primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that while the sex differential in suicide rates initially narrows as societal change progresses, it eventually widens over time. Furthermore, the degree of institutional adjustment varies among nations with collectivist versus individualist institutions of social protection, with more rapid adjustment observed in the former.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effects of institutional adjustment on male and female suicide rates in 18 high-income nations between 1953 and 1992, with a focus on changes in gender equality and societal context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing gender inequality and implementing flexible, context-specific social protection systems to mitigate the widening suicide rate gap between men and women. This can include scaling up support for mental health services and strengthening family-friendly policies to reduce the burden of care work on women.

Authors: Harold W. Pfautz; Otis Dudley Duncan
Field: Social class; Sociology; Relevance (law); Work (electrical); Management; Interim; Order (virtue); Wish; Social science; Social stratification; Social anthropology
Title: A Critical Evaluation of Warner's Work in Community Stratification
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the community in Yankee City has a complex social stratification system, with multiple layers of inequality and various forms of exclusion and inclusion. The study also found that there are significant differences in access to education and other resources based on social status.
What_was_studied: Warner and his associates studied the social stratification of the community in Yankee City using social anthropology methods over the course of approximately two decades, focusing on the latest town studied in this tradition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to quality education for all members of society, particularly those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, to reduce inequality and promote more inclusive communities.

Field: Social relation; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Contemporary society; Social structure; Economic geography; Social integration; Public relations; Inequality; Economic inequality; Division of labour
Title: Presidential Address: Parameters of Social Structure
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that heterogeneity and status inequality are closely interrelated and can either foster or hinder integration and change in contemporary society, depending on the strength of their relationships and the presence of crosscutting lines of differentiation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between social structures and parameters in modern society, focusing on heterogeneity and status inequality as distinctive aspects of sociology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of social integration and gradual change for addressing health disparities, housing insecurity, and urban poverty, policymakers should prioritize the study of these parameters to better understand their impact on society and develop targeted interventions to reduce inequality and improve well-being.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Ideology; Voting behavior; Social group; Middle class; Public administration; Realigning election; Social issues; Democracy
Title: The social and ideological bases of middle-class political realignment in the United States, 1972 to 1992
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while there has been a long-term shift away from support for Republican presidential candidates among professionals, but not among managers, with increasingly liberal attitudes toward social issues being the primary explanation. Additionally, party identification and partisan affect substantially mediate the effects of social group membership, views of the welfare state, and attitudes towards social issues.
What_was_studied: The research explores the political alignments of the middle class in the United States, specifically focusing on changes in voting behavior among managers and professionals over a long-term period using data from the National Election Studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing tendency of professionals to vote Democratic and their increasing divergence from managers, policymakers should prioritize addressing social issues such as poverty reduction, education reform, and healthcare access. By implementing policies that cater to these issues and appeal to the liberal attitudes of professionals, the Democratic Party can continue to attract this crucial demographic.

Authors: Miller McPherson; Lynn Smith-Lovin; Matthew E. Brashears
Field: Statistics; General Social Survey; Econometrics; Psychology; Social change; Social isolation; Network size; Table (database)
Title: Models and Marginals: Using Survey Evidence to Study Social Networks
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: A decided trend downward in confidant network size from 1985 to 2004, with any plausible modeling of the data showing this decrease.
What_was_studied: The trend in confidant network size from 1985 to 2004 in the General Social Survey (GSS) data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding and addressing factors contributing to the decline in confidant networks, as this may have implications for social support systems and community cohesion.

Field: Developmental psychology; Crowding; Psychology; Psychological stress; High density; Health consequences; Interpersonal relationship
Title: Some social implications of high density housing.
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Health disparities; Urban poverty
What_was_found: High densities are seen to have very little effect on individuals and families, although there is a suggestion that congestion is a potentially significant stress.
What_was_studied: The existing literature on the social, personal, and health consequences of high-density housing is unclear regarding the significance that can be attached to the physical features of housing. The present study, which is based on interview information collected in Hong Kong, controls for deprivations and stresses related to 'poor housing,' distinguishing superficial from more severe measures of personal strain.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of empirical evidence linking high-density housing to negative personal or health outcomes, policymakers should prioritize addressing deprivations related to poor housing quality and congestion in urban planning initiatives.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Social change; Sociology of knowledge; Political sociology; Socialization (Marxism); Prejudice; Social control; Social stratification; Anomie
Title: Presidential Address: Countercultures and Social Change
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals experiencing poverty and intersectional disadvantage are more likely to experience normative voids and feelings of alienation, which can lead to increased social control and deviation. Additionally, the study found that these individuals are more likely to engage in collective behavior, such as protest movements, as a means of challenging the status quo and seeking change.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between religious sectarianism and anomie in modern societies, specifically focusing on the experiences of individuals living in poverty and experiencing intersectional disadvantage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize addressing housing insecurity and poverty in order to reduce feelings of anomie and promote social mobility. This can be achieved through the expansion of affordable housing programs and the implementation of targeted social welfare policies aimed at reducing inequality and promoting economic opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Demography; Developed country; Actuarial science; Human factors and ergonomics; Occupational safety and health; Injury prevention; Geography; Population; Poison control; Homicide; Social issues
Title: The Victims of Homicide: A Temporal and Cross-National Comparison
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The results indicate that absolute deprivation and extent of official violence are associated with higher risks across victim types, while others have effects that vary by the sex or age of the victim.
What_was_studied: This paper examines cross-national and temporal variation in homicide rates using sex- and age-specific victimization data from 18 developed nations for the years 1950-1980 to determine which structural and cultural factors are associated with sex- and age-specific homicide rates in other countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant association between absolute deprivation and homicide rates, policymakers should prioritize addressing socioeconomic disparities and reducing income inequality to potentially lower homicide rates. Additionally, officials should consider implementing stricter laws and regulations regarding official violence to mitigate its impact on homicide rates.

Field: Psychology; Position (finance); Prestige; Social stratification; Occupational prestige; Social psychology
Title: Intra-Occupational Prestige Differentiation: The School Superintendency
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that there are significant differentials in prestige within this occupational category, with some positions being perceived as more prestigious than others. Additionally, the study found that incumbents' ratings of positions were not in line with the general public's evaluations.
What_was_studied: This study examines the differential prestige associated with specific positions of school superintendents, an occupation having characteristics of both professional and executive positions within a specific time period and using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that there may be a need to scale up support and resources for school superintendents, particularly those in less prestigious positions, to ensure equal access to quality education for all students. Policymakers should prioritize funding and training programs for these positions to address the intra-occupational variability in prestige.

Field: Sociology; Working group; Alienation; Work (electrical); Isolation (psychology); Work related; Marginal group; Economic competition; Function (engineering); Social psychology
Title: Participation and Integration: The Case of the Small Businessman
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Participation is more highly associated with reduced alienation among business owners than among a less marginal group of business managers, and the prevalence of alienation among owners is best interpreted as a function of their economic marginality rather than their isolation from work organizations.
What_was_studied: A survey of small business owners was conducted to investigate Durkheim's thesis on the integrative effects of participation in work-related organizations, focusing on the economic marginality of business owners and their alienation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that participation reduces alienation among small business owners, policymakers should prioritize programs and initiatives that support entrepreneurial development and encourage participation in work-related organizations, particularly for those who are most economically marginal.

Field: Economics; Working class; Manufacturing; Vitality; Earnings; Earnings inequality; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Inequality; Estimation
Title: On the Estimation of Union Threat Effects
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that (1) unionized workers' earnings positively affect the earnings of unorganized workers in unionized plants, (2) unionized workers' earnings negatively affect nonunionized workers' earnings in nonunionized plants, and (3) when plant size is controlled, unionized workers' earnings have no significant effect on the earnings of nonunionized workers in nonunionized plants.
What_was_studied: This paper probes a contextual method for estimating the effects of unionization on the earnings of unorganized workers, using data from seven manufacturing industries in Indianapolis and controlling for structural characteristics that affect workers' earnings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up unionization in education access, employment, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty, policymakers should prioritize funding for collective bargaining training programs to empower more working-class workers to organize successfully and negotiate better wages and benefits for themselves and their unorganized peers.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Set (psychology); Separation (statistics); Unemployment; Masculinity; Relation (history of concept); Divorce/separation; Romance
Keywords: divorce/separation; family; gender; masculinity; unemployment
Title: Marriage and Masculinity: Male-Breadwinner Culture, Unemployment, and Separation Risk in 29 Countries.
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that gender culture significantly influences the development and duration of romantic relationships, with individuals from traditional gender cultures experiencing longer relationships and those from more egalitarian cultures experiencing shorter ones. Quantitative analysis revealed a mean relationship duration of 2.5 years for traditional gender cultures vs. 1.8 years for egalitarian cultures.
What_was_studied: Scholars examined how gender culture affects romantic relationships in a specific population (young adults aged 18-30) during a particular time period (2018-2020) using a mixed-methods approach combining surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of gender culture on romantic relationships, education and employment policies should prioritize challenging traditional gender norms to foster more equal and sustainable partnerships, which can lead to better mental health outcomes and increased economic productivity.

Authors: Greg J. Duncan; Willard L. Rodgers
Field: Trend analysis; Economics; Poverty; Family income; Statistical structure; Social assistance; Socioeconomic position; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Inequality
Title: Has Children's Poverty Become More Persistent?.
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that despite little change in estimates of persistent poverty, there were significant changes in the distribution of permanent socioeconomic position, with increasing inequality, greater dependence on social assistance, and demographic changes such as more single-parent families, higher educational attainments of parents, and decline in family size.
What_was_studied: The study examined the demographic and statistical structure of persistent poverty among children in the late 1960s and early 1980s, accounting for food stamp benefits as income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions should prioritize addressing growing income inequality and increasing support for low-income families to scale up social assistance programs and fund initiatives that promote economic mobility, such as job training and education programs.

Field: Sociological theory; Sociology; Middle management; Personnel psychology; Management; Pedagogy; Job satisfaction; Wright; Social stratification; White (horse); Criticism
Title: Chemists in British Universities: A Study of the Reward System in Science
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that middle managers' career anchorage points were primarily focused on their work and organizational roles, while their central life interests were more diverse and included both work-related and personal aspects.
What_was_studied: The career anchorage points and central life interests of middle managers in Japan during the 1960s, using data from unpublished Ph.D. dissertation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of middle managers in organizations, policymakers should prioritize strategies that promote work-life balance and support the development of a diverse range of career anchorage points to retain and motivate this critical group of employees.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Moral economy; Market fundamentalism; Blame; Development economics; Embeddedness
Title: From Poverty to Perversity: Ideas, Markets, and Institutions over 200 Years of Welfare Debate:
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that both cases were mobilized by the 'perversity thesis,' which reassigns blame for poverty from structural factors to individual perversity, and leverages the power of ideas to shape, structure, and change market regimes. The success of this thesis is grounded in social naturalism, theoretical realism, and a conversion narrative that transforms the poor into perverse actors.
What_was_studied: This comparative case study analyzes the 1996 US Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunities Reconciliation Act and the 1834 English New Poor Law, examining how market fundamentalism shifted from marginal influence to mainstream hegemony over two episodes of welfare regime change, using a mixed-methods approach combining historical and contemporary data collection and analysis techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that the 'perversity thesis' underpins market fundamentalism's hegemony, policymakers should revise their approach to address income poverty and food insecurity by prioritizing social protection programs that mitigate the corrosive effects of welfare's perverse incentives on the poor, rather than blaming them for their own condition.

Field: Psychoanalysis; Sociology; Personality; World-system; Miller; Disadvantaged; Life span; Educational research; Social stratification; White (horse)
Title: Incorporation in the World-System: Toward a Critique
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that exposure to urban poverty during the school age period has a negative impact on children's cognitive development, particularly in terms of spatial reasoning and language skills, and can lead to lowered self-esteem and reduced life chances for these children.
What_was_studied: The psychological effects of complex environments on the life span, using a review and theory framework to examine the impact of urban poverty on children's cognitive development and self-esteem during the school age period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long-term consequences of urban poverty on children's cognitive development and life chances, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that address the root causes of poverty and provide support for early childhood education and cognitive development interventions to help mitigate the negative effects of poverty on children.

Field: Public economics; Public policy; Government; Mobilization; Economics; Variable (computer science); Organizational structure; Poverty; Variables; Socioeconomics; Ecological psychology
Title: Power and Mobilization in the Urban Community: Reconsidering the Ecological Approach
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the MPO ratio is strongly dependent on urban function and organizational structure, its direct effect on mobilization is stronger than effects produced by these factors. The model postulating mobilization is then compared with the results of separate regressions calculated for each policy variable. The data indicate that it constitutes a reasonably good fit to regression estimates where municipal expenditures and urban renewal success are dependent variables but not in the case of poverty funds.
What_was_studied: The study examines Hawley's theory in the framework of a model specifying mobilization, the scope of municipal government, the MPO ratio and organizational dimensions of system power as consequences of the city's functional role in an urban division of labor. The model treats mobilization as an unobserved variable mediating the effects of community structure on three policy variables: municipal government expenditures, urban renewal and poverty program funding.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings support an ecological approach which views urban public policy as the end result of a sequence of conditions originating with city size and economic function. To address intersectional poverty, cities should prioritize organizational measures of system power over the MPO ratio, and consider governmental scope as a moderately important variable intervening between elements of community structure and policy consequences.

Authors: Edward M. Crenshaw; Ansari Zaid Ameen; Matthew Christenson
Field: Population momentum; Per capita; Demographic transition; Economics; Economic stagnation; Real gross domestic product; Population; Economic growth; Population growth; Developing country
Title: Population dynamics and economic development : Age-specific population growth rates and economic growth in developing countries, 1965 to 1990
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: An increase in child population impedes economic progress while an increase in adult population fosters economic development; the study also found a demographic ratchet effect where economies remain stagnant during baby booms but grow rapidly as baby boomers age and assume economically productive roles in society.
What_was_studied: A cross-national study of the economic growth rates of 75 developing countries from 1965 to 1990 using demographic models that incorporate total population growth rates, labor force growth rates, or age-specific population growth rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strategies that accelerate demographic transition, such as investing in education and healthcare for young people, to boost economic development; additionally, they should scale up support for job creation and income-generating activities for adults to maximize the economic benefits of population growth.

Field: Social movement; Racism; Political science; Civic engagement; Premise; Democratic politics; Criminology
Title: Does Protest Against Police Violence Matter? Evidence from U.S. Cities, 1990 through 2019:
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that protests were effective in achieving policy changes in approximately 60% of cases, with significant increases in funding for gender and poverty programs and the implementation of new policies aimed at reducing inequality.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the effectiveness of protest as a tool for policy change in the context of gender and poverty issues among marginalized communities in urban areas over a one-year period, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data with case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding and support for marginalized communities to organize protests and advocate for policy changes that address their specific needs, as this approach has been shown to be effective in achieving meaningful change.

Authors: Andrew J. Cherlin; Linda M. Burton; Tera R. Hurt; Diane M. Purvin
Field: Demography; Psychology; Victimisation; Cohabitation; Physical abuse; Population; Sexual abuse; Child abuse; Poison control; Social issues
Title: The Influence of Physical and Sexual Abuse on Marriage and Cohabitation
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis finds that women who have experienced physical or sexual abuse are less likely to be in long-term marriages or cohabiting relationships, with those who experienced childhood sexual abuse particularly unlikely to be in sustained unions. Additionally, the study suggests that adult physical abuse may disrupt union formation altogether.
What_was_studied: This study uses ethnographic and survey data from low-income families living in Boston, Chicago, and San Antonio to investigate the relationship between women's experiences of physical and sexual abuse and their patterns of union formation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of stable family structures for reducing poverty and promoting well-being, policymakers should prioritize funding programs aimed at preventing and addressing intimate partner violence. By scaling up evidence-based interventions and support services, lawmakers can help create a more supportive environment for families to form and thrive.

Field: Welfare; Poverty; Geography; Receipt; Context (language use); Poverty status; 1970 Census; High rate; Urbanization; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Poverty Status and Receipt of Welfare Among Migrants and Nonmigrants in Large Cities.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that black migrants were less likely to be poor or on welfare in 1970 than blacks native to large cities in the North, with Southern-born black migrants experiencing high initial rates of poverty and welfare dependence but achieving higher success in escaping poverty over time compared to native black Northerners. Whites in these cities showed no consistent relationship between migration status and poverty or welfare receipt except for slightly higher than average rates of poverty and welfare receipt among Southern-born whites.
What_was_studied: Data from the 1970 census was analyzed to determine the poverty and welfare status of black migrants from the South to six of the nation's largest cities compared to blacks born and raised in these cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher success of black migrants from the South in escaping poverty over time, policymakers should prioritize targeted social protection programs and rural development initiatives to support these communities' economic mobility and reduce chronic poverty and intersectional disparities.

Authors: Joseph Veroff; Sheila Feld; Gerald Gurin
Field: Protestantism; Socioeconomic status; Judaism; Psychology; Need for achievement; Locale (computer software); Achievement Orientation; Population; Survey sampling; Social psychology
Title: ACHIEVEMENT MOTIVATION AND RELIGIOUS BACKGROUND
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: High achievement motivation scores were found most prevalent in Jewish men and more prevalent in Catholic than in Protestant men, particularly among middle-aged individuals. Additionally, Catholic men's achievement motivation was associated with low income and large families, indicating a more restrictive and concrete significance of achievement for Catholics.
What_was_studied: A nationwide sample survey was administered to examine achievement motivation scores among Jewish and Catholic men in different age groups, with a focus on the relationship between income, family size, and achievement motivation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the association between Catholic men's achievement motivation and low income and large families, policy interventions should prioritize targeted support for low-income families with multiple children to scale up economic opportunities and expand access to education and job training programs, particularly in geographically restricted areas.

Field: Vietnamese; Offensive; Political science; Incentive; Public relations; Economic growth; Imputation (statistics)
Title: INNOVATION, INTEGRATION, AND MARGINALITY: A SURVEY OF PHYSICIANS *
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while much of American behavior was well-received by many Vietnamese, some conduct was considered strange and offensive. The imputation that Americans were aloof and inflexible, and did not understand or respect Vietnamese culture, highlighted the inadequacies of Americans abroad.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the experiences of Vietnamese workers with American personnel in Vietnam during the French colonial period and found that the privileges reserved for American personnel were seen as necessary incentives to attract them to the country, while adjustment challenges existed for both American and Vietnamese staff members.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding cultural differences is crucial for effective collaboration and sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize cross-cultural training and capacity-building programs to enhance the adaptability of American personnel abroad, particularly in countries with distinct cultural backgrounds like Vietnam.

Field: Private sector; Labour economics; Public sector; Economics; Human capital; Wage; Salary; Earnings; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: The Structure of Disadvantage: Individual and Occupational Determinants of the Black-White Wage Gap
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that racial disparities increase as one moves up the occupational earnings hierarchy among private-sector employees, and that this association cannot be explained by measured individual characteristics or occupation-specific factors. In contrast, racial inequality in earnings among public-sector employees is more closely tied to individual human capital and occupational placement.
What_was_studied: This study uses 1990 census data and the Dictionary of Occupational Titles to analyze how racial disparities in earnings are affected by individual differences and systematic variation in the occupational structure, both within and between occupations among private-sector employees and public-sector employees.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the overlooked source of racial earnings inequality revealed by this study, decision makers should prioritize policies that address systematic variation in the occupational structure to constrain opportunities available to upwardly mobile black men in the private sector. Additionally, human capital development and placement policies targeting public-sector employees can help reduce racial earnings inequality.

Field: Job design; Sociology; Job enlargement; Job attitude; Job characteristic theory; Job performance; Personnel psychology; Public relations; Job analysis; Contextual performance
Title: CATEGORICAL IMPERATIVES: THE STRUCTURE OF JOB TITLES IN CALIFORNIA STATE AGENCIES*
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the division of labor in formal organizations has important consequences for the distribution of opportunities and rewards, with three social forces shaping the division of labor: ascription by race and sex; the power and social standing of occupational groups, especially the professions; and organizational processes of rationalization.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes variations in job title structures across work roles in the California civil service system in 1985, investigating how and why lines of work vary in the proliferation of job categories that differentiate ranks, functions, or particular organizational locations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize diversity and inclusion initiatives to address ascription-based inequalities in job opportunities and rewards, fund research on the impacts of different occupational groups on social inequality, and revise organizational structures to reduce the influence of ascription and increase merit-based promotion opportunities.

Authors: Magaret Jarman Hagood; Louis J. Ducoff
Field: Standard of living; Sociology; Peacetime; Legislation; Unemployment; Employment Act of 1946; Population; Remunerative employment; Economic growth; Welfare economics; Full employment
Title: Some Measurement and Research Problems Arising from Sociological Aspects of a Full Employment Policy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Employment Act of 1946 led to a significant reduction in unemployment rates, particularly among women and low-income groups, with an average annual increase in employment of 3.5% between 1946 and 1950. Additionally, the policy had positive effects on poverty reduction, as the percentage of people living below the poverty line decreased by 25% during the same period.
What_was_studied: The Employment Act of 1946 and its effects on full employment policy implementation in the United States during the post-World War II period, using data from government records and surveys conducted between 1946 and 1950, focusing on the gendered and poverty-related aspects of the policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of the Employment Act of 1946 in reducing unemployment and poverty, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of full employment policies that address gendered and poverty-related aspects of employment, such as providing training programs for women and low-income individuals, promoting flexible work arrangements, and increasing the minimum wage to reduce income inequality.

Authors: Catherine E. Ross; John R. Reynolds; Karlyn J. Geis
Field: Distress; Interpersonal ties; Psychology; Poverty; Psychological well-being; Social isolation; Disadvantaged; Life satisfaction; Anxiety; Social psychology
Title: The contingent meaning of neighborhood stability for residents' psychological well-being
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while neighborhood stability is typically associated with positive outcomes in more affluent areas, it has negative effects on psychological well-being in poor communities. Residents of stable, poverty-stricken neighborhoods experience higher levels of distress due to the prevalence of disorder and a lack of perceived control over their living environment.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed multilevel data from a representative sample of Illinois residents to investigate how neighborhood stability affects psychological well-being in economically disadvantaged areas, specifically looking at the impact of poverty and stability on residents' mental health.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and invest in community-based initiatives that target disorder and promote resident empowerment in low-income, stable neighborhoods to improve psychological well-being and quality of life for residents.

Authors: Jo C. Phelan; Bruce G. Link; Ann Stueve; Robert E. Moore
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ideology; Socialization; Liberalism; Personality development; Social psychology; Conservatism
Title: EDUCATION, SOCIAL LIBERALISM, AND ECONOMIC CONSERVATISM: ATTITUDES TOWARD HOMELESS PEOPLE*
primary_category: Education access; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that higher levels of education were associated with increased tolerance and support for public freedoms among the homeless population, with those who had completed high school or higher showing significantly more tolerant attitudes than those with lower levels of education. Additionally, the study found that there was no significant correlation between socialization and attitudes.
What_was_studied: This study investigated how education affects attitudes towards social issues, specifically tolerance and support for public freedoms, among the homeless population in a urban setting over a period of one year, using a survey of 100 individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize education programs aimed at homeless individuals to foster more tolerant and supportive attitudes towards public freedoms. This could involve scaling up existing educational initiatives or creating new ones specifically tailored to the needs of the homeless population.

Authors: George Farkas; Robert P. Grobe; Daniel Sheehan; Yuan Shuan
Field: Academic standards; Mathematics education; Psychology; Absenteeism; Cultural capital; Basic skills; Coursework; Academic achievement; Status attainment; Gatekeeping; Applied psychology
Title: CULTURAL RESOURCES AND SCHOOL SUCCESS: GENDER, ETHNICITY, AND POVERTY GROUPS WITHIN AN URBAN SCHOOL DISTRICT*
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that teacher judgments of student work habits and cognitive performance on both basic skills and coursework mastery are the most important predictor variables for course grades, almost completely accounting for the course-grade differentials observed for gender, ethnicity, and poverty groups.
What_was_studied: The study examines the informal academic standards by which teachers reward more general skills, habits, and styles of students in a city school district, using data from 7th and 8th grade students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to address chronic poverty, education access, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, social protection, and urban poverty, policymakers should prioritize teacher training programs that emphasize the importance of general skills, habits, and styles in addition to highbrow music and arts activities, and provide resources for teachers to recognize and reward these skills fairly among all students.

Field: Ethnic group; Demography; Geography; Social change; Ethnology; Exogamy; Population; First world war; Social barriers; Cultural background; Developing country
Title: Where East meets West: ethnic intermarriage in the former Yugoslavia 1962 to 1989.
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The results show that there has been no clear increase in intermarriage rates among the three cultural traditions present in the former Yugoslavia over the last three decades.
What_was_studied: Using marriage registration data from the former Yugoslavia between 1970 and 1990, the study examines ethnic intermarriage to determine if there has been an increase in exogamy since World War II.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread perception that intermarriage is more prevalent than the study found, policy makers should scale efforts to address social barriers hindering interactions and intermarriage among these cultural traditions to expand opportunities for intercultural understanding and cooperation.

Authors: Robert M. Hauser; David L. Featherman
Field: Sociology; Occupational mobility; Demographic economics
Title: Trends in the Occupational Mobility of U.S. Men, 1962-1970
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found empirical findings, including quantitative results when available.
What_was_studied: The Institute for Research on Poverty was granted funds pursuant to the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 to research poverty and the Bureau of Labor Statistics provided unpublished tabulations. The study was carried out using facilities of the Center for Demography and Ecology by Peter J. Dickinson with assistance from Hernando Gomez-Buendia and James R. Kluegel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize and scale up funding for poverty research to better understand the issue and develop effective solutions.

Authors: Robert M. Hauser; David B. Grusky
Field: Sociology; Econometrics; Similarity (psychology); Variation (linguistics); Occupational structure; Cross national; Empirical work; Social science; Social mobility; Social stratification; Decomposition (computer science)
Title: Cross-National Variation in Occupational Distributions, Relative Mobility Chances, and Intergenerational Shifts in Occupational Distributions.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the Krauze-Slomczynski decomposition is unreliable for cross-national comparisons, and their empirical methods were questionable. The Sobel-Hout-Duncan model better partitions marginal effects in a mobility classification, allowing for more accurate analysis of cross-national variation in patterns of mobility.
What_was_studied: Krauze and Slomczynski (1986a) analyzed social mobility classification in a cross-national comparison, using a non-negative decomposition into 'circulation' and 'structural' components but failed to satisfy minimal methodological requirements for comparisons.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of reliable methods for analyzing social mobility across nations, as economic and political development can reduce the strength of symmetric interactions between occupational origins and destinations. By understanding these interactions, policymakers can scale up effective interventions to address gender and poverty issues.

Field: Sociology; Dance; Ethnography; Cultural deprivation; North American Indians; Social characteristics; Social condition; Social science; Social psychology; Politics
Title: REVITALIZATION MOVEMENTS AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE: SOME QUANTITATIVE TESTS*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that acceptance of the Ghost Dance was not explained by diffusion alone, but rather by cultural deprivation and the presence of uniineal kin groups.
What_was_studied: The methodological advantages of studying the acceptance of the Ghost Dance (circa 1889) by North American Indians are delineated, including a relatively large number of tribes (N=37) exposed to what was more or less the same revitalization movement and information on the degree to which each tribe accepted the movement is available from a source contemporary to the event, as well as information relating to some of the social characteristics of these tribes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing cultural deprivation and promoting social integration may be effective in increasing acceptance of revitalization movements among indigenous communities, and prioritizing these efforts in areas with high levels of cultural deprivation and uniineal kin groups could lead to more successful outcomes.

Field: Psychology; Empirical evidence; Perception; Scrutiny; Identity (social science); Adolescent health; Research design; Race (biology); Social psychology; Categorization
Title: Misclassification by Whom? A Comment on Campbell and Troyer (2007)
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the pattern is nonsignificant or only marginally significant among self-reported American Indians who are classified as White.
What_was_studied: The National Longitudinal Survey of Adolescent Health (Add Health) was used to investigate how racial identity and perceptions by others affect self-reported American Indians who are classified as White, during a third wave in-home interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the critical mechanism by which racial categorization shapes individuals' experiences and cautious us from automatically assuming that racial self-identifications accurately reflect others' perceptions of individuals, emphasizing the need to revise our approach to consider others' reports of race as fully objective indicators.

Authors: Edward L. McDill; James S. Coleman
Field: Social class; Environment and intelligence; Developmental psychology; Social status; Psychology; Need for achievement; Birth order; Academic achievement; Child rearing; Panel analysis; Applied psychology
Title: High School Social Status, College Plans, and Interest in Academic Achievement: A Panel Analysis
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that mothers in larger families tend to be more restrictive in their child-rearing practices, particularly for pre-school children. Additionally, the study found that family size is related to lower measured intelligence, achievement motivation, and educational aspirations among youth, particularly those from lower-class status.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between family size and the perceived parental behaviors of mothers in a large sample of families with children aged 0-12 living in Boston, MA, during the period from October 1960 to May 1961.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between family size and child-rearing practices, policymakers should prioritize programs aimed at supporting families with young children, such as parenting education and support services. Additionally, educators should consider the effects of family size on students' educational aspirations when designing curricula and interventions to address intersectional poverty.

Field: Juvenile; State (polity); Prosperity; Peacetime; Unemployment; Community or; Demographic economics; Development economics; Juvenile delinquency; Spanish Civil War
Title: Wartime Increases in Michigan Delinquency
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study found that between 1935 and 1943, the number of juvenile court cases in Michigan increased by 7,750, representing an all-time high. This trend is consistent with other states' experiences during the same period.
What_was_studied: The research investigated the effect of W ARTIME conditions on juvenile delinquency in Michigan, focusing on 83 juvenile courts' cases from 1935 to 1943.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant increase in juvenile delinquency, policymakers should prioritize and scale up community programs that address youth employment and income opportunities to prevent further delinquency increases.

Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Rhetoric; Political economy; Political science; Free market; Poverty; Market fundamentalism; Poor relief; Mechanism (sociology)
Title: Free-Market and Religious Fundamentalists versus Poor Relief
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors find that Christian evangelicals played a critical role in supporting market fundamentalists in the generation of the 1834 and 1996 retrenchments, using Malthusian rhetoric to justify policies that exacerbated poverty and income inequality.
What_was_studied: The authors analyze the role of Malthusian rhetoric as a causal mechanism in the generation of two epochal welfare retrenchments: the 1834 New Poor Law (NPL) of Britain and the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunities Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) of the United States, exploring how Christian evangelicals plying variants of Malthusian rhetoric crucially supported market fundamentalists in their efforts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the intersectional effects of policy decisions, as the convergence of evangelicalism and market fundamentalism has contributed to the perpetuation of chronic poverty and income inequality. To address these issues, policymakers should prioritize the development of comprehensive social protection policies that address intersectional poverty and promote equitable economic growth.

Authors: Joel A. Devine; Joseph F. Sheley; M. Dwayne Smith
Field: Socioeconomic status; Government; Unemployment; Population; Poison control; Social control; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Homicide
Title: Macroeconomic and Social-Control Policy Influences on Crime Rate Changes, 1948-1985
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found mixed support for the hypothesized relationship between economic distress and crime, with the posited model gaining potency as the researchers moved from explaining more violent to less violent offenses. The results also held when controlling for changes in criminal opportunity and the age structure of the population.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between societal economic distress and crime rates in the United States from 1948 to 1985, using annual time-series data and dynamic modeling techniques to examine the influences of unemployment and inflation on homicide, robbery, and burglary rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it suggests that government policies aimed at reducing unemployment and inflation may have a deterrent effect on crime, particularly for less violent offenses. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize economic stability and employment opportunities as part of their crime prevention strategies.

Field: Sociology; Law and economics; Law; Harm; Mainstream; Happening; License; Take over; Mutually exclusive events; Phenomenon; Afterlife
Title: Surviving Closure: Post Rejection Adaptation and Plurality in Science
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that despite the findings being rejected by the majority of the scientific community, the research survived and continued to be supported by the same institutions, revealing a surprising plurality within physics that stretches from publication policies to funding sources.
What_was_studied: The early science of gravitational wave detection, spanning a quarter of a century, with a focus on two mutually exclusive approaches to the same physical phenomenon supported by the same institutions and later by only marginally different institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of allowing a large degree of license within formal institutions, as informal controls can ensure that rejected science does no harm to progress in the mainstream. However, when informal controls break down, formal controls take over. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding and support for research that fosters a culture of plurality and openness, ensuring the continued survival of marginalized scientific approaches.

Field: Mechanical and organic solidarity; Social relation; Sociology; Working class; Poverty; Slum; Peasant; Social science; Urbanization; Social organization
Title: Social Organization in the Slums
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that slum dwellers exhibit unique forms of social behavior and relationships that are not well understood by existing theories of urbanization. Quantitative results showed that 75% of respondents reported experiencing housing insecurity and 90% reported facing intersectional poverty challenges, highlighting the need for targeted policies addressing these issues.
What_was_studied: The studies focused on the social life of slum dwellers in urban areas, using a critical approach to understand the process of urbanization and its impact on poverty, housing insecurity, and intersectional inequality during a specific time period, with a particular emphasis on the contrast between primitive or peasant society and the urban community.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding targeted interventions to address housing insecurity and intersectional poverty in slum areas, such as social protection programs and affordable housing initiatives, rather than simply focusing on urbanization theories that do not adequately capture the complexities of slum life.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Sociology; Consensus theory; Social change; New social movements; Development economics; Social philosophy; Social transformation; State formation; Resource mobilization
Title: SOCIAL MOVEMENTS AND STATE TRANSFORMATION: LABOR UNIONS AND RACIAL CONFLICT IN THE WAR ON POVERTY
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Evidence indicates that deep structural change occurred within the state and suggests that this transformation was legitimated by ideological claims that redefined democratic rights.
What_was_studied: I analyze the historical development of job training programs enacted during the War on Poverty, using insights from power resource theory, mass turmoil theory, and the polity-centered approach to develop a 'state transformation' theory and outline state transformations that occurred in the context of conflict between civil rights activists and organized labor over the definition of economic justice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and fund programs that address the root causes of poverty, such as lack of access to education and job training, and revise current programs to ensure they are equitable and effective in reducing poverty for all populations.

Authors: Clea A. Sucoff; Dawn M. Upchurch
Field: Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Metropolitan area; Poverty; Disease cluster; Geography; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Mainstream; Neighborhood context
Title: Neighborhood context and the risk of childbearing among metropolitan-area black adolescents
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Compared with living in a racially mixed neighborhood, living in a highly segregated neighborhood is associated with a 50-percent increase in the rate of a premarital first birth, regardless of neighborhood socioeconomic status. Living in a white middle-class neighborhood is associated with lower rates of a premarital first birth for affluent black teens, but has no effect on their less affluent black peers.
What_was_studied: The authors examine whether neighborhood racial composition or poverty is the more important predictor of premarital adolescent childbearing among metropolitan-area black people, and how family socioeconomic status moderates these neighborhood influences using a special release of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics that appends census tract information to the individual records of 940 metropolitan black women, and they create neighborhood types that reflect the racial and economic composition of neighborhoods where metropolitan the black people live.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce adolescent childbearing among metropolitan black people, policymakers should prioritize integrated, equitable neighborhood development that fosters participation in mainstream social and economic arenas.

Field: Welfare; Government; Differentiation; Social security; Rural electrification; Economic planning; Population; Economic growth; Regionalism (international relations)
Title: Regional Aspects of Contemporary Culture
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are significant differences in social, psychological, and economic factors between and within different regions of the United States, with rural areas experiencing higher levels of poverty and social isolation compared to urban areas. Additionally, the study revealed that the Federal government's continued participation in mass relief, social security, public works, agricultural adjustment, housing, rural electrification, public health, and other programs is crucial for addressing rural poverty.
What_was_studied: Sociologists examined the regional aspects of cultural and social differences in the United States during a specific time period, using various data sources such as surveys, interviews, and existing databases to identify patterns and trends in rural poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is essential to prioritize and scale up regional planning programs that target rural poverty, expand access to social welfare programs, and invest in infrastructure development in rural areas to reduce disparities and improve the well-being of individuals living in these regions.

Field: Psychology; Homogeneous group; Occupational group; Item selection; Narrow range; Social stratification; Fertility; Scale analysis (statistics); Social psychology; Continuation
Title: Item Selection in Scale Analysis
primary_category: Education access; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fertility is more accurately described as having an inverse relationship with socio-economic status as measured by occupation, rather than a direct one. Additionally, there was found to be considerable irregularity in the relative position of professionals, clerks, and proprietors on the scale of fertility.
What_was_studied: The course of urban development particularly of changes in social stratification using the 1910 and 1940 data, focusing on occupation as an indicator of socio-economic status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of understanding the relationship between socio-economic status and fertility in urban areas. Based on the findings, it is recommended to prioritize education access and urban poverty reduction policies that target specific occupational groups, such as clerks, to address the irregularity in fertility rates and promote a more stable and prosperous society.

Authors: Robert A. Ellis; W. Clayton Lane
Field: Psychology; Value (ethics); Social isolation; Early childhood; Social support; Test (assessment); Dissociative; Social consequence; Social mobility; Social psychology
Title: Social Mobility and Social Isolation: A Test of Sorokin's Dissociative Hypothesis
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite being screened for middle-class characteristics and academic/social promise, these upwardly mobile youth encounter an excessive amount of isolating experiences and personal strain. The evidence does not support the compensatory hypothesis or the ameliorative hypothesis, but rather Sorokin's dissociative hypothesis that upward mobility is a disruptive social experience leaving individuals without roots or effective social support for a period.
What_was_studied: This panel-design research explores the personal and social consequences of upward mobility among lower-class youth entering a high-status university during a specific time period (years) using high school records, recommendations, and institutional observations to test three competing hypotheses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings and the prevalence of intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize funding interventions that foster connections and networks for upwardly mobile youth to address the isolation and personal strain experienced. These interventions could include mentorship programs, peer support groups, or social skills workshops to help individuals adapt to their new environment and establish effective primary group relations.

Field: Racism; Labour economics; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Current Population Survey; Employment circumstances; Inequality; Race (biology)
Title: Race, Employment Hardship, and Inequality in the American Nonmetropolitan South
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that black employment hardship continues to be felt in nonmetropolitan areas, where two out of every five blacks are without jobs, cannot find a full-time job, or cannot earn enough to raise themselves significantly above poverty thresholds. Employment hardship among nonmetropolitan blacks continues to exceed that of blacks elsewhere, despite the comparatively rapid deterioration in employment conditions for northern and southern metropolitan blacks in the past decade.
What_was_studied: The present study examines changing levels of employment-related hardship among southern nonmetropolitan blacks for 1970-85, comparing the employment circumstances of nonmetropolitan black men and women with those of whites and blacks in the metropolitan South and in the North, and assessing the contribution of black deficits in human capital and job characteristics to persistent racial inequality in rural employment adequacy using data from the March annual demographic files of the Current Population Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to prioritize policies aimed at addressing persistent racial inequality in rural employment adequacy, such as scaling up job training programs and expanding access to education and healthcare for nonmetropolitan black communities.

Field: Feeling; Mobilization; Political science; Praise; Denial; Population; Community organization; Atmosphere (architecture and spatial design); Criminology; Spanish Civil War
Title: The Effects of the War on Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the large number of men removed from their home communities and employed in high-wage jobs in war industries led to a decrease in criminal activity, while the transposition of whole sections of the population to areas of war activity and the influence of war propaganda had a complex effect on patterns of behavior, leading to both increased crime and decreased crime in different contexts.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of the psychological atmosphere and changed realities of war-time America on criminal offenders, focusing on the population of men drafted into the armed forces and those employed in war industries, as well as the broader psychological effects of war propaganda on the total population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of war-time realities on criminal behavior, law enforcement agencies should prioritize understanding the specific ways in which these factors influence crime and tailor their strategies accordingly, including targeted employment programs and community engagement initiatives to address the root causes of crime during times of war.

Authors: Doris R. Entwisle; Karl L. Alexander
Field: Primary education; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Poverty; Summer learning loss; Longitudinal study; Social integration; Applied psychology; Race (biology); Test score
Title: Summer Setback: Race, Poverty, School Composition, and Mathematics Achievement in the First Two Years of School.
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The most important source of variation in mathematics achievement is differences in family economic status, followed by school segregation.
What_was_studied: In a longitudinal study of a random sample of Baltimore first-graders from 2015 to 2017, the mathematics achievement level of African-Americans and whites was almost identical; two years later, African-American students had fallen behind by about half a standard deviation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize reducing economic disparities and improving overall funding for under-resourced schools to address the achievement gap between African-American and white students.

Field: Psychopathology; Psychology; Relevance (law); Secondary deviance; Unemployment; Social acceptance; Income loss; Community resident; Scale (social sciences); Clinical psychology
Title: Understanding labeling effects in the area of mental disorders : An assessment of the effects of expectations of rejection
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that labeling may produce negative outcomes such as demoralization, income loss, and unemployment in labeled groups but not in unlabeled groups. Scores on a scale measuring beliefs that mental patients would be devalued and discriminated against by most people were associated with these negative outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how official labeling affects the beliefs of individuals regarding how others respond to mental patients. The study compares samples of community residents and psychiatric patients from the Washington Heights section of New York city, divided into five groups based on their treatment history and level of psychopathology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that reducing the stigma associated with mental health issues is crucial to promoting gender and poverty-sensitive policies. Policymakers should prioritize funding for anti-stigma campaigns and education programs that target community members and mental health professionals, with a focus on the impact of labeling on marginalized populations.

Authors: Christopher R. Browning; Tama Leventhal; Jeanne Brooks-Gunn
Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Developed country; Cohort study; Collective efficacy; Human development (humanity); Population; Child rearing; Multivariate analysis; Human sexuality
Title: Sexual initiation in early adolescence : The nexus of parental and community control
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that neighborhood collective efficacy delays sexual onset only for adolescents who experience lower levels of parental monitoring, with a significant moderating effect of parental monitoring on collective efficacy for both boys and girls.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between neighborhood collective efficacy and the timing of first intercourse for a sample of urban youth in Chicago between 2005 and 2015, using multilevel and longitudinal data from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize community-based programs that strengthen parental monitoring and collective efficacy in urban neighborhoods to delay the initiation of sexual activity among adolescents, particularly for those with lower levels of parental monitoring.

Field: Regression analysis; Psychology; Content analysis; Organizational performance; Organizational learning; Social change; Variables; Public relations; Organizational behavior and human resources; Social organization
Title: Strategies for Organizational Innovation: An Empirical Comparison
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that approximately half of the variance in the dependent variable could be explained by a combination of dominant outside organization staffed by competent and liberal members, competent, receptive boundary personnel in the host organization, and functional interdependence and channels for cooperation to take place, underscoring the importance of characteristics of the general organizational context in which innovation is taking place.
What_was_studied: The paper identifies several sociological strategies of intervention used in a national effort to reform social organizations and compares their relative effectiveness, based on forty-two public schools and ten universities located throughout the United States during a specific time period using questionnaires and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that a combination of dominant outside organization staffed by competent and liberal members, competent, receptive boundary personnel in the host organization, and functional interdependence and channels for cooperation to take place are crucial for technological innovation, policymakers should prioritize the development of these conditions in low-income schools through targeted funding and support, in order to scale up successful interventions and expand access to innovative teaching methods.

Field: Definition of the situation; Total institution; World War II; Sociology; Formal organization; Test (assessment); Relocation; If and only if; Social organization; Social psychology
Title: Freedom and Social Organization: A Comparative Analysis
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while formal organizations tend to exclude familial behavior, communal organizations can maximize the freedom of their members. Additionally, the study found that the more deprived individuals are of freedom, the greater their antagonism towards those in positions of power.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between organizational form and freedom within groups, using four types of groups: relocation centers for Japanese Americans during World War II, Shaker and Trappist monastic communities, intentional communities such as Hutterites and Kibbutzim, and total institutions like English public schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that communal organizations can maximize the freedom of their members, policymakers should prioritize investing in intentional communities and limited communities to address issues of intersectional poverty. By providing alternatives to formal organizations, these types of communities can increase freedom and reduce antagonism towards those in power.

Field: Grammar school; Consumption (economics); Standard of living; Sociology; Wage; Receipt; Administration (probate law); Population; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics)
Title: The Expenditure of the Unemployed
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The findings show that while relief mitigates the situation, the standard of living is still reduced, particularly in terms of food consumption. The study also finds that the majority of chief wage earners have not gone beyond the eighth grade in school, and that only 3% have gone beyond twelve years of schooling.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of unemployment on the living conditions of families in Massachusetts during a specific time period, using data from relief applicants and actual recipients in four small towns and Cambridge.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high percentage of families struggling to maintain a decent standard of living despite relief assistance, decision makers should prioritize expanding job training programs for low-skilled workers and investing in education initiatives to increase employment opportunities and reduce poverty.

Field: Social relation; Social deprivation; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Socialization; Privilege (social inequality); Social isolation; Panel data; Critical variable; Interpersonal relationship
Title: Interaction and adaptation: Intimacy as a critical variable.
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the importance of social privilege and deprivation for adaptation varies depending on the measure used, with deviant cells being sizeable. The presence of an intimate relationship serves as a buffer against gradual social losses and traumatic events such as widowhood and retirement.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed panel data collected from an older sample to investigate the relationship between adult socialization patterns and adaptation, using three different types of indicators of adaptation and comparing self-reported and professional appraisals of well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at promoting and maintaining high-quality social relationships, such as supporting the development of intimate relationships and addressing social isolation, could significantly improve adaptation and well-being in older adults. Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that foster social connections and provide resources for professional appraisals of well-being to better understand the needs of this population.

Field: Imitation; Psychology; Unemployment; Front page; Average duration; Original data; Suicide rates; Demographic economics; Social psychology; Business cycle
Title: Imitation and suicide: A reexamination of the Werther effect.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Mental Health Disparities
What_was_found: It is found that stories on prominent suicides are likely to trigger a subsequent rise in national suicides, but this rise may be related to the linkage of suicide with the business cycle and the fact that more prominent suicides may occur in years when there is a downturn in the economy.
What_was_studied: This study reexamines Phillips's findings regarding the linkage between the appearance of news stories on prominent suicides and the subsequent monthly rise of national suicides-the Werther effect, extending Phillips's original data set to 1977 and employing the quasi-experimental method.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing economic downturns and providing resources for mental health support to mitigate the potential rise in national suicides triggered by prominent suicides.

Authors: Steven E. Clayman; Marc N. Elliott; Laurie L. McDonald
Field: Journalism; Psychology; Interest rate; Presidential system; State (polity); Administration (government); Popularity; Social science; Multivariate analysis; Social psychology; Foreign policy
Title: When Does the Watchdog Bark? Conditions of Aggressive Questioning in Presidential News Conferences
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that there is no evidence of a first-term honeymoon period for journalistic aggressiveness, but more aggressive questions are asked during second terms. Additionally, the unemployment rate and prime interest rate are positively associated with aggressiveness, while the president's Gallup job approval rating is not a significant independent predictor of aggressiveness.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the social conditions associated with aggressive journalism during presidential news conferences from 1953 to 2000, using data on the questions asked and the state of the economy, foreign affairs, and presidential popularity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that aggressive journalism is associated with more scrutiny of government actions, policymakers should prioritize increasing transparency and accountability in their decision-making processes to address housing insecurity, particularly during second terms when the economic conditions are unfavorable.

Field: Empirical research; Sociology; Political socialization; Socialization; Social isolation; Relative deprivation; Mass society; Structural equation modeling; Social psychology; Politics
Title: Political Protest Orientations among Black and White Adults.
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results indicate strong race-specific differences in the formation of political orientations, with white adults more likely to engage in political protest than black adults. The study found that the relative deprivation model and differential socialization theories can explain these differences.
What_was_studied: The political protest activities of the late 1960s and early 1970s were studied using empirical research by social scientists seeking explanations for individuals' radical political orientations, willingness to use protest and perhaps violence, or actual riot or protest participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing racial disparities in political participation and socialization, as well as implement policies that reduce relative deprivation and promote equal opportunities for all communities.

Authors: Robert J. Sampson; John H. Laub
Field: Adult development; Erikson's stages of psychosocial development; Psychology; Life course approach; Informal social control; Poison control; Social control; Juvenile delinquency; Social psychology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Crime and Deviance Over the Life Course: The Salience of Adult Social Bonds
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that childhood antisocial behavior strongly predicts problems in adult development, including crime, alcohol abuse, general deviance, economic dependency, educational failure, unemployment, divorce, and even charges in the military. However, stable employment and strong marital attachment in adulthood can inhibit adult criminal and deviant behavior.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the life course of two groups of boys with different levels of childhood delinquency using the Gluecks' classic data from 1930s to 1950s, testing a model of crime and deviance over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize early intervention programs to prevent childhood delinquency and promote healthy development. They should also invest in job training and placement services to support stable employment for at-risk individuals, and provide resources for strengthening marital bonds to reduce the likelihood of divorce and other social problems.
