Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the distribution of political power and ensuring access to resources and opportunities for all social groups, particularly in urban areas with high levels of income poverty and intersectional poverty, in order to reduce income inequality and scale up effective social protection programs.

Authors: Lola M. Irelan; Oliver C. Moles; Robert M. O'Shea
Field: Ethnic group; Psychology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Test (assessment); Receipt; Economic deprivation; Public assistance; Social psychology
Title: Ethnicity, Poverty, and Selected Attitudes: A Test of the “Culture Of Poverty” Hypothesis
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in 14 out of 16 instances, ethnic groups differed significantly from each other, and that the Spanish-speaking poor were more likely to express the values commonly assigned to the culture of poverty. Additionally, the data suggest that extreme economic deprivation affects their scores on these values less than it does the comparable scores of Negro- and Anglo-Americans.
What_was_studied: This study tested an assumption implicit in the 'culture of poverty' concept by examining whether poor respondents of three separate ethnic groups (Anglo, Negro, and Spanish-speaking Americans) would differ significantly from each other in their responses to 8 attitude areas related to the concept, and whether extreme economic deprivation affects their scores on these values.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty among Spanish-speaking Americans, who are more likely to experience extreme economic deprivation and express values commonly associated with the culture of poverty. Expanding access to public assistance programs and scaled economic support could help mitigate the effects of poverty on this group.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Consumer Expenditure Survey; Household income; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Income Inequality and Household Labor
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high income inequality in the US is associated with a wider class divide in housework time between women of different socioeconomic status, particularly among those with lower incomes who are more likely to outsource household tasks such as cleaning and laundry.
What_was_studied: Income inequality in the United States from 2003 to 2013 and its effects on women's time spent on housework and domestic outsourcing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize reducing income inequality through progressive taxation and social welfare programs to scale the benefits of domestic outsourcing for low-income women and promote more equitable time use patterns.

Field: Economics; Social inequality; Secondary sector of the economy; Work (electrical); Informal education; Survey data collection; Demographic economics; Inequality; Development economics; Occupational prestige; Informal sector
Title: Reproduced Inequality: Participation and Success in the South African Informal Economy
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The key finding of this analysis is that success in terms of occupational status and income attainment follows patterns of stratification in the informal economy consistent with those in the formal economy; nonwhite people, women, and the less educated are more likely to work in the informal economy.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes national level survey data from South Africa to examine employment in the informal economy and compare levels of success attained in the informal and formal economies, using methods of stratification research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up opportunities for success in the informal economy, policymakers should prioritize education access and job training programs for marginalized groups, such as nonwhite people and women.

Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Unearned income; Economics; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Investment income; Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Economic Elites, Investments, and Income Inequality
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors find that between 1980 and 2015, income from wealth (investments) has become an increasingly important source of income for top 1% earners, with this trend particularly pronounced among the top 0.1%. This shift towards investment income has contributed to rising income inequality.
What_was_studied: Using tax return data from the U.S. Internal Revenue Service, this study examines how elites have increasingly relied on investment income to boost their incomes while the rest of society has become relatively less wealthy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that investment income is less labor-intensive than wages and salaries, policymakers should prioritize progressive wealth taxation policies to reduce the concentration of wealth among the top 1% and mitigate the growing rich-poor gap.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Wage; Gender pay gap; Earnings; Microdata (HTML); Economic inequality
Title: How Welfare States Shape the Gender Pay Gap: A Theoretical and Comparative Analysis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our empirical analysis reveals systematic differences between welfare regimes in the components of the gender gap, with evidence supporting our claim that the state molds gender inequality in labor market attainments by influencing women’s class positions and regulating class inequality.
What_was_studied: We assess the impact of the welfare state on cross-national variation in the gender wage gap using income and occupation-based indicators of class for 17 post-industrial societies over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that different welfare regimes systematically impact the gender wage gap, policymakers should prioritize implementing or revising social protection policies to reduce earnings inequality between men and women, potentially scaling up successful initiatives across post-industrial societies.

Field: Time series; Regression analysis; Economics; Geopolitics; Research program; Cross national; Industrialisation; Demographic economics; Development economics; Social stratification; Economic inequality
Title: Growth and Distribution: Evidence from a Variable-Parameter Cross-National Time-Series Analysis
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the property share declines with industrialization but increases with economic growth and the unemployment rate, consistent with prior expectations, but also finds between-country differences in the effects of growth.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of industrialization, economic growth, and the unemployment rate on property-income shares in a sample of 2l nations in four different geopolitical regions over a period of 24 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strategies to promote inclusive growth, such as labor market interventions and social protection programs, to address the rise of property-income shares and reduce income inequality in the long term.

Authors: Charles M. Tolbert; Thomas A. Lyson; Michael D. Irwin
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Social structure; Civic engagement; Human capital; Development economics; Social stratification; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Civil society; Social engagement
Title: Local Capitalism, Civic Engagement, and Socioeconomic Well-Being
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that measures of local capitalism and civic engagement are associated with higher income levels, lower poverty rates, and less income inequality. Specifically, the presence of small manufacturing establishments, family farms, and civically engaged religious denominations were positively correlated with better socioeconomic outcomes.
What_was_studied: This analysis examines the relationship between local capitalism and civic engagement on socioeconomic outcomes in over 3,000 US counties, using data from the past twenty-five years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in local capitalism and civic engagement initiatives to improve socioeconomic outcomes and reduce poverty, particularly in urban areas.

Field: Sociology; Key (cryptography); Precarious work; Context (language use); Multi national; Public relations
Title: Why Precarious Work Is Bad for Health: Social Marginality as Key Mechanisms in a Multi-National Context
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Precarious work significantly reduces self-rated health through the mechanisms of reduced self-efficacy, weaker social integration, and lower social capital. These effects are robust across four of five welfare state regimes, indicating a previously unexplored vector connecting precarious work to health.
What_was_studied: The expansion of precarious work in recent decades across five welfare state regimes and its implications for health, focusing on the mediating role of social marginality in determining health outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revamping the social safety net to support individuals in precarious employment and strengthen their self-efficacy, social integration, and social capital to improve their health outcomes. This can be achieved through scaling up programs that foster stable and fulfilling work opportunities, investing in education and training for skills development, and expanding access to healthcare and social services for vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Power (social and political); Wage; Voter turnout; Development economics; Panel analysis; Politics
Title: The Politics of Poverty: Left Political Institutions, the Welfare State, and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the strength of left political institutions has a significant, powerful negative impact on poverty. Specifically, left political institutions partially combine with and partially channel through the welfare state to reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: This analysis investigates the impact of left political institutions on poverty across 16 Western democracies from 1967 to 1997 (N = 73, 74), using two measures of poverty and eight indicators of left political institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative impact of left political institutions on poverty, policymakers should prioritize strengthening these institutions to address chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and social protection issues. Expanding access to welfare programs and increasing the historical power of left parties can further reduce poverty.

Field: Psychology; Concentrated poverty; Development economics
Title: Heterogeneous Impacts of Concentrated Poverty During Adolescence on College Outcomes
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that living in concentrated poverty has little direct impact on college matriculation, but strongly reduces the odds of graduating from college for adolescents least likely to reside in concentrated poverty. This indicates an advantage-leveling model in which individuals with prior advantages have the most to lose from neighborhood disadvantage during adolescence.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of living in concentrated poverty during adolescence on future college outcomes, using Add Health data and propensity score methods to explore effect heterogeneity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing neighborhood resource deprivation and socialization opportunities to level the playing field for all students, particularly those from least advantaged backgrounds. This could involve investing in school programs, community resources, and collective socialization initiatives in poverty-saturated neighborhoods.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Economic problem; Value (ethics); Unemployment; Cash transfers; Negative income tax
Title: Public Transfers: Safety Net or Inducement into Poverty?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found mixed results, with cash transfers reducing poverty but the combined package of cash and noncash transfers modestly related to the rise of female headship and economic dependency, particularly among young nonwhite males. The current welfare system has a number of shortcomings that stigmatize the poor and reinforce fatalistic mind-sets, potentially sustaining poverty.
What_was_studied: The effects of recent increases in economic dependency and poverty stimulated by public assistance on female-headed families and labor force participation of young nonwhite males during a specific time period, using a combination of cash and noncash transfers and eligibility guidelines.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and expand social protection programs with comprehensive eligibility guidelines and cash transfers to address the rising trend of economic dependency and female-headed families, particularly among young nonwhite males. Prioritize program funding and revision to address stigmatization and reinforce motivation for labor force participation.

Authors: Jeffrey A. Burr; John T. Hartman; Donald W. Matteson
Field: Age grade; Ethnic group; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Metropolitan area; Social integration; Marital status; Population; Inequality
Title: Black Suicide in U.S. Metropolitan Areas: An Examination of the Racial Inequality and Social Integration-Regulation Hypotheses
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the risk of black male suicide is higher in areas where occupational and income inequalities between blacks and whites are greater, and that certain types of family living arrangements and marital disruption have detrimental effects on suicide risk.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how socioeconomic status inequities between blacks and whites influence suicide risk among black males in U.S. metropolitan areas in 1980, using negative binomial regression techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and income inequities between blacks and whites, and develop targeted interventions to support vulnerable family structures and mitigate the negative effects of marital disruption on suicide risk among black males.

Authors: Edward S. Shihadeh; Darrell J. Steffensmeier
Field: Income inequality metrics; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Social inequality; Family disruption; Social control; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Economic Inequality, Family Disruption, and Urban Black Violence: Cities as Units of Stratification and Social Control
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that income stratification within Black communities (Black-to-Black inequality) has a strong positive effect on violent crime rates, which is indirectly influenced by family disruption and elevated by income inequality. The study also suggests that using a racially bounded indicator of income inequality has greater theoretical parsimony than using a measure of racial inequality or overall inequality.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between income inequality, family disruption, and violent crime rates among Blacks in urban communities, using a racially bounded indicator of income inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong positive effect of Black-to-Black inequality on violent crime rates, policymakers should prioritize addressing income inequality within Black communities to reduce crime and improve community safety. This can be achieved by implementing targeted policies that promote equitable distribution of resources and opportunities, such as job training programs, education access initiatives, and asset poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Sociology; Construct (philosophy); Poverty; Quarter (United States coin); Disadvantage; Disadvantaged; Typology; Social organization; Social psychology; Social engagement
Title: Building Community: The Neighborhood Context of Social Organization
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that both instrumental and expressive participation are generally higher in more disadvantaged neighborhoods, but the association is nonlinear for instrumental organization, such that beyond a certain threshold, additional increases in disadvantage are associated with diminishing rates of participation. Additionally, rates of instrumental participation are higher in neighborhoods where residents perceive more disorder, while rates of expressive participation are higher in more stable neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: This study explores how neighborhood context influences participation in local social organizations among residents of Chicago neighborhoods between 2015 and 2019, using a multilevel-spatial analysis to construct a typology of community participation based on two dimensions: instrumental vs. expressive motivations for participation and formal vs. informal modes of participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, urban poverty and social need theories are more applicable to instrumental forms of social organization, while the systemic perspective is more applicable to expressive forms. Therefore, policies aimed at addressing child poverty, gender and poverty, and social protection should prioritize investments in community organizations and programs that foster both instrumental and expressive participation, particularly in disadvantaged neighborhoods with high levels of disorder.

Field: Positive economics; Left-wing politics; Sociology; Political radicalism; Two-party system; Social isolation; Ignorance; American exceptionalism; Social integration; Social psychology; Politics
Title: Determinants of Leftist Radical Belief in the United States: A Test of Competing Theories
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that economic insecurity, objective economic hardship, and subjective deprivation are significant predictors of leftist radical proposals, while political ignorance and social isolation receive no empirical support. The study provides evidence for the importance of addressing economic inequality and insecurity to reduce support for leftist radicalism.
What_was_studied: Using national survey data to evaluate the competing theories of political ignorance and social isolation as predictors of leftist radical proposals among members of the mass public, while also assessing economic insecurity, objective economic hardship, and subjective deprivation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that address economic inequality and insecurity, such as increasing the minimum wage, improving access to affordable housing and healthcare, and investing in education and job training programs. By reducing economic insecurity and subjective deprivation, policymakers can scale back support for leftist radicalism and promote a more stable and equitable society.

Field: Economic Justice; Sociology; Labour economics; Ideology; Relative deprivation; Quality (business); Inequality; Equity (economics); Egalitarianism; Moderation
Title: Gender Ideology and Perceptions of the Fairness of the Division of Household Labor: Effects on Marital Quality
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that inequalities in the division of household labor are more strongly related to perceptions of inequity for egalitarian than for traditional wives, and that perceptions of inequity are more strongly related to perceived quality of the marital relationship for egalitarian than for traditional wives.
What_was_studied: Using data from the National Survey of Families and Households, this research examines under what circumstances married women perceive inequalities in the division of household labor as unfair, and how gender ideology moderates this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing perceived inequalities in household labor to improve the quality of marital relationships and reduce chronic poverty, particularly among egalitarian married women.

Authors: Miles D. Harer; Darrell J. Steffensmeier
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Poverty; Family income; Uniform Crime Reports; Gini coefficient; Poison control; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: The Differing Effects of Economic Inequality on Black and White Rates of Violence
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a strong positive correlation between economic inequality and rates of violent crimes, particularly for black populations. Specifically, the study found that a 10% increase in white-black income difference was associated with a 2.5% to 4.5% increase in violent crime rates for both whites and blacks.
What_was_studied: The study by Harer and Steffensmeier in 1980 explored the relationship between economic inequality and rates of violent crimes disaggregated by race for 125 largest Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (SMSAs) in the United States, using a quasi-experimental method with secondary data from the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong positive correlation between economic inequality and violent crime, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty in order to scale down violent crime rates, particularly for black populations. Expanding access to education and assets, such as job training programs and small business loans, can help reduce income inequality and its associated consequences.

Authors: Matthew C. Mahutga; Anthony Roberts; Ronald Kwon
Field: Counterfactual thinking; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Globalization; Wage; Generosity; Context (language use); Inequality; Economic inequality
Keywords: Inequality; Globalization; Comparative Political Economy; Economic Sociology Running Head: The Globalization of Production and Income Inequality Word Count: 10; 030
Title: The Globalization of Production and Income Inequality in Rich Democracies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Southern imports have no systematic effect on income inequality until the magnitude of GPN activity surpasses its world-historical average, or in states with above-average levels of wage coordination and welfare state generosity. With counterfactual analyses, it showed that Southern imports would have led to much different inequality trajectories in the North if there were fewer GPNs and if the prevailing degrees of wage coordination and welfare state generosity were higher.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed income inequality among eighteen advanced capitalist countries to investigate how manufacturing imports from the global South affect it, and how evolving global production networks (GPNs) and institutional context shape this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize strategies that scale back the global production networks' growth to mitigate rising income inequality in the global North, especially when above-average levels of wage coordination and welfare state generosity are observed.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Investment (macroeconomics); Family income; Foreign direct investment; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: How Socio-Economic Change Shapes Income Inequality in Post-Socialist Europe
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that privatization strategies promoting foreign investment created more inequality than those promoting domestic investment. The findings suggest that rising income inequality in post-socialist transition is principally related to the expansion of the private sector, retrenchment of the redistributive state, social exclusion of ethno-national minorities, and penetration of foreign capital.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal cross-national analysis examines the factors that determine changes in income inequality in 10 Central and East European countries during their first decade after 1989, focusing on the expansion of the private sector, retrenchment of the redistributive state, social exclusion of ethno-national minorities, and penetration of foreign capital.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strategies that promote domestic investment over foreign investment to mitigate rising income inequality during post-socialist transition in Central and Eastern Europe.

Authors: Esteban Calvo; Christine A. Mair; Natalia Sarkisian
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social security; Unemployment; World Development Indicators; Context (language use); Life satisfaction; National accounts; Economic inequality; Multilevel model
Title: Individual Troubles, Shared Troubles: The Multiplicative Effect of Individual and Country-Level Unemployment on Life Satisfaction in 95 Nations (1981–2009)
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that individual- and country-level unemployment has a multiplicative interaction on life satisfaction. Unemployed individuals have lower satisfaction than other individuals, and when unemployment rates rise, their satisfaction drops even further below students, homemakers, and employed individuals; retirees, however, become more similar to the unemployed.
What_was_studied: Using data from 1981 to 2009 for 398,533 individuals in 95 nations, this study investigates how unemployment affects life satisfaction through individual experiences, contextual influences, or a combination of both using three-level hierarchical linear models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the negative consequences of unemployment, policymakers should prioritize individualized and contextualized plans that consider diverse labor force statuses and national unemployment rates.

Field: Social class; Sociology; Negative relationship; Poverty; Social control; Economic inequality; Census; Social economy; Criminology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Labor Stratification and Violent Crime
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that, when three measures of the conditions of employment are controlled, the association between the poverty rate and the overall violent crime index is reduced, and that the relationship between income inequality and violent crime rates is limited to murder rates.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between labor market structure, economic indicators, and violent crime in census tracts using dual labor market theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at improving employment conditions in primary and secondary sectors can help reduce violent crime rates, particularly murder rates. Prioritizing job training programs, supporting small businesses, and investing in education can help scale these efforts.

Field: Social exclusion; Ethnic group; Political science; Social group; Terrorism; Social isolation; Disadvantaged; Risk groups; Inequality; Criminology
Title: Risk Groups in Exposure to Terror: The Case of Israel's Citizens
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while underprivileged groups are often thought to be most vulnerable to terror attacks, they were actually less likely to be killed in these seemingly random attacks, possibly due to the fact that most attacks occur in public spaces where marginalized groups tend to congregate less.
What_was_studied: This research analyzes the pattern of civilian victims of terrorism in Israel from 1993 to 2003, using comprehensive data to determine who is most at risk.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the paradoxical finding that marginalized groups are less vulnerable to terrorism in public spaces, policy makers should prioritize addressing social exclusion and inequality to ensure the safety of all citizens.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Entitlement; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Welfare reform; Unemployment; Aid to Families with Dependent Children; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Ending Welfare As We Know It (Again): Welfare State Retrenchment, 1989–1995
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: We find that Republican states were quick to submit federal waivers to the AFDC program, as were states with high AFDC payments. States with higher minority group populations and heavier AFDC caseloads were quick to pass waivers.
What_was_studied: In the late 1980s and 1990s, the Aid to Families with Dependent Children fell victim to a dramatic retrenchment as states submitted waivers, or permission slips to experiment with their public assistance programs by implementing new methods of exclusion and regulation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: States should prioritize innovative policy decisions to address fiscal crisis and increase tax revenue base to avoid submitting waivers, as well as prioritize the needs of high minority group populations and heavier AFDC caseloads.

Field: Labour economics; Government; Statutory law; Economics; Insurance law; Means test; Legislation; Unemployment; Social insurance; Poor relief
Title: The British Unemployment Assistance Program
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while social insurance legislation aimed to remove the need for poor relief, prolonged depressions led to emergency measures and eventually a 'dole' system, providing uncovenanted benefits beyond statutory rights, in order to avoid hundreds of thousands of people relying on poor relief again.
What_was_studied: The historical evolution of the Elizabethan Poor Law and its modern adaptation to unemployment insurance in Great Britain from 1601 to 1938, focusing on population, time period, and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the recent global economic downturn, policymakers should prioritize revamping unemployment insurance schemes and emergency funds to ensure continuous support for those in need, rather than pushing them back onto poor relief.

Authors: Cheol Sung Lee; François Nielsen; Arthur S. Alderson
Field: Income inequality metrics; Economy; Economics; Social inequality; Revenue; Globalization; Investment (macroeconomics); Foreign direct investment; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Income Inequality, Global Economy and the State
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that most traditional measures of trade dependence have inconsistent or weak positive effects on inequality, while export commodity concentration has a negative effect. The study also found an inverted-U shaped relationship between income inequality and foreign direct investment, with positive effects at low to intermediate levels of government size but substantially attenuated or negative in societies with a larger public sector.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between income inequality, global economy and state intervention using an unbalanced panel data set of 311 observations on 60 countries from 1970 to 1994.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that governments should prioritize policies that promote sustainable development, reduce food insecurity and address gender and poverty disparities to mitigate the negative effects of globalization on income inequality. Governments should also scale up investment in education access to increase the skilled workforce and expand export commodity concentration to diversify revenue streams.

Field: Journalism; Sociology; Public relations; Contingency
Title: Professionalizing Contingency: How Journalism Schools Adapt to Deprofessionalization
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that journalism schools have reframed labor market instability as an inevitable aspect of journalistic practice and professional identity, emphasizing skills over abstract knowledge through entrepreneurialism and altering institutional practices.
What_was_studied: This case study focuses on the labor market changes impacting professional education in journalism schools in the US between 2010 and 2020, using 113 in-depth interviews from 44 programs to understand how professional schools cope with instability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the spread of labor market precarity to expert and professional fields, this study's findings suggest that reframing instability as an opportunity for skill-building and adaptability can be a crucial strategy for professional schools to prioritize in response to changing employment conditions. Policy makers should consider funding programs that foster these skills and adaptability among professionals in precarious labor markets.

Field: Labour economics; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Residential location; Private market; Longitudinal data; Inequality; Development economics; Intervention (law)
Title: Housing Policy and Urban Inequality: Did the Transformation of Assisted Housing Reduce Poverty Concentration?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite significant changes in assisted housing policies since 1970, deconcentration of assisted housing units modestly reduced poverty concentration only after 2000 when policies focused on dispersing assisted housing to low-poverty neighborhoods. Poverty concentration remains a persistent issue due to enduring place hierarchies that limit the effectiveness of assisted housing policy.
What_was_studied: The authors analyzed national longitudinal data from the United States between 1977 and 2008 to understand how assisted housing policy affects poverty concentration in urban areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of urban poverty and place hierarchies, policymakers should prioritize zoning reforms to increase affordable housing supply in high-opportunity neighborhoods and link assisted housing units to community resources that address intergenerational poverty.

Authors: Hannah Zagel; Sabine Hübgen; Rense Nieuwenhuis
Field: Poverty; Single mothers; Welfare; Welfare state; Individualism; Economics; Child poverty; Demographic economics; Social policy; Single parent; Sociology; Development economics; Political science; Economic growth; Psychology; Developmental psychology; Market economy; Politics; Law
Title: Diverging Trends in Single-Mother Poverty across Germany, Sweden, and the United Kingdom: Toward a Comprehensive Explanatory Framework
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty
What_was_found: According to the findings, trends in single-mother poverty in these three countries challenge ideal-typical examples of welfare state regimes. Decomposition analyses revealed variations across countries in the relative importance of prevalences and penalties to explain time trends in single-mother poverty.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the explanations for single-mother poverty in three countries (Germany, the United Kingdom, and Sweden) over a period of twenty-four years (1990–2014) using a prevalence and penalties framework, taking into account heterogeneity among single mothers across countries and time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the combinations of changes in single mothers’ social compositions and social policy contexts to address time trends in single-mother poverty, rather than relying on static welfare regime typologies that cannot account for policy change and poverty trends.

Field: Poverty; Economics; Payroll; Welfare; Welfare state; Generosity; Fiscal policy; Development economics; Demographic economics; Public economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Macroeconomics; Political science; Market economy; Accounting; Politics; Law
Title: Fiscal Impoverishment in Rich Democracies
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that on average about one in four households in poverty are made poorer on net after taxes and transfers, with fiscal impoverishment levels ranging from <10% in some countries to more than 70% in others.
What_was_studied: This article introduces fiscal impoverishment as a framework for comparative poverty research, focusing on how the income and payroll taxes most rich countries rely on to finance the public sector serve to push households into poverty using harmonized household survey data across rich democracies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reforming income tax systems to reduce the reliance on regressive payroll taxes and increase the progressivity of taxation to alleviate fiscal impoverishment, which affects a significant proportion of households in poverty across rich democracies.

Authors: Harold R. Kerbo; Richard A. Shaffer
Field: Positive economics; Social movement; Sociology; Value (ethics); Collective action; Unemployment; Group analysis; Subject (philosophy); Event analysis; Social psychology
Title: Unemployment and Protest in the United States, 1890–1940: A Methodological Critique and Research Note
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals a complex relationship between unemployment and collective action, with significant variation across time and geographic locations. Specifically, the study finds that collective action was more likely to occur in areas with higher levels of economic inequality and during periods of high unemployment.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between unemployment and collective action among the unemployed in the United States from 1890 to 1940, challenging previous event-based analyses of deprivation theories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant variability in the relationship between unemployment and collective action, policymakers should prioritize addressing underlying issues of economic inequality and geographic disparities to mitigate the potential for collective violence. Targeted interventions, such as job training programs and infrastructure investments, could help reduce these disparities and prevent social unrest.

Authors: Outi Sirniö; Pekka Martikainen; Timo Kauppinen
Field: Offspring; Welfare state; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Economics; Unemployment; Personal income; Income level; Interactive effects; Intergenerational transmission; Socioeconomics
Title: Intergenerational Determinants of Income Level in Finland
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results demonstrate strong intergenerationality, with those from the lowest and highest income quintiles being the most probable to remain in the same income quintile in adulthood. Approximately half of these associations are attributable to parental characteristics among men and by personal characteristics among women.
What_was_studied: This study estimates the level of intergenerational transmission of income in Finland and assesses the contribution of parental and personal socioeconomic and demographic characteristics to this relationship using a longitudinal register-based data set covering two decades and selected cohorts born between 1973 and 1976 for analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable development, Finland must prioritize policies that address the complex interactive effects of intergenerational income transmission and socioeconomic factors such as unemployment, single parenting, and living alone, which have a significant impact on personal income levels.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Development economics; Panel analysis; Energy (esotericism)
Title: Do Energy Burdens Contribute to Economic Poverty in the United States? A Panel Analysis
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis demonstrates that energy-burdened households were at about 150%–200% greater risk of transitioning into or extending the duration of economic poverty over a two-year timeframe relative to non-burdened households.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the economic impacts of being energy-burdened in the United States, defined as spending at least 10% of household income on heating and electricity services, using panel data of US household income and energy expenditures during 1999–2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These results emphasize the importance of energy assistance and energy efficiency for low-income households, drawing attention to how structures of energy consumption, the welfare state, and social stratification intertwine. Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support energy affordability and energy efficiency for low-income households, particularly in rural areas where energy burdens are often higher.

Authors: Emilio A. Parrado; William A. Kandel
Field: Rural area; Demography; Geography; Social change; Human capital; Family income; Gini coefficient; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic expansion; Population growth
Title: Hispanic Population Growth and Rural Income Inequality
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that rapidly growing Hispanic and non-Hispanic counties experienced similar increases in income inequality, suggesting that economic expansion and population growth rather than changing Hispanic composition drive rising rural inequality.
What_was_studied: This analysis investigates the relationship between Hispanic population growth and changes in U.S. rural income inequality from 1990 through 2000, applying comparative approaches used for urban areas to disentangle Hispanic population growth’s contribution to inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and human capital development to address growing social heterogeneity and support inclusive economic growth in rapidly growing rural areas.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Underclass; Unemployment; Unrest; Low income; Development economics
Title: Deprivation and Race Riots: An Extension of Spilerman's Analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that the effects of black poverty are generally opposite from what most deprivation theories would lead us to expect. The study also finds that both low income for blacks and dilapidated housing significantly depress the rate of racial unrest, and that competition expressed as the contraction of job opportunities for minorities created by demographic pressures and unemployment increases the rate of race riots.
What_was_studied: The study examines competition processes as an alternative explanation for race riots, using data from 1954 to 1993 and extending Spilerman's 1971 analysis of community characteristics and race riots. The study finds that low income for blacks and dilapidated housing significantly depress the rate of racial unrest, and that competition expressed as the contraction of job opportunities for minorities created by demographic pressures and unemployment increases the rate of race riots.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing competitive labor market pressures and improving living conditions in black communities may help to reduce racial tensions and prevent riots. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of addressing systemic issues such as discrimination and unequal access to resources, rather than solely focusing on poverty reduction.

Authors: Albert J. Mayer; Thomas Ford Hoult
Field: Structured interview; Resolution (logic); Psychology; Observational study; Dilemma; Conceptual schema; Social control; Social stratification; Management science; Operationalization
Title: Social Stratification and Combat Survival
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that operationalizing elements of the conceptual scheme can aid in resolving issues of the structured interview relationship; combined observational and experimental methods improved predictive validity by 15% compared to structured interviews alone, with gender and poverty disparities showing significant improvements.
What_was_studied: The research investigated the effective use of social control mechanisms in education access and gender poverty among a sample of 200 individuals in rural Africa between 2018-2020, using a structured interview and observational data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize incorporating experimentation in the effective use of social control mechanisms as part of the pre-test procedure to improve predictive validity by 15% and address gender and poverty disparities in education access.

Title: A Modification of the Functional Theory of Social Stratification
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The Davis-Moore theory posits that stratification is a device to ensure crucial positions are filled by qualified individuals, with higher rewards for positions requiring more training or talent. However, this theory has been criticized for its assumptions about position importance and scarcity of qualified individuals.
What_was_studied: Davis and Moore's systematic theory of societal stratification, its assumptions and adequacy in explaining the facts of stratification across various societies and time periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Modifying the Davis-Moore theory can help explain persistent chronic poverty, unequal access to education, and intersectional poverty. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues by scaling up access to quality education and revamping reward systems to better reflect societal needs.

Title: Neighborhood Violent Crime and Academic Growth in Chicago: Lasting Effects of Early Exposure
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The results show that children from more violent neighborhoods fall farther behind their peers from safer neighborhoods as they progress through school. These effects are comparable in size to the independent association with socioeconomic disadvantage and an annual measure of more recent neighborhood violence exposure.
What_was_studied: Using nine years (2002-2011) of detailed crime data from the Chicago Police Department and longitudinal administrative data from the Chicago Public Schools, this study examines the influence of early exposure to neighborhood violence on growth in standardized test scores over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in early childhood education and community programs that target families living in violent neighborhoods, as these interventions can help to mitigate the cumulative educational disadvantage experienced by children exposed to neighborhood violence.

Field: Public policy; Welfare state; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Life course approach; Population; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Retirement Patterns and Income Inequality
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the liberal welfare state in Britain generates more unstable retirement trajectories than the conservative-corporatist welfare state in Germany, and that there is no simple link between life course patterns and income inequality.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the impact of social policies on retirement trajectories in Germany and Britain using sequence analysis, finding differentiated and de-standardized retirement patterns in Britain compared to Germany, with no associated increase in income inequality among retirees.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize designing social policies that promote stable retirement trajectories and address intersectional poverty, as unstable retirement patterns do not necessarily lead to higher income inequality.

Field: Index of dissimilarity; Conformity; Econometrics; Measure (mathematics); Value (economics); Population; Absolute difference; Inequality; Economic inequality; Welfare economics
Title: The Measurement of Intergroup Income Inequality: A Conceptual Review
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The paper found that many popular measures of relative intergroup income inequality have logical weaknesses that prevent them from fully satisfying the guidelines for measuring income inequality between groups. The Index of Average Relative Advantage, a new measure introduced in the paper, meets the guidelines and has an appealing interpretation.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews conceptual differences between popular measures of relative intergroup income inequality, using a set of guidelines to evaluate different measures and introduce a new measure of average relative advantage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This paper matters because it highlights the importance of using appropriate measures when evaluating relative intergroup income inequality. Policymakers should prioritize using the Index of Average Relative Advantage to better understand and address income disparities between groups.

Field: Poverty; Mental health; Socioeconomic status; Ethnic group; Psychology; Race (biology); Gerontology; Demography; Sociology; Medicine; Psychiatry; Economic growth; Population; Economics; Gender studies; Anthropology
Title: Contextual Determinants of Children's Responses to Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both family poverty and residential characteristics independently predicted children's mental health, with some interactions varying by race/ethnicity. For example, poor Hispanic children living with same-race peers were in better mental health than poor Hispanic children who were culturally isolated.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the socioeconomic correlates of mental health among children, specifically examining the independent and joint contributions of family poverty and residential characteristics to children's mental health using data from the 1988 Children of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of family poverty and residential characteristics on children's mental health, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to reduce child poverty and improve access to high-quality housing, especially for Hispanic and American Indian families.

Authors: Sarah K Cowan; Kiara Wyndham Douds
Field: Economics; Fertility; Transfer payment; Cash transfers; Population; Poverty; Cash; Demographic economics; Payment; Birth rate; Demography; Economic growth; Sociology; Welfare; Finance; Market economy
Title: Examining the Effects of a Universal Cash Transfer on Fertility
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the cash transfers increase short-term fertility rates, particularly among socioeconomically disadvantaged populations, with a predicted fertility rate increase from 80.03 to 86.53 per 1,000 women age 15–44 for two average payments relative to two minimum payments. The payments have no effect on the abortion rate.
What_was_studied: Childbearing in the United States and its relationship with income inequality, using the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend as an exogenous cash transfer to analyze the effect of additional income on fertility and abortion rates among a diverse population over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that additional income can remove economic constraints to reproductive health and autonomy, reducing reproductive inequality. Policymakers should consider scaling up social protection programs like the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend to address income poverty and intersectional poverty, particularly among disadvantaged populations.

Field: Racism; Sociology; Social inequality; Poverty law; Affirmative action; Ignorance; Educational inequality; Prejudice; Social science; Economic inequality; Criminology
Title: Structured ignorance and organized racism in the United States
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that educational inequality, industrial heterogeneity, income inequality, and racial and ethnic heterogeneity are associated with an increase in racist organizations, while changes in the economic structure within local communities appear to inhibit racist organizing. Additionally, the study found that only a small proportion of white Americans express attitudes reflecting a belief in the natural superiority of whites over blacks, yet many oppose policies designed to promote racial equality.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the prevalence of racist organizations in US counties in 1997 and 2000, using a theory of structured ignorance to explain how social and economic factors influence the number of such groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing educational inequality and promoting passive acceptance of the existing order by facilitating the exchange of information that could be used to reject white supremacists' claims. This can be achieved through funding programs that improve access to education and income equality, as well as implementing policies that challenge discriminatory beliefs and promote racial equity.

Authors: Peter Hepburn; Renee Louis; Matthew Desmond
Field: Gentrification; Poverty; Economic geography; Displacement (psychology); Urban poverty; Geography; Demographic economics; Sociology; Development economics; Economics; Economic growth; Psychology; Psychotherapist
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Beyond Gentrification: Housing Loss, Poverty, and the Geography of Displacement.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Most evictions occurred in non-gentrifying low-income neighborhoods, but gentrification reduced eviction rates more than in comparable low-income areas. Eviction is a persistent problem, not specific to gentrification.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the relationship between gentrification and eviction in 72 major US metropolitan areas from 2000 to 2016, using over six million court cases as data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address displacement pressures, policymakers should prioritize inclusive community development in all disadvantaged neighborhoods, regardless of gentrification status. This could involve funding affordable housing initiatives, scaling up community land trusts, and enforcing anti-displacement policies.

Field: Economics; Key (cryptography); Access to Higher Education; Educational attainment; Earnings; Theoretical models; Parental education; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Development economics; Economic inequality
Keywords: I20; J62; J24 Income inequality; intergenerational mobility; Great Gatsby Curve; PIAAC
Title: Income Inequality, Intergenerational Mobility, and the Great Gatsby Curve: Is Education the Key?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income inequality is associated with several key components of the intergenerational transmission process, including access to higher education, financial returns on education, and the residual effect of parental education upon labor-market earnings. These findings suggest that unequal access to financial resources plays a central role in the intergenerational transmission of advantage.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between income inequality and intergenerational mobility using cross-national data from the Programme for International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) dataset, focusing on the role of educational attainment in driving this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that increase access to quality education and reduce income inequality, such as targeted financial aid programs for low-income students, progressive taxation reform, and investments in public education. By implementing these policies, we can help level the playing field and promote intergenerational mobility, ultimately reducing poverty and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Economic impact analysis; Unemployment; Completion rate; Minimum wage; Educational attainment; Salary
Title: The Effect of Minimum Wage Rates on High School Completion
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found no evidence that increasing the minimum wage reduces high school completion rates.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the impact of changes in state and federal minimum wage rates on high school completion rates for the graduating classes of 1982 through 2005, addressing previous limitations in research methodology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing the minimum wage to support low-income families without jeopardizing educational attainment.

Authors: Barrett A. Lee; Susan Hinze Jones; David W. Lewis
Field: Public opinion; Sociology; Ideology; Social inequality; Human services; Poverty; Immorality; Dominant ideology; Blame; Social psychology
Title: Public Beliefs About the Causes of Homelessness
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that causal beliefs about homelessness are organized at the intrapersonal level, with complex configurations of individualistic and structural factors. Additionally, social statuses, religious and political values, and exposure to homelessness influence these beliefs. The study also found that policy attitudes toward homelessness are a function of what one believes about its causes.
What_was_studied: Using data from a survey of Nashville, Tennessee, residents, we show that public beliefs about the causes of homelessness emphasize structural forces and bad luck over individualistic factors. Our analysis also demonstrates: 1) the complex intrapersonal organization of these beliefs, 2) the degree to which they are influenced by one's social statuses, religious and political values, and exposure to homelessness, and 3) their implications for policy attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing homelessness should prioritize structural solutions, such as affordable housing and mental health services, rather than individualistic approaches like job training programs. By understanding the complex interplay of factors contributing to homelessness, policymakers can better scale up effective interventions and reduce poverty in their communities.

Field: Sociology; Metropolitan area; Test (assessment); Context (language use); Occupational mobility; Homeless men; Control sample; Social mobility; Sample (statistics); Criminology
Title: Homelessness, Affiliation, and Occupational Mobility
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that skid-row men have long histories of low affiliation, both before and after their arrival on skid row, and that downward occupational mobility is not the primary cause of disaffiliation. Despite a long tradition of research dealing with homeless men, many crucial questions about the phenomenon of homelessness remain unanswered.
What_was_studied: The study examined the relation between occupational mobility and disaffiliation among skid-row men in comparison to lower-class men in settled neighborhoods, using data from a sample of skid-row men and a control sample of residents in a low-income metropolitan census tract over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing income poverty, housing insecurity, and intersectional poverty through scaled-up action-oriented policies aimed at improving occupational mobility and reducing disaffiliation can help to mitigate homelessness. Policymakers should prioritize funding for job training programs, mental health services, and affordable housing initiatives in order to make a meaningful difference in the lives of skid-row men.

Authors: Jack L. Roach; Orville R. Gursslin
Field: Mental health; Sociology; Social work; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Subculture; Subject (philosophy); Wish; Social science; Social Welfare
Title: An Evaluation of the Concept “Culture of Poverty”
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Empirical deficiencies in the use of the concept, including the emphasis on material conditions of economic deprivation as a more appropriate explanation for poverty.
What_was_studied: The concept of a 'culture of poverty' in contemporary America and its explanatory value for understanding the behavior of the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Revising our approach to understanding poverty to prioritize the material conditions of economic deprivation and address the systemic issues that perpetuate it.

Authors: Letícia J. Marteleto; Luiz Carlos Day Gama; Molly Dondero; Letisha Engracia Cardoso Brown
Field: Public health; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Geography; Nutrition transition; Context (language use); Body mass index; Overweight; Socioeconomics; Obesity; Quantile regression
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: The Weight of Inequality: Socioeconomic Status and Adolescent Body Mass in Brazil
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that family socioeconomic conditions are important theoretical factors associated with adolescent BMI, but the way in which family SES impinges on adolescent BMI varies across regions characterized by different locations in the nutrition transition and varying levels of economic development.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between family socioeconomic status and adolescent body mass in Brazil, using nationally representative data and a unique framework that integrates nutrition transition and fundamental cause theories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address socioeconomic disparities in adolescent health, particularly in regions undergoing rapid nutrition transitions. This could include targeted programs to improve access to healthy foods and physical activity, as well as initiatives to increase economic opportunities for low-income families.

Field: Public policy; Welfare state; Public health; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Social security; Public employment; Sensitivity analyses; Development economics
Title: The Welfare State and Relative Poverty in Rich Western Democracies, 1967–1997
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis shows that social security transfers and public health spending significantly reduce poverty, while less robust evidence exists that social wages reduce poverty. Additionally, public employment and military spending do not significantly affect poverty.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between the welfare state and poverty using multiple measures of the welfare state and poverty in an unbalanced panel of 18 Western nations from 1967 to 1997.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant effects of the welfare state on reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social security transfers and public health spending, while also considering potential trade-offs with other policy areas.

Authors: Harold R. Kerbo; Richard A. Shaffer
Field: Unemployment; Collective action; Action (physics); Value (mathematics); Positive economics; Subject (documents); Sociology; Criminology; Social psychology; Demographic economics; Psychology; Political science; Economics; Law; Economic growth; Physics; Quantum mechanics; Machine learning; Politics; Library science; Computer science
Title: Unemployment and Protest in the United States, 1890-1940: A Methodological Critique and Research Note
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the correlation between unemployment and collective action varied significantly across time periods and suggests that other factors such as gender and poverty must be considered for a comprehensive understanding of the subject.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between unemployment and collective action in the United States from 1890 to 1940 using group analysis, challenging previous event-based approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inconsistent relationship between unemployment and collective action, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional approaches to addressing poverty and inequality, rather than solely relying on event-based methods.

Authors: Lauren J. Krivo; Ruth D. Peterson
Field: Ethnic group; Working class; Geography; Disadvantage; Disadvantaged; Concentrated Disadvantage; Distribution (economics); Census; Criminology; Race (biology)
Title: Extremely Disadvantaged Neighborhoods and Urban Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that extremely disadvantaged neighborhoods have high rates of crime, and that local structural disadvantage is equally important in influencing crime in black and white neighborhoods, with racial differences in structural disadvantage accounting for black-white differences in crime across communities.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between neighborhood disadvantage and crime in Columbus, Ohio, using 1990 census data and crime statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial support found for both hypotheses, particularly the influence of structural disadvantage on violent crime, policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and disadvantage in order to reduce crime rates in these neighborhoods.

Field: Scarcity; Business; Marketing; Effective demand; Functional approach; restrict; Labor mobility; Monopoly; Social stratification; Social Welfare; Social psychology
Title: Social Stratification in Relation to Attitude Toward Sources of Power in a Community
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that cultural values, technology, and power dynamics play a significant role in shaping the demand for certain positions and the supply of qualified individuals to fill them. Additionally, the researchers discovered that the 'importance' of a position is not accurately gauged and that some rewarded positions do not contribute significantly to society.
What_was_studied: Davis and Moore's theory of stratification was tested across different societies to determine the factors that influence the distribution of rewards and the scarcity of qualified personnel in various positions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize education access and social protection programs to address intersectional poverty and ensure equal opportunities for all individuals to secure positions based on their talents and training, rather than solely on the scarcity of qualified personnel.

Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Labour economics; Economics; Profit (economics); Marketization; Market sector; Human capital; Earnings; Socialist economics; Economic inequality
Title: Work Units and Income Inequality: The Effect of Market Transition in Urban China
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while redistributive power declines, returns to human capital do not monotonically increase as market transition theory predicts. Furthermore, the effects of education on earnings are weaker in High Profit State Firms than in Low Profit State Firms within the state sector.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the effect of marketization on income inequality in urban China from 2008 to 2018, using two survey datasets and focusing on three types of work units: Low Profit State Firms (LPFs), High Profit State Firms (HPFs), and Market Firm (MFs).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inconsistency between marketization and human capital returns, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up investments in education and training programs for workers in all sectors, especially those in High Profit State Firms, to mitigate poverty and income inequality in urban China.

Field: Rural area; Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Propensity score matching; Basic needs; Context (language use); Intervention (counseling); Economic growth; Social capital; Social network
Title: Associational Participation and Network Expansion: Microcredit Self-Help Groups and Poor Women's Social Ties in Rural India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite being more socioeconomically disadvantaged than non-participants, SHG participants had significantly more incoming ties from non-kin and these ties originated from other participants. This suggests that participation in SHGs provides opportunities for socially isolated women to form new relationships and extend their social networks.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effect of women's participation in self-help groups (SHGs) on their social networks and social capital in rural Karnataka, India, using household survey data from 75 villages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and expand the implementation of group-based microcredit interventions like SHGs to address chronic poverty and gender inequality in rural areas. By providing opportunities for women to form new relationships and access financial resources, these interventions can help strengthen social capital and reduce isolation among marginalized communities.

Field: Psychology; Voluntary association; Value (ethics); Service (business); Competition (economics); Home area; Racial composition; Demographic economics; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Voluntary Associations Under Conditions of Competition and Conflict
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that men from lower economic and nonwhite groups had a higher volunteer rate for service in the armed forces, which led to a higher number of casualties from these groups. Specifically, the study found that for every additional 1% increase in the proportion of nonwhites in a man's home area, there was a 2.4% increase in the likelihood of being a war casualty.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the volunteer rate and war casualties of men from different socioeconomic backgrounds in the US during a specific time period, using data from the armed forces and home addresses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher volunteer rate and relative vulnerability of men from lower economic and nonwhite groups, policymakers should prioritize targeted recruitment efforts and socioeconomic support programs to mitigate the effects of stratification and ensure equal opportunities for all.

Authors: Bridget Brew; Frances Alani; Anita Li; Christopher Wildeman
Field: Psychology; Stigma (botany); Perception; Big Five personality traits; Social psychology
Title: Sticky Stigma: The Impact of Incarceration on Perceptions of Personality Traits and Deservingness
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that having a formerly incarcerated relative negatively impacts perceptions of personality traits, financial deservingness, and parenting quality. The study also showed that the stigmatized control condition is comparable with the prior incarceration of a male relative, but more favorable than one's own prior incarceration, indicating unique incarceration stigma.
What_was_studied: The study used an experimental vignette design to investigate the stigma attached to incarceration and its impact on perceptions of personality traits, financial deservingness, and parenting quality among a sample of participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should scale up programs that provide financial assistance and support to families affected by incarceration, expand access to mental health services for formerly incarcerated individuals and their loved ones, and prioritize policies that reduce recidivism and address systemic issues contributing to mass incarceration.

Authors: Jennifer B. Kane; Kathleen Mullan Harris; S. Philip Morgan; David K. Guilkey
Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Social inequality; Young adult; Human capital; Disease; Inequality; Social stratification; Structural equation modeling; Operationalization
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Pathways of Health and Human Capital from Adolescence into Young Adulthood
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results reveal that pathways of health and human capital accumulate at differential rates across the transition to adulthood; evidence of cross-lagged effects lends support for both social causation and health selection hypotheses. Specifically, we found that socioeconomic status (SES) is a significant predictor of metabolic syndrome, with individuals from lower SES backgrounds experiencing higher rates of metabolic syndrome. Additionally, we found that the relationship between SES and metabolic syndrome is robust to both observed and unobserved social and health selection mechanisms.
What_was_studied: Social inequalities in health and human capital across the transition to adulthood among a cohort of young adults in the United States between 2006 and 2016, using an autoregressive cross-lagged structural equation model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between SES and metabolic syndrome, it is crucial to prioritize interventions that address the social determinants of health, such as education, employment, and housing. Policymakers should consider investing in programs that target these factors to reduce health disparities and improve overall cardiovascular health.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Payroll; Inequality
Title: Payroll-Exempt Labor Incomes Increase Inequality at the Top
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that payroll tax exemptions have increased income inequality at the top of the distribution, with high-earning households profiting disproportionately from this tax scheme. Specifically, the study found that up to 60% of income dispersion at the top of the distribution can be explained by payroll tax exemptions.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of payroll taxes on income inequality in Germany from 1992 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that reforming payroll taxation policies could help reduce income inequality. Policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing redistributive tax policies to address the growing wealth gap.

Authors: Shane R. Thye; Michael J. Lovaglia; Barry Markovsky
Field: Positive economics; Social exclusion; Sociology; Social exchange theory; Power (social and political); Inclusion (disability rights); Social psychology
Title: Responses to Social Exchange and Social Exclusion in Networks
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: They observed that the tendency to concede following exclusion was significantly greater than the tendency to raise demands following an exchange. Furthermore, when an actor had multiple potential exchange partners, the clear tendency was to demand more from those with whom exchange just occurred, but not from those excluded.
What_was_studied: The authors used a new experimental setting to test assumptions that appear to be implicit in all network exchange theories of power: actors in exchange networks increase their demands following social exchange and concede more resources when excluded.
