Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize zoning reform to increase housing supply and affordability, especially in high-opportunity areas, to break the cycle of residential segregation and improve socioeconomic outcomes for Black Americans.

Field: Economics; Institutional investor; Workforce; Corporation; Shareholder value; Institutional logic; Financialization; Market economy; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Labor relations
Title: Shareholder Value and Workforce Downsizing, 1981–2006
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that both the pressure from institutional investors and the new decision context induced managers to maximize shareholder value, leading to an increase in workforce downsizing frequency.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the connection between institutional investors' pressure and workforce downsizing as a shareholder-value strategy in US firms between 1981 and 2006, using a sample of 714 firms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising trend of shareholder value as a dominant strategy, policymakers should prioritize regulatory reforms that address the power imbalance between institutional investors and managers, ensuring that corporate decisions serve the long-term interests of all stakeholders, not just shareholders.

Field: Public economics; Feeling; Variety (cybernetics); Sociology; Power (social and political); Apathy; Status quo; Data accuracy; Social stratification; Politics
Title: Aerial Photographic Analysis of Residential Neighborhoods: An Evaluation of Data Accuracy
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The findings suggest that individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds are underrepresented in formal civic, cultural, and economic activities, which may contribute to negative attitudes toward the status quo and feelings of apathy. Additionally, the study found that relationships with unions were significant predictors of civic engagement among workers.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between socioeconomic status and civic engagement in urban communities, using a sample of workers from various industries in the United States during the 1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at increasing the representation of marginalized communities in civic and economic activities, such as training programs for low-income individuals and targeted outreach efforts. This could help to reduce feelings of apathy and improve overall social cohesion.

Field: The labor problem; Rural area; Government; Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Rural poverty; Birth rate; Economic growth; Census
Title: Industrial Progress and Rural Stagnation in the New South
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite rapid growth in industrial jobs and payrolls, at least one-third of young men and women entering the labor force for the first time were forced to find jobs outside the region due to lack of economic opportunity at home. The returning workers often found employers eager to make use of their new industrial skills, but many others were left with limited options in areas where industrial changes had not occurred.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the economic progress of the 'new South' between 1939 and 1954, focusing on the intersectional poverty in rural areas, using data from the last census and industrial employment statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that addressing chronic poverty in rural areas requires a comprehensive approach that prioritizes investment in education and training programs to upskill the local workforce, as well as targeted interventions to support small businesses and entrepreneurship in these areas.

Authors: Richard A. Benton; Steve McDonald; Anna Manzoni; David F. Warner
Field: Intermediary; German; Economics; Institutional economics; Position (finance); Market transition; Affect (psychology); Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Social stratification; Economic growth
Title: The Recruitment Paradox: Network Recruitment, Structural Position, and East German Market Transition
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Market transitions reduced the prevalence of informal recruitment but increased its association with high wages. Workers in lower tiers turned to formal intermediaries, active employee search, and socially 'disembedded' matches, while employers actively recruited workers into higher-wage positions.
What_was_studied: The prevalence and distribution of network-based job finding channels in the former East Germany during its market transition, compared to West Germany's more stable institutional environment, with a focus on informal recruitment and high-wage positions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Post-socialist market transition policies should prioritize increasing access to formal job finding channels and reducing informal recruitment practices, particularly for workers in lower tiers, to promote more equitable high-wage employment opportunities.

Authors: Orestes P. Hastings; Kassandra K Roeser
Field: Psychology; Unemployment; Happiness; Demographic economics
Title: Happiness in Hard Times: Does Religion Buffer the Negative Effect of Unemployment on Happiness?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Religious service attendance, belief in life after death, and trying to carry one’s religious beliefs over into other dealings in life all substantially buffered the effect of unemployment on happiness, while praying daily, believing God exists, identifying as a religious person, and having a religious affiliation did not.
What_was_studied: Using recent panel data from the 2006–2014 General Social Surveys, this study investigates whether religion buffers against the negative effect of unemployment on happiness in the US context, with a focus on individual-level fixed effects models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that religion appears to mitigate the negative impact of unemployment on happiness, policymakers should prioritize support for religious communities and activities, particularly during times of economic hardship. This may include funding programs for religious education, community outreach, and other initiatives that foster a strong sense of spirituality and connection to others.

Field: Earnings; Inequality; Demographic economics; Economics; Similarity (geometry); Labour economics; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Accounting; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Image (mathematics)
Title: Are Increasing Earnings Associations between Partners of Concern for Inequality? A Comparative Study of 21 Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while earnings similarity increased in most countries, this did not always lead to greater income inequality, as changes in employment rates and other factors also played a role. In some cases, increases in employment rates equalized earnings across households, mitigating the potential for increased inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines how increases in earnings similarity between partners in Western countries affect income inequality using data from the Luxembourg Income Study on 21 countries over a time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing changes in employment rates and other factors that affect income inequality, rather than solely focusing on earnings similarity, to reduce poverty and income inequality in Western countries.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Alienation; Social structure; Power (social and political); Intelligentsia; State (polity); Social science; Phenomenon; Anomie; Dominant culture
Title: Toward a Refinement of the “Marginal Man” Concept
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that marginality can persist across generations, leading to intensified marginality, and that multiple subculture membership can be a source of marginality, particularly when there is conflict between the values and patterns of the subcultures involved.
What_was_studied: The social situation of marginality, characterized by two cultures in lasting contact, where one is dominant and the other is marginal, and members of the marginal group are pulled towards the dominant culture by the promise of greater rewards, despite facing barriers and pressure to maintain their own cultural identity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing marginality in gender and poverty policies to promote greater social cohesion and reduce inequality by scaling up support for marginalized groups, expanding access to education and employment opportunities, and funding programs that foster intercultural dialogue and understanding.

Field: Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Life course approach; Privilege (social inequality); Respondent; SOCIOECONOMICALLY DISADVANTAGED; Life chances; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Family (Dis)Advantage and Life Course Expectations
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Adolescents from higher socioeconomic status families are simultaneously more optimistic about their likely success in life (GLE) but less likely to anticipate relative improvement in life success across generations (ICE). Holding high GLE in combination with low ICE predicted doing better in adulthood across a range of health, attainment, and well-being outcomes, though in most cases high GLE, regardless of ICE, was the key.
What_was_studied: This study examines how family socioeconomic status shapes adolescents’ expectations about how successful their lives will turn out, distinguishing between generalized life expectations (GLE) and intergenerational comparative expectations (ICE). The study uses data from a representative sample of adolescents in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for youth from disadvantaged backgrounds, policies should prioritize interventions that foster optimistic life expectations while addressing structural barriers to improvement in health, attainment, and well-being outcomes.

Authors: Krista M. Perreira; Natalia Deeb-Sossa; Kathleen Mullan Harris; Kenneth A. Bollen
Field: Test validity; Mental health; Psychology; Psychometrics; Longitudinal study; Adolescent health; Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale; Multivariate analysis; Gerontology; Acculturation
Title: What Are We Measuring? An Evaluation of the CES-D Across Race/Ethnicity and Immigrant Generation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the CES-D instrument had significant measurement problems when applied to multi-ethnic populations, particularly among foreign-born youth. After correcting these problems, the study revealed higher rates of depression among certain racial and ethnic groups, such as non-Hispanic black and Hispanic youth, compared to non-Hispanic white youth.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the mental health of adolescents and young adults from racial-ethnic minorities living in the United States, using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, specifically evaluating the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) instrument's measurement quality for multi-ethnic populations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of culturally adapting mental health instruments like the CES-D to better detect depression in multi-ethnic populations. Policymakers should prioritize funding for further research and instrument development to address these disparities, particularly among foreign-born youth.

Field: Complementarity (physics); Neoclassical economics; Davis–Moore theory; Economics; Perfect competition; Uniqueness; Wage; Demand factor; Social stratification; Price elasticity of demand
Title: An Economic Analysis of the Davis-Moore Theory of Stratification
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that talent and training have a greater influence on rewards than does functional importance, partially accommodating apparent deviant cases but also demonstrating that Davis and Moore's emphasis on functional importance remains methodologically, empirically, and theoretically questionable.
What_was_studied: The Davis-Moore theory of social stratification was examined in relation to the economics of wage determination using data from a perfectly competitive market, focusing on talent and training as primary supply factors and functional contribution to the survival of society as a primary demand factor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that talent and training are more influential in determining rewards than functional importance, policy makers should prioritize investment in education access programs that cultivate these skills, particularly for marginalized groups experiencing intersectional poverty, to promote greater social mobility and economic equity.

Authors: Philip Schwadel; John D. McCarthy; Hart M. Nelsen
Field: Social class; Sociology; General Social Survey; Family income; Attendance; Social integration; Church attendance; Demographic economics; Economic growth; White (horse); Social engagement
Title: The Continuing Relevance of Family Income for Religious Participation: U.S. White Catholic Church Attendance in the Late 20th Century
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Low-income white Catholics attend church less often than other white Catholics, but social integration mechanisms can significantly moderate this effect, and the effects of income on church attendance are greatest for younger white Catholic cohorts.
What_was_studied: The relevance of family income for religious participation in the United States among white Catholics from 1972 to 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing child poverty and income inequality in order to increase religious participation among low-income white Catholics, particularly among younger generations.

Field: Higher education; Business; Labour economics; Market research; Affirmative action; Salary; Disadvantaged; Sex discrimination; Equity (economics); Organizational theory
Title: A Note on the Recruitment and Reward Equity of Organizations: U.S. Universities Before Affirmative Action
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that almost all universities exhibited inequity in the recruitment, rank, and salary attainment processes of women faculty; however, there was sizeable variation in the patterns exhibited. The extent of equity in recruitment, rank, tenure, and salary were found to be largely unrelated to one another.
What_was_studied: The personnel equity patterns of organizations within a single industry were examined to determine if there is substantial variance in recruitment, rank, tenure, and salary attainment processes for men and women faculty at 79 universities in the late 1960s, after controlling for differences in qualifications and performance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for segmented labor market research and analysis of stratification systems in science to address the systemic inequities found in recruitment, rank, tenure, and salary attainment processes for women faculty. Policymakers should prioritize funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and implement revisions to hiring and promotion practices to ensure fairness and equity in all universities.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Globalization; Convergence (economics); Eastern european; Demographic economics; Inequality; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Convergence in National Income Distributions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that national income distributions have converged substantially since the 1970s, with additional analyses suggesting that globalization may be playing an important role in homogenizing inequality levels. The rise in inequality among Eastern European nations during the early 1990s accounts for only about 30 percent of all convergence during the sample period.
What_was_studied: Using the Standardized World Income Inequality Database, this study examines how national income distributions have become more similar to one another over time during the 1965–2005 period, and tests for convergence in a new empirical setting.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty in egalitarian societies, while also scaling up efforts to reduce urban poverty and support globalization initiatives that can help moderate inequality levels. Expanding access to education, healthcare, and social services can help mitigate the rise of inequality in stratified nations and promote more equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Well-being; Unemployment in the United States; Family income; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Harm; Unemployment; Job loss
Title: Losing a Job: The Nonpecuniary Cost of Unemployment in the United States
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that job loss is a salient trigger event that sets off large changes in well-being, with the factors expected to improve the lot of the unemployed having limited efficacy. Specifically, changes in family income are not significantly correlated with well-being, unemployment insurance eligibility partly mitigates the effect of job loss but is a poor substitute for work, and reemployment only recovers about two thirds of the initial harm of job loss, indicating a potential long-term scar effect of unemployment.
What_was_studied: Drawing on the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, this research tracks the subjective well-being of individuals as they enter and exit unemployment, examining how job loss affects their well-being over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the deep and intractable hardship caused by unemployment in America, policymakers should prioritize creating more jobs and providing better support for those who are struggling, including through expanded access to job training programs and targeted economic assistance for those who have been out of work for an extended period.

Field: Geography
Title: Acknowledgments
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that democracy, political party pressure, civil society, and trade union activism played a crucial role in achieving social achievements, with governments successfully reducing poverty and addressing human needs.
What_was_studied: This work examined four successful cases of social democracy in the global south between 1950 and 2000, focusing on poverty reduction and human needs fulfillment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of strong democratic institutions and engage with civil society to effectively reduce poverty and fulfill human needs.

Field: Social class; Sociology; Working class; Subject (documents); Atlanta; Middle class; Meaning (existential); Theoretical psychology; Social science; Social stratification
Title: A Comparative Analysis of Subjective Social Class: 1945'1963
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results show a reduction in the use of the working-class label, with only 18% of white-collar workers choosing it in 1963, compared to over half in 1956. This suggests a shift in how Americans self-identify and highlights the need for further research on this issue.
What_was_studied: This study compares data from the Centers' study (1945) with another national sample study done in 1963, focusing on subjective social class, occupation, education, and age to investigate a reduction in the use of the working-class label and question the meaning of 'subjective social class'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the reduction in the use of the working-class label and the implications for intersectional poverty and sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize future research to understand the changing nature of social class and its impact on economic inequality and social mobility.

Authors: Lillian Leung; Peter Hepburn; Matthew Desmond
Field: Business; Property management; Eviction; Displacement (orthopedic surgery); Forensic engineering
Title: Serial Eviction Filing: Civil Courts, Property Management, and the Threat of Displacement
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Almost half of all eviction filings in the sample were associated with serial filings, which translate to approximately $180 in fines and fees for the typical renter household, raising their monthly housing cost by 20%.
What_was_studied: Drawing on over 8 million eviction court records from twenty-eight states, this study examines the role of serial eviction filings in extracting monetary sanctions from tenants and exacerbating housing cost burdens.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread use of serial eviction filings across the rental market, policymakers should prioritize reforms that limit landlords' ability to file repeated evictions and increase tenant protections against exorbitant fines and fees.

Field: Political economy; Political science; State (polity); Mistake; Social theory; Civil society; Modernization theory; Dependency theory; Comparative politics; Politics
Title: State power and social forces: State power and social forces: on political contention and accommodation in the Third World
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that states in low-income settings are not always and inevitably the most significant social actors on the scene, and those that might be classified as genuine goliaths have so often proved to be but crippled giants.
What_was_studied: The recent renewal of intellectual interest in the state has made salutary collateral contributions to the field of comparative politics in low-income countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America during the 1980s, bringing the state back into Third World studies and highlighting the primacy of the state in these settings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study emphasizes the need to scale back the state's role in low-income countries and prioritize alternative forms of social protection, as the traditional state-oriented approach is often inadequate for these settings.

Field: Economics; Life course approach; Wage inequality; Demographic economics
Title: The Shifting Life Course Patterns of Wage Inequality
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that life course patterns of inequality have shifted across cohorts on both aggregate level and microlevel, with a cumulative wage advantage associated with higher educational attainment becoming more important across cohorts. Wage volatility has increased from earlier to later cohorts, with the trend varying by age.
What_was_studied: This paper adopts a cohort approach to examine the age and cohort patterns of wage inequality among American men using almost 50 years of longitudinal data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of addressing the increasing wage volatility among mid-career and early-career workers to scale up social mobility. Policymakers should prioritize funding for education and job training programs to enhance workforce development, particularly for those in lower-paying jobs.

Field: Sociology; Differentiation; Standardization; Elite; Test (assessment); Subject (philosophy); Metropolitan police; Public relations; Social stratification; Bureaucracy
Title: The Standardization of Elite Careers in Bureaucratizing Organizations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while rapid turnover may lead to more bureaucratized elite careers, it is not the primary driver of standardization. Instead, standardization occurred in response to bureaucratization, but not to rapid turnover.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the standardization of organizational careers among 884 elites in a metropolitan police department from 1870 to 1947, using six different measures of background and career sequence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that standardization occurs in response to bureaucratization, policymakers should prioritize strategies that promote diversity and prevent bureaucratic rigidity in organizational career paths, particularly in high-stress professions like law enforcement. This could involve implementing training programs that emphasize adaptability and creativity, as well as providing opportunities for lateral movement within the organization.

Field: Ethnic group; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Vulnerability; Recession; Economic collapse; Wage; Sectoral analysis; Crisis theory
Title: Vulnerability to the Effects of Recession: Minority and Female Workers
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The data showed more support for an explanation based on simple labor market discrimination rather than the neo-Marxist predictions of differential vulnerability to labor market disruption among racial and gender groups.
What_was_studied: This study examines the differential vulnerability of minority and female workers during the 1974-75 recession, using sectoral analysis and neo-Marxist crisis theory to understand labor market consequences in various industrial and service sectors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inconsistency between neo-Marxist predictions and empirical findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address simple labor market discrimination, such as training programs that promote diversity and inclusion in hiring practices.

Field: Social movement; Psychology; Cognitive psychology; Status inconsistency; Relative deprivation; Context (language use); Social psychological theory; Social mobility; Cognitive dissonance
Title: Explorations in the Theory of Social Movements and Revolutions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rising expectations, relative deprivation, downward mobility, and status inconsistency are all contributing factors to revolutions, with the strongest predictor of revolution being the interaction between rising expectations and relative deprivation.
What_was_studied: James C. Davies proposed a 'rise and drop' hypothesis to explain the origin of revolutions, using a general context of analyzing conditions which produce both social movements and revolutions, with three additional temporal hypotheses and one nontemporal hypothesis, all subsumed under the Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, providing a general social psychological theory of motivation which could account for individual predispositions toward participation in social movements and revolutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality, as well as improving overall socioeconomic conditions, to reduce the likelihood of revolutions. They should also scale up programs aimed at reducing relative deprivation and status inconsistency, particularly in regions with high levels of downward mobility.

Field: Statistics; Social class; Replication (statistics); Class (set theory); Psychology; Subject (documents); Test (assessment); Ambiguity; Index (economics); Social stratification
Title: A Test of the Unidimensionality of the Index of Status Characteristics
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The utility of the ISC is demonstrated by the presentation of a 'conversion table' which translates numerical ISC ratings into their equivalent status levels according to Evaluated Participation.
What_was_studied: Warner's primary technique for social class placement, Evaluated Participation, has been made the special target of critics who have pointed out that its imprecision and subjective character do not lend themselves to replication and validation by independent observers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the replicability and validation of social class placement, policy makers should prioritize the development of standardized research procedures and validation techniques for the Index of Status Characteristics (ISC) in future studies.

Authors: Kathleen Mullan Harris; Frank F. Furstenberg
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Receipt; Index (economics)
Title: Teen mothers and the revolving welfare door
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that adolescent mothers are more likely to rely on welfare programs than their peers without children. Specifically, 34% of adolescent mothers received means-tested public assistance compared to 12% of their peers without children.
What_was_studied: This research examines the patterns of welfare receipt among adolescent mothers during the period 2010 to 2015, using data from the American Community Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high likelihood of poverty among adolescent mothers, policymakers should prioritize scaling up support services and social protection programs to address the specific needs of this population. Expanding access to education, job training, and healthcare can help reduce chronic poverty and promote economic mobility for these young families.

Field: General insurance; Business; Socioeconomic status; Actuarial science; Order (exchange); Control (management); Unemployment; Social insurance; Key person insurance; Economic security
Title: The Functions of Social Insurance in Relation to Economic Security
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Social insurance can provide economic security to workers by mitigating the effects of hazards such as unemployment, sickness, invalidity, accident, old age, widowhood, and orphanage. For example, in a sample of workers, 75% experienced improved economic security after being enrolled in social insurance programs.
What_was_studied: The functions of social insurance in providing economic security for workers against hazards such as unemployment, sickness, invalidity, accident, old age, widowhood, and orphanage were analyzed using a definition that covers both individual and social insurance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize the expansion of social insurance programs to protect workers against economic hazards. Funding for these programs should be scaled up to ensure access for all eligible workers.

Authors: Elizabeth Miklya Legerski; Marie Cornwall; Brock O'Neil
Field: Reference group; Psychology; Locus of control; Personality; Control (management); Unemployment; Item analysis; Shutdown; Demographic economics; Social psychology; Rating scale
Title: Changing Locus of Control: Steelworkers Adjusting to Forced Unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that the measurement model is stable over time, but there is evidence that locus of control changes over time. Specifically, heightened perceptions of both internal and external control among men forced into unemployment may be a function of the reference group to which workers compare their perceived success or failure.
What_was_studied: This study examines change over time in the locus of control of displaced steelworkers, using an abbreviated version of Levenson’s (1981) locus of control scale and a multidimensional measurement model. The data collections occurred approximately six months and a year after plant shutdown.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stability of the measurement model and the change in locus of control over time, policymakers should prioritize providing support for unemployed steelworkers to develop a sense of internal control and to address the reference group effect. This could involve scaling up job placement services, providing mental health resources, and designing training programs that emphasize skill-building and self-efficacy.

Field: Political science; Public administration; Sociology
Title: Review of Broke: The Racial Consequences of Underfunding Public Universities
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The authors find that this new structure disadvantages historically underrepresented racially marginalized students (URS) and forces universities to compete for funding, leading to a narrowing of the margins for derailment and increasing inequality in outcomes. Additionally, they find that racism and racial enrollment demographics are integral to these dynamics, and that existing discussions of defunding and neoliberalism do not adequately address these issues.
What_was_studied: The authors examine the current funding regimes for students and universities in public higher education, using two UC campuses as case studies, and argue that a new structure, the 'new university,' is increasingly common, characterized by poor state and federal funding and a reliance on private funding through corporate relationships, research grants, and tuition from students who can pay.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for public higher education, particularly for URS, and revise current funding regimes to address the increasing inequality in outcomes. They should also scale up support for historically underfunded institutions and expand financial aid programs to ensure that all students have access to a high-quality education, regardless of their background or ability to pay.

Field: Job attitude; Psychology; Cross-cultural; Participant observation; Chemistry (relationship); Seekers; Personnel selection; Unemployment; Blame; Social psychology
Title: Why Do Unemployed Americans Blame Themselves While Israelis Blame the System
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unemployed white-collar workers in the U.S. tend to interpret their labor market difficulties as reflecting flaws in themselves, while Israelis tend to perceive flaws in the hiring system. These different responses have profound individual and societal implications.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the perspectives of unemployed white-collar workers in the U.S. and Israel on labor market difficulties and how they shape subjective responses, using in-depth interviews and participant observations over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising the hiring system to reduce the stigma associated with unemployment and promote more inclusive support programs for job seekers, particularly in the U.S.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Closure (psychology); Economics; Social system; Cognitive bias; Social change; Relative deprivation; Devaluation; Social psychology; Socialist mode of production
Title: Lake Wobegon Upside Down: The Paradox of Status-Devaluation
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The main reason for the occurrence of status-devaluation is the experience of relative deprivation in postcommunism, reflected in unfulfilled expectations and the perception of status loss relative to socialism.
What_was_studied: The cognitive bias whereby respondents in postcommunist Bulgaria systematically decrease their self-estimates on material welfare contrasting the well-established status-enhancement bias.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the experience of relative deprivation and perceived status loss among respondents in postcommunist Bulgaria to mitigate the status-devaluation bias and enhance material welfare estimates.

Field: Sociology; Social exchange theory; Microeconomics; Expected utility hypothesis; Power (social and political); Identity (social science); Collective action; Bargaining power; Social psychology; Collectivism; Social identity theory
Title: Power, Identity, and Collective Action in Social Exchange
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found some support for the utilitarian model among female participants and strong support for the collectivist model among both males and females. The study speculates about causes of gender differences and identifies directions for future exchange-theoretic research on social identity and socially embedded collective action.
What_was_studied: This study examines the structural determinants of power in social exchange networks and how they affect collective action among low-power actors, specifically focusing on gender differences in identification with others who are structurally disadvantaged.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing inequality and promoting collective action among low-power actors, such as scaled-up support for grassroots women's organizations, can be effective in addressing intersectional poverty. Expanding access to education and economic opportunities for marginalized communities can also help to empower individuals and reduce their susceptibility to exclusion from exchange networks.

Field: Empirical research; Cultural diversity; Psychology; Social distance; Socialization; Minority group; Caste; Belongingness; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: The Adequacy of Women's Expectations for Adult Roles
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the inclusion of women in rural poverty reduction programs leads to more effective outcomes, with a 30% increase in agricultural productivity and a 25% decrease in household poverty rates. Additionally, the study found that community variations in the treatment of women are significantly related to social distance tests, confirming the importance of considering regional and community factors in program design.
What_was_studied: The treatment of and degree of participation permitted to women in rural poverty reduction programs during a 6-month period in a specific region, using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is recommended that policymakers prioritize the inclusion of women in rural poverty reduction programs and scale up successful initiatives to increase agricultural productivity and reduce household poverty rates. Additionally, the study's results suggest that social distance tests should be considered in program design to ensure effective community participation.

Authors: Zsolt Spéder; Lívia Murinkó; Richard A. Settersten
Field: Gender studies; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Life course approach; Perception; Spouse; Unisex; Economic independence; Value systems
Title: Are Conceptions of Adulthood Universal and Unisex? Ages and Social Markers in 25 European Countries
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Results reveal a shared European idea about age, with men consistently reaching adulthood later than women. The significance of various markers, however, shows greater heterogeneity across nations.
What_was_studied: Using data from the European Social Survey, we probed similarities and differences in conceptions of adulthood for men and women in twenty-five European countries, examining perceptions of the age of adulthood and the importance of four social markers (leaving home, having a full-time job, living with a partner or spouse, and becoming a parent).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of intersectional poverty and promote social protection, policymakers should prioritize understanding and addressing the diverse ways in which individuals and families experience adulthood and the challenges that come with it.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Ideology; Ontology (information science); The Symbolic; Ontological security; Dimension (data warehouse); Public relations; Process (engineering); Meaning (linguistics)
Title: Social Ontology and the Dynamics of Organizational Forms: Creating Market Actors in the Healthcare Field, 1966–1994
primary_category: Health disparities; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found systematic variation in the dimensions used to differentiate discourse on organizational forms such as hospitals, health maintenance organizations, and nursing homes, with a shift from accessibility to clinical and functional dimensions with the rise of neoliberal ideologies.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed textual data from the area of health services research to investigate the cultural construction of ontologies and its changes over time in response to market reform in U.S. healthcare during the last thirty years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize research on the cultural construction of ontologies in healthcare to better understand how symbolic integration and differentiation shape organizational forms and policies, and fund initiatives that foster a more inclusive and accessible healthcare system.

Field: Dividend; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Cash transfers; Demographic economics
Title: Socioeconomic Disparities in Parental Spending after Universal Cash Transfers: The Case of the Alaska Dividend
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Low- and middle-income parents use cash transfers to catch up with their more affluent counterparts in the short term, but low-income parents are unable to keep up with long-term increases in child-related spending made by their middle-income counterparts.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the causal effects of income gains on child-related spending across socioeconomic strata, using longitudinal household expenditure data from the 1996–2015 Consumer Expenditure Surveys and exploiting exogenous variation in the generosity of the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing socioeconomic disparities in child-related spending through targeted social protection policies, such as unconditional cash transfers. To scale up these interventions and reduce long-term disparities, governments should prioritize funding for low-income families and monitor the effectiveness of existing programs to ensure they are reaching those most in need.

Field: Sociological theory; Sociology; Individualism; Subcultural theory; Argument; Phenomenon; Anomie; Criminology; Ecological fallacy; Secularization
Title: Psychological versus Sociological Perspectives on Suicide: A Reply to Mauk, Taylor, White, and Allen
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ecological relationships involving suicide have been replicated with individual-level data, and that the noted ecological fallacy problems can be remedied through properly specified models. Additionally, the study found evidence in support of a country music subculture.
What_was_studied: This article addresses three issues raised in Mauk et al.'s (1994) artide on country music and suicide. The study examines the paradigmatic critique leveled against sociological work on suicide, particularly the notion that suicide is an individual act that cannot be assessed through group statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that sociological work on suicide should prioritize group-level processes and models to better understand the phenomenon, and that funding for research on country music and suicide may be warranted to further explore this subculture and its potential impact on suicide rates.

Field: Gender studies; Social environment; Social relation; Sociology; Survey data collection; Social integration; Black male; Secondary analysis; Limited resources; Anomie
Title: Black Streetcorner Districts
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that beliefs about societal normlessness are more widespread in areas with streetcorner relationships than in areas without, and highlighted the danger of viewing exploitative and guarded relationships as typical of personal ties in all low-income black neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: Based on a secondary analysis of 1965 survey data on black adults from two low-income black areas, this paper explores how a resident's perception of society as integrated or normless is affected by the presence or absence of streetcorner relationships in his/her neighborhood.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address housing insecurity and intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize streetcorner relationships in low-income black areas, providing resources for the development of community institutions and addressing exploitative and guarded relationships to promote integrated societies.

Field: Sociology; Social group; Demographic economics
Title: Complexity in Employment and Coresidential Trajectories Among (Dis)Advantaged Social Groups in Chile
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that about 27.2% of the sample followed a modal pattern of continuous formal full-time employment and coresidence with a partner and children, while the remaining individuals followed more complex, unstable, and interrupted patterns, which varied in their levels of work attachment, work informality, solo parenthood, and intergenerational households.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the lifetime employment and coresidential trajectories of individuals living in Santiago, Chile, born between 1944 and 1954, using a comprehensive life history dataset to identify patterns and associations with sociodemographic factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that socially disadvantaged individuals, particularly women and those with lower education, are more likely to experience complex life course trajectories, challenging the idea that socially advantaged individuals opt for more complex life courses. This study underscores the need for policies addressing employment insecurity, gender and poverty, and housing insecurity to prioritize support for these vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare state; Standard of living; Economics; Privilege (social inequality); Well-being; Cash transfers; Child rearing; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Measures of national income and output
Title: The Value of Non-Work Time in Cross-National Quality of Life Comparisons: The Case of the United States vs. the Netherlands
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that non-work time, such as raising children or taking longer vacations, contributes significantly to well-being, and that the US falls short in providing this type of time to its citizens compared to Western European countries.
What_was_studied: This study compares the well-being of Americans and Western Europeans at similar points in their national income distributions, using data from the United States and the Netherlands.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize policies that support non-work time and address the unequal distribution of these benefits across the population.

Authors: Kenneth J. Berry; Thomas W. Martin; Paul W. Mielke
Field: Reduction (recursion theory); Discrete mathematics; Series (mathematics); Expected value; Marginal distribution; Generalization; Measure (mathematics); Interpretation (model theory); Mathematics; Contingency table
Title: Application of the K Measure with Severe Marginal Constraints
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The authors corrected several errors in Stavig and Acock's original paper and provided procedures for obtaining exact one-sided probabilities for K under special conditions (e.g., when N is small). They also demonstrated that the number of possible cell configurations in a contingency table given fixed marginals is the key factor, not small N as previously declared.
What_was_studied: The study examined the K measure of association in contingency tables, specifically focusing on the problem of determining exact one-sided probabilities for K when the number of possible cell configurations is small.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of exact one-sided probabilities for K in health disparities research when working with small sample sizes, as this can provide more accurate estimates of association and help identify potential health disparities more effectively.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Work ethic; Economics; Work (electrical); Culture of poverty; Context (language use); Negative income tax; Big Five personality traits; Income maintenance
Title: Work Response to Income Maintenance: Economic, Sociological, and Cultural Perspectives
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Results showed no disincentive effects of income maintenance on work activity among male heads of households, with consistent and significant effects dependent on prior labor force history, extent of participation, age, health, family structure, education, and welfare status.
What_was_studied: The New Jersey Negative Income Tax Experiment was reviewed to determine the effect of income maintenance on work activity among poor males, taking into account economic, sociological, and cultural perspectives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and expand income maintenance programs without hesitation, as they do not hinder work activity among the poor. Additionally, interventions should focus on improving access to education and healthcare for those with low levels of human capital.

Authors: Zhenchao Qian; Daniel T. Lichter; Leanna M. Mellott
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Developed country; Economics; Childbirth; Population; Selection bias; Mate choice; Probit model; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: Out-of-Wedlock Childbearing, Marital Prospects and Mate Selection
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Women with unmarried births are more likely to cohabit than to marry and tend to have less-educated and older spouses or partners. White women with unmarried births also tend to have husbands or partners of another race.
What_was_studied: This study applies marital search theory to investigate how out-of-wedlock childbearing affects mate selection patterns among American women using 1980-1995 CPS data, with probit models to account for potential selection bias.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lower socioeconomic status and poorer health outcomes associated with cohabitation, public policy should prioritize programs that encourage marriage among low-income women, especially those who are more likely to have diverse spouses or partners.

Authors: Ive Marx; Lina Salanauskaite; Gerlinde Verbist
Field: Public economics; Economics; Context (language use); Public debate; Positive relationship; Economic inequality; Function (engineering)
Title: For the Poor, but Not Only the Poor: On Optimal Pro-Poorness in Redistributive Policies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The overall relationship between pro-poor targeting and income inequality reduction is very weak, with occasional positive associations but no robust patterns. However, the most redistributive systems contain subsystems strongly targeted to the poor by intent and design. Means-tested systems play a crucial role in bringing about redistributive effectiveness, even if their relative size is small.
What_was_studied: The optimal design of redistributive systems for income poverty reduction in urban areas across gender and intersectional lines, using data from various countries over the past two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the weak overall association between pro-poor targeting and income inequality reduction, policymakers should prioritize means-tested systems to maximize redistributive impact. By embedding benefits for the poor within broader benefit systems that meet wider redistributive needs and rationales, policymakers can scale up effective poverty reduction strategies in urban areas across gender and intersectional lines.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Fugue; Survey data collection; Young adult; Transition (fiction); Unemployment; Adolescent development; Life events
Title: The Search for Adolescent Role Exits and the Transition to Adulthood
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: According to the study, the absence of controls allows adolescents to search for role exits, and the presence of strains pushes them towards such a search. The effects are most pronounced among females whose mothers experience unemployment, with early parenthood being a constrained choice among restricted possibilities.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the search for adolescent role exits and its effects on the timing of first marriage and parenthood in a Canadian community using panel and cross-sectional survey data from the period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that adolescent role exits can have a significant impact on the timing of first marriage and parenthood, policymakers should prioritize providing support systems for families in need to reduce strain and increase access to education and employment opportunities for young women.

Field: Epistemology; Psychology; Set (psychology); Control (management); Unemployment; Meaning (existential); Object (philosophy); Argument; Phenomenon; Analogy; Social psychology
Title: "Gestalt" and Case Study. III. Is Statistical Methodology Applicable to the Study of the "Situation?"
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unemployment is not divisible into units, and that studying the situation as a system is necessary to understand its complexity and interconnectedness.
What_was_studied: Mrs. Sheffield's paper examines the concept of 'the home as a cushioned retreat for the man', exploring how it manifests in different situations and highlighting the need to study the situation as a whole rather than individual units.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality in policymaking, particularly in the context of unemployment. To effectively combat these issues, policies should prioritize a holistic approach that considers the entire system rather than individual units.

Field: Social relation; Sociology; General Social Survey; Individualism; Poverty; Regional variation; Test (assessment); Regional differences; Social psychology; Collectivism
Title: The Poverty of Trust in the Southern United States
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Southerners, especially whites, have lower levels of general trust compared to non-Southerners, after controlling for other factors related to trust. This difference persists even when considering other regional variations.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how collectivist social relations in the Southern United States impact general trust levels among the population, using data from the General Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the impact of trust on social cohesion and community development, policymakers should prioritize interventions that foster collectivist social relations in the South, such as targeted community programs and inclusive economic policies. By addressing regional differences in trust, these efforts can help bridge the intersectional poverty gap and promote more equitable social protection.

Authors: Anna Manzoni; Juho Härkönen; Karl Ulrich Mayer
Field: German; Psychology; Perspective (graphical); Occupational inequality; Educational attainment; Context (language use); Demographic economics; Inequality; Social stratification; Cohort; Social psychology
Title: Moving On? A Growth-Curve Analysis of Occupational Attainment and Career Progression Patterns in West Germany
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study confirms previous findings of limited career progression and permanence in occupational inequality, with educational attainment, class background, and cohort context playing a strong role in shaping career mobility. Additionally, the study finds a substantial gross effect of class background, which is strongly mediated by educational attainment for women but not for men.
What_was_studied: Using multilevel growth-curve analysis, this study examines occupational stratification across West German careers for cohorts born between 1919 and 1971, with a focus on the permanence of inequalities across human lives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing educational attainment and class background inequalities is crucial to improving career mobility and reducing occupational stratification. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives that improve access to quality education, particularly for women, and implement targeted interventions to address the root causes of socio-economic inequality.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Poverty; Ethnology; Child health; Racial differences; Statut socio economique; Family characteristics
Title: Contextual Determinants of Children's Responses to Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that household poverty and residential factors are crucial indicators of the mental health of certain children, regardless of whether they are considered separately or together. Furthermore, the study revealed that Hispanic and indigenous communities were disproportionately affected by these factors compared to black or white communities.
What_was_studied: This study combined an individual approach that considers the level of individual income and a family approach that examines the household's poverty level, as well as residential characteristics, to investigate the influence of socio-economic factors on the mental health of some children. The study collected data in 1988 through an American survey and found that family poverty and residential characteristics are critical indicators of the mental health of some children, regardless of whether these variables are considered separately or interactively.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, it is essential to prioritize funding for programs aimed at reducing child poverty in Hispanic and indigenous communities. Policymakers should revise existing policies to address the specific needs of these communities and scale up successful interventions to improve mental health outcomes for vulnerable children.

Authors: John M. Stahura; John J. Sloan
Field: LISREL; Sociology; Poverty; Unemployment; Property crime; Violent crime; Demographic economics; Legal guardian; Maximum likelihood; Juvenile delinquency
Title: Urban Stratification of Places, Routine Activities and Suburban Crime Rates
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that motivation, opportunities, and guardianship had direct and indirect additive effects on both violent and property crime rates, with a multiplicative effect of the preconditions for crime observed only for property crime. The findings support the 'routine activities' model.
What_was_studied: Suburban crime rates in 1972 and 1980 were analyzed using data from 676 American suburbs to evaluate Cohen and Felson's 'routine activities' theory, with a focus on the direct and indirect additive effects of criminal motivation, opportunities, and guardianship on violent and property crime rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty and unemployment, improving female labor force participation, and increasing police employment and expenditure to combat rising crime rates in suburbs. Additionally, traffic congestion, air pollution, and other urban problems should be addressed to prevent further decay of housing and deterioration of the living environment.

Authors: Steven M. Cohen; Robert E. Kapsis
Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Psychology; Salience (language); Voluntary association; Population; Organizational behavior; Argument; Normative; Social psychology
Title: Participation of Blacks, Puerto Ricans, and Whites in Voluntary Associations: A Test of Current Theories
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that neither the deprivation nor the normative explanation was consistently supported. Black ethnic identifiers did not exhibit higher participatory rates than their more assimilated peers, and lower-class black women were unusually active in organizational membership compared to their male counterparts.
What_was_studied: The study examines the participation of Puerto Ricans, blacks, and whites in New York City in voluntary organizations to test several key postulates from deprivation and normative explanations for high rates of participation among blacks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing chronic poverty and promoting sustainable development should prioritize the unique needs and experiences of marginalized communities, such as lower-class black women, in order to increase participation and address intersectional poverty.

Authors: Charles B. Nam; Mary G. Powers
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Prestige; Distribution (economics); Social stratification; Occupational prestige
Title: Changes in the Relative Status Level of Workers in the United States, 1950–60
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed general stability of occupational status but significant changes for a minority of occupations, with changing numbers of occupants, median age, and education and income levels. Slight declines in scores were observed for persons in most occupations, indicating a shifting occupational distribution that makes positions in higher-status occupations more common and those in lower-status occupations even less privileged over time.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the socioeconomic scores of individuals classified by detailed occupation in 1950 and 1960, providing insights into changes in occupational status over the decade and the shifting occupational distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the need to scale up support for workers in lower-status occupations and fund initiatives that promote mobility into higher-status positions, as well as prioritize policies that address income poverty and ensure fair distribution of resources.

Field: Racism; Political science; Poverty; Legislation; Context (language use); Racial formation theory; Inequality; Development economics; Phenomenon; Census
Title: The Impact of Slavery on Racial Inequality in Poverty in the Contemporary U.S. South
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 1860 slave concentration is related to contemporary black-white inequality in poverty, independent of contemporary demographic and economic conditions, racialized wealth disparities, and racial threat. This suggests that slavery has had a lasting impact on shaping existing U.S. racial inequality patterns.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed county-level U.S. Census data to examine the relationship between slavery and contemporary racial inequality in poverty, using regression and spatial data analysis techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the legacy of slavery to scale up poverty reduction efforts targeting black Americans, particularly in areas with historically high slave concentrations.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Judaism; China; Donation; Benefice; Context (language use); Field (Bourdieu); Immigration; Criminology; Acculturation
Title: Sociology in China
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that traditional forms of benefice persist among American Jews in a new context, with examples including the refusal of destitute parents to accept support from prosperous children and extensive cemetery and burial arrangements. Additionally, the study found that Jews in America contribute heavily to charities and projects, both within the Jewish community and beyond.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the benefice patterns of American Jews during a specific time period, using a combination of private and public data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of traditional benefice patterns among American Jews, policymakers should prioritize addressing health disparities and intersectional poverty by scaling up support for Jewish-led charitable initiatives and expanding the definition of 'community' to include both the Jewish community and non-Jewish individuals and organizations.

Authors: Marie Withers Osmond; Charles M. Grigg
Field: Welfare; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Poverty; Family income; Disadvantage; Family economics; Nuclear family; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Correlates of Poverty: The Interaction of Individual and Family Characteristics
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis reveals substantial interaction effects among the two sets of variables, with sex of the family head being a major conditional variable. For female-headed families, characteristics of the family largely account for variation in family income, work history of the head, and welfare history of the family. For male-headed families, individual characteristics of the family head take precedence over family characteristics.
What_was_studied: This study compares the characteristics of family heads and families in relation to three criteria of family poverty using data from a sample of 561 welfare applicants in four states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant interaction effects between family head characteristics and family characteristics in predicting family poverty, policymakers should prioritize tailored interventions that address the unique needs of female-headed families, such as job training programs and childcare assistance. Additionally, targeted support for male-headed families with low levels of education or work experience is also crucial to address chronic poverty.

Authors: Robin W. Simon; Kathryn J. Lively
Field: Social influence; Mental health; Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Depression (differential diagnoses); Anger; Marital status; Affect (psychology); Social issues; Clinical psychology
Title: Sex, Anger and Depression
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women experience more symptoms of depression when they experience intense and persistent anger, with sex differences in the intensity and persistence of anger contributing to this health disparity. Data showed that women reported more frequent and longer-lasting anger outbursts than men, and that these outbursts were associated with a higher likelihood of depression.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1996 GSS Emotions Module, this study investigates the relationship between intense and persistent anger in women and depression, controlling for sex differences in these emotions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of depression among women, policymakers should prioritize addressing sex differences in the intensity and persistence of anger to scale up effective interventions for mental health disparities. This could involve funding research on gender-sensitive therapies, expanding access to mental health services in low-income communities, or revising health policies to better address women's unique emotional needs.

Field: Sociology; Big Four; Demographic economics
Title: Wealth as One of the “Big Four” SES Dimensions in Intergenerational Transmissions
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that wealth is a distinct dimension of SES that is very different from education, occupation, and income. Parental wealth substantially moderates intergenerational reproduction in other dimensions: the wealthiest have higher reproduction rates in all child outcomes, but in particular for children's income and wealth.
What_was_studied: Recent scholarship on mobility has increasingly incorporated wealth, examining if wealth brings anything new to mobility research or is just a standard socioeconomic status (SES) dimension in disguise, using Swedish administrative registers that contain rich SES measures over individuals' lives for both parents' and children's generations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize addressing wealth inequality alongside education, occupation, and income. Excluding wealth leads to underestimating intergenerational inequality, which can be aggravated by its qualitatively unique status as an SES resource. By scaling up policies aimed at reducing wealth disparities, we can expand access to sustainable development opportunities and address intersectional poverty.

Authors: Kathleen Mullan Harris; Robert A Hummer
Field: Mental health; Life expectancy; Life course approach; Social determinants of health; Psychology; Salience (neuroscience); Health care; Gerontology; Social psychology; Environmental health; Medicine; Economic growth; Economics; Psychiatry; Population; Cognitive psychology
Title: The Increasing Salience of Health in Social Forces Research
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Health research in Social Forces has increased over the past century, with a steady flow of publications since 1970 and more growth and diversity in the twentieth-first-century issues. The trend is driven by the relevance of health status, behavior, and healthcare within societal structures and institutional contexts, the increasing availability of high-quality health data, and the attention to measurement of health.
What_was_studied: The 100-year history of Social Forces, covering the global life expectancy at birth which approximately doubled during that period, with a focus on health-related articles from 1920 to 2000 and their relevance to social behavior, mental health systems, general health status, physical health indicators, and changes over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing importance of health in social and economic life, decision makers should prioritize and fund research on health and its relationship with gender and poverty, as well as expand access to high-quality health data and revise policies that impact mental and physical health systems.

Field: Extended family; Sociology; Poverty; Crime prevention; Middle class; Context (language use); Social control; Criminology; Social organization; Social network
Title: Sweet Mothers and Gangbangers: Managing Crime in a Black Middle-Class Neighborhood
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that dense social networks facilitate informal supervision of youth and enhance the activities of formal organizations, but the incorporation of criminal elements hinders efforts to completely rid the neighborhood of poverty and crime.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study examines how residents in a predominantly Black middle-class neighborhood in Chicago manage the challenges of high poverty and crime rates through dense social networks, while also incorporating gang members and drug dealers into their networks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for community-based programs that foster residential stability and social cohesion in high-poverty, high-crime areas, with a focus on addressing the conflicting effects of dense social networks.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; General Social Survey; Big Five personality traits and culture; Triangulation (psychology); Model minority; Ostracism; Racial formation theory; Social theory; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: The Marginalized “Model” Minority: An Empirical Examination of the Racial Triangulation of Asian Americans
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the American public rates Asians more favorably than blacks in terms of family commitment, nonviolence, and wealth, but that these ratings do not match the predictions of a singular hierarchical approach. Additionally, the study found that whites are more likely to have more favorable views of the relative positions of Asians than blacks.
What_was_studied: This article proposes a shift in race research from one-dimensional hierarchical approaches to multidimensional systems of racial stratification, using the American public's ratings of Asians relative to blacks and whites along two dimensions of racial stratification: racial valorization and civic acceptance/ostracism, based on selected years of the General Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty by scaling up education access for all racial groups and reforming existing systems of racial stratification to reduce discrimination.

Field: Economy; Publishing; Self; Political science; Order (exchange); Workforce; Subject (philosophy); Pride; Outsourcing; Economic inequality
Title: Stand-in Labor and the Rising Economy of Self
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ghostwriters face recognition estrangement and alter the subjects they impersonate, leading to a paradoxical dynamic of taking professional pride in disappearing while reappearing in the act of altering others' selves.
What_was_studied: This article explores the experience of ghostwriters and its implications on the economy of self, using 72 interviews with ghostwriters and publishing industry insiders to show that ghostwriters face recognition estrangement and alter the subjects they impersonate, leading to a paradoxical dynamic of taking professional pride in disappearing while reappearing in the act of altering others' selves.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that many stand-in workers engaged in this growing economy of self might alter the people they impersonate, leading to a situation where calls for authenticity breed adulteration. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize implementing policies that protect the rights and well-being of stand-in workers while ensuring the authenticity of the selves they craft.

Field: Psychology; Work (electrical); Spouse; Exercise time; Work time; Family life; Health implications; Physical activity; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Gerontology
Title: Double Time: Is Health Affected by a Spouse's Time at Work?
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: Husband's long working hours (50+) predict better health for wives due to greater resources, while wives' moderately long working hours (41-49) predict worse health for husbands due to reduced exercise time.
What_was_studied: Using the NLSY79, we examined the health implications of men’s and women’s work time on their spouses, investigating three mechanisms through which spousal hours might affect health: resources from the job, stress, and time for physical activity and exercise.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given persistent inequities in work and family life, policymakers should prioritize family-friendly policies that scale up support for caregiving, expand flexible work arrangements, and fund programs supporting work-life balance to promote health equity.

Authors: Steven L. Nock; Peter H. Rossi
Field: Social status; Attribution; Psychology; Prestige; Marital status; Distribution (economics); Unit (housing); Social stratification; Social psychology; Vignette
Title: Household Types and Social Standing
primary_category: Education access; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that occupation is more important than education, age, or marital status in determining social status evaluations. Additionally, each member of the family contributes differentially to the overall evaluation, with certain characteristics not being important.
What_was_studied: The study examines how different family characteristics contribute to social status evaluations, using a hypothetical vignette families and regression analysis to determine which clues are most important.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policies aimed at improving access to education and reducing rural poverty should prioritize occupation and skill development programs to enhance social status and evaluate the effectiveness of these policies.

Field: Standard of living; Sociology; Demography; Poverty; Cohort effect; Cohort study; Baby boom; Population; Fertility; Cohort
Title: The Baby Boom and Trends in Poverty, 1967–1987
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that every successive generation of white family heads born throughout the baby boom faced an increasingly greater chance of being poor, with those born after the baby boom facing the highest odds of poverty. In contrast, the cohort effect was not statistically significant among blacks.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the relationship between cohort and poverty among whites and blacks in the United States during the baby boom period using data from the 1960, 1970, and 1980 censuses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty among white family heads born after the baby boom, who face the highest odds of poverty, and consider targeted interventions to mitigate the impact of cohort competition on food insecurity and intersectional poverty.
