Field: Epistemology; Meaning (existential); Social life; Human ecology
Title: The Geography of Distinction: The Nation and its Regions 1790–1927
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that marginal communities, as measured by ecological indexes, experience higher rates of intersectional poverty, which can be addressed through targeted policies prioritizing economic empowerment and social inclusion.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the ecological indexes of community life in a specific region over a 5-year period, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up funding for programs aimed at improving economic opportunities and social connections within marginal communities to reduce intersectional poverty rates and promote more equitable community development.

Field: Business; Health care; Negative relationship; Poverty; Social indicators; Medical expenditure; Health resource; Poor people; Socioeconomics; Census
Title: Poor People, Poor Places and Access to Health Care in the United States
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the negative relationship between the prevalence of poverty in communities and access to health care is much stronger for middle- and high-income individuals than for those in lower-income groups. Additionally, the study suggests that individuals may benefit from living among those in similar economic circumstances because they face similar obstacles to obtaining medical care.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Surveys, the U.S. Census Bureau, and the Health Resource and Services Administration, this study investigates the relationship between community-level poverty and access to health care among individuals in different income groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stronger negative relationship between community-level poverty and access to health care for middle- and high-income individuals, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address financial barriers to health care for these groups. This could include increasing funding for programs that provide subsidies for health care expenses or expanding access to community health centers.

Field: Social class; Socioeconomic status; Geography; Slum; Population; Low-Income Population; Urbanization; Sample (statistics); Socioeconomics; Developing country
Title: Slums and Squatter Areas as Entrepots for Rural-Urban Migrants in a Less Developed Society
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The data demonstrates that many young married persons, particularly females, migrate to the city and reside in nonslum neighborhoods as servants, lodgers, or extended relatives. This challenges the notion that rural-urban migrants are confined to slums or low-income areas upon arrival.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Philippines, this research scrutinizes the belief that most rural migrants in developing countries settle in low-income neighborhoods upon arrival in the city, challenging the idea that they are heavily segregated in specific districts or likely to reside in slum communities. The study focuses on a sample of lower-status rural-urban migrants and reveals that patterns persist even when restricting the sample to this group.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to support young married women and their families in accessing safe, affordable housing and employment opportunities outside of slum communities. This can involve funding programs for affordable housing initiatives and vocational training specifically tailored towards this demographic.

Authors: Paul E. Bellair; Vincent J. Roscigno
Field: Sociology; Alienation; Survey data collection; Suburbanization; Unemployment; Poison control; Social issues; Juvenile delinquency; Criminology; Economic restructuring
Title: Local Labor-Market Opportunity and Adolescent Delinquency
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found strong effects of low-wage service-sector concentration and unemployment on the likelihood of both fighting and drug use among adolescents, with these effects persisting even when potential mediators are controlled for.
What_was_studied: This article extends the literature on adolescent delinquency by offering a theoretical framework that integrates insights from labor market and stratification research on one hand and microlevel family and criminological research on the other, drawing on local labor market data and nationally representative longitudinal survey data on adolescents, and using techniques that take into account clustering within hierarchical structures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent effects of low-wage service sector concentration and unemployment on adolescent delinquency, policy makers should prioritize strategies to create more job opportunities and improve wages in these sectors, as well as implement programs to support families and strengthen attachment to parents and school, as a way to reduce adolescent delinquency.

Field: False consciousness; Economic Justice; Sociology; General will; Structuralism; Consistency (negotiation); Power (social and political); Relative deprivation; Social science; Legitimacy
Title: Sociology in its place : and other essays
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that religious beliefs were strongly linked to class, status, and power dynamics, with those in positions of power being more likely to report 'religious' beliefs. Additionally, charismatic legitimacy and one-party rule were found to be significant factors in shaping religious beliefs.
What_was_studied: The sociological explanation of 'religious' beliefs in Ghana, using a mixed-methods approach and data from the 1960s and 1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering power dynamics and structural factors in understanding 'religious' beliefs. To address chronic poverty and intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize policies that address class and status disparities and promote more equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Social relation; Mental health; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Qualitative research; Social isolation; Self-concept; Pejorative; Social theory; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: Multiracial Self-Identification and Adolescent Outcomes: A Social Psychological Approach to the Marginal Man Theory
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Self-identified multiracial adolescents reported more psychological difficulties and lower levels of social participation than monoracial adolescents, but also showed higher levels of active social interaction. These findings challenge previous studies' assumptions that multiracial self-identification is problematic and instead suggest that multiracial youth may be more resilient and socially engaged than previously thought.
What_was_studied: A nationally representative sample of racially self-identified adolescents during the 2010s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing health disparities and intersectional poverty by funding targeted interventions that promote social participation and mental health support for multiracial adolescents, while also scaling up comprehensive anti-poverty programs that address the unique needs of multiracial youth.

Field: Gender studies; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Sovereignty; Action (philosophy); Rivalry; Compensation (psychology); Impracticability; Nationalist Movement; Nationalism
Title: The Ambonese Nationalist Movement in the Netherlands: A Study in Status Deprivation
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Ambonese Nationalist Movement was characterized by affectively charged values and demands for full commitment, and that collective concern about status deprivation provided the movement with a dynamic psychological strength, despite the impracticability of its aims. The study also found that the movement's ideology was expressive of converging dissatisfactions and that the values revolved around and had continuous association with status imagery, both individual and collective.
What_was_studied: This study examines the Ambonese Nationalist Movement in the context of status deprivation and its impact on collective action, using a multidisciplinary approach that includes sociology, psychology, and political science, with a focus on the period between 1950 and 1960 and data collected through surveys and interviews conducted during that time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that collective concern about status deprivation provides dynamic psychological strength for nationalist movements, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and multidimensional poverty in education access to prevent the emergence of such movements. Furthermore, the study's results suggest that revamping educational curricula to include more diverse perspectives and values could help mitigate the appeal of nationalist ideologies.

Authors: John Robert Warren; Rachael B. Kulick
Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; State (polity); Legislation; Exit examination; Unemployment; Academic achievement; Event history; Educational finance; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Modeling States' Enactment of High School Exit Examination Policies
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: States with higher unemployment rates and larger proportions of racial/ethnic minority youth were more likely to adopt high school exit examination policies than similar states.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the adoption of high school exit examination policies in U.S. states between 1980 and 2017, using event history techniques to examine the role of academic achievement, education spending, economic conditions, racial/ethnic heterogeneity, and policy diffusion in explaining adoption timing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that economic conditions and racial/ethnic diversity are strong predictors of HSEE adoption, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions and resource allocation in these areas to ensure equal access to quality education for all students.

Field: Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Opiate; Inequality; Politics
Title: Opiate of the Masses? Inequality, Religion, and Political Ideology in the United States
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that religion acts as a compensatory resource for these groups, providing traditional-values-oriented schemas that shape their politics in accordance with the content of religious belief systems, suppressing what would otherwise be larger group differences in political ideology. Additionally, the study shows that religion provides compensatory resources for lack of social status, not just economic status.
What_was_studied: Using a special module of the General Social Survey, this study investigates how religion affects political ideology among structurally disadvantaged groups such as women, racial minorities, those with lower incomes, and sexual minorities over time and across different regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty by expanding access to religious resources and revamping traditional values-oriented political ideologies to foster emancipatory political values and reduce the opiate effect of religion on marginalized groups.

Authors: Hua Yu Sebastian Cherng; Emily Hannum
Field: Sociology; Poverty; China; Longitudinal study; Household survey; Industrialisation; Development economics
Title: Community Poverty, Industrialization, and Educational Gender Gaps in Rural China
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that community impoverishment, not industrialization, correlates with educational gender gaps; poverty and isolation shape gaps differently at different educational levels; and girls in relatively wealthy households fare better than boys at the transition to high school.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates community impoverishment and industrialization as explanations for educational gender gaps in rural China using a multi-province household survey and a longitudinal study of youth in one impoverished province, considering attributes of poor communities that might shape gaps and the related roles of household and community poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing community impoverishment and its effects on educational gender gaps, particularly in rural areas, by implementing targeted interventions that consider the unique challenges faced by girls and boys in poor households and communities.

Authors: Karyn A. Loscocco; Arne L. Kalleberg
Field: Sociology; Industrial sociology; Cross-cultural; Life course approach; Work (electrical); Social change; Meaning (existential); Population; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Age and the Meaning of Work in the United States and Japan
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that older men are more committed to work than younger men in both Japan and the United States, while there are no age differences in work commitment among Japanese women.
What_was_studied: This paper examines age differences in work commitment and work values among American and Japanese employees using data from 4,567 individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of work commitment for employee well-being and productivity, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that support older workers' continued engagement and retention, such as flexible work arrangements and training programs.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Turnover; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Differential accumulation; Pension; Set-aside; Earnings; Working life; Economic inequality
Title: Education and Contributory Pensions at Work: Disadvantages of the Less Educated
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis clarifies two central pathways associated with educational disparities in DC retirement plans. First, we disentangle the effects of education that operate via a labor market pathway, showing that a worker's earnings level is, by far, the most influential labor market factor associated with participation and contribution amounts. Second, we show an important independent effect of education on not only the decision to participate, but also how much money to set aside when participating, net of earnings and structural position in labor markets.
What_was_studied: Using the Survey of Income and Program Participation linked to W-2 tax records containing respondents' annual contributions to DC retirement plans, we examine how participation in and contributions to DC plans among eligible US workers differ by education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Less educated workers face multiple disadvantages in the accumulation of retirement resources in the context of growing income inequality and changing employment institutions. Policymakers should prioritize programs that scale access to education, enhance earnings potential for low-educated workers, and expand access to retirement savings plans to address the education gap in workplace retirement savings plans.

Field: Demography; Age and female fertility; Breastfeeding; Natural fertility; Family planning; Menstruation; Birth control; Population; Fertility; Medicine
Title: Changes of Natural Fertility and Contraceptive Equivalents
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that prolonged breastfeeding and malnutrition delays the onset of menstruation and lengthens postpartum amenorrhea, resulting in increased fertility. The Perrin-Sheps model showed that if a social group abandons breastfeeding before starting birth control, there will be an appreciable rise in fertility.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of prolonged breastfeeding and malnutrition on fertility in underdeveloped countries, using the Perrin-Sheps model to quantify increases in natural fertility and assess contraceptive needs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of food insecurity and income poverty in underdeveloped countries, policymakers should prioritize birth control initiatives that address these factors to mitigate the potential increase in fertility and population growth.

Field: Statistics; Goodness of fit; Social status; Econometrics; Psychology; Social inequality; Proxy (statistics); Social mobility; Social stratification; Centrality; Occupational prestige
Title: A Structural Model of the Mobility Table
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The new mobility ratio measure yielded by the model provided a useful indicator of association in mobility tables, which can be used to compare different measures of occupational mobility and social standing.
What_was_studied: The 1949 British mobility table was analyzed using a multiplicative model to measure association and eliminate confounding main and interaction effects, providing a parsimonious set of parameters that describe the table and goodness of fit assessment with standard inferential procedures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development and implementation of multiplicative models for mobility tables to provide more accurate measures of association and eliminate confounding effects, leading to better assessments of social inequality and more effective policies to address it.

Field: Maturity (psychological); Social class; Sociological theory; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Sociometry; Sociography; Wife; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Socioeconomic Status and Sociometric Choice
primary_category: Social Protection
What_was_found: The chi-square analysis of the data indicated a complex relationship between socioeconomic rank and choice of close associates, with 'equals' chosen under some conditions and 'superiors' chosen under others. The study found that persons choosing others for close relationships tend to name those of higher socioeconomic status than themselves.
What_was_studied: Quantitative data from four studies were analyzed to test the hypothesis that sociometric choices are directed toward persons of higher socioeconomic status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research suggests that policy interventions aimed at reducing social inequality should prioritize programs that foster diverse, cross-class networks and encourage individuals to choose associates from different socioeconomic backgrounds.

Field: Retrenchment; Public policy; Welfare state; Public opinion; Political economy; Government; Economics; Devolution; Public administration; Legitimacy; Politics
Title: Declining Government Confidence and Policy Preferences in the U.S.: Devolution, Regime Effects, or Symbolic Change?*
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The authors found no significant relationship between government confidence and public support for federal involvement in these policy areas, suggesting that other factors may be more influential in shaping public opinion.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between government confidence and public support for federal involvement in health care and education policy domains over time, using data from 1972 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing economic inequality and social polarization to strengthen public trust in government and support for federal policies aimed at reducing poverty and improving gender equality.

Authors: James D. Cowhig; Calvin L. Beale
Field: Rural area; Standard of living; Socioeconomic status; Geography; Educational attainment; Population; Demographic economics; Census; Nonfarm payrolls; Rural sociology
Title: Socioeconomic Differences Between White and Nonwhite Farm Populations of the South
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there was improvement in socioeconomic status indicators such as income, educational attainment, and housing quality for both white and non-white farm populations between 1950 and 1960, the gap between the two groups widened over the period.
What_was_studied: Data from the Census of Agriculture and the Census of Population and Housing were used to compare socioeconomic status indicators for white and non-white farm populations in 1950 and 1960 in 14 Southern states, showing an improvement for both groups but with widening differences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to scale up support for rural farming communities, particularly for non-white farmers, to address persistent socioeconomic disparities and ensure equal access to resources and opportunities.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Political science; Social fact; Political sociology; Social disintegration; Population; Social stratification; Political ecology; Politics
Title: Is Theory for Demographers
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that areas prone to extremist or radical movements also exhibit high instability of political attitudes, and that religious cleavages and ethnic differences can significantly influence voting behavior.
What_was_studied: Siegfried's research on periphery expansions and contractions in certain regions of France revealed patterns of agrarian unrest and labor movements, depending on various factors such as population changes, economic conditions, and social stratification.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high instability of political attitudes in areas prone to extremist or radical movements, it is crucial to prioritize integrated studies across social sciences to understand the complex factors driving these movements, and to fund targeted interventions that address the underlying causes of social disintegration.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Propensity score matching; Sibling; Grade retention; Context (language use); Cornerstone; Causal effect; Social stratification; Social psychology; Test score
Title: The Scarring Effects of Primary-Grade Retention?: A Study of Cumulative Advantage in the Educational Career
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Early primary grade retention significantly reduces the likelihood of high school completion and college entry, with effects operating mainly through middle school academic achievements and expectations. However, students can continue to recover from the effects of grade retention through early high school, suggesting that interventions aimed at mitigating the long-term consequences of retention should be prioritized.
What_was_studied: The effects of primary-grade retention on high school completion and college entry, using propensity score matching and sibling fixed-effects models to control for confounding factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant and lasting effects of primary grade retention on educational outcomes, policymakers should scale up support for early intervention programs targeting academic achievement and expectations in middle school. By funding evidence-based programs and revising policies that tie educational outcomes to a single test score, we can work towards reducing poverty and gender gaps in education.

Field: Political science; Civic engagement; Collective action; Social citizenship; Collective efficacy; Solidarity; Economic growth; Insurgency; Immigration; Criminology; Politics
Title: Social Citizenship, Integration and Collective Action: Immigrant Civic Engagement in the United States
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that institutional threats to immigrants deterred civic activity, while local restrictive efforts instigated solidarity events and outreach efforts directed at immigrants facilitated community improvement projects.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of civic and political environments on immigrant collective action in metropolitan areas using a data set of over 1,000 events.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that conditions intensifying group boundaries between immigrants and natives and encouraging collective efficacy are important predictors of immigrant civic engagement. Policymakers should prioritize creating inclusive and supportive environments for immigrants to encourage their participation in community improvement projects, which can contribute to sustainable development, intersectional poverty reduction, and employment opportunities.

Authors: George S. Wilson; Vincent J. Roscigno; Matt L. Huffman
Field: Private sector; Racism; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Public sector; Economics; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Discretion; Disadvantaged; Social mobility
Title: Public Sector Transformation, Racial Inequality and Downward Occupational Mobility
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Results from a Panel Study of Income Dynamics sample indicate that the 'new government business model,' characterized by increased employer discretion, has disproportionately disadvantaged African Americans, with narrower racial gaps in the incidence, determinants, and timing of downward mobility found in the public sector relative to the private sector during the pre-reform period (1985–90) eroding during the reform period (2002–07) because of widening racial gaps in the public sector.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed race-based inequities on one socioeconomic outcome – downward occupational mobility – among professionals, managers, and executives in the public sector during the civil rights era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up initiatives to improve workplace-based attainments for African American men, expanding funding and resources for programs aimed at addressing racial inequities in the public sector, and revising 'new governance' reforms to better address these issues.

Field: Social class; Positive economics; Sociology; Status symbol; Set (psychology); Power (social and political); Convergence (relationship); Meaning (existential); Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic system
Title: Social Consequences of the Industrialization of Southern Cities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that status symbols and ranking lag behind the acquisition of economic or political power by as much as one or two generations, and that these symbols can persist after the vanishing of the power which achieved them; the study also found a fundamental convergence between the three ways of classifying the data (status stratification, social mobility, and economic class).
What_was_studied: The relationship between status stratification, social mobility, and economic class in a Latin American urban community over time, using data from multiple sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and social protection policies to reduce inequality and promote sustainable development, as the study's findings suggest that social stratification depends on a complex set of interrelated attributes rather than operating as a function of one variable.

Field: Sociology; Social system; Social group; Structure (mathematical logic); Power structure; Mechanism (sociology); Public relations; Process (engineering); Sample (statistics); Community organization; Management science
Title: Statistical Indexes of the Social Aspects of Communities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Community organization using a formal mechanism like a community council is less effective when there are heterogeneity and complexity in the social structure, lack of administrative know-how, discrepancies between agreed objectives and basic functional prerequisites, obstruction by elements in power structures, and efforts to hurry the process faster than understanding can be developed.
What_was_studied: Private office-holding in community organization, specifically how leaders of different types (i.e., formal and informal) affect the process's effectiveness when a mechanism like a community council is used for special programs or services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that intersectional poverty affects various groups within a community differently, policy makers should prioritize modifications to complex social structures and invest in administrative know-how to ensure community organization processes are effective and inclusive of all stakeholders.

Authors: Vincent J. Roscigno; Sherry Mong; Reginald A. Byron; Griff Tester
Field: Psychology; Ideology; Life course approach; Well-being; Inequality; Social stratification; Economic restructuring; Social psychology; Qualitative property; Conceptualization
Title: Age Discrimination, Social Closure and Employment
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that skilled and semi-skilled workers nearing 50 years old were vulnerable to downward occupational mobility, with explicit ageist stereotypes and supposedly age-neutral ideologies contributing to age discrimination. Quantitative results showed trends toward downward occupational mobility for ageing workers, especially in the face of economic restructuring and global economic pressures.
What_was_studied: Age discrimination in employment between 1988 and 2003, using quantitative and qualitative data to investigate the interactional nature of workplace age discrimination, explicit ageist stereotypes, and supposedly age-neutral ideologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions are needed to address age discrimination in employment, such as scaling up training programs to enhance the skills of older workers, expanding employment opportunities for ageing workers, funding research on effective age management strategies, and prioritizing anti-discrimination policies in the workplace. By taking these actions, we can reduce downward occupational mobility for ageing workers and promote more equitable employment practices.

Authors: Lin Huff-Corzine; Jay Corzine; David C. Moore
Field: Demography; Poverty; Geography; High rate; Regional differences; Mutually exclusive events; Homicide
Title: Southern Exposure: Deciphering the South's Influence on Homicide Rates
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Homicides for total populations and whites were found to be influenced by both poverty and regional differences, while poverty was not related to the homicide rate among nonwhites. The results suggest that subcultural differences may play a role in the high homicide rates of white southerners and blacks.
What_was_studied: State homicide rates for total populations, whites and nonwhites in the United States during an unspecified time period were studied using OLS and ridge regression techniques to analyze the influence of poverty and regional differences on homicides.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings support arguments that addressing chronic poverty, particularly in rural areas, can help reduce homicides. Policymakers should prioritize funding for poverty-reduction programs and revise existing policies to better target these efforts at high-poverty regions.

Field: Psychiatry; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Unemployment; Alcohol abuse; Alcohol; Antecedent (logic); Multilevel model
Title: The Impact of Alcohol, Divorce, and Unemployment on Suicide: A Multilevel Analysis
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that approximately one-third of male suicides in Sweden are attributable to alcohol abuse, and that unemployment has a strong indirect impact on suicide. No relationship was found between divorce and suicide.
What_was_studied: The study examined the relationship between alcohol abuse and suicide in Sweden using ecological and time-series data, with a focus on the role of unemployment and divorce as control variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between alcohol abuse and suicide, policymakers should prioritize funding for substance abuse treatment programs targeting men, particularly in regions with high unemployment rates. Moreover, job creation initiatives should be scaled up to address the indirect impact of unemployment on suicide.

Field: Econometrics; Geography; Population; Additional research; Urbanization; Social stratification; Yield (finance); Urban sociology
Title: Recent Population Trends in the Southeast
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Photographic data were found to be sufficient for reproducing the relative, comparative housing structural characteristics of urban residential neighborhoods, with accurate subarea rankings and category classifications regarding prevalence of single-family homes and density of dwelling-units per block.
What_was_studied: The accuracy and practical utility of an aerial photographic method for assessing urban residential neighborhoods' structural characteristics in the United States during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Urban sociologists should prioritize adapting this method for studying ecological patterning of the urban social stratification system, as it may provide useful data for addressing intersectional poverty in sustainable development strategies.

Authors: Mario Luis Small; Erin Jacobs; Rebekah Peeples Massengill
Field: Business; Health care; Poverty; Access to information; Social indicators; Neighborhood poverty; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Community organization; Resource (project management)
Title: Why Organizational Ties Matter for Neighborhood Effects: Resource Access through Childcare Centers
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that centers provide important resource-access through their ties and that neighborhood poverty does not undermine this capacity, uncovering that organizational ties may help explain the inconsistent results of the neighborhood effects literature.
What_was_studied: This case study examines whether organizations, specifically childcare centers, are less connected if located in poor neighborhoods and whether neighborhood poverty affects their capacity to provide important resource-access to parents through their organizational ties.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding childcare centers in low-income areas to ensure parents have access to important resources and support, as organizational ties provide a crucial link to health care and job information.

Field: Nothing; Psychology; Social group; Perception; Harm; Sanctions; Humiliation; Human sexuality; Juvenile delinquency; Criminology; Social psychology
Title: Danger and the Decision to Offend
primary_category: Asset poverty; Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The researchers found that perceptions about danger are significantly associated with involvement in theft, drug selling, and prostitution among homeless youth, and these effects are independent of perceptions about a crime's excitement, profit, or other returns.
What_was_studied: The study examined the role of pain perceptions in deterring individuals from committing crimes among homeless youth in three major cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the physical harm that offenders may experience as a deterrent to crime, considering that the possibility of pain may be irrelevant to individuals who boldly believe in their unassailability.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Government; Recession; Position (finance); Social Security Act; Social security; Unemployment; Earnings; Economic stability
Title: The Farmer and Social Security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that while the bill aimed to provide social security coverage to all groups, including farmers, it failed to address the unique challenges faced by agricultural workers in accessing medical and hospital services, and the collection of social security taxes was more easily applied to industrial payrolls than farm bookkeeping.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of the Wagner-Murray-Dingell Bill on agricultural workers in the early postwar period, focusing on their access to health insurance, maternity benefits, and unemployment compensation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the vulnerability of agricultural workers to climate change, food insecurity, and rural poverty, policymakers should prioritize revising the Wagner-Murray-Dingell Bill to address these challenges and ensure equitable access to health insurance, maternity benefits, and unemployment compensation for all farmers, including those in vulnerable communities.

Authors: Jennifer A. Ailshire; James S. House
Field: Body weight; Psychology; Young adult; Educational attainment; Body mass index; Weight gain; Younger adults; Inequality; Gerontology; Race (biology)
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: The Unequal Burden of Weight Gain: An Intersectional Approach to Understanding Social Disparities in BMI Trajectories from 1986 to 2001/2002
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results reveal complex interactive effects of gender, race, socioeconomic position and age, and provide evidence for increasing social disparities, particularly among younger adults. Most notably, among individuals who aged from 25-39 to 45-54 during the study interval, low-educated and low-income black women experienced the greatest increase in BMI, while high-educated and high-income white men experienced the least BMI growth.
What_was_studied: Using an intersectional approach to studying inequality and the longitudinal and nationally representative American's Changing Lives study (1986-2001/2002), we examine social disparities in body mass index trajectories during a time of rapid weight gain in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These new findings highlight the importance of investigating changing disparities in weight intersectionally, using multiple dimensions of inequality as well as age, and also presage increasing BMI disparities in the U.S. adult population. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these disparities by implementing targeted interventions to support healthy behaviors among disadvantaged populations.

Field: Sociology; Residence; Institution; Disadvantaged; Earnings; Asian americans; Demographic economics; Economic growth; White (horse)
Title: Are Asian American Women Advantaged? Labor Market Performance of College Educated Female Workers
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that, after controlling for various factors such as field of study, college type, region of residence, and demographic variables, none of the Asian American female groups were advantaged in terms of unemployment, annual earnings, or the number of people supervised. Contrary to popular perception, even native-born Asian American women were not advantaged and were more likely to be unemployed.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the labor market performance of Asian American women using the 2003 National Survey of College Graduates, focusing on unemployment, annual earnings, and the number of people supervised.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and discrimination faced by Asian American women in the labor market. This could involve scaling up job training programs specifically designed for this demographic, expanding diversity and inclusion initiatives in hiring practices, and funding research to better understand the unique challenges faced by this group.

Authors: Christen L. Bradley; Linda A. Renzulli
Field: Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Poverty; Dropout (neural networks); Context (language use); Academic achievement; Student dropout; Drop out; Non completion; Social psychology
Title: The Complexity of Non-Completion: Being Pushed or Pulled to Drop Out of High School
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that for black students, differences in SES explain higher likelihoods of being either pushed or pulled out as compared to white students, while Latino students remain more likely to be pulled out even after controlling for SES. Additionally, the study reveals that SES moderates the relationship between race/gender and being pushed out.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Educational Longitudinal Survey, this study investigates student dropout among black and Latino students in high poverty schools, finding that socioeconomic status (SES) moderates the relationship between race/gender and being pushed out, with higher SES levels detrimental to students of color.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that higher SES levels are detrimental to students of color in high poverty schools, policymakers should prioritize funding and resources for schools with high poverty rates to ensure equitable access to education.

Field: Ethnic group; Odds; Demography; Geography; Self-employment; Unemployment; Country of origin; European union; Demographic economics; Census; Immigration
Title: Self-Employment of Immigrants: A Cross-National Study of 17 Western Societies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that (1) immigrants from non-Christian countries of origin have higher odds of self-employment, (2) higher levels of unemployment among natives increase the odds of self-employment, and (3) self-employment is more frequent among immigrant communities that are small, highly educated and have a longer settlement history.
What_was_studied: This study pooled census data from three classic immigrant countries (Australia, Canada and the United States) and labor-force surveys from 14 countries in the European Union for a cross-national data set to examine the role of immigrants' country of origin, country of destination and combinations thereof (settings or communities) in the likelihood of immigrants being self-employed.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher likelihood of self-employment among immigrants from non-Christian countries of origin and in communities with specific characteristics, policy makers should prioritize funding programs that support entrepreneurship training and resources for these groups to scale up their economic opportunities, expand employment opportunities beyond self-employment, and reduce poverty.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Contingent employment; Stigma (botany); Contingent work; Corporatism; Unemployment; Work history; Occupational prestige
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Better Off Jobless? Scarring Effects of Contingent Employment in Japan
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in a highly segmented labor market like Japan's, the strict separation of labor pools for standard and contingent jobs makes being labeled as a contingent worker particularly detrimental.
What_was_studied: Using work history data from Japan, this study shows that accepting a contingent job delays individuals' transition to standard employment more than remaining jobless, and having a contingent job leads Japanese men to have lower occupational status after they transition back to standard employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize policies that alleviate the stigma of contingent work arrangements and support individuals in transitioning back to standard employment, such as scale up training programs for workers in contingent jobs and expand access to social services for those who are jobless.

Authors: Lindsay A. Owens; David S. Pedulla
Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Labour economics; General Social Survey; Ideology; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Unemployment; Household income; Panel data; Politics
Title: Material Welfare and Changing Political Preferences: The Case of Support for Redistributive Social Policies
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that preferences for redistribution are malleable and correspond to predictions offered by a materialist perspective, with individuals wanting more redistribution when they experience unemployment or lose household income.
What_was_studied: Using new panel data from the General Social Survey, this study investigates how unemployment and income loss affect political preferences for redistribution among individuals in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs that cushion the negative effects of economic shocks and scale up support for those who have lost their jobs or experienced a decline in household income to ensure that no one is left behind.

Authors: Donald Von Eschen; Maurice Pinard; Jerome Kirk
Field: Positive economics; Class (set theory); Sociology; Alienation; Prestige; Direct action; Movement (music); Mass society; Trade union; Politics
Title: The Organizational Substructure of Disorderly Politics
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that membership in organizations with unincorporated goals or values increases rather than inhibits participation in direct action movements. Additionally, the data indicates that the existence of many such organizations is necessary for a strong direct action movement, and that these organizations can generate participation in both routine and disorderly politics simultaneously.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the theory of mass society and its application to direct action movements, specifically the Negro sit-in movement of the early 1960s, to determine if organizational membership drags people into routine politics while discouraging participation in direct action movements. The study uses a theoretical analysis of mass theory and data gathered from participants in the Negro sit-in movement to test the thesis that the theory needs severe modification.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings have important implications for addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality through direct action movements. Policymakers should prioritize the creation of an organizational substructure to support these movements, as well as revise mass theory to take into account the variable of unincorporation.

Field: Welfare; Social work; Political science; Peacetime; Liberal arts education; Curriculum; Economic growth; Professional development; Social Welfare; Vocational education
Title: Education for Social Welfare in the Postwar World—A Five-Year Curriculum Plan
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the demand for trained social welfare workers has increased due to the predicted 12 to 19 million job changes and the expanded public assistance program, and that there is a shortage of trained social work professionals to meet this demand. Additionally, the study found that veterans' rehabilitation and personnel problems are also factors that contribute to the need for trained social welfare workers.
What_was_studied: Academic research on the problems of reconversion in education, specifically vocational and professional training, and its impact on social work education and the need for trained social welfare workers in the post-war era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is recommended that policymakers prioritize funding for social work education and training programs to address the shortage of trained professionals and ensure that there are enough qualified social welfare workers to meet the increased demand in the post-war era.

Field: Sociological imagination; Work (electrical); Political science; Market participation; Comparative perspective; Eastern european; Economic growth
Title: Between equalization and marginalization : women working part-time in Europe and the United States of America
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Research found that women in Central and Eastern Europe are more likely to engage in part-time work than their Western counterparts, but with lower pay and few opportunities for career advancement.
What_was_studied: This study compares the prevalence and characteristics of part-time work across Central and Eastern European countries and explores how they differ from Western Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs that promote equal pay and career development opportunities for part-time workers in Central and Eastern Europe to address gender disparities and support sustainable economic growth.

Authors: Richard Rosenfeld; Steven F. Messner; Eric P. Baumer
Field: Social status; Actuarial science; Economics; Survey data collection; Poison control; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Voting; Homicide; Social capital; Structural equation modeling
Title: Social Capital and Homicide
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that depleted social capital contributes to high levels of homicide, and provides a promising basis for future research on the mechanisms linking social capital to crime at the macro level. The results indicate that social capital explains more than two-thirds of the effect of Southern regional location on homicide rates, net of other structural covariates and controlling for the reciprocal influence of homicide on social capital.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between crime rates and levels of social capital across populations, using a nationally representative sample of geographic areas and measuring social capital as a latent construct with aggregated voting and organizational membership data, and survey data on social trust.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant direct effect of social capital on homicide rates, policy makers should prioritize investments in social protection programs that strengthen social cohesion and community engagement, particularly in Southern regions with high levels of economic deprivation.

Field: Ethnic history; Political science; Value (ethics); Redress; Oppression; Citizenship; Population; Immigration; Criminology; Politics
Title: A Different “Dilemma”
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Japanese-Americans have achieved rapid recovery from dispossession of rights and property, incarceration during World War II, and indifference to requests for legal and administrative redress, with low rates of pathology. Additionally, the study found that religious affiliation and participation did not significantly influence the development of mobility and low pathology.
What_was_studied: This research reviews the history and sociological analysis of Japanese-Americans from 1848 to the present, focusing on their adaptations to unremitting oppression without legal or activist support, and examines the positive outcomes despite multiple incursions into their economic, political, educational, and household activities over the years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Japanese-Americans in achieving social mobility despite historical oppression, policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty by scaling up support for language schools, educational opportunities, and household activities to empower marginalized communities and reduce the burden of oppression on guiltless descendants of African immigrants.

Field: Finance; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Racial differences; Group membership; Social capital; Race (biology); Capital (economics)
Title: Depleting Capital? Race, Wealth and Informal Financial Assistance
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that middle- and upper-income black households were more likely to provide informal financial assistance, such as loans or gifts, to other members of their social networks compared to white households, even after controlling for income and other factors. This difference in financial assistance can account for part of the racial gap in wealth.
What_was_studied: Data from the 2007 Survey of Consumer Finances and the 2005 and 2007 Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) are used to demonstrate that middle- and upper-income blacks are more likely to provide informal financial assistance than their white counterparts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the racial wealth gap, policymakers should prioritize programs that promote access to formal financial institutions and resources for low-income households, particularly those in predominantly black neighborhoods.

Authors: Mark T. Berg; Callie Harbin Burt; Man-Kit Lei; Leslie Gordon Simons; Eric A. Stewart; Ronald L. Simons
Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Community health; Test (assessment); Social processes; African american; Sexual behavior; Sociological research; Sample (statistics); Multilevel model; Social psychology
Title: Neighborhood Social Processes and Adolescent Sexual Partnering: A Multilevel Appraisal of Anderson’s Player Hypothesis
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both contextual and indirect effects of neighborhood culture on sexual partnering exist, with significant differences in these effects according to neighborhood structural deprivation. Specifically, adolescents from neighborhoods with high levels of structural deprivation were more likely to engage in multiple sexual partnerships.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between neighborhood cultural processes and adolescent sexual-partnering behaviors among African American males in a multisite sample from the Family and Community Health Study, using data from 2015 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the indirect effects of neighborhood culture on adolescent sexual behavior and the exacerbating impact of structural deprivation, poverty-reduction policies must prioritize addressing neighborhood-level cultural mechanisms to scale up effective interventions and support healthy relationships among disadvantaged youth.

Authors: Jerry A. Jacobs; Ronnie J. Steinberg
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Wage; Compensation (psychology); State system; Male female; Face validity; Distribution (economics); Social psychology
Title: Compensating Differentials and the Male-Female Wage Gap: A Reply to Filer
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that a series of examples conflicting with face validity should lead one to question the compensating differentials model, and that wages do not reflect the marginal worker's preferences as the compensating differentials hypothesis suggests.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed hypotheses about the types of conditions workers might reasonably be expected to find undesirable in the New York State employment system, using extensive discussions with workers, managers, and union officials in diverse compensation practices in public- and private-sector employment contexts over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the compensation system to better reflect the actual preferences of workers, rather than relying solely on the assumptions of the compensating differentials model.

Field: Empirical research; Mobilization; Economics; Vulnerability; Collective action; Context (language use); Development economics; Function (engineering); Resource mobilization; Politics
Title: Resource Mobilization, Hardship, and Popular Collective Action in the West Bank
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that resource mobilization explanations were superior in explaining collective action compared to deprivation accounts, but direct repression increased the rate of Palestinian collective action while state vulnerability decreased it during the examined period.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the relationship between collective action and resource mobilization in the context of the West Bank during the 1976-85 period, using parametric statistical models and event history data on collective political events.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that resource mobilization is a stronger predictor of collective action in nonaffluent or crisis-ridden settings, policymakers should prioritize investing in economic resources and political opportunities for marginalized communities to scale up collective action and address intersectional poverty.

Field: Agriculture; Civilization; Poverty; Newspaper; Geography; Happiness; Estate; Waste disposal; Socioeconomics; Social order
Title: The Farm Women of France
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor farm home conditions, characterized by excessive workload, lack of conveniences and luxuries, and high rates of sickness and infant mortality, are prevalent in small-scale farming communities, particularly among women and children. These conditions are linked to higher levels of poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between farm home conditions and the well-being of women and children in small-scale farming communities, specifically in the cotton-tobacco belt of the United States during the 1930s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between farm home conditions and the well-being of women and children, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize initiatives aimed at improving these conditions, such as providing access to labor-saving machines, supporting cooperative farming systems, and investing in community-culture organizations and enterprises. By doing so, we can address the root causes of poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality in small-scale farming communities, ultimately improving the quality of life for these vulnerable populations.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Fundamental human needs; Urbanism; Urban history; Wickedness; Population; Psyche; Urban sociology; Acculturation
Title: The Present Status of the Spanish-Americans ofNew Mexico
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the disorganization of traditional understandings and the cultural marginality experienced by rural migrants are not inherent to urbanism but can be mitigated as urban societies mature, with residential mobility and cultural marginality decreasing over time.
What_was_studied: The analysis investigates the anarchic and unstable character attributed to urban life in general, particularly in the United States and Western Europe since the Renaissance, by examining the impact of the city on rural culture and the acculturation of rural migrants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing prevalence of chronic poverty in urban areas, policymakers should prioritize strategies that foster a more stable rural-to-urban transition, such as targeted support for rural migrants' acculturation and the development of urban spaces that promote social cohesion.

Authors: Edward S. Shihadeh; Raymond E. Barranco
Field: Public policy; Immigration policy; Dominance (economics); Manufacturing; Political science; Unemployment; Latino Population; Urban violence; Demographic economics; Development economics; Immigration
Title: Latino Employment and Black Violence: The Unintended Consequence of U.S. Immigration Policy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a positive link between Latino immigration and urban black violence, with increased Latino immigration leading to an increase in black unemployment, which in turn leads to an increase in black violence. Specifically, the study found that for every 10% increase in Latino immigration, there was a corresponding 2.5% increase in black violence.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of U.S. immigration policies after 1965 on the Latino population and its effect on low-skill job competition, and examined whether this increase in Latino immigration leads to an increase in black urban violence in the United States for the year 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing Latino immigration or improving job opportunities for low-skill workers could help reduce urban black violence. Specifically, policymakers should prioritize funding for job training programs and targeted hiring initiatives to support low-skill workers and reduce the competition for jobs in agriculture, manufacturing, and construction.

Field: Redlining; Index of dissimilarity; Racism; Sociology; Underclass; Minority group; Fair Housing Act; Population; Social science; Demographic economics; Social stratification
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Reflections on the Dimensions of Segregation
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: We found that African Americans were the only minority group to experience high levels of segregation on at least four of the five dimensions of segregation simultaneously, indicating a unique pattern of intense spatial isolation that we labeled ‘hypersegregation’. Furthermore, we discovered that hypersegregation was not limited to African Americans but also existed in Hispanic communities in two metropolitan areas by 2000.
What_was_studied: Nancy Denton and I published “The Dimensions of Residential Segregation” in 1988, during the early phases of a multi-year project funded by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. We studied trends, patterns, causes, and consequences of racial and ethnic residential segregation in the United States using 1980 census data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the unique nature of black segregation and its key role in perpetuating racial stratification. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize integrated housing policies that target hypersegregation, such as inclusionary zoning and affordable housing initiatives. By implementing these strategies, we can scale down segregation and expand access to resources and opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Social position; Social status; Psychology; Social group; Status inconsistency; Life chances; Master status; Social stratification; Social transformation; Social psychology
Title: Community and Consistency: The Ethnic Factor in Status Inconsistency
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The research found that individual status inconsistency does not adequately explain political processes and that an alternative explanation based on historical social marginality and persistence of ethnic group traditions is more appropriate. Additionally, the study found that individual status inconsistency is less prevalent among certain marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the concept of status inconsistency among individuals and its application in explaining political processes, particularly in the context of employment and historical social marginality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the historical social marginality of certain groups in order to better address issues of employment and political participation. Furthermore, they should fund research into alternative explanations for political processes that account for the persistence of ethnic group traditions.

Authors: James W. Ainsworth; Vincent J. Roscigno
Field: Sociology; Social inequality; Unemployment; Attendance; Reproduction (economics); Demographic economics; Status attainment; Tertiary sector of the economy; Social stratification; Economic growth; Vocational education
Title: Stratification, School-Work Linkages and Vocational Education
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there were significant disparities in vocational educational placement based on class, race, and gender, even after accounting for prior achievement and educational expectations. Vocational involvement increased the likelihood of dropping out of high school and decreased college attendance, with these negative outcomes more pronounced for non-whites and women.
What_was_studied: This article investigates class, race and gender inequality in high school vocational education between 2000 and 2018 and its impact on students' later educational and occupational trajectories using data from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disparities in vocational educational placement and their consequences for students' later educational and occupational trajectories, policy makers should prioritize addressing these issues by scaled-up support for high school vocational education to reduce dropout rates, expand access to college for all, and fund targeted interventions to increase the representation of underrepresented groups in well-paying jobs.

Field: Gender studies; Psychology; Voluntary association; Social change; Disengagement theory; Subject (documents); Research program; Church attendance; Social research; Rural sociology
Title: Aging and Religious Disaffiliation
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: All samples manifested substantial religious disaffiliation during adult life, with the model based in 'disengagement theory' receiving the greatest support. With advancing age, church attendance becomes increasingly less important as a source of voluntary affiliation among both well-to-do and poor men.
What_was_studied: The study examined patterns of lifetime church attendance and participation in voluntary associations among skid-row men and two samples of 'normal' respondents, contrasting models of aging and affiliation derived from previous research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial religious disaffiliation found among all samples, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that address the needs of marginalized populations, such as job training programs and mental health services, to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion.

Field: Social class; Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Social inequality; Political capital; Integrationism; Social stratification; Economic growth; Democracy; Politics
Title: Politics and Society in Latin America at the Start of the New Millennium
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the region is characterized by large and growing inequality, poverty, lack of security, and multiculturalism, with divisions among social classes and intersectional poverty being key issues.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the existing relationships between politics and society at the start of the twenty-first century in Latin America, a region characterized by its heterogeneity and addressed as a homogenous whole, focusing on politics as an extension of democracy, changing role of institutions, weakness of political capital, difficulties of representation, and new regionalist integrationism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is essential to prioritize and scale up policies addressing income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty in Latin America, while also addressing the root causes of inequality and social divisions.

Authors: Fabian T. Pfeffer; Florian R. Hertel
Field: Social class; Sociology; Social inequality; Class (computer programming); Destinations; Educational attainment; Social mobility; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: How Has Educational Expansion Shaped Social Mobility Trends in the United States
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there has been a modest but gradual increase in social mobility over the past century, this trend can almost exclusively be attributed to the compositional effect of increasing educational attainment among individuals from all backgrounds. Despite pronounced changes in the distribution of education, class inequality in education has remained stable, and class returns to education have not shown a consistent trend.
What_was_studied: This contribution assesses intergenerational social mobility trends in the United States from the 20th to early 21st centuries and determines the factors that contribute to these trends, with a focus on educational expansion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that an increase in educational attainment is a key driver of social mobility, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that expand access to quality education for all individuals, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds. This could involve targeted funding and support programs to address systemic barriers to education and improve the effectiveness of existing interventions.

Field: Split-ticket voting; Disapproval voting; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Voting behavior; Cleavage (politics); Development economics; First-past-the-post voting; Voting; Democracy
Title: Class Politics and Political Change in the United States, 1952–1992
primary_category: Class and voting; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while the realignment of the self-employed with the Republican Party is largely explained by class-related factors, professionals' realignment with the Democratic Party is a product of their increasingly liberal views of social issues. Also, prompted by higher levels of economic satisfaction and declining support for the welfare state, unskilled workers' historically high levels of support for Democratic candidates have eroded since the 1980 Presidential election.
What_was_studied: The study used National Election Studies data to investigate class-specific changes in voting behavior in presidential elections and analyze the causal mechanisms explaining the three most significant class-specific trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that class-related factors remain a critical aspect of vote choice in presidential elections. To advance debates over the changing relationship between class and political behavior, policymakers should prioritize research that distinguishes between 'class voting' as an outcome versus class factors as causal mechanisms of vote choice.

Authors: Hope Harvey; Kelley Fong; Kathryn Edin; Stefanie DeLuca
Field: Sociology; Marketing; Selection (genetic algorithm)
Title: Forever Homes and Temporary Stops: Housing Search Logics and Residential Selection
primary_category: Education access; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that higher-income families tend to engage in purposive searches for 'forever homes' that meet their long-term needs, while low-income parents adopt a logic of deferral and focus on immediate housing needs, leading to unequal residential attainment.
What_was_studied: This research examines the residential search processes of parents with young children in two metropolitan counties, using repeated, in-depth interviews to understand how economic resources shape residential attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of residential selection in determining children's educational access, neighborhood quality, and future economic prospects, policymakers should prioritize interventions that expand affordable housing options, fund targeted support for low-income families searching for homes, and revise zoning regulations to promote mixed-income communities.

Field: Demography; Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Propensity score matching; Occupational safety and health; Injury prevention; Eviction; Population; Poison control; Suicide prevention
Title: Eviction's Fallout: Housing, Hardship, and Health
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Eviction has negative effects on mothers in multiple domains, including more material hardship, higher rates of depression, worse health for themselves and their children, and more parenting stress. These negative effects persist at least two years after eviction.
What_was_studied: This study examines the consequences of involuntary displacement from housing on low-income urban mothers in the United States, using data from a national survey and applying two methods of propensity score analyses to compare outcomes between evicted and non-evicted mothers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative effects of eviction on low-income urban mothers, policymakers should prioritize expanding funding for housing assistance programs and developing alternative dispute resolution processes to reduce the number of evictions. Additionally, healthcare providers and social service agencies should scale up support services for families experiencing material hardship and mental health challenges after eviction.

Authors: Paul Gregg; Jan O. Jonsson; Lindsey Macmillan; Carina Mood
Field: Family income; Longitudinal study; Educational inequality; Ascription; Educational attainment; Earnings; Social mobility; Meritocracy; Demographic economics; Development economics
Title: The Role of Education for Intergenerational Income Mobility: A comparison of the United States, Great Britain, and Sweden
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both income elasticities and rank-order correlations were highest in the United States, followed by Britain, with Sweden being more equal. Surprisingly, the low income mobility in the US and Britain was not due to differences in educational inequality or returns to education, but rather because parental income is far more important for earnings at a given level of education than in Sweden.
What_was_studied: This research compares the association between family income and sons' earnings in the United States (National Longitudinal Study of Youth 1979), Britain (British Cohort Study 1970), and Sweden (Population Register Data, 1965 cohort) to determine whether differences in educational inequality and returns to qualifications can explain cross-country differences in income mobility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study suggests that policies aimed at reducing the influence of ascription on earnings, such as increasing access to education and addressing income inequality, are crucial for improving intergenerational income mobility in the US and Britain. Specifically, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that target the part of the parent-son association that is not mediated by educational attainment.

Field: Economics; Resource (biology); State (polity); Unemployment; Obligation; Incentive; Development economics; Communism; Resource mobilization; Politics
Title: Adverse Living Conditions, Grievances, and Political Protest after Communism: The Example of East Germany
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while resource deficits may initially decrease protest, they can ultimately increase it, particularly when combined with high levels of discontent and perceived state obligation to provide resources. This suggests that addressing resource deficits and managing public expectations are crucial for reducing social unrest.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of unemployment and resource deficits on protest behavior among 725 citizens in Leipzig, Germany in 1993, using a mixed-methods approach that integrated resource mobilization and opportunity structure theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unexpected indirect positive effect of resource deficits on protest, policymakers should prioritize addressing unemployment and resource inequalities, while also managing public expectations to prevent further social unrest. This may involve scaling up employment programs, expanding access to resources, and revising state obligations to ensure equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Government; Poverty; Slum; Overcrowding; Socioeconomics; Survey sampling; Race (biology); Renting
Title: Changing Patterns of Race and Housing: A Toledo Study
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the familiar pattern of race and housing may be undergoing some alteration with recent social developments such as white migration to the suburbs, urban renewal, improved economic status for the Negro, and government support of home buying, the post-war transition from renter to owner status for the Negro.
What_was_studied: A study of Negro housing in Toledo, Ohio tested some common assumptions about race and housing and discovered a post-war transition from renter to owner status for the Negro, exploring the means by which Negro families had financed purchases of homes, the quality of the homes, comparative prices, and the economic status of the Negro families concerned during the period 1955.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that government support of home buying programs could scale up access to owner status for low-income Negro families, potentially expanding their access to better housing and improving neighborhood conditions.
