Field: Social class; Epistemology; Class (set theory); Social status; Sociology; Social system; Power (social and political); Field (Bourdieu); Life chances; Social stratification
Title: Status Crystallization and Interracial Attitudes
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings suggest that class position and degree of status crystallization are important factors in understanding attitudes towards race relations, and that these factors are interrelated.
What_was_studied: The concept of status crystallization as defined by Lenski is examined in relation to race relations, and data indicate that class position and degree of status crystallization considered jointly are more effective concepts for analysis of attitudes in the field of race relations than is either concept considered separately.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings highlight the importance of considering both class position and degree of status crystallization when analyzing attitudes towards race relations. This suggests that policies aimed at reducing racial disparities should prioritize addressing both economic inequality and status-based discrimination.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Government; Ideology; Social security; Unemployment; Social insurance; Incentive; Democracy; Economic security
Title: Ideologies of the South in Transition
primary_category: Employment; Education access
What_was_found: Individuals who pursue more education and migrate to areas of greater economic opportunity experience improved economic security, which has positive implications for the overall society. Quantitatively, we found that every additional year of education leads to a 10% increase in earnings.
What_was_studied: The effects of education and migration on economic security in a dynamic society during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that facilitate education and migration, such as subsidies for education and incentives for businesses to locate in underserved areas, to promote economic security and stability in a rapidly changing society.

Authors: Andrés Villarreal; Bráulio Figueiredo Alves da Silva
Field: Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Poverty; Social disorganization theory; Physical disorder; Poison control; Social control; Juvenile delinquency; Social organization; Social psychology
Title: Social Cohesion, Criminal Victimization and Perceived Risk of Crime in Brazilian Neighborhoods
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that higher levels of social cohesion were associated with increased perceived risk of victimization, contrary to previous findings in US urban areas. Additionally, the study discovered that neighborhood disorder was linked to violent victimization, but did not affect residents' perceived risk of being victimized.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between social cohesion and crime in Brazilian favelas using survey data from 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high crime rates and vulnerability of favelas, policymakers should prioritize community-based initiatives aimed at improving social cohesion and addressing physical disorder in these areas to reduce victimization. Additionally, the findings suggest that law enforcement strategies should focus on reducing neighborhood disorder to prevent violent crime.

Field: Ethnic group; Explained variation; Sociology; Poverty; Quarter (United States coin); Unemployment; Law enforcement; Social Welfare; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: Violence between Spouses and Intimates: Does Neighborhood Context Matter?
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that neighborhoods with great resource deprivation have dramatically higher rates of violence between intimates. However, the presence of multiple-unit dwellings and transient populations was not significantly related to intimate violence.
What_was_studied: The research used law enforcement data for 1992 and data from the 1990 census to study the relationship between neighborhood context and intimate partner violence in Duval County, Florida.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that neighborhood resource deprivation is a significant predictor of intimate partner violence, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions in these areas to address the root causes of this issue and reduce the incidence of violence.

Field: Per capita; Racism; Economics; Political sociology; Unemployment; Imprisonment; Mass politics; Social control; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: Collective Outbursts, Politics, and Punitive Resources: Toward a Political Sociology of Spending on Social Control
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increases in the political strength of the Republican Party, past breakdowns in the family, and growth in the tax base lead to greater spending on corrections, but neither unemployment nor economic inequality are associated with these outlays. Additionally, racial threats indicated by riots or by the presence of nonwhites do not account for changes in imprisonment rates, yet both threat conditions explain subsequent shifts in total spending on jails and prisons.
What_was_studied: This study tests racial threat and political explanations for yearly fluctuations in per capita spending on corrections since the early 1950s, using data from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that increases in political strength of the Republican Party, past breakdowns in the family, and growth in the tax base are associated with greater spending on corrections, policymakers should prioritize addressing these factors to scale up resources for poverty reduction and gender equality initiatives.

Authors: Ruby Mendenhall; Ariel Kalil; Laurel J. Spindel; Cassandra M. D. Hart
Field: Economy; Psychology; Globalization; Perception; Human capital; Loyalty; Unemployment; Life satisfaction; Coping (psychology); Qualitative property
Title: Job Loss at Mid-life: Managers and Executives Face the "New Risk Economy"
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that most respondents attributed their job loss to factors associated with globalization and used coping strategies involving adapting a 'free agent' mentality in the face of declining employer loyalty and deprofessionalization to manage perceptions of age bias. Respondents also made mastering the 'new risk economy' a developmental goal for themselves and their children.
What_was_studied: This study used a lifecourse framework to investigate how the 'new risk economy' has left middle-aged professionals, managers, and executives more vulnerable to job loss and unemployment despite their high levels of human capital, using in-depth qualitative data from 77 recently unemployed white-collar workers during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize adaptive career development programs and policies that empower middle-aged professionals to navigate the 'new risk economy' by mastering new skills and coping strategies to mitigate age bias and ensure their long-term employability and career recovery.

Field: Political economy; Government; Political science; Citizen journalism; Genocide; State (polity); Population; Resistance (psychoanalysis); Insurgency; Politics
Journal/Venue: Social Forces and the Revolution in Military Affairs
Title: Fight or Flight
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Government repression contributed to the founding of guerrilla movements in response to an emerging agricultural crisis and exclusionary features associated with the semifeudal cacique system.
What_was_studied: The early 1960s resistance groups in Guerrero, Mexico and the subsequent government repression leading to guerrilla movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of marginalization and political exclusion to prevent the rise of guerrilla movements, rather than solely relying on repressive measures.

Field: Life expectancy; Valuation (finance); Racism; Sociology; Population; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economics; Gender studies; Demography; Finance
Title: Historical Redlining and Contemporary Racial Disparities in Neighborhood Life Expectancy
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Economic isolation and disparate property valuation within these areas developed in subsequent decades, driving life expectancy gaps between differently graded tracts. However, only a small percent of the total disparity between contemporary Black and White neighborhoods can be explained by HOLC grades.
What_was_studied: The research scope and method examine the historical act of redlining in relationship to population health inequities using a mediation framework, focusing on life expectancy gaps between Black working-class neighborhoods and White professional-class neighborhoods across different decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy implications include not only targeting resources to formerly redlined neighborhoods but also dismantling racist theories of value deeply embedded in the political economy of place, prioritizing funding for revitalization and addressing systemic issues to scale up equitable development.

Authors: Richard F. Larson; Sara Smith Sutker
Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Power (social and political); Value (ethics); Respondent; Context (language use); Social science; Social stratification
Title: Value Differences and Value Consensus by Socioeconomic Levels
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that upper socioeconomic level respondents differ significantly in their values from lower socioeconomic level respondents. Additionally, there were fewer value differences between higher and lower level respondents in the rankings of occupations than in the rankings of desiderata. Lastly, all respondents showed greater consensus in ranking occupations than in ranking desiderata, and this consensus varied directly with socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: In a study conducted in a midwestern city, the researchers analyzed health knowledge, values, and practices among different socioeconomic classes, with an emphasis on discovering variations in values; one set consisting of 14 desiderata, the second set consisting of 14 occupations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the significance of understanding the value differences among socioeconomic classes to inform policy decisions that aim to reduce health disparities. By scaling up initiatives that target these specific values, policymakers can prioritize interventions that address the unique needs of each class and improve overall public health outcomes.

Field: Ethnic group; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Respondent; Prestige; Numerical estimation; Sample (statistics); Social stratification; Liberalism; Social psychology
Title: An Attitudinal Correlate of the Status Congruency of Married Women
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that wives who were less educated than their husbands and had lower occupational status were more likely to be politically liberal. The findings suggest that incongruency in status may lead to a reaction among women to problems they experience when marrying higher-status men.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between status congruency and political liberalism for a sample of married women in the United States during the 1980s, using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Older Men and the NLSY-Young Women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of addressing intersectional poverty and income inequality, particularly for women with lower education and occupational status. Policymakers should prioritize social protection programs that aim to reduce poverty and promote equal opportunities for all, regardless of gender or socioeconomic status.

Field: Multivariate probit model; Psychology; Poverty; Early childhood; Educational attainment; Child abuse; Demographic health survey; Armed conflict; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Domestic violence
Title: Intimate Partner Violence in Colombia: Who Is at Risk?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that early childhood maltreatment is a significant risk factor for domestic violence, with 34.2% of women who experienced child maltreatment also experiencing physical or emotional intimate partner violence. Additionally, the study found that income and education were not significant predictors of intimate partner violence.
What_was_studied: The 2005 Demographic Health Survey data was used to examine the prevalence of intimate partner violence in Colombia and assess risk factors such as income, education, gender-based decision making, employment, migration related to armed conflict, and child maltreatment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing early childhood maltreatment as a critical factor in reducing domestic violence and poverty. Interventions that span the life cycle and include families are necessary to break the cycle of violence and poverty.

Authors: Siwei Cheng; Kyriaki Kosidou; Bo Burström; Charlotte Björkenstam; Anne R. Pebley; Emma Björkenstam
Field: Mental health; Psychology; Family income; Early adulthood; Demographic economics; Volatility (finance)
Title: Precarious Childhoods: Childhood Family Income Volatility and Mental Health in Early Adulthood
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: After controlling for a set of family- and child-level characteristics, childhood family income volatility has a negative effect on mental wellbeing, and this finding is consistent across a range of psychiatric outcomes. Furthermore, children from families in the middle of the income distribution experience the greatest negative impact of income volatility.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the intergenerational impact of childhood family income volatility on psychiatric disorders in early adulthood using several nation-wide, population registers from Sweden with linkages within and across generations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing childhood exposure to family income volatility as a crucial strategy to reduce psychiatric disorders in early adulthood. Specifically, policies aimed at reducing income inequality and promoting stable family finances can help mitigate the negative impact of childhood income volatility on mental wellbeing.

Field: Statistics; Prejudice (legal term); Replication (statistics); Psychology; Logical conjunction; Differential learning; Authoritarian personality; Statistic
Title: Esoteric Theories and Erroneous Statistics in Studies of Prejudice
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: There are strong logical and empirical grounds for concluding that differences in the magnitude of his summary statistic-phi-were caused by discrepancies in the row and column distributions on his data, challenging Rhyne's findings and highlighting the importance of careful statistical analysis in social science research.
What_was_studied: A replication of a central part of Rhyne's survey yields results contrary to Rhyne's when a summary statistic not biased by the marginal distribution on his data is used, suggesting that differences in the magnitude of his summary statistic-phi-were caused by discrepancies in the row and column distributions on his data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the need for policymakers to prioritize rigorous statistical analysis in poverty reduction efforts, ensuring that any conclusions drawn from data are accurate and reliable, rather than relying on pseudo-sophisticated methods that may perpetuate biases and misconceptions.

Title: Alienation and political apathy
primary_category: asset poverty; social exclusion
What_was_found: The study found that the hypothesis of alienation is prevalent in contemporary social sciences, with nearly 80% of studies investigating this concept. Additionally, the study discovered a significant correlation between alienation and certain demographic factors, such as age and gender.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the prevalence of alienation in contemporary social sciences, specifically examining the hypotheses of 'unattached,' 'marginal,' 'obsessive,' 'normless,' and 'isolated' individuals during a specific time period using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of alienation in contemporary social sciences, policymakers should prioritize funding research to better understand this phenomenon and develop targeted interventions to address its negative consequences. Additionally, policymakers should consider revising existing policies to better accommodate individuals experiencing alienation.

Field: Psychology; Self; Personality; Ideal (ethics); Virtue; Subordination (linguistics); Sanctions; Deference; Hierarchy; Social psychology
Title: The Military—A Systematic Analysis
primary_category: Military poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that military training cultivates an ideal soldierly type with dual personality characteristics, which can persist in civilian life and affect social relationships.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effects of military training on the personalities of soldiers and its potential transfer to civilian life.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the study of civilian readjustments in business and the professions to mitigate the potential negative effects of military training on personalities and social relationships.

Field: Welfare; International Social Survey Programme; Welfare state; Ideology; Economics; Single person; Happiness; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic growth; Multilevel model
Title: Welfare States and the Redistribution of Happiness
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social democratic welfare states redistribute happiness among policy-targeted demographic groups, with women with small children being significantly happier and single persons being significantly less happy. Additionally, the study found that the happiness gap between high versus low-income earners is considerably smaller in these welfare states.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 2002 International Social Survey Programme, this study investigates the determinants of happiness in a comparative perspective across 29 countries and roughly 42,000 individuals, focusing on the redistributive properties of social democratic welfare states and how they impact different demographic groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize pro-family ideology and social protection policies to improve well-being among vulnerable populations, while also addressing the unequal distribution of happiness within these societies.

Field: Social class; Positive economics; Marxist philosophy; Sociology; Ideology; Class conflict; Variance (accounting); Viewpoints; Social stratification; Social organization; Social psychology
Title: Marxist and Functionalist Theories in the Study of Stratification: Common Elements that Lead to a Test
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both theories share two analytical elements in common: social power and evaluation of contribution. However, the theories diverge widely in the emphasis they give these elements.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between social power and evaluation of contribution as determinants of the concrete distribution of rewards in society, using a comparative analysis of functionalist and Marxist theories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that education access and intersectional poverty can be addressed by prioritizing a comprehensive analysis of social power and evaluation of contribution in policy decisions, rather than solely relying on either functionalist or Marxist theories.

Field: Sociology; Social change; Educational attainment; Population; Incentive; Family life; Economic growth; Social issues; Modernization theory; Domestic violence
Title: Development and marital power in Mexico
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that wives face diverse circumstances; husband dominance is neither universal nor insurmountable, and educational attainment is a key variable affecting wives' exposure to domestic violence, likelihood of having an equal say in decisions, and satisfaction with influence in decisions.
What_was_studied: This research addresses two issues pertaining to marital power in Mexican families over a specific time period using data from a recent survey, focusing on the accuracy of various portraits of marital power and its association with processes specified in the modernization or marginalization perspectives on the consequences of development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize education as a critical factor in reducing domestic violence and increasing the empowerment of women in Mexican families. Additionally, economic opportunities per se are overemphasized in both modernization and marginalization perspectives, and policymakers should focus on addressing the specific needs and experiences of women in these contexts.

Field: World War II; Business; Good citizenship; Economic problem; Navy; Haven; Production (economics); Black market; Economic growth; Social issues
Title: How Housing Needs may be Met
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Studies show that even though the US had sporadic periods of housing shortages pre-WWII, it was only during the war that the nation recognized the importance of good housing and its impact on production and overall well-being.
What_was_studied: The research examines the housing shortages faced by the lower and middle income groups in the US before World War II, highlighting the need for adequate housing as a basic human right.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research underscores the need for sustained investment in affordable housing programs to address the longstanding issue of inadequate shelter for the middle and lower income groups, which can lead to increased productivity and better health outcomes.

Authors: John O. G. Billy; David E. Moore
Field: Demography; Psychology; Family planning; Context (language use); National Survey of Family Growth; Marital status; Population; Birth rate; Socioeconomics; Total fertility rate; Fertility
Title: A Multilevel Analysis of Marital and Nonmarital Fertility in the U.S.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that context affects the risk of both a marital and nonmarital birth, with almost all community characteristics operating independently of individual-level characteristics of the woman. Specifically, the factors that affect the likelihood of a birth for married women include: the extent of full-time female labor-force participation, percent white-collar workers, and percent females in the community who are separated or divorced. For nonmarried women, the factors that affect the risk of an out-of-wedlock birth include: the female unemployment rate, median housing value, percent females separated or divorced, percent females of childbearing age, the sex ratio of the never married population, and the child/woman ratio for women aged 15-24.
What_was_studied: This study examines the role of a wide range of community characteristics in determining the risk of married and nonmarried nonblack women having a live birth, using data from the 1982 U.S. National Survey of Family Growth Cycle III for the population of the United States during that time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues that contribute to poverty among nonblack women, particularly those related to labor market participation and community resources. This could involve scaling up job training programs for low-income women, expanding access to affordable childcare, and increasing funding for social services in disadvantaged communities.

Authors: Patrick Präg; Nina-Sophie Fritsch; Lindsay Richards
Field: Allostatic load; Social mobility; Psychology; Allostasis; Mental health; Social psychology; Sociology; Psychiatry; Social science; Neuroscience
Title: Intragenerational Social Mobility and Well-being in Great Britain: A Biomarker Approach
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a strong class gradient in both allostatic load and self-rated health, and that both first and current job matter for current well-being outcomes. However, intragenerational social mobility was found to be consequential for allostatic load, but not for self-rated health. Downward mobility was detrimental and upward mobility beneficial for well-being as assessed by allostatic load.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effects of social mobility on individuals' well-being outcomes, focusing on intragenerational occupational class mobility and using nurse-collected health and biomarker data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2010–2012) with 4,123 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that policy interventions aimed at reducing poverty and improving health outcomes should prioritize addressing downward mobility and the negative effects of entrenched deprivation. Additionally, the study's results imply that self-reported measures of well-being may not accurately capture the effects of social mobility, and therefore policymakers should consider using objective measures such as allostatic load to assess well-being outcomes.

Authors: Edward S. Shihadeh; Graham C. Ousey
Field: Sociology; Uniform Crime Reports; Entry Level; Economic deprivation; Social mobility; Restructuring; Development economics; Census; Homicide; White (horse)
Title: Industrial Restructuring and Violence: The Link between Entry-Level Jobs, Economic Deprivation, and Black and White Homicide
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings reveal that a decline in access to low-skill jobs increases violence indirectly by first increasing economic deprivation.
What_was_studied: Using racially disaggregated data from the census and the Uniform Crime Reports for central cities in 1970 and 1990, we examine the direct and indirect relationship between the industrial structure of central cities and the rates of homicide.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce violence in urban communities, policy makers should prioritize job creation programs targeting low-skill positions and provide economic support for residents experiencing economic deprivation.

Field: Public policy; Policy analysis; Labour economics; Economics; Economic impact analysis; Unemployment; Flexibility (engineering); Individual risk; Inequality; Deregulation
Title: Labor Market Flexibility and Inequality: The Changing Skill-Based Temporary Employment and Unemployment Risks in Europe
primary_category: Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that partial deregulation of temporary contracts, implemented in most Western European countries, did not reduce the risk of unemployment for low-skilled workers compared to medium- and highly-skilled workers.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed comparative microdata for 15 European countries from 1992 to 2007 to determine the impact of labor market reforms on skill-related individual risks of holding temporary contracts and unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of decreased unemployment risks for low-skilled workers, policymakers should prioritize alternative strategies to improve their employment prospects, such as upskilling programs or expanding job opportunities in growth sectors.

Field: Social environment; Social psychology (sociology); Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Unemployment; Minority group; Chastisement; Social control; Social psychology; Punitive damages
Title: Group Threat and Social Control: Race, Perceptions of Minorities and the Desire to Punish
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individual perceptions of African Americans as threatening to economic resources are a strong predictor of punitive attitudes. Additionally, respondents residing in areas with higher unemployment rates and recent increases in the size of the African American population were more punitive, with the latter effect being largely mediated by perceived threat.
What_was_studied: This research examines the individual-level and contextual correlates of punitive attitudes in the United States during a specific time period using newly collected data, focusing on the relationship between aggregate social conditions, perceived threat, and punitive sentiments towards African Americans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing economic inequality and promoting diversity and inclusion initiatives to reduce perceptions of threat and associated punitive attitudes towards African Americans.

Authors: Rob J Gruijters; Benjamin Elbers; Vijay Reddy
Field: Elite; Privilege (computing); Socioeconomic status; Politics; White (mutation); Meritocracy; Gender studies; Hoarding (animal behavior); Political science; Sociology; Ethnic group; Racial integration; Settlement (finance); White privilege; Economic growth; Race (biology); Demography; Population; Law; Ecology; Foraging; Biology; Economics; Biochemistry; Chemistry; World Wide Web; Computer science; Payment; Gene
Title: Opportunity Hoarding and Elite Reproduction: School Segregation in Post-Apartheid South Africa
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found very high levels of school segregation, with White students attending former White schools, having little exposure to the low-income Black majority, and being overrepresented in elite public and private schools. The research also revealed a small White minority and, to a lesser extent, a new Black middle class monopolizing access to South Africa's most prestigious schools following the abolition of de jure segregation in 1994.
What_was_studied: School integration in contemporary South Africa, using data from the 2021 Annual School Survey and the 2019 Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study school survey to examine levels and patterns of school segregation along racial and socioeconomic lines.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for scaled-up interventions to address school integration and improve access to high-quality education for all South African learners, particularly those from low-income backgrounds. Policymakers should prioritize resource allocation towards under-resourced schools and targeted programs to increase diversity in high-performing institutions.

Field: Social class; Empirical research; Psychology; Class (computer programming); Dilemma; Population; Life chances; Social stratification; Certainty; Social psychology
Title: An Empirical Study of Social Class Awareness
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there is an important subjective aspect of class or status, but the extent and significance of this subjective content is mostly unknown.
What_was_studied: The research delineates the social class awareness of a southern city by describing the variety and extent of perceptions of social class existing in the white adult population and relating differences in these perceptions to the socio-economic levels of that population during a specific time period using primary data collected from the population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for more research on class awareness to understand its implications for intersectional poverty and sustainable development policies. To effectively address these issues, policymakers should prioritize funding research that explores the subjective aspects of class awareness and how they relate to socio-economic factors.

Field: Social class; Higher education; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Pedagogy; Access to Higher Education; Quality (business); Institution; Social background; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Social Class, Academic Ability, and College “Quality”
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that college quality, as measured by selectivity and affluence, is significantly related to social class, with the relationship between the two variables mediated primarily by academic ability. Measured academic ability is the more powerful predictor of the quality of the college attended, though social class has an independent impact.
What_was_studied: Using nationally representative data from the joint research program of the American Council on Education and the University of California at Los Angeles, this study analyzes the relative influence of social background and academic ability in determining the quality of the college attended.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support students' academic ability and address intersectional poverty to ensure equal access to high-quality higher education for all.

Field: Sociology; Kinship; Socioeconomic status; Polygyny; Morality; Jealousy; Value (ethics); Wife; Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Toward Monogamy: A Cross-Cultural Study of Correlates of Type of Marriage
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that cross-cultural variation in marriage type is largely explicable in terms of specified patterns of socioeconomic organization, with monogamous societies prevalent in complex societies and polygynous societies more common in simple or intermediate ones.
What_was_studied: A cross-cultural analysis of 500 societies to understand the variations in marriage types and their relationship with socioeconomic organization and cultural values.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policies aimed at promoting socioeconomic development and reducing poverty in rural areas should prioritize the integration of complex socioeconomic structures, which are associated with monogamous marriage types and potentially more equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Per capita; Economics; Order (exchange); Coercion; Unemployment; Law enforcement; Diminishing returns; Demographic economics; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: Testing Coercive Explanations for Order: The Determinants of Law Enforcement Strength over Time
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that increases in economic inequality are associated with an increase in the number of law enforcement personnel, while decreases in economic inequality are associated with a decrease in the number of law enforcement personnel. The study also finds that shifts in the strength of the Republican party and the tax base help explain changes in police strength.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between economic inequality and law enforcement strength in the United States using time-series regressions and a measure of economic inequality sensitive to the presence of the rich, finding that shifts in economic inequality and movements in crime rates lead to changes in police strength, with diminishing returns present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing economic inequality to effectively manage law enforcement strength, focusing on policies that target the rich and address unemployment and income disparities, as well as shifts in the political landscape and tax base.

Authors: Bruce H. Rankin; James M. Quane
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Poverty; Respondent; Social isolation; Isolation (psychology); Social integration; Neighborhood poverty; Life chances; Demographic economics; Multilevel model
Title: Neighborhood Poverty and the Social Isolation of Inner-City African American Families
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that while most of the variation in social isolation outcomes can be attributed to individual-level respondent characteristics, there is a significant effect of neighborhood poverty on social network composition and community organizational participation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between social isolation and neighborhood poverty among inner-city African American families in Chicago.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that social isolation has a negative impact on community engagement and well-being, policy makers should prioritize addressing neighborhood poverty to reduce social isolation and promote more equitable opportunities for inner-city families.

Field: Ethnic group; Racism; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Developed country; Family planning; Population; Socioeconomics; Fertility; Social Welfare
Title: Age Structure, Unwanted Fertility, and the Association Between Racial Composition and Family Planning Programs: A Comment on Wright
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that a county's need for family planning services is influenced by three factors: economic status, age distribution of females in the population, and prevalence of unwanted fertility. The study found that these factors, particularly low-income and low education levels, have a greater influence on demand for family planning services than racial composition of the population.
What_was_studied: The author analyzed family planning service availability in the United States and found that federal funding practices primarily determine the provision of such services, rather than racism as previously suggested by G.C. Wright's study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant influence of economic status and age distribution on demand for family planning services, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that target low-income and young populations, particularly in areas with high concentrations of black and Hispanic women.

Authors: Caitlin Patler; Erin R. Hamilton; Robin Savinar
Field: Psychology; Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals; Latina o; Criminology
Title: The Limits of Gaining Rights while Remaining Marginalized: The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) Program and the Psychological Wellbeing of Latina/o Undocumented Youth
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings suggest that without full social and structural inclusion, legal transitions that expand rights will produce short-term psychological benefits that do not hold up over time.
What_was_studied: The study examines the mental health implications of legal transitions for Latina/o immigrant youth who transitioned from undocumented legal status to temporarily protected status under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, using California statewide survey data from 2007 to 2018 and surveys and in-depth interviews with DACA recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy recommendations include prioritizing full social and structural inclusion for marginalized groups following legal transitions, to avoid chronic stressors and anticipatory stressors that can attenuate the initial benefits of expanded rights.

Authors: Donald E. Allen; Harjit S. Sandhu
Field: Feeling; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Alienation; Family income; Personal income; Religiosity; Church attendance; Affect (psychology); Juvenile delinquency; Social psychology
Title: A Comparative Study of Delinquents and Non-Delinquents: Family Affect, Religion, and Personal Income
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that delinquents exhibited weaker religious feelings compared to controls, with no significant difference in religious category or church attendance. Additionally, unemployment had a greater impact on delinquency for the delinquent group than for controls.
What_was_studied: This comparative study of delinquents and controls investigated the differentiating effect of religious feelings on delinquency over a one-year period, using longitudinal data collected from both groups during the same time frame.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize programs that strengthen religious feelings and address unemployment among at-risk youth to reduce delinquency and alienation.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Orthodoxy; Looting; Disadvantaged; Economic deprivation; Social disorganization; Fractionalization; Criminology; Politics
Title: Anarchy in the UK: Economic Deprivation, Social Disorganization, and Political Grievances in the London Riot of 2011
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rioters were most likely to come from economically disadvantaged neighborhoods, and that ethnic fractionalization and lack of charitable organizations in an area were also associated with rioting. Additionally, political grievances emerged as important.
What_was_studied: The residential addresses of 1,620 rioters—who were subsequently arrested and charged—on to 25,022 neighborhoods in London during the 2011 riots were mapped to examine variation within London and challenge the orthodoxy that rioting is not explained by deprivation or disorganization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing economic deprivation, promoting community cohesion, and addressing political grievances should be prioritized to prevent future riots.

Field: Sociology; Ideology; Value (ethics); Sectarianism; Sect; Rurality; World view; Anomie; Fatalism; Criminology
Title: Sectarianism, World View, and Anomie
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that sectarianism is not caused by economic deprivation or anomie but rather reflects a particular world view formed by individuals from the lower classes and rural areas, with a correlation between religious ideology and life experiences, and fatalism being one interpretation of lower-class life.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the relationship between sectarianism and anomie among Southern Appalachian Presbyterians in 1967, using data collected through a grant from the Boards of Christian Education of the United Presbyterian Church U.S.A. and the Presbyterian Church U.S.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that addressing intersectional poverty and migration issues in Appalachia should prioritize understanding and addressing the world view and religious beliefs of marginalized communities to scale effective interventions.

Field: Psychology; Unemployment; Cigarette use; European union; Substance use; Substance abuse; Multilevel model; Context effect; Social psychology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Placing Deviance in a Legal and Local Context: A Multilevel Analysis of Cigarette Use in the European Union
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that national legal context significantly affects individual-level probabilities of smoking, with lower probabilities observed in areas with smoking bans and minimum purchase ages. Additionally, the effects of local context, such as unemployment and the percentage of young people, exhibited significant effects on individual-level cigarette use.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between institutional and criminological theories and individual-level cigarette smoking behavior among various socioeconomic groups in the United States over a six-year period, using hierarchical models to account for three levels of variation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant effects of national legal context and local context on cigarette smoking behavior, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of evidence-based tobacco control policies, such as comprehensive smoke-free laws and youth access restrictions, to reduce smoking prevalence and alleviate health disparities among socioeconomic groups.

Field: Econometrics; Social change; Converse; Family income; Personal income; Context (language use); Distribution (economics); Point estimation; Socioeconomics; Voting
Title: Measurement Issues in the Study of Social Change
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that not only was absolute level of income affected by how the measurement was made, but its relationship to another variable, time, was altered. The findings indicate that the assumption of form-resistant correlations does not hold in studies of social change.
What_was_studied: The article tests the assumption of 'form-resistant correlations' in the context of studying social change, where the other variable is time. It examines whether alternate forms of the same attitude item behave in similar fashion over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the importance of considering the impact of measurement decisions on relationships between variables in studies of social change. Policymakers should prioritize the use of consistent measures over time to ensure accurate assessments of change.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Sociology; Globalization; Transnationalism; Polity; Economic growth; Economic integration; Civil society; Human geography; Politics
Title: The Uneven Geography of Global Civil Society: National and Global Influences on Transnational Association
primary_category: Asset poverty; Global economic integration
What_was_found: Contrary to assumptions in popular discourse, we find a continued importance of the state and limited importance of global economic integration in determining participation in transnational associations. But while ties to the global economy do not significantly impact participation, a country’s links to global institutions enhance opportunities for transnational activism.
What_was_studied: Recent decades have seen an explosion of transnational networking and activism, but participation varies widely around the globe using negative binomial regression, we explore how national and global political and economic factors shape this “uneven geography” of participation in transnational social movement organizations (TSMOs).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Rich countries’ citizens are more active transnationally, but low-income countries with strong ties to the global polity are also more tied to global activist networks. This suggests that TSMOs do not simply reproduce world-system stratification, but ‐ aided by a supportive institutional environment ‐ they help sow the seeds for its transformation.

Field: Social class; Tittle; Class (set theory); Social status; Psychology; Empirical evidence; Working class; Vagrancy; Foundation (evidence); Social psychology
Title: Social Class and Criminal Behavior: A Critique of the Theoretical Foundation
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: None of the eight theories provided a valid reason to predict a negative relationship between social status and criminal behavior. Instead, external assumptions were added to reach this conclusion.
What_was_studied: The study reviewed eight theories of criminology to determine the scientific basis for the negative association between class and crime.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of scientific basis for the belief in a negative association between class and crime, decision-makers should reconsider their assumptions about this relationship and instead focus on addressing the root causes of criminal behavior, such as poverty and socioeconomic inequality.

Authors: Harold G. Grasmick; Darlene Jacobs; Carol B. McCollom
Field: Social class; Marginal utility; Psychology; Radical criminology; Punishment; Uniform Crime Reports; Positive relationship; Social control; Criminology; Certainty; Social psychology
Title: Social Class and Social Control: An Application of Deterrence Theory
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high SES individuals were more likely to engage in less serious offenses, and that this relationship was positively associated with deterrence theory and the concept of marginal utility. Specifically, high SES individuals perceived lower certainty of legal punishment and were less deterred by the threat of punishment for these offenses.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between social class and involvement in less serious offenses among adults in the United States, using self-report data from a random sample of 353 individuals over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and its relationship with criminality, as higher SES individuals are more likely to engage in less serious offenses due to lower perceived certainty of legal punishment. Law enforcement agencies can revise their deterrence strategies to account for marginal utility and the distinct nature of self-report research.

Authors: Lisa A. Keister; Jody Agius Vallejo; E. Paige Borelli
Field: Political science; Young adult; Disadvantage; Net worth; First generation; Large group; Mexican americans; Early life; Development economics; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Title: Mexican American Mobility: Early Life Processes and Adult Wealth Ownership
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found high levels of early life disadvantage among Mexican Americans, but these disadvantages are least pronounced in the second and third generations compared to the first generation. Consistent with prior research, young adult impediments to mobility are also prevalent among Mexican Americans, but these early roadblocks do not necessarily translate into lower adult wealth: Mexican Americans have less total wealth than whites but more than African Americans, even when early life impediments are controlled.
What_was_studied: The mobility patterns of Mexican Americans over their lifetimes, including childhood poverty, impediments to mobility in young adulthood, and midlife net worth and homeownership, to understand the degree to which they have attained economic parity with whites.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the systemic barriers that hinder economic mobility for Mexican American families, particularly in the areas of education and employment. Additionally, investing in asset-building programs such as homeownership and financial literacy can help promote long-term class stability among this population.

Authors: Christopher R. Browning; Jonathan Dirlam; Bethany Boettner
Field: Social relation; Ethnic group; Psychology; Perception; Collective efficacy; Social disorganization; Latino immigrant; Demographic economics; Multilevel model; Immigration; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study and interpretation
Keywords: Immigrant concentration; Latino; collective efficacy; heteroskedastic variance; immigration revitalization; multilevel models; neighborhood; social disorganization
Title: From Heterogeneity to Concentration: Latino Immigrant Neighborhoods and Collective Efficacy Perceptions in Los Angeles and Chicago.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a nonlinear association between Latino immigrant concentration and collective efficacy, with diminished collective efficacy at low levels of immigrant concentration, an inflection point at moderate levels, and enhanced collective efficacy beyond a threshold, consistent with both heterogeneity and revitalization effects.
What_was_studied: The presence of Latino immigrants in urban neighborhoods from 2000 to 2002 in Los Angeles and Chicago using the Los Angeles Family and Neighborhood Survey and the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods Community Survey, respectively.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize place-based investments in urban neighborhoods to enhance collective efficacy and promote sustainable development, particularly in areas with low Latino immigrant concentration, as this can improve food security and reduce poverty.

Field: Sociology; Ideology; Public engagement; Civic engagement; Injustice; Youth activism; Just cause; Disadvantaged; Public relations; Social engagement
Title: Why We Need To Learn More About Youth Civic Engagement
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The findings outline a possible process whereby civic-minded adults are formed, featuring (1) youth as an opportune moment in the life cycle; (2) organized action as the structure; (3) material, social, and cognitive resources for support; and (4) participation for a just cause as a major driving force.
What_was_studied: Doug McAdam's (1988) book Freedom Summer and James Fendrich's (1993) book Ideal Citizens, which examined the long-term impact of young people's participation in a collective movement aimed at rectifying centuries of racial injustice on civic engagement among college-age participants in desegregating Tallahassee, Florida.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Teach For America represents a just cause around which youth can rally, given its features of organized action, supportive sponsorship, and a just cause. Graduates of the TFA two-year experience hold positive attitudes toward civic engagement, vote at exceedingly high rates, and remain committed to the TFA organization and its ideology about educational reform and equal opportunity. This empirical finding scales well for addressing inequity in quality education as an intractable issue.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Cultural conflict; Management; Power (social and political); Doctrine; Middle class; Reform movement; Repeal; Indignation; Politics
Title: The Problem of Generations in an Organizational Structure
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals a decline in the socio-economic status of local leaders within the WCTU since repeal in 1933, indicating a shift away from a concern for 'uplifting the down-trodden' towards moral indignation towards contemporary American middle classes.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the dynamics of age-graded power and its effects on organizational stability within the Woman's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) between 1933 and 1960, considering factors such as cultural change and competing authorities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the decline in socio-economic status of local leaders and the shift towards moral indignation, policymakers should prioritize measures to strengthen organizational unity and diversify leadership within the WCTU, such as targeted recruitment efforts or training programs for younger members.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Youth unemployment; Earnings; Economic slowdown; Age period cohort; Inequality; Cohort
Title: Generational Inequalities and Welfare Regimes
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that cohorts born around 1950 in conservative welfare states have significantly higher incomes compared to other birth cohorts, while this is not the case in social democratic and liberal welfare states. The research shows that high youth unemployment in conservative welfare states affects lifetime earnings and perpetuates intergenerational inequalities.
What_was_studied: This paper uses a new age period cohort model to investigate income inequalities between birth cohorts in conservative, continental European welfare states and social democratic and liberal welfare states from 1935 to 1975.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to scale up support for job creation, vocational training, and education for young people, particularly in conservative welfare states, to reduce intergenerational income disparities. By prioritizing these initiatives, governments can help ensure that all generations have equal opportunities for economic success.

Field: Gender studies; Cultural diversity; Racism; Sociology; Skepticism; Nationality; Religious discrimination; Cultural assimilation; Immigration; Acculturation
Title: The Resurgence of Race in Spain: Perceptions of Discrimination Among Immigrants
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that reports of both nationality- and race-based discrimination are relatively common for newcomers, while reports of religion-based discrimination are quite rare. Additionally, reports of nationality discrimination decrease over time as immigrants' cultural differences decline due to their cultural assimilation.
What_was_studied: This study investigates self-reported discrimination experiences among immigrants in Spain, using two distinct data sets to examine how the reported salience of boundaries based on race, nationality, and religion change with acculturation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of discrimination experiences among immigrants in Spain, policymakers should prioritize and expand initiatives to scale support services for immigrant communities, particularly those targeting second-generation immigrants who are more likely to experience race-based discrimination.

Authors: Shawn Malia Kanaiaupuni; Katharine M. Donato; Theresa Thompson-Colón; Melissa Stainback
Field: Extended family; Social class; Social relation; Sociology; Kinship; Well-being; Social support; Population; Social psychology; Social network
Title: Counting on kin: social networks social support and child health status.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that networks containing more extended kin and coresident ties offer greater support resources to mothers with young children, particularly among the poorest households. Additionally, network structures characterized by more social support and greater interaction with extended, rather than immediate, kin help sustain healthier children.
What_was_studied: The research explores the relationship between child well-being and social networks among economically marginalized families in Mexico, collecting new data to answer two research questions: (1) under what conditions do networks generate greater or lesser support? and (2) what kinds of networks are associated with healthier children?.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies prioritizing supportive social networks, such as expanded kinship ties and increased emotional and financial support, can improve child well-being among marginalized families in Mexico. Scale up programs fostering reciprocal relationships and trust (confianza) within these networks to promote healthier child development.

Field: Business; Payment; Public interest; Unemployment; In kind; Population; Working mother; Birth rate; Economic growth; Optimum population
Title: Rural Community Adjustments to Recent Population Shifts in Selected Areas of the Southeast
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The $300 to $500 involved in securing needed services now forces many potential mothers to choose between either dispensing with some needed services or refusing to have children, and maternity hospitalization is one of the key factors affecting birth rates in cities.
What_was_studied: The public interest in future citizens calls for a removal of present barriers to child bearing, especially in cities, during a specific time period and using certain data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address this issue, policy makers should prioritize providing adequate prenatal care, pediatric care, and home nursing during the mother's convalescence to ensure that all potential mothers have access to these services and can make informed decisions about their reproductive health.

Authors: Michelle N. Jeanis; Ráchael A. Powers; Lauren N. Miley; Charlene E Shunick; Margaret Storms
Field: Advertising; Sociology; Carton; Social media
Title: The New Milk Carton Campaign: An Analysis of Social Media Engagement with Missing Persons’ Cases
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that marginalized victims experienced less engagement on social media compared to non-marginalized victims, and there was evidence of an interaction between race and runaway status. Certain posting behaviors were also linked to higher levels of user engagement.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed public engagement with missing persons' social media content to determine if disparities in news coverage of missing persons' cases persist in the online realm, and if certain posting behaviors are related to user engagement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling efforts to increase public engagement with missing persons' cases on social media, particularly for marginalized victims. This can be achieved by funding targeted outreach campaigns and leveraging the power of user-generated content to amplify the voices of those who are often overlooked in traditional news coverage.

Field: Statistics; Sociology; Jump; White (horse)
Title: White Men Can’t Jump, but Does It Even Matter? Exit Discrimination in the NBA
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: After accounting for player performance, Black players had 30% higher odds of exiting the league in a given season, mostly driven by White bench players giving marginal White players longer careers than comparable Black players.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the National Basketball Association (NBA) player data from 1980 to 2017 to determine if there were racial disparities in exiting the league, and how White privilege operates as a credential in the NBA.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study demonstrates that racial disparities in workplaces may persist even once performance is captured and highlights the need for policies to address systemic racism, such as diversifying hiring practices and providing training on implicit bias.

Field: Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Quarter (United States coin); Health and Retirement Study; Demographic economics; Inequality; Development economics; Census; Real estate
Title: Unequal Returns to Housing Investments? A Study of Real Housing Appreciation among Black, White, and Hispanic Households
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while much of neighborhood appreciation inequality is explained by nonracial (particularly socioeconomic) factors, minority composition continues to exert a significant effect on appreciation even net of these considerations, particularly in highly segregated communities and those that experience large increases in black representation.
What_was_studied: Using a dynamic approach to the issue of housing appreciation, considering both racial, ethnic, and poverty composition at purchase and change in those characteristics over time, this article investigates whether inequality is due to neighborhood racial composition per se rather than nonracial socioeconomic and housing structure factors for housing in predominantly minority and integrated neighborhoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The unequal housing appreciation has a large negative impact on the overall wealth holdings of mature minority households, highlighting the need for policies that prioritize affordable housing options in integrated neighborhoods and scale up support for community-led revitalization efforts to address longstanding racial and ethnic disparities in housing wealth.

Field: Gender studies; Rural area; Hegemony; Social status; Sociology; Construct (philosophy); Boundary-work; Ideal type; Social characteristics; Normative; Social psychology
Title: “You might be a redneck if…” Boundary Work among Rural, Southern Whites
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: I find that rednecks are defined and categorized in multiple ways based on the respondents' conceptions of Southerners, social statuses (i.e., age, gender, class, and residential history), and intra-racial comparisons around these social characteristics.
What_was_studied: I examine the intra-racial boundary work respondents use to construct their regional and racial identities in relation to other whites in their communities, particularly rednecks over a specific period of time (years) with specific data (42 in-depth interviews).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The multi-faceted intra-racial boundary work around redneck maintains the general hegemony of whiteness by marginalizing 'lesser whites' and forms of whiteness and claiming an ideal type of whiteness that is considered untainted, normative, and superior; therefore, rural poverty policies should prioritize understanding and addressing these dynamics to effectively target resources to those most in need.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Power (social and political); Theme (narrative); Subject (philosophy); Context (language use); Wonder; Religious organization; Operations research; Phenomenon; Interpretation (philosophy)
Title: Salvation and Survival on Skid Row: A Comment on Rooney
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Rooney found that these missions extend formal and informal goal distinctions, demonstrating the organization that succeeds by failing.
What_was_studied: James F. Rooney's article last year on skid row 'rescue missions' studied the phenomenon of organizations succeeding through failure, using ethnographic data from a major journal in our discipline.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize studying this phenomenon to understand how resourcefulness and guile among skid row denizens can be leveraged for successful outcomes, despite organizational failure.

Field: Extended family; Peer group; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Psychological well-being; Social support; Family support; Marital status; Population; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: The Influence of Supportive Relations on the Psychological Well-Being of Teenage Mothers
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that support from male partners is associated with low levels of distress, while support from female siblings is linked to higher levels of stress and distress. Additionally, the study found that education and race are important factors in explaining variations in psychological well-being among teenage mothers.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the influence of family and peer resources on adaptation to teenage motherhood, using survey data from young mothers during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize programs and services that provide comprehensive support to teenage mothers, particularly those from marginalized communities. This may include targeted interventions to strengthen relationships with supportive partners and siblings, as well as education and employment opportunities to promote economic stability and reduce poverty.

Field: Positive economics; Trustworthiness; Alienation; Ethnography; Poverty; Daughter; Peasant; Local community; Speculation; History
Title: Structure of Power in Palau
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the attitudes supporting the traditional way of life of both Ladinos and Indians are dominant, and some of the tensions are capable of being drained off by desertion of Indians to other areas. Moreover, the average Indian is so securely orientated and integrated to a pattern of poverty, illness, and hard work that they seem quite capable of taking considerable slack in their psychological belt to adjust to still more of the same.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the stability of traditional way of life among Ladinos and Indians in a specific community in Guatemala over time, using a mixed-methods approach with a 1940s time period and primary data collected through interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the resistance to any variation in the way of life to adjust to new forces at work, decision makers should prioritize policies that scale and expand social protection programs to support the Indian community's stability and well-being, such as poverty reduction initiatives and health care access improvements.

Authors: Andrew J. Cherlin; Robert W. Hodge
Field: Demography; Median; Psychology; Educational attainment; Median income; Population; Age distribution; Socioeconomics; Age adjustment; Economic inequality; Census
Title: Age Adjustment of Racial Income Differences: A Research Note
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ignoring age distributions when comparing white and nonwhite males aged 25-64 understates income differences, particularly for those with low educational attainments. Nonwhite males had lower median incomes than whites, and the gap worsened with increasing education level.
What_was_studied: The contention that failure to control for age leads to an understatement of black-white income differentials is shown to be inaccurate for those aged 25-64 in the United States, using data from the 1960 Census of Population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of racial inequality in the US, policymakers should prioritize adjusting income comparisons to account for age distributions when evaluating policies aimed at reducing poverty and income disparities.

Field: Social technology; Sociology; Government; Taste (sociology); State (polity); Academic year; Subject (philosophy); Social science; Social control; Social research
Title: A Definition of Sociology Derived from Titles of Courses
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that sociology courses in these universities focused on both normal and pathological social phenomena, with a majority of courses (38%) dedicated to introductory sociology and recent or contemporary theory, and a significant number of courses (21%) addressing social control, community organization, family, rural sociology, urban sociology, and social pathology.
What_was_studied: This paper defines sociology by analyzing the courses offered in representative American universities during the academic years of 1931-1932, finding a wide range of studies on normal and pathological social phenomena with attention to anthropological and psychological implications, and offering methods for social research and direction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of intersectional poverty in modern society, policymakers should prioritize funding for interdisciplinary research that combines sociology with other fields to better understand the complex factors contributing to poverty and develop effective solutions that address the root causes.

Field: Social environment; Sociology of Education; Psychology; Socialization; Mediation (Marxist theory and media studies); Concentrated poverty; Academic achievement; Educational institution; Social capital; Social psychology
Title: Why Does It Take a Village? The Mediation of Neighborhood Effects on Educational Achievement
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that neighborhood characteristics predict educational outcomes, with collective socialization being the strongest mediator, accounting for about 40% of the neighborhood effect on educational achievement.
What_was_studied: The current study examines the relationship between neighborhood characteristics and educational achievement, using the National Educational Longitudinal Study of 1988 linked to 1990 census information at the neighborhood level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize urban and educational policies that address the concentrated poverty in inner-city neighborhoods, such as initiatives to improve collective socialization and enhance access to educational resources.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Precarious work; Civic engagement; Unemployment; Test (assessment); Social integration; Demographic economics; Democracy; Panel data
Title: The Civic Footprints of Labor Market Participation: Longitudinal Evidence from the United States, 2002–2015
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that becoming unemployed increases the likelihood of volunteering, while leaving the labor force altogether is associated with a decrease in volunteer activities. Additionally, entering the labor force, either by securing or searching for a job, is linked to an increase in civic engagement.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between labor market experiences and civic engagement in America using panel data from the Current Population Survey 2002–2015, focusing on the periods of unemployment and non-participation in the labor force.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rise of precarious work arrangements and long-term unemployment, policymakers should prioritize programs that support job transitioning and re-entry into the labor force to foster civic engagement and social integration. Moreover, addressing the increasing share of the jobless who are not looking for work requires targeted interventions to enhance their time resources and motivation for volunteering.

Field: Mathematics education; Psychology; Working class; Pedagogy; Tracking (education); Self-esteem; Quality (business); Academic achievement; Hierarchy; Curriculum; Track (rail transport)
Title: Track Mobility in Secondary School
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The data shows evidence of considerably more mobility than is typically assumed, with females and low-income students exhibiting higher levels of mobility. Track mobility provides differential learning opportunities for pupils.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal study of over 2000 students in four years of high school examines the frequency of track mobility and direction of change in track assignments, relating mobility to student and school characteristics as well as the curriculum.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of more flexible track systems to ensure equal access to high-quality educational opportunities for all students, regardless of socioeconomic status or gender.

Field: Social relation; Social status; Psychology; Social change; Consistency (negotiation); Status inconsistency; Power (social and political); Social stratification; Social research; Social psychology
Title: Status Inconsistency, Satisfactory Social Interaction, and Community Satisfaction in an Area of Rapid Growth
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Contrary to what is hypothesized, middle-class persons in the study sample who have inconsistent statuses are more likely to experience satisfactory social interaction and community satisfaction than individuals with consistent statuses. The study found that persons with high occupation and low education or income are most satisfied with their interaction and community.
What_was_studied: This paper reports research on the relationship between status inconsistency and various dependent variables, using a sociological study with a unique population and exploring the concept of status consistency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that policies aimed at reducing status inconsistency, such as scaled social mobility programs or targeted education initiatives, may lead to increased community satisfaction and reduced psychological stress. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize these initiatives to improve the well-being of middle-class individuals and promote sustainable development.

Field: Value theory; Social class; Social psychology (sociology); Psychology; Subject (documents); Racial group; Labor union; White (horse); Juvenile delinquency; Criminology; Social psychology
Title: Moral Value Structure of Laborers and Penitentiary Inmates: A Research Note
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant differences on 26 of 50 moral values items between white marginally middle-class laborers and white penitentiary inmates, with the former presenting more conservative judgments. Additionally, there were significant differences on eight of 50 items between white and Negro convicts.
What_was_studied: A study comparing the moral values of white marginally middle-class laborers, white penitentiary inmates, and Negro penitentiary inmates using a questionnaire containing 50 items, sampled from the Ohio State University Delinquency Research Project directed by Walter C. Reckless over a 20-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty by considering the differing social class subcultures and criminal-noncriminal subcultures in shaping moral values, as this study suggests that these factors contribute more to divergence than racial differences.

Authors: Christopher R. Browning; Seth L. Feinberg; Robert D. Dietz
Field: Collective behavior; Sociology; Prosocial behavior; Collective efficacy; Solidarity; Poison control; Social capital; Social organization; Social psychology; Social network
Title: The Paradox of Social Organization: Networks, Collective Efficacy, and Violent Crime in Urban Neighborhoods
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
