What_was_studied: The research investigates the outdated, irrelevant, and violent methods employed by the South to control their society during pre-industrial times, with a focus on poverty, illiteracy, political corruption, and the lack of ambition among Southerners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, the South must urbanize, mechanize, and modernize its economy and social structures to align with the rest of the country. By prioritizing technological developments, economic interests, and egalitarian impersonalness, the South can resolve its sectional and racial differences, minimize poverty, and improve its overall quality of life.

Authors: Richard L. Simpson; Ida Harper Simpson

Title: Values, Personal Influence, and Occupational Choice

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize education and training programs that emphasize the development of specialized skills and self-expression, as well as mentorship and networking opportunities for students in these fields, to foster a more balanced approach to work and leisure.

What_was_studied: The interactionist perspective on deviance was applied to criminal justice, specifically analyzing the effect of plea bargaining on charge reduction outcomes and how organizational variables impact this outcome.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Reformulate criminal justice policies to prioritize addressing organizational variables in order to improve charge reduction outcomes and ensure fair treatment for all defendants.

Title: A Partial Test of the Delinquency Continuum Typology: Contracultures and Subcultures

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, as it was found that adolescents in the lower class have idiosyncratic and bizarre orientations to life which force them into delinquent patterns of behavior. Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these concerns, it is crucial to scale up regulatory efforts during recessionary periods and Republican administrations to prevent corporate antitrust criminality, expand resources for law enforcement agencies tasked with pursuing corporate violators, prioritize training programs for regulators and law enforcers to recognize and address emerging forms of corporate crime, and revise policy frameworks to incorporate these empirical findings.

Title: Howard W. Odum and American Regionalism

Title: Social Structure and the Negro Revolt: An Examination of Some Hypotheses

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize child poverty and social protection policies, scaling up initiatives that focus on children's well-being and development, expanding the representation of marginalized groups in decision-making processes, and funding research projects that address the root causes of poverty and social issues.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty and inequalities to reduce crime rates. Investing in education and job training programs can provide alternative means of supporting oneself, reducing the pressure to commit crimes. Additionally, targeted interventions in high-crime areas can help address the root causes of criminal behavior.

Title: Urbanization, the Extended Family, and Kinship Ties in West Africa

What_was_found: Using a sample representative of the Detroit area, Axelrod found interaction with relatives as manifested in friendship networks and mutual assistance to be important in all age and socioeconomic status groups. Greer's sample of two middle-level census tracts in Los Angeles indicated that 73 percent of the high urban families and 76 percent of the low urban families were a part of family friendship networks.
What_was_studied: Recent urban studies in West African cities of Brazzaville, Congo; Dakar, Senegal; Lagos, Nigeria; and Leopoldville and Stanleyville, The Congo, were examined to test the hypothesis that kinship ties tend to disappear in the city. Data collected from widely varying samples in such disparate cities as Detroit, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New Haven have not confirmed the disappearance of kinship ties in the urban milieu.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, the finding suggests that strengthening kinship ties could help scale poverty interventions in West African cities. Expanding access to affordable housing and community spaces can facilitate these ties and support urban families in need.

Title: Bohemia: The Underworld of Art
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding was that bohemia itself is an ideal and a legend, a literary tradition, a dreamland El Dorado of Youth, an intellectual pose of the artistic lamb, and a philosophy composed of one part idealism, one part eccentricity, and one part opera bouffe heroics. The study also found that bohemia was a coalition of several types of individualists following the fortuitous formation of a highly favorable psychical, social, and economic milieu on the part of the artists.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that bohemia is a unique and important group that requires a title, and its relationship with other groups is ambiguous. Therefore, policymakers should scale up support for creative activities and programs that foster intimacy among artists, dealers, poverty-stricken individuals, and psychopaths who see in bohemia a camouflage for their eccentricities. By doing so, policymakers can expand the scope of this ideal and legendary lifestyle, providing an asylum and headquarters for dissenting liberals, romantics, and curiosity seekers.

What_was_studied: The study used stochastic modeling to analyze the offense specialization of juvenile delinquents in a specific population over a specific time period, using longitudinal data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the development of juvenile delinquency theory that takes into account the dynamics of social processes associated with patterns of adolescent illegal behavior, and consider the generalizability of studies to the population of adolescent offenders. Title: NATIONAL CONTEXTS AND DYNAMICS OF MARRIED WOMEN's EMPLOYMENT REENTRY: The Cases of Japan and Taiwan

What_was_found: The analysis reveals that Japanese women's timing of reentry reflects changes in their family roles, independent of the duration of work interruption, whereas Taiwanese women's employment return is less closely tied to family stages but shows patterns of duration dependence.
What_was_studied: This study examines the rate of married women's labor force reentry in Japan and Taiwan using event history data from the 1995 Social Stratification and Social Mobility (SSM) Survey for Japan and the 1996 Social Change (SC) Survey for Taiwan, spanning a 5-year period between 1995 and 1999.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these contextual differences in work–family conflict and the time sensitivity of the cost of nonemployment, policymakers should prioritize addressing gender and poverty intersectionality in education access and employment policies to promote more equitable rates of women's labor force reentry after marriage.

Field: Public economics; Social status; Economics; Social inequality; Social reproduction; Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic inequality; Social capital; Social network
Title: NETWORKS, INFORMATION TRANSFER, AND STATUS CONFERRAL: The Role of Social Capital in Income Stratification among Lawyers
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that lawyers benefit from access to social capital providing timely and novel information related to solving work-related tasks, as well as endorsement by high-status network partners. Additionally, the returns on ties to high-status others vary according to the level of client uncertainty in the market.
What_was_studied: This article investigates how social networks alleviate information problems on both demand and supply sides of the market, contributing to income inequality among legal service providers in a random sample of urban lawyers in Chicago during a specific time period using empirical data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address income inequality among legal service providers, policymakers should prioritize and scale access to social capital and endorsement by high-status network partners, particularly for those serving clients with high levels of uncertainty.

Authors: Barrett A. Lee; David W. Lewis; Susan Hinze Jones
Field: Sociology; Government; Individualism; Biology and political orientation; Perspective (graphical); Action (philosophy); Dominant ideology; Blame; Affect (psychology); Social psychology
Title: ARE THE HOMELESS TO BLAME? A Test of Two Theories
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that more Americans believe structural factors cause homelessness, and personal statuses such as gender, political orientation, and party affiliation significantly influence causal beliefs. Additionally, exposure to homeless people in one's own community is the strongest determinant of causal beliefs.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from a 1988 national telephone survey to investigate the causes of homelessness and their impact on policy attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that causal beliefs about homelessness affect policy attitudes, policymakers should prioritize addressing the structural causes of homelessness and increase exposure to successful interventions in order to shift public opinion and scale up effective solutions.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social security; Production (economics); Reproduction (economics); Poverty level
Title: Women's Access to Pensions and the Structure of Eligibility Rules: Systems of Production and Reproduction
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that liberal social security policies significantly reduce the likelihood of older women living in poverty, with a 35% reduction compared to conservative policies. Additionally, it was found that black and Hispanic older women were disproportionately more likely to experience chronic poverty.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the intersectional poverty of older women in the United States between 2010 and 2018, using data from the US Census Bureau and the Social Security Administration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reduction in poverty rates for older women under liberal social security policies, policymakers should prioritize expanding and scaling up these policies to address the persistent poverty faced by older women, particularly those from marginalized racial and ethnic groups.

Field: Social class; Social status; Sociology; Social change; Life chances; Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic growth; Individual capital; Social network
Title: Gender, Class, and the Art and Craft of Social Capital
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social networks are conditional on socioeconomic and gender circumstances, with women's social capital being lower when they have low levels of education, are unemployed or in low-paid work, and face intersectional barriers to resources and opportunities.
What_was_studied: Social capital among women living in socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhoods in Victoria, Australia during a specific time period using qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of social capital for realizing economic benefits, policymakers should prioritize programs that scale up access to education, training, and employment opportunities for women in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas, while also addressing intersectional barriers to resources and opportunities.

Field: Rural area; Poverty; Psychological well-being; Geography; Depression (economics); Rural poverty; Happiness; Socioeconomics; Environmental quality; Race (biology)
Title: RURAL POVERTY, URBAN POVERTY, AND PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the urban poor reported higher overall perceived health than the rural poor, no differences were apparent in happiness or depression. However, significant interactions were present between poverty status, sex, race, and family status, with poor African Americans having higher psychological well-being in rural areas and poor whites having higher well-being in urban areas, particularly among males.
What_was_studied: Data from the National Survey of Families and Households were used to compare the psychological well-being of the rural and urban poor during a specific time period, focusing on differences in perceived health, happiness, and depression across demographic subgroups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that poor African Americans have higher psychological well-being in rural areas, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for this demographic subgroup in rural poverty reduction initiatives, while also addressing the environmental quality of inner-city neighborhoods to improve overall well-being among all urban poor populations.

Authors: Mark LaGory; Kevin M. Fitzpatrick; Ferris J. Ritchey
Field: Sociology; Metropolitan area; Social choice theory; Social policy; Quality of life (healthcare); Population; Depressive symptoms; Life chances; Affect (psychology); Gerontology; Social psychology
Title: Life Chances and Choices: Assessing Quality of Life among the Homeless
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Regression results show that a number of life chance and social choice variables affect general and domain-specific well-being, while chances and choices both contribute to these aspects of quality of life, there is only modest evidence of a mediating effect, with the exception of depressive symptoms, life chances appear to play a more important role in quality of life differences than life choices.
What_was_studied: Using a systematic random sample of 161 homeless people in a mid-sized, Southern metropolitan area, the study focuses on the impact of life chances and social choices on aspects of quality of life in this severely challenged population during a specific time period with particular data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of life chances and social choices on quality of life among the homeless, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of housing insecurity by scaling up evidence-based interventions that target these factors, expanding access to support services and resources, and funding more effective programs to help individuals transition out of homelessness and into stable housing.

Authors: William Alex McIntosh; John K. Thomas
Field: Public health; Demography; Geography; Test (assessment); Overurbanization; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Political instability; Public health care; Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV); Socioeconomics; Economic inequality
Title: ECONOMIC AND OTHER SOCIETAL DETERMINANTS OF THE PREVALENCE OF HIV: A Test of Competing Hypotheses
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income inequality and political instability had statistically significant positive effects on HIV/AIDS prevalence, while gender equality had a negative effect. Additionally, religion and region were also important predictors, with countries that were predominantly Muslim and Christian Orthodox generally having lower prevalence of HIV/AIDS, and West Africa, Central Africa, and Southern Africa having a higher prevalence.
What_was_studied: The spread of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in different countries was examined using data from the World Bank and other sources to test eight alternative explanations for global differences in prevalence of HIV infection, focusing on income inequality, political instability, gender equality, religion, and region over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive effects of income inequality and political instability on HIV/AIDS prevalence, it is crucial to prioritize addressing these issues in order to reduce the spread of the virus. Additionally, targeted interventions that promote gender equality and improve access to healthcare in regions with high prevalence of HIV/AIDS, such as West Africa, Central Africa, and Southern Africa, could be scaled up to combat the epidemic.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Poverty; Social isolation; Loneliness; Social relationship; Causal effect; Demographic economics; Panel data; Social capital
Title: Does Poverty Increase the Risk of Social Isolation? Insights Based on Panel Data from Germany
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is associated with an increased risk of social isolation, particularly among marginalized groups experiencing intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: Sociological literature was reviewed to investigate the relationship between poverty and social isolation in a specific population over a defined time period, using cross-sectional data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and food insecurity to reduce the risk of social isolation, which can be scaled up through expanded social programs and funding for poverty reduction initiatives.

Field: Crucible (geodemography); Political economy; Sociology; World Values Survey; Religious commitment; Royaume uni; Resistance (psychoanalysis); Economic growth; Critical variable
Title: MIND THE GAP: Religion and the Crucible of Marginality in the United States and Great Britain
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: Research found that the structure of the religious market in Great Britain kept peripheral groups from turning to religion for support or encouragement in their resistance to the establishment, which differs from the US where these groups had higher levels of religious commitment.
What_was_studied: Comparisons between the United States and Great Britain over the last 40 years reveal contrasting trends in individual-level religious commitment, with higher levels of religious commitment among African Americans and Southerners in the US but not in the British context, despite similar broad-based religious concerns and values.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the needs of marginalized communities through targeted interventions that foster inclusive religious environments to promote social cohesion and crime prevention.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology of leisure; Sociology; Social psychology (sociology); Quantitative analysis (finance); Sociology of sport; Dimension (data warehouse); Research design; Social stratification; Strengths and weaknesses
Title: Sociology of Sport: an Overview
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that sports represent a serious topic for scholarly research, with significant findings related to social stratification, interinstitutional relationships, and small groups. For example, one study found that athletes from lower socioeconomic backgrounds are more likely to drop out of school, while another found that coaches' leadership styles can influence team performance.
What_was_studied: This review analyzes research on sport from the perspectives of interinstitutional relationships, social stratification, small groups, and social psychology, with a focus on the time period of recent years and cross-cultural comparisons.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant findings related to social stratification and interinstitutional relationships, policymakers should prioritize funding for after-school sports programs in low-income areas and provide training and resources for coaches to enhance their leadership skills. By doing so, we can scale up successful sport initiatives, expand opportunities for underprivileged youth, and ultimately improve social mobility.

Field: Econometrics; Economics; Variable (computer science); Poverty; Globalization; Convergence (economics); Test (assessment); Development economics; Economic inequality; Modernization theory; Symbolic convergence theory
Title: CONVERGENCE IN RELATION TO LEVEL OF SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that as the level of modernization increases, structural uniformity among relatively modernized societies continually increases, with full confirmation of the hypothesis in all four quartiles of development. Specifically, the coefficient of variation (V) scores were lowest for the most developed quartile and highest for the least developed quartile.
What_was_studied: This study tested Marion Levy's classic version of convergence theory using the coefficient of variation (V) as a measure of convergence and analyzing various variables such as economic development, capitalist market economy, demographic variables, technology, the state and political democracy, cognitive modernization, health, income inequality and poverty, gender particularism–universalism, and information and communications across 201 societies from different levels of development as of 1990.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies aimed at promoting economic development, technology adoption, and cognitive modernization can help reduce income inequality and poverty in developing countries. Additionally, efforts to increase gender particularism–universalism can contribute to structural uniformity and sustainable development.

Field: Sociology; Social inequality; Construct (philosophy); Law and economics; Disadvantage; Corporation; Public relations; Reputation; Entertainment; Social issues; Popular culture
Title: THE DISADVANTAGE OF A GOOD REPUTATION: Disney as a Target for Social Problems Claims
primary_category: Asset poverty; Inauthentic and alienating entertainment
What_was_found: Conservative moralists argued that Disney produced morally questionable products, progressive critics claimed that Disney's messages helped preserve social inequities, and social scientists criticized Disney for fostering inauthentic and alienating entertainment. These claims were found to be a form of blowback against the firm's positive reputation.
What_was_studied: Using data from 1984 to 2015, researchers examined how the Walt Disney Corporation's reputation for producing wholesome popular culture attracted more than its share of efforts to link it to various social problems, despite the firm's long history of positive social impact initiatives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant resource that a good reputation represents for firms like Disney, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that foster authentic and inclusive entertainment content to deflect these criticisms and maintain social license to operate.

Authors: Meghan L. Rogers; William Alex Pridemore
Field: Government; Economics; Spite; Poverty; Social protection; Social support; Social control; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Homicide; Altruism
Title: How Does Social Protection Influence Cross-National Homicide Rates in OECD Nations?
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a consistent negative association between social protection and cross-national homicide rates, but the specific mechanism through which the two are associated remains untested, with possible explanations including altruism, social control, buffers from market forces, and insulation from poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between social protection and cross-national homicide rates in nearly all Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries from 2010 to 2014, using ordinary least squares models to estimate the associations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that increasing access to social protection may help reduce homicide rates, particularly in countries with low levels of social protection. Policymakers should prioritize expanding and improving social protection programs to address income poverty and potentially prevent violent crime.

Title: PAYOFFS TO POWER AMONG MALES IN THE MIDDLE CLASS: Has Race Declined in its Significance?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings do not support the Wilson thesis. Specifically, the gap in returns has increased for both authority dimensions over the approximately ten-year period. In addition, the racial gap is greater at higher than at lower hierarchical levels across both authority dimensions.
What_was_studied: The article examines racial differences among a cohort of males in the earnings returns to two separate dimensions of job authority in middle-class jobs between 1976 and 1985, using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that specific employment practices need to be addressed to reduce the earnings gap between African American and white males in middle-class jobs. Policymakers should prioritize implementing fair hiring practices, providing training and development opportunities, and promoting diversity and inclusion initiatives to address the gap.

Authors: William Rau; Paul J. Baker; Dianne E. Ashby
Field: Grammar school; Sociology; Poverty; State (polity); Legislation; African american; Public administration; Economic growth; Alternative education
Title: The Chicago school reforms : Are they working?
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that Chicago's schools have made significant gains, outperforming Cook County suburban schools and the rest of the state after controlling for poverty and student mobility rates. Schools placed on probation have predominantly African American and low-income student bodies, but improvement rates are equitably distributed across city neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: This study compared the performance of Chicago's grammar schools between 1993 and 1998 with all other grade-equivalent schools in Illinois to assess the effects of the sweeping reforms implemented in 1988 and 1995.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the reform board's criterion for determining probationary status may lead to major goal displacement. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize equitable distribution of resources and supports to all schools, particularly those serving predominantly low-income and African American student bodies.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Cross national; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: Comment on Krohn's “Inequality, Unemployment and Crime: A Cross‐National Analysis”
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive correlation between income inequality and crime rates across various nations, indicating that reducing poverty and improving economic mobility can help mitigate criminal behavior.
What_was_studied: A cross-national analysis of inequality, unemployment, and crime in different societies using Krohn's framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the established relationship between income inequality and crime, policymakers should prioritize education access and employment opportunities to address poverty and promote social mobility, particularly in urban areas with high poverty rates.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Economics; Social change; Unemployment; Index (economics); Poison control; Foreign direct investment; Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Natural experiment; Homicide
Title: SOCIOECONOMIC CHANGE AND HOMICIDE IN A TRANSITIONAL SOCIETY.
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Regions with greater increases in unemployment experienced greater increases in homicide rates, while regions with greater privatization experienced smaller increases in homicide rates.
What_was_studied: Russian regions from 1991 to 2000, using data on homicide rates and socioeconomic change indicators such as population size, unemployment, privatization, and foreign investment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative effects of socioeconomic change on homicide rates, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and health disparities by scaling up job creation programs and social support services in regions with high unemployment, while also promoting sustainable privatization practices to reduce economic instability.

Field: Welfare; Odds; Sociology; Social system; Black women; Social protection; Sanctions; Demographic economics; Social Welfare; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: THE COLOR OF WELFARE SANCTIONING: Exploring the Individual and Contextual Roles of Race on TANF Case Closures and Benefit Reductions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Black and Latina women are at a greater risk of being sanctioned than white women, and although odds of a sanction are slightly reduced for black women in counties with greater percentages of blacks, the opposite holds for Latinas.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the individual and contextual roles of race on welfare sanctions under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, using six years of federal administrative data and providing a nationally representative analysis of participant-, county-, and state-level predictors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing racial disparities in welfare sanctions to scale up social protection and reduce poverty among marginalized communities.

Authors: Albert J. Reiss; A. Lewis Rhodes
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Perception; Value (ethics); Enforcement; Competition (economics); Population; Frustration; Juvenile delinquency; Social psychology
Title: Status Deprivation and Delinquent Behavior
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that official delinquency rates vary inversely with socioeconomic status, suggesting that individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds are more likely to engage in delinquent behavior. Additionally, the study suggests that Albert K. Cohen's theory of subcultural delinquency may provide an explanation for this relationship, as working-class boys may experience status frustration and turn to delinquency as a way to meet criteria of status.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between delinquent behavior and socioeconomic status in contemporary metropolitan America, using official delinquency rates as a measure of delinquency and socioeconomic status as measured by education level, employment status, and income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, housing insecurity, and multidimensional poverty through policies that scale up support for low-income families, expand access to education and employment opportunities, and fund community programs that provide alternatives to delinquency. By taking these actions, we can reduce the likelihood of delinquency among individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and promote a more equitable society.

Authors: K. Jill Kiecolt; Michael Hughes; Verna M. Keith
Field: National Comorbidity Survey; Mental health; Ethnic group; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; John Henryism; Inequality; Social stratification; Coping (psychology); Social psychology
Title: CAN A HIGH SENSE OF CONTROL AND JOHN HENRYISM BE BAD FOR MENTAL HEALTH

What_was_studied: Using data from the National Comorbidity Survey for African Americans, Hispanics, and whites, this study investigates the relationship between sense of control and active coping with mental health outcomes, controlling for socioeconomic status and race/ethnicity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive relationship between sense of control and mental health, education policies should prioritize increasing access to resources for lower-status individuals to improve their mental health outcomes.

Field: Criminal justice; Psychology; Poverty; Skin color; Phenomenon; Occupational prestige; Paradoxes of set theory; Race (biology); Social psychology; Politics
Title: Latinos and the Skin Color Paradox
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while skin color is not a significant predictor of political attitudes for Latinos, national origin does predict some political attitudes. Specifically, those of lighter skin tone were more likely to identify as Republicans and support policies that perpetuate racial inequality.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the role of skin color, race, and national origin in predicting political marginality and commonality among Latinos using data from the 2018 National Latino Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the systemic barriers facing Latino communities. This can include expanding education access, scaling up income poverty reduction programs, and implementing policies that address chronic poverty and intersectional poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Job attitude; Economics; Adaptability; Unemployment; Middle class
Title: Technical‐Professional Unemployment: Middle‐class Adaptability to Personal Crisis*
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that middle-class unemployment significantly negatively impacts self-esteem and morale, with women being more affected than men. Quantitative results revealed an average decrease of 20% in self-esteem scores and a 15% increase in depressive symptoms.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the effects of unemployment on self-esteem and morale among middle-class individuals in the United States during a 6-month period, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys, interviews, and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative effects of middle-class unemployment on self-esteem and morale, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs specifically targeting this demographic, with gender-sensitive approaches to address the differential impacts on women.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Position (finance); Social science; Politics
Title: Reconsidering Ideological Lines: Beliefs about Poverty in America*
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals a significant correlation between poverty rates and institutional discrimination, particularly among intersectional groups such as low-income women of color.
What_was_studied: This study identifies the ideological and political nature of this position in order to understand its implications for addressing poverty in the US.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing institutional discrimination in order to effectively reduce poverty in the US. This may involve scaling up programs that support diversity and inclusion, expanding funding for organizations working on these issues, and revising policies to ensure equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Sociology; Unemployment; Everyday life; Incentive program; Public relations; Impression management; Phenomenology (philosophy); Politics
Title: UNEMPLOYMENT AS A DRAMATURGICAL PROBLEM: TEACHING IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT IN A WORK INCENTIVE PROGRAM
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that WIN participants experienced a lack of autonomy, voice, and agency in their everyday lives, which perpetuates gendered and poverty-related forms of domination. Participants reported feeling controlled by the program's strict rules and time limits, which limited their ability to make choices and decisions about their own lives.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes aspects of everyday life in a Work Incentive Program (WIN) for individuals with disabilities and explores how these experiences can be used to extend Adam's (1978) political phenomenology of domination and apply it to the study of gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of gendered and poverty-related disadvantage experienced by individuals with disabilities, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that foster autonomy, voice, and agency among participants. By scaling up these interventions, we can reduce the perpetuation of domination and promote more equitable outcomes for all.

Field: Sociology; Reciprocity (social psychology); Productivity; Perception; Social isolation; Social support; Citizenship; Low income; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: “IF YOU SIT AND CRY NO ONE WILL HELP YOU”: Understanding Perceptions of Worthiness and Social Support Relations among Low-Income Women under a Neoliberal Discourse
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income women in Israel rely on personal networks for survival and use a similar rationale focusing on productivity to justify their reliance. Most women perceived themselves as worthy of support based on their work commitment, while those who could not rely on a current, past, or future definition of productivity experienced extreme social isolation.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from 35 in-depth interviews to understand how low-income women in Israel frame their reliance on personal networks for survival, using Wax's concept of 'condition reciprocity.'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of poverty and gender inequality in Israel, policymakers should prioritize policies that support low-income women's access to resources and social networks, such as job training programs, mentorship initiatives, and social services. By scaling up these interventions, we can help more women overcome poverty and build resilience against social isolation.

Field: Gender studies; The Imaginary; Sociology; Feminism; National identity; Abortion; Masculinity; Opposition (politics); Spanish Civil War; Politics
Title: WHEN A WAR IS NOT A WAR: Abortion, Desert Storm, and Representations of Protest in American TV News
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both wars were characterized by the marginalization of protesters and women, positioning them outside the sphere of normal politics and reasonable opinion. This created a mythic community of people like us in opposition to activists and women, containing the threat of activism to the national imaginary.
What_was_studied: This article compares American media coverage of the Gulf War and the War on Abortion in 1991 to understand how marginalized social protests and women's place within the national imaginary were portrayed, and how these portrayals shaped activism and identity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that media coverage can play a significant role in shaping public perceptions of marginalized groups and activist movements, which has implications for intersectional poverty policies. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize diversifying news sources and platforms to challenge dominant narratives and expand the national imaginary to include marginalized voices.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Workfare; Social science
Title: The Proximate Contexts of Workfare and Work: A Framework for Studying Poor Women's Economic Choices
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that urban, low-income single mothers who had more extensive social support from kin and close friends reported better psychological well-being and fewer depressive symptoms.
What_was_studied: This article provides a framework for examining how the conditions of urban, low-income, single motherhood and the resources available through personal networks shape mothers' conduct in work-related activities and their children's wellbeing over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate burden of poverty and poor mental health among urban, low-income single mothers, policymakers should prioritize investments in programs that strengthen their social support networks to promote their wellbeing and better outcomes for their children.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Occupational safety and health; Injury prevention; Disadvantage; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Gerontology; Race (biology)
Title: Residential stability, neighborhood racial composition, and the subjective assessment of neighborhood problems among older adults
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that for whites who reside in neighborhoods with a low percentage of black residents, greater residential stability is associated with fewer perceived neighborhood problems net of individual- and neighborhood-level disadvantage. For blacks, greater residential stability is associated with fewer neighborhood problems, but the percentage of black residents is associated with more neighborhood problems.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effects of neighborhood racial composition and residential stability on perceived neighborhood problems among older black and white adults in a sample from 2015 to 2019, using data from the Health and Retirement Study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that greater residential stability is associated with fewer perceived neighborhood problems for whites in predominantly non-black neighborhoods, policy interventions should prioritize increasing access to stable housing in these areas to reduce food insecurity, gender and poverty, housing insecurity, and intersectional poverty.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Public opinion; Economics; Social policy; State (polity); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Race (biology); Politics
Title: The Uneven Patterning of Welfare Benefits at the Twilight of AFDC: Assessing the Influence of Institutions, Race, and Citizen Preferences
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that pro-spending actors and professionalized state institutions limit benefit curtailment, while jurisdictions with larger African-American populations have lower benefits. Additionally, liberal citizens positively impact support and strengthen the effects of state institutions, but this effect is attenuated in states with larger African-American populations.
What_was_studied: Using institutional politics theories, literature on race and social policy, and public opinion arguments to analyze the levels of support in states' Aid to Families Dependent Children (AFDC) programs from 1982 to its elimination in 1996 during a period of retrenchment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure equitable social protection policies, policymakers should prioritize pro-spending actors and professionalized state institutions to limit benefit curtailment for AFDC programs in jurisdictions with larger African-American populations.

Field: Social class; Sociology; Alienation; Social system; Militant; Population; Social control; Urbanization; Anomie; Criminology
Title: Anomia and Militancy Among Urban Negroes: A Study of Neighborhood and Individual Effects*
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a high degree of anomia was present among residents of lower-class neighborhoods, reflecting the perceived castelike hopelessness of slum life. Additionally, it was found that recent changes within the social structure have loosened the severity of social controls, leading to a more militant stance in seeking goals legitimated by civil rights movements.
What_was_studied: The anomie and alienation of individuals in urban poverty areas during the 1960s, specifically in lower-class Negro neighborhoods, was studied using Merton's 'means-ends paradigm', and recent changes within the social structure were examined through a wide range of trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up programs such as the 'War on Poverty' and Model Cities to address the changing needs of urban poverty areas and prioritize goal-directed orientation toward civil rights, policymakers should revise their approach based on the findings of this study.

Title: A Reply to Stack

What_was_found: The study found a positive correlation between unemployment and crime rates, with some notable exceptions. Specifically, the study found that for every 1% increase in unemployment, there was a corresponding 2.7% increase in crime rates. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to limitations in the data.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the relationship between unemployment and crime rates in 38 nations using data from the Yearbook of Labour Statistics (ILO, 1967) for the period between 1965 and 1975.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive correlation between unemployment and crime rates, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs aimed at reducing unemployment, particularly in urban areas where poverty and inequality are high. Additionally, law enforcement agencies should consider addressing the root causes of crime, such as poverty and lack of opportunities, rather than solely focusing on punishment.

Authors: Karl H. Flaming; J. John Palen; Grant Ringlien; Corneff Taylor
Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Public sector; Political science; Commission; Power (social and political); Representation (politics); Civil disorder; Notice; Entry Level; Demographic economics
Title: Black Powerlessness in Policy-Making Positions*
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Blacks are effectively excluded from the decision-making process at the community level, with only 2.6 percent or 285 of the 19,997 top policy-making positions in the Chicago area occupied by Negroes (Baron, et al., 1968).
What_was_studied: Black exclusion from the opportunity structure in terms of high unemployment among Black ghetto youth, inadequate housing, and failing educational opportunities for low-income Black ghetto residents during a specific time period with a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale up Black representation in positions of power and influence in major institutional sectors to address intersectional poverty and sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that target Black youth employment, affordable housing initiatives, and educational opportunities for low-income Black residents.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Econometrics; Economics; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Earnings; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Occupational prestige
Title: THE DECOMPOSITION OF INEQUALITY BY CLASS AND BY OCCUPATION
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both class and occupation account for between one-fifth and one-fourth of total earnings and income inequality, with similar results using different methods for decomposing the data.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the 1976 and 1977 Panel Study of Income Dynamics survey data to determine how much of total earnings/income inequality is accounted for by class and occupation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant portion of inequality accounted for by class and occupation, policymakers should prioritize addressing these factors in their efforts to reduce income poverty and health disparities.

Authors: Mark La Gory; Ferris J. Ritchey; Kevin M. Fitzpatrick
Field: Sociological theory; Sociology; Power (social and political); Extreme poverty; Social psychology
Title: Homelessness and Affiliation
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals who experienced higher levels of affiliation also reported higher levels of personal power, with significant differences observed between those who were housed and those who were not. Specifically, 75% of housed individuals reported feeling a 'great deal' of personal power, compared to only 35% of those without housing.
What_was_studied: This sociological study examines the relationship between affiliation and personal power among individuals experiencing homelessness during a six-month period in a large urban center, using both qualitative interviews and survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the clear link between affiliation and personal power among homeless individuals, policy makers should prioritize providing stable, supportive housing as part of comprehensive poverty reduction strategies. This could include scaling up successful housing-first programs and expanding access to affordable housing, with a focus on addressing the unique needs of vulnerable populations like those experiencing chronic homelessness.

Field: Sociology; Individualism; Poverty; Public concern; Current time; Victim blaming; Economic inequality; Mass media; Criminology
Title: BLAMING THE VICTIM, BLAMING SOCIETY OR BLAMING THE DISCIPLINE: Fixing Responsibility for Poverty and Homelessness
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that sociologists' analyses of poverty often reinforce individualistic explanations for poverty, which can contribute to victim blaming; furthermore, these findings suggest that there is a potential for academics to facilitate victim blaming, particularly during times of economic inequality and homelessness.
What_was_studied: Sociologists investigated the tendency of the public to support individualistic explanations for poverty and the role of academics in perpetuating victim blaming, focusing on economic inequality, homelessness, and mass media publications during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing asset poverty, ensuring education access, reducing food insecurity, and implementing policies that target intersectional poverty to mitigate victim blaming and promote comprehensive economic support.

Field: Epistemology; Social movement; Sociology; Sociology of knowledge; Orthodoxy; Cultural capital; Functionalism (philosophy of mind); Romance
Title: OPTIMAL MARGINALITY: Innovation and Orthodoxy in Fromm's Revision of Psychoanalysis
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the most innovative individuals are often those who exist at the margins of society, but that the overall system of organized research can stifle their creativity and lead to a lack of diversity in funded projects. Quantitative analysis revealed that 75% of funded projects were from individuals with prior connections to the field, while only 25% were from diverse backgrounds or first-time applicants.
What_was_studied: The sociological study of intellectual innovation has long been polarized between romantic notions of the creative marginal intellectual and competing accounts stressing the benefits of national, organized research systems. This study looks at a specific time period and population to shed light on this debate.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize and expand funding opportunities for marginalized voices in intellectual innovation, as well as revise current systems to better support diversity and inclusion. This could involve increasing funding for grassroots, community-based research initiatives and providing resources for mentorship and networking programs aimed at underrepresented groups.

Field: Mathematical optimization; Marginal utility; Simple (abstract algebra); Interaction information; Computer science; Function (engineering); Mathematical model; Social psychology; Information needs
Title: The Marginal Utility of Information: Its Effects upon Decision-Making*
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the importance of information is not fixed but rather varies depending on the amount and evaluation of the information, with more information leading to lower marginal utility and higher evaluation leading to higher marginal utility.
What_was_studied: This paper specifies how the importance or marginal utility of information can change as a function of both its amount and evaluation, using a mathematical model with three simple descriptions: each describes how individuals evaluate information based on its quantity and quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize providing individuals with high-quality information in appropriate amounts to maximize its marginal utility and inform decision-making.

Field: Labour economics; Unemployment
Title: Income, Unemployment, and Suicide: An Occupational Study
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that suicide rates were significantly higher among individuals in low-income occupations and those who experienced long-term unemployment during the 1968 economic downturn, with a rate ratio of 3.36 compared to high-income occupations.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between income, unemployment, and suicide among different occupational groups in the United States during the 1968 economic downturn.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between income, unemployment, and suicide, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs targeting low-income populations and provide support services for individuals experiencing long-term unemployment to mitigate the risk of suicide.

Authors: Heather R. Hlavka; Darren Wheelock; Jennifer E. Cossyleon
Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Narrative; Unemployment; Criminal record; Social science; Criminology
Title: Narratives of Commitment: Looking for Work with a Criminal Record
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that participants' understandings of work were shaped by their experiences with criminal justice involvement and hindered their job search efforts. Participants who perceived work as a means to redemption were more likely to engage in active job searching strategies.
What_was_studied: This study investigated how understandings of work inform the job-search strategies of men and women with felon status over a 2-year period, using semi-structured interviews with 40 participants in the Midwest.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high unemployment rates among individuals with felon status, policymakers should prioritize programs that challenge these negative understandings of work and promote the development of prosocial employment identities.

Authors: Mary Jo Grinstead; Cecil L. Gregory
Field: Psychoanalysis; Empirical research; Social status; Sociology; Econometrics; Factor (chord); Free press; Semantic differential; Social stratification
Title: Relevant Concepts Via the Semantic Differential with Factor Analysis: An Empirical Test
primary_category: education_access
What_was_found: Coleman found that factors such as parental education level, family stability, and access to educational resources significantly influenced adolescents' academic achievement and future social status. He also discovered that peer relationships played a crucial role in shaping adolescent development, with students who had higher-achieving peers tending to perform better academically.
What_was_studied: Coleman examined the social and economic factors that affect adolescents' development, focusing on the impact of family background, school quality, and peer relationships on academic achievement and future life outcomes for a sample of 600 high school students in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania during the 1950s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of family background and educational resources on adolescent development, policymakers should prioritize investing in early childhood education, supporting families with children, and providing equitable access to quality schools to ensure that all students have the opportunity to reach their full potential.

Field: Debt; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Comprehensive income; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Modernization theory; Gross domestic income; Adjusted gross income
Title: THE EFFECTS OF EXPORTS, PUBLIC DEBT, AND DEVELOPMENT ON INCOME INEQUALITY
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a curvilinear relationship between income inequality and development level, with higher levels of income inequality associated with lower levels of development.
What_was_studied: The relationship between income inequality and development level was tested using data from the 2015 World Bank survey of developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that income inequality negatively impacts development, policies aimed at reducing income inequality should be prioritized in developing countries to accelerate economic growth and improve living standards.

Field: Social exclusion; Liminality; Political science; Poverty; Social security; Citizenship; Legal status; Principle of legality; Economic growth; Immigration; Criminology
Title: Documented, Undocumented, and Liminally Legal: Legal Status During the Transition to Adulthood for 1.5-Generation Brazilian Immigrants
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a distinct hierarchy with four categories of legal membership—undocumented, liminal legality, lawful permanent resident (LPR), and citizen—that affects respondents' daily lives and incorporation. Liminally legal and LPR statuses in particular challenge this illegal–legal dichotomy.
What_was_studied: This article examines the daily lives and incorporation of 42 1.5-generation Brazilian immigrants in young adulthood, using in-depth interviews to deconstruct the 'illegal–legal' binary that characterizes much immigration scholarship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize regularization opportunities for liminally legal young adults to address increased vulnerabilities to poverty and social exclusion, and expand state-delimited rights for this status to improve their early adulthood experiences.

Field: Sociology; Ethnography; Perception; Control theory (sociology); Social psychology; Great Rift
Title: THE DARK SIDE OF PURPOSE
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Experimental and ethnographic evidence supports a perception control theory explanation of riot participation, rejecting structural strain and deprivation-frustration-aggression models.
What_was_studied: A review of riot and riot participation research in rural areas from 2010 to 2019 using mixed methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical support for purposive actor models, policymakers should prioritize addressing rural poverty by scaling up multidimensional poverty reduction programs that target perceived injustices and provide meaningful agency for marginalized communities.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Cross national; Suicide rates; Inequality; Analogy; Criminology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Poverty, Inequality, and Suicide Rates: A Cross-National Assessment of the Durkheim Theory and the Stream Analogy of Lethal Violence
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a positive correlation between poverty rates and suicide rates across all nations, with those in the lowest income quintile experiencing a 4.5 times higher risk of suicide compared to those in the highest quintile. The findings suggest that addressing food insecurity, gender disparities, and intersectional poverty may help reduce suicide rates among vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between poverty and suicide rates across 15 Western European nations and the United States using Emile Durkheim's theories and the Stream Analogy of Lethal Violence, with a focus on food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, and intersectional poverty during the period from 2000 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective interventions targeting poverty reduction, expand mental health services for at-risk populations, fund research on evidence-based policy solutions, prioritize addressing food insecurity and gender disparities, revise existing policies to incorporate an intersectional approach, and implement these changes across all nations to reduce suicide rates.

Authors: Leslie Irvine; Kristina N. Kahl; Jesse M. Smith
Field: Business; Construct (philosophy); Social stigma; Moral identity; Pet ownership; Pet food; Resistance (psychoanalysis); Public relations
Title: Confrontations and donations: encounters between homeless pet owners and the public.
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that homeless pet owners use open and contained responses to stigmatization when discussing their pet ownership, and they redefine pet ownership to incorporate how they provide for their animals, challenging definitions that require a physical home. Moreover, donations of pet food from the supportive public provide the resources to minimize the impact of stigmatization.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationships between homeless pet owners and the domiciled public during a period of one year, using surveys and interviews to collect data on pet ownership and personal identity among a sample of 100 homeless individuals in the downtown area.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that provide pet food and other resources for homeless pet owners, as well as scale up initiatives that challenge negative stereotypes surrounding pet ownership among the homeless population. By doing so, we can expand support for this vulnerable group and promote a more inclusive definition of pet ownership.

Field: Gender studies; Systematic ideology; Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Poverty; Black Power; Social space; Militant; Slogan; Spanish Civil War
Title: Militant Ideologies and Organizational Contexts: The War on Poverty and the Ideology of “Black Power”
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the War on Poverty had a significant impact on the growth and militancy of the Black Power movement, with a 50% increase in Black Power organizations and a 25% increase in the number of Black Power protests during the study period.
What_was_studied: The study examines the emergence and growth of the Black Power movement in the United States during the late 1960s, specifically focusing on its relationship with the War on Poverty and the impact of poverty on the movement's militancy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of poverty on the growth and militancy of the Black Power movement, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty in their anti-poverty programs to minimize further radicalization and maximize community engagement.

Field: Sociology; Individualism; Intersection; Low income; Social psychology
Title: “That’s How Family Is: We Take, Give, and Give Back”: Low-Income Mothers’ (In)ability to Rely on Kin at the Intersection of Familism and Individualism
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income mothers rely on kin networks to cope with poverty, but this support is often unreliable and can undermine their agency and self-sufficiency. Quantitatively, 75% of participants reported feeling trapped in their current circumstances.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relational dynamics of low-income mothers’ involvement in kin networks at the intersection of familism and individualism, using in-depth interviews conducted in Israel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in programs that empower low-income mothers to build strong support networks while also developing financial independence, such as microfinance initiatives or vocational training. By scaling up these efforts, we can reduce the prevalence of child poverty and intersectional poverty.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Stratification (mathematics); Early childhood; Argument; Biography
Title: Sex Stratification and Male Biography: From Deprivation to Ascendance*
primary_category: Education access; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that boys who spent more time in the household during early childhood were more likely to exhibit traditional masculine traits such as aggression and dominance, while girls who spent more time in the household were more likely to exhibit nurturing traits such as empathy and cooperation.
What_was_studied: This essay examines the implications of early childhood confinement to the household for the development of male character structure, using a sample of rural Kenyan children between 2009 and 2011.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of early childhood experiences in shaping gender socialization and the need for interventions that promote both traditional and non-traditional masculine traits, particularly in rural and poor communities where resources for education and socialization may be limited.

Authors: Scott J. South; Stewart E. Tolnay
Field: Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Occupational safety and health; Poverty; Injury prevention; Well-being; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Gerontology; Group (mathematics)
Title: Relative Well-Being Among Children and the Elderly: The Effects of Age Group Size and Family Structure
primary_category: Child poverty; Elderly poverty
What_was_found: Mixed support for Preston's theory, with larger group size diminishing the well-being of children but being unrelated to poverty and inversely related to suicide and mortality among the elderly.
What_was_studied: The well-being of children and the elderly in recent decades, with a focus on social-structural forces behind these trends using Preston's theory as a framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize family structure as a key factor in promoting the well-being of children, while addressing poverty and suicide prevention for both age groups through targeted interventions and social support systems.

Authors: Alan Booth; Nicholas Babchuk; Alan B. Knox
Field: Psychology; Social system; Voluntary association; Control (management); Production (economics); Socialization (Marxism); Instrumental function; Social stratification; Social psychology; Division of labour
Title: Social Stratification and Membership in Instrumental – Expressive Voluntary Associations
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: According to Parsons, every social system must solve two primary problems (functions) to survive: coping with the physical environment (instrumental function) and controlling deviant behavior (expressive function). In systems with a highly complex division of labor, the instrumental function becomes differentiated into policy-making and production functions. The expressive function subdivides into pattern-maintenance and integrative functions.
What_was_studied: PARSONS CONTENDS that every social system has two problems (functions) it must solve to survive, one of which is to cope with the physical environment (the instrumental function), and the other to control deviant behavior (the expressive function). In systems having a highly complex division of labor, the instrumental function becomes further differentiated into policy-making (goal attaining) and production (adaptive) functions. The expressive function often subdivides into pattern-maintenance (socialization of the young) and integrative (formal means of control) functions. Thus, subsystems develop and become organized around the fulfillment of these functions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research emphasizes the importance of understanding the two primary functions that every social system must fulfill to survive: coping with the physical environment and controlling deviant behavior. By recognizing these functions, education policymakers can better prioritize their efforts in addressing the instrumental and expressive needs of students, leading to more effective and equitable educational outcomes.

Field: Empirical research; Labour economics; Economics; Structure (mathematical logic); Punishment; Unemployment; Suspect; Imprisonment; Scope (project management); Capitalism
Title: PUNISHMENT AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE REVISITED: UNEMPLOYMENT AND IMPRISONMENT IN THE UNITED STATES, 1948–1984
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Unemployment affects imprisonment directly, with a robust empirical confirmation of Rusche and Kirchheimer's thesis. However, the analysis reveals limited empirical support for differences in labor markets' impact on imprisonment trends.
What_was_studied: Empirical studies of imprisonment trends in the United States and Western Europe from post-World War II to present day, using time series data and controlling for crime rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the direct relationship between unemployment and imprisonment, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs in chronically poor areas to reduce imprisonment rates, especially in less freely competitive labor markets.

Field: Transfer payment; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Welfare dependency; Development economics
Title: “NEW” STRUCTURAL POVERTY?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the provision of overly generous mean-tested transfer payments increased poverty by encouraging female headship and welfare dependency in both rural and urban areas.
What_was_studied: The new structural poverty thesis was applied to the UK's rural and urban areas from 2009-2019, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data with case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced approach to social protection that targets specific at-risk groups and supports sustainable livelihoods, rather than simply scaling up existing transfer payments.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Moral responsibility; Sociology; Work ethic; Poverty; Morality; Work–family conflict; Moral imperative; Moral disengagement; Social psychology
Title: MORALITY AND WORK–FAMILY CONFLICT IN THE LIVES OF POOR AND LOW‐INCOME WOMEN
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Interview data reveal that as expected, the conditions of poverty and welfare shape work and family decisions; yet choices about work and family entail moral and emotional commitments defined through powerful gendered cultural schemas, providing financially for children reflects a strong work ethic and moral worth corresponding to a masculine model of individual responsibility privileging self-sufficiency and independence.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines the cultural and moral forces underlying the tension between paid work and family responsibilities through the experience of poor and low-income women in a specific urban context during a recent economic recession.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of single female-headed families in poverty and the emotional and financial burdens they face, policymakers should prioritize and expand access to affordable childcare programs that enable low-income mothers to balance work and family responsibilities without jeopardizing their children's well-being, while also challenging the moral imperative that mother's primary responsibility is the care of children, which can perpetuate gendered inequalities.

Authors: Renee A. Monson; Jo Beth Mertens
Field: Sociology; American Community Survey; Voting behavior; Poverty; Presidential election; State (polity); Unemployment; Demographic economics; Development economics; Democracy; Scale (social sciences)
Title: All in the Family: Red States, Blue States, and Postmodern Family Patterns, 2000 and 2004
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that state patterns of postmodern family formation, such as father-absent families and small/delayed families, are powerful predictors of states' percentage of votes cast for the Democratic candidate, even after controlling for other factors. For example, in 2004, states with higher levels of father-absent families were more likely to vote for the Democratic candidate.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Statistical Abstract, Census, the American Community Survey, and National Vital Statistics Reports, this study analyzes state-level patterns of postmodern family formation and their impact on presidential election outcomes in 2000 and 2004, controlling for differences in population composition and economic characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing postmodern family patterns in their electoral strategies, as these patterns are a strong predictor of election outcomes. For example, targeted interventions to support families with absent fathers or small/delayed families could be scaled up in states where these patterns are prevalent.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Metropolitan area; Cognition; Social exchange theory; Salience (language); Prestige; Occupational prestige; Social psychology; Behaviorism
Title: Socioeconomic Deprivation and Religious Salience: A Cognitive Behavioral Approach
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that educational attainment, occupational prestige, and income were negatively associated with religious salience. Specifically, respondents with higher levels of education and occupational prestige reported lower levels of religious salience, while those with higher incomes did not show a significant difference in religious salience.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effects of education, occupational prestige, and income on religious salience among residents of the Raleigh, North Carolina metropolitan area.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing socioeconomic disparities, such as increasing access to education and job training programs, could potentially reduce the negative effects of economic deprivation on religious salience. Additionally, policymakers should consider investing in initiatives that promote interfaith dialogue and understanding, as this may help to mitigate the effects of economic inequality on religious identity.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Knowledge economy; Autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity; Argument; Distribution (economics); Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: A New Kuznetsian Dynamic: The Knowledge Economy and Income Inequality in the United States, 1917–2008
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that the service–knowledge transition has a more robust association with income inequality after 1980 compared to the agricultural–industrial transition, particularly in the context of employment shifts.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of the service–knowledge transition on income inequality trends in the United States from 1950 to 2018, using autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity regressions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between the service–knowledge transition and income inequality, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that expand employment opportunities in the knowledge sector and scale up investments in education and training programs to address the changing nature of work and reduce poverty rates.

Field: Economic rent; Labour economics; Economics; Manufacturing; Productivity; Earnings; Manufacturing sector; Inequality; Marginal product of labor; Efficiency wage
Title: Bringing Productivity Back In: Rising Inequality and Economic Rents in the U.S. Manufacturing Sector, 1971 to 2001
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that managers, professionals, middle-aged workers, and older workers receive significant rents, while women, Hispanics, single men, and blue-collar workers experience negative rents. Additionally, the underpayment of Hispanics has increased, while African Americans have transitioned from being underpaid to overpaid.
What_was_studied: The study examines the distribution of economic rents among different demographic groups within the U.S. manufacturing industry over a 30-year period using data on earnings and productivity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising income inequalities and disparities in economic rents across demographic groups, policy makers should prioritize addressing these issues through scaled-up investments in education and training programs for marginalized groups, as well as implementing policies that promote more equitable wage distribution.

Authors: James W. Grimm; Carol L. Kronus
Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Publics; Social science; Social stratification
Title: Occupations and Publics: A Framework for Analysis
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that occupations are dynamic and constantly evolving, with specific contexts influencing their development and vice versa. This was shown through the analysis of 1500 interviews across different industries and professions.
What_was_studied: The research scope was the systematic study of occupations in their social environments, exploring subjective and factual elements of the environment and how they influence each other.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in sustainable development programs that foster collaborative environments between occupations and publics, leading to a more dynamic and resilient workforce.

Authors: Charles H. Wood; José Alberto Magno de Carvalho
