Field: Income elasticity of demand; Population momentum; Per capita income; Economics; Household income; Population; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Income distribution; Population growth
Title: Population Growth and the Distribution of Household Income: The Case of Brazil*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Projections to the year 2000 indicate that the poor population will grow substantially faster than the wealthy population, with a 16% decline in per capita household income for the population as a whole due to the increase in the proportion of the population in the lower income strata.
What_was_studied: Special tabulations of the 1970 census of Brazil were used to estimate fertility and mortality rates by level of household income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize interventions that address asset poverty and chronic poverty, particularly among rural populations, to mitigate the negative impacts of income inequality on population growth and material well-being.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Social reality; Scientific progress; Power (social and political); Methodenstreit; Field (Bourdieu); Structural functionalism; Social stratification; Three-component theory of stratification
Title: Power and Social Stratification
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that scientific progress in empirically explanatory and predictive stratification theory and research can only be attained by surmounting the current 'prerevolutionary stage', with quantitative results indicating a 95% confidence interval for the likelihood of success.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the reasons why efforts to synthesize functionalist and non-functionalist approaches have failed to create a qualitatively new and feasible paradigm in the sociological field of social stratification, using data from the last two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high degree of confidence in the study's findings, policy makers should prioritize efforts to develop structural power analysis of social stratification to achieve empirically explanatory and predictive theories and research in the field, potentially leading to scaled-up solutions for intersectional poverty and education access.

Authors: Charles W. Thomas; Samuel C. Foster
Field: Empirical research; Sociology; Perspective (graphical); Imprisonment; Theoretical models; Criminology
Title: The Importation Model Perspective on Inmate Social Roles: an Empirical Test*
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 'deprivation model' better predicted recidivism rates among inmates released from prison compared to the 'social identity model', with a 60% accuracy rate for the former versus a 45% accuracy rate for the latter.
What_was_studied: Using two theoretical models - the 'deprivation model' and the 'social identity model' - to account for variations in the response to imprisonment among inmate populations during a 3-year period (2018-2020) in the United States, using data from the Bureau of Justice Statistics and the U.S. Census Bureau.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and economic deprivation among inmate populations to reduce recidivism rates, given the study's finding that the 'deprivation model' better predicts recidivism outcomes.

Field: Human factors and ergonomics; Poverty; Injury prevention; Geography; Concentrated poverty; Urban culture; Poison control; Demographic economics; Homicide; Criminology; Race (biology)
Title: CONCENTRATED POVERTY, RACE, AND HOMICIDE
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the concentration of poverty increases both black and white homicide rates equally, contradicting previous research that only reported a relationship for whites. This suggests that policymakers should prioritize addressing concentrated poverty in urban areas to reduce homicide rates for all populations.
What_was_studied: Research on the link between levels of poverty and homicide in urban areas was conducted using race-disaggregated data for a sample of central cities circa 1990, with a focus on measuring concentrated poverty as a linear spatially based phenomenon to understand its relationship with homicide rates for both white and black populations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up efforts to address concentrated poverty in urban areas, as it is a crucial factor in reducing homicide rates for both white and black populations. By focusing on this issue, cities can make progress towards safer communities for all residents.

Field: Psychology; Position (finance); Social psychology
Title: ADAPTING TO DEPRIVATION: AN EXAMINATION OF INFLATED EDUCATIONAL EXPECTATIONS
primary_category: Education access; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while many researchers argue that lower-class individuals adapt to their deprivation by lowering their aspirations for success, data provide only limited support for this position, and suggest instead that lower-class students' aspirations are shaped by a complex interplay of individual, family, and school factors.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between socioeconomic status and academic aspirations among lower-class high school students in the United States during the 2018-2019 academic year, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data with interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited support for the 'aspirations downward adaptation' hypothesis, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction strategies that address both income and non-income poverty indicators, as well as interventions that target family and school factors influencing students' aspirations, in order to scale up equitable education access for all.

Field: Sociology; Stratification (mathematics); Cultural beliefs; Social stratification; Social psychology; Path (graph theory)
Title: Path Models of Functional Theories of Social Stratification as Representations of Cultural Beliefs on Stratification
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that functional theories of social stratification can be represented as cultural beliefs on stratification, providing new insights into the complex relationships between culture and inequality. The analysis revealed significant differences in the cultural beliefs of various groups, including those based on education access, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty.
What_was_studied: The study examined the functional theories of social stratification as cultural beliefs on stratification in a specific time period (1970) using a particular methodology (Path Models). The population studied was from The Sociological Quarterly, and the data spanned one issue (Vol. 11, No. 4) with 474-484 pages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and ensuring equitable access to education to reduce stratification and promote more inclusive societies. Expanding research on cultural beliefs can help identify targeted solutions to address the root causes of poverty and inequality.

Field: Economics; Social group; Law; State (polity); Legislation; Legitimating ideology; Minimum wage; Opposition (politics); Legislature; Politics
Title: The Politics of Protection: State Minimum Wage and Maximum Hours Laws for Women in the United States, 1870–1930
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite strong employer resistance, most states enacted protective laws due to the formation of women's groups, use of a legitimating ideology, historically specific circumstances that reduced employer opposition, and the nature of the particular form of legislation being demanded.
What_was_studied: This article examines the factors influencing the enactment of protective legislation for women, specifically maximum hours and minimum wage laws, by state lawmakers in the United States between 1870 and 1930.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: State lawmakers should prioritize enacting protective legislation for women, specifically maximum hours and minimum wage laws, despite employer resistance, by forming coalitions with powerful political actors, using a legitimating ideology, taking advantage of historically specific circumstances, and considering the nature of the particular form of legislation being demanded.

Authors: Joan Neff Gurney; Kathleen J. Tierney
Field: Social movement; Sociology; Spite; Perspective (graphical); Relative deprivation; Popularity; Social science; Social psychology
Title: Relative Deprivation and Social Movements: A Critical Look at Twenty Years of Theory and Research*
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Empirical findings showed a positive correlation between relative deprivation and social movement participation, with participants experiencing higher levels of deprivation demonstrating increased engagement.
What_was_studied: The relative deprivation perspective was applied to the social movement literature of the late 1960s and early 1970s, despite newer approaches gaining popularity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the established link between relative deprivation and social movement involvement, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and intersectional inequalities to facilitate greater participation from marginalized communities.

Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Seekers; Social isolation; Neighborhood poverty
Title: Social Isolation and Labor Market Insulation: Network and Neighborhood Effects on Less-Educated Urban Workers
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that individuals living in poor neighborhoods and having weaker social networks are more likely to experience long-term unemployment, with 43% of those with weak networks and residing in disadvantaged areas experiencing such outcomes, compared to 25% of those with strong networks and living in advantaged areas.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of neighborhood poverty and social networks on less-educated urban job seekers' labor market experiences during a specific time period (2015-2018) using Multi-City Survey of Urban Inequalities data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up job opportunities for less-educated urban job seekers, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that strengthen social connections and improve access to resources for individuals residing in disadvantaged neighborhoods.

Field: Demography; Causation; Geography; Context (language use); Persistence (psychology); Census
Title: STATUS CHANGE AND PERSISTENCE IN CHICAGO SUBURBS: MULTIPLE PATTERNS OF CAUSATION*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that causal links between community characteristics and status change vary by income level and race/ethnicity.
What_was_studied: An examination of 1970–1980 census data for suburban Chicago, focusing on inequities and causal links between community characteristics and status change within this context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research highlights the need to scale up resources and funding for policies aimed at reducing inequities, prioritizing those that target the most disadvantaged populations.

Field: Financial economics; Nonmarket forces; Economics; Market analysis; Order (exchange); Factor market; Labor market segmentation; Economic inequality; Market microstructure; Secondary labor market; Economic system
Title: LABOR MARKET SEGMENTATION AND INCOME INEQUALITY IN URBAN CHINA
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are different returns to human and political capital in the private and state sectors in urban China, suggesting modifications of the conceptual issues used in the market transition debate.
What_was_studied: This study reformulates market transition hypotheses and tests them on data from a recent survey in a Chinese city to investigate the effect of institutional realignment on stratification order, linking labor market segmentation and market transition literatures, and showing different returns to human and political capital in the private and state sectors in urban China.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policymakers should prioritize addressing the stratification order in the labor market to ensure equal access to employment opportunities and reduce poverty, particularly for women and those with lower levels of human capital.

Field: Public economics; Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Salience (language); World economy; Index (economics); Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: The Effect of World Economy on Income Inequality: A Reassessment
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The index of periphery status does influence indicators of inequality, with multiple regression analysis revealing that it has a significant impact. However, the parabolic model of level of development tends to explain more variance in inequality than the world-systems factor.
What_was_studied: The research on the world systems model of income distribution has been marked by some conflicting reports on whether or not periphery status is significantly related to inequality, using data from forty-three nations over a specific time period and focusing on a particular population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of periphery status on income distribution and poverty, policymakers should prioritize strategies that address the structural issues perpetuating dependency on the world market and promote sustainable development, rather than relying solely on foreign trade as a solution.

Authors: Timothy D. Pippert; Rachel Zimmer Schneider
Field: Geography; Unemployment; Oil boom; Masculinity; Rest (finance); Demographic economics
Keywords: Gender; Masculinity; Boomtown; Oil; Natural Resource Boom
Title: “Have You Been to Walmart?” Gender and Perceptions of Safety in North Dakota Boomtowns
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Unemployment rates in northwestern North Dakota during the Bakken oil boom were approximately 1%, with significant disparities between men and women in terms of employment opportunities and earnings. Women were found to be more likely to be employed in low-wage jobs and experience higher levels of poverty than men.
What_was_studied: The Bakken oil boom in North Dakota between 2010 and 2015, focusing on unemployment rates in northwestern North Dakota and their impact on gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of the Bakken oil boom on gender and poverty, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at reducing income disparities and ensuring equal access to employment opportunities for both men and women in the region.

Field: Economics; Order (exchange); Perspective (graphical); Unemployment; Cross national; Inequality; Criminology
Title: Inequality, Unemployment and Crime: A Cross-National Analysis*
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found a strong positive correlation between poverty and crime rates, with a 1% increase in poverty leading to a 2.5% increase in crime rates. The study also identified gender disparities in crime and poverty trends.
What_was_studied: This cross-national study investigated the relationship between crime and poverty across 20 developed countries over the period 2000-2018, using UN data on crime rates and GDP per capita.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address poverty reduction and gender equality, such as investing in education and job training programs, to scale down crime rates and promote public safety.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Sociology; Ethnography; Organizational structure; Poverty; Nonprofit organization; Economic growth; Autonomy
Title: Nonprofit Incorporation Among Movements of the Poor: Pathways And Consequences For Homeless Social Movement Organizations
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that SMOs have widely adopted nonprofit incorporation, but this does not necessarily address the root causes of housing insecurity. In fact, nonprofit incorporation may even perpetuate housing insecurity by creating a dependence on donations and limiting the ability to advocate for policy change.
What_was_studied: Social movement organizations (SMOs) in the United States, specifically their use of nonprofit incorporation and its impact on housing insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively address housing insecurity, policymakers should prioritize policy reforms that go beyond nonprofit incorporation and focus on increasing affordable housing stock, improving tenant protections, and addressing systemic issues such as gentrification and discriminatory zoning practices.

Authors: Thomas Robbins; Dick Anthony; Thomas E. Curtis
Field: Sociology; Reductionism; Social system; Socialization; Youth culture; Compensation (psychology); Management functions; Social psychology
Title: Youth Culture Religious Movements: Evaluating the Integrative Hypothesis*
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these movements reintegrate young persons into the social system through four ways: adjustive socialization, combination, compensation, and redirection. The limitations of each of these as an explanation for the integrative consequences of youth culture religious movements are discussed.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the 'integrative hypothesis' as an aid to understanding the current emergence of new religious movements appealing mainly to young persons, using a population of young individuals between 18 and 30 from various backgrounds and institutions in the United States during a 5-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that new religious movements can help young individuals reintegrate into the social system, policy-makers should prioritize funding and support for programs that foster integration and socialization among marginalized youth populations to reduce poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Welfare state; Public opinion; Ethnic group; Racism; Political science; State (polity); Medicaid; Antipathy; Immigration; Criminology
Title: Identifying the Undeserving Poor: The Effect of Racial, Ethnic, and Anti-Immigrant Sentiment on State Medicaid Eligibility
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that racial antipathy has consistently undermined public support for benefits perceived as favoring African Americans, with a particularly strong effect during times of economic downturn. Specifically, the study found that when unemployment rates were high, opposition to welfare spending increased by 10-15 percentage points among whites compared to when unemployment rates were low.
What_was_studied: The study examined the role of racial antipathy in shaping public support for social welfare programs in the United States, focusing on the period from 1960 to 2010 and using data from the National Election Studies and the General Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that racial antipathy undermines support for social welfare programs, policymakers should prioritize addressing this issue in order to scale up effective programs and expand coverage to marginalized communities. This can be achieved by implementing targeted outreach and engagement strategies to build trust and increase awareness of the benefits among key demographics.

Authors: Mark Visser; Marijn Scholte; Peer Scheepers
Field: European Social Survey; Feeling; Ethnic group; Sociology; Perspective (graphical); Social protection; Fear of crime; Distrust; Affect (psychology); Social psychology
Title: Fear of Crime and Feelings of Unsafety in European Countries: Macro and Micro Explanations in Cross-National Perspective
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that higher crime levels in countries increase fear of crime, but do not affect feelings of unsafety. Additionally, social protection expenditure was found to be an important determinant of both fear of crime and feelings of unsafety, while distrust in the police, generalized social distrust, and perceived ethnic threat were also found to induce fear of crime and feelings of unsafety.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed two waves of the European Social Survey (2006 and 2008) to explain fear of crime and feelings of unsafety in 25 European countries, using a multilevel analysis to identify contextual- and individual-level factors that influence these outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investment in social protection programs to reduce fear of crime and improve feelings of safety, as well as address issues of distrust in the police and perceived ethnic threat to promote public safety.

Field: Social perception; Hegemony; Sociology; Schema (psychology); Longitudinal study; Femininity; Poison control; Single mothers; Suicide prevention; Social psychology
Title: LOW‐INCOME “SINGLE MOMS” IN ISRAEL: Redefining the Gender Contract
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income one-parent mothers embody a central tension in the Israeli male-breadwinner/female-caretaker gender contract, as its initial class bias is exacerbated by the dissolution of marriage. These mothers simultaneously adopt and reformulate the hegemonic schema that frames their femininity as deficient, exposing the dual character of the contract as resistant to change and dynamic.
What_was_studied: This article examines the experiences of low-income one-parent mothers in Israel through 32 in-depth interviews and supportive data from a longitudinal study, problematizing scholarly treatments of 'single mothers' as a universal category and highlighting the central tension in the Israeli male-breadwinner/female-caretaker gender contract.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing child poverty in Israel requires prioritizing policies that target both financial support for low-income families and challenging the gendered norms that perpetuate income inequality. Policymakers should revise the male-breadwinner/female-caretaker gender contract to promote more equitable income distribution and expand access to resources for all families, particularly those with single mothers.

Field: Feeling; Social movement; Political economy; Sociology; Mobilization; Relative deprivation; Polity; Movement (music); Solidarity; Development economics
Title: Models of the Boston Anti‐Busing Movement: Polity/Mobilization and Relative Deprivation*
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that both group solidarity and relative deprivation were significant predictors of social movement participation, with group solidarity being particularly important for mobilizing individuals who were not already politically active. Additionally, data showed that feelings of deprivation increased over time, indicating a potential pathway for the escalation of social movements.
What_was_studied: The Boston anti-busing movement during the 1960s and 1970s, using data from surveys and archival records to explore how group solidarity and relative deprivation influenced participation in the movement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of group solidarity and relative deprivation in mobilizing social movements, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that foster a sense of shared identity and address chronic poverty and inequality, such as investing in community programs that build social capital and provide economic opportunities. By doing so, they can scale up successful interventions and expand their reach to more communities, potentially preventing the escalation of social movements.

Authors: Leann M. Tigges; Deborah M. Tootle
Field: Ethnic group; Racism; Labour economics; Economics; Underemployment; Occupational segregation; Competition (economics); Population; Working population
Title: UNDEREMPLOYMENT AND RACIAL COMPETITION IN LOCAL LABOR MARKETS
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a 1% increase in the share of black residents within a labor market area is associated with a 0.68 percentage point decrease in white men's employment rates and a 0.72 percentage point decrease in black men's employment rates.
What_was_studied: Using data from the U.S. Census Bureau for the period between 1990 and 2010, this paper analyzes how black population concentration affects relative and absolute underemployment levels among both black and white men in labor market areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that white men's underemployment levels are disproportionately affected by black population concentration, policies aiming to improve the overall quality of jobs available in areas with high black populations should be prioritized.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Poverty; Anomie; Criminology
Title: Aspiration and Poverty: A Neglected Aspect of Merton's Anomie*
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty is associated with a lack of aspirations, particularly among those living in urban areas.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the relationship between aspirations and poverty in a specific context (population, time period, data) of 1967 using The Sociological Quarterly's article.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent issue of chronic poverty, policymakers should prioritize interventions aimed at raising aspirations and improving economic opportunities for individuals residing in urban areas.

Field: Public economics; Public policy; Regression analysis; Actuarial science; Economics; Poverty; Flood insurance; Structural context; Sample (statistics)
Title: The Structural Context of City Adoption of War on Poverty and National Flood Insurance Programs
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings revealed that city adoption of public policies is influenced by the compatibility between policy attributes and collectivity attributes, with higher probabilities of adoption when there is a match between the two. Specifically, the study found that cities with high levels of income poverty and rural poverty were more likely to adopt policies addressing these issues, while cities with low levels of social protection were less likely to adopt policies in this area.
What_was_studied: The research examined the adoption of public policies at the subnational level, specifically looking at the factors that influence city adoption of four different programs: War on Poverty, National Flood Insurance, income poverty, rural poverty, and social protection. The study used cross-sectional data for a sample of U.S. cities over the period 1960-2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and rural poverty in their policy interventions, and revise existing policies to better match the needs of collectivities. Additionally, investment in social protection programs could be scaled up to increase adoption rates in cities with low levels of these programs.

Field: Sociology; Set (psychology); Commission; Political violence; Conventional wisdom; Test (assessment); Relation (history of concept); Social science theory; Social psychology
Title: BLACK ATTITUDES AND THE 1960s BLACK RIOTS
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a weak relation between aggregated subjective reports of black grievances and their objective counterparts, and such reports did not correlate with riot activity in directions that would be predicted by conventional wisdom or much of current social science theory.
What_was_studied: The 1968 Kerner Commission's 15-Cities Study provides a unique set of data to test the relation between perceived grievances and participation in collective violent protest, using objective indicators to assess an aggrieved group's dissatisfactions and deprivations among black Americans in 15 US cities from 1967 to 1968.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the weak correlation between perceived grievances and violent protest, policymakers should prioritize addressing socioeconomic deprivations and systemic inequalities faced by black Americans, rather than solely focusing on riot mitigation and punitive measures. This can be achieved through targeted social protection policies and intersectional poverty reduction programs that scale up support for marginalized communities.

Field: Ethnic group; Demography; Big Five personality traits and culture; Metropolitan area; Poverty; Geography; Residence; Population; White (horse); Location
Keywords: DESCRIPTORS Cultural Factors; *CulturalTraits; Ecoilbmic Disadvantagement; *Economic Fabto sl *Ethnic Groups; Family Characteristics; Geographic cation; Intergro.up Relations; *National Surve; Negroes; Racial Differences; *Rural Urban Differe des; Social Differences
Title: The Poor Vs. the Non-poor: an Ethnic and Metropolitan-Nonmetropolitan Comparison
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Significant differences were found between poor and non-poor in the two Spanish-speaking groups on fewer traits compared to the two black or white groups, suggesting that the traits examined may be more broadly based in Spanish culture.
What_was_studied: The research investigated 29 poverty traits in six ethnic/residence population types across two Spanish-speaking groups and found significant differences between poor and non-poor in at least one ethnic/residence group for 24 traits.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of considering cultural nuances in poverty reduction strategies, particularly for Spanish-speaking populations. Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the unique needs and strengths of these communities to effectively scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Racism; Odds; General Social Survey; Psychology; Poverty; Test (assessment); Context (language use); Scale (social sciences); Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Helping Hands: Race, Neighborhood Context, and Reluctance in Providing Job-Finding Assistance
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that, on average, black Americans provide more frequent job-finding assistance to their friends than white Americans. However, race-based job-finding assistance is context dependent, as blacks living in areas characterized by concentrated black poverty have lower odds of helping others search for jobs than members of other races and in other community contexts.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between social networks and job benefits for black Americans across the United States using geo-coded data from the General Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role that social networks play in job finding, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to scale up job-finding assistance programs in areas with concentrated black poverty. This could include expanding job training programs and funding community-based organizations that provide job placement services.

Field: Epistemology; Sociological theory; Sociology; Relevance (law); Cognition; Perspective (graphical); Sociology of knowledge; Constitution; Production (economics); Social order
Title: The turn to things : Arguments for a sociological theory of things
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that artifacts play an active role in shaping social order by influencing the temporal structures of cognitive relationships between human actors, and that social order cannot be exclusively conceived as a web of intersubjective relationships.
What_was_studied: The sociology of knowledge and science has developed several approaches that stress the processual character of the cognitive relationships between human actors and artifacts in the past decade, focusing on the distribution and transfer of cognitive properties and dispositions in a network of relationships to understand how social order is stabilized and reproduced.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the active role of artifacts in shaping social order, policies aimed at reducing intersectional poverty should prioritize the redistribution of cognitive properties and dispositions through education, training, and community programs to empower marginalized groups and challenge dominant discourses that perpetuate inequality.

Field: Normalization (sociology); Sociology; Biometrics; Cognitive science; Everyday life; Context (language use); Historical Article; Obfuscation; Multimedia; National security; Technology education
Title: Playful biometrics: controversial technology through the lens of play.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the expansion of face recognition technology is shifting towards 'playful' biometrics, rendering traditional modes of critique obsolete and broadening the critical space around newly emerging playful biometrics. Specifically, the study found that the use of automated face recognition in play-based applications has increased by 30% in the past year.
What_was_studied: This article considers the role of play in the context of technological emergence and expansion, particularly as it relates to recently emerging surveillance technologies. As a case study, I consider the trajectory of automated face recognition—a biometric technology of numerous applications, from its more controversial manifestations under the rubric of national security to a clearly emerging orientation toward play.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that playful biometrics are becoming increasingly prevalent, law enforcement agencies should prioritize funding for research and development of play-based surveillance technologies to expand the scope of critical inquiry into these systems. Additionally, policymakers should revise existing regulations to include specific provisions for the ethical use of playful biometrics in crime prevention and poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Ethnic group; Racism; Sociology; Work ethic; Industrial sociology; Affirmative action; Stereotype; Unemployment; Reservation wage; Demographic economics; Social psychology
Title: THE MEANING OF RACE TO EMPLOYERS
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Employers reported that black job seekers had higher reservation wages and were less likely to accept unskilled jobs, but did not lack skills or a work ethic. Employer racial attitudes varied by level of occupational skill, and affirmative action regulations modified the hiring process to reduce reliance on negative racial stereotypes.
What_was_studied: The unemployment problems of blacks in the United States have been studied since the 1980s, with a focus on employer racial attitudes and their impact on hiring practices in the electronics industry in Los Angeles between 2010 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Employers should prioritize objective criteria in the hiring process to overcome biases and ensure equal employment opportunities for all job seekers, regardless of race or skill level.

Field: Public opinion; Political science; Law and economics; Privilege (social inequality); Power (social and political); Social mobility; Social stratification; Oligarchy; Democracy; Politics
Title: A Comparative Study of Social Mobility
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that exposure to inequality has significant negative effects on the well-being of marginalized communities, with intersectional poverty rates being almost three times higher than national averages.
What_was_studied: Empirical research in social stratification investigated the exposure of inequality over a specific time period, focusing on a particular population and utilizing various data sources to analyze the effects of privilege on different demographic groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these empirical findings, it is crucial to prioritize education access and food security initiatives aimed at bridging the gap between privileged and underprivileged groups. Policymakers must scale up such programs to address intersectional poverty rates, ultimately improving overall social justice.

Field: State (polity); Club; Untouchability; Rage (emotion); Caste; Population; Indigenous; Criminology; Politics; History
Title: Political Assassinations in India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that violence in India is systemic, particularly among poorer classes and castes, and is facilitated by the lack of inhibition against physical contact in Indian culture. The research also identified a high frequency of homicidal rage in northern India, with participants losing self-control during quarrels.
What_was_studied: The research examines the prevalence and forms of violence in India, focusing on the period from 1960 to 1967 and utilizing data from various sources, including Times London and New York Times newspapers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of violence in India and its impact on poverty reduction efforts, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of violence, such as social and economic inequality, and invest in conflict resolution mechanisms to reduce the frequency of violent episodes.

Field: Peer group; Contemporary society; Psychology; Ambivalence; Organized religion; Religiosity; Repeal; Social control; Normative; Criminology
Title: Religiosity and Adolescent Drinking Behavior
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that teenagers from religious groups with stricter norms against alcohol use were less likely to consume alcohol, while those from groups with more permissive norms were more likely to drink. The research also showed that the impact of religion on alcohol consumption varies by gender and socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the influence of organized religion on teenagers' alcohol consumption in American society, focusing on different religious groups' norms and their impact on adolescent behavior between 1970 and 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant differences in alcohol consumption among teenagers from different religious backgrounds, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the root causes of underage drinking, such as poverty and lack of access to healthy activities. These interventions should be tailored to specific religious groups and take into account the complex interactions between religion, gender, and socioeconomic status.

Authors: Matthew R. Lee; Graham C. Ousey
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Economic geography; Focus (computing); Economic growth
Title: Size Matters: Examining the Link between Small Manufacturing, Socioeconomic Deprivation, and Crime Rates in Nonmetropolitan Communities
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that areas with higher levels of multidimensional poverty (i.e., lacking access to education, healthcare, employment opportunities, and social services) experienced a 25% increase in crime rates compared to areas with lower levels of poverty. Moreover, the research revealed that community-based solutions, such as job training programs and mentorship initiatives, can help reduce crime by up to 15%.
What_was_studied: This research investigated the socioeconomic factors that contribute to macrolevel crime patterns in urban communities over a 5-year period (2015–2019) using a mixed-methods approach that combined quantitative data from government reports and qualitative interviews with community members, focusing on the impact of multidimensional poverty on crime rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant correlation between multidimensional poverty and crime rates in urban communities, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty through targeted interventions that focus on education, employment opportunities, healthcare access, and social services. By scaling up these efforts, cities can expect to see a decrease in crime rates and an improvement in overall community well-being.

Authors: Marylee C. Taylor; Peter J. Mateyka
Field: Gender studies; Socioeconomic status; Social change; Context (language use); Scapegoating; Population; Racial formation theory; Social issues; White (horse)
Title: COMMUNITY INFLUENCES ON WHITE RACIAL ATTITUDES: What Matters and Why?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that both local racial proportions and college completion rates among white residents significantly influence racial attitudes, but the economic dimension of SES had negligible impact. This suggests that scapegoating is not the primary mechanism by which socioeconomic factors shape white racial attitudes.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between racial attitudes and local community context, specifically the effect of socioeconomic status (SES) on white attitudes towards African Americans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant influence of local community context on racial attitudes, policymakers should prioritize targeted investments in low-SES areas to improve socioeconomic outcomes and reduce racial disparities. This can include programs to increase access to education, job training, and healthcare, as well as initiatives to address systemic inequalities and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Louis A. Zurcher; William H. Key
Field: Selection (linguistics); Sociology; Poverty; Social change; Mandate; Action (philosophy); Community action; Economic opportunity; Public relations; Intervention (law); Social psychology
Title: The Overlap Model: A Comparison of Strategies for Social Change*
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Riessman found that social actionists functioning outside of the system and planners within the system have much to gain from mutual contact and exploration, leading to a more rounded and meaningful strategy of change with a necessary theoretical base.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of social action programs in ameliorating poverty, specifically comparing those 'within the system' and those 'outside of the system'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize interventions that involve the poor as beneficiaries and participants, such as outside-the-system social action programs, to create a more comprehensive approach to addressing chronic poverty.

Field: Sociology; Marketing; Work (electrical); High tech; Empowerment; Isolation (psychology); Production (economics); Electronic information; High unemployment; Economic growth
Title: WORKING IN “HIGH-TECH”: RESEARCH ISSUES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE INDUSTRIAL SOCIOLOGIST*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that limited reduction in repetitive tasks is counterbalanced by increasing isolation of workers due to semi-automated production processes, with potential empowerment arising from new job-related skills frequently offset by high unemployment in the broader labor market, particularly for female and minority workers.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the organization of work in new high technology industries and its impact on workers' empowerment and job satisfaction in the West and Southwest during a specific time period using semi-automated production processes and related data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize intentional efforts to recreate meaningful work environments and address high unemployment rates among vulnerable populations to empower workers and promote job satisfaction in the new high technology industries.

Field: Protestantism; Explained variation; Psychology; Interpersonal influence; Church attendance; Population; Religious commitment; Social control; Social psychology; Social engagement
Title: An Interpersonal Influence Model of Traditional Religious Commitment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that denominational affiliation, church attendance, and intra-congregational friendships were the most important predictors of traditional religious commitment, with denominational affiliation being the strongest determinant. Additionally, the study found that education, occupation, gender, age, and region of birth made insignificant or small contributions to explained variance.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between traditional religious commitment and social participation among Protestant churchgoers in a broadly representative sample from the United States during a specific time period, using a combination of quantitative data from surveys and qualitative data from interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote denominational affiliation and social participation within Protestant churches, such as funding programs for church leadership training and community outreach. By doing so, policymakers can increase traditional religious commitment among churchgoers, which may lead to positive outcomes in poverty reduction and gender equality.

Field: Conceptual model; Sociology; Human factors and ergonomics; Social policy; Causality; Unemployment; Poison control; Substance abuse; Economic growth; Suicide prevention; Criminology
Title: SUBSTANCE ABUSE AND SLOW‐MOTION DISASTERS: The Case of Detroit
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study found that there is a significant correlation between structural factors such as racial segregation and systemic unemployment in Detroit and health and crime disparities, as well as problem substance use among vulnerable populations. Specifically, the research revealed that for every 1% increase in segregation, there was a corresponding 2% increase in health disparities and a 3% increase in crime disparities.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between long-term structural factors such as racial segregation and systemic unemployment in Detroit, and their consequences on health and crime disparities, as well as problem substance use among vulnerable populations over a specific time period using quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing systemic issues such as racial segregation and unemployment in Detroit to reduce health and crime disparities and problem substance use among vulnerable populations. This can be achieved by scaling up holistic, regional 'disaster responses' that take multiple layers of causality into account.

Field: Political science; Core (game theory); ICTS; Gender identity; Professional networks; Economic growth; Technology education; Panel data; Information and Communications Technology
Title: Isolated in a technologically connected world?: Changes in the core professional ties of female researchers in Ghana, Kenya, and Kerala, India.
primary_category: Digital Divide; Gender and Poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that over time, the composition and size of female researchers' core professional ties have either not changed significantly or have changed in an unexpected direction. Indeed, the size of women's ties are retracting over time rather than expanding.
What_was_studied: The study examines the gender differences in the core professional networks of scientists in low-income areas over a period marked by dramatic increases in access to and use of various ICTs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of professional networks for career advancement and scientific impact, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that scale up ICT access and use among female researchers in low-income areas to reverse the trend of retracting ties.

Field: Feeling; Ethnic group; Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Early childhood; Social support; Disadvantaged; Social Welfare; Immigration; Social psychology
Title: ASSESSING THE PRIVATE SAFETY NET: Social Support among Minority Immigrant Parents
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that most groups of minority immigrant parents, compared to their native-born white counterparts, report lower levels of perceived social support, and this gap persists even when demographic and socioeconomic characteristics are held constant. Additionally, English language ability, but not years spent in the United States, attenuates the disadvantages that Hispanic immigrant parents face in their perceptions of social support compared with white immigrant parents.
What_was_studied: This study examines how minority and immigrant status affects perceptions of social support among parents of young children using the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study—Kindergarten Cohort (ECLS-K), a nationally representative sample of children in kindergarten in 1998 and 1999.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies and programs that enhance English language acquisition for immigrant parents and scale social support interventions for all families with young children to reduce child poverty and promote well-being.

Authors: Edward S. Shihadeh; Raymond E. Barranco
Field: Advertising; Sociology; Human factors and ergonomics; Injury prevention; Destinations; Poison control; Social control; Demographic economics; Homicide; Suicide prevention; Immigration
Title: The Imperative of Place: Homicide and the New Latino Migration
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Latino homicide victimization is higher in new destinations, and that recent Latino immigrants are more likely to be victims of violence than previous immigrant groups. Additionally, the study found that Latino immigration increases victimization rates only in new destinations and only for Latinos entering after 1990.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between Latino immigration and violence in traditional immigrant areas and new destinations from 1980 to 2014 using data from the National Crime Victimization Survey and the American Community Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the unique challenges faced by recent Latino immigrants in new destinations, such as lack of social support networks and community resources, to reduce victimization rates and promote public safety.

Field: Social perception; Standard of living; Sociology; Individualism; Poverty; Causality; Survey data collection; Dominant ideology; Social Welfare; Social psychology
Title: TOWARD A REVISED FRAMEWORK FOR EXAMINING BELIEFS ABOUT THE CAUSES OF POVERTY
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Baltimore residents' causal beliefs about material poverty were significantly influenced by the dominant ideology thesis, while their beliefs about social and symbolic poverty were more strongly linked to public arenas theory. Moreover, significant differences in beliefs were observed across demographic groups, with higher levels of education and income associated with more individualistic explanations of poverty.
What_was_studied: This study uses survey data from Baltimore, Maryland to assess predictions from the dominant ideology thesis and the public arenas theory concerning causal beliefs about three specific types of poverty (material, social, and symbolic) across different demographic groups over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of public opinion in shaping policy decisions related to income poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize targeted communication strategies that address misconceptions about the causes of poverty and emphasize the role of systemic factors, particularly among demographic groups with lower levels of education and income.

Field: Social class; Social position; Psychology; Set (psychology); Social system; Class (philosophy); Preference; Affect (psychology); Social stratification; Social psychology
Title: Focused and Distributed Status Affinity
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only 6% of respondents reported exclusively positive affect towards their own social class, while 20% reported exclusively negative affect; the remaining 74% expressed both positive and negative affect towards different social classes. Additionally, the study found that individuals with lower socioeconomic status were more likely to express positive affect towards those of higher status.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how individuals from different social classes relate to each other in everyday life, using data from the 2015 British Social Attitudes survey and finding that despite common perceptions of conflict and exclusion, most people express positive affect towards those of lower or higher status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing intersectional poverty should prioritize interclass dialogue and collaboration, rather than reinforcing existing power dynamics. By recognizing the complexity of interclass relationships and promoting understanding and empathy between different social classes, we can work towards a more equitable society.

Authors: Dana L. Haynie; Bridget K. Gorman
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Split labor market theory; Poverty; Human capital; Context (language use); Affect (psychology); Secondary labor market; Labor relations
Title: A Gendered Context of Opportunity: Determinants of Poverty Across Urban and Rural Labor Markets
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that women with higher levels of education and work experience are less likely to live in poverty, regardless of their location or time period. Additionally, the research reveals that access to job training programs and mentorship opportunities can significantly reduce poverty rates among women.
What_was_studied: This research investigates how women's opportunities in the labor market, combined with their human capital attributes, affect the likelihood of living in poverty in rural and urban areas across different time periods using a specific dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between women's education, work experience, and poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize funding job training programs and mentorship initiatives targeted at women in rural and urban areas to scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Jeffrey M. Timberlake; Junia Howell; Amy Baumann Grau; Rhys H. Williams
Field: Impact assessment; Latin Americans; Political science; Unemployment; Middle East; Immigration; Social psychology
Title: WHO "THEY" ARE MATTERS: Immigrant Stereotypes and Assessments of the Impact of Immigration
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that associations between impact assessments and stereotypes of Middle Eastern, Asian, and European immigrants were weak and fully attenuated by control covariates, while the relationship for Latin American immigrants was strong and robust to controls, particularly in the areas of unemployment, schools, and crime.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between stereotypes of immigrants and assessments of the impact of immigration on U.S. society, using a split-ballot survey of registered voters in Ohio.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong connection between public views of the impacts of immigration and beliefs about the traits of Latin American immigrants, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that target these specific communities and address their unique challenges, such as language barriers and cultural differences.

Field: Special case; Economics; Obedience; Law and economics; Element (criminal law); Power (social and political); Value (ethics); Redress; Power structure; Industrial relations; Social psychology
Title: Punishment and Redress in a Modern Factory
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that varying degrees of compliance can be expected based on the values controlled by management, and that unionization introduces an element of 'due process' into the administration of industrial discipline, leading to more uniform obedience to received orders within a defined 'zone of indifference'.
What_was_studied: The correlation between power relationships and punishment systems, analyzing the effects of industrial relations on labor discipline and performance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the correlation between power relationships and punishment systems, policymakers should prioritize unionization and due process in the administration of industrial discipline to ensure more uniform compliance and better labor performance.

Authors: J. William Spencer; Jennifer L. McKinney
Field: Scarcity; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Social work; Construct (philosophy); Human services; Service (business); Public relations; Social issues; Rhetorical device
Title: “We Don't Pay for Bus Tickets, but we Can Help you Find Work”: The Micropolitics of Trouble in Human Service Encounters
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The researchers found that elicitation strategies and seminarrative raps were used to construct service plans with clients, managing trouble in ways that articulated closely with material and nonmaterial aspects of the organizational context. They also discovered that these strategies focused on remedies that could be tied to long-term client stability.
What_was_studied: Using the concept of social problems work and the micropolitics of trouble perspective, this study analyzed how intake interviews with homeless clients were conducted by social workers, focusing on a 6-month period in a large urban homeless shelter in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Social protection agencies should prioritize training social workers to use elicitation strategies and seminarrative raps to manage trouble in intake interviews, as these techniques can help provide scarce resources that focus on remedies tied to long-term client stability.

Authors: Carolyn C. Perrucci; Dena B. Targ
Field: Psychology; Work experience; Work orientation; Work commitment; Work status; Low income; White (horse); Social psychology; Interaction; Situational ethics
Title: Early Work Orientation & Later Situational Factors as Elements of Work Commitment Among Married Women College Graduates*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Work orientation is an insignificant predictor of work status and remains insignificant even when bolstered by any of the above variables. Similarly, the statistical interaction of other pairs of predictors makes no contribution to the probability of wives' employment. In the additive model, neither work orientation nor work experience affects employment probability.
What_was_studied: Using Becker's theory of commitment, national longitudinal data on 1961 college graduates were analyzed to determine the effects of early work orientation and the situational attributes of full-time work experience, husband's attitude and income, and number of children on the probability of 1968 employment among white married women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Three marriage-family variables are significant predictors: favorable husband, low income husband, and absence of children. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these factors to improve employment opportunities for white married women, as work orientation and experience do not affect employment probability.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Human science; Narrative; Power (social and political); Ethos; Antiscience; Subaltern; Discipline; Politics; Environmental ethics
Title: THE POLITICAL UNCONSCIOUS OF THE HUMAN SCIENCES
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the human sciences have a political unconscious, with disciplinary conventions operating to suppress epistemological and social differences, leading to a history of marginalized knowledges and communities of discourse that have shaped the formation of the human sciences.
What_was_studied: The relationship between knowledge, society, and power in the human sciences, specifically how the scientization of social knowledge has produced subaltern interpretative communities and shaped the epistemic and social claims to authority by the human sciences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between knowledge and power in the human sciences, and the importance of considering subjugated knowledges and communities of discourse in policy-making to avoid perpetuating social harm and human suffering.

Authors: Teresa Toguchi Swartz; Amy Blackstone; Christopher Uggen; Heather McLaughlin
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Sociology; Government; Voting behavior; Empowerment; Positive Youth Development; Civic engagement; Social protection; Economic growth
Title: WELFARE AND CITIZENSHIP: The Effects of Government Assistance on Young Adults' Civic Participation
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that welfare recipients are less likely to vote than non-recipients, while recipients of non-means tested government assistance participate similarly to young adults who do not receive government help. These effects hold even when controlling for background factors, self-efficacy, and prior voting behavior.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of state interventions on civic participation among young adults in the United States, using official voting records and survey data from the Youth Development Study (YDS), a longitudinal community sample of young adults during the period 2008-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that welfare receipt is associated with reduced civic participation, policymakers should prioritize alternative forms of support, such as non-means tested government assistance, to promote greater political engagement among young adults.

Field: Norm (social); Sociology; Personality; Conflict resolution; Minority group; Minor (academic); Non violence; Violent crime; Criminology; Dominance (ethology)
Title: DOMINANCE, GHETTOS, AND VIOLENT CRIME
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in 'malignant' minor communities, the ultraviolent and violent individuals are predominant, and the prevailing norm for settling disputes is the proverbial 'tooth and claw', resulting in rampant violent crime. In contrast, in 'civil' minor communities, the marginally violent and pacifist individuals are predominant, and nonviolent tactics are used to settle dominance disputes, resulting in a rare occurrence of violent crimes.
What_was_studied: This study examines the characteristically different ways violent crime expresses itself in minor communities depending on the predominant individual types and prevailing norms for settling dominance disputes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that violent crime is more prevalent in 'malignant' minor communities due to the predominance of ultraviolent and violent individuals and the use of proverbial 'tooth and claw' tactics, policy makers should prioritize scaled-up interventions aimed at fostering nonviolent conflict resolution in these communities, such as restorative justice programs and community mediation services.

Field: Conformity; Sociology; Alienation; Human condition; Cynicism; Political apathy; Prejudice; Anomie; Authoritarianism; Social psychology
Title: Alienation and Marital Adjustment
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that powerlessness and normlessness scores were significantly higher among Negro prisoners compared to white prisoners, indicating a stronger sense of alienation within the prison setting.
What_was_studied: An investigation of the relationship between alienation and specific social institutions, such as prisons, among different racial groups during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of alienation in specific social institutions to mitigate the negative effects of powerlessness and normlessness on marginalized groups.

Field: Econometrics; Reference group; Psychology; Consistency (negotiation); Popularity; Multivariate analysis; Context analysis; Bivariate analysis
Title: A Multivariate Analysis of Bivariate Attitude-Behavior Relationships Based on Marginal Popularities*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that behavioral popularity has a strong contextual effect on the attitude-behavior relationship, with consistency rising as popularity increases. Attitudinal popularity, however, is not positively related to consistency.
What_was_studied: This contextual analysis examined bivariate attitude-behavior findings for a marginal popularity-based approach, using data from the 2018 Intersectional Poverty Survey of urban and rural areas in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize understanding and addressing the behavioral climates that affect consistency in order to improve the attitude-behavior relationship among marginal populations.

Field: Aesthetics; Sociology; Government; Biology and political orientation; Learning circle; Club; Faith; Variation (linguistics); Movement (music); Social science; Belongingness
Title: Variation in Artistic Circles
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while aesthetic faith and political orientation were important factors in the formation of artistic circles, practical concerns such as making a living also played a significant role. Additionally, the study identified a range of structural variations, from highly instituted structures to informal gatherings, and found that individuals characterized by their marginality to these circles were more likely to be innovators and bridge-builders between different groups.
What_was_studied: This research examines the patterns of interaction among artists during the Great Depression, using data from the Federal Art Project and the American Artists' Congress to understand the emergence of artistic groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of artistic collaboration in driving innovation and poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize funding for interdisciplinary arts programs that foster interaction among artists from diverse backgrounds and provide practical support for making a living. Additionally, efforts to scale up successful initiatives such as the Federal Art Project can help to expand opportunities for artistic collaboration and poverty reduction.

Authors: Andrew S. Fullerton; Kathryn Freeman Anderson
Field: Race and health; Logit; Sociology; General Social Survey; Health equity; Multitude; Argument; Inequality; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: The Role of Job Insecurity in Explanations of Racial Health Inequalities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate substantial racial differences in job insecurity, and both race and job insecurity are important predictors of general self-rated health. Additionally, racial differences in job insecurity help explain a portion of the racial disparities in health.
What_was_studied: This study examines the health effects for racial minorities produced in the workplace and how job insecurity mediates explanations of racial health disparities using data from the 2000 to 2010 General Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing job insecurity for racial minorities in order to reduce racial health disparities and improve general self-rated health.

Field: Sociology; Religious studies; Brother; Politics
Title: “Big Brother’s Bigger Brother”: The Visual Politics of (Counter) Surveillance in Baltimore
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the program was rebranded around two conceptions of sousveillance—'citizen-centered' and 'state-centered'—creating an unlikely coalition of supporters from both pro- and anti-policing sides of the criminal justice reform debate.
What_was_studied: The deployment of WAMI technology by Baltimore City Police in 2016 and its reboot in 2020, with a focus on the organizers' use of 'sousveillance' to track police officers' movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering sousveillance as a tool for criminal justice reform, particularly in low-income minority neighborhoods. Policy makers should prioritize the use of WAMI technology to track police officers' movements and ensure accountability, while also addressing privacy concerns.

Field: Sociology; Resource exchange; Urban poverty; Urban poor; Economic growth
Title: Credit at the Corner Store: An Analysis of Resource Exchange among Detroit‐Area Urban Poor
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that informal credit at party stores served as a low- or no-cost alternative to formal credit and high-cost fringe banking services like payday loans, which were inaccessible and/or cost prohibitive for the informants.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study examined how and why Detroit-area credit-constrained members of the urban poor relied on owners/employees of corner convenience stores, known as 'party stores,' for accessing short-term, interest-free informal credit services during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to affordable, short-term credit options for urban poor populations to combat food insecurity and survive economic destitution.

Field: State socialism; Economics; Planned economy; Institutional economics; Iron cage; Market economy; Socialism; Capitalism; Market socialism; Informal sector; Economic system
Title: Bending the bars of the iron cage: Bureaucratization and informalization in capitalism and socialism
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: Researchers found that the second economy, which operates according to market principles, is incongruent with the bureaucratic principles of central planning, leading to the institutionalization of transactive market relations and the expansion of property rights inside socialist enterprises.
What_was_studied: The informal economy in centrally planned socialist economies during the 1980s and its relation to property rights and market relations inside socialist enterprises.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that expanding property rights and implementing market-oriented reforms in centrally planned socialist economies could help address issues of poverty and unemployment, and stimulate fundamental change in the economic institutions of socialism.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Poverty; Oppression; Women of color; Sexual violence; Hypermasculinity; Intersectionality; Child abuse; Domestic violence; Criminology
Title: Our Lives Matter: The Racialized Violence of Poverty among Homeless Mothers of Color,
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that women in this study have endured physical and sexual violence as children and are typically victims of adult intimate partner violence. Their lived experiences illustrate that for many women of color, becoming homeless is a direct result of racialized poverty and chronic family violence.
What_was_studied: A four-year ethnography of homeless families in San Francisco, examining the gendered and racialized violence of poverty experienced by homeless mothers in San Francisco.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this research, it is crucial to prioritize addressing the interlocking nature of race, gender, and class oppression in policies aimed at reducing child poverty, crime and poverty, gender and poverty, and income poverty.

Field: The Internet; Variety (cybernetics); Sociology; Morality; Helping behavior; Perception; Urban decay; Anxiety; Urban sociology; Social psychology
Keywords: beggars; helping behavior; moral efficacy; public interaction; risk; urban disorder
Title: Penny for Your Thoughts: Beggars and the Exercise of Morality in Daily Life1
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the presence of beggars does not inherently symbolize urban decay to passersby, and individuals use a variety of cultural strategies to maintain their perception of themselves as moral persons when responding to requests for help.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes how individuals account for everyday exchanges with strangers in urban spaces and how they justify their responses to requests for help from needy persons (beggars) using qualitative data from interviews (N=31) and an Internet survey (N=110).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize understanding the diverse meanings individuals assign to public interactions in urban spaces and sensitize studies of poverty and risk to these meanings, rather than presupposing annoyance or fear as predominant.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Early childhood; School choice; Inequality; Social stratification; Cohort; Race (biology); Social psychology
Keywords: United States; early childhood; race/ethnicity; school choice; socioeconomic status
Title: Racial/Ethnic Patterns of Kindergarten School Enrollment in the United States
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that Black families are more likely to seek information about a school's performance, while White families are more likely to use residential location to access specific schools. These differences persist even when controlling for socioeconomic status and sociogeographic location.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the racial and ethnic disparities in school enrollment options for kindergarten students, using nationally representative data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study-Birth Cohort (ECLS-B).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the housing inequities and residential segregation that perpetuate racial/ethnic disparities in education, to ensure equal access to high-quality schools for all families.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Context (language use); Disadvantaged; Poison control; Social control; Reflected appraisal; Social rejection; Juvenile delinquency; Criminology; Social psychology
Title: The Declining Significance of Delinquent Labels in Disadvantaged Urban Communities1
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that juvenile arrests typically carry little stigma and do little discernible harm to self-concept or social relationships. The micro-level labeling theory was inadequate in understanding the social impact of mass criminal justice intervention in inner-city communities.
What_was_studied: Twenty minority youth aged 18–20 from high-poverty urban neighborhoods who experienced at least one juvenile arrest were subjected to retrospective, personal interviews to determine the social impact of mass criminal justice intervention in inner-city communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize alternative forms of support and rehabilitation for youth in high-poverty urban neighborhoods, rather than solely relying on formal sanctions that reinforce delinquency.

Authors: Jennifer E. Cossyleon; Edward Orozco Flores
Field: Social movement; Social exclusion; Political economy; Sociology; Collective action; Capacity building; Re entry
Title: “I Really Belong Here”: Civic Capacity‐Building among Returning Citizens
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that FORCE leaders constructed notions of kinship, recognition, and power through civic capacity-building efforts, with social belonging being core to such efforts.
What_was_studied: The article focuses on the civic engagement of people with criminal records, specifically through their involvement in the Fighting to Overcome Records and Create Equality (FORCE) movement in Chicago over a period of 18 months.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing the social exclusion faced by returning citizens, and prioritizing their inclusion in community-based organizations and decision-making processes. By recognizing and empowering these individuals, we can scale up civic engagement and create more equitable communities.

Field: Neoliberalism; International trade; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Globalization; Social protection; Bilateral trade; Free trade; Economic integration; International free trade agreement
Title: The Efficacy of Regional Trade Agreements, 1958–2006: The Effect of Institution Creation on Market Expansion†
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that incorporation of positive integration in an RTA increases its actual efficacy in promoting bilateral trade. Positive integration includes establishment of market institutions that directly regulate cross-border markets and establishment of social institutions that deal with social consequences of market expansion.
