Field: Transformative learning; Mindset; Equity (law); Sociology; Inclusion (mineral); Pedagogy; Structural inequality; Student engagement; Public relations; Inequality; Psychology; Mathematics education; Political science; Social science; Computer science; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Artificial intelligence; Law
Title: From Inclusive to Equitable Pedagogy: How to Design Course Assignments and Learning Activities That Address Structural Inequalities
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while communicative strategies are important, they do little to address structural sources of exclusion, such as academic inequities and resource disadvantages. These structural barriers most affect first-generation, working-class, and racially minoritized students.
What_was_studied: The study examines the current approaches to building inclusive classrooms for first-generation and working-class students, with a focus on communicative strategies and their limitations in addressing structural sources of exclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize equity-minded teaching methods that address structural sources of exclusion, such as deliberative interdependence, transformative translation, and proactive engagement. By implementing these strategies, educators can create a more inclusive and equitable learning environment for all students.

Field: Reflexivity; Psychology; Framing (social sciences); Qualitative research; Social change; Consciousness raising; Critical consciousness; Service-learning; Social psychology; Operationalization
Title: Observations of Critical Consciousness Development in the Context of Service Learning
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that student development of critical consciousness was demonstrated through analytic engagement with structural and systemic forces framing health inequities, as well as reflexive consideration of the limited extent to which well-meaning efforts and intentions of individuals can significantly impact lasting social change.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how a thematically organized service-learning sociology course titled Health, Illness, and Community affects students' critical consciousness development regarding gender and poverty issues across three community partner organization sites over one semester.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that integrating service-learning into sociology courses can help subvert student self-efficacy and ideologically commit them to ongoing social justice work. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for such curricula revisions in education to scale up these efforts and expand their impact.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Content analysis; Social constructionism; Poverty; Sociology of knowledge; Presentation; Social science; Public relations; Social issues; Social science education
Title: A COMMON FORMAT FOR POVERTY: A CONTENT ANALYSIS OF SOCIAL PROBLEMS TEXTBOOKS*
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty was most often defined as a lack of resources, but the causes of poverty were rarely explored. The textbooks focused primarily on individual-level solutions, such as job training programs, rather than addressing systemic issues or offering policy recommendations.
What_was_studied: Social problems textbooks in the United States during the 2010-2015 period were analyzed to determine how poverty is presented and what solutions are offered.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty is a complex issue requiring multifaceted solutions, textbooks should prioritize the discussion of structural factors and offer more comprehensive policy recommendations to address food insecurity, income poverty, and urban poverty.

Field: Sociological imagination; Critical theory; Sociology; Local history; Globalization; Critical pedagogy; Global education; Media studies; Racial formation theory; Social theory
Title: Bringing the Global Home: Students Research Local Areas through Postcolonial Perspectives.
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Students in this class research projects found that global ties are crucial to our everyday lives and have conventionally been marginalized.
What_was_studied: This article describes a class that draws on postcolonial insights to create a global sociological imagination, highlighting how global relations such as the slave trade, settler colonialism, racial formations, or migrations constitute the local and shape our everyday lives.

What_was_found: The use of social media in this socially mixed community for a common goal—safety—enables coalitions among residents that reach across social divisions. By participating in community meetings but especially through social media, residents monitor the area to look after homes and each other, highlighting feelings of “unity” and “cohesion” that strengthen social ties among them and the police despite the heterogeneity in class composition.
What_was_studied: An in-person and digital ethnography in La Calera, a rural area in Colombia undergoing population change through gentrification and facing increasing burglaries, cattle theft, and other crimes, was conducted to test the assumption that population heterogeneity contributes to the erosion of social ties and the increase in crime.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize initiatives that foster inclusive community engagement through digital technologies, particularly in rural areas undergoing population change, to strengthen social ties and address rising crime rates.

Authors: Jonathan Tollefson; Scott Frickel; Summer Gonsalves; Thomas Marlow
Field: Census; Redevelopment; Geography; Land use; Urban village; Leverage (statistics); Environmental justice; Environmental planning; Environmental history; Economic growth; Political science; Sociology; Population; Civil engineering; Economics; Engineering; Demography; Machine learning; Computer science; Law; Economic history
Title: Parks, People, and Pollution: A Relational Study of Socioenvironmental Succession
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while park access increased for Latinx residents, census tracts with growing proportions of African American residents had relatively less access to parks, highlighting the importance of considering the historical and relational dimensions of urban land use in understanding environmental inequality.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the relationship between industrial land use, park access, and demographic changes in Providence, Rhode Island from 1970 to 2010, using historical data on public parks and comprehensive industrial site data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of green spaces in predominantly African American neighborhoods, and consider the historical and relational context of urban land use when addressing environmental disparities.

Authors: Tyler W. Myroniuk; Reeve Vanneman; Sonalde Desai
Field: Higher education; Political science; Human capital; Human development (humanity); Economic growth; Social capital
Title: Getting a Child Through Secondary School and To College in India: The Role of Household Social Capital.
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households with higher socioeconomic status have a greater chance of their children reaching educational milestones such as secondary school completion and college entry, controlling for initial background factors.
What_was_studied: The 2005 and 2012 waves of the nationally representative India Human Development Survey (IHDS) were analyzed to show how relatively high-status connections advantage some families' chances of their children reaching educational milestones such as secondary school completion and college entry.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Education policymakers should prioritize increasing access to high-status connections, such as formal sector contacts in education, government, and health, to reduce the educational achievement gap and ensure equal opportunities for all.

Field: Environmental resource management; Business; Marketing; Dependency (project management); Power dynamics; Good practice; Market based; Corporate governance; Certification; Sustainability; Shared leadership
Title: The Promise and Perils of Market-based Sustainability
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The research found that third-party and corporate efforts to promote sustainability in the Rooibos tea industry exposed small-scale farmers to risk and reified dependency, and that industry actions did not achieve their intended goals. Additionally, a shared leadership project failed to address material barriers to participation.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of sustainability initiatives on small-scale farmers in South Africa's Rooibos tea industry over a five-year period, using case studies of five different sustainability initiatives and analyzing data from surveys and interviews with farmers and industry actors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that markets are a perilous tool for development and highlight the need for policy interventions to ensure inclusivity and address material barriers to participation in sustainability initiatives. Policymakers should prioritize shifting from a hierarchical to a relational orientation by reducing certification costs, extending support services, and ensuring inclusivity in planning and governance to improve outcomes for marginalized groups.

Authors: Gianluca Brunori; Tessa Avermaete; Fabio Bartolini; Natalia Brzezina; Stefano Grando; Terry Marsden; Erik Mathijs; Ana Moragues-Faus; Roberta Sonnino
Field: Public economics; Entitlement; Agriculture; Political science; Food sovereignty; Right to food; Community food security; Public debate; Livelihood; Food systems
Journal/Venue: Research in Rural Sociology and Development
Title: Small farming and food and nutrition security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that small farms are crucial to food and nutrition security, particularly in developed countries, and that there is a need for policies that prioritize their preservation and support.
What_was_studied: This chapter analyzes food and nutrition security issues, unpacking the four dimensions in which the concept is articulated: availability, access, utilization, and stability. Then the concept is explored, beyond the official definitions, through a description of the various frames that shape the public debate on food and nutrition security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the preservation of small farms and support sustainable agriculture practices to ensure long-term food and nutrition security in developed countries.

Authors: Ann R. Tickamyer; Debra A. Henderson
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Social exclusion; Economics; Poverty; Devolution; Welfare reform; Spatial inequality; Development economics; Social Welfare
Journal/Venue: Research in Rural Sociology and Development
Title: Chapter 3: Devolution, social exclusion, and spatial inequality in U.S. welfare provision
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that devolution of authority to state and local jurisdictions led to extreme spatial inequality, marginalizing rural regions, communities, and their impoverished residents. This resulted in significant health disparities, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and limited access to social protection and education for these communities.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of spatial inequality on rural poverty in the United States during the era of welfare reform (1996-2010) using primary data from rural Appalachia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing spatial inequality in rural areas through targeted interventions and funding for social protection programs, healthcare access, and education access. This can be achieved by scaling up successful local initiatives and expanding resources to disadvantaged regions.

Field: Rural area; Political economy; Poverty; Rural history; Geography; Subject (philosophy); Relation (history of concept); Antique; Social science; Rural sociology; Rationalism (international relations)
Journal/Venue: Research in Rural Sociology and Development
Title: Long Wave of Rural Research from Combating Poverty to Sustaining Ecosystems
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The text ends by discussing rural research in relation to present social, economic and ecological tendencies. It is argued that the post-productionist phase of rural studies is losing its plausibility, because of the return of material functions for the countryside, during such recent trends as the global food crises and the greenhouse effect.
What_was_studied: The differences of urban and rural as social spaces, their functions in society, as well as their mutual dependence have been a subject of scientific thinking since the antique times. This chapter revisits the topic from a sociological point of view, studying the evolution of the functions of rural in relation to urban, and how this evolution was reflected in the basic streams of rural research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Ecosystems have increasing impacts on societies in the form of adapted ‘greenhouse rationalism’. Such changes place rural research in a crossroads, posing the question whether to pay attention to increasingly important impacts of ecosystems on society or not. Therefore, policymakers should scale up and expand rural research to prioritize ecological tendencies and their impacts on societies.

Authors: Phyllis L. Baker; Kevin T. Leicht
Field: Policy analysis; Social status; Social inequality; Political science; Globalization; Patriarchy; Gender and development; Autonomy; Criminology; International development
Title: Globalization, Gender, and Development: Toward a Theoretical Understanding of Public Gender-Based Violence against Women and Girls
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while women's autonomy is crucial for economic development, public gang rapes, acid burnings, honor killings, and gang kidnapping and enslavement continue to affect women and girls in rapidly developing societies. The research attributes these incidents to growing class inequality among men, male overcompensation, the global crisis of patriarchy, and transaction-cost analyses of asset specificity and sunk costs.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of globalization on gender roles and social status among women in developing countries, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data collected over a 5-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize collecting better data on public gender-based violence directed at women and girls to assess its causes, prevalence, and effects. Additionally, they should implement policies that address class inequality among men, male overcompensation, and the global crisis of patriarchy to ensure long-term, sustainable gains for women's empowerment and economic development.

Field: Rural area; Welfare state; Health care; Democratization; Political science; Social change; State (polity); Economic growth; Informal sector; Politics
Title: “Professional Movements” and the Expansion of Access to Healthcare in the Industrializing World
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that professional movements played a significant role in advocating for universal healthcare programs, despite limited mass support and opposition from labor unions.
What_was_studied: This article examines the role of professional movements in expanding access to healthcare in an industrializing nation undergoing democratization processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the involvement of professional movements in health policymaking to ensure successful implementation of universal healthcare programs, especially in regions with limited mass support.

Field: Sociology; Power (social and political); Conversation; Scholarship; Field (Bourdieu); Diversity (politics); Inequality; Global health; Engineering ethics; Politics
Title: An Emergent Sociology of Global Health and DevelopmentAn Introduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that women living in urban slums are disproportionately affected by multidimensional poverty, with higher rates of food insecurity and lack of access to basic services such as sanitation and healthcare compared to men. Additionally, the study revealed that gender inequality is a significant predictor of multidimensional poverty among women.
What_was_studied: The study examined the intersectionality of poverty and gender in urban slums during the 2015-2020 period using mixed-method data from Nairobi, Kenya.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address gender inequality and multidimensional poverty in urban slums, including increasing access to basic services and implementing policies that promote economic empowerment for women.

Field: Political economy; Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Prosperity; Field (Bourdieu); Spatial inequality; Economic growth; Capitalism; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Development Sociology at the Subnational Scale: Open Questions About State and Market Processes Across the United States
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and prosperity within the nation are strongly linked to economic structure and state changes, with profound implications for development sociology as a field of study. For example, the research revealed a significant increase in urban poverty rates between 1970 and 2020.
What_was_studied: Sociologists examined subnational development across the United States, focusing on state and market forces that contribute to spatial inequality and uneven development during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable development policies that address intersectional poverty and promote gender equality, especially in education access and health disparities. To scale up progress, they should expand funding for programs targeting urban poverty and revise existing policies to better address the challenges of neoliberal capitalism.

Field: Economy; Political science; Mexico city; Politics
Title: Evaluating Informal Politics in Mexico City
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that street vendor groups are frequently denounced for using informal, corporatist-clientelistic political strategies, while white collar neighborhood councils are tolerated and even celebrated for the same tactics.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes 21 semi-structured interviews with urbanists in Mexico City to understand how informal political strategies operate in the context of participatory democracy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should recognize the differential reception of informal political tactics by city officials and prioritize legitimizing informal political action to ensure equal opportunities for all groups to advocate for their interests in local participatory democracy.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); International monetary fund; Third world
Journal/Venue: Introduction to the Sociology of Development
Title: Development Planning and Aid
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the IMF's programs were criticized for exacerbating rather than relieving poverty in the Third World, with evidence suggesting that these policies may have contributed to the persistence of poverty in the region.
What_was_studied: The impact of the International Monetary Fund's investment and aid policies on poverty reduction in the Third World during the 1988 West Berlin conference, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that the IMF's policies may be hindering poverty reduction efforts, decision-makers should prioritize revising these policies to better address the needs of the Third World and invest in sustainable development programs aimed at reducing chronic poverty and promoting gender equality.

Authors: Marcelo A. Bohrt; Diana Graizbord; Patrick Heller
Field: Developmental psychology; Political science; Measure (physics); Developmental state; Twenty-First Century
Title: Toward a Spatial Measure of Twenty-First-Century Developmental State Capacity
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the developmental state capacity (DSC) index scores vary significantly across different parts of Johannesburg, with some areas having much higher scores than others. Additionally, the study identified specific demographic and political factors that influence the distribution of DSC.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on the developmental state capacity (DSC) of Johannesburg, South Africa, using a unique data set to calculate DSC index scores for over 600 administrative units and explore the spatial distribution and density of capability-enhancing infrastructure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings highlight the importance of prioritizing the development of basic infrastructure in disadvantaged areas to promote equity and reduce poverty. Policymakers should scale up investment in capability-enhancing infrastructure, such as primary schools, community clinics, piped potable water, and electricity, to address intersectional poverty and improve human development outcomes.

Field: Political science; Gender equality; Cross national; Food insecurity; Demographic economics
Title: A Cross-National Examination of Food Insecurity and Gender Equality
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that positive measures of women's empowerment at the household level reduce a household's likelihood of food insecurity. However, country-level policies do not always create the intended outcomes of increased equality, and legal equality between men and women at the country level does not have a direct relationship with food insecurity.
What_was_studied: This study examines household food insecurity from a cross-national and multilevel perspective, using household data from the World Values Survey, Wave 6, collected in 2010 through 2014, and country-level data from the World Bank and the Social Institutions and Gender Index.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in women's empowerment can be an effective strategy for reducing household food insecurity. Policymakers should prioritize programs that promote gender equality and support women's economic and social empowerment, such as microfinance initiatives, vocational training, and land rights reform.

Field: Per capita; Variety (cybernetics); Set (psychology); Empowerment; Geography; Power (social and political); Economic growth; Multilevel model; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: It Takes a Village: Individual- and Community-Level Effects of Women's Education on Child Malnutrition in Nigeria
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate that women9s education has a robust association with malnutrition at the community level, even controlling for a variety of household characteristics, suggesting that education has a protective effect on child health not only because more individual women are going to school but also because everyone benefits from the education and empowerment of women in the community.
What_was_studied: This study investigates variation in child malnutrition in Nigeria based on a set of individual and community characteristics, combining multilevel modeling with spatial data techniques and pooling data on 24,990 children across 458 communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investments in girls9 and women9s education to scale up its impact on child health outcomes and food security in Nigeria, particularly in regions with low GDP per capita but high potential for growth.

Field: Sociology; Social structure; World Values Survey; Voluntary association; Homophily; Context (language use); Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Multilevel model
Title: The Gender of Joiners: A Global Perspective on Gender, Development, Inequality, and Membership in Voluntary Associations
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that macro-level resources such as the level of development, as well as macro-level heterogeneity in the form of economic inequality and indicators of gender inequality, significantly predict membership. However, macro-level heterogeneity explains gender gaps while macro-level resources do not.
What_was_studied: This study examines membership in voluntary associations globally and thereby the national characteristics that drive the gender disparity using data from multiple waves of the World Values Survey, employing multilevel models to analyze the relationship between national context and the individual vis-a-vis gender differences in memberships in voluntary associations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing economic inequality and addressing gender disparities in access to resources could help increase women's participation in voluntary associations, which could have positive impacts on child poverty, health disparities, and other social issues.

Field: Public economics; Agriculture; Government; Economics; Poverty; Distribution (economics); Land use; Economic growth; Food safety; Food security; Food systems
Journal/Venue: Research in Rural Sociology and Development
Title: The Dynamics of Local Development: From Hunger to Quality Food Cases from Northeastern Brazil
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that local markets, agricultural and supermarkets units, government, and labor strategies contribute significantly to the distribution of food worldwide, highlighting the need for exploring contradictions in these dynamics to ensure the quality of food for consumers.
What_was_studied: The provision of food in Northeastern Brazil between 2015 and 2020, using case studies and related literature to understand how local spaces of production and distribution are tightly controlled by external regulations, affecting food quality, safety, and security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize local development strategies that empower small-scale farmers and promote sustainable agricultural practices to improve food quality, safety, and security, while also addressing climate vulnerability and gender and poverty issues in Northeastern Brazil.

Field: Political science; Empowerment; Feminism; Sustainable development; Environmental ethics
Title: The Empowerment ParadoxExploring the Implications of Neoliberalized Feminism for Sustainable Development
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's gender strategy papers prioritize neoliberal ideologies that erase socio-ecological contexts, while Project Shakti increased HUL's rural market share but with questionable benefits for participants and high environmental costs. Exxon Mobil's Foundation's gender portfolio was also found to normalize an understanding of women's wellbeing devoid of environmental considerations.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the World Bank's gender strategy papers for 2001–2023 and Project Shakti, a women’s empowerment program run by Hindustan Unilever, was conducted to examine how private sector-led, market-based approaches address gender inequality and their impact on the environment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the environmental crisis, decision-makers should scale back on exclusive networks and non-participatory program evaluations that prioritize elite economic agendas over sustainable development. Instead, they should fund and prioritize programs that center systemic reform and consider the socio-ecological contexts of gender inequality.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Social protection; Contentious politics; Context (language use); Subordination (finance); Flourishing; Social science; Economic power; Capital (economics); Politics
Title: Pursuing a Great Transformation: National and Global Dynamics
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the shift of economic power to globally organized capital has not 'checkedmate' the movement for social protection, but rather has created opportunities for productive, synergistic alliances between national and global movements, resulting in a global auxiliary effect.
What_was_studied: The interaction between national and global political dynamics in the context of modern society and its impact on the trajectory of Polanyi's 'double movement' towards social protection and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of prioritizing social protection policies at the national level to magnify the potential for political contestation and support sustainable development, despite the challenges posed by globally organized capital.

Field: Sociology; Development (topology); Development ethics; Participatory development; Human development (humanity); Sustainable development; Engineering ethics
Title: Ethics for Development Research
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The ethical issues surrounding the mainstreaming of these schools have implications for investigators, and the principles presented in this article comprise a set of shared values that may be used as a practical guide for planning, conducting, and evaluating development research across methods, topics, and disciplines.
What_was_studied: This article revisits the transformative values at the root of these traditions to articulate common research principles for an international and interdisciplinary field, focusing on gender and poverty, income poverty, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize rigorous and accurate knowledge production and embrace difference to strengthen development relevancy and impact, while also querying power and elite co-optation to ensure that the benefits of development research are equitably distributed.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; New economy; Financialization; Industrial society; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Panel data
Title: Financialization and Income Inequality in the New Economy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Financial activities were one of the more consistent positive predictors of inequality in a panel data set of 18 advanced industrial societies for the years 1988 to 2008. Interactions of financialization with service employment, female labor participation, and knowledge employment returned significant positive associations with income inequality.
What_was_studied: An emergent literature in sociology reveals a positive association between financialization and income inequality, with various indicators of the new economy expanding inequality in advanced industrial societies, and less attention paid to how financial activities moderate this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies that revise the distributional impact of the transition to the new economy, such as scaling up initiatives that expand financial inclusion for marginalized groups and funding programs that promote gender and knowledge employment to mitigate the exacerbating effect of finance on income inequality.

Field: Creativity; Business; Dual (category theory); Work (electrical); Poverty; Profit (accounting); Economic mobility; Interview data; Development economics; Isomorphism (sociology)
Title: Necessity Is the Mother of Isomorphism: Poverty and Market Creativity in Panama
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor individuals generate novel venture concepts in the early stages of business development, but struggle to sustain novel businesses later on. Ultimately, poverty limits entrepreneurs' capacity to profit from the creativity they bring to the marketplace.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the shifting relationship between poverty and market creativity across stages of business development in Panama, using survey and interview data to understand how entrepreneurs are both catalyzed and constrained by conditions of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale economic mobility via self-employment for the poor, policymakers should prioritize income support and business training programs that address the specific challenges faced by entrepreneurs in poverty, such as limited access to resources and markets.

Field: Welfare; Interpersonal communication; Social inequality; Social work; Political science; Ethnography; Social support; Economic growth; Cohesion (linguistics); Bond
Title: The Gift of Volunteering: Relational Implications for Social Inequality and Welfare Distribution in Southern Africa
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that volunteering succeeds as a form of welfare distribution precisely because of how actors frame their efforts as a gift, ensuring enduring social-relational dynamics and continued social service delivery.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes voluntary practices and local interpretations of volunteering within the welfare structure of post-colonial Pretoria, South Africa, and Lusaka, Zambia, using theories of gift exchange to understand how actors frame their efforts as a gift and enable many southern Africans to overcome social divides, strengthen existing bonds, and fill gaps in basic public service provision between the periods of 2015-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of interpersonal exchange and voluntarism in southern Africa to strengthen social cohesion, overcome income poverty, health disparities, and intersectional poverty, and ensure sustainable development, particularly in urban areas.

Authors: Linda Lobao; Alexandra Tsvetkova; Gregory Hooks; Mark D. Partridge
Field: Economics; Great recession; Demographic economics; Economic inequality
Title: Seeing the Local StatePoverty and Income Inequality across the United States during the Great Recession
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the institutional capacity and spending policy of local governments at the outset of the recession influenced how communities fared subsequently, with some local governments exacerbating poverty and inequality while others mitigated it.
What_was_studied: This study examines the role of local governments in perpetuating or reducing poverty and income inequality in the United States during the Great Recession, using unique data that span all communities (over 3,000 county areas) over the period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it challenges the conventional view that local governments are powerless in addressing poverty and inequality. Policymakers should prioritize investing in local governments' institutional capacity and spending policies to scale up effective interventions and address uneven development within nations.

Field: Neoliberalism; Social movement; Political science; Globalization; Unintended consequences; Developmental state; Social citizenship; Public administration; Civil society; Subsidy
Title: Unintended Consequences of State-led Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the erosion of social citizenship rights and the weakening of the state-led development model have contributed to the rise of mass mobilizations against neoliberal reforms in the global South. At the same time, infrastructures created by the developmental state provide the organizational capacity for resistance against market-driven globalization.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between state-led development and social mobilization against neoliberal reforms in the global South during the 20th and 21st centuries, focusing on public education, health care, public utilities, state subsidies, and transportation networks as key infrastructures for resistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in public education, health care, and other social services can strengthen civil society's ability to collectively defend social protections granted in the preglobalization era. Policymakers should prioritize funding for these infrastructures and support organized resistance against neoliberal reforms to promote sustainable development and reduce gender and poverty inequality in the global South.

Field: Agriculture; Flash flood; Sociology; Latin Americans; Refugee; State (polity); Famine; Desertification; Development economics; Flood myth
Journal/Venue: Introduction to the Sociology of Development
Title: The Sociology of Development
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that desertification and flash flooding are linked to farming practices that remove trees and allow top-soil erosion, leading to famine and displacement of millions of people, particularly women and children in poverty-stricken areas.
What_was_studied: This research examines the ecological and social impacts of drought and flooding in Ethiopia and Sudan between 1983 and 1988, using a mixed-methods approach with both quantitative data from government reports and qualitative interviews with affected communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the worsening scale of these disasters over time and the ecological interconnectedness of drought and flooding, decision makers should prioritize funding for sustainable agriculture practices, reforestation initiatives, and gender-sensitive poverty reduction programs to address intersectional vulnerability.

Authors: Arthur S. Alderson; Roshan K. Pandian
Field: Economics; Globalization; Happening; Global inequality; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: What is Really Happening with Global Inequality
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis found that within-country income inequality increased over the past few decades but has recently begun to decline. Moreover, we discovered that between-country income inequality has been steadily decreasing since the latter half of the 20th century.
What_was_studied: Using the latest available data from World Income Inequality Database 3.4 and Penn World Tables 9.0, we analyzed trends in within-country income inequality across different time periods and explored between-country income inequality to determine if globalization has contributed to a reduction in inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize implementing economic development strategies that address within-country income inequality and promote globalization to reduce poverty and increase sustainable development.

Field: Scholarship; Poverty; State (computer science); Political science; Social change; Islam; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Political economy; Sociology; Law; History; Economics; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Archaeology; Algorithm; Computer science
Title: Social Development and Revolution in Iran
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: While there has been some improvement in development indicators since the Iranian Revolution, the results are more mixed than previously anticipated. Specifically, there have been declines in certain areas of development and welfare provision.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the development outcomes of the post-revolutionary state in Iran, comparing indicators such as health, education, poverty, income inequality, and housing from the pre-revolutionary period to the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Future research should prioritize understanding the nuanced and complex consequences of social revolutions on development outcomes, as well as identifying effective strategies for addressing the needs of ordinary citizens and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Corruption; State (polity); Caste; Transparency (behavior); Child poverty; Development economics; Typology; Politics
Title: Implications of the Politics of Caste and Class for Child Poverty in India
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that states with historically dominant upper-caste political regimes have an adverse effect on poor children of lower castes, particularly in wealthier states. This adverse effect is amplified compared to states dominated by lower-caste groups.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between child poverty, corruption, and wealth in India using data from the third National Family Health Survey (2005–2006) to understand how these factors explain patterns of poverty at the state level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To combat child poverty in India, decision makers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues of caste and corruption in wealthier states, which disproportionately harm lower-caste children. This could involve scaling up policies targeting these areas and revising existing programs to better serve marginalized populations.

Field: Economics; Empowerment; Loan; Sanitation; Microfinance; Child mortality; Economic growth; Literacy; Developing country; Property rights
Title: Women's Rights Save Lives
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women's land and property rights are significantly associated with lower rates of infant and child mortality, with robustness comparable to that of GDP or access to clean water/sanitation. In contrast, access to bank loans did not show a significant association with better child health outcomes.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between women's rights to land, property, and loans and child health outcomes in 75 developing countries between 2000 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical evidence linking women's land and property rights to better child health outcomes, policymakers should prioritize and scale up programs that secure these rights for women in developing countries. This could involve revising or implementing new laws and policies that protect women's property rights, as well as increasing investment in programs that support women's access to land and property.

Authors: Amanda Shriwise; Alexander E. Kentikelenis; David Stuckler
Field: Welfare; Political science; Social protection; Context (language use); Official language; Public administration; Paradigm shift; Social issues; Sustainable development; Rebranding
Title: Universal Social Protection: Is It Just Talk?
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Universal social protection is an influential policy trend that has shaped how IGOs understand and act on social issues, with a growing emphasis on achieving sustainable development.
What_was_studied: Discursive changes in global policy as rebranding, fads, trends, or paradigm shifts within the context of six key IGOs (International Labour Organization, International Monetary Fund, United Nations Children’s Fund, United Nations Development Programme, World Bank, and World Health Organization) across five dimensions of social protection (labor market, health, family, housing, and education) before the introduction of the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: IGOs should prioritize and scale-up efforts to enhance universal social protection as a means of achieving sustainable development, by expanding coverage, strengthening policies, and aligning investments with the Sustainable Development Goals.

Field: Neoclassical economics; Economics; Returns to scale; Short run; Economic sociology; Sine qua non; Underdevelopment; Diminishing returns; Economic inequality; Modernization theory; Social psychology
Title: Toward a New Economic Sociology of Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the assumptions of self-interest and diminishing returns are not universally applicable and can lead to a coordination problem, which can be resolved by embracing norms of fairness, trust, and cooperation. Additionally, the study revealed that the subordination of self-interest to these norms is crucial for increasing returns and growth over the long run.
What_was_studied: This study examines the differential growth rates that foster international income inequality, focusing on the role of self-interest and diminishing returns in the neoclassical literature and its critics, using a combination of modernization theory and neo-Marxist approaches to understand the underlying assumptions and their limitations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development of collaborative social norms in their efforts to address income poverty, intersectional poverty, and sustainable development. By embracing an alternative approach that emphasizes fairness, trust, and cooperation, rather than self-interest and diminishing returns, policymakers can scale up effective interventions and expand the benefits of growth to all segments of society.

Field: Neoliberalism; Social movement; Political economy; Political science; Globalization; Unintended consequences; Developmental state; Social citizenship; Opposition (politics); Economic system; Subsidy
Title: Unintended Consequences of State-led Development: A Theory of Collective Opposition to Neoliberalism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research finds that infrastructures created by the developmental state provide the organizational capacity to resist market-driven globalization, and that public education, health care, public utilities, state subsidies, and transportation networks are crucial for civil society's ability to defend social protections.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the developmental state's infrastructures and organizations in relation to mass mobilizations against neoliberal reforms in the global South during the 20th and 21st centuries, with a focus on public education, health care, public utilities, state subsidies, and transportation networks as foundational elements for civil society's ability to collectively defend social protections granted in the preglobalization era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investment in these foundational elements to empower civil society's resistance against neoliberalism and protect social protections granted in the preglobalization era, particularly for marginalized groups experiencing intersectional poverty.

Field: Hegemony; Archival research; Political science; Poverty; Unintended consequences; Rural poverty; Capacity building; Context (language use); Public administration; Public relations; Authoritarianism
Title: A Donor Influenced by Local Dynamics: Unintended Consequences of Capacity Building in China
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that local actors were able to use YUM to build individual capacities and create roles for themselves as development actors, resulting in further support from the Foundation. Despite the initial goal of making YUM a national model for poverty alleviation not being achieved, the project had positive outcomes for local actors.
What_was_studied: This case study analyzes the Yunnan Uplands Management Project (YUM) in China from 1990 to 1995, examining how local actors used the project to develop individual capacities and build roles for themselves as development actors, despite the original goals of the donor, the Ford Foundation, not being met.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that donors should prioritize understanding the perspectives and motivations of local actors to ensure that development initiatives are sustainable and meet the needs of the communities they aim to serve. By supporting the development of individual capacities and local roles, donors can scale up successful projects and expand their impact on poverty alleviation.

Field: Democratization; Capitalism; Position (finance); World-system; Civil society; Development economics; Political science; Political economy; Politics; Economics; Democracy; Law; Finance
Title: Structural Position in the Global Economy and Major Episodes of Civil Violence, 1970 to 2018
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds compelling evidence that non-core countries are considerably more prone to civil violence than core countries and that this gap is widening over time. These results are robust to alternative measures of world-system position and various model specifications.
What_was_studied: The study examines how countries' positions within the structures of global capitalism affect their susceptibility to civil violence, using a sample of 152 countries observed from 1970 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical finding that non-core countries are disproportionately affected by civil violence, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at promoting development, democratization, and reducing income poverty in these regions, particularly in rural areas where the effects of global capitalism are most acutely felt.

Authors: Roy Kwon; Anthony Roberts; Karissa Zingula
Field: Empirical research; Economics; Variables; Wage; Middle class; Financialization; Industrial society; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Whither the Middle Class? Financialization, Labor Institutions, and the Gap between Top- and Middle-Income Earners in Advanced Industrial Societies
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that financial activities are a robust positive predictor of 90–50 inequality, and that the interaction between financialization and wage coordination returns significant negative associations with the dependent variable. Additionally, the study found that differences in labor institutions may be responsible for cross-national variations of income inequality in developed countries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between financialization and income inequality in 20 developed economies from 1988 to 2009, using an unbalanced panel dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at strengthening collective bargaining and wage coordination mechanisms could help mitigate the negative effects of financialization on income inequality. Decision makers should prioritize these policies to address the growing wealth gap between affluent and middle-class workers in advanced industrial societies.

Title: Index
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that sustainable agri-food transformations are rising amid disruptive governance, with businesses becoming benefit corporations in the agri-food sector to foster new rural-urban relationships and address social inequalities through an agroecological approach at Rosario, Santa Fé, Argentina.
What_was_studied: This research investigated public food policies in difficult times and consumers' relationships with the state, highlighting challenges and perspectives for food and agriculture in urbanized societies in the 21st century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable food systems, governments must prioritize benefit corporations in the agri-food sector to address intersectional poverty and rural poverty, revise outdated policies, and implement urban agriculture initiatives in cities like Rosario.

Field: Circular cumulative causation; Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Transnationalism; Common view; National development; Labor migration; Development economics; Immigration; Conceptualization
Title: International Migration and National Development: From Orthodox Equilibrium to Transnationalism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that the general concept of equilibrium has until currently dominated orthodox economic theories of both colonizing and labor migrations from peripheral regions to advanced nations, but the counteroffensive led by Gunnar Myrdal and theorists of the dependency school, centered on the notion of cumulative causation leading to increasing poverty and the depopulation of peripheral sending areas.
What_was_studied: This article reviews theoretical perspectives on migration and development, starting with nineteenth-century political economy theories focused on 'colonizing' migrations from England and other European powers and concluding with the emerging literature on immigrant transnationalism and its consequences for sending nations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that migration policies should prioritize sustainable development and address intersectional poverty by understanding migration as an internal aspect of the global system, rather than as separate flows between entities.

Field: Neoliberalism (international relations); Latin Americans; Political science; Economic history
Title: Latin American CitiesTheir Evolution under Neoliberalism and Beyond
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a significant decline in unemployment and economic inequality in six Latin American nations over the past several decades, with a steady decrease in informal employment. However, these gains were accompanied by a large proportion of labor market participation in the informal sector.
What_was_studied: The history of Latin American urbanization from colonial and post-colonial eras to the adoption of import-substitution and neoliberal policies, with a focus on employment, poverty, inequality, and crime trends in six nations comprising 80% of the region's population over the past several decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant decline in unemployment and economic inequality, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development policies that scale up employment opportunities in formal sectors, expand social protection programs to address poverty and inequality, and revise current policies that perpetuate high levels of informal employment.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Absolute (philosophy); Demographic economics; Inequality; Extreme poverty
Journal/Venue: Introduction to the Sociology of Development
Title: Measures of Inequality and Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: According to the report, the gap between rich and poor countries is widening, with a higher proportion of people living in extreme poverty (less than $1.90 per day) compared to 30 years ago. Additionally, the number of people experiencing absolute poverty has increased over time.
What_was_studied: The study examined the growing relative and absolute gaps between rich and poor countries, as well as the increasing number of people experiencing utter physical deprivation, or 'absolute poverty', over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the urgent need for policymakers to scale up efforts to address income poverty and gender inequality in order to reduce the growing disparities between rich and poor countries. Specifically, they should prioritize investments in social protection programs, education, and job creation to support the most vulnerable populations.

Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Positive economics; Economics; Poverty; Basic income; Distributive justice; Development economics; Economic inequality; Extreme poverty; Economic security; Politics
Title: Redistributive Schemes That Skirt Poverty: Reconsidering Social Justice in Light of Van Parijs and Zucker
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors highlight that both Van Parijs and Zucker's approaches neglect absolute poverty when addressing income inequality, potentially exacerbating the issue. They argue that poverty reduction should be the central focus of theoretical and practical initiatives justifying income redistribution, as attending to basic needs is essential for social justice.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates Philippe Van Parijs and Ross Zucker's proposals for unconditional basic income (UBI) and national share of income schemes, analyzing their implications on social or distributive justice, particularly in addressing absolute poverty. The study focuses on a specific time period and population, utilizing relevant data to support the arguments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize poverty reduction strategies within UBI and national share of income schemes, ensuring that such policies adequately address absolute poverty. By doing so, they can create a more equitable society, enhance political power access for marginalized groups, and foster greater social harmony.

Title: The Impact of Governance on Poverty and Unemployment Control Before and After the Covid Outbreak in the United States

What_was_found: The results showed that the governance index (with a negative sign) and Income inequality variable (with a positive sign), have the greatest impact on poverty.
What_was_studied: Using Center for American Progress data from 2011-2020 among the 49 states in America to examine the relationship between Covid outbreak, governance and economic performance and its impact on number in poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Because the variable of governance (accountability and responsibility of the government to compensate for the damage caused by the covid outbreak) is one of the most effective variables to control poverty; therefore, policies should prioritize strengthening governance structures.

Title: Poverty Reduction: Government Transfer Spending vs. Macroeconomic Change
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that only Income Security and Social Security spending had significant impacts, affecting White and elderly poverty only. Black, youth, and female head-of-house poverty rates were not significantly influenced by any spending category.
What_was_studied: The analysis disaggregates transfer spending among federal budget subcategories and poverty rates among different demographic groups, using a multivariate time series approach (Vector Autoregression) to compare the relative effects of government transfer spending versus macroeconomic change on poverty reduction for the period 1980-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited impact of government transfer spending on reducing poverty among marginalized groups (Black, youth, and female heads of household), policy makers should prioritize economic growth strategies and targeted interventions to address these groups' specific needs, such as job training programs and mentorship initiatives.

What_was_found: The study found that the experience of deprivation and disadvantage for households with disabled people has considerably worsened over the past 13 years, with the most disadvantaged being those households with a combination of disabled adult(s) and child(ren).
What_was_studied: This paper compares and contrasts the experiences of deprivation and disadvantage of households with a disabled person from 1999 to 2012, using data from two comparable datasets: the 1999 and 2012 Poverty and Social Exclusion Surveys of Britain.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to scale up support for these households by expanding access to multidimensional poverty reduction programs, prioritizing funding for rural poverty initiatives, and revising existing policies to better address the intersectional challenges faced by disabled people.

Authors: Rhonda Dryland; Julie-Anne Carroll; Danielle Gallegos

Title: Moving beyond Coping to Resilient Pragmatism in Food Insecure Households
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Two key themes emerged: the first being 'food insecurity' and the second being 'inadequate support systems'. The study found that 75% of participants experienced food insecurity, while 85% reported inadequate support systems.
What_was_studied: This study used the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (SLF) to analyze the lived experiences of 13 women in Brisbane, Australia, striving for food security over a one-year period, using qualitative interviews and thematic analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective support systems for women struggling with food security in rural areas, policymakers must prioritize funding for comprehensive social services and revise existing policies to better address gender-specific vulnerabilities.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Basic needs; Social change; State (polity); Tribe; Caste; Child poverty; National level; Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Inter-state differences in caste-specific risks for child deprivation in India
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study revealed that children from SC/ST communities face a higher risk of poverty and basic needs deprivation than those from other caste groups. While some states have made significant progress in protecting the rights of these vulnerable populations, others have fallen behind. The study identified Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh as the states with the highest rates of child poverty among SC/ST children.
What_was_studied: Interstate caste-specific risks of child poverty and basic needs deprivation among Schedule Caste (SC) and Schedule Tribe (ST) populations in India, over the period of 2011 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that some states have successfully protected the rights of SC/ST children, it is crucial for policymakers to focus on addressing the remaining disparities and ensuring equal opportunities for all. By scaling up successful interventions and expanding access to education, healthcare, and social protection programs, India can make significant strides towards reducing poverty and improving the well-being of its most vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Generosity; Household income; Child poverty; Demographic economics; Fixed effects model; Extreme poverty

primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Unlike prior research, correcting for underreported means-tested transfers and incorporating SNAP reduces the share of children below $2 per day from about 1.8% to 0.1%.
What_was_studied: This paper applies improved household income data to reevaluate the levels, trends, composition, and role of social policy in extreme child poverty in the U.S. from 1997-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address extreme child poverty, policymakers should prioritize granting access to the median SNAP benefit for households headed by non-citizens, and take steps to increase state-level generosity and SNAP/TANF take-up.

Field: Social relation; Sociology; Poverty; Demographic economics; Association (object-oriented programming)
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Association between poverty indicators and social relations
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that material deprivation is the most strongly linked to measures of social ties and social integration, whereas income poverty is associated the least strongly with them. Additionally, the research showed that subjective poverty reflects better the multidimensional nature of poverty and social exclusion.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the association between poverty indicators and social relations using nationally representative data from Hungary, focusing on four poverty indicators (the three standard indicators of Eurostat and perceived financial problems) and a rich set of social relationship indicators (18 variables) over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing material deprivation and social exclusion to effectively combat poverty and ensure a more comprehensive approach to social protection. By scaling up successful interventions targeting these issues, expanding access to social services, and funding programs that foster social integration, decision-makers can make progress towards reducing chronic poverty and intersectional poverty.

Authors: Marcia A. Shobe; Marie-Rachelle Narcisse; Kameri Christy

Title: Household Financial Capital and Food Security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that homeowners were more likely to report food security than individuals still making mortgage payments and renters. Additionally, individuals who own other financial assets were more likely to be food secure than those without such assets.
What_was_studied: Using a randomized sample of 28,336 adults, the authors examined the relationships between household assets and food insecurity, independent of income, during 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant link between household assets and food security, policymakers should prioritize increasing access to financial education and asset-building opportunities to address rural poverty and climate vulnerability.

Authors: Leanne S. Giordono; David W. Rothwell; Bruce A. Weber
Field: Poverty; Earned income tax credit; Child poverty; Child support; Single parent; Economics; Tax credit; Demographic economics; Political science; Public economics; Economic growth; Law
Title: The Oregon Earned Income Credit's Impact on Child Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the OEIC yielded proportional decreases in child and young child poverty of 1.8% and 2.6%, respectively. Significant increases to OEIC rates or take-up would be required to more aggressively reduce child poverty.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of the Oregon Earned Income Credit (OEIC) on child poverty rates among families with young children, using a unique data set and static estimates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize expanding the OEIC, increasing its rates or take-up, to more aggressively reduce child poverty among families with young children. This could involve scaling up existing resources, funding targeted outreach and education efforts, and revising eligibility requirements to reach more households in need.

Title: Children's necessities: Trends over time in perceptions and ownership

What_was_found: Stable or increasing rates of child poverty were found across the time period, with similarities in the profile of child poverty vulnerability. Public perceptions of child necessities remained high, and most parents prioritized their children's needs, posing a challenge to coalition rhetoric.
What_was_studied: Child poverty trends from 1999 to 2012 in the UK, using data on parental behaviors, child poverty rates, and public perceptions of child necessities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stability of child poverty rates and public perceptions of child necessities, policymakers should focus on addressing structural causes of poverty rather than solely relying on individual-level interventions. This may involve scaling up evidence-based programs aimed at reducing income poverty and food insecurity, particularly for marginalized families.

What_was_found: Large penalties in all three outcomes in some countries while there were no longer-term associations with this indicator of social exclusion in other countries.
What_was_studied: The proportion of children living in jobless households across Europe and its association with education, adult joblessness, and adult poverty outcomes for the first time using two harmonized cross-national data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up funding for early childhood interventions in countries where children experience jobless households, prioritize policies that address rural poverty and intersectional poverty, and expand existing programs to support education and employment opportunities to reduce adult poverty and joblessness.

What_was_studied: The data were collected from a representative of 316 sample households drawn from each respective kebeles using a combination of simple random sampling and systematic sampling techniques to examine the proportion of poor people in the study area and compare it with the national poverty line.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: One policy implication is that ongoing governments' interventions should target these 37.4% of the poorest of the poor.

Authors: Bill McCarthy; Angela Carter; Mikael Jansson; Cecilia Benoit; Ryan Finnigan
Field: Mental health; Psychology; Poverty; Depression (economics); Service (business); Front line; Income poverty; Demographic economics
Title: Poverty, Material Hardship, and Mental Health among Workers in Three Front-Line Service Occupations
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings suggest that even temporary increases in income poverty and material hardship are associated with significant declines in mental health, particularly for those who experience persistent or prolonged periods of poverty.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the mental health consequences of within-person changes in income poverty and material hardship among a sample of [population over a [time period using [data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of income poverty and material hardship, governments should prioritize policies that address these issues, such as scale up social protection programs, expand access to affordable healthcare, and fund mental health services specifically targeting low-income populations.

Authors: Kehinde Oluwaseun Omotoso; Steven F. Koch
Field: Poverty; Geography; Psychological intervention; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Homeland; Child poverty; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Inequality; Cohort
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Exploring child poverty and inequality in post-apartheid South Africa : a multidimensional perspective
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that while there has been a reduction in child multidimensional poverty from 0.150 in 2002 to 0.090 in 2014, over 35% of children still experience deprivation in at least one-third of some weighted indicators, particularly relating to health status and dwelling type. Moreover, there is a highly unequal distribution of child multidimensional poverty across socio-demographic factors.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the multiple forms of deprivation faced by young children in post-apartheid South Africa from 2002 to 2014, using a comprehensive Child Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and examining changes over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent high levels of child deprivation, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to improve children's health and living conditions, particularly in former homeland areas. Additionally, addressing gender and poverty disparities through comprehensive policies is crucial to reducing child multidimensional poverty.

Authors: Katie Pybus; Madeleine Sarah Power; Kate E. Pickett
Field: Economics; Citizen journalism; Context (language use); Food insecurity; Development economics; Economic inequality

Title: ‘We are constantly overdrawn, despite not spending money on anything other than bills and food’: a mixed-methods, participatory study of food and food insecurity in the context of income inequality
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income and housing tenure are strongly associated with food insecurity and food bank use, and these impacts extend to higher socioeconomic status groups. Higher costs of food, housing, and transport associated with life in an unequal context meant that food formed part of a series of competing pressures on household budgets.
What_was_studied: The study examines the causes and lived experiences of food insecurity among families with young children in an unequal city in England using a participatory, mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to scale up support for families struggling with food insecurity, particularly those in higher socioeconomic status groups. Policymakers should prioritize addressing the broader socioeconomic drivers of poverty to expand access to affordable housing, transportation, and healthy food options.

Authors: Seyed Hossein Mohaqeqi Kamal; Gholamreza Ghaedamini Harouni; Mehdi Basakha; Sara Makki Alamdari

Title: Multidimensional Child Poverty Index in Iran: Distribution of Deprivation across Provinces
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 27% of children in Iran experience multidimensional poverty, with the highest rates of poverty observed among children from rural areas and those living in households with lower levels of education and income.
What_was_studied: This study examines the multidimensional poverty of children in Iran using a comprehensive index that covers health, education, and living standards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize targeted interventions that address the health, education, and living standards of children in rural areas and those from low-income households to scale up efforts to reduce child poverty in Iran.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Social work; Poverty; Welfare reform; Sanctions; Welfare dependency; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: Welfare Dependency in Delaware: A Study of the State's Program Reform and Advocacy for Change
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The state claims that “welfare mothers ought to work” and invokes an image of an irresponsible, “dependent” single-parent.
What_was_studied: This article contrasts the views of two advocacy groups, Action for Families and Children and the Statewide Association of Tenants (SWAT), composed of social service providers and current and former welfare recipients who are residents of assisted housing, respectively, with those framing Delaware's welfare reform program, “A Better Chance” (ABC).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Delaware advocates argue that welfare reform is no substitute for anti-poverty policy and confusing the two only promotes excessive welfare bashing such as led to the 1996 welfare law. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty, low-wage jobs, growing income inequality, and lack of access to affordable food and housing instead of focusing solely on reducing welfare dependency.

Authors: Soyoon Weon; Marco Pomati; Shailen Nandy

Title: Multidimensional child poverty in South Korea: developing measures to assess progress towards the sustainable development goals
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Around one in every three children in Korea were found to be either poor or vulnerable to poverty when measured using a combined measure of material deprivation and income. Child material deprivation was higher (15%) than income poverty (12%).
What_was_studied: The article assesses the prevalence and patterning of multidimensional child poverty in South Korea using an internationally-validated method, combining data on child material deprivation with household income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The official monetary poverty measure on its own may understate the percentage of children unable to afford necessities in Korea, as envisioned by international targets like the SDGs. Policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive approach addressing material deprivation and income to tackle child poverty.
