Title: 'We should not have to choose between hunger and death': exploring the experiences of primary caregivers of recipients of a South African child cash transfer programme during COVID-19 lockdown in Cape Town, South Africa
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: COVID-19 and particularly the hard lockdown worsened the social, economic, and living conditions of primary caregivers and their children and households, with increases in hunger and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The experiences of primary caregivers of children receiving the Child Support Grant (CSG) in Cape Town during lockdown and how they speak to the limitations of the social protection paradigm and potential for transformative social policy approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to shift to a transformative social policy framework that incorporates production, redistribution, social cohesion, adequacy, and protection to address the inadequacies of the social protection paradigm and provide comprehensive support for low-income families with children.

Authors: Yang Li-xiong; W T Ernest Chui
Field: Rural area; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; China; Basic needs; Rural poverty; Population; Development economics; Economic growth; Rural economics
Title: Poverty Line in China Rural Areas: A Critical Reappraisal
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the official rural poverty line has not kept pace with food price inflation, leading to an underestimation of rural poverty and a widening income gap between urban and rural areas.
What_was_studied: The 1980s rural poverty line in China and its insensitivity to food price changes, resulting in underestimation of rural poverty and increasing income disparity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the rural poverty line to reflect the consumption power of poor farmers in China, scale up efforts to address income disparity, and prioritize policies that benefit rural communities to ensure equitable economic development.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Social exclusion; Top-down and bottom-up design; Sociology; Order (exchange); Poverty; Legitimation; Unemployment; Scale (social sciences)
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Top-down or bottom-up: the real choice for public services
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that top-down approaches tend to categorize individuals based on their circumstances, while bottom-up approaches treat people who have experienced poverty as experts and prioritizes user involvement.
What_was_studied: This article considers two contrasting approaches to reforming public services in order to meet the needs of people living in poverty, specifically focusing on unemployment and parenting policies during a time period of 'cycles of deprivation'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of top-down approaches despite increasing support for bottom-up approaches in other policy areas, decision makers should prioritize funding for and scaling up bottom-up initiatives to better meet the needs of people living in poverty.

Authors: Luis Beccaria; Ana Laura Fernández; Héctor Nájera
Field: Poverty; Latin Americans; Dimension (graph theory); Population; Poverty level; Geography; Measure (data warehouse); Index (typography); Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Sociology; Political science; Economics; Demography; Computer science; Mathematics; Database; World Wide Web; Pure mathematics; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The use of the consensual approach for the improvement of existing multidimensional poverty data in Latin America: an illustration based on data from the City of Buenos Aires
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show a remarkable level of consensus about the necessities of life in the twenty-first century, underline the importance of generating more suitable indicators of deprivation, and show that unmet basic needs-type variables are no longer adequate for measuring poverty in countries like Argentina.
What_was_studied: The study examined the process for producing the first multidimensional poverty measure based on the consensual approach for the City of Buenos Aires, using data from the 2019 Survey of Household Income and Expenditures (SHIE) for the city.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high deprivation rate shown by the valid and reliable poverty index, decision makers should prioritize the development of more comprehensive and multidimensional measures of poverty to better understand the social dimensions of poverty in Buenos Aires and target interventions accordingly.

Authors: Yekaterina Chzhen; Zlata Bruckauf; Emilia Toczydlowska
Field: Political science; Child poverty; European union; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Monitoring progress towards sustainable development: multidimensional child poverty in the European Union
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The proposed measure can be used both for national and EU-wide SDG monitoring without replacing either national or EU-wide indices of material deprivation, finding that child poverty rates range from 13% to 27% across the EU, with the highest rates in Southern and Eastern European countries.
What_was_studied: This paper proposes and evaluates a child-specific multidimensional poverty measure using data from ad hoc material deprivation modules of the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) for the period 2015–2016, focusing on the population of children under 18 years old in the EU.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs targeting children in Southern and Eastern Europe to reduce child poverty rates by at least half by 2030, expanding existing national and EU-wide indices of material deprivation to better capture the multidimensional nature of child poverty.

Field: Metropolitan area; Economics; Recession; Residence; Current Population Survey; Economic hardship; Great recession; Food insecurity; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Food security
Title: Predictors of U.S. Food Insecurity Across Nonmetropolitan, Suburban, and Principal City Residence During the Great Recession
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Digital divide; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that suburban households were more likely to experience food insecurity than non-metropolitan households, and as likely to be food insecure as principal city households. Net of income and other household characteristics.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the 2009 Current Population Survey Food Security Supplement data to determine the likelihood of food insecurity across different residence areas during the Great Recession.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising prevalence of food insecurity in suburban areas, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions and resources to address this issue, particularly in light of the increasing economic hardship spreading to suburbs during times of economic downturn.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Earned income tax credit; Child poverty; Young parents; Single mothers; Poverty rate
Title: The Effects of the Earned Income Tax Credit on Children's Income and Poverty: Who Fares Better?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that for all American children under age 18, the EITC provided a little increase in disposable income (1.2%) but a modest reduction in child poverty (15%). For recipient families with children under age 18, the EITC had a greater impact: a 10% raise in disposable income and a 27% reduction in the poverty rate.
What_was_studied: The fully expanded Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) was examined for its contribution to the economic well-being of low-income families with children in the United States, specifically looking at two measures: the effect on disposable income and the effects on the poverty rate and poverty gap from 1996 onwards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the modest but meaningful impact of the EITC on child poverty, policymakers should prioritize scaling up this program to reach more eligible families, particularly those with single mothers or young parents, welfare families, the extreme poor, and large families who benefit the most from the EITC.

Authors: Felix R. FitzRoy; Jim Y. Jin
Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Poverty; Underemployment; Unemployment; Minimum wage; Basic income; Job guarantee
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: basic income; job guarantee; poverty; unemployment
Title: Basic income and a public job offer: Complementary policies to reduce poverty and unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that a modest basic income combined with job offers below the minimum wage is the most cost-effective policy for comprehensive welfare, particularly for those in precarious or underemployment, while a job guarantee policy fails to support self-employed individuals and those who prefer particular occupations over a JG. Additionally, the study finds that an earned income and good jobs are crucial for addressing income poverty and gender disparities.
What_was_studied: The author investigates the effectiveness of unconditional basic income and job guarantee policies in addressing poverty and income inequality in various demographic groups over a one-year period, using a combination of survey data and case studies from developed economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a combination of modest basic income and job offers below the minimum wage to comprehensively address poverty and income inequality, particularly for those in precarious or underemployment, while supporting self-employed individuals and those who prefer particular occupations through targeted programs and funding.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Sociology; Poverty; Social policy; Welfare reform; Legislation; Living wage; Welfare rights; Public administration
Title: Making Experience Count in Policy Creation: Lessons from Appalachian Kentucky
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Through the strategic use of media and the creation of legislation, activists are able to challenge work first policies and help craft programs that meet local needs.
What_was_studied: In Appalachian Kentucky low-income parents need access to education in order to find living wage employment, and how activists are able to challenge work first policies and help craft programs that meet local needs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address issues of poverty, public assistance policy must take into account the lived experience of low-income parents.

Field: Payment; Political science; State (polity); Child support; Child poverty; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: child maintenance; child support; child poverty; comparative study; lone parents
Title: Child maintenance and child poverty: A comparative analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while child maintenance has a minimal effect on overall child poverty rates, it can significantly reduce poverty among non-widowed lone mother families if they receive maintenance payments. Additionally, countries that guarantee child maintenance payments through the state are more effective in reducing child poverty.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the contribution of child maintenance to reducing child poverty in seven countries with different maintenance schemes: Canada, UK, USA, Germany, Norway, Denmark, and Finland, using Luxembourg Income Study datasets from circa 2004.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the minimal effect of child maintenance on overall child poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize state-guaranteed child maintenance payments to effectively reduce child poverty among non-widowed lone mother families.

Field: Public economics; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Social security; Local government; Proxy (statistics); Median income; Income poverty
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Should we be using social security benefits data as proxies for income poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that income poverty is conventionally defined against percentages of national median income, and out-of-work means-tested benefit claims are valid but incomplete proxies for income poverty. Additionally, there is significant regional variation in the statistical relationship between rates of income poverty and rates of benefit claims.
What_was_studied: The paper analyzes the use of administrative data on means-tested benefits as proxies for poverty rates in the UK, specifically examining their use in allocating funding to local governments and constructing neighborhood deprivation indices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of using administrative data as poverty proxies, decision-makers should exercise caution when relying on these measures to describe spatial differences in poverty. Instead, they should prioritize collecting high-quality, standardized poverty data through surveys or other methods to ensure accurate poverty measurement and targeted policy interventions.

Field: Poverty; Wage; Unemployment; Labour economics; Incentive; Economics; Living wage; Social security; Low wage; Economic growth; Market economy
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Explaining the abolition of the wage stop in the UK
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the wage stop was abolished in the mid-1970s due to concerns within the assistance boards with its administration, rather than solely as a result of lobbying by the Child Poverty Action Group, and that there was a shift in approach emphasizing the supplementation of low wages with social security benefits.
What_was_studied: The historical evolution of the household benefit cap in the UK, particularly its intersections with out-of-work benefits, and the reasons behind its abolition in the mid-1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of the intersections between employment, income poverty, and social protection policies to ensure that any revisions or reforms to these mechanisms take into account the complex needs of recipients and their households.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Minimum wage; Child poverty; Index (economics); Sample (statistics); Panel data; Inflation; Estimation
Title: The Impact of State Minimum Wages on Child Poverty in Female-Headed Families
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The evidence shows that raising the minimum wage significantly reduces child poverty rates by up to 10 percentage points after controlling for other factors.
What_was_studied: This study examines how minimum wages affect child poverty rates in female-headed households across 50 states from 1991 to 2002, using state-level panel data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling up minimum wage policies and indexing them to inflation to address the persistent issue of child poverty in female-headed households, particularly in states with high poverty rates.

Authors: Rajeev Dehejia; Bjorn N. Jorgensen; Raphael Thomadsen
Field: Supply and demand; Wage share; Labour economics; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Unemployment; Minimum wage; Wage regulation; Wage level; Efficiency wage
Title: Optimal Minimum Wage in the Classic Labor Supply-and-Demand Paradigm
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that minimum wage increases have not led to significant job losses or reductions in hours worked, even when considering variations in state minimum wage laws across different regions and industries. Instead, the research suggests that higher minimum wages can improve the well-being of low-income households and reduce poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of minimum wage laws on employment and welfare in the United States, using a combination of microdata and aggregate data from 1979 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize implementing or increasing minimum wage laws to improve employment standards, reduce income inequality, and support the well-being of vulnerable populations.

Field: Debt; Payment; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Household income; Child poverty; Consumer debt; Demographic economics
Title: Debt-Poor Kids
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that around 20% of children in the US have lived in poverty for at least half of their lives since the late 1970s, and that interest payments on consumer debt can significantly underestimate child poverty rates.
What_was_studied: Child poverty in the United States between 1979 and 2019, specifically focusing on how interest payments on prior consumer debt affect government calculations of child poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize revamping how they measure child poverty to better account for interest payments on consumer debt and implement policies to scale up efforts to reduce chronic child poverty.

Field: Economic policy; Payment; Economics; Welfare reform; Universal Credit; Low income; Monetary economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Universal Credit: the impact of monthly payments on low income households
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The conclusion is drawn that, for some claimants, monthly payment of Universal Credit is likely to make money management easier, but for low income households whose current preferences and habits are to budget on a weekly or fortnightly basis, monthly payment of Universal Credit risks undermining the money management strategies which they find effective.
What_was_studied: The article examines the evidence for the widespread concern that moving to a monthly payment system will be detrimental for low income households, reviewing the government's proposals for providing claimants with budgeting support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these concerns, the government should prioritize providing claimants with adequate budgeting support and consider offering flexible payment options to accommodate different household preferences and habits.

Authors: Howard Robert Reed; Matthew Thomas Johnson; Stewart Lansley; Elliott Aidan Johnson; Graham Stark; Kate E. Pickett
Field: Microsimulation; Poverty; Economics; Public economics; Inequality; Basic income; Psychological intervention; Development economics; Economic growth; Engineering; Market economy; Psychology; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Psychiatry; Transport engineering
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Universal Basic Income is affordable and feasible: evidence from UK economic microsimulation modelling1
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Even the fiscally neutral starter scheme would reduce child poverty to the lowest level achieved since 1961 and achieve more than the anti-poverty interventions of the New Labour Governments from 2000. The more generous schemes would make further inroads into the UK’s high levels of poverty and inequality, but at greater cost.
What_was_studied: The distributional impacts of three UBI schemes broadly designed to provide pathways to attainment of the Minimum Income Standard (MIS) were examined using microsimulation of data from the Family Resources Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Fiscal strategies should be prioritized to reduce the up-front deficit of higher schemes, providing a more positive assessment of affordability and impact than critics have assumed.

Field: Poverty; Inequality; Prioritization; Kinship; Economics; Demographic economics; Household income; Child poverty; Labour economics; Economic growth; Geography; Political science; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Archaeology; Management science; Law
Title: First the Children, then the Employed: Deprivation and Intra-household Inequality in Europe
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that parents and the unemployed are the most likely to experience deprivation, and that prioritizing children is nearly universal, with no evidence of an association between income or education and the prioritization of children.
What_was_studied: This paper uses data from 22 European countries to investigate how households allocate resources according to dynamic rules that consider age, gender, kinship, and labor market participation, and how extended co-residency can be a helpful but limited strategy to reduce child poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing child poverty by implementing strategies that protect children and support households with limited resources, such as scaling up extended co-residency programs and expanding access to labor market opportunities for parents.

Field: Poverty; Socioeconomics; Functional illiteracy; Economic growth; Population; Checklist; Human capital; Rural area; Basic needs; Geography; Political science; Medicine; Psychology; Economics; Environmental health; Law; Cognitive psychology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Contribution of Human Capital on Poverty Reduction in Rural Areas of Uganda. A Case of Kisoro District
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Education and training were found to have a significant relationship with poverty reduction in rural areas of Kisoro district, with education explaining 23.2% and training explaining 9.1% of the contribution to poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The study examined the contribution of human capital to poverty reduction in rural areas of Uganda, specifically in Kisoro district, using a cross-sectional survey and triangulating both quantitative and qualitative approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study recommends that public education, research, and development, science and technology, and enabling policies should be sustainably promoted for enhanced productivity, poverty reduction, and development in rural areas of Uganda.

Authors: Miriam Stewart; Jeffrey R. Masuda; Joshua Evans; Nicole Letourneau; Jocelyn Edey
Field: Service provider; Poverty; Respiratory health; Respiratory illness; Low income; Multiple factors; Socioeconomics; Medicine; Coping (psychology); Environmental health
Title: Respiratory Health Inequities Experienced by Low-Income Children and Parents
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty exacerbated challenges related to respiratory conditions, and that participants reported multiple factors contributing to poverty and service providers did not fully understand these challenges.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the challenges experienced by children and parents coping with poverty and respiratory health problems in a sample of 69 low-income families, including the impact of poverty on the management of chronic respiratory conditions and the relevance of service inequities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing food insecurity and income poverty to mitigate the impact of chronic respiratory conditions on low-income families, and healthcare providers should be trained to better understand the challenges associated with poverty and pulmonary problems.

Authors: Jessica W. Pardee; Kevin Fox Gotham
Field: Public economics; Public policy; Private sector; Economics; Control (management); Affordable housing; Section (archaeology); HOPE VI; Inequality; Development economics; Social stratification
Title: HOPE VI, Section 8, and the Contradictions of Low-Income Housing Policy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that recent policy shifts have reinforced market dynamics, resulting in many low-income housing residents being shifted to the private market, causing economic distress for these families. This suggests that lack of access to affordable housing is fundamentally a public policy issue.
What_was_studied: The study looks at the HOPE VI and Section 8 housing programs in New Orleans, LA, to determine if they can be effective anti-poverty strategies, using a system of social stratification approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the contradictions inherent in current housing policy, there should be increased federal funding and prioritization of affordable housing programs, and efforts should be made to revise policies that shift residents to the private market, in order to reduce long-standing poverty and exacerbate inequalities.

Field: Social exclusion; Poverty; Population; Microdata (statistics); Geography; Socioeconomics; Demography; Sociology; Economic growth; Economics; Census
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Poverty and Social Exclusion in Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Nationally, 36.1% of the population were absolute poor, with a higher proportion (40.1%) of population living in rural areas being poor compared to 29.1 % of population living in urban areas. Almost half (48.3%) of the population from religious minority are poor, and persons with disability are also likely to be poor (45.7%). Nationally, 16.6 million people are at risk of social exclusion.
What_was_studied: The study aims to assess the extent of poverty as a dimension of social exclusion; provide poverty estimates for various sub-populations and vulnerable groups; develop a methodology for analyzing social exclusion at the national level; and estimate the number of socially excluded individuals at both national and regional (rural/urban) levels in Kenya, using the methodology developed by Cuesta et al. (2022) and based on Sen's capability approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding the concept of social exclusion and poverty will assist policy makers and other stakeholders develop policies and strategies aimed at creating a society where social inclusion is at the forefront, ensuring that no one is marginalized or left behind due to poverty or other forms of exclusion. This inclusive approach will contribute to equitable and sustainable economic growth, benefiting the entire population and fostering a more just and cohesive society. Therefore, we recommend prioritizing policies and programs aimed at reducing social exclusion and poverty, particularly in rural areas and among vulnerable groups such as religious minorities and persons with disabilities.

Authors: Julie Birkenmaier; Jin Huang; Youngmi Kim
Field: Finance; Consumption (economics); Labour economics; Economics; Recession; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Unemployment; Unbanked; Population; Food security; Moderation
Title: Food Insecurity and Financial Access During an Economic Recession: Evidence From the 2008 SIPP
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that there is no evidence that financial access mitigates food hardship for the unemployed. However, financial access and unemployment are significantly related to food insecurity for the general population.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between financial access, unemployment, and household food insecurity during the economic recession among a sample of 14,417 individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between financial access and food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize expanding financial inclusion programs and services to mitigate the impact of economic downturns on household food security.

Field: Economics; Sensitivity (control systems); Income poverty; Demographic economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The overlap between income poverty and material deprivation: sensitivity evidence for Australia
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that accounting for two of these factors leads to a marked increase in the overlap between poverty and deprivation.
What_was_studied: This study uses Australian data to examine the impact on the overlap between income poverty and material deprivation of data adjustments and three substantive factors: short-run income fluctuations, housing costs, and net wealth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize adjusting income poverty measures to account for short-run income fluctuations, housing costs, and net wealth to better capture material deprivation and target interventions more effectively.

Authors: Nuran Bayram; Serpil Aytaç; Mustafa Aytac; Neslihan Sam; Nazan Bilgel
Field: Social exclusion; Social deprivation; Sociology; Poverty; Life satisfaction; High unemployment; Moderate level; Incidence (epidemiology); Socioeconomics; Structural equation modeling
Title: Poverty, Social Exclusion, and Life Satisfaction: A Study From Turkey
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Approximately 29.0% of the variation in social exclusion could be explained by the effects of age, poverty, and life satisfaction, with young people and those experiencing poverty feeling more socially excluded.
What_was_studied: This cross-sectional study of 2,493 randomly selected participants in Turkey examined the relationships among poverty, social exclusion, and life satisfaction using structural equation modeling during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and improving life satisfaction among vulnerable populations to reduce social exclusion and promote sustainable development in Turkey.

Field: Poverty; Context (archaeology); Negotiation; Sociology; Gender studies; Qualitative research; Welfare state; Welfare; Czech; Low income; Lived experience; Single mothers; Psychology; Developmental psychology; Political science; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Economics; Geography; Social science; Politics; Linguistics; Philosophy; Law; Archaeology; Psychoanalysis
Title: Low-income Roma Mothers Negotiating Mothering in the Context of Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis shows that low-income status is perpetuated through motherhood and that mothering experiences are significantly shaped by the welfare state and structural forces.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on low-income Roma mothers in the Czech Republic during a specific time period, using qualitative interviews to understand how mothering is formed, negotiated and reproduced in the context of poverty. Specifically, we analyzed three characteristics of mothering: othermothering, creating multigenerational households, and teenage motherhood.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the support provided to low-income Roma mothers, the government should prioritize multigenerational household support and expand access to early childhood interventions, such as parenting programs and early learning initiatives.

Field: Survey data collection; Geography; Rural poverty; Variation (linguistics); Multidimensional poverty; Rural ethiopia; Socioeconomics
Title: How Does Multidimensional Rural Poverty Vary across Agro-ecologies in Rural Ethiopia? Evidence from the Three Districts
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that approximately 70% of the population in these agro-ecologies experience multidimensional poverty, with the highest rates found among rural households headed by women (84%).
What_was_studied: This article investigates multidimensional poverty in the agro-ecologies of Ethiopia using survey data collected from 450 households across three agro-ecologies between 2018 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address gender and rural disparities in poverty reduction programs, particularly in the agro-ecologies of Ethiopia.

Authors: Eli Buchbinder; Laura I. Sigad; Roni Strier; Zvi Eisikovits
Field: Gender studies; Distress; Sociology; Judaism; Poverty; Working poor; Faith; Constructive; Meaning (existential); Social psychology; Social constructivism
Title: Working Poor Ultra-Orthodox Jewish Women and Men: Between Economic Distress and Meaning Based on Faith
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that religion demands a set of behaviors and belief systems that hinder the individual's ability to break out of poverty, yet provides an alternative framework of interpretative beliefs that enables positive and constructive social meaning even under economic hardship.
What_was_studied: Twenty in-depth qualitative interviews with ultra-Orthodox working-poor women and men in Israel over a 6-month period reveal the complex role of religion in constructing the working poor, as well as hindering their ability to break out of poverty while providing positive social meaning.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for ultra-Orthodox working poor individuals to break out of poverty while preserving their religious beliefs and values, such as through job training programs and education initiatives that take into account their unique needs and challenges.

Authors: Katie Pybus; Geoff Page; Lynsey Dalton; Ruth Patrick
Field: Political science; Social security; Action (philosophy); Early warning system; Child poverty; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Low income; Public relations; Pandemic
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The Early Warning System: How frontline evidence helps us understand the UK's social security response to COVID-19
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the social security system's response to the pandemic has exacerbated poverty, particularly for families with children. The analysis also revealed significant disparities in health outcomes and food insecurity among claimants.
What_was_studied: Child Poverty Action Group Early Warning System (EWS) case studies reporting social security issues directly from frontline benefits advice workers and benefit claimants in the UK during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize short- and longer-term policy changes to address income poverty, health disparities, and food insecurity among families with children. This includes expanding social security support, scaling up health interventions, and implementing targeted poverty reduction initiatives.

Field: Poverty; Nationality; Demographic economics; Extreme poverty; Economics; Poverty rate; Development economics; Socioeconomics; Geography; Immigration; Economic growth; Archaeology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Poverty, extreme poverty and homelessness in Spain: an analysis for the period 2010–2019
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that deep poverty is not influenced by economic cycles and that high-risk groups such as single person households, households with children, younger individuals, individuals with low educational attainment, and foreign nationals are most susceptible to extreme poverty. Additionally, the study found that individuals in consistent poverty have similar profiles to those experiencing homelessness.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes poverty and extreme poverty in Spain between 2010 and 2020 using various monetary thresholds, measures of severe material deprivation, and combination approaches to determine the determinants of these situations and their link to homelessness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should target public policies towards high-risk groups and prioritize addressing deep poverty and its determinants to prevent further cycles of poverty and homelessness.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; Stakeholder; Rural poverty; Restructuring; Development economics; Economic growth; Civil society; Regionalism (international relations); Social capital
Title: Opportunities and Challenges to Address Poverty in Rural Regions: A Case Study from Northern BC
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: New regionalism has been one outcome of neo-liberal policies as regions experiment with different institutional structures and relationships to compensate for the government withdrawal of programs, but civil society groups have limited capacity to respond to rural poverty due to state diminishment.
What_was_studied: Exploring regional approaches to address rural poverty in British Columbia, Canada, using a descriptive case study of the Robson Valley and 22 key informant stakeholder interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize regional approaches to address rural poverty in British Columbia, Canada, by scaling up innovations and economic development initiatives, funding civil society groups, and revising neo-liberal policies to strengthen the capacity of regions to respond to this complex issue.

Field: Social deprivation; Socioeconomic status; Social inequality; Geography; Local government area; Context (language use); Food supply; Food insecurity; Socioeconomics; Food security
Title: Nutritional Insecurity in Ojo-Lagos Nigeria: Redefining Food security in the Context of Social Deprivation
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Majority (80%) of the sampled households suffered from nutritional deprivation due to their low socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: Food Record Method was used to examine nutritional insecurity among residents of Ojo Local Government Area in Lagos over a 1-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs and address multidimensional poverty, policymakers should prioritize funding for nutrition-focused interventions aimed at the urban poor in Lagos.

Field: Geography; Data-driven; Multidimensional poverty; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Multidimensional poverty in Kolkata’s slums: towards data driven decision making in a medium-sized NGO
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The survey found that nearly 70% of the population lived in poverty, with the most common deprivations being lack of access to clean water, sanitation, and secure housing. The data also showed a significant gender disparity in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The 2019 multidimensional poverty survey of Calcutta Rescue (CR) in Kolkata, India, covering the population's deprivation in various life dimensions and assessing the impact of CR's interventions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: CR's findings suggest that scaling up interventions targeting access to basic services such as water, sanitation, and housing can significantly reduce poverty rates and gender disparities in the slums of Kolkata. Prioritizing these interventions can lead to meaningful improvements in the well-being of the city's most vulnerable populations.

Field: Labour economics; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Feminization of poverty; Household income; Single mothers; Longitudinal data; Multilevel model
Title: To Wed or to Work? Assessing Work and Marriage as Routes Out of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results suggest that marriage and employment improve mothers' household income, but that racial-ethnic differences persist.
What_was_studied: Using longitudinal data for 1992 to 2001 from the Survey of Program Dynamics and multilevel models for change, this article analyzes the relative success rates of each of these strategies, as well as racial-ethnic differences in the effects of each on women's household incomes among women at high risk of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize and expand policies addressing the feminization of poverty, such as job training programs and childcare support for low-income women, particularly those from historically marginalized communities.

Field: Positive economics; Economics; Basic income; Confusion
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Basic income: confusion, claims and choices
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper found that none of the five claims for Basic Income hold up to scrutiny.
What_was_studied: The research analyses the idea of basic income and evaluates five claims made for it regarding poverty reduction, fairness, economic efficiency, compatibility with future labor markets, and political feasibility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should not rely solely on Basic Income as a solution to poverty reduction, but rather consider a range of options and make strategic choices to address poverty effectively.

Authors: S. Ramessur; Boopen Seetanah; Sawkut Rojid
Field: Business; Poverty; Asset (economics); Transport infrastructure; Urban policy; Urban poverty; Urban poor; Sample (statistics); Fixed effects model; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Roads and Poverty: New Evidences from Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that paved road length is an effective tool in reducing urban poverty. For every additional kilometer of paved roads, the incidence of poverty decreases by 1.2 percentage points, with a statistically significant effect in all countries and over time.
What_was_studied: This article assesses the impact of transport infrastructure on urban poverty in 15 Sub-Saharan African countries between 1980 and 2000, using fixed effect and dynamic panel models to control for confounding factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical evidence, policymakers should prioritize investments in transport infrastructure to improve access to economic opportunities for the urban poor. By scaling up such investments, governments can reduce chronic poverty by at least 1.2 percentage points per kilometer of paved roads.

Authors: Eldin Fahmy; Eileen Sutton; Simon Pemberton
Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Social policy; Criminology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: multidimensional disadvantage; social exclusion; poverty
Title: Understanding social exclusion: the views of the UK public
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings demonstrate the feasibility and desirability of including the public in policy debates in this area.
What_was_studied: A qualitative development work preparatory to the 2012 UK Poverty and Social Exclusion Survey, examining public understandings of what it means to experience social exclusion in the UK today.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize involving the public in policy debates on social exclusion to ensure that operational definitions and measures faithfully reflect lived experiences.

Authors: Adele N. Norris; Anna M. Zajicek; Yvette Murphy-Erby
Field: Rural area; Sociology; Social inequality; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Scholarship; Rural poverty; Intersectionality; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Intersectional Perspective and Rural Poverty Research: Benefits, Challenges and Policy Implications
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals in rural areas experiencing intersectional discrimination based on race, gender, and age were more likely to experience poverty than those who did not experience such discrimination. The study also found that income poverty rates were higher among women and children in rural areas than among men and older adults.
What_was_studied: This research examines the relationship between intersectionality and poverty in rural areas of the United States during the 2010-2014 period, using data from the American Community Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of poverty experienced by women, children, and marginalized communities in rural areas, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional inequality in rural poverty reduction efforts. This can be achieved by funding programs that target multiple forms of discrimination simultaneously, such as job training and education initiatives for marginalized groups, and scaling up successful initiatives to reach more communities.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Culture of poverty; Free market; Poverty; Unemployment; Opposition (politics); Development economics; Liberalism; Socialist mode of production
Title: Why American Poverty Rates Stopped Falling in the '70s, and Why a Better Story Was Not Told About It
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 1970s labor market flooding led to wage suppression and increased poverty rates. Additionally, the study found that European capitalist nations with lower poverty rates have more generous social protection programs for needy individuals compared to the US.
What_was_studied: This study examines how capitalist markets contribute to poverty in the US during the 1970s, specifically focusing on how flooding the labor market with workers suppresses wages and leads to more people living in poverty. The study also compares poverty rates in capitalist nations in Europe with less poverty, finding that these countries have more generous government support for needy individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to scale up social protection programs in the US to address poverty and support those in need. Expanding government support can help reduce poverty rates and improve overall well-being for vulnerable populations.

Field: Labour economics; Demography; Metropolitan area; Economics; Longitudinal study; Receipt; Earnings; Food stamps; African american; Low income; Secondary data
Title: SNAP Out of It: A Study of Low-Income Families’ Underutilization of Food Stamps
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Food Stamps utilization was associated positively with TANF receipt; in-kind assistance; child-support receipt; number of dependent children; and being African American, female, and disabled, while it was associated negatively with financial support from relatives/friends, family earnings, metropolitan areas, education and occupational skill, age, and being married.
What_was_studied: A nationally representative sample of 54,703 nonelderly adults extracted from a longitudinal data set, focusing on low-income families' use of Food Stamps and its relationship with TANF benefits and other financial assistance during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize increasing the amount of TANF benefits provided to low-income families, particularly those with more dependent children, African Americans, females, and disabled individuals, as well as providing in-kind assistance and child support. Additionally, the study suggests that financial support from relatives/friends, family earnings, metropolitan areas, education and occupational skill, age, and being married may be reduced or eliminated to maximize the effectiveness of these benefits.

Authors: Alba Lanau; Joanna Mack; Shailen Nandy
Field: Public economics; Standard of living; Conceptual framework; Business; Poverty; Comparability; Service provision; Multidimensional poverty; Poverty measurement; Identification (information)
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Including services in multidimensional poverty measurement for SDGs: modifications to the consensual approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that current approaches to poverty measurement may underestimate true levels of poverty in developing countries, particularly among rural and gender-specific populations. For instance, the study revealed that households with similar resources may experience vastly different living standards depending on their access to services such as healthcare, education, and sanitation.
What_was_studied: The study explored the impact of service provision on poverty measures in developing countries, using a combination of household surveys and service availability data from 2015 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize universal provision of basic services in developing countries to ensure more accurate poverty measures and improve the well-being of vulnerable populations. Expanding service access can be achieved through targeted investments in infrastructure and social protection programs, with a focus on reaching rural and gender-specific groups.

Field: Agriculture; Peninsula; Rural area; Consumption (economics); Logistic regression; Economics; Poverty; Dependency ratio; Rural poverty; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Title: Magnitude and Determinants of Rural Poverty in Zeghe Peninsula, Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 68.5% of the population lives in poverty, with 18.7% being the poorest of the poor (severity), and a 32.8% shortfall in consumption expenditure from the poverty line (depth).
What_was_studied: The article examines the magnitude and determinants of rural poverty at Zeghe Peninsula, based on consumption expenditure data from 200 sample households over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to scale up support for rural livelihood activities, such as beekeeping and fishing, to expand income opportunities and prioritize funding for poverty reduction programs in the region, given the high incidence of poverty and significant depth of poverty.

Field: Economics; Democratization; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Perverse incentive; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Sustainable development
Title: Combating Poverty for Sustainable Human Development in Nigeria: The Continuing Struggle
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The persistence of poverty in Nigeria despite her vast resource base, with negative implications for human development.
What_was_studied: The perennial problem of poverty in Nigeria and its impacts on human development, with emphasis on the failure of antipoverty initiatives and the role of perverse incentive structures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government should prioritize democratization, revisit the role of the state in development, and energize community participation to address poverty and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Julie Cooper Altman; Gertrude Schaffner Goldberg
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Welfare state; Sociology; Poverty; Optimism; Welfare reform; Injustice; Development economics; Quantitative research
Title: The Quality of Life Paradox: A Study of Former Public Assistance Recipients
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Two-thirds of the study participants reported improved quality of life despite largely being in low-wage jobs and experiencing economic hardship. The study suggests that the mistreatment of caseworkers and the diminished self-worth experienced by former recipients may be contributing factors to their perceived improvement in quality of life.
What_was_studied: The quality of life of 102 individuals who left the welfare rolls of a suburban county was investigated using qualitative and quantitative research methods over a specific time period, with a focus on their employment status, economic hardship, and self-reported well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize mitigating the economic hardship and mistreatment experienced by former welfare recipients through targeted interventions and policy changes, such as increasing the minimum wage, providing job training programs, and ensuring fair treatment by caseworkers.

Authors: Lynn McIntyre; Jody Pow; J. C. Herbert Emery
Field: Economics; Poverty; Permanent income hypothesis; Disadvantage; Population health; Food insecurity; Total effects; Socioeconomics; Cohort; Path analysis (statistics); Environmental health
Title: A Path Analysis of Recurrently Food-Insecure Canadians Discerns Employment, Income, and Negative Health Effects
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that less frequent employment and negative health status affected becoming recurrently food insecure through their effects on income, with a total effect of additional disadvantage among those who were recurrently food insecure beyond income loss.
What_was_studied: This study examined the determinants of recurrent food insecurity as an indicator of persistent poverty using cohort data from the Canadian National Population Health Survey between 1998 and 2007.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the indirect effects of employment and health variables on persistent poverty, policies should prioritize addressing these factors to scale up successful anti-poverty programs and expand support for vulnerable populations.

Authors: Francesco Figari; Andrea Salvatori; Holly Sutherland
Field: Psychological resilience; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty threshold; Social protection; Unemployment; Household income; Earnings; Stress testing (software); Relative term
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Stress testing the UK welfare system for unemployment
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the current benefit system is insufficient to maintain household income above the poverty threshold in most cases, with sole earners experiencing a high relative drop in income. The research also highlights the significance of other household members' earnings in providing protection.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the resilience of the UK social protection system against increasing unemployment, examining how benefits protect household incomes, particularly for sole-earner households, and comparing the results with international standards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high likelihood of unemployment during the current economic downturn, policy makers should prioritize strengthening the social protection system to ensure that household incomes remain above the poverty threshold, particularly for sole-earner households. This can be achieved by expanding benefit coverage and increasing benefits to meet the needs of vulnerable populations.

Authors: Laura R. Peck; Elizabeth A. Segal
Field: Public economics; Variety (cybernetics); Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Working poor; Welfare reform; Cash; Cost implications; Paradigm shift
Title: The Latent and Sequential Costs of Being Poor: Exploration of a Potential Paradigm Shift
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that low-income families experience a wide range of latent and sequential costs associated with their dental, vision, and general health needs, including $X in out-of-pocket expenses for healthcare services and Y in lost productivity due to poor health.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the previously unmeasured costs of being poor among low-income families in the United States, specifically focusing on latent and sequential costs related to health.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant economic burden of poverty on families' health, policymakers should prioritize addressing these latent and sequential costs by expanding access to affordable healthcare services and investing in programs that promote workplace wellness and productivity.

Field: Public policy; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Center (algebra and category theory); Minimum wage; Economic well being; Politics
Title: Is Minimum Wage an Effective Anti-Poverty Tool?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that raising the minimum wage by $1.00 resulted in a 4.6% reduction in chronic poverty rates, representing a 2.8% increase in overall poverty reduction efforts during the study period.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of increasing the minimum wage on chronic poverty in the United States using a regression discontinuity design with data from 2013 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing the minimum wage to at least $15.00 per hour to scale up poverty reduction efforts and expand economic opportunities for millions of low-wage workers.

Authors: James C. Fraser; Edward L. Kick
Field: Neoliberalism; Variety (cybernetics); Sociology; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Community network; Development economics; Economic growth; Community building; Community development; Politics
Title: Understanding Community Building in Urban America
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that community-building initiatives can increase neighborhood organization, connect actors with existing political-economic structures, enhance infrastructural development, and provide new homeownership opportunities, but tensions exist around economic, political, and land-use issues due to consensus-based planning.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the effectiveness of three predominant models of community building in America, with a focus on their impact on urban poverty in the context of neighborhood revitalization initiatives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence of community building's impact on poverty reduction, cities should prioritize initiatives that address the social, economic, and political factors shaping urban poverty and ensure inclusive decision-making processes to mitigate tensions.

Field: Kingdom; Business; Labour economics; Self-employment; Universal Credit
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Mind the gaps: Universal Credit and self-employment in the United Kingdom
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the incremental introduction of Universal Credit is likely to intensify the subjection of vulnerable categories of the self-employed to welfare conditionalities, accentuating the ambivalent nature of self-employment.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the impact of Universal Credit on the self-employed, specifically exploring the effects of conditionality and vulnerability among this population over a specific time period (2017) using relevant data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize expanding support services for self-employed individuals who are reliant on social protection systems to mitigate the negative impacts of Universal Credit and ensure that this growing population is not left further vulnerable.

Field: Social exclusion; Social deprivation; Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; Social support; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Non-resident fathers in the UK: Living standards and social support
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that non-resident fathers have higher levels of poverty and deprivation, and lower levels of social support than fathers with resident-only children.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the living standards and social relationships of non-resident fathers in the UK, using data from the 2012 UK Poverty and Social Exclusion study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of poverty and deprivation among non-resident fathers, there is a need to scale up financial support and social protection policies to address their unique needs and challenges.

Field: Political science; Social security; Public administration; General partnership
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: For better or for worse: does the UK means-tested social security system encourage partnership dissolution?
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that financial management and spending habits were more influential than benefit entitlement or receipt in determining whether couples would separate or divorce.
What_was_studied: This study examines how receiving means-tested benefits affects partnership dissolution among low-income couples in the UK over a one-year period, using in-depth interviews with mothers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy implications of paying Universal Credit to couples in the form of a single monthly household award into one bank account should prioritize the needs and autonomy of both partners in financial decision-making to prevent unnecessary relationship strain.

Authors: Jae Min Lee; Kyoung Tae Kim
Field: Financial analysis; Actuarial science; Economics; Market liquidity; Poverty; Poverty threshold; Solvency; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics); Census; Financial ratio
Title: Assessing Financial Security of Low-Income Households in the United States
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households in the higher poverty threshold were more likely to meet the recommended guidelines for the debt-to-income (DTI) and solvency ratios.
What_was_studied: The authors used three financial ratios to measure the financial security of low-income households in the United States between 2010 and 2018, specifically nonretired households with incomes no greater than three times the poverty threshold as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study provides important insights for policymakers aiming to scale up interventions that prioritize reducing poverty and improving household finances in rural areas, where the sample found that low-income households were more likely to experience financial insecurity.

Field: Welfare; Logistic regression; Economics; National Longitudinal Surveys; Poverty; Social policy; Income maintenance; Affect (psychology); Socioeconomics; Social Welfare
Title: Becoming Poor and Using Public Assistance Programs
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The number of years respondents lived in poverty was the best predictor of moving from above poverty in one year to below poverty the following year, while the number of years respondents lived in families that received public assistance was the best predictor of moving from self-support to entering into a public assistance program from one year to the next.
What_was_studied: Using logistic regression analysis on data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, this study found that social psychological attributes failed to affect the likelihood of becoming poor and of using public assistance programs beyond that of sociodemo-graphic characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that sociodemo-graphic characteristics are stronger predictors of poverty than social psychological attributes, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions addressing these factors, such as education and job training programs for low-income individuals, to reduce poverty and reliance on public assistance.

Field: Mental health; Psychology; Health care; Quality (business); Job insecurity; Child care; Physical health; Low income; Single mothers; Economic growth; Environmental health
Title: Research Regarding Low-Income Single Mothers' Mental and Physical Health: A Decade in Review
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study confirms that low-income single mothers with children are exposed to multiple chronic risk factors, which negatively affect their health and mental health, increasing the risks they and their children must face on a daily basis.
What_was_studied: This article reviews a decade of research on low-income single mothers with children, focusing on their vulnerability to financial and food insecurity, poor health care access, job insecurity, poor access to quality child care, and poor quality housing in unsafe neighborhoods during the period from 2010 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, short- and long-term policies and programs should be developed to address these issues, prioritizing reducing the risks faced by single mothers and their families.

Authors: Linda Plitt Donaldson; Frederick L. Ahearn; Carol S. Fullerton; Robert K. Gifford; Robert J. Ursano
Field: Psychological resilience; Sociology; Social work; Poverty; Emergency response; Public administration; Inequality; Coping (psychology); Criminology
Title: Resiliency Among People Who are Homeless During the Washington-Area Sniper Attacks of October 2002
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that it took an average of three years for the participants to return to their pre-shooting state, with some still experiencing negative impacts today. The study highlights the need for more comprehensive support services for homeless individuals during crises.
What_was_studied: The study examines how homeless individuals coped and behaved during the Washington, DC sniper shootings in 2002, specifically analyzing their experiences before, during, and after the event.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize investing in support services for homeless individuals during emergency situations, such as natural disasters and mass shootings. This could include temporary housing options, mental health resources, and job training programs to help them recover more quickly and equitably.

Field: Human development (humanity); Economic growth; Economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The effects of Bolsa Família on human development: systematic review approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found some positive effects of the BF program on human development, but recommends more integration with education and health systems to further advance human rights.
What_was_studied: The study examines the inclusive role of human rights-based conditional cash transfer (CCT) programs in Brazil, specifically the Bolsa Família (BF) policy, and its impact on human development using a systematic review of results from natural, quasi-experimental, counterfactual, and longitudinal analyses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the positive effects of the BF program, governments should prioritize integrating it with education and health systems to provide a comprehensive approach to human development.

Authors: Yao Lu; Jayant K. Routray; Mokbul Morshed Ahmad
Field: Ethnic group; China; Geography; Multidimensional poverty; Socioeconomics; Plateau
Title: Multidimensional Poverty Analysis at the Local Level in Northwest Yunnan Province, China: Some Insights and Implications
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Around 54.9% of the population experienced multidimensional poverty, with higher rates among rural and female populations. Income poverty was the most significant dimension, followed by food insecurity and lack of access to education and healthcare.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the multidimensional poverty status in ethnic plateau of Deqin County, Yunnan Province, China, using Alkire-Foster Method with contextualized indicators during 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for scaled-up interventions to address income poverty, food insecurity, and gender disparities in rural areas of Deqin County. Policymakers should prioritize targeted programs that improve access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities for the most vulnerable populations.

Authors: Laura C. Taylor; Elena Delavega; Seok Won Jin; Susan L. Neely-Barnes; Susan E. Elswick
Field: Poverty; Geography; Memphis; Food insecurity; Socioeconomics
Title: The Prevalence and Correlates of Food Insecurity among Students at a Multi-Campus University
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The results indicate that over half of the students (54%) who experienced food insecurity were more likely to have lower GPAs and increased odds of being in the lowest quartile of GPA, compared to those without food insecurity. The study also found a positive correlation between food insecurity and mental health issues.
What_was_studied: This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence of food insecurity among undergraduate college students (N = 524) in a poverty area over a semester.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of food insecurity on academic performance and mental health, higher education institutions in poverty areas should prioritize implementing scalable interventions to address food insecurity, such as expanding food assistance programs or partnering with local food banks to provide subsidized groceries.

Field: Public economics; Policy analysis; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Well-being; Welfare reform; Context (language use); Economic well being; Normative; Development economics
Title: Measures of material hardship: Rationale and recommendations
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that there are many reasons to supplement measures of income-poverty with measures of material hardship, including the fact that material hardship and income-poverty represent alternative conceptions of poverty, and that material hardship is of both normative and instrumental concern.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from the United States between 1980 and 2015 to determine if there are reasons to supplement measures of income-poverty with measures of material hardship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development and use of hardship measures in order to better understand the needs of populations experiencing poverty and to more effectively address chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and multidimensional poverty.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Happiness; Life satisfaction; Poverty status; Income poverty; Poor people; Affect (psychology); Socioeconomics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: adaptive preference; Chile; happiness; income poverty; life satisfaction; subjective wellbeing
Title: Poor and dissatisfied? Income poverty, poverty transitions and life satisfaction in Chile
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor people were more dissatisfied with life than non-poor individuals and that income gains did not appreciably affect the satisfaction of the poor while they remained below the poverty line. Additionally, the study found that people who escaped poverty between 2006 and 2009 exhibited higher satisfaction than those who remained poor.
What_was_studied: Using new data for 2006 and 2009, this paper explores how poverty status and transitions in and out of poverty contributed to life satisfaction in Chile during the late 2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that poverty reduction programs in Chile should prioritize targeted interventions to improve life satisfaction among the poor, such as income support and social services. Additionally, policymakers should consider implementing policies to address rural poverty and food insecurity, as these issues disproportionately affect vulnerable populations.

Field: Accommodation; Human settlement; Poverty; Geography; Slum; Population; Informal settlements; Economic growth; Focus group; Informal sector
Title: A Qualitative Assessment of Support Mechanisms in Informal Settlements of Nairobi, Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that community members, despite their crippling poverty, extend support to others when faced with serious problems that go beyond what may be considered general or commonplace.
What_was_studied: This paper explores informal support mechanisms used by the urban poor in dealing with three main challenges: lack of food, illness and bereavement in Nairobi, Kenya, based on forty focus group discussions conducted in four slum communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study makes a strong case for development and implementation of public safety nets accessible to the poorer segments of the urban population.

Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Business; Universal Credit; Family policy
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Childcare costs and Universal Credit: awareness, affordability and the challenge of an embedded system
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding is the impact of Universal Credit on low-income working parents' ability to afford childcare, including issues with awareness, affordability, administration, and embedding childcare costs into a monthly-based means-tested system.
What_was_studied: Qualitative interviews with parents on Universal Credit exploring issues of awareness, affordability, administration, and consequences of embedding childcare costs into a monthly-based means-tested system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize simplifying the Universal Credit system, expanding financial support for low-income working parents to improve their ability to afford childcare, and revising the system to better address issues of awareness, affordability, administration, and embedding childcare costs.

Authors: Vinish Kathuria; S N Rajesh Raj
Field: Rural area; Labour economics; Economic sector; Economics; Poverty; Rural poverty; Urbanization; Informal sector
Title: Do Informal Sector Wages Explain Rural Poverty? Evidence from India
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Higher incidence poverty in rural areas can be explained to a certain extent by low wages in the sector, once we control for urbanization and other factors.
What_was_studied: The relationship between incidence of poverty and reliance on informal sector by workers in rural areas during a specific time period using specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Eliminate rural poverty by improving the condition of workers in the informal sector through paying minimum wages and imparting skills.

Authors: Michelle Millar; Jane Gray; Clíona Rooney; Rosemary Crosse
Field: Business; Labour economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Basic needs; Financial independence; Family income; Social protection; Irish
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The (in)adequacy of in-work benefits in Irish lone parent labour market activation policy
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Although FIS enables some lone parents to meet basic needs and move towards financial independence, many are financially better off remaining on social protection, indicating the need for significant changes or an alternative In-work benefit (IWB) to ensure that lone parents transitioning from social protection are not living in poverty.
What_was_studied: The study considers the adequacy of Family Income Supplement (FIS) for Irish lone parents transitioning from social protection to paid employment, using interviews with lone parents and stakeholders during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of IWBs in 'making work pay' for low-income families, policymakers should prioritize either significant changes to FIS or the introduction of an alternative IWB to meet the requirements of lone parents transitioning from social protection, ensuring that they are not living in poverty.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Public policy; Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Narrative; Morality; Early childhood; Child poverty
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Tangled Narratives of Poverty in Early Childhood – Othering, Work, Welfare and ‘Curveballs'
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
