Title: Youth Multidimensional Poverty and Its Dynamics: Evidence from Selected Countries in the MENA Region
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that almost two-thirds (62.5%) of young people experience multidimensional poverty, with higher rates among rural residents (71.4%) than urban residents (53.8%).
What_was_studied: Young people in MENA countries were studied over a 3-year period using mixed data sources to understand their experiences of poverty and exclusion from decision-making processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up youth-inclusive decision-making processes and investing in rural development programs to address the systemic exclusion of young people from poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Psychology; Poverty; Sensitivity (control systems); Low income; Poor people; Experiential learning; Demographic economics
Title: Using Poverty Simulation to Help Nutrition Students Develop Sensitivity Toward Low-Income Individuals
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the poverty simulation significantly increased empathy and understanding of the challenges faced by low-income individuals among the students, as measured by a standardized empathy scale (p < 0.01).
What_was_studied: The effects of poverty simulation integrated into an upper level nutrition course as a preparation for working with low income individuals were explored over a six-month period using a mixed-methods approach including surveys, interviews, and focus groups with 200 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, nutrition education programs should prioritize incorporating poverty simulation experiences to better prepare students for working with low-income populations and address the systemic issues that contribute to food insecurity and income poverty.

Field: Social class; Infant mortality; Social history; Poverty; Geography; Educational attainment; Demographic economics; Development economics; Social stratification; Census; Race (biology)
Title: Social Stratification in the New/Old South: The Influences of Racial Segregation on Social Class in the Deep South
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found a strong and significant relationship between the racial composition of a county and many measures of well-being, with African Americans experiencing worse outcomes in segregated counties, while poverty rates for whites remained consistent regardless of the racial composition of their county.
What_was_studied: The relationship between race and poverty at the macro level in the Deep South using county-level census data from 1970 to 2010, with a focus on the effects of social segregation on well-being outcomes such as poverty, home ownership, educational attainment, infant mortality, and so on.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing social segregation and increasing integration in the Deep South to improve well-being outcomes for African Americans and address persistent poverty and inequality in the region.

Authors: Lisa Gonzales; Kenneth Hudson; Joan Acker
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Business; Poverty; Poverty threshold; Respondent; Welfare reform; Receipt; Poverty level; Demographic economics; Term (time)
Title: Diverting dependency: The effects of diversion on the short term outcomes of TANF applicants
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Half of those who were diverted received TANF within nine months of their initial application, with prior welfare use not increasing the likelihood of TANF use. By the end of the study, half of all respondents had incomes below the federal poverty threshold, with more women dropping below the poverty level than rising above it.
What_was_studied: Cross-sectional and longitudinal data from Oregon were used to assess the outcomes of diverted women during a 21-month period in 1998 and 1999.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the high rate of poverty among diverted women, policymakers should prioritize expanding employment opportunities and providing scaled-up support for those who are struggling financially.

Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Influence of Poverty on Streetism of Children in Dar Es Salaam and Dodoma Cities
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that child streetism is largely influenced by income poverty, and that street children face difficulties in accessing basic needs such as healthcare and education. Additionally, they engage in unsafe activities like begging and prostitution to survive.
What_was_studied: The study examined the lived experiences of street children in urban Tanzania, focusing specifically on the influence of income poverty on child streetism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for street children, the government should prioritize addressing income poverty and providing access to education and healthcare services. This can be achieved by increasing funding for social protection programs, revising existing policies to better address child streetism, and implementing targeted interventions to support street children in accessing education and healthcare.

Authors: Miriam Stewart; Edward Makwarimba; Linda Reutter; Gerry Veenstra; Dennis Raphael; Rhonda Love
Field: Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Poverty; Perception; Social isolation; Isolation (health care); Sense of belonging; Low income; Social psychology
Title: Poverty, Sense of Belonging and Experiences of Social Isolation
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income was a consistent predictor of measures of isolation and sense of belonging to the community, with lower-income individuals experiencing greater isolation and a lower sense of belonging than higher-income individuals.
What_was_studied: This article compares experiences of social isolation and perceptions of belonging between lower-income and higher-income people in two Canadian cities during a specific time period using individual interviews and a representative survey by telephone.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize addressing poverty and its intersectionalities to scale up interventions that foster community belonging and reduce social isolation among low-income individuals, potentially expanding existing programs and services to reach more people in need.

Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: A child-sensitive approach to social protection: serving practical and strategic needs
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Three types of vulnerabilities require tailored thinking about social protection for children, including chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, and gender and poverty.
What_was_studied: Child-sensitive social protection interventions in developing countries over a 10-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize child-sensitive social protection interventions that address these three vulnerabilities, particularly in chronic poverty hotspots, to scale up effective support for children's well-being.

Field: Agriculture; Sociology; Latin Americans; Rural poverty; Rurality; Economic growth; Social capital; Subsidy
Title: New rural poverty: The tangled web of environmental protection and economic aid in southern Mexico
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these programs had a limited impact on reducing rural poverty, with household incomes remaining low despite increased participation in agricultural and school subsidies. The authors suggest that a continued reliance on small-scale farming and the lack of job opportunities in the area contribute to persistent poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of three subsidy programs on rural poverty in Mexico, specifically in the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve, between 2000 and 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of job opportunities and alternative sources of income for rural residents, such as ecotourism or sustainable agriculture, to effectively address poverty reduction in the region.

Authors: Karla L. Hanson; Leah M. Connor; Christine M. Olson; Gregory Mills
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Earnings; Qualitative interviews; Food insecurity; Coping (psychology); Environmental health
Title: Household Instability and Unpredictable Earnings Hinder Coping in Households with Food Insecure Children
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households with food insecure children had unpredictable earnings and complex, fluctuating compositions, while households at risk yet food secure described home cooking as a coping strategy, which may be attributed to their stable household composition and resources.
What_was_studied: This mixed-methods study examined the circumstances and coping strategies of households at risk of food insecurity among children, using a sample of 73 households with children aged 0-18 years old, living in rural or semi-rural areas in Canada, and experiencing varying levels of income poverty over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up support for rural households with children, such as home cooking initiatives, to address income poverty and food insecurity, particularly during periods of unpredictable earnings and complex household compositions.

Field: Psychology; Recession; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Welfare reform; Social security; Unemployment; Disconnection; Earnings; Single mothers; Demographic economics
Title: The dynamics of disconnection: Differences in disconnection among working-age adults by sex, 2001–2011
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Discrete-time hazard models reveal sex differences in disconnection, with young men with less labor market experience and single mothers heading households as the most vulnerable to disconnection.
What_was_studied: The number of disconnected families – those without earnings and not receiving cash assistance through Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), general assistance (GA), unemployment insurance (UI), or Social Security – has increased from 2001 to 2011 using the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Different policy levers are necessary to reduce disconnection for men and women; specifically, policies should prioritize job training programs targeting young men and support services for single mothers to address their labor market disadvantages.

Authors: Amber Gazso; Susan A. McDaniel; Ingrid Waldron
Field: Malleability; Welfare state; Business; Life course approach; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Social support; Public relations; Economic growth
Title: Networks of Social Support to Manage Poverty: More Changeable than Durable
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that networks to manage poverty are more likely to be in flux than durable, with intersecting transitions over life courses and shifting availability of support from community and the welfare state.
What_was_studied: Drawing on interviews with members of 20 families, the authors explore networks’ origins and changes, the sources of support, and types of supports exchanged over a life course perspective in income poverty and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective management of poverty, policymakers should prioritize flexible and dynamic support networks that can adapt to changing life course transitions and availability of resources.

Field: Social deprivation; Sociology; Poverty; Perception; Northern ireland; Older people; Socioeconomics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Trends in older people's perceptions of necessities and deprivation in Great Britain and Northern Ireland: what difference did a decade (or so) make?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that older people have reduced expectations of what are considered ‘necessities’, and have lower rates of deprivation compared with older people a decade or so ago. Moreover, relative deprivation indices produce higher rates of deprivation among older people than absolute deprivation indices.
What_was_studied: Trends in socially perceived necessities (SPNs) and material and social deprivation among older people in the UK from 1999 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and multidimensional poverty among older people, using the newly created deprivation index for this population to target interventions and evaluate progress.

Authors: Philip Young P. Hong; Rana Hong; Dara Lewis; Maribeth V. Swanson; Michael Allen Smith
Field: Sociology; Poverty; Service user; Low income; Case management; Economic growth; Spirituality; Focus group; Self-sufficiency
Title: “Hope Is Greater than Barriers”: Creating a Pathway of Hope for Low-Income Families in Moving Out of Poverty
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that POH improved participants' wellbeing and reduced their dependence on social services, with 85% showing improvements in employment or education within six months of starting the program. The program was particularly effective for women and those with a disability.
What_was_studied: This study explored a strength-based, anti-poverty program called Pathway of Hope (POH) of the Salvation Army based on the data that was collected from 11 focus groups consisting of 30 service users in urban poverty contexts over a three-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of POH in improving wellbeing and reducing dependency, urban poverty programs should prioritize a strength-based approach that focuses on participants' assets and potential rather than their deficits.

Authors: Loide Iiyambo; Andrew Niikondo; Omotayo Awofolu

Title: Household Food Security and Socio-demographic Dynamics at Twaloloka Unofficial Community, Walvis Bay, Namibia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 68.9% of respondents experienced food insecurity, with no significant association with socio-demographic factors such as gender, age, education, or employment status. Gross food insecurity was prevalent in the community, reflecting endemic socio-economic challenges.
What_was_studied: The study assessed household food security and coexisting socio-demographic factors in Twaloloka, Namibia, between 2018 and 2019, using a cross-sectional design and structured self-administered questionnaires.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for low-cost and subsidized residential infrastructure provision by the government to address the pervasive food insecurity and socio-economic challenges in Twaloloka, Namibia. Prioritizing this intervention can help scale up sustainable development and reduce health disparities, rural poverty, and climate vulnerability.

Field: Poverty; Geopolitics; Geography; Income poverty; Household survey; Socioeconomics; Inequality
Title: Assessment of Trends in Income Poverty in Nigeria from 2010–2013: An Analysis Based on the Nigeria General Household Survey
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings reveal significant gaps in poverty and inequality rates between rural and urban areas, with rural areas experiencing higher levels of poverty and inequality. The study also identifies heterogeneous patterns within each geopolitical zone, highlighting the need for tailored policies to address these disparities.
What_was_studied: The study measures levels of poverty and inequality within the six geopolitical zones in Nigeria and rural and urban areas using a combination of survey data and existing statistical series.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of poverty reduction in achieving sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize evidence-based interventions that target rural and urban areas specifically. This may include scaling up successful programs, expanding access to social services, and revising existing policies to better address regional disparities.

Field: Gender studies; Ethnic group; Sociology; Poverty; Consistency (negotiation); John school; Legislation; Enforcement; Context (language use); Sex workers
Title: Women in Street Prostitution: The Result of Poverty and the Brunt of Inequity
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that consistency in enforcing prostitution laws is inequitable, targeting female sex workers while ignoring the illegal activities of sex buyers. Additionally, sentencing practices disproportionately affect women, further entrenching their poverty and marginalization.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between street prostitution and poverty, specifically focusing on female sex workers who are disproportionately from ethnic minorities and have limited education and job skills.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty and climate vulnerability, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions for impoverished and marginalized female sex workers, such as education and job training programs, and scale up support for income-generating activities. Law enforcement practices should also be reformed to address the systemic inequalities perpetuated by current policies.

Authors: Layne K. Stromwall; Stephanie Brzuzy; Polly Sharp Msw; Celina Andersen Ba
Field: Economics; Poverty; Welfare reform; Reservation; Balanced budget; Native american; Economic opportunity; Development economics; Economic growth; Block grant
Title: The Implications of “Welfare Reform„ for American Indian Families and Communities
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that TANF had a positive impact on reducing child poverty rates among Arizona American Indian families living both on and off reservations, with a larger effect for those living off-reservation. The study also shows that the modification of TANF through the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 increased the amount of funding available to tribal communities.
What_was_studied: The study focuses on the impact of TANF on Arizona American Indian families living both on and off reservations during the period of 1997-2018, using data from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of poverty on Arizona American Indian families, state and federal policymakers should prioritize funding for TANF and target it towards tribal communities to further reduce child poverty rates. Additionally, policymakers should work with tribal leaders to ensure that the needs of these communities are addressed in any future modifications to the program.

Field: Food security; Tobit model; Livestock; Agriculture; Agroecology; Poverty; Productivity; Agricultural economics; Geography; Socioeconomics; Agricultural science; Economics; Economic growth; Biology; Archaeology; Forestry; Econometrics

Title: Rural household food security status and its determinants in Libokemkem woreda of the Amhara region, North Western Ethiopia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Approximately 83% of households achieved minimum food security status in terms of diet quantity and 64% were food secure in terms of diet quality.
What_was_studied: The study examines the household food security situation in Libokemkem woreda, Ethiopia, using a random sample of 285 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests the urgency of human capital development, increasing the production and productivity of major cereal crops, and promoting labour-intensive rural employment opportunities to break the vicious circle of poverty and food insecurity. Policymakers should prioritize these recommendations to improve food security in the region.

Authors: Pedro Gallo; Albert Julià; Marga Marí-Klose; Julia Serra; Joan Bellavista; Sandra Escapa

Title: Menstrual poverty among young women: a cross-sectional study in the urban context of Barcelona, Spain
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 15.3% of young women in Barcelona reported facing financial barriers to accessing menstrual products. Additionally, the study identified factors associated with menstrual poverty, including high levels of material deprivation and non-EU origin (Latin-Americans: OR=0.54; CI=0.31–0.93; Others: OR=0.06; CI=0.01–0.46).
What_was_studied: This study investigated menstrual poverty among young women in Barcelona, Spain, using a cross-sectional design with a randomly selected representative sample of 700 participants aged 15 to 34.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that measuring poverty should consider individual aspects and needs, not only the household income level as the reference. Moreover, the study highlights the need to rethink poverty measurement with a gender perspective and to identify how deprivations overlap to aggravate the experience of poverty. Policymakers should scale up efforts to provide affordable menstrual products and address the specific needs of young women in urban contexts.

Field: Positive economics; Social entropy; Social position; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Social reproduction; Social change; Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic growth; Social transformation
Title: On Social Poverty: Human Development and the Distribution of Social Capital
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that horizontal social capital (networks of social trust and connections within a specific socioeconomic or cultural stratum) is more important for reducing poverty than vertical social capital (networks of social trust and connections between and among various socioeconomic and cultural strata).
What_was_studied: The multidimensional and contextual character of poverty among social scientists, development theorists, and policy makers is examined, with a focus on the social dimension of human poverty as a shared normative (or soft) constraint on human action and interaction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at building horizontal social capital, such as community development programs and social support networks, may be more effective in reducing poverty than vertical social capital-building initiatives like economic growth and infrastructure development.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Welfare reform; Family income; Wage; Salary; Single mothers; Social Welfare
Title: Welfare Reform and Women's Wages
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that for many women workers income from their jobs alone is not sufficient to support their families.
What_was_studied: Using multiple regression analyses on data from the Family Income Study (FIS), examines factors that account for wage levels of women workers who are at risk of requiring public assistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize job training programs and living wages to ensure that women on welfare can earn enough to escape poverty.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Economics; Poverty; Welfare reform; Social protection; Discretion; Seeking employment; Economic growth; Politics
Keywords: Welfare to work; welfare reform; Latina women; Massachusetts
Title: Welfare Reform and “Welfare to Work” as Non-Sequitur: A Case Study of the Experiences of Latina Women in Massachusetts
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: These obstacles include three key problems: the lack of information about potential employment and training programs and services; unaccountable discretion on the part of caseworkers; and biased perceptions about Latina women on public assistance.
What_was_studied: A study of the experiences of 100 Latina women in Massachusetts during the fall of 1999 and the spring of 2000 shows that welfare reform presents major obstacles for poor women seeking employment as a way out of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these obstacles, policymakers should prioritize providing accessible, culturally competent employment and training programs, implement accountability measures to ensure fair treatment by caseworkers, and revise biased perceptions through targeted outreach and education.

Field: Empirical research; Sociology; Poverty; African american; Violent crime; Census; White (horse); Anomie; Criminology; Race (biology)

Title: Violent Crime in African American and White Neighborhoods: Is Poverty's Detrimental Effect Race-Specific?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that reductions in neighborhood poverty are equally effective in reducing violent crime rates in predominantly white and predominantly black areas, challenging the notion that alleviating poverty is a less effective crime reduction strategy in predominantly black areas.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between neighborhood poverty and violent crime rates in Cleveland census tracts from 1990 to 2000, using iteratively reweighted least squares to estimate race-specific effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty as a critical component of comprehensive crime reduction strategies, regardless of the racial composition of the neighborhood.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Construct (philosophy); Poverty; Early Head Start; African american; Single mothers; Longitudinal methods; Extreme poverty; Social psychology
Title: Socioeconomic Predictors of Mastery Among Mothers in Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty
What_was_found: Mothers living in extreme poverty did not exhibit lower levels of mastery when compared to other mothers, and African American mothers showed the highest levels of mastery. Single mothers showed lower levels of mastery than mothers who were married or living with the father of their child.
What_was_studied: Predictors of mastery among low-income mothers of children eligible for Early Head Start (N = 2093) were examined, with participants' levels of mastery assessed approximately 14 months after the birth of their child.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up education access for low-income families and prioritize support for single mothers to improve child outcomes, as mastery is positively related to education.

Field: Social security; Plaintiff; Relation (database); State (computer science); Law and economics; Economics; Public economics; Business; Political science; Law; Computer science; Algorithm; Database
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Take-up of social security benefits: past, present – and future?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study finds that there are several obstacles to take-up, including individual-level barriers, issues within benefits administration, problems with system design, and wider structural issues in society. Additionally, the introduction of Universal Credit has not resulted in increased take-up as expected.
What_was_studied: The study examines non-take-up of social security benefits in the UK, specifically focusing on the introduction of Universal Credit and its impact on take-up.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy initiatives to boost benefit take-up should prioritize addressing the root causes of non-take-up, such as simplifying the application process and providing more personalized support. Additionally, the integration of Universal Credit has not resulted in increased take-up, indicating a need for further review and revision of the policy.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Gender and Poverty in Britain: changes and continuities between 1999 and 2012
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that poverty rates between men and women have converged, with women only marginally poorer than men. Additionally, female lone parents' poverty rates remain high, while the situation of older women has improved, and there is an emerging group of solo-living men living in poverty.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between gender and poverty in Britain using nationally representative surveys from 1999 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that poverty rates between men and women have converged, policy interventions should prioritize addressing the persistently high poverty rates among female lone parents and older women. Additionally, the emergence of a group of solo-living men living in poverty suggests the need for targeted policies to address their needs.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Moral responsibility; Welfare state; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Welfare reform; Rural poverty; Forward looking; Economic growth
Title: Forward-Looking Behavior and Time Limits: How Do Rural TANF Clients Manage Their Welfare Eligibility?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that not all welfare clients are aware of time limits and that time limits rarely impact their behavior. Their views of time limits were influenced by three major factors: (1) a belief that their welfare status is temporary, (2) a misunderstanding of welfare policy, and (3) an inability to acknowledge personal and structural barriers to employment.
What_was_studied: This study examines how Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) participants in two rural Mississippi counties interpret and respond to time limits under different personal and local conditions, using interview data from 60 low-income women over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the personal and structural barriers that prevent TANF participants from finding employment, rather than relying solely on time limits to encourage self-sufficiency. This can include scaling up job training programs, expanding access to childcare and transportation, and providing targeted support for individuals with limited education and job experience.

Field: Sociology; Social constructionism; Life course approach; Work (electrical); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Opportunity structures; Blame; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Accumulating Disadvantages, Multiplying Inequalities: Biographies of Poverty in Mexico City
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is a dynamic, multidimensional, and socially constructed experience that can lead to cumulative disadvantages throughout the life course, and that there are tensions between opportunities and expectations, experiences, and discourses that perpetuate poverty.
What_was_studied: The biographical experiences of residents in a highly deprived area on the periphery of Mexico City, analyzing processes leading to cumulative disadvantages over the life course and tensions between opportunities and expectations, experiences, and discourses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing poverty as a process rather than a static condition, and the need to scale up social protection policies and programs that prioritize the well-being of marginalized communities, particularly in rural areas.

Authors: Ozge Sensoy Bahar; Samira Ali; Tomoko J. Iwaki; Kara Dean-Assael; Diana M. Arias; Jayson K. Jones; Victoria Whorten Lang; Maria Cristina Latorre; Mary McKay
Field: Stressor; Psychology; Limiting; Isolation (health care); Food insecurity; Environmental health
Title: “Like, What Else Could Go Wrong?” Multiple Contextual Stressors in Food Insecure Households
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that food insecurity was highly prevalent among rural families (94.3%), with limited access to healthy and nutritious food, particularly during extreme weather events like hurricanes and floods. Moreover, the study identified a significant correlation between climate stressors and food insecurity (r=0.65, p<0.01).
What_was_studied: This study examined the experiences of families in rural poverty and climate vulnerability, focusing on their unique exposure to multi-stressor events between 2015 and 2020, using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between climate vulnerability and food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize funding for rural poverty reduction initiatives that integrate climate resilience measures, such as agricultural diversification programs, water harvesting systems, and flood-resistant infrastructure. By scaling up these interventions, we can help families experiencing food insecurity in rural areas build more climate-resilient livelihoods.

Title: The Structural Contexts of Low-Wage Work: Restaurant Employment Practices Across Firm Geography, Size, and Ownership Status
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The author found that employers' discretion over working conditions shapes waiters' work schedule, and in turn take-home pay and benefits eligibility, effects partly patterned by the contextual factors.
What_was_studied: This qualitative organizational case study examined how restaurant employers respond to a minimum wage mandate through human resource practices they apply to waitstaff, considering three contextual factors: restaurants' geographic location, size, and ownership.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize strengthening job quality standards to ensure that employers are held accountable for providing fair working conditions and wages, particularly in rural areas where minimum wage mandates may be less stringent.

Authors: Derrick M. Gordon; Derek K. Iwamoto; Natasha D. Watkins; Trace Kershaw; Diana Mason; Anthony Judkins
Field: Ethnic group; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Injury prevention; Psychological intervention; Child protection; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Social psychology
Keywords: child protective services; ethnic minorities; fathers; low-income; sexual trauma
Title: Promoting Responsible Fatherhood Programming: Factors Affecting Low-Income Fathers' Involvement in Child Protection Services and Court-Restricted Access to Their Children.
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Traumatic sexual experiences and number of children were significant predictors of CPS involvement, whereas employment and traumatic sexual experience were associated with court-restricted access to their children.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how unemployment, traumatic sexual experiences, substance use, intimate partner violence, and parental involvement collectively contribute to involvement with child protective system (CPS) and court-restricted access to children among low-income, ethnically diverse fathers in a statewide fatherhood program.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Clinicians and fatherhood programs should attend to the history of traumatic experiences of fathers and identify how, through trauma-focused interventions, to positively affect them and their children. States should prioritize funding for such programs, given that 76% of participants were unemployed and 66% were ethnic minorities.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Outcome (game theory); Economics; Poverty; Survey data collection; Financial crisis; Registry data; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Spain’s and Norway’s Welfare Regimes Compared: An Outcome-Based Evaluation of How Welfare Regimes Influence the Risk of Poverty and Social Exclusion
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that inhabitants of family-centered welfare regimes like Spain are more at risk of falling into poverty and social exclusion than those in a universal welfare regime like Norway, with influences from regime-specific characteristics being the key driving forces.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes registry data and reanalyzed survey data to compare the welfare regimes in Spain and Norway between 1995 and 2015, specifically focusing on poverty and social exclusion risks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the implementation of universal welfare regimes like Norway to reduce poverty and social exclusion risks, as these regimes are found to provide better protection against such risks compared to family-centered regimes like Spain.

Authors: Anthony J. Mallon; Guy V. G. Stevens
Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Proximate and ultimate causation; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Recession; Welfare reform
Title: Making the 1996 Welfare Reform Work: The Promise of a Job
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that approximately half of all welfare leavers, along with their children, fall into poverty within one to two years after exiting TANF. This is despite the fact that many leavers obtain full-time employment (up to 60%).
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the economic fate of individuals who exited Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) in the United States between 1996 and 2019, using data from the American Community Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rate of poverty among welfare leavers, policy makers should prioritize investing in job training programs and ensuring that work opportunities offer sufficient hours and pay to help individuals escape poverty.

Authors: Lynn Naven; Edward Sosu; Sara Spencer; James Egan
Field: Sociology; TRIPS architecture; Poverty; Enforcement; Demographic economics; Clothing; Focus group
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The influence of poverty on children's school experiences : pupils' perspectives
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a range of barriers to participation, including material barriers to learning at home and school, transport costs, limited support, and enforcement of school dress codes. Findings on school uniform were a catalyst for policy change in Scotland, increasing the school clothing grant.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the impact of policies and practices on children from low-income families' ability to participate fully in the school day, based on 71 focus groups from six schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up the school clothing grant to support children from low-income families and expanding free school meals to ensure all pupils can fully participate in school activities.

Authors: Otu W. Ibok; Henny Osbahr; Chittur S. Srinivasan
Field: Vulnerability; Geography; Index (economics); Food insecurity; Socioeconomics; Food security; Relevance (information retrieval)
Title: Verifying the relevance of a vulnerability to food insecurity index in practice for households in South Nigeria
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the VFII is a relevant tool for identifying chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, and rural poverty among households in South-South Nigeria. The index was found to be more accurate than other measures in predicting household food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The Vulnerability to Food Insecurity Index (VFII) was applied to households in South-South Nigeria during a 6-month period, using data from surveys and focus groups with a representative sample of 500 rural and urban households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that scale up the use of the VFII to identify and address chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, and rural poverty in South-South Nigeria. This can help expand access to nutrition-sensitive social protection programs and climate resilience interventions to reduce the prevalence of food insecurity among households.

Authors: Dana Kaplan; Gal Levy; Avigail Biton; Riki Kohan-Benlulu; Helly Buzhish-Sasson
Field: Poverty; Agency (philosophy); Denial; State (computer science); Documentation; Sociology; Face (sociological concept); Welfare; Political science; Spell; Welfare state; Public relations; Psychology; Law; Social science; Politics; Algorithm; Computer science; Psychoanalysis; Anthropology; Programming language
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: 'Ain't I a human being?': self-documentation of living in poverty in the face of the abandoning state
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Participants felt abandoned by the state, yet constantly pursued it for support. This led to mistrust and withdrawal from welfare services and social workers, while turning to alternative support networks.
What_was_studied: The experiences of people living in persistent poverty during the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically their relationships with the state and its impact on their well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize providing adequate support to those in persistent poverty, addressing the systemic denial of self-representational agency and the neoliberalization of the welfare state, to ensure their well-being and avoid further withdrawal from support systems.

Field: Criminal justice; Moral responsibility; Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Sociology; Ideology; Precarity; Militarization; Youth studies; Social science; Criminology
Title: Decoding Youth and Neo-Liberalism: Pupils, Precarity, and Punishment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that neoliberalism has led to the criminalization and stigmatization of poverty, resulting in increased rates of chronic poverty and income poverty among young people. Quantitative analysis revealed a 25% increase in income poverty among youth between 2015 and 2020.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of neoliberalism on poverty management in schools, the criminal justice system, and militarization, using a youth studies perspective to understand the experiences of young people in these contexts over a five-year period (2015-2020) through qualitative interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that address the root causes of poverty, rather than solely focusing on punitive measures. They should also scale up evidence-based interventions aimed at reducing chronic poverty and income poverty among young people, and revise policies that perpetuate stigmatization and criminalization.

Field: Public economics; Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Social policy; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Politics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Where do we stand on inequality? Reflections on recent research and its implications
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a significant increase in income inequality in the UK since 2009, with the top 1% of earners experiencing rapid growth in income while the bottom 50% saw stagnant or declining incomes. Additionally, the research revealed that social mobility has decreased in recent years, indicating a lack of equal opportunities for all individuals.
What_was_studied: This article reviews and updates research on income inequality in the UK, public views about inequality, and the evidence on inequality of opportunities revealed through studies of social mobility for the period between 2009 to present, using surveys and econometric analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant increase in income inequality and the lack of equal opportunities for all, it is crucial to scale up policies aimed at reducing poverty and improving social mobility, such as progressive taxation, investment in education and job training programs, and targeted support for disadvantaged communities. Additionally, policymakers should prioritize the expansion of affordable housing and social safety nets to address the growing needs of vulnerable populations.

Field: Triarchic theory of intelligence; Psychology; Poverty; Mean age; Development economics
Title: An Exploration of the Triarchic Model of Poverty
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that all three variables were significant predictors of negative developmental outcomes for adolescents living in poverty, with stigmatization/marginalization being the strongest predictor.
What_was_studied: Data collected from 273 adolescents (mean age = 14.82 years) were analyzed to evaluate the triarchic model of poverty proposed by Phillips (2008), a theoretical framework that accounts for the negative developmental outcomes associated with poverty via three variables: stigmatization/marginalization of the poor, limitations in opportunity structure, and excessive and chronic stress. Results supported the proposed model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity and gender inequality, policies should prioritize improving access to education and job training programs for marginalized communities, scaling up social safety nets to reduce chronic stress, and implementing sustainable development initiatives that target poverty reduction and opportunity expansion.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Social security; Social protection; Socioeconomic inequalities; Inequality; Development economics
Title: PART A: Socio-Economic Inequality in South Africa and the Continual Plight for Social Protection in the Future World of Work
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals a strong correlation between asset poverty and chronic poverty, with individuals experiencing both forms of poverty being more likely to face food insecurity and health disparities. Additionally, the research finds that education access is a critical determinant of income poverty, with those having higher levels of education earning significantly higher incomes.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the socio-economic landscape of South Africa by analyzing the various factors that contribute to inequality and poverty across different populations, time periods, and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between asset and chronic poverty, policy makers should prioritize social protection programs aimed at addressing these forms of poverty. Additionally, expanding access to education can be an effective strategy for reducing income poverty and improving overall socio-economic wellbeing.

Field: Sociology; Blueprint; Law; Welfare reform; Conversation; Legislation; Universal Credit; Policy making
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: Universal Credit; welfare reform; policy making; benefits
Title: Talking Universal Credit : in conversation with Lord Freud, Minister for Welfare Reform
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Universal Credit was turned over five years from an aspirational idea into a detailed blueprint for change and finally into legislation in the form of the Welfare Reform Act 2012, highlighting the intricacies of British policy making.
What_was_studied: This article examines the origins and blueprint for Universal Credit, a welfare reform initiative in the UK from 2010 to 2012 through an interview with Lord Freud, Minister for Welfare Reform at the time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the recent implementation of Universal Credit in a small number of pilot areas at the time of the interview in July 2013 and with the aim of increasing employment and decreasing poverty, decision makers should prioritize monitoring the effectiveness of this initiative to ensure it meets its objectives.

Field: Poverty; Nexus (standard); Child poverty; Demographic economics; Development economics; Economic growth; Political science; Economics; Psychology; Computer science; Embedded system
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Exploring the disability–poverty nexus in children: a cross-national comparative analysis in Europe
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Great differences across Europe in the prevalence of childhood disability, the poverty outcomes of children with disabilities and the poverty-reducing effectiveness of social transfers for them; only a third of European countries are children with disabilities more likely to live in poor households than children without disabilities.
What_was_studied: Cross-sectional survey of child poverty in high-income European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize expanding access to social transfers and employment opportunities for families with children with disabilities, particularly in countries with weak performance for both child poverty and adult employment, to reduce childhood poverty and ensure an adequate standard of living for all children.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Law and economics; Law; Freedom of association; Unemployment; restrict; Argument; Colonialism; Immigration; Politics
Title: States of Violence and the Right to Exclude
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high levels of immigration contribute to poverty and increase unemployment, which supports the restrictionist perspectives.
What_was_studied: The conventional view is that states have some authority in restricting its borders, but others argue for open borders. The study critically evaluates two restrictionist perspectives: Wellman’s (2011) deontological view and Macedo's (2007) threats to the public order argument.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy-makers should prioritize restricting immigration to prevent poverty and unemployment.

Field: Public economics; Business; Free market; Working poor; Food assistance; Food insecurity; Social Welfare
Title: Who Deserves to Eat Well? An Analysis of Equality and Efficiency in U.S. Food Assistance Policy
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that nearly 40% of full-time employed U.S. residents experience food insecurity, yet they are not eligible for SNAP benefits due to their income levels. Additionally, the study revealed that existing food assistance policies prioritize efficiency and cost-cutting over addressing food insecurity equitably and effectively.
What_was_studied: This study examines the prevalence of food insecurity among full-time employed U.S. residents and evaluates the effectiveness of current food assistance policies in addressing this issue, using data from the 2019 USDA Household Food Security Scale and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) participation rates during the same period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding SNAP eligibility to include full-time employed individuals, especially those with lower income levels. This policy change could help alleviate food insecurity among this population and address the systemic inequities in current food assistance policies.

Field: Public policy; Business; Workforce planning; Poverty; Workforce; Workforce development; Disadvantaged; Economic growth; Entrepreneurship; Universal design
Title: Integrating Entrepreneurship Services into Local Workforce Development Systems: Who is Doing It and How
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results suggest that few workforce funds are being used to support entrepreneurship and when they are, it is more likely affluent communities than disadvantaged ones. This could mean that important opportunities for the most disadvantaged residents and communities are being overlooked.
What_was_studied: This study examines how public workforce funds are being used to support entrepreneurship based on survey responses from administrators in four states. The study focuses on the period between 2018 and 2022, using data collected through surveys administered to workforce fund administrators in California, Florida, New York, and Texas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Universal access to the entrepreneurship option can play an important role in helping some of the unemployed achieve self-sufficiency, and policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that support entrepreneurship in disadvantaged communities.

Field: Self-insurance; Health education; Business; Health promotion; Poverty; Health equity; Population; Health policy; Economic growth; Social determinants of health; Environmental health
Title: Poverty, Health Insurance Status, and Health Service Utilization Among the Elderly
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that those who are the most heavily insured use the most health services, but it is less clear whether the favorable effect of health insurance coverage holds for low-income populations.
What_was_studied: This study uses data from the Rand version of the Health Retirement Study spanning the years 2002 to 2010 to examine the extent of heterogeneous use of health services within the population of elderly poor and the degree to which health insurance status moderates the effect of poverty on health service utilization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that health insurance coverage does not have a uniform favorable effect on low-income populations, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to scale up access to affordable healthcare for the most vulnerable groups.

Field: Mental health; Sociology; Nursing; Poverty; Triage; Criminalization; Population; Emergency Shelter; Service (systems architecture); Addiction
Title: Managing Multiple Disadvantages: The Regulation of Complex Needs in Emergency Shelters for the Homeless
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that people facing multiple disadvantages make up the majority of the homeless shelter population on a daily basis, posing significant challenges to practitioners and existing service structures. The author argues that these challenges shape collaboration with “complex-need” clients, triage and case prioritization, and assessments of housing readiness.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of people facing multiple disadvantages (re: poverty, criminalization, discrimination, addiction, health/mental health, disabilities) in homeless shelters, using policy and organizational document analysis as well as 20 in-depth interviews with emergency shelter practitioners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should scale up support for homeless shelters to address the complicated needs of this population, expand services to prioritize triage and case management, and revise existing policies to recognize the challenges posed by multiple disadvantages.

Field: Poverty; Investment (military); Government (linguistics); Development economics; Economics; Business; Economic growth; Political science; Politics; Linguistics; Philosophy; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: The Effect of Government Policies on Investment in Poverty-Stricken Areas in South Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Government policies positively impact investment in poverty-stricken areas, fostering economic revitalization and poverty alleviation through targeted fiscal incentives, infrastructure development, and microfinance initiatives, which attract private sector investment, encourage entrepreneurship, and promote sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This desk study research design analyzed the effect of government policies on investment in poverty-stricken areas through a secondary data collection methodology, focusing on chronic poverty, gender and poverty, and income poverty over a specific time period with accessible online data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up targeted fiscal incentives, infrastructure development, and microfinance initiatives in poverty-stricken areas, policymakers should prioritize investment in these areas, revise existing policies to better address chronic poverty, gender and poverty, and income poverty, and expand successful interventions to promote inclusive growth and sustainable development.

Authors: Martha N. Ozawa; Rebecca Y. Kim
Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social protection; Social insurance; Population; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: The Increasing Income Inequality Among Children
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income inequality among children increased at a faster rate than among adult and elderly groups, with public income transfers becoming less effective in reducing income inequality among children.
What_was_studied: This study investigated changes in income inequality among children from 1969 to 1979, 1979 to 1989, and 1969 to 1989 compared to adults and elderly people during the same periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the increasing income inequality among children, policymakers should prioritize strengthening social insurance benefits and expanding eligibility to mitigate the declining effectiveness of these benefits.

Field: Empirical research; Sociology; Commit; Social policy; Scholarship; Social support; Multivariate analysis; Social Welfare; Bivariate analysis; Criminology
Title: Public assistance and the pressure to commit crime: An empirical challenge to conservative criminology
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found no empirical support for the two conservative hypotheses, but significant empirical support for the hypothesis derived from the liberal tradition. Specifically, there was a negative correlation between public assistance and reported criminal offenses.
What_was_studied: This paper uses bivariate and multivariate analyses to test three hypotheses about the relationship between public assistance and criminal arrests among 104 at-risk women over a specific time period, using a specific dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize and expand funding for programs that provide comprehensive support to at-risk women, including public assistance and crime prevention initiatives.

Field: Geography; Human development (humanity); Always true; Poverty reduction; Health outcomes; Health policy; Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Why does the gap between health outcomes for children in Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan not mirror their economic difference
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while Kazakhstan invests more in healthcare than Kyrgyzstan, both countries prioritize healthcare spending similarly and have similar child health outcomes. However, Kyrgyzstan's health policies focus more on primary healthcare and community-based interventions, which may explain their better health outcomes for children.
What_was_studied: This paper compares the health policies and spending of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan to understand why two countries with significant economic differences have similar health outcomes for children, using a capability perspective built within a concern for human development more broadly.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers in Kazakhstan should prioritize investing in community-based interventions and primary healthcare to improve child health outcomes, rather than solely focusing on increasing healthcare spending.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Racism; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Poverty; Welfare reform; Public assistance; Economic growth; News media
Title: Regulating the Reproduction and Mothering of Poor Women: The Controlling Image of the Welfare Mother in Television News Coverage of Welfare Reform
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the media portrayed women on public assistance as childlike, hyperfertile, lazy, and bad mothers, reinforcing racist stereotypes. The research demonstrates that these stereotypes were used to support policies intended to control poor women's reproduction and mothering.
What_was_studied: This analysis investigates television news coverage of U.S. welfare reform from 1992 to 2007 and explores the controlling image of the 'welfare mother' constructed in media discourse.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of such biased portrayals in media discourse, policymakers should prioritize targeted messaging campaigns to counter these stereotypes and promote more equitable policies addressing child poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Higher education; Common good; Sociology; Poverty; Legislation; Quality (business); Elementary and Secondary Education Act; Economic growth; Education reform; Education policy
Title: Fifty Years Later: Access to Education as an Avenue out of Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite their initial success in improving access to education for disadvantaged groups, the foundations of these critical pieces of legislation have been eroded through continuing attacks on public education at all levels, threatening the doors to quality education for today's young people.
What_was_studied: The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESA) of 1965 and the Higher Education Act (HEA) of 1965, with a focus on their effectiveness in ensuring access to quality education for low-income and minority students over time and across different educational levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: We must prioritize and expand access to quality public education for all, particularly low-income and minority students, by scaling up successful programs and revamping those that have become ineffective, in order to ensure a more equitable society and a brighter future for our young people.

Authors: Laura Smith; Alizah Allen; Rashidah Bowen
Field: Social class; Sociology; Working class; Poverty; Class (computer programming); Perception; Middle class; Class membership; Social psychology
Title: Expecting the Worst: Exploring the Associations Between Poverty and Misbehavior
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results showed that most infractions were considered equally likely to be committed by any social class, but respondents linked class categories with infractions that referred to particular social class experiences. The Poor/Low-Income category was the only one associated with infractions that did not contain class references.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed how people perceive infractions and crimes committed by different social classes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research suggests that policy interventions targeting poverty and intersectional poverty should prioritize addressing class biases in perceptions of misbehavior, especially for crimes that do not contain class references.

Field: Health care; Social inequality; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Medicaid; Social security; Disadvantaged; Economic growth; Documentation
Title: Fixing that Great Hodgepodge: Health Care for the Poor in the U.S.
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that healthcare coverage for the poor in America has been inconsistent, with initial commitment to only certain segments of the poor, such as the aged, blind, disabled, and needy families, while neglecting working-age adults. This has led to the current situation where Medicaid covers these groups but leaves out many others.
What_was_studied: The study examines the evolution of healthcare coverage for the poor in America from the second half of the 20th century, focusing on documentation before 1965 and the development of Medicaid in 1965, highlighting how the program covers specific groups such as the aged, blind, disabled, and needy families, neglecting working-age adults.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this study's findings, it is recommended that the current private and public health insurance mechanisms be scrapped in favor of a more global, non-employment-based health insurance coverage for all Americans to address the inconsistent healthcare commitment to the poor.

Authors: Sandra K. Danziger; Jessica Wiederspan; Jonah A. Douglas-Siegel
Field: Welfare; Economics; Further education; Recession; Well-being; Interim; Welfare reform; Service (business); Economic growth; Duration (project management)
Title: We're Not All Deadbeat Parents: Welfare Recipient Voices on Unmet Service Needs
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Respondents identify unmet needs for further education, health-related challenges, interim unemployment-related services, or concrete help with cyclical low wage work.
What_was_studied: Studies since the 1996 welfare reform found caseload reductions yet little improvements in well being; this article provides qualitative analysis of program experiences a decade later via telephone interviews of Michigan recipients, who identified one of four combinations of needs for services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The depth and duration of joblessness and hardship of the Recession and recent state-level cutbacks underscore the urgency of client-driven policy guidelines to address the diverse challenges of low income families.

Field: Rural area; Psychology; Poverty; Grassroots; Outreach; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Descriptive statistics; Substance abuse; Hazard; Gerontology; Environmental health
Title: Poverty and methamphetamine abuse : A study of AIDS risk behaviors among rural Northern California Women
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: 60 out of 75 respondents regularly used methamphetamine for an average period of 6 years, with a large majority being unemployed and receiving public assistance.
What_was_studied: 75 women respondents with substance abuse histories from rural northern California were studied, with descriptive data presented on their sexual and drug use risk behaviors for HIV transmission.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to expand drug treatment opportunities for women and men, along with grassroots organizing and creative outreach strategies to enhance prevention efforts to address poverty and substance abuse as a means of reducing HIV transmission risk.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Sanctions; Social citizenship; Working age; Universal Credit; Conditionality; Economic system; Punitive damages
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Universal Credit, ubiquitous conditionality and its implications for social citizenship
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that Universal Credit represents a major expansion and intensification of personalised behavioural conditionality, backed by a punitive system of tiered sanctions and fines.
What_was_studied: Between 2013 and 2017 Universal Credit replaces six means-tested working age benefits for a population of millions over five years, using a punitive system of tiered sanctions and fines to intensify personalized behavioral conditionality as a core aspect of twenty-first century UK social citizenship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising the Universal Credit system to ensure it does not further exacerbate poverty and inequality, particularly for vulnerable populations.

Authors: John S. Atkinson; Donna D. Whitsett; Isaac D. Montoya; Tiffany L. Carroll-Curtis; Victoria L. Brown
Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Unemployment; Receipt; Earnings; Population; Substance abuse; Demographic economics
Title: Employment and Income Patterns in a Study of a Chronic Drug Using and Non-Drug Using TANF Population
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Significant increases in employment rates and significant decreases in rates of TANF receipt were observed among both non-chronic drug users and chronic users, but employment was significantly higher in the non-users. While hours worked and earnings increased over time, both groups were working less than full time and may be earning less than needed to overcome poverty.
What_was_studied: The employment, welfare, and earnings patterns of 244 current and recent Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) recipients over a two-year period were examined, with a focus on the impact of chronic drug use.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant increases in employment rates and the potential for promoting drug treatment while preparing recipients to find jobs with higher wages, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up evidence-based programs targeting chronic drug users.

Authors: Rebecca Y. Kim; Younghee Lim; Wonik Lee
Field: Moral responsibility; Health care; Political science; State (polity); Medicaid; Welfare reform; Citizenship; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Immigration
Title: A study of health care coverage among children in immigrant families in the post welfare-reform era
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: State-funded Medicaid and state health care programs significantly decrease the risk of being uninsured for children of immigrants, controlling all other socio-economic-geographical variables. A child's citizenship is also found to be a significant and strong predictor for being uninsured among children of immigrants.
What_was_studied: The Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) has targeted lawful immigrants by imposing a broad range of restrictions on access to federally funded benefit programs, leaving state-funded Medicaid and state health care programs as key determinants of uninsured status for children of immigrants in the 1999 Current Population Survey (CPS) sample.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: State policymakers should prioritize expanding state-funded Medicaid and health care programs for low-income children of immigrants, considering the significant risk reduction of being uninsured. Moreover, policymakers should revise PRWORA restrictions to ensure equitable access to federally funded benefit programs for lawful immigrants.

Authors: Elizabeth A. Segal; Keith M. Kilty
Field: Public policy; Sociology; Social policy; Social change; Power (social and political); Status quo; Welfare reform; Public debate; House of Representatives; Public administration
Title: Political Promises for Welfare Reform
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the language used in speeches prior to the final vote on July 31, 1996, maintained the status quo and further marginalized the poor, particularly women.
What_was_studied: Public debate by policymakers in the House of Representatives before passing PRWORA in 1996 and its impact on language use and policy making to marginalize the poor, specifically women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise their language use to empower vulnerable populations, particularly women, by expanding social protection programs and addressing health disparities to reduce poverty and gender inequality.

Authors: Rebecca Reno; Sheila Barnhart; Patricia Temple Gabbe
Field: Psychology; Poverty; Breastfeeding; African american; Infant feeding; Critical inquiry; Structural barriers; Socioeconomics
Title: A Critical Inquiry of Breastfeeding Attitudes, Barriers, and Experiences of African American Women living in Poverty
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty

What_was_studied: This study analyzed the breastfeeding patterns of low-income African American women in the United States over a six-month period, using data from the WIC Infant Feeding Practices Study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the well-documented benefits of breastfeeding for both mothers and infants, policymakers should prioritize funding interventions that support low-income African American women in initiating and sustaining breastfeeding, such as culturally sensitive lactation support and infant feeding education.

Authors: Fred Brooks; Sara E. Mack; Anna E. Chaney; Kirk Gibson; Mary Caplan
Field: Government; Political science; Welfare reform; Economic growth; Self-sufficiency

What_was_studied: This study analyzed Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) data from the United States between 1996 and 2016 to assess whether the program's primary purpose of helping needy families achieve self-sufficiency has been met.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize revising TANF policies to better address the employment needs of all recipients, particularly those from marginalized communities. This could involve expanding job training programs, increasing funding for support services, and scaling up successful pilot initiatives.

Field: Social exclusion; Psychology; Life satisfaction; Gerontology

primary_category: Intersectional poverty

Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions, such as financial assistance programs and community outreach initiatives, to address food insecurity, income poverty, and urban poverty in this and similar communities globally. Policymakers should prioritize funding for these initiatives to improve the well-being of low-income families and promote more equitable urban development.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Professionals implementing programs to assist low-income mothers should focus on concepts such as mastery and empowerment to buffer the negative effects of stress on depression, and prioritize scaling up these interventions to reach more mothers in need.

What_was_studied: This article draws on data from community-based research in the United States to examine how neoliberal policy approaches impact poverty governance, specifically focusing on market-based logic, individualism, and punitive orientation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to resist the hegemony of neoliberal approaches to poverty policy and prioritize more egalitarian strategies to address chronic poverty, ensure education access, and reduce food insecurity.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Social policy; Law; State (polity); Wage; Minimum wage; Governor; Federal level; Public administration; Legislature; Politics
Title: State Minimum Wage Laws: Examining the Case of Illinois
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The legislative success was a result of a mix of factors including a change in the State's political environment with the election of a new governor, and collaboration between advocates and researchers who provided a rigorous analysis of the potential effects of raising the minimum wage.
What_was_studied: Using Kingdon's agenda setting model, this article analyzes lessons from a case study of Illinois, the first Midwestern state to raise its minimum wage to $6.50 in January 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Illinois' legislative efforts, other states should prioritize similar collaborations to inform their own minimum wage increases.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Gross income; Total personal income; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Household income; Income distribution; Net national income; Adjusted gross income
Title: The Relationship between Income and Net Worth in the United States: A Virtuous Cycle for High- but Not Low-Income Households
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The authors find a reciprocal relationship between income and wealth for high-, but not low-, income households. Results suggest that intragenerational mobility works differently by initial income, which could partially explain the difficulty of escaping poverty and low U.S. support for liberal social welfare policy.
What_was_studied: Using cross-lagged panel models of household income and net worth data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, this study compares the income-wealth relationships of high- and low-income households from 1989 to 2011, adjusting for demographic differences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the reciprocal relationship between income and wealth found in this study, policymakers should prioritize programs that address the root causes of poverty and inequality, such as education and job training initiatives, to help high-income households maintain their wealth and mobility over time. Additionally, targeted interventions for low-income households could be implemented to help them escape poverty and accumulate wealth, potentially reducing the need for costly social welfare programs.
