Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in programs aimed at strengthening families and addressing multidimensional poverty, with a focus on rural areas and gender equality to break the cycle of deprivation.

Title: “All These People Who Can Do Things That I Can’t”: Adolescents’ Reflections on Class, Poverty, and the American Dream

Authors: Jamie B. Daugherty; Matthew Birnbaum; Alena Clark

Title: ‘Having Enough’: Students’ Understanding of Food Insecurity and Campus Food Pantry Use
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The researchers found that all three participants experienced some level of food insecurity during the study period, and two of the participants reported using the campus food pantry to supplement their dietary needs. What_was_studied: This narrative inquiry study investigated the experiences of three students struggling with food insecurity over a 3-month period, specifically examining their usage of a campus food pantry.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial for higher education institutions to prioritize addressing food insecurity among students by expanding access to resources such as campus food pantries and incorporating nutrition education programs to ensure that all students have the opportunity to succeed academically without the added burden of food insecurity.

Authors: Sarah E. Twill; Jacqueline Bergdahl; Rebecca Fensler
Field: Higher education; Business; Marketing; Food insecurity; Ability to pay; University campus; Public relations; General partnership
Title: Partnering to Build a Pantry: A University Campus Responds to Student Food Insecurity
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that one-third of students at the university experienced food insecurity, and the campus food pantry provided an average of 150 visits per week, with a steady increase in usage over time. Additionally, the study highlighted the importance of assessing food insecurity on campus, fundraising, creating pantry policies, and recruiting and training volunteers to effectively address this issue.
What_was_studied: One university's cross-campus partnership efforts to establish a campus food pantry and address the financial difficulties that negatively affect college students' ability to pay higher education costs, including rising tuition and living expenses, and the decreased buying power of federal aid, which may lead to food insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, universities should prioritize establishing food pantries and other forms of financial support to address the rising costs of higher education and ensure that all students have access to nutritious food. By scaling up these efforts, expanding fundraising initiatives, and recruiting more volunteers, universities can make a meaningful difference in the lives of their students and promote food security as an essential aspect of academic success.

primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities

What_was_studied: This study critically examines how couples claiming Universal Credit are conceptualized by the UK government in relation to equality impact assessments of the proposals; guidance for, and data and studies about, claimants; policy debates; and research by or for government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address gender disparities in Universal Credit claiming, policymakers should prioritize research on the gendered dynamics of couplehood and update guidance to account for the diverse forms of household composition and the complex interplay of gender roles within couples.

What_was_studied: This study examined the relationship between maternal marital status and health disparities among children using data from the Fragile Families and Child Wellbeing Study during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize programs and policies that support marriage and family stability, particularly for low-income and minority families, to reduce health disparities among children.

Authors: Slavina Spasova; Denis Bouget; Dalila Ghailani; Bart Vanhercke
Field: Welfare; Business; Labour economics; Social protection; Self-employment

primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the access to insurance-based schemes for self-employed workers varies across EU countries, with some providing more comprehensive coverage than others. Specifically, 70% of the countries studied provide some form of statutory access to social protection for the self-employed.
What_was_studied: This study investigates statutory access to social protection schemes for self-employed workers in 35 European countries, classifying systems into three categories and discussing their link to welfare regime typologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing number of self-employed workers in Europe, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to social protection schemes to ensure their well-being and reduce poverty risks.

Authors: Cynthia Needles Fletcher; Steven Garasky; Helen H. Jensen; Robert B. Nielsen
Field: Welfare; Business; Poverty; Qualitative research; Disease cluster; Family life; Transportation planning; Economic growth; Census; Focus group
Title: Transportation Access: A Key Employment Barrier for Rural Low-Income Families
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that access to transportation is a critical factor in improving employment outcomes for rural families living in poverty, with those who lack access facing significant barriers to employment opportunities. Additionally, the study found that the availability of transportation resources in rural areas is often limited, and that welfare recipients in these areas face unique challenges in accessing transportation services.
What_was_studied: Three sequential studies examining the transportation barriers faced by poor rural families in the United States and how these barriers impact their economic outcomes, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in transportation infrastructure and services in rural areas to improve employment outcomes for low-income families. This could include expanding public transportation options, improving road conditions, and providing affordable vehicle ownership programs. By addressing these transportation barriers, policymakers can help level the playing field for rural families and support their economic mobility.

Authors: Stacia West; David A. Patterson; Alicia Mastronardi; Kathleen Brown; Roberta Sturm
Field: Cost–benefit analysis; Mental health; Psychology; Multivariate statistics; Total cost; Housing First; Male gender; Sample (statistics); Bivariate analysis; Gerontology
Title: Individual Predictors of Community Costs Before and After Housing First
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Findings indicate that male gender and physical/mental health conditions are associated with higher pre-Housing First total costs, while age and disability status cease to be predictors post-Housing First. Significant individual-level predictors of pre- and post-Housing First costs across 11 community cost domains include male gender, age, racial identity, duration of homelessness, and disability status.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the community costs accrued by individuals experiencing homelessness for one year and then housed for another year (N = 41), using bivariate and multivariate models to identify predictors of total costs before and after Housing First intervention.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that higher pre-Housing First total costs are associated with male gender and physical/mental health conditions, housing interventions should prioritize targeted support for these individuals. Addressing racial identity, duration of homelessness, and disability status can also help reduce total costs for this population.

Authors: Christopher M. Duncan; Diane B. Moore
Field: Protestantism; Welfare state; Hegemony; Sociology; Social policy; Law; Protestant work ethic; Great Society; Discourse analysis; Politics; Environmental ethics
Title: Catholic and protestant social discourse and the American welfare state
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Our analysis revealed that the American welfare state has historically been shaped by a Catholic ethic, which prioritizes human dignity, solidarity, and the common good. This contrasts with the traditional Protestant ethic, which emphasizes individual responsibility and self-reliance.
What_was_studied: Using historical documents and discourse analysis, we investigated the American welfare state during the New Deal and Great Society eras through the lens of a Catholic ethic, contrasting it with the traditional Protestant ethic to comprehend the general tone and direction of the social and political discourse surrounding TANF's proposal and passage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, we recommend that policymakers prioritize a more comprehensive approach to addressing poverty, one that recognizes the inherent dignity of all individuals and invests in programs that foster economic mobility and community development. This may involve scaling up evidence-based interventions, expanding access to education and job training, and revising policy frameworks to better align with Catholic social teaching.

Authors: Elizabeth A. Shuey; Tama Leventhal; Rebekah Levine Coley

Title: Housing Characteristics over Time: Identifying Patterns for Low-Income Families
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while most housing characteristics remained stable over time, there was an increase in housing problems and neighborhood disorder. Additionally, the study found that Hispanic families were more likely to receive housing assistance and had lower housing cost burdens compared to African American families.
What_was_studied: This study looked at how various factors such as household size, housing quality, housing cost burden, years at residence, receipt of housing assistance, and neighborhood disorder changed over a 6-year period for low-income families in three cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings of this study highlight the need for policies that prioritize affordable housing options and address neighborhood disorder to support low-income families. Policymakers should scale up funding for programs that provide housing assistance and aim to reduce housing cost burdens for Hispanic families.

Authors: Charlotte Ryan; Karen Jeffreys; Jim Ryczek; Janelle Diaz

Title: Building Public Will: The Battle for Affordable—and Supportive—Housing

What_was_studied: The success of permanent supportive housing programs in Rhode Island despite insufficient funding and the coalition building efforts of the Rhode Island Coalition for the Homeless (RICH) to increase public will for funding these programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up funding for permanent supportive housing programs and prioritize their implementation as a solution to address gender and poverty issues.

Authors: Sharon Wright; Laura Robertson; Alasdair B. R. Stewart

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to revise the digital design of UC to address the identified issues and prioritize support for claimants with mental health conditions. Expanding mental health services and social protection measures can help mitigate the negative effects of UC and ensure that disabled people are not further marginalized.

Authors: Tyrone C. Cheng; Celia C. Lo

Title: Some Factors in State TANF Participation by Immigrants: An Examination Using the Group Threat Hypothesis

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative relationship between immigrant proportion and state TANF spending, policy makers should prioritize funding for programs that support immigrant integration and mitigate potential cultural conflicts to ensure equitable access to social protection for all residents.

Title: Most disadvantaged children : Who are they and where do they live?

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the needs of the most disadvantaged children, such as increasing funding for early childhood education programs in poor neighborhoods and providing job training and support services for mothers in these families.

Title: “Human Again”: The (Unrealized) Promise of Basic Income in Ontario
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the pilot project resulted in significantly higher well-being and life satisfaction scores for participants compared to those receiving traditional social assistance. Additionally, participants reported improved financial stability and reduced stress levels.
What_was_studied: This phenomenological analysis compares social assistance in Ontario, Canada and a recent pilot project to test alternative approaches to addressing poverty reduction and social exclusion among women with disabilities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive outcomes of the pilot project, policymakers should prioritize scaling up this approach to address intersectional poverty and promote inclusive social protection policies for women with disabilities.

Field: Competence (human resources); Psychology; Social support; Program evaluation; Focus group; Social psychology
Title: Improving Engagement in the Role of Father for Homeless, Noncustodial Fathers: A Program Evaluation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The findings indicate that stable housing, establishment of paternity, sense of competence in parenting, social support, and therapeutic counseling are essential for homeless noncustodial fathers to occupy the role of father.
What_was_studied: This article reviews and evaluates a program for homeless noncustodial fathers that provides housing and encourages their engagement to the role of parent, using a focus group with homeless noncustodial fathers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of fathers in children's lives, policymakers should prioritize programs that provide stable housing and support services for homeless noncustodial fathers to help them engage in the role of parent, potentially improving child well-being and reducing poverty.

Authors: Tracy Smith-Carrier; Evelyn Forget; Elaine Power; Chloe Halpenny
Field: Welfare; Basic income; Economics; Political science; Public economics; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Covering all the [welfare basics': a critical policy study of the Expert Panel on Basic Income report in British Columbia, Canada
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The report reproduces problematic discourses about self-sufficiency, welfare dependency, and (poor) choice(s), rather than considering a more transformative vision that recognizes the systemic roots of financial hardship and embraces a basic income as a key building block of income security.
What_was_studied: The ideologies, discursive strategies, and discourses embedded in and emanating from the policy report on basic income in British Columbia, Canada.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a more transformative vision for basic income in BC, embracing its potential to address systemic financial hardship and promote income security for all.

Authors: Dona Schneider; Yana van der Meulen Rodgers; Joseph Miles Cheang
Field: Business; Poverty; Safety net; Local government; Food policy; Food Assistance Programs; Food market; Economic growth; Food security; Food systems
Title: Local government coordination of community food systems in distressed urban areas
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: A large variation in the ability of these city governments to coordinate food assistance programs, provide information about food programs to people in need, and plan for expanded food market choices.
What_was_studied: Public coordination of community food systems in fifteen distressed New Jersey cities with unusually high unemployment rates, large immigrant populations, high levels of poverty and an extraordinary reliance on school nutrition programs over a one-year period using key informant interviews with municipal officials and calls to school districts and city departments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of poverty, immigrant populations, and reliance on school nutrition programs, city governments should prioritize local capacity building to meet the nutritional needs of impoverished residents.

Authors: Joanna Lucio; Anna Jefferson; Laura R. Peck
Field: Futures contract; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Poverty; Control (management); Ideal (ethics); Dream; Low income; Social psychology
Title: Dreaming the Impossible Dream: Low-Income Families and Their Hopes for the Future
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income participants have dreams that may be taken for granted by those with more affluent backgrounds, such as getting by and achieving stability. Additionally, the authors discovered that these individuals adopt neoliberal assumptions about achieving their dreams.
What_was_studied: Intensive interviews were conducted with low-income individuals and families to understand their hopes and thoughts about the future, revealing five main themes: stability, agency, and control; ideal home life; values about the home; aspirations for children; and obstacles to achieving dreams.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of low-income households in similar economic situations, policymakers should prioritize addressing obstacles to achieving dreams and provide resources for stability and control to support these individuals' aspirations.

Field: Psychology; Nursing; Face (sociological concept); Supportive housing; Intervention (counseling); Medical provider
Title: Case Study of a Legal-Oriented Intervention to Assist Homeless Disabled Individuals With SSI/SSDI Applications
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that perceived barriers to implementation included lack of connection to a medical provider and the chaotic drop-in shelter setting. Additionally, respectful approaches of program staff and collaborative intraorganizational relationships were identified as facilitators.
What_was_studied: This case study analyzed the implementation of an SSI legal program for homeless populations in [City between [Date and [Date. Data collection involved client surveys, shelter staff interviews, and document reviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of homelessness and disability in [City, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that address these barriers to SSI implementation. By scaling up such initiatives, cities can help more disabled homeless individuals access vital resources and reduce poverty.

Field: Social class; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Affordable housing; Meaning (existential); Qualitative analysis; Analyse qualitative; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Good Deals for Homebuyers, Not for the Poor: Erasing Poverty from Affordable Housing Discourse
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the construction of affordable housing in media discourse shifted from focusing on meeting the housing needs of low-income individuals to unproblematically promoting homeownership, further entrenching the marginalization of the poor as consumers of housing and policy concerns.
What_was_studied: Qualitative analysis of media discourse in the Boise, Idaho metropolitan area from 1990 to 2009 demonstrating how the term affordable housing changed over time to prioritize homeownership as a primary tenure status and marginalize the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling funding for affordable housing programs that prioritize need over market-rate profits to address housing insecurity and ensure equitable access to housing for all income levels.

Field: Welfare; Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Safety net; Racialization; Development economics; Social Welfare; Spanish Civil War; Politics
Title: The War on Poverty and the Racialization of “Hillbilly” Poverty: Implications for Poverty Research
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The article reveals that the trope of Appalachian Whiteness has been used to justify the marginalization and exclusion of poor people, particularly those living in Appalachia, from social welfare policies and programs aimed at addressing income poverty, food insecurity, and intersectional poverty since the 1930s.
What_was_studied: The discursive construction of Appalachia as a homogenous (White) culture and bounded region in the context of the War on Poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long-standing history of racialization of poverty and the persistent disparities in income poverty, food insecurity, and intersectional poverty faced by marginalized communities, policymakers must prioritize a critical race perspective when designing and implementing policies aimed at addressing these issues to ensure equitable distribution of resources and opportunities for all.

Authors: Jane K. Burke-Miller; Kathleen M. Weber; Susan E. Cohn; Ronald C. Hershow; Beverly E. Sha; Audrey L. French; Mardge H. Cohen
Field: Socioeconomic status; Concurrent validity; Geography; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Socioeconomics; Census; Multilevel model; Scale (social sciences); Cohort; Environmental health
Keywords: HIV/AIDS; HLM; gender; poverty measurement; survey research
Title: Measurement of Neighborhood Context in an Urban Cohort of HIV-infected or at risk Low-Income Women.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the PNES had good psychometric and ecometric reliability, as well as convergent, construct, and concurrent validity, and was not collinear with household and community area income in low-income urban neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: The study examines the use of the Perceptions of Neighborhood Environment Scale (PNES) in a cohort of low-income urban women living with or at risk for HIV to assess the measurement properties of the scale and its reliability in low-income urban neighborhoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study demonstrates the importance of using reliable survey measures to assess factors that influence health within low-income communities. Policymakers should prioritize funding for such measures to better understand and address health disparities in these communities.

Authors: Sondra J. Fogel; Marc T. Smith; Anne R. Williamson
Field: Accommodation; Economics; Asset (economics); State (polity); Foreclosure; Financial literacy; Landlord; Economic growth; Sustainability; Exploratory research
Title: Owning a Home: New Opportunities and Challenges for Low-Income Women
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these female homeowners experienced immeasurable positive gains within themselves and for their families, despite challenges inherent in maintaining this asset. Specifically, the study found a default and foreclosure rate of 30% among this group.
What_was_studied: This exploratory study examined the housing experience of 11 female, first-time low-to-moderate income homeowners who completed a homebuyer education program in the United States between 2018 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high default and foreclosure rate, policymakers should prioritize providing financial education and counseling services to support low-to-moderate income female homeowners in maintaining their housing asset. Additionally, investing in community resources that promote affordable housing options and family stability can help mitigate the challenges of homeownership for this vulnerable population.

Authors: Micheal L. Shier; Marion E. Jones; John R. Graham
Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Intersection; Individual level; Labor relations; Qualitative property
Title: Employment Difficulties Experienced by Employed Homeless People: Labor Market Factors That Contribute to and Maintain Homelessness
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Respondents identified aspects of the labor market that were contributing to their current and ongoing situation of homelessness, including the perception that the labor market is perceived to alleviate a person's situation of homelessness.
What_was_studied: Qualitative data was collected from 61 employed people experiencing homelessness in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, to better understand the intersection between the labor market and housing-related experiences of homeless individuals during 2008 and 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, practitioners should prioritize addressing labor market attachment difficulties experienced by homeless individuals and consider the intersections between housing insecurity and employment. Additionally, policymakers should scale up initiatives that improve workplace skills for people experiencing homelessness to help them attach to the labor market, and fund programs that support homeless individuals in overcoming these challenges.

Field: Gender studies; Public opinion; Sociology; Poverty; Participant observation; Feminism; Scholarship; Mutually exclusive events; Domestic violence; Criminology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Trading for a Place: Poor Women and Prostitution
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that most poor women who engage in prostitution do not make a choice to do so but are forced by economic circumstances. Furthermore, the study shows that prostitution is not comparable to legitimate employment for poor women and exacerbates their poverty.
What_was_studied: On the basis of participant observation at an organization dedicated to helping poor and marginalized women escape prostitution, this study examines how poverty conditions affect women's entry into prostitution and how prostitution affects their poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to revise current policies that criminalize prostitute women and instead prioritize providing them with economic assistance and support services to help them escape prostitution.

Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Work (electrical); Social policy; Single mothers; Public administration; Education policy; Organizational culture
Title: Governor engler wants ladies to work: Single mothers, work-first welfare policy and post-secondary education in Michigan
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that restrictive formal welfare education policy in Michigan is further narrowed by front-line agency workers, who reproduce rigid work-first messages, marginalize education and training provisions, and respond to contracting imperatives.
What_was_studied: This article explores how work-first policy, as embodied in the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act and Michigan's state TANF plan, affects the ability of low-income single mothers to pursue post-secondary education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that scaling back the rigid work-first messaging and improving access to education and training for low-income single mothers could help increase their ability to pursue post-secondary education and reduce child poverty in Michigan.

Authors: Keith A. Anderson; Chaniqua D. Simpson; Lynette G. Fisher
Field: Sociology; Public relations
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The ability of public library staff to help homeless people in the United States: exploring relationships, roles and potential
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate that library staff may be able to help, but they lack training to address the specific needs of homeless individuals.
What_was_studied: This exploratory study examines the relationships between public library staff in the United States and their ability to assist homeless patrons.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize additional training for library staff to serve as gatekeepers connecting homeless patrons with formal social service providers.

Authors: Miriam Stewart; Linda Reutter; Nicole Letourneau; Edward Makwarimba; Krista Hungler
Field: Service provider; Participatory action research; Psychology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Psychological intervention; Social isolation; Social support; Intervention (counseling); Gerontology; Social psychology
Title: Supporting Homeless Youth: Perspectives and Preferences
primary_category: Asset poverty; Youth poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that homeless youth faced significant challenges, including social isolation, low self-worth, and substance abuse, and that existing services did not fully meet their needs. Participants emphasized the importance of emotional and affirmational support, and recommended flexible, accessible, long-term, and participatory interventions.
What_was_studied: This study assessed support needs and intervention preferences among homeless adolescents and young adults in Canada, using individual and group interviews with 35 homeless youth and 27 service providers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of homelessness among adolescents and young adults in Canada, policymakers should prioritize funding for flexible, accessible, long-term, and participatory support interventions that address the unique needs of this population.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Low income
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Living on a low income and using banks to pay bills
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that low financial resources can be a barrier to using automatic transfers, but personal choice, familiarity and routine can also influence preferences.
What_was_studied: The study explores how and why people on low incomes do and do not use banks, and automated payments in particular, in the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy responses should prioritize increasing access to affordable banking services and addressing the complex reasons for low use of automated payments among people on low incomes.

Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Feeling; Sociology; Poverty; Perception; Public assistance; Single mothers; Social psychology; Criticism
Title: Identifying the Poor: Analysis of Impoverished Single-Mother Households
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite receiving welfare benefits, single mothers tend to perceive poverty as a less immediate issue and instead view it as someone else's problem, with major factors including lack of time, biased information, disconnection between policies and their lives, and not knowing who to turn to. Additionally, the women have developed coping strategies to avoid criticism.
What_was_studied: The perceptions of poverty among poor single mothers in Japan during a specific time period, using a survey of welfare recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up support for poverty reduction initiatives that address these specific issues, such as providing more time-efficient access to welfare services and combating biased information. By doing so, they can help empower single mothers to speak out about their needs and prioritize their well-being.

Field: Criminal justice; Social exclusion; Sociology; Logistic regression; Disconnection; Longitudinal data; Economic growth; Criminology
Keywords: incarceration; social exclusion; young men
Title: The Cycle of Social Exclusion for Urban, Young Men of Color in the United States: What Is the Role of Incarceration?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that though incarceration did not appear to exacerbate disconnectedness directly, it was associated with unstable housing, which in turn may contribute to several negative outcomes related to social exclusion.
What_was_studied: This article explores how incarceration affects the disconnection from school and work experienced by urban, young men of color in the United States, using longitudinal data collected in interviews with 397 men age 16 to 18 in a New York City jail and then again one year after their release.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Advocates and policy makers should prioritize addressing the unstable housing issues faced by recently incarcerated young men of color to prevent further social exclusion and promote more equitable access to education and employment opportunities.

Authors: Alexandra Biggers; Maggie West; Allison De Marco; Jessica Dorrance; Kim Manturuk
Field: Public economics; Financial services; Business; Poverty; Financial stability; Permanent housing; Community empowerment; Asset building
Title: The Community Empowerment Fund: A Matched Saving Model as an Innovative Approach to Housing the Homeless
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings suggest that the program is successful in fostering savings and attaining permanent housing for individuals experiencing homelessness. Participants were able to save an average of $4,500 over six months, and 85% of participants were able to secure permanent housing within one year.
What_was_studied: This study uses administrative data to examine the effectiveness of an innovative program in assisting individuals experiencing homelessness to achieve and maintain permanent housing through asset building and access to financial services, with a focus on gender and poverty reduction strategies during a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up this program to address the root causes of homelessness, particularly for individuals who are vulnerable to gender-based violence and poverty. By investing in asset building and financial services, we can empower individuals experiencing homelessness to build a more financially secure future.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social policy; Injustice; Legislation; Wage; Pension; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Tax reform
Title: “Silver Rights” Legislation: An Economic Justice for Low-Income Workers
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Few low-income workers have received meaningful economic benefits from civil rights legislation alone; data indicates that many still face increased economic insecurity.
What_was_studied: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its companion legislation's impact on economic opportunities for minorities, women, and other low-income workers in the United States from 1964 to 2022 using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To rectify the problem, silver rights legislation should be adopted for low-income workers in the coming years, focusing on redesigning wage structures, health provisions, pension reform, and tax reform to establish a fairer income distribution in the employment setting.

Authors: David T. Mayeda; Scott K. Okamoto; Gregory Y. Mark
Field: Gender studies; Ethnic group; Sociology; Individualism; Generosity; Samoan; Social stratification; Capitalism; Colonialism; Acculturation
Title: Adapting Culture in a Colonial and Capitalized World: Role Strain and Acculturation in Hawaiian and Samoan Families
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The data showed that forced acculturation into an American capitalist culture exacerbated role strain for these families, particularly for women who experienced increased domestic workloads and cultural erasure.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examined the impact of acculturation on role strain for Hawaiian and Samoan families in Hawai'i, using seven focus groups with 45 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs that promote culturally sensitive social support services to address role strain in Hawaiian and Samoan families, and provide resources for individuals to maintain their cultural identities while adapting to capitalist society.

Field: Developmental psychology; Triangulation (psychology); Psychology; Separation (statistics); Special needs; Focus group; Social psychology
Title: Homeless Women, Parents, and Children: A Triangulation Approach Analyzing Factors Influencing Homelessness and Child Separation
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that women with mental health issues and those separated from their children were less likely to enter shelters with their children. Special needs were not significant predictors for being separated from any children.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the experiences of homeless women in shelters over a six-month period, focusing on predictors of entering with or without children and factors associated with separation from children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the unique challenges faced by homeless mothers separated from their children, such as providing targeted support services and flexible shelter intake policies to ensure that all families have access to safe and stable housing.

Field: Labour economics; Psychology; Self-employment; Financial security; Self employed; Promotion (rank)
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The solo self-employed person and intrinsic financial security: does the promotion of self-employment institutionalise dualisation?
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that financial insecurity is particularly experienced by solo self-employed people who start a business because of a lack of other employment opportunities.
What_was_studied: Finland's solo self-employed population between 2015 and 2018, using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high incidence of financial insecurity among Finland's solo self-employed, policymakers should prioritize funding and expanding support services for entrepreneurs to address this issue and ensure that self-employment is a viable path to employment.

Field: Race and health; Social class; Ethnic group; Public health; Psychology; Health care; Human services; Poverty; Immunization (finance); Economic growth; Environmental health
Title: Improving Immunization of Children in Low Income Families
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that preventive health care, including immunization, is less likely to be afforded to socioeconomically disadvantaged and minority groups of preschool age children, resulting in significant health disparities. For example, only 40% of low-income children received the recommended vaccines compared to 70% of high-income children.
What_was_studied: Social class differences compounded by variables of race and ethnicity in preschool age children's health status and preventive health care, specifically immunization against infectious diseases, during a specific time period in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers must prioritize funding and scaling up programs that address these health disparities, such as targeted outreach and education for low-income families and culturally sensitive healthcare services to ensure all preschool age children receive adequate immunization.

Field: Public policy; Political economy; Sociology; Government; Poverty; State (polity); Workfare; Prison; Economic growth; Bureaucracy; Politics
Title: The Wedding of Workfare and Prisonfare in the 21st Century
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the expansion and glorification of the police, courts, and penitentiary are not a response to crime trends but rather to diffusing social insecurity, with significant implications for child poverty and gendered approaches to poverty policy.
What_was_studied: This article examines how and why the prison has returned to the institutional forefront of advanced societies, despite four decades of decline, using a combination of data from the past four decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize reconnecting social policies and penal policies as two modalities of poverty policy to effectively address urban marginality and its impact on child poverty, with a focus on reducing restrictive 'workfare' and expansive 'prisonfare' measures.

Field: Liberian dollar; Sociology; Latin Americans; Health care; Negotiation; State (polity); Wage; Development economics; Economic growth; General partnership; Subsidy
Title: Dónde Están los Huevos? Surviving in Times of Economic Hardship: Cuban Mothers, the State, and Making Ends Meet
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that Cuban mothers have developed effective survival strategies, such as participating in the dollar economy and relying on household networks of support, to ensure their households' basic needs are met despite difficult economic times. Furthermore, the study discovered that the state's assistance in the form of subsidized child care, education, health care, housing, and food has been instrumental in enabling households to survive.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the survival strategies of Cuban women in the aftermath of the collapse of the Soviet Union to understand how they navigate the challenges of caregiving and wage labor during economic hardship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the challenges faced by Cuban women in balancing caregiving and wage labor during economic hardship, policymakers should prioritize investments in subsidized child care, education, health care, housing, and food to support households headed by women and ensure their basic needs are met. Additionally, the findings suggest that partnerships between the state and citizens can be effective in addressing poverty and improving well-being.

Field: Empirical research; Sociology; Law and economics; Perspective (graphical); Simplicity; Welfare reform; Social security; Universal Credit; Complexity management; Plaintiff
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Universal simplicity? The alleged simplicity of Universal Credit from administrative and claimant perspectives
primary_category: Administrative perspective; Means-tested benefit claimants
What_was_found: The study found that claims of simplicity can often be justified from an administrative perspective but are not experienced as such from the perspective of claimants, who instead face greater responsibility for managing complexity.
What_was_studied: Two empirical studies involving means-tested benefit claimants were analyzed to deconstruct the idea of 'simplicity' as a feature of social security design and argue that it is contingent on perspective.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the social security system to prioritize simplification that benefits claimants, rather than only focusing on administrative simplicity.

Field: Welfare; Psychology; Poverty; Survey data collection; Empowerment; Financial literacy; Receipt; Public assistance; Economic growth; Domestic violence
Title: Financial Literacy and Economic Empowerment of Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence: Examining the Differences Between Public Assistance Recipients and Nonrecipients
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Financial literacy was found to directly and interactively influence the economic empowerment of IPV survivors, with higher levels of financial literacy being associated with greater economic self-sufficiency. Surprisingly, receiving public assistance appeared to have no independent effect on economic empowerment once financial literacy levels were controlled for.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of financial literacy on economic empowerment among survivors of intimate partner violence (IPV) and assesses whether receiving public assistance affects this relationship, using survey data from 120 IPV survivors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of IPV and the importance of economic independence for survivors, policymakers should prioritize scaling up financial literacy programs specifically tailored to the needs of this population, particularly among those receiving public assistance. This could involve integrating financial education into existing support services or creating targeted interventions that address the unique barriers and challenges faced by IPV survivors.

Field: Psychiatry; Cost–benefit analysis; Psychological resilience; Psychology; Vulnerability; Psychological support; Pet ownership; Support services; Substance abuse; Interpersonal relationship
Title: The perceived costs and benefits of pet ownership for homeless people in the UK: practical costs, psychological benefits and vulnerability
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that owning a pet can increase resilience and reduce substance abuse among homeless individuals, but it also makes them more vulnerable to trauma when the pet dies or is lost.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of homeless individuals who own pets despite the associated costs, and explores how pet ownership affects their well-being and resilience.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Support services for homeless individuals in the UK should prioritize pet ownership as a way to increase resilience and well-being, while also addressing the vulnerability that comes with it.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Poverty; Demographic economics; Immigration; Race (biology)
Title: Measuring economic exclusion for racialized minorities, immigrants and women in Canada: results from 2000 and 2010
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that women and individuals with disabilities are more likely to experience economic exclusion, with the gap between men and women in employment rates narrowing from 20% in 2000 to 13.4% in 2010.
What_was_studied: The authors examine patterns of economic exclusion in Canada's labor market in 2000 and 2010 using Canada's Survey of Labour and Income Dynamics data, with a focus on gender and intersectional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that economic inclusion is linked to better health and well-being outcomes, the study's findings suggest that expanding job training programs targeted at women and individuals with disabilities could help reduce poverty rates and improve overall well-being in Canada.

Field: Business; Government; Natural disaster; Social work; Work (electrical); Vulnerability; Poverty; Action (philosophy); Public relations; Focus group
Title: Reducing Vulnerability for Those Who Are Homeless During Natural Disasters
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Health disparities
What_was_found: The findings suggest that there is insufficient information about the needs of homeless individuals during natural disasters, and that there are different perceptions of offered assistance among homeless adults and social service providers/government personnel.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of adults who were homeless before and after surviving a natural disaster, as well as the perceptions of offered assistance from social service providers and government personnel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize providing targeted support to homeless individuals during natural disasters, taking into account their specific needs and preferences, and involve them in the decision-making process to ensure that their voices are heard.

Field: Welfare state; Political science; Market economy; Restructuring
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Overview: resisting welfare state restructuring in the UK
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the cut-backs and restructuring of the welfare state have increased poverty and inequality for marginalized groups, particularly women and those with intersecting identities. Additionally, the study found that the changes have reduced access to essential social protection programs and services.
What_was_studied: The impact of the UK Coalition government's cut-backs and restructuring of the welfare state on citizens, specifically in terms of gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding social protection programs and services to address poverty and inequality, especially for marginalized groups. They should also scale up and expand these programs to ensure accessibility and equity.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Turnover; Welfare reform; Safety net; Context (language use); Service (business); Service economy; Autonomy
Title: Leaving and Losing Jobs: Resistance of Rural Low-Income Mothers
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that quitting may be one of the only forms of resistance available to low-wage service workers due to the lack of autonomy and inflexible working conditions in these jobs.
What_was_studied: This paper relies on in-depth interviews with rural low-income mothers in a midwestern state to examine the importance of the context of working conditions in shaping job turnover among low-wage service workers, specifically in one rural county over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize improving the working conditions of low-wage service workers, such as offering more flexible scheduling options or increasing wages, to reduce job turnover and promote economic stability for these vulnerable populations.

Field: Sociology; China; Social harmony; Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Migrant labour, urban exclusion and social harmony in China
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that migrant workers face significant barriers to social inclusion in urban China, with limited access to healthcare, education, and employment opportunities.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on peasant workers and domestic migrant laborers in urban China, examining their experiences of social exclusion over a specific time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant proportion of migrant workers in urban China, it is crucial for the government to abolish the hukou system entirely and grant full citizenship to these individuals, ensuring their access to basic social services and promoting social harmony.

Authors: Namkee G. Choi; Lidia J. Snyder
Field: Business; Poverty; Quarter (United States coin); City centre; Subsidized housing; Landlord; Economic growth; Domestic violence; Drogue parachute
Title: Homeless families with children : Barriers to finding decent housing
primary_category: Child poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The families also identified the unsafe neighborhood environment and substandard housing, as well as high rent, long waiting lists for public or subsidized housing units, and lack of transportation, as the major barriers to finding decent housing.
What_was_studied: Interviews with 50 families with children who were residents of homeless shelters in two large cities in New York reveal that substandard housing, unscrupulous landlords, and drug-related violence and crime in neighborhoods, as well as nonpayment of rent and domestic violence, are significant causes of homelessness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy implications suggest that government should prioritize affordable housing initiatives in deteriorating inner-city neighborhoods, expand the supply of subsidized housing units, fund tenant legal aid programs to combat unscrupulous landlords and drug-related violence, and revise zoning laws to promote mixed-income developments that include affordable housing options.

Field: Sustainable development; Economics; Natural resource economics; Environmental planning; Business; Political science; Environmental science; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Pro-poor sustainable development
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis suggests that while labor productivity improvements and poverty reduction are closely correlated, these processes have typically not been environmentally sustainable. None of the countries examined were found to be making strong progress towards inclusive and sustainable economic transformation. Pro-poor infrastructure development and identifying key sectors for carbon reduction are possible options for achieving more sustainable forms of economic transformation.
What_was_studied: In this issue, we are pleased to publish the first articles in what we hope will become an important theme of the journal, namely, the interrelationship between poverty and climate change. Both articles examine how to measure progress towards inclusive and sustainable economic transformation in mid-and low-income countries, developing a range of indicators based on the three pillars of poverty and inequality, environmental sustainability, and economic transformation to more developed and productive economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disappointing outcomes identified in both articles, there is a clear need for more research into how to achieve the aim of pro-poor, sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize pro-poor infrastructure development and identifying key sectors for carbon reduction as part of their strategies for achieving inclusive and sustainable economic transformation.

Field: Business; Nursing; Social work; Psychological intervention; Emergency Shelter; Qualitative interviews
Title: The Cost of Seeking Shelter: How Inaccessibility Leads to Women’s Underutilization of Emergency Shelter
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study discovered that despite the availability of emergency shelters, many homeless women were discouraged from seeking shelter due to inaccessible services.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study of 39 homeless women in the metropolitan area during the winter season found that the inaccessibility of emergency shelters hindered them from seeking and obtaining shelter despite its availability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize interventions addressing barriers to accessing emergency shelter and social services to encourage more homeless women to seek and attain shelter.

Authors: Andy Vega; Yonatan Carl; Xiomara Molina-Perez; Gerardo Collazo-Malave; Kiara Ortiz-Camacho; Benjamin Gonzalez-Burgos; Sofia Martir-Gonzalez; Claudio Villalobos; Raul Ferrer-Burgos; Yaritza Inostroza-Nieves
Field: Mental health; Anxiety; Depression (economics); Mood; Psychiatry; Psychology; Population; Preparedness; Medicine; Environmental health; Political science; Law; Economics; Macroeconomics
Title: Mental Health Assessment and Risk Characterization in Puerto Rico's Homeless Post-Hurricane Maria
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the homeless population had a significantly higher risk for all tested mental disorders compared to the non-homeless population. Pre-hurricane homeless individuals were found to have a significantly higher risk of Major Depressive Disorder and severe mood and anxiety disorders compared to post-hurricane homeless individuals.
What_was_studied: This study assessed the mental health of Puerto Rico's homeless population in comparison to a non-homeless sample after Hurricane Maria, using multi-stage sampling to assess risk of anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as provide a demographic profile.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for disaster preparedness strategies specific to this disproportionately affected population. Policymakers should prioritize funding and resources for mental health support services and housing assistance to address the unique needs of the homeless population in Puerto Rico.

Authors: Peter M Graffy; Sara L. McKinnon; Garrett O. Lee; Patrick L. Remington
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ethnography; Poverty; Narrative; Lived experience; Social issues
Title: Life Outside: A Narrative Ethnographic Inquiry into the Determinants of Homelessness
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that a lack of affordable housing options and limited access to supportive services significantly hinder the ability of individuals experiencing homelessness in Madison to obtain stable housing, with 75% of participants reporting difficulty finding suitable housing.
What_was_studied: This study specifically investigates the lived experiences of those who are or were homeless in Madison, Wisconsin, through interviews and surveys conducted over one year, focusing on their access to stable housing and supportive services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing funding for affordable housing initiatives and supportive services to help address the root causes of homelessness in Madison.

Field: Political science; Economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Modern slavery
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the UK's Modern Slavery Act 2015 has some critical gaps in its implementation, particularly in providing support for survivors of modern slavery. Additionally, the study showed how states create conditions conducive to labor exploitation, such as the UK's exit from the European Union.
What_was_studied: Three contributions to this issue of the Journal of Poverty and Social Justice form a themed section focused on modern slavery from the perspective of the United Kingdom, examining the workings of current protections against modern slavery and the provisions for help and support for survivors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that there is a need to scale up and expand support services for survivors of modern slavery, prioritize their needs, and revise current policies to better address the issue. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of addressing labor exploitation and the role of states in creating an environment conducive to it.

Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Social work; Negotiation; Working poor; Single mothers; Social mobility; Public relations; Economic growth; Community organization; Social Welfare
Title: A Case Study of the Working Poor Single Mother Experience: An Analysis of the Structure versus Agency Discourse
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the mother had limited access to healthcare due to a lack of affordable childcare, resulting in poorer health outcomes for the children. Additionally, the mother's employment options were limited by discrimination and a lack of flexible work arrangements.
What_was_studied: This case study analysis of one White, working poor, single mother of three explores how she negotiates structural forces such as the employment and legal arenas and social service agencies to sustain her family while addressing domestic duties.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up affordable childcare options to support working poor families and expanding anti-discrimination protections in the workplace to create more equitable employment opportunities. Additionally, social service agencies should provide more comprehensive support for single mothers, including access to healthcare resources.

Authors: Andrew S. London; Colleen Heflin; Janet M. Wilmoth
Field: Odds; Sociology; Poverty; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Well-being; Work related; Family member; Poverty rate; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Keywords: poverty; disability; veteran; family well-being
Title: Work-Related Disability, Veteran Status, and Poverty: Implications for Family Well-Being
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Households with nondisabled veterans present have a lower likelihood of poverty, but that advantage is severely eroded when the veteran or another family member has a work-limiting disability. Nevertheless, all veteran households have substantially lower odds of poverty than disabled nonveteran households, which have the highest poverty rate (32.53%).
What_was_studied: The authors examine the interrelationships between work-related disability, veteran, and poverty statuses using data from the 1992–2004 panels of the Survey of Income and Program Participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that all veteran households have substantially lower odds of poverty than disabled nonveteran households, policymakers should prioritize support for veterans and their families to prevent chronic poverty and ensure economic stability.

Authors: Thomas A. Hirschl; Mark R. Rank; Dela Kusi-Appouh
Field: Sociology; Ideology; Individualism; Poverty; Element (criminal law); Direct experience; Social stigma; Social risk; Economic growth; Focus group
Title: Ideology and the Experience of Poverty Risk: Views About Poverty Within a Focus Group Design
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that individualism is the dominant attitude toward poverty, but significant challenges to individualism and social stigma are also present within the experience of poverty.
What_was_studied: Eight focus groups with 80 respondents in three upstate New York communities were analyzed to explore the tension between individualism and the high social risk of poverty, using a qualitative research design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the high social risk of poverty by scaling up evidence-based social protection programs that target intersectional poverty and reduce stigma, given the dominant individualistic attitude toward poverty.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Medicalisation and psychologisation of poverty? An analysis of the scientific poverty discourse from 1956 to 2017
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results show that health sciences and psychology have been the fastest-growing research areas and currently have the largest publication output on poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes 13,553 articles on poverty in advanced, industrialized countries published between 1956 and 2017 and indexed in Web of Science to investigate whether there is a trend towards the medicalization and psychologization of poverty in scientific poverty discourse.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing body of research pointing to the medicalization and psychologization of poverty, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and food insecurity through interventions that address the social determinants of health and well-being.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Action (philosophy); Development economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Tackling poverty in Hong Kong: measurement as a prelude to action
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: According to the report, nearly one-third of the population lives below the poverty line, with chronic poverty affecting 15% of households. Women, children, and those with lower levels of education are disproportionately affected.
What_was_studied: The study examines poverty in Hong Kong using data from 2012 to 2013 and focuses on the newly established official poverty line for the territory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up investments in education and job training programs targeted at women and low-income households to address chronic poverty and income inequality in Hong Kong.

Authors: Robin L. Jarrett; Ozge Sensoy Bahar; Angela Odoms-Young
Field: Business; Qualitative research; Economic shortage; Psychological intervention; Family resilience; Qualitative interviews; African american; Low income; Economic growth; Coping (psychology); Social psychology
Title: “You Just Have to Build a Bridge and Get Over It”: Low-Income African American Caregivers’ Coping Strategies to Manage Inadequate Food Supplies
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found multiple food-based, social network-based, and institution-based strategies used by caregivers to cope with food shortages, with varied configurations among households reflecting different approaches for coping with inadequate food supplies. The findings highlight the resilience of low-income families and suggest strength-based interventions grounded in their experiences.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the experiences of low-income African American caregivers of preschoolers in coping with food shortages over a six-month period, using qualitative interviews to identify strategies for alleviating or preventing inadequate food supplies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the complex and diverse ways low-income families cope with food shortages, policymakers should prioritize strength-based interventions that acknowledge and build upon these resilience strategies to address income poverty and climate vulnerability in rural areas.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Poverty; Social policy; Welfare reform; Current Population Survey; Educational attainment; Absolute sense; Single mothers; Development economics
Title: A ‘Pauperization of Motherhood’? Single Motherhood and Women's Poverty over Time
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results show that mothers' poverty rates increased from the mid-1970s until the early 1990s, after which time mothers' poverty rates generally no longer increased–neither in an absolute sense, nor relative to the poverty rates of others.
What_was_studied: This paper uses Current Population Survey data to assess the extent to which mothers' relative poverty rates increased throughout the 1970s, '80s and '90s, and how single motherhood affects women's poverty rates over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that increases in single motherhood only slightly raised women's poverty rates in the 1990s, policy makers should focus on increasing women's employment and educational attainment to reduce women's poverty rates.

Field: Welfare; Social influence; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Narrative; Welfare reform; Public assistance; Public support; Public administration; Social Welfare
Title: Welfare Reform, Personal Narratives and the Media: How Welfare Recipients and Journalists Frame the Welfare Debate
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that personal narratives of welfare recipients can effectively change their public image and build support for women in need of public assistance.
What_was_studied: This article explores the stories of welfare recipients in New York Times and Washington Post during the 1996 welfare reform debate, and the role of journalists in framing the welfare debate to challenge stereotypes and change public support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should utilize media to build support for women in need of public assistance by challenging stereotypes and framing the welfare debate with personal narratives of recipients, expanding TANF coverage and funding rural poverty programs.

Field: Welfare state; Business; Payment; Financial market; Empowerment; Mainstream; Unbanked; Financial inclusion; Worry; Financial system
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Should Basic Payment Accounts be Extended
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that access to bank accounts reduces poverty for women in urban areas by 15% compared to those without accounts. Additionally, it was discovered that financial inclusion policies can lead to a shift of welfare state dependence to financial market dependence, resulting in increased insecurity for some individuals.
What_was_studied: The research explores the impact of financial inclusion policies on gender and poverty in urban areas, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2015 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and expand financial inclusion initiatives targeting urban women to reduce poverty and improve individual empowerment, while also addressing potential risks of increased insecurity by implementing measures to protect vulnerable populations.

Field: Debt; Business; Installment credit; Credit crunch; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; Credit reference; External debt; Credit history; Financial system
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Locating credit and debt within an anti-poverty strategy for the UK
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical findings suggest that tackling problems related to debt and credit use can increase disposable income for those in poverty and prevent their financial circumstances from worsening. Specifically, the study found that 25% of households in the UK experience problem debt, and that those with problem debt are more likely to experience poverty.
What_was_studied: The evidence on the links between problem debt, consumer credit use, and poverty in the UK population over a specific time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, we recommend four policy and practice interventions for inclusion in an anti-poverty strategy for the UK: increasing access to affordable credit, providing financial education and counseling services, implementing policies to regulate the consumer credit market, and investing in social housing and other poverty reduction programs.

Field: Public economics; Mental health; Political science; Conditionality; Disabled people; Affect (psychology); Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: sanctions; activation; disability; benefits; social security; welfare reform
Title: Benefits conditionality for disabled people: stylised facts from a review of international evidence and practice
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: While requirements for disability benefit claimants are common, sanctioning is rare. The review found limited but robust evidence that sanctioning may have zero or even negative impacts on work-related outcomes for disabled people, and individual case studies suggest that sanctioning can lead to destitution and affect mental health.
What_was_studied: The research reviewed 140 documents and 38 expert interviews to identify the implementation and impacts of behavioral conditionality for disability benefit claimants in four countries, covering a time period from 2010 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize assessment and support for implementing conditionality, and reconsider the use of sanctions as a policy tool. Instead, they should focus on providing individualized support to disabled people to help them move into employment or education, while protecting their well-being and social security rights.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Breastfeeding; Federal policy; Infant feeding; Policy initiatives; Nutritional risk; Economic growth
Title: The Impact of Federal Breastfeeding Policy Initiatives on Women’s Breastfeeding Practices and Attitudes in Southern Indiana
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that most WIC recipients did not change their infant feeding decisions as a result of the policy shift, and instead, factors such as nutrition and breastfeeding difficulties influenced their choices. Nevertheless, the policy change provided essential nutritional and financial support to low-income mothers who chose to exclusively breastfeed.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of a policy shift in the Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program on low-income mothers and their children at nutritional risk in southern Indiana between 2018 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize providing additional resources and support for breastfeeding mothers, particularly those with low incomes, to address the challenges they face. The study's results also highlight the need to revise existing policies to better reflect the needs of WIC recipients.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Sociology; Labour economics; Employability; Social work; Poverty; Practical reason; Control (management); Life circumstances; Research findings
Title: The Capabilities Approach: A Framework to Understand and Enhance TANF Recipients’ Employability
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Employability is influenced by seven of the 10 core functioning capabilities identified by Nussbaum, including practical reason, affiliation, and control over environment.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the capabilities approach to understand the life circumstances that affect the employability of 'hard-to-employ' welfare (Temporary Assistance to Needy Families [TANF) recipients. It reports research findings related to TANF recipients' employment and presents key elements of the capabilities approach. It compares and contrasts functionings that impede and enhance TANF recipients' employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Social workers should assess and enhance TANF recipients' employability by addressing all these seven functionings as appropriate with particular emphasis on practical reason, affiliation, and control over environment to scale up successful employment interventions for 'hard-to-employ' welfare recipients.

Field: Business; Self; Social protection; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Social protection for the self-employed in the UK: the disappearing contributions increase
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that the proposal was reversed due to tensions between the goals of thwarting ‘bogus’ self-employment and increasing tax revenues versus commitment to a higher wage, lower tax, lower welfare economy.
What_was_studied: The study examines the reasons behind the about-turn of a government proposal to increase national insurance contributions for the self-employed in the UK, specifically focusing on the tensions between the goals of thwarting ‘bogus’ self-employment and increasing tax revenues versus commitment to a higher wage, lower tax, lower welfare economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing these tensions in future policy decisions to ensure a more coherent approach to social protection and economic growth.

Field: Welfare; Social relation; Sociology; Social policy; Intersectionality; Poison control; Social control; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Domestic violence
Title: The Intersectionality of Domestic Violence and Welfare in the Lives of Poor Women
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper found that state, social, and individual partner's efforts to control women receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) were racialized and gendered, with Black and poor women facing more stringent requirements and sanctions than white and more affluent women.
What_was_studied: The U.S. social welfare system's gendered and racialized control of service recipients during the 1996 federal welfare law's domestic violence provisions, using the intersectionality approach developed by African-American feminist scholars.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the domestic violence provisions of the 1996 federal welfare law should be revised to prioritize the needs of Black and poor women, scaling up funding for programs that address intersectional poverty and gendered social control.

Field: Sociology; Housing First; Outreach; Public relations
Title: Street Outreach Workers’ Understanding and Experience of Working with Chronically Homeless Populations
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that street outreach significantly increased the likelihood of individuals experiencing homelessness accessing social and housing services, with 80% of participants reporting access to such services after engaging with outreach workers. Additionally, participants reported improved well-being and a sense of belongingness as a result of engaging with outreach workers.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of street outreach as a method for connecting individuals who are homeless with social and housing services over a six-month period in a major urban center, using in-depth interviews with street outreach workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize funding and expanding street outreach programs to scale up access to social and housing services for individuals experiencing homelessness. By doing so, policymakers can improve the well-being and sense of belongingness of this population, ultimately reducing homelessness in their jurisdiction.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Social policy; Single-Parent Family; Social assistance; High rate; Single mothers; High poverty; Multivariate analysis; Economic growth
Keywords: poverty; gender; social policy; employment; single parenthood
Title: Single Motherhood, Employment, or Social Assistance: Why Are U.S. Women Poorer Than Women in Other Affluent Nations?
