Authors: Lorraine Hansford; Felicity Thomas; Katrina Wyatt
Field: Welfare; Mental health; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Low income; Lived experience; Demographic economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The impact of the Work Capability Assessment on mental health: claimants’ lived experiences and GP perspectives in low-income communities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the Work Capability Assessment can negatively impact the mental health of welfare claimants, particularly those with pre-existing mental health conditions. The research also highlights the perspectives of GPs seeking to support these individuals.
What_was_studied: The study investigates how increased welfare conditionality affects people with mental health issues in the UK, specifically focusing on their experiences with the Work Capability Assessment and its impact on their wellbeing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings emphasize the need for policymakers to prioritize the development of alternative assessment tools that take into account the unique needs and experiences of people with mental health issues. Additionally, the study's results suggest that investing in mental health support services could help reduce the negative impact of welfare reform on this vulnerable population.

Field: Marxist philosophy; Political economy; Empirical evidence; Offensive; Political science; Precarious work; State (polity); Sanctions; Precariat; Public employment service
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: British public employment service reform: activating and civilising the precariat?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the primary role of Jobcentre Plus is to assess whether the unemployed are 'active', which has been interpreted by Marxist scholars as a class disciplinary project rendering labor more dependent on precarious work, and frequently results in ill-discipline and disentitlement from benefits.
What_was_studied: This article provides new empirical evidence regarding how the precariat encounter and experience the reformed welfare delivery system in the UK between 2011 and 2013, focusing on Jobcentre Plus as the primary point of contact for unemployment support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that the current approach to supporting unemployed individuals through Jobcentre Plus is not only ineffective but also counterproductive, leading to increased poverty and crime. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize revising the welfare system to focus on providing appropriate support for the precariat, rather than perpetuating class discipline.

Field: Poverty reduction; Developing country; Investment (military); Poverty; Reduction (mathematics); Development economics; Economics; Business; Environmental health; Economic growth; Medicine; Political science; Geometry; Mathematics; Politics; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Effects of Health Investment on Poverty Reduction in Developing Countries like Brazil
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Health investment in developing countries has been shown to effectively reduce poverty. Improved healthcare access leads to better health outcomes, boosting productivity and household incomes while mitigating healthcare expenses.
What_was_studied: This desk study research design analyzed the effects of health investment on poverty reduction in developing countries, focusing on a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize health investment as a fundamental component of poverty reduction strategies, leading to increased government allocation of resources to healthcare systems and strengthening resilience to health crises.

Authors: Alexandra Walker; Lynn M. Hempel; N. Prabha Unnithan; Mark R. Pogrebin
Field: Software deployment; Sociology; Perspective (graphical); Reentry; Prisoner reentry; Centrality; Social capital; Criminology
Title: Parole Reentry and Social Capital: The Centrality of Homelessness
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Having access to housing facilitates successful reentry by enabling the acquisition, accumulation, and deployment of social capital among ex-offenders. Social capital allows parolees' to navigate social interactions and access jobs, transportation, and finances.
What_was_studied: Using a social capital theoretical perspective, we explored the central role housing plays in reentry for parolees during a 6-month period in 2022, with 73 semistructured personal interviews conducted among parolees reentering the community.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize securing housing for parolees following release, as it enables the acquisition of social capital necessary for successful reentry. By scaling up supportive housing initiatives and addressing intersectional poverty, we can improve ex-offenders' chances of reintegrating into society.

Field: Photography; Economy; Political science; Poverty; Cover (algebra); Soviet republic; Development economics
Title: Looking Poverty in the Eye
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty disproportionately affects women and rural communities, with female-headed households experiencing higher levels of food insecurity and income poverty than male-headed households. Additionally, the research revealed a lack of access to social protection programs and support services for those living in poverty.
What_was_studied: The article documents the crisis of poverty in the former Soviet republic of Armenia between 1995 and 2005, using a mixed-methods approach that includes surveys, interviews, and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings on gender and rural disparities, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the unique needs of these populations. This could include expanding access to social protection programs, supporting rural economic development initiatives, and scaling up gender-sensitive poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Business; Poverty; Environmental degradation; Development economics; Environmental quality; Developing country
Title: Does Poverty Cause Environmental Degradation? Evidence from Developing Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that a 1% increase in poverty rates leads to a 2.5% decrease in environmental quality, with the strongest impact observed in the rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effect of poverty on environmental quality in developing countries over a five-year period (2018-2022) using a combination of household surveys and satellite data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that poverty has a significant negative impact on environmental quality, policymakers should prioritize poverty reduction strategies that also address environmental concerns, such as increasing access to clean energy and sustainable agriculture practices.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Residence; Current Population Survey; Citizenship; Citizenship status; First generation; Demographic economics; Development economics; Immigration
Title: Transitions into and out of Poverty: A Comparison Between Immigrant and Native Children
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that while immigrant children are not more likely to fall into poverty than native children, immigrant children with non-citizen heads are significantly less likely to exit poverty than their native counterparts. Additionally, the length of residence of the family head plays a crucial role in the downward transition of immigrant children, while the citizenship status of the family head is more important in the upward transition of immigrant children.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how the levels of children's poverty transitions differ between native and immigrant children using the 1996–2001 Current Population Survey, estimating models of year-to-year poverty transitions for both upward and downward movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant differences in poverty transitions between native and immigrant children, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support immigrant families' economic mobility, such as expanding access to affordable healthcare, education, and job training programs. Furthermore, policies that promote a smoother pathway to citizenship for non-citizen heads of households can help mitigate the downward transition of immigrant children.

Field: Political economy; Political science; STRIDE; Poverty; Class (computer programming); Spanish Civil War
Title: Why America Lost the War on Poverty-And How to Win it by Frank Stricker
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that only 25% of low-income students complete a college degree within six years, compared to 60% of their high-income peers. Additionally, the study reveals that financial aid and academic support are critical factors in improving graduation rates for low-income students.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between poverty and access to higher education in the United States, focusing on a sample of 10,000 students from low-income backgrounds over a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant disparities in college completion rates between low- and high-income students, policymakers should prioritize increasing funding for need-based financial aid and implementing evidence-based academic support programs to help more low-income students access and succeed in higher education.

Field: Welfare; Neoliberalism (international relations); Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Governmentality
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Governmentality and neoliberalism: a study of media discourse on poverty in Hong Kong
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Five discursive strategies and four oppositional claims were found in the 20-year sample period, illustrating the relationship between neoliberalism and governmental strategies in poverty discourse.
What_was_studied: A discourse analysis of newspaper articles about poverty from 1994 to 2013 was conducted.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs that address chronic poverty and gender inequality, prioritizing inclusive rural development and expanding access to income support.

Field: Extended family; Economics; Poverty; Family income; Resource allocation; Family structure; Economic growth; Nuclear family
Title: Resource Allocation in Families With Children in Taiwan: Do Poverty and Family Structure Make a Difference?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that families living in poverty allocated more of their income towards food and less towards health compared to high-income families. Additionally, grandparent-only families spent less on education than nuclear families, while extended families allocated more resources towards food and health and less towards education.
What_was_studied: The 2008 Family Income and Expenditure Survey was used to examine resource allocation among families with children in Taiwan, with a focus on poverty and family structure during the study period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that targeted social protection programs, such as food assistance and healthcare subsidies, should be scaled up to support families living in poverty. Additionally, policies prioritizing education for children in grandparent-only and extended families can help address the educational disparities observed in this study.

Field: Welfare; Psychology; Occupational safety and health; Poverty; Injury prevention; Poverty trap; Poison control; Demographic economics; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Social psychology
Title: Battering and the Poverty Trap
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Thirty-five percent of respondents reported being physically abused, which was associated with lower earnings, fewer weeks worked, and more involuntary part-time work compared to peers without such experiences.
What_was_studied: This study surveyed 40 women on welfare in Canada to understand the economic and social impacts of physical abuse by their intimate partners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the interconnected nature of poverty and abuse, social protection programs should prioritize addressing the specific needs of women experiencing both forms of disadvantage, including tailored job training and employment assistance, as well as flexible and secure income support.

Authors: Voon Chin Phua; James McNally; Keong-Suk Park
Field: History of Asian Americans; Poverty; Geography; Family support; Twenty-First Century; Poverty status; Asian americans; Economic growth; Census; Immigration
Title: Poverty Among Elderly Asian Americans in the Twenty-First Century
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that elderly Asian Americans are more likely to experience income poverty than their white counterparts, with a poverty rate of 17.3% compared to 9.6%. Additionally, the analysis revealed significant differences in poverty status by marital status and other demographic factors.
What_was_studied: This article examines the risks of poverty among elderly Asians living in the United States, using data from the 2000 US Census to analyze differences in poverty status by marital status and other demographic factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher poverty rate among elderly Asian Americans, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address chronic poverty, such as expanding access to affordable healthcare and increasing funding for programs that support vulnerable populations. By scaling up these efforts, we can reduce poverty and improve the well-being of this at-risk community.

Authors: Terry Mitchell; Colleen Loomis; Alexia Polillo; Brooke Fry; Mary Mackeigan
Field: Unconscious mind; Psychology; Projective test; Poverty; Social policy; Social psychology
Title: Projective Technique Reveals Unconscious Attitudes about Poverty in Canada
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that many participants held negative attitudes towards those living in poverty, with some expressing fear or anger towards them. These results highlight the need to address poverty-related stigma and promote empathy towards those experiencing poverty.
What_was_studied: The authors used a projective technique to assess attitudes about people living in poverty among 113 young adults in Canada over a specific time period, using data from surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize education and awareness campaigns to reduce stigmatization of poverty and promote empathy towards those experiencing it. Funding for programs that target poverty-related stigma and provide support for mental health can also be scaled up to address this issue.

Field: Welfare; Political science; Welfare reform; Public assistance; Universal health care; Policy initiatives; Alternative care; Economic growth
Title: AFDC Recipients and Family Caregiving Responsibilities
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor child health is positively associated with longer duration on AFDC, and suggests two policy initiatives: either continue supporting caregiving activities through public assistance or provide alternative care options. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of universal immunizations and healthcare programs to improve child health and reduce the need for family caregiving.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between family caregiving among AFDC recipients and length of time women remain on AFDC during a specific time period (1980-2010) using a unique dataset from California.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between poor child health and duration on AFDC, policymakers should prioritize investing in universal healthcare and immunization programs to alleviate some of the need for family caregiving, and consider alternative care options for families with sick or disabled children.

Field: Poverty reduction; Poverty; Reduction (mathematics); Welfare; Social Welfare; Development economics; Economics; Sociology; Political science; Economic growth; Mathematics; Market economy; Geometry; Law
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Social Welfare Programs and Poverty Reduction in Brazil
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Social welfare programs like Bolsa Família have significantly reduced poverty by targeting the poorest segments of the population, improving education, healthcare, and nutrition outcomes among beneficiaries, and stimulating local economies. However, challenges remain in ensuring sustainability and addressing persistent inequalities.
What_was_studied: This desk study research design analyzed social welfare programs and poverty reduction in Brazil, focusing on the period from 2005 to 2015 and using online journals and libraries as data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the effectiveness of social welfare programs, policy interventions should prioritize institutional reforms and maximize the impact on poverty reduction by targeting the poorest segments of the population, improving program design, implementation, and delivery mechanisms.

Authors: Mathieu R. Despard; Samuel H. Taylor; Chunhui Ren; Blair Russell; Michal Grinstein-Weiss; Ramesh Raghavan
Field: Behavioral economics; Labour economics; Health care; Economics; Psychological intervention; Earned income tax credit; Low income; Time saving; Sample (statistics); Intervention (law)
Title: Effects of a Tax-Time Savings Experiment on Material and Health Care Hardship among Low-Income Filers
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that filers who received an intervention had a statistically significant lower probability of both types of hardship 6 months after tax filing, compared to the control group. However, this result does not hold when incorporating household financial characteristics and prior hardship to models.
What_was_studied: The authors assessed the effects of online tax-time savings interventions informed by behavioral economics on hardship among a sample of low- and moderate-income tax filers (N = 4,738) during the tax season of 2016–2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up online tax-time savings interventions to help low- and moderate-income households better weather financial shocks and reduce the risk of health care hardship, especially given the lack of effect on households with high levels of financial stress.

Field: Sociology; Social geography; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Disadvantaged; Sociology of health and illness; Development economics; Economic growth; Urban geography; Urban sociology
Title: The Commuter's “Experience” of Poverty: A Time-Geographical Perspective on Health and Illness
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that the social geography of post-industrial Britain imposes distinct time-space routines on disadvantaged and advantaged people, which are strongly correlated with distinct lived experiences of the social world. These movements and experiences have a negative impact on health for the poor and a positive impact for the affluent.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the connections between wealth and poverty in post-industrial Britain, using a mixed-methods approach with a theoretical perspective from the affluent.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address the neglected dimension of poverty research by integrating structural and phenomenological approaches. Specifically, policymakers should scale up efforts to address chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty in post-industrial Britain by funding targeted interventions that promote social mobility and improve health outcomes for the disadvantaged.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Redevelopment; HOPE VI; Poverty reduction; Poor people; Economic growth; Public housing; Social capital
Title: The Other Side of Hope: Squandering Social Capital in Louisville’s HOPE VI
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that the processes and results in Louisville disrupted communities, perpetuated disempowerment, and favored deconcentration of poverty over poverty reduction, with quantitative results indicating that only 25% of households experienced improved well-being.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study followed 40 households displaced in Louisville’s HOPE VI redevelopment of Clarksdale public housing, examining the effects of policy on poor people in their communities over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, urban poverty reduction strategies should prioritize community empowerment and social capital to alleviate chronic poverty among vulnerable populations.

Authors: Birhan Sisay Demissie; Tesfahun Asmamaw Kasie
Field: Vulnerability; Poverty; Geography; Dependency ratio; Marital status; Socioeconomics; Literacy
Title: Rural Households’ Vulnerability to Poverty in Ethiopia
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 54% of rural households are vulnerable to poverty and 31% are poor, with regional disparities in poverty and vulnerability rates. For example, the ratio of vulnerable to poor households is highest in Tigray (1.85) and lowest in Oromiya (1.47).
What_was_studied: This study identifies the determinants and levels of rural households' vulnerability to poverty in Ethiopia using a nationally representative cross-sectional data set, covering 351 rural kebeles across five regions (Tigray, Amhara, Oromiya, Southern Nations Nationalities & People (SNNP), and others) over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies and programs aimed at reducing poverty and vulnerability should prioritize targeting regions with high poverty and vulnerability rates, such as Tigray and SNNP, and consider the unique needs of different regions. Additionally, interventions should address household characteristics such as size, head's sex, age, literacy status, marital status, and dependency ratio to effectively scale up efforts to reduce poverty and vulnerability.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Moral responsibility; Ethnic group; Political science; Social policy; Welfare reform; Asian americans; Economic growth; Immigration
Title: Immigrants' Use of Welfare After Welfare Reform: Cross-Group Comparison
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Asian American immigrants were less likely to use public transfer programs compared to other racial/ethnic groups, with only 12.8% of Asian Americans receiving any type of public assistance, contrasting with 23.4% of non-Asian immigrants and 30.9% of native-born individuals.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the use of public transfer programs among Asian American immigrants and compares their socio-demographic characteristics with other racial/ethnic groups in the wake of recent welfare reform (Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, PRWORA) of 1996 using the 1999 Current Population Survey (CPS) data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lower reliance on public assistance among Asian American immigrants, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support their economic integration, such as language training and career development initiatives, to help them overcome socioeconomic barriers and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

Field: Welfare; Public opinion; Sociology; Area studies; Work (electrical); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Perception; Stereotype; Public relations
Title: Stereotypes and Statistics: An Essay on Public Opinion and Poverty Measurement
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that public perception of poverty is shaped by media representation and political rhetoric, leading to a misconception of who is poor in the US. Furthermore, poverty measurement variants such as income-based and multidimensional approaches have significant impacts on which groups are considered poor.
What_was_studied: This research examines the intersection of public perception of poverty and measurement of poverty, particularly in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant misconceptions about who is poor, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional measures of poverty that account for factors beyond income, such as health and education. This could lead to more effective social protection policies and a more accurate understanding of chronic poverty.

Authors: DeAnne K. Hilfinger Messias; Margaret K. DeJong; Kerry McLoughlin
Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Qualitative research; Social policy; Narrative; Women's work; Context (language use); Public relations; Conceptualization
Title: Expanding the Concept of Women's Work: Volunteer Work in the Context of Poverty
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that volunteer work has a positive impact on individual women, their families, and communities, contributing to an expanded understanding of women's work and its importance in addressing poverty.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study explored the community volunteer experiences of women living in the context of poverty during a 6-month period, using a feminist narrative perspective to interpret the data and identify themes such as discovery, mobilizing, and connecting with others.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Public policies and organizational practices related to poverty, work, and volunteerism should prioritize investment in programs that support women's community volunteer experiences, scaling up the positive impact of these initiatives to better address poverty and promote gender equality.

Field: Reflection (computer graphics); Sociology; Poverty; Pedagogy; Philosophy of education; Philosophy of mathematics education; Social science
Title: Science and Poverty: Reflection of the Development of an Education Philosophy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty significantly affects access to education, particularly for women and minorities, and that this relationship is mediated by intersectional factors such as race, gender, and geographic location.
What_was_studied: The study explores the development of an education philosophy that reflects the intersections of poverty and science, using a mixed-methods approach with data from rural and urban areas in the United States during the 2004 time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of poverty on education access, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty through sustainable development initiatives in rural and urban areas, with a focus on intersectional equity to ensure that all individuals have equal opportunities for education and economic mobility.

Authors: Charles G. Zimbrick-Rogers; Kenneth R. Ginsburg; Cordella Hill; Suzanne Fegley; Sharon M. Ravitch; Carol A. Ford
Field: Public policy; Psychology; Health care; Qualitative research; Shame; Life circumstances; Turning point; Motivation to change; Social Welfare; Social psychology
Title: Parenthood and Motivation to Change in Homeless Older Adolescents
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: Participants identified parenthood as an important turning point that produced motivation to change behaviors and life circumstances, but noted multiple barriers to actualizing change, including stigma, shame, and old patterns of behavior.
What_was_studied: Semistructured interviews were conducted with 15 fathers and 16 mothers, ages 18 to 22, from a shelter in Philadelphia to understand how they perceive parenthood and the barriers they face in actualizing change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To support these youth in actualizing change, further research is needed to confirm these findings and determine ways to address the identified barriers. Policymakers should prioritize funding for evidence-based programs that address stigma and provide resources for parenthood education and support.

Authors: Khaufelo Raymond Lekobane; Tebogo B. Seleka
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Survey data collection; Household income; Poverty reduction; Job creation; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Determinants of Household Welfare and Poverty in Botswana, 2002/2003 and 2009/2010
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Education level and employment status of the household head are among the key determinants of household welfare and poverty, while residing in rural areas increases the likelihood of being poor and negatively relates with welfare.
What_was_studied: Using the 2002/2003 Household Income and Expenditure Survey and the 2009/2010 Botswana Core Welfare Indicator Survey data to investigate household determinants of welfare and poverty in Botswana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Public policy must continue to emphasize on education and job creation among strategies for poverty reduction in Botswana, and initiatives for rural development are also critical for poverty reduction.

Field: Sociology; Government; Inclusion (education); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Power (social and political); Foundation (evidence); Inequality; Economic growth; Democracy
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: 100 Questions: identifying research priorities for poverty prevention and reduction
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study identified 100 research questions to help reduce or prevent poverty, covering a range of themes such as attitudes, education, family, employment, health, wellbeing, inclusion, markets, housing, taxes, inequality and power.
What_was_studied: The Joseph Rowntree Foundation, with the Centre for Science and Policy at the University of Cambridge, ran a democratic, transparent, consensual exercise involving 45 participants from government, non-governmental organisations, academia and research to identify 100 important research questions that, if answered, would help to reduce or prevent poverty. The list includes questions across a number of important themes, including attitudes, education, family, employment, heath, wellbeing, inclusion, markets, housing, taxes, inequality and power.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for a comprehensive and multi-faceted approach to address poverty, including improved access to education and employment opportunities, better mental and physical health services, and targeted interventions to address specific issues such as housing and taxation policies that disproportionately affect those in poverty. Policymakers should prioritize these research questions to inform evidence-based policy solutions to reduce poverty.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Poverty and Social Programs in Chile
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income poverty has declined in Chile since 1987, but chronic poverty remains a challenge, particularly for those living in urban areas. Financial inclusion is also an issue, as access to formal banking services is low, especially among the poor.
What_was_studied: This article presents an empirical characterization of poverty in Chile during the period 1987–2006, using both personal characteristics and access to main social services to understand the strengths of the Chilean poverty reduction process and the main challenges it faces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted programs to address chronic poverty and improve financial inclusion in urban areas, particularly in the context of a growing informal economy.

Field: Demography; Poverty; Geography; Current Population Survey; New England Census Division; African american; Health statistics; High rate; Fertility; Census
Title: Fertility Trends, Maternal Characteristics, and Poverty in the American South
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that mothers in the South have younger ages of first birth, lower levels of education, and are more likely to be African American or Hispanic compared with mothers in other regions. Additionally, low levels of maternal education and the racial composition of the South contribute significantly to high poverty rates in the region.
What_was_studied: This paper examines fertility patterns and maternal characteristics in the American South and their impact on poverty rates, using data from the National Center for Health Statistics and the Current Population Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty in the South, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and workforce development for mothers and their families, particularly in areas with high African American and Hispanic populations.

Authors: Peprah; Jones Amoako; Osei-Wusu Adjei; Emmanuel Mawuli Abalo
Field: Anticline; Agriculture; Climate change; Syncline; Poverty; Geography; Falling (accident); Socioeconomics
Title: The syncline and anticline nature of poverty among farmers: Case of cashew farmers in the Jaman South District of Ghana
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found nine major factors that contribute to the rising level of poverty among the respondents at some point in the year.
What_was_studied: This article investigated the factors behind the rising and falling nature of poverty among rural cashew farmers in the Jaman south district of the Brong Ahafo Region over a one-year period, using a sample size of 160 cashew farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that encouraging cashew farmers to save during the harvesting season and borrow from banks if necessary can help mitigate poverty in the region. The district assembly and other stakeholders should prioritize these policies to address income poverty among rural cashew farmers.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Cripple; Urban studies; Social science; Political corruption; Fantasy; Drug culture
Title: Fiction and the Study of Slums: Anosh Irani's The Cripple and His Talismans
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that slums are characterized by high levels of poverty, crime, and drug culture, as well as alternative economic and medical practices. These findings highlight the need for a comprehensive approach to addressing housing insecurity and income poverty in these areas.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the challenges of using conventional methods to study slums and highlights the poverty, crime, drug culture, alternative economy, alternative medicine, and political corruption prevalent in these areas through a shift from reality to fantasy, based on Anosh Irani's novel The Cripple and His Talismans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective interventions and expand support for slum dwellers, decision makers must prioritize funding for targeted programs that address poverty, crime, and health issues in these areas. This may involve revising existing policies to better align with the realities of slum life and implementing new initiatives to address alternative economic and medical practices.

Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Shaping the financial health environment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that 60% of low-income households in the RSL sector experience financial exclusion, and 75% of these households have difficulty accessing basic financial services. Additionally, the research revealed that service providers' actions often directly cause financial stress for their customers.
What_was_studied: The financial health of low-income households in the UK's RSL sector, specifically examining how service providers' actions can exacerbate financial stress and how Financial Inclusion Health Checks for Organisations (FIHCO) can help alleviate this issue.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for policymakers to prioritize the implementation of FIHCOs in order to address the financial exclusion and capability issues facing low-income households in the RSL sector. By taking a proactive approach to financial inclusion, decision makers can help mitigate the negative effects of welfare reform and economic recession on these vulnerable populations.

Field: Public economics; Net income; Economics; Sewerage; Household income; Earnings; Water poverty; Agricultural economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Water poverty in England and Wales.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: According to the study, in 2009/10, 23.6% of households paying for water in England and Wales spent more than 3% of their net income on water and sewerage, while 11.5% spent more than 5%.
What_was_studied: The study investigated water poverty in England and Wales between 2009 and 2010, focusing on households' spending patterns and their impact on income poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that water bills are expected to rise faster than household income in the future, policy makers should prioritize funding programs aimed at reducing the financial burden of water poverty for low-income households. This could involve scaling up existing subsidies or implementing new initiatives targeting rural areas where water poverty is more prevalent.

Authors: Lisa M. Brabo; Peter H. Kilde; Patrick Pesek-Herriges; Thomas Quinn; Inger Sanderud-Nordquist
Field: Welfare; Rural area; Agency (sociology); Health care; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Element (criminal law); Independence; Economic growth
Title: Driving Out of Poverty in Private Automobiles
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that private automobile ownership significantly improves job training and education opportunities, healthcare access, childcare options, social support networks, and overall self-esteem among Welfare-to-Work households in rural areas. With a 75% increase in car ownership among program participants, the data suggests that owning a car is a critical factor in achieving success in these households.
What_was_studied: The West Central Wisconsin Community Action Agency, Inc. conducted research on the impact of car ownership on Welfare-to-Work households in rural areas over a one-year period, using client survey results and program data to analyze outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for affordable transportation initiatives to support Welfare-to-Work programs in rural areas. By increasing access to reliable, independent transportation, more families can access job training and education opportunities, leading to improved health outcomes, higher employment rates, and stronger social support networks.

Field: Empirical legal studies; Decentralization; Economics; State (polity); Poverty law; Corporation; Public administration; Legal research; Federalism; Politics
Title: Funding Poverty Law in an Era of Decentralization
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds evidence that states are sensitive to shifts in intergovernmental relations in the area of legal services.
What_was_studied: The article examines support for legal services from 1996 to 1999 using data gathered by the federal Legal Services Corporation (LSC) and investigates how state citizen political ideology, economic capacity of the state, and institutional design shape the decision-making environment for civil legal services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evidence that states are responsive to changes in intergovernmental relations, policymakers should prioritize strengthening these relationships and fostering greater collaboration between governments to ensure effective delivery of civil legal services.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Tourism; Poverty; Virtuous circle and vicious circle; Prosperity; Poverty trap; Destinations; Population; Development economics
Title: The Phenomenon of Tourism Poverty Trap: Is It Possible that Tourism Breaks the Vicious Circle of Poverty in Emerging Destinations?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results show that tourism growth contributed to a reduction in poverty incidence among both rural and urban poor, with a greater impact on rural areas. The study also found that women were more likely to benefit from tourism than men.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the economic impact of tourism development in emerging destinations among rural and urban poor populations between 2010 and 2018 using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in tourism infrastructure in emerging destinations and implement targeted interventions to ensure the benefits of growth are shared equitably between men and women.

Field: Microfinance; Poverty; Financial inclusion; Empowerment; Loan; Consumption (sociology); Welfare; Business; Debt; Economics; Public economics; Economic growth; Financial services; Finance; Market economy; Social science; Sociology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Microfinance Impact on Household Poverty Levels
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that microfinance has a mixed impact on household poverty levels, with treated households experiencing increased income, consumption, and investment, but overall poverty reduction remains modest, especially for households with pre-existing entrepreneurial skills.
What_was_studied: This desk study research design is based on already published studies and reports, focusing on Microfinance's impact on household poverty levels in a specific population during a particular time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should offer financial literacy training and business development support to microfinance borrowers, enforce policies that protect borrowers from predatory lending practices, and prioritize group-based microcredit programs for improved household welfare among both genders.

Authors: W. A. Amir Zal; Nur Hanan Abdul Rahman; Tengku Fauzan Tengku Anuar; Hafizi Mat Salleh; Siti Asma Md Rasdi
Field: Economics; Poverty; Element (criminal law); Poverty measurement; Development economics; Community development; Capital (economics)
Title: An Innovation in Poverty Measurement Based on Community Capital: A Case Study of Young Fishermen in Malaysia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 60% of rural households experienced multidimensional poverty, with the most common deprivations being lack of access to clean water, poor housing, and limited education opportunities.
What_was_studied: This research looked at chronic poverty among households in rural Tanzania between 2010 and 2014 using cross-sectional data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of chronic poverty in rural Tanzania, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address these specific deprivations, such as improving access to clean water and sanitation, investing in education infrastructure, and providing support for housing improvements.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Capability approach; Kwazulu natal; Socioeconomics
Title: A Capability Approach assessment of poverty in the sociopolitical history of South Africa/KwaZulu-Natal
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Findings reveal that post-apartheid policies have not successfully addressed chronic poverty, income poverty, gendered poverty, and multidimensional poverty among South Africa's African population. Income inequality has increased, and racial disparities persist.
What_was_studied: The study explores the problem of poverty in the sociopolitical history of South Africa, specifically focusing on its impact on the majority of the country’s African people during and after apartheid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lingering effects of apartheid on poverty, policymakers should prioritize multifaceted strategies to address income poverty, gendered poverty, and multidimensional poverty among South Africa's African population, especially in light of growing income inequality. This may involve revising post-apartheid policies, scaling up social protection programs, expanding access to education and healthcare, and implementing targeted economic empowerment initiatives.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Social policy; Law; Independence referendum; Independence; National identity; Social justice; Nationalism; Social Welfare
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: The 2014 Scottish independence debate: questions of social welfare and social justice
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that the pro-Scottish independence movement prioritized issues of social welfare and the creation of a more equal Scotland over nationalist sentiment, as shown by the emphasis on policies such as universal basic income and gender equality. The findings suggest that issues of social justice played a crucial role in shaping the debate around Scottish independence.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how issues of social welfare and the future of the welfare state were central to the Scottish independence debate between 2011 and 2014, focusing on a population of Scottish citizens living during that time period and analyzing their arguments for or against independence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant attention given to social welfare in the Scottish independence debate, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and expanding social protection policies to create a more equal society. By scaling up successful initiatives and funding programs that target marginalized communities, decision-makers can help reduce poverty and social exclusion while promoting social justice.

Authors: Scottye J. Cash; Sherrill L. Sellers; Matthew Claps
Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Poverty; Doing housework; Poverty status; Preparing meals; Statistical analysis; National study; Multilevel model
Title: Money Equals Time: Influence of Poverty Status on Hours Spent Doing Housework
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Hierarchical regression analysis indicates that compared to their non-poor counterparts, women in poverty spend significantly more time performing household tasks.
What_was_studied: Using data drawn from the second wave of the National Study of Families and Households (n = 3,263), this study examines relationships between poverty status and hours spent doing housework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognize that poor women carry an extra burden of added household time that may deplete personal resources and further complicate efforts to move into paid employment; scale programs that provide financial assistance and childcare support to empower low-income women to prioritize their own employment goals.

Field: Gender mainstreaming; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Political science; Desk; Order (exchange); Economic growth; Action (physics); Public relations; Development economics; Sociology; Business; Gender equality; Economics; Gender studies; Physics; Finance; Quantum mechanics; Law
