Title: Oh, SNAP! Poverty Simulations in Social Justice Classrooms: Active and Experiential Learning.
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that students who participated in the SNAP Challenge had improved awareness of power and privilege, as well as increased empathy and adaptive flexibility skills, which are essential for effective social work practice with clients experiencing poverty and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The Supplementary Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Challenge was examined over a period of seven consecutive days among social work students, emphasizing critical self-reflection and analysis of biases through active learning methodologies and simulations, with the aim of improving awareness of power and privilege among future clients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of child poverty, income poverty, and food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize funding for social work education programs that incorporate experiential learning opportunities like the SNAP Challenge to ensure that future social workers are adequately prepared to address these issues with empathy and effectiveness.

Field: Welfare; Psychology; Nursing; Poverty; Social policy; Welfare reform; Population; Poison control; Demographic economics; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence
Title: Poverty, Battering, Race, and Welfare Reform: Black-White Differences in Women's Welfare-to-Work Transitions
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poor battered women have a higher dropout rate when compared to other participants in the job readiness program, with three times more severe enough to seek protective orders. Additionally, while there were no significant differences between Black and White women in reported violence and injury, White women reported higher rates of non-violent abuse such as threats that enforce traditional notions of maternity, domesticity, and economic dependence.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the impact of poverty and battering on women's ability to transition from welfare to work, using data from a short-term job readiness program for Black and White women enrolled at six sites.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and intersectional poverty by scaling up programs that support women's economic empowerment and provide safe spaces for them to seek help without fear of violence or threats. Additionally, social protection policies must be reviewed to ensure they address the unique needs of battered women.

Field: Declaration; Descriptive research; Social work; Human rights; Political science; Poverty; Law; Linguistic rights; International human rights law; Qualitative property
Title: A Descriptive Research Study of Economic Human Rights Violations in America
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that participants experienced over 600 EHRV, including lack of access to employment opportunities and fair wages, inadequate social safety nets, and discrimination based on race, gender, and other factors. Participants also reported experiencing multiple forms of EHRV simultaneously and across their lifetimes.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the experiences of individuals living in poverty and their perceptions of economic human rights violations (EHRV) over their lifetimes, using qualitative interviews with 57 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high frequency and complexity of EHRV experienced by individuals living in poverty, social work practitioners and policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues through targeted interventions and policy reforms to ensure that all individuals have access to their economic human rights.

Authors: Margarida Gaspar de Matos; Tania Gaspar; Bruce G. Simons-Morton; Marta Reis; Lúcia Ramiro
Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Demography; Poverty; Sexual intercourse; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Cape verde; Portuguese; Focus group; Immigration; Gerontology
Keywords: Communication; Information; HIV prevention; Poverty; Ethnicity; Sexual risk
Title: Communication and Information About “Safer Sex”: Intervention Issues Within Communities of African Migrants Living in Poorer Neighborhoods in Portugal
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: Compared with Portuguese adolescents, African migrant teens reported initial sexual intercourse at earlier ages and had higher prevalence rates for having had sex without condoms.
What_was_studied: Data were obtained from a special administration of the Health Behavior in School-Aged Children (HBSC) survey in a special sample of Portuguese schools located in low-income Lisbon neighborhoods with large proportions of African migrants. Survey participants included 919 sixth, eighth, and tenth graders (52.3% female), of whom 19.2% were migrant foreigners from African, Portuguese-speaking countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective prevention programs targeting migrant youth and expand access to sexual health services, prioritizing culturally adapted interventions tailored to the diverse ethnic backgrounds of this population.

Authors: Furjen Denq; Douglas H. Constance; Su-Shiow Joung
Field: Geography; Hazardous waste; Justice (ethics); Environmental justice; Environmental racism; Superfund; Population; Economic growth; Unit of analysis; Environmental planning; Operationalization
Title: The Role of Class, Status, and Power in the Distribution of Toxic Superfund Sites in Texas and Louisiana
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that hazardous waste sites are disproportionately located in communities with higher percentages of minorities and poor, specifically in Texas and Louisiana. The findings showed that 61% of the population living near Superfund hazardous waste sites in Texas and Louisiana were minorities and/or low-income.
What_was_studied: This study reexamines the claim that hazardous waste sites are disproportionately located in communities with higher percentages of minorities and poor in the population in Texas and Louisiana combined, using a multi-dimensional conceptual frame to rectify weaknesses associated with conventional approaches to environmental justice issues during a specific time period with specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of hazardous waste on marginalized communities, decision-makers should prioritize funding for community-led cleanup initiatives and environmental health research in these areas to address the issue of environmental justice. Policy interventions should also focus on scaling up community engagement, expanding data collection and analysis, and strengthening environmental regulations to ensure the protection of vulnerable populations.

Authors: Timothy Patrick Hilton; Susan J. Lambert
Field: Human resources; Intermediary; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Seekers; Workforce development; Disadvantaged; High turnover; Autonomy
Title: Understanding Employers’ Use of Labor Market Intermediaries in Filling Low-Level Jobs: Attracting Retainable Employees or Replenishing High-Turnover Jobs?
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that HR managers are more likely to use LMIs to fill lower-quality jobs, often turning to multiple intermediaries simultaneously. In contrast, when filling higher-quality jobs, managers with autonomy tend to adopt a targeted approach, selecting specific LMIs based on their reputation for referring retainable workers.
What_was_studied: This research looks at frontline human resource managers in Chicago hotels' use of labor market intermediaries to fill job openings over a one-year period, focusing on the distinction between lower- and higher-quality jobs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of high-quality job matches for both employees and employers, policymakers should prioritize efforts to improve the quality of labor market intermediaries and promote targeted recruitment practices for higher-quality jobs.

Field: Poverty; Prosperity; Economic growth; Development economics; Population; Sociology; Urbanization; Political science; Economics; Demography
Title: Sociological and Policy Examination of Poverty-Led Crime in Indonesia: Case Study of (Child) Prostitution
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper highlights the critical role Jakarta plays in shaping the future trajectory of its vast human resources and underscores the urgency for comprehensive policies that prioritize improved education, social welfare, and economic opportunities, particularly for the underprivileged youth.
What_was_studied: This paper engages in the profound dynamics of poverty-led crime in Indonesia, emphasizing its socioeconomically constructed nature and the potential for deliberate deconstruction through targeted interventions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognizing Indonesia's potential for urbanization and economic growth, the paper contends that disciplined citizenship, achievable through incentivizing conventional paths for the younger and underprivileged population, is crucial for the nation's prosperity. Therefore, policymakers must prioritize pro-poor and pro-development strategies to mitigate crime.

Field: Welfare; Competence (human resources); Self-efficacy; Sociology; Poverty; Self-actualization; Welfare reform; Receipt; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Social psychology
Title: "It Still Don't Make You Feel Like You're Doin' It": Welfare Reform and Perceived Economic Self-Efficacy.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that economic self-efficacy was central to these women's perceptions of themselves as economic agents and that welfare receipt, the character of work, and experiences related to parenting in poverty all affected their opportunities for exercising agency.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study investigated the impact of federal welfare reform on the self-efficacy perceptions of 31 young mothers in the United States during a one-year period, using in-depth interviews to explore their experiences with financial choices and agency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize providing financial choices and opportunities for economic agency to young mothers receiving welfare to support the development of their self-efficacy and overall well-being.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Social class; Public opinion; Racism; Sociology; Social policy; Welfare reform; Stereotype; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Welfare-Spending Judgments Through Class, Race, and Gender Lenses: Exploring the Influence of Stratification Beliefs, Racial Attitudes, and Gender Norms
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Studies showed that welfare appraisals are influenced by a person's explanation of poverty, racial inequalities, and gender hierarchies. However, most research focused on only one set of class, race, or gender variables, limiting the theoretical breadth of these inquiries.
What_was_studied: Researchers examined American welfare attitudes among politicians in the 1990s, specifically how class, race, and gender statuses affect these attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that welfare attitudes are influenced by multiple factors, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive approaches addressing poverty and inequality. By considering the intersections of class, race, gender, and other factors, decision-makers can create more effective policies to reduce poverty and improve social protection.

Field: Advertising; Economics; Marketing; Poorhouse; Poverty; Social policy; Cash; Reverse mortgage; Home equity
Title: From House to Poorhouse: An Analysis of Reverse Mortgage Portrayal in Selected Media Advertisements
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The analysis found that most recent advertisements fail to provide a complete picture of mortgage reversion and instead prey upon older adults, especially those living in poverty, by portraying it as a free cash-generating machine dispensing large sums of money with no strings attached.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed reverse mortgage advertisements from the past decade to understand how they present this financial product to older Americans, specifically those living in poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize regulating the language used in reverse mortgage advertisements to prevent predatory targeting of vulnerable older adults, especially those living in poverty.

Field: Underpinning; Typology; Poverty; Sustainability; Sustainable development; Inequality; Corporate governance; Descriptive statistics; Economics; Economic growth; Development economics; Public economics; Political science; Geography; Ecology; Mathematical analysis; Statistics; Civil engineering; Mathematics; Archaeology; Finance; Law; Engineering; Biology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Inclusive, sustainable economic transformation: an analysis of trends and trade-offs
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Five clusters of countries with varying degrees of outcomes across the three pillars of inclusive, sustainable economic transformation. No countries consistently performed well across all three dimensions, but some achieved moderate outcomes.
What_was_studied: A typology to capture varying degrees of inclusive, sustainable economic transformation in low- and middle-income countries using a cluster analysis of poverty and inequality, environmental sustainability, and economic transformation proxied by quantitative indicators between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy implications point to the need to prioritize pro-poor infrastructure development and make certain sectors greener to advance tripartite gains.

Authors: Ann E. MacEachron; Nora S. Gustavsson
Field: Welfare; Economics; Cultural competence; Poverty; Social policy; Indian Child Welfare Act; Foster care; Child neglect; Context (language use); Economic growth
Title: Contemporary Policy Challenges for Indian Child Welfare
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that recent federal policies have challenged or altered ICWA outcomes, particularly through the reemergence of poverty as a risk factor for American Indian families, which may increase the removal rate of Indian children due to perceived child neglect. Additionally, the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act of 1980 and the Adoptions and Safe Families Act of 1997 present challenges to ICWA by ignoring its rationale and protections, while the Multiethnic Placement Act of 1994 explicitly exempts Indian children in recognition of ICWA goals and rationale, but noncompliance with this exemption may undermine the intent of ICWA.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of recent federal policies on the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) outcomes over the last 25 years, focusing on four specific policies: the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act of 1980, the Adoptions and Safe Families Act of 1997, and the Multiethnic Placement Act of 1994.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the reemergence of poverty as a risk factor for American Indian families to prevent an increase in the removal rate of Indian children due to perceived child neglect. Additionally, policymakers should revise or fund programs that address challenges to ICWA posed by recent federal policies, such as ignoring ICWA's rationale and protections.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Power (social and political); Distribution of wealth; Belief system; Inequality; Criminology; Social psychology
Title: Robin Hood revisited : Theft, charity, and the ethics of inequality
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that few individuals chose to transfer wealth through charity or theft when given the opportunity, despite the possibility of saving lives and improving well-being. Instead, subjects prioritized property-protecting ethics over altruistic ethics, even in extreme situations where life and death were at stake.
What_was_studied: The study examined the perpetuation of poverty in two societies with systemic inequalities of wealth and power, using data from 2018 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the systemic inequalities that perpetuate poverty and re-evaluate their approaches to asset redistribution. Existing policies that prioritize property protection over human well-being may need to be revised or expanded to address this issue.

Authors: Jessica Wiederspan; Elizabeth Rhodes; H. Luke Shaefer
Field: Public economics; Public policy; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Safety net; Negative income tax; Service provision; Economic well being; Politics
Title: Expanding the Discourse on Antipoverty Policy: Reconsidering a Negative Income Tax
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The article finds that a NIT could potentially lift 52 million Americans above the poverty line and reduce income inequality, while also addressing current gaps in service provision. Estimated annual expenditures for an NIT are around $300 billion, compared to current expenditures of around $600 billion on major means-tested programs.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the effectiveness of a Negative Income Tax (NIT) in addressing poverty gaps and improving income inequality in the United States, using data from major means-tested programs and comparing it to estimated expenditures for an NIT.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential to significantly reduce poverty and income inequality while addressing gaps in service provision, policy makers should consider implementing a Negative Income Tax (NIT) program as part of a comprehensive social protection system.

Authors: Barbara C. Medley; Marilyn Edelhoch; Qiduan Liu; Linda Martin
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Sociology; Poverty; Mentorship; Welfare reform; Legislation; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Economic security
Title: Success After Welfare: What Makes the Difference? An Ethnographic Study of Welfare Leavers in South Carolina
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that factors related to levels of assistance received, resource utilization, mentorship, and self-help attitudes differentiated the experiences of more successful women from those less successful.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study examined the factors that distinguished women with greater success after welfare from those who were less successful, using a population of post-welfare women in the United States during a specific time period (not provided) and collecting data through interviews and resource utilization measures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize providing comprehensive support services for post-welfare women, such as career counseling, job placement assistance, and mentorship programs, to help them obtain jobs that offer economic security. Additionally, resource utilization measures should be implemented to ensure that women have access to the resources they need to succeed.

Field: Finance; Business; Vulnerability; Poverty; Asset (economics); Corporation; Context (language use); Urban poverty; Fuzzy logic
Title: Determining Poverty Vulnerabilities in Dhaka City Corporation Area: An Asset-based Fuzzy Logic Analysis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 75% of households in Dhaka city are chronically poor and have low levels of resilience to climate shocks, with rural areas being more vulnerable than urban areas. Additionally, the study identified a set of vulnerability indicators that can be used to prioritize interventions aimed at reducing poverty and improving resilience.
What_was_studied: This article presents a list of vulnerability indicators in the context of Dhaka city using an asset-based approach and evaluates the relative vulnerabilities of households using fuzzy logic, focusing on the time period of 2018-2020 and using data from household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize investments in rural development programs, targeting the most vulnerable populations and focusing on asset-building interventions to improve resilience to climate shocks.

Field: Psychology; Unemployment; Anger; Style (sociolinguistics); Population; Anger expression; Job retention; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Anger response style as it relates to gaining and retaining employment in a chronically poor population
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Suppressive (passive) anger response strategies were found to increase job retention for six months, while respectfully expressing anger had no significant difference in job retention compared to aggressive verbal or physical expression of anger.
What_was_studied: The research focused on anger response style in a chronically poor, unemployed population over a six-month period to determine its impact on job employment and retention.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy interventions should prioritize developing suppressive anger response strategies to support employment retention programs for chronically poor and unemployed populations.

Field: Public policy; Economy; Nexus (standard); Economics; Poverty; Community action; Entrepreneurship
Title: Poverty and Entrepreneurship in Developed Economies: Re-Assessing the Roles of Policy and Community Action
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that public policy and community action can significantly increase the likelihood of entrepreneurship among the poor. Policies such as business training programs, access to capital, and regulatory reform can help to reduce income poverty and improve social protection for this vulnerable population.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the entrepreneurial potential of the poor in developed economies and explores how public policy and community action can be leveraged to realize this potential over a one-year period, using data from the United States and Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up successful initiatives and expand support for entrepreneurs in need, policymakers should prioritize funding for community-based programs that foster entrepreneurship among the poor. By implementing evidence-based policies and leveraging local action, governments can make a meaningful difference in reducing income poverty and improving social protection.

Authors: Michael J. Lynch; Paul B. Stretesky; Michael A. Long
Field: Biodiversity; Economics; Poverty; Poaching; Environmental justice; Critical criminology; Blame; Social science; Green criminology; Politics; Environmental ethics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Keywords: Environmental Justice; Radical Political Ecology; Critical Criminology; Brundtland Report
Title: Blaming the Poor for Biodiversity Loss: A Political Economic Critique of the Study of Poaching and Wildlife Trafficking
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the political economy perspective on biodiversity loss highlights the role of capitalist and neoliberal policies in driving environmental degradation, while the poaching perspective often places the blame on local communities and individuals, particularly in the context of poverty and social justice.
What_was_studied: The study examined the political economy of biodiversity loss within criminology and its implications for environmental discourse related to poverty and social justice using a qualitative analysis of 30 peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of biodiversity loss, such as capitalist and neoliberal policies, rather than solely focusing on poaching and local communities, in order to effectively address environmental degradation and promote social justice.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Stigma (botany); Ethnography; Poverty; Embarrassment; Welfare reform; Shame; Inequality; Austerity
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Stigma, shame and ‘people like us’ : an ethnographic study of foodbank use in the UK.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The majority of foodbank users experienced stigma, fear, and embarrassment, which was aggravated by representations in 'poverty porn' television shows. However, when people recognized that 'other people like us' were receiving food parcels, stigma was overcome.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic research was conducted over two years in North East England, exploring the lived experiences of health inequalities among residents in the most and least affluent areas to determine how foodbanks and charitable activities are addressing chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, health disparities, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the use of foodbanks and other charitable activities to address chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, health disparities, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty, policy makers must prioritize funding for these initiatives and revise existing policies to better support those in need.

Field: Sense of place; Political economy; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Social policy; Collective efficacy; HOPE VI; Public administration; Social control; Public housing; Social capital
Title: Flawed Policy Assumptions and HOPE VI
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The findings demonstrated that middle-income families experienced a sense of place and a strong work ethic with similar societal values as other income groups in this society, challenging the policy assumption that culture of poverty can only be disrupted by placing them into lower-income neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: The policy assumption that it is necessary to place middle-income families into lower-income neighborhoods to disrupt a culture of poverty was studied using the HOPE VI redevelopment project located in the Northwest as an example. The study examined collective efficacy, social capital, social networks and self-sufficiency among middle-income families before and after HOPE VI redevelopment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the assumption that middle-income families must be placed into lower-income neighborhoods to disrupt a culture of poverty and instead prioritize investing in community development programs and resources to support collective efficacy, social capital, and self-sufficiency among all income groups.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Product (category theory); Control variable; Ideology; Economics; Poverty; Variables; Medicaid; Social Welfare
Title: Effect of Divorce on State Medicaid Expenditures
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that states with higher prevalence of divorce had lower Medicaid spending as a percentage of gross state product. Specifically, they found that every one percent increase in the prevalence of divorce was associated with a 0.23% decrease in Medicaid spending.
What_was_studied: This article tests the hypothesis that family structure, among other factors, helps explain state variation in social services spending, using data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) and other sources for the period 2001-2005 in a pooled time series, quasi-experimental design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between family structure and social services spending, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at strengthening families, such as marriage education programs or parenting classes, to improve the well-being of vulnerable populations and maximize the effectiveness of social services spending.

Authors: Diane McEachern Msw; Marlene Van Winkle Msw; Sue Steiner

Title: Domestic Violence Among the Navajo
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that poverty, lack of infrastructure and social services, and the legacy of colonization have contributed to an increase in family violence among Navajo women.
What_was_studied: The study examined domestic violence among the Navajo in Northeastern Arizona from 1993 to 2018, using ethnographic interviews and data from the Navajo Nation's Domestic Abuse Prevention Act.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and lack of infrastructure to prevent domestic violence and support Navajo women's well-being.

Field: Microfinance; State (computer science); Socioeconomics; Business; Economic growth; Development economics; Economics; Agricultural economics; Mathematics; Algorithm
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Influence of Microfinance Credits on the Socio-economic Status of Women in Edo State, Nigeria
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that access to microfinance positively influenced women's socioeconomic status (income, occupation, and education), despite some challenges in accessing loans. Clients reported using the credits to meet household needs, expand their businesses, and reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of microfinance loans on women's socioeconomic status, including their income, occupation, and education, using data from 750 female microfinance clients in Edo State over a six-month period, with a focus on differences between microfinance institutions that offer health-related services and those that do not.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize implementing or scaling up microfinance initiatives that offer health-related services to empower women socioeconomically. This could involve increasing funding for such programs, streamlining the loan application process, and ensuring that health-related services are integrated into existing microfinance frameworks.

Field: German; Political science; Poverty; Parallels; Disability insurance; Social security; Action (philosophy); Earnings; Self employed; Demographic economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: Precariousness among solo self-employed workers: a German-Dutch comparison
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The results show that solo self-employed workers are relatively vulnerable in terms of income and disability insurance in both countries, with German solo self-employed workers at a higher risk of poverty in old age compared to the Netherlands.
What_was_studied: This article compares solo self-employment in Germany and the Netherlands, examining the structure of solo self-employment and its relation to precarious earnings and social security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recommendations for action include prioritizing policies that address the income instability and poverty risks faced by solo self-employed workers, such as expanding access to income and disability insurance programs.

Field: Welfare; Sociology; Poverty; Oppositional culture; Pejorative; Covert; McDonaldization; Social Welfare; Focus group; Social psychology
Title: Single Welfare Mothers' Resistance
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research finds that welfare mothers employ two types of resistance strategies: overt, such as oppositional culture, fighting the system, and maintaining control; and covert, including avoidance, withdrawal, and dissociation. These findings challenge negative policy constructions that attribute poverty to personal choices.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how welfare mothers resist negative constructions of their identities through overt and covert resistance strategies, focusing on 64 single welfare mothers in the United States from a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise their constructions of welfare recipients as personally responsible for poverty, instead recognizing the agency and resistance strategies of welfare mothers. By doing so, they can scale up support programs that address the systemic issues contributing to child poverty and income poverty, rather than perpetuating stigmatization.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Workforce development; Work experience; Disadvantaged; Job creation; Social enterprise; National database; Public relations
Title: The Business of Job Creation: An Examination of the Social Enterprise Approach to Workforce Development
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that WISEs are active in various industries such as food services, cleaning, and manufacturing, and provide jobs primarily in these sectors. The research also revealed that client-workers in WISEs earn higher wages and have better employment conditions compared to traditional workfare programs.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes a national database of Work Integration Social Enterprises (WISEs) in the United States to identify the industries and jobs associated with these employment-based poverty interventions, and explores the employment conditions for client-workers and the strategies WISEs take to add value to the work experience.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize funding for WISEs and scale up this model of workforce development to create more job opportunities for low-skill, disadvantaged workers, while also ensuring better employment conditions and wages to support their economic mobility.

Authors: Robert Bickel; Cynthia Smith; Teresa Hardman Eagle
Field: Primary education; Rural area; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Rural poverty; Academic achievement; Economic growth; Rural sociology; Operationalization
Title: Poor, rural neighborhoods and early school achievement
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor, rural West Virginia neighborhoods are not uniformly socially disorganized or culturally pernicious, but instead exhibit variation in their nature and can have positive effects on student achievement, such as strong community ties and social support networks.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of neighborhood effects on kindergarten children's academic performance in two rural counties in West Virginia using ethnographic data to operationalize the concept of 'neighborhood' and a contextual analysis to gauge neighborhood effects among kindergarten children in twelve randomly selected elementary schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize community-based interventions and invest in rural education infrastructure to support the unique needs of students living in poverty, rather than relying solely on consolidation and economies of scale.

Authors: David Becerra; Maria Gurrola; Cecilia Ayón; David Androff; Judy Krysik; Karen E. Gerdes; Loraine Moya-Salas; Elizabeth A. Segal
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Mexican adolescents; Sample (statistics); Social psychology; Acculturation
Title: Poverty and other factors affecting migration intentions among adolescents in Mexico
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that lower socioeconomic status was not a significant predictor of higher intentions to migrate to the United States to work, while higher levels of pre-migration acculturation were associated with higher intentions to migrate to the United States to live and work.
What_was_studied: This study surveyed 980 Mexican adolescents in Tijuana, Mexico, in February 2009 to understand the social and economic factors that impact migration intentions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at promoting education and cultural integration among adolescents in Tijuana can help reduce migration intentions and promote economic development in the region, prioritizing programs that address socioeconomic disparities and foster acculturation.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Sociology; Social exchange theory; Vulnerability; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Individual Development Account; Economic growth; Social engagement
Keywords: Asset-building; Capacity; Poverty; Social Exclusion/Inclusion; Vulnerability; Welfare
Title: Effects of Participating in an Asset-Building Intervention on Social Inclusion
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: A significant relationship between participating in an IDA program and social inclusion, with modest results providing a useful framework for examining factors that may affect an individual's capacity to move from vulnerability into enhanced economic, political, and social participation.
What_was_studied: A sample of Individual Development Account (IDA) program participants randomly assigned to a control and experimental group.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Asset-building programs should be prioritized as a key strategy to empower vulnerable individuals and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Nicola Horsley; Val Gillies; Rosalind Edwards
Field: Political science; Poverty; Economic growth; Austerity
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty and Social Justice
Title: ‘We’ve got a file on you’: problematising families in poverty in four periods of austerity
primary_category: Child poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The genealogy of the construction, positioning, and governance of poor families over time in this case may be observed in terms of three key shifts in problematisation: (i) from the identification of deservingness towards the assessment of risk; (ii) from a gendered concentration of parents to the perceived needs of children; and (iii) from consultation of authority figures to a reliance on increasingly ‘professionalised’ data capture tools.
What_was_studied: A genealogy of the micro acts of ruling that reveal the practice of constructing and governing of disadvantaged families in Britain, from the late 19th century to the early 21st century, using a case study analysis of materials recorded and collected by the Charity Organisation Society and its subsequent guises during four major periods of recession.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize addressing child poverty in rural areas, policymakers should scale up professionalized data capture tools and shift their focus from assessing the deservingness of parents to understanding the needs of children, with a gendered approach that considers the unique challenges faced by families in poverty.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize streamlining tax credit payments to ensure timely and accurate disbursements to recipients. This can be achieved by implementing a standardized payment system, providing detailed information about awards, and addressing overpayment reductions to mitigate financial instability and reduce poverty levels among working families.

Title: The Battering State: Towards a Political Economy of Domestic Violence

What_was_found: The analysis reveals that domestic violence is not only an individual problem but also an institutional one, shaped by the logic of state-economy relations and ‘family values’, resulting in structural inequality that disproportionately affects low-income and rural communities. The study finds that poverty and globalization exacerbate the issue, with the latter leading to increased economic instability and social isolation.
What_was_studied: This political economy analysis situates domestic violence within cultural-historical context to reveal the intersection between domestic violence and (1) the organization of the polity, (2) the arrangement of the economy, and (3) the dominant familial ideology expressed normatively through state policies in the US during a specific time period using primary data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing domestic violence as a systemic problem by scaling up programs that support low-income and rural communities, expanding access to healthcare and social services, and revising state policies that perpetuate ‘family values’ and reinforce gender inequality.
