What_was_studied: The All-Party Parliamentary Inquiry into Hunger in the United Kingdom examined hunger among school-age children and young people during the school holidays, with a focus on the relationship between hunger and free school meals (FSM) over approximately 170 non-school days per year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address holiday hunger, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to free school meals (FSM) during non-term time periods, potentially through partnerships with community organizations and businesses. This could involve funding for outreach programs and infrastructure development, as well as revisions to existing policies to ensure equitable distribution of resources.

Authors: Protus Akujah; Peter Koome; Wanjugu Wachira
Field: Dynamics (music); Geography; Integrated project delivery; Environmental planning; Sociology; Engineering; Project management; Pedagogy; Systems engineering
Journal/Venue: Journal of Poverty, Investment and Development
Title: Implementation Dynamics and Project Delivery: A Case Study of Tullow Oil Exploration in Turkana, Kenya
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that community stakeholder involvement had a statistically significant effect on project delivery (X2=8.161, df=1, p-value = .000 and p-value=.037 <.05 respectively).
What_was_studied: The study investigated the effect of community stakeholder involvement in the implementation process on project delivery by Tullow Oil Exploration Company in South Lokichar Basin, Turkana, Kenya, using a multistage sampling design and both qualitative and quantitative methods for data collection between 2013 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of effective stakeholder engagement in ensuring successful project delivery in resource extraction projects, particularly in marginalized areas. Therefore, policy makers should prioritize legal and regulatory frameworks that enhance stakeholder involvement in decision-making processes to mitigate risks, community resistance, and ensure easier execution of community projects.

Field: Gender studies; Welfare state; Racism; Sociology; Poverty; Cultural reproduction; Context (language use); Basic skills; Resistance (psychoanalysis); Demographic economics; Division of labour
Title: The Welfare State and the Cultural Reproduction of Gender: Making Good Girls and Boys in the Job Corps
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while job training for young African American women emphasized middle-class, homemaking skills, young men received training in the skilled trades, enabling them to challenge racial discrimination in the labor market but concentrating women's labor - paid and unpaid - in the realm of domestic status production and consumption.
What_was_studied: The study explores theoretical arguments about cultural reproduction and resistance in the context of the welfare state, focusing on an historical analysis of the Job Corps program during the War on Poverty (1964-1973) and its gendered effects on young men and women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the welfare state reproduces gender stratification structurally by replicating a gendered division of labor and culturally by inculcating an ideological framework that sustains that division of labor. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize programs that provide job training for young women in the skilled trades and revise existing programs to challenge gendered assumptions about work and domesticity.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Participant observation; Negotiation; Perception; African american; Interview data; Qualitative analysis; Low income; Social psychology
Title: Three-Block Fathers: Spatial Perceptions and Kin-Work in Low-Income African American Neighborhoods
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fathers delineate dangerous spaces and grow increasingly wary of certain social relationships based on their perceptions of ecological processes. Additionally, fathers develop kin-work strategies to secure paternal involvement, including constructing “three-block” safe spaces for family interaction, relying on paternal kin, making use of neutral spaces, and managing complex negotiations with their children's mothers and maternal kin.
What_was_studied: This qualitative analysis of participant observation and life history interview data on 40 low-income African American fathers in Chicago's South Side explores how risky physical and social spaces situate low-income fathers' participation in kin-work systems, with ecological processes—including gang activity, police presence, and poverty—shaping men's daily routines in local neighborhoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding that ecological processes shape fathers' daily routines in local neighborhoods, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up investments in community programs and resources that support paternal involvement, such as neutral spaces for family interaction, to enhance the well-being of low-income African American families living in high-risk environments.

Field: Pregnancy; Teenage pregnancy; Public health; Psychology; Environmental health; Sociology; Medicine; Nursing; Population; Biology; Genetics
Journal/Venue: Contemporary Social Problems in the UK
Title: Teenage pregnancy – a social problem or public health issue?
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that teenage pregnancy rates in the UK are the highest in Western Europe and second only to the US in the developed world, with significant negative consequences for the well-being of the mothers and their children, particularly those from marginalized backgrounds.
What_was_studied: Teenage pregnancy rates in the UK and its social, cultural, environmental, and health dimensions during a specific time period using quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of teenage pregnancy in the UK, there is an urgent need to scale up support services and resources for marginalized communities, expand existing programs to address intergenerational poverty, and prioritize comprehensive sexual health education to break the cycle of poverty and improve overall health outcomes.

Authors: Russell L. Curtis; Louis A. Zurcher
Field: Sociology; Poverty; Voluntary association; Perspective (graphical); Intervention (counseling); Social integration; Poverty level; Low income; Phenomenon; Social psychology
Title: Voluntary Associations and the Social Integration of the Poor
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that lower-class interaction patterns are largely contained within local, intimate settings such as families and immediate neighborhoods. Additionally, it was discovered that poverty intervention programs with self-help and self-direction emphases have a low likelihood of affiliation among low-income individuals.
What_was_studied: Studies of membership in voluntary associations were analyzed to determine the likelihood of affiliation among low-income individuals, specifically those at the poverty level, during a specific time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the low likelihood of affiliation among low-income individuals in poverty intervention programs, it is essential to prioritize program funding and scale existing initiatives that focus on affective rather than utilitarian orientation to increase engagement and improve outcomes for this population.

Field: Mental health; Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Recession; Social isolation; Safety net; Pride; Context (language use); Development economics; Social psychology
Title: Surviving the Great Recession: Growing Need and the Stigmatized Safety Net
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that individuals who lost their jobs experienced a sense of failure and ambivalence about utilizing social safety nets, leading to increased social isolation, self-esteem problems, and mental health issues. Additionally, the stigma associated with dependency exacerbated these issues.
What_was_studied: This qualitative research article looks at the experiences of low-income and poor families during the Great Recession, focusing on their challenges, survival strategies, and emotional wellbeing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long, slow recovery from the Great Recession, policymakers should prioritize expanding and improving social safety nets to address the material and emotional needs of vulnerable individuals and families. Scale-up successful programs that provide comprehensive support, such as job training and mental health services, to help these individuals regain their sense of purpose and dignity.

Field: Social exclusion; Developmental psychology; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Life course approach; Socialization; Adolescent health; Imprisonment; Social integration; Status attainment; Social psychology
Title: Incarceration and Intergenerational Social Exclusion
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 15% of youth are socially excluded, a prevalence similar to administrative estimates of severely 'disconnected' youth. The research combined the logic of a cumulative disadvantage theory and the status attainment paradigm with three waves of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) to examine the effects of father’s imprisonment on the social detainment and exclusion of children during the transition to adulthood.
What_was_studied: This article explores the intergenerational implications of parental incarceration, specifically the troubled transitions of children from adolescence to adulthood during the period of annual decreases in crime rates since the early 1990s, despite increased social exclusion of fathers through imprisonment and further exclusion of young adults through homelessness, health-care uninsurance, and political nonparticipation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the interconnected roles of father’s incarceration and intergenerational educational detainment in producing exclusionary outcomes for children in emerging adulthood, decision-makers should prioritize funding programs that address these issues, such as job training and education initiatives specifically targeting disadvantaged youth.

Authors: George J. Musa; Keely Cheslack-Postava; Connie Svob; Diana Hernández; Huilan Tang; Yuly Duque-Villa; William Keating; Lawrence Amsel; Michaeline Bresnahan; Megan Ryan; Andrea A. Baccarelli; Diddier Prada; Po Huang-Chiang; Christopher Jardines; Lupo Geronazzo-Alman; Renee D. Goodwin; Judith Wicks; Christina W. Hoven
Field: Welfare; Voucher; Mental health; Child psychopathology; Psychology; Social work; Subsidized housing; Public housing; Subsidy; Environmental health
Keywords: Child Psychopathology; Housing Subsidies; Housing Vouchers; Mental Health; Public Housing; Section 8
Title: Mental Health of High-Risk Urban Youth: The Housing Subsidies Paradox.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Adolescents in subsidized housing had more internalizing and externalizing symptoms than those in non-subsidized housing, after controlling for individual characteristics. This suggests that housing subsidies may have a positive impact on mental health outcomes among low-income urban youth.
What_was_studied: The association of housing subsidies with adolescent mental health outcomes among urban, low-income minority youth, using the Stress & Justice Study (S&J) baseline survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant association between housing subsidies and adolescent mental health, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to housing subsidies for low-income families and fund programs that improve the physical quality of the housing environment. This could involve increasing funding for public housing and Section 8 vouchers, as well as providing resources to improve the quality of existing housing stock.

Field: Social work; Psychology; Political science; Law
Title: Introduction to the Special Issue.
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Morton had concluded that Caucasians had larger brains, and therefore higher intellectual capacity, based on the measurement of the cranial capacities of skulls that Gould considered to be biased.
What_was_studied: In the late 1970s, Stephen Jay Gould reviewed the notes used by Samuel George Morton to support his 1839 classification of races and found what he considered to be serious methodological flaws.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Heated debates about the meaning of race, specifically whether it is a biological reality or socially constructed, continue to this day. Therefore, the government should prioritize further research into the nature and extent of group differences in health, taking into account the multifactorial causes and the potential for societal and biological interactions.

Field: Welfare; Functional illiteracy; Poverty; Underemployment; Unemployment; Development economics; Social issues; Developing country; Politics
Title: The Cost of Large Families and of Their Prevention, with Special Reference to Underdeveloped Countries
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that large families are associated with higher rates of poverty, unemployment, and illiteracy, as well as lower life expectancy and increased crime rates.
What_was_studied: The research focused on the relationship between large families and social problems such as poverty, unemployment, illiteracy, ill-health, and crime in a specific population over a particular time period using cross-sectional data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize family planning initiatives and invest in education, employment opportunities, and healthcare for individuals from large families to mitigate the negative impact of population growth on social problems.

Field: Social class; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Social policy; Social change; Population; Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic inequality
Title: Education, Jobs and Inequality: Functional and Conflict Models of Social Stratification in the United States.
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that the expansion of education cannot be explained by changing technical skill requirements of work, and that while inequality in educational attainment has been reduced for the population as a whole and between whites and nonwhites, this has not led to a reduction of economic inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines two competing interpretations of the relation between formal education and the occupational structure, and the dynamics of social stratification in the United States, using data from 1970 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The major implication of this study is that the relationship between education, jobs, and social inequality can be better understood in terms of class structure rather than assumed differences in the characteristics (marginal productivity) of individuals who interact within the constraints of that structure. Therefore, policy should focus on the structural determinants of inequality rather than on the education, training, or some other characteristic of individuals.

Field: Welfare; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Poverty; Diversity (business); Meaning (existential); Low income; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics); Economic growth; Term (time)
Title: The Measurement and Meaning of Poverty
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that caution is necessary when comparing poverty rates across studies using different measures, with measures based on low income and SES differing significantly from those based on welfare status and urban/gender demographics.
What_was_studied: This five-year panel study of a national sample measured poverty in sixteen different ways, comparing income-based, welfare status-based, and multidimensional measures of poverty across urban and gender demographics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these differences, policy makers should prioritize multidimensional measurements of poverty that incorporate both income and non-income factors to ensure a more comprehensive understanding of poverty and inform targeted interventions.

Authors: Kevin J. A. Thomas; Catherine Tucker
Field: Racism; Social work; Political science; Poverty; Recession; Child poverty; Great recession; Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Immigration; Race (biology)
Keywords: Children; Families; Immigration; Poverty; Race
Title: Child Poverty During the Years of the Great Recession: An Analysis of Racial Differences Among Immigrants and US Natives.
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the adverse effects of the recession were most intense in states with significant changes in their populations of Black and Latino immigrant children, and that declines in parental work opportunities were more consequential for poverty among Whites and Asians. Additionally, the analysis showed that family contexts had differential implications for child poverty among Black immigrant and natives during the recession, and that increases in racial child poverty disparities during the recession did not disappear in the years following the downturn.
What_was_studied: The consequences of the Great Recession on the economic experiences of children in the United States during the period 2007-2010, with a focus on immigrant status, racial inequality, and socioeconomic inequalities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the changing immigrant composition of the US child population, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the disproportionate impact of economic crises on vulnerable populations. Additionally, the findings suggest that addressing socioeconomic inequalities and family contexts is crucial to reducing child poverty disparities. Finally, the analysis highlights the need for ongoing monitoring and evaluation of policy interventions to ensure their effectiveness in mitigating the negative consequences of economic downturns.

Field: Sociology; Tax credit; Poverty; Earned income tax credit; Child tax credit; Child poverty; Earnings; Family life; Demographic economics; Tax law
Keywords: Child poverty; Family size; Racial equity; Tax credits
Title: The Efficacy of Cash Supports for Children by Race and Family Size: Understanding Disparities and Opportunities for Equity
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Black and Hispanic children in larger families face higher poverty risks compared to White children in larger families, and that the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and Child Tax Credit (CTC) do not reach a significant portion of these children, exacerbating racial disparities in child poverty.
What_was_studied: This analysis examines the intersectional aspects of disparity in the risk and incidence of poverty among children in the United States, focusing on the impact of larger family size on children's poverty rates, particularly for Black and Hispanic children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy action is needed to address both inequities by expanding access to the EITC and CTC for larger families, particularly those with Black and Hispanic children, and reforming policy structures that disproportionately exclude these families. Closing the poverty gap between larger and smaller families will not suffice; the racial gap in child poverty must also be tackled.

Field: Rural area; Contingency plan; Psychology; Donation; Relative deprivation; Needs assessment; Service personnel; Age cohorts; Public relations; Social Welfare; Gerontology
Title: The Reluctance of the Elderly to Accept Help.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the elderly are reluctant to admit need or accept help, and may even deny using services. They have devised their own model of services, with those perceived to have been earned or which require a donation being most acceptable, and those having a minimum income eligibility being least acceptable.
What_was_studied: This study examines the methodology of needs assessment for elderly individuals and identifies why they do not take advantage of existing programs and services, using 25 in-depth interviews and shorter interviews with clients and service personnel in senior centers, meal sites, and agencies over a certain time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is recommended that social protection policies should prioritize addressing relative deprivation and the social and economic history of age cohorts to increase the acceptance and utilization of existing programs and services for the elderly.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Ethnic group; Sociology; Social work; Poverty; Demographic economics; Shock (economics); Race (biology); Pandemic
Keywords: COVID-19; Child well-being; Families; Poverty; Race
Title: What the COVID-19 Pandemic Reveals about Racial Differences in Child Welfare and Child Well-Being: An Introduction to the Special Issue.
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Black and Latino children experienced higher rates of poverty and food insufficiency compared to white children after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with around three-fourths of these children experiencing poverty prior to the pandemic as well.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates racial/ethnic disparities in child well-being during the COVID-19 pandemic, using data from the United States between 2020 and 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to scale up support for low-income families, particularly Black and Latino families, by expanding social protection policies such as unemployment benefits and food assistance programs. Moreover, policymakers must prioritize addressing the systemic issues that have led to historical mistreatment of these families within the American welfare state.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Precarity
Title: Fired and Evicted: Istanbul Doorkeepers’ Strategies of Navigating Employment and Housing Precarity
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that doorkeepers experience simultaneous job loss and involuntary displacement due to earthquake risk-driven urban transformation, which highlights the interconnectedness of employment and housing market precarities.
What_was_studied: This study examines how doorkeepers in Istanbul navigate double precarity, i.e., the risk of being simultaneously fired and evicted, within the context of urban transformation and shifting policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address housing precarity among the urban working poor, policymakers should prioritize the integration of employment and housing policies, ensuring that precarious labor processes are taken into account in urban transformation plans to prevent simultaneous job loss and displacement.

Authors: David J. Brady; Andrew S. Fullerton; Jennifer Moren Cross
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Working poor; Generosity; Inequality; Probit model
Keywords: poverty; work; working poor; social policy; labor markets
Title: More Than Just Nickels and Dimes: A Cross-National Analysis of Working Poverty in Affluent Democracies
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analyses provide the least support for the economic performance explanation. There is modest support for unified theory as unionization reduces working poverty in some models. However, most of these effects appear to be mediated by welfare generosity. More substantial evidence exists for the demographic characteristics and welfare generosity explanations. An individual's likelihood of being working poor can be explained by (a) a lack of multiple earners or other adults in one's household, low education, single motherhood, having children and youth; and (b) the generosity of the welfare state in which he or she resides.
What_was_studied: Using the Luxembourg Income Study (2009), we analyzed whether an individual is working poor across 18 affluent democracies circa 2000, and if working poverty does not simply mirror overall poverty and there is greater cross-national variation in working than overall poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: We encourage a greater role for the welfare state in debates about working poverty. Welfare generosity does not undermine employment and reduces working poverty even among demographically vulnerable groups.

Field: Economy; Political economy; Economics; Human rights; Consolidation (business); Constitution; Garbage dump; Livelihood; Democracy; Informal sector; Politics
Title: Revolution in the Garbage Dump: The Political and Economic Foundations of the Colombian Recycler Movement, 1986-2011
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that neoliberalism and democratic consolidation created political opportunities for collective organizing, with technical support from NGOs, new human rights provisions, and privatization of waste management spurring recyclers to action.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the Colombian informal recycler movement between 1991 and 2018, focusing on how millions of workers mobilized for labor rights despite extreme marginality and state repression.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the millions of workers involved and the potential for innovative organizing models, policymakers should prioritize funding and supporting NGOs that work with informal recyclers, review and revise waste management policies to protect these workers' livelihoods, and scale up successful organizing strategies to other contexts.

Authors: Trina R. Williams Shanks; Stephanie C. Boddie; Robert Wynn
Field: Public economics; Business; Asset (economics); Earned income tax credit; Asset poverty; Estate planning; Socioeconomics; Community development; Real estate; Economic security; Risk pool
Title: Wealth Building in Communities of Color
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households of color have only 60% of the median wealth of white households, and that this gap is largely due to historically unequal access to resources and opportunities for asset accumulation. Specifically, the researchers found that Black and Hispanic families have significantly lower rates of homeownership, retirement accounts, and small business ownership than white families, which hinders their ability to build wealth.
What_was_studied: Racial disparities in wealth accumulation among communities of color in the United States during the 2010-2019 period using a combination of survey data and financial records.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long-lasting impact of these disparities on economic security and mobility, policymakers should prioritize implementing gap-closing methods that collectively address systemic barriers to asset accumulation in communities of color. Examples include scaling individual and collective strategies such as investing a portion of Earned Income Tax Credit refunds, Individual Development Accounts, and shared risk pools for insurance, housing cooperatives, and venture capital entities.

Field: Positive economics; Philosophy and economics; Economics; Portrait; Sophistication; Morality; Immediacy; Heterodox economics; Art history; Mainstream economics; Schools of economic thought
Title: Morality, Economics and the Market
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found vivid portrayals of working-class dwellings, ranging from ordinary to squalid conditions, highlighting the need for urban poverty policies that address hygiene and living conditions.
What_was_studied: Mid-nineteenth century fiction addressing social discontent and industrial society was analyzed, with a focus on the representation of urban poverty in novels like Mary Barton, North and South, Alton Locke, Sybil, and Felix Holt.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for urban renewal programs that focus on improving living conditions in low-income areas, as poor living conditions are a significant factor in health disparities.

Field: Welfare state; Racism; Economics; Human rights; Legislation; Public sphere; Racial integration; Public administration; Social stratification; Politics; Welfare; State (computer science); Civil rights; Political science; Law; Computer science; Algorithm
Title: Promoting civil rights through the welfare state: how Medicare integrated Southern hospitals.
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Medicare program played a crucial role in promoting racial integration in the healthcare system, with compliance rates being higher than in other institutional spheres. Additionally, the research revealed that the welfare state can promote racial equality when political resources are available to challenge discriminatory practices and when institutions that reproduce systems of oppression are incorporated into the public sphere.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the Civil Rights Act of 1964's impact on racial integration in the healthcare system and how the new Medicare program was leveraged to force compliance with the law, specifically in institutions such as employment and education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of leveraging government programs like Medicare to promote racial integration and equal access to healthcare. Policymakers should prioritize the allocation of resources to ensure continuous and universal benefits, challenge discriminatory practices, and incorporate institutions that perpetuate oppression into the public sphere to achieve racial equality.

Authors: George Wilson; Vincent J. Roscigno; Matt L. Huffman
Field: Public economics; Private sector; Racism; Public sector; American Community Survey; Economics; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Corporate governance; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Racial Income Inequality and Public Sector Privatization
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that new governance reforms have led to a significant erosion of relative racial parity in wages for African Americans compared to whites, particularly in public sector jobs. Additionally, the study finds that these changes have resulted in increased income poverty and child poverty for both men and women.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes wage trends and racial disparities in the public sector between 1979 and 2015 using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), Integrated Public Use Micro Sample (IPUMS), and American Community Survey (ACS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the escalation of discrimination as a core mechanism under new governance, policymakers should prioritize strategies to address income poverty and child poverty among African Americans in the public sector. This could include scaling up job training programs, expanding hiring initiatives for underrepresented groups, and revising hiring practices to reduce bias.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Social status; Sociology; Social reproduction; Cultural capital; Social science; Social mobility; Social transformation; Individual capital; Capital (economics)
Title: Black Cultural Capital, Status Positioning, and Schooling Conflicts for Low-Income African American Youth
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that low-income minority students must navigate and balance both dominant and non-dominant cultural capital within their academic and social lives, which has important implications for understanding how culture affects mobility prospects for marginalized communities.
What_was_studied: This article explores the interplay between dominant and non-dominant cultural capital in the lives of low-income African American students, using in-depth interviews with 44 participants to illustrate how they negotiate differential values placed by educators on these forms of capital.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize integrating non-dominant cultural capital into education access programs to better support low-income minority students' mobility prospects, and fund research on the interplay between dominant and non-dominant cultural capital in marginalized communities.

Field: Welfare; Distress; Sociology; Payment; Metropolitan area; Resource (biology); Aggregate data; Disadvantaged; Sample (statistics); Socioeconomics
Title: The Truly Disadvantaged, Public Assistance, and Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that areas with higher levels of welfare assistance had significantly less effect on crime rates compared to areas with lower levels of welfare assistance.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between welfare benefits and crime rates in a sample of large metropolitan counties in 1990.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in social protection programs to reduce poverty and improve economic conditions, as this can help mitigate the negative impact of resource deprivation on crime rates.

Field: Business; Household debt; Food insecurity; Demographic economics
Title: Household Debt and Children’s Risk of Food Insecurity
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate that medical debt increases odds of household food insecurity even after accounting for key sociodemographic and economic risk factors, while no relationship exists between other forms of unsecured debt and food insecurity. Moreover, although liquid assets decrease the risk of household food insecurity and attenuate the harmful effects associated with unpaid medical bills, few households have enough liquid assets to mitigate the risks associated with medical debt.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 2014 Child Development Supplement (CDS) of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), this study assesses whether unsecured debt, by amount and type of debt, is associated with food insecurity among lower-income households with children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Efforts to prevent medical debt may be essential for eliminating food insecurity among lower-income households with children. Policymakers should prioritize addressing medical debt through targeted programs and policies, such as expanding Medicaid eligibility and supporting community health clinics, to alleviate the financial burden of health care costs on these vulnerable families.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Cleavage (politics); Income Support; Pension; Elderly parents; Public support; Multilevel model
Title: Broad Reciprocity, Elderly Poverty, and the Retiree/Nonretiree Cleavage in the Demand for Public Retirement Income Support
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that higher levels of elderly poverty in a country lead to fewer divides between retirees and nonretirees in supporting public pension provision and spending increases.
What_was_studied: This article investigates cross-national variations in the retiree/nonretiree cleavage regarding pension policy preferences among 30 OECD countries over a 30-year period, using elderly poverty as a structural explanation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing elderly poverty to reduce cross-national variations in pension policy preferences and promote more equitable economic wellbeing for all ages.

Field: Criminal justice; Welfare state; Racism; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Underclass; Argument; Social issues; Criminology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: ISOLATION AND STIGMATIZATION IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF AN UNDERCLASS: THE CASE OF CHICANO GANGS IN EAST LOS ANGELES*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the underclass culture is capable of perpetuating itself without assistance from the white world, and that institutionalized racism operates in education, the job market, the housing market, and the criminal justice system. Additionally, the study discovered that differentiation within poor minority communities is a key factor in the development of deviant behaviors and the reabsorption of members of the underclass into a less deviant or stigmatized segment of the minority poor.
What_was_studied: This study examines the emergence of a predominantly minority urban underclass in American society, using a combination of two approaches: the culture of poverty and institutionalized racism. The research scope includes a case history of Chicano youth gangs, with data collected over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize community-based solutions that address differentiation within poor minority communities. Policymakers should scale up initiatives that focus on reabsorbing members of the underclass into a less deviant or stigmatized segment of the minority poor, and fund programs that target institutionalized racism in education, employment, housing, and criminal justice.

Authors: Colleen Heflin; Rajeev Darolia; Sharon Kukla-Acevedo
Field: Psychology; Educational attainment; Food insecurity; Environmental health
Title: Exposure to Food Insecurity During Adolescence and Educational Attainment
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that exposure to food insecurity during adolescence predicts lower levels of educational attainment by reducing college attendance.
What_was_studied: This study examines the association between food insecurity during adolescence and educational attainment using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics Transition to Adulthood Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the established negative consequences of food insecurity on health and cognitive development in early childhood, this study highlights the need to scale up support for families struggling with food insecurity during adolescence. Policymakers should prioritize interventions that address food insecurity among adolescents, such as expanding school meal programs and increasing access to nutrition education.

Field: Gross domestic product; Political science; Poverty; Human Development Index; Universal Primary Education; Human development (humanity); Child mortality; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Sustainability
Title: Global Human Development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that achieving the MDGs resulted in a significant reduction in extreme poverty and hunger, with 1.1 billion people lifted out of poverty between 1990 and 2015. Additionally, primary education became universal in 84 countries, and maternal mortality rates declined by 47%.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and their effect on chronic poverty in developing countries from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize the achievement of the MDGs in order to scale up poverty reduction efforts, expand access to education and healthcare, fund sustainable development programs, and revise policies that hinder progress towards these goals.

Authors: Martha R. Burt; Barbara E. Cohen
Field: Criminal justice; Psychology; Mental illness; Marital status; Population; Personal problems; Probability sampling; Descriptive statistics; Gerontology; Race (biology)
Title: Differences among Homeless Single Women, Women with Children, and Single Men
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that homeless single women, homeless women with children, and homeless men differ significantly on many variables, such as demographic characteristics, length of current spells of homelessness and joblessness, income and income sources, history of personal problems, patterns of utilization of soup kitchens and shelters, and diet adequacy.
What_was_studied: This article presents descriptive data for homeless single women and women with children, and contrasts it to parallel data for single homeless men, using probability sampling and in-person interviews from the first national study of homeless individuals in U.S. cities of 100,000 or more during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant differences found between homeless single women, homeless women with children, and homeless men, policymakers should prioritize gender-sensitive and family-focused interventions to address the root causes of homelessness among these populations, such as inadequate income and education, mental illness, chemical dependency, and criminal justice involvement.

Authors: Michael L. Benson; John Wooldredge; Amy Thistlethwaite; Greer Litton Fox
Field: Racism; Demography; Human factors and ergonomics; Injury prevention; Geography; Social disorganization theory; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Race (biology)
Title: The correlation between race and domestic violence is confounded with community context
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the apparent correlation between race and domestic violence is confounded with the different ecological contexts typically occupied by African Americans and whites. When comparing similar ecological contexts, the correlation between race and domestic violence is reduced or disappears altogether. Additionally, individual-level risk factors for domestic violence appear to operate similarly for both African Americans and whites.
What_was_studied: Using data from wave 2 of the National Survey of Families and Households and the 1990 U.S. census, this study examines why African Americans appear to have a higher likelihood of engaging in domestic violence than whites, drawing on insights from social disorganization theory and recent research on urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing urban poverty and its related social disorganization factors to reduce domestic violence rates among all populations. By targeting resources towards community-based programs that foster social cohesion and provide support for families in need, we can scale up effective interventions to address this critical issue.

Field: Economy; Consumption (economics); Economics; Natural resource economics; Economic impact analysis; Environmental degradation; Carbon tax; Energy consumption; Greenhouse gas; Social stratification; Energy subsidies
Title: Social Stratification and Environmental Degradation: Understanding Household CO2 Production
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that variation in energy use and carbon emissions among households can be accounted for by social class and life cycle differences in housing, appliances, travel, and lifestyle, with regressive effects of carbon taxes on low- and moderate-income households.
What_was_studied: This analysis explores the social origins of one consumption-based environmental problem (greenhouse gas emissions) in California households and considers the social impact of carbon tax proposals aimed at slowing global warming, using data on household-level energy consumption.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the regressive effects of carbon taxes on low- and moderate-income households, policy makers should prioritize equitably increasing the efficiency of housing and household technology, reshaping residential settlement patterns, and fundamentally improving the transportation system in the United States to address the social origins of consumption-based environmental problems.

Field: Welfare; General Social Survey; Government; Economics; Poverty; Position (finance); Economic hardship; Formative assessment; Development economics; Economic growth; Panel data
Title: The Formative Years, Economic Hardship, and Beliefs about the Government’s Role in Lessening Poverty
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that experiences during late adolescence, increases in macro-level economic hardship, and increases in individual hardship all influence support for government efforts to lessen poverty; however, current objective and subjective economic position is particularly important. Moreover, the study found variation in support across different types of government responses to poverty.
What_was_studied: Using both cross-sectional and panel data from the General Social Survey to examine how past experiences shape an individual's belief about what the government should do about poverty, as well as changes in micro and macroeconomic hardship, between 2008 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing current economic hardship and its impact on public opinion to effectively implement antipoverty policies.

Field: Economics; Unemployment; Middle class; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Economic expansion; Resentment; Inflation; Differential (mechanical device); Politics
Title: Inflation and Social Structure: The United States in an Epoch of Declining Abundance
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economically marginal groups and the middle class are more likely to bear the burden of unemployment, inflation, and decreased economic expansion rates compared to the upper classes. Additionally, the research revealed a likelihood of tensions and conflicts arising due to the differential distribution of economic burdens, which may lead to social resentments and hostilities.
What_was_studied: This analysis focuses on the market situations of the upper classes, the middle class, and some economically marginal groups during a specific time period, using primary data sources such as surveys and government records to answer questions about which groups are most apt to bear the burden of unemployment, inflation, and decreases in economic expansion rates, as well as potential social tensions and responses from domestic and international entities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize policies that address the needs of economically marginal groups and the middle class, such as expanding job training programs, increasing minimum wage, and scaling up social safety nets. By taking these actions, decision-makers can mitigate the negative impacts of economic downturns on vulnerable populations and reduce the likelihood of social unrest.

Field: Sociology; Class (computer programming); Meaning-making; Social psychology
Title: “Sometimes you have to pop them”: Conflict and Meaning-Making in a Parenting Class
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant differences between the frame used by instructors (discouraging all forms of force) and that of parents (who saw force as sometimes necessary and effective), highlighting the importance of considering context and meaning making in anti-poverty interventions.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study examines the tensions between parents and instructors over the use of physical force in disciplining children or in resolving conflicts more broadly among low-income African American mothers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of parenting education programs in addressing childhood poverty, this study's findings suggest that anti-poverty interventions should prioritize understanding the cultural frames that shape parents' and instructors' perspectives on discipline and conflict resolution. By doing so, these interventions can be more effective in addressing the root causes of childhood poverty.

Authors: Harriet B. Presser; Linda S. Salsberg
Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Developed country; Family planning; Population; Birth rate; Fertility
Title: Public Assistance and Early Family Formation is There a Pronatalist Effect
primary_category: Asset poverty
What_was_found: Women in households receiving public assistance desired fewer children than those in non-recipient households.
What_was_studied: The relationship between public assistance and fertility was examined, focusing on the time of early family formation among a representative sample of New York City women who recently had their first child, with interviews conducted twice since their first birth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that untimely births are a significant predictor of public assistance receipt, policymakers should prioritize expanding family planning services and education for low-income women to avoid unintended pregnancies and reduce reliance on public assistance.

Field: Welfare; Sociology; Poverty; Punishment; Prison; Criminology
Title: The Runaround: Punishment, Welfare, and Poverty Survival after Prison
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Formerly-incarcerated men must repeatedly engage with parole, public assistance agencies, transitional housing facilities, and community-based service providers to maintain freedom and access food, shelter, and rehabilitative services. Accessing resources requires the men simultaneously to manage multiple, overlapping entanglements across a fragmented network of bureaucracies.
What_was_studied: Based on 17 months of ethnographic fieldwork and 45 in-depth interviews with formerly-incarcerated men, this article explores how former prisoners navigate criminal justice and welfare bureaucracies in their daily lives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize streamlining and integrating criminal justice and welfare bureaucracies to reduce the 'runaround' effect, which exacerbates poverty, breeds distrust of state authorities, and can precipitate recidivism. Policymakers should scale up support for transitional housing facilities and community-based service providers to help formerly-incarcerated men access resources and achieve long-term economic security.

Field: Higher education; Feeling; Labour economics; Economics; Job satisfaction; Underemployment; Overqualification; Job dissatisfaction; Job involvement; Occupational prestige
Title: THE HUMAN EFFECTS OF UNDEREMPLOYMENT
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that higher education produces increased job dissatisfaction, higher turnover rates, reduced job involvement, impaired co-worker relations, and more emphasis on future aspirations among clerical workers. However, workers of all educational backgrounds are prone to feelings of overqualification and complaints about the nature of workplace control.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effects of underemployment on 32 low-level clerical workers, comparing their educational backgrounds with their attitudes and behaviors during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize education-to-workplace gap interventions to address the issue of underemployment. This includes scaling up job training programs that align with workers' educational backgrounds and providing career counseling services to help workers find more fulfilling jobs that match their skills and aspirations.

Title: Fifty Years Later: From a War on Poverty to a War on the Poor

What_was_found: Poverty was found to be a major social problem facing a relatively affluent America in the late 1950s and early 1960s, with 37 million Americans living in poverty at the time.
What_was_studied: Photographs of poor families taken in rural Appalachia and writings of The New York Times journalist Homer Bigart and seminal books by scholars Michael Harrington and John Galbraith.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for policies that expand opportunities and increase income for those living in poverty, such as investing in education and job training programs, improving access to healthcare, and implementing anti-poverty initiatives in rural and urban areas.

Title: Poverty and Political Movements

What_was_found: The study found a strong linear and positive relationship between short-term changes for the worse in one’s economic conditions and Social Credit support, with unemployment in particular showing a strong positive relationship to support for this political movement. These findings suggest that Soical Credit received disproportionate support from the lower classes, particularly the poor.
What_was_studied: The analysis of the rise of the Social Credit party in Quebec in the federal election of 1962 examined how short-term changes for the worse in one’s economic conditions affect support for this political movement, specifically looking at unemployment within respondents' families.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between economic hardship and support for Social Credit, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and implementing policies that protect the vulnerable to mitigate the appeal of protest movements like Social Credit.

Authors: R. Richard Ritti; Drew W. Hyman
Field: Welfare; Product (category theory); Economics; Poverty; Prosperity; Administration (government); Cheating; Unemployment; Development economics; Economic growth; Politics
Title: The Administration of Poverty: Lessons From The “Welfare Explosion” 1967-1973

What_was_found: The study found that the public assistance caseload increased significantly during this time period, despite low unemployment rates and record economic prosperity, and rejected popular explanations for the growth in the caseload such as mismanagement and welfare cheating.
What_was_studied: The public assistance caseload during the late 1960s, a period of economic prosperity and low unemployment in Pennsylvania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a redefinition of the product offered by the Department of Public Welfare and consider the political environment to address chronic poverty and asset poverty among recipients.

Title: Contradictions in the Gender Subtext of the War on Poverty: The Community Work and Resistance of Women from Low Income Communities
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study shows that community workers challenged narrow interpretations of community needs, bureaucratic organization, and a limited definition of labor, revealing contradictions in state-sponsored employment for low-income women.
What_was_studied: The article assesses the community-based work of low-income women hired by the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 anti-poverty programs and reveals how gendered assumptions, gender-differentiated policies, and the gender division of labor shape state organization and can be resisted.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of current state provisions, urban poverty policies should prioritize funding community-based projects that empower women from low-income neighborhoods to challenge gendered assumptions and bureaucratic organization to address chronic poverty.

What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between housing insecurity and employment instability among predominantly low-income working renters in the United States, using novel survey data collected over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives promoting housing stability to mitigate employment instability and support low-income working renters.

Title: The Psychological Cost of Market Transition: Mental Health Disparities in Reform-Era China
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals whose personal conditions expose them more to the risks and uncertainty brought about by market reform, such as self-employed workers, are more likely to suffer from psychological distress. By contrast, residents in more marketized areas tend to feel more satisfied with their economic conditions and therefore have lower levels of distress.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed survey data collected from a national sample of 3,443 Chinese urban residents in 2005 to investigate the effects of employment conditions, political affiliation, and regional level of marketization on self-reported symptoms of psychological distress during China's post-1978 economic reform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the reduced social protection resulting from China's economic reform contributes to an elevated level of psychological distress. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize revamping social welfare policies to better protect individuals experiencing market-related stress and uncertainty.

What_was_found: The study found that these women have agency in mediating the effects of poverty through alternative family patterns and active roles, suggesting the viability of non-nuclear family arrangements as a strategy for reducing child poverty.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support these women's agency and foster their alternative family patterns to scale up successful strategies for reducing child poverty, particularly in the Southeastern United States.

Authors: Candace Kruttschnitt; Jane D. McLeod; Maude Dornfeld

Title: The Economic Environment of Child Abuse

What_was_found: The results indicate that persistent poverty has no significant effect on the severity of abuse and the observed relationship between current poverty and severity is eliminated once race is controlled. Moreover, while poverty persistence is significantly related to recurrent abuse, virtually all of this effect appears to be explained by factors associated with the stress of economic deprivation.
What_was_studied: The study examined whether poverty persistence is a significant predictor of both severe and recurrent child abuse among 185 substantiated cases of physically abused youth, controlling for the dynamic nature of both experiences over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty persistence has no significant effect on the severity of child abuse and the observed relationship between current poverty and severity is eliminated once race is controlled, policymakers should prioritize addressing the stress of economic deprivation to mitigate recurrent abuse among vulnerable populations.

Field: Gender studies; Social movement; Sociology; Ethnography; Participant observation; Power (social and political); Tent city; Population; Low income; Poor people
Title: The Power of the People: Homeless Protesters in the Aftermath of Social Movement Participation

What_was_found: The study found that local social movements can have a significant impact on low-income people's access to material and non-material resources, with participants reporting improved well-being and increased engagement in advocacy efforts.
What_was_studied: An ethnographic study based on interviews and participant observation with street people three years after a 'tent city' protest was conducted to analyze the impact on homeless participants and examine differences and similarities between poor people's movements and middle-class movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and support for local social movements that empower marginalized communities, particularly those focused on gender and poverty issues, to improve access to resources and address systemic inequalities.

Field: Cultural diversity; Ethnic group; Sociology; Social comparison theory; Social support; Population; Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Multilevel model; Social Welfare; Gerontology

Title: To Compare is to Despair? A Population-Wide Study of Neighborhood Composition and Suicide in Stockholm.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that suicide risk increases with the level of affluence in one's neighborhood, particularly among individuals with low income. Additionally, social welfare recipients are less likely to commit suicide when there are other social welfare recipients in the neighborhood, and suicide risk among immigrants decreases with the proportion of co-ethnics in the neighborhood.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between neighborhood context and socio-demographic attributes on suicide risk using a population-based dataset of all adults living in the greater Stockholm area in the 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing income inequality and ensuring that ethnic minorities have access to social support networks within their neighborhoods to prevent suicide risk.

Field: Social exclusion; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Unemployment; Spatial inequality; Inequality; Development economics; Urban planning; Social issues
Title: Inequalities in European cities
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there has been a significant increase in social and spatial inequality within and between European cities, with poverty, unemployment, and social exclusion on the rise, particularly in declining city and especially inner-city areas. These trends have been driven by recent economic and labor market changes, reinforcing social and spatial divisions.
What_was_studied: This chapter examines the evidence that European cities are becoming more unequal and more socially and spatially segregated and divided, focusing on the growth of inequality, poverty, unemployment, and social exclusion in European cities and the increasing concentration of social problems in poor neighborhoods within cities throughout Europe during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, urban and social policy should prioritize addressing growing social and spatial inequality within and between European cities, including revitalizing declining city and especially inner-city areas while also tackling the underlying causes of poverty, unemployment, and social exclusion. This may involve scaling up successful interventions, expanding access to affordable housing and education, and funding targeted programs to support vulnerable populations.

Authors: Simon Outram; Joseph L. Graves; Jill Powell; Chantelle Wolpert; Kerry L. Haynie; Morris W. Foster; Jessica W. Blanchard; Anna Hoffmeyer; Robert P. Agans; Charmaine D.M. Royal

Title: Genes, Race, and Causation: US Public Perspectives About Racial Difference

What_was_found: The study found that perceived genetic factors were more commonly attributed to general ability among Whites and older respondents, while education was a significant factor in decreasing such views. Additionally, non-White respondents and those of lower socioeconomic status were more likely to believe that general abilities are determined by race.
What_was_studied: This nationally representative survey of the US population investigated how perceptions of ability, athleticism, and intellect are linked to racial categories and whether such perceptions contribute to health inequities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between racial and genetic determinism and health inequities, policy makers should prioritize education and public awareness initiatives targeting these populations to challenge such views and promote social interventions that address systemic barriers to equitable access to healthcare.

Authors: Anne M. Santiago; Margaret G. Wilder
Field: Labour economics; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Suburbanization; Residence; Educational attainment; Latino Population; Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Economic restructuring
Title: Residential Segregation and Links to Minority Poverty: The Case of Latinos in the United States
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that residence in more segregated metropolitan areas was a significant predictor of Latino poverty but not of Latino/Anglo income inequality. Changes in local labor market conditions had little effect on Latino poverty and income inequality, but changing Latino labor force characteristics—particularly increasing educational attainment, declining male labor force participation, and rising female labor force participation—were associated with decreases in poverty and reductions in income inequality. Residence in the Northeast was the most significant predictor of Latino poverty and income inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between residential segregation and rising Latino poverty and income inequality between 1970 and 1980 in 58 metropolitan areas with populations of 25,000 or more Latinos in 1980, using multivariate analysis to assess the effects of increasing and high levels of Latino/Anglo segregation on concentration in inner-city poverty areas, changes in local labor market conditions, and changing Latino labor force characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between residence in more segregated metropolitan areas and increased Latino poverty, urban poverty reduction policies should prioritize integrating Latino communities into less segregated neighborhoods and expanding access to affordable housing. Policymakers should also revise labor market training programs to better address the growing educational attainment of Latinos and reduce gender disparities in employment.

Title: Generating Labor Market Inequality: Employment Opportunities and the Accumulation of Disadvantage
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Inner city mothers and fathers experienced greater employment instability and accumulated large work experience deficits compared to parents nationally, with Black and Puerto Rican men, and Hispanic women experiencing the greatest deficits. Cumulative work experience and education significantly influenced labor market success, with higher employment returns to work experience among minority compared to non-minority men.
What_was_studied: The Urban Poverty and Family Life Survey of Chicago was analyzed to examine race and ethnic differentials in the accumulation of labor market experience over the life course of inner city men and women from 1980 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between cumulative work experience and labor market success, urban poverty reduction strategies should prioritize job training programs and workforce development initiatives targeting inner city minority parents, particularly Black and Puerto Rican men, and Hispanic women, to address their experience deficits and improve their long-term employment prospects.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Public policy; Sociology; Work ethic; Social work; Social policy; Welfare reform; Middle class; Social stratification; Economic growth
Title: How Suburban Families View the Work Orientations of the Welfare Poor: Problems in Social Stratification and Social Policy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that middle-class respondents drew sharp distinctions between themselves and lower-class welfare recipients, with the latter exhibiting less confidence in themselves and greater acceptance of welfare. However, the study also discovered that middle-class respondents mistakenly deny the strong work ethic among the poor, fundamentally misunderstand how high work ethic leads to increased feelings of insecurity, and project for the poor a strong identification of welfare income with income from quasi-illegal sources. These misperceptions support so-called welfare reform emphasizing a strong work requirement and below-poverty level base payments.
What_was_studied: This study examines how middle-class suburbanites perceive the work ethic of lower-class welfare recipients in comparison to their own work orientations, using a mixed-methods approach with 40 interviews and 120 survey responses from adults and teenagers across two urban and two suburban locations in the United States over a six-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should revise welfare reform policies to prioritize social protection programs that address the root causes of poverty, rather than perpetuating stigmatization and misperceptions about the poor's work ethic. By scaling up such programs, we can help reduce chronic poverty, improve education access, and address intersectional poverty.

Title: At the Crossroads and in the Crosshairs: Social Welfare Policy and Low-Income Women's Vulnerability to Domestic Violence

What_was_found: The analysis found that some policies provided protection and security to participants at the expense of others, exacerbating the risk of further abuse for some individuals. However, frontline workers played an important role in mitigating this risk.
What_was_studied: The study explores the impact of abused mothers' interactions with an array of social welfare policy systems on their ability to protect themselves and their children from domestic violence, using ethnographic data collected over a 5-year period in low-income communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding support services and security measures for vulnerable families, while also scaling up training programs for frontline workers to better address the complex needs of abused mothers and their children.

Title: The Unequal Weight of Discrimination: Gender, Body Size, and Income Inequality
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that very obese men face one form of discrimination—statistical discrimination—but that they can overcome initial disadvantages with time. In contrast, obese women's income disadvantages persist over time, suggesting the presence of prejudicial discrimination.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1997–2008 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY97), this study examines how gender interacts with body size to determine income inequalities between obese and nonobese workers, posing two questions: first, is anti-obesity discrimination to blame for income inequalities between obese and nonobese workers? Second, do women and men's experiences of those inequalities differ?.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding of persistent income inequalities between obese and nonobese workers, policymakers should scale funding for weight-related health disparities research and expand support for anti-discrimination policies to protect obese individuals from prejudicial treatment in hiring practices. By prioritizing these measures, we can revise our understanding of how social inequality operates through body size and ultimately reduce income poverty.

Authors: John R. Reynolds; Catherine E. Ross

Title: Social Stratification and Health: Education's Benefit Beyond Economic Status and Social Origins
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that education is one of the strongest predictors of both physical and psychological well-being in both surveys, with positive effects on well-being beyond the access it provides to privileged positions in the economy and higher incomes. Respondents from high and low statuses benefited from more years of education.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1987-1988 National Survey of Families and Households and the 1995 Aging, Status, and the Sense of Control Survey, this study investigates the intergenerational processes by which socioeconomic origins affect adult physical and psychological well-being, comparing the effects of social origins, education, work, and economic status on well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of education in intergenerational socioeconomic mobility and well-being, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to quality education for all, particularly for those from low status backgrounds, to scale up economic opportunities and improve public health outcomes.

Authors: Jennifer L. Lawless; Richard L. Fox

Title: Political Participation of the Urban Poor
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our data revealed two central findings: First, material resources and demographic attributes associated with political participation drove activism even among urban poor respondents. Second, severe economic hardship and formative contact with government agents bolstered the willingness to participate in the political system.
What_was_studied: The political participation of impoverished citizens in one of the poorest congressional districts in the country between 2019 and 2022, using a sample of 462 low-income men and women and combining quantitative and qualitative methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that material resources and government agent interactions affect political participation, decision-makers should scale up social protection programs and fund initiatives that address urban poverty's multidimensional nature. By expanding access to education, healthcare, and employment opportunities while improving government accountability through community outreach and grievance mechanisms, policymakers can boost the political activism and participation of impoverished citizens.

What_was_studied: This chapter synthesizes research on risk factors associated with academic problems for a specific population of students in a given time period using quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up comprehensive mentoring programs to enhance academic outcomes for at-risk students.
