PHQ scores also decreased, although not significantly.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the influence of a community health worker (CHW) diabetes lifestyle intervention on mental health outcomes for African Americans and Hispanics with Type 2 diabetes, collecting data from 164 participants over a 6-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact on mental health outcomes, policymakers should prioritize funding for CHW-led diabetes interventions targeting African Americans and Hispanics with Type 2 diabetes. Such interventions can not only improve glycemic control but also address mental health disparities in these communities.

Authors: Kenneth C. W. Kammeyer; Norman R. Yetman; McKee J. McClendon
Field: Social class; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Geography; Family planning; Population; Birth rate; Socioeconomics; Total fertility rate; Economic growth; Fertility
Title: Family Planning Services and the Distribution of Black Americans
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the percentage of the county population that was black was most highly correlated with the availability of family planning services, even after controlling for poverty, fertility, urbanism, and region. This suggests that underlying racism may have influenced the decision to make family planning services available in U.S. counties.
What_was_studied: Availability of family planning services in U.S. counties during 1968, with a focus on the relationship between service availability and county-level poverty, fertility, urbanism, and racial composition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent disparities in health outcomes between black and white Americans, it is crucial that we prioritize scaling up access to family planning services in areas with high percentages of black populations, particularly in low-income communities.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Ideology; Political socialization; Relation (history of concept); Political system; Style (sociolinguistics); Poison control; Social science; Social issues; Politics
Title: SOCIAL DEVIANCE AND POLITICAL MARGINALITY: TOWARD A REDEFINITION OF THE RELATION BETWEEN SOCIOLOGY AND POLITICS
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that there has been an increase in the use of violence as a political tactic and the development of a revolutionary potential among deviant sub-groups, with marginalized communities at the intersection of poverty and social exclusion being disproportionately affected.
What_was_studied: The study examined the relationship between social deviance and political marginality in the context of intersectional poverty among different sub-groups from 2015 to 2020 using a mixed-methods approach involving surveys, interviews, and content analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is essential to prioritize and scale up support for marginalized communities, revise existing policies to address the root causes of political marginality and violence, and expand data collection and analysis to better understand the intersections between social deviance and political marginality in order to inform targeted interventions.

Authors: Richard Williams; Reynold F. Nesiba; Eileen Diaz McConnell
Field: Debt; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Loan; Competition (economics); Consumer protection; Restructuring; Inequality; Real estate
Title: The Changing Face of Inequality in Home Mortgage Lending
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while minority and low-income groups have made record high gains in homeownership, they are often faced with less favorable loan terms, problematic housing, and a lack of adequate consumer protection from predatory practices, indicating a new inequality in home mortgage lending.
What_was_studied: American homeownership trends from 1993 to 2000, with a focus on subprime and manufactured housing lending in U.S. MSAs and how it relates to racial, ethnic, and geographic inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening consumer protections and ensuring equitable access to affordable housing and credit for all communities, particularly for those who have historically been disadvantaged.

Field: Distress; Dominance (economics); Sociology; Spite; Poverty; Single group; Latino a; Social science; Demographic economics
Title: Urban Hispanic Poverty: Disaggregations and Explanations
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that treating Latinos as a single group is an unsatisfactory approach to analysis, and that disaggregation by group is crucial for interpreting trends in relevant indicators of distress. Additionally, the study highlighted the importance of considering the peculiarities of the processes under which these groups have entered U.S. society when analyzing poverty trends.
What_was_studied: This article examines Hispanic (Latino) poverty in the United States, specifically focusing on its understudy and misunderstanding despite its growing incidence, and how it has received relatively little scholarly attention due to data deficiencies and a dominant focus on black poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing incidence of Hispanic poverty and its unique characteristics, policymakers should prioritize more comprehensive data collection and analysis, as well as targeted policies that acknowledge the differences within the Latino community. By doing so, they can better address the needs of this population and make strides towards reducing poverty rates.

Field: Actuarial science; Economics; Human factors and ergonomics; Injury prevention; Unemployment; Aggregate (data warehouse); Future studies; Poison control; Research evidence; Demographic economics; Suicide prevention
Title: Rates of Crime and Unemployment: An Analysis of Aggregate Research Evidence
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found a consistent and significant positive correlation between property crimes and unemployment during the 1970s, with sub-national levels of aggregation yielding the strongest results. The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize job creation programs and targeted crime prevention strategies in areas with high unemployment rates to address property crimes.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the relationship between unemployment and crime rates across various populations, time periods, and data sources, finding a conditional positive correlation that varies depending on the type of crime and the level of aggregation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the consistent positive correlation between unemployment and property crimes, policymakers should scale up job creation programs and fund targeted crime prevention initiatives in regions with high unemployment rates to reduce property crime rates.

Field: Conformity; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Ideology; Poverty; Elite; Power structure; Criminology; Politics; Deviance (sociology)
Title: The Poverty of the Sociology of Deviance: Nuts, Sluts, and Preverts
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite efforts to show that 'deviants' are not fundamentally different from others, the emphasis on their identity and subculture may defeat this aim. Additionally, certain forms of deviance, especially by the economic and political elite, are often neglected in sociological analyses.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the sociology of deviance in three theoretical and ideological biases: (1) emphasis on the 'deviant' identity and subculture, (2) neglect of certain forms of deviance by the economic and political elite, and (3) lack of exploration of power dynamics in the designation of deviance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these biases, policymakers should prioritize exploring power dynamics in poverty designation and addressing economic and political elite deviance to scale up effective interventions for income poverty.

Field: Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Social policy; Alliance; Material resources; Policy outcomes; Public administration; Politics
Title: When Framing Fails: Ideas, Influence, and Resources in San Francisco's Homeless Policy Field
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the center and left of the policy field shared common diagnostic and solution-oriented prognostic framings, the right possessed superior material resources and political influence, leading to internal divisions and amplified differences in tactical prognostic framings.
What_was_studied: This case study examines the homeless policy field in San Francisco, focusing on how actors' shared framings of homelessness did not lead to cooperative alliances or coherent policies due to differences in tactical prognostic framings and material resources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the importance of considering material resources and political influence when analyzing shared framings in policy fields. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these disparities to create more cohesive and effective policies for addressing homelessness.

Field: Developed country; Geography; Population; Low income; Development economics; Social issues; World population; Population growth; Politics
Title: Recent Trends and Perspectives in World Population Growth
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the population growth rate in low-income pre-industrial countries is higher than previously thought, with more than two-thirds of the total world population living in these areas, and widening economic and social disparities between these regions and economically advanced countries.
What_was_studied: The research examines population trends and their economic and social implications, specifically the accelerating population growth in low-income pre-industrial countries over a particular time period using certain data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for sustainable development programs in low-income pre-industrial countries to scale up economic opportunities and address the widening gap in living standards between these regions and economically advanced countries.

Authors: Kenneth J. Neubeck; Jack L. Roach
Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Welfare reform; Income maintenance; Distribution (economics); Capitalism; Politics
Title: INCOME MAINTENANCE EXPERIMENTS, POLITICS, AND THE PERPETUATION OF POVERTY
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that a national guaranteed income program for the poor may not be effective in reducing poverty due to systemic obstacles such as discrimination and lack of access to resources and opportunities.
What_was_studied: The study examines a series of large-scale government-sponsored income maintenance experiments and their background, general design, and basic findings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing these systemic issues through targeted policies and programs that provide equitable access to resources and opportunities for all individuals, particularly those in poverty.

Field: Ethnic group; Demography; Poverty; Geography; Cumulative Exposure; Neighborhood poverty; Inequality; White (horse)
Title: Racial and Ethnic Inequality in the Duration of Children's Exposure to Neighborhood Poverty and Affluence
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The average black child can spend about 50 percent of her first 18 years in neighborhoods with poverty rates in excess of 20 percent, while the corresponding figures for Latino and white children are about 40 percent and 5 percent, respectively.
What_was_studied: The study estimates racial and ethnic inequality in the amount of time children can expect to live in poor and nonpoor neighborhoods throughout childhood using data from the early-to mid-1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing black/white differences in childhood exposure to neighborhood poverty by increasing access to affordable housing in low-poverty neighborhoods and implementing policies that reduce residential segregation.

Authors: Eleanor P. Wolf; Charles N. Lebeaux
Field: Ethnic group; Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Social policy; Slum; Relocation; Slum clearance; Social life; Poor people; Economic growth
Title: On the Destruction of Poor Neighborhoods by Urban Renewal
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that residents in the low-income Negro neighborhood had substantially less sentimental attachment to their homes and neighborhood compared to previous studies in 'old-style ethnic' areas. Additionally, the study revealed that most 'slum clearance' now occurs in these low-income Negro neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: A study examining the impact of slum clearance on urban renewal in low-income Negro neighborhoods, using data from a Detroit case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers must prioritize adequate rehousing programs for low-income households dislodged by urban renewal projects, as current national programs have not been enacted, to address the issue of housing insecurity and poverty in these communities.

Field: Psychology; Personality; Degree (music); Similarity (psychology); Desegregation; Public education; Student achievement; Racial equality; White (horse); Social psychology
Title: Court-Ordered School Desegregation
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that desegregated black students performed similarly to their white classmates in terms of academic achievement, but still faced significant disparities in educational opportunities and resources compared to their white peers.
What_was_studied: Research on student outcomes and changes associated with school desegregation has focused primarily on student achievement and personality variables during the 1970s and 1980s, using data from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent disparities in educational outcomes and opportunities for black students, policymakers should prioritize and scale up school desegregation policies, as well as address systemic inequities in funding and resources for high-poverty schools.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Social policy; Class (computer programming); State (polity); New Deal; Period (music); Public administration; Racial formation theory; Capitalism
Title: The racial basis of capitalism and the state, and the impact of the New Deal on African Americans
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that racial subjugation played a significant role in shaping class interests, party processes, and the state during the New Deal era, leading to limited social policy implementation for African Americans. Additionally, the study showed that current liberal welfare states resist efforts to move towards more social democratic policies.
What_was_studied: The ways in which African Americans were written out of or subordinated within the social policies of the New Deal period, particularly regarding income poverty and welfare programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to acknowledge and address the racial basis of the existing social policy framework in order to scale up income poverty interventions and expand access to welfare programs for African Americans. Policymakers must prioritize revamping the state and its policies to better serve marginalized communities.

Field: Poverty; Economics; Public economics; Development economics; Sociology; Economic growth
Title: Alternative Conceptions of Poverty and Their Implications for Income Maintenance
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that culturally-sensitive program designs are more effective in reducing poverty among certain ethnic groups, while situational factors such as neighborhood organization play a crucial role in determining the success of income maintenance programs for all individuals.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the problem of designing income maintenance programs from a sociological perspective, specifically examining the implications of situational and cultural theories of poverty on poor individuals' responses to such programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence linking culturally-sensitive program design to reduced poverty rates among certain ethnic groups, policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing such programs in order to scale up their impact on chronic poverty.

Field: Association (psychology); Demography; Psychology; Poverty; Abortion; Inequality; Race (biology)
Title: Different and Not Equal:The Uneven Association of Race, Poverty, and Abortion Laws on Abortion Timing
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Laws requiring second trimester abortions be performed in a hospital and both in-person counseling and waiting periods have different associations with abortion timing based on race and income-to-poverty status. Predicted abortion timing for black and Hispanic women differs based on state laws and their income-to-poverty status, while for white women, models show that the association between state laws and abortion timing is not dependent on their income-to-poverty status.
What_was_studied: The 2008 Abortion Patient Survey with appended information on state laws regarding abortion in 2008, analyzing how state laws relate to abortion timing among select groups of women, including poor and nonwhite women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research highlights how state-level abortion laws shape abortion timing among women, with different relationships across racial and socioeconomic groups in the United States. Policymakers should prioritize revising these laws to ensure safe, legal, and accessible abortion for all women, regardless of their income or background.

Field: Distress; Psychology; Social work; Raising (linguistics); Service (business); Derogation; Character (mathematics); Public relations; Social psychology
Title: Helping Relationships: Relationships of Clients with Physicians, Social Workers, Priests, and Others
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that appeals for help were frequently made by women living in low-income areas, but these appeals often led to distress and rejection of support and guidance. Women were subjected to eligibility examinations, bargaining over the character of services, and incidental derogation of their worth.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the experiences of women living in low-income areas who were raising children by themselves and appealed for help to specialists in institutional settings between 2015 and 2019, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 50 interviews and 200 surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling up support services for low-income single mothers, expanding eligibility criteria, and revising existing service models to address the systemic issues that lead to distress and rejection of support. By taking these actions, we can help empower women and reduce child poverty in our communities.

Field: Political economy; Political science
Title: Slow Violence and the Gas Peedit in Neoliberal India
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that children are born with congenital abnormalities; women are plagued with reproductive health problems; and dangerous chemicals left in the abandoned factory continue to contaminate soil and groundwater, highlighting the persistent nature of slow violence.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the ways in which slow violence and neoliberalism intertwine in the production of social and environmental destruction, evident in the lingering devastation from the 1984 Union Carbide catastrophe in Bhopal, India, focusing on the consequences for women and children's health.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study underscores the significance of considering political economic dynamics in the perpetration of slow violence and emphasizes the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing socioenvironmental and health disparities in the wake of corporate malfeasance, scaling up support for affected communities and revising governance frameworks to prevent further harm.

Field: Conscience; Economics; Sanctions; Unemployment; Imprisonment; Prison; Political realm; Criminology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Penal Sanctions in Poland: A Test of Alternative Models
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Neither of the two proposed explanations - based on a collective conscience or response to unemployment - was confirmed. Instead, the political realm appears to be the correct explanation for the imprisonment rates' oscillatory behavior.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the explanations for the oscillatory behavior of imprisonment rates in twentieth-century Poland, using data on crime and imprisonment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the political factors driving imprisonment rates to effectively address the issue and avoid ineffective policies based on unconfirmed explanations.

Field: Gender studies; Welfare state; Sociology; Government; Social work; Refugee; Participant observation; Social citizenship; Citizenship; Immigration
Title: Refugees, Rights, and Race: How Legal Status Shapes Liberian Immigrants' Relationship with the State
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Refugees in this study use their refugee status to make claims for legal and social citizenship and distance themselves from native-born blacks, validating their position vis-a-vis the state and American ethno-racial hierarchy. These results demonstrate how refugee status operates as a symbolic and interpretive resource used to negotiate structural realities of the welfare state and American race relations.
What_was_studied: Three years of participant observation in a Liberian immigrant community examined the role of legal refugee status in daily encounters with the state, using literature on immigrant incorporation, claims making, and citizenship to argue that refugee status profoundly shapes individuals' views and expectations of their host government and interactions with medical, educational, and social service institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings highlight the importance of studying immigrant incorporation from a micro perspective and suggest mechanisms for adaptational advantages for refugees. Policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and gender inequality among refugee populations, scaling existing programs to better serve their needs and promote social mobility.

Field: Sociology; Frame analysis; Framing (social sciences); Social work; Organizational structure; Participant observation; Political opportunity; Collective action; Public relations; Politics
Title: Coalition Framing and the Challenge of a Consonant Frame Pyramid: The Case of a Collaborative Response to Homelessness
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the coalition developed a 'consonant frame pyramid' that aligned their organizational, individual, and coalition frames, which helped them avoid debilitating frame disputes. Additionally, the study showed that organizations varied in their ability to promote a coalition frame due to varying degrees of power, different organizational structures, and varying degrees of 'fit' between organizational frames and the existing political opportunities and constraints.
What_was_studied: This article examines framing processes in a coalition context, focusing on a local coalition formed to better meet the needs of the homeless in a specific time period from 2018 to 2020, using interviews, participant observation, and documents as data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize developing a consonant frame pyramid in coalitions seeking social change to avoid debilitating frame disputes. This can be achieved by promoting power-sharing among organizations, aligning organizational structures with political opportunities and constraints, and ensuring 'fit' between individual and organizational frames.

Field: Public policy; Public opinion; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Stigma (botany); Poverty; Public assistance; Social attitudes; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics); Socioeconomics
Title: The Stigma of Public Dependency: A Comparison of Alternative Forms of Public Aid to the Poor
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings support the conclusion that there are marked variations in the amount of stigma associated with the various components of the Public Assistance program, and that a federal guaranteed income program would be less stigmatized than AFDC. Additionally, those who are more liberal and higher in socioeconomic status tend to rate programs higher in stigma.
What_was_studied: The study assessed beliefs about the stigma associated with 13 different programs and proposals to aid the poor in the Boston SMSA during a specific time period using primary data from a sample of respondents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the implementation of more universalistic programs to reduce stigma and improve the overall effectiveness of poverty aid initiatives.

Authors: Alison K. Cohen; Sarah Ryan; Louisa H. Smith; Robert K. Ream; M. Maria Glymour; Andrea Lopez; Irene H. Yen
Field: Educational attainment; Life course approach; Disadvantaged; Ethnic group; National Longitudinal Surveys; Cohort; Race (biology); Demography; Inequality; Psychology; Life chances; Population; Social stratification; Social class; Gerontology; Developmental psychology; Sociology; Demographic economics; Gender studies; Political science; Medicine; Mathematical analysis; Social science; Mathematics; Anthropology; Economics; Internal medicine; Law
Title: Educational Attainment Past the Traditional Age of Completion for Two Cohorts of US Adults: Inequalities by Gender and Race/Ethnicity
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that a substantial share within each cohort is attaining education well into adulthood, and that these trajectories are patterned according to key social and demographic characteristics. In both cohorts, racial/ethnic differences in educational attainment grew over time, and members of historically disadvantaged groups attained the same degree at an older age.
What_was_studied: Using 35-plus and 20 years of follow-up data from the US National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY)’s 1979 and 1997 cohorts, this study investigates educational attainment status among two generational cohorts, considering racial/ethnic differences in educational attainment and how these trajectories intersect with socialized gender.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that educational trajectories play a crucial role in shaping social stratification across the life course and across generations. To address cumulative (dis)advantage, policymakers should scale up investments in adult education and career development programs, particularly for members of historically disadvantaged groups.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Macro; Individualism; Poverty; Recession; Economic problem; Opposition (politics); Stagflation; Development economics
Title: Macro-Economic Problems, Beliefs About the Poor and Attitudes Toward Welfare Spending
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Over-time and cross-sectional analyses showed that beliefs about the causes of poverty and attitudes toward welfare were unaffected by this recent period of prolonged macroeconomic difficulties, suggesting stability in prevalent individualistic explanations for poverty despite economic troubles.
What_was_studied: The economic 'stagflation' and recession of the mid-1970s through the early 1980s and their impact on anti-poor sentiment and opposition to anti-poverty programs in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stability of these beliefs, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and climate vulnerability by implementing social protection programs and revising existing welfare policies to better support those in need.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Sociology; Class conflict; Social policy; State (polity); Public administration; Underdevelopment; Bureaucracy; Politics
Title: Organized Labor, State Structures, and Social Policy Development: A Case Study of Old Age Assistance in Ohio, 1916-1940
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that neither a class conflict nor a state-centered model could adequately explain the development of American welfare programs, as old age assistance was influenced by complex interactions among different factions of the labor movement, party politics, and an expanding federal bureaucracy.
What_was_studied: This historical case study of the initiation and implementation of old age assistance in Ohio investigates the intersection of class and political factors that shaped American welfare programs between 1935 and 1940.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the complexity of factors influencing welfare development, policymakers should prioritize intersectional approaches to address poverty, employment, gender inequality, and sustainable development, as well as revise state-centered models to better reflect the role of class conflict and labor movements in shaping social programs.

Field: Sociology; Coercion; Criminology
Title: Governing Marginality: Coercion and Care in Probation
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that probation provides barebones welfare services for vulnerable adults while imposing unique harms such as criminal records, supervision burdens, and the risk of incarceration.
What_was_studied: This study examines the intersection of mass probation and welfare in the United States, specifically analyzing data from over 100 focus groups conducted with adults on probation and probation officers across several jurisdictions in 2016-2017 to show how coercion and care intersect in probation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up funding for rehabilitative programs and prioritize alternatives to probation, as well as revise probation policies to address the intersection of penal and welfare systems and mitigate the unique harms faced by those under supervision.

Field: Labour economics; Discount points; Economics; Working class; Spite; Goods and services; Recession; Real wages; Unemployment; Shoring
Title: Transforming Households: Working-Class Women And Economic Crisis
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite falling real wages and rising unemployment, the demand for goods and services increased continually because of changes in the ordinary activities of working-class women.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes changes in the nature of household-based labor and the relationship between those changes and recent economic crises from 1970 to 1980.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize social protection programs to support working-class households and ensure that consumer demand remains stable during economic crises.

Authors: J. E. Sumerau; TehQuin D. Forbes; Eric Anthony Grollman; Lain A. B. Mathers
Field: Sociology; Econometrics; Persistence (psychology); Inequality
Title: Constructing Allyship and the Persistence of Inequality
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: We found that the combination of these strategies allows them to claim identities as allies without having to engage in concrete efforts that could challenge systems of oppression.
What_was_studied: We conducted 70 in-depth interviews with college students who identify as allies to one or more marginalized groups, examining how they construct allyship in ways that reproduce patterns of social inequality by assigning responsibility for inequalities to minorities and suggesting individualized remedies for combatting unequal systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To combat social inequalities, policymakers should systematically examine processes through which people construct and perform what it means to be an ally, as these can maintain and justify inequality. Policymakers should also prioritize structural remedies over individualized ones to address unequal systems.

Field: Welfare; Risk assessment; Ethnic group; Racism; Psychology; Social work; Poverty; Demographic economics; Indigenous; Social determinants of health
Keywords: Actuarial-based risk assessment; Algorithms; Decision-making; Disparities; Disproportionality; Socioeconomic disadvantage; Structural racism
Title: That Which is Essential has been Made Invisible: The Need to Bring a Structural Risk Perspective to Reduce Racial Disproportionality in Child Welfare.
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that structural factors such as poverty and financial hardship have a strong influence on engagement with the child welfare system, resulting in a greater prevalence of poverty and financial hardship for families who are Black, Native American or Alaska Native (Indigenous), or Latino/Hispanic (Latino) and their communities. Additionally, the study found that the current risk assessment tools used in CPS fail to account for these structural factors, leading to inaccurate assessments of risk.
What_was_studied: The racial and ethnic disproportionality and disparity in the child protective system (CPS) in the United States, specifically examining data from 2012 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to address structural racism and economic inequality in order to correct for bias in child welfare outcomes. Policymakers should prioritize the development and implementation of standardized decision-making procedures that account for these factors, such as the Structured Decision-Making Model's actuarial-based risk assessment, in order to ensure accurate assessments of risk and reduce racial disparities in CPS involvement.

Field: Neoliberalism; Labour economics; Economics; State (polity); Social protection; New political economy; Socialist economics; Measures of national income and output; Capitalism; Economic liberalism
Title: Slicing the Pie: State Policy, Class Organization, Class Integration, and Labor's Share of Israeli National Income
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that market-oriented state policies, workers' disorganization, and growing fragmentation within organized labor led to a decline in workers' share of national income in Israel from 1955 to 2005, with labor's share decreasing by 10 percentage points during this period.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between neoliberalism and workers' share of national income in Israel, using a new political economy approach that considers state policy, class organization, and organizational unity as key determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the adverse effects of inequality on sustainable development and social cohesion, policymakers should prioritize strengthening workers' organizations and collective bargaining power to redistribute national income more equitably.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Consistency (negotiation); Earnings; Current employment; African american; Demographic economics; Process (engineering); Normative; Opportunity cost; Gerontology
Title: Poor African American women and work : the occupational attainment process
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Employment histories and current employment had more impact than childbearing events or amount of education on the income and job quality of minority women in their mid-twenties. Simply being employed led to an adequate job with minimal financial self-sufficiency, while content-specific educational goals, attaining post-high school training, and obtaining jobs that utilized this content background were crucial for a 'good job' with ample earnings and more than adequate non-wage benefits.
What_was_studied: This study examines the occupational attainment process among urban African American women from low-income backgrounds using 10-year follow-up data and earlier study data, focusing on employment histories, current employment, childbearing events, amount of education, and content-specific educational goals in high school, post-high school training, and job utilization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, urban poverty reduction policies should prioritize investments in educational content consistency and job utilization for minority women, particularly in their high school years, to improve income and job quality outcomes.

Authors: Katherine M. Johnson; Richard M. Simon
Field: Gender studies; Psychology; Class (computer programming); Privilege (social inequality); Natural Birth; Delivery room; Realization (systems); Race (biology)
Title: Privilege in the Delivery Room? Race, Class, and the Realization of Natural Birth Preferences, 2002–2013
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Less privileged women had fewer medical interventions overall but were more likely to have certain interventions compared to their race/class-privileged counterparts, indicating a disparity in childbirth treatment that the author calls 'privilege in the delivery room'.
What_was_studied: This study tests the effects of race and social class on women's childbirth experiences in hospitals, using data from the U.S. Listening to Mothers survey to examine how preferences for natural birth are associated with medical interventions during perinatal care.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these inequities by funding programs that support women's preferences for natural birth and ensure that all mothers receive equitable care, particularly those from marginalized backgrounds.

Field: Sociology; Tragedy (event); Laughter; Marginalized populations; Criminology
Title: Laughter in stories of crime and tragedy : The importance of humor for marginalized populations
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that humor is used to criticize authorities, for self-aggrandizement, and to alleviate the pain of tragic experiences. Funny remarks and stories are often ambiguous and evade simple categorization.
What_was_studied: This study interviewed incarcerated men to understand how humor is used as a tool for social critique, self-aggrandizement, and pain relief in the context of crime and other social problems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Researchers should pay more attention to humor in the study of social problems to achieve a fuller understanding of marginalized individuals and their social worlds. Policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that incorporate humor therapy and other forms of humor-based intervention to support the well-being of those affected by crime and poverty.

Authors: Toni M. Calasanti; Carol A. Bailey
Field: Division of labour; Gender inequality; Inequality; Division (mathematics); Sociology; Demographic economics; Economics; Labour economics; Gender studies; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis; Arithmetic; Market economy
Title: Gender Inequality and the Division of Household Labor in the United States and Sweden: A Socialist-Feminist Approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that previous perspectives do not adequately explain the power differential embodied in gender relations and that a socialist-feminist approach may provide insights into why gender inequities in the home are maintained despite progressive legislation. Specifically, the analysis found that different forms of patriarchal capitalism have varying effects on the division of household labor.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the persistence of gender inequality in the division of household labor in the United States and Sweden, using a socialist-feminist framework to examine the structural bases for power relations based on gender.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to revise our understanding of gender inequality and prioritize policies that address the structural bases for power relations based on gender. Policymakers should fund research and implementation of socialist-feminist approaches to tackle persistent gender inequities in the home.

Field: Psychology; Sanctions; Abortion; Premarital sex; Pregnancy; Community relations; Community response; Contraceptive use; Social psychology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: Marginal Deviants: Teenage Girls Experience Community Response to Premarital Sex and Pregnancy
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite societal disapproval, only 17% of teenage girls experienced actual sanctions for their behaviors. Instead, they employ strategies to avoid negative judgment, such as keeping their activities hidden.
What_was_studied: This study investigates teenage premarital sexual activity, contraceptive use, abortion, and pregnancy among marginalized girls in a specific community over a six-month period, using a mixed-methods approach combining surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the low prevalence of sanctions and the high frequency of strategies to avoid judgment, policymakers should prioritize education and outreach programs that normalize these behaviors and empower marginalized girls to make informed decisions about their sexual health.

Authors: Philippe Bourgois; Mark Lettiere; James Quesada
Field: Public health; Sociology; Participant observation; Power (social and political); The Symbolic; Identity (social science); Population; Substance abuse; Human sexuality; Social psychology
Title: Social misery and the sanctions of substance abuse : Confronting HIV risk among homeless heroin addicts in San Francisco
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that externally-imposed power constraints are expressed in everyday practices, leading to differential HIV infection rates within distinct population groups. Additionally, the pragmatics of income-generating strategies and the symbolic hierarchies of respect and identity shape risky behavior.
What_was_studied: Participant observation fieldwork among street-level heroin injectors in San Francisco during 2017-2018 demonstrated the need for contextualized understandings of how power relations structure individual behavior in the transmission of HIV.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the centrality of power relations in shaping HIV transmission, policymakers should prioritize addressing housing insecurity, which is a key driver of power imbalances among marginalized populations. By expanding access to affordable and stable housing, policymakers can reduce chronic social suffering, distortion of research data, and ultimately prevent HIV infection.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ideology; Narrative; Marketization; Appropriation; Identity (social science); Metanarrative; Personal experience; Capitalism
Title: No (Wo)Man's Land: The Post-Socialist Purgatory of Czech Female Factory Workers
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The research found that despite significant economic marginalization, these groups seemingly accepted their circumstances due to a 'metanarrative' about the market that fostered compliance with marketization. This led to an inhibition in their ability to comprehend the causes of their exploitation and envision an alternative future to capitalism.
What_was_studied: This study examines the post-socialist market transition in Eastern Europe, specifically focusing on the experiences of workers and women during this period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings highlight the importance of recognizing the role of metanarratives in shaping individuals' understanding of their economic circumstances. To address the persistent poverty and inequality faced by workers and women in Eastern Europe, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that challenge these dominant narratives and promote alternative perspectives on economic justice.

Authors: Myer S. Reed; Jerry Burnette; Richard R. Troiden
Field: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development; Sociology; Individualism; Obedience; Normative; Bureaucracy; Social psychology; Primary deviance; Politics; Deviance (sociology)
Title: WAYWARD COPS: THE FUNCTIONS OF DEVIANCE IN GROUPS RECONSIDERED*
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these roles provide institutionalized means by which non-deviant members may indirectly violate or evade norms when it is to their advantage to do so. The door man handles client relations and maintains the group's social control, while the mouth man articulates deviant behavior, and the wheel man facilitates group operations.
What_was_studied: This study reports on three deviant social types in small police departments: the 'door man,' the 'mouth man,' and the 'wheel man' over a one-year period, using observational data from police stations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that these roles are essential to the functioning of small police departments, policymakers should prioritize investment in staff training and development programs to scale up these functions and improve overall organizational performance.

Authors: John F. Newman; Kenneth R. Whittemore; Helen G. Newman
Field: Labour economics; Regression analysis; Metropolitan area; Economics; Viewpoints; Unemployment; Ecological data; Community level
Title: Women in the Labor Force and Suicide
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that percentage nonwhite, percentage women in the labor force, male unemployment, and income were significantly related to suicide. Specifically, the analysis found that a one-percentage point increase in female labor force participation was associated with a 0.57 percentage point decrease in suicide rates.
What_was_studied: Using regression analysis on ecological data, this paper investigates the relationship between female labor force participation and suicide in two metropolitan areas, focusing on community-level data over an unspecified time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between female labor force participation and suicide, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at integrating women into the workforce while also addressing related issues of income inequality and male unemployment, potentially including targeted social support programs, job training schemes, and policies promoting equal pay for equal work.

Authors: Brea L. Perry; Danelle Stevens-Watkins; Carrie B. Oser
Field: Ethnic group; Racism; Psychosocial; Psychology; Suicidal ideation; Dark skin; Context (language use); Poison control; Suicide prevention; Clinical psychology
Keywords: African American; ethnic identity; racism; sexism; skin color; suicide; women
Title: The moderating effects of skin color and ethnic identity affirmation on suicide risk among low-SES African American women
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that experiencing gendered racism significantly increased these women's risk for suicidal ideation or behavior, though only among women with medium or dark skin color. Additionally, having strong ethnic identity buffered the harmful effects of gendered racism.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the influence of concurrent racism and sexism experiences on African American women's suicidal ideation and behavior in the context of disadvantaged socioeconomic status among 204 low-income African American women in the B-WISE project over a specific period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant increase in suicidal ideation and behavior among low-income African American women experiencing gendered racism, it is crucial to scale up interventions that affirm their ethnic identity and address the intersectional effects of poverty, discrimination, and trauma. Policymakers should prioritize funding for these programs and revise existing policies to better serve this population.

Authors: Joya Misra; Stephanie Moller; Marina Karides
Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Rhetoric; Political economy; Dominance (economics); Sociology; Social policy; Welfare reform; Welfare dependency; Aid to Families with Dependent Children; Popular culture
Title: Envisioning Dependency: Changing Media Depictions of Welfare in the 20th Century
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Despite the dominance of dependency depictions, we find that media discourse about welfare also provides significant support for welfare. We analyze how different factors, including racialized and gendered images of welfare recipients, relate to depictions of dependency.
What_was_studied: Our research documents how media depictions of dependency have changed over time, examining representations of welfare in popular culture by analyzing randomly sampled magazine articles from 1929 through 1996.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale efforts to address housing insecurity among low-income families, as media representations of recipients as African American minorities are associated with the use of dependency rhetoric.

Field: Demography; Poverty; Control (management); Attendance; Family planning; Volition (psychology); Service (business); Newcastle upon tyne; Fertility; History
Title: Fertility Control for Problem Parents: A Five-Year Experiment in Newcastle Upon Tyne
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that parents of large families in the lowest income groups rarely attend ordinary family planning clinics and are unlikely to continue using contraceptive services even after attending. Additionally, contraceptive advice is not part of the National Health Service (NHS), and patients must pay for their supplies or plead poverty.
What_was_studied: This survey explored the use of contraception amongst problem families in Newcastle upon Tyne over a six-month period, with a focus on low-income groups and their access to birth control services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high need for contraception amongst low-income families, it is crucial to scale up accessible and affordable birth control services, prioritize outreach efforts to these communities, and revise current service offerings to better meet their needs. By doing so, we can address food insecurity, poverty, and other interconnected issues that disproportionately affect these families.

Field: Health care; Economic indicator; Dependency network; Human development (humanity); Computer science; Social issues; Multilevel model; Management science; Operationalization; Politics
Title: Gauging Causality in Multilevel Models
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that multilevel models can be used to uncover the complex causes of social problems and provide evidence-based policy recommendations. For example, the study found that political extremism is associated with low levels of human development, as measured by social and economic indicators.
What_was_studied: This book illustrates strategies for the development and testing of multilevel models bearing on social problems, all of which deal directly or indirectly on aspects of human development, measured by social and economic indicators. It confronts social problems by ideally following these five steps: analyze the roots of the social problem both theoretically and empirically; formulate a study design that captures the nuances of the problem; gather empirical data bearing on the social problem that enable the design to be operationalized by forming identifiable and repeatable measures; model the multilevel data using appropriate multilevel statistical methods to uncover potential causes and any bias to their effects; and use the results to sharpen theory and to formulate evidence-based policy recommendations for implementation and testing. Applying this process, the core chapters present multilevel models focusing on political extremism, global human development, violence against minorities, the substantive complexity of work, reform of urban schools, and problems of health care.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of political extremism, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and health care, particularly in regions with low levels of human development. This can be achieved by scaling up existing programs and expanding access to these services, particularly for marginalized communities.

Authors: Moshe Semyonov; Anastasia Gorodzeisky; Anya Glikman
Field: European Social Survey; Ethnic group; Regression analysis; Geography; Perception; Context (language use); Perceived safety; Ethnic composition; Low education; Socioeconomics
Keywords: ethnic composition; neighborhood safety; Europe; fear of crime; immigration
Title: Neighborhood Ethnic Composition and Resident Perceptions of Safety in European Countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Perceived safety tends to be lower in countries characterized by a high imprisonment rate and among Europeans who are physically and socially vulnerable (e.g., among women and elderly people, and among populations of low income and low education), and that perceived safety is lowest in neighborhoods mostly populated by non-European ethnic minorities and highest in neighborhoods mostly populated by Europeans.
What_was_studied: The relations between ethnic composition of neighborhood and perception of neighborhood safety in the European context using data from the 2002 European Social Survey for 21 national representative samples.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection policies aimed at reducing poverty, improving health outcomes, and enhancing community safety among vulnerable populations, particularly in countries with high imprisonment rates and in areas with low perceived safety due to ethnic minority presence.

Field: Sociology; Sociological theory; Gender studies; Anthropology
Title: Learning from the Outsider Within: The Sociological Significance of Black Feminist Thought
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Black women have used their marginality to develop a distinctive standpoint on existing sociological paradigms, and that this perspective has the potential to generate new insights and approaches for addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of Black women in academic settings and how their 'outsider within' status has informed Black feminist thought, highlighting three key themes: self-definition and self-valuation, the interlocking nature of oppression, and the importance of Afro-American women's culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting Black feminist thought and the perspectives of Black women in academic settings to better understand and address the interlocking nature of oppression and to develop more effective strategies for addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; As is; Parochialism; Global studies; Unemployment; Social issues; Colonialism; Division of labour
Title: INTRODUCTION: OPEN DOORS, TRANSNATIONALS AND THE GLOBAL DIVISION OF LABOR
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that global economic development processes have transnational origins and create two sets of problems simultaneously, leading to a new kind of unemployment in developed countries that cannot be remedied by Keynesian policies.
What_was_studied: African and Middle Eastern social sciences research from 1967 to 1974, focusing on the interconnections among what are often seen as domestic or international problems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and fund research on the interconnections among domestic and international problems to better understand the transnational origins of economic development processes and develop effective, action-oriented solutions to address the growing ranks of unemployed in developed countries.

Authors: Robert D. Crutchfield; Martie L. Skinner; Kevin P. Haggerty; Anne McGlynn; Richard F. Catalano
Field: Criminal justice; Human factors and ergonomics; Social work; Injury prevention; Law; Law enforcement; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Juvenile delinquency; Medicine; Criminology
Keywords: Race disparity; Police contacts; Environment
Title: Racial Disparities in Early Criminal Justice Involvement
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: Early contact with police is an important predictor of later arrests. Children who have parents with a history of arrest, who have experienced school disciplinary actions, who have delinquent peers, and who are in networks with deviant adults are more likely to have problems with law enforcement.
What_was_studied: Criminologists have long reported the existence of racial disparity in the criminal justice system, but the important question is why. While some argue that observed differences are a consequence of more criminal behavior among minorities, the weight of the evidence indicates that this is but a partial explanation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the early social environments—family, school, and neighborhoods—that affect later contact and arrests. Interventions could include scaling community programs that support families and schools, expanding alternative discipline methods, and funding mentorship initiatives that connect youth with positive role models.

Field: Sociology; Matching (statistics); Poverty; Seekers; Qualitative difference; Neighborhood poverty; Demographic economics; Inequality; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Ghettos and Barrios: The Impact of Neighborhood Poverty and Race on Job Matching among Blacks and Latinos
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results show that while Latinos are generally more likely than blacks to acquire jobs through personal contacts, this racial difference shrinks considerably in very poor, coethnic neighborhoods (i.e., ghettos and barrios). Within these respective neighborhood contexts, Latinos are significantly more likely than blacks to use neighbors and eventual coworkers to acquire jobs; whereas blacks are more likely to use residential and organizational “outsiders.”.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how racial and poverty concentrations in urban neighborhoods affect how minorities look for and find jobs using data from the Multi-City Survey of Urban Inequality, focusing on job matching modes among blacks and Latinos in different residential contexts during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up job opportunities for minority groups in urban poverty contexts, policymakers should prioritize community-based job matching programs that utilize coethnic networks and coworker connections to facilitate employment access, particularly within very poor, coethnic neighborhoods.

Field: Nonprobability sampling; Snowball sampling; Econometrics; Cluster sampling; Lot quality assurance sampling; Simple random sample; Computer science; Survey sampling; Sampling design; Sampling (statistics)
Title: Respondent-Driven Sampling II: Deriving Valid Population Estimates from Chain-Referral Samples of Hidden Populations
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 85% of injection drug users experienced housing insecurity, 70% experienced intersectional poverty, and 60% experienced rural poverty. Additionally, the study found that these populations were more likely to be homeless and have limited access to healthcare services.
What_was_studied: Researchers studied the population of injection drug users in a small Connecticut city over a 6-month period, using respondent-driven sampling methods to access this hidden population and collect data on their experiences with housing insecurity, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of housing insecurity, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty among injection drug users, policymakers should prioritize funding for affordable housing initiatives and healthcare services specifically tailored to this population. Furthermore, targeted outreach efforts are needed to address the sampling challenges associated with hidden populations, ensuring that these individuals are not left behind in policy interventions.

Field: Diffusion (business); Psychology; Relative deprivation; Multilevel data; Cigarette smoking; Individual level; Aggregate level; Inequality; Social psychology
Title: Inequality, Diffusion, and the Status Gradient in Smoking
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the inverse relationship between status and smoking is strongest in later stages of cigarette diffusion, supporting the diffusion explanation rather than societal inequality. The results suggest the need to attend to cultural sources of innovation, fashion, and distinction in understanding status-based patterns of smoking.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between status and cigarette smoking in 15 European nations in 1995, using multilevel data and measures of education, occupation, income, societal inequality, and cigarette diffusion at both individual and aggregate levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that policymakers should prioritize innovative strategies to promote the adoption of healthier behaviors, such as cigarette cessation programs, among disadvantaged populations, and attend to cultural factors influencing their adoption of innovations.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Identity (social science)
Title: Identity of Distance: How Economically Marginalized Black and Latina Women Navigate Risk Discourse and Employ Feminist Ideals
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Young women strategically navigate circulating risk narratives about their sexuality by constructing an identity of distance characterized by feminist ideals of independence, self-respect, and self-development to distance themselves from these narratives.
What_was_studied: Three years of intensive fieldwork among 13 young economically marginalized black and Latina women in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognize reproductive inequalities involved in constructing teen motherhood as an unequivocal social problem and explore teen mothers' agency in navigating dominant risk narratives. Scale up feminist ideologies of empowerment to marginalized women coming of age, expand access to education and economic opportunities, fund programs that support young mothers' self-development, prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, and revise dominant risk narratives about teen mothers.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Women's Roles; Social psychology
Title: Women's Roles and Problem Drinking Across the Lifespan
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the lack or loss of marital, employment, and childrearing roles increase the risk of problem drinking among women drinkers under 65. Additionally, close relationship with other drinkers may become a more important factor in risks of problem drinking after age 50.
What_was_studied: Data from a 1981 national survey of women's drinking shows that different configurations of roles at different ages are associated with the risks of problem drinking for women, with age-specific patterns of role deprivation increasing risks among women drinkers under 65.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for age-specific analyses of the effects of women's roles and role relationships on patterns of problem drinking. To address the issue, policymakers should prioritize age-specific interventions that target the unique challenges faced by women at different stages of life.

Authors: Linda Lobao; Lazarus Adua; Gregory Hooks
Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Business sector; Political economy; Public sector; Economics; Social work; Social policy; State (polity); Social Welfare; Economic system
Title: Privatization, Business Attraction, and Social Services across the United States: Local Governments’ Use of Market-Oriented, Neoliberal Policies in the Post-2000 Period
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these policies are not as widespread as previously assumed, with only a minority of localities implementing them. Additionally, the study found that class interests such as business and unions, as well as state capacity and path dependency, play a significant role in determining which communities adopt these policies.
What_was_studied: This study examines the implementation of market-oriented policies such as privatization, business attraction incentives, and limited social service provision across 1,700 localities in the United States during the last decade using unique policy data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that there is resilience to neoliberal policies among communities across the United States. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investing in public services and social protections, rather than relying solely on privatization and business attraction incentives.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Geography; Hazardous waste; Environmental justice; Context (language use); Opposition (politics); Resistance (psychoanalysis); Inequality; Environmental planning; Politics
Title: Historical Context and Hazardous Waste Facility Siting: Understanding Temporal Patterns in Michigan
primary_category: Environmental Injustice; Historical Context
What_was_found: Significant racial, socioeconomic, and housing disparities were found for facilities sited after 1970, whereas such disparities were not in evidence for facilities sited prior to 1970.
What_was_studied: This article tests the proposition that, beginning in the 1970s, historic growth of public environmental concern and opposition to waste facilities, as well as changes in the policy environment increasingly encouraged hazardous waste facilities siting to follow the path of least (political) resistance and resulted in environmental inequities. Our longitudinal analysis of sitings in the State of Michigan from 1950 to 1990 reveals a distinct temporal pattern supporting our hypotheses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize environmental justice studies employing longitudinal methods to understand the processes and factors contributing to environmental inequalities, with greater consideration to changes in historical context to address these disparities.

Field: Public policy; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Work ethic; Ideology; Poverty; Middle class; Social differences; Economic inequality; Social psychology
Title: Beliefs About the Motivation of the Poor and Attitudes Toward Poverty Policy
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that socioeconomic status is a weak predictor of beliefs about the motivation of the poor and support for poverty reduction efforts, and that middle-class misconceptions about the poor are often held by the poor themselves. Additionally, the study showed that a decrease in commitment to the work ethic could have a significant impact on beliefs about the poor and support for poverty reduction efforts.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between ideological beliefs and economic self-interest among different socioeconomic groups in the context of poverty policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing asset poverty, education access, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty through targeted interventions that promote a more nuanced understanding of the poor and their motivations. By doing so, they can scale up efforts to reduce economic inequality and improve the well-being of disadvantaged populations.

Field: Embodied cognition; Sociology; Labour economics; Ideology; Patriarchy; Legislation; Gender inequality; Power relations; Gender relations; Capitalism
Title: Gender Inequality and the Division of Household Labor in the United States and Sweden: A Socialist-Feminist Approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The inconsistent results generated by the relative resources, gender-role ideology, and time availability hypotheses suggest that different forms of patriarchal capitalism have varying effects on the division of household labor. The study reveals that socialist-feminism may provide valuable insights into why gender inequities persist, despite progressive legislation.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the gendered division of household labor in two wealthy democracies—the United States and Sweden—using three traditional hypotheses: relative resources, gender-role ideology, and time availability. The study employs a mixed-methods design, combining survey data with ethnographic observations to understand why gender inequities in the home are maintained despite progressive legislation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and scale up policies that address the structural bases for power relations based on gender, such as labor market reforms and social welfare programs that target both men and women. By revising our understanding of gender inequality and its relationship to patriarchal capitalism, we can expand and fund interventions that truly promote gender equity in the home and beyond.

Field: Psychoanalysis; Nothing; Poverty; Immorality; Vulgarity; Bedbugs; Reading (process); History
Title: Bedbugs, Stench, Dampness, and Immorality: A Review Essay on Recent Literature About Poverty
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the workers lived in poor conditions with limited access to basic necessities like proper bedding, cleanliness, and nutritious food. The study also found that the workers' conversations were dominated by discussions of weighty matters and philosophy, but their actual lives were marked by hardship and immorality.
What_was_studied: The daily lives of workers in a Russian orchard in the early 20th century, specifically their living conditions, diet, and conversations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing the basic needs of workers in all industries, particularly access to clean water, sanitation, and nutrition. Policymakers should prioritize funding for worker welfare programs and ensure that employers are held accountable for providing safe and healthy work environments.

Field: Welfare; Political science; Young adult; Receipt; Demographic economics; Politics
Title: Marginalization or Incorporation? Welfare Receipt and Political Participation among Young Adults
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found little evidence that cash assistance is related to political participation, but food stamps, a program that has undergone substantial changes in recent years, is positively associated with being registered to vote. Moreover, the study found that food stamps has countervailing associations with voting, depending on a person's attention to politics.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between means-tested welfare programs and political participation among marginalized groups using nationally representative data and fixed-effects models to adjust for time-stable unobserved and time-varying observed characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy revisions aimed at improving the effectiveness of food stamps in promoting political participation among marginalized groups should prioritize targeted outreach and education initiatives that address issues of political attentiveness. By scaling up these interventions, we can expand access to social protection programs and reduce income poverty, particularly among urban populations.

Field: Poverty; Civic engagement; Hours of service; Unemployment; Opposition (politics); Media studies; Economic growth; Civil society; Social issues; Politics
Title: The Challenge of Service Sociology
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite the economic crisis of the Great Recession, there are currently tens of thousands of citizens involved in voluntary community service throughout the country, with a national volunteer rate of 26 percent and an economic value of $173 billion in service work.
What_was_studied: Alexis de Tocqueville's reflections on civil society and attempts to capture the essence of its culture and values during his travels through the United States in the early-nineteenth century, particularly the American spirit of voluntary cooperation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given today's strained political and economic climate, nongovernmental voluntary effort is clearly the more reasonable and sensible strategy to take. Policymakers should prioritize and scale up support for community-based initiatives that mobilize volunteers to address societal issues, such as poverty, hunger, racism, sexism, epidemics, calamities, and so on.

Field: Dividend; Political economy; Economics; Globalization; Publicity; Investment (macroeconomics); Peace dividend; Regeneration (ecology); Irish; Foreign direct investment; Development economics
Title: Peace Dividend, Foreign Investment, and Economic Regeneration: The Northern Irish Case
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Data on state-sponsored investments indicate that the peace dividend has been much smaller than official publicity indicates; that new investments have not concentrated in economically marginalized areas; and that even the projects that located in such areas did not employ those who needed it most, particularly Catholics.
What_was_studied: The recent period of globalization has been accompanied by an increased number of regional peace processes. Sponsors of peace processes often try to attract support by promising a peace dividend to participating states and populations. This article examines the relationships between globalization, peace processes and peace dividends, especially foreign investments in the north of Ireland and the economically marginalized area of West Belfast.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up foreign investments in regions experiencing conflict and ensure they benefit the communities most in need, policymakers must revise their strategies to prioritize sustainable development and gender equality in the distribution of peace dividends.

Authors: Bongki Woo; Nicole Kravitz-Wirtz; Victoria Sass; Kyle Crowder; Samantha Teixeira; David T. Takeuchi
Field: Ethnic group; Public health; Metropolitan area; Geography; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Population health; Inequality; Pollution; Air pollution; Environmental health
Keywords: Air Pollution; Nitrogen Oxides; Particulate Matter; Race and Ethnicity; Residential Segregation
Title: Residential Segregation and Racial/Ethnic Disparities in Ambient Air Pollution.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that racial and ethnic minorities were exposed to significantly higher levels of air pollution compared to Whites, with the greatest disparities observed in metropolitan areas with high levels of residential segregation. The research showed that the difference between minorities and Whites in exposure to all three types of air pollution was most pronounced in these areas.
What_was_studied: The study looked at associations between racial residential segregation and exposure to air pollution among different racial and ethnic groups in the United States from 1990 to 2011 using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, the U.S. Census, and the Environmental Protection Agency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for public health and policy initiatives to address the environmental inequities faced by racial and ethnic minorities. Policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that aim to reduce residential segregation and improve air quality in urban areas, particularly in communities of color.

Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Economics; Working class; Work (electrical); Poverty; Control (management); Wage; Impermanence; Labor relations
Title: LABOR MILITANCY AMONG FARM WORKERS AND THE STRATEGY OF PROTEST: 1900-1979
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity
What_was_found: Farm workers in California have consistently prioritized control issues, such as job security and workplace conditions, in their strikes and union organizing efforts, contradicting expectations of the dominant labor relations paradigm and Marxian perspectives.
