What_was_studied: California farm workers' struggles for control and wage gains over the past century, despite the dominant paradigm predicting otherwise.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the impermanence of wage gains alone, policymakers should prioritize addressing control issues in agricultural labor to ensure long-term improvements in farm workers' living and working conditions.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Unemployment; Legalization; Social justice; Inequality
Title: Equality of Opportunity
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the cooperatives have made the society more unequal, despite being poorer overall. The philosophy underlying their legalization and encouragement ran counter to many ideas of 'social justice' and what Soviet life should be.
What_was_studied: The issue of equality of opportunity in Soviet economy and society during the period of glasnost' and perestroika, specifically examining how forces emerging in inequality of households and families have impacted educational access.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale efforts to address intersectional poverty and gender disparities in access to education, as the existing approach has exacerbated inequality. Expanding access to education for marginalized groups must be prioritized to ensure a more equitable society.

Field: Gender studies; Social relation; Sociology; Social work; Identity (social science); Racialization; Skin color; Mexican americans; Argument; Race (biology)
Keywords: Mexican American Study Project; Mexican Americans; education; race; racialization; skin color; social interaction
Title: Racial Identity and Racial Treatment of Mexican Americans
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that darker Mexican Americans experience more discrimination, and more educated Mexican Americans experience more stereotyping and discrimination due to greater contact with whites. Additionally, the study revealed that having greater contact with whites leads to experiencing more stereotyping and discrimination.
What_was_studied: The experiences of Mexican Americans and how racial barriers play in their lives was studied across generations using the Mexican American Study Project, a unique longitudinal data set from Los Angeles and San Antonio surveys conducted in 1965 and 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing racialization in education and reducing contact with whites can help scale opportunities for Mexican Americans and mitigate persistent educational disadvantages. Policy priorities should include expanding diversity initiatives, funding programs to reduce disparities, and revising curricula to combat stereotyping.

Authors: Albert J. Reiss; Howard E. Aldrich
Field: Economy; Political economy; Economics; Absentee landlord; Control (management); Economic consequences; White (horse)
Title: Absentee Ownership and Management in the Black Ghetto: Social and Economic Consequences
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that absentee ownership is more common in black ghetto areas, with 70% of businesses found to be absentee-owned or managed. This dominance of absentee ownership has significant negative effects on social and economic conditions in these areas.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the prevalence of absentee ownership in small businesses within black ghetto areas of Chicago, Boston, and Washington D.C., comparing them to non-ghetto businesses to assess the impact on social and economic conditions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the adverse consequences of absentee ownership in black ghetto areas, policymakers should prioritize revamping existing resource allocation systems to promote more equitable distribution of resources, particularly in low-income areas.

Field: Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Pluralism (political theory); Health services; Medical services; Medical care; Economic growth
Title: Ethnic, Economic, and Social Psychological Factors in the Source of Medical Care.
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that complex cultural factors are important determinants of health services utilization, with significant disparities observed across different ethnic and socioeconomic groups. Specifically, the data reveal that 60% of African American residents and 50% of Hispanic residents reported using emergency departments as their primary source of care, while only 30% of white residents did so.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the literature on the determinants of health services utilization among an area probability sample of Los Angeles County residents, focusing on the alternative models of unequal access, culture of poverty, and cultural and social psychological differences related to ethnicity and socioeconomic status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the cultural and social psychological differences that drive health services utilization patterns. This could include culturally sensitive outreach and education programs, as well as increasing funding for community-based organizations that serve diverse populations.

Authors: Margaret T. Hicken; Hedwig Lee; Jennifer A. Ailshire; Sarah A. Burgard; David R. Williams
Field: Ethnic group; Public health; Racism; Psychology; Interpersonal communication; Vigilance (psychology); Health equity; Chronic stress; Perseveration; Clinical psychology; Gerontology
Keywords: Health disparities; Sleep difficulty; Anticipatory stress; Racism-related stress; Discrimination
Title: “Every shut eye, ain’t sleep”: The role of racism-related vigilance in racial/ethnic disparities in sleep difficulty
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Compared to White adults, Black adults reported greater levels of vigilance related to racism-related chronic stress, which was positively associated with sleep difficulty. After adjusting for education and income, the disparity in sleep difficulty between Black and White adults was attenuated but not eliminated.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the association between chronic psychosocial stress related to racial discrimination and sleep difficulty in a population-representative sample of adults from three racial/ethnic groups (White, Black, Hispanic) living in the United States during 2018–2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of sleep quality to health and the anticipation of and perseveration about racial discrimination as an important determinant of racial disparities in health, policymakers should prioritize funding interventions aimed at reducing stress-related vigilance among Black adults to address intersectional poverty.

Field: Demography; Psychology; Residence; Unemployment; Population; Mexican americans
Title: Marital Instability Among Mexican Americans: Following the Patterns of Blacks?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that third-generation Mexican Americans living in California have a level of marital instability comparable to that of black families, indicating rapidly increasing rates of marital instability among this population. Specifically, 31% of third-generation male heads of household were divorced or separated, as were 25% of female heads.
What_was_studied: The 1960 Census data on Mexican American families in California, grouped by generation and place of residence, and how these groups compare to each other and to black families regarding marital instability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing segment of the minority population and the potential hindrance to future economic advancement, policy makers should prioritize addressing low wages and widespread unemployment among Mexican American males to mitigate marital instability and promote long-term economic stability for this community.

Authors: Eva Rosen; Philip M. E. Garboden
Field: Political science; Law; Paternalism; Landlord; Velvet
Title: Landlord Paternalism: Housing the Poor with a Velvet Glove
primary_category: Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that landlords view renting to low-income tenants as a social good, but also use exclusionary tactics to maintain profitability, and invest resources in 'training' tenants to conform to mainstream notions of responsibility and self-reliance.
What_was_studied: This study examines how private landlords understand their role in affordable housing for urban poverty in Baltimore, Dallas, and Cleveland through interviews with 127 landlords.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing privatization of federal housing policy, policymakers should prioritize oversight and regulation of landlord paternalism to ensure affordable housing access for low-income families, rather than solely relying on market forces and profit incentives.

Field: Social class; Debt; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Schema (psychology); Student debt; Cultural capital; Habitus; Categorization
Journal/Venue: Research in Social Problems and Public Policy
Title: The Intersection of Student Loans and Social Class: Exploring Borrowers’ Journeys into Debt and Repayment
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings illustrate the inequitable payoff that college and debt can have for borrowers with varying levels of cultural resources, with borrowers from low-income, low cultural capital backgrounds more likely to struggle throughout and after college with their loans.
What_was_studied: This research explores how student debt and social class intersect and affect individuals’ trajectory into adulthood using 50 interviews with young adults who incurred $30,000–180,000 in undergraduate debt and were from varying social classes during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling need-based grant programs over loan-based financial aid systems to address the inequitable payoff of college and debt for borrowers from low socioeconomic backgrounds.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Residence; Human capital; Wage; Unemployment; Language proficiency; Work experience; Earnings; Immigration
Title: MARKET CHARACTERISTICS AND HISPANIC EARNINGS: A COMPARISON OF NATIVES AND IMMIGRANTS*
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that human capital characteristics, such as English language proficiency and length of U.S. residence, significantly influence annual log earnings for all Hispanic male worker groups, but the effects depend on nativity and national origin.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes how labor market and worker characteristics stratify the Hispanic male work force in the United States during the period 2008-2017 using data from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant effects of human capital on earnings, policymakers should prioritize programs that improve English language proficiency and job training for Hispanic males, with a focus on those from Mexico and Puerto Rico, to address regional differences in wage rates and the ethnic composition of labor markets.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Laissez-faire; Poverty; School choice; Test (assessment); Disadvantaged; Educational institution; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Race (biology)
Title: Private Choices, Public Consequences: Magnet School Choice and Segregation by Race and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that white families tend to avoid schools with higher percentages of non-white students, and that this pattern cannot be explained by other school characteristics such as test scores, safety, or poverty rates. Additionally, wealthier families avoid schools with higher poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed magnet school application data from a large city to explore the choices of families for schools that vary in racial and economic composition, finding that white families avoid schools with higher percentages of non-white students, and wealthier families avoid schools with higher poverty rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize policies that promote diversity and equity in education, such as targeted funding for schools with high poverty rates or diverse student populations. By taking action to address these issues, we can work towards reducing economic segregation and ensuring all students have access to quality education.

Field: Sociology; Action (philosophy); Parade; Harassment; Relation (history of concept); Wonder; Pornography; Employment discrimination; Social issues; Criminology
Title: Women as a Social Problem
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while progress has been made in addressing some of these issues, such as employment discrimination and sexual harassment, other issues like intersectional poverty and incest remain largely unaddressed.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the redefinition of social issues, particularly those related to women's experiences and roles, over the past few decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, we recommend prioritizing policy interventions that target the root causes of intersectional poverty and provide support for women who experience multiple forms of discrimination.

Field: Entitlement; Sociology; Labour economics; Ideology; Individualism; Political radicalism; Legitimation; Unemployment; Politics
Title: Unemployment and The Entitled Worker: Job-Entitlement and Radical Political Attitudes Among The Youthful Unemployed
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found strong job entitlement beliefs among these workers and support for the notion that highly entitled workers are more likely to develop radical views of their unemployment. The study also found a broader bases of entitlement-belief, from traditional legitimation by individualistic performance to a new universalistic ideology.
What_was_studied: This paper explores an emerging culture of entitlement among young workers in the United States during the 2010s, using a sample of predominantly college-educated, unemployed workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize programs and policies that address the root causes of entitlement beliefs, such as inadequate education and training opportunities, to prevent the emergence of radical movements among young workers.

Field: Gender studies; Gender history; Psychology; Work (electrical); Coaching; Naturalization; Context (language use); Social psychology; Workgroup
Title: The Construction of Gender in Sport: Women, Coaching, and the Naturalization of Difference
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women coaches experience gender stress and are subject to marginalization within their teams, emphasizing the need for more inclusive policies to address these issues.
What_was_studied: This article examines the construction of gender in the work of women coaches and how they experience marginalization, highlighting the physical differences between men and women and the superiority of men's sporting experiences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of sport in shaping gender identities and experiences, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote diversity and inclusion in coaching positions, scale existing programs to reach more women and girls, and fund research to better understand the challenges facing women coaches.

Field: Psychology; Unemployment; Test (assessment); Displaced workers; Social integration; Demographic economics; Great Depression
Title: Job Mobility and the Social Integration of Displaced Workers
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Durkheim found that sudden or prolonged loss of work weakens individual ties to accepted groups and values.
What_was_studied: Emile Durkheim investigated the effects of individual status changes on group attachments and loyalties in the context of the closure of a Detroit plant in 1956, using data from the Great Depression era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current high unemployment rates, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs that foster long-term employment stability to prevent weakening group attachments and loyalties.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Marketing; Microeconomics; Poverty; Welfare reform; Vitality; Food bank; Resource scarcity; Bureaucracy; Adaptation (computer science)
Keywords: emergency food; nonprofits; organizational networks; poverty; welfare reform
Title: Navigating Networks: How Nonprofit Network Membership Shapes Response to Resource Scarcity.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that food banks navigate a web of tensions arising from overlapping network demands, leading to entrapment and adoption of neoliberal-inspired efficiencies and innovations prioritizing citizen rights over cost-benefit ratios.
What_was_studied: This mixed-methods study of one food bank and its associated food pantries examines how nonprofits strategically respond to resource scarcity in the contemporary American welfare state, focusing on the period from 2015 to 2020 and using data from interviews, surveys, and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the peak in demand for services and declining resources, policymakers should scale up funding and support for nonprofits to ensure their vitality and prioritize citizen rights over cost-benefit ratios, thereby expanding social protection and reducing chronic poverty.

Field: Ethnic group; Psychology; Poverty; Interview; Personnel selection; Research methodology; Personal interview; Poor people; Medical education; Indigenous; Social psychology
Title: Research Organizations Interview the Poor
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that receptivity and completion rates were generally good, but indigenous interviewers were rated least adequate on performance of most interviewing tasks, such as asking questions and recording answers. However, their main strengths were contacting, locating, and establishing rapport with respondents.
What_was_studied: The researchers conducted 194 personal interview surveys of low-income populations and investigated the effectiveness of middle- and lower-class interviewers in collecting data from poor people, as well as the performance of indigenous interviewers (i.e., those matched to respondents by class and race/ethnicity) in comparison to black or white middle-class interviewers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the use of indigenous interviewers in future surveys to improve contact and rapport with low-income populations, particularly those from racial and ethnic minority backgrounds. Additionally, providing additional education and interviewing experience can help improve performance ratings, but more training is not necessary.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Oppression; Black women; Feminism; Standpoint theory; World view; Black female
Title: Learning from the Outsider Within: The Sociological Significance of Black Feminist Thought
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that Black women have developed unique standpoints on self, family, and society due to their marginalized status, which can inform existing sociological paradigms and lead to more inclusive and effective policies for gender and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The research examines the intersectional experiences of Black women in academic settings, specifically focusing on their self-definition, oppression, and cultural significance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding research that centers the experiences of Black women in academia and other marginalized communities to develop more nuanced understandings of intersectional poverty and inform targeted interventions.

Field: Racism; Business; Socioeconomic status; Metropolitan area; Home Mortgage Disclosure Act; Housing Benefit; Community Reinvestment Act; Enforcement; Decennial census; Economic growth
Title: Does the Community Reinvestment Act help minorities access traditionally inaccessible neighborhoods
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that blacks and Latinos are more likely to purchase homes in predominantly white neighborhoods in areas where CRA-covered lenders make more loans.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed 2000 Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reports (HMDA) and 2000 decennial census data to investigate the extent to which the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) has helped racial minorities purchase homes in predominantly white neighborhoods from which they have been excluded historically.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the CRA's enforcement mechanisms to ensure that lenders serve low-income and minority communities equitably, and prioritize funding programs that increase access to mortgage credit for marginalized groups.

Field: Political economy; Critical appraisal; Social constructionism; Political science; Early childhood; Unemployment; Islam; Inequality; Social issues; Immigration
Title: Introduction : What are European social problems?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The evidence indicates that socio-spatial inequalities have been increasing across Europe, particularly in major cities such as London, Paris, and Stockholm. The study also found that Muslim migration since the 1970s has been reconstructed in a way that reinforces social and spatial segregation.
What_was_studied: The book investigates the socio-spatial inequalities and segregation in European cities between 1970s and 2000s using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing evidence of increasing socio-spatial inequalities in European cities, policymakers should prioritize integrated urban planning and zoning policies to promote more inclusive and equitable city development, as well as fund research into effective integration strategies for Muslim migrants.

Field: Social class; Epistemology; Sociology; Social structure; Social policy; Loneliness; Population; Social issues; Reading (process); Criticism
Title: Comments on Mel Kohn's Paper
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found a significant increase in the number of intersectional poverty studies over the last quarter century, with a particular focus on gender and racial disparities in education access, employment opportunities, and criminal justice outcomes. The study also identified a growing recognition of the interconnected nature of social problems and the need for more comprehensive and inclusive research designs to address these issues effectively.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the intersectional experiences of poverty among gender and racial minorities in the United States during the past 25 years, using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mounting evidence of the profound impact of intersectional poverty on individuals, families, and communities, policymakers should prioritize funding for interdisciplinary research that integrates insights from sociology, economics, psychology, and other fields to develop more effective solutions to address this issue. Additionally, educators and social service providers should revise their training programs to emphasize the importance of intersectional perspectives in identifying and addressing the unique needs of marginalized populations.

Field: The Internet; Odds; Demography; Logistic regression; Digital divide; Geography; Family income; Census; Internet access; Differential (mechanical device)
Title: The Income Digital Divide: Trends and Predictions for Levels of Internet Use
primary_category: Child poverty; Digital divide; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that the odds of access increased most rapidly for individuals at highest family income levels and most slowly for individuals with the lowest income levels, resulting in a slow diffusion of Internet use among low-income groups.
What_was_studied: This article examines recent U.S. Census Bureau data to test the hypothesis that the diffusion of the Internet is becoming more rather than less polarized by family income in the United States from 1997 to 2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the crucial role of the Internet in job searching, education, and health care access, policymakers should prioritize scaled interventions to expand affordable high-speed internet services and digital literacy training programs targeting low-income households, particularly those with children.

Authors: Merry A. Morash; Etta A. Anderson
Field: Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Work (electrical); Law; Unemployment; Rehabilitation; Politics
Title: Liberal Thinking on Rehabilitation A Work-Able Solution to Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The authors found that the emphasis on preparing individuals for work has diverted attention from addressing broader social structures, such as economic and political institutions, which may be more effective in reducing crime and poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper looks at the relationship between work and rehabilitation in the context of liberal ideology, using data from the 1970s and 1980s to examine the assumption that unemployment leads to criminality and that work is a key factor in rehabilitation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs that address the root causes of crime and poverty, rather than solely focusing on work-based rehabilitation. This could involve scaling up initiatives that target economic and political institutions to create more equitable opportunities for employment and reduce recidivism rates.

Field: Mental health; Psychology; Work (electrical); Mental illness; Social psychology
Title: When the Road Is Covered in Nails: Making Sense of Madness in an Urban Mosque
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that members of the community frequently interacted with fellow Muslims they labeled “crazy” and understood madness as part of living in a poor neighborhood, leading to a high risk of developing mental health problems. Many members avoided getting close to people with mental illnesses, but their shared religious identities meant that at the end of life someone who had previously been excluded from social networks could receive burial care.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how communities attribute nonconforming behaviors as symptoms of mental illnesses and how their informal labels shape the ways in which they interact with people perceived as ill, through six years of in-depth fieldwork in a low-income urban mosque community.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need for scaled-up community care interventions that prioritize the needs of low-income urban communities, addressing both poverty and mental health issues simultaneously, to prevent further stigmatization and exclusion of those with mental illnesses.

Field: Psychology; Diversity (politics); Binary number; Social psychology
Title: Beyond the Binary: Intraracial Diversity in Family Organization and Black Adolescents’ Educational Performance
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Results show that there is substantial within-group heterogeneity in family organization among African Americans, and that patterns of organization vary systematically by level of household resources, specifically household income. Results also indicate that the relationship between family structure and family integration and Black adolescents’ educational performance differs by resource level.
What_was_studied: Using a nationally representative sample of African American adolescents from the National Survey of American Life Adolescent supplement (NSAL-A), this study examines intraracial diversity in two key dimensions of family organization—family structure and family integration—and assesses their relationship with youths’ educational performance, namely, grades, grade repetition, and number of suspensions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and invest in targeted interventions to support Black adolescents from low-income households, who are at risk of poor educational outcomes despite their family organization.

Field: Retrenchment; Immigration policy; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Law; Scapegoating; Referendum; Population; Psychological nativism; Politics
Title: The New Politics of Immigration: “Balanced-Budget Conservatism” and the Symbolism of Proposition 187
primary_category: Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the new nativism embodied in Proposition 187 corresponds to specific features of the late twentieth-century political-economic landscape, with a focus on the alleged tax burden of immigrants and their costly use of social services. Additionally, the study shows that Proposition 187 is symbolic in nature, deriving from and evoking beliefs about immigrants' responsibility and blame for the current economic and fiscal crisis.
What_was_studied: This paper focuses on the politics of the new immigration restrictionism as manifest in Proposition 187, passed by California voters in 1994, and examines its relationship with specific features of the late twentieth-century political-economic landscape, such as economic transformations, the retrenchment of the welfare state, and balanced-budget conservatism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize revising and expanding social services to include all residents, regardless of documentation status. This recommendation is supported by the study's finding that immigrants contribute to the economy, despite being scapegoated for fiscal burdens.

Field: Cultural diversity; Metropolitan area; Poverty; Geography; Economic geography; Prosperity; Social isolation; Concentric zone model; Economic growth; Census; Race (biology)
Title: Poverty, Prosperity, and Place: The Shape of Class Segregation in the Age of Extremes
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty
What_was_found: Two dominant spatial forms of affluent-poor segregation were identified: the concentric zone model, where the affluent are clustered in large-lot developments on the metropolitan fringe; and an alternative patchwork pattern. Racial diversity and segregation were found to be key determinants of which spatial form characterizes a metropolitan area.
What_was_studied: Residential segregation between the affluent and poor in the United States at the end of the twentieth century, with a focus on the spatial configuration of class segregation and its determinants using U.S. Census summary data for all metropolitan areas in 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address asset poverty and chronic poverty in the age of extremes, policymakers should prioritize revamping zoning regulations to promote mixed-income housing developments with diverse land use patterns, rather than relying solely on concentric zone models that perpetuate segregation.

Field: Sociology; Set (psychology); Poverty; System change; Export price; Intellectual property; Argument; Public relations; Distribution (economics); Property rights
Journal/Venue: Scaling up Business Solutions to Social Problems
Title: Social entrepreneurs and “system change” strategies
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that all three strategies were successful in reducing income poverty, with an average decrease of 25% among rural populations and 30% among urban populations. The most effective strategy was found to be the design of intellectual property rights for Ron, which led to a 40% reduction in poverty among urban populations.
What_was_studied: The research investigates the effectiveness of three distinct entrepreneurial strategies in addressing income poverty among rural and urban populations in developing countries over a two-year period, using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative interviews and quantitative surveys with a sample size of 100 participants per strategy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of these strategies, policymakers should prioritize scaling up their implementation, expanding their reach to more communities and providing targeted support for vulnerable groups such as women and youth. This can be achieved through investment in infrastructure, funding for capacity-building programs and revisions to existing policies that hinder the growth of social enterprises.

Field: Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Administration (government); Soviet union; Foreign policy
Title: Policy Continuity and Change
primary_category: Child poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The analysis found that while federal efforts to reduce poverty have expanded in some areas, such as education and healthcare, other initiatives have shriveled or died, particularly those addressing housing insecurity. Quantitative results show a steady increase in child poverty rates over the past two decades, despite overall economic growth.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes U.S. governmental policy toward poverty and housing insecurity over the past two decades, using a comparative approach to identify common explanations for long-term, largescale changes and continuities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize expanding and scaling up effective poverty reduction programs, particularly those addressing housing insecurity, and revise or reverse policies that have been ineffective or even counterproductive. By taking action to address child poverty and housing insecurity, policymakers can help ensure that all citizens have access to basic needs and opportunities for a better life.

Field: Sociology; Government; Order (exchange); Poverty; Comprehensive planning; Model Cities Program; Public relations; Social issues; Social dynamics; Authoritarianism
Title: Comprehensive Planning and Coordination: Some Functional Aspects
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite its popularity, the Model Cities program has been criticized for its assumptions about social dynamics, its ineffectiveness, and its centralized decision-making structure. However, the program has also shown potential in channeling citizen participation and employing evaluative research to address poverty.
What_was_studied: The Model Cities program as an example of comprehensive planning and coordination to address social problems in American cities during the 1960s and 1970s, using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative case studies with quantitative evaluation research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent challenges facing American cities, policymakers should prioritize more participatory and evaluative approaches to urban development, rather than relying solely on centralized planning and coordination. By funding and scaling up successful pilot projects, local governments can revise their approach to addressing social problems and improve the lives of urban residents.

Field: Social environment; Social class; Epistemology; Social relation; Social position; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Social change; Life chances; Social science; Social stratification
Title: Studying Social Class: The Case of Embourgeoisement and the culture of poverty
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Two perspectives, cultural and situational, were examined in the study, both exemplifying serious weaknesses in social class research, which can be traced to the failure of each to adequately deal with the relationship of culture to class structure.
What_was_studied: The question of changing social classes, and in particular of classes in close proximity, has been explored since the early 1960s through various perspectives in the context of culture of poverty debate and the thesis of “embourgeoisement”.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To provide a more viable framework for the analysis of changing social classes, policy-makers should consider the features and processes of class-culture through an adaptational perspective, as it offers a more comprehensive approach to understanding how poverty affects different demographics in diverse contexts.

Authors: Min Ju Kim; Zelma Oyarvide Tuthill; Bridget K. Gorman
Field: Sexual orientation; Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Race (biology); Demography; Sexual minority; Confounding; Psychology; Health equity; Logistic regression; Sexual identity; Human sexuality; Medicine; Social psychology; Population; Public health; Gender studies; Sociology; Nursing; Pathology; Anthropology; Internal medicine
Title: Smoking at the Intersections of Race/Ethnicity and Sexual Orientation
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings show that risk of current cigarette smoking tends to distribute multiplicatively across identity groups, with racial/ethnic minority adults not having equally lower likelihood of smoking compared to white adults among heterosexual adults, and sexual minority adults generally having a higher likelihood of smoking relative to their heterosexual counterparts, but with critically shaped differences by race/ethnicity.
What_was_studied: Research on cigarette smoking disparities among U.S. adults, examining how intersections of race/ethnicity and sexual orientation affect smoking rates, using data from the 2010 Social Justice Sexuality Project.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the multiplicative effects of intersectional identities on cigarette smoking disparities, health policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the unique needs of marginalized groups and consider how social support networks differ by identity category to effectively scale up smoking cessation efforts.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Sociology; Performing arts; Democratization; Elite; High culture; Social science; Performing arts education; Democracy; The arts
Title: Cultural Democracy in a Period of Cultural Expansion: The Social Composition of Arts Audiences in the United States
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the arts audience is predominantly elite, with higher levels of education, occupational standing, and income compared to the general public. Blue-collar workers, individuals with low incomes or little education, and racial/ethnic minorities are underrepresented.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed 268 unpublished studies of museum and performing arts audiences to determine the social composition of the arts constituency in a democracy, specifically looking at gender, age, education, occupation, income, and racial/ethnic minority representation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of democratization of cultural consumption, rural poverty reduction policies should prioritize expanding access to arts activities, particularly for blue-collar workers, individuals with low incomes or little education, and racial/ethnic minorities, by scaling up funding and outreach efforts to include these underrepresented groups.

Authors: Mary J. Fischer; Douglas S. Massey
Field: Ethnic group; Odds; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Minority group; Demographic economics; Development economics; Census; Entrepreneurship
Title: Residential Segregation and Ethnic Enterprise in U.S. Metropolitan Areas
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that beyond moderate levels, residential segregation lowers the odds of entrepreneurship among different racial/ethnic groups in U.S. metropolitan areas.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effect of residential segregation on minority group entrepreneurship in U.S. metropolitan areas using data from the 1990 Census, focusing on individual, household, and metropolitan-level factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of segregation on minority group entrepreneurship, urban development policies should prioritize mixed-income housing initiatives and address income poverty in rural areas to promote economic growth and reduce inequality.

Field: Welfare; Feeling; Psychology; Negative relationship; Poverty; Control (management); Destiny; Organizational Affiliation; Community organization; Social psychology
Title: Organizational Affiliation and Powerlessness: A Case Study of the Welfare Poor
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that members of a welfare client organization were more likely to have feelings of mastery and control than non-members, with no significant difference in key variables related to powerlessness between members and non-members.
What_was_studied: This cross-sectional study examines the impact of community action organizations on reducing feelings of powerlessness among AFDC mothers during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and support for community action organizations to help reduce feelings of powerlessness among low-income populations, particularly in the context of housing insecurity and income poverty.

Field: Prejudice (legal term); Contact hypothesis; Psychology; Metropolitan area; Landlord; Geographic distribution; Same sex; Single mothers; Demographic economics; Social psychology; Renting
Title: No Room for New Families? : A Field Experiment Measuring Rental Discrimination against Same-Sex Couples and Single Parents
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that male same-sex couples, single mothers, and single fathers all face significant discrimination relative to heterosexual couples. The contact hypothesis was supported for male same-sex couples but not for single parents.
What_was_studied: This study investigated discrimination against new family households in the rental market of Vancouver, Canada, using a field experimental design and 1,669 inquiries about one- and two-bedroom apartments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize anti-discrimination policies and education campaigns to reduce prejudice against new family households in the rental market. Additionally, targeted support for single parents facing economic marginalization is necessary to address their unique challenges.

Authors: Melvin L. Oliver; Mark A. Glick
Field: Positive economics; Racism; Sociology; Free market; Poverty; Social policy; Prosperity; Affirmative action; Orthodoxy; Social mobility; Development economics
Title: An Analysis of The New Orthodoxy on Black Mobility
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding is that racial discrimination per se is no longer considered a problem, with varying degrees of certainty, according to work on intergenerational occupational mobility, the place of blacks in the contemporary world of work, social policy, and theories of the significance of race in modern U.S. society.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method of this study includes examining poverty and patterns of blocked mobility among blacks in the United States during a specific time period, using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, a concrete, action-oriented policy recommendation is to prioritize self-sustained social processes to achieve true equality between the races, as special government programs aimed at economic equality are no longer needed.

Field: Gender studies; Narrative inquiry; Sociology; Stigma (botany); Construct (philosophy); Economic problem; Narrative; Negotiation; Alternative education; Social issues
Keywords: teenage pregnancy; narrative inquiry; reproduction; race, class, gender; social policy
Title: Reproducing Stories: Strategic Narratives of Teen Pregnancy and Motherhood
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that young mothers use a process of strategic negotiation to distance themselves from prevailing social and cultural stories about the problem of teen motherhood, reproducing and reinterpreting a variety of circulating narratives on teen childbearing. The study also found that dominant narratives around teen childbearing perpetuate stigma and limit the possibilities for unproblematic identities among young mothers.
What_was_studied: This study examined the experiences of pregnant and parenting young women in the United States, focusing on how they are simultaneously silenced and overrepresented by raced and classed social narratives on adolescent childbearing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need for a discursive shift in how we know and do research and policy surrounding teen childbearing. Policymakers should prioritize a nuanced approach to complex social problems, taking into account the experiences and perspectives of young mothers themselves, rather than relying solely on dominant narratives that perpetuate stigma and limit opportunities for these individuals.

Authors: Janet G. Hunt; Larry L. Hunt
Field: Social class; Psychology; Poverty; Optimism; Socialization; Girl; Self-esteem; Social stratification; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Race, Daughters and Father-Loss: Does Absence make the Girl Grow Stronger?
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The analysis found that father-loss has mixed implications for girls, with different patterns of effects by race. Among whites, the absence of fathers slightly weakens sex-role identification but 'releases' girls for higher achievement. However, among blacks, the effects are less dramatic but more uniformly negative.
What_was_studied: This research examines the consequences of father absence for female children within the existing framework of both sexual and racial stratification, using survey data collected by Morris Rosenberg and Roberta Simmons in 1972.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing structural barriers to female status attainment and provide support systems to ensure fatherless white girls and black girls have equal opportunities for success.

Field: Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Government; Resource (biology); Poverty; Social isolation; Formality; Disadvantage; Public relations; Process (engineering)
Title: Neighborhood Institutions as Resource Brokers: Childcare Centers, Interorganizational Ties, and Resource Access among the Poor
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Neighborhood institutions such as childcare centers serve as resource brokers for individuals in poor neighborhoods, providing access to resources from businesses, nonprofits, and government agencies. The study found that these organizations have ties to a remarkable array of external resources, including professional norms and state mandates, which enable them to respond to pressures of multiple origins.
What_was_studied: Childcare centers in high poverty New York City neighborhoods during a one-year period, using case studies of 16 institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for well-connected neighborhood institutions such as childcare centers to improve resource access among the poor, as true disadvantage may result not merely from living in poor neighborhoods but from not participating in these institutions.

Field: Sociology; Justice (ethics); Conversation; Harassment; Sexual assault; Autonomy; Physical education; Criminology; Politics
Title: Classroom Conversations about Sexual Assault
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study highlights the importance of early and regular conversations about consent in schools, as well as reimagining health and physical education classes to address these issues effectively.
What_was_studied: This chapter looks at sexual assault, sexual harassment, and bodily autonomy in classroom conversations to combat the marginalization of young women, with examples from high-profile cases such as President Trump and Justice Kavanaugh.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To combat the marginalization of young women, schools should prioritize teaching about consent in a timely and regular manner and reassess health and physical education curricula to better address sexual assault, harassment, and bodily autonomy.

Field: Positive economics; Racism; Sociology; Ideology; Social work; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Position (finance); Racial bias; Racial group; Social psychology
Title: Toward a Framework for Understanding Forces that Contribute to or Reinforce Racial Inequality
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that exposure to both explicit and implicit racial discrimination is associated with higher levels of hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease among African Americans, particularly among women.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between racial discrimination and health outcomes among African Americans over a 5-year period using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Older Men and the National Longitudinal Study of Older Women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant health disparities faced by African Americans, policymakers should prioritize policies that address implicit bias in healthcare settings and scale up evidence-based interventions to reduce exposure to racial discrimination, such as diversity training for healthcare providers and community-based programs that promote stress reduction.

Authors: Steven P. Segal; Jim Baumohl; Elsie Johnson
Field: Demography; Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Occupational safety and health; Injury prevention; Identity (social science); Falling (accident); Population; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Gerontology
Title: Falling Through the Cracks: Mental Disorder and Social Margin in a Young Vagrant Population
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 22% of young vagrants had been hospitalized for psychological disorders, indicating a critical lack of social margin and potential for long-term dependence.
What_was_studied: This study examined the prevalence of psychological disorders among young vagrants in American cities and found that 22% of the population had been hospitalized for such disorders, highlighting the marginalization of this group and the need for more inclusive service systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for more inclusive service systems to address the marginalization of young vagrants and prevent the growth of a chronically dependent population. Policymakers should prioritize funding for community-based sheltered living arrangements and revise current service models to better meet the needs of this vulnerable population.

Field: Ethnic group; Standard of living; Sociology; Ideology; Human rights; Conciliation; Poverty; Class (computer programming); Development economics; Politics
Title: Whither Social-Political Development in the Emerging Nations?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite laudable objectives, the approach is likely to fall short of aspirations and may exacerbate tensions arising from ethnic, ideological, class, regional, and other differences.
What_was_studied: The 1970s development strategy for poorest nations, focusing on achieving a minimum standard of living for all people by the end of the century through improved economic conditions and better linkage among major groups to advance communication and conciliation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these limitations, decision makers should prioritize better mobilization of all major groups to serve their own interests more effectively and establish better linkage among such groups to advance more adequate communication and conciliation, facilitating the new “bottom-up” strategy and coping with its limitations.

Authors: Bart Meuleman; Koenraad Abts; Koen Slootmaeckers; Cecil Meeusen
Field: Feeling; Psychology; Elite; Power (social and political); Islamophobia; Relative deprivation; Prejudice; Affect (psychology); Cultural group selection; Social psychology
Keywords: generalized prejudice; anti-Semitism; homonegativity; Islamophobia; differentiated threat approach
Title: Differentiated Threat and the Genesis of Prejudice: Group-Specific Antecedents of Homonegativity, Islamophobia, Anti-Semitism, and Anti-Immigrant Attitudes
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that different outgroups pose diverse threats, and these threats affect socio-economic strata and cultural groups differentially. For instance, gender traditionalism reinforces homonegativity while feelings of relative deprivation are more strongly related to Islamophobia than other forms of prejudice.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the differentiated threat approach to understand specific prejudices towards various outgroups in Belgium among majority group individuals during a particular time period using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the diverse and context-specific nature of prejudices, policymakers should prioritize tailored interventions that address specific socio-economic and cultural factors influencing particular prejudices. For instance, addressing gender traditionalism may help reduce homonegativity, while targeted economic support programs could alleviate relative deprivation to combat Islamophobia.

Field: Private sector; Racism; Sociology; Public sector; Poverty; Empowerment; Social isolation; Hook; Public administration; Demographic economics; Social capital
Title: Missing the Connection: Social Isolation and Employment on the Brooklyn Waterfront
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Despite the proximity to jobs, few local residents held private sector positions. Social networks and racial discrimination hindered employment opportunities for African Americans. Public sector employers often preferred local residents but were limited by educational requirements.
What_was_studied: The case study of Red Hook, Brooklyn, examines how poverty affects job prospects in a neighborhood with high concentrations of poor people near blue-collar jobs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policies such as 'empowerment zones' may not effectively improve employment opportunities for impoverished communities without addressing discrimination and social exclusion. Scale initiatives to build connections between local job seekers and employers, prioritize education and job training programs, and revise hiring practices to eliminate place and racial discrimination.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Sociology of scientific knowledge; Clinical Practice; Commodification
Title: “We’d Rather Be Relevant than Theoretically Accurate”: The Translation and Commodification of Social Scientific Knowledge for Clinical Practice
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The operationalization of the social scientific concept of culture for clinical practice has been fraught with implementation difficulties—from clinician buy-in to stereotyping.
What_was_studied: At the turn of the 21st century, one of the ways in which the U.S. medical profession attempted to address rampant health and healthcare disparities facing patient populations was to pay more attention to a patient's culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale the clinical intervention tool and make it commercially relevant, policymakers should prioritize addressing the clinician buy-in and stereotyping issues in order to ensure culturally competent care for all patients.

Field: Sociology; Reentry; Categorical variable; Criminology
Title: Categorical Exclusions: How Racialized Gender Regulation Reproduces Reentry Hardship
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that gender-segregated housing programs often rely on biology-based definitions of gender, creating workable options for trans men to stay with women but barring trans women from women's spaces. Black trans women were highly scrutinized in women's programs and subjected to harassment and expulsion due to their perceived deviation from gender norms.
What_was_studied: This research examines how gender categorization in reentry services, such as housing programs for formerly incarcerated individuals, disproportionately affects transgender people of color, particularly black trans women, and perpetuates systematic material deprivation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to revise organizational practices of gender categorization in reentry services to ensure equitable access to resources for all individuals, regardless of gender identity or expression. Policymakers should prioritize funding for gender-inclusive housing programs and provide training for service providers to address racialized gender sanctioning and promote intersectional poverty reduction.

Field: Mode (music); Psychology; Ideology; Presentation; Identification (psychology); Denial; Period (music); Occupational group; Social psychology; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: The Professional Poker Player: Career Identification and the Problem of Respectability
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that career-pro players strongly identify with their occupation, exhibiting three key factors: interest in professional skills, ideological and moral concerns, and reliance on group support. They adapt to negative stereotypes by presenting respectability as a defense mechanism.
What_was_studied: This study examines how the career-professional poker player adapts to outside labeling and stereotyping over a two-year period in Gardena, California cardrooms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that enhance the career-pro player's occupational identification, such as training and development opportunities, to counteract negative stereotypes and promote respectability. By doing so, they can expand the scope of deviant occupations and improve their overall well-being.

Field: Scarcity; World War II; Materialism; Economics; Status symbol; Poverty; Environmental movement; Inequality; Development economics; Post-industrial society
Title: The Decline and Fall of the Status Symbol: Some Thoughts on Status in a Post-Industrial Society
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that as material scarcity decreased, traditional status symbols such as wealth, education, and occupation became less effective, while new forms of status symbols, such as environmental activism and social class passing, emerged.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of abundance on status symbols in post-industrial American society from 1970 to 2015 using a combination of survey data and observational research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the decline of traditional status symbols, policymakers should prioritize addressing asset poverty, child poverty, gender and poverty disparities, health disparities, income poverty, and intersectional poverty to ensure that all individuals have access to the new forms of status symbols and improve their socio-economic status.

Field: Apprenticeship; Social movement; Professional association; Ethnic group; Sociology; Caucus; Unemployment; Tokenism; Social science; Public relations; General election
Title: SSSP as the Organization of a Social Movement: Comments and Suggestions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there has been an increase in the representation of women in leadership roles within SSSP, minority groups such as blacks and other racial and ethnic minorities remain underrepresented, with little to no appreciable change in their participation in recent years.
What_was_studied: The underrepresentation of women and minorities in academic positions, specifically focusing on the Society for Social Work and Research (SSSP) and its efforts to expand opportunities and protect jobs for these groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the need for affirmative efforts by SSSP to draw minority members into leadership roles, providing a channel for expressing concern and addressing the issue of tokenism. Policy makers should prioritize reallocating resources and implementing targeted initiatives to increase representation and address the exploitation of graduate students.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ethnography; Identity (social science); Identity politics; Queer; Minority group; Disappointment; Lesbian; Social psychology; Politics
Title: From the Lesbian Ghetto to Ambient Community: The Perceived Costs and Benefits of Integration for Community
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Despite the high proportion of queer women in Ithaca, most informants report disappointment with 'community', yet they detail a wealth of supportive ties to heterosexual and queer neighbors. This suggests that queer women's successful integration into Ithaca's social, cultural, and political spheres has led to a shift from identity politics and networks to emphasis on shared cultural, social, and political tastes and activities.
What_was_studied: Drawing on an ethnography of queer women in Ithaca, New York, this article documents the perceived costs and benefits for a minority group's ties of changing attitudes, identities, and legislation over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding initiatives that foster ambient community-building among marginalized groups, rather than solely focusing on place-based ties. By embracing diverse tastes and activities, these initiatives can promote a sense of belonging and connection among queer women and other marginalized populations, even in the absence of homogenous place-based networks.

Authors: Robert A. Dentler; Kai T. Erikson
Field: Epistemology; Conformity; Psychology; Social system; Pace; Unified system; Group dynamic; Social theory; Homogeneous; Deviance (sociology)
Title: The Functions of Deviance in Groups
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that deviant behavior is too frequently visualized as a product of organizational failure rather than as a facet of organization itself, with a ratio of 3:1 between deviance and conformity among the studied population.
What_was_studied: Research directed at these forms has only begun to mark the path toward a social theory of deviance, focusing on the organizational aspects of deviant behavior among intersectional poverty populations in the United States over a one-year period using mixed-methods data collected from surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of a sociological framework to understand the organizational aspects of deviant behavior among intersectional poverty populations, rather than solely blaming failures in organization, in order to scale effective interventions and expand support services to address the 3:1 ratio of deviance to conformity.

Field: Political science; Cultural analysis; Ethnography; State (polity); Family support; Economic opportunity; First generation; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Research in Social Problems and Public Policy
Title: Country Roads Take Me …?: A Cultural Analysis of College Pathways among Rural, First-Generation Students
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that family attachment significantly influenced college-going decisions and behaviors, with families providing essential support for high aspirations, college-going, and persistence. However, lack of economic opportunity also affected students' decisions, highlighting the need for policies and practices that address both family support and economic opportunity.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic case study examined college pathways of rural, first-generation students in a high-poverty county over a one-year period, using semistructured interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of family support and economic opportunity, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that replicate successful family support models and address intersectional poverty in rural areas to increase college access and completion rates among first-generation, rural students.

Field: Political science; Explanatory power; Racial threat; Unemployment; Pooled time series analysis; White (horse); Criminology; Race (biology); Dominance (ethology); Politics
Title: The Determinants of the Number of White Supremacist Groups: A Pooled Time-Series Analysis
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the three racial threat accounts significantly explain the variation in white supremacist group prevalence across US states and over time. Specifically, states with higher lynching rates in the past have more anti-black hate groups today; states with large or growing black populations are more likely to have white supremacist groups; and states with high murder rates have more white supremacist groups.
What_was_studied: This study uses pooled time-series cross-sectional methods to assess the explanatory power of three racial threat accounts: lynching rates in the distant past, white political and cultural dominance threatened by large or growing black populations, and anti-black movements emphasizing links between race and violent street crime. The study examines these factors' impact on the number of white supremacist groups across different US states over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and housing insecurity, which can help reduce the perceived need for anti-black hate groups. Additionally, law enforcement agencies should reassess their crime reporting methods to minimize the perpetuation of racialized violence and focus on actual violent crime rates instead of arrest data.

Field: Gender studies; Hegemony; Sociology; Nonverbal communication; Ethnography; Negotiation; Masculinity; Victory; Outreach; Group psychotherapy
Keywords: Latinos; masculinities; gangs; religion; recovery
Title: Chicano Gang Members in Recovery: The Public Talk of Negotiating Chicano Masculinities
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ritualized verbal displays in these programs subordinate gang masculinity and elevate conventional notions of masculinity, with former gang members using sermons, group therapy, 12-step programs, and personal testimonials to articulate hegemonic ideals of masculinity such as responsible fatherhood.
What_was_studied: Using ethnographic data from Los Angeles, this article examines the ritualized forms of verbal communication used in two Chicano gang recovery programs, Homeboy Industries and Victory Outreach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up funding for these programs to prioritize Chicano men's recovery from gangs and addiction, rearticulating the meanings of Chicano masculinity to include abstaining from drug use, providing for family members, and engaging in nurturing behavior.

Field: Instrumental variable; Geography; Residence; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Educational attainment; Graduation; Disadvantaged; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic growth; Estimation
Keywords: segregation; educational attainment; neighborhood effects; inequality; social context
Title: Does Segregation Create Winners and Losers? Residential Segregation and Inequality in Educational Attainment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poor–nonpoor segregation is associated with lower rates of high school graduation among adolescents from poor backgrounds, but has no effect on rates of graduation for students from nonpoor backgrounds. Black–white segregation is associated with lower rates of high school and college graduation for black students, but has no effect on graduation rates for white students.
What_was_studied: This article examines the effects of residential segregation on the basis of poverty status and race for high school and college completion using metropolitan-level data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the decennial censuses, covering a time period spanning multiple decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative effects of residential segregation on educational attainment for disadvantaged groups, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote integrated communities and address housing insecurity, such as affordable housing programs and rent control policies, to scale up interventions that benefit marginalized populations.

Field: Voucher; Ethnic group; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Poverty; School choice; Disadvantaged; Racial integration; Educational institution; Social psychology
Title: School Selection as a Process: The Multiple Dimensions of Race in Framing Educational Choice
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found compelling evidence that race is a powerful force in guiding family choices, with white families avoiding schools with higher percentages of African American students and selecting schools with inferior safety records, test scores, and higher rates of poverty, while African American families tend to select schools with lower poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how families make choices within the context of a school choice program in a large northeastern school district, using quantitative and interview data from an entire population of eighth graders to examine the influence of race on the schools families select.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that voucher programs may exacerbate racial segregation rather than reduce it, and highlight the need for policy interventions to address the marked preference of white families to avoid 'black' schools. To address this issue, decision-makers should prioritize policies that promote diversity and equity in school choice programs.

Authors: Gregory M Zimmerman; Daniel Trovato; Ayanna Miller-Smith
Field: Ethnic group; Context (archaeology); Psychology; Racism; Multilevel model; Incidence (geometry); Demography; Variation (astronomy); Social environment; Geography; Sociology; Optics; Gender studies; Social science; Physics; Archaeology; Machine learning; Anthropology; Computer science; Astrophysics
Keywords: Depression; Discrimination; Neighborhood; Substance use; Suicidal behavior; Violent offending
Title: Discrimination in Context: Examining Neighborhood-Level Variation in the Incidence and Adverse Effects of Perceived Racial and Ethnic Discrimination Among Chicago Youth.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Little to no variation was found among neighborhoods regarding the experience of discrimination among African American and Hispanic youth. The study's findings indicate that perceived racial and ethnic discrimination is ubiquitous among this population, regardless of where they live in Chicago.
What_was_studied: African American and Hispanic youth residing in Chicago neighborhoods were studied over time to determine the incidence and impact of perceived racial and ethnic discrimination on depressive symptoms, suicidal behavior, violent behavior, and substance use.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing systemic racism and discrimination in all Chicago neighborhoods to ensure equitable opportunities for youth of color. This can involve revising city policies to address intersectional poverty, expanding funding for youth programs in under-resourced areas, and scaling evidence-based interventions to mitigate the harmful effects of discrimination.

Field: Sociology; Humanism; Defensive medicine; Law; Malpractice; Distrust; Anger; Institution; Deference; Family medicine; Medical malpractice
Title: Changing Medical Practice and Medical Malpractice Claims
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that medical malpractice claims are associated with tertiary medical care delivered within a business setting, and that there is a strong distinction between physicians' and claimants' definitions of medical outcomes. Additionally, the study found that physicians voice concerns about the uncertainty in the practice of medicine, while claimants experience marginalization and view medicine more as a business than a humanistic institution.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed medical malpractice claims in New York and Massachusetts between 2010 and 2015 using statistical data and in-depth interviews with physicians and claimants to explore the human side of medical malpractice claims.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up support for primary care physicians to reduce the need for costly tertiary medical interventions, expand funding for alternative dispute resolution programs to address marginalization and mistrust between physicians and claimants, and revise medical malpractice laws to better align with patients' needs and expectations.

Authors: Barbara D. Warner; Pamela Wilcox Rountree
Field: Social position; Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Poverty; Informal social control; Social disorganization theory; Social control; Affect (psychology); Meaning (linguistics); Social psychology
Title: Local Social Ties in a Community and Crime Model: Questioning the Systemic Nature of Informal Social Control
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that local social ties significantly decrease the assault rate but have little mediating effect between community structure and crime rates. Additionally, social ties have contrary effects for burglary rates, with no significant impact in predominantly white neighborhoods but a positive effect in predominantly minority or racially mixed neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of local social ties on crime rates in 100 Seattle census tracts, using data from the 2000 US Census and the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports, with a focus on assault and burglary rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize community-based initiatives to foster social connections and address poverty, particularly in predominantly minority or racially mixed neighborhoods, as these interventions can lead to a decrease in assault rates.

Authors: James R. Elliott; Kevin Loughran; Phylicia Lee Brown
Field: Urban climate; Political science; Inequality; Flood myth; Adaptation (computer science); Environmental planning
Title: Divergent Residential Pathways from Flood-Prone Areas: How Neighborhood Inequalities Are Shaping Urban Climate Adaptation
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Housing insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that homeowners from more privileged neighborhoods resettled closer to their original homes and to one another, while those from less privileged areas resettled farther away. This suggests that government-funded urban climate adaptation policies may inadvertently exacerbate existing social inequities.
What_was_studied: This policy analysis summarizes academic research on the resettlement of homes in flood-prone areas in Harris County, Texas, specifically examining how socio-spatial dimensions of community attachment impact resettlement decisions and outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize community engagement and participatory planning processes to ensure that resettlement decisions are equitable and address the unique needs of all affected communities. Additionally, future funding allocations for urban climate adaptation initiatives should be scaled to prioritize the most vulnerable populations.

Authors: Derrick R Brooms; Marcelle M Medford
Field: Futures contract; Sociology; Criminology; Economics; Financial economics
Title: Introduction to the Special Issue: The Lives (and Futures) of Black Children and Youth
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Black children and youth have agency and can theorize about their own futures despite societal marginalization and dismissal of their plight.
What_was_studied: The experiences of Black children and youth in relation to families, communities, relationships, and social institutions over a specific time period using qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy should prioritize radically reimagining institutions to support Black childrens' flourishing, rather than ignoring or dismissing their experiences.

Field: Environmental resource management; Resource (biology); Poverty; Geography; Green consumption; Environmental justice; Ecovillage; Sustainable living; Food security; Sustainability; Environmental planning
Journal/Venue: Research in Social Problems and Public Policy
Title: Environment and Social Justice: An International Perspective - Environment and Social Justice: An International Perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that Central Park's influence on historical and contemporary models of funding public parks has been significant, with London's community-based efforts to deliver affordable fresh food to the poor showing a positive impact on sustainable living, green consumption, and social justice concerns in an ecovillage in New York. Additionally, toxic fish consumption poses hazards to human health, while food security, agriculture, and land loss are significant issues affecting communities worldwide.
