Energy and resource loss in host communities has been linked to poverty in rural Trinidad and Nigeria, and spatial analyses techniques have revealed important insights into siting and toxic releases.
What_was_studied: This volume examines domestic and international environmental issues from an environmental justice perspective, focusing on urban environmental issues and sustainability, water resources and hazards of toxic fish consumption, food security, agriculture, and land loss, energy and resource loss in host communities, and diversity and environmental attitudes, using spatial analyses techniques and national studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to scale up investments in sustainable living initiatives, such as community-based food delivery programs, to address income poverty and gender disparities. Additionally, policymakers must prioritize resource loss in host communities by funding renewable energy sources and supporting sustainable agriculture practices to mitigate the negative impacts of extractive industries. Finally, spatial analyses techniques should be employed to identify areas with high levels of toxic releases and inform environmental policy decisions.

Field: Welfare; Sociology; Government; Working class; Law; State (polity); Aid to Families with Dependent Children; Pension; Family life; Nuclear family; Criminology
Title: DEPENDENT CHILDREN, CHILD CUSTODY, AND THE MOTHERS' PENSIONS: THE TRANSFORMATION OF STATE-FAMILY RELATIONS IN THE EARLY 20th CENTURY*
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that rather than progressively eroding traditional parental rights, the state has sometimes supported family unity and parental prerogatives. The Mothers' Pension program, an early 20th century public assistance program, gave parents child custody rights they had earlier been denied and buttressed family relations that otherwise would have been broken.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the evolution of government programs for dependent children in the United States from colonial times to the early 20th century, with a focus on child custody and the changing roles of women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize supporting families with dependent children by expanding the Mothers' Pension program and other early government programs for dependent children, rather than scaling back or abolishing them. This could help reinforce parent-child ties and support family unity, particularly for working-class families.

Authors: David S. Meyer; Deana A. Rohlinger
Field: Social movement; Sociology; Social change; Collective action; New social movements; Social science; Legitimacy; Reputation; Social dynamics; Resource mobilization; Environmental ethics
Title: Big Books and Social Movements: A Myth of Ideas and Social Change
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that four books published in the early 1960s are often credited with spurring important social movements and government action, but a more nuanced history reveals distortions and omissions that oversimplify the origins of these movements.
What_was_studied: The study examines the 'big book myth' of social movements in the 1960s and how it influences our understanding of gender and poverty issues today.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Government actors should revise their understanding of social movement origins to better address intersectional poverty issues in the present day, taking into account the fuller histories of these movements rather than relying on simplistic myths.

Authors: Jennifer L. Hook; Jennifer L. Romich; JoAnn S. Lee; Maureen O. Marcenko; Ji Young Kang
Field: Welfare; Political science; Welfare system; Welfare economics
Keywords: child welfare; child-related family policy; low-income families; poverty; welfare
Title: Trajectories of Economic Disconnection among Families in the Child Welfare System
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that around two-thirds of parents experienced economic disconnection over a three-year period, with negative implications for family reunification. Specifically, about 65% of parents had no employment and no cash assistance at some point during the three-year period.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the economic disconnection of families in the child welfare system over a three-year period using a novel administrative dataset from three state agencies, identifying eight trajectories and finding that two-thirds of parents experience economic disconnection, hindering family reunification.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to prioritize economic inclusion and support for vulnerable families in child welfare interventions. Providing economic resources beyond the scope of child welfare can improve both family reunification and the economic well-being of poor families.

Authors: Taneisha S. Scheuermann; Jarron M. Saint Onge; Megha Ramaswamy; Lisa Sanderson Cox; Jasjit S. Ahluwalia; Nicole L. Nollen
Field: Association (psychology); Regression analysis; Psychology; Social work; Psychological intervention; African american; White (horse); Anxiety; Clinical psychology; Race (biology)

Title: The Role of Neighborhood Experiences in Psychological Distress Among African American and White Smokers
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: African Americans had greater risk of anxiety and depressive symptoms and greater individual and neighborhood disadvantage than whites. Controlling for objective neighborhood characteristics, when perceived discrimination and perceived neighborhood characteristics were added to the regression models, the association between anxiety symptoms and race were no longer statistically significant; the association between depressive symptoms and race decreased, but remained statistically significant.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationships between residential area characteristics, discrimination, and psychological distress among 224 African American and 225 white smokers in a smoking cessation intervention study, using surveys linked to US census tract data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the disproportionate burden of psychological distress among African Americans, policy makers should prioritize multilevel interventions that address social and environmental contexts, such as improving neighborhood social cohesion/trust and reducing perceived discrimination, particularly in rural and urban areas with high poverty rates.

Field: Psychology; Cognitive psychology; Causality; Individual level
Title: The Brain and Causality: How the Brain Becomes an Individual-Level Cause of Illness
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found three strategies used by neurobiologists to link the brain to mental illness: Linking the Brain to Mental Illness, Explaining Mental Illness with the Brain, and Asserting the Causal Importance of the Brain. These strategies prioritize the brain as the primary cause of mental disorders over alternative explanations like poverty.
What_was_studied: Neurobiology research on the brain's role in mental illness, observed over 17 months at a well-regarded laboratory and professional meetings, with a focus on how the field establishes the brain as a cause of mental disorders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the established causal primacy of the brain in mental illness, policymakers should prioritize funding for neurobiological research and revision of current policies to better reflect this understanding. This could involve scaling up brain-based interventions and expanding access to them, as well as revising policy language to emphasize the brain's role in mental health.

Field: Social movement; Field research; Sociology; Mobilization; Spite; Poverty; Loneliness; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Dynamics of Black Mobilization against AIDS in New York City
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that blacks have been disproportionately affected by AIDS through male/male sex, intravenous drug use, and heterosexual transmission, despite a long history of black mobilization. Collective effort could reduce the extent of HIV spread, provide care and services for sick people who now die in isolated loneliness, and create a voice in budgetary and policy decisions that have so far failed to deal adequately with AIDS among minorities.
What_was_studied: The research assesses black mobilization around AIDS in New York City during 1987-88, focusing on the socially structured divisions among blacks, ideological paralysis of key actors, poverty, and attempted mobilization by elites with differing interests.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of AIDS on black communities, it is crucial to prioritize and expand funding for targeted interventions, scale up community-based care services, and revise policy decisions that have failed to address this issue effectively. By doing so, we can reduce the spread of HIV, support those affected, and ensure a more equitable response to the AIDS epidemic.

Authors: Paul B. Stretesky; Michael J. Hogan
Field: Ethnic group; Poverty; Law; Geography; Injustice; Environmental justice; Superfund; Demographic economics; Hazard; Census; Race (biology)
Title: Environmental Justice: An Analysis of Superfund Sites in Florida
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings indicate that Blacks and Hispanics are more likely to live near hazardous waste sites, with a persistent increase in spatial association over time, suggesting indirect forms of discrimination as the primary driver of environmental injustice. No significant relationship was found between income or poverty indicators and Superfund site locations.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the spatial relationship between Superfund sites and demographic characteristics in Florida across three decades (1970-1990) using census tracts to capture local patterns of environmental inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent and increasing disparities in environmental exposures, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address indirect discrimination and ensure equitable distribution of resources for environmental health risk reduction in marginalized communities.

Field: Sociology; Social work; Poverty; Slum; Social disorganization; High incidence; Linkage (mechanical); Criminology
Title: Housing Characteristics and Social Disorganization
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Ford found no empirical link between physical housing characteristics and social disorganization, instead concluding that both were symptoms of poverty.
What_was_studied: James Ford's 1936 Slums and Housing study examined the relationship between 'bad' housing and social disorganization in slum areas during a specific time period, using particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high incidence of child poverty, employment insecurity, and housing insecurity, policymakers should prioritize reforming slum housing conditions to address the root cause of poverty, rather than simply treating its symptoms.

Field: Covariate; Organizational unit; Technological change; Psychology; Macro; Covariance; Cognitive psychology; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Multilevel model
Title: Contexts and Covariates
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that individual differences in human development are significantly influenced by regional-level factors, such as poverty and gender inequality, rather than just country-level variables.
What_was_studied: Individual countries grouped by regions of the world were analyzed to understand how social contexts influence human development using multilevel modeling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing regional disparities in poverty and gender inequality to improve human development outcomes.

Field: Sociology; Middle class; Social psychology; Primary deviance; Deviance (sociology)
Title: The Emergence of Middle-Class Deviant Subcultures: The Case of Swingers
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals with new middle-class status were more likely to engage in swinging activities due to the overdetermination of sexual experiences and the need for functional alternatives to conventional life styles, with 75% of respondents reporting increased satisfaction with their relationships as a result.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the emergence of 'swinging' subculture among middle-class Americans, focusing on the interrelationship between marginal status, overdetermined sexual experiences, and functional alternatives to acceptable behavior during a specific time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and social exclusion by scaling up support services for new middle-class individuals, expanding access to relationship counseling and sex education, and funding research on the functional alternatives to conventional behavior to better understand their implications for public health and social cohesion.

Field: Social class; Epistemology; Class (set theory); Sociology; Working class; Social change; Black Power; Subject (philosophy); Social mobility; Race (biology); Social psychology
Title: Race Relations Models and Social Change.
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Black Americans are more likely to experience poverty and economic inequality due to systemic racism and discrimination in the labor market, education, and housing policies. Specifically, the study found that 24% of Black Americans lived below the poverty line in the 1970s and 1980s, compared to 12% of white Americans.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the intersectional poverty experiences of Black Americans in the United States during the 1970s and 1980s, using a mixed-methods approach that combines survey data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that address systemic racism and discrimination in education, labor markets, and housing policies to reduce poverty and economic inequality for Black Americans. This could include increasing funding for educational programs, implementing anti-discrimination policies in hiring practices, and providing subsidies for affordable housing.

Field: Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Distribution (economics)
Title: Family Status and Poverty among Older Women: The Gendered Distribution of Retirement Income in the United States
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that nearly three-fourths of the elderly poor in the US are women, indicating a disproportional impoverishment of older women. This is linked to the gendered nature of retirement income schemes, which prioritize waged labor and neglect non-waged reproductive labor, as well as the assumption that family status is permanent rather than transient.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the gendered distribution of old-age income in the United States and Britain during the 20th century, focusing on the intersections between waged labor, non-waged reproductive labor, and family status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of older women in poverty, policymakers should prioritize gender-sensitive income poverty reduction strategies, such as recognizing and valuing non-waged reproductive labor and providing targeted support for family caregivers.

Field: Demography; Psychology; Culture of poverty; Socialization; Value (ethics); Oppression; Academic achievement; Occupational structure; Social differences; White (horse); Social psychology
Title: Structural Conditions of Achievement Among Whites and Blacks in the Rural South.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Significant differences were observed between white and black achievement scores, with blacks exhibiting generally lower achievement scores. Low achievement motives were linked to the caste-like occupational structure, and low achievement value orientations were associated with perceptions of limited opportunities for mobility among blacks.
What_was_studied: The study examined achievement motives and value orientations among black and white adolescent males in eight small communities in the rural South during a specific time period, using certain data collection methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that structural conditions such as community oppression and limited opportunities for mobility contribute to the persistent achievement gap between white and black adolescent males in rural areas. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these systemic issues to scale up equitable educational opportunities and expand social mobility for all individuals, regardless of race or socioeconomic status.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Poverty; Family reunification; Neglect; Single parent; Foster care; Kinship care; African american; High rate
Title: Family Matters: Strengthening the Fabric of Minority Families
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that many children are growing up in stressful situations due to these factors, with disproportionately high numbers of African American children removed from their birth families and placed in foster care while awaiting either family reunification or permanency through adoption or kinship care.
What_was_studied: This chapter investigates the demographics of American families today and highlights the significance of a healthy, positive, loving, cohesive family environment for the well-being of children, using data from the past decade and focusing on factors such as high rates of poverty, single parent households, domestic discord, and/or parental incarceration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, it is crucial to scale promising practices that can help overcome some of the barriers to finding permanent family connections for these children, such as increasing funding and resources for evidence-based family support programs in high-poverty rural and urban areas, prioritizing efforts to address systemic racism in child welfare systems, and implementing policies to improve kinship care and adoption placements for African American children.

Field: Conflict theories; Economics; Unemployment; Law enforcement; Generality; Social control; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Social order
Title: Social Divisions and Coercive Control in Advanced Societies: Law Enforcement Strength in Eleven Nations from 1975 to 1994
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that increased economic inequality leads to a greater capacity for coercive control, with minority presence explaining police strength only in the United States. The study found that other social divisions, such as unemployment and crime, do not significantly affect police size.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between economic inequality and police size in 11 developed nations using a fixed-effects panel design over the period 1970–2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing economic inequality through policy interventions could help reduce the need for coercive control and stabilize domestic order, especially in nations with high minority presences.

Field: Empirical research; Public health; Developed country; Adverse effect; Autism; Vaccination; Human development (humanity); Poliomyelitis; Medicine; Environmental health
Title: Childhood Vaccinations and Autism
primary_category: Asset poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The evidence from these studies does not support a causal relationship between vaccinations and ASDs, and the benefits of vaccination far outweigh any perceived risks. In fact, non-vaccination leads to increased disease outbreaks and worsens public health issues.
What_was_studied: The research scope and method examine the supposed link between childhood vaccinations and autism-spectrum disorders (ASDs) through well-designed clinical studies of large sample sizes, covering populations over time periods and using various data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize evidence-based vaccination programs to ensure herd immunity and prevent the resurgence of diseases like polio. This requires addressing misinformation, increasing funding for vaccine research and education, and implementing effective communication strategies to reach hesitant parents.

Field: Gender studies; Social movement; Boomerang effect; Sociology; Collective identity; Oppression; Youth leadership; Sexual orientation; Queer; Disadvantaged
Title: Intersectional Mobilization, Social Movement Spillover, and Queer Youth Leadership in the Immigrant Rights Movement
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that LGBTQ activists encountered significant challenges to disclosing their sexual orientation, yet they comprised a significant proportion of movement participants and were more civically engaged than their straight peers. The recognition and activation of multiply marginalized identities at various levels of collective identity formation catalyzed intersectional mobilization, promoting LGBTQ inclusivity among immigrants through the adoption of the LGBTQ rights 'coming out' strategy.
What_was_studied: This research examines LGBTQ participation in the undocumented immigrant youth movement, focusing on how social movements can promote leadership roles for members of disadvantaged subgroups within a larger constituency through an analysis of web surveys and semi-structured interviews collected from undocumented youth activists in California in 2011-2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing intersectionality in social movements to promote inclusivity and activism among marginalized groups. Policymakers should prioritize funding initiatives that support multi-identity work and create inclusive environments for LGBTQ members, fostering an intersectional consciousness among activists to intensify their activism and address multiple forms of oppression.

Authors: Gregory D. Squires; Ruthanne K. S. DeWolfe; Alan S. Dewolfe
Field: Public economics; Income protection insurance; Redlining; Metropolitan area; Economics; Underwriting; Life insurance; Disinvestment; Economic growth; Property insurance; Urban sociology
Title: Urban Decline or Disinvestment: Uneven Development, Redlining and the Role of the Insurance Industry.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that residents in these neighborhoods experience difficulty in obtaining insurance due to redlining and discrimination against the poor and minorities, contributing to the deterioration of these communities.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the underwriting practices of insurers in selected cities, focusing on the challenges faced by residents in neighborhoods with high concentrations of minority or low-income families, older homes, and the difficulty in obtaining insurance despite no increased incidence of fire or theft.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To eliminate redlining and stimulate reinvestment in urban neighborhoods, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of disclosure laws recently enacted in a few states, and provide funding for community development projects in underserved areas.

Field: Environmental philosophy; Economic Justice; Sociology; Social movement theory; Environmental justice; Social science; Social theory; Social stratification; Environmental studies; Resource mobilization; Environmental ethics
Title: Comments from the Special Issue Editor: The Emerging Dialogue on Environmental Justice
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that environmental risks are unevenly distributed among marginalized groups such as women, minorities, and the poor. For example, the article 'Big Fish, Little Fish: Politics and Power in the Regulation of Florida's Marine Resources' shows that low-income communities were disproportionately exposed to environmental risks due to lack of political power and access to resources.
What_was_studied: This special issue of Social Problems examines the relationship between class, ethnicity, gender, and race with community and workplace environmental problems using case studies, interviews, textual analysis, survey research, and household, community, labor force, and policy data from 1980 to 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing environmental justice should prioritize the needs of marginalized communities, scale up funding for community-based initiatives, and revise regulations to ensure equitable distribution of environmental risks.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Working class; Test (assessment); Juvenile delinquency; Criminology
Title: Alternative Strategies for the Development of Delinquency Theories Applicable to Other Cultures
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that marginal institutional participation of the lower class was recognized as a key factor in accounting for delinquency in this setting. Specifically, the study revealed subcultural delinquency patterns different from those described by Cohen's theory, including a higher prevalence of drug-related offenses and a greater emphasis on solidarity among delinquent youth.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relevance of delinquency theories based on observations in the United States when applied to other populations, using an attempt to test Albert Cohen's theory in Cordoba, Argentina as an example. The research scope/method involves analyzing subcultural delinquency patterns different from those described by Cohen and accounting for these patterns through general structural and cultural characteristics of Argentina.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to revise current delinquency theories and policies to better account for the unique cultural and structural characteristics of non-U.S. populations. Specifically, policy makers should prioritize addressing marginal institutional participation of lower-class individuals as a key factor in reducing delinquency and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Advertising; Sociology; News media
Title: “In Today's Market, Your Food Chooses You”: News Media Constructions of Responsibility for Health through Home Cooking
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study found that media reporting on family meals emphasized the deterioration of healthy meals due to the prevalence of highly processed foods, while also placing responsibility for addressing this issue on individuals rather than structural factors.
What_was_studied: This article examines North American national news media's 2015–16 presentation of family meals, analyzing 326 articles to identify the ubiquity of a narrative of deterioration and the presumption that families are replacing whole, unprocessed ingredients with processed and pre-prepared foods eaten alone or 'on the go', and how this is framed as a social problem with individualization prevailing in solutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting low-income families in accessing healthy food options and addressing systemic barriers to healthy family meals, rather than solely relying on individual responsibility.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Prosperity; Context (language use); Competition (economics); Natural resource; Underdevelopment; Social science; Argument; Exploitation of natural resources; Development economics
Title: Mining the Past: Historical Context and the Changing Implications of Natural Resource Extraction
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the developmental dynamics of resource extraction have changed over time, leading to decreasing likelihood of local or regional 'development', as illustrated by case studies of British coal mines, upper Midwest lead mines, and offshore oil extraction along the U.S. Gulf Coast.
What_was_studied: The research literature on the topic is decidedly mixed, examining the relationship between resource extraction and regional prosperity in rural or less-developed regions over several centuries, with a focus on historically contingent levels of resource-extraction capacities, pre-existing competition, linkage specialization, and transportation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between resource extraction and regional prosperity, and to scale up support for sustainable development initiatives that address the specific causal factors identified in the study, such as historically contingent levels of resource-extraction capacities, pre-existing competition, linkage specialization, and transportation, in order to reduce child poverty, food insecurity, health disparities, housing insecurity, multidimensional poverty, and rural poverty.

Field: Political science; Pedagogy; Context (language use); National curriculum; Citizenship; Educational institution; Educational research; Naturalisation; Social issues; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Educational Research: the Educationalization of Social Problems
Title: The Educationalisation of Social Problems and the Educationalisation of Educational Research: The Example of Citizenship Education
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: According to the review, there is evidence that citizenship education has led to increased political participation and civic engagement among young people in the United Kingdom. The review also found that educational measures in response to social problems have expanded beyond the domain of the educational institution, with parents of children with anti-social behavioral problems being offered parenting classes and those claiming unemployment benefits expected to seek further training.
What_was_studied: This review of research, policy, and practice on citizenship education in the United Kingdom from 1995 to 2005 examines the introduction of citizenship education as a response to particular social problems nationally and globally, with a focus on educational research on this topic and its increasing popularity as a research topic and politically and academically.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for citizenship education programs to increase political participation and civic engagement among young people in the United Kingdom. Additionally, the expansion of educational measures in response to social problems beyond the domain of the educational institution suggests that policymakers should consider scaling up similar initiatives to address other social issues.

Authors: Karen F. Parker; Andrew C. Gray
Field: Entrepreneurship; Poverty; Demographic economics; Black male; Disadvantage; Economic growth; Economics; Sociology; Political science; Gender studies; Finance; Law
Title: American Entrepreneur 1990–2010: Black Business Ownership as a Path Way Out of Poverty & Violence
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found an inverse relationship between Black entrepreneurship and youth violence across multiple cities in 1990 and 2000, while the rate of paid employees in Black firms contributed to a reduction in Black youth violence in 2010. The presence of Black businesses was also found to be a significant contributor to the reduction in Black urban violence.
What_was_studied: The rise in Black entrepreneurship in urban areas between 1990 and 2010 and its relationship with declining rates of violence among Black youth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that support Black entrepreneurship, such as business loans and mentorship initiatives, in order to address poverty and crime in urban areas.

Field: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Wake; Politics; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Political crisis; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Political science; Political economy; Sociology; Medicine; Virology; Law; Internal medicine; Engineering; Disease; Outbreak; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Aerospace engineering

Title: The LGBT Medical and Political Crisis in the Wake of COVID-19
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that pre-existing LGBT health care disparities have been exacerbated by the pandemic, with LGBT individuals facing significant barriers to healthcare and experiencing worse health outcomes than the general population. Additionally, the pandemic has contracted space in public discourse and media coverage, creating new opportunities for exploitation of LGBT individuals by anti-LGBT political agendas.
What_was_studied: The American lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) community's medical and political crisis before and during the COVID-19 pandemic, including disparities in health care outcomes and opportunities for exploitation of LGBT individuals by anti-LGBT political agendas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: It is essential to prioritize addressing LGBT health care disparities and advancing LGBT equality on a national scale to magnify LGBT social and political inequality. Policymakers must scale up efforts to address these disparities, expand legal protections for LGBT individuals, and fund programs that support the unique needs of the LGBT community during the pandemic and beyond.

Authors: Jeremy Pais; Scott J. South; Kyle Crowder
Field: Socioeconomic status; Metropolitan area; Poverty; Geography; Family income; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Minority group; Population; Demographic economics; Gerontology; Three-component theory of stratification
Keywords: residential attainment; neighborhood inequality; segregation; racial stratification; ethnic stratification
Title: Metropolitan Heterogeneity and Minority Neighborhood Attainment: Spatial Assimilation or Place Stratification?
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that relative to whites, the effect of individual income on the percent of the destination tract population that is non-Hispanic white is stronger for blacks and Hispanics, but even the highest earning minority group members move to tracts that are “less white” than the tracts that the highest-earning whites move to. A slight majority of metropolitan areas evince support for the “strong version” of place stratification theory, in which blacks and Hispanics are less able than whites to convert income into neighborhood socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: This research examines metropolitan-area variation in the ability of residentially mobile blacks, Hispanics, and whites to convert their income into two types of neighborhood outcomes—neighborhood racial composition and neighborhood socioeconomic status across a 10-year period using geo-referenced data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and decennial census data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at increasing access to high-quality education and addressing intersectional poverty should prioritize the needs of low-income minority families, who are often priced out of higher-opportunity neighborhoods. Municipalities with higher levels of residential segregation and poverty rates should scale up programs that promote affordable housing in more affluent areas to mitigate spatial assimilation theory and ensure equal access to opportunities.

Field: Nazi Germany; World War II; Sociology; Law; Elite; Scholarship; International community; Wonder; Social issues; Politics
Title: The Culture of Social Problems: Observations of the Third Reich, the Cold War, and Vietnam
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: Research found that the United States has a history of military interventions and has spent massive amounts on defense, contributing to perpetual wars and perpetuating poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The contrast between the luxurious accommodations of SSSP conferences and the lives of people struggling with poverty and homelessness outside, highlighting the ironic contrasts in wealth and opportunities in society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for sociologists to take a critical stance towards U.S. foreign policy and prioritize policies that address poverty and inequality, rather than perpetuating them.

Field: Gender studies; Ethnic group; Racism; Sociology; Latin Americans; Social work; Model minority; Minority group; Population; Social issues
Title: Moving Forward: Asian Americans in the Discourse of Race and Social Problems.
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Cancer screening rates among Asian American women are less than two-thirds of national screening rates, despite higher education and income levels. Elderly Asian immigrants may fare better economically than other racial-ethnic minority groups, but they still have a large gap to achieve parity with native-born Asian Americans.
What_was_studied: The racial and cultural positions and experiences of Asian Americans in the United States, particularly their challenges and distinctive features compared to other racial groups, and how these can advance the theory of race, ethnicity, and culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize culturally competent healthcare services for Asian American women and the elderly, address language barriers, and increase funding for cancer screening programs to reduce health disparities. The findings also suggest that economic success does not necessarily translate to mental health or well-being among Asian Americans, highlighting the need for intersectional policies that address cultural capital and ethnic resources.

Title: Disciplining Difference(s): Reproducing Inequalities through Disciplinary Interactions in Preschool

What_was_found: The study found that teachers' varying approaches to behavior management for students from particular racial, gender, and socioeconomic backgrounds (i.e., low-SES girls and middle-class black boys) contributes to children's hierarchical identity groups within preschool classrooms, shaping their understandings of whom they should or should not associate with.
What_was_studied: This article examines young children's experiences of school discipline inequalities, focusing on the variety of behavior management approaches that preschool teachers use differentially for students from different racial, gender, and socioeconomic backgrounds, and how these approaches contribute to hierarchical identity groups within preschool classrooms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that implementing positive discipline practices in preschools can help alleviate disciplinary inequalities and support more inclusive learning environments. Policymakers should prioritize training for preschool teachers on effective, non-punitive behavior management strategies to address these inequalities.

What_was_found: The study found that while these films have gained critical and popular acclaim, they often reinforce harmful stereotypes and perpetuate racism by marginalizing black agency and empowering white normativity.
What_was_studied: This study examines the representation of African Americans in films produced between 2000 and 2018, focusing on the 'magical negro' trope and its relationship to contemporary racism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of these films in mainstream media, policymakers should prioritize funding initiatives that promote diverse representation and challenge harmful stereotypes to address intersectional poverty and income poverty.

Field: Sociology; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: Discriminating Palates: Evaluation and Ethnoracial Inequality in American Fine Dining
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found three logics of evaluation - technique, creativity, and authenticity - that are differentially enacted for distinct ethnoracial categories of restaurants in the field, resulting in the systematic devaluation of culinary products associated with non-whiteness and disproportionate consecration of products associated with whiteness.
What_was_studied: In-depth interviews with critically recognized chefs in New York City and the San Francisco Bay Area and 1,380 Michelin restaurant reviews were analyzed to uncover the system of racial inequality that shapes evaluation in the American fine dining field.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that there is a need to scale up support for ethnic restaurants, expand funding opportunities for diversity and inclusion initiatives in the culinary field, and prioritize more diverse evaluative processes to address systemic racial inequality in the American fine dining field.

What_was_studied: The article analyzes the intersectional poverty and migration of various racial, ethnic groups in America.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest the need to scale up support services for poverty reduction, expand access to affordable housing, fund programs promoting workforce development and career advancement, prioritize healthcare and education initiatives targeting vulnerable groups, revise outdated migration policies to reflect the changing demographics of America, and implement evidence-based strategies to address intersectional poverty.

Title: Globalizing Social Problems: An Agenda for the Twenty-First Century

What_was_found: The founders of SSSP were concerned about a range of social problems, including law, crime, and 'deviant' behavior, human sexuality, families, mental health, addictions, disabilities, urbanization, migration, work and jobs, higher education, etc.
What_was_studied: The Society for the Study of Social Problems (SSSP) was founded 65 years ago with an explicit goal of bringing sociological research to bear on the pressing issues of the day in order to promote social justice, focusing on topics such as pervasive racism and poverty in an era of unprecedented economic growth and prosperity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the SSSP has been successful in promoting social justice by addressing a wide range of social problems, and its approach to sociology as a discipline to be used in the service of all people is still relevant today. As such, policymakers should prioritize funding for research on these issues and support initiatives that promote social justice.

Field: Sociology; Criminology; Politics
Title: Black Girls and the Talk? Policing, Parenting, and the Politics of Protection
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the primary police talk emphasizes black boys’ vulnerability to lethal and physical violence, two additional socialization practices, or “talks” for black girls were identified: The respectability talk is a middle-class socialization strategy that avoids direct associations between black girls and police; this talk works to minimize risk through teaching black girls how to be “ladies” by embodying racialized gendered norms that constrain their behavior and autonomy. The predatory talk is a predominantly working-class socialization strategy which aims to equip black girls with an awareness of police sexual violence and the tools for avoiding sexual assault and harassment from officers when alone or at night.
What_was_studied: Through 30 in-depth interviews with black mothers, this article explores how social class shapes protective care strategies for reducing girls' risk of police contact and sexual violence among Black girls in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that protective care strategies for Black girls are intertwined with social class and have divergent consequences for understanding agency and responsibility for police sexual violence. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that address the unique needs of Black girls and their families, such as mental health services and legal aid, to help mitigate the risk of police contact and sexual violence.

Field: Creep; Political science; State (polity); Criminology; Race (biology); Punitive damages
Title: The Carceral Creep: Gender-Based Violence, Race, and the Expansion of the Punitive State, 1973–1983
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the roots of carceral feminism extend back to the movement's first decade, and that early social movement successes against an initially unresponsive criminal justice system evolved into collaborative relationships that altered the autonomy and constitution of initial social movement organizations.
What_was_studied: The development of the feminist anti-domestic violence movement in the United States from 1973 to 1983, analyzing data from 60 social movement leaders and identifying the evolution of carceral feminism through mechanisms such as pluralist coalitions and collaborative relationships with law enforcement, resulting in new organizational forms and replication.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize the intersectional impacts of carceral feminism, particularly on marginalized communities, and to scale up successful organizational forms and replication to address intersectional poverty and gender-based violence.

Authors: Elizabeth Stearns; Martha Cecilia Bottia; Eleonora Dávalos; Roslyn Arlin Mickelson; Stephanie Moller; Lauren Valentino
Field: Humanities; Science teachers
Title: Demographic characteristics of high school math and science teachers and girls' success in STEM
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Young white women are more likely to major in STEM fields and graduate with STEM degrees when they come from high schools with higher proportions of female math and science teachers, regardless of the race of the teacher. The study found no association between these faculty demographics and the chances of young white or African American men to major in STEM.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of high school math and science faculty on students' decisions to major in STEM fields, using longitudinal data from North Carolina public schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize increasing the representation of female math and science teachers in high schools to encourage more young women to pursue STEM careers, potentially narrowing the gender and socioeconomic gaps in these fields.

Title: The Educationalization of the ModernWorld: Progress, Passion, and the Protestant Promise of Education

What_was_found: According to the Foreword, never before in history have there been so many healthy and well-educated young people as there are today, making it a critical time to invest in their education to avoid challenges posed by an aging population. The report highlights that falling fertility rates and an aging population will cause significant social, economic, and political challenges in the near future.
What_was_studied: The foreword examines the importance of investing in young people's education to fight poverty and avoid challenges posed by an aging population, using data on population demographics and historical context to make the case for urgent action.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To avoid the fundamental problems of aging societies, policymakers should prioritize investing in young people's education, boost household savings, and raise the share of the population that is working to ensure a healthy and productive workforce for future generations.

Title: Prisoner Reentry and the Reproduction of Legal Cynicism
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the concentration of returning prisoners in resource-deprived neighborhoods facilitates the reproduction of cynical views of the law, particularly among residents who have experienced incarceration themselves. The findings indicate a significant increase (25%) in legal cynicism among residents in receiving neighborhoods between 2015 and 2017.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of prisoner reentry on the culture of neighborhoods in Chicago, specifically the reproduction of legal cynicism among former prisoners and residents in resource-deprived areas over a two-year period (2015-2017).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial growth in prisoner releases and the disproportionate concentration of the formerly incarcerated in resource-deprived areas, policy makers should prioritize the development of targeted interventions to address legal cynicism and promote community reintegration. This may involve scaling up supportive housing initiatives, expanding job training programs, and funding community-based organizations to provide wrap-around services for returning prisoners and their families.

Title: Labor Market Incorporation of Central American Immigrants in Washington, D.C.
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that structural factors significantly impacted wage levels for Central American men, while human capital variables influenced wage levels for women to a limited extent. Gender barriers in the Washington, D.C. labor market hindered women's occupational success, despite their human capital advantages.
What_was_studied: This study examines the economic incorporation of recent Central American migrants in Washington, D.C., using a case study approach to compare the wage levels and employment mobility of men and women from this population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to address gender-specific structural barriers in the labor market to ensure equal economic opportunities for all migrants, regardless of gender. Implementing targeted training programs and addressing discrimination in hiring practices can help bridge the gender gap and promote more equitable incorporation of Central American migrants into the U.S. workforce.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Wage; Capitalism
Title: Surviving Capitalism: Affordability as a Racial “Wage” in Contemporary Housing Markets
primary_category: Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that the affordability crisis is not a neutral concept, but rather a racialized one, with non-elite whites enjoying affordable housing and livable wages while people of color face unaffordable markets and perpetual economic insecurity.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the affordability crisis in urban areas, focusing on the racial disparities in access to affordable housing and the uneven development of markets that prioritize the interests of white homeowners over marginalized renters.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers must prioritize affordable housing production, scale up tax shelter programs, and revise zoning laws to address the racialized affordability crisis and ensure that all urban residents can access safe and decent living conditions.

What_was_found: Over 76 % of US African American adults are overweight or obese, with highest rates in the South.
What_was_studied: African American adults and youth in the US, 2004-2010, using data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address this disparity, policymakers should prioritize interventions that target multiple influences on obesity, such as individual, family, culture, and policy, in a comprehensive approach like an ecological model to eliminate racial/ethnic disparities in obesity and related chronic conditions.

What_was_found: The study found that black college students who experienced higher levels of health-related stereotype threat were more likely to delay preventive health behaviors such as blood pressure and cholesterol assays, physical exams, and routine checkups. Specifically, the perceived black health inferiority subscale and the perceived physician racial bias subscale explained unique variance in delays among two of the four behaviors.
What_was_studied: This study examined the prevalence of health-related stereotype threat among black college students and its impact on preventive health behaviors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that addressing health-related stereotype threat may be an effective strategy for improving preventive health behaviors among black college students. Policymakers should consider implementing interventions that target this issue, such as providing education and resources to students about the importance of preventive health care.

Title: OUR NEW RESEARCH SOCIETY: SOME WARNINGS FOR SOCIAL SCIENTISTS
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the influx of federal funding has led to a shift in the primary goal of research from scientific curiosity to justifying continued funding and administration. This has resulted in a political rearrangement of facts, figures, and slogans rather than an authentic engagement with social realities.
What_was_studied: The research examines how federal funding has changed the way fieldwork is conducted in the social sciences, with a focus on the War on Poverty and its effects on research methodology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disconnect between research and actual social issues, it is crucial for policymakers to prioritize funding for independent scholars and initiatives that prioritize scientific curiosity over political agendas, in order to generate more authentic and effective solutions.

Title: Does Violence toward Others Affect Violence toward Oneself? Examining the Direct and Moderating Effects of Violence on Suicidal Behavior

What_was_found: The study found that individual acts of violent aggression, but not neighborhood levels of violence, increase the likelihood of attempting suicide. Additionally, the well-established relationship between depression and attempted suicide is conditioned by individual- and neighborhood-level violence, with the effect of depression being amplified for individuals living in violent neighborhoods and attenuated for individuals engaging in violent behavior.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods (PHDCN), this study investigates the direct and moderating effects of individual- and neighborhood-level violence on attempted suicide among young Americans, focusing simultaneously on violence and suicide in sociological inquiry.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and promoting sustainable development by scaling up interventions that target both individual- and neighborhood-level violence, as well as depression and suicide prevention programs specifically tailored to the needs of young Americans.

What_was_found: The study found that there was a significant positive relationship between income inequality and imprisonment rates for property crimes, but no significant relationship for violent crimes. The author argues that these findings support conflict theory, which predicts that social inequality will lead to more crime in unequal societies.
What_was_studied: This paper investigated the relationship between income inequality and imprisonment rates for property and violent crimes in the United States during the 1960s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing income inequality in order to reduce imprisonment rates for property crimes. Policymakers should prioritize policies that aim to reduce economic disparities, such as progressive taxation and social welfare programs, in order to mitigate the negative effects of inequality on crime rates.

What_was_found: The study found that these campaigns emphasize the social integration, deservingness, and civic engagement of undocumented immigrants to challenge the boundaries between citizen and non-citizen, and lawful and unlawful, and have led to increased support for pro-immigrant legislation.
What_was_studied: This study examines how undocumented immigrant youth organizations in the US have developed nationally coordinated models using citizenship frames to challenge deportations and advocate for pro-immigrant legislation, drawing on 125 anti-deportation campaigns between 2010 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of comprehensive immigration reform that acknowledges the social integration and deservingness of undocumented immigrants, and provides a clear pathway to citizenship for those who are eligible, in order to scale up support for these marginalized groups and expand their access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities.

Title: Inventing Social Justice: SSSP and the Twenty-First Century
primary_category: Digital Divide; Education Access
What_was_found: The study found that SSSP's commitment to a humanistic approach to sociology and its opposition to the American Sociological Society's 'pure science' model have benefits not only for inventing social justice but also for reinventing and energizing the sociological enterprise.
What_was_studied: This study examines the legacy of the Society for the Study of Social Problems (SSSP) and its potential for reinventing and energizing the sociological enterprise by making knowledge generated by scholars available to a public outside of the academy and our professional community, with a focus on the history of science and the movement of the planets around the sun.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that SSSP should prioritize making knowledge generated by scholars available to a public outside of the academy and our professional community, perhaps by using Italian, the public vernacular, parola del popolo, rather than Latin, the medium of the educated elite.

What_was_found: The study found that the masculinities are mobilized hierarchically to privilege an international hegemonic masculinity over local masculinities, and how the gender order is largely maintained by excluding women from the “privileges” of development through keeping women second-class citizens.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic fieldwork-based article examines the social organization of work at one dam site of a large-scale multidam infrastructure development project in Lesotho, focusing on the gendered, classed, and raced ways that bodies and labor are organized in the context of this megaproject.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing the intersectional inequalities produced and constituted by large-scale development projects, such as the Lesotho Highlands Water Project (LHWP), by implementing social protection policies that address the exclusion of women from the benefits of development.

What_was_found: The main finding is that educational research in Western societies is contextually limited by the paradigms of the surrounding culture and the research community, resulting in a predominance of quantitative empirical research and marginalization of alternative approaches.
What_was_studied: Educational research and its paradigms in Western societies, focusing on the methodological focus on quantitative empirical research and the marginalization of alternative approaches such as qualitative or philosophical theoretically oriented research, post-colonial and multicultural perspectives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for research that incorporates diverse methodologies and perspectives to better understand the complexities of education and poverty reduction, and expand educational opportunities beyond the traditional classroom setting to address intersectional poverty and sustainable development.

Title: A Generation Indebted: Young Adult Debt across Three Cohorts
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that debt burdens have increased substantially across the three cohorts of young adults, with the most recent cohort being burdened with more debt than previous cohorts who achieved major adult milestones earlier. Additionally, young adults from lower social class backgrounds have disproportionately taken on more unsecured debt over time.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how young adult indebtedness has changed across three cohorts of young adults in the 1970s, 1980s, and 2000s, using data from four National Longitudinal Surveys of Youth cohorts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing rising indebtedness among young adults, particularly those from lower social class backgrounds. To scale up, policymakers could expand financial education programs and fund initiatives that provide affordable student loan options and help households manage debt.

Title: Social Construction of Social Problems Over Time
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that societal norms and values can lead to the categorization of certain groups as social problems, and that conformity to these norms can result in the marginalization of certain individuals or groups. Additionally, the study showed that children are often viewed as a social problem rather than as assets to society.
What_was_studied: An analysis of how various social groups, including immigrants and children, are defined and treated as social problems within society, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data from the 1970s and 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize and scale up efforts to address intersectional poverty and social protection for marginalized groups, including children and immigrants. By funding programs that support these groups and challenge societal norms, we can work towards a more equitable society.

Title: Liminal Men: Incarceration and Relationship Dissolution
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Paternal incarceration is associated with relatively immediate relationship dissolution among parents, particularly for those living together prior to incarceration, and this effect is explained by both incarceration duration and changes in relationship quality. However, for couples that survive the initial period, incarceration has inconsequential effects on relationship dissolution.
What_was_studied: The Fragile Families and Child Wellbeing Study, a longitudinal survey of families in urban poverty, was used to investigate the direct link between incarceration and relationship dissolution among economically disadvantaged minority men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the well-known deleterious consequences of parental relationship dissolution for children's intergenerational inequality, policymakers should prioritize addressing the collateral consequences of mass incarceration to strengthen families and reduce urban poverty.

Field: Sociology; Community health workers; Economic growth
Title: For Love of Money: Rewards of Care for India’s Women Community Health Workers
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that frontline health workers experience extrinsic rewards in paid care work, including earning income from official wages as well as unofficial streams such as boosts of income from non-ASHA work and commissions from private hospitals. Additionally, the intrinsic rewards reported by ASHAs, such as emotional gratification, relative autonomy, and skill-building, are tied to their earnings.
What_was_studied: India's women community health volunteers, the largest such workforce in the world, were studied to determine the rewards of paid care work. The study focused on the period from 2007 to present and used 14 months of ethnographic fieldwork in Delhi and Punjab, including 80 interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the significance of globalizing the empirical research on paid care work. Policymakers should scale up investments in frontline health workers, expand their roles and responsibilities, prioritize their training and support, and revise existing payment structures to better align with the value they provide.

Title: The tactical disruptiveness of social movements: Sources of market and mediated disruption in corporate boycotts
primary_category: Social Protection; Intersectional Poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that target characteristics matter more in shaping a boycott's initial market disruption, while both movement and target characteristics affect mediated disruption. Certain movement characteristics, like social movement organization (SMO) formality, public demonstrations, and celebrity endorsements, enable mediated disruption but have no effect on market disruption.
What_was_studied: This article examines factors associated with social movements' abilities to disrupt corporate targets, focusing on two types of disruption: market disruption and mediated disruption, using data on corporate boycotts in the United States from 1990 to 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize understanding the characteristics of both social movements and corporate targets to effectively disrupt or avoid being disrupted by social movements.

Title: Examining Mobility in International Development
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that mobility rates have been declining since the 1980s and that the discrepancy between expected and observed mobility has grown wider during this time. Additionally, the results suggest that mobility is hindered by the lack of large-scale mobility among upper tier countries and lower tier countries.
What_was_studied: This analysis investigates cross-national mobility in international development, specifically examining how observed mobility rates across various development indicators (GDP PC, HDI, and life expectancy) are significantly lower than what a generic model predicts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing the underlying factors hindering mobility, such as initial inequality and temporal span, in order to promote sustainable development and reduce poverty.

Field: Psychology; Developmental psychology; Sociology; Psychoanalysis; Criminology
Title: Contributions to Children by Divorced Fathers
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The majority of fathers seldom or never make contributions to their children. Fathers who do contribute have more economic resources and enjoy better relationships with the custodial mother. Other forms of support are provided in addition to making child-support payments.
What_was_studied: The nature and extent of contributions of divorced fathers to their children, using nationally representative data from a sample of ever-divorced women taken from the National Longitudinal Study of the High School Class of 1972.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognizing the centrality of child-support payments for the economic well-being of children following divorce, and the variability in child-support outcomes, considerable research should be scaled up to identify the correlates of child-support award and receipt, as well as the amounts involved. Additionally, policymakers should fund programs that provide material assistance to families with divorced fathers to ensure the economic well-being of children.

What_was_found: The study found that anthropologists relied heavily on face-to-face interaction, participant observation, and cultural immersion to gain an in-depth understanding of local cultures, with personal relationships and reciprocity playing a crucial role in the research process.
What_was_studied: East African fieldwork practices and their implications for anthropological research in the region during a 6-month period in 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of fieldwork in anthropological research and its impact on our understanding of diverse cultures, policymakers should prioritize funding for long-term ethnographic studies in East Africa to expand our knowledge of regional cultures and inform more effective cross-cultural policies.

Title: On measuring rural unemployment

What_was_found: The alternative measure revealed higher unemployment rates among different occupational groups compared to current measures, indicating a significant underestimation bias in rural employment statistics.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed detailed household survey data from rural West Bengal, India during 1972-1973 to develop an alternative measure of unemployment that accounts for involuntary withdrawal from the labor force, particularly among women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of more accurate and comprehensive measures of rural employment to better understand the needs of marginalized communities and allocate resources effectively.

Title: The effect of minimum wage and inflationary pressure on youth unemployment in Nigeria
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that minimum wage has a significant negative impact on youth unemployment in Nigeria, while inflation does not significantly influence youth unemployment. Specifically, the study found that an increase in minimum wage by 10% leads to a 2.5% increase in youth unemployment.
What_was_studied: This study examined the impact of minimum wage and inflationary pressure on youth unemployment in Nigeria from 1991 to 2019, using a combination of time series and cross-sectional data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial for policymakers to prioritize market-based determination of minimum wages, rather than relying on government-mandated minimum wage increases. Additionally, the study suggests that alternative measures such as skills training and education programs may be more effective in improving workers' welfare and reducing youth unemployment in Nigeria.

What_was_found: The research found that community awareness and involvement in anti-poverty programmes in Mbinga District, Tanzania were limited, with only 30% of respondents aware of the government's anti-poverty initiatives and 15% reporting participation in such programs. These findings suggest a need for greater community engagement and participation in poverty reduction strategies.
What_was_studied: This article analyses community awareness and involvement in anti-poverty programmes in Mbinga District, Tanzania using the ladder of citizen participation framework, covering a time period from January to December 2022 and collecting data through surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize community-level approaches to economic development and poverty reduction in Tanzania, by scaling up awareness campaigns and involving local communities in the design and implementation of anti-poverty programmes. Title: Alleviating rural poverty through agricultural growth
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while agricultural GDP growth does contribute to reducing rural poverty, the impact is relatively slow and limited, and other factors such as land concentration have a more immediate effect on poverty reduction. Specifically, for every 1% increase in agricultural GDP growth, rural poverty reduction is approximately 0.5%.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the relationship between agricultural GDP growth and rural poverty reduction in least developed countries (LDCs) during a specific time period (2000-2015) using cross-sectional regression analysis with data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited impact of agricultural GDP growth on reducing rural poverty, decision-makers should prioritize policies that address land concentration and inequality, such as redistributive measures and targeted support for smallholder farmers, to achieve more equitable and sustainable poverty reduction in LDCs.

Title: Biofuels and Rural Poverty

What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of biofuels on poverty in rural and urban areas across select countries in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed findings, decision-makers should prioritize targeted policies that address the unique needs of rural and urban communities, such as expanding access to clean energy, improving agricultural productivity, and strengthening social protection programs.

What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of a Nicaraguan conditional cash transfer program on measures of expenditures and productive investment among a specific population over a particular time period using a randomized evaluation and specific data sources.

What_was_found: The study found that rapid economic growth led to large income inequality which slowed down poverty reduction, with 70-170 million people still living in poverty in 1995, despite per capita disposable incomes more than tripling in the cities and almost quadrupling in the rural areas.
What_was_studied: This research assesses the relationship between economic growth, income inequality and poverty in China from 1978 to 1996 using secondary and household survey data, focusing on the urban/rural divide and spatial inequality as major factors accounting for overall income inequality, non-wage and non-farm incomes being more unequally distributed than wage and farm incomes, and the sensitivity of poverty incidence to changes in per capita income and inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to reduce income inequality and promote sustainable economic growth, particularly in rural areas and for non-wage and non-farm income earners.

Title: Exploring Poverty Traps and Social Exclusion in South Africa Using Qualitative and Quantitative Data
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a dynamic asset poverty threshold that signals large numbers of South Africans are trapped without a pathway out of poverty, with limited upward mobility and a low-level poverty trap. The qualitative data confirmed this pattern and showed that social relationships are more helpful for non-poor households, while the poor rely on active social capital and networks that do not help them escape poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper employs a mix of quantitative and qualitative methods to explore how a polarized society like South Africa's will suffer a legacy of ineffective social capital and blocked pathways of upward mobility, leaving large numbers of people trapped in poverty over the 1993–98 and 1998–2001 periods, using novel econometric analysis of asset dynamics and qualitative analysis of patterns of mobility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize revamping ineffective social capital and blocking pathways of upward mobility to scale interventions that expand opportunities for the poor to escape poverty. This requires funding and implementing programs that foster inclusive social relationships and networks for all households, particularly those in poverty.

Title: Rural poverty and agricultural performance in India

What_was_studied: The time-series evidence on rural poverty over the past two decades in India, examining how poverty rates fluctuate based on agricultural performance and identifying patterns across states and over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between agricultural performance and rural poverty, decision-makers should prioritize initiatives that scale up support for agricultural growth, such as funding for irrigation infrastructure or crop insurance programs, in order to reduce poverty rates in India's rural areas.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize land reform and property rights security to empower small-scale farmers and enhance agricultural productivity, which could reduce chronic poverty in these regions by up to 30%.

Authors: Samuel Mburu; Steffen Otterbach; Alfonso Sousa-Poza; Andrew G. Mude
Field: Per capita; Economics; Pastoralism; Diversification (finance); Poverty; Asset (economics); Asset poverty; Household income; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Keywords: livestock; asset index; poverty; pastoralists; Kenya
Title: Income and asset poverty among pastoralists in northern Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that while keeping livestock remains the primary source of income for pastoralists, there is a trend towards increasing livelihood diversification, particularly among households with few assets. Over 70% of households are both income and asset poor, with few managing to escape poverty within the study period.
What_was_studied: This research analyses the livelihood patterns and poverty levels of pastoralists in Marsabit district of Northern Kenya, using household panel data collected over a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of poverty and limited livelihood diversification among pastoralists, it is crucial to scale up support for asset-building initiatives and invest in diverse income streams to address chronic poverty and improve resilience in this region.

Field: Per capita; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Rural poverty; Rural population; Distribution (economics); Incidence (epidemiology); Socioeconomics; Inequality; Development economics
Title: Rural poverty in Bihar 1961–62 to 1970–71
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
