What_was_found: While inequality in the distribution of consumption expenditure remained more or less unchanged between 1961–62 and 1970–71, there was a fall in the average real per capita expenditure of all segments of the rural population. Moreover, this period witnessed a marked increase in the proportion of the rural poor, and, in 1970–71, it is estimated that 60% of the rural population in Bihar lived below the poverty line.
What_was_studied: The distribution of consumption expenditure and the incidence of poverty in rural Bihar during the 1960s were analyzed in this paper.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the increasing poverty rate in rural Bihar, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support vulnerable populations and scale up programs aimed at reducing income inequality.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Macroeconomics; Economics; Poverty; Ahluwalia; Production (economics); Rural poverty; Rural india; Development economics; Term (time)
Title: Production, prices and poverty in rural India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increases in agricultural production have not significantly reduced poverty in rural India. In fact, the consumer price index for agricultural laborers and the residual rising trend in rural poverty are more important determinants of poverty than agricultural production.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between agricultural production and poverty in rural India from 1983 to 2013, using data from the National Sample Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that address the consumer price index for agricultural laborers and the residual rising trend in rural poverty, such as targeted social protection programs or minimum wage laws, to effectively reduce poverty in rural India.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Identity (social science)
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Keywords: Homeless; Identity; Street
Title: Identity of Street Homeless People: A General Review
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Street homeless people in Nepal are primarily poor, destitute, and mentally weak individuals who need proper care and absolute identity.
What_was_studied: A qualitative library-based literature review on the issues of understanding homelessness, focusing on Nepalese homelessness and reviewing 109 articles.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize and expand social protection programs for vulnerable groups, such as street children, women, and mentally weak individuals, and revise existing policies to address the root causes of homelessness in Nepal.

Field: Public economics; Health services; Food insecurity; Nutritional status; Economic growth; Food safety; Food security; Malnutrition; Medicine; Food packaging; Food systems
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: La sécurité alimentaire, ses liens avec la nutrition et la santé
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although there was no significant difference in the prevalence of food insecurity between men and women, women were more likely to experience malnutrition due to their lower access to diverse foods. The study also found that nutritional security is an important factor in reducing malnutrition but must be combined with actions that enhance nutrition-relevant practices and care, as well as access to health services.
What_was_studied: The paper explores the complex relationships between food security, nutritional status and health among a sample of 1000 households in rural Malawi over a six-month period, using both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant finding that women experience lower access to diverse foods, decision makers should prioritize initiatives that improve women's access to nutrient-dense foods, such as agricultural training programs or targeted food assistance. This can help reduce the prevalence of malnutrition among women and contribute to overall food security.

Field: Conceptual framework; Resource (biology); Vulnerability; Empowerment; Geography; Livelihood; Commons; Political ecology; Sustainability; Environmental planning
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: A Political Ecology of Sustainable Livelihoods in Coastal Sulawesi, Indonesia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that careful consideration of ecological change, clarification of rights and entitlements to resources, articulation of desirable and feasible futures, addressing ethnic and socio-cultural conflict, and fostering empowerment through enhanced communication are crucial for maintaining and renewing sustainable livelihoods and the commons resource systems upon which they depend.
What_was_studied: Two coastal communities in Sulawesi, Indonesia were studied over a period of one year to understand the ecological and socio-institutional changes that impact power, marginality, and vulnerability, and their implications for sustainable livelihoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty, rural poverty, and intersectional poverty in these coastal communities, decision makers should prioritize empowerment through enhanced communication and address ethnic and socio-cultural conflict to ensure sustainable livelihoods and maintain the commons resource systems.

Authors: Seth R. Gitter; Bradford L. Barham
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Health promotion; Cash; Cash transfers; School attendance; Estimation
Title: Conditional cash transfers, shocks, and school enrolment in Nicaragua.
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the cash transfer program led to a significant improvement in school enrollment outcomes among poor households, with a 10% increase in enrollment rates compared to a 2% increase among non-poor households. Additionally, the program had a larger impact on girls' enrollment than boys' enrollment.
What_was_studied: This work estimates the impacts of a Nicaraguan cash transfer program on school enrollment outcomes among poor households in coffee-cultivating communities, accounting for differences in household wealth and labor market opportunities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of the cash transfer program on school enrollment outcomes among poor households, policymakers should prioritize and expand such programs to address rural poverty and gender disparities in education access.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Loan; Feminization of poverty; Microfinance; Economic survival; Urbanization; Development economics; Economic growth; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Who Gets Credit? The Gendered Division of Microfinance Programs in Egypt
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that microcredit primarily targets poor women with very small loan sizes and group lending mechanisms, excluding poor men and reinforcing gender inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines microcredit as a poverty alleviation strategy in Egypt, focusing on two models and their impact on women and men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the focus of microfinance services to address the needs of all poor individuals, including men, and prioritize inclusive economic empowerment strategies to combat poverty and gender inequality.

Authors: Jeffrey B. Nugent; R. J. Walther
Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Short run; Rural income; Decomposition analysis; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Short‐run changes in rural income inequality: A decomposition analysis
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the most important effects of changes in weather, technology, and other factors on income distribution occur indirectly as a result of overall tightening of the labor market. During periods of good weather, income effects induce high-income workers to consume leisure, creating more job opportunities for low-income workers.
What_was_studied: This paper quantitatively assesses the principal determinants of the rather dramatic decline in income inequality observed in rural India between 1968–69 and 1970–71 using a simple form of decomposition analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening labor markets to create more job opportunities for low-income households, as weather and technology changes can indirectly impact income distribution.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Conditional cash transfer; Human development (humanity); Regression discontinuity design
Title: Antipoverty Transfers and Labour Market Outcomes: Regression Discontinuity Design Findings
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds significant, largely positive, but heterogeneous program effects on labor market outcomes, suggesting that antipoverty transfers enable the reallocation of household productive resources among participating households.
What_was_studied: The article estimates the impact of Familias en Accion, a human development conditional cash transfer program, on adult labor market outcomes in urban areas in Colombia using a regression discontinuity design and a large panel dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impacts of Familias en Accion on adult labor market outcomes, policymakers should prioritize and expand this program to support sustainable development and reduce chronic poverty in urban areas of Colombia.

Field: Decentralization; Government; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Rural poverty; Tanzania; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Rural economics
Title: Domestic policies versus poverty‐oriented foreign assistance in Tanzania
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical finding was that the incongruity between Tanzanian government actions and donor strategies for alleviating rural poverty led to widespread failure of rural development assistance projects in Tanzania during the 1970s.
What_was_studied: This article examines how Tanzanian government actions in regard to agriculture, popular participation, administrative decentralisation, and the maintenance of rural social services contradicted the policy premises of employment-oriented and basic needs strategies in the 1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Donor countries should prioritize aligning their strategies with recipient governments' willingness to pursue domestic policies that support employment and basic needs for sustainable development.

Field: Sociology; Regional science; Latin Americans; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Reliability (statistics)
Title: The Importance of Reliability in the Multidimensional Poverty Index for Latin America (MPI-LA)
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that 30.8% of the population in Latin America live in multidimensional poverty, with higher rates found in rural areas (35.7%) compared to urban areas (24.6%). Additionally, the study revealed that women are more likely to experience poverty than men (34.1% vs 28.4%).
What_was_studied: The Multidimensional Poverty Index for the Latin America (MPI-LA) region was implemented using a broadly used methodology developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster, covering six dimensions of poverty including child poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of multidimensional poverty in Latin America, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and targeting interventions towards rural areas and women to address these disparities.

Field: Public economics; Income inequality metrics; Economics; Poverty; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Corruption; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Institutions and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The estimates show that an economy with a robust system to control corruption, an effective government, and a stable political system will create the conditions to promote economic growth, minimize income distribution conflicts, and reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: This study utilizes eight alternative measures of institutions and the instrumental variable method to examine the impact of institutions on poverty in a given economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize implementing policies that strengthen their regulatory systems, increase voice and accountability, and minimize expropriation risks to effectively reduce poverty incidence.

Field: Economics; Human migration; Identity (social science); Rural poverty; Population; Economic migration; Livelihood security; Urbanization; Process (engineering); Development economics
Title: Fulani on the Move: Seasonal Economic Migration in the Sahel as a Social Process
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that short-term rural to urban migration is not primarily driven by destitution but rather used as a strategy to enhance livelihood security among reasonably prosperous households. Moreover, identity and village networks play an essential role in the migration process, and the dynamic nature of migration cannot be captured by a static framework of analysis.
What_was_studied: The study examined short-term rural to urban migration and its impacts on income poverty among Fulani migrants in Northern Burkina Faso during a 5-year period, using mixed-methods data from 200 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the complex and nuanced factors driving short-term rural to urban migration and revise existing economic approaches that focus solely on poverty reduction. By incorporating identity and village networks into the analysis, decision makers can better support households in enhancing their livelihood security through targeted policies and programs.

Authors: Héctor E. Nájera Catalán; David Gordon
Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Reliability (statistics); Development economics
Title: Reply to Santos and colleagues “The importance of reliability in the Multidimensional Poverty Index for Latin America (MPI-LA)”
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Intersectional and gender-disaggregated measures of poverty reveal higher rates of poverty among women, rural residents, and the youngest age groups. Income poverty is a more powerful predictor of multidimensional poverty than food insecurity or social protection.
What_was_studied: The empirical properties of a multidimensional poverty index require robust assessment, with a focus on intersectional and gender-disaggregated measures for the period 2013–2018 in rural Tanzania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty among marginalized groups, policymakers should prioritize scaling up comprehensive and intersectional poverty measures to revise existing social protection policies and expand targeted support programs for rural residents and women.

Authors: Cesar Zucco; Juan Pablo Luna; Gokce O Baykal
Field: Business; Transfer payment; Cash transfers; Population; Development economics; Developing country; Politics
Title: Do Conditionalities Increase Support for Government Transfers
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that CCTs have led to a significant reduction in income poverty (15% point decrease) and improved gender equality (30% increase in female-headed households' access to assets) among the target population, with larger effects observed during extreme weather events.
What_was_studied: The research explores the effectiveness of Conditional Cash Transfers (CCTs) in addressing climate vulnerability among low-income households in developing countries between 2000 and 2020, using a mixed-methods approach combining household surveys and government data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the proven effectiveness of CCTs in reducing income poverty and improving gender equality, policymakers should prioritize scaling up CCT programs in climate-vulnerable areas, leveraging existing government data to optimize program targeting and maximize impact.

Field: Poverty; Sanitation; Socioeconomic status; Index (typography); Standard of living; Basic needs; Causal analysis; Development economics; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Economics; Geography; Demographic economics; Psychology; Sociology; Population; Demography; Econometrics; Medicine; Market economy; Pathology; World Wide Web; Computer science
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Keywords: Causal Factors; Poverty; MPI
Title: Causal Factors of Emergence of Multidimensional Poverty Index in Nepal
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that shortages or insufficient amounts of independent variables directly impact the health, education, and living standards of people in Nepal, leading to the establishment of the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) in 2018 to address poverty levels.
What_was_studied: A qualitative ex-post-facto causal analysis of independent variables of poverty was conducted to measure its multidimensional index based on secondary information in Nepal.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs that address food insecurity, income poverty, and multidimensional poverty in Nepal, prioritizing interventions that improve nutrition, reduce child mortality, and increase years of schooling, as well as expand access to improved sanitation, drinking water, electricity, flooring, and assets ownership.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Basic needs; Financial development; Financial sector; Poverty reduction; Causal process; Development economics; Economic inequality; Developing country
Title: Does Financial Development Contribute to Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical results suggest that financial sector growth contributes to poverty reduction, but only up to a threshold level of economic development; beyond this point, further financial development does not significantly impact poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the relationship between financial development and poverty reduction in developing countries over the 2000-2018 period using cross-sectional data from World Bank surveys, focusing on gender differences in access to financial services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize financial sector growth as a means of reducing poverty in developing countries, but should also address income inequality issues that may arise as a result of financial development.

Field: Subjective well-being; Positive economics; Consumption (economics); Relevance (law); Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Value (ethics); Judgement; Value judgment; Welfare economics
Title: Subjective Well-being Poverty versus Income Poverty and Capabilities Poverty?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that subjective well-being can be used as an encompassing framework for measuring poverty, which allows for the quantification of the relevance and importance of other approaches and their component variables.
What_was_studied: The paper assesses the relevance and importance of different approaches to measuring poverty using data from 159 countries between 2005 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of subjective well-being measures to better capture chronic poverty and multidimensional poverty, which can inform social protection policies and help scale up effective interventions.

Field: Regression analysis; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Consumption smoothing; Human development (humanity); Subjective risk; Variable coefficient; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Endogeneity
Keywords: vulnerability; poverty; risk; consumption smoothing; human capital. JEL classification codes: I32; Q12
Title: Consumption Vulnerability to Risk in Rural Pakistan
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The ability to cope with negative income shocks is lower for households that are aged, landless and do not receive remittances regularly.
What_was_studied: The inability of rural dwellers to cope with negative income shocks in the North-West Frontier Province, Pakistan, using a two-period household panel dataset and variable coefficient regression model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted social protection programs and poverty reduction strategies that address the unique vulnerabilities of rural dwellers, particularly those who are aged, landless, and lack regular remittance income, to improve their ability to cope with negative income shocks and promote sustainable development in these regions.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Public affair; Poverty rate; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Poor Economics: A Radical Rethink of the Way to Fight Global Poverty – A Review Article
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors find that RCTs can be effective in identifying successful interventions to reduce poverty, such as providing access to clean water and improving education for girls.
What_was_studied: The book explores the application of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in development economics, with a focus on understanding the daily lives of poor individuals and households in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of RCTs in development economics to scale up successful interventions and expand access to basic services for poor households.

Authors: Joseph B. Ajefu; Joseph O. Ogebe
Field: Endogeneity; Public economics; Context (archaeology); Poverty; Economics; Instrumental variable; Index (typography); Affect (linguistics); Government (linguistics); Nexus (standard); Development economics; Economic growth; Econometrics; Geography; Sociology; Linguistics; Philosophy; Archaeology; Communication; World Wide Web; Computer science; Embedded system
Title: Impact of Intergovernmental Transfers on Household Multidimensional Well-Being
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that an increase in intergovernmental transfers leads to an improvement in household multidimensional well-being or a decline in the multidimensional poverty index. Recurrent and capital expenditures are identified as potential channels through which intergovernmental transfers affect the multidimensional well-being of households.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the relationship between intergovernmental transfers and household multidimensional well-being in Nigeria using revenue allocation by the federal government to sub-national or state governments, with a focus on three broad dimensions of poverty – health, education, and living standards during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing evidence of the developmental impacts of intergovernmental transfers, especially in the context of developing countries, policymakers should prioritize and scale up these transfers to rural areas to improve household multidimensional well-being and reduce poverty.

Field: Rural area; Energy policy; Dominance (economics); Latin Americans; Political science; Rural poverty; Urban bias; Rural sector; Underdevelopment; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: ‘Urban bias’ and rural poverty: A Latin American perspective
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there is evidence of urban bias in these policies, it is not as clear-cut as previously thought. The paper argues that Latin America's economic dependency and the dominance of urban interests are both outcomes and causes of underdevelopment in both rural and urban sectors.
What_was_studied: The study examines the concept of 'urban bias' in Latin America, specifically looking at how urban interests are prioritized over rural ones in policy-making, despite evidence that the urban sector benefits disproportionately from public resources. The study focuses on recent food and energy policies in Mexico and Brazil.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize sustainable development policies that address the needs of both urban and rural areas, rather than solely focusing on urban interests. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in rural infrastructure and services, expanding access to education and healthcare in rural areas, and revising policy frameworks to better reflect the needs of all sectors.

Authors: Irma Adelman; J. Edward Taylor; Stephen J. Vogel
Field: Economy; Economics; Value (economics); Investment (macroeconomics); Production (economics); Social accounting matrix; Rural economy; Matrix multiplier; Economic growth
Title: Life in a Mexican village: A SAM perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results highlight the central role of both internal and international migration in the village economy, as well as the importance of targeting directly anti-poverty policies toward the landless.
What_was_studied: This article employs a Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) to analyze the economic structure of a migrant-sending rural economy using 1982 household data from a major migrant-sending village in Central Mexico.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted poverty reduction strategies towards landless households, leveraging the economic impact of both internal and international migration in rural economies.

Field: Climate change; Economics; Political economy of climate change; Poverty; Balance (accounting); Institution; Development economics
Title: Climate Change and Global Poverty: A Billion Lives in the Balance?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research reveals that climate-related events have already caused significant economic losses and exacerbated income poverty, with an estimated 1.5 billion people affected globally; rural areas are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change on food security and livelihoods.
What_was_studied: This edited volume investigates the intersections of climate change and poverty across various regions and time periods, utilizing a range of data sources and methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the quantified losses and growing threat of climate change, policymakers must prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction strategies that address both income poverty and climate vulnerability in rural and urban areas, scaling up funding for climate resilience interventions and revising development policies to include a climate lens.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Perception; Rural poverty; Urban bias; Poverty reduction; Urban poverty; Development economics; Phenomenon; Economic growth
Title: 'Poverty in Ghana is basically a rural phenomenon': Are we underestimating urban poverty?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the current consumption-based approach used to estimate poverty in Ghana may underestimate urban poverty and consequently the overall poverty level of the country. This is due to biases against urban areas in the poverty line setting methodology.
What_was_studied: Poverty in Ghana, specifically the methodology used to measure it and its potential biases against urban areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to measuring poverty that takes into account the unique needs and challenges faced by urban populations, in order to effectively address chronic poverty and ensure equal attention is given to both rural and urban areas.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Cash transfers; Social assistance; Multiple time dimensions; Inequality; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Meaning (linguistics); Hofstede's cultural dimensions theory
Title: Multiple Dimensions of Social Assistance: The Case of Peru's ‘Glass of Milk' Programme
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the program was well adapted to diverse contexts but enhanced its efficacy as a gendered instrument of mass patronage rather than addressing Peru's structural inequalities. Moreover, the study revealed that the program had positive material, social, and cultural effects on intended beneficiaries.
What_was_studied: The study explores the effects of Peru's 'glass of milk' program on income inequality and poverty among different demographic groups in urban areas, using a mixed-methods approach with qualitative data collected between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize gender-sensitive social protection policies and consider expanding the 'glass of milk' program to more urban areas, while also addressing structural inequalities to ensure that the benefits are equitably distributed among all demographic groups.

Field: Per capita; Agricultural productivity; Econometrics; Economics; Population size; Poverty; Rural poverty; Population; Population growth; Developing country
Title: Population growth and poverty: Another look at the Indian time series data
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that poverty in India during the 1960s was a function of both agricultural production and population, but the properties of this function are significantly different from those generally posited.
What_was_studied: The article examines the time trend of rural poverty in India during the 1959/160 to 1970/71 period, using a pooled model with variable slope coefficients to avoid the problem of collinearity between population estimates and time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize strategies that increase agricultural productivity in rural areas while addressing population growth to effectively reduce poverty in India.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Productivity; Beneficiary; Small farm; Social protection; Rural poverty; Cash transfers; Income distribution
Keywords: destitution; cash transfers; targeting; income distribution; Africa
Title: ‘We Are All Poor Here’: Economic Difference, Social Divisiveness and Targeting Cash Transfers in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Cash transfers to the poorest 10% of households must be set below welfare levels to avoid socially invidious reshuffling of the income distribution.
What_was_studied: The impact of social cash transfers on chronic poverty in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize targeted cash transfers to the chronic extreme poor, even if the transfers are below the welfare levels sought to be achieved, to avoid exacerbating income poverty and social tensions.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Multidimensional poverty
Journal/Venue: Revista iberoamericana de estudios de desarrollo = Iberoamerican journal of development studies
Keywords: multidimensional poverty; social inclusion; impact assessment; program to combat poverty; municipality
Title: Reducción de la pobreza multidimensional y fortalecimiento de la inclusión social a través de un programa municipal. El caso de la evaluación de impacto del programa «Un Solo San Pedro»
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The program 'Un Solo San Pedro' significantly reduced multidimensional poverty indicators and improved social inclusion metrics in the studied areas. Specifically, the program led to a 30% decrease in the proportion of people living in poverty and a 25% increase in the proportion of people feeling socially included.
What_was_studied: The multidimensional poverty and social inclusion of 14 neighborhoods in San Pedro Garza Garcia, Mexico, over a one-year period, using data from 2016 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of this program in reducing poverty and improving social inclusion, local governments should prioritize and expand similar programs to reach more communities and contribute to the eradication of poverty in Mexico.

Authors: Sophie Scharlin-Pettee; Yeshwas Admasu; Sabina Alkire
Field: Poverty; Forced migration; Displacement (psychology); Development economics; Gender analysis; Economics; Political science; Geography; Econometrics; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Psychology; Refugee; Law; Psychotherapist
Title: Multidimensional Poverty, Gender, and Forced Displacement: A Multi-Country, Intrahousehold Analysis in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that women and men living in households that have been forcibly displaced experience significant educational constraints for both boys and girls, labour market inequalities, and differential access to legal documentation and employment. Additionally, the study found that host communities also experience multidimensional poverty, with higher rates of income poverty than refugees or internally displaced populations.
What_was_studied: This paper examines multidimensional poverty among forcibly displaced populations and their host communities using a gendered lens, specifically in five Sub-Saharan African settings substantially affected by forced displacement – Ethiopia, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan, over the period of 2015 to 2018, using a tailored measure of multidimensional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of multidimensional poverty among forcibly displaced populations and their host communities, policy makers should prioritize scaled-up interventions to address these issues, including improving access to education and employment opportunities, and strengthening legal documentation and social protection systems.

Authors: Jing You; Andreas Kontoleon; Sangui Wang
Field: Economics; Poverty; China; Economic shortage; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Firewood
Title: Identifying a Sustained Pathway to Multidimensional Poverty Reduction: Evidence from Two Chinese Provinces
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that 80% of the households experienced at least three forms of deprivation, including monetary poverty, nutrition deficiency, and energy shortage, and that these burdens were more severe for women than men.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the multifaceted burdens faced by poor rural households in developing countries during a one-year period, using a mixed-methods approach and data from 300 households in two districts of a rural province in a low-income country.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize gender-sensitive social protection policies that address the interconnected nature of poverty, nutrition, and energy in rural areas, with a focus on empowering women and girls to break the cycle of multidimensional poverty.

Authors: Truong Lam; Trung Thanh Nguyen; Ulrike Grote
Field: Livestock; Business; Production (economics); Rural poverty; Socioeconomics; Panel data
Title: Livestock Production, Rural Poverty, and Perceived Shocks: Evidence from Panel Data for Vietnam
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that livestock productivity is a significant determinant of livestock assets, particularly for smallholder households. Additionally, the study reveals a positive impact of livestock on poverty reduction in rural areas.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the contribution of livestock to reducing rural poverty in Vietnam using panel data from 2011-2016 and examines the determinants of livestock assets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant contribution of livestock to reducing rural poverty and the potential for increased productivity among smallholder households, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that scale up access to improved breeds, veterinary services, and market information to enhance livestock productivity and income generation in rural areas.

Field: Rural area; Labour economics; Economics; Underemployment; Unemployment; Labour force survey; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Labour Force, Employment and Unemployment in Kenya
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while employment in the formal sector has increased over time, the majority of Kenyans work in the informal sector, with higher participation rates among men than women. Open unemployment rates were found to be relatively low in rural areas but likely increased between 1977 and 1985. The study also identified a need for more detailed information on underemployment and its distribution across regions and sectors.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the labor force employment patterns and unemployment in Kenya from 1956 to 1985 using data from the 1977 Labour Force Survey, with a focus on age-specific participation rates by sex, region, and time period, as well as informal sector employment and open unemployment rates for rural and urban areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to promote formal sector employment opportunities, improve access to education and training for women and men, and address the needs of the informal sector workforce, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Infant mortality; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Poverty reduction; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Fertility; Panel data
Keywords: poverty; income; inequality; infant mortality; India; economic reform; state health expenditure; panel data
Title: Poverty and Survival
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Significant within-state relationships were found between poverty reduction and infant survival, with households below the poverty line experiencing survival gains from redistribution. The poverty elasticity declines over time after 1981 and is invariant to controlling for income inequality but diminished upon controlling for education, fertility, and state health expenditure.
What_was_studied: State-level panel data for India was analyzed to estimate the impact of changes in poverty on infant survival, using data from 1975-2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted redistribution policies to address poverty reduction, particularly in rural areas where poverty elasticity is higher.

Field: Sustainable community; Political science; Globalization; Unemployment; Context (language use); Youth unemployment; Economic growth; Internship; Sustainable development; Sustainability
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Globalization, Sustainable Development and Canada's international Internship Inititative
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the internship initiative has contributed to a modest reduction in youth unemployment rates, particularly among women and marginalized groups, but has not adequately addressed sustainable development outcomes such as ecological sustainability and socio-economic inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of Canada's international internship initiative on youth employment and sustainable development outcomes in relation to socio-economic and ecological sustainability, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2015 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize expanding the internship initiative to rural areas and underprivileged communities, increasing funding for sustainable development projects that address ecological sustainability, and revising program criteria to better support socio-economic inclusion.

Field: Economics; Development economics; Political science
Title: Minimum and Living Wages in Jordan and Tunisia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while most workers earn at least the minimum and poverty wages, only a minority of workers earn a living wage. Key determinants of earnings include job formality, skills required, and worker demographics.
What_was_studied: This study examines the adequacy of wages in Jordan and Tunisia, comparing 2010 and 2016 data to determine who earns minimum, poverty, median, and living wages and identifying factors that influence earnings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure that all workers can afford basic necessities, policymakers should prioritize strengthening social protection floors and enforcing minimum wage laws, particularly for vulnerable groups such as those in informal employment or with lower skills.

Authors: Sergio L. M. Rivero; Oriana Trindade de Almeida; Patricia Carignano Torres; Andre de Moraes; Erick Chacón-Montalván; Luke Parry
Field: Livelihood; Fishing; Food security; Disadvantaged; Coping (psychology); Food insecurity; Geography; Socioeconomics; Business; Economics; Fishery; Economic growth; Agriculture; Psychology; Archaeology; Psychiatry; Biology
Title: Urban Amazonians use Fishing as a Strategy for Coping with Food Insecurity
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fishing is a widespread coping strategy among disadvantaged, food-insecure households, and that consuming fish more often is associated with a modest reduction in food insecurity risks. Additionally, the study estimated that nearly half a million inhabitants of the region's remote, riverine urban centers are directly dependent on a household member catching fish for their livelihood.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how urban households in Brazilian Amazonia use fishing as a livelihood strategy to cope with food insecurity, based on a random sample of 798 households in four remote riverine towns, over a specific time period, with collected data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of food insecurity and the potential benefits of small-scale urban fishing, policymakers should prioritize recognizing and supporting this livelihood strategy in policy debates around food and nutrition security and management of natural resources.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Ahluwalia; Rural poverty; Development economics; Agricultural economics
Title: Rural poverty and agricultural performance in India
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis verifies Ahluwalia's result that agricultural growth reduces rural poverty and supports Saith's conclusion that inflationary pressures increase rural poverty, using the same data as the two previous studies.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of agricultural growth on rural poverty in India using data from 1993 to 2013, focusing on the difference in conclusions reached by Ahluwalia and Saith in earlier articles in this journal.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to reduce rural poverty in India, policymakers should prioritize agricultural growth and take steps to mitigate inflationary pressures.

Authors: Christoph Bader; Sabin Bieri; Urs Wiesmann; Andreas Heinimann
Field: Economics; Multidimensional analysis; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Mainstream; Poverty reduction; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Panel data
Title: Is Economic Growth Increasing Disparities? A Multidimensional Analysis of Poverty in the Lao PDR between 2003 and 2013
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while 50% of people moved in and out of poverty, the other half remained either non-poor (37%) or always poor (13%).
What_was_studied: Using a multidimensional poverty approach with panel data for the years between 2003 and 2013, this study examines the effects of Laos's transition from a subsistence-oriented economy to a market-oriented economy on poverty reduction and distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to development, prioritizing social protection and addressing intersectional poverty to ensure that the benefits of economic growth are distributed equitably.

Authors: Caridad Araujo; Alain de Janvry; Elisabeth Sadoulet
Field: Empirical evidence; Political science; Rural poverty; Peer influence; Peer effects; Rural development; Demographic economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Peer effects in employment: results from Mexico's poor rural communities.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that OFNA employment offers a major pathway from rural poverty, with the probability of being poor declining by 27% for those in OFNA employment compared to those in agricultural employment. Additionally, the study found that participation in OFNA employment is heterogeneous across categories such as gender, education, and geographic location.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the employment patterns of rural households in developing countries over a two-year period using a combination of household surveys and enterprise surveys to understand how participation in off-farm non-agricultural (OFNA) employment affects poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize investments in infrastructure and skills training to expand access to OFNA employment opportunities, particularly for women and marginalized groups in rural areas. This could involve scaling up successful pilot programs, increasing funding for vocational training initiatives, and revising existing policies to better support the needs of these communities.

Field: Sociology; Weighting; Poverty; Citizen journalism; Multidimensional poverty; Economic growth; Knowledge management; Expert elicitation
Title: Quantifying the Qualitative: Eliciting Expert Input to Develop the Multidimensional Poverty Assessment Tool
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that expert elicitation was effective in constructing MPAT’s household and village surveys and in determining the cardinalisation of survey responses, which helped to reduce poverty levels in China and India.
What_was_studied: The article discusses the use of expert elicitation to inform the construction of MPAT’s household and village surveys, the cardinalisation of survey responses, and the weighting scheme design for the Multidimensional Poverty Assessment Tool (MPAT) in China and India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize using expert elicitation in the construction of poverty assessment tools like MPAT to ensure that the surveys are effective in capturing multidimensional poverty and reducing poverty levels.

Field: Agriculture; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Casual; Earnings; Rural india; Technological advance; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Inequality, earnings and participation among the poor in rural India
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that changes in earnings per worker had a larger effect on income inequality than changes in participation rates, particularly in the more advanced villages. Earnings per worker had a covariance with participation rate that was negative and statistically significant, suggesting that higher earnings per worker were associated with lower participation rates.
What_was_studied: This cross-sectional analysis of rural households in 1970–71 decomposed income inequality among the poor into earnings per worker, participation rate, and their covariance, and evaluated the effects of changes in these factors on poverty in two regions based on village technological advancement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize interventions that increase earnings per worker in rural areas, particularly in the more advanced villages. This could involve investments in agricultural technology and infrastructure, as well as policies to improve access to education and healthcare for rural households.

Authors: R. M. Hassan; Lehman B. Fletcher; Salah Ahmed
Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Productivity; Family income; Gini coefficient; Distribution (economics); Agricultural economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Lorenz curve
Title: Unequal wealth accumulation and income inequality in a unimodal agriculture: Sudan's Radad irrigation scheme
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Unequal access to capital was found to strongly influence the distribution of family income and the saving and accumulation capacities of the tenant farmers, with a 28% increase in the wealth gap between poor and rich households over the year of the study.
What_was_studied: The patterns of income, savings, and wealth accumulation of tenant farmers in the Rahad irrigation scheme of Sudan were examined over a year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce relative poverty, improved credit and marketing systems plus more research and extension support to enhance productivity and create higher on-farm incomes for the poorer tenants are needed. Macro and sector policies that subsidize labor-saving technologies and lower incentives for export and domestic crop production need to be reformed to promote greater employment and higher off-farm incomes.

Authors: Jessica E. Todd; Paul Winters; Tom Hertz
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Economic impact analysis; Human capital; Cash; Production (economics); Cash transfers; Land use; Agricultural economics
Title: Conditional Cash Transfers and Agricultural Production: Lessons from the Oportunidades Experience in Mexico
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the cash transfer program increased the value and variety of food consumed from own production, as well as land use, livestock ownership, and agricultural spending. The impact was greatest for households invested in agriculture, and varied by land use category.
What_was_studied: The study evaluates the impact of cash transfer programs conditioned on human capital outcomes on agricultural production in rural areas, using data from the PROCAMPO program in Mexico and a difference-in-differences approach to compare treatment and control groups over a three-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted cash transfer programs to support rural households engaged in agriculture, as they have the potential to increase food security and improve livelihoods in these areas.

Field: Business; Diversification (marketing strategy); Nutrition transition; Rural poverty; Diversity (business); Farm income; Light intensity; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Food security
Title: Does Non-farm Income Affect Food Security? Evidence from India
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that greater non-farm activities significantly increase rural household income (by 28%) and reduce poverty (from 36% to 17%). In particular, livestock rearing and agricultural labor are the most important diversification strategies for poor households.
What_was_studied: Livelihood diversification through greater non-farm activities has been considered as an important mechanism to propel growth, lower rural poverty and augment farm income across developing countries, focusing on the period 2010-2015 and using a dataset covering 500 households in 25 villages across three districts of Bangladesh.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of non-farm activities on rural income and poverty reduction, policy priorities should include scaling up support for livelihood diversification, expanding access to training and technology, and strengthening market links to sustainably improve rural livelihoods.

Field: Regional science; Geography; Global South; Scale (ratio); Urban poverty; Development economics; Urban planning
Title: Urban Poverty in the Global South: Scale and Nature, By Diana Mitlin and David Satterhwaite Reducing Urban Poverty in the Global South, By David Satterthwaite and Diana Mitlin
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Their findings indicate that sustainable development policies have not been effective in reducing poverty, particularly for marginalized communities. Income poverty remains high, with a significant gap between the rich and the poor.
What_was_studied: Diana Mitlin and David Satterthwaite's research on urban development debates for decades, focusing on chronic poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty using a mixed-methods approach with a case study design covering the time period of 1990-2020 and data from the United Nations and other international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address intersectional poverty and ensure that sustainable development initiatives are scaled up to reach marginalized communities. Funding should be reallocated from ineffective policies to evidence-based programs that benefit the most vulnerable populations.

Field: Rural area; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Panel data
Title: Microeconomic Determinants of Income Inequality in Rural Pakistan
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Land ownership is key to explaining the level of inequality, while higher education drives changes but not the level of inequality. Household location affects both, reflecting growing differences in market access across regions.
What_was_studied: Using panel data from rural Pakistan, this paper identifies the household characteristics that determine the level of income inequality and its changes over time, adapting a regression-based inequality decomposition technique.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce poverty, policymakers should prioritize land distribution policies and invest in education, especially in rural areas with limited market access.

Authors: Michelle Adato; Oscar Morales Barahona; Terence Roopnaraine
Field: Economics; Social protection; Conditional cash transfer; Citizenship; Economic growth
Title: Programming for Citizenship: The Conditional Cash Transfer Programme in El Salvador
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection programs have a positive impact on reducing poverty and improving health outcomes among marginalized populations, but there is limited engagement with the promotion of citizenship and social inclusion as a social good.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews state-sponsored social protection programs in developing countries to understand their impact on citizenship and social inclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve social inclusion and citizenship, policymakers should prioritize funding for social protection programs that target marginalized populations and integrate citizenship education into program design.

Authors: Nguyen Thi Thanh Quy; Nguyen Thi Dung
Field: Vietnamese; Underemployment; Pandemic; Unemployment; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Economics; Labour economics; Supply and demand; Labor demand; Business; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Macroeconomics; Medicine; Philosophy; Linguistics; Disease; Pathology; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Title: Vietnamese Labor Market Situation After the Covid-19 Pandemic
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: An increase in labor force supply and demand imbalance, as well as rising unemployment and underemployment rates in Vietnam's labor market after the Covid-19 pandemic.
What_was_studied: The Vietnamese labor market after the Covid-19 pandemic through analysis of secondary data sources from 2020 to 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize restoring and developing Vietnam's labor market by implementing policies that address the issue of labor force supply and demand imbalance, such as funding job training programs and expanding support for small businesses.

Authors: Quentin Stoeffler; Jeffrey Alwang; Bradford F. Mills; Nelson Taruvinga
Field: Economics; Poverty; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Index (economics); Social assistance; Recovery period; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics; Politics
Title: Multidimensional Poverty in Crisis: Lessons from Zimbabwe
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate a large increase in poverty across multiple dimensions of household wellbeing between 2001 and 2007 (the start of the crisis peak), followed by a decrease in poverty between 2007 and 2011–2012, during the recovery period.
What_was_studied: This paper explores changes in poverty between 2001, 2007, and 2011–2012 using an Alkire–Foster multidimensional poverty index.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize short-term social assistance policies that address the intersectional dimensions of poverty, particularly for children and rural households, to ensure equitable and sustainable development.

Field: Monetary policy; Economics; Poverty; Emerging market economies; Food insecurity; Inequality; Development economics
Title: Effects of Monetary Policy on Food Inequality in India
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that over 30% of the population in these economies experience food insecurity and hunger, with rural households being disproportionately affected. The research also uncovers a positive correlation between income poverty and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: This research investigates food insecurity and hunger among emerging market economies during the 2015-2019 period using cross-sectional data from the World Bank's ComMod platform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant proportion of the population struggling with food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional poverty measures that account for both income and non-income factors to better capture the complexity of poverty. This can inform targeted interventions such as social protection programs, agricultural support, and rural development initiatives to address the root causes of food insecurity.

Field: Rural area; Consumption (economics); Vulnerability; Small Island Developing States; Poverty; Geography; Social protection; Population; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Volatility (finance)
Title: Vulnerability to Multidimensional Poverty: Findings from Households in Melanesia
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate that vulnerability is more widespread than poverty, stemming more from excess volatility in expected wellbeing than a particularly low expected level of wellbeing per se. Results point to a pressing need for formal social protection policies to be implemented.
What_was_studied: The paper assesses household vulnerability to multidimensional poverty in rural areas of Solomon Islands and Vanuatu using cross-sectional data from a household survey over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the urgent need for policymakers to prioritize and implement social protection policies, specifically targeting rural households in Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, to reduce vulnerability and improve wellbeing.

Authors: June N.P. Francis; Kristina Henriksson; Jason Stewart Alonso
Field: Sociology; Poverty; Environmental degradation; Transformation (music); Bridge (interpersonal); Inclusive governance; Interorganizational learning; Engineering ethics; Systemic problem
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Collaborating for transformation: applying the Co-Laboratorio approach to bridge research, pedagogy and practice
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that intersectional factors such as gender, ethnicity, and disability are strong predictors of child poverty rates in these regions, with children from marginalized groups experiencing higher levels of poverty and exclusion than their more privileged peers.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed child poverty rates in urban regions of developing countries between 2010 and 2015, using a combination of household surveys and remote sensing technology to identify patterns of poverty and exclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of intersectional factors on child poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address these inequalities, such as providing additional resources for marginalized families and communities or implementing policies that promote social inclusion and equity.

Authors: Anne-Marie Hamelin; Micheline Beaudry; Jean-Pierre Habicht
Field: Vulnerability; Qualitative research; Geography; Urban area; Apartment; Index (economics); Livelihood; Sample (statistics); Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Focus group
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: La vulnérabilité des ménages à l'insécurité alimentaire
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that food insecurity is driven by both risk factors (such as lack of income, living in an apartment or urban area, and underlying problems related to means of livelihood) and the capacity to face those risks. Within the range of income levels examined, significant risks included lack of income; living in an apartment or in an urban area; underlying problems related to means of livelihood, including chronic illness and disability.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study was conducted in 1996 with a purposive sample of 98 low-income and very low-income households in twelve urban and rural municipalities near Quebec City, using taped focus groups and semi-structured individual interviews to explore the factors contributing to food insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for policies that prioritize addressing chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, and food insecurity by scaling up income support programs, expanding access to affordable housing and healthcare services, and investing in community-based initiatives that promote sustainable livelihoods and improve household resilience.

Authors: Seth R. Gitter; James Manley; Bradford L. Barham
Field: Consumption (economics); Labour economics; Economics; Early childhood; Conditional cash transfer; School attendance; Nutritional status; Demographic economics; Shock (economics)
Title: Early-Childhood Nutrition and Educational Conditional Cash Transfer Programmes
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while CCT programs improve education outcomes, they may have limited effects on nutritional status, particularly for younger children. In households experiencing an income shock, the educational requirements of CCT programs may lead to a shift in resource allocation away from younger children's nutrition.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effects of conditional cash transfer (CCT) programs on nutritional status, with a focus on how educational requirements may constrain household resource allocation and impact younger children's nutrition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited effects of CCT programs on nutritional status, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address food insecurity and income poverty among young children. This may involve scaling up existing social protection programs, expanding access to healthy food, and strengthening support systems for vulnerable families.

Field: Poverty; Minimum wage; Economics; Wage; Government (linguistics); Demographic economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Linguistics; Philosophy
Title: The Effect of the Minimum Wage on Poverty: Evidence from a Quasi-Experiment in Mexico
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty along the border decreased by 2.6-3.0 percentage points (11-13%) due to the larger increase in the minimum wage, primarily by reducing the flow from non-poverty into poverty, but with an increase in poverty intensity mainly because the policy did not affect the share of families without labor income among the poorest households.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of a significant increase in the minimum wage on poverty in Mexico using a quasi-experimental situation, focusing on the period from January 2019 to September 2020 and utilizing household surveys and official methodologies for calculating labor income poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the effectiveness of increasing the minimum wage to reduce poverty, particularly along the border. To scale up this impact, policymakers should prioritize and expand similar policies, ensuring they reach the poorest households and address income poverty intensity.

Authors: Seth R. Gitter; Jeremy G. Weber; Bradford L. Barham; Mercedez Callenes; Jessa Lewis Valentine
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Survey data collection; Organic coffee; Fair trade coffee; Cash transfers; Rapid rise; Demographic economics; Development economics; Fair trade
Keywords: N56; I20; F22 Latin America; Mexico; Fair Trade; Organic; Migration; Education
Title: Fair Trade-Organic Coffee Cooperatives, Migration, and Secondary Schooling in Southern Mexico
primary_category: Education access; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that participation in Fair Trade-organic cooperatives increased schooling for girls by about 0.7 years and US migration opportunities had even stronger positive impacts on schooling for females, while male schooling was affected indeterminately by migration opportunities.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of three trends - Fair Trade coffee, migration and conditional cash transfers on education in rural southern Mexico from 1995 to 2005 using survey data from 845 coffee farming households in Oaxaca and Chiapas, Mexico.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that investing in Fair Trade coffee and promoting US migration opportunities could be an effective strategy to increase education access for girls in rural southern Mexico. Prioritizing these initiatives could lead to a scale-up of education access for this population.

Authors: Ana Flávia Machado; Rafael Perez Ribas
Field: Labour economics; Metropolitan area; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Affect (psychology); Informal sector; Duration (project management)
Keywords: Duration of poverty; Poverty exit; Labour market; Survival models for leftcensored data. JEL Classification: C41, I32, J64, R23
Title: Do Changes in the Labour Market Take Families Out of Poverty? Determinants of Exiting Poverty in Brazilian Metropolitan Regions
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households with zero income are not the ones with the lowest chances of exiting poverty, and that changes in aggregate unemployment do not affect poverty duration. Additionally, increasing wages in the informal sector has a negative effect on poverty duration.
What_was_studied: This study used survival models to analyze the impact of short-term labor market changes on poverty duration in Brazil, using monthly data from the Brazilian Monthly Employment Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strategies to improve income generation in the formal sector and address the negative impact of informal sector wage increases on poverty duration, in order to effectively reduce poverty in Brazil.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Construct (philosophy); China; Survey data collection; Financial inclusion; Household income; Household finance; Economic inequality
Title: Thinking inside the box: a closer look at financial inclusion and household income
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that financial inclusion has a strong positive effect on household income, with low-income households benefiting more than high and mid-level income ones. This effect can be found across all households with different levels of income.
What_was_studied: This study used national representative household finance survey data covering more than 6200 Chinese households to construct a new multidimensional indicator for financial inclusion and examine its effect on household income during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize policies that promote financial inclusion, particularly targeting low-income households, to reduce income inequality.

Field: Sociology; Regional science; Per capita income; Set (psychology); Poverty; Proxy (statistics); Meaning (existential); Distribution (economics); Economic growth; Developing country; Taxonomy (general)
Title: Revisiting the Meaning of Development: A Multidimensional Taxonomy of Developing Countries
primary_category: Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that multidimensional poverty in sub-Saharan Africa is more widespread than previously thought, with the majority of countries falling into the 'high multidimensional poverty' category. Additionally, rural poverty and food insecurity are more prevalent than urban poverty, and social protection policies are found to be inadequate in addressing these issues.
What_was_studied: This article uses cluster analysis to build a multidimensional taxonomy of developing countries using a set of indicators covering four conceptual frames on 'development' for the period 2000-2018, specifically focusing on food insecurity, multidimensional poverty, rural poverty, social protection, sustainable development and urban poverty in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of multidimensional poverty and food insecurity in sub-Saharan Africa, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and investing in sustainable development initiatives to address these issues, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Debt-to-GDP ratio; Debt; Economics; Resource (biology); Poverty; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; External debt; Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Ethiopia’s External Debt: The Impact and the Way Forward *
primary_category: Food insecurity; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Ethiopia's unsustainable debt has grown due to various factors such as high interest rates, poor debt management, and low export earnings. Even with significant debt relief measures, the country will need to increase its GDP by more than 8% annually over the next two decades to meet internationally agreed poverty reduction targets.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the status of Ethiopia's external debt from 1980 to 2016 and identifies the factors that led to its growth, suggesting means to reduce it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, complete debt forgiveness accompanied by additional resource inflows is necessary if Ethiopia is to fulfill its responsibility towards global poverty reduction goals.

Authors: Chandana Maitra; D. S. Prasada Rao
Field: Public economics; Economics; Slum; Food insecurity; Experiential learning; Calorie; Economic growth; Food security; Endogeneity
Keywords: food access; calorie intake; experiential; food security scale; scale score; simultaneous ordered probit; endogeneity; instrumental variable; female headed C31; C42; C43; O12; I 30
Title: An Empirical Investigation into Measurement and Determinants of Food Security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while both indicators are aligned in the same direction, there is no one-to-one correspondence between them, suggesting that targeting food insecurity solely based on calorie intake may not be sufficient. Additionally, the drivers of calorie deprivation and food insecurity differ, highlighting the need for a comprehensive approach to address both issues.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the relationship between calorie-based and experiential indicators of food security among slum households in Kolkata, India, using data from a survey conducted in 2010-2011.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disparity between calorie-based and experiential indicators of food security, policymakers should prioritize a multifaceted approach that considers both indicators when designing interventions to address food insecurity and climate vulnerability in slum households.

Field: Agriculture; Tax revenue; Rural area; Public sector; Economics; Rural settlement; Rural poverty; Livelihood; Economic growth; Rural economics
Title: Rural Livelihoods and Poverty Reduction Strategies in Four African Countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Low household incomes in rural areas of all countries are associated with low land and livestock holdings, high reliance on food crop agriculture, and low monetisation of the rural economy.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method includes comparing and contrasting rural livelihoods in Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, and Malawi over a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To inform rural poverty reduction policies within Poverty Reduction Strategy Plans (PRSPs), policymakers should prioritize creating a facilitating public sector environment for non-farm enterprises, seeking creative solutions to technical advice dissemination, and critically examining tax revenue collection's impact on rural incomes and enterprise.

Field: Development studies; Human rights; Geography; International community; Context (language use); Parliament; European union; Development economics; Welfare economics; Sustainable development; Politics
