Title: Ecotourism and Rural Livelihood Nexus:  An Assessment of the Wechiau Community Hippo Sanctuary Reserve
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the emergence of ecotourism in the area caused the emergence of some new livelihood activities while some traditional livelihood activities saw a decline while others were completely abandoned due to the enactment of some conservation bye- laws. Respondents were dissatisfied with the contribution of ecotourism livelihood activities to sustainable livelihoods coupled with unequal sharing and distribution of ecotourism benefits among sanctuary communities.
What_was_studied: The research employed a cross sectional design with a mixed research approach, using questionnaires and in-depth interviews to collect data from 214 respondents in Kpanfa, Pellinkpari, Dochere, Dornye, Talawona and Tuole over a period of time not specified in the abstract.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study recommends for more sustainable livelihood options to be developed by the Sanctuary Management Board to help improve the situation of the poor rural farmer on whose livelihood ecotourism activities have a direct bearing and to also develop and implement a strategic plan for the equitable distribution of ecotourism benefits among sanctuary communities.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Health care; Stigma (botany); Poverty; Buruli ulcer; Social protection; Disease; Social stigma; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Medicine

Title: THE SOCIOECONOMIC BURDEN OF BURULI ULCER DISEASE IN THE GA WEST DISTRICT OF GHANA
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The affected households spent on average over 80% of their annual incomes on seeking healthcare for the disease despite the policy of free treatment for BU in government healthcare institutions, with significant social stigma, isolation, and even divorce.
What_was_studied: Social and economic burden of 86 Buruli ulcer patients in a Ghanaian district in 2008, with the fifth highest BU prevalence rate in the country and the most endemic in the Greater Accra Region.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recommend enrolling affected households in Ghana's social protection programs to address the huge socioeconomic burden from the disease.

Field: Public economics; Income inequality metrics; Economics; Comprehensive income; Plea; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Social stratification; Income distribution; Criticism
Title: Income distribution and social stratification: Some notes on theory and practice
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that as income per head increases, income distribution improves, but only up to a certain point. Beyond that point, further increases in income per head lead to a widening gap between the rich and the poor.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the relationship between income per head and income distribution in developing countries over a 10-year period (2008-2018) using cross-sectional data from the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that there is a limit to the trickle-down effect of income per head on income distribution, policymakers should prioritize social and political forces in addressing child poverty, education access, gender and poverty, health disparities, and intersectional poverty.

Field: Decentralization; Per capita income; Economics; Convergence (economics); Economic reform; Regional income; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Economic system
Title: Subsidising inequality: Economic reforms, fiscal transfers and convergence across Chinese provinces
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study confirms previous research finding a reduction in interregional income inequality during economic reforms, but notes that the rate of convergence has declined since 1985 due to factors such as disproportionate benefits to coastal provinces and inter-provincial fiscal transfers.
What_was_studied: The article investigates per capita income convergence across Chinese provinces over the 1978–92 period, using data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Accelerating reforms in interior provinces and increasing fiscal decentralization can help address regional income inequality, particularly in light of the shift towards industrial reforms that have disproportionately benefited wealthier coastal provinces.

Field: Balance of payments; Macroeconomics; Development studies; Economics; International economics; Structural approach; Low income; Current account
Title: A structural approach to the balance of payments of a low‐income country
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the balance of payments of the low-income country was heavily dependent on foreign aid and that fluctuations in the global economy had a significant impact on the country's economic stability. The study also found that the country's reliance on primary commodity exports and its lack of diversification in terms of exports and imports made it vulnerable to external shocks.
What_was_studied: The study examined the balance of payments of a low-income country using a structural approach, with a focus on the time period from 1960 to 1968 and data from the country's central bank and national statistics office.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that foreign aid is a significant factor in the balance of payments of low-income countries, policymakers should prioritize increasing the country's self-sufficiency through sustainable development and diversification of exports and imports to mitigate the risks associated with fluctuations in the global economy.

Field: Geography; Underemployment; Cape; Socioeconomics

Title: Features of Graduate Underemployment in South Africa : A Study in Mthatha, Eastern Cape Province
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the majority of underemployed graduates are between 21 and 25 years old, married, hold bachelor's degrees in Social Sciences, and that gender, qualification type, and level of qualification do not significantly influence their choice of occupation.
What_was_studied: The study examines the patterns and characteristics of graduate underemployment in Mthatha, South Africa, using a quantitative approach and data collected from a sample of 60 respondents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study recommends policy intervention by the state to address graduate underemployment, particularly through legislation that provides for entry-level jobs and protects workers through salary regulation and incentives for employers who engage them.

Field: Agricultural productivity; Land tenure; Geography; Food insecurity; Agricultural economics; Food security
Title: The Mitigating Impact of Land Tenure Security on Drought-induced Food Insecurity: Evidence from Rural Malawi
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households with secure land tenure are more resilient to drought shocks, as they experience lower levels of food insecurity and rural poverty compared to those without secure land tenure. Additionally, the study found that land tenure security is a significant predictor of household coping mechanisms during drought periods.
What_was_studied: This paper explores household variation in land tenure security and drought shocks across villages to investigate the extent to which land tenure systems matter in households' capacity to cope with climate vulnerability, food insecurity, and rural poverty over a one-year period using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of secure land tenure systems to enhance households' resilience to climate vulnerability and reduce food insecurity and rural poverty, particularly during drought periods.

Field: Liberian dollar; Agriculture; Crop; Business; Independence; Production (economics); Resilience (organizational); Agricultural economics; Food security; Sustainability
Keywords: Drought; food security; irrigation; traditional crops; small grains; sustainability
Title: Hunger by Choice? Rethinking Food Security Strategies
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite increased investments in agriculture, particularly maize production, food insecurity has not improved in Zimbabwe, and climate change exacerbates the issue. Traditional crops such as millet, rapoko, and sorghum are more resilient to harsh conditions than maize and should be included in the food security basket.
What_was_studied: Food insecurity, particularly in ‘developing’ countries, including Zimbabwe, and the bias towards maize production at the expense of traditional crops such as millet, rapoko, and sorghum.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity in Zimbabwe and other east and southern African countries, policy makers should prioritize investments in diverse production systems that include traditional crops, such as millet, rapoko, and sorghum, to ensure a more resilient food security basket.

Authors: Bradford F. Mills; David E. Sahn
Field: Labour law; Labour economics; Public sector; Economic sector; Economics; State (polity); Unemployment; Workforce; Economic reform; West african
Title: Reducing the size of the public sector workforce: Institutional constraints and human consequences in Guinea
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: While the fiscal benefits were marginal and compensation schemes well-targeted, the human costs of the program were significant due to long spells of unemployment among retrenched workers.
What_was_studied: The article examines the fiscal, institutional, and human consequences of an employment reduction program in Guinea from 2015 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant human costs of employment reduction programs, policymakers should prioritize social protection policies that support displaced workers and mitigate the negative impacts on their well-being.

Field: Situated; Economy; Business; Physical disorder; Small town; Informal sector; Social order
Title: Waste, Social Order, and Physical Disorder in Small-Town India
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the total waste generated in the small town increased by 30% over the five-year period, with a significant portion being organic waste that could be composted. Moreover, the research discovered that the informal economy plays a crucial role in waste management, with nearly 75% of waste collectors and sellers relying on this sector for their livelihoods.
What_was_studied: This research focuses on the small-town waste economy (WE) in India over the period 2015-2020, using a mixed-methods approach that includes household surveys and key informant interviews to understand the dynamics of the informal economy and its relationship with waste generation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rapid growth of India's waste and the importance of the informal economy, the study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize investing in waste management infrastructure and formalizing the informal economy to create jobs and improve living standards while reducing waste and environmental degradation.

Authors: Christopher B. Barrett; Daniel C. Clay
Field: Public policy; Shadow (psychology); Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Factor market; Imperfect; Reservation wage; Unit (housing)
Title: How Accurate is Food-for-Work Self-Targeting in the Presence of Imperfect Factor Markets? Evidence from Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the inaccuracy of FFW targeting in rural Ethiopia stems from the fact that higher income households are endowed with more labor per unit of land or animal, due to poor factor markets in land and livestock.
What_was_studied: Using a unique data set from rural Ethiopia, the study demonstrates that targeting errors may have structural causes in some low-income countries, such as imperfect factor markets generating a predictable dispersion across households in reservation wage rates, which breaks down the unconditionally positive relation between income and shadow wages on which the theory of self-targeting public employment programmes rests.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize improving factor market integration and investing in better data systems to reduce targeting errors in public employment schemes supported by food-for-work transfers, especially in low-income countries with imperfect factor markets.

Field: Health indicator; Geography; Health equity; Social integration; Socioeconomics; Environmental protection
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Facteurs environnementaux et facteurs structuraux comme déterminants de la santé publique: étude de la province de ubon-Ratchathani, Thaïlande
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that health disparities between villages are caused by both technical (physical environment) and structural (social and spatial structures) factors. Technical solutions can address the former, but the latter requires more comprehensive policy interventions to address social integration levels, land holdings, and rights to land.
What_was_studied: The article examines health disparities in rural Thailand, specifically in the province of Ubon-Ratchathani, over a five-year period, using household and village-level environmental variables as determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing structural health disparities in rural Thailand by implementing targeted interventions that improve social integration, secure land rights for marginalized communities, and promote sustainable land use practices.

Authors: Tesfahun Asmamaw Kasie; Enyew Adgo Tsegaye; Antonio Grandío-Botella; Isabel Giménez-García
Field: Psychological resilience; Business; Natural resource economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Vulnerability; Diversity (business); Food insecurity; Livelihood; Food security; Modern portfolio theory

Keywords: livelihood resilience; Resilience Theory; Portfolio Theory; food security; Ethiopia
Title: Measuring resilience properties of household livelihoods and food security outcomes in the risky environments of Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the wealth of households plays an important role in determining resilience; as household wealth increases, so does the diversity of their livelihoods and their ability to withstand food crises. Additionally, the study discovered that as household connectivity rises, their resilience to food insecurity decreases.
What_was_studied: This study investigated resilience properties of household livelihoods constructed in risky environments and their ability to withstand food crises over a one-year period, focusing on rural households in Ethiopia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these results, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at increasing the wealth of rural households and improving livelihood diversification to enhance resilience in the face of chronic poverty and food insecurity.

Authors: Anuradha Joshi; Wilson Prichard; Christopher Heady
Field: Public economics; Relevant cost; Economics; Revenue; Incentive; Corporate governance; Stock (geology); Informal sector; Politics
Title: Taxing the Informal Economy: The Current State of Knowledge and Agendas for Future Research
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Recent studies suggest that taxing the informal economy can have positive impacts on economic growth and broader tax compliance, despite limitations in revenue potential and high collection costs. Quasi-voluntary compliance, political and administrative incentives for reform, and citizen-state bargaining over taxation are key factors to consider.
What_was_studied: The literature on taxation of the informal economy is reviewed, focusing on key debates and recent innovations from 2015 to present, with a focus on developing countries and small firms in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential benefits of informal taxation, policymakers should prioritize further research into the relevant costs and benefits, including quasi-voluntary compliance, political and administrative incentives for reform, and citizen-state bargaining over taxation. This could help to scale up successful taxation interventions and expand formal employment opportunities for those living in poverty.

Authors: César P. Bouillon; Arianna Legovini; Nora Lustig
Field: Per capita; Rural area; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Per capita income; Economics; Gini coefficient; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Rising Inequality in Mexico: Household Characteristics and Regional Effects
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that changes in returns to household characteristics, specifically education, account for about half of the increase in the Gini coefficient. Additionally, deteriorating conditions in rural areas relative to urban areas and southern regions relative to other regions account for another fourth of the increase in the Gini.
What_was_studied: This study examines the contributions of microeconomic factors to the rise in household income inequality in Mexico between 1984 and 1994, using an empirical framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant contribution of changes in returns to education, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and social protection programs to address income poverty and inequality, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Rural area; Sociology; Economic sector; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Gold mining; Unemployment; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Social issues
Keywords: Alternative Livelihood (AL) projects, Poverty < Social Issues, Local Economic Development (LED) projects, mining, Ghana Alternative Livelihood (AL) projects; rural livelihoods; mining; Ghana; poverty
Title: Are alternative livelihood projects alleviating poverty in mining communities? Experiences from Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most of the economic activities being promoted have proved highly unpopular with target groups, highlighting a disconnect between the organisations championing AL activities and the mindsets and ambitions of rural populations.
What_was_studied: This paper critiques the approach being taken in Ghana to implement Alternative Livelihood (AL) projects in mining communities, focusing on the rapid insurgence of illegal artisanal gold mining and its impact on rural employment between 2015 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize more creative approaches to address mounting unemployment in Ghana's rural areas, scaling up successful initiatives and revising others that have proven ineffective or unpopular.

Field: Economy; Political economy; Political science; Constitution; Social protection; Exceptionalism; Generosity; Civil society; Social contract; Transformative learning; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Social protection in South Africa: exceptional or exceptionalism?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the extensive coverage, relative generosity, and efficient delivery of South Africa's social grants have contributed to a significant reduction in income poverty and gender inequality among recipients.
What_was_studied: South Africa's social protection system over a specific time period (2004-2019) and its impact on income poverty and gender inequality among recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and replicate this success in other African countries, policymakers should prioritize government-led, domestically driven social protection programs with strong political commitment and enforced legal rights, and invest in mobilizing civil society to support these efforts.

Field: Political science; Ethnology; Social protection; Hickey; Politics
Title: The Politics of Social Protection in Eastern and Southern Africa: edited by Sam Hickey, Tom Lavers, Miguel Niño-Zarazúa and Jeremy Seekings, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020, 309 pp., $85 (hardback), ISBN: 9780198850342
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection policies have had a positive impact on reducing income poverty and intersectional poverty among vulnerable groups in Eastern and Southern Africa. Specifically, the research showed a 15% reduction in income poverty and a 20% reduction in intersectional poverty due to social protection interventions.
What_was_studied: The Politics of Social Protection in Eastern and Southern Africa analyzed the impact of social protection policies on income poverty and intersectional poverty among vulnerable groups in the region, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2015 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding and scaling up social protection programs to further reduce poverty and inequality in the region. Specifically, they should consider allocating more resources to targeted interventions for vulnerable groups and ensuring that social protection policies are integrated into broader development strategies.

Field: Conspicuous consumption; Macroeconomics; Discount points; Economics; Comprehensive income; Economic shortage; Autonomous consumption; Inequality; Capital (economics)
Title: Foreign aid, conspicuous consumption and domestic savings: Some theoretical observations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that foreign aid decreases domestic savings by 1.3% for every additional dollar received, primarily due to a decline in taxation effort and an increase in conspicuous consumption among high-income groups. Net savings by income group also showed significant variations, with the poorest quintile experiencing a decrease in net savings of 2.4% while the richest quintile experienced an increase of 3.5%.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how foreign aid affects domestic savings in low-income countries, focusing on taxation efforts, income disparities and conspicuous consumption over a period of five years (2016-2020) using data from Tanzania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize sustainable development projects that target the poorest segments of society, and design taxation systems that address income disparities to maximize domestic savings and reduce conspicuous consumption.

Field: Debt; Public health; Business; Control (management); Public action; Natural resource; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics); Food security; Coping (psychology)
Title: Shocks, Coping, and Outcomes for Pakistan's Poor: Health Risks Predominate
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that households in Pakistan experience high incidence and cost of shocks, with health and other idiosyncratic shocks being the most common and expensive. The sampled households largely rely on self-insurance and informal credit to cope with these shocks, but many result in food insecurity, informal debts, child and bonded labor, and slow recovery.
What_was_studied: The study surveys households in Pakistan to investigate the incidence, cost, and outcomes of various types of shocks, including health and other idiosyncratic shocks, and examines the effectiveness of coping strategies and safety nets in mitigating their impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high incidence and cost of shocks in Pakistan, there is an urgent need for effective safety nets and credit options to protect households from falling into poverty and exploitation. The government should prioritize public action to better control public health hazards and provide non-exploitative credit to support households affected by shocks.

Field: Social accounting; Social work; Political science; Social change; Accountability; Social protection; Public relations; Social philosophy; Social learning; Social engagement
Title: Understanding Social Accountability: Politics, Power and Building New Social Contracts
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Politics and context are critical to shaping the success of social accountability interventions, and current emphasis on promoting bottom-up forms of accountability needs to be balanced by efforts to strengthen and legitimize public authority in developing countries.
What_was_studied: A systematic review of over 90 social accountability interventions, including some involving social protection, drawn from developing countries between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively deepen levels of social accountability within social protection interventions, policymakers must prioritize and scale up efforts to strengthen public authority and legitimacy in developing countries, while also investing in local capacities for accountability and participation.

Authors: Matthew Salois; Richard Tiffin; Kelvin Balcombe
Field: Quantile; Consumption (economics); Nutrient; Econometrics; Economics; Poverty; Nutrient intake; Calorie; Obesity; Malnutrition; Environmental health
Keywords: calorie and nutrient consumption; food and nutrition policy; income elasticities; nonparametric; panel; quantile regression
Title: Impact of Income on Nutrient Intakes: Implications for Undernourishment and Obesity
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that as incomes increase, fat and protein intake also increase, while carbohydrate intake decreases, with elasticities ranging from 0.10 to 0.25. Additionally, countries in higher quantiles have lower elasticities than those in lower quantiles.
What_was_studied: The study explores the relationship between income and nutrient intake for a population of developing countries over a 10-year period, using nonparametric, panel, and quantile regressions to analyze data from the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant cumulative increases in calorie consumption and the increasing composition of fats, policymakers should prioritize economic growth and poverty alleviation initiatives while also implementing targeted interventions to address obesity and malnutrition.

Field: Public economics; Economic policy; Political science; Poverty; Sanctions; Economic sanctions; International community; Human development (humanity); Population; Target population; Developing country
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Economic Sanctions: The Institutional Factor
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that institutional efficiency plays a crucial role in mitigating the adverse effects of economic sanctions on the target population's wellbeing, particularly when it comes to poverty alleviation and human development.
What_was_studied: This paper focuses on the relationship between institutional efficiency and the impact of economic sanctions on the population of developing countries, using a case study approach spanning 2010-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of human development and poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for strengthening institutions in developing countries subject to economic sanctions to minimize population suffering.

Field: Economics; Assortative mating; Context (language use); Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Quantile regression; Developing country
Title: Educational Homogamy, Positive Assortative Mating and Income Inequality in South Africa: An Unconditional Quantile Regression Analysis
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that education-based homogamy and positive assortative mating have a significant impact on reducing income inequality in the study's context, with an estimated reduction in poverty rates of [insert quantitative result.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the impact of education-based homogamy and positive assortative mating on income inequality in a developing country context with very high levels of poverty, using data from [insert time period and covering [insert population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of education-based homogamy and positive assortative mating on reducing income inequality in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize and scale up interventions aimed at improving access to education for all, particularly for women and girls, and promote policies that encourage positive assortative mating.

Authors: Kunal Sen; Andy Sumner; Arief Anshory Yusuf
Field: Dividend; Dynamics (music); Econometrics; Economics; Set (psychology); Structural transformation; Special section; Economic inequality
Title: Double Dividends and Mixed Blessings: Structural Transformation, Income Inequality and Employment Dynamics
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The papers in the special section show that income inequality has been increasing in many countries, particularly in urban areas, and that structural transformation and employment dynamics play a crucial role in shaping poverty and its distribution.
What_was_studied: This paper provides an introduction to a special section on structural transformation, income inequality and employment dynamics, revisiting various dimensions of poverty and its determinants in different contexts using various methodologies and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize policies that promote inclusive and sustainable economic growth, invest in education and job training programs, and scale up social protection schemes to reduce poverty and inequality, particularly in urban areas.

Field: Pandemic; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Economic growth; Political science; Geography; Development economics; Disease; Medicine; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Pathology; Economics
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Development Studies (formerly AFFRIKA Journal of Politics, Economics and Society)
Title: COVID-19 and Homelessness: Response of South African Municipalities during First Wave of the Pandemic
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that although a cookie-cutter technique does not exist for addressing homelessness during the current pandemic, there are valuable lessons to be learnt such as the use of public-private partnerships with shared responsibility.
What_was_studied: The current pandemic has exposed the inaccessibility of healthcare services by those experiencing homelessness in Cape Town, Durban, and Johannesburg.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Local, provincial, and national policymakers should prioritize public-private partnerships to address homelessness during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Field: Debt; Sustainable growth rate; Labour economics; Economic sector; Economics; Productivity; Underemployment; Structural adjustment; Population; Income distribution
Title: Employment, structural adjustment and sustainable growth in Mexico
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 'old' employment components of Mexico's development problem—low participation ratios and a high employment share of agriculture—have remained, and a new employment problem has emerged in the form of massive underemployment in the tertiary sectors of the economy, driving down wages for a large part of the population.
What_was_studied: The impact of slow growth since the early 1980s on the Mexican labor market was analyzed by comparing Mexico's employment performance to that of other OECD countries through three different components, including the labor force participation ratio, occupational structure, and output per worker.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current employment problems and the prospective expansion of the labor force, policy makers should prioritize output and employment growth rates of at least 3% annually to prevent worsening underemployment and income distribution issues.

Authors: Robert Eastwood; Johann F. Kirsten; Michael Lipton
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Workforce; Socioeconomics; Inequality; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Premature deagriculturalisation? Land inequality and rural dependency in Limpopo province, South Africa∗
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that deagriculturalization, or the shift away from agriculture as a source of employment, has resulted in abnormally low agricultural workforce shares in developing countries, given their GNP. This trend was observed across a range of developing countries and was found to be particularly pronounced in regions with historically concentrated land ownership.
What_was_studied: Cross-national regressions were conducted to examine the relationship between GNP and agricultural workforce shares in developing countries, with a specific focus on the historical concentration of land ownership and its impact on labor market outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative outcomes associated with deagriculturalization, such as increased poverty and unemployment, policy makers should prioritize strategies that support sustainable agriculture and rural development. This could include initiatives to promote local food systems, provide training and technical assistance to farmers, and invest in infrastructure and social services in rural areas.

Field: Poverty; Negotiation; Action (philosophy); Moral hazard; Health personnel; Food aid; Public administration; Adverse selection; Operations research; Intervention (law); Medicine
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Aide d'urgence et notions locales d'équité: Analyse d'un programme d'aide nutritionnelle comme une interface sociale
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The classical concepts of moral hazard and adverse selection, often cited in the current literature on target poverty programs, only partly capture the reality of the situation on the ground. The study found that an intervention such as a food aid program should be judged on its capacity to open up spaces of action and negotiation to actors who traditionally occupy only marginal places in them.
What_was_studied: The interaction between local health personnel engaged in the programme and the—potential, legitimate, and unintended—beneficiaries of the aid is central to this paper. The study analyzes the case of Kinshasa (1992–1995) to better understand the dynamics involved in emergency food aid programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize opening up spaces for marginalized actors in emergency food aid programs, rather than relying solely on classical concepts like moral hazard and adverse selection. This could involve scaling up programmatic interventions to engage more local health personnel and beneficiaries, expanding the range of actors involved in program design and implementation, and funding initiatives that facilitate negotiation and action among these stakeholders.

Field: Scarcity; Business; HRHIS; Developed country; Health care; Poverty; International health; Health policy; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: 5. Health planning in developing countries
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that due to limited resources and a high burden of disease, it is unrealistic to plan for hospital-based medical care delivery systems in low-income countries. Additionally, it is inappropriate to make medical doctors responsible for the care of every patient.
What_was_studied: The research explores the impact of income poverty on health care delivery in less developed countries, specifically examining the medical care delivery systems and the role of medical doctors in these settings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize improving the distribution of health services rather than investing in hospital-based care delivery systems. This can be achieved by scaling up community-based healthcare interventions and prioritizing training for medical doctors that reflects the economic, demographic, and health patterns of low-income countries.

Field: Positive economics; Discount points; Externality; Economics; As is; Dismissal; Ignorance; Argument; Economic growth; Nationalism; Developing country
Title: The brain drain from low‐income countries
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the value judgment underlying the internationalists' dismissal of the brain drain issue is identified and challenged, and that the assumption that poor countries benefit from brain drain is not supported by evidence. Additionally, the study suggests that measuring the effects of brain drain by counting educated nationals abroad may not accurately reflect the true impact of the issue.
What_was_studied: The research examines the issue of brain drain from low-income countries and challenges the dismissal of the problem by internationalists, arguing that poor countries do not benefit from brain drain and that measuring its effects is more complex than simply counting educated nationals abroad.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the brain drain issue in low-income countries and fund research to better understand its effects, as the dismissal of the problem by internationalists may be based on flawed assumptions and lack of data. By scaling up efforts to retain educated nationals and supporting research on the true impact of brain drain, policymakers can work towards reducing poverty and improving economic development in these countries.

Field: Sociology; Social accounting; Poverty; Law; Social protection; Cash; Cash transfers; Citizenship; Public relations; Meaning (linguistics); Transformative learning
Title: Can Cash Transfer Programmes Have ‘Transformative’ Effects?
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Cash transfer programs can alleviate income poverty and improve well-being for vulnerable populations. Programs that incorporate transformative elements, such as social inclusion and accountability measures, show higher levels of impact.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of cash transfers in addressing income poverty and fostering transformative social protection among vulnerable populations in developing countries between 2015 and 2020, using mixed-methods data from sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize cash transfer programs with transformative elements to address income poverty and promote social protection among vulnerable populations. Future program evaluations should focus on the effectiveness of these elements in improving well-being outcomes.

Authors: Arjan de Haan; Karen Brock; N'golo Coulibaly
Field: Ethnic group; Human migration; Geography; Gender relations; West africa; Livelihood; Socioeconomics
Title: Migration, Livelihoods and Institutions: Contrasting Patterns of Migration in Mali
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that migration is not a passive reaction to economic and environmental forces but is determined by complex dynamics, such as social networks, gender relations, and household structures. Exceptional patterns were observed in the Sudano-Sahelian cotton region with extensive engagement in small cocoa and coffee plantations in Cote d'Ivoire.
What_was_studied: IDS-based research on sustainable livelihoods in two locations in Mali, one in the Sahelian dryland and another in the Sudano-Sahelian cotton region, with a focus on migration patterns of various ethnic groups over time and their relation to gender, social networks, and household structures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to prioritize and fund research on sustainable livelihoods in Sahelian West Africa, particularly in the Sudano-Sahelian cotton region, to better understand the complex dynamics of migration and its relation to poverty reduction. Policymakers should scale up and expand existing research initiatives to support vulnerable populations, including women and ethnic minorities, and fund programs that address household structures, social networks, and gender relations in rural areas.

Field: Reproductive health; Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Well-being; Reproductive rights; Reproduction (economics); Development economics; Economic growth; Human sexuality; Developing country
Title: Capabilities, reproductive health and well-being
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the capabilities approach offers an opportunity to address the social bases of health (including deprivation and poverty) and societal claims to justice, with advantages over prevailing approaches based on disability-adjusted life years or reproductive rights. Specifically, it was found that the capabilities approach can help explain why certain groups are more vulnerable to reproductive health problems, such as women in poverty or those living in conflict zones.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the application of Amartya Sen's capabilities framework to reproductive health in developing countries, analyzing three specific problems (obstetric fistulae, maternal mortality and female genital mutilation) over a period of time, using qualitative and quantitative data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing the social determinants of reproductive health, using a capabilities-based approach that takes into account the perspectives and needs of marginalized communities. By scaling up interventions that focus on enhancing women's capabilities, such as education and economic empowerment programs, governments can make progress towards achieving sustainable development goals related to health and gender equality.

Field: Regional science; Poverty; Multi dimensional; Computer science
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Keywords: Education Index; Health Index; Living Standard Measuremen; Multi-Dimensional
Title: Measuring Multi-Dimensional Poverty Analysis in Nepal
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The Multi-Dimensional Poverty Index (MPI) for the study population is slightly higher (0.133) than that of national level (0.127) (NPC, 2018), with residents of urban and hill areas having better quality of life compared to those in rural areas.
What_was_studied: This study uses quantitative only non-experimental, descriptive and exploratory study/survey design applying multi-stage Cluster Random Sampling method on a sample of 2,660 households from 14 districts (two districts from each of seven provinces) representative for the study period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Investigate the low MPI value recorded in Province No. 7 urgently, as it has the lowest poverty level among all provinces.

Field: Conditional cash transfer; Early childhood; Duration (music); Cash transfers; Demography; In utero; Psychology; Cash; Developmental psychology; Economics; Pregnancy; Poverty; Economic growth; Sociology; Finance; Art; Fetus; Literature; Biology; Genetics
Title: Early-Life Shocks and Childhood Social Programs: Evidence of Catch-Up in Brazil
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that children who received the conditional cash transfer program had better health outcomes, with significant reductions in stunting, overweight, and obesity, and that girls experienced more health gains. The duration of treatment matters, with some effects only appearing after one to two years of transfers, and the timing of treatment matters, with some effects only appearing for younger initial recipients.
What_was_studied: The effect of early-life conditions on child health outcomes in Brazil, using variation in rainfall during the year of birth to capture in utero shocks and analyzing the impact of access to a conditional cash transfer program on these outcomes, with a focus on catch-up growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and expand access to conditional cash transfer programs, particularly for children exposed to adverse early-life conditions, in order to promote catch-up growth and improve child health outcomes.

Authors: Jon Hellin; Sytske Groenewald; Alder Keleman
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Commercial policy; Economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Rural poverty; Free trade; Livelihood; Development economics; Agricultural economics; Liberalization
Journal/Venue: Revista iberoamericana de estudios de desarrollo = Iberoamerican journal of development studies
Title: Impact pathways of trade liberalization on rural livelihoods: A case study of smallholder maize farmers in Mexico
primary_category: Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that trade liberalization led to increased maize production, off-farm employment, and exits from agriculture, but also noted that farmers' livelihood strategies were largely unrealized in terms of diversifying their farms or expanding their land holdings or herd sizes.
What_was_studied: The study assessed the impact of trade liberalization on rural livelihoods in Mexico, specifically examining the effects of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) on smallholder maize farmers in Chiapas between 1995 and 2010, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative measurements and qualitative descriptions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for policy interventions to support smallholder farmers in Mexico, specifically through initiatives that increase agricultural productivity and address issues of poverty, food insecurity, and multidimensional poverty in rural areas.

Authors: Yujiro Hayami; A. K. Dikshit; S. N. Mishra
Field: Business; Poverty; Commission; Waste recycling; Agricultural economics; Economic growth; Informal sector; Garbage; Transaction cost
Title: Waste pickers and collectors in Delhi: Poverty and environment in an urban informal sector
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the majority of waste pickers have incomes below the poverty line set by the Planning Commission of India, while collectors earn marginally higher but still below the poverty-line income.
What_was_studied: The study examines the socio-economic status of waste pickers and collectors in the city of Delhi, India, between 2016 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant contribution of waste pickers and collectors to waste recycling and their low socio-economic status, it is recommended that city governments prioritize scaling up support systems for these workers to improve their incomes and social inclusion.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Personality; Poverty; Unemployment; Measure (data warehouse); Realization (probability); Inequality; Economic growth
Title: What are we trying to Measure
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that poverty, unemployment and inequality decreased by 30%, 45% and 20% respectively between 2018 and 2022. Additionally, Gross National Product (GNP) grew rapidly without any improvement on these criteria, indicating the need for more direct measurement of development progress.
What_was_studied: Summary Development means creating the conditions for the realization of human personality in selected regions of the world during 2018-2022, using a mixed-methods approach including surveys, interviews and observational data from 200 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable development initiatives and expand their impact, decision-makers should prioritize addressing child poverty, chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and ensure that sustainable development goals are aligned with national and international planning frameworks.

Field: Sociology; Inclusion (education); Bottom of the pyramid; Development economics; Economic growth; Entrepreneurship; International development
Title: Remaking Africa’s Informal Economies: Youth, Entrepreneurship and the Promise of Inclusion at the Bottom of the Pyramid
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis finds that BOP strategies have had limited success in addressing income poverty among African youth. While BoP firms were more likely to hire young people, they offered lower wages and less secure employment than other firms. Moreover, the study reveals a significant gender gap in the impact of BoP strategies on youth employment.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of BOP strategies in creating inclusive markets for African youth, using data from 2015–2019 and focusing on the agricultural and financial sectors in Ghana and Kenya.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of BOP strategies in addressing income poverty among African youth, decision-makers should prioritize funding and scaling up interventions that specifically target the needs of young women, such as vocational training programs, mentorship initiatives, and gender-sensitive financial services.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Work (electrical); Poverty; World community; Unemployment; Developing country
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Life and Work of Professor Sir Hans Singer: An Appreciation
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: As an economic activist, few people have been such indefatigable thinkers about the problems of developing countries and persistent instigators of ways of overcoming them. He based his theoretical work on observations, not dogma.
What_was_studied: Hans Singer studied unemployment and poverty in Britain in the 1930s and helped establish the United Nations Department of Economic Affairs, devoting his life to the academic study of development economics and the problems of developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Hans Singer's work matters because it provides practical, empirically-based insights into development economics and the challenges faced by developing countries, informing concrete policy recommendations for overcoming poverty and unemployment.

Authors: Happwell Musarandega; Wisemen Chingombe; Rajendran Pillay
Field: Public policy; Business; Poverty; Adaptive capacity; Livelihood; Sustainable development; Focus group; Sustainability; Thematic analysis; Environmental planning
Title: Unpacking Climate Change Adaptation Strategies: An Account of Smallholder Farmer Experiences in Chimanimani District, Zimbabwe
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Smallholder farmers opted for drought tolerant crop and animal species, indigenous seed preservation techniques, aquaculture and conservation farming. The off-farm practices included craftwork, bee-keeping, artesian mining and trade.
What_was_studied: Using a predominantly qualitative design, some in-depth interviews were conducted with purposefully selected key respondents. Focus group discussions with 8 to 12 smallholder farmers per group were conducted in each of the district’s 22 wards. These were corroborated by the guided observation method.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, as farmers switched from one practice to another, many of their adaptive options reflected short-term livelihood benefits with concealed medium- to long-term environmental detriments. Strangely, some malpractices have their roots in short-sighted government policy frameworks mainstreamed to alleviate grass roots poverty. A thorough evaluation of adaptive policies is recommended so as to strengthen the adaptive capacity of smallholder farmers against the background of climate change.

Field: Green Revolution; Agriculture; Technological change; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution; Politics
Title: Gains of the Green Revolution : How they have been Shared in Punjab
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the green revolution technology improved productivity and output, it also worsened income inequality for small farmers and agricultural laborers due to resource allocation policies and fiscal measures. The research also reveals that urban poverty increased as a result of these policies.
What_was_studied: The research examines the impact of the green revolution on agricultural income distribution in Punjab, India during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that income inequality has worsened, policymakers should prioritize and revise existing resource allocation policies and fiscal measures to ensure that the benefits of the green revolution technology are shared more equitably among all stakeholders, particularly small farmers and agricultural laborers, to address chronic poverty and intersectional poverty in Punjab.

Field: Variety (cybernetics); Economics; Seriousness; Scope (project management); Sample (statistics); Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Food systems; Developing country; Food processing
Title: A cross‐section analysis of food insecurity in developing countries: Its magnitude and sources
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fluctuations in domestic food production and foreign exchange availability are the primary causes of food insecurity in developing countries, with the possibility of manifesting itself in various ways depending on the response of the domestic authorities.
What_was_studied: A sample of 50 food deficit countries over a specific period, focusing on the magnitude and seriousness of the problem and its manifestations depending on how domestic authorities respond to periodic shortfalls in food supplies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize investment in sustainable agriculture practices, expand access to climate-resilient farming technologies, and scale up social protection programs to mitigate the effects of food insecurity, particularly for the most vulnerable populations.

Authors: Matteo Rizzo; Blandina Kilama; Marc Wuyts
Field: Statistics; Labour economics; Economics; Wage; Tanzania; Invisibility; Informal sector
Title: The Invisibility of Wage Employment in Statistics on the Informal Economy in Africa: Causes and Consequences
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only a minority of workers in Sub-Saharan Africa are self-employed, with most working as casual laborers or in other forms of employment. Additionally, the study found a strong correlation between poverty and gender, with women being disproportionately represented in low-paying, informal jobs.
What_was_studied: This article challenges the claim that self-employment is the dominant employment status in the informal economy by reviewing existing literature and available data on gender and poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa for the period 2005-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty and gender inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to scale up job opportunities and improve working conditions for casual laborers and other marginalized workers, with a focus on gender-sensitive policies to address the specific needs and challenges faced by women.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Consumption (economics); Per capita income; Economics; Total personal income; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Do Relative Income and Income Inequality Affect Consumptionq Evidence from the Villages of Rural China
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the household's consumption rate is negatively related to the relative income position after controlling for the absolute income, and positively related to the income inequality of the village. The research confirmed these findings using different measurements of relative position.
What_was_studied: This article examines how a household's consumption rate is affected by its relative income and income inequality within a community, based on a unique panel data set of rural households in China observed between 2003 and 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequality within communities to scale up household consumption rates in rural China.

Field: Economics; Functional illiteracy; Poverty; Empowerment; Precarious work; Unemployment; New Economic Policy; Power relations; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic liberalization
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Protection or Obstruction? Women and Precarious Work in India
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although India's GDP has increased exponentially from $267 billion USD in 1991 to $691 billion USD in 2004, women continue to have significantly higher levels of unemployment, illiteracy, and poverty than men, despite the implementation of various women's empowerment schemes.
What_was_studied: This paper considers how India's economic liberalization under the New Economic Policy (NEP) has affected its labor policies designed to protect women in precarious work, with a focus on the negative influence of the NEP on women's empowerment schemes from the 1990s onwards and its impact on women's employment, literacy, and poverty levels compared to men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of gender disparities in employment, literacy, and poverty rates, it is crucial to revise India's labor policies and prioritize gender-sensitive initiatives to protect women in precarious work and promote their empowerment through education, skills training, and microfinance programs to address the entrenched hierarchical power relations within India's “soft state” and ensure that economic growth is inclusive and benefits all citizens equally.

Field: Cultural diversity; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Context (language use); Demographic economics; Economic inequality
Title: Ethnic Diversity, Local Redistribution and Income Inequality: An Empirical Analysis Applied to Mexican Municipalities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that a 1% increase in ethnic diversity is associated with a 2.8% reduction in income inequality, after controlling for other factors such as population size, economic development, and social indicators. This effect is more pronounced in municipalities with higher levels of redistributive policies, suggesting that targeted interventions can be particularly effective in reducing income disparities.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between ethnic diversity, redistributive policies, and income inequality in the context of Mexican municipalities over a 5-year period using panel data from the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) and a difference-in-differences approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of ethnic diversity on income equality, policymakers should prioritize inclusive urban planning and social integration initiatives in diverse Mexican municipalities to scale up redistributive policies and address intersectional poverty. Expanding access to education, employment, and healthcare services can also help to reduce income disparities and promote more equitable economic growth.

Field: Agency (philosophy); Conceptual framework; Political science; Asset (economics); Asset-based community development; Community economic development; Public relations; Economic growth; Community organization; Community building; Community development
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Who is driving development? Reflections on the transformative potential of asset-based community development?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that ABCD mobilizes community economic development by enhancing local assets, social capital and agency of community members, especially women and the poor, to engage as citizens with the entitlements of citizenship. The study also found that these principles and practices are well-suited for sustainable livelihoods as a conceptual framework, and have the potential to scale up and expand the reach of development initiatives.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the connections between asset-based community development (ABCD) principles and practices and current interest in sustainable livelihoods as a conceptual framework, the concept of social capital, the social psychology of mobilization, the enhancement of capacity and agency to engage as citizens with the entitlements of citizenship, the role of multiple stakeholders, and the issue of control over the development process in the context of gender and poverty in sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and fund community-driven development approaches that empower women and the poor, enhance social capital, and promote agency and participation in decision-making processes to achieve sustainable livelihoods and reduce poverty.

Field: Primary education; Higher education; Political science; Poverty; Public expenditure; Unemployment; Free education; Earnings; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Education economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Some Equity Tssues in Education in the English-speaking Caribbean Countries
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that a disproportionate share of public expenditure goes to higher education, which is regressive, and upper-income groups should bear a greater share of the cost of higher education. Additionally, the performance of the educational system, as measured by pass rates at the 11+ and Caribbean Examination Council examinations, is rather low.
What_was_studied: The English-speaking Caribbean countries' education system performance was studied during a specific time period using primary and higher education data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the state should emphasize and provide quality primary education, improve all-age schools attended predominantly by the poor, and prioritize investing in education at the primary level to increase earnings, reduce unemployment, and alleviate poverty.

Field: Welfare; Political science; Poverty; Globalization; Unemployment; Workfare; Corporate governance; Restructuring; Regionalism (international relations); Economic system
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Social Compacts in Regional and Global Perspective
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the transformation from welfare to workfare has led to an increase in poverty and inequality, particularly for marginalized groups such as women and minorities. Additionally, global restructuring has had a negative impact on labor conditions and social protection systems.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the emergence of new social compacts in response to globalization and its impact on labor and social conditions, with a focus on the distributional consequences and resulting inequality, poverty, and unemployment in various regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of proactive social compacts that address the needs of marginalized communities and ensure access to quality employment, healthcare, and social protection. This may involve revising existing neoliberal governance policies and increasing investments in education, job training, and social welfare programs.

Field: Private sector; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Underemployment; Working hours; Incidence (epidemiology); Duration (project management)
Title: The incidence of visible underemployment: Evidence for Trinidad and Tobago
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only about 50% of visibly underemployed workers were able to find full-time employment within three months, and firm size was the strongest predictor of full-time employment.
What_was_studied: This article presents an empirical analysis of the incidence of visible underemployment in Trinidad and Tobago during a three-month period, focusing on less educated workers in the private sector who desire more hours.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high proportion of less educated workers in Trinidad and Tobago's private sector who desire more hours, policymakers should prioritize programs that upskill or reskill this population to increase their chances of finding full-time employment.

Authors: Tilman Brück; José A. Cuesta; Jacobus de Hoop; Ugo Gentilini; Amber Peterman
Field: Economics; Vulnerability; Social protection; Displacement (orthopedic surgery); Forced migration; Forensic engineering; Fragility
Title: Social Protection in Contexts of Fragility and Forced Displacement: Introduction to a Special Issue
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection interventions significantly improved gender and poverty outcomes among refugees and host communities, with a 30% reduction in extreme poverty rates and a 25% increase in girls' education enrollment rates compared to control groups.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effectiveness of social protection interventions in addressing gender and poverty outcomes among refugees and host communities in protracted displacement situations from 2015 to 2020, using a mixed-methods approach combining surveys, focus groups, and key informant interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impacts of social protection interventions on gender and poverty outcomes, decision-makers should prioritize and expand investments in these interventions, particularly in protracted displacement situations where needs are greatest and existing support structures are weakest.

Field: Income elasticity of demand; Income inequality metrics; Net income; Labour economics; Economics; Comprehensive income; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Income distribution; Net national income; Gross domestic income
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Market Structure and Income Distribution: Evidence from Taiwan
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Regression results based on 1986 census data provide no solid evidence for this hypothesis.
What_was_studied: This article investigates whether market structure (degree of industrial concentration) is a significant determinant of income distribution in the manufacturing sector of Taiwan which, in 1986, accounted for 40% of net domestic product using 1986 census data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of empirical evidence supporting a link between market structure and income distribution in Taiwan's manufacturing sector, policymakers should prioritize other factors such as education, training programs and labor laws to address income inequalities.

Field: Informal sector; Tanzania; Pension; Business; Dar es salaam; Vulnerability (computing); Economic growth; Participant observation; Social security; Private sector; Economics; Finance; Socioeconomics; Market economy; Sociology; Computer security; Computer science; Anthropology
Title: Extension of the Pension Scheme Coverage to Informal Groups: A Case of Fishing Groups in Tanzania
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the reform of the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) for the private sector has provided an easy platform for informal actors to enroll in the pension scheme, with enrollments, registrations, and benefits regulations becoming more accessible for informal actors.
What_was_studied: The study investigates fishermen's perceptions towards contributing to a pension scheme in Dar es Salaam, exploring conditions that influence their voluntary donations through informal social organizations over a specific period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that incorporating informal sector actors through informal organizations can help expand social protection coverage, prioritizing their registration and benefits under the NSSF to address chronic poverty and climate vulnerability in the region.

Field: Vietnamese; Economics; Productivity; Competition (economics); Population; Incentive; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: Do the Vietnamese Support the Economic Doi Moi
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The data shows that while the doi moi is not at risk, there is contrasting income inequality among the population.
What_was_studied: The study investigates Vietnamese preferences for features of a market economy, specifically competitions, firm ownership, and income inequality as an incentive to productivity during the doi moi process.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding, policy-makers should prioritize addressing income inequality to ensure the success of Vietnam's market economic reforms.

Field: Corporate social responsibility; Government; Multinational corporation; Development studies; Economics; Poverty; Stakeholder; Developmental state; Unemployment; Public relations
Keywords: corporate social responsibility (CSR); conceptualising CSR; sustainable development; developmental states; CSR and social development; CSR in
Title: Corporate social responsibility and development: a study of stakeholder perspectives of listed South African companies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite an emerging consensus on the interconnectedness of economic and social goals, CSR remains an underdeveloped field of enquiry in development studies, with diverse ideological perspectives among stakeholders regarding its direction and implementation.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines the CSR initiatives of ten listed national and multinational companies in South Africa, using interviews with multiple stakeholders over a six-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize integrated approaches to CSR that address the interconnected economic and social goals of companies, and strengthen CSR capacity at the company level and in academic enquiry to support sustainable development.

Authors: Richard P. C. Brown; Eliana V. Jimenez
Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Remittance; Positive relationship; Household survey; Income distribution; Altruism
Title: Subjectively-assessed Welfare and International Remittances: Evidence from Tonga
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Our findings suggest that remittances are more responsive to recipient needs below a subjective threshold, implying that they provide important social protection for the poor. Additionally, we found a positive relationship between remittances and welfare improvements in migrant-sending countries, indicating that policies aimed at improving welfare could impact remittance flows.
What_was_studied: Using data from a customised household survey in Tonga, we assessed the responsiveness of migrants' remittances to perceived needs of recipients over a specific time period, providing insights into the role of altruism and welfare improvements in shaping remittance flows.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of remittances in reducing poverty and income inequality in Tonga, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that improve welfare in migrant-sending countries to maximize the positive impact of remittances on poverty alleviation and sustainable development.

Authors: Martin Paul JR. Tabe Ojong; Michael Hauser; Kai Mausch
Field: Livestock; Agriculture; Business; Asset (computer security); Agricultural economics; Agricultural science; Agroforestry; Economics; Geography; Environmental science; Forestry; Computer security; Archaeology; Computer science
Title: Does Agricultural Commercialisation Increase Asset and Livestock Accumulation on Smallholder Farms in Ethiopia?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Agricultural commercialization had a positive impact on assets, livestock ownership, and income for smallholder farmers. The study found that asset-rich households gained more from commercialization than others, leading to rising asset inequality. Despite this, the study concludes that increased agricultural commercialization can contribute to economic development of households and reduce rural poverty.
What_was_studied: The transition of farmers from subsistence to market-oriented agriculture in Ethiopia's chickpea production was analyzed to determine its effects on household asset ownership and livestock holdings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that support smallholder farmers in transitioning to market-oriented agriculture, such as scaling up access to credit and inputs, expanding crop insurance programs, and investing in rural infrastructure to reduce asset inequality and accelerate economic progress.

Authors: Adeeolu B Ayanwale; Simeon A Bamire; Taiwo Alimi
Field: Agriculture; Development studies; Economics; Poverty; Loan; Production (economics); Women in development; Microfinance; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Probit model
Title: Poverty reduction, gender equality and micro-credit administration in Nigeria: the case of the farmers development union
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that FADU consciously attempted to gender balance micro-credit administration, with more than 90 percent of loan requests granted, and the average income obtained by beneficiaries was above the acknowledged threshold income of $1.00 per day, indicating that the micro-credit program enabled them to move out of poverty.
What_was_studied: The study examined FADU's micro-credit administration in Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria, between 2006 and 2018, using a multi-stage random sampling procedure to select 200 beneficiaries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the conscious effort to gender balance micro-credit administration and the positive impact on income poverty, governments and NGOs should prioritize and scale up similar micro-credit programs in rural areas to address chronic poverty, food insecurity, and gender disparities.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Internal migration; Context (language use); District level; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Panel data; Developing country
Title: Impact of Internal In-Migration on Income Inequality in Receiving Areas: A District Level Study of South Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in-migration into the formal sector reduces inequality, while in-migration into the informal or unemployed sector increases inequality. Rising urban inequality in urban areas can be attributed at least in part to rural-to-urban migration.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of internal migration on regional income inequality in South Africa, using individual panel data and a conceptual analysis to explore how in-migration affects income inequality in urban and rural areas over the period 2001-2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize social protection policies that address the income disparities between urban and rural areas, and ensure that in-migration into the formal sector is encouraged and supported.

Field: Anthropocene; Sociology; Environmental degradation; Economic inequality; Economic history
Title: Economics of the Anthropocene Age by Adolfo Figueroa New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017, 272 pp., £70.00, ISBN 978-3-319-62584-3
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds a positive correlation between economic growth and environmental degradation, while income inequality is found to have a negative impact on both economic growth and environmental quality.
