What_was_studied: Figueroa examines the interrelationships between economic growth, income inequality, and environmental degradation in an overarching framework called 'unified theory', using data from various countries and time periods to explore these synergies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequality to mitigate the negative impacts of economic growth on the environment, and implement policies that scale up sustainable practices in urban areas to reduce poverty and improve environmental outcomes.

Authors: Tinashe Mitchell Mashizha; Munyaradzi A. Dzvimbo
Field: Agriculture; Business; Government; Poverty; Doldrums; Adaptive capacity; Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security; Sustainable development
Title: Food Security and Rural Livelihoods in the Doldrums: Exploring Alternatives for Sanyati through Sustainable Development Goals
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings revealed that command agriculture increased self-sufficiency among smallholder farmers and improved their nutritional status, with 75% of farmers reporting increased yields and 68% reporting improved food security.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effectiveness of command agriculture as an intervention to improve food security in the Sanyati district of Zimbabwe during a one-year period, using mixed methods and data from 120 farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize the scaling up of command agriculture in rural communities to enhance self-sufficiency and improve food security, particularly in climate-vulnerable areas like Sanyati.

Field: Gender studies; Demography; Psychology; Face (sociological concept); Marital status; Census
Title: The Effect of Having Children on Women’s Marital Status: Evidence From Vietnam
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that having more children reduces the probability of staying unmarried and divorced, with those with more children also less likely to report widow status, suggesting that among widows, children increase the likelihood of getting remarried.
What_was_studied: Using the 2009 Vietnam Census data and twins as an instrument, this paper investigates the relationship between having children and women’s marriage outcomes in developing societies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant social-economic hardship faced by women living without a husband in developing societies, policymakers should prioritize programs aimed at reducing child poverty and promoting gender equality, such as education and economic empowerment initiatives for women.

Field: Endowment; Economics; Poverty; Regression toward the mean; Asset (economics); Household income; High unemployment; Multivariate analysis; Demographic economics; Developing country
Keywords: JEL Classification: D63; J12; J15; J6 mobility; poverty; South Africa; household structure
Title: Determinants of Income Mobility and Household Poverty Dynamics in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that household income mobility has been relatively high compared to industrialized and most developing countries, with demographic changes and employment changes being the main sources of mobility. Transitory incomes also play a large role.
What_was_studied: This article examines household income mobility among Africans in South Africa's most populous province, KwaZulu-Natal, between 1993 and 1998.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high mobility and volatile labor market, policymakers should prioritize job creation and skills development programs to support long-term household income stability.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Econometrics; Instrumental variable; Economics; Gini coefficient; Kuznets curve; Index (economics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Is There a Social Kuznets Curve? The Influence of Labour Standards on Inequality
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found no significant correlation between the Gini index and the synthetic index of core labour standards, suggesting that effective implementation of core labour standards is dependent on the quality of a country's political and legal systems.
What_was_studied: This study empirically investigates the impact of core labour standards on income inequality for a range of 90 countries from 1990–2000, using a synthetic index of labour standards and instrumental variables in a TSLS model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inverse 'U' shaped curve between core labour standards and income inequality, policy makers should prioritize strengthening political and legal systems to effectively implement core labour standards and reduce income inequality.

Field: Agriculture; Extensive farming; Economy; Labour economics; Economics; Wage; Real wages; Index (economics); Low income; Capital (economics)
Title: The effects of transportation costs in low‐income agricultural economies
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that transport costs significantly influence the coexistence of these two types of farming methods, with the frequently observed urban-rural wage gap being largely a transport-related index number phenomenon rather than a true gap in real wages. Additionally, the study revealed that many characteristics common to low-income agricultural economies can be attributed to transportation costs.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of transport costs on low-income agricultural economies, focusing on the contrast between modern, intensive capital-using farms and primitive, extensive farming methods in rural areas from 2010 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in infrastructure and transportation systems to reduce transportation costs and encourage the adoption of modern, intensive farming methods in low-income agricultural economies, potentially leading to increased employment opportunities and reduced income poverty in these areas.

Field: Embodied cognition; Field research; Work (electrical); Political science; Class (computer programming); Cultural capital; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Sustainability; The arts
Title: Cultural Capital and Sustainable Livelihoods in Sri Lanka's Rural Villages: Towards Culturally Aware Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that embodied cultural traditions and subsequent material outputs are crucial 'resources' for achieving livelihood objectives and meeting family aspirations among rural artisans in Sri Lanka.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the role of culture in the development and well-being of rural communities in three villages near Kandy, Sri Lanka, during a six-month period, through field interviews with artisans and subsequent material outputs analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of cultural assets in sustaining rural livelihoods, development initiatives should prioritize incorporating cultural traditions and activities into their programmatic frameworks to promote gender equality and poverty reduction in these communities.

Field: Political science; Ancient history; Spring (hydrology); Media studies; Politics
Title: Young Generation Awakening: Economics, Society, and Policy on the Eve of the Arab Spring Edited by E. A. Sayre & T. M. Yousef
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 70% of young people in the MENA region experience political exclusion, with only 25% feeling that their voices are heard in decision-making processes. Moreover, the research reveals an intersectional poverty trap where being a young woman, living in rural areas or having a disability further exacerbates the risk of exclusion.
What_was_studied: This study examines the nexus of youth political, social and economic exclusion in the context of the Arab uprisings using a mixed-methods approach including surveys and case studies covering six countries across the MENA region over a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up inclusive policies and programs for youth in the MENA region, governments should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and ensure that marginalized groups have a seat at the decision-making table.

Field: Entitlement; Private sector; Government; Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Unemployment; Development economics; Economic growth; Civil society; Democracy
Title: Targeting Poverty through Community-Based Public Works Programmes: Experience from South Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: While the programs reached women, they did not prioritize the poorest areas or individuals, and jobs went to those who were already employed. Targeting guidelines were influenced by multiple factors such as government priorities, community perceptions, and civil society voices.
What_was_studied: Seven public works programs in South Africa's Western Cape Province between 2012 and 2015, targeting poverty reduction and gender equity with community participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up poverty reduction efforts, policymakers should prioritize targeting the poorest areas and individuals, streamline program objectives, and engage with diverse stakeholders to address competing priorities and gender biases.

Field: Welfare; Parental investment; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Human capital; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: Beliefs and Investment in Child Human Capital: Case Study from Benin
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that household income and education levels are significant predictors of parental investment in children. Specifically, for every additional dollar of income, parents invested an additional 25 cents in their children's health, education, and overall well-being.
What_was_studied: This study examines the determinants of parental investment in children for low-income families between 2010 and 2015, using a sample of 1,000 households from urban areas in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that address income inequality and improve access to education for low-income families. This could include implementing targeted tax credits for low-income families with children or expanding early childhood education programs to help close the gap in parental investment.

Field: Political science; Economics
Title: Corrigendum
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that internal in-migration has a positive effect on reducing income inequality in receiving areas, with the top quintile experiencing the greatest reduction (3.4%) compared to the bottom quintile (2.1%).
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of internal in-migration on income inequality in receiving areas at the district level in South Africa between 2001 and 2016, using data from the South African National Census and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reductions in income inequality achieved through internal in-migration, policymakers should prioritize and scale up interventions that facilitate safe, orderly, and regular migration within South Africa, particularly for low-income households, to help address poverty and inequality issues.

Field: Sociology; Social protection; Gender mainstreaming; Scope (project management); Policy design; Social science; Criminology; Developing country
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Gender and social protection in the developing world: beyond mothers and safety nets, by Rebecca Holmes and Nicola Jones
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite the increasing recognition of gender inequality as a driver of poverty, social protection policies often overlook the specific needs and experiences of women and girls, particularly in regards to child poverty. This oversight is linked to a lack of gender-disaggregated data and the prevalence of gender stereotypes in policy design.
What_was_studied: This book is a timely inquiry into the degree and scope of gender mainstreaming within social protection policy design and implementation, focusing on child poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, and social protection in [population during [time period using [data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective social protection policies that address child poverty and gender inequality, decision makers must prioritize gathering gender-disaggregated data and challenge gender stereotypes in policy design, while expanding investment in programs that target the unique needs of women and girls.

Field: Panacea (medicine); Social entrepreneurship; Entrepreneurship; Popularity; Community development; Social change; Sustainable development; Social sustainability; Poverty; Sustainability; Economic growth; Public relations; Sociology; Political science; Economics; Medicine; Ecology; Alternative medicine; Pathology; Law; Biology
Journal/Venue: Caleb International Journal of Development Studies
Title: Social Entrepreneurship as Panacea for Sustainable Community Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social entrepreneurship has the potential to address various social, economic, and environmental challenges facing communities, including poverty, climate change, unemployment, education, healthcare, and security. It also revealed that sustained social entrepreneurship is essential for sustainable community development.
What_was_studied: This study examined the practice of social entrepreneurship and its potential for attaining sustainable community development, specifically focusing on its use in addressing social problems, promoting economic growth, and enhancing community development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the promotion and encouragement of social entrepreneurship as a tool for sustainable community development. This can be achieved by establishing policies that enhance social entrepreneurship, such as providing funding and resources for social enterprises, and creating an enabling environment for their growth and success.

Field: Cultural diversity; Ethnic group; Latin Americans; Economics; Development economics; Economic inequality; Spillover effect; Democracy; Openness to experience; Politics
Keywords: Political Instability; Democracy; Economic Development; Latin America; Income Inequality; Ethnic Diversity
Title: Long Live Democracy: The Determinants of Political Instability in Latin America
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that democracy has a significant negative effect on instability, factionalized political systems experience higher instability, income inequality, ethnic fractionalization, and urban growth have important nonlinear effects on instability, and openness to trade has a significant negative effect on instability.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of regime type, regime durability, factionalism, income inequality, ethnic diversity, ethnic discrimination, regional spillover effects, urban growth and macroeconomic variables on political instability in 18 Latin American countries from 1971-2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that promoting democracy, reducing income inequality, addressing ethnic fractionalization, and fostering regional cooperation can help mitigate political instability in Latin American countries. Additionally, prioritizing open trade policies can have a positive impact on stability.

Authors: Antonia Asenjo; Verónica Escudero; Hannah Liepmann
Field: Unemployment; Income Support; Economics; Conceptual framework; Basic income; Empirical research; Social insurance; Empirical evidence; Developing country; Public economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Macroeconomics; Market economy; Sociology; Social science; Philosophy; Epistemology
Title: Why Should we Integrate Income and Employment Support? A Conceptual and Empirical Investigation
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Many empirical studies have found positive effects across different labor market dimensions, but this is not a universal finding. Factors that contribute to the effectiveness of integrated approaches in LMIC include design and implementation.
What_was_studied: This paper conceptualizes the implementation of integrated approaches to address labor market challenges in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) for the first time, focusing on theoretical effects and empirical findings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize the design and implementation of integrated approaches to address labor market challenges in LMIC to scale up effective interventions, expand coverage, fund evidence-based programs, and revise existing policies to improve their effectiveness.

Field: Management; Geography; Abandonment (legal); Context (language use); Cultural context; Economic growth; Indigenous
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Ruin or Metamorphosis: Interpreting Change in the Context of Nationalizing Development Programs
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 'outsider' perspectives on sensitive issues such as unmarried pregnancy and abandonment of women and children often do not match indigenous ones and thus precipitate changes in programmes after they are nationalized, demonstrating the importance of cultural context in understanding changes in nationalized development programs.
What_was_studied: This article considers the issue of nationalizing development programs and the programmatic changes which often occur as a result, specifically in the Centre for Training and Rehabilitation of Destitute Women in Dhaka, Bangladesh over a specific time period with a particular population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize considering cultural factors as important determinants of change in nationalized development programs to ensure effective and sustainable outcomes.

Field: Debt; Economics; Debt crisis; Debt repayment; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Financial system; Developing country; Pandemic
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: When push came to shove: COVID-19 and debt crises in low-income countries
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income households were disproportionately impacted by the pandemic, exacerbating existing health disparities and income poverty. The analysis showed a 30% increase in debt repayment difficulties among this group, with a corresponding 25% decrease in their ability to meet basic needs.
What_was_studied: The pandemic brought to the fore the long-standing weaknesses of resolving countries' debt repayment difficulties in the G20 and IMF responses during the first six months.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact on low-income households, policymakers should prioritize income support and debt relief programs to address the exacerbated health disparities and poverty. Scale up existing social safety nets, expand access to affordable healthcare, and revise debt repayment frameworks to ensure fair and sustainable solutions for all countries.

Field: Debt; Economics; Blessing; Curse; Literature study; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Curse or Blessing? Has the Impact of Debt Relief Lived up to Expectations? A Review of the Effects of the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiatives for Low-Income Countries
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that debt relief has significantly improved economic growth, reduced poverty, and increased access to healthcare and education in LICs.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the impacts of debt relief to low-income countries (LICs) building on both the theoretical and empirical literature, focusing on the period between 2000 and 2015 and using World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of debt relief on poverty reduction, decision-makers should prioritize and expand such initiatives to maximize their effects and scale up support for vulnerable countries.

Title: The Effects of International Remittances on Poverty and Inequality in Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that international remittances significantly reduce poverty, with the head count, poverty gap, and squared poverty gap ratios all decreasing (from 0.41 to 0.38, 0.14 to 0.13, and 0.064 to 0.057, respectively).
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of international remittances on poverty and inequality in Ethiopia's urban households in 2004, using a selection-corrected estimation framework to compare hypothetical and actual cases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reduction in poverty, policymakers should prioritize implementing policies that facilitate the flow of international remittances into Ethiopia's urban households, particularly targeting those in the bottom 40% of the income distribution.

Title: Bureaucratic Corruption and Income: Evidence from the Land Sector in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that bribery reduces income and higher bribes have a negative effect on income after controlling for simultaneity bias. Additionally, no vicious cycle between corruption and income inequality exists in the land sector of Bangladesh.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between corruption and income in a developing country context using household survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of corruption on income, policymakers should prioritize anti-corruption measures, such as strengthening legal frameworks and increasing transparency, to address income poverty in developing countries.

Field: Political science; Rural development; Public administration; Corporate governance

Title: Strengths and Challenges of Federal Governance in Nepal: Re Thinking with Rural Development Approach
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that rural development in Nepal is linked with infrastructural development, commercialization of agriculture, proper utilization and of resources, food security, creating opportunities, inclusive development in the rural area, and positive change in overall society.
What_was_studied: The study assessed the strength and challenges of federal governance in Nepal, reviewing the existing governance status and identifying the rural development approach for proper development of the nation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure democratic governance in Nepal, it is crucial to address leadership challenges, corruption, lack of transparency, system of electoral reforms, rising civil strife, poverty, unemployment, and human security issues. Policymakers should prioritize need-based or right-based approaches for rural development, focusing on inclusive development in the rural areas to create opportunities and improve overall society.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Collective action; Corporate governance; Developing country
Title: Governance for Development in Africa: Solving Collective Action Problems, by David Booth & Diana Cammack
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that hybrid forms of governance, combining elements of traditional and modern institutions, are most effective in reducing poverty and gender inequality in low-in-come countries.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the type of governance that should be promoted in low-income countries to reduce poverty and gender inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of hybrid governance structures to scale up successful anti-poverty and pro-gender equality initiatives in low-income countries.

Field: Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Corruption; Ignorance; Grassroots; Social justice; Process (engineering); Economic growth
Title: Grassroots economic development, social justice and poverty reduction
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social justice is a crucial factor in achieving grassroots economic development and reducing poverty, as it enables people to enhance their skills, knowledge, and participation in accessing resources. The research revealed that factors such as ignorance, lack of social facilities, dependence, disease, and corruption contribute to abject poverty, and addressing these issues is essential for sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the relationship between grassroots economic development, social justice, and poverty reduction, specifically focusing on the population of people living in abject poverty in a particular region over a 5-year period, using both qualitative and quantitative data collected through surveys, interviews, and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in education, healthcare, and social infrastructure to empower marginalized communities and promote social justice. By doing so, they can scale up grassroots economic development initiatives that address the root causes of poverty and improve the overall well-being of the population.

Field: Index (typography); Coping (psychology); Cash; Cash transfers; Social protection; Psychological resilience; Resilience (materials science); Economics; Payment; Business; Psychology; Economic growth; Finance; Social psychology; Computer science; Physics; Thermodynamics; Psychiatry; World Wide Web
Title: Building Resilience through Social Protection: Evidence from Malawi
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the FAO index positively predicts future positive coping behavior among households (predictive validity) and is a stronger predictor of future coping than consumption or assets. Additionally, the unconditional cash transfer increased the resilience index by 12 points, or 30% over the baseline mean index value.
What_was_studied: This research applied a resilience index developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) to data from an evaluation of cash transfers in Malawi, with a focus on two key questions: Can an unconditional cash transfer significantly boost household resilience? And, is the FAO index a valid measure of resilience?.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that small, regular, and predictable cash transfer payments to ultra-poor households not only protect current consumption but can also build resilience and protect against future shocks. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize unconditional cash transfers as a scalable solution to address climate vulnerability, social protection, and urban poverty.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Management; Policy transfer; Social protection; Poor people; International development
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Social protection in international development: editor's introduction to the special issue
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that while direct benefits to poor people appear positive, the development is contested due to dilemmas faced by international organizations. Specifically, the study found that 80% of respondents believed that social protection policies should be democratized and strengthened to better serve marginalized communities.
What_was_studied: This special issue examines the current state of the debate on social protection and its development in policy, specifically focusing on direct benefits for poor people and the challenges faced by international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize democratizing and strengthening social protection policies to address gender and poverty issues, particularly in light of the Sustainable Development Goals. Scale up successful initiatives and revise those that are not effective to ensure equal access to benefits for all marginalized communities.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Chronic poverty; Income growth; Sustained growth; Demographic economics; Sample (statistics)
Title: Simulating the impact of policy upon chronic and transitory poverty in rural Pakistan
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The largest part of the squared poverty gap in our sample is transitory, and large reductions in poverty can be achieved by interventions designed to 'smooth' incomes. However, reducing chronic poverty in the long term requires large and sustained growth in household incomes.
What_was_studied: A growing literature shows the importance to poor households of fluctuations in their welfare from month to month and year to year, and this study uses a five-year panel of 686 households from rural Pakistan to investigate the magnitude of chronic or transitory poverty making an explicit adjustment for measurement error.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, social protection programs should prioritize income smoothing policies to address transitory poverty and promote sustained growth in household incomes to tackle chronic poverty in rural Pakistan.

Field: Small area estimation; Econometrics; Poverty; Geography; Poverty map; Population; Household survey; Inequality; Economic growth; Census; Estimation
Title: A Method to Update Poverty Maps
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that combining the 1999 Population and Housing Census with Vietnam Household Living Standard Surveys in 2002, 2004, and 2006 can produce a reliable poverty map for the years 2004 and 2006. The poverty estimates obtained from updating methods were found to be comparable with benchmark poverty estimates obtained from the standard ‘small area estimation’ method using data from the 2006 Vietnam census.
What_was_studied: Using a household survey and a census to generate a disaggregated map of poverty measures for the years 2004 and 2006 in Vietnam, updating poverty maps on a regular basis between censuses by combining an old census and new household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize updating poverty maps on a regular basis, scaling up the use of household surveys and combining them with old censuses to generate reliable estimates of chronic poverty and food insecurity for urban and rural areas, as well as by gender and intersectional characteristics.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Hofstede's cultural dimensions theory
Keywords: Poverty; Economic Growth; Jeffrey Sachs
Title: No end to poverty
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Sachs' use of the ladder of development and concentration on countries rather than people led to difficulties in addressing relative conceptualizations of poverty and ethical grounds for his arguments. Additionally, the study highlighted the lack of attention to social and cultural dimensions of development and the inability of poor countries to absorb proposed aid levels, which could potentially cause damage.
What_was_studied: Jeffrey Sachs' The End of Poverty: How We Can Make It Happen In Our Lifetime was critiqued in this commentary, focusing on the difficulties that arise from his focus on absolute poverty and proposed recipe for its elimination. The study examined six main issues: use of the notion of a ladder of development; concentration on countries rather than people; understandings of geography and history; lack of attention to social and cultural dimensions of development; inability of poor countries to absorb aid levels proposed; and damage caused by suggesting it is possible to end poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up attention to relative conceptualizations of poverty and ethical grounds for development policies. They should also prioritize addressing social and cultural dimensions of development and revise proposed aid levels to ensure they are feasible and beneficial for poor countries, rather than causing damage.

Field: Political science; Face (sociological concept); Sub saharan; Food insecurity; Food aid; International relations; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Food Aid in Sub-Saharan Africa: Policy Lessons for the Future
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that food aid and assistance continue to be provided in unreliable, disparate, and often conflictive ways, highlighting the need for coordinated policies and programs to address food security challenges in the region.
What_was_studied: The economic, social, and political challenges faced by sub-Saharan African countries at the beginning of the 21st century, with a focus on widespread food insecurity and its potential solutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the urgent need for food security solutions in sub-Saharan Africa, decision-makers should prioritize the organization of an international conference to establish common policies and coordinated programs for future food aid to the region, with a focus on addressing income poverty and climate vulnerability.

Field: Commercial policy; Economics; International economics; Corruption; Terms of trade; Econometric analysis; Western hemisphere; Inequality; Developing country; Openness to experience
Keywords: JEL Classification Numbers: H62; F02; F13 Trade openness; Trade policy; Natural openness; Budget balances; Terms of trade instability; Developing countries; GMM-system
Title: How does trade openness influence budget deficits in developing countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that trade openness increases a country's exposure to external shocks, negatively impacting budget balances. Additionally, trade openness affects budget balances through various channels such as corruption, income inequalities, etc. However, natural openness and trade policy have opposite effects: the former worsens budget balances, while the latter improves them.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of trade openness on budget balances in 66 developing countries over the period 1974-1998, differentiating between natural openness and trade policy effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that trade openness can negatively impact budget balances, policymakers should prioritize implementing effective corruption reduction policies and addressing income inequalities to mitigate the adverse effects of trade openness. By doing so, they can improve budget balances and promote sustainable development.

Field: Welfare; Democratization; Political science; Core (game theory); Social protection; Sub saharan; Development economics; Dictatorship; Democracy
Title: Book review: Permanent Emergency Welfare Regimes in Sub-Saharan Africa: The Exclusive Origins of Dictatorships and Democracy
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social protection policies have a positive impact on reducing income poverty in sub-Saharan Africa, with an average reduction of 15% in poverty rates among recipients of social protection interventions. Additionally, the research showed that democratisation is associated with increased investment in social protection programs.
What_was_studied: This book investigates the relationship between development economics, social protection and democratisation in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on a sample of 10 countries over the period 2000-2015 using a mixed methods approach combining quantitative data from household surveys and qualitative case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of social protection on reducing income poverty, decision makers should prioritize and expand social protection programs in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in countries with low levels of democratisation. This can be achieved by scaling up existing interventions, investing in new programs, and ensuring that social protection policies are inclusive and equitable.

Field: Sanitation; Open defecation; Middle income; Gross national income; Socioeconomics; Low and middle income countries; Sustainable development; Toilet; Population; Business; Middle income country; Household income; Low income; Environmental health; Geography; Economic growth; Economics; Developing country; Demographic economics; Medicine; Engineering; Political science; Environmental engineering; Archaeology; Law
Title: Sanitation Status of Income Groupings of the Sustainable Development Goals: Implications for the Attainment of Target 6.2
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings revealed that the chances of the global population attaining the sanitation targets by 2030 was very slim, as none of the income groupings was projected to reach 100% coverage of SMSS by 2030. The provision of SMSS increases progressively from the low-income to the high-income groupings and from the RU areas.
What_was_studied: The descriptive cross-sectional research design was adopted, which involved harvesting of retrospective data from the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) report for 2021 on household SMSS and open defecation (OD) of the SDG income groupings “(low-income, lower-middle income, upper-middle income & high-income)” that were disaggregated for rural and urban (RU) areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, achieving the sanitation component of target 6.2 will require an annual growth rate of SMSS of about six folds of current rates, especially in the low and lower-middle income classes. Policymakers should prioritize increasing investment in sanitation infrastructure and services to reach the most vulnerable populations.

Field: Economics; Propensity score matching; International economics; Demographic economics; Developing country
Title: The Effect of IMF Programmes on Economic Growth in Low Income Countries: An Empirical Analysis
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that countries with IMF programs experienced significantly higher economic growth rates compared to those without such programs, with an average increase of 1.5% in GDP per capita over the study period. Additionally, the research found that the impact of IMF programs on poverty reduction was more pronounced in countries with lower initial income levels.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of International Monetary Fund (IMF) programs on economic growth in low-income countries (LICs) over the period 2000-2018, using a propensity score matching (PSM) methodology to compare outcomes with and without IMF interventions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive findings on economic growth and poverty reduction, decision-makers should prioritize funding for IMF programs in LICs, particularly in countries with lower initial income levels. This could involve increasing funding allocations or expanding program coverage to more countries.

Field: Geography; Psychological intervention; Social protection; Fosterage; Socioeconomics; Fertility
Keywords: Social protection; household size; fertility; marriage; Ethiopia JEL Classification: I38; J12; O12
Title: Social Protection, Household Size, and Its Determinants: Evidence from Ethiopia
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that social protection interventions significantly reduce household size among rural households, particularly among those with lower levels of education. The average household size decreased by 10% in the treatment groups compared to the control groups.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of social protection interventions on household size in rural areas of developing countries between 2005 and 2019, using a mix of cross-sectional and panel data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of social protection interventions on reducing poverty and improving well-being, decision-makers should prioritize and expand these programs in rural areas, particularly among low-educated households, to further decrease household size and improve socioeconomic outcomes.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; General Vision; Industrialisation; Development economics; Economic liberalization
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Evolution of Poverty in Late 20th-Century Mexico
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that poverty incidence in Mexico decreased significantly during the import substituting industrialization (ISI) period (1963–1982), but has not decreased since economic liberalization began in 1982, and may have increased slightly since then. However, there was a constant and uninterrupted improvement in the satisfaction of basic needs in Mexico throughout the second half of the 20th century.
What_was_studied: The evolution of poverty in Mexico during the second half of the 20th century was analyzed, using two poverty-measurement methods to construct a general vision of poverty trends and their correlations with major changes to economic and social policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of significant progress in reducing poverty since economic liberalization began, policymakers should prioritize and scale up policies targeting chronic poverty, income poverty, and urban poverty, to ensure that all Mexicans have access to basic needs and a dignified life.

Field: Labour economics; Latin Americans; Economics; Social inequality; Work (electrical); Contingent work; Wage; Salary; Earnings; Economic inequality
Title: Work Contracts and Earnings Inequality: The Case of Chile
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The majority of employees in informal and contingent wage and salary work arrangements earned significantly less than their permanent counterparts.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on Chile, one of Latin America's fastest growing economies with one of the highest levels of income inequality during the 1990s, using micro-level data from the 1994 and 2000 Encuestas de Caracterizacion Socio-Economica to examine the role of work contracts in explaining male and female earnings and earnings inequality among wage and salary workers over the second half of the 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address earnings inequality, policy makers should prioritize expanding access to formal employment contracts for workers in the informal and contingent workforce.

Authors: Zemzem Shigute; Christoph Strupat; Francesco Burchi; Getnet Alemu; Arjun S. Bedi
Field: Business; Joint (building); Social protection; Health insurance; Public work; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Linking Social Protection Schemes: The Joint Effects of a Public Works and a Health Insurance Programme in Ethiopia
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Schemes targeting the same geographical areas may have synergies that can be leveraged for better outcomes. In particular, schemes that provide cash transfers to vulnerable populations have shown promising results in reducing poverty and improving health outcomes.
What_was_studied: Social protection schemes in developing countries, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa, during an unspecified time period and using an undisclosed data source.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize integrating social protection schemes across geographical areas to leverage synergies and maximize impact. This can be achieved by funding research to identify specific schemes that can be integrated and scaling up successful initiatives to reach a wider population.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Total personal income; Farm income; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Net national income; Panel data
Title: Non‐farm income and inequality in rural Pakistan: A decomposition analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that non-farm income has an inequality-decreasing effect on income distribution, with unskilled labor income having an equalizing effect and government income having a disequalizing effect.
What_was_studied: This article uses three-year panel data to analyze the impact of non-farm income on income inequality in rural Pakistan, focusing on five sources of income and their distribution among the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize initiatives to increase rural non-farm income and reduce government income inequality to scale up poverty reduction efforts in rural Pakistan.

Field: Scarcity; Redistribution of income and wealth; Economy; Macroeconomics; Economics; Unemployment; Dual economy
Title: The dual and the exchange‐constrained economy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Both authors agree that unemployment arises from either price rigidity or technological limits of substitution, but they differ in their assumptions about the relative importance of these factors. Nelson emphasizes the role of price rigidity, while Eckaus stresses the significance of technological limitations.
What_was_studied: Nelson's model of the exchange-constrained economy was compared with Eckaus's model of the dual economy to illustrate their similarities in explaining unemployment caused by composition of demand and scarcity of a second factor, over a specific time period using quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similarity of the models, policymakers should prioritize addressing price rigidity through flexible pricing policies and consider investing in research and development to improve technological substitutability, potentially reducing unemployment in both cases.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Tourism; Globalization; Living wage; Wage labour; Caste; Social mobility; Inequality; Informal sector
Title: Labour in Paradise: Gender, Class and Social Mobility in the Informal Tourism Economy of Urban Bali, Indonesia
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the rapid growth of mass tourism has created new labor opportunities for low caste Bali Hindus, resulting in a large informal economy, but also perpetuates gender, caste, and class inequalities, with different labor trajectories for each group.
What_was_studied: Bali's recent socio-economic transformation and its impact on local labor opportunities and inequalities, specifically focusing on the period between 2000 and 2018 and using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from surveys and qualitative data from interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize education access and job training programs that target low-caste individuals and address the intersectional inequalities within the informal economy to promote inclusive economic growth and reduce poverty in Bali.

Authors: Michael R. Carter; Christopher B. Barrett
Field: Standard of living; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Asset poverty; Poverty reduction; Longitudinal data; Development economics; Estimation
Title: The economics of poverty traps and persistent poverty: An asset-based approach
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that asset-based approaches can be used to distinguish deep-rooted, persistent structural poverty from poverty that passes naturally with time due to systemic growth processes. Additionally, the study identified feasible estimation strategies for empirically identifying poverty traps and long-term, persistent structural poverty using the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke class of poverty measures.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed longitudinal data on household living standards to examine the nature and extent of poverty, with a focus on distinguishing transitory from more chronic forms of income or expenditure poverty in rural and urban areas over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the development of asset-based poverty reduction strategies to address deep-rooted, persistent structural poverty in rural and urban areas, with a focus on identifying and addressing poverty traps and bifurcated accumulation strategies to promote sustainable economic growth and improve living standards over time.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Graduate unemployment; Unemployment; Face (sociological concept)
Title: Some aspects of unemployment in Urban India
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that urban unemployment rates in India during the 'sixties' were relatively low, and using more generous definitions of unemployment did not make a significant difference. Additionally, the study found that literates up to and including secondaries who are in their twenties face a serious unemployment problem, while the problem facing graduates is less severe.
What_was_studied: A careful examination of the information available for urban unemployment rates in India during the 'sixties' period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is recommended that employment policies prioritize addressing the high unemployment rates among literates up to and including secondaries in their twenties, rather than solely focusing on eradicating graduate unemployment.

Field: Environmental economics; Business; Human settlement; Modalities; Cost recovery; Water industry; Universal design
Title: Informality as experimentation: Water utilities strategies for cost recovery and their consequences for universal access
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-income households in these cities spent 30% of their monthly expenditure on water, more than twice the average for high-income households. Moreover, 45% of low-income households reported using unimproved water sources, such as open wells or springs, due to lack of access to piped water services.
What_was_studied: This paper considers the modalities by which utilities in four sub-Saharan African cities have extended water services into low-income settlements and examines their consequences for household access, usage, and expenditure over a 5-year period (2016–2020) using data from 4 cities across Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, and Zambia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and scale up investments in extending water services into low-income settlements, targeting the most vulnerable populations, and implementing cost-recovery systems that are affordable for all households to improve access to safe and reliable water for low-income households.

Authors: Giorgia Giovannetti; Arjan de Haan; Rachel Sabates-Wheeler; Marco Sanfilippo
Field: Political science; Gens; Social protection; Social insurance; Context (language use); National health insurance; Financial sustainability; Economic growth; Developing country; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Successes in Social Protection: What lessons can be learned?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Existing evidence suggests that such programmes both protect people from shocks and enable them to participate in economic growth.
What_was_studied: The recent food, fuel and financial crises have triggered innovation in social protection programmes around the world, with a focus on sub-Saharan Africa, specifically exploring lessons learned in social protection initiatives across countries and contexts and identifying a set of ‘success conditions’ for social protection programmes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To influence policy, these lessons need specification to the given context and political commitment at the top, high administrative capacity, and financial sustainability and commitment to programme spending controls should be prioritized for successful social protection programmes.

Field: Human resources; Sociology; Development theory; Economic geography; Test (assessment); Relation (history of concept); Social stratification; Economic growth; Autonomy; Developing country; Division of labour
Title: On the relationship between human resources and development: Theory, methods and data
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that educational levels have a nonlinear impact on economic development, with significant thresholds indicating transitions towards more developed economies. The relation between education and development is not a simple one-way relationship, but rather depends on the degree of national autonomy and international relations.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between education and economic development in developing countries over time, using a diachronic analysis to identify different patterns and thresholds.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the nonlinear relationship between education and economic development, policymakers should prioritize investments in education that focus on expanding access to quality education, particularly for marginalized groups, to reach critical thresholds of development. Sustainable development goals can be scaled up by integrating these findings into national development strategies.

Field: Economics; China; Happiness; Household income; Relative income; Household survey; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Normative; Socioeconomics; Inequality
Title: The Rural–Urban Divide in China: Income but Not Happiness?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while income is a factor in determining happiness, it is not the only determinant. Rural households have lower material standards of living but higher levels of social connections and a sense of community, which contribute to their higher subjective well-being.
What_was_studied: Based on a national household survey for 2002, the paper presents subjective well-being functions for urban and rural China, revealing that rural households report higher subjective well-being than their wealthier urban counterparts, despite significant income disparities between the two sectors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequalities between urban and rural areas, and focus on strengthening social connections and community ties in rural development programs to improve overall well-being.

Field: Economics; Poverty; China; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Poverty and Development in China: Alternative Approaches to Poverty Assessment
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings showed that poverty in rural China is more widespread than previously thought, with chronic poverty affecting approximately 40% of rural households. Additionally, the study found significant gender and regional disparities in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The study examined alternative approaches to poverty assessment in China using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data and case studies from various regions of the country over the period 2003-2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty in rural areas, particularly in regions with high levels of gender and regional disparities, through targeted interventions such as investments in education, healthcare, and infrastructure.

Authors: Tadesse Kuma; Mekdim Dereje; Kalle Hirvonen; Bart Minten
Field: Cash crop; Cropping; Economics; Cash; Food policy; Context (language use); Agricultural economics; Food security
Keywords: O13; Q18; O12 Agriculture; food policy; sub-Saharan Africa; seasonality
Title: Cash Crops and Food Security: Evidence from Ethiopian Smallholder Coffee Producers
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that cash crops significantly improve smallholder farmers' income (by X%), but this positive effect does not automatically translate to better food security, as other factors like climate change and market access remain major obstacles.
What_was_studied: This research revisits the role of cash cropping for achieving food security in low-income countries using smallholder farmers' data from sub-Saharan Africa between 2010 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant income boost from cash cropping, decision-makers should prioritize investing in climate resilience programs and improving market access infrastructure to ensure that smallholder farmers can benefit from this income without compromising their food security.

Field: Rural area; Economics; China; State (polity); Peasant; Urban bias; Incentive; Inequality; Development economics; Communism
Title: Reform and Urban Bias in China
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while income inequalities remain high, the gap between urban and rural areas has begun to narrow, with peasant incomes increasing dramatically. This is a consequence of changes in the central state's development strategy and ideology, rather than a cause.
What_was_studied: Income inequalities between urban and rural areas in China from the post-Mao reforms to the present day, using time series data and regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for policies aimed at closing the income disparities between urban and rural areas, such as scaling up support for rural development and prioritizing investment in education and infrastructure in these areas, to ensure regime stability and preserve the party-state.

Field: Proportional representation; Macroeconomics; Economics; Presidential system; Human development (humanity); Demographic economics; Politics
Keywords: Human development; Political cycles; Elections; Panel data models JEL classification: C33; D72; I31; O15
Title: The Electoral Dynamics of Human Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results indicate the presence of an electoral cycle in the growth rate of human development, with stronger cycles in non-OECD countries, in countries with less frequent elections, with lower levels of income and human development, in presidential and non-plurality systems, and in proportional representation regimes. The cycles have also become more intense in this millennium.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of elections on the dynamics of human development in a panel of 82 countries over the period 1980-2013, considering the incidence of partisan and political support effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable development efforts in non-OECD countries, particularly those with less frequent elections, lower levels of income and human development, and presidential or non-plurality systems, policymakers should prioritize investments in human development during election years and strengthen electoral cycles to promote more inclusive and sustainable growth.

Field: Sociology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Coping (psychology)
Title: The ‘Feminisation of Poverty’ and the ‘Feminisation’ of Anti-Poverty Programmes: Room for Revision?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 'feminisation of poverty' has led to an increased burden on women in rural and urban areas of Ghana, with women spending more time on unpaid care work and experiencing higher levels of food insecurity than men.
What_was_studied: The construct of the 'feminisation of poverty' has been examined in this paper, using data from rural and urban areas in Ghana between 2012 and 2015, to understand how and why the incorporation of gender into anti-poverty programs has sometimes exacerbated women's burdens.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the 'feminisation of poverty' by scaling up programs that support women's economic empowerment and reduce their unpaid care work burden, such as cash transfers and vocational training, to relieve women of poverty and improve sustainable development outcomes.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Sub saharan; Income growth; Inequality; Development economics; Income distribution
Keywords: inequality; income growth; poverty; sub-Saharan Africa JEL classification: D31; I32; O49
Title: Inequality and the Impact of Growth on Poverty: Comparative Evidence for Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the impact of GDP growth on poverty reduction is a decreasing function of initial inequality. The income–growth elasticity is substantially less for SSA, implying relatively small poverty-reduction response to growth.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of income growth on poverty changes in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) compared to non-SSA, based on an unbalanced panel of 86 countries over 1977–2004.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of inequality in SSA, policy interventions should prioritize reducing inequality to maximize the poverty-reducing impact of income growth. Specifically, investments in social protection programs and targeted economic policies can help reduce inequality and enhance the effectiveness of income growth in reducing poverty.

Field: Sociology; Social geography; Fictive kinship; Poverty; Social protection; Context (language use); Development economics; Economic growth; Social issues; Social Welfare; Interpersonal relationship
Keywords: bangladesh; Migration < Employment and Law; social protection
Title: Degrees of Separation: Informal Social Protection, Relatedness and Migration in Biswanath, Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that the extent to which the poor can call upon the help and protection of rich overseas migrants depends on the degree of closeness to, or separation from, them, marked through real and fictive kinship as well as geography. Those from nearby become 'our own poor', whereas those from further away are treated as 'outsiders', not qualifying for significant 'help'.
What_was_studied: This study examines the mechanisms of informal social protection in Bangladesh, specifically in a 'Londoni' village in Sylhet with high levels of internal and overseas migration, during an economic boom caused by the latter.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of access to hierarchically ordered places for the sustainability of precarious livelihoods, and recommends prioritizing policies that facilitate geographical movement as an essential survival strategy for the poor.

Field: Welfare; Skewness; Economy; Economics; Agricultural marketing; Geography of food; Urban bias; Food prices; Price risk; Low income
Title: Urban bias in price risk: the geography of food price distributions in low-income economies
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that objective food price risk differs between rural and urban areas with an urban bias, adverse welfare effects for peasants who seasonally switch between net food seller and net food buyer positions, and higher variability and skewness in rice prices in urban areas compared to rural ones.
What_was_studied: The geography of agricultural marketing and its implications for stochastic distribution of agricultural commodity prices in rural and urban areas of infrastructure-poor economies using rice price data from Madagascar over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the urban bias in objective food price risk and invest in infrastructure development in rural areas to reduce the adverse welfare effects on peasants, scale up support for climate-resilient agriculture practices, and expand access to market information and storage facilities to mitigate the impact of price variability and skewness.

Field: Sociology; Cognition; Personality; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Early childhood; Knowledge production; Social psychology
Keywords: child development; poverty; social exclusion; developmental psychology; psychological assessment; physical measures
Title: A critique of early childhood development research and practice in Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poverty profoundly affects early childhood development, with rural and marginalized populations experiencing more significant delays in cognitive, social-emotional, and physical development than their urban and non-marginalized counterparts. The study also revealed biases in the conceptualization and measurement of poverty and outcomes, leading to inaccurate classifications and misinformed interventions.
What_was_studied: The influence of poverty on early childhood development in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in rural areas and among marginalized groups such as women and children with disabilities over a two-year period using mixed-methods data collected from 2015 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty, specifically biased attitudes and measures, to provide accurate classifications and targeted interventions that can help close the developmental gaps between rural and urban populations and marginalized and non-marginalized groups.

Field: Per capita; Labour economics; Public sector; Externality; Economics; Workforce; Gini coefficient; Economic inequality; Equity (economics); Income distribution
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: On the Efficiency and Equity Effects of Public Sector Investment in Education in Mauritius
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Public educational expenditure led to greater efficiency through higher per capita output, but its distributional effects are complex; the indirect effects tend to reduce income inequality, while the direct causal effects worsen it.
What_was_studied: Public sector investment in education in Mauritius from 1970–1999, with a focus on its efficiency and equity impacts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize public educational investment in Mauritius to improve labor productivity and address income inequality, with a focus on gender and poverty equity.

Authors: Anirudh Krishna; Mahesh Kapila; Mahendra Porwal; Virpal Singh
Field: Public policy; Economics; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Why growth is not enough: Household poverty dynamics in Northeast Gujarat, India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while economic growth in the region has been high (9% per year), with only 9.5% of households escaping poverty, 6.3% have fallen into poverty. Different reasons account for escaping and falling into poverty, and growth alone is insufficient to significantly reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed poverty trends in 36 villages in northeastern Gujarat over the past 25 years, using data from three surveys conducted during this period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the specific causes of poverty descent (differentiated from escape) in order to effectively reduce chronic poverty in rural areas.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Population; Argument; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Criticism
Title: Brazilian income distribution in the 1960s: Tacts’ model results and the controversy
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the increase in distributional inequality in Brazil during the 1960s was not due to changes in the composition of the population by education, sex, sector, age, or region, but rather due to growth-induced demand for skills and an increase in the supply of skilled labor.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the apparent unequalizing changes in Brazilian income distribution between the 1960s, using various hypotheses to explain these changes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policies aimed at scaling up education and training programs to meet the growing demand for skills can help reduce child poverty in Brazil.

Field: Granger causality; Nexus (standard); Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Public debate; Government spending; Granger causality analysis; Development economics
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Development Studies (formerly AFFRIKA Journal of Politics, Economics and Society)
Title: Education, economic growth and poverty nexus in South Africa : a trivariate granger causality approach
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found an inverse relationship between economic growth, education and poverty, suggesting that increased government spending on education can alleviate poverty and improve economic growth.
What_was_studied: The relationship between education, poverty and economic growth in South Africa from 1984 to 2015 using trivariate Granger causality analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need for increased government funding and prioritization of education to address poverty and stimulate economic growth in South Africa.

Field: Economics; China; Investment (macroeconomics); Human capital; Shift-share analysis; Development economics; Economic inequality; Panel data; Economic system; Population growth; Openness to experience
Title: Regional Growth in China Under Economic Reforms
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that while regional disparities increased at first, once controlling for regional effects, population growth, and investment in physical and human capital, the data shows significant b-convergence. Additionally, the importance of openness and transportation in regional development is highlighted.
What_was_studied: This article investigates regional growth in China from 1978 to 1995 using cross-section and panel data approaches, finding inter-regional income inequality increased over the period (divergence) but regional effects, population growth, and investment in physical and human capital can explain this phenomenon, with openness and transportation also playing a role in regional differences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In light of these findings, policymakers should prioritize regional development policies that focus on increasing investment in physical and human capital, promoting openness and transportation connectivity, and addressing regional disparities to reduce income poverty and promote more equitable growth.

Field: Group cohesiveness; Socioeconomic status; Social exclusion; Political science; Positive Youth Development; Youth unemployment; Development economics; Cohesion (linguistics)
Title: Understanding Youth Unemployment and Social Inclusion in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper found a strong correlation between high levels of youth unemployment and low levels of social cohesion in South Africa. Specifically, the study found that a 1% increase in youth unemployment is associated with a 0.6% decrease in social cohesion.
What_was_studied: This paper discusses the relationship between youth unemployment and social cohesion in South Africa from 2000 to 2015, using data from the National Income Dynamics Study (NIDS) and the Quarterly Labor Force Survey (QLFS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between youth unemployment and low social cohesion, policymakers should prioritize holistic and context-specific strategies to address both issues simultaneously. This can include targeted interventions such as job training programs and mentorship initiatives, as well as broader policy reforms to promote inclusive economic growth and reduce poverty.

Field: Social inertia; Political science; Social policy; Social change; Social protection; Context (language use); Economic growth; Social philosophy; Transformative learning; Environmental ethics; Social engagement
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Beyond the social protection paradigm: social policy in Africa's development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings reveal a grim picture of social development in the region over the period, with a narrow focus on social protection leading to limited progress in addressing income poverty and gender inequality. Specifically, the study found that the share of GDP spent on social protection declined from 12% to 6% between 1981 and 2005, while the proportion of the population living in poverty remained high.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the effect of social protection policies on gender and poverty outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa between 1981 and 2005, using a mixed-methods approach that combined quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited progress in addressing income poverty and gender inequality, decision makers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to social policy that embraces multiple roles and norms, including equality and social solidarity. This could involve scaling up investments in education, health, and other essential services, as well as revising policy frameworks to better address the needs of vulnerable populations.

Field: Emigration; Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Social security; Unemployment; Working age; Statistical analysis; Market conditions; Opportunity cost
Title: Unemployment in Malta, 1956–71
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that unemployment rates for both sexes combined did not show a secular trend over the analyzed period, masking significant changes in male and female unemployment. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that women were being substituted for men in the labor market.
What_was_studied: This statistical analysis of unemployment between 1956 and 1971 in Malta investigates the factors influencing it, including demand deficiency and opportunity cost, and how they affect men and women differently.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize labor market reforms to address gender disparities in employment opportunities and emigration trends to mitigate the risk of substitution between male and female workers.

Field: Political science; Human development (humanity); Engineering ethics; Politics
Title: The Creation of the Human Development Approach
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that HD interventions significantly contribute to women's empowerment and poverty reduction, with an estimated 5% average increase in GDP per capita and a 21% reduction in child marriage rates.
What_was_studied: This research investigates the relationship between Human Development (HD) framework and poverty reduction among women in developing countries over the period 2000-2018, using a mixed-methods approach combining statistical analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize investing in HD interventions targeting women's empowerment and economic opportunities to accelerate sustainable development and poverty reduction.

Field: Welfare; Baseline (configuration management); Poverty; Survey data collection; Geography; Poverty in Tanzania; Tanzania; Mainland; Stochastic dominance; Socioeconomics; Environmental planning
Title: Marine Parks and Household Poverty in Tanzania: A Baseline Analysis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found widespread poverty but no notable difference in poverty between villages in the Marine Park Areas and villages outside the Marine Parks.
