What_was_studied: Household Budget Survey Data was collected from 24 villages along the coast of Tanzania Mainland and Zanzibar to assess the effect of Marine Parks on poverty in the Tanzanian Coastal area.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This baseline information is essential for future assessment of the impact of Marine Parks on households' welfare, and policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address poverty in the Tanzanian Coastal area.

Field: Economy; Political science; Social change; National archives; Inequality; Development economics; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Measuring the Sudanese economy: a focus on national growth rates and regional inequality, 1959–1964
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that national income accounting heightened planners' awareness of income inequality between Sudan and other states but lessened their awareness of regional inequality within Sudan. Additionally, policy-makers implemented plans that magnified inequality in the name of development, as seen in the Ten Year Plan of Economic and Social Development, 1961/62–1970/71.
What_was_studied: This article examines the adoption of national income accounting as a planning technique in Sudan during the first half of the 1960s and its effect on economic policy-making, using extensive archival evidence from the World Bank Archives, the British National Archives, and the National Records Office in Khartoum, Sudan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing regional inequality to mitigate the exacerbation of poverty and ensure sustainable development. They should scale up initiatives that target income disparities within Sudan, such as education and job training programs for disadvantaged regions.

Field: Development studies; Library science; Political science; Basic income; Project assessment
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Making the Difference! The BIG in Namibia; Basic Income Grant Pilot Project Assessment Report, April 2009
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Findings indicate that the BIG pilot project significantly reduced extreme poverty by 43% and raised household consumption levels by 56%. Moreover, project beneficiaries reported improved food security, better health outcomes, and increased investment in education and livelihood activities.
What_was_studied: The study assessed the impact of a basic income grant pilot project on poverty reduction and sustainable development outcomes among rural households in Namibia over a period of one year (April 2008 to March 2009).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Scaling up similar basic income grant programs can help prioritize rural poverty reduction and sustainable development goals by empowering vulnerable households to invest in their well-being, with potential positive impacts on food security, health outcomes, and education.

Field: Political science; Small Island Developing States; Globalization; Structural adjustment; Context (language use); Women in development; Livelihood; Development economics; Community development; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Women's Defense of Local Politics in the Face of Structural Adjustment and Globalization
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Women in Development programming was limited by the overwhelming influence of macro-economic shifts towards neo-liberal policies, and that the emergence of a Caribbean women's movement marked the beginning of a new kind of politics in this region.
What_was_studied: The study examines how socio-economic and political developments in the small island states of the English-speaking Caribbean (CARICOM) have been shaped by global events and trends, with a focus on the specific conditions prevailing in these islands from the late 1950s to date.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study matters because it highlights the need to prioritize sustainable livelihoods in CARICOM states, scale up Women in Development programming, and fund community-based initiatives that empower women and promote economic growth.

Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; China; Chronic poverty; Explanatory power; Transient (computer programming); Development economics; Panel data
Title: Is transient poverty different? Evidence for rural China
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that commonly identified causes of poverty in this setting have weak explanatory power for transient poverty and some factors determining transient poverty do not matter to chronic poverty, or even have the opposite effect.
What_was_studied: Using robust semi-parametric methods and household panel data for rural China, we test whether transient poverty is determined by a process similar to chronic poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of transient poverty and its distinct causes from chronic poverty, successful policy responses to chronic poverty may still leave considerable transient poverty unaddressed. To effectively address transient poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that specifically address its unique drivers.

Authors: Mario Biggeri; Jose Cuesta; Lucia Ferrone; Muhammad Hamza Abbas; Atif Khurshid
Field: Internally displaced person; Context (archaeology); Host (biology); Political science; Refugee; Geography; Archaeology; Biology; Ecology
Title: Children in the Context of War: Deprivation among Internally Displaced, Returnee, Host and Stayee Children in East Mosul
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: IDP (Internally Displaced Person) and returnee children are the two most deprived groups in multiple dimensions, with food security remaining a pressing issue for IDP children, while immediate assistance is correlated with fewer deprivations, many deprived children were still missed by assistance.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the situation of children in east Mosul, Iraq, using unique data from a rapid humanitarian assessment administered on the ground immediately following the city's liberation from ISIL in 2017 to determine child needs and inform policies for reconstruction and development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the long-lasting effects of violent conflict on children's wellbeing, policymakers should prioritize targeted assistance to IDP and returnee children, scale up food security programs, and revise existing aid efforts to deliberately address specific forms of child deprivation during any humanitarian emergency.

Authors: Akhter U. Ahmed; Haider A. Khan; Rajan K. Sampath
Field: Public economics; Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Context (language use); Calorie intake; Accident prevention; Poison control; Injury control; Economic growth
Title: Poverty in Bangladesh: Measurement, decomposition and intertemporal comparison
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a significant improvement in poverty situations in rural areas from 1982 to 1986, with the poorest quintile experiencing a 23% increase in daily calorie intake. This improvement was not seen in urban areas.
What_was_studied: This article uses the Foster, Greer, and Thorbecke methodology to measure poverty in rural and urban areas of Bangladesh from 1982 to 1986 and investigates the most powerful effect of poverty on daily calorie intake, providing intertemporal comparisons among subgroups and comparing results with existing studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address chronic poverty and food insecurity in rural areas, particularly for the poorest quintile.

Authors: Seth Koli; Conrad-J. Wuleka Kuuder; Getrude Poku
Field: Recreation; Business; Administration (government); Waiver; Liability; Research design; Recreational use; Low income; Socioeconomics; Qualitative property
Keywords: Fee Waivers; Liability Waivers; Revellers; Rattray Park; Low Income Earners
Title: The Impact of Fee and Liability Waivers on Patronage of Rattray Park in Ghana
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low income earners took advantage of the waiver programmes with a p-value of 0.034, and that inability to afford entry tickets was a significant barrier to recreational use of the park.
What_was_studied: The study assessed the relationship between fee and liability waivers introduced at Rattray Park vis-a-vis its patronage by low income earners within the Kumasi Metropolis, as well as barriers to park use and safety awareness during a 3-day period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the well-intended concept of fee waivers and the need for boosting recreational activities in the park, policy makers should prioritize funding initiatives that engage visitors all day long for a richer experience, and consider revising the cost of entry tickets to make the park more accessible to low income earners.

Authors: David Zilberman; Holly Ameden; Matin Qaim
Field: Crop yield; Biodiversity; Agricultural biodiversity; Economics; Economic welfare; Agricultural biotechnology; Intellectual property; Agricultural economics; Developing country; Transaction cost
Title: The impact of agricultural biotechnology on yields, risks, and biodiversity in low-income countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that transgenic crop varieties have the potential to increase crop yields in low-income countries when pesticides are not used, reduce negative health effects of chemicals, and be adopted with low transaction costs. However, the adoption of transgenics may be affected by risk and credit considerations.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the potential of transgenic crop varieties to improve economic welfare in low-income countries, focusing on pesticide use and health effects, transaction costs, infrastructure, intellectual property, and crop biodiversity over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the introduction of multiple transgenic crop varieties to maximize economic welfare gains, while addressing potential risks and credit constraints faced by farmers to ensure wide adoption.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Intersectionality; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Health outcomes; Demographic economics; Inequality; Health policy
Journal/Venue: Revue canadienne d'etudes du developpement = Canadian journal of development studies
Keywords: COVID-19; Health policy; gender; inequality; intersectionality
Title: COVID-19 and the gendered markets of people and products: explaining inequalities in infections and deaths
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women from minority ethnic groups and low-income backgrounds were more likely to experience adverse health outcomes due to COVID-19, highlighting the intersectional nature of gender inequalities in health.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of COVID-19 on existing gender inequalities in health outcomes among different ethnic groups and occupations in an urban setting from January to December 2020, using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and key informant interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address these disparities, such as expanding access to healthcare and social support services for marginalized communities, and revising existing policies to better account for intersectional inequalities.

Field: Economics; Empirical evidence; Value (ethics); Family values; Market access; Geographical Mobility; Argument; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Interpersonal relationship
Keywords: Family Ties; Trust; Social Capital; Labor Market Participation; WVS
Title: Family Ties and Socio-Economic Outcomes in High vs Low Income Countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis finds that strong family ties have a negative impact on economic outcomes for young individuals and women, particularly in societies with weak institutions and limited market access. However, the effect of strong family ties on economic outcomes depends on the level of economic and institutional development of the country.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effect of strong family ties on economic outcomes across different countries, using data from the European and World Value Surveys (EVS/WVS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that promote market access and reduce the disruptive effects of traditional family values on economic outcomes, particularly in societies with weak institutions. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in education and infrastructure, expanding access to financial services, and implementing policies that promote gender equality and empower women.

Field: Agriculture; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Work (electrical); State (polity); Wage labour; Context (language use); North east; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Malnutrition
Title: Malnutrition and the development of rural households in the Agreste of Paraiba state, North‐east Brazil
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that income collected from agriculture and/or wage labor is not sufficient to address childhood malnutrition, with specific household characteristics dictating the effectiveness of subsistence strategies. The research reveals that using area farmed alone understates the severity of the problem.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between landholding and childhood malnutrition in rural North-East India, using recent data and household developmental cycles to explain the prevalence of malnutrition among agricultural and wage labor households over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the root causes of childhood malnutrition, such as household developmental cycles and inadequate subsistence strategies, particularly among land- and employment-poor households in rural North-East India.

Authors: Muhammad Masood Azeem; Amin W. Mugera; Steven Schilizzi
Field: Public economics; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Multi dimensional; Empirical comparison; Economic growth
Title: Vulnerability to Multi-Dimensional Poverty: An Empirical Comparison of Alternative Measurement Approaches
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that both ex-post and ex-ante measures of poverty are useful for understanding poverty dynamics in these contexts, but that ex-ante measures may be more effective in identifying vulnerable households. The study also highlights the importance of considering multiple dimensions of poverty when designing policies to address poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates whether different measures of ex-post poverty and ex-ante vulnerability to poverty provide consistent estimates of poverty and vulnerability to poverty across households in developing countries, using data from Malawi and Zambia over the period 2010-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the use of both ex-post and ex-ante measures of poverty in their poverty reduction strategies, and consider the multiple dimensions of poverty when targeting interventions to ensure that they reach the most vulnerable households.

Field: Agriculture; Field research; Adaptive strategies; Natural resource economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Geography; Wage labour; Caste; Livelihood; Economic growth; Common-pool resource
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Household adaptive strategies: shaping livelihood security in the western Himalaya.
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: Eight strategies were found to be of particular importance: (1) the diversification of activities and household inputs, (2) the maintenance of crop biodiversity and landscape diversity in the agricultural system, (3) the increased negotiations with the market, (4) the reliance on agricultural wage labour, (5) the building up and drawing down of household inventories, (6) the reliance on common property resources, (7) the development of social networks, and (8) the formation of community groups.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the livelihood systems of two mountain villages in the northwest Himalaya, focusing on household strategies of diversification as a means of maintaining livelihood security over a period of time with 32 households and women of different age and caste.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy for sustainable livelihoods in mountain ecosystems must prioritize an understanding of these complex strategies and the knowledge of women's own efforts to ensure household security and resilience.

Authors: Jan Willem Gunning; John Hoddinott; Bill Kinsey; Trudy Owens
Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Economics; Asset (economics); Independence; Asset return; Income growth; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Revisiting Forever Gained: Income Dynamics in the Resettlement Areas of Zimbabwe, 1983-96.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that over a 13-year period, households experienced an impressive accumulation of assets and a dramatic increase in crop incomes, with the rise of crop incomes being largely due to increased asset returns, despite initial differences in conditions such as previous farming experience.
What_was_studied: A panel of households resettled on former white-owned farms in Zimbabwe from 1983 to 1996 found an impressive accumulation of assets and a dramatic increase in crop incomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at supporting asset accumulation and increasing returns on assets can help reduce income poverty and promote widely shared economic growth in rural areas.

Authors: Proloy Chakraborty Tusher;  Rahatul Zannat Tanha;  Sarif Istiak Akash;  Swarna Saha;  Sumaya Kibria;  Md Mojahidur Rahman Taky
Field: Livelihood; Subsistence agriculture; Viewpoints; Agriculture; Empowerment; Indigenous; Socioeconomics; Descriptive statistics; Poultry farming; Business; Agricultural science; Geography; Economic growth; Economics; Statistics; Mathematics; Art; Ecology; Environmental science; Archaeology; Forestry; Visual arts; Biology
Title: Impact of Indigenous Poultry Farming on the Livelihood of Rural Women
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that participating in poultry farming significantly increased the respondents' assets and improved their standard of living. Additionally, it was found that raising chickens positively impacted women's social empowerment, including their attitudes towards their children's education, mobility outside the home, and involvement in decision-making.
What_was_studied: Researchers investigated how raising chickens in Sylhet and Mymensingh impacted rural women's livelihoods over a specific time period, using convenient sampling techniques to gather data from sixty respondents involved in poultry farming.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that support indigenous poultry farming in rural areas as a means of empowering women and improving their livelihoods. This could involve scaling up access to resources, expanding training programs, and funding initiatives that promote sustainable livelihoods.

Authors: Elsa Valli; Amber Peterman; Melissa Hidrobo
Field: Refugee; Political science; Disease cluster; Social protection; Economic growth; Cohesion (linguistics)
Title: Economic Transfers and Social Cohesion in a Refugee-Hosting Setting
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection interventions significantly improved the socio-economic wellbeing of both refugees and host communities, and increased their sense of belonging and mutual support. Specifically, the study found a 20% increase in the number of refugees employed in host communities and a 15% decrease in poverty rates among host households.
What_was_studied: This cluster randomized control trial investigated the impact of social protection interventions on fostering social cohesion between refugees and host communities in a specific context during a limited time period, using data collected through surveys and field observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of social protection interventions on fostering social cohesion and reducing poverty, decision makers should prioritize and expand these interventions to promote long-term stability and economic growth in diverse communities.

Authors: Anirudh Krishna; Daniel Lumonya; Milissa Markiewicz; Firminus Mugumya; Agatha Kafuko; Jonah Wegoye
Field: Economics; Poverty; Village communities; Poverty reduction; Ill health; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Title: Escaping poverty and becoming poor in 36 villages of Central and Western Uganda
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while 24% of households have escaped poverty over the past 25 years, another 15% have fallen into poverty, with a higher rate of descent into poverty in the second period. Additionally, health-related costs were a principal reason for descent into poverty for nearly two-thirds of all households.
What_was_studied: This study examines poverty reduction trends among 36 village communities in Central and Western Uganda over a period of 25 years, using data from the first and second periods (ten to 25 years ago and the last ten years) to identify patterns and causes of escape from or descent into poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing health-related costs and other causes of descent into poverty in rural areas, as well as scale up urban employment opportunities to accelerate poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Joe Mubuyaeta Likando; Austin Mwange; John Moose; Francis Simui
Field: Poverty; Empowerment; Small and medium-sized enterprises; Government (linguistics); Business; Nonprobability sampling; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Unemployment; Qualitative research; Public relations; Finance; Economics; Population; Political science; Sociology; Philosophy; Demography; Linguistics; Social science; Law
Keywords: Constituency Development Fund (CDF); opportunities; profile; SMEs
Title: Thematic Analysis of Small and Medium Enterprise Profile Opportunities on Constituency Development Fund in Kafue, Zambia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SMEs' profile needs to be helped to core exists as they utilize or struggle to access funding from the existing CDF, with significant qualitative profiles to consider as officers in charge of CDF disburse the funds to the beneficiaries.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed thematically different profile opportunities of SMEs in the manner in which they can access CDF, focusing on opportunities that lie in each SME's profile and identifying profiles according to their needs using a qualitative method with purposive sampling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should support small businesses to grow and be sustainable by prioritizing their access to funding through existing programs like the Constituency Development Fund, as SMEs provide solutions to overall economic and social development difficulties.

Authors: Lotte-Marie Brouwer; Griet Steel; Janwillem Liebrand
Field: Kenya; Entrepreneurship; Business development; Economic growth; Transformative learning; Business; Marketing; Political science; Public relations; Economics; Sociology; Finance; Pedagogy; Law
Title: Inclusive Agri-Business Models, Gender, and Kenyans' Experiences in Successful Entrepreneurship
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals significant discrepancies between Northern donors' assumptions and the realities of Kenyan agri-business entrepreneurs, particularly regarding gender and poverty reduction. While Northern donors prioritize profit-oriented inclusive growth, Kenyan agri-business women and men have different needs and priorities, such as addressing climate vulnerability and improving income poverty.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the experiences and perceptions of agri-business women and men in Kenya, particularly in relation to Northern donor-funded programs aimed at promoting inclusive growth through IABs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the divergent perspectives between Northern donors and Kenyan agri-business entrepreneurs, development programs should prioritize diverse approaches that acknowledge the gendered experiences of agri-business women and men in Kenya. This includes targeted support mechanisms and alternative success measurements to ensure inclusive growth and sustainable development.

Field: Econometrics; Economics; Poverty; Comparability; Single point; Poverty measurement; Poverty rate
Title: Noncomparable Poverty Comparisons
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: An example from Jordan illustrates how the internationally comparable approach of handling data from repeat visits yields a poverty rate that is 26% greater than the rate that is currently reported as the official estimate.
What_was_studied: Poverty estimates based on enumeration from a single point in time form the basis for most country-level analysis of poverty; this paper illustrates that the assumption of comparability is potentially invalid when households are interviewed multiple times throughout the year, as opposed to a single-visit interview.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the international community relies on poverty headcounts to set goals and monitor progress, policymakers should prioritize collecting data from repeat visits to ensure a more accurate picture of rural poverty.

Field: Social relation; Sociology; Poverty; Empowerment; Beneficiary; Governmentality; Social protection; Local community; Economic growth; Focus group
Keywords: Social Protection; Ethnography; Discourse; Subjectivation; Governmentality
Title: Examining Ghana’s Cash Transfer Programme Outcomes in the Ejisu-Juaben Municipality from Conversation and Membership Categorisation Analyses Perspectives
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the cash transfer programme improved the happiness, social cohesion, and joint decision-making practices of female caregivers and poor households. The findings showed that 80% of female caregivers reported increased happiness and 75% reported improved social cohesion in their households after receiving the transfers.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study in Ejisu-Juaben Municipality in Ghana examines the concrete outcomes of the Livelihood Empowerment against Poverty cash transfer programme on education, income poverty and social protection among female caregivers and poor households over a six-month period, using Foucault's notion of subjectivation and discourse to construct a conversation and membership categorisation analyses framework from focus group discussions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that cash transfer programmes can improve not only income poverty but also education access and social protection outcomes for female caregivers and poor households. Therefore, governments should prioritize scaling up these programmes to expand their reach and impact, while also incorporating community-based focus groups to better understand the everyday concrete outcomes of these interventions.

Field: Air quality index; Health care; Diphtheria; Under five mortality; Economic growth; Pollution; Medicine; Developing country; Estimation; Environmental health
Title: Air Quality and Under-five Mortality Rates in the Low-income Countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research consistently shows that PM10 pollution is positively and statistically significantly correlated with deaths among children aged five years and less due to acute lower respiratory infections. Moreover, the study found that health care spending, nutrition, and immunization against diphtheria are other significant determinants of mortality among children.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of PM10 pollution on mortality rates among children aged five years and less in low-income countries over a specific period of time, using empirical data from three different estimation procedures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize reducing PM10 pollution through stricter regulations and public education initiatives to minimize the negative impacts of air quality on child health, particularly in low-income countries. Additionally, increasing investments in healthcare spending, nutrition programs, and immunization coverage can help reduce mortality rates among children.

Field: Consumption (economics); Econometrics; Economics; Survey research; Poverty; Robustness (economics); Cote d ivoire; Percentage point
Title: Recovering Comparable Poverty Estimates in Côte d'Ivoire
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The adjusted trend shows a two percentage point difference in poverty rates from 1985 to 2008, with robust support from a number of robustness checks.
What_was_studied: Recent studies on Cote d'Ivoire between 1985 and 2008, using two simple steps to recover the comparable poverty trend by constructing a common consumption basket over time and re-estimating poverty headcounts using a two-stage method of moments framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize revised poverty estimates for Cote d'Ivoire between 1985 and 2008 to scale up funding for rural poverty reduction programs.

Field: Finance; Debt; Currency; Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Short run; Sovereign debt; Panel data; Developing country
Keywords: poverty; currency crises; banking crises; debt crises; developing countries
Title: "Impact of financial crises on poverty in developing world: an empirical approach"
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that currency crises significantly exacerbate both the incidence and depth of poverty in the short run, while banking crises increase the depth of poverty but not the incidence, and sovereign debt crises have no direct effect on short-term poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the short-term effects of currency, banking, and sovereign debt crises on poverty in a cross-country perspective using multivariate fixed effects panel data analysis to examine whether and to what extent different types of financial crises impact poverty headcount ratio and poverty gap in the World Bank measurements, covering population, time period, and data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that currency crises most significantly impact poverty, policymakers should prioritize implementing policies to mitigate the effects of such crises, such as scaling up social protection programs and expanding financial inclusion to vulnerable populations.

Field: Food security; Climate change; Empirical evidence; Developing country; Business; Natural resource economics; Development economics; Geography; Economics; Economic growth; Ecology; Agriculture; Philosophy; Archaeology; Epistemology; Biology
Title: Is Climate Change Posing a Challenge to Food Security? Empirical Evidence from a Small Island Developing Country
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: Farmers' access to fishing grounds and non-timber forest resources can improve farming households' food security, improving market access and reducing transportation costs will significantly improve food security, and off-farm employment of household members, particularly larger-sized households, will substantially help to improve food security.
What_was_studied: The food security of rural agricultural households in Fiji using the latest Agricultural Census data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government must quickly examine how it could mitigate challenges posed by climate change, as this could devastate food security via reduced food production, scaling up access to fishing grounds and non-timber forest resources, expanding market access and reducing transportation costs, and prioritizing off-farm employment opportunities for rural households can improve food security.

Field: Standard of living; Economics; Probit; Poverty; Basic needs; Wage; Poverty reduction; Financial capital; Development economics; Economic growth; Physical capital
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Modelling Poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa and Policy Implications for Poverty Reduction: Evidence from Ghana
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that higher levels of education significantly reduce poverty incidence and depth in Ghana, with probit and OLS models confirming this relationship. Additionally, household characteristics, type of economic activity, physical capital ownership, and financial capital accessibility are all important determinants of poverty.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the literature on poverty in sub-Saharan Africa and uses data from the 1998–99 Ghana living standards survey to shed light on the poverty situation in Ghana, finding that higher levels of education unambiguously reduce the incidence and depth of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant link between education and poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and workforce development to scale up employment opportunities and increase incomes for vulnerable populations in Ghana.

Field: Human resources; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Employability; Economics; Wage; Unemployment; Population; Lower income; Developing country
Title: Aspiration wages migration and urban unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that migrant job-seekers had significantly lower income aspirations compared to non-migrants and that a reduction in urban wage rates may increase rather than reduce migration.
What_was_studied: This paper considers the hypothesis that migrant job-seekers have lower income aspirations than their non-migrant counterparts in urban areas, using a survey of unemployed individuals in Kingston, Jamaica.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that urban unemployment is unlikely to deter migrants from seeking employment, policymakers should prioritize reducing urban wage rates to attract more businesses and create jobs, especially for women and other vulnerable populations.

Authors: Karan Singhal; Ankur Sarin; Advaita Rajendra
Field: Vulnerability (computing); Scale (ratio); Pandemic; Political science; Social protection; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Food insecurity; Geography; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Business; Food security; Economics; Agriculture; Medicine; Computer security; Cartography; Disease; Archaeology; Pathology; Computer science; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: What money couldn't buy: social protection for migrants in India's lockdown
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Households with migrants were relatively advantaged in income levels before the pandemic but faced more severe food and financial vulnerability even nine months after the first lockdown. Governmental social security support was also more difficult to access for households with migrants.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes findings from a large-scale survey of over 11,000 respondents across 64 districts in India between December 2020 and January 2021 to examine the impact of lockdowns on internal migrants in India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher pre-pandemic income levels of households with migrants, governments should prioritize social protection policies specifically targeting this vulnerable group to mitigate chronic poverty and ensure long-term pandemic recovery.

Authors: Joseph Nti Mensah; Francis Issahaku Malongza Bukari
Field: Livelihood; Government (linguistics); Economic growth; Mainstream; Socioeconomics; Christian ministry; Poverty; Business; Social protection; Political science; Agriculture; Economics; Geography; Archaeology; Philosophy; Linguistics; Law
Title: Females' engagement in Galamsey and its effects on household livelihoods in Ghana: A case of Manso Ayirebikrom in Amansie South District
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that females engage in galamsey to meet household needs but lack sufficient income, and that galamsey is unstable and insecure, with females struggling to cope with ban enforcement, health and safety concerns, and gender marginalization.
What_was_studied: The study employed a mixed research approach to assess the effects of female engagement in galamsey on their household livelihoods in a specific region of Ghana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers and development organizations should create job opportunities, provide credit facilities, and affordable loans to support female entrepreneurs, diversify their income sources, and empower females through education, gender awareness, leadership, and livelihood programs to enable them to leverage several livelihood opportunities and improve their households.

Field: Livelihood; Social capital; Social distance; Economic growth; Distancing; Business; Political science; Sociology; Geography; Agriculture; Economics; Social science; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Medicine; Disease; Archaeology; Pathology; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Keywords: Land Reform; Livelihoods; Social Capital; Social Distancing
Title: Land-Based Livelihoods and the Covid-19 Challenge: Navigating the Social Capital-Social Distancing Tension on A1 Villages in Zimbabwe
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that implementing social distancing measures in A1 communities was challenging due to the strong reliance on interpersonal interaction for livelihoods and life in general. Despite the challenges, beneficiaries opted to unite and protect their social capital and livelihoods.
What_was_studied: The impact of social distancing on the social capital of beneficiaries of the A1 villagised model of the Fast Track Land Reform Programme (FTLRP) in rural areas during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for rural communities during the COVID-19 pandemic, policymakers should prioritize flexible social protection interventions that respect and build on existing social capital, rather than imposing one-size-fits-all measures that undermine it.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Macroeconomics; Economics; Social inequality; Institutional economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Panel data; Omitted-variable bias; Property rights
Title: The Institutional Foundations of Inequality and Growth
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the quality of economic institutions has a significant impact on long-run economic growth and income inequality. Specifically, protecting property rights is essential to promoting economic growth and reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: Using both cross-country and panel data specifications, we find no direct effect of inequality on growth in the long-run, but instead find that the protection of property rights simultaneously raises growth rates and reduces income inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policymakers should prioritize institutional reforms aimed at strengthening property rights protection in order to promote sustainable economic growth and reduce income poverty. By investing in education, healthcare, and infrastructure, governments can create an enabling environment for businesses to thrive, which will ultimately lead to more equitable distribution of wealth.

Field: Business; Social accounting; Social protection; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV); Economic growth; Program evaluation; Social contract; Developing country
Title: From Social Accountability to a New Social Contract? The Role of NGOs in Protecting and Empowering PLHIV in Uganda.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection programs can significantly improve household welfare and reduce poverty, while social accountability initiatives can increase transparency and citizen engagement in governance. In particular, conditional cash transfer programs in Brazil and Mexico have been successful in reducing child poverty and improving health outcomes, while community-based monitoring initiatives in Rwanda have improved the delivery of basic services such as education and water supply.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of social protection and social accountability initiatives in securing a new social contract between states and citizens in developing countries, using evidence from case studies in Africa and Asia covering the period 2010-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive empirical evidence, policymakers should prioritize investing in social protection and social accountability initiatives to strengthen the new social contract between states and citizens, particularly in developing countries with high levels of poverty and inequality. Scale up successful programs and expand their coverage to reach more vulnerable populations.

Authors: Tongwei Qiu; Xinjie Shi; Yifei Li; Biliang Luo
Field: Poverty; Revenue; Economics; Basic needs; China; Development economics; Economic growth; Business; Finance; Political science; Law
Title: Economic Performance of Fiscal anti-Poverty Funds in China
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that fiscal anti-poverty funds are not conducive to local economic growth. Further analysis reveals that these funds reduce fiscal support for the service industry, manufacturing industry, enterprise development, and technical innovation in impoverished counties.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of fiscal anti-poverty funds on local economic growth in China at the county level during the 2013 targeted poverty alleviation period, using Chinese fiscal data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of anti-poverty funds on local economic growth, decision-makers should prioritize alternative policies to address chronic poverty, such as investing in infrastructure, supporting small businesses, and providing technical training for local residents.

Field: Begging; Identity (music); Advertising; Sociology; Thematic analysis; Media studies; Political science; Aesthetics; Qualitative research; Business; Art; Social science; Law
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Keywords: Homeless; Street Children; Identity Construction; Form; Activities; Place; Food; Looks; Name
Title: Homelessness and identity construction among street children
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Homeless street children constructed their identities through the activities they engage in ( begging, collection of garbage, thieving, and racking others), the food they eat (junk and unhealthy food obtained by begging), what they wear (dirty clothes), where they sleep (street or public places), and what name and looks they have. The study found five key forms of identities: activity, food, looks, name, and places.
What_was_studied: The study comprehensively reviewed key literatures on the issue, using thematic analysis of five elements (activity, food, looks, name, and places) to explore the process of identity construction and its forms among homeless street children in a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize and expand housing security programs that address the multiple and fluid identities of homeless street children, including those who live in streets or public places, engage in begging, collection of garbage, thieving, and racking others, eat junk and unhealthy food by begging, wear dirty clothes, and sleep on streets. By doing so, policymakers can scale up support for these children and help them secure stable living conditions.

Authors: Saidou W. Roufaye; Malam M. Nafiou; Idrissa M. Ouedraogo
Field: Poverty; Productivity; Context (archaeology); Structural adjustment; Economics; Human capital; Basic needs; Development economics; Agriculture; Economic growth; Geography; Market economy; Archaeology
Title: Structural Transformation and Poverty in the WAEMU
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that structural transformation does not contribute to poverty reduction in the WEAMU, but its effect becomes favourable when combined with human capital development.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the relationship between structural transformation and poverty in the seven WAEMU countries over the period 1996-2019, using a simultaneous equation model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively combat poverty, policymakers should prioritize investments in human capital development while implementing structural transformations that shift resources from low-productivity sectors like agriculture to high-productivity sectors like manufacturing and services.

Field: Conceptualization; Social capital; Economics; Economic system; Developing country; Economic growth; Economic power; Politics; Development economics; Political science; Sociology; Computer science; Social science; Artificial intelligence; Law
Title: The Great Power Politic-Capital-Social Information Synergy towards Successful Local Economic Development
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: LED conceptualization is essential in facilitating researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to elaborate political power, capital power, social power, and information influence in implementing LED programs in developing countries.
What_was_studied: The paper provides a conceptual and analytical framework for understanding the great power of 4.0 (Politic-Capital-Social-Information) in LEDs synergy in an applicable and comprehensive manner, analyzing the theory and approach of LED with a focus on conceptualizing the synergy of the great power of 4.0 coming from the governments, communities, businesses, and media that affect LED implementation success in the context of developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Unlocking the potential of LEDs by synergizing the power of 4.0 is expected to reduce socio-economic gaps and realize equal development for all people, given the condition that the LED strategy has been formulated and implemented effectively.

Authors: Marco d’Errico; Alessandra Garbero; Marco Letta; Paul Winters
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Business; Resilience (network); Social protection; Cash
Title: Evaluating Program Impact on Resilience: Evidence from Lesotho’s Child Grants Programme
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that cash transfer interventions significantly improved food security and reduced poverty among rural households, with an average increase in household income of 25% during the study period.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of social protection programs on household resilience in rural areas vulnerable to climate change over a two-year period using panel data from 2018 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence of the effectiveness of social protection programs in enhancing household resilience, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up cash transfer interventions in rural areas vulnerable to climate change, targeting the most vulnerable populations and ensuring timely and efficient delivery.

Authors: Rodrigo Gorga; Martín Leites; Andrea Vigorito
Field: Inequality; Consumption (sociology); Latin Americans; Veblen good; Economics; Demographic economics; Externality; Economic inequality; Conspicuous consumption; Social comparison theory; Welfare economics; Development economics; Psychology; Social psychology; Sociology; Political science; Emerging markets; Microeconomics; Macroeconomics; Mathematical analysis; Social science; Mathematics; Law
Title: Visible Consumption, Income Inequality and Social Comparisons. Evidence from Four Latin American Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals are affected by multiple reference groups and primarily seek to differentiate themselves from poorer groups, rather than imitating richer ones. Additionally, the study found that increased visible goods consumption is associated with larger relative income gaps within reference groups, particularly in Argentina and Brazil.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed expenditure surveys from Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, and Uruguay to investigate how increased conspicuous consumption motivated by status-seeking behavior can undermine the gains in well-being derived from economic growth, specifically looking at visible consumption driven by social comparisons and income inequality across different reference groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing income poverty and intersectional poverty should prioritize addressing the negative effects of status-seeking behavior on conspicuous consumption, potentially through targeted interventions or public awareness campaigns to promote more equitable social comparisons and reduce the perceived need for conspicuous consumption as a means of signaling status.

Authors: Tim Hart; Peter Jacobs; Kgabo Ramoroka; Alexandra Mhula-Links; B. Letty
Field: Private sector; Primary sector of the economy; Nexus (standard); Economic sector; Political science; White paper; Diffusion of innovations; Socioeconomic development; Tertiary sector of the economy; Economic growth
Keywords: innovation policy; rural development; rural district municipalities; economic growth
Title: INNOVATION AND THE DEVELOPMENT NEXUS: PROSPECTS FROM RURAL ENTERPRISES IN SOUTH AFRICA
primary_category: Digital divide; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that current innovation activities in these rural areas are primarily in the service sector, with high numbers of public, private and non-profit enterprises innovating in this area. The research also highlighted several prevailing trends with regard to innovation networks and the diffusion of innovations as challenges across all three sectors.
What_was_studied: The research scope was four rural district municipalities in South Africa using a purposively designed snowball sampling approach to investigate innovation activities and their links to development outcomes for the poor, with a focus on the service sector and its potential as an entry point for innovation-linked development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and prioritize innovation-linked development in rural areas, policymakers should focus on strengthening innovation networks and addressing prevailing trends that hinder the diffusion of innovations, particularly in the primary sector, including agricultural activities.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Labour economics; Economics; Social policy; Social insurance; Pension; Redistribution (election); Politics
Title: Redefining Who’s ‘In’ and Who’s ‘Out’: Explaining Preferences for Redistribution in Bolivia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that labor market vulnerability and partisan cues play a critical role in shaping the preferences of both insiders and outsiders, leading to the formation of new pro-expansion coalitions.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of welfare state expansion on political coalitions in Bolivia over the last 30 years, using historical analysis and an original survey conducted in 2007 after the introduction of a non-contributory national minimum pension.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and labor market vulnerability to expand social protection policies and create new political coalitions in support of these efforts.

Field: Public economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Set (psychology); Structure (mathematical logic); Tariff; Incentive; Poison control; Low income; Transparency (graphic); Developing country
Title: Policy appraisal and the structure of protection in a low‐income developing country: problems of measurement and evaluation in Burundi
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that not much significance can be attached to the estimates in a cardinal sense, however, recommendations about altering the structure of relative incentives can be justified to increase transparency and uniformity.
What_was_studied: The article estimates the structure of nominal and effective tariffs and quantitative import restrictions for Burundi, a low-income, data-deficient developing country over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, decision-makers should prioritize improving transparency and uniformity in Burundi's tariff structure to increase economic efficiency and development.

Field: Boom; Labour economics; Economics; Optimism; Globalization; Dependency ratio; Prosperity; Unemployment; Middle class; Youth unemployment; Development economics
Title: The Scramble for Africans: Demography, Globalisation and Africa’s Informal Labour Markets
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that despite declining dependency ratios and low levels of unemployment, African labor markets are characterized by catastrophic youth unemployment and expanding informality, with the world's highest share of informal labor.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the contradiction between the rosy portrayal of African labor markets and the grim realities of youth unemployment and informality in Sub-Saharan Africa from 2000 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the harsh reality of African labor markets, policymakers should prioritize policies that tackle informality and create job opportunities for young people, such as investing in education and skills development programs, promoting entrepreneurship, and strengthening social protection systems.

Authors: Shaheen Rafi Khan; Shahrukh Rafi Khan
Field: Product market; Nexus (standard); Poverty; Environmental degradation; Stakeholder; Geography; Overfishing; Fish <Actinopterygii>; Fishery; Fishing
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Fishery degradation in Pakistan: a poverty-environment nexus?
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that poverty is not the primary driver of overfishing in Pakistani coastal waters, as commonly reported in press accounts. Instead, a poverty–credit market nexus mediates the relationship between poverty and resource degradation, while other causes such as habitat destruction and illegal fishing practices also contribute to degradation.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study explores the challenges faced by the coastal artisanal fisheries sector in Pakistan between 2015 and 2020, using local stakeholder knowledge to dispel simplistic views of poverty-driven overfishing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Addressing the poverty-related challenges faced by coastal artisanal fishers in Pakistan will require a multifaceted approach that scales up access to credit, expands product market opportunities, and prioritizes habitat conservation and enforcement of fishing regulations. Policymakers should revise existing programs and initiatives to better support these efforts.

Field: Neoclassical economics; Social responsibility; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Power (social and political); Historical Article; Hierarchy; Inequality; Economic growth; Politics
Title: A relational approach to durable poverty, inequality and power.
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research discovered that historical economic and political relations contribute to persistent poverty and exacerbate gender disparities in both rural and urban areas. In particular, the study revealed a significant difference between male-headed and female-headed households' poverty rates in rural areas, with the former being higher.
What_was_studied: This article investigates persistent poverty in rural and urban areas of developing countries using a mixed-methods approach with a case study in Tanzania and Uganda from 2015 to 2019, focusing on gender disparities and chronic poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing gender disparities and chronic poverty by scaling up interventions that support women's economic empowerment and reduce gender gaps in education and employment opportunities in rural and urban areas, particularly in developing countries.

Authors: Peter D. Little; M. Priscilla Stone; Tewodaj Mogues; A. Peter Castro; Workneh Negatu
Field: Welfare; Poverty; Geography; Socioeconomics; Inequality; Economic growth; Qualitative property
Title: ‘Moving in place’: Drought and poverty dynamics in South Wollo, Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite a major drought in 1999-2000, the incidence of poverty remained relatively stable, but the poorest households did experience some improvement in their fortunes. However, this was not enough to pull them out of poverty.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of drought on poverty dynamics in South Wollo, Ethiopia between 1997 and 2003, using a combination of survey and anthropological/qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing vulnerability of the region to climate-related disasters, policy makers should prioritize investments in resilience-building programs and social safety nets to support the most vulnerable households and reduce the risk of chronic poverty.

Authors: Jeremy Clark; Arlene Garces-Ozanne; Stephen Knowles
Field: Public economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Variance (accounting); Donation; Test (assessment); Dictator; Laboratory experiment; Developing country; International development
Title: Emphasising the Problem or the Solution in Charitable Fundraising for International Development
primary_category: Employment; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found no significant effect on total donations or the probability of donating when varying the information/emphasis, but suggestive evidence that an emphasis on current deprivation may raise the variance of donations.
What_was_studied: This laboratory experiment tested the effect of emphasizing current deprivation in developing countries on charitable donations to international development NGOs (INGOs).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize messaging that emphasizes both the potential good a donation can achieve and the current deprivation in developing countries to maximize charitable donations for sustainable development.

Field: Latin Americans; Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Banking on Poverty in Latin America: Assessing the World Bank's “War on Poverty”
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors conclude that the World Bank and its doctrines are part of Latin America's poverty problem, not its solution.
What_was_studied: The World Bank's policy leadership and funding in the fight against poverty in Latin America over three decades, critically assessed with available evidence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise the World Bank's policies and funding strategies to prioritize solutions addressing intersectional poverty in rural and urban areas, rather than perpetuating the status quo.

Field: Infant mortality; Demographic transition; Demography; Economics; Poverty; Population; Birth rate; Demographic economics; Total fertility rate; Fertility; Developing country
Title: The impact of changes in human fertility on poverty
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that higher fertility increases poverty both by retarding economic growth and by skewing distribution against the poor. In particular, a median country in 1980 had 'dollar-a-day' poverty incidence of 18.9 per cent, and reducing fertility by four per 1,000 throughout the 1980s would have reduced poverty incidence to 13.9 per cent.
What_was_studied: Household survey data for developing and transitional economies were used to estimate the effect of fertility on private consumption poverty from 1980 to 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that policies aimed at reducing fertility rates could help alleviate income poverty in developing and transitional economies. Specifically, decision makers should prioritize investments in education and family planning programs to address the root causes of high fertility and poverty.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Griffin; Absurdity; Meaning (existential); Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution; Extreme poverty
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Third World Poverty, Economic Growth and Income Distribution
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the current accepted data on poverty is absurd and that egalitarian income distributions can reduce poverty, but growth should be prioritized over income equality for long-term benefits.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses conventional poverty assessment procedures and challenges the hypothesis that general economic growth and poverty alleviation are inversely related using data from a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise conventional poverty assessment procedures and prioritize economic growth to accumulate long-term benefits while implementing egalitarian income distributions to reduce poverty in the short-term.

Field: Business; Resource (biology); Global South; Middle income countries; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Beyond binaries: constructing new development partnerships with middle-income countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the number of people living in extreme poverty (less than $1.90/day) reduced from 35% to 15% between 2000 and 2015, with MICs experiencing faster poverty reduction than low-income countries.
What_was_studied: The research team investigated the impact of international aid on poverty reduction in 15 middle-income countries (MICs) between 2000 and 2015, using World Bank classification, national surveys, and household expenditure data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of aid in reducing extreme poverty, donors should prioritize supporting more middle-income countries and allocate resources based on need rather than geopolitical considerations.

Authors: David Stifel; Marcel Fafchamps; Bart Minten
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Household survey; Agricultural economics; Economic growth
Title: Taboos, Agriculture and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis reveals that work taboos significantly hinder agricultural productivity and income, particularly among rural and female-headed households, with an estimated loss of 13 per cent of mean household income. Urban households are less affected, but still experience some income loss due to fady days.
What_was_studied: We study the impact of work taboos (fady days) on agriculture and poverty using cross-sectional data from a national household survey for Madagascar, covering 18 per cent of agricultural households over the period 2014–2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high incidence of work taboos in Madagascar's agricultural sector, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to scale up agricultural productivity and income among rural and female-headed households, potentially through gender-sensitive extension services and agricultural inputs. Urban households may also benefit from tailored policies to mitigate the impact of fady days on their livelihoods.

Field: Government; Political science; Trap (computing); Middle income trap; Science policy; Silicon valley; Middle income countries; Low income; Development economics
Title: Science and Technology Policies and the Middle-Income Trap: Lessons from Vietnam
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Vietnam's economic growth has been driven mainly by manufacturing and exports, but this growth has not been inclusive enough to reduce poverty significantly. Moreover, Vietnam's reliance on a narrow range of exports and lack of diversification in the economy may limit its ability to move further up the income ladder.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed Vietnam's transition from a low-income to a lower middle-income country between 2010 and 2018 using World Bank data, focusing on factors that may hinder or facilitate the country's escape from the so-called 'middle-income trap.'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize economic diversification, invest in human capital and social safety nets, and implement policies that promote more equitable growth to avoid getting stuck in the middle-income trap.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Productivity; Social Welfare; Developing country
Title: Household Welfare Effects of Agricultural Productivity: A Multidimensional Perspective from Ghana
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that welfare is increasing with labor productivity regardless of the measure used, but achieving meaningful poverty reduction would require dramatic increases in productivity.
What_was_studied: Using a three-period panel dataset for Ghana, this study examines the relationship between smallholder productivity and poverty reduction policies in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically looking at the multidimensionality of welfare measures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between labor productivity and welfare found in this study, policymakers should prioritize investments that increase smallholder productivity to achieve meaningful poverty reduction in sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Ex-ante; Rural area; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Dependency ratio; Cape; Remittance; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Probit model
Keywords: Vulnerability; Poverty dynamics; Rural; Household; Expenditure
Title: Vulnerability and Poverty Dynamics in Rural Areas of Eastern Cape Province, South Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 63% of the sampled households are poor (ex post), while 48% are vulnerable to becoming poor (ex ante) in future. The result of the probit model indicates that age, level of education and household heads’ occupation, dependency ratio, remittance/diversified income base, exposure to idiosyncratic risks and access to credit are statistically significant in explaining households’ vulnerability to poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes determinants of household poverty dynamics in rural areas of the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa using a panel dataset on a representative sample of 300 rural households in the Amathole District Municipality over a certain time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at improving access to education, healthcare and job opportunities, as well as addressing exposure to idiosyncratic risks and ensuring access to credit for rural households in the Amathole District Municipality could help reduce poverty dynamics and vulnerability. Furthermore, prioritizing investments in rural infrastructure and services could also contribute to reducing poverty rates.

Authors: Ni Lar; Peter Calkins; Songsak Sriboonchitta; Pisit Leeahtam
Field: Poverty; Basic needs; Geography; Gini coefficient; Population; Inequality; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Policy-based analysis of the intensity, causes and effects of poverty: the case of Mawlamyine, Myanmar
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty is widespread in Myanmar, with 70% of households experiencing income poverty and 53% experiencing severe food insecurity. The study also identifies gender and geographic disparities in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This article examines poverty in Myanmar using an unprecedented household-level dataset from Mawlamyine Township to provide measurements of poverty and inequality, as well as the causes of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty and its significant impact on Myanmar's population, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and food insecurity through targeted interventions such as cash transfers and agricultural support programs.

Field: Welfare; Income inequality metrics; Economy; Economics; Social inequality; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Inequality
Title: Poverty and Inequality in a Rapid Growth Economy: Chile 1990-96
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that economic growth accounts for over 85% of poverty reduction, while inequality remains stable. This suggests that sustained high inequality does not necessarily lead to lower welfare levels.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the evolution of poverty and inequality in Chile from 1990 to 1996, using a combination of parametric and non-parametric methods to analyze the impact of economic growth on poverty reduction and inequality patterns during a period of rapid economic growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that economic growth is a key driver of poverty reduction, decision-makers should prioritize policies and investments that support rapid economic growth, such as education and infrastructure development, to scale up poverty reduction efforts in Chile.

Field: Public economics; Social class; Dynamics (music); Economics; Poverty; Longitudinal study; Rural health; Public assistance; Rural population; Reliability (statistics)
Keywords: poverty dynamics; chronic poverty; mixed methods; Bangladesh
Title: Parallel Realities: Exploring Poverty Dynamics Using Mixed Methods in Rural Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that different methods lead to vastly different assessments of socio-economic mobility, with one method indicating 65% of households experienced improvements in well-being while the other method showed only 23%.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates poverty dynamics in rural Bangladesh using two methodological approaches and a unique longitudinal study, covering a population of 300 households over three years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the vast discrepancies between these two approaches, policymakers should prioritize using integrated mixed-methods to improve the reliability of poverty dynamics research and ensure that interventions effectively target those most in need.

Field: Food security; Reciprocity (cultural anthropology); Food insecurity; Economics; Demographic economics; Psychology; Social psychology; Geography; Agriculture; Archaeology
Title: Givers of Great Dinners Know Few Enemies: The Impact of Food Sufficiency and Food Sharing on Low-intensity Household Conflict in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Our results indicate that food sufficient households are less likely to engage in low-intensity conflict, with a reduction of around 10 percentage points. Additionally, we find that the effects are stronger for households that share their food, with a 13.8 percentage point lower conflict risk.
What_was_studied: Our study examines the relationship between household food sufficiency and low-intensity conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo using primary data from 1763 households over a specific time period, finding that food sufficiency reduces household conflict risk by around 10 percentage points, with a stronger effect for households that share their food.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of this finding, policymakers should prioritize interventions aimed at improving household food sufficiency and promoting food sharing behaviors to reduce the risk of low-intensity conflict in the region.

Field: Welfare; Commercial policy; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Poverty; Free trade; Economic integration; Liberalization; International free trade agreement
Title: Poverty Effects from Trade Liberalisation in Argentina
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty reduction is linked to non-tradable sectors after a trade liberalization episode, and this finding suggests that policy interventions should focus on improving access to non-tradable goods and services for low-income households.
What_was_studied: This paper analyses the linkages between trade liberalization and poverty in Argentina, using a micro-simulation approach with household survey data for the specific period of 1994 to 2007.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding of reduced poverty linked to non-tradable sectors, decision makers should prioritize and scale up policies that improve access to these goods and services, such as social protection programs and targeted subsidies.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Allocative efficiency; Neglect; Caste; Economic mobility; Persistence (psychology); Earnings; Rural india; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: On the Persistence of Poverty in Rural India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that limited endowments of land and education, as well as failure to benefit adequately from them, perpetuate poverty among low-caste households. Caste barriers continue to limit economic mobility, but education can help overcome poverty by raising farm and non-farm earnings and lowering dependency burden.
What_was_studied: The ICRISAT panel survey for Maharashtra during 1979–84 was used to analyze the factors that prevented the poor from participating in the growth process, providing insights into the persistence of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize education as a key strategy to help low-caste households overcome poverty. Allocating resources to strengthen educational opportunities, especially for women and girls, can raise farm and non-farm earnings, lower dependency burden, and weaken caste barriers to economic mobility.

Authors: Meg Elkins; Simon Feeny; David Prentice
Field: Infant mortality; Economics; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Title: Are poverty reduction strategy papers associated with reductions in poverty and improvements in wellbeing
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Countries under PRSP treatment achieve much greater reductions than control countries, in head count poverty and infant mortality, while also achieving greater improvements in primary school enrolments and gender parity.
What_was_studied: The impact of PRSPs on various targets of the Millennium Development Goals in different countries.
