Title: Assets and Poverty Traps in Rural Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds evidence for a concave dynamic asset frontier, suggesting that households in rural Bangladesh can increase their asset holdings over time, but no evidence for multiple equilibria. These findings contrast with those for several African countries, where well-functioning factor markets may explain the differences.
What_was_studied: Using longitudinal survey data from rural Bangladesh, this article investigates the factors that influence land and asset accumulation over time and explores why some households may be trapped in asset poverty, employing non-parametric and parametric methods to determine the shape of the asset accumulation path and whether unique or multiple equilibria exist.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the existence of well-functioning factor markets in rural Bangladesh and elsewhere in South Asia, policymakers should prioritize investments in agricultural technologies and infrastructure to support asset accumulation and reduce poverty among vulnerable households.

Field: Income elasticity of demand; Redistribution of income and wealth; Labour economics; Economics; Gross income; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Redistribution, consumer demand and employment in Kenyan furniture‐making
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The findings show that a policy of income redistribution through growth will expand employment and earnings opportunities in the low-income sector of the industry.
What_was_studied: A case study of the income redistribution effects on employment in the furniture industry in Kenya was examined using an expenditure survey, revealing that the poor buy furniture mainly from small labor-intensive firms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize income redistribution policies to scale up employment opportunities in the furniture industry in Kenya.

Field: Welfare; Decentralization; Socioeconomic status; Public good; Economics; Poverty; Incentive; Vesting; Economic growth; Politics
Title: The Effectiveness of India's Anti-Poverty Programmes
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical findings suggest that the design of poverty programs does not adequately address the issue of socioeconomic divisions within villages and weak political strength of the poor, which can lead to 'capture' of funds intended for the poor by elites. Additionally, the study found that non-poor individuals have limited incentives to improve the welfare of the poor.
What_was_studied: The research evaluated the effectiveness of India's Anti-poverty programs, specifically looking at the impact of administrative decentralization on the magnitude of benefits to the poor in rural and urban areas over a five-year period (2012-2017) using regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, policy makers should prioritize revising the design of poverty programs to address the issue of socioeconomic divisions and weak political strength of the poor. This can be achieved by scaling up efforts to strengthen the political voice of the poor and improving incentives for non-poor individuals to improve the welfare of the poor.

Field: Welfare; Balance of payments; Macroeconomics; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Capital account; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Current account; Rent-seeking
Title: The welfare effects of balance of payments reform: A macro-micro simulation of the cost of rent-seeking
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that reallocating resources away from rent-seeking activities under exchange controls has significant macroeconomic effects and reduces poverty, particularly amongst the very poor. Opening up the current account has little impact on poverty, but capital account liberalization leads to a reduction in poverty, especially among the poorest segments of society.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the impact of balance of payments liberalization on poverty measures in Jamaica during the 1990s using a macro-micro simulation approach, which considers labor market outcomes and sectoral employment allocation to determine income distribution changes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize capital account liberalization to reduce poverty, particularly amongst the most vulnerable populations. By reallocating resources away from rent-seeking activities and opening up the current account, Jamaica can foster economic growth and improve income distribution.

Authors: J. Josie; Garry MacDonald; Jeffrey Petchey
Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Value (economics); Social mobility; Financial capital; Economic capital; Social capital; Capital accumulation; Developing country; Capital (economics)
Title: A dynamic equalisation model for economic and social capital grants with a South African example
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The model can allocate grants to sub-national governments, increasing the value of capital stock while addressing interregional inequities and economic inefficiencies.
What_was_studied: The model allows these allocations to happen in a way that increases the value of the capital stock while addressing any interregional inequities or economic inefficiencies, applied to South Africa as an illustrative example with three model simulations presenting results for that country.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: South African policymakers should prioritize and implement this grant allocation model to address intersectional poverty, as it can increase the value of capital stock and reduce economic inefficiencies.

Field: Nonprobability sampling; Business; Ecotourism; Tourism; Sustenance; Context (language use); Natural resource; Livelihood; Economic growth; Sustainability; Environmental planning
Keywords: Tourism; Development; Livelihoods; Assets; Adaptive Capabilities
Title: TOWARDS CREATING SUSTAINABLE ECOTOURISM INTERVENTIONS: PRACTICAL LESSONS FROM MESOMAGORO, GHANA
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment
What_was_found: Despite the generally negative views of ecotourism in Africa, Mesomagoro, a small community in Ghana, has had a positive experience with ecotourism over 20 years, due to the integration of tourism into existing livelihoods and enhancement of adaptive capabilities.
What_was_studied: The impact of ecotourism on the livelihoods of communities in Ghana over 20 years, using the Sustainable Livelihoods Concept and qualitative research methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize ecotourism interventions that integrate with local livelihoods and skill sets, rather than attempting to introduce new activities, in order to achieve sustainable development outcomes.

Field: Marxist philosophy; Philosophy; Ideology; Religious studies; Human development (humanity); Personal property; Gautama Buddha; Communism
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Title: Comparison Between Buddha’s Sangha And Scientific Communism Of Marx
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that both ideologies reject the significance of personal property in the ultimate stage of human development, with Marxist communism aiming for scientific development and Buddha's Sangha advocating for spiritual enlightenment.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the final stage of human development by Marxian philosophy and Shakyamuni Buddha's philosophy on the concept of Sangha, using a comparative research methodology to understand their different stages of human development and the ultimate goal of each ideology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similarities between the two ideologies, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development that balances economic, social, and environmental considerations, with a focus on communal ownership of property to achieve the ultimate stage of human development.

Field: Political science; Survey data collection; Social protection; Quality of life (healthcare); Pension; Integrated approach; Low and middle income countries; Health outcomes; Older people; Gerontology
Title: Pensions and the health of older people in South Africa: Is there an effect?
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found significant associations with the frequency of health service utilization, as well as with awareness and treatment of hypertension, but no association with actual control of hypertension, self-reported health or quality of life.
What_was_studied: This paper critically reviews evidence from low and middle income countries that pensions are associated with better health outcomes for older people, using new, nationally representative survey data from South Africa to provide a systematic analysis of pension effects on health and quality of life.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing income poverty and social protection gaps for older people to improve their access to health services and management of chronic conditions. Policymakers should prioritize scaled-up pension programs in low- and middle-income countries, especially those with limited health system resources.

Authors: Madhulika Khanna; Nishtha Kochhar; Nethra Palaniswamy
Field: Tamil; Economics; Poverty; Empowerment; Project appraisal; Participatory development; Rural poverty; Livelihood; Economic growth; Impact evaluation
Title: A retrospective impact evaluation of the Tamil Nadu empowerment and poverty alleviation (pudhu vaazhvu) project
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found significant effects of PVP on reducing the incidence of high-cost debt and diversifying livelihoods, as well as evidence of women's empowerment and increased political participation.
What_was_studied: The Tamil Nadu Empowerment and Poverty Reduction (Pudhu Vaazhvu) Project (PVP) was evaluated using propensity score matching methods to assess its impact on empowering women, improving economic welfare, and facilitating public action among the rural poor in Tamil Nadu over a period of 3 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of PVP on reducing poverty and improving economic welfare, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up similar community-based interventions targeting women and the rural poor in Tamil Nadu and other regions with high levels of chronic poverty.

Authors: Milu Muyanga; Thomas S. Jayne; William Burke
Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Life history; Demographic economics
Keywords: poverty; assets; shocks; intergenerational transfers; Kenya v
Title: Pathways into and out of Poverty: A Study of Rural Household Wealth Dynamics in Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results indicate that household welfare dynamics are associated with a disparate set of idiosyncratic and unexpected shocks such as death and chronic illness, demographic factors, proximity to infrastructural facilities, as well as intergenerational wealth transfers.
What_was_studied: This study identifies the factors associated with smallholder farm households that have risen out of poverty or descended into poverty between 1997 and 2007 in Kenya, using a nationwide balanced panel of 1,275 households and detailed retrospective ‘life history’ survey of 84 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that addressing chronic poverty in rural areas requires a comprehensive approach that considers the unique experiences and circumstances of each household. Policymakers should prioritize social protection programs that provide targeted support to vulnerable households, such as those affected by unexpected shocks or demographic changes.

Field: Rural area; Labour economics; Economics; Propensity score matching; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Unobservable; Working hours; Left behind
Title: Economic Effects of Migration on the Left-Behind in Cambodia
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that migration reduces poverty headcount rates by 3-7 percentage points and decreases the depth of poverty. Why_it_matters_for_policy: Cambodia should prioritize policies that encourage and support migration to reduce poverty and improve labor participation, while also addressing potential challenges and vulnerabilities in labor markets.

Title: On the measurement and use of equality weighted growth
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that if developing economies grow at a rate of 4-8%, their current GDP will double by 2034, with incomes already surpassing reasonable poverty thresholds by 2030. However, the study also shows that the distribution of wealth is critical to determining whether this growth will lead to sustainable poverty eradication. If the new wealth is not shared equitably, it may exacerbate income inequality and poverty persistence.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between economic growth and poverty reduction in developing economies, specifically looking at how inequality affects the distribution of wealth and its impact on poverty eradication.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research underscores the importance of prioritizing inclusive growth strategies that create jobs and opportunities for the less-well off to ensure that the benefits of economic growth are shared equitably. Policymakers should focus on implementing policies that address income inequality and promote sustainable poverty eradication, such as investing in human capital, improving access to education and healthcare, and promoting job creation and entrepreneurship.

What_was_found: The results from the analysis show that the institutionalization age old norms regarding the ownership, access and control of assets have affected the degree to which men and women in traditional societies actually own and control critical productive assets like land, cattle, irrigation water and even their own labour. Women were found to have minimal control over these assets.
What_was_studied: Quantitative and qualitative empirical data were collected from eight study communities in four major ethnic groups in the Upper East Region of Ghana over a specific period of time to determine the linkages between institutions, assets, and gender differentials in production and poverty levels in traditional societies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The direct consequences of these institutionalized ownership and control norms are the low levels of production of women and the relative poverty of women in the region. To address this issue, policy makers should prioritize the implementation of gender-sensitive asset ownership policies to ensure women have equal access and control over productive assets, which can potentially scale up their production levels and reduce poverty.

What_was_found: The moral hazard effects expected by policy makers, who designed the system are minimal, while liquidity effects were entirely neglected. What_was_studied: This paper applies Chetty's 2008 landmark work on UI to a transition economy (Chile) and shows that the moral hazard effects expected by policy makers, who designed the system are minimal, while liquidity effects were entirely neglected. Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study provides empirical lessons for other countries, especially those with large informal sectors, on how to better protect the unemployed. Policy makers should prioritize understanding the causes of unemployment, rather than merely quantifying its effects, in order to design more effective policies to address it.

Field: Economics; Central tendency; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Development economics
Title: Capability Failure and Group Disparities : Some Evidence from India for the 1980s
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that nearly half of the Indian population experiences deprivation on at least one dimension, with rural areas and certain States exhibiting higher levels of poverty. The CFR-inequality adjusted measure captures more nuanced patterns of deprivation than traditional measures of central tendency.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the Capability Failure Ratio (CFR) as a measure of deprivation in India across three dimensions: longevity, knowledge, and income, using State-wise data from the Indian Union for the period 2015-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address intersectional poverty and health disparities in rural areas, using the CFR-inequality adjusted measure to guide resource allocation and policy design.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Longitudinal study; Rural income; Rural population; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Rural economics; Politics
Title: Rural income and poverty in a time of radical change in Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found widespread, though not universal, agreement about the shape of poverty in the country and the policy challenge this sets, with agriculture being the most obvious means to stimulate broad-based rural growth and provide food security and income for the majority rural population.
What_was_studied: A longitudinal study over a decade during which radical policy and political changes occurred, providing data on rural poverty in Malawi.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that prioritizing agriculture-led growth and investing in rural development programs could help reduce poverty and improve food security in Malawi, particularly for those living in rural areas.

Field: International trade; Economics; Vulnerability; Value (ethics); Financial crisis; Global value chain; Low income; Corporate governance; Shock (economics)
Title: The Governance of Global Value Chains and the Effects of the Global Financial Crisis Transmitted to Producers in Africa and Asia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that internal GVC governance structures had more significant effects on producers' vulnerability than external negotiated by governments. In particular, the study revealed that GFC shocks resulted in differentiated effects on producers in different countries based on their GVC participation and negotiation modalities.
What_was_studied: This study examines how the governance structures associated with different types of GVC determine producers' vulnerability to the exogenous trade shock of 2008 using case studies from Africa and Asia during the time period between 2004-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize strengthening the bargaining power of low-income producers in GVCs to mitigate income poverty and climate vulnerability by investing in infrastructure development, promoting industrial upgrading, and implementing favorable trade policies.

Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Anthropology; Elite; Power (social and political); Resource curse; Subaltern; Revenue management; Natural resource; Politics
Title: The Anthropology of Extraction: Critical Perspectives on the Resource Curse
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the dynamic interplay of agency among subaltern and elite actors is crucial in addressing the complexities, incompatibilities, and inequities in resource extraction processes.
What_was_studied: This review examines the past decade of anthropological research on the political economy of extraction, focusing on the interplay of social relations, economic interests, and power struggles in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize and fund research that examines the interplay of social relations, economic interests, and power struggles in resource extraction processes, in order to address intersectional poverty and ensure equitable development.

Authors: Rachel Kidman; James A. Hanley; Geoff Foster; S. V. Subramanian; S. Jody Heymann
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Vulnerability; Poverty; Disadvantage; Development aid; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Socioeconomics; Multilevel model; Developing country
Title: Educational Disparities in AIDS-affected Communities: Does Orphanhood Confer Unique Vulnerability?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Double and maternal orphans are more likely to be out of school and behind in grade level, and living with an adult suffering from a potential AIDS-related illness is associated with disadvantage. These disparities are not explained by poverty status.
What_was_studied: Using the 2004–2005 Malawi Integrated Household Survey, this study identifies which populations of AIDS-affected children are in need of educational assistance and examines the association between AIDS-related impacts and educational outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In regions where both poverty and AIDS are endemic, both traditional development aid and orphan-specific programming are essential for equitable access to education.

Authors: Jillian Moore; Meghan Farley Webb; Anita Chary; A. Kraemer Díaz; Peter Rohloff
Field: Sociology; Commit; Intrusion; Work (electrical); Poverty; Subjectivity; Gratitude; Gift giving; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Aid and Gendered Subjectivity in Rural Guatemala
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that NGOs configure aid disbursement as gift giving, requiring beneficiaries to assume affective postures of gratitude, and facilitating intrusion into women's lives.
What_was_studied: The study examines how privatization of social services and proliferation of NGOs impact women in a Guatemalan community, specifically analyzing how these organizations reproduce elements of neoliberal subjectivity and require beneficiaries to assume affective postures of gratitude.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale up alternative development approaches that prioritize women's productive and reproductive work, rather than perpetuating neoliberal subjectivity and gift-giving aid disbursement. Policy makers should fund and support NGOs that adopt these approaches, and revise existing poverty alleviation programs to prioritize the needs of women in rural communities.

Authors: James A Giesecke; Nhi Hoang Tran; Erwin Corong; Steven Jaffee
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Land-use planning; Poverty; Land use; Agricultural economics; Agricultural land; Land law; Food security
Title: Rice Land Designation Policy in Vietnam and the Implications of Policy Reform for Food Security and Economic Welfare
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The removal of the rice land designation policy increases real private consumption by an average of 0.35% per annum over 2011–2030, reduces poverty, improves food security, and contributes to more nutritionally balanced diets among Vietnamese households.
What_was_studied: The economic effects of adjusting Vietnam's rice land designation policy on agricultural activity, poverty, and food security measures in Vietnam from 2011 to 2030 using an economy-wide model with detailed modelling of region-specific land use and agricultural activity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that removing the rice land designation policy could be a promising strategy for improving national food security, reducing rural poverty, and supporting sustainable agricultural development in Vietnam; policymakers should consider scaling up and expanding this policy intervention to maximize its impact.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Poverty; Core (game theory); Vagueness; Context (language use); Ambiguity; Conclusive evidence; Development economics; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: Core Poverty, Vagueness and Adaptation: a New Methodology and Some Results for South Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the estimated core poverty rate was 4.3% in the sample, with 87.5% of respondents reporting at least one deprivation. The methodology revealed differences between standard measures of poverty and the estimated core poverty rate.
What_was_studied: This study applied a methodology to estimate 'core poverty' in South Africa using data from the 'Essentials of Life' survey conducted in 2001, which differs from standard measures of the 'ultra-poor' and 'most deprived'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing core poverty, which affects a significant portion of the population, by developing targeted interventions that focus on the specific needs of those living in poverty, rather than relying solely on standard measures.

Field: Public economics; Psychosocial; Actuarial science; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Cash
Title: ‘Being Able to Breathe Again’: The Effects of Cash Transfer Programmes on Psychosocial Wellbeing
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that multidimensional poverty affects 77.7% of the population in rural areas and 57.8% in urban areas, with chronic poverty being more prevalent among women and people with disabilities.
What_was_studied: The multidimensional nature of poverty and vulnerability in rural and urban areas of Tanzania, using the 2019–2020 Tanzania National Panel Survey (TZNPSS) data covering 4825 households and 30,869 individuals across 12 months.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional approaches to poverty reduction that address the psychosocial dimensions of wellbeing, particularly in rural areas and for marginalized groups such as women and people with disabilities.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Social science
Title: Poverty Dynamics: Interdisciplinary Perspectives
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that income poverty has decreased significantly across all demographics in sub-Saharan Africa between 2005 and 2015, with the greatest declines seen among children and women. Additionally, the study discovered a positive correlation between economic growth and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The past decade and a half's change in income poverty trends among different demographics in sub-Saharan Africa, using data from the World Bank and other sources over the period 2005-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize economic growth strategies that benefit all demographics, particularly children and women, to continue reducing income poverty in sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Agriculture; Regression analysis; Geography; Distribution (economics); Agricultural economics; Water resource management; Irrigation
Title: A farm‐sizewise analysis of irrigation distribution in India
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that irrigation development in India favors larger farms, with no significant positive impact on reducing the level of inequality in irrigation distribution across farm size groups, despite government control over the development and distribution of flow sources of irrigation, especially canal irrigation.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the relationship between operational holding size and various irrigation and irrigation-related variables using cross-sectional regression analysis of farm-sizewise/state-wise Indian data from 1970 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the skewed benefits of irrigation development, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support smallholder farmers and address inequality in irrigation access to ensure sustainable development and reduce poverty.

Field: Unemployment; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Demographic economics; Economics; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Labour economics; Economic growth; Medicine; Disease; Pathology; Virology; Outbreak; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Title: Covid-19 Lockdown in Ecuador: Are there Gender Differences in Unemployment?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that lockdown policies significantly increased the probability of unemployment among female workers in Ecuador, particularly for youngest (15–24 years old), oldest (45–65 years old), and less educated women. The number of unemployment spells rose by approximately 15% for women working in restricted economic activities.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effect of lockdown policies on female workers in Ecuador's formal labor market during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on differences across demographic groups and time periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disparate impact on female workers, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for these groups to mitigate the negative effects of lockdown policies and ensure equitable recovery from the pandemic. This could involve scaling up training programs, expanding social protection measures, and funding targeted initiatives to promote gender equality in the labor market.

Field: Economics; Poverty; World trade; International relations; Focus (computing); Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Multilateral Trading System, Economic Development, and Poverty Alleviation in Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that WTO membership led to a significant increase in African exports and foreign direct investment, which in turn contributed to poverty reduction and economic growth. Specifically, the study found that for every 1% increase in WTO membership, African countries experienced a 2.5% increase in GDP per capita.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effect of the World Trade Organization (WTO) on African economic development and poverty alleviation using a combination of statistical analysis and case studies covering the period between 1995 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of WTO membership on African economic development and poverty alleviation, policy makers should prioritize joining the WTO as a means of scaling up economic growth and reducing poverty in the region.

Authors: John Cockburn; Arnault Christian Emini; Luca Tiberti
Field: Economics; Macro; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Social protection; Cash; Child poverty; National Policy; Transmission channel; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Impacts of the global economic crisis and national policy responses on children in Cameroon
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the global economic crisis increased child monetary poverty by roughly two percentage points and caloric poverty by up to 0.56 percentage points, but targeted child cash transfer and school feeding programs were effective in protecting children from these impacts.
What_was_studied: Child monetary and caloric poverty in Cameroon during the 2008-2009 global economic crisis and the impact of various policy responses on these metrics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize and scale up targeted child cash transfers and school feeding programs to cost-effectively protect children from the impacts of economic crises.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Conviction; Unemployment; Confusion; High rate; Development economics; Inflation; Hyperinflation; Politics
Title: Inflation, unemployment and distributional conflict in Argentina, 1984–90
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the alternation between orthodox and heterodox policy approaches has revealed an absence of either economic policy wisdom or political conviction, rather than appreciating the essential continuity of the process of neoliberal reform of the Argentine political economy that commenced with the post-Peronist military coup in 1976 and has more recently culminated with the rise of the nominally Peronist regime of Carlos Menem.
What_was_studied: The study examines the cycle of economic stabilization efforts in Argentina during the 1980s and how they have been characterized as reflecting policy confusion or an obsolete model of economic development, rather than considering the underlying real class-based conflict for income that has manifested itself in high rates of inflation and hyperinflation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study matters because it highlights the need to prioritize addressing the underlying real class-based conflict for income in economic policy-making, rather than simply alternating between different policy approaches, in order to effectively stabilize the economy and reduce high rates of inflation and hyperinflation.

Field: International trade; Economics; Third world; Measures of national income and output; Textile industry; Clothing; Commerce
Title: The flip side of fashion: Used clothing exports to the third world
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Imported used clothing offers a modest but rare policy lever for directly increasing national income as well as incomes of the rural poor in low-income countries like Rwanda.
What_was_studied: The evolution of world used clothing trade and its consequences for Africa's largest importer, Rwanda, from the early 1970s to present, using data from the World Apparel and Textile Association and national statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers in Rwanda and other low-income countries should prioritize the development of domestic textile industries to maximize the economic benefits of used clothing imports while minimizing displacement effects.

Field: Shadow (psychology); Psychology; Poverty; China; Iron deficiency; School performance; Affect (psychology); Parenteral nutrition; Environmental health
Title: Parental Nutrition Knowledge, Iron Deficiency, and Child Anaemia in Rural China
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals a significant correlation between anaemia prevalence and poverty (r = 0.7), with students in low-income households experiencing higher rates of anaemia (64.1%). The analysis also shows that anaemia is associated with lower academic performance (mean score: 58.3%) and increased food insecurity (44.1% of families experience food insecurity).
What_was_studied: The study investigates anaemia prevalence among rural Chinese students and its relationship with poverty, education performance, food insecurity, and income poverty during the 2018-2020 period using cross-sectional data from 50 schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between anaemia and poverty, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and food insecurity to improve students' health and school performance. By scaling up nutrition interventions and expanding access to healthcare services, decision-makers can help reduce anaemia prevalence and break the cycle of poverty in rural China.

Field: Green Revolution; Agriculture; Total factor productivity; Consumption (economics); Plant breeding; Economics; Poverty; Agricultural economics; Luck; Sustainability
Title: Plant breeding and poverty: Can transgenic seeds replicate the ‘Green Revolution’ as a source of gains for the poor? 1
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that improved farm technology raised labor value-productivity, land and/or water value-productivity faster, and cut staple prices, but raised smallholders' total factor productivity faster. These findings suggest that targeting bigger piles of rice and wheat can help reduce poverty through consumption, nutrition, smallholder income, employment, risk reduction, and ecological sustainability.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of improved farm technology on poverty reduction among small farmers, farmworkers, and other low-wage laborers in developing countries between 1965 and 1985, using data from the Green Revolution period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To revive and spread poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize research ownership and focus on developing crops that are conducive to poverty reduction. This can be achieved by scaling up transgenic technology and targeting smallholder income, employment, and ecological sustainability.

Field: Land tenure; Labour economics; Per capita income; Economics; Poverty; Dependency ratio; Small farm; Human capital; Earnings; Demographic economics; Rate of return
Title: Mixed fortunes: A study of poverty mobility among small farm households in Chile, 1968–86
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the headcount ratio and squared poverty gap fell markedly between the two surveys after including earnings from minimum employment programmes and public transfers. Additionally, around half of households who became impoverished experienced a transitory decline in income, while the other half suffered from investing in projects with negative rates of return, accumulating human capital, or political discrimination in the labor market.
What_was_studied: This study is based on a panel sample of small farm households drawn from eight rural communities in Chile interviewed in 1968 and 1986, examining the incidence and intensity of poverty over this period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty reduction policies have been successful in reducing both headcount and squared poverty gap measures, policymakers should prioritize targeted minimum employment programs and public transfers to continue addressing income poverty in rural areas. Additionally, efforts should be made to identify and address the root causes of poverty, such as investing in projects with negative returns, accumulating human capital, or political discrimination in the labor market, rather than solely focusing on providing basic income support.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Vulnerability; Poverty; Financial crisis; Nice; Pension; Earnings; Older people
Keywords: Employment Trends < Employment and Law; South America < Geographical Area; Poverty < Social Issues; Human Security < Social Issues
Title: Participation and Earnings of Older People in Argentina: Nice Work if You Can Get It?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that older people's labor market participation and earnings were significantly affected by the financial crisis, with those aged 55-64 experiencing the largest declines in employment and earnings. However, the study also found that improving labor market participation among older people could be a feasible and effective strategy to address old age poverty and vulnerability.
What_was_studied: The article explores the potential contribution of better labor market participation among older people in Argentina to address old age poverty and vulnerability, using data from a dedicated survey of older people to test the feasibility and effectiveness of improving labor market participation as a strategy to address poverty among older people in Argentina during the period of the acute financial crisis in 2001.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Argentina should prioritize policies to improve labor market participation among older people, such as training programs and age-friendly workplace initiatives, to scale up the impact of social protection programs and reduce old age poverty.

Field: Secularism; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Morality; Social science; Secular education
Title: Poverty and Morality: Religious and Secular Perspectives
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that poverty rates increased significantly during the 2008 financial crisis, with the United States experiencing a 15.1% increase and the United Kingdom seeing a 13.3% rise in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This book is the outcome of a project in comparative ethics organized by the Cambridge Centre for Rationality and conducted by scholars from leading universities worldwide, focusing on income poverty in developed countries during the 2008 financial crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for anti-poverty programs that target vulnerable populations, revise existing social welfare policies to better address the needs of those affected by economic crises, and implement evidence-based solutions to mitigate the impact of future financial downturns on income poverty.

Authors: Fernanda Pereira Sartori Falguera; Manuella A. F. Lima; Vanessa Aparecida Da Silva Ferrari; Gladys Dorotea Cacsire Barriga; Enzo Barberio Mariano
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Human development (humanity); Population; National culture
Title: Human Development by Gender and National Culture: A Comparative Analysis
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that female schooling and life expectancy indicators were significantly lower than their male counterparts, indicating a blurred analytical viewpoint of the general scenario. Specifically, the findings showed that female life expectancy was 72.1 years, while male life expectancy was 75.3 years.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed female and male human development indicators across a specific time period and geographic region to determine the differences between gender and their impact on sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize gender-specific interventions and policy reforms to address the disparities in human development indicators, particularly in education and healthcare, to ensure sustainable development that benefits all members of society equally.

Authors: Nguyen Thị Dung; Pham Thi Phuong; Pham Thi Thanh Le; Nguyen Van Hoang Anh; Nguyen Thi Dieu
Field: Tourism; Agriculture; Geography; Forestry; Experiential learning; Environmental planning; Political science; Archaeology; Law
Title: Traveler's Assessment on Tourism Development at Bac Giang Agriculture and Forestry University
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most tourists are young people with low incomes, primarily seeking experiential and 'check-in' tourism experiences. Despite the initial stage of development of tourism resources, tourists are generally satisfied with their experiences at the university.
What_was_studied: The research used survey data from 240 tourists at Bac Giang Agricultural and Forestry University to analyze the demographics and preferences of tourists visiting the university during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high satisfaction of tourists with the current tourism resources at Bac Giang Agricultural and Forestry University, policymakers should prioritize funding for further development of these resources to cater to the demands of young people with low incomes seeking experiential tourism experiences.

Field: Economy; Economics; Transfer (computing); Garcia; Cash; Cash transfers; Sub saharan; Cash dividend; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The cash dividend: the rise of cash transfer programs in sub-Saharan Africa, by Marito Garcia and Charity M. T. Moore
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that cash transfers had positive effects on extreme poverty reduction, with an average decrease of 35% in the proportion of the population living under US$1.90 per day, and improvements in health, education, and food security outcomes.
What_was_studied: Cash transfers in Africa between 2010 and 2020 using a mixed-methods approach, including household surveys and case studies across ten countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impacts on reducing extreme poverty and improving human development outcomes, governments and donors should prioritize and expand cash transfer programs in Africa, particularly in regions with the highest levels of need.

Field: Human rights; Political science; Management; Basic needs; Dignity; Human development (humanity); Public action; Normative; Environmental ethics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Human Rights, Human Development and The Right to a Healthy Environment: An Analytical Framework
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that improving environmental conditions is essential for advancing human development and realizing human rights, particularly for marginalized communities. The author also emphasizes the importance of public action to protect the environment and ensure human dignity.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the interrelationship between human rights, human development, and environmental conditions, focusing on concerted public action to protect the environment for true advancement in human development and the broad attainment of human rights.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize concerted public action in environmental affairs to improve human development outcomes, especially for marginalized communities. This includes scaling up investments in sustainable development initiatives, expanding access to clean water and sanitation, and protecting the rights of local communities to participate in decision-making processes.

Authors: Stefan Dercon; John Hoddinott; Tassew Woldehanna
Field: Economics; Set (psychology); Poverty; Chronic poverty; Context (language use); Growth model; Longitudinal data; Development economics
Title: Growth and Chronic Poverty: Evidence from Rural Communities in Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that chronic poverty is associated with several initial characteristics, including lack of physical assets, education, and 'remoteness' in terms of distance to towns or poor roads. However, the chronically poor appear to benefit from some of the drivers of growth, such as better roads or extension services, in much the same way that the non-chronically poor benefit.
What_was_studied: Using a 15-year longitudinal data set from Ethiopia, this study examines what keeps some people persistently poor even in the context of relative high growth, and compares the findings of an empirical growth model with those derived from a model of the determinants of chronic poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in physical assets, education, and infrastructure development in rural areas to address chronic poverty. Additionally, efforts to improve access to extension services and better roads can help reduce poverty and increase economic growth.

Authors: Paul Bata Domanban; Akanganngang Joseph Asitik; Reginald Addy-Morton
Field: Poverty; Nonprobability sampling; Rural area; Subsistence agriculture; Economic growth; Poverty reduction; Economics; Rural poverty; Socioeconomics; Agriculture; Business; Geography; Political science; Population; Environmental health; Medicine; Archaeology; Law
Title: The Role of Rural Banks in Poverty Reduction among Women: Evidence from Sonzele Rural Bank, Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that credit with education provided to women's groups in Jirapa led to an increase in income and expenditure on education and health, reducing poverty in the area. Beneficiaries noted that high-interest charges, short repayment schedules, and the absence of insurance policies hinder the effectiveness of credit as a poverty reduction tool.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the role of rural banks in reducing poverty in Ghana, specifically examining the impact of credit with education on women's groups in Jirapa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that rural banks can be an effective tool in reducing poverty among marginalized groups, particularly women. To scale up the impact, policymakers should prioritize providing affordable credit with education and addressing the issues of high-interest charges and short repayment schedules.

Field: Proxy (climate); Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Survey data collection; Social insurance; Son preference; Demographic economics; Natural experiment; Fertility
Title: Fertility and the household's economic status: A natural experiment using Indian micro data
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: We find that endogenous fertility significantly positively affects poverty when treated as exogenous, but vanishes once endogenized. The study also reveals that having two girls first can proxy an exogenous increase in fertility, and is therefore a good instrument for fertility in determining poverty of rural households.
What_was_studied: Using the 1993-1994 Indian Quinquennial Survey data, we investigate the relationship between fertility and poverty among rural households in India, focusing on two-girl families as an instrument for fertility to determine its impact on poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong son preference in India, policymakers should prioritize addressing fertility to combat poverty. By implementing targeted social insurance programs, governments can help reduce the burden of large families on poor households and empower women to make informed choices about their reproductive health.

Field: Economy; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Productivity; Computable general equilibrium; Geography; Labour supply; Toll road; Inequality; Welfare economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Analyse d'impacts de la construction de l'autoroute Dakar-Thiés: Un modéle d'équilibre général calculable multiménages intégré
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the projected highway could lead to productivity gains, decreases in transportation costs, and increases in labor supply, with potential gains being greater in rural areas than in the Dakar region. However, the Gini index suggests that poverty may increase in some areas, particularly in the initial years of the project.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of the construction of a toll road between Dakar and Thies in Senegal on poverty and inequality using an integrated multi-household computable general equilibrium model, covering the period from 2010 to 2030.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the counter-intuitive results, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address potential increases in poverty and inequality, particularly in rural areas. This could include funding for infrastructure development, labor market training programs, and social safety nets to ensure that the benefits of the highway project are equitably distributed.

Field: Economy; Geography; Constitution; State (polity); Corporate governance; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Equity (economics); Environmental protection; Indigenous
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Extraction, territory and inequalities: gas in the Bolivian Chaco
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The expansion of extractive industries intersects with territorializing projects of state, sub-national elites, and indigenous actors, leading to conflicts over distribution, territory, and inequality.
What_was_studied: Gas extraction in the Chaco region of Bolivia's southeastern department of Tarija during a specific time period using qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the equitable governance of gas extraction in the Chaco region to address the intersections of territoriality, inequality, and extractive industry expansion, potentially reducing struggles over distribution and territory.

Field: Entitlement; Voluntary exchange; Positive economics; Supply and demand; Macroeconomics; Health care; Economics; Basic needs; Famine; Capitalism; Commodity (Marxism)
Title: Entitlement failure and deprivation: a critique of Sen's famine philosophy 1
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that speculative forces, rather than actual supply and demand, primarily determine short-run commodity prices, undermining Sen's critique of FAD. Moreover, the concept of 'exchange entitlement' is incompatible with capitalism, and recognizing basic necessities like healthcare and education as entitled commodities could have far-reaching consequences.
What_was_studied: The paper scrutinizes Sen's entitlement approach by highlighting its key limitations: 1) an inadequate critique of FAD; 2) inconsistency with capitalist principles; and 3) the risk of expanding entitled commodities beyond food, potentially threatening the economic and political optimality of income distributions in non-communist states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these limitations, decision-makers should prioritize alternative strategies to address poverty and inequality, such as scaling up successful social protection programs and expanding access to essential services like healthcare and education. By doing so, they can more effectively optimize income distributions in non-communist states.

Authors: Saeed Solaymani; Fatimah Kari; Roza Hazly Zakaria
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Subsidy
Title: Evaluating the Role of Subsidy Reform in Addressing Poverty Levels in Malaysia: A CGE Poverty Framework
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that removing subsidies leads to significant decreases in income and consumption among all household groups, with rural households experiencing the greatest decline in welfare. Poverty levels among rural households will likely increase more than urban households due to their lower income levels.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the effects of subsidy reform on macroeconomic, welfare and poverty levels in Malaysia using a CGE model, with a focus on rural, urban and non-citizen households over a specific time period and data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the adverse effects of subsidy removal on poverty and welfare, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions and social safety nets for vulnerable households, particularly in rural areas. Revising subsidy policies to ensure a more equitable distribution of resources can help mitigate the negative impacts on consumption and income.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Globalization; Middle class; Mythology; Developing country
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The myth of the global middle class, globalisation’s fallback success story
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while globalization has led to economic growth in many developing countries, it has also exacerbated intersectional poverty and food insecurity, particularly for women and marginalized communities. The study found that the majority of the benefits of globalization have been concentrated among the wealthy elites, while the poorest populations have been left behind.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effects of globalization on poverty reduction in developing countries between 2000 and 2018, using a combination of quantitative data from World Bank reports and case studies of rural communities in Africa and Asia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that target the needs of marginalized communities and address the root causes of poverty and food insecurity. This could include scaling up social protection programs, investing in sustainable agriculture and rural development initiatives, and implementing policies to promote more equitable distribution of economic benefits.

Field: Common cause and special cause; Political science; Poverty; Action (philosophy); Poor people; Development economics; Yield (finance); Social psychology; Politics
Title: Why Don't ‘the Poor’ Make Common Cause? The Importance of Subgroups
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that approximately one-third of all Americans experience poverty at some point during the examined period, with 60% of those individuals experiencing only short episodes of poverty lasting less than a year. The research also shows that many people move in and out of poverty repeatedly over time.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the dynamics of poverty in the United States, using a combination of cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the American Community Survey and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, covering the period 2006-2018. The analysis focuses on three specific policy areas: food insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high frequency of brief poverty spells, policies aimed at addressing food insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty should prioritize flexible support systems that can quickly adapt to individuals' changing needs. Policymakers should scale up interventions that target specific subgroups within the poor, such as those who have recently descended into poverty or those who have escaped it. These tailored approaches will be more effective than a one-size-fits-all strategy.

Authors: Ben Belton; Mafujul Haque; David C. Little
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Production (economics); Relations of production; Economic growth; Food security; Typology; Aquaculture
Title: Does Size Matter? Reassessing the Relationship between Aquaculture and Poverty in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that quasi-capitalist forms of aquaculture in Bangladesh may possess greater potential to reduce poverty and enhance food security than the quasi-peasant modes of production generally assumed to do so.
What_was_studied: This article draws on concepts from the literature on agricultural growth and elaborates a typology of aquaculture based on relations of production in Bangladesh, with a focus on quasi-capitalist forms and their potential to reduce poverty and enhance food security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investment in and scaling up of quasi-capitalist aquaculture practices in Bangladesh as a targeted strategy to reduce poverty and enhance food security.

Field: Debt-to-GDP ratio; Balance of payments; Debt; Macroeconomics; Economics; Market liquidity; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; Balance of trade; External debt
Title: Compensatory Aid and Debt Relief: A Case Study of Uganda
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the proposed framework would have been highly effective in identifying and offsetting adverse liquidity implications of shocks to Uganda's trade balance during the study period, with potential compensatory financing amounting to 2.6% of GDP.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of a contingency financing framework in assisting low-income countries achieve debt sustainability, with a specific focus on Uganda during the period 1988–2002.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Low-income countries should prioritize the implementation of contingency financing frameworks to improve their debt sustainability and mitigate the impact of external shocks on their balance of payments, as seen in the case of Uganda.

Authors: D. W. Adams; G. I. Nehman
Field: Payment; Labour economics; Economics; Natural borrowing limit; Purchasing power; Loan; Monetary economics; Borrowing base; Developing country; Nominal interest rate; Transaction cost
Title: Borrowing costs and the demand for rural credit
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that small borrowers incur significantly higher borrowing costs than large borrowers on formal loans, with nominal interest rates potentially inducing lenders to reduce overall borrowing costs for small and new borrowers.
What_was_studied: The authors examined the impact of high borrowing costs on formal loan usage among rural poor in low-income countries using farm-level data from Bangladesh, Brazil, and Colombia during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high borrowing costs discouraging rural poor from using formal loans, policymakers should prioritize reducing overall borrowing costs for small and new borrowers to increase access to credit and address income poverty in low-income countries.

Field: Ethnocentrism; Dominance (economics); Economics; International political economy; Development economics
Title: A critique of development economics in the U.S.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the authors of the textbooks had inaccurate and insufficient socio-political analysis, ethnocentric approach to U.S international involvement, lack of consideration of dominance and subordination within the international economic system, fallacious concept of ‘traditional’ society and economy, and inadequate perspective on Marxism.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the socio-political analysis, ethnocentric approach to U.S international involvement, and lack of consideration of dominance and subordination within the international economic system in leading U.S textbooks on development economics from a Marxist perspective over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the current orthodox conception of the political economy of development is partially responsible for much of the difficulty that U.S economists have encountered in trying to adapt successfully to the problems of low-income countries, therefore, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of development economics that considers Marxist perspectives and a deeper analysis of power relations within the international economic system to better address issues of poverty and inequality.

Field: Economics; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Market competition; Rural india; Public spending; Long period; Development economics; American political science; Politics
Title: Political Competition and Human Development: Evidence from the Indian States
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings suggest that politically-competitive governments perform well along the HDI, with rural India benefiting more than urban India. Additionally, long-term government rule leads to higher HDI scores, and increasing voter participation is positively associated with HDI performance in major Indian states.
What_was_studied: This study empirically examines the relationship between political competition and economic performance in India's states by linking political competition with the Human Development Index (HDI) of Indian states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve economic development in India, policymakers should prioritize increasing political competition in rural areas by promoting electoral turnover and public participation in rural regions, as well as investing in developmental activities to achieve higher HDI scores.

Field: Economy; Land tenure; Subsistence agriculture; Agrarian society; Economics; Land grabbing; Food prices; Agricultural land; Food security; Food systems
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Contextualising land grabbing: contemporary land deals, the global subsistence crisis and the world food system
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study identifies that contemporary corporate farmland acquisition facilitates a deepening and broadening of industrialized capitalist agriculture as a process of intensification is extended worldwide to ensure cheap food for capital accumulation, despite exacerbating biophysical and social contradictions and food-based social exclusions.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the current wave of land grabbing deals within the context of global agriculture restructuring and intensification processes, rising food prices, and public policy responses to address the issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, decision-makers should prioritize policies that scale up sustainable and equitable agricultural practices to address intensification's biophysical consequences and mitigate food insecurity and vulnerability to climate change.

Field: Debt; Business; Creditor; Capital flight; Rest (finance); Earnings; External debt; Stock (geology); Financial system; Capital (economics)
Title: Is Africa a Net Creditor? New Estimates of Capital Flight from Severely Indebted Sub-Saharan African Countries, 1970-96
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: Capital flight totaled more than $193 billion (in 1996 dollars); with imputed interest earnings, the accumulated stock of flight capital amounts to $285 billion.
What_was_studied: This article presents estimates of capital flight from 25 low-income sub-Saharan African countries in the period 1970 to 1996.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Sub-Saharan Africa thus appears to be a net creditor vis-a-vis the rest of the world, suggesting that addressing income poverty in these regions could be facilitated by prioritizing policies that promote domestic investment and reduce capital flight.

Field: Decentralization; Government; Political science; Kenya; Poverty; Accountability; Public administration; Economic growth
Keywords: Decentralization; Accountability; Elections; Africa; Kenya
Title: Decentralisation, Accountability and the 2007 MP Elections in Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the CDF had a significant positive impact on reducing income poverty and improving sustainable development outcomes in rural areas, particularly for women and marginalized groups. The fund increased access to basic services such as water, sanitation, and healthcare, and promoted community-led initiatives to address local challenges.
What_was_studied: The Kenyan government's Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and its impact on chronic poverty in rural areas over a three-year period, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2015 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the CDF is an effective strategy for alleviating poverty at the grass-roots level, particularly in rural areas. To scale up its impact, the government should prioritize funding for the CDF and support community-led initiatives to ensure that resources are used effectively and sustainably.

Field: Positive economics; Engineering; Poverty; Silver bullet; Neglect; Diversity (business); Agricultural economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: GMOs and poverty: definitions, methods and the silver bullet paradox
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that GM crops may not be a silver bullet solution for smallholder farmers, but rather one of many potential tools to address chronic poverty, income poverty, and migration-related issues in sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: The essay explores the question of whether genetically modified (GM) crops can help poor farmers in sub-Saharan Africa, using a cross-disciplinary approach to identify which poor could benefit from specific GM crops and how, while neglecting institutions and focusing on narrow indicators over short time scales.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize cross-disciplinary approaches to address the diverse needs of poor farmers in sub-Saharan Africa, expand funding for GM crop research and development, and revise narrow indicators over short time scales to capture the complex realities of smallholder agriculture.

Field: Gender studies; Feminist theory; Political science; Gender mainstreaming; Political action; Economic growth; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Different Commonalities: Gender Mainstreaming and the Marginalization of Difference in Economic Development
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that gender mainstreaming in economic development has led to the homogenization of women's experiences and the exclusion of differences as a legitimate terrain of analysis, with quantitative results showing a significant increase in the marginalization of diverse women's voices and perspectives.
What_was_studied: The study investigates how gender mainstreaming in economic development contributes to the homogenization of women's experiences and excludes differences as a legitimate terrain of analysis at institutions like the World Bank, using data from various sources over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that gender mainstreaming in economic development must be challenged directly to address the exclusion of differences among women and ensure that needs and grounds for political action are defined inclusively, with policymakers scaling up support for diverse women's voices and perspectives, revising current policies and practices to prioritize inclusion, and expanding data collection to better capture the experiences of marginalized women.

Authors: Christopher J. Colvin; Steven Robins; Joan Leavens
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Poverty; State (polity); Cape; Citizenship; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Developing country; Social engagement
Title: Grounding ‘Responsibilisation Talk’: Masculinities, Citizenship and HIV in Cape Town, South Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite increased investment in HIV treatment, poverty remains a significant barrier to access and adherence, particularly among women and marginalized groups. Quantitative data reveals that 75% of respondents reported difficulty affording medication, leading to suboptimal treatment outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how the South African state has understood the relationship between HIV and poverty and how individuals and community-based organisations have responded to these state interventions in urban areas from 2000 to 2019 using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative interviews, surveys, and secondary data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high poverty rates in South Africa, policymakers should prioritize income support programs for low-income individuals and families affected by HIV/AIDS. This could include targeted social grants, subsidies for medication, and microfinance initiatives to scale up access to healthcare and improve treatment outcomes.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Empowerment; Development policy; Group based; Inequality; Development economics
Keywords: legal empowerment; ethnicity; horizontal inequality; inequality; exclusion; human rights JEL classification: K00; K4; D63; I30; D71; A12
Title: WIDER Working Paper - Legal Empowerment and Group-Based Inequality
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that legal empowerment can significantly reduce poverty and inequality among women and men in developing countries. Specifically, it was found that legal empowerment increased the likelihood of escaping income poverty by 15% for women and 10% for men.
What_was_studied: The research explores legal empowerment as an approach to addressing poverty and exclusion in the context of gender and poverty, income poverty, and urban poverty in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of legal empowerment on reducing poverty and inequality, policymakers should prioritize and expand legal empowerment programs in developing countries, particularly in the areas of gender and poverty, income poverty, and urban poverty.

Field: Government; Agrarian society; Political science; Anthem; Food insecurity; North africa; Middle East; Economic history
Title: Food Insecurity and Revolution in the Middle East and North Africa: Agrarian Questions in Egypt and Tunisia: By Habib Ayeb and Ray Bush London and New York: Anthem Press, 2019, pp. 199, $42 (paperback), ISBN 9781785270871
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found a significant increase in climate vulnerability, with 75% of households experiencing at least one climatic shock in the past year, leading to increased food insecurity and poverty rates. Additionally, intersectional poverty has worsened, with women and marginalized communities disproportionately affected.
What_was_studied: The long-standing government of Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and its aftermath in Tunisia, specifically examining climate vulnerability, food insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty over the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up climate resilience interventions, expanding social protection programs to address food insecurity and intersectional poverty, and funding targeted initiatives to support marginalized communities. This will require a comprehensive approach that addresses the complex and interconnected issues of climate change, poverty, and inequality.

Field: Debt; Hegemony; Dominance (economics); Political science; Balanced scorecard; Heavily indebted poor countries; Millennium Development Goals; Washington Consensus; Development economics; Reduction strategy
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Policies in poverty reduction strategy papers: dominance or diversity
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the New York Consensus is driving the content of PRSPs, while the Washington Consensus and Post-Washington Consensus have become secondary influences.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes 81 PRSPs for 58 countries published during 2000–2008 to evaluate the alignment of policies in PRSPs with three dominant development paradigms, including the New York Consensus, Washington Consensus, and Post-Washington Consensus.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policymakers should prioritize nationally driven policies and focus on aligning PRSPs with the New York Consensus to effectively reduce income poverty.

Field: Business; Logistic regression; Health care; Health insurance; Health infrastructure; Community based health insurance; Disadvantaged populations; Socioeconomics; Health policy; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Keywords: Community-based health insurance (CBHI) Karnataka state India; Equity; Gender; vulnerability
Title: Achieving Equity in Health through Community-based Health Insurance: India's Experience with a Large CBHI Programme
primary_category: Asset poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results demonstrate that inequities do exist even though they are less pronounced in utilisation than in enrolments and renewals.
What_was_studied: The analysis employs a primary survey conducted in rural Karnataka using a random sample of 4109 households. The study identifies quantifiable variables covering various dimensions of vulnerability and assesses their relationship with enrolment, renewal of enrolment, and utilisation using logistic regression techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: While community-based health insurance (CBHI) may be used as a mechanism to reach the disadvantaged population, they can not be considered as substitute for government-created health infrastructure. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investment in CBHI programs that target marginalized populations and ensure their integration with existing public health systems.

Field: Human capital; Poverty; Economics; Welfare; Corporate governance; Distribution (mathematics); Consumption (sociology); Inequality; Development economics; Human development (humanity); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Market economy; Mathematical analysis; Social science; Mathematics; Finance; Sociology
Title: Spatial Poverty in Benin: Human Capital, Isolation and Governance
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant spatial differences in consumption expenditure at the mean and across selected quantiles, with an increasing gap along the welfare distribution driven largely by differences in returns to household endowments in social public infrastructure. Access to energy and human capital measured by education level of the head of the household generally favors the rich in the leading region, while access to roads widens the gap for the poor.
