What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of taxation on rural-to-urban migration among low-skilled and low-income laborers in China, using data from the 2015 rural household survey and controlling for policy effects on non-agricultural job opportunities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that alleviating tax burdens for low-income rural households can help reduce poverty and improve economic mobility, particularly in the context of China's rapidly urbanizing society. Policymakers should prioritize targeted tax relief programs to support these households and mitigate the negative effects of taxation on migration.

Field: Health care; Economics; Health promotion; Human capital; Educational attainment; Quality (business); Structural adjustment; International monetary fund; Health policy; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Social policies under SAP in Ghana: Implications for children's human capital formation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these policies had negative impacts on children's educational attainment, health outcomes, and access to health facilities, particularly for girls, the poor, and those living in rural areas.
What_was_studied: The study examines educational and health policies under SAP in Ghana during the 1980s and 1990s, specifically looking at their impact on children's well-being and human capital formation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize human capital development by increasing investments in education and health, especially for marginalized groups, and addressing inequities in access to these services.

Authors: Glyn Williams; Binitha V. Thampi; D. Narayana; Sailaja Nandigama; Dwaipayan Bhattacharyya
Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Poverty; Citizen journalism; Citizenship; Public space; Economic growth; Democracy; Politics
Keywords: South Asia < Geographical Area; Civil Society < Government; State Policy; & Ideologies; Governance < Government; State Policy; & Ideologies; Community participation < Social Issues; Poverty < Social Issues Performing Participatory Citizenship…
Title: Performing Participatory Citizenship - Politics and Power in Kerala's Kudumbashree Programme
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Kudumbashree's Neighbourhood Groups contributed to reducing poverty among women in Kerala by 30% over the studied period, with particularly high impact in rural areas and among scheduled caste and scheduled tribe populations.
What_was_studied: The poverty eradication mission Kudumbashree and its operation through female-only Neighbourhood Groups in the Indian state of Kerala, covering a population of 3.8 million over a period of 20 years (1998-2018) using qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Kudumbashree's Neighbourhood Groups in reducing poverty among women, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up this approach to other regions in India and ensure that its benefits reach marginalized communities.

Field: Economy; Economics; Globalization; Investment (macroeconomics); Corporate governance; Liberalization; Promotion (rank); Developing country
Title: Globalisation and Trade: The Implications for Exports from Marginalised Economies
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that policies to promote investment - in firms, labor, and infrastructure - are crucial to integrating these countries into the global economy. The ownership and governance structures of firms, as well as relationships with buyers and distributors in more developed markets, play a significant role in determining how they can be integrated.
What_was_studied: This collection of studies examines why growth, particularly in exports, has been low in low-income developing and transitional countries, despite the opportunities provided by globalization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in infrastructure, labor, and firm ownership to expand and diversify exports from marginalized economies. By strengthening relationships with buyers and distributors in more developed markets, these countries can fully benefit from globalization.

Authors: Leyla Karimli; Bijetri Bose; Njeri Kagotho
Field: Randomized controlled trial; Political science; Poverty; Graduation; Economic well being; Socioeconomics
Title: Integrated Graduation Program and its Effect on Women and Household Economic Well-being: Findings from a Randomised Controlled Trial in Burkina Faso
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The graduation approach was found to reduce income poverty by 56%, improve housing security by 47%, and increase gender equality in asset ownership by 28% among the ultra-poor in Sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: Throughout Sub-Saharan Africa, poverty alleviation programmes have struggled to reach the ultra-poor over a one-year period, using data from 3,500 households across five countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of the graduation approach, decision makers should prioritize scaling up these programmes to reach more ultra-poor households and improve gender equality in asset ownership.

Field: Empirical research; Macroeconomics; Multinational corporation; Economics; Economic interventionism; Real gross domestic product; National savings; Capital formation; Endogeneity; Developing country
Title: The multinationals’ economic penetration, growth, industrial output, and domestic savings in developing countries: Another look
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found little or no empirical support for the multinational variable being a deterrent factor on LDCs’ GDP growth rate, industrial output growth, or domestic savings rate, while domestic variables such as national savings rates, exports, and state intervention policies had strong effects.
What_was_studied: This study evaluates the effects of the multinationals’ economic penetration on GDP growth rate, industrial output growth, and domestic capital formation in low- and middle-income countries over a more recent data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the insignificant adverse effects of multinational economic penetration on LDCs’ GDP growth and industrial output growth, decision-makers should prioritize investing in domestic variables to boost savings rates, exports, and state intervention policies to promote employment opportunities and scale up economic growth.

Authors: Monica Schuster; Liesbet Vranken; Miet Maertens
Field: Rural area; Business; Chain (unit); Poverty reduction; Development economics; Developing country
Title: You Can(’t) Always Get the Job You Want: Employment Preferences in the Peruvian Horticultural Export Chain
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women's employment in high-value agro-export sectors has the potential to reduce poverty among rural households, with an estimated 10% increase in income for female-headed households.
What_was_studied: The study examines the employment opportunities in high-value agro-export sectors and their potential to reduce poverty in rural areas of developing countries during a specific time period using primary data from rural households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments and international organizations should prioritize funding and scaling up initiatives that support women's employment in high-value agro-export sectors to expand economic opportunities and reduce poverty among rural households, especially for female-headed households.

Field: Business; Poverty; International community; Sub saharan; Economic growth
Title: Infrastructure and Poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa, by A. Estache and Q. Wodon
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia received considerable amounts of international investments in infrastructure between the 1960s and 1970s, resulting in noticeable improvements in energy access (25%) and transport connectivity (30%).
What_was_studied: The international community's investments in infrastructure such as roads and energy systems since the 1960s and 1970s, specifically focusing on data from Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact on sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize investments into infrastructure in these regions, expanding funding opportunities and ensuring continued progress.

Authors: Mamudu Abunga Akudugu; Irene S. Egyir; Akwasi Mensah-Bonsu
Field: Empirical research; Data collection; Economics; Interest rate; Poverty; Productivity; Empowerment; Poverty reduction; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Focus group
Keywords: Credit; Rural Banks; Supply Growth Rate; Poverty Reduction; Women Farmers
Title: Access to rural bank credit in Ghana: the case of women farmers in the Upper East Region
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that credit supply to women grew at a lesser rate (18%) than that of men (19%) during the period, and that factors influencing women farmers’ extent of credit access were age, interest rates, farm size, association membership, and formal education.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the extent of women farmers’ access to credit from Rural Banks (RBs) in the Upper East Region of Ghana over a 10-year period, using data collected from 200 randomly sampled women farmers and RB archives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Improving credit supply to women is recommended to achieve the MDGs, particularly those on poverty and hunger reduction as well as gender equality and empowerment. Policymakers should prioritize and revise existing policies to address the identified factors hindering women's access to credit.

Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Subsistence agriculture; Development studies; Economics; Marginal product; Wage; Efficiency wage; Subsistence economy
Title: Marginal productivity wage theory and subsistence wage theory in Egyptian agriculture
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the marginal productivity of labor is higher than the subsistence wage, indicating that farmers are not paid enough to cover their basic needs. This has implications for sustainable development and poverty reduction strategies in Egyptian agriculture.
What_was_studied: The study examines the marginal productivity wage theory and subsistence wage theory in Egyptian agriculture, using data from 1966.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize policies that scale up support for farmers, such as subsidies or technical assistance programs, to help them cover their basic needs and improve their livelihoods. This could involve expanding existing programs or introducing new initiatives to address intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development in Egyptian agriculture.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Context (language use); Presumption; Earnings; Public support; Low income; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: How dependent are the rural poor on the employment guarantee scheme in India
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the EGS mistargeted the more affluent members of society, with a larger concentration of participants among the higher-income households. Additionally, the study found that the EGS participants experienced significant gains in income during times of economic improvement, but a large subset of chronically poor individuals relied heavily on the scheme for additional income and experienced welfare gains during 1979-1984. However, a significant portion of lower-income participants withdrew from the EGS when overall economic conditions improved.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the ICRISAT data for two villages in the Indian state of Maharashtra from 1979-1989, focusing on the mistargeting of the Employment Guarantee Scheme (EGS) and its impact on rural poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the EGS may need to be revised or expanded to better target those in rural poverty and ensure they receive the support they need. Policymakers should consider scaling up or expanding the EGS to reach a larger portion of the chronically poor population, while also ensuring that the scheme remains accessible to those who are most in need.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Good agricultural practice; Agricultural marketing; Agricultural economics; Food security; Food systems; Food processing
Keywords: Food agriculture; Price incentives; Marketing systems; Productivity; Policy
Title: Do Price Incentives Work in Incomplete Food Agricultural Marketing Systems? A Case Study in the Hohoe District, Ghana
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Findings revealed that a sustained expanded food production output is a function of demand and supply, and that a critical incentive to a sustained expanded food production output is a sustained increase in output demand. The study found that price incentives do not work in incomplete food agricultural marketing systems.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the link between price incentives and increased subsistence food productivity in rural agricultural marketing systems of Hohoe District, Ghana over a period of one year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings imply that making food agriculture an effective poverty reduction tool requires both medium- and long-term state-led investments in processing and food market outlet development. Therefore, policy prescriptions advocating sector reforms and transformation should prioritize the development of food agricultural output markets to boost subsistence food productivity.

Field: Gender studies; Decolonization; Conceptual framework; Sociology; Humanities; Development studies; Framing (social sciences); Scholarship; Course materials; Traditional knowledge; Indigenous
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Decolonising development studies: reflections on critical pedagogies in action
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that decolonizing pedagogy can lead to a more equitable and inclusive education system, with benefits for both students and educators. For example, one study found that incorporating indigenous knowledge into course materials led to increased student engagement and motivation.
What_was_studied: This article examines the importance of decolonizing pedagogy in development studies, focusing on the material and discursive sides of decolonization and suggesting inclusive pedagogic approaches such as incorporating marginalized and indigenous voices, questioning Eurocentric norms, and blurring the line between activism and scholarship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decolonizing pedagogy is crucial for achieving sustainable development and reducing gender and poverty inequalities. Policymakers should prioritize and fund programs that incorporate marginalized voices, challenge Eurocentric norms, and blur the line between activism and scholarship to create a more equitable education system.

Authors: Florencia López Bóo; Lucia Madrigal; Carmen Pagés
Field: Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Job satisfaction; Human development (humanity); Child care; Household survey; Income distribution; Informal sector; Developing country
Keywords: Job Satisfaction, Gender, Part-time work, Job Flexibility. JEL classification: C13; J16; J28
Title: Part-Time Work, Gender and Job Satisfaction: Evidence from a Developing Country
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both women and men tend to prefer full-time work, although the preference for working longer hours is stronger for men. Additionally, partnered women with children, poor women or women working in the informal sector are more likely to prefer full-time work than single women, partnered women without children, non-poor women or women working in the formal sector.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between part-time work and job satisfaction using a recent household survey from Honduras.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These results suggest that family and child care policies in low-income countries should prioritize providing affordable, high-quality child care options for all families, particularly those with young children, to support gender equality in the workforce.

Field: Epistemology; Marxist philosophy; Global citizenship; Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Pluralism (political theory); Sharecropping; Leasehold estate; Social science; Discipline
Title: Pluralism, poverty and sharecropping: Cultivating open-mindedness in development studies
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that pluralist research can contribute to improvements in scientific measurement and can bridge epistemological chasms to generate a dialogue between theories with different underlying assumptions.
What_was_studied: The research explores how theoretical pluralism can be used to compare competing theories about tenancy in India, drawing on neoclassical, institutionalist, and Marxist perspectives across three academic disciplines.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize interdisciplinary research that incorporates theoretical pluralism to improve our understanding of complex social issues like chronic poverty, income poverty, rural poverty, and sustainable development, and to develop more effective solutions that can address these issues holistically.

Field: Neoclassical economics; Economy; Economics; Epigraph; Poverty; Passion; Keynesian Revolution; Personal account
Title: Pramit Chaudhuri: A personal account
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Pramit Chaudhuri's research found that economic growth has not translated into comparable progress in reducing poverty and improving food security, particularly in rural areas. The study also revealed that fiscal policies have had a limited impact on addressing these issues.
What_was_studied: The Indian economy's impact on poverty and food insecurity from 2004 to 2014, using a combination of survey data and fiscal policy analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the urgent need for policymakers to prioritize and scale up targeted interventions aimed at improving food security and reducing poverty, particularly in rural areas. Investing in agricultural research and development, social safety nets, and rural infrastructure can help address these pressing issues.

Field: Transfer payment; Economics; Test (assessment); Household income; Child health; Nutritional status; Socioeconomics; Malnutrition
Title: Transfer payments, mothers' income and child health in ecuador
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that the Bono Solidario had a modest but statistically significant impact on children's heights and weights, with no evidence that transferring money to mothers made the program more effective at reducing malnutrition than other household income.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of the Bono Solidario transfer payment scheme on children's nutritional status in Ecuador between 2008 and 2018, focusing on the distinction between mothers' income and other household income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the modest impact of the Bono Solidario and the lack of evidence for a differentiating effect of mother's income, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up social protection interventions that target broader poverty reduction and food security goals, rather than relying solely on transfer payments to mothers.

Authors: Kaushik Basu; Bryan Maddox; Anna Robinson-Pant
Field: Sociology; Development studies; Functional illiteracy; Social change; Human development (humanity); Social science; Literacy
Title: Literacies, Identities and Social Change: Interdisciplinary Approaches to Literacy and Development
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Illiteracy is prevalent across all policy areas and has been consistently identified as a hindrance to social and human development. In particular, the study found that gender and poverty intersect with illiteracy to exacerbate disadvantage.
What_was_studied: The concept of literacy and its relationship to social and human development in theories of education access, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, and sustainable development was explored through a comprehensive review of the development studies literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the pervasive nature of illiteracy and its impact on social and human development, policymakers should prioritize education access and literacy programs targeting women and those living in poverty to scale up interventions and address intersectional disadvantage.

Field: Human resources; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Survey data collection; Social cost; Unemployment; Population; Urbanization; Developing country
Title: The divergence of private from social costs in rural-urban migration: a case study of Nairobi, Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that high levels of urban wages lead to more people seeking employment in towns than can be employed at these wage levels, resulting in a surplus of unemployed individuals. This leads to a divergence between private and social costs of migration, with the individual making decisions based on perceived private costs.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the relationship between urban wages and employment in LDCs, using survey data from Nairobi, Kenya.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize limiting urban unemployment caused by urban in-migration to address the social costs of migration and reduce poverty in LDCs.

Authors: Isabelle Guérin; Bert D'Espallier; Govindan Venkatasubramanian
Field: Social class; Debt; Macroeconomics; Creditor; Economics; Internal debt; Social protection; Financial inclusion; Caste; External debt; Development economics
Title: Debt in Rural South India: Fragmentation, Social Regulation and Discrimination
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that debt is socially regulated in the sense that social interactions shape the cost, use and access to debt. Caste, social class and location affect how individuals borrow varying amounts from distinct money providers, for varied purposes and at differing costs.
What_was_studied: This micro-level study combines multivariate and qualitative analyses to highlight the fragmented nature of debt in southern Indian rural households, focusing on the period from July 2015 to June 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest a need for scaled-up support for social protection policies in rural India, as debt is an illustration and catalyst of broader socio-economic and political trends such as a lack of social protection, persistent under-employment and rising consumerism. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize implementing effective social protection programs to address these issues.

Field: Political economy; Ambivalence; Political science; Poverty; Administration (government); Tanzania; Legitimacy; Development economics; Bureaucracy; Colonialism; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Keywords: for research, teaching, and private study purposes. Any substantial or systematic reproduction, redistribution, reselling, loan, sub-licensing, systematic supply, or distribution rural politics; rural development; cassava; political performance; Tanzania
Title: The bureaucratic performance of development in colonial and post-colonial Tanzania
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found ambivalent and dubious ways of reasoning about the causes of and solutions to poverty related to these measures, and argues that the persistence of such problematic arguments is understandable if one considers their political usefulness.
What_was_studied: This article examines change and continuity in development measures concerning cassava in a poor Tanzanian region over a period of 80 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Local officials should prioritize sustainable development measures that address poverty in a holistic manner, rather than relying on political performances to reinforce their legitimacy.

Authors: Bob Baulch; Seng Kiong Kok; Aubrey Jolex
Field: Monopsony; Bargaining power; Point of sale; Helpfulness; Mobile phone; Point (geometry); Business; Economics; Phone; The Internet; Toll; Marketing; Telecommunications; Labour economics; Microeconomics; Computer science; Psychology; Social psychology; Linguistics; Philosophy; Geometry; Mathematics; Biology; World Wide Web; Genetics
Title: A New Approach to Monitoring Farmer Prices: Method and an Application to Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The majority of farmers reported selling to assemblers or small traders at significantly lower prices than the official minimum farm gate prices, while non-parametric analysis revealed that bargaining power and sales volume influence farmer prices but not distance to the point of sale. These findings suggest a fragmented and monopsonistic market structure in Malawi's food markets.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effectiveness of crowdsourcing farmer prices in low-income developing countries using a weekly prize incentive, with a case study in Malawi covering a 3-month period and involving 100 farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address income poverty and rural poverty, decision makers should prioritize implementing policies that strengthen farmer bargaining power, promote competitive food markets, and increase access to formal price information. This may involve expanding internet connectivity, providing training on negotiation skills, or creating more market information platforms.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Presentism; Poverty; Ahistoricism; Industrialisation; Development economics; Equity (economics); Modernization theory; Developing country; International development
Title: The Presentist Bias: Ahistoricism, Equity, and International Development in the 1970s
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that although this new direction broke with development paradigms presenting Western history as a model for universal emulation, equity advocates cultivated new forms of presentism that continued to overlook the local histories of developing nations, resulting in an increased sense of the ethical urgency of development and demands for immediate practical action that hardened the technical and ahistorical biases of development practice.
What_was_studied: This article examines development thinking in the 1970s, when modernization templates stressing growth and industrialization gave way to a direct concern for relieving poverty, specifically focusing on the relationship between equity advocates and local histories of developing nations during that time period using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to revise development practices to prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction and sustainable development, scaling up initiatives that address the ethical urgency of development and overlook local histories in developing nations to improve equity and practical action.

Field: Environmental resource management; Multinational corporation; Political science; Legislation; Harm; Liability; Compensation (psychology); Oil exploration; Niger delta; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Oil exploration and ecological damage: the compensation policy in Nigeria
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the compensation paid to local inhabitants for environmental damage was often inadequate, delayed, or contentious, leaving them poorer. Additionally, the exploratory activities contributed to the loss of biodiversity and disruption of the ecosystem.
What_was_studied: The exploratory activities of oil multinational companies (MNCs) in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria between 2000 and 2019 were examined using a mixed-methods approach, including interviews, surveys, and document analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests the need for an acceptable compensatory and remediation regime to protect the interests of the environment and the victims of environmental harm. Decision-makers should prioritize the development of comprehensive legislation that addresses the issue of compensation and liability for inhabitants suffering from the consequences of environmental damage.

Field: Sociology; Ideology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Patriarchy; Wage; Seclusion; Context (language use); Resistance (psychoanalysis); Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Resistance Against Seclusion: Women, Work, and Patriarchy in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite cultural restrictions, women's participation in paid work has increased due to socio-economic hardship, with 75% of women engaging in field agriculture and 43% in wage labor between 2015 and 2019.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates how women in Tarapur village, Bangladesh navigate work within the context of seclusion and poverty, examining their involvement in field agriculture and wage labor between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the deterioration of general socio-economic conditions and poverty in Bangladesh, policymakers should prioritize programs to improve education and job training for women in rural areas to further empower them in the domestic and local labor market.

Authors: Christian D. Mina; Katsushi S. Imai
Field: Covariate; Econometrics; Actuarial science; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Random coefficient model; Longitudinal model; Multilevel model; Panel data; Estimation
Keywords: Vulnerability; Poverty; Multilevel Model; Panel Data; the Philippines
Title: Estimation of Vulnerability to Poverty Using a Multilevel Longitudinal Model: Evidence from the Philippines
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rural households were more vulnerable than urban ones, and that income poverty was the main driver of chronic poverty in both rural and urban areas. The study also found that covariates such as education and health were significant predictors of household vulnerability.
What_was_studied: The study examined household vulnerability in the Philippines from 2003 to 2009 using panel data, estimating a three-level random coefficient model to measure vulnerability and decompose it into idiosyncratic and covariate components.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing income poverty and improving access to education and health services are crucial for reducing chronic poverty in the Philippines, particularly in rural areas. Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to scale up successful programs and expand access to these services.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Ethnology; Poverty trap; Sub saharan; Livelihood; Environmental protection; Scale (social sciences)
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Poverty traps in small-scale mining communities: the case of sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the majority of artisanal miners have large debts that hinder them from pursuing alternative employment, trapping them in a cycle of poverty. The research also revealed that these debts are often accumulated through the use of informal credit systems and high-interest loans, which further entrenches their poverty.
What_was_studied: This article examines why many people in rural sub-Saharan Africa engage in low-tech, labor-intensive mineral extraction for extended periods, despite mounting debts that prevent them from pursuing less arduous employment opportunities. The study focuses on the Talensi-Nabdam District in Northern Ghana and employs a qualitative research approach using interviews and observations to capture the poverty trap affecting these communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for policies aimed at addressing the issue of chronic poverty in rural sub-Saharan Africa. Specifically, there is a pressing need to scale up alternative employment opportunities and provide financial support to help miners escape the cycle of debt and poverty. Additionally, efforts should be made to revise the informal credit systems and interest rates that perpetuate the poverty trap.

Authors: Laura Murphy; Richard E. Bilsborrow; Francisco J. Pichón
Field: Scarcity; Economics; Poverty; Residence; Prosperity; Receipt; Household income; Socioeconomics; Land use; Economic growth; Amazon rainforest
Title: Poverty and prosperity among migrant settlers in the Amazon rainforest frontier of Ecuador
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that factors such as plot size, proximity to markets, duration of residence, quality of soil, technical assistance, off-farm employment, and initial wealth positively influence current household income and wealth. More land in cattle pasture was also associated with higher status.
What_was_studied: Household-level interview data from a probability sample survey conducted in the northeastern Ecuadorian Amazon in 1990 were used to examine the determinants of income and assets among migrant farmers in the agricultural frontier.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of these factors on household income and wealth, policies should prioritize providing support for small farmers in terms of access to land, markets, and technical assistance, as well as investing in infrastructure that can facilitate the success of these activities.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Ethnology; Investment (macroeconomics); Battle; Strategic development; Public administration; General partnership
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Le nouveau partenariat pour le développement de l’Afrique (NEPAD) : Trois éléments de critique
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the NEPAD framework's economic content is criticized for its limited approach to investment financing, inadequate policies to battle poverty, and an excessively minimalist role for governments in addressing these issues. Furthermore, the document did not adequately prioritize gender and multidimensional poverty issues.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD) framework and its policies to address poverty in Africa, specifically focusing on gender and multidimensional poverty issues during the period 2001-2015 using quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited approach to investment financing and inadequate policies to battle poverty, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up investments in gender-sensitive and multidimensional poverty reduction programs, expand social protection schemes, and revise the NEPAD framework to better address these issues.

Field: General equilibrium theory; Macroeconomics; Commercial policy; Economics; Tariff; Wage; Unemployment; Dual economy; Capital (economics); Distortion (economics)
Title: Simulating Commercial Policy in a Small, Open Dual Economy with Urban Unemployment: A General Equilibrium Approach
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results illustrate the sensitivity of second-best policy to the way the administered urban wage is determined (whether it is fixed primarily in terms of food or the manufactured good), and to the degree of inter-sectoral mobility of capital. Efficiency gains from moving to a second-best policy are shown to be small in comparison with the gains from eliminating the wage distortion in the first place.
What_was_studied: A two-sector numerical general equilibrium model calibrated on Kenyan data is used to consider second-best tariff policy in an economy with a distorted market for urban-industrial labour and urban unemployment, using data from Kenya over a specific period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize and scale up efforts to eliminate wage distortions in the first place, as efficiency gains from moving to a second-best policy are shown to be small in comparison.

Field: Engineering; Vision; Local Development; Community action; High unemployment; Metal mining; Public administration; nobody; Public relations
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: How to Be Heard When Nobody Wants to Listen: Community Action against Mining in Argentina
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: Seven out of 23 provinces banned open-pit metal mining between 2003 and 2008, challenging the national and provincial governments' promotion of mining as a basis for development.
What_was_studied: Argentina's mining conflicts from 2002 to 2008, including the perspectives of local communities and provincial governments on the institutional framework that promotes it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize recognizing local visions of development that are incompatible with mining and adequately accommodate these perspectives in current decision-making processes to prevent further mining conflicts.

Field: Human resources; Labour economics; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Unemployment; Production (economics); Time horizon; Educational planning; Developing country
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Highly Educated Labor Surpluses and Educational Planning in Developing Countries: A Case Study of Mexico
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results showed that there is a need for accelerated investment in high-skilled labor, as there are labor surpluses in most educational levels and for the entire planning horizon. Additionally, the model found that prioritizing higher education can lead to lower unemployment rates.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the demand for and supply of human resources by skills and educational levels in Mexico using a multisectoral planning model, covering the period from 2015 to 2035 and using data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in high-skilled labor and accelerating educational attainment to address labor surpluses and reduce unemployment rates, particularly in the long term.

Field: Consumption (economics); Political science; Production (economics); Social planning; Distribution (economics); Economic growth; Malnutrition; Social organization
Title: 6. Nutrition and social planning
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that improving the life of vulnerable sectors of the community is crucial to addressing nutritional deficiencies and promoting overall well-being. Specifically, the prevalence of protein-calorie malnutrition among children under five was found to be high, with 43% of children experiencing stunting and 16% experiencing wasting.
What_was_studied: The study examined nutrition and nutrition planning in West Budama county, Eastern Uganda, focusing on protein-calorie malnutrition among children under five over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address nutritional deficiencies and improve the life of vulnerable sectors of the community, policymakers should prioritize investments in nutrition planning that take into account the specific needs and characteristics of West Budama county. This includes considering factors such as food insecurity, gender and poverty, and intersectional poverty when developing policies to address malnutrition.

Authors: Shubhashis Gangopadhyay; Robert Lensink; Bhupesh Yadav
Field: Public economics; Economics; Randomized controlled trial; Transfer (computing); Cash; Cash transfers; In kind; Beneficial effects; Development economics; Food security; Intervention (law)
Title: Cash or In-kind Transfers? Evidence from a Randomised Controlled Trial in Delhi, India
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that unconditional cash transfers have no negative impact on food security and allow households to diversify their diets with non-cereal products.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effects of unconditional cash transfers on food security in Delhi, India, during a six-month period among 1,400 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these results, policymakers should consider scaling up unconditional cash transfer programs as a more effective approach to improving food security than traditional food security interventions.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Harmonization; Economic system; International development; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Le Modèle de développement intégré: vers une harmonisation des orientations stratégiques de l'aide au développement
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the IDM's emphasis on strategic selectivity in development practices can lead to a harmonization of practices that may not always prioritize reducing poverty, particularly for marginalized groups such as women.
What_was_studied: The Integrated Development Model (IDM) of the International Financial Institutions and its impact on gender and poverty in the context of sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize gender-sensitive and inclusive development strategies to ensure that sustainable development initiatives effectively address poverty reduction for all populations, including women.

Field: Treatment and control groups; Imitation; Government; Psychology; Cost effectiveness; Economic growth; Literacy; Malnutrition; Spillover effect; Social learning; Environmental health
Title: Learning and Behavioural Spillovers of Nutritional Information
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Results from a difference-in-differences analysis show that nutritional knowledge increases among neighboring untreated mothers relative to a control group, and they exhibit learning spillovers, changes in dietary behavior, and reduced food expenditure regardless of their level of literacy.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the effect of recipe books on reducing malnutrition in children aged three to six years in government day-care centers in urban slums in Chandigarh, India, during a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive spillover effects of recipe books on reducing malnutrition among children, policymakers should prioritize scaling up this intervention to more urban slums in India, particularly targeting mothers with low literacy levels.

Authors: Cristiana Simāo Seixas; Brian Davy; Wardie Leppan
Field: Political science; Management; Community-based conservation; Community action; Poverty reduction; Biodiversity conservation; Economic growth; Community organization; Community building; Community development; General partnership
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Community-Based Conservation and Development: Lessons Learned from the 2004 Equator Prize
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Successful initiatives had factors such as motivation and commitment of individuals concerned, participation, partnership, and cooperation, funding, and capacity-building in organization and management.
What_was_studied: Common features of successful community-based conservation and development initiatives among 24 finalists of the 2004 Equator Prize program were analyzed, focusing on community organization and cross-scale institutional linkages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize community-based conservation and development initiatives that promote gender equality and sustainable development by investing in capacity-building, funding, and cross-scale institutional linkages.

Authors: Stein T. Holden; Klaus Deininger; Hosaena Ghebru
Field: Land tenure; Labour economics; Economics; Allocative efficiency; Land reform; Land registration; Landlord; Certification; Land use; Agricultural economics; Renting
Title: Tenure Insecurity, Gender, Low-cost Land Certification and Land Rental Market Participation in Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Land certification initially enhanced land rental market participation, especially among female-headed households.
What_was_studied: The low-cost approach to land registration and certification of restricted property rights implemented in Ethiopia in the late 1990s and its effects on the allocative efficiency of the land rental market.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize land reforms to improve market development and poverty reduction in Africa, targeting female-headed households to enhance their participation in the land rental market.

Authors: Laurie Parsons; Sabina Lawreniuk; John Pilgrim
Field: Pragmatism; Economics; Poverty; Social change; Power (social and political); Flexibility (personality); Systematic process; Development economics; Phenomenon; Systems theory
Title: Wheels within Wheels: Poverty, Power and Patronage in the Cambodian Migration System
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Cambodian migration is an adaptable but highly patterned process rapidly reordering the Kingdom’s cities and villages alike, with evidence concerning how these structures constitute a vessel of social change from urban to rural areas.
What_was_studied: This article presents evidence for an adjusted and refocused systems theory of labour migration in Cambodia, specifically examining how migration may be understood as a multi-scalar phenomenon characterised by pragmatism and flexibility, with traditional rural norms undergirding the systematic process of labour movement, and constituting a vessel of social change shaping both urban and rural areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for rural development programs that target the undergirding role of traditional rural norms in shaping and mediating the systematic process of labour movement, in order to scale up and expand the positive impact of labour migration on social change in Cambodia.

Field: Demography; Psychology; Position (finance); Test (assessment); Daughter; Population; Demographic surveys; Nutrition Indexes; Socioeconomics; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: Parental Preferences for Nutrition of Boys and Girls: Evidence From Africa
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that mother's schooling has a larger impact on daughter's than son's nutrition, and father's education favors son's nutrition. Specifically, the study found that an additional year of mother's education increases the likelihood of a girl being well nourished by 14%, while the same increase for a boy is only 6%.
What_was_studied: This article models the determinants of pre-school age malnutrition in Africa using the Demographic Health Surveys, specifically examining the differences in the impact of mother's and father's education on the nutrition of boys and girls between 2010 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in girls' education can have a stronger impact on reducing child malnutrition, particularly in Africa. Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize programs and policies that improve girls' access to education, such as scaling up school construction and teacher training in rural areas.

Field: Currency; Economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); International economics; Tourism; Earnings; Developing country
Title: International tourism and export instability
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Although tourism has high growth rates and is a significant source of foreign currency receipts, it did not lead to a substantial decrease in the instability of export earnings for most developing and industrialized countries studied. In fact, some countries experienced an increase in earnings instability due to tourism.
What_was_studied: The research examined the contribution of international tourism to the economies of low-income countries and assessed whether diversification into this sector can stabilize export earnings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that tourism has limited potential to stabilize export earnings, policymakers should prioritize diversification into other sectors to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development in these economies.

Field: Business; Accommodation; Tourism; Poverty; Service (business); Academic community; Pro poor; Livelihood; Economic growth; Hospitality industry
Keywords: Pro-poor Development; Accommodation Facilities; Tourism; Employment; Poverty Alleviation
Title: PRO-POOR TOURISM POTENTIALS OF GHANA: The Contribution of Accommodation Facilities to Poverty Alleviation in the Wa Municipality
primary_category: Child poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that all 15 hotels surveyed were locally owned, provided employment to a diverse workforce, sourced products locally, and helped guests discover regional attractions. The finding suggests that promoting local service production can aid poverty reduction and improve livelihoods in the area.
What_was_studied: This study examined the contribution of accommodation facilities to tourism development in Ghana's Wa Municipality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the study's findings, policymakers should prioritize supporting local accommodation facilities to continue 'charting' a path of 'local service production,' thereby contributing to poverty alleviation and enhancing livelihoods in Ghana's Wa Municipality.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Complementarity (molecular biology); Child labour; Unemployment; Production (economics)
Title: Evidence on substitutability of adult and child labour
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Adult males appear to be complementary with, while adult females are substitutes for child labor, though the employment effects of banning child labor are inconclusive.
What_was_studied: Employment in Egypt's economy between 2000 and 2010 using a flexible form production function fitted to data on Egypt's economy, with an analysis of the substitutability of child and adult labor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that adult females are substitutes for child labor, policymakers should prioritize programs that support adult female employment and income generation to offset potential negative effects of banning child labor.

Authors: Christopher Cramer; Deborah Johnston; Bernd Mueller; Carlos Oya; John Sender
Field: Welfare; Agriculture; Payment; Labour economics; Relevance (law); Economics; Qualitative research; Statistical analysis; Poverty reduction; Rural people; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Fairtrade and Labour Markets in Ethiopia and Uganda
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Fairtrade does not effectively improve the welfare of the poorest rural people, with participants receiving relatively poor pay and non-pay working conditions in research sites dominated by Fairtrade producer organizations.
What_was_studied: Four years of fieldwork in Ethiopia and Uganda investigating the impact of Fairtrade on rural labor markets and poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize alternative strategies to address income poverty and improve labor market outcomes for rural communities, rather than relying solely on Fairtrade.

Authors: Ayush Agrawal; Chitwan Lalji; Debayan Pakrashi
Field: Human development (humanity); Socioeconomics; Hinduism; History
Title: He Has Gone to a Better Place, but She Has Not: Health Status of Hindu Widows in India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the health gap between the richest and the poorest households in India has increased over time, with a 10% difference in self-reported health outcomes between the two groups in 2011-2012, up from a 4% difference in 2004-2005.
What_was_studied: The study uses individual and household-level data from two rounds of the India Human Development Survey (IHDS) to estimate the health gap between different socioeconomic groups in India over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant increase in health disparities over time, policymakers should prioritize addressing asset poverty and sustainable development to reduce health inequalities in India.

Field: Human Development Index; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Mortality rate; Pandemic; Public health; Per capita; Per capita income; Index (typography); Human development (humanity); Global health; Population; Demography; Development economics; Environmental health; Geography; Economic growth; Medicine; Economics; Disease; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Nursing; Pathology; Sociology; World Wide Web; Computer science
Keywords: Aging Population; COVID-19 Mortality Rate; Full Vaccination Rate; HDI
Title: Effects of the Human Development Index on COVID-19 Mortality Rates in High-Income Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The outcomes demonstrate a strong negative correlation between COVID-19 mortality rate and HDI, with a significant (p = 0.013) negative association after controlling for health heterogeneities including aging population, full vaccination rate, GDP per capita, UHC, out-of-pocket burden, and stringency index.
What_was_studied: 41 high-income countries across the world were analyzed based on updated data until April 1, 2022, to explore the correlations and associations between COVID-19 mortality rate and human development index (HDI).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Improving human development capacity should be a vital priority for all countries to better protect global public health, as reductions in the COVID-19 mortality rate depend to a great extent on enhancing human development capacity.

Field: Field (mathematics); Entertainment; Political science; Sociology; Economic growth; Development economics; Economics; Mathematics; Pure mathematics; Law
Title: Entertainment-Education for Better Health: Insights from a Field Experiment in India
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that health entertainment-education successfully increased health knowledge by 16 percent, with these gains persisting almost one year later. However, there were no observed impacts on health behaviors. Additionally, financial incentives did not appear to have any effects.
What_was_studied: This paper used a field experiment in India to study the efficacy of health entertainment-education, particularly through films that show role models and draw on emotions, in increasing health knowledge and behavior among low-income individuals over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of entertainment-education, particularly through films that show role models and draw on emotions, as a potent delivery channel for health education campaigns in low-income settings. By doing so, they can increase health knowledge among low-income individuals, which may lead to lasting, positive change in health outcomes.

Field: Technological change; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Substitution effect; Production (economics); Methods of production; Industrialisation; Comparative advantage
Title: Employment effects of output and technological progress in Malaysian manufacturing
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that domestic demand and export expansion have almost equal influence on industrial employment, with any negative impact on employment due to a shortfall in exports being neutralized by appropriate policy choices. However, the substitution effect of using technology- and capital-intensive production led to a displacement of labor, which was largely compensated for by an increase in labor utilization.
What_was_studied: The growth in industrial employment in Malaysia from 1980 to 2005 and the effects of withdrawal of GSP privileges and technological advancements on labor-intensive industries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize export expansion and domestic demand to maintain employment growth in labor-intensive industries, while also implementing appropriate policies to mitigate the negative impact of technological advancements on labor displacement. This could include funding training programs for workers to adapt to new technologies and scale up support for small and medium-sized enterprises to increase their competitiveness in domestic and export markets.

Field: Economic policy; Labour economics; Economics; Market failure; Productivity; Unemployment; Competition (economics); Economies of scale; Foreign direct investment; Tertiary sector of the economy; Capital (economics)
Title: Labour and Its Discontents: The Consequences of Orthodox Reform in Venezuela and Mexico
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Untheorized increases in precarious informal work, unemployment, and emigration as well as a growing breach between wages and productivity followed trade, capital, and labor market reforms and the prescribed macro stabilization policies.
What_was_studied: The negative impacts of orthodox liberalization policies on labor in Venezuela and Mexico were representative of outcomes elsewhere in Latin America from 1990 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise orthodox liberalization policies to address the growing informal work and productivity gap, prioritizing job creation and fair wages to reduce poverty and inequality in Latin America.

Field: Land tenure; Political science; Poverty; Social change; Land reform; Opposition (politics); Armed conflict; Inequality; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The peace of the oligarchs: land distribution and the Guatemalan peace process
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that few substantial changes have resulted from the land reform agreements, and the majority of agreements remain stalled, with a lack of political will and limited institutional capacity as the main reasons for non-realization.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the events and parties responsible for the non-realization of land reform in Guatemala since the 1996 UN-brokered peace agreements, using a mixed-methods approach with a case study design, focusing on the time period between 2000 and 2018, and drawing on qualitative data from key informant interviews and quantitative data from household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to scale up efforts to strengthen institutions and prioritize land reform policies to address poverty and inequality in Guatemala. The government should allocate more resources and funding towards land reform initiatives, and prioritize their implementation to ensure sustainable development and reduce urban poverty.

Field: Business; Work (electrical); Poverty; China; Production (economics); Project organization; Institutional support; Economic growth; Informal sector; Community development
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Women and Informal Work in China: Reflections on Two Poverty Alleviation Pilot Projects
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that unequal levels of institutional support by agencies and local governments lead to different outcomes for women's participation in poverty alleviation projects, with more support leading to greater recognition of women's contributions to community development.
What_was_studied: Using a comparative case study approach, this paper investigates the experiences of women in two poverty alleviation pilot projects in rural China and identifies the institutional support that is essential to women's participation in these projects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the benefits of these projects, policymakers should prioritize providing equal institutional support to all agencies and local governments involved in implementing poverty alleviation policies, recognizing the critical role that women play in community development, particularly through their work in the informal sector.

Authors: Marilyn Porter Retired; Rose George Mbezi
Field: Economics; Poverty; Tanzania; Gender relations; Transmission (mechanics); Economic growth; Fishery; Fishing
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: From Hand to Mouth: Fishery Projects, Women, Men and Household Poverty
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that improved fishing incomes for men do not automatically benefit their families due to complex household patterns such as polygamous and serial marriages and women-headed households, which disrupt the transmission of resources from the fishery to the household.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of fisheries knowledge and practices on poverty alleviation in two Tanzanian fishing communities over a one-year period, using data from household surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of household relations in determining how resources are transmitted, policy interventions should prioritize a careful analysis of social, and especially gender, relations in the household when addressing poverty alleviation through fisheries development.

Authors: Linus Ugwu Odo; Dennis S. Aidolekhai
Field: Data collection; Sociology; Perspective (graphical); Power (social and political); Power structure; Face (sociological concept); Pride; Population; Process (engineering); Economic growth
Keywords: Community; development; gender; integrate; population; power
Title: Community Power Structure: The Gender Perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women's potential contributions to societal development are often neglected due to archaic traditions about their status in society, resulting in wasted potential for national development.
What_was_studied: The study examined the perceived or real marginalization of women in Nigeria's development process and how it hinders societal progress.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Accordingly, decision-makers should prioritize and fund initiatives that empower women to contribute meaningfully to Nigeria's progress, such as education and economic programs targeting women.

Field: Debt; Economics; Balance of trade; Unemployment; Production (economics); Domestic sector; Debt repayment; Sri lanka; Monetary economics
Title: Trade, taxes and debt repayment in Sri Lanka
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: A 10% tax on the import sector generated the largest net savings on trade balance, but also caused a decline in economic growth by 3%, and the burden fell heavily on the domestic sector.
What_was_studied: The research estimated the cost of taxing the export, import or domestic sectors of Sri Lanka to reduce the national debt using a simple GNP model and simulated the effects of taxing for debt servicing over the period 1977–87.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce the national debt, policymakers should prioritize taxing the import sector while considering the potential impacts on economic growth and domestic production.

Field: Development studies; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Representation (politics); Context (language use); Family life; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Politics
Title: GENDER, VULNERABILITY AND THE POLITICS OF DECISION-MAKING IN GHANA: THE CASE OF THE UPPER EAST REGION
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women in the Upper East Region are more vulnerable than men, with women experiencing all thirteen characteristics of vulnerability identified by the GPRS, including extreme poverty and exclusion from decision-making processes at the household, community, and district/regional levels. Additionally, the study discovered that women have greater care responsibilities than men, which further contributes to their vulnerability.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the gender implications of vulnerability in relation to decision-making processes in Ghana's Upper East Region between 2004 and 2006, using data from the Ghana Poverty Reduction Strategy (GPRS) and examining the characteristics of vulnerable individuals as defined by the GPRS.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize gender-sensitive policies and programs aimed at reducing chronic poverty and climate vulnerability in the Upper East Region, specifically targeting women's empowerment and participation in decision-making processes to ensure their needs and perspectives are taken into account.

Field: Emigration; Health care; Economics; Poverty; Environmental degradation; Country level; Affect (psychology); Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Effects of Poverty, Environmental Degradation, and Gender Conditions on South—to—North Migration
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found a non-linear relationship between income and emigration rates at the source country level, with several other variables such as economic growth, education level, and access to health care helping to explain migration rates. Additionally, evidence emerged that gender conditions and environmental degradation may be associated with South-to-North migration rates.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the evidence on how poverty, environmental degradation, and gender conditions affect migration, and then tests some of the hypotheses that emerge using emigration rates from low- and middle-income countries to wealthier industrial countries over the time period of 1980 to 2015 with data collected through surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize investments in education and economic growth, as well as addressing gender and environmental issues, to reduce emigration rates from low- and middle-income countries to wealthier industrial countries.

Authors: Javier E. Baez; Leonardo Lucchetti; Maria Eugenia Genoni; Mateo Salazar
Field: Storm; Consumption (economics); Natural disaster; Poverty; Geography; Agatha; Tropical cyclone; Climatology
Keywords: JEL Classification: I3; J2; O1 economic development; natural disasters; consumption; poverty; human capital
Title: Gone with the Storm
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals substantial negative effects, particularly among urban households. Per capita consumption fell by 12.6%, raising poverty by 5.5 percentage points (an increase of 18%).
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the causal consequences of Tropical Storm Agatha (2010) on household welfare among urban households in Guatemala during the period of June 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs and expand their coverage to vulnerable populations to mitigate the impacts of natural disasters on household welfare, particularly in urban areas.

Field: Technological change; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Employment growth; Manufacturing employment; Decomposition analysis; Social issues
Title: Trade, Technology and Employment in South Africa
primary_category: Digital divide; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that trade and technological change had a negative impact on employment in South Africa, but these factors only partially explain the low rate of employment growth.
What_was_studied: The paper considers the impact of trade and technological change on both the level and skill composition of manufacturing employment in South Africa from the early 1990s to date, using a Chenery-type decomposition analysis of employment change and labour demand functions estimated econometrically.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize initiatives to support the development of skills that are resistant to technological change and promote the adoption of digital technologies to improve productivity in the manufacturing sector, in order to address the high levels of unemployment in South Africa.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Collective bargaining; Wage; Real wages; Unemployment; Trade union; Bargaining power; Informal sector; Efficiency wage
Title: Wage determination in Brazil: The growth of union bargaining power and informal employment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the reduction in state regulation of collective bargaining has led to the development of a system of wage determination characterized by rent sharing and insider trade union bargaining power, resulting in real wages that are increasingly inflexible with respect to movements in open unemployment.
What_was_studied: This article examines wage determination in Brazilian manufacturing during the 1980s and early 1990s, using data from a specific time period and population of workers to identify trends and patterns in wage setting and labor market conditions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that employment costs of successful counter-inflationary strategies may be severe, highlighting the need for policymakers to prioritize and expand social protection programs to mitigate the impact on vulnerable populations and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Decentralization; Political science; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Local government; National level; West africa; Economic growth; Politics
Keywords: Decentralization; Assemblywomen; Women's Empowerment; Local Government; Political Participation
Title: Women in Politics in Ghana: A Study on Local Government in the Greater Accra Region
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that low income and educational status, as well as lack of confidence due to the misconception that politics is for men, are significant barriers to women's participation in Ghanaian politics. The study also found that only 12% of assembly members in local government are women.
What_was_studied: Women's participation in politics in Ghana was studied using primary data collected through questionnaires and interviews during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To deepen women's political participation, there should be sensitization programs to change the misconception that politics is for men and economic empowerment of women through education and income support to enable them to compete favourably with their male counterparts in politics.

Authors: Gregory S. Amacher; William F. Hyde; Bharat R. Joshee
Field: Agriculture; Consumption (economics); Deforestation; Economics; Crop residue; Production (economics); Dependant; Household income; Energy source; Agricultural economics
Title: Joint production and consumption in traditional households: Fuelwood and crop residues in two districts in Nepal
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women play a larger role in collection in the district dependant on production from common forestlands, while men and agricultural capital are more important inputs in the district dependant on production from private lands. Additionally, demand elasticities for fuelwood, combustible agricultural residues, and improved stoves were measured by household income group, with all price and income demand elasticities less than one.
What_was_studied: This article measures household production of and demand for fuelwood and fuel substitutes in two districts in Nepal during 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to address deforestation in Nepal, policies should prioritize the empowerment of women and support for sustainable agricultural practices, as well as the adoption of improved stoves and alternative fuel sources for low-income households.

Field: Urban agglomeration; Productivity; Labour economics; Wage; Developing country; Demographic economics; Economics; Economies of agglomeration; Population; Economic growth; Economic geography; Demography; Sociology
Title: Urban Agglomerations and Wage and Self-employment Jobs in Ethiopia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals a negative association between town population size and the share of self-employment workers; specifically, a log increase in town population size lowers the probability of engaging in self-employment by 7.9 percentage points. Female, young, and less-educated workers are more likely to work with wage jobs in larger towns.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between urban agglomerations and employment modes in one of the least urbanized low-income countries, Ethiopia, using an instrumental variable approach and worker-level cross-sectional data from 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To promote economic development in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize urbanization and the transition from self-employment to wage jobs, particularly for female, young, and less-educated workers. This could involve investing in infrastructure and education, streamlining business regulations, and targeting job training programs.

Field: Rural area; Sociology; Built environment; Subsistence agriculture; Human settlement; Public debate; Natural resource; Economic growth; Permaculture; Sustainability
Title: Ethnographic insights on rural sustainability; homestead design and permaculture of Eastern Cape settlements in South Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article makes comparisons to some of the founding principles of permaculture theory and practice to suggest that current agricultural practices and homestead (umzi, plural imizi) settlement patterns follow closely to 'permaculture ideals' in theory and practice.
What_was_studied: This article considers the prevalence of sustained agricultural practices (particularly large scale gardens of the homestead) and questions current public debate that permaculture strategy is foreign to South Africa. The paper speaks on recent ethnographic work by the author in rural parts of the Eastern Cape, or the former Transkei.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: An argument is made that the rural Xhosa homestead has developed much more to the tune of achieving sustainability for its occupants, as many continue to build to accommodate subsistence agriculture. Natural resources of the area also continue to be utilized and collectively shared. Therefore, scaling up and expanding these homestead practices could help address income poverty in rural areas.

Field: Welfare; Decentralization; Consumption (economics); Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Household survey; Development economics
Keywords: decentralisation; welfare; local government; capacity; poverty alleviation
Title: How Important is the Capacity of Local Governments for Improvements in Welfare? Evidence from Decentralised Uganda
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds suggestive evidence that both household consumption and school enrolment are positively related with the level of capacity of district governments.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between decentralization and welfare by examining the role of local governments' capacity for household consumption and school enrolment in Uganda using household survey data covering a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in strengthening local governments' capacities to improve household consumption and school enrolment outcomes, particularly in areas with low capacity levels.

Field: Welfare; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Work (electrical); Anecdotal evidence; Ethiopian Orthodox; Rural ethiopia; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Development economics; Estimation
Title: Does Observance of Religious Holidays Affect Agricultural Productivity and Household Welfare? Evidence from Rural Ethiopia
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
