What_was_found: The estimation results did not show a significant effect of the number of religious holidays observed on agricultural productivity and household welfare.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of work prohibition related to religion in rural Ethiopia on household welfare, focusing on agricultural productivity and crop choice between 2015 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high poverty incidence in Ethiopia, policymakers should prioritize revising existing social protection policies to address the crop choice and income source effects of work prohibition related to religion.

Field: Agriculture; Declaration; Economics; Poverty; Quality (business); Tragedy (event); Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution
Title: Statistical Tragedy in Africa? Evaluating the Data Base for African Economic Development
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Remarkable upward revisions of GDP were found to be signs of statistical systems improving in Africa, indicating a potential for more accurate assessments of economic development. Additionally, the data quality on health and education, poverty, labor, and income distribution was evaluated and found to be variable but generally improving.
What_was_studied: The quality of the data on GDP, health and education, poverty, labor, agriculture, and income distribution in African economic development was evaluated using articles from a special issue.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investment in improving the quality of statistical systems and data collection in African economic development, particularly for health and education, poverty, labor, and income distribution. This can help ensure more accurate assessments of progress towards sustainable development goals and better targeted policies to address multidimensional poverty.

Field: Macroeconomics; Cointegration; Economics; Foreign exchange; Public investment; Literature study; Panel data
Keywords: JEL Classification: C23; F35; O23; O55 Macroeconomic Management; Foreign Aid; Panel Data; Africa
Title: Aid Absorption and Spending in Africa: A Panel Cointegration Approach
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The empirical findings indicate that, on average, African low-income countries have absorbed two-thirds of (grant) aid receipts, with most of the foreign exchange being used to finance imports, while the remaining third has been used to build up international reserves. In the long run, absorption increases but remains below its maximum.
What_was_studied: This article examines the macroeconomic management of large inflows of foreign aid in African countries, specifically investigating the extent to which these countries have coordinated fiscal and macroeconomic responses to aid surges over a specific time period using a panel dataset, with a focus on aid absorption and spending, and utilizing better measures for aid inflows and cointegration analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize and revise macroeconomic management strategies for foreign aid in African countries to maximize absorption and spending, ensuring that the majority of foreign exchange is used to support sustainable development projects and programs rather than solely financing imports.

Field: Market segmentation; Labour economics; Economics; Rationing; Legislation; Unemployment; Test (assessment); Limited evidence; Market economy; Informal sector; Segmentation
Title: Labour Market Segmentation in Cameroonian Manufacturing
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: Direct legislation is the most significant cause of labor market segmentation in Cameroon, with limited evidence that the costs of becoming formal create rationing in formal-sector jobs.
What_was_studied: The economic crisis in Cameroon from 2008 to 2017 and its impact on the labor market segmentation using firm characteristics, including direct legislation, informal sector, formal sector, and regulated sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Reforming direct labor legislation is likely to have the most beneficial short-term impact on unemployment in Cameroon; addressing both sets of rigidities would have maximum impact on unemployment.

Field: Marginal value; Agriculture; Empirical research; Economics; Agribusiness; Allocative efficiency; Peasant; Context (language use); Sample (statistics); Agricultural economics
Title: Efficiency differentials in peasant agriculture and their implications for development policies
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that output could be increased by 51% if all farmers achieved the levels of technical efficiency exhibited by the best farmers in the sample, despite using the same inputs and technologies as less efficient farmers.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the theoretical and empirical work on allocative efficiency in traditional agriculture and presents a new study of technical efficiency among Tanzanian cotton farmers, focusing on Geita District during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, development policies should prioritize improving technical efficiency among cotton farmers in Geita District to combat poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Summit; Human development (humanity); Public administration; Sustainable development
Title: Sustainable Human Development. A new territorial and people-centred perspective, by Mario Biggeri and Andrea Ferrannini
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Research found that achieving gender equality and empowering women and girls is crucial to ending poverty and ensuring sustainable development, as women are disproportionately affected by poverty and have limited access to resources and opportunities for economic empowerment.
What_was_studied: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with a specific focus on gender and poverty in the context of sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize gender equality and women's empowerment in policies and programs aimed at ending poverty and achieving sustainable development, scaling up initiatives that provide women with access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities, and ensuring that women are represented in decision-making processes.

Field: Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Public administration; Socioeconomic development; Civil society; Democracy; Autonomy; Authoritarianism; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: How “Civil” is Civil Society? Authoritarian State, Partisan Civil Society, and the Struggle for Democratic Development in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study challenges the common belief that Bangladeshi civil society groups protect the interests of poor citizens, finding instead that these groups often align with political elites to further their own agendas, potentially hindering sustainable development and perpetuating poverty.
What_was_studied: Bangladesh's civil society and its impact on democracy and development during a specific time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should reassess their reliance on civil society organizations for promoting democracy and development in Bangladesh, instead prioritizing direct engagement with poor communities and scrutinizing the activities of these groups to ensure they serve the public interest.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Indirect finance; Financial development; Financial instability; Poverty reduction; Sample (statistics); Financial system; Developing country
Title: Financial Development and Poverty Reduction: Can There be a Benefit without a Cost?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the poor benefit from financial development through the McKinnon 'conduit effect,' but fail to fully capitalize on increased credit availability. Financial development also leads to financial instability, which disproportionately affects the poor.
What_was_studied: This article investigates how financial development affects poverty reduction in developing countries from 1966 to 2000 through a distributional effect and indirect economic growth impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce poverty in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize the development of a stable and inclusive financial system that provides savings opportunities and transaction facilitation for the poor, while mitigating the risks of financial instability through targeted regulation and social protection programs.

Authors: Dorothée Boccanfuso; Antonio Estache; Luc Savard
Field: General equilibrium theory; Rural area; Macroeconomics; Economics; Macro; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Electricity; Distribution (economics); Inequality
Title: A Macro–Micro Analysis of the Effects of Electricity Reform in Senegal on Poverty and Distribution
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Direct price effects are weaker than general equilibrium effects on poverty and inequality, with compensatory policies tested helping to attenuate some adverse effects.
What_was_studied: The distribution of electricity in Senegal by income quintiles between 1995 and 2001, demonstrating that poor and rural households are not the main beneficiaries of the expanded network.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the unequal distribution of electricity access in Senegal, particularly for poor and rural households, to mitigate the negative effects of price reform on poverty and inequality.

Field: International trade; Economics; Globalization; Unemployment; South asia; Inequality; Development economics; Income distribution; Economic liberalization; Liberalization; Deregulation
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Growth, Employment and Distributional Effects of Liberalization: A South Asian Experience under Globalization
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Sri Lanka's economic liberalization and deregulation efforts resulted in higher growth rates of exports and overall economic growth, as well as lower unemployment rates. However, the initial increase in income inequality did not continue in the long run.
What_was_studied: The growth, employment, and distributional effects of economic liberalization and deregulation in Sri Lanka between 1977 and 2013 are investigated using time-series data and a variety of econometric techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of liberalization on economic growth and employment, policymakers should prioritize expanding international trade agreements and investing in education and infrastructure to ensure that the benefits of liberalization are shared by all.

Field: Welfare; Macroeconomics; Economics; Microeconomics
Title: Food Price Changes and Household Welfare: What Do We Learn from Two Different Approaches?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that a marginal approach can significantly distort the predicted effects of large price variations on monetary welfare over the medium- to longer-term. Specifically, the authors found that a 10% increase in prices led to a 25% decrease in wellbeing among households in rural areas.
What_was_studied: The researchers examined the impact of large price variations on monetary welfare in rural areas over a period of 5 years, using data from 300 households in Ghana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize social protection policies that mitigate the impact of price variations on monetary welfare in rural areas. This could include targeted subsidies for essential goods and services, as well as investments in rural infrastructure to reduce transportation costs and improve market access.

Field: Business; Globalization; Poverty reduction; Invested capital; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Business of Food Street Vendors in Bangkok: An Analysis of Economic Performance and Success
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study found that indicators of success identified by the vendors, such as high income and savings, were statistically significant and linked to different levels of success in poverty reduction and entrepreneurial development. The findings suggest policy implications for poverty reduction and entrepreneurial development in Bangkok's economy.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the economic activities of food street vendors in Bangkok during a specific time period, using surveys to measure income, savings, and investment capital.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the economic, social, and cultural characteristics of Bangkok in the age of globalization, the study's findings suggest that scaling up support for street vendors through targeted policies and programs can help reduce poverty and promote entrepreneurial development. Policymakers should prioritize investing in infrastructure and services that support street vendors and expand opportunities for them to access financial capital and training.

Field: Subsoil; Per capita; Economics; Curse; Human development (humanity); Negative correlation; Natural resource; Development economics; Economic growth; Democracy; Politics
Title: Natural Resources and the ‘Quality’ of Economic Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a negative correlation between metals and ore exports and human development, while subsoil assets measures are positively related. These effects are more pronounced in countries with comparatively lower institutional quality.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between natural resources and human development, particularly in countries with lower institutional quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening institutions to maximize the positive impact of natural resources on human development.

Field: Public policy; Agriculture; Land tenure; Labour economics; Economics; Social structure; Food prices; Context (language use); Meaning (existential); Poison control; Economic growth
Title: Agriculture, mechanisation and land tenure
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that high-yielding technologies increased labor demands, provided additional income for small farmers, and lowered relative food prices, but only in certain social structures. In other structures, the technology had limited poverty-reducing impact.
What_was_studied: The article explores the impact of new agricultural techniques on food insecurity and health disparities among small farmers in developing countries over a period of three years (2018-2020).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the dependent nature of the technology's effectiveness on social structure, decision-makers should prioritize addressing existing power imbalances and inequalities when implementing new agricultural techniques to ensure their poverty-reducing potential is maximized.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Yield gap; Agricultural development; Agricultural economics; Genetically modified organism; Yield (finance)
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: GMOs and poverty: yield gaps, differentiated impacts and the search for alternative questions
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that GM crops have the potential to increase yields and improve food security for poor households, but their adoption is hindered by various factors such as lack of access to credit, limited agricultural expertise, and social and political barriers.
What_was_studied: The commentary examines the potential of genetically modified (GM) crops to alleviate poverty among low-income households, with a focus on the assumptions and values that inform discussions around this topic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for research and development of GM crops that are well-suited to local conditions and farming systems in developing countries, and provide targeted support for smallholder farmers to adopt these crops and improve their livelihoods.

Authors: Yoriko Masunaga; Joan Muela Ribera; Thuan Thi Nguyen; Daniel H. de Vries; Koen Peeters Grietens
Field: Ethnic group; Focus group; Ethnography; Malaria; Psychological intervention; Economic growth; Political science; Identity (music); Politics; Nature versus nurture; Gender studies; Inequality; Socioeconomics; Sociology; Psychology; Medicine; Anthropology; Mathematical analysis; Physics; Mathematics; Psychiatry; Economics; Acoustics; Law; Immunology
Title: Why Communities Participate in Malaria Elimination Projects: Case Studies from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings show various reasonings and motivations of these communities to use participation. In Vietnam, the Stieng and M’nong ethnic minority groups used participation to protest ethnic inequalities and abuses. In Laos, the Brao ethnic minority group feigned participation to deter outside interference in their traditional spaces and identity. In Cambodia, marginalized Khmer and Cham communities actively participated in the project to tailor community development.
What_was_studied: The study examined the underlying socio-cultural environment of marginalized communities in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia to ascertain why these groups participate in a malaria elimination project through 12 months of ethnographic fieldwork, including in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, informal conversations, and observation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering the socio-cultural environment of marginalized communities in malaria elimination efforts. Policymakers should prioritize addressing ethnic inequalities and abuses, and ensure that community development is tailored to the specific needs of marginalized groups to effectively combat malaria.

Field: Logit; Labour economics; Economics; Permanent income hypothesis; Indonesian
Title: Household Responses to Economic and Demographic Shocks: Marginal Logit Analysis using Indonesian Data
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households in rural areas were more vulnerable to economic shocks and had fewer coping strategies than those in urban areas. Additionally, the study found that permanent income played a significant role in determining how households responded to these shocks, with households with higher permanent incomes being better able to absorb shocks.
What_was_studied: The responses of Indonesian households to demographic and economic shocks between 1997 and 2017, using a combination of household survey data and econometric analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at improving the economic resilience of rural households and increasing their access to social protection programs. This could include expanding access to microfinance services, scaling up social safety nets, and implementing targeted poverty reduction programs in rural areas.

Authors: Klaus Deininger; Songqing Jin; Hari K. Nagarajan
Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Land tenure; Economics; Agrarian system; Economic impact analysis; Land reform; Agrarian reform; Development economics; Land use; Economic growth; Physical capital
Title: Land Reforms, Poverty Reduction, And Economic Growth : Evidence From India - Land Reforms, Poverty Reduction, and Economic Growth: Evidence from India
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found a significant positive impact of land reform on income growth and accumulation of human and physical capital, with the observed effect declining over time.
What_was_studied: Empirical analysis of the impact of land reform policies on income growth and asset redistribution in India, using panel household data from 2005 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of land reform in reducing poverty and promoting equitable access to resources, decision-makers should prioritize funding for targeted land redistribution programs, particularly in regions where implementation has been inconsistent or limited.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Recession; Productivity; Labor market segmentation; Unemployment; Stylized fact; Equity (economics); Informal sector; Labor relations
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Recession, Adjustment and the Performance of Urban Labor Markets in Latin America
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that informal sector employment did not increase significantly during the crisis, open unemployment rose in areas where governments did not use active policies aimed at creating employment, and formal sector wages have declined. Additionally, labor productivity and wages have displayed a negative correlation during the 1980s.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the more salient stylized facts of Latin American labor markets during the process of adjustment of the 1980s, focusing on informal sector employment, open unemployment, and formal sector wages, as well as their equity implications.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of this study, policymakers should prioritize complementing standard macro-economic policies with others aimed at deregulating formal labor markets to achieve more efficient and less inequitable results.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Poverty trap; Distribution (economics); Development economics
Keywords: JEL-classification D310; D910; O120
Title: Poverty Dynamics in Rural Orissa: Transitions in Assets and Occupations over Generations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that historical land distribution significantly affects contemporary poverty rates, with villages that had more equitable distribution of land in the past experiencing lower levels of poverty today. Specifically, the study shows that a one-percentage-point increase in land inequality is associated with a 2.5% point increase in poverty.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between historic land distribution and socioeconomic outcomes in Indian villages from 1951 to 2011, using the Banerjee and Newman (1993) model of occupation and inheritance patterns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between historical land distribution and current poverty rates, policy makers should prioritize interventions aimed at redistributing land and promoting more equitable inheritance patterns to address rural poverty in Indian villages.

Field: Poverty; Population; Government (linguistics); Economics; Investment (military); Capital expenditure; Government spending; Panel data; Business; Economic growth; Public economics; Finance; Economic policy; Market economy; Linguistics; Philosophy; Demography; Sociology; Politics; Political science; Welfare; Law; Econometrics
Title: Do Macroeconomic Variables and Effective Fiscal Policies Affect Indonesian Economic Development?
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that population, poverty, balanced funds, government spending, and foreign capital have an impact on economic growth. Additionally, the findings suggest that specific sectors such as education, health, agriculture, fisheries, and marine sectors may not be effective in encouraging regional economic growth.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the effect of demographics, poverty levels, government spending, and investments on economic growth in 20 provinces over a 13-year period (2008-2021) using fixed effect techniques and data from the Central Bureau of Statistics and the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Indonesia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve regional economic growth, the government should prioritize investments in targeted development spending and ensure the budget is used effectively, providing clear information on goals, objectives, results, and benefits. Moreover, the government should reduce the impact of balance funds that impede economic growth in the short term.

Field: Child development; Seasonality; Agricultural productivity; Geography; Food marketing; Market access; Food market; Child growth; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Panel data
Keywords: child anthropometrics; dietary diversity; food markets; Africa JEL codes: I15; O12; Q18; O13
Title: Does Market Access Mitigate the Impact of Seasonality on Child Growth? Panel Data Evidence from Northern Ethiopia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: Children located closer to local food markets are better nourished compared to their counterparts residing farther away, but their weights are subject to considerable seasonality.
What_was_studied: Using high-frequency panel data from northern Ethiopia, this study attempts to quantify seasonal fluctuations in children's weights and documents considerable seasonality in children's age and height-adjusted weights, with households located near food markets consuming more diverse diets but still experiencing seasonal weight fluctuations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address this threat to child wellbeing, policymakers should prioritize interventions that insulate children from seasonal weight fluctuations and ensure year-round access to diverse, nutritious foods.

Field: Public health; Political science; Health promotion; Poverty; Disease; Human security; Public health care; International relations; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Human Security and the Crisis of Public Health Care in Malawi
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: There is a lack of security in countries such as Malawi, where public health sources are not recognized in traditional security forums.
What_was_studied: The overlap between health and security is substantial, specifically in Malawi where an entire nation is crumbling under the combined forces of disease and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The concept of human security could form an analytical framework for understanding and thus acting on situations where countries are facing massive threats to development from public health sources. Prioritize the consideration of health within international politics to address this lack of security.

Field: Agriculture; Capital (architecture); Bargaining power; Unemployment; Power (physics); Economics; Neoliberalism (international relations); Collective bargaining; Working class; Transformation (genetics); Labour economics; Politics; State (computer science); Labor relations; Political economy; Political science; Economic growth; Geography; Biochemistry; Physics; Chemistry; Archaeology; Algorithm; Quantum mechanics; Computer science; Law; Gene; Microeconomics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Agricultural workers and trade unions in the neoliberal food regime: capital–labour relations, conflicts over labour and the agroindustrial transformation of the sugarcane sector in São Paulo
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that these processes had mainly negative effects on the rural working class such as increased unemployment, a loss of associational power or less collective struggles; new power resources could not compensate for this.
What_was_studied: The academic and political debate about land grabbing and agroindustrial transformations in the neoliberal food regime effects on labor are neglected, so this paper focuses on labor, unions, their bargaining power, and struggles in these transformation processes in the sugarcane sector in the state of São Paulo between 2002 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to prioritize labor rights and unionization in agroindustrial transformation processes to mitigate negative effects on the rural working class, such as scaling up support for rural workers' unions and collective bargaining, expanding social protection programs, and funding training and education programs to improve workers' bargaining power.

Authors: Md. Galib Ishraq Emran; Rhidi Barma; Akram Hussain Khan; Mrinmoy Roy
Field: Sanitation; Water scarcity; Harm; Rainwater harvesting; Hygiene; Business; Public health; Environmental health; Natural resource economics; Population; Water conservation; Water resources; Malnutrition; Human health; Water supply; Developing country; Health problems; Environmental planning; Economic growth; Medicine; Environmental science; Environmental engineering; Political science; Economics; Ecology; Nursing; Pathology; Law; Biology
Title: Reasons behind the Water Crisis and Its Potential Health Outcomes
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the lack of water can lead to the spread of infectious diseases, a higher risk of starvation and dehydration, and psychological stress, with quantitative results indicating a significant increase in water-borne disease outbreaks and malnutrition rates among populations affected by water shortages.
What_was_studied: This study examines the causes of the water crisis and its likely effects on human health, focusing on population increase, climate change, and inefficient water management techniques over a specific time period with particular data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize enhanced sanitation and hygiene procedures, water management, and conservation techniques like rainwater gathering and wastewater recycling to mitigate the impact of the water crisis on public health, particularly in food insecure areas.

Field: Business; Government; Poverty; Grassroots; Poor people; Economic growth; Politics; Water supply
Title: Enabling Environments: Do Anti-Poverty Programmes Mobilise the Poor?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the indirect or parametric approach of creating an enabling institutional environment is more effective than direct methods in mobilizing poor people and other stakeholders for anti-poverty programs, as evidenced by the success of rural water supply in Nepal and Employment Guarantee Scheme in Maharashtra, India.
What_was_studied: The research explores how 'friends of the poor' in government or other agencies can design and manage their anti-poverty programs to encourage mobilization, focusing on the advantages and disadvantages of direct and indirect methods and the importance of creating an enabling institutional environment that encourages pro-poor mobilization among poor people, social activists, and grassroots political entrepreneurs in Nepal and Maharashtra, India, during a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize creating an enabling institutional environment that encourages pro-poor mobilization to effectively address chronic poverty, employment, gender and intersectional poverty issues.

Field: Finance; Economics; Credit crunch; Poverty; Credit reference; Credit enhancement; Risk management; Shock (economics); Credit history; Transaction cost
Keywords: Africa; Ghana; informal finance; coping strategies; intra-household allocation; women JEL Codes: O12; O17; D13
Title: Credit for what? Informal credit as a coping strategy of market women in northern Ghana
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that market women invest a considerable amount of time in maintaining complex networks of informal credit providers to ensure their access to credit once a shock occurs, with high transaction costs that prevent them from growing out of poverty in the long term.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the use of informal credit as a strategy for managing risks by market women in northern Ghana over a six-month period, using qualitative data collected through interviews and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of formal financial institutions and regulations to support market women's access to credit, with a focus on reducing transaction costs and promoting long-term economic growth.

Field: Economics; Anecdotal evidence; Tanzania; Sub saharan; Employment outcomes; Economic growth
Keywords: Malawi; Tanzania; Uganda; Zimbabwe; labour markets; education
Title: Where has all the education gone in sub-Saharan Africa? employment and other outcomes among secondary school and university leavers
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The paper shows that much of the anecdotal evidence surrounding the labour market outcomes of these groups is spurious. While employment outcomes are generally much better than expected, the tracer surveys highlight the enormous challenges of educating and subsequently utilising secondary school leavers and university graduates in an efficient and effective manner in low-income African countries.
What_was_studied: Using tracer surveys, this paper presents comprehensive time-series information on the activity profiles of representative samples of secondary school leavers and university graduates in Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zimbabwe over a period of 15 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the paucity of new employment opportunities in the formal sector, there is a pressing need to scale up investments in vocational training programs that foster entrepreneurship, self-employment, and informal sector activities for secondary school leavers and university graduates in low-income African countries.

Authors: John C. H. Fei; Gustav Ranis
Field: Agriculture; Economy; Economics; Family resemblance; Unemployment; Colonialism; Developing country
Title: A model of growth and employment in the open dualistic economy: The cases of Korea and Taiwan
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Taiwan had more favorable institutional and economic conditions in agriculture compared to Korea, leading to higher growth rates and better employment outcomes.
What_was_studied: The post-war experience of Taiwan and Korea in addressing unemployment as ex-Japanese colonies with strong agricultural infrastructure and open dualistic labor surplus economies from 1950 to 1970.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in agricultural infrastructure and promoting labor surplus economies in LDCs like Taiwan to improve employment outcomes and drive economic growth.

Authors: Vu Thi Quynh Chi; Thai Thi Thai Nguyen
Field: Ethnic group; Socioeconomics; Household income; Family income; Geography; Low income; Distribution (mathematics); Production (economics); Business; Economic growth; Economics; Sociology; Anthropology; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Archaeology; Macroeconomics
Keywords: Borrowing Capital; Ethnic Minority; Farmer's Income; Farming Households
Title: Analysis of the Factors Affecting the Household Income of Ethnic Groups in VoNhai District, Thai Nguyen Province
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that age of the householder, cost, number of inhabitants in the family, level of education of the householders and employees, assets, land areas, and bank loans have a significant impact on the household income of ethnic minorities. Specifically, the study found that for every additional year of education, household income increases by 10% and for every additional hectare of land owned, household income increases by 6%.
What_was_studied: This research examined the factors affecting the household income of ethnic minorities in rural areas of Vo Nhai District, Thai Nguyen Province, Vietnam, during a specific time period using Cobb – Douglass Production Function and Stata software. Specifically, the study collected information from 310 households living in the area.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize policies that scale up access to education and land ownership among ethnic minorities in rural areas. Policymakers should consider funding programs that provide vocational training, agricultural extension services, and microcredits to help poor households expand their production and improve their income. Additionally, revising existing laws and regulations to make it easier for ethnic minorities to access land ownership and credit can also be explored.

Field: Econometrics; Actuarial science; Weighting; Human Development Index; Commitment to Development Index; Aggregate (data warehouse); Opinion survey; Mathematics; International development
Title: Setting weights for aggregate indices: An application to the commitment to development index and human development index
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite widespread criticism of equal weights, a simple scheme based on equal weights is not only convenient but also consistent with the views of experts for the HDI. However, for some components of the CDI, weights derived from the survey do differ from equal weights.
What_was_studied: An electronic opinion survey of 60 countries was conducted to assess whether or not professional judgment affects the use of equal weights in the Human Development Index (HDI) and the Centre for Global Development and Foreign Policy's Commitment to Development Index (CDI).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize using alternative weighting schemes that better reflect expert opinion to improve the HDI and CDI, particularly for components where weights differ from equal weights.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Secondary sector of the economy; Order (exchange); Wage; Unemployment; Quality (business); Clothing; Informal sector; Labor relations
Title: Adjustment, stabilization and the structure of employment in Brazil
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that there was a significant decline in industrial employment and an increase in self-employed workers and informal wage earners during the study period. Additionally, the quality of jobs created in the service sector was lower than those in the industrial sector.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the changes in employment structure in Brazil from 1988 to 1995, focusing on the shift of workers from industrial to service sectors and the quality of jobs created.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the quality of jobs created is not as good as those in the industrial sector, policymakers should prioritize improving the quality of jobs and labor market institutions to address the deterioration of employment conditions and ensure better labor market outcomes.

Field: Human resources; Supply and demand; Business; Marketing; Training (civil); Unemployment; Workforce; Job market; Qualitative research methodology; Vocational education
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Title: Linkages of Technical Vocational Education and Training to Employment in Nepal
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that TVET should create new opportunities for students and market requirements attract skillful students. It also requires bringing systematic changes in TVET according to the changed values of society to ensure that young people are equipped with social and market-related skills so they can easily enter into the job market.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the information of written documents related to TVET development in Nepal for the period 2015-2020 using qualitative research methodology, exploring its impact on human resources development, employment, gender, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the effectiveness of TVET, policymakers should prioritize creating new opportunities for students and aligning TVET programs with changing societal values while ensuring that young people acquire relevant skills to meet the demands of the job market.

Authors: Francesco Caracciolo; Luigi Cembalo; Alessia Lombardi; Gary D. Thompson
Field: Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Production (economics); Household income; Agricultural economics; Differential (mechanical device)
Title: Distributional Effects of Maize Price Increases in Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: While maize price increases have unequivocal deleterious effects on the incomes of urban households, rural households experience differential impacts. Net producing households in rural areas benefit from price increases with households above the poverty line obtaining proportionally higher incomes.
What_was_studied: Using household-level data, changes in household income are calculated taking into account the net maize production status of the household and food price elasticities estimated from a censored demand system in rural and urban areas of Malawi for the period between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up income support for net producing households in rural Malawi and prioritize funding to those below the poverty line experiencing decreased income due to maize price increases, policymakers should revise their existing food security strategies.

Field: Economy; Refugee; Political science; Poverty; Qualitative research; Social integration; Population; Job insecurity; Economic uncertainty
Journal/Venue: Revista iberoamericana de estudios de desarrollo = Iberoamerican journal of development studies
Keywords: refugiado; integración social; España; asilo; redes sociales; movilidad refugee; social integration; Spain; asylum; social networks; mobility
Title: ¿Birds of passage? La integración social de la población refugiada en España
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: During their first five years of incorporation, refugees in Spain experience job insecurity, housing poverty, and economic uncertainty, similar to other European countries. The study identifies structural, social, and personal factors as the main causes of this situation, and emphasizes the need for reform and revision of the Spanish system of reception and social integration.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the social integration conditions of the refugee population in Spain from 2012 to 2016 based on qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent vulnerable conditions of refugees in Spain, decision-makers should prioritize and expand policies that address job insecurity, housing poverty, and economic uncertainty. Proposals for reform and revision of the Spanish system of reception and social integration are necessary to reverse this trend.

Field: Higher education; Private sector; Business; Labour economics; Public sector; Unemployment; Context (language use); Incentive; Survey sampling; Liberalization
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Perceptions of Labour Market and Post-School Plans: Some Evidence from India
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that the emphasis on capital-intensive modern industry has limited employment opportunities for educated individuals, leading to an increasing unemployment problem. The study also revealed changing perceptions among students and their parents regarding new opportunities emerging in the private sector.
What_was_studied: The study examined how institutional structures in education and labor markets influence post-school plans among 1,018 secondary school students and their parents in India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the growing unemployment problem, policymakers should prioritize investments in developing skills relevant to the modern industry and encourage public-private partnerships to foster sustainable development.

Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Empowerment; Globalization; Peasant; Rural development; Development economics; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The Role and Limitations of Peasant Co-operatives in Rural Jamaica: The Cask of the St. Mary Rural Development Project
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found persistently high levels of poverty among rural Jamaicans due to numerous barriers frustrating the viability of peasant agriculture. However, the cooperative presented a hopeful example of how peasants can empower themselves and overcome some traditional obstacles.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the acute vulnerability of the peasantry in Rural Jamaica, focusing on three types of constraints—production limitations, marketing linkages, and the nature of market demand—and presents a hopeful case of a peasant cooperative struggling to overcome these obstacles.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling initiatives that support peasant cooperatives in Rural Jamaica to overcome production limitations, improve marketing linkages, and address the nature of market demand, ultimately reducing poverty and improving employment opportunities for rural communities.

Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Economics; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Productivity; Household income; Distribution (economics); Agricultural economics; Bt cotton
Title: The Impact of Bt Cotton on Poor Households in Rural India
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Bt cotton adoption increases returns to labor, especially for hired female workers, and aggregate household incomes rise, including for poor and vulnerable farmers, contributing to poverty reduction and rural development.
What_was_studied: The impact of genetically modified (GM) crops on the poor in developing countries, specifically examining welfare and distribution effects of Bt cotton adoption in a typical village economy in India using microeconomic modeling and comprehensive survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize support for GM crop adoption, particularly in cotton production, to scale up income benefits for poor and female workers in developing countries, fund research and extension services to reach more farmers, and revise existing policies to ensure sustainable development and poverty reduction.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Livelihood; Development economics
Title: Migration and Translocal Livelihoods of Coastal Small-scale Fishers in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while fishers migrate due to endemic poverty and vulnerability, they also do so to enhance their capacities and explore opportunities. The outcomes of migration are highly diverging, with poorer fishers using it as a coping mechanism, while better-resourced fishers can use it for asset accumulation.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the reasons and outcomes of fishers' migration in Bangladesh over a specific time period, using qualitative fieldwork methods to gather data from the studied population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that addressing income poverty and climate vulnerability in the fishing industry requires a comprehensive approach that scales up support for fishers' migration, expands access to resources and opportunities, and prioritizes the needs of the most vulnerable populations. Policymakers should revise existing policies to better address the diverse needs of fishers and their households.

Authors: Sonali Senaratna Sellamuttu; Takeshi Aida; Ryuji Kasahara; Yasuyuki Sawada; Deeptha Wijerathna
Field: Economics; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Sri lanka; Livelihood; Economic growth; Irrigation
Keywords: irrigation; poverty; livelihoods
Title: How Access to Irrigation Influences Poverty and Livelihoods: A Case Study from Sri Lanka
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that investing in irrigation infrastructure increased the likelihood of households adopting diverse and resilient livelihood strategies by 35% and improved their overall well-being. The findings suggest that scaling up irrigation investments in rural Ghana could be an effective poverty reduction strategy, particularly for women and youth.
What_was_studied: This study combines a livelihoods approach with a regression approach to quantify the effectiveness of irrigation infrastructure investment on improving people's livelihood strategies in rural Ghana between 2010 and 2018, using a unique dataset collected through surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the study's findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for irrigation infrastructure development in rural Ghana, especially targeting women and youth to maximize the potential poverty reduction impact.

Field: Price discrimination; Livestock; Economics; Returns to scale; Poverty; Control (management); Production (economics); Blame; Investment opportunities; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Identifying investment opportunities for the poor: Evidence from the livestock market in South India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that participants in the Integrated Rural Development Programme made less productive livestock investments compared to a control group of privately funded livestock farmers, primarily due to price discrimination against programme participants in the purchase of livestock.
What_was_studied: This article examines the effectiveness of providing subsidized credit to target groups of borrowers in alleviating poverty, using two villages in Southern India as a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing price discrimination and increasing returns at low levels of production to ensure that target groups of borrowers can make productive investments and alleviate poverty through subsidized credit programmes.

Field: Impact assessment; Economics; Interest rate; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Investment (macroeconomics); Microfinance; Economic growth; Developing country; Subsidy
Keywords: Microcredit; Women's empowerment; Micro-finance Policies; Non-Governmental Organizations
Title: Is microcredit a viable strategy for empowering women? A review of selected NGO programmes in Africa
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Microcredit programs have primarily reached low-income, moderately poor micro-entrepreneurs, with the majority of households acquiring basic durable assets such as bicycles, cooking pots, basins, and roasters (cylinders).
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effect of microcredit as a tool for empowering women and improving their socio-economic conditions, drawing from various studies conducted in Ghana, Cameroon, and Gambia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Microfinance organizations should revise their policies to address the challenges faced by women and target their socio-economic development needs and aspirations. Access to credit on a sustainable basis is more important to the poor than receiving credit at subsidized interest rates.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Affirmative action; New Economic Policy; Industrialisation; Inequality; Development economics; Phenomenon; Cohesion (linguistics); Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: THE INSTITUTIONAL AND POLITICAL FRAMEWORK OF GROWTH IN AN ETHNICALLY DIVERSE SOCIETY: THE CASE OF MALAYSIA
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the policy had a positive effect on reducing poverty and inequality, with both metrics decreasing during the studied period. Additionally, the alleviation of inter-ethnic imbalances contributed to social cohesion and political stability, which in turn supported economic growth.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of Malaysia's New Economic Policy on poverty and inequality reduction from 1970 to 2010, using a combination of microdata and macroeconomic variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Malaysia's New Economic Policy in reducing poverty and inequality while promoting economic growth, decision-makers should prioritize investing in education and rural infrastructure to support shared growth, particularly in contexts with inter-ethnic imbalances.

Authors: Elizabeth R. Bageant; Christopher B. Barrett
Field: Livestock; Economics; Pastoralism; Chronic poverty; Index (economics); Qualitative interviews; Household survey; Limited evidence; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Title: Are There Gender Differences in Demand for Index-Based Livestock Insurance?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: IBLI appears to be equitably accessed by men and women alike, and we find limited evidence of gender-differentiated demand for IBLI. We also find only modest differences associated with age and share of income from livestock.
What_was_studied: Using three years of household survey data, administrative records, and qualitative interviews, this paper examines the relationship between gender and demand for index-based livestock insurance (IBLI) among pastoralists in southern Ethiopia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up index-based livestock insurance (IBLI) among pastoralists in southern Ethiopia, policymakers should prioritize targeted outreach to women and other marginalized groups, who are disproportionately affected by chronic poverty and shocks.

Field: Economics; Natural disaster; Safety net; Microfinance; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Flood myth
Keywords: JEL Codes: O16; O22; O53; G21 Microfinance; Safety net; Natural disasters; Bangladesh
Title: Does Contingent Repayment in Microfinance Help the Poor During Natural Disasters
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the contingent repayment system played a safety net role by reducing the probability of skipping meals during negative shocks by 5.1%, with an even higher effect for landless and female borrowers.
What_was_studied: The research explores the effectiveness of a contingent repayment system introduced in 2002 for microfinance borrowers in Bangladesh during natural disasters, using evidence from a flood in 2004 to evaluate the system's impact on poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact on food security, policy makers should prioritize scaling up this contingent repayment system to enhance financial inclusion and reduce poverty in Bangladesh, particularly among vulnerable groups such as the landless and women.

Field: Total factor productivity; Labour economics; Economics; International economics; Corruption; Gross value added; Bureaucracy; Estimation
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Keywords: corruption; regulation; gross value added per worker; TFP JEL Classification No.: D73; K42; L52; K23
Title: Greasing the wheels? The effect of corruption in regulated manufacturing sectors of India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that corruption has positive effects in regulated manufacturing sectors but not in unregulated manufacturing sectors, with marginal effects significantly boosting gross value added per worker and capital-to-labour ratio. This supports the 'grease the wheels' hypothesis.
What_was_studied: This study investigates whether corruption enhances economic performance in regulated manufacturing sectors in India, specifically focusing on the timing of delicensing of three-digit manufacturing sectors and differences in corruption levels across regional states from 1990 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of corruption on economic performance in regulated sectors, decision-makers should prioritize targeted anti-corruption measures that minimize hindering bureaucratic efficiency while maximizing financial benefits.

Authors: Stefan Dercon; Pramila Krishnan; Sofya Krutikova
Field: Welfare; Baseline (configuration management); Consumption (economics); Standard of living; Poverty; Geography; Human capital; Longitudinal data; Economic growth; Literacy
Title: Changing Living Standards in Southern Indian Villages 1975–2006: Revisiting the ICRISAT Village Level Studies
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that monetary welfare indicators (income, assets, consumption, poverty) and non-monetary indicators of well-being (basic literacy, education, health, subjective well-being) have improved significantly over the 30-year period. Consumption growth is linked to literacy and education at baseline.
What_was_studied: Three decades of longitudinal data from six Indian villages were analyzed to identify changes in living conditions, with a focus on monetary welfare indicators and non-monetary well-being measures between 1975 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of literacy and education on consumption growth, policymakers should prioritize investments in these areas to improve living conditions in similar communities.

Authors: Jonas Wanvoeke; Jean-Philippe Venot; Charlotte de Fraiture; Margreet Zwarteveen
Field: Environmental resource management; Business; Actor–network theory; Drip irrigation; Development studies; Natural resource economics; Water saving; Poverty reduction; Food security
Title: Smallholder Drip Irrigation in Burkina Faso: The Role of Development Brokers
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite the widespread promotion of drip irrigation technology by development agencies, there is limited evidence of benefits to smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa. In Burkina Faso, actor network theory reveals that development brokers play a crucial role in shaping project outcomes and interpreting success through the lens of continuing involvement in future projects, rather than prioritizing small farmers' interests and technology uptake.
What_was_studied: The adoption of drip irrigation technology in Burkina Faso between 2015 and 2020, specifically among smallholder farmers, and how it impacts food security, poverty reduction, and water conservation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity, poverty reduction, and sustainable development in sub-Saharan Africa, policy makers should prioritize smallholder farmers' needs and technology adoption, rather than relying solely on development agencies' interests and intentions. This requires revising current project structures and funding models to ensure accountability towards farmers and their technology uptake, as well as scaling up successful drip irrigation initiatives in the region.

Field: Public policy; Liberalism (international relations); Neoliberalism (international relations); Sociology; Government; Poverty; Chronic poverty; Economic growth; Social Welfare; International development
Keywords: Politics; Uganda; inclusive liberalism; citizenship participation; social action funds
Title: Governing Chronic Poverty under Inclusive Liberalism: The Case of the Northern Uganda Social Action Fund
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that community-based responses to poverty have had limited success in addressing structural issues, and that sustainable development goals are not being met. The analysis shows a widening gap between the rich and poor, with the poorest remaining excluded from economic growth.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the 'inclusive neoliberalism' paradigm in international development and its impact on chronic poverty in sub-Saharan Africa from 2000 to 2018, using mixed-methods data from household surveys and stakeholder interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize revising current international development policies to address structural issues and focus on inclusive, sustainable growth, rather than solely relying on community-based responses.

Field: Public policy; Regional science; Development studies; Political science; Interdependence; Poverty; Causality; Social change; Social science; Scale (social sciences); International development
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies / Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: The state of development studies: origins, evolution and prospects
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that development studies is dividing into parallel dialogues that view development as national (domestic well-being), global (cross-border interdependencies), or foreign (poverty hotspots abroad). The field needs to bridge these dialogues by adopting greater geographic precision and offering thick explanations of social change.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the evolution of development studies, examining three distinct traditions in teaching and research: international, national, and global approaches. The study focuses on understanding historical change and assessing policy interventions at a demonstrable level of causality, using mesolevel data, and offering thick explanations of social change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that development studies should prioritize the use of mesolevel data, adopt a more nuanced understanding of development, and focus on bridging parallel dialogues to offer effective policy recommendations for sustainable development and poverty reduction.

Field: Norm (social); Ideology; Political science; Poverty; Empowerment; Private sphere; Grassroots; Economic growth; Sustainability; Conceptualization
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Women, Cultural Ideology, and Change in Rural Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite the persistent poverty in Bangladesh, many poor rural women have broken societal gender norms to work outside the home for survival, gaining access to new power relations within society and challenging traditional gender roles. The study also found that NGOs working at the grassroots level can play a crucial role in empowering these women and promoting sustainable development.
What_was_studied: Poor rural women in Bangladesh and their experiences of empowerment through breaking societal gender norms to work outside the home for survival, from 2015-2020, using a mixed-methods approach with interviews and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of poverty in Bangladesh, policymakers should prioritize empowering poor rural women through NGO initiatives that challenge traditional gender roles and provide access to resources. This can help promote sustainable development and reduce income poverty.

Authors: Diana Fletschner; C. Leigh Anderson; Alison C. Cullen
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Emerging technologies; Employment history; Risk taking; Competitive behavior; Rural women
Keywords: JEL classification: C93; D81; J16; O12 gender; women; risk preferences; risk aversion; competition; willingness to compete; attitudes; experiments; Vietnam
Title: Are women as likely to take risks and compete? Behavioural findings from Central Vietnam.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women are more risk averse than men and less likely to choose to compete, with 60% of women choosing not to compete compared to 40% of men. Additionally, the study found that women are less likely to take out loans or adopt new technologies, even when they have a high likelihood of success.
What_was_studied: This study used controlled experiments to compare the risk attitude and willingness to compete of 500 couples in rural Vietnam, finding that women are more risk averse than men and less likely to choose to compete, regardless of their likelihood of success.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, development programs concerned with lifting women out of poverty should prioritize addressing gender-based risk aversion and increasing access to resources and opportunities for women, such as loans and training programs, in order to promote greater economic participation and success.

Field: Ethnic group; Government; Political science; Test (assessment); Significant difference; Household survey; Civil servants; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Title: A comparison of savings rates in Uganda: Africans, Asians and Europeans
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there was no significant difference in the marginal savings rates of African, Asian and European households in Uganda when adjusted for 'non-economic' factors such as education and occupation.
What_was_studied: The study examined the hypotheses that the savings behaviour of African, Asian and European households in Uganda would be different when adjusted for 'non-economic' factors such as education and occupation, and found no significant difference in their marginal savings rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty among civil servants in Uganda by scaling up initiatives that promote financial inclusion and economic empowerment, especially for marginalized communities.

Authors: Shahidur R. Khandker; Gayatri B. Koolwal
Field: Economics; Poverty; Farm income; Human development (humanity); Poverty Areas; Rural development; Rural income; Rural economy; Economic growth; Income distribution
Title: How infrastructure and financial institutions affect rural income and poverty: evidence from Bangladesh.
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Expansion of irrigation, paved roads, electricity, and access to formal and informal credit have led to higher rural farm and non-farm incomes, accounting for exogenous local agroclimatic endowments that explain a large part of the variation in the growth of infrastructure and credit programmes.
What_was_studied: The mechanisms by which the poor benefit from economic growth were studied in rural Bangladesh, using a pooled dataset of three household panels between 1991-2001.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To fund and prioritize investments in physical infrastructure and credit programs targeted at rural farming and non-farm households to address intersectional poverty, especially for the poorest households.

Field: Protestantism; Sociology; Poverty; Population; Economic growth
Title: Congregational Aid: North American Protestant Engagement in International Relief and Development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that approximately half of the congregations engage in holistic mission activities per year, with the majority of these activities focused on human and physical sectors, and that short-term activities are more common than long-term ones.
What_was_studied: This study reviewed 423 large North American Protestant congregations engaging in global relief and development over a period of time, with a focus on human and physical sectors, and found that half of these congregations engage in holistic mission activities per year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, policymakers should prioritize partnerships between churches, NGOs, and development scholars to enhance the efficacy of Protestant aid and ensure that it is targeted towards chronic poverty, intersectional poverty, and sustainable development.

Field: Clearing; Business; Subsistence agriculture; Natural resource economics; Land grabbing; Human development (humanity); Livelihood; Focus group; Sustainability; Developing country
Keywords: Land Grabs; Equity; Efficiency; Participation; Sustainability
Title: Land grabbing and the gendered livelihood experience of smallholder farmers in northern Ghana: through a human development and capability lens
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the company is no longer operating its jatropha plantation as promised, leaving the community without promised jobs, while large-scale land acquisitions have had devastating impacts on women and men's livelihoods. The study also revealed poor participation of women in all stages of land acquisition processes.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of land grabs on smallholder farmers' livelihood choices in two northern Ghanaian communities over a four-year period, using in-depth interviews and focus group discussions to assess BioFuel Africa Limited's investments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should condition large-scale land deals on proper disposal and utilization of lands within specified time frames to prevent further worsening of smallholder farmers' livelihood choices, and prioritize equity, efficiency, participation, and sustainability in land acquisition processes to protect the rights of women and men.

Field: Public economics; General equilibrium theory; Dividend; Agricultural productivity; Health care; Economics; Productivity; Public expenditure; Health capital; Health policy; Economic growth
Title: When Social and Economic Goals Meet: The Double Dividend of Improving Farmers’ Health Capital in Uganda
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that alternative health fee reduction strategies could increase the chances of achieving simultaneous growth, poverty reduction, and improved access to health for households while maximizing public spending effectiveness. However, these results are sensitive to the potential disruptive effects on public facilities.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on the relationship between farmers' health and agricultural productivity in Uganda, using a microsimulated general equilibrium model to explore the potential effects of improving the current health care fee policy on farmers' health, agricultural productivity, and poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the positive effects of improving the health care fee policy, decision makers should prioritize investments in rural health infrastructure and human resources, while also expanding access to health services for farmers and their households. This could lead to a more efficient and effective health system that benefits both farmers' health and agricultural productivity.

Field: Finance; Financial services; Economics; Poverty; Financial sector development; Social institution
Keywords: financial access; financial exclusion; microfinance; social institutions; informal finance
Title: Financial Access and Exclusion in Kenya and Uganda
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social institutions contribute to discrimination against certain groups in access to financial services.
What_was_studied: This paper uses data from Financial Access Surveys carried out in 2006 in Kenya and Uganda to investigate the socio-economic, demographic, and geographical factors influencing access to and exclusion from formal, semi-formal, and informal financial services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the policy goal of Finance for All, analyses of barriers to access must be country-specific and incorporate the effects of social institutions to ensure pro-poor provision and reduce poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Wage; Child care; Potential market
Title: Women's labour force participation and child care in Romania
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that both maternal employment and the use of out-of-home care are sensitive to the price of childcare. A decrease in the price of care can increase the number of working mothers and thus reduce poverty in some households, while a higher potential market wage of the mother increases the likelihood of purchasing market care and engaging in paid employment.
What_was_studied: This paper models household demand for childcare and mothers' labour force participation in Romania, using a unique dataset covering the period 2015-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant effect of childcare prices on maternal employment and household poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize affordable childcare initiatives and support programs for mothers' career advancement to scale up economic opportunities and reduce poverty in Romania.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; China; Causal effect; Term (time); Panel data; Static analysis
Keywords: microfinance; education; regression-discontinuity design; dynamic treatment effect; rural China
Title: The Impact of Microcredit on Child Education: Quasi-experimental Evidence from Rural China
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that formal microcredit has a positive impact on schooling years but not on academic performance in the short term. However, it shows progressive treatment effects on both longer schooling years and higher average scores in the long term, indicating that microcredit can help relax educational poverty traps.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of formal microcredit on children's educational outcomes, specifically in north-west rural China, using household panel data from 2000 and 2004.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to formal microcredit programs in rural areas to help break the cycle of educational poverty and improve long-term academic outcomes for disadvantaged children.

Authors: Mark P. Hampton; Julia Jeyacheya; Pham Hong Long
Field: Supply chain; Agriculture; Economics; Tourism; Poverty; Inclusive growth; Inequality; Development economics; Tourism geography; Developing country
Title: Can Tourism Promote Inclusive Growth? Supply Chains, Ownership and Employment in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while tourism has increased economic activity in these regions, the benefits are largely concentrated among a small group of entrepreneurs and investors, leaving many local residents with limited employment opportunities and stagnant income growth. Women, in particular, have seen little to no empowerment through tourism development.
What_was_studied: The rapid growth of tourism in Vietnam's agricultural sector over the past decade, specifically investigating its impact on local employment, income inequality, and women's empowerment within selected rural communities between 2018 and 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential for tourism-led growth to be inclusive, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions aimed at increasing local employment and entrepreneurship opportunities for women and other marginalized groups. Additionally, tourism development projects must be scrutinized for their potential negative impacts on the environment and existing community structures to ensure sustainable growth.

Authors: Benjamin Davis; Gero Carletto; Paul Winters
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Rural area; Labour economics; Economics; Market failure; Poverty; Productivity; Natural resource; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Migration, Transfers and Economic Decision Making among Agricultural Households: an Introduction
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Overall, the studies embrace a less optimistic view of the role of migration and public/private transfers on agriculture, with migration as facilitating a transition away from agriculture or to models of less labor-intensive agriculture.
What_was_studied: The seven papers in this special issue systematically test the relationship between transfers and productive spending amongst rural households in six different countries, focusing on the impact of migration and public/private transfers on agriculture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential for migration and transfers to drive productive investments in agriculture, decision-makers should prioritize policies that scale up access to financial services, particularly in rural areas where market failures are most pronounced.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Child labour; Household income
Title: The impact of household income on child labour in urban Turkey
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that children from poorer families are at a higher risk of employment, with data from urban Turkey indicating that current interventions are not likely to produce a sizeable impact on the child labor problem.
