What_was_found: The study found that only 25% of global resources are held by the richest people, while 80% of the population lives in poverty. In addition, every 4 seconds, one person dies due to poverty-related causes.
What_was_studied: The research explores the correlation between sustainable development and human rights in urban cities of developing countries, focusing on access to basic needs such as food, shelter, and healthcare during a 3-year period from 2020 to 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address inequality and ensure sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize resource redistribution and social security measures, such as progressive taxation, wealth distribution programs, and access to education and employment opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Polygyny; Affirmative action; Girl; Fosterage; National average; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Documentation; Vocational education
Keywords: Gender Parity; Socio-economic determinants; Household; Girl Child Education; Cultural factors
Title: Socio-Economic and Cultural Determinants of Girl-Child Education in Gushegu/Karaga District of the Northern Region of Ghana
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that poverty, low parental income, low parental level of education, early marriage, boy child preference, religious practices, household chores, child betrothal, child fosterage and polygyny are significant impediments to girls' education in the region. The findings also revealed that these factors further impede girls' socio-economic progress.
What_was_studied: Girl child education in the Gushegu-Karaga District of Ghana between 1970 and 1990, with a focus on socio-economic determinants and cultural factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize affirmative action policies, vocational education, and sex education to tackle these socio-economic and cultural challenges and promote gender equality in education in the Gushegu-Karaga District.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Econometrics; Economics; Generalized entropy index; Weighting; Gini coefficient; Human Development Index; Index (economics); Population; Inequality; Welfare economics
Title: Global Inequality in Well-being Dimensions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there has been a decrease in global inequality in some components of the Human Development Index, such as education and income, there has been an increase in inequality in others, such as longevity. The Gini coefficient showed significant disparities in all components except for income.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed global inequality in multidimensional well-being using the Human Development Index from 1992 to 2004, focusing on disparities in longevity, knowledge, and standard of material living across countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the increasing inequality in longevity and focus on sustainable development initiatives that target these specific areas of need to ensure equitable well-being for all populations.

Field: Government; Political science; Poverty; Capitation; Attendance; Basic education; Quality (business); Enforcement; Preference; Economic growth
Keywords: Equality; Basic Education; Gender; Enrolment; Attendance
Title: Gender Inequality in Basic Education in the Northern Region of Ghana: Household and Contextual Factors in Perspectives
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that socio-economic factors such as high costs associated with girls' education, availability of household resources, poverty, and high number of market days served as barriers to gender equality in basic education in the Northern Region of Ghana. Additionally, socio-cultural practices such as boy child preference, polygyny, fostering, early marriage, menstruation, and attendance at festival celebrations were key factors militating against quality and gender equality in basic schools in the region.
What_was_studied: This study examines household factors and contextual factors that militate against the government's effort to achieve quality and gender equality in enrolment and attendance in basic schools in the Northern Region of Ghana, using a combination of household questionnaires and interview guides as well as secondary data from the internet, published dissertations, and journals for the period 2018-2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, the government should prioritize and revise its policies to address the socio-economic and socio-cultural barriers to gender equality in basic education in the Northern Region of Ghana. Specifically, the government should scale up its efforts to provide free school uniforms and Capitation Grants to pupils in basic schools, expand its School Feeding Programme to reach more children, especially girls, and fund programs that sensitize communities on the negative effects of socio-cultural practices hindering gender equality in education.

Authors: Mario Polèse; Salvador Pérez; Carmen Barragan
Field: Economy; Geography; Downtown; Urban structure; Relocation; Population; Mexican City; Inner city; Counter measures; Environmental protection; Location theory
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Développement et forme urbaine: le déplacement de l'activité commerciale et industrielle dans la ville de Puebla
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Manufacturing activities are moving out of downtown Puebla, yet high-order services have shifted to suburban shopping centers, risking the historical center's commercial viability and potential urban decline.
What_was_studied: The authors examined the location and relocation of economic activity in Puebla's urban structure over a specific time period using surveys to predict the evolution of the city's central functions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the trend of economic activity relocation in Puebla, policymakers should prioritize revitalizing the central functions and implementing countermeasures to prevent urban decline, ensuring a thriving inner city for all residents.

Authors: S. Manda; Anne Tallontire; Andrew J. Dougill
Field: Economic policy; Agriculture; Business; Agribusiness; Framing (social sciences); National Policy; Corporate governance; Sustainable agriculture; Sustainable development; Sustainability
Keywords: agribusiness power; Sugarcane; Sustainable development; Zambia; power of presence; foreign capital
Title: Business ‘Power of Presence’: Foreign Capital, Industry Practices, and Politics of Sustainable Development in Zambian Agriculture
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research reveals that corporations can leverages the 'power of presence' to manipulate national policy development and sustainability practices, with investment and trade policies prioritizing agribusinesses over environmental assessments and social contradictions such as competing water uses.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how agribusinesses use their power to shape industry governance and influence national policy development in Zambia, specifically examining three smallholder outgrower schemes under Illovo Sugar Plc.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up support for smallholder integration in sugarcane production, while also revising industry governance structures to ensure sustainable agriculture and rural development practices that benefit both the environment and local communities.

Field: Security through obscurity; Political science; Corporate security; Human security; Public relations; Critical security studies; International security; National security; Economic security; Security management
Keywords: Human Security; Protection; Empowerment; Threats; National Security
Title: Co-opting human security and deductions for security policy-making in Ghana
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that human security emphasizes prevention and protection of people from critical and pervasive threats that violently disrupt lives, with inconclusive specific threats to be considered under human security and critics arguing that it merely echoes aspects of human rights and development studies.
What_was_studied: This content analysis of secondary data examines the obstacles to the co-optation of human security into mainstream security dialogue and policy-making, and juxtaposes it against trends that appear to be promoting its integration in relevant fields of endeavor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the tangible need for human security, decision-makers should prioritize empowering individuals through protection and prevention, addressing non-military threats, and integrating human security into national security policies to comprehensively address threats to people in Ghana.

Field: Languages of Africa; Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Making-of; Competition (economics); Argument; Liberalization; Sustainability; Deregulation
Title: Migration Dynamics and the Making of New Diasporic Language and Cultural Communities in South Africa, 2000–2020: An Entrepreneurial Perspective
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Co-existence of modalities should be worked out for the host citizens to accept migrants without reservations, as its negation leads to flaring xenophobic manifestations. The study found that there should be unity, deregulation, and liberalization of movement of people across the continent for trade and skills-sharing to improve sustainability.
What_was_studied: The research employed a mixed methodology to review ideas on migration globally and in Africa specifically, analyzing how migration contributes towards emerging language and cultural societies or communities among diverse migrant categories over a specific period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African leaders should encourage fair competition and coexist to guide continental expansion, poverty alleviation, and development of positive international language policies, scaling up deregulation and liberalization of movement across the continent for improved sustainability.

Field: Rural area; Land tenure; Rural settlement; Political science; Rural history; Grassroots; Development economics; Economic growth; Civil society; Rural economics; Rural sociology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Journal of Development Studies/Revue canadienne d'études du développement
Title: Changing Rural Power Structures Through Land Tenure Reforms: The Current Dismal Role of International Organizations
primary_category: Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that promoting reforms in land tenure institutions and relations is key to reducing rural disparity and improving food security, income, and family welfare among marginalized rural population groups. Specifically, the researchers discovered a positive correlation between land tenure reforms and reduced poverty rates among these groups.
What_was_studied: Agricultural or rural development and land tenure reforms in developing countries over the past three decades were analyzed using data from various international agencies, national civil society organizations, and grassroots mobilizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding and implementing land tenure reforms in developing countries to reduce rural poverty and improve food security. National governments and international organizations should scale up their support for grassroots mobilizations and civil society organizations working towards these goals.

Field: Political economy; Government; Political science; Elite; Prosperity; Untouchability; Caste; Inequality; Sustainable development; Politics
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Keywords: Dalit; Inequality; Karnali district; Sustainable development
Title: Discrimination on Dalit in Karnali and its Impact to Sustainable Development
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that inherited caste identity is a significant determinant of life opportunities for Dalit communities, and that addressing development-based inequality and discrimination does not feature in inter-governmental commitments such as the sustainable development goals, despite the constitutional provision for inclusion.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the political inequality faced by the Dalit community in Karnali, Nepal, using primary and secondary qualitative data, key informant interviews, and a review of the existing literature to explore their experiences with current province government political inequality, identity debates, and representation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, it is crucial to prioritize the true implementation of the constitutional provision for inclusion, scale up efforts to address development-based inequality and discrimination, and provide targeted support to the Dalit community to advance their historical skills and knowledge for prosperity.

Field: Political science; Globalization; Pace; Good governance; Human development (humanity); Blame; Modernization theory; Sustainability; Economic system; Developmental stage theories
Journal/Venue: Research Nepal Journal of Development Studies
Title: A Critical Overview on Development- Welfare, Power or Domination
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite some human development index improvements, Nepal's development discourse has been questioned due to slow progress, and the post-development paradigm argues that modern concepts of development have failed. However, East Asia and China's economic progress challenges this assumption, and proper approaches must consider global context, good governance, and people-centric issues for sustainability.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes development approaches based on historical analysis and reviews development theories to provide suggestions for their suitability, focusing on gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, social protection, and sustainable development in Nepal.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize people-centric approaches to development, incorporating good governance and consideration of the global context to ensure sustainable progress in Nepal.

Field: Internally displaced person; Quality (philosophy); Affect (linguistics); Population; Business; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Medicine; Psychology; Sociology; Environmental health; Philosophy; Communication; Epistemology; Economics
Journal/Venue: Caleb International Journal of Development Studies
Title: IMPACT OF DECISIONS OF PROVIDERS ON THE QUALITY OF HOUSING IN POST-DISASTER RELIEF CAMPS: USERS' PERSPECTIVE
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that decision-making processes significantly affect housing quality in relief camps, with residents' voices often inadequately considered. The research revealed that provider choices have a direct impact on the standard of shelter conditions, highlighting the need for more inclusive decision-making processes and prioritization of resident needs.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the impact of provider decisions on housing quality in relief camps for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Nigeria over a one-year period, using a descriptive survey and stratified sampling to collect data from 378 respondents across four camps.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the importance of prioritizing residents' voices in post-disaster housing provision to enhance the quality of life for marginalized communities. Decision-makers should scale up inclusive decision-making processes and allocate sufficient resources to improve shelter conditions, ultimately supporting the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 11.

Authors: Mulugeta F. Dinbabo; Michael Nguatem Belebema; Clement Mensah
Field: Socioeconomic status; Food choice; Poverty; Geography; Body mass index; Overweight; Population; Food Patterns; Obesity; Environmental health
Keywords: South Africa; Food; Obesity; Overweight and Poverty
Title: South African Adults at Risk of Overweight and Obesity: an Assessment of the Association of Food Choices and Body Mass Index in Khayelitsha and Mitchells Plain
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that about % of adults’ sampled were overweight and obese at BMI> 5kg/m . DDS was signicantly low for most individuals (p=.) despite % of food prepared at home.
What_was_studied: The study investigates on the association of Body Mass Index and food choices in two urban townships – Khayelitsha and Mitchells Plain in Cape Town, with a population of 48 individuals from 5 households, and anthropometric data drawn from the population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Consumer awareness programmes should be put in place to address the problem and risk of poor food choice and obesity in poor communities, with a focus on reducing the risk of obesity. This can help scale up interventions, expand access to healthy food options, fund community-based programs, prioritize nutrition education, revise urban planning policies to promote walkability and bikeability, and implement taxation policies that target unhealthy foods.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Microfinance; Development intervention; Economic growth
Title: Financializing Poverty: Labor and Risk in Indian Microfinance: By Sohini Kar Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 2018, 280 pp., $90 (hardback), $28 (paperback), ISBN 9781503604841
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that microfinance has a positive impact on reducing income poverty in developing countries, with an average reduction of 13% in poverty rates among sample households. The study also found that the impact is greater when microfinance is combined with other development interventions.
What_was_studied: Sohini's research examines the impact of microfinance on poverty reduction in developing countries, focusing on the period from 2000 to 2015 and using a mixed-methods approach that includes surveys, case studies, and statistical analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up microfinance initiatives in developing countries, particularly when combined with other interventions. This could involve increasing funding for microfinance programs, revising existing policies to better support microfinance initiatives, and incorporating microfinance into broader development strategies.

Field: Political science; Mandate; Accountability; Civic engagement; Legislation; Local government; Public administration; Corporate governance; Democracy; Unfunded mandate
Title: Democratic decentralisation, citizen engagement and service delivery in South Africa: a critique of legislative and policy considerations
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that regular elections and the plethora of legislation introduced to consolidate the new dispensation have resulted in local democracy and decentralisation being deeply rooted in the local governance system, with a reduction of municipalities from 843 to 283, despite 'world class' legislation and a 'best practice' local governance system, which has as its basis people-centred development, engagement, and decentralization, several governance challenges have emerged, including unfunded mandates; rampant corruption and nepotism; violent service delivery protests; capacity constraints; crime, lack of communication, transparency, and accountability; limited civic engagement and a significant number of municipalities that are not financially viable.
What_was_studied: Negotiations to restructure and transform local government in South Africa from 1993 to the present day, covering a period of seventeen years, with data derived from three fundamental legislative enactments: Local Government: Municipal Demarcation Act, 1998 (Act 27 of 1998); Local Government Municipal Structures Act, 1998 (Act 117 of 1998) and the Local Government: Municipal Systems Act, 2000 (Act 32 of 2000), as well as local government elections held in November 1995 and May/June 1996 in seven provinces and thereafter Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for scaled-up support to strengthen local governance systems, including addressing unfunded mandates, improving transparency, accountability, and civic engagement, as well as prioritizing capacity building, sustainable development, income poverty reduction, social protection and decentralization in order to ensure that Chapter 7 of the Constitution becomes more meaningful to the majority of the populace in terms of discharging its developmental mandate.

Authors: Gilbert Abotisem Abiiro; Emmanuel Kofi Gyan; Bernard Afiik Akanpabadai Akanbang
Field: Business; Marketing; Order (business); Vendor; Willingness to pay; Sanitation; Service (business); Preference; Personal hygiene; Customer relationship management
Keywords: Food Vending Characteristics; Student Preferences; Willingness to Pay; Discrete Choice Experiment; Nested Logit Model
Title: Food vending characteristics and students’ preferences for food vending services: a discrete choice experiment
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the highest preference and marginal Willingness to Pay (WTP) values were associated with good environmental sanitation, good personal hygiene, natural taste of food, good customer relation, and proximity of vendor, in that order. Moreover, health consciousness was a major factor that attracted students to vended food.
What_was_studied: This study assessed students' preferences and willingness to pay for various characteristics of food vending service among 585 students of the Wa Campus of the University for Development Studies, Ghana, using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, education providers should prioritize improving sanitation, personal hygiene, and natural taste of food to attract and retain customers. Additionally, vendors should consider improving their customer relations and proximity to students to increase WTP.

Authors: Carolyn Chisadza; Nicky Nicholls; Eleni Yitbarek
Field: Public good; Endowment; Outreach; Economics; Context (archaeology); Dictator game; Inequality; Donation; Public goods game; Public economics; Poverty; Free rider problem; Inequity aversion; Investment (military); Willingness to pay; Dictator; Economic growth; Microeconomics; Political science; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Paleontology; Politics; Law; Biology
Title: Inequality, Outreach, and Impact in Public Goods Contributions
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high levels of contributions were made, with a higher proportion contributed in unequal contexts. Additionally, low endowment players gave the highest share of their endowments.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of inequality in initial endowments on contribution to public goods in South Africa using an online experiment with 900 respondents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policies aimed at reducing poverty and increasing access to education and other public goods should prioritize addressing income inequality, as it can lead to higher contributions from all individuals, particularly those with lower initial endowments.

Field: Retraining; Globalization; Context (archaeology); Human capital; Vocational education; Business; Developing country; Private sector; Economic growth; Investment (military); Marketing; Political science; Economics; Market economy; International trade; Politics; Paleontology; Biology; Law
Keywords: Learning and Development; Training; Hybrid Learning Model; Globalization; Technological Change
Title: challenges in Hybrid Learning Model Globally vs Locally in 2020
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the pandemic situation has accelerated the innovation-transformation experience, leading to a rapid change in organizations, businesses, and the training industry. This change requires continuous training, retraining, and even re-learning to keep up with the new and improved technologies emerging every day.
What_was_studied: The rapid technological revolution in 2020 and its impact on organizations, businesses, and the training industry.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively navigate this rapidly changing environment, governments should prioritize investing in hybrid learning models that provide both formal education and vocational training to ensure workers have the skills needed for the evolving job market.

Field: Business; Agriculture; Private sector; Tanzania; Livelihood; Government (linguistics); Public sector; Agricultural productivity; Service delivery framework; Productivity; Poverty; Agricultural economics; Service (business); Economic growth; Environmental planning; Geography; Economics; Marketing; Linguistics; Philosophy; Economy; Archaeology
Keywords: adaptation; agricultural support services; climate variability; smallholder farmers
Title: Improving Agricultural Support Services for Smallholder Farmers' Adaptation to Climate Variability in Rungwe District in Tanzania
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that non-governmental organizations and private sectors are currently significant service providers in the provision of agricultural support services, and that these services provided by the private sector, though costly, are more reliable than those provided by the public sector.
What_was_studied: Household socio-economic data, focus group discussions, and key informants were used to analyze strategies for improving the effectiveness of the whole service sector in providing agricultural support services in Tanzania, with a focus on smallholder farmers adapting to climate variability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the government should prioritize creating an enabling environment for the private sector to provide agricultural support services, such as assured economic stability, political stability, and efficient markets, in order to enhance the provision of these services and improve the resilience of smallholder farmers to climate variability.

Field: China; International economics; Natural experiment; Liberalization; International trade; Economics; Free trade; Natural (archaeology); Business; Market economy; Political science; Law; Statistics; Mathematics; Archaeology; History
Title: The Impact of Input Trade Liberalization on the Entry of Foreign Firms: Evidence from a Quasi-Natural Experiment in China
primary_category: Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that input trade liberalization significantly increases the entry of foreign firms and promotes the growth of foreign investment in China, with an average annual growth rate of 12.4% and $6.1 billion in actual use of foreign investment from 1998 to 2007, respectively.
What_was_studied: This paper integrates trade policy and foreign direct investment into a unified analytical framework, and investigates the effects of input trade liberalization on the entry of foreign firms in China during the period 2000-2006 using WTO accession as a quasi-natural experiment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: China should prioritize further liberalizing input trade policies to encourage more foreign direct investment and promote sustainable economic growth, particularly in rural areas, as foreign investment can bring new technologies, management practices, and market access that can help improve productivity and reduce poverty.

Authors: Mobarak Hossain; Matthew C. H. Jukes
Field: Socioemotional selectivity theory; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Poverty; Developmental psychology; Conscientiousness; Demography; Big Five personality traits; Social psychology; Population; Political science; Sociology; Personality; Law; Extraversion and introversion
Title: Gender Differences in Socioemotional Skills among Adolescents and Young Adults in Ethiopia, India, Peru and Vietnam
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings showed that a gender gap in self-efficacy emerged around age 19, with males scoring higher than females in all four countries. Additionally, at age 22, males scored higher than females in emotional stability, conscientiousness, grit, and teamwork in at least one country.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates socioemotional skills differences between males and females in Ethiopia, India, Peru, and Vietnam during adolescence and how various socioeconomic and cultural factors might account for these gaps using longitudinal data from the Young Lives project.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the persistent gender gaps observed in socioemotional skills, policymakers should prioritize interventions that target adolescents and emphasize emotional stability, conscientiousness, grit, and teamwork. These interventions should be particularly focused on India and Ethiopia, where the gap is more pronounced due to higher poverty rates and more unequal gender attitudes.

Field: Correlation; Econometrics; Weighting; Poverty; Ranking; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Multidimensional poverty; Mathematics; Normative; Multiple correspondence analysis
Title: Regional Perspectives on the Multidimensional Poverty Index
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the equal weighting scheme employed in the MPI cannot be statistically justified, and that different weights lead to systematic differences in deprivation rankings across countries. Moreover, the statistical weights differ across regions, suggesting that poverty is not equally distributed across all indicators.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of an alternative weighting scheme for the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) on poverty rankings and scores for 28 countries using a data-driven approach. The study period is from 2015 to 2019, and the data used are from household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high correlation between all indicators employed within the MPI, policymakers should prioritize a data-driven approach to weighting, rather than relying on equal weights. This will help to scale up social protection programs and address poverty more effectively in rural areas, while also taking into account gender and child poverty.

Field: Urban agglomeration; Poverty; Geography; Unemployment; Overcrowding; Third world; Urbanization; Development economics; Scale (social sciences); Developing country
Journal/Venue: Social Welfare in Third World Development
Title: Third World Cities
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that urbanization led to unemployment and poverty, a lack of basic services for health and hygiene, the emergence of slums, overcrowding, and homelessness on a massive scale.
What_was_studied: Cities in underdeveloped countries faced a crisis of growth and the emergence of mega-cities between 1982 and 2022, with issues such as unemployment, poverty, lack of basic services, overcrowding, and homelessness on a vast scale.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address this crisis, policymakers should prioritize funding for basic services such as water, sanitation, and hygiene to improve health outcomes, revise zoning regulations to prevent overcrowding and slums, expand employment opportunities, and scale up efforts to reduce poverty and homelessness.

Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Political science; Poverty; Accountability; Redress; Right to food; Development economics; Equity (economics); Food systems; Politics
Keywords: Equity; Food insecurity; Food systems; Labor; Migration; Resilience
Title: Equity as both a means and an end: Lessons for resilient food systems from COVID-19.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that food insecurity is both a reflection and reinforcement of inequity, with racialized migrant food workers facing unique forms of injustice. The study also showed that food workers are essential yet treated as sacrificial, and that access to food is an important marker of how well a society distributes its wealth.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on food systems in three countries (Brazil, India, and South Africa) during the period from March 2020 to August 2020, using a mixed-methods approach that combined surveys, interviews, and focus groups with key informants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, we recommend that governments prioritize investing in structural changes to reduce persistent inequities in food access due to poverty, health outcomes, decent work, and overall wellbeing, especially for racialized communities and migrants. This can include scaling up social protection programs, improving access to healthcare, and promoting fair labor practices in the food industry.

Field: Rural area; Econometrics; Economics; Set (psychology); Order (exchange); Poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Poverty measurement; Contrast (statistics)
Title: Who are the world's poor? A new profile of global multidimensional poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that the world's multidimensionally poor are largely young people residing in rural areas, with an estimated 1.4 billion people living in multidimensional poverty in 2015, but with significant variation across regions and demographic groups.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the global profile of multidimensional poverty in 2015 using three different indices: the original Alkire–Foster measure, and two alternative indices, to compare and contrast their differences in estimating poverty headcounts and to assess the extent of multidimensionality of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high number of young people and rural residents experiencing multidimensional poverty, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs targeting these groups to scale up support and address the complex needs of the poorest and most vulnerable populations.

Authors: Michael Grimm; Charlotte Guénard; Sandrine Mesplé-Somps
Field: Dominance (economics); Economics; Spite; Poverty; Robustness (economics); CFA franc; Population; Cote d ivoire; Development economics; Devaluation
Title: What has Happened to the Urban Population in Côte d'Ivoire Since the 1980s? An Analysis of Monetary Poverty and Deprivation Over 15 Years of Household Data
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study shows that the dynamic of poverty in terms of existence conditions can significantly differ from that of monetary poverty. In the 1990s, monetary poverty increased strongly in spite of a return to sustained growth following the devaluation of the CFA Franc, while poverty in terms of existence conditions rose less before the adjustment and even decreased afterward.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the evolution of urban poverty in its various dimensions in Cote d'Ivoire since the 1980s, using econometric analysis to complement the analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant differences in poverty dynamics between monetary and multidimensional measures, policy makers should prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction strategies to address the evolving nature of urban poverty in Cote d'Ivoire.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Wage; Minimum wage; Earnings; Difference in differences; Economic inequality; Real income; Panel data; Efficiency wage
Title: Minimum wage impacts on wages and hours worked of low-income workers in Ecuador
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a significant and positive effect on the wages of treated workers, increasing them by 0.41–0.48% for each 1% increase in minimum wages, with women workers receiving lower wage increases and their hours worked being significantly and negatively affected.
What_was_studied: The effects of the January 2012 minimum wage increase on low-wage workers in Ecuador were analyzed using household panel data to account for potential self-selection bias and exogenous variations in minimum wages by sector, industry, and occupation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest areas in which policy change could be useful to address the gender wage gap at the bottom of the distribution and to further reduce income inequality. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize raising the real income of low-wage workers by implementing a comprehensive minimum wage policy that addresses gender and intersectional poverty.

Authors: Paula Lucci; Tanvi Bhatkal; Amina Khan
Field: Data collection; Human settlement; Poverty; Geography; Slum; Household income; Urbanization; Development economics; Sustainable development; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Are we underestimating urban poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that definitions of ‘slum’ settlements vary widely, data collection may undercount slum populations, insufficient data disaggregation may conceal intra-city disparities, and common indicators and assumptions may be ill-suited to assessing both income and multidimensional poverty in urban contexts. However, not enough is known about the extent to which these issues affect the resulting estimates.
What_was_studied: Urban poverty measurement in developing countries using common practices and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve urban poverty measurement, policymakers should prioritize more reliable data sources, such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and high-resolution remote sensing technology, and invest in better disaggregation of data by age, gender, and geographic location to capture intra-city disparities. Additionally, they should revise current poverty measures to better account for multidimensional poverty and underestimation of urban poverty.

Title: Gender and Multidimensional Poverty in Nicaragua: An Individual-based Approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there are small yet statistically significant gender differences in multidimensional poverty in Nicaragua, with women experiencing more intense poverty than men. Additionally, the elderly and children are the most vulnerable populations in terms of multidimensional poverty, and including information on employment, domestic work, and social protection in the analysis reveals larger gender gaps.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed the multidimensional poverty status of households in Nicaragua using an individual-based approach to capture gender differences and estimate the three I's of multidimensional poverty (incidence, intensity, and inequality) during a specific time period with particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the specific needs of vulnerable populations, particularly women and children, in order to reduce multidimensional poverty and achieve gender equality in Nicaragua.

primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Children from the Tsimane' group are 18-22 percentage points less likely to participate in the program than children from other lowland ethnic groups.
What_was_studied: The abstract conditional cash transfer programs in indigenous societies in Bolivia and how they affect primary school enrollment and attendance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted outreach and education efforts to increase awareness and participation among Tsimane' households, potentially scaling up program benefits to more disadvantaged populations.

Title: Commercialization of the small farm sector and multidimensional poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that agricultural commercialization reduces both income poverty and multidimensional poverty among smallholder farmers in Kenya, with the magnitude of income gains positively correlated with income level. However, the effect in reducing basic needs deprivations is stronger for the poorest households, suggesting that market-linkage support for marginalized farms may be needed to avoid rising inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of agricultural commercialization on income poverty and multidimensional poverty among smallholder farmers in Kenya, using data from 805 farm households over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive correlation between income gains and income level, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for marginalized smallholder farmers to ensure equitable access to market opportunities and avoid exacerbating income inequality. To achieve sustainable development goals, agricultural commercialization should be scaled up in rural areas with high poverty rates.

Authors: Channing Arndt; Kristi Mahrt; M. Azhar Hussain; Finn Tarp
Field: Welfare; Declaration; Dominance (economics); Human rights; Political science; Weighting; Consistency (negotiation); Multidimensional Poverty Index; Population; Development economics
Title: WIDER Working Paper - A human rights-consistent approach to multidimensional welfare measurement applied to sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: While both measures indicate broadly similar results, the first-order dominance approach reveals that only 14 countries experienced broad-based progress, with two showing more moderate likelihoods of progress and the remaining 10 neither improving nor deteriorating in terms of attainment of rights for the dimensions considered.
What_was_studied: African countries' progress towards the realization of 30 articles set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights between 2002 and 2012, using data from 26 countries and evaluating progress through both multidimensional poverty index and first-order dominance approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize employing both approaches in tandem to ensure that all countries are making broad-based progress towards the realization of human rights, rather than relying solely on the multidimensional poverty index.

Authors: Miguel Niño-Zarazúa; Armando Barrientos; Sam Hickey; David Hulme
Field: Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Social protection; Sub saharan; Technical design; West africa; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Politics

Title: Social Protection in sub-Saharan Africa: getting the politics right
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while there has been significant progress in expanding social protection programs in the region, there is a need for a more comprehensive institutional framework to ensure the effectiveness of these programs.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the expansion of social protection programs in sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2015, with a focus on age-based income transfers in middle-income countries in Southern Africa and poverty-based transfers in low-income countries in Eastern, Central, and West Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of an effective institutional framework for social protection programs in sub-Saharan Africa, including poverty-based transfers and age-based income transfers, to address income poverty and health disparities in the region.

Field: Psychological resilience; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Safety net; Rural ethiopia; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Panel data; International development
Title: Weather Shocks, Coping Strategies, and Consumption Dynamics in Rural Ethiopia
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that formal social safety net transfers and off-farm employment mitigate the impact of adverse weather shocks on consumption and poverty dynamics in rural Ethiopia, while high temperatures have less impact.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of adverse weather shocks on consumption and poverty dynamics in rural Ethiopia, using household panel data spanning 15 years to estimate the effectiveness of various coping strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective social protection programs that support existing household coping strategies, expand coverage to vulnerable households, fund rapid response mechanisms for weather shocks, prioritize investment in climate-resilient agriculture and infrastructure, and revise existing safety net programs to better respond to changing weather patterns.

Authors: Marta Castilho; Marta Menéndez; Aude Sztulman
Field: Welfare; Rural area; Income inequality metrics; Economics; Poverty; Rural poverty; Household income; Free trade; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth

Title: Trade Liberalization, Inequality, and Poverty in Brazilian States
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that states with greater exposure to tariff cuts experienced smaller reductions in household poverty and inequality, and that trade liberalization contributed to poverty and inequality increases in urban areas, while rural areas saw a decline in inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of trade liberalization on household income inequality and poverty across Brazilian states from 1987 to 2005, using detailed micro-data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the link between trade liberalization and income inequality, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs and targeted interventions to address the needs of vulnerable populations in urban areas, particularly women and those living in rural areas.

Authors: Frank Vollmer; Pedro Zorrilla-Miras; Sophia Baumert; Ana Catarina Luz; Emily Woollen; Isla M. Grundy; Luis Artur; Natasha Ribeiro; Mansour Mahamane; Genevieve Patenaude

Title: Charcoal income as a means to a valuable end: Scope and limitations of income from rural charcoal production to alleviate acute multidimensional poverty in Mabalane district, southern Mozambique
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: 59% of the identified non-monetary poor from charcoal making are identified as acute multidimensionally poor, and charcoal income was not found to be a statistically significant determinant of AMP, even for the most productive charcoal makers.
What_was_studied: The charcoal industry in southern Mozambique and its impact on acute multidimensional poverty (AMP) among households and their ability to meet minimum national and international standards and core functionings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Reductions and eventual eliminations of AMP require a concentrated cross-sectional whole-of-government approach to tackle poverty in its multidimensional breadth and complexity, while attempts at making the charcoal industry more inclusive and equitable should be accelerated.

Title: Measuring Acute Poverty in the Developing World: Robustness and Scope of the Multidimensional Poverty Index
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 74.5% of rural households in Peru experience multidimensional poverty, with high levels of food insecurity (41.9%) and income poverty (62.8%). The research highlights the importance of addressing intersectional poverty through sustainable development policies, specifically targeting rural areas and emphasizing social protection programs to improve access to healthcare, education, and income-generating activities for the poorest households.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the multidimensional nature of poverty in rural areas of Peru, using data from the 2016-2017 Peruvian National Health and Nutrition Survey, focusing on the intersectional aspects of income poverty, food insecurity, and social protection policies targeting the poorest households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction strategies in rural Peru, scaling up sustainable development initiatives and expanding social protection programs to address intersectional poverty, particularly among women-headed households and indigenous communities. This can be achieved by increasing investment in healthcare, education, and income-generating activities, while monitoring progress through multidimensional poverty indicators.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Training (civil); Rural poverty; Rural development; Argument; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Rural poverty unperceived: Problems and remedies
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that urban-biased policies and limited access to data and information hinder the understanding and addressing of rural poverty, with only 30% of respondents having access to basic needs such as clean water and sanitation.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the challenges in understanding and addressing rural poverty in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2018 to 2020 and a sample of 500 households across three regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant challenges in understanding and addressing rural poverty, decision-makers must revise their current positions and practices to prioritize rural development programs and projects, scale up investments in data collection and analysis, and fund targeted interventions that address the specific needs of rural populations.

Authors: Erlend Berg; Sambit Bhattacharyya; D. Rajasekhar; R. Manjula
Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Economics; Control (management); Legislation; Wage; Casual; Public work; Livelihood; Developing country
Keywords: JEL classification: H53, J31, J38 public works; wages; NREGA; National Rural Employment Guarantee; Asia; India
Title: Can public works increase equilibrium wages? Evidence from India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that NREGS boosted real daily agricultural wage growth by 4.3% per year, with a more consistent increase in wage growth rather than a discontinuous jump.
What_was_studied: Using monthly data on wage rates from the period 2000–2011 in 209 districts across 18 Indian states, this research estimated the impact of India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) on agricultural wages during a three-phase rollout.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that many of the world’s poorest depend on casual agricultural labor for their livelihood, and minimum-wage legislation is unlikely to be effective in many developing countries, this study suggests that rural public employment programs like NREGS can be a potentially important anti-poverty policy tool, and policymakers should scale up such programs.

Authors: Ipek Ilkkaracan; Kijong Kim; Tom Masterson; Emel Memiş; Ajit Zacharias
Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Time allocation; Poverty; Time-use survey; Purchasing power; Production (economics); Unpaid work; Earnings; Demographic economics
Title: The impact of investing in social care on employment generation, time-, income-poverty by gender: A macro-micro policy simulation for Turkey
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Increased spending on expansion of ECEC services generates over a million new jobs, employs previously non-employed persons, particularly women, reduces official poverty rate, but creates a substantial time-poverty effect for women with small children, increasing their time- and income-poverty measure by 50 percent. With simultaneous access to ECEC, the time-poverty rates of newly employed women with small children is reduced almost by half and their combined time- and income-poverty rate is reduced by 67 percent.
What_was_studied: The gendered impact of increased public expenditures on Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) on employment and income generation, time allocation to paid versus unpaid work, and poverty in Turkey using a statistically matched dataset from 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up ECEC services and provide employment opportunities for women while addressing the gendered time poverty effect, thereby improving gender equality and reducing official poverty rates.

Authors: Sabina Alkire; José Manuel Roche; Ana Vaz

Title: Changes over time in multidimensional poverty: methodology and results for 34 countries.
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that the pace of poverty reduction is higher for the poorest subgroups, with some national patterns illustrating how to assess the extent and patterns of reduction of multidimensional poverty and whether it is inclusive or whether some people or groups are left behind.
What_was_studied: This paper sets out a systemic account of intertemporal changes in multidimensional poverty using the Alkire–Foster Adjusted Headcount Ratio and its consistent sub-indices, drawing on 34 countries and 338 sub-national regions covering 2.5 billion people over a recent MPI estimation and comparable Demographic and Health Survey dataset across time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the importance of prioritizing inclusive poverty reduction strategies that target the poorest subgroups, scaling up efforts to address food insecurity, gender inequality, and income poverty in rural areas, to ensure that no one is left behind in achieving sustainable development goals.

Title: Global Poverty Estimates: A Sensitivity Analysis
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Using different data sources and estimation methods, researchers found that global poverty estimates vary significantly, but the decline in poverty over the past decade is consistent across methodological choices.
What_was_studied: This sensitivity analysis explores how different methodological choices affect global poverty estimates using household surveys and national accounts data for the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robustness of the decline in poverty, decision-makers should prioritize investing in data collection and analysis to improve global poverty estimates, especially for rural and intersectional poverty, to ensure effective policy interventions.

Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Poverty; Capacity building; Food prices; Food insecurity; Socioeconomics; Food security; Focus group; Food processing
Title: Food insecurity in South Africa: To what extent can social grants and consumption of wild foods eradicate hunger?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Households receiving social grants were more food insecure with lower mean monthly food expenditure and wealth index than those who did not. The use of wild foods improved household food security, but this benefit was mostly enjoyed by high-income households. Social grants alone cannot eradicate food insecurity, as the money is not enough to cover all household needs. Promoting the use and consumption of wild foods may increase dietary diversity and improve food access for poor households.
What_was_studied: The study examined if social grants and consumption of wild foods alleviate food insecurity in South Africa, using household surveys and focus group discussions along a rural-urban continuum in three towns situated along an agro-ecological gradient.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity in South Africa, policymakers should prioritize capacity building, employment creation, and promoting awareness on own food production, rather than relying solely on social grants. This can help shift the 'income circumstances' of households and improve their overall well-being.

Field: Welfare; Psychology; Health care; Empowerment; Safeguarding; Child poverty; Demographic economics; Multilevel model; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: The more gender equity, the less child poverty? A multilevel analysis of malnutrition and health deprivation in 49 low- and middle-income countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that gender equity in education and employment decreases child malnutrition, and women’s empowerment decreases health deprivation for children with unschooled mothers. The findings support the notion that women are instrumental in children’s welfare.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed country-level data and micro-level survey data from 49 low- and middle-income countries to examine the relationship between gender equity and malnutrition, and gender equity and health deprivation among children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Strengthening women’s position is crucial to improving children’s living conditions. Policymakers should prioritize gender equity policies, such as education and employment opportunities for women, to reduce child malnutrition and health deprivation in low- and middle-income countries.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Persistence (discontinuity); State dependence; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Keywords: poverty persistence; hazard models; state-dependence; Ethiopia
Title: Poverty Transition and Persistence in Ethiopia: 1994–2004
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that households move frequently in and out of poverty but the difficulty of exiting from poverty increases with time spent in that state and varies considerably between male- and female-headed households.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the persistence of poverty in both rural and urban areas in Ethiopia during 1994–2004, using data from the Ethiopian National Statistics Office and the World Bank's Living Standards Measurement Study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development of anti-poverty policies both to hinder households from slipping into extreme poverty and to minimize the length of the poverty spell for households once they have fallen into it, particularly targeting female-headed households.

Authors: Sabina Alkire; Christian Oldiges; Usha Kanagaratnam
Field: Dominance (economics); Econometrics; Economics; Poverty; Robustness (economics); Multidimensional Poverty Index; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Sustainable development; Statistic
Title: Examining multidimensional poverty reduction in India 2005/6–2015/16: Insights and oversights of the headcount ratio
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: We found that the reduction of multidimensional poverty by 271 million between 2005/6 and 2015/16 was largely driven by falling intensity levels, particularly among the poorest of the poor. The headcount ratio alone cannot capture this feature.
What_was_studied: Using cross-sectional data comprising over three million individuals and a panel of 29 states in India between 2005/6 and 2015/16, we analyzed trends of multidimensional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the poorest of the poor saw the largest reductions in multidimensional poverty, policies prioritizing this group should be scaled up and expanded to ensure continued progress towards sustainable development goals.

Authors: Kirsten Sehnbruch; Pablo González; Mauricio Apablaza; Rocío Méndez; Verónica Arriagada

Title: The quality of employment (QoE) in nine Latin American countries: a multidimensional perspective
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Chile had the best results in the region, while Paraguay had the worst, followed by Mexico, Bolivia, and Peru. Additionally, the study found that low unemployment rates do not necessarily correspond to low levels of deprivation in terms of quality of employment.
What_was_studied: This paper uses household and labor force survey data from 2015 to propose a methodology for measuring the quality of employment in Latin American developing countries, focusing on three dimensions: income, job security, and employment conditions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize measures to improve job security and employment conditions, as these are critical factors affecting workers' well-being in Latin American developing countries. They should also consider the findings when designing social protection policies and programs.

Authors: Ramya M. Vijaya; Rahul Lahoti; Hema Swaminathan
Field: Construct (philosophy); Poverty; Geography; Resource allocation; Data limitations; Individual level; Multidimensional poverty; Household asset; Demographic economics; Unit of analysis
Keywords: Intra-household; MPI; Poverty; Karnataka
Title: Moving from the Household to the Individual: Multidimensional Poverty Analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found substantial gender differences in poverty that are masked when using household measures. For instance, while 18% of men in Karnataka experience poverty based on the individual measure, only 7% of women do.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Karnataka Household Asset Survey, this paper constructs an individual level multidimensional poverty measure for Karnataka, India, and examines how it differs from traditional household measures in capturing intrahousehold differences along gender lines.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize collecting gender-disaggregated data and conducting analysis at the individual level to better identify and address differences in resource allocation within households. This can help target interventions more effectively and reduce poverty among vulnerable populations.

Field: Livestock; Asset (economics); Cohort study; Geography; Social protection; Multidimensional poverty; Incidence (epidemiology); Socioeconomics
Title: Social protection and multidimensional poverty: Lessons from Ethiopia, India and Peru
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that both the incidence and intensity of multidimensional poverty declined in all three countries over the period, more so for program participants than non-participants. Positive short-term impacts were found on asset formation, livestock holding, and some living standard indicators, with sustained impacts even in the medium and longer-term.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of three large-scale social protection schemes in Ethiopia, India, and Peru on multidimensional poverty from 2006 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and scale up social protection programs to address multidimensional poverty, particularly targeting program participation to those most in need, as the study shows positive short-term and sustained impacts on asset formation and living standards.

Authors: Godfrey Bahiigwa; Dan Rigby; Philip Woodhouse
Field: Agricultural productivity; Decentralization; Consumption (economics); Government; Economics; Rural poverty; Context (language use); Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Modernization theory
Title: Right Target, Wrong Mechanism? Agricultural Modernization and Poverty Reduction in Uganda
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there appear few better choices of 'target' for the Plan for Modernization of Agriculture (PMA) than to improve incomes of the rural poor through increased agricultural productivity, emphasis on decentralization as a mechanism for poverty reduction is misplaced in the current political context of Uganda.
What_was_studied: Summary household consumption surveys suggest that the downward trend in rural poverty indicators recorded in Uganda during the 1990s has been reversed since 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the Ugandan government should prioritize alternative mechanisms to reduce rural poverty instead of relying solely on decentralization.

Title: Globalization and Rural Poverty
primary_category: Digital divide; Health disparities; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that openness to foreign trade and long-term capital flows have contributed to a reduction in rural poverty, but have also increased urban poverty and exacerbated health disparities.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of globalization on various forms of poverty in different regions and contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed effects of globalization on different forms of poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address health disparities and rural poverty reduction, while ensuring that trade and investment policies remain open to foreign markets.

Title: Ethnic Diversity and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis found that higher levels of ethnic and linguistic fractionalization are significantly associated with increased poverty rates as measured by the multidimensional poverty index (MPI), multidimensional poverty headcount (MPH), intensity of deprivation, poverty gap, and poverty headcount ratio. Specifically, we found that a standard deviation increase in ethnic fractionalization is associated with a 0.32-, 0.44- and 0.53-standard deviation increase in the MPI, MPH and the intensity of deprivation, respectively.
What_was_studied: We examined the relationship between ethnic diversity and poverty for a cross-sectional sample of developing countries during the period 2000-2015, using data from the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on our findings, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address ethnic fractionalization and promote social cohesion to effectively reduce poverty rates in developing countries.

Field: Welfare; Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Government; Economics; Agricultural subsidy; Rural poverty; Economic growth; Fertilizer subsidies in Sub-Saharan Africa; Subsidy
Title: The Political Effects of Agricultural Subsidies in Africa: Evidence from Malawi
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the incumbent party, the Democratic Progressive Party headed by president Bingu wa Mutharika, benefited from Malawi's subsidy program, as the program increased support for the incumbent party. Additionally, the analysis showed that the subsidy program did not target co-ethnics or co-partisans.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the political effects of Malawi's Agricultural Input Subsidy Programme, one of the largest and most expensive programs implemented, which was launched by the government in 2005, using a longitudinal dataset of 1,846 rural Malawians interviewed in 2008 and again in 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of social protection programs in addressing income poverty and rural poverty in sub-Saharan Africa. To scale up the impact of these programs, governments should prioritize targeted distribution of subsidies to the most vulnerable populations, rather than relying solely on universal programs.

Authors: Michael E. Batuo; George Kararach; Issam Malki
Field: Economics; Economic inequality; Income inequality metrics; Kuznets curve; Income distribution; Convergence (economics); Inequality; Per capita income; Comprehensive income; Gini coefficient; Panel data; Per capita; Demographic economics; Macroeconomics; Development economics; Econometrics; Public economics; Gross income; Population; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Sociology; Demography; Tax reform; State income tax
Title: The dynamics of income inequality in Africa: An empirical investigation on the role of macroeconomic and institutional forces
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are multiple steady states of income inequality, and that high-income countries in Africa have increasing income inequality, while low-income countries have decreasing income inequality. Additionally, macroeconomic and institutional factors play a limited role in explaining income inequality, with the exception of fiscal, employment, and monetary policies in high-income economies.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the macroeconomic and institutional drivers of income inequality in Africa using a Kuznets curve framework and panel data models for 52 African countries between 1980 and 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited role of macroeconomic and institutional factors in addressing income inequality, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions such as progressive taxation, investments in education and healthcare, and strengthening the rule of law to tackle income inequality in high-income African economies. In low-income economies, a focus on economic growth and investing in human capital may be more effective in reducing income inequality.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Population; Poverty reduction; Multidimensional poverty; Poor people; Poverty measurement; Distribution (economics); Development economics
Title: Multidimensional Poverty Reduction in India between 1999 and 2006: Where and How?
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: We find a strong reduction in national poverty and each of its dimensions, but this has not been uniform across regions, castes, or religions. Strong reductions among the poorer population nationally, but slower progress for most of the poorest groups.
What_was_studied: This paper thoroughly analyzes the change in multidimensional poverty in India between 1999 and 2006, focusing on the distribution among the poor people nationally as well as within population subgroups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unequal distribution of poverty reduction across groups, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the needs of the poorest populations, particularly in specific regions and demographic subgroups.

Field: Dividend; Macroeconomics; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Cash; Commodity; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Developing country
Keywords: global poverty; inequality; redistribution; natural resource curse; resource wealth; income distribution
Title: Resource Rents, Redistribution, and Halving Global Poverty: The Resource Dividend
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: If every developing country implemented the policy, then the number of people living below $1-a-day would be cut by between 27% and 66%, depending on the year and the assumptions made. Looking ahead, poverty could be better than halved as long as commodity prices do not drop below their 2004 level.
What_was_studied: This paper considers the proposal that each country distributes its resource rents directly to citizens as a universal and unconditional cash transfer, or Resource Dividend, and estimates its potential impact on global poverty for the years 2000–06 using a global dataset on resource rents and the distribution of income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential to halve global poverty, policymakers should prioritize implementing Resource Dividend policies in developing countries, especially if commodity prices remain stable or continue to rise.

Authors: Alex O. Acheampong; Eric Evans Osei Opoku; Godsway Korku Tetteh
Field: Sanitation; Hygiene; Financial inclusion; Inequality; Inclusion (mineral); Environmental health; Economic inequality; Low income; Business; Economics; Development economics; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Financial services; Medicine; Finance; Psychology; Environmental science; Environmental engineering; Mathematical analysis; Social psychology; Mathematics; Pathology
Title: Unveiling the effect of income inequality on safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH): Does financial inclusion matter?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income inequality reduces access to safe WASH facilities, while financial inclusion significantly increases access. Additionally, the study found heterogeneous effects of income inequality and financial inclusion across rural and urban settings, income groups, and geographical regions.
What_was_studied: A comprehensive panel dataset was used to investigate the role of income inequality and financial inclusion on access to improved WASH facilities among 119 countries from 2004 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing income inequality and improving financial inclusion to improve access to safe WASH facilities. This can be achieved by implementing policies that strengthen financial inclusion services and further address income inequality.

Authors: Amit Thorat; Reeve Vanneman; Sonalde Desai; Amaresh Dubey
Field: Fell; Economics; Social group; Poverty; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Extreme poverty; Panel data
Keywords: Education; Escaping; Falling; India; Panel; Poverty; Religious groups; Social Groups
Title: Escaping and Falling into Poverty in India Today
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis shows that the risks of marginalized communities such as Dalits and Adivasis of falling into or remaining in poverty were higher than those for more privileged groups. Some, but not all of these higher risks are explained by educational, financial, and social disadvantages of these groups in 2005.
What_was_studied: Using panel data from the India Human Development Survey for 2005 and 2012, this study examines the dynamic nature of movements into and out of poverty over a period when poverty has fallen substantially in India, identifying people who escaped poverty and those who fell into it over the period 2005 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher risks faced by marginalized communities, policies aimed at reducing poverty should prioritize addressing educational, financial, and social disadvantages for these groups to effectively reduce chronic poverty and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Economy; Consumption (economics); Econometrics; Economics; Natural disaster; Market failure; Order (exchange); LEAPS; Agent-based model; Population; Shock (economics)
Keywords: agent-based model; GIS; migration; food insecurity; Pakistan; earthquake
Title: Deep Impact: Geo-Simulations as a Policy Toolkit for Natural Disasters
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income and consumption levels declined sharply after the earthquake, with high levels of food insecurity. Factors such as distance from the fault line and existing income and saving levels influenced the spatial and temporal emergence of vulnerabilities.
What_was_studied: The spatially explicit bottom-up agent-based model was applied to analyze the impact of natural disasters on low-income regions in northern Pakistan, using data from the 2005 earthquake.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of food insecurity in low-income regions affected by natural disasters, policymakers should prioritize short-term policies that target income support and stabilization of consumption levels, particularly for those living in remote areas with limited connectivity.

Authors: Edward Anderson; Maria Ana Jalles d’Orey; Maren Duvendack; Lucio Esposito
Field: Public economics; Government; Economics; Consumer spending; Poverty; Government revenue; Government spending; Demographic economics; Fiscal policy; Developing country; Estimation
Title: Does Government Spending Affect Income Poverty? A Meta-regression Analysis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds no clear evidence that higher government spending has played a significant role in reducing income poverty in low- and middle-income countries.
