To scale up these effects, policymakers should prioritize and expand cash transfer programs in rural areas, particularly targeting child support grants to impoverished households.

Field: Refugee; Livelihood; Agriculture; Urban agriculture; Geography; Disadvantaged; Economic growth; Political science; Sustainable development; Poverty; Development economics; Socioeconomics; Sociology; Economics; Archaeology; Law
Title: Flowers in the dark: The contribution of rooftop urban agriculture to human well-being in the Ein El-Hilweh Refugee Camp, Lebanon
primary_category: Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our findings suggest that rooftop urban agriculture contributes considerably to more sustainable livelihoods of Palestinian women and their families in the refugee camp by enabling them to develop natural and human capital as the basis for increasing their food security while protecting natural resources.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the livelihood effects of rooftop urban agriculture for Palestinian women in Ein El-Hilweh, Lebanon's largest refugee camp, using a mixed-method approach combining document analysis and a survey of ten female participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Rooftop urban agriculture thus is a low-threshold tool for refugees in protracted displacement that enhances their well-being over the medium term. Scale up this initiative to catalyze social improvement in other protracted refugee situations in the Middle East and elsewhere.

Authors: Achim Ahrens; Marine Casalis; Dominik Hangartner; Rodrigo Sánchez
Field: Psychological intervention; Cash; Immigration; Business; Development economics; Economics; Demographic economics; Public economics; Political science; Medicine; Finance; Nursing; Law
Title: Cash-based interventions improve multidimensional integration outcomes of Venezuelan immigrants
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The CBI increased the IPL-24 index -an overall measure of immigrant integration capturing several dimensions -by at least 0.12 standard deviations.Moreover, the CBI boosted self-employment by 2 percentage points and raised the intention to emigrate from Peru by 1.2 percentage points.
What_was_studied: Since 2015, over 7 million Venezuelans have been forced to leave their homes, seeking refuge predominantly in neighboring countries across Latin America and the Caribbean.The displacement is typically accompanied by vulnerability and marginalization, yet there is a scarcity of actionable evidence on how to alleviate poverty among immigrants and refugees and facilitate their economic, political, and social integration.This study evaluates the impact of a cash-based intervention (CBI) on multidimensional integration outcomes of highly vulnerable Venezuelan immigrants, predominantly women, residing in Peru.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up cash-based interventions (CBI) targeting highly vulnerable Venezuelan immigrants, prioritizing women, to facilitate their economic, political, and social integration in Peru and across the region.By expanding access to CBI programs, governments can address multidimensional poverty and promote self-reliance among marginalized immigrant and refugee families.

Field: Public policy; Development studies; Political science; Poverty; Basic income; Degrowth; Development economics; Indigenous; International development; Politics
Title: Radical transformation or technological intervention? Two paths for universal basic income
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite best intentions, the radical potential of Basic Income may be jeopardized without critical engagement and nuance around questions of power, and that BI may become another technological quick-fix of development and policy interventions.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the potential of Basic Income (BI) to address poverty and economic insecurity, using two case studies: a proposed BI for Indigenous Australians and support for UBI by high-net-worth individuals in California's Silicon Valley.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize critical engagement and nuance in the implementation of Basic Income programs to ensure that they address issues of power and coloniality, rather than simply providing a technological solution to poverty.

Authors: Heather Randell; Chengsheng Jiang; Xin-Zhong Liang; Raghu Murtugudde; Amir Sapkota
Field: Agricultural productivity; Climate change; Monsoon; Extreme weather; Geography; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Global health; Agricultural land; Food security
Keywords: Food security; Nepal; climate change; drought; earthquake; landslides
Title: Food insecurity and compound environmental shocks in Nepal: Implications for a changing climate.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rainfall anomalies had differing effects on food insecurity based on the severity of earthquake exposure. Minimal earthquake exposure was not associated with increased food insecurity, while greater rainfall was positively associated with food insecurity in steep, mountainous areas due to landslides disrupting food aid distribution and damaging agricultural land.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses how earthquake exposure followed by monsoon rainfall anomalies affect food insecurity in Nepal, using data from the 2016 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey and spatial variation in exposure to environmental shocks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering compound environmental shocks when addressing food insecurity. Policymakers should prioritize targeted support for households in vulnerable mountainous regions, scaling up effective food aid distribution networks to mitigate the impacts of climate change.

Field: Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Corruption; Terrorism; Domestic terrorism; Relative deprivation; Gini coefficient; Sample (statistics); Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: Income inequality, redistribution and domestic terrorism
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Higher levels of income inequality are associated with more domestic terrorism, mainly through the ill effects of income inequality on institutional outcomes (e.g., corruption).
What_was_studied: The effect of income inequality on terrorism for a sample of 113 countries between 1984 and 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize redistributive policies to reduce domestic terrorism by improving institutional conditions.

Authors: Dipti Gupta; Frédéric Ghersi; Saritha Vishwanathan; Amit Garg
Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Natural resource economics; Renewable energy; Population; National accounts; Greenhouse gas; Sustainable development; National wealth; Fossil fuel
Title: Achieving sustainable development in India along low carbon pathways: Macroeconomic assessment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that achieving low-carbon development can accommodate yearly economic growth of 5.8% from 2013 to 2050, despite high investment costs, due to improvement in the trade balance and shifts towards low-carbon products and services of higher value-added.
What_was_studied: This study examines the macroeconomic consequences of achieving development along low-carbon pathways in India, focusing on the period from 2013 to 2050 and using a hybrid modeling architecture that combines strengths of bottom-up and top-down models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that India should prioritize and scale up its low-carbon development efforts to address income inequality and poverty, while also ensuring a sustainable future for its growing economy. Policies should focus on reconciling the interests of entrenched businesses in retreating sectors with emerging low-carbon technologies and industries.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Legislation; Real wages; Minimum wage; Enforcement; Context (language use); Informal sector; Developing country; Impact evaluation
Title: Minimum wages for domestic workers: impact evaluation of the Indian experience
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the minimum wage legislation had a positive impact on real wages in the short run but did not have any long-lasting effects. Additionally, the legislation did not seem to affect the probability of employment as a domestic worker over the short or long term.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the impact of minimum wage legislation on wages and employment opportunities in India's informal sector between 2004 and 2012 using a combination of matching procedures and difference-in-difference estimation methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that most workers' wages remained below the minimum wage, policymakers should prioritize strengthening enforcement mechanisms to ensure fair labor practices and expand coverage to more informal sector workers.

Authors: Edwin Goni; Humberto Lopez; Luis Servén
Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Income inequality metrics; Taxable income; Economics; Gross income; International economics; Tax policy; Household income; Development economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Keywords: fiscal redistribution; income inequality; fiscal reform
Title: Fiscal Redistribution And Income Inequality In Latin America - Fiscal Redistribution and Income Inequality in Latin America
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that the differences in income inequality before taxes and transfers between Latin America and Western Europe are modest, but the fiscal system in most Latin American countries is of little help in reducing income inequality. Additionally, fiscal redistribution is achieved mostly through transfers rather than taxes.
What_was_studied: This paper documents the performance of Latin American fiscal systems from the perspective of income redistribution using newly-available information on the incidence of taxes and transfers across the region during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This highlights the need for fiscal reforms across the region to further social equity, prioritizing the restructuring of tax systems and improving the targeting of expenditures to address income poverty and health disparities.

Authors: Bianca Stumbitz; Suzan Lewis; Abigail Kyei; Fergus Lyon
Field: Business; Statutory law; Developed country; Reciprocity (cultural anthropology); Work (electrical); Element (criminal law); Breastfeeding; Economic growth; Informal sector; Developing country
Title: Maternity protection in formal and informal economy workplaces: the case of Ghana
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The findings show a range of measures related to pregnancy, maternity leave, family-friendly flexible working conditions, breastfeeding, and childcare. While large formal economy organizations mostly offer MP measures corresponding to regulatory entitlements, women working in small informal economy businesses often only benefit from informal MP support.
What_was_studied: This paper explores different forms of maternity protection (MP) found in various forms and sizes of enterprise in Ghana, specifically how workplaces in the formal and informal economy manage MP and how reciprocity shapes workers' access to different forms of MP support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the important roles of reciprocity and relationships built on trust as conditions for family-friendly MP provisions, particularly in the informal economy workplaces. Policymakers should prioritize and expand these informal MP supports to ensure all working women in Ghana have access to adequate maternity protection.

Field: Public economics; Baseline (configuration management); Economics; Poverty; Revenue; Beneficiary; Climate Finance; Population; Economic inequality; Sustainable development
Title: Can the Paris deal boost SDGs achievement? An assessment of climate mitigation co-benefits or side-effects on poverty and inequality
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a full implementation of the emission reduction contributions stated in the NDCs is projected to slow down the effort to reduce poverty by 2030, especially in countries with relatively more stringent mitigation targets and higher policy costs, while the impact of climate policy on inequality remains very limited.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the potential synergies and trade-offs between emission reduction policies and sustainable development objectives, specifically looking at the impact of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) on poverty eradication (SDG1) and reduced income inequality (SDG10) in a reference scenario and under a climate mitigation policy with alternative revenue recycling schemes, using an empirical analysis and modelling exercise to estimate future trends of poverty prevalence and inequality across countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that financial support for mitigation action in developing countries through an international climate fund could reduce poverty at the aggregate level, but the country-specific effect depends on the relative size of funds flowing to beneficiary countries and their economic structure, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of the Paris Agreement and its climate finance tools to maximize the benefits of climate action for sustainable development.

Field: Public policy; Business; Globalization; Social protection; Context (language use); Development economics; Social Welfare; Population growth; Crowding out; Developing country
Keywords: (JEL D64, H31, H55, J14, J22, J26, O15, O16, R2) life cycle, retirement; social protection; developing countries; crowdout effect; inter vivos transfers
Title: Do Public Program Benefits Crowd Out Private Transfers in Developing Countries? A Critical Review of Recent Evidence
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while social protection programs have expanded in LMICs, there is a risk of displacement of informal mechanisms for risk-protection, potentially leading to social welfare loss if the displacement is considerable. Specifically, the study identifies heterogeneous treatment effects by important socio-economic characteristics.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the crowd-out effects of public policies in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) over the last three decades, focusing on social protection programs in response to rapid globalization, rising inequality, population growth, and longevity gains.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given poverty reduction objectives and careful program targeting that accounts for potential crowd-out effects, there may well be a net social gain from expanding social protection programs in LMICs. Policymakers should prioritize program design that balances the need for poverty reduction with the risk of displacement of informal support systems.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Capital asset; Asset (economics); Rural poverty; Peasant; Economic growth; Civil society; Sustainability; Social capital; Economic system
Keywords: sustainable livelihoods; assets; social capital; peasants; Latin America; Andes
Title: Capitals and Capabilities: A Framework for Analyzing Peasant Viability, Rural Livelihoods and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that people's access to productive resources, such as land and technology, is a crucial factor in reducing rural poverty and ensuring sustainable development. The findings also indicate that social capital plays a significant role in expanding asset bases and improving livelihood outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes rural livelihoods in Latin America based on five types of capital assets and their sustainability, with a particular focus on social capital as an asset that enables access to resources and actors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of productive resources and social capital in rural poverty reduction, decision-makers should prioritize policies that scale up access to these assets, such as land reform programs and investments in technology and social infrastructure.

Authors: Dominik Hartmann; Miguel Guevara; Cristian Jara-Figueroa; Manuel Aristarán; César A. Hidalgo
Field: Income inequality metrics; Macroeconomics; Econometrics; Economics; Social inequality; Income in kind; Economic complexity index; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Net national income; Gross domestic income
Title: Linking Economic Complexity, Institutions, and Income Inequality
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that countries exporting complex products have lower levels of income inequality compared to those exporting simpler products. This relationship is robust even after controlling for aggregate measures of income, institutions, export concentration, and human capital.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between a country's productive structure and income inequality using a combination of econometric, network science, and economic complexity methods to analyze data from 150 countries over 45 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize investments in complex product development and diversification to reduce income inequality, particularly in countries with high levels of export concentration in simple products. By focusing on the development of more sophisticated products, policymakers can promote structural transformation and economic growth that benefits a broader segment of society.

Authors: Ben D'Exelle; Alistair Munro; Arjan Verschoor
Field: Contingency; Investment (military); Contingency plan; Economics; Agriculture; Public economics; Geography; Political science; Management; Philosophy; Linguistics; Archaeology; Politics; Law
Title: Agricultural investment behaviour and contingency: Experimental evidence from Uganda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Perceived contingency influences investment behavior; perceived contingency can be readily changed, leading to sub-optimal investment in agriculture and contributing to rural poverty.
What_was_studied: Investment decisions of poor farmers in Uganda during a time of low contingency (e.g., weather fluctuations, pests) using an experiment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address rural poverty and promote agricultural investment, policy should prioritize increasing farmers' awareness of contingency in their decision-making processes.

Field: Agriculture; Agency (sociology); Randomized experiment; Marketing; Political science; Poverty; Fence (finance); Context (language use); Field (Bourdieu); Developing country
Title: How experimental research in agriculture has gone from lab to field
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that randomized field experiments in agriculture can lead to significant improvements in income, food security, and gender empowerment for smallholder farmers in developing countries. For example, the study found that a program aimed at improving rice production in Cambodia increased women's participation in rice production by 25% and their income by 18%.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of randomized field experiments in agriculture, specifically on gender and poverty outcomes, in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the potential of randomized field experiments in agriculture to scale up gender-sensitive interventions that address poverty in developing countries. Policymakers should prioritize funding for such interventions and adapt the methodology to better suit the challenging context of developing country agriculture.

Authors: Tolu I.A. Olarewaju; Tomasz Mickiewicz; Jagannadha Pawan Tamvada
Field: Quantile; Economics; Wage; Minimum wage; Glass ceiling; Middle income; Demographic economics; Income distribution; Selection (genetic algorithm); Entrepreneurship
Title: The Returns to Occupations: The Role of Minimum Wage and Gender in Nigeria
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that although the majority of employers experience labor wage premiums throughout the income distribution, self-employed own account individuals experience a wage penalty at the lower quantiles of the income distribution where paid workers reap benefits from minimum wage guarantees, suggesting that minimum wage legislations may push individuals with low skills into self-employment.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the economic returns to being employers, paid workers and self-employed own account individuals in a lower middle income economy using quantile regressions while accounting for selection using Heckman selection models during a specific time period with particular data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of self-employment on poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize education and training programs to improve the skills of low-income individuals and consider revising minimum wage legislation to protect workers' rights.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Per capita income; Instrumental variable; Economics; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Fractionalization
Keywords: Inequality; Ethnic Fractionalization; Growth JEL Codes: O11, O15, O16
Title: Inequality and Fractionalization
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that ethnic fractionalization has a negative impact on per capita income, schooling, and institutional quality, even after controlling for income inequality. Moreover, the findings suggest that income inequality does not have a significant effect on these outcomes when ethnic fragmentation is properly treated as an endogenous variable.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between ethnic fragmentation and socioeconomic development outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa between 1990 and 2010, using instrumental variables estimation to control for endogeneity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing ethnic fragmentation and promoting inclusive economic growth strategies to improve development outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa, rather than solely focusing on income inequality.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Aggregate income; Economics; Social inequality; Total personal income; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Demography, Growth, and Global Income Inequality
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that global income inequality will reach its lowest point in 2027 before rising again, driven by both economic and demographic forces. GDP per worker was a better predictor of income levels than GDP per capita, highlighting the importance of demographics in income inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines global income inequality trends from 1980 to 2030 using GDP per worker and demographic data to forecast future patterns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the long-term rise in global income inequality after 2030 by focusing on sustainable development, intersectional poverty reduction, and social protection programs that address the needs of diverse populations.

Field: Public economics; International trade and water; Scarcity; Per capita; Economics; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Economic growth; Water scarcity; Utilitarianism; Operationalization
Title: Water and Human Development
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that both EA and CA strengthen the case for the human right to water, highlighting the need to address water inequalities and prioritize the needs and interests of marginalized communities. Furthermore, the research finds that operationalizing CA and EA poses challenges but is necessary to break down false distinctions between water for domestic and productive purposes.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the human development approach to the water 'crisis', focusing on the application of the entitlements approach (EA) and capabilities approach (CA) to water inequalities in various regions, using a mixed-methods research design with a time period of 2015-2020 and data from surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize a human development approach to water policy, scaling up efforts to address water inequalities and ensure equitable access to clean water for all communities, especially marginalized ones. This can be achieved by revising current water policies to incorporate the entitlements and capabilities approaches and increasing funding for water infrastructure and education programs in marginalized areas.

Field: Inequality; Economic inequality; Economics; Property crime; Affect (linguistics); Income distribution; Income inequality metrics; Econometrics; Distribution (mathematics); Demographic economics; Yield (engineering); Bayesian probability; Public economics; Positive economics; Criminology; Sociology; Violent crime; Statistics; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis; Materials science; Communication; Metallurgy
Title: Revisiting the Income Inequality-Crime Puzzle
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate a statistically significant but economically insignificant true effect of inequality on crime, ranging between 0.007 and 0.123 using UWLS FAT-PET and advanced methods. In essence, if there is an impact of inequality on crime, it is, at best, minimal.
What_was_studied: This meta-analysis based on 1,341 estimates drawn from 43 studies in economics journals examines the relationship between income inequality and crime across different populations, time periods, and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited impact of income inequality on crime, policy efforts should focus more on addressing other factors that contribute to criminal behavior, such as poverty, education, and mental health. Additionally, future studies should consider including more comprehensive measures of income inequality, such as those sensitive to changes in the middle and top of the distribution.

Authors: Eleanor Fisher; Ramlatu Attah; Valentina Barca; Clare O’Brien; Simon Brook; Jeremy Holland; Andrew Kardan; Sara Pavanello; Pamela Pozarny
Field: Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Beneficiary; Human capital; Social protection; Cash transfers; Livelihood; Development economics; Social Welfare
Title: The Livelihood Impacts of Cash Transfers in Sub-Saharan Africa: Beneficiary Perspectives from Six Countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: A small but predictable flow of cash improves strategic livelihood choices and stimulates productive investments, including through positive effects on beneficiary entry into risk-sharing arrangements and networks for economic collaboration.
What_was_studied: This cross-case analysis using original qualitative data on beneficiary perspectives from six African countries examines whether and how cash transfers (CTs) go beyond welfare objectives to promote livelihoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of household vulnerability and labor constraint in mediating CT livelihood impacts, policy makers should prioritize targeting the most vulnerable households and ensuring effective program implementation to consolidate livelihood outcomes. Additionally, incorporating beneficiary perspectives can bring realism to the influence of CTs on both immediate survival and long-term livelihood choices.

Authors: Monica K. Kansiime; Justice A. Tambo; Idah Mugambi; Mary Bundi; Augustine M. Kara; Charles Owuor
Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Poverty; Respondent; Social security; Household income; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Shock (economics); Food security
Keywords: COVID-19; Coping strategies; Dietary quality; Food security; Probit model; Social security
Title: COVID-19 implications on household income and food security in Kenya and Uganda: Findings from a rapid assessment.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: More than two-thirds of the respondents experienced income shocks, leading to worsened food security and reduced consumption of nutritious foods, with income-poor households and those dependent on labor income being more vulnerable. Farmers were less likely to experience food insecurity compared to other respondent categories.
What_was_studied: This study assessed the implications of the COVID-19 pandemic on household income and food security in Kenya and Uganda using online survey data from 442 respondents over a specific time period, focusing on income shocks, food security, and dietary quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Government responses should focus on structural changes in social security, building strong financial institutions, and ensuring the resilience of food supply chains to support the recovery of businesses in the medium term and cushion members pushed into poverty by such pandemics. Savings and loan groups can help mitigate income shocks and reduce food consumption.

Authors: Pierre André; Esther Delesalle; Christelle Dumas
Field: Agricultural productivity; Payment; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Production (economics); Tanzania; Conditional cash transfer; Demographic economics; Opportunity cost; Developing country
Title: Returns to farm child labor in Tanzania
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: One day of child work leads to an increase in production value by roughly US$0.89. Children enrolled in school work 26 fewer days than nonenrolled children.
What_was_studied: This paper studies one of these opportunity costs: we estimate the agricultural productivity of children aged 10 to 15 years old using the LSMS-ISA panel survey in Tanzania during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up universal education, policymakers should prioritize compensating enrolled children for loss in income with monthly payments of $1.92. This can be achieved through a complete simulation of a hypothetical conditional cash transfer.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Income Support; Right to work; Cash transfers; Basic income; Workfare; Developing country
Title: Guaranteed employment or guaranteed income
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The evidence suggests that the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act has had a limited impact on reducing poverty, despite pro-poor targeting, with work often being rationed by local leaders and the poverty impact being small when all costs are considered.
What_was_studied: The paper critically reviews the arguments for and against both employment guarantees and income guarantees when viewed as rights-based policy instruments for poverty reduction in a developing economy, focusing on India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and its impact on poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize incentive-neutral, universal and/or state-contingent transfer schemes over workfare programs like the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act to reduce poverty more effectively in developing economies.

Authors: Channing Arndt; Rui Benfica; James Thurlow
Field: Economics; Natural resource economics; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Agricultural policy; Agricultural economics; Income distribution; Biofuel; Food security; Food processing
Keywords: Biofuels; gender; growth; poverty; land abundance; Africa
Title: Gender Implications of Biofuels Expansion in Africa : The Case of Mozambique
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Biofuels investments accelerate GDP growth and reduce poverty, but intense female labor use in feedstock production leads to a stronger trade-off between biofuels and food availability, and skills shortages among female workers limit poverty reduction. Modest improvements in women's education and food crop yields can address food security concerns and ensure broader-based benefits from biofuels investments.
What_was_studied: This study uses a gendered dynamic CGE model to assess the implications of biofuels expansion in a low-income, land-abundant setting, with Mozambique as a representative case, comparing scenarios with different gender employment intensities in producing jatropha feedstock for biodiesel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize education and food production initiatives to maximize the benefits of biofuels investments for women and address food security concerns.

Field: Agriculture; Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Absolute (philosophy); Population; Economic growth; Political risk; Scale (social sciences); Human ecology
Title: The Nature and Extent of World Poverty
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that over half of the world's population suffers from absolute deprivation, with the number growing yearly due to population growth.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the state of global undernourishment, ill-health, inadequate housing, and illiteracy from 1960 to 2000, using data from United Nations organizations such as the Food and Agricultural Organization and the World Health Organization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments must prioritize addressing income poverty and health disparities on a greater scale than ever before to combat these issues and provide adequate resources for all individuals.

Field: Agriculture; Macroeconomics; Latin Americans; Economics; Macro; Chain (unit); Rural poverty; Policy decision; Trickle down; Economic system; Transaction cost
Title: Meso-Economic Filters Along the Policy Chain: Understanding the Links Between Policy Reforms and Rural Poverty in Latin America
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the 'meso-economy' plays a crucial role in filtering policy decisions and market signals, with three levels of filters intervening along the policy chain. Specifically, the paper identifies the importance of understanding the roles played by these filters to address income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, and urban poverty.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the 'meso-economy' concept, clarifying its definition as encompassing market mechanisms and administrative procedures that impact policy decisions and market signals at the household level, using a synthesis of macro-, meso-, and micro-economic perspectives and reviewing three main bodies of literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize analyzing and addressing the 'meso-economy' role in filtering policy decisions and market signals to effectively address income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, and urban poverty. This can be achieved by scaling up the use of meso-economic analysis, expanding research on the 'meso-economy' concept, and funding policies that target these filters to improve the efficiency of policy interventions.

Authors: Alan de Brauw; Daniel O. Gilligan; John Hoddinott; Shalini Roy
Field: Rural area; Labour economics; Economics; Conditional cash transfer; Propensity score weighting; Demographic economics; Percentage point; Differential (mechanical device)
Keywords: conditional cash transfer programs; education; Bolsa Famı ´lia; Brazil; girls' schooling
Title: The Impact of Bolsa Família on Schooling
primary_category: Education access; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the program significantly increased school participation among girls (by 8 percentage points) and grade progression (by 10 percentage points), with larger effects in rural areas and among older girls. Few significant impacts were found among boys.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of Brazil's Bolsa Familia program on schooling outcomes of children aged 6-17 in rural and urban areas, using longitudinal household data and propensity score weighting methods over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of the Bolsa Familia program on girls' schooling outcomes, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support girls' education in rural areas, particularly among older girls.

Authors: Channing Arndt; Roberta Distante; M. Azhar Hussain; Lars Peter Østerdal; Pham Lan Huong; Maimuna Ibraimo
Field: Welfare; Econometrics; Complementarity (molecular biology); Dimension (data warehouse); Child poverty; Population; First order; Household survey; Mathematics; Dominance (ethology)
Title: Ordinal Welfare Comparisons with Multiple Discrete Indicators : A First Order Dominance Approach and Application to Child Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The approach developed in this study allows for making welfare comparisons between populations with multidimensional discrete well-being indicators, and it was applied to household survey data from Vietnam and Mozambique. The findings showed that the majority of households in both countries experienced multidimensional poverty, and there were significant differences in well-being levels across different dimensions and populations.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed household survey data from Vietnam and Mozambique to compare welfare levels across populations with multidimensional discrete well-being indicators observed at the micro level between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's approach and findings provide a new perspective on multidimensional poverty and welfare comparisons between populations. Based on the results, policymakers should prioritize addressing food insecurity and social protection policies to scale up support for vulnerable households and improve overall well-being levels.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Sanctions; Economic sanctions; Population; Economic inequality; Democracy; Duration (project management)
Keywords: Economic sanctions; Income inequality; Target states. JEL Codes: D31; F51; O15
Title: The Impact of Economic Sanctions on Income Inequality of Target States
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic sanctions significantly increase income inequality, with financial and trade sanctions having different effects. The adverse effect of sanctions on income inequality is more pronounced when sanctions last longer.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of economic sanctions on income inequality in 68 target states from 1960 to 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust empirical evidence that sanctions exacerbate income inequality, policymakers should prioritize alternative measures to address international conflicts and human rights abuses, such as targeted aid programs or diplomatic initiatives. This could involve scaling up investments in education access, gender and poverty reduction programs, and urban poverty alleviation initiatives to offset the adverse effects of sanctions.

Field: Politics; Human settlement; Political science; Development economics; Economic growth; Geography; Economics; Archaeology; Law
Title: Political settlements analysis and the study of pro-poor development: Laos and Rwanda compared
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Both countries have achieved significant reductions in multidimensional poverty through large-scale investments in social services and centralized, ideologically committed ruling coalitions. However, economic growth has been misdirected towards extractive industries and high-end services, leading to limited employment opportunities, increased inequality, and vulnerability to land pressures and climate change.
What_was_studied: The article examines the political settlements analysis framework to understand pro-poor economic development in Laos and Rwanda, focusing on employment, social provision, and poverty reduction strategies over the past two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize pro-poor development strategies that focus on sustainable agriculture, productive employment, and social protection programs to address income poverty, intersectional poverty, and health disparities in Laos and Rwanda.

Field: Latin Americans; Exploit; Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Social protection; Cash; Population; Distancing; Development economics
Keywords: COVID-19; Compliance; Lockdown; Poverty; Work mobility
Title: Poverty and COVID-19 in Africa and Latin America.
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that work-related mobility was significantly lower in high-poverty regions compared to other regions during the first lockdown period, and that higher poverty has induced a faster spread of the virus.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between work-related mobility and poverty during the COVID-19 pandemic in 242 regions of nine Latin American and African countries from March 2020 to May 2020, using Google mobility data and poverty statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that social protection measures in the form of food or cash transfers should be complementary to physical distancing measures to attenuate the difference between poor and non-poor regions in terms of exposure to the virus. Policymakers should prioritize targeted support for vulnerable populations to mitigate health disparities and ensure that no one is left behind.

Authors: Alan de Brauw; Daniel O. Gilligan; John Hoddinott; Shalini Roy
Field: Social class; Business; Socioeconomic status; Latin Americans; Family planning; Conditional cash transfer; Population; Demographic economics; Durable good; Developing country
Title: The Impact of Bolsa Família on Women’s Decision-Making Power
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Bolsa Familia significantly increased women's decision-making power regarding contraception in aggregate, with specific effects in urban households where it also increased women's power in spheres related to children's school attendance and health expenses, household durable goods purchases, and contraception use. In rural households, no such increase was found and there may even be a reduction in women's decision-making power.
What_was_studied: The effects of Brazil's Bolsa Familia program on female decision-making power in urban and rural households, using data from 2001 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeting social protection programs like Bolsa Familia towards female beneficiaries to scale up the scope of increasing women's intrahousehold decision-making power, especially in urban areas. Expanding program coverage and improving its design could be a key strategy for addressing multidimensional poverty and gender inequality in Brazil.

Field: Poverty; Extreme poverty; China; Development economics; Basic needs; Geography; Population; Culture of poverty; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Political science; Socioeconomics; Economics; Sociology; Demography; Archaeology; Law
Journal/Venue: Atlas of Sustainable Development Goals 2018: From World Development Indicators
Title: No poverty: End poverty in all its forms everywhere
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The number of people living in extreme poverty has decreased by over one billion since 1990, though the world's population has grown. Today, more extreme poor live in Sub-Saharan Africa than South Asia and East Asia & Pacific combined.
What_was_studied: This study examines the changing geography of extreme poverty between 1990 and 2013, with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and regional distribution shifts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize sustainable development efforts and address chronic poverty, policymakers should focus on targeting support toward the poorest populations in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the largest number of extreme poor now reside.

Authors: André Cieplinski; Simone D'Alessandro; Chandni Dwarkasing; Pietro Guarnieri
Field: Economics; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Labour economics; Unpaid work; Economic inequality; Inequality; Basic income; Income distribution; Aggregate income; Working time; Redistribution of income and wealth; Work (physics); Wage; Demographic economics; Care work; Macroeconomics; Unemployment; Economic growth; Mathematics; Mechanical engineering; Mathematical analysis; Market economy; Engineering
Title: Narrowing women's time and income gaps: An assessment of the synergies between working time reduction and universal income schemes
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while working time reduction directly reduces the amount of unpaid work done by women, it does not address time poverty. Universal income schemes, particularly care income, reduce gender inequality in terms of income but do not affect the wage gap between men and women.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of policy mixes on reducing time poverty and the gender income gap in Italy using Eurogreen, a macrosimulation model, and comparing two policy mixes: working time reduction and universal income schemes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize universal income schemes that target care work to address time poverty and promote gender equality in Italy.

Authors: Nithya Natarajan; Andrew Newsham; Jonathan Rigg; Diana Suhardiman
Field: Livelihood; Framing (construction); Foregrounding; Popularity; Sustainability; Sustainable development; Sociology; Political science; Globalization; Development studies; Geography; Agriculture; Ecology; Law; Archaeology; Philosophy; Linguistics; Biology
Title: A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century
primary_category: Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article highlights problems of theory, method, scale, historical conceptualisation, politics, and debates on decolonising knowledge.
What_was_studied: This paper proposes a reformulation of the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (SLF) fit for the 21st century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and fund research that incorporates a structural, spatially-disaggregated, dynamic, and ecologically-coherent approach to framing rural livelihoods.

Field: Sociology; Cognition; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Young female; Positive relationship; Family health; Phenomenon; Social psychology; Moderation
Keywords: Psychology of discrimination; children survival; gender; India
Title: The Missing Link Between Parents’ Preferences and Daughters’ Survival: The Moderator Effect of Societal Discrimination
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the positive marginal effect of wanted daughters on their survival decreases with higher societal discrimination against young females, suggesting that alleviating poverty alone may not be sufficient to reduce sex-based discriminatory practices and that multidimensional interventions are required.
What_was_studied: The premature mortality of female children in many countries and the effect of son preference on their survival, using data from the third round of the National Family Health Survey in India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize intersectional poverty reduction strategies that target both economic and societal factors to address the systemic gender bias that perpetuates child mortality. Interventions aimed at improving cognitive and noncognitive skills among young females can help mitigate the negative effects of discrimination and promote survival.

Authors: Ross Warwick; Thomas R. Harris; David Phillips; Maya Goldman; Jon Jellema; Gabriela Inchauste; Karolina Goraus-Tanska
Field: Public economics; Tax revenue; Business; Goods and services; Poverty; Revenue; Social protection; Cash; Cash transfers; Extreme poverty
Keywords: Cash transfers; Inequality; Microsimulation; Redistribution; Taxation; Value-added tax
Title: The redistributive power of cash transfers vs VAT exemptions: A multi-country study
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Although preferential VAT rates reduce poverty, they are not well targeted towards poor households overall. Existing cash transfer schemes are better targeted but generally have limited coverage.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the effectiveness of such policies in six LMICs using tax-benefit microsimulation models incorporating input–output tables, allowing us to estimate the impact of exemptions on consumer prices due to VAT embedded in supply chains.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: A UT funded by a broader VAT base would create large net gains for the poorest households, reducing inequality and most measures of extreme poverty in each of the countries studied. Such reforms therefore warrant consideration for LMICs as they pursue Domestic Revenue Mobilisation and broader development objectives.

Field: Product market; Development studies; Economics; Trade barrier; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Contract farming; Estate; Foreign direct investment; Development economics
Keywords: JEL Classification: F14; F16; I3; Q12; Q13; Q17 trade, poverty, standards, vertical coordination, contract farming
Title: Trade, Standards, and Poverty: Evidence from Senegal
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Exports grew sharply despite increasing standards, contributing importantly to rural incomes and poverty reduction. Tightening standards induced a shift from smallholder contract farming to integrated estate production, altering the mechanism through which poor households benefit: through labor markets instead of product markets.
What_was_studied: The vegetable export chain in Senegal between 2000 and 2015 using company and household survey data to quantify the income and poverty effects of high-standards trade and integrate labor market effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize integrating labor market effects in trade agreements and standards to ensure that high-standards trade contributes to poverty reduction in rural areas.

Authors: Florence Bétrisey; Christophe Mager; Stephan Rist
Field: Ecosystem management; Economics; Culture of poverty; Natural resource management; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Commodification of nature; Sustainable management; Natural resource; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Local views and structural determinants of poverty alleviation through payments for environmental services: Bolivian insights
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that PES schemes can increase both natural resource conservation and social justice in marginalized areas, but the benefits are not always distributed equitably. The research highlighted the importance of considering a relational understanding of poverty to better address the complexities of poverty alleviation.
What_was_studied: A Bolivian Payment for Environmental Services (PES) scheme was analyzed to understand the poverty alleviation implications of natural resource management initiatives, using a relational understanding of poverty that considers local views and structural determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize PES schemes that consider a relational understanding of poverty, ensuring that the benefits are equitably distributed and that natural resource conservation is combined with social justice initiatives to address chronic poverty in marginalized areas.

Authors: Zora Kovacic; Josephine Kaviti Musango; Lorraine Amollo Ambole; Kareem Buyana; Suzanne Smit; Christer Anditi; Baraka Mwau; Madara Ogot; Shuaib Lwasa; Alan C. Brent; Gloria Nsangi; Hakimu Sseviiri
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Development studies; Economic geography; Settlement (litigation); Population; Corporate governance; Urban planning; Phenomenon; Focus group
Title: Interrogating differences: A comparative analysis of Africa’s informal settlements
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings show gender asymmetries in urban poverty and the intricate links between energy choices, health and economic status.
What_was_studied: This paper explores what differences reveal about the governance of informal settlements through a comparative analysis of three different informal settlements in Sub-Saharan Africa, using an urban societal metabolism approach based on questionnaires and focus group discussions in Enkanini (Stellenbosch, South Africa), Mathare (Nairobi, Kenya), and Kasubi-Kawaala (Kampala, Uganda).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding differences leads to the formulation of modest and localised goals, which are better able to take into account the complexity of urban informality. Governance should prioritize analyzing informal settlements at multiple levels of analysis: the individual, the household and the settlement.

Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Public finance; Order (exchange); Poverty; State (polity); Tax policy; Aid effectiveness; Double taxation; Fiscal policy
Title: Fiscal Composition and Aid Effectiveness: A Political Economy Model ☆
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that a broadening of the tax structure in low-income countries is crucial for effective aid and economic growth. The study reveals a positive correlation between tax effort and poverty reduction indicators, with a one percentage point increase in tax effort resulting in a 0.45 percentage point decrease in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between tax effort and aid effectiveness in low-income countries over a 10-year period, using panel data from 1996 to 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the effectiveness of aid in reducing child poverty, urban poverty, and income poverty, policymakers should prioritize broadening the tax structure in low-income countries, scaling up tax collection efforts, and investing in diversified taxation systems.

Field: Welfare; Consumption (economics); Standard of living; Economics; Minimum wage; Compliance (psychology); De facto; Demographic economics; Developing country
Title: Minimum wage compliance and household welfare: An analysis of over 1500 minimum wages in India
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that non-compliance rates can be as high as 90% for some unskilled workers in India, and that minimum wage increases lead to higher wages and consumption, but the positive effects are reduced in low compliance regimes.
What_was_studied: The study examines the consequences of imperfect compliance with minimum wage regulations in India from 1999 to 2011, using data on unskilled workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving compliance with minimum wage regulations to ensure that the intended benefits of minimum wage policies reach workers effectively, especially in low-compliance regimes.

Field: Fell; Labour economics; Per capita income; Economics; Real wages; Unemployment; Employment growth; Inequality; Income distribution; Extreme poverty
Keywords: Costa Rica; employment; economic growth; income distribution; labor market
Title: Employment and economic growth in Costa Rica
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that Costa Rica's economic growth has had favorable consequences for the labor market and income distribution, with employment growth keeping pace with labor force growth, improving job quality, and reducing poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines Costa Rica's economic growth over the past 25 years and its impact on labor market and income distribution outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and scale up economic growth strategies that benefit all segments of society, especially in times of crisis, to maintain positive labor market and income distribution outcomes.

Authors: Jeffrey Althouse; Louison Cahen-Fourot; Bruno Carballa-Smichowski; Cédric Durand; Steven Knauss
Field: Environmental degradation; Economics; Value (mathematics); Reproduction; Resource curse; Investment (military); Economic geography; Ecology; Natural resource economics; Development economics; Biology; Political science; Natural resource; Machine learning; Politics; Computer science; Law
Title: Ecologically unequal exchange and uneven development patterns along global value chains
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds three distinct patterns of development and GVC insertion: 'curse of GVC marginalization', 'ecologically perverse upgrading', and 'reproduction of the core'. The results confirm the asymmetry in ecological degradation between high-income and low-income economies, but also reveal that environmental asymmetries are driven by differences in how countries participate in GVCs.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the relationship between participation in global value chains (GVCs) and ecologically unequal exchange (EUE) across 133 countries from 1995 to 2015, using principal components analysis and clustering analysis to identify patterns of development and environmental impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that countries with a higher capacity to capture value from GVC participation should prioritize ecologically-efficient processes to mitigate the negative impact of EUE on domestic ecological degradation. Moreover, marginalization from GVCs constitutes a barrier to socio-economic benefits and should be addressed through targeted policies to promote sustainable development.

Authors: Arild Angelsen; Pamela Jagger; Ronnie Babigumira; Brian Belcher; Nicholas J. Hogarth; Simone Bauch; Jan Börner; Carsten Smith-Hall; Sven Wunder
Field: Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Total personal income; Poverty; Income shares; Household income; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Net national income; Developing country
Keywords: forests; household income surveys; inequality; poverty
Title: Environmental income and rural livelihoods: a global-comparative analysis.
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that environmental income accounts for 28% of total household income, with 77% coming from natural forests. Additionally, the poor rely more heavily on subsistence products such as wood fuels and wild foods, and on products harvested from natural areas other than forests.
What_was_studied: This paper presents results from a comparative analysis of environmental income from approximately 8000 households in 24 developing countries collected by research partners in CIFOR's Poverty Environment Network (PEN) over a specific period of time, with a focus on the household level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of prioritizing policies that support sustainable forest management and rural livelihoods to address poverty and food insecurity in developing countries. Specifically, policymakers should scale up investments in sustainable forest management and rural development programs to increase environmental income for low-income households.

Authors: Anand Sahasranaman; Luís M. A. Bettencourt
Field: Rural area; Standard of living; Socioeconomic status; Geography; Poverty trap; Population; Urbanization; Socioeconomics; Urban geography; Service delivery framework
Title: Life between the city and the village: Scaling analysis of service access in Indian urban slums
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that slums in larger cities attract more migrants and offer, on average, higher levels of service access than those in smaller cities. Slums also provide greater access to services than rural areas, which may explain why larger Indian cities have remained attractive to rural populations in terms of living standards.
What_was_studied: Using Census of India data, this study analyzed the growth and persistence of slums in fast-developing Indian cities between 1991 and 2011 to determine if living conditions in slums constitute a path to human development or a poverty trap for much of the population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address urban inequity and ensure that all residents have access to basic services like water, sanitation, and electricity, policymakers should prioritize investments in public service delivery in northern, central, and eastern Indian cities, where service access is, on average, poorer than in southern and western India.

Field: Caste; Discretion; Poverty; Local government; Economics; Politics; Public good; Public economics; Economic growth; Public administration; Political science; Microeconomics; Law
Title: Clientelistic politics and pro-poor targeting: Rules versus discretionary budgets
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that targeting of anti-poverty programs was progressive both within and across gram panchayats (GPs), while the targeting of public goods was not, indicating clientelistic opportunism of upper level officials. The SFC-rule based formula resulted in allocations that were less progressive than the observed allocation.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the consequences of replacing the observed allocation of local government program budgets based on discretion of higher level officials with a grant allocation determined by a formula recommended by the 3rd West Bengal State Finance Commission (SFC) based on measures of village need in rural India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that switching to a formula-based grant system may not improve pro-poor targeting, and instead, alternative formulae with varying weights on GP characteristics could marginally improve pro-poor targeting. This highlights the need for careful consideration of allocation mechanisms to ensure equitable distribution of resources and address poverty in rural India.

Field: Scarcity; Agriculture; Consumption (economics); Business; Resource (biology); Crop diversity; Agricultural economics; Food security; Food systems; Food processing
Title: “Food aid is killing Himalayan farms”. Debunking the false dependency narrative in Karnali, Nepal
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results showed no indication of 'dependency' as alleged in the narrative. Despite the free/concessional food transfers, the local farms have not only maintained diverse traditional crops but also exhibited recent agricultural innovation, resulting in an increase in on-farm crop diversity. On average, local grains contribute about 65% of the total local consumption, indicating a well-embedded diet pattern with the local food system.
What_was_studied: A mixed-method study conducted in Humla, a highly food-insecure district in western Nepal to examine the dependency narrative surrounding food aid and its impact on local agriculture and diet patterns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, we argue that removing food aid in the guise of 'dependency' will directly affect many poor farmers' food access and leave an increased number of Himalayan farmers vulnerable to food insecurity in the face of emerging environmental and socio-economic stresses. To mitigate these risks, policymakers should prioritize climate-resilient agriculture, fund local agricultural innovation, and scale up sustainable development initiatives in the Himalayan region.

Authors: Michael Grimm; Peter Knorringa; Jann Lay
Keywords: Informality; Entrepreneurship; Capital; Managerial Ability; Targeting; West-Africa JEL codes: D22; O17
Title: Constrained Gazelles: High Potentials in West Africa's Informal Economy
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that even among lower-tier entrepreneurs, profitability can be quite high, with 25% of respondents generating profits above the national average. Additionally, the research identified a distinct group of 'constrained gazelles' who face significant barriers to growth but have the potential to scale up with targeted support.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the profitability and growth potential of entrepreneurs in the informal sector of seven West African countries over a one-year period, using a unique dataset combining structural and macroeconomic indicators.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize providing targeted support to 'constrained gazelles' in the informal sector, such as access to finance and training programs, to help them overcome growth barriers and scale up their businesses. This could lead to increased employment opportunities and reduced income poverty in the region.

Authors: Tira Foran; James R.A. Butler; Liana J. Williams; W. J. Wanjura; Andy Hall; Lucy Carter; Peter Carberry
Field: Agriculture; Conceptual framework; Sociology; Agroecology; Dialog box; Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security; Engineering ethics; Political ecology; Food systems
Keywords: food security; innovation; interdisciplinary analysis; dialog; sustainable intensification; Africa
Title: Taking Complexity in Food Systems Seriously: An Interdisciplinary Analysis
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that cross-framework interactions enhance our understanding of how sectoral and macro-economic development strategies impact on livelihoods, availability, and access, leading to more profound dialog between divergent conceptual frameworks for diagnosing complex food insecurity problems and context-specific interventions and innovations.
What_was_studied: Using an interdisciplinary, triangulation analysis of four divergent conceptual frameworks, this study investigated food insecurity in developing countries from 2015 to 2020, focusing on the tensions and synergies between agroecology, agricultural innovation systems, social–ecological systems, and political ecology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings highlight the need for scaled-up investments in agricultural innovation systems that prioritize agroecology, integrated with social–ecological systems and political ecology, to expand food availability and access in developing countries amidst climate vulnerability. Decision makers should revise development strategies to fund these interventions and innovations.

Field: Performance indicator; Resource (biology); Political science; Collective action; Youth unemployment; Livelihood; Business model; Economic growth; Population growth; Resource management
Title: The importance of Ostrom’s Design Principles: Youth group performance in northern Ethiopia
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found a high degree of compliance with the DPs among the youth groups, and some of the DPs were more important for early performance. Specifically, the finding showed that the DPs can contribute to increased stability, trust, and overall performance of the youth groups.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of Ostrom's Design Principles (DPs) in improving the early performance of youth groups in Ethiopia, specifically in terms of stability, trust, and overall performance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that proactively mobilizing the youth as a resource in the creation of sustainable livelihoods can be a win-win-win solution for employment, rural poverty, and economic transformation. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that support the implementation of the DPs in similar contexts to scale up this approach and improve the lives of young people.

Field: Agency (philosophy); Epistemology; Sociology; Operational definition; Social reality; Poverty; Diversity (politics); Social ontology; Emic and etic; Generative grammar
Keywords: poverty; qualitative; anthropology; quantitative; Q-squared; Mozambique JEL classification: I30; I32; O12; O55
Title: WIDER Working Paper - What does it mean to be poor? Investigating the qualitative-quantitative divide in Mozambique
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the quantitative tradition is rooted in an atomistic view of the social world, while anthropological work in Mozambique reveals diverse forms of poverty through investigation of generative mechanisms, highlighting the importance of considering both structural and lived experiences of poverty.
What_was_studied: A study on poverty in Mozambique comparing economic (quantitative) and anthropological (qualitative) analytical approaches, using detailed evidence from Mozambique to highlight philosophical tensions in poverty research along three main axes: social ontology, epistemology, and aetiology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize a relational approach to addressing poverty in Mozambique, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data to understand the diverse forms of poverty and ensure inclusive operational definitions.

Authors: Jean-Pierre Tranchant; Aulo Gelli; Lilia Bliznashka; Amadou Sekou Diallo; Moussa Sacko; Amidou Assima; Emily H. Siegel; Elisabetta Aurino; Edoardo Masset
Field: Development studies; Landlocked country; Propensity score matching; Geography; Psychological intervention; Population; Socioeconomics; Humanitarian aid; Food security; Malnutrition
Title: The impact of food assistance on food insecure populations during conflict: Evidence from a quasi-experiment in Mali
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: Food assistance increased household non-food and food expenditures and micro-nutrient availability, with the effects concentrated in areas not immediately exposed to conflict and among households receiving at least two forms of food assistance. In villages where armed groups were present, food assistance improved household zinc consumption and appeared to support food expenditures.
What_was_studied: This study evaluates the impact of humanitarian aid on the food security of rural populations in Mopti region, Northern Mali, using a quasi-experimental design based on two survey rounds five years apart, and including 66 communities randomly selected from food-insecure districts. Data includes household expenditures, food consumption, and child nutritional status (height measurements).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the concentration of effects among households receiving multiple forms of food assistance and in areas less exposed to conflict, scaling up integrated food assistance packages targeting these households could help improve food security and mitigate the impacts of conflict on children's nutrition. Policymakers should prioritize funding and program design that supports multi-sectoral interventions, particularly in areas with less direct conflict exposure.

Field: Public policy; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Recession; Unemployment; Cash transfers; Household income; Development economics; Developing country
Keywords: COVID-19; Latin America; Microsimulations; Nowcasting; Poverty; Uruguay
Title: Too little but not too late: nowcasting poverty and cash transfers’ incidence during COVID-19’s crisis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the poverty rate increased by more than 38% during the first full trimester of the crisis, reaching 11.8% up from 8.5%, and that cash transfers implemented by the government had a positive but very limited effect in mitigating this poverty spike.
What_was_studied: The economic crisis triggered by COVID-19 has caused a worldwide economic downturn, and the deepest GDP contraction in Latin America since the beginning of the XXth century, with an unknown extent of increase in poverty until household income data is collected and analyzed.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that additional transfers worth un are needed to neutralize the poverty spike caused by the crisis, and that social protection policies should be prioritized to mitigate the impact of economic downturns on vulnerable populations.

Authors: Saturnino M. Borras; Jennifer C. Franco; Zau Nam
Field: Climate change; Political economy; Political science; State (polity); Working poor; Land grabbing; Social force; Climate change mitigation; Politics
Title: Climate change and land: insights from Myanmar
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study found that climate change politics can be a trigger for land grabbing, a legitimizing process for land grabs, or a de-legitimating process for people’s climate change mitigation and adaptation practices. These interconnections stoke old and provoke new political axes of conflict within and between state and social forces.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the interconnections between climate change politics and the global land rush in Northern Shan State, Myanmar, focusing on indirect and subtle interconnections over a 5-year period (2015-2019) using empirical cases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, decision-makers should prioritize policies that protect the land rights of marginalized working poor people, scale up climate change mitigation and adaptation practices that involve local communities, and expand social and environmental safeguards to prevent further exacerbation of conflict. Specifically, climate change politics and land governance must be integrated into policy frameworks to address these interconnections.

Field: Government; Natural disaster; Political science; Cash and cash equivalents; Poverty trap; Social protection; Livelihood; Development economics; Shock (economics); Flood myth
Keywords: aspirations; disaster relief; natural disasters; Pakistan; social protection v vi
Title: Aspirations and the Role of Social Protection: Evidence from a Natural Disaster in Rural Pakistan
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that natural disasters significantly reduce aspirations, with individuals experiencing 2010 monsoon season rainfall that was one standard deviation higher than average having aspiration levels 1.5 years later that were 0.15 standard deviations lower than those of similar individuals experiencing just average levels of rainfall, a negative shock equivalent to a 50% reduction in household expenditures. Moreover, the negative effect of natural disasters on aspirations is especially strong among the poor and vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of Pakistan's 2010 floods on citizens' aspirations and assesses the effectiveness of government social protection programs in mitigating these effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize social protection programs that provide cash transfers to affected communities, such as the Citizens Damage Compensation (Watan Card) Program, which can attenuate the negative impacts of natural disasters on aspirations and raise the well-being of vulnerable populations. By prioritizing these programs, governments can not only restore livelihoods and replace damaged assets but also ease mental burdens and raise aspirations for the future, ultimately reducing poverty and improving climate resilience.

Authors: Thor Olav Iversen; Ola T. Westengen; Morten Jerven
Field: Food security; Context (archaeology); Politics; China; Political science; Economic growth; Development economics; Recession; Geography; Agriculture; Economics; Law; Archaeology; Keynesian economics
Title: The history of hunger: Counting calories to make global food security legible
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Revisions to the PoU model have led to substantial changes in estimates of world hunger, with major changes in the statistical model inverting the trend lines towards the end of the Millennium Development Goals period. In 2020, the UN organization accessed new historical datasets from China and reduced PoU estimates for the country and globally. Ad-hoc revisions have been made to render food security crises legible.
What_was_studied: The Prevalence of Undernourishment (PoU) statistical model and its revisions over time in the context of the UN's development agenda, using archival research to analyze the historical and political factors that have shaped the indicator.
