Why_it_matters_for_policy: The inconsistent and uncertain nature of the PoU estimates highlights the need for greater transparency in the data and modelling basis for the indicator, and underscores the necessity of critical research on food insecurity quantification. Policymakers should prioritize more multifaceted approaches to measure food insecurity and ensure access to national household survey data from countries with high levels of undernutrition.

Authors: Marina Korzenevica; Catherine Fallon Grasham; Zoé Johnson; Amleset Gebreegzabher; Samrawit Mebrahtu; Zenawi Zerihun; Sonia Ferdous Hoque; Katrina Jane Charles
Field: Precarity; Negotiation; Context (archaeology); Empowerment; Independence (probability theory); Sociology; Entrepreneurship; Gender studies; Economic growth; Political science; Geography; Economics; Social science; Statistics; Mathematics; Archaeology; Law
Title: Negotiating spaces of marginality and independence: On women entrepreneurs within Ethiopian urbanization and water precarity
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women entrepreneurs face significant challenges in accessing water for their businesses, leading to a lack of control over their enterprises. The research also discovered that these women develop their businesses through the simultaneous presence of various, multilevel spaces of marginality/paradoxical spaces and articulation of independence as control over one's business and body.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the daily struggles and embodied experiences of low-skilled women entrepreneurs in informal economies of a small town in Ethiopia, specifically how they negotiate their independence through spatiality and the impact of water on their ability to develop their businesses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for water infrastructure in informal economies to support women-owned enterprises and promote gender equality.

Authors: Philip H. Brown; Adam Daigneault; Emilia Tjernström; Wenbo Zou
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Ethnic group; Psychology; Natural disaster; Social protection; Endogenous preferences; Loss and damage; Affect (psychology); Indigenous
Title: Natural Disasters, Social Protection, and Risk Perceptions.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Being struck by an extreme event substantially changes individuals' risk perceptions as well as their beliefs about the frequency and magnitude of future shocks, with sharply distinct results for the two ethnicities in the sample, indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians. Indo-Fijians exhibited a change in risk perceptions and beliefs consistent with previous research on risk attitudes and risk perceptions, while there was little to no impact on those same measures for indigenous Fijians.
What_was_studied: The impact of exposure to the December 2012 Cyclone Evan on Fijian households' risk attitudes and subjective expectations about the likelihood and severity of natural disasters over the next 20 years, using a randomized natural experiment approach and data from 486 Fijian households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding belief biases and how they vary across social contexts can help decision makers design policy instruments to reduce over-investment in preventative measures at the cost of other productive investments, particularly in the face of climate change.

Field: Extended family; Racism; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Redress; Context (language use); Solidarity; Inequality; Development economics; Social dynamics
Title: Normalizing necessity? Support networks and racial inequality in Namibia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that racial inequality shapes support practices and meaning, with black Namibians viewing support among family members as a necessary act to redress economic imbalances stemming from former discriminatory policies, while white Namibians view support to worse off others as an act of choice primarily involving socially distanced contacts. The study found that racial inequality has normalized a sense of support as a necessity for black but not white Namibians.
What_was_studied: This paper explores how support practices might be shaped by or respond to structurally inherited inequalities in the Namibian context, comparing support practices of black and white Namibians across various age groups, gender, and socioeconomic standing, using primary network data to assess racial inequality as a social dynamic within the space of practising solidarity towards others and evaluating whether providing worse off others corresponds to consequences of former discriminatory practices under the apartheid regime.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing chronic poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty in the Namibian context requires prioritizing policies that target structural inequalities and promote equitable access to resources and opportunities for all groups. Policymakers should scale up initiatives that foster support networks across socioeconomic standing and racial backgrounds to address unequal dynamics and adverse inclusion within these practices.

Field: Welfare; Human resources; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Path dependence; Human development (humanity); Social Welfare; Economic system; East Asia
Keywords: CORE Metadata, citation and similar papers at core; ac; uk
Title: A comparative welfare regime approach to global social policy
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that many poorer, partially capitalized societies rely informally on various clientelist relationships for security, and that formalizing rights to security through de-clientelization strategies is a stepping stone to protecting people against the insecurity of markets.
What_was_studied: The framework of welfare state regimes in rich capitalist countries is redefined and applied to regions and countries with problematic states and imperfect markets, using a comparative typology of regimes (welfare state, informal security, insecurity) that captures the relationships between social and cultural conditions, institutional performance, welfare outcomes, and path dependence. The study compares different regions of the world (East Asia, South Asia, Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa) and finds that many poorer, partially capitalized societies rely informally on various clientelist relationships for security, and that formalizing rights to security through de-clientelization strategies is a stepping stone to protecting people against the insecurity of markets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize de-clientelization strategies to protect people's security in poorer, partially capitalized societies, and scale up formal security provision to address the insecurity of markets.

Field: Soil conservation; Ecology; Environmental degradation; Geography; Investment (macroeconomics); Tanzania; Land user; Livelihood; Social issues; Environmental planning
Keywords: environmental degradation; soil conservation; structuration theory; highlands; Thailand; Tanzania
Title: A Framework for Understanding On-farm Environmental Degradation and Constraints to the Adoption of Soil Conservation Measures: Case Studies from Highland Tanzania and Thailand
primary_category: Sustainable Development; Environmental Degradation
What_was_found: The study found that diverse factors contribute to a lack of investment in conservation measures in these areas, including limited access to information, lack of awareness about soil conservation practices, and limited economic benefits for land users.
What_was_studied: The study uses structuration theory to investigate the social causes of environmental degradation and factors affecting land user decision-making in soil conservation, using case studies from the Uluguru Mountains in central-eastern Tanzania and the Chiang Dao District in the Northern Highlands of Thailand, covering a time period of unspecified duration with data collected through interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in communication and education campaigns to increase awareness about soil conservation practices, provide economic incentives for land users to adopt sustainable farming methods, and support the development of culturally appropriate soil conservation technologies to address the diverse social causes of environmental degradation in these areas.

Authors: Bas van Ruijven; Frauke Urban; René M.J. Benders; Henri Moll; Jeroen P. van der Sluijs; Bert de Vries; Detlef P. van Vuuren
Field: Environmental resource management; Environmental economics; Consumption (economics); Economics; Renewable energy; Electrification; Energy modeling; Kuznets curve; Income distribution; Sustainability; Developing country
Title: Modeling Energy and Development: an Evaluation of Models and Concepts
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The evaluation found that the IPCC/SRES models can capture the broad concepts of energy and development, but improvements are needed to better account for issues such as traditional fuels, electrification, economic structural change, income distribution, and informal economies.
What_was_studied: The IPCC/SRES models' results for Asia were evaluated to identify broad concepts of energy and development, the energy ladder, and the environmental Kuznets curve, and to assess improvements that can be made in modeling issues like traditional fuels, electrification, economic structural change, income distribution, and informal economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize developing more comprehensive energy models that account for these issues to ensure sustainable development in developing countries, particularly in the context of gender and poverty.

Authors: Christopher M. Bacon; William A. Sundstrom; Iris T. Stewart; David Beezer
Field: Outbreak; Agriculture; Qualitative research; Geography; Organizational Affiliation; Food insecurity; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Coping (psychology)
Title: Vulnerability to Cumulative Hazards: Coping with the Coffee Leaf Rust Outbreak, Drought, and Food Insecurity in Nicaragua
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study found that certain household capacities are significantly related to shorter periods of seasonal hunger: households with larger farms, with off-farm employment, and that produce more than half of their food, maintain more fruit trees, and harvest more coffee reported fewer lean months. Additionally, the study found evidence consistent with path dependence in how households cope with a sequence of environmental hazards.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates how seasonal hunger is related to smallholder organizational affiliation, farm and farmer characteristics, and post-hazard household-level coping strategies in the highlands of Central America, using a survey of 368 households completed in 2014, qualitative research, hydro-climatic data analysis, and integrating multiple challenges such as coffee leaf rust outbreaks starting in 2011 and droughts beginning in 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies prioritizing farmer institutions promoting subsistence-oriented production could help reduce chronic poverty and climate vulnerability in the region, particularly for smallholder farmers who are more susceptible to environmental hazards.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Productivity; Population; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Developing country; International development
Keywords: Agricultural Productivity; Inequality; Multidimensional Poverty; Pro-Poor Growth; Rwanda; Sub-Saharan Africa JEL classification: E6; I3; O1
Title: Looking at Pro-Poor Growth from an Agricultural Perspective
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that pro-poor growth in Rwanda has been characterized by impressive income growth, education improvements, and health gains, with the poor experiencing higher productivity growth in agriculture than non-poor households. However, the poor still struggle with low land productivity and labor productivity compared to their wealthier counterparts.
What_was_studied: The article examines the relationship between agricultural productivity and poverty reduction in developing countries, using Rwanda as a case study over three time periods (1999–2001, 2005–06, and 2010–11).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of agricultural productivity in reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize interventions aimed at improving land productivity and labor productivity among the poor, such as targeted agricultural extension services, infrastructure investments, and education programs focused on vocational skills and entrepreneurship.

Authors: Anagaw Mebratie; Robert Sparrow; Zelalem Yilma; Getnet Alemu; Arjun S. Bedi
Field: Social exclusion; Business; Socioeconomic status; Government; Health insurance; Quality of care; Community based health insurance; Waiting time; Adverse selection; Socioeconomics
Keywords: Community based health insurance; adverse selection; social exclusion; Ethiopia
Title: Enrollment in Ethiopia's Community-Based Health Insurance Scheme
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Enrollment reached 45.5% with no significant correlation to socioeconomic status, but food-insecure households were more likely to enroll. Past expenditure was a significant predictor of enrollment, while quality of care and waiting time significantly influenced enrollment. Focus groups highlighted concerns about provider favoritism towards uninsured households.
What_was_studied: The Ethiopian government's Community-Based Health Insurance scheme enrollment patterns from June 2011 to December 2012 in a specific population, focusing on socioeconomic status, chronic diseases, self-assessed health status, past expenditure, quality of care, and provider favoritism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in quality healthcare infrastructure, reducing waiting times for medical professionals, and addressing food insecurity to increase uptake of community-based health insurance schemes in vulnerable populations.

Field: Political science; China; Lead (geology); Rural development; Central china; Distribution (economics); Livelihood; Economic growth; Sustainability; Politics
Title: Historicizing Sustainable Livelihoods: A Pathways Approach to Lead Mining in Rural Central China
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that shifting mining practices are tied to institutional and political economic contexts, with changes in livelihood resources and strategies. The study also revealed a longitudinal analysis that resolves contradictory accounts of whether mining aids or hinders development, and whether local communities are victims or beneficiaries of such development.
What_was_studied: This article adopts a 'pathways to sustainability' approach to study lead mining in rural China, through an in-depth case study, it reveals how shifting mining practices are tied to institutional and political economic contexts, cost-benefit distribution, and changes in livelihood resources and strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that consider the interplay between institutional and political economic contexts, cost-benefit distribution, and changes in livelihood resources and strategies to ensure that mining practices benefit local communities and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Joshua W. Deutschmann; Agnieszka Postepska; Leopold Sarr
Field: Public economics; Service quality; Business; Tariff; Willingness to pay; Contingent valuation; Rural electrification; Quality (business); Service (business); Bidding
Title: Measuring willingness to pay for reliable electricity: Evidence from Senegal
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Households and firms are willing to pay a premium over current tariffs for high-quality electricity service without outages, but WTP for marginal service improvements is significantly lower than WTP for uninterrupted service, suggesting that any increase in electricity tariff must be accompanied by substantial quality improvements.
What_was_studied: A nationally representative survey in Senegal to understand households' and firms' willingness to pay for electricity service quality improvements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in the electricity sector to improve service quality and reliability, rather than simply increasing tariffs, to maximize WTP from households and firms. This can be achieved through multi-round bidding games that emphasize the importance of design choices in eliciting WTP.

Authors: David Neumark; Luis Felipe Munguia Corella
Field: Economics; Minimum wage; Demographic economics; Interpretation (philosophy); Developing country; Meta-analysis
Title: Do minimum wages reduce employment in developing countries? A survey and exploration of conflicting evidence
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Studies with more features predicting negative effects (vulnerable workers, formal sector, strongly enforced minimum wage laws, and binding minimum wages) have consistently found negative employment effects, while studies with fewer or no such features have found mixed or no evidence of disemployment effects.
What_was_studied: Employment effects of minimum wages in developing countries using various data sources and research methods, focusing on vulnerable workers, formal sector, strong enforcement, and binding minimum wage laws across different countries and time periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the systematic heterogeneity in study findings, policymakers should prioritize institutional factors and enforcement when implementing minimum wage laws to avoid negative employment effects on vulnerable workers, particularly in formal sector jobs and countries with strong legal frameworks.

Field: Economic policy; Agriculture; Economics; International economics; Food supply; Food insecurity; Food aid; Food security; Opportunity cost; Coping (psychology); Developing country
Title: The Decline of Food Aid: Issues of Aid Policy, Trade and Food Security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that changing circumstances since the mid-1980s raised questions about the effectiveness of these international arrangements to cope with an extremely serious and widespread period of food insecurity, due to sharp price variability in world markets for cereals and other foodstuffs and barriers to food security imposed on developing countries by the world agricultural trade regime.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of international arrangements in coping with food insecurity after the 'world food crisis' of 1972–4 and the subsequent 'African food crisis' in the late 1980s, focusing on cereal markets and budgetary tightening in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that scaling up social protection programs and strengthening international cooperation are essential to address food insecurity, especially in light of the increasing frequency and severity of climate-related disasters.

Authors: Justice A. Tambo; Mathews Matimelo; Mathias Ndhlovu; Fredrick Mbugua; Noah Phiri
Field: Integrated pest management; Agricultural productivity; Crop; Business; Productivity; Socioeconomics; Crop protection; Food security; Sustainable development; Yield (finance)
Title: Gender-differentiated impacts of plant clinics on maize productivity and food security: Evidence from Zambia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Participation in plant clinics boosted maize yield and income by 14% and 27%, respectively, for both male and female farmers. However, the effects were disproportionately greater for male farmers, with female farmers achieving smaller gains. Female household heads and spouses also had different impacts.
What_was_studied: Gendered impacts of plant clinics on maize productivity and food security among smallholder farmers in Zambia over a one-year period, using gender-disaggregated plot-level data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity and bridge the gender gap in agricultural productivity, policy makers should scale up plant clinic services and ensure that female farmers have equal access to technology adoption and pest management strategies, while also providing additional support for female household heads and spouses.

Field: Psychological resilience; Sociology; Vulnerability; Environmental degradation; Elite capture; Harm; Public sphere; Development economics; Commons; Economic growth; Political ecology
Keywords: BWDB, Bangladesh Water Development Board; CDS, Coastal Development Strategy; GBM, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Meghna river basins; GHG, greenhouse gas; MOEF, Ministry of Environment and Forests; NAPA, National Adaptation Program of Action; UNFCCC, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
Title: Bamboo Beating Bandits: Conflict, Inequality, and Vulnerability in the Political Ecology of Climate Change Adaptation in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that climate change policies in Bangladesh have led to the capture of land by elites, exclusion of marginalized communities from decision-making processes, encroachment on public commons such as forests and farmland, and entrenchment of class and ethnic hierarchies, trapping the poor and powerless into a predatory patronage system.
What_was_studied: Bangladesh's climate change adaptation efforts were researched through semi-structured interviews and a literature review, revealing how processes of enclosure, exclusion, encroachment, and entrenchment hinder the country's ability to address climate change vulnerability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address climate change vulnerability in Bangladesh, policymakers must prioritize inclusive and participatory planning processes that empower marginalized communities and prevent further enclosure, exclusion, encroachment, and entrenchment of existing power dynamics.

Authors: Jerome Monne; Céline Louche; Christophe Villa
Field: Public economics; Herd behavior; Rural area; Financial services; Externality; Economics; Herding; Poverty; Microfinance; Economic growth; Location
Keywords: microfinance institutions; location decisions; uncertainty; rational herding; panel Poisson regression
Title: Rational Herding toward the Poor: Evidence from Location Decisions of Microfinance Institutions within Pakistan
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that MFIs are mostly located in urban and semi-urban areas and hardly reach the poorest rural areas, driven by uncertainty faced by MFIs in their location decision. Additionally, the study identified three main reasons for the spatial clustering of MFIs: common attraction factors, payoff externalities, and herd behavior.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the spatial distribution of microfinance activities in rural areas of Pakistan, using data from almost all microfinance institutions (MFIs) in the country over a specific time period to determine if these activities reach the poorest areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up microfinance activities in rural areas to improve financial inclusion and reduce intersectional poverty. This can be achieved by providing subsidies or financial incentives to MFIs operating in poorer areas, as well as implementing policies that encourage herd behavior among MFIs towards these areas.

Field: Economics; Food Consumption Patterns; Foreign exchange; Food insecurity; Export price; Urbanization; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Developing country; Volatility (finance)
Journal/Venue: Structural Change, Economic Interdependence and World Development
Title: Food Security: A Stabilisation Problem for Developing Countries
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that food insecurity has become a central explicit policy goal for most low- and middle-income countries within the last decade due to interrelated factors such as an explicit commitment by governments to stabilize domestic prices and consumption patterns, rapid urbanization, increased dependence on imported cereals, and increasing volatility of export prices of cereals.
What_was_studied: The study examines food security in low- and middle-income countries over the last decade, focusing on factors such as government commitment to stabilize domestic prices and consumption patterns, urbanization, dependence on imported cereals, and export price volatility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize investing in social protection programs to address food insecurity, particularly in rural areas where the majority of the population resides.

Authors: Melissa Hidrobo; John Hoddinott; Neha Kumar; Meghan Olivier
Field: Livestock; Consumption (economics); Economics; Asset (economics); Social protection; Quality (business); Animal source foods; Agricultural economics; Economic growth; Food security; Developing country
Title: Social Protection, Food Security, and Asset Formation
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Social protection programs improve both the quantity and quality of food consumed by beneficiaries, with an average increase in food consumption value of 13% and caloric acquisition by 8%. Additionally, these programs lead to increased asset holdings such as livestock, non-farm productive assets, farm productive assets, and savings.
What_was_studied: Social protection programs in sub-Saharan Africa between 1995 and 2015, focusing on their impacts on food security outcomes and asset formation among vulnerable populations during the last two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant nutritional benefits of increasing animal source food consumption in vulnerable populations, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs to improve food security and asset formation among these communities.

Authors: Dewan Arif Rashid; Lisa C. Smith; Tauhidur Rahman
Field: Socioeconomic status; Economics; Food insecurity; Consumer demand; Diet quality; Socioeconomics
Title: Determinants of Dietary Quality: Evidence from Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study finds that while male education has a positive effect, female education has a substantially stronger influence on dietary quality. Additionally, female household headship is associated with lower dietary quality compared to male headship.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the determinants of dietary quality in Bangladesh using data from a nationally representative household expenditure survey conducted in 2000, with a focus on gender differences in education's impact on dietary quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between female education and dietary quality, policymakers should prioritize programs that promote female education and address the unique constraints faced by female-headed households to improve food security in Bangladesh.

Field: China; Communism; Distribution (mathematics); Economic geography; Political science; Economic system; Development economics; Economy; Economics; Politics; Law; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics
Title: The impact of Communist Party membership on wealth distribution and accumulation in urban China
primary_category: Asset poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that although the average wealth gap between CCP and non-CCP households remained substantial and consistent throughout the period, there were significant shifts in the returns structure of party membership over time, with the highest wealth premiums now concentrated at the bottom of the distribution, primarily due to CCP households at the lower end of the net wealth distribution possessing housing assets with higher values compared to those owned by non-CCP households.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the evolution of the wealth gap between Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and non-CCP households in urban China from 1995 to 2017, using unconditional quantile regression to analyze variations in premiums of party membership across the wealth distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing asset poverty and health disparities in urban China may require targeted policies to support low-income CCP households in accumulating wealth and reducing their reliance on housing assets, while also promoting more equitable distribution of wealth among all households.

Authors: Sijia Xu; Abu S. Shonchoy; Tomoki Fujii
Field: Parity (mathematics); Economics; Stipend; Quality (business); Conditional cash transfer; Educational resources; Educational quality; Demographic economics; Developing country; International development
Title: Assessing gender parity in intrahousehold allocation of educational resources: Evidence from Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a strong pro-female bias in enrollment decisions, but contrasting pro-male biases in the allocation of total education expenditure and the share of the total education expenditure on core components such as private tutoring. The findings highlight a contradictory gender gap in the intrahousehold allocation of educational resources.
What_was_studied: This study examines the intrahousehold allocation of education expenditure in Bangladesh, using four rounds of nationally representative household surveys to investigate gender parity in education quality and its determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study underscores the importance of minding the gender gap in education quality and implementing complementary policies to address it in developing countries. Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to promote girls' secondary school enrollment and on-time completion, while also addressing the pro-male biases in intrahousehold allocation of educational resources.

Authors: Ricardo Godoy; Jonathan Bauchet; Jere R. Behrman; Tomás Huanca; William R. Leonard; Victoria Reyes-García; Asher Rosinger; Susan Tanner; Eduardo A. Undurraga; Ariela Zycherman
Field: Inequality; Consumption (sociology); Indigenous; Economics; Socioeconomics; Longitudinal study; Asset (computer security); Demographic economics; Geography; Scale (ratio); Economic inequality; Demography; Sociology; Social science; Ecology; Mathematical analysis; Statistics; Mathematics; Computer security; Cartography; Computer science; Biology
Title: Changes in adult well-being and economic inequalities: An exploratory observational longitudinal study (2002–2010) of micro-level trends among Tsimane', a small-scale rural society of Indigenous People in the Bolivian Amazon
primary_category: Asset poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there was a rise in total asset wealth, but a decline in caloric and protein consumption. Economic inequalities were non-trivial and varied between years, with asset inequality varying less than income inequality.
What_was_studied: A longitudinal dataset of nine years (2002–2010) from a horticultural-foraging society of Indigenous People in the Bolivian Amazon (Tsimane') was used for an exploratory analysis of micro-level trends in indicators of well-being and economic inequalities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing asset poverty and housing insecurity among Indigenous communities in the Bolivian Amazon to ensure equitable access to resources and improve well-being. Scale up locally grounded indexes of well-being to monitor micro-level changes in well-being and income inequality, and fund programs that support food security and traditional asset ownership.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Labour supply; Pension; Human development (humanity); Population; Demographic economics; Fixed effects model; Fertility
Title: Does the old-age pension scheme improve household welfare? Evidence from India
primary_category: Food insecurity; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that IGNOAPS participation increased consumption expenditure, food and non-food expenditure, and assets while reducing household labor supply. These effects were only observed when the recipients were women. However, the study also found that the poverty-reducing effect deteriorated in 2011-2012 after the government made several changes to the program's specifications in 2007.
What_was_studied: India's elderly population between 2004 and 2012 using household longitudinal data from the India Human Development Survey, with a focus on the impact of Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS) on household welfare indicators such as consumption expenditure, income, assets, and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that social protection programs like IGNOAPS can be effective in reducing poverty among the elderly, particularly when targeted towards women. To scale up the impact, policymakers should prioritize targeting such programs towards women and ensure that program specifications are regularly reviewed to maintain their effectiveness.

Field: Political science; South–South cooperation; Developmental stage; Economic growth; Christian ministry; Intension; Developing country; Politics
Keywords: Foreign aid; New donors; Aid allocation; South-South Cooperation; India
Title: The Needy Donor: An Empirical Analysis of India’s Aid Motives
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that commercial and political self-interests dominate India's aid allocation, with the importance of political interests being significantly higher for India than for all donors of the Development Assistance Committee. Additionally, countries geographically closer were favored, and countries at a similar developmental stage were more likely to enter India's aid program.
What_was_studied: Aid commitments by India's Ministry of External Affairs to 125 countries between 2008 and 2010 were analyzed to understand why poor countries provide aid to other developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that India should prioritize sustainable development and social protection in its aid allocation, rather than purely commercial or political interests. To scale up the impact of its aid, India should expand its aid program to include more countries at a similar developmental stage and prioritize geographically closer countries.

Authors: M. Yusof Saari; Erik Dietzenbacher; Bart Los
Field: Income inequality metrics; Ethnic group; Labour economics; Social accounting; Economics; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Capital (economics)
Keywords: income distribution; social accounting matrix (SAM); structural decomposition analysis; ethnic groups
Title: Sources of Income Growth and Inequality Across Ethnic Groups in Malaysia, 1970–2000
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that export expansion and changes in labor and capital inputs are the primary drivers of income growth, with varying effects across rural and urban areas, skilled and unskilled workers, and major ethnic groups. The combination of these two factors is a dominant explanation for rising income inequality in Malaysia.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the sources of income growth for major ethnic groups in Malaysia from 1970 to 2000 using input-output structural decomposition analysis on social accounting matrices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address widening income disparities, policymakers should prioritize investments in human capital and physical infrastructure, especially in rural areas and among marginalized groups, while ensuring fair labor practices and targeted social protection programs to mitigate the impacts of globalization and technological change.

Authors: Corey Lang; Christopher B. Barrett; Felix Naschold
Field: Public economics; Econometrics; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Equity (finance); Integrated approach; Intervention (law); Estimation
Keywords: JEL classification: R12; O2; C15; I32 geographic targeting; assets; poverty maps; spatial variation; Uganda
Title: Targeting maps: An asset-based approach to geographic targeting
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that asset-specific transfer schemes would improve with a spatially targeted strategy, and that poverty maps can be overlaid with the maps of marginal returns to identify candidate areas for intervention. Results are consistent with independent empirical findings.
What_was_studied: This paper focuses on estimating marginal returns to assets across subpopulations in Uganda during a specific time period using small-area estimation methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize a spatially targeted strategy for asset-specific transfer schemes in Uganda, scaling up the approach to cover more subpopulations and expanding its application to other development areas.

Field: Psychology; Risk perception; Empirical evidence; Fear of crime; Social disorganization theory; Inequality; Economic inequality; Multilevel model; Endogeneity; Social psychology
Title: Do inequalities predict fear of crime? Empirical evidence from Mexico
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a strong positive linear relationship between municipal income inequality and fear of crime, with emotive and behavioral dimensions being more impacted than the cognitive dimension. Additionally, education inequality was found to have a positive impact on feeling of unsafety (emotive dimension) and risk perception (cognitive dimension), but to a lesser extent.
What_was_studied: This study combines multiple datasets to investigate the causal impact of local income and education inequalities on individuals' fear of crime, with a focus on the Mexican case and using an innovative index of fear of crime composed of three dimensions: emotion, cognition, and behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing income and education inequalities through targeted policies and interventions can help reduce individuals' fear of crime, particularly in emotive and behavioral aspects. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and scale-up initiatives aimed at reducing inequality and improving socioeconomic conditions in vulnerable communities to enhance public safety and well-being.

Authors: Bob Rijkers; Caterina Ruggeri Laderchi; Francis Teal
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Productivity; Investment (macroeconomics); Unemployment; Production (economics); Earnings; Labor intensity; Unit (housing)
Title: Who Benefits from Promoting Small Enterprises? Some Empirical Evidence from Ethiopia
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The program did not lead to the adoption of different technologies or increased labor intensity among participating firms, but there was an earnings premium for program participants, who tended to be relatively well-educated, with the highest premium for those at the bottom of the earnings distribution.
What_was_studied: The impact of the Addis Ababa Integrated Housing Development Program on technology adoption, labor intensity, and earnings among small enterprises constructing low-cost housing using novel technologies in Ethiopia between 2015 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that small firms create more jobs per unit of investment and that the jobs so created are concentrated among the low-skilled and hence the poor, policymakers should prioritize programs supporting small enterprises in the construction sector to address employment and poverty reduction in Addis Ababa, while also exploring alternative technologies and labor market interventions to increase productivity and earnings for the lowest-skilled workers.

Authors: John K. Pattison-Williams; Jeremy Haggar; John Morton
Field: Tamil; Government; Poverty; Asset (economics); Geography; Interim; Tribe; Socioeconomics; Focus group; Thematic analysis
Title: Intergenerational perceptions of household wellbeing in India’s Western and Eastern Ghats
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: We found that most households had a positive perspective regarding their wellbeing over time; when divided into research locations, the Odisha site was the most optimistic, the Kerala site had no consensus position, and the Tamil Nadu site was most pessimistic. Despite ongoing social and economic marginalization of Scheduled Tribe households, these households had similar wellbeing perceptions as non-Scheduled Tribe households.
What_was_studied: Using qualitative information from focus group discussions and a survey instrument, we explored wellbeing trajectories among three generations of respondents in three communities in the Western and Eastern Ghats over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in sustainable development schemes to address poverty alleviation strategies, targeting asset inheritance and government schemes as key factors influencing wellbeing among current generations. By understanding the evolving forms of significant events between generations, policymakers can scale up effective interventions that improve the wellbeing perceptions of these communities.

Authors: Yuko Nakano; Takuji W. Tsusaka; Takeshi Aida; Valerien O. Pede
Field: Agriculture; Business; Econometric model; Hectare; Productivity; Emerging technologies; Agricultural extension; Rural poverty; Agricultural science; Panel data
Title: Is farmer-to-farmer extension effective? The impact of training on technology adoption and rice farming productivity in Tanzania
primary_category: Digital divide; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Key findings indicate that while the key farmers’ technology adoption rates rose immediately after the training, those of the non-trained ordinary farmers caught up belatedly. As the technologies disseminated, the paddy yield of the key farmers increased from 3.1 to 5.3 tons per hectare, while the yield of the ordinary farmers increased from 2.6 to 3.7 tons per hectare.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the technology dissemination pathways among smallholder rice producers within a rural irrigation scheme in Tanzania, using a unique five-year household-level panel data set to estimate difference-in-differences models and examine how social and geographical network influences adoption of technologies by ordinary farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study suggests the effectiveness and practical potential of farmer-to-farmer extension programs for smallholders in SSA as a cost-effective alternative to conventional farmer training approaches, with the potential to increase productivity, alleviate rural poverty, and address food insecurity across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Business; Vulnerability; Tourism; Poverty; Social protection; Domestic policy; Population; Development economics; Developing country; Pandemic
Keywords: COVID-19; Migration; Pacific; Remittances; Social protection; Tourism; Vulnerability
Title: Bubble in, bubble out: Lessons for the COVID-19 recovery and future crises from the Pacific
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Social protection systems are less common in the Pacific than elsewhere, making it more challenging for the region to address the economic impacts of COVID-19 without plunging a significant portion of the population into poverty. Aggressive travel restrictions and effective domestic policy responses have helped spare many Pacific countries from the worst impacts of the virus, with ten countries reporting no confirmed cases.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 pandemic and 22 developing countries in the Pacific, particularly their social protection systems and how they have fared in comparison to other regions worldwide.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unique challenges faced by the Pacific region in managing the COVID-19 pandemic, there is an opportunity for the region to pilot and test strategies that can safely allow tourism, migration, and remittances to resume, helping to address underlying vulnerabilities before the next crisis.

Authors: Philippe Bocquier; Christophe Jalil Nordman; Aude Vescovo
Field: Private sector; Economics; Vulnerability; Underemployment; Earnings; West africa; Demographic economics; Development economics; Bargaining power; Income distribution; Informal sector
Keywords: Vulnerability; working conditions; compensating differentials; earnings; informal sector; West Africa
Title: Employment vulnerability and earnings in urban West Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Quantitative, distributional, and qualitative analyses show that vulnerability compensating mechanisms are mainly observed in the informal sector, at the upper tail of the earnings distribution, and particularly when there is visible underemployment. Employment vulnerability is not compensated for the poorest workers in the private sector.
What_was_studied: This article develops indicators of vulnerability in employment in seven economic capitals of West Africa and studies their links with individual incomes between 2010 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize protecting the most vulnerable workers, expand social protection policies to cover the informal sector, and scale up support for small businesses and entrepreneurship to address long 'job queues' and weak institutional protection of workers in the formal sector.

Authors: Armand Sim; Daniel Suryadarma; Asep Suryahadi
Field: Cognitive skill; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Human capital; Minimum wage; Educational attainment; Family life; Life skills; Endogeneity
Keywords: child labor; human capital; skills; health; Indonesia. JEL Classifications: I12; I21; J13; J22; O15
Title: The Consequences of Child Market Work on the Growth of Human Capital
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that child labor negatively affects mathematics skills and pulmonary function but not cognitive skills and educational attainment. Furthermore, the type of work matters; those who work outside of family business have lower educational attainment than those working for family business.
What_was_studied: The paper measures the effect of child market work on the long-term growth of human capital, focusing on the output of the human capital production: mathematics skills, cognitive skills, pulmonary function, and educational attainment in a rich longitudinal dataset from Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS) over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that address child labor in specific contexts to ensure that children can develop their cognitive skills and educational attainment, as well as maintain good pulmonary function and mathematics skills to improve long-term human capital growth.

Field: Infant mortality; Economics; Democratization; Regime change; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Democracy; Liberalization; Panel data; Politics
Title: Political liberalization and human development: Dynamic Effects of Political Regime Change on Infant Mortality across Three Centuries (1800-2015)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Error correction models were applied to extensive time-series cross-sectional data collected from 172 countries, revealing that political liberalization is more likely to increase equal access to public services immediately but reduces infant mortality rates in the long run.
What_was_studied: Using newly collected panel data on infant mortality rates from 1800 to 2015 from 172 countries, this study tests the theoretical expectations that political liberalization encourages policymakers to adopt poverty-alleviating policies and reduce infant mortality rates over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study suggests that policymakers need to invest tirelessly in advancing political liberalization to continue improving human well-being in developing countries, scaling up poverty-alleviating policies and prioritizing long-term human development.

Authors: Benjamin K. Sovacool; May Tan-Mullins; Wokje Abrahamse
Field: Disaster recovery; Political economy; Business; Development studies; Natural disaster; Environmental degradation; Corporate governance; Political ecology; Emergency management; Politics
Keywords: Political ecology Political economy Enclosure Resistance Disaster relief Climate change adaptation Exclusion Related academic disciplines Resource economics; geopolitics; political geography; political science; economic geography Human geography; ecology; political geography; sociology; peasant studies Environmental sociology; law; jurisprudence; philosophy; ethics; energy policy Development studies; development economics; political geography; political science; International political economy
Title: Bloated bodies and broken bricks: Power, ecology, and inequality in the political economy of natural disaster recovery
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that disaster recovery projects often excluded marginalized groups from decision-making processes and led to the encroachment of private interests into public assets, resulting in entrenched inequalities and environmental degradation. Specifically, it was found that only 30% of the $108 billion in federal funding for Katrina recovery went to low- and moderate-income households, while 70% went to higher-income households and businesses.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the inequitable effects of disaster recovery efforts following Hurricane Katrina in the United States between 2005 and 2015, using a mixed-methods approach combining political economy, political ecology, justice theory, and critical development studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize equitable disaster recovery policies that empower marginalized communities, scale up funding for affordable housing and social protection programs, and strengthen environmental regulations to prevent encroachment and environmental degradation. By taking these actions, we can mitigate the adverse effects of disaster recovery efforts and build more resilient and equitable communities.

Authors: Yonas Alem; Gunnar Köhlin; Jesper Stage
Field: Welfare; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Position (finance); Persistence (psychology); Material consumption; Development economics; Panel data; Probit model
Keywords: JEL Classification: I32; O12 Ethiopia; subjective poverty; dynamic probit
Title: The Persistence of Subjective Poverty in Urban Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite declining consumption poverty rates, subjective poverty remained largely unchanged. Households with a history of past poverty continue to perceive themselves as poor even if their material consumption improves, and the relative economic position of households is a strong determinant of subjective poverty.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed 15 years of panel data to investigate the persistence and correlates of subjective and consumption poverty in urban Ethiopia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively address poverty in urban Ethiopia, policies should prioritize improving the relative economic position of households, especially those with a history of past poverty, and consider the subjective experience of poverty in addition to objective measures.

Authors: Lisa C. Smith; Marie T. Ruel; Aida Ndiaye
Field: Rural area; Socioeconomic status; Geography; Tanzania; Nutritional status; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: Why is Child Malnutrition Lower In Urban Than In Rural Areas? Evidence From 36 Developing Countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there were no significant differences in the nature of the socioeconomic determinants between urban and rural areas, marked differences in the levels of these determinants and caring practices for children and women favored urban areas, suggesting that lower urban malnutrition is due to more favorable socioeconomic conditions leading to better caring practices.
What_was_studied: This study compares the socioeconomic determinants of child nutritional status in urban and rural areas to determine why urban malnutrition rates are lower.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize improving the overall socioeconomic conditions in rural areas and invest in programs that support better caring practices for children and their mothers to reduce malnutrition rates.

Authors: Rudi Purwono; Wahyu Wisnu Wardana; Tri Haryanto; M. Khoerul Mubin
Field: Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Chronic poverty; Index (economics); Demographic economics; Inequality; Panel data
Title: Poverty dynamics in Indonesia: empirical evidence from three main approaches
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the spell approach tends to underestimate chronic poverty, with approximately 6.7% of total households experiencing chronic poverty. The component approach indicates that around 11.07% of total households were classified as chronically poor, while the EDE poverty gap approach suggests that poverty in Indonesia is mainly chronic at 92% of the total component of poverty.
What_was_studied: This study reexamines poverty dynamics in Indonesia using three approaches: the spell approach, the component approach, and the equally distributed equivalent (EDE) poverty gap approach on household panel data from the National Socio-Economic Survey of Indonesia (Susenas) 2008 and 2010, and also the FGT index.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high percentage of chronic poverty found in this study, policy makers should prioritize addressing income poverty and food insecurity, particularly in education access to help reduce inequality and break the cycle of poverty.

Authors: L. Jamila Haider; Wiebren J. Boonstra; Garry D. Peterson; Maja Schlüter
Field: Public economics; Environmental resource management; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Sustainability science; Poverty trap; Diversity (business); Sustainable development; Sustainability; Discipline
Title: Traps and Sustainable Development in Rural Areas: A Review
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poverty traps are not solely driven by individual or household factors but also by complex social-ecological interactions, such as the gendered distribution of labor and assets, land degradation, and external drivers like climate change and market fluctuations.
What_was_studied: The concept of a poverty trap—commonly understood as a self-reinforcing situation beneath an asset threshold—has been very influential in describing the persistence of poverty and the relationship between poverty and sustainability in rural contexts, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative household surveys with qualitative interviews and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty traps are not solely driven by individual or household factors but also by complex social-ecological interactions, it is crucial to prioritize integrated interventions that address these underlying dynamics, such as sustainable agriculture practices, gender-sensitive asset distribution, and climate change adaptation strategies.

Authors: Mani Nepal; Rajesh Kumar; Madan S. Khadayat; Eswaran Somanathan
Field: Business; Metropolitan area; Value (economics); Price premium; Context (language use); Hedonic pricing; Low income; Agricultural economics; Municipal solid waste; Developing country
Title: Value of cleaner neighborhoods: Application of hedonic price model in low income context
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that city residents place a high price premium (between 25% and 57%) on cleaner neighborhoods and less (−11%) on open drains, indicating that better waste management will bring high returns to homeowners and the municipality in cities where the tax base includes the assessed value of property.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effects of municipal solid waste collection services at the neighborhood level on housing property values using the hedonic price model with a sub-sample of nationally representative household survey data from urban areas and primary data collected from one of the metropolitan cities in Nepal during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for improved municipal solid waste collection services and revise zoning regulations to encourage more sustainable urban development to increase housing property values and reduce poverty in developing cities.

Authors: Gustav Ranis; Frances Stewart; Alejandro Ramirez
Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Human development (humanity); Investment rate; Demographic economics; Income distribution
Keywords: Human Development; Economic Growth; Cross-country Statistics 70-92; Resource Allocation; Income Distribution; Poverty; Productivity; Health; Technology; Education JEL Codes: O10; O11; O15; O57
Title: Economic Growth and Human Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found a significant, bi-directional relationship between EG and HD, with public expenditures on health and education, particularly for females, being a crucial factor in the chain from EG to HD. Additionally, the investment rate and income distribution were identified as important drivers in the reverse direction, from HD to EG.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between economic growth (EG) and human development (HD) across different countries over a 30-year period, using cross-country regressions to identify key drivers and reinforcing mechanisms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong sequencing implications of these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in health and education, particularly for women, to foster sustainable development and break the vicious cycles of poverty. Sequencing should be given careful consideration to ensure the best possible outcomes.

Field: Multivariate statistics; Economics; Univariate; Predictive power; Financial crisis; Vulnerability index; Index (economics); Warning system; Monetary economics; Developing country
Title: Exogenous Shocks and Growth Crises in Low-Income Countries: A Vulnerability Index
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: The index has high in-sample and out-of-sample predictive power, particularly explaining well the growth crises observed in LICs during the global financial crisis.
What_was_studied: This paper develops a new index which provides early warning signals of a growth crisis in low-income countries (LICs) during large external shocks, using multivariate regression analysis and a univariate signaling approach to map information from a parsimonious set of underlying policy, structural, and institutional indicators into a composite vulnerability index for the period 1995-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high predictive power of the composite vulnerability index, decision makers in low-income countries should prioritize structural reforms that address policy, structural, and institutional indicators to prevent growth crises exacerbated by external shocks.

Field: Purchasing power parity; Economics; Poverty; Purchasing power; Lagging; Public expenditure; Development aid; Development economics; Population growth; International development
Title: Can the World Cut Poverty in Half? How Policy Reform and Effective Aid Can Meet International Development Goals - Can the World Cut Poverty in Half? How Policy Reform and Effective Aid Can Meet International Development Goals
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research reveals that poverty in developing countries, particularly in Asia, is expected to decrease by half by 2015 if past trends continue. However, poverty reduction in Africa will be slower. The study suggests that efficient aid and policy reforms can significantly contribute to reducing poverty in lagging regions.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the reduction of poverty in developing countries, specifically in Asia and Africa, during the 1990s and projects the trend to 2015, highlighting the potential impact of effective aid and policy reforms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the projected decline in poverty, policymakers should prioritize effective aid and policy reforms to accelerate poverty reduction in Africa and ensure that the gains made in Asia are replicated elsewhere.

Authors: Sonja Radosavljevic; L. Jamila Haider; Steven J. Lade; Maja Schlüter
Field: Public economics; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Poverty trap; Economic dynamics
Title: Implications of poverty traps across levels
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty traps are often multidimensional and involve cross-level interactions between farmers' habits, community decisions, and biophysical factors, which can hinder or mislead development efforts if not properly understood. Specifically, the research showed that 70% of farmers in the study areas were stuck in poverty traps, and that neglecting key interactions can lead to incorrect assessments and potentially inadequate alleviation strategies.
What_was_studied: Recent research on poverty traps in rural and urban areas of developing countries during the 2018-2020 period, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys, focus groups, and biophysical data collection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to addressing chronic poverty, including considering the biophysical and economic dynamics of farmers' habits and community decisions. Developing targeted interventions that take into account these interactions can help break the cycle of poverty traps and improve the effectiveness of sustainable development efforts.

Field: Economic efficiency; Environmental economics; Water use; Economics; Microeconomics; Tariff; Water pricing; Water tariff; Household income; Equity (economics); Subsidy
Title: Evaluating the Performance of Alternative Municipal Water Tariff Designs: Quantifying the Tradeoffs between Equity, Economic Efficiency, and Cost Recovery
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The results show that increasing block tariffs perform poorly in terms of targeting subsidies to low-income households, especially when cost recovery is low and the correlation between water use and household income is high.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the impact of alternative municipal water tariff designs on financial self-sufficiency, equity, and economic efficiency in a hypothetical community of 5,000 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address health disparities related to access to clean water and sanitation, municipal water utilities should prioritize financial self-sufficiency targets that maximize subsidies for low-income households, while also considering the impact of tariff designs on economic efficiency and equity.

Authors: Cheryl R. Doss; Zachary Catanzarite; William Baah-Boateng; Hema Swaminathan; Carmen Diana Deere; Louis Boakye-Yiadom; J Y Suchitra
Field: Data collection; Psychology; Valuation (finance); Gender gap; Monetary value; Property value; Full sample; Demographic economics
Title: Do men and women estimate property values differently
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Overall, the distribution of monetary values reported by women tends to be narrower than that reported by men.
What_was_studied: Using nationally representative data from Ghana and Ecuador and for the state of Karnataka, India, we analyze whether men and women provide different responses to questions about the monetary value of their home.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding has implications both for data collection efforts and for measures of the gender wealth gap. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize revising data collection methods to account for potential biases in valuation responses and ensure that measures of wealth inequality accurately reflect the experiences of all individuals.

Field: Vietnamese; Economics; Poverty; Survey data collection; Poverty map; Rural development; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Census; Social Welfare
Title: Generating Disaggregated Poverty Maps: An Application to Vietnam
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Vietnamese poverty is concentrated in the north and in districts furthest from the coast and cities, with high poverty rates estimated for 21.6% of rural households.
What_was_studied: This study uses data from Vietnam to illustrate a method for generating disaggregated poverty maps by estimating the relationship between poverty and household indicators using survey data and census data on those same indicators for each of the 543 rural districts in Vietnam during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that targeted interventions should prioritize northern and more remote areas to effectively address poverty in Vietnam, and policymakers should scale up survey data collection and mapping techniques to improve poverty measurement and targeting.

Field: Standard of living; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Agricultural diversification; Measuring poverty; Rural poverty; Poverty gap index; Structural adjustment; Development economics
Title: The sectoral structure of poverty during an adjustment period : evidence for Indonesia in the mid-1980s
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while aggregate poverty decreased during the period, gains to the poor were unevenly distributed across regions and sectors, with the rural sector in key regions playing a crucial role in Indonesia's success in alleviating poverty. The growth of off-farm employment and crop diversification were also important factors in reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: The authors examine the structure of poverty in Indonesia by sector of employment during the adjustment period from 1984 to 1987, and how it changed over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role that rural areas and off-farm employment played in reducing poverty, the government's adjustment program should prioritize investments in these areas to ensure continued progress in alleviating poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Deed; Multilevel regression; Bureaucracy; Voting; Subsidy; Property rights; Politics
Keywords: Mexico; hedonic model; housing deed; housing demand; property rights
Title: Where do Property Rights Matter More? Explaining the Variation in Demand for Property Titles across Cities in Mexico
primary_category: Food insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that houses without deeds are roughly five percent less valuable than otherwise similar houses with full deeds, but this premium varies widely across cities. More educated households value deeds more, and having a deed is more valuable for larger houses in neighborhoods with less vacancy and higher infrastructure quality.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the variation in property rights value to housing in Mexico's urban markets between 2012 and 2014, with a focus on the differences between cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that funds intended to subsidize titling should be redirected to places where titles are worth more. Policymakers should reconsider framing property-titling programs as poverty alleviation, as low-income households would benefit more from subsidies for housing and residential infrastructure improvements. The federal government should prioritize reducing the costs of transferring property.

Field: Government; Economics; Economic interventionism; Productivity; Competition (economics); Structural organization; Economic growth; Informal sector; Thematic analysis; Operationalization
Keywords: Waste Pickers; Co-Production; Santiago; Recycling; Waste Management; Informal Economy
Title: Unleashing Waste-Pickers’ Potential: Supporting Recycling Cooperatives in Santiago de Chile
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive association between the level of government support and waste pickers' sustainable performance, suggesting that further government intervention is needed to support a stronger structural organization for the waste-picker recycling system.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed waste pickers' sustainable performance in Santiago de Chile between 2019 and 2022 using a thematic analysis of 40 in-depth interviews and multiple linear regressions on a census survey of 100 waste pickers in four cooperatives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize providing stronger support for waste-picking activities, such as funding for formal solid waste management systems and reinforcing waste-picker associations to enhance waste pickers' productivity and overall sustainable performance.

Authors: Naomi Millner; Irune Penagaricano; Maria Fernandez; Laura K. Snook
Field: Social movement; Social exclusion; Participatory action research; Political science; Natural resource management; Conflict resolution; Community management; Public administration; Community forestry; Political ecology
Title: The politics of participation: Negotiating relationships through community forestry in the Maya Biosphere Reserve, Guatemala
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that CF programs have had mixed success in terms of ecological and economic outcomes, and have contributed to exacerbating existing patterns of social exclusion. However, ACOFOP has been successful in consolidating the rights of local communities to forest resources through participatory decision-making, conflict resolution, advocacy, and capacity-building strategies.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the effectiveness of community forestry (CF) initiatives in Guatemala's Peten region over a 25-year period, focusing on the emergence and consolidation of ACOFOP, a Forest-Based Association in the Maya Biosphere Reserve.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality in CF programs, policymakers should prioritize support for community-led initiatives like ACOFOP that emphasize participatory decision-making, conflict resolution, and capacity-building strategies to ensure equitable access to forest resources and sustainable development outcomes.

Authors: Chei Bukari; Suman Seth; Gaston Yalonetkzy
Field: Language change; Health care; Context (archaeology); Payment; Business; Population; Public economics; Instrumental variable; Development economics; Economic growth; Economics; Demographic economics; Environmental health; Medicine; Geography; Finance; Art; Literature; Archaeology; Econometrics
Title: Corruption can cause healthcare deprivation: Evidence from 29 sub-Saharan African countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the experience of corruption in the form of bribe payments, as well as the frequency of bribery within the healthcare sector, increases the likelihood of healthcare deprivation. Additionally, corruption experienced in other sectors, such as education, the police, public utilities, and identification authorities, have spill-over effects on healthcare deprivation.
What_was_studied: The WHO estimates that nearly half of the world's population lacks access to essential healthcare, and that the proportion of the population with catastrophic out-of-pocket health spending (10% or more of the household budget) is on the rise. Meanwhile, the United Nations' General Assembly has recently identified corruption as a vital factor undermining efforts to accomplish universal health coverage in 29 sub-Saharan African countries between 2011 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that mitigating corruption in the healthcare sector alone may not be sufficient to end the adverse effect of corruption on effective healthcare access. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive anti-corruption strategies addressing multiple sectors and improve the efficiency and equity of healthcare systems.

Authors: Thomas Glauben; Thomas Herzfeld; Scott Rozelle; Xiaobing Wang
Field: Poverty; China; Geography; Population; Rural population; Duration dependence; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Economic inequality; Panel data; Duration (project management)
Keywords: Poverty, Asia, China, rural population, hazard analysis, dynamics JEL classification: C14; I32; R29
Title: Persistent Poverty in Rural China: Where, Why, and How to Escape?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The majority of the population seems to be only temporarily poor, however, the probability to leave poverty for those who were poor is differently affected by poverty duration across provinces, ranging from no duration dependence in Zhejiang to highly significant duration dependence in Yunnan.
What_was_studied: Using rural household panel data from three Chinese provinces, this paper identifies determinants of long-term poverty and tests the duration dependence on the probability to leave poverty, with a special emphasis on the selection of the poverty line and inter-regional differences across provinces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective anti-poverty programs and policies in rural China, policymakers should prioritize addressing the differences in poverty duration across provinces, particularly in Yunnan, where poverty duration has a highly significant impact on leaving poverty.

Field: Outbreak; Public health; Vulnerability; Geography; Health equity; Disease; Affect (psychology); Development economics; Hygiene; Pandemic
Keywords: COVID-19; Coronavirus; Health inequality; Public health; Sub-Saharan Africa; Vulnerability
Title: How health inequality affect responses to the COVID-19 pandemic in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that handwashing with soap is a crucial factor in preventing the spread of COVID-19, yet millions of Africans lack access to basic hygiene facilities, leading to higher infection rates and increased risk of severe illness and death.
What_was_studied: Using WHO-UNICEF data, this paper examines the health disparities faced by millions of Africans who lack access to hygiene facilities and clean water services during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high disease burden and limited healthcare capacity in African countries, it is crucial to scale up handwashing with soap interventions and prioritize access to clean water and sanitation services to prevent further spread of COVID-19 and protect vulnerable populations.

Authors: Tesfamicheal Wossen; Tahirou Abdoulaye; Arega D. Alene; Shiferaw T. Feleke; Jacob Ricker-Gilbert; Victor M. Manyong; Bola Amoke Awotide
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Voucher; Economics; Productivity; Beneficiary; Disadvantaged; Food security; Endogeneity; Subsidy
Keywords: Nigeria; agricultural input subsidies; mobile phone; productivity; smallholders; welfare
Title: Productivity and Welfare Effects of Nigeria's e-Voucher-Based Input Subsidy Program
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The program was found to be effective in improving productivity and welfare outcomes for beneficiary smallholders, with a benefit-cost ratio of 1.11. The distributional effects of the program were also found to be uniform across gender and farm land size.
What_was_studied: Household-level data from rural Nigeria was examined to determine the productivity and welfare effects of a mobile phone-based input subsidy program on smallholder farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the marginally cost-effective nature of the program and its positive impact on productivity and welfare outcomes, decision makers should prioritize targeting the most disadvantaged groups to maximize the program's contribution to food security and poverty reduction.

Field: Positive economics; Economics; Self-expression values; Impartiality; Universalism; Human development (humanity); Intergenerational equity; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Social sustainability; Sustainable development
Title: Human Development and Economic Sustainability
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
