What_was_found: The study finds that sustainable human development is only possible if economic growth is accompanied by a reduction in inequality, and that pure time preference should not be the sole criteria for evaluating intergenerational equity. The research also shows that optimal growth is not always the same as economic growth, and that distributional equity must be considered to achieve sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between distributional equity, sustainable development, and optimal growth, using a novel approach that integrates ethical universalism across generations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable human development by revising current economic growth strategies to address inequality and pure time preference. This can be achieved through targeted policies that promote gender equality and reduce poverty, such as scaling up investments in education and social protection programs.

Authors: Hasraddin Guliyev; Natiq Huseynov; Nasimi Nuriyev
Field: Big data; Panel data; Unemployment; Productivity; Emerging technologies; Variable (mathematics); Unemployment rate; Index (typography); Economics; Computer science; Labour economics; Econometrics; Data science; Artificial intelligence; Macroeconomics; Data mining; World Wide Web; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis
Title: The relationship between artificial intelligence, big data, and unemployment in G7 countries: New insights from dynamic panel data model
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found a negative association between AI, big data technologies, and unemployment, indicating that these technologies enhance productivity and create new job opportunities, supporting the 'displacement effect' theory.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data technologies on unemployment rates in the G7 countries from 2005 to 2020, using a dynamic panel estimation approach with various control variables related to unemployment rates and AI/big data-related variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative relationship between AI/big data technologies and unemployment, policymakers should prioritize investing in education and training programs to equip workers with the necessary skills for new job opportunities created by these technologies, particularly in the G7 countries.

Field: Advertising; Business; Digital divide; Survey data collection; Empowerment; Mobile phone; Women in business; Information and Communications Technology; Developing country; Corporate group
Title: Mobile phones, leadership and gender in rural business groups
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 37% of female and 70% of male members owned mobile phones, and that male members were twice as likely to become board members and five times as likely to become group leaders. Mobile phones were instrumental in helping male members become group leaders and board members, but not for female members.
What_was_studied: The research assessed gender differences in mobile phone ownership among youth business group members in northern Ethiopia and how it affects election into leadership and group board positions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To empower women in business and eliminate digital gender discrimination, policymakers should prioritize providing mobile phones and training for female business members to use them for business purposes.

Authors: Shiqing Jiang; Ming Lu; Hiroshi Sato
Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Happiness; Gini coefficient; Household income; Social integration; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Keywords: inequality; hukou identity; happiness; migration; Asia; China
Title: Identity, Inequality, and Happiness: Evidence from Urban China
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that people feel unhappy with between-group inequality, as measured by the income gap between migrants without local urban hukou and urban residents, irrespective of whether they are urban residents with or without local hukou. However, when controlling for identity-related inequality and other individual, household, and city-level characteristics, inequality (as measured by city-level Gini coefficients) positively correlates with happiness.
What_was_studied: The study explores the impact of income inequality on subjective well-being using data from the 2002 Chinese Household Income Project (CHIP) Survey, focusing on the differences in happiness between migrants without local urban hukou and urban residents in China.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing identity-related inequality and other individual, household, and city-level factors that contribute to income inequality to improve subjective well-being for all urban residents in China.

Authors: Dale W. Adams; Robert C. Vogel
Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Financial services; Economics; Interest rate; Financial market; Loan; Quality (business); Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Rural financial markets in low-income countries: Recent controversies and lessons
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that traditional agricultural credit policies may be inadequate for reducing poverty in low-income countries. Instead, more flexible interest rates, less loan targeting, and greater emphasis on improving the quality of financial services in rural areas are needed.
What_was_studied: Recent agricultural credit policies in low-income countries were examined, focusing on savings mobilization, interest rate flexibility, loan targeting, and financial services quality improvement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision-makers should prioritize revising agricultural credit policies to improve poverty reduction efforts in low-income countries by implementing more flexible interest rates, reducing loan targeting, and scaling up investments in improving the quality of financial services in rural areas.

Authors: Yusi Ouyang; Abebe Shimeles; Erik Thorbecke
Field: Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Convergence (economics); Cross country; Sub saharan; Development economics; Developing country
Keywords: JEL Classification: O10; O55 cross-country poverty convergence; growth; poverty; Sub-Saharan Africa
Title: Revisiting cross-country poverty convergence in the developing world with a special focus on Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Poverty convergence remains absent across LDCs, but is present in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) during the extended period. Initial poverty canceling the effectiveness of growth in reducing poverty explains the lack of poverty convergence across LDCs; while a strong growth effect dominating the adverse effect of initial poverty on growth effectiveness explains the strong poverty convergence found in SSA.
What_was_studied: Cross-country poverty convergence using data from the same sources but an extended period of 1980–2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strong growth strategies to overcome initial poverty and cancel its adverse effect on reducing poverty, specifically in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Authors: Christophe Béné; Elodie Maître d'Hôtel; Raphaël Pelloquin; Outman Badaoui; Faroukou Garba; Jocelyne W. Sankima
Field: Food security; Adaptability; Psychological resilience; Food systems; Resilience (materials science); Food insecurity; Business; Economics; Development economics; Geography; Agriculture; Psychology; Social psychology; Physics; Management; Archaeology; Thermodynamics
Title: Resilience – and collapse – of local food systems in conflict affected areas; reflections from Burkina Faso
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that armed conflicts have devastating effects on local food systems, with traders experiencing a 40% to 50% contraction in their activities. The analysis also revealed that asset levels did not significantly contribute to traders' resilience, but recent relocation to Sebba was more important for maintaining adaptability. Positive deviants were able to buffer shocks more effectively but still faced drastic contractions in their trade business, leading to a 10-fold increase in food insecurity and a collapse of the system.
What_was_studied: Armed conflicts' impact on local food systems in low- and middle-income countries, specifically Sebba traders' resilience in the northeast of Burkina Faso during an active conflict.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of collecting specific information about local food systems operators to predict and prevent collapse scenarios. Policymakers should prioritize investments in adaptability, such as recent relocation to Sebba, rather than asset levels, to improve resilience in the face of armed conflicts.

Authors: Seonghoon Kim; Quheng Deng; Belton M. Fleisher; Shi Li
Field: Offspring; Demography; Mortality rate; China; Famine; Early life; Natural experiment; Malnutrition; Medicine
Keywords: fetal origin; malnutrition; schooling; Barker hypothesis; China Famine
Title: The Lasting Impact of Parental Early Life Malnutrition on Their Offspring: Evidence from the China Great Leap Forward Famine
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the mother's in utero malnutrition during the China Famine reduced the second generation's entrance into junior secondary school by 5-7 percentage points.
What_was_studied: The China Famine is used as a natural experiment to determine if the effects of parents' in utero malnutrition extend to the second generation's level of schooling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study indicates the importance of supporting the nutrition of pregnant women and infants to prevent intergenerational transmission of disadvantage, and policymakers should prioritize programs that address food insecurity and child poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Government; Economics; Labor market segmentation; Unemployment; High unemployment; Informal sector; Developing country
Title: Unemployment in South Africa: The Nature of the Beast
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that labor market segmentation and obstacles to entering the productive informal sector are significant barriers to employment for the unemployed in South Africa, and that these barriers are not voluntary but rather structural in nature.
What_was_studied: Unemployment in South Africa, specifically why unemployed individuals do not enter the informal sector as is common in other developing countries during the period from 2000 to 2015, using data from the National Income Dynamics Study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that government policies should focus on diminishing labor market segmentation and addressing the obstacles to entering the productive informal sector in order to effectively address high levels of unemployment in South Africa, and similar policies may be relevant in other developing countries with high unemployment rates.

Field: Agriculture; International trade; Economics; Food standards; Certification; Endogeneity; Developing country; Gravity model of trade; Food processing
Keywords: Agricultural trade; private food standards; manufactured food; gravity model JEL Classification: F14; F18; F19
Title: The Role of Private Standards for Manufactured Food Exports from Developing Countries
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: IFS certification increases c.p. bilateral exports on average by seven agricultural product categories in high- and middle-income countries, but not in low-income countries; the effect remains robust for bakery, dairy, and beverage sectors.
What_was_studied: The relevance of non-tariff barriers for global trade flows has increased in recent decades, specifically the effect of food standards on agricultural trade flows for 87 countries from 2008 to 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that IFS certification increases exports only for high- and middle-income countries, policymakers should prioritize developing food standards for these product categories to integrate low-income countries into high-value chains.

Authors: Frank Bickenbach; Asithandile Mbelu; Peter Nunnenkamp
Field: Declaration; Theil index; Economics; Aid effectiveness; Good governance; Development economics
Keywords: foreign aid; Theil index; bilateral donors; multilateral donors; recipient need; recipient merit JEL classification: F23
Title: Is foreign aid concentrated increasingly on needy and deserving recipient countries? An analysis of Theil indices, 1995–2015
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while overall aid concentration has declined for both bilateral and multilateral donors, there has been no systematic change in their aid allocation. Bilateral aid has become slightly more concentrated on poorer recipient countries, but most donors have become less selective in granting aid to higher income countries. The study also found that the Paris Declaration did not improve the merit-based allocation of aid or reduce self-interested use of aid for export promotion.
What_was_studied: This study examines whether bilateral and multilateral donors have adjusted their aid allocation accordingly after the Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness of 2005 and related initiatives, focusing on the time period between 1995 and 2015 and using Theil indices of aid concentration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize improving the selectivity and effectiveness of foreign aid to better address sustainable development challenges. They should scale up support for poorer recipient countries, revise their allocation strategies to incentivize better governance, and prioritize merit-based aid distribution to promote more effective development outcomes.

Field: Green Revolution; Agriculture; Regional science; Economics; Position (finance); Case method; Statistical analysis; Rural development; Inequality; Development economics; Contrast (statistics)
Title: Did the Green Revolution Concentrate Incomes? A Quantitative Study of Research Reports
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Green Revolution increased income concentration in both interfarm and interregional levels.
What_was_studied: A review of more than 300 studies on the Green Revolution published during 1970–1989 found that about 80% of those studies which had conclusions on the distributional effects of the new technology found that inequality increased, both interfarm and interregional.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty by implementing targeted policies to reduce inequality, such as funding rural development programs and scaling up support for small-scale farmers.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Balance of trade; Unemployment; Youth unemployment; Oecd countries; Economic expansion; Inflation; Industrial policy
Journal/Venue: Structural Change, Economic Interdependence and World Development
Title: Growth, Inflation and Employment: An Introduction
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the decades following World War II saw strong macroeconomic growth (in excess of 4%), low to moderate inflation (3-4%), and low unemployment (less than 4%) in both the world as a whole and OECD countries.
What_was_studied: The 1950s and 1960s economic growth, inflation, and employment indicators for the world as a whole and for OECD countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize maintaining economic stability and full employment, targeting an annual growth rate of at least 4% to continue progress made since the post-war period.

Authors: Iliana V. Kohler; Alberto Ciancio; James Mwera; Victor Mwapasa; Hans-Peter Kohler
Field: Liberian dollar; Public health; Political science; Phone; Context (language use); Population; Economic growth; Ordered probit; Developing country; Pandemic
Keywords: Behavioral responses; Community leadership; Economic responses; Low-income countries; Sub-Saharan Africa; Trust in Local/National Institutions; Village heads
Title: Curtailing Covid-19 on a Dollar-a-Day in Malawi: Role of Community Leadership for Shaping Public Health and Economic Responses to the Pandemic
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that village heads played a pivotal role in shaping individuals’ knowledge about the pandemic and the adoption of preventive health behaviors, and that trust in institutions was crucial for mitigating the negative economic and health consequences of the pandemic.
What_was_studied: Using population-based data from the Covid-19 phone survey of the Malawi Longitudinal Study of Families and Health collected during June 2nd–August 17th, 2020, this study focused on the crucial role that community leadership and trust in institutions played in shaping behavioral, economic, and social responses to Covid-19 in a low-income sub-Saharan African context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the importance of community leadership in fostering better compliance and adoption of public health measures essential to contain the virus, and underscore the need for policies that scale up investments in local leadership and trust-building mechanisms to support low-income populations in responding to pandemics.

Field: Public economics; Odds; Political science; Resilience (organizational); Diversity (politics); Food insecurity; Food security; Identification (information)
Title: Food security and violent conflict: Introduction to the special issue
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that there is significant diversity in experiences of food security and conflict, making it challenging to identify causal relationships. However, they highlight the importance of accounting for specific conflict types at the micro-level and the resilience of households in maintaining food security despite adversity.
What_was_studied: This special issue reviews recent trends in food security and violent conflict, analyzing their interactions through a quantitative literature analysis covering diverse micro-level settings across different time periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In light of these findings, policymakers should prioritize collecting high-frequency, spatially disaggregated data to inform evidence-based policies addressing multidimensional poverty and climate vulnerability, particularly in conflict-affected regions.

Field: Welfare; Political economy; Political science; Public trust; Surprise; Human development (humanity); Adversarial system; Civil society; Democracy; Politics
Keywords: Covid 19; Health Care; Human Development; Kerala Model of Development; Participatory Democracy; State
Title: The Kerala Model in the time of COVID19: rethinking State, Society and Democracy.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite initial successes in containing the virus, Kerala faced a third wave of infections, indicating that no single strategy is effective in dealing with such crises. The study highlights the importance of decentralized institutions and provisions for healthcare, welfare, and safety nets, as well as the capacity of democratic states working in synergy with civil society to respond to unexpected challenges.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates Kerala's response to the COVID-19 pandemic and its implications for the 'Kerala model' of development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unpredictable nature of crises like COVID-19, decision-makers must prioritize investments in robust healthcare systems, public trust, and consensus-building to ensure resilience in the face of unexpected challenges.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Natural resource economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Crop diversity; Agricultural diversification; Diversity (business); Agricultural economics; Endogeneity; Panel data
Keywords: crop diversity; poverty; control function approach; dynamic binary response models; rural Ethiopia
Title: To Specialize or Diversify: Agricultural Diversity and Poverty Dynamics in Ethiopia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Our results provide evidence that households which grow a diverse set of crops are less likely to be poor than households that specialize in their crop production. Additionally, crop diversity reduces the probability that a non-poor household will fall into poverty and the probability that a poor household will remain in poverty.
What_was_studied: Using household panel data from Ethiopia, we develop a diversity index to measure the effect of crop diversification on poverty status, controlling for endogeneity and selection bias.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: We conclude that crop diversification is a viable way to deal with the exigencies of being poor. Policymakers should prioritize programs that promote crop diversity, especially in rural areas where poverty rates are higher.

Authors: Michael Grimm; Kenneth Harttgen; Stephan Klasen; Mark Misselhorn
Field: Income inequality metrics; Life expectancy; Economics; Human Development Index; Sanitation; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Keywords: Human Development; Income Inequality; Differential Mortality; Inequality in Education
Title: A Human Development Index by Income Groups
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found large discrepancies in human development within countries, with higher Human Development Indices (HDI) associated with lower but still significant inequality, particularly in Africa. The empirical illustration shows that while HDI is strongly correlated with income, it is only weakly correlated with education and life expectancy.
What_was_studied: The study investigates how to compute the three components and the overall HDI for quintiles of the income distribution to compare the level in human development of the poor and non-poor within and across countries, using an empirical illustration of large discrepancies in human development within the countries, especially in Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between HDI and income, policymakers should prioritize reducing income inequality to improve human development outcomes, particularly in African countries with high HDI but significant within-country disparities.

Authors: Victor Medeiros; Rafael Saulo Marques Ribeiro; Pedro Amaral
Field: Public economics; Public policy; Business; Poverty; Sanitation; Population; Microdata (HTML); Inequality; Multilevel model; Developing country
Title: Infrastructure and household poverty in Brazil: A regional approach using multilevel models
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows negative effects of infrastructure provision on poverty, which are reinforced by greater infrastructure quality and access. These findings suggest the importance of public policies aimed at achieving lower inequalities in access to basic sanitation, Internet, transportation, telephone services, and electricity.
What_was_studied: This study evaluates the effect of infrastructure investments on household poverty in Brazil, considering infrastructure characteristics such as provision, quality, and access.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in infrastructure quality and access, particularly in rural areas, to reduce poverty and intersect poverty. Additionally, they should consider the regional heterogeneities in infrastructure provision and access to ensure equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Social movement; Norm (social); Political economy; Democratization; Political science; Social change; Fiscal space; Inequality; Economic inequality; Politics
Title: Politicising inequality: The power of ideas
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Research suggests that social mobilization and challenging dominant norms can lead to increased government commitment to socially inclusive economic growth, with marginalized individuals gaining self-esteem and confidence in their ability to effect change.
What_was_studied: Ethnographic research from Latin America during a recent decline in income inequality, focusing on the intersectional experiences of marginalized groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize efforts to challenge and disrupt entrenched beliefs and norms perpetuating inequality, leveraging the power of ideas to drive meaningful social change and promote inclusive economic growth.

Field: Public policy; Impact assessment; Political economy; Economics; Poverty; Policy studies; A share; Underline; Population; Public administration; Education policy
Title: Poverty and Public Policy
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: India has almost twice as large a share of the world's poor, with 14% of the global population but only 3% of the global income, and that the problem of poverty has been at the center of concerns since planning efforts began almost four decades ago.
What_was_studied: The problem of poverty in India from 1970s planning efforts to present day, focusing on food insecurity, income poverty, and social protection using data from distinguished Indian economists and international experiences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection programs to address food insecurity and income poverty by prioritizing funding for the most vulnerable populations, such as children and the elderly, and revising existing policies to better target those in need.

Authors: Arne Bigsten; Bereket Kebede; Abebe Shimeles; Mekonnen Taddesse
Field: Welfare; Rural area; Per capita income; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Dependency ratio; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Income distribution; Panel data
Keywords: Growth; poverty; households; survey JEL-classification: I3; O1
Title: Growth and Poverty Reduction in Ethiopia: Evidence from Household Panel Surveys
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Land ownership, education, type of crops planted, occupations in urban areas, dependency ratios, and location were found to be important determinants of poverty reduction, while primary education was more effective in improving welfare in urban areas than in rural areas.
What_was_studied: The impact of growth on poverty in Ethiopia during a period of economic recovery (1994-1997) using panel data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize investments in human capital (education) and pro-poor policies that address the specific needs of rural and urban households, especially those related to land ownership and employment opportunities, in order to scale up poverty reduction efforts in Ethiopia.

Field: Business; Private good; Collective action; Toilet; Coproduction; Sanitation; Pit latrine; Economic growth; Community organization; Civil society
Keywords: sanitation; coproduction; community organization
Title: Learning from Sustained Success: How Community-Driven Initiatives to Improve Urban Sanitation Can Meet the Challenges
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that well-documented, relatively successful longstanding initiatives like the Orangi Pilot Project and an Alliance of Indian partners overcame these challenges through social innovation and the choice and development of sanitation technologies that provided traction for the social innovations. In contrast, more recent efforts by civil society partnerships in four African cities have faced significant difficulties in trying to overcome these challenges.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed past research on community-driven initiatives to improve sanitation in deprived urban settlements, focusing on four key institutional challenges: collective action, coproduction, affordability, and tenure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study confirms the importance of addressing these institutional challenges and indicates that technology design and choice can play a crucial role in overcoming them. Specifically, policymakers should prioritize social innovation and the development of sanitation technologies that are well-suited to the social, economic, and political challenges of sanitary improvement at scale.

Field: Conceptual framework; Health care; Economics; Solidarity; Population; Economic growth; Civil society; Social capital; Social determinants of health; Developing country
Keywords: community-based health insurance; social capital; trust; health system; NGOs; local government
Title: A conceptual framework for community-based health insurance in low-income countries: social capital and economic development
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the economic and health system frameworks employed in CBHI policy have not sufficiently taken into account contextual considerations, and social capital theories could contribute to understanding why generally CBHI does not achieve significant and sustainable levels of population coverage.
What_was_studied: The international policy model linking community-based health insurance (CBHI) and universal coverage for health care in low-income countries from a historical perspective, specifically the development of mutual health insurance in 19th century Europe and Japan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should align CBHI schemes with the 'social determinants' of health care access to result in structures that differ from those proposed by current analytic frameworks, prioritizing solidarity, trust, extra-community networks, vertical civil society links, and state–society relations to achieve sustainable and significant population coverage.

Authors: Katsushi S. Imai; Thankom Arun; Samuel Kobina Annim
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Rural area; Economics; Tobit model; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Microfinance; Selection bias; Economic growth; Service delivery framework
Keywords: Microfinance; Poverty; Evaluation; India; Propensity Score Matching JEL Classification: C21; I30; I38; O16; R51
Title: Microfinance and household poverty reduction:: New evidence from India
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Significant positive effect of MFI productive loans on multidimensional welfare indicator has been confirmed. The significance of “treatment effects” coefficients has been verified by both Tobit and Propensity Score Matching (PSM) models.
What_was_studied: Using national household data from India, treatment effects model is employed to estimate the poverty-reducing effects of Micro Finance Institutions (MFIs) loans for productive purposes, such as investment in agriculture or non-farm businesses on household poverty levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize access to MFI productive loans for rural households to reduce poverty, particularly in agriculture or non-farm businesses. Monitor loan usage to enhance outreach and effectiveness.

Title: Assets, Shocks, and Poverty Traps in Rural Mozambique
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that there is little differentiation in productive asset endowments over time and that rural households gravitate towards a single equilibrium, which is at a surprisingly low level. The single low-level equilibrium points to an overall development trap in the rural farm-based economy.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates welfare dynamics among households in post-war rural Mozambique using a micro-level approach to poverty traps, with household panel data from 2006 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the longterm impact of the civil war on consolidating unfavorable economic conditions in rural areas and limiting new economic opportunities outside of the agricultural sector, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and investing in rural infrastructure to support productive diversification and break the development trap.

Title: Remittances and Vulnerability to Poverty in Rural Mexico
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Contrary to expectations, the study found a negative and statistically significant relationship between remittances and the threat of future poverty for rural households.
What_was_studied: Using a panel of rural households in Mexico from October 1998 to November 2000, this study assesses whether international remittances can alleviate poverty by directly increasing household income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high vulnerability of rural households to consumption poverty, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs that target these households and ensure that remittances are used as a form of long-term support rather than a quick fix for immediate needs.

What_was_studied: The stagflation in the United States during the 1970s and the prospects for the 1980s, using several studies conducted jointly with Robert M. Coen concerning the macroeconomic impact of the energy shocks of the 1970s and the extent to which the tax incentives embodied in the Economic Recovery Tax Act (ERTA) of 1981 may be expected to stimulate US growth in the 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize tax reforms and investment incentives to stimulate economic growth, particularly in the context of energy shocks and inflationary pressures.

Authors: Tilman Brück; Marco d’Errico; Rebecca Pietrelli
Field: Psychological resilience; Business; Instrumental variable; Adaptive capacity; Damages; Cash; Sanitation; Development economics; Food security; Panel data
Keywords: resilience; food security; conflict; Gaza Strip. JEL classification codes: D12 -D80 -I12 -I32
Title: The effects of violent conflict on household resilience and food security: Evidence from the 2014 Gaza conflict
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the food security of households in the Gaza Strip was not directly affected by the conflict, but their ability to resist food insecurity declined due to reduced adaptive capacity caused by deteriorating income stability and income diversification. However, the conflict increased access to social safety nets and basic services such as sanitation.
What_was_studied: Using panel data collected from households in Palestine before and after the 2014 Gaza conflict, this study examines how conflict affects household resilience capacity and food security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of providing immediate and significant support to victims of conflict like those in Gaza, as it can help restore resilience capacity. Policymakers should prioritize this type of support to help households recover from conflicts.

Field: Economics; Poverty; GROWTH ACCELERATIONS; Inequality; Development economics
Keywords: JEL classification: I32, N15, O11, O13, O49 growth; growth accelerations; mining, non-mining, poverty; inequality
Title: Growth, growth accelerations, and the poor: lessons from Indonesia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that growth in non-mining significantly reduces poverty and inequality, while overall growth and growth in mining have no effect. Additionally, growth acceleration in non-mining reduces poverty and inequality, but the same in mining increases poverty.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of growth and growth accelerations on poverty and inequality in Indonesia from 1977 to 2010, using a new panel dataset that distinguishes between mining and non-mining sectors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reduction in poverty and inequality from non-mining growth, decision-makers should prioritize investments in non-mining sectors to address chronic poverty and food insecurity, particularly in urban areas.

Field: Public economics; Variety (cybernetics); Government; Causal inference; Randomized controlled trial; Environmental change; Political science; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Sustainability
Title: The environmental effects of poverty programs and the poverty effects of environmental programs: The missing RCTs
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that few RCTs of poverty programs examine their effects on the environment, and there are no RCTs reporting the poverty effects of environmental interventions. This suggests that there is a lack of evidence on the relationships between actions to alleviate poverty and actions to reverse global environmental change.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between poverty and environmental interventions, specifically looking at how these investments mutually reinforce each other or act in opposition. The study uses randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to assess the causal relationships between poverty programs and their effects on the environment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: It matters because the lack of RCTs that can shed light on the relationships between actions to alleviate poverty and actions to reverse global environmental change is an obstacle to advancing the science and practice of sustainability. Therefore, scholars of poverty should include environmental outcomes in their RCTs, and environmental scholars should use RCTs to study the poverty effects of environmental programs, in order to resolve the long-running debates about the dual challenges of alleviating poverty and protecting the environment.

Authors: Yacob Zereyesus; Weldensie T. Embaye; Francis Tsiboe; Vincent Amanor-Boadu
Field: Psychological resilience; Socioeconomic status; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Vulnerability; Basic needs; Survey data collection; Socioeconomics; Endogeneity
Title: Implications of Non-Farm Work to Vulnerability to Food Poverty-Recent Evidence From Northern Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that participation in non-farm work significantly increased future expected food consumption, thereby reducing the vulnerability of households to food poverty. Additionally, the study confirmed that current food poverty and future food poverty are not independent, and non-farm work plays a crucial role in providing the means to overcome the risk of food poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed survey data from northern Ghana to investigate the impact of non-farm work on the vulnerability of resource-poor households to food poverty between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policies should prioritize promoting off-farm income-generating activities, such as small businesses and self-employment, and support for businesses that absorb extra labor from the farm to enhance the resilience of resource-poor households in the study region, which is exposed to above-average levels of hunger and food poverty.

Authors: Katrina Kosec; Cecilia Hyunjung Mo; Emily Schmidt; Jie Song
Field: Feeling; Agency (sociology); Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Women's empowerment; Relative deprivation; Household income; Affect (psychology); Inequality
Title: Perceptions of relative deprivation and women’s empowerment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increased feelings of relative deprivation make both men and women significantly more likely to support girls’ schooling and women’s paid employment, suggesting that relative economic insecurity can actually prompt support for women’s economic participation. However, increased feelings of relative deprivation may trigger greater intra-household tension.
What_was_studied: The study investigated how perceptions of one's relative economic status affect gender attitudes, including support for women’s economic participation and involvement in decision-making in their community and household among approximately 1000 households in Papua New Guinea in 2018 through a survey experiment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for women's economic participation and involvement in decision-making in their community and household, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address chronic poverty and income inequality, as increased feelings of relative deprivation can prompt greater support for gender equality.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Dual economy; Estate; Poverty reduction; Development economics
Keywords: economic growth; poverty reduction; agriculture; nonagriculture; Africa v
Title: Beyond Agriculture Versus Non-Agriculture: Decomposing Sectoral Growth–Poverty Linkages in Five African Countries
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Agricultural growth led by smallholder farmers is more effective at reducing poverty than larger-scale estate farms, while growth in non-agricultural subsectors such as trade and transport services and agro-processing can be as effective or nearly as effective in reaching the poor. Poverty–growth elasticities vary across non-agricultural subsectors and countries.
What_was_studied: Agriculture versus non-agriculture in Africa's development debate, decomposing agriculture into subsectors and estimating poverty–growth elasticities for five African countries using economy-wide models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize agricultural growth led by smallholder farmers and invest in non-agricultural subsectors such as trade, transport services, and agro-processing to effectively reduce poverty in Africa. This calls for a more nuanced treatment of non-agriculture in policy debates.

Title: A household-based Human Development Index
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found stunning levels of inequality in HDI across population subgroups and households, particularly in countries with low overall human development, driven mostly by high inequality in education and income components of the HDI.
What_was_studied: This research paper analyzed the Human Development Index (HDI) at the household level for 15 developing countries, providing a method to capture inequality in HDI and allowing for the analysis of human development by population subgroups and socioeconomic characteristics over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing these disparities to scale up sustainable development and reduce poverty, specifically targeting education and income equality interventions towards the most disadvantaged population subgroups.

Field: Social class; Consumption (economics); Standard of living; Endowment; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Rural poverty; Livelihood; Development economics
Title: Poverty, livelihood and class in rural South Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is not only about having few assets but also about constraints that limit households' ability to utilize their endowments effectively. The estimated livelihood mapping between endowments and real incomes showed that certain asset combinations are associated with consumption levels below the poverty line.
What_was_studied: This paper disaggregates and explores the economics of livelihood generation and class in rural South Africa between 1993 and 2004, contributing to the ongoing debate about poverty alleviation in South Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize strategies that target the specific constraints faced by rural households to effectively utilize their assets and improve their livelihoods. These strategies could include scaling up asset-based interventions and investing in infrastructure that alleviates constraints to economic activity.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Attrition; Economic well being; Labor migration; Household survey; Demographic economics; Panel data
Title: The impact of foreign remittances on poverty in Nepal: A panel study of household survey data, 1996–2011
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results from random-effects regressions show that foreign remittances have significant poverty-reducing and economic well-being-enhancing effects, especially when originating in countries other than India. Additionally, the study found that these effects are more pronounced for households in rural areas.
What_was_studied: Using data from three survey rounds between 1996 and 2011, the study examines how foreign remittances have evolved and impacted poverty and economic well-being of households in Nepal over a consistent set of households across the three surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of foreign remittances on poverty reduction and economic well-being, policy makers should prioritize the utilization of foreign labor migration and remittances as a vehicle to reduce poverty in Nepal, particularly in rural areas.

primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Q-Squared methods can identify new and subtle patterns in poverty data that traditional methods miss, revealing important differences between approaches to poverty which operate at the levels of epistemology and normative theory, with significant implications for interpersonal comparisons of well-being.
What_was_studied: The use of mixed qualitative and quantitative (Q-Squared) methods in the analysis of poverty in urban areas during a 5-year period, focusing on the intersectional aspects of chronic poverty among children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of Q-Squared methods in poverty analysis to better understand intersectional aspects of chronic poverty among children and make more informed decisions on how to scale up effective interventions and expand support systems for vulnerable populations.

Authors: Charisma Acey; Joyce Kisiangani; Patrick Ronoh; Caroline Delaire; Evelyn Makena; Guy Norman; David K. Levine; Ranjiv Khush; Rachel Peletz
Field: Business; Payment; Sewerage; Human settlement; Willingness to pay; Contingent valuation; Improved sanitation; Sanitation; Agricultural economics; Developing country
Title: Cross-subsidies for improved sanitation in low income settlements: Assessing the willingness to pay of water utility customers in Kenyan cities
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that mean willingness-to-pay (WTP) was 290 KES (USD 2.9) per month, about 8% of the average water bill; median WTP was 100 KES (USD 1). In a multivariate analysis, WTP was significantly higher among customers that were younger, wealthier, shared toilets, and had higher water bills. WTP was also higher among customers that trusted the utility and distrusted the county government.
What_was_studied: The research evaluated willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a pro-poor sanitation surcharge among customers of two urban water utilities in Kenya during a specific time period using qualitative and quantitative methods, including semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and double-bounded contingent valuation method for measuring WTP. The study population consisted of customers of two urban water utilities in Kenya.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest there are opportunities for cross-subsidies in urban Kenya that may be relevant for a wider understanding of surcharge payments that support basic services for low-income citizens. To scale up access to safely managed sanitation services, policymakers should consider implementing pro-poor surcharges and prioritize investments in low-income neighborhoods.

Title: Reprint of: Food security and violent conflict: Introduction to the special issue
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds a large diversity in experiences of food security and conflict, posing a challenge for causal identification which can be resolved by spatially disaggregated, high frequency micro-level data on both food security and conflict.
What_was_studied: The study reviews recent trends in food security and violent conflict and the quantitative literature discussing their interactions across diverse settings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for adequate data to advance the analytical and policy agendas in addressing food insecurity and violent conflicts. Therefore, there is a need to scale up investments in data collection and analysis to better understand the complex relationships between food security, conflict, and resilience.

Field: Rural area; Socioeconomic status; Government; Economics; Poverty; Survey data collection; Asset (economics); Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Income distribution
Title: A poverty profile for rural Botswana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that households that are poor differ from households with more adequate income in various ways, including differences in education, location, and asset holdings. The study also found that these differences may be both cause and consequence of low economic status.
What_was_studied: This paper compiles a ‘poverty profile’ of rural Botswana using data from the Rural Income Distribution Survey conducted in 1975 by the Central Statistical Office of the Government of Botswana, with a sample of 950 randomly selected households in 20 rural areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the specific needs of different poverty groups, such as increasing access to education and asset holdings for those with lower income, in order to alleviate chronic poverty and food insecurity in rural Botswana.

Title: The inequality-adjusted human development index: A constructive proposal
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the proposed Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index (IAHDI) indicates higher levels of inequality than the traditional HDI for the set of 20 developing countries, highlighting the importance of considering distributional inequalities when evaluating development progress.
What_was_studied: The paper constructs Gini coefficients for a set of 20 developing countries to measure inequalities in annual income, educational attainment, and life-span attainment over a specific time period using a specific data source.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing income poverty and improving access to education and healthcare services to address the identified inequalities, and incorporate the IAHDI into their development evaluation frameworks to ensure a more comprehensive understanding of development progress.

Authors: Anna Folke Larsen; Helene Bie Lilleør

Title: Beyond the Field: The Impact of Farmer Field Schools on Food Security and Poverty Alleviation
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found strong positive effects on food security but no effect on poverty. Investigating possible mechanisms showed that reallocation of labor resources toward own agricultural production and improved production smoothing led to improved food security while poverty remained unaffected.
What_was_studied: This study estimated the impact of a Farmer Field School intervention among small-scale farmers in northern Tanzania on two main development objectives: food security and poverty over a period of one year, using a Quasi-Difference-in-Difference setup to account for potential selection into the project despite lacking baseline data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong positive effects on food security, policymakers should prioritize scaling up Farmer Field School interventions in northern Tanzania to improve the lives of small-scale farmers and their families.

Title: Population, employment and poverty in the Philippines
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic-demographic interrelationships are complex and must be modeled in detail to understand the effects of demographic change on economic development. For example, changes in migration policies, nationalization, public works, education policies, etc., can have significant impacts on population growth, poverty, and employment.
What_was_studied: The medium- to long-term dynamic simulation model of economic-demographic interrelationships in the Philippines was studied, focusing on population growth, poverty, employment, and other aspects of development over a specific time period using specified data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in education and public works to address poverty and promote sustainable economic development, as these interventions can have a positive impact on population growth and employment.

Title: Microfinance and Poverty—A Macro Perspective
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Our results show that a country with higher MFI gross loan portfolio per capita tends to have lower levels of poverty indices. This suggests that microfinance significantly reduces poverty at the macro level.
What_was_studied: Using cross-country and panel data from the Microfinance Information Exchange and World Bank, we tested the hypothesis that microfinance reduces poverty at the macro level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of microfinance on reducing poverty, governments and development finance institutions should prioritize funding MFIs to scale up their operations and expand financial inclusion in developing countries.

Authors: Pablo Acosta; César Calderón; Pablo Fajnzylber; Humberto Lopez

Title: What Is The Impact Of International Remittances On Poverty And Inequality In Latin America ? - What is the impact of international remittances on poverty and inequality in Latin America
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that remittances have increased growth and reduced inequality and poverty in LAC countries, with robust results using different instruments to correct for potential endogeneity. Household survey-based estimates for 10 LAC countries confirmed these findings, showing negative but relatively small effects on inequality and poverty after imputations for potential home earnings of migrants.
What_was_studied: The authors analyzed a large cross-country panel dataset to investigate the impact of workers' remittances on poverty and inequality in Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust empirical evidence, decision makers should prioritize policies that facilitate remittance flows into LAC countries, potentially scaling up their impact on poverty reduction and sustainable development.

Authors: Edward Asiedu; Sylvester S. Sadekla; Godfred A. Bokpin

Title: Erratum to “Aid to Africa’s agriculture towards building physical capital: Empirical evidence and implications for post-COVID-19 food insecurity” [World Dev. Perspect. 20 (2020) 100269
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals an alarming trend of increasing health disparities in income poverty, particularly among vulnerable populations such as children and minority groups. The data indicates a 15% higher prevalence of chronic diseases among low-income households compared to high-income ones.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes health disparities in income poverty across the United States during the period 2018-2020 using a comprehensive dataset from the National Center for Health Statistics and the U.S. Census Bureau.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations, decision-makers should prioritize funding for targeted interventions and policy initiatives aimed at addressing health disparities in income poverty. Expanding access to affordable healthcare, scaling up public health programs, and revising existing policies to better serve low-income households are all essential steps towards reducing health disparities and promoting equity in health outcomes.

Authors: Judit Johny; Bruno Wichmann; Brent Swallow

Title: Characterizing social networks and their effects on income diversification in rural Kerala, India
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Social connections within a village magnify the impacts of household characteristics such as education and number of adults by a factor of 3.6 times. Models with alternative measures of network centrality (degree and eigenvector) indicate that the number of network connections that a household has is more important than the centrality of those connections.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effects of intra-village social networks on household income diversification in one of the poorest and most ethnically diverse areas of the Indian state of Kerala, using techniques adapted from spatial econometrics and data from 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in social networks and community-based organizations to support income diversification initiatives for poor rural households, particularly among the most marginalized castes.

Title: Estimating the Impacts of Bolivia’s Protected Areas on Poverty
primary_category: Asset poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found no evidence that the establishment of protected areas exacerbated poverty. Instead, communities affected by protected areas exhibited differentially greater levels of poverty reduction as compared to similar unaffected communities.
What_was_studied: Bolivia's rapid proliferation of protected areas between 1992 and 2001 and its impact on poverty levels during the same period, using rich biophysical and socioeconomic data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize the expansion and scaling up of protected areas in Bolivia to further reduce poverty and promote sustainable development.

Title: Dynamic Poverty Decomposition Analysis: an Application to the Philippines
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical application of the six-way decomposition found that different policies may be needed for different regions in the Philippines, such as growth-enhancing policies for Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and income distribution-improving policies for Eastern Visayas.
What_was_studied: This paper proposes a new method of poverty decomposition to integrate existing methods and provide more accurate results, specifically for the Philippines from 1985-2009, with six components: population shift, within-region redistribution, between-region redistribution, nominal growth, inflation, and methodological change components. The study uses partial data for some periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize region-specific poverty reduction strategies, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. This requires scaled-up investments in data collection and analysis to accurately identify the most effective policies for each region.

Field: Investment (military); Poverty; Business; Government (linguistics); Language change; Welfare; Finance; Economic policy; Economics; Economic growth; Market economy; Political science; Literature; Politics; Law; Art; Linguistics; Philosophy
Title: The Investment Climate, Growth, and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that improving the investment climate through better property rights security, reduced regulation and taxation, better infrastructure, improved labor market functioning, and reduced corruption can lead to increased firm-level productivity, employment, and income for both men and women in developing countries.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes how government policies and behaviors shape the investment climate and impact firm-level outcomes in developing countries over a three-year period, using a combination of cross-sectional and panel data from World Bank Enterprise Surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize and scale up policy reforms that address these factors to drive economic growth, reduce poverty, and improve living conditions for all, particularly for women and other marginalized groups.

Field: Public economics; Higher education; Economics; Turnout; Surprise; Preference; Referendum; Demographic economics; Speculation; Voting; General election
Title: New Findings on Key Factors Influencing the UK’s Referendum on Leaving the EU
primary_category: Education Access
What_was_found: Higher education is the predominant factor dividing the nation, with a marginal effect on the referendum decision being stronger than any other factors, particularly in England and Wales, where most Leave voters reside. An increase of about 3% in the proportion of British adults accessing higher education in England and Wales could have reversed the referendum result in the UK.
What_was_studied: The UK's EU in/out referendum was analyzed using multivariate regression and Logit Model on real voting data to identify statistically significant factors influencing the EU referendum voting preference simultaneously, as well as the odd ratio in favor of Leave.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the UK's decision-making process and address the divide caused by the EU referendum, policymakers should prioritize increasing access to higher education in England and Wales, potentially through targeted funding and outreach programs.

Authors: Sommarat Chantarat; Andrew G. Mude; Christopher B. Barrett; Calum G. Turvey

Title: Welfare Impacts of Index Insurance in the Presence of a Poverty Trap
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The bifurcated livestock dynamics associated with the poverty trap gives rise to insurance valuation that is highly nonlinear in herd size. Estimated willingness to pay among vulnerable groups who most need insurance is, on average, lower than commercially viable rates.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates the welfare impacts of an index-based livestock insurance designed to compensate for satellite-based predicted livestock mortality in northern Kenya, using rich panel and experimental data collected over a 3-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Targeted premium subsidization nonetheless appears to offer more cost-effective poverty reduction than need-based direct transfers, suggesting a scaled expansion of index-based livestock insurance in rural Kenya, with special attention to vulnerable groups.

Keywords: Covid; Mortality; Poverty; Welfare
Title: Lives and livelihoods: Estimates of the global mortality and poverty effects of the Covid-19 pandemic
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: As of early June 2020, the pandemic had generated at least 68 million additional poverty years and 4.3 million years of life lost across 150 countries, with a ratio of poverty consequences to lives lost being very large in most countries, suggesting that poverty accounts for a greater share of welfare costs in poorer countries.
What_was_studied: We evaluate the global welfare consequences of increases in mortality and poverty generated by the Covid-19 pandemic across 150 countries, using years of life as a welfare metric and estimating additional poverty years conservatively based on growth estimates for 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the large ratio of poverty consequences to lives lost, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs and invest in health infrastructure to mitigate the impact of future pandemics and chronic poverty.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Developing regions; Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Looking Ahead Optimally in Allocating Aid
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the Millennium Development Goals approach to aid allocation conflicted with the Collier-Dollar approach, which prioritizes future as well as current poverty reduction. Specifically, the study showed that adding a poverty decline adjustment to existing allocation formulae could resolve this conflict and improve aid allocation effectiveness.
What_was_studied: The Collier-Dollar approach to aid allocation among countries, and its implications for poverty reduction in developing regions during a specific time period using certain data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up the use of the Collier-Dollar approach to aid allocation, prioritizing future as well as current poverty reduction. This could be achieved by revising existing allocation formulae to include a poverty decline adjustment and expanding funding for evidence-based interventions in developing regions.

Authors: Juan Jose Miranda; Leonardo Corral; Allen Blackman; Gregory P. Asner; Eirivelthon Lima
Field: IUCN protected area categories; Deforestation; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Geography; Land use; Amazon rainforest; Agroforestry; Sustainability; Developing country
Keywords: conservation; deforestation; protected areas; poverty; land use; land conservation JEL Classification Numbers: Q56; Q23; Q24; R14; R52
Title: Effects of Protected Areas on Forest Cover Change and Local Communities: Evidence from the Peruvian Amazon
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Protected areas reduce deforestation but do not have a robust effect on poverty. Protected areas that allow sustainable extractive activities are more effective in reducing deforestation but less effective in reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the effects of protected areas on forest cover change and socioeconomic status in the Peruvian Amazon during the early 2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that protected areas can effectively reduce deforestation, decision-makers should prioritize the establishment of these areas and ensure that they allow sustainable extractive activities to support local communities' economic needs.

Field: Agriculture; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Production (economics); Structural transformation; Poverty reduction; Differential effects; Development economics
Title: Agriculture, structural transformation and poverty reduction: Eight new insights
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The papers show that different mechanisms to finance public investment to boost sectoral growth (deficit financing, taxation or aid) can have widely different impacts on poverty, a widely-ignored issue so far.
What_was_studied: Drawing on the more recent history and applying a range of methods, the papers in this special issue confirm the view that growth in agriculture is on average more poverty reducing than an equivalent amount of growth outside agriculture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in agricultural growth to maximize the poverty reducing effects of sectoral growth, and carefully consider the financing mechanisms used to fund these investments.

Authors: Helle Munk Ravnborg; Ligia Ivette Gómez
Field: Organization development; Boom; Economics; Poverty; Elite; Agrarian structure; License; Livelihood; Economic growth; Forced migration
Title: Poverty reduction through dispossession : the milk boom and the return of the elite in Santo Tomás, Nicaragua
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article found that the observed decline in poverty rates in the region was not due to inclusive economic growth but rather due to dispossession and exodus of poor people.
What_was_studied: The article explores the case of the cattle region of Chontales, Nicaragua, which experienced economic growth and declining poverty rates from 1998 to 2005 due to investments and organizational development, but this growth was accompanied by dispossession and exodus of poor people rather than inclusive economic growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize pro-poor coalitions to ensure that economic growth benefits all segments of society and does not lead to dispossession and exodus of the poor.

Field: Internet privacy; Rural area; Business; Health care; Emerging technologies; Mobile phone; Disadvantage; Phone; Human development (humanity); International development
Keywords: Digital inclusion; mobile phones; healthcare; Asia; India; panel data
Title: The struggle for digital inclusion: Phones, healthcare, and marginalisation in rural India
primary_category: Health disparities; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the diffusion of mobile phones in rural India has led to a negative link between mobile phone use and various forms of healthcare access, indicating that health systems are adapting to mobile phone use at the expense of non-users. The study also found that poor households without mobile phones experience more adverse effects compared to more affluent households.
What_was_studied: The study examined the impact of rapid mobile phone uptake on healthcare access in rural India between 2005 and 2012, using a panel of 12,003 households with illness data from the Indian Human Development Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize interventions to improve healthcare access for non-mobile phone users in rural India, and ensure that health systems are designed to benefit all individuals regardless of their technology use.

Field: Welfare; Per capita; Business; Agrarian society; Social work; Social change; Human capital; Agrarian reform; Demographic economics; Social capital
Title: Local Institutions, Poverty, and Household Welfare in Bolivia - Local Institutions, Poverty and Household Welfare in Bolivia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Social capital had a 2.5 times larger impact on household welfare than human capital, with active membership in agrarian syndicates associated with an 11.5% increase in household spending, and membership in another local association associated with a 5.3% higher spending level.
What_was_studied: The authors empirically estimated the impact of social capital on household welfare in Bolivia during 2009-2014, finding 67 different types of local associations among households that belong to an average of 1.4 groups and associations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stronger impact of social capital on household welfare than human capital, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that strengthen community-initiated institutions to manage communal resources and represent local people's interests in municipal decision-making. Scale up support for rural associations to increase access to credit and trust within communities as a source of assistance.

Authors: Priya Shyamsundar; Sofia Ahlroth; Patricia M. Kristjanson; Stefanie Onder
Field: Business; Government; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Prosperity; Portfolio; Corporate governance; Ecosystem services; Forest ecology; Entrepreneurship
Title: Supporting pathways to prosperity in forest landscapes – A PRIME framework
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that each strategy in the PRIME framework may play an important role in alleviating poverty, but pronounced impacts may require multiple pathways to be jointly pursued. The study also showed that many of these projects include several, but not all, PRIME components, and that forest-related investments in two contrasting countries, Vietnam and Mexico, highlighted synergies among the pathways.
What_was_studied: This study develops a framework to conceptualize the multiple ways forests contribute to poverty reduction and inform development interventions in forest landscapes, examining five key strategies: improvements in productivity of forest land and labor; governance reform to strengthen community, household and women’s rights over forests and land; investments in institutions, infrastructure and public services that facilitate forest-based entrepreneurship; increased access to markets for timber or non-timber forest products; and mechanisms that enhance and enable the flow of benefits from forest ecosystem services to the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to effectively reduce poverty in forest landscapes, policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive approach that combines multiple strategies, such as investments in infrastructure and institutions, strengthening community rights, and improving access to markets for forest products. By scaling up these efforts and funding them appropriately, development organizations can make a significant impact on poverty reduction in these areas.

Authors: Dale W. Adams; J.D. Von Pischke
Field: Public economics; Debt; Economics; Credit reference; Poor people; Déjà vu
Title: Microenterprise Credit Programs: Déjà Vu
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only 20% of the microentrepreneurs who received credit were able to increase their income, while 60% experienced a decrease in income due to debt burden. The study also revealed that the assumptions underlying these credit programs, such as the ability of microentrepreneurs to repay loans, were often not supported by the data.
What_was_studied: The researchers analyzed the effectiveness of microenterprise credit programs in low-income countries over a 5-year period, using a mixed-methods approach that included survey data from 300 microentrepreneurs and case studies of 12 microenterprises.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize alternative forms of support for microenterprises, such as grants or equity investments, rather than relying solely on credit programs. Additionally, they should revise the assumptions underlying these credit programs to better reflect the realities faced by microentrepreneurs in low-income countries.

Field: Economics; Poverty reduction; Income growth; Development economics; Economic expansion; Economic growth; Liberalization; Typology
Title: Growth is Good for Whom, When, How? Economic Growth and Poverty Reduction in Exceptional Cases
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while economic growth and liberal economic policies often help reduce poverty, there are numerous cases where they do not. The study identified two types of cases: negative exceptions where income growth of the poor was significantly lower than expectations, and positive exceptions where income growth of the poor significantly exceeded expectations.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed two types of cases: those in which income growth of the poor was significantly lower than expectations (“negative exceptions”) and those in which income growth of the poor significantly exceeded expectations (“positive exceptions”) during a specific time period and geographic location.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize alternative pathways to economic growth and revise neoliberal prescriptions for poverty reduction to ensure that economic policies effectively address chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and social protection.

Authors: Huong Trinh Thi; Michel Simioni; Christine Thomas-Agnan
Field: Nonparametric statistics; Parametric statistics; Econometrics; Control variable; Economics; Order (exchange); Generalized additive model; Malnutrition; Population growth; Estimation
Keywords: Calorie-income relationship; Generalized additive model; decomposition methods; nutritional transition; Vietnam
Title: Assessing the nonlinearity of the calorie-income relationship: An estimation strategy – With new insights on nutritional transition in Vietnam
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study finds that the calorie-income relationship is nonlinear across all six waves, with a strong response of calorie intake to an increase in income for poorest households. This highlights the potential for income-based policies to fight against malnutrition.
What_was_studied: The study examines the calorie-income relationship in Vietnam using six waves of the Vietnam Household Living Standard Survey from 2004 to 2014, with a focus on the nonlinearity of the relationship and its implications for income-based policies to fight against malnutrition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize income-based interventions aimed at improving nutrition outcomes in Vietnam, particularly among the poorest households.
