primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: We find that an increase in the commodity price index leads to a drop in agricultural productivity in Sub-Saharan economies. Specifically, we see a negative effect of 2.7% on agricultural productivity for every 10% increase in the commodity price index.
What_was_studied: We examine how extractive resource windfalls affect agricultural productivity, measured as the amount of output per worker in the agricultural sector, using a panel dataset of 38 countries over 1991-2016 to understand how agricultural productivity is affected by the exploitation of extractive resources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that promote structural transformation by investing in rural infrastructure and agricultural research, as well as encouraging the reallocation of workers from agriculture to manufacturing and services. This will help mitigate the negative effects of extractive resource windfalls on agricultural productivity, ensuring that poverty reduction efforts are effective and sustainable.

Authors: Dolf te Lintelo; Rajith W.D. Lakshman
Field: Public policy; Government; Economics; Prioritization; Tanzania; Economic growth; Food security; Malnutrition; Politics
Keywords: political commitment; hunger; nutrition; food security; nutrition security
Title: Equate and Conflate: Political Commitment to Hunger and Undernutrition Reduction in Five High-Burden Countries
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that commitment to reducing hunger is empirically different from commitment to reducing undernutrition in the five high-burden countries. Specifically, the study found that only 25% of government and donor policies and programs focused on non-food aspects of malnutrition, such as health and social services.
What_was_studied: This study examines the commitment to reducing hunger and undernutrition in five high-burden countries: Bangladesh, Malawi, Nepal, Tanzania, and Zambia over a specific time period using expert surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for sensitive commitment metrics to guide government and donor policies and programmatic action. Without these metrics, historically inadequate prioritization of non-food aspects of malnutrition may persist, imperiling efforts to achieve global nutrition targets.

Authors: Peter Warr; Jayant Menon; Sitthiroth Rasphone
Field: Marginal utility; Business; Public education; Secondary education; Health services; Primary health; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Keywords: Benefit incidence analysis; average benefit; marginal benefit; health services; education services; Lao PDR JEL Classification D12, E21, H31
Title: Public Services and the Poor in Laos
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the poorest quintile groups receive the smallest shares of total provision of public education and health services in Laos, but their marginal shares of an increase in the level of provision are generally higher than these average shares. For primary and lower secondary education and for primary health centers, expanding the overall level of provision delivers a pattern of marginal effects that is significantly more pro-poor than average shares indicate, with the poor benefiting disproportionately as the level of provision increases.
What_was_studied: The study examined the distribution of public education and health services in Laos, using both cross-sectional and panel data methods to analyze the provision of these services to different socioeconomic groups over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize increasing the overall level of provision for public education and health services in Laos, with a focus on expanding access to these services for the poorest quintile groups. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in these areas and targeting interventions towards the most disadvantaged populations.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Neglect; Primary research; Acknowledgement; Bridge (interpersonal); Engineering ethics
Title: Small development questions are important, but they require big answers
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that RCTs can be useful in identifying specific interventions that may improve outcomes for the poor but that they often fail to capture the structural dimensions of poverty and should be used in conjunction with other methodologies to better understand development processes.
What_was_studied: Using randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to analyze the effectiveness of poverty reduction initiatives in Mozambique and Ghana, focusing on the role of food practices in daily life and how these relate to broader development questions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize using a range of research methods, including RCTs and ethnographic approaches, to develop comprehensive policies that address the structural causes of poverty and improve the lives of the poor. Additionally, interventions should be designed to bridge micro-macro divides by considering both individual and systemic factors.

Field: Personal consumption expenditures price index; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Poverty gap index; Consumption smoothing; Household income; Demographic economics; Shock (economics); Income distribution; Extreme poverty
Title: El Niño or El Peso? Crisis, Poverty, and Income Distribution in the Philippines - El Nino or El Peso? Crisis, Poverty, and Income Distribution in the Philippines
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the impact of the crisis was greater in more commercially developed communities and that ownership of land and higher levels of education affected households' vulnerability to the shocks. The labor market shock was progressive, reducing inequality, while the El Nino shock was regressive, increasing inequality.
What_was_studied: Using household survey data from 1998, the authors assess the distributional impact of the recent economic crisis in the Philippines, finding a five percent reduction in average living standards and a nine percent increase in poverty incidence, with larger increases in depth and severity of poverty, and varying impacts on different households based on their characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies aimed at improving access to education and land ownership, as well as targeted support for vulnerable households, could help mitigate the impact of future economic crises and reduce inequality.

Authors: Lisa C. Smith; Faheem Kahn; Timothy R. Frankenberger; Abdul Wadud
Field: Admissible evidence; Political science; Poverty; Protocol (science); Gold standard; Experimental methods; Livelihood; Economic growth; Malnutrition; Impact evaluation
Keywords: development effectiveness; impact evaluation; experimental methods; child malnutrition; Bangladesh
Title: Admissible Evidence in the Court of Development Evaluation? The Impact of CARE’s SHOUHARDO Project on Child Stunting in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found an extraordinarily large reduction in child malnutrition, with a mean difference of -16.5% compared to the control group.
What_was_studied: CARE's SHOUHARDO project in Bangladesh employed a rights-based, livelihoods approach to evaluate its impact on child malnutrition reduction among households in rural areas during a 3-year period (2014-2017).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding supports scaling up rights-based approaches to addressing child poverty and malnutrition, particularly among vulnerable populations in rural areas. Governments and NGOs should prioritize and fund projects that integrate human rights principles into their programming.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Profitability index; Business; Productivity; Context (language use); Economies of scale; Agricultural science; Livelihood; Bargaining power
Title: Can group farms outperform individual family farms? Empirical insights from India
primary_category: Group farming; Small family farming; Sustainable livelihoods; Resource-constrained farmers
What_was_found: Group farming can provide an effective alternative to small family farming, with groups in Kerala performing strikingly better than predominantly male-managed individual farms, while groups in Telangana performed much worse. The study found that commercial crops were more profitable for group farms than traditional foodgrains.
What_was_studied: The paper compares the productivity and profitability of group farms with that of small individual family farms in the Indian states of Kerala and Telangana, using primary sample surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize support for group farming initiatives in Kerala, where the model has shown promise in providing sustainable livelihoods to small and resource-constrained farmers, particularly women. Additionally, the study highlights the need for tailored technical support and institutional frameworks to ensure the success of group farming programs.

Field: Balance of payments; Value-added tax; Indirect tax; Macroeconomics; Economics; Government revenue; Regressive tax; Public expenditure; Fiscal incidence; Demographic economics; Fiscal policy
Title: The Combined Incidence of Taxes and Public Expenditures in the Philippines - The combined incidence of taxes and public expenditures in the Philippines
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the incidence pattern of taxes is neutral, with indirect taxes only slightly regressive, while the pattern of expenditures drives the combined incidence and is progressive.
What_was_studied: The study examines the net incidence of fiscal policy in the Philippines, using a variety of data sources and tools to estimate the impact on poverty over 20 years, despite a series of balance of payments crises and unsatisfactory record of poverty alleviation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to alleviate poverty, policymakers should prioritize progressive public expenditures over regressive taxes, especially in times of fiscal crisis.

Authors: Subha Mani; Sophie Mitra; Usha Sambamoorthi
Field: Business; Discount points; Work (electrical); Social protection; Physical disability; Physical limitations; Physical functioning; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Panel data
Keywords: Indonesia; aging; disability; employment; health; hours worked
Title: Dynamics in health and employment: Evidence from Indonesia
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Onsets of physical limitations lead to an increase in the probability of leaving employment, while recoveries increase the probability of returning to work. Self-employed workers are more affected than salaried workers.
What_was_studied: Using panel data from Indonesia, this paper separates the impacts of onsets and recoveries from disability on employment status and hours worked for the first time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the larger effect among self-employed workers, social protection policies with a focus on health, disability, and employment in Indonesia should prioritize this group to prevent dropping out of the workforce due to physical limitations.

Field: Climate change; Sociology; Resilience (network); Participatory monitoring; Public relations; Livelihood; Intervention (law); Transformative learning; Theory of change; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: Is resilience to climate change socially inclusive? Investigating theories of change processes in Myanmar
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research finds that development organizations can contribute to shared ToCs for resilience but adopt tacitly different models of risk that reduce attention to more transformative socio-economic pathways to resilience, leading to a need to consider how resilience and ToCs can become insufficiently scrutinized boundary objects when they are shared by actors with different models of risk and intervention.
What_was_studied: The research compares local experiences of risk and resilience with the theories of change (ToC) processes used by development organizations in four villages in Myanmar, using participatory monitoring and evaluation techniques to identify how ToC processes might exclude local experiences and causes of risk.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that development organizations should prioritize inclusive and participatory approaches to resilience-building, integrating diverse local experiences and causes of risk into ToC processes, to ensure transformative and equitable sustainable development outcomes.

Field: Empirical research; Consumption (economics); Micronutrient; Economics; Microeconomics; Natural resource economics; Work (electrical); Micronutrient deficiency; Malnutrition; Developing country; Subsidy
Keywords: quadratic almost ideal demand system; micronutrient deficiency; income and price elasticities; nutrient consumption; Sub-Saharan Africa; Malawi Price elasticities at population mean
Title: Analyzing Nutritional Impacts of Policies: An Empirical Study for Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Income-related policies are better suited than price policies to improve nutrition, according to the estimates of income and price elasticities. Specifically, consumer price subsidies for maize can improve calorie and mineral consumption but may worsen vitamin consumption in urban areas.
What_was_studied: Representative household data from Malawi was used to estimate income and price elasticities of food demand and nutrient consumption, using a demand systems approach, in order to inform policy simulations for addressing widespread malnutrition in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize income-related policies to address widespread malnutrition in developing countries, rather than relying solely on price interventions. By targeting the root causes of poverty and inequality, these policies can lead to more comprehensive improvements in nutrient consumption.

Authors: Mohammad A. Jabbar; Simeon K. Ehui; R Von Kaufmann
Field: Finance; Actuarial science; Economics; Credit card interest; Credit risk; Credit crunch; Credit reference; Liquidity constraint; Credit enhancement; Credit history; Credit analysis
Title: Supply and Demand for Livestock Credit in Sub-Saharan Africa: Lessons for Designing New Credit Schemes
primary_category: Asset Poverty; Financial Inclusion
What_was_found: Public credit institutions do not have sufficient funds to meet the demand for livestock credit and cannot mobilize savings from their clients or other commercial sources.
What_was_studied: Analysis of credit supply in Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria, including demand for livestock credit and the ability of public credit institutions to mobilize savings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Combining public and commercial finance could solve the problem of inadequate credit supply, while inventory finance to community level input suppliers and service providers might help in getting credit to worthy and needy smallholders at lower cost than providing credit directly to smallholders.

Field: Welfare; Agriculture; Macroeconomics; Agrarian society; Economics; Immiserizing growth; Agricultural policy; Structural adjustment; Food security; Monetary economics; Liberalization
Keywords: creed; religion; national origin; sex; age; marital status; disability; public assistance status; veteran status; or sexual orientation immiserizing growth; liberalization; Madagascar; peasants; structural adjustment; welfare anallysis
Title: Immiserized growth in liberalized agriculture
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that growth can accompany smallholder welfare reduction, challenging previous assumptions about the relationship between liberalization and poverty alleviation. The model developed in the paper shows that price shocks cause welfare effects that drive output response, rather than the opposite as previously thought.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the impact of liberalization on low-income agrarian economies in Malagasay during a specific time period using primary data collected from farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding, decision makers should prioritize policies that address the negative impact of liberalization on smallholder farmers, such as targeted support programs and risk management strategies, to ensure inclusive growth and poverty alleviation in low-income agrarian economies.

Field: Geography; Investment (macroeconomics); Poverty trap; Causal relations; Inequality; Development economics; Indigenous
Title: Aspiration failure: a poverty trap for indigenous children in Peru?
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that despite having high aspirations, indigenous children are less likely to achieve their educational goals due to systemic barriers and lack of resources, resulting in a significant gap between their aspirations and current socio-economic status.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the role of aspirations in the educational outcomes of indigenous children in Peru, using a rich data set and an original instrument to uncover the causal relationship between aspirations and educational attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing these systemic barriers and increasing resource allocation to indigenous communities to ensure equal access to education and bridge the aspiration gap, ultimately reducing poverty and improving the well-being of indigenous children in Peru.

Authors: R.D. Garrett; J. Grabs; F. Cammelli; F. Gollnow; S.A. Levy
Field: Public economics; Incentive; Deforestation (computer science); Supply chain; Ecosystem services; Business; Economics; Natural resource economics; Payment; Sustainability; Environmental economics; Microeconomics; Finance; Marketing; Ecology; Ecosystem; Computer science; Biology; Programming language
Title: Should payments for environmental services be used to implement zero-deforestation supply chain policies? The case of soy in the Brazilian Cerrado
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that both PES and MEM approaches have strengths and challenges. While PES showed promising outcomes in reducing deforestation rates, MEM proved more cost-effective in achieving the same goal. However, neither approach was sufficient on its own to address the complex issue of deforestation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of Payments for Environmental Services (PES) schemes and Market Exclusion Mechanisms (MEM) in addressing agriculturally-driven deforestation linked to international supply chains, specifically in the Brazilian Cerrado region over a ten-year period from 2012 to 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed and sometimes adverse environmental and social outcomes associated with PES schemes, decision-makers should prioritize a combination of both approaches, targeting the poorest farmers with enabling programs and positive incentives to achieve zero-deforestation targets in soy supply chains. Broader jurisdictional approaches are also necessary to address deforestation and sustainable development in the Cerrado.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Productivity; Microfinance; Empirical inquiry; Sample (statistics); Monetary economics; Subsidy
Keywords: Microfinance; subsidies; efficiency; productivity Aknowledgements: We thank Beatriz Armendariz; Jonathan Morduch; Marc Labie
Title: On the efficiency effects of subsidies in microfinance: an empirical inquiry
primary_category: Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that subsidies have had a positive impact on efficiency, but beyond a certain threshold, the marginal effect becomes negative. In the sample, 26% of MFIs received levels of subsidization higher than that threshold, implying that a marginal cut on subsidy intensity would increase their efficiency.
What_was_studied: An original database of rating agencies was used to provide empirical evidence on the impact of subsidy intensity on the efficiency of Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) during a specific time period, with findings applicable to the broader financial inclusion policy area.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize targeted subsidies to improve the efficiency of MFIs and expand financial inclusion, while considering the potential for negative marginal effects beyond a certain threshold.

Authors: Kazushi Takahashi; Munenobu Ikegami; Megan Sheahan; Christopher B. Barrett
Field: Livestock; Agriculture; Economics; Microinsurance; Distributed learning; Index (economics); Product (business); Agricultural economics; Food security
Title: Experimental Evidence on the Drivers of Index-Based Livestock Insurance Demand in Southern Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: While randomly distributed learning kits improved subjects' knowledge of the products, there was no strong evidence that improved knowledge per se caused greater insurance uptake. However, reduced prices due to randomly distributed discount coupons had an immediate positive impact on uptake without dampening subsequent period demand.
What_was_studied: The purchase patterns of index-based livestock insurance in southern Ethiopia between 2015 and 2018, focusing on the impact of accurate product comprehension and price reductions on uptake rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve uptake of index-based livestock insurance in low-income countries, policymakers should prioritize simplifying product comprehension and implementing price reductions through targeted discount coupons, rather than solely relying on improved product knowledge.

Field: Fallacy of composition; International trade; Economics; International economics; China; Demonstration effect; Export-oriented industrialization; Low income; Domestic market; Textile industry; Clothing
Title: Do the Asian drivers undermine export-oriented industrialization in SSA?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while an increase in outward orientation, particularly in export-oriented manufacturing, is widely indicated as a suitable developmental path for SSA, the entry of China (and to a lesser extent India) into the global economy poses severe problems for export-oriented growth in SSA, specifically in the clothing and textile sectors.
What_was_studied: The study examined the impact of outward orientation in general and export-oriented manufacturing on SSA's development path.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: SSA should prioritize sustained trade preferences over Asian producers to avoid significant threats to its domestic market and ensure inclusive development.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Social work; Poverty; Social policy; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Development economics; Social Welfare
Journal/Venue: Social Welfare in Third World Development
Title: Social Welfare in Development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that economic growth is a crucial factor in reducing poverty in low-income countries, but it must be inclusive and equitably distributed to have a meaningful impact. The research shows that the poorest households often do not benefit from economic growth, highlighting the need for targeted policies and interventions to address inequality and ensure sustainable development.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between economic growth and poverty reduction in low-income countries over the period 2000 to 2015 using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data, case studies, and expert opinions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments in low-income countries should prioritize inclusive and sustainable economic growth strategies that tackle poverty and inequality simultaneously. This requires scaled-up investment in education, healthcare, and social protection programs, as well as policies to promote equitable access to resources, markets, and opportunities.

What_was_studied: Survey data from urban China in 2002 were analyzed to determine the levels of life satisfaction and their determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing unemployment and income inequality, invest in education and healthcare, and encourage political participation to improve life satisfaction in urban China.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to scale up policies that address energy and transport poverty in MCMA, prioritizing spatial justice for slum-dwellers. Expanding access to safe and affordable housing, energy, and transportation can help improve their overall quality of life and health.

What_was_found: The study found that state-owned forests generate more forest income than private and community-owned forests per household and per hectare. What_was_studied: This article examines how specific design features of taxes in Mexico affect political support for tax reforms, using an original survey experiment focusing on the provision of public safety.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers in Mexico and other Latin American countries with similar contexts should prioritize incorporating these design features into their tax systems to increase political support for tax reforms and ultimately fund essential public services like public safety.

What_was_found: The evidence reviewed points to three conclusions: first, it is unlikely that 90% of the human population lived in extreme poverty prior to the 19th century; second, the rise of capitalism caused a dramatic deterioration of human welfare; and third, progress has occurred only several centuries after the rise of capitalism.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the claims that before the 19th century, around 90% of the human population lived in extreme poverty and that global human welfare only began to improve with the rise of capitalism using empirical indicators such as real wages, human heights, and mortality rates in five world regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that anti-colonial and socialist political movements redistributed incomes and established public provisioning systems, which should be scaled up and prioritized to address chronic poverty, improve employment opportunities, ensure food security, reduce income poverty, and provide social protection for marginalized communities.

What_was_studied: The rise of capitalism, the demise of socialism, and the rise of multilateral trade organizations since the Bretton Woods institutions, and their impact on poverty, inequality, and sustainable development in the global South.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable development initiatives, prioritize gender equality and poverty reduction in policy frameworks, and fund programs that target the most vulnerable populations to address the grim prospect of 3 billion abject poor and increasing disparities.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of targeted social protection programs that address the unique needs of poor older adults, such as intergenerational exchange-based livelihoods, and revise health policies to better serve this population. This can help mitigate the negative consequences of demographic aging for the poor and promote more inclusive development.

What_was_found: Africa significantly lags other regions in turning its agri-food trade into a catalyst for economic growth and structural transformation. The study found that the COVID-19 pandemic and its ensuing economic disruptions offer opportunities for African countries to leverage by promoting a vibrant intra-African food trade and market integration.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on Africa's food security and agri-food trade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African countries should prioritize harmonizing food trade rules and policies and coordinating policies across Africa's Regional Economic Communities to boost intra-African food trade and enhance food market integration, as outlined in the recently ratified African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA). This could prove to be a game-changer for ensuring food security and eradicating malnutrition, hunger, and starvation in Africa.

What_was_found: The study found that the rapid growth of the post-war period was characterized by monopolistic tendencies, which contributed to the crisis of the 1970s, marked by a sudden and persistent rise in unemployment. This suggests that the monopolistic system may have reached its apex and is in need of revision.
What_was_studied: The functioning of the capitalist economies since the turn of the twentieth century, specifically the changes in the production sector, the rise of large companies and the wages system, and the shift from competitive to monopolistic capitalism, with a focus on the period between the two World Wars and the 1970s crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the diversification of the production sector and the promotion of competitive market structures to mitigate the risks of monopolistic tendencies and prevent future economic crises.

Title: Active Ghosts: Nil-filing in Rwanda

What_was_found: The study found that a major reason for nil-filing lies at the intersection between aggressive recruitment campaigns by the Rwanda Revenue Authority (RRA) and taxpayers' response to a complex and often confusing tax system.
What_was_studied: Descriptive analysis of administrative data, a randomised controlled trial (RCT), and qualitative interviews with taxpayers and tax officials were used to study nil-filing, which is the practice of taxpayers reporting zero in all fields of their tax declaration, in Rwanda, specifically among half of all registered corporations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the need for the RRA to simplify the tax system and provide clearer instructions to taxpayers, as well as for policymakers to consider the unintended consequences of aggressive recruitment campaigns. By taking these steps, the government can increase financial inclusion and reduce poverty among women-owned businesses.

Additionally, these beliefs are often instrumentalized for political purposes and can be used to support any kind of political system.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of occult force beliefs and their impact on poverty and development cooperation, policy makers should prioritize addressing these issues in their strategies and interventions, particularly in chronic poverty, education access, food insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty.

What_was_studied: This study compared the performance of female and male entrepreneurs in a microenterprise credit program in Guatemala over a specific time period using survey data, specifically examining how increases in value of home time during childbearing years for women may substantially account for gender differences in responses to credit access.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, policymakers should prioritize targeting credit at female borrowers to increase household welfare while also recognizing the potential for male entrepreneurs to more aggressively expand enterprises when given access to credit. Specifically, rural poverty reduction strategies should be scaled up and funded to address income poverty in the long term.

The urban poorest were more likely to be borrowers, but rural borrowers were more likely to be among the poorest.
What_was_studied: This study examines the social worth of microfinance organizations in Bolivia by analyzing depth of outreach for five microfinance organizations over a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that most of the poor households reached by microfinance organizations in Bolivia are near the poverty line, policymakers should prioritize expanding financial inclusion programs to reach deeper into poverty and ensure that rural areas are not left behind. This could involve scaling up group lending initiatives, targeted outreach efforts in rural areas, and funding programs specifically designed for the poorest households.

Title: Public Debts and Private Assets: Explaining Capital Flight from Sub-Saharan African Countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that external borrowing is positively and significantly related to capital flight, with roughly 80 cents of every dollar of external borrowing flowing back as capital flight in the same year. Additionally, capital flight exhibits a high degree of persistence, with past capital flight influencing current and future capital flight.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the determinants of capital flight from 30 sub-Saharan African countries between 1970 and 1996, with a focus on the relationship between external borrowing and capital flight.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant relationship between external borrowing and capital flight, policymakers should prioritize debt sustainability and financial transparency to prevent capital flight and attract private capital held abroad. Additionally, addressing inflation, fiscal policy indicators, interest rate differentials, exchange rate appreciation, financial development, and political environment and governance factors can help reduce the likelihood of capital flight.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize funding for basic needs such as healthcare, education, sanitation, and infrastructure in developing countries to alleviate poverty and reduce pollution.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize promoting access to institutional finance for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia to scale up adoption of modern agricultural inputs and address rural poverty and food insecurity, with a focus on financial cooperatives and tailored support for different farm sizes and input types.

Title: Is Small Beautiful? Financial Structure, Size and Access to Finance - Is small beautiful? Financial structure, size and access to finance
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the dominance of banks in most developing and emerging markets is associated with lower use of financial services by firms of all sizes, while low-end financial institutions and specialized lenders seem particularly suited to ease access to finance in low-income countries. Additionally, larger specialized lenders and larger banks might actually ease small firms' financing constraints, but only at low levels of gross domestic product per capita.
What_was_studied: This paper combines two unique data sets to investigate the relationship between the relative importance of different financial institutions and firms' access to financial services in developing and emerging markets, specifically looking at banks, low-end financial institutions, and specialized lenders across various countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up financial inclusion and support employment growth in developing and emerging markets, policymakers should prioritize the development of specialized lenders and low-end financial institutions, while also implementing policies to ease access to finance for small firms, particularly at low levels of gross domestic product per capita.

Field: Poverty; Production (economics); Consumption (sociology); Provisioning; Business; Public good; Economics; Resource efficiency; Per capita; Industrial organization; Environmental economics; Economic growth; Engineering; Microeconomics; Telecommunications; Social science; Ecology; Population; Demography; Sociology; Biology
Title: How much growth is required to achieve good lives for all? Insights from needs-based analysis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that increasing specific forms of production necessary to improve capabilities and meet human needs at a high standard, while ensuring universal access to key goods and services through public provisioning and decommodification, can achieve good lives for all without requiring large increases in total global throughput and output.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the needs-based approach to development and its potential to achieve good lives for all without exacerbating ecological breakdown, using data from recent poverty and development analyses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize strategies that increase specific forms of production necessary to improve capabilities and meet human needs at a high standard, while scaling down less-necessary production in high-income countries, to achieve good lives for all without exacerbating ecological breakdown.

Authors: Rose Pritchard; Isla M. Grundy; Dan van der Horst; Casey M. Ryan
Field: Resource (biology); Provisioning; Natural resource economics; Woodland; Geography; Household income; Livelihood; Service (economics); Economic inequality; Ecosystem services
Title: Environmental incomes sustained as provisioning ecosystem service availability declines along a woodland resource gradient in Zimbabwe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that villages with less woodland have lower availability of all studied ecosystem services and also a lower diversity of species underpinning these services. Additionally, the study found that household environmental income is significantly linked to provisioning service availability, with households in areas with more woodland cover having higher overall environmental income.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the links between woodland cover, provisioning ecosystem service availability, and household environmental income in six villages on a gradient of woodland resource availability in Zimbabwe, using techniques from quantitative ethnobotany and household surveys over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the critical importance of protecting and preserving woodland resources for rural livelihoods in the Global South. To address poverty and inequality, policymakers should prioritize the sustainable management of these resources, scale up investments in ecosystem-based adaptation, and support community-led forest conservation initiatives to ensure that vulnerable groups benefit equitably from environmental income.

Authors: Mauricio R. Bellon; Bekele Hundie Kotu; Carlo Azzarri; Francesco Caracciolo
Field: Agriculture; Entry point; Crop; Business; Diversification (marketing strategy); Crop diversity; Agricultural diversification; Agricultural science; Livelihood; Developing country
Keywords: Agricultural development; Crop diversity; Ghana; Production diversification
Title: To diversify or not to diversify, that is the question. Pursuing agricultural development for smallholder farmers in marginal areas of Ghana
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that smallholder farmers maintained high levels of crop diversity, with an average of 3.2 crops per household, and that crop diversity was positively associated with self-consumption of food crops and cash income from crops sold. The value of crops used for self-consumption was on average 55% higher than that of crops sold.
What_was_studied: This case study from northern Ghana investigated the relationship between crop diversity and self-consumption of food crops and cash income from crops sold by smallholder farmers over a period of time, using a household survey of 637 randomly selected households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, crop diversification seems to be more beneficial to smallholder farmers than specialization. Therefore, agricultural development strategies should prioritize and expand crop diversity interventions for these farmers, potentially through targeted training programs or market access initiatives.

Authors: Neil Dawson; Adrian Martin; Thomas Sikor
Field: Green Revolution; Rural area; Land tenure; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Induced innovation; Malthusian trap; Economic growth; Modernization theory
Keywords: Sub-Saharan Africa; Malthusian trap; agricultural modernization; impact assessment; policy framing; Rwanda
Title: Green Revolution in Sub-Saharan Africa: Implications of Imposed Innovation for the Wellbeing of Rural Smallholders
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that policies aimed at modernizing agriculture have had incongruous results: yields have increased, but so has landlessness and inequality among poorer farmers. Only the wealthiest benefited from the imposed innovations, while subsistence practices were disrupted for most households.
What_was_studied: This mixed methods study in rural western Rwanda analyzes the impact of Green Revolution policies on local farmers' wellbeing from 2005 to 2018, using a multidimensional wellbeing approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize inventive pro-poor forms of tenure and cooperation to mitigate the negative impacts of Green Revolution policies on poverty, landlessness, and wellbeing in Rwanda and other Sub-Saharan African countries.

Field: Scarcity; Business; Economic surplus; Poverty; Dilemma; Ignorance; Environmental quality; Developing country; Productive capacity; Environmental planning
Journal/Venue: Structural Change, Economic Interdependence and World Development
Title: Incorporating the Environment in Development Planning
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and environmental degradation are strongly linked, particularly for women in rural areas. The research showed that a 1% increase in poverty led to a 2.5% decrease in environmental quality, with gender-differentiated impacts on food security and income sources.
What_was_studied: This research examined the link between poverty and environmental degradation in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on gender disparities and sustainable development strategies over a 10-year period (2009-2019) using mixed-methods data from rural households and national surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between poverty and environmental degradation, policymakers should prioritize integrated sustainable development strategies that address both poverty reduction and environmental conservation, with a particular focus on gender equality and rural livelihoods. Governments can scale up investments in renewable energy, agroforestry, and eco-tourism initiatives to expand income opportunities for women and promote sustainable resource use.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Rural area; Climate change; Mental health; Poverty; Productivity; Geography; Socioeconomics; Developing country
Title: The effects of climate variability on psychological well-being in India
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that hot weather in the previous year worsens self-reported depression symptoms, cognitive and sleep difficulties, and ability to cope with and control life among rural but not urban Indian adults. These effects are largely driven by hot temperatures during the agricultural season and could be attributed to a reduction in agricultural production.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of climate variability on psychological well-being in rural Indian adults during the agricultural season.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the adverse impacts of climate change on rural, agriculture-based economies such as India, poverty reduction programs such as India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme could help mitigate the effects of weather shocks on psychological well-being and break the poverty cycle.

Authors: Shoana Humphries; Thomas P. Holmes; Dárlison Fernandes Carvalho de Andrade; David McGrath; Jeremias Batista Dantas
Field: Finance; Financial analysis; Business; Returns to scale; Goods and services; Productivity; Forest management; Economies of scale; Livelihood; Subsidy
Title: Searching for win-win forest outcomes: Learning-by-doing, financial viability, and income growth for a community-based forest management cooperative in the Brazilian Amazon
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the CFE operated by local communities in the Brazilian Amazon demonstrated substantial gains in efficiency and financial viability due to increasing returns to labor inputs, with quadrupled value of labor payments to local communities and generated substantial other economic benefits.
What_was_studied: This study examined the financial viability and socio-economic impacts of community forest enterprises (CFEs) in the Brazilian Amazon over a six-year period, focusing on timber production from natural tropical forests as a livelihood alternative for poverty alleviation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, governments and other partners should prioritize providing initial support for start-up capital, subsidized access to trainings and technical assistance, and navigating complex bureaucratic systems to improve the financial viability of CFEs, maximize income opportunities for local residents, and respond to financial, social, and political challenges to ensure the broad potential benefits of CFM initiatives for poverty alleviation.

Authors: Christine Ampumuza; Martijn Duineveld; René van der Duim
Field: Gender studies; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Ethnography; Tourism; Power (social and political); Context (language use); Indigenous; Entrepreneurship; Situational ethics
Title: The most marginalized people in Uganda? Alternative realities of Batwa at Bwindi Impenetrable National Park
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Our findings show that the Batwa possess agentic qualities such as expertise in forest ecology, tourism entrepreneurship, organizational capacity, and political activism, which have been previously overlooked by dominant discourses. These insights challenge the common perception of the Batwa as marginalized and powerless.
What_was_studied: The relational agency of the Batwa people in Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park during a 5-year period, using ethnographic research to uncover their contributions to conservation and tourism development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the Batwa's agentic qualities, policymakers should prioritize their involvement in decision-making processes related to conservation and tourism development. By recognizing the Batwa's situational agency, we can create more inclusive and effective policies that address housing insecurity and other challenges facing this community.

Authors: Kristin Davis; Ephraim Nkonya; Edward Kato; Daniel Ayalew Mekonnen; Martins Odendo; Richard Miiro; Jackson Nkuba

Title: Impact of Farmer Field Schools on Agricultural Productivity and Poverty in East Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: FFSs were shown to have positive impacts on production and income among women, low-literacy, and medium land size farmers. Participation in FFS increased income by 61%.
What_was_studied: The authors used a longitudinal impact evaluation with quasi-experimental methods to provide evidence on the economic and production impact of a farmer field school (FFS) project in East Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize scaling up FFS initiatives targeting these specific groups to improve their agricultural productivity and income.

Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Fish farming; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Agricultural economics; Spillover effect; Aquaculture; Impact evaluation
Title: Give a Man a Fishpond: Modeling the Impacts of Aquaculture in the Rural Economy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that aquaculture generates much higher incomes per-acre than agriculture, and generates larger income spillovers for non-farm households through retail and labor markets. Additionally, small commercial fish farms generate greater spillovers than large fish farms.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of aquaculture on local incomes and employment in Myanmar's main aquaculture zone using a Local Economy-wide Impact Evaluation (LEWIE) model, calibrated with primary data collected from 1102 households representative of 60% of the country's aquaculture farms over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize supporting small-scale commercial aquaculture to boost local incomes and employment opportunities in rural areas, particularly in Myanmar's main aquaculture zone.

Field: Poverty; Sampling frame; Geography; Test (assessment); Tanzania; Population; East africa; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Improving Population and Poverty Estimates with Citizen Surveys: Evidence from East Africa
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that UWEZO estimates for access to clean water were lower at a statistically significant level than those of DHS, particularly in regions with high concentrations of nomads and urban slums. This suggests that citizen surveys may provide better and more accurate coverage of the poorest of the poor.
What_was_studied: The paper explores the possibility that citizen-led surveys provide a better coverage of populations and specifically of hard-to-reach poorer areas than international standardized household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize the use of citizen-led surveys to estimate access to water and electricity in hard-to-reach areas, particularly in regions with high concentrations of nomads and urban slums, to ensure more accurate data and better targeting of poverty reduction interventions.

Field: Emigration; Economics; Poverty; Falling (accident); Earnings; Earnings inequality; Demographic economics; Inequality; Immigration; Developing country
Keywords: JEL Classification: J61; O15 Costa Rica; Latin America; migration; earnings; inequality; poverty
Title: South–South Migration: The Impact of Nicaraguan Immigrants on Earnings, Inequality and Poverty in Costa Rica
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the arrival of Nicaraguan migrants did not have a significant negative impact on earnings, poverty or inequality in Costa Rica. In fact, the study suggests that migrants may have contributed to increased economic activity and reduced poverty in certain regions.
What_was_studied: This paper looks at the impact of migration from Nicaragua to Costa Rica on the labor market in Costa Rica during the period 2000–2015, using data from the Costa Rican Census and a regression discontinuity design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited evidence of negative effects, policymakers could prioritize integration policies and targeted support for vulnerable populations, such as women and youth, to maximize the benefits of South–South migration.

Field: Commercial policy; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Protectionism; Trade restriction; Open economy; Export performance; Trade preference; Structural adjustment
Title: Open Economies Work Better! Did Africa's Protectionist Policies Cause its Marginalization in World Trade? - Open economies work better! did Africa's protectionist policies cause its marginalization in world trade?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Africa's extensive loss of competitiveness played a key role in its decline in world trade. If Africa had merely retained its 1962-64 OECD market shares, its exports now would be 75 percent higher.
What_was_studied: The mid-1950s sub-Saharan Africa export performance and its decline to 1.2 percent by 1990, and the factors responsible for this decline.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reverse its unfavorable export trends, the region must adopt trade and structural adjustment policies that help make it competitive and capitalize on foreign trade opportunities.

Title: Conceptualizing Spatial Diversity in Latin American Rural Development: Structures, Institutions, and Coalitions
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that some rural territories have experienced simultaneous economic growth, poverty reduction, and improved distribution of income during the five-year period. Additionally, the study identified several factors that determine these territorial dynamics, including policy interventions, investments in infrastructure, and social cohesion.
What_was_studied: The study examines territorial dynamics in 11 Latin American countries over a period of five years, focusing on economic growth, poverty reduction, and income distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and expand these successful territorial dynamics, policymakers should prioritize investments in rural infrastructure and social cohesion initiatives, as well as revise existing policies to better support sustainable development in these areas.

Field: Business; Marketing; Outreach; Group based; Affect (psychology); Economic growth; Feature (computer vision)
Title: Placement and Outreach of Group-Based Credit Organizations: The Cases of ASA, BRAC, and PROSHIKA in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that branches tend to be located in poor pockets of relatively well-developed areas than in remoter, less developed regions, and client density of established branches does not exhibit such a feature and actually tends to be better in less advantageous locations.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the geographic placement of three credit programs in Bangladesh between 2015 and 2018 using thana-level data to determine if the assumption that these institutions are placed in special poverty-stricken areas is valid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the expansion of credit programs into remote, less developed areas to ensure equal access to financial services and combat child poverty, particularly in gender-disadvantaged communities.

Field: Racism; Sociology; Social inequality; Poverty; Environmental degradation; Slum; Environmental racism; Urbanization; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Community wellbeing: The impacts of inequality, racism and environment on a Brazilian coastal slum
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the perceptions of slums, systemic racism, growing inequality, environmental pollution, and environmental disasters negatively impacted community wellbeing. However, targeted measures by the community association and beneficial governmental policy measures helped to reduce these detrimental effects.
What_was_studied: The article applies the 3-dimensional wellbeing lens to examine factors that affect wellbeing in Vila dos Pescadores, a slum community in Cubatao, Southeast Brazil, over a specific period of time using data from multiple sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for scaled-up support for slum communities in addressing environmental hazards and social concerns such as exclusion, poverty, urbanization, and inequality. Policymakers should prioritize community leadership in implementing social programs and community facilities to improve livelihoods and wellbeing.

Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Poverty; Open economy; Production (economics); Constructive; Economic reform; Development economics; Liberalization
Title: Peru's return toward an open economy: Macroeconomic complications and structural questions
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the liberalization program had exceptionally high costs, with potentially constructive changes interacting adversely with each other, leading to worsened production, employment, and exports, and an increased risk of persisting strains of poverty and violence.
What_was_studied: The Peruvian program of stabilization and liberalization initiated in August 1990 and its effects on employment and income poverty in the country during a specific time period, using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize alternatives to the current liberalization program, such as those used in Chile, to address income poverty and promote sustainable economic recovery.

Field: Geography; Human capital; Stunted growth; Context (language use); Sanitation; Human waste; Developing country; Impact evaluation; Open defecation; Environmental health
Keywords: child health; sanitation coverage; open defecation; India
Title: Sanitation and child health in India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that sanitation coverage plays a significant and positive role in height growth during the first years of life, particularly for girls. Specifically, the study shows that an increase of one standard deviation in sanitation coverage leads to approximately 0.45 cm higher height-for-age z-score among girls.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effects of sanitation coverage and usage on child height for age in a semi-urban setting in Northern India, focusing on girls in particular.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of sanitation coverage on girl's height growth, policymakers should prioritize increasing sanitation access and usage in semi-urban areas like the one studied here, as such an intervention is not only effective in reducing child stunting but also targets girls explicitly.

Authors: Marco Letta; Pierluigi Montalbano; Richard S.J. Tol
Field: Effects of global warming; Agriculture; Climate change; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Yield gap; Tanzania; Demographic economics
Title: Temperature shocks, short-term growth and poverty thresholds : Evidence from rural Tanzania
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding shows that temperature shocks have a negative and significant impact on household growth only if their initial consumption lies below a critical threshold, slowing income convergence among households. Agricultural yields and labor productivity are the main transmission channels.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method is an analysis of the relationship between rural household consumption growth and temperature shocks in Tanzania using the LSMS-ISA Tanzania National Panel Survey from 2008 to 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, closing the yield gap and modernizing agriculture is crucial for adaptation to the negative impacts of global warming, and policymakers should prioritize these interventions to support poor farming households in coping with climate change.

Field: Public economics; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Poverty reduction; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Development economics; Income distribution
Keywords: Pro-Poor Growth; Inequality; Non-Income Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Latin America; Bolivia JEL classification: O12; I32; O46
Title: Economic Growth and Poverty Reduction: Measurement Issues using Income and Non-Income Indicators
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that an absolute definition of pro-poor growth is more suitable when analyzing the rate of pro-poor growth, while a relative definition has merits when defining the state of pro-poor growth. Additionally, the extension of the toolbox to non-income indicators greatly improves our understanding of the distribution of change in these indicators and their linkages with income poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper extends the pro-poor growth toolbox to non-income indicators and applies it to Bolivia, examining the distribution of change in non-income indicators, linkages between progress in income and non-income dimensions of poverty, and incidence of progress in non-income outcomes along the income distribution during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of a comprehensive pro-poor growth toolbox that includes non-income indicators to better understand the distribution of poverty and design more effective interventions to address it, particularly in the context of chronic poverty and intersectional poverty.

Authors: Daniela Zapata; Dante Contreras; Diana Kruger
Field: Ethnic group; Latin Americans; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Falling (accident); Domestic work; Low education; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Indigenous
Title: Child Labor and Schooling in Bolivia: Who's Falling Behind? The Roles of Domestic Work, Gender, and Ethnicity
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The study finds that girls are 51% more likely than boys to be out of school and working, with indigenous children, particularly girls, being the most vulnerable to future poverty and exclusion due to low education.
What_was_studied: This analysis investigates the role of gender and ethnicity in the work-school tradeoff among school-aged children in Bolivia, using domestic chores as a measure of child labor and considering time use data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of child labor, including limited access to quality education for indigenous children, to prevent long-term poverty and exclusion.

Field: Consumption (economics); Buffer stock scheme; Marginal propensity to consume; Economics; Revenue; Productivity; Investment (macroeconomics); Fiscal policy; Monetary economics; Volatility (finance)
Keywords: JEL Classification Numbers: E21; E22; E62; D91 volatility; precautionary saving; buffer-stock; investment; oil exporters; fiscal policy
Title: Oil Exporters’ Dilemma: How Much to Save and How Much to Invest
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that precautionary saving is sizable and the marginal propensity to consume out of permanent shocks is below one, in contrast to the predictions of the perfect foresight model. The optimal investment rate is high if productivity in the tradable sector is high enough.
What_was_studied: The allocation of oil revenues among consumption, saving, and investment in oil-exporting countries during the 2000s, using a precautionary saving and investment model under uncertainty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers in oil-exporting countries should prioritize investments in the tradable sector, particularly when productivity is high, to maximize the long-term benefits of oil revenues and mitigate the risks of income volatility.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Aid effectiveness; Poverty reduction; Politics; Transaction cost
Title: International coordination and the effectiveness of aid
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper finds that better donor coordination via concentration to fewer partner countries and a shift from project aid to programme-based approaches can reduce transaction costs by up to 30% and potentially increase poverty reduction by up to 50% through optimized allocation across countries.
What_was_studied: This paper discusses and seeks to quantify the effects of improved donor coordination on aid effectiveness, focusing on empirical estimates of transaction cost reductions and poverty reduction potential through reallocation across countries for the period 2000-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the severe political implementation constraints, decision makers should prioritize coordinated reallocation of aid resources to maximize poverty reduction gains, scaling up programme-based approaches and optimizing allocation across chronic poverty hotspots.

Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Convergence (economics); Territorial development; Inequality; Development economics; Income distribution; Scale (social sciences); Spatial econometrics
Title: A Large-Scale Mapping of Territorial Development Dynamics in Latin America
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results largely support spatial convergence of mean household incomes, although the estimates indicate it has been slow. Territorial inequality is found to be persistent and reduces the pro-poor effect of local income growth.
What_was_studied: This paper examines changes in per-capita income, monetary poverty, and income distribution in 9,045 subnational administrative units of nine Latin American countries between the mid-1990s and mid-2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, territorial development policies in Latin America seem well warranted, with a focus on reducing persistent territorial inequality to amplify the positive effects of local income growth.

Field: Rural area; Business; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty reduction; Rural infrastructure; Poor quality; Livelihood; Economic growth; Rural economics; Developing country
Title: The effect of infrastructure access and quality on non-farm enterprises in rural Indonesia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the quality of roads and electricity significantly impacts both employment opportunities and income levels in rural areas. Specifically, households with access to better quality infrastructure had higher levels of non-farm employment and income.
What_was_studied: The study used data from 4,000 households in rural Indonesia to investigate how the quality of two key types of infrastructure—roads and electricity—affects non-farm employment and income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve economic growth and reduce poverty in rural areas, policymakers should prioritize investments in high-quality infrastructure such as roads and electricity, which have the potential to generate employment opportunities and increase income levels for households.

Authors: Claudia Eger; Graham Miller; Caroline Scarles
Field: Agency (philosophy); Sociology; Social cognitive theory; Pedagogy; Participant observation; Empowerment; Capacity building; Context (language use); Meaning (linguistics); Social learning
Title: Gender and Capacity Building: A Multi-layered Study of Empowerment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that girls' education leads to an incipient change in perceptions of what girls and women can be and do, instilling the image of educated women in community consciousness.
What_was_studied: This study examines the interplay between social learning, relational agency, and culture in understanding empowerment and education acquisition in rural Berber villages in Morocco.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings recommend scaling up girls' education in rural Berber villages to revise perceptions of gender roles and empower women, which is critical for sustainable development and poverty reduction.

Authors: Mohamed El Hedi Arouri; Cuong Nguyen; Adel Ben Youssef
Field: Welfare; Rural area; Economics; Natural disaster; Poverty; Resilience (network); Household income; Natural hazard; Distribution (economics); Development economics
Keywords: Natural hazards; disasters; resilience; poverty; household welfare; Vietnam JEL codes: O12; Q54; D12
Title: Natural Disasters, Household Welfare, and Resilience: Evidence from Rural Vietnam
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: All three types of disasters considered (storms, floods, and droughts) have negative effects on household income and expenditure. Households in communes with higher mean expenditure and more equal expenditure distribution are more resilient to natural disasters.
What_was_studied: The study uses commune fixed-effects regressions to estimate the effect of natural disasters on welfare and poverty of rural households in Vietnam between 2010 and 2018, and subsequently examines household and community characteristics that can strengthen resilience of households to natural disasters.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize providing access to micro-credit, internal remittances, and social allowances to strengthen the resilience of households to natural disasters, particularly in communes with lower mean expenditure and more unequal expenditure distribution.

Authors: Klaus Deininger; Songqing Jin; Mona Sur
Field: Agriculture; Economy; Economic sector; Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Value (economics); Investment (macroeconomics); Inequality; Barriers to entry
Title: Sri Lanka's Rural Non-farm Economy: Removing Constraints to Pro-poor Growth
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that value added in the informal non-farm sector amounts to 80% of agricultural GDP, and participating households' incomes are significantly higher than those of non-participating households. Barriers to entry are low, and the impact of non-farm development on inequality is modest, suggesting a large potential contribution to growth and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This survey of rural enterprises in Sri Lanka explores the characteristics of the informal non-farm sector and identifies obstacles to its expansion and productivity between 2013 and 2018, using a sample of 3,947 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant potential for growth and poverty reduction in the informal non-farm sector, policymakers should prioritize investment in infrastructure and targeted support for new startups and existing enterprises, particularly small ones, to enhance productivity and expand opportunities for rural households.

Field: Rural area; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Global South; Fish consumption; Pro poor; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Food security; Aquaculture
Title: Is Aquaculture Pro-Poor? Empirical Evidence of Impacts on Fish Consumption in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the rapid expansion of commercial aquaculture has led to a decrease in fish prices, resulting in increased fish consumption among extreme poor and moderate poor consumers and those living in rural areas. These outcomes are closely linked to the pro-poor nature of national economic growth during this period.
What_was_studied: Using nationally representative data from Bangladesh, this study analyzes changes in fish consumption from 2000 to 2010, with a focus on the impact of rapid commercial aquaculture expansion on poverty reduction and food security among extreme poor and moderate poor consumers and those living in rural areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for aquaculture development programs that target extreme poor and moderate poor households in rural areas, with a focus on maintaining the pro-poor nature of economic growth. Revise existing policies to ensure that the benefits of aquaculture are equitably distributed among all income groups and geographic locations.

Title: Economic Inequality and HIV in Malawi
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive association between HIV infection and inequality at both the neighborhood and district levels, but no effect of individual poverty. Additionally, the relationship between HIV and inequality was linked to risky sex, gender violence, and return migration, but not to bad health, gender gaps in education or women’s market work.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between economic inequality and HIV infection among young Malawian women using multilevel models and data from 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing economic inequality and its relationship to HIV infection among young Malawian women. This could involve scaling up interventions that target risky sex, gender violence, and return migration, while also ensuring access to education and healthcare for all.

Title: The Welfare Impact of Land Redistribution: Evidence from a Quasi-Experimental Initiative in Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found positive effects on several productive outcomes of beneficiaries, while no effects were found with respect to access to social services. Evidence of heterogeneous effects by gender and inheritance systems was also observed.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of a joint Malawi/World Bank land program on household well-being in developing countries, using household panel data combined with a quasi-experimental program design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize decentralized market-based approaches to land redistribution, as these programs have been shown to positively impact household well-being in developing countries. Specifically, efforts should be scaled up to reach a larger population and address food insecurity, while also ensuring access to social services is not neglected.

Title: Geography of Gender Gaps: Regional patterns of income and farm nonfarm interaction among male- and female-headed households in eight African countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that gender gaps are absent in 17 of the regions regardless of the overall regional income level, suggesting that poverty nor growth in general discriminates against female-headed households. However, specific regional contexts may cause gender discrimination.
What_was_studied: Household level data from 21 regions across eight African countries collected in 2002 and 2008 were analyzed to understand production dynamics, market participation, and nonfarm linkages, with a focus on gender-based income gaps across African production systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the specific regional contexts that lead to gender discrimination and develop targeted interventions to address these issues, such as scaling up successful nonfarm linkage strategies and expanding access to market opportunities for female-headed households.

Title: Shocks, Individual Risk Attitude, and Vulnerability to Poverty among Rural Households in Thailand and Vietnam☆
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals who experienced adverse shocks, such as poverty and vulnerability, were more risk-averse than others, even when controlling for socio-demographic variables. This perpetuates vulnerability to poverty through its effect on risk attitude.
What_was_studied: More than 4,000 households in Thailand and Vietnam were surveyed to determine their risk attitudes and the impact of adverse shocks on those attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy should prioritize case-specific design of risk-coping strategies to address the findings of this study and reduce chronic poverty in vulnerable populations.

Authors: Sven Wunder; Arild Angelsen; Brian Belcher
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Foraging; Wilderness area; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Privileged access; Livelihood; Agricultural economics; Agricultural revolution; Developing country
Title: Forests, Livelihoods, and Conservation: Broadening the Empirical Base
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The steady environmental income flows come often from public forests and are extracted by men and women alike, but inflexible supplies from nature, physical hardship of harvesting, and low returns limit their role as safety nets and pathways out of poverty.
What_was_studied: Millions of rural smallholders in the developing world and their income from foraging forests and wildlands over 10,000 years after the Agricultural Revolution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Privileged access to high-quality environmental resources can become a strong local conservation motive, prioritizing the sustainable use of forests and wildlands is crucial in scaling up support for rural smallholders' income and promoting conservation efforts.

Authors: Timothy J. Hatton; Jeffrey G. Williamson
Field: Emigration; Economics; Poverty; Demographics; Stock dynamics; Third world; Development economics; Developing country

Title: Are third world emigration forces abating
primary_category: Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Emigration pressure has recently been abating and may even decline in the future, with a shift towards African emigrants and away from Hispanic ones.
What_was_studied: Emigration pressure from the developing world to the United States since 1970 based on economic and demographic fundamentals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing source country demographics, education, poverty, and migrant stock dynamics to mitigate emigration pressure and promote sustainable development in the long run.
