Title: Viewpoint – Handwashing and COVID-19: Simple, right there…?
primary_category: Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Over 26% of the global population has no access to a handwashing station in the home; for many low-income countries this proportion rises to over 50%. In other instances, the water is unaffordable or the supply has been shut off on account of unpaid bills.
What_was_studied: Population: global population; time period: over a century; data: access to handwashing stations and water supply.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In the current crisis and its aftermath, it is imperative for governments and donors to prioritize and generously fund affordable, reliable, and accessible water services in underserved regions of the world. More than ever before, this is a foundational investment for health, dignity, and development.

Authors: Fiona Lambe; Ylva Ran; Marie Jürisoo; Stefan Holmlid; Cassilde Muhoza; Oliver Johnson; Matthew Osborne
Field: Conceptual framework; Behavior change; Sociology; Emerging technologies; Psychological intervention; Context (language use); Service (systems architecture); Knowledge management; Service design; Complex adaptive system
Title: Embracing complexity: A transdisciplinary conceptual framework for understanding behavior change in the context of development-focused interventions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that individuals' experiences of a new technology or service are shaped by contextual factors, such as social norms, access to information, and the availability of support systems. Additionally, the research showed that a diverse range of actors operate at different levels within complex social-ecological systems, which can either support or hinder lasting behavior change.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the adoption of new technologies and services among vulnerable populations in Kenya and Zambia, using a mixed-methods approach that combines behavioral insights with service design principles to support lasting behavior change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the contextual factors that influence the adoption of new technologies and services among vulnerable populations. By using a service design approach that incorporates behavioral insights, development interventions can be better tailored to support lasting behavior change and improve the livelihoods of these individuals.

Authors: J. Salcedo Cain; Rana Hasan; Rhoda Magsombol; Ajay Tandon
Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Poverty; Population; Cost effectiveness; Demographic economics; Inequality; Development economics; Income distribution; Economic liberalization
Title: Accounting for Inequality in India: Evidence from Household Expenditures
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that returns to education have significantly risen in the urban sector, particularly for households engaging in education-intensive activities and occupations, driving the observed increase in inequality during 1993–2004. These findings suggest that economic liberalization policies implemented in the 1990s may be linked to these increases in returns to education.
What_was_studied: This research utilizes household-level consumption expenditure data from India to investigate the evolution of inequality between 1983 and 2004, finding that inequality increased during the latter period but not at the expense of reductions in poverty, which are more pronounced in urban areas and linked to increases in returns to education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the link between returns to education and urban poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions aimed at improving access to quality education for low-income households, particularly those residing in urban areas.

Authors: Natàlia Caldés; David Coady; John A. Maluccio
Field: Public economics; Cost efficiency; Latin Americans; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Human capital; Cost analysis
Title: The Cost of Poverty Alleviation Transfer Programs: A Comparative Analysis of Three Programs in Latin America
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that one program stands out as the most cost-efficient, with an administrative cost share of only 8.4% compared to 23.6% and 27.9% for the other two programs. This finding highlights the importance of detailed cost analysis to assess program effectiveness.
What_was_studied: This comparative study of three similar poverty alleviation programs in Latin America examines their cost efficiency between 2015 and 2020, using a replicable methodology that analyzes program cost structures in detail.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high share of administrative costs in these programs, policymakers should prioritize and expand the most cost-efficient program to reach more beneficiaries and scale up its impact, while revising the other two programs to improve their cost efficiency.

Title: Globalization, local ecosystems, and the rural poor
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that trade liberalization and international technology transfers can lead to loss in resilience of ecosystems, exacerbating poverty among vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: This paper studies the effects of globalization on the resilience of semi-arid savanna ecosystems in sub-Saharan Africa, and how these changes impact poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty and climate vulnerability, policymakers should prioritize institutional and ecological resilience by scaling up support for local knowledge and traditional institutions in resource use patterns.

Authors: Klaus Deininger; Daniel Ayalew Ali; Stein T. Holden; Jaap Zevenbergen
Field: Land tenure; Business; Land reform; Land administration; Land grabbing; Land registration; Land titling; Certification; Economic growth; Land law
Title: Rural Land Certification In Ethiopia : Process, Initial Impact, And Implications For Other African Countries - Rural Land Certification in Ethiopia: Process, Initial Impact, and Implications for Other African Countries
primary_category: Education access; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while many African countries have adopted highly innovative and pro-poor land laws, lack of implementation thwarts their potentially far-reaching impact on productivity, poverty reduction, and governance.
What_was_studied: A representative household survey from Ethiopia, covering a short period where certificates were issued to more than 20 million plots.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Ensure sustainability and enhance impact by scaling up successful registration processes like Ethiopia's cost-effective first-time registration, prioritizing resources for implementation support, and revising laws to address the challenges hindering productivity and poverty reduction.

Authors: Jing You; Katsushi S. Imai; Raghav Gaiha
Field: Rural area; Nutrient; Economics; Poverty; Household income; Agricultural economics; Obesity; Endogeneity; Quantile regression; Estimation

Title: Declining Nutrient Intake in a Growing China: Does Household Heterogeneity Matter?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while economic growth has increased income for many households, it has not necessarily led to improved nutrition. In fact, the study shows that rising income tends to reduce inequality in macronutrient intake, but this is driven by increases in nutrient intake for the urban poor and falls in nutrient intake for the rural non-poor.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the changes in nutrient intake among Chinese households from 1989 to 2009, using household-level data to explore how economic growth affects nutrition poverty and inequality in macronutrient intake.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the link between economic growth and nutrition poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the specific needs of the urban and rural poor, such as subsidies for healthy foods or agricultural support programs to increase local food availability.

Field: Sociology; Citizen journalism; Psychological intervention; Civic engagement; Status quo; Public sphere; Focus group; Social psychology; Civics; Qualitative property
Title: Why Might Information Exacerbate the Gender Gap in Civic Participation? Evidence from Mali
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings revealed that a randomly assigned civic education course widened the gender gap in civic activity, with increased participation among men and decreased participation among women. The study also showed that qualitative data collected through focus groups and interviews revealed mechanisms by which the intervention generated negative consequences for women.
What_was_studied: The research team investigated civic engagement and participation in Mali among men and women to assess how resource constraints affect women's political involvement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing discriminatory gender norms to ensure that resource investments in civic education do not exacerbate existing inequalities. Future participatory interventions should be more attuned to the social constraints faced by women and other marginalized groups.

Field: Public economics; Supply chain; Private sector; Dominance (economics); Business; Government; Productivity; Value (economics); Context (language use); Portfolio
Title: Designing interventions in local value chains for improved health and nutrition: Insights from Malawi
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while maize dominates diets, rural households are willing to consume other nutritious foods like leafy greens, tree fruits, and dried fish. However, addressing supply and demand constraints along local value chains will require carefully sequenced interventions.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews research on nutrition-sensitive value chains in developing countries, focusing on food supply and demand conditions in rural Malawi over a year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To advance health and nutrition goals, policymakers should prioritize collaborative efforts between NGOs, government agencies, and the private sector to address supply and demand constraints in local value chains, deepening learning among stakeholders.

Field: Welfare; Business; Government; Transfer payment; Per capita income; Natural disaster; Asset (economics); Wage; Demographic economics; Subsidy
Title: Benefiting From Disaster? Public and Private Responses to the Wenchuan Earthquake
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Health disparities; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that asset and income losses were substantial, but the overwhelming government response resulted in mean income per capita 17.5% higher in 2008 than in 2007, and a decline in poverty rates from 34% to 19%.
What_was_studied: This household survey-based study examines the impact of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake on rural households' welfare in seriously affected areas, using distance from the epicenter as an instrument for earthquake damage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong positive statistical relationship between lost value of housing and other assets due to the earthquake and increases in income per capita and government transfers received, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for rural households affected by natural disasters, and consider using distance from the epicenter as an instrument for earthquake damage when designing interventions.

Field: Discount points; Economics; Work (electrical); Labor income; Job loss; Gender inequality; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Income level; Demographic economics; Pandemic

Title: Gender Inequality during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Income, Expenditure, Savings, and Job Loss
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Women are 24% more likely to permanently lose their jobs due to the COVID-19 outbreak than men, and expect a 50% greater decline in labor income. Women also reduce current consumption and increase savings in response to the outbreak.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 outbreak's impact on gender inequality in income, expenditure, savings, and job loss across six countries with varying geographical locations and income levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these gender gaps in economic outcomes, decision-makers should prioritize policies that address women's disproportionate job loss and income decline, such as targeted financial assistance, job training programs, and support for women-led businesses.

Field: Ideology; Health care; Political science; Social protection; Settlement (litigation); Community management; Population; Legitimacy; Economic growth; Politics
Title: The political path to universal health coverage: Power, ideas and community-based health insurance in Rwanda
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the commitment to expanding health insurance coverage was made possible by a dominant political settlement, with CBHI being chosen as part of the broader efforts of the regime to foster its legitimacy through rapid socio-economic development. Additionally, the study found that the programme's design was compatible with the political economy of the country and incompatible with the ideas of the ruling coalition, making it more likely to run into political obstructions.
What_was_studied: Rwanda's community-based health insurance (CBHI) program, which covers over 75% of the population and is a critical component of the country's universal health coverage (UHC) efforts, was found to be successful due to a dominant political settlement that prioritized rapid socio-economic development and the ruling coalition's core ideology, rather than purely relying on objective interests of rulers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Poor countries should not solely rely on pure CBHI models based on voluntary enrolment and community management to achieve UHC, as these models may not be compatible with the political economy and ideology of the ruling coalition. Instead, they should prioritize a comprehensive approach that includes both CBHI and other health financing strategies to expand access to healthcare.

Field: Public economics; Social exclusion; Social inequality; Human rights; Social policy; Social rights; European Social Charter; Free education; International development

Title: Social Rights and Economics: Claims to Health Care and Education in Developing Countries - Social rights and economics : claims to health care and education in developing countries
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The policy consequences of rights overlap considerably with a modern economic approach, both skeptical that electoral politics and de facto market rules provide sufficient accountability for service provision, advocating intrasectoral reforms to strengthen the hand of service recipients. Differences exist in procedures for service delivery, outcomes assessment, long-term deprivation consequences, tradeoff metrics, and behavioral distortions from subsidies.
What_was_studied: The author analyzes contemporary rights-based and economic approaches to health care and education in developing countries, assessing their foundations and uses in development, outlining an economic approach to improving services, and highlighting differences, similarities, and hard questions between the two approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Advocate for modern economic approaches to health care and education services in developing countries, prioritizing intrasectoral reforms to strengthen the hand of service recipients, fund and expand these services, scale up effective delivery methods, and revise policies addressing long-term deprivation consequences.

Field: Cognitive skill; Poverty; Early childhood; Household income; Human development (humanity); Population; Development economics; Income distribution; Immigration

Title: Seasonal Migration and Early Childhood Development
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that mother's migration has a positive effect on early cognitive development, attributed to changes in income and intra-household empowerment gains offsetting potential negative effects from temporary lack of parenting.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of seasonal migration on early childhood development in a poor, shock-prone region of rural Nicaragua over a specific time period using unique data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential for increased opportunities in seasonal migration due to higher South-South mobility, policymakers should prioritize investments in early childhood development to positively affect long-term poverty reduction.

Authors: Faizal Rahmanto Moeis; Teguh Dartanto; Jossy Prananta Moeis; Mohamad Ikhsan
Field: Welfare; Agriculture; Per capita; Economics; Human capital; Conventional wisdom; Labor mobility; Family life; Agricultural economics; Agricultural land
Keywords: Agriculture land; Labor mobility; Lewis’ dual sector theorem; Poverty dynamics; Structural Transformation
Title: A longitudinal study of agriculture households in Indonesia: The effect of land and labor mobility on welfare and poverty dynamics.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Moving out of agriculture sectors significantly increased the welfare of poor agricultural households, especially during the period of 2000-2007, but this is not the case of 2007-2014. Movement out of agricultural sectors decreases the probability of being always poor by 13.5 percentage points.
What_was_studied: We scrutinize the last three waves of the Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS) to analyze the existence of the dual theorem and examine the effect of moving out of agricultural sectors on the welfare of poor agricultural households in Indonesia during two distinct periods: 2000-2007 and 2007-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that moving out of agriculture does not guarantee better welfare for farmers in a more advanced economy, governments and development organizations should prioritize shifting farmers to formal non-agricultural sectors and investing in their human capital skills to ensure improved well-being. Additionally, keeping farmland ownership, modernizing agriculture, and raising investment in human capital should be the main concerns in agricultural development.

Authors: Emilio Colombo; Lorenzo Menna; Patrizio Tirelli
Field: Finance; Applied economics; Public good; Economics; Unemployment; Population; Market participation; Large sample; Dynamic stochastic general equilibrium; Informal sector
Keywords: Financial crises; Informal Economy; labor market frictions; endogenous participation JEL codes: E26; E32; G01
Title: Informality and the labor market effects of financial crises
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: Financial crises lead to a drop in official market participation and an increase in informal employment, with strong persistence. The informal sector acts as a buffer during bad times but also amplifies the crisis for the official economy. In less developed economies, financial crises cause a relatively stronger reallocation of inputs towards less efficient sectors and expose a larger fraction of the population to the adverse effects of informality.
What_was_studied: A large sample of countries during financial crises to investigate the effects on key labor market indicators, including official and unofficial employment, unemployment, and participation rate.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize measures to support formal employment and reduce reliance on informal work, particularly in less developed economies. This could include investing in education and training programs, improving access to finance for small businesses, and implementing policies to address financial market frictions and promote labor market flexibility.

Field: Economics; International economics; Short run; Computable general equilibrium; Context (language use); Individual country; South asia; Free trade; Linkage (mechanical)
Keywords: trade liberalisation; economic growth; regional disparities; computable general equilibrium model; South Asia; India
Title: Does Trade Liberalization Promote Regional Disparities? Evidence from a Multiregional CGE Model of India
primary_category: Income poverty; Regional disparities
What_was_found: In the short run, trade liberalization has a beneficial impact on the rich and fast-growing middle-income states and a marginal or negative impact on the poor states.
What_was_studied: The link between trade liberalization and regional disparities in the Indian economy over the last few decades using a single-country multiregional Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The Indian government should prioritize funding and implementing policies that address regional disparities to maximize the benefits of trade liberalization, particularly in poor states.

Field: Private sector; Market segmentation; Economy; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; restrict; Earnings; Endogenous Factors; Inequality; Criticism
Title: Labour Market Segmentation: Evidence From Cyprus
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Cyprus labor market is segmented by sex, with women earning lower wages than men; and by employment sector and firm size. The study also shows that these segments operate to erect barriers that restrict access of workers to high-wage segments.
What_was_studied: The existence of labor market segmentation (LMS) in Cyprus, and how it relates to sex, employment sector, and firm size.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of LMS on poverty and inequality, decision makers should prioritize policies that address the gender wage gap and promote access to high-wage jobs in the public sector, such as targeted training programs for women and equal pay legislation.

Authors: Thomas Gries; Manfred Kraft; Daniel Meierrieks
Field: Economics; Empirical evidence; International economics; Financial market; Causality; Capital deepening; Financial deepening; Sub saharan; Economic growth; Openness to experience
Keywords: Financial Markets; Economic Growth; Openness; Hsiao's Granger Causality; Sub-Saharan Africa; JEL Classification: C32; O16; O55
Title: Linkages between Financial Deepening, Trade Openness and Economic Development: Causality Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found limited support for the popular hypothesis of finance-led growth, with financial deepening and trade openness having only marginally influenced economic development. The investigated countries have failed to benefit from financial deepening.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between financial deepening, trade openness, and economic development in 16 sub-Saharan African countries using the Hsiao-Granger method to test for causality over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritizing sustainable development strategies that prioritize gender equality and poverty reduction, rather than solely relying on financial or trade sector development, is crucial for sub-Saharan African countries to achieve meaningful economic growth and development.

Authors: Peter Newton; Angelo Eduardo Angel Gomez; Suhyun Jung; Timothy Kelly; Thiago de Araújo Mendes; Laura Vang Rasmussen; Júlio César dos Reis; Renato de Aragão Ribeiro Rodrigues; Richard Tipper; Dan van der Horst; Cristy Watkins
Field: Environmental resource management; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Forest restoration; Livelihood; Greenhouse gas; Amazon rainforest; Sustainable development; Theory of change; Environmental planning
Title: Overcoming barriers to low carbon agriculture and forest restoration in Brazil: The Rural Sustentável project
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The project's innovative design and theory of change offer insights into possible mechanisms for promoting forest restoration on private lands in the tropics, with participating farmers reporting an average increase of 12% in their agricultural productivity and a 30% reduction in deforestation rates.
What_was_studied: The Rural Sustentavel project in the Brazilian Amazon and Atlantic Forest biomes, which aimed to decrease greenhouse gas emissions, reduce poverty, and promote sustainable rural development by restoring deforested and degraded land and facilitating the uptake of low-carbon agricultural technologies among farmers over a two-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the project's success in promoting sustainable rural development and reducing poverty while decreasing greenhouse gas emissions, decision-makers should scale up this model to other regions of Brazil and prioritize the integration of low-carbon agricultural technologies into national development strategies to promote sustainable food systems.

Field: Psychology; Work (electrical); Mediation; Poverty; Beneficiary; Psychological intervention; Community engagement; Premise; Sanitation; Social psychology
Title: Life of a PAI: Mediation by willingness and ability for beneficiary community engagement
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that willingness and ability of the beneficiary community to engage with PAIs have a direct impact on the performance of these interventions, with ability being more influential than willingness. Additionally, the study identified an evolving interface between willingness and ability throughout the PAI lifecycle.
What_was_studied: The research focused on the effectiveness of Poverty Alleviation Interventions (PAIs) in East India during a two-year period, using mixed-methods data collection and analysis techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize community engagement and participation in the design, delivery, and evaluation of PAIs, particularly in regards to the ability of beneficiaries to effectively utilize the resources provided. This can be achieved by scaling up successful PAI models, expanding resources and support for community-led initiatives, and revamping project evaluation methods to better capture community response.

Authors: Francesco Cecchi; Adriana Garcia; Robert Lensink; Bruce Wydick
Field: Coaching; Production (economics); Index (typography); Poverty; Baseline (sea); Agriculture; Milk production; Quality (philosophy); Business; Economics; Economic growth; Political science; Geography; Management; Animal science; Archaeology; Biology; Macroeconomics; Philosophy; Epistemology; World Wide Web; Computer science; Law
Title: Aspirational hope, dairy farming practices, and milk production: Evidence from a randomized controlled trial in Bolivia
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the treatment group had significant increases in both an aspirational hope index and a business goals index (0.20σ and 1.07σ, respectively), as well as an increase in quality-enhancing practices (1.07σ), but no significant increase in milk production.
What_was_studied: This controlled experiment studied the impact of aspirational hope on dairy farmers' practices in Bolivia over a three-month period, using coaching sessions and an inspiring documentary to increase aspirations related to dairy production among 531 farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of fostering aspirational hope among farmers to enhance their business practices and quality of production, especially among those with high levels of intrinsic motivation. To scale up this intervention, policymakers should prioritize funding for coaching sessions and inspirational media, targeting specifically dairy farmers in Bolivia.

Authors: Ira Irina Dorband; Michael Jakob; Matthias Kalkuhl; Jan Christoph Steckel
Field: Per capita; Climate change; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Revenue; Carbon price; Low and middle income countries; Demographic economics; Economic inequality
Title: Poverty and distributional effects of carbon pricing in low- and middle-income countries – A global comparative analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that carbon pricing has progressive distributional effects in low-income countries, with an average benefit for households with incomes below USD 15,000 per year. The analysis also showed that differences in energy consumption patterns among income groups are the primary determinant of distributional outcomes.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the distributional implications of carbon pricing for different income groups in 87 mostly low- and middle-income countries, using a consistent dataset and method to assess the expected incidence of moderate carbon price increases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the progressive benefits of carbon pricing in low-income countries and the potential for raising domestic revenue and reducing economic inequality, policymakers should prioritize implementing carbon pricing policies that target energy consumption patterns to mitigate climate change while addressing poverty and inequality.

Authors: Andrew Dorward; Jonathan Kydd; Jamie Morrison; Ian Urey
Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Agrarian society; Economics; Psychological intervention; State (polity); Rural poverty; South asia; Development economics; Economic growth; Liberalization
Title: A Policy Agenda for Pro-Poor Agricultural Growth
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite the historical significance of agriculture in reducing poverty, contemporary agricultural growth faces new difficulties, including endogenous issues in today's poor rural areas, global changes, and policy environment changes emphasizing liberalization and state withdrawal. The study also found that active state interventions were crucial in supporting critical stages of agricultural market development, but their benefits in institutional development are often overlooked while their high costs are more visible.
What_was_studied: Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia were studied to determine the prevalence of very poor rural people and the challenges facing agricultural growth in poverty reduction in poor agrarian economies during the 21st century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize active state interventions in supporting critical stages of agricultural market development to reduce poverty in rural areas. This can include funding for infrastructure, scaling up successful programs, and revising policy environments to better support agricultural growth.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Survey data collection; Productivity; Context (language use); Corporate governance; Product innovation; Developing country
Title: Technology Adoption and Employment in Less Developed Countries: A Mixed-Method Systematic Review
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The effect of technology adoption on employment is skill-biased, more likely to be observed when technology adoption favors product innovation over process innovation, and less likely to be associated with employment creation in low-income countries and when the evidence is related to farm employment as opposed to firm/industry employment.
What_was_studied: The implications of technology adoption for productivity, income and welfare in less developed countries (LDCs) have been studied widely, but the relationship between technology adoption and employment has received less attention. This systematic review evaluates the diverse yet sizeable evidence base that has remained below the radars of both reviewers and policy makers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up technology adoption in LDCs, policymakers should prioritize investments in product innovation and strengthen governance and labor-market institutions to mitigate the negative effects of international trade and weak forward and backward linkages on employment creation.

Authors: Ronnie Babigumira; Arild Angelsen; Maarten L. Buis; Simone Bauch; Terry Sunderland; Sven Wunder
Field: Agriculture; Clearing; Deforestation; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); High forest; Livelihood; Agricultural economics; Developing country
Keywords: land-use change; deforestation; poverty; smallholder farmers
Title: Forest Clearing in Rural Livelihoods: Household-Level Global-Comparative Evidence
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 27% of sampled households had converted forest to agriculture during the previous 12 months, clearing on average 1.21 ha.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the factors that influence rural household decisions to clear forestland, using a large dataset of 7172 households from 24 developing countries over a 12-month period, finding that male-headed households with abundant labor and living in recently settled areas with high forest cover tend to clear more land, but regional peculiarities are prevalent, and households with medium to high asset holdings and higher market orientation are more likely to clear forest than the poorest and market-isolated households, questioning popular policy narratives about poverty-driven forest clearing.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted asset-building programs and market integration initiatives to support rural households with medium to high asset holdings and higher market orientation in their efforts to avoid deforestation, while also addressing regional peculiarities and the role of male labor abundance in forest clearing.

Authors: Sophia Baumert; Janet Fisher; Casey M. Ryan; Emily Woollen; Frank Vollmer; Luis Artur; Pedro Zorrilla-Miras; Mansour Mahamane
Field: Agriculture; Land use, land-use change and forestry; Rural area; Business; Poverty; Prosperity; Investment (macroeconomics); Production (economics); Intensive farming; Agricultural economics
Title: Forgone opportunities of large-scale agricultural investment: A comparison of three models of soya production in Central Mozambique
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that small-scale farmers had higher income levels than large-scale commercial operations, and medium-scale emergent farmers had higher income levels than small-scale farmers. Additionally, the study found that all three soya production models resulted in decreasing land availability.
What_was_studied: In Central Mozambique, a study of soya production models found that large-scale plantations lead to localized land scarcity, while small- and medium-scale productions provide greater socio-economic benefits such as on-farm employment and work opportunities along the local value chain.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize support for small- and medium-scale soya farming to maximize local socio-economic benefits and minimize negative effects on food production and access to land.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Propensity score matching; Poverty; Context (language use); Child health; Sri lanka; South asia; Demographic economics; Development economics; Anthropometry
Keywords: Welfare Programs; Child Health; Matching Methods; South Asia; Sri Lanka JEL Classification: H53; I12; I38
Title: Welfare grants and their impact on child health: The case of Sri Lanka
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper finds that Samurdhi improves the height-for-age z-score of a child from a grant-receiving family by roughly 0.40 standard deviations with the impact driven mainly by children between six, and 36 months of age, compared to if they did not receive the grant. It also improves weight-for-height z-scores by around 0.45 standard deviations of children aged 36–60 months.
What_was_studied: The study looks at the Samurdhi Program in Sri Lanka, and uses household data for 1999/2000 to determine whether an exogenous increase in income in the context of a poverty alleviation program has an impact on child anthropometric outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These results are important for Sri Lanka, where child nutrition is a cause for concern; policymakers should prioritize the expansion of Samurdhi and similar programs to improve child health outcomes.

Authors: Chukwumerije Okereke; Alexia Coke; Mulu Geebreyesus; Tsegaye Ginbo; Jeremy J. Wakeford; Yacob Mulugetta
Field: Sociotechnical system; Political science; Green economy; Adaptive capacity; Innovation system; Industrialisation; Climate change mitigation; Sustainable development; Sustainability; Economic system
Title: Governing green industrialisation in Africa: Assessing key parameters for a sustainable socio-technical transition in the context of Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis identifies clear articulation of the imperative for climate change mitigation and economic growth, strong high-level government commitment to a greening agenda within the context of accelerated industrialisation, and a nascent innovation system that is beginning to evolve according to these priorities.
What_was_studied: The conception and implementation of green industrialisation in Ethiopia, one of the world's poorest nations, where an ambitious Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy has been created alongside a multi-sectoral Growth and Transformation Plan (GTP).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the availability of cross-border resources for purposive sustainability transition within low-income countries and prioritize coordinated efforts between different stakeholders to address ongoing tension between addressing climate change and promoting economic growth.

Field: Sociology; Voting behavior; Political socialization; Citizen journalism; Socialization; Context (language use); Public relations; Civil society; Democracy; Politics
Title: Democratic Talk in Church: Religion and Political Socialization in the Context of Urban Inequality
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that exposure to political information in churches is common, especially in evangelical churches and low-education neighborhoods. Non-partisan civic norms are more frequently discussed than partisan messages, leading to increased knowledge of the local campaign and higher turnout rates. Messages encouraging a 'conscientious vote' have a particularly strong impact on political information in low-education neighborhoods, helping to equalize political information across the urban environment.
What_was_studied: The article investigates how civic education in churches affects political socialization and participatory orientations among citizens in new and developing democracies, specifically in low-income and low-education neighborhoods of a Brazilian city during a municipal election campaign.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inclusive nature of churches and their high frequency of interaction, development professionals should prioritize partnerships with churches to scale up civic education initiatives in low-income and low-education neighborhoods. By funding and implementing such programs, decision makers can help close knowledge gaps and promote participatory orientations among citizens, fostering more equitable and informed democratic participation.

Field: Agriculture; Economies of agglomeration; Economy; Urban agglomeration; Economics; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Internal migration; Structural transformation; Urbanization; Development economics
Keywords: Structural transformation; Urban agglomeration; Economic growth; Poverty; Africa
Title: Can Cities or Towns Drive African Development? Economy-wide Analysis for Ethiopia and Uganda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Urban agglomeration is an important source of long-term growth and structural transformation, but investing in cities does not greatly reduce national poverty over the short-term; agricultural growth is more effective, albeit with slower national growth.
What_was_studied: Rapid urbanization in Ethiopia and Uganda from 1990 to 2010 using dynamic economy-wide models that capture both traditional aspects of the debate (growth linkages and foreign trade) and benefits from urbanization (internal migration and agglomeration effects).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these trade-offs, policymakers should prioritize investments in both urban and rural development to achieve sustainable and inclusive economic growth, with a focus on supporting smallholder farmers and agro-processing industries to reduce poverty and inequality over the long-term.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Empowerment; Accountability; Nongovernmental organization; South asia; Economic growth; Developing country
Keywords: NGOs; accountability; empowerment; India; South Asia; values
Title: Accountability for Empowerment: Dilemmas Facing Non-Governmental Organizations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that NGO values have a significant impact on the effectiveness of downward accountability mechanisms for empowerment outcomes among poor women. Specifically, NGOs with a strong focus on participatory democracy, human rights, and social justice were more likely to have successful empowerment outcomes.
What_was_studied: The accountability of NGOs in empowering poor women in India, using case studies from various organizations and time periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding NGO programs that prioritize these values and incorporate downward accountability mechanisms to ensure the most effective empowerment outcomes for poor women in developing countries.

Authors: Jose E. Gomez-Gonzalez; Jorge M. Uribe; Oscar M. Valencia
Field: Economics; Fiscal policy; Fiscal union; Inflation (cosmology); Financial crisis; Monetary economics; Sophistication; Macroeconomics; Social science; Physics; Sociology; Theoretical physics
Title: Does economic complexity reduce the probability of a fiscal crisis?
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that a country's economic complexity significantly reduces the probability of a fiscal crisis, with a one-point increase in the Economic Complexity Index reducing the risk by half. This effect is robust across low-income, emerging, and advanced economies.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between a country's productive structure sophistication and its likelihood of experiencing a fiscal crisis, using a comprehensive dataset of 172 countries spanning over 200 fiscal crisis episodes between 1995 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize increasing economic complexity to reduce fiscal vulnerability and contribute to macroeconomic stability, which is a fundamental condition for sustainable development.

Authors: Jaclyn Yap; Vandana Chaudhry; Chandan Kumar Jha; Subha Mani; Sophie Mitra
Field: Public policy; Interpreter; Applied economics; Political science; Audit; Pledge; Public relations; Sign language; Sustainable development; Pandemic
Keywords: Audit; COVID-19; Disability; Information; Press briefings
Title: Are responses to the pandemic inclusive? A rapid virtual audit of COVID-19 press briefings in LMICs.
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only 65% of countries had a sign language interpreter (SLI) present in COVID-19 press briefings and conferences, with lower proportions in low-income countries (41%) and Sub-Saharan African countries (54%). None of the international organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO), had an SLI present during COVID-19 press briefings.
What_was_studied: The study examined COVID-19 press briefings and conferences issued by governments and international organizations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) during Feb-May 2020 to assess inclusivity for hearing-impaired communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for all countries and international organizations to prioritize accessibility in their COVID-19 press briefings, by including a sign language interpreter, to uphold the sustainable development pledge of 'no one gets left behind.'.

Authors: Anne M. Larson; Juan Pablo Sarmiento Barletti; Nicole Heise Vigil
Field: Empowerment; Accountability; Indigenous; Equity (law); Stakeholder; Corporate governance; Public relations; Political science; Inclusion (mineral); Economic growth; Sociology; Business; Social science; Economics; Ecology; Finance; Law; Biology
Title: A place at the table is not enough: Accountability for Indigenous Peoples and local communities in multi-stakeholder platforms
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that IPLCs perceive multi-stakeholder forums as having potential to address inequality but also identified accountability failures. The findings suggest that greater strategic attention is needed to ensure the collective action and counter power required to hold more powerful actors accountable.
What_was_studied: This comparative study analyzed 11 subnational multi-stakeholder forums aimed at improving land and forest use practices in Brazil, Ethiopia, Indonesia, and Peru between 2015 and 2019, with interviews from over 50 Indigenous Peoples and local communities (IPLCs) forum participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address rural poverty and housing insecurity, decision-makers must prioritize empowering marginalized groups, such as IPLCs, by revising multi-stakeholder forums' accountability structures and fostering collective action to ensure more equitable resource governance.

Field: Decentralization; Sociology; Human rights; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Economic growth; Civil society; Community forestry; Sustainability; International human rights law
Keywords: rights; institutions and the environment; governance; forests; Thailand
Title: In the Eyes of the State: Negotiating a “Rights-Based Approach” to Forest Conservation in Thailand
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper argues that efforts to support rural livelihoods through community rights have been undermined by a state that frequently supports commercial interests or opposes decentralization to minority groups.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the 'rights-based' approach to equitable development in Thailand's 'Community Forestry Bill', examining conflicts concerning watershed forests and mangroves, and how civil society organizations may negotiate rights within wider public spheres.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting community rights in forest reserve areas to address chronic poverty and environmental sustainability, and revise the Community Forestry Bill to better support rural livelihoods.

Authors: M. Surchat; M. Irakoze; R. Hansmann; S. Kantengwa; M. Konlambigue; L. Späth; B. Wilde; J. Six; P. Krütli
Field: Work (physics); Production (economics); Business; Scrutiny; Circular economy; Compost; Sorting; Municipal solid waste; Operations management; Waste management; Engineering; Economics; Political science; Mechanical engineering; Ecology; Biology; Computer science; Law; Macroeconomics; Programming language
Title: Jobs in the circular bioeconomy under scrutiny: The challenging reality of compost production in Rwanda
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the work can be considered relatively decent compared to national references, except for insufficient social protections and occupational safety. Workers reported being rather satisfied with their jobs, although workers employed in composting were significantly less satisfied than others. The findings highlight the importance of household-level waste separation for improving not only worker safety but also nutrient recovery.
What_was_studied: This study examines biowaste recycling in Rwanda, focusing on the working conditions of waste recyclers and their satisfaction, with the purpose of assessing decent work opportunities for those employed in the sector. The research surveyed 63 workers from three compost production and three biowaste processing companies over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize decent work opportunities in the biowaste recycling sector. Ensuring adequate social protections and occupational safety for workers can be achieved by scaling up waste sorting at the household level, expanding waste collection services, and funding training programs that promote sustainable waste management practices.

Authors: Lucila Carbonell; Pascale Hofmann; Nevana Srikissoon; Luiza C. Campos; Sandile Mbatha; Monica Lakhanpaul; Vishnu Mabeer; Ine Steenmans; Priti Parikh
Field: Sanitation; Business; Poverty; Context (archaeology); Sustainable development; Improved sanitation; Millennium Development Goals; Environmental planning; Economic growth; Economics; Political science; Geography; Engineering; Environmental engineering; Law; Archaeology
Title: Localisation of links between sanitation and the Sustainable Development Goals to inform municipal policy in eThekwini Municipality, South Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there are significant linkages between sanitation and all 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including 83 synergies, 49 risks, and 4 trade-offs.
What_was_studied: Significant strides have been made in eThekwini Municipality, Durban, towards achieving Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG6) but with 27% of households lacking access to basic sanitation in 2020, challenges remain.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in sanitation can have co-benefits across multiple SDGs, including poverty reduction, sustainable development, and climate action. Therefore, eThekwini's Water and Sanitation unit should prioritize funding efficient solutions that address existing risks and enhance community acceptance.

Authors: Hitoshi Nagano; Jose A. Puppim de Oliveira; Allan Kardec Barros; Altair da Silva Costa Júnior
Field: Gross domestic product; Health indicator; Per capita; Health care; Economics; Kuznets curve; Population; Health policy; Economic growth; Blood pressure
Keywords: Economic development; Health policy; Heart risk factors, blood pressure; Kuznets Curve
Title: The ‘Heart Kuznets Curve’? Understanding the relations between economic development and cardiac conditions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a positive correlation between low-income countries and an inverted-U shaped curve, or a 'Heart Kuznets Curve', where as country income rises, people tend to change their diets and habits, have better access to health services and education, which affects blood pressure. However, the latter two may not offset the rise in blood pressure until countries reach a certain income.
What_was_studied: The relationship between income and blood pressure in 136 countries from 1980 to 2008 was analyzed using regression and statistical analysis by Pearson's correlation (r).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Investing early in health education and preventive health care can avoid the sharp increase in blood pressure as countries develop, scaling up interventions to reduce cardiovascular risk factors and prioritize health equity in sustainable development policies.

Field: Environmental resource management; Field research; Participatory action research; Sociology; Applied anthropology; Natural resource management; Participatory rural appraisal; Participatory GIS; Food security; Agroecosystem analysis; Environmental planning
Title: The origins and practice of participatory rural appraisal
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: PRA has emerged as a powerful method for analyzing local knowledge and planning community development projects, particularly in the areas of natural resources management, agriculture, poverty, and social programs, and health and food security.
What_was_studied: Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) describes a growing family of approaches and methods to enable local people to share, enhance, and analyze their knowledge of life and conditions, to plan, and to act. PRA has sources in activist participatory research, agroecosystem analysis, applied anthropology, field research on farming systems, and rapid rural appraisal (RRA).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that PRA can effectively enable local people to plan and act on their own behalf, decision makers should prioritize funding and scaling up PRA initiatives in intersectional poverty reduction strategies.

Authors: Marie-Luise Matthys; Sushant Acharya; Sanjaya Khatri
Field: Agriculture; Cash crop; Business; Citizen journalism; Perspective (graphical); Well-being; The good life; Face (sociological concept); Commercialization; Economic growth
Title: “Before cardamom, we used to face hardship”: Analyzing agricultural commercialization effects in Nepal through a local concept of the Good Life
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that while commercialization reduced physical and financial hardship, it did not necessarily lead to an overall improvement in the Good Life for all groups, particularly for women and marginalized castes. The study highlighted the need for a more nuanced approach to evaluating agricultural change and the importance of considering local perspectives.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the effects of commercialization policies on smallholder agriculture in East Nepal over a five-year period, using a local concept of the Good Life to measure outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize inclusive, multidimensional assessments of agricultural change, rather than solely relying on limited indicators. By doing so, they can better address the needs of marginalized groups and ultimately reduce poverty and improve sustainable development outcomes.

Authors: Luciane Lenz; Anicet Munyehirwe; Jörg Peters; Maximiliane Sievert
Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Electricity; Beneficiary; Investment (macroeconomics); Willingness to pay; Electrification; Developing country
Keywords: Energy access; diff erence-in-diff erences; electrifi cation; mixed-methods; Sub-Saharan Africa
Title: Does Large-Scale Infrastructure Investment Alleviate Poverty? Impacts of Rwanda’s Electricity Access Roll-Out Program
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The EARP has been remarkably effective in increasing the connection numbers among all beneficiary types, yet consumption patterns remain low and there is only weak evidence for impacts on classical poverty indicators such as income, health, and education. However, electrification has resulted in a considerable reduction in dry-cell battery consumption with potential environmental benefits.
What_was_studied: The objective of the United Nations Sustainable Energy for All initiative (SE4All) is to provide electricity by 2030 to the 1.1 billion people in developing countries that hitherto lack access, with a focus on Africa and using the Rwandan Electricity Access Role-Out Program (EARP) as one of the largest examples.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To inform the way forward within the SE4All endeavor, more research is needed to compare on-grid and off-grid electrification with respect to impact potentials, costs, and people’s willingness to pay. Policymakers should prioritize electrification programs that maximize connections among all beneficiary groups while taking into account the long-term consumption patterns and environmental impacts.

Authors: Sachiko Ozawa; Sarah K. Laing; Colleen R. Higgins; Tatenda T. Yemeke; Christine C. Park; Rebecca Carlson; Young Eun Ko; L. Beryl Guterman; Saad B. Omer
Field: Cognitive development; Psychology; Cognition; Systematic review; Educational attainment; Academic achievement; Earnings; Low and middle income countries; Demographic economics; Cognitive test
Keywords: Cognition; Cognitive ability; Earnings; Educational attainment; Returns
Title: Educational and economic returns to cognitive ability in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The empirical finding suggests that higher cognitive ability increases the probability of school enrollment, academic achievement, and educational attainment across LMICs, with a standard deviation increase in cognitive test scores associated with a 4.5% increase in wages.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examined the relationship between early cognitive ability and future educational and economic outcomes in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) from 2000 to present, using a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of quantitative studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in early cognitive development can play a critical role in improving educational and economic outcomes in LMICs. Therefore, policy makers should prioritize and scale up interventions aimed at enhancing early childhood cognitive development, particularly in low-income countries with the least evidence.

Field: Rural area; Socioeconomic status; Vulnerability; Poverty; China; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Literacy; Intervention (law); Developing country
Keywords: developing countries; education; eyeglasses; poverty; vision
Title: Poverty and Proximate Barriers to Learning: Vision Deficiencies, Vision Correction and Educational Outcomes in Rural Northwest China
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant unmet need for vision correction, socioeconomic gradients in vision correction, greater vulnerability to vision problems among higher socioeconomic status and more academically engaged children, and significant favorable effects of vision correction on math and literacy performance and class failure.
What_was_studied: Using the Gansu Survey of Children and Families (2,000 children; 100 rural villages) and the Gansu Vision Intervention Project (a randomized trial; 19,185 students, 165 schools, two counties), we analyze the unmet need for vision correction in poor communities in low- and middle-income countries, focusing on rural Northwest China.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant unmet need for vision correction in poor communities, governments and NGOs should prioritize scaling up low-cost, effective vision interventions to improve education outcomes and reduce socioeconomic disparities.

Field: Econometrics; Unobservable; Human development (humanity); Capability approach; Mutual influence; Computer science; Latent variable; Structural equation modeling; Operationalization
Keywords: capability approach; structural equation model (SEM); human development; education; living conditions; Bolivia
Title: Estimating Basic Capabilities: A Structural Equation Model Applied to Bolivia
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a strong interdependence between these capabilities and confirmed the role of exogenous factors such as wealth and education in their determination. The research provided individual capability indices constructed from estimation results, analyzing their empirical distributions.
What_was_studied: The research applied a structural equation model to Bolivian data from 2007-2018, examining two 'basic' capability domains related to children: knowledge and living conditions, capturing their mutual influence and the role of exogenous factors in their determination.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that sustainable development policies targeting multidimensional poverty reduction in rural areas should prioritize investments in education and wealth redistribution initiatives to address the interdependence of capabilities related to children's knowledge and living conditions.

Authors: Masamitsu Kurata; Kazushi Takahashi; Akira Hibiki
Field: Psychological intervention; Child health; Respiratory illness; Aerodynamic diameter; Fully developed; Ambient air pollution; Prenatal exposure; Air pollution; Medicine; Environmental health
Title: Gender differences in associations of household and ambient air pollution with child health: Evidence from household and satellite-based data in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results show that (1) the use of solid fuels is associated with respiratory illness among girls but not boys, (2) prenatal exposure to ambient PM2.5 is associated with stunting in boys but not girls, and (3) postnatal exposure is associated with stunting in both genders.
What_was_studied: This study examines how prenatal and postnatal exposures to ambient particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter of 2.5μm or less (PM2.5) along with household use of solid fuels are correlated with child health in Bangladesh, combining individual-level data from nationally representative surveys with satellite-based high-resolution data on ambient PM2.5.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The main policy implications are that interventions against HAP would be more effective by targeting girls, and interventions against AAP should also target pregnant women. In sum, our findings highlight the importance of protecting women from air pollution and achieving Target 3.9 of the Sustainable Development Goals.

Authors: Jason C. Young; Michael P. Gilmore
Field: Environmental resource management; Knowledge-based systems; Participatory action research; Descriptive knowledge; Sociology; Context (language use); Participatory GIS; Corporate governance; Indigenous; Knowledge management; Geospatial analysis
Title: Participatory Uses of Geospatial Technologies to Leverage Multiple Knowledge Systems within Development Contexts: A Case Study from the Peruvian Amazon
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that PGIS methodologies effectively engaged marginalized groups, particularly women, in decision-making processes, leading to more inclusive and democratic forms of development. Additionally, the study found that these approaches can be used to transform historically unjust governance practices, rather than simply folding new subjects into existing power structures.
What_was_studied: Participatory approaches to development, specifically Participatory Geographic Information Systems (PGIS) methodologies, were examined in the context of a case study with the Maij community in Tanzania, focusing on gender and poverty outcomes over a 5-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of PGIS methodologies in development projects to ensure more inclusive and democratic decision-making processes, particularly in addressing gender and poverty outcomes. By funding and scaling these approaches, practitioners can meaningfully engage marginalized groups and transform unjust governance practices.

Authors: Martin Flatø; Raya Muttarak; André Pelser
Field: Agriculture; Vulnerability; Poverty; Geography; Spouse; Household income; Earnings; Socioeconomics; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Wet season
Keywords: climate variability; economic vulnerability; female-headed household; poverty; South Africa
Title: Women, Weather, and Woes: The Triangular Dynamics of Female-Headed Households, Economic Vulnerability, and Climate Variability in South Africa
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that female-headed households are more vulnerable to climate variability than other household types, with single female-headed households being particularly vulnerable due to lower initial earnings and limited access to protective social networks or coping strategies. Widows, never-married women, and women with non-resident spouses are also found to be more vulnerable.
What_was_studied: Female-headed households in South Africa and their differential vulnerability to climate variability over three waves of the National Income Dynamics Survey from 2006 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted support for female-headed households in South Africa, particularly those in districts where rainfall has a large effect on agricultural yields. This support could include scaled-up social protection programs and climate-resilient agriculture initiatives to help mitigate the impacts of climate variability and reduce intergenerational poverty.

Authors: Carol J. Pierce Colfer; Ramadhani Achdiawan; James M. Roshetko; Elok Mulyoutami; E. Linda Yuliani; A. Mulyana; Moira Moeliono; H. Adnan;  Erni
Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Sophistication; Empowerment; Power (social and political); Quality of life (healthcare); Life chances; Affect (psychology); Development economics; Economic growth; Domestic violence
Keywords: Asia; Indonesia; food; money; life chance; violence
Title: The Balance of Power in Household Decision-Making: Encouraging News on Gender in Southern Sulawesi
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women play a significant role in decision-making processes related to agriculture, food, money, life chances, and attitudes toward domestic violence, indicating a high level of social sophistication and democratic elements within these groups. Additionally, the study identified three areas requiring greater attention for equitable landscape management: ascertaining and accounting for women's spheres of decision-making, expanding men's involvement in care activities, and enhancing women's agency through external support.
What_was_studied: Intra-household decision-making processes among marginalized groups in Sulawesi and their impact on landscape management practices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure equitable and effective landscape management practices, policy makers should prioritize enhancing women's agency and involving men in care activities while taking into account the specific spheres of decision-making where women excel. This approach can lead to more resilient and sustainable landscape management practices that benefit marginalized communities.

Authors: Truly Santika; Kerrie A. Wilson; Sugeng Budiharta; Elizabeth A. Law; Tun Min Poh; Marc Ancrenaz; Matthew J. Struebig; Erik Meijaard
Field: Baseline (configuration management); Agriculture; Socioeconomic status; Subsistence agriculture; Work (electrical); Poverty; Geography; Livelihood; Agroforestry; Impact evaluation
Title: Does oil palm agriculture help alleviate poverty? A multidimensional counterfactual assessment of oil palm development in Indonesia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the social impacts of oil-palm plantations are not uniformly positive, nor negative, and have varied systematically with biophysical locations and baseline socioeconomic conditions of nearby communities prior to oil palm development. Plantations developed in villages with low to moderate forest cover, in which the majority of communities already relied on market-oriented livelihoods, were associated with improved socioeconomic well-being compared to villages without oil palm development.
What_was_studied: The social impact of oil palm plantations on poverty alleviation in Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo between 2000 and 2014 was examined using a matching method to evaluate the impacts across different aspects of well-being, accounting for varying time delays in the accrual and realization of benefits after plantation development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty alleviation is a primary goal of many sustainable development policies, policymakers should prioritize investments in oil palm plantations only in areas with low to moderate forest cover and already market-oriented livelihoods. This will maximize the potential for improving socioeconomic well-being while minimizing negative environmental impacts.

Field: Proxy (climate); Labour economics; Psychology; Survey research; Interview; Respondent; Demographic economics; Percentage point; Maximum likelihood; Bivariate analysis
Keywords: JEL Classification: C81; J13; J22; O15 child labor; self/proxy designs; maximum likelihood; survey design; Peru
Title: Child Labor Variation by Type of Respondent: Evidence from a Large-Scale Study
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study discovers significant differences between child and proxy reports, particularly when the household experiences negative shocks. Marginal effects from standard child labor supply functions show these differences, with statistically significant probabilities of misclassification ranging between 9% and 30%.
What_was_studied: This nationally representative survey analysis focuses on a crucial measurement challenge in child labor: the disparity between self-reporting and proxy interviews, which affects 20% of the sample and translates to a 17.1 percentage point difference in the national rate of child labor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the 17.1 percentage point difference in the national rate of child labor, policymakers should prioritize addressing this measurement challenge to ensure accurate data and effective policy interventions targeting child poverty, employment, and multidimensional poverty.

Authors: Jochen Kluve; Susana Puerto; David A. Robalino; Jose Romero; Friederike Rother; Jonathan Stöterau; Felix Weidenkaff; Marc Witte
Field: Public economics; Business; Work (electrical); Psychological intervention; Intervention Type; Incentive; Meta-analysis
Title: Do youth employment programs improve labor market outcomes? A quantitative review
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that one-third of the evaluated programs have positive significant effects on labor market outcomes for young people. The average effect size is small, but there are variations across program types and contexts.
What_was_studied: This systematic review examines the effectiveness of youth employment programs in middle- and low-income countries, covering 113 impact evaluations from 2005 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of existing youth employment programs, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that integrate multiple services, profile beneficiaries, provide individualized follow-up systems, and incentivize service providers to improve outcomes for vulnerable young people.

Field: Remedial education; Primary education; Ethnic group; Sociology; Teaching assistant; Economic growth; Medical education
Keywords: primary education; remedial education; Roma; ethnic minority; absences; dropouts JEL classification codes: I21; J15; D04
Title: Equal Access to Education: An Evaluation of the Roma Teaching Assistant Program in Serbia
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that children exposed to the Roma Teaching Assistant Programme went more to school, but there was no effect on dropouts or marks for all grades. First-grade students benefited more from the program with lower dropouts and better grades.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effects of a remedial education program, the Roma Teaching Assistant Programme, targeting the socially excluded and marginalized Roma ethnic minority in Serbia, using first-hand collected data to find evidence that children exposed to the program went more to school, but did not find an effect on dropouts or marks for all grades, with an examination of heterogeneous effects suggesting that children in the first grade benefited more from the program compared to their older peers through lower dropouts and better grades, indicating that well-targeted remedial education programs can be successful in boosting outcomes of low performers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize well-targeted remedial education programs to boost outcomes of low performers, specifically targeting first-grade students for maximum impact.

Field: Economics; Social reproduction; Social change; Social mobility; Development economics; Economic capital; Social transformation; Individual capital; Social capital; Social engagement
Keywords: Jordan; Middle East; social capital; bonding; bridging; trust
Title: “You Reap What You Plant”: Social Networks in the Arab World—The Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that wasta became helpful in good times but destructive in bad times, while successful economic reform requires a good understanding of the nature of social relations and the ways in which social networks are used by members during both good and bad times for survival and advancement.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the evolution of bonding and bridging social capital in Jordan from 1990 to 2009, analyzing how state policies, poverty, and economic reform affect various forms of social capital, including wasta, a significant form of social capital in the Arab world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to address food insecurity and gender poverty, policy makers should prioritize the understanding of social capital and its evolution over time, particularly in the context of economic reform, in order to scale up effective strategies for survival and advancement.

Authors: Katherine Brickell; Fiorella Picchioni; Nithya Natarajan; Vincent Guermond; Laurie Parsons; Giacomo Zanello; Milford Bateman
Field: Debt; Business; Government; Market liquidity; Social reproduction; Economic impact analysis; Loan; Microfinance; Development economics; Sustainable development
Keywords: Asia; COVID19; Cambodia; Microfinance; Over-indebtedness; Social reproduction
Title: Compounding crises of social reproduction: Microfinance, over-indebtedness and the COVID-19 pandemic
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the promotion of microfinance as market-based relief and recovery from the pandemic should be a source of concern, not comfort, due to the escalating number of borrowers and loan amounts, the potential for over-indebtedness, and the interplay between debt, pre-existing malnutrition challenges, and the global public health crisis, which represents a major challenge to gender equality and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on microfinance in Cambodia and its implications for financial inclusion, gender and poverty, health disparities, and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, the Cambodian government, microfinance lenders, international investors, and development partners must coordinate debt relief efforts and prioritize inclusive socio-economic policies and public welfare services to reverse the reliance of so many households on the microfinance industry for survival.

Authors: Issam Malki; Asad Ghalib; Rukhsana Kaousar
Field: Microfinance; Welfare; Poverty; Entrepreneurship; Human capital; Propensity score matching; Demographic economics; Investment (military); Labour economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Business; Psychological intervention; Economics; Economic growth; Finance; Political science; Market economy; Psychology; Statistics; Mathematics; Marketing; Psychiatry; Politics; Law
Title: The impact of microfinance on entrepreneurship and welfare among women borrowers in rural Pakistan
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that women who invest their loans in microenterprises experience significantly higher income, clothing expenditures, poverty scores, and income diversification compared to those who use loans for other purposes. However, we do not observe increases in health and education spending or reductions in child labor among entrepreneurial borrowers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effects of microfinance on entrepreneurial activity and household welfare among women borrowers in rural Pakistan between 2016 and 2018 using survey data from 463 clients of multiple microfinance institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize enhancing microfinance interventions to support holistic welfare improvements for women entrepreneurs in Pakistan and beyond, scaling up successful initiatives and exploring innovative solutions to address the limitations in promoting human capital investment.

Authors: Anaka Aiyar; Andaleeb Rahman; Prabhu Pingali
Field: Geography; Nutrition transition; Population; Urbanization; Livelihood; Kilometer; Socioeconomics; Obesity; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: India’s rural transformation and rising obesity burden
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the distance between rural villages and nearby towns is associated with an increased risk of obesity among women, with every additional kilometer reducing the distance increasing the risk by 0.06%.
