This resulted in approximately 3000 rural women becoming at-risk for obesity for every kilometer reduction in rural-urban proximity, with a higher burden in towns with a population of over 50,000 and among lower socioeconomic classes.
What_was_studied: The incidence of rural obesity in India from 2005 to 2016 and its relationship with urban proximity, socioeconomic status, and state-level economic development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the looming dual burden of malnutrition in developing countries like India, policies that promote dietary diversity can help mitigate the rising obesity rates in rural areas, especially among vulnerable populations such as women and lower socioeconomic classes. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize nutrition interventions that support diverse and balanced diets to address both under- and overnutrition.

Field: Selection (linguistics); Causal inference; External validity; Perspective (graphical); Data science; Affect (psychology); Replication (computing); International development; sort
Title: How the cases you choose affect the answers you get, revisited
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Importance of theoretically-informed attention to the selection of experimental sites to generalize findings from single experiments in global development and poverty alleviation studies, and that combining experiments with case study and comparative methods can provide more robust insights.
What_was_studied: The use of experiments in the study of global development and poverty alleviation, using case studies and causal inference to reflect on the selection of experimental sites and improve external validity through replication and combination with other methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize theoretically-informed selection of experimental sites and combine experimental methods with case studies and comparative research to improve external validity in global development and poverty alleviation initiatives, to scale up effective interventions and expand their reach to more populations.

Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Human capital; Development aid; Aid effectiveness; Foreign direct investment; Marginal product of capital; Invested capital; Monetary economics; Crowding out; Physical capital
Title: Does Foreign Aid Increase Foreign Direct Investment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study shows that investing in complementary inputs such as public infrastructure and human capital through aid increases the marginal productivity of capital, which attracts FDI. However, aid that is invested directly in physical capital can crowd out private investments.
What_was_studied: This paper looks into how aid and foreign direct investment (FDI) interact to impact economic development in low-income countries, with a focus on gender and poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that aid invested in complementary inputs leads to increased FDI and economic growth, policymakers should prioritize these types of investments to maximize the efficiency of foreign capital inflows. This could involve scaling up investments in public infrastructure and human capital, especially in low-income countries with high gender disparities.

Field: Livestock; Economics; Natural resource economics; Pastoralism; Genetic erosion; Dynamism; Option value; Diversity (politics); Livelihood; Development economics; Property rights
Keywords: animal genetic resource; property rights; poverty; pastoralists; option value; India; South Asia
Title: Property Rights and the Management of Animal Genetic Resources
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that local property rights systems are essential to conserve AnGR diversity. The poor's livelihoods depend on marginal lands where adaptive characteristics of livestock are maintained, but these systems are breaking down and leading to genetic erosion.
What_was_studied: The study explores the local property rights systems in poor communities for animal genetic resources and their impact on AnGR diversity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Society should prioritize the conservation of AnGR option values through livestock husbandry by the poor. Policies should be scaled up and expanded to support the poor's property rights systems in marginal areas to preserve adaptive characteristics of livestock and prevent genetic erosion.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Social science research; Pro poor; Longitudinal data; Development economics; Economic growth; Human geography
Keywords: Africa; Zambia; pro-poor agricultural growth; rural differentiation; social science research
Title: African Re-Agrarianization? Accumulation or Pro-Poor Agricultural Growth?
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Pro-poor agricultural growth so far is concentrated to particular villages, where it is highly inclusive.
What_was_studied: Household level longitudinal data from smallholder households in eight African countries for the period between 2002 and 2008 using a mixed methods social science approach to complement traditional economic approaches with a spatial perspective.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Devise strategies that can enhance growth also in marginal areas and prioritize these areas for funding and policy interventions to scale up inclusive growth.

Field: Environmental economics; Business; Prioritization; Sanitation; International Futures; Human development (humanity); National development; Secondary level; Sustainable development; International development
Title: Are we on the right path to achieve the sustainable development goals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the world will make only limited progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals with our current set of policy priorities, with 43 percent of country-indicators already reaching target values by 2015 and 53 percent projected to achieve them by 2030.
What_was_studied: This paper explores a dynamic 'middle-of-the-road' baseline global development scenario using an integrated assessment model to evaluate progress toward target values on nine indicators related to six human development SDGs for 186 countries between 2015 and 2030.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for a significant shift in domestic and international aid policies and prioritization to address persistent development issues such as access to safe sanitation, upper secondary school completion, and underweight children. Special focus should be given to 28 particularly vulnerable countries that are not projected to achieve any of the nine human development related target values.

Field: Subsistence agriculture; Agriculture; Poverty; Sample (material); Business; Poverty reduction; Agricultural economics; Economics; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Geography; Chemistry; Archaeology; Chromatography
Title: Village networks and entrepreneurial farming in Uganda
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that farmers who have more friends and relatives who adopted new crops or improved seeds before are more likely to adopt these technologies themselves. Additionally, the study found that support from friends and relatives in the form of gifts or loans increases the likelihood of adoption.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of social networks on farmers' propensity to adopt new crops or improved seeds in rural Uganda, using two waves of data from a sample of farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in information and support networks for farmers to increase the adoption of new crops and improved seeds, which can help reduce poverty and food insecurity in rural Uganda.

Authors: Andrea Cattaneo; Anjali Adukia; David L. Brown; Luc Christiaensen; David K. Evans; Annie Haakenstad; Theresa McMenomy; Mark Partridge; Sara Vaz; Daniel J. Weiss
Field: Urbanization; Economic growth; Operationalization; Poverty; Corporate governance; Rural area; Natural resource; Urban planning; Social Welfare; Geography; Environmental planning; Political science; Economic geography; Business; Economics; Ecology; Philosophy; Epistemology; Finance; Law; Biology
Title: Economic and social development along the urban–rural continuum: New opportunities to inform policy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that access to urban centers is crucial for economic and social development in rural areas, with implications for policymakers to prioritize investments in infrastructure and services that connect rural areas to urban centers of different sizes. Moreover, the study showed that urban centers depend on their rural hinterlands, highlighting the importance of a more geographically nuanced perspective on development.
What_was_studied: The economic and social development of nations relies on their population having physical access to services and employment opportunities, specifically focusing on the interconnections between urban and rural areas, and how a new publicly available dataset operationalizing the concept of catchment areas can shed light on policymaking across various development fields.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in infrastructure and services that connect rural areas to urban centers of different sizes to support economic and social development, and take into account the interconnections between urban and rural areas when making decisions across various development fields.

Authors: Katrin Hofer; Michael Wicki; David Kaufmann
Field: Political science; Public participation; Economic growth; Public administration; Economics
Title: Public support for participation in local development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found strong support for public participation among the study participants, with higher support levels for more inclusive and interactive processes. Participants were also aware of the transaction costs of participation but still expressed support for it.
What_was_studied: This study examined people's perspectives on public participation in local development in Bramfischerville, a low-income residential area in Johannesburg, using an original face-to-face vignette survey experiment (n = 502) and group interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong support for public participation in local development among low-income residents, decision-makers should prioritize and fund more inclusive and interactive participatory processes to scale up public participation in local development and advance sustainable development.

Field: Ebola virus; Securitization; Population; Political science; Legitimacy; Criminology; Economic growth; Development economics; Sociology; Law; Disease; Medicine; Business; Politics; Economics; Demography; Financial system; Pathology
Title: How epidemics affect marginalized communities in war-torn countries: Ebola, securitization, and public opinion about the security forces in Liberia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that experiences with securitization during the 2014 Ebola Virus epidemic in Liberia led to increased perceptions of police discrimination and disrespect among individuals from marginalized communities, resulting in a decline in demand for police services. Additionally, direct contact with soldiers enhanced feelings of safety only among those who did not witness abuse.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how perceptions of security forces change among individuals from marginalized communities during an epidemic and the impact this has on their demand for police services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing perceptions of discrimination and disrespect among marginalized communities during epidemics to maintain trust in security forces and ensure effective policing. Policymakers should prioritize community engagement and outreach programs to address these concerns and ensure equitable access to security services.

Authors: Jane E. Freedman; Mina Rakotoarindrasata; Jean de Dieu Randrianasolorivo
Field: Reproductive health; Economy; Sociology; Order (exchange); Poverty; Transactional sex; Sexual exchange; Gender inequality; Inequality; Transactional leadership
Title: Analysing the economies of transactional sex amongst young people: Case study of Madagascar
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that TS relationships amongst young women in Madagascar are increasingly normalized and involve blurred boundaries with other forms of sexual exchange. The study also revealed the complexities of the meanings and pathways into TS, which go beyond economic necessity.
What_was_studied: This article examines the social and economic determinants of transactional sexual (TS) relationships in Madagascar during a specific time period, using primary data collected through interviews and surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the situation of young women engaging in TS in Madagascar, poverty reduction programs and services addressing their sexual and reproductive health needs should be prioritized and scaled up, with a particular focus on reducing income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty.

Authors: Gong Cheng; Javier Díaz-Cassou; Aitor Erce
Field: Gross domestic product; Debt; Creditor; Economics; International economics; Poverty; Club; Restructuring; Inequality; Present value
Title: Official debt restructurings and development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The progressive introduction of new terms of treatment gradually turned the Paris Club from an institution primarily concerned with preserving creditors' claims into an instrument to foster development in the world's poorer nations, among other objectives. Our study finds that more generous restructuring conditions involving nominal relief are associated with an acceleration of per capita GDP growth and with a reduction in poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: A dataset covering more than 400 Paris Club agreements to provide a comprehensive description of the evolving characteristics of these operations and study their impact on debtors over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the implementation of more generous debt restructuring conditions to foster development and reduce poverty and inequality in poorer nations, as these findings suggest that such actions can lead to accelerated economic growth and improved well-being for these populations.

Field: Technological change; Business; Human Development Report; E-learning (theory); Information and communication technologies for development; Index (economics); Knowledge management; Information and Communications Technology; Developing country
Keywords: technology creation; infrastructures; human skills; development index
Title: A New Indicator of Technological Capabilities for Developed and Developing Countries (ArCo)
primary_category: Digital divide; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The ArCo index revealed preliminary correlations with GDP, suggesting its potential as a useful tool for policymakers to assess technological capabilities and their impact on economic growth.
What_was_studied: This paper devises a new indicator (ArCo) of technological capabilities that accounts for developed and developing countries by considering three main components: the creation of technology, technological infrastructures, and human skills development over time, with eight subcategories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of human skills in technological fields, invest in infrastructures that support innovation, and fund research to improve the creation of technology, as these factors are crucial for economic growth, as indicated by the ArCo index.

Authors: Bart Minten; Lalaina Randrianarison; Johan F.M. Swinnen
Field: Welfare; Supply chain; Business; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Productivity; Globalization; Contract farming; Agricultural economics; Developing country
Title: Global retail chains and poor farmers: evidence from Madagascar.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Small farmers who participate in contracts with supermarkets have higher welfare, more income stability, and shorter lean periods compared to those not participating. Additionally, there are significant effects on improved technology adoption, better resource management, and spillovers on the productivity of the staple crop rice.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed primary data collected to measure the impact of supermarkets on small contract farmers in Madagascar.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize supporting small farmers in developing countries by providing them with access to modern retail supply chains, as this can lead to improved welfare, income stability, and productivity.

Field: Neoclassical economics; Geography; Realm; Economic analysis; Social production; Natural resource; Process (engineering); Phenomenon; Waste management; Inclusion (disability rights)
Journal/Venue: Structural Change, Economic Interdependence and World Development
Title: Natural Resources and Socio-economic Effects of Recycling
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that recycling has universal historical characteristics and is a kind of emulation of nature itself, with important implications for the limits to growth in the twentieth century.
What_was_studied: The social production process and its historical characteristics as they relate to recycling, focusing on the twentieth century and its limits to growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings on the universal historical characteristics of recycling and its impact on limits to growth, policymakers should prioritize the inclusion of this problem in the realm of political economy and consider strategic tools to address it.

Authors: Ximena Peña; María Alejandra Vélez; Juan Camilo Cárdenas; Natalia Perdomo; Camilo Matajira
Field: Per capita income; Geography; Investment (macroeconomics); Human capital; Overcrowding; Land titling; Natural resource; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Developing country
Keywords: Afro-descendants; Collective property; Colombia; Ethnic community; Land titling Q15, Q24, R52, N36, N56 Afro-descendientes; Propiedad colectiva; Colombia; Comunidades étnicas; Titulaciones de tierras Códigos JEL: Q15, Q24, R52, N36, N56
Title: Collective Property Leads to Household Investments: Lessons From Land Titling in Afro-Colombian Communities
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Our study found that the collective land titling process in the Choco region of rural Colombia resulted in significant improvements in socioeconomic outcomes for Afro-descendant communities. Specifically, we found an average increase of 15% in household income per capita, a 10% decrease in extreme poverty rates, a 20% increase in housing investments, a 15% increase in primary education attendance rates among children, and a 10% decrease in housing overcrowding.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of collective land titling on Afro-descendant communities in rural Colombia, specifically in the Choco region, during a 5-year period. Using a comparison of rural districts in titled and untitled areas with similar observable characteristics, we find that collective land titling leads to an increase in average household income per capita, a decrease in extreme poverty, increased investments in housing, higher primary education attendance rates among children, and a decrease in housing overcrowding.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize the expansion of collective land titling programs to other Afro-descendant communities in rural Colombia. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in land titling and strengthening local governance structures to support the implementation of these programs. By doing so, policymakers can help reduce chronic poverty, promote sustainable development, and improve the overall well-being of Afro-descendant communities in rural Colombia.

Field: Sociology; Human development (humanity); Gender gap; Sub saharan; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Democracy; Politics
Keywords: JEL Classification: D01; J16; O38; O55 Support for democracy; gender gap; policy priorities; institutions
Title: Why Are Women Less Democratic Than Men? Evidence from Sub-Saharan African Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Using data for 20 Sub-Saharan African countries, we test whether the gap is due to individual differences in policy priorities or to country-wide characteristics. We find that controlling for individual policy priorities does not offset the gender gap, but those women who are interested in politics are more democratic than men. Furthermore, our results indicate that the gap disappears in countries with high levels of human development and political rights.
What_was_studied: A substantial literature has examined the determinants of support for democracy and although existing work has found a gender gap in democratic attitudes, there have been no attempts to explain it. In this paper we try to understand why females are less supportive of democracy than males in a number of countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for democracy among women, policymakers should fund programs that increase their political engagement, such as voter education and mobilization initiatives. Additionally, efforts to improve human development and political rights can help close the gender gap in democratic attitudes.

Authors: Altaaf Mechiche-Alami; Jihad Yagoubi; Kimberly A. Nicholas
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Cash crop; Land tenure; Business; Natural resource economics; Natural resource; Agricultural land; Food security; Sustainability
Title: Agricultural land acquisitions unlikely to address the food security needs of African countries
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Agricultural Land deals in Africa are unlikely to address the identified food security needs of 38 African countries; only likely to meet the needs of seven countries. Also, they are at risk of increasing land pressures and conflicts or deforestation on 83% of the acquired area.
What_was_studied: Agricultural land deals in Africa and their potential to address food security needs of 38 African countries between 2000 and 2010 based on indicators of food availability, accessibility, stability, and utilization, and the characteristics of locations where the deals happen (population density, land cover, and distance to markets).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, agricultural investments should be elaborated in consultation with local communities and marginalized groups to sustainably support their socio-ecological systems; governments should prioritize food security needs over foreign investors' interests.

Authors: Hannah R. Bassett; Jacqueline Lau; Christopher Giordano; S. Suri; Sahir Advani; Sonia Sharan
Field: Supply chain; Business; Adaptive capacity; Resilience (organizational); Flexibility (engineering); Domestic market; Livelihood; Shock (economics); Fishery; Scale (social sciences)
Keywords: Adaptive capacity; COVID-19; Global seafood distribution system; Resilience; Small-scale fisheries; Supply chain
Title: Preliminary lessons from COVID-19 disruptions of small-scale fishery supply chains
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Actors in the SSF supply chain shifted focus to local and regional distribution channels and leveraged flexibility, organization, and learning to re-purpose pre-existing networks and use technology to their advantage in response to COVID-19 disruptions.
What_was_studied: The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and associated mitigation measures disrupted global systems that support the health, food, and nutrition security of billions of people, including the small-scale fishery (SSF) sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The initial impacts from COVID-19 highlight the risks of over-reliance on global trade networks and suggest supporting local and domestic networks, bolstering financial wellbeing and security within the domestic market before and during such large-scale disruptions to build resilience in the face of future macroeconomic shocks.

Authors: Klaus Deininger; Songqing Jin; Fang Xia
Field: Agricultural productivity; Land tenure; Labour economics; Economics; Productivity; Land reform; Rural poverty; Development economics; Land use; Agricultural land; Land management
Title: Moving off the Farm: Land Institutions to Facilitate Structural Transformation and Agricultural Productivity Growth in China - Moving off the farm: Land institutions to facilitate structural transformation and agricultural productivity growth in China
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Land tenure insecurity discourages households from quitting agriculture, while the recognition of land rights through formal certificates encourages temporary migration of rural labor, with both factors having a large impact on productivity (at about 30 percent each).
What_was_studied: An 8-year panel of 1,200 households in six key provinces to explore the impact of government land reallocations and formal land-use certificates on agricultural productivity growth and household exit from agriculture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognizing land rights and increasing access to non-agricultural opportunities can boost productivity and encourage households to exit from agriculture, supporting successful structural transformation and continued economic attractiveness of rural areas. Policymakers should prioritize secure land tenure and expand non-agricultural employment opportunities to sustain poverty reduction and economic growth.

Authors: Hanna Freudenreich; Anastasia Aladysheva; Tilman Brück
Field: Extreme weather; Cold weather; Climate change; Geography; Demography; Population; Shock (circulatory); Climatology; Environmental science; Environmental health; Medicine; Meteorology; Biology; Ecology; Sociology; Geology; Internal medicine
Title: Weather shocks across seasons and child health: Evidence from a panel study in the Kyrgyz Republic
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities
What_was_found: Children under 20 months are most severely affected by all three types of early life weather shocks, with cold shocks experienced in winter increasing the probability of stunting, particularly for households that mainly rely on electricity for indoor heating. The study finds no rural/urban differences but does find seasonal effects of shock exposure.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes how different weather shocks (cold winter, drought, excessive rainfall) affect the probability of stunting in children under five in Kyrgyzstan, using a rich three-wave representative household panel dataset and location-matched weather data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address child malnutrition in areas with frequent power cuts during winter, particularly in households that rely on electricity for indoor heating. This could include providing alternative heating sources and supporting nutrition programs for young children.

Authors: Jan Duchoslav; Edwin Kenamu; Jack Thunde
Field: Cash transfers; Government (linguistics); Politics; Cash; Political science; Economics; Development economics; Food security; Political economy; Business; Geography; Agriculture; Finance; Linguistics; Philosophy; Archaeology; Law
Title: Targeting hunger or votes? The political economy of humanitarian transfers in Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the government targeted humanitarian transfers at marginal constituencies, prioritizing political considerations over need, with no evidence that this strategy was successful in increasing ruling party candidates' votes in subsequent elections.
What_was_studied: The study examines the targeting of humanitarian transfers in Malawi following an exceptionally poor harvest in 2015/16, focusing on direct cash and food transfers distributed in response to drought and using household survey data and remotely sensed measures of drought alongside the results of the 2014 and 2019 parliamentary elections.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of prioritizing need over political considerations when distributing humanitarian transfers to ensure effective response to food insecurity and malnutrition, and calls for scaling up social protection programs to mitigate the impact of climate-related disasters on vulnerable populations.

Title: Epidemics, Pandemics, and Social Conflict: Lessons from the Past and Possible Scenarios for COVID-19
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The conditions giving rise to scapegoating and persecution of minority groups, including migrants, and the milder or more severe forms of scapegoating that may result from epidemics and pandemics.
What_was_studied: The economic and social dynamics of historical and more recent epidemics and pandemics from the plagues of Antiquity to modern-day outbreaks like Ebola, including how different groups in society interact and cooperate to survive and prosper.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize research on epidemics, pandemics, and social conflict to understand how COVID-19 may affect these dynamics and inform policies that address chronic poverty, health disparities, and intersectional poverty.

Authors: Ashwini Deshpande; Deepti Goel; Shantanu Khanna
Field: Economics; Wage; Gender discrimination; Male female; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Karma

Title: Bad Karma or Discrimination? Male-Female Wage Gaps among Salaried Workers in India
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the gender log wage gap at the mean was 55% in 1999–2000 and 49% in 2009–10, but this change was not statistically significant. The bulk of the gender wage gap is unexplained, possibly discriminatory, and the discriminatory component of the gender wage gap also increased over the decade.
What_was_studied: This study used nationally representative data from the Employment–Unemployment Surveys in 1999–2000 and 2009–10 to explore gender wage gaps among Regular Wage/Salaried (RWS) workers in India, both at the mean and along the entire wage distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that women in India face a significant wage gap, particularly at the lower end of the wage distribution. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing policies that target discrimination and promote equal pay for equal work.

Title: Private Donations, Government Grants, Commercial Activities, and Fundraising: Cointegration and Causality for NGOs in International Development Cooperation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that a marginal dollar spent on fundraising yields almost five dollars in new donations in the long run, with government grants crowding in private donations and commercial revenues crowding out donations.
What_was_studied: The study examined the determinants of private donations to US-based NGOs engaged in international development cooperation for the period between 2003 and 2013, using panel cointegration and causality techniques to analyze the interactions between private donations, government grants, commercial revenues, and fundraising expenditures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing government grants to US-based NGOs engaged in international development cooperation, as this can lead to a significant increase in private donations. Additionally, the study's results suggest that NGOs should focus their fundraising efforts on long-term, sustainable sources of revenue, rather than relying solely on short-term commercial revenues.

Authors: Nancy L. Johnson; Chiara Kovarik; Ruth Meinzen-Dick; Jemimah Njuki; Agnes R. Quisumbing

Title: Gender, Assets, and Agricultural Development: Lessons from Eight Projects.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: All projects were associated with increases in asset levels and other benefits at the household level; however, only four projects documented significant, positive impacts on women's ownership or control of some types of assets relative to a control group, and of those only one project provided evidence of a reduction in the gender asset gap.
What_was_studied: Eight mixed-method evaluations of the impacts of agricultural development projects on individual and household assets in seven countries in Africa and South Asia between 2006 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of assets for poverty reduction and the positive development outcomes associated with women's control of assets, agricultural development programs should prioritize incorporating gender and assets into the design, implementation, and evaluation of interventions to improve outcomes for women and reduce the gender asset gap.

Field: Relevance (law); Poverty; Process management; Psychological intervention; Accountability; Foundation (evidence); Incentive; Cost effectiveness; Argument; Computer science
Title: Improving learning and accountability in foreign aid
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that most aid evaluations are superficial, positively biased, and/or poorly timed, highlighting the need for more rigorous and independent assessments. Additionally, it reveals that evaluation should be oriented to cost effectiveness to enhance the professionalism of foreign aid and hasten an end to poverty.
What_was_studied: The research evaluates the effectiveness of foreign aid projects using the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) criteria and explores the potential for independent and consistent evaluation to improve learning and accountability in the sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the effectiveness of foreign aid, policymakers should prioritize independent and consistent evaluations that focus on cost effectiveness, providing a stronger foundation in evidence and incentive environment for aid managers to make decisions that maximize the impact of their interventions.

Authors: Anna Minasyan; Peter Nunnenkamp; Katharina Richert
Field: Per capita; Economics; Poverty; Aid effectiveness; Quality (business); Index (economics); Corporate governance; Sample (statistics); Development economics; Economic growth; International development
Keywords: donor ranking; quality-adjusted aid; income effects; DDD analysis JEL classification: F35
Title: Does aid effectiveness depend on the quality of donors
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Significant and quantitatively important treatment effects for quality-adjusted aid after the introduction of the Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness in 2005, while unadjusted aid did not have significant treatment effects. Recipient countries with increased high-quality aid inflows benefit in terms of increasing GDP per capita, and the quality of aid matters most when accounting for delayed effects.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of foreign aid in alleviating poverty and stimulating economic growth in recipient countries, with a focus on the impact of aid quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Donor countries should prioritize providing high-quality aid to recipient countries, as this leads to significant increases in GDP per capita and long-term economic growth. Monitoring and evaluating the quality of aid inflows is crucial to ensuring that foreign aid is effective in reducing poverty and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Light industry; Capital intensity; Economics; Heavy industry; Factors of production; Infant industry; Factor endowment; Industrial organization; Industrialisation; Income distribution
Journal/Venue: Appropriate Technologies for Third World Development
Title: Some Practical Constraints on the Use of Appropriate Technologies in Turkish Industrial Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that developing countries with abundant labor resources should prioritize light industries and agriculture, as these sectors have higher labor intensity and lower capital intensity, leading to more efficient use of resources and better employment outcomes. Moreover, the study discovered that export-oriented development strategies are more effective in promoting economic growth than import substitution strategies.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between factor endowments and optimum factor mix in developing countries, specifically focusing on light industries, agriculture, and export-oriented development strategies during a 10-year period from 2000 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for light industries and agriculture, scale up support for export-oriented development strategies, and revise existing policies to promote more equitable income distribution and sustainable development.

Authors: Melissa Leach; Nicholas Nisbett; Lídia Cabral; Jody Harris; Naomi Hossain; John Thompson
Field: Agriculture; Political science; Food politics; Food policy; Livelihood; Equity (economics); Sustainability; Food systems; Politics; Environmental ethics
Title: Food politics and development
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study highlights the interconnected nature of food systems and sustainable development, emphasizing the need for a more holistic approach that considers the political and social dynamics shaping food policies and practices. It also underscores the significance of inclusive structural transformation in achieving sustainable development goals, particularly in addressing climate vulnerability, gender and poverty disparities.
What_was_studied: This review article examines the interrelationship between food and sustainable, equitable development, focusing on the political aspects of food systems in different contexts and the role of state-society relations, science and technology, and rural livelihoods in agri-food systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of food systems in development, decision-makers must prioritize a more integrated approach to sustainable development that addresses the political economy of food production, distribution, and consumption. This includes investing in inclusive agricultural innovation systems, scaling up support for smallholder farmers, and funding research on climate-resilient crops and sustainable food technologies to support equitable transformation of agri-food systems.

Field: Offspring; Demography; Psychosocial; Psychology; Young adult; Girl; Middle childhood; Growth faltering; Age differences; Longitudinal data
Title: Stunting later in childhood and outcomes as a young adult: Evidence from India
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that there are significant gender-based biases in growth faltering later in childhood disfavoring girls and becoming newly stunted as an adolescent is strongly correlated with poorer relationships with peers. Additionally, the study found that a girl experiencing stunting in middle childhood or adolescence (even if they were not stunted at age 8 or eventually moved out of being stunted by age 19) significantly correlates with offspring being shorter and thinner than the offspring of girls never stunted.
What_was_studied: The paper looks at patterns of growth faltering and catch up among around 1000 children from middle childhood through adolescence to young adulthood in Andhra Pradesh and Telengana, India between 2002 and 2013, using Height for Age Difference (HAD) and Height for age z-scores (HAZ).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the importance of addressing nutritional deprivation and its intergenerational consequences. Policymakers should prioritize scaling up nutrition-sensitive interventions, expanding access to healthy food and nutrition education, particularly for adolescent girls, to ensure optimal growth and development.

Authors: Tariq Omar Ali; Mirza Hassan; Naomi Hossain
Field: Forbearance; Political economy; Government; Political science; State (polity); Harm; Moral economy; Incentive; Legitimacy; Politics
Keywords: Bangladesh; Covid-19; Moral economy; Social protection; State capacity
Title: The moral and political economy of the pandemic in Bangladesh: Weak states and strong societies during Covid-19
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite a growing capacity of the Bangladeshi state in the past decade, the pressures to sustain legitimacy with the masses forced the state and its frontline actors to tolerate lockdown rule-breaking, resulting in a failure to ensure a fair and timely distribution of relief. Additionally, the study found that the weakness of the Bangladeshi state contrasts with the strength of widely shared ‘moral economy’ views within society, which provided powerful ethical and political justification for citizens' failures to comply with the lockdown, and for officials' forbearance in its enforcement.
What_was_studied: This study examined the reasons why Bangladesh was unable to sustain a lockdown deemed necessary to contain the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, using original qualitative mobile phone-based research in six selected communities and drawing on theories about state capacity to make and enforce policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address child poverty, health disparities, and sustainable development in Bangladesh, policymakers should prioritize investing in state capacity to enforce policies effectively, particularly in the areas of coercion and control over lower factions within political society, while also ensuring a fair and timely distribution of relief. Additionally, they should consider addressing the strong 'moral economy' views within society to promote compliance with public health measures.

Keywords: Community-driven Development; Social Capital; Field Experiments JEL classification C93; D03; I38; O12; O22
Title: Community-Driven Development and Social Capital: Evidence from Morocco
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The program increased contributions to public goods but had no impact on interpersonal trust or altruism. The study suggests that a shift from centralized to local decision-making may enhance community responsibility but may not positively affect all forms of social capital.
What_was_studied: The impact of community-driven development programs on social capital in rural Morocco, as measured by public goods games, investment games, and dictator games among a sample of 105 communities over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize community-driven development programs in rural areas with high poverty rates, as these programs can increase contributions to public goods and promote a sense of community responsibility. However, they should also be aware that such programs may not universally improve all forms of social capital.

Field: Inflow; Cohesion (chemistry); Immigration; Demographic economics; Community cohesion; Refugee; Unemployment; Political science; Geography; Economics; Economic growth; Law; Chemistry; Organic chemistry; Meteorology
Title: Forced Migration and Social Cohesion: Evidence from the 2015/16 Mass Inflow in Germany
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found mixed evidence of an impact on social cohesion, with no significant effect except for a negative effect on donations to charity. Areas with high vote shares for the populist party AfD experienced greater anti-immigrant sentiment and a concern about crime following the inflow.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of a large and sudden inflow of asylum seekers on social cohesion in Germany between 2015-2016, using individual- and county-level panel data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions should prioritize addressing the root causes of anti-immigrant sentiment and promoting inclusive social cohesion, particularly in areas with high AfD support. Funding programs that foster intercultural dialogue and community engagement could help mitigate negative attitudes towards asylum seekers and promote a more inclusive society.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Experimental economics; Productivity; Expected utility hypothesis; Prospect theory; Demographic economics; Financial risk management; Endogeneity; Risk aversion
Title: Does Market Experience Attenuate Risk Aversion? Evidence from Landed Farm Households in Ethiopia
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that market experience attenuates risk aversion: farm households with greater market experience are more risk tolerant. Results are robust to using several alternative specifications and controlling for possible self-selection into trade.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the effect of market experience on risk aversion for landed farm households in Ethiopia between 2016 and 2017, using lab-in-field experimental data to measure risk aversion and controlling for internal mobility, out-migration, and other potential unobservables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To increase the productivity and efficiency of farm households, policies should prioritize providing market experiences to rural households, especially those with historically low mobility.

Authors: Adriana Garcia; Robert Lensink; Maarten Voors
Field: Business; Poverty; Empowerment; Well-being; Access to finance; Microfinance; Sierra leone; Financial capital; Development economics; Sustainable development
Title: Does microcredit increase aspirational hope? Evidence from a group lending scheme in Sierra Leone
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Significant positive associations with both aspirational hope and economic welfare were found, suggesting that microcredit can play an important role in reducing internal psychological constraints and contributing to the realization of the SDGs.
What_was_studied: A cross-sectional dataset of 1295 women in Sierra Leone between 2018 and 2020 to evaluate the effectiveness of microcredit in alleviating internal psychological constraints such as aspirational hope.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize microcredit interventions to empower women and alleviate poverty in rural areas, as they have been shown to increase both aspirational hope and economic welfare. Expand access to finance for women living within 4 km of a Microfinance Institution branch to scale up the positive effects.

Field: Accountability; Multinational corporation; Corporate governance; Social accounting; Business; Politics; Harm; Public administration; Political science; Accounting; Finance; Law; Accounting information system
Title: "I will sample until things get better – or until I die." Potential and limits of citizen science to promote social accountability for environmental pollution
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social accountability initiatives are rarely effective in improving environmental governance in low-income countries due to political capture and limited capacity. Additionally, the study identified the Deka River as being heavily polluted by mining activities, with scientific data strengthening community monitors' advocacy for a cleaner environment.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the impact of mining activities on human health and ecosystems in low-income countries, specifically focusing on the coal mining area of Hwange in Western Zimbabwe, and employed a citizen science approach to identify sources and extent of pollution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, pro-accountability networks involving multinational enterprises with responsible procurement approaches should be prioritized to address the issue of low accountability in captured states, and corporate governance regimes must shift from risk management to developmental logic to effectively address environmental governance challenges.

Authors: Jonas Vestby; Halvard Buhaug; Nina von Uexkull
Field: Economic model; Per capita; Sector model; Dual (category theory); Economics; Productivity; Civil Conflict; Labor mobility; Demographic economics; Opportunity cost
Title: Why do some poor countries see armed conflict while others do not? A dual sector approach
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access
What_was_found: Replacing GDP per capita with indicators of sector size and relative productivity improves the predictive performance of common civil war models, with countries having a comparatively productive modern sector being less conflict prone than those at similar income levels with lower RLP ratios.
What_was_studied: The relationship between economic structures and conflict risk among low-income countries using a unique 10-sector dataset of economic activity among 40 countries across the world since 1969.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in modern sectors and focus on improving relative labor productivity to reduce the risk of civil war, especially among low-income countries.

Authors: S. Manda; A. Tallontire; A.J. Dougill
Field: Public economics; Inclusion (education); Political science; Social group; Interdependence; Value (ethics); Value capture; Contract farming; Land use; Centrality
Title: Outgrower schemes and sugar value-chains in Zambia: Rethinking determinants of rural inclusion and exclusion
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the terms and conditions of inclusion in sugar value chains are crucial in shaping diverse outcomes for smallholders, highlighting the complexity of intersectional poverty and the importance of considering social-cultural dynamics beyond market imperatives to improve the impacts of outgrower schemes.
What_was_studied: This study was conducted in Mazabuka's sugarbelt region in Zambia and examined the inclusion of smallholders in sugar value chains, focusing on two contrasting outgrower schemes to determine the determinants of smallholder inclusion and how various terms and conditions affect different local groups' interests, reactions, and pathways for capturing value.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the effectiveness of outgrower schemes in reducing income poverty and food insecurity, policymakers and practitioners should recognize and address the diverse interests and reactions of local groups, investing in institutions and policies that prioritize inclusive value capture and mitigate the risks of land-grabbing.

Field: Agriculture; Alternative investment; Survey data collection; Geography; Dynamism; Wage; Intensive farming; Selection bias; Agricultural economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Keywords: agriculture; commercial farming; Mozambique; structural transformation JEL classification: O13; Q12; Q18
Title: WIDER Working Paper - Can commercial farming promote rural dynamism in sub-Saharan Africa? Evidence from Mozambique
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that commercial farms are highly selective in their locations, preferring areas close to existing infrastructure and markets, and that the presence of a commercial farm is associated with moderately higher incomes among neighbouring smallholders but a lower incidence of wage employment. The effects vary according to the type of commercial farming in place, with more inclusive models generating larger benefits.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the economic impact of commercial farming investments on smallholders in Mozambique over four periods, using survey data covering all large commercial farms and a nationally-representative sample of 6000 smallholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the selective location and varying effects of different commercial farming models, policy-makers should prioritize investments in more inclusive models, such as outgrower schemes, to maximize economic benefits for smallholders in developing countries.

Field: Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Agency (philosophy); Food security; Randomized controlled trial; Malnutrition; Socioeconomics; Agriculture; Demography; Medicine; Economic growth; Geography; Economics; Sociology; Social science; Surgery; Archaeology
Keywords: 3DE, Three domains of empowerment; Agency; Agriculture; DHS, Demographic and Health Survey; FAARM, Food and Agricultural Approaches to Reducing Malnutrition; GAAP2, Gender, Agriculture, and Assets Project–Phase 2; GPI, Gender Parity Index; Gender equity; Homestead food production; IFPRI, International Food Policy Research Institute; ODK, Open Data Kit; OR, Odds Ratio; RCT, Randomized controlled trial; SDG, Sustainable Development Goal; Self-efficacy; WEAI, Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index; Women’s groups; pro-WEAI, project-level Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index
Title: Impact of a homestead food production program on women's empowerment: Pro-WEAI results from the FAARM trial in Bangladesh.
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Compared to controls, women in the FAARM intervention group had levels of agency similar to men and much higher than women in the control group (Odds Ratio [OR 7.7, p < 0.001), with greater intrinsic and collective agency but not instrumental agency. More women in the intervention group found intimate partner violence unacceptable (OR 3.5, p < 0.001), had greater ownership of assets (OR 2.6, p = 0.001), better control of income (OR 1.8, p = 0.042), higher levels of group membership (OR 14.0, p < 0.001), and membership in groups they considered influential (OR 166.8, p < 0.001).
What_was_studied: The effect of nutrition-sensitive agricultural programs on women's empowerment and agency in rural Bangladesh, using a cluster-randomized controlled trial with 885 participants approximately four months after the end of the intervention.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Our results provide additional rationale for women-led agricultural projects to improve gender equity and empowerment, which can help address child poverty, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, gender and poverty, multidimensional poverty, and social protection challenges.

Field: Consumption (economics); Labour economics; Per capita income; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Investment goods; Receipt; Remittance; Rate of return; Physical capital

Title: Remittances, Household Expenditure and Investment in Guatemala - Remittances, Household Expenditure and Investment in Guatemala
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Households receiving remittances actually spend less at the margin on consumption-food and consumer goods and durables-than do households receiving no remittances. Instead, they spend more on investment goods like education, health, and housing.
What_was_studied: The author uses a large household data set from Guatemala to analyze how the receipt of internal remittances (from Guatemala) and international remittances (from the United States) affects the marginal spending behavior of households on various consumption and investment goods over the period 2015-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in education and human capital development to boost local economic development and create new income and employment opportunities for skilled and unskilled workers.

Keywords: Children’s educational outcomes; Clean fuel; Maternal time-investment; Piped water; Rural India; Unpaid work
Title: Lack of access to clean fuel and piped water and children’s educational outcomes in rural India
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results showed that children aged 6–14 years living in households that rely on free collection of water and cooking fuel have lower mathematics scores and benefit from lower educational expenditures compared to children living in households that do not collect water and fuel. Additionally, the study found that gender inequality in the burden of unpaid work affects child outcomes, with boys' outcomes being particularly low in households where women bear a disproportionate burden of collection.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the relationship between access to piped water and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and children's educational outcomes in rural India, using data from the second round of the India Human Development Survey (2011–12).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in clean fuel and piped water may not only improve health outcomes but also have positive effects on children's educational outcomes. Policymakers should prioritize such investments, particularly in rural areas where access to these resources is limited, and aim to reduce gender inequality in unpaid work burdens.

Authors: Amin Karimu; Justice Tei Mensah; George Adu
Field: Rural area; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Empirical evidence; Energy poverty; Response rate (survey); Energy source; Level data; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Estimation
Keywords: JEL Classification: C14; O13; Q41; Q42 Fuels; cooking; households; development; energy poverty; Ghana
Title: Who Adopts LPG as the Main Cooking Fuel and Why? Empirical Evidence on Ghana Based on National Survey
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that socioeconomic and demographic factors such as income, education, access to urban infrastructure, and location of the household are key drivers of households' choice of LPG as the main cooking energy source. The evidence shows that urban households with better socioeconomic and demographic factors are more likely to adopt LPG relative to rural households and those with poor socioeconomic and demographic factors.
What_was_studied: The study examines the factors that influence the adoption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) as the main cooking fuel in Ghana using household-level data from the last two nationwide household surveys (GLSS 5 & GLSS 6).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest a policy dichotomy between rural and urban dwellers for effective adoption of LPG as the main cooking fuel. Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions in rural areas to increase access to LPG and improve socioeconomic and demographic factors.

Title: Civil Society and Gender Mainstreaming: Empirical Evidence and Theory-Building from Twelve Post-Conflict Countries 2005–15
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings reveal specific data, transitional justice, and governance challenges in war-affected states as policy actors press for heightened attention to issues such as the effects on women of war-induced poverty, human rights violations, and women’s empowerment in state reconstruction and peace-building.
What_was_studied: This twelve-country study examines civil society perspectives on the implementation of the Participative Democratic Model (PDM) of gender mainstreaming in post-conflict states, using critical discourse analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the aftermath of war accentuates frame misalignment between civil society and governing elites, policy actors should prioritize adapting the PDM to the specificities of war-affected states, through a Transformative Model (TM) of Participative Mainstreaming in Post-conflict States, which engenders.

Title: The place of agricultural research in the development of sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that SSA's agricultural research scientists cost more but produce less than their counterparts outside of SSA, and the region has neglected many important crops such as cassava while overstressing export crops. Moreover, socioeconomists have been underrepresented in research design, and domestic funds have been insufficient and unreliable to support international and capital-account AR efforts.
What_was_studied: Agricultural research in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) during the past few decades has had excellent returns outside of SSA, but SSA itself has not benefited as much due to various challenges such as small country size, dispersed research stations, high turnover rates, and European biases in research priorities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve agricultural research in SSA, policymakers should concentrate on a few key problems and crops, prioritize poverty-oriented research design, and provide steady commitment to funding. This could involve increasing investment in AR, revising research priorities to better address local needs, and incorporating socioeconomic perspectives into the design of research projects.

Authors: Kate Hampshire; Tawonga Mwase-Vuma; Kassahun Alemu; Albert Abane; Alister Munthali; Tadesse Awoke; Simon Mariwah; Elita Chamdimba; Samuel Asiedu Owusu; Elsbeth Robson; Michele Castelli; Ziv Shkedy; Nicholas Shawa; Jane Abel; Adetayo Kasim

Title: Informal mhealth at scale in Africa: Opportunities and challenges.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: Our findings confirm the limited reach of ‘formal’ compared with ‘informal’ mhealth: while only 15% of CHWs surveyed were using formal mhealth applications, over 97% reported regularly using a personal mobile phone for work-related purposes in a range of innovative ways.
What_was_studied: Using data from Ghana, Ethiopia and Malawi, we document the reach, nature and perceived impacts of community health-workers' (CHWs') 'informal mhealth' practices, and ask how equitably these are distributed.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers need to engage seriously with this emergent health system, and to work closely with those on the ground to address sources of inequity, without undermining existing good practice.

Authors: Sophie Plagerson; Leila Patel; Tessa Hochfeld; Marianne S. Ulriksen
Field: Private sector; Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Social policy; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social change; Policy transfer; Social protection; Social contract
Title: Social policy in South Africa: Navigating the route to social development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The current direction of social policy is described as the result of a compromise between two distinct alternative paradigms whereby the statist transformative and market-oriented residual paradigms are held in tension.
What_was_studied: This paper reflects on the trajectory of social policy in South Africa (1994–2017) and on which policy levers present opportunities for cross-country policy transfer, in order to address current social development challenges.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize hybrid policy overlap between these bifurcated ideological, political, and institutional frameworks, for example around social transfers and corporate social investment, to address current social development challenges.

Authors: Inga Mareike Nienkerke; Amit Thorat; Anthony Patt
Field: Livelihood; Agriculture; Transformative learning; Poverty; Geography; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Business; Development economics; Economics; Sociology; Pedagogy; Archaeology
Title: From distress migration to selective migration: Transformative effects of agricultural development on seasonal migration
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The Wadi program boosted agricultural productivity, reduced the intensity and frequency of seasonal migration, and had spillover effects on whole villages, indicating the potential for integrated farming systems to transform livelihoods and places of seasonal migration. Participants migrated less frequently and for shorter durations than non-participants.
What_was_studied: Seasonal migration among rural poor households in India's states of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Karnataka from a mixed-methods perspective over a four-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up the Wadi concept to enhance local economies, reduce chronic poverty, and enable development from distress to selective migration, as this study's findings suggest significant benefits for rural livelihoods and sustainable development.

Authors: Phillip H. Ross; Paul Glewwe; Daniel Prudencio; Bruce Wydick
Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Optimism; Self-esteem; Educational attainment; Causal effect; Demographic economics; Vocational education
Title: Developing educational and vocational aspirations through international child sponsorship: Evidence from Kenya, Indonesia, and Mexico
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: We find that sponsorship increased indices of self-esteem (0.25sd), optimism (0.26sd), aspirations (0.29sd), and expected years of completed education (0.43 years). Sponsorship increases actual grade completion by 0.56 among children at the time of the survey, and mediation analysis suggests that the impact of sponsorship on aspirations is likely to mediate higher levels of grade completion.
What_was_studied: This paper seeks to ascertain whether the impacts of child sponsorship on educational outcomes may occur through elevated aspirations among sponsored children, using an age-eligibility rule applied during program rollout to identify causal effects and studying 2022 children in Kenya, Indonesia, and Mexico.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and expand child sponsorship programs as a means of addressing food insecurity, ensuring education access, and contributing to sustainable development. By elevating aspirations among children, these programs can help the poor alleviate internal constraints that prevent them from escaping poverty.

Authors: Debasis Barik; Sonalde Desai; Reeve Vanneman
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Health care; Economics; Negative relationship; CLARITY; Human development (humanity); Longitudinal data; Economic growth
Keywords: Adult mortality; Asia; India; SES; health; hypertension; morbidity; wealth
Title: Economic Status and Adult Mortality in India: Is the Relationship Sensitive to Choice of Indicators?
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results show that mortality between the two waves is strongly linked to the economic status of the household at wave 1, regardless of the choice of indicator for economic status. However, the negative relationship between economic status and mortality varies for individuals already suffering from cardiovascular and metabolic conditions, depending on the specific marker of economic status used.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between economic status and mortality in a national sample of 132,116 Indian adults aged 15 years and above, using data from two waves of the India Human Development Survey (IHDS) conducted in 2004-2005 and 2011-2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between economic status and mortality, policy makers should prioritize interventions that increase access to healthcare and nutrition for low-income households, such as expanding public health insurance programs and implementing targeted food subsidies. Additionally, efforts to reduce poverty and improve overall economic well-being can help reduce mortality rates over the long term.

Authors: O. Sarobidy Rakotonarivo; Jette Bredahl Jacobsen; Helle Overgaard Larsen; Julia P. G. Jones; Martin Reinhardt Nielsen; Bruno Ramamonjisoa; Rina Mandimbiniaina; Neal Hockley
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Ex-ante; Payment; Economics; Cash; Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation; Context (language use); Forest protection; Content validity
Keywords: welfare impacts; compensations; REDD+; choice experiment; validity; Madagascar
Title: Qualitative and Quantitative Evidence on the True Local Welfare Costs of Forest Conservation in Madagascar: Are Discrete Choice Experiments a Valid ex ante Tool?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs) outcomes vary with conservation experience. Households more experienced with forest protection are less willing to trade-off rights to clear forest for swidden agriculture with any compensatory interventions, while less experienced households highly favor support for alternative agricultural techniques and a secure right to clear one hectare of forest.
What_was_studied: A case study of a new REDD+ project in eastern Madagascar was used to explore the validity of Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs) in low-income settings by examining whether the estimates of welfare costs derived from DCE are affected by respondents' prior experience of conservation and whether DCE results have high theoretical and content validity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering prior conservation experience when designing compensation schemes for protected areas in low-income settings. Policymakers should prioritize support for alternative agricultural techniques and secure land tenure rights to ensure effective welfare impact assessments.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Public infrastructure; Affirmative action; Space (commercial competition); Caste; Proxy (statistics); Affect (psychology)
Keywords: Discrimination; Affirmative action; Quota; Inequality; Caste; India JEL D63; D74; J15; O12; O53
Title: Don’t Touch My Road. Evidence from India on Affirmative Action And Everyday Discrimination ☆
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that ongoing SC quotas reduce the likelihood of caste-based exclusion for members of the Scheduled Castes (SCs) by about one fifth, but the effect is not persistent and disappears with the end of the SC quota.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effect of electoral quotas on group-based discrimination in India, using a measure of caste-based exclusion from public infrastructure and exploiting the rotation of quotas across space and time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the temporary nature of the quota's effect on discrimination, policy-makers should prioritize alternative strategies to address intersectional poverty, such as scaling up existing infrastructure and expanding access to public services for marginalized communities.

Authors: Mohammad Rezaul Karim; Mohammad Tarikul Islam; Bymokesh Talukder
Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Government; Cash flow; Status quo; Unemployment; Workforce; Financial crisis; Remittance; Development economics
Keywords: COVID-19; Migrant workers; National economy; Remittance; Unemployment, Bangladesh
Title: COVID-19′s impacts on migrant workers from Bangladesh: In search of policy intervention
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that migrant workers contribute approximately USD15 billion to the economy of Bangladesh annually, but the COVID-19 pandemic has intensified numerous socio-economic crises such as joblessness, financial crisis, and social discrimination for these workers and their dependents.
What_was_studied: Migrant workers from Bangladesh in other countries and their dependents back in Bangladesh during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the urgent need to provide financial security and social safety nets to migrant workers and their dependents, both in host countries and back in Bangladesh. The government of Bangladesh should prioritize providing financial support as a short-term strategy and designing a comprehensive plan with a detailed database of all migrant workers as a long-term solution to address the socio-economic impacts of COVID-19.

Field: Business; Empowerment; Workfare; Human development (humanity); District level; Demographic economics; Domestic violence
Title: Domestic violence and workfare: An evaluation of India’s MGNREGS
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The introduction of the MGNREGS mitigates the effect of adverse rainfall shocks on officially reported domestic violence crimes at the district level by 8 to 22 percent.
What_was_studied: Using the phased implementation of MGNREGS across districts in India from 2006 to 2008, the study examines how India's workfare program mediates the effect of income shocks on domestic violence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in workfare programs like MGNREGS to mitigate the impact of income shocks on domestic violence, particularly in rural areas where the scheme is more effective.

Authors: David I. Harvey; Neil Kellard; Jakob B. Madsen; Mark E. Wohar
Field: Monetary policy; Vector autoregression; Macroeconomics; Economics; Interest rate; Relative price; Prebisch–Singer hypothesis; Stock market; Index (economics); Commodity (Marxism)
Keywords: Primary commodities; Prebisch-Singer hypothesis; Economic growth; Interest rates; Structural breaks; VAR. JEL Classification: O13; C22
Title: Long-Run Commodity Prices, Economic Growth, and Interest Rates: 17th Century to the Present Day
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that commodity prices have a downward trend with breaks over the entire industrial age, providing clear support for the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis. Additionally, there is evidence that commodity prices Granger cause income and interest rates, and interest rates Granger cause commodity prices.
What_was_studied: This study examines the historical relation between commodity prices, economic activity, and interest rates in the long run, using a new aggregate index of commodity prices, GDP series such as World, Chile, China, UK, and US, and stationary VAR modeling movements around trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that loose monetary policy has tended to support higher commodity prices, and commodity price movements have an asymmetric country effect on economic activity. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize monitoring and managing commodity prices to address child poverty and income poverty in developing countries.

Field: Fell; Debt ratio; Macroeconomics; Government; Economics; Empirical evidence; Involuntary unemployment; World economy; Oecd countries; Great Depression
Journal/Venue: Towards a Socio-Liberal Theory of World Development
Title: The Future of the Socio-Liberal Model
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that a socio-liberal development strategy can lead to short-term boosts in economic growth rates in OECD countries from 1975 to 1983, but raises concerns about long-term stability issues due to high government savings and public debt ratios.
What_was_studied: This chapter analyzes the long-term implications of a socio-liberal development strategy and its feasibility, focusing on economic growth stability issues in OECD countries from 1975 to 1983 using Keynesian strategies that avoid high government savings and risk higher public debt ratios, while promoting institutional integration into the capitalist world economy and encompassing interest organizations to stabilize economic growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize enhancing institutional integration into the capitalist world economy, promoting encompassing interest organizations, and stabilizing economic growth through Keynesian strategies that avoid high government savings and risk higher public debt ratios to achieve sustainable development.

Field: Social accounting; Political science; Empowerment; Social change; Accountability; Public administration; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Service delivery framework
Keywords: accountability; legal empowerment; health; rights-based approaches; service delivery; governance
Title: Legal Empowerment and Social Accountability: Complementary Strategies Toward Rights-based Development in Health?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study finds that integration of social accountability and legal empowerment strategies can lead to increased community participation, improved healthcare service delivery, and stronger governance structures. In Uganda, for example, community scorecards were used to track healthcare services, leading to a 32% increase in facility-based deliveries.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the integration of social accountability and legal empowerment strategies to improve healthcare services for marginalized populations in four countries (Macedonia, Guatemala, Uganda, India) over a 3-year period (2015-2018).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the promise of integration in advancing social change, policymakers should prioritize funding and support for multi-pronged accountability strategies that empower marginalized communities and improve healthcare service delivery.

Authors: Ishita Chatterjee; Ian Li; Marie-Claire Robitaille
Field: Constitution of India; Political science; Human development (humanity); School education; Reading skills; Policy initiatives; Incentive program; Economic growth; Central government
Title: An overview of India’s primary school education policies and outcomes 2005-2011
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: While progress has been made in terms of infrastructure provision and enrollment, other aspects have either seen no progress or have worsened over time, with notably numerical and reading skills of children 8 to 11 years old worsening over time. Better performing states are generally in the South and in the extreme North.
