What_was_studied: This paper reviews the progress of India's primary schools over the period 2005-2011 as public educational undertaking shifted more from the center to the states, using two waves of the Indian Human Development Survey conducted in 2005 and 2011 to track the progress of primary schools in terms of infrastructure upgrade, teachers' quality, the costs of education, enrollment, and learning outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the abysmal results nationwide, policymakers should prioritize investing in teacher training programs, specifically targeting early grade reading and numeracy skills, and scale up successful initiatives in the South and extreme North.

Field: The labor problem; Vision; Political science; Poverty; Negotiation; Household income; Sub saharan; Sierra leone; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth
Keywords: 'crisis of youth'; child labour; artisanal and small-scale mining; livelihoods; poverty; Sierra Leone
Title: Re-Thinking the Child Labor “Problem” in Rural sub-Saharan Africa: The Case of Sierra Leone’s Half Shovels
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article argues that children’s participation in the rural economy not only generates much-needed household income but is the only way in which they can earn the monies needed to attend school, with quantitative results indicating that 75% of child miners reported an increase in their households’ income as a result of their involvement.
What_was_studied: Child miners – or “half shovels” as they are locally known – are both directly and indirectly involved in small-scale gold extraction in Kono District, Sierra Leone’s main diamond-producing area, over a period of time, using qualitative and quantitative data collected from fieldwork carried out in and around the Kono mining village of Bandafayie.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: A blind and uncritical acceptance of international codes and agreements on child labor could have an adverse impact on children and, by extension, poor communities in rural Sierra Leone. Therefore, the findings suggest that Western notions of “progress” and development should be re-evaluated to match up with the complex realities or competing visions of local people, and policymakers should prioritize programs that support the involvement of children in the rural economy while ensuring their safety and access to education.

Field: Agriculture; Macroeconomics; Instrumental variable; Economics; Poverty; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Income distribution; Endogeneity; Panel data; Developing country
Title: Estimating the Relative Benefits of Agricultural Growth on the Distribution of Expenditures
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that growth in agricultural income is more beneficial for poorer deciles, with an estimated elasticity 3-4 times larger than for non-agricultural activities. This effect is most pronounced in the middle range of the income distribution.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between the sectoral composition of aggregate economic growth and poverty in developing countries, focusing on the impact of agricultural growth on the expenditures of poorer households compared to other sectors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that agricultural growth has a disproportionate positive impact on poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize investments in rural development and agricultural productivity, particularly in the poorest countries.

Authors: Timo Kuosmanen; Xun Zhou; Sheng Dai
Field: Per capita; Macroeconomics; Economic cost; Economics; Empirical evidence; Inefficiency; Greenhouse gas; Climate change mitigation; Quantile regression; Kyoto Protocol
Title: How much climate policy has cost for OECD countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The actual abatement cost per capita has been very modest, much lower than predicted in the late 1990s.
What_was_studied: A panel of 28 OECD countries' greenhouse gas abatement costs per capita from 1990 to 2015 using a novel data-driven approach based on convex quantile regression.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This calls for more ambitious climate change mitigation strategy in the future.

Authors: Ira Irina Dorband; Michael Jakob; Jan Christoph Steckel; Hauke Ward
Field: Subsidy; Economics; Equity (law); Consumption (sociology); Sanitation; Poverty; Revenue; Population; Cash transfers; Business; Public economics; Natural resource economics; Economic growth; Finance; Social science; Demography; Environmental engineering; Sociology; Political science; Law; Market economy; Engineering
Title: Double progressivity of infrastructure financing through carbon pricing — Insights from Nigeria
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that lower-income households would bear a smaller consumption burden from carbon pricing than high-income households, while enjoying greater gains from uniform cash transfers or access to improved water, sanitation, electricity, or telecommunication infrastructure.
What_was_studied: This paper estimates the distributional effects of carbon pricing and cash transfers on households within and between income groups in Nigeria, using environmental-extended input-output data and detailed household survey data for the period 2015–2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize recycling carbon pricing revenues into basic infrastructure development and social safety nets to disproportionately benefit the overall poorer rural population, due to larger initial access gaps.

Authors: Xudong Rao; Terrance M. Hurley; Philip G. Pardey
Field: Agriculture; Econometrics; Developed country; Economics; Oaxaca decomposition; Benefit–cost ratio; Model parameter; Internal rate of return; Agricultural economics; Developing country; International development
Title: Are agricultural R&D returns declining and development dependent?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that after accounting for methodological changes and other study attributes that have varied over time, the contemporary returns to agricultural R&D investments are as high as ever. Additionally, a Oaxaca decomposition reveals that regional differences in study attributes tend to result in higher IRR estimates in developed countries, whereas developing versus developed country differences in the marginal effects of the attributes on the estimated IRRs tend to result in higher estimates in developing countries.
What_was_studied: Using a newly updated and expanded global database of estimated returns to agricultural R&D and a robust statistical methodology, the study evaluates both the time trend (i.e., increasing or decreasing) and regional developmental differences in the reported returns to agricultural R&D investments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high returns to agricultural R&D investments, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up investments in this area, particularly in developing regions where the returns are highest.

Authors: Nicolas Hamelin; Sonny Nwankwo; Ayantunji Gbadamosi
Field: Public policy; Political science; Poverty; Corruption; Social marketing; Transparency (behavior); Population; Development economics; Social issues; Social psychology; Developing country
Title: Social marketing and the corruption conundrum in Morocco : an exploratory analysis
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The campaign managed to raise awareness among the public by about 60%, changed perceptions about corruption with a modest but significant 8.2% increase, and increased intention to change proclivity towards corruption by 20.8% compared to the non-exposed population; family influence was reported as the main predictor of intention to change.
What_was_studied: The growing incidence of corruption in Morocco between 2017 and 2020 using a social marketing campaign to change public perceptions and behaviors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between high levels of corruption and underdevelopment in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of social marketing campaigns to address corruption, particularly in Morocco where the issue is stunting positive development. By leveraging family influence as a predictor of intention to change, future campaigns can be tailored to effectively reach and engage this critical demographic.

Authors: Kaleab Kebede Haile; Eleonora Nillesen; Nyasha Tirivayi
Field: Public economics; Counterfactual thinking; Economics; Probit; Poverty; Crop insurance; Investment decisions; Climate risk; Product (business); Risk aversion
Keywords: Weather index-based crop insurance Endogenous risk preferences Experimental risk elicitation Endogenous switching probit Sub-Saharan Africa Ethiopia Boschstraat 24; 6211 AX Maastricht; Netherlands
Title: Impact of formal climate risk transfer mechanisms on risk-aversion: Empirical evidence from rural Ethiopia
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The ESP model shows that farmers who purchased WICI are less likely to be risk-averse compared to non-purchaser farmers. Non-purchasers would have reduced their risk-aversion if they had taken up the insurance product. Additionally, WICI has a positive and statistically significant effect on farmers' real-life risk-taking behavior, as exemplified by mineral fertilizer use.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of smallholder farmers' access to weather index-based crop insurance on their risk preferences in Ethiopia, using survey and experimental data collected from 2017 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Formal climate risk transfer mechanisms can positively influence rural household farm investment decisions by reducing individual risk-aversion, potentially contributing to poverty alleviation and economic development within agrarian economies exposed to recurrent and severe climate shocks. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize scaling up access to weather index-based crop insurance and other formal climate risk transfer mechanisms in rural areas.

Field: General partnership; Amazon rainforest; Civil society; Livelihood; Corporate governance; Politics; Sustainable development; Environmental governance; Political science; Economic growth; State (computer science); Business; Economics; Geography; Ecology; Archaeology; Finance; Law; Biology; Agriculture; Algorithm; Computer science
Title: Transnational partnerships, domestic institutions, and sustainable development. The case of Brazil and the Amazon Region Protected Areas program
primary_category: Child poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: ARPA has built upon the infusion of significant domestic resources and relied on a conductive political environment and pre-existing initiatives, with domestic institutions acting as arbiters of transnational influence to support state and sub-state institutions and ambitious conservation priorities.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes ARPA's institutional and political effects in Brazil, drawing on extensive documentary analysis and field work to examine the materialization of a range of capacity-strengthening and environmental impacts alongside institutional and distributional effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up ARPA's success in sustainable development, funding for domestic resources and capacity-building should be prioritized, and local communities and civil society organizations should be more meaningfully incorporated into the program to address socio-economic components and poverty alleviation.

Authors: Festus A. Asaaga; Mark Hirons; Yadvinder Malhi
Field: Public economics; Agriculture; Land tenure; Business; Investment (macroeconomics); Sustainable land management; Investment decisions; Context (language use); Service (economics); Sustainable development
Title: Questioning the link between tenure security and sustainable land management in cocoa landscapes in Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings showed that different types of SLM investments were undertaken by farmers, even those who perceived their tenure rights as insecure. However, the relationship between tenure security and SLM investments was mediated by other important non-tenurial factors such as access to credit, modernized agricultural inputs, and targeted extension service support.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between land tenure security and sustainable land management (SLM) adoption among smallholder farmers in Ghana, using a tripartite conception of tenure security to examine factors affecting investment decisions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that land tenure policies can deliver a range of outcomes pertaining to land conservation investments. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize redesigning context-specific and appropriate land-use policy interventions that address barriers to SLM adoption in emerging contexts like Ghana and SSA generally, with the aim of scaling up SLM practices to accelerate poverty reduction and achieve sustainable development.

Field: Behavior change; Business; Poverty; Reciprocity (social psychology); Equity (finance); Behavior change communication; Public relations; Focus group; Social capital; Economic security
Keywords: Behavior-change communication; Health and nutrition; Non-governmental organizations; Self-help groups; Social capital; South Asia
Title: Self-help groups as platforms for development: The role of social capital.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Theoretically, SHGs are a promising platform for health messaging, however this is largely dependent on SHG norms of attendance, which itself is closely tied to socioeconomic conditions and social capital. Sites with more mature SHGs had greater economic security allowing more active participation in the intervention than sites with more poverty and young SHGs.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the efficacy and equity of Women-led self-help groups (SHGs) as platforms for delivering health or livelihoods interventions in eastern India, through analyzing 64 interviews and 6 focus group discussions collected from an agriculture and behavior change intervention delivered through SHGs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the use of SHGs as development platforms, funding agencies and governmental bodies should prioritize building social capital among SHG members by providing substantive benefits for membership, such as economic security, before introducing new interventions. This will lead to greater trust and reciprocity between SHGs and the implementing organization, allowing for more successful incorporation of new activities into their agenda.

Field: Government; Social distance; Geography; Mobile phone; Population; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Livelihood; Inequality; Development economics; Pandemic
Keywords: Africa; Covid-19; Inequality; Mobility; Social Distancing; South Africa
Title: Life Under Lockdown: Illustrating Tradeoffs in South Africa’s Response to COVID-19
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: South Africans in all provinces reduced their mobility substantially in response to the government's lockdown orders, with particularly high compliance in the hardest hit provinces. Statistical regression analysis shows that such mobility reductions are significantly and negatively associated with COVID-19 growth rates two weeks later.
What_was_studied: Using anonymized mobile phone data to analyze mobility patterns across all provinces during the initial stages of the pandemic and examining how this relates to COVID-19 growth rates two weeks later.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments and other development-focused organizations should seriously consider how to offset the costs faced by already marginalized populations, as the country's response may deepen preexisting divides. Prioritize measures to contain the spread of disease alongside policies that address income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty to ensure an equitable recovery.

Authors: Vong Nanhthavong; Sabin Bieri; Anh-Thu Nguyen; Cornelia Hett; Michael Epprecht
Field: Proletarianization; Livelihood; Agrarian society; Wage; Poverty; Labour economics; Business; Economics; Economic growth; Agriculture; Geography; Politics; Political science; Archaeology; Law
Title: Proletarianization and gateways to precarization in the context of land-based investments for agricultural commercialization in Lao PDR
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Land-based investments create a significant absolute number of jobs, but former land users were offered predominantly low-skilled and seasonal jobs; the effects of these investments on rural employment are uneven depending on degrees of land and resource dispossession, the extent of job creation, and the availability of alternative opportunities in the region.
What_was_studied: Drawing on a recent, unique national dataset on land concessions in Lao PDR, this paper uses an agrarian political economy lens to investigate how land-based investments live up to the expectation of rural transformation from resource- to wage-based livelihoods through the generation of employment and contribution to poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The promotion of land-based investments as an approach for rural development, particularly along the gradient of transforming resource- to wage-labor based livelihoods, is ineffective without concurrent opportunities within and beyond the agricultural sector to absorb the labor reallocated from traditional livelihoods; enforcing labor regulations, including restrictions on hiring foreign labor, compliance with minimum wages, and relevant skills transfer are essential to minimize precarization and increase benefits for local people.

Authors: Liesbeth Colen; Damiaan Persyn; Andrea Guariso
Field: Capital intensity; Economic sector; Economics; International economics; Foreign ownership; Expropriation; Soviet union; Foreign direct investment; Market economy; Financial risk; Sunk costs
Title: Bilateral Investment Treaties and FDI: Does the Sector Matter?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that BITs are more effective in sectors with higher sunk costs, such as manufacturing and energy, as they provide a legal commitment to the fair and equitable treatment of foreign investors, decreasing investment risk and attracting foreign investors.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the effectiveness of Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) in attracting foreign direct investments (FDI) across different sectors of the economy in 13 countries of the former Soviet Union and Central and Eastern Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To maximize the development impact of FDI, governments should prioritize BITs in sectors with high sunk costs and politically sensitive foreign ownership, as they have been found to be most effective in attracting employment-generating and technology-transferring investments.

Field: Hegemony; Variety (cybernetics); Development studies; Political science; Poverty; Citation; Social Sciences Citation Index; Subject (philosophy); Social science; Sustainability
Title: The contemporary development discourse: Analysing the influence of development studies’ journals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis found that the four journals converged on topics related to aid, poverty, sustainability, and development challenges, but had limited influence in shaping the development discourse due to a high proportion of disconnected articles with self-citations and a preponderance of Anglo-Saxon academia in scientific production.
What_was_studied: This bibliometric analysis of four development journals in the Social Sciences Citation Index between 2000 and 2015 explores the cross-disciplinary nature of the field of development studies, with a focus on identifying the main areas of research, citation networks, and influential articles, countries, and institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening the coherence and influence of development journals in shaping the contemporary development discourse, particularly by increasing the representation of diverse perspectives and institutions to address the existing Western hegemony.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Dividend; Business; Public good; Empirical evidence; Public infrastructure; Cash transfers; Earnings; Productive capacity
Title: Productive effects of public works programs: What do we know? What should we know?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that PW programs can induce productive investments via income and insurance effects when the program is sufficiently reliable and long-term, and can also have positive welfare effects by raising wages. However, there is limited evidence on the productive effects of public infrastructure generated by PW programs, and potential adverse effects on labor markets must be taken into account.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of Abstract Public Works (PW) programs in reducing poverty and improving productive capacity among poor households in developing countries, specifically comparing PW programs to Cash Transfer programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed evidence on the effectiveness of PW programs relative to Cash Transfer programs, policymakers should prioritize investments in PW programs that generate substantial investments among the target group, particularly if there is clear evidence that private-sector wages are below equilibrium wages. Additionally, further research is crucial to understand and quantify the productive effects of public infrastructure generated by PW programs.

Field: Green Revolution; Agriculture; Business; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Adaptive capacity; Climate risk management; Context (language use); Livelihood; Shock (economics)
Keywords: Adaptation; Agricultural intensification; Climate change; Institutions; Livelihoods; Vulnerability
Title: Smallholders' uneven capacities to adapt to climate change amid Africa's 'green revolution': Case study of Rwanda's crop intensification program.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that smallholders' adaptive capacities differed across livelihood groups, with wealthier households able to adapt through commercial agriculture while poorer households were left behind due to deactivation of local risk management institutions. The study also found that access to capitals such as land, labor, and nonfarm income was crucial for smallholders to employ alternate livelihood practices.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how development transitions and cross-scale social-environmental processes shape smallholder adaptive capacities and adaptation pathways in Rwanda over a multi-season period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize reformulating agricultural development policies with careful attention to how power structures and entrenched social inequalities can lead to uneven adaptive capacities among smallholder households. This can involve scaling up access to capitals, strengthening local risk management institutions, and ensuring that all smallholders have equal opportunities to adapt to climate change.

Field: Decentralization; Government; Economics; Incentive; Corporate governance; Argument; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Common-pool resource; Resource management
Title: Decentralization and Participation: The Governance of Common Pool Resources in Nepal’s Terai
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that individuals with greater access to government offices related to decentralization policies and those who are economically and socially better-off are more likely to participate in user groups created by state officials. Additionally, the study found a negative correlation between education and participation levels.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the participation of economically and socially better-off households in community-level user groups for environmental decentralization programs in Nepal's Terai region using data from protected areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that for decentralization policies to be successful on equity issues, it is important to build institutional mechanisms that encourage poorer and more marginal households to access government officials, improve access to educational opportunities, and create incentives to promote more interactions between less powerful rural residents and government officials. Policymakers should prioritize these measures to ensure that decentralization policies benefit all members of society equitably.

Authors: Kathrin Durizzo; Edward Asiedu; Antoinette van der Merwe; Attie van Niekerk; Isabel Günther
Field: Government; Social distance; Political science; Poverty; Risk of infection; Misinformation; Population; Socioeconomics; Hygiene; Pandemic
Keywords: Covid-19; Ghana; Lockdown; Mitigation measures; South Africa; Urban poor
Title: Managing the COVID-19 pandemic in poor urban neighborhoods: the case of Accra and Johannesburg.
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite citywide lockdowns, about 25-40% of people still report attending large gatherings, 10-20% report receiving guests at home, and 30-35% report leaving the house more than once per week.
What_was_studied: This survey of over 1,400 poor households in two African cities found that the urban poor engage in appropriate hygiene practices and social distancing during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite lacking infrastructure or facing poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively mitigate COVID-19 risks among the urban poor, governments should invest in public infrastructure that supports social distancing and provide financial support for those facing poverty to ensure they can follow WHO safety regulations.

Field: Rural area; Labour economics; Economics; Time allocation; Energy poverty; Spouse; Working time; Electrification; Rural electrification; Shock (economics)
Keywords: rural electrification; labor supply; developing countries; joint decision making; bivariate hurdle model; copulas JEL Classification: C3; C31; C35; D1; J22; O13
Title: Rural Electrification and Household Labor Supply: Evidence from Nigeria
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that electrification increases the working time of both spouses, but the joint analysis emphasizes only a positive effect of electrification on husbands' working time. Additionally, the study highlights the significance of considering within-household relationships in assessing the impact of electrification on labor supply decisions.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the effect of electrification on labor supply decisions within rural households in Nigeria using data from the 2010-2011 General Household Survey, focusing on husband-wife data and accounting for dependence in spouses' labor supply decisions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that neglecting the effect of electrification on the spouse of the individual examined may lead to an incomplete assessment of how the individual has been affected by this common shock on both spouses. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize electrification in rural areas and consider within-household relationships when evaluating the impact of electrification on labor supply decisions.

Authors: Rachel Carmenta; Federico Cammelli; Wolfram Dressler; Camila Verbicaro; Julie G. Zaehringer
Field: Agriculture; Development studies; Natural resource economics; Geography; Damages; Environmental justice; Livelihood; Land use; Food security; Ecosystem services
Title: Between a rock and a hard place: The burdens of uncontrolled fire for smallholders across the tropics
primary_category: Environmental Justice; Rural Poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that smallholder farmers experience significant material and non-material burdens due to uncontrolled fires, including infringements on food security, health, livelihoods, social relations and prohibitive fire policies. The study found that these burdens are not adequately addressed by current climate change and biodiversity loss narratives.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the place-based burdens of uncontrolled fires on smallholder farming communities in the tropics, using empirical data from four case studies in Brazil, Madagascar and the Philippines over a 10-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the ecological integrity of tropical forests, policy makers should prioritize equitable responses to uncontrolled fires that recognize the place-based burdens on smallholder farming communities. Policies should be designed to avoid prohibitive fire policies and support resilient agricultural practices that enhance food security and social wellbeing.

Authors: Sebastian Schneider; Jens Eger; Martin Bruder; Jörg Faust; Lothar Wieler
Field: Public opinion; Public health; Government; Political science; Survey data collection; Solidarity; Development economics; Sustainable development; Developing country; Politics
Keywords: COVID-19; Coronavirus; Development assistance; Global solidarity; Public opinion; Trust in government
Title: Does the COVID-19 pandemic threaten global solidarity? Evidence from Germany
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite the challenges posed by the pandemic, there was little negative effect on public support for development assistance during the first wave, likely due to high levels of trust in government. However, as worries recur and trust decreases, global solidarity may wane.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on developed and developing countries' economies, politics, and public health systems, and how it might affect sustainable development progress.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize maintaining and strengthening trust in government to ensure continued support for development assistance during the pandemic and beyond.

Field: Consumption (economics); Crop; Business; Productivity; Biofortification; Micronutrient deficiency; Staple food; Household income; Agricultural science; Food security
Keywords: Africa; Control function approach; Impact; Instrumental variables; Iron-biofortified beans; Rwanda
Title: The impact of iron-biofortified bean adoption on bean productivity, consumption, purchases and sales.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: Adopting iron-biofortified beans increased household yield by 20% to 49%, and the consumption of beans from own production by 0.64 months (19–20 days), reduced the length of time beans were purchased for consumption by 0.73 months (22–23 days), and increased the likelihood of selling beans by 12%.
What_was_studied: The effect of adopting iron-biofortified beans on household nutrition and income in Rwanda over a 12-month period was studied using ten iron-biofortified bean varieties released between 2010 and 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the continued adoption of iron-biofortified beans to improve household nutrition via two channels: increasing iron intake and improving household income for purchasing nutritious foods. Additionally, the availability of iron-dense food in markets benefits households that purchase beans.

Field: Dozen; Rondo; Great Divergence; State (polity); Free trade; International studies; Industrial Revolution; Mythology; Classics; History
Journal/Venue: Theory and Methodology of World Development
Title: Debunk Mythology, Reorient Reality
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite the participation of renowned historians and economists, the discussion exclusively focused on characteristics of Britain and other countries, with no mention of the global political economy's structure, operation, and transformation, which were critical to Britain's rise and decline in world economic primacy.
What_was_studied: The Great Divergence in the 19th century and its implications for world economic primacy, using a comprehensive dataset of conference proceedings from the Luxembourg Institute for European and International Studies in 2002.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a comprehensive understanding of the global political economy and its structural changes to inform effective strategies for sustained economic primacy, rather than relying solely on characteristics of individual countries.

Authors: Emanuel Deutschmann; Lorenzo Gabrielli; Ettore Recchi
Field: Politics; Enforcement; Economic geography; Business; International trade; Economics; Political science; Development economics; Law
Title: Roads, rails, and checkpoints: Assessing the permeability of nation-state borders worldwide
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Europe and Africa have the most permeable borders, while the Americas have the least. Additionally, the study revealed a curvilinear relationship between economic development and border permeability: Borders of very rich and very poor countries are highly permeable, whereas those of moderately prosperous nation-states are significantly harder to cross.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the permeability of 312 land borders globally using transport infrastructure and political checkpoints as indicators, covering a population of approximately 7.9 billion people over a time period of 2015-2020 and utilizing data from OpenStreetMap and the World Food Programme.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize investments in transport infrastructure and checkpoints to increase the permeability of borders, particularly in densely populated areas and moderately prosperous nation-states. By doing so, they can facilitate trade, reduce economic inequality, and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Harriet Elizabeth Smith; Daniel Jones; Frank Vollmer; Sophia Baumert; Casey M. Ryan; Emily Woollen; Sá Nogueira Lisboa; Mariana Carvalho; Janet Fisher; Ana Catarina Luz; Isla M. Grundy; Genevieve Patenaude
Field: Business; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Production (economics); Household income; Rural development; Rural income; Livelihood; Charcoal; Energy (esotericism)
Title: Urban energy transitions and rural income generation: Sustainable opportunities for rural development through charcoal production
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that the size of the urban market affects the type of rural producer and their scales of production, with larger-scale producers being wealthier and less dependent on charcoal income, while small-scale producers rely more heavily on charcoal income, contributing over 95% of household incomes.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the charcoal sector in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on rural producers supplying two differentially sized urban markets in Mozambique over a specific time period, using 767 household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the predicted growth of smaller urban areas and associated higher demand for charcoal, policymakers should prioritize equitable production systems that incorporate the importance of charcoal production for rural livelihoods, targeting better-targeted interventions to support rural poverty alleviation and sustainable development.

Authors: Nicolette Duncan; Sanjiv de Silva; John Conallin; Sarah Freed; Michael Akester; Lee J. Baumgartner; Matthew McCartney; M. Dubois; Sonali Senaratna Sellamuttu
Field: Business; Framing (social sciences); Natural resource economics; Poverty; Fisheries management; Inclusive growth; Elite capture; Livelihood; Food security; Sustainable development
Title: Fish for whom?: Integrating the management of social complexities into technical investments for inclusive, multi-functional irrigation
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite technical solutions existing to minimize irrigation's impact on inland fisheries, there is a fundamental disconnect between the technical application of such 'solutions' and distribution of benefits to marginalized groups targeted by SDGs 1, 2, 3, and more. Insufficient recognition of social contexts underpins this disconnect, highlighting the need for investments in social processes that enable inclusive growth, multi-functionality, and sustainable food security.
What_was_studied: Abstract Irrigation investments in South East Asia between the 1960s and 2010s, with a focus on Myanmar and Cambodia, were examined through a literature review and key informant interviews to understand their impact on inland fisheries and how technical solutions can be applied to minimize these impacts while considering the social context of marginalized groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the role of irrigation in adapting to a changing climate while maintaining landscape integrity and multi-functionality, policymakers should prioritize investments in social processes that enable inclusive growth, multi-functionality, and sustainable food security, rather than solely focusing on technical infrastructure design.

Authors: Matilde D'Amelio; Paola Garrone; Lucia Piscitello
Field: Dummy variable; Multinational corporation; Economics; Electricity; Energy poverty; Context (language use); Foreign direct investment; Development economics; Panel data; Economic system; Developing country
Title: Can Multinational Enterprises Light up Developing Countries?: Evidences from the Access to Electricity in sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that FDI promotes access to electricity in developing countries with weak institutions, particularly when the FDI originates from institutionally underdeveloped countries. These findings challenge the common idea that a regulatory authority is essential for providing infrastructure.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the role of multinational enterprises (MNEs) and foreign direct investments (FDI) in improving access to electricity for local communities in developing countries between 2005 and 2011, using a dataset of 1,547 observations from sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these results, policymakers should prioritize partnering with MNEs and encouraging FDI to enhance access to electricity in developing countries, particularly in regions with weak institutions. This could involve creating regulatory frameworks that incentivize investment while ensuring accountability.

Authors: James E. Prieger; Catherine Bampoky; Luisa Blanco; Aolong Liu
Field: Macroeconomics; Developed country; Economics; Corruption; Venture capital; Proxy (statistics); Population; Monetary economics; Developing country; Entrepreneurship
Title: Economic Growth and the Optimal Level of Entrepreneurship
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a marginal increase in the entrepreneurship rate in developing countries has a positive effect on growth, while in developed countries there is no evident growth penalty. Supplemental results suggest that this is because in developed countries, entrepreneurship is now close to its optimal level, whereas in developing countries, the optimal rates of entrepreneurship are much higher.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM), we examine data from developed and developing countries to estimate the 'growth penalty' over 2003–11 when a country's entrepreneurship deviates from its optimal level, accounting for heterogeneity among countries in the optimal entrepreneurship rate, in the growth penalty from deviating from that optimum, and in other factors affecting growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and scale up initiatives that promote entrepreneurship in developing countries, such as access to venture capital and R&D capabilities, to maximize growth and reduce poverty.

Authors: Juan Bonilla; Rosa Castro Zarzur; Sudhanshu Handa; Claire Nowlin; Amber Peterman; Hannah Ring; David Seidenfeld
Field: Government; Economics; Empowerment; Beneficiary; Women's empowerment; Cash transfers; Marital status; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Scale (social sciences); Developing country
Keywords: Africa; Zambia; cash transfers; decision making; women’s empowerment
Title: Cash for Women's Empowerment? A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of the Government of Zambia's Child Grant Program
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Women in beneficiary households made more sole or joint decisions across five out of nine domains, but the impact translated into relatively modest increases in the number of decision domains a woman is involved in, on average by 0.34 (or a 6% increase over a baseline mean of 5.3).
What_was_studied: The Government of Zambia's Child Grant Program, a poverty-targeted, unconditional transfer given to mothers or primary caregivers of young children aged zero to five in three rural districts over four years, was evaluated through a mixed-methods study combining a longitudinal clustered-randomized control trial and in-depth interviews with women and their partners stratified on marital status and program participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the potential for unconditional cash transfer programs to improve the financial and intrahousehold status of female beneficiaries, but additional design components may be needed for transformational change; therefore, policymakers should prioritize scaling up such programs while addressing entrenched gender norms that limit women's empowerment.

Authors: Paola Velasco-Herrejon; Thomas Bauwens; Martin Calisto Friant
Field: Conceptual framework; Political science; Energy transition; Ecological modernization; Context (language use); Energy source; Sustainable development; Indigenous; Sustainability; Environmental ethics
Title: Challenging dominant sustainability worldviews on the energy transition: Lessons from Indigenous communities in Mexico and a plea for pluriversal technologies
primary_category: Digital divide
What_was_found: The study found that the Zapotec sustainability worldview differs significantly from modernist visions of sustainability, with conflicts and misunderstandings arising around wind energy projects. The Zapotec worldview emphasizes reciprocity, relationality, and place-based knowledge, while modernist visions prioritize technical efficiency, economic growth, and top-down decision-making.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the contrast between modernist and Indigenous sustainability worldviews in the context of wind energy developments within the territory of three Zapotec communities located in southern Mexico, using a mixed-methods approach involving 103 interviews, six focus groups, and participant observation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that inclusive and just energy transitions require recognition of diverse sustainability worldviews and technologies that embrace ontological and epistemological diversity. Policymakers should prioritize co-design, co-production, and co-ownership of technologies by the inhabitants of the socio-cultural territory in which they are embedded to ensure a pluriversal energy transition.

Field: Rural area; Poverty; Social protection; Public trust; Local government; Grassroots; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Economic growth
Keywords: COVID-19; Governance; India; Local institutions; Panchayats; Social protection
Title: The local governance of COVID-19: Disease prevention and social security in rural India.
primary_category: Health disparities; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that local governance was instrumental in bridging the gap between the need for rapid response to the pandemic and local realities in these states, with mid-level bureaucrats playing a crucial role in coordinating responses. Additionally, Kerala's investment in democratic local government and incorporation of women within grassroots state functions built a high degree of public trust and cooperation with state actors, allowing for an ethic of care in the implementation of state responses.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the COVID-19 response in three Indian states - Rajasthan, Odisha, and Kerala - during the early months of the pandemic, examining how local governance played a critical role in coordinating responses and addressing health disparities, rural poverty, and social protection measures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings emphasize the importance of investing in local governance and cross-sectoral collaboration to effectively respond to health crises like COVID-19, particularly in rural areas with limited infrastructure and resources. Policymakers should prioritize building trust and cooperation with local communities, incorporating gender perspectives, and adopting an ethic of care in their responses to ensure the long-term success of disease control and livelihood support measures.

Authors: Simplice A. Asongu; Jacinta C. Nwachukwu
Field: Public economics; Information asymmetry; Government; Actuarial science; Economics; Empirical evidence; Mobile phone; Quality (business); Good governance; Monopoly; Corporate governance
Keywords: JEL Classification: G20; O38; O40; O55; P37 Mobile phones; Governance; Africa
Title: The Mobile Phone in the Diffusion of Knowledge for Institutional Quality in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a positive effect of mobile phone penetration on good governance in Sub-Saharan Africa, with the net effects being positive for the most part. Additionally, countries with low levels of governance were found to be catching up with their counterparts with higher levels of governance.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of mobile phone penetration on good governance in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2012, using three complementary knowledge diffusion variables (innovation, internet penetration, and educational quality) and 10 governance indicators.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that increasing mobile phone penetration and improving knowledge diffusion can help improve good governance in Sub-Saharan Africa. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investments in mobile infrastructure and education to enhance reach, access, adoption, cost-effectiveness, and interaction, which can help reduce information asymmetry and monopoly that create conducive conditions for bad governance.

Field: Public economics; Proxy (climate); Political science; Poverty; Basic needs; Sanitation; Left behind; Normative; Domestic violence; Sustainable development
Keywords: Canada; Methodology; Mortality; Poverty; Sustainable Development Goals; United Nations
Title: Classifying Sustainable Development Goal trajectories: A country-level methodology for identifying which issues and people are getting left behind.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 78 of the 169 SDG targets are quantifiably assessable at the country level, with 43 of these targets being measurable through a systematic approach to establishing 'proxy targets'. The study also found that Canada is on course to succeed on 18 indicators, but is falling short on 33 indicators and making little progress on 12 indicators.
What_was_studied: The study examines the use of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for empirical analysis at the country level, with a focus on the SDGs' normative ambition of 'no one left behind', and assesses Canada's progress towards achieving the goals using a methodological framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings of this study suggest that approximately 54,000 Canadian lives are at stake and millions of people are being left behind on issues such as poverty, education, intimate partner violence, and access to water and sanitation. Therefore, it is crucial for policymakers to prioritize addressing these issues and make concerted efforts to achieve the SDGs in order to ensure that no one is left behind.

Authors: Sacha Ruzzante; Ricardo Labarta; Amy M. Bilton
Field: Public economics; Agriculture; Land tenure; Regression analysis; Natural resource management; Poverty; Productivity; Agricultural machinery; Developing country
Title: Adoption of agricultural technology in the developing world: A meta-analysis of the empirical literature
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that farmer education, household size, land size, access to credit, land tenure, access to extension services, and organization membership positively correlate with the adoption of many agricultural technologies. Technologies in the categories of improved varieties and chemical inputs are adopted more readily on larger farms, while agricultural credit can positively influence adoption but should be measured with whether farmers are credit-constrained rather than simply having access to credit.
What_was_studied: A meta-analysis of 367 regression models from the published literature to identify variables that regularly explain adoption across technologies and contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these observations, policy makers should scale up investments in education and extension services, expand access to credit, and prioritize land tenure reform to increase adoption of agricultural technologies and reduce poverty in rural areas.

Authors: Frederico Brandão; George C. Schoneveld; Pablo Pacheco; Ima Vieira; Marc Piraux; Dalva Maria da Mota
Field: Supply chain; Deforestation; Business; Natural resource economics; Transnational governance; Contract farming; Context (language use); Incentive; Corporate governance; Sustainable development
Title: The challenge of reconciling conservation and development in the tropics: Lessons from Brazil’s oil palm governance model
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that oil palm expansion in Brazil avoided deforestation but failed to optimally enhance smallholder participation in the sector, with significant differences in performance between farmers. Only 17% of farmers were very successful, while 12% were highly unsuccessful.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the impact of oil palm cultivation on gender and poverty outcomes in Brazil between 2010 and 2018, using a mixed-methods approach combining primary data from smallholder farmers and existing literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize aligning domestic governance frameworks with transnational initiatives to reconcile social, environmental, and economic objectives in the oil palm sector. This can be achieved by scaling up successful smallholder programs, expanding support for gender and poverty reduction, and funding research on best practices for sustainable commodity production.

Field: Empirical research; Heuristics; Bayesian inference; Experimental economics; Data science; Context (language use); Casual; Computer science; Sample (statistics); Information processing
Keywords: Experimental economics; India; Learning heuristics; Technology adoption
Title: Can differences in individual learning explain patterns of technology adoption? Evidence on heterogeneous learning patterns and hybrid rice adoption in Bihar, India.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that only about 25 percent of farmers in the sample could be characterized as pure Bayesian learners, with the majority of farmers relying on present-biased learning or first impressions when making decisions about adopting hybrid rice. Additionally, the study found that pure Bayesian learning was more cognitively taxing and required a longer memory and more complex updating processes.
What_was_studied: The study examines the adoption of hybrid rice in rural India, focusing on how individuals' learning processes affect their decision to adopt the technology, and how these processes differ across space and time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at increasing adoption of hybrid rice in rural India should prioritize targeted education and training programs to improve farmers' understanding of the technology, as well as provide incentives for farmers to engage in experimentation and learning. Additionally, policymakers should consider providing credit and financial support to farmers to help them overcome the cognitive barriers associated with pure Bayesian learning.

Field: Political economy; Democratization; Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Unemployment; Citizenship; Social contract; Sustainability; Politics
Title: The Dynamics of the Egyptian Social Contract: How the Political Changes affected the Poor
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The analysis shows the persistence of the same wellbeing priorities, problems, and unfulfilled aspirations, especially in employment, income generation, housing, and education, indicating the repeated failure of the state to enact a new social contract that addresses these needs.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal study tracks the wellbeing priorities, unfulfilled aspirations, problems, and perceptions on the social contract of individuals in Manshiet Nasser and Menia over a ten-year period (2006–2015) adopting a social contract approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the post-revolutionary economic crises disproportionately affected poor communities, particularly female-headed households in urban areas and young informal workers, highlighting the need for more inclusive policies to address socio-economic rights. The current social contract's failure to fulfill these needs may jeopardize long-term political stability in Egypt, underscoring the urgency of revising the social contract to prioritize economic opportunities and social justice.

Field: Sociology; Indigenous rights; Free, prior and informed consent; Obligation; Active citizenship; Corporate governance; Public relations; Indigenous; Exclusive right; International human rights law
Keywords: This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International licence Newcastle University ePrints -eprint.ncl.ac.uk FPIC; participation; indigenous rights; natural resources; ethnicity; Bolivia
Title: The Politics of Indigenous Participation Through “Free Prior Informed Consent”: Reflections from the Bolivian Case
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the implementation of FPIC can have unintended consequences, and consultation can sometimes embed existing social, cultural, and economic tensions.
What_was_studied: Empirically, it examines a recent attempt to establish more participative forms of resource and development governance for indigenous communities in Bolivia through Free Prior and Informed Consent/Consultation (FPIC).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize inclusive participation by ensuring clear guidelines for who is entitled to participate in FPIC processes and addressing existing power imbalances to promote more equitable management of natural resources.

Authors: Anna Erwin; Zhao Ma; Ruxandra Popovici; Emma Patricia Salas O’Brien; Laura Zanotti; Eliseo Zeballos Zeballos; Jonathan Bauchet; Nelly Ramirez Calderón; Glenn Roberto Arce Larrea
Field: Pastoralism; Geography; Adaptive capacity; Environmental justice; Intersectionality; Livelihood; Demographic economics; Inequality; Scale (social sciences); Politics
Title: Intersectionality shapes adaptation to social-ecological change
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social-ecological changes are perceived and experienced differently by individuals and groups within the agricultural sector, depending on their intersecting identities. For example, ‘unskilled’ women diversified their income through day-labor in agriculture, while ‘unskilled’ men had more options for income diversification. Migrants who are also renters had access to water; however, migrants who lived in informal settlements lacked water access. Pastoralists over 50 faced more difficulties pursuing income diversification and labor migration than younger populations with similar livelihoods.
What_was_studied: This study examines how people in the Caylloma Province of Peru adapt to social-ecological changes such as decreasing water supplies and rapidly retreating glaciers, focusing on how intersecting identities like gender and age shape these adaptations at the individual, household, and district scales, based on 130 semi-structured interviews with agricultural actors and participant observations in district and regional meetings across four districts over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing intersectional poverty in chronic poverty reduction efforts, as individuals and groups within heterogeneous communities face unequal adaptation opportunities due to their intersecting identities. Therefore, scaling up and expanding public adaptation spaces, such as irrigation commissions, to include Spanish-speaking men who own land, Quechua speakers, women, and migrants is essential to ensuring that all members of these communities have equal access to resources and opportunities for adapting to social-ecological changes.

Field: Welfare; Government; Political science; Accountability; Local community; Trade union; Public administration; Corporate governance; Civil society; Administrative law
Keywords: Administrative law; Covid-19; Fiscal sociology; Governance; India; Social funds
Title: Unfreezing unspent social special-purpose funds for the Covid-19 crisis: Critical reflections from India.
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: Approximately US$ 4.2 billion (INR 310 billion) came from a vast pile of unspent social special-purpose funds.
What_was_studied: This paper presents a brief analysis of two preliminary case studies of specific social special-purpose funds in India during the COVID-19 pandemic between January 2020 and virtual pursuit following the lockdown.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should focus on the institutional design, decision-making, and accountability structures for the flow and distribution of COVID funds, rather than merely emphasizing their collection, as such funds are likely to mushroom following the pandemic.

Field: Agency (philosophy); Subjective well-being; Feeling; Psychology; Dignity; Humiliation; Life satisfaction; Human development (humanity); Shame; Social psychology
Keywords: subjective well-being; agency; human dignity; capabilities. JEL Classification: D14; G2
Title: Agency, Human Dignity, and Subjective Well-being
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that agency and shame are important predictors of life satisfaction, comparable in magnitude to the effect of income variables. Additionally, the study found that capabilities that measure freedoms and social inclusion are aligned with well-being measures, supporting the view of human development as an integral process.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between life satisfaction and two 'hidden dimensions' of development - agency and human dignity - using a novel nationally representative survey of Chilean households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize interventions that advance agency, reduce shame and discrimination, and promote social inclusion to improve life satisfaction and human well-being in Chile.

Authors: Hanna Berkel; Christian Estmann; John Rand
Field: Transparency (behavior); Corporate governance; Nexus (standard); Compliance (psychology); Legitimacy; Business; Rule of law; Quality (philosophy); Politics; Legislation; Conditionality; Government (linguistics); Public economics; Accounting; Economics; Law; Political science; Finance; Psychology; Social psychology; Philosophy; Linguistics; Epistemology; Computer science; Embedded system
Title: Local governance quality and law compliance: The case of Mozambican firms
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that perceived improvements in transparency positively affect firms’ compliance with existing legislation, and requests from provincial government officials for firms to comment on local regulations seem to be especially important for law abidance. Legitimacy is independently associated with compliance, but does not seem to mediate or moderate the quality of governance.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how the quality of governance (defined as comprising three dimensions: transparency, legal security and infrastructure quality) is related to firm-level compliance with business laws and regulations in the case of Mozambique during 2013-2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that low compliance rates impede economic growth and human development, decision makers should prioritize initiatives that improve transparency, legal security, and infrastructure quality to increase firms' compliance with business laws and regulations in Mozambique. Requesting firm comments on local regulations can also positively impact law abidance.

Field: Electrification; Rural electrification; Economics; Panel data; Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Human capital; Productivity; Ordinary least squares; Estimation; Demographic economics; Agricultural economics; Econometrics; Development economics; Economic growth; Geography; Electricity; Engineering; Archaeology; Electrical engineering; Management
Title: Association between rural electrification and agricultural output: Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive significant association between rural electrification and agricultural output, with the relationship being conditional on the quality of institutional factors and factor inputs of a country. Additionally, the study found that the association between rural electrification and agricultural output is negative for factor inputs such as land and labor.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the association between rural electrification and agricultural output at the macro level using panel data on 43 Sub-Saharan African countries from 1990 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in rural electrification, particularly in countries with weak institutional quality. By doing so, they can enhance the productivity of labor in the agricultural sector and promote economic growth.

What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of post-conflict minerals-for-development reforms on poverty reduction in Sierra Leone, focusing on the diamond sector's mining cooperatives scheme (2005) and the Diamond Areas Community Development Fund (DACDF) in Kono District from 2005 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limits of mineral-led poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize interventions that address power imbalances and promote decentralized governance to complement mining activities in chronic poverty hotspots like Kono District. This could involve scaling up community-based initiatives, expanding access to education and health services, and investing in sustainable livelihoods beyond mining.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed results of the 'assault on poverty' initiative, decision makers should prioritize strengthening advisory, technical assistance, and economic research functions to better address chronic poverty in client countries.

What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between income inequality and social contention in urban areas, using a mixed-methods approach with longitudinal data from 2015 to 2018 and a case study of three cities in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant correlation between income inequality and social contention, decision makers should prioritize policies aimed at reducing poverty and income disparities in urban areas, particularly those that address intersectional factors such as race and gender. This can include funding programs targeting low-income families, expanding access to affordable housing and healthcare, and implementing community-based initiatives to promote social cohesion and reduce inequality.

What_was_found: While the MDG agenda has been successful in rescuing the Millennium Declaration from oblivion, it has not expanded the development narrative beyond economic growth. Poverty remains a multi-dimensional phenomenon, but its quantification remains one-dimensional, reinforcing a money-metric perspective. The agenda has been cut back to a standard set of macroeconomic, sectoral or institutional reforms of a technical nature, despite the need for fundamental transformations in society driven by domestic politics and local actors.
What_was_studied: The origin and effectiveness of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty globally from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the growing inequities within countries, policymakers should prioritize intersectional poverty reduction and scale up sustainable development initiatives that incorporate multi-dimensional poverty measures and prioritize domestic politics and local actor engagement.

What_was_studied: This article examines the pattern of minimum wage changes in Malawi and some of their effects during a specific time period using Ministry of Labour survey data.

What_was_studied: The effects of Ghana's national Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) on poverty within the country's subsistence economy, specifically examining the impact of policies associated with the programme on the growth of informal, poverty-driven artisanal gold mining and the marginalization of its impoverished participants over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the government should prioritize the expansion of large-scale gold mining through foreign investment, while also implementing policies that protect the rights and interests of impoverished artisanal gold miners. This can be achieved by simplifying regulations and policies for artisanal operators, providing support for infrastructure development, and increasing access to finance and technology to enhance productivity.

What_was_studied: In a wide-ranging and thought-provoking contribution to this journal, Professor Keith Griffin (2003) examines the lack of effective democratic institutions at the global level to govern market forces and perpetuate global income inequality and poverty, particularly in low-income countries.
