Title: What do the World Bank's Poverty Assessments teach us about Poverty in Sub‐Saharan Africa?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while poverty assessments acknowledge other factors in identifying the poor, they overemphasize income-poverty defined against an arbitrary poverty line, often ignoring historical perspectives, political contexts, and international dimensions such as debt and commodity price trends. The study also found that the number of poor people in Africa will continue to rise if policies are not put in place to address the situation.
What_was_studied: Poverty Assessments were carried out for 25 countries in sub-Saharan Africa between 1990 and 1996 to understand who the poor are, why they are poor, and what can be done to reduce poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to poverty reduction strategies, taking into account historical and political contexts, international dimensions, and income-poverty defined against an arbitrary poverty line. Policymakers should prioritize addressing the causes of poverty, such as debt and commodity price trends, rather than solely focusing on recent economic growth.

Field: Principal (computer security); Economics; Poverty; Working poor; Structural adjustment; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Structural Adjustment and Poverty Alleviation: An Interpretative Survey
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that adjustment programs have varying impacts on poverty, with the urban working poor experiencing disproportionate negative effects, while rural areas often experience positive outcomes. However, there is a tendency to overemphasize negative outcomes and neglect other factors influencing poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the effects of adjustment programs on poverty, focusing on urban and rural areas, using a mixed-methods approach with time series data from 1980 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively address poverty, policymakers must prioritize long-term strategies that integrate adjustment programs within a cost-minimizing framework, while ensuring national governments take principal responsibility for anti-poverty objectives and international financial institutions support these efforts with targeted funding and expertise.

Field: Public policy; Ethnic group; Sociology; Subsistence agriculture; Stigma (botany); Okavango delta; Affect (psychology); Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Interconnectedness
Title: The Shaping of San Livelihood Strategies: Government Policy and Popular Values
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the economic marginalization of San people is compounded by their ethnic background, leading to limited access to resources and opportunities for subsistence. The analysis also highlighted the importance of considering institutional factors in regulating livelihood strategies and the need to challenge stereotypes associated with San people.
What_was_studied: The livelihood strategies of San people in three villages on the northern peripheries of the Okavango Delta in Botswana over a period of time, using qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the economic marginalization of San people, scale up support for their subsistence practices, and revise policies that perpetuate their social and political exclusion to ensure sustainable poverty reduction and equitable development.

Field: Social relation; Sociology; Horticulture; Agrarian society; Poverty; Social alienation; Obligation; Contract farming; Social practice; Legitimacy; Development economics
Title: Gender and Witchcraft in Agrarian Transition: The Case of Kenyan Horticulture
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that men's failure to compensate their wives for horticulture production has given rise to a string of witchcraft allegations and acts, as the wealth engendered by horticultural commodities comes up against cultural norms of marital obligation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the social effects of contract farming of export horticulture among smallholders in Meru District, Kenya during the 1980s and 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that addressing gendered power imbalances within households is crucial to reducing child poverty in contexts of agrarian transition. Policymakers should prioritize programmes and policies that promote fair distribution of income within households and challenge cultural norms that perpetuate gender inequality.

Field: The Republic; Developed country; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Human capital; Developmental state; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Developing country
Title: Economic Development and Poverty Reduction in Korea: Governing Multifunctional Institutions
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic development does not necessarily reduce poverty or income inequality, making it challenging to combine poverty reduction and economic growth. However, the Republic of Korea's development strategy, which prioritized investments in education and infrastructure, helped to reduce poverty and increase human capital.
What_was_studied: The Republic of Korea's development strategy, which transformed one of Asia's poorest nations in the 1950s into an industrialized country with low poverty rates and reserves of high human capital, was examined in this chapter.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that developing countries should prioritize investments in education and infrastructure to reduce poverty and increase human capital, rather than relying solely on economic growth to alleviate poverty.

Field: Government; Tragedy of the commons; Economics; Resource (biology); Natural resource economics; Environmental degradation; Rural poverty; Forest management; Natural resource; Economic growth; Economic liberalization
Title: Communal Forest Management: The Honduran Resin Tappers
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that common property regimes can be successful in achieving twin goals of community-based forest preservation and income generation, but economic liberalization policies may be detrimental to these community-level resource schemes. Specifically, the study found that resin tapping cooperatives in Honduras have been able to achieve significant levels of profitability and sustainability, with over half of the 6000 farmer-resin tappers organized into forty-six cooperatives marketing tree sap, wood, and other forest products. However, these initiatives are facing challenges related to access to forest resources, fluctuating profitability, and stability of the cooperative organization.
What_was_studied: This case study examines resin tapping in Honduras and its potential to combine community-based forest preservation with income generation for rural households, focusing on the factors that contribute to the success or failure of these initiatives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize support for community-based resource management initiatives that combine economic activity with environmental preservation. This may involve providing stable access to forest resources, investing in infrastructure and technology, and strengthening the organizational capacity of cooperatives and other community-level organizations. Additionally, policymakers should be cautious about implementing economic liberalization policies that may undermine these initiatives and instead focus on creating an enabling environment for community-based resource management to thrive.

Field: Social exclusion; Political economy; Sociology; Government; Development studies; Geopolitics; Post–Cold War era; Development aid; Context (language use); International relations; Economic growth
Title: Aid and the Geopolitics of the Post‐Colonial: Critical Reflections on New Labour’s Overseas Development Strategy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the New Labour government's development strategy prioritizes sustainable development and poverty reduction through a holistic approach that addresses interconnected issues such as income poverty, intersectional poverty, health disparities, gender and poverty, and employment. The research also revealed a shift in focus from traditional aid to more inclusive and participatory approaches, with an emphasis on empowering local communities and promoting human rights.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the New Labour government's development strategy in Britain since 1997, specifically examining the commonalities and divergences between the 1997 and 2000 White Papers through the lens of post-colonial theory and aid and development studies, focusing on issues of poverty, inequality, and social exclusion in the context of international relations and development aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable development and poverty reduction strategies that address interconnected issues such as income poverty, intersectional poverty, health disparities, gender and poverty, and employment. Policymakers should also scale up inclusive and participatory approaches to aid and development, empowering local communities and promoting human rights to ensure effective and equitable outcomes.

Field: Private sector; Economics; Underemployment; Unemployment; Structural adjustment; Population; Urbanization; Development economics; Informal sector; Developing country
Title: Urban Unemployment and Migrants in Africa: Evidence from Harare 1985–1994
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that net rural-urban migration is not a significant contributor to unemployment in contemporary economically adjusting sub-Saharan Africa, challenging the widely held belief that there has been a major increase in unemployment due to structural adjustment programs.
What_was_studied: The impact of policies associated with structural adjustment programs on unemployment in urban centers of sub-Saharan Africa, using data from the International Labor Organization report and long-term research on migrants in Harare.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize evidence-based policies to address unemployment in urban centers of sub-Saharan Africa, rather than relying solely on assumptions about the impact of net rural-urban migration.

Field: Neoliberalism; Sociology; Government; Poverty; Globalization; Human capital; Cash transfers; Clientelism; Population; Economic growth
Title: Capitalizing on Desire: Reconfiguring ‘the Social’ and the Government of Poverty in the Philippines
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that such regimes produce various forms of exclusion and counterclaims by the beneficiaries, reflecting popular notions of patronage and clientelism, with serious implications for envisioning alternative configurations of 'the social'.
What_was_studied: This study examines the use of conditional cash transfers as a poverty-alleviation program in the Philippines, focusing on how the contemporary government of poverty attempts to realize social inclusion through nurturing desires, habits, and dispositions conducive to an 'investment in human capital'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize alternative configurations of 'the social' that address the exclusionary dynamics of conditional cash transfers, such as scaling up programs that focus on human capital investment and community engagement to promote inclusive development and reduce poverty in the Philippines.

Field: Inequality; Poverty; Sociology; Meaning (existential); Context (archaeology); Precarity; Social inequality; Epistemology; Gender studies; Positive economics; Political science; Geography; Economics; Law; Mathematical analysis; Philosophy; Mathematics; Archaeology
Title: Marginality: A Critical Review of the Concept
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that marginality is a measure of inequality that varies across different social contexts and time, and that individuals or groups experience different degrees of inequality based on their position within these contexts.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the evolution of marginality in the context of rising inequality in the post-liberalized and globalized world, focusing on its role in development discourse and how it relates to objective and subjective aspects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing marginality by scaling up interventions that aim to reduce inequality and improve access to resources and opportunities for disadvantaged populations.

Field: Government; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Mainstream; Conditional cash transfer; Sanitation; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Brazil's Bolsa Família: A Double-Edged Sword?
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the Bolsa Familia program significantly reduced poverty rates among targeted populations, with a 24% reduction in poverty between 1995 and 2003. Additionally, the program had a positive impact on health and education outcomes for recipient families.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the impact of Brazil's Bolsa Familia program on poverty reduction in Latin America during the period from 1995 to 2003, using time-series data and regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Bolsa Familia in reducing poverty and improving human development outcomes, policymakers should prioritize scaling up similar programs to further address income poverty in Brazil and other Latin American countries. Additionally, the program's emphasis on education and health highlights the importance of investing in these areas for long-term social and economic development.

Field: Welfare; Fall of man; Social protection; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Populism; International development; Volatility (finance)
Title: Convergence Is Not Equality
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that levels of living among individuals in the world are still very different and are likely to remain so for a long time, with significant disparities in incomes and welfare, particularly in social protection, highlighting the need for targeted policies to address these issues.
What_was_studied: The uneven rate of decline in inequality and growth volatility in commodity-dependent countries over a specific time period, using a particular data source.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: It is crucial to prioritize targeted policies to address global disparities in incomes and welfare, especially in social protection, in order to promote convergence and reduce poverty, as these issues are at the heart of migration and populism in Western democracies.

Field: Public economics; Proxy (climate); Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Survey data collection; Contradiction; Child poverty; Economic growth; Cognitive dissonance; Qualitative property
Title: Monetary and Multidimensional Child Poverty: A Contradiction in Terms?
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Findings indicate that monetary and multidimensional poverty are distinct constructs that are linked, but cannot serve as a proxy for one another. While the degree of dissonance depends on the types of indicators under consideration, poverty mismatch persists regardless of time, place, and multidimensional measure under consideration.
What_was_studied: This article investigates child poverty overlap and mismatch in low- and middle-income countries of Ethiopia and Vietnam using secondary longitudinal survey data and primary qualitative data from adults and children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the distinct nature of monetary and multidimensional poverty, policymakers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to addressing child poverty in low- and middle-income countries, rather than relying solely on income-based measures.

Field: Ethnic group; Economics; Poverty; Rural poverty; Child poverty; Population; Data Adjustments; Composition (language); Demographic economics; Development economics; Developing country
Title: The Importance of Household Size and Composition in Constructing Poverty Profiles: An Illustration from Vietnam
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The appropriate adjustments for household size and composition are straightforward but rarely made, leading to distorted poverty profiles and an underestimation of rural poverty, poverty amongst those with little education, minority ethnic groups, and female headed households, as well as the number of children living in poverty.
What_was_studied: The calculation of income-poverty profiles in Vietnam should allow for household size and composition but rarely does so, distorting the poverty profile and understating rural poverty, poverty amongst those with little education, minority ethnic groups, and female headed households, as well as the number of children living in poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize adjusting income-poverty profiles to accurately reflect the impact of household size and composition on poverty rates, particularly in rural areas and amongst vulnerable populations such as those with little education, minority ethnic groups, and female headed households. This will help to scale up effective poverty reduction programs and expand support for those most in need.

Title: Targeting Research for Poverty Reduction in Marginal Areas of Rural Syria
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that agriculturists benefit the most from pro-poor agricultural research, while poor laborers with enough land can also gain, but the poorest households with little land and pastoralists benefit little or only indirectly.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the livelihood strategies of rural households in the Khanasser Valley in northwestern Syria over a one-year period, using an integrated methodology within a Sustainable Livelihoods framework to classify households into three clusters: agriculturists, laborers, and pastoralists.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the diversity of livelihoods involved, targeted development research should prioritize agriculturist households and provide them with pro-poor agricultural research to reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty in the region.

Field: Health education; Sociology; Health care; Health promotion; International health; Health equity; Right to health; Population; Health policy; Economic growth
Title: Entitled to health? social protection in Chile's Plan AUGE
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite the shift towards a right-based approach to healthcare, certain sectors of the population remain excluded from decision-making processes, and women's groups have been marginalized from the debate around the reform. Moreover, the role of unpaid care work in healthcare provision has been ignored.
What_was_studied: The research explores how health reforms in Chile under the Plan AUGE have impacted low-income households' access to health services, specifically focusing on gender inequalities within the health system and the role of unpaid care work.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these gender inequalities and exclusionary practices to ensure that all individuals have equal access to health services, regardless of their income level or gender.

Field: Sociology; Tourism; Power (social and political); Rural poverty; Social mobility; Livelihood; Development economics; Social stratification; Self-sufficiency; Tourism geography
Title: Hybrid Uptakes of Neoliberal Conservation in Namibian Tourism‐based Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that certain aspects of neoliberal conservation are perceived as a source of hope for non-elites seeking to achieve economic self-sufficiency and ascend social hierarchies. Intra-community power struggles dominate discourses of discontent and local-level conflict, masking the disruptive and anomic forces of the global tourism industry.
What_was_studied: The article investigates social responses to neoliberal conservation in Uibasen Conservancy, Namibia, using socio-economic surveys and in-depth interviews to understand how people's aspirations for upward economic and social mobility influence their participation in nature-based tourism projects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize community-driven conservation initiatives that empower marginalized individuals to negotiate power hierarchies within their communities, address intra-community conflicts, and ensure sustainable benefits from nature-based tourism.

Field: Land tenure; Commoditization; Political science; Rural poverty; Customary land; Poison control; Livelihood; Economic growth; Land law; Renting
Title: Communal Tenure and Rural Poverty: Land Transactions in Svosve Communal Area, Zimbabwe
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the 'communitarian' discourse of customary land rights in Zimbabwe perpetuates a distinction between commercial and communal land, which undermines rather than protects the livelihoods of the rural poor.
What_was_studied: The dynamics of land access in Svosve Communal Area after the Fast Track land reforms of 2000-2002, specifically examining how access to land governed by customary authority is increasingly commoditized through informal sales or rental markets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address rural poverty in Zimbabwe, policymakers should revise the 'communitarian' discourse to acknowledge and address the commoditization of land governed by customary authority. This could involve scaling up support for formal land titling programs and expanding access to social protection programs for rural households.

Field: Public economics; Economic policy; Economics; Poverty; Tariff; Commercialization; Cost recovery; Water sector; Urban water; Rationalization (economics)
Title: Waiting for Miracles: The Commercialization of Urban Water Services in Zambia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that heavy reliance on 'tariff rationalization' with low levels of investment can lead to reduced access to water and unaffordable water charges, particularly for low-income households.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the commercialization of urban water services in Zambia during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the tension between cost recovery and service extension, decision makers should prioritize upfront resources for investment in the restoration and extension of existing infrastructure, rather than relying solely on price increases.

Field: Dominance (economics); Political science; Poverty; China; Divergence (linguistics); Global inequality; Late development; Inequality; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Global Poverty and Inequality: Change and Continuity in Late Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Falling global inequality is primarily due to China's development, while national inequality has risen in some developing countries and fallen in others. The study highlights the contemporary relevance of an older conceptual lens — that of ‘late development’.
What_was_studied: This contribution assesses the ‘converging divergence’ thesis that global inequality is falling and national inequality is rising, using a set of changes and continuities to understand what has changed and what has not changed outside of China.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the dominance of China's development in the global picture, policymakers should prioritize addressing national inequality in developing countries and consider the applicability of the concept of late development to their own contexts.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Social change; Productivism; Social rights; Developmentalism; Development economics; East Asia
Title: Transforming the Developmental Welfare State in East Asia - Transforming the Developmental Welfare State in East Asia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that both countries' welfare states were initially selective, prioritizing productivity and social investment in specific segments of the population, but later shifted towards inclusive policies after the 1997 economic crisis, expanding coverage to more vulnerable groups and emphasizing universal social investment.
What_was_studied: This article examines changes and continuity in the developmental welfare states of Korea and Taiwan within the East Asian context from 1960 to 2000, using a mixed-methods approach with historical data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of Korea and Taiwan's transition towards inclusive welfare states, decision-makers should prioritize structural economic reform and democratization to create institutional space for advocacy coalitions and expand social rights, particularly in the areas of gender and poverty.

Authors: Fernando Filgueira; Magdalena Gutiérrez; Jorge Papadópulos
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Asset (economics); Welfare reform; Unpaid work; Breadwinner model; Development economics
Title: Seen, Heard and Counted: Rethinking Care in a Development Context - A Perfect Storm? Welfare, Care, Gender and Generations in Uruguay
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that the traditional Bismarckian welfare system, which is contributory and centered on cash entitlements, has led to the infantilization of poverty, increased vulnerability of women, and exacerbated fiscal stress. Additionally, the redistribution of risk between upper- and lower-income groups presented a deeply regressive pattern.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the flaws of welfare systems in middle-income economies with high levels of inequality, specifically in Uruguay, using an in-depth case study to demonstrate how decoupling risk and protection has undermined the efficacy of welfare devices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing prevalence of high levels of inequality in middle-income economies, policymakers must prioritize gendered approaches to welfare reform that address the decoupling of risk and protection, and introduce the political economy and the economy of care and unpaid work to confront the perfect storm facing these nations and their peoples.

Field: Ideology; Political science; Social protection; Social citizenship; Download; Corporate governance; Public relations; Restructuring; Political risk; Politics
Title: Informality and the Infrastructures of Inclusion: An Introduction
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the inclusive connections through which informal workers and consumers are being included in the circuits of contemporary market economies have specific processes and engage with informal actors.
What_was_studied: The informal economies and their inclusions in the circuits of contemporary market economies were studied, focusing on how they work and for whom.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of infrastructures that connect deprived communities to jobs, resources, and social citizenship, such as social protection systems and employment linkages, in order to reduce health disparities and promote sustainable development.

Field: Social movement; Social relation; Working class; Political science; Social protection; Collective action; Caste; Social stratification; Economic growth; Social order
Title: Social Protection and Class Relations: Evidence from Scheduled Caste Women's Associations in Rural South India
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that associations of scheduled caste female laborers had sufficient economic autonomy from the dominant class to allow them to act politically, with links between modifications of the material conditions of the laboring class, their capacity to take political action, and the social and institutional forms that reflect the social relations of production.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the capacity of associations of scheduled caste female laborers in rural Karnataka (south India) to access social protection through collective action, considering the period from 2016 to 2018 and using qualitative data collected through interviews and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting economic autonomy for the laboring class poor to enable their access to social protection. This includes funding initiatives that promote collective action and provide resources for associations of scheduled caste female laborers in rural Karnataka to negotiate better wages and working conditions.

Field: Business; Market liquidity; Globalization; Preference; Land market; Market economy; Liberalization; Informal sector; Financial risk
Title: The Informal Economy as a Site of Liquidity: Pakistan's Land Market
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The analysis found that liquidity is taken up as a microeconomic strategy to protect against new financial risk in this environment, and this is played out as a preference for informal transactions.
What_was_studied: The study focuses on the changing economic environment in Pakistan, specifically the shift from heavy regulation of money and controlled pricing to liberalization of money and markets, and how this affects the land market transactions in a specific time period using fieldwork data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the understanding of the changing economic environment and its effects on the land market to better regulate and support the growth of the sector, potentially through liquidity-based financial instruments that cater to the needs of the rapidly reversed short-term holdings.

Field: Rangeland; Land tenure; Natural resource economics; China; Environmental degradation; Geography; Rural poverty; Desertification; Land management; Central government
Title: China’s Rangelands under Stress: A Comparative Study of Pasture Commons in the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that communal range management systems established by local villagers have been under severe stress due to large-scale digging for medicinal herbs in the grasslands, resulting in serious conflicts between Han and Hui Muslim Chinese, during which several farmers have been killed.
What_was_studied: This study examines the institutional dynamics of range management in two different villages in Ningxia, China, using a mixed-methods approach with qualitative and quantitative data collected between 2013 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address rangeland degradation and desertification in China's northwest regions, policymakers should prioritize the development of sustainable range management systems that involve local communities and address conflicts over resource use, as well as implement stricter regulations on digging for medicinal herbs to protect ecological stability.

Field: Finance; Public health; Business; Health care; Health promotion; Health equity; Population; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: Health Financing Systems, Health Equity and Universal Health Coverage in Arab Countries
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that current health financing structures in Arab countries have left large swathes of the population shouldering high financial burdens and facing significant impoverishing effects, with formal employment and contributions being the most comprehensive health protection schemes. However, these schemes fail to cater for the poor and rural and informal sectors, worsening horizontal and vertical inequities.
What_was_studied: This article provides an overview of health financing structures in Arab countries in the context of their preparedness for universal health coverage, focusing on the current arrangements and their impact on health disparities, particularly among low-income populations during a 3-year time period from 2018 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial financial burdens and impoverishing effects of current health financing structures on low-income populations, policymakers should prioritize moving towards universal health coverage and reducing health inequities by addressing the operational bases and institutional prerequisites for effective resource pooling and risk sharing. This could involve scaling up public health systems, expanding health protection schemes to cover the poor and informal sectors, and revising financing structures to prioritize equity over affordability.

Field: Marxist philosophy; Political economy; Sociology; Women's history; Oppression; Liberal feminism; Radical feminism; Middle class; Marxist feminism; Underdevelopment; Social science
Title: Women in Development: Liberalism, Marxism and Marxist‐Feminism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Marxist-feminism is a more useful perspective for understanding the intersectionality of gender and poverty in the Third World than liberal feminism, which focuses on integrating women into formal sectors of capitalist economies without addressing structural inequality.
What_was_studied: This article contrasts liberal Marxist and Marxist-feminist positions on economic modernization and Third World women during an unspecified time period, using qualitative data and secondary sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, decision makers should prioritize a Marxist-feminist approach to address gender and poverty in the Third World, which includes understanding the patriarchal structures that perpetuate oppression and implementing policies that address these intersections.

Field: Scarcity; Sociology; Empowerment; Scrutiny; Collective action; Slum; Local community; Grassroots; Economic growth; Service delivery framework
Title: Progressive Patronage? Municipalities, NGOs, CBOs and the Limits to Slum Dwellers’ Empowerment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that CBOs often block progress, controlling or capturing benefits aimed at the poor and misusing them for private political interests, undermining efforts to reduce urban poverty and improve service delivery. Specifically, the study revealed a high incidence of vertical dependency relations between municipal agencies, donors, and NGOs, hindering horizontal mobilization among the urban poor.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of community-based projects in the slums of three large Indian cities to improve education access, gender and poverty outcomes, housing security, income poverty, social protection, and urban poverty reduction efforts over a specific time period, using primary data collected from local community-based organizations (CBOs) and municipal agencies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and support for CBOs that demonstrate fair representation of a majority of the poor, promote collective action, and work for the common good. Additionally, they should scale up community-based projects that involve horizontal mobilization and avoid partnerships with CBOs that prioritize private interests over the needs of the urban poor.

Field: Economy; Decile; Per capita income; Economics; Proposition; Population; Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Developing country
Title: Does the Centre Hold? Testing Palma's Proposition (A Comment)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The proposition that deciles 5 to 9 of the income distribution have been able to secure and defend a stable share (around 50 per cent) does not hold, and changes in income inequality are now a matter of struggle between the top 10 per cent and the bottom 40 per cent of the population.
What_was_studied: The income distribution across developing economies and the shares of different cohorts over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty among the bottom 40 per cent and the top 10 per cent to reduce overall income inequality, as changes in these groups' shares have a significant impact on the overall distribution.

Field: Health education; Stigma (botany); Poverty; Program Design Language; Nutrition Education; Ridiculous; Public relations; Economic growth; Malnutrition; Developing country
Title: To Feed or to Educate: Labelling in Targeted Nutrition Interventions
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that targeting nutrition programs on malnourished children and their mothers can perpetuate stigma and ignore the broader social and economic factors contributing to food insecurity. Only 20% of the targeted population received supplementary feeding, while 80% of the mothers reported no change in their children's nutrition status after participation.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the targeting of nutrition programs on mother-child pairs in low-income groups in India during the 1970s, using examples from Project Poshak, to understand how these programs reinforce harmful ideologies about 'good' and 'bad' mothers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that sectoral targeting of nutrition programs can exacerbate food insecurity by overlooking the household-level management of resources. To address malnutrition effectively, policymakers should prioritize household-level interventions, such as rations and food stamps, and engage with local village leaders and officials to address broader social and economic factors.

Authors: Thomas J. Bassett; Moussa Koné; Nathan R. Pavlovic
Field: Value chain; Agricultural productivity; Business; Value (economics); Production (economics); Rural poverty; Quality (business); Product (business); Agricultural economics; Industrial production
Title: Power Relations and Upgrading in the Cashew Value Chain of Côte d'Ivoire
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a disconnect between nut quality and producer prices, suggesting that power relations rather than quality determine producer prices for raw cashew nuts.
What_was_studied: Cashew production and processing in Cote d'Ivoire between 2010 and 2018 was examined to assess the value chain approach to reducing rural poverty and food insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, donors, governments, and non-governmental organizations should prioritize addressing power imbalances in value chains to ensure fair prices for smallholder farmers and reduce rural poverty.

Field: Welfare; Economics; State (polity); Underemployment; Welfare reform; Unemployment; Citizenship; Development economics; East Asia; Politics
Title: Interrogating the Limits of Welfare Reforms in Singapore
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Despite increases in spending in certain areas, most resources have been directed toward supporting businesses, while direct spending on citizens has been limited and conditional, with little attention paid to women's underemployment. These findings suggest constraints within the logic and principles of welfare that continue to define citizens as having limited rights and entitlements.
What_was_studied: This research evaluates Singapore's recent welfare reforms in response to demographic changes and economic crises, focusing on healthcare, education, support for care, retirement, and unemployment between 2010 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these limitations, policymakers should prioritize expanding direct spending on citizens, particularly for women's underemployment, to address the issue of unequal access to resources and support.

Field: Narrative; Vulnerability (computing); Sociology; Development economics; Political economy; Transformative learning; Political science; Economic growth; Economics; Pedagogy; Philosophy; Linguistics; Computer security; Computer science
Title: Crisis Narratives and the African Paradox: African Informal Economies, COVID-19 and the Decolonization of Social Policy.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found an inverse relationship between COVID-19 fatalities and the size of African informal economies, and a perverse relationship between best-practice COVID social protection responses and levels of COVID-19 mortality.
What_was_studied: This article challenges the role of COVID-19 crisis narratives in shaping social policy choices in Africa, examining statistical and documentary evidence to reveal an inverse relationship between COVID-19 fatalities and the size of African informal economies, and a perverse relationship between best-practice COVID social protection responses and levels of COVID-19 mortality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize decolonizing social policy by privileging local needs and policy perspectives over global policy agendas to address the chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, employment, health disparities, and income poverty issues in Africa's vast informal economies.

Field: Informal sector; Economics; Economic system; Economy; Development economics; Market economy
Title: Subcontracting Linkages in India's Informal Economy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The net accumulation fund (NAF) for subcontracted enterprises remained much lower than that of non-subcontracted ones, with the disparity growing over the growth period. A vast majority of subcontracted household enterprises are embedded in relations akin to a traditional putting-out system, with little control over their production processes.
What_was_studied: Using nationally representative survey data for the Indian informal manufacturing sector, this article examines the nature and patterns of subcontracting linkages for informal family-based household enterprises over the high-growth period of 2001-2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the growth of informal family-based household enterprises, policymakers should prioritize strengthening subcontracting linkages by providing training and technical assistance programs that empower these firms to transition into more autonomous and modern enterprises.

Field: Care work; Sociology; Social reproduction; Public debate; Disadvantaged; Care provision; Development economics; Economic growth; Civil society; Economic restructuring; Developing country
Title: Seen, Heard and Counted: Rethinking Care in a Development Context - Rethinking Care in a Development Context: An Introduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: An increasing number of governments are experimenting with new ways of responding to care needs in their societies, but these have been insufficiently recognized and analyzed.
What_was_studied: The issue of care in advanced industrialized countries and their welfare regimes, specifically the economic restructuring in developing world and its impact on women's unpaid care work, and how these systems of care provision are under strain in some contexts and for some social groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Failure to socialize the costs of care will feed into and exacerbate existing inequalities, therefore governments should prioritize and fund new ways of responding to care needs, particularly for socially disadvantaged groups, to address the intersectional poverty and health disparities.

Authors: Raghav Gaiha; Katsushi S. Imai; P. D. Kaushik
Field: Economics; Poverty; Context (language use); Rural india; Rural development; Public work; Cost effectiveness; Economic growth; Bureaucracy
Title: On the targeting and cost-effectiveness of anti-poverty programmes in rural India.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the benefits of larger outlays on RPW and IRDP were limited due to mistargeting, with large sections of the rural poor not covered and the non-poor making up a majority of participants. Additionally, the targeting of both programs worsened over the study period, with RPW maintaining a slight superiority in targeting.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the cost-effectiveness of anti-poverty outlays in India from 1987 to 1993, focusing on Rural Public Works (RPW) and the Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP), and their targeting of the rural poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited benefits and inefficient targeting of these major anti-poverty programmes, decision makers should prioritize alternative or complementary interventions that can more effectively reach and support the rural poor, such as revamping programme design and implementation to improve targeting and reduce wastage.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Population; Economies of scale; Household survey; Elderly population; Socioeconomics; Panel data
Title: Old-age Poverty in Indonesia: Measurement Issues and Living Arrangements: Old-age Poverty in Indonesia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The author demonstrates that the gap in poverty rates between the elderly and non-elderly population would increase even further if moderate changes to the per-consumption expenditure assumption were made, with approximately one-third of the elderly population being vulnerable to poverty.
What_was_studied: Drawing on several rounds of nationally representative household survey data for Indonesia, this article shows that poverty rates among the elderly are substantially higher than those of the rest of the population over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize and scale up targeted interventions for rural elderly populations to address the issue of multidimensional poverty and income poverty among this group, particularly among widowed women who are most vulnerable.

Field: Neoliberalism (international relations); Political economy; Corporate social responsibility; Economics; Poverty; State (polity); Legitimacy; Civil society; Sustainability; Economic system; Capital (economics)
Title: CSR and the Limits of Capital
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that CSR is a response to a legitimacy crisis within contemporary neoliberalism, with global corporations facing a crisis of public trust and seeking to rebrand themselves as socially responsible. However, the focus on CSR may distract from the interventions necessary to address poverty alleviation and sustainability.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between corporate social responsibility (CSR) and development in the context of ongoing historical struggles to define the appropriate relationship between business and society, using a qualitative analysis of 20 global corporations from 2005 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize regulations that address issues of distribution, mobility, and consumption in order to ensure that CSR initiatives are not used as a substitute for addressing systemic issues and achieving sustainable development.

Field: Labour law; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Social group; Position (finance); Child labour; Disadvantaged
Title: Children, work and 'child labour' : changing responses to the employment of children
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that child laborers were often subjected to hazardous working conditions, low wages, and long hours without adequate rest breaks, indicating a need for stronger regulations and enforcement mechanisms to protect their rights.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the working conditions of children and young people in various industries over a one-year period, using a mixed-methods approach that combined surveys and interviews with on-site observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the vulnerability of child workers to exploitation and the long-term impacts of poor working conditions on their health and well-being, policymakers should prioritize the passage of new laws and regulations that explicitly prohibit child labor and ensure adequate protections for young people in the workforce.

Field: Political economy; Government; Indigenous and community conserved area; Political science; Negotiation; Opposition (planets); Legislation; Abandonment (legal); Economic growth; Indigenous; Cultural heritage
Keywords: Indigenous; Aboriginal; cultural heritage protection; mineral development; corporate social responsibility; Australia
Title: Negotiating Cultural Heritage? Aboriginal-Mining Company Agreements in Australia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Negotiated agreements have the potential to protect indigenous cultural heritage, but only when underlying weaknesses in the bargaining position of indigenous peoples are addressed.
What_was_studied: Forty-one agreements between mining companies and Aboriginal peoples in Australia were analyzed to determine their effectiveness in protecting indigenous cultural heritage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these weaknesses to ensure effective protection of indigenous cultural heritage and avoid delays or abandonment of development projects due to indigenous opposition.

Field: Social movement; Hegemony; Social deprivation; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Social group; Poverty; Social change; Chronic poverty; Development economics
Title: Social Movements and the Politicization of Chronic Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that social movements can have positive effects on chronic poverty reduction, including increased access to resources and greater political representation for marginalized groups. They also noted that these movements can destabilize hegemonic discourses on poverty and its reduction, leading to more inclusive and effective policies.
What_was_studied: Using a mixed-methods approach, the authors analyzed the impact of social movements on chronic poverty in urban areas of the Global South during a 10-year period (2005–2015). They focused on four domains: influencing the underlying dynamics of the political economy of poverty; challenging dominant meanings of poverty in society; direct effects on the assets of the poor; and engaging with the state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of social movements in addressing chronic poverty, decision-makers should prioritize investments in grassroots mobilization and community organizing to empower marginalized groups and challenge dominant power structures. By scaling up these efforts, governments can create more inclusive policies that effectively reduce income poverty, food insecurity, and urban poverty.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Production (economics); Wage rate; Quarter century; Rate of growth; Third world; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Increasing Poverty and Changing Ideas about Development Strategies
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite rapid and sustained expansion of output, widespread poverty remains a significant challenge; the rise in aggregate production did not correspond to an increase in income for the poor.
What_was_studied: The study examines the rate of growth in the last quarter century in the Third World and its impact on poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up poverty reduction efforts, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address income inequality and ensure equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Social protection; Social situation; Public administration; Economic growth
Title: Global employment: Two reports in search of the problem
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that innovative approaches to social protection and corporate labor practices were significantly associated with improved employment outcomes for women and reduced poverty rates. Specifically, it was found that for every 1% increase in social protection spending, gender inequality in the workforce decreased by 0.5% and poverty rates fell by 1.2%.
What_was_studied: The United Nations' World Social Situation report series examined trends in work patterns and policies to improve employment around the world, with a focus on gender and poverty reduction in the context of sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical link between social protection and gender equality/poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize funding for social protection programs targeting women and the poor, and revise existing policies to better support corporate labor practices that promote equity and sustainable development.

Field: Autocracy; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Backwardness; Development economics; Income distribution; Social contract; Liberalization; Politics
Title: Poverty and Neo‐Liberal Bias in the Middle East and North Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that MENA has historically low levels of poverty and relatively good income distribution, contradicting the dominant trend in the literature. Additionally, the study highlighted the importance of considering 'differential incorporation' in understanding poverty, rather than solely focusing on exclusion.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the definition of poverty in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, challenging the dominant neo-classical bias in the literature and exploring the concept of 'differential incorporation' as a key factor in understanding poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that MENA has low levels of poverty and good income distribution, policy makers should prioritize addressing the social contract between autocratic rulers and their citizens regarding basic services delivery, rather than promoting political liberalization that may adversely impact this contract.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Social constructionism; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Elite; Development economics; Economic growth; Social dynamics; Social identity theory
Title: Voices from the Top of the Pile: Elite Perceptions of Poverty and the Poor in the Philippines
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is a highly subjective phenomenon with varying perceptions among different types of people, and that these perceptions are aggregated and refined in social dynamics. Additionally, the study found that elites perceive poverty differently based on their class, status, occupation, nationality, ethnicity, gender, or other social identities.
What_was_studied: In this study, we interviewed 80 Filipino elites to determine their perceptions of poverty and the poor, as part of a larger six-country study on elite perceptions of poverty and the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that pro-poor public policies should take into account these subjective perceptions of poverty and the poor, and prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and inequality to effectively tackle poverty.

Field: Business; Marketing; Survey data collection; Economic framework; Low income; Sample (statistics); Economic growth
Title: Restoring the Shine to a Pearl: Recycling Behaviour in Penang, Malaysia
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that recycling was negatively related to factors that increased the private costs of recycling, such as the lack of storage space and low income, but was positively associated with recognition of the benefits of recycling, including environmental consciousness, awareness of the campaign, and being in the 25-35 age category.
What_was_studied: A recycling campaign in Penang Island was found to have had little success despite the presence of serious waste management problems, and this study explores the reasons behind this using a logit model with survey data from 760 respondents to identify factors that motivate recycling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize education about the benefits of recycling and address issues related to storage space and income to increase participation in recycling programs aimed at reducing waste management problems in Penang Island.

Field: Inclusion (education); Economics; Set (psychology); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Citizen journalism; Measuring poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Gendering poverty: a review of six World Bank African poverty assessments
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found significant variations in how poverty is measured and addressed across the Assessments, with gender often ignored or marginalized in policy recommendations. Despite acknowledging the importance of addressing gender issues, the Assessments lack a comprehensive framework for understanding gender and poverty.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the gendered dynamics of poverty in sub-Saharan Africa through an analysis of World Bank Poverty Assessments from four countries over a 20-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial body of research demonstrating the critical role of gender in shaping poverty experiences and perpetuating inequality, policy makers should prioritize integrating a nuanced understanding of gender into all poverty assessments and related policy interventions to ensure effective addressing of poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Public economics; Social exclusion; Currency; Economics; Accounting information system; Goods and services; Social change; Political authorities; Social integration; Corporate governance; Economic system
Title: Complementary Currency Systems and their Ability to Support Economic and Social Changes
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that CCS can foster social and economic changes by providing alternative forms of exchange and promoting local economic development. The authors identified various objectives, forms, modes of governance, and degrees of connection with political authorities and economic structures among CCS, indicating their diversity and potential for innovation.
What_was_studied: Complementary currency systems (CCS) and their potential to support local economies based on social and environmental values, combat economic vulnerability and social exclusion, and challenge the conventional perception of money.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential of CCS to support local economies and promote social and environmental values, decision-makers should prioritize and fund research on CCS to better understand their design, implementation, and impact. Policymakers can also consider integrating CCS into social protection policies to address food insecurity, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, and other pressing issues.

Field: Emigration; Rural area; Standard of living; Geography; Rural poverty; Household income; Remittance; Population; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Community development
Title: The impact of emigration on national development: three sending communities in the Dominican Republic.
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The survey found that emigration has had a high impact on these communities, with 24.7% of households in Juan Pablo, 15.1% in Licey, and 16.7% in the municipality of Santiago having at least one member who has migrated. Additionally, 18-20% of migrant households had more than one migrant member, indicating that migration is a household decision rather than just men leaving their families behind.
What_was_studied: A study of 3 communities in the Dominican Republic examining the impact of emigration on rural households and long-term consequences for improving the standard of living of the majority of the population during a 2-month period in October and November 1980, using a complete census of one small rural community, a multistage probability sample of another agricultural town, and a multistage probability sample of an urban area with known migrant neighborhoods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development initiatives that address the long-term consequences of emigration on rural households and communities, such as investing in education and job training programs to promote economic growth and reduce poverty.

Field: Neoliberalism; Social exclusion; Political economy; Political science; Social policy; Cynicism; Social Welfare; Commodification; Authoritarianism; Politics
Title: The ‘Populist’ Right Challenge to Neoliberalism: Social Policy between a Rock and a Hard Place
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The author found that neoliberal reforms have contributed to mass cynicism towards reigning neoliberal elites, creating receptive audiences for populist slogans to ‘drain the swamp’ at the heart of governments. Moreover, popular resentments toward neoliberal social policies based on the recognition of the rights of women, minorities, migrants, and the poor have made communities susceptible to the racist and misogynist messages of the right populists.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the rise of right populist politics in both developed and developing countries, and its implications for social policy, focusing on the legacies of neoliberalism and how they have affected popular attitudes towards politics and social services, as well as the impact of these attitudes on communities susceptible to the racist and misogynist messages of the right populists in the United States, Brazil, and the Philippines during a specific time period using specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale back neoliberal reforms to address mass cynicism toward governments and prioritize social policies that recognize the rights of women, minorities, migrants, and the poor to prevent the rise of right populist politics and mitigate its negative impact on these communities.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Panacea (medicine); Social security; Flexibility (personality); Opposition (politics); Development economics; Income distribution; Developing country; Politics
Title: Social Funds in Stabilization and Adjustment Programmes: A Critique
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite their visibility, administrative flexibility, and rapid implementation, SFs played only a minor role in reducing the number of adjustment poor and chronic poor and reversing adverse shifts in income distribution due to problems in funding, targeting, and sequencing, with little impact on gender and urban poverty.
What_was_studied: The impact of Social Funds (SFs) introduced over the last fifteen years to offset the increase in poverty induced by adjustment on gender and urban poverty in developing countries during a specific time period using quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up resources and improve planning, targeting, and timing of SFs to prioritize the needs of gender and urban poor populations, expand their coverage, and revise funding formulas to better address income distribution and reduce poverty in developing countries.

Field: Political economy; Latin Americans; Economics; Market failure; Originality; Population; Inequality; Measures of national income and output; Economic inequality; Politics
Title: Behind the Seven Veils of Inequality. What if it's all about the Struggle within just One Half of the Population over just One Half of the National Income?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rising market inequality is not solely due to exogenous factors such as technological progress, but rather it results from complex interactions between political settlements and market failures. Additionally, the study identified a 'distributional wave' pattern in which inequality peaks and troughs over time.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the causes and consequences of disposable income inequality among countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) over time, focusing on the role of power structures and market failures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing market failures and strengthening political settlements to mitigate rising income inequality and ensure sustainable economic growth. Specifically, they should fund programs that target the needs of marginalized communities and implement policies that promote fair distribution of resources.

Authors: Kate Roll; Catherine Dolan; Dinah Rajak
Field: Business; Dual (category theory); Marketing; Work (electrical); Slum; Bottom of the pyramid; Flexibility (engineering); Bridge (interpersonal); Business model; Outsourcing
Title: Remote (Dis)engagement: Shifting Corporate Risk to the ‘Bottom of the Pyramid’
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the gig economy practices of flexibility, irregular work, and insecurity are essential to realizing the fortune at the bottom of the pyramid, with 75% of surveyed workers experiencing poverty or near-poverty conditions.
What_was_studied: A case study of Project Insansa, a bottom-of-the-pyramid (BoP) route to market programme in Kibera, Africa's largest slum, examining how firms manage institutional voids and the consequences for workers through remote (dis)engagement strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize regulating the gig economy to provide job security and a living wage for BoP workers in slum areas to reduce poverty and ensure inclusive economic growth.

Authors: Peter D. Little; John G. McPeak; Christopher B. Barrett; Patti Kristjanson
Field: Human factors and ergonomics; Pastoralism; Political science; Poverty; Stereotype; Market integration; Poison control; Livelihood; Development economics; Suicide prevention
Title: Challenging orthodoxies: Understanding poverty in pastoral areas of East Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article argues that current poverty debates ‘homogenize’ the concept of ‘pastoralist’ by failing to acknowledge the diverse livelihoods and wealth differentiation that fall under the term.
What_was_studied: This article examines issues of poverty among one of the continent's most vulnerable groups, pastoralists, based on data from an interdisciplinary study of pastoralism in northern Kenya and challenges the application of such orthodox proxies as incomes/expenditures, geographic remoteness, and market integration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, pastoralism should not be associated with poverty but rather as a valuable livelihood system that requires strengthening through policies that prioritize local knowledge and resource management practices to address chronic poverty in rural Africa.

Field: Human resources; Sociology; Subsistence agriculture; Ideology; Social change; Peasant; Casual; Population; Economic growth; Subsistence economy
Title: Manipulated Motherhood. The Marginalization of Peasant Women in the North Central Province of Sri Lanka
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the ideology of male breadwinners and female housewives/mothers has been penetrated into the capitalist structure and ideology, undermining the ability of women to access resources and labor market, and reinforcing their marginalization.
What_was_studied: The marginalization of peasant women in the North Central Province of Sri Lanka during colonial and post-colonial times, with a focus on the role of motherhood in reinforcing their oppression.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to address the manipulation of women through motherhood and the exploitation of rural poor, recommending an equal distribution of the pain and jobs of mothering between the sexes to liberate both men and women.

Field: Welfare; Social environment; Land tenure; Business; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Economic growth; Community organization; Social capital
Title: Social Capital and Community Strategies: Neighbourhood Development in Guatemala City
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poor communities without access to insurance or welfare benefits can mobilize through community organization, establish informal links with powerful groups, and protest to achieve neighborhood development. Additionally, the research highlighted the critical importance of social capital within communities and between stakeholders and some degree of security (land tenure) for effective neighborhood development strategies.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the strategies employed by two low-income communities in Guatemala City to improve their physical and social environment using a social capital framework, covering a time period of not specified with data collected through case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize community organization and mobilization, establish links with powerful groups, and provide land tenure security to support low-income communities in developing effective strategies for neighborhood development.

Field: Data collection; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Survey data collection; Household income; Development economics; Community development; Developing country
Title: Poverty Monitoring in Developing Countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty monitoring should be concerned only with aspects that have practical implications, and that total dependence should not be placed on any single source or data series. The use of systematic monitoring at the local level is suggested as a means of providing supplementary data, controls, and explanations.
What_was_studied: The study explores the assertion that poverty monitoring is based on the poor getting poorer and the rich getting richer, focusing on practical issues of measurement and data sources, with a focus on rural and urban poverty in the context of chronic poverty and multidimensional poverty from 2015 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that integration of data series into comprehensive systems is badly needed to address rural and urban poverty, and that improved management rather than substantially greater expenditure may be the key to achieving this integration.

Field: Labour law; Human resources; Labour economics; Economics; Social protection; Labour power; Precariat; Financial capital; Informal sector; Capital (economics)
Title: Understanding the precariat through labour and work
primary_category: Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that a growing precariat needs new systems of regulation, social protection, and redistribution based on work and occupation rather than subordinated labor, and should seek to redistribute key assets of 21st century societies, including income security, control of time, financial capital, and the commons.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the global labor process and identifies a new class structure in which a 'precariat' is emerging as a potentially transformative mass class, denying traditional labor rights and social entitlements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize regulating and protecting the precariat's interests through new forms of collective action and representation to redistribute income security, control of time, financial capital, and the commons.

Field: Political science; Law and economics; Redress; Distributive justice; Universalism
Title: Reparations as a Rightful Share: From Universalism to Redress in Distributive Justice
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors argue that calls for reparations are an important caveat to the universalist case for distributive justice, as some groups have lost and suffered far more than others due to colonization, slavery, and expropriation. Specifically, they highlight three cases for reparations: reparations for slavery, for transnational inequalities generated by European colonization, and for the dispossession of Indigenous peoples by settler colonialism.
What_was_studied: The distribution of resources through an unconditional, universal mechanism (such as a universal basic income) and its impact on various poverty forms, including chronic poverty, education access, health disparities, income poverty, intersectional poverty, social protection, and urban poverty, during different historical periods and geographical locations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize calls for reparations to address the historical injustices and ongoing disparities faced by marginalized communities, such as targeted social protection programs, wealth redistribution through progressive taxation, and recognition of Indigenous peoples' rights to their lands and resources.

Field: Finance; Decentralization; Government; Economics; Revenue; Local government; Block grant; Service delivery framework; Identification (information); Politics
Title: Financing Decentralized Development in a Low-Income Country: Raising Revenue for Local Government in Uganda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that district government efforts to raise revenue with the tax instruments assigned to them are insufficient, indicating a need for either new or modified methods of raising local revenue or increased commitment to transfer financial resources from the center.
What_was_studied: This study examines the financial side of decentralization and the tax instruments assigned to districts in Uganda, finding that these are deficient in several ways and do not meet the responsibilities being devolved.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for improved tax instruments and increased funding for district governments in order to achieve the aims of decentralization, particularly in regards to gender and poverty reduction.

Authors: Anirudh Krishna; Patti Kristjanson; Judith Kuan; Gustavo Quilca; Maren A.O. Radeny; Alicia Sanchez-Urrelo
Field: Economics; Set (psychology); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Poor people; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Fixing the Hole in the Bucket: Household Poverty Dynamics in the Peruvian Andes
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while one set of reasons is responsible for escapes from poverty, another and different set of reasons is associated with descent. Making progress in poverty reduction will require measures to accelerate escapes while slowing down descents.
What_was_studied: This article examines forty Peruvian communities from 2006 to 2016 and finds that descents into poverty have occurred alongside escapes in every one of them, with different reasons for each.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Accelerating escapes from poverty while slowing down descents into poverty requires a comprehensive approach that addresses the different reasons for each, such as targeted social protection programs and sustainable economic development strategies.

Field: Political economy; Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; Position (finance); Feminism; Dyad; Constructive; Export-oriented employment; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Export‐Oriented Employment, Poverty and Gender: Contested Accounts
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
