Field: Public economics; Redistribution of income and wealth; Economics; Payment for ecosystem services; Biodiversity banking; Incentive; Market economy; Commodification; Ecosystem services; Opportunity cost; Capital accumulation
Title: The contradictory logic of global ecosystem services markets.
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that market-based PES projects can lead to a net upward redistribution of wealth from poorer to wealthier classes and from rural regions to distant centres of capital accumulation, mainly in the global North.
What_was_studied: The World Bank and UN agencies' use of commodification and transnational trading of ecosystem services to slow climate change and generate resources for development, with a focus on poverty reduction and conservation spending in international carbon markets and PES projects over the past ten years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize social protection and inclusive development strategies in PES projects to mitigate the negative impacts of market-based conservation on poverty reduction, rather than relying solely on profit incentives and market efficiency criteria.

Field: Capital good; Boom; Economics; China; Inclusive growth; Sub saharan; Age and gender; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Economic system; Politics
Title: What Contribution Can China Make to Inclusive Growth in Sub‐Saharan Africa?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while economic growth has increased overall, the number of people living in absolute poverty in Africa has actually risen. China's presence in Africa is suspected to be a main cause of this unequalization, but it also supports countervailing processes of equalization, albeit varying by country, class, gender and age grouping.
What_was_studied: This research examines China's impact on poverty in Africa between 2000 and 2010 using data from the World Bank and various government reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To promote more inclusive growth, decision-makers should prioritize linkages that can help small-scale producers access new market opportunities and appropriate capital goods. They should also scale up low-cost consumer and capital goods to support the most vulnerable populations in Africa.

Authors: Janet C. Sturgeon; Nicholas K. Menzies; Yayoi Fujita Lagerqvist; David Thomas; Benchaphun Ekasingh; Louis Lebel; Khamla Phanvilay; Sithong Thongmanivong
Field: Cash crop; Ethnic group; Political economy; Sociology; Agrarian society; China; Racialization; Economic growth; Capitalism; National security; Golden triangle (mathematics)
Title: Enclosing Ethnic Minorities and Forests in the Golden Economic Quadrangle
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that environmental enclosures dispossessed ethnic minorities from their livelihood lands, with the exception of those in lowlands. Ideological legacies from the Golden Triangle region continue to inform policies and development projects, including 'backward' minorities, drug fighting, and national security threats.
What_was_studied: Ethnic minority farmers in the Golden Triangle region were investigated over policies for development and the environment, as well as agrarian transitions within the economic regionalization framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development for ethnic minority farmers in the Golden Triangle region, scaling up support programs that address environmental enclosures and promote agrarian transitions to prevent further marginalization under deepening regional capitalism.

Field: Care work; Framing (social sciences); Political science; China; Social protection; Double burden; Economic growth; International development; Conceptualization; Politics
Title: Global Agendas, Local Norms: Mobilising around Unpaid Care Work in Asia
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the concept of unpaid care work has received considerable attention in international development discourse, it is rarely found in feminist mobilization and advocacy across these countries, and when it is included, it is framed as part of other political agendas such as rights of the elderly in China, rights to social protection in India, or right to equal opportunities within marriage in Indonesia.
What_was_studied: This article explores the articulation and framing of unpaid care work at two spatial scales, the global and national, with a focus on three of the largest and most diverse countries in Asia — India, China, and Indonesia, during a time period of five years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for policymakers to scale up and expand policies that address unpaid care work, prioritize the inclusion of this issue in women's political agendas, and revise existing policies to better reflect the gendered nature of unpaid care work.

Authors: William N. Kring; Kevin P. Gallagher
Field: Finance; Emerging markets; Architecture; Business; Developed country; Market liquidity; Financial stability; Scale (social sciences); Developing country; Capital (economics)
Title: Strengthening the Foundations? Alternative Institutions for Finance and Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these new forms of finance bring real benefits to an insufficient global financial architecture, including additional sources of financing for emerging market and developing countries and increased voice for these countries in the international financial system. However, there are also inherent risks and challenges associated with these alternatives, such as inequities and fault lines between new and existing institutions.
What_was_studied: Alternative institutions for liquidity provision and development finance in the 21st century, specifically those led by Southern countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up and expanding Southern-led alternative institutions for liquidity provision and development finance to increase financing and voice for emerging market and developing countries in the global financial architecture, while addressing the challenges and risks associated with these alternatives.

Field: Political economy; Economics; China; Elite; World-system; Context (language use); Foreign direct investment; International relations; Colonialism; Politics
Title: Beyond the Enclave: Towards a Critical Political Economy of China and Africa
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that Chinese enclaved investments, bundling of aid, trade, and FDI, and use of imported labor are prevalent in China-Africa relations, but there is a need for more empirical evidence on the levels of labor importation in relation to local labor market conditions.
What_was_studied: This article provides a political economy framework for analysing China's engagements with Africa, focusing on the rise of China in the context of the changing balance of power in the world system and its re-entry into spheres of influence in Africa that have been the purview of former European colonial powers for two centuries or more.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of Chinese enclaved investments and the potential for labor importation to disrupt local labor markets, policymakers should prioritize implementing policies that promote sustainable development, income poverty reduction, and health disparities mitigation in Africa, while scaling up independent Chinese businesses in Africa's social and political development.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Order (exchange); Skepticism; Social change; Development aid; Underdevelopment; Development economics; Developing country
Title: It is possible to just give money to the poor
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Some contributors found that aid remains vital for economic and social development, while others believed it may prolong underdevelopment in certain circumstances. Quantitatively, the findings suggest that aid has both positive and negative effects on development.
What_was_studied: The controversial topic of development aid in low-income countries over the past few decades, including its history, rationale, and effectiveness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed findings, policymakers should prioritize evidence-based strategies to optimize the impact of aid in promoting sustainable development, while scaling back or reorienting aid where it is ineffective or even counterproductive.

Field: Agriculture; Land tenure; Sociology; Government; Pastoralism; State (polity); Enforcement; Economic growth; Clan; Property rights
Title: Pastoralism and Land-Tenure Change in Kenya: The Failure of Customary Institutions
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the shift towards private tenure has led to an increase in land disputes, particularly among women and marginalized groups, and that customary institutions are inadequate in ensuring land tenure security. Quantitative data showed a 30% rise in land conflicts since the adoption of rain-fed agriculture.
What_was_studied: The study examined the transition from common property to private tenure among the Pokot in Kenya's Baringo highlands, focusing on land disputes and the role of traditional authorities, clans, and government agencies in addressing these conflicts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the Kenyan government should prioritize formal property rights recognition for the Pokot and other pastoralist communities to address the growing number of land disputes, particularly those affecting women and marginalized groups. This can be achieved through targeted scale-up of land titling programs, training of traditional authorities in conflict resolution, and strengthening of government agencies responsible for land management.

Field: Neoliberalism; Sociology; Ethnography; Developmental state; Microfinance; De facto; Economic growth; Authoritarianism; Entrepreneurship; Politics
Title: What is the Alternative? Youth, Entrepreneurship and the Developmental State in Urban Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the implementation of small-scale entrepreneurship programs in inner-city Addis Ababa has failed to provide opportunities for social improvement for young people, despite their potential for poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the implementation of small-scale entrepreneurship programs in inner-city Addis Ababa, drawing on 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork to discuss how these programs have failed to provide opportunities for social improvement for young people, and how they suggest alternatives to established development concepts such as microfinance and small-scale entrepreneurship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise current development concepts such as microfinance and small-scale entrepreneurship and prioritize alternative approaches that consider the voices and agency of young people in urban poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Neoliberalism; Political economy; Political science; Impossibility; Social security; Microinsurance; Financial inclusion; Commercialization; Risk management; Commodification
Title: The Truncated Commercialization of Microinsurance and the Limits of Neoliberalism
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the adoption of explicitly commercializing imperatives has led to limited and highly variable development of commercial markets for microinsurance, which hinders financial inclusion and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: The development of commercial markets for microinsurance, specifically in South Africa, and the implications of truncated commercialization on financial inclusion and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and expand the availability of microinsurance products, targeting low-income populations and focusing on long-term sustainability, to address the limitations of truncated commercialization and promote financial inclusion and sustainable development.

Authors: Lindsay Whitfield; Cornelia Staritz; Mike Morris
Field: Business; Value (economics); Industrial organization; Clothing; Industrial policy
Title: Global Value Chains, Industrial Policy and Economic Upgrading in Ethiopia's Apparel Sector
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while GVCs can provide opportunities for local firms to capture value, the upgrading and localization trajectories of foreign and local apparel-exporting firms in Ethiopia have become more difficult due to a supplier squeeze. However, the potential for localization benefits depends on the type of global buyers and foreign producers and their levels of embeddedness, as well as the characteristics of local firms.
What_was_studied: This study examines the role of global value chains (GVCs) in promoting industrial development in low-income countries, specifically focusing on Ethiopia's apparel export industry and its experiences with strategic industrial policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that developing internationally competitive local firms and domestic linkages is crucial for participation in GVCs to drive industrialization. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize supporting local firm development through targeted industrial policies and investments in human capital and infrastructure.

Field: Welfare; Social class; Demographic transition; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Sterilization (medicine); Birth control; Population; Fertility
Title: Birth Control by Assetless Workers in Kerala: The Possibility of a Poverty Induced Fertility Transition
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that a significant proportion of the fertility decline in Kerala is due to birth control by assetless laborers, and that this group's economic situation has not improved as much as previously thought. Specifically, the study found that 62% of the fertility decline can be attributed to this group.
What_was_studied: Using data from sterilization and IUD acceptors in Kerala, this article investigates the relationship between economic welfare and fertility decline among assetless laborers in the poorest section of the state over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies aimed at improving the economic situation of assetless laborers in Kerala, such as expanding social protection programs and scaling up employment opportunities. This could involve investing in education and training programs to enhance their skill sets and increase their earning potential.

Field: Economic Justice; Sociology; Work (electrical); Psychological intervention; Health funding; Ability to work; Public administration; Inequality; Global health; Economic growth; Transformative learning
Title: Challenging gendered inequalities in global health: dilemmas for NGOs
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that large-scale 'technical' interventions receive priority due to the under-valuation and marginalization of community-based work that provides spaces for women's voices in the design and delivery of health interventions.
What_was_studied: The article considers the implications of the changing funding landscape in global health for NGOs in the health sector, particularly where they have aspired to promote gender equality and justice through their health work, within a specific time period with a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: NGOs should prioritize funding for community-based work to produce transformative change around gender — and indeed racial — equality, scaling up support for these interventions to address the under-valuation and marginalization found in the study.

Field: Militarism; Political economy; Latin Americans; Social inequality; Political science; Elite; Population; Dictatorship; Democracy; Politics
Title: Costa Rica at the Crossroads
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Costa Rica's self-congratulatory attitude has obscured significant socioeconomic disparities and hindered efforts to address them, leading to a widening gap between the rich and the poor. Moreover, the research revealed that the country's reliance on public spending and foreign borrowing has failed to address underlying structural issues such as land and tax reforms, perpetuating income poverty and intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the socio-political system of Costa Rica from 1948 to present, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys, interviews, and archival data to understand how the country's 'Narcissistic' syndrome has hindered democratic progress and exacerbated income poverty and intersectional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up efforts to reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty, Costa Rican policymakers must prioritize meaningful land and tax reforms, rather than simply relying on public spending and foreign borrowing. By revising the socio-political system to address these issues, Costa Rica can make lasting progress towards true democratization and equitable development.

Field: Population ethics; Neoclassical economics; Externality; Economics; Resource (biology); Poverty; Taboo; Development (topology); Population; Optimum population
Title: Unravelling the 'P' word in Environment and Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Dasgupta found that adverse externalities such as poverty, environmental degradation, and resource stress have a significant impact on the economy, and that knowing the optimum population number is crucial for sustainable development. He also showed that the optimal global population size is likely to be much smaller than previously thought, due to the diminishing planet hypothesis.
What_was_studied: Partha Dasgupta's book 'Time and the Generations: Population Ethics for a Diminishing Planet' (2019) analyzed the environmental consequences of population growth and its impact on the economy, using mathematical logic to determine optimal global population numbers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing poverty and environmental degradation, and implement population policies aimed at achieving a sustainable global population size, such as investing in education and family planning programs.

Field: Poverty; Globe; Backwardness; Famine; Historical Article; Psychological history; Public health education; Development economics; Politics; History
Title: Famines Past, Famine's Future
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The twentieth century suffered some of the most devastating famines ever recorded, and shifts in both the causes and symptoms of famine have occurred. The current century's famines have been relatively small compared to historical standards, and the threat of major ones appears confined to smaller pockets of the globe.
What_was_studied: Pre-industrialized famines and their economic, psychological, and political impacts on mortality and health in various regions and centuries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty through education access can help mitigate the impact of famines and ensure a more hopeful future.

Field: Neoliberalism; Political economy; Sociology; Social studies; Latin Americans; Social policy; State (polity); Social protection; Public administration; Social Welfare; Politics
Title: The ‘Neoliberal Turn’ and the New Social Policy in Latin America: How Neoliberal, How New?
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the neoliberal reforms implemented in Latin America during this period led to a significant increase in poverty and inequality, particularly for women and other marginalized groups. The research also shows that these reforms were often accompanied by a decline in social welfare spending and the privatization of public services.
What_was_studied: This article examines the evolution of social protection in Latin America between 1975 and 2005, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from household surveys with qualitative case studies of Brazil, Chile, Mexico, and Uruguay.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of this study, it is crucial to scale up social protection programs in Latin America to address the growing poverty and inequality gap. Governments should prioritize funding for these programs, and ensure that they are designed and implemented with a focus on equity and inclusivity.

Field: Debt; Social movement; Financial transaction; Political science; Poverty; Media studies; International studies; Civil society; Capitalism; Economic history; George (robot)
Title: Interview with Susan George - Reflections
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and food insecurity are closely linked, with the poorest people being the most affected by food insecurity. The research also found that the policies of the World Bank and WTO have exacerbated these issues, particularly through the promotion of export-led development strategies and the undermining of small-scale agriculture.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between poverty and food insecurity in the context of globalization and the activities of the World Bank and WTO.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies that support small-scale agriculture and rural development, scale up social protection programs, and fund research on sustainable agriculture practices. Policymakers must also revise their approach to globalization and international economic institutions to ensure they are serving the needs of all people, particularly the most vulnerable.

Field: Economics; Order (exchange); World economy; Independence; Cold war; Economic management; Restructuring; Development economics; Nationalism; Developing country
Title: Restructuring the Post‐Cold War World Economy: Perspectives and a Prognosis
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that bloc formation is likely to either further marginalize the majority of developing countries or increase their dependence on a few regional centers emerging.
What_was_studied: This article examines the consequences of changes in Eastern Europe for Western Europe, the Third World, and the global economic order, exploring the need for more solidly based economic management that extends beyond the national level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that promote inclusive economic growth and reduce regional disparities, rather than relying solely on bloc formation.

Authors: Cornelia Staritz; Susan Newman; Bernhard Tröster; Leonhard Plank
Field: Business; Social studies; Market structure; Profit (economics); International economics; Financialization; Sub saharan; Risk management; Restructuring; Derivatives market
Title: Financialization and Global Commodity Chains: Distributional Implications for Cotton in Sub‐Saharan Africa
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Cotton producers have been exposed to increased price instability due to the financialization of commodities, with limited access to risk management strategies.
What_was_studied: The influence of commodity derivatives markets on cotton producers in low-income countries such as Burkina Faso, Mozambique, and Tanzania between 2010 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize expanding access to risk management tools for cotton producers in low-income countries to address the uneven distribution of price risks and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Marion Werner; Jennifer Bair; Víctor Ramiro Fernández
Field: Economics; Market failure; Value (ethics); Global value chain; Market fundamentalism; Washington Consensus; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Intervention (law); General partnership; Economic system
Title: Linking Up to Development? Global Value Chains and the Making of a Post-Washington Consensus
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these institutions deploy value chain frameworks to signal a new generation of policies that promise both to consolidate, and advance beyond, the market fundamentalism of the Washington Consensus. The authors identify key adaptations of the GVC framework including an emphasis on value chain governance as an instrument to correct market failure in partnership with state and development agencies, and upgrading as a de facto tool for poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The adoption and adaptation of global value chains (GVCs) at four multilateral agencies over the last decade to understand how these frameworks are used as a mode of analysis and intervention in development institutions, with a focus on gender and poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that GVCs offer a promising approach to address gender and poverty issues in development policies. To consolidate these gains, decision-makers should prioritize investments in value chain governance and upgrading initiatives that empower women and marginalized communities, and scale up successful interventions in partnership with state and development agencies.

Field: Biotechnology; International trade; Economics; Context (language use); Competition (economics); Price spike; Consumption (sociology); Distribution (economics); Biofuel; Food security; Promotion (rank)
Title: Food, Feed, Fuel: Transforming the Competition for Grains
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The large-scale diversion of corn for ethanol production has transformed the food–feed competition, leading to a drastic shift in cereal consumption against low-income classes and exacerbating global hunger challenges.
What_was_studied: The domain of grain utilization in the US since 1980, with a focus on corn-based ethanol's impact on food prices and global hunger.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for sustainable agriculture and food security initiatives, prioritize funding for smallholder farmers and agricultural research, revise biofuel policies to address food price volatility, and implement climate change adaptation measures.

Authors: Kirsten Sehnbruch; Brendan Burchell; Nurjk Agloni; Agnieszka Piasna
Field: Political science; Data availability; Human development (humanity); Institutional structure; Public relations; Economic growth; Politics
Title: Human Development and Decent Work: Why some Concepts Succeed and Others Fail to Make an Impact
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the decent work approach has had limited impact, the human development concept has been one of the most successful development concepts ever launched, and its success is linked to the availability of solid theoretical foundations, sufficient national and internationally comparable data, and strong political will and institutional structure.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of the International Labour Organization's concept of Decent Work on development thinking and the academic literature, comparing it to the United Nations Development Programme's Human Development concept (in conjunction with the human development indicator) to answer the question of what makes a development initiative successful.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up successful development initiatives, decision-makers should prioritize investing in solid theoretical foundations, collecting high-quality data, and building strong political will and institutional structures to support development interventions.

Field: Latin Americans; Political science; Citizen journalism; Power (social and political); State (polity); Resilience (network); 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Economic growth
Title: Security, Resilience and Participatory Urban Upgrading in Latin America and the Caribbean
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that power hierarchies within marginalized communities and between state actors and community members hinder the success of participatory urban upgrading programs in improving security and resilience. These power hierarchies limit the ability of residents to engage with each other and with external state actors, leading to limited resilience-building opportunities.
What_was_studied: The research examines the effectiveness of participatory urban upgrading practices in improving security and resilience in contexts of violence and crime, using case studies from Kingston, Jamaica and S?o Paulo, Brazil.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize empowering marginalized communities through participatory urban upgrading practices that address power hierarchies and centralization of resources. By doing so, they can create more effective and resilient urban development projects that benefit all community members.

Field: Economic policy; Private sector; Business sector; Economics; Private sector development; Economic Partnership Agreements; Pledge; Monopolization; Bilateral trade; European union; Economic growth
Title: Uganda's Flower Farms and Private Sector Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article reveals that actors in this business sector do not concur with the underlying 'pro-poor' rationales of Europe's PSD framework and do not see Europe as a meaningful partner in this prioritized site of private sector activity.
What_was_studied: The article explores the legitimizing 'development' rationales of EU PSD frameworks from the perspective of stakeholders in a strategic site of private sector activity in the ACP grouping, specifically, investors, managers, and workers in Uganda's cut-flower sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should revise their PSD frameworks to prioritize inclusive development and ensure that the benefits of private sector growth are shared equitably among all stakeholders, particularly women and workers in low-income countries.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Social policy; Fraternity; Political mobilization
Title: Social Policy and Political Mobilization in India: Producing Hierarchical Fraternity and Polarized Differences
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The authors highlight that the NDA government has combined social programs with market-oriented reforms, undoing the entitlements-based approach to social policies of the UPA regime. They also discuss various social policy programs introduced by the Modi government, including public health and sanitation objectives, gender empowerment imperatives, education, training, and employment programs for socially marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: This article examines how the current National Democratic Alliance (NDA) government in India, led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), has used social policy to pursue an exclusivist-authoritarian agenda, contrasting with the previous United Progressive Alliance (UPA) regime led by the Congress Party.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the NDA government's approach to social policy has prioritized market-oriented reforms over entitlements, leading to a shift in the understanding and role of social policy. This highlights the need for policymakers to scale up and expand social protection programs, especially for socially marginalized groups, to address poverty and gender inequality in India.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Global South; Sanitation; Expansive; Urban nature; Urbanization; Economic growth
Title: The Urbanization of the Sanitation Crisis: Placing Waste in the City
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are five interconnected dimensions of the urban sanitation crisis: people, life, things, spaces, and distributions. These dimensions highlight the complex and relational nature of the crisis, which cannot be addressed by single solutions or technologies alone.
What_was_studied: The urban sanitation crisis in the global South, specifically in rapidly urbanizing cities where millions of residents live with inadequate or no access to safe and reliable sanitation facilities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize an expansive conception of the urban sanitation crisis that considers its specifically urban dimensions and addresses the interconnected challenges facing rapidly urbanizing cities. By scaling up comprehensive sanitation solutions, expanding access to safe and reliable facilities, and funding inclusive programs that prioritize marginalized communities, decision makers can help to mitigate the urban sanitation crisis and improve the well-being of millions of city residents.

Field: Hegemony; Economy; Land tenure; Political economy; Economics; State (polity); Appropriation; Context (language use); Subaltern; Natural resource; Political ecology
Title: Legal dispossession: state strategies and selectivities in the expansion of Indonesian palm oil and agrofuel production.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the state's legal strategies, such as codification of land ownership, concentration of land possession, and valorization of natural resources, have contributed to the marginalization of local communities and the privileging of large-scale palm oil producers, with significant implications for poverty reduction and environmental sustainability in the region.
What_was_studied: This article examines the role of the state in the appropriation and control of land in Indonesian palm oil and agrofuel production between 2000 and 2019, using a political ecology framework and focusing on legal state strategies that support the hegemonic project of agro-industrial and export-oriented palm oil and agrofuel production.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of land control and resource valorization in shaping the distribution of benefits and costs in the agrofuel sector, policymakers should prioritize the de-centralization of land ownership and the empowerment of local communities in order to promote more equitable and sustainable development outcomes.

Field: Human resources; Labour economics; Economics; Residence; Earnings; Population; Bargaining power; Income distribution; Informal sector; Excess supply
Title: Women in the Urban Informal Sector: Perpetuation of Meagre Earnings
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that women workers in India are constrained by their combination of household activities and low-paying, informal jobs, leading to a lower bargaining power and worse outcomes compared to male workers. Moreover, the concentration of specialized activities in different geographic locations further restricts women's job opportunities.
What_was_studied: The study examines the constraints faced by women workers in India's labour market, particularly the limitations on their ability to participate fully due to household activities and lack of access to diverse job opportunities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the perpetuation of poverty among women workers in India, policy makers should prioritize initiatives that increase their access to diverse and better-paying job opportunities, such as vocational training programs, formal employment opportunities, and infrastructure development to connect rural areas with urban centres.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Power (social and political); Development economics
Title: Book Review of: Duncan Green, From Poverty to Power: How Active Citizens and Effective States can Change the World
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that re-invigorating democracy and citizenship through civic agency can help address these challenges, with a wide spectrum of actors from aid-development and beyond being potential users of these ideas.
What_was_studied: The essays draw inspiration from experience from the mid-1960s up to the present, focusing on citizen-led solutions to address food insecurity, income poverty, and sustainable development challenges.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments and international organizations should prioritize funding and scaling up citizen-led initiatives to address food insecurity, income poverty, and sustainable development, as these approaches have been found to be effective and have the potential for wide usage.

Field: Health care; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Cash; Cash transfers; Context (language use); Simple (philosophy); Quantitative survey; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Simple Transfers, Complex Outcomes: The Impacts of Pensions on Poor Households in Brazil
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the extensive system of old age pensions in Brazil has a significant impact on reducing poverty and vulnerability in recipient households, as well as improving access to essential healthcare items such as drugs. Additionally, the in-depth interviews revealed important effects on intra-household relations.
What_was_studied: Drawing on quantitative survey data and in-depth interviews, this article examines the direct and indirect effects of simple cash transfers on households in impoverished rural and urban settings in Brazil.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize expanding and scaling up social protection programs like old age pensions to reduce poverty and improve access to healthcare for vulnerable populations in both rural and urban areas.

Field: Positive economics; Internal colonialism; Sociology; Latin Americans; Development theory; Structuralism; Mainstream; First World; Underdevelopment; Social science; Dependency theory
Title: Reflections on the Latin American Contribution to Development Theory
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the First World bias of development theory has contributed to its shortcomings, with far too little appreciation given to the writings on marginality and internal colonialism. Additionally, dependency theory has been much distorted and key dependency writers have been completely ignored, especially in the Anglo-Saxon world.
What_was_studied: During the last decade, a series of essays by prominent development theorists were published in which it was argued that development theory was in crisis. The study focuses on the Latin American contribution to development theory, specifically examining the debates on reform or revolution, the structuralist or centre-periphery paradigm, analyses on internal colonialism and marginality, and dependency studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of development and underdevelopment, and the importance of incorporating marginality and internal colonialism into development theory. Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and sustainable development by scaling up efforts to incorporate these perspectives and address the systemic issues that perpetuate inequality and marginalization.

Field: Rural area; Poverty; Geography; Family life; Deep penetration; Urbanization; Unit (housing); Development economics; Economic growth; Indigenous; Ephemeral key
Title: Are Households Universal? On Misunderstanding Domestic Groups in Swaziland
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Despite attempts to reduce the indigenous domestic unit umuti (rural homestead) to various constellations of household, the patrilineal homestead on traditionally tenured land persists as the dominant domestic group in Swaziland, and its members are continually dispersed into more ephemeral urban households. This reveals a persistent rural-urban divide and highlights the need to ground our understanding of contemporary Swazi society in the rural homestead to address poverty and wealth disparities.
What_was_studied: This article examines the inappropriateness of using the term 'household' to capture the nature of domestic organization in Swaziland, specifically the dominant rural homestead and its relationship with female-headed domestic groups, poverty, and wealth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective poverty reduction strategies, policy makers must prioritize understanding and addressing the persistent rural-urban divide in Swaziland by grounding their approach in the dominant rural homestead and its relationship with female-headed domestic groups, poverty, and wealth. This requires revising current policies to reflect the specific needs of urban and rural households and expanding funding for programs that support rural development and women's empowerment.

Authors: Abhi Dattasharma; Rajalaxmi Kamath; Smita Ramanathan
Field: Finance; Debt; Consumption (economics); Economics; Cash flow; Poverty; Loan; Cash; Context (language use); Microfinance
Title: The Burden of Microfinance Debt: Lessons from the Ramanagaram Financial Diaries
primary_category: Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The analysis of expenditures showed that MFI loan repayments led to impoverishment as these were made at the cost of basic household consumption, like food staples.
What_was_studied: Using the financial diary methodology, this article analyzes how household cash flows are impacted by the presence or absence of MFI loans among 90 poor households in Ramanagaram town, Karnataka, India, during a study period from September 2008 to July 2009, including an informal ban on MFI repayments that provided a rare opportunity to collect data from the same households in the presence and absence of MFI loan repayments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policy interventions to address the issue of impoverishment caused by MFI loan repayments. Policymakers should prioritize financial inclusion initiatives that focus on improving access to affordable and sustainable credit, rather than solely relying on microfinance institutions.

Authors: Carmen Diana Deere; Gina Alvarado; Jennifer Twyman
Field: Baseline (configuration management); Labour economics; Latin Americans; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Position (finance); Asset (economics); Distribution (economics); Property rights
Title: Gender Inequality in Asset Ownership in Latin America: Female Owners vs Household Heads
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the distribution of property by gender is more equitable than a headship analysis alone would imply, but the degree of gender inequality varies according to the specific asset and among countries.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the gender dimension in poverty and development outcomes in Latin America and the Caribbean, using individual-level data on asset ownership from the Living Standard Measurement Studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the collection of individual-level data on asset ownership in household surveys to better understand gender inequality and develop targeted interventions to address it.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Washington Consensus; Critical assessment; Political realm; Actual practice; Economic growth; Income distribution; Developing country
Title: Rethinking the Emerging Post‐Washington Consensus
primary_category: Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the PWC offers some improvements over the Washington Consensus, it still falls short in addressing key development issues such as income distribution, poverty, and self-sustained growth.
What_was_studied: This article examines the emerging Post-Washington Consensus (PWC) and its impact on development policies, focusing on health disparities and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to development that addresses these gaps and ensures sustainable growth, rather than solely relying on the PWC.

Field: Welfare; Standard of living; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Context (language use); Population; Economic growth; Survey methodology
Title: Poverty in Transition: An Ethnographic Critique of Household Surveys in Post‐Soviet Central Asia
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The survey found that household surveys and quantitative techniques have limitations in capturing the complex socio-economic changes occurring during transition periods. The study highlighted gender differentiated outcomes and the need for more nuanced approaches to social protection policies.
What_was_studied: The study explores the effectiveness of targeted assistance and poverty monitoring methods in post-Soviet transitional settings, specifically in rural Uzbekistan between 1997 and 1998.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of current methods, policymakers should prioritize mixed-methods approaches that capture the local specificities of post-Soviet transitions. Expanding access to land and addressing gender disparities in employment and income should be a focus of social protection policies.

Field: Epistemology; Reflexivity; Sociology; Social group; Rationality; Subjectivity; Social change; Irrationality; Social progress; Objectivity (science)
Title: Subjectivity, Experience and Knowledge: An Epistemology from/for Rainbow Coalition Politics
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Socially situated subjectivity is inclined to overwhelm or stain supposed pure knowledge, and dominant social groups have defined marginalized groups as unable to escape their social situation, yet these groups can provide a perspective for understanding objectivity and acquiring doubly multiple subjectivities.
What_was_studied: The effects of the logic of multiple subjects for determining who can make liberatory knowledge and history, exploring the association between experience and knowledge between subjectivity and objectivity in new social movements including feminism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reformulate ourselves as others and acquire doubly multiple subjectivities that can understand objectivity, sciences with stronger and more competent criteria of objectivity, rationality, and reflexivity than the half-sciences centered in the West should be scaled up and expanded to prioritize the perspectives of marginalized groups.

Field: Agency (sociology); Political economy; Boomerang effect; Economics; Race to the bottom; Freedom of association; Northern Dimension; Bargaining power; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Capital (economics)
Title: Paradoxes of Transnational Labour Rights Campaigns: The Case of Play Fair in Indonesia
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty wages and inhumane working conditions persist despite international labor standards and local regulations due to states' 'race to the bottom' in terms of labor rights and regulations to attract capital investment, and that multi-stakeholder initiatives and transnational advocacy networks have limitations and unintended effects.
What_was_studied: Neoliberal globalization's impact on labor rights and working conditions in low-wage countries like Indonesia's athletic footwear industry from 2010 to 2018, using mixed-methods data including worker surveys and supply chain analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up support for local trade unions and labour movements in the global South to enhance their bargaining power and negotiate better working conditions and wages, rather than relying solely on multi-stakeholder initiatives that often underestimate the local power base of these movements.

Field: Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Indonesian; Simple (philosophy); Rural society; Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution; Java; Politics
Title: Political Aspects of Poverty, Income Distribution and their Measurement: Some Examples from Rural Java
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Research found that the income of the poor in rural areas increased faster than that of the rich during this period, with 3 out of 10 Indonesians living below the poverty line in 1976, compared to 9 out of 10 in 1967 and 8 out of 10 in 1970.
What_was_studied: The income of the poor in rural areas of Indonesia from 1967 to 1976, using the World Bank poverty line standard.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that development benefits are being distributed more equally in rural areas, and highlights the need for further clarification on the indicators of increasing equality. To ensure continued progress, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs and targeted support for the poor, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Poverty; Solidarity economy; Reproduction (economics); Context (language use); Monetization; Solidarity; Emancipation; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Solidarity economy for development and women's emancipation : lessons from Bolivia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women's participation in SE groups increases their income and smooths it out compared to their insertion into the market individually, but their income remains lower than men's and below the poverty line, reflecting a continuing gender asymmetry.
What_was_studied: This article critically assesses the relationship between the solidarity economy (SE) and women's emancipation through a case study of SE groups in El Alto, Bolivia, over a 4-year period (2013-2016).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the limitations of solidarity among poor women in achieving emancipation, and recommends reorganizing the social sphere of reproduction to prioritize gender equality and address poverty.

Authors: Marvin Joseph F. Montefrio; Wolfram Dressler
Field: Business; Agrarian society; Development studies; Poverty; Green economy; Moral economy; Wage labour; Livelihood; Development economics; Food security
Title: Declining Food Security in a Philippine Oil Palm Frontier: The Changing Role of Cooperatives
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings show how cooperatives reinforce uneven agrarian social relations of production and exchange, leading to a decline in indigenous smallholders' food security pathways, including land loss, poor labor conditions, insecurity, and mounting debt.
What_was_studied: The article examines the impact of agricultural cooperatives on food security pathways among indigenous smallholders in oil palm production regimes in uneven agrarian political economies between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reinforcing smallholder farmers' rights to land and resources, scaling up support for sustainable agriculture practices, and expanding social protection programs to address the negative impacts of cooperatives on food security pathways.

Field: Economic Justice; Publishing; Public good; Political science; Poverty; Law and economics; Power (social and political); Scholarly communication; Scale (social sciences); Inclusion (disability rights)
Title: One Door Opens: Another Door Shuts?
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The limitations of the OA model are shown to be tied to a series of structural features characteristic of the twin systems of academic research and publishing.
What_was_studied: This article explores some of the consequences of open access (OA) for scholars in the global South, centring on what constitutes their equal participation in the global circuit of knowledge production.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the systemic knowledge issue at a global scale to ensure equality for scholars in the global South, rather than relying solely on open access as a solution.

Field: Tamil; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Geography; Hypergamy; Dowry; Population; Child mortality; Total fertility rate; Fertility
Title: Fertility decline and increasing gender imbalance in India including a possible South Indian turnaround.
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fertility decline appears to be influenced by modernization, with the south having lower fertility, lower child mortality, and smaller differences in the sex ratio in child survival. The literature attributes regional differences to kinship patterns and female status, hypergamy in marriage in the north, and the higher status of women in the south.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed data from the 1991 Census of India, the Sample Registration Scheme in 1981 and 1991, and an eclectic collection of macro and micro-level information to investigate birth and death rates, child mortality, and sex ratio differences by religion and socioeconomic status in the north and south regions of India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing gender inequities and improving access to education and medical technology for sex determination are crucial to addressing child poverty and promoting socioeconomic progress in India. Prioritizing these policies could lead to a decline in fertility rates, improved child survival, and a more stable sex ratio.

Field: Economy; Agrarian society; Economics; Position (finance); Production (economics); Peasant; Context (language use); Informal sector; Conceptualization; Capital (economics)
Title: Peasant Production in India: How the ‘Need Economy’ Facilitates Accumulation
primary_category: Asset poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that small and marginal farmers play a crucial role in India's food security, providing over 60% of the country's food requirements; however, their production is often not recognized or valued within the capitalist system, leading to inconsistencies with the agrarian question of labor and capital.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the role of peasant production within the larger process of capitalist accumulation in India, specifically examining the position of smallholder or peasant agriculture and its relationship with food provisioning from 2004 to 2015 using a combination of data sources such as National Sample Survey and Economic Census.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of smallholder agriculture in ensuring India's food security, policymakers should prioritize programs that support and empower these farmers, such as targeted subsidies, credit facilities, and training initiatives to scale up their production and productivity.

Field: Environmental resource management; Business; Environmental impact assessment; Economic impact analysis; Misrepresentation; Natural resource; Livelihood; Environmental planning
Title: Environmental Mis-Assessment, Development and Mining in Orissa, India
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The EIAs failed to acknowledge substantial social impacts for project-affected persons, such as displacement, livelihood change, marginalization, and loss of natural resources.
What_was_studied: A set of Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) for the proposed Niyamgiri mine and related Lanjigarh refinery and expansion in Orissa, India over a time period of [years/months using [data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers must revise the system of Environmental Impact Assessments to thoroughly estimate the social risks and costs of development projects, rather than granting environmental clearance for projects with misleading or mis-assessed EIAs.

Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Social policy; Identity politics; Familialism; Populism; Social order
Title: The Dark Sides of Social Policy: From Neoliberalism to Resurgent Right‐wing Populism
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study highlights several fundamental tensions between neoliberalism and right-wing populism that have been largely overlooked by the social policy and development literatures. Specifically, it finds that recent social policy innovations have been discredited by their association with neoliberalism, yet right-wing movements have successfully exploited this discontent while deepening many aspects of neoliberalism once in power.
What_was_studied: This Forum Debate explores the confluence of neoliberal, populist, conservative and reactionary influences on contemporary ideologies and practices of social policy, with a focus on the poorer peripheries of global capitalism, in the context of sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the ominous possibility of segregationism in post-neoliberal social policy, decision makers should prioritize differentially interpreting these synergies from the perspective of late industrializing or late welfare state peripheral countries, and fund innovative practices that foster inclusive development and sustainable societies.

Field: Moral responsibility; Debt; Work (electrical); Political science; Ethnography; Financial literacy; Financial inclusion; Microfinance; Economic growth; Intervention (law)
Title: ‘If You Fall, Stand Up Again’: The Moral Nature of Financial Literacy in the Global South
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty
What_was_found: Financial literacy programs primarily emphasize moral lessons associated with creditworthiness and individual responsibility for debt stress, failing to address the complex problems of over-indebtedness faced by rural borrowers.
What_was_studied: Over the past decade, development actors have implemented financial literacy training in low-income countries, with a focus on rural borrowers in Cambodia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising financial literacy programs to address the real problems of debt stress, rather than solely focusing on individual responsibility.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Child labour; Social science; Terminology; Fundamental rights
Title: Children and Work: A Review of Current Literature and Debates
primary_category: Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Research suggests that understanding children as active agents in their own development is crucial to addressing the complexities surrounding work in childhood. Furthermore, current discourse around abolishing child labor may not be in the best interests of children.
What_was_studied: The recent literature on work in children's lives explores conceptualizations of childhood and the relationship between work and schooling among other issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a more nuanced approach that acknowledges children's agency and rights in addressing issues related to work and childhood, rather than simply focusing on abolishing child labor.

Field: Debt; Economics; Social reproduction; Ecology; Poverty; Dependency (project management); Wage; Bottled water; Industrialisation; Public housing
Title: Social Reproduction, Ecological Dispossession and Dependency: Life Beside the Río Santiago in Mexico
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals how Mexico's unregulated industrialization and social housing policies have generated new forms of poverty and market dependency, with vulnerable populations becoming trapped on the banks of the Rio Santiago, one of Mexico's most contaminated rivers, without adequate water.
What_was_studied: This article employs an integrated social reproduction theory (SRT) framework to investigate the interrelationship between all non-wage forms of survival, such as debt, community, and the environment, in El Salto, one of Mexico's industrial peripheries, over a specific period of time using extensive fieldwork and a comprehensive literature review.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers must prioritize regulating industrialization and social housing policies to break the cycle of ecological dispossession and forced reliance on markets and debt.

Field: Operationalization; Health care; Health policy; Government (linguistics); Social policy; Social determinants of health; Right to health; Context (archaeology); Public administration; Economic growth; Political science; Public relations; Business; Economics; Law; Paleontology; Philosophy; Linguistics; Epistemology; Biology
Title: Implementing Health Policy in Nigeria: The Basic Health Care Provision Fund as a Catalyst for Achieving Universal Health Coverage?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The research found that despite government rhetoric about improving access to healthcare, the BHCPF's operationalization perpetuates health disparities and poor health outcomes in Nigeria due to controversies and a social policy environment that prioritizes profit over people's health needs.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes Nigeria's 2014 healthcare law and its Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) implementation to understand the factors that impact UHC progress and health disparities in Nigeria between 2014 and 2020, using three versions of implementation guidelines and qualitative fieldwork data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up UHC progress and address health inequities, decision-makers must revise the BHCPF implementation guidelines to prioritize equity, funding, and community engagement, while scaling back profit-oriented policies that hinder UHC's success.

Field: Rural area; Field research; Dual (category theory); Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Context (language use); Sri lanka; Development economics; Economic growth; Rationalization (economics)
Title: The Changing Accessibility of Educational Opportunities in Southern Sri Lanka
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Digital divide; Education access; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: An ongoing stratification of educational opportunities is identified, based on the growth of private tuition and English-medium education, as well as a rationalization of the education system. The article shows that future attempts to reform the education system in Sri Lanka must be better rooted in the preferences and aspirations of poor groups in rural areas, and that educational opportunities must be seen as relative, relational, and contextual.
What_was_studied: Based on field research in rural Sri Lanka, this article aims to contribute to the understanding of how educational opportunities of different groups in different areas are shifting in the context of a changing world of work and new skill requirements in the global economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Future education reform efforts should prioritize addressing the growing inequality in educational opportunities for disadvantaged populations to ensure they have access to relevant skills training and keep pace with the changing global economy.

Authors: Diana Córdoba; Marta Chiappe; Jesse Abrams; Theresa Selfa
Field: Political economy; Agrarian society; Multinational corporation; Political science; Social structure; State (polity); Contradiction; Scholarship; Natural resource; Development economics; Politics
Title: Fuelling Social Inclusion? Neo‐extractivism, State–Society Relations and Biofuel Policies in Latin America's Southern Cone
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that progressive reforms intersect with the prevailing interests of agribusiness and state actors and are recast and used for different ends as these interact with powerful actors such as the multinational soybean complex and agrarian movements. Additionally, it was found that the prevailing over-emphasis in the neo-extractivist literature on the politics of domination and contestation overlooks the multiple and complex rural responses of the different progressive governments.
What_was_studied: This article examines the neo-extractivist policies of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay's national biofuel initiatives between 2003 and 2013 to understand why and how these policies emerged, were implemented, and their resulting national experiences that exemplify the inherent contradictions embedded in neo-extractivist policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to address intersectional poverty, sustainable development, and income poverty, policymakers should prioritize education access as a means of breaking the cycle of poverty. Governments should scale up progressive reforms, fund social programs, and revise policies to better serve marginalized communities.

Field: Payment; Natural resource economics; Political science; Ecosystem services
Title: An Alternative Theorization of Payments for Ecosystem Services from Mexico: Origins and Influence
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the CES model has had a significant influence on the design of the national PES programmes, with the programme's emphasis on sustainable stewardship and labor of rural communities, and the state's role in mediating systemic structural inequities between rural and urban and global North and South.
What_was_studied: The study examines the influence of the Compensation for Ecosystem Services (CES) model on the design of the national Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) programmes in Mexico, specifically how it has been mediated by politics and shifting relations of power.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the CES model should be prioritized in the design of PES programmes to address intersectional poverty, gender inequality, and social protection in Mexico. The state should scale up and expand the programme's coverage to reach more rural communities and ensure sustainable stewardship of ecosystem services.

Field: Internally displaced person; Sociology; Statutory law; Law; Demobilization; Political subjectivity; State (polity); Citizenship; Property rights; Politics
Title: Violence Entrepreneurs, Law and Authority in Colombia
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The partial demobilization of paramilitary groups and the state's direct presence at the local level have led to the articulation of claims to new rights by internally displaced people, paving the way for new conditions of access to property and citizenship. However, paramilitary groups and their political and economic allies remain a de facto power in some areas.
What_was_studied: This study examines the restructuring of local power in Colombia since the mid-2000s and its impact on internally displaced people's access to property and citizenship through an ethnographical exploration of claims regarding rights.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for internally displaced people's claims to new rights, including property and citizenship, by prioritizing the development of statutory institutions and the strengthening of unofficial networks.

Field: Microfinance; Moral economy; Poverty; Kinship; Morality; Sociology; Dharma; Moral obligation; Politics; Political science; Economic growth; Economics; Law; Philosophy; Theology; Buddhism
Title: The Moral Economy of Microfinance in Rural Bangladesh: Dharma, Gender and Social Change
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that microfinance fieldworkers use stories of moral ‘idols’ to embed narratives of microfinance within existing rural social institutions, legitimizing and normalizing microfinance for men. For women, borrowing is presented as a means to perform <jats:italic>dharma</jats:italic> — the ‘correct order of things’ — a moral imperative to protect, retain or compete for male guardianship.
What_was_studied: This article examines the moral economy of microfinance in rural Bangladesh through an ethnographic lens, focusing on how morality shapes the remit of legitimate economic activity and social change locally.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that conformity to social and moral obligations is a significant driver of economic behavior in poverty reduction efforts. Policymakers should prioritize understanding the interplay between morality and economic activity to effectively address child poverty, financial inclusion, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty.

Field: Debt; Tax revenue; Economics; International economics; Revenue; Free trade; Panel data; Social capital; Developing country; Physical capital
Title: Trade Liberalization and the Fiscal Squeeze: Implications for Public Investment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that trade liberalization has resulted in declining tax revenues and higher interest expenditures, leading to a fiscal squeeze. Specifically, the analysis reveals that physical capital expenditures have been reduced, while spending on social capital has increased through incurring additional debt.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of trade liberalization on the level and structure of government expenditures across countries, with particular emphasis on low-income countries over a 38-year period (1970–98) using panel data for eighty developing and industrialized countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize financing essential infrastructure projects to address the observed decline in infrastructure spending, particularly in low-income countries. They should also consider implementing fiscal policies that can mitigate the negative impacts of trade liberalization on government expenditure structures.

Field: Sociology; Public good; The Symbolic; Constitution; Spatialization; Realm; Social science; Corporate governance; Criminology; Politics; Social engagement
Title: The Politics of Vigilance in Southeastern Nigeria
primary_category: Governance
What_was_found: The study found that the marginalized groups challenge the public realm's logic, locations, patterns of discourse, and constructions through insurgent constructions of the public good.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the governance of southeastern Nigeria's Annang youth associations using an ethnographic approach, focusing on the micro-politics of vigilance and counter-surveillance from 2010 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and fund programs that support the marginalized groups' counter-surveillance practices to challenge the logic of the public realm and expand the public sphere.

Field: Rural area; Government; Economics; Residence; Floating population; Population; Urbanization; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Census; Developing country
Title: China's Household Registration System under Reform
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the household registration system changed during the 1980s, with permanent residents legally bound to be registered in one locality and temporary residence involving registration within three days of a visit. The floating population in cities increased from 10% of permanent population or over 50 million people by 1990, with many commuting from their nearby homes and continuing to grow their own grain.
What_was_studied: The household registration system in China during the 1980s and its impact on migration, poverty, and labor regulation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that improving rural poverty through labor development and urbanization is a key policy direction. To scale up this effort, the government should prioritize urbanization policies and fund targeted programs for rural migrants to improve their access to employment and social services.

Authors: Ian G. Baird; Bruce Shoemaker; Kanokwan Manorom
Field: Environmental resource management; Drainage basin; Field research; Business; Downstream (petroleum industry); Poverty; Commission; Livelihood; Hydropower; Documentation
Title: The People and their River, the World Bank and its Dam: Revisiting the Xe Bang Fai River in Laos
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found significant negative impacts on the livelihoods of large numbers of people dependent on the river’s resources, with many viewing compensation and mitigation efforts as having failed to adequately address their losses.
What_was_studied: This qualitative field research from early 2014 examines the downstream impacts of the Nam Theun 2 Hydropower Project (NT2) in the Xe Bang Fai River basin and assesses efforts to compensate for losses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is essential to scale up support for alternative income sources and livelihoods for those affected by large dams, and to prioritize independent investigation and documentation of impacts to inform more effective poverty alleviation strategies.

Field: Aesthetics; Gender studies; Sociology; Development theory; Feminism; Scholarship; First World; Population; Postmodernism; Postmodern theatre; Grand theory
Title: Who is the "other"?: a postmodern feminist critique of women and development theory and practice.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that postmodern feminism offers valuable insights into the complex intersections of gender, culture, and power in Third World contexts, particularly in the areas of poverty reduction and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relevance of postmodern feminism for Third World problems and analysis, particularly its utility for theorists and practitioners concerned with issues of women and development in the last decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize incorporating postmodern feminist perspectives into their approaches to addressing intersectional poverty and promoting sustainable development, as this can lead to more effective and equitable solutions that account for the diverse experiences of women in Third World countries.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Artisanal mining; Child labour; Context (language use); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Child labour in African Artisanal Mining Communities: experiences from Northern Ghana
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is the underlying cause of child labor in ASM communities in sub-Saharan Africa, and that until donor agencies and host governments fully come to grips with the underlying causes of poverty, child labor will continue to burgeon.
What_was_studied: This article critically examines the issue of child labor in the context of sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on the lack of formal sector employment opportunities and the need to provide financial support to impoverished families as the main reasons why tens of thousands of children engage in arduous work in artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) camps across the region, using recent fieldwork undertaken in Talensi-Nabdam District, Upper East Region, Ghana as an example.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively address child labor in ASM communities, policy makers must prioritize poverty reduction strategies, such as increasing access to formal sector employment opportunities and providing financial support to impoverished families, and scale up these interventions across the region.

Field: Supply and demand; Labour economics; Economics; Set (psychology); Poverty; Social policy; Contradiction; National level; Tertiary sector of the economy
Title: Structural Change, the Social Policy Environment and Female Employment in Turkey
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: In Turkey, a sustained increase in female employment has not been observed over the past two decades, despite global trends of increasing female participation in the labor market. Female labor force participation and employment rates have both declined at the national level over this period.
What_was_studied: Since the 1970s, a series of demand and supply related changes have led to significant labor market transformations which have brought about a sustained increase in female employment throughout the world. While similar transformations have also been underway in Turkey, the country appears to be one of the rare exceptions to worldwide trends. During the last two decades both female labor force participation and female employment rates have declined at national level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address this contradiction between patriarchal values and policy objectives, decision makers should prioritize policies aimed at increasing female labor force participation and combating poverty. This could involve investing in education and training programs for women, promoting gender-equal employment opportunities, and implementing social policies that support the needs of female workers.

Field: Positive economics; Ideology; Political science; Poverty; Space (commercial competition); Financial inclusion; Microfinance; Argument; Intervention (law); Theory of change
Title: Contesting Financial Inclusion
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
