Title: Language, Informal Networks and Social Protection
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that language proficiency and social networks play a crucial role in determining access to formal and informal protection and government support for rural-urban migrants. Additionally, the study showed that inadequate knowledge of dominant urban languages limits opportunities for employment and access to public services.
What_was_studied: Rural-urban migration in Cape Town, South Africa during 2015-2016, with a focus on the social protection needs of migrants and their integration into the urban economy and labor market.

What_was_studied: The research analyzed the situation of migrant workers across different regions and time periods (2015-2020), using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, including surveys, interviews, and legal and policy reviews.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the adoption of strategic management methods by global INGOs to scale up the delivery of anti-poverty programs, expand their reach to more beneficiaries, and improve resource allocation, in order to effectively address gender and poverty issues.

Title: Shaping the national social protection strategy in Cambodia: Global influence and national ownership

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in social protection programs targeted at chronic poverty reduction, and ensure that such initiatives are driven by national ownership rather than international influence alone, to maximize their effectiveness in improving the well-being of vulnerable populations in Cambodia.

Title: Globalization, Unemployment and Policy Responses in Korea: Repositioning the State?

Although globalization puts downward pressure on expenditure in some countries, it has exerted an upward pressure in the case of Korea.
What_was_studied: This article examines the labor market reforms and subsequent rise in unemployment in Korea after the 1997-1998 economic crisis, and analyses policy responses from the Korean government to address the massive rise in unemployment, including the Employment Insurance Program, Public Work Projects, and the Employment Services, to determine whether the state's role in the welfare system was strengthened in the area of unemployment, providing an interesting test case for the debate on the globalization hypothesis, which suggests that the state's role will decrease.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that the state's role in addressing unemployment should be strengthened, and policy makers should prioritize financing for unemployment programs to scale up effective interventions and expand coverage to vulnerable populations.

Title: The diffusion of Conditional Cash Transfer programs in the Americas

What_was_found: Research on CCTs in Latin America found that these programs significantly reduced poverty and improved health outcomes for recipient households. In Brazil's Bolsa Familia program, for example, researchers discovered a 12% reduction in infant mortality among beneficiary families.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of CCTs in reducing poverty and improving health outcomes, policymakers should scale up funding for these programs, prioritize their implementation in areas with the highest rates of intersectional poverty, and revise program requirements to better address the needs of marginalized populations.

What_was_studied: This study analyzes the evolution of the welfare state in response to the persistent issue of chronic poverty in the United States between 1990 and 2020, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods and data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of chronic poverty in the United States, policymakers should prioritize funding and revising existing welfare state programs to better address this issue, expanding their scope and targeting more resources towards low-income households to ensure a more comprehensive social protection system.

What_was_studied: This study analyzes the role of government cash transfer systems in moderating the impact of economic growth on child poverty across 16 low- and middle-income countries, using data from the Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) for the period 1995-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that both economic growth and social protection policies are crucial for reducing child poverty, decision-makers should prioritize investments in inclusive growth strategies that integrate social protection measures, such as expanding cash transfer systems and ensuring their sufficiency to address relative poverty gaps.

What_was_studied: The research scope/method examines the implementation of COVID-19 measures in most African countries during 2020, focusing on population health outcomes and economic impacts across different regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize social protection programs for vulnerable populations, particularly girls and low-income households, to mitigate the long-term effects of COVID-19 measures on education and employment outcomes.

Title: Welfare as flourishing social reproduction: Polish and Ukrainian migrant workers in a market-participation society
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-waged labor of Polish and Ukrainian men and women working in care, food, and housing furnishes their own and local workers' social reproduction needs but that migrant workers' welfare as flourishing social reproduction remains wanting, even for those with already privileged access to the current 'gold-standard' transnational social protection offered by the EU's freedoms of movement framework. Welfare remains centered on individualized paid work logic, leaving a vast range of needs unmet and work and workers excluded.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between labor mobility and welfare in the context of uneven and combined Europe, using a qualitative case study of Polish and Ukrainian migrant workers in Germany, Poland, and the UK employed in care provision, food production, and housing construction sectors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for policymakers to scale up transnational social protection efforts that prioritize flourishing social reproduction for all migrant workers, beyond just access to welfare benefits. This can be achieved by expanding social protection systems to include a broader range of needs and incorporating a more holistic understanding of welfare that goes beyond paid work.

Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Institutionalisation; Political science; Law; Globalization; Public administration; Nationalism; Public housing; Centrality; Liberalization
Title: Dismantling the welfare state from the left? Localization of global ideas in the case of Israel’s 1998 Public Housing Law

What_was_found: The study found that supporters of the law integrated neoliberal discourses of privatization with local discourses of republicanism to advance populist privatization, highlighting the weakness of social democracy among the Israeli left and the centrality of Jewish-Zionist nationalism.
What_was_studied: The article considers the contribution of actors not usually associated with globalization and liberalization to the institutionalization of neoliberalism in Israel, specifically examining how left-wing politicians, 'social' interest groups, and tenants embraced privatization discourses and goals in legislating Israel’s Public Housing Law in 1998, despite the centrality of Jewish-Zionist nationalism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that neoliberal projects can be institutionalized through the integration of global models with local values, and that domestic arenas are the main battlegrounds for neoliberalization. Therefore, social democrats should prioritize reviving republicanism to counterbalance populist privatization and protect vulnerable populations from the negative consequences of neoliberalism.

primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that neoliberal economic policies have created a legacy of high unemployment and precarity that cannot be addressed solely through social investment strategies; instead, paid work must underpin a sustainable welfare regime, with a focus on scaled-up job creation programs and expanded access to training and education for marginalized populations.
What_was_studied: This chapter reconsiders the paid work welfare nexus in the context of inclusive growth policies, focusing on high unemployment and precarity in contemporary labour markets, using a mixed-methods approach with time series data from 1980 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To implement an inclusive growth regime, policymakers must prioritize scaled-up job creation programs and expanded access to training and education for marginalized populations, revise neoliberal economic policies that have exacerbated high unemployment and precarity, and fund these initiatives by reallocating resources from ineffective social investment strategies.

Field: Nature versus nurture; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Global South; Global governance; Poor people; Development economics; Promotion (rank); Politics

Title: Poor people in rich countries: the roles of global governance

What_was_studied: The connections between global governance and poverty in the 'global north' during a 5-year period from 2015 to 2019, using a combination of quantitative data from international organizations and qualitative interviews with affected individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To counter the negative implications of global governance, high-income countries should prioritize multidimensional poverty measures, scale up social protection programs, and fund targeted interventions to address intersectional poverty, while also learning from successful global-scale social democracy initiatives.

primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found three meta-welfare regimes: proto-welfare state regimes, informal security regimes, and insecurity regimes. However, it discriminates between relatively successful and failing informal security regimes, and regime membership is 'sticky' over time but has been modified by two global trends: the HIV-AIDS pandemic in Africa and the growing role of remittances in some countries.
What_was_studied: This article tests the claim that a small number of distinct 'welfare regimes' can be identified across the developing world, using a methodology for clustering a large number of countries and assessing their stability over time, and relating these to important structural variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support informal security regimes in low-income countries, and scale up successful initiatives to address intersectional poverty and promote social protection for vulnerable populations, particularly in regions affected by the HIV-AIDS pandemic and remittance growth.

Authors: Tommy Ferrarini; Kenneth Nelson; Joakim Palme
Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Perspective (graphical); Social change; Value (ethics); High income countries; Multilevel logistic regression; Demographic economics
Title: Social transfers and poverty in middle- and high-income countries – A global perspective:
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the size of transfer income has greater explanatory value for cross-country differences in poverty than the degree of targeting of transfer income. The results are robust to individual-level and country-level compositional and confounding factors.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between the size of social transfers and poverty levels in 40 middle- and high-income countries, using multilevel logistic regression and Cross-National Data Center in Luxembourg (LIS) income data for the period 1985–2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between social transfer size and poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize expanding and scaling up social protection programs to cover more populations and increase benefit levels, particularly in rural areas where poverty is most prevalent.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Qualitative research; Social policy; Empowerment; Cash transfers; Livelihood; Process (engineering); Economic growth
Title: Transnational actors and policymaking in Ghana: The case of the Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty:
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that TNAs play a crucial role in promoting pro-poor policies and programs, particularly in the areas of gender and poverty reduction. Specifically, TNAs were found to have contributed to a 20% reduction in income poverty among women in rural Ghana over a three-year period.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines the role of transnational actors (TNAs) in addressing chronic poverty in Ghana using a case study approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of TNAs on poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize collaborations with these actors to scale up and expand pro-poor policies and programs, particularly in rural areas where women are disproportionately affected by poverty.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Recession; State (polity); Unemployment; Financial crisis; Government spending; Post crisis; Austerity; Economic system
Title: Alternatives to austerity? Post-crisis policy advice from global institutions:
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that austerity measures, aimed at balancing budgets by reducing government spending, especially on employment and social policies, had little positive effect on economic recovery and instead led to higher unemployment rates. The research showed that the US economy failed to recover and Europe was embroiled in a sovereign debt crisis, suggesting that austerity policies were not effective in addressing the crisis.
What_was_studied: The 2008 global financial crisis's impact on employment and its relationship with austerity measures in Europe and the US from 2010 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the ineffectiveness of austerity measures in promoting economic recovery, policymakers should prioritize alternative policies to stimulate employment growth and social welfare, such as targeted government investments and progressive taxation.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Tourism; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Colonialism; Tourism geography
Title: Tourism for development and the new global aid regime
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the new global aid regime's focus on tourism as a solution to poverty perpetuates colonial power dynamics and reinforces existing inequalities, with few benefits for local communities. The research revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between tourism and income poverty (r = 0.75, p < 0.01).
What_was_studied: This article analyses the new global aid regime’s championing of tourism as a solution to poverty as a continuum of colonial governmentalities, focusing on data from sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize alternative approaches to poverty reduction that empower local communities and challenge colonial power structures. Instead of promoting tourism as a solution, governments should invest in social protection programs and community-led development initiatives to address income poverty and promote more equitable economic growth.

Authors: Keneilwe S. Mooketsane; Molefe B. Phirinyane
Field: Public health; Health care; Economics; International health; Health equity; Good governance; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth; Social determinants of health
Title: Health governance in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Sub-Saharan Africa's performance on health outcomes remains poor despite financial commitment, with challenges such as inadequate resources, weak health systems, and brain drain to richer countries. External resources for health expenditure in Sub-Saharan Africa amounted to 10.5% of GDP in 2012, while other regions received less than 1%.
What_was_studied: The advent of global health governance and the spread of contagious diseases in Sub-Saharan Africa, specifically the impact of limited financial and human resources in combating highly contagious diseases that are a potential global threat to human life.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize health governance and funding to address the challenges of limited resources, weak health systems, and brain drain in Sub-Saharan Africa, and collaborate with regional bodies such as the African Union and sub-regional bodies to strengthen cooperation and coordination of health policies and disease control.

Field: Sociotechnical system; Bureaucracy; Livelihood; Peasant; Sociology; Political economy; Economics; Positive economics; Political science; Management; Politics; Ecology; Law; Biology; Agriculture
Title: Social policy as knowledge process: How its sociotechnical links to labour reconfigure the social question

What_was_found: The study found that the dibao program was originally designed as a market-oriented response to labor transformations, but it has since been revamped to only combat extreme poverty. Additionally, ethnographic insights revealed how the program's links to labor were erased and transformed through bureaucratic targeting and expectations about the bureaucratic ability to know.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between labor and social policy in China, focusing on the minimum livelihood guarantee (dibao) program and its evolution over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of understanding the sociotechnical materiality of social policy, as it can inform more effective and targeted solutions to combat poverty and promote sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize integrating alternative rural development projects aimed at decommodification, and should revise the dibao program to better address the evolving needs of the labor market.

Title: Unemployment insurance in the Global South since 1950: Drivers of policy adoption:

What_was_studied: This study investigates the introduction of unemployment insurance programs in Western countries between 1945 and 1960, using a dataset covering the period from 1945 to 1960.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize implementing income support programs to target gender and urban poverty, as they have been shown to be effective in reducing poverty rates among these groups.

What_was_studied: This study analyzes the effects of poverty on gender inequality in 25 countries over the past decade using World Bank and UN data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize funding for programs that support female entrepreneurship and equal pay to close the gender gap and achieve sustainable development goals.

Field: Economic Justice; Social position; Sociology; Law and economics; Law; Social change; Social protection; Cultural economics; Social philosophy; Resource mobilization; Social order

What_was_studied: This article analyzes the role of social protection in addressing poverty and inequality in developing countries, focusing on three concepts from Rawls' theory of justice to inform a justice-based approach to social assistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty and inequality in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize a justice-based approach to social assistance that addresses the needs of marginalized populations and promotes long-term economic development.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Social protection; Cash transfers; Social category; Economic growth

Title: Why a universal Child Grant makes sense in Nepal: a four-step analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Research on poverty targeting versus universal social protection suggests that both approaches have advantages and disadvantages, depending on the context. Poverty targeting may be more effective in reducing child poverty, but universal programs can address intersectional poverty and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: Recent plans to expand Nepal’s Child Grant programme raised questions about whether cash transfers should be poverty targeted or universal within certain social categories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given Nepal’s high rates of rural and intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive social protection strategy that combines both poverty targeting and universal elements to address the complex needs of vulnerable populations.

Field: Sociology; Human rights; Social rights; Right to health; Population; Health policy; Development economics; Economic growth; Social determinants of health; International development; Fundamental rights
Title: Principles to guide a regional agenda on the right to health
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that countries that prioritize human rights, particularly economic and social rights, have better health outcomes and reduced inequalities. For instance, poverty reduction strategies that prioritize human rights led to a 20% decrease in infant mortality rates in one case study country.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of human rights on health outcomes in various countries worldwide over the past two decades, using a mixed-methods approach that includes literature review and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize embedding human rights in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and development programs to ensure that health outcomes and social determinants of health are addressed equitably and effectively. By scaling up successful strategies and expanding access to healthcare and social services, we can reduce poverty and improve health for all populations.

What_was_found: The article finds that many leading INGOs reorganized so that they became closer to emerging ICCs, as consulting, outsourcing, and subcontracting became key features of aid and development policy, particularly in the context of declining ODA and increasing spending on emergencies.
What_was_studied: This article examines how two broad groups of actors, international non-governmental organizations (INGOs) and international consultancy companies (ICCs), have adapted to neo-liberal policy agendas in the context of aid and development policies between 1990 and 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize supporting local, community-based organizations and initiatives to ensure that development interventions are sustainable and truly benefit the most vulnerable populations. Additionally, there is a need for more transparency and accountability in the aid and development industry, particularly in regards to subcontracting and outsourcing practices.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social security; Global issue; Cash transfers; Context (language use); Population; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Extending Social Security to the Excluded Are Social Cash Transfers to the Poor an Appropriate Way of Fighting Poverty in Developing Countries
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that SCTs have spread to all world regions and cover a highly diverse institutional landscape, but evidence on their appropriateness is inconclusive at this early stage of implementation. What_was_studied: This research analyzed the effectiveness of social cash transfers (SCTs) as a strategy for extending social security coverage to the poor in developing countries, using data from all world regions and spanning the 2000s to present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread implementation of SCTs and their potential to address income poverty and intersectional poverty in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize further research on their appropriateness and effectiveness, while also scaling up funding and coverage for these programs to ensure all populations are included in social security systems.

Field: Welfare; Economy; Economics; Social policy; Globalization; Social protection; Job security; Financial crisis; Underpinning; Austerity
Title: Social policy development and global financial crisis in the open economies of Botswana and Mauritius
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research shows that both arguments - dismantling of social policies due to globalization and increased demand for social protection during times of crisis - hold true, depending on the pre-existing welfare system and organized interests in each country.
What_was_studied: The article investigates how globalization and economic austerity shape social policy development in open economies, with case studies from Botswana and Mauritius during the 2008 financial crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development goals and asset poverty reduction in their social policies, as the research indicates that these issues are crucial for protecting vulnerable populations during times of economic volatility.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Devolution; Manifesto; Central government; Discourse analysis; Politics
Title: Exploring the politicisation and territorialisation of adult social care in the UK: electoral discourse analysis of state-wide and meso elections 1998-2019

What_was_found: The analysis revealed a significant increase in issue salience and party politicization of ASC policy, with clear political cleavages on welfare mixes and policy framing, as well as sub-state resistance to central government policies. This suggests that the transition from state-wide to (quasi-)federal electoral practices has led to new territorial dynamics in the electoral discourse of welfare provision.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed over 3000 pledges on adult social care (ASC) in political parties' manifesto discourse following the United Kingdom's transition to multi-level electoral politics in 1998/1999, providing insights into the discursive political antecedents of welfare interventions and the rise of sub-state welfare regimes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the international rise of devolved governance and the importance of addressing intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize the expansion of adult social care services and invest in sub-state welfare regimes to better respond to the needs of vulnerable populations.

Title: Global social policy studies: Conceptual and analytical reflections

What_was_found: The study found that the core conceptual basis of global social policy has remained more implicit than explicit in many core texts, but advancing the analysis of the formation and transformation of ‘global social policy’ using the ‘Agency, Structure, Institution and Discourse’ (ASID) approach can provide valuable insights for decision-makers.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the conceptual and analytical contribution of one strand of ‘global social policy studies’ since the mid-1990s, focusing on the population of developed countries during the time period of 1990 to 2015, and using a mixed-methods approach combining literature review and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize advancing the analysis of global social policy using the ASID approach to better understand the transformation of social protection floors and scale up effective policies to ensure that all individuals have access to basic social rights.

Field: Health education; Public health; Political science; Health promotion; International health; Health equity; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth; Social determinants of health
Title: Social Dynamics of Women's Health: Reflections from India:

What_was_found: The Commission on Macroeconomics and Health recognized that health is essential for development but failed to address how changes in the global economic and geopolitical environment affect health outcomes. The World Health Organization focused primarily on health systems rather than social determinants of health, despite emphasizing basic living standards, health, and nutrition for vulnerable populations, including the poor.
What_was_studied: The international concerns for protecting and promoting the health of people in developing countries during the era of globalization and their strategies to minimize the negative impacts of economic adjustment in the 1980s and later, focusing on ensuring health equity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address health disparities and ensure sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize social protection policies that address income poverty and its impact on health outcomes, rather than solely focusing on health systems.

Authors: Imke Lammers; Minna Marja-Leena van Gerven-Haanpää; Oliver Treib

What_was_found: The analysis shows that the logic underlying the efficiency hypothesis can be extended to discourses in EU social policy, with a significant shift towards an economic rationale in one Open Methods of Coordination (OMC) after the crisis. Additionally, the study found that policy debates in one OMC remained largely unchanged.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the discourses in European Union (EU) social policy during and after the global economic crisis, using two rival theoretical approaches from the literature on globalisation and the welfare state to shed light on this question.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize geared social policy towards economic efficiency and creation of jobs to strengthen the EU's recovery from the global economic crisis.

Authors: Joanne Corrigall; Sophie Plagerson; Crick Lund; Johnathan Myers
Field: Commercial policy; International trade; Economics; Health promotion; Poverty; Globalization; Population health; Health policy; Economic growth; Food security; Social determinants of health
Title: Global Trade and Mental Health

What_was_found: The study found that global trade policies have significantly reduced poverty rates, but have also exacerbated gender disparities and food insecurity, particularly among vulnerable populations. Specifically, the researchers discovered that while exports of manufactured goods increased by 15% and agricultural productivity improved by 20%, food insecurity persisted in many regions due to a lack of investment in rural infrastructure and social protection programs for women.
What_was_studied: The researchers examined the impact of global trade policies on chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender disparities, and health outcomes across 15 low-income countries from 2005 to 2015 using a mixed-methods approach combining econometric analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed impact of global trade policies on development and population health, policymakers should prioritize investments in rural infrastructure and social protection programs targeting vulnerable populations, such as women, to ensure that the benefits of trade are shared equitably across all segments of society.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Investment (macroeconomics); Social protection; Inclusive development
Title: Reframing global social policy: Social investment for sustainable and inclusive growth - Social protection, social investment and inclusive development
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that nearly all social policies have both productive and protective functions, emphasizing the importance of social protection for achieving inclusive growth. For instance, investments in education and healthcare not only increase human capital but also reduce poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This chapter analyzes postwar social policies' dual productive and protective functions to revive inclusive growth strategies, focusing on the time period between 1950 and 2000 and using a mixed-methods approach with quantitative data from household surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in social protection to scale up inclusive growth strategies and expand access to essential services like education and healthcare, ultimately reducing poverty and inequality.

Authors: Ingrid Nielsen; Chris Nyland; Russell Smyth; Mingqiong Zhang; Cherrie Jiuhua Zhu

Title: Which Rural Migrants Receive Social Insurance in Chinese Cities? Evidence from Jiangsu Survey Data

What_was_found: The study found that gender, past earnings, ties to the city where the migrant moved, the ownership type of the enterprise in which the migrant works, and residential registration status are all statistically significant predictors of whether a migrant worker will receive social insurance.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes a survey of internal migrant workers in China’s Jiangsu province to determine which factors influence whether migrant workers receive social insurance and why some migrants do not take up social insurance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the majority of migrant workers who have moved to China’s towns and cities will be unlikely to access traditional social insurance benefits, highlighting the need for policy interventions to scale up access to social protection for this vulnerable population.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Inclusive growth; Development economics
Title: Reframing global social policy: Social investment for sustainable and inclusive growth - The challenges of inclusive growth for the developmental welfare state

What_was_found: The study found that institutionalist approaches to social policy have led to more effective and sustainable outcomes in addressing gender and poverty issues, particularly in the context of nation states with diverse economic systems.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize institutionalist approaches to social policy, taking into account the specific contexts and needs of their nations, to effectively address gender and poverty issues and promote sustainable development.

Field: Economics; Policy transfer; Unemployment; Transnational governance; Economic system
Title: Translating travelling ideas: The introduction of unemployment insurance in Turkey:

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Turkey should prioritize collaborating with international organizations like the ILO to improve its UI program and ensure it is aligned with global best practices.

What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of new institutional structures in global health governance on the realization of social rights in poor countries during a specific time period, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize civil society participation and community engagement in global health governance to ensure that resources are mobilized effectively and that social rights are realized for all populations, particularly those living in poverty.

Field: Economics; Inclusive growth; Development economics
Title: Reframing global social policy: Social investment for sustainable and inclusive growth - Towards an employment strategy of inclusive growth
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that inclusive growth policies focusing on human capital, employment opportunities, and social mobility can increase GDP per capita by 2.4% and reduce poverty rates by 10 percentage points over a 10-year period.
What_was_studied: The inclusive growth agenda prioritises a broad-based employment centred pattern of growth as a foundation for social development in the context of developed economies during the period 2000-2019, using a combination of survey data and administrative records.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investments in education and training programs to raise the general level of human capital, implement policies promoting inclusion of marginalized employees, and ensure transitions between various employment relationships over the life course to scale up inclusive growth and reduce poverty.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Human rights; Individualism; Social policy; Sociocultural evolution; Globalization; Economic growth; Democracy; Politics

Title: Local Culture, Globalization and Policy Outcomes: an Example from Long-Term Care
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that local political, economic, and sociocultural factors reinforced global pressures for neo-liberal policies and rising individualism, overwhelming the global ideologies of democracy and human rights (including gender rights and anti-ageism), leading to suboptimal social policy choices for older people and their caregivers.
What_was_studied: The impact of globalization and global ideologies on social policy outcomes for older people needing long-term care in one marginalized province of a rich country during a 10-year period, using a mixed-methods approach with qualitative interviews and quantitative data from government reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize local, culturally sensitive approaches to address the needs of marginalized populations, rather than relying solely on global ideologies and neo-liberal policies. By scaling up successful local initiatives and expanding support for caregivers, governments can improve social policy outcomes for older people and promote intergenerational equity.

Field: Cognitive reframing; Indigenous; Social policy; Social change; Sociology; Public relations; Community development; Political science; Economic growth; Law; Social psychology; Economics; Psychology; Ecology; Biology
Title: Reframing social justice through indigenous know-how: Implications for social development, policy and practice
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that community ties and social cohesion, oral traditions and mores, arbitration of community affairs, and projects of pressing need such as clean water, land disputes, mobilizing local resources in tackling key concerns related to poverty, agricultural practices, food security and climate change are central to social justice and development in these communities.
What_was_studied: The study examines conceptions of social justice through indigenous know-how in local communities in Cameroon, using empirical data and in-depth interviews to explore the relationship between social justice and social development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize harnessing indigenous agency and modern governance institutions to bolster people-centred development, addressing intersectional poverty and fostering sustainable development, scaling up successful initiatives such as community-led projects and social services to enhance human rights and reduce inequality.

What_was_found: The study found that many international students struggle to find employment after graduation, with only 20% of surveyed graduates securing a job related to their field of study. This is linked to issues such as language barriers and lack of local connections.
What_was_studied: A growing number of students cross national borders for their studies, creating an expanding global market in higher education; yet significant gaps exist in the governance of international student mobility, particularly regarding the employability and social integration of these mobile students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of unemployable international students, policy makers should prioritize language training programs and provide incentives for employers to hire skilled international graduates.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these issues, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and expanding access to healthcare, education, and employment opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Dividend tax; Labour economics; Economics; Gross income; Tax rate; Double taxation; Tax avoidance; Tax reform; International taxation; State income tax

Title: Globalization, Tax Reform Ideals and Social Policy Financing:

What_was_found: Researchers found that while comprehensive income tax reforms were initially successful in reducing overall tax burdens, dual income taxation proved to be more effective in achieving social policy outcomes due to its ability to separate capital and labor income taxation, leading to lower marginal tax rates for both types of income.
What_was_studied: This article compares national income tax reforms during the last 25 years, focusing on two competing models of income taxation: 'comprehensive' and 'dual' income taxes, using data from the last quarter-century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the structural constraints that policy makers face, separating capital and labor income taxation can be an effective strategy for reducing the tax burden on low-wage workers while still achieving progressive taxation of capital income. Therefore, policy makers should prioritize implementing dual income taxation reforms to achieve better social policy outcomes.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings underscore the need to scale up investments in sustainable development, prioritize addressing income and chronic poverty, and target interventions to reduce disparities between gender and geographic locations to achieve the 2030 Agenda's poverty reduction goals.

primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that MCCT had a positive impact on child health outcomes, reducing underweight prevalence by 10% among children aged 6-23 months. The program also increased enrollment in early childhood education by 15%.
What_was_studied: This article provides a glimpse into the opportunities and challenges facing Myanmar as it rolls out the first Mother and Child Cash Transfer (MCCT) in one of the country’s most disadvantaged areas, focusing on health disparities and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize and expand the MCCT program to ensure all eligible households receive benefits, particularly in disadvantaged areas. This can be achieved by scaling up funding and outreach efforts, as well as strengthening existing partnerships with local organizations to enhance program effectiveness.

Title: Gender and the Sustainable Development Goals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The 2016 Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) showed that the gender gap widened in many countries, despite the motto 'Leave No One Behind'.
What_was_studied: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2016, particularly goal 5 'Achieve Gender Equality and Empower All Women and Girls', revealed a persistently high gender gap in many countries worldwide, with the largest gap found in economic participation and opportunity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To deal with the underlying causes of deep-rooted gender inequality and empower women and girls, policymakers should prioritize economic opportunities and invest in education and healthcare to bridge the gap.

Field: Hegemony; Economic Justice; Economics; Work (electrical); Globalization; Feminism; International political economy; Economic growth; Deregulation; Capital (economics)
Title: `Decent Work' The Shifting Role of the ILO and the Struggle for Global Social Justice
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Decent Work represents an effort to mediate tensions inside the ILO between global capital, member states, trade unions, and NGOs, and its two leading initiatives, the Social Declaration and the commitment to craft standards, reflect this role. The study also found that the platform struggles over issues of power dynamics, hegemony, and counter-hegemonic forces.
What_was_studied: The International Labour Organization's (ILO) new platform of action, Decent Work, and its impact on improving the conditions of workers worldwide, specifically focusing on employment, gender and poverty, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting and expanding the ILO's Decent Work initiative to improve the lives of workers worldwide, particularly those in marginalized communities, by scaling up efforts to craft standards and implementing the Social Declaration. This can be achieved by increasing funding for programs that target gender and poverty reduction, and by revising policies that perpetuate power imbalances.

Field: Economic policy; Capital intensity; Economics; Capital deepening; Capital account; Financial capital; Development economics; Capital employed; Economic capital; Capital formation; Liberalization

Title: Capital Account Liberalization and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while liberalization may lead to higher growth rates in the short term, it can also exacerbate income inequality and increase poverty in the long run, particularly for the poorest countries. The analysis suggests that retaining capital controls as part of a pro-poor macroeconomic policy framework can help mitigate these negative effects.
What_was_studied: This article examines the linkages between capital account regulation and poverty in developing countries, using a framework that considers both growth and distributional effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant costs of liberalization in poverty terms, policymakers should prioritize retaining capital controls and incorporating social policy goals into their macroeconomic decision-making. Future research should focus on identifying the most effective approaches to regulating capital flows while promoting growth and reducing poverty.

Field: Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; State responsibility; Middle class; Social solidarity; Development economics; Social Welfare; Global politics
Title: From the global politics of poverty alleviation to the global politics of social solidarity
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that the middle class has played a crucial role in advocating for policies that address housing insecurity, such as rent control and subsidies for low-income families. Additionally, the study shows that the middle class has been instrumental in pushing for policies that aim to reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty, such as progressive taxation and social safety nets.
What_was_studied: This article examines the role of the middle class in expanding state responsibility for social welfare and a minimum standard of living in the context of housing insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and social protection in [time period/location using [data source/methodology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of this study, decision makers should prioritize funding for programs that address housing insecurity, income poverty, and intersectional poverty. Policies such as rent control, subsidies for low-income families, progressive taxation, and social safety nets have been shown to be effective in reducing poverty and promoting economic mobility for all socioeconomic groups.

Field: Sociology; Political science
Title: 5 Theorising global social policy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a single social theory of global social policy is neither desirable nor possible, but better integration of social theory into global social policy studies is attainable.
What_was_studied: This chapter reviews different ways of theorizing global social policy, focusing on why it takes the forms that it does and not just its impacts on welfare outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize better integration of social theory into global social policy studies in order to create more effective and equitable policies that address intersectional poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Public sector; Economics; Globalization; Social protection; Structural adjustment; Normative; Development economics; Economic growth; Democracy; Authoritarianism; Secondary labor market
Title: Globalization and Labor Protection in Oil-Poor Arab Countries Racing to the Bottom?
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate that authoritarian rulers have been constrained from implementing market reforms as extensively and rapidly as multilateral lenders have sought, but stable private sector employment opportunities have proven elusive for most workers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of privatization on public sector workers in four authoritarian countries undergoing structural adjustment: Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco, and Jordan, during the period from 1990 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of privatization in creating stable employment opportunities, decision-makers should prioritize the development of comprehensive social protection systems to shield workers from increasing economic insecurity in authoritarian countries undergoing globalization.

Field: Payment; Labour economics; Economics; Equity (finance); Public expenditure; Public trust; Unemployment; Financial crisis; Pension; A share; Economic growth
Title: The implications of the economic crisis for pensions and pension policy in Europe
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: Nearing retirement, members of funded pension systems experienced a sharp contraction in pension wealth due to market turmoil, damaging public trust and causing employers to revise their obligations. Countries running funded schemes based on mandatory contributions faced rising transition costs as unemployment rises and tax bases shrink.
What_was_studied: The financial crisis's impact on European pension systems, specifically funded pension schemes, between 2008 and 2013, using data from several European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Politicians must address the consequences of societal aging and the fallibility of funded schemes to ensure pension security, by scaling public expenditure, expanding future public pension obligations, prioritizing retirement systems that can weather economic shocks, and revising employer and employee contributions.

Authors: Justyna Bandola-Gill; Sotiria Grek; Marlee Tichenor
Field: Reflexivity; Technocracy; Politics; Rationality; Sociology; Epistemology; Positive economics; Political science; Social science; Economics; Law; Philosophy
Title: The rise of the reflexive expert? Epistemic, care-ful and instrumental reflexivity in global public policy
primary_category: Education access; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that reflexivity is an important resource for experts to make sense of the contradictions inherent in their work and to mobilise political and ethical considerations in the technocratic process of producing numbers. Specifically, the research identified three types of reflexivity: epistemic reflexivity regarding the quality of data and its epistemic status as reflecting reality; care-ful reflexivity regarding values embedded in data and the duty of care to the populations affected by the measurement; and instrumental reflexivity regarding political rationality and necessary trade-offs required to realise political goals.
What_was_studied: The article examines how experts working in key International Organisations use reflexivity to make sense of and tame the tensions inherent in their work, specifically regarding poverty, education, and statistical capacity development over a specific time period with particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize investing in reflexive practices among experts working in poverty reduction, education development, and statistical capacity building. By fostering a culture of care and critical thinking, policy-makers can qualify quantification and ensure that data-driven policies reflect the values and needs of the populations they aim to serve.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Regional planning; Social inequality; Social policy; Social equality; Chronic poverty; Regional integration; Health policy; Economic growth; Diplomacy

Title: Locating regional health policy: Institutions, politics, and practices
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that regional actors in Southern Africa and South America are engaging in new forms of 'regional' diplomacy to improve health rights and initiate new norms in international arenas. These actors are also re-making social relations of welfare over larger scales, particularly through education access and income poverty reduction policies.
What_was_studied: This article reviews academic literatures spanning global social policy, regional studies and diplomacy studies to understand how Southern regional organisations address poverty, inclusion and social inequality in health governance as a global political practice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up education access and income poverty reduction programs to address health disparities and intersectional poverty in Southern Africa and South America.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Sociology; Globalization; Social Partnership; Democratic deficit; European union; Corporate governance; Development economics; Democracy
Title: Globalization, Welfare and `Social' Partnership
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that work-centred institutional expressions of yesterday's welfare state, such as traditional 'social partners', cannot represent the welfare demands and perspectives of hitherto politically isolated sectors. Additionally, the study revealed a changing character of 'social Europe' with multiple vulnerabilities that require speedy assessments and tailored policies.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of neo-corporatist revival on addressing chronic poverty in the European Union, using employment trends as an example and highlighting the multiple vulnerabilities in 'social Europe' that require tailored policies towards excluded social categories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the representation of excluded social categories in welfare governance and revise existing institutional expressions of welfare state to address chronic poverty in the European Union.

Authors: Shaffa Hameed; Lena Morgon Banks; Sofoora Kawsar Usman; Hannah Kuper

Title: Access to the Disability Allowance in the Maldives: National coverage and factors affecting uptake
primary_category: Child poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that 25.6% of people with disabilities in the Maldives receive the Disability Allowance, with coverage lowest for women, older adults, people living in the capital (Malé), wealthier households, and people with sensory impairments.
What_was_studied: A mixed-methods study exploring coverage of the Disability Allowance in the Maldives, an unconditional, non-means tested cash transfer (2000 MVR or US$130 per month) among people with disabilities and factors affecting uptake across a nationally representative population-based survey and qualitative research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To increase coverage of the Disability Allowance, governments should prioritize outreach efforts to under-served populations such as women, older adults, those living in urban areas, and people with sensory impairments.

Title: The Impact of Social Policies on Income Distribution and the Labour Market in Italy
primary_category: Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Social policies did not suffer real cuts until 1983 despite slowed expansion after 1975, and most recent changes in the income distribution reflect the effects of recession. However, improvements can be discerned in the lowest decile owing to transfer policies targeted on families during the 1970s.
What_was_studied: Italian social policies targeting poverty from 1975 to 1983 and their impact on income distribution during the same period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize expanding social programs and targeted transfers to improve poverty reduction and income distribution.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Intrusion; Nursing; Social policy; Psychological intervention; Ambiguity; Family health; Unit (housing); General partnership
Title: Families 'at risk' and the family nurse partnership: the intrusion of risk into social exclusion policy
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The FNP shows promise in improving parenting skills, reducing child abuse and neglect, increasing employment rates, and encouraging mothers to pursue further education. Specifically, the study found that for every pound invested in the program, there is a return of up to 13 pounds in reduced social expenditure.
What_was_studied: This article considers why the family nurse partnership (FNP) has been promoted as a means of tackling social exclusion in the UK, specifically among low-income first-time mothers during pregnancy and the first two years following birth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the promising results of the FNP, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up this program and investing in its continued development to address intersectional poverty among vulnerable populations. This could involve increasing funding for existing FNP programs or exploring opportunities to expand the program's reach and effectiveness.

Title: Solidarity and reciprocity in the social investment state : what can be learned from the case of Flemish school allowances and truancy?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research reveals that this policy shift has led to increased emphasis on individual responsibility and quid pro quo, which may result in the exclusion of already marginalized groups. The study found that only 58% of single parents receiving school allowances were able to meet the new reciprocity standard, indicating a potential erosion of social protection for vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how the shift from a passive welfare state to an active social investment state in Belgium (Flanders) has affected vulnerable populations, specifically those living in poverty and experiencing intersectional discrimination.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In light of these findings, policy makers should prioritize revamping the social investment state's approach to empowerment and activation, ensuring that it does not inadvertently exacerbate existing social exclusions. This could involve scaling up targeted support programs for disadvantaged groups and expanding eligibility criteria for existing social protection schemes.

Authors: Espen Dahl; Tone Fløtten; Thomas Lorentzen
Field: Social exclusion; Ethnic group; Sociology; Poverty; Friendship; Median income; Development economics; Norwegian; Panel data; Social capital
Title: Poverty Dynamics and Social Exclusion: An Analysis of Norwegian Panel Data
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor people are more likely to see friends regularly than non-poor, but this is primarily caused by some third factor such as work activity or ethnicity, and not by poverty per se. Additionally, the poor are less likely to participate in civic organizations compared to the non-poor, regardless of where the poverty line is drawn and the duration of poverty.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between poverty and social exclusion in a dynamic perspective using four waves of panel data from 1997 to 2000, focusing on two dimensions of social exclusion (lack of friendship relationships and lack of participation in civic organizations) and two aspects of poverty (poverty duration and poverty gradation).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty duration and gradation have a stronger impact on social exclusion than previously thought, policies aimed at reducing poverty should prioritize addressing these aspects to effectively combat chronic poverty, intersectional poverty, and gender and poverty issues. Implementing anti-poverty programs that focus on job creation, education, and skill development can help scale up interventions and expand opportunities for those in need.

Title: The impact of using an income supplement to meet child poverty targets: evidence from Scotland
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The analysis finds that the SCP can technically meet the child poverty targets, but the necessary payment of £165 per week, amounting to a total government cost of £3 billion per year, poses significant political and economy-wide barriers. Additionally, the study shows that the marginal gain in reducing child poverty decreases as the payment increases, with the most effective payments being those between £40-80 per week.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of the Scottish Child Payment (SCP) in reducing child poverty in Scotland, specifically exploring the impact of different payment amounts on poverty reduction and identifying potential policy-mix options to achieve the 2030/31 targets set by the Scottish Government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the ambitious child poverty targets set by the Scottish Government, a policy-mix approach combining the SCP with targeted cash transfers and other support programs is recommended to effectively reduce child poverty while minimizing the economic and political costs. Expanding the SCP and exploring alternative payment structures should be prioritized to maximize poverty reduction while balancing fiscal sustainability.

primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the shrinking population of smokers is increasingly drawn from those occupying subordinate positions in the gender and class hierarchies, with pronounced intra-group differences in smoking behavior associated with material disadvantage and heavier caring responsibilities.
What_was_studied: The decline in smoking prevalence in Britain during the 1990s was analyzed using a mixed-methods approach, focusing on gender and socio-economic disparities among women caring for young children in manual households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the clear links between social inequality and smoking behavior, decision makers should prioritize targeted interventions addressing gender and socio-economic disparities to reduce smoking prevalence and support health equity.

Authors: Robert E. Leu; René L. Frey; Brigitte Buhmann
Field: Economic policy; Aggregate income; Per capita income; Economics; Gross income; Fiscal incidence; Demographic economics; Income distribution; Net national income; Gross domestic income; Adjusted gross income

primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that direct taxes reduce income inequality, while indirect taxes increase it; however, the net effect of all taxes is to reduce income inequality. Additionally, social welfare expenditures have a larger redistributive effect than other government expenditures.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of government policies on income distribution and poverty in Switzerland, using the first nationwide representative Income and Wealth Survey 1980, focusing on the redistributive effect of taxes and expenditures on income distribution in Switzerland.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investments in social welfare programs and targeted tax policies to address income poverty and promote gender equality, particularly in urban areas.

Authors: Mia Hakovirta; Christine Skinner; Heikki Hiilamo; Merita Jokela
Field: Business; Developed country; Work (electrical); Order (exchange); Poverty; Social security; Receipt; Child poverty; Social assistance; Demographic economics
Title: Child Poverty, Child Maintenance and Interactions with Social Assistance Benefits Among Lone Parent Families: a Comparative Analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the potential of child maintenance to alleviate poverty among lone parent families may not be fully realized due to hidden mechanisms within interactions between child maintenance and social security systems, such as the operation of a child maintenance disregard, which can work as effective cost recovery tools for the state but have no poverty reduction impact.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of child maintenance to reduce child poverty among lone parent families in receipt of social assistance in Australia, Finland, Germany, and the UK between 2013 and 2018 using the LIS dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers must understand how these hidden mechanisms work to effectively reduce child poverty among lone parent families. They should prioritize policy reforms that address these issues, such as revising the child maintenance disregard to ensure that all payments received are used to support the family's well-being and alleviate poverty, rather than offsetting other fiscal costs.

Title: ‘Every Town Should Have One’: Emergency Food Banking in the UK
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The data presented demonstrate some of the ways in which the Foodbank model and those who run the projects navigate the tension between addressing symptoms rather than ‘root causes’ of poverty and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The research embeds the phenomenon of the growth of Foodbanks within a social policy research context, examining recent and on-going shifts in the social policy context, notably the importance of welfare diversification under previous Labour governments (1997–2010) and the current public spending cuts, welfare restructuring, and Big Society rhetoric of the Conservative−Liberal Democrat Coalition government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Harness and prioritize the human rights-based approach to food experiences in response to the simultaneous growth in emergency food initiatives and significant upheavals in social policy and welfare provision, especially given the findings' implications for climate vulnerability and food insecurity.

Field: Form of the Good; Welfare state; Economic Justice; Economics; Law; Exposition (narrative); Oppression; Christianity
Title: Rescuing the Good Samaritan: An Exposition and a Defence of the Samaritan Principle in the Welfare State
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper provided an exposition of Samaritanism and defended its role in the modern Welfare State, challenging non-Christians to put their rationale for helping the needy on an equally secure footing as that provided by Christianity. The study found that Samaritanism can provide a more comprehensive approach to addressing health disparities and social protection needs of vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: Catholics in the modern Welfare State were found to have a 'preferential option for the poor' through Samaritanism, which has been largely untheorized in the debate about justice models, such as righting the twin wrongs of exploitation and oppression.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up initiatives that embody Samaritanism, such as community-based programs focused on the whole person, including their physical, emotional, and spiritual well-being. By doing so, they can expand access to healthcare and social services for marginalized populations, ultimately reducing health disparities and improving overall well-being.

What_was_studied: The United Nations Development Program (UNDP) estimates that around one billion people worldwide live under conditions of extreme poverty with under one dollar per day, and at least one billion people live in relative poverty. This study focuses on the situation of global poverty between 1990 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial for local governments to prioritize interventions that target specific groups of the poor, allocate resources adequately, and scale up development plans to address the persistent issue of poverty. Title: Unemployment and Income Protection: How do Better-Earning Households Expect to Manage Financially?
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that state benefits figure only marginally, private insurances to a limited extent, and savings slightly more as sources of income protection for better-earning households in the event of unemployment; however, there is little evidence of strategic planning.
What_was_studied: Sixty-one interviews with couples in the UK to understand how better-earning households expect to cope financially with the risk of unemployment and to what extent they plan ahead for a possible loss of earnings.

Authors: Jin Huang; Minchao Jin; Suo Deng; Baorong Guo; Li Zou; Michael Sherraden

Title: Asset Poverty in Urban China: A Study Using the 2002 Chinese Household Income Project
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the asset-poverty rate in urban China is 12.4%, with a liquid asset-poverty rate of 6.3%. Additionally, the study found that the asset-poverty gap ratio is five times that of the income-poverty rate in urban China, and most households in asset poverty have zero liquid assets or negative net worth.
What_was_studied: Using the 2002 survey data from the Chinese Household Income Project (CHIP), this study investigates asset poverty rates in urban China and finds that while asset poverty rates are lower than those of developed countries, most households in asset poverty have zero liquid assets or negative net worth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize asset building as an integral part of the anti-poverty agenda to protect the poor from economic hardship and provide them with opportunities for economic growth. This could involve expanding access to financial services, such as savings accounts and microloans, and implementing policies that encourage asset accumulation, such as tax incentives for retirement savings or housing subsidies.

Title: Material deprivation and social exclusion of children: lessons from measurement attempts among children in Israel
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The results show it is possible to develop valid and reliable child-centered material deprivation and social exclusion measures that can help policy makers decide on priorities and create policies that better meet the needs of children.
What_was_studied: The research used data from the first wave of the International Survey of Children's Well-being in Israel among twelve-year-olds to develop and test two alternative measures of child poverty: a material deprivation index and a social exclusion measure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up the use of these alternative measures to better understand the scope and nature of child poverty, fund targeted interventions to address material deprivation and social exclusion among vulnerable populations, and prioritize a more comprehensive approach to reducing child poverty that goes beyond income-based measures.

Authors: Elena Bárcena-Martín; M. Carmen Blanco-Arana; Salvador Pérez-Moreno

Title: Social Transfers and Child Poverty in European Countries: Pro-poor Targeting or Pro-child Targeting?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Countries with higher intent to target children experience lower child poverty rates, even more so than targeting lower incomes. Multigenerational households are associated with lower child poverty protection in countries with lower pro-child targeting.
What_was_studied: Children's poverty risk in 30 European countries, using a multilevel framework to compare pro-poor and pro-child targeting approaches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize pro-child targeting in social transfer systems to protect children from poverty, especially in countries with high prevalence of multigenerational households. Expanding social protection coverage and scaling up existing programs can help reduce child poverty.

What_was_found: The empirical finding contradicts the unemployment trap-theorem, as most people re-entered the labor market after a relatively short period of receiving Sozialhilfe. Specifically, 60% of recipients found employment within 12 months.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the German Social Assistance (Sozialhilfe) data from the Socio Economic Panel (GSOEP) between 2009 and 2015, focusing on the recipients' labor market decisions after receiving Sozialhilfe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize and expand support for job placement programs to help recipients transition back into the labor market more quickly.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unreliability of relying solely on one measure of poverty, policy makers should triangulate results from multiple measures to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of poverty and develop targeted interventions that address the unique needs of different populations.
