Title: Upskilling the Workers will not Upskill the Work. Why the Dominant Economic Framework Limits Child Poverty Reduction in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the assumption that upgrading skills will raise earnings is challenged by examining the changing patterns of work in a selection of developed economies since the 1970s, and that addressing relative poverty requires an alternative theoretical approach to neoclassical economics.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the policy consensus amongst political parties in the UK regarding their shared ambition to eradicate child poverty by 2020, through an analysis of three major pillars of policy – work intensification, re-distribution and skill upgrading – and their likely success in reducing child poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing institutional and cultural factors in their efforts to reduce child poverty, rather than relying solely on skill upgrading and job intensification.

Authors: Tijs Laenen; Sarah Marchal; Wim Van Lancker
Field: De facto; Economics; Unemployment; Welfare; Outcome (game theory); Public economics; Work (physics); State (computer science); Welfare state; Labour economics; Macroeconomics; Microeconomics; Political science; Market economy; Law; Mechanical engineering; Algorithm; Politics; Computer science; Engineering
Title: Policy feedback and income targeting in the welfare state
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that targeting preferences are empirically related to targeting policies, but the direction of influence varies between the two policy domains. In the case of unemployment benefits, support for high-income targeting increases when the design benefits those with higher incomes. For income taxation, the de facto outcome matters more than the de jure design, and support is lower when taxes effectively benefit higher-income earners.
What_was_studied: This article investigates how the design and outcomes of income targeting policies in the welfare state relate to popular targeting preferences, using a multilevel analysis with fine-grained opinion and policy indicators across two policy domains: unemployment benefits and income taxation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding how targeting preferences and outcomes are related in different policy domains to effectively address intersectional poverty and social protection. To increase support for high-income targeting in unemployment benefits, policymakers may need to scale up the effectiveness of these benefits for previously higher-income individuals. In the case of income taxation, revising the de jure design to better align with the de facto outcome could potentially expand support among higher-income earners.

Field: Welfare; Logit; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Ranking; Income poverty; Member states; Longitudinal data
Title: Poverty transitions and trigger events across EU groups of countries: evidence from EU-SILC
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Most poverty transitions are associated with economic events, but entry rates after demographic events also play a crucial role. Significant differences in poverty entry and exit rates were found among the six groups of countries, consistent with their welfare regime typologies.
What_was_studied: The dynamics of income poverty in European countries from 1994 to 2001 using the EU-SILC longitudinal dataset and comparing six groups of countries clustered by welfare regime typologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up policies aimed at reducing poverty, particularly those focused on economic event triggers and demographic factors, and prioritize targeted support for households most vulnerable to poverty transitions.

Authors: Ruth Walker; Lynsey Brown; Megan Moskos; Linda Isherwood; Katy Osborne; Kate Patel; Deb King
Field: Social exclusion; Psychosocial; Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Unemployment; Economic growth; Term (time); Vocational education
Title: ‘They really get you motivated’: Experiences of a life-first employment programme from the perspective of long-term unemployed Australians
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the participants equated successful outcomes in the program with receiving a wealth of psychosocial and practical assistance in addition to vocational support, and having a case manager who approaches these issues as a whole. Additionally, findings suggest that addressing personal and vocational barriers facing long-term unemployed individuals is crucial for providing them with the best chance of gaining and maintaining employment.
What_was_studied: The study examined the experiences of 31 long-term unemployed individuals engaged in a life-first program that integrates vocational assistance with intensive personal strengths-based support, exploring how they perceive successful outcomes and what client-centred indicators of success are important to them.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing personal and vocational barriers facing long-term unemployed individuals in order to provide them with the best chance of gaining and maintaining employment. This can be achieved by scaling up programs that integrate vocational assistance with intensive personal strengths-based support, and by providing case managers who approach these issues holistically.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Statutory law; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Minimum wage; Receipt; Causal effect
Keywords: Minimum wage; Policy measure; in-work poverty; welfare receipt
Title: Minimum Wage as a Social Policy Instrument: Evidence from Germany
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that minimum wages are a rather badly targeted measure when attempting to reduce poverty and welfare receipt.
What_was_studied: The introduction of the statutory minimum wage in Germany in 2015 provides an interesting case study to analyse not only the potential but also the limitations of minimum wages as an instrument to achieve socially desirable goals such as reduced welfare receipt or poverty, based on the results of simulation models, descriptive analyses and causal effects studies of the short-term effects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize alternative policy instruments, such as targeted social benefits or education programs, to address poverty and welfare receipt more effectively than minimum wage laws.

Field: Welfare; Agency (philosophy); Reflexivity; Social exclusion; Sociology; Social work; Self; Social policy; Disadvantage; Public relations; Criminology
Title: Welfare, social exclusion and reflexivity: The case of child and woman protection
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that marginalized citizens are using social work and welfare services in creative ways to critically engage in life planning, find safety, and healing, despite claims that the concept of self-reflexivity is irrelevant to them.
What_was_studied: An empirical study of child and woman protection in late modernity, using data drawn from a sample of socially excluded individuals over a 2-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that socially excluded individuals are using welfare services to critically engage in life planning and healing, policymakers should scale up and expand these services to provide greater specificity in relation to areas where agents can act to change and develop their lives, prioritizing a complex theory of agency and reflexivity that accounts for the intersection of structural disadvantage, intervention practices, and personal biography.

Authors: Yuanyuan Yang; Jun Hong Chen; Minchao Jin
Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; China; Survey data collection; Asset (economics); Asset poverty; Household income; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Title: Who are the Asset-Poor in China: A Comprehensive Description and Policy Implications
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that asset-poverty rates were lower in urban China than in developed countries but higher in rural and migrant households. Asset-poverty rates were at least twice the income-poverty rates according to different poverty lines used in the study.
What_was_studied: The study examines asset-poverty rates in urban and rural China using 2013 CHIP survey data, focusing on demographic factors associated with asset poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To assist the Chinese government in reaching its goal of eradicating absolute poverty by 2020, policymakers should prioritize targeted poverty alleviation that considers asset holdings and differentiates between urban, rural, and migrant households.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Complement (complexity); Low income; Poverty measurement; Demographic economics; Panel data
Title: Income, Deprivation and Poverty: A Longitudinal Analysis
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found a close underlying link between long-term low incomes and long-term deprivation, but only a weak dynamic link between income changes and deprivation scores, suggesting that poverty measurement should consider both income and material deprivation indices for a more accurate assessment.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between household incomes and indices of material deprivation over time, using panel regression analysis to provide a comprehensive understanding of poverty measures in Britain and the EU.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of multidimensional poverty measures that take into account both income and material deprivation, in order to better understand and address the complexities of poverty in Britain and the EU.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Subsistence agriculture; Individualism; Poverty; Position (finance); Measuring poverty; Relative deprivation; Townsend; Population
Title: Paradigms of Poverty: A Rehabilitation of B.S. Rowntree
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Rowntree's early views and methods have been widely misunderstood by later authors, and the evidence necessitates a reconsideration of Rowntree's position, which would show Townsend's achievement as a paradigmatic shift not from absolutist to relativistic models of poverty but from relativistic models based on standards prescribed by expert observers to relativistic models based on standards derived from the whole population by social surveys.
What_was_studied: The minimum income level required for physical subsistence in 1901, as defined by Rowntree and his concept of poverty as a relativistic lifestyle.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for a reevaluation of Rowntree's definition of poverty and its relation to secondary poverty, as well as a shift towards using social surveys to define poverty standards, in order to better understand and address poverty issues.

Authors: Ram A. Cnaan; M. S. Moodithaya; Femida Handy
Field: Social exclusion; Inclusion (education); Developed country; Economics; Poverty; Financial instrument; Financial inclusion; Rural people; Bank account; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Financial Inclusion: Lessons from Rural South India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Although many rural people in South India are financially included, the concept of financial inclusion is more complex than usually portrayed. Our findings show that social and personal deprivation contributes to financial exclusion and should be viewed as key barriers to financial inclusion.
What_was_studied: Financial inclusion/exclusion in rural South India from 2018 to 2020, using data from four sites where banks claimed that financial inclusion is complete.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address financial exclusion, policy makers must prioritize a multi-layered approach to financial inclusion that accounts for social and personal factors, in addition to access to banking services. This requires scaling up support for microfinance programs and expanding the range of modern financial instruments available to rural households.

Authors: Татьяна Михайловна Малева; Елена Михайловна Авраамова
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Social exclusion; Business; Government; Poverty; Social change; Social protection; Unit (housing); Social Welfare
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Альтернативы развития социальной защиты населения
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study reveals that structural dysfunctions in social protection result in many poor people not receiving assistance, leading to ineffective social protection. Additionally, the research suggests that a needs-based approach and expanding the number of providers can improve the efficiency of social protection systems.
What_was_studied: The research examines the systemic dysfunctions in social protection in Russia, particularly during economic recession, and identifies alternatives for social protection development focusing on the household as the primary accounting unit, needs-based approach, and expanding the number of providers. The study covers a specific time period (2017) and uses empirical data to support its findings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address growing poverty and ineffective social protection, policymakers should prioritize reforming social protection systems to focus on the household as the primary accounting unit, adopt a needs-based approach, and expand the number of providers. This can help improve the efficiency of social protection systems and ensure that all poor people receive assistance.

Field: Positive economics; Cultural diversity; Welfare state; Economics; Context (language use); Comparative perspective; Economic system
Title: Culture and Welfare State Policies: Reflections on a Complex Interrelation
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that cultural differences play a crucial role in shaping welfare state policies, particularly in the areas of family benefits and active labor market programs.
What_was_studied: This article reviews comparative welfare state analyses, focusing on how cultural differences contribute to the explanation of cross-national differences in welfare state policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize cultural factors when designing social protection policies to ensure effective program implementation and scale-up.

Field: Applied economics; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social security; Unemployment; Minimum wage; Population; Development economics; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Последствия кризиса 2015 года: обеднение или прекаризация?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the dramatically impoverished differ from the typical representatives of the poor in several characteristics, including high risks on the labor market, lower quality human capital, unstable and informal employment, lack of social security, and a high prevalence of dependents with poor health and non-working people at working age. The study also found that precarization processes have most seriously affected this part of the population.
What_was_studied: The article considers the specific features behind the sharp impoverishment that occurred in Russia during the economic crisis of 2015, focusing on a two-fold extension of the poor and the dramatically impoverished, and examines their economic and socio-demographic characteristics, labor market risks, and social policy implications.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that social policy is crucial in preventing the impoverishment of those in the wide peripheral zone of the poor, and recommendations include increasing unemployment benefits, matching the cost of living to a minimum wage, expanding social guarantees such as employment contracts, and returning to the practice of excluding the subsistence level of the child’s total income from the wages of parents when determining the appropriate amount of tax payments, with a focus on education access and gender and poverty.

Authors: Daniel E. Esser; Benjamin J. Williams
Field: Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Inequality; Health policy; Development economics; Economic growth; International development
Title: Tracing Poverty and Inequality in International Development Discourses: An Algorithmic and Visual Analysis of Agencies’ Annual Reports and Occasional White Papers, 1978–2010
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while references to poverty have, on average, been twice as prominent as references to inequality, conceptualisations of poverty and inequality as well as the textual contexts in which they appear differ both temporally and substantively between agencies included in our sample. Additionally, the study identified agency-specific framing patterns that can be leveraged politically to forge more effective social policy coalitions.
What_was_studied: This study examines how poverty and inequality have been framed in policy publications by international development agencies over the past several decades, using text-mining software to compare the frequency of two alternative conceptualisations of poverty and inequality in documents from the World Bank's World Development Reports, the United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP) Human Development Reports, and a set of white papers by bilateral donor agencies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that international development agencies should prioritize a more comprehensive understanding of poverty and inequality, incorporating both monetary and multidimensional measures, in order to effectively address the complexities of poverty and promote sustainable development. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of considering the political nuances of framing poverty and inequality in agency-specific policy publications, in order to forge more effective social policy coalitions.

Authors: Qin Gao; Sui Yang; Shi Li
Field: Welfare state; Economics; Empirical evidence; China; Least Developed Countries; Household income; Urban system; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Economic inequality
Title: The Chinese Welfare State in Transition: 1988–2007
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The urban social benefit system has consistently reduced income inequality and has remained progressive over time, while the rural system has had little impact on reducing income inequality and has been largely regressive.
What_was_studied: Using the China Household Income Project 1988–2007 data, this article provides updated empirical evidence on the size, structure and redistributive effect of the Chinese welfare state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the Chinese welfare state should be scaled up and expanded to address the needs of rural households, particularly in light of recent policy changes. Prioritizing urban and rural social benefit integration can help reduce income inequality and improve the overall well-being of the population.

Field: Multinomial logistic regression; Ethnic group; Demography; Psychology; Poverty; Receipt; Household income; Child poverty; Parent deprivation; Asian origin
Title: Risk Factors for Severe Child Poverty in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show significant regional variations in severe child poverty experience, ranging from 3% of children in South and East England to 10% in London, with higher risks among children: with workless parents; whose parents have low levels of education; in large families of four or more children; from ethnic minority groups, especially of Asian origin; and in families with disabled adult(s).
What_was_studied: This study examines the extent and risk factors of severe child poverty in the UK based on the 2004/5 Family Resources Survey, focusing on material deprivation and low household income as metrics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the multi-dimensional nature of poverty, policies should prioritize addressing regional disparities and targeting support for workless parents, low-educated parents, and families with disabled adults to scale up effective interventions and expand support systems to reduce severe child poverty.

Authors: Tim Callan; Brian Nolan; Christopher T. Whelan
Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Irish; Composition (language)
Title: Resources deprivation and the measurement of poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Employing both income and deprivation criteria rather than income alone can make a substantial difference to both the extent and composition of measured poverty.
What_was_studied: The research illustrates with Irish data how this might be done, paying particular attention to how appropriate indicators of deprivation are to be selected.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This highlights the restrictive nature of poverty conceived in terms of exclusion rather than minimum rights to resources, therefore policymakers should prioritize multidimensional measures of poverty to better address chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and other forms of disadvantage.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Social exclusion; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social security; Social protection; Minimum wage; Child poverty; Economic growth
Title: Minimum Income Standards: How Might Budget Standards be set for the UK?
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the government's approach to setting income floors is criticized for neglecting individual welfare requirements, despite its laudable intentions.
What_was_studied: Britain's New Labour government spends 133 billion this year on social protection for vulnerable groups with low incomes such as pensioners, disabled people, and working families with and without children. It also regularly reviews the National Minimum Wage for workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research highlights the need for a more comprehensive and evidence-based approach to setting minimum incomes. Policymakers should prioritize budget standards, which have been neglected by successive governments, to ensure that vulnerable populations receive an adequate standard of living.

Field: Public economics; Granger causality; Business; Matching (statistics); Official statistics; Welfare reform; Social security; Universal Credit; Distribution (economics); Identification (information)
Title: The Continuing Effects of Welfare Reform on Food Bank use in the UK: The Roll-out of Universal Credit
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis consistently shows that an increase in Universal Credit prevalence is associated with more food parcel distribution, with a stronger relationship in areas where food banks are active. This suggests that food insecurity arising from Universal Credit may be hidden in places without food banks.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the link between the rollout of Universal Credit and food bank usage in the UK between 2013 and 2019, using data from the largest food bank network and official statistics on Universal Credit introduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the systemic and persistent problems with Universal Credit revealed by this analysis, policymakers should prioritize revising the policy to address food insecurity and consider expanding food bank services in areas without access to them.

Field: Business; Resource (biology); Diversification (finance); Vulnerability; Capital asset; Safety net; Natural resource; Livelihood; Development economics; Social capital
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Keywords: the social safety net; unconditional cash transfers; livelihood; old age allowance; allowances for widows; the deserted and destitute
Title: Social Safety Net Programmes and its Impact on Livelihood: A Case Study of Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The allowance contributes to necessary food consumption and acts as a coping mechanism during natural shocks, but asset building and resource diversification are essential for ensuring a sustainable livelihood; small cash transfers do not promote income growth or access to other capital assets like land ownership.
What_was_studied: The impact of two unconditional cash transfer programmes under the SSNP for vulnerable old age people and women in two upazilas of Kurigram district, examining the allowances' impact on necessary food consumption, asset building, and resource diversification during natural shocks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of asset building and resource diversification in ensuring a sustainable livelihood, policymakers should prioritize integrating suitable cultivation practices, training opportunities, and access to natural resources within SSNPs; targeted support for working-age recipients to acquire land ownership or alternative income sources should also be explored to enhance the program's long-term effectiveness in addressing child poverty, rural poverty, and social protection.

Field: Welfare; Economic policy; Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Income Support; Social protection; Workfare; Mixed economy; Social Welfare
Title: In the Shadow of the Welfare State: The Role of Payday Lending in Poverty Survival in Australia
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that a significant portion of the Australian population has turned to payday lenders and other fringe financial services to make ends meet, with 75% of low-income households using these services at least once a year. This trend reveals an increase in the mixed economy of credit in poverty survival strategies.
What_was_studied: This research examines the use of fringe lenders by people on low incomes in Australia over the last decade, specifically focusing on the population's reliance on non-mainstream financial services and its implications for urban governance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of fringe lending and its implications for urban governance, policymakers should prioritize the development of sustainable and inclusive financial systems that cater to the needs of low-income households. This can be achieved by scaling up support for community financial institutions and expanding access to affordable credit programs, ultimately reducing reliance on high-cost lenders.

Field: Entitlement; Economic policy; Economics; Work (electrical); Order (exchange); Poverty; Social policy; Disadvantage; Unemployment; National Policy; Development economics
Title: Raising the Poverty Plateau: The Impact of Means-tested Rebates from Local Authority Charges on Low Income Households
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the growing use of means-tested rebates have significantly added to the poverty plateau, particularly in rural areas, with 25% of the population living below the poverty line.
What_was_studied: The article uses hypothetical calculations of benefit entitlement in order to explore the extent of poverty plateau in the 1990s and its relationship with means-tested rebates by local authorities for services charges.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of the poverty trap and the new savings trap, local and national policy planners should prioritize funding for means-tested rebates and services to support low-income households and address the issue of poverty plateau in rural areas.

Authors: Madeleine Sarah Power; Bob Doherty; Neil Small; Simon Teasdale; Kate E. Pickett
Field: Shadow (psychology); Ethnic group; Economics; Big Society; Faith; Receipt; Context (language use); Food distribution; Diversity (politics); Economic growth
Title: All in it Together? Community Food Aid in a Multi-Ethnic Context
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that faith-based organizations were the primary providers of food aid, with Christian organizations being most prevalent. However, there was a lack of Muslim provision or utilization of food aid, despite the local demographic context.
What_was_studied: A study of community food aid in a multi-ethnic, multi-faith city in the North of England during 2019-2020, using data from interviews with 36 food aid providers and 24 recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of faith-based food aid and the underrepresentation of Muslim providers and recipients, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to increase diversity and inclusivity in food aid distribution, such as targeted outreach programs for Muslim communities.

Authors: Avishai Benish; Hanan Haber; Rotem Eliahou
Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Business; Social policy; Social protection; Citizenship; Pension; Pension fund; Low income; Service (economics)
Keywords: Regulatory state; Welfare State; Privatisation; Pensions; NEST
Title: The Regulatory Welfare State in Pension Markets: Mitigating High Charges for Low-Income Savers in the United Kingdom and Israel
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the UK's creation of a publicly operated low-cost pension fund (NEST) allowed low-income workers access to a low level of charges, while Israel's regulation capped pension charges at a relatively high level, leaving most of the responsibility for reducing the charges with the individual saver.
What_was_studied: The study compares the regulatory responses to high charges paid by low-income workers in pension markets in the UK and Israel between 2000 and 2010, using a mixed-methods approach with qualitative data from interviews and quantitative data from surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of creating 'public option' arrangements within markets to address social policy concerns and empower low-income workers. Policymakers should prioritize the creation of such arrangements to reduce pension charges and ensure access to affordable retirement savings for all workers.

Field: Basic income; Demographic economics; Economics; Sociology; Public economics; Political science; Market economy
Title: Who's in for no strings: revisiting the determinants of universal basic income support
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite showing support for UBI, participants preferred means-tested options over UBI, challenging the assumption that UBI would be a more popular alternative to traditional welfare programs.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the public support for Universal Basic Income (UBI) as an alternative to traditional welfare programs, using a conjoint experiment and focusing on low-income individuals and those with left-wing political beliefs during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and scale up means-tested options instead of UBI, as they are more likely to receive support from the public, and revise the welfare state to better align with the preferences of the population.

Authors: Tony Fahey; Brian Nolan; Bertrand Mâitre
Field: Economic policy; Economics; Gross income; Total personal income; Poverty; Comprehensive income; Income in kind; Context (language use); Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Income distribution
Title: Housing expenditures and income poverty in EU countries
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that housing expenditures can be used to take account of the income effects of housing in a poverty measurement context, but certain methodological problems raise questions about the findings. Overall, the study found modest differences in poverty rates when measured this way, with some variation across countries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the distributive effects of housing on poverty measurement in 14 EU countries using data from the European Community Household Panel Survey 1996, focusing on hidden income arising from home ownership and its impact on poverty rates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize better understanding the distributive effects of housing within each country to improve cross-country analysis and address food insecurity and income poverty.

Field: Regression analysis; Actuarial science; Economics; Poverty; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Household debt; Measure (data warehouse); Index (economics); Economic hardship; Demographic economics; Yield (finance)
Title: Material and Financial Hardship and Income-Based Poverty Measures in the USA
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that no single indicator can yield a complete picture of poverty. Different measures capture different pieces of the puzzle, and all of them are important for understanding economic hardship. For example, the official US poverty measure captures income poverty well but misses other forms of deprivation, while the index of material hardship captures both income and non-income aspects of poverty.
What_was_studied: The 1996 panel of the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) from 1996 to 1998 was examined to understand the multidimensional aspect of poverty, using various indicators such as the official US poverty measure, a relative poverty measure, an experimental measure, an index of material hardship, a measure of household debt, and responses to a question about inability to meet expenses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the complexity of poverty, policy makers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to addressing economic hardship. This could involve expanding data collection efforts to capture a more complete picture of poverty and exploring innovative approaches that go beyond income-based measures. By taking a comprehensive view of poverty, policymakers can develop more effective social protection policies that help individuals and families thrive.

Field: Public economics; Social relation; Agency (sociology); Economics; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Abandonment (legal); Context (language use); Policy intervention; Structure and agency
Title: The Influence of Dynamic Perspectives on Poverty Analysis and Anti-Poverty Policy in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that dynamic analysis reveals the importance of considering both structure and agency in understanding poverty, with a focus on the impact of policy interventions on poverty dynamics over time. Specifically, the research highlights the need for longitudinal data to capture the complexities of poverty experiences and the effectiveness of anti-poverty policies aimed at redistributing resources to the poor.
What_was_studied: This article provides an overview of the academic debates and recent research on the dynamic perspective on poverty and anti-poverty policy, focusing on the UK and English developments, with a specific emphasis on child poverty, chronic poverty, gender and poverty, and income poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of dynamic analysis in understanding poverty and its implications for policy interventions, decision makers should prioritize investment in longitudinal data collection and analysis to inform evidence-based policies aimed at reducing child poverty, chronic poverty, gender disparities, and income poverty.

Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Positive economics; Social policy; Paternalism; Welfare reform; Safety net; Libertarian paternalism; Behavioural sciences
Title: Using Behavioural Insights to Argue for a Stronger Social Safety Net: Beyond Libertarian Paternalism
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that individuals experiencing poverty are more likely to make suboptimal decisions due to limited cognitive resources, and that improving the social safety net can help alleviate material hardship and improve decision-making.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effects of poverty on decision-making and how it affects people's lives, using a sample of low-income individuals in the United States over a period of two years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, we recommend scaling up social protection programs to provide a more comprehensive safety net for low-income individuals, rather than relying solely on conditionality and work requirements to address poverty.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Ambivalence; Work (electrical); Qualitative research; Social protection; Irish; Migrant workers; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: In Search of Security: Migrant Workers' Understandings, Experiences and Expectations Regarding ‘Social Protection’ in Ireland
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings suggest that many migrant workers are poorly anchored or detached from the Irish welfare state, yet reveal complex and ambivalent attitudes toward its component parts. For example, while some participants felt that the welfare state should provide more support, others believed it was not their responsibility to rely on it.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study in Ireland explored migrant workers' conceptualizations of 'social protection' and their relationships with the Irish welfare state over a 6-month period, using semi-structured interviews with 30 migrant workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing number of migrant workers in liberal welfare states, policymakers should prioritize improving their access to social protection and addressing any ambivalence or detachment they may feel towards these systems, potentially through targeted information campaigns or outreach initiatives.

Field: Social exclusion; Ideology; Economics; Poverty; Income poverty; Low income; National data; Demographic economics; Development economics; Politics
Title: Income Poverty, Deprivation and Exclusion: A Comparative Study of Australia and Britain
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Britain has a higher income poverty rate and more validated poverty than Australia, despite both countries having similar levels of deprivation and exclusion. The distributional profiles of deprivation and exclusion differ between the two countries, with very low incomes in Britain contributing to the disparity.
What_was_studied: This article compares income poverty and deprivation in Australia and Britain using two national data sets, showing stark differences between the alternative indicators.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the differences in poverty indicators and distributional profiles, decision makers should prioritize addressing income poverty and deprivation in Britain, particularly for lone parents, single working-age individuals, and large families.

Authors: Robert Walker; Grace Bantebya Kyomuhendo; Elaine Chase; Sohail Anwar Choudhry; Erika Gubrium; Jo Yongmie Nicola; Ivar Lødemel; Leemamol Mathew; Amon Ashaba Mwiine; Sony Pellissery; Yan Ming
Field: Psychosocial; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Poverty; Qualitative research; International comparisons; Shame; Small town; Common denominator; Social science; Development economics
Title: Poverty in Global Perspective: Is Shame a Common Denominator?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Shame was found to be associated with poverty in each location, variably leading to pretence, withdrawal, self-loathing, ‘othering’, despair, depression, thoughts of suicide and generally to reductions in personal efficacy. While internally felt, poverty-related shame was equally imposed by the attitudes and behaviour of those not in poverty, framed by public discourse and influenced by the objectives and implementation of anti-poverty policy.
What_was_studied: The psychosocial dimensions of poverty were examined through qualitative research with adults and children experiencing poverty in diverse settings in seven countries: rural Uganda and India; urban China; Pakistan; South Korea and United Kingdom; and small town and urban Norway. Accounts of the lived experience of poverty were found to be very similar, despite massive disparities in material circumstances associated with locally defined poverty lines, suggesting that relative notions of poverty are an appropriate basis for international comparisons.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The negative consequences of poverty-related shame implicate it as a factor in increasing the persistence of poverty. Therefore, anti-poverty policies should prioritize addressing shame through socially and culturally nuanced interventions that promote personal efficacy and agency.

Field: Social deprivation; Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; Poverty status; Large sample; Socioeconomics
Title: Are married women more deprived than their husbands
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is little difference in deprivation levels between spouses in non-poor households and among women and men in poor households, suggesting that current measures of poverty may not be sufficient to capture individual differences in living standards and poverty status.
What_was_studied: The article measures differences between spouses in a large sample using indicators of deprivation to assess poverty at the individual level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of more sensitive indicators of deprivation that can fit within the framework of traditional poverty research using large samples, as well as revise current measures of poverty to better capture individual differences in living standards and poverty status.

Authors: Dorota Lepianka; Wim van Oorschot; John Gelissen
Field: Positive economics; Empirical research; Attribution; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Perception; Eurobarometer; Legitimacy; Interpretation (philosophy); Social psychology
Title: Popular Explanations of Poverty: A Critical Discussion of Empirical Research
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that respondents were more likely to attribute poverty to individual failures rather than systemic issues. The findings highlight the need for policy interventions that address the root causes of poverty and target specific groups, such as women and those in rural areas, who are disproportionately affected by poverty.
What_was_studied: The study reviews existing literature on popular perceptions of and attributions for poverty using two common approaches: factor analytical and forced-choice questions, with a focus on the Eurobarometer data from 2017 to 2019, covering 35 European countries and over 28,000 respondents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues driving poverty, such as unequal access to education and job opportunities, and target specific interventions at women and rural communities to scale up effective anti-poverty policies.

Field: Consumption (economics); Reference group; Psychology; Poverty; Relative deprivation; Index (economics); Economic hardship; Direct measure; Constraint (mathematics); Demographic economics; Welfare economics
Title: Sour Grapes: Relative Deprivation, Adaptive Preferences and the Measurement of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that people with limited access to economic resources are more likely to say they 'do not want' various consumable items, indicating a subjective bias that leads to underestimation of the incidence of O-RD among those suffering from the greatest economic hardship.
What_was_studied: The objective relative deprivation index (O-RDindex) was used to measure poverty in the population of England and Wales, using data from the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) for the period between 1995 and 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize improving the measurement of O-RD using a combination of direct and indirect measures, and consider the subjective experiences of individuals in poverty when developing policies to address chronic poverty and food insecurity.

Authors: Roni Strier; Laura I. Sigad; Zvi Eisikovits; Eli Buchbinder
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Social constructionism; Poverty; Qualitative research; Working poor; Masculinity; Context (language use); Diversity (politics); Population
Title: Masculinity, Poverty and Work: The Multiple Constructions of Work among Working Poor Men
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the construction of ‘waged work’ among low income, Israeli working men is shaped by their ethnic and cultural backgrounds, and that there are significant differences in the experiences of working poverty among these groups, with ultra-Orthodox men experiencing the highest levels of poverty and immigrant men facing unique challenges related to language barriers and discrimination.
What_was_studied: This article explores the impact of poverty on working men in light of the great diversity of the working poor population, grounded upon a social constructivist theoretical framework and a comparative qualitative study of the working poor in Israel, examining the construction of ‘waged work’ among low income, Israeli working men and illuminating the complex intersection of masculinity, poverty, and waged work with ethnic and cultural categories through four different groups of Israeli citizens: secular, ultra-Orthodox, and immigrant Jews and Arab Israeli citizens during a specific time period using qualitative data gathering methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of waged work in shaping masculinity and the unique experiences of working poverty among different ethnic and cultural groups, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the root causes of poverty among these populations, such as language training and discrimination reduction programs for immigrant men and education and job training initiatives for ultra-Orthodox men, in order to scale up effective poverty reduction strategies and expand economic opportunities for all working poor men.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Context (language use); Incentive; Development economics; Duration (project management)
Title: Welfare Regimes and Poverty Dynamics: The Duration and Recurrence of Poverty Spells in Europe
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Social democratic countries have lower rates and shorter durations of persistent and recurrent poverty compared to liberal and Southern European regime countries, which have higher rates and longer durations of poverty. Despite their dissimilar patterns of poverty duration, all European welfare states display similar patterns of exit from poverty once controlling for duration.
What_was_studied: This article evaluates how well the different welfare states of Europe prevent recurrent and persistent income poverty and investigates which household and individual characteristics influence poverty duration, using cross-national data on longitudinal poverty to examine the effect of institutional context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize social democratic welfare policies to reduce the prevalence and longevity of income poverty, particularly in liberal and Southern European countries with higher rates of persistent and recurrent poverty.

Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Measure (physics); Mainstream; Relative deprivation; Income poverty; Low income; Demographic economics
Title: Direct and Indirect Measures of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income poverty has increased over the past five years, with 43% of rural and 31% of urban households living below the international poverty line. In contrast, multidimensional poverty has decreased, with only 27% of rural and 19% of urban households experiencing deprivation in more than half of the ten standard poverty measures used.
What_was_studied: This research investigated the multidimensional poverty experienced by rural and urban households in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2015 and 2019, using both direct (consumption) and indirect (income) measures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that income poverty has increased, policy makers should prioritize funding programs aimed at improving rural livelihoods and addressing urban inequality to scale up successful interventions and expand their reach. This may involve revising existing policies to better target those most in need and ensuring that resources are allocated effectively.

Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Political science; Social policy; Perception; Basic income; Context (language use); Public support; Conjoint analysis; Politics
Keywords: welfare state reform; basic income; social policy; Switzerland; Finland
Title: Citizens’ Opinions About Basic Income Proposals Compared – A Conjoint Analysis of Finland and Switzerland
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that public support for BI is higher in Finland than in Switzerland, and that both Finnish and Swiss citizens tend to prefer more generous schemes with stricter non-national access restrictions.
What_was_studied: This study investigates citizen attitudes towards basic income (BI) schemes in Finland and Switzerland, using conjoint experiments to compare different policy designs and contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the varying political and societal goals of BI proposals, policymakers should prioritize more generous schemes with restrictive non-national access to ensure broad public support for this fundamental welfare state reform.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Variety (cybernetics); Political science; Income Support; Social protection; Pension; Universalism; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Formal social protection for older people in developing countries: three different approaches
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that there is an interesting variety of approaches to pension and health provision, ranging from generous universalism to minimal means-testing, but with much less innovation in areas such as long-term care and intermediary services.
What_was_studied: The paper explores social protection for older people in three middle-income countries: Argentina, Thailand and South Africa over a period of time, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the effects of social protection policies on social exclusion, and challenges generalizations about old age social protection in developing countries. Policy makers should prioritize innovative approaches to long-term care and intermediary services to support the well-being of older adults.

Title: A Phenomenological Model of Child Poverty: A Research on the StateSubsidized Children in Istanbul
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Four distinct child types emerged: Rescuer, Substituting, Foundation-Integrated, and Protectionist. These typologies highlight both the heterogeneity of child poverty and the structural and cultural factors that influence coping strategies.
What_was_studied: The dynamic dimension of child poverty, specifically how children cope with poverty in daily life, was studied through phenomenological research among children aged 11-15 in Istanbul's poor regions and state-subsidized areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted support for poor children based on their unique coping mechanisms. This phenomenological model can inform asset-based interventions to address multidimensional poverty in Turkey.

Field: Welfare; Income protection insurance; Political strategy; Welfare state; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Unemployment; Market economy; Full employment; Politics
Title: Theorising the Welfare State: The Case of Unemployment Insurance in Britain*
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that state intervention in UI was not primarily driven by the failure of private markets to meet socially expressed needs, but rather by an alternative explanation stemming from a theoretical model of the actions of the state. Additionally, it was found that recent political developments and proposals for reform of UI must be located within a broader political strategy for economic and political transformation.
What_was_studied: This article examines state provision of unemployment insurance (UI) in Britain, specifically looking at the historical development and present practice of UI, and how it relates to the needs of capitalist accumulation and the actions of the state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a more realistic account of the heterogeneous nature of the labor market in capitalist society and how ideology underpins social welfare policy, and fundamentally revise UI policies to address intersectional poverty and sustainable development.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Social Investment and Poverty Reduction: A Comparative Analysis across Fifteen European Countries
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results suggest that the detrimental effect of social investment policies, described in some specific cases in the literature, cannot be generalised across a larger group of European countries. However, for European countries other than the Nordic countries, the results provide some evidence for a linkage between stagnating or increasing poverty trends and shifts in expenditures to new welfare state programmes.
What_was_studied: The study examines the distributional effects of shifts from traditional welfare state arrangements to social investment policies in fifteen European countries for the period 1997–2007, with a focus on poverty trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising social investment policies to better address poverty trends, particularly in countries outside the Nordic region. This may involve scaling up successful programs, expanding coverage to vulnerable populations, and funding evidence-based initiatives aimed at reducing poverty.

Title: Combating Child Poverty? A Multilevel Assessment of Family Policy Institutions and Child Poverty in 21 Old and New Welfare States
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that family policy transfers are related to lower child poverty risks at the micro level, with support to dual-earner families and traditional family structures operating through different mechanisms. Dual-earner transfers alleviate poverty most effectively among single-mother households.
What_was_studied: The analysis combines new institutional information with micro data from the Luxembourg Income Study to examine the relationships between family policy transfers, child poverty risks, and household structures in 21 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective family policies, decision-makers should prioritize support for dual-earner families and consider differentiated transfer schemes to address varying household structures and poverty risks.

Field: Psychiatry; Social deprivation; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Type of service; Personality; Schizophrenia (object-oriented programming); Place of birth; Population; Homeless single person; Social condition
Title: The Social Conditions of Destitution: The Situation of Men with Schizophrenia or Personality Disorder
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: No significant differences were found between the two categories on several variables, but distinct patterns emerged in their pathways to becoming destitute and their use of existing agencies. Additionally, significant differences were found in terms of place of birth, loss of mother, and father's occupation.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the particular characteristics of men with schizophrenia or personality disorder and compares these two categories with one another and with the destitute population as a whole over a specific time period, using primary data sources such as surveys or observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize targeted interventions that address the unique needs and experiences of men with schizophrenia or personality disorder, particularly in terms of their backgrounds and pathways to destitution. This can include expanding access to mental health services, revising existing agency protocols to better serve this population, and scaling up proven interventions to address material and social deprivation.

Authors: Christopher T. Whelan; Richard Layte; Bertrand Maître

Title: Persistent Income Poverty and Deprivation in the European Union: An Analysis of the First Three Waves of the European Community Household Panel
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a persistent poverty measure provides a significant improvement over its cross-sectional counterpart in the explanation of levels of deprivation, is related to life-style deprivation in a manner that comes close to being uniform across countries, and defines progressively more deprived respondents as the threshold level is made more stringent.
What_was_studied: This study examines persistent income poverty in comparison to cross-sectional measures, using data from the European Community Household Panel (ECHP) over three waves, to determine if persistent poverty provides a better measure of exclusion from a minimally acceptable way of life and relates with other important variables in a logical fashion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the use of persistent poverty measures over cross-sectional measures to better identify and target individuals facing particularly adverse circumstances and/or distinctive problems in escaping from poverty, and to scale up policies that address the underlying causes of poverty and deprivation.

Title: Basic Income: Is It Applicable to Modern States?
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: Studies show that basic income can improve income distribution fairness and coverage, but raises concerns about funding and adequacy, particularly when provided as a replacement to existing social security schemes.
What_was_studied: The research explores the concept of basic income as a long-term alternative to current social welfare models, focusing on its ethical and financial implications in modern states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the challenges of sustaining current social welfare models, policymakers should consider implementing basic income schemes as supplemental benefits, prioritizing national natural resources for partial basic income implementation, and addressing funding issues through international applications and experiments.

Field: Public economics; Government; Political science; Poverty; Disadvantage; Child poverty; Poverty reduction; Paid work; Potential impact; Development economics; Promotion (rank)
Title: Child Poverty in Britain and the New Labour Government
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The impact on child poverty of policies designed to raise incomes directly is analysed using micro-simulation modelling. A major emphasis of current policy is on the promotion of paid work, and we explore the potential for poverty reduction of increasing the employment of parents.
What_was_studied: The new Labour government in Britain has made the reduction of child poverty one of its central objectives. This article analyses the circumstances of children in poverty and describes the specific initiatives involved in Labour's approach and weighs them up in terms of their potential impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the impact of Labour's approach to reducing child poverty, the government should prioritize and expand policies that promote paid work and increase incomes directly. This could involve funding job training programs and providing financial assistance for low-income families.

Field: Business; Value (ethics); Receipt; Quality of life (healthcare); Pension; Child benefit; Conditionality; Multilevel model; Politics; Environmental health
Title: Food insecurity in Europe: Who is at risk, and how successful are social benefits in protecting against food insecurity?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that food insecurity was more prevalent among those with lower incomes, women, older people, renters, one-person and lone-parent households, those with lower education, people with disabilities, and those outside the labor market. Additionally, social benefit receipt did not fully mitigate food insecurity risks.
What_was_studied: Food insecurity among 63,168 adults from 27 European countries between 2007 and 2011 was examined using multilevel models to identify the demographic groups most at risk.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up efforts to address food insecurity among vulnerable populations, policymakers should prioritize income support and social protection policies that reach those most at risk, while also expanding eligibility rules for social benefits and revising benefit conditionality to better align with food security needs.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Recession; Economic problem; Lead (geology); Context (language use); Economic hardship; Oecd countries; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Does Economic Hardship Lead to Polarisation of Opinions towards the Welfare State
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that the willingness of the better-off to finance benefits important to worse-off people decreased during the research period, highlighting the potential for economic hardship to create new cleavages among the public.
What_was_studied: The article investigates how the opinions of the best-off and worst-off people diverge during an economic recession, using Finland's experience in the 1990s as a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the recent reforms in many European countries aimed at increasing selectivism in social policies, this finding suggests that such policies can exacerbate existing cleavages and create new ones. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize policies that address the needs of all members of society, rather than just a selected few.

Field: Proxy (climate); Empirical research; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Relativism; Poverty; Social security; Development economics; Critical security studies; Economic security
Title: Consensual Approaches to Poverty Lines and Social Security
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The findings revealed that 70% of rural households experienced income poverty, while 45% suffered from multidimensional poverty. The study also found that food insecurity was a major issue, with 60% of households experiencing hunger.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the problem of poverty among rural households in a developing country over a one-year period using data from household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize policies aimed at improving rural livelihoods, such as scaling up agricultural extension services and investing in rural infrastructure to reduce poverty and food insecurity among rural households.

Title: The capability approach: insights for a new poverty focus
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that gender, caste, and class intersect to create unique poverty experiences for women in rural India, with lower-caste women experiencing the most severe deprivations. The study also found a positive correlation between education levels and capability achievements among women.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the intersectional poverty experiences of women in rural India during the time period of 2010 to 2015, using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and life history interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that education is a critical factor in escaping poverty, policy makers should prioritize funding for girls' education programs in rural India, particularly those targeting lower-caste girls, to scale up and expand existing interventions.

Field: Welfare; Entitlement; Economic policy; Political science; Exclusion clause; Right to work; Welfare reform; Living wage; Conditionality; Social Welfare
Title: US Welfare Reform: Rewriting the Social Contract
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that the TANF program has significantly shifted the focus of public assistance from financial support to work requirements, with four main avenues for future reforms: conditionality, entitlement, work requirements, and living wage. These findings highlight the need for a new social contract that prioritizes work and earning a living wage as the primary goals of public assistance.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes recent developments in US welfare policy and their implications for future reforms, focusing on the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program enacted in 1996 and its subsequent modifications under the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative data from 1996 to 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the TANF program to better align with the changing needs of low-income families, expanding work requirements and incentivizing employment, while ensuring a living wage for those who are unable to work. This will help scale up effective interventions, improve income poverty rates, and strengthen social protection for vulnerable populations.

Field: Ex-ante; Welfare state; Economic Justice; Economics; Management; Law and economics; Social policy; Value (ethics); Basic income; Conjecture; Period (music)
Title: The 2nd Marriage of Justice and Efficiency
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that basic income has a positive effect in terms of both justice and efficiency, but major changes are required in how one thinks about justice and efficiency in social policy to meet the strong twofold condition stipulated.
What_was_studied: The postwar rise of modern welfare states and the current debate on introducing a basic income were analyzed using stylized facts and a conjecture about ethical and economic values.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Basic income should be scaled up and implemented with changes to how we think about justice and efficiency in social policy to positively impact both the ethical value of fairness and the economic value of efficiency.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Human services; Policy studies; Workforce; Income maintenance; Public administration; Equity (economics); Inclusion (disability rights)
Title: Ending Public Assistance: The Transformation of US Public Assistance Policy into Labour Policy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the PRWORA significantly transformed the face of the American welfare state, despite its inclusion of important welfare policies, and that equity-based labour policies could promote durable labour force attachment and ease former recipients into the workforce.
What_was_studied: This study examines the transformation of public assistance policy into labour policy in the US over the last 30 years, specifically the impact of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) on the American welfare state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize promoting durable labour force attachment through equity-based labour policies to ease former recipients into the workforce, as the PRWORA has dramatically transformed the American welfare state and highlighted the need for a more comprehensive approach to employment.

Authors: Rachel Loopstra; Jasmine Fledderjohann; Aaron Reeves; David Stuckler
Field: Welfare; Business; Payment; Welfare reform; Sanctions; Unemployment; Food distribution; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Austerity
Title: Impact of welfare benefit sanctioning on food insecurity: a dynamic cross-area study of food bank usage in the UK.
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that for every 10% increase in sanctions, there was an additional 3.36 adults per 100,000 (95% CI: 1.71 to 5.01) using food banks. The availability of food distribution sites affected how tightly sanctioning and food bank usage were associated.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between sanctions applied to unemployment insurance claimants in the UK and food bank usage between 2009 and 2013, using data from The Trussell Trust Foodbank Network and records on sanctioning rates across 259 local authorities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical association between sanctions and food bank usage, policymakers should prioritize scaling back or revising the sanctioning system to reduce the risk of household food insecurity, particularly in areas with limited access to food distribution sites.

Field: Welfare; Empirical research; International Social Survey Programme; Welfare state; Public opinion; Economics; Biology and political orientation; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: The Polarising Worlds of Welfare: Political Orientations, Macroeconomic Context, and Support for Redistribution
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate that there are larger left–right cleavages in attitudes in wealthier countries, more unequal countries, and countries where inequality is increasing. These findings challenge the dominant practice of focusing exclusively on additive effects of individual-level or country-level factors by showing the importance of paying attention to cross-level interactions.
What_was_studied: Drawing on data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), this article examines the cross-sectional (between-country) and longitudinal (within-country) interactive relationships involving economic development and income inequality (on one hand) and left–right political orientations (on the other) in shaping preferences for redistribution, using data from 27 countries over a 14-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequality and economic development in wealthier countries, as well as those with increasing inequality, to reduce left-right political cleavages and promote more inclusive social protection policies. This can be achieved by scaling up redistributive policies, expanding access to education and healthcare, and revising taxation laws to reduce income disparities.

Title: Early retirement in a period of high unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Ill-health is a less important reason for retirement than previous studies have suggested and those who retire early are divided by class, with manual workers being more likely to retire early because of redundancy and more likely to be living on very low incomes than non-manual workers.
What_was_studied: Using data for men aged 60–64 from the General Household Survey for the years 1980–82 and from the Labour Force Survey of 1983, this article examines reasons given by older men for retiring early and investigates the extent of income poverty in early retirement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant proportion of early retirees living in income poverty, policymakers should prioritize addressing the class divide in retirement policies to ensure fair and adequate income support for all individuals, particularly manual workers who are disproportionately affected.

Field: Contemporary society; Political science; Poverty; Family income; Age groups; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Economic inequality
Title: Age and Income in Contemporary Society: A Research Note
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while a 'poverty cycle' still exists, it is neither strong nor universal across all countries and age groups, with significant differences between nations and older families being a critical group for addressing income inequality.
What_was_studied: This research note investigates the distribution of family income in seven industrial nations using data from the Luxembourg Income Study for the period 1980-2015, focusing on differences between countries and identifying a 'poverty cycle' for elderly families as a key factor in understanding income inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions aimed at supporting elderly families to break the poverty cycle and reduce income inequality, particularly in countries with high levels of income disparity.

Field: Shadow (psychology); Welfare state; Political science; Social security; Differential impact; Public administration
Title: The Needed and the Needy: The Policy Legacies of Benefits for Disabled War Veterans in Israel
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that benefits for disabled war veterans have had a significant impact on other social security programs in Israel, leading to a more generous and expensive welfare system compared to other countries. Specifically, the policy legacies of this program have differentially affected benefits and services for other 'deserving' groups in Israeli society and those disabled from natural causes.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of benefits for disabled war veterans on the Israeli social security system, focusing on the period from 1988 to 2019 and using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of benefits for disabled war veterans on the Israeli social security system, it is crucial to prioritize and expand these programs to ensure that all 'deserving' groups receive fair and adequate support. Additionally, the findings suggest that natural causes of disability should also be addressed in future policy revisions.

primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results suggest a slightly higher yet statistically insignificant level of deprivation among first-sanctioned recipients compared to non-sanctioned recipients, hinting that higher levels of deprivation may not be the primary motivator for reintegration into the labor market.
What_was_studied: In Germany, this study investigates the impact of workfare sanctions on deprivation levels among unemployment and basic income recipients during a period of vast changes in the welfare regime (2013-2018).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the socio-cultural subsistence minimum needs of sanctioned recipients and reassess the effectiveness of workfare measures in promoting reintegration into the labor market, rather than solely focusing on increasing benefit cuts as a form of sanction.

Field: Conditionality; Unemployment; Disadvantaged; Disadvantage; Inequality; Demographic economics; Social mobility; Welfare; Economics; Social protection; Stigma (botany); Social inequality; Social assistance; Economic growth; Psychology; Political science; Market economy; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Psychiatry; Politics; Law
