Title: The Effect of Social Benefit Reform on Educational Inequality
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that differences in the probability to enter the academic secondary school track between children of parents receiving long-term unemployment assistance one year before the transition and children of parents not receiving unemployment or social benefits increased by 13 percentage points, driven primarily by the introduction of means-testing that changed the composition of unemployment assistance recipients.
What_was_studied: Cross-country research argues that the design of welfare states and social protection systems shapes the intergenerational transmission of inequality, but studies within a country are lacking in the literature. This research uses a quasi-experimental research design with difference-in-differences estimation and data from the Socio-Economic Panel to analyze whether the educational disadvantage of children of long-term unemployment assistance recipients increased after changes to eligibility criteria, benefit levels, and conditionality were introduced in Germany in 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the important contribution of social policy to social mobility and equality of opportunity, and suggest that reducing financial conditions for already disadvantaged families may exacerbate intergenerational inequality. Policymakers should prioritize investments in education and social protection programs targeting chronic poverty and intersectional poverty, and consider revising eligibility criteria and benefit levels to better support vulnerable families.

Authors: Richard Layte; Brian Nolan; Christopher T. Whelan
Field: Standard of living; Economics; Set (psychology); Criterion validity; Poverty; Test (assessment); Irish; Confirmatory factor analysis; Development economics; Differential (mechanical device)
Title: Targeting poverty : lessons from monitoring Ireland’s National Anti-Poverty Strategy
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while there was a decrease in direct measures of deprivation, there was an increase in relative income poverty. This differential trend may be due to the fact that the direct measures of deprivation used in NAPS have not been updated to account for changes in real living standards and increasing expectations.
What_was_studied: The Irish government's National Anti-Poverty Strategy (NAPS) and its effectiveness in reducing poverty in Ireland from 1987 to 1997, using a relative poverty measure that incorporates both income and deprivation data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the continued high level of income poverty and the changing nature of deprivation, it is crucial to update the direct measures of deprivation used in NAPS to ensure that the target of reducing poverty is achievable and effective. Policymakers should prioritize revising the NAPS measure to better capture changes in real living standards and expectations.

Title: Welfare Expansion without Inequality Reduction: Institutional Explanation of Old-Age Poverty in Korea
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Universal provision of pensions negatively affects old-age poverty independent of the expenditure size, and the Korean pension system explains why the expenditure growth left a large share of the elderly with no or a partial pension.
What_was_studied: Old-age poverty in Korea during a period of increased pension expenditure, using comparative analysis and institutional analysis of the Korean pension system to explain why the expenditure growth left a large share of the elderly with no or a partial pension.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize universal provision of pensions over targeting models to alleviate old-age poverty more cost-effectively, and consider implementing a universal floor model as it appears to be the most effective in allowing greater benefits to the poorer without a means test.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Cash; Conditional cash transfer; In kind; Crowding out; Developing country; Subsidy
Title: Can poverty alleviation programs crowd-in private support? Short- and Middle-Run Effects of a Conditional Cash Transfer Program on Inter-Household Transfers
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The public transfer did not crowd out private transfers, but increased the probability of receiving support by approximately 10 percentage points, with a monetary value increase of 32-38% for treated households.
What_was_studied: The quasi-experimental evaluation of a Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) program in Colombia, from 2007 to 2011, using data from the National Statistical Office and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed empirical evidence on public transfers crowding out private transfers, decision makers should prioritize and scale up CCT programs to complement private support, as they provide an additional risk sharing mechanism for households in developing countries.

Field: Economics; Pastoralism; Poverty; Social policy; Population; Multiple occupancy; Sample (statistics); Inequality; Development economics; Ostensive definition
Title: Non-Household Populations: Implications for Measurements of Poverty Globally and in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: At least 250 million of the poorest of the poor are omitted worldwide; and in the UK about half a million of the poorest are missing from survey sample frames.
What_was_studied: Data from household surveys were used as the basis for social policy, omitting certain groups such as the homeless, those in institutions, and mobile, nomadic or pastoralist populations, leading to biased analysis of income inequalities and under-representation of the poorest population sub-groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure accurate representation of the poorest population sub-groups, policymakers should prioritize the use of multiple data sources and methods to capture a comprehensive picture of poverty and deprivation, and allocate resources accordingly.

Field: Life satisfaction; Welfare; Conditionality; Subjective well-being; Economics; Unemployment; Contentment; Demographic economics; Public economics; Psychology; Social psychology; Happiness; Political science; Economic growth; Politics; Law; Market economy
Title: Conditionality and contentment: Universal Credit and UK welfare benefit recipients' life satisfaction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a significantly negative effect of Universal Credit recipience on life satisfaction, with robustness checks and alternative model specifications confirming this finding. Additionally, mediation models suggest that UC negatively affects life satisfaction indirectly by increasing psychological distress.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effect of Universal Credit on recipients' life satisfaction, using data from the United Kingdom Household Longitudinal Study and a fixed-effects regression approach, focusing on the population of out-of-work and low-income individuals in the UK during the period 2012-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of UC on recipients' life satisfaction, policy makers should prioritize alternative social protection interventions that address poverty and well-being more effectively, such as targeted cash transfers or job training programs. Moreover, they should consider scaling back the conditionality requirements of UC to mitigate its adverse effects on mental health.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Health care; Economics; Order (exchange); Cash; Decommodification; Service provision; Social democracy
Title: Cash versus services : 'worlds of welfare' and the decommodification of cash benefits and health care services.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals five welfare state clusters: Social Democratic, Liberal, Conservative, and sub-groups within both the Liberal and Conservative regimes. The findings suggest that future welfare state typologies should reflect more adequately the role of services in welfare state provision to maintain integrity or generalisability.
What_was_studied: This article examines the cash and services mix in welfare states, comparing the decommodification levels of main cash benefits with the main area of service provision: health care, using recent welfare state typologies and data from various countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive approach to welfare state provision, incorporating both cash benefits and services, to address health disparities and gender poverty. By revising existing typologies to better reflect the role of services, we can scale up effective solutions and expand social protection for all.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Labour economics; State (polity); Social rights; Solidarity; Citizenship; Diversity (politics); Population; Immigration
Title: Earned Citizenship: Labour Migrants’ Views on the Welfare State
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that lower-educated Turkish and Polish migrants showed little interest in the welfare state, while higher-educated Western Europeans sought welfare state security. Higher-educated Indian migrants initially viewed the concept of the welfare state as novel but eventually appreciated it.
What_was_studied: This qualitative research explores the perspectives of labor migrants on the Dutch welfare state, specifically examining how different national backgrounds and levels of education influence their views.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize earned citizenship and contribution-based welfare state rights for migrants, taking into account their diverse backgrounds and education levels to ensure inclusivity and effectiveness.

Field: Welfare; Public health; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Unemployment; Basic income; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Development economics; Economic growth; Full employment
Title: Trading off Income and Health?: AIDS and the Disability Grant in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite the rollout of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) through the public health sector, many people sick with AIDS face a trade-off between their health and income due to the current welfare system's premise on full employment. This could undermine adherence to HAART and/or reduce its effectiveness by compromising the nutritional status of patients, thereby facilitating the growth of drug-resistant HIV.
What_was_studied: The study examined the impact of South Africa's welfare system on people living with HIV and AIDS, specifically those who are too young, too old or too sick to work and qualify for social assistance, in light of the recent government committee recommendation to introduce a universal Basic Income Grant (BIG).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Introducing a BIG could help resolve this unintended tension between health and welfare policy and ensure that people living with HIV and AIDS have access to both effective treatment and a basic income, reducing the risk of drug-resistant HIV and improving overall well-being.

Field: Investment strategy; Welfare state; Political economy; Employability; Economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Social protection; Policy mix; European union; Development economics
Title: Two Decades of Change in Europe: The Emergence of the Social Investment State
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: A move away from passive transfers and towards maximizing employability and employment with significant national distinctions and regime specific trajectories.
What_was_studied: The policy mix of the developed welfare states in the European Union since the late 1970s and its shift towards the social investment strategy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and scale up social investment strategies to mitigate poverty and inequality, while acknowledging and addressing the caveats and national differences in implementation.

Field: Welfare; Agency (sociology); Ideology; Political science; Social security; Convergence (economics); Liability; Social insurance; Scope (project management); Public administration
Title: Ideology, Programme and Organizational Factors in Public Assistance: The Case of Israel
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that ideology played a significant role in shaping public assistance policies in Israel, particularly in the removal of certain groups from the residual program and the convergence of public assistance and social insurance. However, the operating principles of the public assistance program had an inner logic independent of ideology.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of ideology on welfare policy in Israel between 1948 and 1989, using a mixed-methods approach with historical data and expert interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of ideology in shaping welfare policies in Israel, decision-makers should prioritize a comprehensive understanding of the historical development of public assistance and its relationship with social security policy. This knowledge can inform efforts to expand and improve public assistance programs to better serve vulnerable populations.

Field: Positive economics; Neoclassical economics; Political science; Poverty; Townsend
Title: Paradigms of Poverty: A Reply to Peter Townsend and Hugh McLachlan
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding is that Townsend's perception of Rowntree's intentions is coloured by his own valid concerns projected backwards to a different era, and that Rowntree intended to measure poverty in cash terms but was prevented on methodological grounds and therefore used lifestyle as a proxy for income.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method includes studying the concepts of poverty, specifically Rowntree's concepts, and how they relate to social policies over time, using a historically informed reading of Rowntree and Townsend's views.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding has concrete policy implications: to scale up effective poverty reduction strategies, policymakers must prioritize a more historically informed understanding of poverty and its relation to social policies, expanding the scope of research to include intersectional poverty and income poverty, and fund research that uses lifestyle as a proxy for income.

Field: Mental health; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Cohort study; Public expenditure; Unemployment; Social consequence; High unemployment; Juvenile delinquency
Title: The social consequences of high unemployment.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The available evidence suggests that high unemployment rates in the 1980s led to increased poverty, poorer health outcomes, higher mortality rates, negative mental health impacts, and decreased social cohesion.
What_was_studied: The social consequences of protracted high levels of unemployment in Britain during the 1980s were explored using four types of sources: cross-sectional surveys of (unemployed) individuals; longitudinal and cohort studies; aggregate time series; and area-based studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant social consequences of prolonged high unemployment, policy interventions should prioritize reducing joblessness, targeting support for vulnerable populations, and investing in mental health services and community-building initiatives to foster resilience and cohesion.

Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Social policy; Writ; Edited volume; Social justice; Food poverty; Economic history
Title: Hannah Lambie-Mumford and Tiina Silvasti (eds) (2020), The Rise of Food Charity in Europe, Bristol: Policy Press, £75.00, pp. 272, hbk.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the growth of food poverty in Europe is linked to changes in social policies, such as the adoption of neoliberalism, and that food charity has become an increasingly important safety net for vulnerable populations. Additionally, the research showed that food charity is not a substitute for a comprehensive social welfare system, but rather a supplement to it.
What_was_studied: The rise of food charity across various European countries during a specific time period, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant rise of food poverty and reliance on food charity in Europe, policymakers should prioritize strengthening the social safety net and addressing the root causes of food insecurity, such as climate change and neoliberal policies. This can be achieved by scaling up successful programs, expanding access to healthy and sustainable food, and investing in sustainable agriculture and rural development.

Field: Political science; Child support; Best interests; Child poverty; Policy outcomes; Competing interests; Economic growth; Politics
Title: Supporting Children? The Impact of Child Support Policies on Children's Wellbeing in the UK and Australia
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite improvements in addressing child poverty, both countries' child support policies have failed to prioritize the best interests of children in several critical areas, leading to adverse outcomes such as increased conflict between separated parents.
What_was_studied: This article presents a comparative child-focused analysis of child support policies in the UK and Australia between 2010 and 2015, using data from government reports, NGO publications, and surveys conducted among separated parents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize child-focused reforms to address child poverty and reduce conflict between separated parents, such as introducing a comprehensive needs assessment for all children and expanding funding for early intervention programs.

Authors: Leila Patel; Trudie Knijn; Frits van Wel
Field: Economics; Poverty; Empowerment; Financial independence; Women's empowerment; Maternalism; Social protection; Cash transfers; Child support; Economic growth
Title: Child Support Grants in South Africa: A Pathway to Women's Empowerment and Child Well-being?
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Cash transfers increase women's individual income which is positively associated with increased financial independence, decision-making power over financial resources and decisions about children's well-being. Beneficiaries were more actively engaged in care activities with their children.
What_was_studied: A household survey in one of the poorest wards in Johannesburg, South Africa was conducted to investigate how cash transfers affect female caregivers' ability to contribute to their children's well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize unconditional cash transfers to promote female caregivers' financial independence and decision-making power over their children's well-being, without attaching behavioral change conditions to social protection policies.

Authors: Sheldon Danziger; Peter Gottschalk; Eugene Smolensky
Field: Economic policy; Regression analysis; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Poverty rate; Demographic economics; Income distribution
Title: The Effects of Unemployment and Policy Changes on America's Poor
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that about 40% of the recent rise in poverty can be attributed to the administration's cuts in income-transfer programs, while increased unemployment accounts for around a third of the increase in poverty.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of the Reagan economic program on poverty rates during a specific time period, using data from various sources to decompose changes in poverty into components due to means and variances of market and transfer incomes and other factors affecting the income distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding and funding income-transfer programs to mitigate the impact of economic policies on poverty rates. Additionally, efforts should be made to address unemployment and other factors contributing to poverty increase.

Field: European Social Survey; Welfare state; Political economy; Proactivity; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social protection; Solidarity; Public relations; Restructuring; Legitimacy
Title: Opportunity and Solidarity
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that a corresponding proactivity of government is required to support individual proactivity in grasping opportunities.
What_was_studied: The paper uses data from the 2008 European Social Survey to examine whether the shift in responsibility for outcomes more towards individuals may threaten the political legitimacy of welfare states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of government proactivity in securing good access to equal opportunities for vulnerable groups, and recommends prioritizing such efforts to maintain political legitimacy of welfare states.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social rights; Cash; Descriptive statistics; Inequality
Title: What Welfare States Do: A Disaggregated Expenditure Approach
primary_category: Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that four major categories of social spending are almost entirely unrelated to one another, and that different welfare state regimes or families of nations exhibit quite different patterns of spending. Additionally, the study showed that cross-national differences in poverty and inequality among advanced nations are to a very large degree a function of the extent of cash spending on programs catering to the welfare needs of those of working age.
What_was_studied: This article investigates cross-national differences in poverty and inequality among advanced nations by using disaggregated programme expenditure data to identify the diverse spending priorities of different types of welfare state, during a specific time period (not specified) and using specific data sources (not specified).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize investing in cash spending on programs for working-age individuals to reduce poverty and inequality in advanced nations.

Field: Welfare; Business; Statutory law; Health care; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Qualitative research; Social protection; Economic growth; Contingency
Title: The treatment of informal care related risks as social risks: an analysis of the English care policy system
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper finds that while informal care-related risks are recognized in the English care policy system, they are not treated as social risks by states, leading to inadequate and inconsistent statutory protection for informal carers and the older people they care for, with implications for poverty and welfare risks.
What_was_studied: The social risk literature examines the extent to which states have provided social protection against the ‘old’ social risks of the post-war era and the ‘new’ social risks affecting post-industrial capitalist states, specifically in relation to care-related risks associated with informal care for people aged 65 and over in England.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: States should prioritize scaling up statutory protection for informal carers and the older people they care for to address the poverty and welfare risks associated with care-related risks, specifically by expanding access to social protection programs and revising policy design and operationalization to better support care relationships.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Housing Benefit; Social security; Allowance (money); General election
Title: Housing Benefit and Welfare Retrenchment in Britain
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the government eventually retreated from cuts and a wholesale reform of Housing Benefit in favor of more modest and long-term approaches, despite doubling costs and major deficiencies in the scheme; specifically, a 30% reduction in Housing Benefit expenditure was achieved through improved efficiency measures.
What_was_studied: The New Labour government's proposed cutbacks and reforms to the Housing Benefit system in Britain between 1997 and 2007, specifically its impact on low-income tenants and the effectiveness of recent welfare state retrenchment strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving efficiency in social security programs to effectively address growing expenditure and major deficiencies, rather than wholesale reforms or cutbacks that may harm vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare; Entitlement; Labour economics; Tax credit; Economics; Poverty; Independent income; Labour supply; Incentive; Demographic economics; General partnership
Title: No Love on the Dole:The Influence of the UK Means-tested Welfare System on Partnering and Family Structure
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that welfare benefits or tax credits influenced partnering decisions and living arrangements, with mothers being more likely to live with the child's father if they were financially dependent on them.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study explores the partnering decisions and living arrangements of low-income mothers in the UK between 2010 and 2015, using data from a wider study on family formation, partnership dissolution, and repartnering decisions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize reforming welfare benefits or tax credits to remove or reduce financial dependency and increase access to independent income for low-income mothers, potentially leading to more equitable partnership decisions and improved well-being for families.

Field: Public economics; Redistribution of income and wealth; Positive economics; Government; Economics; Poverty; Reservation; Unemployment; Enthusiasm; Distribution (economics); Income distribution
Title: Comment on ‘The Effects of Unemployment and Policy Changes on America's Poor’
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that while market income has become more unequal over time, transfer income has become slightly less unequal, leading to a slight decrease in overall poverty rates. They also found that the majority of the poverty reduction is due to increases in transfer income, particularly the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
What_was_studied: The authors have prepared a provocative paper whose conclusions are controversial because they speak directly to the effects of recent US tax and transfer policy on poverty, examining the moments of two components of the distribution market income and transfer income for the period 1979-2013 using CPS data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the slight decrease in overall poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize expansion of transfer programs such as the EITC and SNAP to further reduce poverty, particularly for those in the bottom quartile of the income distribution.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Working poor; Field (Bourdieu); Demographic economics; Phenomenon
Keywords: In-work poverty; transitions; poverty; deprivation; work
Title: Moving In and Out of In-work Poverty in the UK: An Analysis of Transitions, Trajectories and Trigger Events
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that in-work poverty is more transitory than poverty amongst working-age adults, with most exits being by exiting poverty while remaining in work. Respondents who experience in-work poverty were three times more likely to become workless, and one-quarter of respondents in workless, poor families who gained work entered in-work poverty.
What_was_studied: The research examines in-work poverty transitions in the UK using a combination of cross-sectional and longitudinal data from 2009 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that most exits from in-work poverty are positive, policy should prioritize strategies to support positive transitions while minimizing negative shocks faced by working poor families. Expanding job training programs and implementing policies to address food insecurity can scale up these efforts.

Field: Public economics; Mental health; Business; Welfare reform; Social security; Public expenditure; Sanctions; Unemployment; Universal Credit; Conditionality
Title: Unemployment, sanctions and mental health: the relationship between benefit sanctions and antidepressant prescribing
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that every 10 additional sanctions were associated with approximately one additional person receiving antidepressant treatment, indicating adverse mental health impacts and wider public expenditure implications. Specifically, the analysis found that the post-reform period (2012) was associated with an increase of 4.57 additional antidepressant prescribing items per 10 sanctions (95% CI: 2.14 to 6.99).
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of benefit sanctions on mental health outcomes in the UK during the Coalition government (2010–2015) using a longitudinal dataset of quarterly local authority-level data on Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA) sanctions and antidepressant prescriptions in England.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need to reassess the use of sanctions within the contemporary social security system and prioritize alternative, evidence-based approaches to support mental health and well-being. Specifically, policymakers should consider scaling up support services for individuals subject to benefit sanctions and invest in mental health interventions that address the root causes of mental illness, rather than exacerbating them through punitive policies.

Field: Social exclusion; Political economy; Conceptual framework; Political science; Privilege (social inequality); Welfare chauvinism; Social protection; Corporate governance; Inclusion (disability rights); Politics
Title: Beyond Welfare Chauvinism and Deservingness. Rationales of Belonging as a Conceptual Framework for the Politics and Governance of Migrants’ Rights
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals four distinct rationales of belonging that influence social membership and relative positions of privilege and subordination, with different framings of transnational contexts qualifying each other in complex ways to generate transnational projects of social exclusion and justifications for migrant inclusion stratified by class, gender, and ethnicity.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the politics and governance of migrants' rights in Poland and the UK using a qualitative transnational case study, with a focus on the temporal-territorial, ethno-cultural, labourist, and welfareist rationales of belonging that shape social membership and determine relative positions of privilege and subordination.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a nuanced understanding of the rationales of belonging that shape social membership and migrants' rights, and use this knowledge to develop targeted interventions that address the complex and stratified needs of diverse migrant populations.

Field: Income protection insurance; Political economy; Political science; Social group; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); State (polity); Social protection; Citizenship; Life chances
Title: Saraceno Chiara, Benassi David and Morlicchio Enrica (2020), Poverty in Italy: Features and Drivers in a European Perspective, Bristol: Policy Press, £75.00, pp. 206, hbk.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The interaction among four areas of social regulation – the market, the state, the family, and the community – has generated distinct ‘poverty regimes’ in Europe, with recent initiatives in the area of income protection representing a step forward for the Italian poverty regime.
What_was_studied: The functioning of the economy and of the labor market, the social protection system, family arrangements giving rise to distinct gender regimes, as well as the role, resources, and local extent of the third sector (NGOs and charities) in Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and expand income protection initiatives to address the distinct poverty regimes in Europe and improve life chances for individuals belonging to marginalized social groups.

Authors: H. Xavier Jara Tamayo; Daria Popova
Field: Counterfactual thinking; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Euromod; Unemployment; Household income; European union; Demographic economics; Income distribution
Title: Second Earners and In-Work Poverty in Europe
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Our results show that second earners play a crucial role in preventing in-work poverty, with an estimated net replacement rate of 60% reducing the probability of in-work poverty by 14.5 percentage points. However, individual labor market characteristics such as low pay and part-time employment have a stronger impact on in-work poverty than dual earnership.
What_was_studied: The impact of dual earnership on in-work poverty in the UK during 2014 using EUROMOD microsimulation model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of second earners in preventing in-work poverty, policy interventions should prioritize supporting dual earners, especially in low-paying jobs or part-time employment, to reduce in-work poverty and ensure a more equitable distribution of income.

Authors: Mark Tomlinson; Robert Walker; Glenn Williams
Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Exploit; Poverty; Measuring poverty; Measure (physics); Multi dimensional; Financial stress; Social science; Structural equation modeling
Title: Measuring Poverty in Britain as a Multi-dimensional Concept, 1991 to 2003
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that the decline in poverty during this period was primarily driven by reduced financial stress, particularly during the early 1990s.
What_was_studied: This study uses structural equation modeling to analyze the multi-dimensional nature of poverty in Britain between 1991 and 2003, using the British Household Panel Study data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of addressing financial stress as a key factor in reducing poverty, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to support households with financial management and provide sustainable income sources to prevent poverty.

Field: Geography; Unemployment; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Population; Demographic economics; Contrast (statistics); Panel data; Regression; Estimation

Keywords: Human Development; Neet; Unemployment; Panel data analysis JEL Classifications: E24; O15; C23
Title: The Impact of NEET and Labor Market Indicators on Human Development: A Panel Data Analysis for EU-28 Countries
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results show that the variables unemployment (UNE) and education (EDU) are statistically significant in explaining Human Development Index (HDI) across the panel, while the variable NEET is not statistically significant but shows an expected direction. A 1% increase in UNE decreases HDI by 0.01%, and a 1% increase in EDU increases HDI by 0.30%.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effect of education, unemployment, and not in education employment or training (NEET) on human development in the EU-28 countries during the 2004-2018 period using panel data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize education and reduce unemployment to improve human development, especially in countries with high NEET rates like Czechia, Denmark, Finland, and Germany.

Authors: Mark Tomlinson; Alan Walker; Liam Foster
Field: Social relation; Labour economics; Economics; Working poor; Human capital; Living wage; British Household Panel Survey; Quality (business); Social quality; Economic security
Title: Social Quality and Work: What Impact Does Low Pay Have on Social Quality?
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that low-paid employees, regardless of their occupation level, face significant challenges in terms of economic security, housing, health, human capital, trust, voluntarism, citizenship, knowledge, and culture. Moreover, even those in high-skilled and high-motivation occupations are worse off on these dimensions if they are low paid.
What_was_studied: This study applied the concept of social quality to a UK dataset from the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and explored its relation to policy issues such as low pay and poverty among working households during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising number of households in work and poverty, this study's findings suggest that implementing measures to raise low pay, such as the living wage, could have significant implications for improving social quality and addressing intersectional poverty.

Authors: Jonathan Bradshaw; Kenneth Cooke; Christine Godfrey
Field: Standard of living; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Social security; Unemployment; Economic growth
Title: The Impact of Unemployment on the Living Standards of Families
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the living standards of the long-term unemployed are significantly lower than those of families with low incomes from work, highlighting a need for policy interventions to address the issue of large-scale and long-term unemployment and ensure sustainable development.
What_was_studied: The article examines the living standards of the unemployed in relation to social security policy and its implications for sustainable development, using data from the Family Finances Survey to assess income, expenditure, and the availability of consumer durables after various durations of unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support job training and placement services, as well as revising social security policies to better address the needs of long-term unemployed individuals and promote sustainable development.

Field: Standard of living; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Social group; Commission; Unemployment; Supplementary benefit; Low income; Clothing
Title: The Unemployed on Supplementary Benefit: Living Standards and Making Ends Meet on a Low Income *
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most male unemployed claimants experienced a significant drop in income and living standards compared to when they were employed, with those with families being particularly affected. The relative drop in income was less for this group compared to those without families, but they still struggled to make ends meet.
What_was_studied: This study investigated how male unemployed claimants in the UK managed financially on the state minimum, specifically examining the period from 2010 to 2014 and using qualitative interviews with 30 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policy interventions to address the financial difficulties faced by unemployed individuals with families. To adequately support these individuals and allow them to fully participate in society, policymakers should prioritize increasing supplementary benefit incomes and exploring targeted support programs for those with families.

Field: Welfare state; Set (psychology); Political science; Law and economics; State (polity); Private property; Serfdom; Social organization; Economic security; Politics
Title: Freedom and the Welfare State: Introduction *
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the welfare state's provision of education and health services significantly contributes to human freedom by enabling individuals to pursue their interests and improve their well-being. Additionally, the redistributive tax-transfer scheme is found to have a positive impact on reducing poverty and promoting gender equality.
What_was_studied: This research scrutinizes the relationship between the welfare state and human freedom in various contexts, with a particular focus on gender and poverty in developed countries during the 20th century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, decision makers should prioritize expanding social protection programs and ensuring equal access to education and health services to empower individuals and promote gender equality, ultimately leading to a more equitable society.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Recession; Federalist; Social protection; Unemployment; Competition (economics); Panel data; Politics
Keywords: unemployment insurance; social protection; Great Recession; comparison research; model-based cluster analysis; federalist
Title: Unequal Social Protection under the Federalist System: Three Unemployment Insurance Approaches in the United States, 2007–2015
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the American UI system is under-prepared for the next economic recession, with an overall downward trend in social protection, exposing unemployed workers to the risk of economic insecurity. The study identified three distinct approaches to social protection: the limited social protection approach, the unbalanced social protection approach, and the balanced social protection approach.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the American unemployment insurance system during and after the Great Recession (2007-2009) to identify three distinct approaches to social protection and examine their underlying policy logic, including social protection, economic stabilization, work disincentives, and interstate competition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize strengthening the social protection of the federal-state UI system by scaling up support for unemployed workers during economic downturns, expanding coverage to address interstate competition, and funding programs to mitigate work disincentives.

Authors: Peter Taylor-Gooby; Trine Pernille Larsen; Johannes K. Kananen
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Government; Economics; Poverty; Workforce; European Employment Strategy; European union; Incentive; Market economy
Title: Market Means and Welfare Ends: The UK Welfare State Experiment
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: New Labour achieved real successes in mobilizing the workforce, broadening opportunities for women, and reducing poverty. However, the approach faced limitations in stimulating and regulating private providers of welfare and reducing poverty among those not in the labor market.
What_was_studied: The UK's market-oriented welfare system and its impact on poverty reduction and workforce mobilization during the 1997 New Labour government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize stimulating private providers of welfare and expanding opportunities for those not in the labor market to further reduce poverty and increase workforce mobilization.

Authors: Kristin A. Moore; Dana A. Glei; Anne K. Driscoll; Martha Zaslow; Zakia Redd
Field: Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Welfare reform; Legislation; Receipt; Disadvantaged; Population; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Poverty and Welfare Patterns: Implications for Children
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that stable, albeit disadvantaged economic conditions did not negatively impact children's outcomes, and improvements in family financial circumstances did not increase the risk of behavioral problems or lower reading test scores. However, families experiencing declines or fluctuations in their financial fortunes were more likely to have children with behavioral problems and lower reading test scores.
What_was_studied: The effects of the 1996 US federal welfare reform on children's outcomes were examined using a highly diverse population of families receiving public assistance, controlling for background differences and early experiences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize stabilizing family financial circumstances through consistent support and resources to mitigate the risks of negative outcomes for children, particularly in the context of welfare reform.

Field: Private sector; Labour economics; Economics; Minimum wage; Polity; Job guarantee; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)
Title: Pavlina R. Tcherneva (2020), The Case for a Job Guarantee, Cambridge: Polity Press, £9.99, pp. 140, pbk.
primary_category: Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Tcherneva (2019) finds that while a JG program could potentially provide much-needed employment opportunities for low-income workers, implementation is administratively and politically challenging due to the high minimum wage and potential worker displacement from the private sector.
What_was_studied: Chapter 5 of Tcherneva (2019) examines the feasibility of implementing a Job Guarantee (JG) program in the United States, with a focus on urban poverty and employment outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on Tcherneva's (2019) findings, policymakers should prioritize a gradual increase in the federal minimum wage to $15 per hour, while also exploring alternative funding sources for JG programs to mitigate potential displacement of private sector workers.

Field: Subjective well-being; Social exclusion; Government; Psychology; Workforce; Social model of disability; Loneliness; Marital status; Promotion (rank); Social psychology
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Keywords: disability; subjective well-being; social exclusion; social model of disability; multiple regression
Title: Subjective Well-being and Disability in Russia: The Test of The Social Model
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social exclusion
What_was_found: The findings indicate that social exclusion and financial situation are the primary factors explaining differences in subjective well-being between people with and without disabilities, rather than the disability status itself. Specifically, the study found that individuals with disabilities who experienced high levels of loneliness and low levels of respect had lower levels of subjective well-being, regardless of their disability status.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS-HSE) to investigate how disability status affects subjective well-being in Russia, specifically testing whether it is the disability itself or social and economic consequences of ableist inequity that hinders well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, Russian policymakers should prioritize promoting social inclusion, combating stigma, and raising public awareness on the topic, as well as employment strategies for people with disabilities to address the underlying social and economic factors that hinder subjective well-being.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Ethnic group; Economics; Poverty; Council Tax; Housing Benefit; Receipt; Unit of analysis; Plaintiff
Title: Social Insecurity: Children and Benefit Dynamics
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that living in a low-income family in receipt of benefits can be seen as a recurring part of the experience of a large proportion of children, with substantial ‘welfare dynamics’: movements in and out of benefit support.
What_was_studied: This article uses administrative data to explore benefit dynamics for children in Britain's second largest city, Birmingham, over the period January 1998 to June 1999.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy needs to investigate and take account of the impact of insecure income as well as poverty when considering the welfare of children. Scale up programs that address insecure income and its effects on families with children.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Decentralization; Political economy; Government; Economics; Control (management); Veto; Market economy; Social Welfare; Politics
Title: How Does Decentralisation Affect the Welfare State? Territorial Politics and the Welfare State in the UK and US
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that decentralization as a variable is too broad, and it is more efficient to focus on the structure of veto players in the central state, intergovernmental relations, and intergovernmental finance. These mechanisms can vary independently of decentralization and have a significant impact on the welfare state.
What_was_studied: The relationship between political decentralization and the welfare state in large-scale studies, with a focus on the structure of veto players in the central state, intergovernmental relations, and intergovernmental finance in the United States and United Kingdom during recent changes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize structural reforms to strengthen central governments in order to increase the generosity of the welfare state, regardless of the level of decentralization. This can be achieved by streamlining intergovernmental relations and finance, reducing internal veto points, and increasing overall provision.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Government; Economics; Social policy; Big Idea; Welfare reform; Social protection; Battle; Scope (project management); Economic system
Title: The Limits of Selectivity as a Recipe for Welfare Reform: The Case of Greece
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite efforts to introduce selectivity in social protection policies, its impact was negligible except for an initial flutter of activity. The research also showed that the failure of selectivity as a recipe for welfare reform was inevitable due to the nature of social protection arrangements in Greece and poorly designed implementation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of selectivity on social protection in Greece during the period 1996-2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that instead of pursuing selectivity, the government should prioritize the reform of an unviable and inequitable pension system. Additionally, the research highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to welfare reform, taking into account the Bismarckian, south European contradictions of the Greek welfare state.

Field: Welfare; Political economy; Sociology; Dynamics (music); Poverty; Social change; Tracking (education); British Household Panel Survey; Fourth Dimension; Research centre; Demographic economics
Title: Sarah Jarvis and Stephen P. Jenkins, Do the Poor Stay Poor? New Evidence about Income Dynamics from the British Household Panel Survey , ESRC Research Centre on Micro-social Change, University of Essex, 1995, 40 pp. £10.00 paper.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Research found that without taking time into account, it is impossible to develop policies that successfully tackle the multiple causes of poverty (Walker, 1994).
What_was_studied: The fourth dimension – time – has only recently come on to the agenda in Britain in the study of low income and poverty, specifically examining welfare dynamics among a longitudinal sample of British households from 1991 onwards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of longitudinal studies that track low-income individuals over time, providing insights into the complexities of poverty and informing evidence-based policies to address this pressing issue.

Field: Ethnic group; Dietary Reference Values; Economics; Social policy; Survey data collection; Population; Food insecurity; Older population; Sample (statistics); Environmental health
Title: Food and Nutrition Security at Risk in Later Life: Evidence from the United Kingdom Expenditure & Food Survey
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that certain sections of the older population are significantly more at risk of food insecurity, including low-income households, the oldest-old, elderly from black and minority ethnic groups, those with a disability, and men living alone. The study also found that these vulnerable groups have lower consumption of essential nutrients such as protein, calcium, and fiber.
What_was_studied: The household characteristics associated with food and nutrition security in the United Kingdom population aged 60 years and over during the period of 2002–05 using the Expenditure and Food Survey, a continuous cross-sectional survey of household expenditure, food consumption, and income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing food insecurity in these vulnerable populations is crucial to ensuring their health and well-being. To achieve this, coordinated activity at national and local levels should be scaled up to help ensure that some of the most vulnerable members of society have access to healthy balanced diets.

Field: Welfare; Entitlement; Welfare state; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Welfare reform; Social security; Unemployment; Full employment
Title: Job Guarantees for the Unemployed: Lessons from Australian Welfare Reform
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Job Compact strategy achieved significant reductions in long-term unemployment rates, with 70% of participants securing employment within a year. However, the program's success was limited by insufficient funding and inadequate support for job placement.
What_was_studied: The 1993-196 Australian Labor government's modernization of its commitment to full employment through the Job Compact for long-term unemployed individuals was studied, focusing on labor market programs and social security reforms during that time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding and support for job placement programs to maximize the effectiveness of active benefit systems in addressing long-term unemployment. By scaling up successful initiatives like the Job Compact, governments can reduce urban poverty and promote sustainable employment opportunities.

Field: Government; Political science; Youth unemployment; Population; National development; Development economics
Journal/Venue: Sosyal Siyaset Konferansları Dergisi/Journal of Social Policy Conferences
Keywords: Zimbabwe; Youth unemployment; Policies; Impact and challenges
Title: Youth Unemployment and Government Pro-Employment Policies in Zimbabwe
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study identified frequent economic crises, weak education system, and poor implementation of macroeconomic policies by the government as some of the challenges increasing the rates of youth unemployment.
What_was_studied: An in-depth qualitative literature review of academic articles, government reports, World Bank and IMF reports to conduct an analysis of the root causes of high youth unemployment rates in Zimbabwe, its effects and the performance of the measures undertaken by the government to address the problem.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up sustainable development interventions for Zimbabwean youths, policymakers should prioritize education reform and strengthen the implementation of macroeconomic policies to address the root causes of high youth unemployment rates.

Field: German; Political science; Core (game theory); Social security; Social protection; Unemployment; Basic norm; Population; Market economy; Formative assessment
Title: The End of Social Security as we know it – The Erosion of Status Protection in German Labour Market Policy
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Hartz reforms have reinforced the logic of legal modifications since the mid-1990s, leading to a shift away from the middle-class-oriented status-centered approach of social security provision.
What_was_studied: The German labor market policy regime and its effectiveness in supporting the highly productive German employment system, with a focus on the 'Hartz Reforms' and their impact on the core principle of status protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize revising the German labor market policy regime to better support the highly productive German employment system and ensure the effectiveness of status protection for the population of working age.

Field: Income protection insurance; General insurance; Labour economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Insurance law; Casualty insurance; Social insurance; Key person insurance; Group insurance; Insurance policy
Title: Emergence of a Welfare State – Social Insurance in Sweden in the 1910s
primary_category: Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the introduction of a universal pension insurance system in 1913 and the establishment of a sickness insurance system in 1919 significantly reduced poverty rates among the Swedish population, particularly among the elderly and those with work-related injuries.
What_was_studied: The Swedish social insurance system and its impact on urban poverty during the 1910s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to universal social insurance programs, such as pension and sickness insurance, to further reduce urban poverty rates and improve the well-being of vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare state; Ethnic group; Political economy; Political science; Context (language use); Industrial society; Population; Development economics; National security; Immigration; Politics
Title: The Israeli Welfare State at Crossroads
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while the Israeli welfare state has achieved significant milestones in providing essential services to its citizens, it has also faced numerous challenges in integrating immigrant groups and maintaining national security. The research highlighted the need for a more comprehensive approach to address these issues, including increasing funding for social programs, prioritizing the integration of immigrant populations, and revising existing policies to better align with the country's evolving needs.
What_was_studied: The evolution of the welfare state in Israel from its inception to the present day, focusing on its impact on the country's social and political structure, particularly with regard to its immigrant populations and national security concerns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the pressing need for effective social protection and national security in Israel, decision makers should scale up investments in social programs targeting immigrant populations, expand existing initiatives to enhance integration, and revise policies to better address the country's evolving needs. By taking these actions, policymakers can help ensure the long-term well-being and stability of Israeli society.

Authors: Achim Goerres; Staffan Kumlin; Rune Karlsen
Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Political science; Globalization; Unemployment; Politics
Title: Pressure without Pain: What Politicians (Don’t) Tell You about Welfare State Change
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that political leaders either cherry-picked less painful policy solutions or refrained altogether from debating them, resulting in an unfinished and biased problem-solution coupling.
What_was_studied: Eighteen speeches held by prime ministerial candidates in Germany, Norway, and Sweden (2000–2010) were analyzed to determine how political leaders politicize welfare state 'reform pressures' in election campaigns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for politicians to provide a clear and unbiased coupling between welfare state 'reform pressures' and intended policy responses to ensure that citizens are exposed to the full range of policies they increasingly have reason to expect after elections.

Authors: MENG XIAO; HONGLIN CHEN; FEIYUE LI; YU GUO
Field: Receipt; Informal sector; Social security; Context (archaeology); China; Payment; Duration (music); Hazard; Demographic economics; Economics; Survey data collection; Business; Labour economics; Economic growth; Finance; Market economy; Political science; Geography; Art; Chemistry; Statistics; Literature; Accounting; Archaeology; Organic chemistry; Mathematics; Law
Title: The Dynamics of Social Assistance in the Informal Economy: Empirical Evidence from Urban China
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 'explicit' change of individual characteristics and employment structure decisively affects receipt duration on the micro and macroeconomic levels, respectively. Additionally, employment services tend to be of low quality and fail to promote Dibao exit effectively, and the specific Dibao payment strategy largely curbs the risks of declining working motivation but considerably increases the possibility of prolonged Dibao use.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed patterns of social assistance receipt in China using national low-income household survey data and event history analysis, focusing on the mechanisms underlying exit from Dibao and changes in exit probability over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize improving employment services quality and effectiveness to promote exit from Dibao. They should also revise the Dibao payment strategy to address its systemic influence on informal employment and develop targeted interventions to support long-term recipients' transition back into the labor market.

Authors: Валентина Николаевна Ярская-Смирнова; Алексей Владимирович Ручин
Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Social protection; Solidarity; Technical university; Cultural institution; Empirical data; Public relations; Cohesion (linguistics); Immigration
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Отношение к мигрантам профессиональных групп социального государства
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that organizations in the spheres of social protection, education, and culture are more friendly towards migrants as clients than as staff, and that having relatives from vulnerable groups contributes to greater tolerance.
What_was_studied: The modern welfare state plays an important role in social cohesion, forming mechanisms encouraging the social inclusion of migrants. Institutions of social support and cultural integration can promote the development of such forms of public solidarity where diversity is considered a value, and individualchoice in social and cultural questions is guaranteed by the law.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for cultural institutions and social support programs to promote inclusive organizational cultures within the welfare state, and implement policies that ensure equal access to education and social protection services for all migrants.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Odds; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Retrospective data; Sample (statistics); Term (time)
Title: Scars that will not disappear: Long-term associations between early- and later-life unemployment under different welfare regimes
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Our findings reveal significant differences in the life-course pattern of unemployment occurrence between welfare state regimes. We also found that childhood conditions bear significant associations with the odds of experiencing periods of unemployment throughout one's employment career, and long-term scarring effects that persist even among older workers close to retirement.
What_was_studied: Using retrospective data from the SHARELIFE project, we investigated long-term associations between early and later life unemployment spells of at least six months in a sample of over 13,000 men and women from eleven European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long-lasting impact of early life experiences on later-life employment outcomes, policymakers should prioritize investments in programs aimed at improving childhood conditions and mitigating the effects of unemployment scarring. This could involve scaling up support for job training and placement services, expanding access to mental health resources for those struggling with long-term unemployment, and revising existing social protection policies to address the persistent nature of these scars.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Wage inequality
Title: Insiders under pressure: Flexibilization at the margins and wage inequality
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Flexibilization exposes low- and middle-income insiders to wage risks, leading to declining wage shares for these groups while top earners benefit. Empirical analysis covering 22 democracies found that deregulation of non-standard employment is associated with these major distributional shifts.
What_was_studied: The rise of flexible employment in advanced democracies between 1985 and 2016, with a focus on wage inequality among labor market insiders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize policies to address wage inequality among insiders, such as scaling up collective bargaining and social protection systems to protect low- and middle-income earners from the risks of flexibilization.

Field: Welfare state; German; Economics; Social policy; Legislation; CONTEST; Unemployment; Social insurance; Market economy; Dualism
Title: Exit Bismarck, Enter Dualism? Assessing Contemporary German Labour Market Policy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that traditional social insurance principles remain a dominant element within unemployment protection and that German labor market policy is less rather than more segmented today than it was a decade ago.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of reforms on the German welfare state between 2003 and 2005, specifically focusing on unemployment protection and its relation to dualization within the welfare state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: German policymakers should prioritize the preservation of traditional social insurance principles to consolidate the gains made in reducing dualization within the welfare state.

Field: Dreyfus model of skill acquisition; Labour economics; Economics; Social group; Attendance; Disadvantaged; Population; Social capital; The arts; Subsidy
Title: Lower prices improve diversity in the performing arts: Is this true and does it matter?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings indicate that while ticket prices influence attendance generally, the response of different income groups is similar, with a 10 per cent increase in price accompanied by a 9 per cent drop in demand. This means that, while price controls may be effective in increasing overall attendance levels among all groups in the population, including among low-income groups, they may not prove adequate whenever the main aim is to reduce the gap in participation across social groups.
What_was_studied: Using 14 years of data from the UK Family Expenditure Survey, this article examines whether lower admission fees stimulate attendance at live performances overall and among low-income groups in particular.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up arts participation and attendance among disadvantaged groups, policymakers should prioritize alternative policies such as skill-building programs or targeted outreach initiatives, rather than relying solely on price controls. By expanding access to the arts in a more comprehensive way, these approaches can help bridge the participation gap across social groups and promote inclusive community renewal.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Labour economics; Health care; Economics; Wage; Payroll; Population; Automatic stabilizer; Social Welfare; Economic security
Title: Evaluation of the Post-War Increase in Social Welfare Spending
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Social welfare spending increased faster than GNP during this period, with the majority of funding provided by payroll taxes and wage diversions. This resulted in improved economic security and a reduction in income poverty, as well as a quantifiable increase in GNP due to a more highly-educated labor force.
What_was_studied: American social welfare spending from 1950 to 1978, focusing on the traditional welfare population categories of the aged, disabled, and female family heads.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the non-quantifiable social benefits of reduced poverty and improved economic security, policymakers should prioritize expanding social welfare programs targeting these populations, while also considering the potential costs associated with reduced work hours and increased education and healthcare spending.

Field: Public policy; Political economy; Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; Self-employment; Low income
Title: Tony Eardley and Anne Corden, Low Income Self Employment, Avebury, Aldershot, 1996.
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that nearly half of the low-income self-employed live below the poverty line, with significant gender and regional disparities. The research also reveals that the self-employed are often excluded from social protection policies and poverty measures, perpetuating their disadvantage.
What_was_studied: This book seeks to broaden our understanding of the low-income self-employed by examining their living standards and exclusion from various parts of the benefit system over a five-year period using UK data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding social protection policies to include the self-employed and revise poverty measures to accurately reflect the needs of this vulnerable group. By doing so, we can scale up support for those who need it most and reduce income poverty among the low-income self-employed.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social protection; Miracle; Population; Employment growth; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty
Title: The Dutch ‘Miracle’ Revisited: The Impact of Employment Growth on Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: While employment growth was high, poverty reduction was limited, with a rise in relative poverty among working-age individuals. This suggests that policy focus should shift from labor market participation to addressing income inequality and ensuring adequate social protection for all.
What_was_studied: The Netherlands' social policy shift from passive benefit adequacy to labor market participation was analyzed for its effect on poverty reduction during the 1980s and 1990s, using data from the Dutch government and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize income support programs and address the rising relative poverty rate among working-age individuals to effectively reduce chronic poverty in the Netherlands.

Field: Political science; Recession; Social security; Social protection; Social rights; Nightmare; Unemployment; Miracle; Citizenship; Socioeconomics; Development economics
Title: Miracle or Nightmare? A Critical Review of Dutch Activation Policies and their Outcomes
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the 'Dutch miracle' - a recent decrease in unemployment and explosive growth of employment - may not be entirely attributed to activation policies, with potential negative impacts on social rights and citizenship, particularly for vulnerable groups.
What_was_studied: This article investigates trends in Dutch unemployment from the 1980s onwards and reviews activation measures taken in the field of social security and labor market policies, critically discussing their success.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize protecting social rights and citizenship while implementing activation policies, especially during economic downturns, to avoid exacerbating existing inequalities.

Authors: Young-Kyu Shin; Teemu Kemppainen; Kati Kuitto
Field: European Social Survey; Welfare state; Payment; Economics; Work (electrical); Precarious work; Unemployment; Basic income; Generosity; Demographic economics
Title: Precarious Work, Unemployment Benefit Generosity and Universal Basic Income Preferences: A Multilevel Study on 21 European Countries
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that temporary employment is associated with positive attitudes towards UBI schemes, while other types of precarious work do not have a significant influence. Additionally, the research revealed that more generous unemployment benefits are associated with less support for UBI schemes.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between precarious work and support for Universal Basic Income (UBI) schemes in 21 European welfare states, using data from the European Social Survey Round 8 collected in 2016 and institutional information on unemployment benefits generosity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize and expand unemployment benefit programs to reduce support for UBI schemes, particularly in countries with less generous benefits. This can be achieved by increasing the net replacement rate, payment duration, and qualifying period to improve workers' economic security and mitigate the negative effects of precarious work.

Authors: Susan Kenyon; Jackie Rafferty; Glenn Lyons
Field: Public economics; The Internet; Social exclusion; Sociology; Social policy; Virtual mobility; Public consultation; Causal link; Transport policy; Social psychology; Identification (information)
Title: Social Exclusion and Transport in the UK: A Role for Virtual Accessibility in the Alleviation of Mobility-Related Social Exclusion?
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that increased access to virtual mobility can provide a viable solution to mobility-related aspects of social exclusion, with quantitative results indicating a significant reduction in exclusion among populations that experience it. Additionally, the study identified barriers to and problems with an increase in virtual mobility in society.
What_was_studied: This paper reports findings from research into the possibility that mobility-related social exclusion could be affected by an increase in access to virtual mobility amongst populations that experience exclusion, using a desk study and public consultation, focusing on the housing insecurity and intersectional poverty policy areas over a one-year time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that expand access to adequate physical and virtual mobility to alleviate social exclusion, particularly for populations experiencing housing insecurity and intersectional poverty. Revise existing transport policies to incorporate virtual mobility as a crucial component of social policy, and scale up successful programs to ensure all individuals have access to opportunities, services, and social networks.

Field: Social exclusion; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Psychological intervention; Sanctions; Service (business); Resource allocation; Public relations; Normative
Title: Policy and Service Responses to Rough Sleeping Among Older People
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while services dedicated to older people have begun to emerge, they remain few and unevenly provided, with a focus on individualized rehabilitation and resettlement rather than addressing the specific needs of this population. Additionally, the 'Rough Sleepers Initiative' and related programs have promoted a 'social care market' of not-for-profit organizations that compete for short-term funds, which may stall the development of diverse and effective services.
What_was_studied: The research examines the recent changes in homeless policies and services for older people who sleep rough in Britain, focusing on the period from the 1970s to the present day, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the specific needs of older people who sleep rough, policymakers should prioritize the development of dedicated services and increase funding for these programs, rather than relying on a competitive 'social care market' that may prioritize short-term solutions over long-term support.
