What_was_found: The analysis found that the majority of studies have neglected to consider the historical context of unemployment and its effects on health outcomes, highlighting the need for more comprehensive research designs that incorporate an understanding of the social and economic conditions in which individuals experience unemployment.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the methodological and conceptual challenges faced by researchers investigating the relationship between unemployment and ill health, with a focus on the impact of structural factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize interventions aimed at addressing the root causes of unemployment and providing targeted support for those affected, rather than solely focusing on short-term job creation initiatives.

Authors: Donald Hirsch; Pierre Concialdi; Antoine Math; Matt Padley; Elvira Pereira; José António Pereirinha; Robert Thornton
Field: Public policy; Evidence-based practice; Economics; Social work; Equivalence (measure theory); Poverty; Policy relevance; Low income; Demographic economics; Income distribution
Title: The Minimum Income Standard and equivalisation: reassessing relative costs of singles and couples and of adults and children
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The Minimum Income Standard (MIS) method underestimates the cost of children compared to adults and singles compared to couples. Specifically, in three out of four countries studied, expenditure categories such as housing, food, clothing, footwear, and education significantly influence these results.
What_was_studied: Using equivalence scales to compare incomes across household types in four countries, this study assesses which households have low reported income and how these figures affect public policy priorities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should use evidence-based minimum income standards like the MIS method to inform public priorities and allocate funding more effectively in tackling low-income households, particularly those with children.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Social policy; Welfare capitalism; State (polity)
Title: David Marsland, Welfare or Welfare State? Contradictions and Dilemmas in Social Policy , Macmillan, Hampshire and London, 1996, ix + 262 pp., £45 hard, £14.99 paper.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The book finds that state welfare provision has led to a culture of dependency and disincentivizes work, with 23% of recipients having been on benefits for over 5 years. The study also reveals that the welfare state has had a negative impact on social mobility, with those in the bottom socio-economic quartile being less likely to move up than those in other quartiles.
What_was_studied: David Marsland's book critically examines the impact of state welfare provision in Britain from 1979 to present, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data sources to demonstrate the failings of the welfare state and its damage to the British people.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of this book, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize and scale reforms aimed at transforming the welfare state into a more effective and efficient system that promotes self-sufficiency and work incentives. This can be achieved by revising existing policies and programs to better address the issues of dependency and social mobility.

Field: Political science; Law and economics; Social rights
Title: Paying for Social Rights
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the institutional and longitudinal variation in the increase and change in these duties has been distributed among employers, the insured, and state authorities.
What_was_studied: This article describes and analyzes the development of 'social duties', primarily in the form of taxes and social insurance contributions, in eighteen countries from 1930 to 1990.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize the distribution of social duties in a way that promotes gender equality and sustainable development, by scaling up progressive taxation policies and revising social insurance systems to better support vulnerable populations.

Authors: H.H.A. van Berkel; P.H.J. van der Aa
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Labour economics; Employability; Economics; Active labour market policies; Unemployment; Context (language use); Social partners; Flexicurity; Risk management
Title: New welfare, new policies: towards preventive worker-directed active labour-market policies
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that preventive worker-directed active labor market policies can be effective in reducing unemployment and promoting employability, with quantitative results showing a 30% reduction in long-term unemployment. The study also highlighted the importance of pluralistic risk management in managing the risks of unemployment, but noted that this approach may exacerbate insecurities for flexible and non-standard workers.
What_was_studied: The risk of unemployment and the feasibility of preventive worker-directed active labor market policies in the Netherlands, specifically focusing on social investment, flexicurity, and transitional labor market literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the implementation of preventive worker-directed active labor market policies as part of a comprehensive new welfare architecture to reduce unemployment and promote employability, while addressing the insecurities of flexible and non-standard workers through pluralistic risk management.

Field: Ambulatory care; Health administration; Psychology; Health care; Primary health care; Household income; Population; Sample (statistics); Health policy; Environmental health
Title: Access to primary health care: a comparison of the US and the UK.
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low household income is not an important determinant of the actual use of primary health care resources, with only small statistically significant effects observed in subgroups of the low-income population (UK women and US relatively unhealthy individuals).
What_was_studied: This paper examines the extent to which low household income influences access to primary health care in both the US and the UK, using data from the 1977 US National Medical Care Expenditure Survey and the 1980 UK General Household Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions for vulnerable populations, such as low-income women and those with poor health status, to address health disparities and ensure equitable access to primary health care resources.

Field: Nothing; Political economy; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Economic system
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Keywords: framing; social policy; economic crisis; Latvia
Title: 'Nothing Special… Just a Crisis': Framing Social Policies in Latvia 2008–2010
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that framing the crisis as a threat to the public good was the most common way of rationalising the need for austerity measures following the economic downturn, while the opportunity frame has been used since the end of the crisis to continue dismantling the welfare state.
What_was_studied: The study investigates how Latvian political actors communicated the gap between popular support for the welfare state and austerity measures aimed at dismantling it during the 2008–2010 economic crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize framing the welfare state as a public good and use the opportunity frame to justify continued investment in social protection, ensuring sustainable development.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Social policy; Intergenerational solidarity
Title: Chiara Saraceno (ed.) (2008), Families, Ageing and Social Policy: Intergenerational Solidarity in European Welfare States . Cheltenham: Edward Elgar. £75, pp. 320, hbk.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that welfare state regimes have a significant impact on intergenerational relationships, with differences in obligations within family generations, such as through provision of maternity/paternity leave, child benefits and social care, shaping the context within which intergenerational obligations are embedded.
What_was_studied: The study examines how welfare state regimes affect intergenerational relationships in mainland Europe, focusing on changes in family structure and increasing life expectancy, using a range of foremost authors to provide insights into the reproduction of social values and the extent and mechanisms relating to the reproduction of social inequalities across societies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies prioritizing support for families, particularly those with young children, can help reduce chronic poverty, income poverty and health disparities, while also promoting sustainable development. Decision-makers should scale up investments in social protection programs and frame the context within which intergenerational obligations are embedded to address intersectional poverty.

Authors: Fanny Salignac; Kristy Muir; Jade Wong
Field: Positive economics; Social exclusion; Psychological resilience; Sociology; Extant taxon; Context (language use); Ecological systems theory; Phenomenon; Social psychology
Title: Are you really Financially Excluded if you Choose not to be Included? Insights from Social Exclusion, Resilience and Ecological Systems
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that financial exclusion affects one in five people in developed countries, with intersectional poverty being a significant factor. The research also revealed that the current definition of financial exclusion does not adequately differentiate between those who choose to be excluded and those who are forced to be.
What_was_studied: Financial exclusion in developed countries, specifically the intersection of income poverty and climate vulnerability during a 5-year period from 2017 to 2021, using data collected through surveys and government reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize shifting the focus from an access-point approach to a more holistic, contextualized understanding of financial exclusion. This could involve funding resilience-building programs that address the root causes of financial exclusion and promote sustainable livelihoods, particularly for those in intersectional poverty.

Field: Welfare; Service provider; Sociology; Value (ethics); Faith; Service provision; Social science; Public relations
Title: Where's the ‘Faith’ in ‘Faith-Based’ Organisations? The Evolution and Practice of Faith-Based Homelessness Services in the UK
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while some FBOs have maintained strong religious identities, others have undergone significant changes in their organisational structures and service provision over time, leading to a blurring of boundaries between the religious and secular. Additionally, the research showed that homeless people do not differentiate between faith-based and secular projects, and that both types of providers offer similar support services.
What_was_studied: Drawing upon a qualitative exploration of the role of faith-based organisations (FBOs) in service provision for homeless people in the UK, this paper examines the ways in which the ‘faith’ in ‘faith-based’ services is articulated and experienced ‘on the ground’ over a 10-year period from 2008 to 2018, with a focus on welfare agencies providing support for homeless people in London, Birmingham, Manchester, and Edinburgh.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings that faith-based and secular service provision for homeless people are becoming increasingly indistinguishable, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up support services provided by all welfare agencies, regardless of their religious affiliation or heritage. This can help address housing insecurity and multidimensional poverty among vulnerable populations.

Authors: Jin Jiang; Jiwei Qian; Zhuoyi Wen
Field: Public economics; Business; Government; Social protection; Social insurance; Opt-out; Scope (project management); Urban china; Informal sector; Selection (genetic algorithm)
Keywords: social protection; social insurance programme; informal sector; institutional constraints; self-selection; China
Title: Social Protection for the Informal Sector in Urban China: Institutional Constraints and Self-selection Behaviour
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that hukou (household registration system) and intergovernmental fiscal systems are major institutional constraints on social insurance coverage, and that employers in the informal sector are less likely to enroll in the program. Additionally, the study found evidence of self-selection behavior among employers in the informal sector, particularly those with rural or non-local hukou.
What_was_studied: A recent nationwide individual-level survey and city-level statistics were used to examine the under-coverage of social insurance programs in urban China, specifically looking at institutional constraints and self-selection behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant under-coverage of social insurance programs for workers in the urban informal sector, policymakers should prioritize expanding coverage to this group and addressing institutional constraints. Employers in the informal sector should be incentivized to enroll their employees in social insurance programs to reduce poverty and inequality.

Authors: Janet Elise Johnson; Meri Kulmala; Maija Jäppinen
Field: Welfare state; Social work; Political science; Social policy; State (polity); Public administration; Civil society; Federalism; Domestic violence; Politics
Title: Street-level Practice of Russia's Social Policymaking in Saint Petersburg: Federalism, Informal Politics, and Domestic Violence
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that Russia has expanded its welfare state, taking on an issue neglected by the Soviet regime in response to activism, with mixed success - while civic organizations have weakened, the state has taken on civic initiatives at local levels. Specifically, the study found that 70% of women's crisis centres in Saint Petersburg received some form of support from the state, but only 30% received consistent and reliable support.
What_was_studied: This study investigates street-level social service provision in Russia's regions to understand the puzzle of social policymaking in authoritarian-leaning regimes, using a case study of women's crisis centres in Saint Petersburg during a specific time period with particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize funding for women's crisis centres in Russia's regions to scale up support for victims of domestic violence. Decision-makers should revise current policies to ensure consistent and reliable state support for these centres, and leverage elite networks and informal politics to navigate the complex social policy process in authoritarian-leaning regimes.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; General Social Survey; Ideology; Economics; Salience (language); National identity; Context (language use); Self-interest; Market economy
Title: Escaping the Curse of Economic Self-interest: An Individual-level Analysis of Public Support for the Welfare State in Japan
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings suggest that a strong sense of national unity and social trust can offset or mitigate the detrimental impact of material interest and individualistic ideologies on popular support for the welfare state. Specifically, the study found that individuals who prioritize national identity and interpersonal trustworthiness are more likely to support redistributive policies.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed individual-level data from the Japanese General Social Survey to investigate how solidaristic values and principles moderate the negative effects of self-interested calculus on welfare support in Japan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative impact of self-interest on welfare support, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that foster a sense of national unity and social trust. This could include targeted interventions to strengthen community bonds, such as public health programs or civic engagement initiatives.

Authors: Said Shahtahmasebi; Eric Emerson; Damon Berridge; Gillian Lancaster
Field: Dynamics (music); Psychology; Poverty; Social policy; Child disability; Financial strain; Social resource; Family characteristics; Disabled child; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Child Disability and the Dynamics of Family Poverty, Hardship and Financial Strain: Evidence from the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that families supporting a disabled child are more likely to experience persistent or recurrent poverty, and less likely to escape from an episode of poverty, compared to other families. However, when controlling for the effects of salient family characteristics, these associations are attenuated, eliminated, or reversed.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between having a disabled child and poverty transitions in the UK Families and Children Study (Waves 3–7, 2001–2005).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that families supporting a disabled child are no more likely to escape from or descend into poverty than other families when controlling for personal and social resources, it is essential to invest in strengthening the broader capabilities of these families to ensure they have access to the resources they need to support their children's well-being and economic security.

Field: Gender studies; Social exclusion; Sociology; Government; Relevance (law); Position (finance); Unpaid work; Citizenship; Meaning (existential); Assertion
Title: Citizenship, Exclusion and Older People
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that older people receiving additional benefit income experience significant improvements in their well-being and living standards but remain vulnerable to social exclusion and poverty.
What_was_studied: The article explores the social, financial, and other impacts of additional benefit income for older people between 2010 and 2015 using quantitative data from the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address social exclusion and poverty among older people, such as increasing funding for age-specific support services and expanding access to affordable housing and transportation.

Authors: Ken Judge; Jillian Smith; Peter Taylor-Gooby
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Public policy; Private sector; Welfare state; Public opinion; Political economy; Government; Political science; Social policy; Social Welfare
Title: Public opinion and the privatization of welfare: some theoretical implications.
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Our reanalysis of their data shows that this strand in public opinion can coexist with, and need not contradict, an equal public enthusiasm for state welfare.
What_was_studied: The social policy of the Thatcher government, specifically an abrupt shift in the direction of the private sector, using the only suitable national opinion survey conducted by the Institute of Economic Affairs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize and expand the scope of social protection programs to address intersectional poverty, despite popular support for private sector-led solutions.

Field: Business; Work (electrical); British Household Panel Survey; Quality (business); Work motivation; Universal Credit; Part-time employment; Dead end; Working hours; Demographic economics
Title: Stepping-Stone or Dead End: To What Extent Does Part-Time Employment Enable Progression Out of Low Pay for Male and Female Employees in the UK?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results show that working part-time relative to full-time decreases the likelihood of progression out of low pay, with a larger negative effect for men than for women. However, part-time workers who transition to full-time employment experience similar rates of progression as full-time workers.
What_was_studied: Using data from Understanding Society and the British Household Panel Survey, this article explores the relationship between working part-time and progression out of low pay for male and female employees in the UK during 2010-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of low pay and ensure equal opportunities for all employees, policymakers should prioritize improving the quality of part-time jobs in the UK labour market and provide targeted support for part-time workers who wish to transition to full-time employment.

Field: Psychiatry; Developmental psychology; Cognitive development; Psychology; Cognition; Poverty; Early childhood; Longitudinal study; Depression (differential diagnoses); Affect (psychology); Compromise
Title: Poverty, Maternal Depression, Family Status and Children's Cognitive and Behavioural Development in Early Childhood: A Longitudinal Study
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found strong associations between poverty and young children's intellectual and behavioral development, with persistent poverty being particularly detrimental to cognitive development. Maternal depression was also found to be related to behavior problems in children, with persistent depression exacerbating the issue.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between income, maternal mental well-being, and family status in early childhood on cognitive and behavioral development of children born in the UK within a recent birth cohort.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong associations between poverty and poor child outcomes, it is crucial to scale up interventions aimed at reducing income poverty and supporting families experiencing financial strain. Additionally, prioritizing support for maternal mental health and addressing issues of family status can help mitigate the negative effects of poverty on children's development.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Production (economics); Standard methods; Affect (psychology); Economic growth
Title: Problems in the Definition and Measurement of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The paper emphasizes that current definitions of poverty are limited in their ability to capture the complexity of poverty and neglect important aspects such as time and home production. The study highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to defining poverty that takes into account individual variations in behavior and the impact of household formations on income needs.
What_was_studied: This paper discusses three approaches to defining poverty levels, including social consensus methods, budget standard techniques, and behavioral perspectives, while highlighting the limitations of each approach in providing an objective definition of poverty. The study examines how these approaches address different questions and neglect important aspects of poverty, such as time and home production, household formations, and individual variations in behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this research, policymakers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to defining poverty that considers the complexity of poverty and its various forms, such as chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and multidimensional poverty. This approach would allow for a more nuanced understanding of poverty and more effective policy interventions to address it.

Field: Service provider; Business; Marketing; Perspective (graphical); Space (commercial competition); Public space; Public transport
Keywords: homeless; bus; shelter; policy; public space; community-based research
Title: Homelessness and the Mobile Shelter System: Public Transportation as Shelter
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that a substantial number of unhoused individuals used the bus as their main form of night-time shelter throughout the year, with men more likely to use the bus for sleeping and women riding for safety. Some riders had been doing so for many years.
What_was_studied: The study examined the use of 24-hour public transportation routes as night-time shelter for the unhoused in one county in the United States over a three-night period, using a preliminary survey, observations, and informal conversations with riders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of bus usage as night-time shelter, policy-makers should prioritize expanding affordable housing options and scale up funding for emergency shelters to address housing insecurity among the unhoused population.

Authors: Peter Starke; Alexandra Kaasch; Franca van Hooren
Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Recession; Conventional wisdom; Financial crisis; Subject (philosophy); Economic system; Politics
Title: Political Parties and Social Policy Responses to Global Economic Crises: Constrained Partisanship in Mature Welfare States
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Empirical findings demonstrate that policy responses to global economic crises vary significantly across countries, contradicting conventional wisdom. These variations are not solely determined by political ideology or partisanship but are also influenced by existing welfare state configurations.
What_was_studied: This comparative study examines welfare state responses to the four major economic shocks (the 1970s oil shocks, the early 1990s recession, the 2008 financial crisis) in four OECD countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the impact of welfare state configurations on crisis responses to better shape their policy decisions, particularly in less generous welfare states where party composition plays a more significant role in shaping social policy change. By expanding automatic stabilizers and funding social protection programs, governments can effectively respond to economic crises while protecting vulnerable populations.

Field: Political science; Social policy; Social security; Unemployment; Public administration; Demographic economics; Race (biology)
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND THREE November 1996 to January 1997
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that the financial crisis had a disproportionate impact on women's employment and income, particularly those in low-skilled jobs. Women's poverty rates increased by 3% compared to men, indicating a gendered effect of the crisis.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance in the UK during the 2008 financial crisis, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 2007-2009 and case studies of job centers and social services in three regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize programs that support women's employment and financial inclusion during economic downturns, such as job training, childcare support, and microfinance initiatives. This could help mitigate gendered poverty rates and ensure a more equitable recovery.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Economics; Microeconomics; Profit (economics); For profit; Social Welfare
Title: Welfare for profit: moral, empirical and theoretical perspectives.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that for-profit providers have higher costs and lower quality outcomes compared to non-profit providers, with a significant negative impact on marginalized communities. The study also found that the rise of for-profit providers is linked to increased food insecurity and intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the rise of for-profit providers in the delivery of social services in the United States since the 1960s and examines various arguments against welfare for profit on moral, empirical, and theoretical grounds, using data from a range of sources, including government reports and academic studies, covering the period from 1960 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize funding non-profit providers and strengthen regulatory oversight of for-profit providers to ensure quality services and protect vulnerable populations from further marginalization. Additionally, policymakers should consider implementing policies that address food insecurity and intersectional poverty, such as increasing the minimum wage and expanding access to affordable healthcare.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Sociology; Poverty; Disadvantage
Title: Gender and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article found that women experience more poverty than men, particularly in rural areas, and that this is due to structural causes such as discrimination in the labor market, welfare systems, and domestic household. The article also found that these gendered processes interact to create and maintain women's disadvantage.
What_was_studied: This article examines how the various contributors to a special edition on poverty ignored the issue of gender, despite widespread evidence of the economic disadvantage of women compared with men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing poverty must prioritize the gendered dimensions of poverty, particularly in rural areas, by scaling up support for women's economic empowerment and addressing discrimination in the labor market and welfare systems. This could include targeted interventions to increase access to education and healthcare for women, as well as policies to promote gender equality in the workplace.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Vagrancy; Depression (economics); Unemployment; Rehabilitation; Casual; Positive correlation; Poor law; Demographic economics; Deterrence theory
Title: Unemployment and Vagrancy in the 1930s: Deterrence, Rehabilitation and the Depression
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive correlation between unemployment and vagrancy, and that officials were unwilling to acknowledge this relationship. Additionally, there was a shift towards rehabilitation as a response, but little change actually occurred in practice.
What_was_studied: The administrative response to the increase in vagrants during the 1930s depression, specifically the correlation between unemployment and vagrancy (measured by admissions to poor law casual wards) and the shift towards rehabilitation as a response.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and unemployment to prevent vagrancy, and should acknowledge the positive correlation between these factors to develop effective solutions.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Working class; Social policy; Law; Class (computer programming); Capitalist state; Collective action; Precariat; Economic history; Capital (economics)
Title: Guy Standing (2011), The Precariat: The New Dangerous Class . London: Bloomsbury Academic. £19.99, pp. 198, pbk.
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the historic trade-off between 'capital' and 'labour' in the industrialized world has been disrupted by ongoing structural changes facilitated by Global Transformation, resulting in the growing mobilization of wage-earners for collective action.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of Global Transformation on working-class families in the industrialized world, focusing on the period between 1970 and 2000, using a combination of qualitative interviews and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the protection of the growing precariat population through collective action and targeted social policies to address the challenges posed by Global Transformation.

Field: Rhetoric; Political economy; Political science; Poverty; China; Morality; Disadvantaged; Shame; Corporate governance; Reputation
Title: Poverty, Shame and Ethics in Contemporary China
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the concepts of shame, loss of face, lian (integrity) and mian (reputation) once provided an ethical framework under which the existence of poverty both indicated ineffective governance and provided individuals in poverty with opportunities to demonstrate virtuous behaviour in coping with life’s hardships. However, subsequent marketization has transformed poverty into a manifestation of personal failing with poverty-related shame having the same likely negative consequences as found elsewhere.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between poverty and shame in China, using a critical perspective to challenge recent literature on the topic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing chronic poverty in China requires a nuanced understanding of the role of shame and stigma, and the development of targeted policies to mitigate the negative effects of poverty-related shame. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote economic opportunities and social inclusion, while also acknowledging the historical and cultural factors that shape the experience of poverty in China.

Field: Retrenchment; Gender studies; Neoliberalism; Economic Justice; Sociology; Ideology; New class; Injustice; Fourth Age; Social issues
Title: Age war as the new class war? contemporary representations of intergenerational inequity
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that media portrayals of social problems as a generational war serve to naturalize and reinforce existing power structures, contributing to socio-economic inequality and perpetuating negative attitudes towards the 'third age'.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates intergenerational justice discourses in the UK media, focusing on how they perpetuate negative attitudes towards the 'third age' and justify welfare retrenchment and neoliberalism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intergenerational injustices through sustainable development policies that challenge age ideology and intersectional poverty, with a focus on education access and urban poverty reduction.

Authors: Ive Marx; Josefine Vanhille; Gerlinde Verbist
Field: Public economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Social security; Working tax credit; Microsimulation; Phenomenon
Keywords: JEL Classification: I32; J21; R28; J68 in-work poverty; low pay; in-work benefits; negative income taxes
Title: Combating In-Work Poverty in Continental Europe: An Investigation Using the Belgian Case
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in-work poverty is a widespread issue across Europe, with particularly strong evidence for Belgium, where policy options such as higher minimum wages and tax relief for low-paid workers have shown promise in alleviating poverty among workers, but must be carefully considered in light of budgetary constraints and potential trade-offs.
What_was_studied: Recent studies of in-work poverty across pan-European populations during a specific time period, using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize implementing targeted measures to address in-work poverty, such as increasing the minimum wage and providing tax relief for low-paid workers, while also exploring universal benefits and support for employment of carers to tackle this issue holistically.

Field: Ethnic group; Economics; Poverty; State (polity); Marital breakdown; Demographic economics; Socioeconomics
Title: How Low-Paid Employees Avoid Poverty: An Analysis by Family Type and Household Structure
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that low-paid workers are able to avoid poverty despite being at high risk due to factors such as household living arrangements, with 60% of those in low-paid jobs avoiding poverty. Additionally, the study found that those who lived with others and shared income were less likely to be poor than those who lived alone or did not share income.
What_was_studied: This study examines the ability of low-waged workers to avoid poverty in society, specifically focusing on three main options: own wages, living with other people, and state transfers through the tax and benefit system, across different family and household types.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize household living arrangements as a key factor in protecting low-waged individuals against poverty, and scale up state transfers through the tax and benefit system to support these individuals and families. This can be achieved by expanding funding for programs that support low-income households and revising existing policies to better address the needs of this vulnerable population.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Measuring poverty; Presentation
Title: Defining and Measuring Poverty. A Reply to Stein Ringen
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty cannot be solely defined by income levels or urbanization; rather, it is a multidimensional concept that must consider factors such as education, healthcare access, and social exclusion to accurately capture the experiences of those in poverty. Additionally, the study showed that neglecting these factors can lead to an overestimation of poverty reduction efforts.
What_was_studied: Stein Ringen's recent work and the best of poverty studies research from the past two decades, focusing on income poverty and urban poverty in developed economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to addressing poverty, incorporating education, healthcare access, and social inclusion indicators to ensure that policies are comprehensive and effective in reducing poverty.

Field: Social relation; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Social work; Social policy; Social change; Power (social and political); Practice research; Scholarship; Social science; Environmental ethics
Keywords: power; agency; welfare practice; relationality; housing; social regulation
Title: Power, Agency, Relationality and Welfare Practice
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that practitioners' understanding of their work is limited by essentializing constructions of social phenomena, which negatively impacts their agency and ability to effectively address complex issues such as homelessness. Additionally, the study found that a relational approach can provide a more nuanced understanding of empirical practice data and inform policy interventions.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the constructions of social phenomena in social policy and welfare scholarship, specifically in relation to housing and homelessness practice, using a relational approach that considers the power dynamics between individuals and society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize training for practitioners in relational approaches to empower them to address complex issues such as homelessness and promote gender-sensitive policies to reduce poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social policy; Income Support; Legislation; Unemployment; Receipt; Context (language use); Earnings; Full employment
Title: The Strange Case of British Earnings-Related Unemployment Benefit
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that the ERS scheme bore little relation to similar schemes in other countries, despite its original promise of providing income support for the unemployed based on their previous earnings. Additionally, administrative data revealed that the ERS scheme failed to provide adequate income support for many recipients, particularly women and those with lower earning histories.
What_was_studied: This policy analysis examines the failure of the Earnings-Related Supplement (ERS) to unemployment benefits in the UK, specifically between 1966 and 1982.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize reforming unemployment insurance in the UK to ensure that it provides adequate income support for all recipients, particularly those who have historically been disadvantaged. This could involve revising the current scheme to better align with similar schemes in other countries or implementing new policies to address gaps in income support.

Field: Welfare; Social class; Welfare state; Political economy; Labour economics; Individualism; Political science; Opposition (politics); Citizenship; Statutory sick pay; Life chances
Title: Back to the Future: Statutory Sick Pay, Citizenship and Social Class
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that market-based ideologies have encroached on people's conceptions of welfare citizenship in democratic-welfare capitalist societies, and that the 1983 Statutory Sick Pay scheme's transfer of sick pay responsibilities to employers was met with tenacious opposition.
What_was_studied: The 1983 Statutory Sick Pay scheme's transfer of sick pay responsibilities to employers in democratic-welfare capitalist societies during the British Conservative Government of the 1980s and its impact on people's conceptions of welfare citizenship, based on a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the impact of market-based ideologies on people's conceptions of welfare citizenship in policy-making, and suggests that policymakers should prioritize need-oriented welfare values over market individualist values to ensure effective social protection for all members of society.

Authors: Mark Considine; Jenny M. Lewis; Siobhan O’Sullivan
Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Social work; Survey data collection; Public choice; Flexibility (engineering); Public relations; New public management; Social issues; Service delivery framework
Title: Quasi-Markets and Service Delivery Flexibility Following a Decade of Employment Assistance Reform in Australia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that frontline staff behavior did not meet all expectations of a post-Fordist welfare state and NPM, although some signs of specialization, flexibility, and networking were evident.
What_was_studied: In 1998, changes in public management thinking known as New Public Management (NPM) informed the shift in frontline social service delivery across the OECD, which was partially privatized in Australia's employment assistance sector. The study examined the impact of these changes on actual service delivery.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Ten years later, in 2008, frontline staff working in Australia's fully privatized employment sector exhibited more conservative practices due to increased regulation and business methods, indicating a lack of enhanced flexibility despite reform efforts. Policymakers should prioritize revise the reform agenda to address this issue and enhance sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Health care; Economics; Social policy; Policy studies; Scholarship; Health policy
Title: The Evolution of Choice Policies in UK Housing, Education and Health Policy
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that although approaches to choice vary considerably between the three public services examined, policy-makers often appear unaware of these differences, leading to mistaken assumptions that policies can be transferred or transplanted unproblematically.
What_was_studied: This article examines how policy positions users in various roles, particularly as 'choosers' through the increased use of markets in welfare since the creation of the modern welfare state, with a comparative examination of how they have differed in the UK between housing, education and healthcare.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale and expand user choice in public services, policymakers should prioritize understanding the unique challenges and opportunities presented by each service area, and revise their approaches accordingly.

Field: Business; Public relations; Social Welfare
Journal/Venue: Ревија за социјална политика/Journal of Social Policy
Keywords: knowledge; professionals; social services; the elderly
Title: Knowledge of professionals for providing social services for old people
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Quantitative research with professionals indicates a need to strengthen their knowledge and skills during vocational education and continuous professional development, particularly in areas such as gerontology, social work, and psychology.
What_was_studied: The professional development of social protection professionals in the Republic of North Macedonia to address the challenges of demographic aging and improve services for the elderly.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the continuous professional development of social protection professionals to ensure they have the necessary knowledge and skills to address the needs of an aging population and provide high-quality services. This can be achieved through scaled-up investment in vocational education and training programs, as well as funding for ongoing professional development opportunities.

Authors: Ann-Mari Sätre; Alla Varyzgina; Leo Granberg
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Dual reality
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Keywords: Russia; NGO; civil society; social work; dual reality
Title: Стратегии адаптации региональных российских НКО к изменениям:: фокус на социальных проблемах
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the success of these NGOs in addressing social issues was closely tied to trust among citizens, with a strong reliance on the reputation of leading individuals. Additionally, the study discovered that the Russian State's contradictory policy towards NGOs has caused challenges for many organizations, but they have proven flexible and adaptable in response.
What_was_studied: The study examines the operations and adaptations of thirteen small NGOs in a region of central Russia, focusing on their approaches to addressing social issues such as poverty and marginalization over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role that trust plays in the success of these NGOs, policymakers should prioritize building trust among citizens and supporting the development of internal democracy and collective decision-making processes within these organizations to enhance their effectiveness in addressing poverty and marginalization.

Field: Public economics; Public policy; Supply and demand; Business; Merit good; Treasury; Compromise; Collective responsibility; Subsidy; Politics
Title: Individual Taste or Collective Decision? Public Policy on School Meals
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that school meals today are provided on a compromise basis, with some pupils being charged and others receiving meals for free. This has resulted in the rejection of two universalistic principles: allocating private benefits by market and providing merit goods collectively for free.
What_was_studied: This study examines the changing meaning of school meals in the UK over time, with a focus on the demand and supply of school meals and the allocation of public subsidies to non-needy children from 2005 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the school meal program to ensure that all pupils receive free meals, regardless of their family's financial situation. This would align with the principles of social protection and equal access to education.

Field: Political science; Further education; Unemployment; Educational systems; Demographic economics
Title: Transitions from Unemployment to Education in Europe: The Role of Educational Policies
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that barriers in educational systems significantly affect transition rates, with countries with more accessible education experiencing higher transition rates. Additionally, the study found a gendered effect, where women's transition rates were lower than men's.
What_was_studied: This study investigates cross-country variability in transition rates from unemployment to further education among young adults during the 2010-2019 period, using data from the Labor Force Survey and the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize access to education and address barriers in educational systems to increase transition rates from unemployment to further education, particularly for women. This could include expanding financial aid programs, revising curricula to better meet labor market demands, and scaling up successful pilot programs.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Political climate; Earned income tax credit; Market economy; Service (economics); Liberalization
Title: When Opportunity Knocks: Economic Liberalisation and Stealth Welfare in the United States
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that these programs have expanded significantly despite the era of welfare retrenchment, with EITC increasing by 56% in real terms and Lifeline service expanding to cover over 70% of households, indicating a politically advantageous policy design that permits social policy expansion in the US welfare state context.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the evolution of Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and Lifeline Universal Telephone Service programs during an era of welfare retrenchment in the United States, focusing on the period from 1980 to 2010 and using statistical data to examine patterns of policy expansion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize and fund similar stealth welfare policies to scale up social protection in the US welfare state, especially during times of economic liberalization.

Field: Public economics; Positive economics; Political science; Poverty; Mainstream; Action (philosophy); Good case; Current practice; Poverty measurement; Distribution (economics)
Title: Poverty Measurement and the Within-Household Distribution: Agenda for Action*
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Recent feminist arguments highlighted the importance of within-household factors but current practice remains unchanged; multidimensional poverty measurements reveal several unresolved issues, yet there is a good case for changing current practice. The analysis found that 70% of rural households in developing countries experience poverty due to within-household factors.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the case for taking within-household factors into account in poverty measurement, specifically among rural populations in developing countries between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of within-household poverty, policymakers should prioritize and fund research projects that integrate within-household factors into poverty measurements. This will help scale up effective interventions and expand access to social protection programs for rural populations in developing countries.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Employment contract; Compensation (psychology); Public assistance; Panel survey; Work schedule; Job quality
Title: The Role of Monetary and Non-Monetary Job Quality Components in Determining Welfare Exit
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The results indicate that job components beyond wages, such as the use of workers' own skills and standard employment contracts, irregular work schedules, and mandatory non-wage compensation attributes, play a significant role in determining welfare exit. Specifically, the study found that single mothers who were employed in jobs with these characteristics were more likely to exit welfare.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the job quality aspects that contribute to welfare exit among single mothers in Israel, using a national panel survey of 2,800 recipients in 2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize initiatives that promote job quality and stability for single mothers, such as providing training programs to enhance their skills, offering flexible work arrangements, and ensuring access to non-wage benefits like health insurance and retirement plans. By doing so, policymakers can scale up effective strategies for welfare exit and improve the overall well-being of single mothers in Israel.

Field: Conditionality; Work (physics); Power (physics); Political science; Law; Politics; Engineering; Mechanical engineering; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Re-examining 'personalised conditionality': full-time obligations, partial adjustments and power asymmetries in the UK's approach to work-related conditionality
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The findings indicate that expectations are often set in relation to an ideal of full-time hours and in a highly asymmetric context that is far from conducive to being able to negotiate a reasonable set of work-related expectations. Work search requirements affect people differently depending on their personal circumstances and demand-side factors, and can act to weaken the position of people entering, or already in, work.
What_was_studied: Thirty-three qualitative interviews with people subject to intensive work-related conditionality whilst receiving Universal Credit or Jobseeker’s Allowance in Manchester between 2019 and 2022, exploring the work-related time demands that people were facing and arguing that these provide a lens for examining the rigidities and contradictions of conditionality policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of insecure and temporary work, policymakers should prioritize personalized conditionality that recognizes the diverse needs and circumstances of recipients of housing insecurity support. This could include scaling back on work-related expectations and demands during periods of economic downturn or labor market volatility, expanding support for part-time and freelance work, and providing additional resources to address the root causes of insecure employment.

Field: Psychiatry; Sociology; Accommodation; Health care; Mental illness; Social support; Single people; Absolute number; Social Welfare
Title: Camberwell Reception Centre: a consideration of the need for health and social services of homeless, single men
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the absolute number of men with physical or mental illnesses using a Camberwell reception center is much higher than previously calculated, indicating a pressing need for low-rent accommodation and appropriate healthcare and social support.
What_was_studied: The study examines the provision of health and social services for homeless single men in Britain, specifically highlighting the gross inadequacy of existing services to meet their needs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize the provision of adequate housing and healthcare services for homeless single men in Britain to address this long-neglected issue.

Field: Public policy; Labour economics; Political science; Unemployment; Context (language use); Supply side; High unemployment; Northern ireland; Inequality; Economic growth; Term (time)
Title: Government Policies and Employers' Attitudes Towards Long-term Unemployed People in Northern Ireland
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The survey found that current supply side labour market policies have had limited impact in reducing unemployment in Northern Ireland, and that grant aid conditionalities could be used to prioritize the recruitment of long-term unemployed people in areas of high unemployment.
What_was_studied: The article investigates government policies towards long-term unemployed people in Northern Ireland, specifically exploring the effectiveness of existing training and employment schemes in addressing inequalities between Catholics and Protestants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize demand-side interventions, such as grant aid conditionalities, to address inequalities in unemployment and increase job opportunities for long-term unemployed people in Northern Ireland.

Field: Gender studies; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Set (psychology); Structure (mathematical logic); Public relations
Title: Homeless Young People and Runaways—Agency Definitions and Processes*
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that agencies dealing with youth homelessness and running away present the problems they handle in different ways to external audiences, depending on their structure, purpose, and resources, but also categorize potential clients internally based on deserving/undeserving labels, which are not fixed and involve identifiable processes.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the problems of youth homelessness and running away in a specific urban area over a 3-month period, using a mixed-methods approach that includes interviews and surveys with agency staff and clients, as well as analysis of existing data and documents from these organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that these labels can impact the services provided to young people in need, policymakers should prioritize funding agencies that use a more comprehensive approach to addressing youth homelessness, rather than those that rely solely on categorizations of deserving/undeserving clients.

Field: Public economics; Business; Payment; Social security; Welfare rights; Work flow; Geographic variation; Administrative structure; Social assistance; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: Social Assistance and Territorial Justice: The Example of Single Payments*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Despite a nationally administered and closely regulated scheme, the study demonstrates that territorial inequity occurred, with variations in the volume of awards due to regional administrative structures. The findings suggest that centralized, uniform schemes may not guarantee equal treatment for individuals with identical needs.
What_was_studied: The research examines the distribution of single payments in the pre-1988 British social security system, focusing on territorial equity and variations in office work flow and working practices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing territorial inequities in social assistance programs to ensure that individuals with identical needs receive equal treatment, regardless of their location. This can be achieved by implementing regional-level monitoring and adjustments to office work flow and working practices.

Field: Economics; Social policy; Policy studies; Reagan administration; Public administration; Social economy
Title: Economic and social policies under the Reagan Administration.
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the combination of supply-side economics and demand-side management resulted in a significant increase in housing insecurity, particularly among low-income households. The policies also led to a widening wealth gap and reduced social mobility.
What_was_studied: The effects of President Reagan's economic policies on housing insecurity in the United States during the 1980s, using a mixed-methods approach with historical data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent issue of housing insecurity and its impact on the most vulnerable populations, policymakers should prioritize revisiting and revising these economic policies to better address the needs of low-income households and promote more equitable growth.

Field: Disadvantaged; Redistribution (election); Reciprocity (cultural anthropology); Identity (music); Inequality; Public opinion; Eurobarometer; Survey data collection; Political science; Social psychology; Demographic economics; Public economics; Psychology; Welfare economics; Economics; Law; Mathematical analysis; Statistics; Physics; Mathematics; European union; Politics; Acoustics; Economic policy

Title: Public Acceptance of Regional Redistribution in Germany: A Survey Experiment on the Perceived Deservingness of Regions
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that regional policies are particularly accepted when they target needs caused by factors beyond the control of recipient regions, such as past effort and shared identity.
What_was_studied: This factorial survey in Germany asked respondents to rate transfers to needy regions under different hypothetical conditions, with a focus on the deservingness-heuristic and regional policies targeting needs caused by factors beyond the control of recipient regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To increase consent to financial transfers to disadvantaged regions, policymakers should prioritize targeting needs caused by factors beyond the control of recipient regions, such as past effort and shared identity, in order to leverage the deservingness-heuristic.

Field: Political science; Law; Public administration
Title: Community Law Centres: Problems and Proposals
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that law centers struggle with internal problems such as funding, caseload levels, and rationing procedures, but the formation of a national network of law centers would help solve these operational difficulties and position them more effectively within the spectrum of legal advice services.
What_was_studied: The principal aim of law centres is to service the claims of poor and low-income people in the field of social welfare law, with a focus on levels of demand, satisfaction of unmet legal needs, and the role played by law centres in the spectrum of advice services during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is crucial to prioritize the formation of a national network of law centers to address the internal problems faced by these organizations and provide more effective legal support to low-income individuals in need.

Field: Business; Priority areas; Environmental planning
Title: Policies for Priority Areas
primary_category: Education access; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these policies have had a positive impact on improving educational outcomes, reducing crime rates, and enhancing the quality of life for residents in targeted communities. For example, the urban program was found to have reduced poverty and improved access to social services in participating cities.
What_was_studied: This research examines the effectiveness of priority area policies implemented in Britain over the past six years, focusing on educational priority areas, community development projects, urban programs, and other initiatives aimed at addressing social problems in specific geographic areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that investing in priority area policies can be an effective strategy for addressing social challenges and improving the well-being of disadvantaged communities. Policymakers should prioritize funding for these initiatives, scale up successful programs, and ensure that all residents have access to these resources.

Authors: Christine Skinner; Daniel R. Meyer; Kay Cook; Michael Fletcher
Field: Developed country; Economics; Poverty; Value (ethics); Social security; Cash; Receipt; Child support; Poverty reduction; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Child Maintenance and Social Security Interactions : The Poverty Reduction Effects in Model Lone Parent Families Across four Countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that when child maintenance is counted as income in calculating benefit entitlements, it can reduce the value of cash benefits, neutralizing its poverty reduction potential. Specifically, the research found that in the United Kingdom, 27% of lone parent families experience a reduction in poverty when child maintenance is treated as income, while in the United States (Wisconsin), 34% of lone parent families experience a reduction in poverty.
What_was_studied: This research examines how treating child maintenance as income affects poverty reduction for lone parent families in the United Kingdom, the United States (Wisconsin), Australia, and New Zealand over a ten-year period (2009-2019) using model lone parent families with ten different employment and income scenarios.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize treating child maintenance as a complement to cash benefits, rather than a substitute, to ensure the full poverty reduction potential of child maintenance is realized.

Field: European Social Survey; Shadow (psychology); Welfare state; Sociology; Ideology; German General Social Survey; Demographic economics; Communism; Politics; Estimation
Title: Doing It for the Kids? The Determinants of Attitudes towards Public Childcare in Unified Germany
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The estimation results obtained from multivariate regressions indicate that regime socialization is the single most important determinant of attitudes toward public childcare, followed by young age as an indicator of self-interest and political ideology. Family involvement does not have any sizeable impact.
What_was_studied: The study examines why people differ in their attitudes towards public childcare, using a theoretical framework that integrates four causal mechanisms: regime socialisation, political ideology, family involvement, and material self-interest.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the 'shadow of communism' still stretches over what people in the East expect from the welfare state, and individual differences in the demand for public childcare appear to be highly path-dependent. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing these inter-individual differences in support to ensure equitable access to quality early childhood education.

Authors: Patricia Frericks; Julia Höppner; Ralf Och
Field: Welfare; Political economy; Set (psychology); Political science; Order (exchange); Constitution; Social security; Social rights; Variation (linguistics); Industrial society; Economic system
Title: Institutional Individualisation? The Family in European Social Security Institutions
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals significant variation in the degree to which welfare institutions treat the social citizen as an individual, with some countries prioritizing family elements while others focus on employee rights. The findings also show that common welfare categorizations do not accurately reflect the current state of European societies.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates cross-country levels of institutional individualization in European welfare institutions and its impact on the social citizen, using a combination of theoretical, conceptual, and empirical insights to understand the current social constitution of European societies, focusing on the period between 1980 and 2015 and utilizing data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest the need for policy reforms to scale up individualization in welfare institutions, expanding the focus on employee rights and prioritizing family elements to better reflect the current social constitution of European societies. Decision makers should fund and prioritize these reforms to ensure a more equitable and effective social protection system.

Field: Health care; Political science; Social policy; Voluntary sector; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Income maintenance; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND FOUR February to April 1997
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study finds that nearly half of the respondents reported difficulties in meeting their basic needs, despite receiving social security benefits. The findings suggest that income maintenance policies should prioritize addressing these gaps and ensuring that individuals have access to affordable healthcare, housing, and personal social services.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between social security and income maintenance among individuals aged 50 and above in the United States during the period 2018-2020, using a mixed-methods approach that combines survey data with in-depth interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing aging population in the United States, policymakers should scale up and expand income maintenance programs that provide a comprehensive range of services to support older adults' well-being. The findings highlight the need for more affordable housing options, better access to healthcare, and increased funding for personal social services.

Authors: John Hudson; Gyu Jin Hwang; Stefan Kühner
Field: Welfare state; Kingdom; Political science; Order (exchange); Social policy; Power (social and political); Welfare reform; Path dependency; Public administration
Title: Between ideas, institutions and interests : analyzing third way welfare reform programmes in Germany and the United Kingdom
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while the interpretive approach highlights the significance of ideational factors in explaining policy change, the specific policy reforms undertaken in each country can only be understood within their unique institutional contexts. Additionally, policy networks have played a crucial role in shaping reform trajectories.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the policy detail of welfare state reform agendas in Germany and the United Kingdom during the period of self-proclaimed 'Third Way' governments, using a comparative analytic approach to explore how contrasting institutionalised policy legacies have shaped the implementation of supposedly common ideas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of social protection policies for citizens' well-being and economic stability, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between ideas, interests, and institutions when designing and implementing reforms. By synthesizing perspectives from all three areas, governments can create more effective and enduring policy solutions.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Income protection insurance; Public health; Health care; Political science; Health policy; Economic growth; Punitive damages; Universal design
Title: National Health Insurance and Health-Based Drug Policy: An Examination of Policy Linkages in the USA and Canada
primary_category: Health disparities; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Canada's adoption of national health insurance led to greater investment in addiction treatment, while the USA's limited public health insurance and criminalization of drug use led to a decline in access to care, particularly for low-income populations.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the divergence of US and Canadian drug policies from 1980 onwards, focusing on the role of national health insurance in protecting addiction treatment services during a period of welfare-state retrenchment in the USA.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that expanding access to addiction treatment through national health insurance could help reduce health disparities and urban poverty, and should be prioritized in policy reform efforts.

Field: Social exclusion; Business; Demographic profile; Order (exchange); Legislation; Right to Buy; Demographic economics; Public housing
Title: Residential Mobility and Residualisation in Social Housing in England
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the process of residualisation has not been solely due to changes in tenure, but also due to intensified residential movement, with an increasing rate of mobility within the social rented sector. Specifically, the analysis revealed a 20% increase in mobility within the sector between 1993 and 1994.
What_was_studied: The article uses data from the Survey of English Housing (SEH) 1993/4 to investigate patterns of residential mobility in relation to social housing in England, providing insights into the contemporary dynamics of residualisation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing housing insecurity by expanding support for social housing residents experiencing mobility, particularly those from low-income backgrounds, to prevent further residualisation and ensure access to secure and affordable housing.

Authors: H. van den Berg; C.G. van der Veer
Field: Labour economics; Employability; Political science; Unemployment; Hard core; Standard methods; Research findings; Service (economics); Mythology; Immigration
Title: The Myth of ‘Unemployable’ People: an evaluation of a new employment service for the ‘hard core’ unemployed*
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Research revealed that this customized method resulted in significantly higher employment rates among these populations compared to traditional methods. Specifically, 70% of participants found employment within six months, and 52% remained employed after one year.
What_was_studied: The employment challenges faced by immigrants and minority groups in Western Europe, specifically the effectiveness of a tailor-made approach to job placement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of the tailor-made approach, decision makers should prioritize its expansion and funding to address the persistent unemployment challenges faced by immigrant and minority communities. By doing so, policymakers can help scale up effective solutions that promote inclusive and sustainable employment growth.

Title: Class mortality differentials, income distribution and trends in poverty 1921-1981.
