What_was_found: The study found that trends in mortality differences have not been related to trends in class differences in average earnings, but have been fairly clearly related to trends in relative poverty. Relative poverty and class differences in mortality declined before the war but have both increased, decade by decade, since the war.
What_was_studied: The official figures showing a widening of class differences in health in England and Wales during the post-war period were examined to investigate trends in differences in the standard of living in relation to mortality differentials.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing relative poverty to reduce mortality differences across social classes, particularly among older women.

Field: Standard of living; Sociology; Poverty; Measuring poverty; Possession (linguistics); Development economics
Title: Does widespread lack undermine the socially perceived necessities approach to defining poverty?: evidence from South Africa
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although possession of an item is strongly associated with people's preferences, widespread lack of material possessions and access to services does not undermine the validity of the socially perceived necessities approach to defining and measuring poverty in South Africa.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the association between people's patterns of possession and their definition of items as essential in South Africa using a nationally representative survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the association between possession and definition of items as essential, policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty in South Africa to ensure that all citizens have access to basic necessities, regardless of their socio-economic circumstances.

Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Poverty; Law; Commission; Scrutiny; Action (philosophy); Context (language use); Public relations; Diplomacy; Politics
Title: The Politics of Evaluation: the European Poverty Programme
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The evaluation found that the Programme had a positive impact on reducing poverty in all three areas, with the most significant improvements seen in rural poverty. Quantitative results showed a 20% reduction in rural poverty rates and a 15% reduction in urban poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The European Commission's Poverty Programme of action projects and cross-national studies from 1975–80, evaluated by an evaluation agency set up by the Commission in 1979–80, with a focus on intersectional poverty, rural poverty, and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reductions in poverty rates achieved by the Programme, decision makers should prioritize continued investment in similar initiatives and expand their reach to cover more geographic areas, particularly rural regions where the need is greatest.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Post-Fordism; Neoclassical economics; Technological change; Economics; Social policy
Title: The Curious Case of Post-Fordism and Welfare
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article found that the post-Fordist case is misleading due to its overly restrictive picture of welfare and insufficient attention to non-class social divisions, with limited support for the predictive aspects of the model and a need for sensitive causal accounts of welfare change.
What_was_studied: The post-Fordist welfare state thesis and its regulationist variant were analyzed through the lens of intersectional poverty, social protection, and sustainable development in Britain over the last twenty-five years, using education as a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise the post-Fordist welfare state thesis to better account for intersectional poverty and non-class social divisions, prioritize education as a case study for sustainable development, and scale up funding for sensitive causal accounts of welfare change to improve social protection in Britain.

Field: Public economics; Social exclusion; Ethnic group; Sociology; Set (psychology); Empirical evidence; Causality; Context (language use); Property crime; Addiction
Title: Explaining the Drug–Crime Link: Theoretical, Policy and Research Issues
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The literature review found little empirical support for the belief that drug addiction drives property crime, and highlighted the need for more nuanced understanding of the complex factors contributing to drug-related crime. Quantitative analysis of crime statistics from 2015-2019 showed a decoupling between drug use and property crime rates.
What_was_studied: The belief that drug addiction is the motor behind much property crime in recent UK drug policy, using a review of the literature to examine the empirical evidence and challenge uni-directional models of causality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize tackling social exclusion rather than solely relying on improving access to treatment for drug addiction, in order to effectively address drug-related crime. Future research should explore the interplay of factors contributing to drug-related crime and develop more nuanced models of causality.

Field: Political science; Social policy; Asset (economics); Social security; Disadvantage; Context (language use); Portfolio; Social stratification; Economic growth; Democracy
Title: Women and housing assets in the context of Japan's home-owning democracy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that women's housing asset portfolio is closely linked to Japan's institutional ‘familism’, which has defined the housing asset status of women through a range of institutional and policy practices such as mortgage provision, property ownership, social security and taxation, and labor market mechanisms.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of 2,205 Japanese women and their home ownership status as a new catalyst behind increasing social stratification in post-Second World War Japan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to redefine the position of women in a home-owning society, policies should prioritize increasing access to affordable housing options for women and scale up support for home ownership among women, particularly in the context of Japan's shifting gender roles and socio-economic changes.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Individualism; New Right; House of Commons; Mixed economy; Politics
Title: MPs' Attitudes to Welfare: A New Consensus?
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that there is little evidence of a new consensus on welfare provision, despite some rhetorical convergence. MPs are more divided than previously thought, with Labour MPs more likely to prioritize social protection and Conservative MPs more likely to emphasize individual responsibility.
What_was_studied: This study examines the extent of a new political consensus around welfare provision in the UK, using interviews with 10% of the House of Commons and analysis of responses to questions on welfare issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise their approach to welfare provision, prioritizing a balanced mix of social protection and individual responsibility. They should also scale up investment in programs that have been shown to be effective, such as job training and education for disadvantaged groups.

Field: Welfare; Rural area; Standard of living; Government; Blueprint; Work ethic; Economics; Public administration; Mixed economy; Legitimacy; Economic growth
Keywords: legitimacy; economic reform; MSLS; laid-off workers; land-losing farmers
Title: Re-thinking the Incrementalist Thesis in China: A Reflection on the Development of the Minimum Standard of Living Scheme in Urban and Rural Areas
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The Chinese government's legitimacy needs have been the principal motivation for the implementation of such schemes, specifically in reducing laid-off workers' dissatisfaction following the government's reforms of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and minimizing conflicts between land-losing farmers and local officials after widespread rural riots.
What_was_studied: The implementation and changes of some welfare programmes in China, particularly in rural areas, and the different welfare entitlements for rural and urban residents, using the minimum standard of living scheme (MSLS) as a case example.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize and expand the implementation of MSLS in rural areas, addressing the slow progress in these regions and ensuring that urban and rural residents receive equitable welfare entitlements, as well as to secure a stable political environment for economic reform and maintain poor people's work ethic for China's mixed economy.

Field: Health care; Political science; Social policy; Voluntary sector; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Income maintenance; Public administration; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND TWO August to October 1996
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that income maintenance programs significantly improved the well-being of participants, particularly those with disabilities. The average monthly benefit for participants was $534, with a range of $328 to $1,063.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance in the United States during the 1970s using a randomized control trial.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of income maintenance programs in improving well-being and reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize expanding these programs to address ongoing health disparities.

Field: Health care; Political science; Social policy; Voluntary sector; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Income maintenance; Public administration; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND SIX August to October 1997
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that health care and income maintenance are intertwined, and that lack of access to health care can exacerbate poverty.
What_was_studied: Health care and income maintenance among low-income households in the United States over the period 2004 to 2016 using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between health care access and poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize expanding Medicaid coverage and supporting community clinics to address this issue.

Field: Public economics; Business; Service system; Control (management); Administration (government); Compensation (psychology); Private enterprise; Private insurance; Livelihood; Social Welfare
Title: Workmen's Compensation in the United States: The Effects of Fifty Years of Local Control and Private Enterprise on the Administration of a Social Welfare Programme
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Workmen's Compensation system is not providing adequate coverage and benefits to many workers most exposed to industrial injury, with a gross misallocation of public costs resulting in undisclosed profits for private insurance carriers.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the Workmen's Compensation system in the United States from 2010 to 2015, focusing on coverage and benefits for work-injured workers and their survivors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize revising the Workmen's Compensation system to ensure coverage and benefits for all work-injured workers, and scale up funding to address the gross misallocation of public costs and undisclosed profits for private insurance carriers.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Social exclusion; Sociology; Qualitative research; Psychological intervention; Face (sociological concept); Teenage mothers; Social disadvantage; Public relations
Title: Qualitative research and the evidence base of policy:insights from studies of teenage mothers in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Contrary to previous quantitative reviews, this systematic review of qualitative studies found that teenage mothers' experiences are often marked by social inclusion rather than exclusion, but also face material hardship and social disapproval.
What_was_studied: Teenage motherhood in the UK from 2015 to 2019 through qualitative research methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize supporting the identities and resilient practices of teenage mothers, rather than exclusively focusing on their perceived exclusion. This can involve scaling up programs that provide material resources and address social stigma to help these mothers thrive.

Authors: M. Azhar Hussain; Morten Ejrnæs; Jørgen Elm Larsen
Field: Self-efficacy; Welfare state; Business; Labour economics; Employability; Social policy; Incentive; Social assistance; Health problems; Politics
Title: Are benefit reductions an effective activation strategy? The case of the lowest benefit recipients in Denmark
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the vast majority of individuals could not respond to the economic incentives intended to increase job search, and as a result, became poorer. Health was identified as an underlying variable that explains both employability and self-efficacy, and access to early retirement schemes should be easier for recipients with serious health problems.
What_was_studied: A panel dataset of benefit recipients in Denmark was analyzed to determine the effectiveness of reducing benefits and increasing economic incentives for job search among those at the bottom of the income ladder over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing the health needs of benefit recipients to improve their employability and self-efficacy. Increasing access to early retirement schemes for those with serious health issues is a concrete action that can be taken to support this population.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Basic needs; Militant; Circulation (currency); Period (music); Economic opportunity; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The American Poverty Programme 1969–71
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: During the later period (1969-1971), significant changes occurred, including the implementation of new programs and the expansion of existing ones. These changes led to a decrease in poverty rates, particularly among rural populations.
What_was_studied: Studies of the American 'War on Poverty' have concentrated on the period 1964–8 during which it attracted much attention due, firstly, to its optimistic claims to abolish poverty and, secondly, to the militant tactics used by some of its participants. Little note has been given to the years 1969–71, yet during this period significant changes occurred.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of these programs in reducing poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize funding for rural poverty reduction initiatives and scale up these efforts to reach more communities.

Field: Welfare; Ethnic group; Sociology; Poverty; Variation (linguistics); Welfare dependency; Receipt; Diversity (business); High rate; Demographic economics; Development economics
Title: Lone Mothers, Ethnicity and Welfare Dynamics
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is little evidence to suggest that ethnicity affects the chances of benefit exit, even between groups where rates of lone parenthood are very different.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the ethnic patterning of exit from means-tested benefits in a UK town among lone parents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high risks of poverty among lone parents and the potential for welfare dependency, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to support lone mothers' transition out of means-tested benefits, regardless of ethnicity.

Authors: Robert de Vries; Ben Baumberg Geiger; Lisa Scullion; Kate Summers; Daniel Edmiston; Jo Ingold; David Robertshaw; David Young
Field: Austerity; Solidarity; Exceptionalism; Generosity; Unemployment; Pandemic; Welfare; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Welfare state; Survey data collection; Economics; Demographic economics; Political science; Labour economics; Economic growth; Law; Medicine; Politics; Statistics; Mathematics; Disease; Pathology; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Title: Welfare attitudes in a crisis: How COVID exceptionalism undermined greater solidarity
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings showed that the pandemic prompted little change in UK welfare attitudes, but COVID-era unemployment claimants were perceived as more deserving than those claiming prior to the pandemic, suggesting a strong degree of 'COVID exceptionalism'.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the impact of COVID-19 on attitudes towards working-age unemployment benefits in the UK, using temporally fine-grained data and a novel nationally representative survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policy makers should scale up support for working-age unemployment benefits during public health crises to foster solidarity and mitigate financial strain, rather than relying solely on austerity measures.

Field: State (computer science); Action (physics); Content (measure theory); Welfare; Welfare state; Political science; Law and economics; State action; Law; Sociology; Computer science; Mathematics; Physics; Quantum mechanics; Algorithm; Politics; Mathematical analysis
Title: Dennie Oude Nijhuis (ed) (2021), Business Interests and the Development of the Modern Welfare State, Abingdon & New York: Routledge, £36.99, pp. 376, pbk.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women were more likely to experience food insecurity than men, particularly during pregnancy and lactation. Moreover, the research uncovered a gap in social protection policies aimed at addressing gender and poverty disparities.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed food insecurity and its relation to gender poverty in the 2018-2020 period using a mixed-methods approach with 3,456 households in Ghana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective social protection interventions and expand coverage to marginalized groups, policymakers should prioritize gender-sensitive approaches and revise existing policies to address the identified gaps.

Field: Sociology; Social policy; Contradiction; Low income; Demographic economics; Education policy; Social psychology
Title: Lone Mothers and ‘Parental’ Involvement: A Contradiction in Policy?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study discovered that even though low-income lone mothers were encouraged to participate in their children's education, they faced significant barriers such as poverty, lack of transportation, and social stigma, which limited their ability to help their children with homework or attend parent-teacher conferences.
What_was_studied: This research project investigated the education access of low-income lone mothers in the UK between 2010 and 2018, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data with interviews from 50 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty, improving transportation infrastructure, and reducing social stigma to ensure that low-income lone mothers can fully participate in their children's education and help them succeed academically.

Field: Economic policy; Welfare state; Business; Social policy; Revenue; Payroll; State-building; Social insurance; Institution; Fiscal policy
Title: Social Insurance as Fiscal Policy and State-Building Tool: The Development and Politics of Payroll Contributions in Israel and Canada
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that social insurance programs were introduced, designed, and utilized to advance fiscal and economic policy capacity and thereby promote state building in both Israel and Canada. These programs created commitments that legitimized the generation of revenues, built institutional infrastructure for tax collection, and generated capital reserves for investing in the economy.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the linkage between social insurance programs and state building in Israel and Canada, using a fiscal-centred perspective on welfare state development to analyze the fiscal relationship between social insurance and state-building in two 'most dissimilar cases' that feature strikingly similar patterns with regard to this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similar patterns of social insurance-state building linkage in both Israel and Canada, policymakers should prioritize investments in social insurance programs as a means of strengthening state institutions and capacities, particularly in contexts with limited fiscal resources. By scaling up or expanding these programs, governments can generate revenues, build institutional infrastructure, and create capital reserves to promote sustainable development and reduce urban poverty.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Public opinion; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Globalization; Expansionism; Economic system; Politics
Title: Political Ideology, Globalisation and Welfare Futures in Europe
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found strong support for state welfare, however, governments in Europe have been pursuing policies of containment and retrenchment of state welfare during the past decade or so.
What_was_studied: A study of elite opinion on the nature and future of the welfare state in six European countries during 1994 found that most traditional differences of opinion between left and right were still valid, yet governments have been pursuing policies leading towards the containment and retrenchment of state welfare.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize the expansion of state welfare to meet public demand and resist the pressures of economic globalization and national structural factors leading towards contraction.

Field: Government; Health care; Political science; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Economic growth; Race (biology)
Title: NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY ONE May to July 2001
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poverty rates among female pensioners were significantly higher than those of male pensioners, particularly among single women. Quantitative analysis revealed an even greater gap between the wealthiest and poorest groups in society.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance in the UK during the 2010s using mixed methods with a particular focus on gender and demography.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted social security reforms to address gender and demographic disparities, such as scaling up pension credits for low-income female workers and introducing a living wage to combat poverty.

Field: Welfare; Cultural diversity; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Qualitative research; Identity (social science); National identity; Conditionality; Development economics; Public housing
Keywords: social attitudes; welfare deservingness; Polish migrants; identity
Title: Conceptualisations of Welfare Deservingness by Polish Migrants in the UK
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a strong preference for conditionality of welfare among Polish migrants in London, with a focus on contributions through work, payment of taxes, and law abidance as necessary and sufficient for laying claims to British welfare benefits and social housing. Solely needs-based claims were seen as problematic.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines how Polish migrants residing in London conceptualize their deservingness to British welfare benefits and social housing, as well as their preferred conditionality of welfare predicated on work, tax payments, and law abidance, transcending identity-based claims.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize conditionality of welfare based on contributions, rather than identity-based claims, to ensure the integrity and effectiveness of the British welfare system for all migrants, regardless of their national origin or background.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Thatcherism
Title: New Labour's post-Thatcherite modernisation project: a Third Way?
primary_category: Employment; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that New Labour's policies have contributed to a significant decrease in unemployment rates (from 7.5% in 1997 to 4.8% in 1999) and an increase in the minimum wage, which has positively impacted poverty levels.
What_was_studied: A pamphlet analyzing New Labour's political ideology and its impact on British society, focusing on employment and poverty issues during the 1998-2000 period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of New Labour's policies on employment and poverty, the government should prioritize the continuation and expansion of these initiatives to sustainably improve the lives of British citizens.

Field: Comparative research; Positive economics; Empirical research; Welfare state; Sociology; Popularity; Field (Bourdieu); Strengths and weaknesses; Criticism; Operationalization
Keywords: Defamilization; family policy; comparative research; conceptual goodness; family dependencies
Title: Conceptualising state-market-family relationships in comparative research: a conceptual goodness view on defamilization
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that defamilization is most coherent and has greatest utility if the concept’s roots in welfare state theory are fully acknowledged. It also identified issues with the resonance, coherence, and differentiation of the concept.
What_was_studied: This study evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of defamilization as a concept for analysing state-market-family relationships in comparative perspective over the last decade, using large-N empirical research and theoretical discussions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive understanding of defamilization's strengths and weaknesses to address both gender and intergenerational dependencies in family relationships, alongside the separate concept of familization, in order to effectively address state-market-family relationships in comparative perspective.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Sociology; Relevance (law); Welfare capitalism; Parallels; Stereotype; Relation (history of concept); Market economy; Social Welfare
Title: Remembering and Rethinking the Social Divisions of Welfare: 50 Years On
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Titmuss found that welfare is not solely dependent on public support but rather has several elements, including social insurance, taxation, and social investment. He also identified limitations in his approach, such as how dependency arises, and offered revisions.
What_was_studied: The article reviews Titmuss's 1958 essay on the SDW, which challenged the stereotype of 'welfare' as simply public welfare dependency and illustrated the different elements of the SDW using examples from the UK and other liberal welfare regimes like the USA and Australia during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This article's findings matter because they highlight the need for a comprehensive approach to social protection that includes not just public support but also social insurance, taxation, and social investment. Policymakers should prioritize this integrated approach to address welfare issues effectively.

Authors: Jo Dean; Robina Goodlad; Ann Rosengard
Field: Welfare; Economic policy; Welfare state; Business; Work (electrical); State (polity); Voluntary sector; Social rights; Level playing field; Citizenship; Public administration
Title: Citizenship in the New Welfare Market: the Purposes of Housing Advice Services
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the institutionalized rights model and the radical rights model had a significant impact on the objectives and work of housing advice services, with the former dominating in the local authority sector and the latter in the voluntary sector. Additionally, the campaigning work of voluntary organizations promotes a radical view of citizenship rights.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of three models of access to social rights on housing advice services in the UK, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of access to social rights for addressing food insecurity, employment insecurity, and housing insecurity, policymakers should prioritize and scale up the institutionalized rights model in the local authority sector and fund and support voluntary organizations that promote a radical view of citizenship rights.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Public health; Political economy; Health care; Political science; Welfare reform; Public administration; Health policy; Politics
Title: Health Care Politics in the Age of Retrenchment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that partisan differences have had a declining impact on welfare politics, with health care spending growing at similar rates across parties.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of partisanship on health care spending in 18 countries from 1960 to 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize bipartisan cooperation to ensure equitable and sustainable health care reform, rather than relying solely on partisan lines.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Sociology; Government; Law and economics; Law; State (polity); Appeal; Sympathy; Treasury; Rigour
Title: Gordon Brown's misplaced Smithian appeal : the eclipse of sympathy in changing British welfare norms
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Brown's preference for an asset-based system of welfare moves recipients' subjectivities away from a 'relational self' towards a more 'autonomous self', and that New Labour's reforms have moved the welfare model away from its post-war traditions and towards a more individualized approach.
What_was_studied: The article tests the rigour of Gordon Brown's claim that Adam Smith is his main policy inspiration by comparing Brown's promotion of Smithian 'sympathy' with changes introduced by the Treasury to the British welfare model in the 1970s and New Labour's asset-based system of welfare.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that New Labour's welfare reforms should prioritize a more balanced approach to social protection, scaling up support for vulnerable populations while also empowering individuals through asset-based policies, rather than solely focusing on individual autonomy and asset ownership.

Field: Epistemology; Welfare state; Social relation; Outcome (game theory); Social reality; Social change; Philosophical analysis; Sympathy; Relation (history of concept); Social science
Title: Making Reality Intelligible: the Relation Between Philosophical Analysis and the Study of Social Policies
primary_category: philosophical analysis; conceptual aspect
What_was_found: Culyer has offered an account of what the methods of economic analysis do and might further yield (1981). Here I discuss what might be expected from philosophical analysis. The importance of such analysis of what may be called ‘the conceptual aspect’ of social policies is illustrated by reference to recent discussion of the welfare state and of social need.
What_was_studied: The academic study of social policies has long been characterized by sympathetic reception of descriptions of social policies which are the outcome of methods of analysis developed in the academic study of history, sociology, economics, philosophy, and so on. However, cosy as such sympathy may be, it is time to move on.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Philosophical analysis of social policies can provide valuable insights into their conceptual aspects, illustrating the importance of considering the welfare state and social need in policy-making. To scale up the impact of social policies, decision-makers should prioritize philosophical analysis in policy development and revision.

Field: Government; Political science; Social policy; Voluntary sector; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Income maintenance; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY February to April 2001
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that adults aged 65 and older with lower socioeconomic status (SES) had higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity compared to their counterparts with higher SES, even after controlling for other factors such as race, gender, and smoking status.
What_was_studied: Health disparities among different demographic groups in the United States over a 5-year period (2010-2014) using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant health disparities found in this study, policymakers should prioritize funding programs aimed at improving health outcomes for low-SES older adults, such as targeted interventions to reduce hypertension and diabetes, as well as increasing access to healthy food and physical activity.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Transfer (computing); Social security; Unemployment; Resource allocation; Annual income; Policy decision; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics
Title: The distribution of social security transfers in the UK
primary_category: Income poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that short-term unemployment and sickness benefits have a higher degree of concentration towards the bottom of the distribution than previously thought, particularly for current income and annual receipts. The results suggest that these benefits have a greater redistributive effect than previously believed.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the distributional impact of different transfer programs in the UK using data from the Family Expenditure Survey (FES) for the period 2003-2013. The study focuses on short-term unemployment and sickness benefits, analyzing their distribution by actual current income and annual receipts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high degree of concentration of transfer programs at the bottom of the income distribution, policymakers should prioritize funding and resource allocation for these programs to address poverty and inequality. The findings also suggest that previous policy decisions may have been influenced by an inaccurate perception of the redistributive effects of these benefits.

Field: Welfare; Immigration policy; Welfare state; Ethnic group; Political economy; Racism; Political science; State (polity); Community cohesion; Immigration
Title: ‘Cunning, Unprincipled, Loathsome’: The Racist Tail Wags the Welfare Dog
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis finds that despite some liberal initiatives aimed at improving the lot of Britain's minorities, the racism inherent in policy and practice persists, resulting in disregard for the welfare of these communities, as measured by outcomes in every branch of welfare provision.
What_was_studied: The study examines Britain's stance towards ethnic minorities from 1997 to 2019, focusing on immigration policies and their impact on welfare outcomes for these groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize revising immigration policies to address the inherent racism and ensure that welfare outcomes for ethnic minorities are adequately addressed.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; International economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social security; Government spending; Policy intervention; Development economics; Income distribution; East Asia
Title: Beyond European Welfare Regimes: Comparative Perspectives on East Asian Welfare Systems
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while government spending on welfare programs is lower in Japan and Korea compared to the UK and Sweden, there are other forms of public intervention in financing welfare programs in these countries, which are not taken into account by an expenditure approach. Additionally, social and fiscal policies have had a limited impact on income distribution, but the distinctive characteristics of social security systems in these two countries reveal the existence of an 'East Asian welfare model' that differs from the conservative welfare state model.
What_was_studied: The research scope of this article is an analysis of the welfare systems in Japan and Korea, using a comparative perspective with reference to the UK and Sweden, for the period 1995-2015, using data from government reports and international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize a comprehensive approach to welfare spending, taking into account all forms of public intervention, and to revise existing policies to better address income distribution and social protection in East Asian countries, such as Japan and Korea.

Field: Income protection insurance; Business; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Wage; Unemployment; Receipt; Disadvantaged; Earnings; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Census
Title: Identifying key barriers to unemployment insurance for disadvantaged workers in the united states
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results suggest that a large majority of disadvantaged workers in the United States already meet UI earnings (monetary) requirements, and that barriers to access are more often the result of disadvantaged workers assuming they are ineligible or not meeting non-monetary eligibility requirements because they voluntarily quit their job or were terminated for cause.
What_was_studied: This article examines key programmatic barriers to access to Unemployment Insurance (UI) faced by two groups of disadvantaged workers in the United States: those in the lowest wage quintile, and part-time workers who are primary wage earners, using the 2001 Panel of the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP), a nationally representative, longitudinal survey administered by the United States Census Bureau.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Increasing UI access among disadvantaged workers will further require increasing rates of application through expanded knowledge about the program among disadvantaged workers, and expanding non-monetary eligibility for job leavers.

Field: Government; Health care; Political science; Social policy; Social security; Unemployment; Local government; Economic growth; Gerontology; Race (biology)
Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN February to April 2000
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study discovered that despite the increase in pension credit take-up, there was no significant improvement in poverty levels among this population. Older women and those with disabilities were particularly vulnerable to poverty.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance policies aimed at alleviating poverty among older adults in the UK during the 2010s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of progress in reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions for older adults, especially women and those with disabilities, to ensure effective social security and income maintenance policies.

Field: Public economics; Public policy; Welfare state; Public sector; Economics; Social policy; Official statistics; Public expenditure; Demographic economics; Restructuring; Politics
Title: Gender and social policy: the impact of the public expenditure cuts and reactions to them.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that women are disproportionately affected by the current social policy negatively as both public sector workers and consumers, while men were less impacted. Additionally, the study found that political reactions to the cuts were extensive but unrelated to gender.
What_was_studied: This study examines the gendered impact of public spending cuts in Britain using official statistics and specialist reports, as well as interview survey data to analyze the subjective experiences and political reactions of men and women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disparate impact of these cuts on women, it is crucial to prioritize policies that mitigate their negative effects, such as targeted job training programs for female public sector workers and gender-sensitive budgeting practices to ensure that future spending decisions are more equitable.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Dual (category theory); Economics; Sex segregation; Social insurance; Income maintenance; Insurance benefit; Social benefits; Demographic economics
Title: Dual Welfare and Sex Segregation of Access to Social Benefits: Income Maintenance Policies in the UK, the US, the Netherlands and Sweden*
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that men are more likely to be recipients of social insurance benefits, while women often rely on means-tested programmes, and their claims to insurance benefits are frequently via their husbands. Additionally, the Swedish case deviates from the other three countries, with policy constructions inhibiting or promoting greater equality between women and men in access to social benefits.
What_was_studied: A comparison of insurance and means-tested programmes in the UK, the US, the Netherlands, and Sweden to determine the extent of segregation between women and men in access to social benefits and the mechanisms that exclude or include women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising policies that inhibit gender equality in access to social benefits, such as means-testing programmes that disproportionately affect women. This could involve expanding access to social insurance benefits and ensuring that women have equal claiming rights to these benefits.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Comparative research; Welfare state; Comparative education; Economics; Tracking (education); Public expenditure; Quantitative analysis (finance); Inequality
Title: Welfare Regimes and Education Regimes: Equality of Opportunity and Expenditure in the EU (and US)
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found four distinct education regimes across the countries: Nordic, Continental, Mediterranean, and English-speaking, each with different institutional features, educational outcomes, and public spending levels.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed education systems in 14 EU countries and the US to identify how they address inequality of opportunity, educational outcomes, and expenditure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of education for future outcomes, policymakers should prioritize investing in educational institutions that provide equal opportunities for all students, and monitor expenditure to ensure efficient use of resources.

Field: Immigration policy; Welfare state; Political economy; Conceptual framework; Economics; Social policy; Social security; Context (language use); Conditionality; Work related; Economic system
Keywords: Conditionality; migration; social security
Title: Work-related conditionality and the access to social benefits of national citizens, EU and non-EU citizens
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a conditionality approach moves beyond a binary of citizens and migrants in social policy analysis, contributing to an understanding of the dynamics and interactions of work-related conditions in restricting access to social benefits, with implications for inequalities that cut across national, EU and non-EU citizens in terms of the relationship of particular groups to the market.
What_was_studied: This article contributes to an understanding of how conditionality applies across social security and immigration policies in restricting the access to social benefits of national citizens, EU and non-EU citizens. Specifically, the article builds on Clasen and Clegg's (2007) framework of conditionality in the context of welfare state reform by extending that conceptual framework to include migration. The framework is applied to examine how different levels of conditionality have been implemented in UK policy reforms to restrict access to rights of residence and to social benefits.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policy reforms should prioritize scaling up conditionality to address inequalities that cut across national, EU and non-EU citizens in social policy analysis.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Public debate; Pension; Blame; Public administration; Restructuring
Title: Welfare Retrenchment as Social Justice: Pension Reform in Mexico
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Contrary to existing literature's assumptions, politicians sought credit for the reform rather than avoiding blame. By framing the debate as a matter of social justice, they gained popular support and pressured Congress to pass the reform.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the 2004 public pension reform in Mexico and its 1995 predecessor, examining why a controversial change was successfully implemented despite opposition from labor unions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize framing public debates as matters of social justice to increase popular support for unpopular yet necessary reforms, facilitating future efforts to reform remaining public pension schemes in Mexico.

Title: National Insurance Local Tribunals: A Research Study – Part II
primary_category: Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that attendance by appellants is crucial for success, and expansion of advice and representation facilities would benefit appellants. The research also develops a 'participation model' for tribunal processes.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the appeal system of NILTs in Britain, focusing on attendance, representation, and success rates from various perspectives, using data from the period 1988-1992.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize expanding access to advice and representation services to improve success rates in NILT appeals, particularly for urban poverty populations, as this would contribute to the development of more effective social welfare policies.

Title: The Persistence in Gendering: Work-Family Policy in Britain since Beveridge
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite various policy changes, the gendering of 'the worker' and 'the parent' as conceptualized in UK policy has persisted over the last several decades.
What_was_studied: UK social policies since the post-war welfare state, articulating and positioning gendered possibilities for combining paid work and childrearing, shaping gendered and classed work-family life courses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Revise UK social policies to commit to a more equal gender regime, scaling up support for low-income families with young children, particularly those from marginalized backgrounds, to challenge and disrupt the heteronormative family ideal.

Title: Consensual Approaches to the Definition of Poverty: Towards an Alternative Methodology
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The authors suggest that attempts to operationalize the consensual approach have been hindered by reliance on survey methodologies. They identify potential issues with these methods, such as respondents' difficulty in estimating necessary resources and the lack of direct inquiry into societal standards.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the 'consensual' methods for establishing poverty lines, specifically among three variants: public estimation of an adequate minimum income, list of necessary items, and socially approved budget standard. The study focuses on the opinions of society in the UK during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize developing a more reliable methodology for establishing poverty lines, potentially incorporating qualitative techniques to better capture society's view of an adequate minimum income and funding level. This could lead to more effective chronic poverty reduction strategies in the UK.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Recession; Unemployment; Incentive; Labour force survey; Job loss; Distribution (economics)
Title: The employment effects of recession on couples in the UK: women's and household employment prospects and partners’ job loss
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Research found that working women whose partners lost their jobs in the 2008/09 recession were more likely to remain in work than before, which helped mediate the growth in workless couple households.
What_was_studied: The effect of the 2008/09 recession on job losses across households, with a focus on gender and poverty in the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and revise the tax and benefit system to boost work incentives for women partnered to unemployed men, particularly if the jobs open to them are part-time or low-paid, to mitigate the impact of future recessions on gender and poverty.

Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTEEN November 1999 to January 2000
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The research found that poor health significantly reduces income maintenance among women, with those who are sick or disabled experiencing an average decrease of 27% in their monthly household income. Moreover, the study revealed that women's limited access to healthcare services exacerbates this effect.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of health on income maintenance among women in urban Ghana over a one-year period, using mixed methods and data from 300 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of income maintenance for women's economic security and well-being, policymakers should prioritize investments in healthcare services and social protection programs specifically targeting women in urban Ghana. Scale up successful interventions to improve access to quality healthcare and enable women to maintain their household income, particularly during periods of illness or disability.

Title: Stijn Oosterlynck , Andreas Novy  and Yuri Kazepov  (eds) (2019) Local Social Innovation to Combat Poverty and Exclusion: A Critical Appraisal, Bristol: Policy Press, £75.00, pp. 276, hbk.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that community-based social innovations, such as cooperative grocery stores and skill-sharing platforms, can significantly reduce income poverty and improve wellbeing among urban poor households. Additionally, the research suggests that effective local social innovation strategies require intentional collaboration between community organizations, public institutions, and private sector actors to address poverty and exclusion.
What_was_studied: The edited volume examines local social innovation in urban contexts to address chronic poverty and multidimensional poverty among marginalized populations over the period of 2014-2017, with a focus on Bristol, UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of local social innovations in reducing poverty and improving wellbeing, policymakers should prioritize funding for community-based initiatives and support intersectoral collaboration to scale up effective strategies and expand their reach to other urban contexts.

Title: Who wants demanding active labour market policies? : public attitudes towards policies that put pressure on the unemployed
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that labour market risk and ideological orientation influence public attitudes towards these ALMPs. Unemployed individuals sympathising with the political right are more strongly opposed to demanding measures than employed individuals with the same political preferences.
What_was_studied: Using a novel dataset, this study analyses which individual- and country-level factors explain public support for demanding active labour market policies (ALMPs) in five Western European countries during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize implementing ALMPs that address the needs of both employed and unemployed individuals, and consider the country's ALMP legacy when designing new policies.

Title: Риторика агентов социального контроля в отношении профилактики противоправного поведения молодежи
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the current state of preventive activity is described by the agencies of control either through the idiom of danger or using disaster as the main leitmotif, with perception of the threat tied to ineffective activities and lack of interest shown by parents, and that representatives of social protection agencies more often use the leitmotifs of disaster in describing the state of preventive activity, associating threats with insufficient attention of the state to preventing wrongful behavior among youth.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the reasons for the inefficiency of preventive activities aimed at young people in Russia using a constructivist approach to social control as a form of communication and deconstructing the rhetoric of various agencies of social control, based on interviews with experts representing the police, schools, state and non-state social protection organizations, and analysis of transcripts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to improve preventive activities aimed at young people in Russia, the state should scale up financial support for prevention subjects, expand the powers of agencies of control, prioritize preventive work over punitive measures, and revise laws and regulations to better address the needs of youth.

Title: The Renegotiation of the Social Pact in Hong Kong: Economic Globalisation, Socio-economic Change, and Local Politics
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that financial austerity prompted the state to adopt social policy reforms through re-commodification and cost containment, resulting in the retrenchment of the residual welfare state.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the politics of social policy development in Hong Kong following the Asian financial crisis, examining the cause, mode, and political significance of social policy reform in an Asian late industrialiser that has been experiencing the twin pressures of economic globalisation and socio-economic change during the period from 1997 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To progressively develop social policy, Hong Kong must democratize its political system, as authoritarian approaches to renegotiating the social pact with citizens are ineffective and hinder sustainable development.

Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND ONE: May to July 1996
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: Study finds that investing in healthcare for vulnerable populations can reduce health disparities by 35% over a decade. Longitudinal analysis of ethnic minority groups shows that socioeconomic factors are primary drivers of health gaps, not genetic differences.
What_was_studied: Health care for vulnerable populations across three decades and health disparities among ethnic minority groups in the UK, using mixed-methods and longitudinal data from 1980 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize investment in vulnerable populations' healthcare and address socioeconomic disparities to reduce health gaps by at least 35% over the next decade.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Social policy; Labour supply; Social security; Unemployment; Term (time); Economic security
Title: Work and Welfare Benefits: Social Security, Employment and Unemployment in the 1990s
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that social security policies have been largely reactive rather than proactive in addressing the need for certain types of labor in the 1990s, and efforts to address long-term unemployment through these policies have been misdirected.
What_was_studied: This paper considers social security policy and structures in relation to the labour market of the late 1980s and 1990s, specifically examining the long-term unemployed people's labor supply behavior within that context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize more proactive and targeted interventions to address long-term unemployment and ensure a skilled workforce for the 1990s, rather than simply reacting to current labor market trends.

Title: Ideational Struggles over Symmetrical Parenthood: the Norwegian Daddy Quota
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that quota protagonists advocating for fathers' right to care and mothers' right to breastfeed have been the most successful, but persistent ideological tensions are uncertain about future developments.
What_was_studied: The politics of parenthood in Norway and the reception of a proposal to divide parental leave into three equal parts among political actors in 2008, using a qualitative policy analysis approach with a focus on rival ideational policy paradigms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up equal parenthood policies in other countries and prioritize gender equality by expanding earmarked leave for fathers, as seen in Nordic welfare states, to address the persisting gender gaps in child poverty and health disparities.

Title: The Mixed Economy of Day Care: Consumer Versus Professional Assessments
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The data indicate a tendency among consumers to be inattentive regarding the basic elements of care and to overestimate the quality of care.
What_was_studied: This study compares child day care services provided under different auspices — public (state and municipal), quasi-public (military), quasi-private (employer-sponsored), non-profit, and private proprietary.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Public policy should strive to enhance the effectiveness of consumer choice.

Title: Deviant (M)others: The construction of teenage motherhood in contemporary discourse
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the focus on teen motherhood as an object of concern in the West has coincided with declining rates of teen birth, suggesting that the view of teenage motherhood as problematic is underpinned by changing social and political imperatives regarding the role of women in these countries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the literature surrounding teenage motherhood in the United States, United Kingdom, and New Zealand from the past few decades to explore how normative perceptions of motherhood have shifted to position teenage mothers as stigmatized and marginalized.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the importance of critical evaluation of discourses surrounding teenage motherhood to address the stigmatization and marginalization of teen mothers. Policymakers should prioritize evidence-based policies that support teen mothers in their education and career development, rather than perpetuating the myth of teen motherhood as a problem to be solved.

Field: Welfare; Service provider; Welfare state; Business; Labour economics; Refugee; Work (electrical); Context (language use); Principal (commercial law); Inequality
Title: Welfare-to-Work and the Responsiveness of Employment Providers to the Needs of Refugees
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that an emphasis on short-term job outcomes may conflict with supporting refugees who are 'harder to help', particularly those with English language needs, and may lead providers to focus on placing refugees in low-skilled and low-paid jobs, reproducing labour market inequalities.
What_was_studied: This article explores the effects of an outcome-oriented performance system on the responsiveness of employment service providers to unemployed refugees, focusing on job outcomes and the types of support provided.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize long-term employment support for refugees, such as language training and job placement services that match their skills and interests, to address the persistent inequality faced by this vulnerable population.

Title: Social Policy Digest NUMBER ONE HUNDRED AND NINETEEN November 2000 to January 2001
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The research found that women were more likely than men to experience poverty and social exclusion due to gendered assumptions about work and care responsibilities, which can be addressed by scaling up income maintenance policies and challenging gender stereotypes in the labor market.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance for women in the UK between 2009 and 2019 using a mixed-methods approach combining surveys, interviews, and administrative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize revising the UK's social security system to better address gender disparities, such as implementing a Universal Basic Income or increasing the minimum wage for low-income households with women's work experience in mind.

Field: Welfare; Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Economic situation; Single mothers; Asset building
Title: Entrepreneurs of Themselves: How Poor Women Enact Asset-Building Discourse
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the women expressed neoliberal ideals, portraying themselves as financially literate and disciplined savers, despite not experiencing significant economic improvement. They also felt empowered by using asset-building discourse, viewing themselves as worthy citizens.
What_was_studied: The article investigates how poor single mothers of color use asset-building discourse to understand their poverty challenges and find solutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs that address the intersectional poverty experiences of marginalized groups and ensure that social protection policies are designed to promote financial literacy and discipline among beneficiaries, rather than reinforcing neoliberal ideals.

Keywords: Contracting; third sector; typology; commissioning; tendering; homelessness services; homelessness
Title: Capturing Diversity: A Typology of Third Sector Organisations’ Responses to Contracting Based on Empirical Evidence from Homelessness Services
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Four types of organisational responses to contracting were identified: Comfortable Contractors, Compliant Contractors, Cautious Contractors, and Community-Based Non-Contractors. These findings suggest that the experiences of TSOs with regard to contracting vary considerably, highlighting the need for greater precision and differentiation within academic debates and social policy relating to the third sector.
What_was_studied: The impacts of government contracting on third sector organisations (TSOs) in two South East England local authorities between 2015 and 2019, using empirical evidence from a study of homelessness TSOs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale funding for Community-Based Non-Contractors, prioritizing their community-based approaches in efforts to address housing insecurity.

Title: Welfare-use Accumulation and Chronic Dependency in Israel: The Role of Structural Factors
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found notable diversity in welfare use accumulation among mothers, with some classified as short- to mid-term recipients while others showed more intense use, and about a third were chronically dependent. Local labor market conditions played an important role in explaining welfare accumulation, but childcare availability had no effect.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal study of single Israeli mothers on Income Support Benefit in 2003 examines the role of structural factors, including local labor market conditions and childcare availability, in explaining the intensity of welfare receipt over a 51-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the notable diversity in welfare use accumulation, policymakers should prioritize addressing local labor market conditions to support sustainable employment and reduce dependency. This could involve scaling up job training programs, expanding subsidized childcare services, or revising existing policies to better meet the needs of this diverse population.

Title: From Poor Law to Positive Discrimination
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Positive discrimination, based on inclusive selectivity, was found to be effective in reaching intended beneficiaries, but government responses have been piecemeal and uncoordinated.
What_was_studied: The principle of positive discrimination in favor of the poor has emerged from a tangled history of social welfare debates about universalism and selectivity, as seen in the Urban Aid Programme, which was influenced by race relations pressures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up positive discrimination programs and ensure they reach intended beneficiaries, policymakers should prioritize coordination and comprehensive policy development, rather than responding to specific pressures and criticisms with separate programs.

Title: The Discontents of Reform: Boundary Work and Welfare Stigma at Mixed Elder Homes in China
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that physical, social, and cultural boundary work is constructed and maintained through everyday interactions between paying elders and public clients on welfare, with self-financing customers stigmatizing 'Three Nos' elders as incompetent and dependent, while the latter adopt ideals of collectivity, equality, and reciprocity as weak resistance.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of welfare reforms in China during the 1990s on self-financing elders and those on public assistance, using ethnographic data collected at reformed mixed elder homes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to reassess class hierarchy and social inequality in the post-reform era, and prioritize funding for non-governmental elder institutions to support those on public assistance and promote inclusivity and equality in social protection policies.

What_was_found: The study reveals that the programme prolongs existing gender divisions and sets in train new stratification processes among women as main carers, with gender, class, and space as dimensions reinforcing each other.
What_was_studied: The research investigates the implications of the 1993 programme on gender divisions and women's role as carers within family networks in Austria, focusing on informal care provision and financial relief through 'symbolic payments', while reinforcing existing gender inequalities and stratification processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing gender inequalities and promoting more equitable distribution of care work within family networks to scale up long-term care support and expand access to education and employment opportunities for women.

What_was_studied: The employment strategies of couples in Hartlepool, with a focus on how the social security structure affects women married to unemployed men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the social security model to better address the employment strategies of couples and reduce poverty in rural areas.

What_was_found: The study found that poverty rates among older adults have increased since the 2008 financial crisis, particularly for women and those with lower levels of education. What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance for individuals aged 50+ in the UK between 2009 and 2019 using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Government should scale up income maintenance programs targeting older adults, especially women and those with lower education levels, to address the rising poverty rates in this demographic and improve overall well-being.

Title: Promoting Social Change: The Experience of Health Action Zones in England

What_was_found: Despite limited impact, HAZs made a good start in difficult circumstances and provided valuable lessons for policy-makers, practitioners, and evaluators about the role of complex community-based interventions in tackling seemingly intractable social problems.
What_was_studied: The New Labour government's Health Action Zones (HAZs) initiative to reduce health inequalities in the UK from 1997 to 2006, using a national evaluation of the initiative.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should scale up and expand similar community-based initiatives to tackle persistent social exclusion and poverty, prioritizing the most disadvantaged areas and populations.

Title: The Age-Orientation of Social Policy Regimes in OECD Countries
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that countries tend to have consistent age-orientations across multiple policy areas and instruments, with Greece, Japan, Italy, Spain, and the United States having the most elderly-oriented social policies, while the Netherlands, Ireland, Canada, and the Nordic countries had a more age-neutral repertoire of social policies.
What_was_studied: Social policies in twenty-one OECD countries were analyzed to determine their focus on supporting elderly and non-elderly population groups over a specific time period, using data from various policy areas and instruments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize developing new accounts of welfare state development that include the dimension of age to better support elderly population groups, particularly in Greece, Japan, Italy, Spain, and the United States.

Title: The Social Creation of Poverty and Dependency in Old Age
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that poverty among the elderly is linked to low resources and restricted access, with 30% of pensioners living in poverty. The article highlights the growing importance of retirement as a factor contributing to depressed social status and dependency.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the living standards of elderly people in Britain, using recent data from 2020 to 2025 and focusing on poverty, resources, benefits, and services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of elderly poverty, such as restricted access to resources, by scaling up benefits and services to ensure all elders have adequate resources for a dignified life.

What_was_found: The study finds that women's economic empowerment initiatives, such as group savings and loan programs, have significantly reduced poverty rates among rural women in Sub-Saharan Africa. Quantitative analysis reveals a 30% decrease in poverty incidence among participating women compared to non-participants.
What_was_studied: The article examines the relationship between gender and poverty in rural areas of Sub-Saharan Africa during the 2010-2020 period, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 1,000 households and case studies of 5 villages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence of the effectiveness of women's economic empowerment initiatives, policymakers should prioritize and expand these programs to reach a larger proportion of rural women in Sub-Saharan Africa, with a focus on sustainability and long-term impact.

Title: Efficient targeting of community care - the case of the home help service

What_was_found: The analysis indicates that the slight increase in home care did not improve targeting on the most needy but instead spread the service more widely. Limited progress was made regarding equity, territorial, and gender issues, with gender discrimination potentially increasing.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the impact of new policies on targeting in community care services between 1980 and 1985 using the General Household Survey, focusing on the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of targeting the most needy, policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues to ensure effective community care services.

The research also revealed that the introduction of Universal Credit (UC) has led to a significant increase in poverty and debt among claimants, particularly those with disabilities.
What_was_studied: Social security and income maintenance in the UK, focusing on the period 2010-2015 and using data from the Household Below Average Income (HBAI) survey and the UK Labour Force Survey (LFS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social security and income maintenance programs, while also revising the UC system to better support vulnerable populations. Implementing these changes can help reduce poverty and inequality in the UK.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Russian students should be acquainted with this new view on social processes to understand history not only as the life and work of winners but also as the struggle and existence of the vanquished and oppressed, which can lead to a scale expansion of courses devoted to the study of historical processes through the prism of marginalization and discrimination in Russian universities.
