Title: Mutual Obligation, Participation and Popularity: Social Security Reform in Australia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis indicates that there is support for mutual obligation for the young and long-term unemployed but not for others, such as the older unemployed, those caring for young children, and those with a disability.
What_was_studied: The research explores the impact of mutual obligation on unemployment in Australia during a 10-year period using a national survey of public opinion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, the government should prioritize reducing unemployment and providing support for those who are struggling to participate in the labor market, especially for long-term unemployed individuals and those caring for young children.

Field: Economic policy; Public policy; Government; Economics; Public finance; Social policy; Tax policy; Economic recovery; Unemployment; Fiscal policy
Title: What are the Distributional Consequences of the Socialist Government Policy in France
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that while the socialist government aimed to reduce income disparities and improve the well-being of the poor through active social and tax policies, actual developments led to a shift in focus towards fighting inflation and improving industrial investment and competitiveness, resulting in changes in poverty reduction strategies. Furthermore, the study highlights a widening wealth gap between 1982 and 1983.
What_was_studied: The study investigates French economic and social policies implemented over the past four years, focusing on income and wealth inequalities, poverty reduction strategies, and their impacts on various demographic groups, specifically during the period from May 1981 to June 1982 and between 1983 and present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing wealth inequalities and adjust poverty reduction strategies to better serve marginalized populations, such as women and the poor, who have been disproportionately affected by these changes. Furthermore, investing in social programs targeting these groups could help mitigate the negative impacts of economic policies on poverty and wealth disparities.

Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Government; TRIPS architecture; Social group; Tourism; Basic needs; Social support; Population; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Социальный туризм в России: потенциальные туристы и доступные возможности
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households with elderly people face the most difficulties in organizing vacations, and that support for socially vulnerable groups is often oriented towards the disabled but almost all groups receive some form of support. Additionally, the unavailability of tourist trips affects not only poor households but also well-off ones, highlighting the importance of developing social tourism initiatives.
What_was_studied: The article examines the issue of access to tourist services and its relation with inequality in Russia, using data from the Survey of Income and Participation of the Population in Social Programs and regulations to determine which groups are most excluded from social tourism initiatives and why.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize and scale up social tourism initiatives to address inequality in access to travel, particularly targeting households with elderly people and those living in urban areas. Regulations should be reviewed and revised to ensure support for all socially vulnerable groups, not just the disabled.

Field: Business; Poverty; Microdata (statistics); Marital status; Economic growth; Developing country
Keywords: JEL Classification: D12; D64; F35; L31 charitable donations; overseas development; NGOs
Title: Who gives charitable donations for overseas development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that individuals with higher incomes are more likely to donate to overseas causes, and that women are less likely to donate than men. Additionally, the study discovered a positive relationship between individuals' attitudes towards poverty in developing countries and their likelihood of donating to overseas causes.
What_was_studied: This study investigates charitable donations to overseas causes from individuals in the UK using survey microdata, focusing on socio-economic correlates and attitudes towards poverty in developing countries during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequality and gender disparities to increase charitable donations to overseas causes, as well as consider the importance of attitudes towards poverty in developing countries when designing development assistance programs.

Field: Ideology; Political science; State (polity); Sick leave; Administration (government); Social protection; Associate professor; Institution; Public administration; Schools of economic thought
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Экспертиза временной нетрудоспособности в СССР и постсоветской России: врачи на службе государства в управлении трудовыми ресурсами
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the institution of temporary disability examinations has undergone limited modifications since the fall of the USSR, with the main changes being in the language and format of the documents. The study also found that medical providers view the examination as a tool for rational distribution of labor resources rather than social protection.
What_was_studied: The Soviet model and modern organisation of temporary disability examinations in Russia, focusing on the period 1930-1980 and comparing the regulations and practices of the USSR and the Russian Federation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the institution of temporary disability examinations should be re-evaluated and potentially revised to better align with current attitudes towards work and employment in Russia. The study's conclusions can inform policy decisions related to employment and education access, such as scaling or expanding the examination system, revising regulations, or prioritizing funding for alternative social protection measures.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Latin Americans; Political science; Poverty; Human capital; Cash transfers; Social pension; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Doing a Bit more for the Poor? Social Assistance in Latin America
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that these programs had mixed results and claims about positive outcomes were sometimes exaggerated. The social pension program in Brazil was found to have a positive impact on poverty reduction, while the Oportunidades program in Mexico had a positive impact on human capital.
What_was_studied: The experiences of three social assistance programs in Latin America: Oportunidades in Mexico, Jefes y Jefas de Hogares in Argentina, and Brazil's social pension, were compared by the researchers, focusing on their administrative effectiveness and impacts on poverty, human capital, and household and gender dynamics between 2006 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed results and limited potential for substantially reorienting welfare systems and promoting equitable public policies, decision-makers should prioritize rigorous evaluations of social assistance programs and focus on scaling up successful initiatives while revamping ineffective ones.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Political economy; Sociology; Voluntary action; Work (electrical); Turnover; State (polity); Flexibility (personality); Social polarization; Intervention (law)
Title: Labours of Love: Voluntary Working in a Depressed Local Economy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that 57% of respondents reported engaging in some form of volunteer activity, with many citing a desire for structure and routine in their lives. The study also discovered that volunteering provided a sense of purpose and belonging among participants.
What_was_studied: This study examines how people deprived of jobs seek to re-create positive working lives for themselves through voluntary work in depressed local economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of voluntary work in these communities, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support and expand opportunities for informal work, as well as provide resources for training and education to enhance the skills and employability of those participating.

Authors: Hans Peeters; Annelies Debels; Gert Verschraegen; Jos Berghman
Field: Economics; Social work; Pension regulation; Social security; Legislation; Flexibility (personality); Unemployment; Flexicurity; Pension; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Flexicurity in Bismarckian countries? Old age protection for non-standard workers in Belgium
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that part-time employment leads to lower first-pillar pensions, while temporary unemployment and career interruptions do not affect pension benefits. Workers with contractual flexibility and job mobility are discriminated against in the second pillar, and non-standard workers do not compensate for lower pension protection through increased participation in the third pillar.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the Belgian pension system's responsiveness to increasing flexibility in the labor market, focusing on differences in old age protection for standard and non-standard workers between 2007 and 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest a need to reassess the system of 'assimilated' periods to ensure fair pension protection for all workers, and policymakers should prioritize revising existing regulations to address discrimination against non-standard workers in the second pillar.

Field: Mathematical proof; Advertising; Standard of living; Sociology; Mores; Middle class; Feed back; Normative; Extreme poverty; Criminology
Title: Criminalising Survival: Images and Reality of Street Children
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Street children in Southern societies face challenges in maintaining a minimum standard of living due to lack of support from parents and governments, resulting in higher rates of poverty, crime, and housing insecurity compared to their peers in Northern societies.
What_was_studied: The lives of street children in Southern societies during a six-month period, using mixed methods and data from interviews, surveys, and observational research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues that contribute to child streetism, such as poverty, lack of education, and limited job opportunities, by scaling up support programs and resources for these children to ensure their basic needs are met and provide a more secure future.

Field: Welfare; Standard of living; Econometrics; Reference group; Economics; Equivalence (measure theory); Goods and services; Poverty; Well-being; Welfare economics; Social engagement
Title: Family size equivalence scales and survey evaluations of income and well-being.
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that income-based equivalence scales are commonly used to set poverty lines for different families, and that tax and transfer systems include equivalency scales within their structure. The research also identified methodological limitations and assumptions that can affect the estimation of equivalence scales, such as reference group effects.
What_was_studied: This article examines different methods for determining relative need (economic resources) as it varies with different family composition, focusing on income equivalence scales for social policy purposes in the context of OECD countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of addressing income poverty in OECD countries, policymakers should prioritize the development of more accurate and comprehensive equivalence scales to ensure equal standard of living for all families, regardless of their composition. This may involve revising existing poverty lines, expanding the scope of tax and transfer systems, and investing in data collection and analysis to better capture the needs of diverse family types.

Field: Aesthetics; Unconscious mind; Imitation; Sociology; Narrative; Associate professor; Context (language use); Field (Bourdieu); Cultural studies; Politics
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Keywords: искусство аутсайдеров; методология; теория дискурса; стратегии; тактики
Title: Тактики «маргиналов»: к проблеме методологии аутсайдерского искусства (постсоветский кейс)
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: Her study identifies the most common tactics used by outsiders in their creative process, such as the tactics of assigning (poaching), capturing 'the place of the other', alerting or imitation strategies, manipulation, and usage of weakness. These findings show that 'poaching tactics' are developed in the assigning of the official meta-narrative, with visual manifestations through a 'capture narrative', borrowing content from literature, TV, and 'high art'.
What_was_studied: Anna Suvorova’s research examines the problem of finding a relevant methodology for outsider art studies, which cannot be described with standard approaches usual in this field, such as the concepts of the unconscious and that of formal and semiotic analysis. Instead, she considers the discursivity of outsider art and its significant relationship with external fields like art, popular culture, and politics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research matters because it highlights the importance of understanding outsider art tactics to develop effective policies for rural poverty. Policymakers should prioritize supporting local art initiatives that empower marginalized communities and provide them with tools to capture their narratives and challenge dominant discourses.

Field: Cultural diversity; Political economy; Political science; Representation (politics); Space (commercial competition); Content (Freudian dream analysis); Face (sociological concept); Public sphere; National Policy; Population
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Soviet in Form, National in Content: Central Asian Migrants in the Cultural Infrastructure of Moscow
primary_category: Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the self-presentations of people of Central Asian origin on various public platforms in Moscow largely involve performing the role of ambassadors of a homogenous 'national culture', which allows them to achieve guaranteed recognition from both the host site and their compatriots, and legitimizes their presence in the public sphere.
What_was_studied: This study examines the self-presentations of people of Central Asian origin on various public platforms in Moscow and how they legitimize their presence in the public sphere as agents of the 'dialogue of cultures'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of recognizing and addressing the symbolic marginalization faced by migrants in urban poverty reduction strategies, and prioritizing the creation of 'safe spaces' for them to express their cultural identities without facing daily troubles associated with labor migration.

Field: Welfare; Secular state; Sociology; Social policy; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social support; Religiosity; Generosity; Social psychology; Politics
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Религия и социальная справедливость: обзор исследований влияния религиозности на предпочтения относительно социальной политики
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that religion significantly influences individual redistribution preferences by creating the overall cultural context and setting standards for helping those in need, with differences in welfare attitudes between followers of different religious traditions and between religious and non-religious individuals.
What_was_studied: This literature review focuses on religion as a cultural predictor of welfare attitudes, examining differences in welfare attitudes between followers of different religious traditions and between religious and non-religious individuals in contemporary Europe, using existing studies to analyze how religion can shape individual attitudes towards social policy and influence redistribution preferences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing the role of religion in shaping welfare attitudes and redistribution preferences to better tailor social policy interventions and support programs for vulnerable populations, particularly in the context of employment, gender, and poverty reduction.

Field: Sociology; Media studies; Economic history
Title: Vincent­Jones, P. (2006) The New Public Contracting: Regulation, responsiveness, relationality. Oxford: Oxford University Press. pp. 406, £60.00, hbk
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the falsificationism of Popper was an 'ideal typification' of science and not representative of how science actually works in practice. Additionally, the study showed that bodies of 'good' science are resilient to attack and can withstand repeated errors before being replaced by a different research program.
What_was_studied: Sociology of science was studied to understand how scientists interact and make sense of the physical world, specifically focusing on the philosophy of Karl Popper and its limitations in explaining scientific practice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding matters because it highlights the importance of understanding the limitations of objective theories of science and recognizing the subjective and relative nature of scientific knowledge. This understanding can inform policy decisions related to intersectional poverty by acknowledging the complexity and nuance of social issues and the need for diverse perspectives and approaches.

Field: Psychology; Nursing; Dependency (project management); Gerontology
Title: Hotel and dependency costs of residents in old people's homes.
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the size of the home beyond which costs do not fall with scale provides for up to 50 places (equivalent to an average daily census of 46 residents), and that dependency costs are large enough to be important in comparisons of alternative forms of care, but smaller than hotel components.
What_was_studied: This study compared the costs of providing residential care for elderly clients with different levels of dependency, using data from a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is important to prioritize estimates of costs for clients with different levels of dependency when comparing alternative forms of care, and to consider the size of the home in terms of capacity and cost-effectiveness.

Authors: Татьяна Сергеевна Киенко; Руфина Михайловна Рудакова
Field: Subjective well-being; Feeling; Personal boundaries; Psychology; Ambivalence; Optimism; Happiness; Quality (business); Anxiety; Gerontology
Journal/Venue: The Journal of Social Policy Studies
Title: Субъективное благополучие пожилого жителя российского дома-интерната
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the residents experienced a range of emotions, including happiness, self-confidence, and a sense of control over their lives, but also anxiety about their future and a lack of life goals and prospects. They also faced specific challenges such as dependence on outside help, immobility, and a sense of static life.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the subjective well-being of 68 elderly residents in a large nursing home in Rostov region, Russia over a period of time, using structured and semistructured interviews to gather data on their experiences and perceptions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that creating conditions and developing technologies to maintain independence, freedom, and mobility, as well as providing an accessible environment and expanding social connections beyond the physical and social boundaries of nursing homes, can help improve the subjective well-being of elderly residents in these facilities. Policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing such interventions to address the intersectional poverty faced by this population.

Title: Grandparent Care: A Key Factor in Mothers' Labour Force Participation in the UK
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that grandparent-provided childcare raises the labor force participation of mothers with a child of school entry age on average by 12 percentage points and raises the participation of the group of mothers who use grandparent childcare by 33 percentage points compared to the situation if they did not have access to this care.
What_was_studied: Using data from the UK's Millennium Cohort Study, a nationally representative sample of children born in 2000, biprobit and instrumental variables (IV) analysis of mothers’ participation (given the social construction of caring responsibility) identifies a significant causal effect of grandparents’ childcare on mothers' labor force participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Grandparent-provided childcare has a substantial impact on the labor market in the UK, an impact that may not be sustainable with forthcoming changes to the state pension age. Therefore, policymakers should scale up support for grandparents providing childcare, expand access to affordable childcare, and prioritize social care services to ensure intergenerational fairness.

Authors: Manos Matsaganis; Maurizio Ferrera; Luís Capucha; Luis Moreno
Field: Welfare; Economy; Economics; Spite; Poverty; State (polity); Field (Bourdieu); Social assistance; Legitimacy; Development economics; Politics
Keywords: Poverty; Social assistance; Minimum incomes; Southern Europe
Title: Mending Nets in the South: Anti‐poverty Policies in Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Significant innovations in anti-poverty policies have taken place in these countries over the past two decades, with the introduction of minimum income schemes in Portugal and certain Spanish regions, and ongoing experiments in Italy. However, social safety nets remain frail due to institutional and political constraints.
What_was_studied: The marginal role of social assistance and the absence of minimum income programs in four southern European countries (Greece, Italy, Portugal, and Spain) from 1990 to 2000, using data from national surveys and policy reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and expand these minimum income programs to address chronic poverty and intersectional inequality, prioritizing their funding and political support, and revising existing policies to better address the unique needs of vulnerable populations.

Field: Social entropy; Social exclusion; Political economy; Social position; Sociology; Social group; Social change; Public administration; Social philosophy; Social transformation; Social order
Title: Social Exclusion and Double Jeopardy: The Management of Lone Mothers in the Market–State Social Field
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Employment activation programs like Ontario Works reinforce social exclusion by keeping women in their place through ideological practices that perpetuate gendered power imbalances and limit economic opportunities for single mothers.
What_was_studied: The social exclusion of women who parent alone in Ontario, Canada, over a six-month time period from 2018 to 2019, using data from Ontario Works, an employment activation program for social welfare recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up alternative income support policies for single mothers, expand the scope of employment activation programs to include training and mentorship opportunities that prioritize equity and inclusion, and revise program eligibility criteria to address gendered power imbalances.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Redundancy (engineering); Economics; Unemployment; Oecd countries; Social democracy
Title: Comparing Formal Unemployment Compensation Systems in 15 OECD Countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Southern European countries have comparable formal unemployment compensation systems to Continental-corporatist countries when considering occupational welfare programs like redundancy pay, contradicting the common view of weaker protection in these countries.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes unemployment compensation programs of 15 OECD countries across four country clusters, examining their strength and how they compare to each other and to occupational welfare schemes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similar strength of unemployment compensation systems across country clusters, policymakers should prioritize integrating occupational welfare schemes into their broader social protection strategies to enhance support for workers and reduce poverty risks.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Social policy; Tax policy; Minimum wage
Title: Aiming to keep poor Mexican families at the breadline (but no higher): The effects of minimum wage, tax, and social policy changes between 1994 and 2012
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Social policy changes primarily subsidized the drop in real minimum wage, leaving poor families at best at similar income levels. Strict targeting mechanisms and limited coverage of social insurance programs exacerbated poverty issues.
What_was_studied: Welfare policy in Mexico from the mid-1990s to present, focusing on social protection programs and their effects on poverty levels among various population groups during an era of economic strategy change and taxation reform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social assistance programs and expand their coverage to include all eligible population groups, prioritizing a living wage and revising strict targeting criteria to ensure the most vulnerable are lifted out of poverty.

Field: Public economics; Positive economics; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Social change; Social protection; Convergence (relationship); Empirical data
Title: Indications of Social Policy Convergence in Europe
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there is evidence of convergence in social policy integration across European countries, particularly in the areas of active and passive labour market expenditures. The empirical data showed an increase in social protection expenditures across the board, with a higher rate of growth in certain countries.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews definitions and typologies of the welfare state to explore the extent of convergence in social policy within Europe, with an empirical focus on 'social protection' expenditures and taxation regimes from 1980 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that there is potential for further integration and coordination of social policy initiatives at the supranational level to address gender and poverty disparities and promote sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize the expansion of active labour market programs and consider revising taxation regimes to support these efforts.

Field: Political science; Cash; Supportive housing; Tertiary Prevention; Public assistance; Secondary prevention; Economic growth; Intervention (law); Subsidy; Politics
Title: Homelessness Prevention Policy: A Case Study
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that primary homelessness prevention measures were most effective in reducing homelessness rates, particularly when intervening in the housing market and providing cash assistance. However, these measures were not consistently implemented across different time periods and policy frameworks.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of Israel's homelessness prevention policies from 1948 to 2010, using a case study approach to identify best practices and areas for improvement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize primary homelessness prevention measures, such as intervening in the housing market and providing cash assistance, to effectively reduce homelessness rates. By scaling up these efforts and ensuring consistent implementation, governments can make a meaningful difference in addressing housing insecurity.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Sociology; Population; Argument; Social issues; Public housing; Criminology
Title: Single Homelessness as Social Exclusion: The Unique and the Extreme
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that single homelessness is characterized by the inability of a section of the socially excluded population to access welfare services and social housing, and that 'homelessness' does not exist as a discrete social problem with unique characteristics and causes.
What_was_studied: Recent research on single homelessness and rough sleeping considered the issue using the concepts and language of social exclusion, analyzing the new literature to determine if single homelessness can be viewed as a product of social exclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of social exclusion to prevent single homelessness and rough sleeping, rather than solely focusing on providing temporary shelter and support services.

Field: Social exclusion; Consumption (economics); Sociology of leisure; Labour economics; Economics; Social policy; Time-use survey; Household income; Social engagement; Social identity theory
Title: Social Participation and Family Welfare: The Money and Time Costs of Leisure in Australia
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that low-income individuals have limited access to leisure goods and services, and that after controlling for working hours, household income has no significant effect on available leisure time. Additionally, a leisure-time poverty line was established based on half-median leisure time, which showed that certain groups are excluded from leisure participation due to time constraints.
What_was_studied: Australian Household Expenditure Survey data was analyzed to investigate how income affects leisure participation and the impact of gender and hours of employment on available leisure time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To alleviate social exclusion from leisure participation, policies should prioritize increasing access to leisure goods and services for low-income individuals, as well as addressing time constraints through flexible work arrangements and childcare support. Additionally, the findings suggest that income alone is not a reliable indicator of leisure participation, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive approach to addressing social exclusion.

Authors: Gerard Redmond; Roger Patulny; Peter Whiteford
Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Income Support; Financial crisis; Household income; Child poverty; Economic growth
Keywords: Child poverty; Global Financial Crisis; income support; Australia; lump-sum payments
Title: The Global Financial Crisis and Child Poverty: The Case of Australia 2006–10
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the policy response reduced child poverty in the short term, rates of relative child poverty have not fallen in the longer term due to moderate support for families with children in longer-term policies.
What_was_studied: The impact of the Australian government's policy response to the global financial crisis (GFC) on child poverty in Australia between 2008 and 2013, using data from the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and expand support for families with children to address persistent child poverty.

Field: Welfare; Social class; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Working class; Social policy; Social protection; Fourth World; Argument; Economic growth
Keywords: Australia; New Zealand; Social class; Social democracy; Welfare state analysis
Title: The Working Class and Welfare: Francis G. Castles on the Political Development of the Welfare State in Australia and New Zealand Thirty Years On
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that Australasian social policy has been shaped by a radical wage-earning model, which prioritizes the protection of workers' rights and has resulted in distinctive path-dependent systems of social protection. Specifically, the study finds that labor market regulation has played a crucial role in reducing poverty and inequality in both countries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the evolution of welfare policies in Australia and New Zealand during the 20th century, focusing on labor market regulation and social protection systems, with a particular emphasis on gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gender and intersectional poverty gaps, decision-makers should prioritize strengthening labor market regulation and social protection systems to ensure equal pay for equal work, address discrimination, and support inclusive economic growth. This may involve scaling up successful policies, expanding coverage to marginalized populations, and funding targeted interventions to address poverty and inequality.

Field: Positive economics; Economics; Construct (philosophy); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Relative deprivation; Subject (philosophy); Townsend; Index (economics); Development economics; Politics
Title: The Political Arithmetic of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study questions the validity of Townsend's attempts to update the measurement of poverty and criticizes the construction of a deprivation index. It also highlights the limitations of statistical measurements of poverty and deprivation, suggesting that these measures are unsatisfactory and unconvincing.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the concept of poverty and specifically the measurement of 'relative deprivation' in the UK, using data from 2008/2009 to 2013/2014 and focusing on three policy areas: chronic poverty, income poverty, and multidimensional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of current poverty measures, decision-makers should prioritize alternative approaches to capturing the complexity of poverty, such as multidimensional indices that account for various dimensions of deprivation, rather than relying solely on income-based measures.

Field: Social exclusion; Social position; Sociology; Social inequality; Social work; Social change; Social mobility; Social stratification; Economic growth; Social engagement
Title: Social Exclusion, Inequality and Social Work
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and inequality are strongly linked, with relative poverty contributing to exclusion from economic and social norms. Additionally, the research showed that financial deprivation is a key factor in individuals approaching or being referred to social services.
What_was_studied: This paper explores pragmatic and idealist arguments concerning whether or not the poor need social work, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data from Britain over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is essential to prioritize advocacy over social control when addressing poverty and inequality. Policymakers should scale up support for social services, expand access to education and employment opportunities, and fund programs aimed at reducing food insecurity and health disparities.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Vulnerability; Poverty; Working poor; Unemployment
Title: Jobless or Working Poor in the Kyrgyz Labour Market: What Role for Social Policies?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that individuals with lower education levels and women were more likely to experience extreme vulnerability, including high risks of unemployment, long-term unemployment, discouragement, low wages, and precarious jobs. Other groups at risk included people with disabilities, those living in rural or depressed areas, young people, and internal migrants.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the vulnerability of various groups in the Kyrgyz labor market, specifically focusing on the working poor and precarious workers, using data from the Kyrgyz Poverty Monitoring Survey (1997-1998).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the large overlap between work and poverty in the Kyrgyz labor market, effective social policies should prioritize addressing the vulnerability of these groups, particularly by providing education and job training programs, targeted employment support, and social protection initiatives.

Authors: Johanna Greiss; Bea Cantillon; Tess Penne
Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Trojan horse; Dilemma; Food bank; Food aid
Title: The Fund for European Aid to the Most Deprived: A Trojan horse dilemma?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that FEAD bears resemblance to a contemporary ‘Trojan horse’: it is welcomed by the Member States as a deceptively innocent EU gift but it might in the long run support the role of the EU as an agent that plugs gaps within national social protection schemes, and provides social protection to European citizens, particularly in the context of food aid in most EU countries.
What_was_studied: The 'Fund for European Aid to the Most Deprived' (FEAD) financing instrument and its budgetary scope in relation to national welfare state efforts, as well as its potential contribution to shifting responsibilities from the national to the European level, using a comparative approach with the United States' Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that FEAD could potentially contribute to shifting responsibilities from the national to the European level, therefore, decision makers should prioritize and scale up FEAD funding to address poverty and social exclusion in the EU, and consider expanding its scope to cover more vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Unemployment; Generosity; Compensation (psychology); Perverse incentive; Panel data
Title: Incomes after Job-loss in the United States: From Programme Rules to Panel Data
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis shows how the income effects of job loss vary across job losers and suggests that the role of unemployment compensation programs in supporting incomes may be overstated.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes income transfers after job loss in the United States and European countries using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) and other international organizations, focusing on the comparative evidence on US welfare state generosity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising unemployment compensation programs to better support low-income individuals experiencing job loss and address the nuanced variations in income effects across job losers.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Economics; Work (electrical); Limiting; Poverty; Annual income; Term (time)
Title: Welfare States: A Response to John Veit–Wilson
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that societies with a guaranteed annual income had significantly lower rates of poverty, indicating that the welfare state can be an effective tool in reducing poverty. Additionally, the study found that the welfare state can be particularly effective in reducing deep poverty and improving overall well-being.
What_was_studied: The article 'States of welfare: a conceptual challenge' examined the effectiveness of the welfare state in reducing poverty in various societies, focusing on those that have implemented a guaranteed annual income and comparing them to those that have not.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of a guaranteed annual income to scale up social protection and reduce poverty in their societies. This approach has the potential to significantly improve the lives of millions of people and help achieve the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

Authors: Peter Saunders; Vera M. Y. Tang
Field: Sociology; Poverty; Socioeconomics
Title: Adult and child deprivation in Hong Kong
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that more than one-third of households in Hong Kong experienced deprivation, with children being disproportionately affected. The findings also revealed disparities between children identified as living in households identified as deprived according to information provided by adults and those whose deprivation status reflects their own views.
What_was_studied: The application of Townsend's deprivation approach to provide estimates of poverty in Hong Kong using data from the second wave (conducted in 2015–2016) of the Trends and Implications of Social Disadvantages in Hong Kong survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for further improvements in health service provision and social security benefits to address poverty in Hong Kong. Policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty, health disparities, and multidimensional poverty by expanding coverage and adequacy of health services and social security benefits to ensure that all households, particularly those with children, have access to the resources they need to thrive.

Authors: Peter Saunders; Hung Wong; Wo Ping Wong
Field: Social deprivation; Standard of living; Government; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Commission; Social security; Socioeconomics; Development economics; International studies
Title: Deprivation and Poverty in Hong Kong
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that around 30% of the population experienced deprivation in at least two items, 18% in at least four items, and 10% in at least eight items. Deprivation rates were highest for basic health needs such as dental care and glasses.
What_was_studied: The study examined the living standards of the poorest in the Hong Kong community using a new deprivation study that identified 35 basic needs items and found high rates of deprivation, particularly among those receiving Comprehensive Social Security Assistance (CSSA), people affected by disabilities, and recent migrants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for the government to set a poverty line and develop targeted policies to address deprivation, particularly among vulnerable groups such as CSSA recipients, people with disabilities, and recent migrants. Policymakers should prioritize funding for healthcare and social welfare programs to improve living standards and address multidimensional poverty.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Financial literacy; Asset building; Habit; Economic system; Qualitative property; Civil discourse
Title: Contradictory Logics in Asset‐building Discourse: Habits, Identities and Discipline
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that asset-building discourse as enacted by workers is fundamentally contradictory, promoting financial literacy but also disciplining the poor to thoughtlessly save out of habit, with more emphasis on inculcating the habit of saving than teaching economically rational decision-making.
What_was_studied: A case study of a matched savings program in the USA, focusing on how frontline workers enact asset-building discourse and its implications for addressing poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that asset-building policies may reinforce neoliberal approaches to addressing poverty by disciplining the poor rather than addressing systemic issues; policymakers should prioritize revising these policies to focus on economically rational decision-making and addressing poverty's root causes.

Authors: David W. Rothwell; Leanne S. Giordono; Jennifer Robson
Field: Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Asset poverty; Cross national; Country differences; Development economics
Title: Public income transfers and wealth accumulation at the bottom: Within and between country differences in Canada and the United States
primary_category: Asset poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that asset poverty rates varied over time in both countries, but were higher in the less generous US welfare state. Additionally, income transfer share was positively related to asset poverty in Canada but not in the US, and counterfactual estimates suggested a substitution effect in Canada where higher levels of transfers may crowd out private asset accumulation.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between the welfare state and private wealth accumulation in Canada and the United States using nationally representative wealth surveys from 1998/1999 to 2016, with a focus on household asset poverty defined as financial asset levels below three-month adjusted income poverty threshold.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the more generous Canadian welfare system has led to higher levels of private wealth accumulation, and policymakers should consider prioritizing income support programs to address asset poverty and promote economic mobility.

Field: Welfare; Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Wage; Minimum wage; Legislature; Politics
Title: The Politics of ‘Minimum Wage’ Welfare States: The Changing Significance of the Minimum Wage in the Liberal Welfare Regime
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that the retreat of the English-speaking welfare states from their postwar compromises has led to a politicization of minimum wage policies, driven by legislative action and activist campaigns from below. This has resulted in higher minimum wages, which have the potential to shift the burden of addressing inequalities from fiscally-strained governments to employers.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between minimum wage policies and poverty reduction in five English-speaking liberal welfare states over the period 1980 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the implementation of higher minimum wage policies as a predistributive strategy to address poverty and inequality, rather than relying solely on social protection programs.

Field: Social exclusion; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; International comparisons; Czech; Social condition; Income poverty; Market policy; Demographic economics
Title: Poverty, Social Exclusion and Social Policy in the Czech Republic
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Material deprivation, as well as concentration of poverty within specific population groups, is high, with the unemployed facing the highest risk of poverty. Social policy measures in effect reinforce this pattern: while the benefit system is highly redistributive and effectively eliminates income poverty among households of employed persons and among pensioners, incomes of persons outside paid employment are protected less effectively.
What_was_studied: The analysis is mostly based on data from the Czech Survey on Social Conditions of Households (2001; 27,000 respondents); Eurostat data provide a benchmark for making international comparisons. The poverty rate in the Czech Republic is among the lowest in Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: We argue that although this practice is effective at present, it is not sustainable in the long term. Therefore, policy makers should prioritize targeting groups which are facing the highest risk of labour market exclusion and poverty through adequate Labour market policy measures.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Class (set theory); Economics; Global South; Social rights; Truism; Dimension (data warehouse); Social stratification
Title: Levels or worlds of welfare? Assessing social rights and social stratification in Northern and Southern countries
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while there are indeed qualitative differences between welfare states, not all countries fit neatly into the original three worlds. Additionally, the study identified a conceptual issue in welfare regime research: regimes are not just defined and measured in terms of different logics of welfare provision but also take into account degrees of welfare stateism.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed 45 countries in the Global North and South to determine whether there are different types of welfare states beyond the original three worlds identified by Esping-Andersen, using data on social rights and social stratification from the period 2010–2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed results and the conceptual issue identified, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of welfare states and their variations beyond the original three worlds. This could involve funding further research on the subject, revising current policy frameworks to account for the qualitative differences found, and scaling up social rights and social stratification data collection efforts to improve comparability across countries.

Field: Social exclusion; Social deprivation; Psychology; Poverty; Friendship; Meaning (existential); Economic integration; Inclusion (disability rights); Autonomy; Social psychology
Title: Excluding Children: Autonomy, Friendship and the Experience of the Care System
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Children in the public care system experience high exclusion risks due to restricted social and economic integration, which affects their capacity for developing social networks. Friendship is crucial for these children's well-being and future poverty prevention efforts should prioritize facilitating relational resources.
What_was_studied: The relational aspects of poverty among children in the public care system were explored through in-depth interviews to understand the meaning of friendship for this group and how social relationships can mitigate future poverty risks, even when material resources are limited.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should scale up funding for programs that foster peer connections, leverage technology to enhance social networks, and revise care system policies to prioritize inclusion and support for children in the public care system to mitigate future poverty risks.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Pension; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: Inequalities and poverty risks in old age across Europe: The double‐edged income effect of pension systems
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found considerable poverty and income inequality in old age across Europe, with notable differences between countries. For instance, poverty rates are low due to encompassing basic pensions in Dutch and some Nordic multipillar systems, while Bismarckian pensions such as in Germany reproduce inequality and medium-level poverty.
What_was_studied: Using recent EU-SILC data (2017/18), a comparative analysis of poverty rates and income inequality in old age shows important cross-national variations that need to be seen in context of market-related inequalities but also the specific pension system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high poverty risks in Beveridge systems like the United Kingdom and Switzerland, policymakers should prioritize enhancing minimum income provision for public pension systems to reduce poverty risks, while also revising pension architectures to address reproduced inequality acquired during working life.

Authors: Yin Zhang; Hung Wong; Ji-Kang Chen; Vera M. Y. Tang
Field: Psychology; Interpersonal communication; Mediation; Poverty; Social support; Social acceptance; Income poverty; Social psychology
Title: Comparing income poverty gap and deprivation on social acceptance: A mediation model with interpersonal communication and social support
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results of structural equation modeling reveal that deprivation significantly negatively impacts social acceptance, which can be mitigated by two significant mediators of interpersonal communication and social support.
What_was_studied: This household survey (N=1,202) in Hong Kong investigates the relationship between poverty and social exclusion, using deprivation as a more powerful indicator than income poverty to specify the negative relations of poverty with interpersonal communication, social support, and social acceptance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing deprivation as a more effective approach to reducing poverty and improving social acceptance, rather than solely focusing on income-based measures.

Field: Labour economics; Discount points; Economics; Poverty; State (polity); Social security; Generosity; Pension
Keywords: Social Security; Public Pensions; Retirement; Poverty; Retirement Policies
Title: Evaluating the Possible Impact of Pension Reforms on Elderly Poverty in Europe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that reforms have significantly decreased pension generosity, with moves to link benefits to contributions making systems less progressive, raising adequacy concerns for certain groups. The need for ensuring better access to labor markets, adequate crediting arrangements, and minimum pensions is strengthened.
What_was_studied: The article assesses the impact of pension reforms on pension wealth since the 1990s using hypothetical cases and estimates of prospective pension transfers, focusing on changes in benefit indexation to provide additional insights into the adequacy of pensions for certain groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the adequacy concerns of pension reforms, policymakers should prioritize ensuring better access to labor markets, implementing adequate crediting arrangements, and providing minimum pensions to protect vulnerable groups.

Field: Welfare state; Psychology; Social policy; Political psychology; Big Five personality traits; Affect (psychology); Social psychology; Neuroticism
Title: Taking social policy personally: How does neuroticism affect welfare state attitudes?
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that neuroticism is a significant predictor of dissatisfaction with the social security system and feelings of financial insecurity across multiple need contexts, but it does not affect support for state provision. Specifically, the study found that neurotic individuals are more likely to experience financial insecurity and dissatisfaction with social security programs, yet they also appear to need these programs more.
What_was_studied: Using cross-sectional data from the German Socio-Economic Panel, this study investigates the relationship between neuroticism and attitudes towards the welfare state, specifically examining how neurotic individuals perceive social security provision in various need contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions addressing financial insecurity and dissatisfaction with social security programs among neurotic individuals. This may involve scaling up existing support services or expanding program eligibility to better meet the needs of this vulnerable population.

Field: Retrenchment; Economic policy; Private sector; Welfare state; Public sector; Economics; Revenue; Cost of living; Market economy; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Narrowing of Public Responsibility in Finland, 1990–2010
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while welfare state programs are popular among the Finnish population, large one-time cutbacks have not been possible beyond the immediate aftermath of the economic crisis; instead, the retrenchment has been achieved through slow, gradual weakening of social programs and tax cuts that have left proportionally more in the hands of the wealthier, resulting in a drastic reversal in the trend of income inequality.
What_was_studied: The public responsibility in Finland has narrowed over the past 20 years while the private sector has increased; this study examines how the welfare state retrenchment has been achieved through slow, gradual weakening of social programs and tax cuts that have disproportionately benefited the wealthy, leading to a drastic reversal in the trend of income inequality in Finland from 1990 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing income poverty and intersectional poverty through targeted social programs and progressive taxation to reverse the trend of rising income inequality and ensure equitable access to resources for all Finns.

Authors: Griet Roets; Rudi Roose; Maria De Bie; Lien Claes; Geert Van Hove
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Economics; Social work; Work (electrical); Poverty; Empowerment; Context (language use); Public relations; Function (engineering)
Title: Pawns or Pioneers? The Logic of User Participation in Anti‐poverty Policy‐making in Public Policy Units in Belgium
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that employing users with experience of poverty as experts in public policy units can be an effective strategy for implementing and monitoring anti-poverty policies, particularly in the areas of chronic poverty and gender and poverty. The study also showed that the participation of these individuals can help to improve the responsiveness and quality of public services, but may also risk their use as mere pawns or acquiring a tragic-optimistic outlook on life.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of involving service users with experience of poverty as experts in public policy units to implement and monitor anti-poverty policies in Belgium.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the effectiveness of involving service users in public policy units, decision makers should prioritize funding for programs that employ experts with experience of poverty, expand existing programs to reach more individuals and communities, and revise policies to ensure that these individuals are not used as mere pawns but rather as pioneers in the implementation of anti-poverty strategies.

Authors: Wolfgang Ludwig-Mayerhofer; Olaf Behrend; Ariadne Sondermann
Field: Social class; Welfare state; Business; Labour economics; Class (computer programming); Power (social and political); Unemployment; Compensation (psychology); Public employment service; Administration (probate law)
Title: Activation, Public Employment Services and their Clients: The Role of Social Class in a Continental Welfare State
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Social class is a significant factor in client outcomes, and earlier research has overemphasized the role of frontline staff as 'street-level bureaucrats'.
What_was_studied: This article investigates how public employment service (PES) staff deal with their clients under a continental regime of activation in Germany, based on interviews with both PES staff and unemployed clients during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that social class is a strong predictor of client outcomes, policymakers should prioritize targeted support for marginalized groups and revisit the training provided to PES staff to ensure they are equipped to address diverse client needs.

Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Fiscal incidence; Economic reform; Welfare system; Economic inequality
Title: The performance of the Australian welfare system in a time of neoliberal economic reform
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Australian welfare system grew in size and redistributive quantum, while wage levels rose strongly and unemployment rates fell, resulting in a small increase in income inequality but no change in wealth inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of neoliberal economic policy reforms on the Australian welfare system and socioeconomic egalitarianism between the mid-1980s and the global financial crisis of 2007–08.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding the Australian welfare system to address rising income inequality, while also revising economic policies to ensure they do not disproportionately benefit the wealthy at the expense of low- and middle-income households.

Field: Empowerment; Poverty; State (computer science); Politics; Social protection; Perception; Social policy; Livelihood; Political science; Public relations; Public administration; Economic growth; Economics; Psychology; Law; Ecology; Algorithm; Neuroscience; Computer science; Biology; Agriculture
Title: From policy to politics? Exploring feedback effects of social protection on state‐citizen relations in Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds positive resource and interpretive/policy learning effects on state-citizen perceptions and interactions, with these impacts being higher among beneficiaries with previously limited access to or negative perception about the state. Additionally, the study highlights the ideational and relational impact of social protection by arguing that when implemented well, social policies can generate political feedback effects beyond their poverty reduction and human development impacts.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of Ghana's Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty cash transfer programme (LEAP) on state-citizen relations in two implementation districts, using a mixed methods approach and focusing on beneficiaries with limited access to or negative perception about the state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of social protection programs like LEAP in a way that fosters policy learning opportunities for reconfiguring the perceptions of and interactions between the state and citizens, particularly among marginalized groups.

Field: Welfare; Entitlement; Political spectrum; Sociology; Social policy; Welfare reform; Cash; Aid to Families with Dependent Children; Public administration; Economic growth; Punitive damages
Title: The Second Phase of US Welfare Reform, 2000–2006: Blaming the Poor Again?
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that TANF ended automatic individual entitlement to public assistance, established a five-year time limit for receiving cash assistance, and promoted a punitive approach towards welfare recipients. Additionally, cash assistance was temporary and granted as a favour to low-income mothers who were required to comply with various behavioural requirements.
What_was_studied: This article examines the evolution of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program since 1996, focusing on its transformation from Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) and the implementation of the Work First Approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that TANF's Work First Approach has been successful in promoting work among welfare recipients, but has also led to increased poverty and inequality. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize expanding funding for TANF and revising the program's approach to better support low-income families.

Field: Welfare state; European social model; Nexus (standard); European Social Survey; Race to the bottom; Convergence (economics); European integration; Political science; European union; Corporate governance; Welfare; Social integration; Social policy; Social protection; Multi-level governance; Public economics; Economics; Economic system; Political economy; Economic growth; Globalization; International trade; Law; Finance; Politics; Computer science; Embedded system
Title: Citizens' expectations about social protection in multilevel governance: The interplay between national and supranational institutions
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that generous national welfare provision fuels expectations of a race to the bottom for social protection levels, while higher receipts from EU Structural Fund programs and individual trust in EU institutions raise expectations of upward convergence in social standards.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between European integration and the welfare state from the perspective of public opinion in 18 EU countries, using data from the European Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening national welfare states and investing in EU-level social protection initiatives to address citizens' concerns about the potential negative impacts of European integration on social standards.

Authors: Maggie Lau; David Gordon; Mary Zhang; Jonathan Bradshaw
Field: Public policy; Empirical research; Agency (sociology); Social deprivation; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Poverty; Longitudinal study; Household income; Child poverty
Title: Children's and adults' perceptions of child necessities in Hong Kong
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Adults were significantly more likely than children to believe that almost all material and social deprivation items were necessities for children, highlighting the importance of incorporating children's views into our understanding of child poverty.
What_was_studied: Child poverty and child well-being in East Asia during the 2010s, using a consensual deprivation approach to compare adult and child perspectives on necessities of life in Hong Kong.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize including children's perspectives in their understanding of child poverty and incorporate child-led measures to better capture the needs of children.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Social deprivation; Economics; Social inequality; Generosity; Disadvantaged; European union; Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Inequality
Title: Welfare Generosity in Europe: A Multi‐level Study of Material Deprivation and Income Poverty among Disadvantaged Groups
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that welfare generosity significantly moderated the risk of both material deprivation and income poverty among disadvantaged groups. Specifically, the risk of material deprivation and income poverty decreased as welfare generosity increased, with few exceptions. Additionally, the study found that individuals who experienced combinations of limiting long-standing illness and either low education or non-employment had lower absolute levels of material deprivation and income poverty in more generous welfare states.
What_was_studied: The 2009 European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions surveys were analyzed to determine whether welfare generosity moderates the risk of income poverty and material deprivation among disadvantaged groups, including people with ill health, low education, and lack of employment in 27 and 28 European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize investing in generous welfare states to reduce social inequalities and buffer the worst-off from material deprivation and income poverty, particularly among disadvantaged groups such as those with ill health, low education, and lack of employment. By scaling up these efforts, policymakers can help ensure that all individuals have access to essential resources and opportunities for a dignified life.

Field: Welfare; Political science; Spite; Unemployment; Family support; Research findings; Development economics
Title: Social and Material Deprivation among Unemployed Youth in Northern Europe
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found diverging tendencies within the Nordic countries and converging trends between the different systems, with family support playing a crucial role in preventing deprivation in all countries.
What_was_studied: This article examines deprivation among unemployed young people in six countries, using a comparative survey of 8,654 participants over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of deprivation among young unemployed people, policymakers should prioritize investing in family support programs to mitigate the negative effects of unemployment and poverty.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Culture of poverty; Urban anthropology; Poverty; Basic needs; Unemployment; Urbanization; Development economics; Industrial policy
Title: The State, Institutional Transition and the Creation of New Urban Poverty in China
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the state as the manipulator of institutions and policies does matter in the creation of new urban poverty, and that cleavages between the old and new institutions further intensify it.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on new urban poverty in China under market transition and discusses the causes of poverty creation, examining the adjustment of industrial policy, the reform of state-owned enterprises, evolution of the household registration system, and the transformation of the welfare state between 1990 and 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rise of new urban poverty in China, policymakers should prioritize the evolution of household registration systems and the transformation of welfare states to better address the needs of those affected by market transition.

Field: Economics; Poverty; China; State (polity); Social security; Action (philosophy); Unemployment; Market economy; Process (engineering); Rationalization (economics)
Title: Social Security Reform in China’s Transition to a Market Economy
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the fragmented nature of China's social security system has led to significant disparities in coverage and benefits, particularly for rural residents, and that reform efforts have had limited success in addressing these issues due to financial pressures and conflicting policy priorities.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the evolution of China's social security system and its challenges in addressing issues such as housing insecurity and sustainable development, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data from the period 1980-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing housing insecurity and urban poverty challenges in China, policymakers should prioritize revising the social security system to provide more equitable coverage and benefits, particularly for rural residents, and allocate additional resources towards sustainable development initiatives.

Field: Economic policy; Political science; Guaranteed minimum income; Austerity
Title: Safety nets in (the) crisis: The case of Greece in the 2010s
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while austerity measures reduced the provision and capacity of social protection, there were also significant advances in protecting against extreme poverty. The system of social safety net that has emerged is leaner but more effective than before.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the transformation of the Greek social safety net in response to the Eurozone crisis (2010-2019) using a mixed-methods approach and data from national statistics, surveys, and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising levels of poverty and inequality, policymakers should prioritize funding for effective social protection programs, scale up successful initiatives, and revise austerity measures to ensure a robust safety net for all Greeks.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Social protection; Social rights; Unemployment; Social mobility; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: Welfare State Changes and Outcomes – The Cases of Portugal and Denmark from a Comparative Perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite improvements in many social domains in Portugal, problems of inequality remain deeply embedded in the country's social and institutional structures, resulting in steadily increasing income inequality. In contrast, Denmark's well-developed welfare state and de-commodification of social rights contributed to a more equitable distribution of resources and opportunities.
What_was_studied: This research compares the impact of changes in crucial domains of social policy on income inequality in Portugal and Denmark from the mid-1980s to the financial crisis of 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening and expanding social protection policies in Portugal to address deeply ingrained issues of inequality, while Denmark can consider scaling up its successful welfare state model to further reduce income disparities.

Field: Public policy; Labour economics; Psychology; Tax credit; Work (electrical); Wage; Child poverty; Cohort; Typology; Subsidy
Keywords: maternal employment; employment trajectories; wage progression
Title: Employment and Wage Trajectories for Mothers Entering Low-skilled Work: Evidence from the British Lone Parent Cohort
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that only one-third of mothers were able to maintain stable employment over the decade, while another third remained at home and a third followed unstable pathways between work and nonwork.
What_was_studied: This article uses the British Lone Parent Cohort to examine employment trajectories for up to 560 mothers with a youngest child under five at the start of the period, from 1991 to 2001.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that maternal employment is seen as a central plank in the campaign against child poverty, this study highlights the need for policy interventions to support mothers in low-skilled employment and facilitate their progression to higher-skilled and better-paid jobs. Policymakers should prioritize job training programs and flexible work arrangements to help women balance work and family responsibilities.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Social exclusion; Economic Justice; Sociology; Ideology; Poverty; Development economics; Social Welfare; Politics
Title: The Local Politics of Inclusion: The State and Community Safety
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while both countries saw increasing rates of youth crime, British local agencies were more successful in deploying policies to offset social exclusion through their connections with national institutions, unlike the French case where community policing was less effective due to a lack of resources and institutional commitment.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the role of local state agencies in offsetting the social exclusion of marginalized communities in two British and French communities between 1990 and 2005 using crime data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising rates of youth crime across economies, decision-makers should prioritize resource allocation for local state agencies to deploy policies that connect marginalized communities with national institutions, leveraging their existing commitments to social welfare projects to ameliorate economic marginalization and reduce social exclusion.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Investment (macroeconomics); Human capital; Unemployment; Poor relief
Title: The (changing) consideration of social investment in the design of welfare benefits: The case of poverty relief in Austria
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the three elements of social investment (improving human capital, enhancing employability, and enhancing employment integration) were particularly relevant in reforming social assistance, but the changes implemented were incoherent and did not support the hypothesis of an ever-increasing significance of social investment. The main triggers for reform were the political ideologies of (changing) governments.
