Field: European Social Survey; Policy analysis; Welfare state; Political science; Social protection; Context (language use); Market integration; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Commodification
Keywords: Nordic and Baltic countries; disability policies; employment of disabled people; Labour Force Survey; public employment services; non-discrimination
Title: Labour Market Integration and Equality for Disabled People: A Comparative Analysis of Nordic and Baltic Countries
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings highlight better employment and social protection outcomes for disabled people in the Nordic countries, but point to policy challenges in both blocks. National processes of (de)commodification and stratification affect disabled people differently and this may disrupt our assumptions about welfare state comparisons.
What_was_studied: The analysis examines the employment situation of disabled people in three Nordic and three Baltic countries during a specific time period using policy analysis and European social survey data to compare outcomes for disabled people in each country and in binary comparison between Nordic and Baltic countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: National policies make a difference, and non-discrimination policies are not enough. A focused mix of regulatory and redistributive measures is needed to improve employment and social protection outcomes for disabled people. Policymakers should prioritize and expand these measures to ensure sustainable development and equal opportunities for all.

Field: Debt; Tax deduction; Economics; Sanctions; Conditionality; Welfare; Poverty; Creditor; Public economics; Social security; Labour economics; Political science; Law; Economic growth; Macroeconomics; Market economy; Gross income; Tax reform; State income tax; Politics
Title: Indentured: Benefit deductions, debt recovery and welfare disciplining
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that deductions are central to understanding low-income life in the UK, with increasing indebtedness and an Inverse Care Law, whereby social security performs worst for those who need it most. Additionally, qualitative longitudinal ethnographic fieldwork showed how deductions affect the lives and trajectories of low-income claimants over time, weaponizing debt and pushing people away from the labor market.
What_was_studied: The UK social security system's deductions and their effects on low-income benefit claimants during a cost-of-living crisis, using mixed methods and data from the period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the social security system's deduction policies to address the poverty-debt trap and push people towards the labor market, rather than further financializing benefit claimants and their entitlements.

Field: Finance; Business; Health care; Poverty; Health equity; Healthcare system; Restructuring; Health policy; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Universal design
Title: Healthcare in India: Changing the Financing Strategy
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that public investment in the health sector is dismally low, with only one-fifth of health expenditure being publicly financed, leading to a significant proportion of out-of-pocket expenses and exacerbating health disparities. Specifically, the study finds that India's healthcare financing model leads to a skewed distribution of healthcare resources, with rural areas and low-income households facing the greatest challenges in accessing healthcare services.
What_was_studied: The study investigates healthcare financing in India and its impact on equity in access to healthcare, focusing on the time period from 2004 to 2016 and utilizing data from various national surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the large-scale poverty and inequities in access to healthcare, the study emphasizes the urgent need for strengthening public investment and expenditure in the health sector, prioritizing universal access mechanisms that factor in the private health sector. Policymakers must scale up public financing for healthcare, expand coverage and benefits for marginalized populations, and revise existing policies to ensure equitable access to quality healthcare for all.

Authors: Lorenza Antonucci; Hyojin Seo; Martin Strobl
Field: Welfare; Psychological intervention; Labour economics; Spillover effect; Welfare state; Economics; Unemployment; Quality (philosophy); Active labour market policies; Workfare; Economic growth; Medicine; Market economy; Political science; Macroeconomics; Philosophy; Epistemology; Psychiatry; Politics; Law
Title: Quantity over quality? How economic factors and welfare state interventions affected job insecurity and job quality before, during and after the economic crises
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that active labor market policies (ALMPs) and passive labor market policies (PLMPs) have a positive effect in reducing job insecurity across skill groups. ALMPs and PLMPs also improved several dimensions of job quality, but mostly among manual/low-skilled workers, while they had a negative effect on work pressure that mostly affected medium- and high-skilled workers.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of macroeconomic variables and welfare state interventions on job insecurity and job quality in 24 European countries from 1995 to 2021.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the reach of ALMP and PLMP interventions, policymakers should prioritize investing in these programs to improve job quality for all workers, particularly for lower-skilled workers.

Field: Allowance (engineering); Legislature; Modernization theory; Poverty; Path dependence; Odds; Political science; Clientelism; Political economy; Sociology; Economics; Law; Politics; Democracy; Medicine; Operations management; Logistic regression; Internal medicine; Microeconomics
Title: All in, against all odds. Path shift in family policy via cross‐party agreement: the case of the Single Universal Allowance reform in Italy
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Fresh empirical evidence of the path-shifting scope of the reform marked a rupture with the longstanding weak model of income support, indicating a significant reduction in child poverty and food insecurity rates, particularly among women and marginalized communities.
What_was_studied: The introduction of the Single Universal Child Allowance in 2021 and its impact on child poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality in Italy from 2021 to 2023 using a mix of quantitative data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up the Single Universal Child Allowance to combat persistent gender and socio-economic disparities in Italy, expanding coverage to all eligible families and addressing lingering implementation challenges.

Authors: Ciara Fitzpatrick; Alexandra Chapman; Siobhán Harding
Field: Politics; Political science; Northern ireland; Sociology; Ethnology; Law
Title: Social policy in a political vacuum: Women's experiences of hunger during the <scp>Cost‐of‐Living Crisis</scp> in <scp>Northern Ireland</scp>
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The research found that women routinely skipped meals, experienced feelings of shame and guilt associated with struggling to feed their children, and had difficulties purchasing food, indicating a fundamental problem with food insecurity.
What_was_studied: This study examines the experiences of women on low incomes in Northern Ireland during the Cost-of-Living Crisis (2022-2024) to understand increasing food insecurity and its implications for realizing their human right to an adequate standard of living.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure compliance with international human rights obligations, policy change is necessary to prioritize addressing the root causes of food insecurity for women and children in Northern Ireland, particularly during times of economic crisis.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Welfare reform; Right to food; Safety net; Public debate; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security
Keywords: Food banks; Food security; Welfare; Rights
Title: Food Banks and Food Security: Welfare Reform, Human Rights and Social Policy. Lessons from Canada?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Food banks have emerged as a key frontline response to food poverty and inequality in Canada, but their institutionalization undermines the state's obligation to respect, protect, and fulfill the human right to food. The study found that while food banks provide essential support to those in need, they also perpetuate the commodification of social assistance and enable governments to neglect food poverty and nutritional health and well-being.
What_was_studied: The growth of food banking in Canada over the past twenty years and its role in addressing food poverty and inequality, with a focus on advancing the human right to food and assessing the effectiveness of food banks in achieving food security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and expand food banking services in Canada, prioritizing public education and advocacy to address the root causes of food poverty and inequality. Governments should revise their welfare reform policies informed by neo-conservative ideology and instead prioritize the human right to food, ensuring that all individuals have access to nutritious food and achieving food security.

Field: Welfare state; Social policy; Sociology; Economics; Corporatism; Politics; Economic system; Positive economics; Political science; Market economy; Law
Title: The 'two lives' of Esping‐Andersen and the revival of a research programme: Gender equality, employment and redistribution in contemporary social policy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study highlights the importance of understanding the relationship between full employment and equality, and how countries belonging to different regimes have dealt with this challenge. Additionally, it emphasizes the need for a holistic approach to social policy that takes into account factors related to the international context, such as the expansion of the market logic and questions of exchange, inflation, and debt.
What_was_studied: This article reviews Gøsta Esping-Andersen's major books and summarizes key concepts and insights related to employment, social stratification, and the double bind of the welfare state in a post-industrial era, with a focus on two regimes: 'the foundations, or the welfare state between states and markets' and 'the demographic turn'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current challenges in achieving both full employment and equality, policymakers should prioritize a holistic approach to social policy that considers the international context and takes into account factors related to the market logic. This could involve scaling up successful policies, expanding support for job creation and training programs, and revising outdated regulations that hinder progress towards these goals.

Authors: Katrin Gasior; Gemma Wright; Helen Barnes; Michael Noble
Field: Vulnerability (computing); Social protection; Shock (circulatory); Natural disaster; Poverty; Adaptive capacity; Microsimulation; Natural experiment; Public economics; Development economics; Business; Economics; Indonesian; Climate change; Economic growth; Computer security; Geography; Engineering; Medicine; Ecology; Statistics; Mathematics; Meteorology; Computer science; Transport engineering; Internal medicine; Biology; Linguistics; Philosophy
Title: Adaptive social protection in Indonesia: Stress‐testing the effect of a natural disaster on poverty and vulnerability
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The existing system generally performs well in lifting people out of poverty in normal times but does not sufficiently help them prepare for and cope with shocks, with large households, households with more than two children, people in their 20s and 80s, and individuals with a disability being especially vulnerable.
What_was_studied: The study used the tax-benefit microsimulation model INDOMOD to analyze the adaptiveness of the Indonesian social protection system by simulating an income shock caused by a natural disaster and testing reforms to the existing social protection system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To better target those identified as needing more support and reduce the impact of income shocks caused by natural disasters, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of Adaptive Social Protection reforms, which would require a substantial increase in social spending.

Field: Conditionality; Sanctions; Punitive damages; Normative; Corporate governance; Context (archaeology); Sociology; Political science; Political economy; Economics; Law; Politics; Paleontology; Finance; Biology
Title: 'Show me you're trying, that's all…': Exploring the discursive impact of punishments and incentives in the <scp>Welsh</scp> homelessness system as 'controlled conditionalities'
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite changes to homelessness law in Wales, Wacquantian-style punitive conditionality is perceived as largely irrelevant by those engaged in administering the system, while 'controlled conditionalities' operate through abandonment of welfare citizens and curating a desire in applicants to be recognized as normative and compliant.
What_was_studied: Extended interviews with 98 actors within the Welsh homelessness system to investigate how conditionality operates through sanctions to further an agenda of creating a context responsibilisation and empowerment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for policymakers to scale up social protection programs that prioritize empowerment over punitive conditionality, expanding support for those experiencing chronic poverty and housing insecurity.

Authors: Chris Nyland; Russell Smyth; Cherrie Jiuhua Zhu
Field: Public economics; Human resources; Payment; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Empirical evidence; Social security; Social protection; Enforcement; Evasion (ethics)
Title: What determines the extent to which employers will comply with their social security obligations? Evidence from Chinese firm-level data
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that larger firms with a higher proportion of state ownership were more likely to evade social protection payments, while smaller private firms were more compliant. Additionally, the study found that employers who took on more risk were less likely to evade contributions.
What_was_studied: This paper examines employer responses to social protection regulations enacted by the government in Shanghai, using firm-specific data collected between 2010 and 2018. The study investigates the relationship between firm characteristics, employer behavior, and compliance mechanisms to contain contribution evasion by employers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that enforcement agencies should prioritize monitoring and penalizing larger firms with state ownership, and offer incentives for smaller private firms to encourage compliance. By targeting these strategies, policymakers can improve social protection contribution rates and ensure fair distribution of resources.

Field: Decentralization; Government; Economics; State (polity); Context (language use); Economic growth; Communism; Indigenous; Liberalization; Politics
Title: Between Decentralized Planning and Neo-liberalism: Challenges for the Survival of the Indigenous People of Kerala, India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study shows that the withdrawal of the state from the social and economic sectors has adversely affected these communities, and the new programme implemented by the Congress Party-led government has not been successful in enabling them to resist exclusion and move out of their states of deprivation.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effects of decentralization on indigenous communities in Kerala under different political regimes from 1996 to 2001, focusing on the impacts of neo-liberal policies on their lives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the state should prioritize and scale up support for indigenous communities, expanding their role in planning and implementing projects at the local level to address their exclusion and deprivation.

Field: Welfare state; Ethnic group; Political science; Welfare reform; Social security; Unemployment; Incapacity Benefit; Turkish; Demographic economics; Normative; Economic growth
Keywords: Activating welfare state; Incapacity; Work resumption; Migrant workers; Transitional labour markets; Netherlands
Title: Back to Work after Incapacity Benefit: Differences between Ethnic Minority and Native Dutch Workers
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that resumption of work after incapacity benefit is even more the exception for migrant workers with a Turkish or Moroccan ethnic background, despite having favourable personal characteristics such as low educational level, and that this difference cannot be explained by unfavourable personal characteristics of Turkish or Moroccan benefit claimants.
What_was_studied: This article examines the possible ethnic differences in resumption of work following incapacity benefit in the Netherlands, using a unique register data file from Statistics Netherlands that contains information about all incapacity benefit claimants in 1999.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that there are other explanations possible for different outcomes between ethnic groups, such as differences in work motivation, lack of 'transition facilities' in companies, and differential treatment by employers or social security officials, and policy makers should be careful of explaining different outcomes between ethnic groups by (alleged) cultural phenomena. Therefore, policy interventions should prioritize addressing these structural factors to promote equal opportunities for all workers, regardless of their ethnic background.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Public opinion; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Work Programme; State (polity); Workfare; Market economy; Politics
Keywords: Workfare; Welfare state; Social class; Political parties; Social attitudes; Public opinion
Title: Foundations of the Workfare State – Reflections on the Political Transformation of the Welfare State in Britain
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Work Programme has had a negative impact on employment outcomes for participants, with only 3.6% of participants finding work lasting at least 6 months, compared to 10.4% in the control group. Additionally, the study found that participants experienced high levels of stress and stigma as a result of participating in the programme.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of the Work Programme on working-age welfare and out-of-work benefits in Britain between 2010 and 2015, using a mixed-methods approach that includes interviews and survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial that policymakers revise the Work Programme's mandatory community work provisions to prioritize job training and placement services, rather than punitive regulatory practices. By scaling up successful job training initiatives and expanding support for long-term unemployed individuals, we can improve employment outcomes and reduce poverty in Britain.

Field: Cultural diversity; Welfare state; Sociology; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Narrative; Development economics; Multiculturalism; Immigration; Politics; Pessimism
Keywords: Welfare state; Multiculturalism; North America
Title: The Multicultural Welfare State: International Experience and North American Narratives
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The evidence suggests more complex relationships than often assumed, with OECD countries with large foreign-born populations not experiencing more difficulty in sustaining their welfare states, but rapid immigrant community growth between 1970 and 2010 leading to lower rates of growth in social spending. Robust multiculturalism policies do not systematically exacerbate this tension, and the United States and Canada exhibit different patterns, with racial diversity weakening support for redistribution in the US but immigration, multiculturalism policies, and redistribution representing a stable political equilibrium in Canada.
What_was_studied: The impact of ethnic diversity on support for the welfare state in Western democracies between 1970 and 2010, analyzing immigration and multiculturalism policies in OECD countries, specifically in the United States and Canada.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy choices do seem to matter, and premature conclusions based on the US experience alone should be avoided. To scale up social protection, intersectional poverty reduction strategies should prioritize inclusive multiculturalism policies that foster integration and address discrimination, ensuring that redistribution is sustainable and equitable across diverse populations.

Authors: Rebecca Patrick; Kay Cook; Hayley McKenzie
Field: Welfare; Actuarial science; Human factors and ergonomics; Political science; Occupational safety and health; Poverty; Child support; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Criminology
Title: Domestic Violence and the Exemption from Seeking Child Support: Providing Safety or Legitimizing Ongoing Poverty and Fear
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Women in Australia who fear ongoing or renewed abuse as a result of seeking child support are eligible for an exemption. However, the exemption policy does not necessarily provide the intended protection of women and children from ongoing abuse and poverty.
What_was_studied: This article examines the experience of low-income women on welfare in Australia and the process of seeking child support from a violent ex-partner, contrasting this with research from the United States and the United Kingdom.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise the current exemption policy to ensure that it effectively protects women and their children from ongoing abuse and poverty, by addressing the complex interaction of personal, cultural, and structural forces that hinder the process of seeking child support for women who have experienced violence.

Authors: Marcel Lubbers; Claudia Diehl; Theresa Kuhn; Christian Albrekt Larsen
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Ideology; Political science; Residence; Family values; Country of origin; Government spending; Demographic economics; Social Welfare
Title: Migrants' support for welfare state spending in Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that migrant groups' preferences for welfare state spending vary strongly across groups, residence countries, and welfare spending domains. Even when controlling for socio-demographic differences and standard ideology measures of attitudes to regulation of the economy and family values, significant differences remain.
What_was_studied: This research examines differences in attitudes towards government spending among migrant groups and natives in three residence countries: Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands, using data from the Migrants' Welfare State Attitudes project to explore how support for government spending can be explained by self-interest explanations of welfare state attitudes and differences in ideological position.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the diverse preferences for welfare state spending across migrant groups and residence countries, policymakers should prioritize comparative analyses of country-of-origin and residence-country provisions to better understand the underlying causes of these differences. This could inform targeted policies that address specific needs and foster greater social cohesion.

Authors: Claire Curran; Tania Burchardt; Martin Knapp; David McDaid; Bingqin Li
Field: Mental health; Sociology; Systematic review; Multidisciplinary approach; Computer processing; Population sampling; Social science; Management science; Information science
Title: Challenges in Multidisciplinary Systematic Reviewing: A Study on Social Exclusion and Mental Health Policy
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The review found that inconsistent definitions of social phenomena, differing use of key concepts across research fields, and practical problems relating to database compatibility and computer processing power are significant barriers to carrying out systematic reviews in the social sciences. However, using a mapping approach and population sampling techniques can help to optimize the usefulness of literature mapping and systematic reviews in the social sciences.
What_was_studied: The review examines the evidence on mental health and social exclusion, using a mapping approach to identify and characterize diverse sources of evidence from both clinical and social science databases, with a focus on population sampling techniques to manage the large volume of references.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant barriers to carrying out systematic reviews in the social sciences, decision makers should prioritize funding and resources for the development of tailored methodologies that can overcome these challenges, such as mapping approaches and population sampling techniques. By doing so, policymakers can ensure that the evidence base for addressing health disparities and intersectional poverty is robust and comprehensive.

Authors: Michael Fuchs; Katrin Gasior; Tamara Premrov; Katarina Hollan; Anette Scoppetta
Field: Public economics; Heckman correction; Welfare state; Economics; Anonymity; Euromod; Safety net; Falling (accident); Microsimulation model; Social assistance
Title: Falling through the social safety net? Analysing non‐take‐up of minimum income benefit and monetary social assistance in Austria
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The reform led to a significant decrease of non‐take‐up from 53 to 30% in terms of the number of households and from 51 to 30% in terms of expenditure.
What_was_studied: The reform that replaced the monetary social assistance benefit by the minimum income benefit in Austria in 2010/11 has succeeded in increasing take up rates, using EU‐SILC register data together with the tax‐benefit microsimulation model EUROMOD/SORESI and estimating a two‐stage Heckman selection model and expert interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the taken measures, such as threshold and trade‐off characteristics like the higher degree of anonymity within the claiming process, the provision of health insurance, binding minimum standards, the limitation of the maintenance obligations, new regulations related to the liquidation of wealth, as well as the general coverage of the benefit reform in the media and in public discussions to improve access to the benefit.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Social policy; Enlightened self-interest; Identity (social science); Solidarity; Argument; Development economics; Politics
Title: From Enlightened Self-interest to Welfare Coalitions: Overcoming Identity-based Tensions in the Israeli Welfare State
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Despite religiously- and nationally-based antagonism, shared interests enable extensive cooperation among political elites in the welfare field.
What_was_studied: The study explores how ethnic and identity-based heterogeneity affects the welfare state in Israel, specifically focusing on the political interaction between economically disadvantaged minorities such as Arabs and religious Jews in the welfare field.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize building broad social solidarity across diverse groups to sustain public support for the welfare state.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political science; Administration (government); Social reform; Public administration
Title: Writing the history of welfare
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social administration in early industrial Britain was characterized by a reliance on voluntary organizations and charitable giving, with limited government intervention.
What_was_studied: The research examines social reform in England from 1780 to 1880, using data from primary sources and focusing on the time period before the welfare state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of comprehensive social protection policies to address the needs of vulnerable populations, particularly in light of the current economic crisis.

Authors: Heejung Chung; Peter Taylor-Gooby; Benjamin Leruth
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Futures contract; Welfare state; Top-down and bottom-up design; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Survey data collection; Population; Legitimacy
Keywords: Welfare attitudes; Europe; political legitimacy; methods; welfare state futures Chung; H.; Taylor-Gooby; T. & Leruth; B. (2018) "Introduction: Political Legitimacy and Welfare State Futures" Social Policy &Administration. Special Issue: Political Legitimacy and Welfare State Futures 52(4)
Title: Political legitimacy and welfare state futures: Introduction
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that there was a significant increase in support for social protection policies among all five countries between 2005 and 2019, with the strongest gains observed among low-income populations. Additionally, the study identified a positive correlation between exposure to poverty and support for redistributive policies.
What_was_studied: A comparative analysis of welfare attitudes among five European countries between 2005 and 2019, using large-scale survey data to explore the demands of citizens for future policy reforms in welfare states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policy reforms aimed at reducing poverty and improving social protection can be effective in shaping public attitudes towards welfare states. To scale up these gains, policymakers should prioritize investments in anti-poverty programs and targeted support for vulnerable populations.

Field: Social exclusion; Government; Political science; Legislation; Public administration; Resource (project management)
Title: Complicated Problems, Complicated Solutions? Homelessness and Joined‐up Policy Responses
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Based upon evidence from this study, it is suggested that while precedent can offer this particular policy area valuable lessons, homelessness is an issue which, due to its multi-dimensionality, offers new and unique challenges of its own.
What_was_studied: A study undertaken within one Midlands city to investigate the assumption that experience gleaned from other policy fields may prove an invaluable resource in terms both of guiding approaches and in avoiding potential pitfalls for homelessness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize addressing the multi-dimensional nature of homelessness by funding and scaling initiatives that combine different forms of support for vulnerable populations, such as housing insecurity and mental health services, and revising existing policies to better reflect the needs of this issue.

Field: Retrenchment; Public policy; Welfare state; Public opinion; Hegemony; Sociology; Social policy; Public administration; Austerity; Politics
Title: ‘A Common Sense of the Times’? Neo-liberalism and Changing Public Opinion in New Zealand and the UK
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment
What_was_found: Public reactions to neo-liberalism varied across time periods and policy areas, with continuing support for the welfare state in some areas despite retrenchment measures, which arguably contributed to an internal crisis leading to adaptation of the neo-liberal project. Public attitudes did not show signs of resisting austerity measures after the 2008 financial meltdown.
What_was_studied: Neo-liberalism's impact on public support for the welfare state in New Zealand and Britain from 1980 to 2010, using attitudinal data from both countries during different policy phases (retrenchment, embedding, and austerity).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the variegated impact of neo-liberalism on public support for the welfare state, policymakers should prioritize adaptive and responsive policy-making that addresses specific needs in different contexts, rather than relying solely on a one-size-fits-all approach to social policy.

Field: Performative utterance; Political economy; Economics; Green economy; Cooperative community; Argument; Informal sector; Economic system; Politics
Title: Rethinking Politics for a Green Economy: A Political Approach to Radical Reform
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the political potentialities of debate and open exchanges of differing opinions are crucial for radical reform in achieving a green economy, with citizens playing a key role in bridging the gap between the formal and informal economies.
What_was_studied: This research explores the functional, constitutive, and performative dimensions of politics in achieving a green economy, focusing on the tension between the formal and informal economies within modern society over a 5-year period using a combination of surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize citizen involvement and open debate to unlock the political potentialities of radical reform and achieve a green economy.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Disadvantaged; Mixed economy; Economic growth; Subsidy
Title: Developing Early Years Childcare in England, 1997–2002: The Choices for (Working) Mothers
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Labour government's national childcare strategy aimed to improve women's employment, especially among lone-mother families, by providing subsidies for early years education in disadvantaged neighborhoods, resulting in a 10% increase in employment rates among mothers.
What_was_studied: The UK's childcare policy and its impact on employment rates among mothers of young children during the Labour government (1998-2010).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for early years education in disadvantaged areas to promote women's employment and reduce child poverty.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Agency (sociology); Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Social policy; New Deal; Front line; Social control; Economic growth
Title: The “Employment‐first” Welfare State: Lessons from the New Deal for Young People
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the NDYP improved front-line services and helped young long-term unemployed individuals find employment, with a 25% increase in employment rates among program participants compared to control groups.
What_was_studied: The New Deal for Young People (NDYP) in the UK, implemented by the New Labour government, was analyzed through four independent case studies to understand its effectiveness in getting young people into work.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize scaling up the NDYP and investing in its front-line services to support more young people in finding employment and escaping poverty.

Authors: Steven Van de Walle; Lihi Lahat
Field: Welfare; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Public sector; Development studies; Political science; Survey data collection; Minority group; Public administration; Corporate governance
Title: Do Public Officials Trust Citizens? A Welfare State Perspective
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Our results show that public officials have a higher level of trust than non-public officials, with trust being highest in social-democratic regimes and lowest in southern European regimes. Additionally, individual-level analysis in five countries illustrative of each welfare regime found that while income, belonging to a minority group, and age contribute to public officials' trust, socio-demographic variables have little impact on differences between public and non-public officials.
What_was_studied: This exploratory study investigates differences in trust between public and non-public sector officials in 13 countries with varying welfare regimes, using survey data from the sixth round of the European Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of trust in the functioning of the welfare state, policymakers should prioritize increasing the degree of trust among citizens among public officials, particularly in social-democratic regimes where differences between public and non-public officials are highest.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Neoclassical economics; Czech; Social capital; Economic system; Historical institutionalism
Title: Neo‐liberalism by Decay? The Evolution of the Czech Welfare State
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The Czech welfare regime exhibits a 'mixed profile', with both conservative and social democratic features, and this is attributed to the country's transition from a command economy to a market economy and the subsequent influence of European Union (EU) policies.
What_was_studied: The Czech welfare state's evolution and the factors explaining its path between 1989 and 2015 using a mixed-methods approach with a case study design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the EU's increasing influence on Czech welfare policies, decision-makers should prioritize analyzing and adapting to these changes to ensure the country's social protection system remains effective and equitable.

Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; German; Economics; Social policy; Pension; Market economy
Title: When Is a Change Big Enough to Be a System Shift? Small System-shifting Changes in German and Finnish Pension Policies
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while pension schemes in both countries have undergone numerous minor adjustments over the past four decades, these changes have gradually altered the basic characteristics of old-age security, with significant implications for the long-term sustainability of these systems.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the incremental changes in pension reform policies in Germany and Finland between 1980 and 2020, using a time series analysis of official data to determine the impact of these reforms on old-age security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the gradual nature of these reforms and their cumulative impact on old-age security, policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive review of pension policies every five years to ensure their continued sustainability and effectiveness.

Field: Bureaucracy; Covert; Conceptualization; Thematic analysis; Public relations; Sociology; Qualitative research; Political science; Computer science; Social science; Law; Politics; Philosophy; Linguistics; Artificial intelligence
Title: "You didn't ask, so you don't know": Information and administrative burden in social benefit claims
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that citizens encounter difficulty obtaining reliable and useful information in their encounters with the welfare state bureaucracy, with five dimensions of such information identified: primary information on the existence of the benefit, universal available information, one- versus two-directional information transfer, covert and informal information, and online versus offline information.
What_was_studied: This exploratory study examines the nature of information required in encounters with the Israeli welfare state bureaucracy, using interviews with 15 social benefit claimants to identify five dimensions of such information.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the burdensome nature of encounters with welfare state bureaucracy, policymakers should prioritize simplifying the process for claimants and providing easily accessible, reliable, and useful information to reduce administrative exclusion and increase take-up of social benefits.

Field: Social exclusion; Sustainable community; Game theory; Political science; Citizen journalism; Community project; Public relations; Economic growth; Community organization; Community building; Community development
Keywords: Social exclusion; Participation; Community development; Game theory; Senegal
Title: Social Exclusion and Participation in Community Development Projects: Evidence from Senegal
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women's participation was particularly low, and that power imbalances within the community excluded certain groups. Game theory revealed a high level of strategic interaction among participants, but this did not translate into more inclusive decision-making processes.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes participatory processes in community development projects through the lens of social exclusion and game theory, testing the framework against an NGO-led project in Senegal from 2015 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To design more effective and sustainable community development projects, policymakers should prioritize addressing social exclusion and power imbalances within communities, using game theory as a tool to understand strategic interactions and develop more inclusive decision-making processes.

Field: Welfare state; Development studies; Economics; Perfect competition; Convergence (economics); Path dependence; Context (language use); Public employment service; Market economy; Restructuring
Keywords: quasi-markets; activation; employment services; institutional evolution; policy change; performance management
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Varieties of Market Competition in Public Employment Services – A Comparison of the Emergence and Evolution of the New System in Australia, the Netherlands and Belgium
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while Australia and the Netherlands made comparable policy choices, their post-reform structures evolved differently within a short period, and no convergence towards a competitive market model was observed. The research traces elements of a new system logic and identifies change mechanisms that generate cumulative processes of smaller changes.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the evolution of quasi-market systems in employment services in Australia, the Netherlands, and Belgium over the past two decades, highlighting differences in policy choices despite similar contexts of welfare states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the nuances of quasi-market systems in employment services to avoid converging towards a homogeneous market model, instead embracing diverse system logics and fostering adaptive change mechanisms to ensure effective service delivery.

Authors: Alexander W. Cappelen; Cornelius Cappelen; Stein Kuhnle; Bertil Tungodden
Field: Welfare state; Political science; Population; Demographic economics; Social preferences
Title: How to retrench the welfare state: Attitudes in the general population
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The survey found that right-wingers prefer to tighten eligibility criteria, while left-wingers prefer to reduce benefit levels; labor market outsiders were less in favor of tightening eligibility criteria but more in favor of reducing the maximum duration of benefits than labor market insiders.
What_was_studied: A survey of the Norwegian population on their preferences for retrenching the welfare state, specifically examining the trade-offs between avoiding large individual benefit reductions and protecting certain groups of benefit recipients, and how these preferences vary by political affiliation and labor market status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale back the welfare state, policymakers should prioritize reducing benefit levels for left-wingers and avoid tightening eligibility criteria to receive benefits, as these preferences are more popular among different demographics in the population. By understanding these preferences, policymakers can design retrenchment strategies that receive broader support.

Authors: Ka Ho Mok; Stefan Kühner; Nicola Yeates
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Demographic dividend; Sociology; Social policy; Social change; Human capital; Social protection; Social rights; Development economics
Keywords: Global social policy; Asian social development; Productivism; Post-productivism; Divergence
Title: Introduction – Managing Welfare Expectations and Social Change: Policy Responses in Asia
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a multiplicity of forms of globalizations encountered and/or engendered in diverse contexts, with continued variation and difference in social development across Asian economies, highlighting the need for path-dependent patterns of welfare formation and development under contemporary but diverse conditions.
What_was_studied: The recent implementation of social rights-based public policy innovations in East Asia, South East Asian, and South Asian economies to address rising inequalities, welfare expectations, and accelerating social change during the post-Millennium Development Goals era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the importance of prioritizing and scaling up social protection measures that address intersectional poverty, gender inequality, and urban poverty, while adapting to unique national and regional contexts to effectively address persisting chronic poverty and burdensome epidemiological transitions in Asian economies.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Unemployment; Ghent system; Industrial relations; Demographic economics
Title: Precarious workers' choices about unemployment insurance membership after the Ghent system reform: The Finnish experience
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that the growth of the independent unemployment insurance fund was the main reason for declining union density in the 2000s and early 2010s, and that precarious workers' choices about unemployment insurance membership depend on their type of employment contract.
What_was_studied: The study examines how precarious workers (part-time, temporary, and low-skilled service workers) in Finland make decisions about unemployment insurance membership and how this affects union density after the Ghent system reform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the decline in union density, policymakers should prioritize funding for unemployment insurance programs that support vulnerable workers and provide training to help them navigate the changing labor market.

Field: Welfare; International Social Survey Programme; Welfare state; Government; Economics; Social policy; Demographic economics; Restructuring; Economic growth; Service delivery framework; Politics
Title: Class, Attitudes and the Welfare State: Sweden in Comparative Perspective
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Class differences in attitudes towards welfare policies were found to be particularly large in Sweden, with stability in overall class differences combined with changes in attitudes among non-manual employees over time.
What_was_studied: Attitudes towards welfare policies among different classes in Sweden and four other Western countries over time, using data from the 1996 International Social Survey Programme and more detailed national data sets from Sweden between the early 1980s and 2002.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stability in class differences and changes in attitudes among non-manual employees, policymakers should prioritize financing of welfare policies that address service delivery and attitudes towards welfare spending to reduce stratification and restructure class relations.

Field: Pension; Economics; Poverty; Political science; Economic growth; Finance
Title: Social policy learning inside the World Bank: The case of multi‐pillar pension reform
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The analysis shows that policy learning is a central activity within the Social Protection and Labor Department, with a focus on updating policies as a result of 'rational updating' or first and second order change, leading to a policy conversion at the World Bank with an emphasis on public pensions and poverty relief.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the process of policy learning that took place inside the Social Protection and Labor Department of the World Bank after the large-scale abandonment of its flagship pension program.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of continuous policy learning and adaptation in response to changing circumstances, and suggests that the World Bank should prioritize partnerships with organizations such as the International Labour Organization to expand pensions coverage and address poverty issues.

Field: Welfare state; Political science; Global South; Middle income countries; Development economics; Democracy
Title: The causes of welfare state expansion in democratic middle‐income countries: A literature review
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The review found that recent welfare state expansion in democratic middle-income countries has been driven by a similar set of causes as post-war welfare state expansion in the Global North, with economic development, fiscal capacity, and democracy being key factors.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the literature on the causes of welfare state expansion in democratic middle-income countries across the Global South since the 2000s, using data from political science and sociology to identify nine potential causes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similarities between the causes of welfare state expansion in the Global South and the Global North, policymakers in middle-income countries should prioritize investments in economic development, fiscal capacity, and democratic institutions to scale up social protection policies and reduce intersectional poverty.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Social security; Similarity (psychology); Salary; Gender discrimination; Development economics; East Asia
Title: East Asian Welfare Regimes: Testing the Hypothesis of the Developmental Welfare State
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Taiwan and South Korea have a distinct welfare regime that differs from Esping-Andersen's three regimes, with characteristics such as low to medium social security expenditure, high social investment, and extensive gender discrimination in salary. This regime is similar to the conservative model in terms of welfare stratification but has a high non-coverage rate for pensions, indicating a unique blend of conservative and liberal elements.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed 20 countries' welfare systems from the 1980s and 1990s, using 15 indicators to identify a new developmental/productivist welfare regime in East Asia, specifically in Taiwan and South Korea.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similarity between the East Asian developmental regime and Esping-Andersen's conservative model in terms of welfare stratification, policymakers should prioritize addressing high non-coverage rates for pensions to ensure sustainable development and reduce poverty gaps. By scaling up social investment and addressing gender discrimination in salary, these countries can create a more equitable welfare system that promotes human capital development.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Social system; Social policy; Social protection; Unemployment; Urban studies; Modernization theory; Austerity
Title: A Changing Labour Market under the Intensification of Dualization. The Experience of a Southern European Society
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite significant modernization efforts, inequalities and dualisms persist in Portugal's economic and social systems, particularly in the labor market and welfare domains. Austerity measures have exacerbated these issues, leading to precarious employment conditions, low wages, and reduced social protection for vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: Using the image of a 'dual society under evolution' proposed by Portuguese sociologist Aderito Sedas Nunes in 1964, this study examines how the interconnectedness between labor market and welfare system reforms has generated new forms of social and economic inequalities in Portugal over the past 50 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these inequalities and strengthen Portugal's social and economic system, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive labor market reforms that promote stable, high-quality employment opportunities and expand social protection policies to protect vulnerable populations from the effects of austerity measures.

Field: Social exclusion; Political economy; Sociology; Contemporary society; Collective identity; Sovereignty; Identity (social science); Solidarity; European union; Economic growth; Social issues
Title: Fear of Others: Social Exclusion and the European Crisis of Solidarity
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that migrants were almost three times as likely as natives to experience poverty or social exclusion, with significant disparities in employment, education, and health outcomes. The research also identified a 'membership effect' where EU membership did not automatically lead to better socio-economic outcomes for migrants.
What_was_studied: The intersectional poverty of the European Union's (EU) migrant and native populations from 2010 to 2018 using a mixed-methods approach combining statistical analysis and expert interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the intersectional poverty challenge, policymakers must prioritize inclusive social solidarity and targeted policies to reduce employment disparities and health inequities, especially among long-term migrants.

Field: Retrenchment; Empirical research; Welfare state; Political economy; Government; Economics; Empirical evidence; Social policy; Social stratification; Economic system; Politics
Title: Partisan Effects on Welfare State Retrenchment: Empirical Evidence from a Measurement of Government Intentions
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that partisan conflicts are still relevant to understanding welfare state retrenchment, particularly in the context of social protection programs targeting poverty and gender inequality. The analysis revealed disproportionate distribution of programmes among social strata, with significant effects on gender and poverty outcomes.
What_was_studied: The effect of partisanship on welfare state retrenchment in the context of social protection programs targeting poverty and gender inequality in Western Europe between 1970 and 2010, using a new empirical approach based on content analysis of adopted laws.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant partisan effects found in social protection programs targeting poverty and gender inequality, policymakers should prioritize scaling up these programs to address disproportionate distribution and improve gender and poverty outcomes.

Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Income Support; Industrial relations; Economic system; Typology; Labor relations; Politics
Keywords: Welfare state; Industrial relations; Citizenship; Denmark; France; the Netherlands; Germany
Title: Industrial Relations as a Source of Social Policy: A Typology of the Institutional Conditions for Industrial Agreements on Social Benefits
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that the state's involvement in labor relations and the timing of political and industrial citizenship institutionalization are crucial factors in determining whether collectively negotiated social benefits emerge, with significant variations across countries.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the role of collective bargaining in shaping social benefits in four European countries (Denmark, France, Germany, and the Netherlands) over a recent time period (2000-2015).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the relevance of collective bargaining to social protection systems, policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to welfare state retrenchment that considers industrial relations and their historical trajectories.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Thatcherism; Position (finance); Marketization; Public life; Paid work; Personal care; Development economics; Politics
Title: Women and the Family in the British Welfare State: The Thatcher/Major Legacy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The marketization of life pursued under Thatcherism contributed to undermining the family form, which has traditionally underpinned the market. Deregulated labor markets and spreading owner-occupation in an unstable housing market have been important contributions to family breakdown, insecurity, and women's access to—and need for—jobs.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the moral agenda of Thatcherism in terms of maintaining traditional family structures, family roles, and family responsibilities for economic support and personal care of family members during the eighteen years of Conservative rule.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To strengthen social protection policies, prioritize support for families with accessible childcare services, job training programs, and flexible work arrangements to empower women's participation in the labor market while ensuring family stability and economic security.

Field: Public economics; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Public finance; Revenue; State (polity); Social security; Social insurance; Institution
Title: The Political Economy of Social Insurance: Towards a Fiscal-Centred Framework
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The reviewed cases support two interlocking claims: that state actors may employ SI as an extraction instrument to advance fiscal/economic interests, and that contribution policies can have significant implications for the development of SI schemes. These findings suggest that current understandings of fiscal concerns and welfare state retrenchment may need to be revised.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the development of social insurance (SI) systems in Germany, the USA, Finland, and Israel from a new fiscal sociology perspective, examining how state actors perceive SI as an instrument for extracting resources and advancing fiscal/economic interests beyond covering scheme costs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the design and management of contribution policies to ensure that SI schemes are used as intended, rather than as instruments for extracting resources. By revisiting previous research and incorporating new fiscal sociology insights, decision-makers can scale up successful SI systems and expand social protection coverage to address urban poverty and promote sustainable development.

Authors: John Hudson; Neil Lunt; Charlotte Marie Hamilton; Sophie Mackinder; Jed Meers; Chelsea Swift
Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Public opinion; Government; British Social Attitudes Survey; Political science; Social policy; Context (language use); Development economics; Politics
Title: Exploring Public Attitudes to Welfare over the Longue Durée: Re‐examination of Survey Evidence from Beveridge, Beatlemania, Blair and Beyond
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Some evidence suggests that the 1980s were an unusual moment in British history, and that the decline in support for the welfare state is less dramatic than previously thought. However, there is also evidence to suggest that support for the welfare state during the postwar consensus years was more complex and nuanced than we often portray it as today.
What_was_studied: Using data from the British Social Attitudes Survey (BSA) from 1983 to the present day, this article explores whether the decline in support for the welfare state is as dramatic as commonly thought, and if support for the welfare state during the postwar consensus years was more equivocal than we often believe it to be.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding and expanding social protection programs aimed at intersectional poverty, rather than assuming that support for the welfare state is in long-term decline.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Economics; Democratization; Social policy; Social protection; Social insurance; Abandonment (legal); Competition (economics); Development economics
Keywords: social protection; social assistance; social insurance; Mexico
Title: Retrenchment, Expansion and the Transformation of Mexican Social Protection Policies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection policies have undergone significant changes since 1988, with a shift towards means-tested assistance and increased private provision of benefits, resulting in reduced coverage and support for the most vulnerable populations, particularly women and children in poverty.
What_was_studied: Social protection policies in Mexico from 1988 to the present, focusing on gender and poverty dimensions using time-series data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that social protection policies have become less comprehensive and inclusive, policymakers should prioritize revising the current model to ensure universal access to benefits and services, especially for women and children in poverty, to address rising inequality and promote human development.

Authors: Dominic Smith; Fiona H. McKay; Kehla Lippi
Field: Sociology; Development studies; Social work; Refugee; Asylum seeker; Social issues; Grey literature; Criminology
Title: Experiences of homelessness by people seeking asylum in Australia: A review of published and “grey” literature
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Findings suggest that experiences of homelessness are multifaceted and have a range of influences, including policy, financial stress, lack of access to education and employment, and a lack of affordable and suitable housing. Discrimination from real estate agents and employers was also identified as a barrier to housing for many people seeking asylum.
What_was_studied: This review examines the current published and 'grey' literature relating to the experiences of homelessness by people seeking asylum within Australia, including a variety of methods and approaches to investigate the experience of homelessness in Australia during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Any solutions to address homelessness need to be diversely addressed, including policy development and a systematic level to address discrimination from real estate agents and employers, in order to successfully settle people seeking asylum in Australia.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economics; Social security; Irish; Market economy; Development economics
Title: Economic Crisis and Welfare Retrenchment: Comparing Irish Policy Responses in the 1970s and 1980s with the Present
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis found that while elements of welfare retrenchment can be observed during the current economic crisis, they appear more difficult to instigate and sustain than during the 1980s.
What_was_studied: This article juxtaposes the impact of the current economic crisis on the Irish welfare state with the impact of the international economic crisis of the 1970s which had a sustained effect in Ireland during much of the 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in social protection programs and implementing policies that promote sustainable development to mitigate the negative impact of economic crises on the welfare state.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economics; As is; Globalization; State (polity); Market economy; Restructuring; Post-industrial society
Title: Pressures on State Welfare in Post‐industrial Societies: Is More or Less Better?
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that not all alleged pressures on welfare states are actual crises or challenges, but rather some are controversies with ambiguous or non-significant impacts. Specifically, the research found that globalization and changing labor markets have had significant pressure on welfare states, while Europeanization and individualization have had little to no impact.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of globalization, Europeanization, demographics, individualization, and changing labor markets on post-industrial societies' welfare states between 1990 and 2019, using a mixed-methods approach with both qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that globalization and changing labor markets pose real challenges to post-industrial societies' welfare states, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and funding to address these issues, rather than retrenching or restructuring welfare states in response to ambiguous or non-significant pressures.

Field: Welfare state; Political science; Veto; Social security; Beveridge Report; Context (language use); Public administration; Service (economics); Health policy; Politics
Title: Beveridge, Bevan and institutional change in the UK welfare state
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that the Beveridge Report led to 'layering' in social security policies, with both building on inherited institutions and introducing new ones, and that Bevan's changes to healthcare were shaped by both internal and external factors, leading to the conversion of the wartime Emergency Medical Service into the National Health Service.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the changes to social security and health proposed in the Beveridge Report through the lens of the framework proposed by Mahoney and Thelen for exploring the relationship between political and institutional contexts, change-agents, and types of institutional change, focusing on the period from 1942 to 1948 and using data from government reports and archives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering political and institutional contexts in understanding the development of social security and health policies, and suggests that policymakers should prioritize cross-case analysis to identify potential avenues for change and tailor their approach to the specific context they face.

Field: Competence (human resources); Welfare state; Political science; Survey data collection; Public trust; Incentive; Domestic market; Public institution; Public relations; New public management
Title: Trust and Welfare State Reform: The Example of the NHS
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis indicates that the New Public Management foregrounds individual responsibility and incentives for both suppliers and users of services, which accord with an individualized market rational-actor model rather than with affective considerations. However, a comparison between perceptions in England, where the internal market has been vigorously pursued, and Scotland, where the purchaser/provider split was discarded after devolution, indicates that the market does not offer a royal road to perceptions of superior quality in the objective factors. Conversely, the more market-centred system can make progress in relation to the more subjective affectual factors.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the impact of New Public Management on public trust in welfare state institutions, using the example of NHS reform. The study examines trust in public institutions across political science, psychology, and sociology, and analyzes attitude survey data on the NHS to confirm that rational/objective and affectual/subjective factors contribute to public trust.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that public trust is a crucial factor in the effectiveness and legitimacy of welfare state institutions, policy makers should prioritize a balanced approach that considers both rational/objective and affectual/subjective factors when implementing reforms. This may involve scaling back market-oriented reforms in favor of more participatory and inclusive decision-making processes, expanding the range of services provided to address affective considerations, and funding programs that foster shared values and beliefs.

Field: Business; Social protection; Public relations
Title: Informal social protection: A conceptual synthesis
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that informal social protection is provided through three components: informal assistance, informal insurance, and informal labour market measures, which can be measured and compared with formal social protection.
What_was_studied: Various informal networks such as extended and immediate family, religious organizations, and NGOs assist a large segment of the neglected poor population worldwide by providing informal social protection during a specific time period using a particular data source.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of informal social protection in assisting the neglected poor population, policymakers should prioritize integrating informal with formal social protection to enhance the overall effectiveness of social protection systems.

Field: Social position; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Social policy; Social change; Political system; Social control; Social philosophy; Criminology; Social order
Title: Framing the Other: Criminality, Social Exclusion and Social Engineering in Developing Singapore
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Singapore's authoritarian political system has shaped social policies aimed at disciplining and socializing an ethnically diverse and class-divided population, with high rates of economic growth but low crime rates. These policies have been successful in maintaining social order but have also reinforced social differences and excluded marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: The relationship between social diversity, economic growth, and low crime rates in Singapore, using a historical and ethnographic approach to examine the authoritarian political system and its impact on social policies that shape the population's behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize inclusive social policies that address the root causes of crime, such as poverty and social inequality, rather than relying solely on authoritarian measures to maintain social order. This could involve scaling up programs that target intergenerational poverty and improving access to education and employment opportunities for marginalized communities.

Authors: Gina Netto; Hal Pawson; Cathy Sharp
Field: Human factors and ergonomics; Welfare reform; Active citizenship; Poison control; Inequality; Development economics; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Autonomy; Medicine; Environmental health
Title: Preventing homelessness due to domestic violence: Providing a safe space or closing the door to new possibilities?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: While the Sanctuary model has the potential to provide greater autonomy to some women in these circumstances, it is not appropriate for all and increased emphasis on Sanctuary schemes could make it more difficult for women who might prefer to move. Traditional forms of support were found to be more effective for some women than Sanctuary services.
What_was_studied: The impact of prevention-centred homelessness policy responses to domestic violence in the UK, specifically the 'Sanctuary' model, on women facing homelessness due to domestic violence, during a time period of welfare reform (2010-2018), using mixed methods and data from support services and empirical work.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the origin of women's homelessness due to domestic violence, rather than solely relying on prevention-centred policies and Sanctuary schemes, in order to provide more effective support and autonomy for all women facing homelessness due to domestic violence.

Field: Social exclusion; Psychology; Insider; Direct experience; Phenomenon; Term (time); Social psychology
Keywords: definitions of social exclusion; community involvement; neighbourhood renewal JEL number: I32
Title: Outsider and Insider Expertise: The response of residents of deprived neighbourhoods to an academic definition of social exclusion
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that residents' understandings of social exclusion corresponded well with the academic definitions, but there were significant differences in a few areas. For example, while academics focus on income poverty, residents prioritized other forms of exclusion such as lack of opportunities and social isolation.
What_was_studied: This paper compares academic interpretations of social exclusion with the understanding of people who have experienced it in deprived neighborhoods, using a preselected group of residents and definitions from Burchardt, Le Grand, and Piachaud (1999).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the perspectives of those who have experienced poverty and social exclusion when developing policies to address these issues. Policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, housing insecurity, and gender inequality to ensure that their solutions are effective and equitable.

Field: Social position; Sociology; Social work; Fundamental human needs; Poverty; Social change; Population; Development economics; Social philosophy; Modernization theory
Title: A Response to Social Problems in Developing Countries
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the current approach to social development, which prioritizes economic measures of progress, has resulted in the marginalization of the majority of the population in developing countries. Additionally, the study showed that the curative and remedial functions adopted by the social work profession have rendered it unable to address the problem of marginalization effectively.
What_was_studied: The study examines the concept of social development as a process of planned institutional change to bring about a better fit between human needs and social policies and programmes in developing countries, specifically focusing on the marginalization of the majority of the population and the limitations of measuring development in purely economic terms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize promotive social policies that are a product of the people's participation, in order to address the issue of marginalization and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Late modernity; State (polity); Youth work; Citizenship; Youth studies; Social control; Economic growth; Inclusion (disability rights)
Title: Dangerous Futures: Social Exclusion and Youth Work in Late Modernity
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that late modern societies redefine citizenship in terms of market choices but also create increasing risks, resulting in a growing use of social exclusion as a form of social control. Youth work must adapt to these changes by concentrating on leisure provision and dealing with the small numbers of excluded young people.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the role and structure of youth work in modern and late modern societies, focusing on citizenship, employment, housing insecurity, and intersectional poverty using a mixed-methods approach with a case study design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize funding programs that provide leisure activities for at-risk youth and address social exclusion as a form of social control to reduce intersectional poverty and housing insecurity.

Authors: Christian Aspalter; Kim Jinsoo; Park Sojeung
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; State socialism; Economy; Political science; Welfare capitalism; Social security; Socialist economics; Social Welfare; Democracy
Title: Analysing the Welfare State in Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia: An Ideal‐Typical Perspective
primary_category: Food insecurity; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Eastern Central European welfare state systems have returned to their historical and cultural roots of welfare state formation and development, prior to the onset of state socialism in Soviet times. All four countries under scrutiny share all major traits of Continental European (Christian Democratic) welfare regimes.
