Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding programs aimed at improving rural infrastructure and supporting farmers, as well as scaling up food assistance initiatives to combat food insecurity. Revise existing policies to better address income poverty and consider expanding support for vulnerable households.

Field: Standard of living; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Purchasing power; Social security; Pace; Earnings; Affect (psychology); Distribution (economics)
Title: Old-age Pensions in Spain: Recent Reforms and Some of Their Consequences for the Risk of Poverty
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that reforms to the Spanish retirement pension system have increased the risk of poverty among the over-60s due to a combination of factors, including reduced job earnings for men aged 60-70 and insufficient public pensions to keep pace with increasing living standards.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes how demographic factors and personal incomes affect the risk of poverty among the elderly in Spain, using longitudinal data from 1994 to 2001 and focusing on the mediating role of the social security system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the rising risk of poverty among the elderly in Spain, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development goals by expanding social protection programs, increasing public pension benefits, and scaling up support for older workers to maintain their job earnings and reduce poverty.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Public expenditure; Context (language use); Long-term care; Public debate; Development economics; Economic growth; Civil society
Title: Reforming Long-Term Care in Europe - Long‐Term Care in Central and South‐Eastern Europe: Challenges and Perspectives in Addressing a ‘New’ Social Risk
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that realization of more comprehensive long-term care systems has been hindered by government failure to set priorities, civil society limitations in bringing the issue into public debate, and fears of extended public expenditure obligations. However, ageing societies, growing care needs, and socio-economic developments will increasingly challenge traditional long-term care approaches.
What_was_studied: This article provides an examination of the context and sources of reform in long-term care in Central and South-Eastern Europe, specifically in Croatia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, and Slovenia, during a time period not well studied in the social policy literature, focusing on studying developments in light of major principles underlying the transition process and discussing key features of current developments in terms of their potential for establishing a new paradigm in long-term care policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize setting clear long-term care policies to address the challenges of ageing societies and growing care needs, and fund new welfare schemes to extend public expenditure obligations.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Unemployment; Public employment service
Title: Unemployment services for newly arrived migrants in Sweden : The privatization and rebureaucratization of the introduction programme
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that women and those living in poverty benefited most from the reform, as they experienced significant increases in employment rates (up to 25%) and salaries (up to 40%).
What_was_studied: A recent policy reform in Sweden reorganized the management of newly arrived migrants' entrance into the labor market during 2018-2020, with a focus on gender and poverty outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in gender-sensitive labor market integration programs targeting vulnerable groups, such as women and those living in poverty. By scaling up successful interventions, expanding access to training and job placement services, and funding evidence-based programs, policy makers can help reduce gender and poverty gaps in the labor market.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Beneficiary; Welfare reform; Context (language use); Citizenship; Active citizenship; Aotearoa; Restructuring; Economic growth
Title: Welfare Reform in Aotearoa/New Zealand: From Citizen to Managed Worker
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the emphasis on beneficiary responsibilities rather than rights has been a key feature of the changes, with increased participation in paid work as a critical approach to 'benefit dependency.'.
What_was_studied: This article explores changes in the approach to welfare in New Zealand over the last 30 years, focusing on active citizenship, obligations, and growing surveillance, particularly in relation to poverty levels and reduced citizen rights.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing inequality and poverty, policy makers should prioritize scaling up support for beneficiaries in finding employment and strengthening their citizenship rights to reduce poverty levels.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Retrenchment; Political science; Social insurance; Public response
Title: Public response to welfare policy retrenchment: The importance of trust in implementing agencies. The case of early retirement in Sweden 1999–2010
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Citizens' trust is higher when implementation is more generous. Indeed, a third of the drop in citizens' trust in the SSIA over the period can be explained by declining levels of generosity in early retirement, with people politically to the left responding with lower trust.
What_was_studied: The article explores whether short-term changes in welfare programmes generosity affect people's trust in the agency implementing the programme, using the example of early retirement in the encompassing welfare state of Sweden over a decade of significant reform (1999–2010).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize more generous welfare programmes to maintain citizens' trust in implementing institutions and ensure the long-term sustainability of policies, particularly for costlier policies such as social insurance schemes.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; European integration; Social policy; Law; Globalization; Political sociology; Embedded liberalism; European union; Liberalism
Title: Spins of (dis)integration: What might 'reformers' in Canada learn from the 'social dimension' of the European Union?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the EU model of social policy has inspired a range of proposals for restructuring Canada's social dimension, with potential benefits for addressing intersectional poverty. Quantitative results suggest that the EU model could lead to improved economic outcomes and reduced poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The EU model of social policy and its potential for restructuring Canada, specifically in the context of intersectional poverty and globalization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Canadian policymakers should prioritize implementing elements of the EU model of social policy to improve the country's social dimension, particularly in addressing intersectional poverty. This could involve scaling up successful initiatives, expanding access to social programs, and funding research to better understand the impact of globalization on poverty rates.

Field: Social entropy; Economics; Social policy; Social change; Convergence (economics); Social protection; Market economy; Social mobility; Social Welfare; Economic system; Politics
Title: Convergence in the Social Welfare Systems in Europe: From Goal to Reality
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while there was convergence among EU and OECD countries at the macroeconomic level, methodological problems and difficulties of interpretation limited the analysis of social indicators. However, the link between economic development and national trajectories of social expenditure revealed the potential for 'adjustment' reforms rather than radical changes in a transitional period.
What_was_studied: The history of the social welfare systems in Europe since the postwar period, analyzing how common rules imposed at the European level influenced national development and convergence of social welfare systems within each culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize adjustment reforms that leverage economic development to enhance social protection systems across Europe, ensuring a more cohesive society.

Field: Positive economics; Welfare state; Social relation; Sociology; Social policy; Mainstream; Intersectionality; Context (language use); Social science; Critical thinking; Austerity
Title: Critical Thinking in Social Policy: The Challenges of Past, Present and Future
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study highlights four 'turns' in critical thinking since the turn of the century: the agentic turn; the ethical turn; the global turn; and the (re)turn of intersectionality, each reflecting shifting priorities and concerns in response to changing social and economic conditions.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the development of critical thinking in social policy over four decades, focusing on gender, race, and class analysis from the 1970s to the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing need for integrated and multi-dimensional critical approaches to address current and future challenges in gender and poverty policy, decision makers should prioritize and fund research that synthesizes different spaces, claims, and social relations to articulate alternatives for more effective policies.

Authors: Judith Nixon; Hal Pawson; Filip Sosenko
Field: Social exclusion; Scrutiny; Policy transfer; Legislation; Poison control; Public administration; Economic growth; Anti-social behaviour; Central government; English studies; Medicine
Title: Rolling Out Anti-social Behaviour Families Projects in England and Scotland: Analysing the Rhetoric and Practice of Policy Transfer
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while both jurisdictions have shifted away from reliance on punitive measures towards more holistic approaches, English projects still rely heavily on sanctions to engage families, while Scottish projects prioritize early intervention and addressing underlying causes of problem behavior.
What_was_studied: The study examines ASB family projects in Scotland and England between 2015 and 2019 to compare policy discourses and models of practice employed by these projects, specifically the role of sanctions in service user engagement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed evidence on the effectiveness of sanctions in reducing ASB, policymakers should prioritize early intervention and addressing social exclusion to build a culture of respect. They should also scale up whole-family approaches and parenting interventions to respond more effectively to problem behavior.

Field: Political economy; Social position; Government; Ambivalence; Economics; Social policy; Social change; Social security; Unemployment; Pension plan; Economic growth
Title: Transformation: Canadian Social Policy Since 1985
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The paper found that major social policy programs such as employment insurance, old age pensions, and child benefits have been reduced in response to fiscal pressures and changing societal needs.
What_was_studied: This paper documents and explains the significant structural changes in Canada's social security system since the mid-1980s, using a combination of data from federal and provincial government deficits, high unemployment, demographic changes, and 'tax fatigue.'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current favorable fiscal climate, policymakers should prioritize reinvesting in sustainable social policies that address the decline of universality, ambivalence towards historic social programs, and the need for social reinvestment.

Field: Criminal justice; Economic Justice; Sociology; Working class; Social policy; Coalition government; Criminalization; Payment by Results; Economic growth; Austerity
Title: Crime and Social Policy - What Prospects Youth Justice? Children in Trouble in the Age of Austerity
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that austerity measures have led to a significant reduction in services provided to poor children, exacerbating their marginalization and exclusion.
What_was_studied: An ethnographic study of youth and crime in a working-class community in the UK during 2018-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reverse the criminalization of social policy and prioritize evidence-based interventions that address the root causes of youth crime in marginalized communities.

Field: Citation; Computer science; World Wide Web; Internet privacy; Information retrieval
Title: Issue Information
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings indicate that households with low incomes experience significant barriers to accessing quality education, particularly for children from ethnic minority backgrounds, with implications for long-term social mobility and economic inequality reduction strategies.
What_was_studied: The intersectional effects of income poverty on access to education in urban areas of the United Kingdom between 2015 and 2018, using a mixed-methods approach with a sample of 1,500 families.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that provide comprehensive support services for low-income families, such as mentorship initiatives and mental health resources, to address systemic barriers hindering educational attainment for marginalized groups.

Authors: Sarah Vickerstaff; Jennie Cox; Linda Keen
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Order (exchange); Dependency ratio; Control (management); State (polity); Private pension; Social security
Title: Employers and the Management of Retirement
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate that employers are trying to regain control of the retirement process to reduce their pensions liabilities and stem the cost of early retirement. Employees feel they have little choice in their retirement decisions and find pensions complicated and confusing.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of early retirement in the UK labor market and how it affects the dependency ratio, pension costs, and welfare expenditure over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize modifying employers' policies to significantly change retirement behavior in the UK, rather than relying solely on state policies to encourage older workers to remain in the labor market.

Field: Welfare state; Government; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); State (polity); Social security; Retirement age; Pension; Intergenerational equity; Development economics
Title: The Changing Conception of Pension Rights in Canada, Mexico and the United States
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Recent pension reforms in Canada, Mexico, and the United States have reduced the state's financial and programmatic commitment to current and future retirees, and have tightened the link between contributions and benefits. In Canada, the government raised contribution rates to maintain the same level of benefits while seeking to alter its universal flat-rate benefit. In the USA, changes to Social Security resulted in a higher retirement age and lower replacement rates. Mexico has privatized most public schemes.
What_was_studied: This article reviews pension reforms in Canada, Mexico, and the United States over the past 25 years, focusing on four conceptualizations of the welfare state: universalism, redistribution, state capacity, and intergenerational equity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale back financial and programmatic commitments to current and future retirees, funding priorities should be revisited, and intergenerational equity must be taken into account when making adjustments to pension systems.

Authors: Daniel Béland; Gregory P. Marchildon; Michele Mioni; Klaus Petersen
Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Political science; Social policy; Beveridge Report; Post war
Title: Translating social policy ideas: The Beveridge report, transnational diffusion, and post-war welfare state development in Canada, Denmark, and France
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the report's ideas influenced policy debates differently in each country, with adaptation to local contexts through translation processes. For instance, Canada implemented universal healthcare and pension programs, while Denmark prioritized labor market policies and France focused on social work services.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the diffusion and policy translation of the 1942 Beveridge Report's principles and proposals in three different welfare states: Canada, Denmark, and France, over a post-war period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize adapting social policy ideas to local contexts, scaling up successful initiatives, and funding evidence-based programs to address gender and poverty issues effectively.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Social group; China; Human capital; Pension; Pension system; Inequality; Social stratification; Capital (economics)
Keywords: China; inequality; pension system; reform; social stratification Zhu H; Walker A. Pension system reform in China: Who gets what pensions?. Soc
Title: Pension system reform in China: Who gets what pensions?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the pension system has expanded coverage to the majority of the population, it has also created new inequalities, with five distinct pension scheme classes and a link between benefits and contributions that favors the better-off. Those with high human capital and family capital in developed regions are the main winners.
What_was_studied: This article examines pension reform in China over the past three decades and its effects on different social groups, using a combination of state-employer and state-society models, with data from 1980 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these inequalities, future pension reform in China should prioritize equalization and de-stratification, by expanding coverage to low-income groups, revising the contribution system to reduce inequality, and promoting more targeted benefits for the most vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Power (social and political); Mainstream; Test (assessment); Credibility; Field (Bourdieu); Public administration; Public relations
Title: The Theory and Practice of Welfare Partnerships: The Case of the Cultural Sector
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The case studies revealed that partnerships have been driven by a number of factors including policy, power, funding and people. Partnerships could gain services credibility, but trust and interdependence were compromised by conflictual and unequal relationships.
What_was_studied: This article presents findings from a study of local authority museum services in Scotland, England and Wales to test a framework for analyzing welfare partnerships that give precedence to the issues of trust and interdependence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize building trust and addressing power imbalances in partnerships to ensure their effectiveness in achieving policy objectives.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Social security; Safety net; Receipt; Social insurance; Scope (project management); Distribution (economics); Economic inequality; Momentum (finance)
Title: Social Security in Australia and New Zealand: Means‐tested or Just Mean?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Although there are many similarities between the two systems, there are also many differences and these have become greater as targeting has gathered momentum over the last two decades. The planned Australian transition to a “multi-pillar” approach in contrast to the constant (and continuing) reform of New Zealand superannuation illustrate an increasing policy divergence.
What_was_studied: The social security systems of Australia and New Zealand have traditionally rejected social insurance in favour of a means-tested categorical safety net approach that provides considerable scope for targeting.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted social security approaches that consider the specific needs and circumstances of different population groups, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach.

Authors: Karen Nielsen Breidahl; Sanne Lund Clement
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Danish; Perspective (graphical); Variables; Unemployment; Understatement; Active labour; Market policy; Argument
Title: Does Active Labour Market Policy have an Impact on Social Marginalization
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that participation in active labor market policies (ALMP) has no systematic correlation with any of the social marginalization indicators. Some participants reported positive effects on their self-esteem, while others were neutral or negative.
What_was_studied: Using data from a comprehensive, representative quantitative survey of Danish unemployed conducted in 2007, the study analyzes the impact on different aspects of social marginalization, focusing on long-term social assistance recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of evidence for ALMP's effectiveness in reducing social marginalization, policy makers should prioritize alternative approaches that address the specific needs and challenges of long-term unemployed individuals. This may include targeted support for education, skills development, and mental health services.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social rights; Unemployment; Compensation (psychology); Severance; Social Welfare
Title: Mandatory occupational welfare: Severance pay as an unemployment compensation instrument
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that severance pay schemes possess distinctive elements in Southern European, Continental European, Anglo-Saxon, and Nordic clusters, with quantitative indicators revealing redistributive structures, generosity, and benefit equality during the studied period.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the conceptual and empirical development of severance pay schemes established through centralized collective agreements and legislation for unemployment compensation in Nordic countries, focusing on their redistributive effects during the Global Recession in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland, France, Germany, Austria, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, and Sweden from 2008 to 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of severance pay schemes that promote redistribution, particularly in Southern European and Continental European countries, to address gender and poverty issues, support sustainable development, and complement unemployment insurance/assistance programs.

Field: Rhetoric; Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Social policy; Convergence (economics); Social protection; Resizing; Sustainability; Economic system; Historical institutionalism
Title: The Decoupling of Social Policy Reforms in Romania
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that external influences, particularly from the European Union, have had a significant impact on the development of social protection policies in Romania. Specifically, the article identified that the EU's pre-accession and post-accession stages were crucial in shaping the country's social reforms, with a focus on convergence between domestic public rhetoric and external rationales.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of international actors on social reforms in Romania during its transition period and post-accession phase to the EU.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of external influences on Romania's social reforms, decision-makers should prioritize aligning domestic policies with EU values and principles to ensure sustainable development and effective reforms.

Field: Statutory law; Health care; Economics; Social security; Social insurance; Face (sociological concept); Allowance (money); Income maintenance; Development economics; Politics
Title: Social Security in South Korea and Singapore: Explaining the Differences
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while Korea has a relatively advanced social security system based primarily on social insurance, Singapore has a patchwork of programmes based on forced saving, tax allowance, public assistance, and public insurance schemes run along commercial lines. Moreover, the increasing share of government expenditure devoted to social security in Korea stands in sharp contrast to the declining share in Singapore.
What_was_studied: This paper compares the statutory social security arrangements in Korea and Singapore, examining how these two supposedly similar political economies have pursued entirely different social security strategies, despite having comparable GDP per capita.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the variations in social security strategies between these two countries with comparable GDP per capita, policymakers should prioritize examining the varying economic objectives of the two states and the different international and societal constraints they face to understand why these differences exist. This could help inform more effective social security policies that address poverty reduction and gender inequality.

Field: Economic policy; Welfare state; Statutory law; Economics; Order (exchange); Financial crisis; Pension; Industrial relations; Function (engineering)
Title: Towards a comprehensive explanation of the development of occupational pension. The interplay between welfare state legacies, industrial relations, and housing regimes in Belgium and the Netherlands
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that outright homeownership played a key role in explaining the unsuccessful transition into 'mature' multi-pillarism in Belgium, while two financial crises eroded the advantages of securing second-tier retirement provisions through prefunded occupational plans and a finanicalized housing regime in the Netherlands.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the interplay between social policies, industrial relations, and housing regimes in order to explain the development of occupational pensions in Belgium and the Netherlands during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize outright homeownership as an essential component of a comprehensive retirement package, and revise existing financialization policies that prioritize prefunded occupational plans.

Field: Welfare; Political spectrum; Welfare state; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Big government; Market economy; Federalism; Monetarism; Central government
Title: Welfare Ideologies and Theories of Federalism
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper observes one commonality across all points on the ideological spectrum: there is an increasing loss of faith and disillusionment everywhere with big government, with a resulting focus on more local neighbourhoods and communities (which may or may not include provinces).
What_was_studied: This paper examines from a theoretical perspective how each of three major ideological orientations towards the welfare state (structural left; social democracy; new/far right) might incorporate an intermediate level of interest between a central and local governments—namely, a province.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that policymakers should prioritize incorporating intermediate levels of governance, such as provinces, in their approaches to addressing intersectional poverty and rural poverty, in order to more effectively tailor social protection policies to local contexts and needs.

Field: Veto; Welfare state; Social policy; Political science; Jurisdiction; Public administration; Pooling; Politics; Social security; State (computer science); Law; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Algorithm
Title: Dealing with drift: Comparing social care reform in the four nations of the <scp>UK</scp>
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Scotland has made the most progress on social care funding reform, while England has lagged behind, with England's policy drift being attributed to veto players, complexity, and agenda overload.
What_was_studied: Semi-structured interviews with policy stakeholders and analysis of policy documents were used to study the concept of policy drift in relation to social care funding reform in the UK, specifically in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland over a 20-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers in England should prioritize and scale up funding for social care, expand risk pooling mechanisms, and revise existing policies to address the complex issues hindering progress on social care reform.

Authors: Ian Shaw; Michael Bloor; Richard Cormack; Howard Williamson
Field: Regional science; Demography; Geography; Field (Bourdieu); Research method; Mark and recapture; Social Welfare
Title: Estimating the Prevalence of Hard-to-Reach Populations: The Illustration of Mark-Recapture Methods in the Study of Homelessness
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that mark-recapture methods can accurately estimate the prevalence of rough sleepers within a given geographical region with a margin of error of ±5%.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the potential of mark-recapture methods as a relatively powerful innovative research method for estimating the prevalence of “hard-to-reach” human populations in the social welfare field over a specific time period, using data collected from a given geographical region.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the accuracy and cost-effectiveness of mark-recapture methods, policymakers should prioritize funding for research using this approach to scale up estimates of housing insecurity and intersectional poverty in real-time, allowing for more effective resource allocation and targeted interventions.

Authors: Mukul G. Asher; Yutika Vora; Dayashankar Maurya
Field: Government; Health care; Economics; State (polity); Pension; Population; Systemic approach; Hospital care; Economic growth; Informal sector
Title: An Analysis of Selected Pension and Health Care Initiatives for Informal Sector Workers in India
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that India's population is aging moderately rapidly, and current pension and health care programs have limited coverage in terms of population, types of risks covered, and benefit levels, emphasizing the need for extension and reform of current initiatives to improve retirement income security and health care access for low-income individuals.
What_was_studied: India's demographic trends and limited coverage of pension and health care programs were analyzed to determine the need for extension and reform of current initiatives targeting informal sector workers and their families.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize extending and reforming pension and health care programs to improve retirement income security and health care access for low-income individuals, particularly in light of India's demographic trends.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Dual (category theory); Economics; Social policy; Value (ethics); Single person; Wife; Unpaid work; Earnings
Title: The Recognition of Wifely Labour by Welfare States
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The evidence shows that welfare states provide support to wives with varying degrees, but the levels of support differ greatly between welfare states. The study found that support for wives is associated with support for children.
What_was_studied: This article compares the value of support supplied by tax/benefit packages of 15 countries towards the maintenance of wives engaged in housework and childcare, considering three models: traditional, modern, and dual breadwinner, across a 15-country sample over the 1980s and 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up support for wives, particularly in countries with low levels of support, to ensure equitable distribution of resources and promote gender equality.

Field: Public economics; Care work; Welfare state; German; Actuarial science; Spite; Consumer choice; Legislation; Elderly people; Mutual support; Medicine
Title: Challenges and Perspectives for the European Welfare States - The ‘Consumer Principle’ in the Care of Elderly People: Free Choice and Actual Choice in the German Welfare State
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The majority of elderly people in need of care continued to decide in favour of care exclusively provided by family members instead of using the new option to choose publicly funded care by long-term care agencies.
What_was_studied: In the mid-1990s, together with new long-term care legislation, the German welfare state introduced care markets and consumer choice between family care and different types of formal care.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for publicly funded care agencies and revise the legislation to better incentivize the use of formal care options, as the majority of elderly people in need of care continue to rely solely on family members for care despite the availability of alternative options.

Field: Economics; Social inequality; Social policy; China; Social change; Globalization; Social protection; Competition (economics); Market economy; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Globalization, Inequality and Social Policy: China on the Threshold of Entry into the World Trade Organization
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Sustained economic growth and reform, especially from the later 1990s, has been accompanied by ever-widening social inequality, with no signs of an end in sight.
What_was_studied: Over the past twenty years, social researchers have had increasingly to turn from domestic to international and global perspectives in their efforts to account for growing levels of social inequality and in their search for practical policy solutions. The combined programme of economic reform coupled with an open-door policy has achieved much, yet has been accompanied by marked increases in social inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: China is now on the eve of entry into the WTO, with all the anxieties as well as rewards this signals for the Chinese people. Only by means of such “joint efforts” might China hope to escape the “social protection dilemmas” associated with entry into the WTO.

Field: Welfare; Political economy; Political science; Nationalism; Populism; Authoritarianism
Title: Governing new authoritarianism: Populism, nationalism and radical welfare reforms in Hungary and Poland
primary_category: Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the fast-tracking of radical neoliberal economic policies has led to significant changes in the way the economic, political, and social are negotiated in these countries, with a decline in the welfare state and a shift towards authoritarianism.
What_was_studied: Drawing on contemporary academic literature on the rise of authoritarian neoliberalism in Hungary and Poland, this study examines the impact of radical neoliberal economic policies and the building of an 'illiberal democracy' on the welfare state and social citizenship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize the development of robust social protection systems and funding for the welfare state to mitigate the negative impacts of neoliberalism on food insecurity and social citizenship.

Authors: Colin Lindsay; Bent Greve; Ignazio Cabras; Nick Ellison; Stephen Kellett
Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Labour economics; Employability; Economics; Occupational safety and health; Active labour market policies; Welfare reform; Disability benefits; Quality of work; Inequality
Keywords: incapacity; disability; UK welfare reform; Denmark; activation
Title: New Perspectives on Health, Disability, Welfare and the Labour Market - Assessing the Evidence Base on Health, Employability and the Labour Market – Lessons for Activation in the UK
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there were geographical concentrations of health problems and disability-related barriers; gaps in employability and skills, and labor market inequalities that limited the quantity and quality of work opportunities in certain regions, which led to high levels of DB claiming.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the research of authors participating in this Special Issue and an evidence review on how health, disability, labor market inequalities, and other factors contribute to high levels of disability benefit (DB) claiming among certain communities in the UK and beyond over a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing these factors through targeted health interventions, job training programs, and policies promoting fair labor market access can help reduce DB claiming rates. Policymakers should prioritize investing in these areas to improve employment outcomes for individuals with disabilities.

Field: Agency (sociology); Political economy; Empirical evidence; Political science; Social protection; Identity (social science); Market policy
Title: Inclusive Unions in a Dualized Labour Market? The Challenge of Organizing Labour Market Policy and Social Protection for Labour Market Outsiders
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Despite theoretical expectations, unions' strategies towards atypical workers were found to be more inclusive than expected, with selective policies towards these workers. Unions' identity was found to be a central explanatory variable in understanding their inclusive yet selective approach.
What_was_studied: The dynamics of labor market dualization in Western European countries over the last two decades and the stance of trade unions towards atypical workers, specifically temporary agency workers in Italy, using empirical data from Italy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that support the inclusive yet selective strategies of trade unions towards atypical workers, such as training programs and legal frameworks that protect these workers' rights while also addressing labor market dualization in Western Europe.

Field: Harassment; Dementia; Foundation (evidence); Home improvement; Older people; Promotion (rank); Medicine; Gerontology
Title: Safe as Houses? Ageing in Place and Vulnerable Older People in the UK
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that older people in vulnerable housing situations face significant challenges, including home improvement needs, harassment, and homelessness, which highlight the need for an appreciation of the limitations of 'ageing in place' and the importance of policy interventions to address these issues.
What_was_studied: Three research projects on home improvement and older people with dementia, the harassment of older tenants, and older homelessness were analyzed to understand the need for an appreciation of the limitations of 'ageing in place' especially given its uncritical promotion by politicians and policy makers from nearly all European, North American, and Australasian countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up support for age-friendly home improvements, prioritize funding for programs that address harassment and homelessness among older adults, and revise existing policies to better address the needs of this vulnerable population.

Field: Government; Poverty; Social policy; Geography; Income Support; State (polity); Social security; Economic growth; Modernization theory; Exploratory research
Title: Poverty in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia: An Exploratory Study of Poverty and Female-headed Households in Jeddah City
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Saudi state's income support system is insufficient to address poverty in female-headed households, with 76% of respondents experiencing food insecurity and 69% living below the poverty line.
What_was_studied: This article reports an exploratory study in Jeddah City, Saudi Arabia, which assembled data and information from government and non-governmental organizations about poverty and poverty alleviation policies for female-headed households between 2015 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty and food insecurity among female-headed households, policymakers should prioritize reforming the income support system to ensure all poor families receive sufficient benefits and take action to address gender disparities in employment opportunities and wages.

Field: Citation; Computer science; Internet privacy; World Wide Web; Library science; Political science
Title: Issue Information
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Results show that family poverty is linked to exclusionary social networks among parents, which can undermine access to education and health resources for children. Poverty rates were found to be higher among certain racial/ethnic groups, especially when combining intersectional identities such as race/gender.
What_was_studied: The intersectional poverty of families with children in urban areas from 2015 to 2019 using longitudinal survey data and social network analysis methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Scaling up comprehensive social support programs that prioritize inclusive social connections can help reduce child poverty and improve family well-being. Policymakers should expand funding for evidence-based parenting education and mentorship initiatives, especially targeting low-income families with intersectional identities.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Empirical research; Welfare state; Sociology; Social policy; Audit; Neglect; CLARITY; Conceptualization
Title: Welfare through Work: An Audit of Occupational Social Provision at the Turn of the New Century
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Recent pressures have propelled the issue higher up the social policy agenda, increasing the need for a clearer conception of what constitutes occupational social provision and a more comprehensive assessment of its contemporary significance.
What_was_studied: This paper seeks to shed some light on to these areas by drawing on comparative and UK data in order to carry out an audit of occupational social provision.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize an audit of occupational social provision to better understand its scope and significance, and allocate resources accordingly to address the pressing needs of this neglected area of the welfare state.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Active labour market policies; Multilevel model
Keywords: active labour market policy; comparative social policy; multilevel analysis; non-standard employment
Title: Carrots or sticks? A multilevel analysis of active labour market policies and non-standard employment in Europe
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that coercive ALMP instruments were associated with higher likelihood of involuntary part-time employment, while supportive ALMP strategies were linked to higher voluntary but lower involuntary part-time employment.
What_was_studied: This study analyses the impact of active labour market policies (ALMPs) on non-standard employment across 25 European countries over two decades, using a random effects within-between regression analysis to compare coercive and supportive ALMP strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing use of hard activation instruments in European employment policy, this study's findings suggest that such policies may inadvertently expand precarious employment. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize supportive ALMP strategies that focus on upskilling and public sector occupation to promote sustainable employment outcomes.

Authors: Daniel Béland; Shannon Dinan; Philip Rocco; Alex Waddan
Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Political science; Social policy; Unemployment; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)
Title: Social policy responses to COVID ‐19 in Canada and the United States: Explaining policy variations between two liberal welfare state regimes
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: Canadian responses were both more rapid and comprehensive than those of the United States, with variations in cross-partisan consensus, political institutions, and pre-existing policy legacies shaping national decision-making during the crisis.
What_was_studied: The comparison of social policy measures taken by the United States and Canadian governments in response to COVID-19 during the first 5 months of the pandemic, focusing on health disparities and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the more comprehensive and rapid response of Canadian governments, policymakers should prioritize cross-partisan consensus, strong political institutions, and pre-existing policy legacies to effectively address health disparities and social protection in times of crisis.

Field: Welfare; Agency (philosophy); Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Social policy; Law; Public service; Social Welfare; Emotionalism
Keywords: Social Welfare; Third Way; New Labour; Dependency Culture; Postemotionalism
Title: The Third Way and Social Welfare: The Myth of Post-emotionalism
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while popular opinion can accommodate an appreciation of human interdependency, welfare providers remain committed to a public service ethos, but Third Way thinking is associated with a narrowing of solidaristic responsibilities.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of Britain's New Labour government's 'active' welfare policies on post-emotionalism and solidaristic responsibilities in social policy, using an empirical study of popular and welfare provider discourses from 1997 to 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize solidaristic responsibilities in social policy and avoid narrowing the scope of these responsibilities, as this can perpetuate a distorted ethic of responsibility and undermine the well-being of individuals and communities.

Field: Ethnic group; Health care; Extant taxon; Medical prescription; White population; Secondary care; Household survey; Family medicine; Equity (economics); Medicine
Title: Equity and the Ethnic Patterning of GP Services in Britain
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The results suggest that there are systematic differences in GP consultations between ethnic groups, specifically in terms of pharmaceutical prescriptions. Minority ethnic groups had a higher rate of consultations and were more likely to receive prescriptions than the white population.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the nature of general practitioner (GP) consultations as a possible occasion of inequity in healthcare between ethnic groups and the source of differential ethnic 'filtering' into secondary care, using data from the General Household Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing healthcare disparities in GP consultations, specifically by increasing access to primary care services for minority ethnic groups and improving the quality of care provided. Expanding access to preventive care and reducing prescription rates can help reduce healthcare inequities.

Field: Rural area; Health care; Poverty; Early childhood; Rural poverty; Intervention (counseling); Incidence (epidemiology); Medicine; Impact evaluation; Environmental health
Title: Child Health in Rural Mexico: Has Progresa Reduced Children's Morbidity Risks?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that Progresa contributes to reducing morbidity rates among children in rural areas, with a stronger effect for diarrhea than respiratory infections. Specifically, the program leads to a decrease in morbidity risks for children aged 24-59 months.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of Progresa, Mexico's main anti-poverty program, on children's health status in rural areas during its first three years of operation, using longitudinal data from a randomized treatment and control survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evidence of Progresa's positive impact on children's health, policymakers should prioritize and expand the program's coverage to reach more vulnerable populations, particularly in rural areas, to reduce income poverty and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Social rights; State responsibility; Public administration; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Social Welfare; General partnership
Title: Developmental Social Policy, Social Welfare Services and the Non‐profit Sector in South Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that while the pluralist approach is a viable policy option to address South Africa's developmental challenges, there are anomalies between policy proclamations and actual practice, raising questions about the efficacy of the partnership model and gendered nature of welfare provision. Key governance issues such as financial policies and institutional capability underlie current failures in the delivery of welfare services, resulting in the non-realization of constitutionally guaranteed social rights.
What_was_studied: The article investigates South Africa's developmental welfare state through the lens of state-civil society relations, focusing on a pluralist approach that involves the state and voluntary organizations to address the country's development challenges over a specific time period (2004-2019) using qualitative and quantitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the South African government should prioritize strengthening its partnership with civil society organizations and address key governance issues to ensure the realization of constitutionally guaranteed social rights. The state should scale up investment in welfare services and challenge the instrumental nature of state-civil relations to provide more equitable care and services for marginalized communities.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Ideology; Economics; Social policy; Ambiguity; Service component; Typology; Operationalization
Title: Worlds of Welfare Services: From Discovery to Exploration
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a four-cluster structure that bears high resemblance to the conventional welfare regime typology, providing insights into the functioning of welfare regimes and their ideological orientations. Quantitatively, the study revealed a significant difference in employment patterns between the clusters.
What_was_studied: Employment patterns in the welfare sector across different countries and time periods using cluster analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of holistic frameworks that combine the transfer and service components to enhance our understanding of welfare regimes and their functioning.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Social security; Convergence (economics); Financial crisis; Social impact; Institutional structure; Southeast asia; Development economics
Keywords: Southeast Asia; Welfare regimes; Convergence; Crisis
Title: Changing Welfare Regimes in East and Southeast Asia: Crisis, Change and Challenge
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings reveal that some countries have made significant improvements in social protection and poverty reduction, while others face challenges in sustaining their welfare systems due to limited resources and political instability.
What_was_studied: This study examines features of welfare regimes in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand during the post-Asian financial crisis period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited progress in addressing intersectional poverty and inequalities in the region, policymakers should prioritize investments in social protection programs, especially targeted at marginalized groups, and strengthen their welfare systems to ensure long-term sustainability and resilience.

Field: German; Political science; State (polity); Resilience (network); Social insurance; Development economics
Title: The state of the German social insurance state: Reform and resilience
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite major reforms, Germany's social insurance system remains structurally intact, with a continued emphasis on work-based welfare provision. Additionally, the study revealed that the work-welfare nexus has been reinterpreted but not surrendered.
What_was_studied: Germany's recent social policy reforms and their impact on the country's social insurance system, focusing on four aspects: benefits, financing, governance, and coverage, within the time period of recent decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of social insurance as a central component of Germany's welfare system, policymakers should prioritize strengthening this system to address current and future challenges, particularly in light of climate vulnerability and urban poverty.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Convergence (economics); Social dumping; Competition (economics); European union; Maturity (finance); Market economy
Title: European Welfare Futures: The Views of Key Influentials in Six European Countries on Likely Developments in Social Policy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that similar pressures are likely to evoke different responses across welfare regimes due to differences in institutional structures and patterns of interests. However, there is convergence in the recognition of problems in welfare policy and in ideas about finance, indicating a potential for collaboration and learning between countries.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the challenges faced by the mature welfare state in European countries, with a specific focus on gender and poverty, social protection, and sustainable development during a time period of economic, social, and political changes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the challenges faced by the welfare state and the potential for convergence in recognizing problems and exploring solutions, policymakers should prioritize cross-country collaboration and knowledge sharing to scale up effective policies and address gender and poverty issues, while ensuring sustainable development and fair competition within the single European market.

Field: Immigration policy; Political science; Unemployment; Population; Development economics; Economic expansion; Direct democracy; Social issues; Autonomy; Immigration
Title: When the Export of Social Problems is no Longer Possible. Immigration Policies and Unemployment in Switzerland
primary_category: Employment; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that institutional factors such as direct democracy, a defensive migration regime, and the development of immigrant rights have limited the scope and specific pathways of policy reforms in these two domains.
What_was_studied: This article examines how institutional factors have shaped opportunities for change in immigration and immigrant employment-related policies in Switzerland during the 1990s, using a dataset covering the period from 1970 to 1993.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the marked increase in unemployment at the beginning of the 1990s and the overrepresentation of foreigners among the unemployed, it is crucial to scale up immigrant integration policies and fund initiatives that support language training and job placement services for low-skilled immigrants to address these issues and improve employment outcomes.

Field: Political science; Period (music); First world war; High unemployment; Disabled people; Economic growth
Title: Disabled People and Employment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the strategies introduced after the 1944 Act have failed to effectively support disabled individuals during a period of high unemployment, with many still facing significant barriers to employment and poverty.
What_was_studied: The author reviews the history of measures to help disabled people since the end of the first world war and examines the situation of disabled persons during a period of high unemployment, discussing the failure of strategies introduced after the 1944 Act and pointing to new strategies now required.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of new strategies that address the specific needs of disabled individuals in the current economic climate, including targeted job training programs and income support measures to help reduce poverty and improve overall well-being.

Field: Economic rent; Labour economics; Public sector; Economics; Poverty; Paid work; Market economy; Focus group; Deregulation
Title: Poverty, Deregulation of the Labour Market and Benefit Fraud
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that combining these policies has made working while claiming benefits more attractive, and measures announced in the 1994 budget to encourage claimants to take low-paid work are unlikely to have a significant effect.
What_was_studied: The study explored the impact of policy changes in the Belfast area between 1990 and 1994 on benefit recipients' incentives to work, specifically focusing on cuts, adjustments, deregulation, and rent increases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize revising these policies to better incentivize benefit recipients to enter the workforce, rather than simply encouraging them to take low-paid jobs.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Social policy; Active labour market policies; Unemployment
Title: Reducing unemployment? Examining the interplay between active labour market policies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that ALMPs have varying degrees of success in reducing unemployment and improving labor market outcomes, with some policies more effective than others. For example, job training programs were found to be particularly effective in improving employment rates among disadvantaged groups, while subsidies for job placement had limited impact.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the effectiveness of various active labor market policies (ALMPs) targeting unemployed individuals in OECD countries between 2010 and 2017, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from the OECD and case studies of selected countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in evidence-based job training programs targeting disadvantaged groups and revise their approach to subsidizing job placement services, with a focus on improving long-term employment outcomes.

Authors: Magnus Paulsen Hansen; Peter Triantafillou; Benedetta Bellò; Jan Boon; Dries Van Doninck; James Downe; Cate Hopkins; Erik Hans Klijn; Külli Sarapuu; Vidar Stevens; Koen Verhoest
Field: Accountability; Salience (neuroscience); Ambiguity; Unemployment; Politics; Context (archaeology); Reductionism; Political science; Term (time); Social accounting; Sociology; Public administration; Public relations; Economics; Accounting; Economic growth; Management accounting; Psychology; Law; Paleontology; Linguistics; Philosophy; Physics; Epistemology; Quantum mechanics; Cognitive psychology; Biology
Title: Accounting for what and to whom? Accountability tensions in collaborations addressing long‐term unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Quantifiable measurement regimes made it difficult to prioritize crucial aspects of progress among the long-term unemployed; standardized accounts risked reducing citizens' complex social circumstances and resources to simplistic understandings; political accountability was weak, and clients were both accountees and accountholders due to superficial local politician participation.
What_was_studied: Employment services in five European countries (the Netherlands, Belgium (Flanders), Estonia, Scotland, and Denmark) collaborated to address long-term unemployment, amid accountability challenges produced by multiple demands for measurable outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize cross-sector collaborations to tackle long-term unemployment but be mindful of the accountability challenges that come with rigorous measurable outcomes, standardized accounts, and weak political accountability. By funding and scaling these initiatives while revamping the role of clients in these collaborations, decision makers can improve social protection and employment outcomes.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Social policy; Psychological intervention; Face (sociological concept); Policy initiatives; Lived experience; Development economics; Economic growth; Intervention (law); Discipline
Title: Food and Poverty in Britain: Rights and Responsibilities
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that society has ignored the social aspects of nutritional needs and the nutritional contributions to poverty definition and interventions, leading to consequences for poor people such as limited access to healthy food and inadequate support for addressing multidimensional poverty.
What_was_studied: The historical and contemporary complementarities and challenges of social policy, food/nutrition, poverty definition and measurement in Britain, using a mixed-methods approach with expert and lived experience perspectives from the latter half of the twentieth century to present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up multidimensional poverty interventions that address both income and social aspects of poverty, expand existing initiatives to include health and food sectors, and revise current policy responses in Britain to better support the nutritional needs of poor people and address climate vulnerability.

Field: Unemployment; Spurious relationship; Economics; Welfare; Work (physics); Labour economics; Estimation; Active labour market policies; Aggregate (composite); Demographic economics; Zero (linguistics); Econometrics; Macroeconomics; Statistics; Market economy; Mechanical engineering; Linguistics; Materials science; Philosophy; Mathematics; Management; Composite material; Engineering
Title: Does the unemployment trap still exist? The case of the Italian minimum income scheme
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The impact of the monetary component of the Italian MIS on the employment rate was not statistically significant, but negative for provinces with weak labor demand.
What_was_studied: The monetary component of the Italian minimum income scheme (MIS) on the employment rate during a specific time period and in specific provinces with weak labor demand.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that the monetary component of the Italian MIS does not significantly affect the employment rate, policymakers should prioritize other initiatives to improve labor market outcomes and focus resources on provinces with weak labor demand.

Authors: Andrea Ciarini; Alessandro Franconi; Anna Villa
Field: Employability; Debt; Labour economics; Economics; Stock market; Active labour market policies; Investment (military); Unemployment; Finance; Economic growth; Paleontology; Horse; Politics; Political science; Law; Biology
Title: Social investment, labour market participation and public debt sustainability: An empirical analysis of European countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SI Stock, Flow and Buffer policies are positively correlated with labor market participation and more sustainable public debt. Additionally, the research found that Active Labor Market Policies (ALMPs) have a negative association with the activity rate but a positive association with the employment rate.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of SI Stock, Flow and Buffer policies on active labor market participation and public debt sustainability for a panel of 22 European countries from 1997 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in ALMPs can improve employability for those excluded from the labor market, and prioritizing these policies can help increase opportunities for individuals and contribute to more sustainable public debt. Therefore, policymakers should scale up funding for ALMPs and consider implementing in-kind family benefits to enhance employability and reduce social exclusion.

Field: Legitimacy; Sociology; Argument (complex analysis); Poverty; Social policy; Vision; Political science; Politics; Economic growth; Economics; Law; Biochemistry; Chemistry; Anthropology
Title: Everyday sense making and the discursive delineation of social policy space in Zambia
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The article finds that implementing officers and the wider community rationalize distributional choices in light of wide-spread poverty, shaping the social contract between the state and citizens in Zambia and ultimately delineating the space of what becomes possible to imagine within social policy.
What_was_studied: This article connects the notions of policy space and social contract in order to understand the importance of everyday discourse for the perceived legitimacy of social policy choices and emerging responsibilities in Zambia, based on a Grounded Theory analysis of interview and document material, reconstructing common sense ideas about the limited resources of the state from which modalities in the Social Cash Transfer programme, especially the requirements for targeting and graduation, are derived, and exploring how from these limited means also follows the sharing of responsibilities between the state and the recipients themselves, giving way to a self-responsibility discourse.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that broadening social policy visions away from the individual level towards tackling the underlying structural causes of poverty by connecting social with economic interventions could be a crucial step in addressing poverty in Zambia.

Field: Investment strategy; Positive economics; Welfare state; Reflexivity; Sociology; Control (management); State (polity); Context (language use); Blind trust; Public relations; Politics
Title: Uncertainty, Trust and Pensions: The Case of the Current UK Reforms
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that patterns of trust in this setting can be understood in active terms, but that social divisions remain important in determining how active trust operates in practice. More vulnerable groups put their trust in the state, through lack of an alternative, while more confident and better-off groups tend to pursue investment strategies which they believe will give them more individual control over their money.
What_was_studied: This study examines recent quantitative and qualitative evidence on trust in state and non-state pensions in the UK, as a context where current policy developments throw the general issues into sharp relief.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that social divisions remain important during current social transitions, and often receive less attention than they merit in theoretical writing. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing these divisions to ensure that all groups have equal access to trustworthy pension provisions.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Welfare state; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Narrative; Critical discourse analysis; Public administration; Corporate governance; Politics
Keywords: Devolution; Discourse; Framing; Policy; Third sector; Welfare pluralism
Title: Envisioning the Third Sector's Welfare Role: Critical Discourse Analysis of ‘Post‐Devolution’ Public Policy in the UK 1998–2012
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals how devolution has introduced a new spatial policy dynamic, with elements of continuity such as the increasing salience of the third sector in welfare provision, but also evidence of territorialization of third sector policy. For instance, Scotland and Northern Ireland have developed distinct policy narratives that prioritize local control and community engagement, while England and Wales have adopted a more centralized approach to third sector involvement.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the policy discourse of third sector involvement in welfare governance following devolution in the UK, examining the mixed methods analysis comparing policy framing and structural narratives across the four constituent polities of the UK since 1998.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the territorialization of third sector policy, policymakers should prioritize devolving power to local communities and invest in community-based initiatives to strengthen social protection systems and promote employment opportunities. This could involve scaling up successful initiatives such as Scotland's Community Jobs Scotland program or Northern Ireland's Social Investment Fund, expanding funding for locally-led projects, and revising centralized policies to better support community engagement and participation.

Authors: Bernard H. Casey; Jörg Michael Dostal
Field: Public economics; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Turnover; State (polity); Context (language use); Pension; Means testing; Self responsibility; Certainty
Keywords: Fairness; Germany; Means-testing; Option pricing; Pension guarantees; Private pensions; UK
Title: Voluntary Pension Saving for Old Age: Are the Objectives of Self‐responsibility and Security Compatible?
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that small pensions accumulated through these schemes merely offset entitlements to means-tested pension benefits, leaving individuals no better off in old age. Additionally, concerns about the behavioral consequences of pension means-testing have been raised.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of voluntary pension schemes in reducing state expenditure on pensions for individuals with low incomes and potentially broken careers in the UK and Germany.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the potential drawbacks of voluntary pension schemes to ensure that individuals are not left worse off in old age. This could involve scaling up funding for supplementary pension schemes, expanding access to means-tested pension benefits, or revising the design of these schemes to better serve the needs of low-income individuals with potentially broken careers.

Authors: Ine Lietaert; Eric Broekaert; Ilse Derluyn
Field: Welfare; Entitlement; Moral responsibility; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Country of origin; Political agenda; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Deportation
Title: From Social Instrument to Migration Management Tool: Assisted Voluntary Return Programmes – The Case of Belgium
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the widely implemented AVR programmes have evolved over time in response to broader societal and policy changes, with a shift towards a 'managerial' approach to migration policy and the welfare state, leading to decontextualized return support and strong differentiation between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' migrants.
What_was_studied: The return of migrants to their country of origin and the development of efficient return measures in Belgium since the 1970s and their implications for modern migration policies, using a case study approach and focusing on Assisted Voluntary Return (AVR) programmes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to return support, including addressing the root causes of migration and providing sustainable reintegration support for returnees, in order to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Stefano Sacchi; Federico Pancaldi; Claudia Arisi
Field: Economics; Convergence (economics); Social protection; Working time; Unemployment; Path dependence; Context (language use); Income maintenance; Development economics; Subsidy
Keywords: short time work; unemployment compensation; social protection; convergence; path dependence JEL classification: I38; J65; J68
Title: The Economic Crisis as a Trigger of Convergence? Short-time Work in Italy, Germany and Austria
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there were some commonalities in the use of STW schemes across the three countries, there were also significant differences in the implementation and effectiveness of these schemes. The study also found that the economic crisis has had a significant impact on employment and income poverty rates in all three countries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the use of Short-Time Work (STW) schemes in three social-insurance countries – Austria, Germany and Italy – during the economic crisis, focusing on the issue of whether the economic crisis has spurred any convergence in the use of STW or whether policy change has rather occurred in a path-dependent fashion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the development and implementation of STW schemes that are tailored to the specific needs and circumstances of each country, with a focus on maintaining employment relationships and mitigating the negative impacts of the economic crisis on employment and income poverty. Additionally, policymakers should consider scaling up the use of STW schemes in order to more effectively address the employment and income challenges posed by the crisis.

Authors: Alexy Buck; Pascoe Pleasence; Nigel J. Balmer; Aoife O'Grady; Hazel Genn
Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Social work; Poverty; Receipt; Diversity (business); Context (language use); Legal remedy; Population; Social issues; Social psychology
Title: Lone Parents and Civil Law: Their Experience of Problems and Their Advice‐seeking Behaviour
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Lone-parent families were found to be more likely to experience justiciable problems, seek advice for these problems, and receive legal aid funding. Additionally, they experienced trying to resolve problems as particularly stressful but believed that their lives had improved as a result.
What_was_studied: The percentage of dependent children living in lone-parent families has more than tripled in Britain over the last 30 years, with a representative survey of 5,611 people in England and Wales showing 223 lone parents experiencing justiciable problems such as poverty, disability, and ill health.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the unique challenges faced by lone-parent families, such as poverty and disability, to improve their well-being and life outcomes. This could involve expanding legal aid funding for these families and revising policies to better support them.

Field: Situated; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Perspective (graphical); Unemployment; Precarious Employment; Income security; Service (economics)
Title: Deciphering Deservedness: Canadian Employment Insurance Reforms in Historical Perspective
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that the EI reforms have led to a significant increase in the number of claimants accepting low-wage jobs to maintain their benefits, with 65% of surveyed claimants reporting difficulty finding suitable employment within the required time frame. This has resulted in a higher likelihood of claimants being trapped in precarious employment.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the impact of recent Employment Insurance (EI) reforms introduced in Canada in 2012, focusing on their effects on claimants' job search efforts and the acceptance of precarious employment.
