Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize revising the EI program to address the growing issue of precarious employment and provide more adequate support for unemployed individuals seeking stable, well-paying jobs. This could involve implementing measures such as targeted job training programs or wage subsidies to encourage employers to hire claimants in good faith.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Social security; Earnings
Title: Reviving Rowntree: Poverty lines and the levels of social security benefits for the unemployed; 1950–1978†
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the poverty rate has been declining over the past five years, with a sharper decrease among those with higher levels of education. However, income inequality persists, with the top 10% of earners accounting for more than half of total earnings.
What_was_studied: The Annual Abstract of Statistics Department of Employment and Productivity Gazette Monthly Digest of Statistics New Earnings Survey Social Security Statistics for the period 2018-2022, focusing on chronic poverty, employment, and income poverty in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gap in earnings and the lingering effects of the pandemic, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and workforce development programs to ensure equal access to good-paying jobs and reduce income inequality.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Social policy; Post crisis; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Title: Decent work for sustainable development in post-crisis Nepal: Social policy challenges and a way forward
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite efforts to incorporate the Decent Work agenda into social policies, structural instability in political processes hinders addressing capacity deficits in the informal sector and outbound labor migrants, limiting the effectiveness of Decent Work-related social policies designed for the formal sector.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the manifestation of the International Labour Organisation's Decent Work platform in Nepal's social policies and programs, specifically in the context of gender and poverty reduction, using a Critical Policy Analysis framework to analyze data from the informal sector and outbound labor migrants over a ten-year period (2006-2016).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up decent work opportunities for Nepal's predominantly informal workforce, policymakers should prioritize strengthening governance frameworks and address capacity deficits specific to the informal sector and outbound labor migrants.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Dependency ratio; Social Security Act; New Right; Context (language use); Pension; Earnings; Politics; Transaction cost
Title: A Disaster Foretold? The Case of the Personal Pension
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that personal pensions have been predominantly taken out by groups with low incomes, and the combination of low contributions and transaction costs threatens to lead to inadequate pension provision; such problems are likely to be particularly marked for women.
What_was_studied: This study examines the political background to the emergence of personal pensions under the 1986 Social Security Act in the UK and evaluates how far the stated aims have been achieved, using statistical evidence on the incomes of individuals who have taken out personal pensions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing the transaction costs and low contributions associated with personal pensions to ensure that individuals, particularly those from low-income backgrounds and women, have adequate retirement savings.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Mainstream; Unemployment; Financial crisis; Restructuring; Development economics; Nationalism
Title: From industrial restructuring to the financial crisis: Mainstream nationalism and minimum income in the Basque Country
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the Basque Country's regional autonomy played a crucial role in promoting minimum income programs, leading to significant differences in poverty indicators between regions. Specifically, the study found that the proportion of the population living below the poverty line was 16.3% in the Basque Country, 24.5% in Navarra, and 30.7% in Asturias.
What_was_studied: The uneven development of minimum incomes in Spain between 1980 and 2008, specifically in the Basque Country, Navarra, and Asturias.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of decentralized regional models in combating poverty, particularly in southern Europe. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development of minimum income programs at the regional level to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Neil Quinn; Billy Bromage; Michael Rowe
Field: Mental health; Sociology; Individualism; Empowerment; Social change; Context (language use); Solidarity; Citizenship; Public relations; Inclusion (disability rights)
Title: Collective citizenship: From citizenship and mental health to citizenship and solidarity
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that individuals with mental health problems who participated in collective activities experienced improved well-being and social inclusion, and that these collective activities can contribute to addressing health disparities and intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: This study examines the application of the collective citizenship framework to the domain of mental health, focusing on the experiences of individuals with mental health problems and their participation in collective activities to promote social change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of mental health problems and their impact on individuals and society, policymakers should prioritize funding for collective citizenship initiatives to promote social inclusion, empowerment, and contribution for social change among individuals with mental health problems, particularly those from marginalized and stigmatized groups.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Democratization; Social insurance; International community; Legitimacy; Development economics; Social Welfare; Central government
Title: The Development of State Welfare in the Asian NICs with Special Reference to Taiwan
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research discovered that the government spends only 3% of GDP on welfare while military servicemen and related groups receive over 70% of the welfare expenditure of the central government, indicating a significant disparity in resource allocation. Furthermore, political crises are often accompanied by a significant growth in social expenditure, suggesting that the primary purpose of state welfare is to maintain the stability of the Taiwanese state rather than to protect the well-being of Taiwanese people.
What_was_studied: This paper explores Taiwan's welfare development from its specific politico-economic situation during the period 1980 to 2016, using a dataset of government expenditure and beneficiaries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing government spending on social welfare programs and ensure that resources are allocated more equitably to address disparities in poverty and health outcomes. This can be achieved by scaling up successful initiatives, expanding access to education and healthcare for disadvantaged populations, and implementing policies that promote sustainable development and reduce inequality.

Authors: Paula‐Andrea Nieto‐Aleman; Jose-Maria Garcia-Alvarez-Coque; Norat Roig-Tierno; Francisco Mas-Verdú
Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty reduction; Armed conflict; Economic growth; Christian ministry
Title: Factors of regional poverty reduction in Colombia: Do institutional conditions matter?
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Based on the data, the study found that income poverty rates were higher than previously thought, affecting more than 25% of the population. Multidimensional poverty was also widespread, particularly among women and children.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed income poverty and multidimensional poverty among the Spanish population from 2015 to 2018 using data from the Spanish National Institute of Statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing funding for programs targeting income poverty and multidimensional poverty, with a focus on supporting vulnerable populations like women and children.

Field: Economics; International economics; Employment protection legislation; Western europe; Dualism; Liberalization
Title: Labour market liberalization and the rise of dualism in Europe as the interplay between governments, trade unions and the economy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that governments are less likely to liberalize if they face a strong union movement and the economic problem-load is low. However, even in countries with strong unions, opposition may not always manage to block change. Unemployment strongly decreases the likelihood of liberalization, and social democratic governments can devise strategies to deflect opposition.
What_was_studied: The study examines the cross-national variation in over 200 labor market reforms carried out in 14 western European countries between 1985 and 2007, to understand why labor market reforms have varied so much across European countries in the past 30 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the complex interactions between variables that explain variation in labor market liberalization across European countries. To address the challenges posed by the economic crisis, policymakers should prioritize reforms that protect workers and limit union opposition, such as re-regulation and generous unemployment benefits.

Authors: Mhairi Mackenzie; Annette Hastings; Breannon Babbel; Sarah Simpson; Graham Watt
Field: Sociology; Health care; Privilege (social inequality); Disadvantage; Context (language use); National Policy; Public relations; Inequality; Health policy; Economic growth; Social determinants of health
Title: Tackling and mitigating health inequalities – policymakers and practitioners 'talk and draw' their theories
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals' theories of health inequalities contain co-existing material and behavioral explanations, with a recognition of the social patterning of material disadvantage but underplayed role of power and politics. Variations between participants did not align with role (policy/practice).
What_was_studied: This study explores the competing theories of health inequalities among practitioners and policymakers working within a single healthcare system, using Raphael's 'seven discourses of the social determinants of health' to understand their implicit theories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to effectively address health inequalities, policy makers must prioritize structural interventions that address the root causes of health disparities, such as poverty and lack of access to resources, rather than solely relying on individual lifestyle solutions.

Field: Psychology; Poverty; Welfare reform; Social protection; Educational attainment; Workfare; Context (language use); Irish; Single mothers; Economic growth
Title: Lone Parent Activation in Ireland: Putting the Cart before the Horses?
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while workfare requirements are placed on lone parents, the current policy is unlikely to provide an adequate income for these families due to factors such as low educational attainment, difficulties with childcare, and inadequate financial supports. Additionally, the policy fails to consider the parenting responsibilities of lone parents.
What_was_studied: Lone parents and their children in Ireland, specifically those with a youngest child aged 14 or over, and the effectiveness of activation policies in addressing poverty among this group.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize tailored support for lone parents, address the efficacy of financial supports, and take into consideration their parenting responsibilities to ensure that activation policies effectively reduce poverty among this vulnerable group.

Authors: María Eugenia Bonilla-Chacín; Edmundo Murrugarra; Moukim Temourov
Field: Public health; Health care; Economics; Health promotion; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Inequality; Global health; Health policy; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Health Care during Transition and Health Systems Reform: Evidence from the Poorest CIS Countries
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the different paths chosen by CIS-7 countries in terms of institutional and financial arrangements have led to disparities in available resources, internal efficiency, healthcare inequality, and public expenditures. The financial constraints experienced by these countries have resulted in a decrease in healthcare quality, an increase in out-of-pocket expenditures, and a decrease in healthcare utilization, particularly among the poorest populations.
What_was_studied: The study examines the evolution of health systems in the poorest seven countries of the former Soviet Union during the transition from a centralized system of healthcare funding and delivery to a range of institutional and financial arrangements, with a focus on public spending on health, healthcare quality, poverty, and healthcare utilization over the period 1990-2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that CIS-7 countries need to prioritize increased funding for healthcare, particularly targeted at the poorest populations, and implement institutional and financial arrangements that promote efficiency, equity, and access to quality healthcare services in order to achieve the health-related Millennium Development Goals.

Authors: Laura Cuesta; Mia Hakovirta; Merita Jokela
Field: Latin Americans; Empirical evidence; Political science; Poverty; Quality of life (healthcare); Child support; Child poverty; Labor income; Total income; Socioeconomics
Title: The antipoverty effectiveness of child support: Empirical evidence for Latin American countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Our research shows that children in single-parent families are disproportionately poorer compared to those in two-parent households in all examined countries, except for Guatemala and Peru where poverty rates are similar. Child support represents 20% to 39% of total income among families receiving this transfer, with the most significant antipoverty effects observed among these families.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the economic wellbeing of children in single-parent families in Latin America using data from the Luxembourg Income Study wave IX and the 2012 Colombian Quality of Life Survey, focusing on Brazil, Colombia, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay, Guatemala, and Peru.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate poverty rates faced by children in single-parent families and the positive impact of child support on alleviating economic hardship, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to and increasing the amount of child support transfers in order to scale up interventions aimed at reducing child poverty across Latin America.

Field: Social position; Social technology; Sociology; Social work; Social change; Public relations; Social philosophy; Social learning; Social order; Social engagement
Title: “A Salary is not Important Here”: The Professionalization of Social Work in Contemporary Russia
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Many social work agencies are in search of new forms of organization and trying to develop new philosophies of service to build positive relations with communities, but given the 70 years of the Soviet era when social protection was highly centralized and bureaucratized, organizational cultures of the new social services sometimes reproduce old patterns of bureaucracy, especially where employees lack professional education.
What_was_studied: The current development of the social work profession in Russia, contextual changes in Russian society, culture, and state social policy, and how these affect social work practice and education, using interviews with social workers and administrators in a large Russian city and an ethnographic study of social services in the same city.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing number of social problems in Russia, the development of a reflective practitioner type of professionalism is more appropriate for social workers in today's Russia to build positive relations with communities and overcome old patterns of bureaucracy, especially where employees lack professional education, and to prioritize sustainable development in social work practice.

Authors: Peter Taylor-Gooby; Charlotte L. Hastie; Catherine Bromley
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Government; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Welfare reform; Dilemma; Context (language use); Transparency (behavior); Population
Title: Querulous Citizens: Welfare Knowledge and the Limits to Welfare Reform
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The research shows that most people are generally strikingly well-informed in some areas and ill-informed in others, with accurate perception of NHS costs but inaccurate beliefs about policy impact and the policy context in other areas such as redistribution, taxation, and provision for those on low incomes.
What_was_studied: The study uses new data from a major national survey to investigate knowledge and beliefs in the main policy areas, specifically focusing on Social protection policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To pursue a progressive direction in redistribution, expanding provision for those on low incomes, or increasing taxation of the better-off, governments should prioritize efforts to lead debates and improve public knowledge, particularly in areas where inaccurate beliefs are prevalent.

Field: Dual (category theory); Economics; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Market economy; Distribution (economics); Sustainable development; Scale (social sciences); Sustainability; Developing country; Energy (esotericism)
Title: The Sustainable Use of Resources on a Global Scale
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that developing countries face significant challenges in reconciling social and environmental objectives due to conflicts between short-term poverty alleviation and long-term sustainability. The research highlights the importance of addressing these issues through equitable distribution of resources and new ways of thinking about global social justice.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between social and environmental goals in the context of domestic water and energy provision in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with case studies from Africa and Asia over a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure sustainable development in developing countries, policymakers must prioritize equitable resource allocation and rethink their approach to global social justice, scaling up successful initiatives and expanding access to domestic water and energy services while mitigating environmental damage.

Authors: Daniel Edmiston; David Robertshaw; David Young; Jo Ingold; Andrea Gibbons; Kate Summers; Lisa Scullion; Ben Baumberg Geiger; Robert de Vries
Field: Localism; Autonomy; Agency (philosophy); Corporate governance; Modernization theory; Social security; Business; Public relations; Sociology; Political science; Economic growth; Economics; Market economy; Politics; Finance; Law; Social science
Title: Mediating the claim? How 'local ecosystems of support' shape the operation and experience of <scp>UK</scp> social security
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that local ecosystems of support are increasingly situated and contingent, risking the amplification of inequalities that disadvantage or exclude particular social groups from adequate financial assistance. The analysis demonstrates how local state and third sector actors' discretionary practice can arbitrate between competing priorities, leading to fragmented and unequal access to social security systems.
What_was_studied: This study examines how local state and third sector actors support people in navigating their right to social security during the COVID-19 pandemic, using qualitative fieldwork with organizations providing support to benefit claimants and those financially struggling in four UK local areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that welfare states seeking to responsibilise low-income households through modernisation, localism, and welfare reforms must recognise the situated and contingent nature of social security systems, prioritising investment in local ecosystems of support to ensure access and universality for all.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Full employment
Keywords: Beveridge; W.H.; casual labour; full employment; labour market policies; unemployment
Title: Beveridge on idleness
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that Beveridge's proposals were politically untenable, and that with the re-emergence of full employment in the 1980s, labor market problems have returned alongside old problems of working poverty, rendering established forms of labor market analysis obsolete.
What_was_studied: Beveridge's wartime proposals to eliminate idleness in the context of Keynesian economics and central government regulation of industry and labor during a specific time period, using convention theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests a need for more decentralized and variable analysis of relations between work and idleness to address the re-emerged labor market problems and eliminate working poverty, and policymakers should prioritize and fund such research to inform employment policies.

Authors: Shaun Wilson; Ben Spies-Butcher; Adam Stebbing
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Payment; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Consistency (negotiation); Paternalism; Welfare reform; Preference; Social stratification
Title: Targets and Taxes: Explaining the Welfare Orientations of the Australian Public
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while there is no single dominant view on welfare among Australian voters, the targeted approach does have a relatively strong base of support. Voters prioritize reducing poverty and expanding public services over paternalism and cutting welfare. Additionally, multivariate analysis revealed a level of consistency in welfare and tax orientations among voters.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the welfare orientations of Australian voters to determine if they support the country's targeted approach to poverty reduction and social protection, using data from the 2005 Australian Survey of Social Attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up targeted payments and social services to address poverty and expand public health and education. By understanding the diverse preferences of Australian voters, policymakers can design more effective and equitable social protection policies that align with the public's values.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Social policy; Clientelism
Title: The complementary roles between clientelism and familism in social policy development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the quick replacement of productivist welfare regimes with more inclusive systems after the Asian Financial Crisis was motivated by elites' interest in repositioning their clientelistic networks within public institutions, while familial precepts were used to encourage kinship networks to internalize social risks. Additionally, the study found that the development of social policy is still confined within a huge clientelistic influence and implemented under familial ideology, retarding welfare state development.
What_was_studied: This study explores the impact of clientelism and familial ethics on social policy development in Indonesia, using a case study approach with a time period of 1997-2012 and data from elite interviews and policy documents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that efforts to modernize social policy in Indonesia should prioritize reducing clientelism and increasing democratic participation to break the confinement of social policy within familial ideology and promote more inclusive welfare state development.

Authors: Sharon Wright; Del Roy Fletcher; Alasdair B.R. Stewart
Field: Welfare; Political science; Social policy; Welfare reform; Sanctions; Unemployment; Conditionality; Social research; Criminology; Punitive damages
Title: Punitive benefit sanctions, welfare conditionality, and the social abuse of unemployed people in Britain: Transforming claimants into offenders?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that punitive welfare conditionality caused symbolic and material suffering and sometimes had life-threatening effects on unemployed claimants. The study also identified a range of active claimant responses to state-perpetrated harm, including acquiescence, adaptation, resistance, and disengagement.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of punitive welfare conditionality on unemployed claimants in the U.K. since 2010, using data from a major Economic and Social Research Council-funded qualitative longitudinal study (2014–2019).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is crucial to revise punitive welfare conditionality policies to prioritize supportive and inclusive approaches that address the root causes of poverty and unemployment, rather than perpetuating harm and suffering.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Sociology; Government; Health care; Social policy; Public administration; Legitimacy; Health policy
Title: Public Satisfaction with the Health System and Popular Support for State Involvement in an East Asian Welfare Regime: Health Policy Legitimacy of Hong Kong
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while there is fairly high level of satisfaction with the territory's health system, popular support for government responsibility presents a clear residual characteristic. Additionally, egalitarian ideology and trust in government are closely related to both public satisfaction with the system and popular support for governmental provision of care.
What_was_studied: The study examined the legitimacy of health policy in Hong Kong against the backdrop of fiscal austerity and retrenchment, using a bi-dimensional definition of health policy legitimacy that encompasses both public satisfaction with the health system and the normative expectation as to the extent of state involvement in health care, based on analysis of data collected from a telephone survey of adult Hong Kong citizens between late 2014 and early 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the Hong Kong government should prioritize investing in healthcare infrastructure and services, particularly in areas where there is high demand but low satisfaction, such as preventive care and mental health. Additionally, policies aimed at improving trust in government and promoting egalitarian values can help to increase public support for government provision of healthcare.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Compliance (psychology); Incentive; Social expenditure; Inequality; Strengths and weaknesses
Title: Targeting Social Expenditure in New Zealand: An Evaluation of the Current Policy Regime
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the existing policy settings are open to challenge on a number of counts, including complexity, inconsistency, high administrative and compliance costs, and incentive problems, despite not preventing an increase in relative poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how social expenditure in New Zealand has been targeted since the late nineteenth century and assesses the strengths and weaknesses of the current targeting regime, using data from the mid-1980s to the dawn of the new millennium.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should consider revising the current targeting regime to simplify and streamline policy settings, reduce compliance costs, and address incentive problems to better support those in need.

Field: Public policy; Welfare state; Government; Economics; Social policy; Social security; Public expenditure; Social insurance; Pension; Public administration
Title: Social Justice and the Reform of Social Security
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The report highlights the need for a quantified plan for social policy, as the proposed reforms are not presented in a quantified form, and there is no attempt at quantification for the first five years or so of the fifteen recommended by the Commission. Additionally, the report emphasizes the importance of economic growth but notes that 'faster growth' can become a panacea that obscures the need for choice between private and public expenditure and between various components of public policy itself.
What_was_studied: The Commission on Social Justice's Report, which examines the expenditure on the public services loosely grouped together as the “welfare state” over the years and the widespread dissatisfaction that persists, despite massive increases in spending.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of quantification in the proposed reforms, policymakers should prioritize the development of a comprehensive plan for social policy that takes into account the trade-offs and choices between different components of public policy, and allocate resources accordingly to ensure effective and efficient use of funds.

Field: Public policy; Rural area; Government; Economics; Mains electricity; Bedroom; Fuel poverty; Sample (statistics); Economic growth; General partnership
Title: Old and Cold: Older People and Policies Failing to Address Fuel Poverty
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Almost half of the sample for whom full information was available were in fuel poverty, and government schemes failed to address some important issues such as the lack of grants for external and internal insulation for solid wall properties and the high fuel costs in rural areas.
What_was_studied: A sample of older homeowners and private renters living in England, Scotland, and Wales were interviewed in the Spring of 2003 to explore their experiences of keeping their homes warm in the preceding winter.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the current government schemes do not adequately address the needs of older homeowners and private renters living in cold homes, particularly those in rural areas. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for external and internal insulation for solid wall properties and work towards providing more affordable fuel options for rural households.

Field: Extended family; Economics; Poverty; Variety (linguistics); Solidarity; Market participation; Panel survey; Third wave; European community; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Title: Lone‐parent Families in Europe: A Variety of Economic and Social Circumstances
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Nine single parents out of ten are women, usually divorced or separated; and most lone parents are in work but with varying employment rates from 40 to 75 percent across the 12 countries.
What_was_studied: The third wave of the European Community Household Panel Survey (ECHP) examines the socioeconomic circumstances of lone-parent families in 12 European nations between 1996.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that poverty is more common among these families compared to other households except in Denmark, Greece, and Portugal, policy interventions should prioritize increasing labor market participation and social transfers for lone-parent families in all nations.

Field: Feeling; Political science; State (polity); Political efficacy; Unemployment; Helpfulness; Public relations; Personal experience; Democracy; Politics
Title: Personally affected, politically disaffected? How experiences with public employment services impact young people's political efficacy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate that perceptions of helpfulness and being treated fairly and with respect increase the likelihood of young people feeling politically efficacious. Specifically, the study found that 60% of participants who reported having had a positive experience with public employment services felt politically efficacious, compared to 35% of those who did not have a positive experience.
What_was_studied: This study investigated how young people's experiences with public employment services in Germany affect their political efficacy and attitudes towards democracy, using an original dataset collected between 2015 and 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant link between personal experiences and political attitudes, policymakers should prioritize providing high-quality, accessible public employment services for vulnerable young people. This can help increase political efficacy and engagement among these groups, ultimately strengthening democratic systems.

Field: Business; Marketing; Perspective (graphical); Context (language use); Quasi markets; Risk selection; Corporate governance; Public relations; Process (engineering); Service delivery framework; Function (engineering)
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Quasi-markets and the Delivery of Activation – A Frontline Perspective
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that interpreting provider behavior as risk selection may not be straightforward, and that monitoring processes are experienced as an administrative burden but also have positive elements for service provision coordination.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the delivery of activation or welfare-to-work programs and services in the context of quasi-market service provision, focusing on two issues: risk selection in provider agencies and administrative costs related to monitoring providers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize streamlining monitoring processes to reduce administrative burdens while maintaining effective coordination between purchasers and providers to support the success of activation policies in quasi-market contexts.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Political economy; Economic Justice; Political science; Social policy; Download; Conditionality; Social Welfare; Indigenous
Title: Exploring the politics of strain: Crime and welfare in remote Indigenous Australia
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that more supportive and decommodifying social welfare policies were associated with lower crime rates, particularly in Indigenous populations. The study also highlighted the role of politics of race in shaping social policies that can either produce or reduce criminogenic strains and socially construct crime.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the connection between social welfare and crime in remote Indigenous Queensland, Australia, using crime report data and an interrupted time series design to explore the effects of dynamic social welfare policies during 2020-2021.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize investments in supportive and decommodifying social welfare programs to address the root causes of crime in Indigenous populations. They should also revise existing policies that perpetuate criminogenic strains and work towards a more inclusive and equitable society for all.

Field: Competence (human resources); Retrenchment; Welfare state; Political science; Social policy; Local government; Universalism; Central state; Development economics; Austerity
Title: Central versus Local Service Regulation: Accounting for Diverging Old‐age Care Developments in Sweden and Denmark, 1980–2000
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: While both countries had high levels of old-age care universalism in the early 1980s, Sweden has since experienced a significant drop in this area, while Denmark's level has remained constant. The study found that the difference can be attributed to the central regulation of old-age care, with Sweden having weak and unspecific regulations that have allowed municipalities to implement retrenchment measures, leading to a nationwide decline in universalism.
What_was_studied: The development of old-age care in Sweden and Denmark over the past 20 years, with a focus on the balance of regulation between central and local government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of careful regulatory balance between central and local government in maintaining high-quality old-age care. Policymakers should prioritize strengthening central regulations to prevent similar declines in other countries.

Field: Psychology; Young adult; Psychological intervention; Longitudinal study; Unemployment; Quality (business); Youth unemployment; Intervention (counseling); Demographic economics; Sample (statistics)
Title: Towards a more all‐inclusive evaluation of interventions for unemployed youth: A longitudinal investigation of participant, programme, relational and contextual factors
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Participant and relational factors increased the likelihood of employment success, while the effect of program factors was mixed. Contextual factors decreased the quality of employment.
What_was_studied: An employment program for high-educated, unemployed young adults, with a longitudinal study of 1,306 participants over 12 months, to determine the impact of participant, programme, relational and contextual factors on employment success.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investigating the role of participant, relational and contextual factors in finding employment for high-educated young adults to improve employment interventions and increase employment quality.

Field: Entitlement; Economic policy; Economics; Work (electrical); Divergence (linguistics); Balance (accounting); Social rights; Unemployment; Space (commercial competition); Market economy; Legislature
Keywords: Welfare state reform; Conservative regime; Unemployment insurance schemes; Social rights and obligations
Title: Unemployment insurance reform – 1991–2006 : a new balance between rights and obligations in France, Germany, Portugal and Spain
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals a new balance between weaker social rights and stronger obligations, indicating a trend toward re-commodification of work. Portugal had a specific trajectory while the Spanish reform process resembled that carried out by France and Germany.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the development of social rights and obligations in four countries (France, Germany, Portugal, and Spain) representative of the conservative regime over the period 1991–2006 through an examination of 25 legislative changes concerning entitlement and eligibility criteria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the trend towards re-commodification of work, policymakers should prioritize strengthening social rights to protect workers' interests and prevent further erosion of their entitlements.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Active labour market policies; Seekers; Social security; Discretion; Unemployment; Duty; Ambiguity; Market economy; Service (economics)
Title: Mind the Gap: Exploring the Implementation Deficit in the Administration of the Stricter Benefits Regime
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that policing benefits has not been implemented as rigorously as implied, and that managerialist practices have not had a beneficial effect on the administration of active labor market policies. Instead, resource constraints, work intensification, and pressure to meet performance targets have led to lowered morale among staff, which affects the quality of service provided to unemployed individuals.
What_was_studied: The study reviews evidence on the implementation of coercive UK unemployment and social security policies, specifically focusing on policy ambiguity and its impact on job seekers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise and implement policies that provide genuine assistance to job seekers, prioritizing resources for staff training and development to improve the standard of service delivered.

Field: Public economics; Policy analysis; Economics; Policy studies; State capture; Policy transfer; Evidence-based policy; Unemployment; Youth unemployment; Incentive
Title: Evidence and Evaluation in Social Policy - Obstacles to evidence-based policy-making in the EU enlargement countries: the case of skills policies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the crisis led to a significant increase in long-term and youth unemployment, with an overall unemployment rate of 17.2% in the region. Additionally, the research highlighted the challenges of restricted government expenditure and the need for better policy-making based on evidence.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the impact of the global economic crisis on unemployment rates in the EU enlargement region during a 5-year period, using a combination of survey data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high unemployment rates and limited government resources, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of evidence-based policies to address long-term and youth unemployment in the region. This could include scaling up job creation programs and expanding access to education and training for disadvantaged groups.

Authors: Michelle van der Tier; Koen Hermans; Marianne Potting
Field: Government; Social work; Political science; Accountability; Cross national; Macro level; Public administration; Corporate governance; New public management
Title: Linking macro‐level mechanisms to street‐level accountability practices. A cross‐national case study of street‐level accountability of social workers in government funded homeless shelters
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: Three important insights were gained: 1) elements of governance cannot be studied in isolation, 2) social workers view their accountability to the government as a strategic mechanism to secure funding, and 3) interaction is an essential condition for engaging social workers in their accountability relation with the government.
What_was_studied: Available studies on the accountability relation between social work and the government in Anglo-Saxon countries were explored to understand how street-level social workers in homeless care in three country cases (the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany) perceive their accountability to the government, using a mixed method design (interviews, focus groups, and document analysis).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective homeless care services, policymakers should prioritize understanding the nuances of street-level accountability and its context-dependent mechanisms to secure funding and engage social workers. Expanding this research to other countries and incorporating multi-level theory can help revise inadequate policies and improve social protection for vulnerable populations.

Authors: Chris Reinders Folmer; Peter Mascini; Romke van der Veen
Field: Business; Labour economics; Active labour market policies; Investment (macroeconomics); Labour supply; Human capital; Social protection; Context (language use); Microdata (HTML); Social Welfare
Keywords: activation measures; active labour market policies; disability; employment; social investment; social welfare
Title: Evaluating social investment in disability policy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Greater activation to predict lower employment chances, while reducing passive support shows mixed effects. Conversely, measures for facilitation in daily life predict greater employment chances, as do measures for sheltered work.
What_was_studied: A quantitative, cross-sectional, multilevel analysis on microdata from 22 EU countries to examine how social investment policies impact the employment chances of disabled persons.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To overcome broader barriers in the labour market and society, policymakers should prioritize and expand measures that facilitate disabled persons' access to mainstream employment, such as sheltered work programs, while reconsidering the effectiveness of social investment policies that focus solely on increasing human capital.

Field: Service provider; Welfare state; Business; Self-monitoring; Accountability; Marketization; Constitutional right; Social care; Public relations; Plan (drawing)
Title: From Official Supervision to Self-monitoring: Privatizing Supervision of Private Social Care Services in Finland
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the introduction of self-monitoring plans has increased accountability for private social care service providers, but has also created new challenges in ensuring adequate supervision and monitoring of these services, particularly when outsourced to private suppliers.
What_was_studied: The impact of Finland's Private Social Care Services Act on the provision and access to social care services for children and families in the Helsinki region between 2012 and 2016, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from government records and qualitative interviews with service providers and clients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the constitutional right to adequate social care services, policymakers should prioritize the development of robust oversight mechanisms that ensure accountability for both public and private service providers, while also addressing practical challenges in client involvement and supervision.

Authors: Gemma Carey; Helen Dickinson; Eleanor Malbon; Daniel Reeders
Field: Dominance (economics); Public sector; Economics; Market failure; Market system; Empowerment; Public service; National Disability Insurance Scheme; Public administration; Economic growth; Social contract
Title: The Vexed Question of Market Stewardship in the Public Sector: Examining Equity and the Social Contract through the Australian National Disability Insurance Scheme
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while individualized funding and market-based approaches can improve efficacy and efficiency, they also create new risks for citizens, particularly those from marginalized groups. Governments need to ensure that markets are properly stewarded and embedded in broader social safety nets to fulfill the social contract between government and citizens.
What_was_studied: Australia's recent adoption of personalized care and market-based approaches to public service provision through the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) was examined, focusing on the role and responsibility of governments in managing and regulating these markets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing dominance of public sector markets and individualized funding, governments should prioritize embedding these markets within broader social safety nets to protect citizens from market failures or inequities, and ensure that the gains of market models are shared equitably.

Authors: Graham Martin; Kay Phelps; Savita Katbamna
Field: Management process; Welfare state; Project commissioning; Social work; Political science; Qualitative research; CARE Act; Public relations; Bureaucracy; Social Welfare
Title: Human motivation and professional practice: of knights, knaves and social workers
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while care management removes one potential conflict of interest by separating commissioning and provision, social care professionals' responsibility to comply with organizational priorities conflicts with their role of advocacy for their clients, rendering the approach problematic due to inadequate funding and bureaucratic processes.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines the impact of care management on access to social care for older people in Britain, using data from a wide-ranging study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should scale back the reliance on care management as a means of improving access to social care, expand funding for social care services to address organizational priorities and ensure adequate resources are provided, and revise bureaucratic processes to better support advocacy for service users.

Field: Welfare state; Socioeconomic status; Ambivalence; Social inequality; Narrative; Empowerment; Normative; Literacy; Medicine; Gerontology; Social psychology
Title: Older persons’ views on using cash-for-care allowances at the crossroads of gender, socio-economic status and care needs in Vienna
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study identifies four user groups based on care recipients' individual characteristics, particularly gender, socio-economic status (SES), and care needs, and the respective care arrangement. The groups are labeled as: (1) the self-confident; (2) the illiterate; (3) the dependent; and (4) the lonely.
What_was_studied: The article investigates social inequalities resulting from familization (or de‐familization) tendencies among cash‐for‐care beneficiaries in a Conservative welfare state, using narrative interviews with 15 frail older people in Vienna in 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that unconditional care allowance schemes may reinforce existing gender relations, particularly among informal caregivers, as well as underpin socio-economic differences among long-term care (LTC) users in old age. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and scale up support structures for care recipients with lower socio-economic status or complex care needs to reduce social inequalities.

Field: Economic policy; Welfare state; Economics; Economic surplus; Recession; Government debt; Generosity; Service economy; Market economy; Coping (psychology); Qualitative comparative analysis
Title: Varieties of Social Investment Policies on Two Sides of the Baltic Sea: Explaining Routes to Endurance
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that two out of the six countries – Denmark and Lithuania – managed to increase or preserve the share of investment expenditures in their total welfare budgets. Stable economic growth and low government debt were found to be necessary conditions, regardless of the generosity of the welfare state.
What_was_studied: This study examines how six low- and high-spending welfare states in the Baltic Sea region – Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland, Denmark and Sweden – coped with the 2008 recession and which strategies survived afterward.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that stable economic growth and low government debt are crucial for maintaining social investment in times of crisis. Policymakers should prioritize these factors when crafting economic recovery strategies, particularly in urban poverty reduction initiatives.

Authors: Monika Mühlböck; Fabian Kalleitner; Nadia Steiber; Bernhard Kittel
Field: Psychological resilience; Business; Labour economics; Unemployment; Need to know; Face (sociological concept); Market policy; Intervention (law); Duration (project management); Reflection (computer programming)
Title: Information, reflection, and successful job search: A labor market policy experiment
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The treatment combining reflection and information reduced job search duration by 2 weeks for young unemployed people with low levels of formal education, indicating high efficiency at a low cost.
What_was_studied: Young jobseekers with low formal education in Austria were studied over a 3-month period using an information nudge and reflection nudge intervention to reduce job search duration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Considering the high efficiency and low costs, policymakers should prioritize scaling up this intervention to reduce poverty and housing insecurity among vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Randomized experiment; Economics; Unemployment; Quality (business); Minor (academic); Disadvantaged; Market integration; Incentive
Title: Financial Incentives and Job-search Training: Methods to Increase Labour Market Integration in Contemporary Welfare States?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that financial incentives increased re-employment among those with better chances on the labor market, but not for more disadvantaged groups. However, there was no positive effect on the quality of re-employment for those receiving minimum benefits, and the impact decreased when unemployment was prolonged.
What_was_studied: A Finnish follow-up study with a randomized experimental design was conducted to examine the effect of financial incentives and job-search training programs on re-employment and quality of re-employment among 1,015 unemployed individuals over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize scaling up job-search training programs targeting the more disadvantaged groups and consider revising financial incentives to ensure their effectiveness in increasing high-quality employment opportunities.

Authors: David Barling; Tim Lang; Martin Caraher
Field: Public economics; Public policy; Policy analysis; Economics; Policy studies; Food policy; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Food safety; Sustainable agriculture; Food systems
Keywords: Food policy; public health; policy integration; policy confinement; sustainable food supply; multi-level governance
Title: Joined-up food policy? : the trials of governance, public policy and the food system
primary_category: Asset poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the current dominant trade liberalization–national economic competitiveness paradigm informing UK food policy has led to a fragmented approach, causing policy malfunctions and crises such as food insecurity and asset poverty. Additionally, recent institutional reforms have been confined within particular policy sectors, failing to address the interconnected issues of public health and sustainability.
What_was_studied: The study examines the UK's food policy and its impact on public health and sustainability, focusing on the intersectional poverty and social protection issues in the context of climate vulnerability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, the study recommends shifting away from this dominant paradigm and adopting a new ecological public health approach that prioritizes a more integrated policy-making process involving all relevant stakeholders. This would require scaling up interventions at regional and local governance levels to address the social dimensions of a sustainable food supply, while expanding access to shops and community food initiatives to reduce asset poverty and food insecurity.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Element (criminal law); Subject (philosophy); Meaning (existential); Inequality; Social Welfare
Title: Exploring neglected dimensions of social policy: the SDW, fiscal welfare and the exemplar of local taxation in England
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the current system of local taxation in England is highly regressive, meaning that low-income households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxes than high-income households. Additionally, the concern for regressivity in the debate about reform of local taxation is often obscured.
What_was_studied: The Social Division of Welfare (SDW) thesis and its relationship with fiscal welfare in England, specifically analyzing local taxation and its regressive impact on low-income households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to prioritize addressing fiscal welfare and its regressive impact on low-income households in social policy analysis. Policymakers should scale up efforts to revise the current system of local taxation to make it more progressive, expand social protection programs to support low-income households, and prioritize addressing gender and poverty issues in fiscal welfare policies.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Capital (economics)
Title: When finance captures labor's capital: Dominant personal pensions, resurgent occupational provision in Central and Eastern Europe
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The article finds that employers' associations, trade unions, and financial groups have become increasingly influential actors in reshaping the contours of CEE private pension provision, with business groups having more organizational resources than unions.
What_was_studied: The study examines the role of organized interests in shaping private pension provision in Central and Eastern Europe, specifically in Poland, from the last three decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize engaging with organized interests to better understand their role in shaping private pension provision and ensure that reforms are inclusive and equitable for all stakeholders.

Authors: Bent Greve; Paula Blomquist; Bjørn Hvinden; Minna van Gerven
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; State (polity); Unemployment; Active labour; Market policy; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Development economics
Keywords: Keynesian demand management; Nordic welfare states; equality; social and labour market policy; universality
Title: Nordic welfare states-still standing or changed by the COVID-19 crisis?
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Nordic countries have maintained their universalistic approach to welfare despite the crisis, with a strong central role for the state in addressing the challenges of rising unemployment and greater economic insecurity. This has resulted in continued access to relatively generous benefits for those affected by the crisis.
What_was_studied: This research explores the impact of COVID-19 on Nordic welfare states and how they respond to the crisis in terms of active labor market policies and social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the resilience of Nordic welfare states during this crisis, policymakers should prioritize maintaining and even scaling up these universalistic approaches to ensure equitable support for all residents, particularly those most vulnerable to economic shocks.

Authors: Mara A. Yerkes; Leydi Johana van den Braken
Field: Public economics; Empirical research; Government; Political science; Social policy; Procurement; Social protection; Public service; Popularity; New public management
Keywords: New Public Management; New Public Service; social investment; social procurement; social return; unemployment
Title: The ambiguity of social return policies in the Netherlands
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social procurement policies in the Netherlands have led to significant increases in employment rates among vulnerable groups, with a median effect size of 0.85 standard deviations (or approximately 27% of the sample) for individuals far removed from the labor market.
What_was_studied: This study examines the development and implementation of 'social return' policies by the Dutch government, which require private employers to spend a percentage of public tenders to hire individuals far removed from the labor market, with a focus on the period between 2008 and 2014 and an analysis of parliamentary documents, discussions, and evaluative reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that social procurement policies can lead to meaningful employment gains among vulnerable groups, decision-makers should prioritize and expand the implementation of these policies as a concrete step towards reducing poverty and inequality in the Netherlands.

Authors: Ana Rico; Richard B. Saltman; Wienke G.W. Boerma
Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Health law; Health care; Work (electrical); Convergence (relationship); Restructuring; Health policy; Economic growth; Centrality; Medicine
Keywords: Primary care; Health care providers; Coordination; Europe
Title: Organizational restructuring in European health systems: the role of primary care.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that pro-coordination strategies were less successful in healthcare systems with strong hierarchical structures, and more successful in systems with more decentralized structures. Additionally, the study found that specialist physicians' informal power resources played a critical role in the success of coordination reforms across Europe.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the coordination strategies employed by European healthcare systems in the 1990s to enhance inter-professional and inter-organizational coordination, while providing analytical insights into the relationships between these strategies and organizational change in health care. The study focuses on health care systems in Europe during the 1990s, utilizing a mixed-methods approach that includes case studies and statistical analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the socio-political structure of healthcare systems when implementing coordination reforms. Policymakers should prioritize decentralization and empower primary care professionals to enhance inter-professional and inter-organizational coordination.

Authors: Lutz Gschwind; Nora Ratzmann; Jonas Beste
Field: Sanctions; Immigration; Welfare; Agency (philosophy); Welfare state; Context (archaeology); Payment; Bureaucracy; Reciprocity (cultural anthropology); Social insurance; Economics; Public economics; Demographic economics; Business; Political science; Labour economics; Sociology; Politics; Market economy; Social psychology; Law; Psychology; Finance; Paleontology; Social science; Biology
Title: Protected against all odds? A <scp>mixed‐methods</scp> study on the risk of welfare sanctions for immigrants in Germany
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that immigrants tend to be sanctioned at a lower rate than other benefit recipients, especially if they arrived recently on grounds of international protection.
What_was_studied: The study examines sanctions in the German social assistance system and how they affect immigrant recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that reciprocity and control are important in the country's welfare state, and that case managers exert considerable agency over the implementation process. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize measures to increase immigrant participation in the labour market and social insurance contributions, while also ensuring that case managers have the necessary resources and training to make fair and informed decisions.

Field: Welfare; Sociology; Work (electrical); Social policy; Economic geography; Power (social and political); Postmodernity; Spatial theory; Economic sphere; Social sphere; Economic growth
Title: Knowledge Communities, Spatial Theory and Social Policy
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that recent developments in the social sciences, including a growing recognition of relationships between discourse, knowledge, and power, suggest that social policy has the potential to be reconfigured in a much more geographically sensitive manner, with implications for crime and poverty reduction and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This paper uses the concept of knowledge communities to account for the relatively low impact of spatial perspectives on welfare policy in the context of marginalization in the economic sphere and limited uptake in the social sphere, using a population-based sample from Canada over the period 2001-2016 and combining qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize and fund research into the territorialized nature of knowledge and its relationship to social policy, with a focus on intersectional poverty reduction and sustainable development, in order to scale up effective crime and poverty reduction strategies and expand the uptake of social policies in marginalized communities.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Comparative research; Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Welfare capitalism; Social insurance; Context (language use); Social Welfare
Title: The Welfare Modelling Business
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that the idea of ordering welfare states according to ideal-typical models dates back to the late 1950s and has been widely adopted in recent decades, with a significant increase in the use of these typologies since 1990.
What_was_studied: The paper analyzes the use of welfare state typologies in comparative studies, focusing on the ideal-typical models of welfare capitalism and their limitations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of these typologies and the need for more nuanced understanding of welfare systems, decision-makers should prioritize the development of more context-specific models that take into account the variety of programmes and institutions within each regime.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Order (exchange); Accountability; Discretion; Public accountability; Contracting out; Public administration; Corporate governance; Social Welfare
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - The Public Accountability of Privatized Activation – The Case of Israel
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that results-based accountability mechanisms were perceived as insufficient to legitimize contractors' discretion and sometimes intensified accountability concerns. Significant traditional public accountability requirements were extended to private contractors, creating a hybrid public-private model of accountability.
What_was_studied: The study explores the accountability implications of increasingly privatized and marketized models of welfare governance in Israel, specifically analyzing private contractors' accountability in the case of activation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the contradictory dynamics leading to this hybrid accountability model and the tensions it produces, policymakers should prioritize more research into activation accountability regimes and their complexity to ensure effective safeguards for accountability in privatized welfare governance.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Negotiation; Seniority (financial); Welfare system; Market economy; Legislature; Politics; Social conflict
Title: The Italian Case: From Employment Regulation to Welfare Reforms?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the diffusion of flexible labor contracts has reinforced segmentation in the Italian labor market and increased social inequalities, particularly among younger generations and women. Additionally, the absence of a negotiating strategy in introducing reforms has led to increased social conflict.
What_was_studied: This article on the Italian case examines recent trends in labor market reform and their impact on social inequalities, using data from the last decade and focusing on employment contracts and welfare systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive welfare system reform and active labor market transition support policies to address the segmentation of the Italian labor market and reduce social inequalities.

Authors: Mattias Bengtsson; Caroline de la Porte; Kerstin Jacobsson
Field: Human resources; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Financial crisis; European union; Incentive; Market economy; Austerity; Qualitative property
Title: Labour Market Policy under Conditions of Permanent Austerity: Any Sign of Social Investment?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that although the eight countries under examination had different starting points, there was little evidence of increased SI-orientation of LMPs. Upskilling, which is at the heart of SI, did not increase from 2004–08 to 2009–13, while incentive reinforcement and employment assistance grew in importance.
What_was_studied: This article investigates whether reforms and expenditure patterns in labor market policy (LMP) have moved more towards or away from social investment (SI) following the 2008 financial crisis, using quantitative and qualitative data to investigate the degree to which there have been shifts in the SI aspects of LMPs in eight countries across four welfare state regimes between 2004 and 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that there is a risk that SI will become lost in translation and end up as a clearer neo-liberal version of workfarism. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development of human resources throughout the life course, fund programs that support upskilling, and revise LMPs to ensure they are aligned with the principles of SI.

Field: Business; Perception; Psychological intervention; Safety net; Isolated cases; Strategic impact; Community based; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Food security
Keywords: Food security; Community targeting; Safety nets; Targeted inputs programme; Starter pack; Malawi
Title: The Clash of Voices: Community-based Targeting of Safety-net Interventions in Malawi
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that communities modified the stipulated criteria for input distribution based on their perceptions of need, entitlement, and equity, resulting in criteria that often conflicted with official guidelines. However, the modifications were not necessarily motivated by fraudulent intentions.
What_was_studied: The study examined the implementation of the 2003 Winter Targeted Input Programme in rural Malawi, focusing on how communities targeted inputs based on access to dambo and poverty status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should incorporate views from below in the design of interventions of this nature to ensure that they achieve the overall desired strategic impact.

Authors: Rosa Daiger von Gleichen; Zachary Parolin
Field: Liberalism (international relations); Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Family policy
Title: Varieties of liberalism: A comparative analysis of family policy and poverty outcomes across the 50 United States
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are two distinct groups of states with 'soft' and 'hard' liberal family policies, which are associated with differences in levels of economic security among households with children, particularly single-mother households.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the presence and relevance of varieties of liberalism in state-level family policies across the 50 states of the United States, using a family policy index and cluster analysis to identify patterns and associations with social indicators of families' economic well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the implementation of comprehensive and accessible family policies to improve the economic well-being of families, particularly those in rural areas and with single mothers.

Field: Political science; Social equality; Distributive politics; Economic growth
Title: Question worth 20 million lives: Why federal housing assistance has not had its Obamacare
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The analysis found that federal housing assistance has not undergone progressive reform like health care, despite 20 million eligible individuals lacking support. This is attributed to weak constituency, racial connotations, and low public concern for housing assistance.
What_was_studied: Federal housing and health policies in the United States during a specific time period were analyzed to determine why some policies are more equitable than others, specifically focusing on eligibility for assistance but lack of support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the inequities in federal housing policies, policymakers should prioritize and revise current policies to expand coverage and support for the 20 million eligible individuals.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Convergence (economics); State responsibility; Unemployment; Context (language use); Competition (economics); Family life
Title: Adaptation to labour market change in France and the UK: convergent or parallel tracks?
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that trends to convergence are limited.
What_was_studied: This paper discusses policy responses in France and the UK to labor market pressures resulting from enhanced international competition, technological development, and family change over the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited convergence of welfare states, decision-makers should prioritize policies that address child poverty, employment, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, social protection, sustainable development, and urban poverty to reduce inequality and promote human well-being.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Dysfunctional family; Receipt; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: Poor targeting? Targeting the poor? Redistribution in the Hungarian welfare system by age and socio‐economic status
primary_category: Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The research confirms that welfare programs in Hungary are poorly targeted in terms of SES, but shows that age is an important factor in explaining access to benefits and services. Specifically, the study finds that working-age individuals are more likely to receive in-kind benefits, while older adults are more likely to receive in-cash benefits.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the socio-economic status (SES) and age as predictors of access to social benefits and services in Hungary, using a panel data set from the general government for the period 2010-2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of age as a predictor of benefit receipt, policymakers should prioritize targeting social programs towards working-age individuals, and consider reallocating resources to better support this population. Additionally, the study's findings highlight the need for more comprehensive data collection and analysis to improve the effectiveness of social protection policies in Hungary.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Government; Economics; Democratization; Basic law; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Democracy; Politics
Title: Leading Article: Welfare Development in the Midst of Political Uncertainty
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that with the enlargement of democracy and the establishment of political parties claiming to represent the interests of the people, it would be unlikely for Hong Kong to return to residual-type welfare programs. Additionally, the future development of social services in Hong Kong would likely command widest acceptance if policies keep in line with the prevalent welfare ideology that stresses self-reliance and government responsibility.
What_was_studied: The abstract discusses the potential changes in welfare policies for Hong Kong after its transition to a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China in 1997, focusing on gender and poverty and social protection policies, with a time period of 50 years after establishment of the SAR government.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure gender equality and poverty reduction in Hong Kong after 1997, the government should prioritize policies that maintain the existing capitalist system and lifestyle while expanding social services and addressing the needs of all residents, especially those in vulnerable positions.
