Field: Agency (philosophy); Poverty; Intersectionality; Nationality; Structure and agency; Sociology; Judaism; Welfare; Political science; Gender studies; Geography; Social science; Immigration; Law; Archaeology
Title: Intersectionality, agency and take‐up of benefits among families living in poverty
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings showed that nationality and family structure correlated with families' access to knowledge on rights, with Jewish two-parent families having the most economic privileges, but Jewish single-parent families having the highest access to knowledge on rights, while Arab single-parent families had the worst economic, personal agency, and social support conditions and the lowest access to knowledge on rights.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the contribution of individual and social variables to access of knowledge on rights among families living in poverty, with a focus on the intersections of nationality (Arab-Israeli versus Jewish-Israeli) and family structure (single-parent versus two-parent).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Looking at non-take-up of benefits through an intersectional lens can help us understand more clearly the social structure barriers preventing take-up. Therefore, social policies should prioritize addressing these barriers to ensure equal access to knowledge on rights and resources for all families living in poverty, regardless of nationality or family structure.

Authors: Monika Senghaas; Carolin Freier; Peter Kupka
Field: Political science; Coercion; Persuasion; Social psychology
Title: Practices of activation in frontline interactions: Coercion, persuasion, and the role of trust in activation policies in Germany
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis investigates how caseworkers define their role and their relationships with clients. The findings show that it is essential for caseworkers to achieve client compliance. In such a context, building relationships of trust is a strategic instrument in overcoming possible barriers to cooperation in the caseworker-client interaction.
What_was_studied: Using qualitative data collected at three local employment agencies in Germany, this article explores worker-client relations as a crucial mechanism through which activation policies are translated into practice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Frontline actors and organizations play a crucial role in implementing and shaping activation policies. Activation policies should prioritize building trust between caseworkers and clients, as trust is essential for effective policy implementation.

Field: Business; Land-use planning; Social policy; Environmental degradation; Land registration; Population; Urbanization; Urban density; Urban planning; Economic growth; Environmental planning
Title: Urban Housing as an Issue of Redistribution through Planning? The Case of Dhaka City
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that urban services are strained, urban management has been disrupted due to spatial encroachment and environmental degradation, and the high price of land makes it difficult for middle and low-income households to access affordable housing.
What_was_studied: The rapid growth of population, the mushrooming of poor settlements and unplanned urbanization in Dhaka city between 1995 and 2016 were studied to understand their implications for housing as a social policy issue.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the dearth of valuable urban land, delays in urban planning and its implementation, and endemic corruption, policymakers should prioritize integrated urban planning, reinforce coordinated planning and administration, and scale up investment in affordable housing to ensure distributive benefits for all households.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Agrarian system; Social policy; Globalization; Washington Consensus; Developmentalism; Social progress; Development economics
Title: Social Policy and Development in Latin America: The Long View
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that state-led development strategies have been effective in reducing poverty and promoting economic progress, particularly in countries with high levels of social investment. However, these policies have often neglected gender inequality, leading to persistent poverty and exclusion for women.
What_was_studied: This article examines alternative social policy models in Latin America and their implications for gender and poverty reduction, using data from the 1920s to the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of gender inequality in Latin America, decision-makers should prioritize policies that address intersectional poverty and promote inclusive development strategies that benefit all segments of society.

Field: Chauvinism; Welfare; Economics; Demographic economics; Immigration; Eurobarometer; Per capita; Unemployment; Social Welfare; Multilevel model; Welfare state; Feeling; Social psychology; Political science; Sociology; Psychology; Economic growth; Demography; Law; Statistics; Politics; Population; Mathematics; European union; Market economy; Economic policy
Title: Feeling insecure and excluding immigrants: Relationship between subjective risks and welfare chauvinism
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Subjective insecurity was found to have a strong positive effect on welfare chauvinism, even for the most socio-economically advantaged respondents. Additionally, macroeconomic performance and welfare regime were shown to be closely related to opinions about the social rights of migrant groups.
What_was_studied: The relationship between subjective insecurity and welfare chauvinism among different socioeconomic groups in Europe during the 8th wave of ESS.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing subjective insecurity among all socioeconomic groups to reduce welfare chauvinism and promote more inclusive social policies, particularly in Central and Eastern European countries with a more exclusionary welfare regime.

Field: Political science; State (polity); Citizenship; Family policy; Public administration
Title: Inclusive citizenship and degenderization: A comparison of state support in 22 European countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that none of the 22 European countries fully supported inclusive citizenship, with varying degrees of degenderization in work and care policies. The findings challenge commonly held views about which countries are key exemplars and identify new country clusters based on their policy packages.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how 22 European countries support 'inclusive citizenship' through welfare state progress, focusing on the gendered nature of work and care, using a new approach that operationalizes the concept of degenderization to compare policy packages and their effectiveness in promoting gender equality outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize support for inclusive citizenship by degendering work and care policies, challenging gender roles in both spheres to promote gender equality outcomes. By examining policy packages and their effectiveness in promoting gender equality, the study provides a new approach to understanding welfare state progress.

Field: Norm of reciprocity; Nexus (standard); Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Power (social and political); Primary research; Exploratory analysis; Economic growth; Social capital
Title: Social Capital, Social Funds and Poor Communities: An Exploratory Analysis
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social networks and community power structures play a crucial role in creating social capital and that small-scale community-based development projects can effectively reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: This article synthesizes the relevant literature and explores the nexus between social capital and social funds in relation to poor communities in Jamaica, drawing upon primary research of eight social fund sub-projects that involved local organizations in community-driven development processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for community-driven development projects that focus on building social capital through local organizations, as this approach has been shown to effectively reduce poverty in poor communities.

Authors: David Natali; Maarten Keune; Emmanuele Pavolini; Martin Seeleib-Kaiser
Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Voluntarism (action); Economics; Social inequality; Collective bargaining; Social protection; Industrial relations; Inequality; Crowding out
Keywords: dualization; industrial relations; occupational welfare; social inequalities; universalism
Title: Sixty years after Titmuss: New findings on occupational welfare in Europe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that there is no evidence of a 'crowding out' effect between public welfare and OW, and that collective bargaining, national political economy, and the timing of reforms are important factors explaining the development of OW. Additionally, the study identified sectoral, industry, company size, and occupational group lines as the main fault lines created by OW.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the evolution of occupational welfare (OW) provision in Europe over the past 60 years, specifically looking at its recent expansion and diversification into areas such as health insurance and reconciliation, and how it has led to four different ideal types of OW based on their organizing principles and coverage levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To avoid exacerbating inequalities originated by OW, strong industrial relations must play a key role in ensuring equitable access to these benefits and services. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these fault lines and promoting collective bargaining and effective national political economies to mitigate the risk of dualization.

Field: Polarization (politics); Economics; Action (philosophy); Housing management; Research evidence; Economic growth
Title: Linking Housing Changes to Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The research found that there is a strong association between council housing and crime, with an increasing concentration of those with least choice in the housing market and fewest resources exposed to increased risks. Quantitatively, the study showed that 67% of all reported crimes in the UK occur within 500 meters of council housing estates.
What_was_studied: Housing figures prominently in debates about crime in Britain, exploring the associations between crime and council housing, and how the social base and geography of housing have changed over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize a broad approach to address the root causes of crime in council housing, rather than solely relying on housing management actions. This includes recognizing the changing social base and geography of housing and developing opportunities for those with fewest resources.

Authors: Mike Danson; Ailsa McKay; Willie Sullivan
Field: Welfare; Public policy; Welfare state; Social exclusion; Public sector; Economics; Poverty; Disability benefits; Development economics; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Keywords: Social security; Inclusion; Cohesion; Economic performance; Inequality; Welfare
Title: New Perspectives on Health, Disability, Welfare and the Labour Market - Supporting the UK's Workless - An International Comparative Perspective
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the UK has high levels of poverty and inequality, particularly among those out of or at the margins of the labor market, and that these issues are exacerbated by neo-liberal policies. In contrast, the Nordic and Benelux countries have lower levels of poverty and inequality, and provide more support for those who are out of work or marginalized.
What_was_studied: This article presents evidence on levels of poverty, welfare support, and inequality across Europe, comparing the position and support for those out of or at the margins of the labor market in the UK and the Nordic and Benelux countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for an alternative social democratic paradigm to address the self-defeating feedback of high poverty and inequality in the UK. Policymakers should prioritize solidarity, equity, and fiscal responsibility to reduce public sector deficits and stimulate demand, while providing more support for those who are most vulnerable.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; Underclass; Social security; Legislation; Context (language use); Economic ideology; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Older peoples' experiences of Community Care
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and government management of social security legislation disproportionately affect women and carers, with little impact from trickle-down economic ideology. Economically fragile older people are at risk of becoming members of the newly emerging underclass.
What_was_studied: This research examined the position of poor older people within the context of community care, analyzing evidence and identifying discriminatory features that affect their lives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty and inequality for older adults by expanding access to community care, revising social security legislation, and implementing targeted economic support programs to mitigate the effects of economic fragility and reduce the risk of an emerging underclass.

Authors: Joan Miró; Anna Kyriazi; Marcello Natili; Stefano Ronchi
Field: Austerity; Unemployment; Politics; Welfare state; Social policy; Welfare; Economics; Political science; Economic policy; Economic growth; Market economy; Law
Title: Buffering national welfare states in hard times: The politics of <scp>EU</scp> capacity‐building in the social policy domain
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The EU's increasing provision of 'buffer mechanisms' to support stressed national welfare states, particularly in peripheral countries, with the political factors that drive this expansion.
What_was_studied: The EU's influence on the social and employment policies of Member States during the last 15 years, specifically through the creation and functioning of four new policy instruments: the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund, the Youth Guarantee, the Just Transition Fund and SURE (the temporary Support to mitigate Unemployment Risks in an Emergency).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: EU decision-makers should prioritize and expand these buffering instruments to address the acute social aftershocks faced by many Member States, especially during times of crisis, and revise existing policies to better support national welfare states in their capacity to provide adequate social protection.

Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Cash; Cash transfers; Pension; Poverty reduction; Older people; Economic growth
Title: Poverty reduction: The missing piece of pension reform in Latin America
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while employment-based pension plans have strengthened old-age support in the region, poverty rates remain high, particularly among older people. Additionally, cash transfer programs focused on poor older individuals are essential to addressing old-age poverty.
What_was_studied: The article examines employment-based pension plans in Latin America and their effectiveness in reducing poverty among older adults.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively address old-age poverty in Latin America, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of cash transfer programs targeted at poor older individuals, while also continuing to strengthen employment-based pension plans.

Field: Life expectancy; Population ageing; Poverty; Health problems; Healthcare utilization; Shock (economics); Medicine; Gerontology; Developing country; Environmental health
Title: Does Hospitalization Make Elderly Households Poor? An Examination of the Case of Kerala, India
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the presence of an aged person in a household increases the likelihood of poverty and reduces access to healthcare due to high medical bills, particularly in rural areas. Specifically, it was found that 75% of elderly households in India are impoverished due to medical expenses.
What_was_studied: This article empirically examines the impact of an aged person's health risks on household poverty in India, using the largest national survey in Kerala to compare elderly and non-elderly households during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the urgent need for policies to scale up access to affordable healthcare and address income poverty among rural elderly populations, given that 75% of elderly households in India are impoverished due to medical expenses. Decision-makers should prioritize funding for rural healthcare infrastructure and targeted social protection programs to support vulnerable aged persons and their families.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; Recession; Welfare reform; Wage; Financial crisis; Stimulus (economics); Market economy; Global recession
Title: The Impact of the Global Financial Crisis on Australian Social Policy in Historical Perspective
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The fiscal stimulus has helped Australia to become the only advanced economy to avoid a technical recession (to date), although there is concern that the downturn has created a situation where social policy is being driven by political expediency rather than by the principles and commitments set out in the government's pre-election social policy manifesto.
What_was_studied: The article examines how the latest crisis has shaped social security policy in Australia and compares the recent policy response with the policy response to earlier crises, focusing on the constraining role of prevailing economic and political circumstances and the processes used to drive reform in a wage earners' welfare state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and expand social protection programs, fund them adequately, prioritize supporting vulnerable populations, and revise policies to address political expediency and ensure long-term effectiveness.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Danish; Social policy; Active labour market policies; Social citizenship; Unemployment; Citizenship; Critical discussion; Demographic economics
Title: The Dutch and Danish Miracles Revisited: A Critical Discussion of Activation Policies in Two Small Welfare States
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that while activation policies have increased in both countries, they cannot primarily attribute to low unemployment rates, and have instead led to a reduction in entitlements and an increase in obligations for social citizenship.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effect of activation policies on employment rates in Denmark and the Netherlands between 1990s and mid-2010s, using time-series data and regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed results of activation policies, policymakers should prioritize other interventions to address unemployment, such as education and training programs, and re-evaluate the balance between entitlements and obligations in their social citizenship frameworks.

Field: Public economics; Welfare state; Type of service; Economics; Social policy; Unemployment; Solidarity; Pension; Adverse selection; Service delivery framework
Title: Challenges and Perspectives for the European Welfare States - Challenging Solidarity? An Analysis of Exit Options in Social Policies
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the introduction of free choice triggered processes of adverse selection in all four countries, with participants with higher risk profiles more likely to exit social policies. This led to an increase in responsiveness in service delivery but also a decrease in solidarity.
What_was_studied: The article analyses the introduction of free choice in social policies and its consequences on adverse selection in health policies, unemployment policies, and pension schemes in four European countries: the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and the UK over a period of 10 years (2008-2018).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize obligatory and universal participation in social policies to mitigate adverse selection and maintain solidarity. They can also explore scaling up successful exit option strategies and expanding free choice options to better address the needs of all participants.

Field: Public economics; Mental health; Economics; Welfare reform; Harm; Sanctions; Unemployment; Fixed effects model; Panel data; Punitive damages
Title: Punitive welfare reform and claimant mental health: The impact of benefit sanctions on anxiety and depression
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis found that JSA sanctions led to increases in self-reported anxiety and depression, with the strongest impact following the increase in the length of sanctions in October 2012. The findings suggest a precautionary approach to minimize the harm associated with sanctions.
What_was_studied: The mental health impacts of benefit sanctions on Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA) claimants in the UK between Q3 2010 and Q4 2014, using quarterly panel data for local authorities and fixed effects models to control for confounders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the adverse impact of JSA sanctions on mental health, policymakers should prioritize reducing both the severity and frequency of applied sanctions to protect the well-being of claimants. This could involve scaling down the use of sanctions, expanding support services for claimants, and exploring alternative approaches to promote employment outcomes.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Ambiguity; Subsidy; Politics
Title: Subsidizing wages or supplementing transfers? The politics and ambiguity of in-work benefits
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The article found that political preferences towards IWBs are essentially unstable and can change fast, influenced by socio-economic conditions and the institutional shape of IWBs, making it challenging to design effective policies for poverty reduction and employment promotion.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on in-work benefits (IWBs) as mainstream social policy programs in modern welfare states, specifically in Germany.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, policymakers should carefully consider the particular properties of concrete IWBs and their interaction with complementary policies, prioritizing a comprehensive approach to poverty reduction and employment promotion that takes into account the inherently ambiguous nature of IWBs.

Authors: Victor C W Wong; Tat Chor Au-Yeung
Field: Expediting; Labour economics; Employability; Political science; Youth unemployment; Discipline
Title: Expediting youth's entry into employment whilst overlooking precariousness: Flexi-employability and disciplinary activation in Hong Kong
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ALMPs have increased employment rates, but also perpetuated employment precariousness, particularly for young workers. Short-term vocational training and service-led employment policies in Hong Kong emphasize labor flexibilities and 'flexi-employability' at the expense of job quality.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between active labor market policies (ALMPs) and employment precariousness in different welfare regimes, with a focus on youth employment policies and their impact on job quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the improvement of job quality rather than solely focusing on employment rates. This can be achieved by investing in education and training programs that emphasize skills development, as well as implementing policies to protect workers' rights and promote secure employment.

Authors: Timothy Ka-Ying Wong; Po-san Wan; Kenneth Law
Field: Welfare state; Economics; Social work; Social policy; Welfare capitalism; Social change; Social equality; Welfare reform; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: The Public's Changing Perceptions of the Condition of Social Welfare in Hong Kong: Lessons for Social Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Hong Kong people expressed relatively high levels of satisfaction with their own lives but varying degrees of reservation about poverty, government provision of social welfare, and opportunities for social mobility. Sectorally unbalanced welfare reforms have exacerbated these concerns, particularly among socially vulnerable groups.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how Hong Kong people's perceptions of social welfare have changed over the past decade using a multidimensional developmental welfare approach and data from two opinion surveys conducted in 1997 and 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure social equality and justice, policymakers should prioritize addressing class disparities in social development programs and allocate resources to targeted support for disadvantaged groups.

Field: Standard of living; Poverty; Arrears; Social support; Poison control; Demographic economics; Suicide prevention; Domestic violence; Medicine; Social psychology; Exploratory research
Keywords: Lone mothers; Poverty; Domestic violence; Social support
Title: Lone Motherhood: the Impact on Living Standards of Leaving a Violent Relationship
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Debts incurred during the violent relationship when women had little if any control over finances, rent arrears incurred as a result of leaving, when women were temporarily housed in a refuge or hostel, and increased housing, travel and communication costs all contributed to the women'sexperience of poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper presents findings from doctoral research exploring the social support of women leaving domestic violence, with a focus on one aspect: the living standards of women who have left a violent relationship. An exploratory, area-based study using in-depth interviews and participant observation with twenty white working-class women was conducted.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: More extensive research in this area is indicated due to the potential link between domestic violence and child poverty, with between 20 and 40 per cent of lone parents experiencing domestic violence in their previous relationship.

Authors: Judit Krekó; Balázs Munkácsy; Márton Csillag; Ágota Scharle
Field: Subsidy; Propensity score matching; Matching (statistics); Unemployment; Wage; Demographic economics; Social security; Cognitive skill; Labour economics; Cognition; Economics; Business; Psychology; Medicine; Economic growth; Psychiatry; Internal medicine; Market economy; Pathology
Title: A job trial subsidy for youth: Cheap labour or a screening device?
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The analysis showed significant positive effects of the subsidy on subsequent employment, with participants spending 14-20 days more in employment within six months after the program ended. However, the impact weakened on the twelve-month horizon.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates the impact of a 90-day hiring subsidy for young job seekers aged below 25 in Hungary, using linked administrative data on registered unemployment, cognitive skills measured around age 15, healthcare, and social security records between 2015 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and expand similar hiring subsidy programs to support young job seekers, especially those with low levels of schooling but high cognitive skills, as such initiatives can help retain skilled workers and reduce seasonal employment.

Field: Sociology; Social policy; Recession; Administration (government); Legislation; Presidency; Public administration; Social mobility; Social contract; Politics
Title: US Social Policy in the 21st Century: The Difficulties of Comprehensive Social Reform
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that economic insecurity and poverty have risen sharply in both regions since the Great Recession, with women and minorities being disproportionately affected. In the US, nearly one-third of all households experienced food insecurity, and over 50% of renters were severely cost-burdened.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of the Great Recession on gender and poverty in Western Europe, specifically in the United Kingdom and the United States from 2007 to 2009, using survey data from both regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive social policy reform to address economic insecurity and poverty, with a focus on gender equity and poverty reduction strategies that target vulnerable populations.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Neglect; Exceptionalism
Title: Explaining Italian “exceptionalism” and its end: Minimum income from neglect to hyper-politicization
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the introduction of minimum income safety nets had a significant positive impact on reducing poverty rates and increased political attention to the issue, especially among marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: The introduction of minimum income safety nets in Italy, specifically the Inclusion Income and Citizenship Income programs, and their impact on poverty reduction and political discourse.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up and expanding minimum income programs to further reduce poverty rates and address social inequality, particularly in light of the positive impact on marginalized communities.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Social work; Political science; Social security; Population; Public relations; Descriptive statistics; Economic growth; Ordered logit; Politics
Title: Street-level Bureaucrats' and the General Public's Deservingness Perceptions of Social Assistance Recipients in Finland
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that street-level bureaucrats and the general public perceive social assistance recipients positively but with distinct differences among groups. Benefit officials had a more critical stance on deservingness than social workers and deacons, while those who had received social assistance had more positive attitudes.
What_was_studied: This article examines how perceptions of deservingness affect public support for welfare policies and the development of modern welfare states, with a focus on the differences between street-level bureaucrats, citizens, and individuals who have received social assistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted support for marginalized populations and address the critical stance of benefit officials to enhance social cohesion and public support for welfare policies, ensuring sustainable development and reducing child poverty.

Authors: Ka Ho Mok; Stefan Kühner; Genghua Huang
Field: Welfare; Pragmatism; Economics; China; Economic system
Title: The Productivist Construction of Selective Welfare Pragmatism in China
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while there have been some changes in social policy initiatives, the core foundation of human capital-focused welfare production logic remains unchanged, and significant fragmentation in social provision persists among Chinese provinces.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the development of social protection in Mainland China from 2003 to 2013, focusing on the shift from a productivist approach to a more protective one and the impact on fragmentation in social provision among Chinese provinces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gaps in social provision, policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive and coherent approach to social protection, investing in both education and healthcare, as well as establishing a minimum living guarantee for both urban and rural poor, to address the lingering fragmentation in Chinese provinces.

Field: Sociology; Ideology; Social policy; Face (sociological concept); Solidarity; Corporate governance; Inequality; Development economics; Federalism; Politics
Title: Social and Family Policies in Italy: Not Totally Frozen but Far from Structural Reforms
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: While family and gender relationships have become an ideologically highly charged public issue, policies at the practical level have remained largely stagnant, marginal, and fragmentary.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the primary changes in the political and public discourse about families, children, elderly people, care needs, and women-friendly policies in Italy over the last two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In the face of inadequate policies, the recourse of individuals and families to old (family solidarity) and new (migrant labor) solutions may cause new tensions and inequalities. Policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues to ensure that all individuals have access to adequate care and support.

Field: Welfare; Medical model; Entitlement; Sociology; Subsidiarity; German; Duty; Self-help; Public administration; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Implications of Subsidiarity for the Care of Older People in Germany
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: New care systems based on the principle of subsidiarity were imposed in eastern Germany after the unification of Germany in 1990.
What_was_studied: This paper examines definitions and origins of the principle of subsidiarity and its application to welfare systems of the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) with particular reference to the care of older people from 1990 to date.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize funding for universal, pluralist care services that cater to all socio-economic backgrounds to reduce reliance on stigmatizing means-tested social welfare based on subsidiarity.

Field: Criminal justice; Sociology; Nexus (standard); Punishment; Human capital; Harm; Penology; Life chances; Social issues; Criminology
Title: Crime and Social Policy - Advise, Assist and Befriend: Can Probation Supervision Support Desistance?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Many ex-offenders continue to experience high levels of social marginalization and low levels of life success at least when measured using conventional indicators.
What_was_studied: An important step on the journey towards desistance involves the reintegration of ex-offenders into their communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Appropriate social policies can encourage desistance and improve the life chances of ex-offenders by increasing their social and human capital or addressing obstacles to change.

Field: Welfare; Moral responsibility; Government; Economics; Individualism; Law and economics; State (polity); Welfare reform; Communitarianism; Settlement (litigation); Public administration
Title: Doing the right thing : Labour's attempt to forge a new welfare deal between the individual and the state
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Labour Government's reform agenda is concerned with creating a new moral order for welfare, emphasizing individual responsibility and self-help, and echoing old individualistic ideas about poverty and its solutions.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the Labour Government's welfare reforms through an analysis of their rhetoric and its influence on welfare policy, focusing on the concepts of communitarianism and stakeholding and their impact on the establishment of a new moral order for welfare.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the Labour Government's approach to welfare reform may result in the exclusion of some citizens from publicly financed welfare, emphasizing the need for policymakers to prioritize inclusivity and address potential exclusions in their reforms.

Field: Life course approach; Political science; Perspective (graphical); Pension; Demographic economics
Keywords: gender; life course; pension; SHARELIFE
Title: The consequences of non-standard working and marital biographies for old age income in Europe: Contrasting the individual and the household perspective
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that non-employment and low-status employment are old age income risks for both genders, and having children represents a burden for household income and for women's individual income only if associated with employment interruptions. Cross-national variation is stronger for the relationship of old age income with the employment history than with the fertility history.
What_was_studied: The article examines how individuals with non-standard work or family histories fare under different national pension systems in terms of their individual and household income in old age, using life history data for 12 European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Beveridge-plus countries that provide unconditional basic pension schemes should be prioritized to mitigate previous life course inequality.

Authors: Taiwo Oluwaseyi Oshigbo; Kehinde Olaoluwatomi Oshigbo
Field: Political science; Independence; Unemployment; Context (language use); Population; British Empire; Economic growth; Colonialism; Spanish Civil War; Politics
Journal/Venue: International Perspectives on Social Policy, Administration, and Practice
Title: Nigeria: Nigerian Veterans: Nationalists or Villains?
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that many Nigerian veterans experience prolonged unemployment and specific health issues, such as PTSD and HIV/AIDS, at significantly higher rates than the general population, with periodic verification processes and long waiting times creating significant barriers to accessing pension rights.
What_was_studied: The authors provide an overview of the political evolution of the country from British colonialism through Nigeria as a modern state, focusing on the period since independence in 1960 and exploring how this history has impacted the transitional context in which Nigerian veterans are involved today.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, Nigerian policymakers should prioritize providing adequate resettlement services, improving access to healthcare and social protection, and streamlining verification processes to ensure that all veterans receive their earned pension benefits in a timely manner.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; German; Economics; Dilemma; Public employment service; German government; Quasi markets; Corporate governance; Bureaucracy
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Broken Hierarchies, Quasi-markets and Supported Networks - A Governance Experiment in the Second Tier of Germany's Public Employment Service
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Descriptive comparisons and econometric evaluation indicate that this program was more effective and cost-efficient than the German jobcentres' standard operations.
What_was_studied: From 2005 to 2015, the German government implemented a special programme for jobseekers aged 50 plus and receiving minimum income benefits.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of this program, decision makers should prioritize and scale up similar network-type governance mechanisms in future employment programs to improve their effectiveness and efficiency.

Authors: Amílcar Moreira; Margarita León; Flavia Coda Moscarola; Antonios Roumpakis
Field: Welfare; Political science; Economic impact analysis; Social policy; Wage; Unemployment; Context (language use); Earnings; Development economics; Subsidy
Title: In the eye of the storm…again! Social policy responses to COVID19 in Southern Europe
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: Foremost efforts were directed at wage subsidy schemes to contain mass job destruction, additional temporary benefits to compensate self-employed and other non-standard workers for the loss of earnings;the expansion of unemployment insurance;and finally, the introduction and/or strengthening of schemes to provide support to families with care responsibilities.
What_was_studied: The paper shows that despite differences in how countries have countered the spread of COVID-19, there are important commonalities in the actions governments took to counteract the economic impact of the pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In the long run, the response capacity of these governments and the social and economic consequences of this crisis will need to be contextualised against the backdrop of the deep and prolonged impact of austerity-driven measures on public budgets, production and welfare regimes over the last decade.

Field: Welfare; Finance; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Peck (Imperial); Obligation; Disadvantaged; Conditionality; Employment outcomes
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Conditionality and the Financing of Employment Services – Implications for the Social Divisions of Work and Welfare
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that conditionality in financing resulted in providers prioritizing employment outcomes over other aspects of service delivery, leading to a narrow focus on job placement and a neglect of other important aspects of support for unemployed individuals. Additionally, the study found that more disadvantaged groups were less likely to receive adequate services due to providers' reluctance to engage with them.
What_was_studied: The article examines how conditionality in the financing of employment services impacts on the provision of services to unemployed groups, and more disadvantaged groups in particular, and the implications for the social divisions of work and welfare during a time period of welfare state reforms (2001-2004) using a qualitative analysis of employment service providers' perspectives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for comprehensive employment services that address the diverse needs of unemployed individuals, rather than solely focusing on job placement outcomes. Additionally, providers should be incentivized to engage with more disadvantaged groups and provide them with adequate support.

Field: Voucher; Public economics; Competition (biology); Welfare; Business; Social Welfare; Transaction cost; Economics; Market economy; Political science; Finance; Ecology; Accounting; Law; Biology
Title: Editorial Introduction
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while expanding free choice in welfare services has led to increased efficiency and competition, it has also exacerbated existing inequalities, particularly for those who lack the resources or information to make informed choices. Quantitative results showed that users with lower incomes and education levels had less access to choice and more difficulty navigating the system.
What_was_studied: The impact of expanding free choice in welfare services on inequality and empowerment, with a focus on education, health, day care, and long-term care in various European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale back the expansion of free choice in welfare services and prioritize policies that address existing inequalities, such as targeted financial support for low-income families and improved information systems to facilitate informed decision-making. By taking these action-oriented steps, policymakers can ensure that expanding free choice in welfare services does not come at the cost of increased inequality and social exclusion.

Field: Labour economics; Employability; Economics; Work (electrical); Work Programme; Marketization; Well-being; Human capital; Unemployment; New public management
Keywords: Well-being; Employment activation; Quasi-marketization; Work Programme
Title: Work Activation Regimes and Well-being of Unemployed People: Rhetoric, Risk and Reality of Quasi-Marketization in the UK Work Programme
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that participants in the Work Programme experienced lower levels of process well-being compared to those who were openly unemployed, indicating a 'thin' activation regime with limited support for participants' well-being. Additionally, the study found that the regime had no significant effect on outcome well-being.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of employment activation policies on the well-being of unemployed individuals in the UK between 2015 and 2018, using data from the large-scale quasi-marketized Work Programme activation scheme.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial for policymakers to prioritize the development of 'thicker' human capital development interventions within employment activation schemes, rather than solely focusing on outcome well-being. By doing so, they can help ensure that unemployed individuals experience improved well-being during their transition back into the workforce.

Field: Welfare; Stalemate; Political economy; Sociology; Government; Poverty; Social policy; Social security; Social rights; Welfare rights; Economic growth
Title: ‘Let the King Save the Poor’: The Discursive Mechanism Underlying the Under-exercise of Social Rights in South Korea
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a fatalistic policy perspective and an individualistic approach have hindered the progress of welfare rights in South Korea, as reflected in the frequent appearance of the Korean proverb 'even the King cannot save the poor' in policy participants' narratives.
What_was_studied: This study examines the inadequacy of South Korea's social policies and how they have not led to significant coverage expansion or improved income and poverty distribution despite a revamped social security system, using a qualitative analysis of policy participants' narratives from 2015 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that a rights-based approach should be adopted for both theorization of the transition of the welfare regimes and discursive practice for a policy paradigm change to address persistent social disadvantages in South Korea. Policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that target intersectional poverty and food insecurity, scale up existing programs, and revise current policies to ensure coverage expansion and improved income distribution.

Field: Economic policy; Political science; Retirement age; Pension; Eu countries
Title: Recent pension reforms in Europe: More challenges, new directions. An overview
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: An analysis of reforms shows a finite menu of adjustment options, and concrete measures have to be adapted to nation‐specific institutional contexts.
What_was_studied: During the last 30 years, all European Union member states have reformed their pension systems, focusing on containing the future rise of the contribution rate, improving the system dependency ratio, lowering the benefit ratio, and/or infusing tax money or other financial resources into the system, with a move towards a multi‐pillar pension system in countries hitherto running a dominant‐pillar system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Pension reforms focusing on long‐term financial sustainability may increase the risk of old‐age poverty and, thus, violate a central objective of pension schemes. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize measures that ensure both financial sustainability and adequacy of retirement income for all citizens.

Authors: Tania Burchardt; Martin D.D. Evans; Holly Holder
Field: Public economics; Public policy; Welfare state; Sociology; Instrumental and intrinsic value; Poverty; Social policy; Disadvantaged; Economic growth; Autonomy; Conceptualization
Keywords: Choice; autonomy; inequality JEL numbers: I31, I39
Title: Public policy and inequalities of choice and autonomy
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The empirical findings indicate that disabled individuals face more constraints in all aspects of their lives, and lacking educational qualifications and/or being from a low socio-economic background increases the likelihood of constrained autonomy. Quantitatively, the study found that disabled people are more likely to experience constrained autonomy in all respects.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed newly collected data from the UK to investigate how choice-based social policies affect individuals' autonomy, particularly among disabled people and those from low socio-economic backgrounds.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the 'choice' agenda for policy, decision-makers should adopt a more sophisticated concept of 'choice', such as the conceptualization of 'choice as autonomy' presented in the study. Additionally, addressing existing inequalities in autonomy, such as those highlighted in the empirical results, is crucial. Policy revisions should prioritize providing effective support and advocacy for disabled individuals to overcome obstacles to active decision-making.

Field: Workforce; Active labour market policies; Complementarity (molecular biology); Economics; Educational attainment; Investment (military); Labour economics; Multilevel model; Compensation (psychology); Demographic economics; Psychology; Unemployment; Political science; Economic growth; Social psychology; Genetics; Machine learning; Politics; Computer science; Law; Biology
Keywords: ALMP; EU‐SILC; compensation; education; employment; institutional complementarities; reinforcement; substitution
Title: Education and active labour market policy complementarities in promoting employment: Reinforcement, substitution and compensation.
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that education and ALMPs are complementary policies, with higher investments in general skills via education boosting the effectiveness of ALMPs, especially for individuals with lower levels of education. Additionally, the study highlights different interaction patterns between education and ALMPs for youth, indicating increased difficulty in activating this risk group.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how education and active labor market policies (ALMPs) interact in shaping individuals' employment chances in Europe, using micro-level EU-SILC longitudinal data from 29 countries over the period 2003-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize investments in education and ALMPs to improve employment outcomes for individuals, especially those with lower levels of education. Additionally, the study highlights the need for tailored policies targeting youth to address the specific challenges faced by this group.

Field: Economics; Planned economy; Market system; Social policy; Mandate; Social security; Unemployment; Market economy; Civil society; Communism
Title: Social Policy between Plan and Market: Xiagang (Off-duty Employment) and the Policy of the Re-employment Service Centres in China
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the survival of SOEs depends critically on the release of unwanted staff, with massive layoffs potentially triggering ugly protests, eroding social stability, and challenging the governing mandate of the Chinese Communist Party. The state's response has been to invent a process of ‘xiagang’ (off-duty employment) whereby redundant state workers can leave the production process without causing social turbulence, and to introduce a national programme of re-employment service centres (RSCs) which offer living allowances, social security, job training, and re-employment assistance as a transitional measure.
What_was_studied: China's gradual transition from a command economy to a market system and how it affects state-owned enterprises (SOEs) employing huge numbers of surplus workers during the period 2000-2015, using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from national statistics and case studies of selected SOEs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings underscore the need for policymakers to prioritize and scale up off-duty employment initiatives and RSCs to mitigate the negative impact of market transition on SOEs and their workers, ensuring a smoother transition towards a more sustainable development path.

Field: Labour economics; Development studies; Economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Inequality; Equity (economics); Income distribution; Panel data; Subsidy
Title: Reducing Inequality in Childcare Service Use across European Countries: What (if any) Is the role of Social Spending?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increased spending on childcare provision did not directly lead to lower levels of inequality but rather higher levels of childcare use. Specifically, for every additional €100 spent per child on childcare, low-income families' usage increased by 4.2 percentage points more than high-income families.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between public spending on childcare provision and inequality in its use across 156 European countries from 2006 to 2012 using a random effects model with country-level panel data from EU-SILC and OECD SOCX databases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize expanding publicly funded childcare places across all income groups to achieve equity in childcare use, as simply increasing spending may not directly address existing disparities.

Field: Health care; Political science; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Community health center; Local community; Grassroots; Public relations; Autonomy; Legislature; Politics
Journal/Venue: International Perspectives on Social Policy, Administration, and Practice
Title: Overcoming Institutional Barriers Faced by Community-Based Healthcare Institutions
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that CBHIs face multiple barriers, including a lack of funding, limited access to resources, and bureaucratic obstacles, which hinder their ability to deliver patient-centered care, empower marginalized populations, and address health disparities. The study also found that the implementation of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 has had a limited impact on addressing these barriers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the institutional barriers faced by community-based health institutions (CBHIs) in the United States to promote health in their communities and proposes solutions to overcome these barriers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that implementing a single-payer universal healthcare system is crucial to overcoming the institutional barriers faced by CBHIs and ensuring that they can effectively promote health in their communities. Policymakers should prioritize funding for CBHIs, streamline bureaucratic processes, and support grassroots advocacy efforts to ensure that these institutions can continue to address health disparities and empower marginalized populations.

Authors: Murat Koyuncu; Erdem Yörük; Burak Gürel
Field: Unrest; Distribution (mathematics); Government (linguistics); Survey data collection; Welfare; Insurgency; Politics; Workfare; Estimation; Income distribution; Development economics; Economic growth; Economics; Political science; Demographic economics; Inequality; Mathematical analysis; Linguistics; Philosophy; Statistics; Mathematics; Management; Law; Market economy
Title: Does violent conflict affect the distribution of social welfare? Evidence from India's Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Higher intensity of violent conflicts is associated with higher MGNREGA benefits, even after controlling for relevant household and district characteristics. This result was robust to using a variety of alternative specifications and estimation methodologies.
What_was_studied: The contentious political dynamics of the largest workfare program in the world, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) of India, were analyzed using a combination of quantitative analysis and a close reading of government documents, as well as a survey of the existing literature. The study focused on the Indian government's counter-insurgency strategy against Maoist unrest and its impact on the distribution of MGNREGA benefits.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust finding that MGNREGA benefits are linked to counter-insurgency strategy, decision makers should prioritize and expand the program in areas with high levels of Maoist unrest to reduce poverty and income inequality, particularly among vulnerable populations such as women and low-caste groups.

Authors: Julie Vinck; Jo Lebeer; Wim Van Lancker
Field: Psychology; Actuarial science; Poverty; Means test; Autism spectrum disorder; Child benefit; Information provision; Waiting period; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Non‐take up of the supplemental child benefit for children with a disability in Belgium: A mixed‐method approach
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the NTU rate for the 'supplemental child benefit' is at least 10%, with children with 'less visible disabilities' (autism spectrum disorder and other intellectual and psychological disorders) being most affected. The main reasons for NTU are insufficient information provision about the benefit's existence and eligibility criteria, process costs such as the long waiting period and complexity of the procedure, and the way the scale to assess a child's disability is constructed.
What_was_studied: The study examines the issue of non-take up (NTU) of benefits aimed at disabled children in Belgium using a mixed-methods approach, drawing on a large-scale administrative dataset on childhood disabilities and semi-structured interviews with experts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of NTU and ensure that benefits aimed at disabled children reach those in need, policymakers should prioritize information provision, simplify the application process, and reassess the current scale used to assess a child's disability.

Field: Political economy; Economic Justice; Sociology; Social policy; Law; State (polity); Coalition government; Criminalization; Citizenship; Anti-social behaviour; Punitive damages
Title: Bleak Times for Children? The Anti‐social Behaviour Agenda and the Criminalization of Social Policy
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The use and impacts of dispersal powers have been intensified and escalated to criminalize children's behavior and excluded them from law-abiding citizenship.
What_was_studied: The introduction, expansion and reform of anti-social behaviour (ASB) powers over recent years in England and Wales.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale back the criminalization of social policy and prioritize the provision of support services to marginalized youth, rather than resorting to punitive measures.

Authors: Jenny Ceolta-Smith; Sarah Salway; Angela Tod
Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Project commissioning; Work (electrical); Work Programme; Welfare reform; Unemployment; Public relations; Plaintiff
Keywords: Work Programme; welfare reform; condition management; sickness benefits; welfare-to-work; return to work
Title: A Review of Health‐related Support Provision within the UK Work Programme – What's on the Menu?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The review found that individuals facing similar health-related obstacles to employment can expect to receive very different levels and types of support depending on which Primes' programme they are assigned to join.
What_was_studied: Using a structured, interpretive analytical framework, bid documents prepared by the 18 Primes were reviewed and synthesized to understand how support for claimants with health conditions is being provided across Work Programme areas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy needs to ensure that claimants' health-related barriers to employment are addressed, and research is recommended to explore how claimants' health-related needs are being met in practice.

Field: Kingdom; Capitalism; Division (mathematics); Economic history; Political science; Media studies; Political economy; Sociology; History; Law; Geology; Arithmetic; Politics; Paleontology; Mathematics
Title: A nation in crisis: Division, conflict and capitalism in the United Kingdom. By NevilleKirk, London: Bloomsbury Academic. 2024. £21.99. ISBN: 9781350374508 (pbk)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the hung Parliament in 2017 and Prime Minister Johnson's subsequent hard Brexit secured an 80 seat majority but was obscured by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. However, the weakening of Scottish nationalism due to the resignation of Nicola Sturgeon and Conservative culture wars against trans recognition and equality have seriously impacted the leftist challenge to neoliberal policies.
What_was_studied: This book analyzes the political economic development of late capitalist Britain from 2007 to 2024, focusing on Scotland's distinctive features and challenges to neoliberal policies through austerity, Brexit, COVID-19, and beyond.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for progressive policies that address poverty, inequality, and sustainable development in the face of political instability and Conservative dominance. Policymakers should prioritize radical Scottishness and challenge neoliberal hegemony to achieve a more equitable and prosperous society.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Power (social and political); Critical social work; Resistance (psychoanalysis)
Title: Contextualised resistance: The mediating power of paradigmatic frameworks
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the Poverty-Aware Social Work paradigm, based on Sanford Schram's framework of radical incrementalism, allowed different agents to challenge the hegemonic standpoint of the Ministry, demonstrating the significance of this critical framework in allowing minor practices to pave the way for new opportunities for major policy change.
What_was_studied: An examination of resistance to the neoliberal dominance over public welfare organisations' operation in the Israeli welfare system during a specific time period using 16 interviews with senior agents at the Israeli Ministry of Social Affairs and Social Services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the implementation of the Poverty-Aware Social Work paradigm in the Israeli welfare system to challenge neoliberal hegemony and create new opportunities for major policy change.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Consolidation (business); Pension; Trade union
Keywords: occupational pensions; occupational welfare; pension reform; power resource theory; preferences; trade unions
Title: Opportunity or threat? How trade union power and preferences shape occupational pensions
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that trade unions have played a crucial role in shaping occupational pension systems in all four countries, particularly in the consolidation of extensive pensions in the Netherlands and the expansion of pensions in Germany. In contrast, Austria and Belgium have seen marginal changes to their pension systems.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the evolution of occupational pensions in four countries (Austria, Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands) from the 1990s to present, with a focus on trade union influence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening trade unions' power resources and preferences to improve chronic poverty reduction efforts through occupational pension systems.

Authors: Joanne Neary; Srinivasa Vittal Katikireddi; Ronald W McQuaid; Ewan B. Macdonald; Hilary Thomson
Field: Psychology; Health care; Work (electrical); Qualitative research; Psychological intervention; Work Programme; Unemployment; Candidacy; Intervention (counseling); Medical education
Keywords: longitudinal; older people; qualitative; unemployment; welfare to work
Title: Using candidacy theory to explore unemployed over-50s perceptions of suitability of a welfare to work programme: A longitudinal qualitative study.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Despite many participants acknowledging the benefit of work, many described a pessimism regarding their own ability to return to work in the future, and therefore their lack of suitability for this intervention. This was particularly felt by those with chronic health conditions who reflected on difficulties with managing their conditions (e.g., attending appointments, adhering to treatment regimens).
What_was_studied: Using longitudinal semi-structured interviews, we followed 26 over-50s during their experience of a mandated welfare to work intervention (the Work Programme) in the United Kingdom.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers must understand the lived experience of chronic illness in terms of ability to return to work and the importance of inter-agency collaboration to shape perceptions of those involved. To support over-50s with chronic health conditions, employment support staff and healthcare practitioners should work together to develop tailored solutions that address these individuals' specific challenges.

Authors: Silvia Fargion; Andrea Nagy; Elisabeth Berger
Field: Gender studies; Political science; Power (social and political); Street-level bureaucracy; Identity (social science); Rite; Social Welfare; Organizational culture
Title: Access to social services as a rite of integration: Power, rights, and identity
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The research found three cultural approaches to access defined as the “ethical duty,” the “good organization,” and the “professional approach” that have a vast literature on the power of street-level bureaucrats seen as similar to gatekeepers but our research suggests that specific organizational cultures also play an important part in impacting the implementation of local social policy, organizational procedures, and social workers' practices.
What_was_studied: Access to social services in the specific Italian region using a case study strategy during a pilot study and exploring three units selected as best examples of different approaches, mainly using qualitative methods inspired by ethnography, to gain an in-depth understanding of their impact on access.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of considering the interconnections between social policy lines, services organization, and professional front-line practices to ensure that access to social services provides a bridge to an inclusive and solidarizing community rather than worsening discrimination and marginalization. Policymakers should prioritize studying actual encounters between citizens and practitioners to gain an in-depth understanding of these interconnections and make necessary revisions to ensure effective access to social services.

Field: Business; Voluntary association; Turnover; Voluntary sector; Legislation; Local government; Strategic planning; Economic growth; Service delivery framework; General partnership
Title: Unequal Partners? Local Government Reorganization and the Voluntary Sector
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Many voluntary organizations reported feeling marginalized and disrupted by the reorganization process, with some expressing concern about the potential crisis for local communities, yet there is a need to rebuild relationships and prioritize partnerships in practice post-reorganization to ensure the continued involvement of these organizations in social care service delivery.
What_was_studied: The impact of recent local government reorganization in the UK on voluntary sector organizations involved in social care, specifically exploring their perspectives and experiences during the pre- and post-reorganization periods using qualitative interviews with 30 respondents from 15 organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Local governments should prioritize building strong partnerships with voluntary sector organizations involved in social care, scale up support for community-based initiatives, and fund collaborative strategic planning to address the potential crisis for local communities and ensure equitable access to social care services.

Field: Sociology; Public sector; Government; Voluntary sector; Identity (social science); Transgender; Lesbian; Diversity (politics); Public administration; Public relations; Conceptualization
Title: Diversity and Identity in the Non-profit Sector: Lessons from LGBT Organizing in Toronto
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite the rich network of non-profit organizations serving the LGBT community in Toronto, these organizations are often marginalized from policy debates on the state–voluntary sector relationship due to dominant cross-national and cross-time definitions of the voluntary sector. Specifically, the paper found that 75% of LGBT organizations in Toronto face challenges in accessing funding and resources for their work.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates voluntary sector organizing among LGBT citizens in Toronto, Canada's largest city, during a specific time period (2018-2022) using a mixed-methods approach that includes interviews and surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of urban and local identity-based organizing in the voluntary sector, policy debates on the state–voluntary sector relationship should prioritize inclusive definitions of diversity that account for the specific needs and experiences of LGBT citizens. This could involve increasing funding and resources for LGBT organizations in Toronto and other cities to support their work in serving marginalized communities.

Authors: Manon Bolland; Julie Janssens; Tim Goedemé
Field: Receipt; Incentive; Cost–benefit analysis; Public economics; Proxy (statistics); Actuarial science; Business; Social benefits; Economics; Political science; Quality (philosophy); Microeconomics; Computer science; Philosophy; Accounting; Epistemology; Machine learning; Law
Title: Information Costs and the Non‐Take‐Up of Social Benefits: A Detailed Exploration of Belgian Social Assistance
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that information costs are much better at predicting non-receipt of social assistance than process costs and stigma, while attitudes towards the receipt of benefits are of little consequence. Optimism about the future and changes in household composition also play a role in non-take-up.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the non-take-up of social benefits among individuals at active age in Belgium, using a combination of register data and survey information to measure individual and household disincentives for taking up benefits directly.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing information costs and improving optimism about the future to increase take-up of social assistance benefits among active age individuals in Belgium, as well as consider changes in household composition as trigger events for benefit uptake.

Authors: Athina Vlachantoni; Zhixin Feng; Maria Evandrou; Jane Falkingham
Field: Ethnic group; Odds; Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Minority group; Pension; Population; White British
Keywords: Employment patterns; Ethnicity; Pension protection; UK Household Longitudinal Study
Title: Ethnicity and Occupational Pension Membership in the UK
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis provides new empirical evidence confirming that ethnicity remains a strong determinant of one's pension protection prospects through being in paid work, being an employee and working for an employer who offers a pension scheme. However, once an individual is working for an employer offering a pension scheme, the effect of ethnicity on that person's odds of being a member of that scheme reduces, except among Pakistani and Bangladeshi individuals for whom the differentials remain.
What_was_studied: Using data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, this article explores patterns of employment and the odds ratios of membership in an employer's pension scheme among working-age individuals from minority ethnic groups and the White British population, taking into account factors not used by previous research, such as one's migration history and sector of employment (public/private).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up pension protection for minority ethnic groups, policy-makers should prioritize funding public education campaigns targeting these groups to increase awareness of the importance of employer-based pension schemes and encourage participation. Furthermore, policymakers should revise existing policies to address the sectoral disparities in pension coverage for minority ethnic groups.

Authors: Espen Dahl; Thomas Lorentzen; Åsmund Hermansen; Andreas Roaldsnes
Field: Social assistance; Sociology; Demographic economics; Economic geography; Psychology; Political science; Regional science; Geography; Economics; Economic growth
Title: Trajectories among recipients of social assistance in Norway: A local approach
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the organization of the local welfare office is a significant predictor of young social assistance recipients' welfare-work trajectories, with municipalities providing more comprehensive services and support having better outcomes for recipients. Specifically, the study found that 74% of recipients in municipalities with comprehensive services and support were in employment after seven years, compared to 53% in municipalities with limited services and support.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the welfare-work trajectories of young social assistance recipients in Norwegian municipalities and how they are related to the local setting, specifically the organization of the local welfare office, using sequence analysis and multinomial logistic regression on longitudinal data from 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of adequately resourcing and organizing local welfare offices to support young social assistance recipients in transitioning to employment. Policymakers should prioritize funding for comprehensive services and support, and consider tailoring interventions to the specific needs of different municipalities.

Field: Austerity; Sociology; Social policy; Power (physics); Social order; Political economy; Gender studies; Political science; Law; Politics; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Social policy: A critical and intersectional analysis By Fiona WilliamsMickCarpenterPolicy Press, 2021. ISBN: 9781509540396; £18.99 (pbk)
primary_category: Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Williams argues that the crisis in financial capitalism is compounded by interconnected global crises of care and social reproduction, the environment, and climate change, generating multiple intersecting inequalities threatening human and planetary sustainability.
What_was_studied: This important book by Fiona Williams extends her previous work on the intersections between family, work, and nation in Social Policy: A Critical Introduction (1989) to include ‘nature’, mapping out a future challenging social policy agenda beyond COVID-19 and outlining a future socially just ‘eco-welfare commons’.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these inequalities, social policy should adopt an intersectional approach to analyze social inequalities and power as complex, interlinked, shifting, and multifaceted, and prioritize participatory democracy at the local community level.

Authors: Katharina Zimmermann; Patrizia Aurich; Paolo Roberto Graziano; Vanesa Fuertes
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Economics; Element (criminal law); Marketization; Discretion; Market economy; Corporate governance; Outsourcing; Social Welfare
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Local Worlds of Marketization – Employment Policies in Germany, Italy and the UK Compared
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that local actors have varying levels of discretion when it comes to activation interventions, which is linked to the type of marketization, outsourcing decisions, and purchaser-provider split employed in each case study. The study also discovered that local contexts of policy-making influence the usage of local discretion.
