What_was_studied: The article examines the interlinked aims of increasing employment rates and integrating formerly excluded groups into the labor market in European countries over the past two decades, with a focus on local-level policy discretion and marketization of employment and social services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize providing varying levels of discretion for local actors in activation policies, taking into account their suitability and willingness to become marketized, in order to increase employment rates and effectively integrate formerly excluded groups into the labor market.

Field: Active labour market policies; Mental health; Unemployment; Subsidy; Context (archaeology); Wage; Virtuous circle and vicious circle; Psychological intervention; Labour economics; Population; Demographic economics; Economics; Business; Psychology; Medicine; Psychiatry; Economic growth; Environmental health; Market economy; Paleontology; Macroeconomics; Biology
Title: On the effects of active labour market policies among individuals reporting to have severe mental health problems
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that ALMPs not only improve labor market integration for unemployed individuals with severe mental health issues but do so more effectively than for other unemployed individuals.
What_was_studied: The study examines the long-term causal effects of active labor market policies (ALMPs) on the labor market integration of individuals with self-reported severe mental health issues, comparing estimates to those without such issues using unique combined survey and administrative data from 2010 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up ALMPs targeting individuals with severe mental health issues to improve their labor market integration and reduce health disparities.

Authors: Sioned Pearce; Helen Blakely; David Frayne; Ian Rees Jones
Field: Sociology; Ideology; Social policy; Accountability; Hierarchy; Argument; Civil society; Engineering ethics; Community development; Politics
Title: Evaluation in reinforcing and resisting hierarchical relations between state and civil society
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that evaluation is a means of defining and producing contested constructions of value, securing vertical accountability, and constructing itself as a lost savior with untapped potential for safeguarding the integrity of an initial political ideology.
What_was_studied: This critical exploration of evaluation within a state-led anti-poverty program examines the accounts of 25 community development workers over 17 years (2001–2018) to argue that evaluation also reinforces hierarchical power relations between the state and civil society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for more inclusive evaluation practices and the development of alternative heterarchies in the evaluation of social policy, premised on processes of co-production and collaboration, to address the power imbalances and ensure that anti-poverty programs are effective in sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Latin Americans; Economics; Government revenue; Revenue; Social security; Promotion (rank); Crowding out
Title: Crowding Out or Welfare Promotion? How Foreign Aid Affects Social Expenditures in Latin American Welfare Systems
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that foreign aid has a limited impact on welfare expenditure in Latin American countries. Specifically, only health care expenditures in middle-income countries were found to decrease slightly as a result of aid inflows. Social security and education expenditures were not affected.
What_was_studied: This study examines fiscal responses by Latin American welfare states to the inflow of foreign aid, specifically looking at whether overall aid and aid targeted at the social sector substitute public welfare provision, using a time-series cross-section analysis of 19 Latin American countries for the period 1980–2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited impact of foreign aid on welfare expenditure, policymakers should prioritize domestic resource mobilization and targeted social sector spending to effectively address poverty and promote economic development in Latin American countries.

Field: Entitlement; Health care; Political science; Irish; Public health care; Public administration; Inequality
Title: “The only equality is the pain”: An exploration of the Irish policy sphere's approach to “access” and “entitlement” in health care
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that the policy aspirations of equality that underpin the HC structures surrounding access and entitlement in Ireland have created conflict and policy ambiguity, particularly in the two-tier system of public-versus-private access to HC services, resulting in growing gaps of inequity between higher and lower socio-economic groups in society.
What_was_studied: This paper critically analyzes how overarching policy goals and practices surrounding access and entitlement to health care (HC) have been dominated by a conflicting system of libertarian and equity-based principles in Ireland, focusing on the period from the Poor Laws era to modern times, using empirical evidence and interviews with key stakeholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should revisit the policy aspirations of equality to achieve greater health outcomes and create a more equal society by scaling up publicly funded HC towards lower-income groups and the most vulnerable in Irish society.

Field: Sociology; Mainstreaming; Phase (combat); Poverty; Gender and development; Context (language use); Women in development; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; International development
Title: Trickle-down or Rising Tide? Lessons on Mainstreaming Gender Policy from Colombia and South Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that South Africa's experience represents a third and distinguishable phase in the establishment of national machineries for the advancement of women, characterized by an internally driven process with less aid dependence and strong support from international women’s networks, leading to the most progressive approach to advancing gender equality worldwide.
What_was_studied: The establishment of national machineries for the advancement of women in South Africa and Colombia between 1976 and 2018, using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up gender-sensitive development programs in South Africa, and adopt a similar internally driven approach to establishing national machineries for women's empowerment in other countries.

Field: Criminal justice; Economic Justice; Ambivalence; Economics; Voluntary action; Work (electrical); Service (business); Public administration; Public relations; General partnership; Punitive damages
Title: Probation Partnerships, Voluntary Action and Community Justice
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while progress has been made in developing partnerships with voluntary organizations, the Probation Service has been ambivalent about this policy due to fears of privatization. Additionally, the study found that the vision for the Service has been lost and replaced by a more punitive approach.
What_was_studied: This study examines the marginalization of the Probation Service in England and Wales since 1991, specifically looking at how politicians have changed their minds about the role of the Service in the criminal justice system and how this has impacted partnerships with voluntary organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize partnerships with voluntary organizations in order to provide alternative visions for the criminal justice system and address the marginalization of the Probation Service. By expanding these partnerships, policymakers can scale up effective interventions and improve outcomes for offenders.

Field: Welfare; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Human services; New Deal; Political structure; Great Society; Public administration; Autonomy; Politics
Title: Office of Economic Opportunity: U.S.A.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the OEO's innovative approach to social administration, which bypassed traditional channels, was undermined by both the U.S. political structure and traditional politics as usual, limiting its effectiveness in addressing chronic poverty.
What_was_studied: The Office of Economic Opportunity's social policies and their effectiveness in addressing chronic poverty during the 89th Congress (1965-1966).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the political context when implementing innovative social policies to address chronic poverty. Policymakers should prioritize bypassing traditional channels and exploring alternative approaches to achieve meaningful progress in this area.

Field: Sociology; Vulnerability (computing); Welfare; Welfare state; Ideology; Retrenchment; Public relations; Political science; Public administration; Law; Politics; Computer security; Computer science
Title: Women, Vulnerabilities and Welfare Service Systems, Routledge Advances in Social work. Kuronen, M., Virokannas, E., & Salovaara, U.Oxon, UK: Routledge, 2021.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that vulnerability is produced and reproduced by welfare service systems that fail to acknowledge the complexity of women's vulnerable situations; by professionals, practitioners, and systems which (mis)interpret and (mis)represent the women's survival and coping strategies.
What_was_studied: The retrenchment of welfare systems across the Western world and its impact on marginalized women, with a focus on the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States between 2000 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the pressing need for substantial and sustained investment in holistic, integrated, and gender-sensitive welfare systems to address the situational and fluid nature of vulnerability. Policymakers should prioritize the development of comprehensive social protection policies that acknowledge the complexities of women's experiences and provide adequate support to marginalized women.

Field: Political science; Debit card; Colonialism; Commerce
Keywords: Settler Colonialism; Income Management; Welfare conditionality; Indigenous policy; Australia
Title: Settler colonialism in Australia and the cashless debit card
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the card restricting cash and purchases aimed to instill 'responsible behavior' such as getting a job, accumulating private property, and succeeding in English education, while the state legitimized assimilation through provoking narratives of First Nations dysfunction, depoliticizing poverty and colonization, constructing evidence around the policy's success, and constructing ideas of 'community' to regulate who speaks and who is overlooked. However, there was resistance and pushback in the trial site.
What_was_studied: A 13-month study examining the Cashless Debit Card trial in North West Australia's East Kimberley region, targeting First Nations subjectivities through behavioural conditions on social security payments to assimilate Indigenous Australians into the capitalist economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that assimilation attempts continue to affect Indigenous Australians today, but there are also signs of resistance and pushback. Policy makers should prioritize decolonizing approaches to address intersectional poverty and focus on evidence-based solutions that empower First Nations communities, rather than perpetuating assimilation through behavioral conditions.

Authors: Sonja Blum; Lenka Formánková; Ivana Dobrotić
Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; Political economy; Development studies; Economics; State (polity); Unemployment; Freedom of choice; Workfare; Market economy; Austerity
Title: Family Policies in ‘Hybrid’ Welfare States after the Crisis: Pathways between Policy Expansion and Retrenchment†
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while the pre-crisis policy pathways were continued during the crisis, there were significant changes in the framing of these reforms, with diverse paradigms related to national-specific contexts and austerity measures being introduced. The Czech Republic focused on neo-liberal policies, Slovenia strengthened the social dimension of family policy, and Austria combined social investment and 'freedom of choice' paradigms.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes family policy reforms in Austria, the Czech Republic, and Slovenia between 2009 and 2013 to determine how countries reacted to the economic crisis and whether the crisis led to new policy pathways and ideas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that countries should consider a more balanced approach to family policy reforms during economic crises, combining social investment and freedom of choice paradigms, rather than solely focusing on negative residual measures. This could help mitigate the negative effects of the crisis on national welfare states.

Authors: James Rees; Adam Whitworth; Eleanor Carter
Field: Public economics; Payment; Economics; Work (electrical); Qualitative research; Work Programme; Conditionality; Payment by Results; Incentive; Public relations; Plaintiff
Keywords: Conditionality; Creaming and parking; Employment services; Payment by results; Welfare-to-work; Work Programme
Title: Contracting-out Welfare Services: Comparing National Policy Designs for Unemployment Assistance - Support for All in the UK Work Programme? Differential Payments, Same Old Problem
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that creaming and parking are prevalent and systematically embedded within the Work Programme, driven by intense cost-pressures and overly diverse claimant groups. Specifically, 63% of providers reported engaging in creaming behaviors, while 58% reported parking claimants.
What_was_studied: The UK's Work Programme, a fully outsourced welfare-to-work provision, over the period 2011-2016 and its effectiveness in mitigating creaming and parking behaviors among providers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, the Department for Work and Pensions should scale up differentiated payment levels to better incentivize providers to serve vulnerable claimants. Additionally, the government should expand support for claimants with complex needs to reduce provider parking behaviors.

Field: Temporality; Economics; Poverty; Development economics; Economic inequality
Keywords: economic inequality; poverty; temporality; wealth
Title: The long and short of it : The temporal significance of wealth and income
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 'poor' participants primarily experience money as flows of income, which constrain long-term orientations, while 'rich' participants experience money both as flows of income and a stock of wealth, enabling long-term planning and control over the future.
What_was_studied: Comparing qualitative interviews with individuals at opposite ends of the income and wealth distributions in the UK, this study examines how temporal dimensions shape the experience of poverty and richness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the form of economic resources affects one's ability to plan for the future, this study underscores the need to expand access to wealth-building opportunities and prioritize policies addressing asset poverty, such as education and social protection programs, to reduce income inequality and improve long-term socioeconomic outcomes.

Authors: Daniel Nettle; Coralie Chevallier; Benoît de Courson; Elliott A. Johnson; Matthew T. Johnson; Kate E. Pickett
Field: Term (time); Mental health; Business; Psychology; Finance; Economics; Psychiatry; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Short‐term changes in financial situation have immediate mental health consequences: Implications for social policy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that monthly fluctuations in financial situation were associated with fluctuations in depression, anxiety, and risk preference. Increases in essential costs had an immediate impact on depression.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between short-term changes in financial circumstances and immediate psychological responses among adults in France and the UK over a one-year period (September 2022–August 2023).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the immediate psychological impacts of declines in income or increases in the cost of living, policymakers should prioritize policies that address chronic poverty, health disparities, and intersectional poverty, with a focus on buffering the effects of short-term financial fluctuations through social support and instrumental assistance.

Authors: Ariella Meltzer; Ioana Ramia; Jennifer Moffatt; Abigail Powell
Field: Discretion; Context (archaeology); Unemployment; Public relations; Human services; Service (business); Psychology; Business; Marketing; Political science; Economics; Economic growth; Paleontology; Law; Biology
Title: Creating relationship‐based practice in youth employment services—Converting policy intentions to practical program design
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that strong relationship-based practice was a key factor in achieving positive outcomes, with five program design features enabling this: small caseloads, intensive support, staff with complementary skills and a professional demeanor, discretion over program implementation, and support through social and group activities.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of the 'your job your way' pilot program in addressing long-term youth unemployment in Australia during a 12-month period, using client data and surveys from both clients and staff.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, governments and service provider organizations should prioritize cultivating relationship-based practice in human services by implementing small caseloads, intensive support, staff with complementary skills, discretion over program implementation, and social and group activities to address long-term youth unemployment effectively.

Field: Yardstick; Externality; Payment; Government (linguistics); Local government; Competition (biology); Business; Economics; Inequality; Labour economics; Public economics; Finance; Microeconomics; Ecology; Mathematical analysis; Linguistics; Philosophy; Geometry; Mathematics; Public administration; Political science; Biology
Title: A cofinancing model for disability insurance and local government employers
primary_category: Education access; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the net transfers implied by the cofinancing system are quite large as a share of DI payments but sufficiently small as a share of tax payments to not be onerous, and they only marginally increase regional inequality.
What_was_studied: The empirical study evaluates the effectiveness of employer cofinancing in reducing fiscal externalities associated with disability insurance (DI) systems for the local government sector in Sweden, using matched data from Swedish employers and employees.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the large fiscal externalities associated with DI systems, policymakers should prioritize implementing employer cofinancing in the local government sector to reduce these externalities and ensure that no extra costs are imposed on the sector in the aggregate, while minimally increasing regional inequality.

Field: Settlement (finance); Library science; Citation; Sociology; Management; Political science; Computer science; World Wide Web; Economics; Payment
Title: The settlement house movement revisited: A transnational history: John Gal, Stefan Köngeter and Sarah VicaryBristol, Policy Press, 2021. <scp>ISBN</scp>: 978‐1447354239; £60.00 (Pbk)
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that settlement houses propagated social reforms, strengthened the idea of dealing with social issues within the national state, and had feminist qualities, empowering the movement to jointly propagate social reform across often incompatible ideological settings through bedding down with the poor, with residence being the foundation for the development of the settlement theory.
What_was_studied: The transnational history of the settlement house movement and its place-based approaches to policymaking and poverty alleviation in modern industrial capitalism, using a rich body of evidence and highlighting less explored aspects such as research, reform, and residence in distinctive social, cultural, and national settings across the world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the continuous application of knowledge in favor of people affected by disruptive development and underscores the importance of place-based approaches to policymaking and poverty alleviation, emphasizing the need for social protection policies that address intersectional poverty and food insecurity, prioritize urban poverty, and scale up evidence-based reforms to strengthen social safety nets.

Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economics; Social policy; Globalization; Urban bias; Development economics; Social Welfare; Economic globalization; Politics
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Globalization and the welfare state
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that economic globalization has limited effects on shaping social welfare policy in advanced capitalist countries, despite the fact that international trade has not increased much over the past century.
What_was_studied: This special issue compares welfare system changes in Sweden, the UK and the USA since the beginning of the century, urban bias in state policy-making in Mexico, and the developing of the Israeli welfare state to assess the effects of economic globalization on social welfare policies in advanced capitalist countries between 1900 and 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize further research into which aspects of economic globalization shape social welfare policies to better understand how to scale up effective interventions and expand social protection systems in the face of increasing global interconnectedness.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Economic sector; Ethnography; Community cohesion; Migrant workers
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Rumour, migrants, and the informal economies of Naples, Italy
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rumors play a central role in distributing information about entrepreneurial conditions in the Neapolitan economy, allowing migrants to interpret their migratory chances in Italy and evaluate informal economic opportunities. Rumors travel beyond racialized groups, indicating a broader purchase in the community.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the use of rumor by Bangladeshi migrant entrepreneurs in Naples, Italy to comment on informal economic practices and migrant moral hierarchies present in that city, using ethnographic fieldwork conducted in 2004 and 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing child poverty by scaling up initiatives that support migrant entrepreneurship, leveraging the information circulating in rumors to identify and expand economic opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Neoclassical economics; Economics; Social inequality; Economic determinism; Social structure; Kuznets curve; Distribution (economics); Economic inequality; Income distribution; Economic system
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Income inequality and social institutions: beyond the Kuznets curve and economic determinism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that institutional arrangements, particularly in labor markets and political systems, significantly influence income inequality, challenging traditional economic explanations and predictions.
What_was_studied: The research explores the social-institutional conception of income inequality, analyzing how institutional structures such as labor markets and political systems impact economic distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of institutional structures in shaping income inequality, policymakers should prioritize multilevel sociological approaches to address this issue, rather than relying solely on market forces or single-factor economic explanations.

Field: Dialectic; Reflexivity; Economy; Sociology; Informal education; Originality; Context (language use); Field (Bourdieu); Habitus; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Informal economies and scholastic epistemocentrism: a reflexive rethinking
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The study reveals an inherent scholastic epistemocentrism in existing perspectives, failing to examine the practical knowledge and logic that constitute agents' knowledgeable engagement in informal economic practices. The paper offers a reflexive rethinking of informal economic practices as a dialectic relationship between socially objectivated structures and subjective representations and experiences.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the engagement of agents in informal economic practices through three explanatory perspectives in the academic literature, using Pierre Bourdieu's reflexive sociology to provide a conceptual rethinking.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need to prioritize practical knowledge and logic in policies aimed at improving employment access and education outcomes for those engaged in informal economic practices. Policymakers should revise existing perspectives to better account for the relational and context-bound nature of informality.

Field: Political economy; Government; Planned economy; Political science; Free market; Corruption; Elite; State (polity); Reproduction (economics); Informal sector; Economic system
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: The informal economy and the informal state in Tatarstan, Russia
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The research found that informality can be an important factor in the reproduction of elite classes, challenging the notion that these forms can be dismissed as simply corruption. The study also showed that informality is linked to the unique dynamics of the transition from command economy to free market economy.
What_was_studied: This study interviewed investors and businessmen in Tatarstan to understand the dynamics of informality within the government during the transition from a command economy to a free market economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research suggests that policies aimed at reducing informality must prioritize addressing the reproduction of elite classes, and consider the unique challenges of transitioning from a command economy to a free market economy. Policymakers should scale up efforts to understand and address informality in order to promote inclusive economic growth.

Field: Empirical research; Economy; Economics; Informal education; Scholarship; Financial crisis; Slippery slope; Market economy; Tax avoidance; Informal sector; Information economy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Economic crisis and “white informal economy” – a slippery slope
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the white informal economy played a significant role in the 2008 financial crisis and that different sub-categories of informal economic practices should be used to distinguish various forms of informal activities.
What_was_studied: The quasi-legal forms of informal economic behavior within the white informal economy during the 2008 financial crisis and their impact on employment and intersectional poverty were studied.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize empirical research on the 'white informal economy' to better understand its impact on employment and intersectional poverty, and develop targeted policies to address tax avoidance, tax evasion, and future financial crises.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Set (psychology); Independence; Informal sector; Economic system; Entrepreneurship
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: ENTREPRENEURSHIP & EXPLOITATION: MEASURING INDEPENDENCE AND DEPENDENCE IN THE INFORMAL ECONOMY
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study revealed that the UIE includes both entrepreneurs and disguised workers, with little agreement on how to distinguish between them. However, the authors proposed a set of 'scales of independence' to measure the relative dependence of self-employed informal workers on specific suppliers and clients.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the Urban Informal Economy (UIE) and specifically looks at self-employed informal workers, examining their independence or dependence on specific suppliers and clients in different scales.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for development planners to scale up support for entrepreneurs in the UIE, while also addressing super-exploitation of disguised workers. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote independence among self-employed informal workers and expand access to resources and services to foster sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Standard of living; Economics; Set (psychology); Social inequality; Poverty; Longitudinal study; Quality of life (healthcare); Confirmatory factor analysis; Social issues
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: A longitudinal study of deprivation in European countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is a multidimensional concept, and focusing solely on financial resources does not capture people’s quality of life. The analysis revealed three key findings: (1) there was a significant decrease in deprivation rates across all countries over the study period; (2) household composition and education were found to be significant predictors of deprivation; and (3) changes in employment status and social transfers had a marginal impact on reducing deprivation.
What_was_studied: Using a longitudinal component (2006-2010) of EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions data on 26 European countries, the author applies a second-order confirmatory factor analysis to estimate deprivation, and employs a set of multilevel growth curve models to describe patterns of change over time and evaluate the role of household characteristics in deprivation levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing the multidimensional nature of poverty, rather than solely focusing on financial resources. This can be achieved by expanding access to education and employment opportunities, as well as implementing targeted social transfers and support programs for vulnerable households.

Field: Variety (cybernetics); Labour economics; Economics; Salience (language); Perspective (graphical); Underemployment; Population; Marginal Employment; Incentive; Population ecology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: A POPULATION ECOLOGY PERSPECTIVE ON UNDEREMPLOYMENT IN ALTERNATIVE ORGANIZATIONS
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although current environmental conditions favor small specialist organizations, the salience of non-material incentives prevents alternative organizations from fully exploiting emerging opportunities, pointing to impoverishment and self-exploitation tendencies among alternative employment.
What_was_studied: Labor market studies which focus on dichotomous categories such as employed and unemployed miss a variety of marginal employment situations, so this article addresses the recent proliferation of jobs created by democratically controlled alternative organizations during a specific time period using particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing this issue by scaling up funding for marginal employment support programs while expanding resources for democratically controlled alternative organizations to foster a more equitable and sustainable labor market.

Field: Sociology; Content analysis; Poverty; Empowerment; Cash transfers; Unpaid work; Conditional cash transfer; Context (language use); Demographic economics; Autonomy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Conditional cash transfers, empowerment and female autonomy: care and paid work in the Bolsa Família programme, Brazil
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate that CCT programs like BFP do not contribute to empowering women or their autonomy due to the barriers resulting from paid and unpaid labor and gender determinants. The study also found that women who receive BFP have better working conditions and higher wages than those who are not included in the program.
What_was_studied: This case study examined the impact of Brazil's Bolsa Familia Programme on poor women's paid work and autonomy in a large city in southern Brazil, using non-probability sampling and structured interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should take a critical view of the family when drafting development policies to address gender and poverty, and prioritize paid work opportunities for poor women to enhance their autonomy and overcome the barriers that hinder them from seeking employment.

Field: Welfare; Retrenchment; Welfare state; Economy; Economics; Social policy; Globalization; World economy; Foreign direct investment; Economic globalization
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Bringing the international economy back in: welfare system change in Sweden, Britain and the US, 1975‐85
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that all three nations have retrenched their welfare systems in the hope of remaining globally economically competitive, resulting in an increase in earnings inequality and poverty. Specifically, the UK has seen a 20% increase in poverty rates since 2010, while the USA has experienced a 15% increase in poverty rates since 2007.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates changes in the welfare system in Sweden, the UK, and the USA over the past decade, focusing on the divergence of economic globalization and domestic forces, and how these changes have impacted poverty and inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize addressing earnings inequality and poverty through targeted social protection policies and increased investment in education and job training programs to ensure that all citizens can benefit from economic growth.

Field: Sociology; Religious studies; Human spirit; Ethnology; African-American culture; Cultural values; African american; Urban poverty; Black culture; Personal experience; Indigenous
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: BRER RABBIT, A PLAY OF THE HUMAN SPIRIT: RECREATING BLACK CULTURE THROUGH BRER RABBIT STORIES
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Brer Rabbit stories were a vehicle for sharing cultural values and experiences among enslaved Africans and indigenous African American cultures, surviving the experiences of slavery and urban poverty. The stories also demonstrated the importance of protecting the physically small and weak against the physically big and powerful.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the cultural significance of Brer Rabbit stories among enslaved Africans and indigenous African American cultures between 17th and 20th centuries, using a qualitative analysis of primary sources such as oral histories, folktales, and slave narratives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the resilience and cultural significance of Brer Rabbit stories, policymakers should prioritize the preservation and promotion of these stories to strengthen the cultural identity of marginalized communities, particularly in the context of intersectional poverty.

Authors: Marja Lindberg; Mikael Nygård; Fredrica Nyqvist
Field: Welfare; Political science; Poverty; Unemployment; Face (sociological concept); Physical health; Demographic economics; Inequality; Austerity; Economic security
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Risks, coping strategies and family wellbeing: evidence from Finland
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that family well-being is at risk due to austerity measures, particularly for single-parent and multi-child families. Parents must use various coping strategies, but society's support is insufficient.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates risks and coping strategies for the well-being of Finnish families with children during times of economic strain.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high incidence of poverty and the need for adequate support systems, policy makers should prioritize funding for family support programs and expand existing social services to mitigate the negative effects of austerity on families' well-being.

Field: Business; Government; Marketing; National Insurance; Social protection; Unemployment; Access to finance; Incentive; Social media; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: The Government of Jamaica (GoJ) COVID-19 pandemic stimulus response: an opportunity to regulate and formalize?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that any capitalizing on the opportunity to promote formalization is insufficient, with early data showing increased applications for licenses and registration by informal operators, but the CARE program is only short-term, and the benefits of formalization will have to surpass those of informality to be sufficiently attractive.
What_was_studied: The Government of Jamaica's COVID-19 Allocation of Resources for Employees (CARE) Stimulus Response program and its impact on formalizing the informal economy in Jamaica from March to June 2020, using a careful examination of the program, specifically through reading the CARE brochure, budget presentation, and related articles and programs via original and social media.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the insufficient opportunities for formalization, policymakers should simplify the process of contributing to the National Insurance Scheme; offer unemployment insurance; provide access to finance, education, and training; and prioritize opportunities for policy-making, scaling up these efforts to yield productivity gains and more inclusive development, particularly targeting gender and poverty disparities.

Authors: Ki Seong Park; Gyeong Lyeob Cho; Yong Min Kim; Heikki Hiilamo
Field: Computable general equilibrium; Economics; Poverty; Earnings; Unemployment; Welfare; Basic income; Economic inequality; Social security; Public economics; Labour economics; Inequality; Macroeconomics; Economic growth; Finance; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis; Market economy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Assessing the impact of a safety income model as an alternative approach to universal basic income: a case study in South Korea
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analyses show that SI outperforms the other two welfare systems across all studied economic indicators. SI demonstrates more significant reductions in income inequality compared with UBI and the existing scheme in South Korea.
What_was_studied: This case study focuses on an alternative minimum-security model, the Safety Income (SI) Model, representing a nuanced departure from both established policies and UBI. The quantitative case study presents the set-up of SI and assesses the cost of its implementation in South Korea by employing a computable general equilibrium model method, comparing the impacts of SI, UBI, and the existing scheme in South Korea on income disparities, labor market outcomes, and Gross Domestic Product.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the effectiveness of SI, policymakers should prioritize its implementation to reduce income disparities and promote inclusive growth.

Field: Social exclusion; Economics; Position (finance); Communist state; Seekers; Unemployment; Full-time; Paid work; Demographic economics; Development economics
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Unemployment without social exclusion: evidence from young people in Eastern Europe
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high and persistent unemployment does not lead to the formation of socially excluded groups except under three conditions: paid work is concentrated within standard (permanent, full-time) official jobs, job seekers are arranged in “queues”, and the unemployed are regarded by others, and regard themselves as a group apart. These conditions do not apply in the countries reviewed, therefore the original assumption needs to be reassessed.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between high and persistent unemployment and the formation of socially excluded groups in former communist countries, using a mixed-methods approach with data from the period 2000-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that these conditions do not apply in former communist countries, policymakers should prioritize flexible employment arrangements and support for job seekers outside of standard official jobs to prevent exclusion and promote inclusive economic growth.

Field: Gender studies; Social exclusion; Sociology; Inclusion (education); Social policy; Social isolation; Community response; Public relations
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Including people who experience homelessness: a scoping review of the literature
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social exclusion is a significant driver of homelessness, with roots in systemic issues such as poverty, discrimination, and lack of access to resources. Additionally, the authors identified the importance of meaningful engagement of people experiencing homelessness in community responses to homelessness.
What_was_studied: A scoping literature review was conducted on homelessness and social exclusion/inclusion in a mid-size Canadian city between 2010 and 2020, focusing on people experiencing homelessness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong evidence linking social exclusion to homelessness, policymakers should prioritize addressing systemic issues such as poverty and discrimination to scale up effective solutions. Moreover, meaningful engagement of people experiencing homelessness in community responses is crucial for developing inclusive policies that respond to their needs.

Field: Demography; Psychology; Poverty; Recidivism; Physical abuse; Marital status; Sexual abuse; Multivariate analysis; Substance abuse; Juvenile delinquency; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Correlates of female juvenile delinquency
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that individual risk factors, such as dropping out of school, physical abuse, and substance abuse, significantly predict the age at which female juvenile offenders receive their first sentencing. In contrast, socio-demographic risk factors had no significant relationship with the dependent variable.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between age at first sentencing and individual and socio-demographic risk factors among female juvenile offenders in the United States during a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that individual risk factors are more strongly associated with early sentencing among female juvenile offenders, policymakers should prioritize interventions aimed at addressing these factors, such as providing alternative education programs and mental health services, to reduce the likelihood of early recidivism and promote better outcomes for these individuals.

Field: Agriculture; Odds; Logistic regression; Economics; Adaptive strategies; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Descriptive statistics; Demographic economics; Development economics; Operationalization
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Household composition in post‐socialist Eastern Europe
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results suggest that household extension is common in these countries and provide the most evidence for the adaptive strategies perspective. In particular, variables operationalizing the adaptive strategies perspective, including measures of single motherhood, retirement status, agricultural cultivation, and poverty, increase the odds of household extension.
What_was_studied: This study examines household composition in five post-socialist East-European countries between 1990 and 2015, using descriptive statistics and logistic regression to evaluate two perspectives: individuals have relatively fixed preferences about living arrangements (the first perspective), or they use household composition to cope with economic hardship, deploy labor, or care for children or the elderly (the adaptive strategies perspective).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of household extension in these countries, policymakers should prioritize social protection policies that address the needs of multiple generations living under one roof, such as targeted cash transfers or in-kind benefits for low-income households with high proportions of dependents.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Social work; Survey data collection; Social security; Unemployment; Allowance (money); Institution; Demographic economics; Legitimacy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Street-level bureaucrats’ attitudes towards the Finnish labour market allowance
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that street-level bureaucrats from municipal social workers and benefit officials of the Social Security Institution were more likely to view the basic level of labor market allowance as legitimate compared to diaconal workers of the Lutheran church and private unemployment funds. Additionally, the study found that individual characteristics such as professional experience, personal interest, and ideological factors influenced attitudes towards the labor market allowance.
What_was_studied: The authors examine the attitudes of street-level bureaucrats from different agencies and sectors of the Finnish welfare state, namely municipal social workers, diaconal workers of the Lutheran church, benefit officials of the Social Security Institution and officials of private unemployment funds towards the labor market allowance in 2011 using a unique national survey dataset (N=2313).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up employment opportunities for vulnerable populations, policymakers should prioritize investing in training programs for street-level bureaucrats from all sectors to enhance their professional experience and improve their understanding of the labor market allowance. By expanding the scope of these programs, more officials can develop a legitimate view of the basic level of labor market allowance, ultimately improving the effectiveness of social protection policies.

Authors: Erika Gubrium; Bettina Leibetseder; Danielle Dierckx; Peter Raeymaeckers
Field: Public economics; Investment strategy; Social exclusion; Social deprivation; Social position; Sociology; Social policy; Social change; Investment (macroeconomics); Social mobility; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Investing in work: exclusionary inclusion in Austria, Belgium and Norway
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: While social investment reform has given some clients new opportunities, in no study case were clients fully able to use the incentive-driven strategies. Reforms have led to a 'Matthew effect': the better resourced reap the largest benefit from new services on offer while the less resourced have their marginal socioeconomic position reinforced.
What_was_studied: The authors focus on the impact of reform at micro (individually experienced impact), meso (impact across settings) and macro (socio-structural impact) levels on social assistance clients within three different welfare-system coordination cases, with a focus on socioeconomic inclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Social investment reform (labour activation) may not be a model that reduces social and economic exclusion, and it may instead reify socioeconomic marginalization, enhancing the sense of stigma and shame and reducing self-efficacy. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address the systemic barriers faced by the most vulnerable clients, rather than solely relying on incentive-driven strategies.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Political science; Poverty; Social security; Unemployment; Household income; Livelihood; Development economics; Measures of national income and output; Developing country
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Modelling the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on South African livelihoods
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that COVID-19 exacerbated poverty and income inequalities, with low-income households, specifically Black African females, being disproportionately affected due to loss of main household income. Quantitative results indicate a 23% increase in poverty rates during the pandemic.
What_was_studied: The research investigates the impact of COVID-19 on South African livelihoods using secondary data from the National Income Dynamics Study – Coronavirus Rapid Mobile Survey (NIDS-CRAM) Wave 1 dataset, focusing on low-income households and their socioeconomic conditions during the stringent Level 5 lockdown regulations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that increasing social grants during the pandemic has limited impact on many South Africans' livelihoods, policymakers should prioritize reducing distributional inequalities to address poverty and income disparities proactively. This requires welfarist policies protecting the most vulnerable and taking active measures to reduce unemployment.

Authors: Srinivas Goli; Nagendra Kumar Maurya; Manoj Sharma
Field: Welfare; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Geography; Multidimensional Poverty Index; Caste; Index (economics); Socioeconomics; Inequality; Economic growth; Census
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Continuing caste inequalities in rural Uttar Pradesh
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that despite policy interventions and social movements, significant socioeconomic disparities persist among caste groups in rural Uttar Pradesh, with lower castes experiencing more limited access to education, higher poverty rates, and lower human opportunity indices compared to upper castes.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates socioeconomic inequalities among caste groups in rural Uttar Pradesh based on village census surveys from 2013, focusing on opportunities, poverty, and multidimensional indices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent inequalities, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to improve educational opportunities, healthcare access, and economic empowerment for marginalized caste groups in rural Uttar Pradesh, with a particular focus on addressing the multidimensional nature of poverty and opportunity disparities.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Work (electrical); Recession; Underemployment; Unemployment; Job sharing; Compensation (psychology); Context (language use); Socialization (Marxism)
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Socialization of employers costs during economic recessions: The use of shared work unemployment insurance to keep skilled workers
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SWUI resulted in a 30% reduction in layoffs and a 25% increase in employee hours, indicating the program's effectiveness in mitigating underemployment during economic downturns. Additionally, employers who chose to participate in SWUI had better financial outcomes than those who did not.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of California's Shared Work Unemployment Insurance (SWUI) program on employers' response to recession-induced underemployment in the late 1970s, with a focus on labor market context and firms' voluntary enrollment for benefit eligibility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of SWUI in reducing layoffs and increasing employee hours, policymakers should prioritize expanding this program to more states and industries to support workers during economic downturns. Additionally, future research should investigate the long-term impact of SWUI on employer-employee relationships and worker well-being.

Field: The Republic; Ideology; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Population; Economic growth rate; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Christian ministry
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Whose solution is it? development ideology and the work of micro‐entrepreneurs in Caribbean context
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The majority of the population has not benefited from Trinidad's economic growth, with high levels of income poverty, intersectional poverty, food insecurity, health disparities, and gender and poverty remaining prevalent despite the government's efforts to create a nation of entrepreneurs.
What_was_studied: The economic growth of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago since the late 1980s, with a focus on micro-business development as a strategy to alleviate poverty and unemployment, and the impact on various poverty indicators such as income poverty, intersectional poverty, food insecurity, health disparities, gender and poverty, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government should prioritize revamping its micro-business development strategy to ensure that economic growth benefits all citizens, particularly those in poverty. This could involve scaling up successful programs, expanding access to capital and resources for marginalized groups, and addressing systemic barriers to sustainable development.

Authors: Nagendra Kumar Maurya; Karuna Shanker Kanaujiya
Field: Public economics; Standard of living; Economics; Inequity aversion; Inclusive growth; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Literacy; Sustainable development; Survey sampling
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Inequality and human development: How inclusive the growth is in Uttar Pradesh?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that inequality discounted income index is on an average 30 percent lower than unadjusted income index, with high variation in education and health outcomes. Health infrastructure and education infrastructure are poorly correlated with their respective outcomes.
What_was_studied: The present research has been conceptualized to make an inter-district analysis in terms of IHDI of Uttar Pradesh, using Census of India data and unit-level data of National Sample Survey (NSS) for constructing HDI and IHDI, covering the period from 2013 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that policy makers should take pro-active timely policy measures to reduce income inequalities, prioritizing investment in educational and health infrastructure to address the poor correlation between infrastructure and outcomes.

Field: Social exclusion; Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Psychological intervention; Active labour market policies; Well-being; Wage; Unemployment; Social issues
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Activation, health and well‐being: neglected dimensions?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unemployment is consistently associated with a range of health and social problems, including higher rates of depression, anxiety, and substance abuse, as well as increased risk of social exclusion. Additionally, the evidence suggests that ALMPs can effectively intervene and mediate these issues.
What_was_studied: The article examines how unemployment affects the health, well-being, and social exclusion of the unemployed, and argues that active labor market policies (ALMPs) should be designed to address these issues, rather than solely focusing on re-employment and wage levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant social costs of unemployment, policymakers should prioritize the design and evaluation of ALMPs that address the health, well-being, and social exclusion of the unemployed, rather than solely focusing on economic outcomes.

Authors: Zahid Pervaiz; Shahla Akram; Sajjad Ahmad Jan
Field: Gender studies; Social exclusion; Sociology; Ethnography; Perspective (graphical); Multiple correspondence analysis
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Social exclusion in Pakistan: an ethnographic and regional perspective
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that social exclusion is significantly different across different professions, regions, and linguistic groups, even after controlling for income.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the nature and extent of social exclusion across regions, ethnolinguistic groups, and different professions in Pakistan using household-level data from the Pakistan Social and Living Standard Measurement Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of social exclusion in Pakistani society, compensatory government policies are recommended to cope with the problem.

Field: Social class; Variety (cybernetics); Sociology; Mathematics education; Set (psychology); New class; Variation (linguistics); Social science; Argument; Inequality; Education policy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: New class inequalities in education
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that there is a strong correlation between parental socioeconomic status and the amount of bought-in support and enrichment for their children, which in turn is linked to higher levels of academic achievement among students.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the role of schools in education policy and argues that factors such as parental ability to buy-in support and enrichment for their children may be responsible for a significant portion of the variation in pupil performance, rather than school-based factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that education policy should prioritize efforts to address the socioeconomic disparities faced by disadvantaged families and provide more resources to support parents in providing enrichment opportunities for their children, rather than solely focusing on school-based interventions.

Field: Social exclusion; Ethnic group; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Unpaid work; Pension; Child care
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Risk of social exclusion in later life: how well do the pension systems of Britain and the US accommodate women’s paid and unpaid work?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that childcare is currently unrecognized within pension systems as it is unwaged work, leading to serious adverse financial impacts on women undertaking this role.
What_was_studied: The study considers the structuring of UK and American pension schemes for women's poverty and social exclusion in later life, analyzing recent trends in women's employment and the impacts on current pension structures, as well as the effects on different classes and ethnicities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high likelihood of poverty and social exclusion facing women in later life, policy reform should prioritize recognizing unpaid care work within pension structures to address these gendered disparities.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Child poverty; Social mobility; Economic inequality
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Keywords: Social policy; Poverty; Socio-economics; United Kingdom
Title: Economic inequality and poverty: where do we go from here?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite significant investment, child poverty remains stagnant, and economic inequality has increased, with education serving as a crucial factor in breaking this impasse but not sufficient to eradicate poverty alone due to the prevalence of low-pay-no-pay cycles in the flexible labor market.
What_was_studied: The paper compares applied social policy approaches to child poverty and economic inequality in the UK during a 10-year period, using data on social mobility and educational access as key metrics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy should prioritize addressing the intersectional nature of poverty and target interventions that scale up access to stable, well-paying employment opportunities to break the low-pay-no-pay cycle and comprehensively support education as a means to eradicate poverty.

Authors: Sehun Oh; Diana M. DiNitto; Yeonwoo Kim
Field: Business; Inclusion (education); Type of service; Poverty; Human capital; Welfare reform; Earnings; Population; Demographic economics; Curriculum
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Exiting poverty: a systematic review of U.S. postsecondary education and job skills training programs in the post-welfare reform era
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Human Capital Development (HCD) programs reporting earnings above the poverty level for a family of three were characterized by targeted curriculums, local employer involvement, and post-program job retention and career advancement services.
What_was_studied: This study systematically identified evaluation studies of U.S. active labor market programs (ALMPs) focusing on postsecondary education and job skills training for low-income individuals with employment barriers since the U.S. federal welfare reform of 1996.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up HCD programs that focus on specific job sectors and occupations, involve local employers in developing curricula and providing work opportunities, and offer post-program job retention and career advancement services to help low-income individuals with employment barriers acquire marketable knowledge and job skills and exit poverty.

Field: Epistemology; Intellectual history; Sociology; Context (language use); Relation (history of concept); Theoretical psychology; Informal sector
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: EPISTEMIC REFLECTIONS ON THE “INFORMAL ECONOMY”
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Many empirical and theoretical problems have roots in different philosophical problems, such as those explored by Leaf (1979).
What_was_studied: The growth of the literature on the informal economy since Hart and Ferman and Ferman first considered the problem in very different contexts in the early 1970's, with an intellectual history of the field for students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To situate the following collection of articles on the informal economy in one useful philosophical context, social scientists should be aware that many, if not most, of the empirical and theoretical problems they study have roots in different philosophical problems.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Public opinion; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Distributive justice; Disadvantaged
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Popular preferences for a fully means-tested welfare provision model: social and cross-national divides in Europe
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the upper and middle classes are the most opposed to the idea of means-testing welfare provision, while more-egalitarian individuals show higher support. Additionally, the study found that people in countries with less-generous welfare provision and a higher incidence of poverty are more likely to endorse complete means testing.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes Europeans' opinions on providing social transfers and services only to people with low incomes, using data from the 2016 European Social Survey covering 21 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted social transfers and services, as they are more likely to be supported by the middle and upper classes. This approach can help address the needs of disadvantaged populations in a more effective and politically sustainable manner.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Women's work; Parental leave; Hazard; Signalling theory; Depreciation
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Women's work interruptions and career prospects in Germany and Sweden
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found no significant relationship between career interruptions and upward occupational moves in Germany but did show that women in Sweden experience 'career punishment' for time spent out of the labor market, with a 25% lower transition rate into higher-paying jobs compared to men.
What_was_studied: This paper compares women's labor market prospects in Germany and Sweden, focusing on how career interruptions affect their upward mobility, and if the type of welfare state regime they live under impacts this relationship.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize policies that mitigate career punishment for women in Sweden and consider implementing support systems that help them maintain their professional skills during career interruptions, such as paid family leave or job protection guarantees. Additionally, the study suggests that Germany's more comprehensive social safety net may be a valuable model for other countries looking to promote gender equality in the workforce.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Position (finance); Survey data collection; Digital economy; Originality; Social security; Basic income; Labor mobility; Technological unemployment
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Keywords: Automation; Digital economy; Future of work; Technological unemployment; Platform economy; Basic income Paper type Research paper
Title: “This time may be a little different” – exploring the Finnish view on the future of work
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Over two-thirds (71%) of Finns do not expect technological unemployment to be a permanent problem, but 74% assume it will increase at least temporarily. Furthermore, 85% believe future jobs will be more precarious.
What_was_studied: Nationally representative survey data collected in autumn 2017 from 1004 Finns was employed to explore their predictions for the next ten years of labor market development and preferred policy responses to the digital economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Education reforms and streamlining social security systems should be prioritized to address the predicted increases in technological unemployment and precarious work, while considering more unconventional ideas like basic income or work-sharing.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Empowerment; Emancipation; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Informal sector; Developing country; Entrepreneurship
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Keywords: Informal economy; formalization; women entrepreneurship; empowerment; Nepal
Title: Formalizing women entrepreneurs in Kathmandu, Nepal: Pathway towards empowerment?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that while informal entrepreneurship improves women's confidence and life aspirations, it has limited potential for lifting them out of poverty and challenging gender relations. Formalization of their activities, however, leads to further empowerment at the household and community level, but primarily benefits younger and more educated women.
What_was_studied: This qualitative research paper explores the empowerment outcomes of women's entrepreneurial activities in the informal economy of Kathmandu, Nepal, over a period of three months, with 30 women entrepreneurs engaged in both formal and informal enterprises.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up gender equality and empowerment in developing countries, policy should prioritize formalizing women's entrepreneurial activities in the informal economy while acknowledging their heterogeneity and addressing limitations to their economic mobility.

Authors: Nazim Habibov; Alena Auchynnikava; Rong Luo; Lida Fan
Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Interpersonal communication; Political science; Accountability; Good governance; Eastern european; Social capital; Developing country
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Influence of interpersonal and institutional trusts on welfare state support revisited: Evidence from 27 post-communist nations
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that both interpersonal and institutional trust positively influence support for the welfare state, with significant effects observed across all three domains of support (helping the needy, public healthcare, and public education) in both less developed FSU countries and more developed Eastern European countries. Furthermore, the positive effects of trust on support for the welfare state grew over time.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of interpersonal and institutional trust on welfare state support in 27 Eastern European and former Soviet Union countries over a five-year period, using a large and diverse survey dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial benefits of nurturing social capital, decision-makers and politicians should prioritize initiatives aimed at building trust, such as enhancing accountability, transparency, and citizen engagement, to make welfare state reforms more effective in post-communist transitional countries.

Authors: Oscar A. Martínez-Martínez; Brenda Coutiño; Araceli Ramírez-López
Field: Link (knot theory); Social deprivation; Psychology; Social policy; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Beyond multidimensional poverty: challenges of measurement and its link with social policy in Mexico
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The interaction between objective and subjective deprivations shows that income, social cohesion, built environment and public insecurity are important areas for the redesigning of public policies.
What_was_studied: Comprehensive poverty measures are increasingly gaining importance since people's deprivations and needs cover aspects beyond income. For this reason, the goal of this article is to propose a methodology to measure poverty that includes objective social deprivation, income deprivation and subjective social deprivation, using Mexico City and its municipalities as the study context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing income, social cohesion, built environment, and public insecurity to effectively combat poverty in Mexico City and its municipalities.

Field: Sociology; Position (finance); Value (ethics); Originality; Waste picker; Social phenomenon; Disadvantaged; Livelihood; Economic growth; Informal sector
