Title: Can social inclusion policies promote financial inclusion?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that social inclusion policies do not have a significant effect on financial inclusion. Also, the older population is less likely to own an account at a formal financial institution in low- and medium-income countries that have strong environmental sustainability policies and institutions.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effect of three social inclusion policies on financial inclusion in 48 low- and medium-income countries using a panel fixed effect regression methodology, with data from 2000 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should consider how social and environmental policies and programs can be designed to promote financial inclusion for older individuals in their countries, as the findings suggest that policies established to promote environmental sustainability may discourage the older population from keeping their wealth in formal financial institutions.

Field: Economy; China; Geography; Domestic trade; Treaty ports; Empire; Urban history; Population; Urbanization; Economic growth; Communism
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: CHINA'S URBANISATION UNDER COMMUNIST RULE, 1949–1982
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: After the Opium War in 1842, China's treaty ports experienced disproportionate growth, concentrating the country's urban population in central and coastal areas, leading to epidemic levels of unemployment, crime, prostitution, and drug addiction.
What_was_studied: China's urban history dating back more than 2000 years, specifically the impact of foreign conquest and treaty ports on urban population distribution and social pathologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the historical concentration of social pathologies in China's rapidly expanding cities, decision makers should prioritize decentralization strategies to restrict urban growth and purge big cities of these issues to improve intersectional poverty outcomes.

Authors: Barbara A. Zsembik; Greg L. Drevenstedt; C. Preston McLane
Field: Ethnic group; Socioeconomic status; Health care; Political science; Poverty; Well-being; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Household income; Demographic economics; Gerontology; Economic security
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Economic well-being among older Latinos
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that older Puerto Ricans report lower median incomes, higher poverty rates, and disproportionate enrollment in the state health insurance program compared to older Cubans and Mexican Americans. Additionally, the results show that access to health care is most limited among older Cubans.
What_was_studied: This research examines ethnic variation in the economic well-being of older Latinos, using data from the 1990 Latino sample of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the 1988 National Survey of Elderly Hispanics to investigate differences in median income, poverty rates, and health insurance coverage among older Cubans, Mexican Americans, and Puerto Ricans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unique economic profiles of each Latino ethnic group, policymakers should prioritize policies guarding economic security for older adults, tailoring these policies to the specific needs of each group. For example, targeted programs addressing the disproportionate enrollment in state health insurance programs among older Puerto Ricans could be implemented.

Field: Redistribution (election); Typology; Positive economics; Welfare state; Empirical research; Sociology; Economics; Epistemology; Political science; Law; Politics; Philosophy; Anthropology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Family in societal redistribution: a theoretical inquiry
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Approaches to redistribution are shaped by distinct concepts of equal or unequal exchange, the relevant actors they identify, and different understandings of the economy. These distinctions are central to understanding the position of family in societal redistribution.
What_was_studied: This paper theorises family as a redistributive principle, focusing on its relevance in modern societies and the major theoretical concepts of redistribution that shape approaches to it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This paper provides a theoretical groundwork for theoretical and empirical investigations of societal redistribution and for better comprehending its international variation, indicating that policymakers should prioritize and revise their approaches to include the significance of family in modern societies.

Authors: Päivi Mäntyneva; Eeva-Leena Ketonen; Heikki Hiilamo
Field: Originality; Pandemic; Inclusion (mineral); Social policy; Welfare; Grey literature; Public economics; Political science; Value (mathematics); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Public relations; Sociology; Social science; Economics; Medicine; MEDLINE; Qualitative research; Computer science; Law; Disease; Pathology; Machine learning; Infectious disease (medical specialty)
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Keywords: Scoping review; Welfare states; Social policy; COVID-19; Comparative studies Paper type Literature review
Title: Initial social-policy responses to the COVID-19 pandemic in the Global North – A scoping review
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that social policy measures were directed specifically at working-age people to minimize income loss and save jobs, while care-related responsibilities necessitated the expansion of current policies and the implementation of new instruments. Despite differences in responses between universalistic and residual welfare states, the influence of welfare regimes on COVID-19 social policy measures remains unclear.
What_was_studied: This scoping review analyzed comparative studies on social policy measures implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic in Global North welfare states and considered their potential influence on responses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the accumulation of scientific knowledge in the area of social policy measures, there is a need for systematic reviews to identify new research topics and knowledge gaps and inspire new research questions and hypotheses. To address the unequal distribution of care responsibilities during the pandemic, policymakers should prioritize expanding current policies and implementing new instruments to support working-age individuals and minimize income loss.

Field: Racism; Sociology; Ideology; Individualism; Affirmative action; Desegregation; Prejudice; Racial formation theory; Social stratification; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: IDEOLOGY AND RACIAL STRATIFICATION: A THEORETICAL JUXTAPOSITION
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that adherence to individualist explanations of poverty was associated with lower perceived levels of racial discrimination in employment, but also with more negative attitudes toward affirmative action programs. These findings suggest that class ideologies play a significant role in shaping beliefs about racial inequality and support for policies aimed at addressing it.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the limits of attitudinal and structural approaches to understanding racial stratification, and explores how incorporating ideological factors can synthesize these perspectives. The study analyzes the relation between adherence to individualist explanations of poverty, perceptions of racial discrimination in employment, and attitudes toward affirmative action programs to illustrate the power of class ideologies in shaping beliefs about racial inequality and vice versa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of class ideologies in perpetuating racial inequality, policymakers should prioritize policies that target both individualist explanations of poverty and structural barriers to economic mobility. This may involve scaling up education and job training programs, expanding access to affordable housing and healthcare, and funding initiatives that promote diversity and inclusion in the workplace.

Authors: Javeed Ahamed Golandaj; Srinivas Goli; Kailash Chandra Das
Field: Social responsibility; Demography; Psychology; Perception; Human development (humanity); Old age assistance; Social institution; Family life; Older population; Adult population; Gerontology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Living arrangements among older population and perceptions on old age assistance among adult population in India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 85% of older individuals lived with their children, while only 2% lived alone. Most women respondents expected their sons to live with them and provide financial and emotional support in old age.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the living arrangements among older people and their perceptions of old age support in India using India Human Development Survey (IHDS) data from 2004-2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize strengthening social safety nets and family support systems for older individuals, particularly in rural areas where the majority of the elderly population resides.

Authors: Richard J. White; Patricia Burke Wood
Field: Political science; Computer science
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Guest editorial
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that diverse and spontaneous forms of everyday activism have been highly influential in recent years, carrying an important presence and influence beyond traditional forms of organized resistance, such as membership-based, coordinated hierarchical organizations (e.g. Trade Unions, NGOs).
What_was_studied: This study explores the role of organization in social movements and other forms of activism, focusing on diverse and spontaneous forms of everyday activism, such as anti-government and anti-austerity protests, Occupy movement, Black Lives Matter movement and student-led protests against higher tuition fees and the rampant commodification of higher education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding matters because it highlights the importance of alternative forms of governance and radical democracy in challenging entrenched economic, political, social and environmental crises, and inspiring new expressions of identity, relationships, resistance and solidarity into being. Therefore, it is crucial to prioritize and fund these grassroots movements, support their self-organization and horizontality, and scale up their influence in shaping a more desirable, practical and enactable future.

Field: Welfare; Public opinion; Political science; Poverty; Cash; Conventional wisdom; Solidarity; Conditionality; Population; Development economics
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Public attitudes towards the poor in the South Caucasus: a matter of solidarity and conditionality
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The majority of the population in Azerbaijan and Georgia would consent to paying higher taxes or reducing public services if their governments used the extra resources to provide cash assistance to more poor people, but in Armenia the level of solidarity is considerably lower.
What_was_studied: The paper is based on an analysis of data from the tenth round of the Caucasus Barometer survey, one of the most reliable sources of public opinion data in the region during a specific time period, focusing on the population of Azerbaijan and Georgia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted social assistance programs for vulnerable populations in the South Caucasus, particularly in Armenia where there is less public support, and ensure that these programs are conditioned on active job searching to maximize self-sufficiency and long-term success.

Authors: Roseann Giarrusso; Du Feng; Qian wei Wang; Merril Silverstein
Field: Grandparent; Feeling; Psychology; Social change; Well-being; Longitudinal study; Solidarity; Normative; Social psychology; Qualitative property
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: PARENTING AND CO‐PARENTING OF GRANDCHILDREN: EFFECTS ON GRANDPARENTS' WELL‐BEING AND FAMILY SOLIDARITY
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that grandparents who parent or co-parent their grandchildren tend to be younger and less healthy than non-parenting grandparents, but there was no statistically significant decline in psychological, physical, or financial well-being nor in normative or marital solidarity after grandparents begin to caregive. The majority of grandparents show stability or improvement in overall psychological well-being, but some show decline.
What_was_studied: This research examines how grandparents who 'parent' or 'co-parent' their grandchildren differ from other grandparents and the extent to which parenting or co-parenting affects grandparents' psychological, physical, and financial well-being and feelings of family solidarity over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing number of grandparents raising their grandchildren due to issues within the parental generation, policymakers should prioritize support for grandparent caregivers through programs such as employment assistance, healthcare services, and financial aid to ensure their well-being and ability to provide stable care for their grandchildren.

Field: Social position; Sociology; Social work; Social policy; Social change; Social stratification; Economic growth; Social philosophy; Social order; Social engagement
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: THE MEANING OF SOCIAL POLICY AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that social policy has had a significant impact on social structure, particularly in reducing poverty and improving access to education and medical care. In the US, for example, the Great Society programs led to a 20% reduction in poverty rates between 1963 and 1968.
What_was_studied: The impact of social policy on social structure during the past decade, focusing on three Anglophone countries (the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia) with a particular emphasis on the Great Society initiative in the United States and Labour Governments in the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of prioritizing social policy initiatives to address poverty and inequality. Governments should scale up successful programs, expand access to education and healthcare, and revitalize urban and rural areas to create a more equitable society.

Authors: Andrés Biehl; Andrea Canales; Viviana Salinas; Guillermo Wormald
Field: Latin Americans; Life course approach; Political science; Order (exchange); Human capital; Social protection; Social insurance; Work experience; Demographic economics; Autonomy
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Gender differences in retirement in Chile and Uruguay
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Main findings support labor market explanations of gender differences in retirement. Work experience, human capital and contribution densities largely explain the chances of retirement and economic autonomy among elderly women.
What_was_studied: The article analyses how labor market and family resources shape the access of women and men to social insurance by investigating the likelihood of retirement after reaching the legal age of retirement, using the Longitudinal Social Protection Survey (LSPS), a biannual or triennial longitudinal survey carried out in six Latin American countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up economic autonomy among elderly women, policy makers should prioritize programs that increase work experience, human capital, and contribution densities for women in the labor market.

Field: Employability; Economics; Quality (business); Population; Public relations; Business model; Curriculum; Economic growth; Sustainability; Vocational education; General partnership
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Towards building a skill based society in India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The research found that neither public nor private training institutions have been able to deliver quality skills training and employability services at affordable costs to the target populations, suggesting a need for PPPs to address this challenge.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the contribution of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in skill building and employability training to making quality services accessible at affordable prices for poor and marginalized sections of India's population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the potential of PPPs in skill building and employability training to scale up access to quality services at affordable prices for poor and marginalized populations. Policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that promote public-private partnerships in this area to address skills gaps and unemployment among vulnerable groups.

Authors: Jitendra Gouda; Kailash Chandra Das; Srinivas Goli; Ladumai Maikho Apollo Pou
Field: Public economics; Performance management; Theil index; Economics; Human development (humanity); School education; Anova test; Physical infrastructure; Social care; Economic growth; Bivariate analysis
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Government versus private primary schools in India: An assessment of physical infrastructure, schooling costs and performance
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that private primary schools outperform government schools in terms of physical infrastructure, schooling costs, and student performance. Additionally, the study revealed that physical infrastructure and schooling costs have a significant impact on student performance in both private and public schools.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the disparities between government and private primary schools in India regarding physical infrastructure, schooling costs, and student performance using India Human Development Survey (IHDS) data from 2005 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investment in physical infrastructure and affordable schooling options to enhance student performance, particularly in underprivileged communities. This could involve increasing funding for school infrastructure, implementing policies to regulate private school fees, or exploring alternative, low-cost educational models.

Authors: L. Janelle Dance; Dae Young Kim; Thomas Bern
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Poverty; Status group; Social isolation; Mainstream; Urban culture; Institution; Extreme poverty; Criminology; Urban sociology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Street culture in Cambridge, Massachusetts?: the perceptions of “poor”, “at‐risk” teens near Harvard
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that even in the absence of extreme poverty and social isolation from mainstream institutions, youths in Cambridge perceive vulnerability to illicit street cultural activities due to social dislocation spillover effects from larger central cities and a desire for peer respect through status group affiliation. Additionally, the study discovered that some students in Cambridge are affected by illicit street cultural activities because of the relative nature of social dislocation and the amplification of experiences among youths in relatively poorer neighborhoods.
What_was_studied: Researchers investigated the relationship between social dislocation and youth involvement in illicit street cultural activities in Cambridge, Massachusetts, focusing on a specific population of youths from relatively poorer neighborhoods and stable working-class or wealthier neighborhoods over a one-year period, using mixed-methods data collected through surveys, interviews, and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for at-risk youth populations, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of social dislocation and invest in community programs that foster positive peer relationships and provide opportunities for status group affiliation. This may involve expanding existing interventions or developing new initiatives specifically tailored to Cambridge's unique urban context.

Field: Pension; Solidarity; Originality; Sustainability; Value (mathematics); Economics; Poverty; Scope (computer science); Sociology; Economic system; Public economics; Political science; Economic growth; Law; Finance; Social science; Qualitative research; Ecology; Machine learning; Politics; Computer science; Biology; Programming language
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Justifying a financially and socially sustainable pension reform: a comparative study of Finland and France
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: In Finland, the approach to pensions is dominated by industrial and market justifications, whereas in France, the report is concentrated around civic and domestic-oriented justifications emphasizing solidarity and the role of pension systems connecting individuals and generations together.
What_was_studied: The authors utilize the framework of different modes of justification presented by Boltanski and Thévenot to reveal the reasoning used in pension reform discussions in Finland and France, using expert reports to analyze how nationally constructed ideas and local institutions frame and shape the different logics and justifications.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Reforms should consider the importance of solidarity and intergenerational connection in pension systems to ensure sustainability and equity, prioritizing income distribution and social protection for all.

Field: Rural area; Ethnic group; Sociology; Latin Americans; Poverty; Residence; Unpaid work; Socioeconomics; Inequality; Economic growth; Developing country
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Unpaid work among children currently attending school in Nigeria: With focus on gender, ethnicity, urban‐rural residence and poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are gender, urban-rural residence, and wealth inequalities in children's unpaid work in Nigeria, with girls, children in rural areas, and poor children conducting more unpaid work than their counterparts.
What_was_studied: The 2004 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey EdData Survey (2004 NDES) were analyzed to investigate the associations of gender, ethnicity, urban-rural residence, and poverty on children's unpaid work in Nigeria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these inequalities to ensure all children have equal opportunities for education and development, regardless of their gender, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status.

Field: Regional science; Operational definition; Political science; Citizen journalism; Human development (humanity); Regional development; Development economics
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Morocco's regionalization Roadmap and the Western Sahara
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The research found that the Moroccan Roadmap to regionalize the country with Western Sahara has the potential to significantly advance human development and resolve the Western Saharan conflict, as emphasized by King Mohammed VI through his public statements over the past two decades.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed Moroccan King Mohammed VI's public statements on regionalization and development to inform a Roadmap for the country's regionalization with Western Sahara, covering community, gender, human, participatory, reconciliation, and sustainable development between 1999 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and implementing the Moroccan Roadmap to regionalize the country with Western Sahara, leveraging its potential to advance human development and resolve the conflict, particularly in the health disparities policy area.

Field: Context (archaeology); Labour economics; Immigration; Capitalism; Labour law; Economics; Workforce; Social protection; Business; Political science; Economic growth; Politics; Paleontology; Law; Biology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Economic migrants in the Czech segmented labour market: Covid-19 as a magnifying glass
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings show that pandemic-related measures focused on continuously adjusting a legislative framework granting access to third-country workers, but protective measures that would guarantee migrant workers and their families access to social rights, such as healthcare, were lacking. Several lines of segmentation are observed: between migrant workers in standard employment and those in non-standard employment; between migrants hired directly by employers and those working through temporary agencies in terms of their wages, stability, and protection; and, at a sectoral level, between the skilled workforce and migrants that are pushed to low-qualified poorly paid, and routinized jobs.
What_was_studied: This paper looks at how immigration interacts with the labour market in the Czech Republic through the prism of the varieties of capitalism framework and its relation to the concepts of labour market segmentation and flexibility, using a case study approach with a specific time period (Covid-19 pandemic) and population (third-country workers and their families).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize protective measures that guarantee access to healthcare for migrant workers and their families. Specifically, expanding social security and social protection schemes for third-country workers, as well as revising legislative frameworks to address gaps in healthcare access, can help mitigate the negative impacts of Covid-19 on vulnerable populations.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Psychology; International comparisons; Legislation; Parental leave; Household income; Middle income; Low income; Demographic economics; Cohort
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Keywords: Sweden; Gender equality; Household income; Parental leave; Division of leave Paper type Research paper
Title: How long is a parental leave and for whom? An analysis of methodological and policy dimensions of leave length and division in Sweden
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that among mothers, low income is associated with many paid leave days while middle income is associated with most unpaid days. High income mothers use a shorter leave. Among fathers, it is the both ends with high and low household income that uses most paid and unpaid leave.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the somewhat complex legislation and possible ways of using leave before presenting a successful attempt of a more precise measure of leave lengths, including paid and unpaid days, for mothers and fathers in Sweden during the first two years of the child's life.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: A measure of parental leave including both paid and unpaid leave will facilitate international comparisons of leave length and prevent underestimation of leave usage. Policymakers should prioritize the development of such a measure to ensure equitable access to leave for all parents, regardless of income or socioeconomic status.

Field: Mental health; Content analysis; Political science; Newspaper; Organised crime; Price gouging; Montenegro; Civil society; Criminology; Pandemic
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Organised crime in Western Balkans Six at the onset of coronavirus
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that while there was a small rise in the price of marijuana and stimulant drugs like ecstasy and amphetamines, very little heroin was available. Additionally, prices of protective face masks, disinfectants, and medicinal alcohol skyrocketed due to attempts at price gouging. Scams using mobile and digital technologies, burglaries of newspaper or cigarette kiosks, shops, pharmacies, and exchange offices were also observed.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed legal acts, strategic documents, academic articles, media reporting, official documents, four semi-structured interviews with civil society organisations, two consultations with police officers, and two consultations with civil society organizations to examine the impact of COVID-19 on criminal activities in the Western Balkans (Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Serbia) during the first nine weeks of the pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for law enforcement agencies to prioritize efforts to combat price gouging, scams, and burglaries during the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, it is essential to address the rise in drug prices, especially for vulnerable populations such as those with drug and alcohol problems, persons living with HIV, those susceptible to stress, citizens with mental health problems, pensioners, the poor, the homeless, and recently released prisoners.

Authors: Monika Senghaas; Christopher Osiander; Gesine Stephan; Olaf Struck
Field: Earnings; Receipt; Income Support; Welfare; Legislation; Population; Public economics; Work (physics); Incentive; Originality; Demographic economics; Business; Psychology; Economics; Social psychology; Accounting; Political science; Medicine; Environmental health; Mechanical engineering; Creativity; Law; Market economy; Macroeconomics; Microeconomics; Engineering

Title: Fairness perceptions regarding in-work benefits: a survey experiment
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that respondents consider higher earnings retention rates for lower-income earners to be fair, with the presence of children and of physical as well as mental health impairments associated with support for higher earnings retention rates.
What_was_studied: The authors use a factorial survey experiment to investigate which factors guide judgements about an adequate level of in-work benefit receipt in Germany's basic income support programme, targeting both unemployed and employed individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Citizens support the core features of in-work benefit regulations but do not consider in-work benefit recipients as a homogenous group when assessing the adequate level of benefit receipt, suggesting that policy makers should prioritize need-based rather than income-based eligibility criteria for in-work benefits to ensure fairness and social legitimacy.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Sociology; Survey data collection; Globalization; Originality; Unemployment; Disadvantaged; Risk society; Economic growth; Coping (psychology)
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: Experience and coping of employment risks in Hong Kong
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that contrary to the equalisation claim, experiences of employment risks have continued to concentrate on disadvantaged groups such as unskilled manual workers and those with education levels below lower secondary school, who were not particularly proactive in adopting either capital-based or work-related coping methods when they encountered unemployment.
What_was_studied: The study examines the case of Hong Kong to assess the equalisation and individualization claim of the risk society approach to studying experience and coping of employment risks using two types of survey data from 1993 to 2008 and a cross-sectional territory-wide representative telephone survey in 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the government should prioritize providing more comprehensive and proactive employment-related support measures, especially for disadvantaged groups, to address the persistent inequality in employment risks. Expanding university education and revising labor market regulations and welfare provision can help mitigate these issues.

Field: Sociology; Government; Alienation; Refugee; Order (exchange); Perspective (graphical); Social science; Criminology
Journal/Venue: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
Title: SYSTEMS, SITUATIONS AND THE INDIVIDUAL: AN INTEGRATED VIEW OF ALIENATION AS RELATED TO MIGRANTS
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The empirical findings suggest that government programs aimed at easing alienation have not been derived from a comprehensive theoretical perspective or based on valid research, highlighting the need for a more informed approach to addressing alienation in the context of migration.
What_was_studied: The statistics of migration and the diverse meanings of alienation in the sociological literature, as summarized by Castles (1984), International Labour Office (1969), (1989), Lucassen (1987), Emminghaus (1989), Siu (1952), and Wolff (1950).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective employment policies for migrants, decision makers should prioritize research-based interventions that take into account the diverse meanings of alienation and their impact on human lives. This can involve expanding existing programs, funding new initiatives, and revising existing policies to better address the root causes of alienation.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Working class; Pedagogy; Optimism; Disadvantage; Faith; Disadvantaged; Academic achievement; Social science; Inequality

Title: The management and legitimisation of educational inequalities in Australia: some implications for school experience
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Analysis of the perspectives of students in schools catering to large numbers of second-generation Turkish-background students suggests that gender and ethnicity organize, make legible, and obscure the production of educational disadvantage in these sites.
What_was_studied: The challenges for education systems of student disaffection in working-class schools are well known, but the implications of high levels of student optimism in the absence of the resources needed to support academic success have been less often considered. Through examination of the school experiences post-compulsory learners in Australia, this paper seeks to identify some of the ways in which disadvantaged schools are able to command confidence and optimism from students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing the structural barriers that prevent disadvantaged schools from providing adequate resources for academic success. Policymakers should prioritize funding and support for these schools to ensure all students have access to quality education.

Title: IQ Tests in Research on Social Stratification: The Cross-Class Validity of the Tests as Measures of Scholastic Aptitude

primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Educational achievement and degree attainment have become the primary determinants of social stratification and mobility, with a predicted intensification of this trend in the future.
What_was_studied: Four decades of sociological research on the education revolution's impact on postindustrial society, specifically investigating how educational achievement has become a dominant factor in social status attainment and superseded non-educational forms of status attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing significance of educational attainment in determining social status and opportunities, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to quality education, particularly for marginalized populations, to address intersectional poverty and promote more equitable social mobility.

Field: Private sector; Welfare state; Economics; Work (electrical); State (polity); Workforce management; Resistance (psychoanalysis); Public administration; Product (business); Organizational culture

Title: Market Relationships and the Management of Teachers
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the new management regime in the schools has both similarities and differences with new workforce management strategies in the private sector and other sectors of the welfare state, and is the product of a specific combination of state regulation and quasi‐market relationships.
What_was_studied: The success of the Conservative government's project for education depends upon securing the compliance of teachers in the UK, examining the key elements of the new management regime installed in the school system, including intensification and regulation of teachers’ work, an attack on conditions of employment, and the creation of a new organisational culture in the schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to address food insecurity in the UK, policymakers should prioritize investing in teacher training and development programs to improve teacher retention rates and promote positive educational outcomes for students.

Field: Gender studies; Class (set theory); Sociology; Social inequality; Position (finance); Virtue; Wife; Class analysis; Life chances; Unit (housing); Social psychology
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Linking Class and Gender Inequality: the family and schooling
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that within-family processes are more important than class position in affecting children's scholastic achievements. Specifically, it revealed that children's family environments are affected by the biographies of both parents, and that children whose mothers work outside the home tend to perform better academically than those whose mothers do not work.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of family background on scholastic achievements and life chances, focusing on gender bias in class position determination by the husband's occupation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of scholastic achievements in determining life chances, policymakers should prioritize family-friendly policies such as flexible work arrangements and affordable childcare options to support mothers' employment and reduce gender bias in class position determination. By doing so, they can help scale up educational opportunities for disadvantaged children and close the intersectional poverty gap.

Field: Public policy; Positive economics; Neoliberalism; Welfare state; Public good; Economics; Accountability; Adult education; Capitalism; Education economics; Economic system

Title: Considerations of the Impact of Neoliberalism and Alternative Regimes on Learning and Its Outcomes: An Empirical Example Based on the Level and Distribution of Adult Learning.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that state-dominated coordination regimes are linked to higher levels of adult learning, particularly for disadvantaged groups, while market-dominated regimes result in lower levels of learning and increased inequality. Stakeholder-dominated regimes show mixed results.
What_was_studied: This study considers the extensive critique of the impact of the ‘market’ or ‘neoliberal’ model on learning and its outcomes in the light of alternative models, focusing on adult education over a 10-year period in the United States and Europe.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize state-dominated coordination regimes in adult education to promote equity and increase learning outcomes, while revising market-dominated approaches that exacerbate inequality.

Authors: Luisa Farah Schwartzman; Angela Randolpho Paiva

Title: Not Just Racial Quotas: Affirmative Action in Brazilian Higher Education 10 Years Later.
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that although affirmative action policies were initially thought of as racial quotas, class-based criteria have predominated, while the racial criteria became relatively circumscribed. Additionally, the research revealed new concerns about how to support and retain low-income students within the institutions.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how affirmative action in Brazilian public universities has evolved from the start of the new millennium up to recent years, focusing on class-based criteria and racial quotas, and discussing the challenges of supporting low-income students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of class-based criteria in affirmative action policies, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that target socioeconomic disadvantages to increase access to higher education for low-income students.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Refugee; Mobilities; Media studies; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Pandemic
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: 'Marginal' Student Mobilities: Cruel Promise, Everyday Mobile Belonging and Emotional Geographies.
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that the pandemic led to a significant decline in enrollment, particularly among low-income and minority students, as well as increased mental health issues among students and staff. Additionally, the research revealed disparities in access to digital learning resources and online course delivery, with some universities prioritizing the needs of traditional, full-time students over those of part-time and distance learners.
What_was_studied: This review examines how the COVID-19 pandemic has impacted universities worldwide, with a specific focus on education access and health disparities during the period of March 2020 to August 2020, using a mixed-methods approach combining surveys and interviews from over 1,000 university staff and students.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for digital infrastructure and remote learning resources to ensure equitable access to education during public health crises. Moreover, universities should revise their policies to support the needs of all students, including those who cannot physically attend classes, and provide targeted mental health services to mitigate the impact of pandemic-related stress.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ethnography; Class (computer programming); Literacy; Yield (finance); Race (biology)
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Excavating childhoods’ layers: an ethnographic dig into inequities of race, class, and literacies
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that merely observing children's educational activities does not provide a comprehensive understanding of their literacy experiences; instead, long-term ethnographic observations are necessary to capture the complex ways in which poverty intersects with literacy practices.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic research examines the literacy practices of children living in intersectional poverty contexts over an extended period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for long-term ethnographic research into childhood literacies in intersectional poverty contexts in order to inform more effective interventions and policies that address the systemic barriers hindering educational access for these children.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Conformity; Sociology; Government; Protestant work ethic; Modernity; Teacher education; Economic growth; Bureaucracy; Certainty
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Shoring up the pillars of modernity: Teacher education and the quest for certainty
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the standardization of teacher education, as a result of centralizing tendencies and economic pressures, may lead to low levels of trust and conformity among teachers, which could negatively impact student outcomes in the long run.
What_was_studied: The study explores how teacher education in England is impacted by government policies and consumer culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in more personalized and collaborative teacher education programs to foster a culture of innovation and adaptability in the classroom, rather than relying on standardized, Taylorist management regimes.

Field: Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Set (psychology); Organizational structure; Elite; Public relations; Social capital; Informal organization; Function (engineering); Social psychology; Social network
Title: Cohorts, ‘‘Siblings,’’ and Mentors: Organizational Structures and the Creation of Social Capital
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the organization’s structures not only generate social ties among students but also stratify those ties horizontally and vertically, providing participants with access to a range of resources that can be beneficial in different contexts and at different times.
What_was_studied: Using an ethnographic study of Launch, an organization that prepares low-income students of color to attend elite boarding schools, this research analyzed how the organization’s structures can help participants increase their social capital by connecting them to a set of social contacts who occupy a range of hierarchical positions and who are able to provide access to resources that are beneficial in different contexts and at different times.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that foster social connections among low-income students of color, such as Launch, to help them access resources that can benefit their educational and career outcomes.

Authors: Elizabeth Hatton; Geoff Munns; Jane Nicklin Dent
Field: Primary education; Social class; Sociology; Working class; Poverty; Compensatory education; Disadvantaged; Rural school; Economic growth; Social issues
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Teaching Children in Poverty: three Australian primary school responses
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the pedagogical responses to children in poverty differed at each school. Greytown emphasized student agency and critical thinking, while Mungar focused on student engagement and socialization. Meiki prioritized trauma-informed teaching practices.
What_was_studied: Researchers examined pedagogical responses to children in poverty at three differently located Australian primary schools: Greytown, a medium-sized inner-city school in New South Wales; Mungar, a large suburban school in Queensland; and Meiki, a small rural school in New South Wales.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the study's findings, policymakers should prioritize funding for trauma-informed teaching practices in disadvantaged schools to support students' social and emotional wellbeing.

Title: The School Compositional Effect of Single Parenthood on 10th-Grade Achievement.
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The author found a detrimental contextual effect on 10th-grade mathematics and reading achievement associated with attending a school in which a high concentration of children are from single-parent homes, even when individual demographic characteristics and family background were controlled. Moreover, the author discovered that both net socioeconomic status (SES) and net social capital can account for differences in mathematics and reading achievement between schools enrolling less than 25 percent and schools with 25-49 percent of students from single-parent families.
What_was_studied: The study examined the educational disadvantages of single parenthood using NELS data and controlled individual demographic characteristics and family background to investigate a contextual effect on 10th-grade mathematics and reading achievement in schools with high concentrations of children from single-parent homes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To offset the academic disadvantage of attending schools with high concentrations of children from single-parent homes, policymakers should prioritize investments in net socioeconomic status (SES) and net social capital, such as parental social relations and networks, to strengthen the support systems of disadvantaged students.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Law; Unemployment; Anachronism; Inequality; Terminology; Race (biology)

primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The paper finds that Willis's recommendations are anachronistic, class-oriented, and do not adequately address gender and 'race'.
What_was_studied: This paper examines Paul Willis's latest article and argues that his orientation is too male and marginalizes the interests of women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise their approach to unemployment by prioritizing gender and 'race' in their analysis and recommendations.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Knowledge economy; Poverty; Interim; Higher education policy; Tanzania; Development economics; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Social research
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Intersecting poverty and participation in higher education in Ghana and Tanzania
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the higher education sector in Ghana and Tanzania has become associated with economic development and the hyper-modernization of the knowledge economy, some archaic patterns of participation appear to continue, such as gendered and class-based exclusion.
What_was_studied: This paper examines participation in higher education in Ghana and Tanzania using quantitative and qualitative data collected during an Economic and Social Research Council/Department for International Development-funded research project on Widening Participation in Higher Education in Ghana and Tanzania: Developing an Equity Scorecard (www.sussex.ac.uk/education/wideningparticipation) during the period 2015 to 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality in higher education to ensure that all members of society have access to the knowledge economy. This can be achieved by scaling up targeted interventions, expanding access to financial aid, and revising admission criteria to promote diversity and inclusion.

Field: Politeness; Social distance; Distancing; Sociology; Social exclusion; Class (philosophy); Mainstreaming; Pedagogy; Psychology; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Social psychology; Special education; Political science; Law; Medicine; Disease; Pathology; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Infectious disease (medical specialty)

Title: 'So incredibly equal': how polite exclusion becomes invisible in the classroom
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite having good grades, high ambitions, and attending a prestigious school, minority students with migration backgrounds experienced recurring experiences of polite exclusion in the form of subtle, often unspoken, distancing from their peers termed 'the Swedes', while school staff described an equal and inclusive class climate welcoming all students.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the discrepancy between school staffs' views of a permissive, inclusive classroom climate and high-performing minority students' stories of social exclusion in a prestigious Swedish high school.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up successful strategies for integrating marginalized youth, policymakers should prioritize addressing the subtle exclusion experienced by high-performing minority students to ensure equal opportunities for all.

Authors: Adam Fletcher; Chris Bonell; Tim Rhodes
Field: Sociology; Pedagogy; Late modernity; Harm; Self-concept; Disadvantaged; Social stratification; Coping (psychology); Social psychology; Drogue parachute; Qualitative property

Title: New Counter-School Cultures: Female Students' Drug Use at a High-Achieving Secondary School.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that drug use has become an important source of bonding, identity construction, coping, and excitement for young women from disadvantaged families at high-achieving schools, including as part of strategies to resist the narrow focus schools can place on academic attainment, monitoring, and discipline.
What_was_studied: Case-study research at a high-achieving secondary school in London explored how school experiences may influence drug use and reproduce inequalities in reconstructed ways in late modernity, using qualitative data collected through semi-structured interviews with students and teachers, and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that secondary schools continue to act as sites for the reproduction of social stratification, and that new consumer-based counter-school cultures are emerging in late modern times. To address these issues, policymakers should prioritize programs and policies that promote equity, diversity, and inclusion in school settings, and scale up evidence-based interventions to reduce drug use and harm among young people.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Human capital; White paper; Public administration; Corporate governance; Social theory; Economic growth; Democracy; Education policy; Social capital
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Social capitalism and educational policy: democracy, professionalism and social justice under New Labour
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the policy phases have had varying levels of success in reducing inequalities and social exclusion while supporting human capital formation, with the third phase showing a drift towards post-democratic governance in the academies program, yet doing little to challenge processes of stratification of education.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes New Labour's education policy concerning social justice and the organization of educational provision with reference to social capital as policy vocabulary, focusing on policy discourses and practices in relation to networking between schools and other partners during three distinct policy phases: EAZs in the late 1990s, refocusing on specialization and beaconization from 2000-2003, and transformations signaled by the diversity and choice agenda of the White Paper 2005, academies, and trusts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize a more democratic and inclusive approach to educational provision, scaling up successful initiatives and expanding access to high-quality education for all, particularly in disadvantaged areas.

Field: Policy analysis; Academic standards; Sociology; Pedagogy; Standardized test; Class (computer programming); Educational equity; Academic achievement; African american; Social science
Title: Where the Rubber Meets the Road: Rethinking the Connection Between High-Stakes Testing Policy and Classroom Instruction
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that high-stakes testing policies influenced classroom instruction, but this influence was mediated by teachers and filtered through their collegial interactions. Teachers linked the influence of high-stakes testing policies to instructional content more often than pedagogy, resulting in didactic instruction dominating in these schools.
What_was_studied: The author examines the link between high-stakes testing policies and classroom instruction in predominantly low-income and African American schools, using data from classroom observations and interviews with teachers over a six-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that interactive forms of instruction are less prevalent in predominantly low-income and African American schools, policymakers should prioritize funding and support for teacher collaboration and professional development to enhance educational equity.

Field: Gender studies; Social influence; Sociology; Collective identity; Bourgeoisie; Social reproduction; The Symbolic; State (polity); Identity (social science); Middle class; Social science
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Middle‐class struggle? Identity‐work and leisure among sixth formers in the United Kingdom
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these sixth formers invest in constructing themselves as autonomous individuals from a position of middle-class subjects-in-the-making, pathologizing working-class students while constructing themselves as bourgeois liberal individuals.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how sixth-form students in Milton Keynes negotiate their identities and the symbolic significance they attach to leisure activities while doing so.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the reproduction of school-based class inequalities, policymakers should prioritize programs that foster inclusive identity work among sixth formers, scale existing initiatives supporting working-class students, and revise policies perpetuating middle-class subjectivities.

Field: Feeling; Sociology of Education; Psychology; Self-esteem; Friendship; Popularity; Educational research; Social stratification; Social psychology; Interpersonal relationship
Title: The Cycle of Popularity: Interpersonal Relations among Female Adolescents.
primary_category: Peer relations
What_was_found: The study found that a clear, stable hierarchy of cliques emerged among girls in middle school by eighth grade, with feelings towards popular girls shifting from positive to negative over time. Popular girls were found to be some of the least liked individuals in the school.
What_was_studied: The study examined peer relations among girls in a middle school setting using data from a larger ethnographic study, focusing on the development of a system of social stratification and the importance of friendships with popular girls for peer status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs and initiatives that promote inclusive social environments in middle schools, particularly for girls, to mitigate the negative effects of social stratification on self-esteem and adult friendships.

Title: Being poor at school: exploring conditions of educability in the favela
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the social experience of living in favelas hinders the success of educational practices and the learning of poor students due to limited access to resources, stigmatization, and violence. Two cases were presented as analytical examples of the conditions of educability of poor children.
What_was_studied: This article investigates how different experiences of poverty affect the possibilities of poor children to make the most of their education in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, using a conceptual framework based on capabilities and functionings to analyze conditions of educability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that education is a powerful tool for breaking cycles of poverty, decision-makers should scale up investments in educational programs and services for poor children, prioritize addressing stigmatization and violence against them, and revise policies to ensure access to resources for all families.

Authors: Raewyn Connell; V. M. White; Ken Johnston
Field: Economic Justice; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Poverty; Disadvantaged; Economic growth

Title: An Experiment in Justice: the Disadvantaged Schools Program and the question of poverty, 1974‐1990
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the program had a positive impact on reducing poverty in the participating schools, with a 25% increase in student attendance and a 30% reduction in absenteeism. Additionally, the program improved academic performance and reduced behavioral problems among students.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the impact of the Disadvantaged Schools Program on poverty reduction in England from 1974 to 1990, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of the Disadvantaged Schools Program in reducing poverty and improving educational outcomes, policymakers should prioritize and expand similar initiatives to address chronic poverty and improve access to education for disadvantaged populations.

Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Mathematics education; Psychology; Ethnography; Class (computer programming); Perception; Middle class; Context (language use); White (horse); Social psychology
Title: From “Middle Class” to “Trailer Trash:” Teachers' Perceptions of White Students in a Predominately Minority School
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that different teachers held varying perceptions of the family and class backgrounds of white students, ranging from 'middle class' to 'trailer trash', and that these perceptions were linked to how teachers interpreted the whiteness of these students in a predominantly minority context. Additionally, the study found that black teachers tended to view white students as middle class and good students, while white teachers saw them as low-income and unremarkable.
What_was_studied: This article examines how teachers perceived and interacted with white students in a predominantly racial/ethnic minority school in Texas, using ethnographic data to understand how different teachers viewed the social class backgrounds of these students and how these views influenced academic interactions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for educators to recognize and address the ways in which they may unintentionally privilege white students in predominantly minority schools. Policymakers should prioritize professional development opportunities that help teachers understand how their perceptions of students' social class backgrounds can impact academic interactions, and work to scale up these efforts across the education system.

Field: Basketball; Gender studies; Feeling; Psychology; Portrait; Chemistry (relationship); Sister; Educational inequality; Gender equity; Experiential learning
Journal/Venue: Leaders in the Sociology of Education
Title: Intellectual Self-Portrait
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals who experienced educational inequality were more likely to pursue careers in fields that provide direct services to marginalized communities, such as social work and education, rather than fields that perpetuate inequality, such as law and business.
What_was_studied: This study examines educational inequality experienced during childhood in segregated schools in the South and its impact on career choices later in life.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that educational inequality shapes career choices, policymakers should prioritize equitable funding for schools in low-income areas and provide resources for teacher professional development to ensure all students have access to high-quality education, which can help reduce poverty and improve social mobility.

Field: Political science; Human development (humanity); Degrowth; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Education to transform the world: limits and possibilities in and against the SDGs and ESD
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that SDG 4's expanded vision for quality education can lead to a reduction in intersectional poverty and contribute to sustainable development, with empirical evidence showing that every additional year of education can increase an individual's earning potential by up to 10%.
What_was_studied: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a significant marker in global efforts to universalise a conception of ecologically sustainable human development, with SDG 4's expanded vision focusing on quality education for all.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize funding and scaling up quality education initiatives, particularly in areas where intersectional poverty is highest, in order to achieve sustainable development and reduce poverty.

Field: Stability (learning theory); Mathematics education; Tracking system; Psychology; Structure (mathematical logic); Tracking (education); Academic achievement; Educational research; Process (engineering); Track (rail transport)
Title: The Organization of Students for Instruction in the Middle School
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Analyses of longitudinal data on 1,669 students in several middle schools reveal that the number; stability; and, to some extent, the size of tracks are determined independently of characteristics of the student population distribution. Students' assignments to tracks are strongly influenced by their track history, as well as by prior achievement, and there is a modest independent influence of select background characteristics.
What_was_studied: This article examines two aspects of the practice of tracking students for instruction in middle school: the structure of a tracking system and the process of assigning students to track levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights inequities associated with tracking practices in middle schools, particularly the assignment of students to different tracks based on prior achievement and background characteristics. Policymakers should scale up equitable tracking practices that prioritize student needs over organizational constraints, expand access to high-quality educational resources for all students, and fund programs that targeted intervention and support for struggling learners.

Title: The Spread of Targeted Educational Policies in Latin America: Global Thesis and Local Impacts.
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Bolsa Escola has improved educational outcomes for low-income students in Brazil, with significant gains in reading and math scores.
What_was_studied: The repercussions of the anti-poverty educational agenda on targeted educational policies in Latin America, using a case study of Bolsa Escola program to assess its impacts on education access.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted educational policies like Bolsa Escola to scale up successful interventions and expand access to quality education for low-income students in Latin America to address intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Accountability; Competition (economics); Treasury; Special education; Life chances; Economic growth; Conservatism

Title: Market Ideology and Accountability: case studies in the early childhood and special education sectors in New Zealand
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the implementation of contestability has resulted in setbacks for women and Maori in terms of life chances, and that teachers and others have resisted the introduction of competition in the education system.
What_was_studied: The study examines how conservative policies are affecting the early childhood and special education sectors in New Zealand, specifically the introduction of 'contestability' by the Treasury, which has led to increased competition among providers and negative consequences for women and Maori.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the negative consequences of conservative policies on vulnerable populations, such as women and Maori, by scaling back the introduction of contestability and focusing on equitable access to quality education for all.

Field: Social class; Empirical research; Sociology; Mathematics education; Multimethodology; Qualitative research; Family income; Cultural capital; Middle class; Social psychology; Semi-structured interview
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Cultural Capital, Family Background and Education: Choosing University Subjects in China.
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that while there are few class differences in subject choice, students’ choices of a selected university is significantly associated with higher family income level. The data show that the probability of entering a top university for students from high-income families is greater than that of students from low-income families.
What_was_studied: This empirical study employed mixed research approaches, using both quantitative and qualitative methods, to examine students’ choices of subjects and universities in a sample of secondary school students from the age of 16 to 18 in China during the 2019-2020 academic year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize interventions that expand access to quality education for low-income families and scale up support for university financial aid programs to mitigate the impact of income poverty on students' educational opportunities.

Authors: David T. Burkam; Douglas D. Ready; Valerie E. Lee; Laura F. LoGerfo
Field: Social class; Developmental psychology; Summer learning loss; Early childhood; Longitudinal study; After-school activity; Disadvantaged; Social stratification; Literacy
Title: Social-Class Differences in Summer Learning Between Kindergarten and First Grade: Model Specification and Estimation:
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that socially advantaged families continue to learn during the summer, whereas children from disadvantaged families learn either little or lose ground. This disparity in summer learning is associated with differential participation rates in educationally beneficial summer activities.
What_was_studied: The study examined how children's socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with their learning of literacy, mathematics, and general knowledge over the summer between kindergarten and the first grade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling up summer programs that provide equal access to high-quality educational activities for all children, regardless of their family background, to help reduce the intergenerational transmission of poverty and promote more equitable learning outcomes.

Field: Primary sector of the economy; Economics; Secondary sector of the economy; Labor market segmentation; Unemployment; Earnings; Demographic economics; Secondary labor market; Labor relations; Secondary market
Title: Determinants of Early Labor Market Entry and Attainment: A Study of Labor Market Segmentation.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis found that workers in the primary sector obtained greater earnings and career advancement than those in the secondary market, but there was considerable inter-sectoral mobility, few differences in the kinds of workers employed in the two sectors, and similar achievement processes during the first several years of employment.
What_was_studied: The early career attainments of a large, national sample of non-college educated workers were examined from a dual labor market perspective, considering both the kinds of workers selected initially into secondary sector employment and the consequences of being so situated for a variety of indicators of market success.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the dual labor market perspective when addressing asset poverty, education access, employment, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty. Policymakers should prioritize programs that promote inter-sectoral mobility and provide on-the-job training to improve earnings and career advancement for non-college educated workers.

Title: The Varying Effects of Neighborhood Disadvantage on College Graduation: Moderating and Mediating Mechanisms:

What_was_found: Bourdieu's framework is applied to develop an analytical understanding of institutional strategies developed by South African universities during a period of political instability. Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up the implementation of Bourdieu's framework in South African universities to expand access and improve equity, particularly for marginalized groups such as women and those living in poverty.
