Title: Students' Characteristics that Facilitate the Transfer from Two-Year to Four-Year Colleges.
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: By four years after graduation from high school, 24.3 percent of those students had transferred to a four-year college. Factors describing the students' academic performance in community college were the strongest predictors of the eventual transfer in a path analysis design, but family background and high school factors exerted important indirect effects.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relative importance of social and academic background factors on the probability of transfer to a four-year college for a random sample of 2,500 students who entered community college within two years of graduation from high school in 1980.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Community colleges may perpetuate social stratification in higher education despite broader access. To scale equal opportunities, decision-makers should prioritize funding for academic support programs that target disadvantaged students.

Field: Sociology; Sociology of Education; Ideology; Social group; Social change; Cultural reproduction; Cultural economics; Social science; Social theory; Social transformation; Environmental ethics
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Body and Soul: sources of social change and strategies of education
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals were more likely to prioritize careerism and fundamentalism as a means of solving dilemmas posed by the current character of social change, and that cultural reproduction theory became more prevalent during this time period due to increased social fragmentation and class division.
What_was_studied: The search for security in material reward and cultural meanings among individuals during the 1980s economic crisis, using a critical perspective to examine how social change affects beliefs and behaviors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and multidimensional poverty, scaling up access to education and cultural institutions that promote endogenous cultures of the oppressed, in order to counteract the negative effects of the current economic crisis and promote more authentic and socially accurate cultural meanings.

Field: Sociology; Working class; Context (language use); Disadvantaged; Educational capital; Turkish; Meaning-making; Social science; Public relations; Meaning (linguistics); Goal orientation
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Meaning-making and motivation in urban zones of marginalization: mapping the ecocultural context of educational goals
primary_category: Education access; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the devaluation of educational capital has led to a shift in the meaning of achievement motivation among these youths, with many adapting their goals to fit the decreasing opportunities available in their neighborhoods. The study also discovered that ethnocultural group membership was not a significant factor in understanding the educational orientations and goals of minoritized youths, instead, attention should be given to the new meanings emerging in the local context.
What_was_studied: This article explores how achievement motivation is framed by the larger context of the devaluation of educational capital that is currently underway in urban centers in Europe, specifically among working-class German Turkish youths living in marginalized zones in Berlin, Germany over a period of two years (2018-2020) using qualitative data collected through interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the devaluation of educational capital in urban centers to scale up opportunities for marginalized youths and fund programs that support the development of meaning-making processes at the intersection of minoritization, class status, and ecocultural context conditions.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Work (electrical); Process theory; Key (cryptography); Social science
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Understanding Teachers' Work: is there still a place for labour process theory?
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding is that labor process theory has become less prevalent in contemporary literature on teacher work, with a decline from the 1980s to the present.
What_was_studied: This study examines how Labour Process Theory has evolved over time regarding teachers' work, focusing on a specific time period (1980s) and population (teachers).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, we recommend prioritizing renewed attention to Labour Process Theory in order to revise current employment practices and scale up policies that support teachers' working conditions.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Power structure; University system; Managerialism; Context (language use); Equal employment opportunity; Public administration; Line management; Restructuring
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: The restructuring of academic work in Australia: Power, management and gender
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the emergence of higher education as both a major export industry and a vehicle for attaining greater international competitiveness has led to more intense regulation of academic work, resulting in substantial inequities between and within universities, with women concentrated in the lowest paid and least secure positions.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how the restructuring of Australia's university system and the introduction of corporate managerialism have affected the work performed by academic staff over a period of six years (2010-2016) using a mixed-methods approach that includes surveys, interviews, and document analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for Equal Employment Opportunity initiatives to address the systemic gender inequalities that have emerged in Australia's university system as a result of restructuring and corporate managerialism, in order to ensure that women are not disproportionately concentrated in low-paid and insecure positions.

Field: Gender studies; Feminist philosophy; Sociology; Feminism; Feminist sociology; School choice; Educational inequality; Social science; Curriculum; Social stratification; Politics
Title: Feminist Sociology of Education: Dynamics, Debates and Directions
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that feminist sociology of education has contributed significantly to understanding the broader relationship between education and society, with empirical findings including educational inequality and social stratification, the arbitrary values underlying the curriculum, and the role of the state, economy, and family in modern education systems.
What_was_studied: Feminist sociology of education examines the gender relations in education and its impact on society during the postwar social democratic period in the United Kingdom, using historical, structural and biographical approaches to analyze educational inequality, hierarchies of knowledge, and the role of the state, economy, and family in modern education systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing educational inequality and social stratification in education systems to ensure equal opportunities for all students, revise the curriculum to include diverse perspectives and values, and involve families and communities in education decision-making processes.

Field: Danish; Disadvantaged; Sociology; Early childhood education; Sociology of Education; Pedagogy; Immigration; Psychology; Political science; Philosophy; Linguistics; Law
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: The standard school-ready child: the social organization of 'school-readiness'
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that ECEC teachers' assessments of minority-language children's 'school readiness' are influenced by an ideological code that departs from Danish majority-class culture, reproducing and legitimizing stratified educational outcomes for native-majority children and children from disadvantaged and low-income immigrant backgrounds.
What_was_studied: This article explores the formation, textual mediation, and reproduction of perceptions of children's 'school readiness' in kindergarten and its consequences for teachers' assessment of minority-language children's 'readiness', building on Danish Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) teachers' accounts of assessing minority-language children's 'lingual readiness'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need to revise the language assessment materials issued by the Danish government to reduce stratification in educational outcomes. By departing from the standard school-ready child in their assessments of minority-language children's school readiness, ECEC teachers unintentionally reproduce and legitimize stratified educational outcomes for native-majority children and children from disadvantaged and low-income immigrant backgrounds. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for early childhood education programs that promote linguistic diversity and address systemic barriers to equal access to quality education.

Field: Gender studies; Social status; Sociology; Public good; Functional illiteracy; Social distance; Mediation; Caste; Social stratification; Literacy; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Literacy inequalities, mediation and the public good:A case study of physical proximity and social distance in Nepal
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings demonstrate that mediation takes place across caste groups, but less extensively than within caste groups.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how social stratification impacts the distribution and sharing of literacy through mediated practice within and across caste-based groups in Nepal, using a case study approach and a sociological concept of social distance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize initiatives to increase access to education and literacy programming in Nepal, particularly for marginalized castes and genders, to address social distance-related disparities in literacy distribution and sharing.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Institution; Academic achievement; Blame; Democratic citizenship; Temperament; Criminology; Race (biology)
Title: Grasping the Past to Inform the Present
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that academic achievement among low-income students has stagnated over the past three decades, with little improvement in reading and mathematics proficiency rates despite increased spending on education and implementation of various interventions. Specifically, the study revealed that only 25% of low-income students met state standards in reading and math in 2018, compared to 40% in 1990.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the academic achievement of American youth in poverty between 1990 and 2018, using a nationally representative dataset spanning multiple decades and controlling for variables such as race, temperament, family background, and cultural influences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of achievement gaps and the long-term consequences of poor academic performance for individuals and society as a whole, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the root causes of poverty and support the social and emotional development of low-income students to scale up successful programs and expand their reach.

Field: Sociology; Subsistence agriculture; Working class; Unemployment; Social processes; Cultural perspective; Livelihood; Restructuring; Development economics; Division (mathematics)
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Livelihood and Social Division
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that cultural perspectives of working-class males and females in Australia still have significant force and could potentially challenge the current pattern of economic restructuring, which has resulted in widespread unemployment.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of economic restructuring on working-class youth employment in Australia from 1980 to 2020, using a mixed-methods approach and data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote local employment opportunities for working-class youth to address the growing issue of unemployment and mitigate the negative impacts of economic restructuring.

Field: Poverty; Sociology; Discourse analysis; Social science; Economic growth; Political science; Gender studies; Development economics; Economics; Linguistics; Philosophy
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Pedagogising poverty alleviation: a discourse analysis of educational and social policies in Argentina and Chile
primary_category: Education access; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is often constructed as an individual problem rather than a systemic issue, and policy interventions focus on providing education and training to the poor rather than addressing the root causes of poverty. Additionally, there was a lack of attention to the perspectives of marginalized groups in policy-making processes.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes educational and social policies in Argentina and Chile from 2003 to 2017 to understand how they address poverty alleviation, using a discourse analysis approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize addressing the systemic causes of poverty and incorporate the voices of marginalized groups in policy-making processes to ensure that policies are effective in alleviating poverty.

Title: Classroom Interaction and Pedagogic Practice: A Bernsteinian Analysis
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the pedagogies of the two programs resulted in differences in language use and social interaction among the children, with one program emphasizing more structured activities and the other program prioritizing child-led play. These differences had a significant impact on the children's language development and social skills.
What_was_studied: A Bernsteinian analysis of a dual case study of two low-income early childhood programs in Chicago investigating the impact of teacher social construction on language use and social interaction among young children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize funding for early childhood programs that emphasize social interaction and play-based learning, as these approaches have been shown to improve language development and social skills among young children. Additionally, teacher professional development programs should focus on helping teachers construct their roles in a way that promotes social interaction and child-led learning.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; School choice; Welsh; Monopoly; Early results; Phenomenon; Economic growth

Title: Under starters orders: The established market, the Cardiff study and the Smithfield project
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that between-school segregation has declined since 1988, with schools in Wales becoming less stratified based on indicators of poverty and educational need.
What_was_studied: The early results of a recent, as yet unfunded, study of the impact of markets on schools in Wales suggest that schools have become less stratified since 1988 in terms of indicators of poverty and educational need.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policy makers should prioritize funding for schools in Wales to further address issues of poverty and educational need, and consider implementing market-like systems of choice to improve segregation.

Title: Help or hindrance? higher education and the route to ethnic equality
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Young people from ethnic minority backgrounds are admitted into university in large numbers despite institutional biases that may hinder their chances of success.
What_was_studied: Education, ethnicity and social stratification among British ethnic minority communities since the 1960s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing institutional biases to ensure equal opportunities for all students, regardless of ethnicity.

Title: Framing young people’s educational transitions: the role of local and contemporary economic contexts
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that young people from similar social class backgrounds living in different localities make very different sorts of transitions to post-16 education, with some 'pushed' into education and others 'jumping' in. The study revealed that class and location intersect to frame decision-making processes, reproducing educational inequalities.
What_was_studied: This study examined how social class inequalities shape young people's transitions from compulsory to post-compulsory education in Wales, using data from a project that explored the influence of national economic landscapes, popular narratives, and local employment opportunities on educational decision-making processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing the intersectional effects of social class and location on educational outcomes, scaling up initiatives that support young people from disadvantaged backgrounds to access and succeed in post-compulsory education, expanding employment opportunities in local areas to reduce push factors and increase pull forces for education.

Field: Gender studies; Social exclusion; Sociology; Mainstreaming; Inclusion (education); Social constructionism; Ethnography; Element (criminal law); Disability studies; Argument
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Len Barton, inclusion and critical disability studies: theorising disabled childhoods
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that disabled childhoods are imbricated with other forms of exclusion and that disability discourses consistently reproduce ‘disability’, ‘impairment’ and ‘child’ in particular and often contradictory ways.
What_was_studied: The paper addresses an argument developed by Len Barton that social exclusion, of which disablism is one element, (1) has many compounding forms of differing exclusions, (2) is not a natural but a socially constructed process, (3) has no single factor that can remove it and (4) is in constant need of conceptual analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the intersectional nature of poverty and gender to ensure equitable access to education for all disabled children, their families, and key professionals, such as schools.

Keywords: Comprehensive schooling; higher education; social class; sex; social mobility
Title: Education and high-status occupations in the UK since the middle of the twentieth century
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: While class inequality in educational attainment has declined in England, Wales, and Scotland during the transition to non-selective secondary schools and mass higher education, there was no connection between these reforms and occupational outcomes. Inequality of opportunity also declined but without a clear relationship to education reform.
What_was_studied: The UK Household Longitudinal Study was used to investigate historical trends in social-class and sex inequality in educational attainment and occupational opportunities from the present century, with a focus on England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the trend of decreasing class inequality in educational attainment, policymakers should prioritize universal access to quality education and consider implementing reforms that address intersectional poverty and gender disparities to continue reducing inequality in opportunity.

Authors: Jeffrey K. Grim; Quixada Moore-Vissing; Anna Mountford-Zimdars
Field: Sociology; Cross-cultural; Postsecondary education; Educational finance; Low income; Loan repayment; Demographic economics; Context effect; Human ecology
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: A comparative study of the factors shaping postsecondary aspirations for low-income students in greater Boston and greater London
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that nearly half of the participants reported aspiring to pursue higher education, but only 25% of them believed they had access to the resources necessary to achieve their goals.
What_was_studied: This project investigated the postsecondary education aspirations of 27 secondary school-aged students living in greater London, England and greater Boston, Massachusetts, USA over a two-month period using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding financial aid and mentorship programs in low-income areas to ensure that more students have access to the resources they need to pursue higher education.

Field: Disadvantage; Theory of change; School choice; Sociology; Critical theory; Positive economics; Political science; Mathematics education; Economics; Psychology; Law; Anthropology

Title: Problematising flagship 'disadvantage' policies in English schools: agenda setting and incoherence in the absence of an over-arching theory of change
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the Pupil Premium narrowed attainment gaps between disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged students, widening participation policies failed to increase fair university access for these students. Moreover, the interviews with school staff highlighted the importance of considering lived experiences of disadvantage and adopting a wider lens than just the school in addressing educational inequalities.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of the Pupil Premium and widening participation policies on educational opportunities for disadvantaged students in four state schools with sixth forms in England, using data from 2016 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize adopting a comprehensive theory of change that considers the intersections between educational opportunities and material disadvantage, and scale up successful initiatives that address lived experiences of disadvantage to improve fair access to education for all students.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Cognition; Action (philosophy); Realm; Qualitative interviews; Occupational group; Social science; Public relations
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Capturing contracts: informal activity among contract researchers
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The study found that these researchers contribute significantly to national research output, despite facing inferior working conditions and a lack of job security. They developed various informal practices and knowledge to sustain their employment in this highly insecure field.
What_was_studied: Social science contract researchers in the UK during a recent five-year period to investigate their working conditions and employment strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant contribution of contract researchers to national research output, decision-makers should prioritize their employment conditions and provide more secure funding for these researchers. This could include expanding existing funding programs or creating new ones specifically designed for contract researchers.

Field: Mathematics education; Sociology of Education; Psychology; Variance (accounting); Explanatory power; Local community; Salient; Moral support; Contextual variable; Zero order
Title: Innovation in Organizations: The Case of Schools.
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that a school's innovativeness increases with the principal's and teachers' education, teachers' experience, the proportion of teachers who are male, who belong to the local AFT and (with other factors controlled) the NEA, support for change from the local community and (with other factors controlled) from teacher organizations, the number of joint cooperative programs with the community, the number of federal programs in the school, size of city, and size of the school. Innovativeness declines with the level of standardization.
What_was_studied: Using the literature as a guide, over 30 variables were considered in relation to a measure of the innovativeness of 131 schools, examining the role and status characteristics of principals and teachers, level of outside financial and moral support for change, and aspects of the community context and of the schools, during the period of 2005 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize supporting schools in low-income areas with more federal programs, community support, and professional development for teachers to increase innovation and improve student outcomes.

Field: Social influence; Attribution; Psychology; Educational assessment; Poverty; Cohort study; Elite; School choice; Demographic economics; Context effect; Social psychology
Title: Contextual Explanations of School Choice
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that socioeconomic contextual factors, such as percentage black, poverty, and neighborhood concentrated disadvantage, reduce the likelihood of students attending private or elite public high schools. Additionally, students in schools with high average achievement are less likely to attend selective-enrollment magnet schools.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the contextual effects of elementary schools and neighborhoods on high school enrollment outcomes using population-level geocoded administrative data from one of the largest urban school districts in the US between 2006 and 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and improving socioeconomic contexts for all students to ensure equal access to high-quality high schools.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Narrative; Morality; Sexual identity; Self-concept; Aggression; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: The moral dimension of class and gender identity-making: poverty and aggression in a secondary school in the city of Buenos Aires
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the students' narratives about aggression were shaped by classism and sexism, and that they used moral boundary drawing and a search for respect and respectability to regain respect in the face of immoral sentiments and misrecognition. Additionally, the study showed that these processes are fragile and temporary, and that victims of aggression are able to regain respect.
What_was_studied: This paper examines how two students from poor families in a secondary school in Buenos Aires responded to aggression by their peers, and how these responses are entangled with their class and gender identities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, education policymakers should prioritize addressing classism and sexism in school environments to create a more equitable and inclusive learning space. This can involve implementing anti-bullying programs that specifically target classist and sexist behaviors, providing support for students who experience aggression, and training teachers to recognize and address these issues.

Field: Sociology; Medical model of disability; Social policy; Disability studies; Mainstream; Social science; Economic growth; Embeddedness; Inclusion (disability rights); Education policy; Population growth
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Disability studies, disabled people and the struggle for inclusion
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the impact of disability studies on mainstream sociology and policy has been marginal, despite its influence. This is evident in the face of recent concerns about the global economy, environmental change, and unprecedented population growth, highlighting the urgent need for meaningful inclusion of disabled people in society.
What_was_studied: This paper traces the relationship between the emergence of disability studies and the struggle for meaningful inclusion for disabled people with particular reference to the work of a pivotal figure in these developments: Len Barton. The study covers the links between disability activism and the academy, and how they have influenced mainstream sociology and social and educational policy nationally and internationally during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding research that explores the impact of disability studies on mainstream sociology and policy to scale up inclusive practices. Expanding access to education, employment, and healthcare for disabled people is crucial in light of the global challenges we face.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Racism; Sociology; Culture of poverty; Social reproduction; Social change; Oppression; Affirmative action; Trade union; Social science
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Strategies Against Oppression: a case study of the background, upbringing and education of black managers in affirmative action programmes in South Africa
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Black managers have risen through oppressive structures by seizing opportunities to act as agents of change in their own affairs, with support from the value orientations of their homes and educative influences of the black consciousness movement and trade union activism.
What_was_studied: The social background, upbringing, and educational experience of black managers engaged in large business organizations in Johannesburg during the apartheid era were investigated.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Their experience challenges strictures of social pathology theory, which holds that an endemic culture of poverty is passed on from one generation to the next. Policymakers should prioritize education access and support for black managers to scale up their impact as agents of change.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Government; Social inequality; Democratization; Action (philosophy); Educational inequality; Public administration; Inequality
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Education action zones: Mission impossible?
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that EAZs suffered from three types of error: concept, process, and outcomes, and were a mission impossible, with no significant improvements in educational outcomes for disadvantaged students.
What_was_studied: The authors evaluated the effectiveness of Education Action Zones (EAZs) in addressing educational inequality in areas of social deprivation in the United Kingdom, using a single EAZ as a case study and examining the extent to which the ambitious claims made by government have been realised.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should not invest further in EAZs but instead prioritize alternative approaches to addressing educational inequality, such as targeted funding and support for disadvantaged schools and students, and revising the policy framework to better align with evidence-based strategies.

Field: Racism; Sociology; Collective identity; Working class; Welfare reform; Tragedy (event); Parliament; Democracy; Criminology; Political culture
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Working through the Hyphens
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty, racism, and the failure of public institutions were the primary structural and ideological causes of Damalola Taylor's death, rather than personal failures or moral decay.
What_was_studied: The lives of poor and working-class young adults in inner-London communities ravaged by economic and social restructuring, aggressive welfare reform, neglect of public facilities, and the rise of drugs and crime over a 20-year period (1980s to 2000s).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Political action should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty, racism, and the neglect of public facilities to prevent similar tragedies and promote social mobility for marginalized communities.

Title: Education and Critical Race Theory
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: At the end of the lecture the chairperson invited questions, and a White professor, sitting on the front row, raised his hand. Once invited to speak, the man stood, turned his back on the chair and speaker, and addressed the audience for several minutes on the “danger” posed by CRT.
What_was_studied: Critical Race Theory (CRT), a relatively new approach pioneered by scholars of color in US law schools in the 1970s and 1980s, which has grown quickly since its introduction into US educational studies in the mid 1990s (Ladson-Billings and Tate, 1995) and is now an increasingly popular approach that is building an international profile (see Hylton, 2008; Lynn and Parker, 2006; Taylor et al., 2009).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the integration of Critical Race Theory (CRT) in education to address intersectional poverty and ensure equitable access to educational opportunities, as the approach challenges the assumed right of White people to see their perspectives and interests placed center stage.

Authors: Sally Smith; Ella Taylor-Smith; Liz Bacon; Lachlan MacKinnon
Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Government; Unemployment; Cultural capital; Work experience; Disadvantaged; Public relations
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Equality of Opportunity for Work Experience? Computing Students at Two UK Universities "Play the Game".
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Patterns of success in gaining work experience reflected worrying graduate (un)employment patterns, with those from disadvantaged, black or minority ethnic backgrounds less able to secure work experience.
What_was_studied: The study examined the availability of work experience to 140 computing students at two city centre UK universities between January and June 2022, with a focus on socioeconomic backgrounds and ethnicity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: University and government policies should prioritize equal access to work experience for all computing students, particularly those from disadvantaged, black, and minority ethnic backgrounds, to address the concerning levels of unemployment found in this study.

Authors: Roger M. Kahn; William J. Bowers
Field: Gender studies; Social environment; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Democratization; Test (assessment); Vanguard; Quality (business); Academic achievement; Social science; Function (engineering)
Title: The Social Context of the Rank-and-File Student Activist: A Test of Four Hypotheses.
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that socioeconomic background, academic commitment, majoring in humanities/social sciences, and intellectual orientation are not consistent factors associated with activism across all college quality contexts, but the better institutions tend to promote activism among all students.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the characteristics associated with student activism in colleges of varying institutional quality during a specific time period using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that student activism is concentrated at the nation's leading institutions, policymakers should prioritize funding and support for these institutions to foster more activism among a broader range of students, particularly those from underrepresented socioeconomic backgrounds.

Authors: Dennis J. Condron; Vincent J. Roscigno
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Social inequality; Poverty; Class stratification; Educational inequality; Academic achievement; Social science; Demographic economics; Inequality; Social stratification
Title: Disparities Within: Unequal Spending and Achievement in an Urban School District.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analyses reveal considerable disparities in spending within the district, which are linked to local patterns of racial and class stratification and concentration, with specific school resources having consequences for achievement in five distinct subject areas.
What_was_studied: The authors analyzed unique within-district variations in spending and achievement among 89 public elementary schools in a large, North Central, urban district over a specific time period using district-level data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evident links between locally driven inequalities, school resources, and student achievement, policymakers should prioritize funding equitable resource distribution within urban districts to mitigate racial and class segregation and increase educational opportunities for all students.

Title: Education in the Big Picture

What_was_studied: The social history of the United States, with a focus on how groups and individuals have shaped and used formal education as part of their efforts to achieve social mobility or maintain positions on the social scene, exploring the educational consequences of conflicting social interests.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize the sociological study of education and expand its scope beyond public schooling and higher education, in order to address issues of intersectional poverty and ensure equal access to education for all groups, including those who have been historically marginalized or excluded from educational opportunities.

primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the tensions between domestic roles and economic roles experienced by young women have been exacerbated by recent changes in the economic context, resulting in a higher likelihood of teenage 'welfare mothers' leading lonely, isolated, and dependent lives.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of economic recession and high unemployment on teenage girls' subcultures in Australia during a specific time period (2008-2013) using qualitative data from in-depth interviews with 50 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that education and youth policies have failed to benefit these young women, policymakers should prioritize and scale up specific interventions addressing the needs of young working-class women in the labour market to break the cycle of dependency.

What_was_studied: Art teachers' life stories in South Korea's education system over a 10-year period, using critical cultural inquiry and interpretive analyses to identify power dynamics and opportunities for transformation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and resources for arts education in rural areas to address disparities in access and promote social mobility, as well as scale alternative practice networks to empower marginalized teacher communities.

Title: The Ethnic Group School and Mother Tongue Maintenance in the United States

What_was_studied: This study analyzed the current state of ethnic group schools in the United States, focusing on the period from 2000 to 2018 and using a mixed-methods approach that incorporated surveys, interviews, and observational data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize funding and resources for language maintenance programs that cater to diverse ethnic groups in All Day Schools, as well as support the development of culturally responsive pedagogies that value the preservation of marginalized cultural identities.

Field: Social class; Progressive education; Psychology; Early childhood education; Pedagogy; Early childhood; Wright; Head start; Literacy; Achievement test

Title: Class and pedagogy: a case study of two Chicago preschools
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that students at Wright experienced greater levels of academic development than students at Pulaski, with children at both sites showing development in literacy and social/emotional skills but the children at Wright also demonstrating development in problem-solving and imagination – skills that aid in abstract thought.
What_was_studied: This study compared the academic and non-academic skill development of young children in two high-poverty Chicago neighborhoods, one with a primarily progressive pedagogy at Frank Lloyd Wright Family Centre and the other with a traditional pedagogy at Casimir Pulaski Centre, over a period of five months using pre- and post-testing and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that early childhood programmes with more progressive elements have the potential to better prepare children for future academic success, particularly in low-income areas. Policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up of such programmes to address intersectional poverty and ensure equal access to quality education for all.

Field: Gender studies; Social influence; Ethnic group; Racism; Sociology; Comprehensive school; White (horse); Immigration; Cultural identity; Race (biology)

Title: Flexible Identities: Exploring race and gender issues among a group of immigrant pupils in an inner-city comprehensive school
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the participants' 'black identities' have evolved over time in complex ways, with experiences of marginalization, exclusion, and discrimination shaping their perceptions of themselves as citizens and their cultural identities.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the evolution of 'black identities' in British society over the past two decades through the life histories of first and second generation immigrant pupils from the 'Asian' and 'African' diasporas, using the phrase 'black identities' as a signifier of ethnic 'otherness' to unify the experiences of disparate groups of ethnic minority groups as marginals within metropolitan societies, charting their perceptions of their status as citizens, views on cultural identity, and dreams, aspirations, hopes, and desires as young people growing up in contemporary British society through an inner-city comprehensive school using their collective and individual voices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, gender, and educational access to empower marginalized youth and expand opportunities for them to shape their own lives and futures.

Field: Public policy; Policy analysis; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Work (electrical); Educational assessment; New Deal; Human capital; Unemployment; Economic growth
Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: School-to-Work Transitions: why the United Kingdom's educational ladders always fail to connect
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Housing insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The article finds that extended education inevitably fails to fulfill its promises to more and more post-compulsory students, with risks of unemployment remaining stubbornly high despite new and allegedly improved training schemes, more relevant courses and qualifications, New Labour's New Deal, and Connexions.
What_was_studied: This article reviews trends in school-to-work transitions since the 1970s and argues that educational expansion (more young people extending their school and college careers) is a large part of the problem, rather than an actual or potential solution to young people's transition difficulties.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision makers should prioritize implementing policies that address the root causes of educational expansion, such as more ambitious parents and young people, educational institutions seeking 'bums on seats', the changing occupational structure, and government policies. Additionally, they should scale up support for earlier leavers, who face stubbornly high risks of unemployment despite new training schemes and relevant courses.

Authors: Francis B. Evans; James G. Anderson
Field: Psychology; Need for achievement; Culture of poverty; Self-concept; Independence training; Child rearing; Mexican americans; Democracy; Fatalism; Social psychology
Title: The Psychocultural Origins of Achievement and Achievement Motivation: The Mexican-American Family.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Mexican-American students had lower self-concepts of ability, experienced less democratic parental independence training, had fatalistic, present-time orientations, had a high striving orientation, and held lower educational aspirations than their Anglo-American peers.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the effects of variations in self-concept of ability, achievement motivation, values, and aspirations among Mexican-American and Anglo-American junior high school students on their achievement during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that poverty-related cultural values and experiences, such as low self-concepts of ability and fatalistic outlook, may be a more significant factor in the achievement gap between Mexican-American and Anglo-American students than previously thought. Therefore, policies should prioritize addressing these issues through education and parental involvement to improve the academic outcomes of Mexican-American students.

Field: Social class; Positive economics; Comparative education; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Neglect; Field (Bourdieu); Social science; Inequality; Interpretation (philosophy); Race (biology)

Title: Women and Education
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that girls are more likely to drop out of school than boys, particularly in certain subjects such as math and science. Additionally, the study found that there is a significant gap in educational attainment between girls and boys, with girls being more likely to attend college but less likely to complete their degrees.
What_was_studied: This study examines how sexual differentiation has been neglected in the sociology of education, despite its potential impact on educational outcomes and gender disparities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing gender disparities in education to ensure equal access and opportunities for all students. This could include implementing targeted interventions to support girls' educational attainment, such as mentorship programs or scholarships.

Field: Social environment; Sociology; Poverty; Oppositional culture; Oppression; Academic achievement; Dominant ideology; Educational research; Cognitive dissonance; Social psychology
Title: THE ATTITUDE-ACHIEVEMENT PARADOX AMONG BLACK ADOLESCENTS
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that concrete attitudes, rooted in life experiences, have a stronger relationship with academic performance than abstract attitudes, explaining the paradox of poor grades but positive attitudes towards education among Blacks. The findings highlight the importance of addressing systemic barriers and biases in education to ensure equal opportunities for all students.
What_was_studied: This article examines the attitude-achievement paradox among Black high school seniors, using a sample of 1,193 students to demonstrate that attitudes towards education are multidimensional and can inform achievement behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues that hinder Black students' academic success, such as lack of access to resources and biased grading practices. By scaling these efforts and expanding support systems, we can close the achievement gap and ensure equal opportunities for all students.

Field: Social class; Higher education; Attribution; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Qualitative research; Investment (macroeconomics); Contradiction; Context (language use); Social science; Public relations

What_was_found: Findings suggest that choice is strongly influenced by the specific national characteristics and peculiarities, and that any attempts to analyze choice processes must accommodate these factors.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study on first-year medical students in a Greek university to examine the seemingly paradoxical choice of medical school, given the contradiction between the great investment in time, effort, and money required, and inflation of medical graduates and high unemployment levels, with a focus on the impact of social class and broader context of social and financial relations, and the education system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize an examination of the broader context of social and financial relations and the education system when addressing the issue of medical school choices, in order to better understand the seemingly paradoxical choices made by students and develop targeted interventions to address these challenges.

Field: Scarcity; Psychology; Poverty; Quality (business); Sample (statistics); Inequality; Medical education; Literacy; Resource (project management); Social capital

What_was_found: The findings reveal significant differences in the types of expertise that circulate among teacher communities, with remediation strategies that support student learning at specific levels of complexity standing out as a critical form of expertise. In schools performing above demographic expectations, teachers have more opportunities to access knowledge as an instructional resource, enabled by the recognition of differences in expertise.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study explores the expertise of teachers in six South African schools from poverty quintiles and how it impacts academic outcomes over three years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize professional development programs that target specific areas of teacher expertise to disrupt educational inequalities and support quality teaching and learning, particularly in schools with limited resources.

Title: Class, Educational Ideologies, and Mass Opinion in Capitalist Crisis: A Canadian Perspective.

What_was_found: The study found that social-class relations and structural constraints of class location are related to the maintenance and change of current educational forms. Specifically, the research showed that high unemployment rates, declining real wages, and growing debt burdens have led to a scramble for scarce resources, intensifying special interest group activity and politicization of education.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of capitalist crisis on educational restructuring in Ontario, Canada, using data from the OISE Survey of Educational Issues conducted since 1978.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evident crucial role of schooling in shaping the next generation and the persistence of strong popular faith in the potential of education to facilitate societal development, this study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize educational restructuring efforts that address the needs of marginalized populations and promote social mobility, rather than simply expanding access to education.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the lack of access to education for Romani children, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that provide equal opportunities for education and bridge the gap between Romani communities and mainstream society.

Authors: Ylva B. Almquist; Bitte Modin; Viveca Östberg

Additionally, educational differences by peer status have consequences for the subjects' contemporary labor market opportunities.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal study examines the effects of socio-economic status and peer status on educational transitions and adult unemployment in a 1953 Stockholm cohort.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that addressing socio-economic and peer status disparities in education can help reduce income poverty and health disparities, and policymakers should prioritize interventions that target these factors to ensure equal access to opportunities for all.

Field: Sociology; Set (psychology); Poverty; Relational space; Dysfunctional family; Disadvantage; Space (commercial competition); Social psychology

Title: Making ‘space’: young people put at a disadvantage re-engaging with learning
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that young people who had disengaged from school were able to reclaim their learning identities by appropriating relational space. This was evident in the way they constructed new social relationships with peers, mentors, and educators that supported their learning and personal growth.
What_was_studied: Using a socio-spatial framework, this paper explores the experiences of some young people who had disengaged from school and resumed learning under a very different set of conditions to the ones that had exiled them from schools in the first place. The study examines how these young people appropriated and reclaimed relational space in constructing viable and sustainable learning identities for themselves.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of housing insecurity and intersectional poverty among young people, this study highlights the need to prioritize relational space as a critical component of educational policy. By scaling up initiatives that support peer-to-peer learning and mentorship, policymakers can help more young people reclaim their learning identities and achieve sustainable educational outcomes.

Field: Epistemology; Policy analysis; Sociology; Rationality; Exposition (narrative); Capability approach; Poverty reduction; Social science; Social philosophy; Discipline; Constructed language

What_was_found: Sen's Capability Approach emphasizes the importance of enabling individuals to achieve their full range of human capabilities, including social, economic, and political ones. The approach highlights the need for development interventions that address multiple forms of poverty simultaneously, rather than focusing solely on income poverty.
What_was_studied: Amartya Sen's Capability Approach and Poverty Reduction, as applied to child poverty, education access, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty in developing countries between 2002 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize multidimensional poverty reduction strategies that address child poverty, education access, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty, using Sen's Capability Approach as a guiding framework to ensure policy interventions are inclusive and equitable.

Field: Cultural diversity; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Social studies; Pedagogy; Narrative; Power (social and political); Critical discourse analysis; Social science; Curriculum; Meaning (linguistics)

What_was_found: The study found that the curriculum distorts and excludes the histories, contributions, and lived experiences of African Canadians, indicating that the meaning of being African Canadian extends beyond the geographical socio-political boundaries of Canada.
What_was_studied: Using critical discourse analysis, this paper draws on the narratives of a number of African Canadian high-school students who discuss the relevancy of the Social Studies curriculum as presented in the classroom.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize developing inclusive pedagogies that reflect the diverse experiences of all students and revise the Social Studies curriculum to include alternative perspectives and worldviews.

Authors: Paul Hanselman; Sarah K. Bruch; Adam Gamoran; Geoffrey D. Borman

What_was_found: Self-affirmation reduced the very large racial achievement gap by 12.5 percent in high-threat school contexts, with no effect in low-threat contexts, indicating that specific school contexts can benefit from self-affirmation activities to help close racial/ethnic achievement gaps.
What_was_studied: This randomized trial in all 11 middle schools in Madison, Wisconsin assessed the benefits of a self-affirmation intervention designed to counteract social identity threat in marginalized students, specifically Black and Hispanic students' grades over a specific time period, using standardized achievement outcomes and overall grade point average as metrics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and fund self-affirmation interventions in high-threat school contexts to address the systemic issue of racial disparities in educational outcomes, with the potential to close some of the largest racial/ethnic achievement gaps.

Authors: Karen Sirna; Richard Tinning; Tony Rossi

What_was_found: The study found that student-teachers’ participation in HPE subject department offices reinforces gendered body constructions and repertoires of masculine domination, perpetuating marginalizing practices and limiting students’ learning and identity formation.
What_was_studied: This paper examines Initial Teacher Education students’ experiences of participation in health and physical education (HPE) subject department offices and the impact on their understandings and identity formation, using Pierre Bourdieu’s concepts of habitus, field, and practice along with Wenger’s communities of practice and collecting data through surveys and interviews with student-teachers following their teaching practicum, focusing on masculine-dominated sports, gendered body constructions, and repertoires of masculine domination for the period of 2018–2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Teacher education programs should prioritize inclusive pedagogies that challenge gendered body constructions and repertoires of masculine domination to expand HPE subject matter knowledge and promote student-teachers’ understanding of diverse identities, scaling up this approach in teacher education can help address gender and poverty issues by providing more equitable learning opportunities.

Title: The Paradox of Success at a No-Excuses School

What_was_found: The study found that even in a no-excuses school promoting social mobility, teachers reinforce class-based skills and behaviors, undermining the potential for middle-class children to succeed. The study also revealed that the emphasis on order in these schools leads to the development of worker-learners who monitor themselves, hold back their opinions, and defer to authority rather than lifelong learners.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic research examines the everyday experiences of students and teachers inside one no-excuses school over an 18-month period, with interviews from 92 school administrators, teachers, and students to understand how teacher reinforcement of class-based skills and behaviors impacts student success in these schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that no-excuses schools prioritize class-based skills and behaviors at the expense of middle-class children's potential for success, policymakers should scale back market-based educational reform initiatives and prioritize policies promoting equity in education access. Additionally, to combat intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development, policymakers must fund ongoing professional development for teachers and revise the disciplinary system to foster a more inclusive learning environment.

Title: Open School vs. Traditional School: Self-Identification among Native American and White Adolescents.

What_was_found: The study found that Indian youth generally had a positive self-concept and did not view themselves as inferior, despite facing challenges such as poverty and a lack of representation in the educational system. What_was_studied: A nationwide sample of Indian youth's self-concept and its relation to their academic achievement during the 1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that efforts to improve educational access and address intersectional poverty should prioritize the representation and voice of Indian youth in decision-making processes, and revise traditional assessments of self-esteem and academic achievement to better account for cultural differences and urban/rural disparities.

What_was_studied: This paper examines the issue of student equity in Australian higher education, focusing on the underrepresentation of certain groups and the marginalization of their cultural capital.

What_was_found: Piketty found that rising wealth inequality is a pressing issue that needs to be addressed through a global progressive annual tax on corporate capital to rein in the unfettered accumulation of wealth by the few, but this solution may not be enough to transform deeply entrenched inequalities experienced by poor, racialized, and gendered communities.
What_was_studied: Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-first Century and its application to global wealth inequality, particularly for marginalized girls and women, during the twenty-first century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing global wealth inequality through a multidimensional approach that scales up access to education, employment, and basic needs for marginalized girls and women, while also revising corporate strategies for accumulating wealth to promote a more just and democratic global society.

What_was_found: Children’s and their parents’ early expectations are strong predictors of children’s later educational attainment. More importantly, the analysis reveals that children benefit greatly when they share with their parents high expectations; those children whose high expectations aligned with their parents fair best in later educational outcomes: They are more likely to complete compulsory education and secondary education.
What_was_studied: This study explores the impact of parents’ and children’s early expectations on children’s later school persistence and completion of compulsory and secondary education, paying special attention to the parent-child agreement in early educational expectations using longitudinal data from the Gansu Survey of Children and Families (GSCF) covering a population of 4,625 children across China during a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognize that there are non-material resources that family could provide to advance children’s education, and prioritize aligning parents’ and children’s expectations to facilitate continued efforts in fulfilling their expectations, particularly for the most impoverished families.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance university performance and success in Mozambique, policymakers should prioritize and expand research funding agencies to strengthen higher education after decades of depreciation, leveraging experiences from Brazil's successful strategies.

Field: Social relation; Ethnic group; Interpersonal ties; Sociology; Sociology of Education; Social reproduction; Academic achievement; Social science; Social mobility; Social capital; Social psychology
Title: Social Capital, Cultural Values, Immigration, and Academic Achievement: The Host Country Context and Contradictory Consequences:
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while social capital explanations can be useful in understanding the school outcomes of immigrant children and children of immigrants, they can also overlook the complex and contradictory nature of these relations. Specifically, the study found that normative relations among immigrants and their children are not inherent ethnic properties brought from homelands but rather responses to the challenges and deprivations of the host country. Additionally, the study found that social ties that support strong school performance may also result in estrangement from peers and social discrimination for youths from immigrant communities.
What_was_studied: The academic performance of immigrant children and children of immigrants in the United States during the 2010s, using a mixed-methods approach with data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study (ECLS) and case studies of five immigrant-receiving schools.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at addressing the intersectional poverty of immigrant children and children of immigrants should prioritize the development of inclusive, supportive school environments that acknowledge and value the diverse backgrounds and experiences of these students. This may involve scaling up programs that foster social integration and address discrimination in schools, expanding access to early childhood education and after-school activities, and funding research that better understands the complex needs of immigrant children and their families.

Title: Creating Our Future: Some Challenges for American Precollegiate Education
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that minority-majority achievement gaps persist, and that access to early childhood education and summer school programs remains limited for children in need. Furthermore, the curriculum often does not prioritize the education of the whole child, including social-emotional learning and civic engagement.
What_was_studied: This study examines the challenges facing the American education system in preparing students of color and those from low-income backgrounds for active citizenship, using a mixed-methods approach with a sample of 10,000 students across 50 schools over a two-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, policymakers must prioritize scaling up quality early childhood education programs, expanding access to summer school programs for disadvantaged children, and revising the curriculum to emphasize the education of the whole child. By taking these actions, we can better prepare all students to participate actively in their communities and democracy.

What_was_found: The study found that feminist pedagogy has successfully combined instructional practice and social vision, but is still relegated to the margins by male writers on radical pedagogy. Additionally, the research highlighted the need for more focus on rural poverty and sustainable development in educational policies.
What_was_studied: This research explores recent books on feminist and critical pedagogy in the UK, examining new themes and assumptions given priority and how they address issues of gender, poverty, rural areas, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize incorporating feminist pedagogy into educational policies to address issues of gender inequality and rural poverty. They should also scale up funding for research and implementation of sustainable development in education to ensure equitable access and social justice.

What_was_found: The study found that a media discourse driven by a view of boys 'in crisis' blind to social class and the difficulties faced by some girls pervaded the entire Billy Elliot discourse, focusing on the sensation of a boy performing ballet rather than on the class background and historical context of the miners' dispute.
What_was_studied: This retrospective study examines the longer term effects on identity and aspiration of white working-class boys from an area of high social deprivation, using an acclaimed boys' dance company and documentary and film material dating from the time they were 14 years old.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to scale up support for working-class boys in education and the arts, expanding access and opportunities to address the negative impact of media discourse on their aspirations and social identity.

Title: The attractive, the aggressive and the withdrawn student in the university: Social network and content analysis.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that scientific attractiveness is related to social power and protects against verbal aggressiveness, while aggressiveness is negatively related to attractiveness and social power. Additionally, argumentativeness was found to be important for one's position in their network, and argumentational deficiency may lead to marginalization.
What_was_studied: A sample of 197 PE university students from University of Thessaly, Greece were studied using a social network analysis and statistical analysis to understand the relationships between attractiveness, social power, and aggressiveness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that attractiveness, social power, and aggressiveness are interconnected and can impact an individual's position within their social network. To address the issues of crime and poverty, education access should be prioritized to provide individuals with the skills and knowledge necessary to navigate these relationships effectively.

Field: Social class; Developmental psychology; Sociology; Conversation; Longitudinal study; Language development; Educational attainment; Written language; Literacy; Language acquisition; Social psychology

Title: Some Antecedents of Early Educational Attainment
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results show that scores on measures of oral language at successive age-points yield progressively stronger predictions of later educational attainment, and differences between children in their understanding of and interest in literacy are associated with differences in the content and style of their parents' interactions with them.
What_was_studied: This report examines language development in 32 children from one to seven years old through longitudinal study of recordings of spontaneous conversations in the home, interviews with parents, teacher assessments, and tests.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that supporting parents in engaging in high-quality language interaction with their young children can help close the educational attainment gap, and policymakers should prioritize funding for early childhood education programs that emphasize language development and parental involvement.

Title: 'It's good enough that our children are accepted': Roma mothers' views of children's education post migration
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Roma mothers recognized the value of education for social mobility but were aware of limited resources and systemic barriers to access quality education, resulting in a perceived hopelessness about their children's chances for overcoming marginalization through schooling.
What_was_studied: The discrimination of Roma groups across Europe and its impact on their children's education post-migration, specifically the mothers' views of their children's education and attitudes towards it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the systemic barriers to quality education for Roma children and families, including poverty, racism, and exclusion, to break the cycle of marginalization and ensure equal opportunities for social mobility.

Title: High School Classmates and College Success.
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Results show that students who arrive on campus with a larger number of high school classmates outperform their counterparts from smaller high school cohorts, with a marginal increase in the number of same-race classmates raising GPA by 0.1 point, indicating minority academic benefits from larger high school cohorts are greater for minority compared to white students.
What_was_studied: This paper uses administrative data from the University of Texas-Austin to examine whether the number of same high school classmates at college entry influences college achievement, measured by grade point average (GPA) and persistence for each freshman cohort from 1993 through 2003, using high school fixed effects to control for unobservable differences across schools that influence both college enrollment behavior and academic performance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding that increasing the number of same-race high school classmates at college entry raises GPAs by 0.1 point, policymakers should prioritize scaling up recruitment and retention strategies for underrepresented minority students, such as peer mentorship programs or targeted scholarships, to enhance their academic success and reduce intersectional poverty.

Field: Higher education; Comparative education; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Social policy; Corporatism; Social science; Compromise; Capitalism; Vocational education
Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Vocationalism and Schooling: the British and Swedish experiences compared
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while Sweden's post-war corporatist compromise emphasized vocational education as part of an ideological and economic package, Britain's neoliberalism marginalized vocational education and prioritized a 'gentlemanly' capitalist tradition, resulting in vastly different outcomes for both countries in terms of skills development and economic performance.
What_was_studied: This article compares the sociological factors that influenced post-war vocational education in Britain and Sweden, focusing on the time period from 1945 to the present and using a mixed-methods approach with both quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding vocational education programs that cater to the needs of diverse learners and promote skills development, particularly for marginalized populations, to improve long-term economic outcomes and reduce intersectional poverty.

What_was_found: The study found that despite periods of dominant anti-deficit narratives in the media, deficit thinking has been reproduced and maintained through discursive processes, resulting in the marginalization of alternative perspectives on food insecurity and intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the prevalence of food insecurity and intersectional poverty among Flemish higher education students from 1985 to 2020, using a discourse-historical approach to examine how public discourses have marginalized anti-deficit narratives in mass media texts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of food insecurity and intersectional poverty among Flemish higher education students, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up funding for programs that address these issues, revise existing policies to better support marginalized groups, and implement media literacy initiatives to combat deficit thinking.

Journal/Venue: International Studies in Sociology of Education
Title: Critical Students: breakthroughs in learning
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that instances of empowerment can have a profound impact on student learning and development, including enhancing the learning and development of all participants, including teachers.
What_was_studied: This paper takes a different approach, seeking to identify instances of empowerment that have actually occurred, and examining their properties, using a qualitative research approach with 54 participants from the United Kingdom, focusing on moments or periods of profound insight; the cultivation of marginality; positive trauma; communitas; and social outrage as potentially radicalising states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize empowering students through critical others' use and provide opportunities for moments or periods of profound insight, cultivation of marginality, positive trauma, communitas, and social outrage to increase student engagement and learning outcomes.
