Journal/Venue: British Journal of Sociology of Education
Title: Understanding inequalities through childhood studies
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that schooling can become implicated in projects of colonialism, nationalism, and reform, distinguishing between the figure of the child as a focus for the national imaginary and the lives of actual children. Furthermore, they discovered that these inequities can be traced across historical and cross-cultural contexts, revealing how education can be used as a tool for social reproduction or transformation.
What_was_studied: This interdisciplinary field of childhood studies has drawn contributions from across university curricula, examining how family life, culture, economy, history, and politics intersect to produce stark inequities in educational performance and life chances, particularly for children living in poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that to address the current 'war on woke', we must prioritize intersectional approaches to understanding childhood poverty and its intersections with other forms of inequality. This requires scaling up efforts to understand how education can be used as a tool for social reproduction or transformation, funding research that examines these complex dynamics, and revising policies that perpetuate inequities.

What_was_found: The study found that 71.5% of students reported experiencing physical victimization, and that such victimization was associated with lower academic achievement, as measured by the Chinese version of the Progress in International Reading Literacy Survey (PIRLS).
What_was_studied: This study examines the prevalence of shadow education in rural middle schools in China and its impact on educational outcomes, using a multilevel analysis of student victimization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing shadow education in rural China to improve academic outcomes and reduce victimization.

Title: "Family Keepers" or "Career Seekers": Understanding the Life Experiences and Educational Trajectories of the Young Chinese Restaurant Owners in the United States
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that there were two types of participants based on their family backgrounds and educational attainments: 'family keepers' who saw ethnic business ownership as a way to sustain their families, and 'career seekers' who regarded the ethnic business as a jumping-off point toward a new career. The study also found that immigrants develop different transnational habitus within which they constantly reframe distinct mechanisms to evaluate their ethnic, family, and human capital for upward social mobility.
What_was_studied: This study investigated how Chinese restaurant owners in Western New York negotiate their education opportunities, family solidarity, and social identity during their migration for success in the United States through in-depth interviews with nine participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that educating immigrant entrepreneurs about the benefits of education and career advancement could lead to increased upward social mobility and reduced intersectional poverty. Policymakers should prioritize funding for educational programs and resources specifically tailored to meet the needs of immigrant entrepreneurs.

What_was_found: The authors found that plantation agriculture was negatively associated with school-enrollment rates and manufacturing employment depressed demand for education, while child agricultural workers could attend school during slack periods. What_was_studied: This analysis of educational participation in 1910 uses the example of the South to further an understanding of general processes of American schooling, focusing on the social organization of production and policies of local governments and their effects on both the supply and demand for education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the social organization of production and local government policies to increase access to education for all children, particularly those in plantation areas and those employed in manufacturing jobs.

What_was_found: The main finding is that taking a gap year can lead to an increase in post-materialist values among young people, particularly in developed European countries.
What_was_studied: The study examines the trajectories of students who defer entry to university in Lithuania using semi-structured interviews and rational choice theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that encourage gap years for students, as this can lead to the development of post-materialist values and a more informed and engaged citizenry.

Title: Grounding the Regime of Precarious Employment: Homeless Day Laborers' Negotiation of the Job Queue
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that agency loyalty is produced by the reliable contingency of supply-side processes, revealing the ways in which homeless workers coproduce the regime of workplace discipline that regulates the temporary labor process and contribute to the reproduction of the industry's micro-foundations.
What_was_studied: This ethnography examines the lives of homeless day laborers in the temporary labor industry over a period of six months (2017-2018) through interviews and observations, focusing on how they negotiate the job queue and comprehend the regime of workplace discipline that regulates the process.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To better understand how the labor process is regulated at the micro-level, policy makers should prioritize studies that move beyond worker grievances or strategies to combat anonymity and instead focus on the supply-side processes that homeless day laborers use to comprehend and negotiate the job queue. This can help scale and expand the industry's micro-foundations, improving employment opportunities for this important subset of workers.

Authors: Brian C. Thiede; Daniel T. Lichter; Scott R. Sanders
Field: Multivariate statistics; Actuarial science; Economics; Construct (philosophy); Poverty; Working poor; Current Population Survey; Index (economics); Highly sensitive; Conceptualization
Title: America's Working Poor Conceptualization, Measurement, and New Estimates
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that the latent construct of working poverty is most highly correlated with empirical measures of working poverty that include part-time or part-year employment and that use poverty thresholds adjusted for differences in cost of living across states and urbanization, with estimated national rates of working poverty ranging from 2% to nearly 19% and being highly sensitive to alternative assumptions.
What_was_studied: This article addresses measurement challenges that have stymied contemporary research on the working poor by reviewing previously used measurement schemes and discussing conceptual assumptions that underlie each, using 2013 March Current Population Survey data to estimate national- and race-specific rates of working poverty using over 125 measures, and developing a working poverty index derived from the results.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study matters because it highlights the need to scale up efforts to address intersectional poverty among workers, particularly those in part-time or part-year employment, by expanding poverty thresholds adjusted for differences in cost of living across states and urbanization, prioritizing targeted interventions to support these workers, and revising existing measures of poverty to better capture the complex realities of working poverty.

primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both unemployment and parental financial support have negative consequences for youth's self-efficacy.
What_was_studied: Applying a hierarchical modeling strategy to longitudinal data from the Youth Development Study, we find that both unemployment and parental financial support have negative consequences for youth's self-efficacy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the personal psychological resources of young adults, policy should prioritize increasing job opportunities for them to achieve diverse markers of adulthood, thereby undermining their sense of confidence and independence.

What_was_studied: Using pre-COVID and COVID-19 era data of the working-age population in Israel, this study investigated the effect of the COVID-19 recession on the construct of precarious work, specifically the relationship between employment instability and employment-contingent outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest a need to revise the conceptualization and operationalization of the precarious work construct to better account for the effects of economic downturns. Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support employment stability and provide targeted assistance to individuals most vulnerable to employment instability, such as those in low-income households or those with limited education.

What_was_found: Even discounting the impact of income mobility, the United States exhibits the highest level of permanent income inequality among industrialized countries. Older workers and individuals at the bottom of the income distribution have faced significantly worse income prospects than common in many European countries.
What_was_studied: Using longitudinal income data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the European Community Household Panel, this study reassesses cross-national differences in social stratification and assesses the impact of income mobility on permanent income inequality in industrialized countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize education access, employment opportunities, and social safety nets to address intersectional poverty and promote income mobility for disadvantaged populations.

What_was_studied: This study analyzes gender differences in wage-related workplace law violations among a sample of employed individuals in the United States between 2010 and 2018, using data from the American Community Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant gender disparities in wage-related workplace law violations found in this study, policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing policies that scale up worker protections and expand access to legal recourse for victims of wage theft, particularly for immigrant women who experience higher rates of violations.

What_was_found: The analysis found that worker control schemes are more likely to succeed in countries with strong democratic institutions, a large middle class, and high levels of social mobilization. What_was_studied: The institutional context of late and marginal capitalist development in Peru, Chile, and Mexico was analyzed with respect to the political and economic role of the state, interest articulation, and trade union organization over a 20-year period, using quantitative data from official sources and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize strengthening democratic institutions, investing in education and social services, and supporting worker-owned cooperatives to scale up successful schemes of industrial democracy and promote sustainable development.

What_was_studied: This research reviewed the current state of international labor politics and examined the prospects of leading organizations, focusing on North America, to understand why globalization has not produced transnational labor organizations, using a world-system perspective.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revitalizing labor unions to address the decline of the welfare state and ensure sustainable development by scaling up international labor politics and coordinating efforts to strengthen unionization globally.

What_was_found: Academic mothers experienced a 'motherhood penalty' in terms of lower patent involvement and fewer patents compared to childless women or mothers in industry, but this gap was closed when controls for past involvement were applied. What_was_studied: Gender and motherhood dynamics among professional scientists in the US during 2008-2015, with a focus on patenting activity as a metric of academic productivity.

What_was_studied: This comprehensive handbook provides an overview of the key developments in various labor market contexts and in the analyses of these that have occurred during the two decades since the publication of the 1981 volume Sociological Perspectives on Labor Markets.

Authors: Franklin D. Wilson; Marta Tienda; Lawrence L. Wu

Title: Race and Unemployment: Labor Market Experiences of Black and White Men, 1968-1988:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that Black workers are more likely to experience longer periods of unemployment than their White counterparts, and that the racial gap in unemployment persists even when controlling for education and other factors. The findings suggest that differential access to employment opportunities by region, occupational placement, labor market segmentation by race, and labor market discrimination play a significant role in perpetuating the persistent racial gap in unemployment.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the persistent gap in unemployment rates between Black and White workers in the United States, despite narrowing educational attainment differences, and explores the underlying reasons for this phenomenon using data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) for the period 1976-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of racial disparities in unemployment rates despite narrowing educational attainment gaps, policymakers should prioritize place-based policies that target high-unemployment regions and support job creation programs that address labor market segmentation by race. Moreover, efforts to combat discrimination in hiring practices can help reduce the racial gap in unemployment rates and promote more equitable access to employment opportunities.

What_was_found: The analysis found that the Holland classification scheme replicates the segmentation of women into low-paying occupations, even after controlling for education, job tenure, and age. In contrast, male wage earners were found to be significantly segregated away from low-income, predominantly female occupations.
What_was_studied: This article explores the gender model of job research instruments based on the Holland Occupational Classification scheme and its impact on the segregation of women into low-paying occupations, using data from the 1973 Quality of Employment Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that current models of 'work' and job counseling tests and techniques may reinforce the economic disadvantages for women. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize the development of gender-neutral instruments and consider revising the Holland classification scheme to reduce the segregation of women into low-paying occupations.

Authors: Steven H. Lopez; Lora A. Phillips
Field: Neoliberalism; Labour economics; Ideology; Political science; Unemployment; Collar; Great recession; Restructuring; White (horse)
Title: Unemployed: White-Collar Job Searching After the Great Recession:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that white-collar workers are more likely to accept neoliberal labor market restructuring because they believe it will benefit them in the long run, despite evidence that it may harm their well-being and job security in the short term.
What_was_studied: A burgeoning literature on white-collar unemployment and job searching has sought over the past two decades to explain why white-collar workers embrace neoliberal labor market restructuring, and why they often fail to challenge or resist it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize programs that promote worker rights and well-being, rather than simply accepting neoliberal labor market restructuring as inevitable.

Title: Brave New Workplace Technology and Work in the New Economy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study finds that while technological innovations improve certain aspects of working life, they also disrupt others, such as increased job insecurity and the need for retraining. Additionally, the research highlights the need for education reform to address shifting skill demands.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effects of technological change in the workplace over time and its relevance to ten core issues, including flexibility, skill requirements, technological unemployment, educational needs, and occupational safety.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize education and training programs that help workers adapt to technological change and mitigate its negative impacts on job insecurity. By scaling up such initiatives, we can ensure a smoother transition into the New Economy.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Economic sector; Secondary sector of the economy; Work (electrical); Permanent employment; Work history; Male workers; Social stratification
Title: The Japanese Permanent Employment System: Empirical Findings
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The findings suggest that besides firm type, industrial sector and occupation are also important in determining work career in Japan.
What_was_studied: Using the 1975 Japanese Social Stratification and Mobility Survey work history data, the author examines the extent to which Japanese male workers stay with their first employers and how retention rates differ in sectors of the economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives promoting job mobility across sectors and occupations to enhance employment opportunities for Japanese workers.

Field: Psychology; Reciprocal; Deference; Qualitative evidence; Emotion management; Public relations; Inequality; Private law; Social psychology
Title: Reciprocal Emotion Management: Working Together to Maintain Stratification in Private Law Firms
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that pursuit of professionalism by paralegals leads to their display of deference to attorneys and acceptance of having deference withheld, which perpetuates their marginal or inferior status in law firms, as demonstrated through qualitative data from interviews and observations of paralegals' daily interactions.
What_was_studied: The concept of reciprocal emotion management is introduced and its role in the reproduction of status inequality in the workplace is illustrated through qualitative evidence, focusing on the three norms of professionalism, deference, and caretaking in paralegals' daily interactions with attorneys within a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaled implementation of training programs to address the three norms and promote more equitable status relationships between paralegals and attorneys in law firms, as well as expand funding for research on reciprocal emotion management in workplace settings to better understand its role in perpetuating status inequality.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Precarious work; Unemployment; New economy
Title: Unemployment Experts: Governing the Job Search in the New Economy:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that job search strategies are often ineffective for workers in precarious employment, resulting in longer unemployment spells and increased likelihood of poverty. Quantitative results showed that 75% of participants experienced poverty or near-poverty conditions during the study period.
What_was_studied: Recent sociological research on unemployment and job searching has focused on how workers are socialized to accept the terms of an increasingly precarious economy, using a population of individuals experiencing unemployment in the United States between 2010 and 2015, and employing both qualitative interviews and quantitative survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty among workers in precarious employment, policymakers should prioritize funding for job training programs specifically tailored to these individuals. This intervention could include skills development for more effective job searching and networking, as well as mentorship opportunities to foster connections with more stable employers.

Authors: Anthony Gary Dworkin; Janet Saltzman Chafetz; Rosalind J. Dworkin
Field: Psychology; Relevance (law); Alienation; Work (electrical); Variables; Tokenism; Absolute size; School teachers; Argument; Social psychology
Title: The Effects of Tokenism on Work Alienation among Urban Public School Teachers
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Despite the absence of specific reference in the literature to worker alienation as an outcome of token status, an argument was presented drawing upon this research tradition and discussions of marginality to link this dependent variable to tokenism. Limited support for the relevance of status concerns was found, only in sex tokenism. Absolute size appears to have negligible effects.
What_was_studied: Existing theories of the effects of relative numbers and tokenism on worker behaviors and attitudes were reviewed, focusing on the populations of workers in education access, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty over a specific time period with qualitative data collected through surveys and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale education access and address intersectional poverty and urban poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that address the marginality of specific groups in the workplace, rather than simply increasing the absolute number of workers.

Field: Sociology; Polity; British literature; Social science; Social stratification; American literature
Title: The Sociology of the Professions Dead or Alive
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: Unlike the American literature, the British literature contains four distinctive characteristics that differentiate it from the American literature, with a focus on inter- and intraprofessional conflicts, the relationship between the professions and the polity, the link between the professions and social stratification, and theoretical roots in classic ideas such as Marx and Weber.
What_was_studied: The recent British literature on the sociological study of professions was reviewed, showing an active area of research and theorizing with important lessons for American students of the professions, focusing on inter- and intraprofessional conflicts, the relationship between the professions and the polity, the link between the professions and social stratification, and theoretical roots in classic ideas such as Marx and Weber.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The realities examined in the British literature suggest that the professions will continue to play a crucial role in shaping income poverty policies, and policymakers should prioritize inter- and intraprofessional conflicts, the relationship between the professions and the polity, and the link between the professions and social stratification in order to effectively address income poverty.

Authors: Joseph J. Simoni; Richard A. Balla
Field: Psychology; Poverty; FAVORABLE RESPONSE; Social psychology; Deviance (sociology)
Title: The Mexican Medicine Huckster He Must Be Doing Something Right
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the medicine huckster presents an extremely favorable response to social psychological factors operative within a subculture of poverty, suggesting that this deviant role is not marginal but rather interstitial within Mexican society.
What_was_studied: The study examines the deviant occupation of medicine huckstering in a Mexican context, focusing on the subculture of poverty and its impact on the prevalence of this phenomenon.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the underlying social and economic factors that contribute to poverty and the prevalence of medicine hucksterism, such as expanding access to affordable healthcare and education, in order to reduce the appeal of this deviant occupation.

Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Industrial sociology; Work (electrical); Unemployment; Earnings; Inequality; Economic inequality; Race (biology); Labor relations
Title: The State of Work (and Workers) in America
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unemployment significantly reduces men's earnings, but not women's. Unemployed women actually experience a boost in earnings compared to employed women.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from the American Community Survey to investigate how employment and unemployment affect earnings and wealth inequality in the United States over the period 2013-2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gender gap in unemployment rates and the unequal impact of job loss on men's and women's earnings, policymakers should prioritize programs that help women enter and stay in the workforce, such as affordable childcare and flexible work arrangements.

Field: Labour economics; Organizational architecture; Economics; Representation (politics); Unemployment rate; Bank rate; Democracy
Title: Female and Minority Employment Patterns in Banks: A Research Note
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Controlling for prior employment composition, community characteristics (labor force composition, unemployment rate, and percentage Democratic) were generally found to be more influential than organizational characteristics in accounting for variations in minority employment patterns, but not female employment patterns.
What_was_studied: The representation of women and minorities in the internal labor markets of 24 large U.S. banks from 1990 to 2018 was examined using a comparative organizational design.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize community-level factors when addressing gender and racial disparities in employment outcomes, particularly in the financial sector. By understanding the role of community characteristics in shaping employment opportunities, policymakers can target interventions to improve access to managerial and professional positions for underrepresented groups.

Authors: Barbara S. Okun; Amalya L. Oliver; Orna Khait-Marelly
Field: Private sector; Welfare state; Sociology; Labour economics; Public sector; Judaism; Family-friendly; Childbirth; Affect (psychology); Argument
Title: The public sector, family structure, and labor market behavior : Jewish mothers in israel
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women in the public sector were more likely to continue working after childbirth than those in the private sector. Additionally, the study showed that previous employment in the public sector significantly interacted with childbearing, resulting in higher likelihood of continuing work.
What_was_studied: This research article analyzes the impact of public and private sector employment on Jewish Israeli women's labor market behavior after childbirth, using panel data from the years 2003 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of interactions between previous sector of employment and childbearing behavior, policymakers should prioritize providing 'family-friendly' employment opportunities in the public sector to encourage women's paid labor in the years following childbirth, ultimately reducing child poverty rates.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Adaptability; Rigidity (psychology); Collective bargaining; Wage; Unemployment; Salary; Wage bargaining; Efficiency wage
Title: European Rigidity Versus American Flexibility? The Institutional Adaptability of Collective Bargaining
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite having higher wage rigidity than the United States, many European countries did not experience excessive wage growth, and some coordination forms even performed better than the U.S. Additionally, labor market actors in most European countries were found to be responsive to their bargaining system's performance, adapting it if necessary to avoid overshooting wages.
What_was_studied: The unified theory of European labor markets was analyzed using empirical analysis spanning from 1971 to 1998, focusing on wage coordination patterns across European countries and their adaptation to overshooting wages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize adapting and improving labor market institutions in Europe, rather than simply focusing on reducing wage rigidity. By understanding the diverse bargaining patterns and responsiveness of labor market actors, policymakers can better address intersectional poverty and employment issues in Europe.

Field: Unemployment; Labour economics; Technological change; Inequality; German; Task (project management); Economics; Demographic economics; Business; Economic growth; Management; History; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Archaeology; Macroeconomics
Title: Who is Replaced by Robots? Robotization and the Risk of Unemployment for Different Types of Workers
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while low- and medium-skilled workers are not at increased risk of unemployment due to robotization, high-skilled workers have a significantly lower unemployment risk. Additionally, the study reveals that occupations with highly substitutable tasks are more vulnerable to job displacement in industries with heavy investment in robots.
What_was_studied: The research examines the impact of robotization on employment outcomes across various skill levels and occupations in the German manufacturing industry over a specific time period, using worker-level data combined with information on industrial robot investments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize upskilling and reskilling programs for high-skilled workers and targeted support for workers in highly substitutable occupations to mitigate the negative impacts of robotization on employment inequality. Furthermore, investments in industrial robots should be scaled back to slow the rate of job displacement.

Authors: Arthur G. Cosby; John K. Thomas; William W. Falk
Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Self-concept; Educational attainment; Black male; Demographic economics; Status attainment; Goal orientation
Title: Patterns of Early Adult Status Attainment and Attitudes in the Nonmetropolitan South
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both white and black youth had unrealistic and optimistic attitudes towards their future occupational and educational attainment, despite the availability of opportunities. White youth tended to have slightly higher aspirations and expectations than black youth, but both groups showed similar patterns of overestimation.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from a survey of Southern, nonmetropolitan youth to understand patterns of congruency and deflection in occupational and educational attitudes and attainment among 427 white and 268 black males from six Deep South states during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to scale up interventions that address the unrealistic expectations and aspirations of young people in poverty-stricken areas. By funding programs that provide realistic career guidance and opportunities, policymakers can help close the gap between expected and actual attainment, ultimately improving the lives of disadvantaged youth.

Authors: Mariah Mantsun Cheng; Arne L. Kalleberg
Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Order (business); Permanent employment; Demographic economics; Social stratification; Economic growth
Title: How permanent was permanent employment?: Patterns of organizational mobility in Japan, 1916-1975
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that macrohistorical events and postwar economic developments affected permanent employment, with differences by firm size and occupations. Mobility differences were most marked among young workers, with white-collar, large-firm workers having the lowest mobility and blue-collar, small-firm workers having the highest. This order was reversed as workers aged, resulting in a similar number of total employer changes over the life for both groups.
What_was_studied: Using work histories in three Japanese social stratification and mobility surveys, this study investigated assertions about permanent employment and measured its extent, as well as the number of employers typical employees would have during their worklife.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale up policies that support permanent employment, particularly among young workers and those in blue-collar, small-firm jobs. To expand access to stable employment, policymakers should prioritize vocational training programs and fund initiatives that support entrepreneurship and job creation in these sectors.

Field: Sociology; Demography; Social policy; Cohort study; Social security; Unemployment; Disability benefits; Social Welfare; Cohort; Social engagement
Title: Cohort differences in men's late-life labor force participation
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Results using an age-period-cohort model indicate that a substantial portion of cohort differences may be attributed to changing levels of social security benefits, the proportion of workers receiving disability benefits, and the unemployment rate. The results also indicate larger cohort differences among Blacks and rural residents.
What_was_studied: This article uses the 1964 to 1992 March Current Population Survey data to examine cohort differences in men's late-life labor force participation for the 1895-1934 birth cohorts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for older workers in need of disability benefits, expand access to social security programs, prioritize job training and placement services for rural residents, and revise unemployment policies to address the needs of an aging workforce.

Field: Conceptualization; Sentence; Sociology; Empirical research; Work (physics); Psychology; Mathematics; Linguistics; Statistics; Philosophy; Mechanical engineering; Engineering
Title: Corrigendum
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that between approximately 6.4 and 8.0 million working family heads were poor in 2012, and between 20 and 24 million persons lived in poor families with a working head.
What_was_studied: Thiede et al. (2015) examined the concept of poverty among working individuals and families in the United States, using two preferred measures—based on well-justified conceptual and empirical criteria—to estimate the number of poor working family heads and persons living in poor families with a working head for the year 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the large number of working poor individuals and families in the United States, policymakers should prioritize the scale-up of multidimensional poverty reduction programs that target both income and non-income dimensions of poverty, such as education and health access, to improve their well-being and alleviate intersectional poverty.

Authors: Sarah Damaske; Adrianne Frech; Hilary Wething
Field: Unemployment; Demographic economics; Economics; Life course approach; Labour economics; Psychology; Economic growth; Social psychology
Keywords: labor market; life course; stratification; unemployment
Title: The Life Course of Unemployment: The Timing and Relative Degree of Risk.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Our novel methodological approach reveals that 73% of full-time workers spend much of their 20, 30, and 40s with a relatively low risk of unemployment. The remaining sizable minority varies in the timing and relative degree of their unemployment risk.
What_was_studied: We use the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 to identify group-based trajectories of unemployment risk as workers age in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the importance of addressing employment precarity, particularly for men and Black workers who are disproportionately at risk of higher unemployment. Policymakers should prioritize programs that provide stable job opportunities and support for long-term unemployment to reduce the risk of labor market constraints.

Authors: Monder Ram; Paul Edwards; Trevor Jones
Field: Labour law; Social relation; Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Order (exchange); Negotiation; Minimum wage; Salary; Informal sector
Title: Staying Underground: Informal Work, Small Firms, and Employment Regulation in the United Kingdom:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that the NMW had little effect on firms operating in the informal economy, with informality deeply embedded in relations of work that continued to reproduce themselves, despite the tacit negotiation of order among employees and employers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effect of the National Minimum Wage (NMW) on firms operating in the informal economy in the United Kingdom, using evidence from 17 firms and a negotiation of consent within the labor process approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of the informal economy and its social relations of work, rather than relying solely on neo-liberal or marginalization theses. This could involve scaling up support for alternative forms of worker organization and collective bargaining, expanding access to social protection programs for workers in the informal sector, and funding research into the specific challenges faced by women in the informal economy.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment
Title: The Effects of Unemployment on the Probability of Suffering a Disability
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that an individual's unemployment is a useful predictor of subsequent disability, with a 2.4% increase in the incidence rate of disability for each additional month of unemployment. However, aggregate countywide measures of unemployment did not help predict an individual's probability of becoming disabled.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between unemployment and disability using a large national longitudinal data set from the United States, covering a 10-year period (2008-2018) and including information on over 35,000 individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant association between unemployment and disability, policymakers should prioritize job creation programs targeting vulnerable populations, such as low-skilled workers or those living in areas with high unemployment rates. Additionally, existing disability benefits should be reviewed to ensure they adequately address the needs of those who become disabled due to unemployment.

Field: Welfare state; Economics; Institutional model theory; Globalization; Wage; Unemployment; Demographic economics; Immigration; Economic system; Business cycle; Comparative sociology
Title: Institutional, Economic, or Solidaristic? Assessing Explanations for Unionization Across Affluent Democracies:
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The findings generally support the institutional model, with left parties and gent systems remaining influential, but ghent is less robust. Workplace access is a more significant indicator of centralization than neo-corporatism or wage coordination. Right cabinet significantly weakens unionization, while inflation, unemployment, economic growth, international trade, and investment do not influence unionization.
What_was_studied: This multilevel analysis of employed workers in 18 affluent democracies using the late 1990s World Values surveys examines how institutional factors, economic conditions, and workplace access affect unionization across nations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening left parties and gent systems, promoting workplace access, and resisting right cabinet influences to support unionization and protect workers' rights in affluent democracies.

Field: Product market; Labour economics; Metropolitan area; Economics; Residence; Panel Study of Income Dynamics; Unemployment; Selection bias; Secondary labor market; Nonfarm payrolls
Title: Local Labor Market Structure and Male Employment Stability in Large Metropolitan Areas
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The structural features of the labor market of residence were among the more important determinants of hours worked for black men, such as living in service-oriented metropolitan areas, and government participation in local labor and product markets stabilized their employment experiences. For white men, their labor supply was chiefly determined by the status of their occupations and whether or not they received unemployment benefits.
What_was_studied: The stability of employment (total hours worked) is a critical (but sometimes ignored) variable in the stratification process in American society, using a sample of male household heads from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics who participated in the labor force for at least 49 weeks in 1976.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize investing in local labor market interventions and government participation to stabilize employment experiences for black men.

Field: Social class; Subjective well-being; Economics; Position (finance); Class (computer programming); British Household Panel Survey; Unemployment; Fixed effects model; Social psychology; Identification (information)
Title: Unemployment and Subjective Well-Being: A Question of Class?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The negative effect of job loss on subjective well-being is highest for individuals who are in the middle classes prior to becoming unemployed.
What_was_studied: This analysis examines whether social class position affects the negative change in subjective well-being experienced from unemployment, using theory on work identification and work conditions to formulate hypotheses on the differential impact of entering unemployment from different social classes, with data from 14 waves of the British Household Panel Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact on middle-class individuals, policymakers should scale up support programs targeting this group, expand existing resources to address intersectional poverty, and prioritize job placement services that consider work conditions and identify opportunities for skill development, as well as fund initiatives that address gendered and class-based disparities in employment.

Field: Political economy; Economic Justice; Sociology; Poverty; Globalization; Collective bargaining; Leverage (negotiation); Trade union; Service (economics); Economic growth; Politics
Title: Public Dramas and the Politics of Justice Comparison of Janitors’ Union Struggles in South Korea and the United States
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unions are staging public dramas that redefine a particular labor dispute into broader violations over justice, with two key factors: cultivating associational power and symbolic leverage.
What_was_studied: The author analyzes how one group of low-wage, nonstandard service workers is transforming their structural marginality into new sources of moral and material leverage through comparative ethnographic case studies of university janitors in South Korea and the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize strengthening social protection programs to address the increasing poverty and inequality resulting from the expansion of low-wage, nonstandard service work, and fund initiatives that support worker associations and collective bargaining to amplify their moral and material leverage.

Field: Competence (human resources); Labour economics; Economics; Disadvantage; Unemployment; Educational attainment; Native-Born; Market return; Immigration; Acculturation
Title: Do Country-Specific Skills Lead to Improved Labor Market Positions? An Analysis of Unemployment and Labor Market Returns to Education among Immigrants in Sweden.
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite having similar language skills and educational attainment as native Swedes, immigrants still face a higher risk of unemployment. The research finds that these factors do not substantially reduce the risk of unemployment, suggesting that discrimination may play a role.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between speaking Swedish, education, and partnership with native Swedes and unemployment among immigrants in Sweden during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing discrimination in hiring practices to bridge the gap in labor market rewards between immigrants and native-born Swedes. This could involve implementing blind hiring processes and providing training for employers on unconscious bias.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Set (psychology); Work (electrical); Welfare reform; Postsecondary education; Low income; Affect (psychology)
Title: Lessons From the Policy World How the Economy, Work Supports, and Education Matter for Low-Income Workers
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: These volumes found that many low-earners perform jobs with adverse work conditions that adversely affect their well-being. However, the analysis could benefit from additional consideration of the specific nature of these jobs and how they impact workers' lives.
What_was_studied: Employment scholars interested in jobs and workers at the lower end of the labor market have much to learn from recent policy-oriented research volumes authored by work and employment scholars. These volumes focus on how shifts in the macroeconomy, work supports, and postsecondary education affect the well-being of workers both on and off the job.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize incorporating job quality indicators into their research and policy decisions to better understand the impact of employment on low-earners' well-being. This could include measures such as job insecurity, low pay, long working hours, and lack of benefits.

Field: Precarity; Neoliberalism (international relations); Stigma (botany); Earnings; Workfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Disability benefits; State (computer science); Welfare; Disability studies; Sociology; Economics; Political science; Political economy; Psychology; Gender studies; Social security; Market economy; Psychiatry; Accounting; Algorithm; Politics; Computer science; Law
Title: Disability and the State Production of Precarity
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Disability benefits set at low levels, yet means-testing limits earnings, channeling people with disabilities into low-wage jobs. Contradictory imperatives attached to state funding incentivize placement in temporary jobs, producing a precarious labor force.
What_was_studied: Ethnographic fieldwork in a job training program for people with psychiatric disabilities during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize scaled up funding for job training programs that prioritize long-term career development and living wages to address the contradictions in the welfare state treatment of disability and mitigate labor market precarity.

Field: Labour economics; Psychology; Work (electrical); Black women; Unemployment; Educational attainment; Work experience; Social attitudes; White (horse)
Title: Determinants of the Increasing Work Attachment of Married Women
primary_category: Employment; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that lessening family responsibilities, higher educational attainment, improved health, and rising unemployment rates were the most important factors contributing to the trend toward greater work attachment among married women in their late thirties. Specifically, the proportion of white women with a strong work attachment increased from 46% in 1966 to 63% in 1976, while the proportion of black women increased from 28% to 45% during the same period.
What_was_studied: Between 1966 and 1976, the proportion of married women in their late thirties who exhibited a strong attachment to the labor force was analyzed, focusing on factors that have encouraged or prevented strong attachment, for white and black women in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing number of married women in their late thirties participating in the labor force, policymakers should prioritize programs and policies that support their continued work attachment, such as flexible work arrangements, childcare support, and education and training opportunities. By doing so, we can scale up the economic contributions of these women and promote gender equality.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Prosperity; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Capitalism; Social Welfare
Title: Pathways Out of Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings from these books provide strong support for the importance of strategies that address the structural rather than individual dynamics of poverty, with evidence suggesting that microenterprise programs and governmental social welfare and employment policies are effective in reducing poverty and improving economic prosperity for marginalized populations.
What_was_studied: This essay reviews three books that explore the feasibility of different avenues out of poverty through an analysis of low-wage labor markets, microenterprise programs, and governmental social welfare and employment policies aimed at inequality and poverty reduction in the context of child poverty, chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, employment, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty over a period of time using qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize strategies that address the structural dynamics of poverty, such as microenterprise programs and governmental social welfare and employment policies, in order to reduce child poverty, chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, and income poverty while improving economic prosperity for marginalized populations.

Field: Sociology; Set (psychology); Organizational structure; Control (management); Popularity; Professionalization; Social science; Public relations; Process (engineering); Sample (statistics); Restructuring
Title: Professionalizing Body Art: A Marginalized Occupational Group’s Use of Informal and Formal Strategies of Control
primary_category: intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study findings depict a situation where occupational practitioners pick and choose among informal and formal strategies in order to restructure themselves in response to threats to their control.
What_was_studied: This analysis applies the concept of control to professionalization strategies used by a sample of body art practitioners in King County, WA over a 3-year period, using interviews and surveys to gather data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up support for marginalized occupations by expanding the range of professionalization strategies available, in order to protect control over two spheres related to business.

Field: Economic policy; Blueprint; Economics; China; State (polity); Job security; Unemployment; Undoing; Incentive; Restructuring; Development economics
Title: Perestroika in the USSR and China Motivational Lessons
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The research found that state support for enterprises and guaranteed employment led to inefficient resource allocation, which was addressed by Perestroika plans. These plans aimed to undo the relationship between state support and guaranteed employment, but leaders' expectations of inflation and unemployment have put these plans on hold.
What_was_studied: The study analyzes the economic reforms of USSR and China from 1985 to 1990 using a mixed-methods approach, combining econometric analysis with case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: U.S. firms can learn from the Soviet and Chinese experiences by prioritizing incentive-based reforms to address resource misallocation, rather than relying solely on guaranteed employment.

Field: Social class; Psychology; Perception; Job satisfaction; Underemployment; Overqualification; Scholarship; Volition (psychology); Opting out; Social psychology
Title: Willful Versus Woeful Underemployment: Perceived Volition and Social Class Background Among Overqualified College Graduates:
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings demonstrate that workers differ markedly in their perceptions of overqualification, with some reporting involuntary overqualification and struggling to find better work, while others narrate their overqualification experience as voluntary, with some seeing it as a temporary period of exploration and others as potentially permanent and opting out of the typical postcollege career path.
What_was_studied: This article challenges a key assumption of underemployment scholarship: that the modal underemployed worker is involuntarily underemployed, using in-depth interviews to analyze one particular type of underemployment among college graduates - overqualification, and focusing on how perceptions of overqualification vary by social class background.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering social class background in understanding underemployment experiences and policy interventions aimed at improving employment opportunities for college graduates should prioritize addressing the diverse needs and aspirations of this population, such as exploring alternative career paths or providing temporary flexibility in the labor market.

Field: Welfare; Ethnic group; Labour economics; Economics; Industrial sociology; Poverty; Social policy; Social isolation; Earnings; Social network
Keywords: poverty; gender; employment; welfare; networks
Title: How Low-Income Women Find Jobs and its Effects on Earnings
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Although most low-income urban women find jobs through strongly tied informal contacts (a method usually associated with lower quality jobs), tie strength has no effect on earnings.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on how low-income urban women find work and the effect it has on subsequent earnings between 2015 and 2018, using data from the U.S.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the social resource perspective is supported by an earnings penalty associated with unemployed contacts, policymakers should prioritize investing in job training programs and formal employment sources to address the earnings disparity faced by less-skilled female workers.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Working group; Economic shortage; Unemployment; Idealism; Rationalization (economics)
Title: The Political Economy and Technical Control of Work Humanization in Sweden During the 1970s and 1980s
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that managers were motivated by both idealism and labor shortages/protests, and that the production system is a sophisticated form of technical control. Additionally, the innovation produced mixed outcomes for labor and employers, with unemployment rising in the late 1970s and 1980s.
What_was_studied: This article closely examines the Swedish production system's incorporation of autonomous work groups from its emergence in the early 1970s to its reversion in the 1980s, with a focus on managerial motivations and technological control, as well as labor outcomes and employer interests during this period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the mixed outcomes and the potential for both humanization and rationalization within the production system, policymakers should prioritize supporting flexible, autonomous work groups to address food insecurity, while also monitoring employment trends and technological advancements to ensure equitable outcomes.

Authors: Carroll Seron; Susan S. Silbey; Erin A. Cech; Brian Rubineau
Field: Gender studies; Hegemony; Sociology; Ideology; Sex segregation; Undergraduate engineering; Meritocracy

Title: “I am Not a Feminist, but. . .”: Hegemony of a Meritocratic Ideology and the Limits of Critique Among Women in Engineering:
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women engineering students experience marginality in the classroom, feel excluded from social activities, and are more likely to leave the field than their male counterparts. The findings suggest that gendered power dynamics and stereotypes affecting women's belonging and career choices exist in engineering education.
What_was_studied: The study examines the experiences of undergraduate engineering students at four universities to understand how gender shapes their educational experiences and career aspirations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for policy interventions to address systemic barriers and biases in engineering education, prioritizing inclusive classroom environments, diversifying extracurricular activities, and providing targeted support for women students to encourage their retention and career advancement in engineering fields. Policymakers should scale up funding for programs that promote gender equity and diversity in STEM fields to address the leaky pipeline of female talent.

Authors: Susan M. Hauan; Nancy S. Landale; Kevin T. Leicht
Field: Ethnic group; Labour economics; Political science; Poverty; Public use; Human capital; Microdata (statistics); Urban environment; Puerto rican; Work effort
Title: Poverty and Work Effort among Urban Latino Men
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research documents sizable ethnic differences in rates of working poverty and ascertains that labor force attachment clearly reduces the risk of poverty for men, but levels of attachment do not explain ethnic differences in poverty among workers.
What_was_studied: This research examines the extent of poverty among working men in urban labor markets and analyzes differences in the risk of working poverty among Mexican, Puerto Rican, Cuban, and non-Latino White men using data from the 1990 Public Use Microdata Sample.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address persistent poverty among working men in urban areas, policymakers should prioritize policies that increase labor market attachment, such as job training programs and mentorship initiatives, for all ethnic groups to reduce the risk of poverty and promote economic mobility.
