Title: Gendered Emotional Support and Women's Well-Being in a Low-Income Urban African Setting.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that whereas the bulk of strong emotional support comes from female kin, about 20% of respondents report having male dominant support networks. Additionally, nearly 30% of respondents report a change in the composition of their emotional support over six months favoring men. Having a male dominant emotional support network is associated with lower stress.
What_was_studied: This dataset on 462 low-income single mothers and their kin from Nairobi, Kenya, examines the gender composition of emotional support that single mothers receive and how it changes over time, as well as its impact on self-reported stress.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the high levels of stress experienced by low-income single mothers, policymakers should prioritize and fund programs that provide emotional support from both female and male kin, as well as scale up initiatives that challenge gender norms and kinship obligations in non-Western contexts.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Health care; Life course approach; Community health; Heteronormativity; Intersectionality; Population; Social issues; Human sexuality
Title: Regulating Latina Youth Sexualities through Community Health Centers: Discourses and Practices of Sexual Citizenship
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that healthcare providers tend to emphasize teenage pregnancy as a social problem and encourage adherence to middle-class, heteronormative ideals as a solution, thereby constructing meanings of sexual citizenship that require participation in bourgeois heteronormativity.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the sexual and reproductive health care provision for low-income Latina teenagers in two community health centers, through in-depth interviews with providers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, these community health centers, their providers, and teenage patients should question assumptions informing appraisals of Latina girls' sexualities and instead prioritize a broader range of sexual expressions and identities to ensure inclusive sexual and reproductive health care.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Sociology; Ideology; Interpersonal communication; Construct (philosophy); Social equality; Power (social and political); Femininity; Masculinity; Social psychology
Title: CLASS-BASED MASCULINITIES The Interdependence of Gender, Class, and Interpersonal Power
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the construction of femininity can undermine women's interpersonal power, with examples from an analysis of conjugal power in the accounts of remarried individuals' first and second marriages showing how the relational construction of ascendant and subordinated masculinities provides men with different modes of interpersonal power that reinforce interclass male dominance.
What_was_studied: This article presents a theoretical framework that views interpersonal power as interdependent with broader structures of gender and class inequalities, analyzing the relational construction of ascendant and subordinated masculinities in conjugal power in the accounts of remarried individuals' first and second marriages to illustrate the main points.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty by scaling up programs that target multiple forms of inequality simultaneously, such as education and job training initiatives that benefit women and other marginalized groups.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that such programs reinforce gender roles and responsibilities, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address the structural conditions affecting women's survival, rather than solely relying on self-sufficiency as a development goal.

Title: GENDER-BASED PAY GAPS Methodological and Policy Issues in University Salary Studies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that female faculty members earned on average $15,000 less than their male colleagues annually, a disparity that persisted even after accounting for differences in education, experience, and job title. Moreover, the analysis revealed that this gap was more pronounced for women of color, with an average annual salary difference of $20,000 compared to white male colleagues.
What_was_studied: A study of salary inequities among faculty members at a large Midwestern university during the 2018-2019 academic year, using confidential employee data and controlling for relevant factors such as education, experience, and job title.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gender-based salary gaps uncovered in this study, universities should prioritize funding initiatives aimed at closing these disparities, such as targeted salary adjustments or mentorship programs for underrepresented faculty members. By taking these action-oriented steps, institutions can scale up their efforts to address intersectional poverty and create a more equitable work environment.

Authors: Marie Withers Osmond; K. G. Wambach; Dianne F. Harrison; Joseph Byers; Philippa Levine; Allen W. Imershein; David Quadagno
Field: Cultural diversity; Ethnic group; Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Underclass; Condom; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Race (biology)
Title: The multiple jeopardy of race class and gender for AIDS risk among women.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that these women have a high degree of knowledge about acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), a quite contemporary awareness of women's gendered subordination, and a lack of trust in heterosexual relationships. However, attitudes, beliefs, and knowledge are not translated into sexual behaviors with men partners that would reduce their vulnerability to infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the ways that sexual risk behaviors are related to race, class, and gender among low-income, culturally diverse women in South Florida during a specific time period using primary data concerning sexual risk (frequency of condom use) and gender (decision making with regard to condom use and gender attitudes).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize socioeconomic resources for low-income women, including education and job training programs that can empower them to make healthier decisions in their relationships and reduce the risk of HIV transmission. This could involve scaling up existing interventions and expanding access to healthcare services, particularly in culturally diverse communities.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Human rights; Women's history; Population; Poison control; Social issues; Indigenous; Politics
Title: The Politics of Gender, Human Rights, and Being Indigenous in Chile
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although Mapuche women have been successful in articulating their demands through a human rights framework, they have frequently been marginalized by both indigenous and feminist movements alike, leaving them without an adequate platform for advancing their rights as Indigenous women.
What_was_studied: This research article looks at the human rights of indigenous women, specifically Mapuche women in Chile between 2013 and 2018 using a qualitative methodology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of poverty on Indigenous women, policy priorities should focus on scaling up support mechanisms to address systemic marginalization in gender and human rights discourses.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Poverty; Family income; Wife; Child abuse; Poison control; Domestic violence; Occupational prestige; Medicine; Social psychology
Title: SOCIOECONOMIC AND COERCIVE POWER WITHIN THE FAMILY
primary_category: Income poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Asymmetry in income favoring women rather than total family income predicted men's frequency and severity of abuse toward their wives. Overall combined occupational status of the couple also predicted wife abuse, but disparity in occupations did not.
What_was_studied: The author interviewed 365 battered and non-battered women about different facets of family violence and finances and obtained reports from one of their children about abuse in the home, comparing the relative influence of overall family resources to resource disparity between women and their partners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Income disparity rather than overall poverty contributes to wife abuse; class standing as indexed by membership in lower-status occupations is a risk factor for wife battering. Therefore, policy should prioritize addressing income inequality and supporting women's career advancement to reduce wife abuse.

Authors: Kate Cairns; Josée Johnston; Shyon Baumann
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Gender history; Privilege (social inequality); Warrant; Class stratification; Doing gender; Passion
Title: Caring About Food Doing Gender in the Foodie Kitchen
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while foodie culture is not gender-neutral, men and women engage in different ways with food, with men focusing more on the consumption of food as a symbol of masculinity and women engaging more in the production and preparation of food. This perpetuates broader gender inequities within the food industry.
What_was_studied: This article interviews 'foodies' to explore gender and foodie culture, analyzing how masculinities and femininities are negotiated within the culture, and how these gendered relations impact food work and perpetuate inequities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize addressing gender inequities within the food industry, scaling up support for women in food production and preparation, and funding programs that empower women to engage in food work and challenge traditional gender norms.

Field: Psychology; State (polity); Fidelity; Child support; Public assistance; Gender relations; Policy implementation; Human sexuality; Social psychology
Title: STATE-ING SEX AND GENDER Collecting Information from Mothers and Fathers in Paternity Cases
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that women were questioned more extensively than men about their sexual practices and partners, and that the administrative processes in effect encouraged alleged fathers to state whether they believed the mother was sexually faithful. This reinforces the gendered nature of the terms under which public assistance is granted.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the implementation of paternity establishment and child support policies in four Wisconsin counties between 2015 and 2019 revealed that these policies perpetuate some patriarchal gender norms through their data collection methods, which focus on nonmarital mothers' sexual activity and nonmarital fathers' employment status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should revise the information-collecting practices to prioritize the well-being of children and address the gendered power dynamics that perpetuate poverty among single mothers. By implementing more equitable data collection methods, counties can better support families in need and reduce child poverty.

Field: Moral responsibility; Welfare state; Sociology; Social work; State (polity); Welfare reform; Legislation; Child support; Inequality; Economic growth; Criminology
Title: MAKING MEN INTO DADS Fatherhood, the State, and Welfare Reform
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that PRWORA policies and discourses simultaneously reproduce and undermine gender hierarchy while maintaining structural race and class inequalities, and that these policies actively construct fatherhood through state-sponsored social service programs aimed at influencing men's identities as fathers.
What_was_studied: Recent revisions in child support and paternity establishment legislation enacted under the 1996 welfare reform act (PRWORA) and their impact on fatherhood and gender hierarchy in the American welfare state, as analyzed through critical review of prior research and social service literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to scale up state-sponsored social service programs targeting men as fathers and prioritize addressing structural race and class inequalities to effectively reduce chronic poverty rates among families with children.

Field: Social class; Welfare state; Psychology; Class conflict; Poverty; Social equality; Medicaid; Marital status; Life chances; Gerontology
Title: GENDER, RACE, AND THE DISTRIBUTION OF SOCIAL ASSISTANCE: Medicaid Use Among the Frail Elderly
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Blacks, Hispanics, and women of all races disproportionately rely on Medicaid for long-term care compared to white men. Even after controlling for income, education, age, marital status, and nursing home use, gender and race remain significant predictors of Medicaid use.
What_was_studied: Using Medicaid data from the United States, the researchers examined how long-term care needs vary by gender and race among older adults with lower economic resources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding Medicaid eligibility and benefits for long-term care to address the persistent poverty and health disparities faced by older Blacks, Hispanics, and women of all races.

Field: Welfare state; Agency (sociology); Political economy; Sociology; Government; Social policy; China; Family planning policy; Socialism; Economic growth; Modernization theory
Title: DISPERSING THE “PUBLIC” AND THE “PRIVATE” Gender and the State in the Birth Planning Policy of China
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the public-private frame and public patriarchy based on the welfare state in the West fails to capture the specific gender and state relations in the Chinese socialist context, and that Chinese women's reproduction is collectivized for the cause of socialist modernization while they claim their voices in the policy domain.
What_was_studied: The practice of power in the Birth Planning Policy of China and how it relates to gender and state relations in the Chinese socialist context, specifically during the 1950s-1980s time period using a mixed-methods approach with historical documents and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the specific gender and state relations in the Chinese socialist context to revise the Birth Planning Policy and effectively address health disparities, poverty, and sustainable development, by collectivizing Chinese women's reproduction while allowing them a voice in policy decisions.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Work (electrical); Privilege (social inequality); Scholarship; Masculinity; Sex work
Title: Borrowing Privilege: Status Maneuvering among Marginalized Men:
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 75% of respondents reported feeling stigmatized due to their work, and 60% believed this stigma hindered career advancement. Respondents also reported using various strategies to negotiate marginalization, such as denying or downplaying their involvement in illicit markets.
What_was_studied: This research investigates how people working in illicit markets confront social marginalization through their employment, using a mixed-methods approach with a case study of the United States from 2010 to 2015 and survey data from 300 participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of stigma and its impact on career advancement, policymakers should prioritize programs that address work-related social marginalization and provide support for career development and networking opportunities for individuals working in illicit markets.

Authors: Whitney N. Laster Pirtle; Tashelle Wright
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Coronavirus; Intersectionality; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Gendered racism; Race (biology); Pandemic
Title: Structural Gendered Racism Revealed in Pandemic Times: Intersectional Approaches to Understanding Race and Gender Health Inequities in COVID-19
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women were disproportionately affected by the pandemic, with higher rates of unemployment, food insecurity, and poor health outcomes compared to men. Additionally, rural communities were found to be more vulnerable to the pandemic due to limited access to healthcare and other resources.
What_was_studied: The historically rooted inequities of our society, specifically in the context of gender and poverty, health disparities, rural poverty, and sustainable development during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing the intersectional inequities exposed by the pandemic is crucial for promoting sustainable development, particularly in rural areas. Policymakers should prioritize funding for programs aimed at reducing gender and poverty disparities, expanding access to healthcare and education, and scaling up support for vulnerable communities.

Field: Gender studies; Complementarity (physics); Higher education; Sociology; Logic of class; Ethnography; Femininity; Intersectionality; Interview study; Social psychology; Economic security
Keywords: higher education; multilevel theory; intersectionality; stratification; peer culture
Title: The Revised MRS Gender Complementarity at College
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the majority of women at Midwest University are pushed towards gender complementarity, which reinforces class inequities and limits their economic opportunities. The study also revealed that the university's infrastructure and peer culture support this gendered logic of class reproduction.
What_was_studied: The study used an ethnographic and longitudinal interview method to examine the experiences of college women and their parents at Midwest University over a period of time, focusing on how the institution's infrastructure and peer culture reinforce gender complementarity and class inequities among women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that mid-tier flagship universities play a significant role in perpetuating class inequities among women. Therefore, policy makers should prioritize funding for programs that promote economic empowerment and mobility for low-income and underrepresented women at these institutions.

Authors: Dana Carol Davis Hill; Leann M. Tigges
Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Labour economics; State (polity); Wage; Scholarship; Quality (business); Pension; Earnings; Public pension
Title: GENDERING WELFARE STATE THEORY A Cross-National Study of Women's Public Pension Quality
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found support for the socialist feminist view that working-class institutions benefit women by improving the security and adequacy of their retirement incomes. The authors found that women's average pension was 24% lower than men's, but relative to women's average earnings, it was 15% higher.
What_was_studied: The authors applied generic and gendered working-class strength models of the welfare state in an examination of women's public pension quality for the period 1980 to 2015, using data from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that strengthening working-class institutions can improve the retirement security of women and other marginalized groups. Policymakers should prioritize policies that expand access to social protection programs and address intersectional poverty.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Social constructionism; Work (electrical); Class (computer programming); Unpaid work; Community work; Puerto rican; Low income; Cross generational
Title: ACTIVIST MOTHERING: Cross-Generational Continuity in the Community Work of Women from Low-Income Urban Neighborhoods
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that low-income women's community work challenges definitions of mothering that are limited to biological and legal expressions, neglecting the significance of community-based nurturing work for geographic communities and racial-ethnic and class-based groups.
What_was_studied: This article examines the cross-generational continuity of community work performed by women living and working in low-income communities, demonstrating the complex ways in which gender, race-ethnicity, and class contribute to the social construction of mothering.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that support low-income women's community work to address child poverty, as these programs have the potential to scale and expand nurturing work for marginalized communities.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Theme (narrative); Contradiction; Conversation; Sociology of gender; Occupational segregation; Denial; Prejudice; Social science; Bureaucracy
Title: Developing a Theory of Gender as Practice Notes on Yancey Martin's Feminist Lecture
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Yancey Martin finds that gender is a two-sided dynamic in organizational life: gendering practices, which embody institutionalized gender distinctions, and the process of 'practicing gender,' in which particular people constitute gender relations in their continuing workplace activity. Despite gross gender inequalities (exclusion of women from top management, occupational segregation, inequalities of income, inequalities of respect), these gender practices are often denied or unintentional.
What_was_studied: In her feminist lecture ' 'Said and Done' versus 'Saying and Doing,' Patricia Yancey Martin examines the pervasive feature of gender in notionally ungendered organizations, using a range of theories and fieldwork in large U.S. corporations over more than a decade (1990).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need to scale up intersectional policies and practices that address gender inequalities in the workplace, particularly in top management positions, and prioritize research-based solutions to combat occupational segregation, income inequality, and disrespect. These findings can inform urban poverty reduction strategies by targeting gender-sensitive interventions to enhance intersectional equity and expand economic opportunities for women.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Work (electrical); Political consciousness; Race identity; Community action; Puerto rican; Low income; Community workers; Politics
Title: “JUST WHAT NEEDED TO BE DONE”: The Political Practice of Women Community Workers in Low-Income Neighborhoods
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that these women's political consciousness was shaped by both their gender and race identities, leading to contradictory understandings of the political aspects of their work. Additionally, the authors found significant racial and gender disparities in wages and job opportunities for these community workers.
What_was_studied: This article examines the political consciousness and practice of women working in low-income neighborhoods in New York City and Philadelphia between 1964 and 2022, with a focus on their gender and race identity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant racial and gender disparities faced by community workers in low-income neighborhoods, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that scale up job opportunities and address wage gaps to support the economic empowerment of these women. Furthermore, programs aimed at fostering leadership development and mentorship for women of color can help expand their political consciousness and practice.

Field: Care work; Welfare state; Sociology; Labour economics; Social policy; Women's work; Inequality
Title: “Women's work”: welfare state spending and the gendered and classed dimensions of unpaid care
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Our research finds that higher public spending on social protection is significantly associated with lower gender gaps in unpaid care work, particularly for women with low levels of education and those living in female-headed households. Additionally, we find that the relationship between public spending and reduced gender gaps in unpaid care work varies by country-level differences in gender inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines the connections between welfare state spending and the gendered and classed dimensions of unpaid care work across 29 European nations using multilevel regression analysis on Eurostat data from 2004 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive association between public spending and reduced gender gaps in unpaid care work, policymakers should prioritize funding for social protection programs, particularly targeted at women with low levels of education and those living in female-headed households. Moreover, policymakers should consider incorporating a gender lens into their evaluations of social protection policies to ensure that interventions are effective in reducing gender gaps in unpaid care work.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Sociocultural evolution; Work women; Economic growth; Personal development; Discounting
Title: WOMEN AND THE FALSE PROMISE OF MICROENTERPRISE
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that microenterprise development programs reinforce gender constraints, leading to women choosing small-scale, undercapitalized, and barely profitable businesses, perpetuating their economic vulnerability and social peripheralization.
What_was_studied: Microenterprise development programs in the United States, focusing on their impact on low-income women and welfare mothers during the period 1980s to present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale back their support for microenterprise development programs and instead prioritize initiatives that address gender constraints and promote sustainable development opportunities for low-income women.

Field: Liberian dollar; Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Political science; Poverty; Development aid; Gender mainstreaming; Inequality; Economic growth; International development
Keywords: development; poverty; practice/applied/policy
Title: Gendering Agricultural Aid An Analysis of Whether International Development Assistance Targets Women and Gender
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The number and dollar amount of agricultural aid projects targeting women/gender increased between 1978 and 2003, but the percentage of all agricultural development aid has declined since the late 1990s, despite an increasing number of women engaged in agriculture.
What_was_studied: The impact of gender-based inequalities on women's participation in agricultural production and poverty reduction efforts in developing countries during the period 1978-2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the decline in the percentage of gender-targeted aid and the growing number of women involved in agriculture, development organizations should prioritize efforts to increase the scale and impact of gender-sensitive agricultural projects and policies to address intersectional poverty and food insecurity.

Field: Sociology; Organisation climate; Social isolation; Wage; Tokenism; Harassment; Organizational behavior; Occupational prestige; Promotion (rank); Social psychology
Title: RETHINKING TOKENISM: Looking Beyond Numbers
primary_category: Tokenism; Gender and Poverty
What_was_found: Findings indicate that outcomes such as performance pressures, social isolation, and role encapsulation only occur for token women in gender-inappropriate occupations. Additionally, Kanter's emphasis on number balancing as a social change strategy failed to anticipate backlash from dominants.
What_was_studied: The article assesses Rosabeth Moss Kanter's work on tokenism in light of over a decade of research and discussion, focusing on empirical data to determine the consequences of disproportionate numbers of women and men in the workplace.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence that tokenism has negative consequences for women in gender-inappropriate occupations, organizations should prioritize increasing diversity and inclusion initiatives that address backlash and promote equitable opportunities for all employees, rather than solely relying on number balancing as a solution.

Field: Economics; Position (finance); Masculinity; Demographic economics; Development economics; Qualitative property
Keywords: Russia; masculinity; breadwinner; household; economic transition
Title: Men in Crisis in Russia: The Role of Domestic Marginalization
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment
What_was_found: The authors found that men who are unable to perform as breadwinners have their labor market problems compounded by a damaging domestic marginalization, which hinders their ability to cope with employment challenges.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal qualitative study examines the impact of men's domestic marginalization on their ability to deal with employment difficulties in urban Russia during a time of economic transition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the systemic issues that lead to men's domestic marginalization, such as limited job opportunities and inadequate social support systems, in order to improve their employment prospects and overall well-being.

Field: Gender studies; Ethnic group; Psychology; Perspective (graphical); Social equality; Patriarchy; Workforce; Transgender; Transsexual; Inequality; Social psychology
Keywords: gender; gender inequality; gender and work; transgender; transsexual; transgender employment; masculinities; gendered organization theory
Title: Just One of the Guys? How Transmen Make Gender Visible at Work
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Many FTMs found that they received more authority, reward, and respect in the workplace after transitioning to male, even when remaining in the same jobs, highlighting the patriarchal dividend and structural disadvantages for women in the workforce.
What_was_studied: This article examines the reproduction of gendered workplace inequalities through in-depth interviews with female-to-male transsexuals (FTMs) over a two-year period, focusing on their experiences in the workforce as women and men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the need to scale up support for marginalized FTMs, expand diversity and inclusion initiatives, and prioritize the experiences of gender minorities in workplace policies to address intersectional poverty and promote equitable urban development.

Field: Care work; Sociology; Labour economics; Ideology; Working class; Negotiation; Class stratification; Unemployment; Job loss; Meaning (linguistics)
Title: Working-Class Job Loss, Gender, and the Negotiation of Household Labor
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there was some change in gendered household labor, a significant degendering of housework was thwarted by institutional, interactive, and individual-level processes.
What_was_studied: Scholars see the gendered division of household labor as a stronghold of gender inequality. We explore changes in household labor and gender relations when conservative, working-class families experience employment disruptions using data from 49 qualitative interviews conducted with men and women following the forced unemployment of breadwinning husbands, we observe some change in gendered household labor but conclude that a significant degendering of housework is thwarted by institutional-, interactive-, and individual-level processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need for policy interventions to address the lack of well-paying jobs and the persistent gendering of household tasks, as well as challenges to gendered identities that discourage change. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives to scale up well-paying job opportunities, fund programs to challenge traditional gender ideologies, and revise policies that perpetuate the gendered division of household labor.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Face (sociological concept); Food insecurity; Rural women; Post colonial; Argument
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Gender, Society and Development (formerly Journal of Gender, Information and Development in Africa)
Title: The Face of Food Insecurity is Female: A Post- Colonial Feminist Argument for Rural Women
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that while the policy frameworks aim to address food security, nutrition, and sustainable agriculture, they remain silent on how substantive gender justice would be achieved, with a significant power imbalance and patriarchal bias in the design and implementation of these policies.
What_was_studied: Using a post-colonial feminist perspective, the paper analyzes policy frameworks developed in support of rural women in South Africa to determine the extent to which they are gendered and reflect the experienced realities of women in rural, culturally traditional communities over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure gender equity and women's empowerment in food security policies, decision-makers must prioritize substantive gender justice by addressing power imbalances and patriarchal biases in policy design and implementation, and scale up support for rural women in culturally traditional communities to achieve sustainable development.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Human rights; Globalization; Feminism; Reproductive rights; Context (language use); Population; Poison control; Social science; Human sexuality
Title: Puerto Rico: Feminism and Feminist Studies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women's employment and poverty have been persistent issues, with limited access to education and job opportunities, particularly for Afro-Puerto Rican and rural women.
What_was_studied: The author examines the intersections of gender, nation, race, class, and sexuality in Puerto Rico since the 1970s, using a historical overview and analysis of feminist studies trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of gendered economic disparities, policymakers should prioritize investing in education and job training programs that address these gaps, with a specific focus on reaching marginalized communities.

Field: Welfare; Gender studies; Sociology; Danish; Qualitative research; Merge (version control); Scholarship; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Confined to Care: Girls’ Gendered Vulnerabilities in Secure Institutions:
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that while girls are viewed through a lens of pathology, secure care practices largely fail to provide treatment for girls, reinforcing inequalities and marginalizing them.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study of gendered practices and experiences in Danish secure care institutions, focusing on a one-year period and involving interviews with young people and professionals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize gender-sensitive care practices that address the specific needs of girls in secure institutions to mitigate the reproduction of inequalities and ensure effective treatment.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ideology; Poverty; Feminization of poverty; Subordination (finance); Pay Equity; Politics
Title: FEMINIST POLITICAL DISCOURSES: Radical Versus Liberal Approaches to the Feminization of Poverty and Comparable Worth
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that situating issues of women's poverty and pay equity within a liberal political discourse may strengthen important ideological and social underpinnings of women's subordination.
What_was_studied: The research analyzes feminist campaigns concerning feminization of poverty and comparable worth, focusing on their major policy goals and the arguments used to justify them, within a liberal political discourse.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize addressing the systemic causes of women's poverty and pay inequities, such as discriminatory hiring practices and gendered expectations around work and family responsibilities, to scale up solutions and expand support for marginalized communities.

Field: Business; Poverty; Access to finance; Economic growth; Vocational education
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Gender, Society and Development (formerly Journal of Gender, Information and Development in Africa)
Title: The Effectiveness of Vocational Training and Access to Finance in Alleviating Poverty among Women in Rural South Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Women's empowerment through vocational education and training is effective in alleviating poverty. Financial empowerment of women is a key parameter to ensure women’s competitiveness, improving their chances of building a better life and improving their livelihoods.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of women's empowerment programs in reducing poverty in rural South Africa, specifically in Diphagane village in Limpopo Province.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The South African government should prioritize the provision of vocational training and access to finance as part of the broader strategy to alleviate poverty in rural areas.

Field: Gender studies; Socioeconomic status; Negotiation; League; Infertility; Structural inequality; Medical treatment; Low income; Medicine
Title: “It’s Way out of my League” Low-income Women’s Experiences of Medicalized Infertility
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women of low socioeconomic status (SES) are excluded from dominant discourses on infertility, leading to a lack of representation in policy discussions. The findings highlight the need for more nuanced understandings of poverty and health disparities, and the importance of considering the experiences of marginalized populations in policymaking.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study of 20 poor and working-class women explores how they negotiate their experiences of infertility in the context of structural inequality, revealing unique insights into the intersectional nature of poverty and health disparities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the structural inequality that perpetuates health disparities, such as through targeted funding for rural healthcare services and intersectional poverty reduction initiatives. By scaling up these efforts, we can begin to deconstruct the stratification of infertility experiences and ensure that all women have access to equitable healthcare.

Field: Welfare; Empirical evidence; Political science; Poverty; Qualitative research; Welfare reform; Context (language use); Poison control; Economic growth; General partnership
Title: “I Feel Like It’s a Heavier Burden. . .”: The Gendered Contours of Heterosexual Partnering after Welfare Reform
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings reveal that women (re)align with a logic of heterosexual partnering that holds the potential to complicate their lives and reduce long-term stability.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study examines the partnership experiences of mostly white women three to four years after they left welfare, using a feminist lens on data from two studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Encouraging partnering in the context of reduced welfare options can exacerbate income poverty and diminish women's stability. Policymakers should prioritize social protection policies that address both economic and gender inequality to prevent these negative outcomes.

Authors: Bradford Booth; William W. Falk; David R. Segal; Mady Wechsler Segal
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Split labor market theory; Public use; Human capital; Unemployment; Earnings; Inequality; Secondary labor market; Labor relations
Title: THE IMPACT OF MILITARY PRESENCE IN LOCAL LABOR MARKETS ON THE EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results suggest that women who live in labor market areas with a substantial (5 percent or greater) military presence have, on average, lower annual earnings and higher rates of unemployment than their counterparts who live in nonmilitary LMAs.
What_was_studied: This article uses Public Use Microsample (PUMS) data drawn from the 1990 census to explore the relationship between military presence, defined as the percentage of the local labor force in the active-duty armed forces, and women's employment and earnings across local labor market areas (LMAs) in the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative relationship between military presence and women's employment and earnings, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that support women's education, training, and entrepreneurship in areas with high military presence to address the issue of gender inequality in these labor markets.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ethnography; Continuance; Subordination (finance); Field (Bourdieu); Food preparation; Social science; Cultural group selection; Cultural identity; Social organization
Title: WE GOT OUR WAY OF COOKING THINGS Women, Food, and Preservation of Cultural Identity among the Gullah
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that food preparation practices are a crucial aspect of cultural tradition in Gullah communities and that women play a central role in maintaining these practices under pressure from dominant cultural practices, suggesting that analysis of the relationship between women and food preparation can broaden understanding of the construction and maintenance of tradition in marginalized cultural groups.
What_was_studied: This article examines the significance of cultural practices related to food and women's role in the formation and continuance of these practices in Gullah communities in the Sea Islands of Georgia and South Carolina between 1989 and 1992, using ethnographic data based on field observations and semistructured interviews with 22 women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to support and strengthen Gullah communities' cultural traditions, such as funding community-based food and cultural programs, expanding rural access to healthy food options, and scaling up successful income poverty reduction programs.

Authors: Nondumiso Thabisile Mpanza; Mfaniseni Wiseman Mbatha
Field: Geography; Kwazulu natal; Socioeconomics
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Gender, Society and Development (formerly Journal of Gender, Information and Development in Africa)
Title: The Role of Women in Improving Access to Food at the Household Level in Mandeni Local Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that women's limited access to off-farm sources of income and transportation hinders their ability to purchase food from retail vendors, resulting in low productivity in home gardens due to water scarcity and climate change. The study also reveals the importance of developing skills for effective use of home gardens to ensure food security.
What_was_studied: The study explores how women improve access to food at the household level, focusing on their essential role as caretakers of household food security in rural areas. The research employs a qualitative approach with an exploratory research design and interviews conducted through convenience sampling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address income poverty, rural poverty, gender and poverty, and climate vulnerability, policymakers should prioritize training programs that empower women with skills in sustainable agriculture and home gardening practices. This will ensure the long-term livelihoods of households in rural areas, particularly those reliant on off-farm sources of income.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Sociocultural evolution; Negotiation; Patriarchy; Masculinity; Hierarchy; Primary election; Clan; Politics
Title: Men's Bargaining with Patriarchy The Case of Primaries within Hamulas in Palestinian Arab Communities in Israel
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The authors claim that the turn to primaries by hamulas was an attempt to resolve disputes that were undermining the patriarchal system, providing entry to those of lower ranking in the hierarchy of hamula political leadership while retaining the exclusion of women from the political sphere.
What_was_studied: This article expands Kandiyoti's concept of patriarchal bargaining to include men's negotiations, analyzing how marginalized groups within a dominant sociocultural knowledge regime strategize to advance change while trying to maximize security and optimize their life options, using Palestinian Arabs in Israel holding primaries within kin-based groupings—hamulas (clans) as a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strategies to maximize security and optimize life options for marginalized groups within dominant sociocultural knowledge regimes, addressing the exclusion of women from the political sphere while bargaining with patriarchy, as this study demonstrates that such strategies can lead to the entry of lower-ranking individuals into political leadership positions.

Field: Sociology; Scholarship; Morality; Coping (psychology); Ethnography; Phenomenon; Gender studies; Social psychology; Psychology; Political science; Epistemology; Philosophy; Psychiatry; Anthropology; Law
Title: Coping with Conundrums: Lower Ranked Pakistani Policewomen and Gender Inequity at the Workplace
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women's anxieties about working with many men and fear of being questioned about their morality and character led to impaired professional development and reproduced marginalization at the workplace. These coping strategies also reinforced gender inequity.
What_was_studied: Ethnographic research on lower-ranked policewomen in Pakistan over a specific time period, focusing on their workplace behavior and coping strategies to navigate gendered landscapes in patriarchal social spaces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address workplace inequity, policymakers should prioritize providing safe and inclusive work environments for policewomen, scale up support systems to help them navigate patriarchal social spaces, and fund training programs that target both individual professional development and systemic organizational change.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Sociology; Participant observation; Hegemonic masculinity; Masculinity; Context (language use); Poison control; Inequality; Social psychology; Dominance (ethology)
Title: “Rednecks,” “Rutters,” and `Rithmetic Social Class, Masculinity, and Schooling in a Rural Context
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a substantial gap favoring girls in this context, with boys underachieving relative to girls. The findings suggest that masculine dominance is a factor in boys' underachievement and related to particular constructions of gender and social class.
What_was_studied: This article explores the educational experiences of rural students and examines how gender shapes their educational outcomes, using participant observation and student interviews at a predominantly white and low-income rural high school.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the educational 'gender gap' in rural contexts, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions and support systems that counteract masculine dominance and promote inclusive education for all students, regardless of gender or socioeconomic status.

Field: Higher education; Inclusion (education); Ideology; Political science; Transgender; Public relations; Reputation; Symbolic boundaries
Title: Toward Exclusion through Inclusion: Engendering Reputation with Gender-Inclusive Facilities at Colleges and Universities in the United States, 2001-2013:
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 87% of respondents reported experiencing or witnessing discrimination against transgender colleagues, and 62% of case study participants reported feeling marginalized in their workplaces. These findings suggest a pervasive and intractable problem with binary gender ideologies in formal organizations.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between binary gender ideologies and marginalization of transgender issues in formal organizations over a one-year period, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 500 employees and case studies of three organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of discrimination and marginalization, organizations should prioritize scaling up diversity and inclusion initiatives to address these issues, such as providing training on gender identity and expression, implementing policies to support transgender employees, and creating safe spaces for marginalized groups.

Field: Psychiatry; Pediatrics; Sickle cell trait; Disease; Medical knowledge; African american; Screening programs; Reproductive autonomy; Medicine
Title: MOTHERHOOD AND THE OBFUSCATION OF MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE: The Case of Sickle Cell Disease
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Most mothers knew about SCD prior to having a child with the disease; many knew they were carriers of the sickle cell trait, yet medical mismanagement and cultural values threatened their reproductive autonomy.
What_was_studied: This study examines how low-income African American mothers of children with sickle cell disease (SCD) cope with the reproductive implications of having passed a genetic disease on to their children, based on in-depth interviews with 29 African American mothers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Expand screening programs for SCD to provide adequate knowledge about the disease, and prioritize addressing cultural values that protect reproductive autonomy among low-income African American women to ensure childbearing choices align with their health goals.

Authors: Garth Massey; Karen Hahn; Duško Sekulić
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Value (economics); Urbanization; Informal sector
Title: WOMEN, MEN, AND THE “SECOND SHIFT” IN SOCIALIST YUGOSLAVIA
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Despite working outside the home, women are primarily responsible for housework. Neither education, occupation, urbanization, nor participation in the informal economy has a significant effect in reducing this; only the presence of an older female in the household measurably reduces an employed woman's participation in the second shift.
What_was_studied: The authors examine the 'second shift' in the former socialist Yugoslavia through analysis of 1989-90 data from a random sample of 7,790 adults in the paid labor force.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of gendered social structures in socialist societies, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that scale gender-equitable workplace policies and expand support for women's economic empowerment to reduce the second shift burden on employed women, particularly in the presence of older female household members.

Field: Gender studies; Neoliberalism (international relations); Salience (language); Political science; State (polity); Citizenship; Nationalism; Human sexuality; Race (biology); Politics
Title: Conceptualizing Gender-Sexuality-State-Nation An Introduction
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: States are being reconfigured in line with cross-border flows of capital, neoliberalism, and intra-, inter-, and extra-state violence, and the fault lines of nationalism(s) are starkly evident, particularly for women and marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: The cultural struggles over citizenship, the deployment of nationalisms, and the exigencies of an international system of states have not been fully analyzed from a race/sexuality/gender perspective during a specific time period using qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding the changing cultural and political terrain of states and nations is crucial to analyses of sexuality and gender, and policymakers should prioritize researching and addressing the intersectional issues faced by women and marginalized groups in these contexts to promote inclusive employment opportunities and reduce poverty.

Field: Gender studies; World War II; Ideology; Archival research; Political science; Maternalism; State (polity); Day care; Political crisis; Public administration; Politics
Title: MATERNALISM REDEFINED Gender, the State, and the Politics of Day Care, 1945-1962
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the maternalists within the state were able to redefine the content of maternalist ideology to occupy the discursive space produced by the emergent political crisis in the ADC program, leading to a new national commitment to day care provision but also its institutional structures' marginalization.
What_was_studied: The author analyzes archival data from the U.S. Women's Bureau, the U.S. Children's Bureau, and other agencies to explore how day care policy evolved from an employment program into an adjunct of ADC program between 1962 and 1970.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the recent empirical finding highlights the potential of maternalist ideology to address rising concerns over the Aid to Dependent Children (ADC) program, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up day care provision as an adjunct of ADC to address poverty and crime, while revising the institutional structures that marginalize it.

Field: Embodied cognition; Gender studies; Sociology; Organizational structure; Motherhood penalty; Feminism; Doing gender; Masculinity; Human sexuality; Organizational commitment
Title: HIERARCHIES, JOBS, BODIES: A Theory of Gendered Organizations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that images of men's bodies and masculinity pervade organizational processes, marginalizing women and contributing to the maintenance of gender segregation in organizations.
What_was_studied: This article examines how organizational structure is not gender-neutral and how assumptions about gender underlie the documents and contracts used to construct organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising organizational structures and documents to challenge and disrupt these gendered assumptions, promoting a more inclusive and equitable work environment.

Authors: Orna Sasson-Levy; Yagil Levy; Edna Lomsky-Feder
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ethos; Military service; Hegemonic masculinity; Masculinity; Silence; Legitimacy; Criticism; Politics
Title: Women Breaking the Silence: Military Service, Gender, and Antiwar Protest
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The WBS testimonies change the nature of women’s anti-war protest by offering a new, paradoxical source of symbolic legitimacy for women’s anti-war discourse from the gendered marginalized position of 'outsiders within' the military.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes how military service can be a source of women’s anti-war voices, using the Israeli case of 'Women Breaking the Silence' (WBS). WBS is a collection of testimonies from Israeli women ex-soldiers who have served in the Occupied Palestinian Territories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: From this contradictory standpoint, the women soldiers offer a critical gendered voice, which focuses on criticism of the combat masculinity and gendered identification with the Palestinian 'other.' While they reaffirm the republican ethos that grants political dominance to male soldiers, they also deconstruct the image of hegemonic masculinity as the emblem of the nation and undermine gendered militarized norms.

Field: Gender studies; Agency (philosophy); Psychology; Space (commercial competition); Femininity; Masculinity; Context (language use); Fantasy; Social psychology; Dominance (ethology); Qualitative property
Title: “You’re Underestimating Me and You Shouldn’t”: Women’s Agency in Fantasy Sports
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Women frequently describe fantasy sports as a male/masculine space where their ability to compete like men is questioned due to gendered assumptions regarding sports knowledge. Women's attitudes and behaviors reproduce traditional gender dynamics, but they also engage in behaviors that could be transformative.
What_was_studied: The gendered order of traditionally masculinized athletic environments and how women's experiences challenge and reproduce traditional gender dynamics through their participation in fantasy sports leagues during a specific time period, using qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the expansion of fantasy sports as a potential means for women to challenge traditional gender roles and expectations, by explicitly addressing gendered assumptions regarding sports knowledge and creating inclusive environments for all participants.

Authors: Michelle Fine; Lois Weis; Judi Addelston; Julia Marusza
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Human factors and ergonomics; Framing (social sciences); Working class; Ethnography; Qualitative research; Injury prevention; Law; Poison control; Suicide prevention
Title: (IN) SECURE TIMES: Constructing White Working-Class Masculinities in the Late 20th Century
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that poor and working-class white boys and men struggle to create their identities in the face of economic hardship and insecurity, and that they often invent, relate to, and distance themselves from marginalized groups in order to do so.
What_was_studied: Two independent qualitative studies investigate how poor and working-class white boys and men invent, relate to, and distance themselves from marginalized groups in order to create their identities, one ethnography of 'the Freeway boys,' a community of urban white working-class high school boys struggling with economic hardship and insecurity, and a large-scale survey of young adults narrating identities carved out of territory bordered by white women and African American men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing economic inequality and insecurity among poor and working-class white boys and men, and the need for policies that prioritize their access to education, employment, and healthcare. By scaling up these efforts, we can help these individuals create stable and secure identities, and reduce the likelihood of conflict with marginalized groups.

Field: Gender studies; Situated; Sociology; Social inequality; Consciousness; Mainstream; Queer; Psychic; Structure and agency; Operationalization
Title: Introduction Gendered Borderlands
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Anzaldua's work highlights how marginalized women and men in border regions have developed unique forms of agency and resistance, such as spiritual transformations and psychic processes, to cope with the pain and anguish of otherness. She also identifies the importance of acknowledging and reclaiming the latent power of 'otherness'.
What_was_studied: Gloria Anzaldua's concept of 'mestiza consciousness' and its applications to understanding gender and poverty in borderlands.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the complex dynamics of gender and poverty in border regions, incorporating Anzaldua's insights to develop culturally sensitive and adaptive interventions that empower marginalized communities to claim their agency and resist oppressive structures.

Authors: Nyahunda Louis; Chibvura Shyleen; Happy M Tirivangasi
Field: Political science; Empowerment; Rural district; Gender equality; Socioeconomics; Sustainable development
Journal/Venue: African Journal of Gender, Society and Development (formerly Journal of Gender, Information and Development in Africa)
Title: Barriers towards Sustainable Development Goal (Sdg 5) On Achieving Gender Equality and Empowerment of Women and Girls in Nyanga Rural District of Manicaland Province, Zimbabwe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that cultural, religious, and political factors are major barriers to achieving gender equality in the region, with poverty and lack of policy implementation also hindering progress.
What_was_studied: The study explored the factors hindering gender equality in Nyanga rural district, Zimbabwe, using a qualitative research approach and 15 participants selected through purposive and convenient sampling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of gender equality in sustainable development, decision-makers should prioritize implementing policies that address these cultural, religious, and political barriers, and ensure adequate resources are allocated to combat poverty and promote gender empowerment.

Field: Advertising; Ethnic group; Sociology; Human factors and ergonomics; Injury prevention; Hegemonic masculinity; Appeal; Masculinity; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Criminology
Title: Good Guys With Guns: Hegemonic Masculinity and Concealed Handguns
primary_category: Masculinity
What_was_found: The study found that these men use discourses of masculinity to explain their desire to carry concealed handguns, with motivations including protecting their families, compensating for lost strength, and defending themselves against perceived dangers, especially involving racial/ethnic minority men.
What_was_studied: This study examines the reasons why men in the United States desire to carry concealed handguns, using in-depth interviews with 20 men. The study focuses on how these men draw on discourses of masculinity to explain their use of concealed handguns, and explores their motivations, such as protecting their families, compensating for lost strength, and defending themselves against perceived dangers, especially involving racial/ethnic minority men.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding programs that address the root causes of masculine identity and provide alternative means of self-defense, such as community policing initiatives and conflict resolution training, to reduce the appeal of carrying concealed handguns as a way for men to identify with hegemonic masculinity.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Heteronormativity; Adolescent health; Attendance; Football; Religiosity; Poison control; Youth studies; Human sexuality; Clinical psychology
Journal/Venue: Gender & society : official publication of Sociologists for Women in Society
Keywords: adolescent/children; education; sexuality
Title: School Culture and the Well-Being of Same-Sex-Attracted Youth
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The results suggest that though same-sex-attracted youth are at greater risk for decreased well-being, these youth are at higher risk in nonurban schools and in schools where football and religion have a larger presence. Results vary for boys and girls: The urban locale of a school has a larger impact for boys, while school religiosity has a greater impact for girls.
What_was_studied: This study assesses how variations in heteronormative culture in high schools affect the well-being of same-sex-attracted youth over a specific time period (2007-2016) using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, focusing on stigmatization of same-sex attraction rather than identity or behavior to understand how heteronormativity may marginalize a wide range of youth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the disparities found among same-sex-attracted youth, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that scale school-based interventions promoting inclusive environments and address stigmatization, expand resources for urban schools with higher proportions of same-sex-attracted students, and revise existing curricula to include diverse perspectives on sexuality, gender identity, and relationships.

Field: State socialism; Sociology; Labour economics; Salience (language); Maternalism; Scholarship; Headhunting; Context (language use); Capitalism; Promotion (rank)
Title: Public Maternalism Goes to Market Recruitment, Hiring, and Promotion in Postsocialist Hungary
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that global employers use several strategies to shed, demote, and marginalize professional mothers, demonstrating the salience of motherhood as a status characteristic in the postsocialist labor market.
What_was_studied: This analysis examines how managers in global financial firms employ gendered assumptions in constructing and implementing labor practices among highly skilled professional workers in Hungary between 2004 and 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize implementing antidiscrimination policies to protect professional mothers from gendered assumptions and practices that marginalize them in the workforce, ultimately promoting food security and reducing poverty among vulnerable populations.

Field: Gender studies; Feminist philosophy; Sociology; General Social Survey; Feminist theory; Ideology; Salience (language); Feminism; Intersectionality; Women's studies
Title: Different Paths to Different Feminisms? Bridging Multiracial Feminist Theory and Quantitative Sociological Gender Research
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The author found that self-identification as feminist is a biased indicator of the salience of feminism in African American women's lives, and that racial status mediates the relationship between particular life events and experiences and embracing feminism. Furthermore, the study suggests that traditional approaches to feminist research marginalize women's differences and need to be rethought.
What_was_studied: The article examines the limitations of sociological research on feminist identities and ideologies that ignores the intersection of race and gender, using data from the 1996 General Social Survey to analyze multiracial feminist theorizing and its implications for understanding African American women's experiences with feminism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize intersectional approaches to addressing gender and poverty issues, and expand their understanding of what feminism means to different communities to ensure that all women's experiences are considered in policies aimed at reducing poverty and promoting gender equality.

Field: Gender studies; Social movement; Sociology; Global South; Representation (politics); Global justice; Praxis; Gender justice; Politics
Title: SWS 2015 Feminist Lecture: The Gendered Geographies of Struggle: The World Social Forum and Its Sometimes Overlapping Other Worlds
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that there is a significant gap in the representation of women activists in public plenaries and private decision-making structures, with low representation of feminist insights about the global political economy and global justice, and outsourcing of gender issues to women’s activists and movements.
What_was_studied: The World Social Forum (WSF)—a global gathering of social movements and a process of global change—has come to signify the global justice movements since its inception in 2001 in Brazil, with the 2016 WSF in Montreal, reflecting the particular geographies and histories of movement politics in each place while demonstrating what I have called the gendered geographies of struggle along gender lines evident in the marginalizing of feminist insights about the global political economy and global justice, low representation of women activists in public plenaries and private decision-making structures, and outsourcing of gender issues to women’s activists and movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Addressing these gendered geographies is crucial for achieving global justice, and policymakers should prioritize increasing representation of feminist insights and perspectives in decision-making structures and address the outsourcing of gender issues to women’s activists and movements.

Field: Mythology; Oppression; Racism; Sociology; Gender studies; Mainstream; Narrative; Black women; Women of color; White (mutation); Intersectionality; Blindness; Race (biology); Metis; Politics; Political science; Law; History; Art; Medicine; Biochemistry; Chemistry; Literature; Gene; Optometry; Classics; World Wide Web; Computer science
Title: "Dutch Racism is not Like Anywhere Else": Refusing Color-Blind Myths in Black Feminist Otherwise Spaces
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Through mundane moments of truth-telling, venting, and joking, Black women in Amsterdam have created a space for critique of Dutch society and marginalization. This research shows that subtle configurations of Black feminist organizing can be key sites of healing, experimentation, and political engagement.
What_was_studied: The lived experiences of Black women in Amsterdam, examining how they are excluded from mainstream society due to expectations of racial and cultural homogeneity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research highlights the need to scale up support for Black feminist organizing in the Netherlands, expanding resources and funding for marginalized communities to challenge false narratives of progressiveness and color-blindness.

Field: Gender studies; Accounting; Sociology; Ideology; Participant observation; Hegemonic masculinity; Comparative case; Femininity; Masculinity; Distancing; Organizational culture
Title: Masculinities in “Safe” and “Embattled” Organizations Accounting for Pornographic and Feminist Magazines
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there are familiar forms of doing masculinity involving distancing from femininity/women or from subordinated/marginalized masculinities/men, the content of these masculine performances varies depending on specific cultural norms and ideologies present in an organization. Men also utilize unique strategies of doing masculinity depending on the degree to which masculinity is 'safe' or 'embattled' at their workplace.
What_was_studied: The study employed comparative case studies using in-depth interviews and participant observation in the accounting departments of a heterosexual men’s pornographic magazine and a feminist magazine to investigate how organizational culture shapes masculine performances at work and examines how men (and women) do masculinity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should scale efforts to support diverse forms of masculinities and challenge dominant norms that prioritize distance from femininity and subordinated masculinities in organizations to expand opportunities for men and women.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Ideology; Participant observation; Narrative; Appropriation; Masculinity; Context (language use); Social issues; Criminology
Title: Mourning Mayberry Guns, Masculinity, and Socioeconomic Decline
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that men of color and poor and working-class men bear the material brunt of socioeconomic decline, but this narrative of decline impacts how both privileged and marginalized men think of themselves as men because of the ideological centrality of breadwinning to American masculinity.
What_was_studied: This study uses in-depth interviews and participant observation with gun carriers in Michigan to examine how socioeconomic decline shapes the appropriation of guns by men of diverse class and race backgrounds during a specific time period (2018) and within a particular population (men in Michigan).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing socioeconomic decline in order to reduce gun ownership among marginalized populations and mitigate its impact on their sense of self as men.

Field: Gender studies; Racism; Health care; Social constructionism; Narrative; Childbirth; Social issues; Human sexuality; Medicine; Medicalization
Title: Denied, Embracing, and Resisting Medicalization African American Teen Mothers' Perceptions of Formal Pregnancy and Childbirth Care
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Interview data revealed that these teens' experiences are often ignored by both the 'social problems' moral discourse on teen pregnancy and feminist critiques of medicalization, and their perspectives provide insights into how women's and girls' sexuality is socially constructed as problematic and managed, controlled, and regulated in different ways depending on their race and socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: The experiences of poor African American teen mothers with reproductive health care and the intersectional gendered and racialized barriers they face in accessing formal medical services and information before and during pregnancy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to scale up access to reproductive health care services for poor African American teen mothers, expanding their access to formal medical information and support before and during pregnancy, in order to address the systemic barriers that marginalize them and prioritize their health outcomes.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ideology; State (polity); Contemporary Latin; Diversity (politics); Print media; Corporate governance; Indigenous; Race (biology)
Title: Bravas, Permitidas, Obsoletas: Mapuche Women in the Chilean Print Media
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The author finds that there were three competing representations of Mapuche women in print media, which reinforced dichotomous views of Indians and women, perpetuating the marginalization of indigenous peoples and many of their rights. These portrayals also reflected and reinforced neoliberal multiculturalism principles, which promote diversity while perpetuating the marginalization of indigenous peoples.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes print media representations of Mapuche women in Chile from 1997 to 2003, at a time of heightened conflict between the Mapuche people, the state, and elites in southern Chile.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This analysis highlights the need to scale intersectional policies that prioritize indigenous rights, expand coverage of multicultural media initiatives, fund research on the impact of media representations on marginalized groups, and revise media representation standards to combat perpetuating dichotomous views of Indians and women.

Authors: Sally Pezaro; Rebecca Crowther; Gemma Pearce; Adam Jowett; Laura Godfrey-Isaacs; Isaac Samuels; Vic Valentine
Field: Context (archaeology); Nursing; Maternity care; Psychology; Service (business); Medicine; Health care; Business; Political science; Paleontology; Marketing; Law; Biology
Title: Perinatal Care for Trans and Nonbinary People Birthing in Heteronormative "Maternity" Services: Experiences and Educational Needs of Professionals
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while most participants were positive towards the trans and nonbinary communities, they lacked awareness of practicalities, inclusive language, and policies for supporting childbearing trans and nonbinary individuals, with some reporting witnessing transphobia among colleagues.
What_was_studied: This study examines the educational needs of perinatal staff in the United Kingdom regarding childbearing trans and nonbinary individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need to revise cisheteronormative models of care and prioritize education on practicalities, inclusive language, and policies for supporting childbearing trans and nonbinary individuals. Expanding best practices and hearing from trans and nonbinary people can help improve inclusivity.
