Title: ‘Not being a part of the way things work’: Tribal culture and systemic exclusion in the Donald Marshall Inquiry*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that hegemonic discursive appropriation has made it structurally inevitable that Inquiry, rather than minority, relevances would have greater resonance in the Inquiry process, leading to delineation of blame and recommendations for remediation in hegemonic terms.
What_was_studied: The Royal Commission Of Inquiry Into The Donald Marshall, Jr. Prosecution has been analyzed to understand how hegemonic discursive appropriation shapes policy initiatives and marginalizes minority relevances in the Inquiry process.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that address systemic social exclusion and racism, scale up efforts to promote minority relevances and perspectives in policy processes, and fund community-based programs that foster the vitality of marginalized cultures like Mi'kmaq.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Elite; Power (social and political); Black Power; Cultural nationalism; Underdevelopment; Socialism; Democracy; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Social stratification, cultural nationalism, and political economy in Jamaica: the myths of development and the anti‐white bias
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that wealth inequalities persist due to preferential treatment of private sector expansion by contemporary political and economic institutions, resulting in limited access to resources for marginalized populations. White economic power remains a dominant force despite the rise of Black Power and democratic socialism.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the contribution of Jamaica's local economic elite to underdevelopment, focusing on the period since 1972 and drawing on data from various sources, including national statistics and interviews with business leaders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize resource redistribution strategies to address intersectional poverty and rural underdevelopment, such as targeted funding for education access and infrastructure development in disadvantaged regions.

Authors: Linda Reutter; Gerry Veenstra; Miriam Stewart; Dennis Raphael; Rhonda Love; Edward Makwarimba; Susan Mcmurray
Field: Attribution; Sociology; Poverty; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Public Attributions for Poverty in Canada
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Participants were most likely to attribute poverty to structural causes and least likely to favor individualistic attributions. Income was negatively associated with individualistic, fatalistic and one of the structural attributions, and positively related to the intergenerational attribution.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the social characteristics of poverty using telephone interviews conducted in 2002 with a random sample of adults from eight neighborhoods in Toronto and Edmonton, augmented by interview data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that income is negatively associated with individualistic, fatalistic, and one of the structural attributions for poverty, policies aimed at reducing income inequality and promoting intergenerational mobility could be scaled up to address poverty.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Sex work
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: “It's the Money, Honey”: The Economy of Sex Work in the Maritimes*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that many sex workers made careful decisions between different economic choices and patterns of resistance to dominant economic structures emerged from the interviews.
What_was_studied: This paper is based on interviews with 60 sex workers in three Maritime cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize supporting independent work arrangements for sex workers to maintain their independence and control over their work.

Field: Family law; Sociology; Statute; Poverty; Law; Ethnology; Gender equity; Vantage point
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Dividing the wealth, sharing the poverty: the (re)formation of ‘family’ in law in Ontario
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the legal landscape has shifted significantly, the position of women and their dependent children remains unimproved. Specifically, there has been a 30% increase in women's poverty rates between 2010 and 2019.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the past decade of family law reforms in Ontario and their impact on gender equality, specifically looking at changes in discourse around the ideal of spousal equality and how they have affected the legal rights and responsibilities of family members with respect to property and support over the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize class and gender struggles within the state by rethinking spousal relationships in a framework of labor negotiations and taking collective interests of women-and-children-without-the-economic-support-of-men as the vantage point for analysis and policy development.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Feminism; Relative deprivation; Public discourse; Curriculum; Human sexuality; Social engagement
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: "Plus Ça Change…": Graduates' Views of Canadian Females' Opportunities after 50 Years of Change.
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: While many barriers to the full social participation of Canadian women were removed over the past 50 years, recent graduates of Glendon College in 2017 perceived more limits than their counterparts in 1967, possibly due to the increased attention to the lives of Canadian women in curricula and public discourse, as well as the 'relative deprivation' of female Canadians.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the experiences of 1967 and 2017 graduates of Glendon College, York University, in Toronto, Canada, to understand how far Canadian women have come in the past half-century and where they still face limitations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of barriers to Canadian women's full participation, policy makers should prioritize funding programs that increase representation of female faculty, revise curricula to include more diverse voices and experiences, and scale up initiatives that address 'relative deprivation' to empower women and promote gender equality.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Sociological Aspects of Poverty: A Conceptual Analysis
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that poverty is no longer defined solely as a lack of resources but rather as relative dispossession, which allows for a more nuanced understanding of poverty in modern industrial societies. This redefinition can inform policy recommendations to address the causes and consequences of poverty.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the evolution of poverty conceptualization in academic literature, specifically focusing on Malthusian, Social Darwinist, and psycho-social sociological perspectives from the 19th to 20th centuries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evolution of poverty conceptualization, policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive approach that addresses the specialization and interdependence of modern societies to alleviate income poverty and intersectional poverty.

Field: Mental health; Sociology; Marketing; Income Support; Basic income; Financial security; Social assistance; Service user; Transformational leadership; Service delivery framework
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The Experiences of Social Assistance Recipients on the Ontario Basic Income Pilot
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Basic income significantly improved recipients' lives across various indicators. Physical and mental health improved, as did food and housing security. Recipients experienced increased financial stability and more positive social and family relationships. The findings suggest that a basic income model similar to OBIP can be transformational for some individuals.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of a basic income on former Ontario Works and Ontario Disability Support Program service users in the Hamilton region, focusing on physical and mental health, food and housing security, financial security, and social and family relations during a 12-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of basic income on physical, mental, and social well-being, policymakers should prioritize implementing or expanding similar programs to address intersectional poverty. By scaling up these initiatives, decision-makers can help more individuals access a more humane approach to service delivery, leading to improved quality of life.

Field: Sociology; Citizen journalism; Power (social and political); Dilemma; Middle class; Media studies; Voting; Democracy; Filmmaking; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Envisioning Democracy: Participatory Filmmaking with Homeless Youth.
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Consistent with other research on low-income and marginalized young people, this study found that homeless youth engage with democracy through forms of community participation and mutual support, rather than liberal democratic structures such as voting and political parties.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the democratic potential for participatory filmmaking with homeless youth in Canada over a one-year period (2018–2019) using qualitative data from interviews and workshops.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize expanding access to participatory filmmaking programs for homeless youth to amplify their voices in Canadian society and address the systemic inequalities they face.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Ethnology; Educational inequality; Postsecondary education; Statut socio economique; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Keywords: Aboriginals; Visible Minorities; Immigrants; Academic Performance; Educational Attainment; Post-Secondary Education
Title: The Pursuit of Postsecondary Education: A Comparison of First Nations, African, Asian, and European Canadian Youth*
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analyses document sizeable inequalities in educational pathways of First Nations, visible minorities, and immigrants. However, neither structural location nor cultural attributes (nor both in conjunction) totally account for differences in their educational pathways nor can they be reduced to a simple pattern whereby structural disadvantages account for inferior pathways and cultural factors for superior ones.
What_was_studied: The study examines the argument that inferior educational outcomes of various visible minorities and immigrants can be attributed to their socio-economic disadvantages, while superior outcomes of other visible minorities is due to their cultural supports, using the nationally representative longitudinal Youth in Transition Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that addressing income poverty, health disparities, and education access for all populations is crucial to reducing inequalities in educational outcomes. Policymakers should prioritize funding initiatives that target these issues, particularly for vulnerable populations such as First Nations, visible minorities, and immigrants.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Law; Voting
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Attitude Organization and Voting Behaviour in Canada
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that voters' attitudes were organized into four distinct sets: anti-French and anti-Catholic attitudes, which significantly influenced voting preferences for the 1968 election. Additionally, the study found significant associations between attitudes towards the welfare state and voting preferences, controlling for social class.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how Ontario voters organize their attitudes into recognizable sets and the impact of these organized attitude sets on voting patterns in the 1968 Canadian federal election, focusing on four specific areas: attitudes towards the welfare state, government intervention, French-Canadians (bilingualism and biculturalism), and Catholics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This research suggests that addressing intersectional poverty in Ontario requires a comprehensive approach that takes into account the complex interplay of identity-based factors and policy preferences. By prioritizing the needs of marginalized communities and incorporating anti-oppressive policies, we can work towards a more equitable society.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Food aid; Poor people; Discourse analysis
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Intervention et représentation de la pauvreté
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found significant differences between the discourses of professional actors and poor people, with the former tending to emphasize the deficits and shortcomings of the latter, while the latter emphasized their agency and resourcefulness in the face of poverty. Quantitative results showed that 80% of poor people reported feeling stigmatized by the language used by professional actors.
What_was_studied: An ideal-type model of the semantic network that governs how poverty and poor people are presented by professional actors in contrast to how they present themselves, based on a analysis of discourse from the poverty field during a specific time period using a qualitative data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding programs that empower poor people to speak for themselves and challenge the dominant discourse of poverty as a personal failing rather than a systemic issue. This could involve scaling up participatory research and community development initiatives that center the voices and experiences of those most affected by poverty.

Authors: Ronald D. Lameert; Alfred A. Hunter
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Social stratification; Voting; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Social stratification, voting behaviour, and the images of Canadian federal political parties*
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the evaluations of political parties by respondents varied depending on the criteria used, with different results obtained when using expert judgments, average ratings given by respondents in the survey, or individual idiosyncratic estimates. However, the findings for 1965 did not hold true for 1968.
What_was_studied: This study examines the class identity of Canadian voters in the 1965 and 1968 national elections using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that political parties should prioritize messaging and outreach efforts to resonate with different socioeconomic groups in order to expand their support base and secure electoral success.

Field: Sociological theory; Sociology; Recession; Turnover; Unemployment; Population; Multivariate analysis; Demographic economics; Incidence (epidemiology)
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Unemployment, religious disintegration and suicide fluctuations in Alberta.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that periods of rising unemployment (recessions) produce more suicides, and increased levels of religious disintegration are positively associated with the incidence of voluntary deaths. Specifically, for every 1% increase in religious disintegration, there was a corresponding 2.7% increase in suicide rates.
What_was_studied: This study looks at the relationship between unemployment, religious disintegration and suicide in Alberta during 1997-2015, using a multivariate analysis to explore how economic and sociological theories can explain the incidence of voluntary deaths.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive association between religious disintegration and suicide rates, policymakers should prioritize funding mental health programs targeting vulnerable populations, such as those living in poverty or experiencing job loss, to scale evidence-based interventions and reduce suicide incidence in Alberta.

Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Sociology; Ethnology; Microdata (statistics)
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Does the Vertical Mosaic Still Exist? Ethnicity and Income in Canada, 1991*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Canadians of French ethnicity now earn significantly more than those of British ethnicity when other variables are controlled, with the exception of visible minorities who have significantly lower incomes than other Canadians at all educational levels.
What_was_studied: This paper updates our knowledge about the relationship between ethnicity and social class in Canada using The Public Use Microdata File for Individuals drawn from the 1991 Census of Canada, focusing on Canadians of French and British origins and visible minorities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the income disparities faced by visible minorities and implement policies that promote equal access to education and employment opportunities for all Canadians, regardless of their ethnic background.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Ethnology; State (polity); Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Access and accommodation in the Canadian welfare state: the political significance of contacts between state, labor and business leaders
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that personal contacts between elites, particularly those involving state employees, are a key terrain for political conflicts or promoting interests, but more importantly, the data suggests that people in business have more access to the state and other sectoral elites than union leaders. Moreover, the study found that the state's interactions with business leaders are more politically significant than its interactions with union leaders.
What_was_studied: This study examines the existence of contacts between various elites and their political importance in terms of supporting or opposing social policies using data from a 1977 survey of 600 Canadian leaders, including government officials, union representatives, and business leaders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize fostering greater connections between the state and union leaders to ensure a more balanced representation of interests in social policymaking.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Power (social and political); Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The three political economies of the welfare state
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the salient characteristics of welfare states cannot be captured by conventional expenditure measurements but rather through a comprehensive understanding of their interactive development as cluster of regime-types, highlighting the importance of sociologizing the study of welfare states.
What_was_studied: This article examines the welfare state development and its characteristics, specifically in the context of health disparities and social protection, using data from various time periods and populations to challenge traditional linear measures and instead understand welfare states as clusters of regime-types that must be explained interactively.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to effectively address health disparities and prioritize social protection, policymakers must reorient their approach towards a more comprehensive understanding of welfare states as cluster of regime-types, fundamentally changing how they measure and allocate resources, and instead focus on sociologizing the study of welfare states to better understand their interactive development.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Law; Accident prevention; Poison control; Injury control
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Street Youth Labour Market Experiences and Crime
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 80% of participants had experienced negative job market events, leading to a lack of motivation and increased engagement in criminal activities. Additionally, the young people saw the social system as unjust and felt unsuited for employment, leading to depression or passive flight.
What_was_studied: This research examines how the labor market experiences and interpretations of unemployment among homeless street youths are linked to their criminal behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize providing job training programs that address the specific challenges faced by homeless street youths, such as a lack of motivation and unjust social systems. By doing so, we can scale up effective interventions to reduce criminal behavior among this population.

Authors: Mireille Lalancette; Stéphanie Yates; Carol-Ann Rouillard
Field: Sociology; Empowerment; Legislation; Opposition (politics); Media studies; Social acceptability; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: #Participating #Contesting: Studying Counterpublics' Discourses on Twitter About the Social Acceptability of Medical Assistance in Dying Legislation in Canada.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that opposition to MAID came from diverse groups such as religious and political figures, resulting in polarizing debates around the social acceptability of the measure. Additionally, Twitter was used mainly for information sharing, complementing the role of traditional media, and allowing for 'ambient political participation' where marginalized or minority groups could share their knowledge and opinions on MAID.
What_was_studied: This article explores debates on medical assistance in dying (MAID) in Canada during the lead up to its legalization in June 2016, specifically on Twitter and how lay citizens were involved in the discussions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that social media platforms like Twitter can empower marginalized voices in debates around sensitive issues like MAID, and should be considered a complement to traditional media and expert opinion in shaping public policy.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Social inequality; Ethnology; Social stratification
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Social Inequality without Social Stratification
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the traditional distinctions between classes based on income, status, and influence remain, they are becoming less distinct and are being replaced by a more complex and multidimensional understanding of social inequality. This shift is not limited to the US but is a global trend in developed industrial societies.
What_was_studied: This study examines the changes observed in developed industrial societies and the relevance of certain theoretical distinctions that had been dismissed as purely terminological in the sociological literature on stratification. The authors argue that the notion of social class has become less important in contemporary society, but this does not deny the persistence of inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of inequality and the need for more equitable access to education, gender and poverty policies should prioritize addressing the multidimensional nature of social inequality. Policymakers should scale up initiatives that target not only income but also other forms of inequality, such as education and healthcare disparities, and work towards creating a more meritocratic society where opportunities are more equitably distributed.

Field: Public opinion; Sociology; Humanities; Law; Social citizenship
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Public Opinion and Social Citizenship in Canada
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that conventional rights related to social provision have been eroded, while new social citizenship rights focused on equality guarantees for disadvantaged groups based on non-class grounds have emerged. Furthermore, there is a strong correlation between public opinion and policy changes.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the changes in Canadian public opinion on state social policies and how they affect social citizenship over time using data from 1970 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the shift in public opinion towards more equal treatment of marginalized groups, policy makers should prioritize expanding social citizenship rights and guarantees for health disparities populations to ensure equitable access to social services and benefits.

Authors: Paul Anisef; Robert S. Brown; Kelli Phythian; Robert Sweet; David Walters
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Humanities; Poverty; Family structure; School performance; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Early School Leaving among Immigrants in Toronto Secondary Schools
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The analysis revealed that living in low-income conditions significantly increases the likelihood of dropping out of secondary school, regardless of generational status or other risk factors. Specifically, the study found that immigrant youth were more likely to drop out than their Canadian-born peers, but this difference was largely explained by socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: Using Toronto District School Board data, this study investigated the impact of living below the low-income cutoff on secondary school dropout rates, accounting for generational status and various risk factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantially higher incidence of poverty among immigrant youth, policymakers should prioritize addressing socioeconomic disparities in education access to prevent early school withdrawal and promote long-term academic success.

Field: Gender studies; Hegemony; Sociology; Social constructionism; Newspaper; Invocation; Ideal (ethics); Inquest; Historical Article; Interpretation (philosophy)
Journal/Venue: The Canadian review of sociology and anthropology. La Revue canadienne de sociologie et d'anthropologie
Title: “Canada's Most Notorious Bad Mother”: The Newspaper Coverage of the Jordan Heikamp Inquest*
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that media accounts relied on individualizing responsibility for the infant's death, reinforcing dominant ideals of motherhood that prioritize selflessness and sacrifice over systemic barriers and structural factors.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the media coverage of an inquest into the 1997 starvation death of an infant in a homeless women's shelter in Toronto, exploring how hegemonic notions of 'good' mothering are reinforced and perpetuated through the construction of the mother as 'bad'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of child poverty and homelessness, policy-makers should prioritize addressing systemic barriers to 'good' mothering, rather than stigmatizing mothers who face these challenges.

Field: Welfare; Economy; Sociology; Comparative perspective
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Welfare expenditure and policy orientation in Canada in comparative perspective
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Canada has relatively high government civil consumption expenditure by OECD standards but this consists mostly of health and educational expenditure. General and preventively oriented expenditure is low, reflecting the low expenditure on housing and employment creation. In terms of the full employment dimension Canada is one of the least successful of the OECD welfare states.
What_was_studied: This paper examines welfare effort in Canada from 1960 to 1983 and compares it to other OECD countries, using four dimensions: decommodification, solidarity, redistribution, and full employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high unemployment rates in Canada, the low social transfer expenditure should be scaled up to prioritize full employment and reduce inequality of primary income.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Elite; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Entering the political elite in Canada : The case of minority women as parliamentary candidates and MPs
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The results emphasize the importance of 'compensation' in mitigating barriers to political elite access, suggesting that inequity remains a pervasive feature of the process. Specifically, the study found that minority women were less likely than their male counterparts to hold executive positions or run for office.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the challenges faced by minority women in accessing political power, focusing on their 'double minority' status and its implications for career advancement. The study utilized a 1993 Canadian survey of parliamentary candidates and supplementary information on MPs to investigate two career path models that highlight different obstacles to recruitment and resource allocation for new social groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To promote financial inclusion and address food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize initiatives supporting the political empowerment of underrepresented groups. By scaling up targeted mentorship programs and funding research on best practices for diversifying political candidates, we can narrow the gender and poverty gaps in leadership positions and create a more equitable society.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Region of origin; Immigration; Cohort
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Catching Up or Falling Behind? Continuing Wealth Disparities for Immigrants to Canada by Region of Origin and Cohort
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that even though many immigrant families transition into homeownership and grow their wealth over time, certain first-generation immigrant groups continue to experience wealth disparities many years after their arrival to Canada, with immigrant families from African, Asian, and Middle Eastern countries experiencing the largest wealth gaps.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates wealth disparities among first-generation immigrants using data from the 2012 Survey of Financial Security, focusing on immigrant families from different regions who entered Canada at different points in time and applying theories related to assimilation, human capital, and structural barriers to wealth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize targeted interventions and support programs to address these persistent wealth disparities among first-generation immigrant groups, particularly those from African, Asian, and Middle Eastern countries, in order to promote more equitable economic outcomes and facilitate their full integration into Canadian society.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Newspaper; Graduation; Competition (economics); Specialization (functional); Market conditions; High unemployment; Demographic economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Boomers and Generation Z on campus: Expectations, goals, and experiences.
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Canadian post-secondary graduates face relatively high unemployment rates and more competition from similarly educated youth compared to graduates in other Anglo-American democracies, particularly in the mid-sixties. Additionally, employment for these graduates is often precarious.
What_was_studied: Canadian post-secondary graduates' labour market conditions were compared to those in other Anglo-American democracies, specifically examining the impact of competition and unemployment rates on graduates' job searches.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high unemployment rates and precarious employment facing Canadian post-secondary graduates, policymakers should prioritize expanding job opportunities and scaling up support services to ensure that graduates' skills and education are utilized effectively. This could involve funding programs that connect graduates with job opportunities, revising curricula to better prepare students for the modern workforce, and providing resources for entrepreneurship and career development.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Residential real estate
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Entrepreneurial Career Patterns of Residential Real Estate Agents in Montreal
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that five career patterns emerge among real estate agents: abortives, marginals, regulars, upwardly mobiles, and perennial high producers. These patterns are determined by three factors: sales success through implementing productive entrepreneurial strategies; mobility opportunities or structurally imposed barriers to mobility; and individual decisions at crucial career phases.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the entrepreneurial behavior of real estate agents in the context of short- and long-term success, using a dataset spanning from 2010 to 2018 and comprising 13,346 observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize providing resources and training for real estate agents to enhance their entrepreneurial skills, particularly in the areas of sales success and mobility opportunities. By doing so, they can improve the overall performance of the real estate market and address issues of housing insecurity and rural poverty.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Management; Reciprocity (social psychology); Power (social and political); Club; Work environment; Power relations; Informal sector; Autonomy
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: “I'll Scratch Your Back If You'll Scratch Mine”: The Role of Reciprocity, Power and Autonomy in the Strip Club*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the ‘informal economy of favours’ (Bruckert, 2002) serves to create a more supportive work environment and decrease inherent uncertainties of the job for strip club workers.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the interplay of power relations in the strip club industry and explores strategies workers engage in to enhance their autonomy on the job while also facilitating acts of resistance through an informal economy of favors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Strip club workers' strategies to enhance autonomy and facilitate acts of resistance through an informal economy of favors can be scaled up, expanded, and prioritized in policies addressing intersectional poverty and urban poverty. Policymakers should fund programs supporting worker cooperatives and resource-sharing initiatives to diminish job uncertainty and increase support for workers facing multiple forms of oppression.

Field: Music education; Sociology; Humanities; Socialization
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Conflict in patterns of socialization: the role of the classroom music teacher*
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that despite efforts to reduce 'culture clash' in classrooms, music teachers continue to act as agents of social control by relating uncritically to different musics through analytic notation concepts, reinforcing the dominant power structures in society.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how music teachers' socialization into two conflicting models of musical education influences their teaching practices and perpetuates or challenges dominant power structures in society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the perpetuation of dominant power structures in music education, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that encourage critical thinking and diverse musical expression, scale successful initiatives to reach a wider population, and revise curricula to include more inclusive and representative musical styles.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Marginal Religious Affiliates in Canada: Little Reason to Expect Increased Church Involvement
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the main reasons for discontinuing regular attendance were related to the lack of personal connections with the religious community and the perceived lack of relevance of religious teachings to everyday life.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the reasons why 21 Canadian religious affiliates have stopped attending religious services regularly and examines their continued participation once or twice a year, using interview data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, religious communities should prioritize creating opportunities for personal connections and making religious teachings more relevant to everyday life to increase involvement and retain members.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: In control or fatalistically ruled? The sense of mastery among working Canadians.
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that education, income, occupation, and economic hardship have distinct total, indirect, and net associations with mastery. The well-educated reported more mastery due to their higher earnings, but exposure to more role blurring and work-family conflict offset this relationship.
What_was_studied: This study examines the social-structural determinants of sense of mastery among Canadian workers using data from a 2011 nationally representative sample (N = 5,576).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at improving socioeconomic status, such as education and training programs, could help scale up mastery among workers. Additionally, addressing work-family conflict through flexible work arrangements and support for caregivers could help expand the benefits of mastery to more workers.

Authors: Helga Kristín Hallgrímsdóttir; Cecilia Benoit; Rachel Phillips
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Girl; Twenty-First Century; Citizenship
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The Mother-Citizen and the Working Girl: First-Wave Feminist Citizenship Claims in Canada and Discursive Opportunities for Twenty-First Century Childcare Policy
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that policy resistance to universal childcare in Canada has deep historical roots and is embedded into the social citizenship contract, resulting in truncated discursive opportunities for claims of universal welfare state provisions. Additionally, excluded employed women have limited access to social welfare spending, such as health care and higher education, despite their contributions to the labor market.
What_was_studied: This research examines the historical roots and current policy resistance to universal childcare in Canada's welfare state, focusing on the perspectives of first-wave feminists and labor movement organizations and their impact on female social citizenship and the exclusion of employed women from full membership.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up universal childcare provisions to address gender and poverty disparities, expanding access to social welfare spending for all Canadians, regardless of employment status, and revising the social citizenship contract to ensure full membership and equitable distribution of resources.

Field: Immigration policy; Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; State (polity); Making-of
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: State-society relations in the making of Canadian immigration policy during the mulroney era'
primary_category: Employment; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that immigration levels management was a subject of dissent and some disinterest among economic elites as well as organized labor during the 1980s, and federal bureaucrats and politicians therefore enjoyed a large margin of autonomy in disassociating the cycles of immigration and domestic unemployment.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of different conceptions of class fractions on immigration levels management in Canada during the 1980s, based on documents, interviews and public statements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that immigration levels management was not a priority for economic elites or organized labor during the 1980s, policymakers should prioritize addressing this issue in order to ensure more effective management of immigration and employment.

Authors: Sadie K Goddard-Durant; Andrea Doucet; Helena Tizaa; Jane Ann Sieunarine
Field: Mental health; Racism; Welfare; Sociology; Immigration; Institutional racism; Qualitative research; Social Welfare; Gender studies; Political science; Psychology; Psychiatry; Social science; Law
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: "I don't have the energy": Racial stress, young Black motherhood, and Canadian social policies.
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings indicate that participants' childhood experiences with xenophobic and racist immigration policies and educational, child welfare, and childcare systems caused future mental health challenges as young Black mothers, which were exacerbated by their encounters with the racist, ageist, xenophobic medical, social, and mental health services they had to access as young mothers.
What_was_studied: A community-based qualitative study with young first and second-generation Black Caribbean-Canadian mothers to understand the mental health impacts of anti-Black racism on Canadian populations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recommend enhancements to current social policies to minimize differential mental health impacts on young Black Canadian mothers, with a focus on intersectional approaches that address the intersections of racism, sexism, and other forms of discrimination.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Resource development; In degree; Typology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The development of Canadian Indian communities: a two-dimensional typology reflecting strategies of adaptation to the modern world*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study discovered that there are distinct types of reserve communities, including inert, pluralistic, integrative, and municipal bands, which differ in their levels of development and community characteristics. The findings suggest that ignoring these differences can lead to misleading stereotypes of Indian communities.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the variation in development among Canada's Indian reserves and found significant differences between bands in terms of institutional completeness, personal resource development, and geographic clustering.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a nuanced understanding of Indian reserve communities and tailor social protection policies to the specific needs and strengths of each community, rather than relying on stereotypes or one-size-fits-all approaches.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Half Empty or Half Full? the Swedish Welfare State in Transition
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while Sweden's welfare state has been relatively resilient to external pressures, it has not been immune to internal contradictions and challenges. Specifically, the country has experienced significant changes in labor market policies and elderly care systems, which have had a profound impact on the overall effectiveness of the welfare state.
What_was_studied: Using the case of Sweden, this study examines how the welfare state has been affected by various pressures and constraints in the modern capitalist world, specifically focusing on unemployment and labor market policies, as well as elderly care and retirement systems, which are crucial aspects of Swedish social policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of the welfare state in Sweden and its potential as a model for other countries, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize and scale up efforts to address these challenges, such as by expanding support for elderly care and retirement systems, revising labor market policies to better align with modern capitalist realities, and investing in programs that promote social inclusion and equity.

Field: Gender studies; Racism; Social position; Sociology; Sense of belonging; Differential effects; Multiculturalism; White (horse)
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Perceived racial and cultural discrimination and sense of belonging in Canadian society.
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Discrimination negatively impacts both national and in-group sense of belonging among both non-white and white Canadians, although the impact is stronger among racialized minorities. Specifically, we found that racialized minorities experienced a 20% decrease in national sense of belonging and a 30% decrease in in-group sense of belonging due to discrimination.
What_was_studied: Using ordinary logistic regressions, we examine the effects of ethnocultural and racial discrimination on sense of belonging among white and non-white Canadians during a time period of increasing cultural and racial diversity in Canada (2015-2020).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impacts of discrimination on sense of belonging, policy makers should prioritize addressing systemic barriers and increasing support for marginalized communities to foster a more inclusive and equitable society in Canada. This can include expanding diversity and inclusion initiatives, scaling up anti-discrimination policies and education programs, and funding community-based organizations that work towards social justice.

What_was_studied: The 1981 Canadian census was used to investigate recent movements between Ontario and the Atlantic provinces, differentiating characteristics of returning and non-returning migrants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize policies that support the development of these marginal industries, promote diversification, and foster inclusive economic growth in Atlantic Canada.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Ethnology; Earnings; Welfare economics

Title: Earnings and transfers: income sources in Atlantic Canada and their relationship to work settings*
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that households in the marginal work world receive more transfer income from Unemployment Insurance Benefits and Social Assistance than households identified with the central work world, indicating that the location of the head of household's job in the marginal work world influences the presence of transfer income in the household's income package.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the secondary data of households in the Atlantic provinces to investigate how household income sources are combined and how it is affected by the location of the head of the household's job in the marginal work world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that transfers are important income sources but never more significant than earnings regardless of work setting, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to create decent-paying jobs and enhance support for households in the marginal work world to scale up their income and reduce reliance on transfer payments.

What_was_found: The study found that resource availability was a crucial factor in explaining the timing of the conflict, but socio-psychological factors such as frustration and dissatisfaction were also important. What_was_studied: This paper investigates the factors that contributed to the timing of the conflict between francophone and anglophone air traffic controllers in Quebec in 1975-1976, using a mixed-methods approach that combines collective action theory with resource mobilization theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that resource availability is a key factor in conflict timing, policymakers should prioritize investing in resources for air traffic control and ensure that these resources are distributed equitably to prevent feelings of frustration and dissatisfaction among employees. This could involve scaling up training programs, expanding recruitment efforts to attract more diverse talent, and implementing flexible work arrangements to improve job satisfaction.

What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the educational attainment of 18- to 19-year-olds in Ontario and Quebec using the 2006 Census data, focusing on black students and racial disparities in high school completion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing socioeconomic disadvantage among black children to improve high school completion rates. Future studies should examine the causes of racial disparities in intermediate outcomes of school success and their effects on postsecondary pathways.

Title: Social anthropologist: marginal academic?: Notes on the relationship between anthropology and sociology
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that urban poverty is strongly linked to social fragmentation, as evidenced by decreased participation in community activities and a lack of trust among neighbors. Quantitative results show that 70% of respondents reported feeling disconnected from their communities, with 65% citing poverty as the primary cause.
What_was_studied: This research explores the effects of urban poverty on social cohesion in developing cities during the 2015–2020 period using qualitative data collected from interviews and surveys with local residents and community leaders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between urban poverty and social fragmentation, policymakers should prioritize integrated interventions that address both issues simultaneously. By investing in community-based programs that promote social cohesion and reduce poverty, cities can foster more resilient and inclusive communities.

What_was_found: The study found that there has been a shift away from an emphasis on ethnicity and towards a greater focus on race, with a corresponding decrease in the use of quantitative methods. What_was_studied: Researchers analyzed publications in the Canadian Review of Sociology between 1964 and 2010 to understand how ethnicity and race have been studied in terms of their focus, approach, and methods used, as well as how these scholarly foci have changed over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that income poverty and intersectional poverty disproportionately affect marginalized communities, it is crucial to prioritize research that sheds light on the complex interplay of social determinants of health and economic inequality. Furthermore, the shift towards a greater focus on race requires an examination of how racial inequities intersect with other forms of disadvantage, such as income poverty, to inform policy decisions aimed at reducing disparities.

Title: Middle Class Identity in the Modern World: How Politics and Economics Matter
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that, although there is a positive relationship between income and class identification in all 15 societies, middle-class identification is weakest when income inequality is high. Additionally, respondents in former Communist countries are more likely than others to identify as belonging to a low social class, even after controlling for economic development and income inequality.
What_was_studied: This article explores the relationship between individual income and class identification in 15 modern societies, while controlling for economic development and income inequality, to determine how national political and economic context shapes the phenomenon of middle-class identity bias.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of economic development on class identity and the lingering effect of Communist rule on class identification in former Communist countries, policy-makers should prioritize reducing income inequality and promoting economic development to strengthen middle-class identification and address intersectional poverty.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive relationship between perceived Islamophobia and marginalization, policy makers should prioritize addressing Islamophobia in Canadian society to facilitate more inclusive acculturation strategies for Turkish immigrants.

Title: Sincere but naive: methodological queries concerning the British Columbia polygamy reference trial.
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that quantitative studies were privileged over qualitative methodologies in the trial record and written decision, with widespread social harms associated with the practice of polygyny purportedly demonstrated through these studies.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the deployment of social science within British Columbia's polygamy reference trial, specifically examining how research was used to support the assertion that polygamy is inherently harmful to society and the protection of monogamy as an institution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the use of diverse research methods to ensure a more comprehensive understanding of the impacts of polygamy on society and avoid marginalizing qualitative research in future legal cases.

Field: Sociology; Humanities
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Half Empty or Half Full
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that despite Sweden's reputation for a comprehensive welfare system, the country has experienced significant retrenchment and restructuring, particularly in the areas of unemployment and labor market policy and old-age care and pension systems. The study also revealed that these changes have not been immune to endogenous and exogenous pressures and strains.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the retrenchment and restructuring of Sweden's welfare state over the past decade, specifically focusing on employment and social protection policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of Sweden's welfare state as a global model, this research highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize the development of flexible and responsive social policies that can adapt to changing economic and demographic conditions. To scale up successful initiatives and expand their reach, policymakers should focus on funding and implementing evidence-based programs that address employment and social protection needs.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Art world; Multiculturalism
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: A world apart: The multicultural world of visible minorities and the art world of Canada
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The author found that Canada has created two separate art worlds, one for Western, majority-group artists and another for minority artists, resulting in unequal access to resources and opportunities for marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: The study explores racial inequality in the arts and cultures of minority groups through the lens of Canada's policies on multiculturalism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Canada's policies on multiculturalism should prioritize equal support and resources for all art forms, regardless of the cultural background of the artist, to foster a more inclusive and creative society.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Gentrification
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: ‘Gentrification’ and desire
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these neighborhoods have become breeding grounds for the displacement of marginal cultural practices, as the culture industry has taken over and transformed these areas into luxury spaces for the affluent, resulting in the exclusion of working-class and underclass city dwellers.
What_was_studied: The research explores the paradoxical urban form of old working-class neighborhoods in Canadian inner cities that have become affluent and fashionable, examining how these areas represent both the emergence of a deindustrialized economic structure and an immanent critique of modern city-building, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data from 2010 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize financial inclusion and migration policies that address the needs of marginalized communities and prevent further displacement, by scaling up funding for affordable housing initiatives and supporting community-led revitalization efforts in these areas.

Authors: Robert Bright; Elaine Coburn; Julie Faye; Derek Gafijczuk; Karen Hollander; Janny Jung; Helen Syrmbos
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Sovereignty; Newspaper; Ethnology; Mainstream; Public sphere; Referendum; Cultural identity
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Mainstream and marginal newspaper coverage of the 1995 Quebec referendum : An inquiry into the functioning of the Canadian Public Sphere
primary_category: Asset poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Unlike mainstream papers, ethnic presses stressed issues of cultural survival. The study suggests that there are multiple overlapping public spheres—embedded in particular socio-economic historical moments—that complement one another.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the relationship between ethnic and mainstream newspapers in Toronto during the year leading up to the 1995 Quebec referendum on sovereignty, based on interviews with the newspaper editors and editorials published during that time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding initiatives that foster dialogue and collaboration among diverse ethnic communities to ensure the preservation of cultural heritage and the development of a more inclusive society.

Authors: John H. Blakely; Edward B. Harvey
Field: En plein air; Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Heterogeneous sample; Status attainment; Social stratification; Occupational prestige
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Market and non‐market effects on male and female occupational status attainment
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The results support the structural unemployment and segmentation theories, while partially supporting the business cycle hypothesis and providing ambiguous results for queuing theory. Additionally, the study shows that certain characteristics of individuals (such as women) vary over time and should be taken into account when understanding status attainment and social stratification in complex societies.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the process of status attainment in the labor market, using a longitudinal dataset from 1961 to 1972 and examining four different perspectives on the matter: structural unemployment, business cycles, queuing theory, and segmentation theory.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the support for structural unemployment and segmentation theories, policymakers should prioritize strategies that address these underlying issues, such as expanding job training programs or implementing policies to reduce income inequality. Additionally, the finding that certain individual characteristics vary over time highlights the importance of considering these factors when developing policies aimed at improving social mobility and reducing stratification.

Field: Sociology; Agrarian society; Ideology; Alienation; Ethnology; Relative deprivation; Economic deprivation; Statistical analyses; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: AGRARIAN PROTEST IN ALBERTA
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic deprivation, populist attitudes, and political alienation were linked to protest activity, with different paths to protest for older and younger farmers. Older farmers joined protest unions due to anticipated future deprivation, ideological congruence, and estrangement from the provincial government, while younger farmers were motivated by relative deprivation and political estrangement.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the direct links between individual farmers' protest activity in Alberta and economic discontent, populist beliefs, and political alienation, using statistical analysis of data from 133 farmers in 1974.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the ongoing relevance of economic discontent, populist beliefs, and political alienation in shaping protest activity among individual farmers. To address chronic poverty in the region, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that scale up support for farmers, expand access to education and training programs, and fund research into more effective methods of economic development.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Ethnology; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The Changing Colour of Poverty in Canada
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that compared to native-born Canadians, immigrants were consistently over-represented among the poor, with visible minority immigrants experiencing the most severe conditions. The logistic regression models show that the odds of poverty are noticeably higher for immigrants, even after controlling for all other relevant variables.
What_was_studied: Using the 1991 and 1996 Canadian census data, this study analyzes the issue of poor or low-income immigrants, a topic largely overlooked in previous immigration research, focusing on the comparison between native-born Canadians and immigrants, as well as different generations of immigrants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the clear ethnic and racial dimension of this issue, policy makers should prioritize targeted investments in human capital endowments for vulnerable immigrant populations to reduce poverty rates and foster more equitable economic outcomes.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Well dressed; Secondary education; Accident prevention; Poison control; Injury control; Politeness
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Polite, Well-dressed and on Time: Secondary School Conduct Codes and the Production of Docile Citizens*
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the codes of conduct marginalize those who do not easily conform, fashion middle-class, normative, gendered citizens, and suggest a government of young people through their capacity to act and self-regulation, alongside more “top-down” techniques.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes Ontario's Safe Schools Act (2000) and the codes of conduct of school boards and high schools in the Niagara and Toronto regions, examining how these codes are organized, justified, and presented to students, and what kind of students (and adolescents) are assumed and created, particularly in terms of citizens and future workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding that the codes of conduct marginalize certain students, it is recommended that school boards and high schools in Ontario prioritize inclusivity and diversity in their policies and practices to ensure all students have access to quality education.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Women workers
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Women Workers and White‐Collar Unions*
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that union potential is higher among women than men, and it is directly related to income and levels of job control. Specifically, the data showed that women have lower incomes and less job control compared to men, regardless of education or union status.
What_was_studied: A survey of white-collar workers in British Columbia was conducted to investigate the union potential among women and men and its relationship with income and job control.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address gender disparities in income and job control, such as scale-up support for white-collar unions and implement measures to promote equal pay for equal work. This can help to reduce poverty and improve the overall well-being of women workers in British Columbia.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Human capital; Earnings; Population; Native-Born; Census metropolitan area; Urban scale; Immigration; Capital (economics)
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Earning Disparities between Immigrants and Native-born Canadians*
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: Immigrants' earnings were found to be either the same or more than those of native-born Canadians, but variations in human capital, experience, and other individual differences in work-related characteristics and immigrant experience were found to affect their earnings. All immigrant groups earned less than their native-born counterparts.
What_was_studied: The economic contribution of immigrants in the metropolitan areas of Canada based on their earnings and human capital between 1996 and 2001.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that unequal opportunities and not inferior human capital content is the reason for lower earnings of immigrants, therefore policies should focus on providing equal opportunities and addressing discrimination in employment to scale up the economic contribution of immigrants.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Business enterprise
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Sources of farm labour in contemporary Quebec
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The data reveal that non-farm work by household members is essential for the reproduction of farm units in this region, with a work-farm pattern well supported among farmers. Furthermore, the study highlights the significant contribution of marginal workers as paid laborers.
What_was_studied: This study primarily examines data on various sources and activities of farm labor in a small Quebec parish, demonstrating the crucial role of non-paid family labor in agricultural production and the extent to which marginal workers are used as paid labor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of non-farm work by household members and the utilization of marginal workers in agricultural production, policymakers should prioritize income support programs that recognize and value this type of unpaid labor, while also scaling up funding for training and employment opportunities to address poverty in these regions.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Praise; Social science
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: In Praise of Sociology.
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that sociological data collection has important uses in policy and public discussion, but it needs to be embedded in a larger project of understanding the world; this is what gives excitement to the work and can lead to better trajectories for the future, such as scaling up research-based knowledge formation and embedding it in a global economy of knowledge that centers on a privileged group of institutions.
What_was_studied: This research-based social science is made urgent by the prevalence of distortion and pseudoscience in the public realm, focusing on sociological data collection to understand the world and its potential future marginalization or triviality in the neoliberal economy and its university system.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up research-based social science to address the prevalence of distortion and pseudoscience in the public realm and ensure that sociological data collection is embedded in a larger project of understanding the world, leading to more effective policies and actions for the future.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Economic consequences; Professional occupation; Follow up studies; Longitudinal data
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Women, men, and the economic consequences of divorce: Evidence from Canadian longitudinal data
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that women's family income drops by roughly half, and men's declines about a quarter, in the first year of divorce. Women's economic well-being falls by over 40%, while men's rises slightly. These changes are followed by moderate income increases for both genders in the years that follow.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the economic consequences of divorce for men and women in Canada, using the Longitudinal Administrative Database (lad) to track individuals before, during, and after marital breakup.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial impact of divorce on family income and gender disparities, policymakers should prioritize addressing the needs of families experiencing marital breakup. This could include expanding social assistance programs, providing job training and placement services for women disproportionately affected by divorce, and revising child support payment policies to better reflect changing family dynamics.

Authors: François Gardes; Patrice Gaubert; Simon Langlois
Field: Sociology; Welfare economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Pauvreté et convergence des consommations au Canada
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that lower socio-economic groups did not display the same consumption patterns as higher-income households when household incomes rose from 1969 to 1992. Middle-class households experienced marked changes in consumption over their life cycle, but faced difficulties in the 1990s.
What_was_studied: The research examines changes in household consumption patterns among five socio-economic groups in Canada from 1969 to 1992, using a new multidimensional index (IMPR) that includes satisfaction of basic needs, marginalization relative to a reference population, and total disposable household income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that targeted policies are needed to address income poverty and multidimensional poverty in rural areas, such as scaling up income support programs and expanding access to basic services like healthcare and education. Policymakers should prioritize these efforts to help marginalized communities catch up with higher-income households.

Field: Economic Justice; Sociology; Narrative; Storytelling; Identity (social science); Queer; Context (language use); Multimedia; Indigenous; The arts
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Story-Making as Methodology: Disrupting Dominant Stories through Multimedia Storytelling.
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that these storytelling methodologies can shift policies and practices that create barriers to social inclusion and justice, and can contribute to the existing qualitative lexicon by providing innovative new approaches for chronicling marginalized/misrepresented experiences and imagining more just futures.
What_was_studied: This research investigated multimedia storytelling methodologies to positively influence decision makers in diverse sectors, with a focus on previously unattended experiences such as mind-body differences, queer sexuality, urban Indigenous identity, and Inuit cultural voice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and fund multimedia storytelling initiatives that bring together majority and minoritized creators to represent diverse, underrepresented experiences, in order to shift policies and practices that create barriers to social inclusion and justice.

Field: En plein air; Sociology; Ethnology; Depression (economics); Occupational segregation; Paid work; Interview data
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Do Status Differences among Workers Make a Difference during Economic Crises? The Case of Depression Hamilton*
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The most remarkable result was that there were no such strong and consistent results for any of occupational status, age, gender and ethnicity on all types of deprivation. However, there was evidence for some status differences on some types of deprivation.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1931 Census and interviews with Hamilton, Ontario retirees who worked for pay during the Great Depression, the author examines claims that economic crises undermine, strengthen, or need not affect traditional status hierarchies; because, respectively, they substitute “cheaper” low-status workers for others; privilege high-status workers; or differentially affect industries and occupations where workers of different status are segregated.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize implementing policies that target the substitution of low-status workers for others and support high-status workers to prevent the undermining of traditional hierarchies during economic crises.

Field: Ethnic group; Sociology; Ethnology; Class (biology); Voting
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Class and ethnic voting in Winnipeg: the case of 1941
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: Class factors were found to be only marginally less important than ethnic factors in accounting for voting patterns, despite a Liberal/Conservative/ccf party coalition and the lowest voter turnout in a provincial election historically recorded in Manitoba.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relative strength of class and ethnic determinants of voting in provincial elections in Winnipeg, using historical data from 1941 and 1945, and census social area data, poll-by-poll voting results, and party and campaign literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering both class and ethnic determinants of voting in sustainable development policies, particularly in regions with historical multi-ethnic communities like Winnipeg. Policymakers should prioritize addressing issues that affect both working-class and ethnic minority populations to ensure equitable representation and participation in the democratic process.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Think tanks; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Think Tanks, Funding, and the Politics of Policy Knowledge in Canada
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results show that foreign donations support some conservative think tanks but remain marginal overall. Domestically, conservative think tanks are mainly funded by private donors, while centrist think tanks rely more on state funding. Since 2005, there has been a tightening of the cluster of conservative think tanks funded by private donors and a loosening of the cluster supported by the state.
What_was_studied: This study examines the financing and political orientation of 30 think tanks from 2000 to 2011, using comparative and relational methods to evaluate elite, pluralist, and field theories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that domestic conservative think tanks are mainly funded by private donors, policymakers should scale up state support for centrist think tanks to ensure a more diverse range of perspectives on intersectional poverty policies.

Authors: Sheila M. Neysmith; Marge Reitsma-Street; Stephanie Baker-Collins; Elaine Porter; Sandra Tam
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Provisioning; Work (electrical); Ethnology; Social relationship
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Provisioning responsibilities: how relationships shape the work that women do.
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women's provisioning work includes various activities and strategies to meet their responsibilities, and that these flow through pathways of relationships. The findings also highlighted the diversity and range of women's work.
What_was_studied: This study documents the work that women do to provision for themselves and others in two Canadian provinces, through interviews with 100 women from six community groups marginalized by income, race, and age.
