Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that support women's provisioning work and empower them to engage in civil society, such as scaling up support programs for community groups and organizations led by marginalized women, expanding access to affordable childcare and healthcare, and funding research on the social and economic impact of unpaid care work.

Authors: Scott Davies; Clayton Mosher Mosher; Bill O'Grady
Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Wage; Real wages; Unemployment; Earnings; Demographic economics; Inequality
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Educating Women: Gender Inequalities among Canadian University Graduates*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results show that gender became a weaker predictor of these outcomes, with the female-male earning ratio growing from 84% to 91% over this period, but a notable wage gap remained in later cohorts.
What_was_studied: This paper compares male versus female income and unemployment for three cohorts of university graduates between 1978 and 1988, using data from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the persistence of gender segregation within occupations that result in disparate earning trajectories. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize programs that promote equal career opportunities for women and men, such as mentorship initiatives and targeted training programs.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Jamais vu; Dentistry; Professional practice; Dental practice; Dental education
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Gender and Women's Employment in the Male‐dominated Profession of Dentistry: 1867–1917*
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite being never excluded from the profession, women in dentistry experienced marginalization and encouragement to pursue sex-typed behavior and roles, similar to those in medicine.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on women's experiences in the male-dominated profession of dentistry in Ontario between 1867 and 1917, examining their entrance into the profession, education, and practice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this research, policy makers should prioritize addressing gender disparities in professional education and practice to promote more inclusive work environments for all professionals.

Field: Psychology; Sociology; Positive economics; Epistemology; Economics; Philosophy
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Black life, complexities, nuances, and insights.
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite recent efforts to address anti-Black racism, Black Canadians continue to face significant barriers to employment, education, health, and other social outcomes. Data showed that Black people are underrepresented in certain fields such as education and employment, and that they experience higher rates of poverty, unemployment, and incarceration.
What_was_studied: The legacy of systemic anti-Black racism in Canada and its effects on Black Canadians' employment, education, health, and other social outcomes, as well as the effectiveness of recent equity, diversity, inclusion, and decolonization initiatives aimed at addressing these issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent disparities faced by Black Canadians, it is crucial to scale up equity, diversity, inclusion, and decolonization initiatives to address systemic anti-Black racism in employment, education, health, and other social outcomes. Policymakers must prioritize funding and resources for these initiatives to ensure that Black Canadians have equal access to opportunities and resources.

Field: Ethnic group; Census; Population; Race (biology); Health equity; Pandemic; Geography; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Political science; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Sociology; Gender studies; Health care; Medicine; Disease; Pathology; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Law
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Themed section introduction: Emerging research on racial/ethnic inequality in Canada.
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Racial/ethnic disparities in vulnerability to the pandemic were difficult to assess due to limited data availability, with Indigenous peoples and immigrants experiencing higher levels of discrimination in smaller and mid-sized communities, and Asian men facing sexual racism both online and offline.
What_was_studied: The health, social, and economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic on population groups in Canada, particularly by race/ethnicity, using high-quality individual-level data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address racial/ethnic disparities in health outcomes and social relations during the pandemic, policymakers should prioritize collecting more detailed race-based data, expanding access to education and employment for marginalized groups, and funding research that explores the intersections between race/ethnicity, immigration, and technology use in cyberspace.

Field: Sociology; Negotiation; Dependency (project management); Accident prevention; Poison control; Injury control; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Negotiating the Dependency/Nurturance Tightrope: Dilemmas of Motherhood and Disability*
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that disabled mothers are often caught in a dilemma between nurturance and dependency, with limited access to resources and social support. Moreover, the study reveals that negative conceptions of dependence can exacerbate their challenges, leading to poverty and vulnerability.
What_was_studied: This study explores the challenges faced by disabled mothers in rural areas of developing countries, specifically examining how normative femininity and gendered expectations of motherhood affect their experiences of poverty and vulnerability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the specific challenges faced by disabled mothers in rural areas, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions providing resources and social support to help them balance nurturance and dependency. Moreover, efforts to challenge negative conceptions of dependence can help scale up these initiatives and expand their reach.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Cape; Workfare; Cousin
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Workfare's Cousin: Exploring a Labour-force Enhancement Experiment in Cape Breton*
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: L'analyse presentee ici avance l'idee que, en depit du discours public officiel, la conception du programme n'apporte que peu d'avantages a la collectivite locale et a ses citoyens le plus dans le besoin, mais vehicule des avantages ideologiques importants pour l'etat.
What_was_studied: Cet article etudie la structure de l'un de ces programmes, parraine par le gouvernement federal, dans la region de la province la plus marginale sur le plan economique, Cape Breton, aupres des beneficiaires de paiements de transfert gouvernementaux.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Le gouvernement devrait prioriser le soutien communautaire et les programmes de formation professionnelle pour les beneficiaires de paiements de transfert gouvernementaux dans la region de Cape Breton, afin d'améliorer significativement la situation économique et sociale de cette région marginale.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Social policy; Food bank
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Housing affordability, social policy and economic conditions: Food bank users in the Greater Toronto Area, 1990-2000
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The analysis confirms that social assistance rate reductions and housing costs are factors contributing to the decline in post-shelter income available to food bank users.
What_was_studied: This paper examines trends in social and economic correlates of food bank usage in the Greater Toronto Area between 1990-2000 through annual interviews with users.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize addressing affordable housing problems and ensuring stable social assistance benefits to reduce economic vulnerability among already marginalized families.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; French
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Quantitative methods and contemporary sociology in francophone Quebec
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Quantitative studies were found to be marginalized within Quebec francophone sociology, with limited scope in terms of population, time period, and data, and an overreliance on pre-existing methodologies.
What_was_studied: The study demonstrates the limited scope of quantitative analysis in the official activities of Quebec francophone sociologists, with few researchers publishing quantitative articles and focusing on specific subject matters such as the Quebec context and elaborate theoretical frameworks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of multidimensional poverty in Quebec, policymakers should prioritize the development of quantitative methods tailored to the local context, expanding the scope of sociological research beyond a few select subject matters and elite theoretical frameworks to better understand the complexities of poverty and social exclusion.

Authors: Carl J. Cuneo; James E. Curtis
Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Ascription; Occupational prestige
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Social ascription in the educational and occupational status attainment of urban Canadians
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social ascription plays a strong role in determining respondents' occupational status in Canada, with family background having different effects on men and women and on francophones and anglophones. Mother's education has the strongest effect on respondent's education among French males, while family size has a greater negative impact on education among anglophones than among francophones.
What_was_studied: This paper reports on an extension of the Blau-Duncan model to urban Canadian samples and additional independent variables, applying it to four subsamples of urban Canadians by gender and language, and exploring how social ascription affects respondents' education and occupation attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that policies aimed at improving education access and reducing poverty in urban Canada should prioritize addressing the ascriptive effects of social background, particularly for women and those from language minority communities. Interventions targeting family background variables such as mother's education and family size may be necessary to scale up educational attainment and reduce occupation-based poverty.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Residence; Maximization; Economic deprivation; Welfare economics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Maximization, Marriage, and Residence among the So*
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: Les resultats montrent que le betail alloue a la dot est une utilisation secondare des ressources, et que les So realignent leurs mecanismes dallocation des ressources lorsque les resources deviennent rares.
What_was_studied: L'etude a etudie les ramifications economiques de la date et de la residence post-nuptiale chez les So du Nord-est de lOuganda au cours d'une periode de 12 ans, en utilisant des données de terrain collectees aupres de 300 foyers So.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: En basant nos politiques sur la theorie de la maximisation, nous pouvons prioriser l'allocation des ressources pour la construction de residences durables et resistantes au changement climatique, ce qui permettra aux So de continuer a vivre dans leur habitat traditionnel.

Field: Market segmentation; Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Social mobility
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Labour market segmentation and social mobility in a Canadian single-industry community†
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there was only minor mobility differences between the Canadian labor force and Fort McMurray's labor force, workers in core sector firms experienced different mobility patterns than those working in peripheral sector firms.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the occupational mobility opportunities in Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada, focusing on a 1979 sample of male residents and their socio-economic status changes over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that scale socio-economic opportunities for residents of Fort McMurray and other single-industry towns to improve their gender and poverty outcomes.

Field: Nous; Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Making-of; Chose; Face (sociological concept); Humanity
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Matters of Scale: Sociology in and for a Complex World
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The article found that the traditional nested vertical hierarchy of the micro to macro binary is not sufficient for understanding the complex world we live in, and that attending to ambiguity and the unfinished making of our contemporary world can provide valuable insights for discussions about the economy, the future of humanity, and how to organize society.
What_was_studied: This article explores how sociology can make sense of our increasingly complex world by reconsidering the scale(s) of our relations and actions, treating them as multiple and produced in practice, and paying attention to the connections between sites, fields, and terrains.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To better understand and address intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize a multiscale approach that considers the complex intersections of social, economic, and political factors in different sites, fields, and terrains, and fund research that can provide valuable insights for making informed decisions.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Citizenship
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Women's Changing Relations to the State and Citizenship: Caring and Intergenerational Relations in Globalizing Western Democracies*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a contradiction between the gendered shrinking of welfare states and women's dramatic increases in paid work, as well as growing concerns about social cohesion. Additionally, it was discovered that deepening marginalization of women parallels growing concerns about social cohesion.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the evolution of women's relations with the state in three sociological perspectives: 1) women and welfare states; 2) recent citizenship literature; and 3) social cohesion, based on the premise that the state can invest in women's rights and protect them in the context of shrinking states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize investing in women's rights and protections, as well as addressing the gendered implications of shrinking welfare states, in order to promote sustainable development and social cohesion.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Ethnology; Criminal behaviour; Accident prevention; Job placement; Poison control; Injury control
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Labour‐Market Problems and Crime in the Transition from School to Work*
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Employment; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that labor market problems such as unemployment and job instability may lead to criminal behavior, especially when combined with certain attitudes and beliefs about the workplace. The presence of delinquent friends also played a role in the development of criminal behavior during this transition period.
What_was_studied: This longitudinal panel study examined the transition from school to work among Canadian youth, focusing on how labor market problems and social influences affect criminal behavior over a four-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize education and employment programs that address labor market problems and provide young adults with positive social influences to prevent criminal behavior. Governments should also consider implementing policies that reduce poverty, improve access to education, and provide job training and placement services to help young adults successfully transition into the workforce.

Field: Sociology; Ethnology; Context (language use); Subordination (finance); Common property; Regional development; Historical evidence; Underdevelopment; Fishing
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Common property rights and regional subordination in a staples economy: the rise and decline of the British Columbia coastal fishing community, 1880–1981
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: Historical evidence demonstrates how the common property and perishable qualities of the fishing resource combined with processor and harvesting capital to fuel a brief economic heyday along the rural coast earlier in this century, resulting in the creation of a number of coastal fishing communities.
What_was_studied: The emergence and decline of the British Columbia hinterland coastal fishing society between 1880 and 1981 was examined to identify the reasons for its existence and eclipse, using historical evidence from the British Columbia fisheries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for sustainable development strategies that prioritize the unique resource properties of the staple and the specific needs of coastal communities to ensure the long-term survival of these communities.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Humanities; Ethnology
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Factory to faculty: socioeconomic difference and the educational experiences of university professors.
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that several measures of socioeconomic background were significant predictors of academic experiences, with working-class faculty members being particularly hyper-aware of how their background affected their educational trajectories.
What_was_studied: This study surveyed a random sample of full-time university professors at all 95 Canadian universities to analyze the impact of socioeconomic background on their experiences within university and graduate school.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to shift focus away from apolitical discussions of diversity and towards promoting inclusivity for those from working-class or lower-income backgrounds. Policy makers should prioritize funding programs that support students from disadvantaged backgrounds and revise hiring practices to promote diversity in the academic workforce.

Field: Anthropocene; Sociology; Anthropology; Resource scarcity; Environmental sociology
Journal/Venue: Canadian review of sociology = Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: An Environmental Sociology for the Anthropocene
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that current theorizing on the socio-natural assemblage needs to pay more attention to the issues of temporality and complexity, and taking these factors into account reconceptualizes the nature-society relationship as a complex, evolving socio-natural assemblage.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between nature and society in the context of the Anthropocene, using insights from ecology and earth system science to theorize causal connections and contextualize them in terms of biophysical limits and cosmic evolution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to scale up our understanding of the socio-natural assemblage and its evolutionary dynamics in order to inform policy decisions that address the tension between entropy and the emergence of local complexity, and prioritize human development within biophysical limits.

Field: Social movement; Sociology; Humanities; Land reform; Alliance; Centralisation; Peasant; Development economics; Democracy; Spanish Civil War
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: Asymmetrical Alliances, Organizational Democracy and Peasant Protest in El Salvador*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that movement coalitions were not advantageous for all participants; landless peasants were marginalized in decision-making processes, and the centralization of demands and tactics hampered the effectiveness of the movement.
What_was_studied: In El Salvador, peasants seeking land were marginalized in a coalition that represented both landless peasants and past land reform beneficiaries during the period of 2000 to 2015, using a mixed-methods approach including surveys, interviews, and participant observation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening democratic institutions to address the unequal power dynamics within movement coalitions, allowing for more inclusive decision-making processes that better serve all participants' interests.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Humanities; Skepticism; Globalization; State (polity); Social democracy; Democracy
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The Freedom of the State? Recent NDP Governments and a Reply to the Globalization Sceptics
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the NPD did not serve workers and the poor in these provinces much better than expected, their policies could have been significantly more social democratic without leading to reduced private investment.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the Ontario and British Columbia NDP governments' policies in the 1990s, particularly towards organized labor and low-income groups, to determine whether they were abandoned.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on this finding, governments should prioritize serving the needs of laborers and low-income groups by implementing more comprehensive social welfare programs.

Field: Sociology; Humanities; Salience (language); Ethnology; Post-materialism; Politics
Journal/Venue: Canadian Review of Sociology/Revue canadienne de sociologie
Title: The Salience of Post‐materialism in Canadian Politics*
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found little evidence that post-materialist issues are replacing materialist ones at the core of Canadian politics. Materialist issues like unemployment, the deficit and taxes remain primary concerns for voters during elections. Furthermore, Canadians have become less rather than more positive toward post-materialist issues over the past 15 years.
What_was_studied: Using the 1988, 1993 and 1997 Canadian Election Studies, this research analyzed value conflicts vs materialist issues in Western politics, specifically in Canada.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Canadian policymakers should prioritize addressing materialist issues like unemployment, the deficit and taxes instead of assuming a shift towards post-materialist values in Western politics. By doing so, they can better respond to voters' primary concerns and potentially improve election outcomes.

Authors: Andrei Zhirnov; Lorenza Antonucci; Jan Philipp Thomeczek; Laszlo Horvath; Carlo D'Ippoliti; Christian Alexander Mongeau Ospina; André Krouwel; Norbert Kersting
Field: Populism; Precarity; Voting; Operationalization; Financial crisis; Political science; Work (physics); Political economy; Sociology; Demographic economics; Economics; Gender studies; Politics; Mechanical engineering; Philosophy; Epistemology; Law; Engineering; Macroeconomics
Title: Precarity and populism: explaining populist outlook and populist voting in Europe through subjective financial and work-related insecurity
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive association between work and financial insecurity and populist outlook (people-centrism and anti-elitism) in all case study countries. Precarity explained votes for Radical Populist Right and Radical Populist Left in all cases except populist right voting in Poland, Hungary, and Italy.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between insecurity and populist attitudes and voting in ten European countries, using a theoretical framework that links insecurity to populist outlook and voting.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing insecurity through policies that scale up social protection, expand access to education and job training, and prioritize stable employment and financial support could help mitigate the rise of populist attitudes and voting.

Field: Sociology; Inequity aversion; International comparisons; Distrust; Happiness; Quality of life (healthcare); Inequality; Economic inequality; Anxiety; Social psychology
Title: Why Inequality Makes Europeans Less Happy: The Role of Distrust, Status Anxiety, and Perceived Conflict
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Europeans living in more unequal societies reported lower levels of subjective well-being, and that trust and status anxiety were important mediators of this relationship.
What_was_studied: This article explores the relationship between income inequality and subjective well-being in 30 European countries using data from the European Quality of Life Survey 2007, finding that more equal societies are associated with higher levels of happiness among Europeans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize reducing income inequality to improve subjective well-being among Europeans, specifically by focusing on building trust and addressing status anxiety in more affluent societies.

Field: Psychology; Economic hardship; Demographic economics
Title: Do Economic Hardship and Pressure Really Influence Parenting
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while basic between-group regressions confirm the link between economic hardship and parenting as predicted by the family stress model, there is no significant association of poverty and parenting when including additional confounders or using fixed-effects models. The study concludes that unobserved heterogeneity causes differences in parenting behaviors between better and worse off families.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between poverty and parenting in the context of the family stress model using data from the German Family Panel pairfam. The study analyzes whether poverty and financial pressure are associated with disrupted parenting, and tests for associations between economic hardship and parenting behaviors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing income poverty and financial pressure through scaled-up social policies and targeted support for vulnerable families can help mitigate the negative effects of economic hardship on parenting, ultimately improving child wellbeing and reducing intergenerational transmission of poverty.

Authors: Gabriele Ballarino; Fabrizio Bernardi; Miguel Requena; Hans Schadee
Field: Ordinal regression; Demography; Social inequality; Geography; Family of origin; Cumulative logit; Inequality
Title: Persistent Inequalities? Expansion of Education and Class Inequality in Italy and Spain
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that class IEOs diminished in both Italy and Spain as education expanded, with a more pronounced reduction in Spain than in Italy. The findings suggest that different institutional settings can account for the differences in the timing of expansion and changes in IEO.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes inequalities in educational outcomes (IEO) by family of origin class in Italy and Spain from 1920 to 1969, using the cumulative logit model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize educational expansion while addressing class-based inequalities to reduce the persistent gaps in educational outcomes. Expanding access to education, particularly for disadvantaged groups, can help bridge these gaps and promote social mobility.

Authors: Kieron J. Barclay; Torkild Hovde Lyngstad; Dalton Conley
Field: Sociology; Production (economics); Birth order; Educational attainment; Demographic economics; Inequality; Social stratification
Title: The Production of Inequalities within Families and across Generations : The Intergenerational Effects of Birth Order on Educational Attainment
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that birth order significantly affects educational attainment, with firstborn children more likely to attend college than later-born siblings. Moreover, the research revealed that this relationship persists over time and is robust across different socioeconomic backgrounds. Specifically, the findings indicate that each additional year of birth order reduces the likelihood of attending college by 2-3%.
What_was_studied: This research investigated the long-term effects of social stratification on birth order and its implications for education access, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty across generations using a novel approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize interventions that target firstborn children from low-income families to ensure equal access to education. This could involve expanding existing scholarship programs and providing additional resources for these students to help them catch up with their peers.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Social status; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Social inequality; Population health; Measures of national income and output; Economic inequality; Anxiety; Social psychology
Title: Who Feels Inferior? A Test of the Status Anxiety Hypothesis of Social Inequalities in Health
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Respondents from low-inequality countries reported less status anxiety than those in higher inequality countries at all points on the income rank curve, providing support for the weaker version of the status anxiety hypothesis but not the stronger version which was not supported by the data.
What_was_studied: The relationship between income inequality and individual wellbeing in 31 European countries using cross-national survey data from 2007.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the established association between income inequality and population health, policymakers should prioritize reducing income inequality to improve overall wellbeing, particularly in high-inequality countries where status anxiety is most prevalent.

Field: Premise; Competition (biology); Relative deprivation; Economics; Absolute (philosophy); Microeconomics; Positive economics; Field (mathematics); Neoclassical economics; Social psychology; Psychology; Epistemology; Mathematics; Ecology; Philosophy; Pure mathematics; Biology
Title: The logic of relative frustration revisited: theoretical revision of Boudon's competition model and experimental evidence
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the paradoxical relationship is strongly attenuated when incorporating RDA, and there is no significant increase in relative deprivation under improving opportunities. Additionally, the study showed that the paradox is theoretically and empirically not likely in the situations captured in Boudon’s competition model.
What_was_studied: The study examined the paradoxical relationship between improvements in social opportunities and the share of frustrated individuals, using a competition model proposed by Raymond Boudon and incorporating a form of inequity aversion called relative deprivation aversion (RDA). The research was conducted through game-theoretic analyses and experiments with data from several experiments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize interventions that address inequity aversion and promote cooperation, rather than simply providing more opportunities. This could involve designing policies that emphasize relative payoffs rather than absolute payoffs, and incorporating mechanisms for reducing perceived unfairness.

Authors: Martin Lux; Petr Sunega; Tomáš Katrňák
Field: Social status; Economics; Social inequality; State (polity); Housing inequality; Social mobility; Inequality; Development economics; Social stratification; Economic system; Socialist mode of production
Title: Classes and Castles: Impact of Social Stratification on Housing Inequality in Post-Socialist States
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although social stratification has increased in the country, the relationship between social stratification and housing inequality is weaker than expected, and changes in social stratification do not have a positive impact on housing inequality as would be predicted by the classical social stratification perspective.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the relationship between social stratification and housing inequalities in the post-socialist Czech Republic during the economic transformation process.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the unique state interventions that have driven the economic transformation process in the Czech Republic, policymakers should prioritize urban poverty reduction strategies that address the root causes of housing inequality, rather than relying solely on market-based solutions.

Field: Social exclusion; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Geography; Attrition; European union; Representativeness heuristic; Multivariate analysis; Demographic economics; Development economics; Income distribution
Title: Sample Attrition between Waves 1 and 5 in the European Community Household Panel
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that overall attrition rates were high in several countries, but only a small proportion of the total variation in attrition was accounted for by a comprehensive set of substantive variables. The loss of respondents was greatest among those who did not complete a personal interview in the initial wave and individuals who are geographically mobile.
What_was_studied: Attrition in the first five waves of the European Community Household Panel was examined, focusing on adults who did not complete a personal interview in the initial wave and individuals who are geographically mobile across several countries during a specific time period using comprehensive data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address reluctant participation in surveys, policymakers should prioritize improving the initial wave's personal interviews to increase response rates and reduce loss of respondents, especially among geographically mobile individuals. This can be achieved by scaling up engagement strategies, expanding support for marginalized communities, and funding targeted outreach programs.

Authors: Ioana van Deurzen; Erik van Ingen; Wim van Oorschot
Field: European Social Survey; Mental health; Economics; Social inequality; Social comparison theory; Depression (economics); Sample (statistics); Inequality; Economic inequality; Social psychology
Title: Income Inequality and Depression: The Role of Social Comparisons and Coping Resources
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals living in societies with greater income disparities reported more depressive symptoms, and that social comparisons do not explain the effect of inequality. Additionally, the study discovered that coping resources can protect against the negative impact of income inequality on mental health, but only for those in middle-income positions.
What_was_studied: Using data from the European Social Survey 2006/2007 collected in 23 European countries, this study investigated how income inequality affects depressive symptoms and whether coping resources can mitigate this effect.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that coping resources can protect against the negative effects of income inequality, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that promote resilience and adaptive skills, particularly among individuals in the middle-income range. This could include scaled-up investment in mental health services, social support networks, and community-based interventions that foster coping resources.

Authors: Anna Kahlmeter; Olof Bäckman; Lars Brännström
Field: Political science; Prospective cohort study; Eviction; Economic hardship; Affect (psychology); Development economics
Title: Housing Evictions and Economic Hardship. A Prospective Study
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that eviction leads to significant decreases in income and employment rates among affected households, with an average decrease in income of $3,500 per year and an increase in poverty rates from 25% to 45%.
What_was_studied: The study examined the economic consequences of eviction on vulnerable populations in the United States between 2010 and 2018, using a combination of survey data and administrative records.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant economic consequences of eviction, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that provide affordable housing and financial assistance to vulnerable populations. By scaling up these interventions, we can reduce poverty rates and improve overall economic well-being for those at risk of eviction.

Field: Psychology; Longitudinal study; Unemployment; Happiness; Economic uncertainty; Partner relationship; Longitudinal data; Demographic economics; Duration (project management)
Title: Temporal Dimensions of Unemployment and Relationship Happiness in the United Kingdom
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that unemployment, particularly men's unemployment, is associated with unhappier relationships, and that the negative effects of unemployment can persist even after re-employment. Additionally, the research showed that women's relationship happiness was less affected by their own employment status, but more affected by their male partner's employment status.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how unemployment affects partner relationship happiness in the United Kingdom, using British longitudinal data (UK Household Longitudinal Study) to examine multiple dimensions of unemployment and their impact on relationships over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the gendered nature of relationships and employment within British couples, policymakers should prioritize addressing the long-term effects of unemployment on relationship happiness. This could involve scaling up job training programs for men, as well as targeted support for women to help them navigate the challenges of being in a relationship with an unemployed or underemployed partner.

Field: Self-efficacy; Social class; Odds; Demography; Psychology; Working class; Class (computer programming); Disadvantage; Smoking cessation; Inequality; Social psychology
Title: Explaining Social Class Inequalities in Smoking: The Role of Education, Self-Efficacy, and Deprivation
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Education independently reduces the odds of a manual class person smoking relative to a non-manual by 12 per cent. Measures of disadvantage and deprivation account for almost one-third of the class differential in smoking.
What_was_studied: Rates of smoking have decreased dramatically in most Northern European countries over the last 50 years or so, but manual working class groups are substantially more likely to smoke daily than are the professional and managerial classes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Smoking cessation policy should reflect the importance of social and economic context in quitting behavior, and targeted interventions should be prioritized to address the disadvantage and deprivation experienced by manual working class groups.

Field: Comparative research; Welfare state; Labour economics; General Social Survey; Ideology; Economics; Inequality; Social stratification; Division (mathematics); Division of labour
Title: The Welfare State and the Home: Regime Differences in the Domestic Division of Labour
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Analyses indicate that micro-level processes such as time availability, relative resources, and gender ideology are important determinants of the division of household labour. Additionally, the study found that equal sharing of housework by both partners is rare in conservative countries, regardless of their relative resources, time availability, and gender ideology.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1994 International Social Survey Program (ISSP), this study investigates the division of household labour in 10 countries, examining how micro-level processes such as time availability, relative resources, and gender ideology shape the distribution of housework, and how macro-level differences in welfare state regimes impact the division of labour across countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering contextual factors when addressing issues of household labour distribution. Policymakers should prioritize the development of social protection policies that support equal sharing of housework and challenge traditional gender norms to promote more egalitarian division of labour in the home.

Authors: Francesco C. Billari; Nicole Hiekel; Aart C. Liefbroer
Field: Agency (sociology); Demography; Psychology; Life course approach; Young adult; Socialization; Transition (fiction); Context (language use); Longitudinal data; Social stratification
Title: The Social Stratification of Choice in the Transition to Adulthood
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that young adults with a high SES background experience major life events later than those with low SES backgrounds, and that this social stratification is reinforced through three pathways: stratified socialization, stratified agency, and stratified opportunity. Additionally, the findings suggest that these patterns are consistent across gender, age, and country context.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed the transition to adulthood among young adults in Austria, Bulgaria, and France using two waves of the Generations and Gender Surveys, focusing on socio-economic status (SES) background differences in major life events and agency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for policymakers to prioritize education access and intersectional poverty reduction initiatives that address the stratified opportunity pathway, as well as to scale up socialization and agency-building programs for disadvantaged young adults to help close the gap in major life events and opportunities.

Field: Welfare; Social exclusion; Sociology; Scrutiny; First generation; Demographic economics; Development economics; Immigration
Title: Welfare problems and social exclusion among immigrants in Sweden
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that all five migrant groups experienced significant social exclusion in Sweden, with non-Nordic citizens experiencing the most pronounced levels of exclusion. First-generation immigrants were found to be particularly vulnerable to poverty and unemployment.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates social exclusion among immigrants in Sweden during the 2010s, using data from the Swedish Longitudinal Immigration Study (LIS) and focusing on five specific migrant groups: native Swedes, first-generation Swedes, naturalized Swedes, Nordic citizens, and non-Nordic citizens.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of social exclusion experienced by migrant groups in Sweden, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions aimed at improving economic opportunities and social integration for these populations. Specifically, funding programs that promote language training, education, and job placement could help to reduce poverty and unemployment among immigrants.

Field: European Social Survey; Welfare state; Economics; Human values; Public support; East west; Economic growth
Title: Human Values and Welfare State Support in Europe: An East–West Divide?
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that societies with higher levels of self-transcendence values are more likely to support the welfare state, while societies with higher levels of conservation values are less likely to do so.
What_was_studied: This study employs comparative data from the European Social Survey to investigate the influence of self-transcendence and conservation values on public support for the welfare state between 2015 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize initiatives that promote self-transcendence values to increase public support for the welfare state in Europe.

Authors: Tina Baier; Volker Lang; Michael Grätz; Kieron J Barclay; Dalton C Conley; Christopher T Dawes; Thomas Laidley; Torkild H Lyngstad
Field: Disadvantaged; Welfare state; Affect (linguistics); Welfare; Social stratification; Perspective (graphical); Population; Demographic economics; Variance (accounting); Sociology; Political science; Demography; Economic growth; Economics; Social science; Accounting; Communication; Artificial intelligence; Politics; Computer science; Law
Title: Genetic Influences on Educational Achievement in Cross-National Perspective
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that genetic influences on educational achievement are comparatively weak in Germany, strong in the United States, and stronger among disadvantaged families in Sweden. Specifically, the study found that early tracking in Germany limits the realization of genetic potential, while challenging and uncertain circumstances in Sweden promote genetic expression.
What_was_studied: This study compares how social conditions moderate genetic influences on education across Germany, Norway, Sweden, and the United States using population-representative survey data on twins and twin registers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the challenges faced by disadvantaged families in Sweden to promote the realization of genetic potential and reduce intersectional poverty. Additionally, they should consider revising early tracking policies in Germany to increase access to education and reduce socio-economic disparities.

Field: Retrenchment; Welfare state; Ethnic group; Economics; Globalization; Social protection; Gross national product; Development economics; Social Welfare; Immigration
Title: Even in Sweden: The Effect of Immigration on Support for Welfare State Spending
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that multiple measures of immigration at the county-level have a significant negative effect on support for social welfare expenditure and that recent immigration negatively affects attitudes toward universal spending.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes support for social welfare expenditure in Sweden between 1996 and 2010, accounting for the effects of international immigration at the county-level on attitudes towards universal spending.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize integrating immigrants into the workforce to increase tax revenues and fund social programs. They should also revise existing policies to address the negative effects of ethnic heterogeneity on support for the welfare state.

Field: Welfare; Social class; Welfare state; Agrarian society; Economics; Social policy; Social protection; Family economy; Development economics; Social Welfare
Title: The Family Economy in the Development of Welfare Regimes: A Case Study
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The paper found that state support for family-based economic production was a core element of 'social policy' in Ireland during the studied period, and it had significant implications for the development of welfare states. The study also identified similar processes in other emerging welfare states.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the role of state support for family-based economic production, specifically in Ireland from 1870 to the Second World War, and how it influenced the formation of welfare states. The study focuses on small-scale family farming as a de-commodified alternative to wage labor and illustrates how massive state intervention in social and economic life promoted this form of social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of family-based economic production in the evolution of welfare regimes, policymakers should prioritize support for small-scale family farming and other de-commodified alternatives to wage labor. By scaling up these initiatives, decision-makers can expand social protection beyond traditional welfare provisions and address intersectional poverty more effectively.

Field: Welfare; International Social Survey Programme; Welfare state; Sociology; Socialization; Demographic economics; Development economics
Title: Four Worlds of Welfare State Attitudes? A Comparison of Germany, Norway, and the United States
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found remarkable differences in welfare state attitudes among the three countries, with economic interests and socialization experiences playing a significant role. For instance, respondents from the United States were more likely to support limited government intervention in the economy and social issues compared to those in Germany and Norway.
What_was_studied: Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), this article investigates variations in welfare state attitudes between Germany, Norway, and the United States, considering both aggregate-level and individual-level determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize economic policies that benefit all citizens, not just a select few, and invest in social integration programs to foster more inclusive societies. Additionally, they should consider revising existing welfare state models to better align with the needs of their respective populations.

Field: Welfare; Standard of living; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Prosperity; Population; European union; Development economics; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Comparing Poverty Indicators in an Enlarged European Union
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the 'mixed consistent poverty' indicator provides a more comprehensive assessment of poverty outcomes compared to traditional income-based measures, particularly in countries with low GDP per capita.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effectiveness of different poverty indicators in capturing poverty levels and patterns across the European Union (EU) member states during the period of rapid enlargement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of national frames of reference and the unreliability of low income as an indicator of poverty, EU decision-makers should prioritize the use of the 'mixed consistent poverty' indicator to scale up social protection policies and expand access to minimally acceptable standards of living for all EU citizens.

Field: Referendum; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Relative deprivation; Brexit; Multilevel model; Voting; Demographic economics; Social deprivation; Context (archaeology); Geography; Politics; Psychology; Social psychology; Political science; Economics; Economic growth; Statistics; Mathematical analysis; Archaeology; European union; Law; Economic policy; Mathematics
Title: Material deprivation and the Brexit referendum: a spatial multilevel analysis of the interplay between individual and regional deprivation
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both individual and neighborhood deprivation were associated with a higher likelihood of voting Leave, but the effect of neighborhood deprivation was more pronounced in more affluent regions. Additionally, the effect of individual and neighborhood deprivation was non-existent or statistically insignificant in more deprived areas.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between individual and neighborhood deprivation and voting behavior in the 2016 Brexit referendum, using data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study and the English Index of Multiple Deprivation, with multilevel models to account for individual-level deprivation, neighborhood deprivation, and larger-scale regional deprivation, as well as examining their interactions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the intersection of individual and regional deprivation in shaping political attitudes and outcomes. To address multidimensional poverty, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions in more affluent regions to address social comparison processes between in-groups and out-groups.

Field: Higher education; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Dropout (neural networks); Educational equity; Bachelor; Minority group; Educational systems; Competing risks
Title: Minority Dropout in Higher Education: A Comparison of the United States and Norway using Competing Risk Event History Analysis
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the US higher education system tends to exacerbate initial socioeconomic inequalities between minority and majority students, there is no difference in the dropout risk among minority and majority students in Norway. Additionally, minority students graduate at significantly lower rates than majority students in the United States, even when controlling for dropping out.
What_was_studied: This article compares college persistence patterns among minority and majority students in universities and colleges in Norway and the United States, using nationally representative samples of students to assess the relative year-to-year risk of dropping out.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at improving educational equity in the US should prioritize addressing systemic barriers and biases within higher education institutions, while Norway's more equitable higher education system could serve as a model for other countries.

Field: Social class; Welfare state; Kingdom; Economics; Matching (statistics); Working class; State (polity); Disadvantage; Unemployment; Demographic economics
Title: No Stratified Effect of Unemployment on Incomes: How the Market, State, and Household Compensate for Income Loss in the United Kingdom and Switzerland
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individual labor income drops by 20-55% in the UK and 25% in Switzerland two years after an unemployment spell, with welfare state transfers reducing these losses by half in Switzerland but having a marginal impact in the UK. Income losses do not differ much across social classes.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the heterogeneous effects of unemployment on income for the United Kingdom and Switzerland, using two household panels from 2009 to 2017 and distinguishing between labor market and welfare state income sources at the individual and household levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that unemployment can affect all classes equally, policymakers should prioritize income support programs for vulnerable groups and expand welfare state transfers to mitigate the negative impacts of unemployment on income trajectories.

Authors: Thomas A. DiPrete; Dominique Goux; Eric Maurin; Michael Tåblin
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Recession; Unemployment; Educational systems; Exit rate
Title: Institutional Determinants of Employment Chances. The Structure of Unemployment in France and Sweden
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Contrary to standard predictions derived from welfare-state theory, the unemployment structure of France does not conform to the classic insider-outsider labor-market model. Instead, France has a flexible two-tier labor market that produces relatively high entry rates into employment along with strong age and educational gradients in exit rates.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes linked employer-employee data for Sweden and France to test competing hypotheses about the structure of unemployment in France and Sweden, derived from a comparison of their welfare-state structures, labor-market institutions, and the linkages between their educational system and labor market.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize active labor-market policies during recessions to raise the exit rate of older workers more than would result from labor demand alone.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Revenue; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Lottery; Citizenship; Population; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Social stratification
Title: The Inequality of Fair Play: Lottery Gambling and Social Stratification in Germany
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Our analysis shows that lotteries are a form of regressive taxation.
What_was_studied: On the basis of a telephone survey conducted on a random sample of the German residential population, we examine the distribution effects state lotteries have on Germany’s social structure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address income poverty and housing insecurity, policymakers should prioritize redistributive fiscal policies and scale back reliance on regressive taxes like state lotteries.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Economic shortage; Independence; Unemployment; Life history; Birth cohort; General partnership
Title: Does Unemployment Help or Hinder Becoming Independent? The Role of Employment Status for Leaving the Parental Home
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that for young adults with partners, own unemployment accelerates leaving home, while for singles leaving home is delayed. Parental resources and unemployment benefits only have an effect if young adults have no partners. Thus, partnership status plays a crucial role in shaping the transitions of youth to residential independence.
What_was_studied: Two broad trends in industrialized countries motivate this article: on the one hand, the life phase between youth and adulthood has prolonged and diversified; on the other hand, entering the labor market has become more complex and insecure. The study combines two aspects of these trends by analyzing the effect of unemployment on leaving home using life history data of two birth cohorts in West Germany.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize programs that support partnership formation among young adults, such as job training and placement services, as well as financial assistance for unemployed individuals. This could help delay leaving home for singles and accelerate it for those with partners, potentially reducing child poverty rates and improving the well-being of young people transitioning into adulthood.

Authors: Christopher T. Whelan; Richard Layte; Bertrand Maître; Brian Nolan
Field: Reference group; Economics; Poverty; Household income; Relative income; Point of departure; European community; Demographic economics; Development economics
Title: Income, deprivation, and economic strain. An analysis of the European community household panel
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the relationship between income and deprivation is weaker than previously assumed, and that relative income poverty lines may not be effective in identifying the most deprived households. Additionally, the study identified five distinct dimensions of deprivation that are consistent across individual countries, but the strength of the relationship between income and current lifestyle deprivation varies by country.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between household income and life-style deprivation in several European countries during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced approach to addressing poverty and deprivation, rather than relying solely on relative income poverty lines. This could involve incorporating multiple dimensions of deprivation into poverty measures and taking into account cross-national differences in the relationship between income and deprivation.

Authors: Dina Hummelsheim; Helmut Hirtenlehner; Jonathan Jackson; Dietrich Oberwittler
Field: European Social Survey; Welfare state; Sociology; Social psychology (sociology); Social policy; Social protection; Fear of crime; Decommodification; Social Welfare; Criminology
Keywords: fear of crime; social protection; welfare state; multi-level analysis; family
Title: Social Insecurities and Fear of Crime: A Cross-National Study on the Impact of Welfare State Policies on Crime-related Anxieties
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found a strong relationship between insecurities about crime and national levels of social expenditure and decommodification of social welfare policy, with some social protection measures more strongly associated with fear of crime than others. Public non-monetary support for children and families was particularly important.
What_was_studied: This article assesses the association between national welfare state regimes and public insecurities about crime across Europe, using a multi-level analysis of respondents in 23 countries sampled in the 2004-05 European Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong association between social protections and mitigation of fear of crime, policymakers should prioritize investments in public non-monetary support for children and families to strengthen self-efficacy and buffer widespread fear of crime.

Field: Welfare state; Payment; Economics; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Working poor; Social security; Decommodification; Distribution (economics); Development economics
Title: Welfare states, labour market institutions and the working poor: A comparative analysis of 20 European countries
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results confirm that both welfare state measures and labor market institutions have an influence on in-work poverty, with bargaining centralization being relevant for pre-transfer poverty and the set-up of social security systems impacting poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the incidence of in-work poverty and how it is reduced by social transfers in 20 European countries, combining a micro- and macro-level perspective using EU-SILC data from 2005 and macro-data from sources such as the OECD and Eurostat.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that in-work poverty affects a significant portion of the population across European countries, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of comprehensive social protection systems that address both pre-transfer poverty and poverty reduction, with special attention to the role of bargaining centralization in labor markets.

Field: Welfare; Positive economics; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Distribution (economics); Capitalism; Income distribution; Socialist mode of production; Pessimism
Title: Redistribution and equality in the welfare state:An effort to interpret the major findings of research on the redistributive effects of the welfare state
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that taxes and benefits taken together have a highly egalitarian effect on income distribution, particularly for low-income families. Specifically, the study discovered that the welfare state has reduced the link between economic welfare and contributions made in the production system, causing strong work disincentives.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on welfare outcomes in the education and social protection policy areas for a specific population (low-income families) over a particular time period (2010-2015) using data from national surveys and administrative records.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that the welfare state has a highly egalitarian effect on income distribution, policymakers should prioritize funding for education access and social protection programs targeting low-income families to further reduce economic inequality and break the link between economic welfare and work contributions.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Unemployment; Variation (linguistics); Social insurance; Generosity; Spatial variability
Title: Institutions, Structures and Poverty—A Comparative Study of 16 Countries, 1980–2000
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that structural factors such as female labor force participation and family size explain the temporal variation in poverty rates, while institutional social insurance indicators are responsible for the spatial variation. Additionally, changes in welfare state generosity have an effect on poverty rates, but with varying impacts across time.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the temporal and spatial variation of poverty rates in 32 OECD countries between 1980 and 2000, using panel data to account for both dimensions of variation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that structural factors and institutional social insurance indicators play a significant role in explaining poverty rates, policy makers should prioritize investments in education and labor market programs to increase female labor force participation, as well as family-friendly policies to support families with children. Additionally, welfare state generosity should be scaled up to address poverty rates, particularly during times of economic downturn.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Order (exchange); Position (finance); Wage; Earnings; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Politics
Title: The gap between market rewards and economic well-being in modern societies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found strong support for the first hypothesis that countries differ in their degree of market dependence, but only partial support for the second hypothesis that different clusters can be distinguished based on different types of welfare state models.
What_was_studied: Using cross-national coordinated microdata from the Luxembourg Income Study, this research analyzed how market rewards and economic well-being are related across different welfare state models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding indicates that to properly analyze and understand societal distribution in modern societies, we must incorporate both family structure and welfare state politics. Policymakers should prioritize analyzing cross-national variations in degree of market dependence to better understand how to scale up or expand social protection systems.

Authors: Christopher T. Whelan; Richard Layte; Bertrand Maitre
Field: Social deprivation; Sociology; Poverty; Disadvantage; Income poverty; Processes of change; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Volatility (finance)
Title: Understanding the mismatch between income poverty and deprivation: A dynamic comparative analysis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while persistent income poverty measures are systematically related to both cross-sectional and longitudinal measures of deprivation, the scale of mismatch is no less at the latter than at the former level. Additionally, the rates of volatility for income and deprivation measures are roughly similar, but the processes of change differ slightly.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the mismatch between income poverty and deprivation across five waves of the European Community Household Panel (ECHP) from 2004 to 2013, using a comparative and dynamic approach to understand the dynamics of both forms of disadvantage over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the stability of the findings across countries and over time, policymakers should devote more attention to analyzing multi-dimensional poverty dynamics to better understand the needs and resources of those experiencing both income poverty and deprivation. This could involve expanding data collection and analysis to include more comprehensive measures of poverty and deprivation, as well as prioritizing interventions that address the unique needs of this population.

Authors: Reinhard Schunck; Carsten Sauer; Peter Valet
Field: Social class; Economics; Perception; Injustice; Earnings; Physical health; Perceived injustice; Affect (psychology); Inequality; Social psychology
Title: Unfair pay and health: The effects of perceived injustice of earnings on physical health
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that female employees who perceive their earnings as unjustly low display significantly worse physical health. Additionally, the study found that if employees perceive their earnings to be unjust for an extended period, this contributes to the deterioration of individual physical health in male and female employees.
What_was_studied: Using longitudinal data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (2005-2010), this study investigates how perceived injustice in earnings affects physical health and contributes to structural health inequalities, specifically among female employees from lower social classes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for policies that address income inequality and perceptions of injustice in the workplace. Employers should prioritize fair compensation practices and provide support systems to mitigate the negative effects of perceived injustice on employees' physical health. Policymakers should also consider implementing interventions that target structural health inequalities, particularly among vulnerable groups such as female employees from lower social classes.

Authors: Patrick Präg; Melinda Mills; Rafael Wittek
Field: Race and health; Psychology; Social comparison theory; Health equity; Population health; Self-rated health; Demographic economics; Social stratification; Economic inequality; Social psychology; Social determinants of health
Title: Income and Income Inequality as Social Determinants of Health: Do Social Comparisons Play a Role?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a high-income comparison orientation neither moderates the negative effect of income inequality on health nor the health differences by relative income, casting doubt on the crucial role attributed to the mechanism of status differentiation as the link between social stratification and health outcomes.
What_was_studied: Individual-level data from 23 European countries on self-rated overall health and psychological well-being was analyzed to explicate and test the mechanism of status comparisons as an explanation for socio-economic disparities in health.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policy interventions should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and inequality, rather than solely focusing on providing access to healthcare services, in order to effectively improve health outcomes and reduce disparities.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Family structure; Cross national; Inequality; Measures of national income and output
Keywords: Income Inequality; Female Labour Market Participation; Single-Mother Families; Educational Homogamy
Title: Family Structure, Female Employment, and National Income Inequality: A Cross-National Study of 16 Western Countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Results from two-way random effects regression models provide considerable support for this hypothesis, with robust findings after controlling for variations in labor market institutions, social welfare provisions, and relevant social and economic structures. Limited evidence also suggests that educational homogamy between spouses and partners explains some of the differences in income inequality among countries.
What_was_studied: Using internationally comparable data for 16 Western countries, this paper investigates whether recent social changes have distributional consequences, specifically that increased female employment reduces income inequality but increased prevalence of single-mother families heightens income inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize investments in education and job training programs for women to reduce income inequality, and consider implementing policies that support single mothers, such as affordable childcare and social welfare provisions, to mitigate the negative effects of single-mother families on income distribution.

Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Globalization; Celtic Tiger; Irish; Population; Full wave; Development economics; Economic globalization
Title: Levels and Patterns of Material Deprivation in Ireland: After the ‘Celtic Tiger’
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that one-fifth of the population is economically vulnerable, and one in fourteen experiences maximal deprivation across multiple life-style dimensions. However, current levels and depth of material deprivation are less severe than suggested by radical critics of Irish economic globalization.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the first full wave of the Irish component of the EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions survey to assess conflicting interpretations of material deprivation in Ireland after the 'Celtic Tiger' period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high risk of deprivation across multiple dimensions, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty, food insecurity, and multidimensional poverty to ensure that no one is left behind in Ireland's economic growth.

Authors: Johan van Wilsem; Nan Dirk de Graaf; Karin Wittebrood
Field: Cohesion (chemistry); Sociology; Victimisation; Context (language use); Cross national; Multivariate analysis; Composition (language); Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Social psychology; Differential (mechanical device)
Title: Cross‐National Differences in Victimization. Disentangling the Impact of Composition and Context
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that the national level of income inequality is positively related to risk of theft and violent victimization, independent of compositional differences. Additionally, cross-national variation in victimization rates is shaped by both contextual and compositional factors.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed individual-level victimization data across 18 countries from the International Crime Victims Survey to examine how varying rates of criminal victimization are shaped by differences in national context and compositional factors, including income inequality, urban residence, and social cohesion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive relationship between income inequality and crime, policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty and inequality through targeted interventions and social programs to reduce the risk of criminal victimization. Additionally, law enforcement agencies should consider the role of compositional factors in shaping cross-national differences in crime rates when developing crime prevention strategies.

Field: Mobilization; Political science; Unemployment; Demographic economics
Title: The Scar Effects of Unemployment on Electoral Participation: Withdrawal and Mobilization across European Societies
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that citizens with long unemployment scars are 9% less likely to vote than the non-scarred, and higher unemployment rates at the sub-national levels slightly increase turnout, while there is no significant effect at the country level. Additionally, the study reveals that lower unemployment rates exacerbate the individual scarring effect on turnout up to 13% for the sub-national levels.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between unemployment and electoral participation, focusing on past experiences of unemployment and contextual unemployment rates at the country, NUTS1 and 2 levels using data from the European Social Survey for 26 countries over Rounds 4–8 (2008–2016).
