Title: Migration, Class Attainment and Social Mobility: An Analysis of Migrants’ Socio-Economic Integration in Italy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The results show that migrants are penalized in the Italian labor market, remaining largely 'trapped' in the working class. This inclusion at the bottom of the class structure reduces their heterogeneity by education and by social origin. Moreover, their penalty increases during the career, except when they move from the non-standard to the standard working class.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the socio-economic integration of ethnic minorities in Italy, combining the literature on migration with research on social stratification and analyzing the ethnic penalty on occupational attainment and career mobility.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing the ethnic penalty in the labor market to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion among migrant populations. This could involve scaling up education and training programs, expanding access to employment opportunities, and funding targeted initiatives to support the socio-economic integration of migrants.

Field: Labour economics; Political science; Unemployment; Graduation; Youth unemployment; Difference in differences; Economic growth; Capitalism; Social transformation; Vocational education; Socialist mode of production
Title: Social Transformation and the Transition from Vocational Education to Work in Hungary: A Differences-in-differences Approach
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The authors found that the substitution of employer-provided training with school-based training increased male vocational school graduates' unemployment rate by 10 percentage points within the first two years after graduation, indicating lower job quality.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the impact of shifting training provision from employers to vocational schools on labor market entry and job quality for male vocational school graduates in Hungary between 1994 and 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high youth unemployment rates in many countries, policymakers should prioritize institutional frameworks that support employer involvement in vocational training to ensure effective integration of young people into the labor market.

Authors: Patricia McMullin; Frances McGinnity; Aisling Murray; Helen Russell
Field: Cognitive skill; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Home learning
Title: What You Do Versus Who You Are: Home-Learning Activities, Social Origin and Cognitive Skills among Young Children in Ireland
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there is a social gradient in vocabulary development even at age 3, with the largest gaps for mothers’ education. Family income, mothers’ education, and social class are also associated with vocabulary independently, though these associations are reduced by adding all three measures simultaneously. The extent of HLAs helps explain a very small part of the education differences and none of the income or social class differences in vocabulary.
What_was_studied: This article explores the role that home-learning activities (HLAs) play in the relationship between social origin and cognitive development using an Irish birth cohort study, Growing Up in Ireland.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in home-learning activities may help compensate for disadvantage and reduce the gap in vocabulary development between high- and low-income children. Policymakers should prioritize programs that support HLAs, such as parental education and family income support, to promote sustainable development and reduce child poverty.

Authors: Maurice Gesthuizen; Heike Solga; Ralf Künster
Field: Competence (human resources); Socioeconomic status; Economics; Unemployment; Educational attainment; Cross national; Cognitive competence; Statut socio economique; Demographic economics; Status attainment; Economic growth
Title: Context Matters: Economic Marginalization of Low-Educated Workers in Cross-National Perspective
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that educational differences in socio-economic status attainment are larger in countries with low average competence, unfavourable social composition, and small low-educated groups. The study also showed that negative social selection, cognitive competence selection, and discredit contribute to the economic marginalization of low-educated workers.
What_was_studied: This article examines the economic marginalization of low-educated individuals in different countries, focusing on the displacement mechanism and additional causes such as negative social selection, negative cognitive competence selection, and discredit.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the economic vulnerability of low-educated individuals, policymakers should prioritize education expansion in countries with low average competence, unfavourable social composition, and small low-educated groups. Additionally, they should fund programs aimed at reducing negative social selection, cognitive competence selection, and discredit among low-educated workers.

Field: Labour law; Economic policy; Labour economics; Economics; Employment protection legislation; Unemployment; Legislation; Youth unemployment; Job security; Business; Demographic economics; Political science; Economic growth; Law; Work (physics); Mechanical engineering; Engineering
Title: Employment Protection Legislation and the Youth Labour Market
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study suggests that deregulating job security provisions may lower youth unemployment, while deregulating temporary contracts at high levels of job security provisions may increase youth unemployment rates and lower employment rates.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of employment protection legislation on youth unemployment and employment rates in Western Europe from 1980 to 2008, differentiating between job security provisions and regulations on temporary contracts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the suggestive evidence of increased youth unemployment rates and lower employment rates when deregulating temporary contracts at high levels of job security provisions, policy makers should prioritize careful consideration of EPL regulations to address the issue of youth unemployment.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Mathematics education; Survey data collection; Degree (music); Bachelor; Novelty; Bologna Process; Meaning (linguistics); Panel data
Title: The Introduction of Bachelor Degrees and the Under-representation of Students from Low Social Origin in Higher Education in Germany: A Pseudo-Panel Approach
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the reduction in the length of study did not increase participation from low social origins.
What_was_studied: In the course of the Bologna Process, European higher education systems have experienced major reforms, particularly in Germany, where the length of study for a first-level degree (Bachelor) was reduced, along with the introduction of a second-level degree (Master's), with the goal of increasing access to higher education for under-represented groups such as those from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize alternative measures to expand access to higher education for under-represented groups, such as targeted financial support and outreach programs, rather than relying solely on degree structure reform.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Standard of living; Economics; Generosity; Decommodification; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Commodification; Scale (social sciences); Politics
Title: Directions of Decommodification: Gender and Generosity in 12 OECD Nations, 1980–2000
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that increases in women's employment and political representation, as well as declining fertility, are positively associated with decommodification outcomes. Nation-level differences were also significant, suggesting the importance of considering gender in future research on decommodification.
What_was_studied: The decommodifying capacity of states and its relevance for gender in a changing world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize increasing women's employment and political representation to improve decommodification outcomes and reduce gender disparities in health and economic wellbeing.

Field: Finance; Net income; Job attitude; Economics; Work (electrical); Flexibility (personality); Unemployment; Full-time; Incentive; Fixed cost
Keywords: JEL Classification: I38; J32; J64 Unemployment traps; incentives; job attitudes
Title: Unemployment Traps: Do Financial Disincentives Matter?
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate large disincentive effects for some groups, especially low-paid women. In 1996, 6% of Danish men and 13% of women had lower disposable net income if working full time compared to unemployment benefits.
What_was_studied: Based on a panel survey merged with administrative registers, the study calculates precise measures of economic incentives for labor-force participants between employment and unemployment insurance benefits, with a focus on low-paid women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant disincentive effects, policymakers should prioritize addressing financial incentives to increase labor-force participation, particularly among low-paid women. This could involve scaling up training programs and expanding support for job seekers.

Field: Welfare; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Social integration; Population; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Immigration
Title: Immigrants’ Attitudes towards Welfare Redistribution. An Exploration of Role of Government Preferences among Immigrants and Natives across 18 European Welfare States
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while immigrants have more favorable views of welfare than non-immigrants, these are largely due to their disadvantaged position in society and not because they perceive welfare as a pull factor for migration. Furthermore, the study discovered that immigrants' opinions on welfare closely follow those of the non-migrant population of the country they reside in, indicating strong social integration at the opinion level.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between immigrants' opinions on government support and their level of social integration in European countries using the 2008 'Welfare Attitudes' module of the European Social Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that immigrants' opinions on welfare are not driven by a desire for pull factors, policymakers should prioritize integrating immigrants into the host society through social protection policies that address their disadvantaged position. This could involve expanding access to education and employment opportunities, as well as funding initiatives that promote intercultural dialogue and understanding.

Field: Subjective well-being; Economics; Hysteresis (economics); Unemployment; Happiness; Life satisfaction; Job loss; Demographic economics; Shock (economics); Panel analysis
Title: Does Unemployment Hurt Less if There is More of it Around? A Panel Analysis of Life Satisfaction in Germany and Switzerland
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found no evidence that being unemployed in a region with high unemployment rates is any less harmful than being unemployed in a region with low unemployment rates. Additionally, the negative impact of unemployment on individuals' well-being does not diminish over time or with repeated episodes of unemployment.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the existence of a habituation effect to unemployment in Germany and Switzerland between 1984 and 2009, using individual-level data from the German Socio-Economic Panel and the Swiss Household Panel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize measures to reduce the duration and frequency of unemployment spells, rather than relying solely on the assumption that habituation may mitigate the negative effects of unemployment.

Authors: Tak Wing Chan; Gunn Elisabeth Birkelund; Arne Kristian; Øyvind Wiborg
Field: Social class; Social position; Social status; Sociology; Life chances; Social mobility; Social stratification; Norwegian; Social psychology; Multidimensional scaling
Title: Social Status in Norway
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: We found that social status in Norway is more equitably distributed than in the UK, with a similar contour of the status order but different relationships between social status and education, income, and social class.
What_was_studied: Using register data on married and cohabiting couples in contemporary Norway, we estimate a status order by applying multidimensional scaling to contingency tables and find that social status is more equitably distributed than in the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the empirical relevance of the class–status distinction and suggests that policymakers should prioritize equitable distribution of social status in Norway by scaling up education and income opportunities for all individuals, regardless of their background.

Field: Sociology; Demography; Social inequality; Social mobility; Generative grammar; Demographic economics; Operationalization
Title: Mobility Regimes and Generative Mechanisms: A Comparative Analysis of Italy and the United States
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that general resources and objective desirability of classes account for most of the variation in mobility propensities observed in both countries, with women being less likely to inherit their father's business compared to men. Additionally, Italy displays higher class inequality in terms of mobility chances compared to the United States.
What_was_studied: This paper compares intergenerational mobility regimes in Italy and the United States in the 1980s using a hybrid log-linear model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the evidence of class inequality and gender disparities in mobility chances, policymakers should prioritize policies aimed at increasing access to general resources and reducing the objective desirability of classes to enhance intergenerational mobility and reduce poverty, particularly for women.

Field: Odds; Labour economics; Work (electrical); Political science; Training (civil); Unemployment; Quality (business); Continuing education; European community; Affect (psychology)
Title: Does it Work? The Effect of Continuing Training on Labour Market Outcomes: A Comparative Study of Germany, Denmark, and the United Kingdom
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The results suggest that the impact of training varies across the three countries, with Denmark showing the highest effectiveness in reducing unemployment spells and increasing upward occupational mobility.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of continuing education and training for adults on labor market performance in Germany, Denmark, and the United Kingdom during a specific time period using data from the European Community Household Panel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in high-quality continuing education and training programs to enhance labor market outcomes for adults in Germany, Denmark, and the United Kingdom.

Field: Odds; Sociology; Mathematics education; Matriculation; Social inequality; Attendance; Educational attainment; Hierarchy; Demographic economics; Inequality; Vocational education
Title: Reforms, Expansion, and Equality of Opportunity
primary_category: Education access; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while the reforms increased access to education for working-class students, they did not significantly reduce class inequalities in educational attainment. The study also discovered a decline in the effects of father's education on completing lower levels of education.
What_was_studied: Using data from the 1960s Italian educational reform, this study analyzes how the expansion of middle school and university access affected class inequalities in educational attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the reforms did not effectively address class inequalities, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to improve access and retention for disadvantaged students. This could include expanding scholarships, mentorship programs, and early intervention strategies to address socio-economic disparities.

Authors: Siddartha Aradhya; Raffaele Grotti; Juho Härkönen
Field: Unemployment; Immigration; Demographic economics; Current Population Survey; Disadvantage; Persistence (discontinuity); Economics; Turkish; Population; Demography; Sociology; Geography; Political science; Economic growth; Linguistics; Philosophy; Geotechnical engineering; Archaeology; Engineering; Law
Title: Unemployment persistence among second-generation immigrants
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Past unemployment increases the probability of current unemployment more among second-generation Middle-Eastern, Turkish, and Southern European immigrants compared to ancestral Swedes due to higher baseline levels of unemployment.
What_was_studied: Unemployment dynamics of the ancestral population and second-generation immigrants in Sweden over an early working career using correlated dynamic random-effects logit models to study the effect of past on current unemployment (g genuine state dependence) among 10 second-generation immigrant groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing past unemployment experiences among second-generation immigrant groups to reduce the labour market consequences of higher baseline unemployment rates, specifically among Middle-Eastern, Turkish, and Southern European immigrants.

Authors: Irma Mooi-Reci; Bart F.M. Bakker; Matthew Curry; Mark Wooden
Field: Psychology; Work ethic; Empirical evidence; Work (electrical); Unemployment; Educational attainment; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Inequality; Pessimism
Title: Why parental unemployment matters for children's educational attainment: Empirical Evidence from the Netherlands
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both mothers' and fathers' changing attitudes towards work, specifically becoming more pessimistic, negatively impacted their children's educational attainment. Additionally, the study found a direct negative effect of fathers' unemployment duration on their children's educational attainment.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of parents' unemployment on their children's subsequent educational attainment, specifically looking at the mediating role of changing work ethics during spells of unemployment using a sample of 812 Dutch children who experienced parental unemployment during the early 1980s economic crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at supporting parents' employability and work ethic during periods of unemployment can help mitigate the negative impact of parental unemployment on children's educational attainment. Specifically, policies that scale up job training programs for parents, expand access to childcare services, and prioritize early intervention to support parents' mental health could help reduce the intergenerational transmission of poverty.

Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Logistic regression; Position (finance); Temporary work; Longitudinal study; Unemployment; Youth unemployment; Multivariate analysis; Poisson regression
Title: History Dependence in Youth Unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Previous spells of unemployment were the strongest predictor of later periods of unemployment, with structural features such as employment sector and working conditions being more important than individual problems in explaining recurrent unemployment. Multivariate analyses showed that structural variables were more significant than individual factors.
What_was_studied: A theoretical model to explain recurrent periods of unemployment from youth to adulthood, based on a longitudinal study of nearly 2,000 young people in Norway over the period 1985-1993.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of structural and cultural factors on recurrent periods of unemployment, policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues to reduce poverty and housing insecurity among young people. This can include funding programs that provide job training, education, and placement services, as well as scaling up initiatives that promote flexible and secure employment opportunities.

Authors: Lewis R. Anderson; Erzsébet Bukodi; Christiaan W. S. Monden
Field: Labour economics; Psychology; Lead (geology); Versa; Job loss; Dissolution
Title: Double Trouble: Does Job Loss Lead to Union Dissolution and Vice Versa?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that job loss and union dissolution have modest and non-significant prospective associations with one another, and that unemployment appears to increase risk of union dissolution, particularly for men. No support was found for a connection between being divorced/separated and subsequent job loss.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between job loss and union dissolution in the UK using longitudinal data to address three limitations of previous research, including unmeasured confounders, neglect of the distinction between job loss and unemployment, and failure to account for the duration of unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the negative impact of major life events on both the labour market and family relationships by implementing policies that provide support for individuals experiencing job loss or union dissolution, such as training programs and financial assistance for job seekers, as well as counseling and mediation services for couples experiencing relationship difficulties.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Life course approach; Political science; Social democracy
Title: Intergenerational Educational Mobility and Life Course Economic Trajectories in a Social Democratic Welfare State
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that earnings trajectories clustered into two groups based on educational destination, not educational origin, suggesting that mobility trajectories in the Swedish labor market do not follow a strong advantage pattern and are instead explained by the attainment of human capital. However, complementary analyses of mid-life wealth suggested more support for cumulative advantage, with those having high-educated parents having much higher levels of wealth.
What_was_studied: We test a prediction of cumulative advantage theory about enduring life cycle effects of educational mobility on earnings using Swedish population registers covering birth cohorts between 1953 and 1955, studying the long-term economic consequences of intergenerational educational mobility and analyzing earnings trajectories of Swedish men and women in each educational mobility category over most of their working-age life course.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the effectiveness of the Swedish welfare regime in regulating and suppressing inequality in the labor market, suggesting that policymakers should prioritize investments in education and social protection to scale up these successes.

Field: Multinomial logistic regression; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Event (probability theory); Economic independence; Retrospective data; Pays bas
Title: Union Dissolution, Unemployment and Moving Out of Homeownership
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that separation has a particularly strong effect on dropping out of owner-occupation, with women having a consistently higher probability than men. Additionally, the study found that later moves are caused by a decline in resources rather than direct changes in the household situation.
What_was_studied: Using multinomial regression analysis on retrospective data for the Netherlands, this study examines how events such as union dissolution and unemployment affect homeownership, with a focus on gendered differences in economic independence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the gendered disparities in economic independence and homeownership, policymakers should prioritize policies that scale up resources for women, such as job training programs and financial assistance for unemployed women. Additionally, policymakers should revise housing policies to better support women who experience separation-related drops in resources.

Authors: Jani Erola; Hannu Lehti; Tina Baier; Aleksi Karhula
Field: Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Early life; Social stratification; Gerontology
Title: Socioeconomic Background and Gene–Environment Interplay in Social Stratification across the Early Life Course
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Genetic influences were strongest in education and weakest in income, and always strongest among those with the most advantaged socioeconomic background, independent of the socioeconomic indicator used. Shared environment influences were negligible for all outcomes.
What_was_studied: Finnish register-based data on 6,529 pairs of twins born between 1975 and 1986 was used to study how genetic influences differ by parents' socioeconomic standing and when in a child's life course parents' socioeconomic standing matters for genetic influences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Stratification scholars should therefore emphasize the importance of the non-shared environment as one of the drivers of the intergenerational transmission of social inequalities.

Field: Sociology; Crowding; Judaism; Unemployment; Occupational mobility; High unemployment; Mass migration; High rate; Demographic economics; Development economics; Immigration
Title: Immigrant employment and occupational mobility in a context of mass migration : Soviet immigrants in Israel
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that the Israeli labor market is more saturated in the 1990s than in the 1970s, leading to high rates of unemployment among immigrants, particularly among male immigrants from high-status occupations. Additionally, there is significant downward occupational mobility for employed immigrants.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the employment and occupational mobility patterns of Soviet Jewish immigrants in Israel during two distinct migration waves: the moderate wave of the 1970s and the enormous wave of the late 1980s and 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of unemployment and downward occupational mobility faced by Soviet Jewish immigrants, it is crucial to scale up job training programs and funding opportunities specifically tailored to their needs. This can help mitigate the negative impacts of mass migration on stratification systems and promote more equitable economic outcomes.

Field: Labour economics; German; Economics; Recession; Unemployment; West germany; Crowding out; Business cycle
Title: Crowding-out of Unskilled Workers in the Business Cycle: Evidence from West Germany
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The analysis finds evidence for crowding-out at the worker inflow: during recessions, the chances of securing a low-skilled job deteriorate more extensively for unskilled individuals than for skilled workers, indicating increased competition between unskilled and skilled workers for low-skilled jobs. However, no evidence for crowding-out at the worker outflow was found.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the question of whether and how cyclical crowding-out contributes to the disproportionate increase in unemployment among the less educated during recessions, using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (GSOEP) for the period 2005-2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize programs that upskill or reskill the less educated to increase their chances of securing better-paying jobs during economic downturns. Additionally, policies aimed at reducing labor market segmentation and improving job matching for low-skilled workers could help mitigate the negative effects of cyclical crowding-out.

Authors: Wout Ultee; Jos Dessens; Wim Jansen
Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Unemployment; Marriage market; Non employment; Individual level; Inequality; Phenomenon
Title: Why does unemployment come in couples? An analysis of (un)employment and (non)employment homogamy tables for Canada, the Netherlands and the United States in the 1980s
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that wives of unemployed husbands had a higher chance of unemployment than wives of employed husbands. Data showed that this phenomenon persisted even after controlling for education and other factors.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between spousal unemployment and marital status among wives in Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, and the USA during the first half of the 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent couple effects observed in this study, policymakers should prioritize interventions aimed at addressing both labor market and marriage market inequalities to mitigate poverty and reduce income disparities.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Psychological intervention; Opportunity structures; Productive aging; Religious freedom; Older people; Multilevel model; Social psychology; Politics
Title: Societal Determinants of Productive Aging: A Multilevel Analysis across 11 European Countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The results partially support hypotheses regarding the relationship between specific macro-level variables and individuals' productive engagement at older ages. While our measure of societal images of aging does not exhibit statistically significant associations with any of the activities considered here, our hypotheses concerning a positive relationship between greater political and religious freedom as well as the provision of welfare state services and older individuals' propensity to engage in productive aging are largely confirmed.
What_was_studied: Based on micro-data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, we estimate logistic multilevel models for individuals' engagement in formal volunteering, informal helping, and caring across 11 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that societal images of aging, political and religious freedom, and the provision of welfare state services can influence older individuals' participation in productive activities. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote positive aging and encourage older adults to engage in meaningful activities, such as volunteering, helping others, or caring for family members.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Collective bargaining; Educational attainment; Wage inequality; Inequality
Title: Occupations and British Wage Inequality, 1970s–2000s
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while most wage inequality is within occupations, it is inequality between occupations that accounts for the majority of the 'massive rise' in wage inequality. Additionally, trends in between-occupation inequality cannot be explained by fundamental labor market changes such as rising educational attainment and declining collective bargaining.
What_was_studied: British wage inequality trends from 1980 to 2017 were analyzed using decomposition methods to understand the between- and within-occupation components of wage inequality, with a focus on the relationship between occupations and growing wage inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing growing between-class inequality to mitigate the widening gap in British wage inequality. This could involve revamping education access and employment opportunities for disadvantaged classes, as well as implementing policies to strengthen collective bargaining and reduce the negative effects of labor market changes on inequality.

Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Work (electrical); Unemployment; Age groups; Distribution (economics); Linkage (mechanical)
Title: Age and Labour‐Market Chances in International Comparison
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found divergent patterns of age concentration in unemployment rates across countries, indicating that different institutional mechanisms affect the transition from education to work and work to retirement for various age groups. For instance, in Germany and Sweden, youth unemployment is lower than adult unemployment, while in Spain and the USA, there is a higher incidence of unemployment among older workers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between institutional mechanisms and unemployment distribution across age groups using a life-course theory of transitions embedded in linkage structures, with international data from the USA, Germany, Sweden, Spain, and Japan covering the period 1985-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the varying patterns of age concentration in unemployment rates, policymakers should prioritize the development of institutional mechanisms that support smooth transitions from education to work and work to retirement for all age groups. This can include strengthening job training programs, promoting flexible work arrangements, and investing in lifelong learning opportunities to scale up employment opportunities for youth and older workers alike.

Field: Private sector; Labour economics; Economics; China; Productivity; Human capital; The Conceptual Framework; Incentive; Meritocracy; Social stratification; Economic system
Title: Rise of Meritocracy in Poland: 1982–2008
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The analysis found that market-oriented reforms have shifted the allocation of rewards towards meritocracy and individual attainments, as evidenced by the rise in returns to university education. Additionally, managers and professionals experienced growing benefits, and privatization distinguished between private and state sector workers with more significant income advantages in the private sector.
What_was_studied: This article investigates whether social stratification in Poland adheres to the market transition framework proposed by theorists for post-communist countries, focusing on returns to human capital and merit-based achievements between 1982 and 2008 using national surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize expanding access to higher education to increase returns to human capital and foster a meritocratic society, as well as consider privatization-based income disparities between public and private sectors when making decisions.

Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Sociology; Unemployment; Occupational commitment; Social psychology; Social network; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: The Concentration of Unemployment Families and Social Networks : A Question of Attitudes or Structural Factors?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a high concentration of unemployment within families and social networks in Sweden.
What_was_studied: This article studies the concentration of unemployment within families and social networks in Sweden based on two random samples consisting of ca. 47 000 young people and ...
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of targeted employment programs for young people in Sweden, particularly those from low-income families and marginalized communities.

Field: Public economics; Counterfactual thinking; Welfare state; Econometrics; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Public expenditure; Flat rate; Social insurance; Earnings; Distribution (economics)
Title: On the counterfactual problem of welfare state research: How can we measure redistribution?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that welfare states with flat rate benefits and proportional taxation have higher income inequality than those with progressive taxation and positive income-related benefits. Additionally, public expenditure on primary and secondary education reduces income poverty and intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of welfare states on income inequality in developed countries, using theoretical models, numeric simulations, and empirical analysis to identify sources of bias in the pre/post approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, decision makers should prioritize progressive taxation policies, invest in public education to reduce inequality, and consider redistributive effects of welfare states when designing social protection systems to ensure fair distribution of resources.

Authors: Kenneth Nelson; Ida Borg; Rense Nieuwenhuis; Susanne Alm
Field: Rental housing; Fractionalization; Economics; Politics; Welfare state; Citizenship; Government (linguistics); Welfare; Demographic economics; Power (physics); Renting; Public economics; Political science; Market economy; Ethnic group; Linguistics; Philosophy; Physics; Quantum mechanics; Law
Title: The political determinants of housing benefits
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that the strength of left governments is positively associated with the size of housing benefits, but this association is conditional on the relative size of rental housing and the fractionalization of the party system.
What_was_studied: This paper applies power resource theory to analyze the political determinants of housing benefits in 31 affluent democracies from 2001–2018, using new housing benefit data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the expansion of housing benefits to address rising inequality and ensure that all citizens have access to safe and affordable housing.

Field: Welfare state; German; Economics; Observational study; Staffing; Context (language use); Family policy; Federal republic of germany; Demographic economics
Title: Do hiring practices penalize women and benefit men for having children? Experimental evidence from Germany
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Job recruitment processes penalize women but not men for having children, with quantitative results indicating that women were less likely to be invited for an interview than men, even after controlling for qualifications and experience.
What_was_studied: The effects of parenthood on hiring processes in the prototypical conservative welfare state, specifically in Germany, using a field experiment and examining the likelihood of motherhood penalties in hiring.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding of motherhood penalties in hiring, policy makers should prioritize scaling up diversity and inclusion initiatives in the German labor market to address discrimination against women with children.

Authors: Maria Vaalavuo; Maarten van Ham; Timo Kauppinen
Field: Multinomial logistic regression; Labour economics; Socioeconomic status; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Economics; Residence; Disadvantaged; Population; Economic integration; Immigration
Title: Income mobility and moving to a better neighbourhood : an enquiry into ethnic differences in Finland
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that upward income mobility is connected to exit from low-income areas, but the effect is stronger among native-born Finns than among those with an immigrant background. This suggests that policies improving labour market opportunities of immigrants and reducing constraints for spatial integration are needed to decrease ethnic residential segregation.
What_was_studied: The spatial concentration of immigrants in disadvantaged neighbourhoods may hinder their opportunities for social and economic integration. This study analyses intra-urban residential mobility from low-income neighbourhoods into non-low-income neighbourhoods among immigrants and native-born residents in three urban regions in Finland, using longitudinal register data for the 2004–2014 period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings imply that policymakers should prioritize and fund initiatives that improve the labor market opportunities of immigrants and reduce constraints on their spatial integration, such as affordable housing in non-low-income neighborhoods. By doing so, they can scale up successful strategies to decrease ethnic residential segregation.

Field: Public economics; International Social Survey Programme; Welfare state; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Survey data collection; Human capital; Research design; Oecd countries; Economic growth; Division of labour
Title: Education Funding and Individual Preferences for Redistribution
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that individuals in countries with high levels of private spending on education are less willing to support government-induced redistribution, suggesting a potential trade-off between private and public investment in human capital formation and social solidarity.
What_was_studied: Using International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) data from 20 OECD countries to investigate the relationship between education financing and preferences for redistribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize and scale up investments in public education, particularly in countries with high levels of private spending on education, to foster a more equitable social safety net and support for redistributive policies.

Field: Positive economics; Welfare state; Public opinion; Sociology; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Scholarship; Insider; Self-interest; Social mobility; Operationalization
Title: Self‐interest, Social Beliefs, and Attitudes to Redistribution. Re‐addressing the Issue of Cross‐national Variation
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Using demographic variables, we find cross-country differences in the social bases of support for redistribution that confirm predictions of welfare-state scholarship. The gap between married and unmarried people is unimportant in universalist regimes; the insider/outsider cleavage is more important in conservative and specific skills systems; class matters more in liberal regimes.
What_was_studied: Stefan Svallfors' 1997 conclusion that patterns of attitudes towards redistribution are essentially the same across welfare-state regimes, using demographic variables to improve model specification and identify cross-country differences in the social bases of support for redistribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the cross-country differences in the social bases of support for redistribution to better tailor social protection policies to their specific contexts. In particular, they should focus on addressing the insider/outsider cleavage and class differences in liberal regimes to ensure effective redistribution.

Authors: Jörg Hartmann; Karin Kurz; Holger Lengfeld
Field: Left-wing politics; Political economy; Political science; Modernization theory
Title: Modernization Losers’ Revenge? Income Mobility and Support for Right- and Left-Wing Populist Parties in Germany
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that support for the AfD is highest among those with stable incomes and those who perceive their incomes as having been unstable, while support for die Linke is highest among those who experienced absolute income gains and those who perceive their incomes as having been upwardly or downwardly mobile.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between income changes and support for populist parties in Germany using longitudinal data from the SOEP survey in 2016, focusing on objective and subjective measures of deprivation and economic mobility among different socioeconomic groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address subjective economic dissatisfaction and promote inclusive economic growth, rather than simply relying on blanket measures to address rising populism.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Comparative research; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Variables; Generosity; Development economics; Social Welfare
Title: Welfare Regimes and Attitudes Towards Redistribution: The Regime Hypothesis Revisited
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The empirical analysis provided mixed support for the hypothesized relationship between welfare regimes and support for redistribution.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates why comparative research on welfare state attitudes has failed to establish a link between welfare regimes and popular support for redistribution in 13 Western European countries from the first two waves of the European Social Survey, using data on total public social spending, benefit generosity, and the weight of social services relative to total public social expenditure.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize operationalizing welfare regimes using a range of theoretically defining characteristics, such as total public social spending, benefit generosity, and the weight of social services relative to total public social expenditure, to better understand the relationship between welfare regimes and popular support for redistribution in Western Europe.

Field: Market segmentation; Ethnic group; Labour economics; Economics; Human capital; Unemployment; Population; Restructuring; Panel data; Immigration
Title: Last Hired, First Fired? The Unemployment Dynamics of Male Immigrants in Germany
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that immigrant populations face a higher risk of unemployment, particularly guest workers, recent newcomers from outside the EU and ethnic Germans, which is largely due to unfavourable labour market allocation and over-representation in vulnerable occupations and economic branches.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the unemployment dynamics of various immigrant groups in Germany during the second half of the 1990s using German Socio-Economic Panel data, comparing guest workers, ethnic Germans, immigrants from the EU-15 or other western industrialized countries, non-EU immigrants and second-generation immigrants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize improving human capital among immigrant populations and addressing labour market segmentation to reduce the risk of unemployment. Additionally, they should scale up support for second-generation immigrants to promote better employment outcomes.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Schema (psychology); Comparability; Law; Presupposition; Dream; Related research; Social stratification
Title: The CASMIN project and the American dream
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The authors found that their model of 'core social fluidity' provided a better explanation for the persistence of inequality than existing theories, with implications for policies aimed at reducing poverty and improving economic mobility. They also found empirical support for the FJH-hypothesis, suggesting that economic mobility is shaped by both structural factors and individual agency.
What_was_studied: The authors analyzed data from the Common Content component of the CASMIN project to respond to critiques by Hout and Hauser and Sorensen on their work, focusing on issues of data comparability, their model of 'core social fluidity', and empirical results relevant to the evaluation of the FJH-hypothesis within an intersectional poverty framework for the United States during the 1970s and 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of poverty and inequality, policymakers should prioritize funding research on 'core social fluidity' to develop targeted interventions that address the systemic barriers facing marginalized communities. This research can inform efforts to scale up successful programs, expand economic mobility opportunities, and revise existing policies to better address intersectional poverty.

Authors: Anette Eva Fasang; Silke Aisenbrey; Klaus Schömann
Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; German; Economics; Life course approach; Context (language use); Employment history; Marital history; Gender inequality; Longitudinal data
Title: Women’s Retirement Income in Germany and Britain
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that single women have higher retirement income than continuously married women in both countries, but there are significant cross-country differences. In the corporatist-conservative German welfare state, marriage over the life course leads to greater dependence on a male breadwinner in retirement than in the liberal British welfare state.
What_was_studied: This article analyses women's retirement income in the context of two distinct welfare states, using longitudinal data for women born between 1930 and 1940 from the German Socio-Economic Panel and the British Household Panel Study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions should prioritize addressing the gendered nature of retirement income, particularly in corporatist-conservative welfare states like Germany. This could involve scaling up programs that support women's employment and financial independence, such as training and education initiatives, as well as expanding social protection schemes to better support single women and those who have been married multiple times.

Field: Welfare state; Political economy; Ideology; Economics; Position (finance); Elite; Elite theory; Variation (linguistics); Public relations; Norwegian; Politics
Title: Ideological integration and variation within the private business elite in Norway
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the private business elite in Norway is largely ideologically integrated, with members opposing key elements of the Norwegian welfare state model and preferring non-socialist parties. CEOs and board chairmen were found to be more conservative than other leaders.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the ideological and political integration of Norway's private business elite during the 2000-2014 period using empirical analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the private business elite is a significant stakeholder in Norway's economy and society, this study suggests that policymakers should prioritize engaging with the elite group to ensure that policy decisions align with their interests and preferences to promote sustainable development.

Field: Social class; European Social Survey; Class (set theory); Sociology; Market system; Survey data collection; Demographic economics; Development economics; Social stratification; Voting; Politics
Title: A New Dimension of Social Stratification in Poland? Class Membership and Electoral Voting in 1991–2001
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that class membership significantly impacts voting behavior in Poland, with the association remaining unchanged across time and across party lines. The findings suggest the emergence of a new dimension of social stratification in post-communist Central and Eastern Europe.
What_was_studied: Using Polish survey data on respondents' voting behavior in elections of 1991, 1994, 1997, and 2001, this study investigates whether class divisions increased as post-communist societies transitioned to a market system, with a focus on Poland.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of class divisions in shaping voting behavior in Poland, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty and education access to scale up opportunities for marginalized communities and reduce class-based political polarization.

Field: Higher education; Sociology; Life course approach; Access to Higher Education; Educational inequality; Educational attainment; Inequality; Social stratification; Economic growth; Horizontal and vertical
Title: Educational Expansion and Its Consequences for Vertical and Horizontal Inequalities in Access to Higher Education in West Germany
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that unequal opportunities to access postsecondary and tertiary institutions remain constant at a high level, and social background effects have not changed over time for the choice of field of study.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effect of educational expansion on inequalities in tertiary education in Germany using four school-leaver surveys from 1983, 1990, 1994, and 1999, focusing on access to postsecondary and tertiary institutions and horizontal choices of fields of study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the ongoing expansion of secondary and tertiary education, policymakers should prioritize interventions that target the persistent inequalities in access to higher education and ensure equal opportunities for all students, regardless of their social background.

Field: Economy; Political science; Property (philosophy); Elite; Czech; Restitution; Eastern european; Social stratification; Socialism; Communism
Title: Did the Transformation to Post-Communism in Eastern Europe Restore Pre-Communist Property Relations?
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that continuity between the pre- and post-communist period with respect to property ownership can be attributed to three factors: (1) property holdings remaining intact throughout the communist period; (2) the restitution of property to the original owners or their heirs in the post-communist period; and (3) the achievement of high-status occupations during the communist period, which facilitated the acquisition of property during that period. Business ownership in post-communist Eastern Europe is linked directly to pre-communist property holding only in Hungary and Bulgaria.
What_was_studied: Using data from Szelenyi and Treiman's 1993 six-nation survey of Social Stratification in Eastern Europe, the study investigates how the transformation from socialism affected property relations in five Eastern European countries (Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia) during the pre- and post-communist periods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of pre-communist property ownership on business ownership in Hungary and Bulgaria, policymakers should prioritize restitution policies that return property to its original owners or their heirs. By doing so, they can enhance the odds of attaining elite occupations during the communist period, which may ultimately lead to greater economic opportunities and social mobility in post-communist Eastern Europe.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Receipt; Educational attainment; Life chances; Income distribution; Social Welfare
Title: Change over Time in the Intergenerational Transmission of Social Disadvantage
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a systematic impact of parental income at all levels of the income distribution, with those originating in the poorest families not standing out as a marginal group. The prevalence of youth employment, teenage motherhood, and low educational attainment decreases over time, while receipt of welfare benefits is more stable. However, intergenerational transmission of social disadvantage does not decline over time if we focus on relative inequality.
What_was_studied: The impact of parental income on social disadvantage in Norway across three decades and four forms of disadvantage (receipt of welfare assistance, unemployment, low educational attainment, and teenage motherhood) was studied using data from a maximum of 30 complete birth cohorts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social mobility opportunities and reduce income poverty, Norway should prioritize policies that target the systematic impact of parental income at all levels of the distribution, such as expanding access to education and job training programs for disadvantaged youth, funding mentorship and networking opportunities for low-income individuals, and revising welfare assistance programs to address intergenerational transmission of poverty.

Authors: Tak Wing Chan; John H. Goldthorpe
Field: Social class; Positive economics; Social status; Sociology; Friendship; Or education; Occupational structure; Status hierarchy; Life chances; Social science; Social stratification
Title: Is There a Status Order in Contemporary British Society?Evidence from the Occupational Structure of Friendship
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found one dimension of the friendship occupational structure that can be plausibly interpreted as reflecting a hierarchy of status, with clear continuities from historical and earlier sociological research, and showed that the status order is distinct from income, education, and socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: This paper considers whether it is still possible to identify a status order in contemporary Britain, analyzing the occupational structure of friendship and presenting empirical results that show a gender-neutral status hierarchy with clear continuities from historical and sociological research, and examining the connection between status and income, education, and class.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that retaining the Weberian distinction between status and class in social stratification research can reveal insights into the articulation of the class structure and the status order, potentially informing policy decisions to scale, expand, or prioritize initiatives aimed at reducing poverty and improving life chances for marginalized populations.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Ideology; Economics; Social inequality; Context (language use); Managing money; Public spending; Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Economic system
Title: Economic Inequality In and Outside of Marriage: Individual Resources and Institutional Context
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that overall levels of economic inequality in a country significantly shape the likelihood of couples having equal versus unequal financial arrangements. Additionally, all three measures of economic inequality - national income inequality, public spending on social programs, and ideological support for inequality - were significantly related to how couples manage their money.
What_was_studied: Cross-nationally comparative data from 15 countries was used to examine the relationship between economic inequality at the national level and the likelihood of couples having equal or unequal financial arrangements, considering gendered contexts and various measures of economic inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need to address economic inequality at the national level to promote equal financial arrangements in marriage. Policymakers should prioritize reducing income inequality, increasing public spending on social programs, and challenging ideologies that support inequality to create a more equitable society.

Authors: Gordon Marshall; Stephen E. Roberts; Carole B. Burgoyne; Adam Swift; David A. Routh
Field: Social class; Sociology; Social inequality; Class (computer programming); Sex segregation; Life chances; Social mobility; Unit (housing); Social psychology; Class formation
Title: Class, Gender, and the Asymmetry Hypothesis
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the unit of class composition is the household in advanced capitalist societies, but not in post-communist states, suggesting that processes of sociopolitical class formation may be different in East and West.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews three interconnected issues that have been central to the controversial problem of describing the relationship between class and gender in advanced capitalist societies and post-communist states, using cross-national data on the relationships between class identities, voting behavior, and the social class standing of male and female partners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the differences in class formation processes between East and West to inform targeted interventions addressing intersectional poverty and gender inequality, particularly in post-communist states.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Position (finance); State (polity); Wage; Disadvantage; Microdata (HTML); Intervention (law)
Title: Winners and losers: The consequences of welfare state policies for gender wage inequality
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that welfare state policies interact with socio-economic position: they limit the economic rewards of highly skilled women, but do not adversely affect, and by some measures actually benefit those who are less skilled.
What_was_studied: Cross-national studies of the impact of welfare states on gender inequality tend to overlook socio-economic divisions among women. This article challenges the implicit assumption that welfare states have uniform effects on the economic attainments of women, arguing that the impact of state intervention is necessarily conditioned by women’s relative advantage or disadvantage in the labour market, using Luxembourg Income Study microdata for 21 advanced countries to analyze gender wage gaps among highly skilled and low-skilled men and women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Highlighting the advantages and disadvantages of social policies for different groups of women, this article concludes that more research is needed to explore differentiated approaches to reconciling work and family, rather than addressing universal work-family tensions. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives tailored to specific socio-economic groups of women to maximize the effectiveness of social policies.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Separation (statistics); Longitudinal study; Unemployment; Cox proportional hazards regression; Market position; Hazard
Title: Does Union Dissolution Lead to Unemployment? A Longitudinal Study of Health and Risk of Unemployment for Women and Men Undergoing Separation
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that individuals who experienced union dissolution were more likely to become unemployed compared to their married/cohabiting counterparts. Additionally, the study revealed gender differences in the impact of union dissolution on labor market position, with men experiencing a higher risk of unemployment than women.
What_was_studied: Using the Swiss Household Panel (SHP) study data from 1999 to 2004, this paper analyzes the effects of union dissolution on employment outcomes for both men and women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize programs that support individuals who have experienced union dissolution, particularly men, to mitigate the negative impacts on their employment outcomes. This could include providing training and education programs to help individuals adapt to changing labor market conditions.

Authors: Klarita Gërxhani; H. van de Werfhorst
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Negative relationship; Social inequality; Informal education; Position (finance); Survey data collection; Human capital; Post communist; Informal sector
Title: The Effect of Education on Informal Sector Participation in a Post-Communist Country
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a strong negative relationship between education and informal sector participation, with education shaping broad civic attitudes that explain more of this relationship than the human capital factor. Additionally, the effect of education was found to be independent of income, suggesting that education shapes moral values independently of socioeconomic status.
What_was_studied: This article examines participation in the informal economy in Albania during the post-communist transition period, focusing on the impact of education and other individual, social, and institutional factors on participation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative relationship between education and informal sector participation, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to quality education for all individuals, particularly those in low-income communities, to reduce poverty and promote sustainable economic growth.

Authors: Frances McGinnity; Antje Mertens; Stefanie Gundert
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Transition (fiction); Unemployment; Subject (philosophy); Life history; West germany; Term (time); Function (engineering)
Title: A bad start? Fixed term contracts and the transition from education to work in West Germany
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment
What_was_found: The researchers found that beginning with a fixed-term contract did not clearly signal a bad start in the German labor market. After five years, the unemployment rates of those who started with fixed-term contracts and permanent contracts converged.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of fixed-term contracts on labor market integration in Germany using life history data, focusing on high-skilled and low-skilled labor market entrants from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up training programs for both high-skilled and low-skilled workers to improve their chances of securing permanent employment contracts. Additionally, the government should consider revising regulations to better support the transition from school to work.

Authors: Tianjian Lai; Haley McAvay; Mirna Safi
Field: Socioeconomic status; Unobservable; Immigration; Disadvantage; Endogeneity; Legal status; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Demographic economics; Salience (neuroscience); Sociology; Political science; Geography; Economics; Econometrics; Psychology; Demography; Law; Mathematical analysis; Population; Mathematics; Cognitive psychology
Title: Diverging pathways: the effects of initial legal status on immigrant socioeconomic and residential outcomes in France
primary_category: Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that refugees have lower household incomes and are more likely to live in immigrant-dense neighborhoods, despite controlling for observable premigratory characteristics. The findings indicate long-term civic stratification mechanisms beyond sorting into legal status categories.
What_was_studied: A large-sample survey of migrants in France, Trajectories and Origins (TeO), examining the effects of initial legal status on socioeconomic attainment, specifically household income, neighborhood disadvantage, and concentration in immigrant neighborhoods, using a unique data set with rich premigratory information and instrumental variable design to correct for endogeneity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to scale up support for refugees and address the socioeconomic disparities they face, particularly in terms of income and neighborhood disadvantage. Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions, such as job training programs and affordable housing initiatives, to help refugees overcome these challenges and achieve sustainable economic mobility.

Authors: Martin Neugebauer; Marcel Helbig; Andreas Landmann
Field: Developmental psychology; Mathematics education; Psychology; Key (music); Disadvantage; Western world; Educational systems; Causal effect; Same sex; Mythology; Objective test
Keywords: Education; Gender Inequality; Teacher Gender; Boy Crisis; Feminization of
Title: Unmasking the Myth of the Same-Sex Teacher Advantage
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found virtually no evidence of a benefit from having a same-sex teacher for boys or girls, suggesting that calls for more male teachers in primary school to address the growing disadvantage of boys are not supported by the data.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed large-scale data from IGLU-E in Germany to investigate whether having a same-sex teacher affects student outcomes, specifically for typical 'male' and 'female' subjects and objective test scores and subjective teacher grades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at improving educational outcomes for all students, rather than focusing solely on increasing the number of male teachers.

Authors: Anna Baranowska-Rataj; Björn Högberg; Laura Bernardi
Field: Microdata (statistics); Unemployment; European union; Demographic economics; Economics; Inequality; Eu countries; Psychology; Economic growth; Sociology; Demography; Mathematical analysis; Population; Mathematics; Census; Economic policy
Title: Parental unemployment and adolescents' subjective wellbeing—the moderating role of educational policies
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that parental unemployment is associated with lower subjective wellbeing among adolescents, but the magnitude of this association varies depending on access to financial support for participation in education. Adolescents who receive educational allowances and who live in countries with broader access to such support are less harmed by parental unemployment.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between parental unemployment and subjective wellbeing of adolescents across countries with different educational policies, using multilevel modelling and data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that providing educational allowances and prioritizing access to education can mitigate the negative impact of parental unemployment on adolescent wellbeing. Policymakers should consider scaling up these interventions to support vulnerable families during economic crises.

Field: Economics; Cohabitation; Institution; Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: The accumulation of wealth in marriage: over-time change and within-couple inequalities
primary_category: Asset poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that wealth premiums are lower during early years of marriage but increase steadily thereafter, with the majority concentrated in housing wealth. Additionally, there is a pronounced within-couple wealth gap prior to marriage during pre-marital cohabitation that remains stable over time in marriage.
What_was_studied: Using high-quality data from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (2002, 2007, 2012, and 2017), this study investigates the accumulation of personal wealth of husbands and wives over time in marriage, focusing on the development of within-couple wealth inequalities during pre-marital cohabitation and after entry into marriage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of a growing wealth gap within couples and the majority of wealth concentrated in housing, urban poverty reduction policies should prioritize affordable housing initiatives to scale up access to affordable housing for low-income households, especially during pre-marital cohabitation.

Authors: Diederik Boertien; Francisco Perales; Léa Pessin
Field: Lesbian; Disadvantaged; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Educational attainment; Sexual identity; Variation (astronomy); Identity (music); Gender studies; Sociology; Demography; Human sexuality; Economic growth; Economics; Physics; Acoustics; Social science; Astrophysics
Title: Does intergenerational educational mobility vary by sexual identity? A comparative analysis of five OECD countries.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that gay and lesbian people have higher educational attainment than heterosexual people in all five countries, with greater rates of upward educational mobility among gay/lesbian individuals. However, there were few differences between heterosexual and bisexual people.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between sexual identity and intergenerational educational mobility in five OECD countries using representative data and coarsened exact matching.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize policies that scale up access to education for disadvantaged sexual minorities, such as funding programs targeting intersectional poverty and supporting sustainable development.

Field: Economics; State (polity); Seekers; Unemployment; Variation (linguistics); Youth unemployment; Educational systems; Oecd countries; Cross national; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Explaining Cross-national Variation in Youth Unemployment Market and Institutional Factors
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that youth unemployment is high in regulated labor markets where employers are restricted in their freedom to dismiss unsuitable workers, but low in liberal labor markets and countries with strong educational systems that provide clear signals about job seekers' abilities and skills.
What_was_studied: This study examines the variation in youth unemployment among OECD countries and identifies institutional and economic factors that contribute to this variation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize implementing labor market reforms that promote flexibility and mobility for both employers and employees, as well as investing in education systems to improve the quality of job matching. Additionally, addressing gender and poverty issues through targeted programs can help reduce youth unemployment.

Field: Unemployment; Turnout; Socialization; Politics; Grievance; Argument (complex analysis); Relevance (law); Feeling; Survey data collection; Panel data; Empirical evidence; Demographic economics; Labour economics; Economics; Political science; Sociology; Social psychology; Psychology; Economic growth; Law; Biochemistry; Chemistry; Statistics; Philosophy; Mathematics; Epistemology; Voting; Econometrics
Title: Unemployment, workplace socialization, and electoral participation: evidence from Sweden
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Significant but modest negative effects of both unemployment in general and job loss, particularly among the young; socialization at workplaces with high colleague participation mitigates the effect.
What_was_studied: The effects of unemployment on electoral participation in Sweden during the 1930s and a pandemic using extensive panel data to investigate causal relationships.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize policies that address grievances and socialize disadvantaged groups into electoral participation, such as job creation programs targeting the young and those who have lost relatively well-paid jobs, to combat intersectional poverty in times of economic crisis.

Field: Labour economics; Discount points; Economics; Unemployment; Research question; Educational attainment; Negative response; Low education; Phenomenon
Title: Unemployment Persistency, Over‐education and the Employment Chances of the Less Educated
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that although jobs with low educational requirements have decreased, they still constitute a significant proportion of all jobs. Moreover, the study reveals that over-education in these jobs has increased, and changed selection patterns into this group contribute to poor employment chances for the less educated. The study also shows that periods of low general demand for labor exacerbate these issues.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between unemployment persistency and employment difficulties for the less educated in Sweden from 1976 to 2000, using empirical data to determine whether reducing jobs with low educational requirements can improve their chances of employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve employment opportunities for the less educated, policies should prioritize job creation in fields that do not require high levels of education, and provide training programs to address over-education and changed selection patterns.
