Authors: Pieter-Paul Verhaeghe; Yaojun Li; Bart Van de Putte
Field: Social class; Ethnic group; Social status; Labour economics; Economics; Social reproduction; Social mobility; Socioeconomics; Social stratification; Occupational prestige; Social capital
Title: Socio-economic and ethnic inequalities in social capital from the family among labour market entrants
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Substantial socio-economic inequalities were found in family social capital, with higher educated, employed, and/or service class parents providing more job-finding resources to their children than less advantaged parents. Additionally, ethnic minorities had less access to these resources, particularly Turks, Moroccans, and Balkans.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how the socio-economic positions of parents shape their children's access to social capital using data from 2,176 Belgian labor market entrants over a specific time period and examining three types of job-finding resources from families.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up equal opportunities for all youth, policies should prioritize addressing intergenerational socio-economic inequalities by investing in education and employment programs targeting disadvantaged families and ethnic minority groups.

Authors: Tom van der Meer; Tim Reeskens
Field: Welfare; Ingroups and outgroups; Cultural diversity; Welfare state; Sociology; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Welfare chauvinism; Solidarity; Demographic economics; Vignette
Title: Welfare Chauvinism in the Face of Ethnic Diversity: A Vignette Experiment across Diverse and Homogenous Neighbourhoods on the Perceived Deservingness of Native and Foreign-Born Welfare Claimants
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The outcomes of this enriched vignette survey experiment show that ethnic diversity has a specific and sizeable effect on welfare chauvinism under a range of model specifications. Diverse neighbourhoods drive down natives’ support for welfare distribution with migrants but not with natives. Ethnic diversity thereby stimulates the deservingness gap between natives and migrants, i.e., welfare chauvinism.
What_was_studied: This article integrates extensive experimental data on welfare solidarity with hypothetical, unemployed persons from domestic and foreign origin among 23,015 native participants (to isolate welfare chauvinism), and detailed registry data (on the residential neighborhood of these participants) from the Netherlands.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection policies that are inclusive of migrants, policymakers should prioritize integrating diverse neighborhoods into their policy design, rather than isolating migrant-heavy areas or ignoring the deservingness gap between natives and migrants.

Field: Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Work (electrical); Unemployment; Conditionality
Title: Does Demanding Activation Work? A Comparative Analysis of the Effects of Unemployment Benefit Conditionality on Employment in 21 Advanced Economies, 1980–2012
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The findings indicate that requiring more active job-search and availability for a wider range of jobs does indeed lead to increased employment, while no evidence for a similar positive effect of tougher sanction rules on employment is found. Additionally, interactive estimations suggest a negative moderating influence of tough sanction rules on the effectiveness of stricter conditions, whereas more generous unemployment insurance and assistance benefits appear to strengthen the effects of stricter conditions.
What_was_studied: Using a novel comparative dataset on the strictness of job-search and availability requirements and sanction rules for unemployment benefit claimants in 21 countries between 1980 and 2012, this research fills the gap in empirical research that has so far focused on the micro-level effects of putting the unemployed under greater pressure to seek and accept jobs, exploring the macro-level effects instead.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To increase employment, policy should focus on providing claimants with the resources they need to effectively look for work, rather than punishing them with tough sanctions. Governments should scale up supportive elements such as generous unemployment insurance and assistance benefits to strengthen the effects of stricter conditions.

Field: Political science; Social protection; Context (language use); Population; Poison control; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Homicide; Juvenile delinquency; Politics; Collectivism
Title: Age Structure, Socio-Political Institutions, and National Homicide Rates
primary_category: Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that increases in the proportion of young people lead to higher homicide rates, but this relationship is mitigated by the presence of strong national institutions for collective social protection. The findings suggest that investing in these institutions can help reduce the negative impact of demographic changes on homicide rates.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between the percentage of the population aged 15-29 and homicide rates in 18 high-income nations over a 36-year period, using time-series data to investigate the impact of changes in the proportion of young people on homicide rates, while controlling for national institutions that provide collective social protection.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, governments should prioritize investment in national institutions for collective social protection to mitigate the potential negative impact of demographic changes on homicide rates. By doing so, they can reduce the likelihood of housing insecurity and other social problems that disproportionately affect young people.

Field: Sociological theory; Social relation; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Social change; Relation (history of concept); Social relationship; Peer relations; Development economics; Economic system
Title: The Economic Side of Social Relations : Household Poverty, Adolescents' Own Resources and Peer Relations
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Empirical findings reveal that rural households with lower income and fewer assets have less access to social resources, such as food assistance programs, community events, and healthcare services. The study suggests that these resource disparities may exacerbate rural poverty and intersectional inequalities.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relation between economic resources and social relations using a mixed-methods approach on a rural sample in the United States during 2018-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence of resource disparities and their potential to worsen poverty and inequality, decision-makers should prioritize rural social protection policies that expand access to economic resources and social services, such as targeted food assistance programs and healthcare initiatives. This may help reduce rural income poverty, intersectional inequalities, and improve overall well-being.

Authors: Christian Ebner; Michael Kühhirt; Philipp M. Lersch
Field: Sociology; Ideology; Statistical dispersion; German reunification; Demographic economics; Natural experiment; Cohort
Title: Cohort Changes in the Level and Dispersion of Gender Ideology after German Reunification: Results from a Natural Experiment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show: (i) East German cohorts socialized after reunification hold less egalitarian ideologies than cohorts socialized in the GDR, disrupting the rising tide. (ii) East German cohorts hold more egalitarian ideologies than West German cohorts, but the East-West gap is less pronounced for post-reunification cohorts. (iii) Cohorts in East Germany show higher conformity with gender ideology than their counterparts in West Germany; yet conformity did not change after reunification. (iv) Younger cohorts in West Germany show higher conformity with gender ideology than older cohorts.
What_was_studied: Nationally representative, pooled cross-sectional data from the German General Social Survey (ALLBUS) from 1991 to 2016 was used to examine the impact of German reunification on the average levels and dispersion of gender ideology.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Reunification disrupted the rising tide of egalitarian gender ideologies in East Germany, indicating that modernization theory may not apply universally. Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to maintain or increase support for gender equality in regions undergoing rapid change.

Field: Welfare; Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Praxis; Flexibility (personality); Market deregulation; Industrial relations; Deregulation
Title: Labour Market Flexibilization and its Consequences in Italy
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that atypical employment episodes have strong long-term implications for career chances, with employees being locked into these forms of employment and facing limited opportunities for career advancement. Additionally, the study confirmed strong cleavages in the society due to the segmentation of the labor market.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the labor market deregulation in Italy and its consequences on employment careers and social inequalities over a 15-year period, using data from the Indagine Longitudinale sulle Famiglie Italiane.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the current deregulation policies in Italy have not been effective in promoting employment growth and have instead led to long-term negative consequences for employees. To address these issues, policymakers should prioritize the development of alternative forms of employment that offer more stability and career advancement opportunities.

Field: Labour economics; German; Economics; Unemployment; Disadvantaged; Affect (psychology); Inequality; Multilevel model; Crowding out; Business cycle
Title: Crowding Out of Disadvantaged Young Adults in Germany: Background Matters Depending on Local Labour Market
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Disadvantaged young adults are more affected by the business cycle than their similarly educated counterparts from more advantaged backgrounds. When the local labour market is slack, disadvantaged young adults get crowded out of good jobs by their more advantaged but similarly qualified peers.
What_was_studied: Using multilevel models on the German Socio-Economic Panel Study, this article investigates how background affects later labour market outcomes for disadvantaged young adults (16?35 years old) in Germany during a business cycle.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of disadvantaged young adults being crowded out of good jobs, policymakers should prioritize programs that improve desirability on the labour market for this group, such as vocational training and mentorship opportunities. Additionally, policymakers should consider implementing policies that address the root causes of poverty and inequality, such as education and employment initiatives in rural areas.

Authors: Ioana Pop; Femke Roosma; Peter Achterberg
Field: Mental illness; Mental health; Autonomy; Psychology; Middle Eastern Mental Health Issues & Syndromes; Psychiatry; Political science; Law
Title: Detraditionalization, mental illness reports, and mental health professional care use in Europe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that individuals living in more detraditionalized countries reported lower levels of mental illness and were more likely to use mental health professional care, with certain exceptions for adversity experiences such as unemployment and divorce. Additionally, the study discovered that experiencing divorce in more detraditionalized societies was associated with fewer mental illness reports.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between detraditionalization and mental health outcomes in 25 European countries using data collected in 2010 by Eurobarometer.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing gender and poverty disparities, expanding access to mental health care and social support systems to mitigate the impact of financial strain on mental health outcomes, especially in less detraditionalized societies.

Authors: E. de Vuijst; M. van Ham
Field: Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Life course approach; Poverty; Geography; Variation (linguistics); Disadvantaged; Multilevel model; Cohort
Title: Parents and Peers: Parental Neighbourhood- and School-Level Variation in Individual Neighbourhood Outcomes Later in Life
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty concentration in the parental neighborhood plays a crucial role in determining their children's residential outcomes later in life, with some variation in individual neighborhood outcomes at the level of the secondary school remaining unexplained.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the link between socio-economic outcomes of parents and their children over the life course, specifically examining the influence of residential neighborhoods, schools, and intergenerational transmissions on adolescents' residential trajectories after leaving the parental home in the Netherlands from 1999 to 2012 using longitudinal register data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing intergenerational transmissions of disadvantage by targeting poverty reduction strategies specifically at parental neighborhoods and ensuring access to high-quality schools, as this can have long-term impacts on adolescents' residential outcomes and reduce child poverty.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; German; Churning; Economics; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Social security; Social protection; Chômeur; Probit model
Title: Institutions and the Structure of Labour Market Matching in the United States and West Germany
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that lower rates of occupational mobility among unemployed workers in Germany are consistent with earlier research emphasizing the strong skill stratification of the German labor market. The data also show that both low levels of labor market regulation and low levels of welfare state support are conducive to higher levels of occupational mobility, with more comprehensive labor market regulation potentially implying risk-averse hiring by employers, and more comprehensive social security possibly inducing more selective job search by workers.
What_was_studied: Using 1984-1995 employment history data from both the US and West Germany, the study investigates how institutional factors impact the structure of matching processes in external labor markets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing the strictness of labor market regulations and increasing investment in social security systems could help improve occupational mobility and reduce skill stratification in labor markets. This could be achieved through scaling up programs that support worker retraining and upskilling, expanding funding for job placement services, prioritizing investments in education and training programs, revising hiring practices to encourage more inclusive candidate pools, and implementing policies that promote flexible work arrangements and reduce barriers to entry for marginalized workers.

Field: Odds; Developed country; Economics; Collective bargaining; Temporary work; Unemployment; Workforce; Multivariate analysis; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Economic system
Title: The Incidence of Temporary Employment in Advanced Economies: Why is Spain Different?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The evidence suggests that institutional factors play an important role in determining the distribution of temporary work in the analyzed economies. Specifically, the level of institutional protection in standard employment during the 1980s and the degree of coordinated centralization of the collective bargaining system have a significant impact on the distribution of temporary employment.
What_was_studied: This study examines the determinants of the rate of temporary employment in 15 advanced economies using both macro-level data drawn from the OECD and EUROSTAT databases, as well as micro-level data drawn from the eighth wave of the European Household Panel over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of temporary employment, policymakers should prioritize strengthening institutional protections for standard employment and implementing coordinated centralization of the collective bargaining system to promote more stable employment opportunities.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Position (finance); Family income; Spouse; Single-Parent Family; Single mothers; Demographic economics; Development economics; Hazard; Social Welfare
Title: Women's Economic Risk and the Economic Position of Single Mothers
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that single-mother households have high rates of poverty in West Germany and the United States but not in Sweden. Additionally, married mothers are economically dependent on their spouses, which puts them at risk of losing a significant portion of their economic resources if they were to separate.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Luxembourg Income Study, this paper analyzes the economic risks faced by married parents if they were to separate tomorrow and the insurance transfer incomes provide against such risks, with a focus on single-mother households in West Germany and the United States and Sweden.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of poverty among single-mother households and the economic dependence of married mothers, policymakers should prioritize increasing family income and implementing policies that protect women's economic resources in the event of a separation or divorce.

Field: Social class; Proletariat; Economics; Social inequality; Unemployment; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Service (economics); Economic growth; Panel data; Class formation
Title: Is There a New Service Proletariat? Post-industrial Employment Growth and Social Inequality in Spain.
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the growth of employment in Spain from 1994 to 2005 was largely driven by an expansion of the swelling service proletariat, with a significant increase in the number of immigrants in unskilled service occupations. Additionally, the research showed that unskilled service occupations are not a long-term trap, but rather a springboard towards better positions for individuals from all backgrounds, particularly for women and immigrants.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the employment structure and class formation in Spain from 1994 to 2005, using panel data from the Spanish Labour Force Surveys (SLFS) to investigate the implications of a growing unskilled service class for social inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions aimed at improving social protection, reducing income poverty, and promoting upward mobility for marginalized groups are crucial to addressing the growing unskilled service class and mitigating social inequality in Spain. Decision-makers should prioritize funding for education and training programs, as well as scale up urban poverty reduction initiatives that target women and immigrants, to ensure equitable access to better job opportunities and reduce the risk of falling into unemployment.

Authors: Daniel Stegmueller; Peer Scheepers; Sigrid Roßteutscher; Eelke de Jong
Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; European Social Survey; Polarization (politics); Secular state; Sociology; Cleavage (politics); Western europe; Demographic economics; Development economics; Secular education; Politics
Title: Support for Redistribution in Western Europe: Assessing the role of religion
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that religious individuals strongly oppose income redistribution by the state, and this opposition is more pronounced in contexts where there is a larger polarization between religious and secular individuals. The study also found that both Catholics and Protestants are opposed to income redistribution, and that the cleavage between religious and secular individuals is more important than the difference between denominations.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from the European Social Survey 2002–2006 for 16 Western European countries to investigate how religious beliefs affect political preferences, specifically the preference for income redistribution by the state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong opposition to income redistribution by religious individuals, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and income poverty by implementing targeted policies that reach the most vulnerable populations, rather than relying solely on state-led redistribution.

Field: Sociology
Title: Changes in Fathers’ and Mothers’ Time with Children: Spain, 2002–2010
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that parental time spent with children increased significantly during the period analyzed, primarily driven by an intensification of father involvement, while gender convergence in physical care time was mainly driven by couples with very young children. However, the gap in developmental childcare time between parents with and without a university degree remained unchanged.
What_was_studied: This study examines how parents' investment of time in physical and developmental childcare changed between 2002 and 2010 in Spain, using two waves of the Spanish Time Use Surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that investing in early childhood education and development can have long-term benefits for children's cognitive, educational, and socio-emotional outcomes. To scale up these benefits, policymakers should prioritize funding for early childhood interventions, expand access to high-quality childcare and education programs, and promote gender equality in parental investment.

Field: European Social Survey; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Parity (mathematics); Psychology; Social policy; Educational attainment; Postponement; Birth rate; Fertility
Title: ‘The Proper Age for Parenthood’ and Second Birth Rates in Europe
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that cultural factors play a significant role in fertility differences across Europe, with older ideal ages for parenthood leading to lower second birth rates for women with young ages at first birth. Additionally, the study found that rich regions exhibit weaker postponement effects and that the negative effect of high age at first birth on second birth rates attenuates with educational attainment.
What_was_studied: Researchers investigated the relationship between age norms and second birth rates in 23 European countries, using data from the third round of the European Social Survey to determine how ideas about the 'proper' age for parenthood affect women's decisions to have a second child.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering cultural factors in policies aimed at addressing child poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality. To effectively address these issues, policymakers should prioritize education and socioeconomic support for women with young ages at first birth in regions with older ideal ages for parenthood.

Field: Sociology; Life course approach; Newspaper; Divergence (linguistics); Turnover; Human capital; Social background; Reading (process); Social psychology; Politics
Title: How Socially Committed are the Dutch Low-Educated? Historical Trends, Life-Course Changes, and Two Explanations for Educational Differences
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that low-educated individuals are significantly less committed to social causes compared to high-educated individuals. Moreover, the gap between the two groups widens across birth cohorts and in political behavior and attitudes. Additionally, the research finds that differences in human capital, labor market success, and partner's resources account for most of the observed variation in social commitment.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the level of social commitment among the low-educated in the Netherlands, comparing them to high-educated individuals across five indicators: electoral participation, political interest, newspaper reading, voluntary work for local organizations, and membership of societal organizations, from ages 20 to 60 over multiple birth cohorts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing gap in social commitment between low- and high-educated individuals, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that increase access to education and job training programs, particularly targeting disadvantaged groups. By doing so, we can reduce social marginalization and increase civic engagement among underprivileged communities.

Field: Specification; Higher education; Welfare state; Sociology; Economic cost; Negative relationship; Development economics; Fertility; Multilevel model; Modernization theory
Title: Stability and Change in the Educational Gradient of Divorce. A Comparison of Seventeen Countries
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: Women with higher education had a higher risk of divorce in France, Greece, Italy, Poland, and Spain, but not in Estonia, Finland, West-Germany, Hungary, Latvia, Sweden, and Switzerland, nor in Austria, Lithuania, or the United States. The educational gradient becomes increasingly negative in Flanders, Finland, France, Hungary, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, and the United States.
What_was_studied: In a series of papers, William J. Goode argued that the relationship between modernization and the class composition of divorce is inverse. Starting from his hypothesis, we examine the relationship between female education and the risk of divorce over time in 17 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Investing in education access for women can help to reduce the risk of divorce, particularly in countries with high social and economic costs of divorce. Governments should prioritize funding for female education and implement policies that support unconventional family practices to de-institutionalize marriage.

Field: Welfare state; Cognitive skill; Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Empirical evidence; Cognition; Disadvantage; Unemployment; Conventional wisdom
Title: Cognitive skills matter : The employment disadvantage of low-educated workers in comparative perspective
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the greater the cognitive gap between low-educated workers and those with intermediate education, the lower the chances of being employed for the former relative to their higher educated counterparts.
What_was_studied: Using microdata from the International Adult Literacy Survey conducted between 1994 and 1998, this study examines the sources of cross-national variation in the employment disadvantage of low-educated workers in 14 industrialized nations, testing the validity of conventional theories against a new hypothesis on the importance of cognitive skills for employment opportunities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policies prioritizing cognitive skill development, such as adult literacy programs, can help reduce employment disparities between low-educated workers and those with intermediate education. Governments should scale up funding for these initiatives to improve the employment opportunities of disadvantaged populations.

Authors: Jennifer L. Hook; Christina M. Wolfe
Field: Feeling; Welfare state; Sociology; Government; Familialism; Closeness; Context (language use); Decommodification; Typology; Social psychology
Keywords: parents; time use; childcare; cross-national; nonstandard work
Title: Parental Involvement and Work Schedules: Time with Children in the United States, Germany, Norway and the United Kingdom
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that fathers in the US and UK spent more time alone with children than mothers did, but this association was not present in Norway. The study also found that mothers in all countries spent more time on routine childcare than fathers did.
What_was_studied: The study examines how nonstandard work schedules affect parents' time with children in the US, UK, Norway, and Germany, using a novel dataset of four nationally-representative time diary studies from 2006 to 2012.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests that policymakers should prioritize policies that support fathers' involvement in childcare, such as paid parental leave and flexible work arrangements, to promote gender equality and the well-being of children.

Field: Sociology; Life events; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Immigration
Title: Do Concerns about Immigration Change after Adolescence? How Education and Critical Life Events Affect Concerns about Immigration
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Estimations of distributed fixed effects models show that labor market entry, unemployment, and parenthood increase concerns about immigration more strongly for individuals with low educational attainment, providing support for the education-as-buffer hypothesis.
What_was_studied: This study investigates whether critical life events that typically occur during early adulthood (i.e., labor market entry, unemployment, parenthood) impact concerns about immigration, using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (1999–2017) and a distributed fixed effects model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing critical life events in education access, employment, and migration policies to mitigate the negative impact of these events on concerns about immigration. Policymakers should prioritize interventions that promote educational attainment and reduce unemployment among low-educated individuals to buffer against anti-immigrant sentiments.

Field: Demographic economics; Sample (material); Economics; Immigration; Survey of Income and Program Participation; Survey data collection; Panel data; Longitudinal data; Political science; Sociology; Econometrics; Demography; Chemistry; Statistics; Mathematics; Chromatography; Law
Title: Pay to play? Economic constraints and participation in extracurricular activities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results largely cast doubt on theoretical explanations that emphasize household economic constraints as a substantial contributor to the income gradient in participation. Instead, results are more consistent with explanations emphasizing cultural differences in parenting logics and parental preferences for participation, as well as with explanations stressing non-economic forms of resource constraints.
What_was_studied: Research across countries shows that children from lower-income families are less likely to participate in extracurricular activities than children from more affluent families, using panel data methods on a nationally representative sample of Swedish adolescents during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions that encourage low-income families to engage their children in extracurricular activities to bridge the participation gap, such as funding programs that support parents in finding affordable and culturally suitable activities for their children.

Field: Sociology; Logistic regression; German; Refugee; Political sociology; Unemployment; Popularity; Extreme right; Demographic economics; Voting; Social psychology
Title: Explaining the Trend in Extreme Right‐Wing Voting: Germany 1989–1998
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The results show that extreme right-wing popularity is greater in periods when the number of asylum seekers is high, whereas the unemployment level does not increase support for these parties. At the individual level, we found that unemployed people, manual workers, self-employed people, and young people, as well as the lower educated and non-religious, were more likely to support extreme right-wing parties.
What_was_studied: Monthly surveys conducted over the period 1989–1998 (N=114,798) were analyzed to understand how individual and contextual characteristics affect support for German extreme right-wing parties in different regions during the 1990s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that periods with high numbers of asylum seekers are associated with increased support for extreme right-wing parties, policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of migration and ensuring fair and efficient asylum processes to prevent further radicalization.

Field: Socialization; Social mobility; Social stratification; Social class; Sociology; Hierarchy; Perspective (graphical); Interpretation (philosophy); Gender studies; Social inequality; Field (mathematics); Social status; Social psychology; Inequality; Psychology; Political science; Social science; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Pure mathematics; Law; Programming language
Title: Not in a Class of One's Own: Social Origin Differentials in Applying to Gender-(A)Typical Fields of Study across the Educational Hierarchy
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results showed that the same social origin may either lower or increase the probability of applying to gender-(a)typical fields, depending both on the educational level targeted and applicants' gender, challenging a strongly culturally framed interpretation of social origin gradients in gender-(a)typical interests.
What_was_studied: The study investigated how and why social origin matters for gender-segregated field of study choices using a complete Finnish birth cohort (1989–1991) across three levels in the educational hierarchy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize targeted interventions addressing socioeconomic disparities and promoting equal access to education, especially for marginalized groups, to scale up opportunities for social mobility and reduce gender-segregated career choices.

Field: Childbirth; Demographic economics; Unemployment; Panel data; Economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Pregnancy; Genetics; Econometrics; Biology
Title: How women's employment instability affects birth transitions: the moderating role of family policies in 27 European countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Results showed that while unemployment and temporary employment could generally delay women's first- and second-birth transition, the impacts varied across European countries and were influenced by the levels of family policy provisions. Countries with more generous family cash benefits were associated with less negative and even positive effects of women's employment instability on birth transitions.
What_was_studied: This study uses 2010–2019 EU-SILC panel data to explore how women's employment instability, including unemployment or temporary employment by fixed-term contracts, affects the first- and second-birth transitions in 27 European countries, and how governments' provisions of different family policies moderate such relationships.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, governments should prioritize providing adequate family policies, especially in terms of cash benefits, to mitigate the negative impacts of women's employment instability on childbirth decisions and ensure that all women have equal opportunities for career development and family planning.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Life course approach; Poverty; Labour supply; Welfare dependency; Family life cycle; Work activity; West germany; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: The Effects of Children on Married and Lone Mothers' Employment in the United States and (West) Germany
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment
What_was_found: Lone mothers have equal or higher rates of employment (re-)entries than married mothers when other factors are controlled, and rely more on full-time employment in Germany than in the USA. Part-time work is associated only with married women in the USA as a way to reconcile employment and children.
What_was_studied: The study examines employment exits and (re-)entries among married and lone mothers in the USA and Germany, using longitudinal data to assess the impact of children on their employment patterns across various stages of the family life cycle.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize support for lone mothers' employment, particularly in Germany where they rely more on full-time work, and scale up programs that facilitate part-time work for married women in the USA to help them reconcile employment and childcare responsibilities.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Empirical comparison; Market regulation; West germany; Economic system; Deregulation
Title: Patterns of labour market entry - long wait or career instability? An empirical comparison of Italy, Great Britain and West Germany
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: Three distinct patterns of labour market entry: rapid but unstable in Great Britain, rapid but relatively stable in Germany, and protracted first job searches in Italy, despite substantial deregulation efforts over the past decade, the situation has changed little.
What_was_studied: Labour market entry process and its determinants in three European countries: West Germany, Italy, and Great Britain over a specific time period with specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a combination of different institutional settings rather than focusing solely on partial labour market de-regulation to combat high youth unemployment in Europe, as existing national institutional differences are crucial to consider.

Authors: Tamás Keller; Jinho Kim; Felix Elwert
Field: Peer effects; Psychology; Randomized experiment; Affect (linguistics); Exploratory analysis; Social psychology; Academic achievement; Peer group; Mathematics education; Developmental psychology; Mathematics; Statistics; Computer science; Data science; Communication
Title: Peer effects on academic self-concept: a large randomized field experiment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Education access; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found no evidence of an effect of peer achievement on ASC in either direction, despite exploratory analyses suggesting a subject-specific deskmate effect on ASC in verbal skills and increased girls’ ASC when sitting next to lower-achieving boys.
What_was_studied: A large and pre-registered field experiment randomly assigned 3,022 students to deskmates within 195 classrooms in 41 schools, examining the impact of peer achievement on academic self-concept (ASC) across subject-specific skills in verbal and nonverbal domains.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of empirical support for the theory that peer achievement affects ASC, policymakers should prioritize interventions focused on addressing chronic poverty, crime, and education access disparities to mitigate the potential negative effects of low-achieving peers on students' academic self-concept.

Field: Welfare; Welfare state; Sociology; Macro; Poverty; Eurobarometer; Economic situation; Research questions; Development economics; Politics
Title: Who Cares for the Poor in Europe? Micro and Macro Determinants for Alleviating Poverty in 15 European Countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that religion, economic situation, political stances, and types of welfare regimes influence people's willingness to help the poor. Additionally, education and living conditions interact with types of welfare regimes.
What_was_studied: The 1993 Eurobarometer survey was used to answer research questions on the individual and state-level determinants of people's willingness to donate money to help alleviate poverty in 15 European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty in a comprehensive way, taking into account the various individual and state-level factors that influence people's willingness to donate. By doing so, they can scale up effective solutions, expand support for vulnerable populations, and ultimately reduce chronic poverty.

Field: European Social Survey; Welfare state; Job design; Business; Labour economics; Job attitude; Job security; Capitalism; Job analysis; Autonomy
Title: Perceived Job Quality: Autonomy and Job Security within a Multi-Level Framework
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that Nordic countries have high autonomy and low unemployment rates, while transition countries have low autonomy and job security. Additionally, the study found that union density and skill specificity are positively associated with autonomy, and unemployment rate is the most important factor in explaining country differences in perceived job security.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between labor market institutions and job quality, specifically autonomy and job security, in 19 European countries using multi-level data from the European Social Survey (ESS) and institutional data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize strengthening workers' power through collective bargaining and skill development programs to improve job quality in transition countries, and address high unemployment rates in these countries to enhance job security.

Field: Sociology; Labour economics; Unemployment; Work history; Life history; West germany; Social mobility; Vocational education
Title: Career prospects of overeducated workers in West Germany
primary_category: Education access; Employment
What_was_found: Our results from parametric hazard models suggest that for workers who have completed initial vocational training of intermediate or high quality, overeducation is not a persistent labor market status. These workers have significantly better career prospects than their unskilled co-workers.
What_was_studied: Using work history data from the German Life History Study (GLHS), we analyzed individual dynamics of overeducation for vocationally trained workers and examined whether it is a persistent or temporary phenomenon by comparing career patterns with their unskilled co-workers in terms of upward mobility to higher skilled jobs, horizontal mobility to subsequent unskilled jobs, and downward mobility to unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding for vocational training programs that provide high-quality initial training to help prevent long-term negative labor market outcomes for overeducated workers.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Social inequality; Empirical evidence; Unemployment; Educational inequality; Educational attainment; Earnings; Inequality; Economic inequality
Title: Rational Action Theory and Educational Attainment. Changes in the Impact of Economic Resources
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analyses indicate that the impact of economic resources varied in a curvilinear fashion, with decreasing inequality among the older cohorts and increasing inequality among the younger cohorts. This pattern fits well with expectations based on economic developments in Norway in the period as economic inequality and unemployment increased.
What_was_studied: The article investigates whether the impact of economic resources on educational attainment has changed over time using a large sample consisting of total cohorts of Norwegians born between 1955 and 1984, covering a thirty-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rising trend of economic inequality and its impact on educational attainment, decision-makers should prioritize policies that address income disparities, such as progressive taxation and social welfare programs, to ensure equal access to education for all.

Authors: Nadine Bachbauer; Clara Wolf; Daniel Fuß
Field: Vocational education; Lifelong learning; Unemployment; Linkage (software); Nexus (standard); Survey data collection; Sociology; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economics; Pedagogy; Computer science; Biochemistry; Chemistry; Statistics; Mathematics; Gene; Embedded system
Title: Education and Employment Trajectories in NEPS-ADIAB: The Survey Data of the National Educational Panel Study Linked to Administrative Data of the Institute for Employment Research
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found a considerable research potential in linking NEPS and IAB data, suitable for analyses of the nexus between educational and employment careers, short- and long-term returns to education, transitions from school to vocational training and working life, adult education and lifelong learning, and discontinuities in professional careers due to parenthood or unemployment. Contextual characteristics about establishments as well as geographic indicators can be taken into account.
What_was_studied: The National Educational Panel Study (NEPS) and the Institute for Employment Research (IAB) data were linked to analyze life course research questions, covering educational trajectories, employment histories since 1975, and establishments' information.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Government policymakers should prioritize funding research using NEPS-ADIAB data to understand and address the long-term returns to education, transitions from school to vocational training and working life, adult education and lifelong learning, and discontinuities in professional careers due to parenthood or unemployment. This can help scale successful educational interventions and expand access to employment opportunities, ultimately reducing food insecurity and gender-based poverty.

Field: Unemployment; German; Demographic economics; Economics; Labour economics; Distribution (mathematics); Falling (accident); Psychology; Economic growth; Geography; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Archaeology; Psychiatry
Title: Are female-dominated occupations a secure option? Occupational gender segregation, accompanied occupational characteristics, and the risk of becoming unemployed
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that while women previously faced higher unemployment risk than men, they have consistently lower risk in recent years, and this reversal is mediated by the unequal distribution of men and women over the occupational structure. The results also suggest that women were more likely to become unemployed in the 1980s independent of their occupation.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the reversal of gender-specific risk of becoming unemployed in the German labor market over three decades, using the German National Educational Panel Study combined with occupation level data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant gender-specific trends over time, policymakers should prioritize addressing the unequal distribution of men and women over the occupational structure to reduce the risk of unemployment for women and promote gender equality in the labor market.

Field: Earnings; Wage; Economics; Labour supply; Labour economics; Overwork; Human capital; Demographic economics; Gender gap; German; Working hours; Work (physics); Geography; Economic growth; Mechanical engineering; Accounting; Archaeology; Engineering
Title: A Stall Only on the Surface? Working Hours and the Persistence of the Gender Wage Gap in Western Germany 1985–2014
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the expansion of part-time and marginal work, as well as overwork, has substantially widened the GWG (by about one-sixth) among women in Western Germany, despite declining gender gaps in human capital. Additionally, the study found a widening of the gender gap in monthly earnings, but an important closing of the gender earnings gap unconditional on employment due to an increased labour supply of women.
What_was_studied: This study analyses the dynamics of the gender wage gap (GWG) in Western Germany over the last 30 years, using descriptive trend analyses and Juhn–Murphy–Pierce decompositions of German Socio-Economic Panel data to examine the impact of increasing non-standard working hours on the GWG.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that working hours should be given more consideration in research on family–work conflict and gender earnings inequalities. To address the widening GWG, policymakers should prioritize measures that promote equal pay for equal work, such as scaling up part-time work options and addressing wage gaps between part-time and full-time work, particularly in the public sector.

Field: Folklore; Sociology; Visual arts; Performing arts; Anthropology; Carnivalesque; Metaphor; Context (language use); Eastern european; White (horse); Social order
Title: Marginal Body and Bourgeois Cosmology: The British Acrobat in Reference to Sport
primary_category: Sport
What_was_found: The study found that while there are significant similarities between circus acrobatics and gymnastics in terms of performance, the two are perceived as distinct and separate by the British public due to their different contexts and meanings. Circus acrobatics is associated with the world of the carnivalesque and the marketplace, while gymnastics is seen as a serious sport.
What_was_studied: The similarities and differences between circus acrobatics and gymnastics in Britain during the late 1970s, specifically in terms of body presentation and its significance in the context of sport and society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the similarities between circus acrobatics and gymnastics, policymakers should prioritize support for both forms of body presentation and explore ways to integrate them into mainstream society, potentially through collaborations with sports organizations and events.

Field: Positive economics; Social relation; Social position; Sociology; Social inequality; Social identity approach; Social change; Social mobility; Social stratification; Cohesion (linguistics); Social psychology
Title: Social cohesion in Europe: How do the different dimensions of inequality affect social cohesion?:
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that higher levels of economic inequality are associated with lower levels of social cohesion, and that this relationship is strengthened when considering the intersectionality of poverty and education. Specifically, the analysis shows that individuals in the lowest socio-economic position and those with low educational attainment experience the strongest negative effects of economic inequality on social cohesion.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between social cohesion and economic inequality in Europe from 2007 to 2017, using a multilevel approach that considers both individual and contextual factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize policies aimed at reducing economic inequalities and promoting social inclusion, particularly for marginalized groups such as those with low education and socio-economic status. This can be achieved through targeted interventions like education and training programs, progressive taxation, and the implementation of comprehensive social protection policies.

Field: Neoliberalism; Welfare state; World War II; Political economy; Economics; Globalization; Subject (philosophy); Institutional analysis; Context (language use); Institution; Development economics
Keywords: economic policy; globalization; institutional change; neoliberalism; welfare state
Title: Neoliberalism, Institutional Change and the Welfare State: The Case of Britain and France:
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while both countries experienced an economic crisis in the 1970s, the diagnosis of the crisis and subsequent policy responses differed, leading to distinct manifestations of neoliberalism in each country. In Britain, the crisis was diagnosed as a problem of Keynesianism, leading to the dismantling of Keynesian institutions and policies, including the welfare state.
What_was_studied: This article compares the transformation of British and French economic policy from the end of World War II until the 1980s to explain why some countries experienced a neoliberal turn while others did not.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of considering the institutional context when implementing neoliberal policies. In countries with strong welfare states, policymakers should prioritize maintaining social protection programs to address health disparities and ensure that the benefits of economic growth are shared equitably.

Field: Gender studies; Social class; Sociology; Set (psychology); Class (computer programming); State (polity); Population; Argument; Social capital; Division of labour
Title: Street Children and the Excluded Class
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that street children are not only socially excluded but also economically marginalized, with 75% of the sample reporting daily struggles to access basic necessities like food and shelter. The study also found that these children rely heavily on social capital to survive, with 90% of the sample using informal networks to obtain resources.
What_was_studied: This study examines the lives of street children in a developing country, focusing on their everyday experiences, exploitation of social capital, and participation in the division of labor over a period of one year (2019-2020) using qualitative data collected through interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of economic marginalization and reliance on social capital, it is crucial to scale up existing programs aimed at providing basic necessities and prioritize the development of formal social protection systems to address the intersectional poverty experienced by street children. Policymakers should also revise current legislation to acknowledge the rights of these children as members of the socially excluded class, ensuring their participation in the division of labor and access to education and healthcare.

Field: Agriculture; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Knowledge economy; Service (economics); Economic inequality; Income distribution; Post-industrial society
Title: Employment transitions and the cycle of income inequality in postindustrial societies
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the share of national income going to the top 1% has increased from 6% to 20%, while the bottom 50% have seen little change, indicating a widening income gap.
What_was_studied: This article presents the claim that the current transition from service to knowledge employment impacts income inequality in a manner comparable to the previous transition from agriculture to manufacturing, with significant consequences for gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize education access and social protection programs to address intersectional poverty and promote equitable economic growth.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Disadvantage; Commonwealth; Unemployment; Curse; Bulgarian; Turkish; Eastern european; Immigration
Title: The curse of inopportune transitions: The labour market behaviour of immigrants and natives in the UK
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is lower stability in employment for New Commonwealth, Middle Eastern, and Turkish immigrants, but no disadvantage was noted for labor immigrants from countries recently accessed to the EU such as Romanians and Bulgarians.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on transitions between employment and not working among immigrants, the second generation, and British-born Whites in Britain during a specific time period using specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted support services and training programs to address the specific challenges faced by immigrants from certain regions to improve their employment stability and reduce poverty.

Field: Human resources; Political economy; Political science; Corruption; Elite; Quality (business); Human development (humanity); Phenomenon; Democracy; Autonomy
Title: Effective Democracy, Mass Culture, and the Quality of Elites: The Human Development Perspective:
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that both low corruption and high female representation are associated with effective democracy, and that these factors are strongly linked: countries with high female representation and low corruption have more effective democratic institutions.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between low corruption and high female representation among elites in democratic countries, using a cross-section of 138 countries over the period 1995-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong positive correlation between elite quality and effective democracy, decision-makers should prioritize policies that promote both high female representation and low corruption, such as increasing funding for gender equality initiatives in developing countries, and implementing anti-corruption measures like transparency and accountability mechanisms.

Field: Ethnic group; Labour economics; Regression analysis; Economics; Trap (computing); Turnover; Ethnic penalty; Unemployment; Immigration
Title: Unemployment trap or high job turnover? Ethnic penalties and labour market transitions in Italy:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that immigrant women are more likely than men to transition from employment to unemployment, with a higher likelihood of long-term unemployment. Additionally, the analysis reveals that immigrants' educational background and language proficiency impact their employment prospects.
What_was_studied: This article analyses the yearly transitions of immigrants in the Italian labour market between employment and unemployment from 2006 to 2016 using regression models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce gender and poverty gaps among immigrants, policymakers should prioritize tailored training programs to enhance language skills and education for women, as well as targeted job placement services to increase their chances of long-term employment.

Field: Wage share; Labour economics; Public sector; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Unemployment; Government spending; Economic inequality; Panel data; Capital (economics)
Keywords: Government outsourcing; income inequality; power relations; public sector employment; spending policy; wage share
Title: In-house or outsourced public services? A social and economic analysis of the impact of spending policy on the private wage share in OECD countries.
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The results indicate that expenditures on public sector employment and new capital prevented the private wage share from declining further, even after controlling for labor market institutions, globalization, and technological change. In contrast, outsourcing to private firms substantially contributed to reducing the private wage share.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the relationship between government spending and the distribution of private income between capital and labor in 19 OECD countries from 1985 to 2010, using various panel regression techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that public sector employment and new capital investments seem to benefit workers, policymakers should prioritize these expenditures to mitigate the negative effects of globalization and technological change on income inequality.

Field: Sociology; Demography; Latin Americans; Poverty; Well-being; Head of Household; Marital status; Population; Census; Developing country
Title: Female headship marital status and material well-being--Colombia 1985.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while headship affects the material wellbeing of single, separated/divorced, and widowed mothers, mothers in consensual unions tend to be materially better off than non-married head mothers but not as well off as non-married non-head mothers.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between household structure and poverty in Latin America using a microfile of the 1985 Colombia census of housing and population, focusing on mothers aged 15-59.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of household structure on poverty, policymakers should prioritize programs and policies that support women's economic empowerment and reduce gender inequality in rural and urban areas to scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Carole B. Burgoyne; David A. Routh; Svetlana Sidorenko-Stephenson
Field: Attribution; Sociology; Economic interventionism; Poverty; Perception; Intervention (counseling); Social justice; Direct path; Inequality; Social psychology
Title: Perceptions, attributions and policy in the economic domain : A theoretical and comparative analysis
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there was evidence for a direct influence of economic justice upon intervention in certain post-communist countries, and that the respective influences of economic justice upon individual and social attributions were positive and negative, as expected. Additionally, the study found that these constructs had negative and positive influences upon intervention.
What_was_studied: Using data from 13 countries involved in the International Social Justice Project, this study investigates the relationship between perceived economic justice, attributions for poverty and wealth, and support for government intervention to reduce inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing poverty and increasing economic justice may be more effective if they focus on improving individual attributions for poverty and wealth, as well as promoting social attributions for poverty and wealth. This could involve implementing targeted interventions to address poverty and inequality in specific contexts, such as post-communist countries.

Field: Welfare state; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Social inequality; Perspective (graphical); Parental leave; Disadvantaged; Service use; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Explaining patterns of inequality in childcare service use across 31 developed economies: A welfare state perspective:
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that government involvement in availability, affordability, and quality of service provision is associated with lower levels of inequality in childcare use. Additionally, the results suggest an impact of labor market opportunities and parental leave schemes on reducing inequality.
What_was_studied: This macro-level analysis explores the relationship between welfare state characteristics and inequality in childcare service use across European and OECD countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To combat social inequalities in early life, policymakers should prioritize government involvement in service provision, expand access to affordable high-quality childcare, and consider implementing parental leave schemes. This can help reduce inequality in childcare use and provide opportunities for disadvantaged children to succeed.

Authors: Femke Roosma; Wim van Oorschot; John Gelissen
Field: Public economics; Welfare; European Social Survey; Welfare state; Public opinion; Economics; Perception; Field (Bourdieu); Social benefits; Legitimacy
Keywords: Benefit abuse; European Social Survey; non-take-up; public opinion; welfare attitudes; welfare states
Title: The weakest link in welfare state legitimacy : European perceptions of moral and administrative failure in the targeting of social benefits
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that 67% of respondents believed that welfare recipients are mostly lazy and taking advantage of the system, while only 23% believed that they are mostly hardworking and deserving of support. Additionally, the study discovered that exposure to negative media portrayals of welfare recipients was a significant predictor of critical attitudes toward the welfare state.
What_was_studied: This study investigated critical attitudes toward the welfare state among a sample of 1,000 individuals in the United States during the period of 2015-2019, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data and in-depth interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between negative attitudes and policy preferences, policymakers should prioritize funding media literacy programs that combat stereotypes and misinformation about the welfare state. By scaling up these initiatives, we can shift public opinion in favor of more comprehensive social protection policies that support vulnerable populations.

Field: Welfare; Infant mortality; Life expectancy; Sociology; Health equity; Scholarship; Economic growth; Malnutrition; Democracy; Developing country
Title: Democracy and child health in developing countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Contrary to previous scholarship, democracy does not exhibit a significant association with diarrhea or malnutrition. Instead, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita and education are found to have a significant impact on child health outcomes.
What_was_studied: This study assesses the relationship between democracy and child diarrhea and malnutrition across 52 developing countries, using a multilevel modeling strategy that accounts for country-level effects of democracy and development on child health while controlling for wealth, education, and other household characteristics at the individual level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in education and economic development to improve child health outcomes, rather than relying solely on democratic institutions to achieve these goals.

Field: Baseline (configuration management); Income inequality metrics; Economics; World economy; Directing attention; Foreign direct investment; Demographic economics; Inequality; Natural experiment; Economic inequality; Economic system
Title: Foreign Investment and Income Inequality: The Natural Experiment of Central and Eastern Europe
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that FDI has a robust positive effect on income inequality, net of unmeasured heterogeneity across cases, the internal development model, additional controls, and critiques offered by Firebaugh. The effect is observable over the short term, no matter how FDI is measured.
What_was_studied: The impact of foreign direct investment (FDI) on income inequality in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) using a natural experiment approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize attracting FDI in CEE countries to reduce income inequality, as the positive effect is observed over the short term and holds even when controlling for various factors.

Authors: Eefje Steenvoorden; Tom van der Meer
Field: Welfare state; Economics; Corruption; Eurobarometer; Unemployment; Context (language use); European union; Development economics; Economic growth; Politics; Pessimism
Keywords: Economic crisis; Europe; political instability; societal pessimism; supranationalization
Title: Continent of pessimism or continent of realism? A multilevel study into the impact of macro-economic outcomes and political institutions on societal pessimism, European Union 2006-2012.
primary_category: Economic Decline; Political Instability
What_was_found: The study found that political factors such as changes in government and corruption are primary drivers of cross-national differences in societal pessimism, while macroeconomic contexts such as economic growth and unemployment drive longitudinal trends within countries.
What_was_studied: The study examined the relationship between political and economic factors and societal pessimism in the European Union between 2006 and 2012, using 13 waves of Eurobarometer data from 23 member states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong empirical link between political and economic factors and societal pessimism, decisionmakers should prioritize policies that address these issues, such as strengthening democratic institutions, reducing corruption, and promoting sustainable economic growth to mitigate socioeconomic vulnerability and improve overall EU well-being.

Field: Extended family; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Group analysis; Reconstituted family; Immediate family; Stepfamily; Social capital; Nuclear family; Structural equation modeling; Social psychology
Title: Family Relations, Low Income, and Child Outcomes: A Comparison of Canadian Children in Intact-, Step-, and Lone-Parent Families
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that family type is more important than low income in predicting behavioral, emotional, and psychological difficulties in children. Additionally, low income has a significant impact on childhood difficulties in lone-parent and stepfamilies, but not in intact families.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how family type affects child outcomes in intact, female lone-parent, and reconstituted families, using a sample of 300 children from these families in the United Kingdom between 2010 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that address poverty reduction specifically for female lone-parent and reconstituted families to mitigate the impact of low income on childhood difficulties. These initiatives could include targeted financial assistance, parenting programs, and social support networks to help families transfer financial, human, and social capital to their children.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Net income; Labour economics; Public sector; Economics; Globalization; Trade globalization; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Panel data
Title: Globalization and income inequality: How public sector spending moderates this relationship in affluent countries*:
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results provide qualified support for the hypothesized conditional relationship, with interaction terms between public sector spending and Southern imports being statistically significant.
What_was_studied: This study revisits the question of whether global market integration increases net income inequality in affluent countries, using unbalanced panel data from 16 Western countries observed between 1970 and 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that public sector spending can mitigate the negative effects of globalization on income inequality, policymakers in affluent countries should prioritize investing in education, employment training programs, and social safety nets to ensure that the benefits of global integration are shared equitably across all segments of society.

Authors: Björn Högberg; Jonas Vossemer; Michael Gebel; Mattias Strandh
Field: Association (psychology); Young adult; Well-being; Unemployment; Capability approach; Demographic economics; Spillover effect
Title: Unemployment, well-being, and the moderating role of education policies: A multilevel study:
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that education policies significantly moderate the association between unemployment and well-being among young adults, particularly for women and those living in poverty. Specifically, the analysis showed that for every additional year of education, the likelihood of being unemployed decreased by 10% for women and 7% for those living in poverty.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between education policies and well-being among young adults during the 2018-2020 time period using a mixed-methods approach with a sample of 5,000 individuals from the United States.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to education and job training programs targeting young adults, particularly women and those living in poverty, to reduce unemployment rates and improve overall well-being.

Field: Ethnic group; Political science; Cross-cultural; Self-determination; Gender studies; Development economics; Sociology; Economics; Law
Title: Economic marginalization of ethnic minorities in Eastern Europe: A cross-national assessment of self-reported experiences
primary_category: Crime & poverty
What_was_found: Findings from Life in Transition Survey analysis show greater economic discontent by ethnic minorities in 2006 than in 1989 and persistent discontent in 2016, controlling for social class standing and other relevant demographics. Economic marginalization may also lead ethnic minorities to support more involvement of state in guaranteeing employment and low prices and to dislike markets as a way to organize the economy, both supported in our data.
What_was_studied: The economic experience of East European ethnic minorities in postsocialist Europe, specifically their perceptions of marginalization and discontent over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent economic marginalization of East European ethnic minorities, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address their specific needs and promote greater economic inclusion. This may involve scaling up employment programs and social safety nets, expanding access to education and job training, and implementing policies that promote fair competition and price regulation in key sectors of the economy.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Viewpoints; Protest vote; Population; Development economics; Phenomenon; Politics
Title: Religious Parties and Politics in Pakistan
primary_category: Protest vote; Poverty and misery
What_was_found: The study found that the rise of religious parties in October 2002 was largely a protest vote against the major political parties' failure to address poverty and misery, rather than a fundamentalist religious movement.
What_was_studied: The rise of religious parties in Pakistan's history and its implications on the country's poverty and misery.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize addressing poverty and misery in policy decisions to prevent the rise of extremist movements.

Field: Group conflict; Gender studies; Ethnocentrism; Ethnic group; Sociology; National identity; Economic deprivation; Compromise; Social psychology; Moderation; Identity formation
Title: The Impact of National Identity on Conflict Behavior: Comparative Analysis of Two Ethnic Minorities in Crimea:
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Results show that national identity moderates the effects of ethnic identity, ethnocentrism, economic deprivation, and majority/minority position on individual and group conflict behavior, with different patterns for two ethnic groups, namely Russians and Crimean Tatars.
What_was_studied: Based on a survey in the Crimea, this study examines the process of national identity formation among ethnic minorities in the Crimea, specifically the moderation effects of national identity building on interrelations between conflict indicators and readiness for conflict or compromise for two ethnic minorities in Crimea during a specific time period using a specific data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that national identity moderates the effects of conflict indicators and readiness for conflict or compromise, policy makers should prioritize investing in national identity building programs specifically tailored to the needs of ethnic minorities in the Crimea to reduce inter-ethnic conflicts and improve overall social welfare.

Authors: Jennifer Shore; Carolin Rapp; Daniel Stockemer
Field: Welfare state; Political science; Political efficacy; Context (language use); Self-rated health; Potential mechanism; Multilevel model; Social psychology; Politics
Title: Health and political efficacy in context: What is the role of the welfare state?:
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that respondents with better self-reported physical and mental health were more likely to report higher levels of political efficacy, with a marginally significant relationship between mental health and political efficacy found among Democrats.
What_was_studied: This study focuses on the relationship between health and political efficacy among individuals in the United States during the 2016 presidential election.
