Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of political efficacy in democratic engagement, policymakers should prioritize investments in public health interventions to promote physical and mental well-being, particularly among Democratic voters.

Authors: Vincent Corluy; Ive Marx; Gerlinde Verbist
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Residence; Unemployment; Citizenship; Labour force survey; Market position; Probit model; Immigration
Keywords: citizenship; employment probability; selection effect; naturalization premium
Title: Employment chances and changes of immigrants in Belgium: The impact of citizenship
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Citizenship acquisition is associated with better labor market outcomes for non-Western immigrants in general, with a 'citizenship premium' found in Belgium.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of citizenship acquisition on the labor market position of immigrants in Belgium, using Labour Force Survey data for 2008 and probit regression to estimate static and dynamic employment probabilities and unemployment risks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Belgium should prioritize simplifying citizenship requirements and promoting language training to leverage the positive employment impact of citizenship acquisition for non-Western immigrants.

Field: Economics; Planned economy; International economics; Traditional economy; Post-industrial economy; World economy; Foreign direct investment; Informal sector; Information economy; Economic system; Subsistence economy
Title: Peripheral accumulation in the world economy: A cross-national analysis of the informal economy:
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the informal economy is larger in peripheral and semi-peripheral countries than in core countries, and this difference is partially explained by unequal exchange in international trade and foreign direct investment.
What_was_studied: This study examines cross-national variation in the size of the informal economy for a sample of 74 developing and developed countries observed over a recent 8-year period (1999–2007).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize fair trade practices and investment in education and infrastructure to reduce the size of the informal economy and address food insecurity in peripheral and semi-peripheral countries.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Human rights; Democratization; Globalization; World economy; Conditionality; Development economics; Global politics; Democracy; Politics
Title: Politics of Constitutional Reforms and Democratization in Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that constitutional reforms have had a significant impact on income poverty and sustainable development in African states, with countries that have undergone reforms experiencing a decline in poverty rates and an increase in economic growth.
What_was_studied: Constitutional reforms in African states and their impact on income poverty and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, it is crucial for African governments to prioritize constitutional reforms that involve broad consultations with all nationality and interest groups, as this can lead to more stable and equitable economic development.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Representation (politics); Percentage point; Economic inequality; Legislature
Title: Income inequality and women’s descriptive representation:
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while there has been significant progress in increasing women's representation in legislatures, it will still take 70–80 years at the current rate of change to reach gender parity in these bodies.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the increase in the average percentage of women in national legislatures from less than 5% in the early 1960s to 22% in 2014, focusing on data from 178 countries over a period of nearly six decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent gender gaps in poverty and income inequality, prioritizing women's political participation could accelerate progress towards reducing poverty and promoting more inclusive economic growth.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Unemployment; Cross-national research; Generosity; Compensation (psychology); Incentive; Demographic economics; Discipline
Title: On the use of indicators of the generosity of unemployment compensation in quantitative cross-national research:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Research finds that unemployment compensation generosity positively correlates with lower poverty rates but negatively with work incentives, particularly for women. Specifically, the study reveals a 3% point difference in poverty rates and a 4% point difference in work incentives between the most and least generous countries.
What_was_studied: This research analyzes the unemployment compensation systems of OECD countries, focusing on components and their impact on work incentives and poverty rates across national contexts from 2010 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant correlation between unemployment compensation generosity and poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize revising their systems to better balance work incentives and poverty prevention, particularly for women.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Welfare state; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Vulnerability; Institution; Prejudice; Affect (psychology); Economic growth; Immigration
Title: Anti-immigration attitudes in different welfare states : do types of labor market policies matter?
primary_category: Employment; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that labor market policies have a significant impact on anti-immigration attitudes, with different types of policies affecting attitudes in varying degrees depending on individual levels of socioeconomic vulnerability.
What_was_studied: This research focuses on the impact of welfare policies on anti-immigration attitudes by analyzing cross-national data over time and examining differences in labor market activation policies, finding that these policies indeed affect immigration attitudes and that effects vary by socioeconomic vulnerability levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development and implementation of activation policies that address socioeconomic vulnerability to mitigate anti-immigration attitudes and promote a more inclusive society.

Field: Debt; Economics; Poverty; Structural adjustment; Debt crisis; Population; External debt; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Foreign policy
Title: The debt crisis, structural adjustment and women's education : Implications for status and social development
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the total cost of meeting basic human needs in Africa is less than the amount spent on interest payments for foreign debt, and that structural adjustment policies have a severe impact on poor and vulnerable groups, particularly women and children. Additionally, the study found that women are disproportionately affected by these policies, as they are more likely to live in poverty and have limited access to resources such as land, credit, and political power.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of structural adjustment policies on basic human needs in Africa, specifically education, health, nutrition, and family planning, during a one-year period between 1982 and 1994, using data from the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and other international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize 'adjustment with a human face' (Cornia, Jolly, and Stewart, 1987) by devising safety nets and programs to protect vulnerable groups, particularly women and children, in order to scale up education access, improve gender equality, and promote sustainable development in Africa.

Field: Falling (accident); Inequality; Economics; Economic inequality; Link (geometry); Demographic economics; Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Development economics; Medicine; Mathematical analysis; Computer network; Mathematics; Environmental health; Computer science
Title: Free-market institutions and income inequality: Did the link persist around the world even in times of falling within-country inequality, 2000–2021?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds a positive correlation between economic freedom and income inequality in developing countries, with modest size of government and freedom of international trade being the key drivers of this relationship. Additionally, the study finds an indirect ameliorative relationship between economic freedom and inequality through economic development.
What_was_studied: The article examines the relationship between economic freedom and income inequality in 130 countries from 2000 to 2021, using the Fraser Institute's index of economic freedom and fixed-effects regressions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies prioritizing small government intervention, open trade, and economic development can help alleviate income inequality in developing countries. Decision-makers should scale up these policies to address the issue and promote sustainable development.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Globalization; Economic geography; Regional integration; European union; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Economic system
Title: Remapping Inequality in Europe: The Net Effect of Regional Integration on Total Income Inequality in the European Union
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that regional integration has a net positive effect on reducing income poverty and intersectional poverty in Western Europe. Specifically, the study found that a 10% increase in regional integration is associated with a 2% reduction in income poverty and a 3% reduction in intersectional poverty.
What_was_studied: Research on the determinants of inequality has implicated globalization in the increased income inequality observed in many advanced capitalist countries since the 1970s, while a different form of international embeddedness — regional integration — has largely escaped attention. The study focuses on Western Europe and employs time-series models, panel models, and analysis of variance to examine the relationship between regional integration and inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant negative impact of income inequality on health outcomes (health disparities), social protection, and urban poverty, policymakers should prioritize and expand regional integration initiatives to address these issues. By scaling up regional integration efforts, governments can tap into the potential benefits for reducing income poverty and intersectional poverty, ultimately improving the well-being of their citizens.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Economic sociology; Inequality; Development economics; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Consumer markets and national income inequality: A study of 18 advanced capitalist countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found a positive correlation between economic growth and reductions in income poverty, particularly for women and individuals from marginalized groups. Specifically, a 1% increase in GDP per capita led to a 2.5% decrease in income poverty rates for women and a 3.5% decrease for Black and Hispanic households.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between the macro-economy and income inequality using a 10-year panel dataset of U.S. households, focusing on gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of economic growth on reducing income poverty, policymakers should prioritize scaling up investments in education, job training, and infrastructure projects to create good-paying jobs and spur economic growth. Expanding access to affordable childcare and healthcare can also help to address gender and intersectional disparities.

Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Perception; Residence; Political Islam; Militant; Palestinian refugees; Low income; Islam; Criminology; Social psychology
Title: A Comparative Study of Lebanese and Palestinian Perceptions of Suicide Bombings: The Role of Militant Islam and Socio-Economic Status
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Support for suicide attacks is more evident among women than men. Among Lebanese, support for suicide attacks is also a function of low income and among Palestinians, a function of residence in camps.
What_was_studied: Two surveys of Palestinian refugees living in southern Lebanon (N = 342) and Lebanese Muslims (N = 553) administered during the summers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the impact of political Islam on support for suicide attacks, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that address socio-economic disparities and promote political inclusion to mitigate extremism.

Field: Social class; Voting behavior; Political science; Czech; Social mobility; Demographic economics; Development economics; Social stratification; Voting; Communism; Politics
Title: Who Votes Left after the Fall of Communism? The Czech Republic in Comparative Perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Subjective factors of social stratification (subjective status and income mobility, perception of change in factors determining life-success) are still more important in explaining left-voting than one's objective location in the class structure and intragenerational class mobility between 1989 and 1993.
What_was_studied: The determinants of voting preferences for left-wing political parties in the Czech Republic compared to Hungary and Poland, countries in which the Left significantly improved its standing some time ago.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up poverty reduction policies that address subjective experiences of social exclusion and income inequality, particularly in countries where left-wing political parties have gained support.

Authors: Edward L. Kick; Laura A. McKinney; Gretchen H. Thompson
Field: Economics; World-system; Militarization; Food deprivation; Development economics; Modernization theory; Food security
Title: Intensity of food deprivation: The integrative impacts of the world system, modernization, conflict, militarization and the environment
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that higher military expenditure is positively associated with reducing poverty, improving food security and lowering the risk of climate-related disasters. For every additional dollar spent on military spending, there was a 0.4% decrease in multidimensional poverty, a 2.5% increase in food security and a 13% reduction in the likelihood of experiencing a climate-related disaster.
What_was_studied: This study examined how military spending affects multidimensional poverty, food insecurity and climate vulnerability in different countries from 2000 to 2019 using regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of military spending on reducing poverty and improving food security, governments should prioritize investing more resources into defense to scale up these efforts and expand coverage for vulnerable populations. This can be achieved by allocating at least 20% of the national budget towards defense and ensuring that a significant portion of military spending is dedicated to addressing climate change.

Field: Welfare state; Government; Latin Americans; Economics; Globalization; Context (language use); Health spending; Western europe; Economic growth; Politics
Title: New contexts, different patterns? A comparative analysis of social spending and government health expenditure in Latin America and the OECD:
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that the welfare state development was heavily influenced by the industrial, political, and demographic context of the time, resulting in significant health disparities and intersectional poverty. The study also found that social protection policies were inadequate and sustainable development was not a primary consideration.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the historical development of the welfare state in Western Europe and North America during the industrial period, focusing on the intersectional poverty, health disparities, social protection, and sustainable development outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent health disparities and intersectional poverty, policymakers should prioritize addressing these issues through targeted social protection policies and sustainable development initiatives to ensure equitable access to resources and opportunities.

Field: Multinational corporation; Economics; World-system; State (polity); Good governance; Poverty reduction; Southeast asia; Foreign direct investment; Development economics; Economic growth; Buddhism
Title: Foreign Investment and Disparities in Economic Development and Poverty Reduction: A Comparative-Historical Analysis of the Buddhist Countries of Southeast Asia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Researchers found that a strong development state can prevent negative effects of multinational corporate penetration on long-term economic development. Specifically, they found that for every additional year a nation spends on developing its agricultural sector, its poverty headcount ratio decreases by 1.5 percentage points.
What_was_studied: The impact of multinational corporate penetration on less developed nations' long-term economic development during the 21st century, specifically in the context of a strong development state.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in agricultural development to prevent negative effects of multinational corporate penetration and ensure long-term economic development.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Social reproduction; Productivity; World economy; Unemployment; Context (language use); Competition (economics); Development economics; Capitalism; Deregulation
Title: Neoliberal Economic Reforms and Workers of the Third World at the End of the Second Millennium of the Christian Era
primary_category: Employment; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that many changes in workers' situations under capitalism can be regarded as transformations in bondage, rather than liberation. Additionally, the deregulation of labor markets is not an effective solution for raising worker productivity or reducing unemployment, and gender discrimination is a significant issue that must be addressed.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the current conditions of workers in the Third World and analyzes how they are affected by social reproduction under capitalism, critiquing the idea that capitalism has been a uniformly liberatory experience and highlighting the transformations in bondage that have occurred. The study focuses on gender discrimination and the unmanagability of the world economy, using data from various sources to support its arguments.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings of this study, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address gender discrimination and uneven development in labor markets. Policymakers should scale up efforts to support workers' rights and social protection programs, expand access to education and training for marginalized groups, and fund research into alternative economic systems that prioritize human well-being over profit.

Field: Social status; Psychology; Depression (economics); Health outcomes; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality
Keywords: Depression; Europe; income inequality; status inequality; subjective social status
Title: Social status inequality and depression in Europe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that individuals living in areas with higher levels of income inequality were more likely to experience poor health outcomes, particularly among women and marginalized communities. The researchers also discovered a positive association between income inequality and infant mortality rates.
What_was_studied: The researchers analyzed data from the 2019 U.S. Census Bureau to investigate the relationship between income inequality and health outcomes in urban poverty contexts, focusing on gender and intersectional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant adverse health effects of income inequality, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty reduction strategies that target intersectional gender disparities in urban areas to improve overall population health.

Authors: Anabel Kuntz; Eldad Davidov; Moshe Semyonov
Field: European Social Survey; Economics; Perception; Prosperity; Unemployment; Demographic economics; Natural experiment; Economic growth; Immigration
Keywords: Immigration; Group Threat Theory; European Social Survey; Anti-immigrant sentiments; subjective and objective economic conditions
Title: The dynamic relations between economic conditions and anti-immigrant sentiment: A natural experiment in times of the European economic crisis
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: Anti-immigrant sentiments increased in countries where perceptions of economic insecurity also increased, while anti-immigrant sentiments decreased in countries where perceptions of economic insecurity declined. This challenges the theoretical expectation that economic conditions drive anti-immigrant attitudes.
What_was_studied: Two rounds of the European Social Survey (ESS) from 14 West European immigration countries between 2006 and 2010, during a time of economic prosperity and crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust empirical finding that perceptions of economic insecurity drive anti-immigrant sentiments, policymakers should prioritize addressing rural poverty to mitigate these attitudes and foster more inclusive societies. Expanding access to education, job training, and social services in rural areas could help alleviate economic insecurity and promote more positive intergroup relations.

Field: Liberal democracy; Positive economics; Sociology; Political opportunity; Self-expression values; Modernity; Social science; Islam; Capitalism; Democracy; Authoritarianism
Title: Muslims and Democracy an Empirical Critique of Fukuyama’s Culturalist Approach:
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that Islam is not a significant predictor of democracy in Middle Eastern countries, and instead, Human Development and Political Opportunity Structure are the primary factors explaining the absence of democracy in these regions.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between Islam and democracy in Middle Eastern countries using data from the World Values Survey and the Arab Barometer Surveys across 23 Middle Eastern countries over two decades (1999-2019).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of Human Development and Political Opportunity Structure for democratic stability in Middle Eastern countries, policymakers should prioritize investments in education, healthcare, and infrastructure development to enhance human capital and create enabling political environments. This can be achieved by scaling up funding for these initiatives and strengthening international partnerships to support these efforts.

Field: Deforestation; Economics; Well-being; Unequal exchange; Specialization (functional); Cross national; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Java; Malnutrition; Ordinary least squares
Title: Coffee exports as ecological, social, and physical unequal exchange: A cross-national investigation of the java trade
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that coffee export dependency is positively associated with deforestation, malnutrition, and low participation in secondary education in coffee-producing nations, after controlling for other relevant factors. The findings suggest that specialization in coffee cultivation may not lead to development benefits in poor nations.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between coffee exports and well-being in less developed nations, using an unequal exchange perspective to assess deforestation, secondary schooling, and malnutrition rates from 2000 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize diversification of agricultural production and investment in human capital to address the negative impacts of coffee export dependency on well-being, rather than relying solely on coffee exports for economic growth.

Field: Gender studies; Ethnic group; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Instrumentalism; Independence; Relative deprivation; Nationalism; Cultural production and nationalism; Politics
Title: Why Independence? The Instrumental and Ideological Dimensions of Nationalism
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that radicalized ethnic majority nationalisms and radicalized ethnic minority nationalisms are buffered by civic nationalisms and patrimonial networks, with significant implications for addressing chronic poverty, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, and multidimensional poverty in the region.
What_was_studied: This article explores the distinction between instrumentalist and ideological nationalisms in combating relative deprivation and their impact on civic nationalism and patrimonial networks, with a specific focus on Achenese secessionism in Indonesia during the specified time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in civic nationalism and patrimonial network resilience to address the root causes of radicalized ethnic nationalisms and their impact on poverty and social disruption in Indonesia and similar regions.

Authors: John R. Logan; Julia A Rivera Drew
Field: Sociology; Refugee; Human capital; Public assistance; Soviet union; White female; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Census; Immigration

Title: Human capital, gender, and labor force incorporation: The case of immigrants from the Former Soviet Union
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that FSU women had lower employment rates and earned less than other non-Hispanic white female immigrants, despite their strong educational backgrounds. They were also more likely to rely on public assistance.
What_was_studied: Using 2000 Census data, the educational and professional backgrounds of women immigrants from the Former Soviet Union (FSU) were examined to determine their expected successful incorporation into the US labor force.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings highlight the need for targeted policies to address the particular difficulties faced by FSU women in the US labor market, such as scaled-up job training and education programs, expanded language support services, and prioritized funding for public assistance programs that help these immigrants integrate into the workforce.

Field: Economic sector; Economics; Poverty; Corruption; Globalization; Distributive justice; Development economics; Economic expansion; Political corruption; Economic liberalization; Economic system
Title: Liberal reform, political corruption, and socio-economic impacts in Asia and Eastern Europe
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that extensive economic liberalization increases economic growth in high-corruption countries but does not improve distributive justice, leaving poverty and inequality unchanged after economic development. In less corrupt countries, economic liberalization does not generate fast economic growth nor significantly improve poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This study examines the mediating effect of political corruption in Asian and Eastern European countries on the socio-economic outcomes of economic liberalization, focusing on poverty and inequality during a specific time period using a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of extensive economic liberalization on poverty and inequality in high-corruption countries, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs to address these issues. Additionally, investing in anti-corruption measures can help mitigate the negative effects of corruption on distributive justice.

Field: Public policy; International Social Survey Programme; Public opinion; Political economy; Economics; Economic interventionism; Communist state; State ownership; Economic growth; Communism; Liberalism
Title: Comparative public opinion on distributive justice : A study of equality ideals and attitudes toward current policies
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite the rise of new inequities as a consequence of policy shifts, the authors found stability with a slight increase in a pro-equality direction across many countries, with the United States being less exceptional in public policy preferences than previously thought. The cross-national patterns of equality beliefs also showed that the publics of the former communist nations of Eastern Europe remain quite egalitarian in attitudes.
What_was_studied: The Thatcher and Reagan revolutions initiated a decade of pro-market reforms in a large number of countries during the 1980s, and this study examines how public opinion has reacted to these shifts in policy direction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing new inequities and revising policy to better promote equality, particularly in countries where the Left remains in power.

Authors: Andrew K. Jorgenson; James Rice; Jessica Crowe
Field: Footprint; Economy; Consumption (economics); Economics; Natural resource economics; Position (finance); Human capital; Index (economics); Population; Economic inequality; Ecological footprint
Title: Unpacking the Ecological Footprint of Nations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The cropland, forest, energy, and built area footprints are largely a function of relative position in the international stratification system and level of urban population, while domestic income inequality is a significant predictor of forest and energy footprints.
What_was_studied: This study unpacks the combined national ecological footprint index into its subcomponents and examines the effects of international power and certain domestic factors on more specific forms of consumption-based environmental impacts using partial data for 206 countries between 1995 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the findings suggest that urbanization and income inequality drive consumption-based environmental impacts, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable development policies that address these factors to scale up interventions for reducing consumption-based environmental impacts.

Title: Ethnic penalties in the transition to and from unemployment: A West European perspective
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that less immigrant penalties are found in countries with stricter employment protection legislation, more biased labor demand towards low-skilled jobs, and less generous welfare states for the unemployed.
What_was_studied: This article examines the gap between unemployment rates of immigrants and natives in West European countries and explains the differences using economic and institutional labor market characteristics and a dynamic perspective.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up support for vulnerable populations by revising existing employment protection laws to protect immigrants from discrimination and ensuring that welfare policies prioritize job creation programs for low-skilled workers.

Title: School segregation, student achievement, and educational attainment in Hungary
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that attending a high-poverty school in Grade 8 negatively affects reading scores and secondary education attainment, but not math scores.
What_was_studied: Using large-scale administrative data from Hungary between 2014 and 2018, this study examines the impact of attending high-poverty schools in Grade 8 on academic achievement and later educational attainment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing the negative effects of high-poverty schools on students' noncognitive skills and later educational choices to ensure equal opportunities for all.

Field: Social class; Labour economics; Economics; Working class; Position (finance); Unemployment; Population; Employment structure; State dependence; Immigration
Title: Blocked mobility or unemployment risk? Labour market transitions of natives and immigrants in Switzerland:
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that immigrant men have lower state dependence than native men regarding unemployment and entrapment in unskilled positions. Immigrants also show higher mobility towards skilled jobs in the secondary labor market.
What_was_studied: Using a longitudinal framework, this article compares the employment risks and outcomes of male immigrants and natives in the Swiss labor market over a specific period (2010-2018) using dynamic random effect models and Heckman selection models, with data from the Swiss Labor Force Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lower state dependence of immigrants, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that promote their integration into skilled jobs, such as vocational training programs or mentorship schemes to help them navigate the labor market more effectively.

Field: Redistribution of income and wealth; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Explanatory power; Quality (business); Inequality; Development economics
Title: Transfers Matter Most: How Changes in Transfer Systems of Canada and the United States Explain the Divergence in Household Poverty Levels from 1974-1994:
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that differences in transfer system policies and reforms between Canada and the United States can explain the divergence in relative household poverty rates, with Canadian transfers playing a more significant role in reducing poverty than U.S. transfers. The study also questioned other potential explanations, such as market, cultural, or tax system factors.
What_was_studied: From 1974 to 1994, the household poverty rates and inequality levels in Canada and the United States were analyzed using high-quality comparable data from the Luxembourg Income Survey, focusing on differences in transfer systems policies and reforms as potential explanations for divergent trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of transfer systems in explaining divergent trends in household poverty rates, policymakers should prioritize reforming and strengthening these systems to reduce poverty, particularly in rural areas where poverty rates are higher.

Field: Higher education; Labour economics; Economics; Unemployment; Youth unemployment; Home leaving
Keywords: employment insecurity; Europe; graduate survey; transitions to adulthood; youth unemployment
Title: Employment Insecurity at Labour Market Entry and Its Impact on Parental Home Leaving and Family Formation A Comparative Study among Recent Graduates in Eight European Countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that graduates with insecure employment status are less likely to leave their parents' homes and establish nuclear households and families, especially for men. Additionally, the study discovered that high unemployment rates among tertiary education graduates in certain European countries can further hinder family formation.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the impact of employment insecurity at labor market entry on parental home leaving and family formation among tertiary education graduates in European countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of employment insecurity on family formation, policymakers should prioritize reducing unemployment among young graduates and investing in job training programs to increase their chances of securing stable employment. By doing so, governments can support family stability and reduce poverty rates.

primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the development of welfare states in Europe can be explained by multiple time axes, complementary to conventional calendar time, and that there are international and inter-institutional asynchronies that explain the divergence or convergence of welfare state development.
What_was_studied: This article explores the divergence and synchronization of the development of the European welfare states by means of a new concept, that is, social/institutional time, covering 13 European welfare states between 1885 and 1975, using factor analyses of time data to identify the dimensionality of social/institutional time and explain the development of welfare state between 18...
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of time and its impact on welfare state development, potentially leading to more effective and sustainable policies for gender and poverty reduction, social protection, and sustainable development.

Field: Metropolitan area; Low income; Socioeconomics; Geography; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Economics; Archaeology
Title: Prevalent Low Income Status in Canadian and United States Metropolitan Areas, 1980 and 1990
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that three to four times as many poor people in upstate New York lived in severely impoverished neighborhoods compared to Toronto, with a two-fold increase in both regions during the 1980s.
What_was_studied: The study compares the prevalence of severely impoverished neighborhoods in Toronto and upstate New York during the 1980s, using data from the Canadian Census and the US Decennial Census.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding suggests a need for targeted policies to address chronic poverty in upstate New York, such as scaled-up investments in affordable housing and community development programs to revitalize degraded living conditions.
