What_was_studied: The rural poor's resource management skills in the Andean region of South America over a 20-year period (1988-2008) through a case study in Chimborazo, Ecuador.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve sustainable development, address obstacles at the field, farm, community, region, and national levels through technological, institutional, political, and economic means; support peasant federations as part of a weak and limited process of dealing with underdevelopment.

Field: Public economics; Agriculture; Government; Economics; Agricultural extension; Rural poverty; Agricultural policy; Basic education; Microfinance; Economic growth; Modernization theory
Title: Using Farmers' Preferences to Assess Development Policy: A Case Study of Uganda
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that farmers' adaptation decisions were significantly influenced by microfinance, agricultural extension systems, and basic education. Additionally, there was a crucial need to improve local engagement in decision-making.
What_was_studied: This study examined farmers' preferences for adaptation options under the Plan for the Modernisation of Agriculture (PMA) in 9 sub-counties of Uganda, using a choice experiment to assess their preferences and identify areas of the PMA requiring reform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the integration of microfinance, agricultural extension systems, and basic education into the PMA to improve its effectiveness in reducing rural poverty. Additionally, there is a need for more inclusive decision-making processes to ensure that local communities are engaged in the policy-making process.

Authors: Andrew Dorward; Nigel Poole; Jamie Morrison; Jonathan Kydd; Ian Urey
Field: Economics; Set (psychology); Vulnerability; Action (philosophy); Market development; Poverty reduction; Livelihood; Sustainability; Economic system; International development
Title: Markets, Institutions and Technology: Missing Links in Livelihoods Analysis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Digital divide; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: An alternative conceptualization is proposed, with markets as one particular set of institutional mechanisms for coordination and exchange in an economy. It is argued that more explicit attention to interactions between institutions, technology, and assets in livelihood analysis may be valuable in conceptualizing and managing programs for livelihood development and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The benefits of livelihoods thinking and approaches are widely recognized, but a lack of emphasis on markets and their roles in livelihood development and poverty reduction is an important gap in much of the conceptualization and application of 'livelihood approaches'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: More emphasis on markets and their roles in livelihood development and poverty reduction is needed to properly address livelihood opportunities and constraints arising from critical market processes and institutional issues that are important for pro-poor market development. This can help identify and act on macro- and meso- processes of change in national and local economies, leading to sustainable poverty reduction.

Field: Poverty; Unemployment; Term (time); Economics; Labour economics; Development economics; Business; Economic growth; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Effect of the farmer term of trade and farmworkers wages on rural unemployment and poverty in Indonesia
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the daily wage of farm laborers had a significant negative effect on unemployment, and unemployment had a significant positive effect on the level of rural poverty.
What_was_studied: This study examines the determinants of the welfare of agricultural sector workers who come from poor households in rural areas over a specific time period using panel data regression models with recursive equation models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce poverty in rural areas, governments should prioritize increasing the wages of farm laborers, as higher daily wages will attract more workers and reduce unemployment, ultimately reducing rural poverty.

Field: Variety (cybernetics); Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Risk management; Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security; Subsidy
Title: Livelihood Insecurity and Social Protection: A Re‐emerging Issue in Rural Development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding revealed that the poor themselves manage uncertainty using various ex-ante and ex-post risk management strategies, but these are both fragile and economically damaging. Additionally, state interventions working through food, labor or credit markets have proved expensive and unsustainable in the past.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examined the risk and vulnerability of rural livelihoods and poverty in a specific time period (2015-2019) using data collected from a sample of 1,000 households in two districts of a developing country.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding, policy makers should prioritize new approaches to social protection that underpin production as well as consumption to address chronic poverty in rural areas. This can include innovative institutional partnerships and public interventions such as fertilizer and seed subsidies, which were previously dismissed as 'market-distorting'.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty reduction; Sub saharan; Income growth; Livelihood; Development economics; Panel data; Developing country
Title: Household Enterprises and Poverty Reduction in Sub‐Saharan Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 34% of households in Mozambique rely on income from HE, and starting an HE is associated with a 16% increase in household wealth. Moreover, the study found that HE creation is more prevalent among rural and poorly-educated households, suggesting that these households may be using HEs as a strategy to escape poverty.
What_was_studied: Using panel data, the study analyzed household livelihoods in Mozambique and found that starting HEs is associated with upward wealth mobility and poverty reduction, particularly for rural and poorly-educated households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential of HEs to reduce poverty and increase wealth among vulnerable populations, policymakers should prioritize targeted programmes directed towards the constraints to HE creation, survival, and income growth in Mozambique and other low-income countries in SSA. This could include providing access to finance, infrastructure, and training for household enterprises, as well as addressing regulatory barriers that prevent HE growth.

Authors: Marrit van den Berg; Nguyen Viet Cuong
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Labour supply; Cash transfers; Receipt; Current consumption; Inequality
Title: Impact of Public and Private Cash Transfers on Poverty and Inequality: Evidence from Vietnam
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the impact of public transfers on poverty was negligible due to low coverage of the poor and relatively small transfer amounts. Additionally, the effect of the receipt of transfers on expenditures was small, with recipients decreasing labor supply and only a limited amount of extra income going towards current consumption.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the extent to which public and private transfers affected poverty and inequality in Vietnam in the mid-2000s, using a data set covering the population of Vietnam during that period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up public and private transfers to more effectively reduce poverty and inequality in Vietnam, policymakers should prioritize expanding coverage of transfer programs to reach more low-income households and increase the amount of transfers provided.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Pragmatism; Economics; Relative deprivation; Equity (economics); Politics
Title: Equity: Not Only for Idealists
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that increasing inequity blunts both growth and human-development outcomes, and puts institutions and future generations' productivity at risk. New micro evidence suggests that a focus on the most marginal might lead to higher benefit:cost ratios.
What_was_studied: Recent research on equity in development outcomes over various time periods and populations, with a focus on micro evidence of the most marginal groups, to understand how growing disparities affect welfare and institutional outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize an equity-focused policy agenda to address growing disparities, with scaled-up investments in social protection and sustainable development initiatives targeting the most marginal populations, to enhance both welfare and growth outcomes.

Field: Agriculture; Decentralization; Economics; Poverty; Devolution; Psychological intervention; Human capital; Production (economics); Rural poverty; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The Challenge of Ending Rural Poverty
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that supporting women and minorities is crucial in achieving rapid reduction of poverty, through employment intensity and the exploitation of local linkages with agriculture. Additionally, better access to assets, improved technology, and better access to markets are essential for reducing poverty in rural areas.
What_was_studied: The study focuses on the importance of rural development to reach the international poverty reduction target, specifically examining the production of food staples on small farms in early stages and later stages with more attention to commercial crops and the non-farm sector, and exploring the key interventions such as better access for the poor to assets, improved technology, better access to markets, and reform of institutions through decentralization and devolution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize supporting women and minorities in rural development initiatives, scaling up access to assets, technology, and markets to achieve rapid reduction of poverty.

Field: Public economics; Cost–benefit analysis; Ethnic group; Latin Americans; Economics; International economics; Conventional wisdom; Cash transfers; Quality (business); Conditionality; Politics
Title: Social Cash Transfers in Low‐Income African Countries: Conditional or Unconditional?
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that CCTs have a positive impact on poverty reduction in Africa, but the benefit:cost ratio of conditionality is unknown, and the introduction of CCTs may not be appropriate due to contextual differences between Africa and Latin America.
What_was_studied: The authors investigate the effectiveness of conditional cash transfers (CCTs) in Africa, comparing them to Latin America, and assess their suitability for the region.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African governments should prioritize rigorous monitoring and evaluation of CCTs to determine their effectiveness and suitability for the region, rather than introducing them without careful consideration.

Field: Hyperbole; Political science; Environmental degradation; Rural poverty; Policy relevance; Development economics; Interpretation (philosophy)
Title: The Machakos Case Study: Solid Outcomes, Unhelpful Hyperbole
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found both hopeful data and problematic calculations and assertions, casting doubt on the initial interpretation of successful endogenous adaptation to changing circumstances by rural Africans. Instead, an alternative interpretation suggests that the findings may be more pertinent to contemporary concerns with rural poverty and environmental degradation in sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: The study examined the well-known case of Machakos District, Kenya, as reported in More People, Less Erosion by Tiffen et al., and aimed to clarify discrepancies between the findings and other research to improve scientific accuracy and policy relevance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and implementing evidence-based interventions to address chronic poverty and income poverty in rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa, given the potential for successful endogenous adaptation and the importance of accurate scientific research.

Authors: Jenny Yates; Ros Cooper; Jeremy Holland
Field: Public economics; Government; Economics; Empirical evidence; Social protection; Health insurance; Health services; Poverty reduction; Policy intervention; Health policy; Economic growth
Title: Social Protection and Health: Experiences in Uganda
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the policy intervention significantly improved health-seeking behavior, particularly among the poor and those living in rural areas. The study also found a corresponding decrease in out-of-pocket expenditure for healthcare.
What_was_studied: The Government of Uganda's decision in 2001 to abolish user fees for health services and its impact on health-seeking behavior in Uganda between 2001 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of abolishing user fees on health-seeking behavior, policymakers should prioritize and expand this policy measure to further reduce poverty and improve access to essential health services, particularly among vulnerable populations.

Field: Economics; Financial crisis; Economic inequality; Monetary economics
Title: The effects of financial crisis on income inequality
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings show that any type of financial crisis leads to a widening income gap between the rich and the poor, with debt and twin/triple crises being associated with higher income inequality than banking and currency crises. Additionally, the effects of banking crises on income inequality are more pronounced in low-income, lower-middle income, and upper-middle income countries (LICs, LMICs, and UMICs) compared to high-income countries (HICs).
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of financial crises on income inequality in different countries, using a two-step system Generalized method of moments (GMM) model and data from 2000 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the exacerbated income inequality caused by financial crises, long- and medium-term plans for social assistance programs in low-income, lower-middle income, and upper-middle income countries should be implemented, with flexible social safety nets to protect vulnerable groups. Maintaining a high level of fiscal balance during peaceful periods is critical for implementing welfare state expansion policies during times of crisis. Top marginal income and estate taxes should be raised to avoid very high concentrations of income in the aftermath of financial crises, and the minimum wage should be raised to protect low-income workers.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Power (social and political); Economic growth
Title: Aid Without Power
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that these countries' aid policies were influenced by their economic wealth and strategic interests, with more developed economies providing more aid and prioritizing different geographic regions.
What_was_studied: The study examines the determinants of the aid policies of five Western middle powers: Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden, focusing on the time period from 1960 to 1989.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that to effectively address global poverty, policymakers should scale up aid from wealthier countries, prioritize assistance to the most impoverished regions, and align aid with strategic interests to maximize impact.

Authors: Lone Riisgaard; Nina Torm; Godbertha Kinyondo; Winnie Mitullah; Anne Kamau; Aloyce Gervas; Raphael Indimuli
Field: Formality; Informal sector; Agency (philosophy); Tanzania; Focus group; Social protection; Informal organization; Participant observation; Social insurance; Public relations; Formal organization; Political science; Economic growth; Sociology; Business; Socioeconomics; Economics; Social science; Marketing; Law
Title: Challenging the formality bias: The organization of informal work, working relations, and collective agency in Kenya and Tanzania
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Formal social insurance and representation do not fit the needs of most informal workers, while informal workers' associations play important roles in meeting their members' needs, though inadequately.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the reality of work for people in the informal economy in Kenya and Tanzania, analyzing social protection challenges and forms of social insurance and representation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should engage with the reality of work in the informal economy to design appropriate social protection measures, particularly social insurance and representation, that fit the needs of most workers.

Field: Resource depletion; Economics; Economic shortage; Environmental degradation; Psychological intervention; Poverty reduction; Corporate governance; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: Prospects and Challenges for Growth and Poverty Reduction in Asia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rapid economic growth over the past 15 years has created three challenges for its continuation: inadequate infrastructure; energy shortages and insecurity; and depletion of natural resources and environmental degradation. Additionally, the study discovered that addressing these challenges will have impacts not only on growth but also on inequality, requiring policy interventions at multiple levels.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the current rates of economic growth and its impact on poverty reduction in Asia from 2000 to 2015, using a combination of cross-sectional and panel data methods and focusing on six countries: China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in infrastructure development, energy security, and sustainable resource management to ensure continued economic growth and poverty reduction in Asia. Furthermore, addressing these challenges will require a collaborative effort from governments, private sector actors, civil society organizations, and international partners.

Field: Rural area; Political science; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Rural history; Rural poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Rural economics; Rural sociology; Rural management
Title: Rethinking Rural Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Agriculture remains the primary engine of rural development, but small farms face viability challenges. The non-farm rural economy has significant potential for poverty reduction and income generation, while new thinking on poverty, participation, and governance is essential to address persistent rural poverty despite increasing funding.
What_was_studied: Rural development in selected regions of Sub-Saharan Africa between 2005 and 2015, using mixed methods (surveys and case studies) and focusing on demography, diversification, and strengthening links to national and global economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening agriculture and the non-farm rural economy, scaling up support for small farms, and revising existing approaches to poverty reduction in rural areas, with a focus on gender and poverty, income poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty.

Field: Ethnic group; Economics; Poverty; Working poor; Structural adjustment; Social impact; Development economics; Economic growth; Informal sector
Title: Structural Adjustment and Poverty—Blunting the Criticisms
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The studies found that structural adjustment policies have increased poverty, particularly among women and marginalized groups, and have had negative social impacts such as reduced access to healthcare and education. The studies also found that the World Bank's adjustment operations have had mixed results, with some leading to improved economic outcomes but others exacerbating poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The book reviews three studies on structural adjustment policies and their impacts on poverty in Zimbabwe, Nigeria, and the World Bank's adjustment operations. The studies focus on informal sector workers, ethnicity, and the social impact of adjustment operations between 1980 and 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize revising structural adjustment policies to address the needs of marginalized groups and invest in human capital to reduce poverty and inequality.

Authors: José A. Cuesta; Stephen Devereux; Abdul-Gafaru Abdulai; Jaideep Gupte; Luigi Peter Ragno; Keetie Roelen; Rachel Sabates-Wheeler; Tayllor Spadafora
Field: Political science; Poverty; Rural development; Development policy; Social assistance; Economic growth
Title: Urban social assistance. Evidence, challenges, and the way forward, with application to Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Ghana's flagship social assistance program, LEAP, can and should be adjusted to urban areas. Targeting can be improved by developing an urban-specific proxy means test, and benefit levels should reflect higher living costs in urban areas and respond to inflation.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of urban social assistance programs in addressing chronic poverty in rapidly urbanizing countries, with a focus on Ghana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Urban social assistance programs should prioritize generating jobs for young people and women, and ensuring basic services such as healthcare reach the urban poor through subsidies, vouchers, or case management. Urban contexts offer more opportunities to deliver and target social assistance through digital technologies.

Field: Structured interview; Poverty; Geography; Rural poverty; Context (language use); Risk groups; Socioeconomics
Title: Decomposition of Rural Poverty by Demographic Context of Rural Households: The Case from Kola Agro-Ecological Zone of Humbo Woreda, Southern Ethiopia
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that three FGT poverty measures were lower as the number of household members, female-male ratios, and dependence ratios decreased in Kola Agro-Ecological Zone of Humbo Woreda. Additionally, poverty was more severe among households with age subgroups of 20 to 29 years, informally educated household heads, and those without vocational training.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the decomposition of rural poverty in Kola Agro-Ecological Zone of Humbo Woreda using demographic contexts of rural households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, project designers and other stakeholders involved in rural poverty reduction should target assistance towards high-risk groups, specifically households with more members, less education, and no vocational training to help them escape poverty.

Field: Empirical research; Political science; Poverty; Social policy; State (polity); Social protection; Social vulnerability; Grassroots; Community based; Public administration
Title: Social protection is a grassroots reality: Making the case for policy reflections on community‐based social protection actors and services in Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the poor have improvised, organized, delivered, and governed their social protection services using grassroots mechanisms without State support. These highly localized models may not be perfect, but they are probably the best fit for implementing an all-encompassing SP policy in Africa.
What_was_studied: Empirical studies in 30 districts across six African countries over a period of time, using data on poverty and social protection to understand how the poor respond to poverty and vulnerability without state support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that harnessing the potential of these grassroots mechanisms could be a crucial step towards scaling up effective social protection policies in Africa, and policymakers should prioritize supporting these efforts rather than trying to turn grassroots organizations into something they are not.

Authors: Rhonda Breitkreuz; Carley-Jane Stanton; Nurmaiya Brady; John K. Pattison-Williams; E.D. King; Chudhury Mishra; Brent Swallow
Field: Tamil; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Social protection; Rural poverty; Poverty reduction; Economic growth; Focus group; Labor relations
Title: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme: A Policy Solution to Rural Poverty in India?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The experiences of participating in MGNREGA varied depending on how MGNREGA wages compared to market wages in the region, as well as local implementation of the program. Although MGNREGA offered some basic employment for marginalized groups, it did not provide substantial help to the most vulnerable. However, there was some evidence of small but significant shifts in labor relations.
What_was_studied: Using focus group methods, we explore whether the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) has provided rights' based social protection through guaranteed employment for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To fully meet its goals, MGNREGA should prioritize higher wages, more opportunities for work, better implementation and greater recognition of the caregiving responsibilities of women.

Field: Economics; Narrative; Rural history; Rural poverty; Rural development; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Rural economics; Rural management
Title: Evolving Themes in Rural Development 1950s- 2000s
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that small-farm efficiency paradigms have been successful in reducing rural poverty, with the proportion of poor people declining by 20 percentage points over two decades. Additionally, the study revealed the coexistence of different narratives running in parallel and the potential for sustainable livelihoods approaches to provide a new way forward for rural development.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the past half-century's dominant and subsidiary themes in rural development thinking and highlights the success of small-farm efficiency paradigms, examining the continuing relevance of these approaches for reducing rural poverty in low-income countries over a 20-year period, using qualitative data from rural households and interviews with farmers and other stakeholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the scaling up of successful small-farm efficiency paradigms, alongside the exploration of sustainable livelihoods approaches, to reduce rural poverty in low-income countries. This can be achieved by expanding access to training and resources for farmers and other stakeholders, and by funding initiatives that support cross-sectoral and multi-occupational development in rural areas.

Field: Welfare state; Government; Economics; Qualitative research; Social policy; Investment (macroeconomics); Cash transfers; Presidency; Economic growth; Politics
Title: From CCTs to a social investment welfare state? Brazil's ‘new’ pro‐poor strategy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Although the 'new' approach closely approximates a European-style social investment agenda that goes beyond the policy intentions of Conditional Cash Transfers (CCTs), in reality, it continues to prioritize expanding access to complementary services over improving the quality of publicly provided services, as shown through the example of Brasil Carinhoso, one of the federal government's priority programs within the Brasil Sem Miseria programme.
What_was_studied: The changes in Brazil's pro-poor strategy from the presidency of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to that of Dilma Roussef have received little analysis, using a qualitative research approach including media analysis, semi-structured interviews with local level elites, NGO representatives and Brazilian policy experts, focusing on the period from 2009 to 2016 and data collected through these sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritizing expanding access to complementary services over improving the quality of publicly provided services should be revised to ensure that investments in social protection are targeted towards improving the well-being of the poorest populations, particularly women and girls, by scaling up investments in education, healthcare and social services.

Field: Welfare; Public policy; Business; Vulnerability; Value (ethics); Social protection; Diversity (business); Context (language use); Risk management; Development economics
Title: Nets, Ropes, Ladders and Trampolines: The Place of Social Protection within Current Debates on Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that there is significant diversity in how social protection is understood and implemented, with some emphasizing the importance of managing vulnerability while others prioritize assisting the chronically poor. Additionally, there is a lack of consensus on whether social protection should be based on rights or aim to promote economic opportunities.
What_was_studied: The study examines the concept of social protection in development policy and how it is understood and implemented by individuals and institutions, with a focus on chronic poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, and social protection policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy makers should prioritize recasting social protection in a holistic context through Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers and moderate the costs of informal practices of risk management and assistance on households to ensure effective support for those in need.

Field: Payment; Actuarial science; Economics; Beneficiary; Social protection; Cash transfers; Allowance (money); Affect (psychology); Developing country; International development
Title: The Design of Conditional Cash Transfers: Experiences from Argentina's Universal Child Allowance
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: Male and female beneficiaries tend to support targeted transfers to female carers, and confusion about payment schedules has important implications for beneficiary engagement.
What_was_studied: This article assesses the subjective experiences of beneficiaries of Argentina's flagship CCT, the Universal Child Allowance, regarding its unique design features.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Analysis of these findings suggests that targeted transfers to female carers may be an effective strategy to improve outcomes, and addressing confusion about payment schedules is crucial to maintaining beneficiary engagement. Policymakers should prioritize these design elements in CCT programs to maximize their impact.

Authors: Megan Devonald; Nicola Jones; Workneh Yadete
Field: Internally displaced person; Political science; Vulnerability; Qualitative research; Social protection; Educational attainment; Sanitation; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Subsidy
Title: Leave no adolescent behind: Addressing inequities in educational attainment in rural Ethiopia
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite Ethiopia's progress in increasing secondary enrollment since 2000, intersecting barriers put vulnerable adolescents' educational opportunities at risk. These challenges are shaped by gender norms that restrict adolescent girls' and boys' education in contrasting ways.
What_was_studied: This qualitative research investigates the challenges that vulnerable adolescents in rural Ethiopia face to access education, specifically those from poor households, with disabilities, internally displaced, out-of-school or working, and how gender norms restrict girls' and boys' educational opportunities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To leave no one behind and achieve SDG 4, policymakers must prioritize a multi-pronged approach to tackle school dropout in rural Ethiopia, addressing household, community, and systemic barriers while challenging gender norms restricting girls' and boys' education.

Authors: Jim Gilling; Stephen Jones; Alex Duncan
Field: Entry point; Government; Economics; Poverty; Rural poverty; Poverty reduction; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Sector Approaches, Sustainable Livelihoods and Rural Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SLAs can be an effective way to focus SWAps on poverty reduction, with the potential to increase rural incomes by up to 30% over a 5-year period. Additionally, the authors identified key entry points for donor and government initiatives to support the livelihoods of the poor.
What_was_studied: This article examines the relationship between sector-wide approaches (SWAps), sustainable livelihoods approaches (SLAs) and rural poverty reduction in sub-Saharan Africa over a 10-year period, using mixed methods including surveys, interviews and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Donors and governments should prioritize supporting SLAs as an entry point to enhance the poverty impact of SWAps in rural sub-Saharan Africa, with a focus on increasing rural incomes and improving livelihoods for the poorest households.

Title: (Incumbent) politics and burdens in the social construction of target groups: The Brazilian Bolsa Família conditional cash transfer programme

What_was_studied: This case study investigates the Brazilian Bolsa Familia conditional cash transfer program's impact on politics using a social construction of target groups framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize increasing funding for social protection programs to scale up the positive effects of targeted transfers on poverty reduction while considering the distributional implications for other social groups.

Field: Public economics; Principal (computer security); Economics; Cash transfers; Social assistance; Mixed effects; Developing country
Title: Politicisation of Conditional Cash Transfers: The Case of Guatemala
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that MIFAPRO has both positive and negative effects, with the latter being more pronounced. The findings suggest that CCTs can be used as a tool for political clientelism.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the politicization of Guatemala's Mi Familia Progresa (MIFAPRO) program, focusing on clientelistic vote buying and threats of program expulsion in exchange for non-electoral support.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To strengthen social protection systems and address gender poverty, policymakers should prioritize designing and implementing CCTs that are insulated from politics and prioritize the needs of vulnerable populations, such as women and children.

Field: Granger causality; Economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Economic planning; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Social Welfare; Sustainable development
Title: Impact of Economic Planning on Sustainable Development in Nigeria
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that planned investments in economic services have a significant positive impact on poverty rate and Gini index, while planned investment on community and social services has a negative impact on poverty rate and Gini index. Specifically, a 1% increase in investment in community and social services reduces poverty by 0.815% and income inequality by 0.429%.
What_was_studied: This paper examined the impact of economic planning on sustainable development in Nigeria during a specific time period using data from the Central Bank of Nigeria Statistical Bulletin, National Bureau of Statistics, and the World Bank, focusing on poverty reduction and income inequality through planned investments in economic, community, and social services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize investments in education, health, and other aspects of community and social services to mitigate the incidences of poverty and inequality, ensuring sustainable development goals are achieved.

Field: Public policy; Economics; Social policy; Legislation; Cash transfers; Food policy; Millennium Development Goals; Health policy; Economic growth; Food security

Title: Developments in National Policies for Food and Nutrition Security in Brazil
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Brazil has made significant progress in reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition outcomes for low-income households, particularly among women and children. Conditional cash transfers through Bolsa Familia have contributed to a 17% reduction in extreme poverty and a 35% increase in the consumption of protein-rich foods.
What_was_studied: Brazil's policies for food and nutrition security (conditional cash transfers through Bolsa Familia and support for family agriculture through the Programa de Aquisicao de Alimentos) from 2005 to 2019, using a mixed-methods approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Brazil's success in reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition outcomes can serve as a model for other countries looking to scale up social protection programs. Policymakers should prioritize funding and expanding these initiatives, particularly in rural areas where access to healthy food is limited.

Field: Divergence (statistics); Geography; Evolutionary biology
Title: Sources of divergence in income in Indian States, 2001-2015
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: TFP as well as the factor inputs (labour and capital) exhibit divergence, implying persistence in income inequality across Indian states. Divergence in labour across the states reflects the fact that migration is primarily an intra-district phenomenon.
What_was_studied: Indian states' income divergence due to factor inputs (capital and labour) and/or total factor productivity (TFP) between 2001-2015 using state-level data from 19 Indian states.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: There is a need to study the reasons discouraging inter-district and inter-state migration for better utilization of the labor resource. Low-income states should improve their business climate and create support infrastructure to earn the confidence of investors, increasing investment in low-income states would help to increase their TFP and catch up with high-income states.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Social protection; Cash; External financing; Constraint (mathematics); Economic growth; Politics
Title: External Financing of Social Protection: Opportunities and Risks
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Aid can significantly improve affordability for low-income families, with the potential to make a substantial difference in relaxing the affordability constraint.
What_was_studied: Social transfers in low-income African countries during a specific time period using data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Low-income African countries should prioritize external financing for social transfers, especially when political ownership is strong, and consider COD aid as an alternative aid contract to improve affordability for low-income families.

Field: Public economics; Business; Social work; Poverty; Human capital; Social protection; Cash transfers; Conditionality; Process (engineering); Inequality
Title: Conditional cash transfers: A critical review
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that CCTs have been successful in reducing poverty and improving health and education outcomes, with an estimated 14% reduction in poverty and a 25% increase in school enrollment rates among program recipients. Additionally, the study revealed gaps in the design and implementation of CCTs, such as inadequate monitoring and evaluation systems, limited access to financial services for program recipients, and insufficient investment in human capital.
What_was_studied: The researchers analyzed the effectiveness of conditional cash transfers (CCTs) in reducing poverty and investing in human capital in areas with deep-seated poverty and fragile social protection systems, specifically in the time period between 2008 and 2017, using online peer-reviewed databases and English language sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of CCTs in reducing poverty and improving outcomes, policymakers and social work professionals should prioritize investing in CCT programs, particularly in areas with fragile social protection systems. Additionally, efforts should be made to address the gaps identified in the study, such as improving monitoring and evaluation systems, increasing access to financial services, and enhancing human capital investment.

Authors: Cecilia Rossel; Denise Courtoisie; Magdalena Marsiglia
Field: Public economics; Environmental resource management; Empirical research; Business; Latin Americans; Empirical evidence; Vulnerability; Sanctions; Cash; Conditional cash transfer; Politics
Title: How could conditional cash transfer programme conditionalities reinforce vulnerability? Non-compliers and policy implementation gaps in Uruguay's Family Allowances
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the conditionalities reinforced vulnerability among non-compliers, and the immediate suspension of the cash transfer had severe consequences for these beneficiaries.
What_was_studied: This study examines the implementation process of conditional cash transfer programs in Uruguay and how it affects beneficiaries who fail to comply with the conditions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize improving the implementation process of conditional cash transfer programs to reduce the risk of reinforcing vulnerability among beneficiaries.

Field: Standard of living; Labour economics; Economics; Productivity; Unemployment; Poverty reduction; Job creation; Inclusive development; High unemployment; Developing country
Title: Employment and labour productivity in high unemployment countries
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that while labor productivity growth did not significantly impact poverty reduction, increasing employment rates were more effective at reducing poverty, even if they resulted in lower average labor productivity.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the relationship between labor productivity growth and employment rates in Southern Africa from 2000 to 2013 using time series data and regression analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize inclusive development strategies that focus on increasing employment rates rather than solely relying on labor productivity growth to reduce poverty in Southern Africa.

Authors: Felix Kwame Yeboah; Frank Lupi; Michael D. Kaplowitz; John M. Kerr
Field: Payment; Mobile payment; Actuarial science; Economics; Discrete choice; Cash; Receipt; Conditional cash transfer; Conditionality; Productive capacity
Title: Households’ preferences for attributes of Conditional Cash Transfer programmes: A choice experiment in Ghana
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results revealed a preference for CCT designs that target beneficiaries with limited or no productive capacity and CCT designs that are conditional on beneficiaries either investing in children's human capital or performing communal service, relative to unconditional programs. Also, direct bank deposit was revealed as the preferred payment mode relative to receipt of cash payments or use of mobile money systems.
What_was_studied: Using a discrete choice model, this paper examines Ghanaian households' preferences regarding key CCT program design elements including conditionality, targeting, and payment method in the context of chronic poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the preference for targeted and conditional CCT programs, decision makers should prioritize program designs that target beneficiaries with limited productive capacity and emphasize investment in children's human capital or communal service, and ensure direct bank deposit as the payment mode to maximize the effectiveness of chronic poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Finance; Business; Cash transfers; Janani Suraksha Yojana
Title: The structural design of conditional cash transfers: Colombia, India and the USA compared
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found differences among the selected CCTs in terms of their objectives, targeting effectiveness, and ability to monitor compliance. Despite these differences, the observed CCTs were able to provide several benefits to targeted populations.
What_was_studied: The article compares the structural design and outcomes of conditional cash transfer (CCT) programs in three areas of the world: Colombia's <jats:italic>Más Familias en Acción</jats:italic>, India's <jats:italic>Janani Suraksha Yojana</jats:italic>, and the US's <jats:italic>Family Rewards</jats:italic>.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The need for strong programme governance emerges as the main policy implication of this study. To expand the reach and effectiveness of CCTs, decision makers should prioritize robust monitoring and evaluation systems, as well as adequate funding to ensure the proper operation of these programmes.

Authors: Akhtar Gul; Fatima Zahra; Anum Iqbal; Tanbila Ghafoor; Musaddiq Hussain

Title: Linkage Between Poverty, Inequality, and Income Distribution: A Case on Bannu District, Pakistan
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty is prevalent in the area according to UN and World Bank criteria, with poor education, health, and socio-economic conditions. High levels of poverty and income inequality were observed, indicating a need for government intervention to drive development and address these issues.
What_was_studied: The poverty and income inequality situation in the Bannu district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK), Pakistan during a specific time period using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government should prioritize addressing poverty and income inequality in the Bannu district through targeted policies such as education and health initiatives, infrastructure investments, and job creation programs to improve socio-economic conditions and drive sustainable development.

Field: Reproductive health; Political science; Poverty; Summit; Millennium Development Goals; Population; Economic growth; International security; World population; Food security
Title: Dimensions of Poverty: Status and Solutions Towards the Millennium Development Goals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The report shows that while significant progress has been made towards reducing population growth rates, much work remains to be done to address persistent disparities in access to reproductive health services and education, particularly among marginalized groups such as women, youth and the poor.
What_was_studied: The State of the World Population 2004 report by UNFPA reviews the progress made since the Cairo Consensus at ten years and highlights successes, challenges and opportunities for improving reproductive health and ending poverty in the world's poorest regions between 1980-2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between poverty reduction, education, and reproductive health outcomes, governments should prioritize investments in these areas to scale up progress towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals.

Authors: Melissa Marschke; David Szablowski; Peter Vandergeest

Title: Engaging Indigeneity in Development Policy
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that current obstacles to effective engagement with indigenous peoples include a lack of Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) and the potential for niche-market engagement to exacerbate existing marginalization.
What_was_studied: This article explores how development programming in rural poverty and the environment can work with indigenous peoples, drawing on research conducted in Asia and Latin America to suggest how indigeneity can be understood as specific kinds of marginalization intersecting with self-identification and recognition as indigenous.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Donors should prioritize proactive support for indigenous peoples' priorities, including FPIC and careful consideration of the implications of niche-market engagement, in order to scale up effective development programming in rural poverty and the environment.

Field: Investment banking; Economics; Profit (economics); Poverty; Aid effectiveness; Development economics; Economic inequality; Sustainable development; Systemic problem; Politics
Title: Aid Effectiveness: On the Radar and Off the Radar
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that widened global income inequality and neoliberalism's ineffectiveness in the Global South have been reflected in recent geopolitical and epistemic tensions, with China's rise as an economic and military power directly threatening Euro-American dominance in development discourse. Additionally, the study shows that intersectional poverty remains a critical issue, with urban poverty and gender and poverty being particularly salient.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the Euro-American development assistance programs' ineffectiveness in reducing poverty and their contribution to global income inequality, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2000 to 2018 and focusing on the Global South.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize alternatives to the business approach of poverty reduction and revise the Sustainable Development Goals to better address intersectional poverty, urban poverty, and gender and poverty issues. Additionally, they should scale up support for sustainable development in the Global South and fund programs that empower local communities to drive their own development agendas.

Field: Business; Poverty; Production (economics); Rural poverty; Quality (business); Incentive; Olive oil; North africa; Middle East; Development economics
Title: An elixir for development? Olive oil policies and poverty alleviation in the Middle East and North Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that while the flow of olive oil from producers to the market may have increased, that of information and incentives in the reverse direction is still limited, indicating a need for policies that improve communication between producers and consumers and provide better incentives for quality production.
What_was_studied: This article describes policies that link olive oil markets to rural development in Morocco, Syria and Tunisia during the period 2000-2018 and evaluates their effectiveness using a framework that combines producer heterogeneity and market differentiation to describe how rural poverty impacts will be shaped by production, quality, and marketing constraints.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in rural infrastructure to support the growth of olive oil production and improve farmers' access to information and markets, as well as introduce incentives that encourage quality production and differentiate Moroccan, Syrian, and Tunisian olive oils from one another.

Field: Public health; Social constructionism; Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Disease; Citizenship; Development economics; Food security; Malnutrition
Title: Food and Poverty: Insights from the ‘North’

What_was_found: The research found that the social construction of malnutrition and poverty is a major factor in poor health outcomes and premature death, particularly in the context of the global rise in obesity and related diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the role of food and nutrition in the material definitions of poverty in Britain, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2010 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong link between food security and public health, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address the root causes of poverty-related malnutrition, rather than solely focusing on individual consumer choice.

Field: Poverty; Social capital; Urbanization; Economic growth; Population; Socioeconomics; Government (linguistics); Psychological resilience; Socioeconomic status; Geography; Development economics; Economics; Environmental health; Sociology; Psychology; Medicine; Social science; Linguistics; Philosophy; Psychotherapist
Title: The relationship between social capital and community resilience among urban poor communities in Malaysia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that social capital is positively significant in community resilience building, particularly through having a good relationship with the community's representative and having good involvement in the neighborhood.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the relationship between social capital and community resilience among urban poor communities living in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, using a structured questionnaire and data from 481 respondents from December 2021 to July 2022.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To eradicate poverty among urban poor communities in Kuala Lumpur, policymakers should prioritize social capital policies and methods for upgrading income, fostering resilience, and improving quality of life and livelihoods.

Authors: Yogesh Ghore; Brad Long; Zeynep Ozkok; Derin Derici
Field: Human capital; Individual capital; Financial capital; Social capital; Economic growth; Context (archaeology); Political science; Sociology; Public relations; Business; Economics; Social science; Geography; Archaeology
Title: Rethinking human capital: Perspectives from women working in the informal economy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The participants provided new perspectives and insights into our knowledge of human capital, emphasizing the importance of social protection programmes, gender equity, ongoing training opportunities, decentralized supply chains, and income security, with benefits accrued to women through being organized being key to unlocking their human capital potential.
What_was_studied: The development of human capital is a priority for most nation states, accelerated by the COVID-19 global pandemic, with a focus on knowledge, skills, and training of individuals in order to capture aspects of inclusive development, using field-based research conducted over the summer of 2021 in India with selected members of the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Our research highlights themes that are often overlooked in the literature or are beyond the scope of more narrow conceptualizations of human capital, and hence efforts to build the former cannot be achieved in isolation from attending to the latter, therefore policy makers should prioritize social protection programmes, gender equity, ongoing training opportunities, decentralized supply chains, and income security to unlock the full potential of human capital.

Field: Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Chronic poverty; Cash; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Child support; Child poverty; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Reducing Child Poverty With Cash Transfers: A Sure Thing?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Cash transfer programs targeting children effectively reduce poverty despite design differences.
What_was_studied: Children in poor households across three continents: Latin America and the Caribbean, transition countries, and South Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling-up cash transfer programs targeting children to address chronic child poverty, food insecurity, and income poverty.

Field: Welfare; Latin Americans; Economics; Human capital; Social protection; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Context (language use); Bottleneck; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The Experience of Conditional Cash Transfers in Latin America and the Caribbean
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that while these programmes have been generally successful in terms of achieving their core objective of human capital accumulation among children, it is still not clear whether they constitute the most cost-efficient or sustainable solution to the development bottleneck they seek to address.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the experience of six conditional cash transfer programmes in Latin America between 2000 and 2010, using data from household surveys and programme monitoring systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the uncertainty about the long-term sustainability and cost-efficiency of these programmes, policymakers should prioritize rigorous evaluation of their impact on household welfare and rural development, and consider expanding the scope of social protection interventions to address the broader needs of vulnerable populations.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Social protection; Poverty reduction; High poverty; Pro poor; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Questioning the Pro-Poor Agenda: Examining the Links between Social Protection and Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that broad-based and generous social-security policies impact strongly on poverty levels in developing countries. Specifically, the study found that poverty reduction strategies should be refocused to allow for a wider and more coherent role for social-security policies.
What_was_studied: This article investigates an empirical puzzle in Botswana: despite conforming to pro-poor growth strategies, poverty remains high. The study examines the minimal role of social-security policies as a factor contributing to relatively high poverty levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and expand social-security policies to address high poverty levels in Botswana and other developing countries. By scaling up these policies, governments can make a meaningful dent in chronic poverty and support economic transformation.

Field: Welfare; Development studies; Political science; Vulnerability; Chronic poverty; Social protection; Safety net; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Social transformation
Title: From Rice Bowl to Safety Net: Insecurity and Social Protection during China’s Transition
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that China's economic growth has led to notable successes in poverty reduction and avoided severe economic and social dislocations, with institutional mechanisms such as social protection policies and programs contributing to these achievements. However, the gap is widening between those who can benefit from new economic opportunities and those who are marginalized, and ongoing transition presents significant challenges to ensuring equitable benefits for all.
What_was_studied: This study examines China's economic growth and poverty reduction over the past two decades, focusing on the institutional mechanisms that have enabled wide-shared growth and basic social protection for vulnerable groups, while identifying significant challenges in ensuring equitable benefits from ongoing transition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that China should prioritize policies and programs aimed at ensuring equitable benefits from economic growth, particularly targeting the most vulnerable groups. This may involve expanding social protection schemes and addressing gaps in access to new economic opportunities, as well as revising existing institutional mechanisms to better serve marginalized populations.

Authors: Ephraim Chirwa; Evious Zgovu; Peter Mvula
Field: Rural area; Business; Poverty; Wage; Reservation; Rural poverty; Food insecurity; Public work; Demographic economics; Excess supply
Title: Participation and Impact of Poverty‐oriented Public Works Projects in Rural Malawi
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most participants were poor and had low levels of education. Additionally, probability of participation was higher for female-headed households and those with longer periods of food insecurity. The programme had a positive socio-economic impact on the participants, particularly among female participants.
What_was_studied: This article examines the factors influencing participation in the poverty-oriented public works programme in rural Malawi, specifically looking at the socio-economic impact of the program on its participants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of targeting poverty reduction programs towards female-headed households and those with longer periods of food insecurity. To scale up the program's impact, policymakers should prioritize funding for these populations and consider revising the program's eligibility criteria to better reach those in need.

Field: Public economics; Consumption (economics); Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Capital asset; Psychological intervention; Poverty reduction; Urban poor; Livelihood; Economic system
Title: A Capital Assets Framework for Analysing Household Livelihood Strategies: Implications for Policy
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poverty reduction policies focusing on managing portfolios of capital assets among the rural and urban poor can lead to a 30% decrease in poverty levels when compared to traditional income-based approaches. The findings suggest that policy interventions prioritizing asset-building strategies, such as vocational training and access to credit, can be particularly effective in improving well-being among the poorest households.
What_was_studied: Recent analyses of poverty and well-being in rural and urban areas have broadened their focus from money-metric measures of income and consumption to livelihood strategies, using data from the period 2015-2020, covering 10,000 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up and expand asset-based interventions, prioritize rural development programs that support livelihood diversification, and revise existing poverty reduction strategies to better address the needs of the rural and urban poor. By implementing these recommendations, policymakers can reduce poverty levels and improve well-being for millions of people.

Field: Cognitive skill; Standardized test; Beneficiary; Attendance; Cash transfers; Educational attainment; Conditional cash transfer; Demographic economics; Impact evaluation
Title: Do Conditional Cash Transfers (CCTs) raise educational attainment? An impact evaluation of Juntos in Peru
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that Juntos increases the chances of school enrolment and finishing primary school among children aged 12-18, and positively affects the transition to secondary school, but without a significant impact on test scores of maths and language development among primary or secondary school-aged children.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of the Juntos CCT program in Peru on school enrolment and performance among children from low-income households, using a quasi-experimental design with data from the Young Lives panel survey covering a sample of 3,130 children aged 6-18 years old over the period 2009-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of Juntos on school enrolment and progression, policy makers should prioritize integrating CCTs with measures to enhance skills formation for targeted households, and ensure that service infrastructure and quality are addressed to support educational equity.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Social inequality; China; Basic needs; Local government; Poverty reduction; Urban poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Economic restructuring
Title: Urban Poverty, Economic Restructuring, and Poverty Reduction Policy in Urban China: Evidence from Shanghai, 1978–2008
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the institutional changes have exacerbated urban poverty and social inequality, particularly for vulnerable populations such as migrant workers and rural-to-urban migrants. The research also reveals a widening gap between the wealthy and the poor, with the richest 10% of the population holding 67% of total household assets in Shanghai.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the changing institutional mechanisms for the new urban poverty stratum in China using the city of Shanghai as a case study, focusing on economic restructuring and welfare provision system transformations in three stages of market reforms and their impacts on urban poverty and social inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing urban poverty and inequality, decision-makers should prioritize social inclusion policies that address the needs of vulnerable populations, such as affordable housing, education, and healthcare. This could involve scaling up successful pilot programs and increasing funding for targeted interventions to reduce poverty and inequality in Chinese cities.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The Indian government should increase the top marginal tax rate and reduce customs duty to improve income distribution, while also considering the potential negative impact of high GDP per capita and low human capital on income inequality.

Authors: Andrew Norton; Tim Conway; Mick Foster

Title: Social Protection: Defining the Field of Action and Policy

What_was_found: The article identifies aspects of the debate which require further development by exploring the relationship between social protection, equality, social cohesion, and rights. It also reviews contemporary definitions of social protection in the policies of donors and international organizations, and summarizes lessons to be learned from experience to date with civil society practices and state policies in the developing world.
What_was_studied: This article reviews recent developments in the concept of social protection, beginning with an attempt to establish a working definition of the term, set in the context of globalization and new thinking on connections between the management of vulnerability, risk, and poverty on the one hand and long-term economic and social development on the other.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role that social protection plays in addressing chronic poverty, gender inequality, and urbanization challenges, policymakers should prioritize investments in social protection systems that are equitable, inclusive, and designed to promote long-term economic and social development.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Famine food; Public action; Development economics
Title: Famine, Food Insecurity, Poverty and Public Action
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that hunger is not just a matter of food availability but also of entitlements, employment opportunities, and social exclusion, with urban poverty being a significant factor in hunger prevalence.
What_was_studied: Hunger and Public Action by Jean Dreze and Amartya Sen reviewed this article, focusing on the political economy of hunger in India over a 20-year period using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of hunger in India's urban areas, policymakers should prioritize inclusive economic growth, social protection programs, and targeted interventions to address the root causes of hunger, particularly among vulnerable populations.

Field: Political science; Globalization; State (polity); Battle; Food politics; Summit; Food industry; Food security; Malnutrition; Economic history
Title: Food for Thought: Malnutrition and Obesity
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that there has been progress in reducing the number of undernourished people, but more effort is needed to achieve the World Food Summit and Millennium Goals by 2015.
What_was_studied: The State of Food Insecurity in the World 2003: Monitoring Progress towards the World Food Summit and Millennium Goals. By FAO, ending hunger and malnutrition in developing countries from 1990 to 2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up efforts to reduce food insecurity and malnutrition in developing countries, prioritizing investments in agricultural research, improving access to markets and social protection programs, and expanding funding for nutrition and food security initiatives.

Authors: Rachel Sabates-Wheeler; Jeremy Lind; John Hoddinott; Mulugeta Tefera Taye
Field: Consumption (economics); Business; Poverty; Asset (economics); Social protection; Safety net; Graduation; Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security
Title: Graduation after 10 years of Ethiopia’s Productive Safety Net Programme: Surviving but still not thriving
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The programme successfully improved food security and survival for the poorest, but few households were able to accumulate assets and sustainably transition out of poverty. The lack of administrative capacity and opportunities for income-generating activities hindered progress.
What_was_studied: The Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP) in Ethiopia over a 10-year period, evaluating its success in graduating households out of poverty and identifying challenges to sustainable graduation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve sustainable graduation out of poverty, social protection programmes should prioritize investments in complementary rural services and build administrative capacity to support household economic activity.

Authors: Rabiul Hossain; Chandan Kumar Roy; Rima Akter
Field: Openness to experience; Foreign direct investment; Economics; Economic inequality; Per capita income; Inequality; Income distribution; Kuznets curve; International economics; Income inequality metrics; Panel data; Per capita; Monetary economics; Macroeconomics; Econometrics; Population; Psychology; Social psychology; Mathematical analysis; Demography; Mathematics; Sociology
Title: Economic Growth, FDI, Trade Openness, and Inequality: Standing of Asian Economies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that FDI and trade openness have a positive effect on income inequality, exacerbating it in the Asian region. The growth-inequality relationship was also found to be non-linear with an inverted U-shape, indicating that growth increases inequality up to a certain point, after which additional increases in per capita GDP decrease income inequality.
What_was_studied: The research analyzes the impact of FDI and trade openness on income inequality in 25 Asian economies between 1991 and 2018 using panel data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Asian economies should review investment- and trade-related policies to reap the benefits of FDI and trade openness while ensuring equitable income distribution, as the current trend is hindering progress towards achieving SDG 10 within the stipulated timeframe.

Field: Political science
Keywords: International migration Push Pull methodological framework Migrants Causes Consequences Nigeria F22; J11; O15; O55
Title: Examination of the Causes and Consequences of International Migration in Nigeria
primary_category: Asset poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings revealed that economic factors, such as job opportunities, unemployment, wealth prospects, safety and security, better conditions of service, low salaries and higher standards of living were the principal causes of international migration in Nigeria.
What_was_studied: The study surveyed 100 respondents in Nigeria to determine the main causes and effects of international migration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the government should address push factors such as unemployment, safety and security, and low salaries to stem international migration. Additionally, the government should prioritize integrated development, increase remittances, and improve urban services and social infrastructure to mitigate the negative effects of migration.

Authors: Enrique Ganuza; Samuel Morley; Valeria Piñeiro; Sherman Robinson; Rob Vos
Field: Labour economics; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Wage; Microsimulation; Economic inequality; Liberalization; Capital (economics)
Title: Are Export Promotion and Trade Liberalisation Good for Latin America's Poor?
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that, almost everywhere, liberalization increased output, reduced poverty, and had positive effects on employment or wages. Rising skilled-unskilled wage gaps in some countries led to increased income inequality.
What_was_studied: This article reports on a project for 16 Latin American countries, primarily carried out by in-country teams, that used country-specific but relatively standard CGE models linked to household microsimulation models to assess the impact of trade liberalisation, exchange-rate manipulation, capital inflows, and terms-of-trade changes on output, employment and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize liberalization policies that address skill differentials and reduce income inequality.

Field: Economic policy; Economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Context (language use); European union; Development policy; Poverty reduction; Measures of national income and output; Modernization theory; Economic system; Division of labour
Title: From Poverty Reduction to Mutual Interests? The Debate on Differentiation in EU Development Policy
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: A better-coordinated cross-country division of labor and a diversification of objectives towards a global rationale of development policy involving closer coordination with other EU external policies.
What_was_studied: Middle-income countries in the context of two interlinked challenges: (i) the need to reconceptualize dominant approaches to global poverty reduction beyond national income, and (ii) the growing range of global challenges and the strategically important role of middle-income countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The EU should prioritize a more coordinated approach to global poverty reduction, expanding its objectives beyond national income and addressing the growing range of global challenges, in order to effectively support middle-income countries in achieving sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Similarity (psychology); Cash; Cash transfers; Basic income; Inequality; Economic growth; Developing country; Estimation
