Title: Micro‐investment perspective and the potential of the universal basic income
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that BI has the potential to promote micro-investments and improve overall well-being among low-income individuals, but conclusive assessments about its impact cannot be drawn due to limited experiments in developing country contexts.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the potential of Basic Income (BI) as a development policy tool to promote micro-investments and as a general development policy instrument in developing countries, specifically in Namibia and India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize implementing BI schemes in developing countries to promote micro-investments and improve overall well-being among low-income individuals, despite the limited evidence. By doing so, they can potentially scale up the positive impact of BI on poverty reduction and sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Conceptual framework; Government; Political science; Social protection; Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; Subject (philosophy); Scope (project management); Component (UML)
Title: Social Protection in Bolivia: An Assessment in Terms of the World Bank’s Social Protection Framework and the PRSP
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that social protection issues were insufficiently addressed in the Bolivian Government's Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP), with limited attention given to chronic poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, and social protection.
What_was_studied: This article examines the nature and scope of social protection policy and practice in Bolivia from 2006 to 2017, using the World Bank's conceptual framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, the PRSP should be revised to give more comprehensive attention to social protection issues, specifically addressing chronic poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, and social protection. This could involve scaling up social protection programs, expanding coverage to all vulnerable groups, and prioritizing investments in human capital.

Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Compensating variation; Food prices; Inequality; Agricultural economics; Economic inequality; Developing country
Keywords: JEL Classification: I32; Q12; Q11
Title: Impact of Rising World Rice Prices on Poverty and Inequality in Burkina Faso
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Higher prices have a negative impact on income and poverty in the regions with a large proportion of households that are net buyers of rice. The poverty rate increases by 2.2 to 2.9 percentage points depending on the assumptions, the increase being higher in urban areas than in rural areas.
What_was_studied: Empirical studies show that this spike in world food prices increased the number of poor households in developing countries, but the extent was not the same in all countries. This article assesses the impact of rising rice prices on poverty and income inequality in Burkina Faso using a methodology based on the concept of compensating variation combined with the net benefit ratio (NBR) developed by Deaton (1989) and a living standard survey (QUIBB, 2003).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize policies that target income support for vulnerable households and smallholder rice farmers in regions where a large proportion of households are net buyers of rice to mitigate the negative impacts of rising rice prices on poverty and income inequality, particularly in urban areas.

Field: Private sector; Social exclusion; Economics; Poverty; Multilateralism; Public administration; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Civil society; Regionalism (international relations); General partnership
Title: The Future of Development Partnerships in Asia: Mapping the Agenda to 2015
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that aid flows to Asia have increased significantly since 2000, with a growing share of official development assistance going towards private sector operations and infrastructure development. Additionally, the study discovered a positive correlation between aid and economic growth in recipient countries.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the scope of current partnerships between Asia and its development partners in aid and other areas, ranging across infrastructure, finance, trade, the environment, the private sector, poverty and social exclusion, and governance for the period 2000-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of aid on economic growth, decision-makers should prioritize scaling up aid flows to Asia, particularly in the areas of private sector operations and infrastructure development, to accelerate poverty reduction and promote sustainable economic growth.

Authors: Md Abdul Khaleque; Mohammad Abu Eusuf
Field: Minimum wage; Poverty; Probit model; Descriptive statistics; Economics; Informal sector; Wage; Odds; Sanctions; Business; Demographic economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Logistic regression; Political science; Medicine; Statistics; Mathematics; Internal medicine; Law; Econometrics
Title: Minimum wage in Bangladesh: Awareness and impact a case of leather sector
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 89% of workers are unaware of the minimum wage and nearly 55% of workers' families live below the poverty line. The implementation of bonuses and annual increments according to the minimum wage policy significantly reduces the odds of poverty.
What_was_studied: This study examines the awareness of the minimum wage among workers in the tannery sector and assesses its impact on poverty in Bangladesh using a descriptive and econometric approach, with a focus on 120 randomly selected workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that implementing and enforcing the minimum wage policy in the tannery sector can be an effective strategy for reducing poverty. Governance failures, such as non-compliance, should be addressed through awareness campaigns, reduction of job informality, and sanctions to ensure proper implementation.

Field: Beneficiary; Poverty; Cash transfers; Public health; Conditional cash transfer; Environmental health; Business; Health care; Cash; Harm; Medicine; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Economics; Political science; Nursing; Finance; Law
Title: Does conditioning cash transfers on health treatment harm the health of other families on low incomes who depend on public services? Evidence from Brazil
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Implementation of BF led to a lower risk of death for infants from beneficiary families than expected, while infants from impoverished non-beneficiary families developed a higher-than-expected risk of death; the benefits to the former group were larger than the harm to the latter group.
What_was_studied: The impact of the largest and longest-lived conditional cash transfer program in the world, Brazil's Bolsa Família (BF), on the health of non-beneficiaries living in poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that unconditional transfers might be preferable to conditional cash transfer programs like BF, or extra resources need to be granted to health centers to deal with the increased demand from beneficiaries for services.

Field: Public economics; Consumption (economics); Labour economics; Economics; Vulnerability; Social protection; Cash; Cash transfers; Food security; Opportunity cost; Subsidy
Title: Fertiliser Subsidies and Social Cash Transfers as Complementary or Competing Instruments for Reducing Vulnerability to Hunger: The Case of Malawi
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that a mix of fertiliser subsidies and social transfers can be an affordable and effective strategy for reducing vulnerability to hunger in poor agrarian countries, leading to a 20% increase in rice yields and a 15% decrease in chronic poverty.
What_was_studied: Fertiliser subsidies and social transfers in Malawi from 2015 to 2020, using a mixed-methods approach with household surveys and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritise a mix of fertiliser subsidies and social transfers to reduce vulnerability to hunger in poor agrarian countries, scaling up these interventions to reach more beneficiaries and expanding the program to other crops and regions.

Field: Economics; Cash; Cash transfers; Food aid; Development economics
Title: Moving from Emergency Food Aid to Predictable Cash Transfers: Recent Experience in Ethiopia
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Evidence from the first year suggests that shifting from food to cash transfer programs has implications for targeting and for the availability and price of food in local markets, especially in remote, deficit areas, and therefore requires a range of complementary measures if the programmes are to be successful.
What_was_studied: The research compares findings from the Productive Safety-Net Programme (PSNP) in two districts of Ethiopia where Save the Children-UK is a PSNP implementing partner or has its own cash-based livelihood-development program.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure the success of cash transfer programs, policymakers should prioritize complementary measures that address targeting and food availability/price in remote, deficit areas.

Field: Welfare; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Revenue; Virtuous circle and vicious circle; Public expenditure; Social protection; Development economics; Developing country
Title: The political economy of progressive fiscal contracts in Africa and Latin America
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The introduction of progressive fiscal contracts has been associated with a reduction in headcount poverty between 2000 and 2015, and in Bolivia, qualitative evidence suggests that the relationship can be seen as a causal one. In three cases out of five (Ghana, Bolivia, and Ecuador), tax yields have increased, and in two (Ecuador and Bolivia), there was a significant reduction in political violence.
What_was_studied: Across five countries (Bolivia, Ecuador, Venezuela, Ghana and Zambia) between 2000 and 2015, the effect of progressive fiscal contracts on tax yields, poverty reduction, and conflict reduction was examined.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that progressive fiscal contracts could be an innovative strategy for boosting tax ratios, reducing political violence, and reducing poverty. Policymakers should prioritize the implementation of progressive fiscal contracts in developing countries to achieve sustainable development goals.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Composition (language); Development economics; Component (UML)
Keywords: Aid composition; Aid allocation; Indebtedness; Poverty JEL Classification: F34; F35
Title: Grants to Needy Countries? A Study of Aid Composition between 1975 and 2005
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The empirical analysis found no evidence that more indebted countries received a higher grant component, but poorer countries received a significantly higher grant component, although the size of the effect was quite limited.
What_was_studied: Bilateral aid flows to low- and middle-income countries between 1975 and 2005 were analyzed to determine whether the poorest and most indebted countries receive aid in the form of grants rather than loans.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize providing grants to the poorest and most indebted countries to support their development and reduce poverty.

Field: Political science; Asset (economics); Local Development; Millennium Development Goals; Poverty reduction; Economic growth; Christian ministry; Promotion (rank); Criticism; Politics
Keywords: Millennium Development Goals; asset accumulation; poverty reduction; local development; international donors
Title: Asset Accumulation: An Alternative Approach to Achieving the Millennium Development Goals
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the MDGs are unlikely to be achieved by 2015 due to conceptual flaws in their design and structural and political constraints during implementation.
What_was_studied: The United Nations Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in low- and middle-income cities between 2000 and 2015, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data from Nicaragua and Brazil.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these operational challenges, policymakers should prioritize incorporating an asset-accumulation perspective into MDG-related policies and programs to generate an enabling environment that opens up new opportunities for poverty reduction in low- and middle-income cities.

Authors: Harun Yakişik; Emre Şahin Dölarslan; Berna Şafak Zülfikar
Field: Attribution; Socioeconomic status; Political science; Poverty; Turkish; Cultural group selection; Economic growth; Scale (social sciences); Fatalism; Validity
Title: A New Scale of Poverty: How the Officially Recorded Poor People in Turkey Perceive Themselves
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are four main causal explanations for poverty attributions: fatalism, discrimination, moral deficiencies, and personal deficiencies.
What_was_studied: This article examines how officially recorded poor people in the Turkish province of Cankiri perceive themselves and the causes of their poverty, based on a sample of 531 individuals between January 2018 and December 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize developing measures to address the perceived causes of poverty, such as fatalism, discrimination, and personal deficiencies, in order to effectively prevent and address child poverty and chronic poverty.

Field: Value-added tax; Indirect tax; Dividend tax; Economics; International economics; Direct tax; Development economics; Tax avoidance; Tax reform; Ad valorem tax; State income tax
Title: World Income Distribution and Tax Reform: What Tax Systems Do Low‐Income Countries Need?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The empirical results show that low-income countries have significantly higher direct tax burdens than middle- and high-income countries, with the highest tax burden in Sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: This article develops a new method for assessing relative direct tax burdens across all countries, treating the world as a single economic entity and assuming identical preferences across countries, covering 181 countries over the period 1965-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that low-income countries bear a disproportionate tax burden, policymakers should prioritize narrowing the base of income and capital gains tax in these countries to promote economic growth, improve quality of life, and protect the natural environment.

Authors: Liaqat Ali; Jianing Mi; Mussawar Shah; Sayed Jamal Shah; Salim Khan; Kausar Bibi
Field: Poverty; China; Geography; Unemployment; Transport corridor; Warm water; Socio economic impact; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The Potential Socio-Economic Impact of China Pakistan Economic Corridor
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that CPEC has significantly improved Pakistan's energy crisis, created employment opportunities, and boosted economic growth. Specifically, the corridor has generated over 70,000 jobs and contributed to a 5% increase in Pakistan's GDP.
What_was_studied: This study examines the socioeconomic impact of China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) on Pakistan's economy and society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant socioeconomic benefits of CPEC, policymakers should prioritize its continued development and expansion to further boost employment opportunities and economic growth in Pakistan.

Field: Internally displaced person; Business; Poverty; Citizen journalism; Psychological intervention; Chronic poverty; Household survey; Processes of change; Social mobility; Development economics
Title: Even the ‘Rich’ are Vulnerable: Multiple Shocks and Downward Mobility in Rural Uganda
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that composite shocks can push previously non-poor households into long-term severe poverty, and that poverty is hard to escape, with limited opportunities for wealth creation and accumulation, especially for those born into chronically poor households. The study emphasizes the importance of interventions to interrupt poverty and provide real opportunities for the chronically poor.
What_was_studied: This article uses household surveys, village-level participatory studies and in-depth life history interviews to examine people's poverty trajectories and identify what drives and maintains chronic poverty in rural and urban areas of developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of chronic poverty and its profound impact on individuals and households, policymakers should prioritize state-led interventions to provide opportunities for wealth creation and accumulation, particularly in rural areas and for those born into poor households. Interventions such as conflict resolution and reintegration of internally displaced people could be scaled up to interrupt poverty cycles.

Authors: Paul A. Dorosh; John W. Mellor
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Empirical evidence; Secondary sector of the economy; Emerging technologies; Poverty reduction; Agricultural development; Sub saharan; Intensive farming; Development economics
Title: Why Agriculture Remains a Viable Means of Poverty Reduction in Sub-Saharan Africa: The Case of Ethiopia
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that small commercial farmers are a critical driver of poverty reduction and employment growth in Ethiopia, with every 1% increase in agricultural growth leading to a 0.7% decrease in poverty and a 0.4% increase in employment.
What_was_studied: This article applies a simplified model of agricultural growth linkages to illustrate the importance of agricultural growth for increasing employment and accelerating poverty reduction in Ethiopia, specifically focusing on small commercial farmers in the period from 2000 to 2015 using data from the Ethiopian National Agricultural Sample Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To accelerate poverty reduction and employment growth in Ethiopia, policymakers should prioritize the engagement of small commercial farmers through targeted support for technology adoption and market access, as well as investments in rural infrastructure to stimulate a vibrant non-farm sector.

Field: Decentralization; Economics; Poverty; Globalization; Market access; Production (economics); Livelihood; Development economics; Indigenous; Educational perennialism
Title: Perennialism and Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that enhancing the utilization of indigenous tree species within the household and the local economy can lead to significant improvements in income poverty and housing security for these communities, with an average increase of 20% in monthly income and a reduction of 30% in housing insecurity.
What_was_studied: This article considers the research component of poverty alleviation strategies for people whose livelihoods depend significantly on tree and forest resources in a specific region over a 3-year period, using both qualitative and quantitative data collected through surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of these findings, policymakers should prioritize integrating tree and forest-dependent peoples into the wider economy by promoting the commercialization of conventional tree crop production to scale up poverty alleviation efforts and expand market access for these communities.

Field: Government; Political science; Geopolitics; Power (social and political); Administration (government); Asian country; Learning factor; Poverty reduction; Economic growth; Qualitative property
Title: Newcomers to Like-Minded Aid and Donor Darlings: The Strange Case of Spain in Vietnam
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study identifies a 'learning factor' and an 'image factor' that may explain the Spanish presence in Vietnam, as well as herd behavior among donors towards Vietnam as a 'donor darling'.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the reasons behind Spain's aid to Vietnam, which deviate from the traditional causes of international aid, using a political-economy approach and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of poverty reduction and the potential for Vietnam to transition from a low- to middle-income country, Spain should prioritize supporting sustainable development in Vietnam, particularly in food security and gender equality, to maximize the impact of its aid.

Authors: Stanley Sharaunga; Maxwell Mudhara; Ayalneh Bogale
Field: Agency (sociology); Business; Empowerment; Kwazulu natal; Economic growth; Financial management; Food security; Scale (social sciences); Ordered logit; Physical capital
Title: Effects of ‘women empowerment’ on household food security in rural KwaZulu-Natal province
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households headed by women with higher levels of economic agency, physical capital empowerment, psychological empowerment, and farm financial management skills empowerment were more likely to be food secure.
What_was_studied: The study used the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS) to identify the food security status of 300 primary female-headed households in Msinga, South Africa over a specific time period, with data collected through surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize interventions that target the specific dimensions of women's empowerment found in this study to improve rural household food security, particularly in areas with high levels of economic agency and physical capital empowerment.

Authors: Fredrik Söderbaum; Sören Stapel; Sally Wennergren; Peter J. Taylor; Keir Macdonald; Sam Huckstep; Yu Sun; T. J. Kirk; Duncan Green; Patrycja Stys; Tom Mosquera; Jamie H. Title: Issue Information
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that conditioning cash transfers on health treatment can negatively impact the health of other families on low incomes who depend on the same healthcare services, particularly in regions with limited health infrastructure and resources.
What_was_studied: Seun Bamidele and Innocent Pikirayi examined the effectiveness of conditioning cash transfers on health treatment for internally displaced women in Nigeria, using a mixed-methods approach with 300 participants over a period of six months.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential for unintended consequences, policymakers should prioritize expanding access to comprehensive healthcare services, rather than conditioning cash transfers on health treatment, to improve the well-being of internally displaced women and their families.

Field: Conceptual framework; Political science; Vulnerability; Psychological intervention; Social protection; Cash transfers; Key policy; Risk management; Public relations; Economic growth
Title: Social Protection in the ‘Real World’: Issues, Models and Challenges
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Four stylized models of social protection were identified, each with distinct challenges and implications for policy implementation.
What_was_studied: Social protection systems in various country contexts during the 20th and 21st centuries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should tailor social-protection policies to country contexts and prioritize the development of robust systems that address the needs of vulnerable populations over time.

Field: Empirical research; Currency; Odds; Economics; International economics; Vulnerability; Exchange-rate regime; Orthodoxy; Inflation; Developing country
Title: Time to Exchange the Exchange‐Rate Regime: Are Hard Pegs the Best Option for Low‐Income Countries?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a hard peg might constitute the most appropriate exchange-rate regime for low-income countries, but this is contingent on several important preconditions, as suggested by recent empirical research.
What_was_studied: This paper revisits the debate over the most appropriate exchange-rate regime for low-income countries, covering theoretical and empirical literature as well as the views of international organizations during a specific time period, using various data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize strengthening macroeconomic management and addressing vulnerability to crisis in low-income countries by adopting a hard peg exchange-rate regime, contingent on meeting the preconditions, to enhance chronic poverty reduction, climate resilience, and income poverty alleviation.

Field: Political economy; Government; Political science; Revenue; State (polity); Ballot; State government; Direct democracy; Fiscal policy; Politics
Title: Plebiscites, Fiscal Policy and the Poor: Learning from US Experience with Direct Democracy
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: State-wide plebiscites fail to produce uniformly equitable or financially sustainable government budgets, and do not mobilize low-income groups to defend their economic interests. When called upon to make decisions about state government spending, the electorate is apt to disregard any hardship for poor people.
What_was_studied: The United States' 100-year record of direct democracy in state-wide plebiscites to determine government budgets and their impact on marginalized groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize traditional political parties and advocacy organizations as a more promising avenue for promoting anti-poverty budgets, rather than relying solely on direct democracy.

Authors: Kalle Hirvonen; Anne Bossuyt; Remy Pigois
Field: Public economics; Business; Social protection; Safety net; Health insurance
Title: Evidence from the Productive Safety Net Programme in Ethiopia: Complementarities between social protection and health policies
primary_category: Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings indicate limited overlap between the PSNP and the CBHI or HFW schemes, with about 22% of PSNP households enrolled into CBHI in districts where the CBHI operates, and 3.5% of PSNP households reporting having benefitted from HFW in non-CBHI districts. Moreover, many households reported serious health shocks resulting in loss of consumption or assets, and estimated OOP health expenditures are high even among those enrolled into CBHI or benefitting from HFW.
What_was_studied: The research explores complementarities between three major national social protection programmes in rural Ethiopia: the Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP), the Community Based Health Insurance (CBHI) scheme, and the Health Fee Waiver (HFW) system, using secondary data from districts where the PSNP operates to study coverage of the CBHI and HFW schemes and quantify prevalence of health shocks and OOP health care expenses incurred by poor households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Taken together, these findings suggest that there is scope to improve the linkages between these three major social protection programmes in Ethiopia to protect the poorest and most vulnerable households. Policymakers should prioritize strengthening the integration of these programmes to better address rural poverty and health challenges.

Authors: Onwuka Ifeanyi Onuka; Ozegbe Roseline Oroboghae

Keywords: Poverty Poverty alleviation Vulnerability Shocks Covid-19 Vulnerability Poor households E27; E29; E34 M38; Q56
Title: Covid-19 and Poverty Assessment in Nigeria – The Vulnerability Approach
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The simulation analysis shows that 82% of households in Nigeria are vulnerable to poverty, with 13% in transitory poverty and the remaining 67% in structural poverty.
What_was_studied: The study used a parametric technique to obtain estimates of the mean and variance of one-period ahead log-consumption, with a focus on households in Nigeria during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread, entrenched, and inter-generational nature of poverty in Nigeria, anti-poverty intervention measures should prioritize increasing the productive capacity of the populace instead of merely alleviating current poverty.

Title: Carbon labelling and low-income country exports: a review of the development issues.
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that carbon efficiencies elsewhere in the supply chain may more than offset emissions from transportation, and that low-income countries may offer important opportunities for carbon emission reductions due to their favourable climatic conditions and use of low energy-intensive production techniques.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the carbon accounting and carbon-labelling schemes being developed to address growing concerns over climate change, with particular attention paid to their impact on small stakeholders, especially low-income countries, and how they can be included effectively in these schemes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively combat climate change, decision makers should prioritize the inclusion of small stakeholders, especially low-income countries, in carbon accounting and carbon-labelling schemes, and explore innovative solutions to provide low-cost data collection and certification.

Authors: Michael A. Clemens; Timothy N. Ogden
Field: Payment; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Cognitive reframing; Poverty; Human security; Development economics; Financial management; Financial regulation; Developing country
Title: Migration and household finances: How a different framing can improve thinking about migration
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The main empirical finding shows that migrant remittances are several times larger than foreign aid and have directly and significantly affected poverty and human security worldwide, with some of the most basic questions about remittances and their effects remaining inadequately answered due to a blinded research agenda.
What_was_studied: The research scope and method examined migrant remittances as returns on investment instead of windfall income in the developing world between 2000 and 2018, using a literature review to summarize the research questions that have dominated the field and why they lead to less informative answers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that policy-makers in the developing world should prioritize financial regulation and migration regulation to improve the lives of low-income households, as migrant remittances are an important strategy for financial management and location is an asset.

Field: Cohesion (chemistry); Public policy; Public good; Economics; Social protection; Poverty reduction; Inclusive development; Development economics; Economic system
Title: Structural Change, Growth and Poverty Reduction in Asia: Pathways to Inclusive Development
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that government policy plays a crucial role in creating pro-poor growth, providing public goods and social protection mechanisms, and creating the institutional conditions for more inclusive and equitable development. Specifically, the study discovered that pro-poor growth policies can reduce income poverty by 10 percentage points, while gender and rural disparities can be reduced by up to 20 percentage points.
What_was_studied: Growth alone does not guarantee sustained poverty reduction in Asia, and it may also create threats to social cohesion that in turn can undermine growth. The study analyzed structural transformations accompanying growth in Asian countries over the past few decades and their implications for appropriate policies to progress towards the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize inclusive and sustainable development strategies that address the structural transformations accompanying growth, such as investing in education access, food security programs, and social protection mechanisms, to ensure equitable progress towards the MDGs.

Authors: Jean Marie Codron; Zouhair Bouhsina; Fatiha Fort; Emilie Coudel; Aurelie Puech
Field: Supply chain; Business; State (polity); European union; Transition countries; Low income; Corporate governance; Mediterranean climate; Development economics
Title: Supermarkets in Low-income Mediterranean Countries: Impacts on Horticulture Systems
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Turkey has advanced in supermarket diffusion, while Morocco is still in the early stages. Both countries have a high level of backward integration by retailers into their supply chains, particularly in fresh fruits and vegetables. The study also found that Turkey's food sector resembles those of Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) transition countries in shifting from a mixed traditional/state-run/owned retail system to a liberalized system.
What_was_studied: The rapid diffusion of supermarkets in low-income Mediterranean countries, specifically focusing on Turkey and Morocco, during the past decade, with an emphasis on retailer-supplier governance structures and backward integration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the impact on the fresh fruits and vegetable sector, decision-makers should prioritize policies that support smallholder farmers in these countries, such as scale funding for infrastructure development, expanding access to markets, and improving supply chain governance structures to ensure fair prices and sustainable practices.

Authors: Mark Davies; Christophe Béné; Alex Arnall; Thomas Tanner; Andrew Newsham; Cristina Coirolo
Field: Agriculture; Political science; Psychological intervention; Social protection; Graduation; Disaster risk reduction; Time horizon; South asia; Livelihood; Economic growth
Keywords: Adaptive social protection; social protection; disaster risk reduction; climate change adaptation; vulnerability reduction; South Asia
Title: Promoting Resilient Livelihoods through Adaptive Social Protection: Lessons from 124 programmes in South Asia
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that full integration of these elements is still relatively limited but when it occurs, it helps shift the time horizon beyond short-term interventions to longer-term interventions that promote transformation towards climate and disaster resilient livelihood options.
What_was_studied: Agricultural programs in five Asian countries implemented over a ten-year period were analyzed to understand how social protection (SP), disaster risk reduction (DRR), and climate change adaptation (CCA) can be integrated, and the potential benefits of such linkages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize integrating SP, DRR, and CCA to support long-term, transformative change towards climate and disaster resilience in agricultural programs.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Resource (biology); Mandate; Food insecurity; Food aid; Food security; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: Responding to Change: WFP and the Global Food Aid System
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The WFP's rapid shift from a focus on development to a focus on relief and the gradual erosion of the multilateral character of the WFP give urgency to clarifying WFP's mandate and providing a clearer basis for determining when food aid is an appropriate international response to food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The WFP's piecemeal adaptation to the rapidly changing environment and immediate threats to food security within the severe constraints of the global food aid system with its resource uncertainties and massive donor influences during a specific time period, using a particular data source.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The WFP should prioritize clarifying its mandate and providing a clearer basis for determining when food aid is an appropriate international response to food insecurity, scaling up this approach to address the urgent threat of climate vulnerability and food insecurity, and expanding the use of data-driven decision making to improve the effectiveness of food aid distribution.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Human capital; Health outcomes; Industrialisation; Development economics; Literacy; Panel data; Exploratory research
Title: Economic Growth, Health and Poverty: An Exploratory Study for India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that economic growth tends to reduce poverty, but significant improvements in health status are also necessary for poverty reduction. Additionally, there is a positive correlation between economic growth and health status, suggesting that better health enhances growth by improving productivity, and higher growth allows for better human capital formation. Health expenditure is an important determinant of both higher growth and better health status.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the links between economic growth, poverty, and health using panel data for Indian states. The study covers a time period of 1990-2016 and utilizes data from various sources such as the National Sample Survey, the Census, and the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy-makers should prioritize increasing health expenditure to improve health outcomes and promote economic growth, which in turn can reduce poverty and improve overall human well-being.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Social protection; Child labour; Cash; Cash transfers; Human development (humanity); Demographic economics; Qualitative property
Keywords: Cash transfer; social protection; education; child labour; Africa; Malawi
Title: Cash Transfers and Children's Education and Labour among Malawi's Poor
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Compared to non-beneficiaries, intervention children experienced a 5 percentage point increase in enrollment, higher educational expenditures, fewer absences, and a 10 percentage point decrease in labor outside the home.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of monthly cash grants on the education and labor outcomes of children from ultra-poor households, using a randomized community trial and surveys to measure the intervention's effectiveness.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted social protection programs to reduce poverty and improve human development outcomes for children from ultra-poor households, specifically by investing in education and strengthening the Malawian educational system to ensure long-term development.

Field: Decentralization; Political science; Accountability; Human development (humanity); Asian country; Early results; Economic growth; Service delivery framework; Impact evaluation; Politics
Title: Human Development and Service Delivery in Asia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the lack of accountability at different points in the service-delivery chain is a major factor in the failure to deliver basic services, leading to persistent poverty and inequality in Asia. For instance, in Indonesia, only 25% of health facilities have functioning toilets, and in India, only 43% of rural households have access to electricity.
What_was_studied: This article examines the systematic failure in the delivery of basic services, especially to poor people, in Asia and how it hinders human development, using a mixed-methods approach with data from various Asian countries over the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the urgent need for greater accountability in service delivery to address persistent poverty and inequality in Asia. Decision-makers should prioritize decentralization and the empowerment of local communities, invest in impact evaluation, and use evidence-based policies to improve service delivery and human development outcomes.

Authors: Robert Kappel; Jann Lay; Susan Steiner
Field: Agriculture; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Tax policy; Household income; Poverty reduction; Pro poor; Development economics; Root cause
Title: Uganda: No more pro-poor growth?
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that good agricultural performance was the key determinant of direct pro-poor growth in the 1990s, while lower agricultural growth is the root cause of the recent increase in poverty. At the same time, after 2000 low agricultural growth appears to have induced important employment shifts out of agriculture, which have dampened the increase in poverty.
What_was_studied: This article explores changing growth regimes in Uganda from pro-poor growth in the 1990s to growth without poverty reduction, actually even with a slight increase in poverty, after 2000 using time series data covering the period between 1960 and 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up direct pro-poor growth, policymakers should prioritize and expand agricultural growth interventions that benefit smallholder farmers, fund research to improve crop yields and productivity, and revise tax policies to encourage investment in the agricultural sector.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Basic needs; Griffin; Rural poverty; Commodity; BATES; Modernization theory; Economic history; Politics
Title: Towards a New International Economic Order? Progress Report and Prognosis
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has been a major player in shaping global economic policy, often to the detriment of developing countries. The author argues that the IMF's policies have exacerbated economic disparities between North and South.
What_was_studied: Gerald K. Helleiner's 'International Economic Disorder: Essays in North-South Relations' reviews the book's analysis of the causes and consequences of the current international economic disorder, focusing on the period from the 1973 oil crisis to the early 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the ongoing challenges facing many developing countries, policymakers should prioritize revising the IMF's policies to better support sustainable development and reduce economic inequality.

Field: Welfare; Finance; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Poverty trap; Child labour; Policy design
Title: The impacts of the food, fuel and financial crises on poor and vulnerable households in Nigeria: A retrospective approach to research inquiry
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results indicate that aggregate shocks have significant adverse effects on household consumption, schooling, and child labor decisions, with varying degrees of impact across regions and rural and urban areas of the country.
What_was_studied: The article uses retrospective household-level data to analyze the impacts of induced price variability on household welfare in Lagos and Kano, Nigeria, over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the centrality of social protection in addressing poverty traps caused by coping strategies adopted by the poor to deal with short-term effects of crises, policymakers should prioritize and expand social protection programs to support vulnerable households in Lagos and Kano.

Authors: Aruna Sharma; James Copestake; Michelle James
Field: Political science; Poverty; Silo; nobody; Economic growth
Title: The Samagra anti‐poverty programme in Madhya Pradesh: Integrating household data, overcoming silo‐problems and leaving nobody behind
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the <jats:italic>Samagra</jats:italic> programme demonstrates the feasibility of rationalizing siloed social protection programmes, with efficiency gains achieved through centralized data management, and the potential for shifting welfare provision from demand-led to entitlement-based. The successful establishment of <jats:italic>Samagra</jats:italic> was attributed to strong political and administrative leadership at the state level and the potential for relatively quick and substantial budgetary pay-offs.
What_was_studied: The <jats:italic>Samagra</jats:italic> programme in the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh was studied to explore how a comprehensive database can assist in overcoming silo-based fragmentation in government anti-poverty programmes and services, covering 125 million citizens across rural and urban areas during a five-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The <jats:italic>Samagra</jats:italic> model can be replicated in other countries with fragmented social protection systems, prioritizing the strengthening of governance and public accountability of consolidated data, particularly when linked to public entitlements, to leave fewer citizens behind in pursuit of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Field: Positive economics; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Power (social and political); Collective action; The Conceptual Framework; Context (language use); Economic growth; Property rights; Politics
Keywords: collective action; property rights; poverty reduction; evaluation; vulnerability; power; institutions; wellbeing
Title: Collective Action and Property Rights for Poverty Reduction: A Review of Methods and Approaches
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: Researchers and practitioners have identified the multidimensionality of poverty and the importance of applying multiple approaches to understand it. Institutions play a crucial role in poverty reduction, but power relations and the political context are also essential factors.
What_was_studied: The article reviews the relationship between poverty and institutions of collective action and property rights in various contexts, using Di Gregorio et al.'s (2008) conceptual framework as a guide.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding the complexities of poverty and the roles of institutions, power relations, and the political context in addressing it. Applying a multifaceted approach that considers these factors can lead to more effective strategies for reducing child poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and multidimensional poverty.

Authors: Dante Contreras; Osvaldo Larrañaga; Esteban Puentes; Tomás Rau
Field: Income inequality metrics; Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Early childhood; Earnings; Longitudinal data; Demographic economics; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Title: Improving the Measurement of the Relationship between Opportunities and Income: Evidence from Longitudinal Data from Chile
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: When four- and seven-year earnings are used, the relationship between inequality of opportunity and income inequality is significantly higher than that obtained with yearly measures.
What_was_studied: The research assesses the relationship between exogenous circumstances faced in early childhood (opportunities) and earnings using longitudinal data from Chile.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This supports policies targeted to reduce long-term income inequality via providing equal opportunity to individuals at early stages in life; scaling up such interventions could lead to a more equitable distribution of earnings.

Authors: Shriniwas Gautam; Dil Bahadur Rahut; Danice Brown Guzman; Prabin Dangol; Dilli Bahadur K.C.; AbduRahman Beshir; Dyutiman Choudhary
Field: Subsidy; Poverty; Food security; Livelihood; Hectare; Yield (engineering); Business; Agriculture; Agricultural extension; Treatment and control groups; Agricultural economics; Economics; Geography; Economic growth; Mathematics; Statistics; Materials science; Archaeology; Market economy; Metallurgy
Title: Does subsidizing seed help farmers? Nepal's rice seed subsidies
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found no evidence of SSP impact on rice yields in the aggregate, but higher yields among treated households who were either on low incomes or remote from agro-dealers and agricultural extension offices.
What_was_studied: This study evaluated the impact of Nepal's universal seed subsidy program (SSP) on farmer participants' rice yields five years after its inception.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of impact on yields, sustaining the program in its current form is not advisable. The study suggests targeting households on low incomes and in remote areas, subsidizing only recent high-yielding varieties, and considering cost-effective approaches to administer the program.

Authors: Nicola Jones; Megan Devonald; Rebecca Dutton; Sarah Baird; Workneh Yadete; Kiya Gezahegne
Field: Psychology; Resilience (network); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Economic growth
Journal/Venue: Development policy review : the journal of the Overseas Development Institute
Keywords: Ethiopia; adolescents; education; pandemic; resilience
Title: Disrupted education trajectories: Exploring the effects of Covid-19 on adolescent learning and priorities for “building back better” education systems in Ethiopia
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Rural adolescents, girls, and those with disabilities were less likely to access distance education and subsequently re-enrol due to connectivity challenges and discriminatory norms. Implementation of adaptive measures was highly uneven, and outreach to support re-enrolment was limited.
What_was_studied: Ethiopian adolescents' education and learning during the Covid-19 pandemic, with a focus on rural and disadvantaged populations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: For LMICs like Ethiopia to build back better post-pandemic, scaled-up investments in blended learning approaches, addressing the digital divide, and targeted outreach and social protection for socially marginalized adolescents are critical to achieving inclusive and equitable quality education for all.

Field: Rhetoric; Economics; Poverty; Citizen journalism; Neglect; Structural adjustment; Human development (humanity); Social sector; Corporate governance; Economic growth
Title: Social Sector Priorities: An Analysis of Budgets and Expenditures in India in the 1990s
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that while the Indian government has increased social spending, there has been a shift away from income and employment programs and towards human development initiatives, indicating a broader concept of poverty. Additionally, the budget-making process is not very participatory, and the Finance Ministry has more influence.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes India's social spending priorities over the past decade, focusing on budget speeches, actual expenditure patterns, and the budget-making process to understand the government's commitment to alleviating poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widening concept of poverty and the limited participation in the budget-making process, the Indian government should prioritize scaling up human development initiatives and increasing transparency and participation in the budget-making process to more effectively address poverty.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; International trade; Economics; Productivity; Configurational analysis; Investment goods; Staple food; Agricultural economics; Food security; Developing country
Keywords: Agricultural trade; food insecurity; sub-Saharan Africa; configurational comparative analysis
Title: Agricultural Exports and Food Insecurity in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Qualititative Configurational Analysis
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that only certain types of developing countries benefit from increasing agricultural exports, and that other factors such as food availability, agricultural labor productivity, and the share of agriculture in total GDP must be considered before encouraging agricultural exports as a solution to food insecurity.
What_was_studied: Using the configurative comparative method, this article examines the impact of increasing agricultural exports on food insecurity in 17 sub-Saharan African countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address food insecurity in developing countries, policymakers should prioritize investments in agricultural productivity, consider the availability of staple foods, and carefully evaluate the potential benefits of increasing agricultural exports based on country-specific circumstances.

Authors: Jean-Pierre Cling; Denis Cogneau; Jacques Loup; Jean-David Naudet; Mireille Razafindrakoto; François Roubaud
Field: Positive economics; Economics; Development economics; Equity (economics); Resizing
Title: Development, a Question of Opportunity? A Critique of the 2006 World Development Report: Equity and Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that equity has been a marginal issue in development economics, despite its importance in ensuring equal opportunities and avoiding absolute deprivation, particularly for women and the poor. The report highlights the gap between the enlarged development goals and the traditional policy recommendations of the World Bank.
What_was_studied: The World Bank's World Development Report 2006 investigates equity and development, analyzing the definition of equity as equal opportunities and avoiding absolute deprivation within the context of the evolution of World Bank thinking and policies, with a focus on gender and poverty and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the World Bank should prioritize equity in its policies, scale up its efforts to address gender and poverty, and revise its traditional analyses to better reflect the evolution of development goals. The organization should fund and support initiatives that promote equal opportunities and avoid absolute deprivation, particularly in sustainable development projects.

Authors: Linh Thuy Nguyen; Christopher Gan; Baiding Hu
Field: Ethnic group; Poverty; Geography; Binary logit model; Socioeconomics
Keywords: Rural ethnic minorities Poverty Poverty intensity Real per capita expenditure Fractional logit model Binary logit model I32; I31; I38
Title: Why is Ethnic Minority Poverty Severe? The Case of Rural Vietnam
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that education, wage-paying employment, housing conditions, and domestic remittances reduce poverty and its intensity, while language barriers, farm size, and overseas remittances influence the poverty intensity but not the likelihood of poverty.
What_was_studied: The study examined the determinants of poverty intensity among rural ethnic minorities in Vietnam using binary and fractional logit models and data from three household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Poverty incidence reduction hinges on development programmes on credit and scholarships. Policymakers should prioritize these programmes in southeast Vietnam, where the likelihood and shortfall of poverty declined, and address language barriers to effectively target poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Clemens Breisinger; Xinshen Diao; Marie-Helen Collion; Pierre Rondot
Field: Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Oil depletion; Financial crisis; Human development (humanity); Population; Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth; Income distribution
Title: Impacts of the Triple Global Crisis on Growth and Poverty: The Case of Yemen
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The growth driven by oil in 2008 did not benefit the poor, and the financial crisis of 2009 raised the poverty rate to 42.8%, up from 34.8% in 2005/6.
What_was_studied: The impacts of the triple crisis on poverty in Yemen using a dynamic CGE model, focusing on the period from 2005/6 to 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize pro-poor policies and investments to address the persistent high poverty rates, particularly in rural areas where almost half the population lives in poverty.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; State (polity); Industrialisation; Economic growth; Civil society; Social Welfare; Scale (social sciences)
Keywords: Growth; Industrialisation; Rural Development; Poverty; Policy Growth; Poverty; Industrial Development; Rural Development; Policy
Title: Pathways to poverty reduction
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found four poverty-reduction pathways: (1) industrialization, (2) rural development, (3) social welfare, and (4) petroleum-generated employment. These pathways resulted in the bottom quintile experiencing an annual increase in income of at least 6% over at least a decade.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes 15 systematically selected national cases of demonstrated rapid poverty reduction, seeking insights into effective approaches to reducing poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and scale up these effective poverty reduction strategies, particularly in rural areas and through social welfare programs, to rapidly reduce poverty and improve economic growth.

Authors: Mathilde Maitrot; Geof Wood; Joe Devine
Field: Political science; Poverty; Structural violence; Resilience (network); Lived experience; Livelihood; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Title: Understanding resilience: lessons from lived experiences of extreme poverty in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that experiences of extreme poverty are not solely a function of systemic, class-based inequality but also intersect with idiosyncratic conditions such as household life cycles, dependency ratios, gender, and age balance, morbidity, ethnic discrimination, and social isolation; four key factors were identified as influencing deep poverty: ill health, intergenerational reproduction, high incidence of female-managed and -headed households, and a lack of income diversity and security.
What_was_studied: A large donor-funded programme in Bangladesh implemented multiple measures designed to graduate individuals and households out of extreme poverty, monitored through socioeconomic surveys, qualitative tracking methods, real-time assessments, and project evaluations, with a focus on the nature of extreme poverty and resilience among the extremely poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings provide fresh insights into policy responses to extreme poverty, suggesting a shift away from a narrow concern with graduation towards a wider focus on resilience, targeting interventions that support individuals (micro level), address the intergenerational reproduction of poverty (meso level), and engage with wider power structures that exploit and neglect poor people (macro level).

Field: Poverty; Welfare; Welfare state; Mainstream; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Sociology; Political science; Development economics; Economics; Politics; Law
Title: Family's roles as a welfare pillar: The case of older persons living in extreme poverty in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Family relationships play a central role in pursuing security and wellbeing for older persons, with reciprocal family systems being crucial in delivering welfare. The study found that all members of the family actively fulfill moral and material expectations to achieve collective goals.
What_was_studied: This article explores the role of families as welfare providers in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), using Bangladesh as a case study, specifically focusing on older persons living in extreme poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and scale up support for informal security regimes, such as family relationships, to improve wellbeing and security outcomes for older persons in LMICs. This can include funding community-based initiatives that strengthen reciprocal family systems and expand access to social protection programs.

Field: Seven Management and Planning Tools; Political science; Millennium Development Goals; Human development (humanity); Poverty reduction; Income group; National development; Adaptation strategies; Economic growth
Title: Millennium Development Goals: Impact on national strategies and spending
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: A high correlation is detected between the income group, PRSP status and ODA reliance of countries, and their propensity to incorporate MDGs in their planning instruments.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the post-2005 national development strategies of 50 countries from diverse income groups, geographical locations, human development tiers and official development assistance (ODA) levels to assess Millennium Development Goal (MDG) absorption into development planning.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Countries that have not integrated MDGs into their national plans were as likely to allocate government funds to social sectors as MDG aligners. This highlights the need for proactive allocation of resources towards poverty reduction and sustainable development efforts, prioritizing support for vulnerable populations and targeting localized adaptation strategies.

Authors: Peter Mollinga; Ruth Meinzen-Dick; Douglas J. Merrey
Field: Economics; Farm water; Poverty; Core business; Human development (humanity); Public administration; Economic growth; Bureaucracy; Sustainability; Developing country; Politics
Title: Politics, Plurality and Problemsheds: A Strategic Approach for Reform of Agricultural Water Resources Management
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that existing approaches to policy and institutional transformation have been inadequate in addressing the complex interplay of actors, institutions, and objectives involved in water management. Specifically, past efforts have relied too heavily on 'social engineering' approaches that fail to acknowledge the inherently political nature of the issue.
What_was_studied: Agricultural water management in developing countries between 2000 and 2018 was assessed to determine why past efforts at reform have achieved little, focusing on poverty alleviation, ecological sustainability, and democratic governance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the urgent need for more effective agricultural water management in developing countries, decision makers should prioritize a fundamentally different approach to policy and institutional transformation. This includes acknowledging the diversity of actors, institutions, and objectives involved and employing 'strategic action' approaches that proactively engage with these complexities.

Authors: Bernhard G. Gunter; Marc J. Cohen; Hans Lofgren
Field: Macro; Political science; Poverty; Optimism; Theme (narrative); Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Analysing Macro‐Poverty Linkages: An Overview
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a positive correlation between economic growth and poverty reduction, with every 1% increase in economic growth leading to a 0.5% decrease in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The analysis of macro-poverty linkages has emerged as an important but contentious area of national and international policy-making, focusing on the connection between macroeconomic policies and poverty reduction over a period of time (2015-2019) using data from various sources including household surveys and national accounts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize policies that promote sustainable economic growth, such as investments in education and infrastructure, in order to effectively reduce income poverty.

Field: Prejudice (legal term); Debt; Economics; Constructive; Face (sociological concept); Co operation; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Sustainable development
Title: Will ‘Emerging Donors’ Change the Face of International Co-operation?
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that DAC aid as a percentage of GDP is likely to decline only slowly from its historically high level, and at least some non-DAC donors are likely to adopt DAC approaches and norms. However, low-income countries have a wider range of financing options, with the risk of prejudicing their debt situation by borrowing on inappropriate terms, postponing necessary adjustments, and wasting resources on unproductive investments.
What_was_studied: This article examines the effect of donor aid on low-income countries' debt situations, using data from 2005 to 2015 and focusing on the DAC (Development Assistance Committee) member states and non-DAC donors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: DAC members should develop constructive dialogue with other bilateral donors based on the recognition that sustainable development and poverty reduction should be the core purpose of aid, and prioritize low-conditionality aid to avoid prejudicing debt situations and wasteful investments.

Authors: Welmah N. Mutengwe; Adrino Mazenda; Moreblessing Simawu
Field: Unemployment; Earnings; Labour law; Work (physics); Minimum wage; Wage labour; Harm; Labour economics; Livelihood; Flexibility (engineering); Labor relations; Economics; Political science; Business; Economic growth; Engineering; Law; Management; Geography; Accounting; Mechanical engineering; Archaeology; Agriculture
Title: Uber's digital labour platform and labour relations in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite numerous constitutional provisions governing DLP and DEL, Uber DLP workers in South Africa are considered independent contractors not entitled to employee benefits, making less than the national minimum wage after platform fees are deducted.
What_was_studied: The study examines the nature of employment through digital platforms in South Africa, specifically Uber's digital labour platform (DLP), to assess its potential to create decent work and the challenges it poses for the Department of Employment and Labour (DEL) in terms of labour law and regulation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: DEL should establish a balance between flexibility and labour standards, update labour laws based on reliable data, and ensure financial stability in the digital age while preserving workers' rights and providing the same protection at work for platform workers as other workers.

Field: Public economics; Business; Work (electrical); Public finance; Accountability; Public expenditure; Parliament; Poverty reduction; Function (engineering); Politics
Title: Managing Development for Results: A Role for Results‐oriented Public Expenditure Management
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Results-oriented approaches to public expenditure management can work in these environments, but not when there is excessive 'informality' and instability. With political will and a strong finance ministry, they have proved valuable tools in ensuring the coherent expansion of pro-poor programmes and their delivery through autonomous local governments.
What_was_studied: Seven countries with mediocre discipline in budget and public finance management and a degree of uncertainty caused by macroeconomic instability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Low-income countries should prioritize strengthening finance ministries and implementing results-oriented approaches to public expenditure management to improve the effectiveness of poverty reduction strategies and secure 'aid for results' from donors.

Field: Agriculture; Business; Natural resource economics; Social protection; Crop insurance; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Climate Variability and the Role of Access to Crop Insurance as a Social‐Protection Measure: Insights from India
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that lack of awareness and complicated agricultural insurance processes deter small and marginal farmers from using crop insurance, but it may help farmers at the household level. Moreover, present adaptation practices may have long-term negative consequences.
What_was_studied: A primary survey conducted in India among small and marginal farmers to determine the efficacy of crop insurance as an adaptation strategy to climate change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective crop insurance schemes that prioritize the needs of small and marginal farmers in India and other developing countries, while also addressing the long-term negative consequences of present adaptation practices.

Field: Environmental economics; Psychology; Accountability; Value (economics); Quality (business); Low income
Title: Testing the feasibility of a value‐added model of school quality in a low‐income country
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty
What_was_found: The model was found to be robust to different empirical specifications and control variables, with potential for providing a clearer signal about learning outcomes in different schools at low cost.
What_was_studied: The study adapted value-added models (VAMS) to the Ugandan context to measure secondary school quality, accounting for student socioeconomic status and testing its robustness using official test score data from Uganda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize implementing this approach in a wide range of low-income countries with similar testing regimes to improve education quality and account for student socioeconomic status, providing parents and teachers with a clearer signal about school performance.

Authors: R. Hope; M. Edmunds; R. McDonnell; M. Rouse; D. Johnstone; E. Kistin; L.F. Vincent
Field: Scarcity; Economics; Poverty; Power (social and political); Human Development Report; Development economics; Water scarcity
Title: Human Development Report 2006: Beyond Scarcity: Power, Poverty and the Global Water Crisis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The Human Development Report 2006 found that power imbalances and unequal access to resources are a major cause of poverty and the global water crisis. Does Foreign Aid Really Work? found that foreign aid can have positive effects on development, but its impact is often limited by political and economic factors. Human Security and the UN: A Critical History examined the role of human security in international relations and found that it has become a dominant discourse in recent years.
What_was_studied: These books reviewed in this article cover various aspects of development, including food security, gender and poverty, income poverty, sustainable development and the role of foreign aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings suggest that addressing power imbalances and ensuring equal access to resources is crucial for reducing poverty and achieving sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize these issues when designing development programs and allocate sufficient funding to support them.

Field: Politics; Cash transfers; Ideology; Government (linguistics); Social policy; Civil society; Presidential system; Cash; Political science; Subsidy; Social protection; Foreign policy; Public administration; Political economy; Economic growth; Economics; Finance; Law; Linguistics; Philosophy
Title: International donors, domestic politics, and the expansion of social cash transfers in Malawi
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Donors were unable to persuade Bingu wa Mutharika's government to adopt social cash transfers, but succeeded with Joyce Banda's administration within two months of her being in office, highlighting the importance of domestic politics and engagement with local politics for successful policy reforms.
What_was_studied: International donors piloted social cash transfers in Africa in the 2000s, with a focus on Malawi and its political context, using a multiple streams framework to trace policy-making for social cash transfers over six years, covering the administrations of two presidents: Bingu wa Mutharika and Joyce Banda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To institutionalize social cash transfers nationally, donors should prioritize engaging with local politics and tailoring their approaches to each country's unique political context.

Field: Nutrient; Business; Micronutrient; Production (economics); Food consumption; Agricultural science; Food systems
Title: Mapping the nutrient adequacy of farm production and food consumption to target policy in Uganda
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that sufficient calories and protein are generally available from farm production, purchases, and transfers, but alarming deficits can be seen in the supply of calcium, iron, and zinc as well as vitamins A and B12. Deficits are especially marked in the North East sub-region.
What_was_studied: This article quantifies nutrient production and consumption by sub-region in Uganda to identify the magnitude and location of gaps left by farm households' own production, market purchases, and food transfers relative to household nutrient requirements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest the need for targeted interventions to increase the availability of calcium, iron, and zinc, as well as vitamins A and B12. Policymakers should prioritize the production and marketing of these nutrient-dense foods in the North East sub-region to address hidden hunger.

Field: Commercial policy; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Poverty; Tariff; Market access; Household income; Free trade; International free trade agreement
Title: Can Trade Help Poor People? The Role of Trade, Trade Policy and Market Access in Tanzania
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that increasing market access for Tanzanian exports could reduce national poverty by up to 5.6% and increase household income by up to 21.5%. Simulation scenarios that swap some poor households into trade-related sectors such as cash cropping or tourism suggest even greater potential gains.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the poverty-reducing effects of trade in Tanzania, using household data and simulated policy changes to project national poverty reductions of up to 5.6% and household income increases of up to 21.5%. The analysis focuses on the potential of trade, trade policy, and market access to reduce poverty among agricultural households, who make up 81% of the poor and account for 88% of the export bundle in Tanzania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize market access and trade agreements to maximize the poverty-reducing effects of trade in Tanzania, particularly in rural areas where most of the poor work in agriculture. By scaling up successful trade initiatives and expanding market access, governments can help reduce chronic poverty, promote financial inclusion, and increase income poverty reduction among agricultural households.

Field: Poverty; Political science; Human rights; Indigenous; International development; Developing country; Democracy; Politics; Economic growth; Economics; Development economics; Law; Ecology; Biology
Title: Book Reviews
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The book provides insights on various issues related to poverty reduction, sustainable development, trade, and global governance.
