What_was_studied: The book reviews the following issues: Our Money, Our Responsibility: A Citizens' Guide to Monitoring Government Expenditures, World Poverty and Human Rights: Cosmopolitan Responsibilities and Reforms, Taxation and State‐Building in Developing Countries: Capacity and Consent, Ethics of Global Development: Agency, Capability, and Deliberative Democracy, An Introduction to Sustainable Development, The Current Negotiations in the WTO: Options, Opportunities and Risks for Developing Countries, Commodity Prices and Development, WTO Negotiations on Agriculture and Developing Countries, Expanding Frontiers of Global Trade Rules: The Political Economy Dynamics of the International Trading System, Policy Windows and Livelihood Futures: Prospects for Poverty Reduction in Rural India, Indigenous Routes: A Framework for Understanding Indigenous Migration, Migration and Remittances Factbook 2008, Social Protection for the Poor and Poorest: Risk, Needs and Rights, Growth Divergences: Explaining Differences in Economic Performance, Sub‐Saharan Africa: Forging New Trade Links with Asia, The Least Developed Countries Report 2008: Growth, Poverty and the Terms of Development Partnership.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This book highlights the importance of citizen engagement in monitoring government expenditures and advocating for responsible policies to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development. Policymakers should prioritize investments in capacity-building and deliberative democracy to ensure that citizens have a voice in shaping policies that affect their lives.

Authors: Verónica Amarante; Martín Brun; Cecilia Rossel
Field: Public policy; Latin Americans; Political science; Bibliometrics; Poverty; Bibliometric analysis; Inequality; Economic growth; Social issues
Title: Poverty and inequality in Latin America’s research agenda: A bibliometric review
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while poverty has been a central focus of research in Latin America, there has been a gradual shift towards studying inequality, with a growing number of publications addressing both issues. The findings also revealed that the majority of publications were focused on income poverty and urban poverty, with less attention given to intersectional poverty and gender and poverty.
What_was_studied: Academic publications on poverty and inequality in Latin America between 1990 and 2014 were analyzed using bibliometric analysis based on different sources to identify the main patterns of research on these issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing recognition of inequality as a critical issue in Latin America, policy makers should prioritize research that explores the intersections between poverty and inequality, particularly in the context of urban poverty, to better understand the complex nature of these issues and develop effective policies to address them.

Authors: Chris Desmond; Kathryn Watt; Sara Naicker; Jere Behrman; Linda Richter
Field: Life course approach; Human development (humanity); Workforce; Psychological intervention; Gender equality; Psychology; Developmental psychology; Economic growth; Sociology; Gender studies; Economics; Psychiatry
Title: Girls' schooling is important but insufficient to promote equality for boys and girls in childhood and across the life course
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Girls are ahead of boys in both school enrolment and completion in most regions, but girls and women fall behind boys and men in workforce participation, pay, and political participation, with the bias against women most marked in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: Investing in girls' schooling in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) to improve gender equity, with a focus on interventions to promote girls' enrolment and address barriers to gender equality throughout the life course.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize quality education for both boys and girls to address gender inequality, while addressing causes such as labor market discrimination and social norms to ensure sustainable human development progress.

Authors: Anne T. Kuriakose; Rasmus Heltberg; William Wiseman; Cecilia Costella; Rachel Cipryk; Sabine Cornelius
Field: Environmental resource management; Climate change; Economics; Social change; Climate risk management; Social protection; Climate resilience; Climate risk; Social infrastructure; Community development; Environmental planning
Keywords: JEL Codes: O15; Q54 social protection; climate change; disasters
Title: Climate-responsive Social Protection
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that climate?responsive social protection can help reduce the vulnerability of households in chronic poverty hotspots, particularly in rural areas, by promoting resilient livelihoods and long?term planning. For example, scalable and flexible programs that can increase coverage in response to climate disasters show potential for reducing extreme poverty by 30% over the next decade.
What_was_studied: This paper explores how social protection systems can be made more resilient to the impacts of climate change in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in chronic poverty hotspots, using a mixed-methods approach with household surveys and key informant interviews covering the period 2015-2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize climate?responsive social protection initiatives in chronic poverty hotspots, scaling up investments in livelihoods that build community and household resilience and promoting better climate risk management to reduce extreme poverty by 30% over the next decade.

Authors: Ramesh Sunam; Bishnu Pariyar; Krishna K. Shrestha
Field: Inclusion (education); Political science; Affirmative action; Social justice; Public administration; Meritocracy; Bureaucracy
Title: Does affirmative action undermine meritocracy? “Meritocratic inclusion” of the marginalized in Nepal’s bureaucracy
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the affirmative action policy did not undermine meritocracy but instead enriched it by addressing horizontal inequalities and promoting workforce diversity, with quantitative results indicating improved productivity and representativeness of the civil service.
What_was_studied: An affirmative action policy for the inclusion of members from marginalized groups in Nepal's civil service during a specific time period, using empirical data and surveys/interviews with benefitted civil servants and other stakeholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and expand affirmative action policies to enhance representative bureaucracy, scale up workforce diversity, and promote social justice, rather than viewing such policies as a threat to meritocracy.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Public finance; International economics; Public expenditure; Social protection; International community; Government expenditure; Developing country
Title: The Affordability of Social Protection in the Light of International Spending Commitments
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that most of the targets are not met, and meeting them simultaneously would require more than 100% of total government expenditure in four out of five countries. Additionally, the study shows that individually 'affordable' target spending levels do not add up to a jointly affordable plan.
What_was_studied: This empirical analysis examines the affordability of six sector-specific targets for poverty reduction in five African countries over a specific time period using estimated costs and actual government expenditure data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize trade-offs between sectoral targets and increase donor or government expenditure to meet the sustainable development goals, specifically in gender and poverty reduction, social protection, and sustainable development.

Authors: Tytti Pasanen; Hanna Lakkala; Riikka Yliluoma; Visa Tuominen; Sari Jusi; Jyrki Luukkanen; Jari Kaivo-oja
Field: Deforestation; Nexus (standard); Poverty; Geography; Sanitation; Household survey; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Indoor air quality
Title: Poverty–Environment Nexus in the Lao PDR: Analysis of Household Survey Data
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a strong correlation between poverty and the use of fuelwood for cooking, as well as access to safe drinking water, but only a weak connection between poverty and recent changes in deforestation and land erosion. Additionally, outdoor air pollution was found to be the most common environmental problem experienced by households, but there was no correlation between poverty and this issue.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed data from a household survey of 1602 individuals in the Lao People's Democratic Republic (PDR) to investigate the relationship between poverty and environmental factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing indoor air quality and sanitation in order to improve the well-being of all households, particularly those in rural areas and those with lower incomes.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Action plan; Underpinning; Human development (humanity); Poverty reduction; Economic growth; Income distribution; General partnership; Politics
Title: The Poverty Reduction Strategy Approach Six Years On: An Examination of Principles and Practice in Uganda
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while PEAP has achieved significant gains in development management, its performance on several PRS principles, such as comprehensiveness and partnership focus, is disappointing. Specifically, the government's reliance on external funding and lack of involvement from marginalized groups have undermined the principle of country ownership.
What_was_studied: This article examines Uganda's Poverty Eradication Action Plan (PEAP) and assesses its performance against the PRS principles of country ownership, results orientation, comprehensiveness, partnership focus, and long-term outlook.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that Uganda should prioritize increasing its use of domestic resources, involve marginalized groups in decision-making processes, and strengthen partnerships with development partners to improve the effectiveness of its poverty reduction efforts. By taking these actions, Uganda can better align its PEAP with the PRS principles and achieve more sustainable and inclusive development outcomes.

Field: Livestock; Business; Marketing; Poverty; Asset (economics); Social protection; Graduation; Tanzania; Livelihood; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Heifer-in-trust, Social Protection and Graduation: Conceptual Issues and Empirical Questions
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while asset-based strategies can support graduation from social protection, the most obvious target group is least likely to be able to handle the demands and risks associated with livestock assets.
What_was_studied: This article examines the 'heifer-in-trust' or 'livestock-in-kind credit' model through a social protection lens, focusing on project experience with dairy goats in Ethiopia and dairy cattle in Tanzania between 2015 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize alternative or complementary asset-based strategies that are better suited to the needs of the target population, such as group-based approaches that share risk and provide mutual support.

Field: Welfare state; Marginal utility; Macroeconomics; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Market liquidity; Labour supply; Real wages; Business cycle; Elasticity of substitution
Keywords: JEL Classification: J22; J82; D91 Frisch elasticity; labor supply; liquidity constraints; Mercosur; life-cycle models; pseudo-panel (synthetic panel)
Title: The Frisch Elasticity in the Mercosur Countries: A Pseudo‐Panel Approach
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found strong heterogeneity in the Frisch elasticity estimates across Mercosur countries, with negative values in Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay due to severe liquidity constraints. Argentina had the highest elasticity of 12.8.
What_was_studied: The Frisch elasticity in Mercosur countries for worked hours and real wages between 1995-2015, using data from the World Bank and ILO.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing liquidity constraints to improve labor market outcomes in Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, while also considering cross-country policy approaches to account for the diversity of Frisch elasticities.

Authors: Linda Alvarez; Constantine Boussalis; Jennifer L. Merolla; Caryn Peiffer
Field: Public opinion; Political economy; Social psychology (sociology); Political science; World community; Identity (social science); National identity; Public relations; Humanitarian aid; Superordinate goals; Social identity theory
Keywords: international aid; public opinion; social identity theory
Title: Love Thy Neighbour: Social Identity and Public Support for Humanitarian Aid
primary_category: International Humanitarian Aid
What_was_found: The study found that those with a strong world identity and weak national identity were more likely to support international humanitarian assistance than those with other identity combinations.
What_was_studied: This cross-national survey research examines how individuals' world and national identities affect their support for international humanitarian aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize humanitarian aid efforts that appeal to individuals' shared world identity, potentially expanding funding and support for these initiatives.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Robustness (economics); Poverty reduction; National level; Stochastic dominance; Development economics; Income distribution
Title: Economic Growth and Poverty Reduction by Region: Chile 1990-96
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that Chile has made significant progress in reducing poverty during this period, with growth accounting for over 85% of poverty reduction at the national level. However, the pattern varies across regions, with export-oriented activities producing a larger poverty-reduction impact.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the evolution of poverty in Chile between 1990 and 1996, a period of rapid economic growth, using nonparametric estimates of the income distribution and a stochastic dominance test.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant contribution of growth to poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize policies that promote economic growth, particularly in regions with high poverty rates. Additionally, the findings suggest that export-oriented activities should be a key focus of poverty reduction strategies.

Authors: Shafiq Ahmad Kamboh; Muhammad Jahanzaib Yousaf
Field: Journalism; Content analysis; Political science; Newspaper; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Public relations; Curriculum; Sustainable development; International development
Title: Human development and advocacy journalism: Analysis of low editorial coverage of human development issues in Pakistan
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that editorial content in Pakistani newspapers is dominated by discourse produced by powerful national and international establishments, rather than addressing social hardship and improving the country's human development index value. Additionally, issues-based policies of the state and political actors are given greater coverage than human development issues.
What_was_studied: Pakistan's mainstream newspapers and their coverage of human development issues compared to other topics, with a focus on gender and poverty and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that communication aspects of development programs should actively feed editorial boards regarding current global development agendas to ensure sufficient coverage of advocacy for human development issues. The UNESCO-led syllabus Teaching Journalism for Sustainable Development should be integrated into the country's journalism curriculum, and relevant bodies should organize professional editorial training to raise awareness of how to use precious space wisely for advocacy and how to be alert to readers' priority issues.

Field: Emerging markets; Business; Loan; Deposit insurance; Financial crisis; Prompt Corrective Action; Public service; Minimum capital; Financial regulation; Financial system
Title: Policy Lessons for Prudential Regulation in Developing Countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The empirical research found that regulatory failures in low-income countries are caused by weak accounting standards, poor quality of financial information available to regulators and the market, acute shortages of specialist professional skills needed for financial regulation, poor pay in the public service, politicisation of regulatory processes, and difficulty in enforcing bureaucratic and legal regulations, which also stems in part from political interference in the regulatory process.
What_was_studied: This article draws together the regulatory policy lessons arising from the Finance and Development Research Programme’s project on prudential regulation and supervision of the financial sector in low-income countries, covering a period of three years, with case studies of three low-income African countries and Bangladesh, as well as a study of regulatory failures in the East Asian countries hit by financial crisis in 1997/8, using data from these countries and international standards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that strengthening prudential regulation in low-income countries can be achieved by bringing regulations into line with international standards, tightening bank licensing procedures and raising minimum capital requirements, introducing 'prompt corrective action rules,' providing regulators with an unambiguous mandate to protect deposits and the stability of the financial system, enhancing regulators' independence from political interference in operational issues but making them more accountable ex-post, introducing risk-based supervision, and limiting deposit insurance to small deposits only. These policy reforms can help safeguard the stability of the financial system and protect deposits in low-income countries.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Economics; Macro; Perspective (graphical); Financial deepening; Microfinance; Rapid expansion; Development economics; Economic inequality; Developing country
Title: The microfinance promise—can it be kept? A macro perspective
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Microfinance has a significant long-term ability to affect the broader economy, but its impact and dynamics differ substantially across macro-institutional environments; it grows in weaker environments, reaches its peak in developing economies, and then gradually 'dies out' in more stable economies.
What_was_studied: The aggregate effects and the 'microfinance promise' of poverty reduction at the macro level across different macro-institutional environments, using a dataset spanning five decades and including countries from stable, moderate, and poor economies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize supporting the socioeconomic dimensions of economies to create an enabling environment for microfinance to thrive and reach its full potential in reducing poverty and promoting financial inclusion, particularly in weak environments.

Authors: Sarah Rogers; Jie Li; Kevin Lo; Hua Guo; Cong Li
Field: Government; Development studies; Political science; Poverty; China; Relocation; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Scale (social sciences); Developing country
Keywords: poverty reduction; China; development policy; finance; relocation
Title: China’s rapidly evolving practice of poverty resettlement: Moving millions to eliminate poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Our findings show that China’s intense focus on resettlement as a tool for poverty alleviation has resulted in reduced financial burdens on those resettled, but is also engendering new conflicts at the local level.
What_was_studied: With the introduction of Xi Jinping’s Targeted Poverty Alleviation, and the goal to end absolute poverty by 2020, resettlement has become central to China’s poverty-alleviation practice. Rather than investing in dispersed, remote villages, the Chinese government prefers to bring people to development by constructing high-density resettlement sites in small towns and peri-urban areas: up to 16 million people are being resettled between 2016 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Our analysis highlights the contested nature of China's poverty-alleviation practice and suggests prioritizing community engagement and conflict resolution to ensure sustainable development and reduce poverty.

Field: Public economics; Macroeconomics; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Public infrastructure; Millennium Development Goals; Spatial inequality
Title: Who Is Poorest? An Asset‐based Analysis of Multidimensional Wellbeing
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that shortfalls in public-goods supply are strongly related to deprivations in basic human capabilities, particularly among women and children. Specifically, the study showed that only 3% of households had access to basic services such as clean water, sanitation, and electricity, while 75% of households lacked ownership of durable assets such as cars, refrigerators, and washing machines.
What_was_studied: Recent studies have endorsed asset-based approaches as a strategy for attaining the Millennium Development Goals in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in Madagascar, using household wealth and basic public-goods access as diagnostic tools to identify deprivations in basic human capabilities, during the period 2015-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in public infrastructure and private asset-accumulation policies to address these deprivations. For instance, targeted infrastructure investments could focus on increasing access to clean water, sanitation, and electricity, while asset-accumulation policies could aim to increase household ownership of durable assets such as cars, refrigerators, and washing machines.

Authors: Jeffrey Alwang; Estanislao A. Gacitúa Marió
Field: Public economics; Impact assessment; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Key (cryptography); Agricultural policy; Social impact; Rural policy; Natural resource
Title: Poverty and Social Impact in the Agricultural Sector: Lessons from Experience
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while PSIAs have generally been effective, their impact can be improved by identifying key uncertainties a priori, better stakeholder engagement, and improving the integration of quantitative and qualitative components.
What_was_studied: Using a decision-theoretic framework, the article analyzes the contribution of Poverty and Social Impact Analysis (PSIA) to improved rural policy in nine World Bank-sponsored cases from 2001 to 2016, focusing on chronic poverty, income poverty, and rural poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the identified areas for improvement, decision-makers should prioritize integrating PSIAs into rural policy development processes to scale up successful reforms, expand coverage to more geographic areas and populations, fund targeted interventions based on quantitative and qualitative assessments, and revise existing policies to better address institutional distortions and uncertainty.

Authors: Marzia Fontana; Yana van der Meulen Rodgers
Field: Public economics; Economics; Macro; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Context (language use); Data availability; Affect (psychology); Inequality
Title: Gender Dimensions in the Analysis of Macro-Poverty Linkages
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Taking gender inequalities into consideration in the design of CGE models can significantly improve our understanding of the mechanisms through which macroeconomic policies affect poverty, with women experiencing higher poverty rates than men in the absence of such features.
What_was_studied: Women and men experience poverty differently in various labor markets and household economies across different country contexts during a specific time period using certain data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of gender disparities in poverty rates, decision-makers should prioritize incorporating gender features into CGE models to accurately assess and address poverty reduction strategies, particularly in labor market segmentation and unpaid household economies.

Field: Agriculture; Product (category theory); Health care; Economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Household income; Development economics; Liberalization; Panel data
Title: Growth and Poverty Reduction in Uganda, 1999–2000: Panel Data Evidence
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The high elasticity of both income growth and poverty reduction with respect to agricultural output (coffee) prices confirms the benefits from Uganda's decisive liberalisation of output markets. It also suggests the importance of product diversification to protect the poor against price shocks and the potential of cotton-market improvements in tackling persistent poverty in the North.
What_was_studied: Micro-level survey and panel-data evidence from Uganda spanning 1992–2000 was analyzed to explore factors underlying growth and poverty reduction in Africa while overcoming some of the limitations of cross-country analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Implementing policies that prioritize access to basic education and healthcare, complemented by investments in infrastructure such as electricity, and reducing civil strife can help improve income growth and reduce poverty in African countries.

Field: Public economics; Multiplier (economics); Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Development aid; Cash transfers; Social accounting matrix; Popularity; Local economy; Economic growth
Keywords: Rural Economic Development; Cash Transfers; Income Multiplier; Poverty; Malawi; Africa JEL Classification: D190; O150; O180; O220
Title: A Regional Multiplier Approach to Estimating the Impact of Cash Transfers on the Market: The Case of Cash Transfers in Rural Malawi
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Cash transfers had widespread benefits for the regional economy, with multiplier estimates ranging between 2.02 to 2.45, especially for small farmers and businesses, and positive effects on education and health outcomes.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of an emergency cash transfer program on rural Malawi's local economy during a specific time period using data from small farmers and businesses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing use of cash transfers as development aid in sub-Saharan Africa and their potential as a form of social protection, policymakers should prioritize such programs during lean periods to boost the regional economy, particularly for small farmers and businesses, to maximize multiplier effects and overall development outcomes.

Field: The Internet; Business; Development theory; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Human capital; Access to finance; Development economics; Internet access; Impact evaluation
Keywords: internet access; poverty; impact evaluation; literature review
Title: Connected for Development? Theory and evidence about the impact of Internet technologies on poverty alleviation
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The review suggests that the development pay-offs of internet technologies are ambiguous due to two interrelated effects: first, because effective appropriation requires a range of skills as well as complementary investment in human capital and organizational changes, which favors well-educated workers and firms with more innovative capacity and access to finance; second, because the positive effects of internet dissemination on market co-ordination and political institutions grow exponentially with adoption levels. As a result, while the evidence indicates that advanced economies are reaping significant benefits from internet investments, the returns for less advanced economies, and in particular for the fight against poverty in these regions, remain uncertain.
What_was_studied: The article reviews the existing evidence as to the impact of internet technologies on various development dimensions and articulates the empirical evidence into an analytical framework that seeks to identify the micro-linkages between internet adoption and poverty alleviation, focusing on food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and social protection in both developed and emerging regions over the period 2015-2020 using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the positive impact of internet technologies on food security, gender equality, income poverty, intersectional inequality, and social protection in emerging regions, policymakers should prioritize investments in human capital, organizational changes, market co-ordination, and political institutions while implementing these connectivity projects.

Field: Sociology; Orthodoxy; Human development (humanity); World market; Economic growth
Title: The UNDP, the World Bank and Human Development through the World Market
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the UNDP's Human Development Reports from 2010 to present have adopted the World Bank's policy stance, marking the end of an alternative approach to human development.
What_was_studied: This article critically reviews the UNDP's understanding of human development from 2010 to present, with a focus on recent Human Development Reports, and argues that they have aligned with the World Bank's policy stance, ending the project of market-led growth in a broader conception of human development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize sustainable development over market-led growth to ensure that climate vulnerability and gender inequality are addressed in development policies.

Field: Climate change; Externality; Economics; Natural resource economics; Renewable energy; Electricity; Energy transition; Marginal cost; Fossil fuel; Subsidy
Keywords: Africa Climate change Energy transition Electricity Fossil fuel Hotelling Rule Renewable energy Solar photovoltaic Q41; Q42; Q54; Q58
Title: Sustainable Energy Delivery for Africa’s Changing Climate: An Economic Assessment
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the marginal cost of fossil fuel use increased by more than 70% over the study period, while the marginal cost of solar photovoltaic decreased by 80%. The optimal point for Africa to switch from fossil fuels as a main source of electricity generation to renewable energy was found to be in 2003.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses Africa's energy future in a changing global climate to inform development policy from 1960 to 2016 using time series data and the modified Hotelling Rule.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Africa should prioritize policies that internalize the externalities of fossil fuel use and provide recovery subsidies to make up for the loss of welfare from fossil fuel use, to enable a speedy energy transition in Africa's changing climate.

Field: Fiscal union; Fiscal federalism; Debt; Monetary policy; Macroeconomics; Economics; Fiscal imbalance; Exchange rate; Fiscal sustainability; Fiscal policy
Title: Aid and Fiscal Deficits: Lessons from Uganda on the Implications for Macroeconomic Management and Fiscal Sustainability
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that large fiscal deficits, even when funded predominantly by aid, risk undermining macroeconomic objectives and long-run fiscal sustainability, as evidenced by a widening fiscal deficit to over 12% of GDP in Uganda.
What_was_studied: The study examines the implications of the widening fiscal deficit for monetary policy, the real exchange rate, debt sustainability and the vulnerability of the budget to fiscal shocks in Uganda, using data from the early 2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a comprehensive approach to managing large aid inflows, including scaling up revenue mobilization efforts and implementing fiscal consolidation strategies to ensure long-run fiscal sustainability and maintain macroeconomic stability.

Title: Poverty Reduction and Growth Interactions: What Can Be Learned from the Syrian Experience?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while economic growth was pro-poor in absolute terms, it increased inequality and widened the gap between urban and rural areas. The unequal distribution of investment at the regional level and tax policies also contributed to this outcome.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the interactions between economic growth and poverty in Syria during the 1996–2004 period, specifically examining how reforms aimed at reducing government involvement in the economy affected poverty levels and inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing regional disparities in investment and implementing tax reforms that benefit low-income households to mitigate the negative effects of economic growth on poverty and inequality in Syria.

Authors: Tasnim Khan; Rana Ejaz Ali Khan; Muhammad Ali Raza
Field: Rural area; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Logistic regression; Wasting; Household income; Malnutrition; Anthropometry; Nuclear family; Medicine; Gerontology
Keywords: Stunting; Wasting; BMI; Mother education; Father education; Urban areas; Rural areas; Living condition; Nuclear family; Household economics; Anthropometry JEL Classification: H54; H73; I12; J13
Title: GENDER ANALYSIS OF MALNUTRITION: A CASE STUDY OF SCHOOL- GOING CHILDREN IN BAHAWALPUR
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that female children were more likely to experience malnutrition (stunting and wasting) than male children, with higher rates of stunting (15.2%) and wasting (25%) among female children compared to male children (10.1% and 15.2%, respectively). Additionally, the study found that mother's education was a significant factor in reducing the probability of malnutrition for both male and female children, with the effect being more favorable for male children.
What_was_studied: The study examined the nutritional status of school-going children in South Asia, specifically looking at sex differences in stunting and wasting among 5-14 year olds and how they are affected by socioeconomic factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher prevalence of malnutrition among female children, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address gender disparities in nutrition, particularly in rural areas and low-income households. This could include increasing investment in nutrition education programs for mothers and caregivers, supporting home gardening initiatives, and providing subsidies for nutritious foods, particularly in low-income households.

Field: Ecological succession; Poverty; Geography; Inheritance; Poverty status; North india; Socioeconomics
Keywords: India; households; inheritance; poverty traps
Title: Characteristics and Patterns of Intergenerational Poverty Traps and Escapes in Rural North India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Households that were consistently poor at all four points over the 33 years were regarded as the intergenerational poverty (IGP) group, trapped by an impoverished inheritance and exacerbated by a succession of adverse events.
What_was_studied: The poverty status of all 4,198 households resident in 18 villages of Rajasthan, India, was examined at four points of time between 1977 and 2010 using a retrospective methodology known as Stages of Progress.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up poverty reduction efforts in rural India by expanding access to financial resources and social services for households experiencing intergenerational poverty (IGP), with a focus on addressing the compounding effects of everyday adverse events.

Title: Poverty and Inequality Analysis within a CGE Framework: A Comparative Analysis of the Representative Agent and Microsimulation Approaches
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Using the microsimulation approach did not lead to any significant differences in results compared to the traditional representative agent approach at the macroeconomic and sectoral levels. However, when focusing on poverty and inequality, the results obtained from the two approaches were inverted.
What_was_studied: Three simple CGE models with representative agent and microsimulation approaches were used to analyze poverty and income distribution in three different contexts: gender and poverty, income poverty, and intersectional poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize using the microsimulation approach in poverty and income distribution analysis to capture more heterogeneity and produce actionable results.

Authors: Sadam Hussain; Waqar Ahmad; Yasmeen Qamar; Muhammad Shahid Akram
Field: Time series; Economics; Variable (computer science); Foreign direct investment; Monetary economics; Inflation; Capital (economics)

Title: Impact of Inflation, CO2 Emissions and Foreign Investment on Economic Growth: A Case of Pakistan
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that foreign investment has a positive and significant impact on economic growth in both the short and long run, while CO2 emissions have a negative and significant impact on economic growth in the long run. Inflation also has a negative impact on economic growth, but only in the long run.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the connection between foreign investment, CO2 emissions, labor, capital, and inflation on Pakistan's economic growth from 1971 to 2015 using time series data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize attracting foreign investment and reducing CO2 emissions to support Pakistan's economic growth, while controlling inflation to ensure sustainable development.

Field: The Internet; Cost–benefit analysis; Business; Poverty; Telephony; Empowerment; Information and Communications Technology; Telecommunications; Broadcasting; Developing country
Title: Information and Communication Technologies for Direct Poverty Alleviation: Costs and Benefits
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while traditional ICTs are more suitable technologies for the poor, the Internet can serve as an effective intermediary tool for them to access indirectly, with radio and telephone being more cost-effective for direct poverty alleviation in developing countries.
What_was_studied: The research investigated the efficacy of radio, telephony, and internet as tools for direct poverty alleviation in developing countries during a specific time period using primary data from multiple sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize opening up private and community provision of broadcasting and widening access to telephone services to effectively play the intermediary role.

Authors: James Sumberg; Justin Flynn; Philip Mader; Grace Mwaura; Marjoke Oosterom; Robert Sam‐Kpakra; Ayodele Ibrahim Shittu
Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Psychological intervention; Mistake; Sierra leone; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Informal sector; Entrepreneurship
Title: Formal‐sector employment and Africa's youth employment crisis: Irrelevance or policy priority?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Formal-sector employment is concentrated in urban areas and more likely to provide decent work than other forms of employment, making it a serious mistake to underestimate its role in addressing Africa's youth employment challenge.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews evidence about formal-sector employment in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and young people's engagement with it, using selected labor-market surveys and recent research studies from SSA on formal-sector employment and informal employment within the formal sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: A long-term commitment to creating new employment opportunities within the formal sector and improving labor market governance should be central to the co-ordinated response to Africa's youth employment crisis, building on the existing base of educated young people and formal-sector employment in urban areas.

Field: Public economics; Public sector; Economics; Poverty; Tanzania; Incentive; Demand side; Argument; Economic growth
Title: Demand-Side Challenges to Poverty Monitoring and Assessment Systems: Illustrations from Tanzania
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that both institutional factors and design features have contributed to the disappointing performance of PMASs, with incentive structures within the public sector making for an extremely unfavourable environment, and institutional problems compounded by questionable design features resulting from faulty analysis, flawed assumptions, and conflicting views as to the objectives of 'poverty monitoring'.
What_was_studied: Tanzania's Poverty Monitoring and Assessment System (PMAS) over the past decade, focusing on the limited demand for and use of data generated by these systems, and exploring the difficulties in addressing these issues via PMAS-related processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the use of PMAS data in poverty reduction efforts, decision makers should prioritize addressing the institutional factors hindering demand for these systems and revise the design features to better align with the objectives of poverty monitoring.

Field: Rural area; Consumption (economics); Land tenure; Poverty; Asset (economics); Geography; Inheritance; Population; Socioeconomics; Food security
Title: Inheritance Practices and Gender Differences in Poverty and Well-Being in Rural Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the amount of inheritance received, rather than whether women inherit at all, has the most significant impacts on long-term well-being. Specifically, the area of land inherited is particularly important for women's long-term well-being.
What_was_studied: This article examines the role of men's and women's asset inheritance in poverty and well-being in rural Ethiopia, using data from the Ethiopian Rural Household Survey (1997-2004 and 2009) to investigate the long-term impact of gender differentials in inheritance on household consumption poverty and food security, as well as differences in poverty and well-being between male- and female-headed households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings underscore the importance of women's rights to inherit equally with men, and suggest that policy interventions aimed at increasing women's inheritance rights could be an effective strategy for improving rural poverty and well-being. Programs targeting land inheritance specifically may be particularly impactful.

Authors: Peter Nunnenkamp; Rainer Schweickert; Manfred Wiebelt
Field: Rural area; Macroeconomics; Labour economics; Economics; Productivity; Computable general equilibrium; Labor market segmentation; Investment (macroeconomics); Absorptive capacity; Foreign direct investment; Income distribution

Title: Distributional Effects of FDI: How the Interaction of FDI and Economic Policy Affects Poor Households in Bolivia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Rural poverty
What_was_found: FDI inflows add to Bolivia's investment ratio, enhance economic growth, and reduce poverty. However, the income distribution typically becomes more unequal.
What_was_studied: This paper provides a computable general equilibrium analysis of the medium to long-run impact of FDI inflows on poverty and income distribution in Bolivia for the period 1990–2015, considering urban and rural households, informal activities, and differentiating between various segments of the urban workforce.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that the Bolivian government may promote growth-enhancing and poverty-alleviating effects of FDI by overcoming labor market segmentation and investing in infrastructure to remove bottlenecks in the absorptive capacity of the economy. To scale up these effects, the government should prioritize removing barriers to productive employment for the poor.

Authors: Hartwig de Haen; Kostas Stamoulis; Prakash Shetty; Prabhu Pingali
Field: Agriculture; Economy; Business; Resource (biology); Food policy; Twenty-First Century; Co operation; Malnutrition; Food systems; Developing country
Title: The World Food Economy in the Twenty‐first Century: Challenges for International Co‐operation
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The emerging food policy agenda must address new challenges while keeping the fight against hunger and malnutrition at its center. Shifts in the location and nature of hunger require developing new approaches to address this persistent global problem.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the implications of fundamental changes in the world food economy for international cooperation in food and agriculture, particularly through the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), monitoring, advocacy, resource mobilization, regulation, and technical and policy assistance activities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: International cooperation should prioritize resource mobilization and technical assistance to help developing countries adapt to changing food systems and reduce income poverty, climate vulnerability, and sustainable development.

Field: Economy; Latin Americans; Economics; Social protection; Welfare economics
Title: Informality and contributory and non-contributory programmes: recent reforms of the social protection system in Uruguay
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that intermediation services significantly improve job placement rates for workers, with an average effect size of 15% (or 1.5 standard deviations) over the sample period.
What_was_studied: The research investigates the impact of labor market intermediation services on job placement outcomes for workers in Argentina during the period 2014-2017, using a unique dataset from the National Employment Service and controlling for individual and job characteristics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of intermediation services on job placement outcomes, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up these services to improve employment outcomes for workers in Argentina, particularly for those with lower levels of education or experience.

Authors: Céline Hoeks; Hossein Azadi; Parisa Rafiaani Khachak; Enrique Troyo-Diéguez; Steven Van Passel; Frank Witlox
Field: Land tenure; Economics; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Land reform; Economic growth; Colonialism; Land law; Sustainable agriculture; Sustainability; Property rights
Title: Reforming Land-Tenure Systems in South Africa: Routes to Socio-Economic and Agricultural Sustainability
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The progress and main limitations of post-apartheid land reform to approach agricultural sustainability and alleviate poverty are discussed, along with different possibilities for future land reform and recommendations for future land-reform policies in South Africa.
What_was_studied: The aim of this article is to examine the best routes to alleviate poverty and retain sustainable agriculture in South Africa, using a theoretical framework that relates land tenure to sustainability and considering three historical periods (pre-colonial, colonial, and apartheid) to explain changes in land tenure and their consequences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up post-apartheid land reform to approach agricultural sustainability and alleviate poverty, decision makers should prioritize and expand the coverage of land reform programs, fund and support small-scale farmers, and revise existing policies to better address the limitations of post-apartheid land reform.

Field: Public economics; Blueprint; Economics; Poverty; Social change; Psychological intervention; Public expenditure; Good governance; Poverty reduction; Corporate governance; Development economics
Title: The Aid Paradigm for Poverty Reduction: Does It Make Sense?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while economic growth can lead to gains for the poor, these gains do not always match the national average, and public expenditure needs to be targeted towards achieving social development. Furthermore, governance reform is critical but there is no simple governance blueprint, and the corruption-growth association need not always be negative.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between economic growth, good governance, and social development in response to the perceived weak results of earlier adjustment reforms in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with case studies from various countries over the past two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision makers should prioritize targeted public expenditure and nuanced governance reforms to achieve sustainable development and reduce income poverty in developing countries.

Authors: Njeri Kagotho; Neema N. Salim; Michele Patak-Pietrafesa; Stavroula Kyriakakis
Field: Sociology; Family farm; Socioeconomics
Title: Inheriting the family farm: Generational wealth transfers in rural Kenya
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The narrative from these focus groups underscores the importance the community places on family-held wealth and how failures in the financial socialization process have compromised the generational wealth-transfer system, leading to the loss of household wealth and the marginalization of vulnerable individuals including women and children.
What_was_studied: A sub-set of intervention participants (n = 58) ranging in age from 20 to 78 were invited to participate in post-test focus group discussions to evaluate a succession curriculum in a farming community in Kenya over a specific period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need to strengthen parental financial capabilities and facilitate access to legal resources to facilitate wealth transfers, as youth unemployment and substance misuse have compromised the generational wealth-transfer system in sub-Saharan Africa.

Authors: Ubong Edem Effiong; Supper Roland Okijie; Nora Francis Inyang
Field: Unemployment; Ordinary least squares; Politics; Variation (astronomy); Demographic economics; Economics; Variables; Estimation; Discouraged worker; Unemployment rate; Economic growth; Political science; Econometrics; Statistics; Physics; Mathematics; Management; Astrophysics; Law

Title: Labor Employment in Western and Central Africa: An Exploration of Economic, Demographic, Social, and Political Indicators
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic variables account for approximately 76.81% of the total variation in labor force participation, while demographic indicators account for about 96.31%. Social indicators explain 88.46% of the overall variation in total unemployment, and political indicators jointly explain 89.75% of the overall variation in total unemployment.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed time series data from 1991 to 2020 on key economic, demographic, social, and political variables influencing labor employment in Western and Central Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To solve the problem of labor employment within the WCA region, decision-makers should prioritize addressing economic vagaries, demographic explosion, and social and political change.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; International development
Title: Eliminating World Poverty: Building Our Common Future
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that income poverty, child poverty, food insecurity, and rural poverty are pervasive issues affecting millions of people worldwide, with unequal access to resources and opportunities exacerbating these challenges. The report highlights that sustainable development is hindered by persistent poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The UK Department for International Development's report examines the extent of poverty globally and identifies key areas for intervention to achieve sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty globally, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up interventions aimed at reducing income poverty, child poverty, food insecurity, and rural poverty. This can be achieved by increasing funding for sustainable development programs and revising existing policies to better address the needs of marginalized populations.

Field: Agricultural productivity; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Productivity; Least Developed Countries; Industrialisation; Economic growth; International development
Title: How countries become rich and reduce poverty: A review of heterodox explanations of economic development
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that developing a country's manufacturing capabilities and improving agricultural productivity are crucial for long-term poverty reduction, and these processes are interdependent. Moreover, industrialization and increased agricultural productivity have been linked to economic transformation and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: Using new and old literature to review the reasons behind poverty differences between countries and the potential of foreign aid in achieving sustainable development goals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in manufacturing and agriculture to stimulate economic transformation and achieve long-term poverty reduction. Foreign aid can play a reasonable role in supporting these objectives by focusing on capacity-building initiatives, particularly in the areas of manufacturing and agricultural productivity.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Geography; Traditional authority; Urban bias; Disadvantaged; Spatial inequality; Development policy; Urbanization; Development economics
Title: Breaking down rural and urban bias and interrogating spatial inequality, evidence from South Africa
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found substantial differences in household composition and access to services and assets across different geotypes, with households located in particular areas facing more vulnerability to poverty.
What_was_studied: This article investigates current socioeconomic disparities within rural and urban areas using 2012 household survey data on South Africa, focusing on differences in household composition and access to services and assets across various geotypes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Development policy should prioritize addressing the specific income-generating constraints that disadvantaged areas face to alleviate poverty.

Authors: Xavier Irz; James Stevenson; Arnold Tanoy; Portia Villarante; Pierre Morissens
Field: Economics; Poverty; Development economics; Equity (economics); Aquaculture
Title: The Equity and Poverty Impacts of Aquaculture: Insights from the Philippines
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Aquaculture benefits the poor in important ways, with the poor deriving a relatively larger share of their income from it than the rich, and provides employment to a large number of unskilled workers. The study also shows that aquaculture represents an inequality-reducing source of income.
What_was_studied: Empirical investigation of aquaculture development's potential to reduce poverty and enhance equity in five coastal communities of the Philippines over a six-month period, using survey data from 148 randomly selected households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical evidence of aquaculture's poverty-reducing potential, decision-makers should prioritize funding and scaling up aquaculture development initiatives in coastal communities, particularly in areas with large labor surpluses, to address chronic poverty and food insecurity.

Field: Public economics; Private sector; Umbrella fund; Economics; Open-ended investment company; Causality; Private equity firm; Investment (macroeconomics); Causal chain; Developing country
Title: Private-Sector Investment in Infrastructure: Rationale and Causality for Pro-poor Impacts
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that there is a possible but not necessary association between private investment, economic growth and poverty reduction, but the causal chain is poorly understood.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the arguments for promoting private investment in infrastructure as a basis for poverty reduction in developing countries, using data from international 'facilities' intended to address impediments to private investment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize developing a comprehensive framework for understanding the causal pathways linking private investment to pro-poor outcomes in order to scale up private investment in infrastructure and reduce poverty in developing countries.

Authors: Sarah Challe; Stamatios Christopoulos; Michael Kull; Louis Meuleman
Field: Nexus (standard); Development studies; Political science; Poverty; Environmental degradation; Information policy; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Title: Steering the Poverty‐Environment Nexus in Central Asia: A metagovernance analysis of the Poverty‐Environment Initiative (PEI)
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty and environmental degradation are closely linked in Central Asia and Tajikistan, with poverty exacerbating environmental issues and environmental degradation perpetuating poverty. Specifically, the study found that 70% of households in rural Tajikistan experience food insecurity, and gender inequality is a significant factor in both poverty and environmental degradation.
What_was_studied: The close and reciprocal ties between poverty and environmental degradation in Central Asia and Tajikistan between 2005-2020, using a mixed-methods approach combining document analysis and stakeholder interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing poverty and environmental degradation in Central Asia and Tajikistan must be done jointly and with a focus on gender equality. Policymakers should prioritize integrating endogenous knowledge into development plans, linking national and local development planning, and improving governance coordination to achieve more inclusive decision-making and ultimately increase the impact of the UNDP-UNEP Poverty Environment Initiative on society and the environment.

Field: Content analysis; Political science; Process management; Human development (humanity); National planning
Title: How can countries improve human development? Four distinct national planning strategies and the challenges for human development ahead
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings reveal that despite varying socioeconomic and political conditions, these countries ultimately articulate similar challenges in their efforts to achieve human development, such as globalization and economic diversification, climate change, rising inequality, ineffective public administration, and demographic changes.
What_was_studied: This article compares the national planning strategies of four countries with distinct approaches to human development, using a deductive approach based on Sen's theoretical framework of five instrumental freedoms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To better understand how national planning strategies can improve human development, decision-makers should prioritize addressing the common challenges of globalization and economic diversification, climate change, rising inequality, ineffective public administration, and demographic changes.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Financial market; Sharif; Independence; Financial integration; Financial sector; Development economics; Economic growth; Liberalization
Title: Strengthening Financial Markets for the Poor
primary_category: Child poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The studies found that liberalization of financial markets has had a positive impact on poverty reduction, with the poorest households experiencing significant improvements in their well-being. Specifically, the research showed that access to credit and financial services can lead to increased income and reduced poverty rates.
What_was_studied: Financial sector reform and its impact on poverty reduction in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Bangladesh, during the period after independence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize financial sector reform and ensure that the benefits of liberalization are shared equitably across all socioeconomic groups. This may involve implementing targeted interventions to increase access to credit and financial services for vulnerable populations.

Field: Architecture; Economics; Convergence (relationship); Rural development; Poverty reduction; Urban policy; Political instability; Development economics
Title: Rural development and the 'new architecture of aid': convergence and constraints
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while there is growing convergence among donors on certain issues, such as gender equality and sustainable development, practical problems persist in managing sector-wide approaches and linking rural and urban policies. Moreover, chronic political instability continues to limit development support in many areas with high concentrations of the poor.
What_was_studied: This article investigates donor practices in relation to three major policy areas—gender and poverty, rural poverty, and sustainable development—in order to identify emerging issues and differences in approach that may impact the effectiveness of pro-poor initiatives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent challenges facing pro-poor initiatives in these areas, decision makers should prioritize strengthening the capacity of local institutions and investing in integrated, sector-wide approaches that address the interconnected nature of gender, poverty, and sustainable development. Additionally, donors should consider innovative strategies to link rural and urban policies and foster greater coordination among different stakeholders to maximize the impact of their support.

Field: Agriculture; Personal boundaries; Economics; Stakeholder engagement; European union; Institutional support; Agricultural development; Public administration; Legitimacy; Economic growth; International development
Title: Policy Coherence for Sustainable Agricultural Development: Uncovering Prospects and Pretence within the Swedish Policy for Global Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found institutional fragmentation and struggles for legitimacy, with the internationally heralded Swedish Policy for Global Development operated largely as a tokenistic instrument, legitimized by the pretence of stakeholder engagement.
What_was_studied: This article examines the prospects for stakeholders in Sweden to implement policy coherence for agricultural development in low-income countries, drawing on experiences from the launch of a national multi-stakeholder platform with the participation of 99 organisations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Sweden should prioritize cross-sectoral dialogues to deconstruct social boundaries which are no longer relevant and improve institutional support to facilitate policy coherence for agricultural development in low-income countries.

Field: Business; Industrialisation; Decision tree; Industrial policy; Environmental planning; Taxonomy (general)
Title: Industrial policy: Clarifying options through taxonomy and decision trees
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that basic issues such as infrastructure and land access are often the binding constraints to growth in these sectors, rather than choices of specific forms of incentives.
What_was_studied: Industrial policy in low-income countries, specifically in the context of Ethiopia's garment, leather goods, and cut flowers sectors over a particular time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy-makers should prioritize addressing these basic issues in order to improve competitiveness in these sectors and promote sustainable development.

Field: Social status; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Property (philosophy); Asset (economics); Spouse; Dimension (data warehouse); Inheritance; Demographic economics; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Inheritance: A Gendered and Intergenerational Dimension of Poverty
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that women are more likely to lose access to assets after their spouse's death, highlighting the gendered and intergenerational dimensions of inheritance. Moreover, the research indicates that inheritance can have a significant impact on economic and social status and mobility, with implications for poverty reduction policies.
What_was_studied: This collection of articles investigates the inheritance patterns and their consequences for women's economic and social status across various populations, time periods, and data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize addressing the gendered and intergenerational dimensions of inheritance to scale up poverty reduction efforts. This could involve revising inheritance laws and practices, expanding access to financial education and resources, and funding programs that support women's economic empowerment.

Authors: Tadashi Hirai; Flavio Comim; Richard Jolly
Field: Political science; Economic stagnation; Praise; Human Development Report; Acknowledgement; Human development (humanity); Capability approach; Engineering ethics

Title: Rescuing human development from a lip‐service syndrome
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals two fundamental challenges: (1) to make more specific the rich concepts of human development and (2) to relate them to the dominant concepts of development.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the challenges in making more specific the rich concepts of human development and relating them to the dominant concepts of development, and motivating and guiding the context-specific choices at the national and regional level.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, policy-makers should prioritize exploring the theoretical and operational implications of Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum's work and adopting a more careful approach to the implementation of the Human Development (HD) approach, with a focus on context-specific choices at the national and regional level.

Field: Public economics; Private sector; Business; Poverty; Management system; Tracking (education); Balance (accounting); Public expenditure; Public spending; Developing country
Title: Is There a Place for Virtual Poverty Funds in Pro‐Poor Public Spending Reform? Lessons from Uganda's PAF
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: VPFs can be useful in identifying the right balance of expenditures in the entire budget, improving the effectiveness and efficiency of existing allocations, and developing better public-sector policies for promoting pro-poor private sector growth.
What_was_studied: The experience of Uganda's Poverty Action Fund and the use of VPFs as a mechanism for tagging and tracking the performance of specific poverty-reducing expenditures in the budget.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Emphasis needs to be placed on identifying the right balance of expenditures in the entire budget, improving the effectiveness and efficiency of existing allocations, and developing better public-sector policies for promoting pro-poor private sector growth to avoid distorting public expenditure allocations and management systems, potentially undermining growth.

Authors: Dyutiman Choudhary; S. P. Kala; N.P. Todaria; Sabyasachi Dasgupta; Michael Kollmair
Field: Business; Value (economics); Cinnamomum tamala; Power relations; Bay leaf; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Agroforestry
Title: Drivers of Exploitation and Inequity in Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFP) Value Chains: The Case of Indian Bay Leaf in Nepal and India
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that bay-leaf VCs are loosely integrated and consist of stakeholders with asymmetrical power relations and different priorities, with traders in India dominating the chains and inappropriate standards leading to the exploitation of small producers and inequity in the chain.
What_was_studied: This article presents the findings of a study that analyzed the Indian Bay Leaf (Cinnamomum tamala) Nees and Eberm value chain (VC) in Uttarakhand, India and Udayapur, Nepal during the period of 2015-2018 using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy measures are suggested for improving coordination and competitiveness in the bay-leaf VC, which could be applied to the NTFP sector as a whole, to address urban poverty by scaling up sustainable and equitable value chains that benefit small producers.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Social protection; Cash transfers; Politics
Title: The politics of promoting social cash transfers in Uganda: The potential and pitfalls of “thinking and working politically”
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The adoption of a 'thinking and working politically' approach by donors enabled the successful promotion of SCTs in Uganda, despite the deteriorating political conditions. However, cash transfers have primarily been adopted as a form of clientelism rather than as a strategy for poverty reduction or improving the social contract.
What_was_studied: Social cash transfer programmes in Uganda between 2010 and 2016, with a focus on donor strategies and their alignment with the country's changing political settlement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of clientelistic practices in SCTs, decision-makers should prioritize strengthening Uganda's political settlement and promoting more progressive forms of politics to ensure that social protection policies effectively address intersectional poverty and support sustainable development.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; State (polity); White paper; Corporate governance; Economic growth; International development
Title: Britain's New White Paper: Making Governance Work for the Poor
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The review highlights the importance of addressing income poverty, social protection, and rural poverty to make progress in reducing child poverty and food insecurity.
What_was_studied: The white paper reviews books on international development to identify effective strategies for reducing poverty, with a focus on governance and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up successful programs and expand access to social protection, governments should prioritize investment in sustainable development and targeted interventions for the most vulnerable populations.

Field: Climate change; Economics; Energy supply; Oecd countries; Poverty reduction; Financial stability; Inequality; Development economics; Extreme poverty
Title: Growth, Poverty Reduction and Development Assistance in Asia: Options and Prospects
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that between 2005 and 2015, poverty rates in Asia declined by 46%, with China and India being the main drivers of this reduction. Additionally, the study discovered that while economic growth has been more rapid in Asia than in any other region, inequality has also risen, particularly in China and India.
What_was_studied: This article examines the pattern of growth and poverty reduction in Asia over the last decade, specifically focusing on how rapid economic growth has led to a significant decrease in poverty rates, yet still leaving the majority of the world's poor living in Asia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rapidly rising middle class in Asian countries, it is crucial to prioritize policies aimed at reducing income poverty and addressing emerging patterns of inequality to ensure sustainable development and equitable growth.

Field: Inclusion (education); Political science; Socioeconomics
Title: Community‐Led Reconstruction, Social Inclusion and Participation in Post‐earthquake Nepal
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that CLR led to limited achievements in terms of greater participation and social inclusion of some hitherto marginalized groups, with women experiencing improved social status and enhanced community solidarity supporting landless people.
What_was_studied: The article examines the community-led reconstruction (CLR) program implemented by ActionAid Nepal after the 2015 earthquakes in Nepal, focusing on the participation and social inclusion of marginalized groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and fund CLR programs that target marginalized groups, ensuring their participation and inclusion in decision-making processes to address deep-seated inequalities and promote democratic social change.

Field: Government; Political science; Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; Aid effectiveness; Good governance; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Civil society; Developing country; Politics
Title: Second‐Generation Poverty Reduction Strategies: New Opportunities and Emerging Issues
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that PRSPs have led to increased government focus on poverty reduction, civil society participation, and donor coordination, resulting in a significant decrease in income poverty rates. However, the approach has limited success in addressing chronic poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effectiveness of Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) in reducing poverty and promoting good governance in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2001 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of PRSPs on income poverty reduction, governments and international organizations should prioritize scaling up the approach to address chronic poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality, through targeted interventions and increased financing.

Field: Political science; Developing regions; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic inequality; Developing country; International development
Title: Attaining the International Development Targets: Will Growth be Enough?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that progress in health and education and poverty reduction in developing regions and transition economies has slowed or reversed since the 1990s, indicating a need for renewed efforts to attain the IDTs set by the DAC.
What_was_studied: The improvement in health and education and poverty reduction in developing regions and transition economies during the late 1980s and early 1990s, as well as the attainability of the International Development Targets (IDTs) set by the OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) in 1996.
