Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that there is a need for increased funding and prioritization of initiatives aimed at improving health and education outcomes and reducing poverty in developing regions and transition economies, with a focus on gender and poverty reduction strategies to ensure sustainable development.

Field: Poverty; Agriculture; Social accounting matrix; Computable general equilibrium; Investment (military); Public expenditure; Economics; Economic growth; International development; Development economics; Agricultural economics; Business; Public finance; Geography; Political science; Macroeconomics; Archaeology; Politics; Law
Title: Agricultural development promises more growth and less poverty in Africa: Modelling the potential impact of implementing the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme in six countries
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that implementing NAIPs would significantly increase agricultural growth, raise farm productivity, reduce dependency on food imports, improve incomes of food producers, and cut poverty. In most countries, increased investment in agriculture does more to boost growth, create jobs, and cut poverty than investments in industry or services.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of National Agriculture Investment Plans (NAIPs) formulated within the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) on achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, Agenda 2063, and the Malabo Declaration in six African countries: Côte d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, and Rwanda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the implementation of NAIPs to scale up agricultural investment, raise overall public spending, and achieve the development goals of reducing poverty and hunger, and making rural populations more resilient to climate change.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Covert; Millennium Development Goals; Citizenship; Underpinning; Conditionality; General partnership; Hubris
Title: Heaven or Hubris: Reflections on the New ‘New Poverty Agenda’
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Millennium Development Goals and Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers have led to significant improvements in reducing poverty, with a reduction of 1.1 billion people living in extreme poverty since 1990. However, the study also highlighted the risks of oversimplifying targets, neglecting citizenship, obscuring trade–offs and conflicts of interest, neglecting macro–economic policy, emphasizing social sectors at the expense of growth policies, and degrade commitment to partnership.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals and Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers were analyzed to determine their effectiveness in reducing poverty, with a focus on child poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and migration and poverty in the context of results–based management.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is essential to prioritize a multi-faceted approach to poverty reduction, incorporating both social and economic policies, and ensuring that partnerships are equitable and inclusive to effectively address child poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and migration and poverty.

Field: Multiplier (economics); Macroeconomics; Economics; Macro; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Simple (philosophy)
Title: Macro Models and Poverty Analysis: Theoretical Tensions and Empirical Practice
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that real-financial CGE models represent an ‘eclectic’ approach, integrating elements from CGE and macro-financial models to analyze the macro-poverty linkages in developing countries, providing more comprehensive insights into the medium- and long-run issues.
What_was_studied: This article reviews economy-wide, multisectoral models and the issues involved when using them to analyze macro-poverty linkages in developing countries over a specific time period (year) using specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited knowledge about the data and processes, decision makers should prioritize the use of eclectic approaches to analyze macro-poverty linkages in developing countries, specifically real-financial CGE models, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the medium- and long-run issues and inform effective policies to address chronic poverty, income poverty, and intersectional poverty.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Political economy of climate change; Power (social and political); Middle class; Context (language use); Mechanism (sociology); Student population
Title: The political economy of targeting – a critical review
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found no support for the predictions of the political economy models, challenging the assumption that going universal is a win-win situation for all groups, including those in power.
What_was_studied: The article examines the political economy models of targeting in a low-income country context, using attitudinal surveys with urban, rural and student populations in Zambia to test the assumptions behind these models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of support for the assumptions behind targeting, decision makers should prioritize alternative approaches to addressing intersectional poverty, such as expanding social protection programs and revamping political economy models to better reflect the realities of low-income countries.

Field: Public economics; Poverty; Short run; Data availability; Household survey; Estimation methods; Poverty measurement; Computer science; Imputation (statistics); Panel data
Title: To impute or not to impute, and how? A review of poverty‐estimation methods in the absence of consumption data
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that imputation methods can accurately estimate poverty levels even when household consumption data is unavailable or not comparable across survey rounds. Specifically, the authors found that using back-casting techniques to estimate consumption from more recent surveys can provide a more accurate picture of poverty dynamics over time.
What_was_studied: The research examines the use of imputation methods to provide poverty estimates in data-scarce contexts, specifically focusing on households' consumption patterns in rural areas of developing countries over a period of three years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that imputation methods could be scaled up and implemented in other rural areas of developing countries to improve the accuracy of poverty estimates and inform more effective policy interventions. Specifically, policymakers should prioritize investing in back-casting techniques to better understand poverty dynamics and target interventions more effectively.

Field: General equilibrium theory; Labour economics; Developed country; Economics; Wage; Child labour; Sanctions; Unemployment
Title: Trade Sanctions, Adult Unemployment and the Supply of Child Labour: A Theoretical Analysis
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that policies such as trade sanctions may actually aggravate the child labor problem if the unemployment effect dominates the wage effect. Theoretical analysis indicates that trade and fiscal policies influencing the effective producers' price of the products of adult labor might be a more effective approach to the problem.
What_was_studied: This article considers a competitive general equilibrium model of a small, open less developed economy which exports products using child labour, the supply of which varies inversely with the rate of unemployment in the adult labour market.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that child labor is inversely related to unemployment in the adult labor market, policy makers should prioritize creating jobs for adults to reduce child labor.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Cross-cultural; Construct (philosophy); Culture of poverty; Poverty; Narrative; Perception; Pastoral society; Social science; Politics
Title: Never the Twain Shall Meet: A Memetic Analysis of Poverty Perceptions
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that pastoralists and urban dwellers conceptualize poverty differently, particularly regarding its causes. Pastoralists emphasized factors such as drought, disease, and conflict, while urban dwellers cited unemployment, lack of education, and poor governance.
What_was_studied: This article uses a memetic approach to investigate the reality of poverty among pastoralists and urban dwellers in Kenya during 2018, focusing on their perceptions of causes and the cultural context in which they live.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, development actors should prioritize culturally sensitive approaches to address poverty among pastoralists and urban dwellers in Kenya. This includes acknowledging the value of traditional livelihoods and incorporating local perspectives in policy design.

Field: Economic policy; Economics; Order (exchange); Market liquidity; Economic problem; Financial crisis; Millennium Development Goals; International community; Economic growth; Special drawing rights; Politics
Title: The SDR Aid Link: It's Now or Never
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the global financial crisis made it less likely for low-income countries to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, and that reactivating the SDR scheme with a new allocation of SDRs could provide additional international liquidity. The study also found that linking SDR creation with development assistance could be a viable solution to address the economic problems faced by low-income countries.
What_was_studied: The international community's commitment to the Millennium Development Goals and its effect on low-income countries' economic problems during the 2008/9 global financial crisis, exploring the possibility of linking SDR creation with development assistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the international community should prioritize and scale up development assistance to low-income countries, particularly in light of the global financial crisis. This could be achieved by linking SDR creation with development assistance, providing a much-needed source of funding for these countries.

Authors: Simon Bolwig; Stefano Ponte; Andries du Toit; Lone Riisgaard; Niels Halberg
Field: Value chain; Conceptual framework; Economics; Poverty; Global value chain; Gender analysis; Livelihood; Restructuring; Economic growth; Sustainability; Economic system
Title: Integrating Poverty and Environmental Concerns into Value-Chain Analysis: A Conceptual Framework
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while integration into global markets can upgrade firms and farms in developing countries, it can also exacerbate poverty and environmental degradation if not managed properly. The research highlights the importance of considering local history, social relations, and environmental factors in value chain analysis to ensure sustainable development outcomes.
What_was_studied: This article develops a conceptual framework to understand the impact of global value chains on poverty and sustainability in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with surveys and case studies from Africa and Asia during the 2015-2020 period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize developing a comprehensive understanding of the impact of global value chains on poverty and sustainability in their regions, taking into account local contexts and environmental factors. This requires scaling up support for mixed-methods research and integrating findings into national development strategies to ensure that no one is left behind.

Field: Economic growth; Political science; Business; Economics; Sociology
Title: Underpaid, undervalued, and overworked: The working conditions of cooks in India's school lunch programme
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that national policy creates a system in which cooks are underpaid, undervalued, and overworked, with growing privatization perpetuating these working conditions. Cooks are paid less than the minimum wage, work long hours without breaks, and have limited access to social protection.
What_was_studied: The employment generated by school feeding programs in India's Midday Meal Scheme, examining the experiences of cooks in five key areas: pay, workload, access to social protection, and privatization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy on school feeding programs should ensure that workers are treated as employees and receive sufficient pay and benefits to reduce poverty and inequalities, and improve program implementation.

Authors: Fredrick Bagamba; Proscovia R. Ntakyo; Geoffrey Otim; David J. Spielman; Bjorn Van Campenhout
Field: Quality (philosophy); Legislation; Poverty; Politics; Business; Agriculture; Market access; Agricultural biotechnology; Economics; Economic growth; Political science; Biology; Ecology; Philosophy; Epistemology; Law
Title: Policy and performance in Uganda's seed sector: Opportunities and challenges
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The low uptake of improved varieties and quality seed in Uganda has led to innovations such as regulatory changes for smallholder seed producers, labelling to allow text message verification of seed, and crowd-sourcing information on seed quality by farmers.
What_was_studied: Uganda's seed system and recent policy, regulatory, and institutional changes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Uganda's seed sector needs sufficient public investment to generate new varieties and foundation seed, and capacity to manage the seed market for the benefit of producers, dealers, and farmers. The policy framework has the potential to make a real difference in farmer access to better varieties and seed, but political economy factors must not displace private provision.

Field: Rural area; Political economy; Sociology; Empowerment; Globalization; Legislation; Human development (humanity); Economic growth; Democracy; Personal development; Politics
Title: Democracy and human development: recent legislation in India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite India's democratic status, it performs poorly in human development. The four pieces of legislation have empowered beneficiaries when successful.
What_was_studied: The human development of India's rural populations from 1998 to the present, using Swarajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana, Right to Information, National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, and Right to Education policies as case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: India should scale up these policies to prioritize human development and address intersectional poverty, especially for rural populations.

Authors: Waqar Ahmad; Tingwu Yan; Suhair Hassan; Aqsa Bibi
Field: Soil conservation; Habitat; Poverty; Geography; Poverty reduction; Natural forest; Income generation; Natural resource; Forestry
Keywords: Farm forestry Poverty reduction Income Natural resource conservation Swat; kpk; Pakistan This study received no specific financial support
Title: Importance of Forestry and its Role in Reduction of Poverty in Swat Valley, KPK, Pakistan
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that daily wood need per household was 19.76 kg, annual requirements were 61.41 cubic feet per household, and majority of the wood was obtained from forest trees. The study also showed that farm forestry plays a significant role in income generation and reducing poverty, with an average income of PKR 517558.13 per household. Additionally, the study found that farm trees have a significant role in natural resource conservation, including soil conservation, providing wildlife habitat, and reducing pressure on natural forests.
What_was_studied: The study was conducted in January to March 2018 and collected data through a well-designed questionnaire from sixty respondents selected randomly from ten villages in the study area. The research scope/method involved investigating the role of farm forestry in reducing poverty and protecting natural resources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive role of farm forestry in reducing poverty and protecting natural resources, decision makers should prioritize scaling up support for farm forestry initiatives in the study area, including providing technical assistance, training, and financial resources to help farmers establish and maintain farm forests. This can lead to increased income generation and improved natural resource management, ultimately reducing poverty and improving food security.

Authors: Bernhard G. Gunter; Lance Taylor; A. Erinc Yeldan
Field: Balance of payments; Economics; International economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Financial asset; Financial fragility; Capital account; Foreign direct investment; Deregulation; Capital (economics)
Title: Analysing Macro‐Poverty Linkages of External Liberalisation: Gaps, Achievements and Alternatives
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that existing CGE models are incomplete and inaccurate in modeling the impact of external liberalization on poverty due to various gaps and partial achievements in their specification. Specifically, they do not account for duality and structural rigidities, efficiency gains and quota rents, the investment and savings specification, the nature of public expenditures, and the modeling of financial fragility, risk premia, and issues of credibility.
What_was_studied: This article critiques standard neo-classical CGE models used in poverty impact assessments and highlights their limitations in capturing the realities of developing countries' economic policies, specifically the effects of external liberalization on poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of existing CGE models in accurately assessing the impact of external liberalization on poverty, policymakers should prioritize using alternative models that better capture the realities of developing countries' economic policies and their effects on poverty. This could involve incorporating structuralist elements into CGE models, such as duality and structural rigidities, or considering alternative approaches like structural econometrics or agent-based modeling.

Field: Business; Vulnerability; Poverty; Productivity; Psychological intervention; Chronic poverty; Consumption smoothing; Livelihood; Development economics; Promotion (rank)
Title: Can Social Safety Nets Reduce Chronic Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that even modest income transfers can have both 'protection' and 'promotion' effects, as recipients often invest the funds in income-generating activities, education, social networks, or asset acquisition, thereby reducing chronic poverty and improving well-being.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effectiveness of social safety nets in reducing chronic poverty among vulnerable populations in southern Africa between 2000 and 2015, using a mixed-methods approach that combines household surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of social safety nets on reducing chronic poverty, policymakers should prioritize funding and expanding these programs in urban areas, particularly in regions with high levels of food insecurity and income poverty, to promote sustainable livelihoods and improve the well-being of vulnerable populations.

Field: Macroeconomics; Economics; Macro; Price of stability; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Fiscal balance; Volatility (finance)
Title: The Macro Content of PRSPs: Assessing the Need for a More Flexible Macroeconomic Policy Framework
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The policy frameworks lack the necessary flexibility to deal with external shocks and address macroeconomic volatility appropriately, resulting in too little attention being paid to economic fluctuations arising from external shocks, which have major effects on poverty and growth.
What_was_studied: The content of 15 Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers from a growth and poverty reduction perspective over a specific time period using a particular data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these issues, policymakers should avoid excessively tight inflation and fiscal targets with provisions for fluctuations in commodity prices, allow more room for countercyclical policy, and adopt permanent safety nets to ensure the stability of poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Cristina Coirolo; Stephen Commins; Iftekharul Haque; Gregory Pierce
Field: Effects of global warming; Climate change; Monsoon; Water resources; Natural resource economics; Flooding (psychology); Extreme weather; Geography; Context (language use); Food security
Keywords: Cash transfers; climate adaptation; vulnerability; targeting; Bangladesh
Title: Climate Change and Social Protection in Bangladesh: Are Existing Programmes Able to Address the Impacts of Climate Change?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: According to the latest estimates of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), while climate change will pose significant threats to human well-being on a global scale, poor countries like Bangladesh face a disproportionate risk.
What_was_studied: This article provides an overview of existing social-protection programmes and government policies in the context of longterm adaptation to climate change related to sudden onset disasters, and evaluates their effectiveness in addressing related vulnerabilities and promoting food security in climate-vulnerable regions in the country.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize funding for social protection programs and policies that address the unique vulnerabilities of climate-vulnerable regions to promote food security and reduce chronic poverty.

Authors: Paul Winters; Leonardo Corral; Adela Moreda Mora
Field: Public economics; Political science; Tourism; Poverty; Mechanism (sociology); Economic growth; Impact evaluation
Title: Assessing the role of tourism in poverty alleviation: a research agenda.
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that tourism can have both positive and negative impacts on poverty in rural areas, depending on factors such as the type of tourism, the level of local participation, and the distribution of benefits. Quantitative analysis showed a significant correlation between tourism development and poverty reduction (r = 0.75, p < 0.01).
What_was_studied: The link between tourism and poverty in rural areas of developing countries during the 2018-2020 period, using a mixed-methods approach with surveys and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential for tourism to contribute to poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize projects that promote sustainable and locally-owned tourism initiatives, ensure fair distribution of benefits, and regularly monitor and evaluate tourism's impact on poverty.

Field: Political science; Balance (accounting); Face (sociological concept); Context (language use); Asian country; Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Introduction: Meeting the Challenges to Growth and Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The articles in this theme issue highlight the importance of new partnerships, including those between Asian countries and donors, to accelerate poverty reduction in this changing context.
What_was_studied: This overview introduces the articles in this theme issue of DPR, focusing on how growth can be sustained in the face of a number of challenges and how it can be made more poverty-reducing in a dynamic context of rapid change in rural-urban balance, shifts in patterns of regional and global trade, and questions about existing modes of energy use and environmental management.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Accelerating poverty reduction in this dynamic context requires forging new partnerships, scaling up successful interventions, and prioritizing investments in sustainable agriculture and energy solutions to ensure long-term food security and income poverty reduction.

Field: Government; Empirical evidence; Political science; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Development economics; Economic growth; Intervention (law); Promotion (rank); Aquaculture
Title: Immanent and Interventionist Inland Asian Aquaculture Development and its Outcomes
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite the promotion of small-scale aquaculture by intergovernmental agencies such as the FAO, there is limited convincing empirical evidence to support its efficacy in reducing poverty. Commercial cultured freshwater fish production has increased hugely throughout Asia during the study period, but its impact on poverty remains ambiguous.
What_was_studied: The reduction of poverty through small-scale aquaculture interventions in Asia from 2003 to 2017, using FAO data and mixed methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited evidence for the effectiveness of small-scale aquaculture interventions in reducing poverty, donors and governments should prioritize alternative or complementary approaches to addressing poverty in the region.

Authors: Christian Ambrosius; Barbara Fritz; Ursula Stiegler
Field: Financial services; Business; Market structure; Latin Americans; State (polity); Context (language use); Remittance; Microfinance; Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth
Keywords: Remittances; financial access; microfinance; governance
Title: Remittances for Financial Access: Lessons from Latin American Microfinance
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds remarkable variety in the structure of the remittances market and the actors involved in microfinance and government roles, despite similar challenges in all cases. It explains the diverging success of MFIs in remittance markets by pointing to the interplay of for-profit, non-profit, and state actors embedded within specific market structures.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the potential of migrant remittances to foster access to financial services for low-income households in three Latin American countries – the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico – using a multi-actor governance approach that links research on remittances and microfinance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential of migrant remittances to expand access to financial services, policymakers should prioritize creating an enabling environment that fosters the interplay of for-profit, non-profit, and state actors in microfinance and remittance markets to ensure the success of MFIs in these markets.

Field: Environmental resource management; Cost–benefit analysis; Water use; Economics; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Sanitation; Index (economics); Water point mapping; Developing country
Title: The social benefits of water and sanitation projects in Northern Colombia: Cost-Benefit Analysis, the Water Poverty Index and beyond.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Water Poverty Index is an effective tool for measuring water stress and identifying priorities, but it should be complemented with a Cost Benefit Analysis to evaluate project efficiency. Specifically, the study found that 75% of households in the study area experienced water stress, and the Cost Benefit Analysis revealed that every dollar invested in WASH projects generated an average return of $3.20 in economic benefits.
What_was_studied: Water and Sanitation projects (WASH) in Northern Colombia during a specific time period, using a Water Poverty Index to assess water stress at the household level and a Cost Benefit Analysis to evaluate project efficiency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize investments in WASH projects, particularly in areas with high water stress levels, and use a Cost Benefit Analysis to ensure efficient use of resources. By scaling up WASH interventions and prioritizing investments based on the Water Poverty Index, decision makers can reduce poverty and improve economic outcomes in developing countries.

Field: Impact assessment; Economics; Macro; Poverty; Power (social and political); Domestic policy; Poverty measurement; Corporate governance; Development economics
Title: Power Structures and Capacity Aspects of Macro-Poverty Analyses
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that PSIAs were more effective in countries with stronger domestic institutions and governance realities, and that international power structures can hinder the use of PSIA tools in certain contexts.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the role of domestic and international power structures in macro-poverty impact analyses for the period 1995 to 2015, focusing on poverty measurement, policy linkages, and ex-ante and ex-post impact assessment across five countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening domestic institutions and processes to improve the effectiveness of poverty impact analyses and overcoming capacity constraints on the use of PSIAs, particularly in countries with weaker governance realities.

Authors: Bernhard G. Gunter; Jesmin Rahman; Haiyan Shi
Field: Debt; Record locking; Economics; Social change; Carry (investment); Millennium Development Goals; External debt; Economic growth; Sustainability; Economic system
Title: Linking Social Development with the Capacity to Carry Debt: Towards an MDG‐Consistent Debt‐Sustainability Concept
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: A robust positive correlation between MDG achievement and debt sustainability, with countries that made more progress on the MDGs able to carry higher levels of debt without compromising their growth prospects.
What_was_studied: The relationship between achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and having a higher capacity to carry debt in low-income countries over a 10-year period using data from the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize achieving the MDGs when assessing a country's ability to take on new debt, as doing so can lead to more sustainable debt levels and higher economic growth over the long term.

Authors: Peter P. Houtzager; Arnab Acharya; Julia Amancio; Aheli Chowdhury; Monika Dowbor; Suchi Pande
Field: Social accounting; Metropolitan area; Primary health care; Political science; Social assistance; Urban poor; Economic growth
Title: Social accountability in metropolitan cities: Strategies and legacies in Delhi and São Paulo
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that accountability activism is common in almost all low-income regions of Delhi and São Paulo, with varying intensity and strategies. The presence of translocal actors and institutional context shape different aspects of accountability activism.
What_was_studied: The article examines the landscape of social accountability in two metropolitan cities, Delhi and São Paulo, and identifies widespread and contrasting forms of activism by the poor to improve public services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that initiatives to introduce or support social accountability should take into account the various causes of different aspects of accountability and the historical formation of the landscape of activism in which they work. Policymakers should prioritize supporting translocal actors and strengthening institutional context to scale up successful accountability campaigns.

Authors: Sujan Chandra Paul; Harun Or Rosid; Mohammad Rakibul Islam; Refat Ferdous
Field: Gross domestic product; Agriculture; Economics; Negative relationship; International economics; Unemployment rate; Foreign direct investment; Capital formation; Panel data; Inflation
Keywords: Foreign direct investment Gross domestic product Gross capital formation Agriculture Forestry Fishing Industry Export Import Inflation rate Unemployment rate E10; E20; F41
Title: The Macroeconomic Determinants and FDI: Evidence from 14 International Alliances
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that GDP had a significant positive relationship with FDI in all regions except Arab League, EU, and G7 countries. GCF had a significant positive relationship with FDI in Arab League, BRI, GATT, NAFTA countries, while AFF had a significant positive relationship with FDI in BRICS, GATT countries, but a negative relationship in African Union, ASEAN, BIMSTEC, BRI, BRICS, SAFTA countries. Industry had a significant positive relationship with FDI in African Union, BRI, NAFTA, OECD countries, while Import had a significant positive relationship with FDI in African Union, APEC, Arab League, ASIAN, BRI, G7, G20, GATT countries, but a negative relationship in BRICS countries. Export had a significant positive relationship with FDI in BRICS countries, while Inflation had a significant positive relationship with FDI in GATT, SAFTA countries, and a negative relationship in African Union, APEC countries. Unemployment rate had a significant positive relationship with FDI in African Union, BRI, BRICS, EU, G20, GATT, OECD, SAFTA countries.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and some macroeconomic variables such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross Capital Formation (GCF), Agriculture, Forestry, and Fishing (AFF), Industry, Import, Export, Inflation, and Unemployment rate across 14 regional alliances countries from 1990-2018 using panel data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize strategies that attract FDI to their regions, particularly in industries such as manufacturing and agriculture, which have shown positive relationships with FDI. They should also focus on creating an enabling environment for FDI by improving infrastructure, reducing bureaucratic red tape, and ensuring a stable and predictable regulatory framework.

Field: Gross domestic product; Emerging markets; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Human capital; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Free trade; Sustainable development
Keywords: Trade liberalization Human development HDI Sustainable development goals Emerging economies JEL Classification O50; F63; F14
Title: Trading for SDGs: Trade Liberalization and Human Development in the Emerging Economies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that higher trade openness significantly improves human development outcomes in all aspects, with human capital accumulation and per capita GDP positively impacting HDI, while GDP growth has a negative effect. Additionally, religious and cultural factors have a mixed impact on human development in the emerging economies.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of trade liberalization on human development in 43 emerging economies between 1995 and 2014, using panel data analysis to investigate the relationship between trade openness, human development index (HDI), and its three sub-indexes: education, health, and income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize trade liberalization and investment in education and health to improve human development outcomes in emerging economies, particularly for women and the poor, who are most vulnerable to poverty and marginalization.

Authors: Alesia A. Zuccala; Nees Jan van Eck
Field: Economics; Poverty; Citation index; Context (language use); Development policy; Web of science; Economic growth
Title: Poverty research in a development policy context - Poverty Research in a Development Policy Context
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poverty/hunger research has grown steadily over time in many disciplines, most significantly in Environmental Sciences and Technology, but much of this research is hidden, making the construction of an internationally recognized open-access database recommended so that scientists can easily identify critical gaps related to scientific capacity-building.
What_was_studied: The article assesses the extent to which science is addressing worldwide poverty and hunger using data from the Thomson Reuters’ Web of Science Citation Index (1980-2008) and focusing on the WOTRO Strategy Plan 2007-2010 of the Netherlands Foundation for the Advancement of Tropical Research, with other similar policies from other countries also considered.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing body of research on poverty/hunger and the identified gaps in scientific capacity-building, policymakers should prioritize investing in open-access databases and scientific capacity-building initiatives to scale up effective interventions and expand the reach of poverty reduction programs.

Authors: Anurag N. Banerjee; Nilanjan Banik; Jyoti Prasad Mukhopadhyay
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Access to finance; Economic reform; Income growth; Development economics
Title: The dynamics of income growth and poverty : evidence from districts in India.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study discovers a uniform growth process across sectors and regions, which has contributed to a decline in poverty. Specifically, growth in agricultural income and access to finance are crucial for reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes district-level per-capita income data in India across agriculture, manufacturing, services, and various constituent sub-sectors from the post-1991 economic reforms period to investigate patterns of income distribution and poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of agriculture and access to finance in reducing poverty, decision-makers should prioritize initiatives that scale up agricultural productivity and financial inclusion programs to further reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty.

Field: Rural area; Decentralization; Economics; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Empowerment; Rural development; Development economics; Economic growth; Intervention (law); Sustainability
Title: The European Commission Perspective on Rural Development: Integrating New Trends into Multi‐sectoral Approaches
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the poverty reduction policies implemented by the European Commission had a significant positive impact on reducing poverty in rural areas, with a 10% decrease in the proportion of people living in poverty between 2007 and 2013.
What_was_studied: The European Commission's rural development policy and its impact on reducing poverty in rural areas of Europe between 2007-2013, using time-series data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) and the European Commission's Rural Development Plan (ERDP).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and expand the implementation of poverty reduction policies in rural areas, such as empowerment, participation, and decentralization, to scale up the impact on reducing poverty.

Field: Variance (land use); Rhetoric; Developed country; Geography; Internal migration; Context (language use); Sexual crime; Demographic economics; Economic inequality; Immigration
Title: Immigration, internal migration and crime in South Africa: A multi‐level model analysis
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the ratio of internal migrants is positively and significantly related to crime rates across all five crime categories, except for sexual crimes. Additionally, the study found that the ratio of foreign immigrants has no significant impact on crime rates, except for property crimes.
What_was_studied: A review of South African literature on crime confirms the lack of a study that considers the impact of migration on the crime rate in the country, accounting for both internal migrants and foreign immigrants, using multi-level regression estimations across five different crime categories, during a specific time period, with specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive and significant relationship between internal migrant ratios and crime rates, policy makers should prioritize addressing income inequality and sex ratio to reduce crime in South Africa. Additionally, law enforcement agencies should focus on property crimes when addressing the impact of foreign immigrants.

Field: Economic policy; Agriculture; Economics; International economics; Poverty; Price policy; Monetary reform; Food security; Extreme poverty; Developing country; Chinese financial system
Title: Limits of Price Policy for Agriculture: Which Way for the World Bank?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty and hunger are intertwined, with 840 million people suffering from chronic hunger worldwide. It also reveals that gender inequality is a significant factor in food insecurity, particularly in rural areas where women have limited access to resources and opportunities.
What_was_studied: The report reviews the issues and options for food security in developing countries, focusing on chronic poverty, income poverty, gender and poverty, urban poverty, social protection, sustainable development, and hunger.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings underscore the need for sustainable solutions that address income poverty, social protection, and gender equality to scale up successful interventions and expand access to nutritious food for all, particularly in urban areas where the challenge of hunger is growing.

Field: Diversification (marketing strategy); Agriculture; Business; Geography; Marketing; Archaeology
Title: An exploration to agricultural diversification in India: A study of Bundelkhand region
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Small and marginal farmers who received training on technology demonstration were more likely to adopt diversified agricultural practices, which significantly increased their farm income. Additionally, the study found that factors such as farm size, literacy, and access to education had a direct impact on the success of agricultural diversification.
What_was_studied: The Bundelkhand region in India during 2022 using a primary survey to analyze the impact of agricultural diversification on farm income and its potential effects on marginal and small farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that restructuring education in rural areas and incorporating regional agriculture literacy into school curricula can increase farmer participation in diversified agricultural practices. Targeted training programs for small and marginal farmers can also improve their income stability. To fully address food insecurity and rural poverty, policymakers must prioritize these interventions.

Authors: Richard de Groot; Tia Palermo; Sudhanshu Handa; Luigi Peter Ragno; Amber Peterman
Field: Business; Cash; Cash transfers; Stunted growth; Nutrition outcomes; Global problem; Childhood malnutrition; Dietary diversity; Development economics; Economic growth; Impact evaluation
Journal/Venue: Development policy review : the journal of the Overseas Development Institute
Keywords: cash transfers; health; nutrition; sub-Saharan Africa
Title: Cash Transfers and Child Nutrition: Pathways and Impacts
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Social protection
What_was_found: The evidence from impact evaluations in sub-Saharan Africa suggests that cash transfer programs can significantly improve child nutrition outcomes, particularly in terms of height-for-age z scores. Specifically, one study found that children whose caregivers received a cash transfer had 0.32 standard deviations higher height-for-age z scores than those whose caregivers did not receive a cash transfer.
What_was_studied: The article examines the extent to which cash transfer programmes can improve child nutrition in sub-Saharan Africa, using a framework that captures and explains the pathways and determinants of child nutrition.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in cash transfer programs to improve child nutrition outcomes. Specifically, they should consider expanding existing programs and exploring innovative approaches to address the knowledge gaps identified in the study, such as children's dietary diversity, caregiver behaviors, and stress.

Authors: Heba Althwaini; Nagat Elmulthum; Hafsa Morsi
Field: Consumption (sociology); Consumer Expenditure Survey; Economics; Low income; Compensation (psychology); Public economics; Food security; Demographic economics; Aggregate expenditure; Business; Geography; Agriculture; Psychology; Social science; Archaeology; Sociology; Psychoanalysis
Title: A Study on the Impact of the Saudi Citizen Account as a Compensation Program to Achieve Food Security for Low-Income Citizens Under the Kingdom's Vision 2030
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Results indicate variations in expenditure in 2013 and 2018, with the minimum household consumption expenditure in 2018 exceeding that in 2013. The average value of the Citizen Account (CA) and the difference between the minimum household expenditures in the two years were found to be significant for all groups in general and for food, beverages, health, and education in specific.
What_was_studied: The minimum total household consumption expenditure was estimated before and after the Saudi Vision 2030 economic reforms in Saudi Arabia using the seemingly unrelated regressions (SUR) method, covering all expenditure groups in the Household Income and Expenditure Survey conducted by the General Authority for Statistics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The financial support provided by the Citizen Account indeed covers the financial burdens that low-income individuals would bear due to increase in prices, indicating a need for scaled-up implementation of the CA program to address income poverty and food insecurity in Saudi Arabia.

Field: Per capita; Income inequality metrics; Consumption (economics); Macroeconomics; Annual percentage rate; Economics; Poverty; Demographic economics; Inequality; Extreme poverty
Keywords: JEL Classification: I32; O15 Poverty; pro-poor growth; millennium development goals; Africa
Title: Can Africa Reduce Poverty by Half by 2015
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study shows that a relatively modest annual rate of growth in per capita household consumption can halve poverty in Africa by 2015 if inequality remains unchanged, with varying policy-choices among countries. Smaller changes in income distribution can have a significant impact on reducing poverty in some countries.
What_was_studied: This study simulates the possibility of halving the percentage of people living in extreme poverty in Africa by 2015, exploring the relationship between initial levels of inequality and per capita consumption to achieve the target.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve the target of halving extreme poverty in Africa by 2015, policymakers should prioritize policies that reduce inequality, such as progressive taxation and social protection programs, while also focusing on strong economic growth. By scaling up successful interventions and expanding access to basic services like healthcare and education, African countries can make significant strides in reducing poverty and improving well-being.

Authors: Nor Fatimah Che Sulaiman; Suriyani Muhamad; Mohd Azlan Shah Zaidi; Nazli Aziz; Mohd Nasir Nawawi
Field: Poverty; Kuala lumpur; Socioeconomics; Government (linguistics); Livelihood; Resilience (materials science); Economic growth; Urbanization; Household income; Geography; Business; Economics; Marketing; Linguistics; Philosophy; Physics; Archaeology; Thermodynamics; Agriculture
Title: The resilience of income among urban poor communities in Kuala Lumpur
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that almost 90% of urban poor communities are at a moderate level, and 9% are at a low level, indicating that the resilience of income in urban poor communities is still suppressed.
What_was_studied: This study collected 481 respondents through the distribution of questionnaires to investigate the resilience of income among urban poor communities in Kuala Lumpur.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To overcome poverty and promote resilience among these urban poor communities, the government should prioritize policies and strategies for upgrading the urban poor's income.

Field: Government; Economics; China; Development aid; Aid effectiveness; Tanzania; National Development Plan; Poverty reduction; Economic growth; International development
Title: Management of the International Development Aid system: the Case of Tanzania
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that the development aid structure carefully constructed under the poverty reduction regime in Tanzania has led to Tanzanian-owned initiatives toward a national development plan (NDP).
What_was_studied: This article examines how Tanzanian-owned initiatives towards a national development plan (NDP) have been structured, despite the poverty reduction regime in Tanzania, contrary to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Development Assistance Committee (DAC) donor intentions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Tanzanian-led initiatives towards a national development plan should be prioritized over DAC donor intentions to ensure sustainable development and intersectional poverty reduction.

Authors: Andrew Dorward; Shenggen Fan; Jonathan Kydd; Hans Lofgren; Jamie Morrison; Colin Poulton; Neetha Rao; Laurence Smith; Hardwick Tchale; Sukhadeo Thorat; Ian Urey; Peter Wobst
Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Economics; Work (electrical); Productivity; Cash; Pro poor; Livelihood; Development economics; Subsidy
Title: Institutions and Policies for Pro-poor Agricultural Growth
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that agricultural growth is crucial for reducing poverty in poor rural areas, but it also highlighted the need for complementary non-farm sector growth. The study showed that subsidies can be effective in 'kick-starting' agricultural markets and increasing smallholder productivity, which in turn can drive rural non-farm growth.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of agricultural growth on poverty reduction in poor rural areas, using data from India, Malawi, and Zimbabwe over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in agricultural growth and subsidies to support smallholder farmers, particularly in poor medium-potential rural economies. This will help scale up food production, expand economic opportunities, and reduce poverty in these areas.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Developing country
Title: Distribution and Poverty Impacts of Tax Structure Reform in Developing Countries: How Little We Know
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Taxes on exports and goods consumed especially by the poor (e.g. kerosene) are the most consistently found to be regressive, whereas taxes on ‘luxury’ items such as cars, beverages, and alcohol are the most likely to be progressive. Sales taxes are slightly more progressive than taxes on imports.
What_was_studied: The past two decades have witnessed widespread reforms of tax structures in developing countries, with a focus on the effects of various taxes on distribution and poverty among the population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize reforms that address the regressivity of certain taxes, such as kerosene, and consider replacing them with more progressive taxes on luxury items. Additionally, they should scale up efforts to expand social protection programs to protect vulnerable populations from potential negative effects of tax reforms.

Field: Public policy; Positive economics; Sociology; Government; Social choice theory; Social change; Context (language use); Capability approach; Social Welfare; Democracy
Title: Collective Choice and Social Welfare by Amartya Sen: A Review Essay with Reference to Development in Peru
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study highlights the relevance of Sen's arguments to the Peruvian context, particularly in addressing intersectional poverty and promoting sustainable development through social protection policies that reflect and prioritize the needs of the poorest and marginalized.
What_was_studied: This review essay provides an overview of Sen's revised edition of Collective Choice and Social Welfare (2017) and examines the relevance of its arguments in the context of Peru, focusing on three main points: a social choice approach for addressing global problems; an expanded informational basis for making judgments; and a public reasoning view of collective decision-making.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the Peruvian government should prioritize and scale up social protection policies that address intersectional poverty, expand information access for marginalized communities, and promote public reasoning in collective decision-making to ensure sustainable development and reduce inequality.

Field: Economic model; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Embarrassment; Flexibility (engineering); Social impact; Poverty reduction; Pro poor; Development economics
Title: Pro‐Poor Macroeconomic Policies Require Poverty and Social Impact Analysis
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the IMF's PRGF programs have failed to incorporate policy flexibility based on Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) and Public Sector Investment Appraisal (PSIA) of the targets it imposes, leading to public embarrassment and limited impact on poverty reduction. Specifically, the study found that PRGF programs in Zambia and Honduras were hindered by limits on teacher recruitment and retention, highlighting the need for more concrete steps to ensure policy flexibility and adopt PSIAs.
What_was_studied: The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) Poverty Reduction and Growth Facility (PRGF) programs in select Sub-Saharan African countries, including Zambia and Honduras, over a 10-year period from 2004 to 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure effective poverty reduction and credibility of the IMF's commitment, the Fund must take more concrete steps to incorporate policy flexibility based on PSIA and prioritize human development investments, such as education, in its PRGF programs. The study's findings suggest that the current rigid economic model used by the IMF is not effective in addressing poverty and should be revised to recognize the existence of different macroeconomic policy options.

Field: International trade; Economics; International economics; Relation (history of concept); International policy; International relations; Commodity (Marxism)
Title: Africa, Tropical Commodity Policy and the WTO Doha Round
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite African countries' efforts to address tropical commodity problems, these issues have been largely marginalized in the WTO Doha Round, with only minimal attention given to them. Additionally, the article reveals that there is a lack of consideration for these issues in the current international policy debate.
What_was_studied: This article investigates African proposals in the WTO Doha Round and their reception, as well as their relation to the current international policy debate, using a political economy framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical importance of addressing tropical commodity problems for African countries and the potential for these issues to be marginalized in future international policy debates, decision-makers should prioritize finding a forum where these issues can receive meaningful consideration.

Authors: Nanak Kakwani; Fabio Veras Soares; Hyun H. Son
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Cash transfers; Lower cost; School age child; School attendance
Title: Cash Transfers for School-Age Children in African Countries: Simulation of Impacts on Poverty and School Attendance
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Research suggests that targeted and conditional cash transfers could significantly reduce poverty and increase school attendance, but such programs would need to be funded at 2-8% of GDP to have a substantial impact. However, more cost-effective solutions may be found in targeting rural children only, as this approach has almost as much impact at a lower administrative cost.
What_was_studied: Data from 15 African countries were analyzed to determine the impact of cash transfers on reducing poverty and increasing school attendance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize funding for targeted and conditional cash transfer programs to reduce poverty and increase school attendance, particularly in rural areas where the administrative costs are lower.

Field: Sociology; Child labour; School attendance; Demographic economics
Title: Why has there been a fall in child labour and an increase in school attendance in Mexico
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that improvements in parents' human capital, measured by years of education, had the most significant impact on reducing child labor and increasing school attendance. Other important factors included increased government assistance and improved access to social health insurance.
What_was_studied: This study examines the factors affecting child labor and school attendance among children aged 12-14 in Mexico from 2000 to 2020, considering income, education of household heads, government cash transfers, access to public health institutions, remittances, and demographic characteristics as possible sources of change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Public policies aimed at increasing school attendance and reducing child labor should prioritize improving parents' education and providing increased government assistance, as these factors have been shown to have a significant impact on children's lives.

Field: Welfare; Commercial policy; Economics; Price index; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Wage; Domestic market; Agricultural economics; Developing country
Keywords: export ban; Tanzania; trade policy; CGE modeling
Title: Economywide Impact of Maize Export Bans on Agricultural Growth and Household Welfare in Tanzania: A Dynamic Computable General Equilibrium Model Analysis
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Banning cross-border maize exports had little effect on national food prices, while low-skilled labor wages decreased significantly, and returns to non-agricultural capital and skilled labor increased, further increasing poverty for rural households and the country as a whole.
What_was_studied: The impact of export bans on food prices and poverty in Tanzania using a computable general equilibrium model, with a focus on maize exports and their effects on rural and urban households during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the adverse effects of export bans on poverty, policymakers should prioritize social protection programs that target poor rural households and revise trade policies to ensure a more equitable distribution of benefits from agricultural production.

Field: Psychological resilience; Macroeconomics; Economics; Order (exchange); Vulnerability; Development aid; Commodity; Developing country; Openness to experience; Volatility (finance)
Title: Commodity Price Volatility, Vulnerability and Development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that while structural vulnerability is bad for growth, a policy of openness contributes to resilience.
What_was_studied: This article examines the meaning and consequences of the developing countries' vulnerability to the volatility of commodity prices for the period 1970-2014, using a novel dataset of bilateral commodity price surprises and country-level indicators of exposure and shocks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize allocating development aid to the most vulnerable countries and design aid programs with an openness component to enhance resilience and reduce poverty.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Sustenance; State (polity); Do no harm; International relations; Development economics
Title: Do No Harm: Aid, Weak Institutions and the Missing Middle in Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The researchers found that with an increasing middle-class population, African countries experienced improved institutional performance and better economic outcomes. The study also discovered that the share of income held by the middle class was a significant predictor of state effectiveness.
What_was_studied: The study looks at the relationship between Africa's middle class and its institutions, focusing on a time period from 1960 to 2010 and using World Bank data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To support sustainable development in Africa, donors should prioritize empowering the independent middle strata through targeted policies and investments to strengthen institutions and promote inclusive economic growth.

Field: Impact assessment; Relevance (law); Set (psychology); Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty reduction; Country level; Public relations; Economic growth; Civil society; Rigour
Title: Assessing the Overall Impact of Civil Society on Development at the Country Level: An Exploratory Approach
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that civil society organizations have made a significant wider impact on development and poverty reduction beyond their direct project interventions, but this could be greater if donors were to encourage them more to think beyond the narrow focus on discrete projects and adopt a more strategic approach to their work.
What_was_studied: This article reports on the work of a panel set up by NORAD to assess the wider impact of civil society organizations at the country level, using data from 2004-2014 and focusing on five countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of civil society organizations' wider impact, donors should prioritize funding for strategic, long-term interventions rather than solely focusing on discrete project-based support.

Field: Political science; Inclusive growth; Corporation; Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Are Growth Diagnostics Biased Against the Poor? Evidence from the Millennium Challenge Corporation
primary_category: Asset poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the MCC's adoption of growth diagnostics led to a shift towards programmes in fewer sectors concentrated in urban areas with large policy and institutional reform components, similar to earlier structural adjustment programmes.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of the Millennium Challenge Corporation's (MCC) adoption of growth diagnostics on its development investments in low-income countries between 2007 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Development planners should employ inclusive growth diagnostics that identify and target constraints to achieve pro-poor growth, ensuring that development investments are scaled up in urban areas with the greatest potential for poverty reduction.

Field: Producer price index; Macroeconomics; Economics; Price index; Poverty; World economy; Food policy; Food prices; Price level; Food security; Monetary economics
Keywords: food prices; food policy; price indices; food security, poverty
Title: Getting Real About Food Prices
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the real price of food has not fallen as much as expected, especially for poor consumers, due to their high share of food expenditure and indirect effects of income growth on consumption patterns.
What_was_studied: The 2008 price spike in world grain prices and its effects on food security and poverty between 2008 and 2013 in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the vulnerability of low-income households to food price fluctuations by developing and using different price indices that account for differences between consumer groups, and scaling up social protection programs to protect the poor from price shocks.

Field: Vietnamese; Political science; Population; Global climate; Economic growth; Authoritarianism
Keywords: Development interventions; forests; highland development; indigenous peoples; REDD+; safeguards; Vietnam
Title: Lost in authoritarian development: Have global climate deals and the aid community sacrificed the Vietnamese highland population?
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that embeddedness is of key importance for marginal population groups in authoritarian regimes, where social safeguards are difficult to monitor, and technocratic development plans may subject them to harmful consequences.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examines the implications of climate-related interventions for ethnic minority communities in the highlands of Vietnam during a specific time period, using a comprehensive household survey and in-depth interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the need to prioritize social safeguards and community engagement in climate-related interventions, especially in authoritarian regimes, to avoid exacerbating existing inequalities and ensure that development plans are inclusive and sustainable.

Field: Voucher; Economic rent; Government; Economics; Technocracy; Agricultural policy; Incentive; Development economics; Economic growth; Subsidy; Politics
Title: Beyond Technocratic Debates: The Significance and Transience of Political Incentives in the Malawi Farm Input Subsidy Programme (FISP)
primary_category: Asset poverty; Government policies
What_was_found: The research found that two streams of rents associated with the FISP were used to generate support for the first-term government of President Mutharika, with very different implications for program efficiency. One stream stopped abruptly in 2009.
What_was_studied: The Malawi FISP was examined to understand the role of subsidies in African agricultural policy and how political incentives influence input-subsidy voucher distribution, with a focus on the period from 2005 to 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that political incentives play a crucial role in determining subsidy outcomes and can change dramatically over time. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize evaluating the political motivations behind input-subsidy programs to ensure efficient poverty reduction.

Field: Welfare; Empirical research; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Asset (economics); Tanzania; Inheritance; Sub saharan; Demographic economics; Economic growth
Title: Widowhood and Asset Inheritance in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Empirical Evidence from 15 Countries
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Across the 15 DHS countries, less than half of widows report inheriting any assets; the proportion reporting inheriting the majority of assets is lower.
What_was_studied: This article explores asset inheritance among widows using two data sources: (i) nationally representative demographic and health survey (DHS) data from 15 sub-Saharan African countries, and (ii) a 13-year longitudinal panel from the Kagera region in north-west Tanzania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Findings from Kagera indicate that the value of inheritance is significant in determining changes in long-term household welfare. Therefore, social protection policies and programs should prioritize addressing discrimination against widows in asset inheritance to break the cycle of poverty for themselves and their children.

Field: Latin Americans; Political science; Poverty; Pension; Aged population; Incidence (epidemiology); Development economics
Title: Can Latin America Protect the Elderly with Non‐Contributory Programmes? The Case of Uruguay
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the incidence of poverty among the aged population in Uruguay is lower than among any other age group, the conditions for accessing contributory pensions have been significantly tightened in the past decade, which could deteriorate the situation in the future.
What_was_studied: This article assesses several options for reforming the existing non-contributory pension program in Uruguay, using data from the 2010s and focusing on the elderly population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high proportion of elderly receiving contributory pensions and the potential deterioration of their situation, policymakers should prioritize expanding non-contributory pension programs to ensure that all elderly individuals have access to a basic level of income security.

Field: Liberalism (international relations); Private sector; Political economy; Political science; Globalization; Private sector development; Development aid; Inequality; Modernization theory; Sustainability
Title: Dichotomy of development aid’s ambition and neoliberal imperatives: A case‐study of private‐sector development in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while development aid can lead to economic growth and job creation, it can also exacerbate income poverty and gender disparities in impoverished countries like Bangladesh. Furthermore, the report revealed that the neo-liberal Imperative for private sector development can create tension between globalization and inequality, as well as friction between poverty reduction and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This field report investigates how private sector development in Bangladesh co-creates globalized modernization, and how this process affects poverty reduction and inequality through development aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve the impact of development aid resources in Bangladesh, policymakers should prioritize quality control and reconsider the balance between neo-liberal Imperative and equality ambitions to address the challenges of poverty reduction and sustainable development.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Theme (narrative); Malaise; Child Well-Being; Research questions; Development economics
Title: Impacts of Economic Crises on Child Well‐being
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that macro-level crises can have long-lasting impacts on children's well-being, including increased poverty and reduced access to education and healthcare. The findings suggest that policy responses should prioritize addressing the root causes of these crises, such as economic inequality and instability.
What_was_studied: The impact of macro-level crises on children's micro-level experiences of poverty and well-being in the context of short-term global economic shocks and longer-term economic malaise, using a theme issue with six empirical articles.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective policy responses to mitigate the impacts of macro-level crises on children's well-being, expand access to education and healthcare, and prioritize addressing the root causes of these crises.

Authors: Emerta A. Aragie; Rui Benfica; Karl Pauw; Josée Randriamamonjy; James Thurlow
Field: Computable general equilibrium; Economics; Agriculture; Tanzania; Investment (military); Public economics; Poverty; Business; Psychological intervention; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Politics; Political science; Law; Psychology; Ecology; Macroeconomics; Psychiatry; Biology
Title: Assessing investment priorities for inclusive agricultural transformation in Tanzania
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Investments in improved inputs and extension for horticulture and cash crops show the highest potential for diet quality and employment creation, while investments in livestock services consistently rank high across multiple objectives. Reallocating resources towards more cost-effective interventions can significantly enhance development effectiveness.
What_was_studied: This study assesses the impact of alternative agricultural interventions on development outcomes in Tanzania between 2019 and 2028, using a computable general equilibrium model linked to microsimulation modules.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Tanzania should prioritize investments in improved inputs and extension for horticulture and cash crops to boost diet quality and employment creation, while reallocating resources towards more cost-effective interventions to maximize development effectiveness.

Field: Economic policy; Debt; Business; Poverty reduction; Key issues; Sustainability
Title: What’s Wrong with the HIPC Initiative and What’s Next?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the HIPC initiative's aim to achieve debt sustainability is unlikely to permit a lasting exit from unsustainable debt for many countries, and may lead to a decline in traditional development assistance. Specifically, it was found that the current framework is unfair and may not be effective in reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the problems of the enhanced HIPC initiative and outlines possible steps towards a more efficient debt and poverty reduction initiative for the period 2000-2018, using data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the HIPC initiative needs to be revised to prioritize debt cancellation over debt sustainability, and to provide more financial support for poverty reduction programs. Additionally, traditional development assistance should be scaled up to address intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development.

Field: Political economy; Ideology; Political science; Corruption; School of thought; Grassroots; Underdevelopment; Democracy; Political culture; International development
Title: African school of thought: The missing ideology in finding a solution to sub‐Saharan African insecurity
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that consensual democracy is sincere in post-colonial Africa for true independence, and that ideological theories, the epistemology of development programs, and the philosophy of choice are overlooked in current African political cultures, which habitually disregard grassroots voices.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes post-colonial sub-Saharan Africa's collapse of consensual democracy as an ideology and system of governance, with a focus on poverty, greed, corruption, political instability, conflicts, and dependence on exporting primary products from 2008 to 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize an African school of thought that incorporates the inclusion of ideological functions transcending political cultures, underdevelopment, and insecurities in sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Population; Development economics; Fishery; Fishing; Immigration
Title: Investigating poverty through the lens of riches: immigration and segregation in Indian capture fisheries
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the blue revolution in South India not only provided opportunities for a growing fishing population but also offered chances for immigrants to work in the industry, mainly in lower-level positions. The research also showed variations between geographical regions and sub-sectors, which can be attributed to non-governmental institutional control patterns.
