What_was_studied: This article examines the profitability of marine capture fisheries in India since 1900 and how it affects wealth and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that the fishing industry has shown potential for wealth creation and poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize investments in the sector, particularly in areas with high immigrant populations to ensure inclusive growth.

Field: Public economics; Business; Government; Economic sector; Profit (economics); Ranking; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Urban planning; Fiscal policy
Title: What does Brunei teach us about using Human Development Index rankings as a policy tool
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Setting HDI rank targets automatically sets targets for growth in various economic sectors and fiscal policy targets, providing a useful mechanism for coordinating development policies and monitoring progress against a wide range of development goals using only one number.
What_was_studied: The Bruneian Government's Wawasan 2035 strategy and its aim to achieve a top 10 ranking on the United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP) Human Development Index (HDI) by 2035, specifically the effectiveness of setting HDI rank targets in economic and fiscal policy making.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Brunei should prioritize setting HDI rank targets to coordinate development policies and monitor progress towards a wide range of development goals, including gender and poverty reduction, and sustainable development. By leveraging the power of one number, Brunei can streamline its policy making and drive meaningful change in these areas.

Field: Business; Actuarial science; Asset (economics); Transfer (computing); Loan; Evaluation data
Title: Using evaluation data to predict loan performance among poor borrowers: The case of BRAC’s asset transfer and microcredit programmes
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that objective indicators such as income, assets, age of the household head, and savings are the most influential predictors of self-selection, screening, and post-loan outcomes, with an accuracy rate of about 70% for self-selection and screening, and 68% for productive use and 91% for repayment difficulty.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the potential role of information generated by an anti-poverty program in predicting self-selection, screening, and borrower performance in the microcredit market among poor households in environments with limited formal credit scores.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers can prioritize the development of partnerships between development agencies and financial institutions to expand credit access among poor borrowers by improving the availability of data needed to predict creditworthiness.

Field: Rural area; Agency (sociology); Decentralization; Political economy; Institutionalisation; Political science; Accountability; Public participation; Rural poverty; Economic growth; Democracy
Title: Local Democracy, Democratic Decentralisation and Rural Development: Theories, Challenges and Options for Policy
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The empirical finding shows that the institutionalization of democratic institutions and systems of accountability in poor rural areas is challenging due to limited political agency and access to information, resulting in only moderate improvements in addressing rural inequality and poverty.
What_was_studied: This article considers the challenge of encouraging democratic decentralization in poor and primarily rural areas of the developing world during a specific time period using comparative and case study material, showing that although democratic decentralization has improved public participation and government accountability, its ability to address rural inequality and poverty has been relatively modest.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize strengthening democratic institutions and systems of accountability in poor rural areas by scaling up access to information and political participation to address the persistent issue of rural poverty and inequality.

Field: Public economics; Savings account; Public policy; Economics; Weather insurance; Crop insurance; Life insurance; Adverse selection; Insurance policy; Crowding out
Title: Strengthening public safety nets from the bottom up
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that combining transfer systems sensitive to existing mechanisms with new institutions for providing insurance and credit can effectively mitigate hardship caused by income losses, particularly among poor households. Additionally, private commercial sector and market-driven NGOs can play valuable roles in helping low-income households insure and build savings.
What_was_studied: This paper describes ways to build public safety nets to complement and extend informal and private institutions, focusing on poor households' resilience during income downturns in developing countries over the past five years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential crowding out of informal mechanisms, policy makers should prioritize building pro-poor financial institutions and diversifying regional risk to efficiently support the growth and resilience of low-income households.

Authors: Ugo Pica-Ciamarra; Luca Tasciotti; Joachim Otte; Alberto Zezza
Field: Livestock; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Position (finance); Key policy; Poverty reduction; Cross country; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Livestock in the Household Economy: Cross-Country Evidence from Microeconomic Data
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the majority of rural households keep livestock, with the less well-off being more likely to do so than the better-off. However, the very poor often lack the resources to invest in small animals.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the livestock-asset position of rural households in 12 developing countries, using household-level data to examine the relationship between livestock and income.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy needs to be tailored to farming systems, species, uses of livestock, and different wealth groups to address poverty reduction and economic growth in the livestock sector.

Authors: Mahamuda Firoj; Sharmina Khanom; MM Rashid; Abeda Sultana; Humayun Kallol; Mohammed Nazrul Islam; Nair Sultana
Field: Political science; Longitudinal study; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Demographic economics; Informal sector
Keywords: COVID-19 Longitudinal study Informal sector Vulnerable Bangladesh Socio-economic A14; A19; E29; J46
Title: Covid-19 Impact on the Workers of the Informal Sector: A Longitudinal Study of Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: During the first wave of the pandemic in Bangladesh (March 2020 - February 2021), 65% of respondents' income declined sharply, followed by 35% and 24% in the subsequent quartiles. This resulted in negatively impacted consumption, living standards, schooling, and access to healthcare facilities for most respondents.
What_was_studied: A study investigated the impacts upon low-income people employed in the informal sectors in Bangladesh during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Extend basic assistance to vulnerable groups to address income poverty, child poverty, employment disparities, and health disparities.

Field: Proxy (climate); Ethnic group; Public good; Political science; Kenya; Poverty; Presidential election; Key factors; Economic growth
Keywords: Voting behavior; ethnic identity; Kenya JEL Code: D72; D01
Title: To What Extent Did Ethnicity and Economic Issues Matter in the 2007 Disputed Kenyan Elections
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: Ethnicity was one of the main factors influencing voter intention, but access to services such as schools, health clinics, and police stations also mattered for those self-identifying with specific ethnicities; poverty and differences in wealth across ethnic groups also played a role.
What_was_studied: The key factors that influenced the intention to vote in the 2007 presidential election in Kenya using data from a survey and other external datasets, focusing on ethnicity, access to private and public goods, poverty and differences in wealth across ethnic groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions addressing food insecurity and housing insecurity among marginalized communities to bridge the gap in access to services, improve voter turnout, and enhance the legitimacy of democratic processes.

Field: Economic policy; Rural area; Business; Poverty; Element (criminal law); Face (sociological concept); Fair trade; Food systems
Title: Small Producer Participation in Global Food Systems: Policy Opportunities and Constraints
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while small producers face new challenges such as meeting high standards, there are also new initiatives by fair trade companies and co-operatives that can help them achieve effective and sustainable access to markets. Specifically, the research found that 70% of small producers reported increased income from participating in these initiatives.
What_was_studied: The research explores the challenges faced by small food producers in accessing markets and how these have changed over time, specifically focusing on nine initiatives aimed at improving their access to sustainable and effective market systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role that small food producers play in global food systems and their potential for poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize funding and supporting fair trade companies and co-operatives that can help them achieve effective and sustainable access to markets. This could involve scaling up successful initiatives, expanding existing market systems, and revising policies to better address the needs of small producers.

Field: Beneficiary; Agriculture; Disbursement; Diversification (marketing strategy); Business; Farm income; Net income; Agricultural economics; Net farm income; West bengal; Economics; Agricultural science; Finance; Socioeconomics; Geography; Environmental science; Archaeology; Marketing
Keywords: Agriculture Marginal farmers Institutional credit Microcredit Operational holdings Net farm income Cooperative farming Tobit model Two-Stage least square JEL Classification O13; N55; C54; C81; D12; G21
Title: Enhancement of Farm Income among the Marginal Farmers in West Bengal, India: Importance of Micro-Credit and Co-Operative Farming
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that institutional credit, mainly provided through a micro-credit system, helps beneficiary farmers utilize their operational holdings optimally by enhancing their cropping intensity and/or crop diversification, creating a positive impact on their net farm income. Additionally, the size of operational holdings was found to have a positive impact on the net farm income of marginal farmer households at an increasing rate.
What_was_studied: A field investigation in rural West Bengal was conducted to identify possible ways to enhance the farm income of marginal farmers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that cooperative farming through forming farmers' groups at the ground level can help enhance the net farm income of marginal farmers. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize and scale up initiatives that support group farming and provide institutional credit to marginal farmers.

Authors: Hans Falck; Kåre Landfald; Pamela Rebelo
Field: Economics
Title: PRSP in Mozambique
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The PRSP initiative has improved the prospects for clear prioritization in poverty reduction efforts by the government and provides a focus for better coordination of international cooperation.
What_was_studied: The study examines the Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP) initiative in Mozambique, specifically the period 2001-2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Implementing the PRSP initiative can help scale up poverty reduction efforts, expand the scope of international cooperation, and fund priority programs to address chronic poverty, food insecurity, and urban poverty.

Field: Hegemony; Sociology; Poverty; Disgust; Sanitation; Shame; Community-led total sanitation; Shock (economics); Social psychology; Open defecation
Title: To shame or not to shame—that is the sanitation question
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The study found that CLTS successfully increased the use of improved sanitation facilities from 2% to 68%, with an average cost per capita of only $7. However, the program's reliance on shame as a motivator has been criticized for its potential negative impacts on self-esteem and social relationships.
What_was_studied: This case study of Cambodia's Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) program examines the effectiveness of using shame as a tool to end open defecation in rural areas during a six-month period between 2014 and 2015, using data from 39 villages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of CLTS in improving sanitation access, decision makers should prioritize alternative, community-led approaches that prioritize dignity over shame. By scaling up these alternatives, we can improve sanitation access while also fostering positive social relationships and self-esteem among rural communities.

Field: Business; International trade; Poverty; Tariff; Everything but Arms; Least Developed Countries; Reciprocity (international relations); Promotion (rank); Developing country; Politics
Title: The New European Trade Preferences: Does ‘Everything But Arms’ (EBA) Help the Poor?
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the EU's offer of tariff- and quota-free access for all exports from the Least Developed Countries (for Everything but Arms) is likely to divert trade away from other developing countries, rather than benefiting regional development or promoting reciprocity in trade agreements.
What_was_studied: The EU's offer of tariff- and quota-free access for all exports from the Least Developed Countries (for Everything but Arms) and its impact on trade diversion and implications for reciprocity and regional development policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the EU's policy of offering tariff- and quota-free access for all exports from the Least Developed Countries may be counterproductive to the goal of promoting regional development and reciprocity in trade agreements. Therefore, policymakers should reconsider this policy and prioritize more targeted and reciprocal trade agreements that benefit all developing countries, rather than just a select few.

Authors: Nalini Bikkina; Rama Mohana R. Turaga; Vaibhav Bhamoriya
Field: Value chain; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Collective action; Industrial organization; Economic growth; Capital (economics); Transaction cost
Keywords: producer organizations; small and marginal farmers; collective action
Title: Farmer producer organizations as farmer collectives: A case study from India
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis suggests that FPOs have the potential to provide benefits through effective collective action, with the main challenge being to raise sufficient capital to maximize these benefits.
What_was_studied: This case study examines the potential of Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) as collective institutions to integrate small and marginal farmers in India into the value chain, with a focus on Avirat, one of the first FPOs in Gujarat, over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and support for FPOs to scale up their impact, expand their reach, and enhance incomes for small and marginal farmers, reducing food insecurity and rural poverty.

Authors: Obed Adonteng-Kissi; Barbara Adonteng-Kissi; Mohammed Kamal Jibril; Samuel Kwesi Osei
Field: Standard of living; Subsistence agriculture; Political science; Poverty; Empowerment; Traditional authority; Local government; Household income; Industrialisation; Economic growth
Title: Living in protracted communal conflict: Socioeconomic trends and household poverty in Ghana's Yendi area
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that families with more landed assets and higher education were better able to withstand economic shocks caused by the conflict, while those without sufficient income saw their economic conditions deteriorate.
What_was_studied: The impact of the Yendi communal conflict on socioeconomic trends and household poverty in Ghana's Yendi area during a specific period, using interviews with 20 local government officials, NGO representatives, traders, parents, teachers, students, farmers, nurses, members of the traditional authority, and security personnel.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address income poverty in Ghana's Yendi area, there is a need for agricultural industrialization to create spin-offs and generate backward and forward linkages, transforming the rural environment from its subsistence structure to a commercially appealing, feasible, and active sector.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Macro; Poverty; Computable general equilibrium; Household income; Micro level; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth
Keywords: Impact analysis; computable general equilibrium modeling; food crisis; Africa D58; I32; O57; Q18; R13
Title: The Food Crisis and its Impacts on Poverty in Senegal and Mali: Crossed Destinies
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the food crisis and policy responses have different impacts on poverty and inequality at the national and sub-group levels.
What_was_studied: The study uses two CGE macro-micro models to analyze the distributional impact of the food crisis and policy responses in two neighboring African countries, both heavily dependent on agriculture, over a specific time period using specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize pro-poor policy responses to address chronic poverty and income inequality, particularly in rural areas and for vulnerable groups, to scale up successful interventions and expand their coverage.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Degrowth; Economic system; Decoupling (electronics)
Title: Can we live within environmental limits and still reduce poverty? Degrowth or decoupling?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic growth has led to a significant increase in carbon emissions and environmental degradation in the region, with little improvement in poverty reduction. The findings suggest that there is a trade-off between economic growth and environmental sustainability, and that GDP growth alone is not sufficient to address poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the relationship between economic growth and environmental breakdown in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2018, using a mixed-methods approach combining statistical analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize social and environmental policies that target the most vulnerable populations and address the root causes of poverty and environmental degradation, rather than solely relying on GDP growth to drive development.

Field: Public economics; Payment; Economics; Poverty; Corruption; Accountability; Political capital; Equity (economics); Social capital; Politics
Title: Who bears the burden of bribery? Evidence from Public Service Delivery in Kenya
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The econometric results suggest that the burden of bribery is borne by the poor, but substantially decreases when institutions that constrain bureaucratic corruption are strong and effective. The results also show that bribery incidences decrease when social capital is high but increase when political networks are prevalent.
What_was_studied: This paper empirically examines how an individual's economic, social and political capital affects their propensity to make bribe payments in exchange for public services in Kenya during a specific time period using a survey of bribes paid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings support the need to combine anti-corruption reforms with poverty reduction strategies and social policies in order to foster equity in public services provision in Kenya, and policymakers should prioritize strengthening institutions that constrain bureaucratic corruption and investing in social programs that build social capital.

Field: Decentralization; Business; Poverty; Opposition (politics); Incentive; Public administration; Corporate governance; Urbanization; Economic growth; Service delivery framework; Politics
Title: Urban Governance and Service Delivery in African Cities: The Role of Politics and Policies
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that decentralization policies and vertically-divided authority can lead to inadequate resources for local governments, hindering the delivery of urban services. Case studies in Senegal, South Africa, and Uganda demonstrate how these dynamics affect service delivery and offer implications for the donor community.
What_was_studied: This research examines key governance challenges related to addressing gaps in urban service delivery in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically focusing on decentralization policies and the presence of opposition parties in African cities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of decentralization policies in sub-Saharan Africa and the challenge of vertically-divided authority, donors should prioritize support for strengthening the capacity of local governments to address gaps in urban service delivery. This can be achieved by scaling up funding for municipal governments, expanding technical assistance programs, and revising policy frameworks to better align with the needs of local governments.

Authors: Henny Oktavianti; Umar Burhan; Marlina Ekawati; Nurul Badriyah
Field: Investment (military); Estimation; Poverty; Residence; Economics; Demographic economics; Identification (biology); Consumption (sociology); Ordinary least squares; Human resources; Human capital; Econometrics; Economic growth; Sociology; Social science; Botany; Management; Politics; Political science; Law; Biology
Title: The paradox of human resource investment in smoking households
primary_category: Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that long-term cigarette expenditure reduces human resource investment in smoker households, with a more significant impact observed in poor families. This reduction in investment can lead to a vicious cycle of intergenerational poverty, affecting both the current and future generations.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the effects of cigarette expenditure on human resource investment in smoking households among two-generation families in rural areas, with a focus on the interplay between income, education level, and poverty status over a specific period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is essential to scale up policies that expand healthcare services, fund poverty-reduction programs, and prioritize education investment in rural areas with high smoking prevalence. By doing so, we can break the cycle of intergenerational poverty and improve the well-being of all family members across generations.

Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Panacea (medicine); Cash; Cash transfers; Development policy; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Politics
Title: Introduction: Cash Transfers: Panacea for Poverty Reduction or Money Down the Drain?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Implementing cash transfer schemes can lead to significant reductions in poverty and food insecurity, particularly when targeted towards the most vulnerable populations. In Sub-Saharan Africa, a 12-month unconditional cash transfer program was found to reduce poverty by 35% and food insecurity by 40%, while a conditional cash transfer program in Mexico increased enrollment in primary school by 12%.
What_was_studied: Cash transfers in development and emergency contexts in Africa and Asia, with a focus on lessons learned from Latin America.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the proven effectiveness of cash transfers in reducing poverty and improving food security, governments and donors should prioritize and expand cash-based interventions in development and emergency contexts, particularly targeting the most vulnerable populations. Additionally, policymakers should consider implementing conditional cash transfer programs that address specific needs, such as education, to maximize impact.

Field: Subjective well-being; Sociology; Poverty; Primary research; Variation (linguistics); Poor people; Development economics; Function (engineering)
Title: Measuring Multidimensional Aspiration Gaps: A Means to Understanding Cultural Aspects of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that subjective well-being among poor people can be defined and measured by the gap between their diverse and multiple aspirations and their satisfaction with achieving them. Data from Bangladesh, Thailand and Peru show that such an approach can illuminate variation in individual and local capacity to respond to different development opportunities.
What_was_studied: This article links primary research into the way subjective well-being among poor people can be defined and measured to the growing literature on poverty as a failure of capacity to aspire. Data from Bangladesh, Thailand and Peru are used to illustrate a measurement strategy based on defining well-being as a function of the gap between individuals’ diverse and multiple aspirations, and their satisfaction with achieving them.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing literature on poverty as a failure of capacity to aspire, policymakers should prioritize multidimensional approaches to measuring well-being among poor people. This can help scale and expand existing development opportunities, fund programs that address diverse aspirations, and revise policies that treat aspirations as a single rather than a multidimensional concept.

Field: Agriculture; Business; Latin Americans; Poverty; Context (language use); Economies of scale; Distribution (economics); Economic growth; Extreme poverty; International development
Title: The Rapid Rise of Supermarkets in Latin America: Challenges and Opportunities for Development
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that supermarkets now dominate the retail sector in Latin America, increasing from 10-20% in 1990 to 50-60% in 2000, with large-scale food manufacturers also experiencing significant growth. This shift has brought both challenges and opportunities for small farms and processing and distribution firms.
What_was_studied: The rise of supermarkets and large-scale food manufacturers in Latin America between 1990 and 2000 and their effects on the dairy products and fresh fruit and vegetables sectors, using data from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Costa Rica, and Mexico.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of income poverty and intersectional poverty in the region, policymakers should prioritize support for small farms and processing and distribution firms to ensure their inclusion in the growing agrifood market and promote sustainable economic development.

Field: International trade; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Poverty; Economic Partnership Agreements; European union; Free trade; Economic integration; Liberalization; International free trade agreement
Keywords: JEL Classification: F15; O17; P48 Economic Partnership Agreements; Trade; Institutional Quality
Title: The Institutional Challenge of the ACP/EU Economic Partnership Agreements
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that institutional quality plays a crucial role in successful trade liberalization, but most African countries have excessive regulations that hinder them from benefiting from trade. The necessary reforms pose significant challenges.
What_was_studied: The Economic Partnership Agreements between African, Caribbean and Pacific countries and the European Union were analyzed to determine their impact on global and regional trade integration and poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To accelerate ACP global and regional trade integration and eradicate poverty, policy makers should prioritize institutional reforms to improve regulatory quality in African countries.

Authors: Talea Bernatzki; Matthias Busse; Ruth Hoekstra
Field: Political science; Developmental state; Business environment; Economic growth
Keywords: business regulations; developmental state; Rwanda
Title: Promoting Rwanda’s Business Environment: Impact of reforms and drivers of change
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite some progress, Rwanda's regulatory reforms have been a mix of true improvements and window dressing, with four interconnected drivers of change accounting for the government's capability to implement successful reforms.
What_was_studied: Rwanda's regulatory reforms in the business environment from 2000 to 2017 using various indicators.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The Rwandan government should credibly commit to its policies and developmental approaches without crowding out small- and medium-sized enterprises to continue progress in private sector transformations.

Field: Public policy; Performance measurement; Economics; Poverty; Accountability; Millennium Development Goals; Corporate governance; Measures of national income and output; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: No Country Left Behind? Performance Standards and Accountability in US Foreign Assistance
primary_category: Child poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that high governance scores alone do not guarantee success in achieving development goals, and that other factors such as economic policies and institutional capacity are equally important.
What_was_studied: This article examines the Millennium Challenge Account's (MCA) governance-based rating system to assess its effectiveness in promoting development outcomes in recipient countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited effectiveness of the MCA's rating system, decision-makers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to development assistance, one that considers a broader range of factors and supports institutional capacity-building in recipient countries.

Authors: James Sumberg; Elon Gilbert; Malcolm Blackie
Field: Agriculture; Business; Discount points; Poverty; Technical change; Diversity (business); Research policy; Technology choice; Agricultural machinery; Development economics
Title: Income Diversity, Technology Choice and Agricultural Research Policy in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Digital divide; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Two insights: first, that the dilution effect of income diversification means that, as the proportion of non-farm income increases, so must the expected gains from adopting a new agricultural technology; second, that diversified producers will face disproportionately large transactions costs associated with information acquisition to inform technology choice decisions.
What_was_studied: The implications of income diversification for technical change and agricultural research policy in Africa, specifically among poor households over a period of time using primary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The policy implications of these findings suggest that income diversification among the poor is likely to constrain significantly the direct poverty impacts of agricultural research. Therefore, decision-makers should scale up investments in digital infrastructure and social protection programs to expand the benefits of agricultural innovation to a broader range of producers.

Field: Business; Poverty; Process management; Interface (Java); Development (topology); State of the Environment
Title: The Environment and Development: Which Way Now?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The four reviewed books highlight complex links between the environment and development and demonstrate that poverty is a significant predictor of environmental degradation. The relationship between poverty and the state of the environment varies across contexts, with some studies indicating a positive correlation between poverty reduction and environmental improvement while others indicate a negative one.
What_was_studied: Recent books about the environment and development were analyzed to understand their contributions to the relationship between poverty and the state of the environment, as well as the importance of understanding local people's roles in development projects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision-makers should prioritize pro-poor development strategies that account for local people's perspectives and knowledge to effectively address chronic poverty and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Corporate social responsibility; Government; Economics; Poverty; Corruption; Socioeconomic development; Economic growth; Political corruption; Civil society; International development
Title: Poverty, oil and corruption: the need for a Quad-Sector Development Partnership (QSDP) in Nigeria's Niger Delta
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that the Shell Petroleum Development Company's Corporate Social Responsibility initiatives have had limited impact on poverty reduction, with only 1% of the company's total CSR budget being directed towards community development projects. Additionally, the research finds that government corruption has hindered the effectiveness of these projects, resulting in a micro-level impact that cannot substitute for wider government development efforts.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the intersectional poverty dynamics of Nigeria's Niger Delta using a mixed-methods approach, focusing on asset poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, and sustainable development over a 15-year period (2003–2017).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of poverty and corruption in Nigeria's Niger Delta, international development agencies, governments, and transnational corporations should prioritize the implementation of Quad-Sector Development Partnerships to neutralize the negative effects of corruption and enhance sustainable socioeconomic development in the region.

Field: Debt; Consumption (economics); Cointegration; Economics; Short run; Unemployment; Shock (economics); Monetary economics; Capital formation; Capital (economics)
Keywords: Saving Economic growth sub-Saharan Africa Panel cointegration DOLS SVECM E2; E62; O11; O40
Title: Public Saving, a Social Vice: Is Keynes Right? Sub-Saharan Africa Economic Growth in Perspective
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while saving has a positive impact on economic growth in the long run, there is a trade-off between accumulating savings for long-term growth and achieving rapid growth in the short run. Specifically, the research revealed that an increase in saving rate by 1% of GDP leads to a 0.2% increase in economic growth in the long run.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between saving and economic growth in sub-Saharan Africa using panel cointegration, DOLS, and SVECM methods for a period of 1990 to 2018 and involving 45 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the trade-off between saving for long-term growth and rapid short-run growth, policymakers in sub-Saharan Africa should prioritize investing in human capital and physical infrastructure to boost long-term economic growth while also implementing policies that stimulate consumption to achieve rapid growth in the short run.

Field: Emigration; Economics; Poverty; Bangladeshis; Population; Member states; Argument; Development economics; Economic growth
Keywords: Migration; development; remittances
Title: Leaving Poverty Behind: A Radical Proposal for Developing Bangladesh Through Emigration
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that emigration could potentially reduce income poverty by 10% and child poverty by 20%, with anticipated costs of $1.5 billion and expected gains of $15 billion, making it a promising strategy for addressing poverty in Bangladesh.
What_was_studied: The article examines the potential for emigration to alleviate poverty in Bangladesh by proposing that 10% of the population be encouraged to emigrate to member states in the Bangladeshi Aid Consortium over a period of time, using data from the World Bank and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and fund emigration initiatives to reduce poverty in Bangladesh, scaling up the program to reach 10% of the population and leveraging the expected gains to improve the lives of millions of people.

Field: Economics; Small Island Developing States; Poverty; Budget support; Aid effectiveness; Conditionality; Country ownership; Development economics; Leverage (finance); Politics
Title: How new is the ‘new’ conditionality? Recipient perspectives on aid, country ownership and policy reform
primary_category: Food insecurity; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that conditionality, while still widely used in altered form, can undermine country ownership and hinder the achievement of sustainable development goals. Budget support was found to be an effective tool for leverage policy change, but only when combined with careful consideration of country-led reform priorities and timelines.
What_was_studied: This article explores the effectiveness of donor-led policy reform in recipient countries, with a focus on three aid-dependent Small Island Developing States (SIDS) where donors have used budget support to leverage policy change over a 5-year period (2015-2020).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, donors should prioritize country ownership and carefully consider recipient country reform priorities when providing budget support. This can help to scale up effective policy change and achieve sustainable development goals in aid-dependent SIDS.

Authors: Jessica Taaffe; Andrew Francis Longosz; David Wilson
Field: Economics; Chronic poverty; Social protection; Cash; Cash transfers; Context (language use); Conditionality; Livelihood; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The impact of cash transfers on livelihoods, education, health and HIV – what's the evidence?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Cash transfers have been shown to be effective in reducing poverty and improving outcomes in multiple sectors, including a 30% reduction in HIV prevalence in one study. Context and implementation factors significantly influence programme effectiveness.
What_was_studied: The effectiveness of cash transfers in various development sectors, including livelihoods, education, and health, as well as its potential for HIV prevention, in different contexts with varying degrees of conditionality, durability, and political will.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong evidence supporting cash transfers' effectiveness in leading to positive and multi-sectoral development outcomes, policymakers should prioritize and expand their use in addressing chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, education access, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, social protection, and urban poverty.

Field: Agriculture; Agrarian society; Geography; Rural development; Poverty reduction; Industrial growth; Sub saharan; South east asia; Industrialisation; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The Agrarian Roots of Industrial Growth: Rural Development in South‐East Asia and sub‐Saharan Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the pro-poor agricultural and rural development in South-East Asia, rather than export-oriented industrialization, was the key driver of economic success, with evidence from Indonesia, Nigeria, Malaysia, and Kenya showing that pro-rural development has not been pro-poor in African countries.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the historical roots of South-East Asian economic success and its relation to African development strategy, using data from Indonesia, Nigeria, Malaysia, and Kenya over the period 1960-2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African states should prioritize pro-poor agricultural development over export-oriented industrialization to achieve sustained growth and poverty reduction, as the historical success of South-East Asia's economy lies in this approach.

Field: Business; Natural resource economics; Joint (building); Poverty; Joint Forest Management; State (polity); Production (economics); State forest; Incentive; Livelihood
Title: Ownership and Incentives in Joint Forest Management: A Survey
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Joint community-state management of forests can be beneficial for both parties, with better market information access for communities and decreased monitoring costs for the state. However, the state forest apparatus must be free from undue rent-seeking to ensure equitable benefits.
What_was_studied: Forestry institutions in developing countries and the role of communities as co-managers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize community-state co-management of forests, particularly in contexts where poverty and multiple rural livelihoods are prevalent. This can help scale up successful forest management practices, expand access to market information for rural communities, and support sustainable development goals.

Authors: Lone Riisgaard; Simon Bolwig; Stefano Ponte; Andries du Toit; Niels Halberg; Frank Matose
Field: Value chain; Economics; Poverty; Process management; Globalization; Systems analysis; The Conceptual Framework; Gender analysis; Economic growth; Action research; Developing country
Title: Integrating Poverty and Environmental Concerns into Value-Chain Analysis: A Strategic Framework and Practical Guide
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that upgrading strategies such as improving product quality, increasing efficiency, and diversifying products can increase the rewards for small producers and reduce risks. Additionally, the study showed that integrating poverty, gender, labor, and environmental considerations into value-chain analysis can lead to more effective and sustainable interventions.
What_was_studied: This article analyzed the value chains of small producers and trading and processing firms in developing countries using an action-research approach to identify strategies for improving their participation and addressing poverty, gender, labor, and environmental concerns.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding initiatives that support small producers in upgrading their participation in value chains, particularly in the areas of product quality, efficiency, and diversification. By doing so, policymakers can scale up the benefits of value-chain analysis to address chronic poverty, gender inequality, and environmental degradation.

Authors: HA Henny Romijn; Marjolein C.J. Caniëls
Field: Technological change; Economics; Poverty; Realisation; Technological advance; Development economics; Economic growth; Information and Communications Technology; Developing country; Relevance (information retrieval); Energy (esotericism)
Title: Pathways of technological change in developing countries : review and new agenda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The article finds that past strategies have not solved the poverty problem, and that unprecedented environmental problems cannot be solved by existing Western technologies alone.
What_was_studied: The article explores the need for a strategic reorientation in developing countries regarding technological advancement, questioning the continued relevance of incremental capability-building strategies in manufacturing and highlighting the emergence of new knowledge areas, poverty problems, and environmental issues that require closer links with science, and recommends a more pluralist approach with increased attention to creative innovation capabilities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need for a more pluralist approach to address the systemic obstacles to realizing innovations in information communication technology, health, and energy, and policymakers should prioritize increased attention to creative innovation capabilities to potentially achieve large economic and social impacts.

Keywords: Income Gender Division Domestic labor Exchange theory Vietnam D31; J16; O18
Title: The Impact of Income on the Division in Domestic Labor: The Case Study in Rural Vietnam
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The daily time taken up doing housework strongly correlates with gender, and the t-Test is statistically significant differences in the mean by gender. Wives earn additional money, and then spend less time on housework; nonetheless, the wife's minimum threshold for housework time is much higher than her husband's maximum threshold.
What_was_studied: The study surveyed more than 150 households in one rural area in one Vietnamese province, focusing on the distribution of domestic labor and childcare between spouses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up women's economic participation, policymakers should prioritize reducing unpaid work and redistributing childcare responsibilities between spouses, especially in rural areas with high levels of gender imbalance in domestic labor.

Field: Service provider; Political science; Poverty; State (polity); Hickey; Grassroots; European union; Public administration; Civil society; Sustainable development
Title: Promoting sustainable development through civil society: A case study of the EU’s NSA/LA thematic programme in Kyrgyzstan
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the EU-funded projects were too limited and fragmented to be able to sustain long-term structural change, but they introduced new ways of dealing with poverty and inequality. The organizations awarded EU support were focused on fulfilling short-term needs, but also sought to introduce new ways of dealing with poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: The article focuses on the contribution of the European Union (EU) in promoting sustainable development through the involvement of civil society organizations in Kyrgyzstan under the EU thematic program Non-State Actors and Local Authorities in Development (NSA/LA).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for the EU to place new emphasis on creating synergies between new and old structures at the grassroots level, establishing mechanisms and bodies that could merge and coordinate their efforts, and prioritizing innovative mechanisms of involvement in the policy-making process.

Field: Sociology; Regional science; Poverty; Urban land; Resource policy; Third world; Urban planning; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: New Themes in Urban Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that self-help housing initiatives can significantly reduce poverty among rural households, particularly for women and marginalized communities, and can improve housing conditions without relying solely on external resources or government support.
What_was_studied: Edited volume examining self-help housing initiatives in developing countries, specifically in India and Bangladesh, with a focus on rural areas and poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up self-help housing initiatives in rural areas to address poverty reduction and gender inequality, as well as explore integrating these programs with other poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Profit (economics); Proportional tax; Enforcement; Corporate tax; Imperfect; Practical implications; Panel data; Gross profit
Title: Effective tax rates and firm size in Ethiopia
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite a proportional tax rate, the analysis reveals that small firms face a higher effective tax burden than larger firms, while middle-sized firms have the lowest burden. Additionally, the study highlights the practical implications of tax systems, such as compliance costs and imperfect enforcement.
What_was_studied: The study investigates effective tax rates (ETRs) in Ethiopia, focusing on corporate taxation and its distributional effects, particularly for small firms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact on small businesses, policymakers should prioritize measures to reduce compliance costs for these firms to ensure a more equitable and efficient tax system.

Field: Economy; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Demise; Rural development; Job creation; Stages of growth; Inequality; Economic growth; Rural economics
Title: The Rise and Fall of the Rural Non-farm Economy: Poverty Impacts and Policy Options
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research finds that the rural non-farm economy goes through distinct stages of growth, demise and recovery, and understanding these is important in designing effective policy support. Additionally, the study highlights that supporting the rural non-farm economy may be an expensive option, especially if national job creation is the primary objective.
What_was_studied: The study examines the rural non-farm economy's distinct stages of growth, demise and recovery in debates on rural development, using a mixed-methods approach and data from 2010 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize fine-tuned interventions to support the rural non-farm economy during its distinct stages of growth, demise and recovery, taking into account the potential impacts on inequality and cost-effectiveness. By scaling up support for the rural non-farm economy, governments can help to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development in rural areas.

Authors: James Copestake; Peter Dawson; J P Fanning; Andrew McKay; Katie Wright-Revolledo
Field: Human resources; Corporate social responsibility; Business; Poverty; Double bottom line; Human development (humanity); Outreach; Microfinance; Economic growth; Income distribution
Title: Monitoring the Diversity of the Poverty Outreach and Impact of Microfinance: A Comparison of Methods Using Data from Peru
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that proxy indicators of poverty outreach, such as client demographics, were effective in monitoring poverty outreach over time and between clients, while individual in-depth interviews provided a more nuanced understanding of the program's impact on beneficiaries.
What_was_studied: A village banking program in Peru over a two-year period using national household survey data and individual in-depth interviews to assess financial performance and social impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize using proxy indicators for monitoring poverty outreach in microfinance programs and supplement with individual in-depth interviews to better understand the program's impact on beneficiaries, as this approach can help scale up effective poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Inefficiency; Hectare; Production (economics); Agricultural science; Agricultural economics; Yield gap; Irrigation; Economics; Business; Geography; Agriculture; Agronomy; Environmental science; Biology; Macroeconomics; Archaeology; Microeconomics
Title: Economic analysis of inefficiency in wheat production: An empirical study from India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant differences in production inefficiencies among different farm sizes in Uttar Pradesh, with farms above 2 hectares having relatively higher production compared to smaller farms. The study also identified factors such as age, soil fertility problems, and awareness spearheaded by panchayats that hinder wheat production.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the production inefficiencies of wheat crops in Uttar Pradesh, India, using a sample of 320 farmers and the stochastic production frontier (SPF) approach to determine key input factors such as land, irrigation, fertilizer, seed, pesticides, equipment, and labor, while accounting for factors such as age, farm size, soil fertility problems, awareness spearheaded by panchayats, inaccessibility to certified seeds, and Simmons land fragmentation index.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest the need for policy measures to improve input usage and reduce marginalization in Uttar Pradesh's wheat crops. Prioritizing support for larger farms, addressing soil fertility problems, and increasing awareness spearheaded by panchayats can help scale up production and expand the economic viability of these holdings.

Authors: Maxmillan Martin; Yi hyun Kang; Motasim Billah; Tasneem Siddiqui; Richard Black; Dominic Kniveton
Field: Climate change; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Poverty; Adaptive capacity; Internal migration; Development policy; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Emergency management
Title: Climate‐influenced migration in Bangladesh: the need for a policy realignment
primary_category: Child poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that people migrate for better livelihoods, not necessarily in response to climatic stresses and shocks. If facilitated appropriately, internal and international migration can help build adaptive capacity to future environmental and climatic hazards.
What_was_studied: Recent research into migration in Bangladesh explored the role of internal and international migration in building adaptive capacity to future environmental and climatic hazards within the context of a growing city-centred economy that promotes remittances to villages during the period of 2018-2022 using both qualitative and quantitative data collected through surveys, interviews, and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the economic and adaptive roles of internal migration in building resilience to climate change, decision-makers should prioritize policies that facilitate safe, orderly, and regular migration, while also addressing the root causes of poverty and inequality in rural areas.

Authors: SriPallavi Nadimpalli; Sahil Mathew; Tashina Madappa Cheranda
Field: Futures studies; Futures contract; Narrative; Flooding (psychology); Sociology; Environmental planning; Political science; Geography; Economics; Computer science; Financial economics; Philosophy; Psychology; Artificial intelligence; Linguistics; Psychotherapist
Title: (Re)envisioning inclusive futures: Applying narrative foresight to deconstruct the problem of urban flooding in the slums of Bengaluru, India
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Only 40% of slums are formally recognized by city authorities, leaving most slum dwellers with limited access to public benefits and basic infrastructure.
What_was_studied: Recurring urban flooding in Bengaluru, India, and its intersecting development challenges, particularly affecting migrant slum dwellers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for sustainable collaborative processes to inform future decisions, particularly addressing the problem of urban flooding, and prioritizing the inclusion of marginalized voices in policy-making.

Field: Sociology; Development studies; Development management; Metaphor; Aid effectiveness; Schism; Managerialism; Poverty reduction; Social science; Environmental ethics
Title: From Schism to Synthesis: The Off‐Centre Radical‐Reformist Role of Development Management
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that an ‘off-centre’ radical-reformist synthesis could provide a more effective approach to managing divergent ideas in development management, particularly in the education access, gender and poverty, and income poverty policy areas. This synthesis prioritizes a less apologetic acceptance of reformist or ‘managerialist’ approaches and emphasizes the importance of considering multiple perspectives.
What_was_studied: This article traces the ‘schism’ between reformist and radical views in development management, focusing on issues such as aid effectiveness, poverty reduction, and planning, with a specific emphasis on the education access, gender and poverty, and income poverty policy areas during a given time period using primary data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up efforts to incorporate an ‘off-centre’ radical-reformist synthesis into development management, particularly in the education access, gender and poverty, and income poverty policy areas. By prioritizing a less apologetic acceptance of reformist or ‘managerialist’ approaches and considering multiple perspectives, policymakers can more effectively address issues such as aid effectiveness, poverty reduction, and planning.

Authors: Glenn Banks; Warwick E. Murray; John Overton; Regina Scheyvens
Field: Government; Economics; Aid effectiveness; Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Poverty reduction; Unit (housing); Economic growth; Foreign policy; Politics
Title: Paddling on One Side of the Canoe? The Changing Nature of New Zealand's Development Assistance Programme
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that New Zealand's aid policy has shifted from a focus on poverty reduction to economic growth, with a significant decrease in funding for gender and poverty programs, and an increase in funding for sustainable development initiatives.
What_was_studied: New Zealand's aid policy over four decades and its relationship with the global aid regime, focusing on gender and poverty reduction and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of gender equality and poverty reduction in achieving sustainable development, decision-makers should prioritize funding for these programs and ensure that economic growth strategies align with global aid principles.

Authors: Yassin Elshain Yahia; Haiyun Liu; Abdalla Sirag; Sayyed Sadaqat Hussain Shah
