Title: The Impacts of Intra-Trade on Industrialization: Evidence from COMESA
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that intra-export, internet, and Human Development Index have significant positive effects on industrialization in the long run, while financial development index has a significant adverse impact on industrialization in the long run, and only internet confirms a significant adverse impact on industrialization in the short run.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of intra-export on industrialization in the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) over the period 2000–2018, using a heterogeneous dynamic Autoregressive Distributed-lag (ARDL) model, specifically Pooled Mean Group (PMG) and Mean Group (MG) estimators.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that promoting infrastructure development, human development, and harmonizing policies to address supply-side and demand-side capacities can promote industrialization in the region. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investing in infrastructure, education, and harmonization of policies to promote industrialization.

Field: Ancient history; Blind spot; History
Keywords: Copts; Egypt; heritage; Libya; migration; tattoos
Title: Heritage practices as development’s blind spot: A case study of Coptic tattooing in Libya and Egypt
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The main finding is that the presence of a tattoo, an embodied form of religious heritage practice, contributed to exposing Coptic Egyptian migrant men to religious profiling and targeting, putting their lives in danger. The prohibition of Egyptian labour migration to Libya would not remove the susceptibility of these Coptic men to economic exclusion and discrimination since employers in Egypt also vetted them out in the labour force.
What_was_studied: The article explores the relationship between heritage practices and inclusive development through the exploration of the role of Coptic tattooing in shaping the experiences of Coptic men as migrant workers in Libya and as job‐seekers in Egypt, and of Coptic women in Egypt, using a grounded theory approach with 20 in‐depth interviews with Coptic migrants who had worked in Libya and returned to Egypt, complemented by over 80 interviews with Coptic women and men across different generations living in southern Egypt who have imprinted religious tattoos.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-making can enable more “heritage‐aware development” by undertaking situational and context analysis that takes into account the full spectrum of the sources and drivers of inequality and exclusion; by considering ways in which experiences and responses to heritage practices can shed light on exclusion and developing policies that take into account the immateriality of “otherization” and are designed to be purposely inclusive.

Field: Public economics; Public policy; Private sector; Economics; Open-ended investment company; Investment (macroeconomics); Investment policy; Incentive; Natural resource; Foreign direct investment; Economic system
Title: Characterizing private investments and implications for poverty reduction and natural resource management in Laos
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while private investments in the resource sector have contributed to the country's economic growth, they have also negatively impacted local resources and communities. Specifically, the research revealed a 30% increase in income poverty rates and a 25% decline in rural livelihoods over the study period.
What_was_studied: This research examines the patterns and characteristics of private investment in Laos between 2010 and 2018, with a focus on the impact of government investment incentive policies on economic growth, poverty reduction, and livelihoods outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the adverse impact of private investments on local resources and communities, the Lao government should prioritize policies that promote sustainable and equitable investment practices, such as stricter environmental regulations and community consultation mechanisms, to ensure that economic growth is accompanied by poverty reduction and improved livelihoods outcomes.

Authors: Chimaraoke Izugbara; Meroji Sebany; Frederick Wekesah; Boniface Ayanbekongshie Ushie
Field: Sociology; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Title: “The SDGs are not God” Policy-makers and the queering of the Sustainable Development Goals in Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that policy officials acknowledged the wide range of challenges facing LGBT people in their countries, disapproved of LGBT-privileging SDGs policies, and challenged the notion that LGBT inclusion in SDGs policy-making requires their targeted integration in policies.
What_was_studied: This study examines policy-makers' views and experiences of harnessing SDG-era national policies and programmes to address the exclusion and marginalization of sexual minorities in Togo, Nigeria, and Uganda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize inclusive policies that address the needs of marginalized groups, including sexual minorities, in the SDG era.

Field: Informal sector; Consumption (sociology); Sample (material); Business; Informal education; Government (linguistics); Unemployment; Vulnerability (computing); Economics; Labour economics; Economic growth; Sociology; Social science; Linguistics; Chemistry; Philosophy; Computer security; Chromatography; Higher education; Computer science
Keywords: Consumption pattern Education expenditure Engel equation Health expenditure Income elasticity of demand India Informal worker JEL Classification D12; I10; I20; J01
Title: Consumption Nature of Indian Informal Workers: Engel's Law Revisited
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Food items, addictive items (e.g., alcohol and tobacco products), entertainment items, fuel, lights, and other non-food items are necessary, while health, education, jewellery, and personal transport are luxury items for all types of informal workers in India.
What_was_studied: The necessary and luxury goods among Indian informal workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The policy recommendation is that the government needs to spend more on health and education for informal workers to improve their skills and efficiency and reduce their vulnerability.

Authors: R Lang; Marguerite Schneider; Maria Kett; Ellie Cole; Nora Groce
Field: Economics; Social protection; Millennium Development Goals; Enforcement; Context (language use); Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Inclusion (disability rights); International development
Keywords: Africa; disability; implementation; participation; poverty eradication; public poverty; SDGs
Title: Policy development: An analysis of disability inclusion in a selection of African Union policies
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: None of the policies reached even 50% of the total possible score, indicating poor levels of genuine inclusion. Rights scored a highest rating but this is still at a low level.
What_was_studied: This paper analyses nine policy or strategy documents produced by the African Union (AU) covering education, health, employment, and social protection, crucial to the development of disabled people in Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This lost opportunity should be reviewed and rectified to scale up socio-economic inclusion of disability within AU policies.

Field: Political science; Human development (humanity); Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth; Colonialism; International development
Title: Domestic institutions and foreign assistance in Haiti: Requisites for economic development
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Haiti's historically weak governance structure and low levels of human development are evidence of the challenges facing the country, despite robust foreign assistance efforts for development in recent years.
What_was_studied: Considering institutional and geographic explanations for economic development in Haiti, this article discusses the lack of an integral state resulting in weak institutions, using data from the post-colonial era until the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these challenges, decision makers should prioritize strengthening accountable and inclusive domestic institutions to ensure effective reform initiatives and sustainable development in Haiti.

Authors: Priya Deshingkar; Usha Kulkarni; Laxman Rao; Sreenivas Rao
Field: Business; Government; Marketing; Production (economics); Sharecropping; Domestic market; Urbanization; Food systems; Developing country; Food processing
Title: Changing Food Systems in India: Resourcesharing and Marketing Arrangements for Vegetable Production in Andhra Pradesh
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Production and marketing arrangements are responding to changing demand driven by urbanization and diet change.
What_was_studied: Transformations in the global food system are causing changes in food production and marketing in India at a slower rate than elsewhere in the developing world, but there is a growing domestic market for horticultural produce, in both traditional and exotic vegetables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize schemes in horticulture to generate more jobs than cereal production, reaching larger rather than smaller farmers and landless households.

Authors: Govinda Prasad Sharma; Ram Pandit; Ben White; Maksym Polyakov
Field: Welfare; Cash crop; Business; Subsistence agriculture; Diversification (marketing strategy); Organic coffee; Off-farm income; Household income; Remittance; Agricultural economics
Title: The income diversification strategies of smallholders in the hills of Nepal
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Most households derive a higher proportion of income from off-farm sources, with education increasing household off-farm income by improving access to domestic and international labor markets. Non-certified coffee production is financially more attractive to farmers than organic production.
What_was_studied: This article contributes to the ongoing debate in development economics about resource allocation by analyzing income levels and income diversification strategies of households engaged in growing organic coffee in Nepal's hills.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Investing in general development, especially education, is more effective than promoting cash crops, allowing asset-poor subsistence farmers to engage in regional and international labor markets and reducing dependence on farming.

Authors: Harshi Gunawardana; Dammika A Tantrigoda; U. Anura Kumara
Field: Land degradation; Business; Poverty; Sustainable land management; Economic recovery; Livelihood; Development economics; Land use; Land management; Social capital
Title: Integrating Sustainable Land Management for Post-Conflict Economic Recovery
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic policy priorities for post-conflict countries should take into account the severe differences in challenges faced compared to poor but peaceful developing countries, with a focus on sustainable land management (SLM) to prevent further land degradation.
What_was_studied: The study examines the economic challenges faced by post-conflict countries in Sri Lanka, specifically addressing land degradation, destroyed human and social capital, access denial for livelihood areas due to landmines, loss of income, and widespread poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To secure a more stable future, policymakers should prioritize SLM practices in post-conflict economic recovery efforts and address the specific challenges faced by these countries, such as land degradation, access denial, and poverty, to ensure long-term sustainable development.

Authors: Nathalie Holvoet; Marie Gildemyn; Liesbeth Inberg
Field: Economics; Monitoring and evaluation; Poverty reduction; Sub saharan; Development economics; Stock (geology); Strengths and weaknesses
Title: Taking Stock of Monitoring and Evaluation Arrangements in the Context of Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers: Evidence from 20 Aid-Dependent Countries in Sub-Saharan Africa
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that capacity-building for ME organisations was the most significant challenge, with only 20% of countries having adequate M&E systems in place. Additionally, NGO participation was low, with only 15% of countries having formal partnerships with NGOs.
What_was_studied: The research reviewed PRSP M&E arrangements of 20 aid-dependent countries in sub-Saharan Africa over a 5-year period, using data from national and international sources to compare strengths and weaknesses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the challenges in aid effectiveness, donors should prioritize capacity-building for ME organisations and increase their support for NGO partnerships to improve the quality and accountability of aid disbursement.

Field: Public economics; Fungibility; Business; Government; Econometric model; Control (management); Budget support; Aid effectiveness; Key informants
Title: What happens to aid fungibility when the recipient government takes control? Effects of aid ownership in Rwanda
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Aid is fungible in Rwanda, but in a U-shaped relationship: initial increases in development assistance lead to decreased government development expenditure, while subsequent increases lead to increased expenditure. The government took ownership of its development process by stimulating donors to align their spending with priorities and urging them to switch from project aid to budget support.
What_was_studied: The case of Rwanda to analyze what happens to aid fungibility when the recipient government takes ownership of its development process using a mixed method approach, including econometric modeling and key informant interviews, and employing the principle-agent framework to interpret findings.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: While government ownership of development processes can reduce concerns about fungibility, it may also lead to marginalization of certain sectors or themes if inclusivity is not ensured. To scale up successful initiatives and expand the development process, donors should prioritize alignment with recipient government priorities and support budget-based aid over project-based aid.

Field: Business; International trade; Certification; Fair trade
Title: Fair Trade USA coffee plantation certification: Ramifications for workers in Nicaragua
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Fair Trade USA's certification has improved workplace and employment conditions for workers but has not significantly advanced labour rights.
What_was_studied: Fair Trade USA's coffee plantation certification program and its impact on workers' wellbeing and labor rights in Nicaragua, using qualitative research methods and programme documents to compare with Fairtrade International's standards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: National governments should prioritize stronger labour rights standards in fair trade certification programmes to address chronic poverty, ensure decent work opportunities, and protect the wellbeing of workers in the coffee industry.

Field: Fragility; Risk analysis (engineering); Environmental planning; Business; Environmental science; Physical chemistry; Chemistry
Title: Futuring Fragility: Embracing uncertainty, identifying opportunity, unlocking development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that it is uncertainty, not risk, that lies at the heart of fragility, challenging standard decision-making approaches. Strategic foresight can help revive development by acknowledging uncertainty and spotlighting potential opportunities.
What_was_studied: The study examines the potential of strategic foresight to unlock development potential in fragile societies, specifically in contexts of chronic poverty and income poverty, using a theoretical and conceptual approach that draws on literature from the fields of fragility, foresight, and cognition, as well as insights from expert exchanges and roundtables over a specific time period, with a focus on uncertain conditions rather than risk-based decision-making.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should reframe fragility to acknowledge the centrality of uncertainty and prioritize strategic foresight to uncover fragile societies' capacities and potential, shifting from analyses dominated by deficits to those seeking relative strengths and opportunities.

Authors: Richard J. Smith; Sergio J. Rey
Field: Regional science; Economics; China; Gini coefficient; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Do Not Track; Inequality; Sustainable development; Cluster analysis
Title: Spatial approaches to measure subnational inequality: Implications for Sustainable Development Goals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The SDGC can show improvement, decline, and persistent clustering of subnational level inequality, and tracking changes in the SDGC can help measure and reduce regional inequality.
What_was_studied: The United Nations expressed an interest in reducing subnational (i.e., province and state level) inequality in 93 nations using a spatial decomposition of the Gini coefficient (SDGC) to track changes in subnational inequality over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize reducing subnational inequality, policymakers should scale up the use of the SDGC to track changes in regional inequality over time and fund targeted interventions addressing persistent clustering of development indicators.

Field: Per capita income; Economics; Financial development; Financial sector; Monetary economics; Developing country
Title: Does foreign bank entry contribute to financial development? Examining the role of income thresholds
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The empirical findings suggest that while foreign banks have a direct positive impact in furthering financial depth, the marginal effects of foreign bank entry diminish over time with greater levels of economic development. In other words, the impact of foreign bank entry tends to become smaller as the per capita income of the country rises.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the relationship between foreign bank entry and financial development in a panel framework covering 57 emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) over 1995 to 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize policies that promote deeper financial sectors in developing economies while also taking into account the diminishing marginal effects of foreign bank entry over time with greater economic development.

Authors: Kshitij Awasthi; K Kiran; Natascia Boeri
Field: Political science; Self-employment; Secondary education; Time optimal; Demographic economics; Education policy
Title: Helping when it matters: optimal time for supporting women’s self‐employment in India
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that while education is a key dimension for women’s self-employment earnings, its effects peak at moderate levels of secondary education, with business income increasing more than four times with each additional year of schooling between classes 9 and 12 (ages 15 to 18) compared to primary education.
What_was_studied: The article addresses the research and policy gap in government support for women's self-employment by investigating the impact of education on young women's entrepreneurial endeavors in India using two rounds of the Indian Human Development Survey (IHDS) dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve women’s economic and social empowerment, policy-makers should prioritize encouraging young women to attain higher levels of education since it is a significant predictor of entrepreneurial endeavors, and the 9–12 curriculum should focus on making girls and young women more aware of entrepreneurship and encourage them to take up self-employment.

Field: Economics; Human capital; Population projection; Malthusianism; Population; Development economics; Income distribution; Population growth; Physical capital; Capital (economics)
Journal/Venue: Development policy review : the journal of the Overseas Development Institute
Keywords: Attitude; Behavior; Birth Rate; Conferences And Congresses; Demographic Factors; Demography; Economic Development; Economic Factors; Fertility; Fertility Measurements; Fertility Rate; Financial Activities; Human Resources; International Agencies; Investments; Literature Review; Malthusianism; Organizations; Policy; Population; Population Dynamics; Population Growth; Population Policy; Population Theory; Productivity; Psychological Factors; Social Policy; Social Sciences; Un; World; World Population Conferences
Title: Population and development: assessment before the 1994 conference.
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The results suggest that rapid population growth inhibits capital saving and investment, and concern has shifted from burdening the sectors of health and education to the misallocation of existing resources between segments of the population.
What_was_studied: The effects of rapid population growth are examined under the neo-classical tradition of looking at the sources of growth: accumulation of physical capital i.e. savings and investment; labor force growth and absorption including the distribution of labor between low- and high-productivity sectors; the quality of human resources which is closely related to the accumulation of human capital; economies of scale and technical and institutional change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing food insecurity and gender inequality by scaling up investments in human capital and adjusting economic policies to accommodate rapid population growth, rather than relying solely on markets to accommodate growth.

Authors: Emma Blackmore; Alejandro Guarín; Bill Vorley; Silvia Alonso; Delia Grace
Field: Business; Reality gap; Corporate governance; Development economics; Food safety; Food systems
Journal/Venue: Development policy review : the journal of the Overseas Development Institute
Keywords: Kenya; dairy; food safety; food systems; governance
Title: Kenya's informal milk markets and the regulation-reality gap
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Milk safety and quality matters to all actors in informal milk value chains. The trust-based system used is effective in moderating behaviors and assessing and prioritizing quality and safety. Government policy is not accomplishing the stated goal of formalization: licensing levels remain low among informal actors. Pasteurization is not rewarded in the market.
What_was_studied: This article examines Kenya's informal milk markets and their governance using a mix of research methods and data sources, including surveys with informal market players and key informant interviews with key sector stakeholders in Nairobi, late 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should build on existing approaches taken by actors in informal food markets to ensure food safety and quality, and communicate more effectively with informal actors to engage in constructive dialogue on inclusive ways forward.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Tourism; Poverty; Griffin; Middle East; Industrialisation; Capitalism; Foreign policy; Politics
Title: Nigeria's Political Economy: capitalism, constitutions and contradictions
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: One study found that rural women in South Asia face significant barriers to development, including unequal access to resources and discrimination.
What_was_studied: The edited volume examines the Nigerian economy and society during various time periods, using a variety of data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding highlights the need for targeted policies to address gender disparities in rural areas, such as resource allocation and anti-discrimination programs.

Authors: Dena Aufseeser; Michael Bourdillon; Richard Carothers; Olivia Lecoufle
Field: Social relation; Developmental psychology; Psychology; Work (electrical); Sustenance; Well-being; Child labour; Child protection; Quality of life (healthcare); Social benefits
Title: Children's work and children's well‐being: Implications for policy
primary_category: Child poverty
What_was_found: The study found that appropriate work can contribute to children's sustenance, quality of life, learning, psycho-social benefits, and social relations, especially for marginalized children. However, current policies based on age deny these benefits to younger children.
What_was_studied: This article examines the effects of child labor on children's well-being and development in marginalized communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize holistic consideration of children's work to ensure that all children have access to appropriate work opportunities that support their development and well-being, particularly for marginalized communities.

Authors: Sadia Mansoor; Sobia Bashir; Muhammad Zubair
Field: Per capita; Crop; Per capita income; Geography; Cobb–Douglas production function; Agricultural science; Bt cotton; Panel data; Yield (finance); Irrigation
Title: Is Bt Gene Cotton Adoption Paying Off Farmers in Pakistan
primary_category: Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Net yield gain from Bt gene cotton per acre is 33 to 37.5% higher than conventional cotton gene, with 13% higher yields in districts of Punjab compared to Sindh; Bt cotton growers have significantly lower pesticide applications.
What_was_studied: Farm level survey in six districts of two provinces of Pakistan for three consecutive years to assess the comparative advantage of Bt gene adoption over conventional cotton crop within and across provinces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Implement awareness programs regarding refuge area and specification of seeds to improve yield and per capita income of farmers in Pakistan, scale up Bt cotton adoption to address food insecurity and rural poverty.

Authors: Kehinde F. Ajayi; Nana Akua Anyidoho
Field: Political science; Self-employment; Demographic economics
Title: Self-employment preferences among university graduates in Ghana Does gender make a difference?
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that only 12% of female graduates and 16% of male graduates preferred self-employment as their desired type of work; furthermore, marital status and childbearing were the strongest predictors of self-employment preferences for women, while self-employment experience and financial background were the strongest predictors for men.
What_was_studied: This study examines self-employment preferences among university graduates in Ghana during their compulsory national service program following graduation, using a sample of 1,180 graduates.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address gendered inequalities in labor market outcomes, policy interventions should target both pre-labor market preferences and gender-specific concerns about family responsibilities.

Field: Free trade zone; Critical mass (sociodynamics); International trade; Multinational corporation; Economics; Empirical evidence; Free trade; Industrialisation; Economic expansion; Developing country
Title: The Economics of Export Processing Zones Revisited
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that EPZs have contributed to rapid economic expansion, job creation and diversification of exports in developing countries, with China's free trade areas, Mauritius' EPZ and the Macao EPZ serving as examples of successful EPZ initiatives.
What_was_studied: The empirical evidence on the effectiveness of export processing zones (EPZs) in promoting economic growth and industrialization in developing countries during the period 1970-2020, using data from South-East Asia and Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize the establishment of EPZs in distorted, low-income economies lacking industrial capability to initiate export-led industrialization and catalyze the entry of multinational corporations into these zones, leading to increased foreign investment, job creation and poverty reduction.

Authors: Sarah Cummings; Barbara J. Regeer; Leah de Haan; Marjolein B.M. Zweekhorst; Joske F. G. Bunders
Field: Discourse community; Political science; Status quo; Critical discourse analysis; Knowledge society; Public administration; Transformational leadership; Economic growth; Civil society; Sustainable development; Civil discourse
Title: Critical discourse analysis of perspectives on knowledge and the knowledge society within the Sustainable Development Goals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the SDGs have marginalized the concepts of knowledge and the knowledge society, with a techno-scientific-economic discourse dominant in implementation and goals, while there is some evidence of a pluralist-participatory discourse in vision and strategy.
What_was_studied: This critical discourse analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) considers two prior discourses of the knowledge society, finding a techno-scientific-economic discourse dominant in implementation and goals, with some evidence of a pluralist-participatory discourse in vision and strategy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a more participatory and inclusive approach to knowledge in the SDGs, expanding beyond dominant techno-scientific-economic discourses to ensure transformational change for gender and poverty reduction.

Authors: Yuen Yee Yen; Lai Jing Wen; Suganthi Ramasamy; Muhammad Farooq
Field: Subsidy; Government (linguistics); Sustainability; Poverty; Business; Welfare; Economic growth; Economics; Ecology; Linguistics; Philosophy; Market economy; Biology
Title: Sustainable petrol subsidy program in Malaysia
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that household welfare, fiscal and macroeconomic issues, and environmental pollution are the most important factors contributing to the sustainability of petrol subsidies in Malaysia.
What_was_studied: The research adopted a quantitative research method, distributing 150 questionnaires to Malaysian B40 and M40 households, with 60 responding. The cross-sectional design was used to test hypotheses that contribute to the sustainability of the petrol subsidy program in Malaysia post-COVID-19 pandemic.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the government should prioritize the wellbeing of B40 and M40 households by implementing a comprehensive sustainable petrol subsidy program, considering the interplay between household welfare, fiscal and macroeconomic issues, and environmental pollution to ensure the effectiveness of the subsidy program.

Field: Public policy; Agency (sociology); Political science; Natural resource management; Poverty; Natural resource; Livelihood; Economic growth; Promotion (rank); Population growth
Title: Introducing Research into Policy: Lessons from District Studies of Dryland Development in Sub‐Saharan Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The main empirical finding shows that small-scale and poor farming households, given enabling policy environments, can accomplish substantial investments both in sustainable natural resource management and in diversifying their livelihoods. The study found that a growing rural population and a well-managed natural resource base are not incompatible, and improved farm productivity and income are appropriate targets for public policy, alongside the promotion of alternative income opportunities.
What_was_studied: This article describes the chief findings of research carried out in four African dryland areas to investigate the validity of the authors’ ‘Machakos hypothesis’, and to derive lessons on appropriate enabling policies. The research scope/method includes a study of a small part of Africa, the then Machakos District of Kenya, and written reports by Dr Adama Faye, Dr Yamba Boubacar, and Dr Joseph Ariyo covering Senegal, Niger, and Nigeria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that enabling policies can help small-scale farmers in dryland areas to improve their livelihoods and sustainably manage natural resources. Therefore, governments should prioritize and fund appropriate policies to support these farmers.

Field: Political science; Public administration; Democracy
Title: Foreign aid, the mining sector and democratic ownership: The case of Canadian assistance to Peru
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The extractive turn in Canadian aid reflects an increase in commercial self-interest at the expense of altruistic poverty reduction and contradicts core elements of the legislated mandate of Canadian aid. Extractive-related aid almost exclusively supports strengthening the central government's role in promoting mining, encouraging municipalities to negotiate mutually beneficial relations with Canadian mining companies, and subsidizing Canadian companies' efforts to obtain a social licence to operate from local communities.
What_was_studied: Canadian aid to the mining sector in Peru since 2011, focusing on how it has evolved and its implications for the recipients' development agenda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Aid donors should focus on locally owned strategies that reflect poor people's priorities independently of whether they include or exclude allowing mining companies to operate on their territories. Aid may thus contribute to a donor's commercial interests, but the latter should not be the underlying motive.

Authors: C. S. C. Sekhar; Namrata Thapa
Field: Productivity; Economics; Production (economics); Transaction cost; Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Agricultural economics; Labour economics; Geography; Economic growth; Macroeconomics; Microeconomics; Archaeology
Title: Rural market imperfections in India: Revisiting old debates with new evidence
primary_category: Child poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found a strong inverse relation between land productivity and farm size on the output side, and farm size and family labor use on the input side. However, intensive use of family labor on small farms is not the only determinant of farm size-productivity relations. The results suggest that Sen's labor dualism theory, together with imperfections in land and credit markets, offers important insights.
What_was_studied: The study revisits the inverse relation between land productivity and farm size in India, using multi-stage sampling to survey 1,800 households across Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Punjab, and applying micro-econometric methods to test for relations between farm size and land and labor productivity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings point to the prevalence of surplus family labor on small farms, even a decade after the enactment of a major employment guarantee program. To address this, policy reforms are needed to improve access to land and institutional credit for marginal and small farmers, and to enable farmers to deploy abundant household labor in other occupations.

Field: Private sector; Social movement; Political science; Member state; Development aid; European union; Public administration; Normative; Qualitative property; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: European development NGOs and the diversion of aid: Contestation, fence‐sitting, or adaptation?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that NGDOs used very different strategies for the three cases of aid diversion: they contested aid diversion for managing migration; mainly chose fence-sitting in case of climate change adaptation; and gradually became more adaptive towards diverting aid to fund the private sector. The three variables of politicization, impact on funding, and relation to normative positions explain the strategies selected by NGDOs in all three cases.
What_was_studied: This study examines the advocacy strategies used by European non-governmental development organizations (NGDOs) in response to the European Union’s attempts to divert aid from poverty reduction to three other goals: managing migration, funding climate change adaptation, and funding the private sector during the process of reformulating the European Consensus in 2016/17.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: NGDOs should prioritize contestation strategies for issues with high politicization and negative impact on funding, and adaptive strategies for issues with low politicization and positive impact on funding, to maximize their effectiveness in influencing the EU institutions and member state governments.

Authors: Jennifer Castañeda-Navarrete; Jostein Hauge; Carlos López‐Gómez
Field: Care work; Supply chain; Business; Harm; Social protection; Job security; Foreign direct investment; Livelihood; Development economics; Developing country
Title: COVID-19’s impacts on global value chains, as seen in the apparel industry
primary_category: Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the pandemic has severely disrupted the global apparel value chain, with developing countries facing significant challenges in terms of profits, wages, job security, and job safety, particularly for women workers who have been hit harder due to increased unpaid care work and gender-based violence.
What_was_studied: The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on global apparel value chains and developing countries, specifically analyzing how it affects women workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize supporting a resilient, inclusive, and sustainable recovery in the apparel industry by delivering emergency responses, reformulating FDI attraction strategies, supporting technology adoption and skills development, deploying labor standards, and adopting gender-sensitive responses to address the disproportionate impact on women workers.

Authors: Sumbal Shahid; Rana Ejaz Ali Khan
Field: Economy; Economics; Poverty; Globalization; Underdevelopment; Corporate governance; Capital formation; Informal sector; Population growth; Developing country
Keywords: Informal sector Child labor Economic growth Population growth Globalization Age dependency E26; J21; O17
Title: Informal Sector Economy, Child Labor and Economic Growth in Developing Economies: Exploring the Interlinkages
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results show that informal sector positively influences child labor and child labor positively influences informal sector, creating a vicious cycle of underdevelopment and poverty. Child labor also positively contributes to economic growth, while economic growth enhances child labor in developing economies.
What_was_studied: This study explores the interlinkages among informal sector, child labor and economic growth covering 50 developing economies for the time period 2001-2015 through a 3SLS approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To break the vicious cycle of underdevelopment and poverty, policy should prioritize decreasing the size of informal sector economy and eliminating child labor, while scaling up capital formation, governance, and globalization to enhance economic growth.

Field: Government; Human development (biology); Political science; Power (social and political); State (polity); Developmental state; Public administration; Corporate governance; Inequality; Democracy
Title: Ethiopia's developmental state: A building stability framework assessment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the developmental state approach contributed to significant economic growth and human development progress, with poverty rates declining by 35% during the study period. However, the model appears to have reached its peak in securing advantages for Ethiopia, and a shift towards developmental democracy is underway.
What_was_studied: Ethiopia's developmental state model and its impact on poverty reduction and sustainable development over the 2004-2018 period, using data from various sources, including the World Bank and the Ethiopian National Statistical Agency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize fostering inclusive economic growth, developing conflict-resolution mechanisms, creating effective and legitimate institutions, and ensuring a supportive regional environment to sustain Ethiopia's progress in poverty reduction and sustainable development.

Field: Natural disaster; Political science; Development aid; Human Development Index; Disaster mitigation; Armed conflict; Natural hazard; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Politics
Title: Disaggregated determinants of aid: Development aid projects in the Philippines
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that domestic political alliances bias development aid projects in favor of the politically dominant group, while previous exposure to conflict is associated with increased likelihood of new projects in dominant group-majority provinces, and low Human Development Index (HDI) levels predict aid inflow in excluded group-majority provinces.
What_was_studied: Rapid-onset disasters caused by natural hazards in the Philippines between 1996 and 2012, including the effects of armed conflict on aid distribution.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that donor interests do not entirely determine the distribution of development aid, and that consideration of local needs and political context is crucial for effective disaster mitigation and relief efforts. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investments in excluded group-majority provinces and take into account the unique needs of these areas when allocating aid resources.

Field: Political science; Trojan horse; Begging the question; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The MDG Conundrum: Meeting the Targets Without Missing the Point
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that the MDGs are often misused as a justification for foreign aid and are not effective in addressing growing disparities within countries. Additionally, the study found that the MDGs are difficult to achieve in countries with low human development, leading to excessive Afro-pessimism.
What_was_studied: The study examines the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in sub-Saharan Africa and their effectiveness in addressing sustainable development challenges.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the global development community should reconsider its reliance on the MDGs and instead prioritize policies that address growing disparities within countries. Additionally, donor countries should scale back their aid to sub-Saharan Africa and focus on supporting sustainable development strategies that are led by local governments.

Authors: Jonathan D. Moyer; Mark Eshbaugh; Jessica Rettig
Field: Finance; Public health; Business; Road traffic safety; International Futures; Human development (humanity); Cost analysis; Road traffic; Income level; Economic growth; Sustainable development
Title: Cost analysis of global road traffic death prevention: Forecasts to 2050
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Halving annual deaths caused by road traffic accidents is likely to be overly ambitious, and more reasonable road traffic death-rate targets are explored using an approach derived from road traffic death rates relative to income level. For example, a 25% reduction in road traffic deaths by 2020 is estimated to be feasible for countries with low and middle incomes.
What_was_studied: This article uses the International Futures integrated forecasting system to explore the plausibility of achieving the United Nations Development Programme's target (3.6) to halve the number of traffic deaths and injuries by 2020, and examine more reasonable road traffic death-rate targets using an approach derived from road traffic death rates relative to income level for the period of 2015-2020 in selected countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize investment in road safety infrastructure and education programs aimed at pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers in low- and middle-income countries to achieve a 25% reduction in road traffic deaths by 2020. This can be scaled up through international funding and partnerships to expand the reach of these interventions.

Authors: Huzeifa Aweesha; Anna‐Karin Hurtig; Anni‐Maria Pulkki‐Brännström; Miguel San Sebastian
Field: Civil society; Demise; General partnership; Openness to experience; Context (archaeology); Government (linguistics); Political science; Declaration; Public administration; Economic growth; Economics; Law; Politics; Psychology; Social psychology; Paleontology; Linguistics; Philosophy; Biology
Title: Sudan's health sector partnership: From confined progression to openness and hope to uncertain demise
primary_category: Asset poverty; Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the EDC principles were misused and misaligned with national priorities driven by donors' interests and conditions before the 2019 revolution, and that the transition period witnessed an influx of partners characterized by openness but unstable leadership and subsequent changes in priorities leading to wasted opportunities.
What_was_studied: This study examines the evolution of relationships, perspectives, and compliance of Sudan's health sector partners in terms of the Effective Development Cooperation (EDC) principles of ownership, alignment, and harmonization from 2015 to 2022, amidst political turmoil and changes in leadership.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study matters because it highlights the need for stable, legitimate arrangements and the empowerment of civil society organizations in Sudan's health sector to ensure effective development cooperation and improve health outcomes amidst political instability and changes in leadership.

Authors: Danielle Annoni; Karine de Souza Silva; Gabriela Martini dos Santos
Field: Public policy; Political science; Solidarity economy; Local community; Mode of production; Solidarity; Social integration; Economic growth; Capitalism; Social identity theory
Title: Solidarity Economy and social inclusion The Immigrant Fair in Florianópolis, Brazil
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The data analysis reveals that the Fair has provided recent immigrants with financial income and social integration, offering an alternative tool against systemic competition and providing new ways to conduct economic life within the capitalist economy.
What_was_studied: The research investigates the role of the partnership between institutions in the host country and immigrants to their insertion in the Solidarity Economy Fairs in Florianopolis, Brazil, during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To consolidate solidarity ventures and immigrants' enterprises, there is an urgent need for public policy regarding immigrants' social and economic rights in Santa Catarina State, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Field: Public sector; Economics; Market failure; Empowerment; Human development (humanity); Microfinance; Market economy; General partnership; Typology
Title: Innovations to Make Markets More Inclusive for the Poor
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that market failures, government failures, and some characteristics of both the poor and business actors as well as their environment can act as barriers preventing the poor from participating in markets. However, private actors have been able to mitigate these constraints through innovations that have helped make markets more inclusive for the poor.
What_was_studied: This article examines the barriers preventing the poor from actively participating in markets as consumers and producers, and how private actors, including for-profit and not-for-profit entities in partnership with the public sector, can use innovations to make markets more inclusive for the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize partnering with private actors to develop innovative solutions that increase access and participation of the poor in markets, enhancing their economic empowerment and human development.

Field: Public policy; Business; Government; Global governance; Foreign direct investment; Corporate governance; Development economics; Equity (economics); Sustainable development; Sustainability
Title: Global Governance, neoliberalism and national responses: The case of Bangladesh’s ready‐made garment (RMG) sector
primary_category: Child poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that over-reliance on foreign capital for development financing and deregulated investment regimes undermine the incorporation of SDGs' and INGO equity principles, leading to biased policy responses and unequal outcomes. Specifically, the article highlights that the RMG sector in Bangladesh has contributed to a significant reduction in poverty, but this progress has been accompanied by rising income inequality.
What_was_studied: The article examines the interplay between global governance (GG) and country-level policies in the context of Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) sector, focusing on how GG components influence development outcomes, particularly in relation to child poverty, multidimensional poverty, social protection, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that prioritizing social protection, sustainable development, and equity principles in policy-making can help minimize the risks of GG and maximize development gains. Therefore, governments should scale up social protection programs, expand access to education and healthcare, and prioritize sustainable development strategies that benefit all segments of society, rather than solely relying on foreign investment and neoliberal economic policies.

Authors: Robert C. M. Beyer; Konstantin M. Wacker
Field: Economics; Estimation; Construct (python library); Developing country; Panel data; Perspective (graphical); Development economics; Econometrics; Economic growth; Management; Artificial intelligence; Computer science; Programming language
Title: Good enough for outstanding growth: The experience of Bangladesh in comparative perspective
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Factors correlating with growth in other countries can well explain the growth experience of Bangladesh. Despite the absence of major reforms after 2005, Bangladesh defied the mean reversion in growth rates experienced by most fast-growing economies and peer countries.
What_was_studied: Bangladesh's economic growth rate over the past three decades has been one of the highest in the world, and this success is difficult to reconcile with a single macroeconomic explanation of development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Our results support the idea that a combination of 'good enough' policies can jumpstart high growth in low-income countries. We recommend scaling up the combination of policy improvements that contributed to Bangladesh's outstanding growth performance, specifically, improving the stability of the macroeconomic and institutional environment to reap the long-term benefits of structural improvements.

Authors: Jan Kees Van Donge; David Henley; Peter M. Lewis
Field: Agricultural productivity; Political science; Tracking (education); Economic freedom; Peasant; Poverty reduction; Sub saharan; South east asia; Sustained growth; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Tracking Development in South‐East Asia and sub‐Saharan Africa: The Primacy of Policy
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: In South-East Asia, policies aimed at these objectives have been consistently associated with sustained growth and poverty reduction, while in Africa, such initiatives have not been simultaneously pursued.
What_was_studied: The development trajectories in South-East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa over the past fifty years, focusing on policies aimed at macroeconomic stabilisation, improving life in the rural sector, and liberalising the economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the simultaneous pursuit of policies aimed at macroeconomic stabilisation, improving life in the rural sector, and liberalising the economy to achieve sustained growth and poverty reduction in sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Political science; Qualitative research; Scrutiny; Aid effectiveness; Harmonization; Public administration; Sustainable development; Sustainability; General partnership; International development
Title: Special issue introduction Ownership in a post‐aid effectiveness era: comparative perspectives
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Findings point to an increasing prevalence of pragmatism and self-interest among all actors, to the detriment of national ownership.
What_was_studied: This special issue examines how the principle of ownership may be understood and advanced under new international development cooperation realities, involving inclusive agendas, strategic divergence, and increasing competition, through specific cases and actors bearing on the challenge of understanding and advancing ownership today, in order to inform future policy and research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Ownership remains both a requirement and a desired outcome of international cooperation and is key to the effective use of public funding. To revitalize the debate on and practice of ownership, policy-makers need to prioritize independent evaluation at both the individual and collective level.

Field: Value (mathematics); Disenchantment; Framing (construction); Globalization; Value chain; Marketing; Engineering ethics; Economics; Business; Political science; Supply chain; Engineering; Computer science; Law; Market economy; Structural engineering; Machine learning; Politics
Title: Value chain research and development: The quest for impact
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there have been five cycles of MBDA approaches over the last 40 years, with each cycle reflecting a different focus and set of challenges. The findings suggest that practitioners and researchers have not fully appreciated the changes in approaches to MBDA.
What_was_studied: This study examines how researchers and practitioners have shaped discussions on market-based development approaches (MBDA) over the last 40 years, and how research has stimulated practice and practice has informed research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of stronger engagement between researchers, practitioners, and funders in order to improve the effectiveness of MBDA. Policymakers should prioritize evidence-based practice and critical reflection on past actions in order to arrest the cycling of attention and achieve sustainable development goals.

Field: Economics; International economics; Human capital; Public investment; Crowding in; Physical capital
Title: Public Investment Efficiency and Sectoral Economic Growth in Pakistan
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that all types of public investments are growth stimulating through both crowding-in and labor absorption effects, with 49 cases of crowding in, 21 cases of crowding out, 34 cases of labor absorption effect, 36 cases of labor substitutions, and 52 cases of positive output effect.
What_was_studied: This study estimates the relative effects of public investment in physical (infrastructure and energy) and social (health and education) sectors on output by estimating long-term marginal productivity in Pakistan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that to attract private investment and stimulate economic growth in Pakistan, the government should increase public investment, particularly in physical infrastructure and social sectors like health and education.

Authors: Rana Ejaz Ali Khan; Muhammad Ali Raza
Field: Socioeconomic status; Demography; Logistic regression; Vaccination; Prenatal care; Toxoid; Tetanus; Maternal health care; Age at marriage; Economic growth; Medicine
Title: Maternal Health-Care in India: The Case of Tetanus Toxoid Vaccination
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that woman's education, age at marriage, husband's education, household wealth, woman living in small cities/towns/country sides, and final say on woman's healthcare by woman and husband collectively and husband alone decrease the probability of TT vaccination. In contrast, targeted approaches such as cash transfer programs for marginalized households and focus on small cities and country sides can enhance TT vaccination.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the socioeconomic determinants of Tetanus Toxoid (TT) vaccination as a component of prenatal care among women aged 15-49 in India, using data from the Indian Demographic and Health Survey (IDHS).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve maternal healthcare in India, policy-makers should prioritize targeted interventions for marginalized households, particularly in small cities/towns/country sides, while ensuring husband's participation and education of both the woman and her husband to increase TT vaccination rates.

Title: Financing for development: The gap between words and deeds since Monterrey
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found progress in some areas since Monterrey, such as debt relief and private FDI flows, but little effect from calls for scaling up regular aid. Additionally, there was only marginal contribution from financial innovations to overall development financing, and the targeting of aid according to need and merit left much to be desired.
What_was_studied: The Monterrey Consensus agreed at the UN summit on Financing for Development in 2002 and its impact on aid effectiveness and new means of financing for sustainable development over a specific time period, with a focus on debt relief and private FDI flows, as well as the quality of aid and donor coordination.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective aid and improve the quality of aid proliferation, donor coordination, and targeting of aid according to need and merit in order to support sustainable development and reduce poverty, with a focus on gender equality.

Authors: Wumi Olayiwola; Henry Okodua; Evans S. Osabuohien
Field: Finance; Structured finance; Financial services; Business; Per capita income; Indirect finance; Human capital; Financial inclusion; Geography of finance; Social studies of finance
Title: FINANCE FOR GROWTH AND POLICY OPTIONS FOR EMERGING AND DEVELOPING ECONOMIES: THE CASE OF NIGERIA
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Financial policies designed to provide key financial functions are present in all three countries, but the efficiency of the financial system varies greatly between them. Access to financial services or financial inclusion is crucial for economic growth, regardless of which sector supplies the funds.
What_was_studied: The concept of “finance for growth” in emerging and developing economies, with a focus on China, South Africa, and Nigeria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To build confidence in the Nigerian financial system, appropriate policy options should be implemented to prioritize access to financial services and financial inclusion.

Authors: Hafidz Wibisono; Jon C. Lovett; Dhimas Bayu Anindito
Field: Trilemma; Electrification; Sustainability; Framing (construction); Political science; Rural electrification; Energy policy; Energy security; Economics; Renewable energy; Economic system; Electricity; Monetary policy; Geography; Ecology; Electrical engineering; Archaeology; Monetary economics; Biology; Engineering
Title: The contestation of ideas behind Indonesia's rural electrification policies: The influence of global and national institutional dynamics
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis reveals an energy trilemma, with contestation between energy access, energy security, and climate change mitigation. The study finds that sustainability has not been a primary topic of debate within the policy subsystem in pre- and post-SDG and NDC periods, but the global deployment of sustainability has triggered the emergence of discursive intermediaries within the policy subsystem who frame global environmental issues to fit into internal debates.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the contestation of ideas within Indonesia's rural electricity policy subsystem during two time periods: pre- and post-SDG and Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) periods, using statements from political actors in national news articles and Discourse Network Analysis to investigate the influence of global agendas on the debate over energy access, energy security, and climate change mitigation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize the narration of implementing renewable energy that emphasizes its benefits over the energy poverty problem while injecting messages related to environmental profit, and give more attention to the issue of decentralization, which has always been the most frequent and mutually connected topic in terms of source utilization and governance.

Title: Spillover of Financial Innovations during Covid-19: A Cross-Country Analysis
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The empirical results demonstrate that the financial innovations spillover is very high during the Covid-19 pandemic, with a total spillover of 49.2% on average based on three months' government bond yield price, and 62% on average when measured through composite financial sector indices.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the cross-country financial innovations spillover during the Covid-19 pandemic among the top ten economies in terms of gross domestic product, from January 1st to July 10th, 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that more than half of the total variance of forecast errors is explained by innovations spillover across countries, implying the need for better guidance to investors, portfolio managers, and policymakers during this economic disaster to make informed decisions.

Field: Numeracy; Psychological resilience; Agency (philosophy); Public relations; Government (linguistics); Literacy; Psychology; Political science; Sociology; Pedagogy; Social psychology; Social science; Linguistics; Philosophy
Title: Building resilience now and for the future: Adolescent skills to address global challenges
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings presented in this special issue address a range of skills, including foundational literacy and numeracy, hard skills in digital literacy, financial literacy, and entrepreneurship, and soft skills, such as critical thinking, confidence, voice, and agency.
What_was_studied: This special issue brings together researchers and practitioners in the field of international education to illustrate how current global challenges shape the types of skills needed to build resilience and offer possible solutions to supporting young people's development of such skills, drawing on both quantitative and qualitative data, including surveys and interviews with students, parents, teachers, school leaders, nonformal education providers, and government officials, most studies presenting evidence from sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: With the special issue, we aim to draw more attention to the need for research and policy that equip youth with relevant skills and see them not just as subjects of the challenges they encounter but also as active agents of change, highlighting the importance of an intersectional lens that addresses not just gender but also other individual and household characteristics, such as student age, disability status, and poverty to support youth resilience and skills development.

Field: Intermediary; Generosity; Bureaucracy; Ethnography; Power (physics); Development aid; Political science; Sociology; Public relations; Media studies; Politics; Business; Law; Marketing; Anthropology; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Aid is not development: The true character of Pacific aid
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Three clear shifts in Australian aid over the last decade: (1) aid has become more politicized, deployed to support Australian interests; (2) aid has been increasingly privatized as much of the aid has been spent through four large Australian and international corporations—with local Pacific companies marginalized; and (3) aid has been increasingly contested by the peoples of the Pacific.
What_was_studied: Seven decades of collective experiences and observations of Australian aid in the Pacific, using ethnographic and auto-ethnographic insights to explore repressed stories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Such changes have encouraged donors to tighten their grip on power, and intermediaries to act as their agents, performing high levels of 'interpretive labor.' Recipients of aid have been left with few options: they can comply with donors, thanking them for their generosity. Aid of this character is not development but rather an unchecked donor-driven system beset by excessive power and control to benefit the system and its agents. It systematically fails to empower Pacific agency and reduce aid dependency.

Field: Work (physics); Beauty; Demographic economics; Training (meteorology); Entry Level; Affect (linguistics); Labour economics; Occupational segregation; Business; Psychology; Political science; Gender studies; Sociology; Economics; Wage; Medicine; Medical education; Engineering; Geography; Mechanical engineering; Meteorology; Law; Communication
Title: Do job aspirations cause job choice? Insights from women entering male‐dominated occupational training in India
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Contrary to conventional wisdom, young women's entry into non-traditional training in Delhi was not a result of their occupational aspirations. Rather, entry into training saw them aspire to the jobs for which they trained.
What_was_studied: Young women's entry into non-traditional training in Delhi was studied to understand how aspirations for non-traditional jobs are formed among them.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should focus on factors that directly affect job entry—for example, having training centres close to where these young women live—and provide opportunities for young women to train. This study raises questions about traditional conceptions of aspirations and prompts future studies to assess whether they apply in other parts of the global South.

Field: Fell; Economics; Poverty; Prosperity; Human development (humanity); Corporate governance; Development economics; Politics
Keywords: global; economic crisis; Africa
Title: IMPACT OF THE GLOBAL FINANCIAL AND ECONOMIC CRISIS ON DEVELOPMENT: WHITHER AFRICA?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the economic crisis resulted in a 60% decline in economic growth in Africa, but improvements in governance helped mitigate the impact. Low-income and 'fragile' countries were resilient despite their dependence on external assistance.
What_was_studied: The global economic crisis' impact on Africa's economic growth from 2008 to 2013 using data from various African countries, with a focus on poverty and human development trends during that time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Africa should prioritize improved governance to ensure continued prosperity, particularly for low-income and fragile countries that critically depend on external assistance. Policymakers must commit to sustainable development practices and invest in human capital to scale up economic growth and address food insecurity and income poverty.

Authors: Valerie Rhoe; Suresh Chandra Babu; William Reidhead
Field: Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Basic needs; Population; Central asia; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Malnutrition; Extreme poverty
Title: An analysis of food security and poverty in Central Asia—case study from Kazakhstan
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the total poverty line captures more of the poor population, and while there are some variations amongst the determinants of poverty under the two poverty lines, the strength of the common determinants is generally weaker when non-food expenditures are included in deriving the poverty line.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the Kazakhstan Living Standard and Measurement Survey to identify a food poverty line and total poverty line for Kazakhstan during the transition from planned to market-oriented economies, with a focus on understanding the magnitude of food insecurity and poverty and their determinants.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address food insecurity and poverty, particularly among those who are most vulnerable to market shocks and economic transition, by investing in social protection programs and sustainable agriculture practices to increase self-sufficiency.

Authors: Wenjing Li; Chuanmin Shuai; Yu Shuai; Xin Cheng; Yue Liu; Fubin Huang
Field: Business; Grounded theory; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Human capital; Index (economics); Livelihood; Sustainable development; Physical capital; Capital (economics)
Title: How Livelihood Assets Contribute to Sustainable Development of Smallholder Farmers
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Psycap is a significant predictor of Humcap and Phycap, which in turn have direct and indirect effects on sustainable livelihoods. Additionally, the study identified key factors and paths affecting smallholder farmers' sustainable livelihoods, including the impact of Phycap and Humcap on a new sustainable livelihood index.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the six capitals of smallholder farmers' household capacity and their relationships with sustainable livelihoods in the Three Gorges Reservoir Region in China, using a hybrid approach of qualitative and quantitative methods and the sustainable livelihood approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize investments in Psycap development programs to enhance smallholder farmers' household capacity and promote sustainable livelihoods. Additionally, policies aimed at improving access to physical capital and human capital for smallholder farmers can have a significant impact on reducing poverty and achieving sustainable development in the region.

Field: Public policy; Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Business relations; Unemployment; Black Economic Empowerment; Mixed economy; Development economics; Politics
Title: State‐business relations and pro‐poor growth in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there was growth-oriented cooperation between the state and business, economic growth remained weak and did not reduce income poverty or unemployment. The state's selective interventions in a mixed economy were not enough to address these issues.
What_was_studied: This research examined the relationship between state and business in post-apartheid South Africa from 1994 to 2010, using a mixed-methods approach with a focus on economic growth, income poverty, and employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent poverty and unemployment, the study suggests that the government should prioritize more pro-poor and inclusive policies, such as labor market regulation and investment in education and infrastructure, rather than relying solely on market-oriented solutions.

Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Economics; Wage; Rural poverty; Household income; Secondary education; Nonfarm payrolls
Title: NONFARM EMPLOYMENT AND INCOMES IN RURAL GHANA
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women are significantly less likely than men to be in wage employment and more likely than men to be in self-employment activities, and that households whose heads have completed secondary education or higher gravitate more toward wage employment. Nonfarm employment appears crucial for alleviating rural poverty in Ghana.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the determinants of participation in nonfarm activities and the impact of nonfarm employment on household income for rural households in Ghana during a specific time period using secondary data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize initiatives to increase access to nonfarm employment opportunities for women and households with lower education levels, particularly in rural areas, to supplement or augment farm income and alleviate poverty.

Authors: Ben Crow; Nichole Zlatunich; Brian Fulfrost
Field: Income inequality metrics; Neoclassical economics; Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Human Development Index; Information and communication technologies for development; Field (Bourdieu); Inequality; Economic growth; Economic inequality
Title: Mapping global inequalities: Beyond income inequality to multi‐dimensional inequalities
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that current understandings of poverty are limited by their reliance on income-based measures, and that new questions and opportunities exist to work towards a fuller understanding of global inequalities. The study also identified significant disparities in health outcomes between urban and rural areas, as well as variations in social protection policies and access to sustainable development opportunities.
What_was_studied: The research examines the multi-faceted nature of global inequalities beyond income measures using a variety of data sources and methods for the period between 1990 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of multidimensional poverty measures that account for health disparities and access to social protection and sustainable development opportunities, particularly in rural areas. This could involve scaling up existing interventions, expanding access to healthcare services, and investing in sustainable development programs that benefit marginalized communities.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Poverty; Mainstream; Microfinance; Livelihood; Development economics; Scale (social sciences); Intervention (law); Sustainability
Title: Microfinance North and South: Contrasting Current Debates
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while microfinance has shown promise in reducing income poverty and improving economic well-being in the South, its emphasis on scale and sustainability may be at odds with its original goal of re-inventing mainstream economic and financial systems to address social, economic, and environmental costs and benefits. Moreover, the study highlights the need for deliberate efforts to address gender inequities in microfinance interventions.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effectiveness of microfinance as a tool for addressing poverty and social exclusion in both North and South, examining the current practices in Southern microfinance and their origins in community banking in the North.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the promise of microfinance in reducing income poverty and improving economic well-being, decision makers should prioritize and fund initiatives that integrate gender-sensitive approaches to ensure equitable benefits for all populations, particularly women.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Passive income; Labour economics; Economics; Comprehensive income; Gross income; Income in kind; Distribution (economics); Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Economic growth, inequality and poverty: An analysis of policy in a two period framework
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that providing income support alone can lead to greater mean income and less poverty and income inequality compared to laissez-faire when income is responsive to educational outlays, while supplementing income support with additional education for the poor can further reduce poverty and income inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes policies aimed at reducing poverty and income inequality within a two-period overlapping generations model, using a balanced budget framework with income in the second period determined by human capital and education investment in the first period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investment in education for the poor and implement income support programs to scale up the reduction of poverty and income inequality, especially when income is responsive to educational outlays.
