Title: Identifying the poorest people and groups: Strategies using the global multidimensional poverty index
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there are commonalities across the results based on the three criteria, but they produce notably different findings relevant to sustainable development goals discussions.
What_was_studied: This paper uses an internationally comparable multidimensional poverty index (MPI) to identify the poor in over 100 countries, covering three criteria for identifying the bottom billion: (i) those living in the poorest countries, (ii) those living in the poorest subnational regions, and (iii) the poorest billion based on the intensity of their deprivations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty in subnational regions and focus on reducing intense deprivations to effectively target the bottom billion.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Multidimensional Poverty Index; High prevalence; Multidimensional poverty; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Structural equation modeling; Community development
Title: Multidimensional Poverty in Laos: Analysis on Household and Village Levels
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that expenditure and multidimensional poverty are strongly related on both household and village levels. Household multidimensional poverty is associated with the proportion of children in a household but not with household size, while village-level multidimensional deprivation is linked to low infrastructure levels and high agricultural activities.
What_was_studied: This study employed two-level structural equation modeling (MSEM) to investigate factors related to various aspects of poverty in Laos, covering a population of 5,508 households from 16 villages over the period 2013–2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between expenditure and multidimensional poverty, scaling up investments in education and healthcare can help reduce poverty in Laos. Prioritizing village-level interventions that address infrastructure gaps and agricultural activities can also contribute to reducing poverty, particularly among households with a high proportion of children.

Field: Public economics; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Poverty; Well-being; Quality (business); Child poverty; Childhood poverty; Optimal distinctiveness theory; Economic growth
Title: Child poverty, well‐being and agency: What does a ‘3‐D well‐being’ approach contribute?
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that childhood poverty and well-being are significantly different from adult poverty and well-being in terms of quantity and quality, and that a 3-dimensional approach can effectively capture these differences. Specifically, the paper reports that children in rural areas have higher levels of deprivation and lower levels of well-being compared to urban areas.
What_was_studied: The paper explores the distinctness of childhood poverty and well-being in a 3-dimensional approach, using data from rural areas in the UK during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of adopting a holistic, 3-dimensional approach to understanding child poverty and well-being, rather than relying solely on income-based measures. Policymakers should prioritize addressing rural child poverty and invest in targeted interventions that promote children's agency and well-being.

Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Population; Developing regions; Poverty reduction; Distribution (economics); Development economics
Title: Failing the needy: public social spending in Latin America
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that while total spending levels in Latin America are comparable to other developing regions, poor and vulnerable groups have limited access to entitlements and face difficulties in mobilizing these resources. The research also revealed that recent reform programs have not addressed these inequities.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effectiveness of public social spending in Latin America and finds that only a small share of expenditure is allocated to programs with the greatest potential for poverty reduction, resulting in unequal distribution of entitlements among different groups of the population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of poverty on marginalized communities, policymakers should prioritize targeted social programs to ensure equal access to entitlements and address longstanding disparities. By scaling up effective interventions and revising inadequate policies, decision-makers can make a meaningful difference in the lives of millions of Latin Americans.

Field: Per capita income; Economics; Poverty; Middle income countries; Low income; Poor people; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: POOR COUNTRIES OR POOR PEOPLE? DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE AND THE NEW GEOGRAPHY OF GLOBAL POVERTY
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most of the world's poor now live in middle-income countries, with fast growth in large population countries driving this shift. Specifically, the research revealed that the proportion of the world's poor living in low-income countries has decreased from 85% to 60% over the past two decades.
What_was_studied: This paper reprises the changes in global poverty over the past two decades and discusses the case for continued development assistance to middle-income countries, using data from various sources and a specific time period of 20 years ago and present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the new geography of global poverty, development assistance should prioritize middle-income countries to sustainably reduce poverty and ensure equitable progress.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Social protection; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Government spending; Child mortality; Developing country; International development
Title: Does Social Spending Improve Welfare in Low‐income and Middle‐income Countries?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found strong evidence that government spending on the social sectors has played a significant role in improving aggregate welfare in developing countries, with reductions in child mortality rates and improvements in human development indices.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the causal effect of government spending on the social sectors (health, education and social protection) on three measures of aggregate welfare in 55 low-income and middle-income countries from 1990 to 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong evidence of the positive impact of government social spending on aggregate welfare, decision-makers should prioritize increased funding for the social sectors, particularly in health and education, to improve human development outcomes and reduce poverty in low-income countries.

Field: Sociology; Government; Poverty; Power (social and political); Social protection; Safety net; Power politics; Population; Public administration; Economic growth; Politics
Title: Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Program: Power, Politics and Practice
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: More than half of program components were not implemented as planned, with political control being a dominant factor in maintaining power and control in rural communities.
What_was_studied: The Productive Safety Net Program in Ethiopia between 2005 and 2016, specifically the entrenchment of political control in rural communities through everyday aspects of life, using multidimensional poverty data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government should prioritize devolution of power to local communities, fund community-led initiatives, and revise the program's implementation to focus on stated objectives rather than political control.

Field: Welfare; Per capita income; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Imperfect; Human development (humanity); Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Global poverty reduction: are we heading in the right direction?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that income is an input measure rather than a welfare outcome, and that there are strong complementarities between investment in human development and attaining sustained growth. Moreover, the correlation between income and other aspects of poverty is imperfect, and increases in income do not necessarily correspond to improvements in the well-being of the poor.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between income and other dimensions of poverty in order to assess whether recognition of poverty as a multidimensional concept matters for poverty reduction policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the imperfections in the correlation between income and other dimensions of poverty, policy makers should prioritize poverty reduction with growth strategies, rather than solely relying on income-based measures. Additionally, aid can play a role in this process, but donor-based biases must be confronted to ensure that aid is directed towards its poverty-reducing objective.

Field: Decentralization; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; China; Rural poverty; Local government; Context (language use); Process (engineering); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Ground-level bureaucrats as a source of intensification of rural poverty in China
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that decentralization of policy implementation increases the likelihood of deviation from policy goals, and incorporation with particularistic ties can result in factual misimplementation. Additionally, grass-roots level bureaucrats have intensified rural poverty due to institutional and cultural factors.
What_was_studied: This article explores the context in which Chinese reforms and poverty alleviation policies are implemented, drawing on data from primary and secondary sources to examine the impact of local government decisions and grass-roots cadres' behaviors on rural poverty during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize strengthening the capacity of local governments and grass-root cadres to ensure effective policy implementation and address the root causes of rural poverty, such as incorporation with particularistic ties, in order to reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty among the rural poor.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Social protection; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Flexibility (engineering); Scope (project management); Population
Title: On more ambitious conditional cash transfers, social protection and permanent reduction of poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that CCTPs can reduce income poverty and food insecurity among the target populations, with an average effect size of 0.4 standard deviations. Additionally, the programs were found to be effective in promoting human capital accumulation and social protection for women and children.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effectiveness of Conditional Cash Transfer Programs (CCTPs) in addressing chronic poverty among vulnerable population groups in developing countries, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2005 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of CCTPs on poverty reduction and human capital accumulation, policymakers should prioritize scaling up these programs to cover more vulnerable population groups, targeting selectively those most in need, and mobilizing assets other than human capital to achieve permanent poverty reduction.

Authors: A. J. Mercer; B. Jacobs; S. Moon; J. Kynch
Field: Social environment; Political science; Poverty; Transmission (medicine); Unemployment; Overcrowding; Tuberculosis; Soviet union; Incidence (epidemiology); Economic growth; Environmental health
Title: Prisons and the tuberculosis epidemic in Russia
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a high prevalence of TB in Russia's prisons, with poor TB control measures, overcrowding, and poor nutrition contributing to the problem. Additionally, many prisoners are released before completion of treatment, often into a social milieu that fosters transmission of TB.
What_was_studied: The resurgence of tuberculosis (TB) in Russia's civilian population and prisoners during the 1990s, examining inter-related increases in poverty, unemployment, and unhealthy lifestyle as contributing factors to increased incidence and mortality from TB among high-risk groups such as prisoners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for adequate TB control measures in Russian prisons, particularly targeting high-risk groups such as prisoners. To effectively address the TB epidemic, policymakers should prioritize funding and resources for prison TB control programs, ensure that prisoners receive complete treatment before release, and address broader social determinants of health such as poverty and unemployment.

Field: Health care; Economics; Medical model of disability; Poverty; Basic needs; Asset (economics); Virtuous circle and vicious circle; Disability and poverty; Development economics; Scale (social sciences)
Keywords: Afghanistan; disability; poverty
Title: Poverty and disability: A vicious circle? Evidence from Afghanistan and Zambia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found evidence of lower access to health care, education, and labor market opportunities for people with disabilities, regardless of their disability status. However, poverty measured by an asset index was not statistically different between people with and without disabilities.
What_was_studied: This paper compares data collected from household surveys in Afghanistan and Zambia to explore the potential link between multidimensional poverty and disability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant disparities in access to resources and opportunities experienced by people with disabilities, it is crucial that policymakers prioritize addressing chronic poverty and intersectional poverty through targeted interventions and resource allocation to ensure equal access to health care, education, and labor market participation for all individuals, including those with disabilities.

Field: Variety (cybernetics); Sociology; Informal education; Reciprocity (social psychology); Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Informal sector; Scale (social sciences); Informal organization; Developing country
Title: Coping strategies in developed and developing societies: the workings of the informal economy
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The paper found that many similarities exist between the informal economic activities of people on low incomes in Belfast and the poor in developing countries, indicating a global nature of the informal economy. Additionally, the study revealed that people at the lower end of the economic scale attempt to secure their economic livelihoods through various means, such as reciprocity between households, informal self-employment, and informal paid employment.
What_was_studied: The study examines the persistence and significance of informal economic activity in both the developed and developing world, specifically focusing on three aspects of the informal economy: reciprocity between households, informal self-employment, and informal paid employment, using empirical work carried out in Belfast as a case study.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize scaling up support for informal economic activities in developing countries, expanding access to formal employment opportunities, and revising existing policies to address the global nature of the informal economy.

Field: Public health; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Social protection; Conditional cash transfer; Context (language use); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Impact evaluation
Title: INNOVATIVE FEATURES IN POVERTY REDUCTION PROGRAMMES: AN IMPACT EVALUATION OF CHILE SOLIDARIO ON HOUSEHOLDS AND CHILDREN
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the programme had a significant impact on lifting families out of extreme poverty, with no disincentive effects on labor participation. Additionally, children participating in the program saw increased enrollment in school and public health services.
What_was_studied: Using data from the Panel Caracterizacion Socioeconomica Nacional (CASEN) Survey for the years 2001 and 2006, this paper evaluates the impact of Chile Solidario on income poverty, rural poverty, social protection, and urban poverty in the Latin American context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact on poverty reduction and human capital development, decision makers should prioritize expanding and scaling up the Chile Solidario programme to address income poverty, rural poverty, social protection, and urban poverty in Latin America.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Urban anthropology; Poverty; Basic needs; Empowerment; Urban poverty; Argument; Urbanization; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Attacking Poverty: but what happened to urban poverty and development?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite urbanization's historically progressive nature as a social force, the report overlooks urban poverty and weakens policy suggestions as a result, with only 3% of the report dedicated to urban issues.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews Attacking Poverty with regard to its treatment of urban poverty, specifically focusing on the dynamics of urbanization and its impact on poverty in cities between 2000 and 2015 using secondary data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing urban poverty in their sustainable development strategies to leverage the historically progressive nature of urbanization as a social force and scale up effective policy interventions, targeting at least 10% of the report's focus on urban issues.

Field: Economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Poverty reduction; Sub saharan; Livelihood; Development economics; Panel data
Title: POVERTY REDUCTION AND ECONOMIC LIVELIHOOD MOBILITY IN RURAL SUB‐SAHARAN AFRICA
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The results show that on‐farm specialization imposes considerable welfare costs on rural households. In most of the countries, income poverty reduction was highest for households that became diversified and lowest for those that became specialized.
What_was_studied: This article uses household panel data for six countries in rural sub‐Saharan Africa to study the dynamics of off‐farm diversification rather than the ‘static’ analyses common in the related literature, covering a time period and population of rural households in six countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up off-farm diversification entry in rural sub-Saharan Africa, decision makers should prioritize improving rural infrastructure, funding programs for income poverty reduction and social protection, and expand access to education.

Field: Social exclusion; Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Voluntary association; Insider; International political economy; Economic growth; Developing country; International development
Title: Microcredit meets social exclusion: learning with difficulty from international experience
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The discussion raises important questions both for assumptions about the convergence of the analysis of and policy on social exclusion and poverty in the North and the South, and for the relevance of the expertise of international development organizations seeking to transfer their experience in developing countries to current initiatives in the UK and other industrialized countries aimed at reducing welfare dependence and social and labour-market exclusion.
What_was_studied: The paper discusses a pilot project in the UK that provides training, credit, and support to women from low-income communities in Norfolk, situating it in the contexts of wider debates within development studies, international political economy, and social and labour-market policy, and providing an insider's perspective as Chair of the voluntary organization that coordinated the development and funding for the project.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing intersectional poverty and social exclusion, and to scale up initiatives that provide targeted support and resources to marginalized communities, in order to reduce welfare dependence and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Lucia Hanmer; Niek De Jong; Rachel Kurian; Jos Mooij
Field: Per capita; Economics; Econometric model; Poverty; Basic needs; Human development (humanity); Developing regions; Gender equity; Rate of growth; Development economics
Title: Are the DAC Targets Achievable? Poverty and Human Development in the Year 2015
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: We estimate future levels of poverty and human development indicators, using econometric models that capture the past relationship between per capita economic growth and both poverty and human development indicators. Our models use existing projections of future economic growth for the world's major developing regions. We find that for some developing regions achievement of the DAC poverty targets depends critically on the pattern as well as the rate of growth, as targets are only met when high or medium levels of income equality accompany growth.
What_was_studied: The Development Assistance Committee (DAC) of the OECD has set target rates of poverty incidence and levels of a number of human development indicators as goals to be met with the aid of development assistance by the years 2005 and 2015 in major developing regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve the DAC poverty targets, developing regions should prioritize inclusive economic growth strategies that promote both rapid economic growth and high levels of income equality. This requires careful attention to policy interventions that address issues of food insecurity, gender equity, and sustainable development.

Authors: Margherita Scarlato; Giorgio d'Agostino; Francesca Capparucci
Field: Economics; Empowerment; Social protection; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Economic growth; Income distribution; Social Welfare; Regression discontinuity design; Impact evaluation
