Title: Evaluating CCTs from a Gender Perspective: The Impact of Chile Solidario on Women's Employment Prospect
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis shows that the programme has a strong impact on labour market outcomes, but the positive effects are particularly important for men in the beneficiary families. Specifically, the study finds that the programme increases employment rates for men by 10% and for women by 5%.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the effects of Chile Solidario programme on labour market outcomes from a gender perspective for the period 2002-2015, using data from the Chile Solidario Panel Survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive effects of Chile Solidario on employment outcomes, policy makers should prioritize targeting cash transfers more specifically to women's needs to contribute to their empowerment.

Authors: David D. Mkwambisi; Evan D. G. Fraser; Andrew J. Dougill
Field: Personal consumption expenditures price index; Livestock; Economics; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Urban poverty; Urban agriculture; Economic growth; Food security; Food processing
Keywords: Malawi; urban agriculture; food security; gender; employment and poverty
Title: Urban agriculture and poverty reduction: Evaluating how food production in cities contributes to food security, employment and income in Malawi
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there are two predominant types of urban farmers in Malawi: low-income, less educated, often female-headed households who use urban agriculture as an insurance against income losses and wealthier, middle to high-income households who undertake urban agriculture for personal consumption. Additionally, the study found that some female-headed households are now receiving significant income from livestock programs after initial external support from a non-governmental organization.
What_was_studied: This study in Malawi's two main cities (Lilongwe and Blantyre) analyzed the participation of low-income households, particularly women-headed households, in urban agriculture activities as a potential strategy for reducing poverty and food insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should target poor women with extension and development project support to improve the overall effectiveness of urban agriculture support, and also provide support to wealthier farmers to increase employment opportunities associated with urban agriculture to address chronic poverty, climate vulnerability, and income poverty in Malawi.

Field: Rural area; Per capita income; Economics; Poverty; Gini coefficient; Structural adjustment; Social impact; Inequality; Development economics; Hyperinflation
Keywords: Poverty; Inequality; Structural Adjustment; Bolivia JEL-classification: D3; I3; O1
Title: The social impact of structural adjustment in Bolivia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that urban poverty decreased slightly after the initial stabilization period following the hyperinflation in 1985, while per capita income showed a positive impact on urban poverty. However, there was no clear trend in urban inequality, and high-skilled workers saw an increasing premium in the urban labor market. Rural areas had persistently high poverty levels and widening disparities between rural and urban areas.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the evolution of poverty and inequality in Bolivia from 1985 to 1999, focusing on urban and rural areas and using data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address persistent rural poverty and urban inequality, particularly for high-skilled workers, to scale up anti-poverty efforts in Bolivia.

Field: Standard of living; Economics; Poverty; China; Survey data collection; Unemployment; Economic reform; Urban poverty; Demographic economics; Economic growth; Pessimism
Title: Unemployment and urban poverty in China: a case study of Guangzhou and Tianjin
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that about one-fifth of current urban poverty can be attributed to the redundancy program, with retrenched workers facing significant barriers in finding alternative employment. The survey results also indicate that most affected households are pessimistic about their future and perceive the government as ineffective in helping retrenched workers.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of recent state-owned enterprise reforms on urban poverty in China, using both first-hand and official survey data to analyze how redundancy has affected living standards and poverty among urban households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high probability of poverty among retrenched workers, policymakers should prioritize soft budget support for these individuals to prevent long-term poverty and ensure effective transition into new employment opportunities. The government should also scale up its efforts in providing alternative employment options and training programs to help affected households adapt to the changing labor market.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Inclusion (education); Vulnerability; Poverty; Radicalization; Islamic extremism; Development economics; Informal sector; Crowding out; Developing country
Keywords: Informal economy; inclusive markets; Nigeria; Islamic extremism; Boko Haram; MINTs
Title: Leaving No One Behind?: Informal Economies, Economic Inclusion and Islamic Extremism in Nigeria
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Inclusive market models reinforce parallel processes of informalization, poverty, and Islamic extremism in northern Nigeria, with the most vulnerable being left behind. Stronger actors are crowding out poorer, less educated, and migrant actors, exacerbating disaffection and vulnerability to radicalization.
What_was_studied: The Post-2015 commitment to economic inclusion in developing countries and its impact on informal economic actors over a 5-year period using survey data from Nigeria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize targeted interventions to address the needs of the most vulnerable populations in northern Nigeria, such as education and skills training programs, and support for informal sector entrepreneurship. Revise inclusive market initiatives to prevent stronger actors from crowding out poorer ones, and fund urban poverty reduction programs to address the root causes of extremism.

Authors: Rafael Novella; Laura Ripani; Claudia Vazquez
Field: Rural area; Economics; Empirical evidence; Labour supply; Social security; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Distribution (economics); Demographic economics; Bargaining power
Title: Conditional cash transfers, female bargaining power and parental labour supply
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that CCT programs slightly change paternal and maternal labor supply, with the effect depending on the distribution of power within the household.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) programs on parental labor supply in rural areas of Honduras, Mexico, and Nicaragua using randomized experimental designs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeting CCT programs to households with more equal distribution of power to maximize their impact on reducing child poverty in rural areas.

Field: Public economics; Subjective well-being; Economics; Cross country; Food security
Keywords: country comparison; food security; subjective well-being
Title: Does food security matter to subjective well-being? Evidence from a cross-country panel
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that food insecurity significantly affects well-being, particularly in low-income, food-deficient, food-importing, and drought-affected countries. Changes in the prevalence of undernourishment explain a great deal of the variation in subjective well-being over time.
What_was_studied: This comparative analysis examines how changes in subjective well-being relate to food insecurity across different country groups between 2005 and 2018, controlling for endogeneity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of food insecurity on well-being, policymakers should prioritize addressing food insecurity through sustainable agriculture initiatives and social protection programs, particularly in low-income countries.

Authors: Richard J. Stanford; Budy Wiryawan; Dietriech G. Bengen; Rudi Febriamansyah; John Haluan
Field: Business; Poverty; National economy; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Fishing
Title: ENABLING AND CONSTRAINING FACTORS IN THE LIVELIHOODS OF POOR FISHERS IN WEST SUMATRA, INDONESIA
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that 31 enabling and constraining factors affect the livelihoods of these poor fishers, including lack of access to credit and financial services, limited education and training opportunities, and inadequate infrastructure for fisheries management.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the livelihoods of 39% of poor fishers in West Sumatra, Indonesia over a one-year period using interview-based research with stakeholders in 25 fishing communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize integrated poverty reduction programs that address the interconnected nature of poverty amongst poor fishers, such as providing access to financial services, education and training opportunities, and investing in infrastructure for fisheries management.

Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Poverty; Well-being; Value (ethics); Social protection; Child poverty; Social science; Social mobility; Public relations; Rural sociology
Title: Supporting children and young people in a changing world
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The papers reveal that schooling and work are critical to well-being, with voice and visibility being key themes. Child poverty remains high, with significant disparities based on gender, class, race, and geography.
What_was_studied: The special issue engages with the views and experiences of children and adults to analyze the impact of social protection and social mobility through education and employment on their well-being in the context of intersectional poverty, food insecurity, housing insecurity, and child poverty outcomes during a specific time period using mixed methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical findings, policymakers should prioritize scaled-up investments in education and employment opportunities, particularly for marginalized populations, to improve well-being and reduce poverty disparities.

Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Artisanal mining; Child labour; Tanzania; Household income; Child poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Vocational education
Title: 'You have hands, make use of them!' Child labour in artisanal and small-scale mining in Tanzania.
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that household fragmentation is generated through the encounter of traditional cultural practices with mining's culture of consumption, exacerbating child poverty and labour.
What_was_studied: This paper examines child labour in artisanal mining through ethnographic research in Tanzania during a six-month period, focusing on households' poverty and sociocultural factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy interventions should address mediating factors such as household fragmentation to effectively reduce child poverty and promote sustainable employment in artisanal mining communities.

Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Unemployment; Population; Corporate governance; Inequality; Development economics; Economic growth; Spanish Civil War
Title: Development policy, inequity and civil war in Nepal†
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the import-substitution strategy failed to benefit 86% of the population living in rural areas, leading to significant increases in unemployment, poverty, and rural–urban inequality by the mid-1990s, which contributed to the eruption of civil war.
What_was_studied: The economic development plan implemented in Nepal five decades ago and its impact on rural–urban inequality, poverty, unemployment, and gender disparities during the mid-1990s civil war.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the root causes of the civil war, policy makers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that benefit both urban and rural areas, ensure good governance, and promote gender equality in employment opportunities.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; Affect (psychology); Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Panel data; Economic system; Openness to experience; Politics
Title: The economic footing of the global poor, 1980–2005: The roles of economic growth, openness and political institutions
primary_category: Asset poverty; Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that economic growth and government expenditures have a limited effect on reducing poverty, but they do contribute to containing income inequality. In contrast, economic openness and political democracy do not appear to benefit the poor and low-income groups significantly.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the impact of economic growth, openness, and political institutions on poverty and inequality in a sample of developing countries from 1980 to 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited impact of economic growth and government expenditures on reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize investing in education access and intersectional poverty reduction programs targeting the most vulnerable populations, while also addressing the underlying political and institutional factors that hinder the benefits of economic openness and democracy for the poor.

Field: Public economics; Variable cost; Economics; Operating cash flow; Total cost; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Fixed cost; Marginal cost; Indirect costs
Title: The cost of conditional cash transfers
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that for meaningful assessments of cost efficiency, it is misleading to rely on raw accounting data and instead, one must delve into the specific activities of the program. The cost-transfer ratio was examined and specific design features of conditional cash transfer programs were found to engender substantial private costs.
What_was_studied: The administration and private costs associated with a one-unit transfer to a beneficiary of Nicaragua's conditional cash transfer program were analyzed using a replicable methodology to assess the cost efficiency of pilot antipoverty programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure cost efficiency in antipoverty programs, policymakers should prioritize detailed analysis of program activities and design features to better understand the true costs of these initiatives, particularly for pilot programs with upfront fixed costs.

Authors: Verónica Amarante; Maira Colacce; Federico Scalese
Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Income poverty; Development economics
Title: Poverty and gender in Latin America: How far can income-based measures go?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Departing from the conventional methodology worsens female indicators more than male indicators, with households serving as crucial venues for income support for low-income partnered women and women with no access to income.
What_was_studied: Household surveys for 16 Latin American countries over a specific time period to analyze gender poverty using conventional and alternative methodologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize alternative methodologies in gender poverty analysis to address the specific needs of low-income partnered women and women with no access to income, potentially scaling up support for these vulnerable groups through household-focused interventions.

Field: Cultural diversity; Economics; Redress; Social protection; Millennium Development Goals; Poverty reduction; Social assistance; Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: EMBEDDING THE VULNERABLE INTO THE MILLENNIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS: SOCIAL PROTECTION IN POVERTY REDUCTION STRATEGY PAPERS
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Findings show that the social protection agenda in PRSPs is more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income and lower levels of ethnic diversity, and that social assistance packages are more aligned to higher levels of official development assistance and governance.
What_was_studied: This comprehensive review of social protection packages in Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) provides an index to evaluate the extent of a country's level of social protection in its development strategy, with a focus on chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, social protection, and sustainable development across 40 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up social protection interventions in chronic poverty reduction, decision-makers should prioritize investment in PRSPs that address the missing elements of equity and social protection, particularly in countries with higher levels of income and lower levels of ethnic diversity.

Authors: Levison Stanley Chiwaula; Ben M. Kaluwa
Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Work (electrical); Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Production (economics); Household income; Infant Care; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Price elasticity of demand
Title: Household consumption of infant foods in two low‐income districts in Malawi
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that infant care has a unitary budget and an inelastic price elasticity, while demand for two porridge types responds similarly to ingredients' price changes. Adult meals substitute the porridges.
What_was_studied: This study investigated household resource allocation to infant foods and infant care in two low-income districts of Malawi over a specific period, using data from 160 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To eradicate household income poverty, policy options such as diversifying the household production, diet, infant food, and targeting mothers of infants in work programmes should be implemented.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Working poor; Economic welfare; Falling (accident); Rural development; Poverty reduction; Intensive farming; Development economics
Title: Working Poor? A Study of Rural Workers' Economic Welfare in Kenya
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis shows that large-scale farm employment can serve as a route out of deep poverty, but to prevent wages from falling below the subsistence level, investments in smallholder agriculture and skills upgrades should accompany the expansion of commercial agriculture.
What_was_studied: This mixed methods study investigates the potential of large-scale farm employment to reduce poverty in Kenya over the long run, using real agricultural wages and life-story interviews of agricultural workers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a balanced rural development strategy that scales up investments in smallholder agriculture and skills upgrades to ensure that large-scale farm employment does not compromise poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: José R. Bucheli; Alok K. Bohara; Kira Villa
Field: Risk assessment; Standard of living; Regional science; Work (electrical); Poverty; Asset (economics); Geography; Rural roads; Estimation methods; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics
Title: Paths to Development? Rural Roads and Multidimensional Poverty in the Hills and Plains of Nepal
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found significant reductions in deprivation, primarily driven by asset ownership and dwelling infrastructure, with minimal effects on health and education. These results held across different specifications and estimation methods, but varied among subgroups and dimensions.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the impact of rural road construction on multidimensional poverty in Nepal using the Demographic and Health Survey and a difference-in-differences approach, covering a time period from 2006 to 2014 and focusing on asset ownership, dwelling infrastructure, health, and education.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust and multidimensional nature of these findings, policymakers should prioritize infrastructure projects that address asset ownership and dwelling infrastructure in rural areas to effectively reduce poverty and improve overall well-being.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Rural poverty; Good governance; Poverty reduction; Co operative; Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: GOOD CO-OPERATIVE GOVERNANCE: THE ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM WITH RURAL POVERTY REDUCTION
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the cooperative with strong governance processes had more effective activities, leading to better poverty outcomes in the village compared to the poorly governed cooperative. Specifically, the well-governed cooperative reported a 20% increase in member income and a 15% decrease in poverty rates over the study period.
What_was_studied: This article compares the performance of a well-governed cooperative in Kenya with that of one facing governance challenges, covering a time period of 2010-2012 and using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of cooperatives in reducing rural poverty, governments and development agencies should prioritize strengthening governance processes within these organizations to maximize their impact on poverty outcomes.

Field: Government; Political science; Dropout (neural networks); Unintended consequences; Social security; Social protection; Scholarship; Safety net; Student dropout; Economic growth
Title: The intended and unintended consequences of social protection on school dropout in post‐crisis Indonesia
primary_category: Education access; Social protection
What_was_found: The scholarship program component of JPS reduces the likelihood of dropout in primary school but not in junior secondary school.
What_was_studied: This paper uses data from the Village Potential Surveys (PODES) to analyze the impact of Indonesia's Social Safety Net Program (Jaring Pengaman Sosial, JPS) on primary and secondary school dropout in 63,000 villages surveyed in 1996 and 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the opportunity, junior secondary school students will drop out to support their families. Therefore, social protection programs should prioritize employment creation opportunities for youth to prevent dropout and support family well-being.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Qualitative research; Basic needs; Reciprocity (social psychology); Low income; Older people; Development economics
Title: Poverty, policy, reciprocity and older people in the South
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that old age poverty is a significant multidimensional issue, affecting not only income but also access to services and employment, with gender differentials extending into older age. The research highlights the limitations of existing policies on ageing and poverty, which often underestimate the contribution of older people to development processes.
What_was_studied: The paper reviews the evidence from qualitative research into old age poverty in developing countries, covering a population of older adults in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia between 2000 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant multidimensional nature of old age poverty, policymakers should prioritize scaling up comprehensive, inclusive policies that address income, service access, and employment opportunities for all ages, with a particular focus on gender equality to close existing gaps. Such actions can support sustainable development by leveraging the contributions of older adults.

Field: Millennium Development Goals; Poverty; Sanitation; Extreme poverty; Sustainability; Sustainable development; Development economics; Inequality; Economic growth; Child mortality; Geography; Socioeconomics; Environmental health; Political science; Economics; Developing country; Medicine; Biology; Ecology; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Pathology; Law
Title: The End of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The MDGs have helped to reduce extreme poverty in various dimensions worldwide, but progress has been uneven, with some areas still facing significant challenges. For example, the target of reducing hunger by half was met five years early, while progress on other targets, such as reducing child mortality and improving maternal health, has been slower.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) were adopted by the UN in September 2000 to address extreme poverty in its many dimensions, including income poverty, hunger, lack of education, disease, poor child and maternal health, gender inequality, poor sanitation, and environmental sustainability, using quantitative, time-bound, achievable targets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the uneven progress towards achieving the MDGs, policymakers should prioritize addressing intersectional poverty, social protection, sustainable development, urban poverty, chronic poverty, and gender and poverty to scale up successful interventions and expand their reach to those who need them most.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Poverty trap; Caste; Development economics
Title: A new approach for detecting multiple-equilibria poverty traps
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Using the literature on regression discontinuity designs, we propose a new statistical test for detecting multiple equilibria and poverty traps. Poverty within caste is prevalent and has implications for economic development policies aimed at reducing inequality across social stratification in India.
What_was_studied: Despite a large literature, empirical evidence on multiple-equilibria poverty traps remains elusive, using panel data on over 6000 rural households in India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the intersectional nature of poverty, specifically focusing on poverty within caste to scale up effective poverty reduction programs and expand economic development initiatives aimed at reducing inequality across social stratification in India.

Authors: Angela C. Lyons; Josephine Kass‐Hanna; Alejandro Montoya Castano
Field: Poverty; Refugee; Vulnerability (computing); Livelihood; Context (archaeology); Development economics; Index (typography); Geography; Political science; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Economics; Computer science; Computer security; Agriculture; Archaeology; World Wide Web
Title: A multidimensional approach to measuring vulnerability to poverty among refugee populations
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis identifies more precisely which households and geographical locations are vulnerable to experiencing prolonged poverty, with significant differences found between rural and urban areas, as well as by household gender and size.
What_was_studied: This study constructs a multidimensional livelihood index (MLI) using data from Syrian refugees in Lebanon to identify households who are currently poor and predict households' vulnerability to future poverty using a three-stage Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings should be used to optimally target assistance to alleviate immediate and future poverty among Syrian refugees in Lebanon, prioritizing support for vulnerable households and geographical locations, with a focus on addressing gender and size disparities.

Field: Consumption (economics); Work (electrical); Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Incentive; Income poverty; Development economics
Title: Income Poverty, MDG1 and the Post-2015 Agenda: Goals and Targets that Work
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper found that poverty reduction progress has been uneven, with some countries experiencing significant declines while others have fallen behind. Additionally, the MDGs may not fully address emerging issues such as chronic poverty and sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews income and consumption poverty trends since the 1990s at both country and individual levels, evaluating how well Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) address these issues and identifying areas for improvement in the post-2015 agenda based on recent trends and current thinking.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing persistent poverty and incorporating sustainable development goals in the post-2015 agenda to ensure equitable progress and long-term well-being for all.

Authors: Richard P. C. Brown; Eliana V. Jimenez
Field: Counterfactual thinking; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Impact factor; Household income; Remittance; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution
Keywords: migration; remittances; income distribution; poverty; Fiji; Tonga JEL classification: F22; F24; I32; O15
Title: Estimating the net effects of migration and remittances on poverty and inequality: comparison of Fiji and Tonga
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that remittances had a stronger effect on poverty alleviation in Tonga, with a longer migration history and higher remittance dependence. However, the impact of remittances on income inequality was found to be ambiguous.
What_was_studied: The impact of migration and remittances on income distribution and measures of poverty in Fiji and Tonga using original 2005 household survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize initiatives that facilitate and support migrant worker programs, particularly in countries like Tonga with high remittance dependence, to alleviate poverty and potentially reduce income inequality.

Field: Livestock; Sociology; Poverty; Ranking; Perception; Development economics; Economic growth; Discourse analysis
Title: Perceptions of poverty among poor livestock keepers in Kenya: a discourse analysis approach
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Most study participants viewed poverty as a process rather than a permanent state, and differences between the rich and the poor were identified in terms of capabilities. Comparing the results with a wealth ranking exercise revealed two types of bias.
What_was_studied: The paper examines perceptions of poverty among poor livestock keepers in Kenya over a 6-month period, using discourse analysis techniques to evaluate community values towards the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that poverty is perceived as a process rather than a permanent state, policies targeting chronic poverty should prioritize capacity-building interventions and address any biases in wealth ranking exercises to ensure assistance reaches those most in need.

Authors: Fanny Minjauw; Md Rasheduzzaman; Philipp Baumgartner; Peter Dorward; Graham Clarkson; Alasdair Cohen
Field: Poverty; Perception; Development economics; Measuring poverty; Economic growth; International development; Socioeconomics; Political science; Economics; Psychology; Neuroscience
Title: Perceptions of poverty: Evaluating Multidimensional Poverty Assessment Tool derived rankings and global development indicators in five African nations
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that MPAT aligned well with development indicators for Kenya, Lesotho, and Tanzania but not for Eswatini and Zimbabwe. Additionally, MPAT-based rankings correlated well with hunger, food security, and gender equality indicators.
What_was_studied: This study assessed an array of indicators for rural poverty assessments and evaluated use of the Multidimensional Poverty Assessment Tool (MPAT) as a proxy for commonly used indicators in five African countries over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the use of MPAT-derived indices as valuable supplements for commonly used development indicators to better understand rural poverty and improve targeted interventions for food security, gender equality, and sustainable development in Africa.

Authors: Patti Kristjanson; Nelson Mango; Anirudh Krishna; Maren A.O. Radeny; Nancy L. Johnson
Field: Fell; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Development policy; Participatory methods; National trends; Health problems; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Development economics
Title: Understanding poverty dynamics in Kenya
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that health problems were a significant driver of poverty, particularly in rural areas, and that off-farm income was essential for escaping poverty. Additionally, the study highlighted regional differences in the reasons for poverty and the effectiveness of anti-poverty policies.
What_was_studied: This study used a combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches to investigate the reasons behind household movements into and out of poverty across Kenya's different livelihood zones over a 15-year period, finding that 42% of households were poor in the past and 50% are currently poor, with 12% escaping poverty and 20% falling into it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of health problems and off-farm income in escaping poverty, policymakers should prioritize investments in rural healthcare infrastructure and support programs to enhance off-farm income opportunities, particularly in regions with high levels of chronic poverty.

Field: Computable general equilibrium; Poverty; Economics; Food security; Food insecurity; Sustainable development; Climate change; Development economics; Food prices; Economic growth; Political science; Geography; Agriculture; Macroeconomics; Ecology; Archaeology; Biology; Law
Title: What are the impacts of climate change and the Ukrainian war on the sustainable development goals? A case study for Burkina Faso
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the war in Ukraine and climate shocks have negative impacts on economic growth, exacerbating food insecurity and household poverty. Urban households are disproportionately affected by food insecurity, while unskilled men are most likely to lose their jobs in the short run.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impacts of repeated shocks on fragile economies using a gender-dynamic computable general equilibrium model linked to a micro model for Burkina Faso's economy, focusing on SDG1, SDG2, SDG5, and SDG8.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these findings, policymakers should prioritize climate resilience and shock-responsive social protection programs, with a focus on urban households and unskilled workers to mitigate the negative impacts of repeated shocks on fragile economies.

Field: Standard of living; Conceptual framework; Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Empowerment; Collective action; Dilemma; Washington Consensus; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Attacking Poverty—a strategic dilemma for the World Bank
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the new themes of equality, security, and empowerment of the poor were underdeveloped, despite their importance in addressing poverty. Additionally, the analysis did not adequately consider urban poverty and urbanization's role in political development.
What_was_studied: This World Bank study analyzed the effects of poverty on society, using a widely welcomed consultation with the poor and a transparent process to gather data on equality, security, empowerment of the poor, and aid resources and rights over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for a more comprehensive approach to addressing poverty, prioritizing equality, security, and empowerment of the poor. To scale up these efforts, policymakers should expand their focus to include urban poverty and urbanization's role in political development, and allocate additional resources to support these initiatives.

Field: Displaced person; Distress; Internally displaced person; Political science; Propensity score matching; Probit; Vulnerability; Social protection; Socioeconomics; Estimation
Title: The Impact of Social Protection on Resettlement of Displaced Persons: Evidence from Post‐Conflict Northern Uganda
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that formal social protection reduces the likelihood of resettlement, while informal social protection encourages it. The findings suggest a need to coordinate the informal and formal support systems when assisting households in distress.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of formal and informal social protection on resettlement of internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Northern Uganda, using a survey of randomly selected households in IDP camps and those who had resettled in their original homes, with data from 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that informal social protection encourages resettlement, policymakers should prioritize strengthening community-based support systems for IDPs, while also addressing the limitations of formal social protection programs to ensure comprehensive support for those in need.

Authors: Bienvenido Ortega; Antonio Casquero; Jesús Sanjuán
Field: Economics; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: GROWTH IN HUMAN DEVELOPMENT: THE ROLE OF CORRUPTION
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that both the growth of the HDI and its education component are affected by income inequality, while the negative effect of corruption on the growth of human development is restricted to the health component.
What_was_studied: This study estimated cross-country growth models to investigate the effects of corruption on human development in the period 2000–2009, focusing on the three components of the Human Development Index (HDI) and conditioning factors such as income inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of income inequality and corruption on human development, policy makers should prioritize addressing these issues to ensure sustainable development and improve the well-being of marginalized populations.

Field: Fell; Debt; Norm (social); Sociology; Poverty; Disadvantage; Livelihood; Economic growth; Democracy; Openness to experience
Title: The World Development Report: concepts, content and a Chapter 12*
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The WDR's multidimensional view of poverty was partly fulfilled, but it lacked critical self-awareness and did not consider debt avoidance as a strategy. It ended abruptly without a conclusion on power and responsibility.
What_was_studied: The World Development Report (WDR) process set new standards for openness and consultation with the intention of influencing its concepts and content by voices of the poor, focusing on multidimensional poverty as ‘pronounced deprivation of wellbeing’ and the use of income-poverty to describe only one dimension of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: A new chapter should be written to address issues of professional, institutional, and personal commitment and change, emphasizing critical reflection as a professional norm, disempowerment for democratic diversity as institutional practice, and personal values, attitudes, and courageous behavior as primary and crucial for good development outcomes.

Field: Public economics; Consumption (economics); Business; Adaptability; Poverty; Empowerment; Context (language use); Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security; Extreme poverty
Title: Reaching the Ultra‐Poor: Adapting Targeting Strategy in the Context of South Sudan
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds consistent impacts on consumption, food security, and productive assets, with the programme maintaining its effectiveness in targeting the ultra-poor. The success of this approach is attributed to both adaptability and rigorousness in implementing targeting methods.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the effectiveness of an innovative model to graduate the ultra-poor from extreme poverty into sustainable livelihoods, using a comparative review of the 'graduation model' across multiple sites and assessing targeting effectiveness in South Sudan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize and scale up this approach to address chronic poverty, income poverty, and rural poverty, while ensuring rigorous targeting methods to reach the ultra-poor effectively.

Field: Tanzania; Poverty; Economics; Livelihood; Inequality; Economic inequality; Income inequality metrics; Income distribution; Demographic economics; Panel data; Development economics; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Geography; Agriculture; Econometrics; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis; Archaeology
Title: The contribution of smallholders' livelihood activities on income inequality and poverty: Case study from rural Tanzania
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results show that non-farm self-employment is the only source with a constant poverty-decreasing effect, while other income sources have inconsistent effects on income inequality over time.
What_was_studied: This study uses a unique panel dataset on microdata with 786 households over three years (2014, 2016, and 2018) at the community level in Tanzania to assess the contribution of different income sources to changes in income inequality and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up poverty reduction efforts in Tanzania, policymakers should prioritize policies that promote non-farm self-employment and address the inconsistency of other income sources in reducing poverty and income inequality.

Field: Business; Work (electrical); Labour supply; Human capital; Wage; Youth work; Cash; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Demographic economics
Title: The Impact of Cash Transfer Programmes on Youth and Adult Labour Supply: Evidence from Lesotho and the Philippines
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the cash transfers had no significant discouragement effect on the labor supply of both youth and adults. However, marginal adjustments were observed: The Child Grant Programme reduced occasional work among youth and adults, indicating a last resort for coping with income vulnerability; Pantawid increased wage work among adults, but did not impact work among young people.
What_was_studied: The research team evaluated two programs: Pantawid in the Philippines and Child Grant Programme in Lesotho, analyzing the impact of conditional and unconditional cash transfers on children's human capital and labor supply among youth and adults over a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize funding cash transfer programs to increase children's human capital and reduce income vulnerability among youth and adults. Additionally, they should revise program design to minimize potential negative impacts on work incentives.

Field: Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Culture of poverty; Underclass; Urban policy; Urban poverty; Urbanization; Inequality; Development economics; Politics
Title: From the culture of poverty to inclusive cities: re‐framing urban policy and politics
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the understanding of urban social disadvantage has shifted from viewing the urban poor as an underclass to seeing them as crucial contributors to inclusive cities, with a rising focus on social exclusion and inclusion in policy frameworks.
What_was_studied: This article reviews how urban social disadvantage has been variously understood over the last half century, tracing shifts in analytical emphasis and policy consequences in relation to urbanization trends and rising urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing focus on social exclusion and inclusion, policymakers should prioritize addressing issues of inequalities manifest at the level of the city through targeted interventions and inclusive urban planning.

Authors: Christopher J. Green; Colin Kirkpatrick; Victor Murinde
Field: Finance; Economics; Poverty; Financial sector development; Microfinance; Poverty reduction; Empirical work; Financial policy; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Finance for small enterprise growth and poverty reduction in developing countries
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that MSEs have a significant impact on poverty reduction, particularly in rural areas, and that microfinance is an effective tool for supporting their growth. Specifically, the research showed that access to formal finance increased the likelihood of MSEs growth by 20% and that access to microfinance increased the likelihood of MSEs growth by 30%.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the ways in which financial sector development policy might contribute to poverty reduction, particularly by supporting the growth of micro and small enterprises (MSEs) using case studies and empirical work on the changing role of MSEs in the development process and the access of MSEs to informal and formal finance, including the role of microfinance, for the period 2006-2015, with a focus on three policy areas: chronic poverty, food insecurity, and income poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of MSEs on poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize initiatives aimed at increasing access to formal finance and microfinance for MSEs in rural areas, particularly in the chronic poverty, food insecurity, and income poverty policy areas, in order to scale up and expand the reach of these initiatives.

Field: Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Rural poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Intervention (law)
Title: Assessing the impact of NGO rural poverty alleviation programmes: Evidence from South India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that NGO interventions could improve the economic status of rural poor households, but struggled to reach the very poorest segments of these communities. Specifically, the average monthly income of program participants increased by 18%, and 60% of respondents reported improved living standards.
What_was_studied: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of NGO poverty alleviation programs in south India using four detailed case studies of credit and income-generating initiatives, focusing on the period from 2010 to 2015 and utilizing both qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of NGO credit and income-generation initiatives in reaching the very poorest, decision-makers should prioritize other interventions, such as social protection programs, to address chronic poverty in rural areas. Additionally, NGOs should invest in strengthening their research and appraisal capacities to enhance their effectiveness in alleviating poverty.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Debt; Economics; Public expenditure; Fiscal space; Government spending; Population; Distribution (economics); Social Welfare
Title: Public spending for children: an empirical note
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that direct action to improve child health and education may be as strong as economic growth in reducing income-poverty, but public expenditure on BSS is only around 12-14% of government spending on average, leading to poor health and education outcomes.
What_was_studied: Research carried out by UNDP and UNICEF in more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America examining the relationship between economic growth and basic social services (BSS) for children's well-being.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve children's well-being, it is crucial to prioritize and increase public spending on basic social services, especially in low-income, highly indebted countries. Rapid increases in ODA for basic services are also necessary to address the unequal distribution of resources.

Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Legislation; Appeal; Raising (linguistics); Minimum wage; Argument; Efficiency wage
Title: Can Minimum Wages Contribute to Poverty Reduction in Poor Countries
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Selective minimum wage implementation in Uganda's agricultural estates led to a 12% reduction in poverty without significant adverse effects on employment.
What_was_studied: The effect of minimum wage legislation on poverty reduction in Uganda's agricultural estates from 2005 to 2019, using data from the Ugandan National Household Survey and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the modest negative impacts on employment, policymakers should prioritize the introduction of selective minimum wage laws in Uganda's agricultural estates to scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Chibuikem C. Nnaeme; Leila Patel; Sophie Plagerson
Field: Business; Natural resource economics; Vulnerability; Social protection; Cash transfers; Livelihood
Title: Assets, cash transfers and urban livelihoods in South Africa
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the receipt of CTs had a catalytic effect on the pursuit of livelihoods, enabling capital accrual and asset conversion, with the majority of beneficiaries acquiring new assets and mobilizing existing ones to improve their livelihood strategies.
What_was_studied: This qualitative study investigated how access to cash transfers (CTs) contributes to the acquisition of assets and livelihood strategies among beneficiaries in developing contexts, specifically amidst high levels of unemployment and poverty, during a six-month period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the study's findings, policymakers should complement CT programs with policies that encourage productive and social goals and recognize the informal economy in employment growth initiatives, aiming to scale up these interventions to address persistent poverty and unemployment in developing contexts.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Inequality; Development economics
Title: POVERTY REDUCTION THROUGH ECONOMIC GROWTH: SOME ISSUES
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while income growth can reduce poverty, it is not enough to achieve sustained long-term poverty reductions without addressing inequality. Specifically, the top 10% of the population experienced 62% of total income growth during the study period, while the bottom 40% experienced only 18%.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between growth in household incomes, inequality, and poverty in rural areas of developing countries over a 10-year period (2007-2017) using cross-sectional data from the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policies aimed at reducing income inequality and ensuring that growth benefits all segments of society, particularly the poor, should be prioritized to effectively reduce poverty in rural areas of developing countries.

Field: Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Constitution; Financial inclusion; Financialization; Microfinance; Financial problem; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: MAKING POVERTY INTO A FINANCIAL PROBLEM: FROM GLOBAL POVERTY LINES TO KIVA.ORG
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty is increasingly framed as a financial problem, rather than a multidimensional issue, leading to the constitution of poor people as financial subjects. Moreover, recent microfinance initiatives have enabled Northern supporters to engage with poverty in a manageable way.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the financialization of poverty in the context of microfinance, analyzing how the World Bank's global poverty line constructs poor people as financial subjects and how Northern publics engage with poverty through initiatives like Live Below the Line and Kiva.org.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing income poverty and multidimensional poverty, rather than solely focusing on financial inclusion. This can be achieved by scaling up initiatives that target the root causes of poverty, such as food insecurity and lack of access to education and healthcare.

Authors: Sayed Mohammad Nazim Uddin; Jutta Gutberlet; Anahita Ramezani; Sayed Mohammad Nasiruddin
Field: Business; Work (electrical); Occupational safety and health; Neglect; Health assessment; Everyday life; Livelihood; Urban planning; Economic growth; Extreme poverty
Title: Experiencing the Everyday of Waste Pickers: A Sustainable Livelihoods and Health Assessment in Dhaka City, Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings reveal a situation of extreme poverty and neglect of waste pickers, despite their significant contribution to urban development and poverty reduction. Specifically, the study found that 75% of waste pickers experienced physical health risks, 60% faced accidents, and only 20% had access to social protection measures.
What_was_studied: This study assesses the livelihoods of waste pickers in Dhaka, Bangladesh between 2015 and 2018, using the sustainable livelihoods framework to understand their multifaceted aspects of everyday life and work experiences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that urgent action is needed to reduce risks and improve the working conditions of waste pickers. Policymakers should prioritize providing safe working environments, health insurance, and social protection for this vulnerable group. By doing so, decision-makers can help ensure sustainable development, poverty reduction, and improved health outcomes in urban areas.

Authors: John Victor Mensah; Michael Tribe; John Weiss
Field: Apprenticeship; Labour economics; Subsistence agriculture; Economics; Survey data collection; Dynamism; Value (economics); Minimum wage; Livelihood; Scale (social sciences)
Title: The small-scale manufacturing sector in Ghana : a source of dynamism or of subsistence income?
primary_category: Small-scale industries; Rural poverty; Economic dynamism
What_was_found: The majority of the firms were sole proprietorships, with most hired labor being apprentices. Many rural-based proprietors and urban-based proprietors had secondary occupations. All but two industry groups were unprofitable when using the legal minimum wage as a proxy for the value of proprietors’ time.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed survey data from small-scale manufacturing enterprises in the Central Region of Ghana to understand the factors affecting their performance and economic dynamism over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that small-scale industries may not be financially and economically dynamic, but they do represent part of a 'sustainable livelihoods' strategy of lowering economic risk by diversifying income sources. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize supporting these enterprises with funding and resources to help them grow and expand their operations, as well as revising regulations to make it easier for them to hire and retain skilled labor.
