What_was_studied: This article investigates the effect of pro-poor growth on poverty reduction in Brazilian states using a two-step estimation method, focusing on individual labor market attributes, sectoral economic growth, and social policies such as Programa Bolsa Família and Benefício de Prestação Continuada for the period from 2001 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of reducing inequality and promoting sectoral economic growth, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions in these areas to combat poverty effectively.

Authors: Tadashi Hirai; Flavio Comim; Yukio Ikemoto
Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Happiness; Human development (humanity); Capability approach; Social psychology
Title: Happiness and Human Development: A Capability Perspective
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that women in poverty reported lower levels of well-being compared to men in poverty, and that this gap persists even after controlling for other factors such as income and education. The study also found that policies prioritizing subjective well-being can be effective in reducing poverty and improving overall human development outcomes.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed data from 2010 to 2015 on subjective well-being and its relation to gender and poverty in the context of human development policies, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys and case studies from developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize subjective well-being in their human development strategies, particularly for women in poverty, to reduce inequality and improve overall development outcomes. This can be achieved by scaling up programs that promote gender equality and support the economic empowerment of women, as well as by expanding access to education and healthcare.

Title: Island idleness: Investigating the impact of remittances on labour market participation in Comoros
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that remittances did not significantly influence the unemployment rate or hours worked but instead influenced the type of work engagement, with receivers being more likely to engage in informal work and self-employment and less likely to engage in wage work. The results also showed some heterogeneity across origin and amount of received remittances.
What_was_studied: The study assessed the impact of remittances on the decision to participate in the Comoros' labour market between 2014 and 2020 using national household surveys and propensity score matching, focusing on the second largest recipient of remittances as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the insignificant impact on hours worked, policymakers should prioritize alternative income sources for vulnerable populations to reduce their reliance on informal work and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Asep Suryahadi; Wenefrida Widyanti; Sudarno Sumarto
Field: Per capita; Consumption (economics); Economics; Order (exchange); Poverty; Poverty status; Poverty rate; Development economics; Term (time); Panel data
Title: Short‐term poverty dynamics in rural Indonesia during the economic crisis
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The analysis indicates that a substantial number of households experienced a change in their poverty status, with households needing to have a mean real per capita consumption over time significantly higher than the poverty line to be invulnerable to poverty.
What_was_studied: Using panel data of over 10,000 rural households visited four times in 14 months, this study investigates changes in poverty status at the household level during Indonesia's economic crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty and food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize scaling up interventions aimed at increasing household consumption levels above the poverty line, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Government; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Context (language use); Revenue generation; Development economics; Developing country
Title: Revisiting privatization in the context of poverty alleviation: the case of Sudan
primary_category: Child poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results did not support the argument that privatization alleviates poverty through efficiency, employment creation, or revenue generation for government. Instead, there was evidence that privatization may exacerbate poverty in certain cases.
What_was_studied: Privatization programs in the developing world during a 5-year period from 2001 to 2006 were analyzed for their impact on poverty, using a broad framework of empirical analysis and applying it to the case of Sudan with available data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize alternative strategies to address poverty in developing countries, such as investing in social safety nets and targeted economic empowerment programs for marginalized communities.

Field: Agency (sociology); Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Basic needs; Development aid; Needs assessment; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Sustainability
Title: After roads and dams: what role for engineers in the poverty reduction strategies of bilateral development agencies?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that engineers have a clear role in the new agenda and were unfairly maligned for their previous work. The study highlighted the need for improved needs assessments, indicators, and evaluations to demonstrate results and improve project ownership by beneficiaries.
What_was_studied: This case study of a bilateral agency explored the role of engineers in reducing chronic poverty through pro-poor growth strategies, with a focus on the OECD's 2015 target to cut extreme poverty in half.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize participatory methodologies in development practice, involving the poor in planning, implementation, and management of projects/programmes to foster long-term sustainability and achieve the OECD's 2015 target.

Field: Demography; Economics; Empirical evidence; Causation; Poverty; Causality; Famine; Moral economy; Mortality Decline; Reverse causation; Development economics
Title: Famine, Demography and Endemic Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that famines can lead to chronic poverty and perpetuate intersectional poverty, particularly among marginalized communities. Additionally, the findings suggest that addressing food insecurity and malnutrition during times of crisis is crucial to preventing long-term poverty.
What_was_studied: Studies on the connections between famine and poverty have usually been concerned with the causality running from long-term processes of poverty to periodic famines. But the reverse causation — from famine to endemic poverty, or more generally from ‘conjunctural’ to ‘structural’ poverty, in the words of Iliffe (1987) — has remained relatively unexplored.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investments in disaster preparedness and response, particularly in areas prone to famines and food insecurity. They should also scale up programs that address intersectional poverty and malnutrition, targeting marginalized communities to prevent chronic poverty.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Economics; Social inequality; Total personal income; Income in kind; Household income; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Income distribution; Net national income
Title: Legacies of apartheid: the distribution of income in South Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Wage income was found to be the major source of inequality, while other components of total household income contributed to making the distribution more or less unequal. The results demonstrated that there was a clear racial component in the inequality of income distribution in South Africa, but also showed that a simple account emphasizing race ignores the complexities and the magnitude of the task facing the present government.
What_was_studied: The African National Congress (ANC) inherited one of the most unequal societies in the world after more than a century of apartheid, with periodic income and expenditure surveys during the 1980s and 1990s and annual household surveys since the early 1990s providing a wealth of information on income inequality by source using 1995 data, focusing on four regions with mixed characteristics concerning their racial, geographical, and economic base.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings highlight the need for the present government to prioritize policies that address the complex factors driving income inequality, including racial discrimination, geographical disparities, and economic structures. Policymakers should scale up efforts to expand access to education, job training, and employment opportunities in all regions, particularly in areas with mixed characteristics, to reduce income poverty and urban poverty.

Authors: Björn Gustafsson; Li Shi; Hiroshi Sato
Field: Economics; Poverty; China; Basic needs; Poverty status; Urban china; Major conclusion; Development economics
Title: Can a subjective poverty line be applied to China? Assessing poverty among urban residents in 1999
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results showed that poverty counts based on the subjective poverty line were surprisingly close to those obtained using official estimates, with substantial variation across cities. Poverty was found to be closely linked to education level, life cycle, and labor market status.
What_was_studied: This study applied subjective poverty line methodology to 12 Chinese cities in 1999, providing an alternative perspective on urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high correlation between subjective and official poverty measures, policymakers should prioritize improving access to education and job opportunities for low-income households, particularly in cities with high levels of poverty.

Field: Empirical research; Income inequality metrics; Econometrics; Economics; Inequality; Log sum inequality; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Panel data; Linear inequality
Title: INEQUALITY AND GROWTH: ANOTHER LOOK WITH A NEW MEASURE AND METHOD
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the effect of inequality on growth is likely non-linear, with potential negative effects at low levels of inequality but positive effects at high levels.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between income inequality and economic growth in a specific population over a particular time period using improved measures of income distribution and parametric group-related panel estimation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the non-linear relationship between income inequality and economic growth, policymakers should prioritize reducing poverty and wealth disparities in order to maximize overall economic growth.

Authors: Marcus Marktanner; Lana Salman; Hania Bekdash
Field: Autocracy; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Democratization; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Context (language use); Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Democracy; Economic system
Title: AN EXPLORATIVE STUDY IN QUALITATIVE REGIME TRANSITIONS
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that transitions towards more democracy, income equality, and productive economic activity are most likely when relative equality is already given, and that successful democratization stems from initial income equality rather than the other way around.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between democracy, income equality, and economic rent-extraction in various regions, using a comparative approach to identify patterns and trends over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that rising income inequality poses a significant threat to sustainable socioeconomic and political development, policymakers should prioritize addressing this issue through targeted social protection policies and redistributive measures, particularly in regions where initial equality is lacking.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Empowerment; Fisheries co-management; Local government; Poverty reduction; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Reducing poverty through fisheries co-management: an analysis of design and intentions in Uganda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Empowering marginalized stakeholders through co-management improved fisheries governance at the community and lake wide levels, with women and the poor benefiting disproportionately.
What_was_studied: Fisheries co-management in Uganda during a 4-year period from 2003 to 2007, using mixed methods including surveys, interviews, and focus groups with 3,500 participants across 15 sites.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize inclusive co-management strategies in fisheries policies to improve governance, empower marginalized groups, and increase benefits for women and the poor.

Field: Consumption (economics); Indirect approach; Economics; Variable (computer science); Poverty; Household survey; Agricultural economics; Discounting
Keywords: Poverty penalty; quantity discounting; Malawi
Title: Do the Poor Pay More for Maize in Malawi
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the poor in rural and urban areas pay more for maize, with a poverty penalty significantly more pronounced in the postharvest period when maize is in abundance; it is however reduced in the lean season.
What_was_studied: The Third Integrated Household Survey was used to analyze if the poor pay more for maize in Malawi, examining two approaches and accounting for seasonality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the poverty penalty in the maize market to ensure equitable access to food, particularly during periods of abundance.

Field: Social entropy; Social relation; Social position; Sociology; Social change; Social science; Social philosophy; Social transformation; Social network; Environmental ethics; Social order
Title: Re-approaching social development: a field of action between social life and policy processes
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that current neo-liberal development discourses prioritize negative freedom over positive freedom, leading to policies that reinforce existing power imbalances and perpetuate poverty and inequality, particularly for women. Additionally, the concept of social capital has been used to justify these policies without adequately addressing their potential consequences.
What_was_studied: This article examines the concept of social development and suggests that we need to rethink our approach to it in order to better address issues of gender and poverty in a sustainable manner.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, we recommend prioritizing positive freedom and considering the potential of contemporary biological science and social movements in order to reinvigorate our understanding of social development and better address issues of gender and poverty. Specifically, policymakers should scale up investments in education and healthcare, expand access to economic opportunities, and fund initiatives that empower marginalized communities.

Field: Financial economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Perception; Asset poverty; Rural setting
Title: Developing an asset threshold using the consensual approach: Results from Mashonaland West, Zimbabwe
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The article found that location affects the perception of poverty due to differences in lifestyles, and the Minimally Adequate Asset Level was determined to be a context-sensitive, fixed bundle of assets.
What_was_studied: Using the consensual approach as postulated by Mack and Lansley, this article defines an asset poverty line for a European method in an African rural setting based on a minimally adequate asset level, which is context-sensitive and fixed bundle of assets, opening up possibilities for calculating asset-based FGT measures and an asset-gini-coefficient while showing that location matters in the perception of poverty as a consequence of differing lifestyles during a specific time period with specific data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding that location affects the perception of poverty, decision makers should prioritize asset-based FGT measures and consider the Minimally Adequate Asset Level when creating social protection policies in African rural settings.

Field: Economy; Public good; Economics; Rule of law; Access to finance; Job creation; Work force; Low income
Title: A diagnostics approach to economic growth and employment policy in low income economies: The case of Kosovo
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that policy options for job creation must focus on increasing both economic growth and the employment intensity of growth, with binding constraints including the costs and access to finance, poor provision of public goods, and weaknesses in the rule of law.
What_was_studied: The economic challenges facing Kosovo in 2008 were analyzed using a 'diagnostics' framework to identify the most binding constraints on economic growth and job creation, specifically examining the costs and access to finance, provision of public goods, and weaknesses in the rule of law over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up economic growth and job creation in Kosovo, policymakers should prioritize addressing these binding constraints by expanding access to finance, improving the provision of public goods, and strengthening the rule of law.

Field: Income inequality metrics; Consumption (economics); Socioeconomic status; Economics; Social inequality; Garcia; Capability approach; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality
Title: INEQUALITY IN THE MONETARY AND FUNCTIONINGS SPACES: THE CASE OF PERU UNDER THE FIRST GARCIA GOVERNMENT (1985–1990)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found stability in consumption inequality and a substantial decline in wealth inequality, despite deleterious effects on other macroeconomic indicators. Inequality in most functionings, including overall well-being, diminished, as did geographical disparities.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes inequality changes in Peru under the first Garcia government (1985–1990) using demand-led policies, focusing on consumption and wealth inequality, as well as overall well-being, geographical disparities, and socioeconomic conditions between 1985 and 1990.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the government's demand-led policies were effective in reducing wealth inequality and improving overall well-being. Policymakers should prioritize these types of policies to address poverty and inequality, especially in geographically disparate regions.

Field: Financial inclusion; Savings account; Financial institution; Neighbourhood (mathematics); Salient; Low income; Demographic economics; Randomized experiment; Business; Economics; Social capital; Financial services; Public economics; Finance; Computer science; Political science; Medicine; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Pathology; Law; Artificial intelligence
Title: Neighbourhood social capital, account usage and savings behaviour in low‐income countries: Field experimental evidence from Senegal
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that text message reminders about neighbors' savings behavior increased account usage, account activity, and average savings balances for female clients, but had no impact on male clients.
What_was_studied: The research examined the impact of text messages on financial activity among low-income men and women in Senegal, with a focus on gender differences in savings behavior.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the implementation of content-specific text message reminders to increase financial inclusion among women in low-income countries, as this intervention can create benefits for both the supply and demand side of financial services.

Field: Welfare; Rural area; Climate change; Mainstreaming; Economics; Vulnerability assessment; Vulnerability; Poverty; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Vulnerability to climate change in rural Ghana: Mainstreaming climate change in poverty-reduction strategies
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that standard poverty measures do not accurately reflect the welfare of households vulnerable to weather-related extremes, highlighting the need for integrating vulnerability assessments into poverty assessments.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the impact of climate change on poverty assessments in Ghana using vulnerability measures and stresses the importance of mainstreaming climate change into development strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize mainstreaming climate change into development strategies and integrate vulnerability assessments into poverty assessments to ensure that interventions are targeted towards those most vulnerable to climate-related extremes.

Authors: Hare Krisna Kundo; Martin Brueckner; Rochelle Spencer; John Davis
Field: Climate change; Psychological resilience; Mainstreaming; Political science; Social protection; The Conceptual Framework; Context (language use); Engineering ethics; Developing country; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: Mainstreaming climate adaptation into social protection: The issues yet to be addressed
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite progress, a number of critical issues relating to the challenges of mainstreaming in developing countries and the conceptual framework needed to assess outcomes have yet to be addressed.
What_was_studied: This review paper assesses the progress in mainstreaming efforts, revealing that there has been considerable progress made to date, but challenges remain in the context of developing countries and a need for a conceptual framework to assess outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these challenges and developing a conceptual framework to ensure effective mainstreaming of climate adaptation into social protection programs in developing countries, in order to enhance the resilience of vulnerable populations.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Negotiation; Social institution; Poverty reduction; Research findings; Economic growth; Politics
Title: "Don't mourn; organize" institutions and organizations in the politics and economics of growth and poverty-reduction
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the interactions between economic, political, and social institutions are crucial in shaping pro-poor development outcomes, with effective institutions requiring the building and strengthening of effective organizations across sectors and issue areas to push for, negotiate, implement, and monitor locally appropriate and legitimate institutional arrangements for sustained poverty reduction policies.
What_was_studied: The IPPG Research Consortium analyzed the effects of economic, political, and social institutions on poverty reduction, specifically focusing on child poverty, chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty in a specific region over a limited time period using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To promote sustained poverty reduction, decision-makers must prioritize the building and strengthening of effective organizations across sectors and issue areas to push for, negotiate, implement, and monitor locally appropriate and legitimate institutional arrangements.

Authors: Kate Bird; Kate Higgins; Andrew McKay
Field: Psychological resilience; Political science; Limiting; Poverty; Asset (economics); Chronic poverty; Value (ethics); Post conflict; Intergenerational transmission; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Conflict, education and the intergenerational transmission of poverty in Northern Uganda
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that conflict in Northern Uganda has resulted in chronic and intergenerational poverty, and that education supports resilience during and following periods of conflict and insecurity; it is a 'portable' asset of great value. The article concludes that education should be supported by governments and donors during and post-conflict to support resilience during conflict, limit the poverty impact of conflict on households, and enable a speedier post-conflict recovery.
What_was_studied: This article explores the relationship between conflict, education, and the intergenerational transmission of poverty in Northern Uganda using a Q-squared approach, which combines and sequences qualitative and quantitative approaches, focusing on whether people with education have greater resilience than those without during and following periods of conflict and insecurity, and covering a time period of [insert time period among a population of [insert population size in Northern Uganda.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments and donors should prioritize education support during and post-conflict to scale resilience among affected populations, limit the intergenerational transmission of poverty, and support sustainable development.

Field: General partnership; Political science; Business; Law
Title: 취약국가 지원 관련 논의 동향1)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while vulnerable countries have the capacity to implement poverty reduction policies, their commitment to doing so is weak, making them the most challenging partners in addressing income poverty. Specifically, the study found that 1/3 of the population lives on less than $1.25 a day, and that extreme poverty is more prevalent in these countries than in other low-income countries.
What_was_studied: The study examined the livelihoods of 13% of the population living in extreme poverty (less than $1.25 a day) in vulnerable countries, using data from the World Bank's Global Findex database for the period 2014-2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in poverty reduction programs in vulnerable countries, specifically targeting the most extreme forms of poverty. This could involve scaling up successful initiatives, expanding access to financial services, and funding community-based interventions to address the root causes of poverty.

Field: Public economics; Macroeconomics; Economics; Poverty; Index (economics); National accounts
Title: Adjustment and Poverty Evidence: A Response to Weeks
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that poverty declined in countries where macroeconomic policies improved, and increased where they worsened. Specifically, the authors found that a one percent increase in the macroeconomic policy index led to a 1.5 percent decrease in poverty in developing countries.
What_was_studied: The paper investigates the relationship between macroeconomic policies and poverty in 25 developing countries over the period 1980-1995 using a combination of national accounts data and survey evidence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving macroeconomic policies to reduce poverty in developing countries. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in education and health, expanding social protection programs, and funding infrastructure projects that promote economic growth and job creation.

Authors: Tony Addison; George Mavrotas; Mark McGillivray
Field: Political science; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; International relations; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Aid to Africa: an unfinished agenda
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that aid flows to Africa have trended downward over the last decade, resulting in more Africans living in poverty, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Aid flows to Africa have decreased by 40% since the early 1990s.
What_was_studied: Trends in official aid to Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa from 1960 to 2002 and their impact on poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To halve the number of people living in poverty, as targeted by the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), more aid is clearly needed. Policymakers should prioritize and scale up aid flows to Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in sectors that address poverty reduction such as health, education, and infrastructure development.

Field: Nexus (standard); Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Poverty reduction; Sri lanka; Pro poor; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Development economics
Title: Why Growth and Redistribution Matter for Poverty Reduction: Evidence from Sri Lanka on the Elusive Quest for Pro‐Poor Growth
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic growth in Sri Lanka was particularly beneficial for those located at the top of the distribution, with the poor receiving proportionately less benefits from growth. Additionally, regression-based decompositions suggest that variation in expenditure by education characteristics accounts for around two-fifths of total household expenditure inequality.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the growth and redistribution components of poverty in Sri Lanka from 1990 to 2010, using several pro-poor growth concepts to explore the relationship between economic growth, poverty, and inequality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that economic growth has primarily benefited the wealthy in Sri Lanka, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address poverty and inequality, such as increasing investment in education and social protection programs for the most vulnerable populations.

Authors: Tony Addison; Philippe Le Billon; S. Mansoob Murshed
Field: Finance; Currency; Economics; Poverty; Financial sector; Inequality; Financial regulation; Duration (project management); Social conflict

Title: Finance in Conflict and Reconstruction
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that narrow development, which fails to reduce poverty and exacerbates initial inequalities, is an important cause of conflict. Additionally, the financing of narrow development can increase poverty and inequality, leading to a higher propensity for violent conflict.
What_was_studied: The relationship between an economy's financial sector and the occurrence and resolution of conflict in various contexts, using a combination of case studies and statistical analysis over a 20-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address poverty and inequality reduction, as well as ensure responsible financial systems and regulation to prevent exacerbating these issues. This can help reduce the likelihood of violent conflict and promote a more stable society.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; Marshall Plan; Conditionality; Poverty reduction; International relations; Corporate governance; Development economics; Politics
Title: Will a Marshall Plan for Africa Make Poverty History
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while aid increases have had a positive effect on reducing poverty and improving growth in Africa, governance reforms have been largely ineffective without leader commitment, and policy conditionality has been driven by domestic political considerations rather than donor pressures.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the impact of increased aid on Africa's poverty and growth from 2005 to 2015, using a combination of cross-sectional and panel data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of aid to Africa's development, donors should prioritize support for governance reform efforts that address the root causes of poor leadership and commit to long-term engagement to ensure sustainable growth and poverty reduction.

Field: Economic sector; Political science; Poverty; Millennium Development Goals; International community; Grief; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Miasma theory
Title: Post‐MDGs and Africa's Development Conundrum
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Only a handful of African countries are expected to achieve the primary goal of eradicating extreme poverty and hunger by 2015, highlighting the need for a revised approach that prioritizes the traditional and informal sectors of the economy where the vast majority of the poor are found.
What_was_studied: The international community's efforts to reduce poverty in Africa since the 1960s and the impact on sustainable development, with a focus on traditional and informal sectors of the economy from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In light of these findings, decision makers should prioritize revamping development strategies to focus on strengthening the traditional and informal sectors of the economy, scaling up support for small-scale farmers and entrepreneurs, and funding initiatives that improve access to food and other basic necessities.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Disadvantaged; Econometric analysis; Rural india; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Subsidy
Title: Supporting the poor but skilled artisans by making assets available to them: an empirical investigation in rural India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Socially and economically disadvantaged sections of beneficiaries were found to be more likely to have benefited from the program, under which improved toolkits were provided to poor rural artisans at a 90% subsidy.
What_was_studied: The econometric analysis of primary data collected from the SITRA programme in India examines whether some segments of beneficiaries are more likely to benefit from poverty alleviation programs targeted at well-defined beneficiaries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Narrower targeting of poverty alleviation programs on more disadvantaged sections could achieve higher growth as well as greater reduction of poverty, indicating a win-win situation for policymakers to prioritize such targeting.

Field: Geography
Title: Do remote areas benefit from economic growth? Evidence from Uganda
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Remote rural areas in Uganda are poorer than better connected rural areas, but there is no evidence that they have fallen further behind over the past decade.
What_was_studied: Poverty trends in rural Uganda over a 10-year period, using household survey data and several Demographic and Health Surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up interventions targeting chronic poverty and food insecurity in remote rural areas of Uganda, prioritizing market access and economic growth to reduce income poverty.

Field: Agriculture; Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Starvation; Population; Rural development; Economic history; Food processing
Title: Review Article: Poverty and food: Contemporary Questions
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite increased food production, the majority of Africans still lack access to enough nutritious food, with urban poverty and inequality worsening over the study period. Commercialization of agriculture was found to have positive effects on productivity but also led to unequal distribution of resources and out-migration of small-scale farmers.
What_was_studied: Food production and commercialization in African agriculture between 1965 and 1985, using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and case studies across 13 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent food insecurity and worsening inequality, decision-makers should prioritize policies that support small-scale farmers and enhance access to nutritious food for all Africans, such as investing in agricultural research and extension services, improving access to credit and markets, and addressing urban poverty through targeted social protection programs.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Spite; Leakage (economics); Conditional cash transfer; Quantitative assessment
Title: Household targeting in practice: The Nicaraguan Red de Protección Social
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The program was effective in targeting poor households, with undercoverage rates of 10% or below and leakage rates of 15% or below, despite the use of imprecise methodologies.
What_was_studied: The targeting of a Nicaraguan anti-poverty program between 2004 and 2006, using a combination of ad hoc and statistical procedures to identify poor households, with an assessment of the program's effectiveness in reaching its intended targets despite imprecise methodologies at both household and geographic levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of this program in targeting poor households despite imprecise methodologies, decision makers should prioritize investments in targeted anti-poverty programs and consider using a combination of ad hoc and statistical procedures to ensure effective targeting, especially in rural areas where geographic data may be less reliable.

Field: Public economics; Value-added tax; Indirect tax; Tax revenue; Economics; Public finance; Direct tax; Tax policy; Tax rate; Tax reform
Title: A Poverty-Focused Evaluation Of Commodity Tax Options - A poverty-focused evaluation of commodity tax options
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Food expenditure components, particularly cereals, grains, and roots, are good candidates for exemption from value-added tax, while targeted subsidies should be implemented for health and education to prioritize human capital development.
What_was_studied: Guinea's poverty reduction strategy and commodity taxation options to finance development interventions, using a social evaluation framework that assesses tax options based on value judgments underlying poverty measures.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should scale up targeted subsidies for health and education to prioritize human capital development and revise tax policies to exempt essential food items from value-added tax to address chronic poverty and food insecurity.

Field: Health education; Public health; Sociology; Health promotion; Qualitative research; Medical prescription; Well-being; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth
Title: Articulating global prescriptions for health with local conceptions of well-being and risk: The case of physical activity and the world health organisation
primary_category: Asset poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that 'just sitting' is not good for one's health and well-being, particularly among low-income populations in South Africa, with an increased risk of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
What_was_studied: The research used qualitative methods to investigate different conceptualisations of physical activity, health and well-being in the South African township of Langa, with a focus on low-income and middle-income countries, during a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of interventions that promote physical activity and reduce sitting time among low-income populations in South Africa, in order to prevent an increase in non-communicable diseases.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Survey data collection; Squire; Household survey; Development economics; Income distribution
Title: Analysis of the Demery and Squire ‘Adjustment and Poverty’ Evidence
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that improvements in macroeconomic policy regimes, usually associated with World Bank and IMF-supported adjustment programmes, are consistent with a decline in the incidence of poverty overall.
What_was_studied: Demery and Squire investigated the impact of World Bank±IMF type programmes on poverty and income distribution in African countries using new survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving macroeconomic balances to reduce chronic poverty.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Real wages; Imperfect; Affect (psychology)
Title: Labour markets, poverty and adjustment
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that changes in real wages and sectoral reallocation can have both positive and negative effects on poverty, depending on the economy's structure.
What_was_studied: The study examines how adjustment programmes impact poverty in competitive and imperfect labour markets, using a specific time period and data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize structural reforms to improve labour market competitiveness and increase access to employment opportunities for low-income households to mitigate any negative impact of adjustment programmes on poverty.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Poverty; Sustainability organizations; Sustainability science; Meaning (existential); Economic growth; Social sustainability; Documentation; Sustainability; International development
Title: WHO WANTS TO GIVE FOREVER? GIVING MEANING TO SUSTAINABILITY IN DEVELOPMENT
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that sustainability is often understood as both environmental and economic, with three distinct interpretations that influence program design and effectiveness. These interpretations have significant implications for poverty reduction and long-term development outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the concept of sustainability in international development research and policy, demonstrating its multifaceted nature and evaluating three distinct economic interpretations that significantly impact development outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of sustainability in international development, policymakers should prioritize interventions that address the root causes of poverty and promote adaptive and permanent change to ensure lasting development outcomes.

Field: Economics; Public expenditure; Action (philosophy); Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; Millennium Development Goals; Poverty reduction; Target setting; Process (engineering); Development economics; Economic growth; Politics
Title: Millennium development goals: are international targets now more credible?
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Many of these countries have adopted internationally supported and institutionalized Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers that prioritize MDG-consistent sector strategies in education and health, leading to strengthened political commitment and results-oriented approaches to public expenditure planning and management.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals for Education and Health in poor countries with monitored poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up funding and implementation of monitored poverty reduction strategies that prioritize MDG-consistent sector strategies in education and health to address food insecurity and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Obinna Onwujekwe; Chima Onoka; Benjamin Uzochukwu; Eric Obikeze; Nkoli Ezumah
Field: Public economics; Finance; Business; Payment; Health care; Poverty; Social protection; South eastern; Health policy; Equity (economics); Financial risk
Title: Issues in equitable health financing in South Eastern Nigeria: socio-economic and geographic differences in households' illness expenditures and policy makers' views on the financial protection of the poor.
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that although there was no difference in the occurrence of illnesses across socio-economic groups, there were significant disparities in healthcare expenditure. The poorest households spent more than twice as much on healthcare compared to the wealthier households, and relied more heavily on out-of-pocket payments.
What_was_studied: This study investigated socio-economic and geographic differences in healthcare expenditure and illness occurrence among South Eastern Nigerian populations over a 6-month period, using both qualitative and quantitative data collected from households and healthcare facilities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs to shield vulnerable populations from the financial burden of illness. Healthcare providers must also revise their payment mechanisms and fee exemption policies to ensure fair access to healthcare for all.

Title: THE EX‐ANTE EFFECTS OF NON‐CONTRIBUTORY PENSIONS IN COLOMBIA AND PERU
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that a NCP program in Colombia and Peru contributes to reducing poverty and inequality among the elderly, particularly in rural areas, at affordable scal costs.
What_was_studied: The study examines the ex-ante effects of implementing a Non Contributory Pension (NCP) program in Colombia and Peru using household survey data to simulate the potential impact on poverty, inequality, scal cost, and the probability of alitation to the contributory pension system among the elderly, particularly in rural areas at affordable scal costs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the potential of NCP programs to reduce poverty and inequality among the elderly, decision-makers should prioritize and expand such programs, particularly in rural areas, to address these issues effectively.

Field: Positive economics; Cultural diversity; Economic Justice; Sociology; Order (exchange); Poverty; Deliberation; Diversity (politics); Development economics; Income distribution; Developing country
Title: Destruction, diversity, dialogue: Notes on the ethics of development
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Market forces are found to be inadequate for resolving the problem of world poverty, with institutions playing a crucial role in economic performance and income distribution, highlighting the need for alternative solutions to address the ethical challenge of acceptability of the world's market-based economic order.
What_was_studied: The persistence of world poverty in the face of increasing global interdependence of economies presents a challenge for ethical deliberation, specifically examining the role of institutions in fundamentally influencing economic performance and income distribution in developing countries over the period 1970-2015 using data from the World Bank and UN agencies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize the development of policies that actively address the persistence of poverty in the face of global interdependence, by fundamentally revising the current market-based economic order and implementing an ethic of development that respects cultural diversity and promotes inter-subjective dialogue.

Field: Sociology; Human rights; Poverty; Empowerment; Accountability; White paper; Gender equity; Gender equality; Development economics; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: The gender and poverty nexus in the DFID White Paper: opportunity or constraint?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while there are efficiency arguments in focusing on poor women, too rigid a link being made between gender and poverty can be dangerous. It also showed that an equity and empowerment focus is crucial for advancing gender equality, but does not automatically address gender relations, and accountability is a two-way street.
What_was_studied: This article considers the implications of the strong poverty focus in the new White Paper for advancing gender equality, looking at poor women in a specific context between 1995 and 1998 using survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize building gender-equitable partnerships to accommodate the participation of poor women, develop new skills and practices among all partners, and recognize accountability as a two-way street to effectively promote women's empowerment and advance gender equality in poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Feeling; Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Perception; Psychological intervention; Shame; Qualitative analysis; Inequality; Social psychology; Environmental ethics
Title: Shame, Poverty and Development Studies
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The collection finds that poverty is not just a lack of resources, but also a source of shame and stigma for those experiencing it. This shame can lead to further marginalization and exclusion of the poor from social and economic opportunities.
What_was_studied: This three-volume collection on poverty and shame in development studies examines the lived experiences, perceptions, and feelings of the poor over a 20-year period, using both qualitative and quantitative data to understand the impact of poverty on individuals and communities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing poverty as a multifaceted issue that requires comprehensive approaches to alleviate shame and stigma. This may involve targeted interventions to improve access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities, as well as addressing social and cultural factors that perpetuate poverty and shame.

Field: Public economics; Positive economics; Cointegration; Economics; Empirical evidence; Low income; Object (philosophy); Politics
Title: Growth and Institutions
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that certain institutional factors, such as low levels of corruption and strong property rights, are positively associated with economic growth, while others, such as high levels of inequality, may be negatively associated with growth. Additionally, the study identified considerable heterogeneity between countries in the nature of the link between institutions and economic activity.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between social and political institutions and economic growth, using a variety of theoretical frameworks and empirical methods to explore alternative conceptions of this link.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant variability in the relationship between institutions and economic growth across countries, policymakers should prioritize efforts to strengthen property rights, reduce corruption, and address inequality in order to promote sustainable economic development and poverty reduction.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Culture of poverty; Market failure; Market system; Poverty; Context (language use)
Title: Why do the poor pay more? Exploring the poverty penalty concept
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the poor pay a higher cost than the non-poor in participating in certain markets, with different causes and forms of the poverty penalty depending on the market, country context, and characteristics of the poor.
What_was_studied: The research examines the poverty penalty phenomenon in various markets and clarifies its subtle and direct ways of marginalizing the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing market failures that exacerbate the poverty penalty, such as lack of access to financial services and information, to scale up inclusive market-based interventions and reduce income poverty.

Authors: Alemayehu Geda; Abebe Shimeles; John Weeks
Field: Baseline (configuration management); Per capita; Aggregate income; Economics; Poverty; Status quo; Distribution (economics); Inequality; Development economics; Panel data
Keywords: Poverty; Growth; Inequality; Distribution of Income; Pro-poor growth; Ethiopia; Africa
Title: GROWTH, POVERTY AND INEQUALITY IN ETHIOPIA: WHICH WAY FOR PRO-POOR GROWTH?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that growth is strongly correlated with inequality, and that implementing a pro-poor growth strategy can have a significant impact on reducing poverty. Specifically, the paper shows that over a 10-year period at a 4% per capita growth rate, poverty would decline from 44% to 26% for distribution-neutral growth (DNG), while equally distributed gains of growth (EDG) would result in a 50% poverty reduction to 15%.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the pattern of poverty, growth, and inequality in Ethiopia over the past decade, using a rich household panel data set.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between growth and inequality, policymakers should prioritize pro-poor growth strategies to address poverty reduction in Ethiopia. By implementing policies that target the poorest segments of society, we can reduce poverty by over half within a decade.

Field: Regional science; Economics; Human Development Report; Economic welfare; Composite index; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Islamic republic; Country level; Development economics
Title: Human development and regional disparities in Iran: a policy model
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that provinces with lower human development indices tend to have higher levels of poverty and gender inequality. Specifically, it was found that 70% of poor people in Iran live in provinces with low human development indices. Additionally, the study revealed a positive correlation between human development index scores and access to basic services such as healthcare and education.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes regional disparities in the Islamic Republic of Iran between 1990 and 2014 using a composite index of education, health, and economic welfare based on data from the Human Development Report of Iran.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize targeted interventions to address regional disparities in education, health, and economic welfare, particularly in provinces with low human development indices. This could involve increasing funding for basic services such as healthcare and education, as well as implementing policies to promote gender equality and reduce poverty.

Field: Standard of living; Economics; Human capital; Unemployment; Eastern european; Foreign direct investment; Market economy; Total fertility rate; Fertility; Panel data
Title: No Eastern and Central European left behind: A cross country regression for fertility, human capital and market economy
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that only tertiary education is correlated with fertility, and that fertility is responsive to a 'business cycle' type of macroeconomic factors, particularly female unemployment. Additionally, foreign direct investment (FDI) as a proxy for new market economy had a negative association with fertility.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed the sharp decline in fertility rates in Central and Eastern European countries during their transition to a market economy using panel data, focusing on education by gender as a proxy for human capital, and including additional economic variables such as unemployment to capture the effect of a declining standard of living.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the low fertility rates in Central and Eastern European countries, policymakers should prioritize investing in education, particularly tertiary education for women, and implement policies to reduce unemployment among women. Additionally, they should consider foreign direct investment as a key factor in promoting economic growth and addressing the declining standard of living, which can help improve fertility rates.

Field: Macroeconomics; Business; Test (assessment)
Title: Leaving No One Behind? A New Test of Subnational Aid Targeting
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis found that aid projects were placed closer to richer people, with a significant effect within countries and administrative regions.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the geographic targeting of aid projects in Nigeria, Senegal, and Uganda from nearly all donors between 2006 and 2015 to determine if aid targets areas of poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that donors should prioritize targeting aid projects towards the poorest areas and populations to ensure no one is left behind in achieving sustainable development goals.

Field: Public economics; Economic efficiency; Agriculture; Economics; Allocative efficiency; Peasant; Scope (project management); Scale (social sciences); Estimation
Title: How credible are estimates of peasant allocative scale, or scope efficiency? A commentary
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The research found that peasant farmers' productivity is significantly lower than previously thought, with an average efficiency score of 60% compared to industrial farmers' scores of 80%. This challenges the Schultzian hypothesis that poor farmers are more efficient due to their limited resources.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the economic efficiency of peasant farmers across different regions and time periods, using a combination of survey data and experimental methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant difference in productivity between peasant and industrial farmers, policymakers should prioritize investing in agricultural technology and training programs specifically tailored for rural farmers to improve their efficiency and food security.

Field: Per capita; Life expectancy; Economics; Functional illiteracy; Short run; Variables; Development aid; Demographic economics; Development economics; Panel data; Developing country
Keywords: foreign aid; education; health; low-income countries
Title: The Impact of Development Aid on Education and Health: Survey and New Evidence for Low-income Countries from Dynamic Models†
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that growth rates or levels of aid per capita have statistically significant, favourable effects on growth rates rather than on levels of life expectancy and illiteracy. Additionally, polynomial distributed lags play a strong role in explaining the great diversity of aid results found in the literature.
What_was_studied: Using panel data models with lagged dependent variables to examine the effectiveness of foreign aid in reducing income poverty, illiteracy, and gender inequality among developing countries from 2000 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize investing in foreign aid programs that focus on growth rates rather than levels of aid per capita. Additionally, they should consider incorporating polynomial distributed lags into their analysis to better understand the effects of foreign aid on poverty reduction and gender equality.

Authors: Channing Arndt; M. Azhar Hussain; Vincenzo Salvucci; Finn Tarp; Lars Peter Østerdal

Title: WIDER Working Paper - Poverty Mapping Based on First-Order Dominance with an Example from Mozambique
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The FOD approach outperformed small-area estimation methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, with a multidimensional conception of welfare that captures the complexities of poverty in Mozambique.
What_was_studied: The research explores a novel first-order dominance (FOD) approach to poverty mapping in Mozambique using census data, accounting for welfare distributions in both levels and trends between 2003 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the advantages of the FOD approach in monitoring and evaluating public expenditures, policy analysts should prioritize its implementation to rigorously assess the impact of anti-poverty interventions on child poverty, food insecurity, rural and urban poverty in Mozambique.

Authors: Greg Regier; Yacob Zereyesus; Timothy J. Dalton; Vincent Amanor-Boadu
Field: Per capita; Rural area; Econometrics; Equivalence (measure theory); Poverty; Geography; Economies of scale; Indifference point; Highly sensitive; Inequality
Title: Do Adult Equivalence Scales Matter in Poverty Estimates? A Northern Ghana Case Study and Simulation
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that overall poverty and inequality measures in northern Ghana are highly sensitive to the use of equivalence scales, with poverty measures for children and the elderly and in urban and rural areas also being sensitive to equivalence scales.
What_was_studied: This study examines the sensitivity of per capita expenditures to several methods of per adult equivalent expenditures to control for economies of scale and household composition in northern Ghana, specifically among children and the elderly in urban and rural areas during a specific time period using simulation analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize the use of per adult equivalent expenditures to control for economies of scale and household composition when assessing poverty and inequality measures in northern Ghana, particularly among children and the elderly in urban and rural areas, in order to more accurately identify those most in need of support.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Negotiation; Power (social and political); Charter; Member states; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Politics
Title: Seven Decades of ‘Development’, and Now What?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper finds that ideas do matter in shaping development agendas and that power dynamics play a crucial role in determining which ideas are adopted and implemented.
What_was_studied: This paper looks at the conceptualization of development agendas and power dynamics within and between the UN member states, the UN secretariat and agencies, and civil society in the context of the UN's sustainable development goals (SDGs) for 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of ideas and power in shaping development policies, decision-makers should prioritize inclusive and participatory processes to ensure that marginalized voices are represented in the SDGs agenda and that gender and poverty reduction targets are met.

Authors: José A. Cuesta; Suzanne Duryea; Fidel Jaramillo; Marcos Robles
Field: Distributive property; Economics; International economics; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Position (finance); Food prices; Development economics
Keywords: food crisis; distributive impacts; simulation; Andean region JEL classification: O20; O18; I30
Title: Distributive impacts of the food price crisis in the Andean region.
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study shows that poverty incidence increased by 2-6 percentage points in the Andean region due to the food price crisis, with significant heterogeneity across household characteristics. The findings suggest that households with a net consumer position were more vulnerable to the crisis than others.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the distributive effects of the recent international food price crisis in the Andean region between 2008 and 2009, using a simple simulation exercise to isolate direct and short-term impacts on poverty across various households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial and variable impacts of the food price crisis on poverty, policymakers should prioritize targeted support programs for vulnerable households, particularly those in net consumer positions, to mitigate the effects of future price shocks and promote sustainable development in the region.

Field: Welfare; Socioeconomic status; Economics; Poverty; Economic reform; Traditional agriculture; Inequality; Development economics; Economic expansion; Spanish Civil War
Title: Economic Reform: Is it Hurting the Poor? A Country Specific Study
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that the 1980s economic reform in Sudan was flawed and did not tap into impulses for equitable economic growth, leading to considerable deterioration on all poverty dimensions, and that alternative broader-based reforms favoring traditional agriculture and processing of its products would have reduced poverty without compromising growth-oriented policies and social equity.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes how and why the welfare of the poor in Sudan changed during the 1980s reform period, using data from that time period to examine poverty dimensions, incidence, intensity, and inequality among the poor, and how external shocks and civil war affected the socioeconomic crisis in Sudan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings suggest that policymakers in Sudan should prioritize broader-based economic reforms that support traditional agriculture and processing of its products to reduce poverty and inequality, rather than solely focusing on growth-oriented policies.

Field: Balance of payments; Demographic transition; Public sector; Economic sector; Real interest rate; Economics; Unemployment; Government debt; Structural adjustment; Development economics; Economic system
Keywords: Africa; Africa South Of The Sahara; Behavior; Demographic Factors; Demographic Transition; Developing Countries; Economic Conditions; Economic Factors; Education; Employment; Estimation Technics; Fertility; Fertility Decline; Health; Macroeconomic Factors; Population; Population Dynamics; Population Projection; Research Methodology; Social Adjustment; Social Behavior; Social Change
Title: Adjustment social sectors and demographic change in Sub-Saharan Africa.
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that economic crises had a negative impact on employment, health, and education sectors in sub-Saharan Africa, with drastic reductions in spending on these sectors leading to declines in manpower development, increases in poverty and inequality, and slowed or stopped social and economic development. The study also found that structural adjustment programs (SAPs) were inadequate solutions to long-term problems and exacerbated the negative impact of economic crises on demographic outcomes.
What_was_studied: The economic crises of the 1980s in sub-Saharan Africa and their impact on employment, health, education, and social protection policies and outcomes over time, using case studies of individual countries as the geographic unit of analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of economic crises on employment, health, education, and social protection policies and outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa, policymakers should prioritize scaling up investments in these sectors to address the lingering effects of the 1980s crises and promote sustainable development. Specifically, policymakers should revise SAPs to better address long-term structural issues and avoid exacerbating demographic challenges.

Field: Economics; Market failure; Poverty; State (polity); Revelation; Washington Consensus; International capital; Development economics; Bureaucracy
Title: Attacking Poverty and the ‘post‐Washington consensus’
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's pursuit of 'security' has forced it to acknowledge widespread market failure in providing social and financial security, leading it to espouse some measures inconsistent with the Washington consensus, such as international capital controls. On the other hand, the old agenda of rolling back the frontiers of the state remains, but with a new twist in WDR 2000 by revealing that 'voices of the poor' are arrayed against bureaucratic abuses.
What_was_studied: The World Bank's pro-poor stance in its most recent World Development Report (WDR) and how it has affected its traditionally free-market attitudes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the World Bank should prioritize measures to address market failures in providing security, particularly in the areas of social and financial security. This could involve implementing international capital controls and acknowledging the need for a more interventionist role by the state in certain contexts.

Field: Welfare state; Sociology; Danish; Community based; Public administration; Process (engineering); Creating shared value
Title: The aid policy process of a ‘humane internationalist’: the Danish example
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the aid policy process in Denmark is driven by a 'humane internationalist' community based on shared values and self-interest among key participants, resulting in an increasing aid budget despite global trends of decreasing aid.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the increasing aid budget of Denmark at a time when other OECD countries are cutting their aid budgets, using concepts from political science to understand the motivations behind foreign aid and contribute to the debate on determinants of foreign aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that community-based values and self-interest drive Danish aid policy, decision-makers should prioritize building and engaging with similar communities to scale up effective foreign aid and address income poverty and sustainable development challenges.

Authors: Ola Hall; Francis Dompae; Ibrahim Wahab; Fred Mawunyo Dzanku
Field: Poverty; Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Predictive power; Welfare; Satellite imagery; Computer science; Scholarship; Field (mathematics); Deep learning; Consumption (sociology); Economics; Economic growth; Social science; Mathematics; Geography; Sociology; Remote sensing; Market economy; Philosophy; Epistemology; Pure mathematics
Title: A review of machine learning and satellite imagery for poverty prediction: Implications for development research and applications
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the most important factors correlated to the predictive power of welfare are the number of pre-processing steps employed, the number of datasets used, the type of welfare indicator targeted, and the choice of AI model. Studies that used stock measure indicators (assets) as targets achieved better performance—17 percentage points higher—in predicting welfare than those that targeted flow measures (income and consumption) ones, and the combination of machine learning and deep learning significantly increases predictive power—by as much as 15 percentage points—compared to using either alone.
What_was_studied: The field of artificial intelligence is seeing the increased application of satellite imagery to analyze poverty in its various manifestations, specifically focusing on welfare and poverty predictions from the combination of machine learning and satellite imagery for a period spanning from 2015 to 2022, using datasets such as World Bank and United Nations data, and targeting indicators like assets, income and consumption, with AI models like logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machines and neural networks in different spatial resolutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investing in AI models that combine machine learning and deep learning for more accurate predictions of welfare, targeting stock measure indicators like assets for better performance, and expanding the use of satellite imagery to more areas and time periods to increase predictive power, especially in the context of addressing child poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, housing insecurity, income poverty, and urban poverty.

Field: Distributive property; Labour economics; Economics; Empirical evidence; Poverty; Human capital; Gender discrimination; Inequality; Unitary state; Politics
Title: The distributive consequences of machismo: a simulation analysis of intra‐household discrimination
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that intra-household gender discrimination significantly worsens poverty and inequality in Chile, with estimates suggesting a substantial increase in these issues under non-cooperative allocation rules dominated by gender discrimination among household members compared to conventional poverty and inequality analyses conducted for the household as a whole.
What_was_studied: Empirical evidence questions the unitary allocation model of the household that underpins the standard measurement of monetary poverty and inequality in Chile, specifically looking at intra-household gender discrimination and its effects on expenditure decisions, nutrition status, and human capital accumulation among household members during a specific time period using recent developments in intra-household bargaining modeling.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing intra-household gender discrimination in order to effectively tackle poverty and inequality in Chile, possibly revising standard measurement methods of monetary poverty and inequality to better account for this issue and consider targeted interventions to address gender discrimination within households.

Authors: Matias Mednik; Cesar M. Rodriguez; Inder J. Ruprah
Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Hysteresis (economics); Unemployment; Demographic economics; Development economics
Keywords: Unemployment hysteresis; unit root test; panel unit root test; crosssection dependence. JEL Classification: C22; C23; E24; J24; J60
Title: Hysteresis in Unemployment: Evidence from Latin America
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings give support to the hysteric dynamic hypothesis for the majority of the countries analyzed.
What_was_studied: This paper tests the hysteresis hypothesis in unemployment for 13 Latin American countries covering the period 1980-2005, exploiting time series and cross sectional variation, allowing for cross section dependence and a different number of endogenously determined structural breakpoints.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The results suggest that macro-stabilization policies should prioritize addressing hysteresis effects to reduce persistent unemployment and improve social protection programs to mitigate the impact on vulnerable populations.

Field: Developmental psychology; Socioeconomic status; Psychology; Cognition; Personality; Poverty; Vitality; Child poverty; Deterministic theory; Childhood poverty; Social psychology
Title: ‘Poor children grow into poor adults’: harmful mechanisms or over‐deterministic theory?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Research shows that childhood poverty can have lasting effects on cognitive, physical, and personality development, but these effects can be mitigated or even reversed with appropriate interventions throughout life.
What_was_studied: Childhood poverty in specific behavioral and biological mechanisms from a developmental psychopathology perspective over a particular time period, using certain data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the long-lasting impact of childhood poverty on socioeconomic attainment, policymakers should prioritize addressing food insecurity, gender inequality, and income poverty in early life to promote sustained prosperity and limit the reach of intergenerational poverty.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Basic service; Core (game theory); Complementarity (molecular biology); Loyalty; Collective action; Urban area; Urban slum; Low income; Economic growth
Title: Standalone, Collective or Both? How Low‐income Urban Households Employ Strategies to Secure Basic Service Access in Hyderabad, India
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that households employ several strategies simultaneously to enhance basic service provision, with little evidence of strategic complementarity between individual and collective strategies. Specifically, the survey showed that 75% of households used standalone strategies, while 60% participated in collective action efforts.
