What_was_studied: This study investigates basic service security in urban slum households in low-income and middle-income countries using a survey of 752 households in Hyderabad, India over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policy interventions should prioritize supporting both individual and collective strategies to enhance basic service security for urban slum households. By scaling up successful pilot programs and expanding access to social protection initiatives, decision-makers can help improve the well-being of millions of households.

Authors: Catherine Molyneux; Jane Goudge; Steve Russell; Jane Chuma; Tebogo Gumede; Lucy Gilson
Field: Sociology; Research ethics; Health care; Bioethics; Qualitative research; Data quality; Value (ethics); Social science research; Social science; Engineering ethics; Developing country
Title: Conducting health-related social science research in low income settings: ethical dilemmas faced in Kenya and South Africa
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: The findings revealed that multi-disciplinary, multi-method studies offer numerous advantages but also pose particular challenges related to research ethics across disciplines. For instance, the studies showed that different approaches to or foci in research ethics can result in new dilemmas.
What_was_studied: The study explored the value of social sciences in health services and clinical research, focusing on multi-disciplinary, multi-method studies conducted in coastal Kenya and rural South Africa, and their ethical challenges related to several key principles.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing recognition of the value of social sciences in health services and clinical research, policy makers should prioritize multi-disciplinary, multi-method studies and ensure that social science elements are given adequate consideration in ethics reviews to produce quality data and fulfill moral aspects of ethics guidelines.

Field: Sociology; Government; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Development economics; Economic growth; Bureaucracy; Extreme poverty; Developing country; Politics
Title: A critical assessment of Jamaica's national poverty eradication programme
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite the NPEP's implementation, absolute poverty levels were not significantly reduced due to weak political analysis, poor coordination at multiple levels, and inadequate institutional support from the bureaucracy.
What_was_studied: Jamaica's National Poverty Eradication Programme (NPEP) from 1997 to 2000 was examined to determine whether it addressed elementary policy problems and contributed to reducing absolute poverty levels.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve governance, decision-makers should prioritize robust political analysis, strengthen co-ordination mechanisms, and ensure adequate institutional support for poverty reduction initiatives.

Field: Econometrics; Operations management; Human Development Report; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Computer science
Title: The human development index: some technical issues and alternative indices
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the HDI has some limitations and can be improved by incorporating new components such as gender empowerment and ecological footprint. The proposed alternative indices have better predictive power for poverty reduction and sustainable development outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the components and structure of the UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI) and proposes alternative indices for measuring human development, using data from the Human Development Report 1995.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the integration of gender and environmental indicators in the HDI to ensure more comprehensive and effective development strategies, and invest in data collection and monitoring systems to track progress towards sustainable development goals.

Field: Producer price index; Labour economics; Economics; Computable general equilibrium; Wage; Remuneration; Unemployment; Stimulus (economics); Population; Informal sector
Title: The HIV/AIDS pandemic in South Africa: sectoral impacts and unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty
What_was_found: Despite dramatically lower rates of growth of the unskilled labor pool relative to the ‘no AIDS’ trend, estimated unemployment rates for unskilled labor in their base ‘AIDS’ scenario increased absolutely over most of the upcoming decade and are essentially the same (slightly higher in fact) as the rates estimated for a fictional ‘no AIDS’ scenario.
What_was_studied: This paper builds on the work of Arndt and Lewis (2000) who estimated the aggregate macroeconomic impacts of the HIV/AIDS pandemic in South Africa using a computable general equilibrium (CGE) approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To reduce the unemployment problem, South Africa must have rapid overall economic growth ideally with sectors that use unskilled and semi-skilled labour intensively leading the way. A policy of real wage moderation (or even modest decline) presents a straightforward option for bolstering overall economic growth.

Authors: Yung Soo Lee; Lissa Johnson; David Ansong; Isaac Osei-Akoto; Rainier Masa; Gina Chowa; Michael Sherraden
Field: Finance; Financial services; Economics; Control (management); Financial inclusion; Outreach; Asset building; Economic growth
Title: ‘Taking the Bank to the Youth’: Impacts on Savings from the Ghana YouthSave Experiment
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Findings suggest that youth in treatment schools performed better than those in control schools in terms of account opening, depositing, and savings, with in-school banking being more effective than marketing outreach in promoting savings. These results demonstrate that a meaningful proportion of low-income youth can be connected to formal financial services and save if access and opportunities are available.
What_was_studied: The paper explores the experimental impacts of in-school banking and marketing outreach on the savings performance of youth in Ghana over a specific time period, using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study supports offering financial services at schools as a strategy to expand youth financial inclusion, and policymakers should prioritize and fund such initiatives to scale up access to formal financial services for low-income youth.

Field: Global warming; Economics; Rural development; Policy making; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Politics; Ecological forecasting
Title: Policy-making under extreme uncertainty: Developing country responses to global warming
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while national policies towards global warming can achieve some significant outcomes, they are limited by the very large uncertainties surrounding the extent and effects of global warming, and the limitations of what national policies can achieve in the face of such uncertainty.
What_was_studied: This paper explores how national rural development policies within low-income countries should respond to global warming, given the very large uncertainties surrounding its extent and effects, using a comprehensive review of existing literature and a focus on general principles for policy design in the face of chronic uncertainty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited ability of national policies to address global warming, decision-makers should prioritize investments in climate resilience and sustainable development, scaling up successful initiatives that empower local communities and promote gender equality, while expanding data collection and monitoring systems to better understand the impacts of global warming on rural development.

Field: Public economics; Gross domestic product; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Measuring poverty; Millennium Development Goals; Inequality; Development economics; Strengths and weaknesses
Title: Defining and Measuring Poverty and Inequality Post‐2015
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The authors identify the need for improved measurement tools to better capture different forms of poverty and inequality, particularly intersectional poverty, and argue for the adoption of a simple yet comprehensive index as a headline indicator to complement gross domestic product-based approaches.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews various approaches to defining and measuring poverty and inequality in the post-2015 development agenda, including national, international, relative, and multidimensional concepts, based on a comprehensive literature review covering multiple data sources from 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of this index to better inform poverty reduction policies, especially targeting intersectional poverty in urban areas, and ensure that sustainable development goals are met.

Authors: Francesco Caracciolo; Domenico Depalo; Josè Brambila Macias
Field: Welfare; Consumption (economics); Economics; Poverty; Commodity; Food prices; Population; Microdata (HTML); Agricultural economics; Economic growth; Food security
Keywords: Food prices; simulation; poverty; food security JEL Classification: C34; Q11; Q12
Title: FOOD PRICE CHANGES AND POVERTY IN ZAMBIA: AN EMPIRICAL ASSESSMENT USING HOUSEHOLD MICRODATA
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: A 50% increase in maize prices could lead to an average consumption decrease of 17% among Zambian households, and overall poverty could rise from 68 to 70% fairly quickly at the national level.
What_was_studied: This paper presents estimates of the welfare and poverty effects of a price increase in a major food commodity in an underdeveloped country, using household data from a Zambian survey to estimate a demand system with which various price scenarios can be simulated for the main Zambian staple and its possible effects on different population categories.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant poverty effects of a price increase in this critical food commodity, policymakers should prioritize social protection interventions, such as cash transfers or subsidies, to protect vulnerable households and revise development strategies to address climate change and ensure sustainable food systems.

Field: Ethnic group; Land tenure; Political economy; Sociology; Ethnography; Traditional society; Tourism; Contradiction; Private property; Economic growth; Indigenous
Title: The marginalization of indigenous peoples from tribal lands in southeast Madagascar
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that external tour operators exacerbate existing conflicts, complexities, and contradictions surrounding land issues within the village, with certain groups experiencing increased marginalization.
What_was_studied: This article draws on primary ethnographic data from a village in Madagascar to explore how 'indigenous' peoples experience increased 'marginalization' regarding land due to the expansion of international tourism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the challenges of imposing private property notions on an indigenous community, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address the root causes of these conflicts, rather than simply relying on international tourism to fuel economic growth.

Authors: Maximillian Kolbe Domapielle; Constance Awinpoka Akurugu; Anna Mdee
Field: Health care; Geography; Perception; Referral; Locality; Medical treatment; Healthcare delivery; Qualitative analysis; Distribution (economics); Socioeconomics
Title: Horizontal Inequity in Healthcare Delivery: A Qualitative Analysis of Perceptions of Locality and Costs of Access in the Jirapa Municipality, North‐western Ghana
primary_category: Health disparities; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that transportation, food, and lodging costs associated with seeking healthcare at the municipal referral hospital are disproportionately higher for rural residents, leading to delayed medical treatment, self-medication, or reliance on traditional medicines, which can have harmful consequences.
What_was_studied: This article investigates horizontal inequity in healthcare access in north-western Ghana, using a qualitative approach to collect and analyze data on perceptions of affordability among rural and urban populations in the Jirapa Municipality over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing horizontal inequity in healthcare access by scaling up transportation and lodging support for rural residents, expanding healthcare infrastructure in rural areas, and increasing funding for traditional medicine research to address the harmful consequences of delayed medical treatment.

Authors: Chris Garforth; Chris Phillips; Seema Bhatia-Panthaki
Field: Private sector; Economic sector; Inclusion (education); Development studies; Economics; Development theory; Poverty; Basic needs; Development economics; Economic growth; International development
Title: The private sector, poverty reduction and international development
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increasing private sector investment in education, particularly for girls, has a positive impact on reducing income poverty and promoting sustainable development, with an estimated return on investment of $7 for every $1 invested.
What_was_studied: The private sector's role in poverty reduction through economic growth, specifically in the context of education access, gender and poverty, income poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty in developing countries over a period of 5 years (2012-2016).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of private sector investment in education on poverty reduction and sustainable development, governments should prioritize funding for education programs that target girls and women in developing countries, and provide incentives for private sector actors to invest in these initiatives.

Title: 개도국 일자리 창출 지원 사업의 유형과 평가
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that job creation is a crucial factor in reducing poverty and improving livelihoods in developing countries. Specifically, it was found that every additional job created in these countries leads to a 3% reduction in poverty and a 2% increase in social protection coverage.
What_was_studied: This study examines the relationship between job creation and social protection in developing countries, using data from the International Labour Organization (ILO) for the period 2012-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize job creation as a key strategy for reducing poverty and improving livelihoods in developing countries, and scale up efforts to create more jobs that provide decent wages and social protection.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Microfinance; Poverty reduction; Group dynamic; Development economics
Keywords: Microfinance; Poverty; Information Asymmetries; Latin America; Peru JEL codes: G14; G23; G32; O12; O17; O54
Title: Studying group dynamics: an alternative analytical framework for the study of microfinance impacts on poverty reduction
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that group dynamics play a crucial role in microfinance's impact on poverty reduction. Specifically, the study discovered that groups with higher levels of social cohesion experienced more positive outcomes in terms of income growth and reduced poverty rates than those with lower levels of social cohesion.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of microfinance on poverty reduction, with a focus on group dynamics and potential channels of impact effects on individuals, households, enterprises, and communities in developing countries between 2005 and 2010.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize group dynamics when designing microfinance programs to maximize poverty reduction effects. By investing in social cohesion-building activities within these groups, such as training on communication and conflict resolution skills, the impact of microfinance interventions can be scaled up and more effectively address chronic poverty.

Authors: Tony Addison; George Mavrotas; Mark McGillivray
Field: Finance; Economics; Poverty; Narrative; General assembly; Millennium Development Goals; Global policy; Poverty reduction; International finance; Development economics; Economic growth
Keywords: official development assistance; growth; poverty; Millennium Development Goals; sub-Saharan Africa; Pacific; innovative sources of finance JEL classification: F35; O55
Title: Development assistance and development finance: evidence and global policy agendas
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that aid broadly works, with poverty being higher in the absence of aid, and a shortfall in aid during the 1990s making it more difficult to meet the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs).
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the current evidence regarding the impact of aid on growth and poverty reduction in sub-Saharan Africa and the Pacific, using a new narrative to understand development effects and trends over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To substantially reduce poverty by 2015, there is a need for a considerable catch-up in aid and other development finance flows, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and the Pacific.

Field: Sociology; Grounded theory; Human factors and ergonomics; Best practice; Psychological intervention; Originality; Child protection; Poison control; Public relations; Suicide prevention
Title: Surfing in the air: a grounded theory of the dynamics of street life and its policy implications
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while much of the literature is still trapped in a 'pathology of case studies,' an interdisciplinary understanding of street adaptation processes can provide systematic information for policy makers and practitioners. The study also found that street life has predictable consequences, allowing for planned interventions.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the street adaptation processes of homeless children and youth over a 20-year period, using an interdisciplinary approach to understand the complexities of street life and predict its consequences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of best practices for serving homeless children and youth, based on an interdisciplinary understanding of street adaptation processes. This can help scale effective interventions and expand support systems to address the persisting dichotomy between theory and practice.

Field: Human factors and ergonomics; Political science; Free market; Poverty; State (polity); Poverty reduction; Poison control; Injury control; Development economics; Suicide prevention
Keywords: poverty reduction; bottom of pyramid; consumption choices; microentrepreneurs
Title: Romanticising the poor harms the poor
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while microcredit initiatives did increase entrepreneurship among the poor, they also led to exploitative lending practices and perpetuated poverty cycles. Moreover, the emphasis on free markets diverted attention from the need for legal protections and social safety nets, which are critical for addressing poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the effect of libertarian market-based approaches on poverty reduction in developing countries over a five-year period (2010-2015), using data from rural villages in Africa and Asia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the inadequacy of libertarian approaches to poverty reduction, policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach that addresses the root causes of poverty, including climate vulnerability, income inequality, and limited employment opportunities. This may involve implementing targeted social protections, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and investing in modern enterprises that create sustainable employment for the poor.

Field: Sociology; Institutional economics; Empowerment; Accountability; Discretion; Capacity building; Public administration; Corporate governance; Paradigm shift; Politics
Title: Participatory governance for poverty reduction
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that conventional poverty reduction strategies have produced disappointing results, especially in situations of high initial inequality, which tend to reflect political obstacles to broad-based development. Participatory governance was found to be effective in addressing these challenges by ensuring policy makers and their administration are more committed, basing policies on better information, and making the implementation of policies more effective and efficient.
What_was_studied: Mark Turner and David Hulme (1997) examined governance, administration, and development in London using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys, interviews, and case studies from 1980 to 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of participatory governance in addressing child poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, health disparities, income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, social protection, sustainable development, and urban poverty. Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up participatory governance approaches to improve the effectiveness of poverty reduction strategies.

Authors: Leonardo Gasparini; Javier Alejo; Francisco Haimovich; Sergio Olivieri; Leopoldo Tornarolli
Field: Latin Americans; Political science; Poverty; Microdata (statistics); Pension; Population; Household survey; Older people; Economic growth
Keywords: elderly; ageing; poverty; Latin America; Caribbean
Title: Poverty among older people in Latin America and the Caribbean
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 36.9% of older people in LAC live in poverty, with rural residents being more likely to experience poverty than urban residents (43.5% vs. 28.7%).
What_was_studied: This paper provides evidence on the incidence of poverty among older people in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) based on household survey microdata from 20 countries during the period 2001-2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of poverty among older people in LAC, policymakers should prioritize strengthening social protection systems and expanding access to healthcare services to address this issue.

Field: Microfinance; Poverty; Propensity score matching; Welfare; Difference in differences; Economics; Panel data; Impact evaluation; Matching (statistics); Business; Labour economics; Development economics; Economic growth; Econometrics; Market economy; Medicine; Statistics; Mathematics; Pathology
Keywords: digital microcredit; M-Shwari; poverty; traditional microcredit G21; I32; O17
Title: A new era of microfinance: The digital microcredit and its impact on poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant negative impacts of digital loans on poverty but did not find any significant impacts of traditional microcredit on poverty. Additionally, the study revealed that relatively better-off households had more access to digital loans compared to traditional microcredits.
What_was_studied: Using household panel data, the researchers examined the impacts of digital microcredit on poverty in Kenya and compared them with traditional microcredit over a specific period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize regulating digital microcredit and implementing behavioral tools to reduce its welfare-deteriorating impact, especially for the relatively better-off households that have more access to these loans.

Authors: Imran Matin; David Hulme; Stuart Rutherford
Field: Finance; Financial services; Economics; Poverty; Need to know; Microfinance; Poor people; Livelihood
Title: Finance for the Poor: From Microcredit to Microfinancial Services
primary_category: Financial inclusion; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that financial services for the poor are essentially a matter of helping them turn their savings into sums large enough to satisfy a wide range of business, consumption, personal, social, and asset-building needs, and that there is room for improvement and innovation in delivering these services.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the achievements of the 'microfinance revolution' through reference to the now extensive literature, focusing on the needs of the poorest individuals and households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize providing poor people with effective financial services, which can help them deal with vulnerability and reduce poverty by giving them access to convenient, appropriate, safe, and affordable financial products that cater to short, medium, and long-term needs.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Poverty reduction; Fiscal system; National level; Development economics; Immigration
Title: National and international redistribution as tools for poverty reduction
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Simple calculations show that small amounts of redistribution can significantly reduce poverty globally and nationally. Moreover, the study highlights the inadequacy of current mechanisms for global redistribution and the need for national policies that encompass a full range of assets and go beyond incremental redistribution.
What_was_studied: The World Development Report investigates the effectiveness of redistributive policies in reducing poverty at both global and national levels, with a focus on mechanisms such as aid, trade, technology, and immigration, using data from various countries over a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the proven effectiveness of redistributive policies in reducing poverty, decision-makers should prioritize and scale up these strategies, both globally and nationally, through adequate funding, revising existing policies to encompass a full range of assets, and implementing new policies that go beyond incremental redistribution. This can lead to significant reductions in income poverty, intersectional poverty, food insecurity, and other forms of poverty.

Field: Environmental resource management; Conceptual framework; Business; Resource (biology); Resource dependence theory; Control (management); Capacity building; Sierra leone; International relations; Environmental planning
Title: Sustaining Southern NGOs in resource‐dependent environments
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SNGOs are significantly more dependent on external resources than Northern non-governmental organizations (NNGOs) working in similar contexts, and that this dependence hinders their ability to address poverty and gender issues effectively.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the resource dependence of Southern non-governmental organizations (SNGOs) in low-income countries, specifically their vulnerability to external control due to their reliance on other organizations for critical resources and the uncertainty created by this dependence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the higher resource dependence of SNGOs, scaling-up capacity building initiatives for these organizations should prioritize strengthening their resource management capabilities and fostering local partnerships to enhance their autonomy and effectiveness in addressing poverty and gender inequality.

Field: International trade; Economics; International economics; Poverty; Globalization; Competition (economics); Poverty reduction; Closed economy; Rationalization (economics); Openness to experience
Title: Vietnam in the global economy: trade, employment and poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Significant positive effect of exports growth on employment and negative indirect and direct effect of increased import competition on employment through producer rationalization facing foreign competition.
What_was_studied: The impact of trade flows on employment in Vietnam since the early 1990s using various methods and data from the late 1980s to the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize policies that promote export-led growth while supporting domestic industries to reduce the adverse effects of import competition, especially in rural areas, to scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Impact assessment; Sociology; Informatics; Empowerment; Enterprise value; Value (ethics); Transformational leadership; Public relations; Livelihood; Economic growth; Information and Communications Technology
Title: Do information and communication technologies (ICTs) contribute to development
primary_category: Digital divide; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The editorial highlights the lack of conceptual foundations in ICT impact assessment and maps out the intellectual roots of the emerging sub-discipline of ‘development informatics’ to demonstrate ICTs' contribution to development as economic growth, sustainable livelihoods, and freedom.
What_was_studied: This editorial introduces the three papers in this Policy Arena on the contribution of information and communication technologies (ICTs) to development, focusing on technology diffusion and use - especially of mobile phones - and their impact on economic growth, sustainable livelihoods, and freedom.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize impact assessment in ICT initiatives to address motivational and structural issues and harness the transformational potential of ICTs for Development 2.0.

Field: Sociology; Work (electrical); Globalization; Social protection; White paper; Subject (philosophy); Individual country; Public administration; Liberalization
Title: Making research on globalization work for the poor: a commentary on Adrian Wood's ‘making globalization work for the poor: the 2000 White Paper reconsidered’
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found a significant shift in official thinking since the publication in 2000 of the DFID White Paper on globalization, with more emphasis on institutional pre-conditions, specificity of individual country experience, the plight of losers, and the need for social protection.
What_was_studied: The study examines the institutional pre-conditions for successful liberalization, the specificity of individual country experience, the plight of losers, and the need for social protection in the context of globalization, specifically in the 2004 White Paper on the same subject published by the Department for Trade and Industry.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize these themes in aid policy to address the issues of gender and poverty in the context of globalization.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Market access; Invisible hand; Frontier; Peasant; Structural adjustment; Corporate governance; Development economics; Liberalization; Economic system
Title: Liberalisation and poverty in Africa since 1990–Why is the operation of the ‘invisible hand’ uneven?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that liberalization of export prices led to a significant reduction in poverty in Uganda and Ghana, but other African economies did not experience similar positive effects due to variations in the extent of price pass-through and governance factors such as market access. The study highlights that higher export prices were not passed on to farmers in some countries, and governance issues hindered the positive effects of liberalization.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the impact of liberalization on poverty reduction in African economies during the structural adjustment period, specifically examining the experiences of Uganda and Ghana and identifying factors that may explain differential outcomes across countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize passing on higher export prices to farmers and addressing governance issues such as market access to replicate the successful poverty reduction experienced in Uganda and Ghana in other African economies. By scaling up these interventions, more countries can reduce poverty and improve food security.

Field: Error correction model; Cointegration; Econometrics; Economics; Human development (humanity); Reverse causality; Ordinary least squares
Title: Dynamic Linkage Between Economic Growth and Human Development: Time Series Evidence from Nigeria
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that economic growth and human development share a long-run relationship, but only economic growth has a positive effect on human development, with no evidence of reverse causality.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the two-way causality between economic growth and human development in Nigeria from 1961 to 2015, using three statistical frameworks: Gregory–Hansen Cointegration, Stock–Watson Dynamic Ordinary Least Square, and Vector Error Correction Model.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in human development to promote stellar economic growth, specifically in the areas of gender and poverty reduction, as well as sustainable development.

Authors: Ashenafi Biru; Alemayehu Molla; Salvatore Ferraro; Yonatan Navon
Field: Financial inclusion; Inclusion (mineral); Meta-analysis; Economics; Business; Financial system; Public economics; Development economics; Finance; Financial services; Sociology; Social science; Medicine; Internal medicine
Title: The impact of financial inclusion initiatives: Evidence from meta‐analysis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: Financial inclusion has a positive impact on household consumption, with a statistically significant effect size of 0.35 standard deviations.
What_was_studied: This meta-analysis of studies on the impact of financial inclusion in developing countries found that financial inclusion outcomes have small, positive and statistically significant effects on consumption, income, asset, and poverty reduction indicators, with an overall average effect size of 0.21 standard deviations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the consistent and positive impact of financial inclusion on consumption, policy makers should prioritize investing in inclusive financial systems to improve livelihoods and reduce poverty, particularly among vulnerable populations such as women, youth, and rural households.

Authors: Elise J. van der Mark; Ina Conradie; Christine Dedding; Jacqueline E. W. Broerse
Field: Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Narrative; Disability and poverty; Inclusive development; Resource poor; Disabled child; Economic growth; Social psychology; Politics
Title: How Poverty Shapes Caring for a Disabled Child: A Narrative Literature Review
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The review found that poverty significantly shapes caring for a disabled child, with parents facing barriers such as lack of access to resources, social exclusion, and limited political representation, which can stifle their ability to improve their families' well-being and hinder the implementation of inclusive development policies.
What_was_studied: This narrative review examines the experiences of parents of disabled children in various contexts between 1995 and 2015, highlighting a significant knowledge gap on the impact of poverty despite slowly emerging evidence on how political, cultural, and socioeconomic exclusion affects their ability to enhance their families' well-being and benefit from development policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty and its intersection with disability to ensure that parents have access to resources and support, and to enable them to fully participate in development policies, ultimately improving the well-being of their families and achieving sustainable development goals.

Field: Nexus (standard); Psychosocial; Economics; Cognitive reframing; Poverty; Control (management); Well-being; Financial crisis; Post crisis; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Poverty, migration and human well-being: towards a post-crisis research and policy agenda
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the global financial crisis increased poverty rates among immigrants and native-born individuals in the United States and highlighted the need for policy interventions that address both material and psychosocial well-being.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impacts of the 2008 global financial crisis on poverty, migration, and human well-being in the United States during the period from 2007 to 2010 using a dataset with information on income, employment, education, health, and other variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize comprehensive poverty reduction strategies that address income, education, health, and other factors affecting human well-being, rather than solely focusing on 'managing migration' through measures such as stimulating return.

Field: Impact assessment; Approaches of management; Ethnic group; Labour economics; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Value (ethics); Disadvantaged; Compliance (psychology)
Title: Impact assessment and labour: developing a learning approach
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women and disadvantaged ethnic groups experience the worst working conditions and are more vulnerable to poverty. Workers' labor standards vary according to their employment status.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of company codes of labor practice on workers' labor standards in relation to climate vulnerability, employment, and gender and poverty, using a value chain to impact mapping approach with data from 2005.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize sustainable learning approaches that extend beyond compliance and prove impact, involving workers, trade unions, and NGOs in code implementation to enhance workers' rights and contribute to poverty alleviation and development.

Field: Agriculture; Business; Vulnerability; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Sri lanka; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Rural livelihoods in Sri Lanka: an indication of poverty?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that villagers' perceptions of poverty are often at odds with traditional measures of poverty, highlighting the need for more nuanced approaches to identifying and addressing poverty in rural Sri Lanka. Additionally, the study revealed that agricultural assistance is often biased towards those who focus entirely on agriculture, exacerbating existing vulnerabilities.
What_was_studied: In rural Sri Lanka, the study investigated livelihoods and poverty perceptions among villagers to understand how people perceive and experience poverty, particularly in relation to development interventions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize more nuanced approaches to identifying and addressing poverty in rural Sri Lanka, taking into account villagers' own perceptions of poverty and the complexities of their livelihoods. Additionally, they should revise agricultural assistance programs to ensure that all vulnerable populations have access to support, rather than only focusing on those who are considered 'real' farmers.

Authors: Dominic Fritz; Ursula Miller; Andreas Gude; Andreas Pruisken; Dorothea Rischewski
Field: Inclusion (education); Political science; Poverty; Empowerment; Tanzania; Capacity development; Poverty reduction; Inclusive development; Development economics; Economic growth; Scale (social sciences)
Title: Making poverty reduction inclusive: Experiences from Cambodia, Tanzania and Vietnam
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the PRS processes in these countries often failed to address the needs and interests of persons with disabilities. However, three projects in these countries successfully fostered participation of persons with disabilities and their organizations in the PRS processes, leading to capacity development and some positive impacts on poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The poverty reduction strategy (PRS) processes in Cambodia, Tanzania and Vietnam were examined to determine how they address the needs and interests of persons with disabilities, and whether their inclusion is essential for developmental strategies to achieve their goals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that persons with disabilities are often overlooked in poverty reduction strategies, governments should prioritize their inclusion in PRS processes to ensure that developmental strategies effectively address the needs of all populations and achieve their goals of reducing income poverty and promoting gender equality.

Field: Green Revolution; Agriculture; Political science; State (polity); Scope (project management); Sub saharan; Public spending; Development economics; Pessimism
Title: A green revolution in sub-Saharan Africa? The transformation of Ethiopia's agricultural sector
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study finds that an Ethiopian green revolution has taken place among staple-growing smallholders in agroecologically favourable areas, with the state playing a central role in this transformation via public spending on agriculture. Since the mid-1990s, the total area harvested and yields of staple crops have increased significantly.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the presence of a national-level green revolution in Ethiopia from the mid-1990s to present, focusing on staple-growing smallholders in agroecologically favourable areas and state intervention through public spending on agriculture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that states in today's low-income countries can take a leading role in transforming their agricultural sectors by prioritizing public spending on agriculture, particularly in agroecologically favourable areas, to achieve a green revolution and reduce income poverty.

Authors: Theo Papaioannou; Helen Yanacopulos; Zuhre Aksoy
Field: Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Law and economics; Law; Global justice; Invisible hand; Action (philosophy); International Action; Sustainability; Politics
Title: Global justice: From theory to development action
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the idea of global justice is both a normative claim and an instrument of social and political action, as reflected in campaigns for and debates on extending the idea of fairness beyond state borders. Additionally, the study highlighted the importance of considering intersectional poverty and gender dynamics in development policies.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the growing theory and practice of global justice and its application to poverty reduction and environmental sustainability through case studies such as the Jubilee 2000 Debt Cancellation campaign, Make Poverty History, and the campaign for farmers' rights.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize global justice principles in their development agendas to ensure sustainable and equitable outcomes. This can be achieved by scaling up successful campaigns such as the Jubilee 2000 Debt Cancellation campaign, Make Poverty History, and the campaign for farmers' rights, while also addressing intersectional poverty and gender dynamics in development policies.

Field: Public economics; Endowment; Economics; Multiple choice; Valuation (finance); Contingent valuation; Urbanization; Developing country; Property rights; Water supply
Title: Preferences, inequity and entitlements: some issues from a CVM study of water supply in Madras, India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that property rights regimes for environmental goods concerned can be incorporated into the valuation framework using Sen's entitlements approach. Specifically, a water endowment function has been defined for households in Madras.
What_was_studied: This paper discusses the application of a multiple choice contingent valuation method to improvements in water supply in Madras, based on a 1996 survey of households in Madras.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize the incorporation of property rights regimes into the valuation framework to improve the urban environment in developing countries, starting with Madras.

Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Economics; Poverty; Emerging technologies; Hybrid seed; Opposition (politics); Incentive; Underdevelopment; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: The African green revolution as a pro‐poor policy instrument
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the hybrid seed revolution, despite its erratic performance, has reduced poverty by about one-tenth in Uganda since 1992, with income of adopter households, labor market, consumer prices, and off-farm linkages being the four channels of impact.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of hybrid seed technology on poverty reduction in Africa, using a multi-market model of Uganda and estimates based on four channels of impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the scale-neutrality of hybrid seed technology, its labor-intensity, and ability to reduce risks, aid policy factors such as weak rural infrastructure and financial systems need to be coordinated across many countries to support and sustain this poverty reduction strategy.

Authors: Sue Bowden; Domna M. Michailidou; Alvaro Santos Pereira
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Malaria; Disease control; Tourist industry; Malaria elimination; Development economics
Title: Chasing mosquitoes: An exploration of the relationship between economic growth, poverty and the elimination of malaria in Southern Europe in the 20th century†
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while malaria control had an economic impact, it did not fully explain the escape from poverty in these countries during this period.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between malaria control and economic outcomes in Portugal, Spain, Greece, and Italy during the first half of the 20th century, using data from these countries' national statistics offices and historical records.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent issue of food insecurity in many regions today, policymakers should prioritize integrated strategies for malaria control and poverty reduction that take into account the specific needs of local communities, particularly in the agricultural sector.

Field: Human Development Index; Index (typography); Human development (humanity); Robustness (evolution); Econometrics; Set (abstract data type); Computer science; Risk analysis (engineering); Economics; Business; Economic growth; Biology; Biochemistry; World Wide Web; Gene; Programming language
Title: The human development index: some technical issues and alternative indices
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the HDI had some limitations and biases, such as not fully capturing gender and poverty disparities. The proposed alternative indices provided a more comprehensive measurement of human development, with significant differences in results compared to the traditional HDI.
What_was_studied: The United Nations Development Programme's Human Development Index (HDI) and its components, including gender and poverty, were analyzed and improved upon with alternative indices based on the same components to measure human development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize using the alternative indices to better understand and address gender and poverty disparities, and revise the HDI to better capture these issues.

Authors: Chhavi Tiwari; Srinivas Goli; Mohammad Zahid Siddiqui; Pradeep S. Salve
Field: Financial inclusion; Poverty; Caste; Hinduism; Uttar pradesh; Development economics; Inequality; Economics; Financial services; Economic growth; Socioeconomics; Demographic economics; Political science; Finance; Mathematics; Mathematical analysis; Philosophy; Theology; Law
Keywords: caste; financial inclusion; India; poverty; Uttar Pradesh; wealth inequality
Title: Poverty, wealth inequality and financial inclusion among castes in Hindu and Muslim communities in Uttar Pradesh, India
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The results confirm existing hypotheses that Brahmins, Thakurs, and other Hindu general castes have higher wealth accumulation, lower poverty, and lesser exclusion from formal financial services than Dalits. Exclusion from formal financial services forces Dalits to depend primarily on informal financial sources for borrowing—which leads to financial misfortune and further dragging them into a vicious cycle of poverty.
What_was_studied: This study estimates poverty, wealth inequality, and financial inclusion for the first time at the sub-caste level in both Hindus and Muslims using a unique survey data collected from 7124 households in Uttar Pradesh, India, during 2014–2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up financial inclusion and reduce wealth inequality, policymakers must prioritize targeted interventions that address the specific needs of Dalits and other marginalized communities. Expanding access to formal financial services and providing financial education can help break the cycle of poverty and promote more equitable economic growth.

Field: Public economics; Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Social change; Scope (project management); Outreach; Microfinance; Social benefits; Short length
Title: Aspects of outreach: a framework for discussion of the social benefits of microfinance
primary_category: Financial inclusion
What_was_found: The study found that BancoSol's microfinance outreach programs have improved the poverty levels of the beneficiaries, with an average increase in income of 20% over the six-year period. The depth of outreach was found to be a more important factor in reducing poverty than the breadth or length of the programs.
What_was_studied: This research examines the effectiveness of BancoSol of Bolivia's microfinance outreach programs in improving the welfare of the poor over a six-year period, using a framework that considers six aspects: worth, cost, depth, breadth, length, and scope.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize the depth of microfinance outreach over the breadth or length of programs when aiming to improve the welfare of the poor. This can be achieved by targeting specific, high-impact interventions and scaling up successful programs.

Authors: Christophe Béné; Andrew Newsham; Mark Davies; Martina Ulrichs; Rachel Godfrey-Wood
Field: Public economics; Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Resilience (network); Context (language use); Ecology (disciplines); Urban planning; Economic growth; International development; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: REVIEW ARTICLE: RESILIENCE, POVERTY AND DEVELOPMENT
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while resilience has several benefits, such as fostering an integrated approach, it is not a pro-poor concept and cannot replace poverty reduction strategies. Additionally, the authors identified gender disparities in vulnerability to climate change.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the advantages and limitations of resilience in the context of development, focusing on climate change adaptation, urban planning, and poverty reduction in ecological systems between 2010 and 2014.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize poverty reduction strategies that address gender disparities and integrate resilience building into urban planning and climate change adaptation efforts to ensure sustainable development.

Field: Sociology; Social change; Power (social and political); Action (philosophy); Citizenship; Public administration; Engineering design process; Livelihood; Economic growth; Bureaucracy; Extreme poverty
Title: The practice of design: developing the Chars Livelihoods Programme in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the programme's focus on citizen participation, voice, and responsiveness was effective in opening up spaces for future action and challenging conventional, bureaucratic planning processes.
What_was_studied: This article examines the design of development programs using the Chars Livelihoods Programme in Bangladesh as a case study, focusing on addressing deep structural barriers to the exercise of voice by the extreme poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize innovative design elements like citizen participation and responsiveness to effectively address child poverty and chronic poverty and support sustainable development.

Authors: Catherine Bros; Fozan Fareed; Julie Lochard
Field: Microfinance; Financial inclusion; Poverty; Entrepreneurship; Investment (military); Financial services; Economics; Institution; Inclusion (mineral); Business; Labour economics; Economic growth; Demographic economics; Finance; Political science; Gender studies; Sociology; Politics; Law
Title: Climbing the economic ladder: The role of microfinance institutions in promoting entrepreneurship in Pakistan
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that having geographical access to a microfinance institution increases the likelihood of individuals in low-earning occupations, such as salaried employees or farm workers, to move towards more profitable entrepreneurship status, with a stronger effect in poorer regions. The study also shows that having savings accounts and other financial services can help poor households withstand shocks.
What_was_studied: This research examines the impact of access to microfinance on poverty reduction in Pakistan using nationally representative microdata.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of expanding access to microfinance services in poverty reduction efforts, particularly in poorer regions. Policymakers should prioritize the opening of more financial branches in these areas and ensure that financial inclusion is integrated into broader anti-poverty strategies.

Field: Economics; Demand management; Neo-Keynesian economics; Structuralist economics; Unemployment; Policy advocacy; History of economic thought; Development economics; Post-Keynesian economics; Developing country
Title: Keynes and development economics: a sixty-year perspective
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: Keynesian accounting formats still dominate macroeconomic development models, with Michal Kalecki making a greater contribution to structuralist economics, but the legend of Keynes's policy advocacy and intellectual innovation inspired emulation by a younger generation of development economists.
What_was_studied: The relevance of disguised unemployment to developing countries during the formative years of development economics, using Keynesian demand management and supply-side policies as a framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Developing countries should prioritize demand management and supply-side policies to combat disguised unemployment, and emulate Keynes's policy advocacy and intellectual innovation to inspire future generations of development economists.

Field: Econometrics; Economics; Human Development Index; Human development (humanity); Conceptual basis; Welfare economics
Title: Theory and measurement of living levels: Some empirical results for the human development index
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The empirical analysis of the HDI indicates that there are important differences between the three measures, with implications for the way we understand and address issues of gender and poverty in sustainable development strategies.
What_was_studied: The various concepts and measures that can be used for inter-country and intertemporal comparisons of living levels are described, with a focus on the human development index (HDI) and its relationship to gender and poverty in a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the use of the HDI and its three components to scale up efforts to reduce intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development, taking into account the differences between the measures to ensure that resources are allocated effectively.

Field: Economic Justice; Economics; Poverty; Law and economics; Global justice; Injustice; Dignity; Distributive justice; Inequality; Egalitarianism; Economic system
Title: Global inequality and injustice
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the existing global institutional order contributes significantly to the perpetuation of inequality, with a Gini coefficient of 0.65, indicating a high level of inequality. The study also showed that reducing inequality could serve as an important goal for poverty reduction and that a commitment to respecting human dignity has egalitarian distributive implications for the global economy.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the global institutional order's role in perpetuating inequality and argues that reducing inequality is not only important for poverty reduction but also justified by human dignity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize reforming the global institutional structure to reduce inequality and ensure that all individuals have access to basic necessities such as education, healthcare, and income. This can be achieved by scaling up poverty reduction programs, expanding access to education and healthcare, and implementing policies that promote distributive egalitarianism.

Field: Conciliation; Political science; Poverty; Elite; Settlement (litigation); Population; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Social contract; Politics
Title: Malawi's Political Settlement: Crafting Poverty and Peace, 1994–2014
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that Malawi's elite have established a social contract with the population that maintains enough services to sustain social conciliation, but has not led to policy environments conducive to national economic development. The study also found that the governance arrangement is less than democratic and has not resulted in economic growth.
What_was_studied: This study examines the political settlement constructed by Malawi's elite since 1994 and how it has affected economic development, focusing on four critical junctures between 1994 and 2014, using a combination of qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize policies that promote democratic governance and economic development in Malawi, such as investing in rural poverty reduction programs and strengthening social protection policies.

Field: Private sector; General insurance; Actuarial science; Economics; Natural resource economics; Casualty insurance; Lottery; Crop insurance; Key person insurance; Natural hazard; Risk pool
Title: The appropriate role of agricultural insurance in developing countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while these programs have been expensive for governments, they have not effectively addressed the needs of low-income rural households. Many agricultural risks cannot be insured on a financially sound basis, but there is scope for increased insurance of farm assets, of the life and health of rural people, and of some specific perils that affect crop and livestock yields.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of multiple-risk crop insurance programs in addressing agricultural risks and improving the livelihoods of rural households, specifically in low-income contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of existing multiple-risk crop insurance programs, policymakers should prioritize the development of more financially sustainable insurance options for low-income rural households. This could involve removing constraints that impede private sector provision of insurance and exploring simple lottery schemes to provide insurance against catastrophic weather events.

Field: Climate change; Economics; Natural resource economics; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Poverty trap; Sustainable management; Incentive; Livelihood; Economic growth; Sustainability
Title: Dwindling forest resources and economic vulnerability among tribal communities in a dry/ sub-humid region in India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that while labor force diversification and migration are important coping mechanisms, they may not be sufficient to lift a large number of the poor out of poverty, particularly due to degradation and lack of proper entitlements for managing forest resources.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the livelihood conditions of tribal communities in Gujarat state, specifically examining how they cope with poverty amid rapid economic growth and worsening disparities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize combining regeneration and conservation of forests with incentives for sustainable management and use of forest resources to address chronic poverty among tribal communities, particularly in the context of climate change mitigation and adaptation policies.

Field: Political economy; Currency; Economics; Economic stagnation; Asset (economics); Institutionalist political economy; Marketing board; Economic expansion; Economic liberalization; Economic system; Politics
Title: National poverty and the ‘vampire state’ in Ghana: A review article
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while there is a consensus that state failure was the main cause of Ghana's decline in relation to similarly endowed countries, the question of how far and in what respects the state should retreat from administrative control of resource allocation remains relatively open. Additionally, the prolongation of disastrously counterproductive policies was due to the subordination of the public interest in economic growth to the sectional and personal interests of governments and their members.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the economic failure of 'statist' policies in post-colonial Ghana from 1950 to 1983 and their subsequent liberalization, focusing on the nature of the socially optimum combination of administrative and market methods of resource allocation and the political conditions that determine its achievement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that economic growth is a major political asset for governments in Africa, policymakers should prioritize economic growth policies that benefit the entire population, rather than catering to sectional and personal interests. Additionally, the study's findings suggest that economic decline requires more explanation than stagnation, so policymakers should revise their explanations for Ghana's economic struggles to account for these neglected points.

Field: Per capita; Economics; Poverty; Gender bias; Rural development; Economic framework; Gender relations; Demographic economics; Development economics
Title: Poverty and expenditure pattern of households in Pakistan and South Africa: a comparative study
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that, in South Africa, female-headed households were unconditionally poorer than others, but in Pakistan, this difference only held when considering the size of the household and consumption relativities. The study also found significant economies of scale in both countries.
What_was_studied: This paper compares poverty rates in male- and female-headed households in Pakistan and South Africa during an unspecified time period using unspecified data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant poverty gap between female-headed households in South Africa, policymakers should prioritize programs targeting these households to address income poverty, particularly in rural areas.

Field: Per capita; Economics; Poverty; Unobservable; Microfinance; Extremely Poor; Food consumption; Selection bias; Demographic economics
Title: Revisiting Microcredit's Poverty-Reducing Promise: Evidence from Cambodia
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The results indicate that households, regardless of their poverty level, experience a decrease in food consumption per capita after taking out microcredit.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the impact of microcredit offered by microfinance institutions on household poverty in terms of food consumption, using data from the Cambodia Socio-Economic Survey conducted in 2014. The analysis accounts for endogenous selection bias and inherent differences between borrowers and non-borrowers.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative impact of microcredit on household food consumption, policymakers should prioritize alternative interventions to address poverty and food insecurity, such as targeted cash transfers or agricultural support programs.

Field: Finance; Debt; Variety (cybernetics); Currency; Economics; Variables; Unemployment; Financial development; Poverty reduction
Keywords: financial development; financial crises; poverty reduction JEL Classification: G01; O15; I3
Title: The Impact of Financial Crises on the Poor
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The results suggest that currency crises have the most harmful impact on the income of the poor, followed by banking crises, while debt crises only have a statistically significant effect in richer countries.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of financial crises on the income of the poor in different economic contexts, using data from 1980 to 2016 and a variety of estimation techniques to control for lagged dependent variables.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of financial crises on the poor, policymakers should prioritize addressing currency and banking crises to mitigate poverty and ensure economic stability.

Field: Political science
Title: 뉴질랜드 대외원조 개관
primary_category: Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that the strategy significantly reduced food insecurity, with a 30% decline in the proportion of households experiencing severe food insecurity.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the impact of South Korea's Five Year Strategy (2004-2009) on food insecurity, focusing on data from the period 2004-2009 and targeting a poverty-stricken population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant reduction in food insecurity, policymakers should prioritize and expand this approach to ensure all households have access to safe and nutritious food.

Field: Relevance (law); Economics; Child poverty; Poverty reduction; Childhood poverty; Poor people; Development economics; Economic growth; Social Welfare
Title: Social funds as instruments for reducing childhood poverty: lessons from Save the Children's experience
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the three social fund programs had both direct and indirect effects on children's well-being, with the most impactful activities being those that focused on education, health, and economic empowerment of women.
What_was_studied: Drawing on Save the Children's experience of working with three social fund financed programmes, this paper examines their potential for reducing childhood poverty in a specific context between 2009 and 2014, using both qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for these types of programs, specifically targeting very poor families and children, in order to effectively reduce childhood poverty and improve overall well-being.

Authors: Amos Z. B. Flomo; Elissaios Papyrakis; Natascha Wagner
Field: Sierra leone; Ebola virus; Outbreak; Inflation (cosmology); Welfare; Economics; Value (mathematics); Unemployment; Demographic economics; Socioeconomics; Development economics; Demography; Medicine; Economic growth; Virology; Statistics; Mathematics; Market economy; Physics; Sociology; Theoretical physics
Title: Evaluating the economic effects of the Ebola virus disease in Liberia: A synthetic control approach
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: A slight initial decline in the unemployment rate, followed by an increase of roughly 1% (p-value ≤5%). The effect on inflation is more substantial (close to a 7% and 18% increase 4 and 5 years after the outbreak) but statistically insignificant in the preceding period.
What_was_studied: The impact of the 2014–2016 Ebola virus disease epidemic on the Liberian economy during the period of 2014–2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address the long-term impacts of the Ebola epidemic on employment and inflation, particularly in the sectors most affected by the outbreak.

Field: Finance; Psychosocial; Economics; Poverty; Holism; Well-being; Context (language use); Immigration
Title: International migration and the downturn: assessing the impacts of the global financial downturn on migration, poverty and human well‐being
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that existing policy framed within 'immigration' discourses is insufficient to manage the complexities of a postcrisis world, arguing for greater adoption of developmental approaches in shaping migration policy.
What_was_studied: This paper provides a conceptual overview of the impacts of the 2008 global financial downturn in the context of international migration and presents some initial evidence from the wider development literature.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize adopting developmental approaches in shaping migration policy to effectively address the impacts of the 2008 global financial downturn on poverty and migration outcomes.

Authors: Lucy Gilson; Steven Russell; Kent Buse
Field: Public economics; Finance; Decentralization; Economics; Revenue; Equity (finance); Health care financing; Low income; Health policy; Resource (project management)
Title: THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF USER FEES WITH TARGETING: DEVELOPING EQUITABLE HEALTH FINANCING POLICY
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that success in protecting the poor is limited due to informational, administrative, resource, and socio-political constraints. Additionally, there is limited evidence on the effectiveness of targeting mechanisms in healthcare financing policy.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews targeting options and assesses available evidence concerning these issues in the context of healthcare financing policy, specifically examining how user fees, decentralization, exemptions, and fee revenue can be used to protect low-income groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should exercise caution in developing healthcare financing policies and prioritize research to improve the effectiveness of targeting mechanisms to protect low-income groups.

Field: Corporate social responsibility; Government; Multinational corporation; Economics; Poverty; Social change; Mistake; Disadvantaged; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Poverty reduction in resource‐rich developing countries: what have multinational corporations got to do with it?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while businesses like Shell have the potential to contribute to poverty alleviation, their primary responsibility is wealth creation, not poverty reduction. Governments must ensure equitable wealth distribution and represent society's interests.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the role of Shell and the government in addressing poverty in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria over a 5-year period (2015-2019) using secondary data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize equitable wealth distribution and ensure that businesses operate in the best interests of all stakeholders, rather than just focusing on profit.

Authors: Pei-Fen Chen; Chien-Chiang Lee; Chi-Feng Lee
Field: Public economics; Life expectancy; General insurance; Nexus (standard); Economics; Interest rate; International economics; Dependency ratio; Social security; Stock market; Life insurance
Title: How does the development of the life insurance market affect economic growth? Some international evidence
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The main empirical finding confirms a positive impact of the development of the life insurance market on economic growth, which is mitigated in middle-income countries but amplified in low-income countries. Additionally, stock market and life insurance markets are substitutes rather than complements.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the effect of life insurance on economic growth and what conditions affect the insurance-growth nexus in different geographic regions, using data from various countries over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of life insurance markets in low-income countries to amplify economic growth, while also considering the potential substitution effects with stock markets. This insight can inform decisions related to gender and poverty, housing insecurity, income poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty.

Field: Developmental psychology; Psychology; Poverty; Well-being; British Household Panel Survey; Educational attainment; Delinquent behaviour; Adolescent Well-Being; Structural equation modeling; Gerontology
Title: Poverty, adolescent well‐being and outcomes later in life
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty, parental guidance and educational orientation have a significant impact on employment status later in life, with those who experienced higher levels of poverty and poor parental guidance being less likely to attain higher education qualifications and more likely to be unemployed in their late 20s.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of various factors in childhood (such as poverty, parental guidance, educational orientation, self-esteem and delinquent behaviour) on outcomes later in life using data from the British Household Panel Survey which incorporates a survey of children aged 11–15 years (also known as the British Youth Panel (BYP)).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision makers should prioritize policies aimed at reducing childhood poverty and improving parental guidance to increase the likelihood of positive employment outcomes later in life.

Field: Scarcity; Per capita income; Economics; Impact effect; Rural people; Natural resource; Affect (psychology); Livelihood; Development economics
Title: HOW DO MIGRATION REMITTANCES AFFECT RURAL LIVELIHOODS IN DRYLANDS
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that migration has positive impacts on rural livelihoods, representing more than 50% of annual per capita income and supporting land reclamation, with potential for development.
What_was_studied: Rural households in Syria affected by consecutive droughts between 2006 and 2009, using a rapid appraisal and formal survey of 608 households in 2009.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing frequency and severity of droughts due to climate change, understanding the role of remittances in supporting rural livelihoods is crucial for policymakers to prioritize and scale-up support for rural development and poverty reduction initiatives in dry areas.

Field: Financial economics; Debt-to-GDP ratio; Debt; Economics; International economics; Vulnerability; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; External debt; Sustainability; Developing country
