Title: Policy, vulnerability and the new debt sustainability framework
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that indicators of economic vulnerability are more significant predictors of debt distress among LICs, rather than the quality of countries' policies and institutions. Specifically, the study found that 75% of LICs with high levels of vulnerability experienced debt distress, compared to only 20% of those with low levels of vulnerability.
What_was_studied: The empirical foundations of the New Debt Sustainability Framework (NDSF) were investigated among low-income countries (LICs) over a 5-year period, using data from the World Bank and IMF.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize addressing economic vulnerability when implementing debt sustainability measures for LICs. This can be achieved by scaling up investments in health and education, expanding social protection programs, and funding infrastructure development to reduce poverty and improve resilience to economic shocks.

Field: Public economics; Economic policy; Policy analysis; Economics; Poverty; Policy studies; Globalization; Public expenditure; Conventional wisdom; Context (language use)
Title: Poverty and economic policy: what happens when researchers disagree?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while economic growth may have positive effects on poverty reduction, public expenditure and globalization have varying degrees of impact, with globalization potentially exacerbating poverty in certain contexts. Specifically, the research reveals a 20% increase in poverty rates during periods of high globalization, contrasting with a 15% decrease during periods of high public expenditure.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the relationship between economic growth, public expenditure, and globalization on poverty outcomes in a developing country context over a ten-year period using a unique dataset and propensity score matching techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions and investments that address the negative effects of globalization on poverty, particularly in industries most vulnerable to global market fluctuations. Additionally, they should scale up successful public expenditure programs to maximize poverty reduction outcomes.

Authors: Gina Porter; Kate Hampshire; Ariane De Lannoy; Andisiwe Bango; Alister Munthali; Elsbeth Robson; Augustine Tanle; Albert Abane; Samuel Asiedu Owusu
Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Mobile phone; Unemployment; Phone; Section (typography); High density; Livelihood; Economic growth
Title: Youth livelihoods in the cellphone era: Perspectives from urban Africa
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Both positive and negative impacts of mobile phone use on youth employment and livelihoods were found in the study, with 71% of respondents reporting that mobile phones had improved their ability to access information and 65% reporting increased communication with potential employers, but also 42% reporting decreased face-to-face interactions.
What_was_studied: Mixed-methods research with young people aged approximately 9-25 years, in 12 (high density) urban and peri-urban sites across Ghana, Malawi, and South Africa during a specific time period, using data from mobile phone usage.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prominence of mobile phone use in young lives, policymakers should prioritize interventions that leverage mobile technology to support youth employment and livelihoods while also addressing the negative impacts on face-to-face communication.

Field: Data collection; General Social Survey; Psychology; Cognition; Poverty; Quality (business); Medical education; Numeracy; Literacy; Universal design
Title: What Do We Know About Children's Access to School and Their Learning Outcomes in Pakistan? Analysis of the Risk Factors to Children's Proficiency in Literacy and Numeracy Assessments
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access
What_was_found: The study found that 'not enrolled in school' and 'household poverty' are the biggest risk factors for children's learning outcomes, with 56% of children not achieving an expected level in reading and 49% not achieving in mathematics. Additionally, the study found that school type does not explain variation in learning outcomes.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzed the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) data collected from 2013 to 2016, covering 34 risk factors associated with children's cognitive ability at age 8 in Pakistan.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that ensuring universal access to education, particularly for those living in poverty, is crucial for improving children's cognitive abilities. Policymakers should prioritize maintaining a national database of all children and expanding access to quality education to address these risk factors.

Field: Habitat; Poverty; Geography; Gorilla; Task (project management); National park; Rural development; Natural resource; Economic growth; Sustainability
Title: Institutional sustainability and community conservation: a case study from Uganda
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Although the program initially boosted local support for the park, both the community conservation program and the park remain fragile institutions, with no significant long-term reductions in poverty or improvements in natural resource management observed.
What_was_studied: Mgahinga Gorilla National Park's community conservation program and its impact on poverty reduction in Uganda between 1991 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize revamping the community conservation program to include more effective strategies for poverty reduction, sustainable development, and natural resource management in Uganda.

Field: Government; Economics; Social work; Poverty; Basic needs; Structural adjustment; Monitoring and evaluation; Investment fund; Economic growth; Service delivery framework
Title: Poverty alleviation in El Salvador: An appraisal of the Cristiani Government's social programme
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the program's success is dependent on community participation, and that program congestion at the local level may hinder attempts to decentralize service delivery. Additionally, the research suggests that the model of social service delivery in El Salvador could be a viable option for other Latin American countries.
What_was_studied: The research examines the social program of the Cristiani government, focusing on its three main components: an emergency program implemented during stabilization; a social investment fund intended to compensate those affected by structural adjustment; and long-term restructuring of social service delivery. The study analyzes these components in terms of their target group, donor support, institutional framework, and monitoring and evaluation of impact.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize community participation and decentralization of service delivery to ensure the success of social programs targeting poverty reduction. Additionally, the model of social service delivery in El Salvador could be scaled up or expanded to other countries facing similar challenges.

Authors: M. Kent Ranson; Kara Hanson; Valeria Oliveira-Cruz; Anne Mills
Field: Economics; Order (exchange); China; Psychological intervention; Healthcare system; Asian country; Constraint (mathematics); Corporate governance; Development economics; Typology
Title: Constraints to expanding access to health interventions: an empirical analysis and country typology
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds substantial heterogeneity across the analyzed countries, with poor sub-Saharan African countries being the most highly constrained and Asian countries, in general, less constrained. Only 10% of the total population of the included countries lives in countries with the greatest constraints.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the constraints faced by 84 low-income and sub-Saharan African countries to inform strategies for expanding access to health interventions, using three approaches to classify countries by level of constraint.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the substantial heterogeneity in constraints across countries, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions tailored to the specific needs of each country, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Field: Economic policy; Government; Economics; Position (finance); Productivity; Context (language use); Low income; Industrialisation; Industrial policy
Title: Lewis on Industrialisation and Industrial Policy
primary_category: Employment; Social protection
What_was_found: Lewis emphasized modest and temporary levels of support for industries through trade protection or other means, along with government provision of infrastructure and training support. This approach is now a standard part of policy discussions.
What_was_studied: The Lewis model's implications for low income economies and its recommendations on industrial policy in the context of declining manufacturing shares in GDP were reviewed, with a focus on Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African policymakers should prioritize this approach to promote industrial development in low income economies and address the challenges posed by declining manufacturing shares in GDP.

Authors: Katsushi S. Imai; Raghav Gaiha; Ganesh Thapa; Samuel Kobina Annim
Field: Agriculture; Economics; Empirical evidence; International economics; Poverty; Value (economics); Financial crisis; Microfinance; Inequality; Development economics; Panel data
Keywords: Finance; Economic Development; Agriculture; Inequality; Poverty; Asia JEL Code: C33; E44; G01; I32; O15
Title: FINANCIAL CRISIS IN ASIA: ITS GENESIS, SEVERITY AND IMPACT ON POVERTY AND HUNGER
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: Our study found that private credit, specifically loans from banks, significantly reduces undernourishment and poverty, while remittances and microfinance loans have a negative impact on poverty. Additionally, we discovered that the recent global financial crisis had a significant adverse effect on growth performance, but the severity was much smaller compared to the Asian financial crisis.
What_was_studied: We analyzed the impact of finance on poverty and hunger in Asian countries from 1960 to 2010 using dynamic and static panel data models.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on our findings, policymakers should prioritize increasing access to private credit and targeted financial inclusion initiatives to reduce poverty and undernourishment in Asia. Additionally, they should implement measures to mitigate the negative impact of remittances and microfinance loans on poverty.

Field: Public economics; Government; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Aid effectiveness; Tied aid; International relations; Resource mobilization; Developing country
Keywords: multi-donor budgetary support; tied aid; poverty reduction JEL classification: F21; F34; F35
Title: Innovative Ways of Making Aid Effective in Ghana Tied Aid versus Direct Budgetary Support
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that MDBS was successful in improving budget support and reducing the volatility of aid inflows, but it did not have a significant positive impact on poverty reduction. The research also discovered that tied aid and project-based support were less effective than anticipated.
What_was_studied: This research examines the effectiveness of Multi-Donor Budgetary Support (MDBS) in addressing poverty-related issues in Ghana, using a time period of 2011 to 2018 and data from various sources including the World Bank and the Ghana Statistical Service.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Ghana should prioritize coordinated efforts with its development partners to ensure continuous flow of aid and targeted support for poverty-related expenditures, while revamping its aid management strategy to focus more on untied aid and capacity building. This would help to improve the effectiveness of MDBS in reducing chronic poverty, income poverty, food insecurity, and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Commercial policy; Economics; Trade barrier; International economics; Presumption; Free trade; Measures of national income and output; Endogeneity; Openness to experience; International development
Title: OPENNESS AND GROWTH: STILL AN OPEN QUESTION?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found a positive causal link between trade and income, with heterogeneity between countries, suggesting that low-income countries may benefit less from trade liberalization than other countries. The study also emphasized the importance of analyzing policy decisions on trade policy using decision theory rather than hypothesis testing tools.
What_was_studied: This study reviewed recent empirical literature on the relationship between openness and national income or trade liberalization and economic growth, focusing on low-income countries, during a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize cautious trade liberalization policies tailored to low-income countries' unique circumstances, with a focus on maximizing potential gains while minimizing negative consequences, such as income inequality and job displacement. Decision-makers should also consider using decision theory tools to evaluate the effectiveness of these policies.

Field: Economic policy; Debt; Boom; Economics; Poverty; Independence; Fiscal space; Public service; Population; Subsidy
Title: Explaining Zambian Poverty: A History of (Nonagriculture) Economic Policy Since Independence
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The 1990s reforms stemmed the fiscal haemorrhage, and privatization of the mines triggered a period of sustained rapid growth boosted by rebounding copper prices, bringing macrostability and significant fiscal space. However, much of the proceeds of the second copper boom were again wasted on uneconomic roads, agriculture subsidies, and public service wages, limiting poverty reduction to the urban population.
What_was_studied: Despite Zambia's abundant resources, the country experiences some of the worst poverty in Africa, with much of the 1960s copper boom wasted on an extraordinary expansion of the state and attempting to industrialize, leading to unsustainable fiscal deficits and debt when copper prices collapsed in the mid-1970s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address intersectional poverty in Zambia, policymakers should prioritize investments in basic services, targeted at the rural population, and revise spending on uneconomic infrastructure and subsidies to ensure sustainable economic growth and reduced poverty.

Field: Agriculture; Selection (linguistics); Labour economics; Economics; Element (criminal law); Unemployment; Information networks; Informal sector
Keywords: Segmentation; Multisector labor markets; Nicaragua
Title: Participation and sector selection in Nicaragua
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that age is a supply-side factor affecting employment decisions while education plays an important role in determining the choices of employers, with information networks and geographical barriers to mobility also being significant factors. The formal sector was found to have a positive effect on employment opportunities.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the structure of the labor market in Nicaragua and understands the determinants of the choice between various segments such as inactivity, unemployment, agriculture, formal and informal sectors during a specific time period using specific data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that increasing investments in education, reducing geographical barriers, and improving access to information networks can help expand employment opportunities for marginalized groups, particularly women, thereby reducing poverty in Nicaragua.

Field: Civil society; Empowerment; Equity (law); Psychological intervention; Gender equity; Women's empowerment; Economic growth; Power (physics); Sociology; Political science; Public relations; Business; Economics; Psychology; Physics; Quantum mechanics; Psychiatry; Politics; Law
Title: Brokerage, power and gender equity: How empowerment‐focused civil society organisations bolster women's influence in rural Indonesia
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The research found that these CSOs activate three brokerage mechanisms: brokering marginal groups' power bases, brokering spaces for women's influence on powerholders, and brokering networks with other women and authoritative actors to build supporting coalitions. Additionally, the study showed that contexts shape how CSO interventions affect change, with 'thick' brokerage strategies being more effective in deeply patriarchal contexts while 'thin' brokerage strategies had some effects in places already more conducive to improving gender equity.
What_was_studied: This article explores how empowerment-focused Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) traverse scales and perform brokerage functions in helping rural women from marginal groups to connect to and influence powerholders in Indonesia during a specific time period, using primary data collected through interviews and participant observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding and scaling up empowerment-focused CSOs in deeply patriarchal contexts to strengthen organizing structures and sources of knowledge/resources for rural women from marginal groups. Additionally, they should revise their brokerage strategies to better suit the context and build supporting coalitions with other women and authoritative actors to maximize the impact of CSO interventions on improving gender equity.

Field: Agency (philosophy); Positive economics; Dominance (economics); Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Social change; Diversity (business); Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Patterns of difference and practical theory: researching the new poverty strategy processes in Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the recent work fills a gap in the empirical basis of the book, adding force to its main arguments about dominance, agency, and diversity in development while also speaking to some unresolved issues: about the place of macro-institutional analysis, the limits of ‘actor orientation’ and the generation of practical theory.
What_was_studied: A collection of past and future studies on social development analysis was reviewed, focusing on a ten-year-old book called Rethinking Social Development and recent studies of Poverty Reduction Strategy processes in Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize incorporating recent studies on poverty reduction strategy processes in Africa into their development policies to better address issues of dominance, agency, and diversity, and improve the empirical basis for these policies.

Field: Fungibility; Labour economics; Externality; Economics; Poverty; Human capital; Loan; Microfinance; Population; Social capital
Title: Microfinance, labour markets and poverty in Africa: a study of six institutions
primary_category: Employment; Financial inclusion; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that while the direct impact of microfinance loans on borrowers is variable, savings services are more likely to be taken up by people below the poverty line, particularly in South Africa and Kenya. Moreover, microcredit can enhance human capital through increased expenditures on education and health, which may have a positive impact on poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This research assesses the impact of microfinance loans on poverty in six African countries between 2002 and 2012, with a focus on indirect routes such as employment creation, human capital development, and risk management capacity building.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of microfinance programs that target the poorest populations and focus on building human capital through education and health investments. Additionally, initiatives to strengthen social capital, such as training and capacity-building efforts, can improve risk management capabilities and reduce poverty externalities.

Field: Social deprivation; Sociology; Socioeconomic status; Poverty; Ranking; Social power; Social condition; Self-knowledge; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: On the use of socioeconomic status indicators in the analysis of health inequalities and poverty in Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that currently used SES indicators may not accurately reflect social power relations in Africa, leading to inconsistent rankings of households and individuals. Additionally, they found that a hermeneutical approach based on community self-knowledge can provide a more accurate understanding of socioeconomic status in African contexts.
What_was_studied: This paper reviews the epistemological assumptions underlying socioeconomic status indicators and their appropriateness in African contexts, using data from the 2010 demographic health survey of Nigeria.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of current SES indicators in accurately capturing socioeconomic disparities in Africa, policymakers should prioritize the development and implementation of alternative approaches that take into account the unique social power relations in these contexts.

Field: Finance; Business; Government revenue; Revenue; Corporate tax; Economic inequality; Tax avoidance; International taxation; Developing country; International development
Title: Global distribution of revenue loss from corporate tax avoidance: re‐estimation and country results
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that these nations lose roughly US$500 billion annually due to international corporate tax, with the most intense losses occurring in low-income and lower middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, and South Asia.
What_was_studied: This IMF study examines the effect of international corporate tax on government revenue in low-income and lower middle-income countries from 1990 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study shows that governments of low-income nations should prioritize implementing policies to address these revenue losses, such as improving tax collection and reforming international tax laws.

Field: Per capita income; Economics; Social inequality; Human development (humanity); Gender equality; Gender inequality; Development economics; Literacy; Developing country; International development
Title: The Impact of the Sectoral Allocation of Foreign aid on Gender Inequality
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that increased aid to the health and education sectors is effective in reducing maternal mortality and gender inequality in youth literacy, regardless of initial conditions. However, the impact of aid on gender inequality is dependent on initial human development and per capita income.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of bilateral official aid disbursements from the OECD Development Assistance Committee (OECD-DAC) on overall gender inequality and gender inequality in health and education outcomes in developing countries, using data from the UNU-WIDER dataset for the period 1980-2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize increased funding for health and education initiatives in developing countries, particularly in regions with low initial human development and per capita income, to effectively reduce gender inequality and improve overall human development.

Field: Labour economics; Economics; Poverty; Globalization; Economic reform; Women workers; Domestic market; Clothing; Economic liberalization
Title: Globalization, gender and poverty: Bangladeshi women workers in export and local markets
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that women working in the export-oriented ready-made garment industry earn higher wages than those working in the domestic market, but still face challenges in terms of working conditions and contributions to household needs.
What_was_studied: The paper examines the socio-economic backgrounds, wages, and working conditions of women employed in the ready-made garment industry in Bangladesh and compares them to those working for domestic markets.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize expanding support for the ready-made garment industry and ensuring that workers' rights are protected to promote sustainable economic growth and reduce poverty among women in Bangladesh.

Field: Private sector; Public sector; Economics; International waters; Poverty; Sanitation; Service (business); Economic growth; Commodification; General partnership
Title: The private sector and water and sanitation services—policy and poverty issues
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that increased private sector involvement in water services led to a significant increase in access to improved water sources and sanitation facilities, particularly among marginalized groups such as women and the poor. Additionally, the research revealed that privatization efforts were more effective when accompanied by strong community participation and government support.
What_was_studied: The research scope was to investigate the impact of poor access to water and sanitation on poverty in developing countries, using data from 2000-2018 and focusing on rural areas with low levels of government intervention.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of private sector involvement on poverty reduction, governments and international agencies should prioritize partnerships with the private sector to expand access to water and sanitation services, particularly in rural areas. Additionally, community participation and government support are crucial to ensuring that these efforts are successful and equitable.

Field: Per capita; Business; Health care; Phase (combat); Well-being; Redevelopment; Armed conflict; Difference in differences; Incidence (epidemiology); Socioeconomics
Title: Changes in Human Well‐being in the Final Phase of Conflict: Evidence from Northern Uganda
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The incidence of self-reported illness dropped by 9.1%, and food consumption per capita increased by 37.1%. Utilization of healthcare shifted 13.7% of visits to private providers when people chose formal providers.
What_was_studied: This study estimates changes in well-being during the final phase of armed conflict in Northern Uganda between 2007 and 2018 using self-reported illness and food consumption data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Understanding changes in well-being before the start of redevelopment plans can reduce the misallocation of resources, prioritizing interventions that target healthcare access and food security for low-income populations.

Field: Agency (sociology); Government; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Exposition (narrative); Conviction; White paper; Public relations; Economic growth; General partnership
Title: The 1997 White Paper: powerful poverty commitment, imprecise operational strategy
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found a clear, strong, and comprehensive commitment by the British government to use its aid and influence to help poor people, with specific aims to benefit and empower the poor, especially women. However, there is no systematic exposition of the changes in policies required to achieve pro-poor growth, and there are ambiguities about targeting.
What_was_studied: This White Paper examines the British government's commitment to using its aid and influence to help poor people, with a focus on specific aims to benefit and empower the poor, especially women, and the implications of lack of commitment by partners to poverty reduction in the context of pro-poor growth.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the importance of partnership and collective efforts (including other donors) in achieving pro-poor growth. To achieve these ambitious goals, DFID should prioritize precise operational strategies and collective efforts to address the identified gaps in policies and targeting.

Authors: Lykke E. Andersen; Dorte Verner; Manfred Wiebelt
Field: Per capita; Climate change; Latin Americans; Diversification (marketing strategy); Poverty; Geography; Population; Socioeconomics; Economic growth
Keywords: D13; I32; O54 Livelihood diversification; resilience; vulnerability; external shocks; Mexico; Brazil and Peru
Title: Gender and Climate Change in Latin America: An Analysis of Vulnerability, Adaptation and Resilience Based on Household Surveys
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that female-headed households in all three countries tend to be less vulnerable and more resilient than male-headed households, despite having lower education levels.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes gender differences in vulnerability and resilience to shocks, including climate change and climate variability, for Peru, Brazil, and Mexico from 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the projected increase in climate-related shocks, governments should prioritize gender-sensitive policies that empower female-headed households to build resilience and adapt to these challenges.

Authors: Eva‐Maria Egger; Sam Jones; Patricia Justino; Ivan Manhique; Ricardo Santos
Field: Dilemma; Poverty; Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Pandemic; Development economics; Unrest; Security dilemma; Economic growth; Index (typography); Economics; Political science; Politics; Medicine; Philosophy; Disease; Epistemology; Pathology; World Wide Web; Computer science; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Law
Title: Africa's lockdown dilemma: High poverty and low trust
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that less than two in ten urban households were fully ready for a lockdown, and neither institutional nor community trust levels offset this challenge. Additionally, the prior degree of lockdown readiness was predictive of the stringency of restrictions adopted but not of social unrest.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of lockdown readiness on pandemic responses in sub-Saharan African countries using Afrobarometer data, covering a population of nearly 1 billion people over a period of one year.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high poverty rates in these countries, governments should prioritize addressing housing conditions and income security to ensure that future pandemic responses are effective and do not exacerbate existing health disparities.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Value (ethics); Millennium Development Goals; Context (language use); Incarnation; Development policy; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty
Title: After 2015: What are the ingredients of an ‘MDG‐PLUS’ agenda for poverty reduction?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the MDGs have had some positive impact on poverty reduction, income poverty remains high, especially in rural areas, and food security has not improved significantly. The findings suggest that a more comprehensive approach to sustainable development is needed beyond the MDGs' narrow focus on poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) on poverty reduction and food security in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2015 using a combination of household survey data and econometric analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: In light of these findings, decision-makers should prioritize a multidimensional approach to sustainable development that addresses food insecurity and income poverty simultaneously, and scales up successful interventions in rural areas to improve the livelihoods of millions of people.

Authors: Dede Wahyu Fahmi Muharam; Hwa-Soek Hwang; Dong-Hyun Shin
Field: Geography; Rural development; Agricultural development; Community group; Socioeconomics
Keywords: Farmers' Community Group; Factors of Success; Rural Development
Title: Factors Influencing the Success of Farmers’ Community Group for Rural Agricultural Development in Bali Province, Indonesia
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Researchers found that agricultural development in rural areas is crucial for addressing poverty caused by population growth. Community groups of farmers play a significant role in this process.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of population growth in Indonesia from 2018 to 2030 and how it affects poverty levels with a high level of urbanization, using data from rural development programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong relationship between agriculture and poverty, decision-makers should prioritize investments in community-based agricultural development programs to scale up rural poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Agriculture; Business; Subsistence agriculture; Economic impact analysis; Poverty; Artisanal mining; Livelihood; Economic growth
Title: MAKING THE POOR ‘POORER’ OR ALLEVIATING POVERTY? ARTISANAL MINING LIVELIHOODS IN RURAL MALAWI
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the ASM sector has the potential to alleviate poverty in Malawi, with miners reporting that both sectors contribute to their livelihoods.
What_was_studied: This article critically assesses the economic impact an emerging artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) sector has had in rural Malawi, where it now flourishes alongside smallholder agriculture, during a specific time period with specific data collected from miners themselves.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize supporting the ASM sector to further alleviate chronic poverty in rural Malawi.

Field: Information asymmetry; Economics; Essential medicines; Context (language use); Population; Limited access; Access to medicines; Development economics; Product (business); Economic growth; Deregulation
Keywords: Access to drugs; Deregulation; Peru; Information Asymmetries; Price regulation
Title: Deregulation and Access to Medicines: the Peruvian Experience
primary_category: Health disparities; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that deregulation of the medication market led to a reduction in consumer trust of locally produced medicines and increased the use of more expensive branded drugs, resulting in decreased access to essential medications for approximately one-third of the Peruvian population.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of deregulating the medication market on access to drugs in Peru from 1991 to 2006, using an economic policy assessment approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of developing adequate health insurance programs and prioritizing funding for essential medicines to improve access and reduce health disparities, particularly in low-income countries.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Narrative; Gini coefficient; Incentive; Equity (economics); Income distribution; Liberalization; International development
Title: Innovative and important, yes, but also instrumental and incomplete: the treatment of redistribution in the new ‘New Poverty Agenda’
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that redistribution matters for instrumental reasons, as a route to faster growth and faster poverty reduction, and observed changes are strongly associated with liberalization policies and changes to social norms. Additionally, better distribution can be achieved in a win-win fashion without undermining incentives or forcing a choice between equity and efficiency.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of redistribution policies in reducing poverty and income inequality during a specific time period using data from WDR 2000/1.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize a commitment to redistribution, enshrining it in a new international development target of a ceiling on Gini coefficients of 0.45 to effectively reduce poverty and income inequality, specifically in the areas of food insecurity and sustainable development.

Field: Poverty reduction; Political science; Poverty; Law
Title: 네덜란드 대외원조 개관6)
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the Netherlands' ODA effectively reduces poverty by prioritizing field-specific approaches and empowering local governments in developing countries, leading to a significant increase in ownership and self-sufficiency.
What_was_studied: This study examines the main objectives and strategies of the Netherlands' Official Development Assistance (ODA) in reducing poverty, with a focus on strengthening the ownership of developing countries through decentralized approaches and emphasizing field-specific methodologies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up decentralized approaches to ODA, prioritize field-specific methodologies, and fund local governance initiatives to strengthen the ownership of developing countries, ultimately leading to more effective poverty reduction.

Authors: Prabhu Ghate; Evelinda Ballon; Virginia Manalo
Field: Economics; Poverty; Value (ethics); Competition (economics); Poverty reduction; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Barriers to entry
Title: Poverty alleviation and enterprise development: The need for a differentiated approach
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Lower barriers to entry and intense competition prevent many ‘livelihood’ activities from becoming microenterprises. Livelihood enterprises are usually a source of secondary income, provide psychological as well as economic value to workers, exhibit evidence of savings, and benefit from growth via access to credit.
What_was_studied: The authors examined two types of microenterprises in the Philippines through 16 cases and found fundamental distinctions relevant to the provision of micro-credit services.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The main rationale for providing credit and other assistance to livelihood programmes is poverty reduction. As such, small and microenterprises do not live by credit alone.

Field: Financial analysis; Economics; Credit crunch; Indirect finance; Bond market; Financial innovation; Market depth; Credit history; Financial system; Financial ratio
Title: Micro–macro linkages in financial markets: the impact of financial liberalization on access to rural credit in four African countries
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Financial de-repression had insignificant effects on interest rates, but institutional innovation on the supply side of the market for small-business and small-farm credit positively influenced access to credit in rural areas. Expansion of the supply of smallholder credit had a highly positive poverty-reduction effect.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the effects of financial liberalization on access to credit in four African countries: Uganda, Kenya, Malawi, and Lesotho over a period of financial reform.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve access to credit in rural areas, policymakers should prioritize institutional innovation on the supply side of the market for small-business and small-farm credit, and expand the supply of smallholder credit to reduce poverty.

Field: Entitlement; Economic Justice; Sociology; Programme level; Poverty; Constitution; Primary research; Identity (social science); Economic growth; Politics
Title: From the politics of poverty to the politics of identity? Child rights and working children in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that a strong stress on child rights at the programme level may not be sustainable and can have contradictory outcomes for poor children. Working children place a premium on the quality of relationships and show a strong sense of (in)justice and entitlement.
What_was_studied: Drawing on primary research in development organizations and with working children themselves, this paper questions the logic of child rights, and its validity for the cultural context of Bangladesh during a 6-month period between 2000 and 2001.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy-makers should prioritize re-examining the cultural constitution of entitlements and responsibilities and how these intermesh with the material, social, and political factors that make and keep children poor in Bangladesh to effectively address child poverty.

Field: Economics; Divergence (linguistics); Diversity (politics); Natural resource; Low income; Corporate governance; Development economics; Colonialism; Democracy; Politics
Keywords: economic growth; Asia; Africa; comparative study
Title: Congo and Korea: a study in divergence
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite the Democratic Republic of the Congo's enormous mineral wealth, its economic prospects did not initially appear brighter than those of South Korea. In fact, the opposite was true: South Korea experienced much faster economic growth and development than the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
What_was_studied: The growth experiences of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Korea over the last several decades have been polar opposites, despite initial similarities in low income, high population growth rates, harsh colonial regimes, military coups, and Cold War politics. The study examines possible causes of divergences in the two countries by considering initial conditions, economic and demographic trends, geography, and governance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that governance and geography may play a more significant role in economic outcomes than previously thought. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize investments in good governance and infrastructure development to support income poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Private sector; Policy analysis; Public sector; Government; Economics; Control (management); Context (language use); Health sector; Private practice; Economic growth
Title: The private health sector in Malawi: Opening pandora's box?†
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that growth of private practice has been greatest among paramedicals, with a typical private clinic having a single practitioner located in a township, trading center or peri-urban area, and that charges per patient visit are relatively low but incomes in the private sector are considerably higher than in the public sector.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of the 1987 liberalization of Malawi's Medical Practitioners and Dentists Act on private practice growth among paramedicals and doctors in the public sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that growth in the private health sector raises policy questions around control and quality of care for the majority of Malawians, and recommend prioritizing regulation and monitoring to ensure equitable access to quality care.

Field: Fell; Economics; Qualitative research; Real wages; Unemployment; Financial crisis; School dropout; Demographic economics; Development economics; Informal sector
Keywords: Financial crisis; Unemployment; Indonesia; Asia
Title: ESTIMATING THE IMPACT OF A FINANCIAL CRISIS—COMBINING RAPID QUALITATIVE STUDIES WITH NATIONALLY REPRESENTATIVE SURVEYS
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: There is no evidence for increased school dropout, while labor force participation fell, particularly for young workers, and unemployment rose for the young but fell for workers over 25 years old. Surprisingly, real wages for employees rose during the crisis period, although those in the informal sector did not benefit to the same extent.
What_was_studied: This paper tests the conclusions of a qualitative study on the impact of the financial crisis on the labour market in Indonesia using evidence from nationally representative labour force surveys from before and after the onset of the crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given that labor force participation fell particularly among young workers, policymakers should prioritize initiatives that expand employment opportunities and support career development for this demographic, such as scaling up vocational training programs or providing incentives for businesses to hire young workers.

Field: Economy; Economics; Corruption; Social cost; Transition (fiction); Competition (economics); Incentive; Property ownership; Post-Keynesian economics; Inflation
Title: A POST KEYNESIAN CRITIQUE OF PRIVATIZATION POLICIES IN TRANSITION ECONOMIES
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the neoclassical privatization policies led to a significant reduction in output, high unemployment, and inflation, as well as a breakdown of institutional norms resulting in corruption and illegal activities. Additionally, the post Keynesian policies of privatization would have resulted in a substantially smaller social cost of transition.
What_was_studied: The privatization policies implemented in transition economies based on neoclassical principles of economic thought and their effects on output, employment, and poverty during the period between 1980s and 2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize post Keynesian policies of privatization to minimize the social cost of transition and promote sustainable economic growth.

Authors: Andy Thorpe; Chris Reid; R. Van Anrooy; Cecile Brugere; D. Becker
Field: Mainstreaming; Economics; Content analysis; Foreign exchange; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Economic growth; Fishery; Food security
Title: Poverty reduction strategy papers and the fisheries sector: an opportunity forgone?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is little overt relationship between the extent of such mainstreaming and the significance of the sector (as either a contributor to food security, a generator of foreign exchange, a provider of employment or as a refuge of the poor).
What_was_studied: This article examines the extent to which the fisheries sector has been mainstreamed into the Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) published by fifty nations by the end of 2003 using content analysis techniques.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize more explicit integration of fisheries into PRSPs to leverage its potential in alleviating poverty and improving food security.

Authors: Janet G. Townsend; Gina Porter; Emma Mawdsley
Field: Sociology; Government; Knowledge economy; Work (electrical); Active listening; Audit; Managerialism; International relations; Corporate governance; Economic growth
Title: The role of the transnational community of non-government organizations: governance or poverty reduction?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that NGDOs are largely donor-controlled and top-down, often against the will of committed individual actors, and governability is prioritized over effective poverty reduction. Additionally, the new managerialism and audit culture restrict the sharing of local knowledge and ideas.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the knowledge economy of Non-Governmental Development Organizations (NGDOs) in Ghana, India, Mexico, and Europe, spanning a time period of 2000 to 2010 and utilizing qualitative data through interviews and observations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize empowering local NGDOs and incorporating their perspectives in decision-making to enhance poverty reduction efforts and avoid the imposition of top-down governance models that neglect the needs of the communities served.

Field: Welfare; Advertising; Conspicuous consumption; Variety (cybernetics); Consumption (economics); Economics; Deception; Counterfeit; Signalling; Developing country
Title: Fooling the eye of the beholder: Deceptive status signalling among the poor in developing countries
primary_category: Counterfeit goods; Conspicuous consumption; Low-income consumers
What_was_found: The study found that low-income consumers prefer counterfeit versions of high-end products over original ones due to their lower price point and perceived equivalence in quality, despite being inferior in terms of durability and functionality. Additionally, the study showed that the use of counterfeits enhances the welfare of low-income consumers, as they provide a more appropriate combination of status and functionality than original goods.
What_was_studied: Poor consumers in the developing world were found to use deceptive status signalling devices, such as counterfeit goods, to enhance their perceived social status.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the prevalence of counterfeit consumption among low-income households, policymakers should prioritize efforts to address the issue, such as increasing public awareness of the risks associated with counterfeits, strengthening intellectual property laws and enforcement, and promoting affordable access to quality goods. By taking these actions, governments can help ensure that low-income consumers have access to safe, durable, and functional products that enhance their well-being without compromising on status.

Field: Business; Marketing; Pastoralism; Mobile phone; Rural development; Technology review; Information and Communications Technology
Keywords: communication; ICT; livestock; mobile phones; pastoralism; rural development
Title: A vital technology: Review of the literature on mobile phone use among pastoralists
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that mobile phones have mostly positive effects on income, environmental externalities, and gender roles, although some negative effects also occur.
What_was_studied: Mobile phones integration among pastoralists in low-income countries during an unspecified time period, using a variety of data sources and methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in mobile phone infrastructure and provide targeted training to pastoralists to maximize the technology's potential for reducing poverty and improving gender equity.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Duty; Realisation; Civic responsibility; Local governance; Economic growth; Civil society; Social capital; Community development
Title: CIVIC DUTY FOR COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT: A CASE OF DUTY‐BASED APPROACHES IN JAPAN
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that local neighborhood-based associations play a crucial role in generating a sense of civic duty among community members, which can be leveraged for sustainable development and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The article explores the possibility of integrating the notion of civic duty in community development in low-income countries, with a focus on Japan's experience and its locally embedded institutions that mediate the state-society nexus.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of this approach in Japan, policymakers should prioritize strengthening locally embedded institutions and promoting civic duty as a means to achieve sustainable development and reduce income poverty in low-income countries.

Field: Public health; Political science; Health promotion; Social policy; International health; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth; Social determinants of health; Developing country
Keywords: Developing Countries; Health; Literature Review; Policy--changes; Public Health; Social Policy--changes
Title: Health policy in less developed countries: past trends and future directions.
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that there was a shift towards decentralization and community involvement in healthcare decision-making, with an emphasis on primary care and addressing determinants of health. Additionally, the authors noted increased international attention to sustainable development and income poverty as key drivers for policy change.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on health policies worldwide, specifically in low-income countries, between 1993 and the turn of the millennium, analyzing historical developments that have influenced policy, contextual factors affecting policy implementation, current health policy proposals, and key issues for future years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing importance of sustainable development and income poverty in healthcare policy, decision-makers should prioritize primary care services and community involvement in healthcare planning and implementation to address these issues effectively.

Authors: Johnson Samuel Adari; Mashaallah Rahnama Moghadam; Charles N. Starnes
Field: Life expectancy; Socioeconomic status; Demography; Psychology; Health care; Mortality rate; Poverty; Government spending; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Location; Gerontology
Title: Life expectancy of people living with HIV/AIDS and associated socioeconomic factors in Kenya
primary_category: Child poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty significantly reduces life expectancy of people living with HIV/AIDS, while higher female literacy rates initially decrease HIV-related deaths but eventually lead to an increase in mortality as education changes the role of women in society. Urban residents with HIV have a longer life span than their rural counterparts, and greater resource endowment improves the chances of extending the lives of the infected people.
What_was_studied: The correlation between socioeconomic factors and life expectancy of people living with HIV/AIDS in urban and rural areas, specifically looking at poverty, female literacy rate, government spending on health care, external grants, geographical location, and HIV prevalence rate over a specific time period with a particular dataset.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up funding for healthcare and social support programs in poverty-stricken areas to improve life expectancy for those living with HIV/AIDS, prioritize education and empowerment initiatives for women to address the unintended consequences of education on mortality rates, and revise urban planning and resource allocation policies to better serve the unique needs of HIV-infected urban residents.

Field: Slum; Human settlement; Informal settlements; Sustainable development; Resource (disambiguation); Work (physics); Economic growth; Domestic violence; Socioeconomics; Political science; Sociology; Poison control; Geography; Human factors and ergonomics; Environmental health; Economics; Population; Medicine; Demography; Mechanical engineering; Computer network; Archaeology; Engineering; Computer science; Law
Title: 'Money is what makes you to be called a man.': The interaction of resource access and gender norms in shaping intimate partner violence in urban slums
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rates of IPVAW are higher in Nairobi slums compared to other human settlements, with the slum environment, economic deprivation, cultural norms, and women's economic roles all contributing to this increased prevalence.
What_was_studied: Using survey and interview data, this study investigated how the environment in a Nairobi slum exacerbates intimate partner violence against women (IPVAW) and explored how economic deprivation, cultural norms, and women's economic roles intersect to perpetuate IPVAW.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address both slum-environment and IPVAW issues, development initiatives should prioritize integrated interventions that tackle the intersecting drivers of IPVAW in Nairobi slums, including economic empowerment for women, cultural norms transformation, and improved living conditions.

Authors: Volker Schöer; Neil Rankin; Gareth Roberts
Field: Labour economics; Economics; Matching (statistics); Seekers; Unemployment; Youth unemployment; Job rotation; Data set (IBM mainframe); Panel data
Title: ACCESSING THE FIRST JOB IN A SLACK LABOUR MARKET: JOB MATCHING IN SOUTH AFRICA
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Accessing jobs through various employment channels is non-random; individual, household, job, and firm characteristics are correlated with the probability of accessing the first job via a particular channel, indicating that firms and/or job seekers select themselves into the use of these channels in their recruitment and job search strategies.
What_was_studied: Using a unique data set of labour market experiences of young African job participants in South Africa, this study investigates job matching in labour markets with mass unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high rates of intersectional poverty and food insecurity in South Africa, policymakers should prioritize funding programs that provide job training and placement services specifically tailored to the needs of young African job seekers, as well as initiatives that target the selective hiring practices of firms in order to scale up employment opportunities for this vulnerable population.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Power (social and political); Double Movement; Context (language use); Resistance (psychoanalysis); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Drivers of development over the next 30 years: Some speculations
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the rise of new middle classes in Asia will have a significant impact on development, but marginalized and excluded groups are unlikely to organize resistance or change structures of power. Poverty will be managed through welfare interventions such as India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of class relationships on development in Asia over the next 30 years and how poverty will be managed through welfare interventions like India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme from 2009 to 2030.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the rise of new middle classes in Asia, governments should prioritize targeted social protection programs to address intersectional poverty and promote inclusive development, funding interventions such as India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme to effectively manage poverty.

Authors: Di McIntyre; Lucy Gilson; H. Wadee; Michael Thiede; Okore Okarafor
Field: Private sector; Public sector; Economic sector; Health care; Economics; Population; Inequality; Health policy; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: Commercialisation and extreme inequality in health: the policy challenges in South Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite efforts to regulate the private sector and strengthen the public sector, little had changed in the South African health system by 2005, with a highly commercialized and fragmented system still present, serving predominantly high-income white populations.
What_was_studied: This paper presents a South African case study analyzing the policy challenges of health sector commercialization, focusing on the period before and after 1994, with data from various sources including surveys and government reports.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To develop an integrated health system built on income-related cross-subsidies, brave leadership and a stronger vision of the relative roles of public and private sectors are required to address the policy challenges posed by health sector commercialization in South Africa.

Field: Deforestation; Business; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Artisanal mining; Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation; Land-use conflict; Forest management; Corporate governance; Livelihood
Title: LOCKING‐IN CARBON, LOCKING‐OUT LIVELIHOODS? ARTISANAL MINING AND REDD IN SUB‐SAHARAN AFRICA
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the adoption of REDD could further marginalize and criminalize the ASM sector, reducing its contribution to poverty alleviation, while deforestation caused by ASM undermines sound forest management and potentially threatens the implementation of REDD.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) and the Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD) initiative in terms of their potential mutual conflict and how it affects poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize cross-sectoral institutions that address the challenges facing both ASM and REDD to ensure poverty reduction strategies are complementary, rather than contradictory.

Field: Economics; Human rights; Law and economics; Preparedness; Obligation; Service (business); Universal service; Economic growth; Water industry; Water supply; Universal design
Title: 'Standpipes and beyond' - a universal water service dynamic
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the universal service obligation concept, which is based on human rights, does not consider the practical realities of achieving universality of networked urban water supply, particularly in slums. The study also found that consumer groups' preparedness to pay and their perception of benefits vary widely.
What_was_studied: The failure of many developing countries' water utilities to provide adequate services to low-income urban populations during a specific time period (2000-2010) using primary data from surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision makers should prioritize a 'universal water service dynamic' approach that allows for transparency and progressive evolution of service obligations based on different consumer groups' preparedness to pay, rather than relying solely on regulation-oriented 'universal service obligation' rhetoric.

Authors: Peter Hangoma; Arild Aakvik; Bjarne Robberstad
Field: Welfare; Income protection insurance; Consumption (economics); Economics; Social protection; Health insurance; Demographic economics; Shock (economics)
Title: Health Shocks and Household Welfare in Zambia: An Assessment of Changing Risk
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Results show that injury was associated with lower consumption and reduced earned income in both periods. Injury almost doubled health expenditure after 2002, an effect which was more modest before 2002. Households relied on informal borrowing and selling assets as self-insurance strategies.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the effect of a disabling health shock, injury, on household health expenditure and welfare in Zambia before and after 2002.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of addressing social protection for households affected by disabling health shocks, specifically in rural areas where access to formal insurance and employment opportunities may be limited. Policymakers should prioritize the expansion of comprehensive social protection programs that not only provide health insurance but also labor income protection to mitigate the negative impacts of injuries on household welfare.

Field: Income elasticity of demand; Standard of living; Per capita income; Economics; Total personal income; Structural adjustment; Human development (humanity); Demographic economics; Economic growth; Developing country; International development
Title: Standards of living, human development indices and structural adjustments in developing countries: an empirical investigation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that while real per capita income grew faster during the adjustment period, the standards of living and human development indices did not improve as expected. The income elasticity of non-income components of human development indices was found to be low for countries that benefited from structural adjustment loans and non-treated countries.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of World Bank structural adjustment programs on human development indices in treated countries between 1980 and 1995.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the low income elasticity of non-income components of human development indices, policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach to sustainable development, scaling up investments in physical standards of living and exploring alternative indicators beyond income growth.

Authors: A Mushtaque R Chowdhury; Abbas Bhuiya
Field: Economics; Poverty; Child survival; Power structure; Family planning; Income level; Healthcare providers; Nutritional status; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: The wider impacts of BRAC poverty alleviation programme in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The program was found to have a positive impact on child survival, nutritional status, expenditure patterns, family planning practices, children's education, rural power structure, and health providers networking relationships.
What_was_studied: The poverty alleviation program of BRAC in Bangladesh was studied over the decades of the 1980s and 90s, using carefully designed studies to assess its impact on selected components of human well-being such as child survival, nutritional status, expenditure patterns, family planning practices, children's education, rural power structure, and health providers networking relationships.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact of the poverty alleviation program on human well-being, policymakers should scale up funding for such programs, prioritize their implementation in rural areas, revise existing policies to incorporate human well-being indicators, and expand their reach to more communities.

Field: Unemployment; Qualitative research; Work (physics); Lived experience; Disabled people; Political science; Economic growth; Psychology; Sociology; Economics; Social science; Applied psychology; Mechanical engineering; Life style; Psychoanalysis; Engineering
Title: Barriers to disability‐inclusive employment in Uzbekistan: A pilot qualitative study of disabled people's lived experiences
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The findings revealed that the current institutional framework restricts disabled people's right to work, with reported levels of disability employment remaining low. Environmental and attitudinal barriers further hinder their ability to access employment opportunities.
What_was_studied: This pilot qualitative study investigated the challenges faced by disabled people in exercising their right to work in Tashkent city and the Tashkent region of Uzbekistan, focusing on the period from January 2018 to December 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure equal opportunities for disabled people in the labor market, policy makers should remove all existing barriers, including the outdated institutional framework rooted in Soviet disability policies, and prioritize accessible infrastructure and education programs to promote inclusive employment practices.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Sub saharan; Affect (psychology); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Institutions and economic performance: Implications for African development
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that weak institutional frameworks hinder economic growth in the region, with an estimated loss of 2% GDP per year due to poor institutions. The study also identifies a positive correlation between good institutions and foreign investment, highlighting the potential for sustainable development through investment in strong institutions.
What_was_studied: The study focuses on the relationship between institutions and economic development in Sub Saharan Africa over the period 2000-2015, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of institutions on economic growth and sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize strengthening institutional frameworks in Sub Saharan Africa to attract foreign investment and scale up economic growth. This can be achieved through targeted investments in institution-building programs, regulatory reforms, and capacity-building initiatives.

Field: Human factors and ergonomics; Political science; Human Development Report; Originality; Human security; Human development (humanity); Poison control; Injury control; Policy making; Public administration
Title: Human security—national perspectives and global agendas: insights from national human development reports†
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that broader definitions of human security are operational for both analysis and policy-making, and that limits to defining a core of high-priority concerns can be set after exploring the concerns of people in specific situations rather than before.
What_was_studied: This paper explores how National Human Development Reports (NHDRs) in 13 countries define and prioritize human security since 1997, with a focus on gender and poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize gender and poverty considerations in their human security strategies, expanding the scope of human security to include these concerns and scale up policies that address them effectively.

Field: Fungibility; Economics; International economics; Poverty; Public expenditure; Democratic consolidation; Resource curse; Natural resource; Sierra leone; Development economics; Democracy
Title: Foreign Sectoral Aid Fungibility, Growth and Poverty Reduction
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The analysis found that democracies only bear fruit after some time, and that good institutions are necessary to turn the resource curse into a blessing. Additionally, the study found that sectoral aid is largely treated as fungible by recipient countries, but the alternative use of aid may be less productive or less socially useful.
What_was_studied: This thesis presents three self-contained essays focusing on empirical questions in growth and development economics, analyzing the effect of democracy on economic development, the relationship between natural resources and growth, and the efficiency of foreign development assistance.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that investing in democratic consolidation and good institutions can lead to long-term economic growth, and that sectoral aid should be targeted towards productive and socially useful sectors to ensure effective poverty reduction and sustainable development.

Field: Public policy; Government; Multinational corporation; Economics; Financial market; Globalization; Gold mining; Economic recovery; Incentive; Economic growth
Title: Ghana's Economic Recovery Programme and the Globalisation of Ashanti Goldfields Company Ltd
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Ashanti's globalization was driven by the government's economic recovery program, specific incentives, and Ashanti's own business strategies. The research demonstrates how a local company in a low-income country could profitably globalize its operations.
What_was_studied: The economic recovery program implemented in Ghana in 1983 and its impact on the globalization of Ashanti Goldfields Company, a local gold mining company, over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of government policies in promoting the globalization of local companies in low-income countries. Therefore, governments should prioritize providing incentives and support for such companies to scale their operations and expand into international markets.

Field: Agriculture; Labour economics; Government; Economics; Investment (macroeconomics); Human capital; Wage; Rural poverty; Intervention (law); Capital accumulation
Keywords: R11; R12; O18 rural development; livelihood strategies; human capital; conditional cash transfers; Oportunidades; Mexico; Latin America rural development; livelihood strategies; human capital; conditional cash transfers; Oportunidades; Mexico; Latin America
Title: Human capital investment and long‐term poverty reduction in rural Mexico
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that investments in education lead to a shift towards non-farm wage employment, with larger effects for households with more assets and those located in urban areas. The magnitude of the impact was also found to be influenced by household assets and location.
What_was_studied: This paper uses administrative data to analyze the economic activities of the Mexican rural poor after receiving the Oportunidades program, specifically focusing on how investments in education affect their shift from agricultural wage employment to non-farm wage employment and how this impact is influenced by household assets and location.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize complementary policies that support education and human capital investment, particularly in rural areas with limited access to resources, to maximize the program's impact on reducing poverty and improving economic outcomes for the rural poor.

Field: Economics; Financial crisis; Affect (psychology); Demographic economics; Inequality
Title: How do migration and remittances affect inequality? A case study of Mexico
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that remittances lower inequality and become more pro-poor over time, strengthening their insurance effects and mitigating some of the negative impact of shocks on the poorest households.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of remittances on inequality in Mexico using household-level information on the receiving side during the 1994 Mexican peso crisis and the global financial crisis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant poverty-reducing effects of remittances, policymakers should prioritize measures that facilitate the flow of remittances to the most vulnerable populations and support their financial inclusion, particularly during times of crisis.

Authors: Teresa Njoroge Mwendwa; Ambrose Murangira; R Lang
Field: Mainstreaming; Political science; Poverty reduction; Inclusive development; National development; Un convention; Public administration; Economic growth
Title: Mainstreaming the rights of persons with disabilities in national development frameworks
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the active involvement of disabled people's organizations (DPOs) is critical for ensuring that poverty reduction strategies are inclusive and address the needs of marginalized groups. For example, in Uganda, DPOs played a key role in advocating for policy reforms to improve accessibility in public transportation, and their involvement was associated with more equitable distribution of resources and greater social inclusion.
What_was_studied: This paper analyses the challenges involved in ensuring that persons with disabilities and their representative organisations are effectively included in poverty reduction strategy plans and national development programmes, using examples from recent practices in Uganda between 2006 and 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role of DPOs in ensuring that poverty reduction strategies are inclusive and address the needs of marginalized groups, governments and development practitioners should prioritize funding and capacity-building for DPOs to enable them to effectively participate in policy-making processes.

Authors: Maureen Mackintosh; Kwadwo Mensah; Leroi Henry; Michael Rowson
Field: Payment; Health care; Economics; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Health equity; Obligation; Development aid; International inequality; Economic growth; Subsidy
Title: Aid, restitution and international fiscal redistribution in health care: implications of health professionals' migration
primary_category: Education access; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: High and sustained levels of migration create a perverse subsidy from poor to rich, worsening international inequality, with an estimated net cost of £2.9 million to the UK NHS annually.
What_was_studied: The migration of health professionals from Sub-Saharan Africa to the UK between 2000 and 2005, using data from the UK's General Medical Council and the Commonwealth Foundation.
