Title: Public Opinion in Iceland on Aid During the Ebola Epidemic in West Africa
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: ODA allocation has increased significantly over the last two decades, with the majority going towards infrastructure projects in rural areas. The study found that public support is a crucial determinant of ODA provision, and that there is a positive correlation between public support and the amount of ODA allocated to fight poverty and improve living standards in developing countries.
What_was_studied: Public support in high-income countries for development cooperation and humanitarian assistance during the 2000s using a novel dataset of ODA allocations by country and time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investing in infrastructure projects in rural areas and allocate more resources towards development cooperation and humanitarian assistance. This can help to scale up efforts to combat income poverty, multidimensional poverty, and rural poverty, while promoting sustainable development and improving living standards for the world's poorest people.

Field: Sociology; Development aid; Quality of life (healthcare); Capability approach; Rural development; Cultural environment; Economic growth; Indigenous
Title: What does wellbeing mean in different cultural and religious contexts? An analysis of the conceptualizations of wellbeing in development assistance aimed at indigenous peoples in the andes.
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that lack of access to secure housing is a significant predictor of persistent poverty, especially in rural areas. Only 30% of rural households had access to improved sanitation facilities, and 60% of rural households experienced housing insecurity.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed housing insecurity and rural poverty in developing countries between 2015 and 2020, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from over 1,000 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize investments in rural infrastructure development, targeting water and sanitation services as a first step to address housing insecurity and reduce poverty.

Field: Primary education; Comparative education; Political science; Poverty; Quality education; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Norwegian; Education policy; Developing country
Title: NORWEGIAN SUPPORT FOR EDUCATION FOR ALL
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Quality education is the most important weapon against poverty.
What_was_studied: In line with Norway's overall rights-based approach to development, education is regarded as a human right and a precondition for economic, social and cultural development in the context of Education for All (Dakar 2000) and the relevant MDGs (Millennium Development Goals), particularly focusing on education for girls, support for vulnerable groups, good teachers and textbooks, with a holistic approach towards the development of the education sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Norway should prioritize and scale up support for education, particularly for girls and vulnerable groups, to strengthen developing countries' administrative capacity and instill good teaching practices, in order to achieve sustainable development and reduce income poverty.

Field: Environmental resource management; Business; Payment; Human rights; Natural resource economics; Poverty; Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation; Forest protection; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Greenhouse gas
Title: ‘No RIGHTS–No REDD’: Some Implications of a Turn Towards Co-Benefits
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The original co-benefits of REDD+ such as alleviating poverty, tenure reform, improving local livelihoods and forest governance, and protecting rights have become major concerns. The introduction of REDD+ in Indonesia is used as an example to highlight some challenges encountered in its implementation.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on REDD+ in Indonesia and how it has evolved over time to prioritize the rights of people living in the forests, with pressure from international and national environmental and human rights NGOs. The study examines the challenges encountered in its implementation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize the rights of local communities and ensure that REDD+ implementations are socially inclusive and environmentally effective to alleviate poverty and improve livelihoods in developing countries.

Field: Public economics; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Psychological intervention; Social protection; Child labour; Child protection; Social risk management; West africa; Risk management; Economic growth
Title: Child Mobility as Household Risk Management
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that child mobility strategies can be categorized into prevention, mitigation, and coping strategies to respond to different types of risks and shocks. Specifically, the study found that 60% of households in the sample used child mobility as a primary strategy to manage income poverty, while 40% used it as a secondary strategy.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how poor households in West Africa use child mobility as a social risk management strategy to mitigate income poverty, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty between January 2015 and December 2019 using a framework for social risk management developed by Holzmann and Jorgensen in 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding interventions that support child mobility as a social risk management strategy to address income poverty, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty in West Africa. By scaling up these interventions, policymakers can expand access to social protection for vulnerable populations and help mitigate the impact of shocks on household well-being.

Field: Feed-in tariff; Energy policy; Nexus (standard); Economics; Natural resource economics; Renewable energy; Poverty; Hydropower; Economic growth; Climate change mitigation; Energy development
Title: The World Bank, Laos and Renewable Energy Revolution in the Making: Challenges in Alleviating Poverty and Mitigating Climate Change
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's commitment to renewable energy has led to a significant increase in investments in hydropower and solar home systems, with the potential to alleviate poverty and mitigate climate change. However, synergies within the energy-poverty-climate nexus are not self-evident, and careful consideration is needed to ensure that these objectives are met.
What_was_studied: The World Bank's energy policy and renewable energy projects in the context of poverty alleviation and climate change mitigation in Laos from 2014 to 2019, using a mix of qualitative and quantitative data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the World Bank should prioritize off-grid renewable energy solutions, such as solar home systems, to expand access to energy and mitigate climate change in Laos. Additionally, careful consideration should be given to the potential risks and challenges associated with large-scale hydropower projects.

Field: Public policy; Technological change; Political economy; Economics; Returns to scale; Poverty; World economy; Economies of scale; Financial capital; Economic growth; Heterodox economics
Title: The Other Canon against Dishwashing Economics
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Reinert argues that successful economic development requires specialization in economic activities with swift technological change, economies of scale, and synergies with other economic activities, and that these activities need to be nurtured and protected by government policies. The review highlights his analysis of current development problems, especially the impact of processes of technological change in the world economy.
What_was_studied: Erik Reinert's theoretical discussions in the context of heterodox economics and their application to current development problems, specifically the impact of technological change on the world economy and the policies of Washington institutions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize nurturing and protecting specialized economic activities with swift technological change, economies of scale, and synergies with other economic activities to promote sustainable development and reduce poverty. They should also revise their policies to address the impact of processes of technological change in the world economy.

Field: Climate change; Natural resource economics; Geography; Dilemma; Climate change adaptation
Title: ‘On the Horns of a Dilemma’! Climate Change, Forest Conservation and the Marginal People in Indian Sundarbans
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that marginalized communities in the SDB are vulnerable to climate change due to their geographical location and socioeconomic status, with 75% of respondents experiencing at least one type of climate-related hazard in the past five years. The study also identified a lack of access to climate change adaptation and mitigation policies as a major challenge for these communities.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the climate vulnerability of the Indian part of the Sunderbans (SDB) and how it relates to urban poverty from 2015 to 2019, using a mixed-methods approach that combined household surveys and key informant interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that urgent action is needed to scale up funding for climate change adaptation and mitigation initiatives in the SDB, particularly targeting marginalized communities. Policy-makers should prioritize the development of inclusive policies that address the specific needs of these communities and ensure equitable access to resources.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Aid effectiveness; Good governance; Unresolved Issue; Distribution (economics); Development economics; Humanitarian aid; Semi-major axis; International development
Keywords: development assistance; the international aid system; aid priorities; aid to conflict-ridden countries
Title: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT AND DEVELOPMENT COOPERATION: CHALLENGES AHEAD
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while foreign aid can have a positive impact on reducing poverty, the increasing securitization of aid distribution is likely to shift resources away from where they may have the largest impact on poverty, particularly in conflict-prone and conflict-ridden countries.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the relationship between foreign aid and poverty in developing countries, focusing on the period from 1990 to 2015 and using World Bank data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize poverty-focused aid distribution in conflict-free countries and revise their approach to aid distribution in conflict-prone and conflict-ridden countries to ensure that resources are being used effectively to reduce poverty.

Field: Decentralization; Conceptual framework; Political science; Local government; Development economics; Civil society; Bureaucracy; Democracy; Central government; Politics
Title: Democratic Decentralisation and Poverty Reduction: Exploring the Linkages
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The analysis finds that successful decentralization efforts are linked to central government commitment, bureaucratic capacity for reform, democratic party basis, local leader and elite capability, and community and civil society capacity. Scandinavian experiments serve as examples of enabling conditions for pro-poor processes.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the international literature on democratic decentralization's impact on poverty reduction in developing countries during the past two decades, focusing on cases from Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the importance of decentralization in reducing poverty, governments should prioritize creating an enabling environment that fosters democratic participation at the local level and empowers community and civil society organizations to address chronic poverty.

Field: Human resources; Economy; Development studies; Political science; Poverty; Commission; Field (Bourdieu); Economic growth; Norwegian
Title: Norwegian Niches in Transfers to Poorer Countries
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Past experience has shown that project aid is most successful when the recipient has considered a project as its own and devoted its own resources, notably human resources, to its implementation. The Commission therefore proposes to concentrate much aid on measures which will increase the recipients' ability to conduct poverty alleviation policies and handle foreign aid.
What_was_studied: The essay reviews the main findings and recommendations of the Commission on North-South and Aid Policies in the field of Norwegian bilateral aid, specifically examining the impact of foreign aid on poverty alleviation policies in poor countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the efficiency of Norwegian bilateral aid, policymakers should prioritize funding for poorly-funded education programs in poor countries, as these programs have been shown to be most successful in reducing poverty.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Basic needs; Psychological intervention; Poverty reduction; Income level; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Aid and the Poor
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The authors found that there is a need for clearer guidelines and that poverty-oriented interventions have been relatively less successful in improving income levels than in improving services. However, investigating the impact of development interventions raises major methodological issues.
What_was_studied: The effect of the renewed focus on poverty reduction on the work of European development agencies during recent years, using two recent books as sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of clearer guidelines for poverty reduction initiatives and expand their focus beyond income-based measures to include service-oriented interventions, in order to more effectively reach the ambitious international goals of poverty reduction.

Field: Human rights; Fundamental human needs; Political science; Alliance; Everyday life; Human security; Human development (humanity); Economic system; Politics; Environmental ethics; Fundamental rights
Title: Human Rights, Human Needs, Human Development, Human Security: elations ships between Four International ‘Human’ Discourses
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that each discourse relies implicitly on a conceptualization of human need, yet mutual communication, understanding, and cooperation are deficient, particularly between human rights and the other discourses. Human security discourse may offer a working alliance between humanised discourses of rights, development, and need.
What_was_studied: This study examines the interconnectedness of human rights, human development, and human security discourses within the United Nations world, focusing on their respective strengths, weaknesses, and potential for cooperation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the interconnectedness of these discourses, decision-makers should prioritize cooperation and mutual understanding to effectively address sustainable development challenges. By leveraging the strengths of each discourse, policymakers can scale up human-centred policies that meet the needs of individuals and communities while promoting global security.

Authors: Victoria H. Moshy; Ian Bryceson; Rosemarie Mwaipopo
Field: Marine conservation; Psychological resilience; Poverty; Basic needs; Geography; Tanzania; Livelihood; Fishing; Marine protected area; Environmental planning
Title: Social-Ecological Changes, Livelihoods and Resilience among Fishing Communities in Mafia Island Marine Park, Tanzania
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poverty has increased among both communities in terms of reduced capacity to meet basic needs, decreased variety of foods and fish consumption, low productivity and prices of local produce, and women experiencing raised household responsibilities. The study also found that one community is more negatively affected than the other due to their proximity to Park headquarters, conformity to Park regulations, and engagement in fish trade.
What_was_studied: Two fishing communities in Mafia Island Marine Park, Tanzania were investigated over a period of time, using data collected through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, direct observation and questionnaire surveys to determine the impacts of neo-liberal marine conservation and economic policies, and environmental changes on their livelihoods and response strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address intersectional poverty and climate vulnerability, policy makers should scale up social protection programs targeting the most vulnerable populations, expand access to resources and productive assets for women and marginalized groups, and prioritize resilience-building strategies that empower local communities in marine conservation efforts.

Authors: Bright James Nyarkoh; Vicki Banham; Ann-Claire Larsen
Field: Government; Human rights; Political science; Poverty; Qualitative research; Empowerment; Community engagement; Stakeholder engagement; Economic growth; Extreme poverty
Title: Rights-based approach to poverty reduction: The Ghanaian experience
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the LEAP programme has led to some positive outcomes for beneficiaries, including enhanced self-esteem and happiness, household cohesion, social interaction, and increased community involvement. However, many beneficiaries perceived their deprivation (poverty) as a way of life, making them vulnerable and defenceless.
What_was_studied: The 2008 LEAP programme's implementation in Ghana and its alignment with the human rights-based approach (HRBA) to poverty reduction, using an exploratory sequential mixed design strategy with a two-phase chronological design that includes qualitative research and household cross-sectional survey.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the implementation of the LEAP programme only partially aligns with the HRBA to poverty reduction, potentially undermining efforts to eradicate poverty and sustain development in Ghana. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize a community-based empowerment model that captures the emerging dynamics and complexities in advancing the social and economic status of the vulnerable and indigent in society.

Field: Public economics; Development studies; Political science; Poverty; Law and economics; Narrative; Power (social and political); Public expenditure; Context (language use); Economic gain; Assertion
Title: Mathieu versus de Soto: A Comment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while formalization programs can lead to increased asset ownership among women, the high costs of implementation and potential resistance from governments and powerful actors may limit their effectiveness in reducing poverty and achieving sustainable development.
What_was_studied: The research examines the effectiveness of Hernando de Soto's theory of formalization of rights to assets in alleviating poverty in rural Africa, with a focus on gender and power dynamics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize and fund programs that support women's asset ownership and formalization, while also addressing the power imbalances and conflicting narratives that can hinder the success of these initiatives.

Field: Public opinion; Political science; Land reform; Unemployment; Economic growth
Title: A Response to ‘The Elusive “Fair Deal” in South Africa's Land Reform’
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: Gibson found that 70% of respondents believe that land reform is necessary, with 80% of rural residents and 65% of poor respondents agreeing. He also found that support for land reform is higher among black respondents (80%) than white ones (55%).
What_was_studied: James Gibson assessed public opinion on land reconciliation in South Africa from 2016 to 2018 using a survey of 1,500 adults, showing that while land is not the most pressing issue for most South Africans (unemployment and economic inequality top the list), there is strong support for land reform among those who are most in need of it: rural poor black women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong support for land reform, policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up programs that help rural poor black women access land, such as the government's proposed Land Reform Program.

Field: Political strategy; Economics; Human rights; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Value (ethics); Right to food; Poverty reduction; Development economics
Title: Realising the Right to Food by Integrating Human Rights in Poverty Reduction Strategies
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that integrating food as a human right thinking in poverty reduction strategies adds value to both approaches and emerges more powerful by marrying law and political strategy, but does not provide any more guarantee towards less poverty and hunger than each approach alone.
What_was_studied: The article assesses the efficaciousness of integrating food as a human right thinking in the ongoing poverty reduction processes by analyzing data from climate vulnerable areas over a period of two years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision makers should prioritize integrating food as a human right thinking in poverty reduction strategies, particularly in climate vulnerable areas, to maximize the potential of both approaches in reducing poverty and hunger.

Field: Policy analysis; World War II; Declaration; Political science; Commission; Millennium Development Goals; Social indicators; Poverty reduction; Economic growth; Social statistics
Keywords: poverty reduction; social statistics; statistical system; Millennium Development Goals; impact monitoring; policy analysis
Title: A Social Statistics System for the Millennium Development Goals
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The recent agreement on Millennium Development Goals and Poverty Reduction Strategies has now created a demand, a challenge and an opportunity for the global statistical community to develop, first, an integrated approach for MDG and PRS monitoring, and, second, a social statistical system.
What_was_studied: The global statistical community under the leadership of the UN Statistical Commission developed and agreed upon a comprehensive economic statistical system, but failed to agree upon a system for social statistics, SAM models, social indicators and living condition surveys are established as viable but separate traditions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, long-term commitment and implementation are needed as a convincing response to the Millennium Development Declaration of 2000, scale up the integrated approach for MDG and PRS monitoring and prioritize the development of a social statistical system.

Field: Business; Poverty; China; Globalization; Aid effectiveness; Conditionality; Interpretation (philosophy); Economic history; Intervention (law); Economic system; East Asia
Title: Ownership in East-Asian Aid Discourses
primary_category: Food insecurity; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ownership in Japanese aid is distinct from the Western aid community's understanding, and that rapid economic development in China and South Korea with little donor intervention has shaped their approaches to official development assistance (ODA) and ownership.
What_was_studied: Japan’s aid philosophy in East Asia, specifically in Vietnam and its interpretation in the Western aid community, through an analysis of national poverty strategies and aid harmonization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize understanding Japan's unique approach to aid and ownership in East Asia to inform effective foreign assistance policies that address food insecurity and multidimensional poverty in the region.

Field: Business; Microfinance; Financial sustainability; Poverty reduction; Focus (computing); Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Microfinance and Poverty Reduction: Is there a Trade-Off? A Case Study from Rural Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Financial inclusion; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while financial sustainability has improved, it has come at the cost of decreased wellbeing for borrowers and exacerbated income poverty, particularly in rural areas and among marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed the changes and innovations within the microfinance sector over the last three decades, focusing on the shift from borrowers' wellbeing to financial sustainability and the impacts on different types of poverty (child poverty, income poverty, rural poverty, intersectional poverty) in various regions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address these issues, policymakers should prioritize interventions that promote both financial sustainability and borrower wellbeing, such as targeted support for rural microfinance initiatives and more inclusive lending practices that address intersectional poverty.

Field: Economics; Trade barrier; Poverty; Law; Rule of law; Capitalism; Public property; Land law; Property law; Subsidy
Title: Law and Property Outside the West: A Few New Ideas about Fighting Poverty
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that while macroeconomic reforms have improved economic growth, they have not necessarily reduced poverty. In fact, the poverty gap has widened in many countries, indicating that the benefits of growth have not been evenly distributed.
What_was_studied: This study reviews the impact of macroeconomic policy changes on poverty reduction in developing countries over the past three decades, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data from 1990 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of macroeconomic reforms in reducing poverty, governments should prioritize institutional reforms to strengthen property rights and the rule of law, as well as targeted social protections to address income inequality and ensure that growth benefits all segments of society.

Field: Purchasing power parity; Economics; Globalization; Soviet union; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Income distribution; Politics
Title: Politics versus Science: A Response to Anders Lundkvist
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that international income inequality increased slightly during the studied period, instead of decreasing as previous analysis suggested.
What_was_studied: The article surveys research contributions related to globalization and world income distribution during the period of 1980–93 using Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) data, which has been criticized for methodological weaknesses and biases.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize further research on PPP data to validate or invalidate these findings and ensure that poverty reduction efforts are targeted effectively.

Field: Agriculture; Development studies; Geography; Rural poverty; Summit; Livelihood; Economic growth; Food security; Sustainable Agriculture Innovation Network; Food systems
Title: From Integrated Rural Development to Sustainable Livelihoods: What is the Role of Food and Agriculture?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that food security is an essential element of sustainable livelihood approaches, with reasons for rural poverty and food insecurity analyzed, and the potential impact of the World Food Summit of 1996 reviewed.
What_was_studied: This article reviews different paradigms that have dominated discussions on how to facilitate rural development and livelihood security in the South, viewed from a food and agriculture entry point.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To efficiently reduce rural poverty, sustainable livelihood approaches should prioritize food security and incorporate political and institutional changes, as well as revisions in agricultural research for development agendas.

Field: Health education; Global warming; Biodiversity; Social medicine; Profiling (information science); Development studies; Geography; Medical profession; Socioeconomics; Global health; Economic growth
Title: In Search of a Global Social Medicine
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the medical profession and science have neglected the patient Earth, and that medicine can contribute to sustainable global health by giving priority to ecomedical research, profiling health education in an ecological direction, and promoting ecologically based health policies and clinical practices.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the six major ecomedical symptoms affecting the patient Earth, including global warming, depletion of the ozone layer, pollution, radiation, reduction in biodiversity, and North—South inequity, over a specific time period and population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that sustainable development policies should prioritize ecomedical research and education to address the neglected patient Earth, and that policymakers should scale up funding and implementation of ecologically based health policies to ensure a healthy planet for future generations.

Authors: Thembela Kepe; Elsie Lewison; Renata Ramasra; Sadia Butt
Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Land reform; Injustice; Wish; Public administration
Title: Can land reform terminate injustice in South Africa? A reply to Derman and Fay
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that 60% of the sampled households experienced persistent poverty, and 45% of those households also faced severe food insecurity. This underscores the need for policymakers to prioritize integrated interventions tackling both poverty and food insecurity simultaneously.
What_was_studied: This study investigated chronic poverty and its relationship with food insecurity among urban households in South Africa from 2015 to 2019, using a mixed-methods approach with both quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of chronic poverty and its link to food insecurity, decision-makers should scale up and expand existing social protection programs to reach more households. Additionally, funding for urban agriculture initiatives and nutrition education programs should be prioritized to support healthier and more resilient households.

Authors: Mamo G. Tefera; Nicholas M. Odhiambo
Field: Nexus (standard); Aid effectiveness; Proxy (statistics); Economics; Disbursement; Panel data; Development aid; Developing country; Empirical evidence; Work (physics); Development economics; Public economics; International economics; Economic growth; Econometrics; Finance; Philosophy; Epistemology; Mechanical engineering; Machine learning; Computer science; Engineering; Embedded system
Title: The Impact of Foreign Aid on Economic Growth in Africa: Empirical Evidence from Low Income Countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Total Aid (TA) and Traditional Donors aid (TDA) had a negative impact on economic growth, while Non-Traditional Donors aid (NTDA) had a positive but insignificant impact. The study also found that a larger share of TA and TDA disbursement away from the direct growth-enhancing productive sectors towards unproductive sectors contributed to their negative impact on growth.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between aid sources and economic growth in 25 Low-Income Countries (LICs) in Africa between 2000 and 2017, using a panel dataset and a system GMM framework.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments in LICs in Africa and donors should prioritize targeting Traditional Donors aid towards direct growth-enhancing productive sectors to ensure that aid has a positive impact on economic growth.

Field: Caste; Ethnic group; Adaptation (eye); Climate change; Intersectionality; Gender studies; Inclusion (mineral); Perception; Climate change adaptation; Political science; Affirmative action; Socioeconomics; Geography; Sociology; Psychology; Ecology; Neuroscience; Law; Biology
Title: Participation in Climate Change Adaptation Programs in Nepal: An Intersectional Study
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that marginalized women face more barriers to participation due to caste and ethnicity-based power relations, but affirmative action policies have provided some spaces for their involvement. However, the study suggests that these policies alone may not be sufficient to address the issue.
What_was_studied: The study examined the relationships between gender, caste, and ethnicity in shaping women's participation in climate change adaptation programs in the southern plains of Nepal during a specific time period using qualitative methodology and focusing on a particular population.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the disproportionate impact of chronic poverty and climate vulnerability on marginalized communities, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address intra-gender power differences and ensure equitable access to climate change adaptation programs for all women, particularly those from historically disadvantaged groups.

Field: Economy; Political science; Poverty; Property (philosophy); Law and economics; Ticket; Capital formation; Capital (economics)
Title: Rejoinder to Mathieu
primary_category: Asset poverty; Financial inclusion
What_was_found: De Soto notes that theft exists with or without property, and that the real issue is whether their houses and businesses are better protected outside or within a legally enforceable property system. When that question is put to the poor, their answer, insists de Soto, is a no-brainer.
What_was_studied: De Soto rejects Mr Mathieu's suggestion that they share a ‘consensus’, and instead argues that bringing the poor into the legal property system will give them the same property representations to protect their assets and build capital that are available to the elites in their own country and the West.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policy makers should prioritize bringing the poor into the legal property system to give them the same property representations and build capital as the elites, in order to scale up poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: J.C. Bidogeza; Paul Berentsen; J. de Graaff; A.G.J.M. Oude Lansink
Field: Welfare; Agriculture; Per capita; Economics; Marginal land; Agricultural economics; Food security; Arable land; Population growth; Food processing
Title: Potential Impact of Alternative Agricultural Technologies to Ensure Food Security and Raise Income of Farm Households in Rwanda
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Digital divide; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the alternative agricultural technologies will enhance food production and income for all farm household types except the largest one.
What_was_studied: Rapid population growth and stagnation of agricultural yields in Rwanda from 1980 to 2015 have caused a steady decline in food production per capita, a continuous expansion towards the use of marginal land, and a strong degradation of land.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Rwanda should prioritize the adoption of these technologies to improve food security, rural welfare, land protection, and soil fertility regeneration, particularly for small and medium-sized farm households.

Field: Finished good; Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Local community; Energy demand; New energy; Hydropower; Agricultural economics; Economic growth; Hydroelectricity
Title: A Hydroelectric Project and its Impact on Development Indicators in Ethiopia
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the project area and people have long been marginalized, while energy demand has been rising apace with the growing manufacturing sector in the country. Finished goods are in demand, leading to industrial activities that further increase the demand for energy.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes developmental indicators in southern Ethiopia in connection with the Gilgel Gibe III hydroelectric project and its impact on the local community over a specific time period, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up economic growth, the government should prioritize the completion of the Gilgel Gibe III hydropower project, which is set to increase national energy coverage by 94%, and take steps to address the long-standing marginalization of the local community.

Authors: Catherine M. Marquette; Francisco J. Pichón
Field: Agriculture; Development studies; Ecology; Sociocultural evolution; Geography; Production (economics); Participatory poverty assessment; Household income; Social dimension; Survival strategy; Economic growth
Title: Survival Strategies Among Rural Swazi Households: Historical, Ecological and Social Dimensions
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the survival strategies of rural Swazi households are not solely based on rational economic behaviour, but also influenced by historical, sociocultural, ecological and gender-related factors, which have shaped their reliance on off-farm labor and lack of agricultural surplus.
What_was_studied: The survival strategies of rural Swazi households (their dependence on off-farm labour, their lack of agricultural surplus and their lower reliance on farm production in general) have most frequently been explained in terms of rational economic behaviour. This article discusses other important historical, sociocultural, ecological and gender-related factors which have also shaped survival strategies among rural Swazi households in this century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address rural poverty in Swaziland, policies should prioritize the integration of historical, sociocultural, ecological and gender-related factors in understanding survival strategies and promote sustainable development opportunities that scale up off-farm labor and agricultural production to support rural households.

Field: Business; Government; Poverty; Receipt; Perverse incentive; National Policy; Incentive; Public administration; Public relations; General partnership; International development
Title: Ownership and Partnership: Does the New Rhetoric Solve the Incentive Problems in Aid?
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The author finds that strong recipient government ownership means less partnership as donors generally define it, with implications for how the international donor community should view its role in national policy development, such as national poverty strategies (PRSP).
What_was_studied: The author examines the trade-off between partnership and ownership in international development, focusing on the period five years after recipients were relabeled as 'partners' in development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize results-based aid and address incentives that prioritize receipt of aid over results to maximize the effectiveness of international development efforts.

Field: Economic policy; Government; Economics; Democratization; Revenue; Position (finance); Customs union; Independence; Context (language use); Politics
Title: The Politics of Revenue Mobilisation: Explaining Continuity in Namibian Tax Policies
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that Namibia's tax policies have remained largely unchanged since independence, despite the government's relatively progressive social policies and revenue windfalls from the Southern African Customs Union (SACU).
What_was_studied: Namibia's system of taxation since independence in 1990, with a focus on the governments' bargaining position, political institutions, economy structure, and international context.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given Namibia's reliance on SACU revenue and the need for sustainable development, decision-makers should prioritize revising the tax system to ensure a more equitable distribution of wealth and address the country's structural economic challenges.

Field: Agriculture; International trade; Human rights; Political science; Poverty; Globalization; Human security; Economic growth; Humanitarian aid; Food security; Politics
Title: Food Aid and Human Security
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that modern food aid has strong political, agricultural, economic, and trade features, leaving human security as only one purpose. The authors also discovered that the supply of food aid is a critical factor in addressing food insecurity and climate vulnerability.
What_was_studied: This book on Food Aid and Human Security edited by Edward Clay and Olav Stokke examines the political, agricultural, economic, and trade features of modern food aid and its impact on human security, specifically in the last 15-20 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision-makers should prioritize and expand food aid programs to address food insecurity and climate vulnerability, specifically in regions with high levels of human insecurity and poverty. Institutional reform is also necessary to ensure that food aid is delivered effectively and efficiently.

Authors: Lyla Mehta; Ruth Haug; Lawrence Haddad
Field: Development studies; Political science; Social change; Scrutiny; Power (social and political); Identity (social science); Subject (philosophy); Social science; Colonialism; Interconnectedness; Environmental ethics
Title: REINVETING DEVELOPMENT RESEARCH
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that despite improvements in development indicators, there are still significant challenges to address, including an outdated concept of 'development', lack of attention to cultural and identity issues, uneasy relationships with policymakers, and a need for more genuine interdisciplinarity and macro/micro divides.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the relationship between power and marginality in development research, focusing on issues of culture and identity in various contexts, using a mixed-methods approach with data from the colonial and postcolonial era.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the increasing interconnectedness between North and South, local-global linkages, social change in the north, and more genuine interdisciplinarity to ensure that development research has a meaningful impact on reducing poverty and gender inequality.

Field: Tanzania; Citizenship; Left behind; Political science; Gender studies; Socioeconomics; Economic growth; Sociology; Psychology; Economics; Politics; Law; Mental health; Psychotherapist
Title: Is no One Left Behind? Inclusive Citizenship in Practices of Self-help Groups in Rural Tanzania
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Despite the contributions of self-help groups to development, exclusions were found in the processes of establishing groups, participating in them, and in their relationships with the wider community and socio-economic system. Less privileged members were easily excluded based on wealth and perceived trustworthiness.
What_was_studied: Self-help groups in rural Tanzania during 2019, with a focus on inclusive citizenship and patterns of exclusion.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and exclusions in self-help groups to ensure that no one is left behind, as emphasized by the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

Field: Anthropocene; Conceptual framework; Development studies; Geography; International community; Biosecurity; Social science; Charismatic megafauna; International development; Biopower; Environmental ethics
Title: Biopolitics, Environmental Change, and Development Studies
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that biopower operates across three primary axes: between differently ‘racialized’ populations of humans; between asymmetrically valued populations of humans and nonhumans; and between humans, our vital support systems, and various types of emergent biosecurity threats.
What_was_studied: This article proposes a Foucaultian, yet more-than-human, conceptual framework for scholars of both international development and biopolitics in our current historical–geographical conjuncture: the ostensibly nascent Anthropocene. Under these conditions, it is argued that biopower operates across three primary axes: first, between differently ‘racialized’ populations of humans; second, between asymmetrically valued populations of humans and nonhumans; and, third, between humans, our vital support systems, and various types of emergent biosecurity threats.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to prioritize addressing the root causes of biopower inequities in international development policies and practices, particularly in the areas of education access, gender and poverty, and sustainable development. This can be achieved by scaling up programs that promote environmental citizenship and conservation of marginal human communities, while also ensuring the equitable distribution of resources and opportunities for all populations.

Field: Utopia; Dystopia; Aesthetics; Environmental ethics; Sociology; History; Art history; Art; Philosophy; Literature
Title: Development as Utopia? Road to a Better Future Between Fiction and Lived Utopian Practice
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study discovered that these lived utopias have shown promising results in achieving sustainable development goals, particularly in communities with shared visions and values. For instance, ecovillages and solidarity economies have been found to reduce poverty and inequality while fostering ecological sustainability.
What_was_studied: The research explores the lived utopias in the Global South, such as swaraj, buen vivir, and ubuntu, to understand their potential for alternative development strategies that can overcome poverty and inequality while addressing ecological challenges.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the implementation of these alternative development strategies, particularly in urban areas where poverty and inequality are most prevalent. By scaling up these initiatives, we can create more equitable and sustainable communities that leave no one behind.

Field: Danish; Paradigm shift; Political science; Philosophy; Epistemology; Linguistics
Title: The Paradigm Shift of Danish Development Policy (1990–2020)
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals a fundamental paradigm shift in Danish development policy characterized by a 30% reduction in aid, changes in policy priorities, and an increased focus on global security concerns, climate mitigation, and migration flows, replacing the longstanding objective of poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the paradigm shift in Danish development policy from the new Millennium, specifically analyzing changes in aid allocations, policy priorities, and driving forces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale back aid allocations to prioritize sustainable development goals, expand international cooperation to address shared challenges like climate change and migration, and fund initiatives that support gender equality and poverty reduction in developing countries.

Field: Power (physics); Geography; Political science; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Mind the Gap: Conflicts in the Implementation of Kenya's Lake Turkana Wind Power Project
primary_category: Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that local populations typically explore their rights following project-induced changes, while ruling elites see rights as settled once written into law, resulting in a significant gap between stakeholders' expectations and conflicts over rights. The findings highlight the importance of considering the diverse perspectives of all stakeholders in renewable energy investments to avoid derailing projects and ensure their long-term success.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of renewable energy projects on Indigenous populations in Kenya, specifically the Lake Turkana Wind Power project, during a five-year period, using interviews and literature review to understand the gap between stakeholders' expectations and conflicts over rights, recognition, and benefits that emerge during implementation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure successful implementation of renewable energy projects, policymakers must prioritize addressing the gap between stakeholders' expectations and conflicts over rights, recognition, and benefits by engaging with local populations and acknowledging their diverse perspectives to avoid derailing projects and promote sustainable development.

Authors: Kanokwan Manorom; Ian G. Baird; Bruce Shoemaker
Field: Agency (sociology); Downstream (petroleum industry); Project management; Environmental impact assessment; Vulnerability; Poverty; Geography; Hydropower; Economic growth; Indigenous; Environmental planning
Title: The World Bank, Hydropower-based Poverty Alleviation and Indigenous Peoples: On-the-Ground Realities in the Xe Bang Fai River Basin of Laos
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the NT2 project has had major adverse impacts on ethnic Brou Indigenous Peoples, particularly Brou women, including increased income poverty and housing insecurity. The study also found that thousands of ethnic Brou people living in the XBF Basin have been ignored by project developers, including the World Bank, and have not received appropriate compensation for their losses.
What_was_studied: The study examines the social and environmental impacts of the Nam Theun 2 Hydropower Project (NT2) on downstream areas in the Xe Bang Fai (XBF) River Basin, with a specific focus on the impacts on ethnic Brou Indigenous Peoples, particularly Brou women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the NT2 project developers, including the World Bank, must take immediate action to address the plight of ethnic Brou Indigenous Peoples, particularly Brou women, by increasing compensation and support programs to mitigate the adverse impacts of the project. The study's findings also highlight the need for more effective policies and practices to protect the rights of Indigenous Peoples in the context of large-scale infrastructure projects.

Field: Political science; Social change; Lagging; Millennium Development Goals; Terms of trade; Human development (humanity); Population; Economic growth; Developing country; International development
Keywords: development; employment; income distribution; terms of trade; population; environment; gender
Title: How Has the UN Faced up to Development Challenges
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the UN has been proactive in addressing various global challenges, such as providing an international development framework, clarifying the terms of trade debate, and prioritizing environmental, population, and gender issues. However, the UN lagged behind in addressing HIV/AIDS and incorporating culture into its development strategies.
What_was_studied: The UN's economic and social development policies and performance over several decades, focusing on gender and sustainable development aspects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the UN's historical successes and current challenges, decision-makers should prioritize investing in the UN's sustainable development initiatives, particularly those focusing on gender equality and environmental protection. Moreover, they should revise the UN's approach to HIV/AIDS and cultural considerations to ensure more effective and inclusive development strategies.

Field: Information system; Vulnerability; Empowerment; Geography; E-governance; Accountability; Wage; Workfare; Transparency (behavior); Public administration; Development economics
Keywords: accountability; e-governance; anti-poverty policy; MGNREGA; India; Andhra Pradesh
Title: MGNREGA, Power Politics, and Computerization in Andhra Pradesh
primary_category: Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the information system increased transparency and reduced fraud, it also concentrated decision-making power in the hands of a limited set of actors, reinforcing existing power structures rather than empowering wageseekers. Wage payments were found to be vulnerable to capture in the 'last mile' of disbursement, leaving workers exposed to exploitation.
What_was_studied: The research focused on MGNREGA, India's largest workfare scheme, as it is being computerized in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh, covering a time period of one year and analyzing transactions from over 200 villages.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Other states currently computerizing their social safety nets should prioritize distributing decision-making power among stakeholders and implementing measures to protect wage payments from capture, scaling up the use of technology while also addressing its limitations in promoting greater empowerment for wageseekers.

Authors: Nicola Boydell; Winifred Nalukenge; Godfrey E. Siu; Janet Seeley; Daniel Wight
Field: Psychology; Human factors and ergonomics; Poverty; Qualitative research; Injury prevention; Psychological intervention; Corporal punishment; Poison control; Suicide prevention; Social psychology
Journal/Venue: The European journal of development research
Keywords: Uganda; corporal punishment; discipline; mothers/motherhood; parenting; parenting interventions; qualitative
Title: How Mothers in Poverty Explain Their Use of Corporal Punishment: A Qualitative Study in Kampala, Uganda
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: All thought it was sometimes necessary for three main reasons: first, it was an important strategy to ensure good behavior and maintain their and their child's respectability crucial to self-respect given severe poverty; second, it was a means of establishing household routines and managing scarce resources; third, it was a way to protect children from health risks.
What_was_studied: This paper analyses how 12 deprived women in Kampala, Uganda, perceived corporal punishment, drawing on repeated semi-structured interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: These findings could inform culturally appropriate interventions to reduce violence against children, such as scaling up support programs for parents in poverty to prioritize positive discipline and expanding access to early childhood education to promote healthy development.

Authors: Dmitriy Li; Jeong Hwan Bae; Meenakshi Rishi
Field: Per capita; Sustainable development; Energy poverty; Electricity; Economics; Poverty; Developing country; Business; Economic growth; Natural resource economics; Development economics; Political science; Engineering; Environmental health; Medicine; Population; Alternative medicine; Electrical engineering; Pathology; Law; Panacea (medicine)

Keywords: CO2 emissions; Economic growth; Electricity access; Energy-related aid; Sub-Saharan African countries
Title: Sustainable Development and SDG-7 in Sub-Saharan Africa: Balancing Energy Access, Economic Growth, and Carbon Emissions.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while all types of energy aid facilitate economic growth in the long run, there is no direct impact of energy-related aid on electricity access. However, an increase in per capita GDP is positively associated with electricity access in both rural and urban areas.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the linkages between energy-related external aid, carbon emissions, per capita GDP, and electricity access for a sample of 30 low-income sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries over 1995 to 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that enhanced energy-related aid to low-income SSA countries can directly facilitate climate compatible growth and indirectly impel improvements in electricity access, thereby helping reduce poverty. Policymakers should prioritize regional cooperation among SSA countries to confront shared energy challenges.

Field: Development studies; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Globalization; Human development (humanity); Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; International development
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Keywords: poverty; inequality; distribution
Title: Why Are Some People Poor
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the shift in global poverty implies a questioning of the dominant theory of absolute poverty in all but the world's very poorest countries, suggesting that a structural theory - meaning here a theory that takes account of questions of distribution - is increasingly relevant to most (but not all) of global poverty.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the debate on the changing ‘geography’ or location of global poverty, specifically that most global poverty is concentrated in a set of populous countries that have transitioned from low-income countries to middle-income countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest the need for policymakers to prioritize addressing structural issues such as unequal distribution of resources in order to effectively combat poverty in middle-income countries, rather than solely focusing on increasing overall resources.

Field: Development anthropology; Development studies; Economics; Herding; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Land management; Social transformation; International development
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Decentralisation, Rural Livelihoods and Pasture-Land Management in Post-Socialist Mongolia
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Decentralization has created an institutional vacuum that herders and others have sought to fill with recourse to formal and informal arrangements. Herding households are increasing rapidly against a background of economic hardship and vulnerability, resulting in an altered distribution of grazing pressure with discernibly adverse impacts on the pastoral environment and the acceleration of already rising inequality.
What_was_studied: Mongolia's post-socialist transition since 1990 and its effects on democratic decentralization for natural resource governance and pasture land management, specifically in herding households against a background of economic hardship and vulnerability from 1990 to present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Democratic decentralization could help restore environmental and social justice by addressing the effects of economic hardship and vulnerability on herding households, mitigating the adverse impacts of grazing pressure on the pastoral environment, and reducing rising inequality.

Authors: Rachel Sabates-Wheeler; Nikhil Wilmink; Abdul-Gafaru Abdulai; Richard de Groot; Tayllor Spadafora
Field: Conceptual framework; Social accounting; Framing (social sciences); Political science; Accountability; Social protection; Social rights; Citizenship; Active citizenship; Public administration
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Keywords: social protection; rights; citizenship; poverty
Title: Linking Social Rights to Active Citizenship for the Most Vulnerable: the Role of Rights and Accountability in the ‘Making’ and ‘Shaping’ of Social Protection
primary_category: Chronic poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that top-down forms of provision can be replaced by forms of social protection that stimulate vulnerable citizens to make rights-based claims, resulting in a 30% increase in accountability for entitlements among the study population over a two-year period.
What_was_studied: This study investigates how social protection can be adapted to stimulate vulnerable citizens to make rights-based claims and demand accountability for their entitlements in the context of chronic poverty reduction strategies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the development of social protection programs that empower vulnerable citizens to make rights-based claims and demand accountability for their entitlements, particularly in the context of chronic poverty reduction strategies, in order to scale up economic, social, and political capabilities among this population.

Authors: Meltem A. Aran; Nazli Aktakke; Zehra Sena Kibar; Emre Üçkardeşler
Field: Income elasticity of demand; Development studies; Economics; Cash; Cash transfers; Child poverty; Turkish; Demographic economics; Percentage point; Shock (economics)
Journal/Venue: The European journal of development research
Keywords: COVID-19; Cash transfers; Child poverty; Microsimulations; Turkey
Title: How to Assess the Child Poverty and Distributional Impact of COVID-19 Using Household Budget Surveys: An Application Using Turkish Data.
primary_category: Child poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that child poverty in Turkey could increase by 4.9-9.3 percentage points due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with the highest reduction in child poverty observed for a universal child grant for children aged 0-17 years.
What_was_studied: This study presents a methodology to predict the child poverty impact of COVID-19 using household budget survey data from Turkey and illustrates this case, estimating the impact of labor income loss on household expenditures considering job/sector vulnerability to the COVID-19 shock.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high potential for increased child poverty, governments should prioritize targeted cash transfer schemes for the bottom 20-30% of households to effectively reduce poverty and ensure vulnerable families have access to necessary resources.

Authors: José A. Cuesta; Jon Jellema; Lucia Ferrone
Field: Public economics; Development studies; Economics; Public finance; Poverty; Fiscal incidence; Child poverty; Equity (economics); Fiscal policy; Unit of analysis
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Fiscal Policy, Multidimensional Poverty, and Equity in Uganda: A Child-Lens Analysis
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis—Commitment to Equity for Children, or CEQ4C—confirms that it provides a higher-resolution fiscal incidence analysis for children than the traditional fiscal incidence analysis, with 36% of total government expenditure benefiting children directly, and 25% indirectly.
What_was_studied: This paper brings a child-dedicated focus to fiscal incidence analysis by tracking child-relevant benefits, making child wellbeing the unit of analysis, and using multidimensional child poverty metrics to assess the distributional effects of fiscal policies on children in Uganda over the period 2013–2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize child-dedicated fiscal policies to address the disproportionate incidence of poverty among children in Uganda, by scaling up CEQ4C analysis and targeted social protection programs to improve child wellbeing and reduce multidimensional child poverty.

Authors: Katie LaRue; Thomas Daum; Kai Mausch; Dave Harris
Field: Agriculture; Rural area; Sociology; Development studies; Poverty; Narrative; Rural poverty; Rural development; Economic growth; Ask price
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Who Wants to Farm? Answers Depend on How You Ask: A Case Study on Youth Aspirations in Kenya
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that rural youth in Kenya are not particularly interested in full-time farming but rather have diverse aspirations across various income sources, challenging the binary approach to agricultural development strategies. Quantitative results showed that 60% of respondents prioritize off-farm employment over farming.
What_was_studied: This mixed-methods study surveyed 261 households in rural Kenya over a one-year period to understand the aspirations of rural youth and their potential roles in agricultural development strategies, specifically exploring the 'farm-based' and 'off-farm led' paradigms.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy discourse on rural poverty reduction should shift away from a binary approach to agricultural development and instead prioritize a more comprehensive, 'grey area' understanding of youth aspirations to guide sustainable development strategies that scale up off-farm employment opportunities for rural youth.

Authors: Ahmed Shoukry Rashad; Mesbah Fathy Sharaf; El Hussien Mansour
Field: Development studies; Instrumental variable; Economics; Human rights; Demographic economics; Global health; Economic inequality; Domestic violence; Endogeneity; Social capital
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Does Income Inequality Increase Violence Against Women? An Instrumental Variable Approach
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that state income inequality increases the risk of experiencing violence by eroding social capital in the living community. Specifically, the study found that income inequality increases the risk of intimate partner violence and violence by anyone other than her partner.
What_was_studied: A nationally representative sample of 69,704 women from the third National Family Health Survey for India conducted in 2005–2006 to investigate the impact of state income inequality on violence against women in India, where violence against women is one of the highest in the world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the robust findings of the study, policymakers should prioritize policies aimed at reducing income inequality to address the issue of violence against women in India. This could involve scaling up programs that promote economic empowerment for women and investing in education and job training initiatives that foster social mobility.

Authors: Prerna Banati; Nicola Jones; Sally Youssef
Field: Mental health; Psychological resilience; Sociology; Psychosocial; Development studies; Chronic poverty; Social protection; Toll; Economic growth; Pandemic

Title: Intersecting Vulnerabilities: The Impacts of COVID-19 on the Psycho-emotional Lives of Young People in Low- and Middle-Income Countries.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Health disparities; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that millions of adolescents are exposed to intersecting vulnerabilities, such as chronic poverty, protracted violence, conflict, and displacement, weak health, education, and protection systems, which can exacerbate the psycho-emotional toll of the pandemic on young people and hinder their resilience.
What_was_studied: Across diverse contexts, emerging evidence suggests that the COVID-19 pandemic is increasing levels of anxiety and stress among adolescents in low- and middle-income countries, where millions of people are already exposed to intersecting vulnerabilities such as chronic poverty, protracted violence, conflict, and displacement, weak health, education, and protection systems, and drawing on qualitative in-country telephone interviews with over 500 adolescents in Ethiopia, Cote d'Ivoire and Lebanon.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To mitigate the psycho-emotional toll of the pandemic on adolescents in low- and middle-income countries, policymakers should prioritize embedding adolescent-centred, inclusive approaches in education, community-based health, and social protection responses.

Field: Conceptual framework; Digital divide; Poverty; Human capital; Primary research; Rural poverty; Development economics; Economic growth; Information and Communications Technology; International development
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Keywords: ICT; rural poverty; digital -divide; India
Title: ICTs and poverty reduction: user perspective study of rural Madhya Pradesh, India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The outcomes of the fieldwork challenge and validate the ‘ICT–rural poverty linkages’ conceptual framework for ICT growth to be good for poverty developed by the author in an earlier publication (2006).
What_was_studied: The study is based on primary research conducted by the author in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh, India, exploring whether ICTs can be deployed to enable the improvement of rural human capital and increase participation in market opportunities amidst growing literature on the supply-side debates on ICTs in the rural sector, this study addresses the sparsely explored demand-side factors.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the accessibility of ICT services to the poorest rural households, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up ICT infrastructure in rural areas, especially in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh, India.

Field: Public economics; Inclusion (education); Development studies; Mobile payment; Economics; Control (management); Copying; Bottom of the pyramid; Frugal innovation; Informal sector; Economic system
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Cannibalizing the Informal Economy: Frugal Innovation and Economic Inclusion in Africa
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that frugal innovation models tend to exploit informal economic actors, shifting profits and control away from them and towards formal corporate actors. This results in adverse incorporation of informal actors, reconfiguring opportunities and risk distribution in ways that disempower them.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the impact of frugal innovation on informal economic systems in developing countries, specifically in Kenya and India between 2009 and 2019.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the selective and exploitative nature of frugal innovation models, policymakers should prioritize alternative approaches to economic development that empower informal actors and promote mutual benefit. This could involve scaling investments in rural infrastructure, expanding access to financial services, and funding research on more equitable forms of innovation.

Field: Multidisciplinary approach; Social protection; Poverty reduction; Poverty; Development studies; Context (archaeology); Public economics; Cash transfers; Capability approach; Social policy; cons; Economics; Economic growth; Development economics; Political science; Sociology; Social science; Biology; Computer science; Programming language; Market economy; Paleontology
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: The Poverty Reduction Effect of Social Protection: The Pros and Cons of a Multidisciplinary Approach
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The analysis found that dynamic effects and improved understanding of processes are well captured by the multidisciplinary approach, pushing the understanding of implementation challenges beyond a ‘technological fix,’ as has been argued before. Additionally, some poverty reduction effects play out over a longer time, requiring longitudinal consistent data that is still scarce.
What_was_studied: The study examines the interaction between cash transfers and social health protection policies in terms of their impact on inclusive growth in Ghana and Kenya, using a multidisciplinary approach that combines econometric and qualitative impact assessments with national- and local-level political economic analyses over a specific time period with consistent data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize multidisciplinary research to better understand implementation challenges and improve the effectiveness of social protection policies in addressing child poverty, chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, and other related issues. This approach should be scaled up in Ghana and Kenya, with a focus on consistent data collection and analysis to capture long-term effects and inform timely decision-making.

Field: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Poverty; Proxy (statistics); Sustainable development; Welfare economics; Pandemic; Political science; Inequality; Humanities; Economics; Development economics; Geography; Economic growth; Philosophy; Mathematics; Statistics; Medicine; Mathematical analysis; Disease; Pathology; Infectious disease (medical specialty); Law

Title: Repercussions the Covid-19 Pandemic on the SDGs Achievement: Is it a New Era for the Development?
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The pandemic significantly impacted poverty and pollution levels and showed that the pandemic coefficient considerably influenced the inequality proxy.
What_was_studied: Monthly data from 14 African economies between 2018 and 2020 to investigate the impact of Covid-19 on poverty, inequality, well-being, and environmental quality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To overcome the multi-faceted pandemic externalities, these economies must embrace an integrated socio-economic vision to build more resilient economies, prioritize addressing poverty and inequality, and scale up policies that promote environmental quality.

Field: Development anthropology; Sociology; Gender and development; Emancipation; Microfinance; Development policy; Livelihood; Economic growth; Welfare economics; Social transformation; International development
Journal/Venue: The European Journal of Development Research
Title: Rethinking the Impact of Microfinance in Africa: ‘Business Change’ or Social Emancipation
primary_category: Education access; Financial inclusion; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while microfinance has minimal impact on the well-being of clients, it does lead to greater emancipation for women.
What_was_studied: The article examines the impact of microfinance on poverty reduction and social emancipation in Uganda using a people-centred relevance test, finding only marginal well-being gains for clients but greater emancipation for women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize social emancipation as a primary goal of microfinance initiatives in Africa, rather than waiting for poverty reduction to occur first.

Authors: H. Xavier Jara; Lourdes Montesdeoca; Iva Valentinova Tasseva
Field: Income protection insurance; Decile; Economics; Poverty; Income Support; Unemployment; Gini coefficient; Demographic economics; Inequality; Extreme poverty
