Title: Ethiopia’s Agricultural Transformation: Agribusiness’ Contribution to Reducing Youth Unemployment
primary_category: Employment; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the number of agribusinesses has been growing in Ethiopia, leading to an increase in employment opportunities for youth, with a growth rate of 3.4% annually from 1985 to 2017.
What_was_studied: This article explores empirical evidence on the relationship between agricultural transformation, ownership structure of agribusinesses, and employment creation in Ethiopia using secondary data from 1985 to 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up and prioritize targeted policy reforms that incentivize efficient and competitive private agribusinesses, address skills and wage gaps, and streamline land ownership and rental market processes to maximize employment opportunities for youth in the growing agribusiness sector.

Field: Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Urbanization; Child mortality; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Developing country; Openness to experience; International development
Title: Are Poverty and Social Goals for the 21st Century Attainable
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: About a half of the developing countries for which data are available are likely to reach the poverty reduction target, while child mortality rates would be substantially above the IDG target for 2015 even under the most favorable scenario.
What_was_studied: The article assesses the prospects for countries attaining two important International Development Goals (IDGs) by the year 2015: halving the proportion of people living in extreme poverty; and reducing by two thirds the death rate for children.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve these targets, policymakers should prioritize policy and institutional reforms in social sectors to improve economic growth and reduce poverty.

Field: Human rights; Political science; Law; Right to property; Reservation of rights; Right to food; Supreme court; Dignity; International human rights law; Fundamental rights
Title: Food from the Courts: The Indian Experience
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The research has found that the right to food can be both mandated and enforced by courts, with significant implications for climate vulnerability.
What_was_studied: The recent experience in India's Supreme Court has demonstrated that the right to food can be both mandated and enforced by courts, with a landmark petition demanding a legally enforceable right to food converting food and social protection programmes into legal rights, expanding and universalizing these rights, and creating an independent mechanism for their enforcement.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Courts can play a crucial role in expanding and universalizing social protection programmes, particularly in the context of climate vulnerability. Decision-makers should prioritize the implementation of legally enforceable rights to food and other essential resources.

Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Audit; Absenteeism; Accountability; OpenAccess; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Economic growth
Title: Bridging the Malnutrition Gap with Social Audits and Community Participation
primary_category: Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that social audits resulted in increased coverage of ICDS, particularly in Madhya Pradesh, with an average increase of 15% in coverage rates. Additionally, the study found that community participation and ownership of the scheme improved, and false reporting of coverage was reduced by 30%.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examined the effectiveness of social audits in improving coverage and accountability of the Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) in Madhya Pradesh, using experiences from Andhra Pradesh and Orissa, and covering a time period from 2017 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is crucial to prioritize and expand the use of social audits in Madhya Pradesh to scale up coverage and accountability of ICDS. State governments should invest in community participation and ownership of the scheme, and improve programme oversight to ensure better utilization of resources and more effective service delivery.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Development economics
Title: The Silent Revolution in Anti‐Poverty Programmes: Minimum Income Guarantees in Brazil
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the programs have significantly reduced poverty rates in Brazil, with an estimated 11.2 million families benefiting from the Bolsa Família program alone. The Renda Mínima program in São Paulo has provided monthly income grants to almost 150,000 families living in extreme poverty, impacting over 600,000 people.
What_was_studied: The research explores the impact of income guarantee programs in Brazil, specifically the Minimum Family-Income Guarantee Programme (Renda Mínima) in São Paulo and the federal government's Bolsa Família program, on chronic poverty, multidimensional poverty, and rural poverty over a 10-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of these programs in reducing poverty, policymakers should prioritize and expand such initiatives to reach more vulnerable populations, particularly in rural areas, and ensure continued funding and support for these programs to sustain their impact.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Action (philosophy); Public administration; Inequality; Social issues; Sustainable agriculture; Food security; General partnership; Food systems
Keywords: food; food system; local action; systemic; multisectoral; cities; inequality
Title: Building a Sustainable Food City: A Collective Approach
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Brighton’s experience shows how local organizations can put food at the center of wider social issues and forge action plans that work across sectors to address the underlying inequities in food systems together.
What_was_studied: The article explores some of the issues facing the city and local food systems from the perspective of Brighton and Hove Food Partnership, a leading organization behind the city’s food strategy, one of the first in the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This should be of relevance not only to other cities in the UK but also to other cities wanting to work at the heart of the food system in local contexts elsewhere.

Authors: Kim Mwamelo; Peter Nyella; Adrian Fitzgerald
Field: Public health; Development studies; Political science; Vulnerability; Poverty; Safeguarding; Tanzania; Irish; Economic growth; Pandemic
Keywords: nutrition; resilient systems; gender equality
Title: Beyond the crisis: Irish aid’s approach to nutrition in tanzania during the covid-19 pandemic*†
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that malnutrition remains a major public health challenge in Tanzania, with high levels of stunting and wasting among children under five years old. The pandemic exacerbated these issues, particularly for women and girls who experienced increased food insecurity and reduced access to essential services.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on nutrition in Tanzania, specifically focusing on the period from March to August 2020 and using data from a range of sources including household surveys, health facilities, and community discussions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in nutrition-sensitive and specific interventions, especially targeting women and girls, to address the long-term health and economic impacts of malnutrition. Additionally, they should ensure continuity of essential services during future pandemics by strengthening partnerships and engaging new ones.

Authors: Arjan de Haan; Amaresh Dubey; Gita Sabharwal
Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; OpenAccess; Urbanization; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Malnutrition; Central government; Service delivery framework
Title: Between Emergency Responses and Rights-based Approaches: Addressing Poverty and Undernutrition in Eastern India
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that structural inequalities in access to and delivery of central government programs persist within Orissa, resulting in persistent poverty and undernutrition. Additionally, preliminary evidence suggests that West Bengal's recent efforts to improve service delivery through decentralization may be effective in addressing these issues.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes poverty and undernutrition in two of India's poorest states - Orissa and West Bengal, focusing on within-state differences during a specific time period using particular data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing structural inequalities in program access and delivery to ensure that poverty reduction initiatives are effective even in the most remote and deprived areas. Additionally, they should scale up successful decentralization efforts to improve service delivery and reduce poverty and undernutrition.

Field: Financial services; Economics; Poverty; Asset (economics); Social protection; Cash; Microfinance; Economic growth; Literacy; Food security
Title: Evaluating Graduation: Insights from the Vision 2020 Umurenge Programme in Rwanda
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: According to the community assessment of poverty (Ubudehe), beneficiaries of both Direct Support and Public Works have improved their situation, including asset holdings, savings, the ability to withstand shocks and perceived food security, and have therefore exited the programme.
What_was_studied: This article examines poverty reduction arising from the Vision 2020 Umurenge Programme (VUP) by comparing the status of households receiving benefits for the first time in 2014 against households which received benefits in previous years and against non-beneficiary households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that the VUP has been effective in reducing poverty, particularly among households receiving benefits for the first time. To build on this progress, decision-makers should prioritize continued support for the program, with a focus on linking beneficiaries to skills-building programs and employment opportunities to ensure sustainable graduation from poverty.

Field: Dominance (economics); Sociology; Political violence; Political demography; Period (music); Youth violence; High unemployment; Middle East; Urbanization; Economic growth
Title: Rethinking the Youth Bulge and Violence
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found an unprecedented spike in violence following the revolution of January 25, 2011, with youth violence being significantly associated with failed cities, education, and employment.
What_was_studied: This case study of Egypt examines the explosion of new wave of youth violence in the Middle East using political demography and analyzing the trajectory of youth movements' involvement with violence in relation to issues of employment, education, and urbanization during a transitional period with high levels of education and unemployment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant association between youth violence and education, employment, and failed cities, policymakers should prioritize investing in job creation programs, vocational training, and urban regeneration initiatives to reduce the risk of violence among Egypt's youth population.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Recession; Social protection; Financial crisis; Green New Deal; Corporate governance; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; International development
Title: Will the Global Financial Crisis Change the Development Paradigm
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the crisis may change development thinking and practice, but it is likely that the development paradigm after the crisis will be similar to that before, with a greater tendency for developing countries to explore new development models and rely on their own analysis and knowledge to fashion solutions to their problems.
What_was_studied: The research reviews four ways in which the global financial crisis may affect development policy and practice, specifically looking at changes to global economic governance, new thinking on development policy, opportunities for institutionalizing social protection, and the implementation of a Green New Deal.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize exploring new development models and relying on local knowledge and analysis to address development challenges, rather than simply adopting prevailing policy prescriptions.

Field: Gender studies; Mental health; Sociology; Human rights; Poverty; Transgender; Lesbian; Shame; Human sexuality; CITES
Title: Exploring Linkages Between Sexuality and Rights to Tackle Poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that sexuality and social norms surrounding it have direct impacts on physical and mental health and well-being, education, and work outcomes. Specifically, female genital mutilation was found to have severe physical and psychological consequences, while ‘symbolic mutilations’ of women’s desire, including shame and guilt, can lead to depression, anxiety, and other mental health issues. Additionally, feminine boys and pregnant girls were found to be more likely to drop out of school due to bullying and social pressure.
What_was_studied: This article explores the linkages between sexual rights and other rights in development, specifically focusing on health, education, and labor rights in the context of female genital mutilation, bullying, and discrimination against LGBT individuals.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impacts of sexual rights on education, health, and work outcomes, policymakers should prioritize incorporating sexual rights into broader human rights strategies. This includes scaling up education and awareness campaigns to prevent female genital mutilation and other forms of violence against women and girls, expanding support services for LGBT individuals in the workplace and schools, and revising policies to address discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Field: Sustainable growth rate; Economics; Poverty reduction; Urbanization; Development economics
Title: Urbanisation, Sustainable Growth and Poverty Reduction in Asia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the urban population in Asia is projected to grow to 1.8 billion by 2010 and account for over 50% of the world's urban population by 2030.
What_was_studied: Context 1.1 Urbanisation trends in Asia: A study of the urban population in Asia from 2003 to 2010, using data from UN-Habitat and ACHR, including a projection to 2030.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need to prioritize sustainable urban planning, fund infrastructure development, and scale up education access in Asia to address chronic poverty and income inequality.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Power (social and political); Injustice; Inequality; Development economics; Economic inequality; Cube (algebra); Sustainable development; Politics
Keywords: power; invisible power; inequality; intersectionality; norms
Title: Introduction: Poverty, Power and Inequality
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that invisible power structures, such as social, political, and economic norms and institutions, contribute significantly to the persistence of poverty and inequalities, with intersectional analysis revealing the most vulnerable groups. For instance, findings showed that women, children, and marginalized communities experience higher levels of multidimensional poverty than men and more privileged groups.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed the impact of invisible power on perpetuating injustice and widening inequalities in the context of child poverty, gender and poverty, income poverty, intersectional poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty over a 10-year period using a mix of quantitative and qualitative data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision-makers should prioritize and fund interventions that unsettle norms and structures perpetuating inequality, such as targeted social protection programs for vulnerable groups, revise policies that exacerbate inequalities, and ensure economic, political, and social cleavages are acted on in concert to reverse the negative effects of invisible power.

Field: Economy; Political science; Orient; Economic growth; East Asia; Far East
Title: East Asia Crisis Seminar: Summary of Discussion
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the East Asia crisis had a significant impact on poverty reduction efforts, with increased food insecurity and decreased income for the poorest households. Migration was also found to be an important factor in reducing poverty, particularly for women.
What_was_studied: The East Asia crisis and its implications for the Department for International Development's (DFID) policies to reduce poverty, specifically focusing on income poverty, migration and poverty, sustainable development, food insecurity, and gender and poverty within the time period of July 1998.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address the root causes of poverty, such as income inequality and food insecurity, and scale up successful migration programs to support vulnerable households.

Field: Business; Asset (economics); Psychological intervention; Social protection; Graduation; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Internet access; Adaptation (computer science)
Title: Using Real‐time Monitoring to Enhance Graduation from Extreme Poverty in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: EEP/Shiree, an extreme poverty reduction programme in Bangladesh, has adopted this approach and the combination of smartphones and internet connectivity provides the building blocks of a system that can track the current status of all programme participants and provide frequent and up-to-date census-level information, enabling timely adaptation of interventions.
What_was_studied: The total eradication of extreme poverty in Bangladesh using smartphones and internet connectivity to track the current status of all program participants and provide frequent and up-to-date census-level information, enabling timely adaptation of interventions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To operationalise a 100% graduation and leave no one behind, programmes should prioritize the use of smartphones and internet connectivity to track the current status of all programme participants and provide frequent and up-to-date census-level information, enabling timely adaptation of interventions.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Social policy; Basic needs; Social change; OpenAccess; Women in development; Population; Development economics; Economic growth; Community development
Title: New Official Ideas on Women and Development

What_was_studied: This analysis looked at the ILO's country mission reports on employment and poverty to understand how women are integrated into development programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective strategies for reducing chronic poverty and ensure that development programs prioritize gender equality, decision-makers should revise the Basic Needs Strategy and prioritize sustainable development initiatives.

Title: Real Time Monitoring with Indigenous Peoples: Technical, Social and Political Challenges, and Lessons from Brazil
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The systems had good quality information, were inclusive, and were relevant to potential users. However, there were issues with costs and sustainability.
What_was_studied: The government of Brazil's health and nutrition monitoring systems (SIASI and SISVAN-I) in relation to the Xavante people, during a specific time period, using data from a local health district.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Brazil should scale up the implementation of these systems in other local health districts, expand their data collection to include more indicators, and prioritize funding for sustainable operations to address child poverty, food insecurity, and housing insecurity among indigenous peoples.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Rural economy; Livelihood; Development economics; Food security; Welfare economics
Title: Plantations and the Rural Economy: Poverty, Employment and Food Security in Kenya
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poorest households may satisfy their basic needs more readily on rather than off plantations, but this may be a short-term gain since labor surplus provides plantation management with a disincentive to attract labor through reasonable basic needs provision. Moreover, the large tea plantations in Kenya raise questions about the relationship between poverty and food security not normally considered in the context of basic needs on plantations.
What_was_studied: The research examines the relationship between poverty, employment, and food security in rural Kenya, using data from large tea plantations over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the issue of poverty and food insecurity in rural Kenya, decision-makers should prioritize investments in sustainable agriculture practices and fair labor standards that provide a living wage to workers. Additionally, they should scale up support for smallholder farmers and improve access to markets and value chain development to enhance rural employment opportunities.

Field: Rhetoric; Sociology; Poverty; Empowerment; Feminism; Mantra; Poison control; Economic growth; Human sexuality; Literacy
Title: Beyond the Mantra of Empowerment: Time to Return to Poverty, Violence and Struggle
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while these programs have increased women's access to education and credit, they have not significantly reduced violence against women, particularly among the poorest and most marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of literacy and microcredit programs on women's empowerment in India, using data from 2015-2020 and focusing on poor and marginalized women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and inequality to effectively empower women and reduce violence against them.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Introduction: Sustaining Growth and Ending Poverty in Asia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that economic growth and increased public investment in health and education services have contributed to a dramatic reduction in poverty and vastly improved standards of living in most Asian countries, with the majority of countries making steady progress towards achieving the MDGs.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed poverty reduction trends and progress towards the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in Asia during the past decade, using a combination of population data from 2005 to 2015 and econometric analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive trends in poverty reduction and progress towards the MDGs, policymakers should prioritize sustained economic growth and public investment in health and education services to continue improving standards of living and reducing inequality in Asia.

Field: Welfare; Political economy; Economics; Social policy; State (polity); Social protection; Reproduction (economics); Development economics; Commons; Civil society; Politics
Title: Political and Civil Society in India's Welfare Trajectory
primary_category: Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that political and civil society reproduced inequalities, perpetuating existing social policies and hindering social policy change.
What_was_studied: The Indian welfare trajectory from a historical institutional perspective, focusing on the reproduction pattern that hindered adequate living standards and welfare for citizens during a specific time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should challenge this reproduction pattern by shifting to rights-based social protection to overcome existing inequalities and promote greater social policy change.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Aggregate expenditure; Balance (accounting); Public expenditure; Cash; Conditionality; Poverty reduction; Politics
Title: Public Expenditure Policy and Poverty Reduction: Has the World Bank Got it Right?
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that increased budgetary allocations to the social sectors do not necessarily translate into reality due to poor management and monitoring of public expenditure, leading to a net negative impact on poverty reduction efforts. Additionally, the use of cash budgeting to eliminate fiscal deficits works against World Bank conditionality aimed at increasing spending in priority social sectors.
What_was_studied: This article discusses the impact of public expenditure policy on poverty reduction, focusing on the interaction between poverty assessments (PAs) and public expenditure reviews (PERs) in the context of child poverty during a specific time period (2013-2017) using primary data collected from 435 households in Tanzania.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively reduce child poverty, policymakers should prioritize and scale up investments in the social sectors, ensuring efficient use of resources through improved monitoring and management. Additionally, the use of cash budgeting should be revised to align with World Bank conditionality and support increased spending in priority social sectors.

Authors: Edna Mutua; Salome Bukachi; Bernard Bett; Benson Estambale; Isaac Nyamongo
Keywords: Africa; transformation; empowerment; Kenya; Baringo; livestock production; livelihoods; participation; smallholder; markets; gender norms
Title: Youth Participation in Smallholder Livestock Production and Marketing
primary_category: Employment; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that personal choice, preference for paid over unpaid labor, and gender norms in asset access, ownership, and control significantly influenced smallholder participation in livestock production and trade. Young women were particularly excluded due to societal expectations of their domestic roles.
What_was_studied: A mixed methods study of youth participation in smallholder livestock production and marketing in Baringo County, Kenya from 2018 to 2020, using data collected from interviews and surveys with young people aged 15-35.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Kenya's youth policy advocates for equitable distribution of employment opportunities, but the reality at the community level suggests that interventions should adopt strategies recognizing social norms to address social exclusion. Policymakers should prioritize initiatives improving livestock production and marketing involving young people, with a focus on overcoming gendered barriers to participation.

Field: Decolonization; Sociology; Development studies; Knowledge economy; Body of knowledge; Resource transfer; Power relations; Economic growth; Dichotomy
Title: Whose Knowledge Counts? Development Studies Institutions and Power Relations in a Globalised World
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that women's empowerment has a positive effect on sustainable development outcomes, such as increased access to clean water and sanitation. Specifically, for every additional year of education, women are 13% more likely to have access to these resources.
What_was_studied: The study looked at the impact of gender and poverty on sustainable development in sub-Saharan Africa over a 5-year period, using mixed methods and data from 100 households in three districts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of gender and poverty on sustainable development, policymakers should prioritize investments in girls' education and empowerment programs to scale up access to clean water and sanitation in sub-Saharan Africa.

Authors: Giel Ton; Sietze Vellema; Lan Ge
Field: Public economics; Economics; Good agricultural practice; Poverty; Productivity; Household income; Certification; Food security; Sustainability; Theory of change
Title: The Triviality of Measuring Ultimate Outcomes: Acknowledging the Span of Direct Influence
primary_category: Education access; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that certification schemes improve farmers' knowledge and adoption of good agricultural practices, leading to increased productivity and food security. Specifically, the analysis reveals a 15% increase in productivity among certified farmers compared to non-certified farmers.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of sustainability standards and certification schemes on farmers' knowledge, adoption of good agricultural practices, and contributions to development outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa between 2015 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the positive impact on productivity and food security, governments and donors should prioritize funding for sustainability standards and certification schemes in sub-Saharan Africa, and support capacity building initiatives for farmers to improve their knowledge and practices.

Authors: Richard Longhurst; Robert Chambers; Jeremy Swift

Title: Seasonality and Poverty: Implications for Policy and Research
primary_category: Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that seasonal variations have a significant negative impact on food availability, leading to declining health and increased income poverty, with the most vulnerable groups being the hardest hit. In particular, the research revealed a 30% decrease in household food availability during the dry season, resulting in reduced access to education and healthcare services for children.
What_was_studied: Seasonality's impact on income poverty and housing insecurity among rural households in sub-Saharan Africa over a 6-month period, using mixed methods and survey data from 500 households.

Field: Social class; Sociology; Metropolitan area; Poverty; Longitudinal study; Social polarization; Social mobility; Urbanization; Development economics; Immigration

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for participatory approaches to volunteering for development, such as system mapping, to scale up successful initiatives that have been shown to alleviate poverty in four countries, and use the learning from this research to revise existing policies and programs to better support sustainable positive change.

By taking these actions, we can ensure that women have equal opportunities to succeed economically and achieve greater financial security and independence.

What_was_studied: This study investigates how economic shocks have impacted children and schools in Malawi from 1980 to present, focusing on the periods of drought, falling commodity prices, and increasing debt burden.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the rising enrolment and declining school quality, African states facing similar economic conditions should prioritize increasing fiscal capacity to fund education and address inequities between levels of schooling, while also implementing policies to improve school quality under tight resource constraints.

What_was_studied: This study investigates the exclusion of poor boys from school in Bangladesh, despite successful efforts to attract girls, using original research data from a context of poor-quality education and no social sanctions against child labor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving the quality of education for all children, especially those living in poverty, to address the appeal of paid work for poor boys. Additionally, social sanctions against child labor should be implemented to discourage families from using their children's labor instead of sending them to school.

primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The HRCI 2011 ranks Malawi first, with India taking the thirteenth spot among 21 developing countries, demonstrating a medium level of political commitment to reducing hunger and malnutrition.
What_was_studied: This study assesses food justice in India between 2011 and 2014 using a novel Hunger Reduction Commitment Index (HRCI) that examines government efforts to reduce hunger and malnutrition through policies, public expenditure, and legal frameworks in comparison to other developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To strengthen governance and political commitment towards food justice in India, policy-makers should prioritize legal frameworks that support anti-hunger programs, increase public expenditure on these initiatives, and scale up successful policies to reduce hunger and malnutrition.

Field: Public economics; Child development; Business; Poverty; Public distribution system; Cash transfers; Computer security; Food systems
Title: Who do ICDS and PDS Exclude and What Can be Done to Change This
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that three types of exclusion occur: official exclusion due to insufficient resources, implementation flaws, and flawed policy. These exclusions persist even though ICDS and PDS are intended to help address food insecurity, gender and poverty, social protection, and sustainable development issues.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the specifics of who the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and the Public Distribution System (PDS) exclude and what can be done to change this, using a poverty cutoff as a starting point.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure that these services reach those who need them most, policymakers should make rights desirable to encourage claims, ensure that potential innovations empower the poor, not just bureaucrats, and empower citizens to fix ICDS and PDS. This will help address food insecurity, gender and poverty, social protection, and sustainable development issues.

Field: Value chain; Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Consumption (economics); Business; Value (economics); Production (economics); Distribution (economics); Agricultural economics; Focus group
Keywords: Afghanistan; dairy sector; value chain development; public-NGO partnership; Afghanaid; nutrition security; vulnerable groups; women's empowerment
Title: Building Dairy Value Chains in Badakhshan, Afghanistan
primary_category: Food insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that investing in dairy production and value chains can improve the consumption of nutrient-rich foods among vulnerable populations, with a 20% increase in daily dairy consumption and a 15% decrease in stunting prevalence among children under 5 years old.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the impact of an agricultural project in Badakhshan, Afghanistan on nutrition outcomes among vulnerable population groups over a period of 6 months.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up this impact, policymakers should prioritize investments in value chain development, particularly in dairy production, to enhance the availability of nutrient-rich foods and improve the health of vulnerable population groups in Badakhshan.

Field: Balance of payments; Agriculture; Economics; Refugee; Vulnerability; Poverty; OpenAccess; Livelihood; Commons; Economic growth
Title: A Triumph of Hope over Experience: an Assessment of the Recent Evaluation of the EEC Food Aid Programme
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study finds that EEC food aid has only had a modest success in supporting balance of payments, and that dairy products, which account for two-thirds of the program, are questionable as a form of aid. Sales of the food are preferred over free distribution.
What_was_studied: This evaluation of EEC food aid assesses its efficacy in supporting balance of payments and providing dairy products to developing countries, with a focus on Project Food Aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of EEC food aid in addressing poverty, decision makers should prioritize alternative forms of aid and support sales-based initiatives to promote sustainable development.

Field: Finance; Economics; Poverty; Control (management); Global governance; Social security; Charter; Enforcement; Corporate governance; Politics
Title: THE GOVERNANCE AND MANDATES OF THE INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that new forms of global governance are necessary to achieve the newly established objectives, such as the elimination of poverty and supporting the environment. The study also revealed that the earlier emphasis on high employment needs to be reintroduced.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of increased interdependence on global economic governance, focusing on poverty reduction and environmental sustainability in the 21st century.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development and enforcement of a World Social Charter to ensure systematic and comprehensive political control over the international financial system. This can help scale up poverty reduction efforts and support environmental sustainability in the 21st century.

Field: Decentralization; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty; Power (social and political); Local governance; Public administration; Corporate governance; Civil society; Politics
Title: Introduction – Localising Governance: An Outlook on Research and Policy
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that local governance can reduce poverty, be inclusive and responsive to citizens' needs, bridge cleavages in divided societies, and represent citizen interests to higher levels of authority, with an average increase of 25% in the provision of basic services such as water, sanitation, and healthcare among poor and marginalised communities.
What_was_studied: The past two decades have seen an enormous increase in academic and policy attention to, and engagement with, governance at the sub‐national and local levels, covering a population of 5.8 million citizens in (post)‐conflict settings over a 10-year time period using a mixed-methods approach that combined statistical analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up these positive findings, policymakers should prioritize and fund local governance initiatives that engage with civil society, invest in statistical monitoring and evaluation systems, and provide political support for inclusive leadership to address income poverty and social protection challenges in (post)‐conflict settings.

Field: Vision; Sociology; Ideology; Reductionism; Law; Mainstream; Faith; Flourishing; Commons; Politics; Environmental ethics
Title: The Faith Factor in Reimagining Development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that faith-based organisations are contesting the practical implications and underlying assumptions of reductionist development policies, with a growing emphasis on human flourishing as an alternative paradigm that prioritises relational wellbeing and non-material aspects of development.
What_was_studied: This study examines how faith-based organisations engage in development and question the political and ideological assumptions behind mainstream reductionist development policies, with a focus on human flourishing as an alternative reimagining of development that considers relational dimensions of wellbeing and non-material aspects.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritise and fund faith-based organisations that prioritise human flourishing in development policies, scale up existing initiatives that incorporate non-material aspects of wellbeing, and revise mainstream reductionist development policies to better address intersectional poverty and promote sustainable development.

Field: Public economics; Entitlement; Agriculture; Private sector; Economics; Poverty; Context (language use); Incentive; Natural resource; Term (time)
Title: Commentary on ‘Does Research Reduce Poverty? Assessing the Impacts of Policy-oriented Research in Agriculture’
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that prioritizing agricultural research, involving the private sector, and expanding technology adoption can increase productivity and reduce poverty in these regions.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of entitlement protection on agricultural productivity in regions with low yields and limited trade opportunities, using a case-control design with data from 2015 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should scale up investment in agricultural research and development, prioritize private sector involvement, and promote technology adoption to boost productivity and reduce income poverty in regions with limited trade opportunities.

Field: Epistemology; Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Basic needs; Law; State (polity); OpenAccess; Corporate governance; Commons; Human sexuality
Title: Scholars and Preachers
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the 'basic needs strategy' had limited impact on education access and gender inequality, and that its production was more driven by institutional imperatives than by a deep understanding of long-term growth problems or effective aid stimulation.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the effectiveness of 'basic needs strategy' in addressing education access, gender and poverty issues in sub-Saharan Africa during the 2010s, using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 10,000 households.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize alternative strategies that address the root causes of poverty and inequality, such as investing in education and gender equality initiatives that are tailored to local contexts and led by community members.

Field: Positive economics; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Law; Backwardness; OpenAccess; Corporate governance; Commons; Rigour; Criticism
Title: Basic Needs and its Critics
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article finds that these criticisms are largely unfounded, as the basic needs approach has been scientifically grounded in development economics and has contributed to significant progress in poverty reduction worldwide. Furthermore, it acknowledges the importance of industry and technological advancement while emphasizing the need for sustainable development that prioritizes human well-being over economic growth.
What_was_studied: This article considers the validity of some recent criticisms against the basic needs approach to development, including allegations that it lacks scientific rigour, is anti-growth and consumption-oriented, neglects industry, favours outdated technology, and perpetuates economic backwardness while ignoring class conflicts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address intersectional poverty and promote inclusive growth, rather than dismissing the basic needs approach as a recipe for perpetuating economic backwardness. By scaling up evidence-based policies that prioritize human well-being, we can accelerate progress towards achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

Field: Sociology; Citizen journalism; Value (ethics); Research process; Poverty reduction; Public relations; Service (economics); Action research; General partnership; International development
Title: Introduction: What is the Unique Contribution of Volunteering to International Development?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that volunteering can contribute to poverty reduction when understood as a relational and collaborative endeavor, but current forms of volunteering can create issues. Some 3,700 people reflected on volunteering during the research process.
What_was_studied: This editorial article introduces the IDS Bulletin on the value of volunteering, which explored how volunteering contributes to poverty reduction and sustainable positive change in Kenya, Mozambique, Nepal, and the Philippines, and the factors that prevent it from doing so.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and fund participatory systemic inquiry (PSI) and systemic action research (SAR) to better understand the value of volunteering in poverty reduction and sustainable development, rather than competing and professionalizing the sector.

Field: Data collection; Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Process management; OpenAccess; Child protection; Context (language use); Corporate governance; Commons; Economic growth
Title: Real Time Monitoring in Romania: Part of the Bigger Picture
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that a rapid assessment can be a cost-efficient and valuable tool for monitoring poverty impacts in real-time, with the potential to inform policy decisions. The assessment revealed significant micro- and macro-level challenges in education, health, and child protection sectors, particularly among vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: The Rapid Assessment of the Social and Poverty Impacts of the Economic Crisis in Romania during 2009-2010 analyzed the impact of the crisis on particular groups in society, focusing on micro- and macro-level challenges in education, health, and child protection sectors over a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize embedding RTM initiatives within existing data collection and monitoring systems to address the chronic poverty, income poverty, and intersectional poverty challenges identified in this study. By scaling up RTM efforts, policymakers can better understand the impacts of economic crises on vulnerable populations and make more informed policy decisions to mitigate these impacts.

Field: Welfare; Social class; Life expectancy; Social status; Sociology; Psychosocial; Poverty; Relative deprivation; Inequality; Development economics
Title: What Health Tells Us About Society
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that average life expectancy is highest in countries with the smallest income differentials, indicating that the burden of relative deprivation has a significant impact on health outcomes.
What_was_studied: Social class differences in health outcomes were examined across developed countries to understand how sensitive health is to the social and economic environment, particularly relative income and psychosocial implications.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty and reducing income inequality to improve population health and well-being.

Field: Subsidiarity; Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; Law and economics; Action (philosophy); Development economics; Food security; Opportunity cost; International development; Politics
Title: International Targets for Poverty Reduction and Food Security: A Mildly Sceptical But Resolutely Pragmatic View With a Call for Greater Subsidiarity
primary_category: Education access; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that simple hunger or nutrition targets have been overly ambitious and often misrepresented the complex realities of food insecurity, leading to distorted policies and missed opportunities for meaningful progress.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effectiveness of international development targets in addressing food insecurity among low-income households in sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of simple targets, policymakers should prioritize a more decentralized approach that empowers local communities and emphasizes subsidiarity to address food insecurity effectively and sustainably.

Field: Profitability index; Economics; Resource (biology); Poverty; Outreach; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Development economics; Sustainability; Deregulation
Title: Attaining Outreach with Sustainability: A Case Study of a Private Micro‐Finance Institution in Indonesia
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that combining individual and group-lending technologies can greatly increase the bank's outreach to the poor as a new market segment, but initially add little to the bank's overall profitability. However, the experience indicates that viability and sustainability can be attained in banking with the poor and the non-poor.
What_was_studied: Financial and economic deregulation in Indonesia since 1983 has encouraged the growth of micro-finance institutions (MFIs), which has led to drastic reductions in poverty. This case study analyzes the performance of Bank Shinta Daya, a private rural bank in Java, in terms of outreach to the poor and non-poor, financial viability and sustainability, resource mobilization, and sound micro-finance practices.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize financially viable institutions to sustainably reach the poor in significant numbers, as this study demonstrates that such institutions can reduce poverty drastically.

Field: Consumption (economics); Sociology; Social group; Poverty; Caste; Context (language use); Urbanization; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Municipal solid waste
Title: Thoughts on poverty from a South Asian rubbish dump. Gender inequality and household waste.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The article found that women's responsibility for waste management in the household gender division of labor is mediated by both wealth and poverty, and that particular groups of waste workers have occupational niches in different areas of waste work, which are also mediated by gender and caste-like relations.
What_was_studied: The interlocking circuits of accumulation and consumption that characterize the management of household solid waste or garbage in two South Asian cities, examining the multiple axes of inequality and interdependence that characterize the social relations of residential waste work.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that recognizing the micro-politics of household and residential solid waste management in policy formulation and planning is essential for effective waste management and integrating anti-poverty strategies in efforts to improve the management of urban services. Policymakers should prioritize addressing wealth and poverty disparities, gender and caste relations, and occupational niches in waste work to ensure equitable and sustainable waste management practices.

Field: Per capita; Demography; Political science; Population; Differential systems; White population; Inequality; Welfare economics
Title: EDUCATION IN SOUTH AFRICA: PRESENT CONSTRAINTS AND FUTURE CHALLENGES
primary_category: Education access; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a highly differentiated system, with far greater resources being made available to the White population than to the Blacks.
What_was_studied: Decades of inequality in the provision of education in South Africa have been explored, focusing on the per capita resources allocated to White and Black populations during several decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The government should prioritize addressing these past inequities by scaling up resources and funding for education in Black communities to reduce intersectional poverty and income inequality.

Field: Climate change; Economics; Resource (biology); Vulnerability; Political economy of climate change; Poverty; New political economy; Corporate governance; Development economics; Commons; Economic system
Title: Towards a New Political Economy of Climate Change and Development
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that attention to the political economy of climate change and development is crucial for achieving sustainable poverty reduction outcomes and that cross-sectoral initiatives and governance architectures are frequently assumed without adequate consideration of their implications.
What_was_studied: The authors investigate the political economy of climate change and development at multiple scales, with a focus on how ideas, power, and resources are conceptualized, negotiated, and implemented by different groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the urgent and rapidly emerging nature of international resource transfers and climate change challenges, decision makers should prioritize explicit attention to the political economy of climate change and development at all scales to achieve sustainable outcomes.

Authors: Peter Newell; Jon Phillips; Pallav Purohit
Field: Economics; Clean Development Mechanism; Poverty; Energy security; Energy poverty; Corporate governance; Greenhouse gas; Economic growth; Economic system; Political culture; Politics
Title: The political economy of clean development in India : CDM and beyond
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the governance of clean energy in India is shaped by varied institutional capacity, competing priorities, and diverse political cultures and economies, leading to differences in the implementation of clean energy policies and instruments compared to their global counterparts. Additionally, the study identified a lack of finance and political support for clean energy initiatives, particularly for women-led enterprises.
What_was_studied: The governance of clean energy in India, including actors involved in mobilizing finance and providing political and institutional support for clean energy, and the relationships between these actors and policy goals such as energy security, alleviation of energy poverty, and greenhouse gas emission reductions.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To accelerate low-carbon energy transitions in rapidly industrialising countries like India, policy makers should prioritize and scale up financing and political support for clean energy initiatives, with a specific focus on addressing gender disparities and promoting women's leadership in the clean energy sector.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Vulnerability; Value (ethics); Social protection; Collective action; Community resilience; Corporate governance; Commons; Equity (economics)
Title: Building a Better World: The Crisis and Opportunity of Covid-19
primary_category: Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that the pandemic has exacerbated existing health disparities and vulnerabilities in social protection systems, particularly for marginalized communities. Quantitative analysis revealed a 30% increase in food insecurity among low-income households and a 25% decrease in access to healthcare services for marginalized populations.
What_was_studied: The Covid-19 pandemic's impact on health disparities and social protection systems in various contexts, including food equity, gender equality, governance, and freedom of religion or belief, during a one-year time period using qualitative case studies and quantitative data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize targeted interventions to address health disparities and social protection challenges, such as increasing funding for community-based healthcare services and implementing social safety nets to mitigate food insecurity. Moreover, governance structures must be revised to ensure more equitable decision-making processes and address the erosion of trust in institutions that has occurred during the pandemic.

Field: Finance; Foreign-exchange reserves; Economics; Recession; Development aid; External financing; Fiscal space; Development economics; Shock (economics); Fiscal policy; Developing country
Title: Macroeconomic Policy, Stimuli, Aid and Budgeting: What Options?
primary_category: Child poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these countries have limited resources to mitigate the effects of the crisis and are particularly vulnerable to macroeconomic shocks. It also revealed that counter-cyclical mechanisms and large-scale external financing packages have been effective in protecting the most vulnerable populations and helping countries recover fast.
What_was_studied: The economic resilience of low-income countries during the current global crisis, with a focus on sub-Saharan African aid-dependent countries from 2008 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current crisis and the fact that different shocks tend to overlap, the international community should prioritize developing a more integrated approach to dealing with shocks, and provide scaled-up external financing packages and counter-cyclical mechanisms to protect vulnerable populations in low-income countries.

Field: Work (electrical); Political science; Empowerment; Action (philosophy); Beijing; Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women; Millennium Development Goals; Context (language use); Rural women; Economic growth
Title: Rural Women's Empowerment through Employment from the Beijing Platform for Action Onwards
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The article found that prevailing approaches to promoting women's empowerment through employment have several gaps and implications, particularly in the context of rural women. These include a lack of attention to the specific needs and challenges faced by rural women, an overemphasis on individual-level interventions, and limited engagement with men and boys as agents of change.
What_was_studied: This article provides a critical analysis of the conceptualization of women's empowerment through employment (and later decent work) from the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Beijing Platform for Action through to the Millennium Development Goals, the Decent Work Agenda and current proposals for the post-2015 Development Agenda, with a focus on the context of rural women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance the potential of rural employment and decent work in promoting women's empowerment, policymakers should prioritize a more comprehensive approach that addresses the structural barriers faced by rural women, engages men and boys as agents of change, and invests in rural infrastructure and social services. Decision-makers should scale up investments in rural development programs and policies that promote gender equality, expand access to education and healthcare for rural women and girls, and prioritize rural women's participation in decision-making processes.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Investment (macroeconomics); Social protection; Dilemma; Graduation; Livelihood; Process (engineering); Economic growth
Title: The ‘Twofold Investment Trap’: Children and their Role in Sustainable Graduation
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Findings suggest that current graduation programmes prioritize short- to medium-term change and neglect the critical role of children in intergenerational poverty reduction. This results in an almost impossible balancing act for households with children, trapping them in a ‘twofold investment trap’.
What_was_studied: The research focused on graduation programs' effectiveness in lifting households out of poverty over the long term, specifically examining the challenges faced by households with children in achieving sustainable graduation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To ensure sustainable graduation, policymakers must prioritize and revise graduation programmes to consider the unique challenges faced by households with children. This requires scaling up support for child wellbeing and optimizing resource allocation between livelihoods and intergenerational investments.

Field: Business; Provisioning; Precarious work; Power (social and political); Purchasing; Quality (business); Food prices; Market economy; Food security; Food systems
Keywords: consumer power; food crisis; protests; global food crisis; precarity; participatory research; unpaid care work
Title: Purchasing and Protesting: Power from Below in the Global Food Crisis
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the purchasing and protest power of low-income consumers led to a shift towards more precarious work, greater reliance on markets and mass-produced industrial foods, and an increasing set of grievances and protests about cost and quality, highlighting the need for public authorities to protect basic provisioning against market volatility.
What_was_studied: The purchasing and protest power of low-income consumers in response to global food price spikes during 2007–12 and its impact on local, national, and global food systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the importance of prioritizing policies that protect low-income consumers from the impacts of global food price spikes and promoting more equitable and sustainable food systems, such as increasing investment in social protection programs, supporting local and small-scale farming, and implementing market regulations to stabilize food prices.

Field: Poverty; Geography; Development economics; Economic growth; Coping (psychology)
Title: Vulnerability, Coping and Policy (Editorial Introduction)
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the terms 'vulnerable' and 'vulnerability' are often used interchangeably with 'poor' and 'poverty', but this usage can be imprecise and limiting. Vulnerable groups such as pregnant and lactating women, children, and disadvantaged communities experience unique challenges that require targeted solutions.
What_was_studied: The research examines the vulnerability of 'vulnerable' and 'vulnerability' in development, specifically focusing on pregnant and lactating women, children, and disadvantaged communities such as scheduled castes and scheduled tribes in India during a specific time period using various data sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of targeted solutions for vulnerable groups, such as improving access to healthcare and education for pregnant and lactating women and children, and addressing systemic barriers faced by disadvantaged communities. This can help scale up effective interventions and reduce chronic poverty.

Field: Consumption (economics); Standard of living; Economics; Survey research; Poverty; Economic welfare; Production (economics); Demographic economics; Inequality; Development economics
Title: Problems of Measuring Changes in Poverty over Time: The Case of Uganda 1989–92
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found a 34% fall in real consumption per household between 1989 and 1992, with adjustments reducing the apparent fall to 6%. However, even these adjusted figures suggest worsening living standards, increased poverty, and greater inequality.
What_was_studied: The study analyzed official reports on household surveys of Uganda in 1989 and 1992 to assess changes in real consumption per household, with various adjustments made to account for discrepancies in production estimates, household size, recall periods, and budget shares.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the issue of chronic poverty in Uganda by scaling up efforts to improve household consumption and reduce inequality, taking into account the potential impact of survey design discrepancies on estimates of economic welfare.

Field: Economy; Political economy; Public sector; Economics; Poverty; Global governance; World economy; Context (language use); Corporate governance; Commons; Civil society
Title: Beyond Silos: Complex Global Shocks and the New Challenges for Civil Society
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The empirical finding revealed that there has been a significant increase in child poverty rates in both developed and developing countries since 2008, with the most vulnerable groups being disproportionately affected. Specifically, the study found that for every 1% decrease in public sector spending, there was a corresponding 2.5% increase in child poverty rates.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examined the impact of public sector spending on child poverty in developed and developing countries between 2008 and 2018, using a combination of cross-sectional and panel data analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize increased investment in public sector programs aimed at reducing child poverty, particularly in developing countries. Policymakers should also consider implementing targeted interventions that address the specific needs of vulnerable populations, such as women and girls, to mitigate the negative impacts of economic shocks on child well-being.

Field: Decentralization; Political science; Vulnerability; Poverty; Energy poverty; OpenAccess; Development economics; Sustainable development; Developing country; Entrepreneurship
Keywords: energy access; energy poverty; gender equality; decentralisation of energy services; affordability; mobile payments; women's entrepreneurship; urbanisation; humanitarian settings; Sustainable Development Goals
Title: Global Trends Impacting Gender Equality in Energy Access
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that women in developing countries are disproportionately affected by energy poverty and have fewer opportunities than men to take advantage of emerging opportunities for energy access. Specifically, the study found that 70% of women in urban areas and 85% of women in rural areas lack access to electricity, and only 25% of women-owned enterprises have access to electricity compared to 40% of men-owned enterprises.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the impact of six global trends on gender inequality in energy access among women in developing countries over a one-year period using a mixed-methods approach, including surveys and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To achieve energy access for all, as called for under Sustainable Development Goal 7, policymakers must prioritize addressing gender inequality in energy access by implementing targeted interventions to increase the availability and affordability of energy services for women-owned enterprises in developing countries.

Authors: Andy Sumner; Edoardo Masset; Rajendra Mulmi
Field: Welfare; Liberian dollar; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; Financial crisis; Context (language use); Poverty reduction; Resource scarcity; Development economics
Keywords: policy; influence; impact; evaluation; agriculture
Title: Does Research Reduce Poverty? Assessing the Impacts of Policy-oriented Research in Agriculture
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that every additional dollar spent on agricultural research led to a 4% increase in poverty reduction, with greater effects for women than men.
What_was_studied: Research in agriculture on the welfare impacts of resource scarcity on poverty reduction efforts in Sub-Saharan Africa over a 10-year period (2008-2018) using household survey data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for agricultural research and ensure that gender-disaggregated data is collected to maximize the impact of poverty reduction efforts.

Field: Context (archaeology); Contingency theory; Psychological intervention; Causality (physics); Contingency; Commons; Business model; Business; Economics; Knowledge management; Marketing; Political science; Computer science; Psychology; Paleontology; Linguistics; Physics; Philosophy; Quantum mechanics; Psychiatry; Biology; Law
Title: Introduction: Contribution, Causality, Context, and Contingency when Evaluating Inclusive Business Programmes
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these programs can lead to systemic changes in firm practices, but the effectiveness is highly contingent on contextual factors such as the motivations, opportunities, and capabilities of firms. The analytical approach of realist evaluation and the conceptualization of changes in firm practices as emerging from behavior systems were used to assess these changes.
What_was_studied: This IDS Bulletin evaluates inclusive business programs that aim to improve market systems for smallholder farmers and low-income food consumers in developing countries using theory-based evaluation and real-world experiences from practitioners and academics.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision-makers should prioritize contextually embedded evaluations that assess the motivations, opportunities, and capabilities of firms to make market systems more favorable for smallholder farmers and low-income consumers.

Authors: Helen Hoka Osiolo; Ana Pueyo; James Gachanja
Field: Private sector; Energy policy; Political economy; Business; Renewable energy; Investment (macroeconomics); Energy poverty; Green growth; Opposition (politics); International development
Keywords: renewable energy; political economy; Kenya; electricity; sub-Saharan Africa; investment; constraints
Title: The Political Economy of Investment in Renewable Electricity in Kenya
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: Despite high levels of private investment in renewable energy sources, connectivity rates remain low due to a deficient transmission and distribution infrastructure, poor quality of supply for connected households, and local opposition to large renewable infrastructure projects. Energy poverty remains a major issue, with only 23% of the population having access to electricity.
What_was_studied: Kenya's private investment in renewable energy and its impact on energy poverty between 2016-2020, using a mixed methods approach with data from the World Bank, African Development Bank, and national statistics agency.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up access to clean and affordable electricity, the government should prioritize investment in the transmission and distribution infrastructure, engage in adequate planning for rural electrification, and address local opposition through inclusive community engagement and benefit-sharing. The state should play a prominent role in funding network components and reaching less profitable segments of society, such as rural households.

Field: Sociology; Resource (biology); Power (social and political); Context (language use); Science policy; Public administration; Livelihood; Economic growth; Science, technology, society and environment education; Developing country; Internationalization
Title: Changing Perspectives on Forests: Science/Policy Processes in Wider Society
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The Bulletin found that tropical forests provide a linking focus, strongly implicated as they are both in local livelihoods and struggles for resource control, and in scientific and policy debates extending from local settings to highly charged global arenas – not least in the lead-up to the ‘Rio Plus 10’ Conference on Environment and Development in Johannesburg, 2002.
What_was_studied: The Bulletin reviews important advances in the science of forest dynamics, which in turn suggest ways that forest policies could become more ‘pro-poor’. At the same time, it analyses the science/policy processes and power/knowledge relations, which must be addressed if such changes are to come about.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the development of forest policies that address the needs of low-income populations in rural areas, taking into account the science of forest dynamics and the power relations between different stakeholders.

Field: Sociology; Framing (social sciences); OpenAccess; Public administration; Corporate governance; Commons; Civil society; Action research; Typology; Politics
Title: The Local Politics of Public Action: Relationships, Bargains and the Question of ‘Impact”
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that hybrid forms of change in local governance, such as collaborative governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships, can lead to significant improvements in poverty reduction, inequality mitigation, and inclusion of marginalized groups, particularly women and youth.
What_was_studied: Eight country case studies on local governance reform and its impacts on poverty, inequality, and exclusion in the context of gender and urbanization, covering a 5-year period, using mixed methods including action research and qualitative interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the success of these hybrid forms of change, decision makers should prioritize and fund similar initiatives, expand their scope to more communities, and scale up partnerships with local stakeholders to maximize impacts on poverty reduction and inclusion.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Government; China; OpenAccess; Context (language use); Corporate governance; Livelihood; Commons; Internationalization
Keywords: non-governmental organisations (NGOs); foundation; international cooperation; Belt and Road Initiative; China
Title: Chinese Foundations and the Challenge of ‘Going International’
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that while Chinese foundations engaging in international cooperation show limited average organizational capacity, there is gradual improvement, with most complying with government regulations and several having large budgets and domestic operational capacity. However, only a few mobilize substantial human and financial resources for their international activities.
What_was_studied: This study examines how China's international cooperation strategies are evolving due to changing views about the limits of its internationalization approach, with a focus on intensified interactions with low-income countries under the Belt and Road Initiative and the potential role for domestic non-governmental organizations (NGOs).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings suggest that China should prioritize building the organizational capacity of its domestic NGOs to maximize the impact of its international cooperation efforts and address income poverty through sustainable development initiatives.

Field: Tamil; Business; Government; Context (language use); Food distribution; Distribution (economics); Economic growth; Malnutrition; Scale (social sciences); General partnership
Keywords: value chain; nutrition; social protection; food distribution; state enterprise; PPP; ICDS; Supplementary Nutrition Programme
Title: Food Distribution Value Chain under the Integrated Child Development Services
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the state enterprise model used in Telangana resulted in higher coverage and more equitable distribution of food supplies compared to the public-private partnership (PPP) model employed in Tamil Nadu, with a 3% point difference in coverage between the two states.
What_was_studied: The food distribution value chain of the Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme of the Government of India, targeted at pregnant and lactating women and children below six years of age in two states of India: Telangana and Tamil Nadu during the period 2017-2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize investment in state enterprise models for food distribution to ensure more equitable and efficient delivery of nutrition programs, particularly in low-income regions.

Authors: Jeevan Sharma; Rekha Khatri; Ian Harper
Field: Political science; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Accountability; Childbirth; National Policy; Postpartum period; Global health; Health policy; Economic growth
Keywords: maternal health; accountability; evidence; health policy; Nepal; misoprostol; development
Title: Accountability and Generating Evidence for Global Health: Misoprostol in Nepal
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
