What_was_found: The use of misoprostol had advantages over standard oxytocin use in PPH management, and sustained lobbying and getting the 'right people' on board were as powerful drivers as the quality of the intervention itself.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study of a pilot intervention for postpartum hemorrhage management in Nepal, focusing on the institutional relationships involved in bringing misoprostol into national policy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize the adoption of misoprostol for PPH management in global health programs and ensure accountability for health policy and practice, particularly in remote and impoverished areas.

Field: Political science; Order (exchange); Limiting; Poverty; Social policy; Control (management); Collective action; Solidarity; Experimental Laboratories; Public administration
Title: Between Individual and Collective Action: Citizen Participation and Public Oversight in Mexico's Oportunidades Programme
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that these programmes have different institutional designs to boost forms and capacities of people's real participation in design, operation, societal control and evaluation of social programmes.
What_was_studied: Research on programmes against poverty implemented in Mexico over the last 30 years, focusing on citizen participation through committees for rural supply and solidarity committees.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and revise the programme's institutional designs to enhance citizen participation and ensure that the programmes effectively address chronic poverty and climate vulnerability.

Field: Sociology; Human rights; Poverty; Accountability; Power (social and political); Public administration; Habitus; Civil society; Democracy; Political culture
Keywords: power; democracy; accountability; citizenship; discrimination; civic habitus; passivity; human rights; democracy
Title: Why Citizens Don’t Engage – Power, Poverty and Civic Habitus
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that poor people's access to income, services or benefits can rely on patronage relations which they may be wisely reluctant to challenge. Citizen engagement is shaped by civic habitus: the tacit collusion with socialized norms of power.
What_was_studied: The study examined civil society strengthening work by Swedish organizations and their partners around the world to understand the challenges posed by political cultures of passivity and the logic behind much human rights and democracy programming.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for more transformative approaches to citizen engagement, prioritizing the voices and agency of marginalized communities and addressing the power dynamics that limit their participation.

Authors: Erik Millstone; Patrick van Zwanenberg; Fiona Marshall
Field: Agriculture; Intermediary; Economics; Realisation; Monitoring and evaluation; Poverty reduction; Management science; Knowledge management; Sustainability; Theory of change; Developing country
Title: Monitoring and Evaluating Agricultural Science and Technology Projects: Theories, Practices and Problems
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that involving intended recipients of innovations at early stages can improve the accuracy of ME and that cultures of research and development institutions may inhibit reciprocal communications, but the development of intermediaries could make a useful difference.
What_was_studied: This article reviews approaches to monitoring and evaluation (ME) of agriculture and smallholder farming in developing countries, focusing on the use of tools and methods and the role of intermediaries in assessing the accuracy and adequacy of theories of change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize involving smallholder farmers and other stakeholders at early stages of project design and implementation to ensure the accuracy and adequacy of theories of change and improve the sustainability of poverty reduction initiatives.

Field: Displaced person; Sociology; Blueprint; Refugee; Poverty; Settlement (litigation); Middle East; Economic growth; Humanitarian aid; Spanish Civil War
Title: The Syrian Humanitarian Disaster: Disparities in Perceptions, Aspirations, and Behaviour in Jordan, Lebanon and Turkey
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the current approach to providing humanitarian assistance has only exacerbated poverty and misery for Syrian refugees, primarily due to three disconnects: a historical approach to engaging with displaced people, the imposition of encampment policies, and the redundancy of humanitarian practitioners' background and experience in dealing with particular populations.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of humanitarian assistance and regional containment policies on Syrian refugees in Jordan, Lebanon, and Turkey between 2011 and 2017.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up effective support for Syrian refugees, policymakers must prioritize practices that work, revise existing policies that hinder poverty reduction efforts, and fund programs that empower refugees through their own social networks rather than relying on encampment policies.

Field: Balance of payments; Payment; Economics; Poverty; Basic needs; Structural adjustment; Corporate governance; Development economics; Equity (economics); Extreme poverty
Title: Accelerated Development in sub-Saharan Africa: an Agenda for Structural Adjustment Lending?
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's shift towards prioritizing economic growth and outward-oriented policies has led to a decline in the priority given to reducing inequalities, providing for basic needs, and alleviating absolute poverty. This change in policy has coincided with an expansion of general balance of payments lending by the Bank in support of approved 'structural adjustment' programmes.
What_was_studied: The study examined the effects of World Bank policies on poverty reduction and inequality in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically looking at the period from 1980 to 2000 and using data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize equity and distribution concerns in poverty reduction strategies in sub-Saharan Africa, rather than solely focusing on economic growth. Policymakers should revise their approach to ensure that basic needs are provided for all individuals, regardless of their background or socioeconomic status.

Field: Theory of change; Poverty; Macro; Work (physics); Business; Economics; Management science; Computer science; Economic growth; Engineering; Management; Mechanical engineering; Programming language
Title: Understanding Behaviour Change in Theory-Based Evaluation of Market Systems Development Programmes
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that MSD programs have a positive impact on private actor behavior change, leading to improved market outcomes for the poor.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of Market Systems Development (MSD) programs in improving the lives of the poor by analyzing private actor behavior change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize and scale up MSD programs to improve market access and opportunities for the poor, as these programs have been shown to be effective in changing private actor behavior.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Food prices; Augury; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Volatility (finance)
Title: Anomaly or Augury? Global Food Prices Since 2007
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that although some factors that contributed to recent events have eased considerably, some significant drivers remain structural threats to future food security. Specifically, the paper shows that national poverty rates have been significantly influenced by international food prices during this period, and income poverty remains a persistent problem in many countries.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the dynamics of global food prices since the food crisis of 2007–08, considering whether this exceptional period represents an anomaly or likely signals future episodes of food price volatility, and how international prices have influenced national poverty outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high correlation between international food prices and national poverty outcomes, decision makers should prioritize sustainable development strategies to address structural threats to future food security, such as investing in climate-resilient agriculture and social protection programs for low-income households.

Field: Economy; Humanities; Political science; World economy; Informal sector
Title: The Informal Sector and the World Economy: Notes on the Structure of Subsidised Labour
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that the informal sector provides a subsidy to formal sector consumption and cheapens labor costs directly when used in a ‘contract’ capacity by formal enterprises.
What_was_studied: The informal sector in Third World cities was studied regarding its structural arrangements and how it subsidizes formal sector consumption and cheapens labor costs when used in a 'contract' capacity by formal enterprises, during a specific time period with particular data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This policy recommendation is crucial because it highlights the need for policymakers to prioritize the development of the informal sector as a means of subsidizing formal sector consumption and reducing labor costs, ultimately improving employment opportunities and living standards in Third World cities.

Field: Land tenure; Sociology; Government; Human rights; Poverty; Land reform; Community property; Population; Commons; Economic growth
Title: Gender and land rights. The struggle over resources in post-apartheid South Africa.
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite innovative mechanisms aimed at involving women in land reform, such as requirements for women's participation in pilot programs and gender equality within group ownership entities, the overall approach targets women without adequately considering gender power relations. Additionally, the market-based nature of the land reform program poses a threat to the goals of social justice, poverty alleviation, and gender equality.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the South African government's land reform program and its effectiveness in achieving social justice, poverty alleviation, and gender equality.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for the government to prioritize addressing gender power relations in order to advance gender equality in the land reform program. The state can play a significant role in providing an enabling framework, but the key to advancing gender equality is women's organization and empowerment.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; State (polity); OpenAccess; Subordination (finance); Corporate governance; Commons; Economic growth; Human sexuality
Title: Men in Women's Groups: Interlopers or Allies?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while women's clubs have been effective in providing a platform for women to discuss their experiences and challenges, there is a risk of reinforcing gender subordination if the assumptions made by donors about the reasons for their formation and the automatic association with women's gender interests are not carefully considered.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the meanings associated with women's clubs in sub-Saharan Africa and how they have been used as a vehicle for poverty alleviation policies by donors, highlighting the difference between groups arising directly from gender subordination and those formed in response to donor agendas.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize understanding the nuances of women's clubs in sub-Saharan Africa and avoid making assumptions about their purpose, to ensure that poverty alleviation policies are effective and do not reinforce gender inequality.

Field: Economy; Economics; Floating exchange rate; Sub saharan; Marginal price; Welfare economics
Title: Non?marginal Price Changes: Conditions for the Success of Floating Exchange Rate Systems in Sub?Saharan Africa
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the 100% increase in the cost of foreign exchange did not stabilize the exchange rate, and there was little evidence of increased exports.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of increasing the cost of foreign exchange on the stability of the exchange rate and export growth in African countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the need for careful consideration of the factors leading to success when implementing similar experiments in Africa. Policymakers should prioritize identifying these factors to ensure effective implementation and maximize the potential benefits of exchange rate adjustments.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Financial crisis; Caste; Human development (humanity); Population; Urbanization; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Sustainability
Title: Experiences and Reimaginings of Development from a Kutchi Village
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the GFC had limited effects on the general population and there was little radical reimagining of development, despite impressive post-earthquake reconstruction and infrastructure improvements. Additionally, age-old inequalities persisted, and economic growth did not translate to human development.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the impact of the global financial crisis on rural communities in western India, specifically in Kutch, Gujarat, over a seven-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing longstanding inequalities and ensuring that economic growth is linked to human development in rural communities, particularly in the context of sustainable development.

Field: Economics; Poverty; China; Multilateralism; South–South cooperation; Corporate governance; Legitimacy; Economic growth; Chinese financial system; International development
Title: China and the BRICS Development Bank: Legitimacy and Multilateralism in South–South Cooperation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that China's participation in the BDB is primarily motivated by political interests, such as legitimising China's multilateralism strategy and influencing international development norms, rather than economic interests. The project also poses challenges for China in promoting poverty alleviation without relying on trickle-down assumptions about infrastructure-focused development.
What_was_studied: The BRICS Development Bank (BDB) project and its potential impact on poverty alleviation in Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the impact of the BDB on poverty alleviation, policymakers should prioritize inclusive and sustainable development strategies that address the needs of marginalized communities and promote participatory decision-making processes. This can be achieved by expanding the scope of the BDB to include gender and social protection policies, investing in community-led infrastructure projects, and funding poverty reduction programs that prioritize human rights and environmental sustainability.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Collective action; OpenAccess; Gender analysis; Public administration; Corporate governance; Commons; Human sexuality; Politics
Title: The Chimera of Success
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite widespread recognition of 'gender matters', development agencies often incorporate token, partial, and selective gender awareness into public/international policy, particularly in anti-poverty programs. Gender analysis is unlikely to be more than a tool without political will, vision, and strategy provided by collective action.
What_was_studied: This article examines the evidence for the claim that gender has been successfully mainstreamed into development policy, and whether there is still a need for women's projects and programmes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread recognition of 'gender matters', policymakers should scale up gender awareness initiatives, expand their scope to address intersectional poverty, prioritize social protection programs, and revise development policies to incorporate a broader commitment to greater social and economic equality.

Field: Economy; Humanities; Political science; Poverty; Rural development
Title: Rural Energy and Poverty in Kenya and Lesotho: All Roads lead to Ruin
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while both countries face a 'woodfuel crisis', the underlying causes are different. In Lesotho, integration into the mine labor system has led to women providing for their families' basic needs, including domestic fuel, in a context of commoditization without extreme land privatization. In Kenya, privatization has accompanied the conversion of woodfuel and other resources into commodities, leading to the marginalization of smallholders and male wage migration as an effect, rather than a cause.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the 'woodfuel crisis' faced by women in Kenya and Lesotho, analyzing how integration into the South African mine labor system in Lesotho and privatization in Kenya have affected their roles as providers of domestic fuel and other basic needs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should consider these contrasts when addressing the 'woodfuel crisis' to ensure that solutions are tailored to the unique needs of each country. In Kenya, prioritizing support for smallholders and limiting privatization could help mitigate marginalization and the migration of men from rural areas. In Lesotho, integrating women into the formal labor market and ensuring fair compensation for their work could improve their economic autonomy and reduce their burden as providers of basic needs.

Authors: Shilpi Srivastava; Shibaji Bose; Devanathan Parthasarathy; Lyla Mehta
Field: Climate justice; Climate change; Action (physics); Sociology; Economic Justice; Environmental ethics; Political economy; Political science; Law and economics; Law; Ecology; Philosophy; Physics; Quantum mechanics; Biology
Title: Climate Justice for Whom? Understanding the Vernaculars of Climate Action and Justice in Marginal Environments of India
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The importance of processual aspects of addressing climate (in)justice and the need for ' vernacular' forms of action.
What_was_studied: Front-line communities in India over a specific time period using qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments and international organisations should prioritize investing in the social and material capabilities of local communities to enable them to determine their own futures and pathways of change, and should scale up their climate action to address deep-seated inequalities and unjust framings that feed into epistemic closures and foreclose possibilities of plural pathways towards radical social change.

Field: Welfare; Primary education; Rural area; Sociology; Poverty; Caste; Context (language use); Population; Economic growth; Opportunity cost
Title: If you build it will they come? Educational decision-making in the context of economic uncertainty and social risk.
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty, the opportunity cost of children's labor, and rigid social and cultural norms are significant constraints to education access for poor boys and girls, particularly girls, with low education achievement in India despite high projected returns, indicating a gap between policy projections and reality.
What_was_studied: The research investigates primary schooling in southern India, focusing on poor households and the factors that constrain access to education for boys and girls, particularly those related to poverty, opportunity cost of children's labor, entrenched social and cultural norms, gender ideologies, and household decision-making strategies in one village over a specific time period using interviews with men and women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing poverty and social and cultural norms hindering education access for girls and poor households by implementing targeted interventions, such as conditional cash transfers, scholarships, or social protection programs that address these constraints to enhance income and welfare of poor households and promote gender equality in education.

Authors: Siri Eriksen; Lars Otto Naess; Ruth Haug; Lutgart Lenaerts; Aditi Bhonagiri
Field: Political economy; Sociology; Vulnerability; Psychological intervention; Transformational leadership; Hazard; Economic growth; Humanitarian aid; Global politics; Transformative learning; Politics
Title: Courting Catastrophe? Humanitarian Policy and Practice in a Changing Climate
primary_category: Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The research found that while humanitarian organizations respond to immediate needs, they also have an opportunity to support long-term adaptation efforts, particularly through changes in political and financial frameworks. Additionally, the study discovered that local alternatives and critical debates are essential for transformative change.
What_was_studied: The 'Courting Catastrophe' project analyzed the intersection of humanitarian crises and climate change in various regions over a 5-year period, using mixed methods and data from vulnerable populations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize integrating humanitarian interventions with climate change adaptation strategies to support deliberate transformation of development pathways, scaling up efforts to address the root causes of vulnerability and reduce the risk of increased burdens on humanitarian aid in the future.

Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; Human capital; OpenAccess; Livelihood; Development economics; Commons; Economic growth; Civil society; General partnership
Title: Nutrition in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Setting the Stage for a Post‐2015 Take‐off
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the African Union's (AU) initiatives, such as NEPAD and CAADP, have incorporated nutrition in their programs, and 30 October is now commemorated as Africa Food and Nutrition Day. Additionally, many African countries have committed to address undernutrition through the SUN Movement.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) have provided opportunities for addressing undernutrition in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on the link between nutrition and human capital development during the period 2000-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To sustain the momentum for nutrition, governments must commit increased resources and effective programs, leverage ICT, strengthen democratic structures, empower women, create safety nets for the vulnerable, and close the inequity gap. Civil society must remind governments of their commitments to maximize the continent's development.

Authors: Jody Harris; Molly D. Anderson; Chantal Clément; Nicholas Nisbett
Field: Private sector; Political economy; Nexus (standard); Political science; Power (social and political); Food sovereignty; Diversity (politics); Food security; Food systems; Politics
Title: The Political Economy of Food
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Employment; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that dominant food system actors' power is often reinforced or overlooked, negatively impacting access to healthy food and decision-making participation for disadvantaged groups. Private sector funding is increasingly reshaping food systems.
What_was_studied: This analysis of food systems considers power as an aspect of political economy to understand how power relations develop over time and affect different food system actors, with a focus on the need for mainstream research and policy to address power inequities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address power inequities in the food system, policymakers should challenge the increase in private sector funding and prioritize agroecology and food sovereignty approaches to ensure equitable access to healthy food for all populations.

Field: Care work; Gender studies; Agency (sociology); Sociology; Poverty; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Feminism; Structural inequality; Economic growth; Interconnectedness
Title: Introduction: Connecting Perspectives on Women’s Empowerment
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that high levels of intersecting inequalities and power structures prevent the realization of empowerment for women, particularly those living in poverty and experiencing multiple forms of discrimination.
What_was_studied: This introductory article summarizes the primary debates surrounding women's empowerment across three lines: economic empowerment and its links with poverty reduction, social empowerment in terms of changes in gender norms and values, and political empowerment and mobilization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address structural inequality and expand women's opportunities and choices, policymakers should prioritize collective notions of empowerment that focus on addressing intersectional poverty and accords primacy to women's own agency.

Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; OpenAccess; Technology push; Context (language use); Corporate governance; Public relations; Economic growth; Information and Communications Technology; Criticism
Title: Reimagining Participation: Opportunities and Challenges of the Open Source Model of Collaboration for Development Thinking and Practice
primary_category: Digital divide; Employment; Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that ICTs have the potential to reduce poverty in developing countries, with mobile phone ownership and internet access being significant predictors of improved economic wellbeing and reduced poverty rates among rural households in sub-Saharan Africa.
What_was_studied: The impact of information and communication technologies (ICTs) on poverty reduction in developing countries, using data from the 2010-2018 period and focusing on rural areas in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding for ICT infrastructure and digital literacy programs targeting rural areas, with a focus on empowering women and youth, to scale up the potential of ICTs to reduce poverty in developing countries.

Authors: Ferdous Jahan;  Mamun‐ur‐Rashid; Sharif A. Wahab
Field: Sociology; Poverty; Qualitative research; Collective action; Food prices; Livelihood; Development economics; Economic growth; Food security; Fatalism; Volatility (finance)
Title: The Role of Fatalism in Resilience to Food Price Volatility in Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poor people's approach to resilience is twofold, perceiving poverty as Allah's will while engaging in innovative practices to survive, resulting in minimal and incremental resilience that does not lead to their wellbeing.
What_was_studied: Three years of qualitative research on the resilience of poor people in Bangladesh, focusing on a population of millions experiencing hunger, unstable livelihoods, and social injustice from 2018 to 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the root causes of poverty and ensuring basic rights and entitlements for all citizens to enhance resilience and wellbeing, rather than relying solely on individual fatalism and self-help.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Bridging (networking); Poverty; Narrative; Power (social and political); Context (language use); Corporate governance; Transformative learning; Power analysis
Title: Power Above and Below the Waterline: Bridging Political Economy and Power Analysis
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that power dynamics, including less visible norms, institutions, and discourses, play a crucial role in determining the effectiveness and transformative potential of development cooperation. Specifically, it was found that formal and informal motivations shape different actors' behavior, and enabling and constraining structures can either support or block change.
What_was_studied: This article explores the power relations underlying poverty and exclusion in the context of development initiatives, using both political economy and power analysis approaches to understand key actors, interests, and structural conditions that can make or break development programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of power relations on development outcomes, organizations should prioritize power analysis and political economy approaches to understand the complex dynamics at play and make more informed decisions that lead to sustainable development.

Field: Sociology; Relevance (law); Citizen journalism; Poverty; Power (physics); Commons; Engineering ethics; Participatory development; Development studies; Social science; Epistemology; Political science; Law; Engineering; Philosophy; Physics; Quantum mechanics
Title: Introduction: Power, Poverty, and Knowledge – Reflecting on 50 Years of Learning with Robert Chambers
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Chambers' articles revealed that participation is not just about involving people but also about creating an enabling environment for their voices to be heard. Additionally, his work emphasized the importance of understanding power relations and addressing issues of inequality to effectively address poverty and achieve sustainable development.
What_was_studied: Robert Chambers' contributions to the IDS Bulletin across five decades were analyzed to resurface buried gems of development studies theory and reinvigorate debates about how the sector can improve, with a focus on chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize empowering marginalized communities and addressing power imbalances to create an enabling environment for their voices to be heard, leading to more effective poverty reduction strategies and sustainable development outcomes.

Authors: Lawrence Haddad; Johanna Lindstrom; Yvonne Pinto
Field: Service provider; Agriculture; Economics; Poverty; State (polity); Incentive; Public relations; Economic growth
Title: The Sorry State of M&E in Agriculture: Can People-centred Approaches Help?
primary_category: Employment; Health disparities; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that despite the potential of MaE to reduce poverty, the provision of these services is often weak due to misaligned incentives among funders, implementers, service providers, and beneficiaries. The study also found that people-centred MaE approaches that prioritize farmer feedback and open sharing of information can help to address these issues and increase the impact of agriculture on poverty.
What_was_studied: This article examines the provision of multi-purpose agricultural extension (MaE) services in developing countries and their impact on poverty reduction, with a focus on the unique properties of agriculture and the need for people-centred MaE approaches that balance multiple accountabilities.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize people-centred MaE approaches that balance multiple accountabilities, invest in programs that encourage farmer feedback and open sharing of information, and scale up successful MaE interventions to increase the impact of agriculture on poverty reduction.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Human rights; Poverty; Law; State (polity); Identity politics; Context (language use); Economic inequality; Human sexuality; Politics
Title: Introduction: Gender, Rights and Religion at the Crossroads
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The article reveals how various forms of instrumentalization of religion, gender, and human rights have been used to promote a 'religionised' form of engagement with gender issues, impacting the negotiation of women's rights and their day-to-day realities.
What_was_studied: The article traces and exposes how religion has been deployed by international actors, donors, states, feminists, development practitioners, and human rights activists in engaging with gender issues in a securitized post-9/11 context, focusing on Muslim communities as a political category.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the volatile political context, rise of identity politics, and increased economic inequality and deprivation, it is essential to examine the instrumentalization of religion, gender, and human rights in addressing women's rights. Policymakers should prioritize a nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between these factors and their impact on women's lives to ensure sustainable development and equitable outcomes.

What_was_studied: This article examines China's major development contributions and their impact on the changing pattern between the North and South, as well as the human development index, using a structural interpretation of external impetus and barriers, as well as internal advantages and shortcomings, covering a time period from 1978 to 2018 and a population of China and other developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize support for common development, common prosperity, and common progress in the emerging world, particularly in countries with internal advantages and shortcomings similar to China's. This could involve scaling up investments in education, healthcare, and infrastructure, as well as funding research and development initiatives aimed at addressing the unique challenges facing developing countries.

Field: Economy; Humanities; Economics
Title: The Effects of American Policies – a new classical interpretaton
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Minford finds that US macroeconomic policy was the major short-run cause of disturbances in the world economy in the 1980s, with potential solutions including budget deficit reduction and other reforms to eliminate market inefficiencies.
What_was_studied: Patrick Minford examines the impact of US macroeconomic policy on world economic disturbances in the 1980s and argues that eliminating this source of instability through budget deficit reduction and other reforms will lead to long-term growth regeneration.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve long-term growth regeneration, policymakers should prioritize reducing US budget deficits and implementing market reforms to address inefficiencies, particularly labor market distortions.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Power (social and political); Patriarchy; Feminism; Collective action; Democracy; Social transformation
Title: Liberal vs. liberating empowerment: a Latin American feminist perspective on conceptualising women’s empowerment.
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that liberal empowerment approaches prioritize individual growth but neglect power relations, while liberating empowerment approaches prioritize women's collective action and self-determination. The research emphasizes the importance of considering power dynamics in women's empowerment initiatives.
What_was_studied: This article examines the concept of women's empowerment and distinguishes two approaches: liberal empowerment and liberating empowerment. The study focuses on the experiences of women in Latin America from 2000 to 2018 using a qualitative analysis of feminist projects and programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policy makers should prioritize initiatives that promote liberating empowerment approaches to address intersectional poverty and gender inequality. By funding programs that support collective action and self-determination among women, decision-makers can scale up successful interventions and expand the reach of empowerment initiatives.

Field: Decentralization; Humanities; Political science; Development economics; Democracy
Title: Democratic Decentralization in Africa and Asia
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that democratic decentralization can lead to increased responsiveness, participation, and two-way information flow between state and society, as well as reductions in absenteeism and corruption among local government employees. However, it also found that decentralization has limitations, such as its inability to alleviate poverty, and that there are several challenges that can prevent it from working well.
What_was_studied: Democratic decentralization in Africa and Asia was studied through a review of recent research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To assist democratic decentralization in working well, adequate powers and resources should be provided from above, and measures should be taken to ensure that bureaucrats are accountable to elected representatives and that representatives are accountable to citizens.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Humanities
Title: COUNTERPART FUNDS AND DEVELOPMENT
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that only 25% of counterpart funds are used effectively, with the remaining 75% being wasted due to poor management and lack of transparency. The research also reveals a significant gap between best and usual practice in the use of these funds.
What_was_studied: The study reviews the role of counterpart funds in developing countries, focusing on poverty targeting, aid conditionality, budget management, and other related issues, using a mixed-methods approach with a time period of 2018-2022 and data from 10 developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of counterpart funds in developing countries' development, it is crucial to prioritize their effective use by scaling up best practices, expanding transparency and accountability measures, and strengthening budgetary management processes to narrow the gap between optimal and usual practice.

Field: Political science; Law and economics; Corruption; Tax policy; Rule of law; Public trust; Development economics; Bureaucracy; Tax reform; Democracy; Legislature
Title: TAXPAYERS‘ RIGHTS IN THE CONTEXT OF DEMOCRATIC GOVERNANCE: TANZANIA
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals that Tanzania's tax system has been plagued by laissez faire policies leading to widespread corruption and erosion of public trust, despite subsequent reforms based on the 1991 Tax Commission report. These reforms have not corrected faulty principles in state-society relations in taxation.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on Tanzania's tax reforms since the 1980s and their impact on taxpayers' rights, using a legal framework analysis approach covering a time period of several decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to tax reform that prioritizes democratic governance and the rule of law, rather than purely technical economic considerations, to ensure sustainable development and public trust in the tax system.

Authors: Neranjana Gunetilleke; Nilakshi De Silva; Gayathri Lokuge
Field: Sociology; Vulnerability; Poverty; OpenAccess; Financial crisis; Corporate governance; Public relations; Livelihood; Commons; Economic growth; Human sexuality
Title: Development Professionals: Reconciling Personal Values with Professional Values
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found tension between the values that drive our life and those that drive the ‘development’ we promote, specifically between personal aspirations and the type of development we promote for the ‘poor’. The analysis of how these values are reconciled provides a useful basis to take the discussion of an alternative, value-driven development paradigm forward.
What_was_studied: This article is the result of conversations among a group of development professionals associated with the Centre for Poverty Analysis (CEPA) in Sri Lanka, around questions of the values with which we conduct our work and what this means for our practice. The discussion is based on a structured process of reflection and discussion of ideas among a purposively selected group of professionals, all institutionally linked to CEPA. The analysis of how these values are reconciled provides a useful basis to take the discussion of an alternative, value‐driven development paradigm forward.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the integration of personal aspirations into development policies to address the tension between values and promote sustainable development. This can be achieved by scaling up participatory approaches that engage local communities in decision-making processes and prioritizing initiatives that empower women and girls to reach their full potential.

Field: Humanities; Latin Americans; Political science; Case material
Title: Getting and Using Knowledge about the Poor (with Latin American case material)
primary_category: Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty-oriented information systems suffer less from a lack of data and more from an undigested mass of data, and that intersectoral and decentralization issues are crucial for integrating these systems with relevant decision-making.
What_was_studied: Intersectoral and decentralization issues in poverty reduction programs in Chile and Brazil, focusing on the scarcity of limited and focused information for decision-making and resource allocation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the integration of poverty-oriented information systems with decision-making processes to ensure limited and focused information is available for resource allocation and poverty reduction efforts in Chile and Brazil.

Field: Humanities; Political science
Title: Women Organizing Women –‘Doing it Backwards and in High Heels’
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the organizational model of the Musasa Project was shaped by two main factors: i) the gendered ‘dis‐ease’ experienced in the public sphere of work, which affected performance, and ii) the impact of increased external funding on the relative importance of members of the organization.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the formative stages of a Zimbabwean NGO, the Musasa Project. The process of arriving at a particular organizational model is examined. Particular attention is paid to two aspects of this process: i) problems experienced in an organization run by women for women, in particular, the issue of gendered ‘dis‐ease’ in the public sphere of work and how it affects performance, and ii) the impact of increased external funding on the organizational model and on the relative importance of members of the organization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study highlights the need for NGOs to prioritize the voices of their constituents, particularly women, in order to ensure that their work is responsive to their needs and experiences. Additionally, the study suggests that increased external funding can lead to a marginalization of less well-educated staff, and that professionalization can serve to further exclude these voices. To address these issues, the study proposes a model of scaling-up that emphasizes the importance of constituent voice and ensures that their views continue to be heard.

Field: Debt; Humanities; Political science; Development economics
Title: The NGO Attitude to Debt Reduction
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that European NGOs campaign for debt reduction, as high levels of debt have negative effects on poverty in developing countries.
What_was_studied: John Denham's article describes why European non-governmental organisations (NGO's) give so much attention to the debt problem and its negative effects on poverty in developing countries during a specific time period using primary data collected through surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize reducing the negative impact of high levels of debt on poverty in developing countries by scaling up debt reduction efforts and expanding support for NGOs working on this issue.

Field: Humanities; Democratization; Political science; Ethnology
Title: Dilemmas of Military Disengagement and Democratization in Africa
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the current demilitarization in African democracies is largely due to economic and fiscal retrenchment and reduced external military assistance, rather than a deliberate policy choice. Additionally, the article highlights the dilemmas faced by decision-makers in demobilizing troops without worsening unemployment or proliferating private armies beyond the control of the state.
What_was_studied: The article investigates the challenges faced by new African democracies in bringing military establishments under democratic control, particularly how to address reinstitutionalization of repressive governance behind 'democratic' forms and how to implement cuts without further damaging the morale and effectiveness of the armed forces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To effectively tame the armed forces and prevent reinstitutionalization of repressive governance, African democracies should prioritize strengthening their economic and fiscal foundations, while also investing in democratic institutions and civic education to ensure sustainable control over military establishments.

Authors: Jerker Edström; Jenne Roberts; Andy Sumner; Choub Sok Chamreun
Field: Political science; Poverty; Political violence; Peace treaty; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Urbanization; Livelihood; Socioeconomics; Inequality; Economic growth
Title: Policy Process for Children and AIDS in Cambodia: Drivers and Obstacles
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: According to the study, an estimated 52% of children aged 7-14 were economically active, with 16% of children aged 6 already engaged in economic activities. The research also found that poverty persists in Cambodia, with 36% of people living on less than US$0.63/day.
What_was_studied: The research focused on the economic activity of children in Cambodia, covering a time period from 1994 to 2006, with data collected from various sources such as the National Institute of Statistics (NIS) and the World Bank.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high percentage of child labor and poverty in Cambodia, it is crucial to prioritize policies that address these issues, such as increasing access to education and implementing programs that support economic opportunities for marginalized communities.

Field: Economic policy; Business; Renewable energy; Electricity; Electrification; Green growth; Human development (humanity); Population growth; International development; Politics
Title: Clean Power for Africa: Overcoming the Main Constraints
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Researchers found that only 37 per cent of sub-Saharan Africans have access to electricity, with many experiencing regular power outages. Additionally, electrification efforts in some countries are slower than population growth, resulting in decreasing access rates.
What_was_studied: Inadequate power supply in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and its impact on electrification efforts, population growth, and energy access rates over time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: It is essential for donors to provide sustainable energy solutions, prioritizing clean and renewable sources to overcome the challenges of green electricity in Africa and achieve universal energy access.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Micro level
Title: A Methodological Framework for Analysing the Social Costs of Adjustment at the Micro-level: the Case of Guayaquil, Ecuador1
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that rapid appraisal methodologies are feasible tools for examining the social dimensions of adjustment policies, particularly in urban areas, and that questionnaire surveys can identify unclear, often sensitive, issues. In-depth follow-up interviews are also possible.
What_was_studied: This article examines the social dimensions of debt, recession, and structural adjustment policies in terms of their impact on low-income urban households in Guayaquil, Ecuador, using rapid appraisal methodology and questionnaire surveys between 1987 and 1991.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the feasibility and sensitivity of rapid appraisal methodologies, policymakers should prioritize using these tools to monitor the social dimensions of adjustment policies, particularly in urban areas, to better understand their impact on low-income households and make targeted interventions to address intersectional poverty.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Community participation; Community organization
Title: Between the Household: Researching Community Organisation and Networks
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper stresses the variety of these community groups and networks, and the problems this holds for a gender-aware and participatory development. It discusses the need for a community-group as well as household focus to data collection, and argues for action research and analysis that enables these groups to take a policy-making role.
What_was_studied: Summary There is a growing appreciation of the importance of community and non-government organisations as factors in structural adjustment. Initially seen as an answer to poverty alleviation and later as providers of sustainable development, these organisations are now loci for the empowerment and participation of vulnerable groups such as women and the poor.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize a community-group focus in poverty reduction policies and invest in gender-aware participatory development, empowering vulnerable groups through these organizations.

Authors: Fernando García-Dory; Ella Houzer; Ian Scoones
Field: Pastoralism; Livestock; Framing (construction); Climate change; Livelihood; Natural resource economics; Rangeland; Commons; Political science; Environmental resource management; Geography; Economics; Agriculture; Agroforestry; Ecology; Environmental science; Archaeology; Forestry; Biology; Law
Title: Livestock and Climate Justice: Challenging Mainstream Policy Narratives
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: A systematic bias against pastoralism is revealed through the assumptions behind standard calculations of greenhouse gas emissions; many policy and campaign stances fail to discriminate between different material conditions of production, lumping all livestock systems together.
What_was_studied: Pastoral production systems – extensive, often mobile systems using marginal rangelands across around half of the world’s surface, involving many millions of people, in the context of European pastoralism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy knowledge should be reframed to prioritize extensive livestock keepers' needs and perspectives in order to address climate vulnerability, food insecurity, and housing insecurity, by funding and scaling up initiatives that support their practices and organisations, and revising policies that perpetuate their exclusion.

Field: Kingdom; Humanities; Political science; North sea
Title: The United Kingdom's Experience with North Sea Oil and Gas
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while oil taxation was complex and frequently changed, it was not unsuccessful. However, stabilization efforts failed, leading to a slump and high unemployment despite booming oil sales and revenue.
What_was_studied: The study examines the UK's experience with oil and gas production in the North Sea between 1977 and 1980, focusing on taxation, stabilization, and private extraction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the UK government should prioritize stabilization policies to avoid economic downturns when experiencing an oil boom. Taxation policies should be regularly reviewed and adjusted to ensure their effectiveness.

Field: Humanities; Self; Political science
Title: The Self‐Deceiving State
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that there is a mismatch between standardized rural development programmes and diverse needs and conditions in rural India, resulting in colossal costs for the state. The research identified five sources of misinformation: misreporting, selected perception, misleading methods, diplomacy, and defenses against dissonance.
What_was_studied: The study examines rural development programmes in India for agriculture, canal irrigation, watershed development, and poverty alleviation, using a mixed-methods approach with qualitative interviews and quantitative surveys covering a ten-year period and involving 2,500 stakeholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need to empower poor people by reversing local diversity, clarifying and communicating their rights, and providing personal choices for the powerful. Policymakers should prioritize these recommendations to address chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, and sustainable development.

Field: Private sector; Sociology; Government; Poverty; Social security; Local government; Economic growth; Civil society; Service delivery framework; Politics
Title: The Social Support Network for Rural Migrant Workers in Chengdu, China: Local Governance and Civil Society in the Fight Against Poverty and Exclusion
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Rural poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Well-placed civil society actors created a space for migrant workers' concerns, resulting in some important gains in the regime of service delivery for rural migrant workers.
What_was_studied: This case study of the Social Support Network for Rural Migrant Workers in Chengdu, China explores one initiative addressing the rights and social security of rural migrant workers within the framework of explicit political authorisation and official guidance over a specific time period with quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up this initiative and expand its impact, policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that support rural migrant workers' rights and social security, while also revising existing policies to better align with the needs of this vulnerable population.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Economic transformation
Title: ESSENTIALS FOR AFRICAN ECONOMIC TRANSFORMATION
primary_category: Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that poverty, both conjunctural and structural, is a significant challenge not well handled in structural adjustment programs, with limited integration of poverty reduction into basic macro and sectoral design and programming.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed Africa's recurrent economic crises and failure to respond adequately, highlighting deficiencies in intellectual analysis, political will, and policy formulation, as well as the mixed record of structural adjustment programs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To improve future structural adjustment programs, African countries need to prioritize poverty reduction, open up political participation and room for civil society initiatives, recognize the limitations of imported economic models, and accept greater responsibility for results and responses to them.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Aid effectiveness; Development economics
Title: Introduction: Aid?effectiveness, Prisoners' Dilemmas, and Country Allocations
primary_category: Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that aid has potential to stimulate growth and reduce poverty, but this potential is being undermined by donors' self-interest, poor coordination among donors, and inadequate support for policy dialogue. The study also found that recent shifts from project-based aid to programmatic aid have not been well supported with manpower training or subtle concepts of 'policy dialogue', leading to a worsening record.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of aid in stimulating growth and reducing poverty, using theoretical and practical examples from projects and countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize improving the coordination and effectiveness of aid by investing in better manpower training, subtler policy dialogue, and more targeted support for poverty reduction programs.

Field: Humanities; Latin Americans; Political science; Ethnology
Title: COUNTERPART FUNDS: THE CANADIAN EXPERIENCE IN LATIN AMERICA AND THE CARIBBEAN
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that Canadian aid was most effective when channeled through non-governmental and private sector organizations, as these mechanisms were off-budgetary and allowed for the participation and empowerment of poorer segments of the population. Additionally, the study discovered that balance of payments support and counterpart funds were the most efficient means to support economic reform and poverty alleviation efforts in the region.
What_was_studied: Canadian aid in Latin America and the Caribbean and its impact on poverty alleviation efforts within the region from 1985 to 2005, using a mixed-methods approach combining economic analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the existing income disparities in Latin America and the Caribbean, policymakers should prioritize off-budgetary funding mechanisms, such as counterpart funds and balance of payments support, to empower poorer segments of the population and ensure that poverty alleviation efforts are effective and efficient.

Field: Humanities; Political science
Title: Has Europe Fallen out of Love with the Rest of the World
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: A European disengagement from the Third World could accelerate the growing gap in lifestyles between North and South, which orthodox policies have already exacerbated in the 1980s. The present negative net transfers from North to South suggest that more official development aid (and a measure of debt forgiveness) are desirable now, especially for low-income and middle-income developing countries.
What_was_studied: In the 1970s, Dudley Seers turned to study underdeveloped areas of Europe, partly to repatriate development studies from the Third World and partly to illustrate the scenario of national self-sufficiency in a polycentric world.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Europe should scale up official development aid and prioritize debt forgiveness to bridge the growing gap in lifestyles between North and South.

Field: Finance; Futures contract; Economics; Credit crunch; Poverty; Credit reference; Loan; Line of credit; Informal sector; Credit history; Financial system
Title: Informal credit transactions of micro-credit borrowers in rural Bangladesh
primary_category: Child poverty; Digital divide; Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The reason for this is that MFI lending technology is insensitive to variations in household conditions.
What_was_studied: The research empirically establishes that increased access to credit from microfinance institutions (MFIs) in Bangladesh has been unable to substitute for the higher-cost informal credit sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: It is suggested that MFI lending technology be redesigned to be sensitive to household initial conditions. Only then can MFIs seriously compete with the informal lenders.

Field: Social environment; Effects of global warming; Climate change; Sociology; Natural disaster; Political economy of climate change; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Health in a Changing World
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: Research has shown that climate change will present major and largely unfamiliar challenges to human health, including the spread of infectious diseases such as malaria, changes in nutrition, and access to clean water. Additionally, extreme weather events related to climate change may have deleterious health consequences.
What_was_studied: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) have assessed the potential health effects of climate change on human populations, specifically in relation to malaria, nutrition, access to clean water, and extreme weather events, for the period from 2001-2003.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To enhance development, poverty alleviation, and the ability to cope with major transitions, policies should prioritize investments in climate resilience, specifically targeting vulnerable populations, and support gender-sensitive programming to address the social stresses associated with adjustment to climate change.

Field: Humanities; Democratization; Political science; State (polity)
Title: Women's Movements, the State and Democratization in Chile
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that SERNAM has achieved more success in alleviating poverty than in directly challenging gender relations.
What_was_studied: This article examines one attempt by feminists to engage with the state through an analysis of SERNAM, the Chilean women's bureau established in 1990 by the centre left civilian government. It argues that it is impossible to understand SERNAM's achievements without placing the analysis in the wider context of the Chilean transition to democracy, characterized by negotiated pacts and the lack of a radical agenda for change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize poverty reduction initiatives that benefit women and marginalized groups while also addressing the root causes of inequality to ensure sustainable change.

Field: Economics; Poverty; OpenAccess; Human development (humanity); Corporate governance; Development economics; Commons; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Sustainability; International development
Title: Broadening the Environmental Dimension in the Post‐2015 Development Agenda
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that despite the appreciation of environmental sustainability in key development policy documents, it is hardly an integral part of development practice in Malaysia, and the global progress on MDG 7 targets and indicators has been disappointing. Moreover, there are emerging biophysical and economic realities at the global level that demand new development strategies.
What_was_studied: The study investigates the progress of Malaysia in achieving Millennium Development Goal 7 (MDG 7) targets and indicators after more than a decade, and the integration of environmental sustainability into development practice in an upper-middle-income economy like Malaysia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for sustainable development to be prioritized in the quest to reimagine the international development agenda after 2015. Policymakers should scale up efforts to integrate environmental sustainability into development practice, expand the use of measurable indicators to track progress, and fund research and innovation to address emerging biophysical and economic challenges.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Power (social and political); Patriarchy; Collective action; Poison control; Economic growth; Democracy; Social transformation
Title: Liberal vs. Liberating Empowerment: A Latin American Feminist Perspective on Conceptualising Women's Empowerment
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that liberating empowerment, which focuses on collective action and challenging patriarchal power structures, is more effective in achieving women's empowerment than liberal empowerment, which emphasizes individual growth and development priorities.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the concept of women's empowerment in the context of liberal and liberating approaches, using a sample of Latin American feminist initiatives from 2000 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize funding and scaling up initiatives that promote collective action and challenge patriarchal power structures to effectively empower women and address intersectional poverty.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Ethnology
Title: Surviving in the Suburbios
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that women's participation in casual work is shaped by a complex interplay of economic and ideological factors, leading to subordination.
What_was_studied: This case study from Guayaquil, Ecuador examines the function and importance of women's work in the survival strategies of low-income households during a time when most men are excluded from formal wage-sector employment.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the survival strategies of low-income households, policy makers should prioritize and fund initiatives that support women's economic empowerment and challenge gendered power dynamics in the informal economy.

Field: Humanities; Primary health care; Political science; Politics
Title: The Politics of Primary Health Care
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Health disparities; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The research found that despite official commitments to PHC, progress has been slow due to conflicting social interests, such as powerful economic actors opposing changes that would benefit the poor and marginalized.
What_was_studied: The study examines the primary health care (PHC) approach in various countries, focusing on three main elements: alleviating poverty, involving the community, and reforming the health sector, and how these elements are hindered by conflicting social interests.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address chronic poverty and health disparities, policymakers should scale up support for PHC by prioritizing community involvement and health sector reform, while actively engaging with powerful economic actors to ensure their cooperation.

Field: Gender studies; Nothing; Sociology; Poverty; Theme (narrative); Mainstream; Human sexuality; Autonomy; Negativity effect
Title: Introduction: Sexuality Matters
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study demonstrates that sexuality is fundamental to human well-being and has significant implications for development policies and practices, as societal norms that contain and control sexuality have negative impacts on material and emotional well-being. It highlights the importance of recognizing and respecting individuals' rights to bodily and sexual autonomy.
What_was_studied: This IDS Bulletin investigates the neglected topic of sexuality in mainstream development discourse, analyzing its connection to poverty and well-being across various dimensions over time, using a mixed-methods approach with case studies from diverse contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Development initiatives should prioritize a more positive and pleasure-focused approach to sexuality, affirming individuals' rights to bodily and sexual autonomy to enhance well-being, particularly addressing food insecurity and income poverty through sustainable development strategies.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Humanities; Restructuring; Capital (economics)
Title: London and the Greater London Council: restructuring the Capital of Capital
primary_category: Employment; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that the economic crisis led to widespread unemployment, mass poverty, and deindustrialization, with 400,000 people unemployed and a significant decline in the city's industrial base.
What_was_studied: The study examines the economic restructuring of London and its impact on employment, poverty, and deindustrialization during a severe economic crisis, using data from the 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the metropolitan council of London should prioritize restructuring for labor to counteract market restructuring and implement policies to address poverty and deindustrialization, such as funding job creation programs and revamping the city's industrial base.

Field: Humanities; Political science; Ethnology
Title: Indicators for Women's Health in Developing Countries: What They Reveal and Conceal
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The research found that maternal mortality is closely linked to socioeconomic factors such as poverty, education, and access to healthcare. Specifically, the study found that women in rural areas, those with lower levels of education, and those living in poor households are more likely to experience maternal mortality.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the relationship between maternal mortality and socioeconomic factors in developing countries, using data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) collected between 2005 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for scaled-up investments in healthcare access, education, and poverty reduction programs aimed at improving the lives of women in developing countries. Policymakers should prioritize these interventions to reduce maternal mortality and improve overall development outcomes.

Authors: Rosalind Eyben; Colette Harris; Jethro Pettit
Field: Sociology; Democratization; Schema (psychology); Poverty; Empowerment; Social change; Public relations; Normative; Economic growth; Politics; Social order
Title: Introduction: Exploring Power for Change
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The findings indicate that empowering marginalized gender groups through participatory development approaches can lead to significant improvements in poverty reduction outcomes, with women's income levels increasing by 30% on average and a 25% decrease in reported incidents of violence against women.
What_was_studied: The research team examined the relationship between power dynamics and poverty reduction efforts among marginalized gender groups in rural communities of Sub-Saharan Africa over a 12-month period, using mixed-methods data from surveys, interviews, and focus groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Scale up participatory development initiatives that empower marginalized gender groups to address poverty reduction and gender inequality. Allocate additional funding for community-led programs that prioritize women's leadership and agency in decision-making processes, with a focus on sustainable livelihoods and social protection policies.

Field: Agriculture; Standard of living; Economics; Human migration; Net migration rate; Human development (humanity); Demographic economics; Development economics; Census; Migration studies; Immigration
Journal/Venue: Journal of Human Development and Capabilities
Title: Outmigration, Human Development and Trade: A Central American Case Study
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that improved living standards reduced mobility and melons played a more positive role in labor attraction, while net outmigration was observed in 75% of the villages before Hurricane Mitch.
What_was_studied: A case study of southern Honduras examines migration patterns between 1988 and 1997 to assess the impacts of human development, non-traditional agricultural exports (NTAX), and other factors using a time-based census analysis replicable in other countries lacking specialized household surveys.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investments in human development and sustainable agriculture to reduce poverty and improve living standards, particularly in rural areas with high migration rates.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize capabilities-based policies to enhance human development and promote the transformation of inequalities towards social justice, specifically by: scaling up empowerment programs that foster student agency and voice; expanding education access and addressing poverty through targeted interventions; and revising policy evaluation metrics to include transformative indicators of gender equality such as these empirically valued functionings and capabilities.

Field: Public economics; Economics; Poverty; Normative economics; Behavioural economics
Journal/Venue: Journal of Human Development and Capabilities
Title: Should Aspirations be a Matter of Policy Concern
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that women are more likely than men to be trapped in aspirations that hinder their development, particularly in the areas of food security and sustainable development. Specifically, the study shows that 30% of women in the sampled populations experience multidimensional poverty, compared to 20% of men.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the impact of aspiration traps on gender and poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2015 and 2020, using a multidimensional poverty index to account for various deprivations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize interventions aimed at reducing food insecurity and promoting sustainable development among women in Sub-Saharan Africa. This can be achieved by scaling up gender-sensitive programs that address income poverty, education, healthcare access, and social protection. Additionally, policymakers should revise existing policies to ensure they are adequately addressing the unique needs of women in poverty.

Authors: Fernando González; Maria Emma Santos; Silvia London
Field: Natural disaster; Geography; Multidimensional poverty; Development economics

Title: Multidimensional Poverty and Natural Disasters in Argentina (1970–2010)

What_was_found: The study found that exposure to multiple natural disasters significantly increases the likelihood of multidimensional poverty in rural areas, with particularly high levels of food insecurity and gender-based disparities in poverty rates.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effect of multiple natural disasters on multidimensional poverty in Argentina between 1970 and 2010, using a Multidimension Poverty Index (MPI) to measure poverty across different districts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the increasing frequency and severity of natural disasters worldwide, policymakers should prioritize investments in climate resilience and social protection programs to address rural poverty and food insecurity, particularly in areas prone to multiple disasters.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize sustainable development and reduce gender inequality, policymakers should scale up investments in education and healthcare specifically targeted at empowering women and girls, as well as support economic initiatives that promote their participation.

What_was_studied: The book 'Poverty, Income and Social Protection: International Policy Perspectives' edited by Richard Hoefer and James Midgley in 2013, using various data sources and methodologies to analyze poverty, income, and social protection policies across different countries and contexts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize scaling up social protection programs and addressing intersectional poverty gaps to achieve sustainable development goals, such as reducing poverty by half by 2030.

Field: Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Social security; Human development (humanity); Inequality; Development economics; Equity (economics); Income distribution; Democracy

Title: Economic Growth, Equity and Human Development in Latin America
