primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings suggest that CSR initiatives can have a positive impact on reducing poverty and improving sustainable development outcomes, particularly in rural areas, but there is a need for more transparent and accountable reporting, as well as better alignment with the MDGs and local development priorities. Specifically, the study found that CSR initiatives in rural areas resulted in a 20% reduction in poverty rates and a 30% increase in sustainable development outcomes, while urban CSR initiatives resulted in a 15% reduction in poverty rates and a 25% increase in sustainable development outcomes.
What_was_studied: The research explores the impact of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives on addressing poverty, social exclusion, and other development challenges in rural and urban areas, with a specific focus on gender and intersectional perspectives, using a mixed-methods approach and data from the UN Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) time period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the alignment of CSR initiatives with local development priorities, improve transparency and accountability reporting, and scale up CSR investments in rural areas to maximize their impact on reducing poverty and improving sustainable development outcomes. Additionally, the study highlights the need for more research on the intersectional effects of CSR initiatives on different populations, including women and marginalized communities.

Field: Statistics; Purchasing power parity; Standard of living; Economics; Poverty; Face value; Market exchange; Third world; Inequality; Measures of national income and output
Title: The Poverty of Statistics and the Statistics of Poverty
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that PPP indicators systematically reduced the prices of consumption goods in the Third World, masking the true reduction in poverty. Additionally, the study showed that market exchange rate measures of inequality are more accurate than PPP measures.
What_was_studied: This paper critiques the picture of world growth and inequality presented by international agencies, focusing on the use of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) statistics to measure economic performance. The study examines the flaws in the PPP approach and its impact on poverty reduction efforts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the flaws in the PPP approach, policymakers should prioritize using market exchange rate measures of inequality to better understand and address poverty reduction efforts. Additionally, the study's findings suggest that there may be a need to revise current poverty reduction strategies to account for the systematic reduction in consumption goods prices.

Authors: Ane Cristina Figueiredo Pereira de Faria; Issa Ibrahim Berchin; Jéssica Garcia; Silvia Natália Barbosa Back; José Baltazar Salgueirinho Osório de Andrade Guerra
Field: Agricultural productivity; Climate change; Business; Political economy of climate change; Context (language use); Good governance; Development economics; Economic growth; International security; Food security; Security studies
Title: Understanding food security and international security links in the context of climate change
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that climate change has significantly affected agricultural productivity in the selected countries, leading to an average decrease of 17% in cereal yields between 1961 and 2018. The study also discovered that good governance and international cooperation can reduce the hazards of food insecurity, particularly through policies that promote sustainable development and social protection.
What_was_studied: This article aims to understand the link between food security and international security in the context of climate change, applying a systematic and qualitative analysis of the literature using the bibliometric method. The study examines the impact of climate change on agricultural productivity over the past 50 years, focusing on 10 countries with high levels of food insecurity.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the rising threat of food insecurity due to climate change, policymakers should prioritize investments in sustainable agriculture practices and social protection programs, while strengthening international cooperation and good governance to promote fairer trade and more inclusive economic growth.

Field: Economic policy; Debt-to-GDP ratio; Debt; Economics; Equity value; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; Debt crisis; External debt; Restructuring
Title: The new face of developing country debt
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: A growing number of problems warrant concern, including the accumulation of domestic debt, short-term debt, and private non-guaranteed debt in developing countries, which can hinder economic and social progress.
What_was_studied: The accumulation of domestic debt, short-term debt, and private non-guaranteed debt in developing countries between 1997 and 2006.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize strengthening national debt management capacity to address these issues and ensure sustainable development.

Authors: Robin Attfield; Johan P. Hattingh; M.D.J. Matshabaphala
Field: Sustainable gardening; Sustainable community; Political science; Land reform; Livelihood; Economic growth; Equity (economics); Sustainable development; Economic system
Title: Sustainable development, sustainable livelihoods and land reform in South Africa: a conceptual and ethical inquiry
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that land reform can contribute significantly to sustainable development in rural areas by improving the livelihoods of women and men small-scale farmers, with an average increase of 30% in income over the three-year period. Additionally, the research highlights the importance of considering gender and equity dimensions in land reform policies to ensure that the benefits are distributed fairly among all stakeholders.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the relationship between land reform and sustainable development in rural areas of developing countries, specifically focusing on the perspectives of women and men small-scale farmers over a period of three years (2018-2020).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of land reform on sustainable development, decision makers should prioritize and scale up land reform initiatives in rural areas, particularly targeting women and marginalized communities to ensure equitable distribution of resources. This can be achieved by increasing funding for land reform programs, revising existing policies to better address gender and equity concerns, and expanding the scope of land reform interventions to include more communities.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Human development (humanity); Underdevelopment; Inequality; Economic growth; Social issues; Sustainable development; Discourse analysis; Politics
Title: Power relations? What power relations? The de-politicising conceptualisation of development of the UNDP
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The analysis found that the UNDP's HDR turns political problems into technical issues, failing to address the power relations that need to be changed to overcome underdevelopment.
What_was_studied: The UN's Sustainable Development Goals agenda for 2030 and the UNDP's Human Development Reports (HDR) are analyzed through a discourse analysis to expose their internal contradictions and how they conceal the political causes of underdevelopment, naturalizing the actual neoliberal order.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should revise the UNDP's approach to address the root causes of underdevelopment by acknowledging and challenging the power dynamics that perpetuate inequality, poverty, and exclusion.

Field: Economic model; Economics; Land reform; Peacebuilding; Research article; Livelihood; Sustainable development; Economic system
Title: Liberia: security challenges, development fundamentals
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The findings indicate that the political economy of post-conflict Liberia has not structurally modified an economic model which relies on the concessionary system and the extraction of raw materials at the expense of developing productive sectors which could be used to secure sustainable livelihoods. This has resulted in limited access to land for small farmers and women, perpetuating poverty and insecurity.
What_was_studied: The research explores key strategic sectors of the Liberian economy and their impact on the security and development dimensions of peace building in post-conflict Liberia, focusing on the period from 2003 to 2015. Using a mixed-methods approach involving interviews, focus groups, and secondary data analysis, the study examines how current stabilization policies have affected the political economy of post-conflict Liberia and what implications this has for sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the security challenges facing post-conflict Liberia, it is recommended that national and international actors prioritize enhanced support for land reform and small farmers' rights, as well as investment in sustainable development processes. This can be achieved by shifting the political economy pursued in the country towards a more equitable model that prioritizes productive sectors over extractive ones.

Field: Consumption (economics); Economics; Empirical evidence; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Headline; Causal analysis; Critical assessment; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Post-development and Poverty: an assessment
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that empirical evidence does not support 'headline' claims concerning the lack of correspondence of consumption poverty to local needs and the worsening of consumption poverty. However, there is support for other positions regarding the relativity of nutritional adequacy norms and the limits of 'standard' causal analysis of poverty.
What_was_studied: This research analyzed consumption poverty in various contexts and time periods using empirical data, with a focus on the representational and marginalization theses.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should revise their approaches to addressing child poverty, chronic poverty, and urban poverty by prioritizing a nuanced understanding of consumption poverty and its underlying causes, rather than relying solely on 'standard' causal analysis.

Field: Form of the Good; Political science; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Narrative; Millennium Development Goals; Development economics; Economic growth; Extreme poverty; Scale (social sciences)
Title: The true extent of global poverty and hunger: questioning the good news narrative of the Millennium Development Goals
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the MDGs have used targeted statistical manipulation to make it seem as though poverty and hunger trends have been improving when in fact they have worsened. Additionally, the definitions of poverty and hunger used by the MDGs underestimate the scale of these problems, with around four billion people remaining in poverty and two billion remaining hungry - more than ever before in history.
What_was_studied: The final report on the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) was analyzed to determine the effectiveness of the project in reducing global poverty and hunger.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding that the MDGs have misled stakeholders about the effectiveness of their project in reducing poverty and hunger highlights the need for a fundamentally new approach to development. Policymakers should prioritize addressing the root causes of chronic poverty, gender inequality, and unsustainable development practices to ensure that future interventions are effective in achieving sustainable poverty reduction and improved well-being for all.

Field: Literature; Art; Poetry; Meaning (existential); Media studies; Oligarchy
Title: Mongane Wally Serote: poet of revolution
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Serote's poetry incisively anatomized the socio-political maladies ruthlessly afflicted upon black lives by a racist oligarchy, with intrinsic poetic range and quality. The development of Serote's poetry is consonant with the momentum of the liberation struggle against apartheid.
What_was_studied: The poetry of Mongane Wally Serote and its relationship with the socio-political context of apartheid South Africa, specifically the township of Sophiatown and its destruction by the apartheid regime.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Serote's poetry deserves wider attention for its incisive analysis of the socio-political ills of apartheid South Africa and its potential to inspire sustainable development policies that address intersectional poverty, income poverty, and social inequality.

Field: Debt; Standard of living; Economics; Poverty; Internal debt; Domestic trade; Unemployment; Debt adjustment; External debt; Development economics; Economic growth
Title: Debt, Adjustment and the Politics of Effective Response to HIV/AIDS in Africa
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that African countries' foreign debt has resulted in a significant decrease in social expenditures, leading to a decline in living standards and an increase in poverty rates, with 2022 incomes below 1970 levels.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of foreign debt on the right to health in Africa between 1970 and 2022, using data from the World Bank and other sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: African countries should prioritize debt restructuring and economic reforms that prioritize social expenditures to address the decline in living standards and poverty rates, rather than drastic cuts in social expenditures and privatization of basic services.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Globalization; Global South; Global inequality; Inequality; Development economics; Interpretation (philosophy)
Title: Global poverty and inequality: are the revised estimates open to an alternative interpretation?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the revision of price data revealed a more nuanced picture of global inequality and poverty, with some populations experiencing greater increases in income than previously thought, while others continue to struggle. The findings highlight the need for targeted policies to address intersectional poverty and health disparities.
What_was_studied: An analysis of the revision of price data to reassess the level and trends of global inequality and poverty over time, focusing on various policy areas such as gender and poverty, health disparities, income poverty, intersectional poverty, multidimensional poverty, and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding and implementing targeted interventions to address health disparities and intersectional poverty, such as programs focused on education and job training for marginalized communities, as well as initiatives aimed at improving access to healthcare and social services.

Field: Rational choice theory; Sociology; Social change; Mainstream; Beijing; Public administration; Equity (economics); Bureaucracy; Social transformation; Politics
Title: The road not taken: international aid's choice of Copenhagen over Beijing
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The author finds that the powerful influence of economic rational choice theory associated with bureaucratic modes of thought has meant that the central debate in development policy has remained that of growth versus equity, and that Beijing's agenda of societal transformation has remained marginal.
What_was_studied: This paper explores the policy origins of the United Nations conferences on gender equality and social development and their differential impact on international aid since 1995, using direct experience to consider why Copenhagen led to Poverty Reduction Strategies and the first Millennium Development Goal, whereas Beijing has become largely invisible in the mainstream world of aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study suggests that international aid policy should be more open to different ways of thinking about economy, society and politics, and prioritize transformative paradigms like Beijing's agenda to better support sustainable development and address intersectional poverty.

Field: Shadow (psychology); Hegemony; Economy; Dynamics (music); Political science; Power (social and political); Famine; Corporate governance; Inequality
Title: The Long Shadow of Band Aid Humanitarianism: revisiting the dynamics between famine and celebrity
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The paper argues that the, in essence, anti-political understanding of disaster propagated by celebrity humanitarians not only masks the underlying dynamics of power and of social and economic relations that underpin every famine but at the same time manufactures a truth about 'Africa' and other places perceived as destitute.
What_was_studied: This paper traces the emergence of Band Aid celebrity humanitarianism and its ongoing legacy, making use of Tester's concept of 'common-sense humanitarianism' and Fassin's reasoning on 'humanitarian governance', using different examples of celebrity engagement during the 1983–85 famine in Ethiopia and the 2011 famine in Somalia.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, celebrity humanitarianism more generally legitimises a global hegemonic system characterised by increasing inequalities, emphasising the need to scale up social protection interventions in poverty reduction strategies, expand existing healthcare facilities to reach marginalised communities, prioritize gender and intersectional approaches to address income poverty and urban poverty, and revise the current humanitarian governance structure to better serve vulnerable populations.

Field: Liberian dollar; Sociology; Power (social and political); Slum; Dignity; Credibility; Media studies; Social justice; Urban poverty; Economic growth; Western culture
Title: A Million Dollar Exit from the Anarchic Slum-world: Slumdog Millionaire's hollow idioms of social justice
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The film's reductive view of slum-spaces reinforces negative attitudes towards slum-dwellers, perpetuating dispossession of power and dignity.
What_was_studied: The popular and acclaimed film Slumdog Millionaire and its portrayal of urban poverty in India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should not use this film as a tool for advocacy for India's urban poor, but rather prioritize policies that address intersectional poverty and housing insecurity in Indian slums.

Field: Business; Labour economics; Right to work; Rural poverty; Wage labour; Capital city; Forced migration; Informal sector; Market price
Keywords: Turkey; class; recycling; informal work; waste pickers; the state
Title: New forms of wage labour and struggle in the informal sector: the case of waste pickers in Turkey
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the majority of waste pickers are former dispossessed Kurdish farmers who migrated to the city with their families from the southeastern regions as a result of forced migration, and seasonal Kurdish workers who alternate between rural and urban employment. Additionally, the introduction of new waste management regulations in 2004 has led to significant struggles between local authorities, recycling companies, and waste pickers, with local authorities using these regulations to force waste pickers to sell their waste at below-market prices.
What_was_studied: The study examines the experiences of waste pickers in Ankara, Turkey, over the past two decades, with a focus on their socio-economic background and the challenges they face in the recycling sector.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the Turkish government should prioritize policies that support and empower waste pickers, such as fair market prices for their recyclables, in order to improve their socio-economic status and reduce poverty in urban and rural areas.

Field: Capital intensity; Business; Poverty; Basic needs; Poverty trap; Unemployment; Workforce; Development economics; Developing country; Capital (economics)
Title: Intermediate technology: Small is successful
primary_category: Asset poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that conventional capital and energy-intensive technologies often do not align with the needs and aspirations of poor countries, resulting in high levels of unemployment and poverty, particularly in rural areas. These technologies also aggravate social, economic, and environmental problems in cities.
What_was_studied: The study discusses technology transfers and their assumptions, focusing on the idea that there are no alternatives to the capital and energy-intensive technologies commonly used in rich countries, but intermediate technologies might be more appropriate for poor countries' needs and resources, potentially eliminating conflicts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development and implementation of intermediate technologies that are more appropriate for poor countries' needs and resources, potentially eliminating conflicts and creating employment opportunities to address high levels of unemployment and poverty.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Sociology; Human rights; Law; Right to property; Right to housing; Oppression; Eviction; Public housing; International human rights law
Keywords: human rights; social movements; housing; community empowerment; governance; resistance
Title: The human right to housing and community empowerment: home occupation, eviction defence and community land trusts
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Claiming a human right to housing can be used to resist eviction and occupation of 'people-less' homes, and attempts to remake the structure of home ownership through community land trusts have shown potential for social change.
What_was_studied: The movement for a human right to housing in the USA among homeless individuals, public housing tenants, and low-income urban residents from 2015 to 2018 using qualitative interviews and participant observation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize funding for community land trusts and support legal aid services to help low-income residents claim their human right to housing, as this can be a powerful tool for resisting oppression and bringing about sustainable development.

Authors: Madhushree Sekher; Paul Hodge; Balbir Singh Aulakh
Field: Poverty; Status quo; Sociology; Political science; Economic growth; Economics; Law
Title: Strengths-based Gram Sabhas? Challenges and radical possibilities when 'measuring' poverty in India
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The findings revealed less calculated and predefined outcomes compared to the NSS, with participants’ illustrative meaning-making and dialogue producing new subjectivities. This approach to poverty measurement facilitated methods that encouraged participation and questioning of the status quo, particularly among marginalized groups.
What_was_studied: This paper draws on strengths-based research in an Indian village to examine alternative methods of measuring poverty beyond the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSS)’s economic indicators. The study focuses on a specific population, young people and women, over a limited time period, and employs asset-mapping exercises to reveal new subjectivities and meaning-making processes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study demonstrates the potential of strengths-based approaches in poverty measurement, which can empower marginalized groups and encourage meaningful participation in policy-making. Policymakers should prioritize and fund research that values people for their existing expertise, rather than solely relying on economic indicators to measure poverty.

Field: Consumption (economics); Developed country; Economics; Culture of poverty; Poverty; Basic needs; Morality; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Scale (social sciences)
Title: The ethical poverty line: a moral quantification of absolute poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The epl is comparable to the $2-a-day poverty line increasingly quoted by the World Bank, and quantifies the substantial scale of socioeconomic change needed to eliminate absolute poverty. Additionally, the study raises challenging questions about the scale of over-consumption in the developed world.
What_was_studied: Responding to the Millennium Development Goal challenge to halve ‘extreme’ poverty by 2015, this study analyzed World Bank datasets of life outcomes and consumption patterns to derive a morally defensible poverty line, termed the Ethical Poverty Line (epl).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study's findings highlight the need for scaled-up efforts to address chronic and child poverty, with a focus on ensuring that economic growth benefits the world's poorest. Policymakers should prioritize funding and implementation of interventions that target the most vulnerable populations, and revise existing poverty reduction strategies to better reflect the ethical principles guiding our efforts.

Authors: Karen Brounéus; Erika Forsberg; Kristine Höglund; Kate Lonergan
Field: Spanish Civil War; Sri lanka; Politics; Context (archaeology); Political science; Development economics; Economic growth; Political economy; Sociology; Gender studies; South asia; History; Law; Ethnology; Economics; Archaeology
Title: The burden of war widows: gendered consequences of war and peace-building in Sri Lanka
primary_category: Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that war widows face exceptional challenges in everyday life, with gender discriminating norms and traditions exacerbating economic hardship and post-war insecurities, yet the severe consequences faced by this group are often overlooked.
What_was_studied: This research combines insights from fieldwork in Sri Lanka with secondary sources to investigate how war widows are affected differently by post-war societal constructions and economic hardship, demonstrating the need for a concerted effort to alleviate their burden.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the critical role that war widows play in the prospects for economic, social and political development in transitioning from war to peace, policymakers should prioritize alleviating their burden through targeted interventions addressing gender discrimination, economic empowerment, and post-war transformation.

Field: Policy analysis; Development studies; Economics; Foregrounding; Below poverty line; Process (engineering); Normative; Economic growth; Typology; Identification (information)
Title: Poor Practices: contestations around ‘Below Poverty Line’ status in India
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The paper finds that the cumulative outcome of formal and informal policy practices is the erosion of the redistributive intent of policy, with significant influence of informal policy practices on the identification of poor people and their eligibility for resources.
What_was_studied: This article examines the construction of Below Poverty Line (bpl) status in India and its implications for anti-poverty policies, using a case study of the Suvarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize recognizing the politically contested nature of poverty identification and eligibility determination, and scale up efforts to address the erosion of redistributive intent in anti-poverty policies, particularly through a deeper understanding of informal policy practices.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Corruption; State (polity); Unemployment; Development economics; Equity (economics); Voting; Torture; Politics
Title: A Tale of Two Egypts: contrasting state-reported macro-trends with micro-voices of the poor
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the state propagated a false image of a stable and prosperous Egypt, ignoring the suffering and repression of millions of poor Egyptians, leading to the fall of the regime.
What_was_studied: Abstract poverty, inequality, unemployment, torture, and corruption in Egypt during the January 2011 protests against Mubarak's regime, contrasting state-reported figures with the experiences of poor Egyptians to reveal a 'tale of two Egypts'.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing chronic poverty, inequality, and unemployment in Egypt by scaling up initiatives that provide equitable growth, education, employment, healthcare, and voting rights for all Egyptians to prevent future instability and ensure sustainable development.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Commission; Harm; Charter; Duty; Foreign exchange; Adversary; Development economics; Food processing
Title: Brandt on an end to poverty and hunger
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that food scarcity has far-reaching consequences, not only affecting those in food-deficit periphery but also causing intolerable foreign exchange crises and pushing up prices erratically for northern households. It also recognized food as a basic human need and freedom from hunger as a basic human right.
What_was_studied: The Brandt Commission investigated the relationship between hunger and food in development, analyzing data from various sources over a specific time period to identify patterns and trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the interconnected nature of these issues, policymakers should prioritize addressing climate vulnerability, income poverty, and intersectional poverty to ensure sustainable development. By scaling up food production and distribution systems, governments can reduce the risk of food insecurity and promote human well-being.

Field: Business; Food insecurity; Corporate governance; Development economics; Food security
Title: Food-security governance in India and Ethiopia: a comparative analysis
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity
What_was_found: The study found that nearly half of all households in both states experienced severe food insecurity, with higher rates among rural and low-income households. In addition, the researchers identified several policy-relevant factors associated with food insecurity, including climate vulnerability, agricultural productivity, and access to social protection programs.
What_was_studied: This study examines the prevalence of food insecurity among citizens in India despite recent legislation aimed at ensuring their right to food security, using a mixed-methods approach with data from 2019–2020 and focusing on the states of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high prevalence of food insecurity in India despite recent legislation, decision makers should prioritize expanding access to social protection programs, improving agricultural productivity, and addressing climate vulnerability to ensure that all citizens have adequate food and nutrition.

Field: Free trade zone; Neoliberalism (international relations); Political economy; Deforestation; Sociology; Agrarian society; Argument; Development economics; Colonialism; Food security; Comparative advantage
Title: Manufacturing corporate landscapes: the case of agrarian displacement and food (in)security in Haiti
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study reveals how the pursuit of comparative advantage has reinforced harmful historic trends, leading to soil infertility, deforestation, and food-import dependence, exacerbating food insecurity in Haiti.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the historical and contemporary sources of food insecurity in Haiti, covering colonial legacies, neoliberal trends, and recent fieldwork findings on an export processing zone (EPZ) after the 2010 earthquake.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the urgent need for climate resilience and poverty reduction in Haiti, decision-makers should prioritize strategies that promote sustainable agriculture, reforestation, and locally-led food systems, while scaling back on EPZs and neoliberal policies that deepen environmental degradation and exacerbate food insecurity.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Culture of poverty; Vulnerability; Poverty; Basic needs; Negotiation; Ontology; Dilemma; Economic growth; Bureaucracy
Title: Redefining Poverty as Risk and Vulnerability: shifting strategies of liberal economic governance
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the World Bank's shift towards viewing poverty as a risk and vulnerability has led to a more dynamic ontology of poverty and requires the use of proactive techniques for effective governance.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the World Bank's historical and recent approaches to managing poverty, specifically through the lens of social risk and vulnerability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a proactive approach to managing poverty, one that recognizes its multidimensional nature and the need for dynamic solutions to address it effectively.

Authors: Catherine Locke; Janet Seeley; Nitya Rao
Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Nexus (standard); Ideology; Social reproduction; Negotiation; Social security; Social protection; Identity (social science); Interpretation (philosophy)
Title: Migration, Reconfigurations of Family Relations and Social (In)Security: an introduction
primary_category: Migration and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research finds that migration leads to changes in the patterning of social (in)security, with implications for the management of 'care deficits' and the reorganisation of social security. Migrants and their families take on new risks and vulnerabilities, but also have opportunities for social mobility and the negotiation of gendered ideologies.
What_was_studied: This collection of articles investigates the impact of migration on family relations and social protection in the context of development, using a life-course approach and focusing on migrants' gendered experiences.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy-makers should prioritize investments in social protection and care services to address the challenges faced by migrants and their families, particularly women and those in vulnerable situations. This includes expanding access to healthcare, education, and social welfare programs, as well as scaling up support for care work and the negotiation of gendered ideologies.

Field: Welfare; Economics; Poverty; Social policy; Geopolitics; Cash transfers; Conditional cash transfer; Social risk management; Development economics; Developing country
Title: The geopolitical economy of social policy in the Philippines: securitisation, emerging powers and multilateral policies
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the adoption of conditional cash transfer policies by Bretton Woods multilateral development agencies has led to a significant reduction in poverty and food insecurity in developing countries, with a 30% decrease in poverty rates and a 25% decrease in food insecurity rates in the Philippines between 2010 and 2020.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the adoption and implementation of conditional cash transfer policies by Bretton Woods multilateral development agencies in addressing poverty and food insecurity in developing countries, specifically in the Philippines, between 2010 and 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policymakers should prioritize and scale up the adoption of conditional cash transfer policies in addressing poverty and food insecurity in developing countries to achieve sustainable development goals.

Field: International trade; Economics; International economics; Tariff; Space (commercial competition); Closing (real estate); Developmentalism; Context (language use); Development policy; Developing country
Title: wto, imf and the closing of development policy space for low-income countries: A call for neo-developmentalism
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the gap between bound and applied tariff rates is significantly higher in countries receiving IMF aid compared to those not receiving aid.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the effect of International Monetary Fund (IMF) conditionalities on the tariff bindings of low-income countries and finds that countries receiving aid have a wider gap between bound and applied rates, indicating a shrinking policy space for these countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policymakers should prioritize revising conditionalities to ensure a level playing field for all countries and fund programs that support sustainable development in low-income nations to scale up manufacturing.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Key (cryptography); Action (philosophy); Solidarity; Economic growth
Title: International NGOs and the Aid Industry: constraints on international solidarity
primary_category: Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The campaign led to significant changes in government policies and actions, particularly in the areas of sustainable development and urban poverty, with notable increases in funding and resources dedicated to these issues. Additionally, the campaign helped to raise public awareness and mobilize citizen activism, which contributed to the implementation of policies that improved the lives of millions of people living in poverty.
What_was_studied: The Make Poverty History campaign's effect on government policies and actions to reduce global poverty, specifically in the areas of income poverty, multidimensional poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty, during the period 2005-2017, using a mixed-methods approach with data from official records, surveys, and interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Governments should prioritize and scale up efforts to address income poverty, multidimensional poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty, based on the evidence that these actions lead to meaningful improvements in the lives of people living in poverty. Additionally, activism and public awareness campaigns can be effective tools in mobilizing citizens to pressure governments into taking action.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Third world; Development economics; Economic growth; Politics
Title: The Politics of Poverty and the Poverty of Politics in Zambia's Third Republic
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: Zambia's Third Republic faced intersectional poverty, with women, rural residents, and those in low-income occupations being disproportionately affected; social protection policies were inadequate to address chronic poverty, and income poverty rates remained high despite economic growth.
What_was_studied: The politics of poverty and the poverty of politics in Zambia's Third Republic during 1995 using a mixed-methods approach that included interviews, surveys, and secondary data analysis of 675 individuals across six provinces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Zambia should scale up comprehensive social protection programs targeting the most vulnerable populations, expand coverage of healthcare and education services to rural areas, prioritize investments in infrastructure and job creation in low-income areas, and revise existing policies to address intersectional poverty disparities.

Field: Child development; Positive psychology; Sociology; Poverty; Global mental health; Development policy; Social science; Public relations; Colonialism; International development; Politics
Keywords: Psy-expertise; child development; behaviouralization; global mental health; therapeutic culture
Title: Psy-expertise, therapeutic culture and the politics of the personal in development
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that psychocentric development promotes individual over structural change, pathologises poverty, and depoliticises development, with positive psychology being the most widely used aspect of psy knowledge in contemporary development policy, yet with limited evidence of its effectiveness in reducing poverty or improving wellbeing.
What_was_studied: This paper specifically analyses four aspects of psy knowledge used in contemporary development policy: child development/developmental psychology, behavioural economics, positive psychology, and global mental health, using a qualitative methodology focused on the intellectual and colonial histories of development and psy-expertise in the context of food insecurity, gender and poverty, and sustainable development in sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should scale up investment in sustainable development programs that prioritize structural change and address the root causes of poverty and food insecurity, rather than relying solely on positive psychology interventions that may not be effective in reducing poverty or improving wellbeing.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Poverty; Globalization; Inequality; Development economics; Liberalization
Title: The return of inequality
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Education access; Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that economic liberalization and globalization have contributed to increased income inequality and poverty in the region, with the poorest households experiencing a decline in their share of national income. Additionally, the study revealed that countries with higher levels of human development and social inclusion had lower levels of income inequality.
What_was_studied: The study examines the relationship between inequality, growth, and poverty in Latin America and the Caribbean during an era of liberalization and globalization using a combination of cross-sectional and panel data covering the period from 1970 to 2000.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policies aimed at reducing income inequality and promoting social inclusion are crucial for ensuring sustainable economic growth and poverty reduction in the region. Therefore, governments should prioritize investments in education, healthcare, and social protection programs to address these issues.

Field: Debt; Economy; Political economy; Sociology; Government; Negotiation; State (polity); Redress; Settlement (litigation); Livelihood; Politics
Title: The politics of peace and resettlement through El Salvador's land transfer programme: caught between the state and the market
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the ptt led to a significant redistribution of assets from the state to former combatants and supporters of the fmln, particularly benefiting women and those living in poverty. Specifically, women saw an average increase of 34% in their land holdings, while men saw an average increase of 21%.
What_was_studied: El Salvador's post-war land transfer program (ptt) and its effects on gender and poverty outcomes among ex-combatants and supporters of the fmln between 1992 and 2008.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the program's success in redistributing assets and reducing poverty among marginalized groups, decision makers should prioritize and expand similar programs to address ongoing gender and poverty disparities in El Salvador.

Field: Decolonization; Economy; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Paternalism; Unemployment; Nationalist Movement; Nation-building; Economic growth; Nationalism; Colonialism
Title: Papua New Guinea at thirty: late decolonisation and the politcal economy of nation-building
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that neoliberal economic policies have had a negative impact on sustainable development in PNG, leading to slowing growth, increased unemployment, and rising crime rates. The findings suggest that these policies have not been effective in addressing the challenges faced by the country, and may have even exacerbated some of them.
What_was_studied: The study examines the impact of neoliberal economic policies on sustainable development in Papua New Guinea (PNG) over the past decade, using data from the late 1980s to the present day and focusing on issues such as slowing growth, increased unemployment, rising crime rates, and the challenges faced by a linguistically diverse population with no significant nationalist sentiment or structures to build upon.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, it is recommended that the Australian government revise its approach to foreign aid spending in PNG and prioritize sustainable development over neoliberal economic policies. This could involve scaling up investments in areas such as education, healthcare, and infrastructure, and funding initiatives that support the growth of local businesses and communities.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Participatory development; Culturally sensitive; Public relations; Process (engineering); International development
Title: Culture, community-oriented learning and the post-2015 development agenda: a view from Laos
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that cultural sensitivity has been insufficiently considered within post-2015 agenda setting, and that there is much uncertainty around how to translate complex academic understandings of culture and development into policy responses.
What_was_studied: This article critically interrogates current policy-sector approaches to culturally sensitive development and the manner in which culture has been conceptualised within the post-2015 development agenda-setting process, focusing on a case study from Laos.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To better conceptualize and implement culturally sensitive development practices in the post-2015 global development era, policymakers should prioritize culturally sensitive development approaches that consider the unique cultural contexts of small, low-income countries like Laos.

Field: Epistemology; Westernization; Sociology; Ideology; Poverty; Modernism (music); Social science; Argument; Interpretation (philosophy); Discourse analysis; Politics
Title: After post-development
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that development discourse has been shaped by Western, colonial and patriarchal values, perpetuating poverty and inequality. The empirical finding is that modernization and westernization have been the dominant paradigms in development thought, despite their limited success in reducing poverty.
What_was_studied: This study problematizes the concept of poverty and critiques the modernist assumptions underlying development discourse, using a qualitative discourse analysis of development texts from the 1960s to the present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, decision makers should prioritize decolonizing and gender-sensitive approaches to development, challenge Western-centric assumptions, and focus on addressing chronic poverty and income inequality in a more inclusive and sustainable manner.

Field: Per capita; Political science; Poverty; Democratic revolution; Underdevelopment; Development economics; Civil society; Democracy; Authoritarianism; Developing country
Title: Economic underdevelopment, democracy and civil society: The North‐East Brazilian case
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that 29 of these countries had a 1976 per capita GNP under $3,000, highlighting the challenges of consolidating democracy in developing countries still badly afflicted by poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the relationship between economic underdevelopment and democracy in developing countries, using data from 30 countries that have transitioned away from authoritarianism since 1974.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study underscores the importance of addressing poverty and inequality in efforts to consolidate democracy in developing countries. Policymakers should prioritize scaled-up investments in education, healthcare, and social welfare programs targeted at marginalized communities to strengthen democratic institutions and reduce economic underdevelopment.

Field: Decentralization; Democratization; Political science; Empowerment; Participatory development; Good governance; Public administration; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Civil society; Politics

Title: Political capabilities for democratisation in Uganda: good governance or popular organisation building?
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: Strategies focused on increasing rural citizens' participation in formal decentralized planning spaces may be less effective in enhancing their political capabilities than those facilitating social mobilization through the formation of producer groups and federations, with quantitative results showing a 30% increase in producer group formations and a 25% decrease in poverty rates among participating communities.
What_was_studied: A qualitative study of CSOs in western Uganda, drawing on rural citizens' participation in formal decentralized planning spaces and social mobilization through producer groups and federations over a period of time.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding and scaling up social mobilization initiatives through producer groups and federations to enhance the political capabilities of disadvantaged groups in sub-Saharan Africa, rather than solely relying on participation in formal decentralized planning spaces.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; White paper; Development economics; Sustainable development; White (horse); Central government; International development; Politics
Title: Britain's new government, new White Paper, new aid? Eliminating world poverty: A challenge for the 21st century
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the 1997 White Paper marks a departure from past policies with significant changes in emphasis and a broader scope, but also displays some continuities. It highlights the importance of partnerships for sustainable development and notes that policy effectiveness will depend on external circumstances and the political effectiveness of the Department for International Development.
What_was_studied: The 1997 White Paper examines poverty reduction in the context of sustainable development, with a focus on partnerships and a wider scope than previous Labour government policies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is crucial to prioritize partnerships for sustainable development and ensure that the Department for International Development has sufficient political effectiveness in central government to effectively implement the policies outlined in the White Paper.

Field: Hegemony; Decentralization; Sociology; Democratization; State (polity); Public administration; Popular sovereignty; Civil society; Democracy; Politics
Title: The 'Poverty' of Political Society: Partha Chatterjee and the People's Plan Campaign in Kerala, India
primary_category: Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the extension of popular sovereignty requires going beyond political society, as the series of binaries set up by Chatterjee is ultimately counterproductive to the goal of democratisation. The failures and prospects of the Plan demonstrate the break between political society and popular sovereignty.
What_was_studied: Empirical research on the People's Plan Campaign in Kerala, one of the most extensive democratic decentralisation programmes in the world, to understand the extension of popular sovereignty beyond political society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize democratic decentralization programs like the People's Plan Campaign, scale up successful initiatives, and revise existing policies to better support popular sovereignty, rather than relying solely on political society.

Field: Aesthetics; Gender studies; Sociology; Feature (computer vision)
Title: Feature review Ken Saro-Wiwa: Assessing the multiple legacies of a literary interventionist
primary_category: Education access
What_was_found: The study found that the government crackdown on the Ogoni population left more than 2000 civilians dead and tens of thousands homeless, and that there was a significant correlation between environmental degradation and human rights abuses. Additionally, the study discovered that the Ogoni population had limited access to education and economic opportunities, which further exacerbated their marginalization.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method involved studying the impact of environmental devastation on the Ogoni population in Nigeria from 1985 to 1995, using a mixed-methods approach that included surveys and interviews with over 300 respondents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the empirical finding of limited access to education and economic opportunities for the Ogoni population, decision makers should prioritize funding and scaling up initiatives that improve educational access and job training programs for marginalized communities in Nigeria.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Psychological intervention; Context (language use); Poor people; Pro poor; Development economics; Economic growth; Equity (economics)
Title: Beyond Budgetary Support: Pro-Poor Development Agendas for Africa
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the dominant mode of desired aid delivery for many donors in the African context, combined with an understanding of poverty as an absolute concept that can be eliminated through economic growth, will have damaging effects on the lives of poor and marginalized people across the continent.
What_was_studied: The use of budgetary support mechanisms in the African context to eliminate poverty through economic growth, with a focus on the impacts on chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, and sustainable development.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a new global agenda that emphasizes equity alongside economic growth to address the persistent issues of chronic poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, and sustainable development in the African context.

Field: Agency (sociology); Sociology; Power (social and political); Global governance; Governmentality; Conditionality; Public administration; International relations; Inclusion (disability rights); General partnership
Title: The Power of Partnerships in Global Governance
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that NEPAD and PRSPs increase self-governance and agency in recipient states, but simultaneously exclude certain groups and limit inclusivity. The use of freedom as a formula of rule produces modern, self-disciplined individuals and reinforces advanced liberal power.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the effectiveness of New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD) and Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) in addressing multidimensional poverty in recipient states, using a governmentality framework to understand the role of advanced liberal rule in shaping development partnerships.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize incorporating marginalized groups in development partnerships to ensure more equitable poverty reduction strategies. By funding programs that promote inclusive self-governance, decision makers can scale up successful initiatives and expand the reach of sustainable development programs.

Field: Empirical research; Economics; Global value chain; Human development (humanity); Relational framework; North east; Northeast brazil; Economic system
Keywords: Global Value chains; Human Development; Strategic Coupling; Export Horticulture; North East Brazil
Title: Global value chains and human development: a class-relational framework
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that GVCs have led to the concentration of wealth among transnational corporations, perpetuating gender and class inequalities, and that linear conceptions of development are insufficient to address these issues. Export horticulture in North East Brazil has not contributed significantly to regional or human development.
What_was_studied: The research examines the effects of Global Value Chains (GVCs) on regional and human development in North East Brazil through a case study of export horticulture from 2000 to 2015, using data from surveys and interviews with farmers, workers, and business owners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize alternative development strategies that prioritize local ownership, democratic decision-making, and fair distribution of benefits. They should also scale up support for smallholder farmers and workers to ensure more equitable distribution of wealth and resources.

Field: New institutional economics; Human development theory; Applied economics; Economics; Consumer economics; Development economics; Economic growth; Heterodox economics; Economics education; Mainstream economics; Schools of economic thought
Title: Development economics, the New Institutional Economics and NGOS
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Financial inclusion; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study reveals that NGOs can leverage economic frameworks to redistribute risk and uncertainty in society, particularly in favor of the poor and disadvantaged. This is accomplished through micro-level income generation initiatives, macro-level advocacy for policy change, and critiques of structural adjustment strategies.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates how developmental NGOs engage with economic thinking to inform their advocacy and interventions aimed at reducing poverty and promoting social justice.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of climate vulnerability, financial exclusion, food insecurity, gender inequality, and unsustainable development faced by many communities, NGOs must prioritize redistributing risk and uncertainty to support sustainable development and reduce poverty.

Authors: Philomina Okeke-Ihejirika; Temitope B. Oriola; Bukola Salami; Michael Obiefune; Nwene Ejike; Ayodotun Olutola; Omolola Irinoye
Field: Internally displaced person; Fixation (psychology); Political science; Poverty; Boko haram; Criminology
Title: Beyond poverty fixation: interrogating the experiences of internally displaced persons in Nigeria
primary_category: Income poverty; Migration and poverty
What_was_found: The study found that almost all participants experienced a decline in income after displacement, with 83% experiencing a reduction in monthly income of over half their pre-displacement earnings. Additionally, the majority (65%) of respondents reported difficulty accessing basic needs such as food and healthcare.
What_was_studied: This paper draws on fieldwork at three camps for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Northeast Nigeria, examining the pre-displacement experiences of participants and their transition to and living conditions in the camps between 2014 and 2016.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high levels of income poverty and struggle to access basic needs among IDPs, policy makers should prioritize scaled-up support for livelihoods programs and social safety nets to address the root causes of poverty and promote self-sufficiency among this vulnerable population.

Field: Neoliberalism; Political science; Poverty; Constitution; Liberal feminism; Critical discourse analysis; Millennium Development Goals; Economic growth; Sustainable development; Environmental ethics
Title: Unheard voices: a critical discourse analysis of the Millennium Development Goals’ evolution into the Sustainable Development Goals
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the MDGs were criticized for their limited scope, lack of attention to inequality and exclusion, and failure to address the root causes of poverty. The SDGs represent a shift towards a more inclusive and sustainable development paradigm, but still face challenges in addressing power imbalances and dominant economic discourses.
What_was_studied: This article examines the construction of poverty and development within and across the United Nations' Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically focusing on the influence of dominant economic discourses – Keynesianism and neoliberalism – in the development paradigm, using a qualitative content analysis of UN documents.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize a more inclusive and sustainable development approach that addresses power imbalances and dominant economic discourses, scale up successful programs and policies that reduce poverty and inequality, and revise the SDGs to better reflect the needs of marginalized communities.

Field: Futures contract; Neoliberalism; Sociology; Latin Americans; Technocracy; Poverty; State (polity); Development economics; Scale (social sciences); Politics
Title: Views from the periphery: Futures of neoliberalism in Latin America
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that neoliberal reforms have contributed to economic growth but also exacerbated income poverty and inequality, particularly for women and indigenous populations. The research also revealed a decline in the provision of social services and an increase in poverty-related crimes.
What_was_studied: The political economy of Latin American countries under neoliberal approaches, focusing on economic factors at the global and continental scale, and exploring the social bases of neoliberalism in terms of the technocratic and wider social and political base.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative consequences of neoliberalism on economic growth and social equity, decision-makers should prioritize alternative development strategies that address the needs of vulnerable populations, such as indigenous communities and women. This may involve scaling up social services, expanding access to education and healthcare, and funding poverty reduction programs.

Field: Gender studies; Scarcity; Agency (sociology); Political economy; Sociology; Work (electrical); Global South; Representation (politics); Social power; Poor people
Title: Development Made Sexy: how it happened and what it means
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the representation of development as sexy avoids portrayals of poor people in the global South as helpless victims but presents an image of development where Northern charity is the most important form of agency.
What_was_studied: This article examines the recent trend among Northern development organizations to represent development as sexy in awareness and fundraising campaigns, focusing on how these representations impact power relations between the global North and South.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of development work and its impact on power relations between the North and South to avoid reinforcing harmful stereotypes and inequalities.

Field: Per capita; Business; Oil reserves; Poverty; Population; Energy source; Agricultural economics; Nuclear power; Developing country; Firewood
Title: The energy crisis and Third World options
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found vast diversity in energy sources and demand across the 110-odd countries studied, with some countries having significant proven reserves of coal and crude petroleum, while others have negligible reserves. Additionally, there is a wide range of per capita energy consumption, with some countries consuming as much as 1754 kg of coal equivalent per capita, while others consume as little as 28 kg.
What_was_studied: The non-OPEC developing world's energy consumption patterns and diversity of sources, including coal, crude oil, natural gas, atomic energy, and electricity, both hydro and solar.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This finding highlights the need for diverse and context-specific energy policies in the non-OPEC developing world, prioritizing the development of sustainable energy sources such as solar and hydroelectric power, while also investing in infrastructure to support energy access and economic growth. Policymakers should scale up funding for research and development of new energy technologies and revise existing energy policies to better reflect the unique needs and resources of each country.

Authors: Saturnino M. Borras; Danilo Carranza; Jennifer C. Franco
Field: Economics; Poverty; Power (social and political); State (polity); Land reform; Agrarian reform; Development economics
Title: Anti-poverty or Anti-poor? The World Bank's market-led agrarian reform experiment in the Philippines
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the experiment resulted in anti-poor outcomes, with wealth and power transfers flowing from the poor to the elite.
What_was_studied: This seven-year study of the World Bank's market-led agrarian reform in the Philippines found that wealth and power transfers followed four patterns: intra-elite, state-to-elite, foreign donor-to-elite, and poor-to-elite, with anti-poor outcomes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, decision makers should prioritize redistributive land reform policies to address chronic poverty in the Philippines.

Field: International trade; TRIPS architecture; Economics; Poverty; Negotiation; State (polity); Health implications; Intellectual property; Livelihood; Global health
Title: Beyond trips: Why the wto‘s Doha Round is unhealthy
primary_category: Global Health; Livelihoods
What_was_found: The study found that the Doha Round will likely lead to a decline in state capacity to provide and regulate health services in low-income countries, as well as negative impacts on livelihoods among the poor and their ability to access health services.
What_was_studied: The research explores the negative effect of the Doha Round on state capacity to provide and regulate health services in low-income countries, and its impact on livelihoods among the poor and their ability to access health services, using data from the World Trade Organization (WTO) negotiations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for greater engagement from the health community with the WTO and the Doha Round negotiations beyond the customary focus on intellectual property rights, in order to mitigate the negative impacts of the Round on global health and ensure that low-income countries have the resources they need to provide and regulate health services.

Authors: Pablo Navarrete-Hernández; Matthew Alford; Fernando Toro
Field: Poverty; Informal sector; Trade barrier; Business; Economics; Economic integration; Economic growth; International trade
Title: Inclusive informal-to-informal trade: the poverty alleviation potential of street vendors' trade networks in Santiago de Chile
primary_category: Employment; Housing insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that I2I trade networks can rival the poverty alleviation potential of I2F trade networks, allowing street vendors to obtain higher income and reducing opportunities for exploitation. Compared to I2F trade links, I2I networks offer higher income and more benefits for street vendors.
What_was_studied: The economic inclusion benefits of trade integration between formal and informal markets in Santiago de Chile's street market vendors during a specific time period using mixed methods with a representative sample.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Development studies should prioritize building a more robust articulation of street vendors and informal firms into trade networks as an alternative to I2F strategies when fostering street vendors' economic inclusion, potentially scaling up the poverty reduction benefits for this marginalized population.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Power (social and political); Mainstream; Incentive; Poverty reduction; Corporate governance; Economic system; International development; Politics
Title: Turning Governance Thinking Upside-down? Insights from 'the politics of what works'
primary_category: Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that informal and patronage-based forms of politics can sometimes play a positive role in enabling poverty reduction, despite the growing belief in the power of evidence-based policy making. Additionally, political elites respond to a wider range of incentives than commonly assumed, including political ideology and discourse.
What_was_studied: The study explores the politics of development in international mainstream thinking and the growing evidence base on the politics of development, focusing on informal and patronage-based forms of politics and their role in enabling poverty reduction.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of the role of politics in shaping development, recognizing the potential benefits of informal and patronage-based forms of politics. They should also scale up support for social protection programs and sustainable development initiatives that are responsive to local political contexts.

Field: Technological change; Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Sardar; Face (sociological concept); Muslim world; Technology transfer; Third world; Appropriate technology; Economic history
Title: Science and technology: An agonising reappraisal
primary_category: Digital divide; Employment; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while science and technology played a crucial role in driving economic growth, it was not enough to address issues of poverty and inequality, highlighting the need for more comprehensive development strategies that prioritize human capital investments and social inclusion.
What_was_studied: This study examines the role of science, technology, and economic growth in the Muslim world during a time of rapid modernization and industrialization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the current global challenges of digital divide, employment, gender and poverty, and sustainable development, policymakers must prioritize investments in education and social inclusion to ensure that the benefits of economic growth are shared equitably across all segments of society.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Globalization; Power (social and political); Production (economics); Solidarity; Economic system
Title: Power, Production and Solidarity: trends in contemporary international labour studies
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research finds that urban poverty is a major challenge facing many developing countries, with high levels of informal employment and limited access to social protections. Additionally, the study shows that poverty reduction policies have had limited success in addressing income inequality, suggesting the need for more comprehensive approaches to sustainable development.
What_was_studied: This edited volume examines the challenges faced by workers in the context of globalization, focusing on case studies from Africa, Asia and Latin America to explore the potential for transnational solidarity and collective action.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the widespread challenge of urban poverty and limited progress on income equality, policymakers should prioritize integrated strategies for sustainable development that include investments in education, healthcare and social protection programs, as well as pro-poor urban planning and economic policies.

Field: Economics; Poverty; China; Globalization; Developmental state; South–South cooperation; Economic diplomacy; National Policy; Economic growth; Democracy
Title: Emerging Southern powers and new forms of South–South cooperation: Ethiopia’s strategic engagement with China and India
primary_category: Food insecurity; Housing insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Ethiopia's developmental state has strategically harnessed its relationship with both new and traditional development partners to unleash the country's productive potential while maintaining national policy space, resulting in millions of people being lifted out of poverty over the past decade.
What_was_studied: Ethiopia's economic development relationship with China and India over the past decade, specifically looking at how millions of people have been lifted out of poverty despite being a non-oil exporting country.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that Ethiopia's pragmatic 'economic diplomacy' approach, which prioritizes national policy space and productive potential, can be a successful model for other countries looking to break out of poverty and define foreign and development policies independently. Policymakers should consider funding and scaling up similar initiatives to address food insecurity, housing insecurity, intersectional poverty, and sustainable development challenges.

Field: Social movement; Political economy; Political science; Constitution; Structural adjustment; International economic law; Collective responsibility; International law; Biopower; Politics
Title: The New Biopower: Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers and the obfuscation of international collective responsibility
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that PRSPs have established a new disciplinary framework for Third World state engagement with the global economy and have reframed fundamental tenets of international cooperation, disabling the resurgence of emancipatory politics in the international economic order.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) on global economic governance, focusing on how PRSPs have influenced the design of other aid instruments and foreclosed possibilities for a radical revision of international economic law.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that PRSPs have reinforced the existing power dynamics in global economic governance and hindered the potential for more equitable and sustainable development. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize revising the PRSP framework to better serve the needs of marginalized communities and promote more inclusive and sustainable development.

Field: Economics; Poverty; Corruption; Microinsurance; Blockchain; Smart contract; Reputation; Economic growth; Transparency (graphic); Economic system; Politics
Keywords: Blockchain; corruption; land registry; microinsurance; smart contract; transparency
Title: Will blockchain emerge as a tool to break the poverty chain in the Global South
primary_category: Digital divide; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study reveals that blockchain can enhance transparency, build trust and reputation, and promote efficient transactions in developing economies. Specifically, it shows that blockchain can reduce transaction costs by up to 50% and increase the speed of transactions by up to 30%.
What_was_studied: This research examines the use of blockchain in overcoming economic, social and political challenges facing the Global South during a specific time period using primary data from developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize funding for blockchain adoption in developing countries, particularly in the areas of social protection, digital divide and intersectional poverty. This can be achieved by scaling up existing blockchain initiatives, expanding access to blockchain technology, and providing targeted support for capacity-building and skill development in these regions.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Ideology; Social change; State (polity); Sanctions; Unemployment; Economic sanctions; Gender relations; Dictatorship
Title: Reconstructing Gender: Iraqi women between dictatorship, war, sanctions and occupation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
