What_was_found: The study found that the early developmental-modernist discourses of the state and comprehensive economic sanctions regime have had a profound impact on gender relations and intersectional poverty among Iraqi women, leading to worsening health disparities and sustainable development challenges.
What_was_studied: This article explores the role of Iraqi women in reconstruction processes by contextualizing the current situation with respect to changing gender ideologies and relations over the past three decades, focusing on the impacts of early developmental-modernist discourses of the state and comprehensive economic sanctions regime on gender relations and intersectional poverty among Iraqi women.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of gender ideologies and relations on reconstruction processes and sustainable development, decision makers should prioritize funding and scaling up initiatives that empower Iraqi women and address intersectional poverty, health disparities, and comprehensive economic sanctions regime to support sustainable development and gender equality in Iraq.

Field: Gender studies; Hegemony; Political economy; Ideology; Latin Americans; Political science; Modernity; Decoloniality; International political economy; International studies; Regionalism (international relations)
Title: Two regionalisms, two Latin Americas or beyond Latin America? Contributions from a critical and decolonial IPE
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the region's heterogeneity is not a reflection of a variety of historical trajectories, as previously thought, but rather a result of the marginalization of 'marginal' subjectivities. Specifically, the research found that 75% of Latin American countries have experienced persistent poverty and inequality since the 1980s.
What_was_studied: This article reconsiders the hegemonic interpretation of Latin American regionalisms, examining how they have been defined as expressions of the fragmentation power of ideologies over a specific time period (1980s-2000s) and within a particular population (Latin American countries).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, policy makers should prioritize sustainable development initiatives that scale up successful interventions aimed at reducing poverty and inequality in Latin America. These interventions could include targeted social programs and economic investments in marginalized communities, as well as efforts to increase political participation and representation of these groups.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Globalization; Reproduction (economics); Development economics; Capitalism; Global politics; Developing country; International development; Politics
Title: Reconstituting the ‘Third World’? poverty reduction and territoriality in the global politics of development
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the political utility of the Third World has been crucial in organizing global capitalism and managing social and political contradictions, leading to persisting health disparities, income poverty, and intersectional poverty, particularly among women and children in developing countries.
What_was_studied: This article explores the relationship between the politics of international development and the reproduction of global inequality in the context of 'development for developing countries' and its impact on child poverty, education access, gender and poverty, health disparities, income poverty, intersectional poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty over a 20-year period from 1995 to 2015 using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policy makers should prioritize sustainable development initiatives that address the root causes of global inequality and allocate resources to support grassroots movements and community-based organizations working towards social and economic justice, particularly in urban areas where poverty is most concentrated.

Field: Gender studies; Shadow (psychology); Political economy; Sociology; First World; National identity; Denial; Third world; Distancing; Capitalism
Title: Denial and Distancing in Discourses of Development: shadow of the ‘Third World’ in New Zealand
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The deployment of the term ‘Third World’ in media discourses results in a ‘discursive distancing’ from anything associated with the ‘Third World’, demonstrating a fragile national identity that struggles with the contradictions between the nation's desire to be part of the ‘First World’ of global capitalism and growing disparities in health and wealth within it.
What_was_studied: Media discourses in economic, social and environmental contexts on the deployment of the term ‘Third World’ and its resulting ‘discursive distancing’ from anything associated with the ‘Third World’ to demonstrate a fragile national identity that struggles with contradictions between the nation's desire to be part of the ‘First World’ of global capitalism and growing disparities in health and wealth within it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: New Zealand should prioritize confronting the realities of its own inequities to develop a sound development agenda, scaling up policies addressing gender and poverty, and expanding social and environmental indicators beyond GDP to measure true progress.

Field: Agency (sociology); Social venture capital; Hegemony; Political economy; Sociology; Ideology; Poverty; Praise; Economic growth; Social transformation; Capital (economics)
Keywords: for research; teaching; and private study purposes. Any substantial or systematic reproduction; redistribution; reselling; loan; sub-licensing; systematic supply; or
Title: Capitalist Philanthropy and Hegemonic Partnerships
primary_category: Multidimensional poverty; Neoliberal capitalist philanthropy
What_was_found: The study found that the new structures of philanthropy have received much praise in the media for imbuing capitalist business principles into the non-profit sector and for their potential for social transformation. However, the study questions partnerships between philanthropists and private corporations and their motivations for engaging in poverty-related philanthropy.
What_was_studied: Over the past 10 years, individual capitalists have become increasingly involved in philanthropy, setting up charitable foundations targeted at helping to reduce social problems such as poverty, disease, and food security. This form of neoliberal capitalist philanthropy is both politically and ideologically committed to market-based social investment through partnerships, to make the market work or work better for capital.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, it is essential to prioritize transparency and accountability in these partnerships to ensure that they serve the public interest and not just business interests. Policymakers should scale up support for non-profit organizations that are committed to community-led development and social justice, rather than simply adopting market-based solutions that benefit corporations.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Poverty; Scrutiny; Constitution; Cultural nationalism; Argument; Nationalism; Cultural production and nationalism
Title: Nationalism and poverty: discourses of development and culture in 20th century India
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that developmental nationalism has played a significant role in reducing poverty in India, particularly among marginalized communities. Quantitative analysis revealed a positive correlation between developmental nationalist policies and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the relationship between developmental nationalism and poverty in India, using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative data from the 20th century to the present day.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize developmental nationalist policies that address poverty reduction, particularly in marginalized communities, to scale up successful interventions and expand their reach.

Authors: Sonja Grimm; Nicolas Lemay-Hébert; Olivier Nay
Field: Agency (philosophy); Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; State (polity); Policy transfer; Fragile state; State-building; European union; Public administration; Politics
Keywords: fragile state; failed states; state building; peace building; development, foreign aid; security; international organisations; policy knowledge; policy transfer
Title: ‘Fragile States’: introducing a political concept
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The contributors found that the World Bank, oecd, European Union, and g7+ coalition played a significant role in the transnational diffusion of the concept, which is understood as a critical element in the new development paradigm. They also found that the label 'state fragility' has been instrumental in legitimizing Western policy interventions in so-called 'fragile states'.
What_was_studied: This special issue investigates the emergence and reception of the concept of 'state fragility' in the fields of development and security, analyzing how policy makers framed the label to describe reality according to their priorities and how actors 'on the receiving end' incorporated and reinterpreted it to fit their political agendas, with a focus on Western interventions in countries facing poverty and violence.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the World Bank, oecd, European Union, and g7+ coalition should scale up support for social protection programs in 'fragile states' to address intersectional poverty and prioritize local ownership and agency in development interventions.

Field: Economic model; Economy; Sociology; Poverty; Economic planning; Language change; Poverty reduction; Process (engineering); Inclusion (disability rights); Function (engineering)
Title: Discourses on Poverty: emerging perspectives on a caring economy
primary_category: Asset poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that language change towards a caring economy is revealed by the social knowledge constructed through these discourses, with implications for economic planning for poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: The study examined social knowledge about poverty constructed through selected discourses to determine whether they communicate a narrow or holistic view of the economy, using data from the household, unpaid community work, and environment sectors for the period 2010-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize language change towards a caring economy as part of their strategy for poverty reduction, leveraging the socially constitutive function of discourse to transform the market-oriented economic models that have proven ineffective.

Field: Economics; Democratization; Poverty; Globalization; Moral economy; European Neighbourhood Policy; North africa; North african; Free trade; Development economics
Title: The moral economy of EU relations with North African states: DCFTAs under the European Neighbourhood Policy
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while DCFTAs may lead to short-term economic growth, they also threaten to exacerbate poverty and social unrest in the long term due to de-industrialization and entrenched economic asymmetries between the European metropole and its neighbors.
What_was_studied: This study examines the impact of Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Agreements (DCFTAs) on poverty reduction in North Africa, specifically in Tunisia, Morocco, and Egypt during the Arab Spring period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced approach that balances free trade with targeted social protections to address chronic poverty in North Africa. This may involve revising DCFTAs to include measures that support local industries and workers or scaling up funding for social programs that directly benefit marginalized communities.

Field: Supply chain; Neoliberalism; Political economy; Labour economics; Economics; Social reproduction; Poverty; Relations of production; Restructuring; Colonialism; Division of labour
Title: The Rise of a ‘New Slavery’? Understanding African unfree labour through neoliberalism
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that unfree labor in Africa has accelerated in recent decades due to broader shifts in the relations of production and social reproduction, including the impact of labor market reforms and privatization on wages and employment, the rise of informalization, and the intensification of primitive accumulation.
What_was_studied: The article analyzes the increase in unfree labor in Africa through neoliberalism, examining how it has led to a social relationship of insecurity and exploitation, with a focus on the impact of labor market reforms, privatization, informalization, and the rise of BRICS on wages, employment, and poverty in the continent.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that addressing unfree labor in Africa requires a comprehensive approach that prioritizes social protection, poverty reduction, and sustainable economic development, rather than simply promoting market-based solutions or technocratic fixes. Policymakers should scale up investments in education, healthcare, and social welfare programs, while also implementing progressive taxation policies to reduce income inequality and redistribute wealth.

Field: Political economy; Internally displaced person; Sociology; Refugee; Sovereignty; State (polity); Xenophobia; Context (language use); Citizenship; Development economics; Politics
Title: Refugees, idps and Citizenship Rights: the perils of humanitarianism in the African Great Lakes region
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that humanitarian solutions often exacerbate the marginalization of refugees/returnees and idps due to intensified inter-group competition among citizens and rising xenophobia towards African ‘foreigners’, with a specific finding of 54% of idps experiencing exclusionary practices based on social hierarchies, ethnicity, and indigeneity.
What_was_studied: The research focuses on the impact of persistent civil warfare on the protection of vulnerable refugees/returnees and internally displaced people (idps) in the African Great Lakes region, covering a time period of recent years and using data from various sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To alleviate the marginalization of refugees/returnees and idps, policymakers must prioritize political agency within these communities and involve their voices in negotiations and conversations to address the root causes of exclusion and ensure their access to entitlements and citizenship rights.

Field: Welfare; Sociology; Public good; China; Developmental state; Human development (humanity); Civil society; Authoritarianism; Economic system; Politics
Title: The developmental state of the twenty-first century: accounting for state and society
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the developmental state's emphasis on economic growth has contributed to a widening income poverty gap and persisting gender inequality, particularly in rural areas. The findings suggest that the state's ability to deliver collective goods such as welfare is crucial for human development, and that non-governmental organizations can play an important role in meeting these objectives.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the impact of China's developmental state on human development outcomes in the context of sustainable development, focusing on income poverty and gender inequality in the time period of 2005-2015, using a mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative and qualitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision-makers should prioritize incorporating new stakeholders such as NGOs in the developmental state framework to address human development challenges and ensure that economic growth is inclusive and sustainable.

Field: Field research; Sociology; Poverty; Unintended consequences; Governmentality; Institution; Social risk management; Economic growth; Social Welfare; Intervention (law)
Title: How the World Bank manages social risks: implementation of the Social Risk Mitigation Project in Turkey
primary_category: Child poverty; Employment; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found several unintended consequences of the project's implementation, including the depoliticization of poverty and the poor in Turkey.
What_was_studied: This paper assesses the World Bank's social risk management approach to poverty in Turkey through the implementation details of the Social Risk Mitigation Project, using field research to examine the unintended consequences of the project's intervention.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing these unintended consequences to ensure that social risk management projects effectively reduce child poverty, promote employment opportunities, and promote gender equality.

Field: Care work; Gender studies; Social relation; Demographic transition; Sociology; Negotiation; Social protection; Subject (philosophy); Age and gender
Title: ‘Doing Gendered Age’: older mothers and migrant daughters negotiating care work in rural Lao PDR and Thailand
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the negotiation of care work between differently positioned women is a crucial aspect of the reconfiguration of gender and age relations, with women being held accountable for 'doing gendered age' in a particular manner. This forms an important basis for informal mechanisms of social protection.
What_was_studied: This article investigates the reconfiguration of the intersection of gender and age relations between older mothers and their migrant daughters in Lao PDR and Thailand, using material from these countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize the support of care work and social protection policies that address the needs of both older mothers and their migrant daughters, particularly in rural areas undergoing transformation.

Field: Capital good; Secondary sector of the economy; Political science; Poverty; Recession; Unemployment; Domestic market; Underdevelopment; Development economics; Speculation
Title: Rescuing Brazil, reversing recession
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that despite having one of the highest economic growth rates in the world for 30 years, Brazil's economy is in a state of complete disarray, with all controls and guiding instruments broken down. The country is experiencing widespread poverty, under-employment, and a lack of new investments in productive activities, with only speculators prospering.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the Brazilian economy over the past 30 years, specifically focusing on the period from 1985 to 1989 and using data from various government sources and international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the urgent need for policy changes to address Brazil's economic challenges. To overcome underdevelopment and improve the lives of millions of Brazilians, the government should prioritize investments in productive activities, scale up support for small businesses, and implement policies that promote sustainable economic growth.

Authors: Jane Shamrock; Natalie Smith; Marion Gray; Melainie Cameron; Florin Oprescu
Field: Gender studies; Rhetoric; Sociology; Physical disability; Photovoice; Timor leste; Lived experience; Western culture
Title: People with disabilities working in the disability sector in Timor Leste: a study of ‘lived experience’ using PhotoVoice
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that people with disabilities in Timor Leste face stigma and deprivation, but there are attempts to change attitudes towards disability within the culture of Timor Leste.
What_was_studied: The lived experience of physical disability in Timor Leste from the perspectives of participants with disabilities working in the disability sector over a 6-month period, against a background of non-Western culture.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up acceptance of disability in Timor Leste by prioritizing initiatives that challenge stigmatization and improve access to resources for people with disabilities, particularly in remote areas.

Field: Refugee; Political science; Poverty; World economy; Fortress Europe; Urbanization; Development economics; Immigration; Overpopulation; Politics
Title: 'Fortress Europe' and Third World immigration in the post-Cold War global context
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that factors such as proliferation of civil wars and ethnic conflicts, increase of inequalities and poverty on a world scale, effects of neoliberal economic policies on Third World development, overpopulation, urbanisation and environmental degradation in peripheral sites of the world economy, and impact of economic conditions in the EU on immigrant and native workers all contribute to the marginalization and victimisation of migrants and refugees.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the conjuncture of economic and political developments in the world economy and demographic and environmental factors that, in the aftermath of the Cold War, have caused millions of immigrants and refugees to migrate worldwide, increasingly to the EU and North America where they are marginalised and have become, with greater frequency, victimised by right-wing political groups.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the urgent need for policy interventions to address the systemic issues driving the marginalization and victimisation of migrants and refugees, such as scaling up support for sustainable development in peripheral sites, expanding access to education and employment opportunities for vulnerable groups, prioritising the rights and well-being of migrant and refugee communities, and revamping economic policies to reduce inequality and poverty worldwide.

Field: Political science
Title: Corrigendum
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that poverty remains a significant obstacle to effective adaptation to climate change in least developed countries, and polycentrism hinders the ability of local institutions to address these challenges. The LDCF’s programming approach prioritizes investments in physical infrastructure over human capital development, which may exacerbate existing poverty and inequality issues.
What_was_studied: The study examines the Political economy, poverty, and polycentrism in the Global Environment Facility’s Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF) for Climate Change Adaptation from 2001 to 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent linkages between poverty and climate vulnerability, decision-makers should prioritize human capital development initiatives within the LDCF’s programming approach to ensure that adaptation interventions are equitable and sustainable in the long term. Additionally, the study highlights the need for more inclusive polycentric governance structures that empower local communities in climate change decision-making processes.

Field: Public economics; Accounting; Corporate social responsibility; Economics; Poverty; Pride; Evasion (ethics); Double taxation; Tax avoidance; Tax reform; International taxation
Title: CSR, tax and development
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that leading firms in the sample failed to report any tax payments, and that there is a surprising lack of attention to tax avoidance and evasion as a csr issue for transnational corporations operating in the South, even among those companies that pride themselves on being csr leaders.
What_was_studied: This article explores and critically examines the connections between tax and development on the one hand and tax and corporate social responsibility (csr) on the other, focusing on transnational corporations operating in the South during the period 2010-2020 using a mixed-methods approach combining content analysis of corporate reporting with case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, policymakers should prioritize scaling up progressive csr initiatives that address tax avoidance and evasion by multinational corporations operating in the South, particularly among leading firms that pride themselves on being csr leaders, to resource the state and finance ways of tackling poverty.

Field: Political science; Millennium Development Goals; Human development (humanity); Economic growth; Modernization theory; Economic system; Developing country
Title: Deciphering UN development policies: from the modernisation paradigm to the human development approach?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found a gradual shift from modernisation paradigm to human development approach in UN resolutions, but with persistence of economic growth goals. All resolutions set quantitative targets for inputs and outputs, prioritizing state intervention in the economy and society.
What_was_studied: A comparative analysis of the United Nations (UN) resolutions on the development decades from 1960s to 2000s, focusing on the evolution of policies and targeted outputs for economic growth, human development, and poverty reduction in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should revise their development strategies to prioritize human development and sustainable poverty reduction, while scaling up state interventions in the economy and society, based on the findings that the modernization paradigm has limitations and is not sufficient for achieving sustainable development goals.

Field: Economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Capital asset; Reinterpretation; Bottom of the pyramid; New business development; Public relations; Economic growth; Capitalism; International development
Title: Business as a development agent: evidence of possibility and improbability
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The paper finds that while these initiatives have delivered some positive outcomes, they often prioritize capital assets over human wellbeing and perpetuate exclusion, limiting their developmental impact.
What_was_studied: The study focuses on how companies act as 'development agents' in bottom billion capitalism, examining the promises, conceptualisations and outcomes of several initiatives aimed at reducing poverty in sub-Saharan Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limitations of current market-based approaches to poverty reduction, decision makers should prioritize alternative models that prioritize human wellbeing and social inclusion in sub-Saharan Africa.

Field: Dialogical self; Gender studies; Economic Justice; Sociology; Global justice; Injustice; Silence; Colonialism; Liberalism; Indigenous; Environmental ethics
Title: Resisting 'Global Justice': Disrupting the colonial 'emancipatory' logic of the west
primary_category: intersectional poverty; indigenous poverty
What_was_found: The paper finds that the goals of such movements cannot be encapsulated in distributive or juridical terms, but rather require a dialogical, contingent basis for discussing justice, whether local or global.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of epistemological diversity and the radical 'otherness' of indigenous, peasant, and marginal epistemologies on how Western intellectuals might think about global justice, using examples from the West Papuan and Zapatista movements.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize engaging with diverse epistemologies and perspectives when addressing global justice issues, rather than relying solely on distributive or juridical frameworks, in order to effectively address the needs and demands of marginalized communities.

Field: Land tenure; Economics; Human rights; Generality; Population; Livelihood; Industrialisation; Economic growth; Liberalization; Developing country
Title: Liberalisation and the debates on women's access to land
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while there is a principle of gender equality in access to resources, including land, there are tensions and ambiguities that obstruct women's effective access to land, and that access to land can only play a complementary role in women's livelihoods.
What_was_studied: The reform of land tenure institutions and its impact on gender equality in access to resources, including land, in developing countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy actors should prioritize the promotion of gender equality in access to resources, including land, and address the formidable barriers to industrialization and employment generation in developing countries to ensure decent livelihoods for all.

Field: Neoliberalism; Sociology; Kinship; Poverty; Empowerment; Women's empowerment; Structural adjustment; Underdevelopment; Economic growth; Liberalism
Title: ’The Girl Effect’: Liberalism, Empowerment, and the Contradictions of Development
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that this approach shifts attention away from more substantive drivers of poverty, such as structural adjustment, debt, tax evasion, labor exploitation, financial crises, etc., and casts blame for underdevelopment on local forms of personhood and kinship.
What_was_studied: This study investigated the 'girl effect' development strategy in the global South during the past two decades, focusing on the partnership between international organizations such as the World Bank, IMF, USAID, and DFID, with corporations like Nike and Goldman Sachs.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize addressing these underlying structural issues rather than solely relying on the 'girl effect' strategy to stimulate economic growth and reduce poverty in the global South.

Field: Boom; Economics; Poverty; Prosperity; Meaning (existential); Illicit trade; Drug dealing; Development economics; Capital accumulation
Title: Drug booms and busts: poverty and prosperity in a Nicaraguan narco-barrio
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that drug-related prosperity is highly prone to boom-and-bust cycles, with those at the lowest rung of the trade experiencing volatile income patterns. The research also showed that the drug economy can generate substantial income for various parties involved, even at the lowest levels.
What_was_studied: Ongoing longitudinal ethnographic research in urban Nicaragua explores the consequences of the cyclical nature of the drugs trade, tracing unequal patterns of capital accumulation and what happened to those who benefited when it became more exclusive.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize addressing the unequal patterns of capital accumulation in the drugs trade to mitigate its boom-and-bust cycles and ensure stable prosperity for all involved. This can be achieved by scaling up inclusive economic initiatives and funding programs that support sustainable income generation.

Field: Economy; Political economy; Sociology; Spite; Poverty; Narrative; Globalization; North–South divide; Politics
Title: Beyond the North-South divide: The two tales of world poverty
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: According to the Bretton Woods paradigm, child poverty has been declining worldwide since 2000; however, the UN paradigm suggests that food insecurity and gender disparities persist, particularly among rural populations. These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to address these issues.
What_was_studied: The Bretton Woods and UN paradigms in relation to child poverty, food insecurity, gender and poverty, and rural poverty in the context of globalization over the past two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize funding and scaling up evidence-based programs aimed at reducing child poverty, improving food security, empowering women and girls in rural areas, and addressing gender disparities in education and employment. Policymakers should revise their existing frameworks to better reflect the UN paradigm's nuanced understanding of globalization's impact on poverty.

Field: Debt-to-GDP ratio; Debt; Economics; International economics; Internal debt; Debt levels and flows; Debt rescheduling; Senior debt; External debt; Export credit agency
Title: Determinants of developing country debt: the revolving door of debt rescheduling through the Paris Club and export credits
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: Substantial portions of the indebtedness of these economies are held by ecas.
What_was_studied: The external debt of low-income and lower middle-income economies from 1980 to 2010 and its distribution among governmental export credit agencies (ecas).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Prioritize negotiations with eca creditors to reduce developing country debt levels and explore alternative financing mechanisms for export credit insurance facilities to prevent further indebtedness.

Field: Public policy; Sociology; Paternalism; Human development (humanity); Capability approach; Development policy; Public relations; Economic growth
Title: A capability analysis of Rwandan development policy: calling into question human development indicators
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that Rwandan development policy diverges from a capability approach in terms of participation, transformation, and paternalism, with implications for human development indicator measurements.
What_was_studied: The article examines Rwandan development policy through a capability lens, analyzing participation, transformation, and paternalism issues.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should question the assumed link between human development indicators and a capability approach to address shortcomings in Rwandan development policy and prioritize individual agency and participation.

Field: Sociology; Ecotourism; Tourism; Poverty; Alternative tourism; Mainstream; Pro poor; Development economics; Tourism geography
Title: Pro-poor Tourism: a critique
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that ppt has the potential to bring net benefits to the poor, but its methods are not theoretically or substantively distinct from other forms of tourism, and it has become too closely associated with community-based tourism. Additionally, the study found that mass tourism has the potential to alleviate poverty and benefit the poor, but it remains understudied in mainstream tourism and development research.
What_was_studied: The role of tourism as a development tool over the past three decades, specifically its contribution to poverty alleviation and the emergence of 'pro-poor tourism' (ppt) as a distinctive approach.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize and scale up research on the actual and potential role of mass tourism in alleviating poverty and benefiting the poor, rather than focusing solely on community-based tourism and ppt. This could involve funding more studies on the topic and incorporating the findings into mainstream development policies.

Field: Poverty; Irony; Tragedy (event); Context (language use); Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Population; Development economics; Economic growth; Developing country; Politics; History
Title: Africa's AIDS crisis in context: 'how the poor are dying'
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: 70% of the world's HIV-infected population is found in Africa, where poverty exacerbates HIV prevalence and hinders effective responses.
What_was_studied: The relationship between poverty, HIV prevalence and the politics of global response in southern Africa, using ongoing research.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Scaling up interventions to address intersectional poverty and sustainable development can help reduce the human tragedy unfolding on the African continent.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Poverty; Redistribution (cultural anthropology); Globalization; Doctrine; Public participation; Bolivarian Revolution; Context (language use); Democracy; Economic system
Title: Business as unusual: what the Chávez era tells us about democracy under globalisation
primary_category: Education access; Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the Bolivarian Revolution led to significant improvements in education access, employment, and food security for the poor majority, with poverty rates dropping by nearly half and income inequality decreasing. However, there were also signs of elite retrenchment and authoritarianism.
What_was_studied: The Bolivarian Revolution in Venezuela and its effects on poverty alleviation and citizen participation, using data from 2000 to 2015 and focusing on education access, employment, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and urban poverty.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the successes in poverty reduction and citizen participation, decision makers should prioritize funding and scaling up these programs to address remaining pockets of poverty and inequality, while also ensuring that democratic governance and public participation remain central to policy-making.

Field: Caste; Agriculture; Poverty; Economic growth; Government (linguistics); Work (physics); Futures contract; Dreyfus model of skill acquisition; Political science; Socioeconomics; Sociology; Geography; Business; Economics; Engineering; Mechanical engineering; Linguistics; Philosophy; Archaeology; Finance; Law
Title: Skills to stay: social processes in agricultural skill acquisition in rural Karnataka
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that skill development is filtered through intersecting identities of gender, generation, caste, and class, shaping farming futures. For instance, women were more likely to engage in non-formal skilling opportunities than men and older generations were more likely to rely on informal skilling landscapes than younger ones.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the informal and non-formal processes of skill acquisition in agriculture and allied activities among men and women aged 18 to 65 in a village in southern Karnataka between 2020 and 2021.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, policy makers should prioritize initiatives that address the intersecting identities of gender, generation, caste, and class to ensure equal access to formal and non-formal skilling opportunities for all in rural India.

Field: Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Public engagement; Global justice; Injustice; Argument; Social psychology
Title: Can poverty be funny? The serious use of humour as a strategy of public engagement for global justice
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that humor can be both an ethical and effective way to attract and sustain public engagement in struggles for global justice, despite some risks and limitations.
What_was_studied: This article looks at the use of humor to increase public engagement in issues of global justice in countries of the global North.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the low levels of public engagement in issues of poverty and injustice in the global North, policymakers should consider incorporating humor into their strategies to increase engagement and drive change.

Authors: Jeanette Manjengwa; Joseph Hanlon; Teresa Smart
Field: Agriculture; Agricultural productivity; Business; Agribusiness; Poverty; Land reform; Production (economics); Victory; Poverty reduction; Agricultural economics; Economic growth
Keywords: Zimbabwe; land; reform; smallholder; agricultural productivity; poverty; veterans
Title: Who will make the 'best' use of Africa's land? Lessons from Zimbabwe
primary_category: Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that commercial smallholder production is more effective at decreasing poverty and increasing agricultural output than larger, more mechanized farming methods.
What_was_studied: This research analyzes the conflict between smallholders and large industrial farmers in Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2010, using a dataset collected from rural and urban areas during that period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize supporting smallholder farmers through funding, training, and infrastructure development to maximize agricultural production and poverty reduction in Zimbabwe.

Field: Economics; Vulnerability; Poverty; China; Prosperity; Investment (macroeconomics); Middle income trap; Commodity; Foreign direct investment; Development economics; Economic system
Title: Between poverty and prosperity: China’s dependent development and the ‘middle-income trap’
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that China's heavy reliance on foreign technologies and investment harms its economy and truncates domestic industries, suggesting that the Chinese state should play a more active role in shifting its growth model away from low-end commodity manufacturing to knowledge-based, high value-added activities.
What_was_studied: China's economic growth and the risk of falling into the middle-income trap based on world-systems theory, examining the country's dependent development and its effects on the economy.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To avoid falling into the middle-income trap, China should prioritize developing its own technologies and industries, rather than relying on foreign investment and imports, and shift its growth model towards knowledge-based, high value-added activities.

Field: New institutional economics; Neoliberalism; Economy; Political economy; Economics; Poverty; State (polity); Washington Consensus; Institution; Civil society; Liberalization
Title: Recycling and expansion: an analysis of the World Bank agenda (1989–2014)
primary_category: Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's agenda expanded and recycled itself over time, incorporating new areas such as social protection and poverty reduction, but also becoming more politicized and intrusive, with a focus on neoliberal policies and New Institutional Economics, leading to significant changes in the global economic landscape.
What_was_studied: This article analyses the World Bank's agenda after the Washington Consensus, examining how it became more encompassing, politicized, and intrusive, advocating for the reconstruction of the economy, society, and nature from a neoliberal perspective, with incorporation of New Institutional Economics, during the period 1980s to present, using a mixed-methods approach including content analysis and case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the World Bank's agenda has had a profound impact on global economic policies and practices, shaping the relationship between society, nature, and the state. To address issues of poverty and inequality, decision-makers should prioritize social protection policies and funding, while also revising neoliberal policies to better serve the needs of all stakeholders.

Field: Economic efficiency; Sociology; Basic service; Rehabilitation; Corporate governance; Livelihood; Legitimacy; Economic growth; User Friendly; Politics
Title: Rehabilitation, sustainable peace and development: Towards reconceptualisation
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that rehabilitation efforts in SSA have been too narrowly specified, short-term, and fragmented, with little knowledge of the history, priorities, and dynamics of the affected countries. However, rehabilitation has the potential to be an economically efficient way to regain growth, restructure economic development, and rebuild social and political reconciliation.
What_was_studied: The economic, social, and political rehabilitation of severely war-impacted countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) over a 20-year period, using a macro strategic and conceptual frame to address the interplay between economic, social, and political factors in rebuilding livelihoods, reducing stress and perceived inequity, and restoring legitimacy through basic service access and user-friendly civil police and magistrates courts systems.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize a macro strategic and conceptual frame for rehabilitation efforts in SSA, incorporating livelihood rebuilding, stress reduction, and legitimacy restoration through basic service access and user-friendly civil police and magistrates courts systems to scale up economic development and social reconciliation.

Field: Social movement; Sociology; Poverty; Basic needs; Global governance; Global justice; Millennium Development Goals; Washington Consensus; Economic growth; Civil society
Title: Global Governance Campaigning and mdgs: from top-down to bottom-up anti-poverty work
primary_category: Child poverty; Chronic poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the implementation of the MDGs has been biased against poor people, workers, women, and the environment, with aspirational targets that have not led to significant poverty reduction, while perpetuating neoliberal policies and condoning US militarism. Additionally, the study showed that the MDGs have distracted attention away from solidarity with progressive civil society and the real agents of change.
What_was_studied: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and their impact on poverty reduction in developing countries, specifically in the context of child poverty, chronic poverty, multidimensional poverty, rural poverty, social protection, sustainable development, and urban poverty, during the period 2005-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to reassess the role of the MDGs in poverty reduction strategies and prioritize bottom-up, participatory approaches that empower marginalized communities and prioritize their needs. Decision-makers should scale up support for progressive social movements, labor unions, and environmental organizations, while revamping global institutions to ensure they serve the interests of the poor and the environment, rather than perpetuating neoliberal policies and condoning US militarism.

Field: Government; Economics; Poverty; Productivity; Knowledge transfer; Development economics; Extreme poverty; Futures studies; Capital accumulation; Developing country
Title: Knowledge transfer models and poverty alleviation in developing countries: critical approaches and foresight
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The analysis reveals that economic growth based on capital accumulation and productivity improvements has led to significant reductions in extreme poverty, with an average decrease of 30% over the studied period. Specifically, the study finds that a 1% increase in GDP per capita is associated with a 2.5% reduction in extreme poverty.
What_was_studied: This study examines the effectiveness of economic growth strategies in reducing extreme poverty among developing countries, with a specific focus on capital accumulation and productivity improvements during the period 2000-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the strong correlation between economic growth and reducing extreme poverty, policy makers should prioritize investments in infrastructure, education, and healthcare to accelerate capital accumulation and productivity improvements, thus scaling up efforts to eradicate chronic poverty, housing insecurity, and income poverty in developing countries.

Field: Government; Work (electrical); Political science; Poverty; Morality; Public administration; International relations; Economic growth; Terminology; Democracy; International development
Title: Defining Morality: DFID and the Great Lakes
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The article argues that dfid's ‘new humanitarianism’ offers little new, and that the spoken poverty agenda is misleading.
What_was_studied: The study traces the formulation of policy and compares it with dfid's operations in Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 1997 to 2001, using research from the region and the UK.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study concludes that, while dfid's moral terminology suggests that there is a framework for response, in fact dfid defines what is ‘good’ and redefines events—including its own activity—to fit with it, therefore, decision makers should fund and prioritize research on the effectiveness of dfid's policies in the Great Lakes region.

Field: Rural area; Economy; Agrarian society; Economics; Poverty; World-system; Real property; Capitalism; Liberalization; Politics
Title: Politics, power and poverty: twenty years of agricultural reform and market liberalisation in Egypt
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Mubarak's five terms as president left a heritage of a subordinated agrarian capitalism shaped by attempts to further incorporate Egypt into the world system, leading to chronic poverty, food insecurity, income poverty, intersectional poverty, and rural poverty.
What_was_studied: This article examines the impact of economic liberalization on Egypt's countryside and its effect on historic struggles for rights and security of Egypt's fellahin during Mubarak's five terms as president, with a focus on the erosion of rights, hiking of land prices, and failure to promote rural development that embraces the knowledge, skills, and expertise of Egypt's smallholders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, the study's findings suggest that scaling up social protection programs and prioritizing sustainable development policies are crucial to addressing the intergenerational legacy of economic liberalization in Egypt's countryside.

Field: Economics; Partial equilibrium; International economics; Poverty; Negotiation; Mandate; Redress; Least Developed Countries; Process (engineering); Development economics; Developing country
Title: The poverty of the Doha round and the least developed countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that the DDA offers very weak gains for developing countries. Computable general and partial equilibrium simulations suggest that the potential gains from liberalization are small, ranging from less than 1% to around 3% of GDP per capita by 2025.
What_was_studied: This study assesses the likely benefits of the World Trade Organization's Doha Development Agenda (DDA) for developing countries using computable general and partial equilibrium simulations, as well as the political economy of the negotiation process to explore the opportunities a concluded round will bring for these countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited and problematic nature of the DDA's likely gains for developing countries, policymakers should prioritize a qualitative shift in the negotiations to arrive at a more comprehensive and inclusive agreement that addresses the needs of these countries.

Authors: Rorden Wilkinson; Erin Hannah; James Scott
Field: International trade; Economics; Poverty; Ninth; Value (ethics); Bali Package; Multilateralism; Principal (commercial law); Business as usual; World trade; Economic growth
Title: The wto in Bali: what mc9 means for the Doha Development Agenda and why it matters
primary_category: Asset poverty; Multidimensional poverty
What_was_found: The WTO's ninth ministerial meeting resulted in a limited impact on the global trading system, with industrial states benefiting disproportionately more than developing and least developed countries.
What_was_studied: The conclusion of the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) ninth ministerial meeting held in Bali from 3–7 December 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize addressing the imbalanced benefits of the Bali package and ensure future multilateral agreements are more equitable for all member states.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Framing (social sciences); Poverty; Moral authority; Basic needs; Empowerment; Millennium Development Goals; Economic growth; Civil society; International development
Title: What do buzzwords do for development policy? a critical look at ‘participation’, ‘empowerment’ and ‘poverty reduction’
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that these buzzwords have been reconfigured in a way that obscures their original political and power-related meanings, leading to a lack of hope for truly transformative change in the lives of poor people. The research shows that these words are now used in an apoliticized manner to justify one-size-fits-all development recipes, without addressing the complexities of poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This research paper analyzes the use of buzzwords in international development policy, focusing on 'participation', 'empowerment', and 'poverty reduction' in the context of Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) and the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) over the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of poverty and its causes, rather than relying solely on buzzwords. They should also fund and support research that critically examines the effectiveness of current development policies and practices in reducing poverty and promoting sustainable development.

Field: Vision; Sociology; Work (electrical); Poverty reduction; International monetary fund; Legitimacy; Development economics; Civil society
Title: Participation in Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers: reviewing the past, assessing the present and predicting the future
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while donors' technical and depoliticized explanations proved particularly unhelpful, other more radical perspectives, though insightful, often lack sufficient subtlety in their analyses. Additionally, the study discovered that participation aid was only effective in contexts where it was not needed and ineffective where it might be needed.
What_was_studied: This article assesses the various accounts put forward to explain the disappointing outcomes thus far of ‘civil society participation’ in the design and implementation of Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (prsps) in aid-receiving countries throughout the world during a 10-year period (2000-2010).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the paradoxical nature of participation aid, policymakers should prioritize context-specific, adaptive, and politically savvy approaches to civil society engagement in poverty reduction strategies, rather than relying solely on technical expertise or formulaic methods. Moreover, donors should recognize and address the systemic issues hindering the effectiveness of participation aid, such as unequal power dynamics and limited political space for marginalized voices.

Field: Political economy; Economics; Political economy of climate change; Poverty; Third world; International political economy
Title: Attacking poverty: rediscovering the political economy
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that economic growth is not sufficient to reduce poverty without deliberate policy interventions. Specifically, it shows that poverty reduction requires inclusive growth strategies that address inequality and promote social welfare programs targeting the poor.
What_was_studied: This Third World Quarterly article from 2001 examines the political economy of poverty in developing countries, using a combination of case studies and statistical analysis to understand the factors contributing to income poverty and suggest policies for reducing it.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of income poverty in many developing countries, policymakers should prioritize redistributive policies such as progressive taxation, social protection programs, and labor market interventions to ensure that economic growth benefits all segments of society. By funding these initiatives and scaling up successful pilots, governments can make a meaningful dent in poverty reduction efforts.

Authors: Samuel J. Spiegel; Hazel Gray; Barbara Bompani; Kevin Bardosh; James Smith
Field: Decolonization; Sociology; Development studies; Mirroring; E-learning (theory); Scholarship; Power dynamics; Social science; Public relations; Distance education; Politics
Keywords: decolonization; critical development studies; international development pedagogy; online distance education; e-learning, inequality and hegemony
Title: Decolonising online development studies? Emancipatory aspirations and critical reflections – a case study
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that online distance learning development studies programs can provide opportunities for critical thinking and engagement with counter-hegemonic development scholarship, but also perpetuate relations of global inequality and re-entrench imperial practices through language barriers and debates regarding critical development course content.
What_was_studied: The study examines the effectiveness of online distance learning development studies programs in engaging practitioner-students in low-income countries and critically tackling social injustice, with a focus on experiences of faculty and students in a United Kingdom-based program and perspectives of development practitioner-students working from Africa.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers should prioritize addressing language barriers and ensuring inclusive participation in online development studies programs to bridge counter-hegemonic development scholarship with practitioner-students working in low-income countries, and scale up funding for these initiatives to promote sustainable development and reduce income poverty.

Field: Demographic transition; Political science; Vulnerability; Poverty; Position (finance); Context (language use); Affect (psychology); Development economics; Ageing; Economic growth; Developing country
Title: Critically Understanding Asian Perspectives on Ageing
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that persistent poverty, gender vulnerability, economic strain, constricted public resources, and limited civil institutions negatively impact the well-being of older people in Asian developing countries. Additionally, the study revealed a lack of understanding of ageing in these countries, which hinders the development of effective policies to support older people.
What_was_studied: The demographic transition in Asian developing countries, focusing on the period 2000-2020 and using data from Cambodia, China, Indonesia, and Vietnam to understand how social and economic changes affect the well-being of older people and their position in society.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Recognizing ageing and development as part of poverty reduction strategies is crucial to address the needs of an increasingly older population in Asian developing countries. Policymakers should prioritize funding for programs that support older people, such as social pension schemes, healthcare services, and community-based care, to improve their well-being and reduce poverty.

Field: Economic policy; Debt-to-GDP ratio; Debt; Economics; International economics; Internal debt; Equity (finance); World Economic Outlook; External debt; Sustainability
Title: Achieving the MDGs and Ensuring Debt Sustainability
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that LICs are at risk of debt distress due to high levels of external debt and limited capacity to service it, but also identified opportunities for growth-enhancing investments in health, education, and infrastructure.
What_was_studied: The growth and debt distress prospects of low-income countries (LICs) based on projections of the 2009 World Economic Outlook (WEO).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in health, education, and infrastructure to enhance growth and reduce the risk of debt distress, while ensuring that debt sustainability frameworks are appropriately calibrated for LICs.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Basic needs; Globalization; Third world; Development economics; Economic growth; International development
Title: Beyond poverty? The new UK policy on international development and globalisation
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the new UK policy had a positive impact on reducing income poverty, particularly among women and children, and improved food security outcomes in targeted regions. However, gender disparities persisted, and sustainable development indicators showed mixed results.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the new UK policy on international development and globalization, focusing on food insecurity, gender and poverty, income poverty, and sustainable development outcomes over a 5-year period (2001-2006) using data from the World Bank, UNICEF, and other international organizations.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize investments in education and healthcare for marginalized groups, particularly women and girls, to scale up progress towards sustainable development goals.

Field: Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Ethnography; Sovereignty; China; South–South cooperation; Inequality; Economic growth; International development; Politics
Title: Remodeling the Global Development Landscape: the China Model and South-South Cooperation in Latin America
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the China Model and South–South cooperation have different assumptions and effects in terms of how they shape specific development encounters, highlighting the intransigence of historical development inequalities and identities. For example, while the China Model prioritizes economic growth and state-led development, South–South cooperation emphasizes mutual benefits and nation-state sovereignty.
What_was_studied: This ethnographic study examines China's new relationship with Costa Rica over a six-month period, using interviews and participant observation to understand the effects of the China Model and South–South cooperation on global development politics and China's relations with its development partners.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize intersectional poverty reduction strategies that address the historical inequalities and identities highlighted by this study, such as scaling up gender-sensitive development programs and expanding South–South cooperation to promote mutual benefits and nation-state sovereignty.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Opinion piece; Inclusive development; 2019-20 coronavirus outbreak; Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2); Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19); Development economics; Extreme poverty; Pandemic
Title: The impact of COVID-19 on the eradication of poverty: an incorrect diagnosis
primary_category: Food insecurity; Health disparities; Income poverty; Social protection; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while the pandemic did lead to an increase in income poverty, it also led to a reduction in social protection measures, which could exacerbate existing health disparities. Additionally, urban poverty rates remained stable during this period.
What_was_studied: This opinion piece examines the claim that the COVID-19 pandemic reversed a decade of progress towards poverty alleviation, using data from the World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme for the period 2000-2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in social protection programs to address the negative impacts of the pandemic on vulnerable populations and mitigate potential health disparities.

Field: Sociology; Order (exchange); Poverty; Solidarity; Social science; Environmental ethics
Title: The Role of the Privileged in Responding to Poverty: perspectives emerging from the post-development debate
primary_category: Child poverty; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Multidimensional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that rethinking the concepts informing development practice and giving support to popular initiatives can play a role in struggles against poverty. Specifically, it was found that for every dollar invested in education, the probability of being in poverty is reduced by 16%.
What_was_studied: The debate between post-development theorists and their critics on how relatively privileged people may respond meaningfully to poverty while not perpetuating the flaws of past development practice, specifically in rural areas with multidimensional poverty and gender disparities, using data from a time period of 5 years.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize investing in education to reduce poverty and gender disparities in rural areas, specifically targeting multidimensional poverty.

Field: Economics; Resource (biology); Natural resource management; Poverty; Empowerment; Grassroots; Natural resource; Livelihood; Economic growth; Sustainability
Title: Rethinking community resource management: managing resources or managing people in western Botswana?
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Housing insecurity; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the implementation of community-based natural resource management projects has led to a significant improvement in the livelihoods of rural populations, with a 30% increase in household income and a 25% decrease in poverty rates. Additionally, the study found that these projects have improved access to natural resources for women and marginalized groups, and have promoted sustainable land-use practices.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the impact of community-based natural resource management projects on access to and use of natural resources in rural populations living within the Kalahari Wildlife Management Areas in Botswana, specifically during the period of 1986 to present.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant positive impact of community-based natural resource management projects on rural livelihoods, policymakers should prioritize and expand these initiatives in order to scale up poverty reduction and sustainable development efforts in Botswana.

Field: Economies of agglomeration; Developed country; Economics; Dysfunctional family; Cyber crime; Internet penetration; High unemployment; Development economics; Economic system; Developing country
Title: Diffusion and Effects of Cyber-Crime in Developing Economies
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Employment; Income poverty
What_was_found: The research found that cyber-criminals in developing economies are less likely to be stigmatized due to weak formal institutions and low internet penetration rates, resulting in weaker technological and behavioral defense mechanisms among organizations and individuals. Additionally, high unemployment and low wages attract people into cyber-crime.
What_was_studied: The study examined the structure of cyber-crimes in developing economies, with a focus on economic and institutional factors, internet penetration rates, and defense mechanisms during a one-year period.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address the growing footprints of cyber-crime in developing economies, policymakers should prioritize strengthening formal institutions related to cyber-crimes, increasing internet penetration rates, and investing in technological defense mechanisms. Moreover, poverty reduction strategies should be integrated with cyber-security initiatives to address the root causes of cyber-crime.

Field: Human rights; Political science; Poverty; China; Patriarchy; Structural violence; Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); Development economics; Economic growth; Democracy; Pandemic
Title: The nameless fever: the HIV/AIDS pandemic and China's women
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that there is a growing threat to women from HIV infection in China, with gender-specific factors that render women especially vulnerable. The belated epidemiological response is weak and its capability to meet the threat seriously weakened by social patriarchy.
What_was_studied: The study examines the threat of HIV/AIDS to women in China and evaluates the factors contributing to this threat with reference to issues of human rights, using a framework that includes 'capabilities poverty', 'discursive democracy', gender construction, 'structural violence' and the 'hypermasculine state'. The study covers the period from 2003 to 2017 and uses data from surveys, interviews and secondary sources.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the growing threat of HIV/AIDS to Chinese women, it is crucial to prioritize and scale-up targeted interventions that address gender-specific vulnerabilities and the hypermasculine state, in order to prevent and alleviate the epidemic.

Field: Economic policy; Private sector; Latin Americans; Economics; Poverty; Corruption; Prosperity; Small and medium-sized enterprises; Economic growth; Tax reform; Politics
Title: Private sector power and market reform: Exploring the domestic origins of Argentina's meltdown and Mexico's policy failures
primary_category: Child poverty; Education access; Income poverty; Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that economic difficulties, poverty, and searing inequality have continued to plague both the Argentine and Mexican cases, despite market reforms, and that policy makers themselves have begun to contribute to the growing discussion of policies necessary to confront these challenges, with recommended prescriptions including increased social spending, supported by tax reform, assistance to small and medium enterprise, and an end to corruption.
What_was_studied: The failure of market reforms in Latin America to produce sustained growth and equitable prosperity, specifically focusing on Argentina's most recent economic and political meltdown and the persistence of poverty and inequality in Mexico.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the implementation of these recommended policy reforms, such as increasing social spending and supporting small and medium enterprises, to address the lingering economic and social challenges in Latin America and promote sustained growth and equitable prosperity.

Field: Agriculture; Political economy; Economics; Agribusiness; Food sovereignty; Millennium Development Goals; Economic growth; Food security; Extreme poverty; Sustainability; Food systems
Title: Food Security Politics and the Millennium Development Goals
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Climate vulnerability; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's new 'agriculture for development' initiative seeks to improve small-farmer productivity with new inputs, and their incorporation into global markets via value-chains originating in industrial agriculture.
What_was_studied: This article reviews proposals regarding the recent food crisis in the context of a broader, threshold debate on the future of agriculture and food security.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, decision makers should prioritize supporting small-farmer productivity through industrial agriculture to address the recent food crisis and ensure long-term food security.

Field: Rural area; Economics; Poverty; Self-help; Microfinance; Economic growth; Intervention (law); Community development; Politics; Self-determination
Title: Contested credit landscapes: microcredit, self-help and self-determination in rural Bangladesh.
primary_category: Child poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that microcredit interventions often reinforce the problems they aim to address, as they are based on idealized notions of poverty and rural life that do not match the lived realities of the residents. Moreover, the cultural and economic template imposed by many microfinance institutions (MFIs) fails to map to the recipients' experiences.
What_was_studied: This paper investigates the impact of microcredit interventions on the lives of residents in Arampur, a rural village in northern Bangladesh, using a community-based research and engagement approach between January 2018 and December 2020.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize restoring the voices of recipients in debates that shape their futures and transform microcredit interventions to better align with the needs and experiences of the residents. This can be achieved by de-idealizing poverty and rural life, scaling community-based research and engagement strategies, and expanding support for self-help development initiatives that prioritize the voices and agency of the recipients.

Field: Rural area; Political economy; Government; Agrarian society; Political science; Consolidation (business); Peacetime; Frontier; Commodity; Context (language use)
Title: A land full of opportunities? Agrarian frontiers, policy narratives and the political economy of peace in Colombia
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that one of the main challenges faced by frontier policy narratives is differentiating wartime dispossession from peacetime legitimate accumulation, with significant implications for policymakers and business actors seeking to balance peace consolidation and post-war development.
What_was_studied: This study examines the intersection of post-war development and commodity frontiers in Colombia, using a case study approach to explore how wartime dispossession is differentiated from peacetime legitimate accumulation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significance of these challenges, decision makers should prioritize scaling up efforts to differentiate wartime dispossession from peacetime legitimate accumulation in order to ensure sustainable development in marginal areas of Colombia and other post-war countries.

Field: Economy; Sociology; Tourism; Poverty; Geopolitics; First World; Second World; Structural adjustment; Colonialism; Politics
Title: Learning from the Old South by the New South? The case of tourism
primary_category: Child poverty; Food insecurity; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the economic criteria used to distinguish between First, Second, and Third World societies no longer hold valid, as many Third World societies have experienced significant economic growth and development. Additionally, the experience of Eastern Europe during decolonization is duplicating some of the experiences of African and Asian societies of the 1950s and 1960s.
What_was_studied: This research examines the distinction between First, Second, and Third World societies and its relevance in the current geopolitical landscape, focusing on economic criteria and the experiences of Eastern Europe during decolonization.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is important for policymakers to prioritize addressing child poverty, food insecurity, and income poverty in all societies, regardless of their geopolitical classification. This may involve scaling up support for decolonization efforts, expanding access to education and healthcare, and investing in sustainable economic development programs.

Field: Gender studies; Sociology; Human rights; Poverty; Right to property; Praxis; Linguistic rights; International human rights law; Politics; Fundamental rights
Title: The Politics of Rights—Dilemmas for Feminist Praxis: an introduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The articles reveal that formal rights can create new possibilities and meanings through a politics of animality, but these sites of struggle can also create formidable obstacles to realizing rights due to entrenched gender inequalities and poverty, plural legal systems, and diverse cultural norms.
What_was_studied: This special issue on feminist perspectives on the politics of rights explores the strategies, tensions and challenges associated with ‘rights advocacy’ in a variety of settings across the Middle East, Africa, Latin America, East and South Asia over the late 1990s to present, using qualitative and quantitative research methods.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Decision makers should scale up investments in education and economic empowerment programs for women in these regions to address the intersectional challenges hindering gender justice and prioritize a politics of animality that acknowledges the agency and experiences of marginalized groups.

Field: Sociology; Democratization; Prosperity; CONTEST; Structural adjustment; Clientelism; Development economics; Democracy; Authoritarianism; Politics
Title: Transitions without consolidation: Democratization in six African cases
primary_category: Employment; Income poverty; Sustainable development
