What_was_found: The study found that these historical conditions pose significant long-term structural hindrances to democratization, including the difficulty in reversing economic decline and generating rising prosperity, as well as the presence of deep ethnic or communal cleavages that undermine mutual trust. Additionally, the limited experience with multiparty democracy and the prevalence of personalism, clientelism, and corruption in previous authoritarian regimes further impede democratization.
What_was_studied: The historical conditions that hinder democratic experiments in certain regions, specifically the low level of economic development and high levels of poverty and illiteracy, as well as the limited experience with multiparty democracy and prevalence of personalism, clientelism, and corruption in previous authoritarian regimes.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given these findings, it is crucial to prioritize economic development and poverty reduction initiatives in order to create a more favorable environment for democratization. Additionally, efforts should be made to address the prevalence of personalism, clientelism, and corruption in order to strengthen democratic institutions and build trust among citizens.

Field: Marxist philosophy; Sign (semiotics); Political science; Poverty; BENGAL; Soviet union; Development economics; Socialism; Communism; General election; Economic history
Title: Communism in Rajiv Gandhi's India
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Crime & poverty; Food insecurity; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The Marxist hope of peaceful transition has regularly proved a false dawn since the 1950s, with a declining share of the vote from a peak of 9.9% in 1971 to 8.5% in 1984, and a decrease in seats from 48 in 1971 to 28 in 1984.
What_was_studied: Indian communism over the past 60 years, focusing on general election performance and voting trends.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistent poverty and toiling masses in India, the communist movement's lack of breakthrough highlights the need for alternative policy approaches to address chronic poverty and food insecurity, prioritizing support for marginalized communities and revamping urban poverty reduction strategies.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Goodwill; Millennium Development Goals; Normative; Economic growth; Momentum (finance); Discounting; International development; Politics
Title: The Millennium Development Goals: challenges, prospects and opportunities
primary_category: Food insecurity; Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found that while progress has been made in some areas, such as a reduction in extreme poverty and an increase in access to education, there is still much work to be done to address widespread poverty, particularly in rural areas. The research also highlighted the importance of addressing intersectional poverty and the need for more inclusive policies that benefit all populations.
What_was_studied: The research analyzed the effectiveness of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in addressing food insecurity, gender and poverty, intersectional poverty, rural poverty, sustainable development, and urban poverty in the past decade.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the persistence of poverty and the ongoing challenges facing the MDGs, it is crucial to scale up efforts to address these issues, particularly in rural areas. Policymakers should prioritize more inclusive policies that benefit all populations and expand access to education and economic opportunities.

Field: Derivative (finance); Neoclassical economics; Systemic risk; Economics; Valuation (finance); Financial market; Realm; Monetary value; Poverty reduction; Development economics; Speculation
Title: Derivative Nature: interrogating the value of conservation in ‘Boundless Southern Africa’
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The paper found that the use of 'derivative nature' has made conservation more susceptible to speculation and increased systemic risk and uncertainty, while doing little to reduce poverty.
What_was_studied: The neoliberal move to appropriate nature into the realm of commodities and price it in monetary terms, and its consequences for poverty reduction and conservation.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize alternative approaches to conservation that prioritize the well-being of local communities and the environment, rather than relying solely on monetary valuation and commodification.

Field: Immigration policy; Sociology; Human migration; Poverty; Historicity; Service (economics); Development economics; Mythology; Politics; Political economy; Immigration; Political science; Irregular migration; Historicity (philosophy); Economics; History; Ethnology; Population; Law; Demography; Classics
Title: The Myth of Invasion: the inconvenient realities of African migration to Europe
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Migration and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that restrictive immigration policies have failed to curb migration and instead have had perverse effects, with migrants being pushed towards informal labor markets and experiencing exploitation and abuse. Moreover, the demand for cheap migrant labor in informal sectors is a key driver of African migration to Europe.
What_was_studied: African migration to Europe and Libya from 2010 to 2019 using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative data from Eurostat, EUMIPE and other sources with qualitative data collected through fieldwork in seven EU countries and two African countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the structural demand for cheap migrant labor in informal sectors to effectively combat African migration to Europe. Rather than focusing solely on border control and development initiatives, a more comprehensive approach is needed that includes regulating the informal economy, providing fair wages and safe working conditions, and addressing the root causes of poverty and conflict in Africa.

Field: Public economics; Actuarial science; Economics; Credit crunch; Poverty; Credit reference; Collateral; Land registration; Argument; Assertion; Developing country
Title: Access to Credit in the Developing World: does land registration matter?
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: Despite the prevalent belief that formalizing property titles increases access to credit, empirical evidence does not support this claim. Land registration has no positive impact on access to credit in developing countries.
What_was_studied: Access to credit in developing countries and its relation to land registration, examined through empirical data from the period 2000-2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the failure of land registration to improve access to credit, decision-makers should prioritize alternative strategies to address poverty and food insecurity, such as investing in rural infrastructure and supporting farmer organizations.

Field: Agriculture; Economics; Gender analysis; Land policy; Economic growth; Land law; Unit of analysis; Promotion (rank); Default; Capital (economics)
Title: Capital, Labour and Land Relations in Africa: A Gender Analysis of the World Bank's Policy Research Report on Land Institutions and Land Policy
primary_category: Employment; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study challenges the notion of 'non-contractible labor' and questions the Report's use of the household as a unit of analysis, highlighting the consequences for households defaulting on rural loans and the failure to address the link between credit markets, reliance on women's unpaid labor, and poverty reduction.
What_was_studied: This paper analyzes the World Bank's approach to land relations in Africa and its gender implications, focusing on the promotion of formal rural credit and the assumption of women's agricultural labor availability.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Advocates of women's rights in Africa should continue to be attentive to land issues and respond to the World Bank's land agenda by challenging the promotion of credit markets that rely on unpaid women's labor, scaling up efforts to address poverty reduction strategies, and prioritizing household-level data collection to better understand the gendered implications of land relations.

Field: Architecture; Hegemony; Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Power (social and political); Development aid; Reproduction (economics); Modalities; Corporate governance; Development economics
Title: Governance, Representation and International Aid
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that representations about aid, its modalities, and dispensations reproduce a hegemonic discourse, with representational authority residing generally on one side of the aid binary. Additionally, the study showed that development aid has shaped self-understandings of donors in relation to recipients and has embedded neoliberal solutions to development.
What_was_studied: The postwar 20th century international aid architecture and its impact on the representational power and authority of aid donors over recipients.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that the current aid architecture perpetuates a hierarchical and asymmetric relationship between donors and recipients, limiting the potential for sustainable development. To address this issue, policymakers should prioritize more equitable and inclusive forms of aid, such as community-led development programs, and scale up initiatives that empower local communities to drive their own development agendas.

Field: Sociology; Poverty; Globalization; Globe; Power (social and political); Development aid; Social justice; Capital flows; Resource transfer; Development economics
Title: NGOs without aid: Beyond the global soup kitchen
primary_category: Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the rapid changes in the world environment over the past two decades have been driven by unprecedented magnitude of capital flows, with the Northern NGOs holding disproportionate power in their relationships with Southern NGOs.
What_was_studied: The past two decades of globalization and capital flows have had a profound impact on the world environment, with uneven distribution and diminishing concessional aid.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need for more genuine partnerships between Northern and Southern NGOs, moving beyond relations premised on aid, to enhance the possibilities of building a stronger global movement for social justice and poverty eradication.

Field: Neoliberalism; Political economy; Sociology; Developmentalism; Solidarity; Opposition (politics); Delegitimisation; Corporate governance; Economic growth; Indigenous; Politics
Keywords: post-development; neoliberalism; Vedanta; NGOs; transnational solidarity
Title: Worlds beyond the political? Post-development approaches in practices of transnational solidarity activism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that these discourses and practices have tended to rearticulate racialized constructions of unspoiled and authentic 'natives' requiring protection, which are historically embedded in colonial practices of governance. This has resulted in the failure to acknowledge indigenous histories of political organization and resistance, and the delegitimization of demands for equality.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the influence of post-development thought on NGO-led activist discourses and practices of transnational solidarity, particularly in the context of the proposed bauxite mining in the Niyamgiri hills in Odisha, India.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, it is crucial to prioritize the inclusion of marginalized voices in decision-making processes and to challenge dominant narratives around development. Policymakers should focus on dismantling concepts that blur the fundamental divide of wealth and poverty, such as 'graduation', 'differentiation', and 'reciprocity'. Instead, they should aim to address North-South relations and promote enlightened leadership to mitigate global disparities.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize sustainable development and socially inclusive economic growth strategies that address the needs of marginalized communities, scale up public investments in essential services like healthcare and education, and revise market-fundamentalist policies that exacerbate inequality and environmental degradation.

What_was_found: The study found that while the internet has the potential to create a global information marketplace and narrow the poverty gap, its development is primarily driven by commerce, leading to a concentration of economic activity and power in one group. Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that to fully realize the potential of the internet as a GII and address poverty and inequality, policymakers must prioritize investments in local resources and infrastructure, promote regional integration, and adopt policies that balance the interests of all stakeholders, rather than solely prioritizing external funding and expertise.

What_was_found: The tendencies in the world economy that caused the conjuncture of the 1930s and produced-out of a breakdown in liberal-economic structures-the onset of depression, fascism, unemployment, and resurgent nationalism, collectively a partial negation of economic globalisation, leading to world war.
What_was_studied: The global transformation now underway not only slices across former divisions of labour and geographically reorganises economic activities, but also limits state autonomy and infringes sovereignty, using a historical example from the 1930s to explain vast changes in the global political economy.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study matters because it highlights the need to revise the colonial theory of underdevelopment and prioritize gender-sensitive policies and programs that address poverty and income inequality in backward regions, particularly in areas with harsh climates.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: The Kerala model may be taken as an early prototype of sustainable development because of improvements in the quality of life, environmental stability, social and economic equality, and the decline in political strife. Why_it_matters_for_policy: Despite these escalating disposal difficulties in industrial countries, the volumes of wastes produced continue to rise; export to Third World countries seems to undermine the ability of tighter local disposal standards to force the reduction of harmful waste production in the first place; forty developing countries have officially banned waste imports in the last two years, and yet more have rejected specific offers.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the high level of popular support for Hamas and the political challenge it poses to the secular nationalism of the PLO, policymakers should prioritize addressing the socio-economic needs of the disenfranchised segment of the population, potentially scaling up poverty alleviation initiatives to counterbalance Hamas's appeal.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: To address sustainable development challenges, policymakers must prioritize improving the livelihoods of the poorest, particularly the African population, by scaling up access to healthcare, education, and economic opportunities to reduce income poverty and intersectional poverty, and funding initiatives that target these issues.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the negative relationship between financial development and pupil:teacher ratios, policy makers should prioritize investments in education as a crucial factor in improving financial inclusion. What_was_studied: This paper examines the social and ecological foundations of groundwater overexploitation and agrarian distress in semi-arid Andhra Pradesh using an approach grounded in political ecology and political economy.

Therefore, addressing this issue requires scaling up support for smallholder farmers and prioritizing policies that strengthen their resilience to debt-driven survival strategies, such as agrarian reforms that promote collective action and community-based resource management.

Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the findings, donors should prioritize stability-enhancing governance interventions that support local reforms in fragile contexts like Guinea. By focusing on citizen engagement and collaborative governance, these interventions can improve state–citizen relations, leading to more stable and prosperous communities.

What_was_studied: This research analyzed the G20 Principles for Innovative Financial Inclusion and its impact on gender and poverty in the context of finance-led capitalism, using a historical materialist lens and data from 2010 to 2018.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize alternative, inclusive financial systems that do not rely on exploitative relationships between lenders and borrowers, such as community-based financial institutions, to address gender and poverty disparities. Additionally, official development institutions should revise their support for finance-led capitalism and instead fund initiatives that promote human well-being over profits.

Authors: Henk J. van Rinsum; Tangwa Godfrey B
Field: Genome; Sociology; Social group; Genomics; Perspective (graphical); Ideal (ethics); Homo sapiens; Diversity (politics); Social science; Genealogy; Typology
Title: Colony of genes, genes of the colony: diversity, difference and divide
primary_category: Intersectional poverty; Health disparities
What_was_found: The paradoxical intermingling of diversity and difference in genomics, with Homo sapiens becoming part of 'natural resources' and the mapping and definition of differences between individuals and groups, but also the moral dimension of this perspective in terms of diversity and difference.
What_was_studied: The study of the genome in complex transnational organisational research arrangements, specifically the perspectives of marginalized communities on genomics and its implications for diversity and difference.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize the perspectives of marginalized communities in genomics research and expand funding for research on the ethical implications of genomics to ensure that the benefits of technoscience are equitably distributed.

Field: The Imaginary; Sociology; Cognitive reframing; Poverty; Negotiation; Globalization; Face (sociological concept); Context (language use); Economic growth; Politics; Environmental ethics
Title: Education, Development and the Imaginary Global Consensus: reframing educational planning dilemmas in the South
primary_category: Education access; Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The research found that there is no consensus on the role of education in development, despite the common assumption in the contemporary policy discourse. Instead, educational planning dilemmas have changed character and now revolve around how to navigate and negotiate in highly complex political landscapes.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed educational planning dilemmas in the context of knowledge-intensive globalization and severe poverty in the South from a historical perspective, using a mixed-methods approach that includes literature review and case studies from various countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lack of consensus on the role of education in development, decision-makers in the South should prioritize navigating and negotiating in complex political landscapes when addressing educational planning dilemmas. This can be achieved by investing in social protection programs that target the most vulnerable populations and by revising educational policies to better address gender and poverty disparities.

Field: Embodied cognition; Gender studies; Field research; Sociology; Ethnography; Poverty; Negotiation; Structural violence; Sierra leone; Inclusion (disability rights)
Title: Embodiment and Emotion in Sierra Leone
primary_category: Crime & poverty; Gender and poverty; Rural poverty
What_was_found: The study found that people in the 'amputee and war-wounded' community face challenges such as poverty, stigma, and limited access to medical care and rehabilitation services, which can have a profound impact on their daily lives and well-being.
What_was_studied: Drawing on in-depth multi-sited ethnographic field research, this article describes how an ‘amputee and war-wounded’ community formed in Sierra Leone after a 10-year civil war from 1991 to 2002.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The study's findings highlight the need for comprehensive support programs that address the physical, emotional, and spiritual needs of individuals affected by conflict. Policymakers should prioritize funding for rehabilitation services, poverty reduction initiatives, and community-based support networks to ensure that these individuals have access to the resources they need to thrive.

Field: Sociological imagination; Situated; Business; Labour economics; Work (electrical); Poverty; Production (economics); Work quality; Working hours
Title: Corporate labour standards and work quality : insights from the agro-export sector of Guanajuato, Central Mexico
primary_category: Employment
What_was_found: The study found that better pay and secondary benefits resulting from corporate labor standards do not necessarily translate to perceptions of better work quality, as many workers prefer work with lower labor standards but more convenient working hours and the ability to engage in family and social activities alongside the job.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes how workers perceive corporate labor standards and related work conditions in the agro-export sector of Northern Guanajuato, Central Mexico, comparing labor standards on local farms to an international fresh vegetable production, harvesting, processing, and export company with explicit corporate labor standards.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize context-specific labor standards and work conditions that enable workers to balance work and personal life, rather than solely focusing on higher pay and better benefits.

Field: Scarcity; Moral responsibility; Positive economics; Sociology; Development studies; Social work; Poverty; Perception; Development ethics; Social psychology; Criticism
Title: ‘Living Well’ while ‘Doing Good’? (Missing) debates on altruism and professionalism in aid work
primary_category: Employment; Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that aid workers experience moral uncertainties and contradictions in their lifestyles and public perception, with significant implications for development ethics, yet there is a scarcity of studies addressing these issues in the field.
What_was_studied: This paper examines the moral dimensions of international aid work through fieldwork in Cambodia, highlighting the uncertainties and contradictions faced by aid workers regarding their lifestyles and the public perception of their work.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize addressing the moral dimensions of aid work to ensure sustainable development and scale up effective altruism practices among aid workers, revising existing ethical frameworks to better serve collective moral responsibilities.

Field: Political science; Poverty; Economic Partnership Agreements; Cotonou Agreement; Context (language use); Good governance; Public administration; Corporate governance; Sustainable development; General partnership
Title: Is the EU's Governance ‘Good’? An assessment of EU governance in its partnership with ACP states
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that while the EU's governance mechanisms have had some positive impacts on sustainable development and poverty reduction in ACP countries, such as increased trade and investment, there are also significant challenges and contradictions, including unequal power dynamics, inadequate resources, and limited institutional capacity. Additionally, the study found that the EU's emphasis on economic partnerships has often taken precedence over social and environmental considerations.
What_was_studied: The European Union's relationship with African, Caribbean, and Pacific (ACP) states since the adoption of the Cotonou Agreement, focusing on governance mechanisms such as Economic Partnership Agreements, the European Development Fund, and Fisheries Partnership Agreements, and assessing their impact on sustainable development and poverty reduction in ACP countries between 2000 and 2015.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, the EU should prioritize more equitable and sustainable development strategies in its relationships with ACP states, such as scaling up support for local economic development and capacity-building initiatives, expanding access to education and healthcare, and revising its partnership agreements to better address social and environmental concerns.

Field: Gender studies; Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Perspective (graphical); Foregrounding; Order (virtue); Third-Worldism; National development; Nationalism; Politics
Title: Human (In)Security and Development in the 21st Century
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that Third Worldism had both positive and negative consequences, with national development being influenced by wider historical and transnational social and political relations, and that a more relational understanding of the history of development is necessary to understand wealth and poverty, order, violence, and conflict.
What_was_studied: This contribution focuses on the political merits and limitations of Third Worldism, examining its impact on world politics through a critical historical analysis, with a focus on development struggles and emancipatory nationalism.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on these findings, decision-makers should prioritize a more relational understanding of development history to address issues of gender and poverty, and implement social protection policies that acknowledge the interconnectedness of wealth and poverty, order, violence, and conflict.

Field: Government; Economics; Budget support; Action (philosophy); Face (sociological concept); Conditionality; Development economics; Democracy; Developing country; Politics
Title: Budget Support and Democracy: a twist in the conditionality tale
primary_category: Food insecurity; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Recent years have seen several incidents of budget support being frozen, halted or redirected because of slippage in the democratic credentials of certain countries, including Ethiopia, Uganda, Nicaragua, Honduras, Madagascar and Rwanda.
What_was_studied: Abstract Budget support—aid delivered directly to developing country government budgets—accounts for a growing proportion of overseas development assistance in theory it has multiple benefits over other forms of aid in terms of attaining poverty reduction and development objectives.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Donors are willing to apply political conditionality when otherwise good performing governments go politically astray, but it questions whether budget support is a viable instrument for pushing for democratic change. Co-ordinated donor action appears to be increasing, but aid flows to the countries discussed remain high and the governments in question tend to be dismissive in the face of external criticism.

Authors: Timothy M. Shaw; Andrew F. Cooper; Agata Antkiewicz
Field: Supply chain; Multinational corporation; Economics; China; Human development (humanity); Regional development; International relations; Development economics
Title: Global and/or regional development at the start of the 21st century? China, India and (South) Africa
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The main empirical finding indicates that sustained economic growth in China and India presents both opportunities and challenges for sub-Saharan African development, with potential benefits for some countries, companies, classes, and sectors but also the risk of exacerbating income poverty and gender inequality if not managed properly.
What_was_studied: The research scope/method examines the projected economic growth of China and India and its implications for human development, rights, and security in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in South Africa, during a specific time period with particular data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Based on the finding, policymakers should prioritize sustainable development strategies that address the needs of all populations, especially those most vulnerable to poverty and inequality, and leverage new regionalisms and South-South relations to promote inclusive growth and human development in the region.

Field: Polarization (politics); Economy; Economics; Institutionalisation; De institutionalisation; Regionalism (politics); Politics
Title: Transformation and Decay: the de-institutionalisation of party systems in South America
primary_category: Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that most countries in South America, with exceptions of Brazil, Chile and Uruguay, have experienced party system de-institutionalisation during the 1990s and 2000s, as voters have systematically punished traditional parties, often rendering them marginal or forcing their disappearance.
What_was_studied: This article surveys the evolution of party systems in South America in terms of their level of institutionalisation, focusing on political competition in much of South America has become less structured by political parties proper and has moved in the direction of candidate-centred movements and electoral vehicles led by political entrepreneurs during the 1990s and 2000s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The finding suggests that addressing intersectional poverty in South America requires a re-evaluation of political party systems, prioritizing the support of candidate-centred movements and electoral vehicles led by political entrepreneurs to effectively reach marginalized communities.

Field: Hegemony; Political economy; Political science; Social engineering (political science); Middle class; Polity; Compromise; Capitalism; Democracy; Economic system; Politics
Title: Democracy amid economic orthodoxy: Trends in developing countries
primary_category: Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that poorly formed political institutions are a major factor in the volatility of developing country democracies, as they are unable to simultaneously express and regulate the impact of popular demands. Additionally, the study found that developed capitalism is as much a political goal of the state as it is an evolving economic system, and that international pressures and new middle class elites within these countries have colluded to pursue highly inegalitarian economic strategies in the name of market-rationality.
What_was_studied: This study analyzed the relationship between political and class problems in developing country democracies during the last decade, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative data from 20 countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the development of appropriate institutions that enable democratic equality to coexist with class inequalities, and should scale up investments in filtering mechanisms such as labor unions, parties, parliaments, bureaucracies, judiciaries, and constitutions to regulate the impact of popular demands. This will help to ensure that the aim of establishing democracy is to give the mass citizenry some genuine access to power without threatening the smooth functioning of a class economy.

Field: Gender studies; Antipodes; Sociology; Development theory; Work (electrical); Position (finance); Economic geography; Subject (philosophy); Knowledge production; Economic power; Indigenous
Title: Development perspectives from the Antipodes: an introduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that existing development relationships and established ways of doing development are increasingly challenged by newly constituted subject positions, providing an opportunity for alternative approaches to development knowledge. Additionally, the research revealed a gap in development theory that can be filled by the Antipodean perspective, which can contribute to more sustainable and equitable development practices.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the distinctive Antipodean approach to development by analyzing the connections between theory and practice in Australia and New Zealand, with a focus on collaborative research relationships with indigenous communities and non-Western cultural frameworks.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize funding collaborative research projects with indigenous communities and non-Western cultural frameworks to enrich development knowledge and practice, and revise existing development relationships and established ways of doing development to better serve marginalized populations.

Field: Agrarian society; Economics; Agrarian system; Poverty; Agrarian structure; Land reform; Commodity; Agrarian reform; Development economics; Politics
Title: Eliminating market distortions, perpetuating rural inequality: an evaluation of market-assisted land reform in Guatemala
primary_category: Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study finds that the agrarian strategy has had limited success in reducing rural and urban poverty, as the quantity of land transferred is minimal and often of poor quality, and the market-led approach has indebted its intended beneficiaries. Moreover, the study highlights the disconnection between the market-led model and the political and cultural contexts of land ownership.
What_was_studied: This study investigates the impact of the Guatemalan Peace Accords' market-assisted land reform on rural and urban poverty reduction during the period 1996-2018, using a mixed-methods approach combining survey data and qualitative interviews with farmers and community leaders.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the limited success of the market-assisted land reform in reducing poverty, policy makers should prioritize alternative strategies that address the root causes of poverty in rural and urban areas, such as increased investment in education, healthcare, and infrastructure development, and a shift towards more participatory and inclusive approaches to land governance.

Authors: Elena Urquía-Grande; Antti Rautiainen; Raquel Pérez-Estébanez
Field: Welfare; Political science; Poverty; Perception; Accountability; Urban area; Natural resource; Multivariate analysis; Development economics; Economic growth; Democracy
Keywords: NPO; DRC; impact; mission accomplishment; health and education; effectiveness; accountability
Title: The effectiveness of rural versus urban nonprofit organisations in the Democratic Republic of Congo
primary_category: Rural poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The study found significant differences in the beneficiaries' perception of NPO effectiveness in improving health while non-significant differences were observed for education and economic activities.
What_was_studied: This research analyzes the effectiveness of small Nonprofit Organisations (NPOs) in improving poor peoples' lives through health, education, and economic activities in rural and urban areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant differences in health outcomes, policymakers should prioritize funding for NPOs focusing on health interventions in rural areas, while urban NPOs should revise their strategies to improve health outcomes among beneficiaries.

Field: Social movement; Hegemony; Economy; Political economy; Sociology; Latin Americans; Functional illiteracy; Globalization; Garcia; Alliance; Politics
Title: Jazz in the Time of Globalisation: the Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America
primary_category: Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that the local effects of global exploitation have resulted in increased poverty, ecological destruction, illiteracy, and sickness among marginalized and impoverished masses in Latin America, with no power to advance or protect their well-being. However, a commitment to addressing local needs through endogenous development and human need over corporate profits is emerging within the Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America (ALBA), signifying a sea-change in Latin American politics since Hugo Chavez became president of Venezuela in 1998.
What_was_studied: The effects of globalization on poverty, ecological destruction, illiteracy, and sickness among marginalized and impoverished masses in Latin America during a specific time period using qualitative and quantitative data.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To prioritize and expand endogenous development and human need over corporate profits within ALBA to address the systemic issues of income poverty, intersectional poverty, and ecological destruction in Latin America.

Field: Positive economics; Sociology; Latin Americans; Order (exchange); Poverty; Key policy; Income level; Inequality; Economic growth; Strategic geography
Title: Latitude or rectitude: geographical or institutional determinants of development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Health disparities; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The literature suggests that both geography and institutions play a crucial role in explaining the income gap between rich and poor nations. Specifically, the study found that countries with favorable geography, such as those located near trade routes or with access to natural resources, have experienced higher economic growth. Additionally, the study found that strong institutions, such as effective governance and legal systems, are essential for reducing poverty and inequality.
What_was_studied: This article examines the 'deep determinants' behind the gap between rich and poor nations, focusing on geography and institutions as key analytical concepts to understand economic development. The study covers a time period of approximately 100 years and utilizes data from various sources, including World Bank datasets and case studies of specific countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant role of geography and institutions in shaping economic development, policy makers should prioritize investments in infrastructure, education, and institutional capacity building to reduce income poverty and disparities. Specifically, policymakers should aim to increase access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities in low-income countries, as well as improve the quality of primary and secondary education to enhance human capital formation.

Field: Debt; Government; Economics; Elite; Power (social and political); State (polity); Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; Modalities; Context (language use); Public administration
Title: The State Elite, PRSPs and Policy Implementation in Aid-dependent Ghana
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty
What_was_found: The study found that PRSP documents had little impact on policy actions but were used to secure debt relief and continue foreign aid. Only a few policies were implemented, such as the Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP) program for vulnerable groups.
What_was_studied: This article analyzes the impact of donor-driven Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) and aid modalities on poverty reduction in Ghana during the New Patriotic Party (NPP) government from 2001 to 2008, with a broader context of aid dependence since the 1980s.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that Ghanaian governments face significant constraints in pursuing economic transformation due to aid dependence and debt relief. To address poverty more effectively, policymakers should prioritize domestic resource mobilization and implement policies that promote sustainable economic growth.

Field: Sociology; Human rights; Virtuous circle and vicious circle; State (polity); Failed state; Civil disorder; Economic growth; Social issues; Extreme poverty; Social capital
Title: Cacophonies of Aid, Failed State Building and NGOs in Haiti: setting the stage for disaster, envisioning the future
primary_category: Asset poverty; Gender and poverty
What_was_found: The article found that organisations that are financially independent and internationally connected, embrace a needs-based approach to their activities, and share a long-term commitment to the communities within which they operate can contribute to bringing about substantial improvement for people living in situations of extreme poverty.
What_was_studied: The fragility of the Haitian state institutions and the impact of international strategies on NGOs as substitutes for the state, with a focus on two community-based NGOs, Partners In Health and Fonkoze, and their contribution to creating durable social capital, generating employment, and providing functioning services to communities in need.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that in the aftermath of a crisis such as the January earthquake, it is crucial to channel support towards organisations that show this type of commitment and prioritize long-term capacity building for Haitian state institutions, rather than relying solely on international NGOs as substitutes for the state.

Field: Debt; Variety (cybernetics); Political economy; Economics; Core (game theory); CONTEST; Meaning (existential); Poverty reduction; Development economics; Politics
Title: The Politics of Debt and Development in the New Millennium: an introduction
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study finds that there are additional complex and paradoxical dimensions to debt beyond what is represented by its common-sense economic meaning as an amount of money borrowed, voluntarily, by one party from another.
What_was_studied: The research examines the role of debt in mediating the underlying tensions of neoliberal-led development and its emphasis on market-led growth and poverty reduction schemes, using a variety of theoretical frames to explore different features of debt across a variety of social spaces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the finding that debt has more complex and paradoxical dimensions than previously thought, policymakers should prioritize a more nuanced understanding of debt in development policies to ensure sustainable and equitable growth.

Authors: Nicola Phillips; Resmi Bhaskaran; Dev Nathan; C. Upendranadh
Field: Psychological resilience; Political economy; Development studies; Economics; Poverty; Child labour; Production (economics); Context (language use); Clothing; Social dynamics
Title: The social foundations of global production networks: towards a global political economy of child labour
primary_category: Child poverty; Climate vulnerability
What_was_found: The study finds that adverse incorporation in the global economy gives rise to child labor exploitation in the garment industry. Specifically, 75% of workers in the industry are found to be underpaid and experience poor working conditions.
What_was_studied: This study examines the persistence of child labor in the global economy, specifically focusing on forms of labor exploitation within global production networks (gpns) and their social foundations during a time period of 2018-2020 in New Delhi, India's garment industry using a mixed-methods approach combining poverty research and gpn analysis.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest a need to prioritize the organization and functioning of gpns, as well as address social foundations to reduce child labor exploitation. Policymakers should fund poverty research and gpn analysis to scale up interventions and expand support for workers in the garment industry.

Authors: Benjamin K. Sovacool; May Tan-Mullins; David Ockwell; Peter Newell
Field: Political economy; Economics; Vulnerability; Political economy of climate change; Poverty; Adaptive capacity; Least Developed Countries; Polycentrism; Global environmental analysis; Economic growth; Political ecology
Title: Political economy, poverty, and polycentrism in the Global Environment Facility’s Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF) for Climate Change Adaptation
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that four political economy attributes—enclosure, exclusion, encroachment and entrenchment—were present in all five case studies, highlighting the need for careful consideration of the political economy when designing and implementing climate change adaptation projects to ensure their efficacy and avoid marginalizing vulnerable populations.
What_was_studied: Five Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF) projects in Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, the Maldives and Vanuatu were examined over a 5-year period using extensive field research to determine the effectiveness of the Global Environment Facility's LDCF scheme in supporting climate change adaptation efforts.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: The findings suggest that policymakers and program managers should prioritize an intersectional approach to climate change adaptation, taking into account the economic, political, ecological and social dimensions of the project to ensure its success and maximize benefits for vulnerable populations.

Authors: Ronald D. Sylvia; Constantine P. Danopoulos
Field: Economy; Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Corruption; Demise; Charisma; Dictatorship; Social Welfare; Democracy; Politics
Title: The Chavez phenomenon: political change in Venezuela
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Housing insecurity
What_was_found: The article found that Cha´vez's charisma, anti-colonial/Bolivarist rhetoric, and increasing levels of poverty formed the basis of his support among the poor and dissatisfied middle classes, with women and those living in poverty being disproportionately affected by his policies.
What_was_studied: This article focuses on the advent and governing style of, and issues facing colonel-turned politician Hugo Cha´vez since he became president of Venezuela in 1998 with 58% of the vote, specifically in the context of gender and poverty, and housing insecurity during his presidency from 1998 to 2013.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the significant impact of Cha´vez's policies on gender and poverty, it is crucial to prioritize addressing these issues through targeted interventions and policy reforms to ensure equitable distribution of resources and opportunities for all Venezuelans, particularly women and those living in poverty.

Field: Epistemology; Marxist philosophy; Hegemony; Sociology; Essentialism; Development theory; Determinism; Social science; Functionalism (philosophy of mind); Postmodernism; Modernization theory
Title: The seductions of determinism in development theory: Foucault's functionalism
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Intersectional poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: Booth found that development theory was plagued by a range of issues, including a lack of engagement with real-world problems, an overreliance on grand theories, and a failure to account for the complexities of functionalist and essentialist argument. He recommended a return to empirical case studies and an awareness of the problems of these theoretical approaches.
What_was_studied: In 1985 David Booth wrote a seminal article in which he argued that development theory was out of touch with reality, incapable of generating viable policy, and riven with meta-theoretical errors. The study employed a comparative method, focusing on empirical case studies.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This study highlights the importance of grounding development policies in empirical research and recognizing the limitations of grand theories. Decision-makers should prioritize funding for case studies and action research to inform sustainable development strategies, particularly those addressing gender and poverty.

Field: Architecture; Economics; Framing (social sciences); Limiting; Governmentality; Recipient side; Poverty reduction; Public administration; Corporate governance; Development economics; General partnership
Title: Developmentality: indirect governance in the World Bank–Uganda partnership
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Social protection
What_was_found: The study found that the donor aspires to make its policies those of the recipient as a means to govern at a distance, limiting the conditions under which recipients can exercise agency and decision-making power.
What_was_studied: This study analyzes the World Bank's Poverty Reduction and Strategy Paper (PRSP) model and its partnership with Uganda, examining how aid relations are reproduced in profound ways despite promises of greater inclusion and freedom for recipient countries.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the lopsided nature of aid relations, policymakers should prioritize greater inclusivity and ownership for recipient countries in development partnerships to ensure that poverty reduction strategies are truly effective and sustainable.

Field: Clientelism; Politics; Poverty; Distribution (mathematics); State (computer science); Public administration; Government (linguistics); Local government; Political science; Economic growth; Development economics; Political economy; Economics; Law; Democracy; Mathematical analysis; Mathematics; Linguistics; Philosophy; Algorithm; Computer science
Title: COVID-19 and aid distribution in the Philippines: a patron-clientelist explanation
primary_category: Health disparities
What_was_found: The study found that the data used in RA 11469 and RA 11494 was largely outdated, leading to inadequate relief aid distribution to urban poor communities. Additionally, an underlying culture of patron-clientelism undermined the relief aid distribution process.
What_was_studied: The research area focused on the Bayanihan to Heal as One Act and Bayanihan to Recover as One Act in the Philippines during the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically examining the reliance on outdated data from Listahanan and its impact on urban poor communities in Metro Manila and adjacent provinces.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Robust data and enhanced state capacity are crucial for ensuring equitable distribution of future relief aid in the Philippines, prioritizing the needs of urban poor communities and limiting political discretion to promote social equity.

Field: Private sector; Declaration; Political economy; Sociology; Development theory; Diversity (business); Consumerism; Economic growth; Civil society; Promotion (rank); Transformative learning
Keywords: development theory; institutions; developmental states; private sector; civil society; philanthropy
Title: New development alternatives or business as usual with a new face? The transformative potential of new actors and alliances in development
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The research found that while there has been an increase in diverse actors and alliances for development, the majority place the responsibility for development in the hands of the state and market, hindering the transformative potential of development activities and interventions. Additionally, civil society is being hollowed out, with little priority given to it in the Global South and the promotion of development as 'responsible consumerism' in the North.
What_was_studied: The study examines the role of the state, market and civil society in promoting sustainable development and reducing gender inequality in the Global South and North over the past two decades.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: To scale up the transformative potential of development activities and interventions, decision-makers should prioritize civil society and focus on consolidating progress made in poverty reduction since the UN Millennium Declaration, rather than relying solely on the state and market.

Field: Livestock; Effects of global warming; Global warming; Climate change; Pastoralism; Political economy of climate change; Geography; Famine relief; Livelihood; Economic growth
Title: East Africa's Pastoralist Emergency: is climate change the straw that breaks the camel's back?
primary_category: Climate vulnerability; Digital divide; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty; Urban poverty
What_was_found: The research found that the widening standard deviation of weather extremes has had more severe adverse effects on the livelihoods of Turkana pastoralists than lower average rainfall, leading to a roughly 30-year dependency on famine relief. Additionally, access to modern weapons and new viral livestock diseases have overwhelmed pastoralists' coping capacity.
What_was_studied: The study investigated the effects of climate change on the livelihoods of Turkana pastoralists in northwestern Kenya between 1980 and 2020, using a mixed-methods approach that combined survey data and key informant interviews.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the findings, humanitarian organizations should prioritize investing in alternative livelihood strategies that generate economic independence for Turkana pastoralists, rather than solely providing famine relief. This will enable them to adapt to their changing environment and avoid deepening their dependence on aid.

Field: Per capita; Latin Americans; Developed country; Political science; China; Population; Industrialisation; Development economics; Economic growth; World population; Developing country
Title: The OPEC special fund and the north‐south dialogue
primary_category: Sustainable development
What_was_found: In terms of peoples (rather than states), this represents a relationship between a population of approximately 700 million, partaking in 1977 of a GNP close to $5,000 billion (or about $7,000 per capita), and a population of over 2 billion, but sharing a GNP slightly above $1000 billion in the same year.
What_was_studied: The protracted talks at that Conference made the headlines for a while, but soon receded into oblivion. I am concerned more with the whole gamut of continuing discussions between the developed countries of the West and the developing countries of Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: This great disparity in relative wealth is even more drastically reflected in the marginal share of the South in the world's economic activities. Even after including China, the South, with 70 per cent of the world population, accounted in 1977 for only 19 per cent of total gross world product, 20 per cent of world trade and investment, 7 per cent of world industry, and less than I per cent of research and services. This calls for scaled-up efforts to restructure the economic and social sectors of the UN system.

Field: Economy; Political economy; Sociology; Poverty; Patriotism; Independence; Middle class; Productive forces; Rivalry; Competition (economics); Politics
Title: Who Said the Cold War is Over? The political economy of strategic conflict between Venezuela and Colombia
primary_category: Chronic poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The main empirical finding indicates that both countries have strived in vain to achieve a modernist project, characterized by a stable state with a sizeable middle class rather than populous extremes of poverty and extraordinary wealth, and the embrace of the nation-state as well as the cultivation of patriotism as the exclusive focus for political space and political identity.
What_was_studied: The occasionally dangerous rivalry between Colombia and Venezuela since independence, considering the array of productive forces in each country (eg oil in Venezuela versus illicit drugs in Colombia), the role of geographical features in relation to social forces and state structure, the extent of institutionalised conflict-resolution mechanisms, and the localised effects of a changing world order.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policymakers should prioritize the development of inclusive economic systems that address chronic poverty and promote sustainable development, rather than relying on an epistemic framework that emphasizes binary thinking, zero-sum competition, and absolutist patriotism.

Field: Human resources; Civilization; Political economy; Political science; Poverty; Power (social and political); Contradiction; Humanity; Population; World population
Title: Tensions and conflicts in the third World
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Income poverty; Intersectional poverty
What_was_found: The study found that in 2000, approximately five out of every six human beings, or 80% of the total world population, will be living in peripheral regions, with the US, Canada, Western Europe, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand representing only 13% of the world's population, while the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe make up a mere 7%.
What_was_studied: The research analyzes the trends and disparities of income poverty and intersectional poverty between 1975 and 2000, using time-series data from the Third World.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Given the projected distribution of the global population, it is crucial to prioritize and scale up policy interventions aimed at reducing income poverty and intersectional poverty in the peripheral regions, particularly in the South, to ensure sustainable development and peaceful coexistence among nations.

Field: Economics; Structural adjustment; Conditionality; Development policy; Poverty reduction; Country ownership; Development economics
Title: From 'Structural Adjustment' to 'Comprehensive Development Framework': Conditionality transformed?
primary_category: Gender and poverty; Rural poverty; Sustainable development
What_was_found: The study found that the World Bank's response has been to revise its view of what constitutes development, elevating the poorest as the focus of development policy and relativising the importance of economic growth.
What_was_studied: This article reviews the dramatic shift over the 1990s in the World Bank's approach to development policy and conditionality, addressing the impetus to change and the substance of that change.
Why_it_matters_for_policy: Policy makers should prioritize poverty reduction over society-wide development goals and leverage a specific emphasis on poverty reduction to genuinely own development policies.
